# Patrologia Latina, volume 2 — English translation

## QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN

### The complete works of Tertullian, presbyter of Carthage

### List of the contents of this volume

The Book of Prescriptions against Heretics.

**First series. Polemical writings of Tertullian the Montanist.** *On the Soldier’s Crown. On Flight in Persecution. Scorpiace against the Gnostics. Against Praxeas. Against Hermogenes. Against Marcion*, five books. *Against the Valentinians. Against the Jews. On the Soul against the Philosophers. On the Flesh of Christ. On the Resurrection of the Flesh.*

**Second series. Moral writings of Tertullian the Montanist.** *On the Veiling of Virgins. Exhortation to Chastity. On Monogamy. On Fasts. On Modesty. On the Pallium.*

**Appendices.** Appendix I. Poems ascribed to Tertullian: *Against Marcion*, five books; *Genesis; Sodom; To a Senator; On Jonah and Nineveh; On the Tree of Life.* Appendix II. A fragment *On the Gods to Be Abominated*, brought to light from the Vatican Library by Jean-Marie Suares of Avignon. Appendix III. Fragments and brief notes from Greek works. Appendix IV. Fragments and notices of lost works. Appendix V. Notes by the Reverend Father Corbinian Thomas, monk of the [Col. 0009] Order of Saint Benedict, on the books *On Baptism* and *On Repentance*, together with his dissertation on the affinity [Col. 0009] between baptism and repentance in Tertullian. Indexes.

## [ON PRESCRIPTIONS AGAINST HERETICS]



## THE BOOK OF [Col. 0011D] QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN ON PRESCRIPTIONS AGAINST HERETICS

[Note:  *On the Prescription of Heretics.* Such is the title in the oldest manuscript of this book, and we think it was given by the  author himself. He says “the prescription of heretics,” because we plead against heretics by the very fact that they are heretics, opposing to them this single exception: that they advance doctrines contrary to the rule. Thus we remove them from every dispute as persons who must not be heard. No other prescription [Col. 0012D] is at issue here. Tertullian himself says in book I *Against Marcion*: “Another little book will maintain this stage of the case, refuting heretics even without a reconsideration of their doctrines, on the ground that they are under the prescription of novelty.” The prescription of heretics is therefore the prescription of novelty, and the text hitherto printed, *On Prescriptions against Heretics*, is less correct. He said “prescription of heretics” in the same idiom in which legal writers say “prescription of fraud,” “of [Col. 0013C] forum,” “of time,” and “of a matter adjudged.” RIG.—*On prescription.* I do not know whether I should explain here what others before us have examined. “Prescription” is taken from forensic usage and means a rebuttal by which the defendant casts aside his adversary’s charge or turns it back upon him (see Ulpian, Digest, on the Julian law concerning adultery). Thus in law the expressions “to cast aside,” “to except against,” and “to bring forward a charge” are common. [Col. 0013D] I would also think that “against heretics,” or “against heresies,” should be read here, not “of heretics.” LE PR. There can be no doubt that “against heretics” is the author’s true reading, for in the conclusion of this    book he says: “We have dealt generally against all heresies by sure, just, and necessary prescriptions.” The very passage cited by Rigaltius from book I *Against Marcion* in support of his position supports ours too: “Another little book will maintain this stage against heretics, who are to be refuted even without reconsideration of their doctrines, because they fall under the prescription of novelty.” For our author does not say “by the prescription of heretics,” but “by the prescription of novelty . . . against heretics.” Moreover, “prescription of heretics” would be ambiguous [Col. 0009A] and could more readily be understood of heretics wishing to prescribe against us than of us, who by our own right may prescribe against anyone. EDITORS, from DE GOURCY’s work.]

## PROEM

 Although no one would deny that Tertullian’s book *On Prescriptions* is by far the finest of all his minor works, and that by this single weapon all the heresies of every age are laid low and utterly destroyed, everyone nevertheless knows the difficult controversy that arises at the very threshold of the work: at what time in particular—before or after the author’s defection to the Montanists—this book was either published or composed.

The common Catholic opinion is that this exceptional work could not have grown within the confines of heresy. One may enumerate the most learned [Col. 0009B] and distinguished men supporting this view: Baronius (at the year 197, no. 11), Tillemont (*Mémoires pour servir à l’Histoire ecclésiastique*, III, note 6  on Tertullian, p. 300 ff.), Dom Rémy Ceillier (*Histoire des auteurs ecclésiastiques*, II, ch. 28, art. VI, p. 395), Fleury (*Histoire ecclésiastique*, II, book V, no. 28), and J. A. Möhler (*Patrologie oder christliche Litterargeschichte*). Since Möhler is more recent and therefore expresses the mind of the others more fully, it is worth quoting his words here: “Such is the spirit of this book, and such the manner in which it is woven throughout, that the sincerity of a Catholic author is evident. For once he had gone wholly over to Montanist tenets and openly withdrawn from the Church, he could no longer have asserted with such weight and integrity of fact and language this chief argument of prescription, [Col. 0010A] by which he himself was afterward vigorously assailed and pierced through by Catholics.”

They are further moved to this opinion by three other arguments:  (1) nothing in this book savors of open heresy; (2) indeed, unmistakable signs show that the author was then joined in communion with the Roman Church; (3) nowhere does he make the slightest mention of a certain Artemon, a most wicked heresiarch who denied Christ’s divinity. It may therefore be inferred that the book was written before Artemon’s time, and consequently before Tertullian’s fall.

Such arguments they ordinarily advance. Yet they do not plainly and adequately overcome Tertullian’s own testimony after his fall, when in the books *Against Marcion* he declares that this work *On Prescriptions* [Col. 0010B] had not yet been published, as is discussed more fully in Dom Lumper’s dissertation placed at the beginning of this edition.

 After weighing the considerations on either side, one must therefore admit a middle path between the two positions, on which the disputants may safely meet and agree. The arguments on both sides seem to compel us to conclude that the work was composed at one time and published at another.

First, we believe that Tertullian conceived this book and wrote its first draft while staying at Rome, when his faith was still whole and he was fierce and exultant, as it were, with a convert’s fervor. He saw all the heresies besieging the Apostolic See from every quarter with united force dashed against the Rock by the single stroke of tradition. At the same time, being closely associated [Col. 0011A] by necessity with the foremost men then flourishing in the City—Caius the presbyter and Hippolytus, above all the illustrious disciples of St Irenaeus —he received from them the books of so great a master. From them too he discovered, adopted, and found proven the most ready way to defeat any innovators without battle or combat: the wholly secure course of traditions and prescriptions. Hence he fixed deep in his mind the plan of dragging the new enemies of truth to judgment and, without examination of the subject or litigation of the cause, expelling them from every suit merely by the force of certain exceptions and sending them away condemned. (Cf. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* II.2, p. 41; Tertullian, *On the Dress of Women* I.6; Jerome, *Illustrious Men* 53.)

When this plan had nearly been executed or was hastening toward completion, [Col. 0011B] there arose—whether from the envy of the Roman clergy, the ungovernable character of Septimius, or the exceedingly fierce spirit of the African—a truly lamentable storm, which  tore him from the ship of the Church and the harbor of Catholic faith and drove him upon the pathless reefs of Montanism. Yet Tertullian remained to some extent an indefatigable defender of truth. When he was now devoting the whole last part of his life to controversies, he did not reject his earlier labors, but published that renowned monument of Catholic prescription.

We have therefore thought it better to place this work midway between the books of Tertullian the Catholic and Tertullian the Montanist, judging [Col. 0011C] that it looks to both faces of his genius and both parts of his life and belongs to each by the same title.

## ARGUMENT

This book may be divided into two parts.  The first weighs five preliminary considerations that pave the way for prescriptions; the second sets forth nine principal methods of prescribing against heresies.

**First part.** First proposition: Heresies must exist, must possess great power, and must achieve much in overthrowing souls. Chapters I–III. Second: Heresies are to be shunned, as worse than dissensions and persecutions. IV–V. Third: Heresy is a choice, and the very thing in which choice is made is the source of condemnation. [Col. 0011D] VI. Fourth: All heresies flow from one of two sources, either secular wisdom or itching curiosity.  VII–XII. Fifth: The rule of faith must be kept whole and never torn apart in controversy. XIII–XIV. [Col. 0012A]

**Second part.** It presents this **first** prescription: heretics are not to be heard in a dispute over Scripture.  XV–XIX. **Second:** the apostles received sound teaching from Christ himself to hand down to posterity, and the churches received it from the apostles; none is to be received from anywhere else. XX–XXVII. **Third:** the Church’s teaching is true because it is one; the heretics’ is false because it is diverse. **Fourth:** that which was handed down first is true and divine. XXIX–XXXI. **Fifth:** the continuous succession of bishops from the apostles is firm testimony to the true Church. XXXII. **Sixth:** our teaching is true, since the apostles certainly do not condemn it [Col. 0012B] but defend it; every other is false, being foreign or unknown to the apostles.  XXXIII–XXXV. **Seventh:** to find the truth the apostolic churches must be consulted, and above all that happy church upon which the apostles poured out their entire teaching together with their blood. XXXVI–XXXVII. **Eighth:** heretics have no right whatever to the Holy Scriptures. XXXVIII–XL. **Ninth:** no truth can coexist with the perverse conduct of heretics; where there is fear of God, there are honorable seriousness, deliberate fellowship, respectful advancement, devout submission, reverent appearance, modest procession, a united Church, and all things belonging to God. XLI–XLV. The final chapters follow, [Col. 0012C] containing a catalogue of heretics; concerning its authenticity see the annotation appended to those chapters. EDITORS.

## ARGUMENT BY JAMES PAMELIUS

Writing against the heretics or heresies then rampant, and seeing that disputations accomplished nothing or little, Tertullian judged that they must be refuted by fixed prescriptions, or without a reconsideration of their doctrines, as he says elsewhere.

## CHAPTER I

Before coming to his subject, he teaches that we ought not to marvel at heresies, since they were foretold.

The condition of the present times [Note:   Junius [Col. 0011D] and the Paris edition insert “brethren”; compare ch. 29.] calls forth this admonition from us as well: we ought not  to marvel [Col. 0012D] at these heresies, either because they exist—for they were foretold as future—or because they overthrow the faith of some; for this is why they exist, so that faith, by undergoing temptation, [Col. 0012D] may [Note:  “might have,” Semler, Venetian, Rigaltius.] also have proof. Most people therefore are vainly and thoughtlessly [Col. 0013A] scandalized by the very fact that heresies have such [Col. 0013D] power. How much [Note:   “How much, if they had not existed!” That is: if they marvel that heresies have such power, how much more would they marvel if heresies had not existed at all! That would deserve far greater amazement, since the Holy Spirit foretold their [Col. 0014C] coming and could not be mistaken. We corrected this formerly very corrupt passage with the help of Agobard’s manuscript, with which the Dijon manuscript [Col. 0013C] also agrees. LE PR.] more, if they had not existed! [Note:   “How great they are,” [Col. 0013C] Semler, Pamelius. Heumann thinks either reading should be deleted.] [Col. 0013C] Since whatever has obtained the condition that it should [Col. 0013C] in every way exist receives, just as it does, the cause for which it exists, [Col. 0013C] so [Note:  “These things” for “so,” Venetian, Rigaltius.] it acquires [Col. 0013C] the power through which it exists and cannot [Note:  “not,” [Col. 0013C] Venetian, de Gourcy, Rigaltius, Pamelius.] fail to exist [Note: [Col. 0013C]  “It is necessary that it can,” Wouwer.].

## CHAPTER II

Rather, they are to be abominated and guarded against, as bringing eternal death and possessing no strength except among those weak in faith.

We do not marvel at fever, allotted among other deadly [Col. 0013C] and torturing [Note:  Others prefer “torturous.”] [Col. 0014C] ends for spending a man’s life [Note:      “By spending the man.” We prefer to retain Rigaltius’s reading, which seems true. Tertullian used *erogo* in several places, evidently in the sense of “destroy”: e.g., “so many innocent persons are spent” (*Apology* 44); “flesh [Col. 0014D] is spent in punishments” (*Resurrection of the Flesh* 8); “the spender of the virgin” (*Modesty* 16). EDITORS, from de Gourcy.], because [Col. 0014C] it exists—for it does exist—nor because it spends a man, for that is why it exists. Likewise, if we dread that heresies, produced for the weakening and destruction of faith, can do this, we must first dread    that they exist; for while they exist they have the power to act, and while they [Col. 0013B] have power they [Col. 0014C] have existence. But fever, as an evil known both from its cause and its power, [Note:   “We abominate rather than marvel.” It is no wonder that so many heresies exist. Just as, if fever strikes, we do not [Col. 0014D] marvel but seek a means of driving it off, so must we deal with heresy and strive by every means that it not grow up. Mark Augustine’s golden words (*Against Julian* III.3): “Wondrous are the things you Pelagians say; new are the things you say; false are the things you say: we marvel at the wondrous, guard against the new, and refute the false.” LE PR.] we abominate rather than marvel at, and as far as we can we guard against it, though its abolition is not in our power. Yet some prefer to marvel that heresies can bring eternal death and the heat of a greater fire [Note:  Variant spelling in Rigaltius, Pamelius, Venetian.] [Col. 0014C] rather than prevent them from being able to do so, although they possess the power of avoidance. Otherwise they will have no power if men merely cease marveling at their power. For either, while men marvel, they [Col. 0014C] are supplied with material for scandal; or because men are scandalized, they marvel, as though the fact that heresies possess such power came from some [Col. 0014A] truth.   A marvel indeed, that evil should have its own strength! Except that [Col. 0014C] heresies possess great strength among those who possess little [Note:  Others read “little.”] strength [Col. 0014C] in faith. In a fight of boxers or gladiators, a man often wins not because he is strong or invincible, but because the defeated man had no strength; so much so that this same victor, afterward matched against a strong man, departs defeated. Heresies likewise derive their strength from the weaknesses of certain people; they have no strength if they encounter a strong faith.

## CHAPTER III

Nor ought anyone to be scandalized if a bishop, deacon, widow, virgin, teacher, or even martyr has fallen from the rule, because faith is not proved from persons, but persons from faith.

  Those simpletons [Col. 0014B] [Note:  “The weaker,” Rigaltius and Venetian, [Col. 0014C] from the very ancient manuscript of Agobard.] are accustomed to build themselves toward ruin from the example of certain persons captured by heresy: “Why did this or that most faithful, prudent, and experienced [Note:  “Most [Col. 0014C] ancient,” Semler, from old manuscripts.] person in the Church go over to that side?” Who, in saying this, does not answer himself that those whom heresies could change ought to be judged neither prudent, nor faithful, nor experienced? And is it marvelous, I ask, that someone formerly approved should afterward fall away? Saul, good above others, was afterward overthrown by envy. David, a good man after the Lord’s heart, afterward became guilty of murder and adultery. Solomon, endowed by the Lord with every grace and wisdom, was led into idolatry [Col. 0014D] by women. [Note:  “For the Son of God alone it was reserved to remain without sin.” It is no wonder that he did not add the most blessed Virgin here beside Christ, since in *On the Flesh of Christ* he wrote of her things less consonant with the theology of later ages. With laudable feeling Augustine said in *Nature and Grace against the Pelagians*: “Concerning the holy Virgin Mary, [Col. 0015C] for the Lord’s honor, I wish no question whatever to be raised when sins are discussed.” RIG.—The ecumenical Council of Trent employed the same exception. EDITORS, from de Gourcy.] For the Son [Col. 0015A] of God alone it was reserved   to remain without sin. What then if a bishop, deacon, widow, virgin, teacher, or even martyr has fallen from the rule [Note: [Col. 0015C]  “From the rule,” that is, from the creed, from the Catholic faith. SEMLER.]? Will heresies therefore seem to possess the truth? Do we prove faith from persons, or persons from faith? No one is wise unless faithful; no one is great unless a Christian; no one, moreover, is a Christian unless he perseveres to the end (Matt. 10:22).

You, as a man, know each from the outside; you suppose what you see, and see only so far as you have eyes. “But the eyes of the Lord,” he says, “are lofty.” Man looks upon the face, God upon the heart (1 Sam. 16:7). Therefore “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19); he uproots the plant which the Father did not plant (Matt. 15:13); he reveals the last from among the first (Matt. 20:16); [Col. 0015C] and he carries the winnowing fan [Note:  “Openly,” Franeker and Paris editions; Junius approves by comparison with *Flight in Persecution*; likewise Irenaeus, Augustine [Col. 0015B] to Macrobius, Arnobius’s annotator, and Juvencus.] in his hand  to cleanse his threshing floor [Col. 0015C] (Matt. 3:12). Let the chaff of light faith fly away as much as it will [Note:  “as much as it wishes,” Semler.] on every blast of temptation: by so much the purer will the mass of wheat be stored in the Lord’s granaries.

Did not some of the Lord’s own disciples turn away in scandal? Yet the others did not therefore think they too must [Col. 0015C] depart from his footsteps. Those who knew him to be the Word of life [Note:  “Who knew him to be the Word of life.” The original text (John 6:69) gives a somewhat different [Col. 0015D] sense, faithfully reproduced by our Vulgate and various Eastern versions. In place of “words of eternal life,” our author preferred to say that Christ is the Word of life. La Cerda noted in his commentary that several Fathers interpreted this scriptural passage just as Tertullian did. EDITORS, from de Gourcy.] and to have come from God persevered in his company to the end, although he calmly offered them the chance to depart too if they wished. It is a lesser thing if some Phygellus [Col. 0015D] and Hermogenes [Note:  “Phygellus and Hermogenes.” Paul, 2 Tim. 1: “You know that all who are in Asia have turned away from me, among whom are Phygellus and Hermogenes.” Ambrose says of them: “They were full of deceit; for they pretended friendship with the apostle so that, by adhering to him, they might learn something from which to calumniate him or instigate others against him.” Tertullian, *Resurrection of the Flesh* 24, counts this Hermogenes among heretics denying the resurrection of the flesh. RIG.], [Col. 0015D] Philetus, and Hymenaeus [Note:  “And Philetus and Hymenaeus.” Paul, 2 Tim. 2: “Their speech spreads like a cancer; among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who fell from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already happened, and overthrew the faith of some.” RIG.] abandoned his apostle (2 Tim. 1:15; 1 Tim. 1:20): Christ’s own betrayer was one of the apostles. Do we marvel if his churches are deserted by some, when the [Col. 0015C] sufferings that follow Christ’s example show us to be   Christians? “They went out from us,” he says (1 John 2:19), “but [Col. 0016A]  they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us.”

## CHAPTER IV

Rather, let us remember both the Lord’s declarations and the apostolic letters, which foretold future heresies and determined beforehand that they must be shunned.

Rather, let us remember both the Lord’s declarations [Col. 0016C] [Note:  “Foretellings,” Rigaltius, Venetian.] and the apostolic letters, which both foretold future heresies and determined beforehand that we must shun them. Just as we do not dread their existence, so let us not marvel that they can do the very [Col. 0016C] thing for which they must be shunned. [Note:  “The Lord teaches,” etc. Blessed Cyprian imitates this passage almost word for word in his book to the heretic Novatian: “The Lord,” he says, “had foretold that many ravening wolves would come beneath sheep’s skins. Who [Col. 0016C] are false prophets but false preachers? [Note:  “Who are false apostles?” The former he took from the Lord’s predictions; this and what follows from the apostolic writings: 2 Cor. 11 and 1 John 2. PAMELIUS.] Who are false apostles [Col. 0016D] but adulterous evangelists? Who [Note:  “Antichrists.” He calls heretics antichrists because, just as the true Antichrist will feign miracles, so do they. Lucas of Tuy, *On the Frauds of Heretics* III.2, should be read. LA CERDA.] are the antichrists, [Col. 0016C] now and always, but Christ’s rebels? Heresies now assail the Church by perversity of doctrines no less than Antichrist will then persecute it by the savagery of persecutions—except that persecution also makes martyrs, while heresy makes only apostates.

Therefore heresies too had to exist so that all the approved might be made manifest (1 Cor. 11:19): those who stand in persecutions as well as [Col. 0016C] those who do not stray into heresies [Note:  “have strayed,” Semler.]. It does not help [Col. 0016C] to understand as approved [Note:  “may help,” Semler; [Col. 0016C] “commands,” Rigaltius, Venetian.] those  who change their faith into heresy, as they perversely [Col. 0016D] interpret for themselves because he said elsewhere: [Note:   “Test everything.” Heretics, says Quintinus, have always pretended—and still pretend—that their opinions, diverging from the customary rule of the Fathers, follow what Christ and his disciples warned should be done. The apostles likewise warned: “Test what is pleasing to God” (Eph. 5:10); “Do not despise prophecies”—that is, interpretations of divine Scripture and declarations of your faith—“but test everything” (1 Thess. 5:21); “Do not believe every spirit, but test whether the spirits  are from God” (1 John 4:1). So now certain [Col. 0017C] idle busybodies reason badly about all the Church’s sacraments, disputing whether they are ancient and quarreling over rites and forms; they say that they wish to investigate, as men once did, whether true things are being advanced, after examining arguments from every side. For, they say, it is written: “Test everything.” Thus by our pride we gradually slide with an all too easy and slippery assent  into [Col. 0017D] heresies. Christian reader, “test everything” and the other statements above were not spoken to everyone. I do not think any unlearned person, if he wishes to walk carefully, can fulfill this command, because it was enjoined upon the wise, not fools. Jerome says these and other pertinent things when interpreting Eph. 5:15, “See how carefully you walk.” Ambrose too should be read on the command to the Thessalonians, “Test everything.” PAMELIUS.] “Test everything; hold fast what [Col. 0017A] is good” (1 Thess. 5:21), as though it were not possible, after testing everything badly, to stumble through error [Col. 0017C] into the choice [Note:   “suggestion,” Semler; Junius conjectures another form; “choice,” Wouwer.] of some evil.

## CHAPTER V

It is determined that heresies must be shunned not only under the names of dissensions and schisms, but also under their own name.

Further, if he rebukes dissensions and schisms, which are undoubtedly [Col. 0017D] evils, and immediately [Note:  “And immediately adds heresies.” *Incontinenti* means “at once.” Justin often says *ex continenti*, as in book V, “that they immediately replace Alcibiades as commander with Conon,” and book VII, “he could not be restrained from immediately deciding the matter in battle.” RHENANUS.] [Col. 0017C] adds heresies (1 Cor. 11:18), by joining them to evils he surely declares heresy an [Col. 0017C] evil, and indeed a greater one, since he says he believed the report of schisms and dissensions precisely because he knew that heresies too must exist. For, in view [Note: [Col. 0017C]  “contempt,” Semler.] of a graver evil, [Col. 0017C] he shows that he readily believed the [Col. 0017B] lesser     ones; certainly he did not believe the evils because heresies were good, but so as to warn that trials of an even worse stamp should not be marveled at—trials which, he said, tended [Note:  “were [Col. 0017C] impending,” Rhenanus, Junius, Paris.] to make all the approved manifest, namely those whom they had been unable to corrupt.

Finally, if the entire chapter aims [Note:  Variant readings: “you may fit”; or [Col. 0017C] a conjectured verb meaning “binds and contains, fitted as though [Col. 0018C] by one bond.”] at preserving unity and restraining separations, while heresies tear men from unity no less than schisms and dissensions, he undoubtedly places heresies under the same condemnation as schisms and dissensions. Thus he does not [Note:  “us,” [Col. 0018C] Venetian.] make those approved who have turned aside into heresies, since above all he rebukes such turning and instructs [Note: [Col. 0018C]  “rebuking and teaching,” Semler, Pamelius.] all to speak one thing and think the same thing (1 [Col. 0017C] Cor. 1:10),   which heresies do not permit.

## CHAPTER VI [Col. 0018A]



For in the Epistle to Titus, when the apostle describes a heretic, he intimates that heresies are so called by a Greek word signifying choice, which a man employs either in founding or adopting them.

I need say no more about this [Note: [Col. 0018C]  Heumann adds “I dispute.”], if it is the same [Note:  “and,” [Col. 0018C] Semler.] Paul who elsewhere numbers heresies among fleshly crimes, writing to the Galatians (5:20), and who advises Titus (3:10–11) to reject a heretical man after the first correction because such a man is perverted and sins, being self-condemned. In almost every epistle, moreover, by repeatedly urging that adulterous doctrines be shunned, he censures heresies, whose works are adulterous doctrines. They are called “heresies” by a Greek word [Col. 0017D] [Note:  “By a Greek word,” namely αἵρεσις (“heresy”), signifies this very thing. EDITORS, from de Gourcy.] derived from “choice,” [Col. 0018B]  which a man uses either in founding or adopting them.

[Note:  “Therefore he said that the heretic [Col. 0017D] was self-condemned.” A little before, he said “being self-condemned,” for which today we read in the apostle “condemned [Col. 0018C] by his own judgment.” But Blessed Jerome both read and explained the former wording, as Quintinus also observed: “The heretic is said to be self-condemned because adulterers, fornicators, murderers, and other offenders are expelled from the Church by priests, whereas heretics pronounce sentence against themselves by withdrawing from the Church of their own choice; this withdrawal appears to be the condemnation of their own conscience.” [Col. 0018D] PAMELIUS.] Therefore he said that the heretic was self-condemned, because he himself chose that in which he is condemned. We are permitted to introduce nothing by our own choice, nor to choose [Col. 0018C] [Note:  “permit,” Semler.] what another has introduced by his own choice. We have the Lord’s apostles as our authorities. They themselves chose to introduce nothing by [Col. 0018C] their own decision, but faithfully delivered to the nations the teaching received from Christ. Therefore, even if an angel from heaven preached otherwise, [Note:  “He would be [Col. 0018D] called anathema by us.” The Holy Spirit had already foreseen it. The Holy Spirit had already foreseen that in a certain [Col. 0018D] virgin, Philumene, [Note:    “In a certain virgin Philumene.” Philumene was an Alexandrian girl possessed by a familiar demon, who told many lies. Apelles afterward violated her and was so blinded by love of this shameless woman that he wrote a book entitled *The Prophecies and Manifestations of Philumene*. See Eusebius, *History* V, and Blessed Augustine, *On Heresies*, to Quodvultdeus. Almost all others deliberately tried to bury this impure little woman in silence. LE PR.] an angel of seduction would transform himself into an angel of light; led by his signs and tricks, Apelles introduced [Col. 0018C] a new heresy.  

## CHAPTER VII [Col. 0019A]



Finally, since heresies themselves are suborned by philosophy, the apostle also prescribed that philosophy must be guarded against under the name of curiosity.

[Col. 0019C]

[Note:  “These are doctrines of men”: diabolical doctrines, born and invented for those whose ears itch—that is, men driven by various fleshly desires, who long to hear novel, curious, and soothing things. Hence they seek teachers who will not bite with the word and resist vices, but flatter them and their desires and scratch their ears by preaching honeyed things [Col. 0019B] popular with the crowd. These are the men Paul foretold in 2 Tim. 4. LA CERDA.] These are [Col. 0019B] doctrines of men and demons, born from the ingenuity of secular wisdom for itching ears (2 Tim. 4:3) [Col. 0019B] [Note:  “Of the world,” Franeker.]. The Lord called that wisdom foolishness and chose the foolish things [Col. 0019B] of the world to confound [Note:  “for the confusion,” Semler.] philosophy itself (1 Cor. 1:27). For it is the material [Note:  Heumann conjectures [Col. 0019B] “mother.”] of secular wisdom, a rash interpreter of the divine nature and dispensation. Heresies themselves are suborned by [Col. 0019B] philosophy.

From it come Valentinus’s aeons, his forms of some [Col. 0019B] unknown kind, and his trinity of man [Note:  Rigaltius, from Agobard’s book: “some unknown infinite [Col. 0019B] things belonging to man.” Compare *On the Soul* 21.]; he had [Col. 0019B] been a Platonist [Note:  “madness,” Junius from certain manuscripts.]. From it comes Marcion’s “better god” of tranquility ; he came from the Stoics. The claim that the soul perishes is adopted [Col. 0019C] from the Epicureans; the denial of the restoration of the [Col. 0020B] flesh is taken from the common school of all philosophers. Where matter is made equal with God, there [Col. 0020B] is Zeno’s teaching; where anything is alleged [Note:  “bound,” Semler.] about a fiery god, Heraclitus intervenes [Note:  Heumann conjectures “discovers.”]. [Col. 0020A] Heretics and philosophers turn over [Col. 0019C] the same material and become entangled in the same examinations: Whence comes evil, and why? Whence man, and how? And, as Valentinus lately proposed, whence God? From an enthymesis and an ectroma, of course.  [Note: [Col. 0020B]  “Ectroma.” Jerome, in his first commentary on Amos, writes [Col. 0019C] that Valentinus calls the last—that is, the thirtieth—of his aeons Christ and ἔκτρωμα, that is, “an abortion.” RHENANUS.]

Poor [Note:  Semler reads [Col. 0019D] “It follows” for “Poor.”] Aristotle [Note:  Gregory of Elvira, *On Faith*: “Do not, unhappy man, collect Aristotle’s artful arguments against Christ the Lord of all creation, while somehow professing yourself a Christian; do not approach the pious confession of the ineffable mystery of God like a deceiving counter, as though you could circumscribe it by the discipline of earthly calculation.” Again: “Where now are those impious sophisms of yours, which you learned under Aristotle, your bishop?” This Baetican bishop of Elvira is no commonplace author; he is numbered among ecclesiastical writers in Jerome’s catalogue. He wrote to Galla Placidia, daughter of Emperor Theodosius, against the Arians. I marvel that this otherwise sufficiently candid man never once names our Septimius, [Col. 0020B] though he everywhere takes much from him. RIG.]! He taught them dialectic: [Col. 0020B] the art of building up and tearing down, slippery in propositions, forced in conjectures, [Col. 0019D] harsh in arguments, a factory of contentions [Note:  “contention,” Semler.], troublesome even to itself, reconsidering everything [Note:  “handling,” Semler.] so that it has handled nothing at all.
 [Col. 0020C]
Hence those fables [Note:  “Hence also those fables.” Quintinus says some thought this warning aimed at the Jews, who continually boasted in their ancestors Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and others. The boast was useless, but bred no question or fables, since every Jew had his true lineage and ancestors well known and undisputed. Some said pagans and their theogony were censured. Tertullian believed the makers of aeons were marked: they divided their aeons into various chambers, showing who was begotten by whom, and pretended that all divinity was contained in them. Cerdo and Valentinus were contemporaries of the apostles and immeasurably disturbed unbelievers with these endless questions. Among such men the apostle names Hymenaeus, Alexander, and Philetus. In my judgment the entire [Col. 0020D] passage concerns the refutation of heretics. Epiphanius understands [Col. 0020D] it so too. The man who twists the passage toward ceremonies, petty human constitutions, and scholastic questions seems to me to calumniate as usual. PAMELIUS.] and endless genealogies [Note:  The Greek uses ἀπέραντοις (“endless”) (1 Tim. 1:3). It marks Jewish ravings and ridiculous inventions. LE PR.], fruitless questions, and words creeping like cancer [Col. 0020B] (1 Tim. 1:4; 3:4; 2 Tim. 2:17–23). Restraining us from these, the apostle explicitly testifies that philosophy must be [Col. 0020B] guarded against [Note:  “having testified,” Semler, Venetian.], writing to the Colossians (2:8): “See that no one circumvent you [Note:  “be one who circumvents you,” Semler.] [Col. 0020B] through philosophy and empty seduction, [Col. 0020B] according to human tradition,” not without the Holy Spirit’s providence.

He had been at Athens and had learned from encounters that this human wisdom, the imitator [Note:  “follower,” Venetian.] and adulterator of truth, was itself divided into manifold heresies by the diversity of mutually [Col. 0020D] opposed sects. What therefore has Athens to do with Jerusalem? What has the Academy to do with the Church? What have heretics to do with Christians? Our instruction comes from Solomon’s Portico [Note:  “From Solomon’s Portico.” Our author opposes Solomon’s Portico to the Stoics’ porch. Both Christ and the apostles often taught in the temple and its portico, called Solomon’s because it was built over the ruins of Solomon’s portico (John 10:23; Acts 3 and 5). EDITORS, from de Gourcy.], [Col. 0020D] and Solomon himself had taught that the Lord must be [Col. 0021C] sought in simplicity of heart (Wis. 1:1). Let those who have produced a Stoic, Platonic [Note:  “And dialectical Christianity.” This is a strong argument that Christians should detest sophistical questions and logical traps that soil religion and theology. [Col. 0021D] Why depend on Plato or Aristotle to be a Christian? Both were pagans and foreign to truth, able to hand down only inventions and impostures. Why mix their opinions or errors with Christian doctrines? Remember the unhappy end, related by Zonaras, of the painter who tried to portray Christ in the same clothing and arms as Jupiter: his hand immediately withered upon the panel. Take care not to unite things entirely contrary. LE PR.] and dialectical Christianity [Note:  Paris [Col. 0020B] reads “Christians”; Rhenanus proposed “preferred to Christianity.”] [Col. 0020C] look to themselves. We have no need of curiosity after Jesus Christ, [Col. 0021A] nor of inquiry after the Gospel. When we believe, we desire to believe nothing further. For this we believe first: that there is nothing further we ought to believe.

## CHAPTER VIII

The saying “SEEK AND YOU SHALL FIND” offers no obstacle, for it was spoken to those by whom Christ had not yet been acknowledged.

I therefore come to that clause which our own people advance for entering upon curiosity [Col. 0021C] and heretics press for introducing scrupulosity [Note:  “curiosity,” Semler.]: “It is written,” they say, “Seek and you shall find” (Matt. 7:7). Let us recall when the Lord uttered this saying. I think it was at the very beginning of his teaching, when everyone [Col. 0021B] still doubted whether he was the Christ, Peter had not [Col. 0021D] yet declared him the Son of God,  and even John had ceased to be certain of him [Note:  Rigaltius interprets: “even after John’s departure.” Macereus rightly takes it of John the Baptist, who, already certain of Christ through the heavenly voice (Matt. 3:17), had ceased to exist—that is, died by Herod’s beheading. But Latinius’s sense, indicated from *On Baptism* 10, pleases better: the spirit of prophecy failed in John after [Col. 0022C] the whole Spirit was transferred to the Lord, so that he later sent to ask whether this was the man whom he had proclaimed and identified (Matt. 11:2). Compare *Against Marcion* IV. PAMELIUS.—Tertullian [Col. 0022D] truly seems in *On Baptism* to have fallen into so absurd an error. Yet at the beginning of Christ’s teaching John had not ceased to exist, as Macereus interprets. EDITORS, from de Gourcy.] [Note:  Heumann: “had asked.”]. It was therefore rightly said then [Note:  This clause is absent from Semler.], “Seek and you shall find,” when he still had to be sought because he had [Col. 0021C] not yet been acknowledged [Note:  Final clause absent from [Col. 0021C] Semler.]. This applies to the Jews, to whom that entire speech of rebuke belongs; they had sources in which to seek Christ.
 [Col. 0021C]
[Note:  “They have Moses and Elijah.” Tertullian reads more than Luke 16 contains, where Greek and Latin have only “They have Moses and the prophets.” Perhaps he was [Col. 0022D] thinking of Moses and Elijah’s appearance on Mount Tabor. PAMELIUS.] “They have,” he says, “Moses and Elijah” (Luke 16:29), that is, the law and prophets who proclaim Christ, just as elsewhere he says (John 5:39), “Search the Scriptures in which you hope for salvation, for they speak of me.” This [Note:  “Here,” Semler.] will be “SEEK AND YOU SHALL FIND.” The sequel too plainly applies to the Jews: “Knock and it shall be opened [Col. 0021C] to you.” The Jews had formerly been with God; afterward, cast out for their offenses, they began to be outside God. The nations, however, had never been with God, but were a drop from a bucket and  dust from a threshing floor, always outside (Isa. [Col. 0021C] 40:15).  How, then, will one who was always outside knock at [Col. 0022A] a place where he never was? What [Note:  “How,” Heumann.] door does [Col. 0021C] he know, through which [Note:  “by which,” Semler.] [Col. 0021C] he was never received or expelled? Is not the man who knows that [Col. 0021C] he was once inside and was driven out more likely to knock [Note:  “knocked,” Venetian.] [Col. 0021C] and know the door [Note:  “at the door [Col. 0021C] which he knows,” Heumann.]?

“ASK AND YOU SHALL RECEIVE” likewise belongs to one who knew from whom to ask, [Col. 0021C] from whom something had been promised—to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob by God, whom the nations knew no more than they knew any promise of his. Therefore he spoke to Israel: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 10:15). He was not yet throwing [Col. 0022C] the children’s bread to dogs, nor yet commanding them to go upon the way [Note: [Col. 0022C]  Semler inserts “of the gentiles.”] of the nations (Matt. 28:19). At the end he commanded them to go teach and baptize the nations, for they would soon receive  the Holy [Col. 0022B] Spirit, the Paraclete, who would lead them into all truth (John 16:13). This he did in their case [Col. 0022C] [Note:  Variant readings: “therefore in that case”; “therefore them.”] [Col. 0022C] [Note:  Junius; others read present tense.]. If the apostles [Col. 0022C] themselves, teachers appointed for the nations, were to receive the Paraclete as teacher, “SEEK AND YOU SHALL FIND” will be still more inapplicable [Col. 0022C] [Note:  Heumann’s reading; others have past tense.] to us, upon whom teaching was to come unasked through the apostles, and upon the apostles through the Holy Spirit. All the Lord’s sayings were [Col. 0022C] indeed set down for all, passing to us through Jewish ears [Note:  “But most were directed to [Col. 0022D] persons”—namely Jews. RIG.]; yet most, being directed to particular persons, established for us an example, not the literal terms of the admonition.

## CHAPTER IX

We, however, who have already believed, must seek nothing else.

I now voluntarily yield from this position: let “SEEK AND YOU [Col. 0022C] SHALL FIND” have been [Col. 0022C] said to everyone. Yet [Col. 0022C] even here one must contend  with sound sense [Col. 0022C] [Notes:  “weigh,” Venetian; variants [Col. 0022D] “sense,” “certain.”] under the governance of interpretation. [Note:  “Under the governance of interpretation,” that is, with reason [Col. 0023C] and rational discipline, which must govern every interpretation. Irenaeus treated this passage [Col. 0023A] in the same sense, [Col. 0023C] II.46. RIG.]  No divine utterance is so unrestrained and diffuse that only the words are defended and the rationale of the words is not established. [Note:  Quintinus [Col. 0023D] cites a similar passage in the Decrees I, q. 1: “Let us not think the Gospel lies in the words of Scripture, but in the sense; not on the surface, but in the marrow; not in the leaves of the [Col. 0023C] sayings, but in the root of reason.” PAMELIUS.] [Col. 0023D]

First I lay this down: Christ established one definite thing [Note:  Macereus correctly interprets this as the one rule or creed of faith, each article being one, certain, and determinate. The Church after the apostles proposed no new article of faith. Although it explained obscure or ambiguous articles more clearly, and divided into several what had been contained in one general article, they are not more articles in reality but only by distinction and explanation. What the ancients knew generally, we know distinctly and particularly, as human curiosity—especially that of heretics attacking the faith—grows daily, along with God’s grace in explaining Scripture; compare Eph. 3:5. PAMELIUS.], which the nations must wholly [Col. 0024C] believe and therefore seek so that, when they find it, they may believe. Inquiry into a single definite institution cannot be infinite. One must seek until one finds, and believe when one has found; thereafter nothing remains but to guard what one has believed, while believing besides that there is nothing else to believe or therefore to seek, since one has found and believed what was established by him who commands no inquiry beyond what he established.

If anyone doubts this, it [Col. 0023C] will be demonstrated that we [Note:  “We,” that [Col. 0024C] is, Catholics. SEMLER.] possess what Christ established.  Meanwhile, [Col. 0023B] confident of the proof, I anticipate the matter [Note: [Col. 0023C]  Variants: “turn beforehand,” “anticipate.”], admonishing certain men that nothing must [Col. 0023C] be sought beyond what they have believed to [Col. 0023C] be what they ought to have sought, lest they interpret [Col. 0023C] “SEEK AND YOU SHALL FIND” without [Note:  Rhenanus read [Col. 0023C] “with no interpreter of rational discipline.”] rational discipline.

## CHAPTER X

Otherwise, if we always seek, we shall never find and never believe.

The rationale of this saying consists in three points: subject, time, and manner—subject, that you consider what must be sought; time, when; manner, how [Col. 0024A] far. What Christ  established must therefore be sought, [Col. 0023C] obviously while you have not found it [Note: [Col. 0024C]  “as long as you have not found,” Junius.], and only until you find. You have found when you have believed: you would not have believed had you not found, nor sought except in order to find. You seek in order [Col. 0024C] to find and find in order to believe. By believing you have fixed the entire continuation [Note:  “Continuation,” that is, duration. SEMLER.] [Col. 0024C] of seeking and finding. The fruit of seeking itself set this limit for you [Note:  “believing,” Rigaltius.]; he who wills you to believe only what he established, and therefore to seek no more, marked out this boundary for you.

But if, because so many other things have been established [Col. 0024C] by others, we must seek as long as we can find, we shall always seek and never believe at all. Where will seeking end? [Note:  “Where the station?” [Col. 0024D] The whole sentence is a military allegory: you have fixed the stakes of your tent and station; let them go no farther. You have reached the fruit of seeking, which God commanded under this limitation; you must seek [Col. 0024B] no farther. A “station” is where soldiers stand and converse. LA CERDA.] Where will belief take its stand? Where will finding be completed? With Marcion? But Valentinus too proposes [Col. 0024C] “SEEK AND YOU SHALL FIND.” With Valentinus? Apelles too will strike me with this saying; [Col. 0024D] so will Ebion and Simon, and every order has nothing else by which to insinuate itself and bind me to it. I shall therefore be nowhere [Note:  Agobard: “It will therefore be”; several conjectures. Albaspinaeus explains: “While I agree with so many that one must seek, I [Col. 0024C] shall never end seeking, which heretics especially [Col. 0024D] desire, so that I may always seek with them as though I had not yet discovered what Christ established and what must be sought and believed.”], while everywhere I am confronted with “SEEK AND YOU SHALL FIND” [Note:  The cited text gives no support to defenders of free examination; it concerns prayers raised confidently to the heavenly Father, who much more than evil human parents gives good [Col. 0024C] things to those who ask him (Matt. 7:11). The cited passages of Luke carry no different sense. EDITORS, from de Gourcy.], as if I were nowhere and had never grasped what Christ established, what must be sought, what must be believed.

## CHAPTER XI

For no one seeks unless he either never possessed or has lost.

One wanders without penalty unless one sins—although to err [Col. 0025A] is to sin; I say, he wanders with impunity who abandons nothing. But if I have believed what I ought to believe and again think something else must be sought, I surely hope that something else may be found. This hope is impossible unless either I had not believed when I seemed to believe, or I ceased believing. Thus, [Col. 0025C] abandoning my faith, I am found a denier.  [Note:  “I am found a denier.” A denier is one who, after finding the well-worn road of truth and accepting Christ’s faith with Catholics, abandons, innovates upon, or changes it before men. Christ will abandon and deny him before the angels. Deniers were therefore expelled from the Church’s communion because they had not endured to the end but defected to pagans or heretics; when they later returned penitent they were admitted only with difficulty, which once caused a great controversy in the early Church. Tertullian [Col. 0025D] therefore levels the grave reproach of “deniers” not only against full defectors to heretics, but also against those wishing to learn something from them. PAMELIUS.]

I will say it once: no one seeks unless he either never possessed or has lost. The old woman had lost one of ten drachmas (Luke 15:8), and therefore sought; when she found it, she ceased seeking. The neighbor had no bread (Luke 11:5), and therefore knocked; when the door was opened and he received it, he ceased knocking. The widow asked the judge to hear her (Luke 18:3) because she was not admitted; once heard, she pressed only thus far. So there is an end to seeking, knocking, and asking. “For to one asking it will be given,” he says, “to one knocking [Col. 0025B] it will be opened, and one seeking will find” (Luke 11:9). Let him who always seeks see to it, because he has not found: he seeks where it will not be found. Let him who always knocks see to it, because it will never be opened: he knocks there [Note: [Col. 0025C]  “there,” Venetian, Pamelius, Rigaltius.] where no one is. Let him who always asks see to it, because he will never be heard [Col. 0025C] [Note:  “is heard,” Semler.]: he asks from one who does not hear.

## CHAPTER XII

If anything still must be sought, let us seek it not among heretics, whom we are forbidden to approach, but from our own people and concerning our own matters.

Even if we still and always had to seek, where ought it be sought? Among heretics, where everything is foreign and opposed to our truth, and whom we are forbidden to approach? [Col. 0026A] What slave expects rations from a stranger—to say nothing of his master’s enemy?  What soldier seeks a gift and pay from kings who are not allies—to say nothing of enemies—unless he is plainly a deserter, fugitive, and rebel? The old woman too sought the drachma within [Col. 0025C] her own roof; the man who knocked beat upon his neighbor’s [Note:  Variant corrupt readings.] door; the widow addressed a judge who, though harsh, was not an [Col. 0025C] enemy. No one can be instructed by that from which he is destroyed; no one is enlightened by him through whom he is darkened. Let us therefore seek among our own people, from our [Col. 0025C] own people, and concerning our own matters, and only what can come into question while the rule of faith remains safe.

## CHAPTER XIII

The rule (or creed) of faith prescribed for us, so that from this point we may [Col. 0026B] profess what we believe.

 The rule [Col. 0025D] of faith is this [Note:  The rule of faith: faith, Κανὼν τῆς ἀληθείας (“rule of truth”), a little body of truth, Σωμάτιον τῆς ἀληθείας (“little body of truth”) in Irenaeus, because the articles constituting a Christian were arranged in the creed as in one body. In the following rule no mention is made of burial or descent into hell, as likewise in the rule at the start of *Veiling of Virgins* or in Irenaeus, as though the mention of the cross—that is, death—included burial and descent. But in *Against Praxeas* the articles include: “He suffered, died, and was buried”; Augustine, *Unfinished Literal Commentary on Genesis* 1: “to be crucified, buried, and rise.” RIG.—Here he calls “rule” what [Col. 0026C] we commonly call the Apostles’ Creed. Some learned men doubted whether it was apostolic, but incautiously. It is certain that the apostles handed down a definite rule of faith, comprised in twelve statements according to their number and called a creed, says Augustine, sermon 181 *On Time*, as he and many ancients attest elsewhere. It is also certain that the creed we now recite, which the Church commands us to believe, has descended from [Col. 0026D] those times by continuous tradition. PAMELIUS.], so that [Col. 0025C] from this point we may profess what we defend [Note:  Formerly read “believe.”]: namely, one altogether believes that there is one God and no other besides the Creator of the world, who [Col. 0026C] produced everything from nothing through his Word, emitted [Col. 0026C] first of all [Note:  “sent down,” Venetian after Rigaltius.]; that this Word, called his Son [Note:  “the Son,” Semler.], was seen in various ways by the patriarchs in God’s name, always heard in the prophets, [Col. 0026D] and lastly brought down by the Spirit and power of God the Father into the Virgin Mary; that it became flesh in her womb, was [Col. 0026C] born of her, and enacted [Note:  “Enacted Jesus Christ,” that is, assumed that human person and did all foretold of Jesus Christ. RIG.] Jesus Christ [Note:  Variants: “existed,” “went forth,” “was man and existed.” I change nothing; compare later, “who may [Col. 0026D] enact believers.”]; thereafter preached a new law and a new promise of the kingdom of heaven; performed miracles; was fastened to a cross; rose on the third day; was taken into heaven and sat at the Father’s right hand; sent the vicarious power of the Holy Spirit to direct believers; and will come in glory to take the saints into the fruit of eternal life and the heavenly promises , and to sentence the profane to eternal fire, after the resurrection of both classes with the restoration of their flesh.

[Note:  “Sat at the right hand of the Father.” God the Father [Col. 0027C] must not be imagined as bounded by human form, with right and left sides, nor his sitting as bent knees; [Col. 0027D] such an image must not be placed by a Christian in a temple, much less in the heart. God’s “sitting” signifies judicial power; “at the right hand” means in highest blessedness, [Col. 0027A] where justice, peace, and joy [Col. 0027D] are. Augustine, *Faith and Creed* VII.14.  RIG., as corrected by the editors.] [Note:  “And to sentence the profane,” etc. Tertullian mentions fire, which is very frequently located in hell. Beza and Calvin hold that there is no fire in hell, but that it signifies the miserable state of the damned. Yet Scripture mentions this [Col. 0027C] fire so frequently that we must necessarily confess fire [Col. 0027D] to exist in hell. LA CERDA.] [Note:  “After the resurrection of both classes”: the pious and impious. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0027C]  “resurrection,” others.]

## CHAPTER XIV

This rule, established by Christ, raises no questions among us except those introduced by heresies and those that make heretics.

This rule, established by Christ as will be proved, raises no questions among us except those introduced by heresies and those that make heretics. So long as its form remains in its proper order, inquire and discuss as much as you like and pour out every desire of curiosity. If something seems to you suspended in ambiguity or veiled in obscurity, there is surely some brother  who is a teacher endowed with the [Col. 0027C] grace of knowledge, someone conversant among the experienced, someone seeking with you [Col. 0027B] but more inquisitively [Note:  Several corrupt variants: “someone,” “something”; Venetian, Rigaltius, Paris, and Pamelius [Col. 0027C] repeat “with you.”]. In the last resort, it is better to remain [Col. 0027C] ignorant lest you know what you ought not, since you know what you ought [Note:  Semler deletes this clause; La Cerda read “since you know what you ought.”]. “Your faith,” he says, “has saved you” [Col. 0027C] (Luke 18:42), not training in the Scriptures. Faith is placed in the rule: you possess the law and salvation from observing the law. Training, however, consists in curiosity and has only the glory arising from zeal for expertise. Let curiosity yield to faith and glory to salvation. At least let them cease clamoring and be still. To know nothing contrary to the rule is to know everything.

Even if heretics were not enemies of truth, even if we were not forewarned to flee them, what sense is there in conferring with men who themselves profess that they are still seeking? For if they truly still seek, they have found nothing  certain as yet [Note:  Paris reads “discovered”; Junius conjectures “certainly,” Franeker “certain [Col. 0027C] indeed,” and Franeker inserts “still further.”]; [Col. 0027C] and therefore, whatever they seem meanwhile to hold, they display their own doubt  so long as they keep seeking. Accordingly, you who likewise seek, looking to men who themselves seek, must necessarily [Col. 0028A] be led into the pit—doubtful by the doubtful, uncertain by the uncertain, blind by the blind (Matt. 15:14).

But when, for the sake of deceiving, they pretend that they are still [Note:  Paris reads “for this purpose.”] seeking, in order to insinuate their treatises into us by implanting [Col. 0027C] anxiety, and then, when they have approached [Note:  “have approached,” Semler.] us, immediately defend the very things which they said must [Col. 0028C] be sought, we must refute [Note:  “reckon,” Venetian, Rigaltius.] them in such a way that they know we are [Note:  “you are,” Venetian.] [Col. 0028C] deniers not of Christ but of them. For while they still seek, [Col. 0028C] they do not yet possess; while they do not [Note:  Semler thinks “not” should be deleted and that after “possess” one should read “and [Col. 0028C] they do not yet believe.”] possess, they have not yet believed and are not Christians. But when they do possess and believe, they nevertheless say that inquiry is necessary in order to defend their belief. Before they defend it, they deny it, because in seeking they confess that they have not yet believed. Therefore those [Col. 0028B] who  are not Christians even to themselves are much less Christians to us. Those who come by deceit—what faith do they discuss? Those who introduce [Note:  “pronounce,” Semler.] truth by a [Col. 0028C] lie—what truth do they champion?

## CHAPTER XV

Now coming to his subject, Tertullian prescribes that heretics are not to be admitted to any dispute concerning the Scriptures.

But they themselves deal with the Scriptures, and from the Scriptures they seek to persuade. [Note: [Col. 0027D] As though, of course, they could speak from some other source about matters of faith. Everyone understands these words as though he were denying that heretics could prove their faith from any writings other than the two Testaments. A different thought, however, occurs to me: namely, that these same words are not stated negatively, and that the Author intends nothing else by them than that heretics sometimes draw even their arguments from the Scriptures, although in proof of their opinion they might adduce the writings of the philosophers, from whom they drew their fabrications, as he demonstrated in chapter 8. In confirmation of the explanation we defend, it may be observed that no question mark is written here, though those who interpret the passage in the contrary sense are compelled to supply one. I must nevertheless admit that the contrary interpretation takes possession of readers’ minds far more readily; but if anyone recalls the Author’s acuteness and skill in expression and keeps them before his mind, he will discover that interpretation to be spurious. ALBASP.] As though, of course, they could speak [Note: [Col. 0028C] “Persuade,” not “speak,” Seml.] about matters of faith from any source other than the writings of the faith? [Note: [Col. 0028D] We have therefore come to the point. Quintinus says that throughout his entire book Tertullian proposed to teach this one thing: that one must neither dispute nor even converse about the Scriptures with the Gnostics. For disputes of this kind harass those who are weak in faith, disturb them, cause them to waver, often carry those who are undecided over to the other side, and cast the weak down into heresy. If these things are not truer than truth itself, let us not cease disputing and writing against heretics, nor fasting and praying against them; yet meanwhile, and everywhere, let us remember that this kind of demon is not cast out except by prayer and fasting. PAM.] We have therefore come to the point; for this was the direction in which we were aiming, and this was what we were preparing by the preface to our address [Note: [Col. 0028C] “Here,” Seml. Rig.] [Note: [Col. 0028C] Seml. deletes “this.”] [Note: [Col. 0028C] Others read “to the address.”] [Note: [Col. 0028C] “The preface,” Seml.]: that from this point onward we may engage upon the very ground on which our adversaries issue their challenge.

They parade the Scriptures, and by this very audacity [Col. 0028C] they immediately unsettle some; in the actual encounter, however, they weary the strong, capture the weak, and send those in between away [Col. 0029A] burdened with doubt. [Note: [Col. 0029C] “This approach, therefore, above all.” He counsels against entering into a contest with heretics—not because he distrusts the ecclesiastical cause as though it were doubtful; far from it—but because heretics insolently abuse Holy Scripture and its legitimate sense in support of their blasphemies. From this the victory becomes doubtful, while the danger to hearers who hear them endlessly trumpeting nothing but Scripture becomes utterly certain. So far, therefore, is frequent ostentation of the Holy Scriptures in these matters from being a mark of true religion, that they should rather be greatly feared, lest they hurl against us what they themselves possess—that is, the filth of blasphemies wrapped in a tissue of divine Scriptures. See Clement of Alexandria, book *Against the Heretics*. LAC.] It is therefore this approach above all that we block: they are not to be admitted [Note: [Col. 0029C] “Are to be admitted,” Seml.] to any dispute concerning the Scriptures. [Note: [Col. 0029D] “If these are those powers of theirs.” The sense is: whether they can use these weapons, or whether the Scriptures are their weapons. ALBASP.] If these are those resources of theirs, so that they may be able to possess them [Note: [Col. 0029C] For “those,” the *Juris Latini* proposes “any”; Seml.] [Note: [Col. 0029C] Heuman deletes “so that they might be able to possess them.”], it must be determined to whom possession of the Scriptures belongs, lest anyone be admitted to them to whom it belongs in no way at all.

## CHAPTER XVI

**First, that our faith owes obedience to the Apostle, who forbids disputation when he prohibited meeting a heretic after one correction.**

I might seem to have introduced this from a counsel of mistrust, or from a desire to establish the case by a different procedure [Note: [Col. 0029D] “I might have introduced.” That is, “I might have seemed to introduce.” SEML.], unless the rationale were firmly established—especially this one: [Note: [Col. 0029C] “Which,” Venet., from the book of Agobard.] that our faith owes obedience to the Apostle, who forbids us to enter into questions, to lend our ears to novel expressions (1 Tim. 6:4), and to meet a heretic after one correction (Titus 3:10), not after a disputation. He so thoroughly prohibited disputation that he designated correction as the reason for meeting the heretic—and this correction only once [Note: [Col. 0029D] “And this correction only once.” On the contrary, the Apostle does not command that a heretical person be avoided except after a first and second correction (Titus 3:10). Moreover, if you observe carefully, the original word, νουθεσίαν (*nouthesian*), signifies a mere admonition, counsel, or persuasion. Both the Syriac and Arabic versions agree with the Greek text; the Vulgate and Arabic, however—[the note is textually confused here]. Yet all the readings agree on this point: that the person of the heretic is not to be avoided until after several admonitions. See the *Polyglot*, vol. V, London, 1657. For charity, and prudence as well, dictate that exhortations, persuasions, and entreaties must by no means be withheld, whoever the person may be and whatever error he may be involved in. This was the purpose of the Gospel and of its divine Author, who impressed nothing more earnestly upon his followers than that they should be gentle, patient, and merciful. That Tertullian possessed a very different disposition is all too certain. EDD., from the notes of DE GOURCY.]; because, of course, he is not a Christian, lest he should be thought deserving of rebuke in the manner of a Christian, once and again and before two or three witnesses (Matt. 18:15–16), since he is to be rebuked precisely for the reason that one must not dispute with him.

## CHAPTER XVII

**Next, that an encounter over the Scriptures accomplishes nothing, since some heresies do not accept them; and if they accept any, they distort them by additions and subtractions, or do not accept them entire; and if they accept them to some extent entire, they devise divergent interpretations.**

Next, an encounter over the Scriptures accomplishes nothing at all, unless it be that one enters upon the overturning of one’s stomach or one’s brain. One heresy does not accept certain Scriptures; and if it accepts any, it does not accept them [Note: [Col. 0030C] “And if it accepts any, it does not accept them entire.” The impudence of our heretics could not have been sketched more elegantly: they admit Scripture and immediately reject it if anything in it obstructs them. They also add their own explanations in order to twist it toward their own meanings, and everywhere they advance nothing but the dreams of sick men, or interpretations of dreams. LE PR.] entire. By additions and subtractions it distorts them to suit the arrangement of its own scheme; and even if it presents them entire to some extent, it nevertheless perverts them by inventing divergent interpretations. A counterfeit meaning [Note: [Col. 0030D] “A counterfeit meaning clamors against it,” etc. That is, a perverse interpretation. *Adulterare* in this sense means “to corrupt” and καπηλεύειν λόγον τοῦ Θεοῦ, “to peddle or adulterate the word of God.” So blessed Paul, 2 Corinthians 5 [the reference is apparently corrupt]. LE PR.] clamors against the truth just as much as a corrupting pen does.

Their various presumptions [Note: [Col. 0029C] “Vain,” Jun.] necessarily refuse [Note: [Col. 0030C] “Wish,” Semler, from Agobard and the Dijon manuscript.] to acknowledge those passages by which they are refuted [Note: [Col. 0030D] “They necessarily refuse to acknowledge those passages by which they are refuted.” So below: “Those whose purpose was to teach differently were compelled by necessity to arrange the instruments of their teaching differently.” RIG.]. They rely upon passages they have composed falsely and those they have seized upon because of their ambiguity [Note: [Col. 0030C] “Began,” Seml. Pam.]. What will you accomplish, however highly trained in the Scriptures you may be, when whatever you defend is denied by the other side, and whatever you deny is defended? For your own part, you will lose nothing but your voice in the contention, and gain nothing but bile from the blasphemy [Note: [Col. 0030C] Seml. reads “a paltry reputation for blasphemy.”].

## CHAPTER XVIII

**Even the person for whose sake you descend into an encounter over the Scriptures will depart more uncertain than before, because denial and defense are evenly matched in the altercation.**

But suppose there is someone for whose sake you descend into an encounter over the Scriptures, in order to confirm him while he is in doubt: will he incline toward the truth, or rather toward the heresies? Moved by the very fact that he sees you have accomplished nothing, with denial and defense established on equal footing by the opposing [Note: [Col. 0030C] “Adverse,” Venet. Rigalt.] side [Note: [Col. 0030C] “Established,” Seml. Pam.; *statu*, Rigalt. Venet.], he will certainly depart still more uncertain after an altercation that is, at the least, evenly matched, not knowing which side to judge heretical. [Note: [Col. 0030D] “These things, assuredly, they themselves also have.” What Catholics, Quintinus says, truly allege against heretics—namely, that they do not understand but corrupt the Scriptures—heretics themselves allege against Catholics. What usefulness, then, can there be in disputing with such people, since—as Jerome most truly said at the end of his book *Against the Luciferians*—heretics can indeed easily be defeated, but cannot be persuaded? Thus, in disputing, you will certainly lose your words, and perhaps the hearer’s soul as well; and in the end you will hear yourself called a heretic. Nor is it a new thing for the faith and religion of Christ to be called “heresy” as an insult by its adversaries, as Jerome attests in his commentary on Titus 3. PAM.] These same charges, assuredly, they themselves [Col. 0031A] have to turn back against us. For they too must say that it is rather we who introduce corruptions of the Scriptures and falsehoods in interpretation [Note: [Col. 0031C] Seml. adds “of them.”], since they likewise claim the truth for themselves.

## CHAPTER XIX

**The sole matter for dispute, therefore, is this: to whom the faith belongs; whose the Scriptures are; and from whom, through whom, and to whom the discipline by which people become Christians was handed down.**

Therefore, no appeal is to be made to the Scriptures, nor is the contest to be established in matters in which the victory is either nonexistent, uncertain, or equally uncertain [Note: [Col. 0031C] From traces of an ancient manuscript, Seml. and Pam. read “not very uncertain,” or “not very certain.”]. For even if a conference over the Scriptures did not turn out in such a way as to leave both sides evenly matched, the order of the subject required that this question be put first—the only one that must now be disputed: To whom does the faith itself belong? Whose are the Scriptures? From whom, through whom, when, and to whom was the discipline handed down by which people become Christians? [Note: [Col. 0031C] “For where it becomes apparent that the truth exists.” A notable passage in favor of Catholics, because among them is found the truth of the Scriptures and their interpretations, and of all Christian traditions. PAM.] For wherever it becomes apparent that the truth of Christian discipline and faith exists, there too will be found the truth of the Scriptures, of their interpretations, and of all Christian traditions [Note: [Col. 0031C] “Of Christians,” Seml. Gourcy.].

## CHAPTER XX

**But Christ handed down to the Apostles the one doctrine of the same faith; they proclaimed it to the nations and founded churches in each city. From these the other churches daily borrow what makes them churches, so that all these many and great churches are that one first Church derived from the Apostles, from which they all come.**

Our Lord Jesus Christ—allow me for the moment to say, whoever he is: the Son of whatever God, man and God composed of whatever substance, teacher of whatever faith, and promiser of whatever reward—while he lived upon earth himself declared what he was, what he had been, what will of the Father he administered, and what he determined that man must do. He declared it either openly to the people or privately to his disciples. From among these he had chosen twelve principal men to remain at his side, appointing them as teachers destined for the nations [Note: [Col. 0031D] “Teachers destined for the nations.” For there was no part of the world, however remote in distance or barbarous in the savagery of its customs, into which the glory of Christ did not most gloriously penetrate. Irenaeus, Justin, Clement, and Origen have treated this matter sufficiently. To this pertains Isaiah’s astonished exclamation in chapter 66, “Who has heard such things?” etc., and that of the royal Prophet: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth.” LAC.].

Accordingly, after one of them had been struck away, as he was departing [Note: [Col. 0031C] “Returning,” Semler. Pam.] to the Father following the resurrection, he commanded the remaining eleven to go and teach the nations, baptizing them [Note: [Col. 0032C] “Baptizing,” Seml.; variant spelling, Pam.] into the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. Immediately, therefore, the Apostles—a name meaning “those who are sent”—took Matthias by lot as the twelfth in Judas’s place, on the authority of the prophecy contained in a psalm of David. Having received the promised power of the Holy Spirit for miracles and utterance, they first bore witness throughout Judaea [Note: [Col. 0031D] “First throughout Judaea.” No one disputes that the Church was first founded at Jerusalem from among the Jews; hence among pagan writers there is almost no distinction between Jews and Christians. LE PR.] to faith in Jesus Christ and established churches. Then, setting out into the world, they proclaimed to the nations the same doctrine of the same faith [Col. 0032B], and thereafter founded churches in every city.

From these churches the others subsequently borrowed—and daily continue to borrow—the shoot of faith and the seeds of doctrine, so that they may become churches. [Note: [Col. 0031D] “From whom the shoot of faith.” Those who have written on agriculture, Quintinus says, call them *traduces*, especially in vines, when several little branches spread from one trunk or one arm of a vine and are led to another place while remaining connected with one another; they do not appear to differ greatly from layers. By a particularly elegant metaphor, Tertullian here calls the transference of faith from one church to another a *tradux fidei*, “a shoot of faith.” The churches, that is, handed down the apostolic doctrine to one another, as though from hand to hand. PAM.] On this account these churches themselves are also reckoned [Note: [Col. 0032C] “Will be reckoned,” Seml.] apostolic, as offspring of the apostolic churches. Every kind must necessarily be classified according to its origin. Accordingly, these many and great churches are that one first Church from the Apostles, from which they all come. Thus they are all first [Note: [Col. 0032C] “The first churches,” Seml. Pam.] and all apostolic, since all together establish their unity as one; since among them there is [Note: [Col. 0032C] Pam. and Seml. delete “since among them there is.”] the communion of peace, the name of brotherhood, and the reciprocal pledge of hospitality. [Note: [Col. 0032D] “The reciprocal pledge of hospitality.” With elegance, Tertullian, an inventor of words, fashioned the verb *contesserare* from *tessera*, and from it *contesseratio*. It signifies a more intimate association made by means of a token. For among the ancients the *tessera* was a token of hospitality, and if someone happened to meet another and showed it, he was immediately recognized. RHEN.] These rights are governed by no other principle than the one transmission of the same sacrament. [Note: [Col. 0032D] “The one transmission of the same sacrament.” That is, of the same creed or rule, the same faith. RIG.—It is very important to observe that the meaning ascribed to this word in Tertullian by the interpreters does not apply here. It is used for the rule of faith, Christ’s commandments, and all the rites and discipline of the Christian religion, but not for an oath. Thus he says that all the churches communicate with one another and enjoy the same right because, of course, they have continued in the faith handed down by the Apostles, and have faithfully preserved and handed it down to posterity. ALBASP.]

## CHAPTER XXI

**From this he therefore formulates another prescription: no preachers are to be accepted except those whom Christ appointed; and consequently that doctrine is to be accepted which undoubtedly maintains what the Church received from the Apostles both by living voice and by letters, the Apostles from Christ, and Christ from God. The testimony to the truth of our doctrine is therefore this: that we communicate with the apostolic churches.**

From this, therefore, we formulate our prescription. If the Lord Jesus Christ sent the Apostles to preach, no other preachers are to be accepted than those whom Christ appointed, because no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son has revealed him; and the Son does not appear to have revealed him to anyone other than the Apostles whom he sent to preach—namely, to preach what he had revealed to them.

As for what they preached—that is, what Christ revealed to them—here too I prescribe that it must be proved in no other way than through those same churches which the Apostles themselves founded by preaching to them, both by living voice, as the saying goes, and afterward through letters. If these things are so, it follows that every doctrine agreeing with those apostolic churches, the mother-churches and sources of the faith, must be reckoned true, since it undoubtedly maintains what the churches received from the Apostles, the Apostles from Christ, and Christ from God. Every remaining doctrine [Note: [Col. 0033C] “Every doctrine, however,” in place of “every remaining doctrine,” Venet. Rig.] must be prejudged false if it savors of anything contrary to the truth of the churches, the Apostles, Christ, and God.

It remains, therefore, for us to demonstrate whether this doctrine of ours, whose rule we set forth above, is classified as belonging to the tradition of the Apostles, and [Note: [Col. 0033C] “From this very fact,” Pam. Seml.] by that very fact whether the other doctrines proceed from falsehood. We communicate with the apostolic churches, because our doctrine differs from theirs in no respect [Note: [Col. 0033C] “No doctrine differs,” Pam. Seml.]. This is the testimony of truth.

## CHAPTER XXII

**The Apostles, however—whatever the opposing party may customarily say to the contrary—both knew and handed down everything; for Christ deigned to explain all the Scriptures to them and sent the Holy Spirit to lead them into all truth.**

But because the proof is so readily available [Note: [Col. 0033C] “Then,” Seml.] that, if it were produced immediately [Col. 0034A], nothing would remain to be reconsidered, let us act for the moment as though it had not been produced by us [Note: [Col. 0033C] “As though produced.” That is, “just as though it had been produced.” EDD.], and allow the opposing party an opportunity to see whether they think they can advance anything to weaken this prescription.

They are accustomed to say that the Apostles did not know everything. [Note: [Col. 0033C] “That the Apostles did not know everything.” The heretics of our own time affirm this very thing about the Fathers. For Hyp. says in the *Method* that they necessarily remained ignorant of many things. Wittacherus says that they erred conspicuously in many matters. No one, so far as I know, has explicitly asserted this about the Apostles. Rather, Kimedon, in *On the Word of God*, fastens the charge upon the Catholics—by what right, let him see. Yet these phantoms are hardly dissimilar, as when Bullengerus says in the German *Decades* that the Apostles did not possess plenary authority.
