LAC.] Driven by the same madness with which they turn what is above downward [*susum jusum*] [Note: [Col. 0034C] Seml. and Pam. read “again” for *susum jusum*.] [Note: [Col. 0033D] “By which they turn it back again.” In Agobard’s copy the reading is, “By which they turn upward back again,” and this is confirmed by the Dijon manuscript. Augustine, *Tractate 8 on the Epistle of John*: “What is upward, you make downward; what is below, you make above. Do you wish to make God downward and yourself upward? You are cast down, not raised up, for he is always above.” And Tractate 10: “Upward you honor me; downward you trample me.” Therefore the text here must read: “Driven by the same madness with which they turn what is above downward.” RIG.], they reverse themselves and say that the Apostles did indeed know everything, but did not hand everything down to everyone. In both cases they subject Christ to reproach [Note: [Col. 0034C] “Bring reproach upon,” Seml.], because he sent Apostles who were either insufficiently instructed or insufficiently straightforward.

What person of sound mind, then, can believe that those whom the Lord appointed as teachers were ignorant of anything, when he kept them inseparably with him in companionship, discipleship, and common life, and privately explained every obscure matter to them, saying that it had been granted to them to know the mysteries which the people were not permitted to understand? Was anything hidden [Col. 0034B] from Peter, [Note: [Col. 0033D] “Was anything hidden from Peter?” Simon Bar-Jona was called Peter by the Lord because he was the first, upon recognizing Christ, to declare: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” This utterance was a profession of the true faith; hence Peter merited hearing that he was the rock upon which Christ would build his Church, for here Peter and rock are the same. RIG., as corrected by EDD.] who was called the rock upon which the Church was to be built (Matt. 16:18–19), who received the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the power of loosing and binding in heaven and on earth?

Was anything hidden from John as well [Note: [Col. 0034D] “Was anything hidden from John as well?” Jerome, preface to Matthew: “Last came John, Apostle and Evangelist, whom Jesus loved most greatly; reclining upon the Lord’s breast, he drank the purest streams of doctrine, and he alone merited hearing from the cross: ‘Behold your mother.’” RIG.], the Lord’s most beloved disciple, who reclined upon his breast, to whom alone the Lord pointed out Judas as the betrayer, and whom he entrusted to Mary as a son in his own place? What did he wish those men to remain ignorant of, to whom he displayed even his glory, as well as Moses and Elijah, and furthermore the voice of the Father from heaven? He did this not as though rejecting the others, but because every word shall stand upon three witnesses (Matt. 18:16).

Were even those men, then, ignorant to whom, after his resurrection, he deigned to explain all the Scriptures on the road? He had indeed once said: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12–13). Yet by adding [Col. 0034C], “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will lead you into all truth,” he showed that those to whom he had promised the attainment of all truth through the Spirit of truth were ignorant of nothing. And he assuredly fulfilled his promise, as the Acts of the Apostles proves by recording the descent of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0034D] “Those who do not accept this Scripture.” Quintinus says that the Manichaeans wholly rejected the book of the New Testament entitled *Acts of the Apostles*. They asserted that the Holy Spirit, the teacher of truth whom the Lord had promised to send to his Apostles, descended from heaven not upon Christ’s Apostles but upon their own arch-Manichaean; and that through their Mani—who came from Persia under Aurelian and first began to rave, that is, nearly three hundred years, certainly more than two hundred and sixty years, after that stupendous and wonderful mission described in chapter 2 of the said Acts of the Apostles—the Spirit was communicated to the world. And because Scripture manifestly refuted their shameless lie, they denied that it had ever been written and condemned the book. Read Augustine, chapter 3 of the book *On the Utility of Believing, Against the Manichaeans*. Montanus had done the same thing earlier and even called himself the Paraclete. Ebion, Cerinthus, Marcion, and others before Tertullian did not accept it. PAM.]

Those who do not accept this Scripture [Col. 0035A] cannot belong to the Holy Spirit, since they cannot yet acknowledge that the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0035C] Pamelius lacks “can belong to the Holy Spirit, since they have not yet.”] [Note: [Col. 0035C] Pam. and Seml. add “Holy.”] was sent to the disciples. Nor can they defend the Church, since they have no means of proving when and from what beginnings this body was constituted. [Note: [Col. 0035C] “For it is so important to them,” etc. These words must be explained, for they are so involved that the interpreters have failed to uncover their meaning. He therefore says that many things are taught and defended by heretics which, although consistent with the true faith, they nevertheless refuse to establish by the authority and protection of Scripture. Their reason, of course, is that from those same passages or books of Scripture their falsehoods might be overturned and exposed to the light. Thus it happens that they reject the book containing the Acts of the Apostles with the greatest advantage to themselves—for *tanti* here means “to such advantage”—because by that book alone the origin and formation of the Church, which they acknowledge, can be demonstrated. Take care not to understand *traductiones* as “corruptions,” with Rhenanus; in Tertullian *traductio* means an illustration, demonstration, or exposure. For in the same author *traducere* means to expose to the light, disclose, or uncover. ALBASP.] For it is worth so much to them to have no proofs of the things they defend, lest the exposures of the things they falsely assert be admitted at the same time. [Note: [Col. 0035D] “Lest the exposures of the things they falsely assert be admitted at the same time.” That is, lest they should at the same time be compelled to permit their falsehoods to be exposed publicly. RIG.]

## CHAPTER XXIII

**For in Peter it was not any ignorance that Paul rebuked, but his conduct.**

To brand the Apostles with some kind of ignorance, they therefore put forward the fact that Peter and those with him were rebuked by Paul. “They were so plainly deficient in something,” they say, “that from this it may also be inferred that a fuller knowledge could afterward have supervened, such as came to Paul and enabled him to rebuke his predecessors.”

Here too we can say to those who reject the Acts of the Apostles: you must first show who this Paul is, what he was before becoming an Apostle, and how he became an Apostle—especially since in other questions they make very extensive use of him. For if he himself professes that he became an Apostle after being a persecutor, this is not enough for anyone who believes only after examination [Note: [Col. 0035C] “To examine,” Venet.; Heuman reads, “Nothing is sufficient without examination.”], since not even the Lord gave testimony concerning himself.

[Note: [Col. 0035D] “But let them believe without the Scriptures.” Those who do not accept the Acts of the Apostles nevertheless believe that Paul was made an Apostle after being a persecutor, though once Acts has been rejected they possess no authentic Scripture attesting this. For if they say that they put faith in Paul when he writes this, Paul cannot be his own witness, since not even the Lord gave testimony concerning himself. But let their faith be so perverse that they believe some things without the Scriptures in order to believe other things against the Scriptures; nevertheless, let them teach, from the allegation that Peter was rebuked by Paul, that Paul introduced a different form of the Gospel beyond that which Peter and the others had previously delivered, etc. RIG.]

But let them believe [Note: [Col. 0036C] Others read “they will believe”; Jun. reads “indeed” for “without.”] without the Scriptures, so that they may believe against the Scriptures. Nevertheless, let them demonstrate, from their allegation that Peter was rebuked by Paul, that Paul introduced another form of the Gospel beyond the one Peter and the others had already delivered.

On the contrary [Note: [Col. 0036C] “And indeed,” Pam.; “But indeed,” Seml.], when Paul had been changed from persecutor into preacher, he was conducted to the brethren by brethren, as one of the brethren, and brought by them to those who had put on the faith from the Apostles. Then, as he himself relates, he went up to Jerusalem for the purpose of becoming acquainted with Peter, in accordance, of course, with the duty and right belonging to the same faith and preaching. For they would not have marveled that a persecutor had become a preacher if he preached something contrary to them; nor would they thereafter have glorified the Lord because Paul, formerly his adversary, had come to them. Accordingly, they gave him the right hand as a sign of harmony and agreement, and arranged among themselves a distribution of office, not a division of the Gospel—not that each should preach something different, but that each should preach to different people: Peter to the Circumcision and Paul to the nations. [Note: [Col. 0036D] “Peter to the Circumcision, Paul to the nations.” Certainly the Apostle of the Circumcision and that other Apostle of the Gentiles were each sent in a special manner to one of the two peoples, but not in such a way that one excluded the other from his own territory. For blessed Peter was also pastor and Apostle of the universal Church, while blessed Paul became all things to all people, Jews and Gentiles alike, that he might win them all for Christ. EDD., from the work of D. DE GOURCY.]

Moreover, if [Note: [Col. 0036D] “Peter was rebuked.” The enemies of the Roman See make a remarkable display of this rebuke of blessed Peter; for from it they think it proved that the Supreme Pontiff is truly liable to rebuke. This is entirely false, at least in matters of faith. For in such matters that κρηπίς (*krēpis*, “foundation”) of the Church can in no way err. In the present case, however, the error—if indeed there was one—concerned conduct, not faith. LE PR.] Peter was rebuked because, after having eaten with Gentiles, he afterward began to withdraw from their company out of regard for certain persons, this was assuredly a fault of conduct, not of preaching. For no other God than the Creator was thereby proclaimed, nor any other Christ than the one born of Mary, nor any other hope than the resurrection.

## CHAPTER XXIV

[Col. 0036B]

**And that the practice giving rise to the rebuke was adopted in view of particular times, persons, and circumstances.**

My condition is not so fortunate—or rather, not so unfortunate—that I should set the Apostles against one another. But because these most perverse men parade that rebuke for the purpose of making the earlier doctrine suspect, I shall answer as though on Peter’s behalf. Paul himself said that he had become all things to all people: a Jew to the Jews, a non-Jew to non-Jews, so that he might win everyone [Note: [Col. 0036C] “Might gain,” Semler.]. Thus, with regard to particular times, persons, and circumstances, they censured certain actions which they themselves likewise committed with regard to particular times, persons, and circumstances. It would be as though Peter were also to rebuke Paul because, although forbidding circumcision, he himself circumcised Timothy.

Let those who pass judgment upon the Apostles see to it. [Note: [Col. 0036D] “It is well that Peter is made equal to Paul even in martyrdom.” Do not suppose that these words are put forward directly by the learned man; the context alone shows that he seems to say them by way of concession, as though he were saying: Grant—although this must not in fact be granted—that Peter and Paul were not equals, or held differing opinions; nevertheless, it must be admitted that they were entirely equal in martyrdom, which they bravely suffered for Christ. LE PR.] It is well that Peter [Col. 0037A] is made equal to Paul even in martyrdom.

But even if [Note: [Col. 0037D] “Paul was caught up as far as the third heaven.” This had also become known to Lucian’s Trypho. For he undoubtedly describes Paul in these words: ἡνίκα δέ μοι Γαλιλαῖος ἐνέτυχεν ἀναφαλαντίας, ἐπίρρινος, εἰς τρίτον οὐρανὸν ἀεροβατήσας, καὶ τὰ κάλλιστα ἐκμεμαθηκώς, etc.—“when a Galilean met me, bald in front, hook-nosed, who had traveled through the air to the third heaven and had learned the finest things,” etc. RIG.] Paul was caught up as far as the third heaven and carried into paradise, where he heard certain things, these cannot be thought to have made him better instructed in another doctrine, since their very nature was such that they were to be disclosed to no human being. But if that unknown something passed into the awareness of any person, and some heresy affirms that it follows this teaching, then either Paul is guilty of betraying the secret, or else another person must be shown to have been caught up into paradise afterward and granted permission to utter what Paul was not allowed even to mutter.

## CHAPTER XXV

**Nor, indeed, did the Apostles preach some hidden gospel.**

But, as we have said, it is the same madness when they indeed acknowledge that the Apostles were ignorant of nothing and did not preach doctrines differing [Col. 0037B] from one another, yet refuse to admit [Note: [Col. 0037C] “But did not,” Pam. Seml.] that they revealed everything to everyone. For they say that the Apostles entrusted some things openly and to all, but others secretly and to a few. Their reason is that Paul too used these words to Timothy: “O Timothy, guard the deposit” [Note: [Col. 0037C] “Keep,” Rigalt.]. And again: “Keep the good deposit.”

What is this deposit? Is it something so secret [Note: [Col. 0037C] “So secret,” Fran. Paris.; “so suitable,” Seml.] that it should be reckoned as another doctrine? Or is it the charge of which Paul says: “This charge I entrust to you, son [Note: [Col. 0037C] “Little son,” Semler.] Timothy”? Likewise, is it the commandment of which he says: “I charge you before God, [Note: [Col. 0037D] ‘Who gives life to all things.’ Following Greek usage: ζωοποιοῦντος (*zōopoiountos*, ‘giving life’). Other manuscripts have ‘who justifies,’ as though the text read δικαιοῦντος (*dikaiountos*, ‘justifying’). LE PR.] who gives life [Note: [Col. 0037C] Others read “who justifies.”] to all things, and Jesus Christ, who testified the good confession before Pontius Pilate, that you keep the commandment” (1 Tim. 6:13)?

But what commandment and what charge? From what is written above and below it will be understood [Note: [Col. 0037C] “He had understood,” Seml.; Rhenanus conjectures “it was to be understood.”] that these words do not hint at some unknown matter belonging to a more remote doctrine [Note: [Col. 0037D] “Of a more remote doctrine,” Rhen.]. Rather, they emphatically command that no doctrine be admitted other than the one Timothy had heard from Paul himself—and, I think, openly [Note: [Col. 0038C] Seml., following Pam., deletes “openly.”]. “Before many witnesses,” he says (2 Tim. 2:2). If they refuse [Note: [Col. 0038C] “Wish,” Paris.; “he advises,” Pam. Seml.] to understand those many witnesses as the Church, it makes no difference, since nothing uttered before many witnesses could have been secret.

Nor, because Paul wished Timothy to entrust these things to faithful people capable of teaching others as well [Col. 0038A] (2 Tim. 2:2), is this statement to be interpreted [Note: [Col. 0038C] Pam. and Semler delete “to.”] as evidence for some hidden Gospel. For when he says “these things,” he means the matters about which he was presently writing. With regard to secret things, however—as matters absent but retained in his own consciousness—he would have said not “these things” but “those things.”

## CHAPTER XXVI

**Although the Apostles did not preach indiscriminately or without due consideration to everyone.**
Moreover, it followed that, when he entrusted someone with the administration of the Gospel, he should add that it was not to be administered indiscriminately or thoughtlessly, in accordance with the Lord’s saying that one should not cast a pearl before swine or what is holy to dogs (Matt. 7:6). The Lord proclaimed this openly, without any indication of some concealed [Note: [Col. 0038C] “Unspoken,” Pamelius, Semler.] mystery. He himself had commanded that, if they had heard anything in darkness and in secret, they should preach it in the light and upon the housetops [Col. 0038B] (Matt. 10:27). He himself had foreshadowed by a parable [Note: [Col. 0038D] “That they should not keep one mina.” Macereus notes here that a *mna*, or mina, was worth ten crowns, which he derived from Budé. Pliny, book XXI, ch. 27, says: “The *mna*, which our people call a mina, weighs one hundred Attic drachmas.” Yet each evangelist—both Luke, who reads μνᾶν (*mnan*, “mina”), and Matthew, who has “talent”—appears not to have understood it as a particular denomination of money, but generically, since a talent, according to the same Budé, was worth sixty minas, which are worth sixty crowns. PAM.—The mina, as we read in the notes to the French translation by the excellent de Gourcy, was worth approximately ninety-three francs. EDD.] that they should not keep one mina—that is, one word of his—hidden away without fruit (Luke 19:20). He himself taught that a lamp is not normally hidden [Note: [Col. 0038C] “Bushel,” Rigault, Venice.] under a bushel [Note: [Col. 0038C] “Blocked,” Semler; “hidden,” Pamelius, François, Rhenanus, Junius.], but set upon a lampstand so that it may shine upon everyone in the house (Matt. 5:15).

The apostles either neglected these things or did not understand them at all [Note: [Col. 0038C] The clause “or did not understand them at all” is absent from Rhenanus’s edition.], if they did not fulfill them but concealed something of the light—that is, of the word of God and [Note: [Col. 0038C] “Of,” Semler.] the mystery of Christ. So far as I know, they feared no one: neither the violence of the Jews nor that of the gentiles. How much more freely, then, did those who did not remain silent in synagogues and public places preach in the Church! Indeed, they could neither have converted Jews nor won over gentiles unless they had set forth systematically what they wished them to believe. [Col. 0038C] Much less would they have withheld anything from Churches that already believed, in order to entrust it separately to a few others.

And yet, even if they discussed certain matters among members of the household, so to speak, it must not be believed that these were matters that introduced another rule of faith, different from and contrary to the one they publicly advanced in the catholic manner [Note: [Col. 0038D] “Different from and contrary to that which they advanced publicly to the catholic Church.” So it is written in the ancient copies. But I think it more correct to read *catholice* adverbially, [Col. 0039C] that is, “in the Church.” For he says that the apostles did not transmit one rule privately, or in a lodging, and another catholically, or in the Church; nor one in secret and another in public. Thus, in the book *On Flight*, persecution is said to occur “catholically” when the Church is shaken and harassed not in part but wholly and universally. So too in book II *Against Marcion*: “catholic goodness,” spread throughout the whole world. And in book IV: “the catholic Jerusalem,” meaning the universal Christian Church. Pagan writers likewise called universal things *catholica*, as Pliny speaks of the *catholica*—the universal principles—of the wandering stars and the *catholica* of lightning. RIG.]: as though they named one God [Col. 0039A] in the Church and another in their lodging; indicated one substance of Christ openly and another in secret; announced one hope of resurrection among all and another among a few. For in their own letters they entreated everyone to say the same and single thing, and that there should be no schisms or dissensions in the Church (1 Cor. 1:10), because whether it was Paul or the others, they preached the same message. Besides, they remembered: [Note: [Col. 0039C] “Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes; No, no.’” These are Christ’s words in Matt. 5, where he forbids swearing in every way, whether by heaven, by earth, or [Col. 0039D] by one’s head. “But let your speech be,” he says, “‘Yes, yes; No, no.’” Although these words were spoken generally to the Jewish multitude, and not specifically to the Twelve, our Septimius nevertheless says that the disciples, or apostles, were admonished by the same words not to handle the Gospel inconsistently. But what does the formula of affirmation, “Yes, yes,” or of denial, “No, no,” have to do with the handling of the Gospel? Septimius plainly seems to have understood that Christ prescribed not merely a simple formula of affirmation or denial, but also meant this: the discourse of all Christians, and much more that of the apostles, is to be commended by an exceptional sincerity of truth, containing nothing rendered doubtful by contrived subtlety and nothing twisted into an equivocal defense. One person is not to say “Yes” and another “No”; rather, all alike are to say “Yes, yes; No, no.” Nor are they ever to intermingle “Yes” and “No,” but clearly to declare that what is, is, and what is not, is not. For whatever [Col. 0040C] goes beyond this—whatever is additionally woven in by artifice—is from evil: it is deceit, or close to deceit. This passage is treated in the same sense in *On the Flesh of Christ* and *Against Praxeas*. RIG.] “Let your speech be: ‘Yes, yes; No, no’; whatever goes beyond this is from evil” (Matt. 5:37), so that, of course, [Note: [Col. 0039B] “Of course” deleted by Semler.] they should not handle the Gospel inconsistently.

## CHAPTER XXVII

### That they also established one rule of faith, both for Churches that were rebuked and subsequently corrected and for those that they commended. [Col. 0039B]

[Note: [Col. 0040C] “If, therefore, it is incredible.” He touches upon the mark of true and apostolic doctrine, which is the most ancient mark of the Church. He therefore says that it is incredible that the apostles were ignorant, as though to say: That doctrine which the apostles knew is the most ancient; all the rest are novel and adulterated, since the apostles did not know them. Hence below, ch. 3: “Yet agreeing in the same faith,” etc. For those who agree in the same faith that the apostles maintained plainly retain their doctrine, as though they were blood relatives of the apostles. Hence Sozomen, book VII, relates that Theodosius, who commanded the leaders of the sects to assemble, then asked whether they thought that the ancient Fathers who had governed the Church before that dissension over religion arose had agreed rightly and had been truly holy and apostolic. When they conceded this, he added the reasoning by which he would restrain the heretics, namely: “Let us therefore examine your doctrine against their writings; if it agrees with them, let it be retained; if not, let it be rejected.” LAC.]

If, therefore, it is incredible either that the apostles were ignorant of the fullness of the proclamation or that they did not disclose the entire order of the rule to everyone, let us see whether perhaps [Note: [Col. 0039C] “Perhaps” deleted by Semler.] the apostles did indeed proclaim it simply and fully [Note: [Col. 0039C] “Plainly,” others.], but the Churches, through their own fault, received it otherwise than the apostles presented it. You will find all these provocations to scrupulous doubt advanced by the heretics.

They seize upon the Churches rebuked by the apostle: “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you?”; and: “You were running so well; who hindered you?”; and the very opening: “I marvel that you are so quickly turning away from him who called you [Note: [Col. 0040B] “His own,” Venice, Rigault.] in grace, to [Col. 0040A] another gospel.” Likewise, it was written to the Corinthians that they were still carnal, being reared upon milk and not yet fit for solid food; and that they thought themselves to know something when they did not yet know as they ought to know. When they bring forward the rebuked Churches, let them also believe that they were corrected. But let them also acknowledge those Churches [Note: [Col. 0040D] “Concerning whose faith, knowledge, and conduct.” At the beginnings of his Epistles, the apostle commends the Romans, Ephesians, and Philippians for their faith and love, which he here calls “conduct.” He commends the Romans particularly for knowledge, saying to them in chapter 15: “For you yourselves are full of love, filled with all knowledge.” PAM.] over whose faith, knowledge, and conduct the apostle rejoices and gives thanks to God. Yet today these share the rights of a single institution with those that were rebuked.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### That what is found as one thing among many must be judged not an error, but a tradition.

Come now: let them all have erred. Let the apostle have been deceived in giving testimony to certain Churches [Note: [Col. 0040B] “To certain Churches” deleted by Rigault, Venice.]. Let the Holy Spirit have regarded none of them, so as to lead it into the truth (John 14:26), although he was sent by Christ and requested from the Father for this very purpose, that he might be the teacher of truth (John 15:26). Let the steward of God, the vicar of Christ, have neglected his duty by allowing the Churches meanwhile to understand one thing and believe another than what [Note: [Col. 0040C] “Which,” Venice, Junius.] he himself was preaching through the apostles. Is it at all credible that so many and such great Churches should all have gone astray into one faith? [Note: [Col. 0040D] “Among many events there is no single outcome.” An accident dispersed among many is not received by everyone in one and the same way. RIG.] Among many events there is no single outcome: error in the doctrine of the Churches ought to have produced variations. But what is found as one thing among many is not an error, but a tradition [Note: [Col. 0040C] “But a tradition” suppressed by Rhenanus, Semler.]. Let someone dare, then, to say that those who handed it down were in error!

## CHAPTER XXIX

[Col. 0041A]

### That it is rather the heresies which have erred, since they are later than the true doctrine.

[Note: [Col. 0041C] “However the error may have occurred.” With the strongest reason I can answer this very thing to the supreme critics of our time, who do not fear to say that the Church has hitherto erred: “If the truth awaited certain Lutherans, Calvinists, or Anabaptists to set it free,” etc. PAM.]

However the error may have occurred, error undoubtedly reigned [Note: [Col. 0041B] “Erred,” Junius, Semler.] for as long as the heresies did not exist [Note: [Col. 0041B] “Are in error,” Junius.]. The truth awaited certain Marcionites and Valentinians to set it free. Meanwhile, the Gospel was preached wrongly, believed wrongly [Note: [Col. 0041B] “Was believed wrongly” omitted by Semler.]; so many thousands upon thousands were baptized wrongly; so many works of faith administered wrongly [Note: [Col. 0041B] “Ministered,” Semler alone against all the others.]; so many mighty works, so many spiritual gifts [Note: [Col. 0041C] “So many mighty works, so many spiritual gifts.” There is no mention here of virtue or charity, but of the power to perform miracles and of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. ALBASP.] wrongly exercised; so many priestly offices, so many ministries [Note: [Col. 0041B] “Mysteries,” Rigault, from Agobard’s book.] wrongly discharged; and, finally, so many martyrdoms crowned in vain [Note: [Col. 0041B] “Wrongly and in vain,” with “crowned” omitted, Semler; “wrongly crowned,” Pamelius, Rigault.].

Or, if these things occurred neither wrongly nor in vain [Note: [Col. 0041B] “Or, if neither wrongly nor in vain” omitted by Semler; “not wrongly,” Venice, de Gourcy.], what sense does it make that the things of God should have run their course [Note: [Col. 0041B] “Should care,” Semler.] before it was known to which God they belonged; that there should have been Christians before Christ was found, and heresy before [Col. 0041B] true doctrine? Yet in everything truth precedes its image; the likeness follows the reality afterward. Moreover, it is absurd enough that heresy should be considered prior in doctrine [Note: [Col. 0041B] “Prior to that doctrine,” Junius; “the prior doctrine,” Wouwer, from [Col. 0041C] an old manuscript.], merely because it is the very doctrine that foretold future heresies and warned that they must be avoided [Note: [Col. 0042B] “Was foretelling,” Venice.]. It was written to the Church belonging to that doctrine—indeed, the doctrine itself writes to its own [Note: [Col. 0042B] “Its own” absent from Rigault, Venice.] Church: “Even if an angel from heaven should preach a gospel other than what we preached to you, let him be anathema” (Gal. 1:8).

## CHAPTER XXX

### That Marcion and Valentinus at first believed the catholic doctrine in the Roman Church under the episcopate of Eleutherus; until, having been expelled once and again because of their restless curiosity, they were finally banished into perpetual separation and disseminated the poisons of their doctrines. And that the same judgment applies to others who cannot prove by mighty works and miracles that they are new apostles.

Where was Marcion then, the Pontic shipmaster and student of Stoicism? Where was Valentinus, the follower of the Platonic sect? For it is agreed that they lived not so very long ago, around the reign of Antoninus, and that at first [Note: [Col. 0041D] “At first believed in the doctrine of the catholic Church.” This is the reading of the most ancient manuscript. “The doctrine of the catholic,” namely, the Church: the doctrine received throughout the whole Christian world—that is, by the universal Christian Church—and distinguished by the name “catholic” from the doctrine of heretics. For among Christians “heresy” is the name for what someone chooses to believe against public conscience or faith—that is, against the common judgment of the Christian nations. ALBASP.] they believed in the doctrine of the catholic Church [Note: [Col. 0042B] “Almost in the catholic doctrine,” Semler.] at Rome, under the episcopate [Note: [Col. 0041D] “At the Roman Church under the episcopate of Eleutherius.” So reads the old copy; and it is important that the writings of ancient authors, especially those of this man, be reproduced even with their mistakes, nor is Septimius accustomed to render with perfect exactness what he takes from other authors. ALBASP.] of the blessed Eleutherius [Note: [Col. 0041D] “Of the blessed Eleutherius.” Even while they were alive, men were called “blessed.” *On Modesty*: “Blessed Pope, you preach.” ALBASP.]. This continued until, because of their perpetually restless curiosity—through which they also shunned the brethren [Note: [Col. 0042B] “Which even the brethren avoided,” Rigault.] [Note: [Col. 0042C] “Which even the brethren avoided.” This is certainly the reading in the manuscript; the sense is that their curiosity was odious even to the Christian laity, so that they were expelled by the common desire of the brethren when the bishop cast them out. RIG.]—they were expelled once and again [Note: [Col. 0042C] “Expelled once and again”: that is, men who, after being admitted to repentance, used it treacherously and inconstantly. Irenaeus also seems to indicate something of this kind where he treats the heretic Cerdo. RIG.]. Marcion in particular was expelled together with the two hundred thousand sesterces that he had brought into the Church. Finally banished into perpetual separation [Note: [Col. 0042B] “Dissension,” Wouwer.] [Col. 0042B] [Note: [Col. 0042B] “Banished,” singular, Semler; likewise, “disseminated,” singular.], they disseminated the poisons of their doctrines.

Later, the same Marcion, having publicly professed repentance [Note: [Col. 0042D] “Having professed repentance”: that is, after he had publicly testified that he repented. ALBASP.], when he had undertaken to meet the condition imposed upon him [Note: [Col. 0042B] “Condition,” with “of repentance” understood, Semler.] [Note: [Col. 0042D] “When he had undertaken to meet the condition imposed upon him”: when he was at the point of fulfilling the condition given to him; when he began to satisfy the condition. RIG.]—namely, that he would be restored to peace if he restored to the Church the others whom he had instructed for perdition [Note: [Col. 0042D] “If he restored the others whom he had instructed for perdition.” Heretics were recalled into the Church more readily than other sinners; but heresiarchs were not granted peace unless they attempted to restore to the Church the others whom they had corrupted. St Cyprian, letter to Antonianus concerning Trophimus; Eusebius, book VI, ch. 35. ALBASP.]—was overtaken by death.

“For there had to be heresies” (1 Cor. 11:19). Yet heresies are not therefore good because they had to exist, as though evil also did not have to exist. For the Lord too had to be betrayed; “but woe to the betrayer” (Mark 14:21)! Let no one [Note: [Col. 0042B] “What,” Semler.] defend heresies on this ground either [Note: [Col. 0042B] “Let them defend,” Venice.].

If [Note: [Col. 0042B] “If,” Semler.] the pedigree of Apelles must also be reviewed, he himself is no older than Marcion, his instructor and forerunner. But after falling into involvement with a woman [Note: [Col. 0042C] “A woman,” same editor.], he deserted Marcionite continence [Col. 0043A] [Note: [Col. 0042D] “Marcionite continence.” Not because Marcion lived continently—for his morals were dissolute—but because he forbade marriage. LE PR.] and withdrew from the eyes of his most holy teacher to Alexandria. Returning from there after some [Note: [Col. 0043C] “Some” added by Wouwer.] years no better than before, except only that he was now no longer a Marcionite, he collided with another woman: the virgin Philumene, whom we mentioned above, but who afterward became an enormous prostitute herself. Deceived by her possessing spirit, he wrote down the “manifestations” (*phaneroseis*) that he learned from her.

There still survive in this world people who remember them, even their own pupils and successors, so that they cannot deny that they are later. And indeed, they are convicted even by their own works, as the Lord said (Matt. 7:16). For if Marcion separated the New Testament from the Old, he is later than what he separated, because he could not have separated it unless it had been united. Its having been united before it was separated, and separated afterward, shows [Col. 0043B] that the separator was later. Likewise Valentinus, by interpreting differently and undoubtedly correcting, demonstrates that whatever he corrects must previously have existed before him as something defective [Note: [Col. 0043C] “May demonstrate that it belonged to another,” Semler.].

We name these men [Note: [Col. 0043C] “Certainly,” Semler.] as the more notorious and more prevalent adulterators of the truth. But there are also some fellow named Nigidius [Note: [Col. 0043C] “Who,” François, Semler.], Hermogenes, and many others who [Note: [Col. 0043C] “Who” deleted by Semler.] still go about perverting the ways of God [Note: [Col. 0043C] Semler inserts “if you wish.”]. Let them show me by what authority they have come forth. If they preach another God, how do they use the possessions, Scriptures, and names of the God against whom they preach? If they preach the same God, how do they preach him differently?

[Note: [Col. 0043D] “Let them prove themselves to be new apostles; let them say that Christ descended again.” Optatus, book III: “But is there another redeemer? Which prophets announced that another was to come? What Gabriel spoke again to another Mary? What virgin gave birth again? Who performed new or different mighty works?” RIG.] Let them prove themselves to be new apostles. Let them say that Christ descended again, taught again in person, was crucified again, died again, and was raised again. For it is in this way that he is accustomed to make apostles [Col. 0043C]: he also gives them the power to perform the same signs that he himself performed [Note: [Col. 0043C] “For so the apostle described it. He is accustomed to make them; moreover, he would give them the power of producing the same signs that he himself produced.” Agobard’s book has this wording here, according to Rigault.] [Note: [Col. 0043C] “He himself,” Semler.].

[Note: [Col. 0043D] “I therefore wish their mighty works also to be produced.” “Mighty works” means miracles. EDD.] I therefore wish their mighty works [Note: [Col. 0044C] “Also” deleted by Semler.] also to be produced—except that I recognize their greatest mighty work, by which they emulate the apostles perversely: the apostles made the living out of the dead [Note: [Col. 0043D] “They made the living out of the dead; these make the dead out of the living,” etc. Bolsec, in his *Life of Calvin*, testifies that this happened to Calvin at Geneva: namely, that he rendered a living man dead. Bellarmine recounts it at length in *On the Marks of the Church*, ch. 14, book IV, *Controversies*, vol. II. LE PR.] [Note: [Col. 0044C] “Raised,” Semler.]; these men make the dead out of the living [Note: [Col. 0043D] “They make the dead out of the living”: they overthrow the weaker faithful. Thus in *Scorpiace*: “And so the weakness which has once been struck breathes out its wounded faith either into heresy or into the world.” RIG.].

## CHAPTER XXXI

[Col. 0044A]

### That what was handed down earlier is therefore true and from the Lord, while what is later is false.

But I shall return from this digression to discussing the priority of truth [Note: [Col. 0044D] “I shall return to the priority of truth and the posteriority of falsehood.” By “priority” he means what existed immediately from the beginning; by “posteriority,” what crept in afterward. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0044C] “To truth,” Franeker.] and the posteriority of falsehood [Note: [Col. 0044C] “To be assigned to falsehood,” Semler.]. Support is also supplied by that parable which places the good seed of wheat, sown by the Lord, at the beginning [Note: [Col. 0044C] “Places first,” Paris, François; “restores in the first place,” Semler.], but afterward introduces the adulteration of barren grass—the tares—by the enemy, the devil (Matt. 13:37, 39) [Note: [Col. 0044C] “Adulterous,” Venice.]. For it specifically symbolizes the distinction between doctrines [Note: [Col. 0044C] “For its part,” Semler.], since elsewhere too the word of God is likened to seed.

Thus the very order makes it manifest that what was handed down first is from the Lord and true, while what was introduced later is foreign and false. This judgment will stand against every later heresy, [Col. 0044B] since no steadfast assurance arising from conscience belongs to them [Note: [Col. 0044C] “And conscience grants,” Semler; “the conscience of steadfastness grants,” Junius.] for defending the truth as their own.

## CHAPTER XXXII

### If, meanwhile, certain heresies have existed from the apostolic age itself, they must be met with the prescription that they disclose the succession of their bishops, running down through successive appointments from the beginning, so that their first bishop has some apostle or apostolic man as predecessor, as in the Churches of Smyrna and Rome. Since they cannot prove this, they are not to be received into communion.

Moreover, if any heresies dare to insert themselves into the apostolic age, so that they may therefore appear to have been handed down by the apostles because they existed under the apostles, we can say: Let them publish [Col. 0044C] the origins of their Churches. Let them unroll the succession of their bishops, running down through successive appointments [Note: [Col. 0044D] “Through successive appointments.” Nothing in the whole doctrine of the ancients is clearer than the succession of the Roman pontiffs; you may learn the rationale of this from St Epiphanius, *Heresies* 27, the question of the Carpocratians. LE PR.] from the beginning [Note: [Col. 0044C] “Running down,” ablative, Semler.], so that their first bishop had as his author and predecessor one of the apostles, or one of the apostolic men who nevertheless persevered with the apostles [Note: [Col. 0044C] “Who persevered,” plural, François.].

[Note: [Col. 0044D] “For in this manner the apostolic Churches present their registers.” “Their registers” means their origins. Thus in book I *Against Marcion*, he called the Church “of apostolic register”; and in *On Monogamy*: “Our register is transferred to Christ.” RIG.] For this is the manner in which the apostolic Churches present their registers [Note: [Col. 0044D] “They present their registers.” Interpreters here think that “registers” must be understood as authority and dignity; I, however, believe that it signifies origin, as may be gathered from various passages and from these words, “every kind is registered according to its origin,” [Col. 0045D] and from *Against Marcion*, book IV, ch. 5: “If you inquire into their register.” ALBASP.]. Thus the Church of the Smyrnaeans [Col. 0045A] [Note: [Col. 0045D] “Thus that of the Smyrnaeans,” etc. Irenaeus, book III, relates that Polycarp was appointed by the apostles in the Church at Smyrna. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0045C] “Having” added by François, Paris.] reports that Polycarp was installed by John. Thus the Church of the Romans [Note: [Col. 0045D] “Thus that of the Romans, Clement.” Jerome, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*: “Clement was the fourth bishop of Rome after Peter, for Linus was second and Cletus third, although most Latin writers think Clement was second after the apostle Peter.” Irenaeus had related that the blessed apostles entrusted to Linus the episcopate of administering the Church; that Anacletus succeeded Linus; and that after him, in the third place from the apostles, the episcopate was conferred upon Clement. RIG.] declares [Note: [Col. 0045C] “Likewise,” Venice; “the same,” Semler.] that Clement was ordained by Peter [Note: [Col. 0045D] “Clement ordained by Peter.” As though Clement exercised the episcopate at Rome while Peter was still alive, and apostolic men were everywhere assigned to various episcopates while the apostles were still performing their apostolic office. Yet we read that immediately after the Lord’s Passion, James the apostle, the Lord’s brother, was appointed bishop of Jerusalem by the apostles themselves, while Peter was already exercising the apostolate in a preeminent manner. Chrysostom says that this occurred because Christ had appointed Peter διδάσκαλον τῆς οἰκουμένης (*didaskalon tēs oikoumenēs*, “teacher of the inhabited world”) (homily on John, ch. 21). This passage of Tertullian plainly shows that the lines from which some think the succession of Roman bishops can be established with certainty are not Tertullian’s. RIG.]. In the same way, of course, the other Churches exhibit those whom they have as shoots of the apostolic seed, men appointed to the episcopate by the apostles [Note: [Col. 0045C] “The apostles,” nominative, Semler.] [Note: [Col. 0045C] “Have,” Latinus, Junius.].

Let the heretics fabricate something of this kind. For what is unlawful to them after blasphemy? Yet even if they fabricate it, they will accomplish nothing. For their doctrine itself, when compared with the apostolic doctrine, will pronounce by its own diversity and contrariety that it has neither an apostle nor an apostolic man as its author. For just as the apostles would not have taught doctrines differing from one another, so apostolic men would not have published doctrines contrary to the apostles—unless those who learned from the apostles afterward preached differently [Note: [Col. 0045C] “Defected and preached,” Semler, de Gourcy.].

They will therefore be tested [Col. 0045B] according to this standard [Note: [Col. 0045C] “Challenged,” Semler.] by those Churches which, although they can present neither an apostle nor an apostolic man as their founder—being much later Churches that are, indeed, established every day—are nevertheless reckoned no less apostolic because they agree in the same faith, [Note: [Col. 0046D] “Because of the consanguinity of doctrine.” Doctrines handed down by one and the same author are consanguineous, as though born of one parent. Thus he himself, in book I of *On the Dress of Women*, spoke of “consanguineous materials.” So too Calcidius speaks of “domestic and consanguineous reasons.” RIG.] because of their consanguinity of doctrine.

Accordingly, when all heresies are challenged by our Churches according to both standards, let them prove themselves apostolic in whatever way they think possible. But they are not apostolic at all; they cannot prove what they are not; nor are they received into peace and communion by Churches that are apostolic in any sense, precisely because, [Note: [Col. 0046D] “Because of the diversity of the mystery.” Here too I shall depart from the interpreters’ judgment when they say that by “mystery” (*sacramentum*) one must understand the oath that the faithful pronounced at the threshold of the Church shortly before they were washed. For in nearly six hundred passages *sacramentum* is used for the Christian faith and religion. ALBASP.] because of the diversity of their mystery of faith, they are in no sense apostolic.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

### Moreover, that they were already both identified and repudiated by the apostles at that time, and that all the remaining heresies took their seeds from them. [Col. 0045C]

Beyond these arguments, I apply an examination of the doctrines themselves that existed under the apostles and were both identified and repudiated [Note: [Col. 0045C] “Repudiated,” François.] by those same apostles. For in this way they will be exposed more easily, when they are found either to have existed already at that time or to have taken their seeds [Col. 0046A] from those which already existed then.

Paul, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians (15:12), censures those who deny or doubt the resurrection. This opinion is peculiar [Note: [Col. 0045D] “First,” Semler, Pamelius.] to the Sadducees; Marcion, Apelles, Valentinus, and any others who undermine the resurrection of the flesh appropriate part of it.

Writing to the Galatians (5:2), he inveighs against the observers and defenders of circumcision and the Law: this is the heresy of Ebion [Note: [Col. 0046C] Semler adds “thus.”].

In instructing Timothy (1 Tim. 4:3), he also brands those who prohibit marriage: Marcion and his follower Apelles teach accordingly.

He likewise touches upon those who said that the resurrection had already taken place (2 Tim. 2:18): the Valentinians affirm this of themselves [Note: [Col. 0046C] “Thus of themselves,” Semler.].

And when he mentions endless genealogies (1 Tim. 1:4), Valentinus is recognizable. In his system, some Aeon or other, of a new and compound name, begets Mind and Truth from his Grace [Note: [Col. 0046C] “And from his love,” Semler.]; these in turn procreate two others, Word and Life; then these generate Man and Church. This is the first Ogdoad [Col. 0046B] of Aeons [Note: [Col. 0046C] “This first [group] is therefore a Decad,” Semler; “in the first Ogdoad,” Paris, François; “of which this is the first Ogdoad, thus far,” Semler.]. From these arise ten other and twelve remaining Aeons with extraordinary names, making a sheer [Note: [Col. 0046C] “Extraordinary,” others.] fable of thirty Aeons.

When the same apostle condemns those who serve the elements, he exposes something of Hermogenes [Note: [Col. 0046C] “A certain Hermogenes,” Semler.], who introduces unbegotten matter and compares it with the unbegotten God. Thus, by making the mother of the elements a goddess, he can serve that which he compares with God.

In the Apocalypse, John commands that those who eat food sacrificed to idols and commit sexual immorality be chastised [Note: [Col. 0046C] “Is commanded,” Paris, Venice, François, Rigault.]. There are others of this kind even now—the Nicolaitans; it is called the Cainite [Note: [Col. 0046D] “Gaian,” Semler.] heresy.

But in his Epistle he particularly calls those antichrists who denied that Christ had come in the flesh and those who did not think Jesus was the Son of God. Marcion claimed the former; [Col. 0046C] Ebion the latter.

The teaching of Simonian magic, moreover, since it served angels, was itself of course reckoned among the idolatries and was condemned by the apostle Peter in Simon himself.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

### And consequently, since these heresies share fellowship with those others in their preaching, they also share fellowship in their condemnation—especially since they were foretold by the apostles. [Col. 0047A]

These, as I judge, are the classes of adulterated doctrines which we learn from the apostles themselves existed under the apostles. Yet among so many varieties [Note: [Col. 0047C] “As varieties,” Semler.] of perversity we find no system that raised a controversy about God, the Creator of the universe.

[Note: [Col. 0047D] “No one dared [suppose] another God,” etc. Here, says Quintinus, you see the advance or progression of the heretics, concerning whom the maxim from the philosophical school is most truly spoken: “A small error at the beginning is greatest at the end.” Twice at the Synod of Gangra we attempted to declare that these foxes are tied together by their tails: namely, that someone guilty of one heresy gradually becomes guilty of the others and is finally burned altogether; for they are linked in a chain. PAM.]

No one dared even to imagine another God. There was doubt about the Son more readily than about the Father, until Marcion introduced, besides the Creator, another God of goodness alone; Apelles made some glorious being of the higher God, the creator of the angels [Note: [Col. 0047C] “An angel,” Semler.], into the God of the Law and of Israel, affirming that he was fiery; and Valentinus scattered abroad his Aeons and traced the origin [Col. 0047B] of God the Creator to the fault of one Aeon.

To these alone—and to these first—was the truth of the Divinity revealed! They had evidently obtained greater favor and fuller grace from the devil, who wished to rival God even in this respect: from doctrines of poison, he himself made disciples superior to their master, something the Lord denied.

Let all the heresies therefore choose for themselves their respective periods—whenever each may have existed, provided that [Note: [Col. 0047C] “Provided not,” Rhenanus; “then not,” Junius; “not,” Wouwer.] it makes no difference which existed when, since [Note: [Col. 0047C] “Since” absent from Rhenanus.] they do not belong to the truth. Those which were not named by the apostles [Note: [Col. 0047C] “Were not under the apostles,” Rhenanus.] certainly cannot have existed under the apostles [Note: [Col. 0047C] François adds “to say that they”; “under the apostles” absent from Rhenanus.]; for if they had existed, they too would have been named, so that they too might be restrained. Those which did exist under the apostles are condemned under their own names [Note: [Col. 0047C] “Are deemed worthy,” Rhenanus.].

Therefore, whether the present heresies are those same heresies in a somewhat more polished form [Note: [Col. 0047D] “Are in some degree more polished.” You hear, says Quintinus, that heresies are crude at first and afterward become more polished. For forty years heresies likewise began to be renovated in such a way that the more skilled a heretic appeared in some sort of Greek and Latin learning, the more applauded and accepted he became: “He speaks purely, elegantly, and neatly.” Hence they gather followers of that eloquence. Heresy, then, is pure, polished, and neat! It is highly reprehensible [Col. 0048C] that even serious theologians are carried away by those expressions and prettinesses of human eloquence. They ask whether the diction is good. Yet we ought to remember that there is no good diction in any Christian which is not at the same time a benediction in Christ Jesus. Let us leave those fine dictiones and rhetorical flourishes to grammarians such as Cresconius, as Augustine did. They do not befit those who handle sacred things sincerely, any more than white lead befits a matron or wrestling oil an ox. PAM.] which were crude under the apostles, they possess their condemnation from that time onward. Or whether the former heresies were one thing and others afterward arose [Col. 0047C] [Note: [Col. 0047C] “Arose” added by François, Paris.], but appropriated certain things from the former [Note: [Col. 0047C] “Certain ones among them,” Rhenanus.], then, because they share fellowship with them in preaching, [Note: [Col. 0048D] “By sharing fellowship with them.” Gelasius I, says the same Quintinus, an African, writes something similar to Tertullian: “Whoever falls into a heresy once condemned involves himself in its condemnation,” 24, q. 1, c. 1. The definitions of the Council of Chalcedon and others have the same bearing, where it is expressly stipulated that it is no longer permissible to doubt matters once defined, but that those who follow their heresy must be condemned with them and must share—as the author puts it—with “condemned heresies,” that is, as Quintinus interprets it, heresies already condemned. Compare *fictitium*, “fabricated,” from *fictum*, “a fabrication”; *donatitium*, “given”; *dedititium*, “surrendered”; and *conductitium*, “hired.” PAM.] they must also share [Col. 0048A] in their condemnation.

This is in addition to the foregoing boundary-line [Note: [Col. 0048C] “Cord,” Junius.] of posteriority, by which they would be prejudged on grounds of age alone even if they shared nothing with those already condemned [Note: [Col. 0048C] “Were shared,” Rhenanus.]. They are all the more adulterated because they were not even named by [Note: [Col. 0048C] “By” absent from Paris.] the apostles. From this it is established all the more firmly that these are the heresies which were at that time still being announced as future.

## CHAPTER XXXV

### That, conversely, none of the prescriptions discussed applies against our doctrine.

Provoked by these definitions of ours and refuted, let all heresies dare to answer—whether later than the Apostles or contemporary with them, provided that they are divergent; whether condemned by them generally or specifically, provided that they were condemned beforehand—and themselves advance any prescriptions of this sort against our rule of faith. [Note: [Col. 0048C] *Qua*, Rhen.] For if they deny its truth, they ought to prove that it too is a heresy [Note: [Col. 0048C] *Esse* is absent from Rhen.], refuted by the same procedure by which they themselves are refuted; and at the same time to show where the truth is to be sought, since it is already established that it is not among them. Our cause is not later; indeed, it is earlier than all: this will be the testimony of the truth, which everywhere holds the first place. [Note: [Col. 0048C] *Praefigitur quod*, Fran., Paris.] It is certainly not condemned by the Apostles; indeed, it is defended by them: this will be the mark of ownership. For by not condemning it [Note: [Col. 0048C] *Enim damnant*, Seml.]—they who condemned [Note: [Col. 0048C] *Quasi*, Wouwer.] every alien teaching [Note: [Col. 0048C] “did not condemn every alien teaching,” Fran., Paris.]—they show it to be their own, and therefore defend it as well.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

For anyone who surveys the apostolic churches, among which the very chairs of the Apostles still preside in their own places, [Col. 0048C] and among them the Roman church, from which authority is also at hand for us—the church where Peter and Paul were crowned—will find that it drank from the Apostles the faith which was their own, [Col. 0049A] by which it seals with water, clothes with the Holy Spirit, and nourishes with the Eucharist.

Come now, you who wish to exercise your curiosity more profitably in the business of your salvation: [Note: [Col. 0049C] “Survey the apostolic churches.” Augustine too enjoins this (*On Christian Doctrine*, book II, ch. 8): “In the canonical Scriptures,” he says, “let us follow the authority of the greater number of Catholic churches; among these, certainly, are those which have deserved to possess apostolic sees and to receive epistles.” RIG.] survey the apostolic churches, among which [Note: [Col. 0049C] “The very chairs of the Apostles still preside in their own places.” It is certainly evidence of veneration that the very chairs of the Apostles still presided in their own places in memory and honor of the Apostles, while their successors sat below them. But in my own opinion it would be more correct to say that by “chairs of the Apostles” are meant the principal churches—namely, those established by the Apostles themselves—which [Col. 0049D] still presided in their own places in Tertullian’s age as the mother churches of the others: such as Corinth in Achaia; Philippi and Thessalonica in Macedonia; Ephesus in Asia; and Rome in Italy. RIG.] the very chairs of the Apostles still preside in their own places [Note: [Col. 0049B] *Praesidentur*, Rhen.]; among which [Note: [Col. 0049D] “Their authentic letters themselves are read aloud.” That is, in the same language in which they had been written by the Apostles, sounding forth the voice of each one. Thus he himself, in the book *On Monogamy*, appeals to Paul’s authentic Greek text. RIG.] their authentic letters themselves are read aloud, sounding forth the voice and [Note: [Col. 0049D] “Representing the face of each one”—insofar, of course, as it is permissible for those reflecting on them to form an image. RIG.] representing the face of each one [Note: [Col. 0049B] Seml., following Rhen., deleted “and … of each one.”]. Is Achaia nearest to you? You have Corinth. If you are not far from Macedonia, you have Philippi; you have the Thessalonians [Note: [Col. 0049B] Seml., following Rhen., deleted “you have the Thessalonians.”]. If you can travel into Asia, you have Ephesus. But if you are near Italy [Note: [Col. 0049B] *Adjiceris*, Rhen.], you have Rome [Note: [Col. 0049B] *Romanam*, Rhen.], [Note: [Col. 0049D] “From which authority is also at hand for us.” Thus in book IV *Against Marcion*: “What the Romans close at hand also proclaim.” RIG.—“From which authority is also at hand for us.” This passage would convict the heretics who deprive the Roman Pontiff of universal authority, restricting it within the jurisdiction of the prefect of the city, which was bounded within one hundred and fifty miles. I shall speak of this elsewhere. I note only that in countless passages the holy Fathers said that blessed Peter was appointed **τῆς οἰκουμένης διδάσκαλον**, “teacher of the inhabited world”; thus Chrysostom, homily on [Col. 0050C] John chapter XXI. Then the Council of Chalcedon, act 16: **ἡ ἐκκλησία Ῥώμης πάντοτε ἔσχε τὰ πρεσβεῖα**, “The Roman Church has always held the first place.” LE PR.] from which authority is also at hand for us [Note: [Col. 0049B] Rhen. adds *statuta*; *ista quam* is absent from the same editor.]. How fortunate is that Church [Note: [Col. 0049C] *Statu felix*, Fran.; *statu tam felix*, Seml.]! [Note: [Col. 0050C] “Upon which the Apostles poured out their entire teaching together with their blood.” By “entire teaching” he means the sum of the whole Christian teaching, which he so often proclaims to consist in courageously enduring martyrdom for Christ’s name: namely, that we should lay down our life for him who has deserved so well of us, since he laid down and expended his own for us, who were not merely undeserving but ill-deserving. LE PR.] Upon it [Col. 0049B] the Apostles poured out their entire teaching together with their blood; [Note: [Col. 0050C] “Where Peter was made equal to the Lord’s passion.” These words certainly attest that Peter saw Rome, as did Paul and John, [Col. 0050D] who is also mentioned here. All, moreover, are made equal to one another in steadfastness under martyrdom. Tertullian says in this book, *On the Prescription of Heretics*: “How fortunate that Peter is made equal to Paul in martyrdom also!” Irenaeus (book III, ch. 1) asserts that Peter and Paul evangelized at Rome and founded the Church; and in chapter 3 he ascribes a magnificent encomium to the Roman Church: “the greatest and most ancient Church, known to all, founded and established at Rome by the two most glorious Apostles Peter and Paul.” LE PR.] where Peter was made equal to the Lord’s passion; where Paul was crowned with John’s [Note: [Col. 0050D] “John’s”—that is, the Baptist’s, whose head was cut off. SEMLER.] manner of death; where the Apostle John, after being plunged into burning oil and suffering nothing, was banished to an island. Let us see what it learned, what it taught, and what token of fellowship it exchanged with the African churches as well [Note: [Col. 0049C] *Contestatur*, Rhen.; *contesseratur*, Pithaeus.].

It knows one God, creator of the universe, and Christ Jesus, born of the Virgin Mary, the Son of God the Creator, and the resurrection of the flesh. It combines the Law and the Prophets with the evangelical and apostolic writings, [Col. 0050A] and from them drinks in [Note: [Col. 0049C] *Importat*, Wouw.; *plantat*, Seml.; *portat*, Rhen.] the faith; that faith [Note: [Col. 0049C] *Fidem eam*, Paris, Fran.; Rhen. omits *eam*.] [Note: [Col. 0050D] “It seals with water”—with baptism, the seal of faith. LE PR.] it seals with water, [Note: [Col. 0050D] “It clothes with the Holy Spirit.” He himself says in the book *On Monogamy*: “But Jesus, the high and great priest of the Father, clothing us from what is his own—for those baptized into Christ have put on Christ—made us priests to God his Father”; and in the book *On Baptism*: “The sealing of baptism, the garment of faith.” LE PR.] clothes with the Holy Spirit, nourishes with the Eucharist, exhorts to martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0050B] *Martyrio*, Fran., Paris, Pam.; *martyrium*, Rig., Venet., Rhen., Seml.], and thus admits no one who opposes this institution. This is the institution—not merely, I say now, the one which foretold the heresies that were to come, but the one from which the heresies went forth. Yet they did not belong to it [Note: [Col. 0050B] “not all belonged to it,” Rhen.], from the moment they were made hostile to it. Even from the kernel of a mild, excellent [Note: [Col. 0050B] *Opimae*, “rich,” Rhen.], and useful [Note: [Col. 0050B] *Suavissimae*, “most pleasant,” Rhen.] olive arises the harsh wild olive; [Note: [Col. 0050D] “And likewise from the poppy of the fig.” Even in the senate Cato did not hesitate to call the fig a fruit. Later, however, legal writers debated whether figs were included under the designation “fruits.” Septimius was by no means unaware that in sacred literature they are called *grossi* (“unripe figs”), but those differ somewhat from the fruit described in Pliny’s account. He therefore preferred to use the name “poppy,” to which the unripe fig is certainly very similar in shape, color, seeds, and milk. RIGALTIUS.] likewise, from the poppy-like bud of the most agreeable and pleasant fig there springs the windy, empty wild fig [Note: [Col. 0050B] Rhen. reads: “from the most pleasant fig there springs the windy, empty wild fig,” and nothing further.]. So too heresies come from our shrub, but not from our stock; from the grain of truth, but rendered wild by falsehood [Note: [Col. 0050C] “They bore fruit from ours, but are not ours: degenerate from the grain of truth and rendered wild by falsehood,” Rhen.; *degeneres vanitatis grano*, “degenerate from the grain of vanity,” Jun.].

## CHAPTER XXXVII

Since, therefore, the truth is adjudged to those of us who walk according to that rule which the Church received from the Apostles, it follows that his proposed argument stands: heretics are not to be admitted to enter into an appeal to the Scriptures, since they are not Christians and consequently have been disinherited from possession of the Christian writings.

If these things are so, so that the truth is adjudged to us—all of us who walk according to that rule which the Church handed down from the Apostles, the Apostles from Christ, and Christ from God [Note: [Col. 0050C] *Accepit*, “received,” Pam.]—then the rationale of our proposal is established, which determines that heretics are not to be admitted [Col. 0051A] to enter into [Note: [Col. 0051C] *Ad eamdem*, “to the same,” Paris; *adeundam*, “to approach,” Rhen.] an appeal to the Scriptures: without the Scriptures we prove that they have no claim upon the Scriptures. For if they are heretics, they cannot be Christians, since what they follow by their own choosing and admit under the name [Note: [Col. 0051C] *Nomina*, “names,” Rig.; *nomen*, Jun.] of heretics is not something they possess from Christ. Thus, since they are not Christians, they acquire no right to the Christian writings. To them it may deservedly be said: Who are you? When and whence did you come? What are you doing on my property, when you are not mine? By what right, Marcion, do you cut down my woodland? By whose permission, Valentinus, do you divert my springs? By what authority, Apelles, do you move my boundaries [Note: [Col. 0051C] Rig., Fran., Paris, and Venet. add: “The possession is mine.”]? Why are the rest of you sowing and grazing here at your own pleasure? The possession is mine; I have possessed it from of old [Note: [Col. 0051C] The same editions add: “I possess it first.”]. I have secure title-deeds from the very [Note: [Col. 0051C] “and the very,” Rhen.] authors to whom the property belonged. I am the heir of the Apostles. [Col. 0051B] Just as they provided in their will, just as they entrusted it in faith [Note: [Col. 0051D] Jun., following legal usage, prefers the single word *fideicommiserunt*, “made it a fideicommissum.”], just as they bound me by solemn adjuration, so I hold it. You they certainly disinherited and repudiated forever, as strangers and enemies. But whence are heretics strangers and enemies to the Apostles, unless from their divergence in teaching, which each one, by his own judgment and against the Apostles, either produced or received?

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

Especially since corruption of teaching could not have succeeded among them without corruption of the documents, through the employment in the Scriptures of subtraction, addition, alteration, and interpolation, whereby one man overturns the Scriptures with his hand and another with an exposition of their meaning.

It is therefore where divergence in teaching is found that adulteration both of the Scriptures and of their interpretations must be reckoned. Those whose purpose was to teach differently were compelled by necessity [Note: [Col. 0051D] *Instituit*, “instructed,” Rhen.] to arrange the documents of the teaching differently. For otherwise they could not have taught differently unless they possessed in a different form the materials through which they taught [Note: [Col. 0051D] Fran. and Paris add *haeresim*, “heresy.”]. Just as corruption of their teaching could not have succeeded among them without corruption of its documents [Note: [Col. 0051D] “without corruption of the documents” is not read in Rhen.’s edition.], so too integrity of teaching could not have belonged to us [Note: [Col. 0051D] Rig. and Venet. add “and by us.”] without the integrity of those documents through which [Col. 0052A] the teaching is treated. For what in our writings is contrary to us? What have we introduced of our own, so that by subtraction, addition, or alteration we might remedy anything found in the Scriptures that was contrary to what already existed [Note: [Col. 0051D] “to it and in the Scriptures,” Rhen.]? What we are, the Scriptures have been [Note: [Col. 0052C] *Haec sunt. Inde scriptura*, Rhen.; “This is what the Scriptures have been from the beginning”; Jun.: “This is what the Scriptures have been from their very beginning; from them”; Wouw.] from their beginning; from them we have our being, before there was anything different [Note: [Col. 0052C] “before there was nothing different,” Rhen.; “in antiquity there was nothing different,” Jun.], before they were interpolated by you.

Since every interpolation must be believed to be later, arising, of course, from a cause of rivalry—which is never either prior to or native to that which it rivals—it is just as incredible to every wise person that we should appear to have introduced an adulterating pen into the Scriptures, since we are both the first and derived from them [Note: [Col. 0052D] “we are from the beginning and the first,” Rig., Venet.], as it is incredible that those who are both later and hostile should not have introduced one. One man overturns the Scriptures with his hand, another with an exposition of their meaning. For although Valentinus [Note: [Col. 0051D] “For although Valentinus.” Quintinus says that the opinions of these two founders of heresies differ concerning which biblical and sacred Scriptures should be admitted. Marcion accepted nothing from the Old Testament; from the New he had selected certain portions and set them out in two books, taking material from the Gospel of Luke while rejecting the others, and from some epistles of the Apostle Paul, cutting out from them whatever did not agree with his doctrine. This is undoubtedly to deny everything. PAM.] appears to use the complete [Col. 0052B] body of documents, he laid hands upon the truth with an intellect no less cunning than Marcion’s [Note: [Col. 0052D] “laid hands upon the truth” is not read in Rhen.’s edition.]. For Marcion openly and publicly [Note: [Col. 0052D] “He used a sword, not a pen.” *Machaera* means “knife” in Greek. For from the sacred corpus he cut away the Acts of the Apostles, the Apocalypse, part of Luke’s Gospel, and part of the Pauline Epistles. RHEN.] used a sword (*machaera*), not a pen, since [Note: [Col. 0052D] “He carried out a slaughter of the Scriptures to suit his own material.” Nothing more apt could have been said against more recent heretics than these words against Marcion; for among them you may see a slaughter of the Scriptures, but one that is varied and inconsistent according to the whim of some yawning or ignorant little man. For although the Church has so often enumerated the canonical [Col. 0053B] books, they nevertheless become utterly deaf. Indeed Calvin (*Institutes*, book I, ch. 7, §§1, 2, 4) writes that it is not for the Church to judge which books possess divine authority, but that this belongs to the secret testimony of the Spirit. Impious words! LE PR.] he carried out a slaughter of the Scriptures to suit his own material. Valentinus, however, spared them, since he did not devise the Scriptures to suit his material, but his material to suit the Scriptures; and yet he took away more and added more, removing even the proper meanings of individual words and adding arrangements of things that do not appear in the text.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

In this they are to be compared with those who are said to have composed Virgil-centos and Homer-centos.

[Col. 0052C] Such are [Note: [Col. 0052D] *Erant*, “Such were,” Rig., Venet.] the devices of the spiritual powers of wickedness against whom our struggle is waged, brothers—a struggle deservedly to be contemplated and necessary for faith [Note: [Col. 0052D] *Contemplandae fidei*, “necessary to the faith that is to be contemplated,” Rhen.], so that the chosen may be made manifest and the reprobate exposed. And therefore they have power and facility [Note: [Col. 0052D] Rig. and Venet. add *in*; *felicitatem*, “success,” Rig., Venet.] in devising and equipping errors—a facility not so very astonishing, as though it were difficult and inexplicable, since even secular literature provides an example of such facility. Today you see [Note: [Col. 0052D] *Quo jus hodie*, Rhen.; *vis hodie*, “you wish today,” Fran., Paris; *qui vis hodie*, “whoever you wish today,” Jun.; *cujus hodie*, “of whom today,” an old manuscript.] [Col. 0053A] a wholly different story [Note: [Col. 0053B] “A wholly different story.” This is a Greek construction: he says *totum aliam*, “a whole different,” that is, different throughout or entirely different. RHEN.] composed from Virgil [Note: [Col. 0053B] *Componit*, “composes,” Jun.], with the subject matter fitted to the verses and the verses to the subject matter.

[Note: [Col. 0053B] “Finally, Hosidius Geta.” Agobard’s manuscript has *Vosidius*; Ursinus’, *Osidius*. In Dio it is written **Γναῦος ὁ Σίδιος Γέτας**, which should be read **Γν. Ὁσίδιος**. A decree of the senate made under the emperor Claudius, when Gnaeus Hosidius Geta [Col. 0053C] and Lucius Vagellius were consuls, is said to have been unearthed at Naples in the year of Christ 1603. It was directed against those who had bought a building for purposes of trade, so that by demolishing it they might acquire more than its purchase price, and by a most bloody form of commerce produce in time of peace the most hostile appearance through the ruins of houses and villas. RIG.—“Hosidius Geta.” The foolish work of this poet has survived to our own times. In manuscripts found by Salmasius it consists of 461 verses, some of which were published by P. Scriverius in his *Collections of the Ancient Tragedians*, after Seneca, pp. 187, 190; the whole, however, was published by Burmann in the *Latin Anthology*, vol. I, pp. 148–186. Some wrongly supposed that this tragedy was the same one to which Ovid gave a similar title, and from which Quintilian, *Institutes of Oratory* VIII.5, took the following little verse:

> I was able to save you: do you ask whether I can destroy you?

For that reason they falsely imagined that our text of Tertullian ought to read “Ovidius” rather than “Hosidius” or “Osidius.” But they would not have fallen into such an error [Col. 0053D] if they had only been willing to observe from the verse cited by Quintilian that Ovid’s *Medea* was composed chiefly in iambics, whereas the extant work consists of hexameters. Others have also invented the claim that the poet Hosidius Geta of whom we are speaking was the suffect consul under the emperor Claudius in the year 48 after Christ’s birth—that is, the same man concerning whom Dio wrote certain things in book IV, whom Reinesius also mentions from an inscription (*Inscriptions*, pp. 475, 477), and whom Doni likewise names (*Marbles*, p. 84). Yet the words Tertullian used indicate rather one of his contemporaries. Furthermore, I can scarcely believe that centos were already in use when Claudius was emperor, a time when Roman literature was still flourishing (Burmann, loc. cit.). For that childish game, which an ancient author’s censure appears to have stigmatized along with other scholastic trifles in this fashion—

> It is disgraceful to produce laborious trifles,  
> And foolish is labor spent on absurdities—

[Col. 0054B] surely did not flourish until literature had already become corrupted. And indeed many other examples could later be added to those employed by Tertullian. Almost two hundred years after him, a certain matron named Proba Falconia, wife of the proconsul Adelphius and born at Horta, an ancient Italian town, published a Latin poem which has indeed been transmitted to us and which, throughout, like Osidius’ *Medea*, consists of verses—or at least half-verses—from Virgil. Its subject, however, is the history of the Old Testament (Fabricius, *Bibliotheca of Medieval and Late Latin*, vol. II, p. 142 ff., Mansi’s edition). Around the same time Ausonius composed an epithalamium filled with wantonness, to which he gave the title *Nuptial Cento*, using exactly the same method. A very large number of poets writing in modern Latin likewise composed Virgilian centos. But since it would be excessively long to list them all, let the reader consult Fabricius if he wishes, *Bibliotheca Latina*, vol. I, pp. 384–386, Ernesti’s edition, although even he passed over in silence Stephen Plurreus, canon regular of the house of Saint Victor and author of a poem on the *Life of Jesus Christ*, a fragment of which may be found under the article “Cento” in the *Dictionary of Trévoux*. EDD., from the work of DE GOURCY.]

Finally, Osidius [Note: [Col. 0053B] *Ovidius Geta*, Fran.; *Osidius Geta*, Paris; *Ovidius ita*, Jun.; *Hosidius Geta*, Rig., Venet.] Geta drew out [Note: [Col. 0053B] *Expressit*, “fashioned,” Rhen.] an entire tragedy, *Medea*, from Virgil [Note: [Col. 0054C] “He drew out an entire tragedy, *Medea*, from Virgil.” That tragedy is in the possession of the distinguished Salmasius, from whose copy some verses were published by P. Scriverius in his *Collections of the Ancient Tragedians*. RIG.]. A relative of mine, in fact, among the other recreations of his pen, expounded the *Pinax* of Cebes from the same poet. [Note: [Col. 0054C] “The *Pinax* of Cebes.” Cebes of Thebes, a Pythagorean by school if we trust Pamelius, wrote three dialogues. The first of these, entitled *Pinax of Human Life*, or *The Tablet*, was long ago printed in Italy, France, and Germany, and was also represented in a painting. It depicts the road to virtue and pleasure and the house of each: a work, says the illustrious Abbé de Gourcy, full of Stoic wisdom. EDD.] Those too are customarily called Homer-centonists who, in the cento manner, stitch together their own works from Homer’s poems, gathering many pieces from here and there into a single body. [Note: [Col. 0054D] “Homer-centos—those who make their own works from Homer’s poems.” An ancient example of this cento art is found in Irenaeus (book I, *Against Heresies*). RIG.] And divine literature is certainly more fertile in its capacity to supply material for any subject whatsoever [Note: [Col. 0053B] *Cujusque*, “each,” Rig., Venet.]. Nor do I shrink from saying that the Scriptures themselves were arranged in this way by God’s will, so that they might furnish materials to heretics, since I read that there must be heresies—which cannot exist without the Scriptures.

## CHAPTER XL

[Col. 0054A]

These things, moreover, are brought about by the same instigation of the devil, who also counterfeits the very realities of the divine sacraments in the mysteries of idols: for example, he baptizes certain people, promises expiation of sins from a bath, marks foreheads, and celebrates an offering of bread.

The next question will be [Note: [Col. 0053B] *Sed quaeritur*, “But the question is,” Rhen.]: by whom is the understanding of those things that promote heresies overturned [Note: [Col. 0053B] *Interpretetur*, “interpreted,” Rig., Venet.]? By the devil, of course, whose role it is [Note: [Col. 0054B] *Pares*, “equal,” Rhen.] to overturn the truth and who counterfeits the very realities of the divine sacraments in [Note: [Col. 0054B] Rhen. and Pam. prefix *in*.] the mysteries of idols.
