He too baptizes certain people—his own believers and faithful, of course; he promises the putting away [Note: [Col. 0054D] “The setting forth of sins.” This is the reading of Agobard’s manuscript. He used *expositio* (“setting forth”) for *depositio* (“putting away”). Cyprian likewise says in his letter to Jubaianus: “He has not set forth his former sins,” that is, “has not put them away.” RIG.] of sins [Note: [Col. 0054B] *Expiationem*, “expiation,” Rhen., Pam.] by means of the bath; and, if I still [Note: [Col. 0054B] *Sic adhuc*, “thus still,” Fran., Paris.] remember [Note: [Col. 0054B] *Memini* is absent from Fran. and Paris.], [Note: [Col. 0054D] “Mithras marks them there upon the forehead”—that is, there in the camp of darkness or of Satan. RIG.] Mithras [Note: [Col. 0054B] *Mithrae*, “of Mithras,” Rhen., Fran., Paris.] there marks his soldiers upon their [Col. 0055A] foreheads; [Note: [Col. 0054D] “He marks his soldiers upon their foreheads”—in imitation, of course, of the sign already in very common use among Christians in Tertullian’s age. For he says in the book *On the Crown*: “Whatever activity our daily life involves, we rub our forehead with the sign of the cross.” It therefore began to be applied so casually that even those who did not abstain from the Circus nevertheless appeared to be bound by reverence for this sign. “For how many of our brothers,” says Augustine, “do we now contemplate and mourn as they go off into empty pursuits and lying madness, neglecting that to which they have been called? If perchance, in the Circus itself, they become frightened for some reason, they immediately sign themselves and stand there bearing on their forehead that which would make them leave if they bore it in their heart,” etc., *Exposition of Psalm I*. It is also permissible, moreover, to suppose that Mithras, or Satan, marked his soldiers upon their foreheads in imitation of Christian anointing. RIG.] he also celebrates an offering of bread, introduces an image of resurrection, and [Note: [Col. 0055C] “Beneath a sword he redeems a crown”—by a mime of martyrdom, which he explains at greater length near the end of the work *On the Crown*. RIG.—“And beneath a sword he redeems a crown.” For an understanding of this, consider what he says in the book *On the Soldier’s Crown* near the end: “When the soldier of Mithras … is initiated in a cave … truly in the camp of darkness, a crown offered to him with a sword interposed, as though in a mime of martyrdom, is then fitted to his head. He is instructed to knock it from his head with his hand and transfer it, if possible, to his shoulder, saying that Mithras is his crown; and from then on he is never crowned. He possesses this as his token for proving himself whenever he is tested concerning his sacred obligation, and he is immediately believed to be a soldier of Mithras if he casts down the crown and says that it is in his god.” EDD.] beneath a sword redeems a crown.

What shall I say of the fact that he also restricts the high priest to one marriage [Note: [Col. 0055C] *Pontificem nuptiis*, Rhen.; *in unius nuptiis*, Hinsaug., from an old copy according to Rhenanus; *in unis nuptiis*, Fran.]? He too has virgins and continent persons. [Note: [Col. 0055D] “Moreover, if we review the superstitions of Numa Pompilius.” Here there is a fine annotation by Audebert Macereus, which we have thought should be translated from the French idiom. “A certain man,” he says, “in a book published not very long ago, entitled *A Brief Commentary on the Sacred Signs, Sacrifices, and Sacraments Instituted by God from the Creation of the World*, charges us with having derived our ceremonies for the most part from Numa Pompilius, and therefore with deserving to have them rejected and mocked. He was deceived,” the same author says, “because he did not consider the cunning of his father and master. For the devil altered them from the Old Testament and handed them down to Numa, so that through them he might be honored and worshiped by Numa and his followers. As for us, who have that Old Testament at hand, even if we omit the tradition of the Fathers, it is more credible that we derived them from it than from the books of Pompilius. Meanwhile, this too must be considered: observance of such ceremonies is pleasing to God, since the devil so zealously affects and counterfeits them.” PAM.]

Moreover, if we review the superstitions of Numa Pompilius; if we consider the priestly offices, insignia, and privileges; the sacrificial ministries [Note: [Col. 0055C] *Sacrificantia*, Rhen.; *sacrificantium et vasa ipsorum si sacrificiorum*, “of those sacrificing, and their vessels, if of sacrifices,” from Ursinus’ manuscript, Rig.], implements, and vessels of their sacrifices; and the minute observances surrounding expiations and vows—has not the devil plainly imitated [Note: [Col. 0056C] “That punctiliousness of the Jewish law.” By *morositas* he means the scrupulousness of Jewish customs and rites. PAM.] that punctiliousness of the Jewish law? He, therefore, who so emulously affected to reproduce in the affairs of idolatry the very things by which Christ’s sacraments are administered, certainly also desired and was able, being the same and acting with the same ingenuity, to adapt the documents of divine realities [Note: [Col. 0056C] “And of the holy Christians.” The meaning of this phrase must be gathered from the things that follow in chapter 44. He calls the Acts and Epistles of the Apostles “the documents of the holy Christians.” ALBASP.] and of the holy [Col. 0055B] Christians—meaning for meaning, words for words, parables for parables—to a profane and rival faith [Note: [Col. 0055C] *Attemperare*, “to accommodate,” Rig., Venet., Fran., Paris.].

And therefore no one ought to doubt either that the spiritual powers of wickedness, from whom heresies also come, were sent by the devil, or that heresies are indistinguishable from idolatry, since they belong to the same author and the same work as idolatry. They either fabricate another god in opposition to the Creator, or, if they confess one sole Creator, they describe him otherwise than he truly is. Accordingly, every falsehood they utter concerning God is, in a certain sense, a kind of idolatry [Note: [Col. 0056C] Rhen.: “Thus every falsehood concerning God—or nation, in a certain sense, sex—is idolatry.”].

## CHAPTER XLI

Finally, there must not be omitted, as a prescription we may advance against them, a description of heretical conduct itself: among them it is uncertain who is a catechumen and who a believer, for they enter alike, listen alike, and pray alike; they mingle the peace indiscriminately with everyone; their women dare to perform exorcisms and perhaps even to baptize; their ordinations are rash; one man is bishop today, another tomorrow; one is deacon today and reader tomorrow, presbyter today and layman tomorrow; for they impose priestly functions even upon laymen.

Nor shall I omit a description of heretical conduct itself: how futile, how earthly, how human it is—without seriousness, without authority, without discipline, as befits their faith. First of all, it is uncertain who is a catechumen and who a believer: they enter alike, [Col. 0056B] listen alike, and pray alike. Even if pagans should happen to come in, [Note: [Col. 0056D] “What is holy to the dogs.” We shall not pass over these words carelessly, for we think they refer to the Eucharist, concerning which he speaks as follows in chapter 25 of the book *On the Shows*: “From the mouth with which you have pronounced ‘Amen’ over that which is holy.” ALBASP.] they will cast what is holy to the dogs and pearls—though not genuine ones—before swine. They wish the overthrow of discipline to be regarded as simplicity, while the care we give to discipline they call pandering. They also mingle the peace indiscriminately with everyone; for it makes no difference to them, however divergent their treatments may be, provided that they conspire to overthrow the one truth. All are puffed up; all promise knowledge. Their catechumens are perfected before they have been instructed [Note: [Col. 0056C] *Educati*, “educated,” Paris.].

The heretical women themselves—how brazen they are! They dare to teach, to debate, to perform exorcisms, to promise healings, and perhaps [Note: [Col. 0056C] *Fortasse an*, Rhen.] even to baptize. Their ordinations are rash, frivolous, [Note: [Col. 0056D] “Inconstant.” All churchmen, whatever their rank might be, were assigned to fixed places; nor were they made bishops or priests for the sake of honor or a livelihood, but were ordained according to the necessity and use of the place or people. Just as they were not permitted to hasten elsewhere and change their sees, so neither could they be removed without cause from their office in the place to which they had been ordained and assigned. Among the heretics, however, sees were changed at will, and, as he says, one man is bishop today, another tomorrow. ALBASP.] inconstant. At one time [Note: [Col. 0056C] *Tunc*, “then,” Rhen.] [Col. 0057A] they appoint neophytes; at another, [Note: [Col. 0057C] “Those entangled with the world.” He means those who held some prefecture among the pagans. For many Christians who had attained some dignity or military rank nevertheless continued to discharge the duties of those honors, and it did not appear right to ordain such men to ecclesiastical honors. ALBASP.] men entangled with the world; at another, apostates from us—so that they may bind them by glory, since they cannot bind them by truth. Nowhere does a man advance more easily than in the camp of rebels, where merely to be present is to earn merit. Thus one man is bishop today, another tomorrow; one is deacon today and reader tomorrow; presbyter today and layman tomorrow; for they impose [Note: [Col. 0057C] *Laici*, “laymen,” Rhen.] priestly functions even upon laymen.

## CHAPTER XLII

In the ministry of the word also, their business is not to convert pagans but to subvert our people; nor do they show reverence to their own presiding officers. Hence schisms among them do not become apparent, however much they differ among themselves from their own rules and even from their own founders.

[Note: [Col. 0057C] “But concerning the ministry of the word.” I do not think he is speaking of the ministry conducted in the churches, since pagans were excluded from it, but of that conducted familiarly at home or elsewhere; for Christians had no greater concern than gradually to instill Christ’s precepts into pagans in order to draw them to the faith. ALBASP.] But what shall I say concerning the ministry of the word, [Col. 0057B] since their business is not to convert [Note: [Col. 0057C] *Evertendis*, “subverting,” Jun.; *convertendis*, “converting,” others.] pagans but to subvert our people? They seek this glory more eagerly: to bring ruin upon those who stand, rather than to raise up those who lie fallen. For their own work does not arise from a structure of their own, but from the destruction of the truth. They undermine our buildings in order to construct their own. [Note: [Col. 0057D] “Take away from them the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and God the Creator, and they have no accusation to utter.” He is marking Cerdon, Marcion, and Apelles, who dared to tear down even those foundations of the Christian religion. For in the *Catalogue of Heretics*, where he speaks of Cerdon, he says: “He rejects the prophecies and the Law; he renounces God the Creator.” Marcion, moreover, was Cerdon’s disciple, and Apelles Marcion’s. He therefore says that the minds of heretics are so constituted that they destroy rather than build. Take away from them the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and God the Creator, and they will have no legal ground on which to plead a case against you because of it; there will be nothing of which they can complain. For they long ago testified that these things in no way belonged to them. RIG.] Take away from them the Law [Note: [Col. 0057C] *In lege*, “in the Law,” Paris.] of Moses, the Prophets, and God the Creator, and they have no accusation to utter. Thus it comes about that they more readily produce the collapse of standing buildings than the reconstruction of fallen ruins. Only for works of this sort do they act humble, flattering, and submissive. For the rest, they do not know how to show reverence even to their own presiding officers.

And this is why schisms among heretics are scarcely [Col. 0057C] apparent: because, when they exist, they do not become apparent. [Note: [Col. 0057D] “Schism is unity for them.” This is the reading of Ursinus’ manuscript, and it is entirely true. There are indeed schisms among heretics, but we notice them less because of their common and completely harmonious disagreement with us. RIG.] Schism is [Col. 0058A] unity for them [Note: [Col. 0057C] *Ipsa*, “itself,” Seml.]. I am lying if they do not even differ among themselves from their own rules, while each man modifies what he has received according to his own judgment, just as the man who handed it down originally composed it according to his own judgment. The development of the thing recognizes its own nature and the customary character of its origin. The Valentinians claimed the same right that Valentinus had, and the Marcionites the same right that Marcion had: to innovate the faith according to their own judgment. Finally, when examined thoroughly, all heresies are found to disagree with their founders on many points. Most do not even have churches; motherless, without a see, orphaned in faith, banished, and without a home [Note: [Col. 0057C] *Quasi sibi late*, Fran., Jun.; *sibi late*, Paris; *sibilatae*, “hissed away,” Rhen.], they wander about.

## CHAPTER XLIII

Their dealings with magicians, mountebanks, astrologers, and philosophers have also been noted; so much so that the index of their untrue teaching [Col. 0058B] is their evil discipline.

It has also been noted [Note: [Col. 0058C] Perhaps *Nota* ought to be read. EDD.] that heretics associate with a great many magicians, with mountebanks, with astrologers [Note: [Col. 0057D] “With a great many magicians, with mountebanks, with astrologers.” No one even slightly acquainted with ecclesiastical history is unaware that the earlier heretics were notorious for magic or associated with Magi. Such were the Gnostics, the Carpocratians, and others. It is likewise beyond doubt that these same magicians were excluded from the communion of the Church, as were mimes, stage performers, mountebanks, itinerant charlatans, and comedians; against them Augustine and Cyprian wrote in many places, as did the councils. LE PR.], and with philosophers—that is, men devoted to curiosity. Everywhere they remember, “SEEK, AND YOU SHALL FIND.” Thus even from the character of their way of life the quality of their faith may be assessed: [Note: [Col. 0058C] “Conduct is the index of doctrine.” In this author, *disciplina* always denotes matters of faith, the sacraments or their use, rites and ceremonies, and the other observances that we keep according to Christ’s precepts; sometimes it is also employed for faith itself. ALBASP.] conduct is the index of doctrine. [Note: [Col. 0058C] “Judge,” RIG., Venetian edition; “thence,” Rhenanus; “doctrine is the index of conduct,” Paris.] They deny that God is to be feared; accordingly, everything is free and unrestrained for them. But where is God not feared, except where he is absent? Where God is absent, no truth exists either; where no truth exists [Note: [Col. 0058C] The words “where no truth exists” are absent from Rhenanus’s edition.], such conduct is deservedly found. But where God is, there is fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom. Where there is fear of God, there are honorable seriousness [Note: [Col. 0058C] “Honorableness,” Rhenanus.], vigilant diligence, [Note: [Col. 0058D] “Vigilant diligence.” He calls that diligence vigilant which always fears lest it sin. RIG.] anxious care, a scrutinized selection, [Note: [Col. 0058D] “A scrutinized selection”—that is, of those to be chosen for ecclesiastical office. This announcement was made by putting forward their names and admonishing the people that, if anyone had any accusation against them, he should prove it by manifest facts. Lampridius relates that Alexander Severus recommended, on the Christians’ example, that this be done when provincial governors were appointed. Such, therefore, was the Church’s scrutinized selection; by contrast, rash ordinations among the heretics are noted above. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0058C] “Addition,” Rhenanus.] [Col. 0058C] deliberate communion, [Note: [Col. 0058D] “Deliberate communion.” He means the communion that he himself describes in the *Apologeticum*: namely, participation in prayer, assembly, and every sacred fellowship. None were admitted to it unless, after prior deliberation, they were found thoroughly approved. RIG.] advancement earned by merit, [Note: [Col. 0058D] “Advancement earned by merit.” He is his own interpreter in the same *Apologeticum*: “Approved elders preside, each of them having obtained this honor not by payment but by testimony.” RIG.] [Col. 0059A] religious submission, [Note: [Col. 0059C] “Religious submission.” “For the sake of the Church’s honor,” he says in the book *On Baptism*, “by whose preservation peace is preserved.” One is called “subject” when he accommodates himself to another, as a son to his father. Thus in the *Apologeticum*: “The father, suffering patiently, disowned the son who had already become submissive.” RIG.] devoted service, [Note: [Col. 0059C] “Devoted service.” Presbyters and deacons serve bishops; scribes, heralds, and attendants serve magistrates. The Glosses of Philoxenus: *apparitores*, ἐκβιβασταί (*ekbibastai*, “executive attendants”). [Col. 0059D] Εἰσὶν δὲ ὑπηρέται τοῖς ἄρχουσιν προσεδρεύοντες (“They are servants who attend upon the rulers”). *Apparitio*, ἐκβιβασμός (*ekbibasmos*, “service”). In this sense our Septimius says in the book *On the Shows* that the ears and eyes serve the spirit: “Since the ears and eyes serve the spirit, the spirit cannot be kept pure when its attendants are defiled.” RIG.] and modest public appearance, [Note: [Col. 0059D] “Modest public appearance.” Christians went out in public with modest dress and expression. ## CHAPTER XLIV

Finally, if perhaps they are not moved by these pleas in bar, he challenges both the heretics and those who lend an ear to them with fear of the future judgment.

Accordingly, these evidences of our stricter discipline [Note: [Col. 0059D] “Of stricter discipline.” This is what he said in the *Apologeticum*: “We reinforce our discipline by repeated inculcation of the commandments.” Hence also the expressions that frequently occur: “discipline to be feared,” “discipline preserved,” “the terror of discipline,” “the tenor of discipline.” By contrast: “the most indulgent, most lax discipline.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0059C] “Stricter things,” Rhenanus; both readings absent from Franeker and Paris.] contribute to the proof of the truth. It is expedient for no one to turn away from it who remembers the future judgment, at which we must all stand before Christ’s tribunal and render an account first of all for faith itself. What, then, will those say who have violated by heretical adultery the virgin faith entrusted to them by Christ? They will allege, I suppose, that neither he nor his apostles ever foretold to them anything [Note: [Col. 0059D] “Concerning late and perverse doctrines.” So, most excellently, Ursinus’s manuscript. Previously, *saevis* (“savage”), which makes no sense. He calls the doctrines of Antichrist “late,” since the consummation of the age will follow Antichrist’s times. In Tertullian’s writings three periods divide all the ages of humankind: Nature, Law, and Gospel. The period of the Gospel is therefore the last, with Antichrist and the end of the age stealing in. RIG.] about the late and perverse doctrines that were to come, nor commanded them to beware of and abominate them. [Note: [Col. 0059C] *Saevis*, Rhenanus; *scaevis*, Junius.] [Col. 0059B] [Note: [Col. 0059C] “What,” Rhenanus.] Let them acknowledge their own fault rather than that of those who so long beforehand equipped us against them. [Note: [Col. 0059C] The word “so” is absent from Rhenanus’s edition; “not beforehand” is read by Paris and Franeker; “their own beforehand,” Junius.] They will add, moreover, many things concerning the authority of each heretical teacher: that those men especially confirmed the credibility of their doctrine [Note: [Col. 0059C] “Confirmed the greatest points of their doctrine,” Rhenanus.], raised the dead, restored the infirm, and disclosed things to come, so that they were deservedly believed to be apostles. [Note: [Col. 0060C] “So that they were deservedly believed to be apostles.” Here Tertullian attacks only fictitious miracles, or tricks of demons; for in this same work, especially chapter 30, he acknowledges that true miracles constitute a certain proof of divine mission, when he challenges the heretics [Col. 0060D] with this victorious demand: “Let them prove themselves to be new apostles. Let them say that Christ descended again, taught in person again, was crucified again, died again, and was raised again; for it is thus that he is accustomed to make apostles.” EDD., from the work of DE GOURCY.] As though it had not also been written that many would come who would perform even the greatest miracles [Note: [Col. 0060C] “Had performed,” Rhenanus.] in order to fortify the deceit of a corrupted proclamation! Will they therefore deserve pardon? But those who, mindful of the Lord’s and the apostles’ warnings, have stood firm and undefiled in the faith [Note: [Col. 0060C] “The faith standing undefiled,” Rhenanus.] will, I suppose, be in danger of losing pardon, when the Lord answers:

> “I had indeed foretold that teachers of deceit would come in my name, and likewise in the names of the prophets and apostles; and I had commanded my disciples to preach the same warning to you. Once for all I had entrusted the Gospel and the doctrine of its rule to my apostles; but, since you would not believe, [Note: [Col. 0060C] In Rhenanus’s edition the words “but, since you would not believe” are prefixed to the words “once for all the Gospel,” etc.] I later chose to change some things in it. [Note: [Col. 0060D] “To change.” Understand this as spoken ironically. EDD.] I had promised the resurrection even of the flesh, but I reconsidered, lest perhaps I should be unable to fulfill it. I had shown that I was born of a virgin, but later this seemed shameful to me. I had said that he who made the sun and rains was my Father, but another and better father adopted me. I had forbidden you to lend an ear to heretics, but I was mistaken …?”

Such thoughts befit those who stray beyond the bounds and do not guard against endangering the faith of truth. [Note: [Col. 0060C] “Other things,” Rhenanus.] [Note: [Col. 0060C] Junius conjectures “faith,” but in our judgment most badly.]

## CHAPTER XLV

[Col. 0060B] Moreover, having at the same time undertaken this design in detail, beginning with Judaism, he reviews all the heretics down to his own times, and first Dositheus, the Sadducees, and the Pharisees.

[Note: [Col. 0060D] “But for the present we have dealt generally against all heresies.” He himself says in the book *On the Flesh of Christ*: “But elsewhere we have already made fuller use of pleas in bar of this sort against all heresies.” EDD.] For the present, however, we have dealt generally against all heresies, which are to be excluded from a conference upon the Scriptures by definite, just, and necessary pleas in bar. [Note: [Col. 0060D] “And necessary pleas in bar.” He calls the pleas in bar “necessary” because, in accordance with them, a judge must necessarily reject any who wish to bring an action. RIG.] For the rest, if God’s grace permits, we shall also reply to certain heresies individually. [Note: [Col. 0060D] “We shall also reply to certain heresies individually.” This he indeed accomplished in the books *Against Marcion*, *Against the Valentinians*, *Against Praxeas*, etc.; but certainly not in the following little work, for in it heresies are merely catalogued, not refuted. RIG.] To those who read these things in the faith of truth [source gap after *ci-*], peace and the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ forever.

[Note: [Col. 0060D] “Against the Heretics ends.” In the Agobard manuscript [Col. 0061C] the book *On the Prescription of Heretics* proceeds no farther, nor is any mention made of the following little work, which begins, “Of those heretics—to pass over the greater number—I shall touch briefly upon a few,” etc. And it will remain [Col. 0061D] ἀκέφαλον (*akephalon*, “headless”), unless we say that it was appended by Tertullian to the work *On the Prescription of Heretics* in such a way that, after that work was completed, someone wrote, “The Prescription of Heretics ends,” and the same person—whoever he may have been, a writer of that age—then placed as the title of the following little work, “Of those heretics”; for he was, of course, about to give a catalogue of those whom he judged should be excluded by the general plea in bar. Then the little work would begin, “For I pass over the heretics of Judaism.” For this reason it is regarded as a portion and continuation of the preceding work, and accordingly is nowhere found cited separately by the author. Its style certainly does not appear unlike that of Septimius. In some copies, however, it precedes the book *On the Prescription of Heretics*. RIG.]

**AGAINST THE HERETICS ENDS**

The following is not found in the very ancient Agobard manuscript.

[Col. 0061A] Of those heretics—to pass over the greater number—I shall touch briefly upon a few. [Note: [Col. 0061D] “For I pass over the heretics of Judaism.” Jerome had read these words when, writing against the Luciferians, he says: “I pass over the heretics of Judaism, who before Christ’s advent had dissipated the law that had been handed down: how Dositheus, leader of the Samaritans, rejected the prophets,” etc. RIG.] For I pass over the heretics of Judaism: Dositheus the Samaritan, I mean, who first dared to reject the prophets on the ground that they had not spoken in the Holy Spirit. I pass over the Sadducees, who, springing from the root of this error, dared in addition to deny the resurrection of the flesh as part of this heresy. I omit the Pharisees, who separated themselves from the Jews by constructing certain additions to the law; hence they were worthy to receive the very name they bear. With these I omit also the Herodians, who said that Herod was the Christ.

## CHAPTER XLVI

He then reviews those who wished to be heretics on the basis of the Gospel: Simon Magus, Menander, Saturninus, Basilides, and Nicolas.

[Note: [Col. 0062C] “I turn to those.” Jerome, in the same work: [Col. 0062D] “I come to those heretics who have mangled the Gospels.” RIG.—“I turn to those,” etc. He now proceeds to speak of the heretics who arose after Christ’s birth and who left the grounds of their madness to later heretics. LE PR.] I turn to those who wished to be heretics on the basis of the Gospel. [Note: [Col. 0062D] “The first of all these is Simon Magus.” He numbers Simon Magus first of all, together with Irenaeus, Epiphanius, etc.] The first of all these is Simon Magus, who in the Acts of the Apostles deservedly received from the apostle Peter a just sentence. He dared to say that he was the supreme Power—that is, the supreme God—and that the world had been established by his angels; [Note: [Col. 0062D] “That he had descended, while straying from a demon, to inquire among the Jews what wisdom was.” These words are extremely corrupt, nor do the manuscripts help. Nevertheless, it seems they ought to be read: “That he, who was Wisdom, had descended to seek the wandering sheep. Among the Jews he in an apparition,” etc. Jerome, *Catalogue of Heresies*: “And therefore, he says, he descended to save the lost sheep. Christ did not suffer among the Jews.” RIG.] that he had descended, while straying from a demon, to inquire among the Jews what wisdom was [materially uncertain text]; that in an apparition of God he had not suffered, but only seemed to have suffered. After him came his disciple Menander, likewise a magician, saying the same things as Simon himself. Whatever Simon had said himself to be, Menander said that he himself was, [Col. 0061C] denying that anyone could possess salvation unless he had been baptized in Menander’s name.

After these came Saturninus. He likewise said that the unbegotten [Note: [Col. 0061C] “Ignoble,” Junius; “among those highest and,” Junius.] [Col. 0062A] Power—that is, God—remained in the highest and those infinite regions above, while angels far removed from him made the lower world. And because a certain radiance of light from above had shone in the lower regions, the angels took care to fashion the human being after that higher likeness, on account of the light’s radiance. [Note: [Col. 0061C] “The likeness of that light, and nothing intervening,” Semler.] This being lay crawling upon the earth; but that light and power, through mercy, [Note: [Col. 0062C] Semler inserts here the words just omitted, in this fashion: “that higher power, through mercy.” Junius, however, has: “into whom that light and that higher power, through mercy, infused the spark of life; this spark is saved, but the rest of the human being perishes.”]—the spark—is saved, while the rest of the human being perishes. [Note: [Col. 0062C] “The remaining part,” Rhenanus.] Christ did not exist in the substance of a body, and only in an apparition did he seem to have suffered; the resurrection of the flesh will in no way occur.

Afterward the heretic Basilides burst forth. He says that there is a supreme God named Abraxas, from whom Mind was created, which in Greek he calls ΝΟΥΣ (*nous*, “mind”). From Mind came the Word; from the Word, Providence; [Col. 0062B] from Providence, Power and Wisdom. From these in turn were made principalities, powers, and angels, and thereafter limitless emanations and projections of angels. By these angels 365 heavens were established, and the world was made in honor of Abraxas, whose name, when calculated, contained this number. Among the last angels, those who made the present world, he places the God of the Jews last—that is, the God of the Law and the Prophets. He denies that this being is God, calling him instead an angel. To him the seed of Abraham fell by lot; and therefore he transferred the children of Israel from the land of Egypt to the land of Canaan. [Note: [Col. 0062D] “More turbulent than all the other angels.” Jerome’s *Catalogue*: “This angel in his insolence exalted himself above the other angels.” RIG.] He was more turbulent than the other angels and therefore frequently stirred up seditions and wars and shed human blood. But Christ came, sent not by him who [Col. 0062C] made the world, but by that Abraxas; he came in an apparition and lacked the substance of flesh. He did not suffer at the hands of the Jews; instead, Simon was crucified in his place. Hence no one should believe in the one who was crucified, lest he confess that he has believed in Simon. Basilides denies that martyrdoms should be undergone. He fiercely opposes the resurrection of the flesh, denying that salvation has been promised to bodies.

Another [Note: [Col. 0063C] “In another manner,” Junius.] heretic, Nicolas, emerged. [Note: [Col. 0063C] “He was one of the seven deacons.” The heresy of the Nicolaitans is touched upon here. Its principal dogma was that marriage was a merely human institution and did not bind consciences, and also that it was lawful to eat things sacrificed to idols without any distinction. Those heretics are referred to in Acts 20 by the words λαλοῦντες διεστραμμένα (*lalountes diestrammena*, “speaking perverse things”). Tertullian in this passage, Saint Epiphanius, *Heresy* 25, Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* 2 and 3, Saint Jerome in the letter concerning Fabian and that to Ctesiphon, Eusebius, Book III, Philastrius of Brescia in his book *On Heresies*, Theodoret, *Heretical Fables*, Book III, Augustine, *Heresy* 5, and innumerable others make Nicolas, one of the seven deacons, the author of this dogma. After so great a consensus of the holy Fathers on this matter, I do not know whether any room for doubt can remain. Yet Saint Ignatius causes me to remain doubtful here and to believe that perhaps Nicolas the deacon was not the author of that sect. For Ignatius, in his letter to the Trallians, writes: φεύγετε καὶ τοὺς ἀκαθάρους νικολαΐτας, τοὺς ψευδωνύμους, “Flee also the impure Nicolaitans, who falsely assume that name.” Add that several of those Fathers speak doubtfully about this Nicolas, upon whom it was easy to cast the blame because of the filthiness of their lives and their utterly corrupt morals. LE PR.] He was one of the seven deacons chosen in the Acts of the Apostles. He says that darkness existed in desire for light, a desire indeed foul and obscene; from this mingling arose things so fetid and unclean that modesty forbids their recital.

For he relates that certain aeons were born of shameful intercourse [Note: [Col. 0063D] “For he relates that certain aeons were born of shamefulness.” Epiphanius: Καὶ ἐκ τούτου τοῦ αἰῶνος τοῦ αἰσχροῦ καὶ τῆς μήτρας γεγονέναι θεούς τε, καὶ τοὺς ἀγγέλους, καὶ δαίμονας, “And that from this shameful aeon and the womb were born gods, angels, and demons.” Hence a most learned man recently advised that the text be read: “For he relates that certain aeons were born of shamefulness,” etc. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0063C] “There are also the remaining obscene things. For he relates that all are certain marks of shamefulness,” Semler. Latinus reads *communes* (“common”) in place of *aeones* or *omnes*.], as well as embraces, execrable minglings, obscene couplings, [Note: [Col. 0063D] “And obscene things joined together”—that is, conjunctions. [Col. 0064C] Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*, says of this very heretic: “Making marriages day and night, he imagined obscene couplings shameful even to hear.” RIG.] and certain things still more shameful than these. He further relates that demons, gods, seven spirits, and other things equally sacrilegious and foul were born from them. [Note: [Col. 0063C] Junius deletes “sufficiently.”] [Col. 0063B] We blush to relate these things and now pass them over. It is sufficient for us [Note: [Col. 0064C] Semler proposes: “Even if we pass them over, it is sufficient.”] that the Lord’s Apocalypse condemned this whole heresy of the Nicolaitans with the most solemn authority of its sentence, saying: [Note: [Col. 0064C] “Because you possess this, you hate the doctrine of the Nicolaitans.” Jerome’s *Catalogue*: “But the Holy Spirit, calling it a heresy, says to the Church: ‘But this you have, that you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans.’” RIG.] “Because you possess this: you hate the doctrine of the Nicolaitans, which I too hate.”

## CHAPTER XLVII

To these he adds the Ophites, Cainites, and Sethites.

To these were also added the heretics called Ophites. For they magnify the serpent to such a degree that they even prefer it to Christ himself. It was the serpent, they say, who gave us the origin of the knowledge of good and evil. Perceiving its power and majesty, they say, Moses set up the bronze serpent, and all who [Col. 0064A] looked upon it obtained health. Christ himself, they further claim, imitates in his Gospel the sacred power of that serpent when he says [Note: [Col. 0064C] “Teaches,” Semler.], “And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.” They bring in the serpent itself to bless their Eucharist. [Note: [Col. 0064C] “They bring it in to bless their Eucharist.” So too Jerome’s *Catalogue*: “And it sanctifies the Eucharist for them.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0064C] “Eucharistic things,” Franeker.]

But the whole setting and doctrine of this error flowed from the following source. They say that from that supreme, primordial aeon several other, lower aeons came into existence; yet an aeon whose name is Jaldabaoth presides over them all. [Note: [Col. 0064C] “Whose name is Jaldabaoth.” This name was drawn from the storehouse of the Nicolaitans, concerning whom Saint Epiphanius, *Heresy* 25, writes: Ἕτεροι δὲ τῶν προειρημένων Ἰαλδαβαὼθ δοξάζουσι, φάσκοντες αὐτὸν εἶναι πρῶτον υἱὸν τῆς Βαρβηλὼ καὶ διὰ τοῦτό φασι δεῖν ἄγειν αὐτῷ τὴν τιμήν, ὅτι πολλὰ ἀπεκάλυψεν· ὅθεν καὶ βιβλία τινὰ ἐξ ὀνόματος τοῦ Ἰαλδαβαὼθ ποιητεύονται ἐκτυποῦντες, “Others among the aforesaid chiefly venerate Jaldabaoth, asserting that he is the firstborn son of Barbelo and that honor ought therefore to be paid to him, as they say, because he revealed many things. Hence they fabricate certain books and circulate them under the name of Jaldabaoth.” Many names of this filthy sort were invented by the Nicolaitans, some of which are recorded in Saint Epiphanius. But, modesty, I violate you by dwelling any longer upon these things. LE PR.]

They say that he was conceived from another aeon mingled with lower aeons; and that afterward, when he wished to struggle upward, he was unable, because of the weight of the matter mingled with him, to reach the higher regions. [Note: [Col. 0064C] “Heavenly things,” Semler; “and closed off the higher regions,” Junius.] Left in the middle, he stretched the whole of himself out [Note: [Col. 0064C] Semler says “himself” should be added.] and so made heaven. [Col. 0064B] Jaldabaoth, however, descended farther and made seven sons for himself. By his expansion he closed off the higher regions, so that, because the angels could not know what was above, they considered him the only God.

Those lower powers and angels therefore made the human being. Because he had been fashioned by weaker and middling powers, he lay crawling like a worm. But the aeon from whom Jaldabaoth had proceeded, moved by envy, infused a certain spark into the prostrate human being; [Note: [Col. 0064D] “Infused a certain spark into the prostrate human being.” Jerome’s *Catalogue*: “Accordingly, the Mother above, wishing to empty Jaldabaoth’s power, caused a spark of power to descend into the human being, and it immediately raised him up so that he stood upon his feet.” RIG.] awakened by it, through understanding he became wise and was able to comprehend the higher regions. Thus Jaldabaoth in turn, moved to indignation, produced from himself a power in the likeness of a serpent. This was the power [Col. 0065A] in paradise—that is, this was the serpent in which Eve had believed as though it were the Son of God. She plucked, they say, from the fruit of the tree, and thereby imparted to the human race knowledge of good and evil. They also hold that Christ did not exist in the substance of flesh, and that no salvation of the flesh whatever is to be hoped for.

Yet another heresy also burst forth, [Note: [Col. 0065C] “Which is called that of the Cainites.” Philastrius, Epiphanius, Augustine, and Damascenus certainly also call them Caians. Finally, Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*, when he joins together the Ophites, Caians, Carpocrates, Cerinthus, and Ebion, appears to have imitated the Author. Clement of Alexandria, however, in *Stromata* 7, calls them Cainites; Irenaeus, more properly, as also Theodoret, calls them Cains, because all unanimously derive the name from Cain. PAM.—“Cainites.” They were so called because they worship and venerate Cain, the fratricide and firstborn of our father, the blessed Adam the first-formed, saying that Cain was possessed of the most powerful virtue. Cain, they say, was produced by one power, namely the devil; but the most blessed Abel was born from another, namely God. The greater power, which was in Cain himself, so prevailed that he killed his brother. They similarly adore Judas the traitor, considering him to possess something divine—to such a degree, indeed, that they regard his detestable crime as a great benefaction. They assert that he foreknew how greatly Christ’s passion would benefit the human race and therefore handed him over to the Jews to be killed. They are also reported to worship the Sodomites, as well as Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, because, after causing a schism among God’s first people, they perished when the earth opened. So true is it that, however wicked or criminal some have at one time been, they have never lacked persons to praise them and commend their crimes. Finally, they blaspheme the Law and God, its author, and deny the resurrection of the flesh. Irenaeus and Augustine, moreover, attribute all Marcion’s errors to them; from this it is readily credible that the Caian heretics had their origin from Marcion. LAC.] which is called that of the Cainites. [Note: [Col. 0066C] “For they too magnify Cain.” Jerome’s *Catalogue*: “They sanctify him.” RIG.] For they too magnify Cain, as though he had been conceived from some powerful force that operated within him. Abel, however, was conceived and begotten from a lower power [Note: [Col. 0066C] “And was therefore found inferior.” Jerome’s *Catalogue*: “And therefore he was killed.” RIG.], and was therefore found inferior.

Those who assert this also defend Judas the traitor, commemorating him as admirable and great [Note: [Col. 0066C] “Commemorating him as admirable and great.” Jerome’s *Catalogue*: “He was more learned than all the apostles.” RIG.] because of the benefits he is boasted to have conferred upon the human race. Some of them think that thanksgiving should be rendered to Judas for this reason. For Judas, they say, perceiving that Christ wished to overthrow the truth, betrayed him so that the truth could not be overthrown. Others argue contrariwise in the following manner. Because the powers of this world did not wish Christ to suffer, lest salvation should be procured for the human race through his death, Judas, taking counsel for humanity’s salvation, betrayed Christ, so that the salvation which was being obstructed by the powers opposing Christ’s suffering could in no way be obstructed; and so that, through Christ’s passion, the salvation of the human race could not be delayed.

That heresy also arose [Note: [Col. 0066C] “Which is called that of the Sethites.” The Sethians—or, as Tertullian prefers, Sethites—were named after Seth, Adam’s third-born son, whom certain Jews were said to venerate, as Augustine reports in *On Heresies*, chapter 19. For they said that Seth was born from the supreme Mother, asserting that she united with the Father above, from which union that divine seed was born as the seed of the sons of God. For among them male and female gods and goddesses are believed to exist. LAC.] which is called that of the Sethites. [Note: [Col. 0065C] Junius prefers “Setthites.”] The doctrine of this perversity is as follows. Two human beings, Cain and Abel, were fashioned by the angels. On their account great disputes and dissensions arose among the angels. For this reason, when Abel had been killed, that Power which was above all powers [Note: [Col. 0066D] “The Power which was above all powers.” In Jerome’s *Catalogue* it is called the “Threefold Power.” RIG.] [Col. 0066A]—whom they declare to be the Mother—wished Seth to be conceived and born in Abel’s place, so that those angels who had created the first two human beings might be emptied of their power as this seed died and was born in the world [materially uncertain syntax].

For they say that the minglings of angels and human beings were unlawful. For that reason the Power whom, as we have said, they declare to be the Mother also brought on the Flood in vengeance, so that the seed of that mingling might be removed and this seed alone, being pure, might be preserved intact. Yet, secretly and covertly, and without the knowledge of that Mother-Power, those who had fashioned the men of that former seed also sent the seed of Ham [Note: [Col. 0065C] “Cain,” Franeker and Paris.] into the ark with those eight souls, so that the seed of wickedness might not perish but, preserved with the others and restored to the earth after the Flood, might grow after their example, spread out, and fill and occupy the whole world. Concerning Christ, however, they hold that he was Seth alone, and that he himself existed on behalf of Seth. [Note: [Col. 0066C] Rhenanus reads: “Not on our behalf alone, but also on his own behalf he himself existed.” Semler: “But also on his own behalf he himself existed.”]

## CHAPTER XLVIII

In addition, Carpocrates, Cerinthus, and Ebion.

[Note: [Col. 0066D] “Carpocrates in addition,” etc. It is evident that Carpocrates was the father of the Gnostics. His errors, however, were extinguished in their cradle. Among his other fabrications, he rejected the Old Testament. I do not determine whether the same man was the founder of both the Gnostics and the Carpocratians. It is certain that a certain worthless woman named Marcellina was the associate or inventor of so many crimes; she worshipped images of Christ, Paul, Homer, and Pythagoras indiscriminately. The emperor Alexander Severus is likewise said absurdly to have bestowed this same worship upon profane divinities together with sacred figures, keeping statues of Abraham and Orpheus, Christ and Apollo, in his shrine. LE PR.] Carpocrates, in addition, introduced the following sect. He says that there is one principal Power in the higher regions, and that from it angels and powers were brought forth. These, being far removed from the higher powers [Note: [Col. 0066C] “Power,” Semler.], fashioned this world in the lower regions. Christ was not born of the Virgin Mary but from Joseph’s seed, and was begotten merely as a human being; nevertheless, he was better than others in his cultivation of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0066D] “Certainly above others in his cultivation of righteousness.” Jerome’s *Catalogue*: “But he possessed the prophetic spirit.” RIG.], [Col. 0067A] and in the integrity of his life. [Note: [Col. 0067B] Semler deletes “of his life.”] He suffered among the Jews. His soul alone was received into heaven, because it was firmer and stronger than the others. From this he would infer—since only the salvation of souls is maintained—that there are no resurrections of the body. [Note: [Col. 0067B] Junius reads “to infer” and “maintained.”]

After him the heretic Cerinthus burst forth, teaching similar doctrines. For he too says that the world was established by those beings; he declares that Christ was born from Joseph’s seed and contends that he was merely a human being without divinity. He also reports that the Law was given by angels and puts forward the God of the Jews not as the Lord but as an angel.

[Note: [Col. 0067B] “His successor was Ebion.” This was the impious man who said that the Blessed Virgin gave birth to a man, not God, and who accepted only the Hebrew Gospel. Against him Saint John, both apostle and evangelist, wrote his Gospel last of all. He did not admit the epistles of Blessed Paul, for he called the Apostle an apostate. Since, moreover, the Ebionites at first thought and spoke basely of Christ—or perhaps because by their heresy they betrayed the poverty of their intelligence—their founder was by some chance called “beggar”; for in Hebrew *Ebion* means “beggar.” LE PR.] His successor was Ebion, who did not agree with Cerinthus in every respect, because he says that the world was made by God, not by angels. And because it is written, “No disciple is above his teacher, [Col. 0067B] nor is a servant above his lord,” he also puts forward the Law, evidently in order to exclude the Gospel and vindicate Judaism. [Note: [Col. 0067C] “And because it is written, ‘No disciple is above his teacher.’” Jerome’s *Catalogue*: “Carpocrates, Cerinthus, and Ebion—these three succeeded one another, teaching that all things should be done according to the Law: circumcision, observance of Sabbaths and Jewish feast days; for Christ observed all these things. They said that it was enough for the disciple to be as the teacher.” Hence it is clear that the words should be punctuated thus: “And because it is written, ‘No disciple is above his teacher, [Col. 0067D] nor is a servant above his lord,’ he also puts forward the Law,” etc. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0067B] “To exist,” Semler.]

## CHAPTER XLIX

Next Valentinus and his followers Ptolemy, Secundus, and Heracleon.

Valentinus the heretic, however, introduces many fables; [Col. 0068A] I shall briefly dispose of them by reviewing them in turn. [Note: [Col. 0067B] “Reviewing” (*circumdicens*), Semler; *circumducens*, Latinus; *circumcidens*, Rhenanus.] For he introduces a Pleroma and thirty Aeons, and sets them out in syzygies, that is, certain pairs. For he says that in the beginning there were Bythos and Silence; from these proceeded the seed—[Note: [Col. 0067B] Chacón deletes “seed.”]—Mind and Truth; from these burst forth Word and Life; and from these in turn were created Man and Church. But from these too, he says, proceeded twelve Aeons; and from Word and Life, another ten Aeons. This [Note: [Col. 0067B] “These,” Semler.] is the triacontad of Aeons, which is constituted [Note: [Col. 0068B] “May be,” Semler; “may be constituted,” Junius.] in the Pleroma from an ogdoad, a decad, and a duodecad. [Note: [Col. 0067D] “But the thirtieth Aeon.” Jerome’s *Index*: “And so the thirtieth roll, which is Wisdom, desired to see the Father.” LE PR.]

But the thirtieth Aeon wished to see that Bythos and dared to ascend into the higher regions of the Pleroma in order to see him. And because it was incapable of beholding his greatness, [Col. 0068B] it fell into a state of deficiency and was almost dissolved, had not the one whom they call Horos been sent [Note: [Col. 0068B] “Had sent,” Semler.] to stabilize it and confirmed it by saying “Iao.” [Note: [Col. 0068B] Semler deletes “Iao.”] [Note: [Col. 0067D] “This he calls utterance.” Something seems to be missing, which may be supplied from what is read in the book *Against the Valentinians*: “He would have come upon his daughter so untimely as even to cry out to her, ‘Iao!’—as though saying, ‘Now then, citizens!’ or ‘By Caesar’s good faith!’ Hence *Iao* is found in the writings.” RIG.—“Apelles pronounces this ‘Io.’” We have restored this exceedingly obscure passage in this way, being led in part by the arguments that Father Hardouin of the Society of Jesus presented in his *Collectanea* (*Mémoires de Trévoux*, April 1724, p. 842 ff.), although he thought that the reading should be not *Apelles* but rather *Apella*. Yet that famous author appears to have suffered a failure of memory, if not of judgment. For he contends that Tertullian intended to allude to Valentinus as a Jew by birth by calling him *Apella* in an appellative sense—that is, “circumcised”—in accordance with Horace’s line [Col. 0068B] (*Satires* I.5.100):

[Col. 0068C] “Let Apella the Jew believe it,

not I.”

But Valentinus was not even a Jew, but an Egyptian, according to the account of St. Irenaeus, Book I, chapter 1 (cf. the *Great Library of the Holy Fathers*, enlarged by Margarin de la Bigne, vol. XXV, fol. 110), and as all historians and lexicographers report. Apelles, however, a disciple of Marcion and himself a heresiarch, was a contemporary of Tertullian, as is evident from this very book, chapter 41; and he could indeed have pronounced IO for IAO, so that, just like Heracleon, who is discussed below in this chapter XLIX, he might appear, through a novel pronunciation, to hold different views.

The learned Jesuit fell into another plainly similar error when he represented Tertullian (p. 845 of the work cited) as speaking of Heracleon as a Jewish man. For our author called Heracleon not “another Jew” but “another heretic.” Moreover, it seems scarcely probable that Heracleon belonged to the Jewish people, since he began to teach in parts of Sicily [Col. 0068D] (consult the *Great Library of the Holy Fathers*, vol. XXVII, fol. 547).

With these qualifications established, I agree with Hardouin that the word IO, just like IA, was a name of God among the Hebrews, though pronounced in a different way. For among them it was always permissible to invoke God’s name not only in the form *ia*, as in *alleluia*, but also as *io*, as in *Johannes* and *Josedec*. Yet everyone knows—although Father Hardouin was mistaken in this too—that the Jews were forbidden to use God’s name in its proper form, and that this name was not simply [Hebrew text absent in the supplied source], as Hardouin maintained—for if that had been so, it would have had to be pronounced *ie* rather than *io*, *iao*, or *ia*—but, in its full letters, [Hebrew text absent in the supplied source], that is, JEHOVAH. Accordingly, it was customary among them to have recourse to the abbreviated form *ia* or *io*, so that reverence for the name might be preserved all the more (cf. Buxtorf, s.v. [entry absent in the supplied source]).

Valentinus preferred to say IAO, perhaps because that form was Egyptian; Apelles, however, said IO, evidently following Hebrew custom; and Heracleon, finally, perhaps used yet another, unknown sound of the word, so that he might appear to hold different views. But Father Hardouin (p. 846) invented the claim that the name (Jehovah) was pronounced as ADONAI. On what foundation he based this assertion is, I think, hidden even from himself, although no learned person is unaware that, out of reverence, God was very frequently called *Adonai* in place of *Jehovah*. Next (p. 847), that most learned man asserted that the genuine origin of the name IAO—he meant JEHOVAH, I believe—was [Hebrew text absent in the supplied source], that is, GOD HIMSELF. But who, provided he has even a slight acquaintance with Hebrew letters, does not know that the word [Hebrew text absent in the supplied source] is the third-person singular future form of the verb [Hebrew text absent in the supplied source] (*havah*), signifying τὸ esse, “to be,” and that the letter [Hebrew letter absent in the supplied source] is nowhere attached to this name? As for the rest of the same writer’s ravings on this passage, especially concerning the word IAOTH (pp. 848–849), we either omit their refutation altogether or defer the reader until such time as we publish—God grant it—the works of St. Irenaeus. (Cf. Tertullian, *Against the Valentinians*, ch. 14; Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book IX; Diodorus Siculus, Book I, p. 84; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book I, toward the end; St. Irenaeus, Book I, chs. 4 and 18; Clement of Alexandria, etc.) EDD.]

Apelles pronounces this “Io.” [Note: [Col. 0068B] “This he calls utterance,” Rigault; all of this, in Semler’s view, should be deleted.] Valentinus says that this Aeon, having fallen into deficiency and being called Achamoth, experienced certain passions of desire and produced matters from those passions. For, he says, it was terrified, became afraid, and was grieved; [Note: [Col. 0068B] “He was grieved,” Semler, with “Aeon” understood.] [Col. 0069A] and from these passions it conceived and brought forth. From this [matter] he made heaven and earth and sea, and everything contained in them. For this reason, everything made by him is weak, fragile, perishable, and mortal, since he had himself been [Note: [Col. 0070C] “Conceived and brought forth from *aporiation*.” *Aporiatio*: hesitation, fear, confusion. Irenaeus: “Then it became terrified and *aporiata*, that is, confused.” LE PR.] conceived and brought forth from *aporiation*—perplexity. Nevertheless, he fashioned this world from the matters that Achamoth had supplied through terror, fear, grief, or sweating. For from terror, he says, darkness was made; from fear and ignorance, the spirits of wickedness and malignity; and from grief and tears, the moist matter of springs, rivers, and the sea.

Christ, however, was sent by that Forefather who is Bythos. Christ was not of the substance of our body, but, bringing down from heaven some sort of spiritual [Col. 0069B] body, passed through the Virgin Mary as water [Note: [Col. 0069C] “Water,” Semler.] passes through a pipe, neither receiving nor borrowing anything from her. He denies the resurrection of this flesh, but affirms that of another. [Note: [Col. 0069C] “But not of another,” Latinus; “of this flesh, but of another law,” Junius; Semler prefers “of another part,” namely, the soul.] He approves some things in the Law and the Prophets and disapproves others—that is, he disapproves them all by rejecting some. He also has a gospel of his own besides these Gospels of ours.

After him appeared [Note: [Col. 0070C] “Ptolemy and Secundus.” These were Valentinus’s successors, as was Heracleon. Of their fables and old wives’ inventions we shall say little, or rather nothing, since their doctrines are examined most fully in St. Epiphanius. LE PR.] the heretics Ptolemy and Secundus, who agree with Valentinus in every respect. They differ on this point alone: whereas Valentinus had invented only thirty Aeons, they added many more. For they first added four, and then another four. And Valentinus says that the thirtieth [Note: [Col. 0069C] “Thirtieth”; alternatively, “thirty,” Semler.] Aeon departed from the Pleroma into a state of deficiency, but these men deny this. For the one who fell into deficiency because of its desire to see the Forefather did not, they say, belong to that triacontad. [Col. 0069C]

There also appeared another heretic, Heracleon, who holds views equivalent to Valentinus’s but wishes to appear to think differently by employing a certain novelty of pronunciation. For he first introduces [Note: [Col. 0070D] “That which he pronounces existed.” Here too something—perhaps a word—appears to be missing. RIG.] “that which he pronounces” as having existed, and then from that Monad two beings, and thereafter the remaining Aeons; and then he introduces the whole system of Valentinus.

## CHAPTER L

[Col. 0070A]

### Marcus Likewise, and Colarbasus

After these men there was no lack of a certain Marcus and Colarbasus, who constructed a new heresy from the Greek alphabet. For they deny that truth can be found without those letters; indeed, they maintain that the entire fullness and perfection of truth is arranged in them. For this reason, they say, Christ declared: “I am Α and Ω.” Finally, [Note: [Col. 0070C] Semler judges that *in* should be added.] Jesus Christ descended—that is, [Note: [Col. 0070D] “The dove came upon Jesus.” I still doubt whether one ought to linger over such trifles; yet, lest we pass over this without comment: among the Greeks, α and ω produce the same number as the WORD περιστερά, “dove”; the number is 801, as stated here. Hence the grammatical trifles of the Marcosians and Colarbasians. LE PR.] the dove came upon Jesus—and since “dove” in Greek is pronounced περιστερὰ (*peristera*), it has [Note: [Col. 0070C] “To have,” Semler.] the numerical value 801. [Note: [Col. 0070D] “These men run through.” These matters are related differently in Epiphanius, *Heresy* 34, from Irenaeus; but labor spent on such absurdities is wasted. RIG.] These men run through ω, ψ, χ, φ, υ, τ, all the way to Alpha Beta [Note: [Col. 0070C] “Alphabet,” Semler.], and calculate ogdoads and decads, so that it would be foolish and idle to set forth [Note: [Col. 0070C] “So as to bring,” Semler.] all their [Col. 0070B] vanities—something that would by now be not merely futile, but even dangerous.

They invent another God besides the Creator. They deny that Christ existed in the substance of flesh. They deny that there will be a resurrection of the flesh.

## CHAPTER LI

### Thereafter Cerdon, Marcion, and Marcion’s Disciples Lucanus and Apelles

To these is added a certain Cerdon. He introduces two first principles, that is, two gods: one good and the other savage—the good god being higher, while the savage god is this world’s creator. He repudiates the prophecies and the Law, renounces God the Creator, and teaches that Christ, the Son of the higher God, came. He denies that Christ existed in the substance of flesh, declares that he existed [Col. 0070C] only as a phantom, and says that he did not suffer at all, but only appeared to suffer; that he was not born of a virgin—indeed, that he was not born at all. He approves only the resurrection of the soul and denies that of the body. He accepts only the Gospel of Luke, and not even the whole of it. Of the Apostle Paul’s Epistles he accepts neither all nor complete versions. He rejects the Acts of the Apostles and the Apocalypse as false.

[Note: [Col. 0070D] After him emerged his disciple Marcion. He had been expelled from the Church by his own father because of fornication. His father was a bishop; and when, despite many supplications, he could not be readmitted to the Church by him, he went to Rome, where he was likewise rejected by the apostolic men. When he perceived this, he began to swear allegiance to Cerdon’s ravings and to embrace his impostures. They also report that when, during the pontificate of Anicetus, he met the blessed Polycarp at Rome and asked whether Polycarp knew him, the blessed Polycarp replied: “I know the firstborn of Satan.” LE PR.]

After him [Col. 0071A] there emerged a disciple of his [Note: [Col. 0071D] “Marcion, the son of a bishop, because of the violation of a certain virgin.” Epiphanius also relates this. Yet Septimius, in the book *On the Prescription of Heretics* and in the books against Marcion himself—where he discusses at length Marcion’s expulsion and his crimes—does not mention the violation of a virgin. It is therefore permissible to suppose that this *Catalogue of Heretics* is not Tertullian’s. For in the book *On the Prescription of Heretics* he even praises Marcionite continence, and at the beginning of the books against Marcion he calls Marcion a castrator of the flesh. Irenaeus likewise notes that Marcion’s disciples appropriated the name of “the continent” and condemned marriage. RIG.] named Marcion, a Pontic by birth and the son of a bishop, who was cast out of the Church’s communion because of the violation of a certain virgin. Seizing upon the saying, “Every good tree produces good fruit, but an evil tree evil fruit,” he attempted to approve Cerdon’s heresy and taught the same things that the earlier heretic had taught before him.

After him there appeared [Note: [Col. 0071D] “A certain Lucanus,” etc. From his own name he had followers called Lucanists. There is also another disciple of Marcion named Lucianus, from whom came the heretical Lucianists. LE PR.] a certain Lucanus, a follower and disciple of Marcion. Proceeding through the same kinds of blasphemy, he too teaches the same things Marcion and Cerdon had taught.

After these comes Apelles, a disciple of Marcion, who, after he had lapsed into the flesh, separated from Marcion. He introduces one God in the infinitely higher regions. This God, he says, created many powers and angels; and accordingly he speaks of another [Col. 0071B] power whom he calls “Lord,” though he makes him an angel. He wishes it to appear that this world was fashioned in imitation of the higher world, and that the angel mingled repentance into this world because he had not made it as perfectly as that higher world had been fashioned.

He repudiates the Law and the Prophets. He says that Christ existed neither as a phantom, as Marcion says, nor in the substance of a real body, as the Gospel teaches; rather, because he descended from the higher regions, in the very act of descending he wove for himself a body made of the stars and the air. At his resurrection, Christ returned to each individual element, during his ascent, what he had borrowed during his descent; and thus, once the several parts of his body had been dispersed, he restored only his spirit to heaven.

Apelles denies the resurrection of the flesh. He uses only the Apostle, and that in Marcion’s version, [Col. 0071C] that is, not the whole. He says that souls alone are saved. He also has his own private and extraordinary readings, which he calls the *Revelations* (*Phaneroseis*) of a certain girl named Philumene, whom he follows as a prophetess. He has, in addition, books of his own entitled *Syllogisms*, in which he seeks to prove that everything Moses wrote concerning God is not true, but false.

## CHAPTER LII

### Then Tatian, and Those Called “According to the Phrygians”: [Col. 0072A] the Party of Proclus and the Party of Aeschines—the Montanists

To all these heretics [Note: [Col. 0072C] “There is added a certain Tatian.” He was a disciple of Justin Martyr, and as long as his teacher lived, he appeared to hold entirely sound views concerning religion and faith; [Col. 0072D] but after Justin’s death, he followed the Aeons and the impious doctrines of Valentinus. LE PR.] there is added another heretic, a certain Tatian. He was a disciple of Justin Martyr; after Justin, he began to hold different views. For his whole system follows Valentinus, with the addition that Adam cannot attain salvation—as though, if the branches are saved, the root were not also saved.

There arose other heretics who are called [Note: [Col. 0072D] “According to the Phrygians.” In a single word, these heretics are called Cataphrygians, because they spread especially through (Lower, Edd.) Phrygia. The originators of that heresy came from that province: Apelles, Montanus, and his prophetesses Prisca, or Priscilla, and Maximilla. They flourished during the reign of Commodus and the pontificate of Soter. LE PR.] “according to the Phrygians”; but their doctrine is not uniform. For some are called κατὰ Proclum, “the party of Proclus,” while others are designated as the party of Aeschines. They have one blasphemy in common and another that is not common but peculiar to themselves.

Their common blasphemy is this: they say that the Holy Spirit was indeed present in the Apostles, but the Paraclete was not; and they say that the Paraclete spoke more through Montanus [Col. 0072B] than Christ uttered in the Gospel—and not only more, but things that were better and greater.

## CHAPTER LIII

### Finally Blastus, Both Men Named Theodotus, Praxeas, and Victorinus

Those who belong to the party of Aeschines have this particular blasphemy: they add the claim that Christ himself is both Son and Father.

In addition to all these there is also Blastus, who wishes covertly to introduce Judaism. For he says that the Passover must be observed in no other way than according to the Law of Moses, on the fourteenth day of the month. But who does not know that the grace of the Gospel is nullified if one brings Christ back under the Law?

[Note: [Col. 0072D] “To these is added Theodotus, a Byzantine heretic.” He was a Byzantine leather-worker. He differs from the other Theodotus of whom Tertullian presently speaks, who was the originator of the Melchizedekians. These heretics said that Christ was inferior to Melchizedek himself, because Melchizedek is said to have been without father and mother, whereas all the Evangelists and the whole of Scripture and tradition attest that Christ had a mother. LE PR.]

To these is added Theodotus, a Byzantine heretic, [Col. 0072C] who, after being arrested for the name of Christ, denied him and did not cease to blaspheme Christ. For he introduced a doctrine in which he said that Christ was merely a man and denied that he was God. He said that Christ was indeed born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin, but was a solitary and naked man, having no authority above others except that of righteousness alone.

After him another heretic named Theodotus burst forth. He too introduced a distinct sect and says that Christ himself was merely a man, alike conceived and born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary; but he says that Christ is inferior [Col. 0073A] to Melchizedek, because it was said concerning Christ: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4). For, he says, Melchizedek is a heavenly power of exceptional grace: Christ acts on behalf of human beings, having become their intercessor and advocate, while Melchizedek acts on behalf of the heavenly angels and powers. For Melchizedek is so much better than Christ that he is *apator*, “without father”; *ametor*, “without mother”; and *agenealogetos*, “without genealogy”; [Col. 0074A] and neither his beginning nor his end has been, or can be, comprehended.

But after all these, a certain Praxeas also introduced a heresy that Victorinus took pains to reinforce. He says that God the almighty Father is Jesus Christ; he contends that the Father was crucified, suffered, and died. Furthermore, with profane and sacrilegious rashness, he asserts that the Father sits at his own right hand.

III, p. 659, of his well-known work (*Memoirs Serving the History of the Church*); Father Tournemine, in the *Journal of Trévoux*, 1703, July–August, p. 311. EDD.]

# QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN: ON THE CROWN

[Note: [Col. 0073B] “On the Crown.” This is the title given to this book in the manuscript of Agobard, [Col. 0074B] not, as commonly, *On the Crown of the Soldier*.

We follow the old hand all the more willingly because, although Septimius took the occasion for writing from the deed of a certain soldier, he nevertheless seeks to deter not soldiers alone, but every Christian without exception, from wearing a crown. [Col. 0075C] RIG.]

(C)

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0073B]

Among the books Tertullian composed during his Montanist period, the first place belongs to the book *On the Crown*, published in the year of Christ 201, as Lumper clearly demonstrated in his introductory dissertation, following the highly learned Noesselt. The occasion for writing this treatise was supplied to its author by the soldier’s deed elegantly related below in the opening. Some Christians censured that deed and reproached the soldier for rashly exposing the Church, which was enjoying a long peace, to danger. They further asserted that wearing this [Col. 0074B] crown was an ornament neither good nor evil by its nature. Tertullian alone, in keeping with his harsh temperament, championed the soldier’s cause by writing the book *On the Crown*. He bitterly assailed the pastors as lions in peace and deer in battle, because to be crowned in this way was a sign of idolatry; and when asked in what passage of Scripture the wearing of such crowns was forbidden, he said that tradition was sufficient.

Accordingly, in this book he exalts tradition and custom to no small degree and offers many noteworthy examples of ceremonies that, he contends, were received from tradition. How rich the book is in memorable matters and ancient customs will be apparent from the synopsis of the whole work itself.

After resolutely establishing that wearing a crown was contrary to Christian custom and tradition, he describes in passing the ceremonies of baptism, the sacraments of the Most Holy Eucharist, offerings for the dead and for the anniversaries of the martyrs, the Lord’s Day, fasting, and the sign of the cross upon the forehead.

Then, returning to his purpose, he attacks the use of crowns altogether. He maintains that it is forbidden even by nature, that it positively reeks of superstitious origins, or at least that it was unfamiliar to the patriarchs, the prophets, the Levites, and also to the temple of God, the ark of the covenant, the tabernacles, and the shrines of the martyrs. Finally, he maintains [Col. 0075B] that no crown should be used, whether a military crown, a triumphal crown, a camp crown, a laurel or golden crown granted to magistrates, a crown of festivity, marriage, or freedmen, or the crown of an athletic contest—since Christ submitted to a garland of thorns, while a crown has been laid up in heaven for Christians. EDD.

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0076A]

Very recently there was a distribution of largesse by our most excellent emperors. [Note: [Col. 0075B] Thus Rhenanus and Gelenius, on the authority of the Gorgias manuscript. Junius, from a manuscript: “when the largesse had been distributed,” etc. Rigault produced the strange reading: “Very recently there took place . . . largesse—the soldiers were being paid off in camp—they approached crowned with laurel.”] [Note: [Col. 0075C] “Our most excellent emperors”: namely, the father Lucius Septimius Severus and his son Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Caracalla, under whom St. Jerome, in *Illustrious Men of the Church*, attests that Tertullian flourished. RHEN.] The soldiers were being paid [Note: [Col. 0075C] “Were being paid.” Understand: with the donative. For largesse has been mentioned; that is, the promised donative was being ceremonially paid or furnished to the soldiers. RIG.] in camp while crowned with laurel.

There one man was brought forward as more truly a soldier of God than the others, more steadfast than his brethren who had presumed that they could serve two masters. [Note: [Col. 0075C] “Could serve two masters”: God and Caesar. RIG.] He alone had his head uncovered, with the crown held uselessly [Note: [Col. 0075C] “With the crown held uselessly in his hand.” He calls “useless” what is unprofitable and inappropriate. Thus, in *To His Wife*: “For us it is useless to beget children”; that is, it is unprofitable and inappropriate for Christians to beget children while a tyrant rages against the Christian name. RIG.] in his hand. By this time the discipline proper to Christians was clearly shining forth even in this act. [Note: [Col. 0076B] “There one man was more truly a soldier of God.”]

Then individuals began pointing him out and mocking him from a distance, and gnashing their teeth at him close by. The murmuring was reported to the tribune. [Note: [Col. 0075C] “The murmuring was reported to the tribune.” So reads the Agobard exemplar. In the Dijon manuscript and the common editions, [Col. 0075D] the reading is: “Immediately the murmuring was reported to the tribune.” Some prefer to punctuate it: “Immediately the murmuring will be reported to the tribune.” But the same thing would then appear to be said twice, for “gnashing their teeth close by” is murmuring. RIG.] And now the man himself had come forward from the ranks.

At once the tribune asked, “Why are you so different in your attire?”

He said that he was not permitted to act as the others did. When pressed to give his reasons, he answered, “I am a Christian.”

O soldier glorious in God! Thereupon a vote was taken and the case adjourned, [Note: [Col. 0075D] “And the case adjourned, and the accused was sent to the prefects.” The old exemplar has precisely this: “And the case ad . . . . . ed, and the accused to the pref.” From this one may suppose that Tertullian wrote: “And the case was adjourned and the accused sent to the prefects.” A case is said to be “adjourned” when its examination is deferred or remitted to another time or another tribunal. Thus, in trials, defendants are condemned, acquitted, adjourned, or “scorched.” Examples of persons condemned or acquitted occur everywhere. Examples of adjourned defendants are found in Livy, Book XIII, concerning Marcus Titinnius: “Twice adjourned, on the third occasion the defendant was acquitted.” And shortly thereafter, concerning Publius Furius, Phillo, and Marcus Martienus: “Both were accused of the gravest crimes and their cases adjourned.” Examples of those “scorched,” that is, brought into danger of capital punishment but neither condemned nor acquitted, are also found, [Col. 0076B] as in the case of Lucius Aemilius Paulus in the same Livy, Book XXII: “He compelled Aemilius Paulus, who had been consul with Marcus Livius, and who had narrowly escaped being scorched by both his colleague’s condemnation and his own, though hostile to the people, hateful to the gods, and offering strong resistance, to stand for office.” Valerius Maximus likewise mentions two “scorched” persons amid inexplicable hesitation, as the examinations were now transferred, now deferred. RIG.] [Col. 0076B] and the accused was sent to the prefects.

There and then he put down his exceedingly burdensome cloak, [Note: [Col. 0076C] “He put down his exceedingly burdensome cloak, inaugurating his relief.” We noted in the *Apologeticum*, p. 7, that military cloaks were resented because of their weight. Taking his occasion from this, Septimius says that this soldier, glorious in God, after laying aside the exceedingly burdensome load of pagan military service, had from that moment begun to be relieved, as soon as he submitted to Christ’s burden, which Christ himself taught was light. RIG.] inaugurating his relief. He removed from his feet the exceedingly troublesome speculator’s boot, [Note: [Col. 0076C] “He removed from his feet the exceedingly troublesome speculator’s boot.” This concerns the military boot, especially that of the soldier who had served among the *speculatores*, a very restless, troublesome, and harsh branch of service, since he wandered here and there, running about, scouting, and carrying reports. Therefore, after the booted *speculator* became a Christian, he removed from his feet that troublesome and burdensome speculator’s boot, and at the same time began to stand upon holy ground—that is, immediately and courageously to face death for Christ’s name and to lead a holy and innocent life, far different from the service of a *speculator*, who also commonly performed the executioner’s work at the tribune’s nod. RIG.] beginning to stand upon holy ground. He returned the sword, which was not necessary even for the defense of the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0076D] “The sword, which was not necessary even for the defense of the Lord.” He alludes to Christ’s words to Peter: “Put your sword into its sheath.” Augustine likewise says of this in the *Letter to Vincentius*: “Peter’s sword is called back into its sheath by Christ and shown that it ought not to have been drawn from the sheath, not even for Christ.” For, as Tertullian says in the book *On Patience*, p. 160: “The Lord’s patience was wounded in Malchus.” And so the Lord cursed the works of the sword for the future. By disarming Peter, he unbelted every Christian. RIG.] (Matt. 26:52).

The laurel also fell from his hand. [Note: [Col. 0076D] “And the laurel became conspicuous in his hand.” For he carried the crown in his hand; accordingly, the laurel became conspicuous in his hand—that is, it was plainly seen there and not on his head, which was uncovered. RHEN.] [Note: [Col. 0076B] “Uselessly in his hand; by now this discipline also shone forth in the Christian. Then individuals began pointing him out and playing mockingly.”] [Col. 0077A] [Note: [Col. 0077C] “Fell,” Wouwer; “became conspicuous,” Junius.]

And now, reddened by the hope of his own blood, [Note: [Col. 0077C] “Reddened by the hope of his own blood.” This is the reading of the most ancient exemplars. Military tunics were red, φοινικοὶ χιτῶνες, “scarlet tunics.” This soldier, having become a Christian, is said to have been reddened, in place of wearing a red tunic, by the hope of his own blood—that is, by the hoped-for purple of martyrdom. Trebellius speaks of “the red-clad military”; and Juvenal uses “red-clad”: “a lizard.” RIG.] shod with the readiness of the Gospel, [Note: [Col. 0077D] “From the equipment of the Gospel.” *Natura* is used substantivally, as above in many passages; that is, the sort of sword the Gospel customarily prepares—namely, a spiritual one. RHEN.] girded with the sharper word of God, wholly armed from the Apostle (Eph. 6:11), and destined to be crowned more fittingly with the white robe of martyrdom, he awaits Christ’s donative in prison.
