Thereafter judgments were passed upon him—I do not know whether they were the judgments of Christians, since they were no different from those of pagans—as upon a reckless and headlong man, eager to die, who, when questioned about his dress, had created trouble for the Name: he alone, of course, was brave; he alone among so many brother-soldiers was a Christian. Clearly all that remains is for those who rejected the prophecies of the same Holy Spirit to plan also to refuse martyrdoms.

Finally, they mutter [Note: [Col. 0077D] “Finally they mutter . . . nor do I doubt that some mutter the Scriptures.” The deed of this most courageous soldier was censured even by his Christian fellow soldiers as an example of imprudent, headlong, and untimely courage. Talk circulated about him as a reckless, impetuous man, eager to die, who, when questioned about his dress, had brought hostility and danger upon the Christian name and by his rashness had nearly overthrown the good and lengthy peace that Christians were then enjoying. Septimius severely rebukes these remarks. “They mutter,” he says, “that the good and lengthy peace they have enjoyed is being endangered. Nor do I doubt that some are also muttering that the Holy Scriptures are already emigrating, unpacking their baggage, and preparing to flee from city to city.” The common reading is: “Nor do I doubt that certain Scriptures are emigrating, gathering their baggage.” But the most ancient manuscript reads: “Nor do I doubt that some the Scriptures are emigrating, gathering their baggage.” Consequently the reading must without doubt be: “Nor do I doubt that some are muttering the Scriptures are emigrating, gathering their baggage.” The verb must be repeated from what precedes: “Nor do I doubt that some are muttering the Scriptures.” RIG.] that the good and lengthy peace they have enjoyed is being endangered. Nor do I doubt that some are muttering that the Scriptures are emigrating, packing their baggage, and preparing [Col. 0077B] to flee from city to city; for they care to remember no other passage of the Gospel.

I know their pastors too: [Note: [Col. 0078D] “I know their pastors too,” etc. He marks the bishops of the orthodox people who had subscribed to the condemnation of the false prophet Montanus as effeminate men and as the first to flee in time of persecution, though they ought to have encouraged the people to martyrdom. Montanus’s false prophecy appears to have commanded and demanded martyrdom. RHEN.] lions in peace, deer in battle. But we shall deal elsewhere with questions concerning confession.

For the present, however, since they also raise this objection—“But where are we forbidden to be crowned?”—I shall address this more immediate substance of the present case, so that those who inquire from the anxious concern of ignorance may be instructed, and those who contend in defense [Note: [Col. 0077C] “In the defense,” Semler.] of wrongdoing may be refuted—especially those Christians who have themselves worn the laurel, for whom this alone is the question, as though an offense that admits of questioning could be regarded as either nonexistent or at least uncertain. Yet that it is neither nonexistent nor uncertain I shall meanwhile demonstrate from this.

## CHAPTER II
[Col. 0077C] I say that none of the faithful knows a crown upon his head [Note: [Col. 0077C] “For the head,” MS. Wouw.] except at a time of trial of this sort. All observe the rule in this way, from catechumens to confessors and martyrs—or even deniers. You may consider whence comes the authority of this custom, which is now the chief question. Yet when it is asked why something is observed, it is meanwhile established that it is observed. Therefore an offense committed against an observance that must now be vindicated by its own title, and sufficiently authorized by the support of consensus, can appear neither nonexistent nor uncertain. [Col. 0078A] Its rationale must indeed be sought, but with the observance preserved—not for its destruction, but rather for its edification (2 Cor. 13:10), so that you may observe it all the more once you are also assured of its rationale.

But what sort of conduct is it for someone to call an observance into question precisely when he has fallen away from it, and then to ask whence the observance derived when he has ceased to keep it? Even if he wishes to appear to call it into question in order to show that he did not offend by abandoning the observance, he nevertheless offended by previously presuming the observance. For if he did not offend by accepting the crown today, he once offended by refusing it.

This discussion, therefore, will not be addressed to those to whom the question does not properly belong, but to those who, from a desire to learn, put forward not a challenge but a request for counsel. For [Col. 0078B] the matter is always being investigated, and I commend the faith that believed [Note: [Col. 0078C] “Believes,” Fran. Paris.] a thing ought to be observed before it learned why (Isa. 7:9). It is easy to demand at once: “Where is it written that we must not be crowned?” But where is it written [Note: [Col. 0078D] “But where is it written?” Here Tertullian argues wonderfully for traditions against the Calvinists and the Magdeburg Centuriators, who asserted far too boldly that this was a dogma of Montanus—an assertion that is false and pure slander. For Montanus, according to Eusebius, *History*, book V, is said to have been the first to propose certain things contrary to tradition. LE PR.] that we may be crowned? For those who demand the support of Scripture on the opposing side thereby prejudge that the support of Scripture ought also to be present for their own side [Note: [Col. 0078C] “Side’s,” Seml.]. For if it is said that one may be crowned because Scripture does not forbid it, the retort will equally be made that one may not be crowned because Scripture does not command it. What will discipline do? Will it accept both, on the ground that neither is forbidden? Or reject both, on the ground that neither is commanded? “But what is not forbidden is freely permitted.” Rather, what is not freely permitted is forbidden.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0078C]

And how long shall we work the saw back and forth along this line, when we possess an ancient observance that has settled the matter by anticipating it? If no Scripture has determined it, custom has certainly confirmed it, and custom undoubtedly flowed from tradition. For how can anything become customary unless it was first handed down? “Even under the plea of tradition,” you say, “written authority must be demanded.” Let us ask, then, whether a tradition, unless [Note: [Col. 0078C] “Not,” Fran. Paris.] written, ought not [Col. 0079A] to be received. We shall certainly deny that it ought to be received if no precedents stand in our way from other observances which, without any instrument of Scripture [Note: [Col. 0079B] “Without any instrument of Scripture, under the title of tradition alone.” Jerome drained this entire discourse for his work *Against the Luciferians*: “Even if,” he says, “the authority of Scripture did not underlie it, the consensus of the whole world on this point would have the force of a command. For many other things observed in the churches through tradition have claimed for themselves the authority of Scripture and law, such as immersing the head three times in the bath, then, after emerging, first tasting the concord of milk and honey,” etc. RIG.], we vindicate under the title of tradition alone and thereafter by the support of custom.

Finally, to begin with baptism [Note: [Col. 0079B] “Finally, to begin with baptism.” In Agobard’s codex only this is read: “Finally, that I may enter the water three times in baptism, there likewise one approaches.” RIG.]: when we are about to enter the water, there itself—and also somewhat earlier, in the church, beneath the hand of the presiding minister—we solemnly testify [Note: [Col. 0079C] “Somewhat earlier, in the church, beneath the hand of the presiding minister, we solemnly testify.” The author of the *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, question 102: “Those who wish to become Christians approach the presiding minister and declare their vows to him. He pronounces the words of ecclesiastical law. If the vows are genuine, they are accepted by the judge.” RIG.] that we renounce the devil, his pomp, and his angels. Then we are immersed three times [Note: [Col. 0079C] “We are immersed three times.” Tertullian himself, *Against Praxeas*, p. 659: “For we are immersed not once but three times, at each name, for each individual person.” Chrysostom indicates that this rite was still in use in his own age, commenting on the words of Luke, Acts 10:16, where the vision presented to Peter is related, τοῦτο δὲ ἐγένετο τρίς, “and this happened three times.” Chrysostom: τὸ δὲ τρίτον τοῦτο γενέσθαι, τὸ βάπτισμα δηλοῖ, “Its happening a third time signifies baptism.” Ammonius on John, chapter 21, where Christ asks Peter three times, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?” says: ἔθος δὲ γέγονεν ἐκ τούτου … τρεῖς ὁμολογίας ἀπαιτεῖσθαι τοὺς μέλλοντας βαπτισθῆναι, “From this arose the custom that three confessions are required of those about to be baptized.” Hence that formula which Pope Stephen II calls rustic, response 14: [Col. 0079D] “In the name of the Father I immerse; and of the Son I immerse; and of the Holy Spirit I immerse.” Vol. II of the *Councils of Gaul*. Thus some trace the origin of one and the same rite to the persons of the most holy Trinity, others to the threefold vision, and others to the threefold interrogation. So uncertain are human minds after they have departed from the simplicity of the beginning. RIG.], answering somewhat more than the Lord laid down in the Gospel. After being received from there, we first taste the concord of milk and honey; and from that day we abstain from the daily bath for an entire week.

The sacrament of the Eucharist [Note: [Col. 0079D] “The sacrament of the Eucharist,” etc. These words indicate that, in Tertullian’s age, the time for receiving the Eucharist was so far removed from mealtime—the time at which it had been instituted by the Lord—that it was received even in the hours before dawn. I shall not contend, however, against those who say it was also received at hours other than those before dawn, provided it was before all food. For this appears to be signified in book II of *To His Wife*: “Will the husband not know what you secretly taste before all food?”—unless it appears rather that even before Tertullian’s age this practice was not fixed, and was performed differently according to each person’s devotion. Certainly the mention of the Lord’s Supper celebrated among the apostles is scanty and obscure, although no sober person would deny that it was indeed celebrated, and very frequently—but, as Tertullian says, at mealtime—and thus that it is included in that breaking of bread which occurs so often. We are led to this view by Paul’s very severe rebuke in 1 Corinthians 11. RIG.], although commanded by the Lord both at mealtime and for all [Note: [Col. 0080B] “Commanded by the Lord for all,” etc.; “nor do we receive it from the hand of anyone but the presiding ministers.” There is a similar passage on the honor of the presiding ministers in *On Baptism*, p. 263: “Accordingly, baptism, being equally God’s property, can be administered by all,” etc. It will be worthwhile to compare the passages, for they shed remarkable light upon one another. RIG.], we receive even in gatherings before dawn, and from the hand of none but the presiding ministers. We make offerings for the dead [Note: [Col. 0080C] “Offerings for the dead.” It is also an invention of the Magdeburg Centuriators that Tertullian derived this doctrine from Montanus. As a foundation for this rite I could adduce against the heretics the evidence commonly cited: namely, the many funeral orations of the holy Fathers for friends, relatives, and even the greatest men in the Church of God. Yet I shall not omit the passage from Cyprian’s Epistle 66, where, in his own name and that of the Council of Carthage, he recalls to the bishops’ memory the decree that, if any brother had appointed a cleric as guardian, no offering should be made for him and no sacrifice celebrated for his falling asleep. It is therefore nothing new that offerings and sacrifices should be made for the dead in the Church of God. LE PR.] and celebrate the anniversaries of their birth-days [Note: [Col. 0080C] “For their birth-days on the annual day,” etc. By “birth-days” he means the solemnities customarily held in honor of the martyrs on the day when, having died to the world, they were born into heaven. Hence “on the annual day” means that we do it every year. LE PR.]. On the Lord’s Day we consider it unlawful to fast or to worship on our knees [Note: [Col. 0079B] Seml. omits “from.”]. We enjoy the same exemption [Col. 0080A] from Easter Day until Pentecost. We are distressed if any part of our cup or even of our bread [Note: [Col. 0080D] “Or even of our bread”: even bread that is not Eucharistic, even ordinary bread. RIG.] is shaken onto the ground [Note: [Col. 0080D] “Any part is shaken onto the ground,” etc. Augustine: “With what great care we attend when the body of Christ is administered to us, lest any part of it fall from our hands to the ground,” etc.; cited in Gratian, I, question 1, *Interrogo*. RIG.]. At every step forward and movement, at every entrance and departure, when putting on our shoes, at the baths, at tables, at the lighting of lamps, on going to bed, on sitting down—whatever activity occupies us—we rub our forehead with the sign of the cross [Note: [Col. 0079B] Seml. rejects “of the cross.”].

## CHAPTER IV

If you demand a law from Scripture for these and other disciplines of this sort, you will find none. Tradition will be presented to you as their originator, custom as their confirmer, and faith [Note: [Col. 0079B] “Of faith,” Rhen.] as their observer. Either you yourself will perceive, or you will learn from someone who has perceived, the rationale that supports tradition [Note: [Col. 0080D] “The rationale that supports tradition.” For without rationale, tradition would be empty. Thus Jerome too, in the passage cited above: “And many other things that are not written have been claimed by reasonable observance.” Nor does the Apostle demand any obedience except reasonable obedience. RIG.], custom [Note: [Col. 0080B] “Tradition [supports] custom,” Fran. Paris.], and faith. Meanwhile, you will believe that some rationale exists to which obedience is owed [Note: [Col. 0080B] “Rendered,” Jun.].

I add [Col. 0080B] one further example, since it will also be appropriate to teach from ancient practices. [Note: [Col. 0080D] “Among the Jews it is so customary.” There survives an entire book, *On the Veiling of All Women of Whatever Race, Rank, Condition, Age, or Dignity*, based upon the Apostle. I suspect that its author is later than this work, because here he adds: “I ask for the law; I defer the Apostle.” For in that work [Col. 0081C] he proves this chiefly by the authority of the Apostle (1 Cor. 11). PAM.] Among the Jews it is so customary for their women to veil their heads that they are recognized by it. I ask for [Col. 0081A] the law; I defer the Apostle (1 Cor. 11:5). If Rebecca, on seeing her bridegroom from afar, seized a veil (Gen. 24:65), private modesty could not make a law—or else it made one only for its own case. Let virgins alone be covered, and only when they are coming to be married, and not before they have recognized their bridegrooms.

If Susanna too, unveiled at her trial, supplies an argument for veiling (Dan. 13:18) [Note: [Col. 0081C] “Veiled,” Seml.], I can say: “Here also the veil was a matter of personal choice. She had come as an accused woman and was ashamed of her disgrace, justly concealing her beauty—or else now fearing to give pleasure.” At any rate, in her husband’s garden walk [Note: [Col. 0081D] “In her husband’s *stadium*.” By *stadium* he means a *hypaethrum*, that is, an open-air or uncovered promenade, which we also call a *xystus* and which was customarily planted with trees for shade. RIG.—“In the *stadium*,” etc. One might read *stibadium*, for this is the name given to turf seats in gardens, including seats made of flowers. But I change nothing, for all pleasant places planted with trees may be called *stadia*. LAC.] [Note: [Col. 0081C] Others read “in the orchard.”], I do not suppose that she who gave pleasure walked about veiled. Grant now that she was always veiled: in her case too I ask for the law governing her attire [Note: [Col. 0081C] “Attire,” Seml.], or in any other case. If I find the law nowhere, it follows that tradition gave this custom to usage, [Col. 0081B] a custom destined in time to obtain apostolic authority through the interpretation supplied by reason.

These examples, therefore, will have declared that even an unwritten tradition can be defended in observance when confirmed by custom, the proper witness that the tradition was once approved, as shown by the persistence of the observance. [Note: [Col. 0081D] “Custom, moreover, even,” etc. Heraldus has already noted (*Digressions*, book II, chapter 3) that this is identical with the statement of Ulpian: “Long-standing custom is commonly observed as right and law in matters that do not descend from writing”; and he adduces the rationale from Julian: “For what difference does it make whether the people declare their will by vote or by the actual circumstances and deeds?” I add Gregory of Nyssa (*On Virginity*, chapter 9), whose words are not remote from Ulpian’s. LAC.] Moreover, in civil matters too, custom is received as law when law is lacking; nor does it matter whether it rests upon writing or upon reason, since reason also commends law. Furthermore, if law rests upon reason, then whatever reason has established will now be law, by whomsoever it was produced. Do you not think it lawful for every believer to conceive and establish something, provided that it accords with God, conduces to discipline, and advances salvation, since the Lord says: “And why do you not judge even of yourselves what is right?” (Luke 12:57)—and this not merely concerning a judgment, but concerning every decision on matters requiring examination?

The Apostle too says: “If you are ignorant of anything, God will reveal it to you” (Phil. 3:15). He himself was accustomed both to supply counsel when he had no commandment of the Lord and to issue certain rulings on his own authority, [Note: [Col. 0081D] “But himself also possessing the Spirit of God.” From this too it may be inferred that this book was written before *On the Veiling of Virgins*. For there he acknowledges that saying (John 16), “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will lead you into all truth,” as fulfilled in Montanus alone. Here, however, he acknowledges [Col. 0082D] the same Spirit of God in the Apostle Paul. Thus the wretched man gradually slipped from one error into another and at last into heresy. PAM.] while himself also possessing [Note: [Col. 0081C] “Himself,” Rhen.] the Spirit of God, the guide into all truth. Accordingly, his counsel and ruling [Note: [Col. 0081C] “Statement,” Seml.] obtained [Col. 0082A] the force of a divine commandment because of the support of divine reason. Demand this rationale now, while preserving respect for tradition, by whatever transmitter it is reckoned to have come. Do not look to the author but to the authority, and especially to that of custom itself. Custom must be honored for the very reason that it may be the interpreter of reason, so that, if God has also given you this rationale, you may then learn whether custom ought not to be observed by you.

## CHAPTER V

But [Note: [Col. 0081C] “Custom, but,” Venet.] why is a greater rationale produced [Note: [Col. 0082C] “Required,” Fran.] for Christian observances, when [Note: [Col. 0082D] “When nature too defends them,” etc. And indeed nature precedes all laws; hence those who sin, sin against nature. Thus Tarquin sinned against the eternal law of nature in his assault upon Lucretia, although no Julian law yet existed, nor any statute concerning rape, according to Cicero, *On the Laws*, book II. LE PR.] nature too defends them [Note: [Col. 0082C] “Although it may defend,” Wouw.], nature being the first of all disciplines? This, therefore, is the first rule to prescribe that a crown is unsuitable for the head.

I think, moreover, that the Lord of nature is our God, who fashioned the human being and arranged within him definite senses for desiring, judging, and attaining the fruits of things, employing the respective members as a kind of organ. He hollowed out hearing in the ears, kindled sight in the eyes, enclosed taste in the mouth, wafted smell through the nostrils, and placed touch as the outermost sense in the hands [Note: [Col. 0082C] “Appraised,” Seml.; “determined,” Rig.] [Note: [Col. 0082D] “Placed touch as the outermost sense in the hands.” That is, he placed touch, the last or outermost sense, in the hands—and indeed at their extremities, for the tips of the fingers perceive and feel differences of touch most acutely. Here he uses *extimum* for *extremum*, as in book II of *On the Dress of Women*, p. 179, where he uses *extimatio* for “extremity.” RIG.]. Through these services of the outer human being [Note: [Col. 0082D] “Through these things that serve the outer human being, the fruits of divine gifts are conveyed by the soul to the senses.” Tertullian’s meaning is this: through these organs—namely, the ears, mouth, eyes, nostrils, and finally the hands—all of which serve and minister to the outer human being, that is, the body, assent or approval of natural things, which were created by God for humanity’s sake, is conveyed from the soul. For it is the soul that hears, the soul that sees, the soul that feels. Accordingly, the ears, eyes, and hands are rightly said to assent on behalf of the sensing soul, since through them the soul hears, sees, and touches. RIG.], which minister to the inner human being, the fruits of divine gifts are conveyed to the soul by the senses [Note: [Col. 0082C] Venet. reads: “Through these things that serve the human being, the fruits of divine gifts are conveyed by the soul to the senses.”].

What fruit, then, comes from flowers? For the proper and certainly the chief substance of crowns is the flowers of the field. “Either scent,” you say, “or color, or both together.” What senses will perceive color and scent? Sight, I suppose, and smell. Which members have been allotted those senses? The eyes, unless I am mistaken, and the nostrils. Use flowers, therefore, by sight and [Col. 0082C] smell, whose fruit they are; use them through the eyes and nostrils, which are the organs of those senses. Their substance has been handed over to you by God; their manner of arrangement comes from the world—although even an extraordinary arrangement does not obstruct their ordinary use. Let flowers be these things for you whether inserted, interwoven, strung on thread, or woven around a rush, provided they are free and loose: objects, namely, of sight and scent.

If by chance you regard a crown as a bundle of flowers gathered into a sequence so that you may carry several at once and use them all together, then by all means put it into your bosom too, if it possesses such purity; scatter it over your couch, if it possesses such softness; and entrust it to your cup, if it possesses such innocence. Enjoy it in as many ways as you perceive it. But what taste of a flower is there upon the head [Note: [Col. 0083C] “What taste of a flower is there upon the head?” For this reason Diogenes, when anointing his feet with perfume, used to say that fragrance vanishes from the head into the air, but from the feet reaches the nostrils. RIG.]? What perception is there of a crown, except only that of a fetter—a place where neither its color is seen, nor its scent inhaled, nor its tenderness appreciated? It is as contrary to nature to seek a flower with the head as a sound with the nostril. Everything contrary to nature deserves among everyone [Note: [Col. 0083D] “Deserves among everyone the mark of a monstrosity.” These words, “among everyone,” are not found in the exemplar and indeed may elegantly be omitted. RIG.] the mark of a monstrosity, but among us also a formal charge of sacrilege against God [Note: [Col. 0083D] “A formal charge of sacrilege.” This alludes to the formal charges and inscriptions of defendants discussed in chapter 1 of *On Idolatry*. Tertullian thus marks out the crime of sacrilege, for this word is often used in a bad sense. Second Council of Seville, chapter 5: “Also with reference to you, not the title of consecration but a formal declaration of disgrace.” LAC.], the Lord and author of nature.

## CHAPTER VI

Do you ask [Note: [Col. 0083C] “Will you ask,” Fran. Paris.] for God’s law, then? You have that law shared by all, publicly displayed in the world, upon nature’s tablets. The Apostle too is accustomed to appeal to these, as when, concerning a woman’s veil, he says: “Does not even nature teach you?” (1 Cor. 11:14). Likewise, when he says to the Romans (2:14) that the nations do by nature the things contained in the law, he indicates both that law is natural and that nature has the force of law.

Moreover, in the earlier epistle [Note: [Col. 0083D] “But also in his own epistle.” Ursinus’s manuscript reads “in the first.” Thus in *The Prescription Against Heretics*, p. 343: “He established in the beginning the seed of wheat sown by the Lord.” RIG.], by affirming that males and females changed their natural use of the created order into an unnatural use with one another, receiving the recompense of their error as reciprocal punishment, he certainly supports natural use [Note: [Col. 0083C] “Supports natural things,” old codex, Rig.] [Note: [Col. 0083D] “Certainly supports natural use.” The old exemplar reads “supports natural things,” which I consider correct. RIG.].

We first came to know God himself according to nature, calling him “the God of gods,” presuming him to be good, and invoking him as judge. Do you ask whether nature ought to go before us in our enjoyment of his creation [Note: [Col. 0084C] “Whether nature ought to go before us in our enjoyment of his creation.” That is, whether we ought to enjoy the things God created in such a way that we follow nature as our guide. By *conditionem* he means what others call “creation.” Thus in book I of *On the Dress of Women*, p. 173: “Incense is God’s creation,” that is, incense was created and made by God. RIG.], lest we be swept away by that means through which God’s rival corrupted the entire creation assigned to humankind for particular uses, together with the human being himself? Hence the Apostle says that creation unwillingly [Col. 0084A] succumbed to vanity (Rom. 8:20) [Note: [Col. 0084C] “Succumbed to vanity.” Rhenanus says that Tertullian uses this, as he often does in other books, in the sense of “yielded” or “was subjected,” as our translator rendered it in Romans 8. A little later, however, on the authority of the Vatican MS. and the codices of Paterniacum and Hirsaugia, we again read “those who indeed perceive that all things belong to God by nature.” For Rhenanus had removed “God.” [Col. 0084D] PAM.], being perverted first to vain uses and then to shameful, unjust, and impious ones.

Thus, too, in the case of the pleasures of public shows, creation has been brought into disrepute by those who indeed perceive by nature that all things from which shows are constructed belong to God, yet lack the knowledge to understand [Note: [Col. 0084D] “Yet lack the knowledge also to understand.” *Deficiunt intelligere* means “they do not understand.” They lack the knowledge by which they might understand. RIG.] that all things have also been altered by the devil. We have, however, treated this subject [Note: [Col. 0084D] “This subject too.” He undoubtedly alludes to his work *On the Shows*, written by him not only in Latin but also in Greek. PAM.] on behalf of our pleasure-loving brethren [Note: [Col. 0084D] “Our pleasure-loving brethren.” This is his name for those Christians who were still held by the attractions of the public shows. He means, however, his two books *On the Shows*. RHEN.] in Greek as well.

## CHAPTER VII

Accordingly, let these crown-wearers now acknowledge [Note: [Col. 0084D] “Let them acknowledge now.” This little word *interim* is not to be taken in Tertullian in its ordinary sense, as though it denoted that something not yet proved was being provisionally assumed; for if you think this you will very often be mistaken. Here he provisionally assumes nothing, since he has already clearly proved the authority of nature. Rather, *interim* here means “already now.” LAC.] the authority of nature: as human beings, under the title of common wisdom [Note: [Col. 0083C] “Endurance,” Rhen.; “parent,” Fran. Paris.]; but as pledges of their own religion [Note: [Col. 0084D] “Pledges of their own religion.” Junius rewrites this as “by the pledge” and explains it in a most alien fashion, perhaps because he did not wish to acknowledge the saints or that they are honored by the scattering of flowers. But let him consider the similar sentence at the beginning of the following chapter: “For now I already hear it being said,” etc. LAC.] [Note: [Col. 0084C] “By the pledge,” Jun.], under the title whereby they worship the God of nature at close hand [Note: [Col. 0084C] “Very closely,” Lat.].

And thus, as though by superabundance, let them also examine the remaining arguments which, in our own particular case, forbid every kind of crowning of the head. For we are also pressed by our participation in natural discipline to turn to the distinctive character of Christian discipline, which must now be defended in its entirety through the other varieties of crowns as well. These appear to have been devised for other uses, since they are constructed from other materials, lest—because they do not consist of flowers, whose use nature has marked out, as with this very military crown of laurel—they should be thought not to fall under the prohibition of our sect merely because they have escaped nature’s prior objection.

I therefore see that the matter must be treated both more carefully and more plainly, from its origins through its development and excesses. Secular literature is necessary for this purpose, for secular matters must necessarily be proved from their own documentary sources. I believe the few sources I have touched upon will suffice.

If there was any Pandora, whom Hesiod records as the first of women, hers was the first head to be crowned by the Graces, when gifts were bestowed upon her by everyone—whence the name Pandora. Our Moses, however [Note: [Col. 0085C] “Our Moses,” etc. That Moses was a shepherd is indicated by the words of Exodus, chapter 4: “Now Moses was tending the sheep of his father-in-law,” etc. By the poetic shepherd, moreover, he means Hesiod, who, while acting as keeper of his father’s sheep at Helicon, saw the Muses and was led by them to Hippocrene, that is, the Horse’s Fountain, whereupon he immediately became an outstanding poet. Hence Ovid’s line:

> Clio and Clio’s sisters did not appear to me  
> As I tended flocks in your valleys, Ascra.

RHEN.], the prophetic rather than poetic shepherd [Note: [Col. 0085C] “Moses, the prophetic rather than poetic shepherd.” Moses and Hesiod were both shepherds: the former prophetic, the latter poetic. RIG.], describes the first woman, Eve, as having more readily bound leaves around her shameful parts than flowers around her temples. There was therefore no Pandora. Indeed, the origin of the crown should be ashamed of its falsehood.

And now, too, from their own truths [the source is elliptical]. For it is established that the Greeks [Note: [Col. 0085C] “Certainly the Greeks.” We judge that this is the correct reading, although the most ancient exemplar reads “the others,” Ursinus’s codex “certain persons,” and Latinus “the blind.” Tertullian says that the Greeks were the authors or elucidators of the subject of crowns, as what follows demonstrates. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0085B] “Certain persons,” cod. Wouw.; “the blind,” Latin.; “the others,” Fran.] were the authors, or at least the elucidators, of the practice. Pherecydes reports that Saturn was crowned before all others; Diodorus says that Jupiter was crowned after the Titans had been defeated [Note: [Col. 0085B] Seml. inserts: “was honored by the others with this gift.”] [Note: [Col. 0085D] “After the aforesaid Titans.” In the printed books and even in the ancient exemplars the words “was honored by the others with this gift” are added. They do not appear to be Tertullian’s. RIG.]. The same author gives fillets to Priapus [Note: [Col. 0085D] “He gives fillets to Priapus.” Agobard’s codex reads *temianias*. RIG.], and to Ariadne a wreath of gold and Indian gems—the workmanship of Vulcan, the gift of Liber, and afterward a constellation [Note: [Col. 0085D] “Ariadne’s wreath of gold and Indian gems.” Hyginus, speaking of the Crown: “This is thought to have belonged to Ariadne and to have been placed among the constellations by Father Liber.” The same author a little later: “It is also said to have been made by Vulcan from gold and Indian gems.” Germanicus: “A crown made by Vulcan’s workmanship from gold and precious gems.” RIG.].

Callimachus placed a vine upon Juno. Thus Agis too presents her statue wreathed with a vine shoot, [Col. 0085B] with a lion’s skin beneath her feet, triumphing [Note: [Col. 0085B] “Exulting,” Jun.] over the spoils of both her stepsons [Note: [Col. 0086B] “Presenting,” Rhen.]. Hercules wears now poplar on his head, now wild olive, now parsley. You have the tragedy *Cerberus*; you have Pindar and Callimachus, who also records that Apollo, after killing the dragon Delphyne [Note: [Col. 0086B] Semler inserts: “for which reason suppliants were crowned among the ancients.”] [Note: [Col. 0085D] “The dragon Delphyne.” Traces of this reading appear in Agobard’s codex. Hesychius: Δελφίς, ὁ ἐν Δελφοῖς δράκων, “Delphis: the dragon at Delphi.” RIG.], put on a laurel crown [Note: [Col. 0085D] “Put on a laurel crown.” In the editions and also in the manuscripts there follows: “for which reason a suppliant.” For suppliants were crowned among the ancients. But I do not think these words belong to Tertullian. I nevertheless restore them if anyone should come demanding the omitted words. RIG.].

Harpocration, with due diligence, argues that Liber—who among the Egyptians is likewise Osiris—was crowned with ivy [Note: [Col. 0086B] “He argues that he inherited.” Pliny, book XVI, chapter 5: “Father Liber was the first of all to place ivy upon his head.” Likewise chapter 24: “Alexander, on account of its rarity, returned victorious from India with his army crowned in this way, after the example of Father Liber,” etc. RHEN.], because it is the nature of ivy to protect the brain from drowsy stupor [Col. 0086A] [Note: [Col. 0086C] “To protect from drowsy stupor.” According to Sextus Pompeius, *helucus* signifies one who is languid and half-asleep and weak from yesterday’s wine, so called from the opening of the mouth and yawning. Tertullian, however, appears to use the word rather for that condition of the head by which we are rendered prone to sleep and which the Greeks call καρηβαρία (*karēbaria*, “heaviness of the head”). Authors have much to say about ivy’s cooling power. RHEN.]. But the populace too acknowledges Liber as the originator of the crown, specifically the laurel crown in which he celebrated his triumph from India, when it calls the days solemnly devoted to him “the Great Crown.”

If you also unroll the writings of Leo the Egyptian [Note: [Col. 0086C] “If you also unroll the writings of Leo the Egyptian.” Augustine, *City of God*, book VIII, chapters 5 and 27, following Alexander, calls this Leo the high priest of the Egyptian rites. Hyginus, under Aries, says that he wrote an account of Egyptian matters. Throughout his *Fables*, the same Hyginus mentions Callimachus, Pherecydes, and others cited here by Septimius.], you will find that Isis was the first to carry around her head the ears of grain she had discovered—a matter belonging rather to the belly. For those seeking more, Claudius Saturninus, the most distinguished commentator on this subject as well, will supply everything [Note: [Col. 0086D] “Claudius Saturninus.” None of his works survives, but I believe this book of Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, to be plainly an epitome of that work. LAC.]. For he has a book *On Crowns*, explaining their origins, causes, types, and solemnities in such a way that you will find no charm of a flower, no delight of foliage, no sod or vine shoot, that was not consecrated to someone’s head.

From this we may be sufficiently instructed how alien we ought to judge the institution of the crowned head, introduced by those whom the world believed to be gods and thereafter administered in their honor. For if the devil, a liar from the beginning, produces the falsehood of divinity in this form too, he undoubtedly also provided in advance the persons through whom the falsehood of divinity would be enacted. What, then, should that thing be regarded as among the people of the true God which was introduced by the devil’s candidates, dedicated to those very candidates from the beginning, and already then initiated into idolatry by idols—and by idols still living? Not that an idol [Note: [Col. 0086D] “Not that an idol is anything.” Tertullian says that idolatry is a falsehood of divinity, which the devil, a liar from the beginning, has produced, so arranging and providing for himself human beings in whom that falsehood might be enacted. For the gods of the nations were human beings whom the nations, after they had died, regarded as gods—whether from eagerness to flatter them, perhaps at the request of their descendants, or in memory of their benefits. This was the most ancient custom of repaying gratitude to benefactors: such persons were enrolled among the divine powers. Nor did Pliny think otherwise about the gods of his own age. Tertullian therefore calls these human beings whom the devil provided for himself—those from whom idols, or thefts and falsehoods of divinity, would be made—the devil’s candidates; while still alive, they already ambitioned to be idols, to have statues erected to themselves, and to be worshiped. [Col. 0087C] He says that all these things must be abhorred by Christians, worshipers of the true God—not because idols or statues are anything, but because the worship that human beings render to idols or statues belongs to demons, God’s rivals. He then adds: “But if the things that human beings do for idols belong to demons, how much more does what the idols themselves did for themselves while they were still alive?” RIG.] is anything, [Col. 0087A] but because the things others do for idols pertain to demons. Moreover, if the things others [Note: [Col. 0087C] “Moreover, if the things others,” etc. The sense appears to be: If the things the gentiles do belong to others within their idols—to Mercury, for example, or Jupiter. He is speaking of sacrifices and immolation. RHEN.] do for idols pertain to demons (1 Cor. 10:20), how much more does what the idols themselves did for themselves while they were still alive? The demons themselves, namely, procured these things for themselves through those in whom they had previously hungered for what they procured [Note: [Col. 0087C] “Had hungered,” Fran. Paris.] [Note: [Col. 0087C] “The demons themselves, namely, procured these things for themselves through those in whom they had previously hungered for what they procured.” He says that the demons procured for themselves idols, statues, incense, and the savor of sacrifices through those human beings in whose minds, while they were still living among mortals, the demons had so settled that through and within them the demons themselves seemed to live and exist among human beings. Thus even before that time the demons themselves had hungered and yearned in those human beings for the entire apparatus of idolatry. The verb “to hunger” is used here for the ardor of vehement desire, just as in the *Scorpiace*, where he says of the saints who had already suffered certain torments in prison: “Having tasted martyrdoms in prison, they hunger for them.” RIG.—“They themselves, namely, procured demons for themselves.” Thus Tertullian himself says in *On the Shows*, p. 95, that from the beginning demons, making provision for themselves, provided among the other pollutions of idolatry those of public shows as well, by which they might draw the human being away from God and bind him to their own honor. RIG.—“They themselves, namely, procured demons for themselves.” *Procurare* with the dative, as in book I *Against Marcion*: “Rivalry, moreover, makes provision for the human being by liberating him,” and in many other passages. RHEN.] [Note: [Col. 0087C] “Before they had procured it,” Pam.].

## CHAPTER VIII
Hold fast to this conviction for the moment, while I repel the assault of the question [Note: [Col. 0088C] “The assault of the question”: its attack. RIG.]. For I already hear it said: “Many other things, too, were produced by those whom the world believed to be gods; yet today they are found in our own uses, in those of the saints of old, in the things of God, and in Christ himself—who, of course, discharged the functions of human life by no other means than these common instruments of human sustenance” [Note: [Col. 0088C] “Human sustenance”: that is, human life. In the same way legal writers speak of “the burdens of maintaining a wife” and of parents “to be maintained” by their children. RIG.].

Let it indeed be so; nor will I yet dispute more remotely about origins. Let Mercury have been the first to expound letters: I will acknowledge that they are necessary both for commercial dealings and for our studies concerning God. But even if he also first stretched strings to produce sound, I will not deny that this device has had dealings with the saints and ministered to God, since I hear David. Let Aesculapius have been the first to investigate remedies: I remember that Isaiah too prescribed something medicinal for the ailing Hezekiah (Isa. 38:21). Paul also knows that a little wine is beneficial for the stomach (1 Tim. 5:23). And let Minerva have been the first to fashion a ship: I shall see Jonah sailing [Note: [Col. 0088C] All the others read “Jonah.”] (Jon. 1:3), and the apostles (Luke 8:2). More than that (Acts 13:4), even Christ will be clothed, and Paul too will have a cloak (2 Tim. 4:13).

If they name some one of the gods of the world as the inventor of each item of furniture [Col. 0088A] and every individual vessel, they must acknowledge Christ reclining on a couch [Note: [Col. 0088C] “Christ reclining on a couch.” Our Sirmond discusses this passage in Epistle 2, Book I of Sidonius, and says that, because Christ reclined, John—who was perhaps the youngest in age—reclined next to Christ, in his bosom. For the arrangement on the semicircular dining couch was such that the first place was given to Christ; then the others reclined, while John was in the last place and therefore rested in Christ’s bosom. Thus, plainly, Christ’s supper was arranged not as painters now represent it, with Christ in the middle and the apostles crowding either side of him, [Col. 0088D] but with him truly at the right-hand end, the others surrounding him, and John bringing up that sacred company; for this reason John reclined at Christ’s side. LAC.]; and also when he brings a basin to his disciples’ feet (John 13:5), when he pours water from a pitcher, and when he girds himself with a linen cloth—the distinctive garment of Osiris [Note: [Col. 0088D] “The distinctive garment of Osiris.” Herodotus is the authority that among the Egyptians it was forbidden to bring woolen garments into sacred buildings; accordingly, they used linen ones. RHEN.].

To a question of this kind I give the same answer everywhere: I indeed admit the common use of practical objects, but appeal to the distinction between rational and irrational things, because passivity [Note: [Col. 0088C] Rhenanus reads “passibility.”] deceives [Note: [Col. 0088D] “Because passivity deceives.” *Passivitas*, that is, the multitude. RIG.], obscuring the corruption of creation by which it has been subjected to futility (Rom. 8:28). For we say that those things alone were suitable for our use, for the use of our predecessors, for the things of God, and for Christ himself, which provide sheer benefits, reliable assistance, and honorable comforts for the necessities of human life [Col. 0088B] [Note: [Col. 0088D] “The necessities of human life”: that is, needs. RIG.]; so that they may be believed to have been inspired by God himself, who first exercised foresight for his human creature, furnished him, and, when appropriate, gave him pleasure. But whatever things have exceeded this order are not suitable for our use—especially those which, precisely for that reason, are recognized neither in the world’s ordinary life, nor in the things of God, nor in Christ’s conduct.

## CHAPTER IX

Finally, what patriarch, what prophet, what Levite or priest or ruler, or, later, what apostle or evangelist or bishop, is found wearing a crown? I think that neither the temple of God itself, nor the ark of the covenant, nor the tabernacle of witness [Note: [Col. 0088D] “The tabernacle of witness.” Just as in the Old Testament it is called the “tabernacle of testimony,” so too in the New; for “testimony” is μαρτύριον (*martyrion*) in the Septuagint. That word is also used for martyrs’ basilicas. Thus the Council of Chalcedon was convened ἐν τῷ μαρτυρίῳ τῆς ἁγίας καὶ καλλινίκου μάρτυρος Εὐφημίας, “in the basilica of the holy and gloriously victorious martyr Euphemia,” as stated in Act 4 of that council. LE PR.], nor the altar, nor the lampstand (1 Kings 6 and 8) was crowned—though crowning would certainly have been appropriate to them both at the solemnity of their first dedication and at the celebration of their second restoration [Note: [Col. 0089C] The Paris edition reads “prior establishment.”]—if it were worthy of God (1 Esd. 5:11; 1 Cor. 10).

Yet if they were figures of us—for we are the temples of God, his altars, lights, and vessels—they also symbolically portended this: that human beings belonging to God ought not to be crowned. The reality must correspond to the image. If perhaps you raise the objection that Christ himself was crowned, for the moment you will hear this brief reply: “Then crown yourself in that manner too; it is permitted.” Yet even that crown of insulting impiety was not decreed by the people [Note: [Col. 0089C] “Yet even that crown of insulting impiety was not decreed by the people.” “The people,” that is, the Jews. RIG.]. It was an invention of Roman soldiers, drawn from a worldly custom which the people of God never admitted, either in the name of public rejoicing or of innate extravagance. They returned from the captivity of Babylon more readily with drums, pipes, and harps than with crowns (1 Esd. 2 and 3); and after eating and drinking they rose up to play without crowns (Exod. 23). For neither a description of rejoicing nor a denunciation of extravagance would have remained silent about the honor or dishonor of a crown. Indeed, Isaiah too says (24:9): “For they drink wine with drums, pipes, and harps.” He would also have said “with crowns,” if this custom had ever existed in the things of God.

## CHAPTER X

Thus, when you advance the claim that ornaments belonging to the gods of the world are also found in the presence of God, in order to vindicate among them the crown of the head for common use, you have already laid down a rule against yourself: that what is not found in the things of God must not be admitted into common use [Note: [Col. 0089C] Semler inserts “among us.”]. For what is so unworthy of God [Note: [Col. 0089C] “For what is so unworthy of God?” The form of this argument is more compact in the manuscript: “For what is so unworthy of God as what is worthy of an idol? As what is also worthy of a dead man?” RIG.] as what is worthy of an idol? [Col. 0089C] And what is so worthy of an idol as what is also worthy of a dead person? For it is characteristic of the dead too to be crowned in this way [Note: [Col. 0089D] “It is characteristic of the dead to be crowned in this way.” Pliny writes that crowns were an honor paid to tombs and the spirits of the dead. RHEN.], since they immediately become idols through the attire and ritual of consecration, which among us is a second idolatry.

Therefore it will belong to those who lack perception to make use likewise of something of which they lack perception—as though they wished to misuse it, if they did not lack perception. But there is no distinction concerning misuse when the reality of use ceases with the cessation of the nature capable of perception. By what faculty could anyone wish to misuse a thing when he has no faculty with which to use it? We, however, are not permitted by the apostle to misuse; he teaches us more readily not to use—except that those who perceive nothing do not misuse either. But the whole matter is empty and is itself a dead work insofar as idols are concerned; it is, however, decidedly alive insofar as demons are concerned, to whom the superstition belongs.

“The idols of the nations,” says David (Ps. 113:4), “are silver and gold; they have eyes and do not see, nostrils and do not smell, hands and do not touch.” Yet it is by these faculties that flowers are enjoyed. But if he declares that those who manufacture idols will become like them, those who use anything in accordance with the adornment of idols are already like them. “All things are clean to the clean” (Titus 1:15); likewise, all things are unclean to the unclean—and nothing is more unclean than idols.

Substances, however, are clean, as things belonging to God, and in virtue of their created condition are available for common use; but the manner in which the use is conducted makes the difference. For I too slaughter a chicken for myself, no less than Socrates did for Aesculapius [Note: [Col. 0089D] “Than Socrates did for Aesculapius.” He ordered this while he was in prison, shortly before he was to drink the poison. RHEN.]; and if the odor of some place offends me, I burn something from Arabia [Note: [Col. 0089D] “I burn something from Arabia.” When speaking about himself, he is even afraid to use the word “incense.” He therefore said, “I burn something from Arabia,” that is, some incense or Arabian fragrance. In the book *Against the Jews*, too, he interprets “the spoils of Arabia” as gold and perfumes. An ancient author cited by Festus says, “It smells Arabian,” that is, of Arabian fragrances. RIG.]; but not with the same rite, attire, or ceremonial apparatus with which it is done before idols.

For if a created thing is polluted by a mere statement [Note: [Col. 0089D] “By a mere statement.” I believe this man, highly skilled in law, was alluding to formulas occurring in jurisprudence, where one frequently reads: “bare possession,” “bare ownership,” “bare claim,” “bare delivery”—that is, respectively, possession unaccompanied by ownership; ownership from which usufruct is absent; a claim in which some debt is entered in the accounts although no cause of indebtedness preceded it; and delivery lacking a just and adequate cause for transferring [Col. 0090D] ownership. Thus a “bare statement” will be one by which a person is admonished by someone who has no authority to admonish, as though that statement were bare of all authority and support. LAC.], as the apostle teaches—“But if anyone says, ‘This has been sacrificed to an idol,’ do not touch it” [Note: [Col. 0090D] “This has been sacrificed to an idol; do not touch it.” This is from the Apostle, 1 Cor. 10:28, where he retained the Greek word εἰδωλόθυτον (*eidōlothyton*), “idol-sacrifice,” in place of what our translator renders “sacrificed to idols.” It is surprising, however, that he reads “Do not touch it,” since the Greek is μὴ ἐσθίετε (*mē esthiete*), which cannot be translated otherwise than our translator does: “Do not eat it.” PAM.]—how much more is it contaminated when you have danced about [Note: [Col. 0090C] “Have danced about” is absent from Pamelius and the Leopold edition.] in the attire, rite, and ceremonial apparatus of idol-sacrifices? So too a crown becomes an idol-sacrifice. For by this rite, attire, and ceremonial apparatus it is sacrificed to an idol by those who originated it; its use is so peculiarly theirs that something not found in the things of God cannot be admitted into common use.

Therefore the apostle cries out: “Flee idolatry” (1 Cor. 10:14)—all of it, certainly, and in its entirety. Survey the forest and see how many thorns lie concealed. Nothing must be given to an idol, and likewise nothing taken from an idol. If reclining in an idol’s temple is foreign to faith, what of appearing in an idol’s attire? “What fellowship has Christ with Belial” [Note: [Col. 0090D] “What fellowship has Christ,” etc. Drogo, bishop of Ostia, expands this with other related passages. Others attribute it to Cassian, *Conferences* XII, chapter 16. LAC.]? And for that reason, flee. For he commands a far-reaching separation from idolatry: one must conduct nothing in proximity to it. Even an earthly dragon [Note: [Col. 0090D] “Even an earthly dragon swallows human beings from afar with its breath.” Pamelius published: “Even an earthly dragon no less swallows birds from afar with its breath.” These words seem to have been taken from what Isidore reports of the basilisk, though they are wholly inapplicable to the dragon. Rhenanus had published something quite different: “Even an earthly dragon swallows the breaths of a human being from afar.” This comes close to the true reading, which we have restored from the manuscript of Agobard: “Even an earthly dragon swallows human beings from afar with its breath.” For here Tertullian is dealing with fleeing idolatry in accordance with Paul’s command to the Corinthians, and he says it must be fled as far away as possible, because the earthly dragon—that is, infernal Satan—swallows human beings even from afar with his breath and blast. He then adds from the First Epistle of John: “John goes further: Little children, guard yourselves from idols.” That is, John traces the matter more deeply and declares that not only idolatry must be fled, but even the idols themselves. RIG.] swallows human beings from afar with its breath.

John goes further [Col. 0091A]: “Little children,” he says, “guard yourselves from idols” (1 John 5:21)—no longer merely from idolatry as an activity, but from their very image. For it is unworthy that you, the image of the living God, should become the image of an idol and of a dead thing [Note: [Col. 0091C] Semler reads “should become.”].

Thus far we have vindicated the peculiar ownership of this attire for idols, both by the title of its origin and by the practice of superstition; and additionally from the fact that, since it is not mentioned among the things of God, it is more and more reckoned an image of those in whose antiquities, solemnities, and rites it is encountered. Finally, even their doors, victims, and altars, and their ministers and priests themselves [Note: [Col. 0091D] “Their ministers and priests themselves.” Pliny relates that crowns initially claimed their designation only among sacred rites and military honors. RHEN.] are crowned (Baruch 6:9). In Claudius you have the crowns of all the priestly colleges.

But we have also inserted that distinction between rational and irrational things, to answer those who defend common use in every case on the occasion of certain examples. For this part, then, it remains to examine the actual grounds for wearing crowns, so that, by showing them to be foreign—indeed, contrary—to our discipline, we may prove that none of them is supported by the protection of reason whereby this kind of attire, and its use too, could be vindicated for common use, even though there are some whose examples are raised against us.

## CHAPTER XI

Indeed, to take up the very case of the military crown, I think it must first be investigated [Note: [Col. 0091D] “It must be investigated whether military service is altogether suitable for Christians.” Since he does not permit a Christian to lend his assistance to a pagan waging war, would he permit a Christian to join himself as a soldier to a Christian who was going to persecute his brothers? Tertullian undoubtedly never believed that Christians would one day clash with one another in arms. RHEN.] whether military service is altogether suitable for Christians. Otherwise, what sense is there in reconsidering incidental matters when the fault lies in what precedes them?

Do we believe that a human oath of allegiance [Note: [Col. 0091D] “Do we believe that a human oath of allegiance…” He alludes to the sacrament and response, or profession of faith, made at baptism. PAM.] may be superimposed upon the divine one, and that after Christ one may pledge allegiance to another lord? May one renounce [Note: [Col. 0091D] “And renounce father and mother,” etc. The word *ejerare* means to disown or renounce. The author’s meaning is that another oath, the military one, must not be superimposed upon the sacrament of baptism. For when a Christian binds himself by the military oath, he appears to renounce God’s law, by which parents are commanded to be loved in accordance with God. LE PR.] father and mother and every neighbor, whom the Law commands to be honored and loved after God (Exod. 20; Lev. 19) [Note: [Col. 0092C] “Whom the Gospel, making none of them dearer than Christ, honored in the same manner.” The old copy reads: “Whom the Gospel, making Christ alone dearer … also honored.” Hence, whether we read “making Christ alone dearer,” or “making none dearer than Christ,” the meaning will be the same. RIG.], and whom the Gospel too, making none of them dearer than Christ, honored in the same manner [Note: [Col. 0092C] “Honored in the same manner.” That is: the Gospel commanded that parents and every neighbor be honored no less than had been prescribed by the Mosaic Law. For the Law ordered them to be honored immediately after God, and the Gospel immediately after Christ. RIG.] (1 Cor. 6; Matt. 5; 1 Cor. 8)?

Will it be permitted to occupy oneself with the sword when the Lord declares that whoever has used the sword will perish by the sword? And will the son of peace take part in battle, when even litigation is unsuitable for him [Note: [Col. 0092D] “When even litigation is unsuitable for him.” He alludes to 1 Cor. 6:7: “Now therefore it is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another. Why do you not rather suffer injury?” Consequently Rhenanus is not wrong in interpreting *litigare*, a jurists’ term, as bringing an action against a person or concerning property before a judge. Yet it must be noted that the Apostle immediately adds in the same passage: “But you commit injury,” etc. PAM.]? Will he administer chains, imprisonment, tortures, and punishments, when he is not even the avenger of his own injuries?

Will he now perform guard duties for another more than for Christ? Or even on the Lord’s Day, when he will not perform them for Christ? Will he keep watch over temples which he has renounced? Will he dine in a place of which the apostle disapproves? Will he defend by night those whom he has put to flight by exorcisms during the day, leaning and resting upon the spear [Note: [Col. 0092D] “Resting upon the spear.” The books published thus far read “upon the *lunchus*.” Livy, Book XLIV: “They stood helmeted, holding their shields upright before them; then, when weary, leaning on their spears and placing their heads upon the rim of their shields, they slept standing.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0092C] The Frankfurt and Paris editions read *lunchus*.] with which Christ’s side was pierced (John 19:34)?

Will he also carry a standard rivaling Christ? Will he request the watchword from a commander after he has already received one from God? When dead, will he be disturbed by the trumpeter’s trumpet, though he expects to be raised by the trumpet of the angel? And will a Christian be burned in accordance with military regulations, when he was not permitted to burn incense [Note: [Col. 0092D] “When he was not permitted to burn.” Incense, that is, to an idol. The Glosses of Isidore define *cremutium* as a whole burnt offering. RIG.], and when Christ remitted for him the deserved punishment of fire?

How many other acts can be observed among the offenses involved in military duties, to be interpreted as transgression? The very act of transferring one’s name from the camp of light to the camp of darkness is transgression [Note: [Col. 0092D] “Is transgression.” The manuscript of Agobard reads “belongs to transgression.” RIG.].

Certainly, if faith finds some men already committed to military service when it comes to them afterward, their case is different: it was so with those whom John admitted to baptism (Luke 3:3), and with the most faithful centurions, the one whom Christ commends (Matt. 8) and the one whom Peter catechizes (Acts 10). Nevertheless, once faith has been accepted [Col. 0092C] and sealed, military service must either be abandoned immediately [Note: [Col. 0092D] “Once faith has been accepted and sealed, it must either be abandoned immediately.” That is, military service must be abandoned. RIG.], as many have done; or every kind of evasion must be employed to prevent anything from being committed against God—which military regulations do not permit either [Note: [Col. 0093C] “Which military regulations do not permit either.” What the manuscript reads, “outside military service,” seems less consistent with Tertullian’s meaning. For this is what he intends: the Christian whom faith finds in military service must either abandon it immediately upon accepting the faith—which military law, that is, the regulations governing military service, does not permit—or must guard by every possible means against doing anything contrary to the Christian faith, which likewise is scarcely permitted under Roman military law; or must endure every extremity for God, to which every Christian pledged himself when he pledged faith to Christ. RIG.]; or, finally, every extremity must be endured for God, something to which civilian faith equally binds one [Note: [Col. 0093C] “Something to which civilian faith equally binds one.” To death, that is. For a Christian civilian—that is, one who is not a soldier—has pledged this to Christ equally with a soldier. What follows suggests this interpretation. RIG.].

For military service will promise neither impunity for sins nor immunity from martyrdom. A Christian is nowhere anything else. There is one Gospel and the same Jesus, who will deny everyone who denies, confess everyone who confesses God, save the life lost for his name’s sake, and, conversely, destroy the life gained in opposition to his name (Matt. 10:39). Before him, a faithful civilian is as much a soldier as an unfaithful soldier is a civilian. The state of faith admits no pleas of necessity [Note: [Col. 0093D] “The state of faith admits no pleas of necessity.” Outside the state of faith, however, they are admitted (*Apology* XLV; *Exhortation to Chastity* VI). Necessity is reckoned as an excuse (*On Idolatry* X). Necessity is put forward as a kind of advocate pleading for pardon (*Apology* IV, VII), and shortly afterward here: “The plea of necessity is exceedingly familiar.” RIG.]. There is no necessity to sin for those whose sole necessity is not to sin.

For a person is also pressed by the necessity of torture or punishment to sacrifice and directly deny the faith. Yet discipline does not connive even at that necessity, because the necessity of fearing denial and undergoing martyrdom is stronger than that of escaping suffering and fulfilling one’s official duty. Otherwise, an excuse of this kind subverts the whole substance of the sacrament, so that it loosens the fastening even for voluntary sins. For even the will could be maintained to be a necessity [Note: [Col. 0093C] Semler reads “could have been.”], since it plainly has something by which it is compelled.

I would lay down this same argument in advance for the other grounds for official crowns, in connection with which the plea of necessity is exceedingly familiar: official posts must either be avoided, lest we fall into sins, or martyrdoms must be endured, so that we may break free from those posts. I shall say no more [Note: [Col. 0093D] “I shall say no more.” The manuscript of Agobard reads “They do no more”; Ursinus, “Let them do no more.” RIG.] concerning the first form of the question, namely the unlawfulness of military service itself, so that the second may receive its answer—lest, if I drive military service out by every means, I have already appealed in vain concerning the military crown.

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0094A]

Suppose, then, that military service is permissible up to the question of the crown. But let us first speak about the crown itself. That laurel is sacred to Apollo or Liber: to the former as the god of missiles [Note: [Col. 0093D] “To the former as the god of missiles.” Relevant here is Plato’s derivation of Apollo from ἀπὸ τοῦ πάλλειν (*apo tou pallein*), that is, “from hurling”; hence also the custom of forming his images with bow and arrows. PAM.]; to the latter as the god of triumphs. Claudius teaches this, while also saying that soldiers were customarily wreathed with myrtle [Note: [Col. 0093D] “Also with myrtle.” Myrtle likewise served in military affairs. When Postumius Tubertus, during his consulship, triumphed over the Sabines—the first of all men to enter the city in an ovation—because he had carried out the affair easily and without bloodshed, he proceeded crowned with the myrtle of Venus Victrix and made that desirable tree acceptable even to enemies. This afterward became the crown of those celebrating an ovation. RHEN.]. For myrtle belongs to Venus, the mother of Aeneas, and not laurel—to her who was also the mistress of Mars, Mars being Roman through Ilia and the Romuli. But I do not believe Venus to be Roman in this respect together with Mars [Note: [Col. 0094C] “But I do not believe Venus to be Roman in this respect together with Mars.” He says: I might believe Mars to be Roman insofar as he begot the Romuli by Ilia; but I do not think Venus Roman insofar as she perceived Ilia as her rival and grieved over her. RIG.], insofar as this involves resentment toward a rival.

When military service is crowned with olive too, the idolatry is directed toward Minerva [Note: [Col. 0093C] The Frankfurt edition reads “Minerva.”], likewise a goddess of arms, but also one crowned from this tree upon making peace with Neptune [Note: [Col. 0094C] “Peace with Neptune.” Since Minerva made peace with Neptune while wearing an olive crown, the olive is therefore a sign of peace. LE PR.] [Note: [Col. 0093C] The Frankfurt and Paris editions read: “Indeed, that military service is crowned with olive derives from Minerva, goddess not only of the arts but also of arms; and that she made peace with Neptune because of this tree,” etc. Junius reads: “But also that she was crowned from this tree after peace was made with Neptune.”]. Among these things the superstition of the military wreath will be both polluted and polluting; and everything is now polluted by its very grounds.

Look at the annual declaration of vows: what does it seem to be? Its first stage is in the headquarters, its second on the Capitol. Hear, after the places, the words: “THEN WE VOWED TO YOU, JUPITER, THAT THERE WOULD BE A BULL WITH ITS HORNS ADORNED WITH GOLD” [Note: [Col. 0094C] “Then we vowed to you, Jupiter, that there would be a bull with its horns adorned with gold.” This is the reading of the old manuscript, which may also be confirmed by the ancient inscription of the Arval Brothers: “WE VOWED THAT THERE WOULD BE A GILDED BULL.” RIG.]. Whose utterance is this? Surely an utterance of denial. Even if the Christian is silent there with his mouth, he has answered with his crowned head.

The same laurel is proclaimed at the distribution of the donative—idolatry that is plainly not free of charge, selling Christ for a few gold coins, as Judas sold him for silver (Matt. 26). Will this be what is meant by, “You cannot serve God and mammon” (Matt. 16:24): to hand your hand over to mammon [Note: [Col. 0094C] Leopold reads “is.”] and withdraw from God? Will this be, “Render to Caesar what belongs to Caesar and to God what belongs to God” (Matt. 22:21): neither rendering the human being to God [Note: [Col. 0094D] “Neither rendering the human being to God.” Yet the human being is God’s coin and image. He therefore says that the Christian, when both a soldier and crowned, does not render the human being to God, because he walks about wearing an ornament dedicated to idols; and that he takes the denarius away from Caesar, because he carries home the donative received from Caesar. Thus he renders neither what is God’s to God nor what is Caesar’s to Caesar. He signifies that military service and the business of battles are unsuitable for a Christian. Battles must be left to Caesar, the crown to the world and Satan; the human being himself, God’s image, must be rendered to God—but pure, free, the servant and soldier of no one but God. RIG.], nor leaving Caesar his denarius?

Is the laurel of triumph constructed from leaves—or from corpses? Is it adorned with metal plates [Note: [Col. 0094D] “Adorned with metal plates.” The old copy reads *lemnis*, “with ribbons.” RIG.]—or with funeral pyres? Is it anointed with perfumes [Note: [Col. 0095C] Hence the Paris edition reads: “with contrasting ribbons, gilded with little plates, with perfumes”; C. Wouwer: “constructed from leaves, adorned with ribbons”; Junius, from a manuscript: “The laurel of triumph is constructed from leaves, on one side with contrasting ribbons, on the other gilded with little plates; it is anointed with perfumes.”]—or with the tears of wives and mothers? Perhaps the wives and mothers of some Christians too, for Christ is also among the barbarians [Note: [Col. 0095C] “For Christ is also among the barbarians.” Trypho in Lucian gave the same answer when Critias asked whether the affairs of the Scythians were a concern to God: “Certainly, if perhaps Christ is also among the nations” (εἰ τύχοι γε Χηστὸς καὶ ἐν ἔθνεσι). RIG.]. Has not the man who has carried upon his head this cause [Note: [Col. 0095C] “Who has carried upon his head this cause”: the triumphal crown—the cause of corpses, funeral pyres, and tears. RIG.] himself also fought?

There is also another military service, that of the imperial households. For they too are called *castrenses*, palace soldiers, and are bound to the duties [Note: [Col. 0095C] “They too are bound to the duties of imperial solemnities.” In Festus we read that soldiers who were not exempt but performed service for the emperor were called *munifices*; those exempt from service were called *beneficiarii*. In Vegetius too, *munifices* are soldiers who perform service, from which those called *immunes* are free. Interpret *munificae*, therefore, as “bound and obligated to the duty of imperial solemnities.” A later age used *munificum* for *munifice*. Paul the Jurist too, in the chapter *Munus*, *On the Meaning of Words*, teaches that *munus* also signifies “official duty”; hence “military duties” and the designation of certain soldiers as *munifices*. RHEN.] of imperial solemnities. But you in like manner are the soldier and servant of another. Even if you are the servant of two, God and Caesar, you certainly cease to be Caesar’s whenever you owe yourself to God—who, I believe, has the stronger claim even in matters common to both.

## CHAPTER XIII

Public occasions crown the public orders with laurels, while magistrates additionally receive golden crowns [Note: [Col. 0095C] Semler inserts “as at Athens, as at Rome,” and says that these words were perhaps added by some interpreter.]. Etruscan crowns are ranked above [Col. 0095B] even these [Note: [Col. 0095D] “Etruscan crowns are ranked above even these.” Thus reads the old copy: *superferuntur illis*, that is, they are considered more noble even than golden crowns. RIG.]. This is the name for crowns distinguished with gemstones and golden oak leaves in honor of Jupiter, which magistrates wear with palm-embroidered robes when escorting the sacred chariots [Note: [Col. 0095D] “When escorting the sacred chariots.” Festus teaches that the *tensa* was a silver vehicle on which the emblems of the gods were carried to their cushioned seats in the circus during the Circensian games. RHEN.]. There are also provincial golden crowns, now seeking heads larger than those of men—the heads of statues.

But your orders and your magistracies, and the very name of your senate, are the Church of Christ. You are enrolled [Note: [Col. 0095D] “Enrolled in the books of life.” Lucian’s Trypho had also heard something of these books, for he says to Critias: “Therefore leave everything alone, so that you too may be enrolled among the good in the heavenly books” (Ὥστε ἔασον ἅπαντα ὡς καί σε ἐν ταῖς ἐπουρανίοις βίβλοις τῶν ἀγαθῶν ἀπογράψωνται). RIG.] in the books of life (Phil. 4; Rev. 13). There your purple is the Lord’s blood, and your broad stripe (*clavus latus*) is in his cross (Matt. 27). There the axe is laid to the trunk [Note: [Col. 0096C] Junius reads “to the roots.”] of the tree (Matt. 3:10); there are the rods [Note: [Col. 0096C] “There are the rods from the root of Jesse.” He says “rods,” alluding to the fasces of Roman magistrates; so it is read in the manuscript of Agobard. RIG.] from Jesse (Isa. 11:1).

Let public horses look to themselves and their crowns. When your Lord wished to enter Jerusalem according to Scripture (Matt. 21), he did not even possess a donkey of his own. “These trust in chariots and these in horses, but we shall call upon the name of the Lord our God” (Ps. 19). We are removed from even residing in that Babylon in the Apocalypse of John (*Apology* 18), much more from its magistrate’s platform [Note: [Col. 0096C] Junius reads “to the platform.”].

The populace too is crowned, now in exultation over the rulers’ successes, now through the particular customs of municipal solemnities; and extravagant display eagerly seizes upon every public rejoicing. But you are a stranger to this world, a citizen of the Jerusalem above. “Our citizenship,” he says (Phil. 3:20), “is in heaven.” You have your own civic rolls [reading *census* for the apparent OCR *sensus*], your own calendars [Note: [Col. 0096C] “Your own calendars.” The *fasti* were books containing the scheme and festivals of the whole year; Tertullian speaks with reference to these. In the Church too there are *fasti*, so do not concern yourself with the calendars and solemnities of municipalities. The passage should indeed be noted as evidence of the Church’s custom of entering the “birthdays”—that is, the deaths—of martyrs in calendars, which in ecclesiastical terminology we call martyrologies. There is an excellent passage on this matter in Cyprian, Epistle 83. LAC.], your own calendars. You have nothing to do with the world’s rejoicings; indeed, you owe the contrary: “For the world will rejoice, but you will mourn” (John 16:20). And, I think, he calls those who mourn blessed (Matt. 5:5), not those who are crowned.

Weddings too crown bridegrooms [Note: [Col. 0096D] “Weddings too crown bridegrooms.” Relevant here is the custom by which a bride, while preparing to go to her husband, would weave a garland from vervain, which was dedicated to Venus, and from flowers and herbs she had gathered herself, and carry it with her; for it was considered a fault to wear purchased wreaths. Likewise, the bridegroom, while awaiting her at home, would crown the door with great ceremony and decorate many things with laurel, as Alexander ab Alexandro attests. PAM.]. Therefore let us not marry pagans, lest they lead us all the way into idolatry, from which marriage among them begins. You have the law from the patriarchs (Gen. 24:3; Gal. 3), and you have the apostle commanding marriage “in the Lord” (1 Cor. 7).

Worldly freedom too crowns its recipients. But you have already been redeemed by Christ—and at a great price. How will the world manumit another’s slave? Even if it appears to be freedom [Note: [Col. 0096C] The Wouwer manuscript reads “may seem.”], the former slavery likewise only appeared to be slavery. All things in the world are imaginary, and nothing is real. For even then, when redeemed by Christ, you were free from human ownership; and now you are Christ’s slave, though manumitted by a human being. If you regard the world’s freedom as genuine, so that you authenticate it with a crown [Note: [Col. 0096C] Latinus, Rhenanus, and the Frankfurt edition read “the crown.”], you have returned to human slavery, which you regard as freedom; you have lost the freedom of Christ, which you regard as slavery.

Surely the occasions of athletic contests must not also be debated [Note: [Col. 0096D] “Surely the occasions of athletic contests must not also be debated.” That is, the games. “Surely the games will not also come into dispute,” he says, “so that one must further ask concerning them whether a Christian ought to avoid them or not?” RIG.], when their very titles immediately condemn them as sacred or funerary? This alone remains: that Olympian Jupiter, Nemean Hercules, poor little Archemorus [Note: [Col. 0096D] “And poor little Archemorus.” Archemorus, the son of Lycurgus, died while still an infant after being injured by a serpent, through the negligence of his nurse Hypsipyle. She had left him in the grass while going to show the spring Langia to the Greeks, who were suffering from thirst. An annual contest was instituted in memory of the boy; and because he died while still an infant, Tertullian calls him “poor little” rather than simply “wretched.” RHEN.], and unhappy Antinous [Note: [Col. 0097C] “Unhappy Antinous.” The emperor Hadrian kept him as his favorite and loved him so tenderly that he named after him the Egyptian city where he also instituted an annual contest in his honor. Hegesippus elegantly committed this affair to writing, as the blessed Jerome reports. RHEN.] should be crowned in a Christian, so that he himself becomes a spectacle—the very thing he ought to watch [Note: [Col. 0097B] Rhenanus reads: “which ought not to be watched.”].

We have, I think, enumerated every occasion. Not one belongs to us: all are foreign, profane, and unlawful, once for all renounced in the profession of the sacrament. For these were the pomp of the devil and the offices of his angels: the world’s honors, solemnities, public favor, false vows, human servitudes, empty praises, shameful glories—and idolatry in all of them, even in the mere conception of the crowns with which all these were wreathed.

Claudius will indeed begin by saying that in Homer’s poems even heaven is crowned with stars—certainly by God, certainly for the human being; therefore the human being himself must be crowned by God.
