In the world, however, brothels [Note: [Col. 0097C] “Brothels too are crowned.” He appears to mean the crowns with which public or private household gods were crowned in individual houses, and therefore in brothels too, etc. PAM.], latrines, bakeries, prisons, gladiatorial schools, the amphitheaters themselves, the stripping-rooms, and the undertakers’ establishments themselves are crowned. How sacred and holy, how honorable and pure [Note: [Col. 0097C] “How sacred and holy, how honorable.” The reading of the Dijon manuscript is attractive: “How sacred and holy, how honorable,” etc. RIG.] this attire may be, judge not from one poetic heaven, but from the practices of the whole world.

A Christian, moreover, will not disgrace even his own door with laurels, if he knows how many gods the devil has attached even to doorways: Janus from *janua*, “door”; Limentinus from *limen*, “threshold”; Forculus [Note: [Col. 0097C] Some read “Forcula,” others “Foreculus.” RIG.] and Carda from *fores*, “doors,” and *cardines*, “hinges”; and among the Greeks, Apollo Thyraeus, “Apollo of the Door,” and the Antelian (*Antelioi*, “facing the sun”) demons.

## CHAPTER XIV
Source/review notes: The transmitted reading “nihil lugubre” (“nothing mournful”) is internally inconsistent with the surrounding argument but has been translated faithfully and marked as contextually suspect.

So far is he from bringing upon his own head an offering to idolatry—[Col. 0098A] indeed, I would now say, to Christ, since “the head of the man is Christ” (1 Cor. 11:3)—a head as free as Christ himself, subject not even to a covering, much less to a binding. Moreover, that which is subject to a covering, the woman’s head, is already occupied by that very covering and has no room for an additional binding; it bears the burden of its humility. If she ought not to be seen with her head uncovered because of the angels, much more, perhaps, would she then scandalize those crowned ones by wearing a crown (1 Cor. 11:10).

[Note: [Col. 0097C] “Much more, perhaps, would she then scandalize those crowned ones.” He alludes to those twenty-four elders crowned with golden crowns, Rev. 4:4. If a woman with uncovered head scandalizes the angels, much [Col. 0097D] more would she with crowned head scandalize those crowned elders. RIG.]

For what is a crown upon a woman’s head but a procuress of beauty, the supreme badge of wantonness, the uttermost denial of modesty, and a compound of enticement? For this reason, too, from the Apostle’s point of view a woman will not be adorned too elaborately, so that she may not even be crowned by an artful arrangement of her hair. Yet he who is both the man’s head and the woman’s countenance (1 Tim. 2:5), Christ Jesus, what garland, I ask you, underwent on behalf of both sexes (Matt. [Col. 0098B] 27:29)? One, I think, of thorns and thistles, as a figure of the sins which the soil of our flesh brought forth for us, but which the power of the cross removed, blunting every sting of death through the endurance of the Lord’s head (Isa. 53:5). Certainly, apart from the figure, the insult is manifest, and the shame and dishonor, together with the savagery entwined in them, which then both befouled and lacerated the Lord’s temples.

This was so that you might now be crowned with laurel, myrtle, olive, some splendid foliage, and—what is more serviceable—with hundred-petaled roses gathered from the garden of Midas,

[Note: [Col. 0097D] “And—what is more serviceable—with hundred-petaled roses gathered from the garden of Midas.” Rhenanus’ first edition reproduced the reading of the Dijon manuscript: *Centauriis quoque roris et hortomi delectis*, which no one doubts is corrupt. The manuscript of Agobard, eaten away in this section, preserved only: *et quod magis v . . . . narint quoq. rosis de horto lectis*. Greater credence should indeed be given to this reading, since that manuscript is on parchment far older than the Dijon copies. We therefore follow Rhenanus’ conjecture and judge that it should be read: *Centenariis quoque rosis de horro Midae lectis*—“with hundred-petaled roses gathered from the garden of Midas”—which comes closer to that ancient reading. Tertullian called the roses “hundred-petaled” from their hundred petals, just as in the *Apologeticum*, p. 7, he speaks of “hundred-thousand-sesterce dinners,” and in the book *On the Pallium*, p. 138, of “platters of a hundredweight.” Most appropriately, moreover, he said that a crown made from roses—a thing for sight and breath, [Col. 0098C] that is, delighting the eyes by its color and the nostrils by its scent—is more serviceable than one made from laurel, myrtle, olive, or any other splendid foliage, which feeds only the eyes. RIG.]

and with lilies of both kinds,

[Note: [Col. 0098C] “And with lilies of both kinds”: white and purple. Concerning these there are famous verses in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* X, where he speaks of Hyacinthus:

> Brighter than Tyrian purple  
> A flower arises and assumes the form of lilies, were not  
> The color purple in these, and silver in those.

The poets therefore tell how purple lilies were born from Hyacinthus’ blood; moreover, they bear the letters AI, AI, marks of mourning and lamentation. But as for the common tradition that those lilies are meant in that very well-known verse of Virgil, “Tell me in what lands,” etc., if we may be permitted a short digression, we shall demonstrate that it is false. And why should it not be permitted to weave ribbons into Tertullian’s little work *On the Crown*?

I certainly laugh at the grammarians clinging to the cross which Virgil, jesting with Asconius Pedianus, revealed that he himself had once set up for them. And who would not laugh at Servius, who, transmitting that story [Col. 0098D] from Asconius, perversely torments himself with the most elaborate trifles?

There are pastoral contests in *Eclogue* III, where Damoetas and Menalcas alternately test against one another what each can achieve in song; at last, wearied by competition, they conclude their humorous quarrel by submitting the dispute to Palaemon’s judgment. Damoetas asks Menalcas:

> Tell me in what lands—and you shall be my great Apollo—  
> The breadth of heaven extends no more than three cubits.

Menalcas strikes back at Damoetas with a similar question:

> Tell me in what lands flowers grow  
> Inscribed with kings’ names; and have Phyllis for yourself alone.

Damoetas had asked where on earth heaven extended only three cubits. Certainly no such place exists, nor can it happen according to the nature of the universe that anywhere on earth the breadth of the heavens above the earth should be contained within a space of three cubits. Menalcas therefore does not solve the proposed question but refutes it with another: “Tell me,” [Col. 0099A] he says, “where on earth flowers grow inscribed with the names of kings?”—of Romulus, that is, Numa, Tullus, Tarquin, and others. Flowers of that kind certainly grow nowhere.

In the third book *Against the Academics*, Augustine says that this is called a Tuscan quarrel, when a proposed question appears to be met not by its solution but by the counterproposal of another. The former jest, “from impossibilities” (*ἐκ τῶν ἀδυνάτων*), is wittily refuted by the latter, “from non-existent things” (*ἐκ τῶν οὐκ ὄντων*).

And perhaps, at the same time, Virgil expressed his longing for the recently lost Roman republic—Suetonius reports that Augustus even entertained plans for restoring it—concealing it beneath the simple jests of rustic men, under this guise: flowers inscribed with the name of kings, whom the Roman people abhorred through hatred of tyrannical license, grow no more truly than there can be found a region of the earth where the [Col. 0099B] breadth of heaven extends only three cubits.

There is no reason to suspect that something more learned is concealed here; nor am I credulous toward the grammarians’ comments, as though Virgil himself had revealed to Cornificius or Asconius that his intention in the verse,

> The breadth of heaven extends no more than three cubits,

was to lash a certain Coelius of Mantua. I do not think so frigid a jest ever entered Virgil’s mind. And the writings about Virgil by those whom they produce as witnesses to their story of Coelius—Asconius and Cornificius, of course—have perished.

“But they are cited by Philargyrius; they are cited by Servius.” We shall presently discuss Philargyrius. Certainly, in the extant Servian material, the passage reads precisely as follows: “Asconius Pedianus says that he heard Virgil say that in this passage he had set up a cross for the grammarians, wishing to test which of them would be found more learned; intending Coelius of Mantua to be understood.”

First, then, what confidence can be placed in a grammarian who offers us these trifles along [Col. 0099C] with solecisms? Next, how absurd is: “wishing to test which of them would be found more learned.” Who could believe that Asconius ever spoke in this way? No: from the Philargyrian material it should be read: “Pedianus says that he heard Virgil say that in this passage he had set up a cross for the grammarians, who would ask whether anything more learned was concealed there.” This, certainly, is Asconius—and nothing further. But some petty grammarian immediately added from his own invention: “The poet, however, means Coelius of Mantua.” In the Servian material too, “intending Coelius of Mantua to be understood” was added by the same hand.

Now the Philargyrian material which we possess is generally purer than the Servian; but here, at any rate, it was interpolated with no greater wisdom. For on the verse, “The breadth of heaven extends three,” etc., it has this note: “Among the ancients there was a very deep well, into which they descended to perform sacred rites. The circle of this well—that is, its uppermost rim, from which they ascertained the year’s yield—measured no more than three cubits.” These are sheer ravings and the dreams of a sick man; no sounder are the explanations that follow concerning a cavern [Col. 0099D] near Etna, or “heaven” meaning the entire world, or “the breadth of heaven” meaning the shield of Achilles. After trifles of this sort, who could promise himself anything better thereafter?

It continues: “Cornificius says that he heard from Virgil himself that he touched upon a certain Coelius of Mantua, who, having exhausted all his resources, left himself nothing except a plot of three cubits for burial. Likewise, Ovid Naso: *torificium*—only so much heaven seems open as the *torificium* is open.” I do not see what good anyone can fashion from these scraps of foolishness.

I rather embrace the opinion of those who judge that there is nothing of Cornificius here, but that the name slipped in through similarity of sound with the word *torificii*, or *orificii*, occurring shortly afterward. And we have already demonstrated from the Servian and Philargyrian materials, whatever their quality may be, that it cannot rightly be inferred that Asconius transmitted something about Coelius of Mantua which he had received from Virgil. What? Did this become known to Cornificius but not also to Asconius, who was among the eminent poet’s intimates and who published a book [Col. 0100A] against his detractors?

Let us therefore reject that stale tale about Coelius of Mantua, admitting only the final note of Philargyrius: “Asconius Pedianus says that he heard Virgil say that in this passage he had set up a cross for the grammarians, who would ask whether anything more learned was concealed there.” What follows—“The poet, however, means Coelius of Mantua”—is no longer Asconius’, but some foolish glossographer’s.

So much for the breadth of heaven. As for the flowers inscribed with the names of kings, the grammarians are mistaken here as well, though much more simply. They all agree in thinking that the hyacinth flower is meant, born first from the blood of that Hyacinthus whom Apollo loved, and afterward from Ajax’s blood. They take these men for kings, although neither answers to the title of king. That is the first point.

Next, [Col. 0100B] no poet’s boldness in inventing myths ever went so far as to say that Hyacinthus’ name was written upon that flower. “Read the Hyacinthus,” says Philostratus, “for it is inscribed” (*Ἀναγνώθι τὸν Ὑάκινθον … γέγραπται* [text uncertain]). But what is read upon it? A king’s name? The name of Hyacinthus? By no means. It is the opening of mourning and lamentation: AI, AI. Thus Ovid, where he speaks of Apollo mourning the boy:

> He himself inscribes his groans upon the petals, and AI AI  
> The flower bears inscribed, and the mournful letter is traced.

Moschus, in the *Epitaph for Bion*:

> Now, Hyacinthus, speak your letters, and yet more AI, AI  
> Take upon your petals.  
> (*Νῦν, Ὑάκινθε, λάλει τὰ σὰ γράμματα, καὶ πλέον AI, AI / Λάμβανε τοῖς πετάλοισι.*)

It is therefore established that what is read upon the hyacinth flower is not Hyacinthus’ name but the beginning of a mournful song, “the prelude to the lament” (*προοίμιον τῆς παρηγορίας* [reading uncertain]), as Palaephatus says, or “the letters belonging to the dirge” (*τὰ ἐπὶ τῷ θρήνῳ γράμματα*), as Pausanias says.

Hence, in this Virgilian verse,

> Tell me in what lands flowers grow  
> Inscribed with kings’ names,

those who wish the names of Hyacinthus and Ajax to be meant [Col. 0100C] must now allow the name of one of their kings to be struck out. They must henceforth defend themselves by Ajax alone and say that Virgil used the plural “names of kings” for “a royal name,” and called a man king who was never king. That this is Virgilian seems to me scarcely probable.

But what if we also strike Ajax’s name from the flower? Ovid appears to stand in the way when he says that a letter common to Hyacinthus and Ajax, boy and man, had been inscribed upon the petals—a mournful letter, that is, or a lamenting inscription, AI, AI—so that for Hyacinthus it is a sign or letter of lamentation, but for Ajax a letter of his name. Yet it will not be difficult to remove this objection if we reflect that those letters denoted mourning or lamentation before Ajax; indeed, that even in Ajax’s case they are employed upon those flowers only by way of mourning, since Ajax’s very name signifies lamentation. From this came Ovid’s opportunity to prophesy that the time would come when the bravest hero would add his mournful name to this already mournful flower. It thus follows that nothing mournful is read upon the Hyacinthus [the source reading is contextually suspect], and certainly nothing [Col. 0100D] royal.

Pliny, book XXI, chapter 11: “The hyacinth is attended by the story of the mourning for the man whom Apollo loved, and of Ajax, its veins running in such a way that the shape of the Greek letters AI, AI, is read inscribed upon it.”

On the mournful name of Ajax, Ajax himself says in Sophocles:

> AI AI! Who would ever have thought that my name  
> Would so accord by name with my misfortunes?  
> For now it is possible for me to cry *aiai* twice  
> And three times.  
> (*AI AI, τίς ἄν ποτ᾽ ᾤεθ᾽ ὧδ᾽ ἐπώνυμον / Τοὐμὸν ξυνοίσειν ὄνομα τοῖς ἐμοῖς κακοῖς; / Νῦν γὰρ πάρεστι καὶ δὶς αἰάζειν ἐμοὶ / Καὶ τρίς.*)

Thus, in the interpreter of Theocritus, *Idyll* X, Euphorion, in mourning for the descendant of Aeacus, addresses the purple hyacinth as “wailing through what is written upon it” (*γεγραμμένα κωκύουσαν*). He was reading upon the hyacinth not the royal name of the descendant of Aeacus, but the mournful song AI AI.

Nor do I think the same letters, AI, should be understood in any other sense upon an ancient gem which displays the image of a human figure changing into a flower and which is kept by that most eminent man Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc. From these considerations, I think, it will become sufficiently clear how empty is the conjecture of [Col. 0101B] those who suppose that what is read inscribed in Greek letters, AI AI, upon the purple lily—the poets’ hyacinth—constitutes “the names of kings” implicitly meant by the little verse of Virgil’s shepherd. RIG.—“With lilies of both kinds and with all violets.” Thus at the end of the book *On the Spectacles* he said that the spectacles were more delightful than “either seating section and every stadium.” The white lilies belong to confessors, the purple to martyrs. RIG.]

[Col. 0099A] and with every kind of violet; perhaps even with gems and gold, so that you may also emulate that crown of Christ [Col. 0100A] which afterward came to him, since he also tasted honeycomb after gall (Luke 24:42). Nor was he greeted by the heavenly beings as King of Glory before he had been condemned to the cross as King of the Jews; first made by the Father a little lower than the angels, and thus crowned with glory and honor (Ps. 8:6; Heb. 2:7).

If because of these things you owe him your head, repay him, if you can, with one such as he offered for yours; or else do not be crowned with flowers if you cannot be crowned with thorns, because you cannot be crowned with flowers.

## CHAPTER XV

Keep God’s own possession undefiled for him. He will crown it if he wishes—indeed, he does wish to; in fact, he invites you: “He who conquers,” he says, “I will give him the crown of life.” You too must “be faithful unto death” (Rev. 2:10). You too must “fight the good contest,” whose crown the Apostle rightly trusts has been laid up for him (2 Tim. 4:7–8).

The angel too receives the crown of victory as he goes forth upon a white horse to conquer (Rev. 6:2). Another is adorned with the encircling rainbow (Rev. 10: [Col. 0101B] 1), a meadow of heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0101B] “And another was adorned with the encircling rainbow, a meadow of heaven.” So the old copy reads. Septimius elegantly and appropriately called the rainbow a heavenly meadow because of its appearance, green like an emerald. For so they are described in the Apocalypse: “and a rainbow round about the throne, in appearance like an emerald” (*καὶ ἶρις κυκλόθεν τοῦ θρόνου ὁμοία ὁράσει σμαραγδίνῳ*). RIG.]

The elders also sit crowned (Rev. 4:4), and with the same gold the Son of Man himself shines above the cloud (Rev. 14:14). If such are the images in vision, what will the realities be when made present? Gaze upon those; smell those.

Why do you condemn your head to a little wreath or a *dracontarium* [Col. 0102A] when it is destined for a diadem?

[Note: [Col. 0101C] “Your head to a little wreath or a *dracontarium*.” The ancients used thinner crowns, Pliny says, calling them *strophia*, whence *strophiola*. Furthermore, *dracontarium* appears to have been a word of that age for a little crown. [Col. 0102B] RHEN.—I, however, think *dracontarium* means a crown made either from the plant *dracontia*, an antidote against poisons mentioned by Pliny, book XXIV, chapter 19, or from the *draconitis* gems discussed by the same Pliny, book XXXVII, chapter 10. PAM.—“Or a *dracontarium*.” *Dracontaria* are little chains of gold, silver, or another material fashioned in the likeness of a serpent. Lucian calls necklaces “serpents”: “the serpents around the wrists or arms” (*τοὺς περὶ καρποὺς ἢ βραχίοσι δράκοντας*). LE PR.]

For Christ Jesus has also made us kings to God and his Father (Rev. 1:6; 5:10).

[Note: [Col. 0102C] “For he has also made us kings to God and his Father.” Septimius very frequently insists upon the exalted dignity of the Christian family, which Justin also extolled splendidly against Trypho the Jew: “We are God’s true high-priestly race” (*ἀρχιερατικὸν τὸ ἀληθινὸν γένος ἐσμὲν τοῦ Θεοῦ*).]

What have you to do with a flower destined to die? You have the flower from the stem of Jesse, upon whom the whole grace of the divine Spirit rested (Isa. 11:1), a flower incorruptible, unfading, everlasting. By choosing him, the good soldier too

[Note: [Col. 0102C] “The good soldier too.” He is speaking about that soldier who had carried the crown in his hand rather than upon his head and was dragged to prison for that reason. RHEN.]

advanced in the heavenly order through divine favor. Blush, his fellow soldiers: you are now to be judged not by him but by some soldier of Mithras. When that soldier is initiated in a cavern—in a camp that is truly one of darkness—a crown is offered to him upon the point of a sword, as though in a parody of martyrdom; it is then fitted to his head, but he is instructed to push it away from his head with his hand and, if possible, transfer it to his shoulder, saying that Mithras is his crown. From that time onward he is never crowned, and he possesses this as his token of authentication [Col. 0102B] if he is ever tested concerning his sacrament: he is immediately believed to be a soldier of Mithras if he has cast away the crown and declared that it is in his god. Let us recognize the devil’s ingenious devices: he lays claim to certain things belonging to God precisely so that he may confound and judge us through the faithfulness of his own servants.

# THE BOOK OF QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIANUS ON FLIGHT IN PERSECUTION (C)

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0101C]

—The book *On Flight in Persecution*, written in the year 202, when persecution was already raging, is still a sign of Tertullian’s very obstinate disposition. [Col. 0101D] In it he openly upholds the Paraclete of Montanus, although he does not yet assail Catholics as “Psychics.”

Not implausibly, recent critics judge this treatise to be the same work which, in *On the Crown*, chapter 1, he promised to publish *On Questions Arising from Confessions*, namely, against pastors who abandoned their flock during times of persecution. A dispute having arisen among Christians as to whether it was permissible during persecution to flee, or to buy off harassment with gold or silver, Tertullian, after discussing something of this question orally, was questioned by a certain intimate acquaintance named Fabius and eventually composed this treatise. In it he attempts at length to prove against the orthodox that God’s ministers must neither flee during persecution nor buy off persecution [Col. 0102C] by paying money. Among other things he argues as follows:

“If it is established from whom persecution comes, [Col. 0102D] we can now take up your question and determine from this very discussion that one must not flee during persecution. For if persecution comes from God, a twofold reason opposes flight: because what comes from God ought neither to be avoided nor can be escaped. It ought not to be avoided, because it is good; for everything that has seemed good to God must necessarily be good.”

—I am reluctant to pursue at greater length the other things which he adds in confirmation of his opinion. Anyone can easily understand that Tertullian is raving there with so foolish an argument, which is most openly contradicted by Christ’s example, by the Gospel in which flight is commanded during persecution, and by the authority of holy men. LUMP.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0103A]

You recently asked, brother Fabius,

[Note: [Col. 0103D] “Brother Fabius.” He calls him brother here by the name common among Christians. Who he was, however, is uncertain. LE PR.]

whether or not one ought to flee during persecution, because some report or other was being announced. There on the spot I replied with something suited to the place and time; but, because of the importunity of certain persons, I carried the only half-treated subject away with me, and shall now report it more fully in writing, since both your inquiry had commended it to me

[Note: [Col. 0103D] “To him,” Semler and Oberthür; “to me,” Rhenanus; “and which,” Junius.]

and the present condition of the times had now imposed it on its own account. For the more frequently persecutions loom over us, the more necessary it is to conduct an examination of how faith ought to receive them.

The examination, however, must be conducted by you who, by not accepting the Paraclete as the guide into all truth, are perhaps deservedly still liable to other questions as well. Therefore [Col. 0103B] we also impose an order upon your inquiry, perceiving that it is first necessary to determine the status of persecution itself: whether it comes from God or from the devil, so that how it should be met may more readily be established. For the examination of every matter is clearer once its author is known.

It is indeed sufficient to lay down as a preliminary rule that nothing happens without God’s will. Yet we shall not immediately, by this proposition, give scope to the other reconsiderations, lest we be drawn away from the present issue if someone replies: “Then evil too is from God, and sin is from God; nothing now belongs to the devil, and nothing even to ourselves.”

The present question concerns persecution. Concerning this, for the moment, I would say that nothing happens without God’s will, considering, first of all, that persecution is worthy of God and, so to speak, necessary—namely, for the approval or rejection of his servants. For what is the outcome [Col. 0103C] of persecution, what other effect does it have, except the approval and rejection of faith, by which the Lord surely examined his own?

Persecution is all an act of judgment, through which a person is adjudged either approved or rejected. Judgment, moreover, belongs to God alone. Persecution is that winnowing shovel

[Note: [Col. 0103D] “That winnowing shovel.” Rhenanus rightly interprets the *pala* as an agricultural implement. For he alludes to Matt. 3, according to a similar version used by blessed Cyprian: “because the Lord will come bearing the winnowing shovel in his hand and [Col. 0104D] will cleanse his threshing floor.” PAM.]

which even now cleanses the Lord’s threshing floor—that is, the Church—by winnowing the confused heap of the faithful, the grain of the martyrs

[Note: [Col. 0104D] “Ripe grain,” Rhenanus.]

and the chaff of the deniers. These are also

[Note: [Col. 0104D] “These too,” Semler, Oberthür, and Leopold.]

the ladders which Jacob dreams of, showing to some an ascent to the heights, to others a descent to the depths.

Thus persecution also begins to be understood as an athletic contest. By whom is the contest proclaimed, except by him who offers the crown and the prizes? You read the proclamation of this contest in the Apocalypse: with what rewards it invites men to victory, especially those [Col. 0103D] who have conquered specifically in persecution, having prevailed in the struggle—[Col. 0104A] in truth, “not against flesh and blood, but against the spiritual powers of wickedness” (Eph. 6:12). You will thus recognize that the control of the contest belongs to the same contest-master who invites men to the prize.

Everything enacted in persecution is the glory of God, who approves and rejects, raises up and casts down. But that which pertains to God’s glory will surely occur by his will. And when is God more believed in than when he is more feared, unless

[Note: [Col. 0104D] “Unless when—in time of persecution the Church,” Latinus.]

in a time of persecution? Then the Church is in a state of alarm; then faith too, on active service, is more watchful and disciplined in fasts, stations, prayers, humility, mutual solicitude and love,

[Note: [Col. 0104D] “In mutual solicitude and love.” By these words he means all the duties of Christian piety toward God and neighbor, and the affections of the faithful toward one another as those who cared for and loved one another—things which even pagans praised and admired, in the *Apologeticum*. RIG.]

holiness, and sobriety. For there is leisure for nothing except fear and hope. Accordingly, from this very fact it is also shown to us that persecution, which makes God’s servants better, cannot be attributed to the devil. [Col. 0104B]

## CHAPTER II

If

[Note: [Col. 0104D] “Since,” Latinus.]

iniquity is not from God but from the devil, while persecution consists in iniquity—for what is more unjust than that the priests of the true God and all

[Note: [Col. 0104D] “All,” Semler, Oberthür, and Leopold.]

the followers of truth should be treated like the most criminal of men?—then persecution therefore appears to come from the devil, by whom the iniquity of which persecution consists is performed.

We must know that, insofar as there is neither persecution without the devil’s iniquity nor a testing of faith without persecution, the iniquity necessary for testing faith provides persecution not with authorization but with service. For God’s will regarding the testing of faith—which is the rationale of persecution—comes first; the devil’s iniquity follows as the instrument of persecution, which is the rationale of the testing. For elsewhere too, to the same degree that iniquity is the rival of righteousness, it is material for bearing witness to that of which it is the rival, so that righteousness may be perfected in iniquity just as power is perfected in weakness (2 Cor. 12:9). For the weak things of the world were chosen by God to confound the strong, and its foolish things to confound the wise (1 Cor. 1:27). Thus iniquity too is employed so that righteousness may be proved, confounding iniquity.

Therefore, because the ministry belongs not to command but to service—the command, namely, is the Lord’s: persecution for the testing of faith; while the ministry

[Note: [Col. 0104D] The words “the ministry—for the instrumentality” were omitted for some unknown reason by Semler and his follower Oberthür.]

is the devil’s iniquity for the instrumentality of persecution—we believe that persecution may perhaps occur through the devil, but not from the devil. [Col. 0104D]

Satan will be permitted nothing against the servants of the living God unless the Lord permits it, [Col. 0105A] either so that he may destroy Satan himself through the faith of the elect, victorious in temptation,

[Note: [Col. 0105D] “Victorious against temptation,” Semler and Oberthür.]

or so that he may expose certain people as having belonged to him—

[Note: [Col. 0105D] “Or so that he may expose certain people as having belonged to him.” That is, so that he may show and demonstrate that those who have forsaken God and deserted to the devil were the devil’s people. RIG.]

those who have deserted to him.

You have the example of Job, upon whom the devil could inflict no temptation unless he had received authority from God—not even against Job’s property, unless the Lord had said: “Behold, I give everything he possesses into your hand; but do not stretch out your hand against the man himself” (Job 1:12). And indeed he did not stretch it out until, after the devil had requested this too, the Lord said: “Behold, I deliver him to you; only preserve his life” (Job 2:6).

Thus he also requested the power to tempt the apostles, since he did not possess it except by permission. For in the Gospel the Lord says to Peter: “Behold,” he says,

[Note: [Col. 0105D] “Satan asked to sift you.” *Cernere* in the sense of “to sift,” which the Greek word *σινιάσαι* means at Luke 22, is also employed by Pliny, book XVIII, chapter 11. PAM.]

“Satan asked to sift you like wheat; but I prayed for you, that [Col. 0105B] your faith might not fail” (Luke 22:31)—that is, lest so much be permitted to the devil that faith would be imperiled. By this it is shown that both things are in God’s hands: both the shaking of faith and its protection, since both are requested from him—the shaking by the devil and the protection by the Son.

And since the Son of God surely has in his own power the protection of faith which he requests from the Father, from whom he receives all power in heaven and on earth (Matt. 28:18), how could the devil possess the shaking of faith in his own hand?

But in the prescribed Prayer,

[Note: [Col. 0105D] “But in the prescribed Prayer.” He calls the prayer which Christ, the expert in heavenly law, dictated to us the “prescribed prayer.” [Col. 0106D] Thus Augustine called it the “prescribed petition,” Sermon 125, *On Time*. RIG.]

when we say to the Father, “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. 6:13)—and what temptation is greater than persecution?—we profess that it comes from him from whom we pray for deliverance from it. For this is what follows: “But deliver us from the evil one” (*ibid.*); that is: do not lead us into temptation [Col. 0105C] by permitting us to the evil one. For we are delivered from the devil’s hands when we are not delivered to him in temptation.

Not even over the herd of swine did the devil’s legion possess power unless it had obtained that power from God—so far is it from possessing power over God’s sheep. I can say that even the swine’s bristles were then numbered before God, much more the hairs of the saints.

The devil appears perhaps to possess a power already his own over those who do not belong to God, once they have been reckoned by God as a drop from a bucket (Isa. 40:15), the dust of a threshing floor,

[Note: [Col. 0106D] “And as spittle, the nations being reckoned.” As worthy contemptuously to be spat upon. RIG.]

and as spittle—the nations thus exposed to the devil as a kind of vacant possession. But over members of God’s household he is permitted nothing by his own power, because examples recorded in the Scriptures demonstrate when he is permitted anything—that is, for what causes.

Either the right of temptation is granted to him for the sake of testing, when he has been challenged or is himself challenging, as in the examples above; or, for the sake of rejection, [Col. 0106A] a sinner is delivered to him for punishment, as to an executioner, as Saul was: “And the Spirit of the Lord,” it says, “departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord shook him and choked him” (1 Sam. 16:14 [cited here as 2 Kings 16:2]). Or it is for the sake of restraint,

[Note: [Col. 0105D] “Cohabitation,” Semler and Oberthür.]

as the Apostle relates (2 Cor. 12:7), that a stake, an angel of Satan, was given to him so that he might be struck with fists.

[Note: [Col. 0106D] “A stake was given to him.” A pale, “a thorn in the flesh” (*σκόλοπα τῇ σαρκί*). Thus, in book V *Against Marcion*, he says that the Creator appointed an angel of Satan to strike his apostle with fists. RIG.—“A stake was given to him”: a thorn, *σκόλοπα*. LE PR.]

Not even this form of power is permitted to the devil for humbling the saints through affliction of the flesh unless it is permitted at the same time so that the power of endurance may be perfected in weakness. For the Apostle himself also delivered Phygelus and Hermogenes to Satan so that they might be corrected and cease blaspheming (2 Tim. 1:15). You now see that the devil more readily receives power even from God’s servants—so far is he from possessing it by right of ownership.

## CHAPTER III

Since, therefore, these examples occur especially during persecutions—[Col. 0106B] seeing that we are then especially approved or rejected, and then especially humbled or corrected—these things must necessarily take place universally by the permission or command of him by whom they also take place in particular; namely, by him who says: “I am he who makes peace and creates evils” (Isa. 45:7), that is, war. For this is the contrary of peace. And what war is there against our peace other than persecution?

If the outcomes of persecution above all bring either life or death, either a wound or healing, you have the author of both: “I shall strike, and I shall heal; I shall make alive, and I shall put to death” (Deut. 32:39). “I shall burn them,” he says, “as silver is burned;

[Note: [Col. 0105D] “Silver, gold,” the Franeker edition.]

and I shall test them,” he says, “as gold is tested” (Zech. 13:9). For when we are burned by the heat of persecution, then we are tested concerning the constancy of our faith.

These will be the devil’s fiery darts [Col. 0106C] (Eph. 6), through which faith’s burning and refining are administered—yet by God’s will. Who could doubt this I do not know, unless it is a plainly frivolous and cold faith which overtakes those who assemble timidly in church.

For you say:

[Note: [Col. 0106D] Rigault adds “he says.”]

“Because we assemble without order,

[Note: [Col. 0106D] Semler and Oberthür add “and.”]

assemble all together, and gather in great numbers at the church, the nations seek us out, and we fear that the nations may be stirred up.”

Do you not

[Note: [Col. 0106D] “Do you,” Rhenanus.]

know that God is Lord of all? If God wills it, then you will suffer persecution; but if he does not will it, the nations will remain silent. Surely you should believe this—if indeed you believe in that God without whose will not even a sparrow worth one penny falls to the earth (Matt. 10:29). We, however, I think, are worth more than many sparrows.

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0106D]

Therefore, if it is established from whom persecution comes, we can now [Col. 0107A] resolve your question and determine from this very preliminary discussion that one must not flee during persecution. For if persecution comes from God, that which comes from God must by no means be fled. This conclusion is upheld by a twofold argument: what comes from God ought neither to be avoided nor can it be escaped. It ought not to be avoided, because it is good. For everything that has seemed good to God must necessarily be good. And was it not for this reason that Genesis repeatedly states, “And God saw that it was good” (Gen. I, passim)—not because he would not have known it was good unless he had seen it, but so that by this expression it might be declared good because it was seen by God? There are indeed many things that come from God and come to someone’s harm. Rather, a thing is good precisely because it comes from God, as something divine and rational. For what is divine that is not rational and good? [Col. 0107B] What is good that is not divine?

But if it appears otherwise to someone’s perception, human perception does not prejudge the objective condition; rather, the condition judges perception. For the condition of each thing is something determinate, and it gives perception the rule that the thing is to be perceived as it actually is. If, then, what comes from God is objectively good—for nothing from God is not good, because it is divine and rational—yet appears evil to perception, the condition will remain secure and the fault will lie in the perception. Chastity, truth, and justice are objectively excellent things, though they displease the perception of many. Is their condition therefore surrendered to perception? So too persecution is objectively good, because it is a divine and rational dispensation, though it displeases the perception of those to whose harm it comes.

Do you see that even that evil has a rationale with God, when someone in persecution is overthrown from salvation, just as that good [Col. 0107C] occurs rationally when someone advances toward salvation through persecution? Unless someone either perishes before the Lord or is saved irrationally, he will not be able to call persecution evil, since even on the side of evil it is good, insofar as it is administered rationally. Thus, if persecution is good in whatever respect, since its objective character is established, we rightly determine that what is good ought not to be avoided, because it is a sin to refuse what is good—all the more so what has seemed good to God. Nor, indeed, can it be avoided, because it comes from God, whose will cannot be escaped.

[Note: [Col. 0107D] “Resolve your question,” etc. *Inducitur*, says Rhenanus, properly means “what is erased”; here *consultationem inducere* means to remove the doubt involved in the question. He explains himself when he adds “and determine.” In what follows there is an excellent reconsideration of the same point. PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0107D] “Upholds”: *depends*, Pamelius, Semler, Oberthür.]

[Note: [Col. 0107D] “Prejudged,” Franeker.]

[Note: [Col. 0107D] “Each one,” Rhenanus.]

[Note: [Col. 0107D] “But gives,” Semler, Oberthür.]

[Note: [Col. 0107D] “In the whole,” Rhenanus, Rigault, Venetian edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0107D] “Rational,” Semler, Oberthür.]

[Note: [Col. 0107D] “And now among evils,” Pamelius.]

[Note: [Col. 0107D] “Among evils it is an equal good,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.]

Therefore those who think one should flee either reproach God with evil, if they flee persecution as an evil—for no one avoids what is good—or consider themselves stronger than God, since they think they can escape if God has willed such a thing to occur.

[Note: [Col. 0108D] “Therefore those who think one should flee.” In the Dijon manuscript: *Eo ad igitur*. In the margin there likewise: *Eo ad*, that is, *adeo* (“to such a degree”). RIG.]

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0108A]

“But,” he says, “I do what belongs to me: I flee, lest I perish if I deny him. It belongs to God, if he wishes, to bring me back into public view even while I am fleeing.”

First answer me this: Are you certain that you will deny him if you do not flee, or uncertain? If you are certain, you have already denied him; for by presuming that you will deny him, you have pledged yourself to that which you presumed. And now you flee in vain lest you deny him, since, if you are going to deny him, you have already done so. But if you are uncertain, why, given the equal uncertainty of your fear concerning either outcome, do you not also presume that you may confess him, and that by not fleeing you may instead be saved—just as you presume that you will deny him, in order that you may flee?

[Note: [Col. 0108D] “By presuming,” Rigault.]

Now either both outcomes are within our power, or the whole matter lies with God. If it is within our power to confess or deny, why do we not presume what is better, namely, that we shall confess? [Col. 0108B] Unless, though you wish to confess, you do not wish to suffer. But to be unwilling to confess is to deny. If, however, the whole matter lies with God, why do we not leave it wholly to his judgment, acknowledging his strength and power—that just as he can bring us back into public view when we flee, so he can also overshadow us when we do not flee, indeed even when we move about amid the people? What sense does it make to honor God in connection with flight, because he can bring you into public view even while you flee, but to dishonor him in connection with bearing witness, by despairing of his power to protect you?

[Note: [Col. 0108D] “Bring forth,” Pamelius, Semler.]

[Note: [Col. 0108D] “For standing firm,” Rhenanus.]

Why do you not rather say, on the side of steadfastness and confidence in God: “I do what belongs to me: I do not depart. If God wishes, he himself will protect me”? It is more properly ours to stand under God’s judgment than to flee under our own.

[Note: [Col. 0108D] “Why”: “How much,” Rhenanus.]

[Col. 0108C] The most holy martyr Rutilius, after fleeing persecution so many times from place to place, and even buying off the danger—as he supposed—with money, was unexpectedly arrested after all the security he had contrived for himself, brought before the governor, torn apart by tortures—I believe as punishment for his flight—and then given to the flames. He ascribed to God’s mercy the suffering he had avoided. What else did the Lord intend to demonstrate to us by this example than that one must not flee, since flight is of no use if God does not will it?

[Note: [Col. 0108D] “The most holy martyr Rutilius.” He suffered in Africa with Silvanus and Maximus, as is clear from the martyrology, where the name is incorrectly given as *Rutilus*. LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0108D] “By the mercy,” Rhenanus.]

## CHAPTER VI

“Rather,” he says, “he fulfilled the command by fleeing from city to city.” For thus a certain man, himself also a fugitive, chose to argue. Such people accordingly refuse to understand the meaning of that pronouncement of the Lord, so that they may use it as a covering for their cowardice, although [Col. 0109A] it had its own persons, times, and causes: “When they begin to persecute you, flee from city to city” (Matt. X, 23).

[Note: [Col. 0108D] “It,” Codex Wouwerianus.]

We maintain that this properly concerns the persons of the Apostles, their times, and their circumstances, as the preceding and following meanings will prove, since they apply only to the Apostles: “Do not go into the way of the nations, and do not enter a city of the Samaritans; but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. X, 5–6).

[Note: [Col. 0109D] “Person,” Pamelius, Rhenanus.]

[Note: [Col. 0109D] The words enclosed in parentheses were added by Pamelius and accepted by Rigault.]

But the way of the nations lies open to us: upon it we were found, and along it we continue to walk until the end. Nor is any city excepted in which we preach throughout the whole world. Neither has special care for Israel been imposed upon us, except insofar as we must preach to all nations. Even if we are arrested, we shall not be brought before their councils [Col. 0109B] or flogged in their synagogues, but will of course be placed before Roman authorities and tribunals.

Thus the Apostles’ circumstances also required the command to flee, since the lost sheep of the house of Israel had to be preached to first. Accordingly, so that the preaching might be completed among those with whom it first had to be completed, and so that the children might receive the bread before the dogs, he therefore commanded them to flee temporarily at that time. This was not for evading the danger posed personally by persecution—for he had, on the contrary, foretold that they would suffer persecutions and taught that these must be endured—but for the advancement of the proclamation, lest, if they were immediately crushed, the dissemination of the Gospel should also be destroyed.

[Note: [Col. 0109D] “Among us,” Venetian edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0109D] “Crushing,” Rhenanus, Semler, etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0110D] “For the name,” Junius.]

[Note: [Col. 0110D] “Condition,” Rhenanus, Junius.]

Nor were they to flee silently into some city, but as men who would proclaim everywhere and therefore suffer persecutions everywhere, [Col. 0109C] until they had filled the cities with their teaching. Finally he says (Matt. X, 23), “You will not complete the cities of Israel.” Thus the command to flee was contained within the boundaries of Judea. But no limitation of preaching to Judea applies to us, now that the Holy Spirit has been poured out upon all flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0110D] “Their teaching,” Pamelius.]

Accordingly Paul and the Apostles themselves, mindful of the Lord’s command, declare this before Israel, whom they had now filled with their teaching: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be delivered to you. But since you have rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations” (Acts XIII, 46). And thence, having themselves turned, as their predecessors had ordained, they went into the way of the nations and entered the cities of the Samaritans, so that indeed their sound might go out into all the earth and their voices to the ends of the world [Col. 0109D] (Ps. XVIII, 1).

If, therefore, the exclusion of the way of the nations and of entrance into the cities of the Samaritans has ceased, why should the command to flee, issued at the same time, not also have ceased? Indeed, from the time when Israel had been filled and the Apostles passed over to the nations, they neither fled from city to city nor hesitated to suffer.

Indeed Paul, who had permitted himself to be lowered through the wall to escape persecution while the command still applied, later, at the conclusion of his office and the fulfillment of the command, [Col. 0110A] refused to yield to his disciples’ earnest entreaties that he not expose himself at Jerusalem to the sufferings Agabus had prophesied there. On the contrary, he said: “What are you doing, weeping and troubling my heart? For I would choose not only to suffer bonds, but even to die at Jerusalem for the name of my Lord Jesus Christ.” And so they all said: “The Lord’s will be done” (Acts XXI, 13–14). What was the Lord’s will? Certainly that he should no longer flee persecution. Otherwise, those who preferred that he avoid persecution could have invoked the Lord’s earlier will, by which he had commanded flight.

Therefore, since even under the Apostles themselves the command to flee was temporary, like the other injunctions, that which ceased among our teachers [Col. 0110B] cannot continue among us, even if it had not been issued specifically to them. Or, if the Lord wished it to continue, the Apostles sinned by failing to take care to flee until the end.

[Note: [Col. 0110D] “Abandoned,” some witnesses, incorrectly.]

## CHAPTER VII

Let us now see whether the Lord’s other decrees agree with a perpetual command to flee. First, if persecution comes from God, what sense does it make for the same one who inflicts it to command that it be fled? If he wished it to be escaped, it would have been better not to send it, lest he seem to transgress his own will. For either he wished us to suffer persecution or to flee it. If to flee, how are we to suffer? If to suffer, how are we to flee?

Again, how great is the inconsistency between the sayings of one who commands flight and invites to suffering, which is the opposite of flight! “Whoever has confessed in me, I too will confess in him before [Col. 0110C] my Father” (Matt. X, 32). How will one fleeing confess? How will one confessing flee? “Whoever has been ashamed of me, I too will be ashamed of him before the Father” (Mark VIII, 38; Luke IX, 26). If I avoid suffering, I put confession to shame. “Blessed are those who have suffered persecution for my name’s sake” (Matt. V, 11). Unhappy, therefore, are those who, by fleeing according to the supposed command, will not have suffered. “Whoever endures to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22). Why, then, when commanding me to flee, do you wish me to endure to the end?

Since so great a diversity of pronouncements does not accord with divine gravity, it is also apparent from these statements that the command to flee possessed at that time the rationale we have explained.

“But,” he says, “the Lord, foreseeing the weakness of certain persons, nevertheless in his humanity also pointed out the harbor of flight.” As if he were not capable of saving during persecution without flight—a protection so shameful, unworthy, and servile—those whom he knew to be weak! On the contrary, he does not cherish the weak but always rejects them, [Col. 0110D] first teaching that persecutors are not to be fled, but rather not to be feared: “Do not fear those who can kill the body, but can do nothing to the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both body and soul in Gehenna” (Matt. X, 28).

And thereafter what does he prescribe for the fearful? “Whoever values his life more than me is not worthy of me”; and, “Whoever [Col. 0111A] does not take up his cross and follow me cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV, 26). Finally, in the Apocalypse he does not offer flight to the cowardly, but assigns them, among the other reprobates, a portion in the lake of sulfur and fire, which is the second death (Rev. XXI, 8).

## CHAPTER VIII

He himself sometimes withdrew from violence, but for the same reason that he had commanded the Apostles to flee: namely, until he should complete his teaching. Once it was completed, I do not merely say that he stood his ground; he did not even desire assistance from the Father in the form of armies of angels, and he even rebuked Peter’s sword.

[Note: [Col. 0111D] “He himself sometimes withdrew from violence.” By various arguments and examples, including even the flight of Christ the Lord, which he explains elegantly, he proves that one must not flee. LE PR.]

He himself did indeed profess that his soul was sorrowful unto death and that his flesh was weak, in order to show you, first, that both human substances existed in him, from the distinctive sorrow of the soul and the weakness of the flesh; [Col. 0111B] lest you interpret either the flesh or the soul of Christ as something different, as certain people have now introduced. Next, having demonstrated their conditions, he wished you to know that in themselves, without the spirit, they have no strength.

And therefore he gives precedence to the words, “The spirit is willing” (Matt. XXVI, 41), so that, considering both conditions of both substances, you may understand that strength of spirit is also within you, just as is weakness of flesh. From this you may now know what you are to do from which source, and which you must subject to which—the weak, namely, to the strong—lest, as you now do, you plead the weakness of the flesh while suppressing the firmness of the spirit.

He too asked the Father that, if it were possible, the cup of suffering might pass from him. You too may ask—but while standing firm as he did, merely asking, and adding what followed: “Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will” (Matt. XXVI, 39). [Col. 0111C] But how will you ask this while fleeing, when you yourself secure for yourself the removal of the cup, doing not what the Father wills but what you will?

## CHAPTER IX

The Apostles certainly taught everything according to God; they wished to proclaim everything as gospel. Where do you show that they renewed the command to flee from city to city? They could not have established anything so contrary to their own examples, commanding flight when they wrote to the churches chiefly from bonds or islands, where they were confined because they confessed the Name, not because they fled it.

[Note: [Col. 0111D] “They reviewed all the matters of the Gospel,” first edition; Rhenanus approves; Junius.]

Paul commands that the weak be supported—certainly not while fleeing, for how could they be supported while absent? Or does he mean that they are to be borne with patiently whenever they stumble through weakness of faith? So too [Col. 0111D] the fainthearted are to be consoled, yet not sent into flight.

But when he admonishes us, “Give no place to evil” (Eph. IV, 27), he does not suggest a plan of flight, but teaches restraint of anger. And when he says that the time must be redeemed because the days are evil (Eph. V, 16), he wishes us to gain time for our sojourn, not through flight, but through wise conduct.

[Note: [Col. 0111D–0112D] “He wishes us to gain time for our sojourn?” By *sojourn* he means our delay in this world. He wishes us to “gain” our sojourn, that is, to count as gain for ourselves every day we pass innocently or, as he says, in wise conduct. RIG.]

Moreover, he who commands us to shine [Col. 0112A] like children of light does not command us to be hidden by flight like children of darkness. He instructs us to stand immovable—certainly not made mobile by flight—and to be girded: for flight, or for advancing to meet the Gospel’s conflict? He also points out weapons that would not be necessary for those about to flee, among them the shield by which you may extinguish the devil’s darts (Eph. VI, 16), doubtless by resisting and receiving the full force of his assault.

Likewise John teaches that we must lay down our lives even for the brethren (1 John III, 16), much more for the Lord. This cannot be fulfilled by fugitives. Finally, mindful of his Apocalypse, in which he had heard the fate of the cowardly, he too admonishes us in the same vein that fear must be cast out. “Fear,” he says, “is not in love. But perfect love casts fear outside, because fear has punishment”—surely the fire of the lake. “But whoever [Col. 0112B] fears is not perfect”—in the love of God, that is. Now who will flee persecution except one who is afraid? Who will be afraid except one who has not loved?

But if you consult the Spirit, what does the Spirit more strongly attest by that utterance? For nearly all its words exhort to martyrdom, not to flight. Let us recall this one as well: “You are exposed to public view,” it says; “it is good for you. For whoever is not exposed before human beings is exposed before the Lord. Do not be ashamed: righteousness brings you into public view. Why are you ashamed when you bear praise? Power comes into being when you are seen by human beings.” Likewise elsewhere: “Do not desire to depart amid beds, miscarriages, and gentle fevers, but amid martyrdoms, so that he who suffered for you may be glorified.”

## CHAPTER X

But some, passing over the divine exhortations, [Col. 0112C] instead apply to themselves that little Greek verse of worldly wisdom: “The man who fled will fight again” (*ἀνὴρ ὁ φεύγων καὶ πάλιν μαχήσεται*)—perhaps so that he may flee again as well. And when will he conquer, who, when he fled, was defeated? Does he prove himself a good soldier to Christ his commander, when, though so fully armed by the Apostle, upon hearing persecution’s trumpet he deserts the day of persecution?

I too will answer with something from the world:

> “Is it, then, so very wretched to die?”  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* XII, 646)

Let him die in whatever manner, either defeated or victorious. For even if he has fallen by denying, he has nevertheless fought against the tortures. I prefer what calls for pity to what calls for shame. A soldier lost in battle is nobler than one saved in flight.

Christian, do you fear a human being—you whom angels ought to fear, since you are to judge angels; whom [Col. 0112D] demons ought to fear, since you have received power even over demons; whom the entire world ought to fear, since in you the world too is judged? You have put on Christ, since you were baptized into Christ. By fleeing the devil, you have depreciated Christ, who is in you. You have rendered yourself a fugitive together with the devil.

But by fleeing, you reproach the Lord with the futility of the counsel of all who flee him. A certain courageous prophet also fled the Lord: [Col. 0113A] he crossed from Joppa toward Tarshish, as though he could sail away from God. But I find him not only in the sea and on land, but even in the belly of a beast, where he could neither die for three days nor even in that way escape God.

How much better is the servant of God who, if God’s enemy threatens, does not flee him but rather despises him, confident, of course, in the Lord’s protection; or, if he fears God, stands all the more beneath his eyes, saying: “He is the Lord; he is mighty; all things are his. Wherever I may be, I am in his hand. Let him do what he wills; I will not depart. And if he wishes me to perish, let him himself destroy me, provided that I preserve myself for him. I prefer to provoke his envy by perishing through his will than his anger by escaping through my own.”

## CHAPTER XI

Every servant of God ought to think and act in this way, even one of lesser rank, so that he may become one of higher rank [Col. 0113B] if he ascends to some degree through endurance of persecution.

[Note: [Col. 0113D] “So that he may become one of higher rank.” Thus in the book *On Baptism* he calls those admitted into the ecclesiastical order “higher persons.” RIG.]

But when the authorities themselves—that is, the deacons, presbyters, and bishops themselves—flee, how will a layman be able to understand the rationale of the saying, “Flee from city to city” (Matt. X, 23)?

[Note: [Col. 0113D] “But when the authorities themselves.” By “authorities” he means the superiors and teachers of the Church, in whose hands lies the authority for governing the Church. In the Glosses of Philoxenus, *auctor* is ἀρχηγός (“leader”), αὐθέντης (“master”); and in the books of the land surveyors, *auctores* is used absolutely for teachers and masters. RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0113D] “The deacons, presbyters, and bishops themselves flee.” He reproaches this disgrace in the book *On the Crown*: “I know their shepherds too—lions in peace, deer in battle.” RIG.]

Thus, when the leaders flee, who from the rank and file will endure them urging him to plant his foot firmly in the battle line?

[Note: [Col. 0113D] “When the leaders flee.” That is, the authorities, as he has just said, and the shepherds who are accustomed to be lions in peace and deer in battle, as he reproaches them in *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter I. To these I add the line of Aristophanes: “At home lions, but in battle foxes” (*Οἴκοι μὲν λέοντες, ἐν μάχῃ δὲ ἀλώπεκες*). LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0113C] “To urge,” Rhenanus, Semler; “to urge that it be planted,” Pamelius.]

Certainly the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. Thus Moses, although Christ the Lord had not yet been revealed, and even though Christ was foreshadowed in himself, said: “If you destroy this people, destroy me together with them” (Exod. XXXII, 32). Moreover, since Christ confirms his own prefigurations, he who flees when he sees the wolf and abandons the sheep to be torn apart is a bad shepherd (John X, 12). Such a shepherd will be cast out of the estate; the wages for his service will be withheld from him [Col. 0113C] as compensation; indeed, restitution for the master’s loss will also be exacted from his former private property. For “to him who has, it will be given; but from him who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away” (Matt. XIII, 12).

[Note: [Col. 0114D] “The wages for his service will be withheld from him as compensation.” That is, as compensation for the sheep torn apart by the wolf through the shepherd’s negligence or treachery, although it had been entrusted to his loyalty and vigilance for an agreed wage for the commission. RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0113C] “Harvest,” Latinus.]

[Note: [Col. 0113D] Some insert “or.” Latinus.]

[Note: [Col. 0113D] “For his own compensation,” Pamelius.]

Thus Zechariah threatens: “Arise, sword, against the shepherds, and tear away the sheep; I will bring my hand upon the shepherds” (Zech. XIII, 7). Against them Ezekiel (Ezek. XXXIV, 2) and Jeremiah also declaim with the same threats, because they not only feed shamefully upon the sheep, feeding themselves instead, but also [Col. 0114A] cause the scattered flock to become prey for all the beasts of the field, since it has no shepherd. This never occurs more than when, during persecution, the Church is deserted by the clergy.

[Note: [Col. 0114C] “And,” Semler, Rhenanus.]

If anyone has also recognized the Spirit, he will hear it denouncing fugitives as well. Moreover, if it is neither fitting nor permissible for those who preside over the flock to flee when wolves rush in—for he who declared such a shepherd evil certainly condemned him, and everything condemned has without doubt been made unlawful—then the superiors of the Church ought not to flee in persecution. Moreover, if the flock were obliged to flee, the superior of the flock ought not to remain, for he would remain without cause to protect a flock that, under the permission to flee, would have no need of such protection.

[Note: [Col. 0114C] “The superiors of the flock ought to remain, since they would remain without cause,” Rhenanus.]

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0114B]

As far as your problem is concerned, brother, you now have both the answer expressing our judgment and the exhortation. Moreover, whoever asks whether persecution ought to be fled must necessarily also anticipate the following question: if it ought not to be fled, may it at least be bought off? I shall therefore volunteer advice to you on this matter too, determining that persecution, which admittedly must not be fled, likewise must not be bought off.

The price makes the difference. Yet just as flight is redemption without payment, so redemption by money is flight. This too is certainly a counsel of cowardice. You buy off what you fear; therefore you flee. You remained standing with your feet, but ran with your money. By the very fact that you stood your ground through payment, you fled.

[Note: [Col. 0114D] “Cowardice,” Codex Wouwerianus.]

[Note: [Col. 0114D] “You remained standing with your feet, but ran with your money.” This concerns the *libellatici*, who offered the judges a certificate in which they professed themselves Christians and therefore declared that they were not permitted to be defiled by the rites of the profane, but bought off the penalty by paying money. The Church treated them not much more leniently than the *lapsi*, or those “who had sacrificed to idols” (*ἐπιτεθυκόσι εἰδώλοις*). LE PR.]

But to buy with money the freedom of your person, whom Christ redeemed with his own blood—how unworthy of God and of his dispensation! He did not spare his own Son [Col. 0114C] for you, so that he might become a curse for us, because “cursed is everyone who hangs upon the tree”; he was led like a sheep to slaughter, and like a lamb before the shearer, so he did not open his mouth; he offered his back to scourges, his cheeks to blows, and did not turn his face away from spitting; he was numbered among the lawless (Isa. LIII) and delivered over to death, even death on a cross. All this was so that he might gain us away from our sins!

The sun gave way to the day of our purchase. In the lower regions was our manumission, and in heaven our formal covenant. [Col. 0115A] The everlasting gates were lifted up so that the King of Glory, the Lord of hosts, might enter (Ps. XXIII, 9), having purchased humanity from the earth—indeed, from the lower regions—for heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0114D–0115D] “The sun gave way to the day of our purchase. In the lower regions was our manumission, and in heaven our formal covenant.” He says that the sun represented the day of our purchase, the day on which Christ the Lord rose from the dead. Thus Sunday gave way to the day of our redemption. Through Christ’s death our manumission was formally completed. Christ dying is the purchaser of the household—himself both purchaser and price. The merchandise and household is humanity. God in heaven is the party receiving the formal promise. Christ, the guarantor and price of our purchase, returning to the Father, carried into heaven the earnest of the entire sum. RIG.]

Who is there now who struggles against him—indeed, who depreciates and defiles his acquisition, procured at so great a cost, namely, by the most precious blood?

[Note: [Col. 0115D] “Indeed, depreciates the merchandise.” By wishing what was redeemed to be valued at a few paltry coins. He calls the human being redeemed by Christ’s blood his “acquisition.” RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0115C] “From the price,” Semler.]

It is therefore now better to flee than to become cheaper, if a human being will not value himself at as much as he cost the Lord. The Lord redeemed him from the angels that rule the world, from the powers, from the spiritual forces of wickedness, from the darkness of this age, from eternal judgment, and from perpetual death. But you bargain over him with an informer, a soldier, or some petty thief of a governor, under the tunic and in the fold of the garment—as the saying goes—as though he were stolen goods, though Christ bought him before the whole world and indeed set him free!

Will you therefore assess this free man at a price and possess him [Col. 0115B] at a price other than that which, as we have said, he cost the Lord—namely, his own blood? Why, then, do you buy Christ from a human being, in the human being in whom Christ dwells?

[Note: [Col. 0115D–0116D] “Why, then, do you buy Christ from a human being, in the human being in whom Christ dwells?” Septimius means this: Why do you buy from a pagan person—an informer, a soldier, or a petty-thief governor—permission for the Christian sect for yourself, yourself, I say, a Christian who, if you are a Christian, have Christ within you? Why do you buy with money the spirit of Christ—that is, permission for you to live as a Christian? Thus Septimius will soon say: “It is not fitting that Christ should have a monetary price.” RIG.]

Simon likewise attempted no different thing when he offered the Apostles money for the spirit of Christ. Therefore this man too, who by redeeming himself redeems Christ’s spirit, will hear: “May your money perish with you, because you thought the grace of God could be obtained for a price” (Acts VIII, 20).

Who would not despise such a denier? For what does that extortioner say? “Give me money”—obviously so that he may not betray the man, since he sells nothing other than what he will supply in return for your payment. When you give, you plainly intended not to be betrayed. Yet if you had not been betrayed, you would have been brought forward. Therefore, by being unwilling to be betrayed, you are unwilling to be brought forward; [Col. 0115C] by that unwillingness you have denied what you were unwilling to be brought forward as being.

[Note: [Col. 0115D] “Nevertheless, a denier,” Rhenanus, Pamelius, Semler; “a thing from the denier,” Latinus; “let him be despised,” Semler.]

[Note: [Col. 0115D] Latinus adds “not.”]

“Rather,” you say, “by being unwilling to be brought forward as what I am, I have confessed that I am what I am unwilling to be brought forward as—namely, a Christian.” Can you therefore claim to be a martyr? To have steadfastly displayed Christ? By buying yourself off, you did not display him. If perhaps you confessed before one person, then by being unwilling to confess before many you denied him.

Your very preservation will judge that the person has fallen away while escaping. The person who preferred to escape has therefore fallen away. Refusal of martyrdom is itself denial. A Christian is saved by money and, for this purpose, has coins so that he may not suffer, while being rich against God. But Christ was rich in blood for him. “Blessed, therefore, are the poor,” he says, “for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 0116A] (Matt. V)—those whose soul alone is held in the treasury.

[Note: [Col. 0116D] “They have only their soul held in the treasury.” Suetonius used the word *confiscatum*, where, in speaking of money “confiscated,” he means money stored in chests (*fisci*). LE PR.]

If we cannot serve God and Mammon, can we be redeemed by God and by Mammon? For who will serve Mammon more than the man whom Mammon has redeemed?

Finally, what example do you employ in support of buying off betrayal? When did the Apostles, harassed by persecutions, free themselves by negotiating with money? They certainly did not lack it: the proceeds of estates were deposited at their feet, and many wealthy believing men and women supplied them with relief as well. When did Onesiphorus, Aquila, or Stephen assist them in this way during persecution?

[Note: [Col. 0115D–0116D] “Negotiating,” added by Rhenanus and Semler. Pithoeus restored the passage thus: “When did the Apostles, harassed by persecutions, free themselves by negotiating with money?” RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0115D] “Negotiating” is absent here in Rhenanus and Semler.]

Indeed, when the governor Felix hoped that he would receive money for Paul from the disciples, a matter about which he also conferred privately with Paul himself, neither Paul paid for himself nor did his disciples pay for him. Those were, of course, the disciples who wept because he persisted in going to Jerusalem and did not guard against the persecutions foretold for him there, but finally said: “The will of God be done” [Col. 0116B] (Acts XXI, 14).

[Note: [Col. 0116C] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür add “nor.”]

[Note: [Col. 0116D] “The will of God be done.” Justin, *Second Apology for the Christians*: “Let that which is pleasing to God come to pass” (*ὃ φίλον τῷ Θεῷ, τοῦτο γενέσθω*). RIG.]

What will was this? Certainly that he should suffer for the Lord’s name, not that he should be bought off. For just as Christ laid down his life for us (1 John III, 16), so must we do for him; and not only for him, but indeed also for the brethren on his account. Teaching this, John pronounced that money was not to be paid even for the brethren, but that one should rather die. It makes no difference whether you ought not to redeem a Christian or purchase one. And that this is indeed God’s will is plain.

Look at the condition of kingdoms and empires, certainly disposed by God, [Col. 0116C] in whose hand is the king’s heart (Prov. XXI, 1). Every day so many means are devised for increasing the treasury—censuses, customs duties, levies, and taxes. Yet never to this day has any such plan been devised concerning Christians, to make them liable for some payment to redeem their lives and sect, although an immense revenue might be reaped from so great a multitude, which is unknown to no one.

[Note: [Col. 0116D] “From the summit,” Pamelius, Paris edition, Franeker.]

[Note: [Col. 0116D] “With the condition arranged,” Pamelius, Franeker, Paris edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0116D] “Nor has any such plan ever yet been devised concerning Christians,” etc. But it is gathered from what is read in Cyprian concerning the *libellatici* that this was done not long afterward. RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0116D] “Under some payment for redemption,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.]

Bought with blood, rewarded with blood, we owe no coin for our head, because Christ is our Head. It is not fitting that Christ should have a monetary price. How could martyrdoms take place for the Lord’s glory [Col. 0117A] if we purchased permission for our sect by a tax? Therefore, whoever bargains for that permission by payment opposes the divine dispensation.

[Note: [Col. 0116D] “Counted,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.]

Since, then, Caesar has imposed upon us no such arrangement for a tax-paying sect, nor could such an arrangement ever be imposed, with Antichrist now drawing near and panting for Christians’ blood, not their money, how can Scripture be cited to me: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s”?

[Note: [Col. 0117C–0117D] “With Antichrist now drawing near.” Judas, similarly extending his work on Daniel’s weeks to Severus’s tenth year, appears to have predicted Antichrist’s advent at that time. The blessed Jerome reports this in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, as does Nicephorus, Book V, chapter 35. In this, says blessed Jerome there, he is convicted of error; but he wrote this because the magnitude of the persecution threatened the immediate destruction of the world. PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0117C] “Can you,” Junius.]

A soldier, informer, or enemy extorts me while exacting nothing for Caesar; indeed, he acts against Caesar when, for payment, he releases a Christian who is guilty under human laws. The denarius I owe Caesar is a different one: it belongs to Caesar and was the subject then under discussion—the tribute coin, owed by taxpayers, of course, not by free persons.

Or how shall I render to God the things that are God’s? Surely, likewise, by rendering his image and coin, [Col. 0117B] stamped with his name—that is, the Christian human being.

[Note: [Col. 0117D] “His image and coin, that is, the Christian human being.” Ignatius, *Epistle to the Magnesians*: “The God-fearing human being is a coin struck by God” (*ὁ θεοσεβὴς ἄνθρωπος, νόμισμον ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ χαραχθέν*). RIG.]

And what do I owe God, corresponding to the denarius owed Caesar, except the blood that his Son poured out for me? But if I owe God both the human being and my blood, and I am now at the time when he demands what I owe him, I plainly defraud God by acting so that I need not pay what I owe. I have admirably observed the command—rendering to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s while denying to God the things that are God’s!

[Note: [Col. 0117C] “But,” Oberthür, Semler, Rhenanus.]

## CHAPTER XIII
But I shall also give to everyone who asks of me (Matt. 5:42). This concerns almsgiving, not extortion. “Who asks,” he says. Now, one who extorts [Note: [Col. 0117C] Oberth., Seml., Pam., and Rhen. read *incutit*, “strikes fear.”] does not ask. One who threatens unless he receives does not request, but extorts. He does not await alms who comes not as one to be pitied [Col. 0117C] but as one to be feared. I shall therefore give in the name of mercy [Note: [Col. 0117C] Rhen. reads *misericordiam*, “mercy.”], not of my timidity—where the recipient honors God and returns a blessing to me, not where he believes that he himself has conferred the greater benefit and, [Note: [Col. 0117D] “Looking upon his booty, he says, ‘It comes from guilt.’” That is, the extortioner, looking upon the coins upon receipt of which he has released a Christian already arrested, says: “This comes from guilt. This,” he says, “is the payment for a criminal whom I released. This is the price of my breach of duty and treachery.”] looking upon his booty, says: “It comes from guilt.”

[Note: [Col. 0117D] “I shall feed even an enemy.” These are the words of a Christian about to negotiate the purchase of immunity from persecution and to offer money to the soldier, informer, or hostile extortioner. The text was previously extremely corrupt. We have restored it from Ursinus’s book. RIG.]

I shall feed [Col. 0118A] even an enemy. [Note: [Col. 0118C] Thus Rig.; Pamel. reads: “Because of guilt I shall be angry even with an enemy.”] But enmities have other grounds. Yet he did not say “a betrayer,” “a persecutor,” or “an extortioner.” For how much more shall I heap coals upon this man’s head if I do not ransom myself?

Likewise, he says, “If anyone has taken away your tunic, yield to him your cloak also.” This applies to one who has sought to take away my property, not my faith. I shall yield even my cloak to one who does not threaten betrayal. If he does threaten it, I shall demand even my tunic back. Every declaration of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0118C] Rigalt. inserted *pronuntiationum*, “declarations”; it is absent from Pam. and Rhen., who direct that *sententiarum*, “sayings,” be supplied mentally.] already has the limits of its own [Note: [Col. 0118C] Pam. reads *suae*, “its own.”] occasion and rule; they do not extend indefinitely or apply to everything. Indeed, the very one who commands that something be given to everyone who asks does not give a sign to those who ask for one. Otherwise, if you think that something must be given indiscriminately to everyone who asks, you seem to me prepared to give—not merely wine to someone with a fever, but even poison or a sword to someone desiring death. [Col. 0118B]

As for “Make friends for yourselves from mammon” (Luke 16), the preceding parable teaches how it is to be understood. It was spoken to the Jewish people, who, after mismanaging the Lord’s account entrusted to them, ought rather to have secured friends than enemies for themselves from the people of mammon—which is what we were—and to have released us from the debts of sins by which we were bound to God, if they imparted to us something from the Lord’s account; so that when they began to fail from his grace, they might flee for refuge to our faith and be received into the eternal dwellings.

For the present, however, suppose some other interpretation of that parable and saying, provided you know that it is not plausible that our extortioners, once brought into friendship through mammon, will then receive us into the eternal dwellings. But what will cowardice not persuade one to believe? [Col. 0118C] As though Scripture both permitted flight and commanded the purchasing of immunity.

Finally, it is not enough if one or another individual is thus rescued.

[Note: [Col. 0117D] “Whole churches have imposed tribute upon themselves collectively.” By joining the sequence of their members, they made up a lump sum of Christian taxes. Thus Optatus, book II, toward the end: “And yet you have compelled these congregations to bend and bow their necks and, by joining the sequence of their members, to make up a mass of penitents.” [Col. 0118D] RIG.]
