Whole churches have imposed tribute upon themselves collectively. I do not know whether it should be lamented or blushed for that, in the registers

[Note: [Col. 0118D] “Of the *beneficiarii* and *curiosi*.” Soldiers appointed by favor of the emperor to definite duties or services were called *beneficiarii*. Thus they attended upon the emperor in carrying out his commands. From their school or corps came the *curiosi*, who were placed in charge of the public post and were also called *stationarii*, since they were stationed at posts. Among other things, the first law in the Code *De Curiosis* enjoins upon these officials that they remember to report crimes to the judges. They therefore sought out and denounced the names of accused persons and brought the accused themselves before tribunals and into court. The ancient account of the martyrdom of Bishop Fructuosus says: “The *beneficiarii* were sent to his house”; and shortly afterward: “The soldiers said to him, ‘Come; the governor summons you,’” etc. The anonymous author of the *Life of Chrysostom* in Suidas writes: “being dragged away by the *curiosi* of the city” (*ἑλκόμενος ὑπὸ τῶν Κουρίοσων τῆς πόλεως*); and Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IX, chapter 9: “the insults and violent extortions of the *beneficiarii*” (*Βενεφικιαρίων ὕβρεις καὶ σεισμοί*). Such offices, however, eventually degenerated into breaches of duty, pillage, and extortion, since the *beneficiarii* and *curiosi* generally connived at [Col. 0119B] the wickedness of thoroughly evil men. For they themselves, corrupted by annual or monthly payments, concealed the crimes of tavern keepers, debauchees, thieves, and pimps, so that they even kept at home registers of such disgraceful arrangements. Since they also carried out the savage commands of emperors, proconsuls, or governors against Christians as though against criminals, Christians too eventually began to pay these men money according to agreed periodic payments. Septimius says that it is shameful and disgraceful to the Christian name that Christians too should be reckoned among those paying tribute in the registers of the *beneficiarii* and *curiosi*, alongside debauchees, thieves, tavern keepers, and pimps. [Col. 0119C] RIG.]

of the *beneficiarii* and *curiosi*, [Col. 0119A]

[Note: [Col. 0119C] “Among tavern keepers and butchers.” Butchers’ shops are found in the literary records, and no one doubts that butchers were registered on the roll of shopkeepers. Thus it might appear to be an error that they are mentioned separately here. Rhenanus indeed testifies that the ancient copies read *janeos* and *juneos*, as though Septimius had used *ganeos* for *ganeonibus*, “gluttons.” For in book II *To His Wife* he joined the den of debauchery to the tavern: “Let him hear something, indeed,” he says, “from the theater, the tavern, and the den of debauchery” (*de scena, de taberna, de ganea*), which in the common editions had previously been corrupted into “from Gehenna” (*de gehenna*). Likewise in Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXVIII, where the text reads, “they cry out through the *Jani* and forums” (*per Janos et fora*), one should read, “through the dens of debauchery and forums” (*per ganeas et fora*). Nevertheless, since we know that Christians of that age so greatly abhorred blood and gore that they most scrupulously abstained even from sausages and other foods of that kind, I can readily be persuaded that Tertullian here excluded butchers from the general designation of shopkeepers [Col. 0119D] in order to heighten the foulness of the business under discussion. RIG.]

among tavern keepers, butchers, and

[Note: [Col. 0119D] “Thieves at the baths”: in *Apology* 44 they are called “robbers of bathers.” A soldier caught stealing at a bath was held in disgrace: final law, Digest, *De furtis nocturnis vel balneariis*. Against such thefts servants called *capsarii*, or *ἱματιοφύλακες* (“clothing guards”), were employed; they also performed other services. Paulus, book III, *De officio praefecti vigilum*. Hence Lucian, *Hippias*: “What further should I mention to you on this point—the wrestling schools and the common arrangements of the clothing attendants?” (*Τί ἄν σοι ἐπὶ τούτῳ λέγοιμι, παλαίστρας καὶ τὰς κοινὰς τῶν ἱματιοφυλαττούντων κατασκευάς*). [Col. 0120B] Some here read *balneariorum*, “of bath attendants,” which amounts to the same thing, although in the Glosses “bath thief” is *βαλανειακλέπτης*. LE PR.]

thieves at the baths, gamblers, and brothel keepers, Christians too are included among those paying tribute.

The apostles, with greater foresight, established this model for the episcopate

[Note: [Col. 0120B] “So that they might securely enjoy their kingdom under the pretext of administration.” The episcopate was already rising into a kingdom, if we believe Septimius writing against the Roman or Catholic Church. I would certainly pay no heed to Ammianus Marcellinus, who in book XXVII reports that it arose from such beginnings, were things still more atrocious not also related in the final words of Sulpicius Severus’s *Sacred History*. RIG.]

so that they might securely enjoy their kingdom under the pretext of administration. [Note: [Col. 0119B] A. Neander conjectures that the word *pacem*, “peace,” has fallen out here and should be restored.] For of course this was the kind of peace

[Note: [Col. 0120C] “Christ commanded that such peace be purchased from soldiers by Saturnalian gifts.” Either *saturnalia* should be written, or *saturnalitia* should be said to mean the gifts that, on the occasion of the Saturnalian festival, Christians sent to the soldiers or officials of the proconsul or governor in order to find them more favorable and merciful.... The Saturnalia were days of gifts and New Year’s presents. Hence Martial, IV:

> Sabellus did not have  
> Saturnalia more fruitful  
> in ten years.]

that Christ, when returning to the Father, commanded to be purchased from soldiers by Saturnalian gifts.

## CHAPTER XIV

[Note: [Col. 0120C] “But how shall we assemble?” (*Πῶς συνάξομεν;*) Irenaeus, book III, chapter 3: “We confound all those who in any way, whether through their own evil self-satisfaction, vain glory, blindness, or corrupt judgment, assemble otherwise than they ought.” Optatus, book II: “For the few who, among more than forty basilicas, had no place in which to assemble should not have been called a flock or a people.” RIG.]

“But how shall we assemble,” you ask, “how shall we celebrate the Lord’s solemn rites?” Just as the apostles did, surely: protected by faith, not by money. If that faith can move a mountain, much more can it move a soldier. Be secured by wisdom, not by payment.

[Note: [Col. 0120C] “For you will not immediately be safe from the people merely because you have bought off the military officials.” Even if, by offering money, you have placated those extortioners, the *beneficiarii* and *curiosi*, and purchased peace from them, you will not immediately be safe from the raging fury of the populace. [Col. 0120D] RIG.]

For you will not immediately be safe from the people merely because you have bought off the military officials. You therefore need both faith and wisdom [Col. 0119B] together for your protection. If they are not employed, you can even lose the immunity you purchased; if they are employed, you will feel no need to purchase immunity.

Finally, if you cannot assemble by day,

[Note: [Col. 0120D] “You have the night, luminous with the light of Christ.” Thus the book of Ursinus. I would remove the following words, “against it,” as improperly inserted. RIG.]

you have the night, luminous with the light of Christ [Note: [Col. 0120B] Rhen. reads “with the light of Christ’s luminous ones”; the codices of Ursinus and Wouwer read “the night luminous with the light of Christ.”] [Col. 0120A] against it. You cannot go around to each individual: let the Church exist for you even in three persons.

[Note: [Col. 0120D] “It is better that you should sometimes not see your congregations than that you should enslave them”—namely, to tributary servitude. RIG.]

It is better that you should sometimes not see your congregations than that you should enslave them. Preserve for Christ his virgin bride. Let no one make a profit from her.

These things, brother, perhaps seem harsh and intolerable to you. But recall that God said: “Let him who can receive it, receive it” (Matt. 19:12); that is, let him who cannot receive it depart. One who fears to suffer cannot belong to him who suffered. But one who does not fear to suffer will be perfect in love—surely the love of God. For perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:18). And therefore many are called, but few chosen (Matt. 22:14). The question is not who is prepared to follow the broad way, but who is prepared to follow the narrow (Matt. 7:13; Luke 13:24).

And therefore the Paraclete is necessary—the guide into every truth, the encourager of every endurance. Those who have received him know neither how to flee persecution nor how to purchase immunity from it, for they possess him who will be there for us: just as he will speak during interrogation, so he will give aid during suffering.

[Col. 0121]

# QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN  
## AGAINST THE GNOSTICS: *SCORPIACE*

[Note: [Col. 0121C] *Scorpiace*. In the codex of Agobard, *Scorpiace* immediately follows the book *On the Prescription of Heretics*. In the common editions this book is entitled *Against the Gnostics: Scorpiacum, on the Good of Martyrdom*. Following the ancient manuscripts, we have called it *Scorpiace*, or *On Scorpiace*. For it is also entitled in this fashion, like *On the Prescription of Heretics* and *On the Exhortation to Chastity*, although in actual fact it is itself a *Scorpiace*, a “Prescription of Heretics,” and an “Exhortation to Chastity.” Tertullian gave this admittedly elegant little work the title *Scorpiace*, after the Greek manner, since the Greeks also speak of a “scorpion antidote” (*σκορπιακὴ ἀντίδοτος*). In the common editions of Jerome, however, the reading *Scorpiacum* occurs in the book *Against Vigilantius*: “Tertullian, a most learned man, writes against your heresy—which long ago erupted against the Church—a notable volume that he calls *Scorpiacum* by a most appropriate name, because it has poured poisons into the Church’s body through a curved wound.” RIG.] (C)

## SUBJECT

[Col. 0121A]

He attacks the Gnostics, who rejected martyrdom, and proves its usefulness and necessity. This book is called *Scorpiace* or *Scorpiacum* because they stealthily deceived the more simple-minded after the manner of scorpions, saying that God does not thirst for the blood of Christians and that Christ does not expect salvation from our death. VENETIAN EDITION.

## CHAPTER I

From something small comes a great evil: the earth exudes scorpions.

[Note: [Col. 0121D] “The earth exudes scorpions.” These words do not seem to me to refer to the nourishment of scorpions drawn from the earth. Rather, they should be explained from the fact that scorpions are not only generated from one another but are also produced from decay, from rotting wood, and even from earth. Thus Nicander’s scholiast on the *Theriaca*: “Scorpions are born not only from one another, but also from rotting wood and crabs” (*Γίνονται δὲ οἱ σκόρπιοι οὐ μόνον ἐξ ἀλλήλων, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀπὸ σεσημμένων ξύλων καὶ παγούρων*). LE PR. and EDD.]

[Note: [Col. 0121B] Pam., Rhen., and Seml. read the singular *scorpium*, “scorpion.”]

As many poisons as there are kinds [Note: [Col. 0121B] Pam., Rhen., and Seml. read *ingenia*, “characters”; Petrus Ciacconius, following Isidore, reads *et genera*, “and kinds.”]; as many forms of destruction as species; as many pains as colors [Note: [Col. 0121D] “As many as the colors.” There are several species of scorpion, named chiefly from their color; Nicander enumerates eight of them in the *Theriaca*. LE PR.]. Nicander describes them in words and pictures.

And yet all have a single violent means of doing harm: by the tail.

[Note: [Col. 0121D] “A single violent motion in them all does harm from the tail.” Pliny: “The tail is always engaged in striking, and it never ceases for a moment to prepare itself, lest it fail when an opportunity arises.” RIG.]

That tail consists of whatever projects from the rear of the body and lashes. Accordingly, [Note: [Col. 0121B] Rhen. and Seml. read *perinde ut*, “just as”; Jun. reads *proinde scorpiis*, “accordingly, in scorpions.”] that sequence of knots belonging to the scorpion, with a fine venomous vein inside it, rises [Col. 0121B] [Col. 0122A] in an arcing attack

[Note: [Col. 0121D] “Rising in an arcing attack.” Jerome imitated this in the preface to Joel: “Though the scorpion rise up and attempt to strike with a curved wound.” [Col. 0122C] RIG.]

and contracts a barbed point at its extremity like an engine of war. [Note: [Col. 0122C] “Like an engine of war”: that is, after the fashion of an engine. RIG.] Hence a military engine that launches missiles by recoil [Note: [Col. 0122C] “Hence also a military engine that launches missiles by recoil.” It is described by Ammianus, book XXIII. RIG.] is also called a “scorpion.”

That point [Note: [Col. 0122C] “That point is also a tube.” Likewise, concerning the gnat, he calls it both a trumpet and a lance in *On the Soul* and book I *Against Marcion*. RIG.] is also a tube, open in its narrowness to the wound and to the venom, which it pours out where it pierces. [Note: [Col. 0121B] Rhen. and Seml. read *id*, “it.”] [Note: [Col. 0122C] “Which it pours out where it pierces.” Isidore touched on this carelessly, as was his custom: “A scorpion is a poisoned arrow discharged from a bow or engine; when it reaches a person, it pours into him the venom with which it pierces.” Thus he transferred to the arrow what Septimius had said about the engine and the animal. RIG.]

The season naturally favorable to this danger is summer [Note: [Col. 0121B] Pam. and Franeq. read *aestus*, “heat.”]; its savagery spreads sail before the south and southwest winds. [Note: [Col. 0121B] Fran. reads *velificabat*, “spread sail.”] Among remedies there are very many natural ones [Note: [Col. 0122B] Pam. reads *naturalia plurimum*; Fran. and Seml. read *naturalium plurimum*, “a great many natural remedies.”]; magic also binds something around the sufferer, while medicine meets it with knife and cup. Some will even drink an antidote beforehand [Note: [Col. 0122B] Jun. reads *jam et*, “even now”; Wouw. reads *quaedam*, “certain things.”], hurrying to secure protection; but intercourse drains it away [Note: [Col. 0122C] “But intercourse drains it away.” That is, the remedy they drank beforehand is exhausted by the heat of sexual passion. He seems to be taking a passing swipe at the lustfulness of his own Psychics, concerning whom he speaks at the beginning of *On Monogamy*. RIG.], and they thirst again.

For us faith is our protection—unless faith itself is struck by hesitation to make the sign immediately, to adjure,

[Note: [Col. 0122D] “By mistrust of immediately making the sign and adjuring.” We have reproduced the reading of the Agobardine codex. Yet the reading found in Ursinus is by no means displeasing: “For us faith is protection, provided that faith itself is not struck by mistrust, by immediately making the sign and adjuring,” etc. RIG.]

and pressing our heel upon the beast.

[Note: [Col. 0122D] “Pressing our heel upon the beast.” The Agobardine reads *unguendi*, “anointing.” I think Tertullian’s hand wrote *urgendi*, “pressing.” To “press the beast’s heel” is the same as to press the beast with one’s heel. He will presently say: “But you, if faith is alert, strike down the scorpion at that very place with an anathema in place of a sandal.” To strike a sandal against the scorpion is to press one’s heel upon the beast. Christ says in Luke 10: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions.” RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0122B] Seml. reads *ungendi*, “anointing.” Cod. Wouw. reads: “by immediately making the sign, adjuring, and anointing.”]

Indeed, in this way [Note: [Col. 0122D] “Indeed, in this way we often assist even pagans”—by immediately making the sign and adjuring. RIG.] we often assist even pagans, having been endowed by God with that power [Note: [Col. 0122D] “Endowed by God with that power”—the power to tread upon scorpions, to press beasts beneath the heel. RIG.] which the apostle first displayed (Acts 28), when he despised the viper’s bite. [Col. 0122B]

What, then, does this pen [Col. 0123A] promise, if faith is safe by its own resources? That faith may likewise [Note: [Col. 0123B] Rhen. and Seml. read *sit, ut et*, “that it may likewise”; Pam. and Fran. read *sit, et*, “that it may be, and.”] be safe by its own resources on other occasions, when it suffers attacks from its own scorpions. [Note: [Col. 0123C] “When it suffers attacks from its own scorpions.” He means heretics of the kind he will presently describe. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0123B] Cod. Wouw. reads: “when it contemplates bitter moderation and these things with its own scorpion.”]

These too are a bitter smallness, [Note: [Col. 0123C] “These too are a bitter smallness.” He now begins to compare heretics with scorpions. Just as he said of scorpions, “From a small thing comes a great evil,” so here he says of heretics, “These too are a bitter smallness.” RIG.] varied in kind, yet armed in a single fashion. They are equipped at a definite time [Note: [Col. 0123C] “They are equipped at a definite time, and no other than one of heat.” Pliny: “The venom in all of them is strongest at midday, when they have grown hot beneath the sun’s burning rays.” RIG.], and that time is none other than one of heat.

Among Christians this heat is persecution. Therefore, when faith grows hot and the Church burns in the image of the bush, then the Gnostics break out, then the Valentinians crawl forth, then all the opponents of martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0123C] “All the opponents of martyrdom.” He indicates the Gnostics and adherents of other heresies who attempted to abolish martyrdom and fought against it. LE PR.] bubble up, themselves burning hot [Note: [Col. 0123B] Pam. and Fran. read *callentes*, “skilled.”] to strike, pierce, and kill. [Note: [Col. 0123C] “Themselves burning hot to strike.” This is the entirely correct reading, since the venom of scorpions becomes inflamed when they grow hot. RIG.]

For they know that many are simple and untrained, some weak, and most Christians only as the wind blows and if authority approves. [Note: [Col. 0123C] “Most, however, are Christians as the wind blows and if authority approves.” “As the wind blows” means borne by the wind, with a favorable wind, according as the wind carries them—according as the opportunity of the time grants or advises it. “If authority approves” means, of course, Caesar, the proconsul, the governor, etc. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0123B] *Et*, “and,” is absent from Pam. and Fran.] They never judge these people more approachable [Note: [Col. 0123D] “They never judge them more approachable than when fear has loosened the entrance to the soul.” He alludes to Juvenal:

> And when the trumpets are heard, their blasts  
> loosen your trembling bowels.

Thus fear loosens not only the belly but also the mind. RIG.] than when fear has loosened the entrance to the soul, especially when some atrocity has crowned the martyrs’ faith.

And so at first, [Col. 0123B] still dragging their tail [Note: [Col. 0123D] “Still dragging their tail”: not yet rising in an arcing attack, not yet piercing with their points, not yet pouring out venom. RIG.], they make a gentle approach through appeals to feeling [Note: [Col. 0123D] “They make an approach”: they draw near gently and softly. RIG.], or lash as though striking empty air:

[Note: [Col. 0123D] “Are innocent people to suffer these things?” These words are spoken in the person of Gnostics approaching simple and fearful believers. Such speakers must henceforth be carefully distinguished from the person of Septimius. [Col. 0124C] RIG.]

“Are innocent people to suffer these things? You would think the man a brother—or even one of the better pagans. Is a sect that troubles no one to be treated like this?”

Then they press the argument: “People perish without cause.” “Perish,” indeed—and “without cause” [Note: [Col. 0124C] “Perish, indeed—and without cause.” These are Tertullian’s words as he indignantly examines the Gnostics’ statements. For they said that those who underwent martyrdom perished, and that they “perished without cause”—as though those devoted to God perished, or as though those suffering for Christ’s name did so without cause! RIG.]—that is the first piercing stroke.

After that they strike outright:

“But simple souls do not know what is written, how it is written, where, when, and before whom confession must be made—except that this is not simplicity but vanity, indeed madness, to die for God.

“And who will save me [Note: [Col. 0124C] “And who will save me, if the one who ought to save me kills me?” The beginning of this clause in the Agobardine codex was erased by age. It appears to have read: “And who will save me, if the one who ought to save me kills me?” RIG.] if the one who ought to save me kills me? [Note: [Col. 0123B] Rhen. and Semler read: “As the one who will save me, if he kills, who...”; cod. Wouw. reads: “And who will save me if he kills, who saves....”]

“Christ died for us once; he was killed once so that we should not be killed. If he demands repayment in kind, does even he now expect salvation from my death?

“Does God demand the blood of people in the world, especially if he rejects that of bulls and goats (Ps. 49:13)? Surely he prefers a sinner’s repentance to his death (Ezek. 18:23). And how does he not desire the death of those who are not sinners?” [Note: [Col. 0124B] Pam. and Fran. read “does not desire the death of sinners.”]

These and any other *admenta*—launching-thongs—[Note: [Col. 0124B] Rhen. and Seml. read *adinventio*, “invention.”] of heretical poisons [Note: [Col. 0124C] “Barbs of heretical poisons.” In the ancient Glosses, *admentum* is *ammentum*, *ἀμμαλόγχης*: “the thong by which the spear is held” (*λῶρόν ἐστιν ὅθεν κατέχεται ἡ λόγχη*). Hence the expression noted above: “He attached a thong to this saying.” [Col. 0124D] RIG.]—whom would they not pierce, at least into doubt, if not into destruction [Note: [Col. 0124B] Pam. and Fran. read *exitum*, “departure.”]? Or at least into bile, if not into death?

But you, if faith is alert, strike down the scorpion at that very place with an anathema in place of a sandal, and leave it dying in its own stupor. [Note: [Col. 0124B] Jun. reads *pure*, “cleanly.”]

But if it has driven the wound deep, [Note: [Col. 0124D] “If it has driven the wound deep”: if the dart, driven into the wound, has penetrated. RIG.] it implants its venom and hastens into the entrails. Immediately all former perceptions grow numb again; the blood of the soul turns cold; through the flesh [Note: [Col. 0124B] Rhen. and Seml. read *caro*, “the flesh.”] the spirit decays [Note: [Col. 0124D] “Through the flesh the spirit decays”: through a corrupt love of mortal life. RIG.]; revulsion at the Name grows bitter.

[Note: [Col. 0124D] “Revulsion at the Name grows bitter.” Cod. Agob. reads *inagrescit*, from *ἀγριάζει*, “grows savage.” Hesychius gives *διαπρίεται*, “is exasperated.” Horace said, “the feasts grow bitter” (*inamarescunt epulae*). The sense is, “it turns sour.” Thus in the *Apology*: “The air turns sour as the decuries belch”; and in book I *Against Marcion*: “He corrupted the whole mass of faith with heretical sourness.” Pliny too spoke of vinegar’s “treachery” or “badness.” Septimius says that revulsion from the Christian name is provoked by this sourness. RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0124B] Cod. Agob. reads *ingrescit*, “enters” or “grows upon.”]

Now the mind itself seeks something into which it may vomit. And thus, once the weakness that has been struck [Note: [Col. 0124B] Rhen. and Seml. read, “when weakness too has been struck.”] breathes out its wounded faith either into heresy or into the secular world. [Note: [Col. 0124D] “Breathes out its wounded faith either into heresy or into the secular world.” That is, our Christian brethren become either heretics or pagans. RIG.]

And now the present state of affairs is the very height of the heat, the dog days of persecution themselves—at the instigation, of course, of the dog-headed one. [Note: [Col. 0124D] “At the instigation, of course, of the dog-headed one”: the devil, who torments the human race with canine envy. RIG.]

Fire has proved some to be Christians, the sword others, and beasts still others. [Col. 0125A] Some, meanwhile, after tasting martyrdom under clubs and claws, hunger for it in prison.

[Note: [Col. 0125C] Rhen. and Seml. read “after tasting martyrdom.”]

[Note: [Col. 0125C] “After tasting martyrdom under clubs and claws, they hunger for it in prison.” That is, they long to complete the martyrdoms that they have only tasted, having been beaten and torn by clubs or claws, as though merely grazed upon the outermost skin. RIG.]

We ourselves, like hares—the appointed quarry—are besieged from afar, while the heretics range about as usual. And so the season has warned me to compound with my pen an antidote readily available against our own little beasts. [Note: [Col. 0125C] Seml. reads: “a *Scorpiacum* against our native little beasts.”]

[Note: [Col. 0125D] “To compound with my pen an antidote readily available against our own little beasts.” We have restored the text by following traces in the exemplar such as these: “Against our native little beasts ... to temper my pen into an antidote for healing.” By “our own little beasts” he means the exceedingly dangerous little heretical scorpions born from those who are not true Christians. Of them he said above, “From a small thing a great evil,” and “a bitter smallness.” Among the serpent kind, scorpions are small and moderate in size; and Tertullian is fond of calling a small thing “moderate.” RIG.]

You who read it have drunk it. The potion is not bitter. [Note: [Col. 0125C] Rhen. and Seml. read “Nor is the potion bitter”; Latinus reads, “For the potion is not bitter.”] If the Lord’s utterances are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb (Ps. 19:10), its ingredients come from them. If God’s promise flows with milk and honey, the things that lead there have this taste.

But woe to those who turn sweetness into bitterness and light into darkness (Isa. 5:20). For those who oppose martyrdom likewise transform salvation into destruction, turning sweetness into bitterness just as they turn light into darkness; and thus, by preferring this most wretched life [Col. 0125B] to that most blessed one, they substitute bitterness for sweetness just as they substitute darkness for light.

## CHAPTER II
But we must not yet discuss the goodness of martyrdom until we have first discussed its obligatory character [Note: [Col. 0125C] “Of its obligatory character,” Ciacconius, Junius]; nor must we learn of its usefulness before its necessity [Note: [Col. 0125C] “Must be stated,” Latinus]. Divine authority comes first: whether God willed and commanded any such thing, [Note: [Col. 0125D] “So that those who deny that it is good may not be persuaded that it is advantageous until they have been subdued.” This is precisely the reading of the Agobard manuscript. Tertullian says that those who deny martyrdom to be good ought not to be persuaded that it is good and advantageous before they have been compelled by the authority of the divine Scriptures to believe that martyrdom is necessary for salvation. For once this has been established, it may readily be obtained from them that they believe it to be not only good but also advantageous and useful. RIG.] so that those who deny that it is good may not be persuaded that it is advantageous [Note: [Col. 0125C] “Toward advantage,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür] until they have been subdued. [Note: [Col. 0126C] It is fitting that heretics should be compelled to their duty, not enticed. The Gnostics said that martyrdoms were neither good nor useful in God’s sight, and therefore were not to be sought by Christians. Septimius says that he must not deal with heretics of that sort by persuading them, through flattering but subtle enticements of argument, that martyrdoms are useful; rather, at the very threshold of the disputation force must be applied, by which they may be driven and compelled to understand that martyrdoms are necessary: for God wills them to be undergone courageously; God commands them. And so he brings to bear the authority of the divine word, the divine forces and resources, the weapons of heaven; he draws up the battle line of the Scriptures. With these swords he compels the heretics to their duty; with these crosses and torments he breaks and subdues their hardness. His words accord with what he said to Scapula: “It is no part of religion to compel religion,” which ought to be embraced voluntarily, not by force. Clearly, in that passage he contends that the kind of force which afflicts or kills a human body must be renounced; and he therefore condemns such force as absurd and useless in matters of this kind, because it indeed produces hypocrites, but by no means religious people, still less Christians. RIG.] It is fitting that heretics should be compelled to their duty [Note: [Col. 0125C] “Until they have been compelled to their duty. Heretics,” Junius], not enticed. Hardness must be conquered, not persuaded. And surely that will be presumed sufficiently excellent which is proved to have been established and commanded by God.

Let the Gospels wait a little while, while I first draw out their root, the Law; while from that source [Col. 0126A] I elicit the will of God—from the same source from which I also recognize God himself. “I am,” he says (Exod. XX), “your God [Note: [Col. 0125C] “The Lord your God,” Pamelius, Franeker edition], who brought you out of the land of Egypt. You shall have no other gods [Note: [Col. 0125C] “Gods” is absent from Rhenanus and Semler] besides me. You shall not make for yourself an image of the things that are in heaven, or on the earth below, or in the sea beneath the earth. You shall not worship them or serve them. For I am [Note: [Col. 0125C] “Am” omitted by Oberthür] the Lord your God.”

Likewise, in the same book of Exodus: “You yourselves have seen that I have spoken to you from heaven. You shall not make for yourselves [Note: [Col. 0125C] “There,” Rhenanus, Semler] gods of silver, and gods of gold you shall not make for yourselves.” In accordance with these words [Note: [Col. 0125C] “For yourselves. In accordance with these words,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür], it is also written in Deuteronomy (VI): “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God [Note: [Col. 0126C] Junius adds “the Lord”] is one”; and: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength.” And again: “You shall not forget the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt and [Note: [Col. 0126C] “From,” Junius] the house of bondage. You shall fear the Lord [Col. 0126B] your God, serve him alone, cleave to him, and swear by his name. You shall not go after foreign gods, from among the gods [Note: [Col. 0126C] “The gods of others and the gods,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür] of the nations that surround you, because your God is jealous [Note: [Col. 0126C] “And the Lord your God is a jealous God,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür] over you, lest [Note: [Col. 0126C] “And lest,” Semler; “so that he may not,” Junius], being angered, he become indignant and destroy you from the face of the earth.”

And when he sets forth blessings and curses, he says: “Blessings [Note: [Col. 0126C] “A blessing and a curse: a blessing,” Pamelius, Franeker edition]” (Deut. XI, 27), “if you heed the commandments of the Lord your God, whatever I command you today, [Note: [Col. 0126C] “A curse if you go astray,” erroneous reading in Pamelius and the Franeker edition] and do not [Note: [Col. 0126C] “Today; and a curse if you do not heed the commandments of the Lord our God, whatever I command you today, and if you go astray from the way,” Junius] go astray from the way which I commanded you, departing to serve other gods [Note: [Col. 0126C] “Gods,” Venetian edition], whom you do not know.”

Concerning their utter eradication everywhere, he says: “You shall utterly destroy all the places in which the nations whom you are to possess as an inheritance served their gods [Note: [Col. 0126C] “Their” is absent from Pamelius and the Franeker edition]: beneath [Note: [Col. 0126C] “Upon,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür] the mountains and hills and beneath every dense tree; [Col. 0127A] [Note: [Col. 0127C] “And beneath every dense tree,” Junius] you shall dig up their altars, overthrow and break to pieces their sacred pillars, cut down their groves, burn with fire the carved images of those gods [Note: [Col. 0127C] “Of those gods,” Franeker edition; “of those goddesses,” Pamelius], and destroy their name from that place.”

He presses the matter still further regarding the time when they had entered the land of promise and destroyed its nations: “Take care that you do not follow them after they have been destroyed from before your face, and that you do not inquire after their gods, saying: ‘Just as the nations act toward their gods, [Note: [Col. 0127C] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür add “so”] so shall I act.’”

And also this [Note: [Col. 0127C] “This” omitted by Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür]: “If,” he says (Deut. XIII), “a prophet should arise among you, or one who dreams a dream, and should give you a sign or wonder, and it should come to pass [Note: [Col. 0127C] “Should come,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür], and he should say: ‘Let us go and serve other gods, whom you do not know,’ do not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer, because the Lord your God is testing you, to see whether [Note: [Col. 0127C] Pamelius and the Franeker edition add “he may know if”] you fear [Note: [Col. 0127C] “Love,” Junius] him with all your heart and all your soul. [Col. 0127B] You shall follow the Lord your God [Note: [Col. 0127C] “The Lord” omitted by Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür], fear him, keep his commandments, hear his voice, serve him, and cleave to him. But that prophet and dreamer shall die, for he has spoken in order to seduce you from the Lord your God.”

[Note: [Col. 0127D] “And also in another chapter.” It is enough to have noted once that even from this it is evident that the division into chapters in editions of the Bible was very different in Tertullian’s age from what it is now, since today this passage is found in the same chapter. This will not seem novel to anyone who has examined the commentaries of the ancient Fathers, especially those of Rabanus Maurus, on almost the whole of Scripture, which survive among my manuscripts. The differing divisions undoubtedly arose [Col. 0128D] because at first Scripture was divided not into chapters, but only into books. PAM.]

And also in another chapter [Note: [Col. 0127D] “Title,” Rigault]: “But if your brother by your father or mother, or your son, or your daughter, or the woman who is in your bosom, or the friend who is a part of your soul, should secretly entreat you, saying: ‘Let us go and serve other gods, whom neither you nor your fathers know, from among the gods of the nations which are near you round about or far away,’ do not consent to go with him, and do not listen to him. Your eye shall not spare [Note: [Col. 0127D] “Feed,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür] him; [Note: [Col. 0128D] “Nor shall you pity or conceal him.” The parchment preserves traces of a different text: “Do not desire . . . you shall save her.” RIG.] nor shall you pity or conceal [Note: [Col. 0127D] “Nor shall you desire or save him,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür] him. You shall surely denounce him; your hands shall be the first against him to kill him, and afterward the hands of all the people [Col. 0127C] [Note: [Col. 0128C] “The hands of your people,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür]; and you shall stone him, and he shall die, because he sought to turn you away from the Lord your God.”

He adds a provision concerning cities as well: if it were established that any of them, through the persuasion of wicked men, had gone over to other gods, all its inhabitants were to be killed, everything in it was to be devoted to destruction, all its spoils were to be gathered into all its thoroughfares, and it was to be burned with fire, together with all its vessels and all its people, in the sight of the Lord God. “And it shall not be inhabited,” he says, “forever; it shall no longer be rebuilt, nor shall anything from what has been devoted to destruction cling to your hands, so that the Lord may turn from the indignation of his wrath.”

He also began the sequence of curses [Col. 0128A] with the execration of idols: “Cursed is the man who makes a carved or molten image, a thing rejected by the Lord, the work [Note: [Col. 0128C] “A rejected work,” Semler, Oberthür] of an artisan’s hands, and places it in a hidden place” (Deut. XXVII, 15).

In Leviticus, however (XIX, 4), he says: “You shall not follow [Note: [Col. 0128C] “Follow,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür] idols, and you shall not make molten gods for yourselves. I am the Lord your God.” And elsewhere: “The children of Israel are my servants and attendants; they are those whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. I am the Lord your God. You shall not make for yourselves things made by hand; nor shall you set up for yourselves a carved [Note: [Col. 0128C] Pamelius and the Franeker edition add “nor”] pillar, nor place a conspicuous stone in your land. I am the Lord your God.”

These, then, are the first things spoken by the Lord through Moses [Note: [Col. 0128C] “They are God’s decrees for all,” Semler, Oberthür], and they plainly apply to all whom the Lord God of Israel has likewise brought out of the Egypt of this most superstitious age and from the house of human bondage. But thereafter [Col. 0128B] every mouth of his prophets resounds with the utterances of the same God, who augments his own law by renewing the same commandments, and who announces nothing first and with such fundamental emphasis as the need to beware of every manufacture and worship of idols. Thus through David: “The gods of the nations are silver and gold; they have eyes and do not [Note: [Col. 0128C] “And do not,” Semler, Oberthür] see; they have ears and do not hear; nostrils, and do not smell; a mouth, and do not speak; hands, and do not touch; feet, and do not walk. Those who make them [Note: [Col. 0128C] Semler, following Rhenanus, omits “them”] and those who trust in them shall become like them.”

## CHAPTER III

Nor do I think it necessary to debate whether God is right to forbid his name and honor from being assigned to a falsehood; whether he is right to refuse to allow those whom he has torn away from the error of superstition to return again to Egypt; or whether he is right not to permit [Col. 0128C] those whom he has chosen for himself to withdraw from him. And so [Note: [Col. 0128C] “Thus,” Semler, Oberthür] neither will he expect [Note: [Col. 0128D] “Will it be expected,” Wouwer manuscript] us to reconsider whether he wished the discipline which he chose to institute to be observed, or whether he rightly avenges its abandonment when he wished it to be observed. For he would have instituted it in vain if he had not wanted it observed; and he would have wished it observed in vain if he had not wanted to vindicate it.

It follows, then, that I must prove these determinations of God against superstitions to have been not only established [Note: [Col. 0128D] “Both established and also vindicated.” So the Agobard manuscript reads; in Ursinus’s book, “promulgated.” RIG.] but also vindicated [Note: [Col. 0128D] “Promulgated,” Wouwer manuscript], since the entire rationale of martyrdoms will rest upon them.

Moses was away with God upon the mountain when the people, unable to endure even his necessary absence, demanded that gods be produced for them—gods which the people themselves would more properly have destroyed [Note: [Col. 0128D] “By which they would more properly have destroyed themselves,” Junius]. [Col. 0129A] Aaron was pressed, and ordered the earrings of their women to be cast into the fire. For in judgment upon themselves they were about to lose the true ornaments of the ears: the words of God. The discerning fire cast the figure of a calf for them [Note: [Col. 0129C] “Poured them abroad,” Wouwer manuscript], thereby reproaching them for having their heart where their treasure also was—that is, in Egypt, which, among other animals, consecrated a certain kind of ox as well. And so three thousand men, slain by their nearest relatives [Note: [Col. 0129C] The Venetian edition lacks “and”], because they had offended their nearest Parent, dedicated both the beginning and the recompense of transgression.

[Note: [Col. 0129D] “In *Arithmoi*.” He retained the Greek word for *Numbers*, just as a little later he has *Kritai* for *Judges*. LE PR.]

In *Arithmoi* (Numbers XXV), when Israel had turned aside at Shittim, they went off to commit fornication with the daughters of Moab; they were invited to the idols so that they might also fornicate in spirit; finally, they ate some of the things polluted by them. Then they also worshiped the gods of that nation and were initiated into Baal-peor. Because of this idolatry also—the sister of adultery—[Col. 0129B] twenty-three thousand, slaughtered by the swords of their own countrymen, made satisfaction to the divine wrath.

After Joshua son of Nun had died (Judges II), they abandoned the God of their fathers and served [Note: [Col. 0129D] “The idols of the Baals and Astartes.” Here *Baalim* means the gods of the nations, or idols; sometimes *Baal* is used for a place. Astarte, of whom very frequent mention is made in the books of Kings, was a goddess of the Sidonians. Cedrenus attests this where he relates that Solomon built temples for the idol of the Moabites and for Astarte of the Sidonians; so does Achilles Tatius at the beginning of *The Loves of Clitophon and Leucippe*: ἔθυον τῇ τῶν Φοινίκων· καλοῦσιν αὐτὴν Ἀστάρτην οἱ Σιδώνιοι, “They offered sacrifice to the goddess of the Phoenicians; the Sidonians call her Astarte.” Suidas, however, says that this abominable idol was the Greeks’ Venus: Ἀστάρτη, ἡ παρ’ Ἕλλησιν Ἀφροδίτη λεγομένη, θεὸς Σιδωνίων, “Astarte, who among the Greeks is called Aphrodite, a goddess of the Sidonians.” [Col. 0130D] You will find the same in Cedrenus. LE PR.] the idols of the Baals and Astartes. The Lord was angered and delivered them into the hands of plunderers; they were plundered by them and sold to their enemies, and they were altogether unable to stand before their enemies. Wherever they went, his hand was against them for evil, and they were grievously oppressed.

After these things [Note: [Col. 0129C] “After,” Rhenanus, Semler], God appointed *Kritai*—“Judges”—over them, whom we understand as censors; but they did not persist in obeying even these. Whenever any one of the Judges died, they returned to sinning more than their fathers, going after the gods of foreigners and serving and worshiping them [Note: [Col. 0129C] “Praying to,” Rhenanus, Semler]. And so the Lord, angered, said: “Since indeed [Note: [Col. 0130D] ‘This nation has transgressed my covenant.’ In the Agobard manuscript the reading is, ‘They, this nation, have transgressed my covenant,’ and a little later, ‘and they have not listened to my voice.’ I do not doubt that this is how Tertullian wrote it. But those who feared the rods of petty schoolmasters altered the text. RIG.] this nation has transgressed [Note: [Col. 0129C] “They, this nation, have transgressed,” Agobard manuscript] my covenant, which I established [Col. 0129C] with their fathers, and has not listened [Note: [Col. 0129C] “Has not obeyed,” Rhenanus, Semler] to my voice, I too will not continue to remove from before them any man from among the nations which Joshua left behind when he died.”

And thus throughout almost all the annals of the Judges, and thereafter of the Kings, he administered his wrath against Israel by preserving the strength of the surrounding nations—through war, captivity, and the yoke of foreigners—whenever they most especially strayed from him into idolatry [Note: [Col. 0130C] “Into idolatry,” Semler].

## CHAPTER IV

If, therefore, this [Note: [Col. 0130D] “If from the beginning it is established that it was forbidden.” It is absolutely certain that idolatry was forbidden as the supreme crime. Hence Tertullian proves in his book *On Idolatry* that all crimes are comprised in that one, beginning the work with these words: “The principal crime of the human race,” etc. Gregory of Nazianzus does not depart from this view in Oration 38, *On Idolatry*: ἔσχατοι τῶν κακῶν καὶ πρῶτοι, “the last of evils and the first.” LE PR.] is established from the beginning—both that idolatry was forbidden by so many and such great commandments, and that it was never committed with impunity, as shown by so many and such great examples—and if no crime is reckoned so presumptuous before God as a transgression of this kind, we must understand without further prompting the purpose of God’s warnings and executions of judgment. Even then it was giving support to martyrdoms, which not only must not be doubted but must also be endured, since by forbidding idolatry it had made room for them. Otherwise martyrdoms would not occur; and God had plainly constructed his authority in advance, willing those things to occur for which he had made room.

For now we are stung concerning the will of God, and [Note: [Col. 0130C] Semler, following Rhenanus, omits “and”] the scorpion redoubles the wound, denying and accusing this will, so that it may either insinuate another God whose will this is not; or destroy our God all the same, because his will is such; or deny that there is any will of God at all, if it cannot deny [Col. 0130B] God himself.

We, however, having elsewhere contended concerning God and the rest of the whole body of every heretical doctrine, now draw beforehand the fixed lines for a single kind of encounter. We defend the will of no God other than Israel’s—the will which made room for martyrdoms through both the commandments by which idolatry was always forbidden and the judgments by which it was punished.

For if the keeping of a commandment [Note: [Col. 0130C] “By keeping,” Pamelius, Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür] suffers violence, this will in some fashion be the commandment’s way of being kept: that I should suffer whatever will enable me to keep the commandment—namely, whatever violence threatens me as I guard against idolatry. And surely he who imposes a commandment exacts obedience. He therefore cannot have been unwilling for those things to occur through which obedience will be established.

I am forbidden to name any other as God, lest even by naming him I should fashion a god with my tongue no less than with my hand; I am forbidden to worship or in any way [Note: [Col. 0130C] “How,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür, Pamelius; “in any way,” Junius] venerate any other besides the one God who so commands. I am also commanded to fear him, lest I be abandoned by him, and to love him with my whole being, so that I may die for him. Serving under this oath of allegiance, I am challenged by enemies; I become their equal if [Note: [Col. 0130C] “If to them,” Rhenanus, Pamelius, Semler, Oberthür; “unless to them,” Latinus] I surrender. In defending this oath I fight to the finish in the battle line; I am wounded, cut down, killed. Who willed such an end for his soldier, if not the one who marked him with such an oath of allegiance?

## CHAPTER V

You have, therefore, the will of my God: this wound has been met. [Col. 0131A] Let us consider another stroke [Note: [Col. 0131C] “Nor,” Latinus], concerning the character of that will.

It would take too long to demonstrate that my God is good—a truth the Marcionites have already learned from us. For the moment it is enough that he is called God, so that he must necessarily be believed good. For whoever [Note: [Col. 0131C] “Who,” Pamelius, Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür] has presumed there to be an evil God cannot remain consistent in both terms: either he will have to deny that one to be God whom he has judged evil, or call him good whom he has pronounced God. Therefore the will of him who, unless he is good, will not be God, will also be good.

The goodness of the very thing that God has willed will prove this as well—I mean martyrdom—for only one who is good has willed what is good [Note: [Col. 0131C] Others read: “Only one who is good has willed what is good”]. I maintain that martyrdom is good in the sight of the same God by whom idolatry is both [Note: [Col. 0131C] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür omit “both”] forbidden and punished. For martyrdom opposes and resists idolatry. Nothing can oppose and resist evil unless it is good [Note: [Col. 0131C] “Be observed,” Franeker edition].

We do not thereby deny that rivalry exists among evils themselves as well as among goods. But the present proposition has a different character. [Note: [Col. 0131C] “For martyrdom does not contend with idolatry over some malice common to both, but through its own grace.” [Col. 0131D] The manuscript reads *malitia* (“malice”), whereas the common editions then read “but through its own grace.” We shall therefore owe one part of the correction to those ancient parchments of Agobard and the other to the common books. For the true reading will emerge if we read: “For martyrdom does not contend with idolatry over some malice common to both, but through its own grace; for it delivers from idolatry.” Tertullian says that martyrdom is good because it opposes the evil which is idolatry, and that it cannot oppose evil unless it is good. He does not thereby deny that opposition, conflict, and rivalry exist among vices or evils themselves; for we sometimes experience greed contending with cruelty, gluttony with lust, since both sides in such cases are evils and vices. But, he says, the discourse which he has undertaken concerning martyrdom’s contest with idolatry has a different character. For martyrdom does not contend with idolatry over some malice common to both, as though it were a contest between two evils as to which is stronger; rather, it contends through its own grace, [Col. 0132C] through its own goodness, because it delivers from idolatry. RIG.]

For martyrdom does not contend with idolatry over some malice [Note: [Col. 0131C] “Military service,” Pamelius, Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür] common to both, but through [Note: [Col. 0131C] “With,” Venetian edition, Semler] its own grace; for it delivers from idolatry. Who will not pronounce good that which delivers from evil? What else is the opposition [Note: [Col. 0131C] “To the adversary,” Rhenanus, Semler, Venetian edition] between idolatry and martyrdom than that between death and life? Life will be assigned to martyrdom in the same measure as [Note: [Col. 0131C] “Insofar as,” Latinus] death [Note: [Col. 0132C] “In the same measure as idolatry is assigned to death”: so it stands in the Agobard book; [Col. 0132D] but in Ursinus’s book, “in the same measure as death is assigned to idolatry.” RIG.] to idolatry [Note: [Col. 0131C] “In the same measure as idolatry is assigned to death,” Rhenanus, Pamelius, Venetian edition, Semler, Oberthür]. Whoever calls life an evil has death available to call a good.

This too is human perversity: to cast away what brings health, embrace what brings destruction, seek what is dangerous [Note: [Col. 0131C] “And everything,” Semler], and wrongly avoid what heals; in short, to desire to die sooner than to be cured. For many also flee the protection of medicine [Note: [Col. 0132C] Semler inserts “who”]: many, indeed [Note: [Col. 0132C] Semler omits “indeed”], are foolish, many are timid and wrongly ashamed.

[Col. 0131C] And plainly there is a kind of savagery in medicine [Note: [Col. 0132C] “Medicine,” Semler], arising from the scalpel, the cautery, [Note: [Col. 0132D] “From the burning of mustard.” Pliny describes the fiery effect of mustard as exceedingly beneficial to the body. Caustic force and burning heat are also attributed to it. RIG.] and the burning of mustard. Yet being cut, cauterized, and stretched [Note: [Col. 0132C] Rhenanus, Pamelius, Semler, and Oberthür add “and bitten”] is not for that reason [Col. 0132A] evil, because it inflicts useful pains. Nor will it be rejected merely because it causes distress; rather, because it necessarily causes distress, it will be applied. The fruit excuses the horror of the procedure.

That man who howls, groans, and bellows beneath the physician’s hands will afterward heap payment upon those same hands, proclaim them supremely skillful, and deny that they were ever savage. Thus martyrdoms too rage fiercely, but for salvation; and God too must be permitted to heal unto eternal life through fires, swords, and every bitter thing.

Yet you will admire the physician even for the fact that he generally applies remedies whose qualities match those of the complaints. He gives aid as though by contraries, bringing relief through the very things by which the patient suffers. For he restrains fevers by burdening them still further with heat; he quenches burning conditions by wasting them through thirst instead [Note: [Col. 0132C] “Restrains,” Rhenanus, Pamelius, Semler, Oberthür]; he gathers up [Note: [Col. 0132C] “Corrects,” Latinus] an excess of bile with every sort of bitter little potion [Note: [Col. 0132C] “Potions,” Rhenanus, Pamelius, Semler, Oberthür]; and he checks a flow of blood by opening yet another small vein.

But will you think God—and indeed a jealous God—deserving of blame if he chose to contend with the cause of the injury and to benefit us by matching it: to dissolve death by death, scatter killing by killing, drive torments away by torments, dissipate punishments by punishments, confer life by taking it away, aid the flesh by wounding it, and save the soul by snatching it away? What you consider perversity is reason; what you regard as savagery is grace: thus [Note: [Col. 0132D] “God heals eternal things by means of momentary things.” So reads the old manuscript. Tertullian says that God, who is cruel and grim for our good because he wills human beings to arrive at the glory of eternal felicity even through the tortures of martyrdom, must be worshiped and loved by us much more than a physician who restores our bodily health only by burning and cutting. He then explains and softens what otherwise seemed harsh and grim. Lucifer of Cagliari apparently wished to imitate this passage in his book *On Despising Death for Christ*: “For although the physician may cut, burn with a cautery, and by the burning of mustard lead the sick man through every pain, nonetheless being cut, cauterized, eaten away, and bitten is not hostile,” etc. But there is a great difference between the two artists. RIG.] God heals eternal things by means of momentary things [Note: [Col. 0132C] “Contemplates,” Rhenanus, Pamelius, Semler, Oberthür].

Magnify God, though grim, for your good. You have fallen into his hands, but you have fallen happily; he too has fallen upon your illnesses. Man always gives the physician his business first: indeed, he himself brought the peril of death upon himself. [Col. 0132C] He had received from his Lord, as from a physician, a sufficiently beneficial discipline according to the law of life: he was to eat from everything, but abstain from one little tree alone, which the physician himself knew to be harmful for the time being. He listened to the one he preferred, broke his abstinence, ate what was forbidden, and, sated with transgression, [Note: [Col. 0133D] “He suffered lethal indigestion unto death.” After the unlawful food, he was afflicted by deadly indigestion. Tertullian uses the same verb in his book *On Fasting*: “suffering indigestion from quails even to the point of cholera.” RIG.] suffered indigestion unto death [Note: [Col. 0133C] “Belched unto death,” Rhenanus, Pamelius, Semler]. He thoroughly deserved, in good faith, to perish [Note: [Col. 0133C] “To have perished,” Pamelius, Semler] altogether, since he had so willed.

But the Lord, restraining the fever of the offense [Note: [Col. 0133C] “When the fever had been restrained,” Semler] until it might be moderated in due time by medicine [Note: [Col. 0133C] “Is moderated,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür], gradually compounded remedies: all the disciplines of faith, themselves set in rivalry against the vice, annulling the word of death by the word of life and wearing away the hearing of transgression by the hearing of devotion. Thus, even when that physician commands man to die, he expels the lethargy of death.

Why is man burdened by suffering now from the remedy what he was not burdened by suffering then from the vice? Does he dislike being killed for salvation, when he did not dislike being killed for destruction? Will he feel nausea at the antidote, who gaped eagerly for the poison?

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0133B]

But even if [Note: [Col. 0133C] “And,” Pamelius, Semler] God had set martyrdoms before us under the name of a contest [Note: [Col. 0133C] “Sets,” Pamelius, Semler], so that through them we might test ourselves against the adversary, and so that man, who was willingly struck down by him, might now strike him down steadfastly, here too the generosity rather than the harshness of God presides.

For having torn man [Note: [Col. 0133D] “From the devil’s maw.” Thus in the book *On the Shows*: “The maw of the devil cast down from on high”; and in the book *On Modesty*: “For whom even every more pleasing circumstance has been snatched from his maw.” RIG.] from the devil’s maw through faith, he then willed to make him also his trampler through courage, so that he might not merely have escaped the enemy but also have conquered him [Note: [Col. 0133C] “Have thoroughly conquered him,” Pamelius, Semler]. He who had called men to salvation loved also to invite them to glory [Note: [Col. 0133C] “Those whom,” Pamelius, Semler; “whom,” Latinus], so that we might rejoice [Note: [Col. 0133C] “So that we who rejoice,” Pamelius, Semler; “we rejoice,” Junius] at being liberated and also exult at being crowned.

With what favor the world celebrates those *agōnes*—competitive festivals and superstitious contests of Greek religions and pleasures—has become clear even to Africa [Note: [Col. 0133C] “Was permitted,” Semler].

[Note: [Col. 0133D] “Even now the individual cities trouble Carthage,” etc., “which has been granted a Pythian contest,” etc. The author appears to have taken from this the occasion for writing the book *On the Shows*: a Pythian contest had been proclaimed for Carthage, and this after the stadium’s old age—that is, after the stadium, the place assigned to contests, had undergone a kind of old age because it had not been frequented for many years. He calls “Pythian contest” the one celebrated at the Pythian games, that is, games dedicated to Pythian Apollo. As for *pyctes*, “boxer,” the word is too well known to require further explanation. PAM.]

Even now the individual cities disturb Carthage with their congratulations because, after its stadium’s old age, it has been granted a Pythian contest. Thus, from antiquity onward, the testing performed in stadiums [Note: [Col. 0133C] “Of pursuits,” Rhenanus, Pamelius, Semler] has been considered supremely worthy: to bring skills into competition, to display [Note: [Col. 0134C] “To weigh,” Rhenanus, Pamelius, Semler, Oberthür] excellence of bodies and voices, with the prize as herald, the spectacle as judge, and pleasure as verdict.

[Note: [Col. 0133D] “Where there are no battles.” For contests are celebrated even in the midst of profound peace. Thus in the book *On the Shows* he called athletes “fattened men because of Greece’s leisure.” RIG.]

Where there are no battles, there are yet some [Note: [Col. 0134C] Semler inserts “there are”] wounds [Note: [Col. 0133D] “Some wounds.” The words must be punctuated as follows: [Col. 0134D] what he means is this: “There are no battles,” because there is no enemy; yet “there are some wounds,” because they contend vigorously and courageously and are wounded. RIG.]: fists shatter, [Note: [Col. 0134D] “Heels batter.” Faber, *Agonistes*, book II, chapter 9, wishes to read *calvae*, “bald heads.” I judge that nothing should be altered. The word *arietant*, “batter,” is also used by other authors. Pliny, book II, chapter 82, says of buildings striking one another in an earthquake: “It is harmless even when roofs rushing together batter one another with contrary impact, since one motion resists the other.” Although, from the word’s etymology, it might seem that this is understood only of rams, Virgil nevertheless writes of bulls in book XII:

“When, turning upon one another, bulls engage in hostile battle…”

They rush against the springs. Of fallow deer also Martial, Book IV, epigram 35. LE PR.] heels batter, cestuses tear, scourges lacerate; yet no one will have reviled the president of the contest because he exposes men to violence, while actions for injury lie outside the stadium. Rather, he will consider what those bruises [Note: [Col. 0134C] *Bruise*, Seml.], bloodshed, and welts procure [Note: [Col. 0134C] *You consider*, Rhen. Pam. Seml. Oberth.]: crowns, of course, and glory, and an endowment, public privileges, civic stipends [Note: [Col. 0134C] *Stipends, citizenship*, Latin.], portraits, statues, and such eternity from fame, such resurrection from memory, as the world can furnish. The boxer himself does not complain that he is in pain, for [Note: [Col. 0134C] *Not*, Rhen. Seml.] he wills it: the crown presses down upon his wounds, the palm conceals his blood; [Note: [Col. 0134D] “Victory swells more than injury.” The Agobardine manuscript suggested this reading. Nor do I doubt that Tertullian wrote precisely this. RIG.] victory swells more than injury [Note: [Col. 0134C] *There are more victories than injuries*, Lat. Jun.; *there has been more victory than injury*, Rhen. Pam. Seml.]. Will you consider injured the man whom you see rejoicing? But [Col. 0134B] not even the defeated man himself will reproach the contest-director with his fall.

Would it be unworthy of God to bring his arts and disciplines out into the open, into this arena of the world, as a spectacle for human beings and angels and all powers? To test flesh and soul in constancy and endurance? To give one person the palm, another honor, another citizenship, another stipends? Even to reject some, and, after chastising them, to remove them in disgrace? Doubtless you will prescribe to God at what times, or by what methods, or in what places he may judge his household—as though it were not fitting for the judge also to render a preliminary judgment.

What now if, under the title of a contest, he had set faith before martyrdoms not merely for its [public] trial, but also [Note: [Col. 0134C] Seml. rejects *also*.] for its own advancement? Ought it not to possess some summit of hope toward which it might direct its zeal and suspend its desire, and which it might strive to ascend, [Col. 0134C] when [Note: [Col. 0134D] “Earthly offices also strive after ranks.” That is, they contend for the dignity of rank, so as to obtain first place. RIG.] even earthly offices strive after ranks? Or how are there many dwellings with the Father, if not according to a variety of merits? How too will star differ from star in glory (1 Cor. 15), unless according to [Col. 0135A] a diversity of rays?

Moreover, even if some manifestation of elevation and splendor [Note: [Col. 0135D] *For the elevation and splendor*, Rhen. Pam. Seml. Oberth.] was therefore fitting for faith, its reward had to be something of such a kind that it would cost [Note: [Col. 0135D] *To cost*, Rhen. Seml. Oberth.] great labor, agony, torment, and death. But look at the compensation: flesh and soul are paid out, and nothing in a human being is dearer than these—the one the hand of God, the other his breath [Note: [Col. 0135D] *Inbreathing*, Rhen. Pam. Seml.]; the very things whose advancement it is are paid out for that advancement [Note: [Col. 0135D] *Prefecture*, Jun.]; the very things that make a gain are expended [Note: [Col. 0135D] *Make a profit*, Rhen. Seml. Oberth.]; the same things are both the price and the reward.

God had also foreseen these weaknesses of the human condition: the adversary’s snares, the deceptions of circumstances, the nets of the world; that even after the washing faith would be imperiled; that most would perish again after salvation—those who had worn out [Note: [Col. 0135D] *Worn-out things*, Jun.] their wedding garment, who had not prepared oil for their torches, who would have to be sought through [Col. 0135B] mountains and forests and carried back upon shoulders. He therefore established secondary consolations, final safeguards: the combat of martyrdom and the washing in blood, henceforth secure. Of its blessedness David says: “Blessed are those whose offenses have been forgiven and whose iniquities have been covered” (Ps. 32:1). “Blessed is the man to whom God has not imputed an offense.”

[Note: [Col. 0135D] Properly speaking, nothing can be charged to martyrs. This passage also relates to the affirmation of purgatory and to that distinction—also discussed above in this author, *On the Soul*, ch. 35—which blessed Cyprian states more openly in Epistle 52 to Antonianus. “It is one thing,” he says, “for someone sent to prison not to depart from it until he pays the last farthing, to be cleansed and purified from sins through long suffering, to be tormented for a long time by fire, and to remain pending until the day of judgment for the judge’s sentence; it is another thing to attain glory immediately, to receive the reward of faith and virtue, to have purified all sins through suffering, and to be crowned by the Lord.” PAM.]

Properly speaking, therefore, nothing can now be charged to martyrs, since in that washing life itself is laid down. Thus love covers a multitude of offenses (1 Pet. 4:8): loving God, namely, with all its strength, with which it fights in martyrdom, and with all its soul (Matt. 22:37), which it lays down for God, it forges the human being into a martyr. Will you judge these remedies, counsels, judgments, and spectacles [Note: [Col. 0136D] “Will you even call them God’s cruelty?” The old copy has *call*. RIG.] to be even God’s cruelty [Note: [Col. 0135D] *Will you indicate*, Jun.; *will you call*, old copy.]? Does God covet human blood? And yet I would dare [Col. 0135C] say: so too does the human being covet God’s kingdom, so too the human being covets certain salvation, so too [Note: [Col. 0135D] Seml. rejects *too*.] the human being covets a second regeneration. No one begrudges a compensation in which the reckoning of either favor or injury is shared.

## CHAPTER VII

Let the scorpion still strike, brandishing the charge that God is a murderer. I shall certainly shudder at the filthy posture of blasphemy reeking from a heretic’s mouth; yet I shall also embrace such a God with the confidence of reason—the same reason by which he himself pronounced himself more than a murderer, speaking in the person of his own Sophia, through the voice of Solomon: “Sophia,” he says (Prov. 9:2), “has slaughtered her sons.” *Sophia* is wisdom. Wisely indeed did she slaughter them, since it was unto life; and rationally, since it was unto glory. O ingenuity of parricide! O craftsmanship of crime! O proof of a cruelty that kills precisely so that the one it has killed may not die!

And therefore [Col. 0136A] what follows? “Sophia is celebrated with hymns at the exits” [Note: [Col. 0136D] *Is sung*, Rhen. Pam. Seml.] (Prov. 1:20), for the exits of the martyrs too are celebrated. “Sophia treats of constancy [Note: [Col. 0136D] *Constancy*, Pam. Fran.] in the streets,” for she slaughters her sons well. “Confident upon the highest walls, however, she speaks,” since according to Isaiah one person cries out here, “I belong to God”; another cries aloud, “In the name of Jacob”; and another writes [Note: [Col. 0136D] *Insubscribes*, Rhen. Pam. Seml.], “In the name of Israel” (Isa. 44:5).

O good mother! I myself desire to be enrolled among her sons, so that I may be killed by her. I desire to be killed, so that I may become a son. But does she only slaughter her sons, or does she also torture them? For I hear God saying elsewhere: “I shall burn them as silver [Note: [Col. 0136D] *Gold*, Rhen. Seml. Oberth.] is burned, and I shall test them as gold [Note: [Col. 0136D] *Silver*, Rhen. Seml. Oberth.] is tested” (Zech. 13:9). Assuredly, through the torments of fires and punishments, through martyrdoms that assay faith.

The Apostle too knows what sort of God he has set forth when he writes: [Col. 0136B] “If God did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us, how has he not also graciously given us all things with him?” You see how divine Sophia slaughtered even her own firstborn and only-begotten Son—one who would assuredly live, indeed who would restore the others also to life. I can say with God’s Sophia: “Christ is he who delivered himself up for our offenses.” Now Sophia has slaughtered even herself.

Words possess wisdom [*sapiunt*] [Note: [Col. 0136D] *By the Word*, Rhen. Seml. Oberth.] not in sound alone, but also in meaning; they must be heard not merely with the ears, but also with the mind. The person who does not understand believes God cruel. Yet even for the one who does not understand, a declaration has been set down to restrain the rashness of understanding otherwise. “For who,” it says (Rom. 11:34), “has known the mind of God? Or who was his counselor, to instruct him? Or who has shown him the way of understanding?”

Yet in the world’s estimation it was permissible for the Diana of the Scythians, [Col. 0136C] the Mercury of the Gauls, or the Saturn of the Africans to be appeased with a human victim [Note: [Col. 0136D] *It was left*, Pam. Fran.]. And in Latium, to [Note: [Col. 0136D] *In*, Pam.] this very day, human blood is offered for Jupiter to taste in the midst of the city; nor does anyone reconsider it, or fail to presume that there is some rationale, or that the will of his god is beyond estimation. If our God too had demanded martyrdoms for himself under the title of a sacrifice proper to him, who would have reproached him with a death-dealing religion, mournful rites, an altar that was a funeral pyre, and a priest who was an undertaker? And who would not instead have reckoned all the more blessed the one whom God had consumed?

## CHAPTER VIII

We therefore take our stand upon one degree of the argument, and upon this alone we issue the challenge: whether martyrdoms have been commanded by God, so that you may believe they were commanded with reason [Note: [Col. 0136D] *By a nation*, Venet.] once you have learned that they were commanded, because God has commanded nothing without reason.

For “the death of his devout ones is honored in his sight,” as [Col. 0137A] David sings (Ps. 115). I do not suppose that this means the ordinary death owed by everyone: [Note: [Col. 0137D] “Indeed, that death is also disgraceful by reason of the charge of transgression.” He says this according to the judgment of all Catholics, who, on the basis of perpetual tradition and the testimony of Scripture, believe that human beings die because they had tasted, contrary to the prohibition, from the tree placed in the midst of paradise which God had excepted. RIG.; the editors emend.] indeed, although just, that death is also disgraceful by reason of the charge [Note: [Col. 0137C] *Charge*, Jun.] of transgression and the desert of condemnation. Rather, it means the death encountered in him [Note: [Col. 0137C] *Is heard*, Seml.] through the testimony of religion and the battle of confession, for righteousness and the sacrament—as in Isaiah (57:1): “See [Note: [Col. 0137C] *See*, singular, Seml.],” he says, “how the righteous man perishes, and no one takes it to heart; righteous men are taken away, and no one notices. For the righteous man perishes from before injustice, and his burial [Note: [Col. 0137C] *Of his burial*, Pam. Rhen. Seml.] shall be held in honor.”

Here too you have both the proclamation and the recompense of martyrdoms. For from the beginning righteousness has suffered violence. As soon as God began to be worshiped, religion incurred envy: the man who had pleased God was killed, and indeed by his brother, so that impiety might the more readily pursue [Note: [Col. 0137C] *Attack*, Seml.] another’s blood, having made its beginning with its own [Note: [Col. 0137C] Seml. inserts *having attacked*.]. Finally, this was so not only of the righteous, but [Col. 0137B] also of the prophets. David is harassed, Elijah put to flight, Jeremiah stoned, Isaiah sawn apart, Zechariah slaughtered between the altar and the temple, leaving the enduring stains of his blood upon the flints. The very conclusion of the Law and the Prophets, called not a prophet but an angel, is beheaded in an insulting execution [Note: [Col. 0137D] “As the payment of a dancing girl.” Dom. Latinius refers us to Festus. There Joseph Scaliger, citing this passage of Tertullian, says that *lucar* denotes the payment of dancers, which Charisius and the glossographers call θεατρικόν (*theatrikón*, “theater-payment”); and that Tacitus too used it in this sense in *Annals* I: “the *lucar* of actors was curtailed in the time of Tiberius,” and Livy in Book III: “the gift of the *lucar* earned,” which was ordered to be sent to Pythian Apollo. This is elegantly expressed, inasmuch as the head of blessed John the Baptist was given as the reward of the dancing girl, whom he calls *saltica* in his own terminology. PAM.] as the payment of a lyre-playing girl [Note: [Col. 0138C] *Dancing girl*, Seml.].

And assuredly those who were moved by the Spirit of God were directed by him toward martyrdoms, so that by now [Note: [Col. 0138C] *Also*, Seml.] suffering the things they had also proclaimed, they might confirm them. Likewise, when the dedication of the royal image pressed the city [Note: [Col. 0138C] *Crowd*, Jun.] into service, the brotherhood of three did not fail to understand what faith—which alone had not been taken captive in them—demanded: namely, that they must die in resistance to idolatry.

[Note: [Col. 0137D] “For they remembered Jeremiah,” etc. Whatever is today contained in the Book of Baruch was once attributed to Jeremiah by the Fathers; and thus they also agreed concerning the canonical authority of that writing. This author agrees with them, citing under Jeremiah’s name what is found in Baruch 6. PAM.]

For they remembered Jeremiah writing to those upon whom that captivity was impending (Baruch 6): “And now you will see the gods of the Babylonians, of gold and silver and wood, carried upon shoulders, [Col. 0137C] displaying terror to the nations. Take care, therefore, that you too do not become like the foreigners and are not seized by fear when you see the crowds worshiping behind and before them; but say in your heart: ‘You, Lord, we ought to worship.’”

And so, with confidence conceived from God, they spoke when, by the vigor of their spirit, they cast off the king’s conditional threats (Dan. 3:16): “We have no need to answer this command of yours. [Col. 0138A] For our God whom we worship is able to rescue us from the furnace of fire and from your hands; and then it will become plain to you that we shall neither serve your idol nor worship your golden image, which you have erected.”

O martyrdom perfect even without suffering! They had suffered enough, they had been burned enough; God protected them precisely so that they might not seem to have given the lie to his power. For Daniel too—[Note: [Col. 0138D] “Daniel, a suppliant to none but God.” He touched upon this history in ch. 5 of *On Idolatry*, though that passage does not agree entirely with this one. For here Daniel is said to be a suppliant to none but God, whereas there he is “submissive to Darius in other matters,” that is, compliant. Yet that kind of obedience concerned secular matters, while here the subject is religion and the worship of the true God. LE PR.] a suppliant to none but God, and for that reason denounced and demanded by the Chaldeans—the shut-up and accustomed savagery of the lions would surely have devoured immediately, if Darius’s worthy confidence concerning God had been destined to prove false.

Otherwise, every preacher and worshiper of God who, when summoned to idolatry, refused obedience had to suffer, also in accordance with the principle by which [Note: [Col. 0138C] *Because*, Seml.] the truth had to be commended both to those then present and thereafter to posterity, since the suffering of its own defenders would bear faithful testimony on its behalf; for no one would have been willing to be killed unless he possessed the truth. Such commandments and examples from the beginning show that faith is indebted to martyrdom.

## CHAPTER IX

It remains—[Note: [Col. 0138D] “Lest antiquity too had its own sacrament.” That is: lest anyone suppose that martyrdoms were ordained in the Old Testament but not the New, by the Law but not by the Gospel. He therefore calls it the sacrament of martyrdom. RIG.] lest antiquity [Note: [Col. 0138D] “Its own sacrament.” That is, one proper and peculiar to antiquity, namely to the Jews, and not also to be shared with Christian newness. RIG.] should have had a sacrament of its own—to examine Christian newness, as though it derived from another God and consequently had a rival discipline as well, whose Sophia did not know how to slaughter her sons. Certainly, there must be in Christ another [Note: [Col. 0138C] Seml. omits *and*.] divinity, will, and school, [Note: [Col. 0138C] Seml. adds *and*, as does the Wouwer manuscript.] which has commanded that martyrdoms either do not exist at all or must be understood otherwise; a Christ who exhorts no one to a crisis of this kind, who promises nothing to those who suffer for him, because he does not wish them to suffer!

And therefore, when setting out the first principles of his commandments, he says: “Blessed are those [Col. 0138C] who suffer persecution for righteousness, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:10). This indeed is addressed without qualification to everyone; then, specifically to the apostles themselves: “You will be blessed when they dishonor and persecute you and say every evil thing against you because of me. Rejoice and exult, because your reward is very great in heaven; for thus their fathers used to treat the prophets also” (Matt. 5:11). Thus [Col. 0139A] he also prophesied that they themselves would have to be killed after the example of the prophets.

And even if he had directed this whole conditional persecution only toward the apostles of that time, yet through them, together with the entire sacrament, the propagation of the name, and the transmission of the Holy Spirit, the discipline of undergoing persecution would also have extended to us, as hereditary disciples and shoots of apostolic seed.
