For again he directs his words to the apostles (Matt. 10:16): “Behold, I send you like sheep into the midst of wolves”; and (v. 17): “Beware of men, for they will hand you over to councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you, and you will be brought before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the nations,” etc. But when he adds (v. 21), “Brother will hand brother over to death, and the father his son, and children will rise up against [Col. 0139B] their parents and put them to death,” he plainly pronounced this iniquity against others as well, since we do not find it among the apostles. For none of them suffered either a brother or a father as betrayer, whereas very many of our people already have.

He then turns back to the apostles (v. 22): “And you will be hated by everyone because of my name.” How much more shall we, who must also be betrayed by our parents? Thus, by means of this very intermingling, arranging his discourse now toward the apostles, now toward everyone, he poured out upon all the same consequence of bearing the name, wherever the name has settled together with the law of the hatred directed against it.

“But the one who endures to the end will be saved” (ibid.). By enduring what, except persecution, betrayal, and killing? For to endure to the end is nothing other than to suffer one’s end. And therefore: “The disciple is not above the master” (ibid., v. 25). Immediately there follows: “Nor is the servant [Col. 0139C] above his lord”; because, since the Master and Lord himself endured persecution, betrayal, and killing, much more will servants and disciples have to pay the same, lest, as though superior, they appear exempted from iniquity—when this very thing ought to suffice them for glory: to be made equal to the Lord and Master in his sufferings.

Building them up for endurance of these things, he warns (ibid., v. 28) that they must not fear those who kill only the body but are unable to kill the soul; rather, fear must be consecrated to him who can kill and destroy both body and soul in Gehenna. Who are these killers of the body alone, except the governors and kings mentioned above? Human beings, I think. And who is master of the soul as well, except God alone? Who is this threatener with fires, except he without whose will not even one of the sparrows [Col. 0139D] falls to the ground—that is, neither one of the two substances of the human being, flesh or soul? For even the number of the hairs is entered in his register (ibid., v. 31).

“Therefore do not fear,” [Col. 0140A] he says above, “for you surpass many sparrows.” He promises that we will fall to the ground not in vain—that is, not without reward—if we choose to be killed by human beings rather than by God.

“Therefore everyone who confesses in me before human beings, I too will confess in him before my Father who is in heaven. And everyone who denies me before human beings, I too will deny him before my Father who is in heaven” (ibid., v. 33). This is, I think, a manifest definition and rationale [Note: [Col. 0139D] *Both a definition and a rationale*, Seml.] both of confession and of denial, even though the formulation differs.

The person who confesses himself a Christian testifies that he belongs to Christ. One who belongs to Christ must necessarily be in Christ. If he is in Christ, he assuredly confesses in Christ when he confesses himself a Christian; for he cannot be this unless he is in Christ. Moreover, by confessing in Christ, one who is in Christ also confesses Christ, since Christ too is in him, inasmuch as he is a Christian. For even if [Note: [Col. 0139D] *As if*, Wouwer manuscript.] you say “day,” you show [Note: [Col. 0139D] *You have shown*, Seml.] the reality of the light that produces the day, though you have not said “light.”

Thus, although he did not pronounce directly, “The one who confesses me,” the act of everyday confession does not differ from the meaning of the Lord’s pronouncement. For the one who confesses what he is—that is, a Christian—also confesses that through which he is what he is—that is, Christ.

Likewise, the one who has denied himself to be a Christian has denied in Christ, by denying that he is in Christ when he denies that he is a Christian; and, by denying Christ in himself when he denies himself to be in Christ, he will also deny Christ himself. Thus both the one who denies in Christ will deny Christ, and the one who confesses in Christ will confess Christ.

It would therefore have sufficed even if the Lord had pronounced only concerning confession. For from the form of confession a preliminary judgment would also be rendered concerning its contrary, namely denial: that the Lord repays denial [Note: [Col. 0139D] *By denial*, Seml.] with denial, just as he repays confession [Note: [Col. 0140D] *By confession*, Seml.] with confession.

And therefore, since in the form of confession the condition of denial is also understood, it is evident that what the Lord pronounced differently concerning denial than concerning confession belongs to another mode of denial, since he said, “The one who denies me,” not “The one who denies in me.” For he had foreseen that this coercion too would very often follow in the assault upon the name: [Note: [Col. 0139D] namely, that the one who had denied himself to be a Christian would be compelled to deny Christ himself as well by blaspheming him. Something of this kind is related by Pliny: those named by an informer as people who called themselves Christians, after being arrested, denied it, and at last even cursed Christ. RIG.] namely, that the one who had denied himself to be a Christian would be compelled to deny Christ himself as well by blaspheming him.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] “Just as not long ago at . . . spice we shuddered when the entire faith of certain persons was assailed in this manner.” Several letters have fallen out of the Agobardine manuscript. I do not approve what is read in the common editions, *pro auspice cum in tota fide quorumdam*. Certainly nothing seems to be missing here except the name of a place. RIG.]

Just as not long ago at . . . spice [Note: [Col. 0140D] *Auspice*, Pam.; but some letters are missing in the Agobardine manuscript.] we shuddered when [Note: [Col. 0140D] Pam. adds *in*.] the entire faith of certain persons was assailed in this manner. [Col. 0140D] It will therefore be futile to say: “Even if I deny that I am a Christian, I shall not be denied by Christ, for I have not denied him himself.” For he will be held equally liable by that denial [Col. 0141A] whereby, in denying himself to be a Christian, and thus denying Christ in himself, he has also denied Christ himself.

There is more: he also threatens shame in return for shame. “The one who is ashamed of me before human beings, I too will be ashamed of him before my Father who is in heaven.” For he knew that denial is fashioned especially from shame: that the condition of the mind rests upon the forehead, and that the wound of shame precedes the wound of the body.

## CHAPTER X

As for those who think that confession was established not here—that is, not within this circuit of the earth, nor along this passage of life, nor among human beings of this common nature—what presumption theirs is against the whole order of things that must be experienced upon this earth, in this life, and under human authorities! [Col. 0141B]

Doubtless, when souls have departed from their bodies and have begun to be examined throughout the individual stories of the heavens [Note: [Col. 0141D] “To be examined concerning the commandment.” To be examined concerning the commandment means to be investigated and tested as to whether we obeyed Christ’s commandment and whether we were constant in confessing Christ’s name before the authorities. RIG.] concerning the commandment [Note: [Col. 0141C] *Having been received*, Rig.; *having been regarded*, old copy; *by admission*, Latin.], and to be questioned about those secret sacraments of the heretics, then confession must be made before the true powers and [Note: [Col. 0141D] “True men,” namely the *Teletoi*, *Abaskantoi*, and *Akinetoi* of Valentinus. In the Agobardine manuscript the words run thus: “true men . . . *letoi*, namely, and *aginetoi* and *abaskantoi* of Valentinus.” Ursinus’s manuscript reads *ageratoi*. Words of this kind are found among the follies of the Valentinians, by which they signified true, perfect, unbewitchable, steadfast human beings: τελείους (*teleíous*, “perfect”), ἀβασκάντους (*abaskántous*, “unbewitchable”), ἀκινήτους (*akinḗtous*, “immovable”). RIG.] true men—namely the *Theletoi*, *Abaskantoi*, and *Akinetoi* [Note: [Col. 0141C] *Aginetoi*, Seml.; *Aegratoi*, Wouwer manuscript, Rig.] of Valentinus!

“For our own people,” they say, “not even the Demiurge himself consistently declared to be true human beings [Note: [Col. 0141C] *The same one will prove by reproaches that steadfast men are true*, Seml.], since he reckoned them the dripping of a bucket, the dust of a threshing floor, spittle, and locusts; he even made them equal to irrational beasts of burden.” It is indeed written so. Yet no other race of human beings besides us must therefore be understood: because it is established that we exist, and he could clothe us in comparison [Notes: [Col. 0141C] *Because*, Seml.; [Col. 0141D] “He could clothe them in comparison.” Thus the Agobardine manuscript; Ursinus’s manuscript has *indicate*. RIG.; [Col. 0141C] *To exist by comparison*, Seml.], while preserving both the distinctive character and the singularity of the race.

For even if life has been corrupted, so that, being judged contemptible, it might be compared with contemptible things, nature has not thereby immediately [Col. 0141C] been abolished, so that another nature might be reckoned under its name. On the contrary, nature is preserved even if life is put to shame. Nor does Christ know any other human beings than those concerning whom he says: “Whom do human beings say that I am?” and, “As you wish human beings to do to you, so do you also to them.” See whether he has preserved the race from whom he both expects testimony concerning himself and toward whom he commands the reciprocal duty of justice.

But if I should demand that those heavenly human beings be shown to me, Aratus would more readily [Col. 0142A] [Note: [Col. 0141D] Aratus will delineate Perseus, Cepheus, Erigone, etc. One may consult the *Phaenomena* of Aratus, whom Cicero too follows in Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*, where he places Cepheus and Perseus after the Lesser Bear. Arnobius says thus of Erigone in Book VII: “Erigone hanged herself with a noose, so that as a maiden she might be among the fiery stars.” Finally, concerning Perseus and Ariadne, Justin Martyr—whom the Author is accustomed to imitate—says in *Apology* I, after he has numbered Perseus among the sons of Jupiter: “What shall we say of Ariadne and those whom they likewise say were received among the stars, just as he was?” PAM.] delineate Perseus, Cepheus, Erigone, and Ariadne for me among the constellations.

But what prevented the Lord from explicitly determining that the confession before human beings was also to be made there where he openly pronounced that his own confession would take place? The wording could thus have been: “The one who confesses in me before human beings in heaven, I too will confess in him before my Father who is in heaven.” He ought to have rescued me from this error of an earthly confession, which he did not wish to receive [Note: [Col. 0142C] *Would not have wished*, Seml.], if he had commanded a heavenly one, since I knew no human beings other than the inhabitants of earth, and since no human being had yet even been seen in heaven at that time.

Further, what credibility is there in such a course of events: that, after my departure, I should be raised [Note: [Col. 0142C] *Taken up*, Seml.] to the realms above and be tested there [Note: [Col. 0142C] *Be tested*, present tense, Seml.], although I could not be placed there unless already tested? [Note: [Col. 0142D] “I should be examined there concerning the commandment.” Thus reads the old copy; this text confirms what we noted above concerning “to be examined concerning the commandment.” RIG.] That I should be examined there concerning the commandment [Note: [Col. 0142C] *Having been received*, Venet.; *by admission*, Seml.], [Col. 0142B] although I could not arrive there unless I were to be admitted?

Heaven lies open to the Christian before the road does, because there is no road to heaven except for the person to whom heaven lies open; the one who reaches it will enter. What gatekeeping powers do you affirm for me, in accordance with Roman superstition: [Note: [Col. 0142D] “Some Janus, Forculus, and Limentinus.” The copy reads “some Barnus.” RIG.] some Janus [Note: [Col. 0142C] *Some Cardus*, Seml.; *some Cardea*, Fran.], Forculus, and Limentinus? What powers do you station at the barriers?

If you have ever read in David (Ps. 24:7), “Lift up your gates, O princes [Note: [Col. 0142C] *Your princes*, Rig. Venet.], and let the eternal gates be raised, and the King of glory will enter”; if likewise you have heard in Amos (9:6), “He who builds his ascent into the heavens and establishes his outpouring upon the earth”—then know that that ascent has henceforth been leveled by the footsteps of the Lord and the entrance henceforth opened by the powers of Christ. No delay or interrogation will confront Christians at the threshold, [Col. 0142C] since they are not to be investigated there, but recognized; not questioned, but admitted.

For even if you still think heaven closed, remember that the Lord left its keys here to Peter, and through him to the Church—keys that each person here, after being questioned and making confession, will carry with him.

But the devil insists that confession must be made there, so that he may persuade us to deny here. Fine credentials, clearly, I shall send on ahead [Note: [Col. 0142D] “Fine credentials.” As though “documents supporting our case.” Thus Book XXIX, ch. *On Gifts*: “adequate credentials.” RIG.]; fine keys I shall carry with me [Note: [Col. 0142D] “Fine keys I shall carry with me”: constancy in the Christian faith. What follows concerning fear is added sarcastically. Tertullian himself says in *On the Soul*: “Your blood is the whole key to paradise.” RIG.]—fear [Col. 0143A] of those who kill only the body [Note: [Col. 0143D] “But do nothing to the soul.” Tertullian is accustomed to speak thus, as we have already observed in the book *Against the Valentinians*. RIG.] but do nothing to the soul! I shall be commended by abandoning this commandment; I shall stand honorably in the heavenly realms, [Note: [Col. 0143D] “I who could not stand in earthly realms”—that is, having fallen from the faith. RIG.] I who could not stand in earthly realms; I shall withstand the greater powers, I who yielded to the lesser; finally, I shall deserve to be admitted, though already excluded.

There is still this to say: if confession is to be made in the heavenly realms, then denial must be made here [Note: [Col. 0143C] *Or*, Seml.]; for [Note: [Col. 0143C] *Assuredly*, Seml.] where the one occurs, there [Note: [Col. 0143C] *In the same place*, Wouwer manuscript, Jun.] both occur, since all opposites come into conflict. Persecution too will have to be carried on in heaven, since it supplies the occasion for confession or denial.

Why then do you delay, most audacious heretic, in transferring the entire order of the Christian ordeal to the realms above, and first of all in locating there the very hatred of the name, where Christ sits at the Father’s right hand? There you will also establish [Note: [Col. 0143C] *You should establish*, Seml.] the synagogues of the Jews, the fountains of persecutions, [Col. 0143B] in which the apostles suffered scourging; and the peoples of the nations, together, indeed, with their circus, where they readily cry out, [Note: [Col. 0143D] “How long must we endure the third race?” Ursinus’s manuscript has “the foul race”; but the Agobardine copy has “the third race.” Tertullian himself, in Book I *To the Nations*, shows that this is perfectly correct: “Plainly,” he says, “we are called the third race. If there is at least some reason among you, I should like you to set forth the first and second races, so that the identity of the third may thereby be established.” RIG.] “How long must we endure the third race?”

But you will also have to produce in that same place our brothers, fathers, sons, mothers-in-law, daughters-in-law, and members of our household [Note: [Col. 0143C] *You will have to*, plural, Rhen. Seml. Oberth.], through whom betrayal has been ordained; likewise kings and governors and armed authorities, before whom the case must be defended [Note: [Col. 0143D] *Fought*, Rhen. Seml. Oberth.].

There will assuredly also be a prison in heaven, deprived of sunlight—or perhaps, contrary to its occupants’ wishes, full of light—and perhaps chains made from the celestial belts, and the very axle that revolves will be the rack. Then, if the Christian is to be stoned, hailstones will be at hand; if burned, thunderbolts are readily available; if slaughtered, the hand [Note: [Col. 0143D] *Office*, Seml. Jun.] of armed Orion will perform the task; if [Note: [Col. 0143D] “If he is to be finished by beasts.” That is, one condemned to the beasts must undergo death, and life must be ended. “Day of finishing” appears in a certain inscription among Gruter’s collections, from Appian: “If she remains until the day of her finishing,” which is said of a widow. *To be finished*: to be consumed. Fabius, Declamation 19: “I consumed my son with beatings and fires.” Ulpian, Book VI, § *But if anyone*: “Not when he was consumed, but when he underwent sentence.” And Book III, *On Punishments*: “The punishment of a pregnant woman who is to be consumed is deferred”; the word commonly added, “condemned,” is an explanatory gloss. RIG.] he is to be finished by beasts, [Note: [Col. 0144D] “The Septentrion will send forth bears.” He carefully considers those constellations which astrologers observe so intently. Here he calls “bears” those which are termed the Septentrions. There are two, the Greater and the Lesser, which because of the arrangement of their stars are called *Triones* and *Septentriones*, and in Greek “wagons,” ἄμαξαι (*hámaxai*). Thus Aratus in the *Phaenomena*—
> “The Bears wheel together, and for that reason are called Wagons.” [LE PR.]

The north will send forth bears, the zodiac bulls and lions. He who endures these things to the end will be saved. [Col. 0143C] Are the end, then, and suffering, and killing, and the first confession also in heaven? And where is the flesh, which is necessary for all these things? Where is the body, which alone can be killed by human beings? Certain reasoning has conveyed these conclusions to us even in the manner of a game; and no one will dislodge the obstacle posed by this prescriptive argument, so as to avoid being compelled to transfer thither the whole course of persecution, the whole fixed preparation of its cause, wherever he has assigned a tribunal to confession. For confession arises from persecution, and persecution ends in confession. [Col. 0144A] Nor can things fail to follow together when they arrange both the entrance and the departure [Note: [Col. 0144C] Seml., following Rhen., deletes “which arrange”], that is, the beginning and the end.

Moreover, hatred of the name will be here; persecution breaks out here; betrayal brings one forward here; interrogation presses one here; the torture chamber rages here; and confession or denial completes this entire course upon earth. Therefore, if the other things are here, confession cannot be elsewhere; if confession is elsewhere, neither can the other things be here. But the other things are assuredly nowhere else; therefore neither is confession in heaven. Or, if they wish there to be another system of heavenly interrogation and confession, they will certainly also have to construct for it an entirely different course, distinct from that arrangement marked out in the Scriptures; and we can [Note: [Col. 0144C] Rig.: “we may be able”] say: Let them see to that, provided that this course of earthly interrogation and confession, proceeding from the material circumstances of persecution and public hostility toward the name, remains secure in the faith proper to it—[Col. 0144B] so that it is to be believed just as it is written [Note: [Col. 0144C] Seml., from Rhen., deletes “so that”], and understood just as it is heard.

Here I uphold the entire course, since the Lord himself assigns no other region of the world. For what does he add after the conclusion concerning confession and denial?

> Do not suppose [Note: [Col. 0144C] Seml., following Rhen.: “let him not suppose”] that I have come to send peace upon the earth; I have not come to send peace, but a sword—

certainly upon the earth.

> For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law; and a man’s enemies will be those of his own household.

For thus it comes about that

> brother will betray brother to death, and a father his son; and children will rise against their parents and cause them to die. And he who endures to the end will be saved

(Matt. 10:34ff.).

So entirely does this whole course of the Lord’s sword—sent not into heaven but upon the earth—also establish confession there, a confession that, by enduring to the end, [Col. 0144C] is destined to suffer death.

## CHAPTER XI

By the same pattern, therefore, we maintain that the other sayings also pertain to martyrdom.

> He who values even his own life more than me is not worthy of me

(cf. Luke 14);

that is, he who would rather live by denying me than die by confessing me.

> He who finds his life will lose it; but he who loses it for my sake will find it.

For the man who has denied Christ thereby finds [Note: [Col. 0144C] Fran.: “will find”] it [Note: [Col. 0144C] Seml.: “by that”; Fran.: “it”], in that he gains his [Col. 0145A] life; but he who thinks that by denial he gains it will lose it in Gehenna [Note: [Col. 0145C] Jun.: “so that”; Seml.: “to gain”]. The man who confesses and is killed, however, loses it for the present, but will find it unto eternal life. Indeed, when governors exhort people [Note: [Col. 0145C] Rhen., Seml., Oberth.: “urge people”] to denial, they say, “Save your life, and do not lose your life.”

[Note: [Col. 0145D] **Save your life.** Similar words of the proconsul Paternus to Cyprian occur in the account of that most courageous martyr’s passion; Augustine also attacks them in his sermon on the same Cyprian. RIG.]

How else [Note: [Col. 0145C] Others: “in what manner”] would Christ speak, except in the manner in which a Christian would be dealt with [Note: [Col. 0145C] Rig., Seml.: “is dealt with”; others: “is being dealt with”]? When, moreover, he forbids his servants to prepare their answer for the tribunal, he instructs them and promises that the Holy Spirit will answer (Matt. 10:20); when he wishes a brother in prison to be visited (Matt. 25), he commands that care be shown to a confessor; and when he affirms that God will avenge his elect (Matt. 15), he consoles them in their sufferings. Even in the parable of the seed [Note: [Col. 0145C] Rig.: “of the word”] after the turf has dried up, he [Col. 0145B] depicts the heat of persecutions [Note: [Col. 0145D] Rig., from an old book: “in persecution”].

[Note: [Col. 0145D] **In the parable of the seed after the turf has dried up.** The exemplar reads: “In the parable of the word after the turf has dried up, he depicts the heat of persecutions.” RIG.]

If these things are not received as they are pronounced, then without doubt they mean something other than what they sound like: one thing will be in the words, another in their meanings, as with allegories, parables, and riddles. Whatever wind of argument, therefore, these scorpions have conceived [Note: [Col. 0145D] Jun.: “whatever poison they have conceived”], with whatever point they have thrust themselves forward, there is now a single line of response: they will be challenged to show whether the events themselves are carried out according to the Scriptures. For something different will be signified in the Scriptures only if that very thing is not found in the events. What is written must come to pass. Moreover, what is written will then come to pass if nothing else [Note: [Col. 0145D] Seml.: “in another manner”; Seml. also reads “and” for “is”] comes to pass.

But see: we are hated by all people on account of the name, just as it is written.

[Note: [Col. 0145D] **On account of the name.** This has been sufficiently discussed in the *Apology*, where we showed from ancient authorities that neither praise nor blame ought to be expected from a mere name. LE PR.]

We are also betrayed by those closest to us, just as it is written; we are brought before the authorities, interrogated, [Col. 0145C] tortured, confess, and are slaughtered, just as it is written (Matt. 10). Thus the Lord declared it. If he declared these things in some other sense, why do they not happen otherwise than [Note: [Col. 0145D] Jun.: “the things which”] he declared—that is, precisely as he declared them? Yet they do not happen otherwise than he declared. Therefore, just as they happen, so he declared them [Note: [Col. 0146C] “Therefore, just as they happen, so he declared them” is deleted by one edition; Venet. substitutes “but also just as”], and so they happen. For they could not have happened otherwise than he declared; nor would he himself have declared them otherwise than he wished them to happen. Thus the Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0146C] Seml. adds “these”] will signify nothing other than what we recognize in the events.

Or [Note: [Col. 0146C] Seml.: “But”], if the things foretold are not yet being done, how are [Col. 0146A] these things being done [Note: [Col. 0146C] Seml., following Rhen., deletes “being done”] which were not foretold? For the things now being done were not foretold, if what was foretold consists of different things and not of the things now being done. But now, because [Note: [Col. 0146C] Ciacc.: “when”] the very things in the events are the things [Note: [Col. 0146C] Seml. adds “also”] in the words, they are believed to have been spoken in another sense. What would happen if they were actually found to have occurred [Note: [Col. 0146D] Seml.: “been enacted”] differently? But this is [Note: [Col. 0146D] Seml.: “will be”] the perversity of faith: not to believe what has been proved, but to presume what has not been proved.

Against that perversity I shall also set this argument: if the things now being done just as they were written are not the very things foretold, then those other things too must not happen just as they were written, lest they too be endangered by the example of the former; for the possibility of one thing in the words and another in the events has indeed been excluded; and [Note: [Col. 0146D] Jun.: “Thus”] it follows that prophecies will not be recognized even when they have come to pass, if they are foretold otherwise than they are destined to happen. And how will things be believed that will not have been foretold, [Col. 0146B] since they will not have been foretold in the manner in which they happen? Thus heretics, by refusing to believe the things foretold as they have been proved, believe things that were not even foretold.

## CHAPTER XII

Who could have known the innermost substance of the Scriptures better than Christ’s own school? The Lord adopted them as disciples for himself, certainly to be taught everything; and he furnished them as teachers for us, certainly to teach everything. To whom would he more readily have explained the figurative form of his speech than to those to whom he revealed the image of his glory—Peter, James, and John—and afterward Paul, whom he made a participant in paradise even before his martyrdom?

[Note: [Col. 0146D] **To whom would he more readily have explained the figurative form of his speech?** That is, the mysteries and sacraments of his discourse, when its meanings withdraw from its literal words, as Tertullian himself speaks in this very work, ch. 15. RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0146D] **Whom he made a participant in paradise even before his martyrdom.** That is, when he was caught up as far as the third heaven and saw things that no one can narrate or express, or even comprehend in thought. LE PR.]

Or did they too write otherwise than they understood, as teachers of deception rather than truth? Peter, at least, writes to the people of Pontus:

> For how great is the glory if you endure when punished not as wrongdoers! For this [Col. 0146C] is grace, and to this you have been called, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you himself as an example, that you might follow in his footsteps

(1 Pet. 2).

And again:

> Beloved, do not be terrified by the burning that is taking place among you as a trial, as though something strange were happening to you. Rather, insofar as you share in Christ’s sufferings, rejoice, so that at the revelation of his glory you may also rejoice with exultation. If you are dishonored in [Note: [Col. 0146D] Seml. deletes “in”] the name of Christ, you are blessed, because glory and the Spirit of God rest [Note: [Col. 0146D] Rhen., Seml., Oberth.: “will rest”] upon you. Only let none of you suffer as a murderer, or thief, [Col. 0147A] or evildoer, or a meddler in another’s affairs. But if one suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; rather, let him glorify the Lord in that name

(1 Pet. 4).

[Note: [Col. 0147D] **A meddler in another’s affairs.** That is, one who attends to concerns belonging to others. LE PR.]

John, moreover, exhorts us even to lay down our lives for our brothers, denying that there is fear in love:

> For perfect love casts fear outside, because fear has punishment; and he who fears is not perfect in love

(1 John 4:18).

What fear is it preferable to understand except the fear that produces denial? What love does he affirm to be perfect except that which drives out fear and inspires confession? With what punishment does he punish fear except that which the denier will incur, when he is to be killed in Gehenna [Note: [Col. 0147C] Seml.: “into Gehenna”] in both body and soul? But if John teaches that one must die for one’s brothers, how much more does he teach that one must die for the Lord—being sufficiently instructed by his own Apocalypse to offer this counsel!

For the Spirit had commanded the angel of the church of the [Col. 0147B] Smyrnaeans:

> Behold, the devil will cast [Note: [Col. 0147C] Rhen., Seml., Oberth.: “casts”] some of your number into prison, that you may be tested for ten days. Be faithful even unto death, and I shall give you the crown of life

(Rev. 2:10).

Likewise, to the church of Pergamum he spoke concerning Antipas, the most faithful martyr, slain in the dwelling place of Satan. Likewise, to the church of Philadelphia, he promised that the man who had not denied the Lord’s name would be delivered from the final trial.

[Note: [Col. 0147D] **Had not denied the Lord’s name.** Compare Rev. 3:10 and 1 Cor. 10:13; and elsewhere, “the devil’s time is short.” SEML.]

Thereafter he promises each conqueror: now the tree of life and exemption from the second death; now hidden manna together with a white stone and an unknown name; now authority over the iron rod and the brightness of the morning star; now to be clothed in white, not to be erased from the book of life, and to become a pillar in God’s temple, inscribed with the name of God and the Lord and of the heavenly Jerusalem; now to sit with the Lord upon his throne—a privilege once denied to the sons of Zebedee.

[Col. 0147C] Who are these most blessed conquerors, if not martyrs in the proper sense? For victories belong to those to whom battles belong, and battles belong to those whose blood is shed. Meanwhile the souls of the martyrs rest peacefully beneath the altar,

[Note: [Col. 0147D] **The souls of the martyrs rest peacefully beneath the altar.** By the term “altar” the earth seems to be signified, since it served as an altar for the immolation of the martyrs. RIG.]

and confidence in vengeance nourishes their patience; clothed in robes, they lay claim to the white radiance of glory until others too complete the fellowship of their glory.

[Note: [Col. 0148D] **And confidence in vengeance nourishes their patience; clothed in robes.** We supplied these words from Agobard’s manuscripts. He says elegantly that the souls of the martyrs, laid beneath the altar in hope of resurrection, rest peacefully and, as though in a meadow of refreshment, nourish their patience with confidence in vengeance. RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0147C] Others: “The souls nourish patience and, clothed in robes, are white.” Seml., omitting several words: “confidence in vengeance [nourishes] whiteness.”]

For once again an innumerable multitude is revealed, clothed in white and distinguished by the palms of victory—evidently those triumphing [Note: [Col. 0147C] Seml.: “triumphal”] over Antichrist. As one of the elders says:

> These are those who come out of that great tribulation; they have washed their garment and made it white in the blood of the Lamb

(Rev. 7:14).

For the garment of the soul is the flesh. Its filth is washed away in baptism, but its stains are [Col. 0148A] made white in martyrdom. Isaiah too promises that what is reddish [Note: [Col. 0147C] Seml.: “red”] and scarlet will become white as snow and wool (Isa. 1:18).

When great Babylon is also described as drunk with the blood of the saints, her drunkenness is undoubtedly supplied by the cups of martyrdom. What the fear of martyrdom will bring upon a person is likewise shown. For among all the rejected—indeed, before all the rest—it is said:

> But for the fearful,

and then for the others,

> their portion is in the lake of fire and sulfur.

Thus in John’s Epistle the fear that love casts outside has punishment (1 John 4:18).

## CHAPTER XIII

The apostle Paul, once a persecutor (Acts 9) who was the first to shed the Church’s blood, afterward exchanged the sword for the pen and turned the blade into a plow: Benjamin’s ravening wolf, who afterward, [Col. 0148B] according to Jacob, himself brought food [Note: [Col. 0148C] Rhen., Seml., Oberth.: “himself also brought food”]. How highly he commends martyrdoms, which had now become desirable even to himself!

Rejoicing over the Thessalonians [Note: [Col. 0148C] Venet. omits “over”], he says:

> So that we may glory in you among the churches of God because of your endurance and faith in all the persecutions and tribulations that you endure as a demonstration of God’s just judgment, so that you may be accounted worthy of his kingdom, for which you also suffer

(2 Thess. 1:3–4).

[Note: [Col. 0148D] **You endure as a demonstration of just judgment.** You await the coming, the manifestation, of the judgment. RIG.]

Likewise, to the Romans:

> And not only so, but we even exult in tribulations, knowing [Note: [Col. 0148C] Rhen., Seml., Oberth.: “by art”] that tribulation perfects endurance, endurance produces tested character, tested character produces hope, and hope does not disappoint

(Rom. 5:11).

And again:

> But if we are children, we are also heirs: heirs indeed of God, but coheirs with Christ, provided that we suffer with him [Note: [Col. 0148C] Others: “that we may suffer with him”], so that we may also be glorified with him. For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that will be revealed in us [Col. 0148C]

(Rom. 8:17).

[Note: [Col. 0148C] Rhen., Seml., Oberth. read: “is to be revealed.”]

And therefore, shortly afterward:

> Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: For your [Note: [Col. 0148C] Agobard’s codex: “your,” feminine form] sake we are put to death all day long; we are accounted as livestock for slaughter. But in all these things we more than conquer through him who loved us. For we are persuaded that neither death nor life, nor power, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord

(Rom. 8:35).

And when enumerating his sufferings to the Corinthians, he certainly prescribed what must be suffered:

> In labors more abundantly, in prisons very frequently, in deaths more often; five times I received from the Jews forty lashes less [Col. 0149A] one, three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned,

and the rest (2 Cor. 11:33).

Even if these appear to be hardships rather than martyrdoms, he nevertheless says again:

> Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in insults, in necessities, in persecutions, and in distresses for Christ’s sake

(2 Cor. 12:10).

Likewise, earlier:

> We who are afflicted in everything, but not confined; who are in need, but not utterly destitute; who are [Note: [Col. 0149C] Jun.: “who also are”] driven by persecutions, but not abandoned; who are cast down, but do not perish—always carrying about in our body the dying of Christ Jesus

(2 Cor. 4:8).

> But even if our outer man is being corrupted,

he says—that is, the flesh, through the violence of persecutions—

> yet the inner man is renewed day by day—

that is, the soul, through hope in the promises.

> For our present, temporary and light tribulation produces for us, beyond all measure upon measure [Note: [Col. 0149C] Rhen., Seml., Oberth.: “in addition, through”], an [Col. 0149B] eternal weight of glory [Note: [Col. 0149C] Others: “will produce”], while we look not at the things that are seen but at those that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporary,

speaking of hardships,

> but the things that are not seen are eternal,

pledging the rewards [Note: [Col. 0149D] Agobard’s codex: “the things promised”].

Writing to the Thessalonians [Note: [Col. 0149D] Fran.: “Philippians”] about his chains, he declared blessed those to whom it had been granted not only to believe in Christ but also to suffer for him:

> Having the same contest which you saw in me and now have heard [Note: [Col. 0149D] Rhen., Seml., Oberth.: “hear”] about

(Phil. 1:29).

[Note: [Col. 0149D] **Writing to the Thessalonians about his chains.** This passage must be corrected to read “to the Philippians,” both because “about his chains” is added—the first Epistle to the Philippians was written from chains, whereas neither Epistle to the Thessalonians was—and because the scriptural testimonies that follow are found at Phil. 1:7 and following. In the first of these, Tertullian retained the Greek word *agōn*, “contest”; in the latter, he confirms the reading of the more accurate Latin codices, which have “I am poured out upon the sacrifice,” instead of the reading of others, “I emulate.” PAM.]

> For even if I am poured out as a libation upon the sacrifice, I rejoice and rejoice together with all of you; likewise, you too rejoice and rejoice together with me

(Phil. 2:17).

You see how he defines the blessedness of martyrdom, for which he establishes a solemn celebration of mutual joy. Finally, when he had come very near the fulfillment of his desire, how exultantly does he write to Timothy at its prospect [Note: [Col. 0150C] Rhen., Seml., Oberth.: “he exults, saying to Timothy”]?

> For I am already being poured out as a libation, and [Col. 0149C] the time of my departure is at hand [Note: [Col. 0150C] Rhen., Seml., Oberth.: “the time of lodging elsewhere presses upon me”]. I have fought the good contest, I have completed the course, I have kept the faith. The crown remains, which the Lord will give me on that day

(2 Tim. 4:6–7)—that is, the day of his suffering.

He himself had said enough earlier:

> The saying is faithful: for if we have died together with Christ, we shall also live together with him; if we endure with him, we shall also reign with him; [Col. 0150A] if we deny him, he too will deny us; if we do not believe, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself

(2 Tim. 2:11).

> Therefore do not be ashamed of the martyrdom of our Lord, nor of me, his prisoner,

because he had previously said:

> For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and sound understanding

(2 Tim. 1:8).

For through power we suffer out of love for God, and with sound understanding when we suffer on account of our innocence. Wherever he commands endurance, what does he have in view more than sufferings? Wherever he tears people away from idolatry, what does he tear away from it in preference to martyrdom?

[Note: [Col. 0149D] **What does he tear away from it in preference to martyrdom?** Tertullian says: Wherever God tears people away from idolatry, what does he tear away from idolatry, to set it immediately in opposition to idolatry, in preference to the martyrdoms of courageous Christians? RIG.]

## CHAPTER XIV

To be sure, he admonishes the Romans to be subject to all authorities (Rom. 13:4–7), because there is no authority except from God, because it does not bear the sword without cause, and because it is God’s ministry [Note: [Col. 0150C] Rhen., Seml., Oberth.: “female minister”]; but it is also, he says,

> an avenger for wrath upon him who [Col. 0150B] does evil.

For he had also prefaced this:

> Rulers are not a cause of fear to good conduct, but to evil. Do you wish not to fear the authority? Do good, and you will receive praise from it. It is therefore God’s minister to you for good. But if you do evil, be afraid.

[Note: [Col. 0149D] **It is therefore God’s minister.** Agobard’s manuscript has, “It is therefore God’s minister . . .” From these traces it is apparent that the text was, “It is therefore God’s ministry,” as above. RIG.]

Thus he does not command you to be subject to the authorities as an opportunity to frustrate martyrdom, but as an inducement to live well, even with regard to them, as though they were assistants of justice and ministers of divine judgment, which even here passes preliminary judgment upon the guilty.

He then proceeds to explain how he wishes you to be subject to the authorities, commanding that you render tax to whom tax is due, and revenue to whom revenue is due—that is:

> the things that are Caesar’s to Caesar, and the things that are God’s to God

(Matt. 22:21).

But the human being belongs to God alone [Note: [Col. 0150D] Rhen., Seml., Oberth.: “God alone; the human being”]. Peter, of course, had spoken in agreement: the king is indeed to be honored, but in such a way that the king is honored when he attends to his own affairs and [Col. 0150C] remains far removed from divine honors. For father and mother too are loved [Note: [Col. 0150D] Fran., Pam.: “diligently”], provided they are not compared with God. But it will not be permissible to love even one’s own life above God.

[Note: [Col. 0150D] **Peter, of course, had spoken in agreement.** *Condixerat* means that Peter had spoken together with Paul, had said things consonant with Paul. So in the book *On the Crown*: “which the pagan faith likewise affirmed together.” RIG.]

## CHAPTER XV

Are even the apostles’ writings, then, mutable [Note: [Col. 0150D] Pam.: “well known”; Jun.: “clouded”]? [Col. 0151A]

[Note: [Col. 0150D] **The apostles’ writings are mutable.** This is the reading in Ursinus’ exemplar, which we followed in the first edition, as though Septimius had spoken of “mutable writings” which meant something other than they sounded, with one thing in the words and another in their meanings. We may now be permitted to change our judgment, since our only concern is the truth. In Agobard’s book Septimius says: “Are the apostles’ writings, then, well known?” That reading must be retained. For after proving, on the authority of the prophets and the Gospel, that martyrdoms must be courageously undergone by Christians, and that this is the Lord’s precept or command, he also proves it by citing the apostles’ writings, and adds: “Are the apostles’ writings, then, well known?” That is: Are they not known, clear, and manifest to everyone? Certainly they are. He immediately presses the point: “Let it indeed be so, that their meanings withdraw from their letters”—as if those writings were not so clear and manifest that they could admit some indulgence in interpretation. Let us come to the events themselves. Let us see what the apostles themselves, the interpreters of their own writings, did. They certainly did not hesitate to expend their lives in martyrdom, since they had no doubt about the Lord’s command. RIG.]

And are we altogether simple souls [Note: [Col. 0151C] **And are we altogether simple souls?** These are sayings—or rather, the stings of scorpions—of the sort mentioned above. RIG.], and doves only [Note: [Col. 0151C] **And doves only.** Not also serpents in prudence. He alludes to Christ’s words in Matthew: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves.” RIG.], who gladly wander astray [Note: [Col. 0151C] **Who gladly wander astray.** Straying through unwary simplicity and flying away from the Lord’s dwelling. RIG.]? I suppose it is from a desire to live.

Let it indeed be so, that their meanings withdraw from their literal words. Yet the sufferings that we know the apostles underwent constitute manifest teaching. This alone I understand as I run through the Acts. I seek nothing further. There are prisons, chains, scourges, stones, swords, assaults by Jews, gatherings of the nations, reports from tribunes [Note: [Col. 0151B] Jun.: variant spelling *ellogia*], audiences before kings, tribunals of proconsuls, and the name of Caesar: these require no interpreter.

That Peter is beaten [Note: [Col. 0151B] Rig.: “is raised up” (*ὑψοῦται*, “is exalted”)], that Stephen is crushed, that James is sacrificed, that Paul is torn apart—these things are written in their own blood.

[Note: [Col. 0151C] **Peter is beaten.** So Agobard’s old exemplar reads. Nevertheless, since the deaths of the apostles are designated in this passage by their kinds of punishment, we judge that Peter’s passion was described by a more expressive word and that the reading here, “is beaten,” is corrupt. We should therefore read “is raised up,” meaning that he is lifted and suspended upon the elevated and erected cross: *ὑψοῦται*, which the common version rendered “is exalted.” John 12 contains Christ’s words, indicating by what death he was to die: *ἐὰν ὑψωθῶ ἐκ τῆς γῆς*, “If I am exalted from the earth.” Sulpicius Severus: “Peter was raised upon the cross.” RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0151D] **Stephen is crushed.** By the onrush of stones, by stoning. RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0151D] **James is sacrificed.** The Lord’s brother, or John’s brother? Herod killed John’s brother with the sword. Luke, Acts 12: *Ἀνεῖλε δὲ Ἰάκωβον, τὸν ἀδελφὸν Κυρίου, μαχαίρᾳ*—“He killed James, the brother of the Lord, with the sword”—which in the martyrologies is understood as beheading and is entirely unsuited to sacrifice. It must therefore be said that James, the Lord’s brother, is designated here. Eusebius, Epiphanius, and Jerome report that he died after being struck in the head with a fuller’s club; but this derives from Hegesippus’ rather foolish and worthless narrative. Nevertheless, as far as the manner of death is concerned, it seems to be confirmed by these words of our Septimius: he would have said that James, the Lord’s brother, was sacrificed because he was slaughtered with a fuller’s club, as though with the mallet or club of a sacrificial attendant. RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0152C] **Paul is torn apart.** His head was separated and cut from his neck. Septimius, in book IV *Against Marcion*, says that separation is the work of the sword; and Luke used *διαμερισμόν* (“division”) for what Matthew called *μάχαιραν* (“a sword”). Paul is therefore torn apart by beheading, which removes the chief part of the body. For this happens to those punished by such a penalty: they do not fall whole, nor lie there as an entire corpse. Indeed, the heads of the beheaded are generally fixed upon a stake or spear. RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0152C] **Is beaten, is crushed, is sacrificed, is torn apart.** Septimius plays upon antitheses. He opposes Stephen to Peter. Peter was raised and elevated upon the cross, whereas Stephen was buried beneath a heap of stones. He then opposes James to Paul. Paul, his head severed, was divided into two parts; but James, sacrificed and dashed to the earth by the blow of a club, fell whole. It was the practice of sacrificial attendants to strike and kill victims in such a way that they did not struggle but fell as though voluntarily. RIG.]

And if the heretic desires the confirmation of the public record [Note: [Col. 0151B] Rhen., Seml., Oberth.: variant form *Commentari*], the documents of the empire will speak, like the stones of Jerusalem.

[Note: [Col. 0152D] **And if the heretic desires the confirmation of the public record.** That is, if he wishes to be instructed also from the evidence of the public archives. So in the book *On Idolatry*: “They wish, of course, for the time of the persecution and the place of the tribunal,” etc. RIG.]

We read the *Lives of the Caesars*: [Col. 0151B] Nero was the first at Rome to drench the rising faith in blood. Then Peter is girded by another when he is bound to the cross. Then Paul attains the birth of Roman citizenship when he is reborn there through the nobility of martyrdom.

Wherever I now read these things, I learn to suffer. It makes no difference to me which teachers of martyrdom I follow—the apostles’ meanings or their [Col. 0152A] ends—except that I also recognize their meanings in their ends. For they would have suffered nothing that they had not first understood must be suffered [Note: [Col. 0151B] Agobard’s codex: “known”].

When Agabus had foretold Paul’s chains even by a symbolic gesture, the disciples wept and begged him not to entrust himself to Jerusalem, but their pleas were in vain. For Paul, inspired by what he had always taught, said:

> Why are you weeping and grieving my heart? For my part, I would choose not only to suffer chains at Jerusalem, but even to die for the name of my Lord Jesus Christ.

And so they yielded, saying:

> Let the Lord’s will be done

(Acts 21:13–14),

confident, of course, that sufferings belonged to God’s will. For they had attempted [Note: [Col. 0152B] Rhen., Seml., Oberth.: “attempted,” corrected form] to hold him back not with the intention of dissuading him, but out of affection: because they longed for the apostle, not because they counseled against martyrdom.

But if Prodicus or Valentinus [Col. 0152B] had then been standing by and suggesting that confession was not to be made before human beings upon earth [Note: [Col. 0152B] Rhen., Seml., Oberth.: “that no attempt should be made”], and indeed less so, lest God thirst for human blood or Christ demand repayment for his suffering as though he himself were to obtain salvation from it [Note: [Col. 0152B] Seml.: “human beings, which not even”], he would immediately have heard from God’s servant what the devil had heard from the Lord:

> Withdraw, Satan; you are a stumbling block [Col. 0153A] to me.

[Note: [Col. 0152D] **That confession was not to be made before human beings upon earth.** These too are the stings of the scorpions mentioned above.]

[Note: [Col. 0152D] **What the devil had heard from the Lord.** Rather, what Peter himself heard, Matt. 16:23. But someone, out of affection for Peter, wished Matthew’s narrative to be understood as though the words for which Christ rebukes Peter had been uttered not so much by Peter himself as by the devil through Peter’s mouth. Chrysostom, however, plainly contradicts this interpretation, as the matter is clear: *οὐκ εἶπεν, ὁ Σατανᾶς ἐφθέγξατο διὰ σοῦ, ἀλλ’ ὕπαγε ὀπίσω μου, Σατανᾶ· καὶ γὰρ ἐπιθυμία ἦν τοῦ ἀντικειμένου, τὸ μὴ παθεῖν τὸν Χριστόν*—“He did not say, ‘Satan spoke through you,’ but, ‘Go behind me, Satan’; for the desire that Christ should not suffer belonged to the adversary.” RIG.]

> It is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve

(Matt. 26:23 [sic]; 4:10).

[Note: [Col. 0153A] **It is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, etc.** This is how the words stand in the exemplar. They contribute nothing, however, to Tertullian’s purpose, and we suppose that they were inserted by the same hand that distorted the preceding rebuke so as to direct it against the devil, removing Peter’s name. RIG.]

But even now he ought to hear this, insofar as, much later, he poured in [Note: [Col. 0153A] Fran.: “those”] these [Col. 0154A] poisons—unlikely not to harm any of the weak [Note: [Col. 0153A] Rig. inserts “unless”] who has not first drunk, or even drunk deeply, this draught of ours from [Note: [Col. 0154A] Fran.: “that”] the faith.

[Note: [Col. 0154A] **Unlikely not to harm any of the weak.** *Nulli facile nisi* stands for *nulli non facile*, “unlikely not to harm anyone.” Septimius chose to speak in this manner. RIG.]

[Col. 0153]

# THE BOOK OF QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN AGAINST PRAXEAS

## SUMMARY

[Col. 0153B]

Praxeas, a Phrygian originating from Asia, had once been cast into prison for the sake of the faith; because of those sufferings—which were not especially worthy of mention—he had become greatly swollen with pride. Nevertheless, he had rendered distinguished service to the Church. For when the pontiff—called Eleutherius by some and Victor by others—was on the point of granting letters of communion to the Montanists, who represented themselves as catholic in the transmitted profession of faith, Praxeas, then arriving from Asia, disclosed the errors of the Montanists that had become notorious in that province, and so prevented those men from deceiving that excellent pontiff.

In the end, his own arrogance destroyed the wretched man. For while he never ceased boasting of the titles of a martyr, he shared the fate common to all the proud and became the unfortunate founder of a new sect. He acknowledged one God in such a way as to abolish every distinction of persons, daring to assert that the Father himself had assumed flesh, had been driven to the cross, and now sits at his own right hand. His followers were called Patripassians or Monarchians because they posited only a single person of the most holy Trinity.

The most excellent work that Tertullian certainly wrote after his own lapse is this treatise *Against Praxeas*, in which he undertakes the defense of the faith of the Trinity; for on this point the Montanists did not disagree with the Catholic Church. In this work Septimius explicitly employs the term “Trinity” and exposes the deception of those heretics who usurp the name “monarchy” in order to persuade the less educated that they are defending the one almighty Creator of the world, while in the meantime making a heresy out of the One.

To establish the distinction between the persons of the Father and the Son, he says that the entire question concerning the Son must be examined: whether he exists, who he is, and how he exists.

> Before all things God was alone . . . because nothing else existed outside him. Yet not even then was he alone, for he had with him his own Reason—the Word, Wisdom—which he afterward sent forth externally, and it became the outward Word.

Tertullian judges that the Word of God should be called *Sermo* (“Speech” or “Word”) only after its outward utterance, or manifestation, made in the creation of the universe, in accordance with the very ancient theologians’ phraseology and manner of speaking. He nevertheless acknowledges that the Word was with God in the beginning. For although God had not yet sent forth his Word, he nonetheless possessed him within himself, together with and in Reason itself, silently thinking and arranging within himself the things that he was soon to speak through the Word.

From this it becomes clear in what sense he said elsewhere:

> There was a time when neither sin nor the Son existed;

namely, with respect to their outward manifestation through the creation of things—especially when he said, “Let there be light.” With respect to inward generation, however, his Son, the Word and Wisdom, was always with God the Father.

Tertullian further shows that the Son is from the Father’s substance and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son; that the Word, who was with God from all eternity and who went forth from him, as it were, to create and govern the world, is a subsistent person, yet is not different in substance from the Father; that it does not therefore follow that there are two Gods and two Lords; and that the Son, not the Father, became human, without ceasing to be God, to such a degree that the properties of human nature were found in Christ. In a word, throughout this treatise he lucidly explains the Church’s faith concerning the mysteries both of the Trinity and of the Incarnation. LUMP.

## CHAPTER ONE
In various ways the devil has rivaled the truth. At times he has sought to shake it by defending it. He champions one Lord, the almighty Creator of the world, so that even from the doctrine of one God he may make a heresy. He says that the Father himself descended into the Virgin [Note: [Col. 0153D] “Virgin,” Semler.], that he himself was born from her, that he himself suffered, and, finally, that he himself is Jesus Christ. The serpent forgot himself, because, when tempting Jesus Christ after John’s baptism, he assailed him as the Son of God; [Col. 0155A] he was certain that God had a Son, even from the very Scriptures out of which he was then constructing the temptation: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves”; likewise: “If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down from here; for it is written that he”—the Father, assuredly—“has commanded [Note: [Col. 0155B] ‘He will command,’ others.] his angels concerning you, that they should bear you up in their hands, lest anywhere you strike your foot against a stone” (Matt. 4:3–6; Ps. 90:11).

Or did he perhaps reproach the Gospels with falsehood [Note: [Col. 0155B] “He will reproach,” Franeker, Paris.], saying: “Let Matthew and Luke see to it; for my part, I approached God himself and tempted the Almighty himself at close quarters. That is why I approached him and why I tempted him. But if he had been the Son of God, perhaps I should never have deigned to tempt him [Note: [Col. 0155C] ‘To have tempted,’ Wouwer.]”? But [Col. 0155B] rather, he himself has been a liar from the beginning (1 John 3:8), as also when he has suborned [Note: [Col. 0155C] “Suborned,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.] one of his own men, namely Praxeas.

For this man was the first to introduce this kind of perversity [Note: [Col. 0155C] “Introduced it at Rome, a man,” etc. He means the provinces nearer the city of Rome. Otherwise Asia itself was partly under Roman rule. RHENANUS.] at Rome from Asia; a man in other respects also restless, and furthermore puffed up by boasting of martyrdom merely because of the simple and brief discomfort of imprisonment. Even if he had surrendered his body to be burned, he would have gained nothing, since he did not possess the love of God (1 Cor. 13:3), whose spiritual gifts he also attacked.

For this same man at that time [Note: [Col. 0155C] “The Roman bishop, who was already acknowledging the prophecies of Montanus.” What are called Tertullian’s heresies prescribed scarcely anything other than sterner martyrdoms, drier fasts, holier chastity—that is, either one marriage or none. In these matters, whatever his fault may have been, he seems to have erred entirely through a more vehement love of virtue. Certainly more serious was his acknowledgment and defense of Montanus’s Paraclete. But Montanus’s school, as Baronius also observes, remained harmless for some time and had disciples so commendable for holiness of conduct, so venerable for the beneficent power of their miracles, and so steadfast in martyrdoms [Col. 0155D] that no one could recognize elsewhere more immediately present manifestations of divine power. And indeed that most learned cardinal rightly judged that Anicetus, then Roman pontiff, acknowledged these gifts of the divine Spirit in people who as yet dissented in nothing from the rule of faith, granted peace to their churches, and, as Tertullian says, sent letters of peace. Nor is there any reason to suspect that Tertullian—a serious man, although then devoted to the party of Montanus—wished to lie about so recent and manifest a historical event, in a work that he was composing against the heretic Praxeas on an article of the catholic faith that ranks among the foremost; especially since a splendid lie, one immediately and easily refuted, would have had no value. Praxeas, therefore, as Tertullian portrays him, did not cease burdening Montanus’s disciples before the pontiff with fabricated allegations, and indeed with accusations that diminished pontifical authority, until the letters of peace or communion already issued, as we have said, were revoked. For this reason some of them, perhaps more offended [Col. 0156C] and indignant than was proper, began to extol and proclaim their Montanus to such a degree that they said that the Holy Spirit had indeed been in the apostles, but not the Paraclete; that their Paraclete had said more through Montanus than in Christ’s Gospel; and not only more, but even better and greater things. This, of course, is what we read concerning those called “According to the Phrygians” in the *Catalogue of Heretics*, which is commonly appended to Tertullian’s book *On Prescription*. These statements sufficiently show that those Phrygians attributed to their Montanus many things that he himself had never claimed for himself. Hence it becomes probable that Tertullian held Montanus’s teaching as it existed at its beginning, when it was acceptable to more austere Christians, rather than as it existed later, when, embroidered with the Phrygian needle by the impostures and frauds of certain followers, [Col. 0156D] it began everywhere to be rejected by the catholic churches. Finally, Tertullian’s extant writings do not persuade us that he ever became foolish “according to the Phrygians”; and the writings that have perished do not seem, while they were still extant, to have persuaded either Cyprian or Jerome of it. RIGAULT.]

compelled the Roman bishop—who was already acknowledging the prophecies of Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla, and, on the basis of that acknowledgment, bringing peace to the churches of Asia and Phrygia—both to revoke the letters of peace already issued and to desist from his intention [Col. 0156A] of receiving the spiritual gifts, by making false assertions concerning those prophets and their churches and by defending the authority of the bishop’s predecessors.

Thus Praxeas managed two pieces of the devil’s business [Note: [Col. 0156D] “Business.” He plays upon the name Praxeas, which could be derived from the Greek πράσσειν (*prassein*, “to do, transact”): thus Semler. EDITORS.] at Rome: he expelled prophecy and introduced heresy; he put the Paraclete to flight and crucified the Father. The Praxean tares had borne fruit [Note: [Col. 0156B] “Had borne fruit,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.], having been sown here also among the many who slept (Matt. 13:26) in simplicity of doctrine. Afterward, when they had been exposed by one whom God willed, they also seemed to have been uprooted.

[Note: [Col. 0156D] Finally, the former teacher had given a written guarantee of his amendment. Praxeas, having changed his opinion, cultivated and accordingly taught the former doctrine, that is, the ancient and true one; indeed, he had also given a written guarantee of his amendment. “The former teacher,” as Graevius reads the remaining words. RIGAULT.] Finally, the former teacher had given a written guarantee of his amendment; and the document remains among the Psychics [Note: [Col. 0156B] Others read “Physicists” here, and likewise “physical” below, but incorrectly.], among whom the affair was then conducted. From that time there was silence. And we, indeed, were afterward separated from the Psychics by our acknowledgment and defense of the Paraclete. Yet those tares had surely [Col. 0156B] shed their seed at that time [Note: [Col. 0156C] “Everywhere,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.]. Thus for a while it lay concealed through hypocrisy, with a deceitful vitality, and now it has broken out again. But it will also be uprooted again, if the Lord wills, through this present treatise; if not [Note: [Col. 0156C] “But if not,” Junius.], on his appointed day all adulterous crops [Note: [Col. 0156C] “Fully grown crops,” Petrus Ciacconius.] will be gathered and, together with the other stumbling blocks, burned in unquenchable fire (*ibid.*).

## CHAPTER II

Accordingly, it is now proclaimed that after a certain time the Father was born and the Father suffered: that God himself, the Lord Almighty, is Jesus Christ. We, however, have always believed—and now believe all the more, as persons [Note: [Col. 0156D] “Better instructed by the Paraclete.” Rhenanus correctly notes that he is speaking of Montanus’s Paraclete, to whom he also wrongly applies John 16:13, “the guide into all truth.” PAMELIUS.] better instructed by the Paraclete, that is, the guide into all truth—in one God indeed, yet under this dispensation, which we call the οἰκονομία (*oikonomia*, “economy”): namely, [Note: [Col. 0156D] “That the one God also has a Son, his Word, who proceeded from him.” He attributes the word “proceeding” to the Son, though the Church made it proper [Col. 0157D] to the Holy Spirit. RIGAULT.] that the one God also has a Son, his Word, who proceeded from him, through whom all things were made, and [Col. 0157A] without whom nothing was made (John 1:3); that this Son was sent by the Father into the Virgin and was born from her, man and God, Son of Man and Son of God, and was named Jesus Christ; that he suffered, died, and was buried according to the Scriptures; that he was raised by the Father and taken back into the heavens [Note: [Col. 0157C] “Into heaven,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.]; that he sits at the right hand of the Father and will come to judge the living and the dead; and that from there, according to his promise, he sent from the Father the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, the sanctifier of the faith of those who believe in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.

That this rule has run its course from the beginning of the Gospel, even before all the earlier heretics—to say nothing [Note: [Col. 0157D] “Before yesterday’s Praxeas.” Thus Persius said “yesterday’s Quirites,” that is, new, recent ones. RIGAULT.] of yesterday’s Praxeas—will be proved both by the very posteriority of all heretics and by the sheer novelty of yesterday’s Praxeas. From this point onward it may equally be prejudged against [Col. 0157B] all heresies [Note: [Col. 0157D] “That whatever is first is true”—namely, taking as the starting point the place where truth began. Thus in the book *On the Prescription of Heretics*: “And so from the order itself it is manifest that what was handed down earlier is the Lord’s and is true.” RIGAULT.] that whatever is first is true, and whatever is later is adulterated.

But while preserving this prescription, a place must nevertheless also be given to renewed examinations, for the instruction and fortification of certain persons, lest every perversity appear to have been condemned without examination, merely by prejudgment—especially this one, which thinks itself to possess the unalloyed truth because it believes that the one God cannot be believed in otherwise than by saying that the very same one is Father and Son and Holy Spirit. It is as though all were not in this way also one, since all are from one, namely through unity of substance, while nevertheless the mystery of the economy is preserved, which arranges the unity into a Trinity, setting forth three: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Three, however, [Col. 0157C] not in condition but in degree; not in substance but in form; not in power but in aspect; yet of one substance, one condition, and one power, because there is one God from whom these degrees, forms, and aspects are reckoned under the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. How, however, [Note: [Col. 0157C] Semler, following Rhenanus, omits “however.”] they admit of number without division, the ensuing examination [Note: [Col. 0157C] “Discussions,” Semler.] will demonstrate.

## CHAPTER III

For all the simple people—not to call them unwise and uneducated, who always constitute the greater part of believers—are alarmed at the economy. The very rule of faith transfers them from the many gods of the age [Col. 0158A] to the one true God, but they do not understand that he is indeed to be believed as one, yet together with his economy. They assume that the number and arrangement of the Trinity is a division of the unity, whereas the unity, deriving the Trinity from itself, is not destroyed by it but administered through it. And so they now loudly accuse us of preaching two and three Gods, while presuming that they themselves are worshipers of one God—as though a unity irrationally gathered into one did not create heresy, while a Trinity rationally considered constitutes truth.

[Note: [Col. 0157D] “We maintain the monarchy,” they say. Μοναρχικήν (*monarchikēn*), that is, “we affirm one God”—rightly indeed, for otherwise we fall εἰς τὴν ἄθεον πολυθέοτητα (*eis tēn atheon polytheotēta*), “into godless polytheism.” Jerome, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, states that Irenaeus composed a book bearing this title: *On the Monarchy, or, That God Is Not the Author of Evils*. Tertullian himself used the word “monarchy” to signify God in Book II of *On the Apparel of Women*: “We must put on this incorruptibility for the new house that the monarchy promises.” RIGAULT.] “We maintain the monarchy,” they say. And even Latins—and even *Opici*—pronounce the sound of the word so precisely [Note: [Col. 0157C] “Throne,” Semler, Rhenanus, Junius.] that you would suppose they understood “monarchy” as well as they pronounce it.

[Note: [Col. 0158D] “Even *Opici*.” That is, barbarians, because they spoke *opice*, that is, barbarously, not in Latin, according to Pliny, Book XXIX, chapter 1. PAMELIUS.—I know that Juvenal said in Satire 6:

> Nor should men heed the words corrected by an Opican crumb.

But here the exemplar reads: “And even Latins, even craftsmen, pronounce the very sound of the word so precisely,” which seems most appropriate to what follows, so that you would suppose they understood “monarchy” as well as they pronounce it. Septimius speaks in just this way in the *Apology*: “Any Christian craftsman both finds God [Col. 0159D] and makes him known.” RIGAULT.]

[Note: [Col. 0157D] “And so skillfully,” Semler; “even craftsmen,” Rigault.]

But Latins strive to pronounce “monarchy,” while even Greeks refuse to understand “economy.” [Col. 0158B] Yet if I have gleaned anything from either language, I know that “monarchy” signifies nothing other than a sole and single sovereignty. Nevertheless, because it belongs to one, monarchy does not prescribe that the one to whom it belongs either must have no son, must have made himself his own son, or must not administer his monarchy through whomever he wishes. Indeed, I say that no dominion belongs so entirely to one, is so singular, is so monarchical [Note: [Col. 0158C] “A monarchy,” Junius.], that it is not also administered through other persons closely associated with it, whom it has itself provided as its officials.

Moreover, if the one whose monarchy it is also has a son, it is not immediately divided, nor does it cease to be a monarchy, if the son too is taken into participation in it. Rather, it continues primarily to belong to him by whom it is shared with the Son [Note: [Col. 0158C] “Himself,” Franeker, Paris.]; and while it belongs to him, it therefore remains a monarchy, since it is held by two who are so united.

Thus, if even the divine monarchy is administered through so many legions and armies of angels, as it is written, “A thousand thousands [Note: [Col. 0158C] “A thousand times ten thousand hundreds of thousands,” Semler; “a thousand thousands, hundreds of thousands,” Latinus.] stood before him, and a thousand times a hundred thousand appeared before him,” it has not thereby ceased to belong to one, so as to cease being a monarchy merely because it is managed through so many thousands of powers. How, then, can God be thought to undergo division and dispersal in the Son and the Holy Spirit, who have obtained the second and third places and are such sharers in the Father’s substance, when he does not undergo this in so great a number of angels, who are indeed so alien to his substance [Note: [Col. 0158D] “The Father’s substance,” Semler; Franeker adds “of aliens.”]?

You reckon as the monarchy’s overthrow its members, its pledges, its instruments, its very strength, [Col. 0159A] and the whole sum of its resources. That is not right. I would rather have you exercise yourself upon the meaning of the reality than upon the sound of the word. For you must understand that the overthrow of a monarchy occurs when another dominion is brought in—one possessing its own origin and independent condition and therefore a rival—when another God is introduced in opposition to the Creator. Then it is an evil, when there are several gods, as among [Note: [Col. 0159D] “Valentinians and Prodicans.” Better than “Proclians,” as Rhenanus has it, although he adduces the Proclianites from Philastrius and Augustine, who say that angels made souls out of fire and spirit, which was also a doctrine of the Seleucians. LE PRIEUR.] the Valentinians and Prodicans [Note: [Col. 0159D] “Prodigals,” Semler; “Proclians,” Paris.]; then it is an overthrow of the monarchy, when it tends toward destruction of the Creator.

## CHAPTER IV

But as for me, who derive the Son from no other source than the Father’s substance, who represent him as doing nothing without the Father’s will and as having received all power from the Father—how can I destroy in matters of faith the monarchy that I preserve in the Son, since it was delivered to the Son by the Father? Let this also be said by me concerning the third [Col. 0159B] degree, because I hold that the Spirit comes from no other source than from the Father through the Son.

See, therefore, whether it is not rather you who destroy the monarchy, since you overthrow its arrangement and dispensation, established in as many names as God willed. Indeed, it so remains in its own condition, although the Trinity is introduced, that it is even to be restored to the Father by the Son. For the Apostle writes concerning the final consummation: “When he delivers the kingdom to God and the Father. For he must reign until God puts his enemies beneath his feet”—that is, in accordance with the Psalm: “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.” “But when all things have been subjected to him”—assuredly [Note: [Col. 0159D] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür omit “assuredly.”] except him who subjected all things to him—“then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all.”

We see [Note: [Col. 0159D] “We seem,” Venetian edition.], therefore, that the Son does not harm the monarchy, although today it is in the Son’s possession, because it both remains in its own condition while in the Son’s possession and will be restored with its condition to the Father by the Son. Thus no one will destroy it on this account if he admits the Son [Note: [Col. 0159D] “Destroy it. The Son,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.], to whom it is established that the monarchy was delivered by the Father and by whom it is one day to be restored to the Father.

By this single passage [Note: [Col. 0159D] “Passage,” that is, a saying, according to Semler. EDITORS.] of the apostolic Epistle, we could already have shown that the Father and the Son are two—not only from the names “Father” and “Son,” but also because the one who delivered the kingdom and the one to whom he delivered it, and likewise the one who subjected and the one to whom he subjected [Note: [Col. 0159D] “And the one to whom he subjected” was absent from Rhenanus.], must necessarily be two.

## CHAPTER V

But because they wish the two to be one, so that the same person may be regarded as both Father and Son, the entire question concerning the Son must be examined: whether he exists, who he is, and how he exists. Thus the reality itself, with the Scriptures and their interpretations supporting it, [Col. 0159D] will vindicate its own form.

Some indeed say [Note: [Col. 0160D] “Some,” Petrus Ciacconius.] that Genesis [Col. 0160A] begins thus in Hebrew: “In the beginning God made a son for himself.”

[Note: [Col. 0159D] “In the beginning God made a son for himself.” Blessed Jerome taught me, at the very beginning of his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, that this passage, which he cites there, can be understood of Christ more according to its sense than according to a literal translation. For the Seventy translators, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated “In the beginning”; and in Hebrew the text reads [Hebrew absent in the supplied text], which Aquila interprets “in the chief part,” and not [Hebrew absent in the supplied text], which is interpreted “in the son.” LE PRIEUR.]

Other arguments, however, derived from God’s own arrangement—from the state in which he existed [Note: [Col. 0160D] “In which he existed”—namely God. SEMLER.] before the establishment of the world until the generation of the Son—lead me not to regard this reading as established.

Before all things, God was alone, being for himself his own world, place, and everything. He was alone because there was nothing else [Note: [Col. 0160D] “Else” is absent from Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.] external besides him. Yet even then he was not alone, for he had with him that which he had within himself, namely his own Reason. For God is rational, and Reason was first within him; and thus all things were from him. This Reason is his consciousness. The Greeks call it λόγος (*logos*), a term by which we also designate “Word.” Hence it has now become customary among our people, through the simplicity of the translation, to say that the Word was in the beginning with God, although Reason is more properly regarded as prior, because God was not “word-bearing” from the beginning but rational even before the beginning; and because the Word himself, consisting in Reason, thereby shows Reason to be prior as his substance.

Yet even so, there is no difference. For although God had not yet sent forth his Word, he nevertheless had him within himself, together with and within Reason itself, silently thinking and arranging with himself what he would soon say through the Word. For while thinking and arranging with his Reason, he was making it into Word, which he treated by means of Word.

To understand this more easily, recognize it beforehand [Note: [Col. 0160D] “From me,” Semler.] from yourself, as from the image and likeness of God (Gen. 1:26). You too possess reason within yourself, since you are a rational creature, made by a rational craftsman and not only made by him but also animated from his substance.
