Observe that when you silently converse with yourself, this very activity is conducted by reason within you, as reason meets you together with word at every movement of your thought and every impulse of your consciousness. Whatever you think is word; whatever you perceive is reason. You must speak it within your mind; and while you speak, you experience the Word as your interlocutor, in whom is this very Reason through which, thinking with him, you speak, and through whom, speaking, you think. Thus in a certain sense the Word within you is a second, through whom you speak by thinking and through whom you think by speaking. The Word himself is another.

How much more fully, then, does this take place in God, whose image and likeness you also are reckoned to be: that even while silent he possesses Reason within himself, and the Word within Reason? I can therefore maintain that I did not rashly lay down beforehand that even then, before [Col. 0160D] the establishment of the universe, God was not alone, since he possessed [Col. 0161A] Reason within himself and, within Reason, the Word, whom he made second to himself by setting him in motion within himself.

## CHAPTER VI

This power and this ordering of the divine consciousness is also shown in the Scriptures under the name of Wisdom. For what is wiser than God’s Reason or Word? Accordingly, hear Wisdom herself as also having been established as a second person. First: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works, before he made the earth, before the mountains were established; before all the hills he begot me” (Prov. 8:22)—that is, establishing and begetting her within his own consciousness.

Then recognize her as standing beside him by reason of her distinctness: “When he prepared the heaven,” she says, “I was there together with him [Note: [Col. 0161D] “Together” is absent from other copies.]; and when he made firm the things above the winds, the clouds on high; and when he made secure the fountains of that which is beneath heaven, I was with him, fitting things together; I was the one in whom [Note: [Col. 0161D] “Whom,” Rhenanus.] he delighted, and daily I rejoiced in his presence.”

For as soon as God willed to bring forth into their own substances and forms the things that he had arranged within himself together with the Reason and Word of Wisdom, he first brought forth the Word himself, who had within himself his inseparable companions [Note: [Col. 0161D] “His inseparable companions,” that is, attendants. As near the end of the book *On Patience*: “When, therefore, the Spirit of God descends, patience, his inseparable companion, accompanies him.” RIGAULT.], Reason and Wisdom [Note: [Col. 0161D] “Reasons, Wisdom,” Rhenanus.], so that through him all things might be made through whom they had been thought and arranged—indeed, through whom they had already been made, insofar as they existed in God’s consciousness. This alone was lacking to them: that they should also be openly recognized and apprehended in their own forms and substances.

## CHAPTER VII

Then, therefore, the Word himself also assumes his form and adornment—sound and voice—when God says, “Let there be light.” This is the perfect nativity of the Word, as he proceeds from God: first established by him for thought under the name of Wisdom—“The Lord established me as the beginning of his ways”—and then begotten for effect: “When he prepared the heaven, I was there together with him.”

Thereafter, by making him equal to himself, from whom by proceeding he became the Son, God made him “the firstborn” (Col. 1:15), as begotten before all things, and “the only-begotten” (1 John 4:9), as alone begotten from God—properly from the womb of God’s own heart, in accordance with the Father’s own testimony: “My heart has uttered the best Word” (Ps. 44:1). Then, rejoicing in him who in turn rejoiced [Note: [Col. 0161D] “To the rejoicing one,” Semler.] in his presence, he said: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7); and: “Before the morning star I begot you.”

So too the Son, speaking in his own person under the name of Wisdom, confesses the Father: “The Lord established me as the beginning of his ways for his works. Before all the hills he begot me.” For although Wisdom here appears to say that she was established by the Lord for his works and ways, elsewhere it is shown that all things were made through the Word, and that without him nothing was made; as again it is written (Ps. 33:6): “By his Word the heavens were established, and by his Spirit all their powers”—assuredly by that Spirit which was within the Word. It is therefore apparent that the one and same power is designated now by the name “Wisdom,” now by the title “Word”: the power that received the beginning of the ways for God’s works, that established the heaven, through which [Note: [Col. 0161D] “Whom,” Franeker.] all things were made, and without which [Note: [Col. 0162D] “Whom,” Franeker.] nothing was made (John 1:3).

No more need be said on this point, as though the reference under the names of Wisdom, Reason, and every divine mind and spirit were not to him who became the Son of God by being begotten through proceeding from God.

“Therefore,” you say, “you grant that the Word is some kind of substance, constructed from spirit and the transmission of Wisdom?” Certainly. For you are unwilling that he should possess substantial existence in reality through the distinctive property of substance, so that he may be seen as a certain reality and person, and may thus, being established by God as second, make two: the Father and the Son, God and the Word.

[Note: [Col. 0161D] “For what, you will say, is the Word except the voice and sound of the mouth and air that has been struck?” So too in the book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, where he discusses the teeth, which, he says, man received so that the articulations of the voice might be marked by their impact. RIGAULT.]

“What is the Word,” you will say, “except the voice and sound of the mouth and—as the grammarians teach—air that has been struck, intelligible to hearing, but otherwise some empty, insubstantial, incorporeal thing?” Yet I say that nothing insubstantial and empty could have proceeded from God, since it was not produced from what is insubstantial and empty; nor can that which proceeded from so great a substance and made such great substances itself lack substance. For the Word himself made the things that were made through him.

How could he himself be nothing, without whom nothing was made? How could one who is insubstantial have produced solid things, one who is empty have produced full things, and one who is incorporeal have produced corporeal things? For although something can at times be made different from that by which it is made, nevertheless nothing can be made through that which is empty and insubstantial.

Is the Word of God, who was called the Son and himself named God, an empty and insubstantial thing—“And the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1)? It is written: “You shall not take the name of God in vain” (Exod. 20:7). He surely is the one who, “being established in the form of God, did not consider equality with God to be robbery” (Phil. 2:6). In what form of God? Surely in some real form, not in none at all.

[Note: [Col. 0162D] “For who will deny that God is a body?” See on this passage Dom Le Nourry, *Dissertation on Tertullian’s Apologeticum*, chapter VII, article 3, volume I of this edition, p. 811 ff. EDITORS.]

For who will deny [Note: [Col. 0162D] “Denied,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.] that God is a body, although God is spirit? For spirit is a body of its own kind, in its own form. But even all those things that are invisible possess before God their own body and their own form, through which they are visible to God alone. How much more, then, will that which was sent forth from his very substance [Note: [Col. 0162D] “Substance,” Rhenanus.] not be without substance!

Whatever, therefore, the substance of the Word was, that I call his person, and for him I claim the name of Son; and when I acknowledge the Son, I maintain that he is second to the Father.

## CHAPTER VIII

If anyone [Note: [Col. 0162D] “This,” Latinus.] supposes [Note: [Col. 0162D] “That I am introducing some προβολή.” By this word, or “prolation,” he explains what the holy Fathers call “generation” when speaking of the Son or Word, who is γενητός (*genētos*, “begotten”), whereas the Holy Spirit is ἐκπορευτός (*ekporeutos*, “one who proceeds”). [Col. 0163D] RIGAULT.] that I am introducing some προβολή (*probolē*), that is, the prolation of one thing from another, as Valentinus does when he produces one Aeon after another from an Aeon, I shall first tell you that truth does not therefore refrain [Note: [Col. 0163D] “Refrain,” Franeker, Paris; “will refrain,” Latinus.] from using this word, and the reality and meaning belonging to it, merely because heresy instead borrowed from truth the material with which it might construct its lie.

The Word of God was brought forth, was he not? Here take your stand with me. If he was brought forth, acknowledge the *probolē* of truth, and let heresy see to it whether it has imitated anything from the truth. The question now is who uses a given reality, and its name, and how.

Valentinus distinguishes and separates his probolai from their author, and places them so far from him that an Aeon does not know the Father. Indeed, the Aeon desires to know him but cannot; it is even almost consumed and dissolved into the remaining substance. Among us, however, the Son alone knows the Father [Col. 0163B] (Matt. 11:27); he himself has revealed the Father’s bosom (John 1:18); he has heard and seen all things with the Father; and he speaks the things [Note: [Col. 0163D] Latinus inserts “to.”] that he was commanded by the Father to speak (John 8:26). He fulfilled not his own will but the Father’s (John 6:38), which he had known from close at hand—indeed, from the beginning. “For who knows the things that are in God except the Spirit who is within him?” (1 Cor. 2:11).

Now the Word was constructed from Spirit, and, so to speak, the Spirit is the Word’s body. The Word, therefore, is always in the Father, as he says, “I am in the Father” (John 14:11); and always with God, as it is written, “And the Word was with God” (John 1:1); and never separated from the Father or other than the Father, because “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

This will be the *probolē* of truth, the guardian of unity, whereby we say that the Son was brought forth from the Father, [Note: [Col. 0163D] “But not separated.” Hence arise so many questions about whether he is a different thing from the Father—which is not conceded—although he is another person. RIGAULT.] but not separated [Note: [Col. 0163D] “Prepared,” Semler.]. For God brought forth the Word, as the Paraclete also teaches, as the root brings forth the shrub, the spring the river, and the sun the ray. For these forms too are *probolai* of the substances from which they proceed.

Nor would I hesitate to call the shrub the son of the root, the river the son of the spring, and the ray the son of the sun, because every origin is a parent, and everything brought forth from an origin is offspring—much more the Word of God, who has also properly received the name of Son. Yet the shrub is not separated from the root, nor the river from the spring, nor the ray from the sun, just as neither is the Word separated from God.

Therefore, in accordance with the pattern of these examples, I profess that I speak of two: God and his Word, the Father and his Son. For the root and the shrub are two realities, but joined; and the spring and the river are two forms, but undivided; and the sun and the ray are two configurations, but coherent. Everything that proceeds from something [Col. 0163D] must necessarily be second to that from which it proceeds; it is not, however, therefore separated from it. But where there is a second, there are two; and where there is a third, there are three.

For the Spirit is third from God and the Son, just as the fruit from the shrub is third from the root; the stream from the river is third from the spring; and the tip of the ray is third from the sun. Yet nothing is estranged from the source from which it derives its distinctive properties. Thus the Trinity, flowing down from the Father through interwoven and connected degrees, neither disturbs the monarchy nor fails to protect the condition of the economy.

## CHAPTER IX

Hold everywhere to this rule that I have professed, whereby I testify that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit are inseparable from one another; and thus you will recognize what is said and in what sense.

For observe: I say that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Spirit another. Every uneducated or perverse person takes this statement wrongly, as though it signified diversity and, from that diversity, extended the separation [Note: [Col. 0164D] “Maintained,” Junius.] of the Father, the Son, [Col. 0164B] and the Spirit. I say this, however, under the compulsion of their contention that the same person is Father, Son, and Spirit, as they flatter the monarchy in opposition to the economy.

Yet I say that the Son is another than the Father not by diversity but by distribution; another not by division but by distinction, because the Father and the Son are not the same, but differ from one another in measure. For the Father is the whole substance;

[Note: [Col. 0163D] “The Son, however, is a derivation.” Rhenanus correctly noted in the margin that Tertullian must be read cautiously here, [Col. 0164D] since, having written long before the Arian heresy, he did not weigh his words with complete precision. Yet his meaning—that the Father, Son, and Spirit are of the same substance—is manifest both from what precedes and from what follows in this book, chapter [number absent in the supplied text]. PAMELIUS.]

the Son, however, is a derivation and portion of the whole, as he himself declares: “Because the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). By him, too, the Son is sung of in the Psalm (8:6) as having been made less [Note: [Col. 0164D] “Younger,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.]: “A little [Note: [Col. 0164D] “By a little,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.] below the angels.”

Thus the Father too is another than the Son, insofar as he is greater than the Son; insofar as the one who begets is one and the one who is begotten another; the one who sends is one and the one who is sent another; the one who acts is one and the one through whom the action is performed another.

It is well that the Lord, when using this word in the person of the Paraclete, signified not division but arrangement: “For I shall ask,” he says (John 14:16), “the Father, and he will send you another Advocate, the Spirit of truth.” Thus he made the Paraclete another than himself, just as we make the Son another than the Father, so that he might show the third degree in the Paraclete, just as we show the second in the Son, for the preservation of the economy.

Does not the very fact that they are called Father and Son mean that one is distinct from the other? Assuredly, whatever all things are called, that they will be; and whatever they will be, that they will be called. The diversity of names cannot possibly be confounded, because neither can the realities whose names they are. “Yes” is yes, and “no” is no; for whatever is more than this comes from evil (Matt. 5:37).

## CHAPTER X
Thus he is either the Father or the Son; and just as day and night are not the same, neither are the Father and the Son the same, such that both might be one and each the other—which is what those most foolish Monarchians desire. [Note: [Col. 0164D] Those most foolish Monarchians. Some Praxeans seemed to deny the Trinity: for they maintained that God the Father had made himself the Son, a doctrine they called the μοναρχία (*monarchia*, “sole sovereignty”) of God, from which they derived their name. LE PR.] “He made himself,” they say, “a Son to himself.” Yet the Father makes the Son, and the Son makes the Father. And those who are constituted by one another can in no way constitute themselves in relation to themselves, so that the Father might make himself a Son to himself, and the Son present himself as a Father to himself. What God has established, he himself also observes. The Father must necessarily have a Son in order to be Father, and the Son a Father in order to be Son; but to have is one thing, and to be another.

For example, in order that I may be a husband, I must have a wife; I shall not myself be my own wife. Likewise, in order that I may be a father, I have a son; I shall not myself be my own son. And in order that I may be a son, I have a father; I shall not myself be my own father. For it is what I have that makes me what I shall then be: I shall be a father if I have a son, and a son if I have a father. But if I myself am what I ought to have, then I no longer have what I myself am: neither a father, because I myself shall be the father; nor a son, because I myself shall be the son. Now, insofar as I must have one of these in order to be the other, if I am both I shall be neither, because I do not have the other. For if I myself am the Son who is also the Father, I no longer have a son, but am myself the Son. Yet by not having a son, since I myself am the Son, how shall I be Father? For I must have a son in order to be Father. Therefore I am not the Son, because I do not have the Father who makes the Son. Equally, if I myself am the Father who is also the Son, I no longer have a father, but am myself the Father. Yet by not having a father, since I myself am the Father, how shall I be Son? For I must have a father in order to be Son. Therefore I shall not be the Father, because I do not have the son who makes the father.

This will be the sum total of the devil’s ingenuity: to exclude each by means of the other, since, by enclosing both in one under the patronage of the monarchy, he causes neither to be possessed—so that he is not Father, since of course he has no Son, and he is not Son, since equally he has no Father. For insofar as he is Father, he will not be Son. Thus those who uphold the monarchy contain neither Father nor Son.

“But nothing is difficult for God.” Who does not know this? And who is unaware that things impossible with the world are possible with God (Matt. 19:26)? “And God chose the foolish things of the world to confound wisdom” (1 Cor. 1:27) [Note: [Col. 0165D] “Wisdom,” Rhen. Seml. Oberth.]: we have read all these texts. “Therefore,” they say, “it was not difficult for God to make himself both Father and Son, contrary to the form handed down among human beings; for neither was it difficult for God to cause a barren woman to give birth contrary to nature, just as it was not difficult to cause a virgin to do so.” Certainly, nothing is difficult for God. [Note: [Col. 0165D] “Difficult,” I have understood; “so,” Seml.] But if we employ this maxim so abruptly in support of our presumptions, we shall be able to fabricate anything whatever about God, as though he had done it merely because he could have done it. Yet because he can do all things, it is therefore not necessarily to be believed that he did even what he did not do; rather, one must inquire whether he did it. [Note: [Col. 0165D] “Therefore,” Rhen. Seml. Oberth.]

God could—so may I be saved—have equipped man with wings for flight, as he also did for kites [Note: [Col. 0166D] “If he had wished,” added by Rhen.]; nevertheless, because he could, it does not follow that he actually did. He could also have extinguished Praxeas and all the heretics together immediately; nevertheless, because he could, it does not follow that he extinguished them. For there had to be kites, and there had to be heretics; there also had to be a crucified Father. By this reasoning something will even be difficult for God—namely, whatever he has not done—not because he could not, but because he did not will it. For God’s ability is his will, and his inability his unwillingness; but what he willed, he both could do and showed that he could. Therefore, because, if he willed to make himself a Son to himself, he could; and because, if he could, he did: you will then prove both that he could and that he willed, if you prove that he did.

## CHAPTER XI

But you will have to prove it from the Scriptures as openly as we prove that he made his Word a Son to himself. For if he names a Son, and the Son will be none other than the one who proceeded from him, while the Word proceeded from him, then the Word will be the Son, not the one from whom he proceeded. For he did not himself proceed from himself. Moreover, when you say that the Father and the Son are the same, you make the same one, who is God, both bring forth from himself and proceed forth. Even if he could have done it, he nevertheless did not do it.

Or else produce the proof I demand, corresponding to my own; that is, show that the Scriptures present the Son and the Father as the same, just as among us Father and Son are demonstrated to be distinct—distinct, I say, not divided. Thus I bring forward what God said: “My heart has poured forth the excellent Word” (Ps. 44:1). You in turn should oppose to this some place where God said, “My heart has poured forth the excellent word,” in such a way that he himself is both the one who poured forth and what he poured forth; both the one who brought forth from himself and the one brought forth—if he himself is both the Word and God.

See, I set forth that the Father said to the Son: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7). If you wish me to believe that he himself is both Father and Son, show that it is stated elsewhere in this manner: “The Lord said to himself, I am my Son; today I have begotten myself”; and likewise: “Before the morning star I begot myself” (Ps. 109:3); and, “The Lord established me as the beginning of his ways for my works; before all the hills I begot myself” (Wis. 8:22); and any other texts of this sort.

Whom, however, did God, the Lord of the universe, fear, so that he would not declare it in this manner if such were the reality? Or did he fear that he would not be believed if he had straightforwardly declared himself both Father and Son? There is, however, one thing he feared: to lie. But he feared himself and his own truth. And therefore, because I believe God to be truthful, I know that he declared no otherwise than he arranged, nor arranged otherwise than he declared.

You, moreover, make him a liar, a deceiver, and one who misleads this faith, if, when he himself was his own Son, he assigned the person of the Son to another, since all the Scriptures display both a manifestation and a distinction of the Trinity. From these also our prescriptive rule is derived: that the one who speaks, the one about whom he speaks, and the one to whom he speaks cannot be regarded as one and the same, because neither perversity nor deception befits God—as would be the case if, when he himself was the one to whom he was speaking, he spoke rather to another and not to himself. [Note: [Col. 0166D] “Was speaking,” Rhen. Seml. Oberth.; “would speak,” Jun.]

Receive, therefore, also other utterances of the Father concerning the Son through Isaiah (Isa. 42:1): “Behold my Son whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom I have been well pleased. I shall place my Spirit upon him, and he will announce judgment to the nations.” Receive also the words addressed to him (Isa. 49:6): “It is a great thing for you to be called my Son, to establish the tribes of Jacob and to turn back the dispersion of Israel. I have appointed you as a light of the nations, that you may be salvation to the end of the earth.”

Receive now also the utterances of the Son concerning the Father (Isa. 61:1): “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me to bring good news to humankind.” Again, to the Father in a Psalm concerning the same matter: “Do not forsake me until I announce your arm to every generation yet to come” (Ps. 71:18). Again, in another Psalm (Ps. 3): “Lord, why have those who oppress me multiplied?” Indeed, almost all the Psalms sustain the person of Christ: they represent the Son speaking to the Father—that is, Christ addressing God.

Observe also the Spirit speaking in the third person concerning the Father and the Son: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. 110:1). Again through Isaiah: “Thus says the Lord to my lord, Christ” (45:1). Again through the same prophet, to the Father concerning the Son: “Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? We proclaimed concerning him: he was like a little child, like a root in thirsty ground, and there was neither form nor glory in him” (Isa. 53:1–2).

These few are taken from many. For we do not seek to unroll the whole of Scripture, since, while calling to witness the full majesty and authority present in its individual chapters, we have a larger engagement with the matter in our treatises. [Note: [Col. 0167D] “We have,” Rhen. Seml. Oberth.] By these few passages, then, the distinction of the Trinity is nevertheless plainly set forth. For there is the one who speaks, namely the Spirit; the Father to whom he speaks; and the Son about whom he speaks. So too the other things that are declared—now to the Father about the Son, or to the Son; now to the Son about the Father, or to the Father; now to the Spirit—establish each person in his own distinctive character.

## CHAPTER XII

If the number of the Trinity still scandalizes you, as though it were not joined together in simple unity, I ask how the unique and singular God speaks in the plural: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26), when he ought to have said, “I shall make man according to my image and likeness,” since he is unique and singular. But also in what follows: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us.” Is he deceiving or jesting, that, although he was one, alone, and singular, he should speak numerically? Or was he perhaps speaking to angels, as the Jews interpret it, since they too do not acknowledge the Son? Or, because he himself was Father, Son, and Spirit, did he therefore, presenting himself as plural [Note: [Col. 0167D] “Displaying,” Wouw.], speak to himself in the plural?

No. Rather, because the Son, the second person, his Word, was already adhering to him, and the third, the Spirit in the Word, he therefore declared in the plural, “Let us make,” “our,” and “us.” With whom, then, did he make man, and to whom did he make him similar? With the Son, indeed, who was to clothe himself with man; and with the Spirit, who was to sanctify man. He spoke as with ministers [Note: [Col. 0167D] “Fellow ministers,” Jun.] and witnesses, from the unity of the Trinity. [Note: [Col. 0167D] “Similar? With the Son,” Rhen. Seml. Oberth.]

Finally, the Scripture that follows distinguishes between the persons: “And God made man; according to the image of God he made him” (Gen. 1:27). Why did it not say “his own,” if there was one who made and no one according to whose image he made? But there was one according to whose image he made: namely, the Son. Since the Son was to be the more certain and truer man, he caused that man who was then to be formed from clay to be called his image—the image and likeness of the true one. [Note: [Col. 0167D] “Of the true,” Rhen. Pam. Seml. Oberth.]

But how is it written concerning the preceding works of the world? First, before the Son had yet appeared: “And God said, Let there be light; and it was made” (Gen. 1:3)—the Word himself being at once the true light that enlightens the human being coming into this world, and through him the worldly light also. Thereafter, with the Word, Christ, standing by and administering, God willed things to come into being, and God made them. [Note: [Col. 0167D] “May have willed,” Rig. Venet.] “And God said, Let there be a firmament; and God made the firmament” (Gen. 1:7); and, “God said, Let there be lights; and God made the greater and the lesser light” (Gen. 1:14–16). The same one who made the former things also made the rest: that is, the Word of God, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made. He himself is God, according to John (1:1): “The Word was God.”

You have two: one who says that it should be made, and another who makes it. But I have already declared how you should understand “another”: as a designation of person, not of substance; for distinction, not division. Otherwise, although everywhere I maintain one substance in three who cohere, nevertheless, by the necessity of the sense, I must speak of the one who commands and the one who acts as “another.” For he would not command if he himself were doing it, since he was commanding that it be done through him. [Note: [Col. 0168D] “For since he commanded, it was to be done,” Lat. Rig.; “since he commanded. Yet he commands it to be done through him,” Jun.] Nevertheless, he was commanding—whereas, if he were one, he would not have been going to command himself—or he would have acted without a command, since he would not have waited for himself to command.

## CHAPTER XIII

“Therefore,” he says, “if God spoke and God made; if one God spoke and another made, two gods are proclaimed.” If you are so obtuse, suppose it for the moment; and so that you may suppose it still more, receive the statement in the Psalm (44:7–8) that speaks of two gods: “Your throne, O God, is forever; the rod of your kingdom: you have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you.” If it speaks to God and affirms that an anointed God was anointed by God, this passage plainly presents two gods. [Note: [Col. 0168D] “But this presents two gods” in place of “the rod of your kingdom,” Seml. Pam.; “it affirms, and this presents two Gods,” Lat.]

Hence Isaiah also says in the person of Christ (Isa. 45:14): “And the Sabaeans [*sabain*], men of lofty stature, will cross over to you, and will follow after you bound by the hands, and will worship you, because God is in you. For you are our God, and we did not know it, the God of Israel.” [Note: [Col. 0168D] “Sabaim,” Fran.; “Seboim,” Seml.] Here too, by saying both “God is in you” and “you are God,” he presents two: the one who was there, and the one in whom he was [Note: [Col. 0168D] “Who were in Christ,” Rhen. Seml. Oberth.]—Christ and the Spirit. [Note: [Col. 0169D] *Spiritum* (“Spirit”), s.; *plus* (“more”), Latin.; *in Christo ex S. plus* (“in Christ from S., more”), Jun. [apparatus wording uncertain].]

More than this, you will find the same number in the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). There is one who was, and another with whom he was. I also read the name “Lord” applied to two: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109:1). And Isaiah says this: “Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53:1). For he would have said “your arm” [Note: [Col. 0169D] “He would not have said ‘his arm’ if...,” Seml.], not “the Lord’s,” if he had not wished the Lord as Father and the Lord as Son to be understood.

Genesis, still more ancient, also says: “And the Lord rained sulfur and fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord out of heaven” (Gen. 19:24). Either deny that these things are written, or who are you to think they should not be understood as they are written—especially those passages whose meaning is not contained in allegories and parables, but in definite, certain, and straightforward statements? [Note: [Col. 0169D] “And” absent from Seml.] But if you are one of those who at that time could not endure the Lord’s showing himself to be the Son of God, and would not believe him to be Lord, remember that it was written against you together with them: “I said, You are gods and sons of the Most High” (Ps. 82:6); and, “God stood in the assembly of gods.” Thus, if Scripture did not fear to call human beings—made sons of God through faith—“gods,” know that it much more justly bestowed the name “God” upon the true and only Son of God.

“Therefore,” you say, “I challenge you, on the authority of these Scriptures, steadfastly to proclaim even today two gods and two lords.” Far be it from us. For we, who by God’s grace examine both the occasions and the reasons of the Scriptures—being especially disciples of the Paraclete, not of human beings [Note: [Col. 0169D] “Especially disciples of the Paraclete, not of human beings.” Unless I am mistaken, he is referring to the Paraclete of the new prophecy. For the followers of Montanus boasted that they were not disciples of human beings, but of the Paraclete. RHEN.]—do indeed define two, Father and Son, and now three with the Holy Spirit, according to the principle of the economy [οἰκονομία, *oeconomia*], which produces number. This is so that, as your perversity infers, the Father himself may not be believed to have been born and to have suffered—a thing it is not permissible to believe, since it was not so handed down.

Nevertheless, we never bring forth from our mouth the expressions “two Gods” and “two Lords”—not as though the Father were not God, the Son God, the Holy Spirit God, and each one God; but because formerly both “two gods” and “two lords” were proclaimed, so that, when Christ had come, he might both be acknowledged as God and be called Lord, because he is the Son of God and of the Lord. For if only one person of both God and Lord were found in the Scriptures, Christ would rightly not have been admitted to the name “God” and “Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0169D] “To” added by Seml.] For no other was proclaimed besides one God and one Lord, and it would have appeared that the Father himself had descended, since “one God” and “one Lord” was read; and his entire economy, which was foreseen and dispensed as the substance of faith, would have been obscured.

But when Christ came and was known by us to be the one who had formerly produced the number [Note: [Col. 0169D] “Is” absent from Seml.]—being made second from the Father, and third with the Spirit, while the Father was now more fully manifested through him—the name of God and Lord was now reduced to unity. [Note: [Col. 0169D] “And,” Seml.] This was so that the nations might pass from the multitude of idols to the one God, and that [Note: [Col. 0170D] “So that,” Seml.] a distinction might be established between worshipers of one divinity and worshipers of a plurality. For Christians had to shine in the world as sons of light, as the light of the world, worshiping and naming one God and Lord.

Otherwise, if, from the consciousness by which we know that the name “God” and “Lord” is fitting for Father, Son, and Spirit, we called them “gods” and “lords,” we should have extinguished our torches and become more timid even before martyrdoms. For an opportunity of escape would then lie open [Note: [Col. 0170D] “Lies open,” Seml.] to us as well [Note: [Col. 0170D] “In every way,” Seml.], if we immediately swore by “gods and lords,” as do certain heretics whose gods are numerous. [Note: [Col. 0169D] Whose gods are numerous. He particularly indicates the Valentinians because of their immense medley of divine Aeons; they were, as it were, shoots and branches of the Gnostics from a corrupt root. LE PR.]

Therefore, I shall by no means say “gods” or “lords”; rather, I shall follow the Apostle, so that if Father and Son are to be named together, I shall call the Father “God” and name Jesus Christ “Lord.” But I shall be able to call Christ alone “God,” as does the same Apostle: “From whom is Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5). For I shall also call a ray of the sun “sun” when considered separately; yet when I name the sun to which the ray belongs, I shall not immediately call the ray “sun” as well. For although I shall not make two suns [Note: [Col. 0170D] “I shall make two,” Seml.], nevertheless I shall reckon both the sun and its ray as two things and two forms of one undivided substance, just as God and his Word, and the Father and the Son. [Note: [Col. 0170D] “As,” Seml.]

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 0170C]

There still supports us, in maintaining two—the Father and the Son—the rule that has defined God as invisible. [Note: [Col. 0170D] “Which,” Seml.] For when Moses in Egypt desired the sight of the Lord (Exod. 33:13, 20) [Note: [Col. 0170D] Moses had desired the sight of the Lord in Egypt. Yet Moses himself relates that he had such a conversation with God not in Egypt but on Mount Sinai in Arabia. We therefore find it remarkable that not even one interpreter or commentator, down to our own times, has noticed this error of Tertullian’s, obvious though it is. EDD.], saying, “If, therefore, I have found favor before you, manifest yourself to me, that I may see you knowingly,” he replied, “You cannot see my face, for a human being will not see my face and live”—that is, whoever sees it will die.

For we find that God was seen by many, yet none of those who had seen him died. God was indeed seen according to human capacity, not according to the fullness of divinity; for the patriarchs are reported to have seen God, such as Abraham and Jacob, and the prophets, such as Isaiah and Ezekiel, and yet they did not die. Therefore, either they ought to have died if they saw him—for “no one will see God and live”—or, if they saw God and did not die, Scripture lies when it reports that God said, “If a human being sees my face, he will not live”; or Scripture lies when it presents God now as unseen and now as seen.

There will therefore be another who was seen, because the same one who was seen cannot be defined as invisible. Consequently, we must understand the Father to be invisible on account of the fullness of his majesty, but acknowledge the Son to be visible according to the measure of his derivation. Similarly, we are not permitted to gaze upon the sun with respect to the very totality of its substance in heaven, but we can endure its ray with our eyes because of the moderated portion extended from it to the earth.

Here, in opposition, someone will wish to contend that even the Son is invisible, as Word and as Spirit; and, by claiming a single condition for Father and Son, he will insist instead that Father and Son are one and the same. [Note: [Col. 0171D] “One,” Seml.] But we have said that Scripture supports the difference through the distinction between visible and invisible. For they also add the following to their argument: “But if it was the Son who was then speaking to Moses, he himself would have declared his own face visible to no one, because he himself was of course the invisible Father under the name of the Son.” And for this reason they wish the same one to be understood as both visible and invisible, just as they understand the same one to be Father and Son: since shortly before, before he had denied his face to Moses, it was written that the Lord had spoken with Moses face to face, as one speaks to his friend. [Note: [Col. 0171D] “And” inserted by Seml.] Jacob likewise said: “I saw the Lord face to face” (Gen. 32:30). Therefore, the same one is visible and invisible. [Note: [Col. 0171D] “And” absent from Fran. Paris.] And because the same one is both, he himself is invisible insofar as he is Father, and visible insofar as he is Son. [Note: [Col. 0172D] “Because also the Son,” Seml.; “the Father was formerly visible,” Jun.]

As though our interpretation of Scripture did not apply to the Son, with the Father set apart in his invisibility! [Note: [Col. 0172D] “Visibility,” Seml.] For we say that the Son also, in his own right, is thus far invisible: insofar as he is the Word and Spirit of God, by the condition of his substance even now, and insofar as he is God, Word, and Spirit. But he was visible before the flesh in the manner in which he says to Aaron and Miriam (Num. 12:6–8): “If there is a prophet among you, I shall make myself known to him in a vision, and I shall speak to him in a dream—not as to Moses. I shall speak to him mouth to mouth in a form,” that is, in reality, “and not in a riddle,” that is, not in an image. [Note: [Col. 0172D] “Because,” Seml.; “who is God as,” Jun.; “as also,” Rig.] As the Apostle also says: “Now we see as through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12).

Therefore, since he reserves his sight and face-to-face conversation with Moses for the future—for this was afterward fulfilled in the retirement on the mountain, as we read in the Gospel (Luke 9:30), where Moses was seen conversing with him—it is apparent that formerly God, that is, the Son of God, was always seen in a mirror, a riddle, a vision, and a dream, by the prophets and patriarchs as well as, thus far, by Moses himself.

And even if the Lord did perhaps speak face to face, nevertheless a human being did not see his face as it truly is, except perhaps in a mirror and a riddle. Finally, if the Lord spoke to Moses in such a way that Moses came to know his face close at hand, how is it that immediately, in the same place, he desires to see his face—which he would not desire if he had seen it? Likewise, how does the Lord deny that his face can be seen, if he had shown it—assuming he had shown it? Or what is the face of God whose sight is denied, if it was the one that had been seen? Jacob says, “I saw God face to face, and my soul was preserved” (Gen. 32:30). The face that kills if it is seen must be another.

Or was it perhaps the Son who was seen, and indeed his face, but this very sight occurred in a vision, dream, mirror, and riddle, because the Word and Spirit cannot be seen except in an imaginary form? [Note: [Col. 0171D] “But he calls his face,” etc. The author introduces this as an argument of the Praxeans; for he also refutes it with the words, “For what father?” etc., showing that the Son should rather be called the face of the Father, and this from Scripture, Lam. 4. PAM.] But he calls the invisible Father his face.

For what, then, is the Father? Will he not be the face of the Son, by designation of the authority that the one begotten from the Father obtains? For is it not also fitting to say of some greater person: “That man is my face,” and “He represents my face”? “The Father,” he says, “is greater than I” (John 14:28). Therefore, the Father will be the face of the Son. For what does Scripture also say? “The Spirit of his person is Christ the Lord” (Lam. 4:20). Therefore, if Christ is the Spirit of the Father’s person, he rightly declared the one whose person he was the Spirit of—that is, the Father—to be his face, namely by reason of their unity. I should indeed be surprised if the Father could be understood as the face of the Son, since he is his head: “For the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11:3).

## CHAPTER XV

If I do not resolve this point by means of questions arising from the Old Scripture, I shall take confirmation of our interpretation from the New Testament, lest you likewise defend as belonging to the Father whatever I attribute to the Son. For behold, both in the Gospels and in the Apostles I find a visible and an invisible God, under a manifest and personal distinction between the condition of each.

John exclaims, as it were: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18). Certainly, then, no one did so in the past either. For by saying that God was never seen, he removed the question of time. The Apostle also confirms concerning God: “Whom no human being has seen, nor indeed can see” (1 Tim. 6:16)—because, of course, whoever sees him will die. Yet these same Apostles testify that they both saw Christ and touched him. [Note: [Col. 0171D] “These same Apostles,” etc. He attributes to the Apostles in the plural what John alone writes in 1 Epistle 1, and soon cites. The reason for this, apparently, is that John spoke in the plural: “What we saw, what we heard, we saw with our eyes, and our hands touched, concerning the Word of life.” Here again, a little later, he changes the order of the words, since both the Greek and the Latin now read: “what we heard, what we saw with our eyes, what we beheld, and our hands touched.” PAM.]

Moreover, if Christ himself is both Father and Son, how was he both seen and unseen? To reconcile this diversity of the seen and the unseen in one, who on the other side will not argue that both statements were rightly made: that he was visible in the flesh, but invisible before the flesh, so that the same one is the Father invisible before the flesh and the Son visible in the flesh? Yet if the same one was invisible before the flesh, how is he also found to have been seen formerly, before the flesh? Equally, if the same one whom flesh later made more fully visible was formerly seen in a riddle, then the Word, of course, who became flesh, is someone other than the one whom no one ever saw—namely the Father, to whom the Word belongs.

Finally, let us examine whom the Apostles saw. “What we saw,” says John (1 John 1:1), “what we heard, we saw with our eyes, and our hands touched concerning the Word of life.” For the Word of life was made both audible and tangible because he was flesh—the one who before the flesh was only the Word, in the beginning with God the Father, not the Father with the Word. For although the Word is God, he is with God, because he is God from God, because he is with the Father, in the Father’s presence.

“And we saw his glory, as of the only-begotten from the Father” (John 1:14)—the glory, certainly, of the Son, namely the visible one, glorified by the invisible Father. And therefore, because [Note: [Col. 0173C] “How,” Seml.] he had called the Word of God “God,” lest [Note: [Col. 0173C] “So that,” Seml.] he lend support to the presumption of his adversaries, as though he had seen the Father himself, he adds more than enough, in order to distinguish between the invisible Father and the visible Son: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18). Which God? The Word? Yet it was declared beforehand, “We have seen, heard, and touched concerning the Word of life.” But which God, then? The Father, of course, with whom, as God, the Word was—the only-begotten Son, namely, who himself expounded him from the Father’s bosom. [Note: [Col. 0173D] “God,” Seml.; “namely” absent from Seml.; “is in the bosom,” Seml.]

He himself was both heard and seen, and, lest he be believed a phantom, was even touched. Paul too beheld him, yet he did not see the Father. “Have I not,” he says, “seen Jesus?” (1 Cor. 9:1). He also called Christ “God”: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5). [Note: [Col. 0173D] “The Lord himself,” Seml.; “through,” Seml.] He too [Note: [Col. 0173D] “He” absent from Seml.] shows the Son of God to be visible, that is, the Word of God, because, having become flesh, he was called Christ.

But concerning the Father he says to Timothy: “Whom no human being has seen, nor indeed can see” (1 Tim. 6:16). He intensifies the statement further: “Who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light.” Concerning him he had also said above: “But to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God.” [Note: [Col. 0173D] “But to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible,” etc. It is worth noting here that not only the blessed Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine, when citing this passage of the Apostle, 1 Tim. 1, but also the present author, read nothing other than “the only God.” From this it is inferred that the word “wise,” which some present-day Greek manuscripts insert, was added from the end of the Epistle to the Romans. Hence Clarius’s correction in that passage was also much too free. PAM.]

Thus we should attribute to the Son the contrary qualities: mortality [Note: [Col. 0173D] “And” inserted by Jun.] and accessibility. Scripture testifies that he died according to the Scriptures (1 Cor. 15:3), and that he was seen by Paul at the last, certainly through accessible light—although Paul himself did not experience even that light [Note: [Col. 0173D] “And” added by Seml.] without danger to his sight; nor did Peter, John, and James experience it without danger to their reason and without stupefaction. [Note: [Col. 0174D] “Nor Peter and John and James without reason and madness.” That is, neither without danger to reason nor without stupefaction. He says “danger to reason” as above “danger to sight,” that is, damage. Ursinus’s book reads, “without a testing of reason”; Pithoeus’s, “without reason and madness.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0173D] “Reasons,” Seml.; “through irrationality,” Fran.; “through wandering,” Rhen. and Jun.; “of reason from stupefaction,” Wouw.] If they had seen not the glory of the Son, which they were capable of suffering, but the Father, I believe they would have died on the spot. For “no one will see God and live.”

If these things are so, it is established that the one seen at the end is the one who was always seen from the beginning, and that the one not seen even at the end is the one who was not seen from the beginning; and thus there are two: the seen and the unseen. Therefore, it is the Son who was always seen, the Son who always held converse, and the Son who always acted, by the Father’s authority and will. For the Son can do nothing from himself unless he sees the Father acting—that is, acting in thought. [Note: [Col. 0174C] “Thinking,” Seml.] For the Father acts in thought [Note: [Col. 0174D] “In thought,” Jun.], while the Son, seeing what is in the Father’s thought, brings it to completion. [Note: [Col. 0174D] “Who,” Venet. Rhen.] Thus all things were made through the Son, and without him nothing was made.

## CHAPTER XVI
Nor should you suppose that only the works of the world were made through the Son, but also those things that God has done since then. For the Father, who loves the Son, has delivered all things into his hand [Note: [Col. 0174D] “Bosom,” Rhen.]; assuredly he has loved him from the beginning and delivered all things to him from the beginning. From that beginning the Word was with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1); to him all power in heaven and on earth was given by the Father (Matt. 28:8). The Father judges no one [Col. 0174C], but has delivered all judgment to the Son (John 5:22)—from the beginning, nevertheless. For when Scripture says “all power,” “all judgment,” “all things were made through him,” and “all things were delivered into his hand,” it permits no exception of time, because “all things” would not be all unless they belonged to all time.

Accordingly, it is the Son who [Note: [Col. 0174D] Seml. adds “also.”] judged from the beginning: striking down the most arrogant tower, scattering [Note: [Col. 0174D] “Destroying,” Seml.] the languages, punishing the whole world with the violence of the waters, and raining fire and sulfur [Note: [Col. 0174D] “Sulfur,” Jun.] upon Sodom and Gomorrah—the Lord [Note: [Col. 0174D] “God from God,” Seml.] from the Lord (Gen. 19:24). For it was he who also always descended to converse with human beings, from Adam down to the patriarchs and prophets, in vision, in dream [Note: [Col. 0174D] “Sleep,” Seml.], in a mirror [Col. 0175A], and in an enigma, always preparing from the beginning the course that he was to follow through to the end [Note: [Col. 0175C] “The infinite things that he was to pursue,” Seml.].

Thus he was always learning [Note: [Col. 0175D] “Thus he was always learning.” So too in the book *On the Flesh of Christ*: “And he was learning,” he says, “to deliver and to judge the human race in the guise of flesh not yet born.” Again, in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*: “They learn the flesh’s immunity.” And presently here: “But he was learning.” In the little book *To the Martyrs*: “Even in peace,” he says, “through toil and hardships they are already learning to endure war.” RHEN.], and no other God could have associated with human beings on earth than the Word who was to become flesh. He was learning, moreover, in order to lay down for us a path to faith, so that we might more readily believe that the Son of God had descended into the world if [Note: [Col. 0175D] “If” absent from Seml.] we knew that something of this kind had also happened formerly. For just as these things were written for our sake, so too were they done for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come down.

Thus even then he was becoming acquainted with human affections, since he was also to assume the very substances of the human being, flesh and soul: asking Adam, as though he did not know, “Where are you, Adam?”; regretting that he had made the human being, as though he had not foreknown it; testing Abraham, as though ignorant of what is in a human being; taking offense at and being reconciled [Col. 0175B] to the same persons. The heretics seize upon any such things as though they were unworthy of God, for the destruction of the Creator, not knowing that these things were appropriate to the Son, who was also to undergo human sufferings—thirst, hunger, tears, birth itself, and death itself. For this reason he was made a little [Note: [Col. 0175D] “Something” absent from Seml.] lower by the Father than the angels (Ps. 8:6).

Yet the heretics, to be sure, will not assign to the Son of God as appropriate even those things that you attribute to the Father himself [Note: [Col. 0175D] “Yourself,” Seml.], as though he had diminished himself for our sake, although Scripture says that one was made lower by another, not that he was made lower by himself. What if, moreover, the one who was crowned with glory and honor [Note: [Col. 0175D] “Glory and honor,” Seml.] was one, and the one who crowned him another—assuredly the Father crowning the Son?

Besides, how could that invisible almighty God, whom no human being has seen or can see; he who dwells in inaccessible light; he who does not dwell [Col. 0175C] in things made by hands; before whose sight the earth trembles and the mountains melt like wax; who grasps the whole world in his hand as though it were a nest; whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is earth; in whom every place exists, while he himself is not in a place; who is the outermost boundary of the universe—how could that Most High have walked in paradise toward evening, seeking Adam; have shut the ark after Noah entered; have refreshed himself beneath the oak beside Abraham; have called Moses from the burning bush; and have appeared as the fourth figure in the Babylonian king’s furnace—although he was called the Son of Man—unless these things had taken place in an image [Note: [Col. 0175D] “Was called, and in an image,” Seml.], a mirror, and an enigma? Of course, even these things would not have been [Col. 0176A] believed [Note: [Col. 0175D] “Had been,” Jun.] of the Son of God if they had not been written; perhaps they ought not to be believed of the Father even though written—of him whom these people bring down into Mary’s womb, set before Pilate’s tribunal, and enclose in Joseph’s tomb [Note: [Col. 0175D] “Tombs,” Seml.].

Their error is therefore apparent from this. For, because they are ignorant that from the beginning the whole course of the divine dispensation has run through the Son, they believe that it was the Father himself who was seen, who met with human beings, who acted, who suffered thirst and hunger—contrary to the prophet’s declaration: “The eternal God will not thirst or hunger at all” (how much less will he die or be buried!)—and thus that the one God, that is, the Father, has always done those things which were done through the Son.

## CHAPTER XVII

They found it easier to suppose that the Father acted in the Son’s name than that the Son acted in the Father’s, although the Lord himself says [Col. 0176B], “I have come in my Father’s name” (John 5:43). Likewise, he says to the Father himself, “I have manifested your name to human beings” (John 17:6). [Note: [Col. 0175D] “Scripture also speaking in agreement.” *Condicere* is used in a novel sense for “to speak similarly” or “to assent.” RHEN.] Scripture also speaks in agreement: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 21:6)—assuredly the Son in the Father’s name.

But the Father’s names [Note: [Col. 0175D] “To the name; and the Father’s name,” Seml.] are also “Almighty God,” “Most High” [Note: [Col. 0176C] “Most High” absent from Seml.], “Lord of Hosts,” “King of Israel,” and “HE WHO IS.” Insofar as the Scriptures teach it, we say that these names were also applicable to the Son, that the Son came under these names, that he always acted under these names, and that under these names he manifested them in himself to human beings. “All things,” he says, “that belong to the Father are mine.” Why not the names also?

When, therefore, you read “Almighty God,” “Most High,” “God of Hosts,” “King of Israel,” and [Note: [Col. 0176D] “HE WHO IS.” The Lord God says, ἐγὼ εἰμὶ ὁ ὤν, “I am HE WHO IS”; and elsewhere: “HE WHO IS has sent me,” etc. Immediately afterward, as an interpretation of this expression, there is appended “he who is,” because many are called sons and are not. Whether that explanation is correct I would not venture to say. For who would believe that the tetragrammaton name Jehovah is signified there, in which, as the rabbis and Kabbalists relate, so many mysteries lie hidden? LE PR.] “HE WHO IS,” see whether the Son also is not indicated by them: “Almighty God” in his own right, because he is the Word of Almighty God and because he received [Col. 0176C] power over all things; “Most High,” because he was exalted at God’s right hand, as Peter proclaims in Acts (2:22); “Lord of Hosts,” because all things have been subjected to him by the Father; “King of Israel,” because the lot of that nation properly fell to him [Note: [Col. 0176D] “Happened,” Jun.; “properly went forth,” Latin.]; and likewise “HE WHO IS,” because many are called sons [Note: [Col. 0176D] Ciaccon. conjectures “gods.”] and are not.

But if they also wish the name “Christ” to belong to the Father, they will hear the answer [Note: [Col. 0176D] “They hear,” Seml.] in its proper place. Meanwhile, let the response already advanced here stand against what they also bring forward from John’s Apocalypse: “I [Note: [Col. 0176D] “Therefore,” Seml.] am the Lord who is [Note: [Col. 0176D] Seml. adds “and who was”; Jun.: “and who was and who is coming.”], and who was, and is coming, the Almighty”; and against any other place where they suppose that the designation “Almighty God” is not also applicable to the Son—as though he who is to come were not [Note: [Col. 0176D] “Is not” absent from Seml.] [Col. 0177A] almighty, when the Son of the Almighty is just as almighty [Note: [Col. 0177D] Seml. adds “the Son of God.”] as the Son of God is God.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Yet Scripture confounds them whenever it establishes that God is one, so that they do not readily perceive this sharing of the Father’s names in the Son. It is as though that same Scripture had not also set forth two as God and Lord, as we demonstrated above. “Therefore,” they say, “because we find two and yet one, both are one and the same, Son and Father.”

Scripture, however, is not in danger, so that you must come to its rescue with your argument lest it appear self-contradictory. It has a rational account both when it establishes one God and when it reveals two, the Father and the Son; and it is sufficient unto itself. It is agreed that the Son is named by it. For, with the Son preserved, it could rightly have defined as one the God whose Son he is. The one who has a Son does not thereby cease to be the one God himself [Col. 0177B], under his own name, whenever he is named without the Son. He is named without the Son when he is defined principally as the first person, who had to be set forth before the name of the Son, because the Father is first made known and after the Father the Son is named.

Thus there is one God, the Father, and apart from him [Note: [Col. 0177D] “Apart from him there is another,” Seml.] there is no other. When he himself makes this declaration [Note: [Col. 0177D] “Inserts,” Seml.], he does not deny the Son but another god; for the Son is not another God from the Father [Note: [Col. 0177D] Jun. adds “God.”]. Finally, inspect the context following declarations of this sort, and you will find that their definition almost always concerns the makers and worshipers of idols: the unity of divinity is to expel the multitude of false gods, while nevertheless possessing the Son, who, insofar as he is indivisible and inseparable from the Father, must be reckoned as being in the Father, even though he is not named.

Indeed, if he had named him, he would have separated him, saying: “There is no other besides me, except [Col. 0177C] my Son.” For he would have made even the Son “another,” by excepting him from the others. Suppose the sun were to say, “I am the sun, and there is no other besides me except my ray.” Would you not have censured [Note: [Col. 0177D] “Would he not have censured,” Seml.] the absurdity [Note: [Col. 0177D] Others read “unity.”], since the ray too is reckoned as being in the sun?

Accordingly, when he says that there is no other God besides [Note: [Col. 0177D] “Through,” Seml.] himself, he says this on account of the idolatry both of the nations and of Israel, and also on account of the heretics, who fashion idols with words just as the nations fashion them with their hands—that is, another God and another Christ. Thus, even when the Father declared himself to be one, he was acting on the Son’s behalf, lest Christ be believed to have come from another God rather than from him who had foretold: “I am God, and apart from me there is no other”; who shows himself to be one, but together with the Son, with whom he alone stretched out heaven.

## CHAPTER XIX

[Col. 0177D] Indeed [Note: [Col. 0177D] “Who,” Seml.], they will seize upon this declaration of his also as an argument for singularity [Col. 0178A]: “I alone,” he says, “stretched out heaven.” With respect to all other powers, he was alone, preparing beforehand against the conjectures of the heretics who maintain that the world was constructed by angels [Note: [Col. 0177D] “Who maintain that the world was constructed by angels,” etc. He is referring to the Valentinians and others like them, as well as the followers of Proclus and the Seleucians. RHEN.] and various powers. They make even the Creator himself either an angel, or else one who, though ignorant, was put forward for external tasks [Note: [Col. 0177D] “Adilla,” Jun.], such as the works of the world.

Or, if he stretched out heaven alone in that sense, how do these heretics perversely presume that he admits no companion, although that Wisdom says: “When he was preparing the heavens [Note: [Col. 0177D] “Heaven,” Seml.], I was there with him [Note: [Col. 0178D] “With him” absent from Seml.]”? And if the Apostle said, “Who has known the mind of the Lord, and who was present at his counsel?” (1 Cor. 2:15), [Note: [Col. 0177D] “Assuredly apart from Wisdom.” The meaning is: when Paul says, “Who was present at his counsel?” he means, “Who apart from Wisdom was present at his counsel—the Wisdom that was there with him?” RHEN.] he assuredly means, “apart from Wisdom” [Note: [Col. 0178D] “Was,” Seml.], who was there with him.

Nevertheless, in him and together with him God was joining the universe together, while the Son was not ignorant of what God was doing. But by “apart from Wisdom” he means “apart from the Son,” who is Christ, the Wisdom and Power of God according to the Apostle, the only one [Col. 0178B] who knows the Father’s mind: “For who knows the things that are in God except the spirit that is in him?”—not one who is outside him [Note: [Col. 0178D] “Him. Therefore he was,” Seml.]. There was therefore one with him who did not allow God to be alone, except in relation to all others.

But then the Gospel too must be rejected, because it says that all things were made by God through the Word, and that without him nothing was made. For, unless I am mistaken, it is also written elsewhere: “By his word the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth [Note: [Col. 0178D] “Of his mouth” absent from Seml.] all their powers.” And the Word, Power, and Wisdom will himself be the Son of God. Thus, if all things were made through the Son, then, in stretching out heaven through the Son, he did not stretch it out alone, except in the sense in which he was alone in relation to all others.

Indeed, immediately afterward he speaks of the Son: “Who else casts down the signs of ventriloquists and divinations from the heart, turns the wise backward, and makes their counsel foolish? Establishing the words of his Son”—namely, by declaring, “This is [Col. 0178C] my beloved Son; listen to him.” Thus, by immediately introducing the Son, he is himself the interpreter of how he stretched out heaven alone: namely, alone together with the Son, just as he is one together with the Son.

Accordingly, the words “I alone stretched out heaven” will also belong to the Son, because the heavens were established by the Word. Because heaven was prepared with Wisdom—that is [Note: [Col. 0178D] “Wisdom in the Word,” Seml.] with the Word—assisting, and all things were made through the Word, it is also appropriate to say that the Son [Note: [Col. 0178D] “To the Son,” Wouw.] alone stretched out heaven, because he alone ministered to the Father’s work.

He will likewise be the one who says: “I am the first, and I am also among the things to come” [Note: [Col. 0178D] “Among the things about to come,” Seml.; “among” absent from Fran.]. The Word, namely, is the first of all things: “In the beginning was the Word”; in which beginning he was brought forth by the Father. The Father, however, having no beginning, since he was brought forth by no one and is unborn, cannot be regarded as first. He who alone always existed could have no position in an order.

Thus, if they thought that the same one must be believed to be both Father and Son in order to vindicate one God, his unity remains intact [Note: [Col. 0178D] “Intact,” masculine, Seml.] [Col. 0179A], because, although he is one, he has [Note: [Col. 0179D] “May have,” Seml.] a Son, who likewise is himself embraced by the same Scriptures. If they do not wish the Son to be reckoned second after the Father, lest being second cause two gods to be spoken of, we have shown that Scripture also mentions two as gods and two as lords. Yet, lest they be scandalized [Note: [Col. 0179D] Others read “might be scandalized.”] by this, we have explained the principle according to which they are not called two Gods or two Lords [Note: [Col. 0179D] “In which Lords,” manuscript of Wouw.], but according to which the Father and the Son are two. This is not by separation of substance but by dispensation, since we declare that the Son is indivisible and inseparable from the Father; another not in status but in degree. And although he is called God when he is named by himself, he does not thereby make two gods, but one, by the very fact that he is entitled to be called God from the unity of the Father.

## CHAPTER XX

[Col. 0179B] But work must still be devoted to refuting their arguments, should they extract anything from the Scriptures in support of their own opinion while refusing to consider the rest, which likewise preserves the rule—and indeed preserves the unity of the divinity and the import of the monarchy.

For just as in the Old Scriptures they retain nothing except, “I am God, and there is no other besides me” (Ps. 45:5), so in the Gospel they defend the Lord’s answer to Philip: “I and the Father are one” (John 14); and, “He who has seen me sees [Note: [Col. 0179D] “Has seen,” Fran., Paris, Rig.] the Father also”; and, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.” They wish the entire body of both Testaments to yield [Note: [Col. 0179D] “Believe,” Seml.] to these three passages, although the fewer ought to be understood in accordance with the greater number. But this is characteristic of all heretics. For because the passages that can be found in the thicket are few, they defend the few against the many [Col. 0179C] and adopt the later against the earlier. Yet the rule established for every matter always [Note: [Col. 0179D] “Always” absent from Seml.] from the beginning prescribes from the earlier and more numerous passages for the later, and assuredly also for the fewer [Note: [Col. 0179D] “In the earlier passages, and prescribes for the later, and assuredly also in the fewer,” Rhen.].

## CHAPTER XXI

Consider, therefore [Note: [Col. 0179D] “How many things prescribe for you.” *Quanta* is used for *quam multa* (“how many”), as more than once previously above.], how many things the Gospel itself prescribes for you [Note: [Col. 0179D] “Prescribe,” plural, Seml.] before Philip’s inquiry and before your entire argument.

First of all, the very opening of John the Evangelist immediately demonstrates that he who was to become flesh had existed previously: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1), “and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” [Col. 0180A]. For if these words may be received in no other way than as they were written, there is unquestionably shown to be one who existed from the beginning and another with whom he existed: the Word to be one, and God [Note: [Col. 0179D] “Of God, another Lord,” Seml.] another—although the Word also is God, but insofar as he is God’s Son, not insofar as he is the Father; one through whom all things were made, and another from whom all things came.

How we use the term “another,” however, we have already explained often. We necessarily say “another” so that we do not say “the same”; yet “another” not as though separated, but another by dispensation [Note: [Col. 0179D] “It is necessary that he not be the same, but not as though separated [Col. 0180D], another by dispensation,” Seml.; “It is necessary that he not be the same, but not as though,” Jun.], not by division.

It is this one, therefore, who became flesh, not the one whose Word he was. It was his glory that was seen [Note: [Col. 0179D] “As of an only-begotten from a father,” μονογενοῦς ἀπὸ πατρὸς. For by the expression “only-begotten” he rendered what appears in John 1. LE PR.] as the glory of an only-begotten from the Father, not as the Father’s own glory. This one alone [Note: [Col. 0180D] “Of one,” Seml.] expounded the Father’s bosom, not the Father his own bosom. For the statement precedes: “No one has ever seen God.”

This same one is also designated by John as the Lamb of God, not the one whose beloved he is. Certainly he is always the Son of God [Col. 0180B], but not the very one whose Son he is. Nathanael immediately perceived this concerning him, as Peter did elsewhere: “You are the Son of God” (John 1:50; Matt. 16:16). He himself confirms that they perceived this correctly: answering Nathanael [Note: [Col. 0180D] “Nathanael,” Rhen.], “Because I said [Note: [Col. 0180D] “He said,” Rhen.] to you, ‘I saw you beneath the fig tree,’ you therefore believe” (John 2:50); and affirming Peter to be blessed, since neither flesh nor blood had revealed it to him—that is, that he had perceived the Father also—but the Father who is in heaven (Matt. 16:17).

By this declaration he established the distinction between both persons: the Son on earth, whom Peter had recognized as God’s Son, and the Father in heaven, who had revealed to Peter that the Christ whom Peter recognized was God’s Son. When he entered the temple [Note: [Col. 0180D] “Into the temple,” Seml.], he called the sanctuary his Father’s house, as a Son. When he says to Nicodemus, “God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have everlasting life” (John 3:16). And again (ibid. 17): “For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him. He who believes in him is not judged; he who does not believe in him has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God.”

When John [Note: [Col. 0180D] “Of” omitted by Ciaccon.] was asked what was happening concerning [Note: [Col. 0180D] “But when John was asked.” He means John the Baptist, whose words are also those that follow in John 3, “The Father loves the Son,” etc.; for thus we have corrected the text in place of “loved.” PAM.] Jesus, he said: “The Father loves [Note: [Col. 0180D] “Loved,” Seml.] the Son, and has delivered all things into his hand. He who believes [Note: [Col. 0180D] “Believed,” Seml.] in the Son has eternal life; he who does not believe in the Son [Note: [Col. 0180D] “Believed in the Son,” Seml.] of God will not see God, but God’s wrath will remain upon him” (John 3:35–36).

Whom, then, did he reveal to the Samaritan woman? If it was the Messiah, who is called Christ, he surely revealed himself [Col. 0181A] as the Son, not the Father, since elsewhere too Christ is called the Son of God, not the Father. Thereafter he says to the disciples: “My purpose is to do the will of him who sent me, so that I may complete his work.” And to the Jews, concerning the healing of the paralytic: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5:17). “The Father and I,” says the Son.

Finally, for this reason the Jews desired all the more to kill him—not only [Note: [Col. 0181D] “Nevertheless,” Seml.] because he was breaking the Sabbath, but because he called God his own Father, making himself equal to God. He therefore said to them at that time: “The Son can do nothing of himself unless he sees [Note: [Col. 0181D] “May see,” Seml.] the Father doing it” (John 5:19). “For whatever he does, the Son likewise does. For the Father loves the Son and has shown him all the things that he has done, and he will show him works greater than these [Note: [Col. 0181D] “These things,” Seml.], so that you may marvel. For just as he raises the dead and gives them life [Col. 0181B], so too the Son gives life [Note: [Col. 0181D] “Will give life,” others.] to whomever he wishes.

“For the Father does not judge, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father. He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent the Son. Amen, amen, I say to you that he who hears [Note: [Col. 0181D] “That even he who shall have heard,” Latin.] my words [Note: [Col. 0181D] “My” absent from Seml.] and believes him who sent me has eternal life; and he does not come [Note: [Col. 0181D] “Will not come,” Seml.] into judgment, but passes [Note: [Col. 0182D] Others: “has passed.” “Has passed”; others: “comes,” manuscript of Wouw.] from death into life. Amen, I say to you that the hour will come when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God; and when they hear, they will live. For just as the Father has eternal life [Note: [Col. 0182D] “Eternal” absent from Rhen.] from himself, so too he gave the Son to have eternal life in himself; and [Note: [Col. 0181D] “He gave him authority to execute judgment, in that he is the Son of Man.” Nearly all manuscripts and interpreters place *quia* (“because”) here, which is easier to understand. For St. Chrysostom did not employ that punctuation, because Paul of Samosata used it. LE PR.] he gave him authority to execute judgment, inasmuch as he is the Son of Man”—through the flesh, namely, just as he is the Son of God through his Spirit.

He further adds: “But I have testimony greater than John’s” (John 5:36–37). “For the works [Col. 0181C] that the Father gave me to complete, those very works bear witness concerning me that the Father sent me. And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness concerning me.” Then, by adding, “You have never heard his voice nor seen his form,” he confirms that it was not the Father but the Son who formerly was seen and heard.

Finally, he says: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you have not received me” (John 5:43). So thoroughly had the Son always existed under the name of God, King, Lord, [Note: [Col. 0182D] “And” absent from Seml.; “and Lord” absent from the manuscript of Wouw.] Almighty, and Most High. When they asked what they ought to do, he answered: “Believe in him whom God sent” (John 6:29). He also affirms that he is the bread which the Father would provide from heaven (John 6:32).

Therefore, everything that the Father gave him would come to him, and he would not reject it, because he had descended from heaven not to do his own will but the Father’s; and the Father’s will was that whoever saw [Col. 0181D] the Son and believed in him should obtain life and resurrection (John 6:35). Moreover, no one could come to him [Col. 0182A] unless the Father drew him [Note: [Col. 0182D] “Unless the Father draws him.” In these seven chapters beginning with Chapter Twenty, he attacks the Monarchians and proves from Scripture that the Son is another than the Father, and therefore that the Father did not make himself the Son. LE PR.]; everyone who had heard and learned from the Father would come to him (John 6:14).

He also adds here, “Not that anyone has seen the Father,” in order to show that the Word, through whom they are taught, belongs to the Father. But when many withdraw from him (John 6:66), and he offers his Apostles the choice whether they too wish to depart, what does Simon Peter answer? “To whom shall we go [Note: [Col. 0182D] “Shall we go,” Fran.]? You have the words of life, and we believe that you are the Christ.” Did Peter believe him to be the Father, or the Father’s Christ?

## CHAPTER XXII

Whose teaching does he say it is, at which they marveled—his own or the Father’s? Likewise, when they debated among themselves whether he himself might be the Christ—assuredly not the Father, but the Son—he says: “You do not even [Note: [Col. 0182D] “But,” Jun.] know me” (John 7:28), “or where I come from; and I did not come of myself, but he who sent me is true, and you [Col. 0182B] do not know him. I know him, because I am from him [Note: [Col. 0182D] “Because I am with him,” Seml.; “because I am from him,” Jun.], and he sent me.” He did not say, “Because I am he, and I sent myself,” but, “He sent me.”

Likewise, when the Pharisees sent men to seize him, he said: “For a little while longer I am with you, and I am going to him who sent me.” And when he denies that he is alone—“But there are I,” he says, “and the Father who sent me”—does he not reveal two, two who are nevertheless inseparable? Indeed, this was the entire substance of his teaching: that there are two who are inseparable.

For when he cites the law confirming the testimony of two persons, he adds: “I bear witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me.” But if there were one, because the Son and the Father were the same, he would not have employed the law’s support, which requires belief on the testimony not of one but of two.

Likewise, when he is asked where the Father was, he answers that neither he nor the Father was known to them [Col. 0182C], thus declaring that two were unknown. If they knew him, they would know the Father—not because he himself was both Father and Son, but because, through their indivisibility, neither can be known or remain unknown without the other.
