“He who sent me,” he says, “is true; and the things I heard from him are those I speak to the world.” Scripture interprets from outside the narrative that they did not understand that he had spoken about the Father, although they assuredly ought to have recognized that the Father’s words were in the Son by reading in Jeremiah (Jer. 1:9): “And the Lord said to me, ‘Behold, I have put my words into your mouth’”; and in Isaiah (Isa. 1:4): “The Lord gives me the tongue of instruction, that I may know when it is fitting to speak a word.”

So too he himself says again: “Then,” he says (John 8:28), “you will know that I am, and that I speak nothing of myself, but as he taught me, so I speak; because he who sent me is with me.” This too is testimony [Col. 0182D] to two indivisible persons.

Likewise, in the dispute with the Jews, reproaching them because they wished to kill him [Col. 0183A], he says: “I speak the things that I have seen in the presence of my Father, and you do what you have seen in the presence of your father”; and, “Now you wish to kill a man who has spoken to you the truth that he heard from God”; and, “If God were your Father, you would love me. For I came forth from God and have come”—and yet they are not separated [Note: [Col. 0183D] “We do not separate,” Seml.], although he said that he came forth, as some seize upon the occasion afforded by this saying. He came forth from the Father as a ray from the sun, a stream from its spring, or a shoot from its seed.

“I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father”; and, “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is the Father who glorifies me, whom you say is your God; yet you do not know him, but I know him. And if I say, ‘I do not know him,’ I shall be a liar like you; but I know him and keep his word.” And when he adds, “Abraham saw my day and rejoiced” [Col. 0183B], he surely demonstrates that it was the Son who formerly was seen by Abraham, not the Father.

Likewise, concerning that blind man, he says that he must do the Father’s works. After the restoration of the man’s sight, he says to him: “Do you believe in the Son of God?” (John 9:35). And when the man asked who he was, by revealing himself he assuredly revealed the Son, in whom he had said the man must believe.

Next, he professes that he is known by the Father and that the Father is known by him. He says that the Father loves him because he lays down his life, since he had received this commandment from the Father. And when asked by the Jews whether he himself was the Christ—God’s Christ, assuredly [Note: [Col. 0183D] “God,” Seml.], for even to this day the Jews await God’s Christ, not the Father himself, since it is nowhere written that the Father would come as Christ—he says: “I speak to you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in the Father’s name themselves bear witness concerning me.”

To what do they bear witness [Col. 0183C]? Assuredly that he was the one about whom they were asking, that is, God’s Christ. Concerning his sheep too, he says that no one would snatch them from his hand: “For what the Father gave me is greater than all things” [Note: [Col. 0183D] Others: “For the Father, who is greater than all, gave them to me”; Jun.: “For the Father who gave them to me is greater than all.”]; and [Note: [Col. 0183D] “I and the Father are one.” He cited these same words from John 10 earlier, in Chapter 20. The Monarchian heretics, however, distorted them, supposing that they established that the Son was not another than the Father, although the words state a unity of essence, not of person. LE PR.]: “I and the Father are one.”

Here, then, the foolish—indeed, the blind—wish to establish their position, failing to see, first, that “I and the Father” signifies two; next, that the final word “are” does not proceed from a single person, since it is expressed in the plural; and then that he says, “We are one,” not “We are one person.” For if he had said, “We are one person,” he might have assisted their position. “One person” appears to signify the singular number.

Yet because there are two, he uses “one” in the neuter gender, not the masculine. This does not pertain to singularity but to unity, likeness, conjunction, and the love [Col. 0183D] of the Father, who loves the Son, and to the obedience of the Son, who obeys the Father’s will. By saying, “We are one, I and the Father,” he shows that those whom he makes equal [Col. 0184A] and joins are two.

So thoroughly is this the case that he adds that he had shown them many works from the Father, none of which merited stoning. And lest they suppose that for this reason they ought to stone him—as though he had wished himself to be understood as God himself, that is, the Father, because he had said, “I and the Father are one”—he shows himself to be God insofar as he is the Son of God, not insofar as he is God himself:

“If,” he says, “it is written in the law, ‘I said, you are gods,’ and Scripture cannot be annulled, do you say that he whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world blasphemes because I said [Note: [Col. 0183D] “He had said,” Seml.], ‘I am the Son of God’? If I do not perform my Father’s works, do not believe; but if I do perform them, and you are unwilling to believe me, believe at least on account of the works. And know that I am in the Father and the Father in me.”

The Father, therefore, was in the Son through the works, and the Son was in the Father; and thus through the works we understand that the Father and the Son [Note: [Col. 0183D] “And the Son” absent from Seml.] are one. So thoroughly did he persist [Col. 0184B] in establishing this entire point: that two nevertheless should be believed to exist in one power, because the Son could not otherwise be believed unless two were believed to exist.

## CHAPTER XXIII
After this Martha confessed him to be the Son of God, and erred no more than Peter (Matt. 16:16) and Nathanael; and even if she had erred, she would immediately have been instructed. For behold: when about to raise her brother from the dead, the Lord looked up to heaven and to the Father: “Father,” he said (John 11:42)—[surely the Son]—“I thank you that you always hear me. [Note: Lat. adds “But.”] Because of these crowds standing around, I have said this, so that they may believe that you sent me.”

And also, in the agitation of his soul: “And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour. Yet it was for this very reason that I came to this hour. But, Father, glorify your name” [Col. 0184C] (John 12:27)—the name in which the Son also was. [Note: Seml. omits “also.”] “I,” he says (John 5:43), “have come in my Father’s name.” The Son’s voice addressed to the Father had, of course, been sufficient. Behold, out of superabundance [Note: Latin reads “abundantly.”], the Father answers from heaven [Note: Fran. reads “answered.”] and bears witness concerning the Son (Matt. 17:5): “This is my beloved Son, in whom I have been well pleased; listen to him.”

Thus also in this saying, “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again” [Note: Seml. and Venet. punctuate: “I will glorify it; again.”], how many persons do you perceive, most perverse Praxeas, if not as many as there are voices? You have the Son on earth; you have the Father in heaven. This is not separation, but divine ordering. Certainly, we know that God is even within the abysses and is present everywhere, though by force and power; and that the Son likewise, as inseparable, is everywhere with him. Yet within the economy itself, the Father willed that the Son should be present on earth, while he himself should be in heaven. Looking up to that place [Note: Seml. reads “which.”], the Son himself both prayed and made requests of the Father; [Col. 0184D] toward that place he also taught us to raise ourselves in prayer: “Our Father who art in heaven” (Matt. 6:9). And although he is also everywhere [Note: Seml. reads “heaven: although”; others add “indeed.”], the Father willed this to be his seat. He made [Col. 0185A] the Son a little lower than the angels (Ps. 8:6) [Note: Seml. reads: “He willed it. The Father made the Son lower.”] by sending him down to earth, though intending to crown him with glory and honor by taking him back into heaven.

He was already granting him these things when he said, “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it.” The Son petitions from earth; the Father promises from heaven. Why do you make both Father and Son liars, if either the Father was speaking from heaven to the Son while he himself was the Son on earth, or the Son was praying to the Father while he himself was the Father in heaven? What sense would it make for the Son likewise to petition himself by petitioning the Father [Note: Seml. reads “should petition” and omits “if”], if the Son was the Father; or, conversely, for the Father to promise himself something by promising it to the Son, if he was the Father? Even if we were thereby to call them two divided beings, as you keep proclaiming, it would be more tolerable to speak of two divided beings than to preach one shape-shifting God.

Accordingly, the Lord then [Note: Seml. reads “now.”] declared to those people [Col. 0185B] (John 12:30): “This voice came not for my sake, but for yours,” so that they might believe in both Father and Son, each under his own names, persons, and locations. But Jesus further cries out and says: “He who believes in me does not believe in me, but believes in him who sent me”—because through the Son one believes in the Father, and the Father is the authority for believing in the Son—“and he who sees me [Note: Rhen. omits “me.”] sees him who sent me.”

How so? Because, of course, “I have not spoken from myself; but the Father who sent me himself gave me a command as to what I should say and what I should speak.” For “the Lord gives me the tongue of instruction, so that I may know when it is fitting to speak the discourse that I speak” (Isa. 50:4). “As the Father has spoken to me, so I also speak” (John 12:50).

John, the evangelist and surely so illustrious a disciple, knew [Col. 0185C] better than Praxeas how these things had been said [Note: Seml. reads “names.”]. Therefore, expressing his own understanding, he says: “Now before the feast of Passover” [Note: “Now before the feast of Passover.” He cites these words from John 13 in transposed order; otherwise he agrees with the remaining text, even reading with the Vulgate translator “in himself,” although the Greek is *ἐν αὐτῷ* (“in him”). PAM. The expression *ἐν αὐτῷ* is certainly not found in our copy, published at Paris in 1549, but, much more correctly, *ἐν ἑαυτῷ*, that is, “in himself,” as in the Vulgate (*Καινὴ Διαθήκη* [New Testament], p. 177, l. 11). Tertullian could therefore have had before his eyes a Greek reading similar to ours, to which the Vulgate was subsequently conformed. EDD.] (John 13:1), “Jesus, knowing that all things had been handed over to him by the Father, and that he had come forth from God [Note: Seml. reads “to be.”] and was going to God.”

Praxeas, however, would have the Father himself come forth from himself and depart to himself, so that the devil put into Judas’s heart not the betrayal of the Son, but of the Father himself. This works well neither for the devil nor for the heretic, because the devil did not effect the betrayal in the Son for his own benefit. For it was the Son of God who was betrayed—the one who was in the son of man—as Scripture adds: “Now the son of man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him.”

What [Col. 0186A] God? Surely not the Father, but the Father’s Word, who was in the son of man, that is, in the flesh, in which he too had already been glorified; but in power and word even before Jesus [Note: Seml. reads “Jesus” in the nominative]. “And God,” he says, “has glorified [Note: Jun. reads “will glorify.”] him in himself”—that is, the Father, having the Son within himself [Note: Seml. adds “whom.”], even though extended down to earth, soon glorified him through the resurrection [Note: Seml. omits “will glorify.”], once death had been conquered.

## CHAPTER XXIV

There were indeed people who even then did not understand. Thomas too was unbelieving for a time: “Lord,” he says (John 14:5), “we do not know where you are going, and how can we know the way?” And Jesus replied: “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me. If you had known me, you would also have known the Father; but [Note: Seml. adds “also.”] from now on you know him and have seen him.”

And now we come [Col. 0186B] to Philip, who, stirred by the hope of seeing the Father, did not understand how he had heard that the Father had been seen: “Show us the Father,” he says, “and it is enough for us.” And the Lord answered: “Philip, have I been with you so long, and you have not known me?”

Whom does he say they ought to have known—for this alone must be examined—as the Father or as the Son? If as the Father, let Praxeas show that during all the time Christ had lived among them he could ever have been—not to say understood, but even supposed—to be the Father. [Note: “All the Scriptures, both the ancient ones,” etc. He alludes to all those ancient Scriptures in which Christ is called God, such as Psalm 2, Isaiah 45, Lamentations 4, and Daniel 9. PAM.] For us, all the Scriptures—both the ancient, which define him as the Christ of God, and the new, which define him as the Son of God [Note: “And the new define him as the Son of God.” Passages of this kind from the New Testament may be found at the beginnings of the Gospels of Mark, Luke, and John, and elsewhere in those same writers; Matthew 4; Acts 2 and 9; the Epistles to the Romans, Galatians, Ephesians, and Hebrews; and finally Revelation 2. PAM.]—establish this beforehand.

This was proclaimed in earlier times; this was declared by Christ himself; indeed, by now it had also been declared openly by the Father himself from heaven, confessing the Son and glorifying the Son: “This is my Son”; and, “I have glorified it and will glorify it.” [Col. 0186C] This was believed by the disciples; this was not believed by the Jews. Desiring them to believe this about himself, at every moment he named the Father, set the Father before them, and honored the Father.

If this is so, therefore, it was not the Father who had lived among them so long whom they had failed to know, but the Son. And when the Lord reproached Philip for not knowing him, he surely wished that one to be recognized whom he reproached them for having failed to recognize for so long—that is, the Son.

It will now also become apparent how the words “He who sees me sees [Note: others read “has seen.”] the Father also” were spoken: namely, in the same sense as the earlier statement, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Why? Because “I came forth from God and have come”; and “I am [Col. 0187A] the way” (John 14:6): “no one comes to the Father except through me”; and “No one comes to me unless the Father has drawn him”; and “The Father has handed all things over to me”; and “As the Father gives life, so also does the Son”; and “If you have known me, you have also known the Father” (John 6:44 and related passages).

According to these sayings, he had shown himself to be the Father’s representative, through whom the Father might both be seen in deeds and heard in words, and might be known in the Son who administered the Father’s deeds and words. For the Father is invisible, as Philip too had learned in the Law and ought to have remembered: “No one shall see God and live.” He is therefore rebuked for desiring to see the Father as though the Father were visible, and is taught that the Father becomes visible in the Son through acts of power, not through a representation of his person.

Finally, if Christ wished the same being to be understood as both Father and Son by saying, “He who sees me sees the Father,” how does he add, “Do you not believe [Note: Seml. reads “Do you not believe” in the singular.] that I am [Col. 0187B] in the Father, and the Father is in me?” For he ought to have added: “Do you not believe [Note: same variant.] that I am the Father?” Or how did he reinforce his point if he did not disclose what he wished to be understood, namely, that he was the Son?

Rather, by saying, “Do you not believe that I am in the Father, and the Father is in me?” he reinforced precisely this point: lest, because he had said, “He who sees me sees [Note: Seml. reads “has seen.”] the Father also,” he should be thought to be the Father—something he never wished to be thought, since he always confessed himself to be the Son and to have come from the Father.

He therefore made clear the conjunction of two persons, so that the Father should not be sought separately as though visibly present to the sight, and so that the Son should be regarded as the Father’s representative. Moreover, he also interpreted how the Father was in the Son and the Son in the Father: “The words,” he says, “which I speak to you are not mine”—surely [Col. 0187C] because they are the Father’s—“but the Father who remains in me performs the works.”

Thus, by the works of power and the words of teaching, the Father who remains in the Son is seen through those things by which he remains and through him in whom he remains. In this very statement the distinctive property of each person appears, when he says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.” And indeed: “Believe,” he says. What? That I am the Father? I do not think that is written; rather: “That I am in the Father, and the Father is in me. Otherwise, believe at least because of the works.” Those works, surely, through which the Father in the Son was seen not by sight, but by understanding.

## CHAPTER XXV

After Philip and the entire substance of this question, John continues to the end of his Gospel in the same mode of discourse, by which Father and Son are distinguished in their own proper identity [Note: Seml. reads “is distinguished.”]. Christ also promises that, when he has ascended to the Father, he will ask the Father for the Paraclete and send him—another Paraclete indeed, though we have already explained in what sense he is another.

Moreover, “He will take from what is mine” (John 16:14), he says, just as he himself takes from what belongs to the Father [Note: “Just as he himself from what belongs to the Father.” The sentence is elliptical, as he has often spoken above; “takes from that which belongs to the Father” is to be understood. Similarly below: “Do you not know,” he says, “that I must be among the things of my Father?” where “things” is understood. RHEN.].

Thus the connection of the Father in the Son and of the Son in the Paraclete produces three who cohere, one from another. These three are one, not one person, in the sense in which it was said (John 10:30): “I and the Father are one”—with reference to unity of substance, not singularity of number.

Continue through the passage, and you will find that the one whom you believe to be the Father is spoken of as acting in the Father’s stead. And you surely suppose the Father, the vineyard keeper, to have been on earth [Note: Jun. reads “and whom.”]. Yet again you acknowledge him to be in heaven when the Son, looking up there, entrusts [Note: Seml. reads “entrusted.”] his disciples to the Father.

But even if it had not been [Note: Seml. reads “is.”] revealed in this Gospel: “My God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46), and, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit,” nevertheless, after the resurrection and the glory [Col. 0188B] of conquered death [Note: Seml. reads “glory”; another variant reads “necessity” as an accusative], when the necessity for every humiliation had been laid aside, he could by then have revealed himself as the Father to that faithful woman who, from love, not from curiosity or the unbelief of Thomas, attempted to touch him. Yet he said (John 20:17): “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father; but go to my brothers”—indeed, even in this he shows himself to be the Son [Note: Seml. reads “because even in this he shows himself to be the Son”], for he would have called them sons if he had been the Father—“and say to them: I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God.”

Is it the Father going to the Father, and God going to God; or the Son going to the Father, and the Word to God? Why, too, does the concluding sentence of the Gospel attest that these things were written, if not “so that you may believe,” it says, “that Jesus Christ is the Son of God”?

Therefore, whatever among these sayings you may think can serve you as proof that Father and Son are the same, you are striving [Col. 0188C] against the Gospel’s definitive declaration. For they were not written so that you might believe [Note: Rhen. inserts “in.”] Jesus Christ to be the Father, but so that you might believe him to be the Son.

## CHAPTER XXVI

Because of Philip’s single statement and the Lord’s answer to him, we see [Note: Rhen. reads “we seem.”] that we have traversed the Gospel of John, lest one statement overturn so many things plainly declared both before and afterward. That one statement must instead be interpreted in accordance with all the others, rather than against them all—and even against its own meaning.

But, not to introduce the other Gospels, which confirm the same teaching [Note: Rhen. reads “faith.”] concerning the Lord’s nativity, it is enough that the one who was to be born of the virgin was announced by the angel himself and expressly defined as the Son of God: “The Spirit of God will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy thing that will be born from you [Col. 0188D] will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

They will indeed attempt to argue here also, but the truth will prevail. “Certainly,” they say, “the Son of God is God, and the power of the Most High is the Most High.” Nor are they ashamed to foist in an assertion which, if it were true, would have been written explicitly. Whom was the angel afraid of, that he did not openly declare, “God will come upon you, and the Most High will overshadow you”?

But by saying “the Spirit of God,” although the Spirit [Note: Fran. reads the accusative “Spirit.”] of God is God, yet without directly naming God, he wished a portion of the whole to be understood, which was to assume the name of Son. This Spirit of God will be the same as the Word. For just as, when John says, “The Word was made flesh,” we also understand the Spirit in the mention of the Word, so here too we recognize the Word under the name of Spirit. For the Spirit is the substance of the Word, and the Word is the operation of the Spirit, and the two are one.

Otherwise, John will confess that one being was made flesh and the angel that another was to become flesh, unless the Spirit is also the Word and the Word the Spirit. Therefore, just as the Word of God is not himself the one whose Word he is, so neither is the Spirit; and even if he is called God, nevertheless he is not himself the one whose Spirit he is said to be. Nothing belonging to someone is itself the one to whom it belongs.

Certainly, when something is from him, and is his precisely because it is from him, it can be something of the same kind as he from whom it comes and to whom it belongs. Therefore, the Spirit of God [Note: Rhen. omits “of God.”] is God, and the Word of God [Note: same omission.] is God, because each is from God; yet neither is himself the one from whom he comes.

But if he is “God of God,” as a substantival entity, he will not be God himself, but God to this extent: because he is from the substance of God himself, by virtue of which [Note: Lat. reads “because”; Rhen. reads “which.”] he too is a substantival entity, and is, as it were, a portion of the whole.

Still more, “the power of the Most High” will not be the Most High himself, because power is not even a substantival entity, as the Spirit is; nor are wisdom and providence. For these are not substances, but attributes of each substance. Power is an attribute of the Spirit, and will not itself [Col. 0189C] be the Spirit.

Therefore, when these realities—whatever precisely they are—the Spirit of God, the Word, and the power, were brought together in the virgin, what is born from her is the Son of God. [Note: Rhen. adds “if.”]

In these Gospels too he himself testifies to this about himself immediately from childhood: “Do you not know,” he says (Luke 2:49), “that I must be among the things of my Father?” Satan also recognizes him as such in the temptations: “If you are the Son of God.” From that point onward the demons too confess it: “We know who you are: the Son of God.” He himself worships the Father. He does not deny that Peter recognized him as the Christ of God.

Exulting [Note: Venet. reads “insulting.”] in the Spirit, he says to the Father: “I confess to you, Father, because you have hidden these things from the wise” (Matt. 11:25). Here too he affirms that the Father is known to no one except the Son. He affirms that the Father’s Son will confess before the Father those who confess him and deny those who deny him. He presents the parable of the son—not the father—sent into the vineyard [Col. 0189D] after several servants, killed by the wicked tenants, and vindicated by the Father. He himself does not know the final day and hour, which are known to the Father alone. He assigns a kingdom [Col. 0190A] to his disciples just as, he says, one was assigned to him by the Father. He possesses the power, if he wished, to request legions of angels from the Father as assistance. He cries out that God had forsaken him and places his spirit in the Father’s hands. After the resurrection, he promises to send his disciples the Father’s promise. Finally, he commands them to baptize into the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit—not into one person. For we are baptized not once but three times, at each name into each individual person.

## CHAPTER XXVII

Why do I linger [Note: Rhen. reads “shall I linger?”] over matters so manifest, when I must address the passages by which they seek to obscure what is manifest? For, hemmed in on every side by the distinction between Father and Son—which we order while preserving their conjunction, like that of sun and ray and of spring and river, yet according to the inseparable number of two and three—they nevertheless attempt to interpret this distinction according to their own opinion. Thus they distinguish both Father and Son within one person, saying that the Son is the flesh, that is, the human being, that is, Jesus; while the Father is the Spirit, that is, God, that is, Christ.

And those who contend that Father and Son are one and the same now begin [Note: “To divide them rather than unite them.” Rhenanus says that Tertullian uses the simple verb *unare*, from which we derive *adunare* and *coadunare*. Although [Col. 0190D] three Vatican manuscript codices read *unire*, we have retained *unare*, since it has a stronger flavor of African usage. PAM.] to divide them rather than unite them. For if Jesus is one and Christ another, the Son will be one and [Note: Rhen. omits the second “one/another.”] the Father another, since the Son is Jesus and the Father Christ. Perhaps they learned such a monarchy from Valentinus: to make two, Jesus and Christ.

But this objection of theirs has already been blunted by what was discussed beforehand [Note: Rhen. reads “reconsidered”]: namely, that the one whom they make the Father is called the Word of God, or the Spirit of God, and the power of the Most High. For these are not themselves the one whose they are said to be, but are from him and belong to him. Nevertheless, they will also be refuted in another way in this chapter. [Col. 0190C]

“Behold,” they say, “it was proclaimed by the angel: ‘Therefore the holy thing that will be born will be called the Son of God.’ Accordingly, the flesh was born, and the flesh surely [Note: Rhen. reads “therefore.”] will be the Son of God.”

No: it was said of the Spirit of God. For certainly the virgin conceived from the Holy Spirit, and what she conceived she bore; therefore, what had been conceived and was to be delivered was what had to be born—that is, the Spirit, whose name will also be called Emmanuel, which is translated “God with us.”

The flesh, however, is not God, so that it should have been said of the flesh, “The holy thing that will be born will be called [Note: Rhen. reads “will be called holy.”] the Son of God.” Rather, the one who was born in it is God, of whom the Psalm also says (Ps. 87:5): “For God was born as man in her, and he built her by the will of the Father.”

What God was born in her? The Word and the Spirit, who was born with the Word by the Father’s will. Therefore, since the Word was in the flesh, we must also inquire concerning this [Note: Latin reads “Finally, this.”]: how was [Col. 0190D] the Word made flesh? Was he transformed, as it were, into flesh, or clothed with flesh? No: he was clothed with it.

For God must be believed immutable and incapable of change of form, since he is eternal. Transformation is the destruction [Col. 0191A] of the former condition. [Note: “Transformation is the destruction of the former condition.” This passage supports transubstantiation, which Catholics affirm in the sacrament of the Eucharist but deny in the assumption of Christ’s humanity, since, according to the Creed of blessed Athanasius, he is one “not by conversion of the divinity into flesh, but by assumption of the humanity into [Col. 0192D] God.” PAM.]

For everything that is transformed into something else ceases to be what it had been and begins to be what it had not been. But God neither ceases to be nor can be something else. The Word, moreover, is God, and “the Word of the Lord remains forever,” surely by continuing in his own form.

If he is not capable of being transformed [Note: Rhen. reads “conformed.”], it follows that he must be understood to have been made flesh in this sense: that he comes to be [Note: Fran. reads “is.”] in flesh, and is manifested, seen, and handled through the flesh. For the other considerations also require that the passage be understood in this way.

For if the Word was made flesh by transformation and alteration of substance, Jesus will now be one substance from two—a kind of mixture of flesh and Spirit, like electrum from gold and silver. He begins to be neither gold, that is, Spirit, nor [Col. 0191B] silver, that is, flesh, since the one is changed by the other and some third thing is produced.

Jesus will therefore no longer be God: for the Word, who was made flesh, has ceased to exist. Nor will he be flesh, that is, man [Note: Rhen. reads “nor man flesh”]; for one who was the Word is not properly flesh [Note: Rhen. reads “because.”]. Thus from both he is neither; he is something else, a third thing far removed from either.

Yet we find him expressly set forth as both God and man, as this very Psalm indicates: “For God was born as man in her, [Note: Rhen. inserts “and.”] and he built her by the will of the Father.” He is assuredly everywhere called both Son of God and son of man, since he is without doubt God and man, with each of the two substances remaining distinct in its own proper identity: for the Word is nothing other than God, and the flesh nothing other than man.

So too the Apostle (Rom. 1:3–4) teaches concerning both his substances: “Who was made,” he says, “from the seed of David.” This will be the man and son of man, who “was designated Son of God according to the Spirit.” This will be God and the Word of God, the Son.

We see a twofold condition, not confused [Note: “Not confused but conjoined in one person,” etc. God and man are, of course, conjoined while the proper identity of each substance is preserved, *οὐχὶ ἐκ συγχύσεως τῆς οὐσίας*—“not from a confusion of the substance.” These words do not seem very far removed from the Creed of blessed Athanasius. LE PR.], but conjoined in one person, Jesus, God and man. Concerning “Christ,” however, I defer discussion [Note: Seml. reads “I discuss.”].

And so fully is the proper identity of each substance preserved that the Spirit performed in him its own activities—that is, powers, works, and signs—while the flesh underwent its own sufferings: hungering under the devil’s temptation, thirsting with the Samaritan woman, weeping for Lazarus, being distressed even to death, and finally dying.

But if he had been some third thing, confused from both like electrum, such distinct proofs of each substance would not appear. Rather, through the interchange, the Spirit would have performed fleshly acts and the flesh spiritual acts; [Col. 0192A] or else [Note: Rhen. reads “or.”] neither fleshly nor spiritual acts would have occurred, but acts of some third form arising from [Note: Venet., Fran., Paris., and Rig. omit “from.”] the confusion.

Indeed, either the Word would have died, or the flesh would not have died, if the Word had been changed into flesh. For either the flesh would have been immortal or the Word mortal. But because both substances, each distinctly, acted in its own condition [Note: Paris. reads “distinct.”], their respective works and outcomes therefore befell them.

Learn, then, with Nicodemus (John 3:6): “What is born in [Note: Latin reads “from.”] the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.” Flesh does not become Spirit, nor Spirit flesh. They certainly can exist in one being. Jesus consisted of these: from the flesh, man; from the Spirit, God. The angel then declared him the Son of God with respect to that part by which he was Spirit, while preserving “son of man” as the designation of the flesh.

So too the Apostle, by calling him the mediator of God and human beings (1 Tim. 2:5), confirmed both substances. Finally, you who interpret the Son of God as the flesh: show what the son of man is. Or will it perhaps be the Spirit? But you wish the Spirit to be regarded as the Father himself, because “God is Spirit”—as though there were not also the Spirit of God, just as the Word is God and there is also the Word of God.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

And so you make Christ the Father, most foolish man, without even examining the meaning of this title—if indeed “Christ” is a name and not rather an appellation; for it means “anointed.” [Note: Rhen. reads “for rather ‘anointed.’”] “Anointed,” however, is no more a name than “clothed” or “shod”: it is a circumstance added to a name.

Suppose that, on the basis of some consideration, Jesus were also called “clothed,” just as he is called Christ from the sacrament of anointing. Would you likewise say that Jesus was the Son of God, but believe that “the clothed one” was the Father?

Now concerning Christ. If the Father is Christ, the Father is anointed, and surely by another. Or, if by himself, prove it. But the Acts of the Apostles do not teach this, in that exclamation of the Church [Note: Rhen. omits “of the Church.”] to God: “For all assembled” (Acts 4:27) “in this city against your holy Son Jesus [Note: Rhen. omits “Jesus.”], whom you anointed—Herod and Pilate together with the nations.” Thus they both testified that Jesus was the Son of God and that the Son was anointed by the Father.

Therefore, Jesus [Note: Seml. reads “the Lord.”] will be the same as Christ, who was anointed by the Father; he will not be the Father, who anointed the Son. So too Peter says (Acts 2:36): “Therefore let the whole house of Israel know with absolute certainty that God has made this Jesus whom you crucified both Lord and Christ”—that is, anointed.

John, moreover (1 John 2:22), brands as a liar the person who denies that Jesus is the Christ; conversely, he says that everyone who believes Jesus to be the Christ has been born of God. Therefore he also exhorts us to believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, so that we may have communion with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.

Thus Paul too everywhere sets forth God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ. When writing to the Romans (1:8), he gives thanks to God through our Lord Jesus Christ. When writing to the Galatians (1:1), he declares that he is an apostle not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father.

And you have all his writings [Note: Rhen. reads “his whole document.”], which declare matters in this way and set forth two: God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father’s Son. They also set forth Jesus himself as the Christ, the Son of God under this second designation as well. [Col. 0193B]

For hence, by the principle that both names belong to one being, namely the Son of God [Note: Rhen. reads “Son.”], either one without the other also belongs to that same being. Whether only “Jesus” is used, “Christ” is also understood, because Jesus [Note: Rhen. adds “Christ.”] is anointed. Or whether only “Christ” is used, the same one is Jesus [Note: Rhen. omits “only” and “Jesus.”], because Jesus is the one anointed.

Of these names, one is proper, the name imposed by the angel; the other is circumstantial, belonging to him by reason of the anointing—provided, however, that Christ is the Son, not the Father.

Finally, how blind is the person who does not understand that even in the name “Christ” another God is indicated, if he ascribes the name Christ to the Father [Note: Seml. reads “the name of Christ to the Father”]? For if Christ is God the Father, he who says (John 20:17), “I ascend to my Father and your Father, and my God and your God,” plainly shows another Father and God above himself.

Likewise, if the Father is Christ, then another is the one [Col. 0193C] who establishes the thunder, creates the Spirit, and announces his Christ among human beings (Amos 4:13). And if “the kings of the earth took their stand, and the rulers assembled together against his Christ” (Ps. 2:2), then another will be the Lord against whose Christ the kings and rulers assembled.

And if: “Thus says the Lord to my lord Christ” (Isa. 45:1), another will be the Lord who speaks to the Father of Christ. And when the Apostle writes (Eph. 1:17), “That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ may give you a spirit of wisdom and knowledge,” another will be the God of Christ Jesus, the giver of spiritual gifts.

Certainly, not to wander through every passage, “he who raised Christ will also raise our mortal bodies” (Rom. 8:11). Thus the one who raises will now be another than the dead Father and the Father who was raised [Note: Rhen. reads “as though another”; Wouw.’s codex reads “surely another”], if Christ, who died, is the Father.

## CHAPTER XXIX

[Col. 0193D]

Let this blasphemy fall silent—let it fall silent. Let it suffice to say that Christ, the Son of God, died; and this only because it is so [Col. 0194A] written. For the Apostle too, when declaring—not without gravity—that Christ died, added [Note: others read “adds.”], “according to the Scriptures,” so that he might soften the harshness of the declaration by the authority of the Scriptures and remove the stumbling block for the hearer.

Yet since two substances are reckoned in Christ Jesus, divine and human; and since it is established that the divine is immortal, just as that which is human is mortal [Note: Jun. reads “it mortal”; Rhen. reads “since mortal”], it is apparent in what respect he calls him dead: namely, insofar as he is flesh, human being, and son of man—not insofar as he is Spirit, Word, and Son of God.

Finally, by saying “Christ died”—that is, “the anointed one”—he shows that what was anointed died, namely, the flesh.

“Therefore,” you say, “when we declare by the same reasoning that the Father died, just as you declare the Son did [Note: Seml. omits “the Father died”; Rhen. reads “we” for “you”], we do not blaspheme against the Lord God; for we say that he died not in his divine substance but in his human substance.”

On the contrary, you blaspheme not only because you say that the Father died, but also because you say that he was crucified. For by transferring to the Father the curse of the crucified, which according to the Law applies to the Son—because Christ became a curse [Note: Fran., Paris., and Rig. read “by a curse.”] for us, not the Father—and by transforming Christ into the Father, you blaspheme against the Father.

We, however, when we say that Christ was crucified, do not curse him, but report the curse of the Law; for the Apostle did not blaspheme when he said this either. Just as something which a subject is capable of having said about it may be said without blasphemy, so if something of which it is not capable is said of it, that is blasphemy.

Nor, therefore, did the Father suffer with the Son. For, being afraid of direct blasphemy against the Father, they hope to lessen it in this way, now conceding that Father and Son are two: if [Note: Rhen. reads “since.”] the Son suffers, the Father suffers with him. They are fools [Col. 0194C] in this too. For what is “to suffer with” except to suffer together with another?

Further, if the Father is incapable of suffering, he is surely also incapable of suffering with another. Or, if he is capable of suffering with another, he is surely capable of suffering. You gain nothing for him even by this fear of yours [Note: Seml. reads “as though dead.”]. You are afraid to call him capable of suffering, though you call him capable of suffering with another.

The Father, however, is just as incapable of suffering with another [Note: Seml. reads “capable of suffering with another.”] as the Son too is incapable of suffering in respect of that condition in which he is God.

But how did the Son suffer, if the Father did not suffer with him? He was separated [Note: Rhen. reads “is separated.”] from the Son, not from God. For even if a river is contaminated by some disturbance, although a single substance flows down from the spring and is not severed from the spring, nevertheless the injury to the river will not extend to the spring.

And although it is the water of the spring that suffers in the river, yet because it suffers not in the spring but in the river, it is not the spring that suffers, but the river which comes from the spring. Thus, even if the Spirit of God [Col. 0194D] could suffer something [Note: Seml. reads “can”; Paris reads “Thus also he who suffers.”] in the Son, yet because it would suffer not in the Father but in the Son, the Father would not be regarded as having suffered.

But it is enough that the Spirit of God suffered nothing in his own proper capacity; for if he suffered anything, he suffered it in the Son, [Col. 0195A] in whom the Father also was [Note: Semler reads “indeed was as Father”], while the Son [Note: Semler reads “in the Son.”] suffered in the flesh—because this has already been discussed [Note: Semler reads “discussed” in agreement with a masculine subject].

Nor will anyone deny it, since even we cannot suffer for God unless [Note: Seml. omits “not”; another Seml. variant reads “if.”] the Spirit of God is in us, who also speaks from within us the words belonging to confession—yet without himself suffering, but enabling us to suffer.

## CHAPTER XXX
Otherwise, if you proceed further [Note: [Col. 0195C] “Proceeding,” Semler.], I shall be able to answer you more severely and bring you into conflict with the Lord’s own declaration, by saying: Why do you inquire about this matter? You have [Note: [Col. 0195C] “He has,” Semler.] him himself crying out in his passion: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Therefore either the Son suffered, forsaken by the Father, while the Father, who forsook the Son, did not suffer; or, if it was the Father who suffered, to what God was he crying out? But this cry belonged to the flesh and [Col. 0195B] the soul—that is, to the man—not to the Word or the Spirit, that is, not to God. It was uttered precisely to show that God is incapable of suffering: he forsook the Son in such a way that he delivered the Son’s humanity over to death. This is also what the Apostle understood when he wrote (Rom. 8:32): “If the Father did not spare the Son.” This too Isaiah had declared beforehand (Isa. 53:6): “And the Lord delivered him up for our transgressions.” Thus he forsook him by not sparing him; thus he forsook him by delivering him up [Note: [Col. 0195D] “Will deliver,” Semler.]. Yet the Father did not forsake the Son, into whose hands the Son committed his spirit. Indeed, he committed it, and immediately died; for while the spirit remains in the flesh, the flesh cannot die at all. Thus, for the Son to be forsaken by the Father was for him to die. It is therefore the Son who both dies (1 Cor. 15:3 ff.) and is raised by the Father, according to the Scriptures. It is the Son who ascends into the heights of heaven, who also descended [Col. 0195C] into the inner regions [Note: [Col. 0196C] “Lower regions,” others.] of the earth. He sits at the right hand of the Father; the Father does not sit at his own right hand. Stephen sees him [Note: [Col. 0196C] “Saw,” François.] while he is being stoned [Note: [Col. 0196C] “Was being stoned,” Rhenanus.], still standing at the right hand of God, as one who was [Col. 0196A] thereafter to sit until (Ps. 109:2) the Father placed all his enemies beneath his feet. He too will come again upon the clouds (1 Cor. 15) of heaven, in the same form in which he ascended. In the meantime, he poured out the gift received from the Father, the Holy Spirit, the third name [Note: [Col. 0196C] “Divine power” (*numen*), Paris.] of the divinity and the third degree of majesty [Note: [Col. 0196C] “And the third degree of majesty” omitted by Semler.], the herald of the one monarchy, but also the interpreter of the economy—if anyone will admit [Note: [Col. 0195] The discourses of the new prophecy: the oracles of Montanus, by which Tertullian was blinded, are indicated here by him. LE PR.] his discourses of the new prophecy—and the guide [Note: [Col. 0196C] “Of the guide,” Rhenanus.] into all truth, which is in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, according to the Christian mystery.

## CHAPTER XXXI

But this matter belongs to the Jewish faith [Note: [Col. 0196C] Semler conjectures “You would press the point”], namely, so to believe in one God that you refuse to number the Son with him, and after the Son, the Spirit. For what difference will there be between us and them [Col. 0196B] except this distinction? What is the work of the Gospel, what is the substance of the New Testament—which fixes the Law and the Prophets as extending only to John—if from that point onward the Father, Son, and Spirit, believed to be three, do not constitute one God? Thus God willed to renew the mystery: that in a new manner he should be believed to be one through the Son and the Spirit, so that God might now be known openly in his own proper names and persons—he who in former times, though proclaimed through the Son and the Spirit, was not understood. Let the antichrists, therefore, who deny the Father and the Son, see to it. For they deny the Father when they say that he is the same as the Son; and they deny the Son when they believe that he is the same as the Father, ascribing to them what they are not and taking away what they are. But whoever confesses that Christ is the Son of God, not the Father, God abides in him, and he in God. We believe the testimony [Note: [Col. 0196D] “Testimony” in the accusative, Semler.] of God, by which he testified concerning [Col. 0196C] his Son: “He who does not have the Son does not have life either” (1 John 5:12). But he does not have the Son who believes him to be anything other than the Son.

[Col. 0195]

# THE BOOK OF QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN AGAINST HERMOGENES

## Synopsis

[Col. 0195D] This Hermogenes was African by nationality and a painter by profession, entirely distinct from the man of whom the Apostle speaks together with Phygelus or Philetus in 2 Timothy 1. Having at first professed himself a Christian, [Col. 0196D] he bore witness to the cunning and deceitful disposition of his nation when, degenerating, he rushed into pagan philosophy and [Col. 0197A] followed the delusions of the Stoics. While still alive, Hermogenes taught that eternal matter existed. He relied upon this principle: God is good and supremely good, and wills to make things good and supremely good just as much as he knows how—indeed, he both wills and devises nothing that is not good and supremely good. . . . Yet evil things are found to have been made by him, certainly not by his choice and will; therefore they must undoubtedly have been made from matter, owing to the defect of some thing. Tertullian replied that Hermogenes introduces two Gods by introducing matter as God’s equal. God, however, must be one; but he cannot be unique if anything is made equal to him, and matter will be made equal to God when it is regarded as eternal. Likewise, God is not almighty if he needed matter, while matter supplied itself to a needy God—one inferior, powerless, and insufficiently capable of making from nothing whatever he wished. Furthermore, if matter is evil and eternal, evil is assuredly unavoidable and necessary; if matter can be changed into good, it is therefore not eternal. Moreover, God is here the author of evil: although he ought to have brought forth from matter either all things or only good things, he also brought forth evil things—either certainly willing evil things to exist, if he could have caused them not to exist, or else unwilling to make all things good, if he willed this but did not do it. LUMP.

## CHAPTER I

For the sake of brevity, we are accustomed to enter a preliminary objection against heretics on the ground of their lateness. For insofar as the rule of truth came first—a rule that also foretold future heresies [Note: [Col. 0197C] “Renounced,” Semler.]—so every later doctrine will be prejudged as heresy, since such doctrines are the things foretold as future by the more ancient rule of truth. The doctrine of Hermogenes, however, is so novel that the man is, indeed, still alive in the present age; and by nature too he is a turbulent heretic, [Col. 0197C] one who [Note: [Col. 0197C] “Regards loquacity as eloquence.” It is a common fault of those in error that they wear out their listeners with their loquacity while wishing to be considered eloquent. “It is the nature of things,” says Symmachus, Book I, Letter 76, “that those who stammer talk more; for, ashamed of their deficiency, they affect abundance.” LE PR.] regards loquacity as eloquence, reckons shamelessness as steadfastness, and judges that slandering individuals is [Col. 0198A] the duty of a good conscience. Furthermore, he paints unlawfully [Note: [Col. 0197C] “He paints unlawfully.” Hermogenes was a painter. He painted unlawfully because, after assuming the name of Christian, [Col. 0197D] he nevertheless painted images of gods—false gods, of course. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0197C] “Freely,” Rhenanus, Junius, Semler. Junius interprets it as “without restraint” or “licentiously.”], marries repeatedly [Note: [Col. 0197D] “Marries repeatedly”: by continually changing wives, for he favored polygamy. RIG.]; he defends the law of God in the service of lust [Note: [Col. 0197D] “He defends the law of God in the service of lust”: he used as a pretext for his lust the law of God, “Increase and multiply.” RIG.—“He defends the law of God in the service of lust,” etc. He defended polygamy, which Septimius detested, in order thereby to find protection for his own crimes; and for this purpose he employed God’s law, which he defiled by painting the most shameful things, and by this practice proved himself guilty of falsification. LE PR.], and by his art holds it in contempt [Note: [Col. 0197D] “By his art holds it in contempt”: that is, by his art he holds that same law in contempt, painting images although the law forbade it: “You shall not make an idol.” RIG.]. Twice a falsifier [Note: [Col. 0197D] “Twice a falsifier, with cautery and pen.” A falsifier with his painter’s cautery, burning waxes of different colors in order to represent images of false divinities; a falsifier also with his pen, corrupting the Scriptures in a heretical manner. RIG.], both with cautery [Note: [Col. 0197D] “Cautery”: because he painted with waxes and burned the painting in with a cautery. This kind of painting was called encaustic painting, or *encaustum*. Pliny XXXV.2; Vitruvius VII.9; Marcianus, Book XVII. Read *De instr.* or *instrumentis*. RIG.] and with pen, he is wholly an adulterer, both in his preaching and in his flesh [Note: [Col. 0198C] “Wholly an adulterer, both in his preaching and in his flesh.” Hermogenes’ flesh was adulterous because it repeatedly married. Flesh that marries so often does not marry but is adulterous according to the law. Hermogenes’ preaching was also adulterous because through his heresy he had corrupted the faith and peace of the Church. RIG.], since he reeks from the contagion even of those who marry [Note: [Col. 0198D] “Since he reeks from the contagion even of those who marry.” He explains what he said above, that Hermogenes was an adulterer in the flesh, since he himself, rutting amid the contamination of frequent marriages, reeked. RIG.]. Nor did Hermogenes himself—the apostolic Hermogenes [Note: [Col. 0198D] “Nor did Hermogenes himself—the apostolic Hermogenes.” Among Paul’s companions was a Hermogenes who shared a name with Septimius’ opponent; he afterward deserted Paul, and thereby Christ. Septimius therefore thrusts upon the heretical Hermogenes the name of the apostolic Hermogenes to signify that he is an apostate, because he too did not persevere in the rule of faith, just as Paul’s Hermogenes did not persevere in the faith. RIG.]—persevere in the rule. But let his person be; my dispute is with his doctrine. He appears to know Christ the Lord differently, not as a different Christ [Note: [Col. 0197C] “He appears to know Christ the Lord, not as another, but otherwise; yet he makes him another,” Vatican codex. “He appears to know Christ the Lord, not as another, differently; yet another,” François, Junius.]; nevertheless, by knowing him differently he makes him another. Indeed, he takes away everything that constitutes God by refusing to admit that he made all things from nothing. For, turning from Christians to philosophers, from the Church to the Academy and the Stoa, he took from the Stoics the doctrine that matter must be placed alongside the Lord: matter that had itself always existed, neither born nor made, having absolutely [Col. 0198B] neither beginning nor end, and from which the Lord afterward made all things.

## CHAPTER II

This first shadow, entirely without light, that most wretched painter colored with the following arguments. He laid down beforehand that the Lord made all things either [Note: [Col. 0198C] Junius, incorrectly, reads “he says.”] from himself, or from nothing, or from something; so that, after showing that he could have made them neither from himself nor from nothing [Note: [Col. 0198D] “Nor from nothing,” etc. Pagan wisdom is utter folly; for Hermogenes had drawn from the Stoic school the doctrine that matter had existed eternally and that God therefore did not make all things from nothing. You will not marvel at this in a pagan philosopher, for, as is stated below, philosophers are the patriarchs of heretics; there he speaks of those who obstinately adhere to the tenets of the pagans. LE PR.], he might establish the remaining alternative: that God made them from something, and that this “something” was matter. He denies that God could have made anything from himself, because whatever the Lord made from himself would have been parts of himself. Yet the Lord, as indivisible, unchangeable, and always the same, could not be divided into parts. Moreover, if he had made anything from himself, that thing would have been something of himself. But both that which was made and that which made it [Col. 0198C] would have to be regarded as imperfect, because the former would be made from only a part, and the latter would make it with only a part. Or, if the whole made the whole, [Col. 0199A] he would have had to be at once whole and not whole: for he would have to be whole in order to make himself, and not whole in order to be made from himself. [Note: [Col. 0199C] “That, moreover,” Junius.] This, moreover, is exceedingly difficult. For if he existed, he would not be made, since he already existed; but if he did not exist, he would not make, since he would be nothing. He who always exists is not made but exists for ever and ever. Therefore he did not make from himself, since his constitution was not such [Note: [Col. 0199C] “Would be made,” Semler; Oberthür considers this reading probable, following Junius.] that he could make from himself.

Hermogenes similarly contends that God could not make from nothing, defining the Lord as good and supremely good, one who wills to make things good and supremely good just as much as he is good; indeed, he both wills and makes nothing that is not good and supremely good. Accordingly, all things ought to be good, and everything made by him ought to be good and supremely good in accordance with his own nature. Yet evil things are also found to have been made by him—certainly not by his choice [Col. 0199B] or will, because, if they were made by his choice and will, he would make nothing inconsistent with or unworthy of himself. What he did not make by his own choice must therefore be understood to have been made through the defect of some other thing, undoubtedly from matter.

## CHAPTER III

He adds another argument: God has always been God [Note: [Col. 0199C] “God has always been God and likewise has always been Lord; he was never not Lord,” Junius.] and also Lord; he was never not God. Yet he could in no way always have been regarded as Lord, just as he was always God, unless there had always existed in the past something of which he was always regarded as Lord. Matter, therefore, always existed for God to be its Lord.

I shall hasten at once to destroy this conjecture of his, which I have thought fit thus far to set out for the sake of those who do not understand, so that they may know that his other arguments can likewise both be understood and refuted. We say that the name “God” has always existed with and [Col. 0199C] within God himself, but not the name “Lord”; for the condition of each name is different. “God” [Note: [Col. 0199C] “But God,” Semler.] is the name of his substance, that is, of the divinity; “Lord,” however, is the name not of substance but of power. His substance has always existed together with its name, which is “God.” “Lord” came afterward, clearly as the designation of a thing that had been added [Note: [Col. 0199C] Junius correctly reads “with the designation of a thing that had occurred,” according to Latinus.]. For from the time when things [Col. 0200A] over which the Lord’s power could operate began to exist, from that time he both became and was called Lord through the accession of power. For God is also Father, and God is Judge; yet he is not therefore always Father and Judge simply because he is always God. For he could not be Father before the Son, nor Judge before an offense. There was, however, a time [Note: [Col. 0199D] “There was a time when,” etc. Everyone will readily recognize that an error must be guarded against in this passage, namely Arianism. For their expression ἦν ὅτε οὐκ ἦν, “there was a time when he was not,” is well known, and these words convey precisely the same meaning. LE PR.] when neither [Note: [Col. 0199C] “And,” Semler, Oberthür.] offense nor Son existed—the former to make the Lord [Note: [Col. 0199C] “God,” Latinus and others.] a Judge, and the latter to make the Lord a Father. So too he was not Lord before the things [Note: [Col. 0199D] “Previously,” Semler.] of which he would become Lord; he was only destined to be Lord at some future time: just as Father through the Son, and Judge through offense, so also Lord through the things he would make to serve him.

Do I seem to you to be engaging in clever argument, Hermogenes [Note: [Col. 0200C] “Do I seem to you to be quibbling, Hermogenes? Scripture vigorously—” or so Junius.]? Scripture vigorously supports us, distinguishing the two names for him and showing each at its proper time. For it immediately names him “God” [Note: [Col. 0200C] “Lord,” Semler.], which he always was: [Col. 0200B] “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” Thereafter, for as long as he was making the things whose Lord he was to become, Scripture employs “God” alone: “And God said,” “and God made,” “and God saw”; nowhere yet does it say “Lord.” But when he had completed all things, and most particularly man himself, who was properly to understand the Lord [Note: [Col. 0200C] “The Lord, and was to understand,” Semler.], he is also designated “Lord” [Note: [Col. 0200C] “Was to be designated,” Semler, Oberthür.]. Then Scripture also added the name “Lord”: “And the Lord God took [Note: [Col. 0199D] “And God took.” What the author observes is indeed true: that God is not called “Lord” until he has completed all things, and especially man himself. Yet even before the Scripture cited here, immediately at the beginning of chapter 2, there occur: “For the Lord God had not caused it to rain,” and “the Lord God planted a paradise”; only then comes, “And the Lord God took the man.” PAM.] the man whom he had formed.” And “the Lord God commanded” [Note: [Col. 0200C] “Commanded,” Semler.]. From that point onward he is “Lord,” whereas previously he was only “God,” from the time when he possessed something whose Lord he was. For he was God to himself; but he was then God to created things when he was also their Lord.

Therefore, insofar as Hermogenes thinks that matter always existed because the Lord always existed, it will instead be established that nothing existed, because it is established that he was not always Lord. I too shall add something for the sake of those who do not [Col. 0200C] understand, of whom Hermogenes is [Note: [Col. 0199D] “Of whom Hermogenes is the finishing line.” In this very work he says that the finishing line is the end of everything. He means that Hermogenes’ foolishness is the end of all foolishness—that is, the highest foolishness, beyond which none exists. RIG.—“Of whom Hermogenes is the finishing line.” In the courses where races were publicly held in ancient times, the beginning and end were marked with lines. Hence whatever is last came proverbially to be called “the finishing line.” Therefore, when Tertullian here calls Hermogenes the finishing line of those who do not understand, take him to mean “the most ignorant of all.” Horace closes his letter to Quintius thus:

> Death is the final boundary-line of things.

At the same time he makes a tacit allusion to Hermogenes’ art, since as a painter he was accustomed to draw lines with a brush. Thus below, speaking of matter, he says: “If it is in a place, it is therefore within a place; if within a place, it is therefore bounded by the place within which it is; if it is bounded, it has a finishing line, which—as far as a painter properly understands—it recognizes as the end of everything whose finishing line it is,” etc. In the book *Against Praxeas*, he calls God the finishing line of the universe. RHEN.] the finishing line; indeed, I shall turn his own *epinoēmata*—afterthoughts [Note: [Col. 0200D] *Epinoēmata*. We have emended the text thus from Ursinus’ book. RIG.]—against him [Note: [Col. 0200C] “I shall turn this against him from his repentance,” Semler, [Col. 0200D] Oberthür.]. For since he denies that matter was born or made, I likewise find that the title “Lord” did not apply to God in relation to matter. Matter must necessarily have been free, since, by having no origin, it had no author; being what it was, it served no one [Col. 0201A] [Note: [Col. 0201C] “It had no thing which it was, serving no one,” Rhenanus, François, Paris; “it had no author of what it was,” Wouwerius, Venice; “it had no thing which it was, and therefore served no one,” Vatican codex; “it had no author of what it was and therefore served no one,” Junius.]. Accordingly, from the moment God exercised his power upon it by making things from matter, from that moment matter submitted to God as Lord; this demonstrates that he had not been Lord for as long as matter existed [Note: [Col. 0201C] “This,” Junius, Latinus; “existed,” Rigault, Venice, more correctly.].

From this point, then, I shall begin to reconsider the subject of matter: Hermogenes equates it with God as likewise unborn, likewise unmade, likewise eternal, set forth without beginning and without end [Note: [Col. 0201C] “Set forth,” Junius and the rest.]. For what other mark belongs to God than eternity? What other condition belongs to eternity than always to have existed and always to exist in the future, by virtue of having neither beginning nor end? If this belongs properly to God, then even if it is ascribed to another, it will no longer be proper to God but common to him and to that to which it is also ascribed. For though there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, in name, yet there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things [Col. 0201B] (1 Cor. 8:5). All the more, among us, whatever belongs properly to God ought to belong to God alone; and, as I have said, it would no longer be proper to him if it belonged to another. But if God is one, what belongs to him must necessarily be unique, so that it belongs to one alone [Note: [Col. 0201D] “For, as I have said, it would no longer be proper to him if it belonged to another; but if God is one, it must necessarily be unique, so that it belongs to one alone,” Junius; “but if God, unique,” codex of Wouwerius.]. Or what will be unique and singular unless nothing is equal to it? What will be supreme unless it is above all things, before all things, and the source from which all things come? [Note: [Col. 0201D] “God alone is God by possessing these things.” God alone is master of these things; he alone possesses them. RIG.] God is God by possessing these things alone, and by possessing them alone he is one [Note: [Col. 0201D] “God alone, by possessing these things, is one,” Semler, Oberthür.]. If another possesses them, there will then be as many gods as there are possessors of divine attributes.

Thus Hermogenes introduces two gods. He introduces matter as equal to God [Note: [Col. 0202C] “He introduces matter when—,” Junius.]. God, however, must be one, because God is that which is supreme; but the supreme will not be supreme unless it is unique, and it cannot be unique if anything is made equal to it. Matter, however, will be made equal to God when [Col. 0201C] it is regarded as eternal [Note: [Col. 0202C] Junius conjectures “when it will be regarded as eternal,” perhaps for “when.”].

## CHAPTER V

“But God is God, and matter is matter”—as though diversity of names prevented comparison when identity of condition is claimed. Let their natures be different and their forms not the same, provided that [Note: [Col. 0202C] “Provided the status of its name,” Semler.] the principle of their condition is one. Is God unborn? Is matter not also unborn? Is God eternal? Is matter not also eternal? Both are without beginning, [Col. 0202A] both without end, both are also authors of the universe—both he who made it and that from which he made it. For matter too cannot but be reckoned an author of all things, since the universe is constituted from it.

How will he answer [Note: [Col. 0202C] The question mark is absent from the editions of Rhenanus and Semler, and more correctly.]? That matter is not immediately comparable to God if it possesses something belonging to God, because, since it does not possess the whole, it does not attain to a complete comparison? What more has he left to God, so that he may not appear to have given everything belonging to God to matter? “Or,” he says, “although matter is thus constituted, God’s authority [Note: [Col. 0202C] Rhenanus conjectured “his principle remains secure”; others, according to Junius, who approves it: “God’s authority and substance remain secure, by which he is regarded as the sole and first author and the Lord of all.”] and substance remain secure, inasmuch as he is regarded as the sole and first author and as the Lord of all.” But truth requires us so to defend one God that whatever belongs to him belongs to him alone. For it will belong to him if it belongs to him alone; and for this reason another god cannot be admitted, since no one is permitted to possess anything belonging to God.

“Then,” you say, “neither do we [Col. 0202B] possess anything belonging to God.” On the contrary, we possess it and shall possess it, but from him, not from ourselves. For we too shall be gods [Note: [Col. 0202D] Others read “gods” (*dii*).], if we have deserved to be those of whom he declared: “I said, You are gods”; and, “God stood in the assembly of the gods” (Ps. 81:1). But this is by his grace, not from our own property, because he alone is the one who makes gods. Matter [Note: [Col. 0202D] “Matter,” Semler.] makes its own that which it possesses in common with God. Or, if it received from God that which belongs to God—I mean the order of eternity—it can be believed both to possess something in common with God and yet not to be a god. But what sort of position is it when Hermogenes confesses that matter possesses something in common with God, yet wishes that which he does not deny matter possesses to belong to God alone?

## CHAPTER VI

He says that God’s position remains secure [Note: [Col. 0201D] “He says that God’s position remains secure, so that he is both alone,” etc. Tertullian reveals a self-contradictory or apparently contradictory sense—ἐναντιοφανές—in Hermogenes, who affirms that God is alone and first, although he does not shrink from saying that matter is coeval and coeternal with him. This is impious and drawn from the storehouse of pagan philosophy. Laertius taught me that Plato admitted two principles of things, God and matter. I marvel at this in him, though in other matters it does not seem unusual to me. LE PR.], so that he is alone, first, the author of all, the Lord of all, and comparable to no one—attributes that he immediately ascribes to matter as well [Col. 0202C] [Note: [Col. 0202D] “Comparable through those things which he is not. He ascribes them to matter also,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.]. “I indeed am God” [Note: [Col. 0202D] “He indeed is God,” in the same editions.], God will testify; and he has sometimes sworn by himself that there is no other like him (Deut. 32:39–40). But Hermogenes will make him a liar, for matter too will be like God: unmade, unborn, having neither beginning nor end.

God will say, “I am first” (Isa. 41, 44, 48) [Note: [Col. 0202D] “God will say: I am first.” This occurs three times in Isaiah, chapters 41, 44, and 48, in these words: “I am first and last.” But the statement “I stretched out heaven alone,” according to the Septuagint, is found in Isaiah 44, where the edition translated from the Hebrew has “stretching out,” preceded by “I, the Lord, completing” or “making all things.” The author also alludes to this when he makes God the author of all. PAM.]. But how is he first when matter is coeval with him? Among those who are coeval and contemporary there is no order—or else [Col. 0203A] matter too is first.

[Note: [Col. 0203D] “‘I stretched out,’ he says, ‘heaven alone.’” Thus Isaiah 44: Ἐξέτεινα τὸν οὐρανὸν μόνος, “I stretched out heaven alone.” And Psalm 104: ὁ ἐκτείνων τὸν οὐρανὸν ὡσεὶ δέρριν, “who stretches out heaven like a hide.” These words are also cited by pagan writers. Thus Trypho to Critias: Εἰ οὐρανὸν ὡς δέρριν ἐξήπλωσε, γῆν δὲ ἐφ’ ὕδατος ἔπηξεν, ἀστέρας ἐμόρφωσεν, “If he spread out heaven like a hide, fixed the earth upon water, and fashioned the stars.”]

“I stretched out,” he says, “heaven alone” (Isa. 44). But he did not do so alone, since he stretched it out together with that from which he stretched it. When Hermogenes asserts that matter existed without prejudice to God’s condition [Note: [Col. 0203D] “That God existed without prejudice to matter’s condition,” Rhenanus, Semler; the codex of Wouwerius has “that God existed without prejudice to matter’s condition,” with Junius’ approval.], see whether we may not reply to him [Note: [Col. 0203D] “See whether he is not mocked by us,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.] that God likewise existed without prejudice to matter’s condition, although the condition of both was common. It will therefore remain secure for matter too that it existed, though with God, just as God too was alone, though with matter. Matter too was first with God, just as God was first with it. Matter too was incomparable with God, just as God was incomparable with it; and it was an author with God and a mistress with God. Thus, by allowing matter to possess something but supposedly not everything, Hermogenes has left God nothing that he has not also conferred upon matter, so that matter is not compared with God, but God rather with matter.

Indeed, since the attributes [Col. 0203B] that we claim as proper to God [Note: [Col. 0203D] “Since the things proper to God,” in the same editions.]—always to have existed, to be without beginning and without end, to have been first and alone, and to be the author of all—also belong to matter, I ask: what different and alien attribute, unlike God’s and thus private to itself, did matter possess, by which it is not compared with God? Since all God’s proper attributes are enumerated in it, these sufficiently prejudge the rest of the comparison.

## CHAPTER VII

If Hermogenes contends that matter is lesser and lower than God and therefore incomparable with him as the greater and higher, I enter the preliminary objection that whatever is eternal and unborn admits no diminution or humiliation. For this is precisely what makes God as great as he is: inferior and subordinate to none, indeed greater and higher than all. For just as other things, which are born or [Col. 0203C] come to an end and therefore are not eternal, once exposed to an end and also admitting a beginning, admit what God does not—by which I mean diminution for the present and subjection—because they were born and made; so God does not admit them precisely because he was neither born at all nor made. But the condition of matter [Note: [Col. 0203D] “And of matter,” Rhenanus, etc.] is of this same kind.

Therefore, since there are two eternal things, unborn and unmade—God and matter [Note: [Col. 0203D] “God and matter” in the dative, Rhenanus and the same other editors, as usual.]—their condition is common for the same reason: they equally possess that which admits neither diminution nor subjection, namely eternity. We say that neither is lesser or greater than the other, neither lower nor higher than the other, but that both stand equally great, equally exalted, [Col. 0204A] and equally possessed of the solid and perfect blessedness that is reckoned as eternity.

For we shall not approach the opinions of the pagans, who, if ever they are compelled to confess God, nevertheless wish there to be other gods beneath him. Divinity, however, admits no degree, since it is unique. If it is also present in matter, because matter is likewise unborn, unmade, and eternal, divinity will be present in both, since nowhere can it be less than itself. How, then, will Hermogenes dare to distinguish matter from God and thus subject it to God—eternal to eternal, unborn to unborn, author to author? Matter dares to say: “I too am first”; “I am before all things”; “I am that from which all things come. We were equals; we existed together; both of us are without beginning and without end; both without author and without God. What God subjects me [Note: [Col. 0204D] Perhaps “to God,” Junius.] to one who is my contemporary and coeternal? If he is called ‘God,’ I too have my own name. Either I [Col. 0204B] am God, or he is matter [Note: [Col. 0204D] “And he is matter,” Junius.], because we are both what each of us is.” Do you therefore think that you have not compared matter with God merely because you supposedly subject it to him?

## CHAPTER VIII

On the contrary, Hermogenes even places matter above God and subjects God rather to matter when he maintains that God made all things from matter. For if God employed it for the works of the world, matter is now found to be superior, since it supplied him with the means of working; and God appears subject to matter, whose substance he needed. For everyone needs that [Note: [Col. 0203D] “That from whose he uses”: an elliptical expression, with “things” or something similar understood. He also used this form of speech in earlier books. In *Against Marcion*, Book V: “If it is understood in the Creator’s.” In the same book: “And it can be opposed from our party’s.” Again, shortly afterward there follows: “He is not lesser than that from whose he uses.” It is an imitation of the Greeks. RHEN.] whose resources he uses; everyone is subjected to that which he needs in order to be able to use it. Likewise, everyone who uses what belongs to another is lesser than the one whose resources he uses; and everyone who permits another to use what belongs to himself is, in this respect, superior to the one whom he permits to use it.

Accordingly, matter itself had no need of God, but [Col. 0204C] offered itself to the needy God [Note: [Col. 0204D] “But it had needed to offer itself to God,” Latinus; “but it offered itself to the needy God,” Junius. “But it offered itself to the needy God, being rich”—codex of Wouwerius; perhaps “but it, being rich, offered itself to the needy God.”], rich, wealthy, and generous as it was, to one who was, I suppose, inferior, powerless, and insufficiently capable of making from nothing whatever he wished. It truly conferred a great benefit upon God, enabling him today to possess that through which he might be known as God and called almighty—except that he is now not almighty, if he also lacks this power: to bring forth all things from nothing.

Matter certainly also rendered some service to itself, enabling it to be recognized together with God as coequal with God, indeed even as his helper. Yet only Hermogenes recognized it, along with [Note: [Col. 0204D] “The philosophers, patriarchs of the heretics.” The author treated this expressly above in *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 7. PAM.—“Patriarchs of the heretics.” In his letter to Ctesiphon, Saint Jerome cites this passage of Tertullian. The same writer, while explaining the words in the prophet Nahum, “it leapt forth like a locust,” says: “For all their doctrines”—he is speaking of heretics—“since they are cold and cannot fly, find a seat and resting place among the thorn-brakes of Aristotle and Chrysippus.” RHEN.] the philosophers, the patriarchs of the heretics. For until now it escaped the notice of the prophets and Apostles—and, I suppose, of Christ as well [Note: [Col. 0204D] “I suppose, of Christ as well,” François, Paris, Rigault; but Junius reads “the prophets, Apostles, and Christ.”].

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0205A]

Hermogenes cannot say that God used matter as its Lord for the works of the world, since a Lord [Note: [Col. 0205C] “God,” Semler, Oberthür.] could not exist over a substance coequal with himself. Perhaps, then, he used it by sufferance. [Note: [Col. 0205D] “And therefore by sufferance, not by ownership.” To take another’s property by sufferance, ownership, or force are expressions used by jurists.
