Not only this passage shows that Tertullian possessed very extensive knowledge of civil law. RHEN.] He used it by sufferance, therefore, and not by ownership. Since it was evil [Note: [Col. 0205C] “Was not,” Semler, Oberthür. “Not” is absent from François, Paris, and Rigault, more correctly.], he nevertheless endured using evil matter, evidently under the constraint of his own limited power, whereby he was incapable of employing nothing as his material. He did not use it by virtue of a power that, had he possessed it as God over matter—which he knew to be evil—would have caused him first to convert it into good [Note: [Col. 0205C] “In the good,” Semler, Oberthür.] as Lord and as good, so that he might then use good matter, not evil. But because he was indeed good, yet was not Lord, he used matter as he found it. He thus revealed that his necessity yielded to the condition of matter, which he would have corrected if he had been its Lord.

This is how Hermogenes must be answered [Col. 0205B] when he argues from dominion that God used matter, though it was a thing not his own, because it had not been made by him. Evil, therefore, now comes from him who, if not the author of evil because he did not make it, was certainly its permitter because he ruled it. But if matter did not belong to him either, so that its evil was not God’s evil [Note: [Col. 0205C] “By which the evil is not God’s,” Semler, Oberthür.], then he used another’s property: either he used it by sufferance, because he needed it, or else wrongfully, because he was stronger than it. For in these three ways the property of others is taken: by right, by favor, or by assault—that is, by ownership, sufferance, or force. Since ownership is unavailable [Note: [Col. 0205C] Rhenanus separates the text here; Semler does not approve.], let Hermogenes choose which befits God: that he made all things from matter [Note: [Col. 0205D] “By sufferance or by force.” Something is said to be done by sufferance when it is extorted by entreaties; for sometimes that which would otherwise have been refused is granted to importunity and troublesome persistence. LE PR.] by sufferance or by force [Note: [Col. 0205C] “Had made,” François.]. Would God, then, not have judged it better to make absolutely nothing than to make by sufferance or force—and that from evil?

## CHAPTER X
[Col. 0205C] Would he not, even if matter had been perfectly good, have judged it equally unseemly for himself to make something from what belonged to another, even though it was good? Quite foolishly, if in this way [Note: [Col. 0205C] “Quite foolishly. And so,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür; “quite foolishly [Col. 0205D] and so,” Junius.] he undertook the world for the sake of his own glory, only to show himself indebted to another’s substance—and one that was not even good. “Then,” he says, “should he have made it from nothing, so that the evils too might be charged to his will?” Great indeed, [Col. 0206A] in all seriousness, [Note: [Col. 0205D] *Bona fide*, that is, “seriously”; thus Petronius in the *Satyricon*: “But now I complain of nothing, now I remember nothing, if you make good your repentance *bona fide*.” And elsewhere—earlier, of course—“when the kisses had been exacted *bona fide*.” Sometimes it means the same as “justly and equitably,” and in this sense *optima fide* is also used; likewise Petronius: “He did not resist, but after we had divided the spoils *optima fide*.” LE PR.] is the blindness of the heretics in advancing an argument of this kind. For they either wish another god, good and supremely good, to be believed in precisely because they consider the Creator the author of evil; or else they set matter alongside the Creator, so that they may derive evil from matter rather than from the Creator. Yet no god whatever can be exempted from this question so as not likewise to be regarded as the author of evil, whoever he may be, if, although he did not make evil himself, he nevertheless permitted it to be made by anyone and from any source whatever.

Let Hermogenes therefore listen—while elsewhere we distinguish the rationale of evil—that in the meantime he too has accomplished nothing by this objection [Note: [Col. 0206D] “By this thrust of his.” That is, by an objection or argument twisted in the contrary direction. LE PR.] of his. For behold: God is found to be, if not the author, at least the supporter [Note: [Col. 0206D] “But the supporter of evil.” As though its defender—or, if you prefer, its dissembler: that is, although God recognizes matter to be evil, he nevertheless makes use of it—as Hermogenes taught—and either confirms its depravity or at least overlooks it. LE PR.] of evil, [Note: [Col. 0205D] Junius conjectures *assectator*, “follower.”] since before the establishment of the world he tolerated so great an evil in preference to good within matter, though, being good and an opponent of evil, he ought to have corrected it. For either [Col. 0206B] he was able to correct it but was unwilling; or he was indeed willing but, being a weak God, was unable. If he was able but unwilling, he himself is evil, because he favored evil; and thus he is already held to be [Note: [Col. 0206D] “Its author”: these words, omitted by others, are added in the Venetian edition and the manuscripts of Wouwer.] its author. For although he did not institute it, nevertheless, since [Note: [Col. 0206C] Rhenanus alone has *qui*, followed by Semler and Oberthür.] it would not have existed had he been unwilling for it to exist, he himself caused that to exist which he was unwilling should not exist. What could be more shameful than this? If he willed that to exist which he himself was unwilling to make, he acted against himself, since he both willed to exist what he was unwilling to make and was unwilling to make what he willed to exist. He willed it to exist as though it were good, and was unwilling to make it as though it were evil. What he judged evil by not making it, he pronounced good by tolerating it. [Note: [Col. 0206C] All read “pronounced.” Junius says *praenuntiavit*, “foretold,” would be clearer.] By tolerating evil as good instead of rooting it out, he has been found its champion: [Note: [Col. 0206C] Semler places a comma here.] wickedly, if by his will; shamefully, if by necessity. God will be either the servant [Col. 0206C] or the friend of evil, since he associates with the evil of matter, to say nothing of his even working from its evil.

## CHAPTER XI

And yet on what grounds [Note: [Col. 0206C] “On what grounds for us?” All read more correctly than Semler, who has: [Col. 0206D] “not from us.”] does Hermogenes persuade us [Note: [Col. 0206D] “That matter is evil?” He had just replied to Hermogenes’ objections as though granting their truth; here, however, he rises against him and demands that he demonstrate that matter is evil and show from whom he derived this claim. LE PR.] that matter is evil? For he cannot avoid calling that [Col. 0207A] evil to which he ascribes evil. For we have established that what is eternal cannot admit diminution [Note: [Col. 0207C] Junius reads *definiimus deminutionem*.] or subjection, [Note: [Col. 0207C] All read “cannot, what is eternal,” except Semler and Oberthür, who read: “but if it is so.”] so that it might be reckoned inferior to another coeternal being. Thus even now we say that evil cannot belong to it, because it cannot thereby be subjected—since what is eternal can in no way be subjected.

But since, on other grounds, it is agreed that what is eternal, like God, is the supreme good—and that it is precisely through being eternal that he alone is God, and thus through being God that he is good—how will evil inhere in matter, which, because it is eternal, must necessarily be believed to be the supreme good? Or if what is eternal can also be susceptible to evil, the same may be believed of God; and Hermogenes has eagerly transferred evil away from God without cause, if evil is compatible with eternity by being compatible with matter.

Moreover, if what is eternal can be believed evil, evil will be unconquerable and insuperable [Col. 0207B] because it is eternal. And thus [Note: [Col. 0207C] “And thus,” Rigault; Junius: “and yet almost in vain.” But Wouwer’s codex reads: “and then we labor in vain … from ourselves; then God too … about to punish. But if,” etc.; Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür: “and nevertheless we in vain.”] we labor in vain to remove evil from ourselves; and God too [Note: [Col. 0207C] Semler has “when”; Latinus, “indeed God too does this in vain.”] commands and enjoins this in vain. Indeed, God has even established judgment in vain, [Note: [Col. 0207C] “Indeed, God has even established judgment in vain.” Since Scripture very frequently mentions God’s judgment, he nevertheless appears to allude specifically to Matthew chapter XXV, since there follow the words, “which God prepared for him and his angels.” The words “by which an end against evil” are, however, exceedingly obscure; they could not be remedied, because the third set of variant readings from the Vatican codex was still lacking here. PAM.—Compare Pamelius’ text with ours. EDD.] though he will surely punish injustice. [Note: [Col. 0207C] “Injustice,” Rigault, more correctly than Rhenanus, whose text has “in which there is injustice.”]

But if there will then be an end of evil [Note: [Col. 0208C] Thus Rigault and Wouwer’s codex; Pamelius, Semler, and Oberthür read “by which an end against evil.”], when its ruler, the devil, has gone away into the fire that God prepared for him and his angels (Matt. XXV), having first been banished into the pit of the abyss (Rev. XX); [Note: [Col. 0207D] “First into the pit of the abyss,” etc. He alludes to Revelation XX: “And he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and cast him”—or banished him, as our author says here—“into the abyss”; or else, according to the author, “into the pit of the abyss.” Unless one prefers to refer it to another passage in the same chapter: “And the devil who deceived them was cast into the lake of fire.” PAM.] when the revelation of the sons of God [Note: [Col. 0207D] “When the revelation of the sons of God,” etc. Here he has in view Romans VIII: “For the expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God; for creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly.” What the Latin translator calls *creatura*, “creation,” Tertullian in his customary manner calls *conditio*, “the created order,” just as he said in chapter 6 of *On the Soldier’s Crown*: “The whole created order unwillingly submitted to vanity.” PAM.] has redeemed the created order from evil—surely that which was subjected [Note: [Col. 0208D] “Has redeemed the created order from evil.” By *conditio* he means all created and fashioned things. Paul, Romans VIII.19: Ἡ γὰρ ἀποκαραδοκία τῆς κτίσεως τὴν ἀποκάλυψιν τῶν υἱῶν τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀπεκδέχεται. Τῇ γὰρ ματαιότητι ἡ κτίσις ὑπετάγη, οὐχ ἑκοῦσα, ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸν ὑποτάξαντα. Ἐπ’ ἐλπίδι ὅτι καὶ αὐτὴ ἡ κτίσις ἐλευθερωθήσεται ἀπὸ τῆς δουλείας τῆς φθορᾶς εἰς τὴν ἐλευθερίαν τῆς δόξης τῶν τέκνων τοῦ Θεοῦ. “For the eager expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God. For creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope that creation itself also will be freed from bondage to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.” Tertullian calls the created human being *conditio*, “created order”; Paul calls it κτίσις, *creation*. Primasius of Hadrumetum: “In the flesh itself Christ conquered sin, so that by his grace he might restore the nature that had been good through creation but was corrupted through transgression.” RIG.] to vanity [Note: [Col. 0208D] “Subjected to vanity,” ματαιότητι, “to futility.” Grotius splendidly explained this passage of Paul, and therefore of Tertullian, in his annotations on Paul’s Epistle. RIG.] (Rom. VIII); [Note: [Col. 0208C] “From evil, surely subjected to vanity,” Franek, from Romans VIII.] when, with the innocence and integrity of creation restored, livestock have made terms [Note: [Col. 0208D] “Livestock have made terms with wild beasts.” So that a common shade or common shelter may enclose sheep and wolves, and they may come together amicably, as though by mutual agreement, in the same place. RIG.] with wild beasts, [Note: [Col. 0208C] Latinus reads “have lived together.”] and [Note: [Col. 0208C] Semler reads “nor.”] little children have played with serpents (Isa. XI.6–7); [Note: [Col. 0208D] “And little children have played with serpents.” This pertains to Isaiah XI: “And a very young child shall put his hand into the den of asps,” etc. Yet here he seems to have read something fuller than what is now read in Greek, and to agree more closely with St. Jerome’s Hebrew and the Chaldean interpretation, which reads: “And the little child shall delight over the hole of asps.” PAM.] when the Father has placed the Son’s enemies under his feet (Ps. CIX)—surely [Note: [Col. 0208C] Semler and Oberthür read “and so.”] the agents of evil—then certainly, if an end belongs to evil, a beginning must also have belonged to it; and [Col. 0207C] matter will have a beginning, since evil has an end. [Note: [Col. 0208C] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “will be.”] [Col. 0208A] For things attributed to evil are reckoned according to the condition of evil.

## CHAPTER XII

Come now, let us believe matter to be evil and supremely evil, namely by nature, just as we believe God to be good and supremely good, likewise by nature. Furthermore, nature must be held certain and fixed: persevering in evil in the case of matter, just as in the case of God it is unconvertible and unchangeable in good. [Note: [Col. 0208C] Namely, because if nature in matter is changed, it will be capable of being changed from evil into good, and in God from good—not into evil. Semler, Oberthür.] Namely, because if nature in matter is changed from evil into good, it will also be capable of being changed in God from good into evil.

At this point someone will say: “Then children of Abraham will not be raised up from stones, the brood of vipers will not produce fruit of repentance (Luke III.7–8), and children of wrath will not become children of peace (Eph. II.3), if nature is [Col. 0208B] not mutable.” You will appeal to these examples rashly, O man, for things that have come into being—stones, vipers, and human beings—do not apply to the case of matter, which is unbegotten. Since their nature has an institution, it can also have a cessation.

But hold matter, once and for all, to have been determined as eternal, as unmade, as unbegotten; and therefore it must be believed to possess an unchangeable and incorruptible nature. This follows even from Hermogenes’ own proposition, which he advances [Note: [Col. 0208C] Junius reads “sets forth.”] when he denies that God could have made anything from himself, because what is eternal is not changed. For, in losing what it had been while through change it becomes what it was not, it would not be eternal; whereas the Lord, being eternal, can be nothing other than what he always is.

By this same definition I shall deservedly strike him back. I find equal fault with matter when from it—evil and supremely evil—even good and supremely good things are made by God: [Col. 0208C] “And God saw that they were good,” and “God blessed them” (Gen. I.[Col. 0209A] 3, 31)—surely because they were supremely good, certainly not because they were evil and supremely evil. Matter therefore admitted change, and if so, it lost the condition of eternity; indeed, it died to its own form. But eternity cannot be lost, because unless it cannot be lost, it is not eternity. Therefore matter could not have admitted change either, because, if it is eternal, it can in no way be changed.

## CHAPTER XIII

And the question will be asked: How were good things made from it, when they were in no way made through change? Whence was there in what is evil and supremely evil a seed of good and supreme goodness? Certainly a good tree does not produce evil fruits, because God too is nothing but good; nor does an evil tree produce good fruits, because matter too is nothing but supremely evil.

Or if we grant matter some seed of good as well, it will no longer be of a uniform nature, that is, entirely evil, [Col. 0209B] but rather twofold, that is, [Note: [Col. 0209D] In the Venetian edition the words “entirely evil, but rather twofold, that is” are absent, doubtless through a typographical error.] of a good and an evil nature. And it will again be asked whether light and darkness, sweetness and bitterness, can agree in good and evil. Or if the diversity of both good and evil could have come together, and matter could have possessed a twofold nature fruitful in both kinds of fruit, then good things themselves will no longer be credited to God, just as evil things will not be charged to matter; rather, each kind, derived from matter’s own property, will belong to matter. In that case we shall owe God neither gratitude for good things nor resentment for evil ones, because he produced nothing from his own ingenuity.

## CHAPTER XIV

By this it will be manifestly proved that he was enslaved to matter. For even if it is said that, although occasioned by matter, he nevertheless brought forth good things by his own choice, as though he had found the good [Col. 0209C] in matter—even though this too is shameful—yet certainly, when he also brings forth evil things from that same matter, by bringing forth at least these not according to his own choice, he serves matter, having nothing else he can do but bring forth evil from evil: unwillingly, surely, insofar as he is good; from necessity, insofar as he is unwilling; and from servitude, insofar as he acts from necessity.

Which, then, is more worthy: that he created evil things from necessity, or from his will? Certainly he created them from necessity if from matter; from his will, if from nothing. For now you labor without cause to prevent God from being established as the author of evils, because even if he made them from matter, they will be attributed to him who made them, precisely insofar as he made them.

Plainly, it makes as much difference whence he made them as if he had made them from nothing; and it makes no difference whence he made them, provided he made them from the source from which it better befitted him to make them. But it better befitted him to make them by his will than from necessity—[Col. 0209D] that is, from nothing rather than from matter. It is more worthy to believe God to be the free author even of evils [Col. 0210A] than their slave. Power of any kind befits him more than impotence.

Even if we grant on this basis that matter possessed no good at all, but that the Lord, if he produced anything good, produced it by his own power, other questions will equally arise. First, [Note: [Col. 0209D] “If good did not exist at all in matter.” Since a good tree does not produce evil fruit, and conversely, by what reasoning, heretic, will you prove that anything good was made from matter, which you make evil? LE PR.] if good did not exist at all in matter, good was not made from matter, since matter did not possess it. Next, if it was not from matter, then it was made from God. If it was not from God either, then it was made from nothing. For this alone remains under Hermogenes’ arrangement.

## CHAPTER XV

Furthermore, if good was made neither from matter, because it did not exist in matter as evil matter, nor from God, because nothing could be made from God, as Hermogenes maintains, good is now found to have been made from nothing, as having been [Col. 0210B] made from no source—neither from matter nor from God. And if good came from nothing, why not evil as well? Indeed, why not everything from nothing, if anything came from nothing? Unless divine power was insufficient to produce everything, though it did produce something from nothing.

Or if good proceeded from evil matter, because it came neither from nothing nor from God, it will follow that it proceeded from a transformation [Note: [Col. 0209D] The Venetian edition wrongly reads “confession.”] of matter, contrary to the denied [Note: [Col. 0209D] All read “contrary to the denied,” except Semler and Oberthür.] possibility of transforming what is eternal. Thus Hermogenes will now deny that good could have arisen from the very source from which it did arise. Yet it must necessarily have proceeded from one of those sources from which he denied that it could proceed.

Moreover, if evil did not come from nothing in order that it might not belong to God, from whose will it would appear to derive, but instead came from matter so that it might belong to that from whose substance it was made, then here too, as I have said, God will be held the author of evil. For with the same power and [Col. 0210C] will he ought either to have brought forth all things good [Note: [Col. 0209D] Rigault and the Venetian edition insert “good” from Wouwer’s codex.] from matter, or to have brought forth only good things—though not all good things—yet he also brought forth evil things: [Note: [Col. 0209D] Junius reads: “or he would have brought forth only good things (though not all good things); or also evil things”; but this is unnecessary.] surely either willing evil things to exist, if he was able to ensure that they did not exist, or unable to make all things good, if he willed this but did not accomplish it. It makes no difference whether the Lord became the author of evil through weakness or through will.

Or what reason was there that, after making good things as one who was good, he should also bring forth evil things as one who was not good, when he did not produce only things congruous with himself? [Note: [Col. 0210D] Latinus reads “as good, as not good.”] What necessity was there, after producing his own work, for him also to attend to matter’s business by bringing forth evil as well, so that he alone might be known as good from the good, [Note: [Col. 0210D] In the other editions the question mark is placed only after “evil.”] while matter might not [Note: [Col. 0210D] Junius reads “so that it might be known.”] be known as evil from the evil? Good would have flourished more fully without the breath of evil. For Hermogenes himself attacks the arguments of certain people [Col. 0210D] who say that evil things were necessary for illuminating good things, which are understood from their contraries.

[Col. 0211A] Therefore either there was no place for bringing forth evil even for that reason; or, if some other rationale requires evil to be introduced, why could it not also have been introduced from nothing? That very rationale would excuse the Lord from being regarded as the author of evil, just as it now excuses him when [Note: [Col. 0211C] *Cum* is inserted in the other editions; Semler says this is better, though he also [Col. 0211D] omits it.] he produces evil things from matter. [Note: [Col. 0211D] *Cum* is absent here from all editions.] If it excuses him, the question is thereby everywhere and from every direction driven to the point that they reject. For by failing to examine the rationale of evil itself and to discern how they may either attribute evil to God or separate it from God, they expose God to numerous and still more unworthy demolitions.

## CHAPTER XVI

Therefore, by way of laying the groundwork for this issue, which may perhaps be reconsidered elsewhere, I for my part define the alternatives thus: either both the good and the evil that God made from matter must be attributed to God, or both must be attributed to matter itself, from which he made them; or both must be attributed to both, [Col. 0211B] because the two parties—the one who made and that from which he made—are mutually bound; or one must be attributed to the one and the other to the other, for there is no third party besides matter and God.

Now, if both belong to God, God will appear to be the author of evil also; but God, being good, will not be the author of evil. If both belong to matter, [Note: [Col. 0211D] Semler and Oberthür read “matter.”] matter will appear to be the womb of good also; but matter that is wholly evil will not be the womb of good. If both belong to both, matter will in this respect too be compared with God, and the two will be partners, equally allied to evil and good; but matter must not be equated with God, lest it produce two gods. If one belongs to one and the other to the other—surely good to God [Note: [Col. 0211D] “Surely to God,” thus Wouwer, correctly; Semler, “surely God”; Rigault, “surely to God.”], and evil to matter—neither evil is attributed to God nor good to matter. Yet God makes both good and evil when he makes them from matter.

If these things are so, [Col. 0211C] I do not know how Hermogenes’ position [Note: [Col. 0211D] Semler reads “Hermogenes.”] can escape, since he thinks that God, [Note: [Col. 0211D] Rhenanus reads “who, God.”] who in whatever manner created evil from matter—whether by will, necessity, or reason—is not the author of evil.

Furthermore, if the author of evil is the one who made it, while matter is plainly his partner through supplying the substance, [Note: [Col. 0211D] “Matter is plainly his partner through the furnishing of substance.” He not infrequently uses this word *suggestus*, sometimes for ornament or the addition of decoration, as here and in *On the Dress of Women*, chapter II: “You should know that you must reject not only the equipment of fabricated and elaborated lust, but also,” etc. Sometimes it means a framework or texture, as in *On the Pallium*, chapter 1, where there is “sacred furnishing.” The glosses do not depart from this meaning, for *suggestus* is rendered by σῆμα, “sign,” and ὕφος, “texture”; and elsewhere ὕφος means woven fabric. Also in the *Apology*, chapter 16: “the array of images.” LE PR.] you now exclude [Note: [Col. 0212C] Rhenanus reads “you excuse.”] the very rationale for introducing matter. For God is nevertheless shown to be the author of evil even through matter, if matter was posited precisely to prevent God from appearing the author of evil.

Matter therefore being excluded, since the rationale for it is excluded, it remains established [Col. 0212A] that God made all things from nothing. We shall see whether this includes evil things too, when it becomes apparent which things are evil and whether the things that you currently suppose evil really are evil. [Note: [Col. 0212D] Rhenanus reads “and meanwhile even the things you suppose,” with punctuation before “meanwhile.”] For he produced these things too more worthily from his own will, by producing them from nothing, than under another’s prejudgment, had he produced them from matter. Freedom, not necessity, befits God. He would better have willed to create evil things from himself than have been unable not to create them. [Note: [Col. 0212D] Latinus inserts “because.”]

## CHAPTER XVII

The status of the one God vindicates this rule: he is not otherwise one unless he is alone; [Note: [Col. 0211D] “Not otherwise one.” Take this rule from Tertullian as one common to others: God is either one or none. For it is impious and damnable to conceive anything equal to God. He alone is Creator and preserver, he alone Lord and arbiter of all things; and, if it is permissible to apply that profane saying to the most solemn of all subjects, οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη, “the rule of many is not good.” LE PR.] not otherwise alone unless there is nothing with him. Thus he will also be first, because all things are after him; thus all things are after him, because all things are from him; thus they are from him, because they are from nothing. In this way the rationale of that Scripture too may stand: “Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who was his counselor? Or whom did he consult? Or who demonstrated to him the way of understanding and knowledge? Who has given to him, so that it will be repaid to him?” (Rom. XI.34–35). No one, surely, because no force, no matter, no nature belonging to another substance was present with him. [Note: [Col. 0212D] Semler reads “will be present.”]

Moreover, if he worked from something, he must necessarily have received from that very thing both counsel and the method of his arrangement, [Col. 0212B] as well as [Note: [Col. 0212D] Junius reads “and the way.”] the way of understanding and knowledge. For he had to work in accordance with the quality of the thing and according to the character of matter, not according to his own will—so much so that he would have made evil things according to a nature not his own, but that of the substance.

## CHAPTER XVIII

If matter was necessary to God for the works of the world, as Hermogenes supposed, God possessed matter far worthier and more suitable—not to be sought among philosophers, but to be understood among the prophets: [Note: [Col. 0212D] “His Wisdom, namely.” He means the Wisdom of God, which so surpasses human minds and thought that all the wisdom of the world is utter foolishness before God. Hence he teaches that this Wisdom must be sought not among the philosophers but among the Prophets. For one who does not know God cannot speak rightly about God, as is the case with the philosophers, whom Septimius calls creatures of vainglory; rather, the prophets and saints were inspired by the Spirit of the same supreme God. LE PR.] namely, his own Wisdom (*Sophia*). [Col. 0212C] For she alone knew the mind of the Lord. “Who knows the things of God and what is in him, except the Spirit who is in him?” (1 Cor. II.11). But Wisdom is Spirit. She was his counselor; she herself is the way of understanding and knowledge (Prov. VIII). From her he made, by making through her and making with her.

“When he prepared heaven,” she says, “I was present with him; and when he made strong the things above the winds—the clouds—and when he established the firm springs [Note: [Col. 0212D] Rhenanus, Semler, and Junius read “mountains.”] of that which is beneath heaven, I was joining things together with him. I was the one in whom he rejoiced, and daily I [Col. 0213A] delighted in his presence” (ibid.): when he delighted after he had perfected the world, and took delight in the sons of men.

Who would not commend her instead as the source and origin of all things, and as the matter of all matters—[Note: [Col. 0213C] “Of matters” is absent from Pithoeus’ book. Rigault. Junius reads “but matter of matters—not,” and says that this was appended from the Hirsau codex on Rhenanus’ authority.] not subordinate to him, not different in condition, not restless in motion, not formless in aspect, but innate to him and his own, orderly and beautiful—as the sort that God [Note: [Col. 0213C] “Of which God could have had need? Needing his own more than another’s,” Semler and Oberthür. The Hirsau codex has “of alien stock”; from this Rhenanus proposed: “his own rather than things of alien stock.”] could have needed, needing what was his own rather than what belonged to another?

Indeed, as soon as he perceived her as necessary for the works of the world, he immediately created and generated her within himself: “The Lord,” she says, “created me as the beginning of his ways for his works; before the ages he established me, before he made the earth, before the mountains were set in place; but before all the hills he generated me; before the abyss [Note: [Col. 0213C] Junius reads “likewise before the abyss.”] I was generated” (ibid.). [Note: [Col. 0213D] “I was generated. Let him recognize.” Rhenanus and Oberthür; Semler reluctantly and with disapproval.]

Let Hermogenes therefore recognize [Col. 0213B] that the Wisdom of God is proclaimed to have been born and created for this very reason: so that we should believe nothing unbegotten and uncreated besides God alone. For if even that which was within the Lord, from him and in him, was not without a beginning—namely, his own Wisdom, generated and created from the moment when she began to be stirred in the mind of God for arranging the works of the world—much more [Note: [Col. 0213D] “It is inadmissible that anything existed without a beginning.” You will learn everywhere and often from Tertullian’s preceding books his use of the impersonal verb *capit*, which among the Greeks is ἐνδέχεται, “it is possible.” Here “it is inadmissible that anything existed” means simply “It cannot be.” RHEN.] is it impossible that anything outside the Lord existed without a beginning.

But if this same Wisdom of God is the Word in respect of meaning—Wisdom—[Note: [Col. 0213D] Junius reads “the Word is meaning, Wisdom”; Pithoeus’ book, “meaning and Wisdom.”] and if “without him nothing was made that was made” (John I.3), just as nothing was arranged without Wisdom, how is it possible that anything besides the Father was older than the Son of God, the Word, the Only-begotten and Firstborn? And in this way it would certainly be more nobly born, to say nothing of the fact that the unbegotten would be stronger than the begotten [Note: [Col. 0214C] Franek inserts “begotten.”], and the unmade more powerful than the made. [Note: [Col. 0214C] Semler and Oberthür read “made thing.”] For that which [Col. 0213C] needed no author in order to exist will be far more exalted than that which had some author in order to exist.

Accordingly, if evil is unbegotten, while the Word of God was born—[Note: [Col. 0214C] Semler and Oberthür read: “unbegotten, that is, the Word of God.”] “For he uttered,” he says, “the best word” (Ps. XLIV.1)—I do not know whether evil can be made subordinate to good, the stronger to the weaker, the unbegotten to the begotten. Thus by this designation too Hermogenes places matter before God, by placing it before the Son. For the Son is the Word, and “the Word was God” (John I.1); and “I and the Father are one” (John X.10)—[Col. 0214A] unless, perhaps, the Son will calmly endure having placed before himself what is equated with the Father.

## CHAPTER XIX

But I shall also appeal to Moses’ original document, from which the opposing party too tries, willy-nilly, [Note: [Col. 0214C] Junius reads *ingratiis*, “unwillingly.”] to support its suspicions, lest it should appear not to be instructed from the source from which it ought. Accordingly, it seized opportunities [Note: [Col. 0214C] Junius reads “opportunities there.”] from certain words, as is generally the custom of heretics: to twist every simple expression.

[Note: [Col. 0213D] “For even the very beginning in which God made heaven and earth.” Whoever interprets Moses’ words, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” as follows seems readily able to resolve all these quibbles: “At the beginning at which heaven and earth came into existence, God created them.” For this is what Moses meant: by the names “heaven” and “earth” he signified the whole universe as created by God. Then he explains in what order and manner each of its principal parts was created. RIG.—Whatever Tertullian and his annotators may have said, many doctors of the Church are nevertheless found who understand Genesis I.1, “In the beginning,” as referring to the Word of God; thus Basil, Ambrose, and others. Others attribute another sense to these words, as may be seen in Cornelius à Lapide or in the *Complete Course of Sacred Scripture*. EDD.]

For they wish even the very “beginning” in which God made heaven and earth to have been something substantival and corporeal, which could be interpreted as matter. We, however, vindicate for each word its own proper meaning: [Note: [Col. 0214C] Semler reads “when we vindicate its proper meaning.”] that *principium*, “beginning,” means an initiation and was appropriately placed in reference to things beginning to be made. For nothing that [Col. 0214B] is to be made can exist without a beginning; indeed, the very moment in which it begins to be made is its beginning.

[Note: [Col. 0214D] “Thus *principium*, or beginning,” etc. It is likely that, in order to indicate this meaning of *principium*, the author therefore elsewhere customarily translates the cited Scripture as “At the commencement God made heaven and earth,” as above in *On Baptism*, chapters 3 and 5. PAM.] Thus *principium*, or beginning, is a word for inception, not the name of some substance.

Now, if God’s principal works are heaven and earth, which he made before all things, the things made first are properly the beginning of his works. [Note: [Col. 0214C] Latinus reads “of the universe.” In his printed *Corrections*, C. Macrus has *universorum*, “of all things.” Junius.] Scripture therefore rightly prefaces its account in this way: [Note: [Col. 0214D] Others read: “Scripture therefore rightly prefaces its account.” Junius: “The things made first are properly the beginning, since they were made first; and Scripture therefore rightly prefaces its account: ‘In the beginning.’”] “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. I.1), just as it would have said, “At the end God made heaven and earth,” if he had made them after everything else.

Or if “beginning” is some substance, then “end” too will be some kind of matter. It is certainly possible for something substantial to be the beginning of another thing that is to arise from it, as clay is the beginning of an earthen vessel and seed the beginning of a plant. But when we thus use the word “beginning” as a term of origin rather than of order, [Col. 0214C] we specifically add mention of the very thing which we wish to be the beginning of another thing.

Otherwise, if we say, for example, “In the beginning the potter made a basin or jar,” “beginning” will no longer signify the material; [Note: [Col. 0214D] All the editors and Junius read “will signify.”] for I have not called clay the beginning, but have indicated the order of the work, because before all else the potter first made the basin and jar and was thereafter going to make the rest. The word “beginning” will pertain to the ordering of the works, not to the origin of the substances.

[Col. 0215A] I can also interpret “beginning” in another way, though still not irrelevantly. [Note: [Col. 0215C] Semler and Oberthür read “They can also.”] For in Greek the word for “beginning,” which is ἀρχή (*archē*), signifies not only order but also sovereign authority. [Note: [Col. 0215D] “For in Greek the word for beginning, which is ἀρχή.” Xenophon, book I *On Government*, Aristotle, *Politics* I, and Plato, *Republic*, also agree with Tertullian concerning the meaning of ἀρχή as “sovereignty.” PAM.]

Hence they call rulers and magistrates ἄρχοντας (*archontas*). [Note: [Col. 0215D] “Hence they call rulers and magistrates ἄρχοντας.” It is noteworthy that, wherever the Greek has ἄρχοντες, the author customarily retains that word in his translation of Scripture, as above in *Against the Jews*, chapter 9, and below in book III *Against Marcion*. For, citing Isaiah chapter I, he says: “He also calls your rulers ἄρχοντας, the *archontes* of Sodom.” Likewise, in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 20, he translates another passage from Isaiah III thus: “He will come into judgment with the elders and the *archontes* of the people.” PAM.] [Note: [Col. 0215D] “They call rulers and magistrates *archontas*.” A man learned in antiquity could not omit this word when speaking of the government of the Athenians. Among them, when Codrus died, the succession of kings came to an end, and the commonwealth was entrusted first to perpetual praetors or magistrates [Col. 0216D] called *archons*, thirteen in number. Afterwards seven were appointed for ten-year terms, and finally annual archons were established. The first archon was Medon, as Pausanias relates in his *Achaica*. Since he was disabled in one foot, his brother Neleus maintained that he could not be appointed ruler at Athens. When the matter was referred to Apollo, he pronounced in favor of Medon. LE PR.]

Accordingly, even under this meaning, “beginning” will be understood as sovereignty and power. For in sovereignty and in power God made heaven and earth.

## CHAPTER XX
But even if the Greek word signifies nothing other than “beginning,” and “beginning” admits no other sense than “commencement,” we must also acknowledge as “commencement” her who says: “The Lord created me [Note: [Col. 0215C] “The beginning of his ways” is absent from Semler and Oberthür. “The manuscripts do not have it,” says Junius, “and it can be absent,” etc.] as the beginning of his ways for his works.” For if all things were made through God’s Wisdom [Sophia], then, in making heaven and earth “in the beginning,” that is, at the commencement, God made them in his Wisdom. Finally, if “beginning” signified matter, Scripture would not have worded [Note: [Col. 0215C] “Arranged,” Semler, Oberthür.] it thus: “In the beginning God made,” but “from the beginning.” For he would not have made them *in* matter, but *from* matter. Of Wisdom, however, it could be said, “in the beginning.” For he first made them in Wisdom, in whom, by thinking and ordering them, he had already made them; because even if he had been going to make them from matter, he had already made them beforehand in Wisdom by thinking and ordering them. For Wisdom was also the beginning of his ways, [Note: [Col. 0215C] “By ordering he had already made them; and thus she was the beginning of the ways, because thought and ordering are Wisdom’s first operation, establishing through thought a way for the works. Hence this authority,” [Col. 0215D] etc. [Col. 0216C] Junius reads thus and defends his reading at considerable length.] because thought and ordering become Wisdom’s first operation, establishing through thought a way for the works. Hence I also claim for myself the authority of Scripture, because, although it shows both God who made and the things he made, it does not likewise attest from what he made them.

For since in every operation there are three principal things—the one who makes, what is made, and that from which it is made—three designations must be given in a proper account of the work: the person of the maker, the kind of thing made, and the form of the matter. If the matter is not stated where both the works and their maker are stated, it is evident that he worked from nothing. For that from which he worked would likewise have been stated, had he worked from anything.

Finally, if I bring in the Gospel as a supplement to the Old Testament instrument [Col. 0216A] [Note: [Col. 0216C] “I shall bring in,” Semler, Oberthür.], in which it should all the more have been shown that God made the universe from some matter, because there it is also revealed through whom he made all things: [Note: [Col. 0216D] “In the beginning was the Word,” etc. It was customary not only for this author but also for the blessed Cyprian to call the Son “the Speech of God” rather than “the Word of God.” Hence the statement in Book II of the *Testimonies against the Jews*, chap. 3: “That Christ is himself the Speech of God,” where he proves this from various Scriptures. PAM.] “In the beginning was the Word”—in which beginning, of course, God made heaven and earth—“and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1). Since, therefore, here too there are manifested the maker, that is, God; the things made, that is, all things; and the one through whom, that is, the Word—would not the proper order also have required an avowal of that from which all things were made by God through the Word, if they had been made from anything? Thus Scripture could not avow what did not exist; and by not avowing it, Scripture sufficiently proved that it did not exist, because it would have avowed it if it had existed.

## CHAPTER XXI

“Therefore,” you say, “if you prejudge that [Col. 0216B] all things were made from nothing because it is not expressly related that anything was made from preexistent matter, take care [Note: [Col. 0216D] “Lest the opposing party.” Above: “Hence the opposing party strives to support its suspicions by faith.” RIG.] lest the opposing party contend that all things were made from matter precisely because it is likewise not openly stated that anything was made from nothing.”

Some arguments can certainly be turned back easily; but they are not therefore to be admitted as equally valid where the grounds of the case differ. For I say that, even if Scripture did not expressly declare that all things were made from nothing, just as it did not declare that they were made from matter, there was not so great a necessity for expressly indicating that all things were made from nothing as there would have been if they had been made from matter. For what is made from nothing is shown, by the very fact that it is not shown to have been made from anything, to have been made from nothing; [Note: [Col. 0216D] “And there is no danger that it may be thought to have been made from something,” etc. He uses this construction with the verb *periclitor* elsewhere also, in imitation of the Greeks, who use the verb κινδυνεύω in this way. [Col. 0217C] “There is no danger,” that is, “it is absent; there is no risk.” RHEN.] and there is no danger of its being thought to have been made from something when that from which it was made is not demonstrated.

But unless something made from something is expressly declared to have been made from that thing, then, because that from which it was made is not shown [Note: [Col. 0216C] *Non* is absent from Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür.], it will first risk appearing to have been made from nothing, because that from which it was made is not stated. Next, even if its condition is such that it cannot appear not to have been made from something, [Note: [Col. 0216C] “To appear to have been made from something,” Semler, Oberthür. Junius reads: “so that it can now appear to have been made from something.”] it will likewise risk appearing to have been made from something entirely different from that from which it actually was made, because the source from which it was made is not set forth.

Thus, even if Scripture had not added that God made all things from nothing (2 Macc. 7:28), supposing that God could not have made them from nothing, it ought in every way to have declared that he made them from matter, if he had indeed [Note: [Col. 0217C] *Etsi* is absent from Semler and Oberthür.] made them from [Note: [Col. 0217C] “Even if from,” Semler, Oberthür.] matter; for the former could be understood absolutely even if it were not expressly indicated, whereas the latter would remain doubtful unless it were indicated.

## CHAPTER XXII

Indeed, the Holy Spirit established this principle for his Scripture: whenever something comes from something else, Scripture also relates whence it comes. [Note: [Col. 0217C] “Let the earth put forth herbage,” he says, etc. We again read this both here and below, chap. 29, following the correction of Latinius, in place of *fructificet*, which Rhenanus had substituted; and all the more because the Greek word βλαστησάτω signifies “let it germinate” or “put forth shoots,” not “let it bear fruit,” as do also the Hebrew and Chaldean words. Moreover, the author more correctly translates the Greek κάρπιμον as “fruitful tree” than does the Latin translator of the Septuagint, who renders it “fruit-bearing.” PAM.] “Let the earth put forth [Note: [Col. 0217C] “Let it bear fruit,” Semler, Oberthür.],” he says, “the herbage of grass, sowing seed according to kind and according to likeness, and the fruitful tree producing fruit, whose seed is within it according to likeness. And it was so. And the earth brought forth the herbage of grass, sowing seed according to kind, and the fruitful tree producing fruit, whose seed is within it according to likeness.”

And again: “And God said: [Col. 0217B] [Note: [Col. 0217D] “Let the waters produce creeping things.” He undoubtedly thought that ἑρπετά was better rendered by “creeping things” than by “reptiles,” as in the Vulgate text, although I would think “reptiles” better. LE PR.] Let the waters produce creeping things having living souls, and flying creatures flying above the earth across the firmament of heaven. And it was so. And God made the great sea-monsters and every living soul among the creeping animals which the waters produced according to their kind.”

Likewise afterward: “And God said: Let the earth produce a living soul according to kind: quadrupeds, creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their kind” (Gen. 1:11ff.).

If, therefore, when God brought forth some things from things already made, he showed through the prophet, and stated, what he brought forth and whence—although we could suppose from what [Note: [Col. 0217C] Repetition of *unde* in Rigault and Wouwerius; Latinius.] they were brought forth [Note: [Col. 0217C] “Suppose,” Rigault, from the Dijon manuscript.], provided they were not from nothing, since certain things had already been made from which they might seem to have been brought forth—if the Holy Spirit expended such care upon our instruction that we should know what proceeded from what, would he not likewise have put us in possession of knowledge [Col. 0217C] concerning both [Note: [Col. 0217D] “Concerning heaven and earth,” etc. That is: the Holy Spirit, who was teaching us the mysteries of heaven, would have informed us concerning the heaven from which created things had come. The same Spirit would also have taught us concerning the earth from which they were created; and thus would have put us in possession of knowledge concerning heaven and earth. LE PR.] heaven and earth by indicating whence he fashioned them, if their origin had been established as deriving from some matter? All the more must he be seen to have fashioned them from nothing, since nothing had yet [Col. 0218A] been made from which he could be thought to have fashioned them.

Accordingly, just as Scripture shows whence those things that were brought forth from something were brought forth, so, by not showing whence other things were brought forth, it confirms that they were brought forth from nothing. “Therefore, in the beginning God made heaven and earth.” [Note: [Col. 0217D] “I adore the fullness of Scripture.” I think no one will deny that this author ascribed a certain veneration to the sacred text; nevertheless, in explaining Scripture he lays down certain principles of his own against which one must be on guard. LE PR.] I adore the fullness of Scripture, by which [Note: [Col. 0218C] “Which,” all the others, according to Junius.] it manifests to me both the maker and the things made. In the Gospel, moreover, I find in addition the Word as the minister and [Note: [Col. 0218C] “I find the Word to be the judge of the ruler.” It should be written, as in the Dijon manuscript: “I find the Word to be the judge of the maker.” RIG.] arbiter of the ruler. But that all things were made from some underlying matter, I have nowhere yet read. Let Hermogenes’ workshop show where it is written. If it is not written, let it fear [Note: [Col. 0218D] “That woe destined for those who add,” etc. It would be the height of audacity to add to or subtract from Holy Scripture. Yet its interpretation must be derived, not from the brains of insignificant men, but only from the decrees of the Church and the studies of the holy Fathers. I add this in order to meet the insolence of heretics, who might believe that they could extract something from this passage to support their follies. LE PR.] that woe which is appointed for those who add or subtract (Rev. 22:18–19).

## CHAPTER XXIII

But he argues from what follows, because it is written: “The earth, however, was invisible and unformed.” [Col. 0218B] [Note: [Col. 0218D] “For he also reduces the name ‘earth.’” Here he approaches more closely to Hermogenes’ error, whose origin he shows to have lain in his belief that matter was designated by the name “earth.” LE PR.] For he also reduces [Note: [Col. 0218C] Rhenanus conjectures “And in the earth’s.”] the name “earth” to matter [Note: [Col. 0218C] *In* is absent from the Frankfurt and Paris editions.], because earth is what was made from it. And he directs the word “was” toward the claim that matter had always existed in the past, unbegotten and unmade. [Note: [Col. 0218D] “Invisible and crude.” Shortly before he had said “unformed” for the Greek ἀκατασκεύαστος; here it is called “crude,” as in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I: “A crude and undigested mass.” LE PR.] He calls it “invisible and crude” because he maintains that matter was formless, confused, and unordered.

I shall indeed refute these opinions of his one by one; meanwhile, however, I wish to answer him as follows. Let us suppose [Note: [Col. 0218C] Junius conjectures, “Let us suppose.”] that matter is demonstrated by these clauses. Yet does Scripture, because it existed before all things, indicate that anything of this kind was made from it? On the contrary, it indicates no such thing. Let matter have existed, to the extent that it—or rather Hermogenes—is permitted this concession; it could both have existed and yet God have made nothing from it, either because it was unfitting for God to have needed anything, or certainly because he is not shown to have made anything from matter.

“Then it would have been purposeless,” you say. Not [Col. 0218C] altogether without purpose. For even if the world was not made from it, a heresy was made from it; and the heresy is all the more shameless because the heresy was not made from matter, but rather the heresy itself made matter.

## CHAPTER XXIV

[Col. 0219A]

I now return to the individual clauses through which he thought matter was signified. First I shall demand an account of the names. For we read one of these, namely “earth”; we do not find the other, namely “matter.” I ask, therefore: since the designation “matter” does not occur in Scripture, how is the appellation “earth” also applied to it, when that appellation is already known in another genus of substance?

All the more should the designation “matter” also have appeared, accompanied by the appellation “earth,” so that I might know that “earth” was a name shared with matter, and so that I would not claim it exclusively for that substance to which it is proper and in connection with which it is better known [Note: [Col. 0219C] “It is known,” Oberthür and Semler, following Rhenanus, who indeed suspected that the reading should be “it is known.”]; or so that, if I wished, I might not be able to share it with any other kind whatsoever, and certainly not with every kind of matter. For when the proper term for the thing to which a common term is assigned does not exist, inasmuch as the thing to which it is assigned does not appear, it will be possible to assign that term to anything else whatsoever. Thus, even if Hermogenes could show that matter was named, he would still have to prove that it was also surnamed “earth,” so that he might thereby claim both terms for it.

## CHAPTER XXV

He therefore maintains that two earths are presented in this passage of Scripture: one which God made in the beginning; the other being matter, from which he made it and of which it was said: “The earth, however, was invisible and crude.”

If I were to ask which of the two should lend the name “earth” to the other, [Note: [Col. 0219C] *Debeat* is omitted by Semler and Oberthür, who add *id*. Junius reads: “which of the two should have the name ‘earth’ applied to which.”] it would of course be said that the earth made from the other derived its designation from that from which it was made, because it is more probable that offspring should be named from its origin than that the origin should be named from its offspring. [Col. 0219C]

If this is so, another question is cast over us: whether it is fitting that this earth which God made should have derived its surname from that out of which he made it. For I hear from Hermogenes and the other matter-affirming heretics that the former earth was formless, invisible, and crude, [Col. 0220A] whereas this earth of ours received form, visibility, and cultivation from God. It was therefore made something different from that from which it was made. Moreover, once made different, it could not share the designation [Note: [Col. 0219C] “With it by name,” Semler, Oberthür.] of that from whose condition it had departed. If “earth” was the proper name of that matter, then this, which is not matter but was plainly made something else, cannot take the alien name “earth,” foreign to its own condition.

“But when matter was made—that is, earth—it shared the name of its origin just as it shared its genus.” [Note: [Col. 0220C] “From earth,” Semler, Oberthür.] Not at all. [Note: [Col. 0220C] “I do not hear,” Pamelius, Paris, Franeker; “not by God,” Rigault, Semler, Oberthür.] For although a potsherd has been formed from clay, [Note: [Col. 0219D] “I shall no longer call it clay, but a potsherd. For fire has stripped away the name of clay.” RIG.] I shall no longer call it clay, but a potsherd; and although electrum has been compounded from gold and silver, [Note: [Col. 0219D] “And electrum, though compounded from gold and silver”: fused through the mingling of both metals. Pliny, Book IX, 40: “Nor is there any end to our corruptions: we delight in extravagance and in doubling luxury by mingling things, and then in adulterating even nature’s own adulterations—as by blending silver with gold to make electrum and adding bronze to these to make Corinthian metal.” He also says that wherever the proportion of silver is one fifth, it is called electrum. RIG.] I shall nevertheless call it neither silver nor gold, [Note: [Col. 0219D] “Yet I shall call it neither silver nor gold, but electrum. For a kind of new body comes into being,” as Gaius says, Book VII, *On Acquiring Ownership of Things*. “A third thing comes into being, blended from both.” So too in the book *Against Praxeas*. RIG.] but electrum. [Note: [Col. 0219D] “But electrum.” Pliny, *Natural History*, Book XXXIII, 4: “All gold contains silver. Wherever the proportion of silver is one fifth, it is called electrum. Electrum is also made deliberately by adding silver; but if this exceeds a fifth part, it does not withstand the anvils.” PAM.]

Whatever departs from the condition of a thing likewise withdraws from its designation, [Note: [Col. 0220C] *Quid*, Paris, Franeker, Rigault; but Junius has *qui*, Semler *quod*.] in accordance with the proper character of its appellation as well as of its condition. How far this earth has passed from the condition of that earth—that is, of matter—is evident at least from the fact that in Genesis this earth receives the testimony of goodness: “And God saw that it was good,” whereas Hermogenes assigns the other to be the origin and cause of evils.

Finally, if this earth is called earth because the other is, why is this not also called matter, because the other is? Indeed, heaven too, and all things, if they consist of matter, should have been called both earth and matter.

Enough concerning the name “earth”—under which he wished matter [Note: [Col. 0220C] “Matter,” Semler.] to be understood—a name which everyone knows belongs to one element, first through nature and then through the teaching of Scripture, [Note: [Col. 0220D] “Unless one must believe that Silenus in the presence of Midas,” etc. Similar is the statement above, chap. 2 of *On the Pallium*: “Let someone else see whether there is another world anywhere—among the Meropes, as Silenus babbles into Midas’ ears, ears well suited to rather tall tales”; and that which Maximus of Tyre has in Discourse 30—if indeed Giraldi cites it correctly in *On the Gods of the Nations*—that Silenus, drunk and bound with snares and chains, foretold various and diverse things to Midas. From this it is also easy to infer that the poet Virgil took from it the subject of his *Eclogue of Silenus*, and that the expression “more ridiculous than Alcibiadean Sileni” also passed into a proverb; Rhenanus somewhere uses that name for the Valentinians’ fantasies because of their rather tall tales. PAM.] unless [Note: [Col. 0220C] Rhenanus and Semler add *si*: “unless if.”] one is to believe that Silenus who, before King Midas, asserted the existence of another world, [Note: [Col. 0220D] “On the authority of Theopompus.” There was more than one Theopompus: one was a historian, another a comic poet who gave one of his plays the title *Silenus*. Whether the poet and historian were the same person I regard as uncertain. The whole story of Midas, however, is derived from Theopompus. Yet Silenus was in fact captured by Midas in the pleasant gardens which he possessed in Macedonia. LE PR.] on the authority of Theopompus. But the same author also reports many gods.

## CHAPTER XXVI

[Col. 0220C]

For us, however, there is one God and one earth, which God made in the beginning. Scripture, beginning to trace the sequence concerning it, first declares that it was made and then explains its quality; just as it first professes that heaven [Col. 0221A] was made—“In the beginning God made heaven”—and then adds its arrangement: [Note: [Col. 0221D] “And he separated between the water that was beneath the firmament.” Here the author plainly takes *infra* to mean “underneath” or “under”; for it can be understood in no other way. The Greek is ὃ ἦν ὑποκάτω τοῦ στερεώματος, “that which was beneath the firmament,” especially since the same expression is translated in Hebrews 2 as “beneath his feet,” just as other translators render it here, “beneath the firmament.” PAM.] “And he separated between the water that was beneath the firmament” (Gen. 1:7) “and that which was above the firmament, and God called the firmament heaven”—the very heaven that he had made at the beginning.

Likewise concerning man: “And God made man; in the image of God he made him” (Gen. 1:27). Then Scripture relates how he made him: “And God fashioned man from the mud of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul” (Gen. 2:7).

And surely this is the proper way to begin a narrative: first to preface, then to pursue; to name, and then to describe. Otherwise it would be absurd if Scripture suddenly disclosed the form and condition of a thing of which it had made no prior mention—not even its name—namely matter: [Note: [Col. 0221C] “It discloses the condition before it relates what it was, before it shows whether it existed; it delineates the shape of the deformed thing, but conceals its name.” Junius thinks it should be read thus.] it first relates what it was like before showing whether it existed; it displays the shape of the deformed thing but conceals its name.

How much more credible is our account: that Scripture appended the arrangement of the very thing whose creation and designation it had already set forth. How complete, indeed, is the sense: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth. The earth, however, was invisible and crude” (Gen. 1:1–2)—the earth, namely, which God made, and which Scripture had just expressly mentioned. [Note: [Col. 0221C] “Had declared,” Semler, Oberthür.]

For the very word “however” (*autem*), like the clasp of a connective particle, has been attached [Note: [Col. 0221C] “Placed beside,” Semler, Oberthür.] to bind together the narrative: “the earth, however.” By this word Scripture returns to the earth of which it had spoken above and binds the sense together. [Note: [Col. 0221D] “Thus remove ‘however’ from here,” etc. A fine interpretation of what the particle “however,” when added in Holy Scripture, signifies. Rhenanus notes a similar passage from *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, below, chap. 40: “Thus the word ‘man’ is in a certain way the clasp joining together the two substances.” PAM.] Indeed, remove “however” from this place, and the structure is dissolved, so that it might then appear to speak of another earth: “The earth was invisible and crude.”

## CHAPTER XXVII

[Col. 0221C]

[Note: [Col. 0221D] “But you, with a nod of the head and an appropriate movement of the finger, raise your eyebrows” [Col. 0222D]. In Rhenanus’ editions and in the Dijon manuscript the reading is: “But you, with a haughty look, a nod of the head, and an appropriate movement of the finger,” etc. RIG.] But you, raising your eyebrows [Note: [Col. 0221D] “With a haughty look and a nod of the head, your fingers appropriately posed,” Junius; “with a haughty look,” Semler, Oberthür.] with a nod of the head and an appropriate movement [Note: [Col. 0221D] “And a movement,” Semler, Oberthür, Pamelius.] of the finger, lifting them higher and as though casting them backward, say: “It *was*”—[Note: [Col. 0221D] “He says,” Junius.] as though it had always existed, unbegotten and unmade, and for that reason must be regarded as matter.

But I, without any theatrical embellishment of my delivery, shall simply answer that “was” can be said of everything, including something that was made, something that came into being, something that at one time did not exist, and something that is not matter. For everything that has existence, from whatever source it has [Note: [Col. 0221D] “Has,” Semler; “may have,” Franeker.] it—whether through a beginning or without a beginning [Note: [Col. 0222C] “Without” is absent from Semler.]—by the very fact that it *is* will also be said to have *been*. Whatever admits the primary form of the verb for a definition will also admit the inflection of the same verb in a narrative. “Is” stands at the head of definition; “was” serves narrative. [Note: [Col. 0222C] “Of narrative,” Junius.]

These are the quibbles and subtleties of heretics, twisting the simplicity of ordinary words into a question [Note: [Col. 0222C] “Into a great question,” Semler.]. A great question indeed—whether the earth which was made also “was”! What must truly be examined is whether being invisible and crude applies to the earth that was made or to that from which it was made, so that “was” belongs to the same subject as the predicate stating what it was. [Note: [Col. 0222C] Thus all editions. The Halle editor suspects that it should read: “to that from which it was.”]

## CHAPTER XXVIII

On the contrary, we shall prove not only that this condition belonged to this earth, but also that it could not have belonged to that other one. For if naked matter [Note: [Col. 0222D] “If matter was naked, subject to God,” Semler, Oberthür. “If naked in this way,” Junius.] lay exposed to God, with no element obstructing it—since as yet nothing [Col. 0222B] existed apart from matter itself and God—it certainly could not have been invisible.

For even if Hermogenes wishes darkness to have existed in the substance of matter—to which clause we shall have to respond in its proper order—even to a human being darkness is visible. The very fact that darkness exists is seen, much more so by God. And surely, if matter were invisible, its quality could in no way be known. How, then, did Hermogenes ascertain that it was formless, confused, and unordered, [Note: [Col. 0222D] “Restless,” Semler, Oberthür. Junius suspects “uncultivated.”] when, being invisible, it lay hidden? [Note: [Col. 0222D] “Or if this was revealed by God.” A passage to be noted against the heretics whom some call “spiritual” or “ecstatic,” who teach that Scripture may be disregarded and reliance placed solely upon revelations. Here the author teaches that they must not be believed unless they prove that this was revealed by God. PAM.] Or, if this was revealed by God, he must prove it.

I also demand to know whether it could have been called “crude.” For surely what is crude is imperfect. Surely nothing can be imperfect unless it has been made. For what has been made insufficiently is imperfect.

“Certainly,” you say.

Therefore matter, which had not been made, could not have been imperfect at all. What was not imperfect was also not crude. Having no beginning, because it had not been made, it also lacked a first rudiment [OCR corrected contextually from *carnit*: “lacked”]. For rudimentary condition is an accident of beginning. But the earth that was made deserved also to be called crude. For immediately upon being made it occupied the place of something imperfect, prior to its perfection.

## CHAPTER XXIX

For God completed all his works in order: first, with the elements uncultivated [Note: [Col. 0222D] “The world uncultivated,” namely; Junius, less well.], he in a manner laid the world open; [Note: [Col. 0222D] “In a manner laying the world open.” *Depalans*, that is, manifesting, showing openly. In Book V *Against Marcion*, he calls the Apostle the *depalator* of divine teaching, that is, its expositor and promulgator. [Col. 0223D] For in Tertullian *depalare* means “to reveal openly.” RHEN.] afterward, once they had been adorned, he as it were dedicated it. [Note: [Col. 0223D] “Afterward, adorning them, as though dedicating it.” Thus in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*: “They prefer that the universe was dedicated by him from underlying matter,” he says; and in *On the Flesh of Christ*. Again in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh* and Book I *Against Marcion*. PAM.]

For he did not immediately fill the light with the sun’s radiance; nor immediately temper the darkness with the solace of the moon; nor immediately mark the heaven with constellations and stars; nor immediately populate the seas [Note: [Col. 0223C] Rhenanus wrongly printed “matter.”] with monsters; nor immediately endow the earth itself with its varied fecundity. Rather, he first bestowed existence upon it; then he filled out its existence so that it was not empty. For Isaiah too says: “He did not make it to be empty, [Note: [Col. 0223D] “But to be inhabited.” He translates literally the words of Isaiah 45, ἀλλὰ κατοικεῖσθαι, “but to be inhabited,” in place of “that it might be inhabited.” PAM.] but to be inhabited” (Isa. 45:18).

Therefore, after it had been made but was still to be perfected, it was meanwhile invisible and crude. It was crude, indeed, by the very fact that it was invisible, being neither perfected for sight nor yet furnished in other respects. It was invisible because it was still covered by waters as by the protection [Note: [Col. 0223C] “Memorial,” Rhenanus.] of generative moisture; in this same form our flesh, which is akin to it, is also brought forth. For David too sings thus: “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness; the inhabited world [Note: [Col. 0223D] “The inhabited world and all who dwell in it.” That the ancient edition of the Psalms published by Faber in the *Fivefold Psalter* is authentic is evident even from this. Whether one reads with Tertullian “the inhabited world of the earth,” or with others “the inhabited world of the lands,” makes no difference, since the single Greek word οἰκουμένη, “inhabited world,” applies indifferently to both. PAM.], and all who dwell in it. He founded it upon the seas and prepared it upon the rivers” (Ps. 23:1–2).

For when the waters had been separated into the hollow [Note: [Col. 0223C] “Into the more hollow recess,” Rhenanus.] of their basins, the dry land that had previously been covered by waters emerged more clearly. [Note: [Col. 0224D] “The dry land emerged more clearly.” Thus in *On the Soul*: “so that they might shine forth as acceptable to each.” Ovid:

> It rose aloft and chose for itself a place upon the summit of the citadel.

RIG.]

From that point it accordingly also became visible, when God said: “Let the water be gathered together into one gathering, [Note: [Col. 0223C] “In one gathering,” Rhenanus.] and let the dry land be seen.” He says, “Let it be seen,” not “Let it be made.” For it had already been made, [Note: [Col. 0224D] “But until then, being invisible, it waited to be seen.” That is, it expected. RIG.] but until then, being invisible, it waited to be seen. The dry land, however—what it was to become through the separation of moisture—was nevertheless earth. “And God called the dry land earth,” not matter.

So too, after it attained perfection, it ceased to be regarded as crude, when God declared: [Note: [Col. 0223C] “Let it bear fruit,” Paris.] “Let the earth put forth the herbage of grass [Col. 0223C], sowing seed according to kind and according to likeness, and the fruitful tree producing fruit, whose seed is within it according to likeness.” Likewise: “Let the earth produce a living soul according to kind: quadrupeds, creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to kind.”

Divine Scripture therefore completed its sequence. To the earth which it had previously declared invisible and crude, [Col. 0224A] it restored both visibility and perfection. But no other matter was invisible and crude. Therefore [Note: [Col. 0223C] An old manuscript of Wouwerius inserts “not.”] matter will afterward be visible and perfect. I therefore wish to see matter, for it has become visible. I wish also to recognize it in its perfected state, so that from it I may pluck the herbage of grass, and from it gather the fruitful tree, [Note: [Col. 0223C] Rhenanus and Semler read: “the fruit tree, and from it.” Rhenanus conjectured [Col. 0224C] “the fruit of the tree”; but Franeker and Paris read, “the fruitful tree producing fruit”; Rigault, however, “the fruitful tree, and from another.”] and so that animals from it may serve my use.

But matter is nowhere; the earth, however, is here [Note: [Col. 0224C] “This,” Franeker, Paris, Pamelius.]—that is, before me. I see it and enjoy it, now that it has ceased to be invisible and crude. Isaiah speaks most clearly of it: “Thus says the Lord who made heaven” (Isa. 45:18): “This is the God who displayed the earth and made it.” Surely he displayed the same earth that he made. How did he display it? Clearly by saying, “Let the dry land be seen.” Why does he command it to be seen unless because previously it was not seen? Thus too, by making it visible and thereby serviceable [Note: [Col. 0224C] “And habitable,” Latinius.], he did not make it to no purpose.

Thus it is proved to us in every respect that the earth which we inhabit is the very same earth that was both made and displayed by God; that no other earth was crude and invisible than the one which was both made and displayed; and therefore that the words “the earth, however, was invisible and crude” refer to the earth which God separated along with heaven.

## CHAPTER XXX

In the same way, what follows will also appear to support Hermogenes’ conjecture: “And darkness was over the abyss, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1:2), as though these confused substances too pointed to evidence of that massive bulk. On the contrary, by defining separately the darkness, the abyss, the Spirit of God, and the waters, Scripture allows nothing confused, nor anything uncertain within a confusion, to be inferred from so distinct [Note: [Col. 0224C] “Different,” Junius, from the Vatican manuscript.] an account [Col. 0224C] of definite and distinguished elements.

More than this: when it assigns their respective positions—darkness over the abyss, the Spirit over the waters—it denied any confusion of substances; for by demonstrating their arrangement, it also demonstrated their distinction.

It is supremely absurd [Note: [Col. 0224C] *Vanitimum*, Rhenanus, Junius, Semler; Junius suspects that some Greek term lies behind it.] that matter, which is introduced as formless, [Col. 0225A] should be asserted to be formless despite the names of so many forms, without stating what that body of confusion actually is—a body which must certainly be believed to be single if it is formless, since that which is formless is uniform. A formless thing, however, which is confused through variety, must necessarily have one appearance; yet it has no appearance, while from many it has one appearance [the transmitted wording is uncertain]. [Note: [Col. 0224D] “It is supremely absurd,” etc. The Vatican manuscript and the edition read *vanitimum*; but because I have found that word nowhere, I prefer the common reading. The things which he shortly calls “kinds” he calls “forms” a little later; therefore the Vatican manuscript’s variant “form” is not attractive. The text should be read interrogatively with Latinius: “If it did not possess them, how is it recognized?” PAM.—The Halle editor suspects that some Greek lies behind Rhenanus’ reading, which he and Junius defend. The index of Tertullianic Latin observes that this is an ancient word derived from *vanus*, “empty,” and signifies that which must chiefly be referred to the emptiness of idols. EDD.]

Besides, either matter possessed within itself these kinds by whose names it was to be understood—I mean darkness, the abyss, the Spirit, and the waters—or it did not possess them. [Note: [Col. 0225C] “Were to be understood, I mean the darkness,” Rhenanus, Semler; Rigault more correctly from Wouwerius’ manuscript.] If it possessed them, how is it introduced as not possessing forms? If it did not possess them, how is it recognized? [Note: [Col. 0225C] “Possesses,” Junius.] [Note: [Col. 0225C] “If, however,” Junius.] [Note: [Col. 0225C] “Is recognized,” Rhenanus, Semler, Pamelius.]

## CHAPTER XXXI
But this point too will certainly be seized upon: that Scripture signifies only of heaven and this earth that God made it in the beginning, but says nothing of the kind concerning the aforementioned forms; and therefore those which are not said to have been made belong to uncreated matter. We shall answer this difficulty as well. Divine Scripture would have spoken sufficiently if it had declared that the principal wholes of things—the heaven and the earth—were made by God, since they necessarily had their own proper contents, which could be understood as included within those principal wholes. Now the contents of heaven and earth at that first time were darkness, the abyss, spirit, and waters. For beneath the earth were the abyss and darkness. If the abyss was below the earth and darkness over the abyss, then undoubtedly both darkness and the abyss were below the earth. Beneath the heaven, however, lay the spirit and the waters; for if the waters which covered the earth were above the earth, and the spirit was above the waters, then both spirit and waters were likewise above the earth. But what is above the earth is necessarily below the heaven. And just as the earth rested upon the abyss and darkness, so the heaven rested upon the spirit and waters, and they were embraced within them.

[Note: [Col. 0225C] Thus Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür. Rigault and the Venetian edition read *Scripturarum*.]

[Note: [Col. 0225C] Rhenanus conjectured that the reading should be *disserit* (“speaks”), and shortly afterward *commendans et coelum*. Others, following Junius, read *si summas*, which is better.]

[Note: [Col. 0225D] Others, according to Junius, give *contempta dantur* from the Vatican codex.]

Thus it is nothing novel that only the containing whole should be named as the sum, while what is contained within it is understood as a part. Suppose, for example, that I say: “The city constructed a theater and a circus; the stage, however, was of such and such a kind, and statues stood above the *euripus*, and an obelisk towered above everything.” Because I did not also expressly declare that these particular forms were made by the city, will they therefore not have been made by it together with the circus and theater?
