Or did I refrain from adding that these particular forms too were made because they were contained within the things which I had previously said were made, and it could be understood both that they were contained and within what they were contained?

[Note: [Col. 0225D] “And statues above the *euripus*.” The Euripus, the strait at Chalcis, gave its name, by resemblance, to the trenches by which the games were surrounded in place of barriers. It afterward came about that *euripus* began to be used for any trench or channel. Pliny the Younger, in his letter to Caninius Rufus: “What of the green and jeweled *euripus*?” Vitruvius, Book VII: “For harbors, promontories, shores, rivers, springs, channels, shrines, groves, mountains, cattle, and shepherds are painted.” RHENANUS.]

[Note: [Col. 0225D] “Above the *euripus*.” In the Circensian games, the *euripus* was a pool or strait. For Hesychius states in these words that it is a receptacle for waters: he calls the *euripus* (Εὐρίπους) a “receiving-place for waters” (δόξας ὑδάτων) [the Greek reading is materially uncertain]. Cassiodorus, Book III, Letter 51: “The *euripus* presents an image of a glassy sea,” whence the expression: “Dolphins swim amid the waters of the sea.” “New shores and artificial rivers” are called *euripi* by Manilius, *Astronomica*, Book IV. See Suetonius, *Julius*, chapter 39. LE PRIEUR.]

[Note: [Col. 0226D] “And an obelisk above everything.” No one doubts that the column called an obelisk stood in the circus. Augustus erected in the circus an obelisk cut by King Semnesertes, 125¾ feet high, apart from the base of the stone. Another stood in the Campus Martius, nine feet shorter, carved by Sesostris. Today the celebrated Vatican obelisk at Rome is of ophite stone; its height is 170 feet, apart from its base, which measures 37 feet. By the work of Domenico Fontana of Como, it was moved from the left side of the Vatican basilica into the middle of the square in the year 1586. Moreover, in *On the Shows*, chapter VIII, its “monstrous mass” is called “the obelisk.” Pliny discusses it in Book XXXVI, chapter 9. LE PRIEUR.]

But let this example be set aside as merely human; I shall take another from the authority of Scripture itself. “God,” it says, “made man from the earth, breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul.” It does indeed name his face here, but did not say that even this was made by God. Later, however, it speaks of his rib, bones, flesh, eyes, sweat, and blood (Gen. II.21, 23; III.5, 29; IV.10), although it did not then signify that these too were made by God. What will Hermogenes answer? Will the members of the human being also belong to matter because they are not individually reported as having been made? Or are these too reckoned as included in the making of the human being? In the same way, the abyss and darkness, spirit and waters, will be members of heaven and earth. For within bodies the members were made, and within bodies the members were named. No element fails to be a member of the element by which it is contained; and all elements are contained either by heaven or by earth.

[Note: [Col. 0226C] Rhenanus read *cui tam vero*, for he conjectured *vero et ossa*. But the Paris edition has *cutem vero*, while the Frankfurt edition, Rigault, Junius, and Pamelius have *costam vero*.]

[Note: [Col. 0226D] “In the making of the human being.” No one should be troubled by the word *factitatio*, derived from a frequentative verb. For in the preceding book as well as in this work, he uses *factitatio* for creation or making. It has an adversative force: “Therefore,” he says, “he understood both that it was made and that whoever made it was the maker of the thing made.” RHENANUS.]

[Note: [Col. 0226C] Others read “were.”]

## CHAPTER XXXII

I would offer this answer concerning the present passage of Scripture, insofar as it appears here to declare only the making of the bodies of heaven and earth. Scripture knew that there would be those who would of their own accord recognize the members within the bodies, and it therefore used brevity. Yet it also foresaw the dull-witted and the captious, who, while ignoring the tacit meaning, would demand a word signifying the making of the members themselves as well. Accordingly, for their sake too, it teaches in other passages that the individual forms were made.

[Note: [Col. 0226C] Rhenanus suspected *commentari*; the Frankfurt, Paris, and Rigault editions read *commendare*, Semler *commentari*.]

[Note: [Col. 0226C] The Frankfurt edition and Pamelius read *sciit*; Rigault and Latinius *scivit*; Semler and Oberthür *scit*.]

[Note: [Col. 0226C] Semler and Oberthür read *significatorum*.]

[Note: [Col. 0226C–D] Semler and Oberthür, without any sense, read: “in other places. You have Wisdom.”]

You have Wisdom saying, “Before the abyss I was begotten”: so that you may believe the abyss too to have been begotten—that is, made—for we too “make” children, although we beget them. It makes no difference whether the abyss was made or born, provided that a beginning is assigned to it, which would not be assigned if it were subject to matter. Concerning darkness, however, the Lord himself says through Isaiah: “I am he who constructed the light and made the darkness” (Isa. XLV.7). Likewise concerning the spirit, Amos says: “He who establishes the thunder and creates the spirit, and announces his Christ among men” (Amos IV.13), showing that the spirit was created which was assigned to the created earth, which moved over the waters, balancing, breathing upon, and animating the universe—not, as some think, signifying that the Spirit is God himself because God is spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0227C] Semler, concerning darkness, has *si materiae subjiciatur, esset*, and proposes reading *subjiciatur esse*.]

[Note: [Col. 0227D–0228D] “For the waters would not have been capable of sustaining the Lord.” At this point he tests the opinion of those who think that the Lord himself is signified by “the Spirit of God.” As though, he says, it were fitting for God’s Spirit to be borne over the waters because of the fluid and unstable nature of water, and God could not have fixed his own waters so that they stood still—which he accomplished when he led Israel across—or made them solid so that they could be trodden upon—which he brought about for the instruction of his disciples’ faith. Yet he supports that common opinion more strongly in *On Baptism*, where he says: “The liquid alone, always a perfect, flowing, simple substance, pure in itself, offered itself as a worthy vehicle for God.” Such is Septimius’s usual practice: he seizes upon every passage of Scripture capable of edification as though divinely inspired. Indeed, he presents this approach in the first book of *On the Dress of Women*, where he excuses his citation of the Book of Enoch; and in *On the Shows* he says broadly that divine Scripture is always distributed wherever, in accordance with the sense of the matter at hand, discipline is also fortified. Yet the truest interpretation of all would seem to be that the words “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters” signify that a certain vital force was present in the waters when they were first created: it was not merely water, but living water, which did not lie inert in sluggish stupor but, quickened by an enduring spirit, was always in motion, lest it ever be said to rest. Our author certainly intimates this on the page of *On Baptism* cited above. Chrysostom, however, speaks most plainly in his *Homily on Genesis* CXI: “What does this statement mean: ‘The Spirit of God,’ he says, ‘was borne above the water’? It seems to me to signify that a certain life-giving energy was present in the waters, and that the water was not simply standing still and motionless, but moving and possessing a certain vital power” (Τὶ βούλεται τοῦτο τὸ εἰρημένον, Πνεῦμα, φησί, θεοῦ ἐπεφέρετο ἐπάνω τοῦ ὕδατος; Ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ τοῦτο σημαίνειν, ὅτι ἐνέργειά τις ζωτικὴ προσῆν τοῖς ὕδασι, καὶ οὐκ ἦν ἁπλῶς ὕδωρ ἑστὼς καὶ ἀκίνητον, ἀλλὰ κινούμενον, καὶ ζωτικήν τινα δύναμιν ἔχον). RIGAULT.]

For the waters would not have been capable of sustaining the Lord; rather, he means that spirit from whom the winds also came into being, as he says through Isaiah: “Because the spirit went forth from me, and I made every breath” (Isa. LVII.26). Likewise concerning the waters the same Wisdom says: “And when he established the firm springs of that which is beneath heaven, I was arranging all things with him” (Prov. VIII.28–29).

[Note: [Col. 0227C] Rhenanus wished to read: “the springs of the waters which are beneath…” Pamelius and the Frankfurt edition read “the springs of that which is beneath heaven”; others, according to Junius, “which are beneath heaven.”]

When, therefore, we prove that these forms too were made by God, even though in Genesis they are merely named without mention of their making, perhaps an answer will be made from the opposite side: “Certainly they were made, but from matter”; so that Moses’ wording, “And darkness was over the abyss, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters,” denotes matter, while the other Scriptures show in scattered passages the forms that were made from matter. Thus, just as earth was made from earth, so the abyss came into existence from abyss, darkness from darkness, and spirit and waters from spirit and waters. And, as we said above, matter could not have been formless if it possessed forms from which other forms were fashioned—except that they were not other forms but those very forms fashioned from themselves. For one cannot admit that they were different when they are presented under the same names; otherwise the divine operation could now appear pointless if God made things that already existed, whereas it would have been nobler if things which did not exist were made.

[Note: [Col. 0227C] Rhenanus and Semler read “are.”]

[Note: [Col. 0227C] Semler and Oberthür omit “from spirit and” and read only “from waters.”]

[Note: [Col. 0227C–0228C] Semler, following Rhenanus, reads *si qua ferant*; all the others accept Rhenanus’s conjecture, “if the things which existed received…”]

[Note: [Col. 0228C] The Frankfurt and Paris editions, following Rhenanus’s conjecture, write “if the things which did not exist were made.”]

Therefore, to conclude: either Moses signified matter when he wrote, “And darkness was over the abyss, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters”; or, when these forms are elsewhere afterward shown to have been made by God, they should likewise have been shown to have been made from the matter which Moses had previously introduced; or, if Moses signified these forms and not matter, I ask where matter has been shown.

[Note: [Col. 0228C] Rhenanus and Semler read “Moses writes”; the Paris edition, “when he writes.”]

## CHAPTER XXXIII

But while Hermogenes finds matter among his own pigments—for he could not find it among the Scriptures of God—it is enough that everything is established to have been made by God, while nothing is established to have been made from matter. Even if matter had existed, we would have believed that it too was made by God, because, by laying down the rule that nothing is unbegotten except God, we would have carried the point.

[Note: [Col. 0228C] Rhenanus, Pamelius, and Semler read “could not”; Paris reads “had not been able”; Frankfurt, “could not sufficiently.”]

Up to this point there is room for reconsideration, until, once the appeal has been made to the Scriptures, the production of matter fails. The summary is straightforward: I find nothing made except out of nothing, because whatever I find to have been made, I know did not exist. Even if anything was made from something, it derives its origin from something already made: thus grass, fruit, animals, and the formation of the human being himself came from the earth; and swimming and flying creatures came from the waters. I shall be able to call such origins “materials” of the things brought forth from them—but materials which were themselves made by God.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

Moreover, that everything came into existence from nothing will finally be confirmed by that divine arrangement which will reduce everything to nothing. For the heaven will be rolled up like a book (Isa. XXXIV.4); indeed, together with the earth with which it was made in the beginning, it will cease to exist altogether (Matt. XXIV.21, 35). “Heaven and earth will pass away,” he says. “The first heaven and the first earth departed, and no place was found for them” (Rev. XXI.1), because, of course, whatever comes to an end also loses its place.

[Note: [Col. 0228C] “Divine” is absent from the Venetian edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0228D] “The first heaven and the first earth departed.” He translated this idiomatically into Latin rather than word for word, because in Revelation XXI one reads παρῆλθεν, that is, “passed away”; then he reads, “and no place was found for them,” instead of the Greek and Latin text, “And the sea is no more.” RHENANUS.]

Thus David also says: “The heavens are the works of your hands, and they themselves will perish” (Ps. CI.26–27). For even if he changes them like a covering, and they will be changed, nevertheless to be changed is to perish with respect to their former state, which they lose while they are being changed.

[Note: [Col. 0229C] Junius reads “and thus he will change.”]

[Note: [Col. 0229C] Semler and Oberthür read “which, while…”]

“And the stars will indeed fall from heaven, just as a fig tree, shaken by a powerful wind, loses its unripe figs” (Rev. VI.13).

[Note: [Col. 0229D] “And the stars will fall from heaven, like a fig tree.” These words are taken from Revelation, where the text reads: καὶ οἱ ἀστέρες τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἔπεσαν εἰς τὴν γῆν, ὡς συκῆ βάλλει τοὺς ὀλύνθους αὐτῆς ὑπὸ μεγάλου ἀνέμου σειομένη, that is: “And the stars of heaven fell to the earth, as a fig tree casts off its unripe figs when shaken by a great wind.” The Greek ὀλύνθοι are what the Latins call *grossi*, that is, figs not yet ripe. Tertullian translated *grossi* as “its unripe fruit”; the Vulgate edition has “its *grossi*,” but the interpretation translated by Tertullian is virtually the same. For an ὄλυνθος or *grossus* is nothing other than a fig which is still hard and unripe. Theodorus Gaza, in his work *On Plants*, calls the wild fig an ὄλυνθος. RHENANUS.]

[Note: [Col. 0229D] “A fig tree loses its unripe fruit.” Rigault reads “its *grossi*.”]

“The mountains, however, will melt like wax before the presence of the Lord” (Ps. XCVII.5), when he rises, namely, to shatter the earth (Isa. II.19). “I shall also dry up the marshes,” he says, “and they will seek water and will not find it” (Isa. XCI.17; XCII.15); even the sea shall be no more.

[Note: [Col. 0229C] The Frankfurt, Pamelius, and Paris editions read “the Ocean.” Rigault, following Rhenanus, retains *hactenus*; so do all later editors.]

[Note: [Col. 0229D–0230D] “And now the sea—thus far,” that is, “It will exist no longer.” So above concerning heaven: “It will cease to exist altogether.” So in *On the Pallium*: “Thus far Sodom.” RIGAULT.—“Even the sea—thus far.” Others have “Ocean” in place of *hactenus*, in which case the sense would be: “Even the Ocean will fail them.” But the word *hactenus* is not unusual in Tertullian, who uses it to mean “it no longer is,” or “will be.” LE PRIEUR.]

Even if someone thinks that all these things should be interpreted spiritually, he will nevertheless be unable to remove the reality that they will occur just as they are written. For if any of them are figures, they must be made from things that exist, not from things that are absent, because nothing can furnish a likeness of something else from itself unless it itself exists as that which furnishes such a likeness.

[Note: [Col. 0229C] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read: “nothing can furnish toward a likeness from itself.”]

I therefore return to the case, which determines that all things produced from nothing will pass into nothing. For God would have made nothing perishable from something eternal—that is, from matter—nor would he have created lesser things from greater, since it is more fitting for him to produce greater things from lesser: that is, something eternal from something perishable, as he also promises for our flesh. He wished already to establish in us this pledge of his power and might, so that we might believe that he also raised the universe from nothing, like something dead—which, of course, it had been, in that it did not exist—so that it might exist.

[Note: [Col. 0229C–D] Rhenanus, Pamelius, and Oberthür read “his powers and authorities”; Junius, “by his power and authority.”]

[Note: [Col. 0230C] Rhenanus and Semler read “will be.”]

## CHAPTER XXXV

As for the remaining condition of matter, although it ought not to be reconsidered—for the first requirement was that its existence should be established—nevertheless, as though it had been established, the sequence must be pursued, so that it may be all the more firmly established that matter does not exist, since not even its remaining condition can be sustained, and at the same time so that Hermogenes may recognize his own contradictions.

“At first sight,” he says, “matter appears to us to be incorporeal; but when investigated by right reason, it is found to be neither corporeal nor incorporeal.” What kind of “right reason” is this, which reports nothing right—that is, nothing certain? For unless I am mistaken, everything must necessarily be either corporeal or incorporeal—granting for the moment that there is anything incorporeal among substances strictly so called, although substance itself is the body of each particular thing. Certainly, after corporeal and incorporeal there is no third thing.

[Note: [Col. 0230C] The last two words are absent from Rhenanus and those who follow him.]

Come, then: let there even be a third thing, which that right Hermogenean reason has discovered, making matter neither corporeal nor incorporeal. Where is it? What is it like? What is it called? How is it described? How is it understood? Reason has reported only this: that matter is neither corporeal nor incorporeal.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

But see: he adds the contrary—or perhaps another reason occurs to him—reporting that matter is partly corporeal and partly incorporeal. Therefore, lest it now be neither, must matter be regarded as both? For it will be both corporeal and incorporeal, contrary to the pronouncement of that “right reason,” which plainly gives no reason for its own judgment, just as the other gives none either.

[Note: [Col. 0230C] Pamelius, Frankfurt, Paris, and Rigault read thus; others wrongly have *reciprocationis* or *reparationis*.]

For he holds that the part of matter from which bodies are produced is corporeal, but that its unregulated motion is incorporeal. “For,” he says, “if it were merely body, nothing incorporeal would appear in it—that is, motion. But if it had been wholly incorporeal, no body would be made from it.”

How much “righter” this reasoning is! Except that, if you draw lines as straight as this reasoning, Hermogenes, no painter is more stupid than you.

[Note: [Col. 0230D] “How much righter this reasoning is! Except that, if you draw such straight lines, Hermogenes…” Here one should note the proverbial expression, borrowed from the painter’s art—which was Hermogenes’—“to draw straight lines”; another such expression is “beyond the line.” PAMELIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 0230C] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür—or rather a follower of their errors—read “sufficient for the reasoning”; Junius reads “reasoning”; others, “this is the reason.”]

For who grants you the right to reckon motion as a second part of substance, when it is not a substantial thing, precisely because it is not corporeal, but rather, if anything, an accident of substance and body—like action, impulse, sliding, falling, and likewise motion? For if something is moved by itself, motion is its action; it is certainly not part of the substance, as you make motion the incorporeal substance of matter.

In short, all things are moved either by themselves, as living beings, or by others, as non-living things. Yet we shall not say that either a human being or a stone is both corporeal and incorporeal because it has both body and motion; rather, we assign to all of them the single form of corporeality alone, which is a substantial thing. If any incorporeal things are present in them—whether their actions, passions, functions, or inclinations—we do not reckon them as portions.

[Note: [Col. 0230D] “As non-living things.” The Vatican manuscript has *inanimata*, but I was unwilling to alter the former reading, since the same word is found below in chapter XCIV and the author habitually uses obsolete expressions of this sort, such as *corporalitas* and *incorpora*. PAMELIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 0230C] Pamelius, from the Vatican codex, reads *inanimata*.]

[Note: [Col. 0230D] “Or their inclinations.” By *libidines* he means appetites and inclinations. Thus in *On Patience*: “Although they disagree among themselves through the various inclinations of sects and rivalries of opinions.” *Libidinibus* means “pursuits.” RHENANUS.]

To what end, therefore, does it serve to arrange one portion of matter as motion, which belongs not to substance but to the condition of substance? For what if it had pleased you to present matter as motionless? Would immobility therefore have appeared to be a second part of its form? In the same way, motion is not such a part. But it will be possible to discuss motion elsewhere as well.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] “But it will be possible concerning motion elsewhere as well.” The verb “to discuss” is understood, unless *licebit* stands for *liquebit*, just as in the preceding book *licuit* stood for *liquit*, that is, “became clear.” RHENANUS.]

[Note: [Col. 0231C] Rhenanus reads “will become clear.”]

## CHAPTER XXXVII

For now I see you returning once more to another kind of reasoning, which is accustomed to report nothing certain to you. For just as you infer that matter is neither corporeal nor incorporeal, so you allege that it is neither good nor evil; and then you add the following argument:

“If,” you say, “it were good, as it had always been, it would not desire God’s ordering; if it were evil by nature, it would not admit of transformation for the better; nor would God have applied any of his ordering to something of such a nature, for he would have labored in vain.”

[Note: [Col. 0231C] Rhenanus reads “that”; the Frankfurt and Paris editions read “just as.”]

[Note: [Col. 0231C] Semler reads “infers.”]

[Note: [Col. 0231C] One reading has “had alleged.”]

[Note: [Col. 0231C–D] Semler and Oberthür read “had added a further argument”; another reading has “you add a further argument.” Rhenanus reads “but if.”]

[Note: [Col. 0231D] The Frankfurt edition reads “in vain” (*in vanum*).]

These are your words, which you ought to have remembered elsewhere as well, lest you introduce anything contrary to them. But since in what has gone before we have already discussed something of the ambiguity of good and evil in relation to matter, I shall now answer only your present proposition and argument. Nor shall I say that here too you ought to have pronounced something definite—either that matter was good, or evil, or some third thing—but merely that you ought to have preserved what it pleased you to pronounce concerning these matters.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] Rhenanus and Semler read “reconsidered.”]

[Note: [Col. 0231D] The same editors read “either good or evil.”]

[Note: [Col. 0231D] Rhenanus and his followers read “not here.”]

For you undo your pronouncement that it is neither good nor evil. When you say, “If it were good, it would not desire to be ordered by God,” you foreshadow that it is evil; and when you add, “If it were evil by nature, it would not admit transformation for the better,” you indirectly reveal that it is good. Thus you have made it akin to both good and evil, although you pronounced it neither good nor evil.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] Rhenanus edits “by adding, he shows,” with the same sense.]

[Note: [Col. 0232C] Rhenanus, Semler, and others add “and.”]

But to refute the argument by which you thought you would confirm your proposition, I also oppose this: if matter had always been good, why would it not have desired to be reformed for the better? What good thing does not desire, wish for, or admit advancement, so that it may become better from good?

[Note: [Col. 0232C] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “But if.”]

[Note: [Col. 0232C] The Wouwer manuscript wrongly reads “desires.”]

Likewise, if it had been evil by nature, why could it not have been converted by God, as by one more powerful, by him who is capable of converting even the nature of stones into children of Abraham (Matt. IV)? You therefore plainly not only compare God with matter, but even subordinate him to it, as though the nature of matter could not have been conquered and subdued for the better by him. But elsewhere you will not deny having admitted that the matter which here you refuse to call evil by nature was evil.

[Note: [Col. 0232C] Rhenanus, Semler, and Pamelius read “the Lord.”]

[Note: [Col. 0232C] Rhenanus and Semler read “could better have been.”]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

Concerning the position of matter, I discuss the same point as concerning its motion, so that it may expose your perversity. You place matter beneath God, and thereby certainly assign it a place below God. Matter is therefore in a place. If in a place, then within a place; if within a place, then bounded by the place within which it is; if bounded, it has an outermost line, which—as befits a painter—you recognize as the limit of every thing that has such an outermost line.

[Note: [Col. 0232C] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “movement.”]

[Note: [Col. 0231D–0232D] “Which, as befits a painter…” This is certainly the passage’s meaning; for *quantum* is used for *in quantum* (“insofar as”), so there is no need to omit that word. PAMELIUS.]

Matter, therefore, will not be infinite, since, while it is in a place, it is bounded by that place, and while it is bounded by it, it admits the place’s outermost line. Yet you make it infinite, saying: “It is infinite because it always exists.”

[Note: [Col. 0232D] Rhenanus and his later followers read “in the place in which…”]

[Note: [Col. 0232D] Junius adds “in which it is.”]

And if one of your disciples should wish to argue that by “infinity” you mean infinity in duration and not in the extent of the body, the statements that follow show, on the contrary, that you mean it to be corporeally infinite, corporeally immense, and uncircumscribed. “Hence,” you say, “it is not fashioned as a whole, but only parts of it.” Thus it is infinite in body, not in time.

[Note: [Col. 0232D] Rhenanus and Pamelius read “infinite.”]

[Note: [Col. 0232D] The Frankfurt edition reads “in duration, not motion.”]

[Note: [Col. 0232D] Rhenanus and the Frankfurt edition read “as corporeally.”]

And you are caught: for you make it infinite in body, although by assigning it a place you enclose it within a place and within the place’s outermost line.

[Note: [Col. 0232D] “And you are caught.” We have noted more than once above that in Tertullian *obducere* and *obduci* mean “to refute” and “to be refuted,” or to catch or be caught asserting contrary and mutually conflicting claims. RHENANUS.—“And you are caught”: so that you cannot escape. RIGAULT.]

Yet why God did not form it all, I do not know, unless because he was either weak or envious. Accordingly, I seek the half of it which was not wholly formed, so that I may recognize what the whole had been like. For God ought to have displayed it openly as a specimen of antiquity for the glory of his work.

[Note: [Col. 0232D] Some add “that.”]

[Note: [Col. 0232D] “A specimen of antiquity.” He means an exemplar. So shortly afterward: “And you want better things to bear the exemplar of worse things.” Similarly, against the Valentinians he uses *sigillarium* in place of *sigillare*. RIGAULT.]

## CHAPTER XXXIX

Let it now be finite, as seems more correct to you, through its transformations and changes; and let it also be circumscribable, since, you say, it is fashioned by God, because it is convertible, changeable, and divisible. “For its transformations,” you say, “show that it is divisible.”

[Note: [Col. 0233D] “They show that it is divisible.” That is, capable of division, though this does not agree with Hermogenes’ earlier words. For he said that God made matter from himself, although God was eternal and indivisible; yet now he thinks that matter divisible, and thus contradicts himself. LE PRIEUR.]

Here too you have strayed from your lines, those which you employed concerning the person of God when you laid down the rule that God did not make matter from himself, because one who is eternal and remains forever, and is therefore immutable and indivisible, could not be divided into parts.

[Note: [Col. 0233D] “You have strayed from your lines.” You have missed the mark. Nor do I think that he was alluding here to that man’s art as a painter; since the words can be understood quite easily without recourse to that allusion, I would think it unworthy of Tertullian to dwell upon it continually. LE PRIEUR.]

[Note: [Col. 0233C] Rhenanus and Semler read “that God.”]

If matter too is reckoned by the same eternity, having neither beginning nor end, by the same reasoning it will be incapable of undergoing division and transformation, just as God is. Placed in fellowship with eternity, it must necessarily share with him the powers, laws, and conditions of eternity.

[Note: [Col. 0233C] Rhenanus wished to read “which.”]

[Note: [Col. 0233C] Rhenanus and Semler read “him with it.”]

Likewise, when you say, “Its parts, however, possess all things together from all things, so that the whole may be discerned from the parts,” you plainly mean those parts which were brought forth from it and which are seen by us today. How, then, do they possess all things from all things—that is, from their former conditions—when the things seen today possess a different condition from what the former things possessed?

[Note: [Col. 0233C] Rhenanus, Semler, and Pamelius read “And.”]

## CHAPTER XL

You say that matter was reformed for the better, necessarily from worse conditions; and you wish better things to bear the exemplars of worse things.

[Note: [Col. 0233C] Rhenanus and Junius read “necessarily from worse things.”]

It was a confused thing, whereas now it is ordered; and you wish the unordered to be represented by the ordered. No thing is the mirror of another thing—that is, of one that is not equal to it.

[Note: [Col. 0233C] Rhenanus and Semler read “is of another,” that is…]

No one at a barber’s has looked upon a mule in place of a human being—unless someone thinks that in this construction of the world, matter, now arranged and adorned, corresponds to matter that is formless and uncultivated.

[Note: [Col. 0233D–0234D] “No one at a barber’s,” etc. He is referring to the custom by which barbers use a mirror; for he adds that the world is the mirror of matter. From this the author also derived the new word *speciatum*, meaning that which appears beautiful in a mirror. For Varro too says in *On the Latin Language*, Book IV: “A mirror (*speculum*) is so called from looking (*speciendo*), because people look there.” PAMELIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 0233C] Rhenanus reads “already arranged and despised,” but thought the reading should be “conceived.”]

What in the world today is formless? What in matter formerly possessed visible form, so that the world should be matter’s mirror? Since among the Greeks the word “world” (*kosmos*, κόσμος) denotes adornment, how does it reflect the image of unadorned matter, so that you may say the whole is known through its parts?

[Note: [Col. 0233C] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “gloomy” in place of “formerly.”]

[Note: [Col. 0233C] Semler notes κόσμος.]

[Note: [Col. 0233C] Rhenanus alone and his followers read “display.”]

Certainly that part too which did not undergo formation will belong to that whole. And above you declared that it was not all fashioned. Therefore, at least this rude, confused, and unordered portion cannot be recognized in the polished, distinct, and ordered things. Nor is it proper to call them parts of matter, since, divided from its form through change, they have departed from it.

[Note: [Col. 0233C] The same source reads “fashioned” in the feminine.]

[Note: [Col. 0233D–0234D] Rhenanus read “and I fled and counted for myself”; he recognized the corruption and proposed the reading which all editors adopted.]

## CHAPTER XLI

I return to motion, to show how slippery you are everywhere. Matter’s motion was unregulated, confused, and turbulent. For thus you also apply the analogy of a pot boiling over on every side.

[Note: [Col. 0234C] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “you will oppose.”]

And how is it elsewhere affirmed by you to be something different? For when you wish to present matter as neither good nor evil, you say: “Thus matter lying beneath had a motion of equal weight, inclining no more toward good than toward evil.” If it was of equal weight, it was no longer turbulent or pot-like, but ordered and balanced—a motion which, being driven by its own choice between good and evil, nevertheless inclined and plunged toward neither side, but was carried with a balanced impulse at, as they say, the middle pivot of the balance.

[Note: [Col. 0234C] Paris reads *cacabatius*; Frankfurt *cacabaceus*.]

[Note: [Col. 0234C] The manuscripts and Junius read “is balanced.”]

[Note: [Col. 0234D] “At, as they say, the middle pivot of the balance.” That is, a motion so balanced that it inclines in no direction and neither side weighs more heavily. For Festus teaches that the *agina* is the hole into which the beam of a balance is inserted and within which it turns. LE PRIEUR.]

[Note: [Col. 0234C] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read, contrary to all the manuscripts, “plunging mediates what they call…”]

You will say: “This is not—this is no turbulence and passivity”; but rather moderation, restraint, and the evenness of a wavering motion which inclines toward neither side.

[Note: [Col. 0234C] Rhenanus, contrary to all the manuscripts, reads “turbulent”; Semler conjectures that the words should be deleted.]

[Note: [Col. 0234D] “This turbulence and passivity.” The old copies read “turbulent.” But “turbulence” is preferable. We have noted in many places, as the subject required, what Tertullian means by “passive.” Here by “passivity” he means dissolution, or disorder and confusion. RHENANUS.]

[Note: [Col. 0234D] “The evenness of motion.” Thus at the beginning of *On the Pallium* he spoke of “the justice of the pallium.” RIGAULT.]

[Note: [Col. 0234C] Junius reads “wavering”; Rhenanus “changing.”]

[Note: [Col. 0234C] Semler and Oberthür read “judging.”]

To be sure, if it inclined this way and that, or leaned more toward one side, it would then deserve to be marked by disarray, inequality, and turbulence.

[Note: [Col. 0234C] Semler, contrary to all the manuscripts, reads “inclined.”]

Furthermore, if its motion was inclined neither more toward good nor more toward evil, it was necessarily conducted between good and evil. From this too it becomes apparent that matter is capable of being bounded: because its motion, inclined toward neither evil nor good, hung within the two and between them, since it tended toward neither; and on this account it was bounded by both.

[Note: [Col. 0234D] “Inclined neither toward evil nor toward good.” That is, inclined neither to evil nor to good. *Pronus* takes the dative. RHENANUS.]

[Note: [Col. 0234C] Rhenanus and Semler read “turned.”]

[Note: [Col. 0234D] Rhenanus and his followers, contrary to all the manuscripts, read “judged.”]

But you also place good and evil in a location when you say that matter’s motion was inclined toward neither of them. For matter, which was in a place, in inclining neither here nor there did not incline toward the places in which good and evil were. By assigning a place to good and evil, however, you make them corporeal by making them local; for things which possess a place must first be corporeal. In fact, incorporeal things would possess no place of their own except in a body, since they occur as accidents of a body.

But matter, in not inclining toward good and evil, was not declining toward things that were either corporeal or local. You therefore err if you wish good and evil to be substances. For you make substances of the things to which you assign places; and you assign places when you suspend matter’s motion between the two regions.

## CHAPTER XLII

[Col. 0235B]

You scattered all your statements so that their mutual contradictions would not shine out from close proximity. But I shall gather and compare them one by one. You assert that matter’s motion is unregulated, and add that matter pursues formlessness; then elsewhere you say that it desires to be ordered by God. Does that which pursues formlessness desire formation, or does that which desires formation pursue formlessness?

You do not wish to appear to equate God with matter, yet you add that matter possesses fellowship with God. “For it is impossible,” you say, “that matter should be adorned by him unless it had something in common with God.” Yet if it had something in common with God, it did not desire to be adorned by him, since through that fellowship it was, of course, a part of God.

Or God too could have been adorned by matter, since he likewise possessed something in common with it. And now in this respect you subject God to necessity, if there was something in matter on account of which he formed it.

You make this common feature between them: that they are moved by themselves and always.

[Note: [Col. 0235D] Rhenanus adds “they are moved” and reads it twice.]

What less do you ascribe to matter than to God? The whole partnership in divinity will amount to this: freedom and eternity of motion. But God moves in an ordered manner, matter in an unregulated manner. Nevertheless it is equally divine, with equally free and eternal motion. Indeed, you grant more to matter, to which it was permitted to move in a way in which God was not permitted to move.

## CHAPTER XLIII
I would also note the following concerning motion. For, according to the analogy of a pot, such, you say, was the motion of matter [Note: [Col. 0235D] “Will be,” Rhenanus, Semler], [Col. 0236A] before it was put into order: coagulated, restless, incomprehensible, because of the excessive violence of its struggle. Then you add: “But it came to rest for God’s ordering, and its ordered motion was incomprehensible because of the sluggishness of unordered motion” [Note: [Col. 0235D] “Unordered,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür]. Above, you ascribe struggle to motion [Note: [Col. 0235D] “To the motion,” Rhenanus and his two followers]; here, sluggishness. Take note [Note: [Col. 0236D] “You take”; above, “you judge,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür] how often you fall away from your account of the nature of matter.

Above you say: “But if matter were evil by nature, it would not have admitted transformation into something better, nor would God have applied any ordering to it; for he would have labored in vain.” You have therefore settled two propositions: that matter was not evil by nature, and that its nature could not have been altered by God. Forgetful of these, you afterward infer [Note: [Col. 0236D] “Inserting,” Rhenanus, against all the manuscripts]: “But when it received ordering from God and was adorned, it ceased from its nature.” If it was reformed into something good, it was certainly reformed from something evil. And if [Col. 0236B] through God’s ordering it ceased from the nature of evil, then its nature ceased; its nature was therefore evil before that ordering, and after its reformation it was able to cease from its nature.

### Chapter XLIV

It remains for me to show how you represent God as having worked. You plainly depart from the philosophers, but also from the prophets. The Stoics hold that God permeated matter as honey runs through the comb. But you say: “No; he does not make the world by passing through matter, but merely by appearing and approaching it, just as beauty acts merely by appearing, and a magnetic stone merely by approaching.”

[Note: [Col. 0235D] “Just as beauty acts.” That is, some instance of beauty. But this reading comes from Rhenanus. Previously the text read: “Beauty, merely appearing, does something.” This is correct. Beauty, merely by appearing, does something—that is, it wounds the mind, as he will presently say. Lucretius, IV:

> But grant that she now possesses however great a beauty of countenance,  
> One in whose every limb the power of Venus is aroused, etc.

(Rigault).]

What resemblance is there between God’s fashioning the world and beauty’s wounding the mind, or a magnet’s attracting iron? For even if God appeared [Col. 0236C] to matter, he did not wound it as beauty wounds the soul; and if he approached it, he did not adhere to it as a magnet does to iron.

Suppose for the moment that your examples are applicable. Certainly, if by appearing and approaching matter God made the world from it, then he made it from the moment when he appeared and from the moment when he approached. Therefore, when previously he had not made it, he had neither appeared to it nor approached it. And to whom is it credible that God had not appeared to matter, which was co-substantial with him in eternity? Or that he had been far from it, whom we believe to be everywhere and to appear everywhere [Note: [Col. 0236D] “On every side,” Latinus]? Even inanimate and incorporeal things sing his praises in Daniel (Dan. III).

[Note: [Col. 0235D] **Inanimate and incorporeal things.** He alludes to the hymn of the three young men in Daniel 3, according to Theodotion’s edition; for St. Jerome correctly noted that it is not found in the Hebrew. St. Cyprian also cites the same hymn under the title “confession” [*exomologesis*] [Col. 0236D] in his books *On the Lapsed* and *On the Lord’s Prayer*. These passages should be noted in support of the canonical authority of that hymn, which the Church also accords it. In the Church it is sung in the sacred rites of the faithful not only now, on the Saturdays of the four Ember seasons, but, from the very beginning of the nascent Church, it was always sung on every solemn occasion. Augustine bears witness to this in Sermon 47, *On Time*—and he also expressly cites it in Letter 186, *On the Saturday Fast*—as does Rufinus, book 2, *Against Jerome*. Jerome replies to him that whatever he had written about it in his preface to Daniel was stated according to the opinion of the Hebrews. What then? The same Jerome, in his letter to Demetrias *On Preserving Virginity*, cites from the prefatory material to that hymn—which likewise is not found in the Hebrew—the statement that the fire blazed up forty-nine cubits. St. Augustine similarly cites from the same prologue, “For you are just in all that you have done to us,” in Letter 122. Pamelius.]

How vast, then, was that space [Col. 0237A] in which God stood so far apart from matter that before the construction of the world he neither appeared nor drew near to it? I suppose he journeyed to it from afar when he first wished to appear and approach it.

### Chapter XLV

But the prophets and apostles do not teach that the world was made by God in this fashion, through his merely appearing and approaching matter—for they never even named any matter. Rather, they teach that Wisdom [*Sophia*] was first created as the beginning [Note: [Col. 0237C] “Beginnings,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür] of his ways for his works (Prov. 8:22); and thereafter that the Word was brought forth, through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made (John 1:3). Finally, “By his word the heavens were established, and by his spirit all their powers” (Ps. 33:6). This Word is God’s right hand, and Wisdom and the Word are the two hands through which he accomplished the things [Col. 0237B] that he fashioned [Note: [Col. 0237C] “And fashioned,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür] (Isa. 48:13). For, he says, “The heavens are the works of your hands” (Ps. 102:26); by these hands he also measured the earth and the heaven with his palm [Note: [Col. 0237C] Rhenanus, and after him, as usual, Semler and Oberthür, read with inverted order: “the heaven, and the earth with his palm”] (Isa. 40:12).

Do not flatter God in such a way [Note: [Col. 0237C] “Not in such a way,” Rhenanus, Semler] that you would have him produced so many and such great substances by sight and approach alone, without establishing them by his own powers. For Jeremiah also commends him in this manner: “God, who makes the earth by his might, prepares the world by his understanding, and by his perception stretches out the heaven” [Note: [Col. 0237C] “The heavens,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür] (Jer. 51:15; Ps. 64:7). These are his powers, by exerting which he created this entire universe. His glory is greater if he labored. Accordingly, on the seventh day he rested from his works (Gen. 2:2)—each act in his own manner.

Or, if he made this world merely by appearing and approaching, did he, when he ceased making it, again [Col. 0238A] cease to appear and approach? On the contrary, from the moment the world was made, God began to appear all the more and to be encountered everywhere. You see, therefore, how all things subsist through God’s operation [Note: [Col. 0237C] “He established all things,” Rhenanus, Semler]: through the might of him who makes the earth, the understanding of him who prepares the world, and the perception of him who stretches out the heaven—not of one who merely appears and approaches, but of one who employs such mighty exertions of his mind: wisdom [*sophia*], might, perception, word, spirit, and power. These would not have been necessary to him [Note: [Col. 0237C] “Will not be,” Rhenanus, Semler] if he had accomplished his purpose [Note: [Col. 0238C] Oberthür, with the same editors, reads “so that by appearing”; Latinus wishes “had been” to be absent] merely by appearing and approaching.

[Note: [Col. 0237C] In the phrase “the might of him who makes the earth,” etc., in Jeremiah 51, the Greek words are **τῇ ἰσχύϊ, τῇ σοφίᾳ, τῇ συνέσει**—“by might, by wisdom, by understanding.” Here and shortly afterward the author renders these as *valentia* (“might,” that is, strength), *intelligentia* (“understanding”), and *sensus* (“perception”). Pamelius.]

These, moreover, are his invisible attributes, which according to the apostle are perceived from the establishment of the world [Note: [Col. 0238C] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür do not insert “from”] through the things he has made (Rom. 1:20) [Note: [Col. 0237C] “His invisible attributes,” etc., in place of: “The invisible attributes of God are seen, being understood through created things from the creation of the world.” Rom. 1. Le Prieur]—not the attributes of some matter or other, but his own capacities of perception. For who has known the mind of the Lord? [Col. 0238B] Concerning this he exclaims [Note: [Col. 0238C] The same editors read: “And he exclaims: O depth”]: “O depth of the riches and wisdom! How undiscoverable are his judgments and untraceable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33).

[Note: [Col. 0237D] **His undiscoverable judgments, and untraceable**, etc. Since all the copies we have seen agree persistently, I think *ininventibilia* (“undiscoverable”) was used just as one might say *incompetibilia*—namely, things that cannot be discovered and known, however much we strive; just as *investigabile* here signifies something that cannot be traced. We must remember that Tertullian is somewhat harsh in rendering Greek expressions, as we have noted in the preceding books. Perhaps, however, this word was once more commonly used. Attending to the force of the Greek term **ἀνεξερεύνητα**, we once thought that *inervibilia* should be read. Rhenanus.—“His undiscoverable judgments,” etc. The Greek has **ἀνεξερεύνητα**, that is, inaccessible and incomprehensible, as the Vulgate reads. Moreover, it makes little difference whether one reads “traceable” or “untraceable” [Col. 0238D], for either can represent the Greek **ἀνεξιχνίαστοι**. Le Prieur.]

What do these words more strongly suggest than that all things were made from nothing—things that could neither be discovered nor traced except by God alone? Otherwise they would be traceable, if they had been sought out and discovered from matter.

Therefore, insofar as it has been established that there was no matter—also because no such matter as is alleged could appropriately have existed—to that same extent it is proved [Note: [Col. 0238C] “Would be proved,” the same editors, against all the manuscripts] that all things were made by God from nothing. The only exception is that Hermogenes, in describing matter in the very condition in which he himself exists—unformed, confused, turbulent, with motion uncertain, precipitous, and seething—while displaying a specimen [Note: [Col. 0238C] “Specimens,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür] of his art, has painted his own portrait.

[Col. 0239]

# The Five Books of Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullian Against Marcion

## Preface

## Historical Synopsis

[Col. 0239A]

Marcion was born at Sinope in Pontus around the year 148, during the reign of Antoninus. At the beginning of his life he made a show of chastity and professed the way of life of monks. His father was a bishop of the catholic communion. Later, having fallen in love with a virgin, he violated her. Because of this incest, therefore, he was expelled from the Church by his own father, a man exceptionally religious, most ardent in his love of truth, and outstanding in the administration of the episcopal office. Although Marcion pleaded with him long and earnestly and sought admission to penance, he obtained nothing from his father by any entreaties.

He therefore went to Rome and approached the elders who had been instructed by disciples of the apostles and were still living, but he sought admission to communion [Col. 0239B] in vain. Consequently, provoked by envy and driven by anger, he said to them: “I shall tear your Church apart and introduce into it an everlasting schism.” Departing from them, he resolved to take refuge in the heresy of the impostor Cerdo (St. Epiphanius, *Heresy* 42).

Cerdo’s doctrines were these: that the God who established the Law was different from the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ; that the latter was good, but the former evil; and that Jesus Christ did not assume true flesh consubstantial with ours, nor was he born of the Virgin Mary. Dupin.

Tertullian composed his work *Against Marcion* after he had fallen into the error of the Montanists, as [Col. 0239C] appears from these words (book 1, chap. 29): “A limit is now placed upon marrying; on the authority of the Paraclete, one marriage in the faith is prescribed.” This is also evident when he mentions the new prophecies and, speaking of certain revelations, writes (book 4, chap. 22): “Concerning this there is a dispute between us and the ‘psychics’”—a distinction that plainly indicates a difference of communion.

Yet these things by no means prevent this work of Tertullian from being called excellent and, as it were, a treasury of more ancient theology. He had first written a short work on this same subject, but in a hurried style, as they say. He afterward recast it with a fuller treatment (book 4, chap. 1) [Col. 0239D], but says that this work too was fraudulently taken from him by an apostate brother. To repair that loss, he labored upon this third version in the fifteenth year of the emperor Severus, A.D. 207. Lumper.

## Overview of the Entire Work

In the first place, therefore, he demonstrates God’s unity and uniqueness, since he proves that it is impossible for there to be two supreme beings. For whoever could admit two could likewise admit more; [Col. 0240A] after two comes plurality, once unity has been overthrown, whereas the number of divinity must, by the highest reasoning, consist in unity.

Moreover, to establish his two principles, Marcion said that the Creator deserved blame, since he would have to be called the author of evils, as Scripture says (Isa. 45:7): “I form peace and create evil.” But Tertullian shows that it is impious, blasphemous, and rash to say of God (chaps. 3–4): “God ought not to have acted thus, and ought rather to have acted thus.”

He then reveals the Creator’s goodness shining forth in all his works, especially in the formation and creation of the first man. Next, he shows the necessity of divine justice in the punishment of evils, in order to restrain the wicked and avert sins committed [Col. 0240B] against God’s command and will (book 2, chap. 13): “For it was not enough that good should commend itself by itself unless there presided some power inspiring fear, which would make even the unwilling seek good and compel them to preserve it.” An unbridled freedom of sinning is therefore laid open to sinners when God is presented to them as one who cannot punish with fire and Tartarus, who cannot be feared—and does not wish to be feared (chap. 16).

“As injustice is evil, so justice is good. Severity, therefore, is good because it is just, if the judge is good—that is, just. So too are all the other good attributes through which the good work of good severity proceeds, whether anger, jealousy, or fierceness—that is, the volitions of God, which we signify by these words, while nevertheless removing [Col. 0240C] far from God all human passions.”

Yet the philosophers and the heretics who followed them, lest they should represent God either as subject to passions or as mutable and consequently corruptible and mortal, imagined him to be altogether without feeling (chap. 16). “It is well,” Tertullian replied, “that it belongs to Christians to believe even that God died, and yet lives for ever and ever. Most foolish are those who predicate divine things from human ones, so that, because passions of this kind are found in man’s corruptible condition, they therefore suppose them to be of the same character in God.”

From these words it is evident that in Tertullian’s age the doctrine of Christ’s divinity and of the unity of the three Persons was established [Col. 0240D] and confirmed. Then, continuing his argument, he adds: “Distinguish the substance, and assign to it its own affections, as diverse as the substances require, even though they seem to share the same names. For we also read of God’s right hand, eyes, and feet; yet they will not therefore be compared with human members merely because they share their designations. . . . God’s goodness is prior according to nature; his severity is subsequent according to cause” (chaps. 13–14).

The first evil, therefore, was sin; punishment followed it, and [Col. 0241A] punishment is called an evil. But these latter evils are of another kind: they are the things by which sins are repaid, though in their own proper character they are good, because they are just, defend good things, oppose transgressions, and in this order are worthy of God.

To disclose the origin of evil, Tertullian establishes the freedom of the human will, saying: “In this very respect man would be reckoned the image and likeness of God—namely, in freedom and power of choice.” But an image is always inferior to its original, and a work inferior to its craftsman; it is therefore by its nature capable of failing (chap. 10). Just as God introduced man into the state of life, so man drew upon himself the state of death. The same must be said of the angel: God made an angel, who transformed himself into a demon.

In this way he solves the objection drawn from the fall of man and the angels to accuse the Creator—namely, [Col. 0241B] that he was guilty either of lack of knowledge and ignorance, if he did not foresee the sin of each, or of malice, if he foresaw it and did not prevent it. For God had to preserve both his faithfulness and his steadfastness in every work. He therefore preserved his work as he had created it—that is, endowed with free choice (chap. 7). For if he had once granted man freedom and power of choice, he had certainly granted him the enjoyment of them by that very institution. The ability to sin, however, is a consequence of this freedom, which God permitted together with its adjuncts—namely, sins and punishments—all of which he afterward turned to the manifestation of his glory.

Proceeding afterward to the Messiah’s mission and incarnation, he says (book 3, chap. 3) that Christ was not to be believed merely on the basis of miracles, but on the basis of the prophets’ prior predictions concerning him, since it had been foretold [Col. 0241C] that many would come, work signs, and display great powers, yet were not therefore to be accepted.

Here he also observes that future events are sometimes announced by the prophets as though they had already occurred (chap. 5), because with God there is no difference of time: eternity directs all times into one uniform state before him. It is characteristic of prophetic foreknowledge that what it foresees, while foreseeing it, it regards as already seen and thus already accomplished—that is, it demonstrates it as something that will certainly come to pass.

To show that God was truly man, not shadowy and phantasmal, he says that if there had not been true humanity in Christ, neither should true divinity be believed in him (chap. 8): “For if that which appeared in Christ was not truly there, and what was there falsely represented itself, then his flesh was not flesh and the man was not man; consequently, Christ as God was not God either. For why should he not also have borne the phantom [Col. 0241D] of God? Shall I believe him concerning his inward substance when I have been deceived concerning the outward?”

That he was a true man is shown by everything we read concerning him in the Gospels: namely, that he both touched others and was touched by them. For it is written that by touching the sick he delivered them; that his feet were touched by the sinful woman and anointed with poured-out ointment; and also that he suffered, died, and yielded up his spirit. After his resurrection he demonstrated that he possessed flesh and bones, commanding them to touch and handle him. Otherwise, if he had not possessed true flesh, he would neither have suffered nor died and therefore would not have risen. Consequently, our faith is vain, and vain also is the apostles’ preaching, for they would be found false witnesses of God.

[Col. 0242A] The Marcionites objected that it was unworthy of Christ to assume flesh. They described that earthly substance as thrust amid filth and called the virgin’s womb a sewer; and they dwelt at length upon the unclean and shameful torments of childbirth and the foul, harmful, and ridiculous issues of delivery (chap. 11).

But Tertullian says that all these are most holy and reverend works of nature. Although Marcion might represent them as unworthy of God, he would nevertheless gain nothing by doing so, for birth will not be more unworthy than death, infancy than the cross, nature than punishment, or flesh than condemnation. “If Christ truly suffered those things, it would have been a lesser thing for him to be born” (chap. 10).

Moreover, if we look to the matter strictly, no substance is worthy for God to put on. Whatever he puts on, he himself makes worthy—provided that there is no falsehood. How, therefore, can it be that he regarded the truth of flesh as a disgrace rather than its falsehood? [Col. 0242B] Indeed, since it had been foretold of Christ that he would be filled with reproaches and covered with confusion, so that he appeared a worm and not a man, it was necessary for him to undergo shame (book 4, chap. 21), so that our salvation might rest upon his disgrace. Since man had felt no shame in worshiping stone and wood, God received satisfaction for the shamelessness of idolatry through the corresponding shamelessness of faith—through a steadfastness that was not ashamed of Christ.

He adds that it was known and established by everyone that Christ was born from the family of David, while the distinction of tribes and families was still preserved among the Jews (book 4, chap. 7), and that this could be found in the census of Augustus, which the Roman archives preserve as a most trustworthy witness to the Lord’s birth.

He called himself the Son of Man while claiming for himself the authority to forgive sins, so that it might be evident that he was at once true God [Col. 0242C] and true man. For Christ could not lie by declaring himself the Son of Man if he were not truly man; nor could he forgive sins if he were not true God. Thus he was the man whom Daniel’s prophecy foretold would receive authority to judge.

But in speaking of Christ’s kingdom, Tertullian shows with perfect clarity that he adhered to the opinion of the chiliasts. This ought not to seem surprising to anyone who considers that he also placed faith in the visions of the Montanists.

To accuse the Creator of all things, the Marcionites chiefly employed the device and deceit of opposing the New Testament to the Old. If they encountered anything either harsh or rather humble in the Law or the Prophets, they treated it as worthless and exaggerated it as something contemptible. But Tertullian showed that those two Testaments [Col. 0242D] had not proceeded from different authors, but from one and the same author, who nevertheless conducted himself differently according to the state and condition of the human race.

At first God promised only lesser rewards, as pledges of the sublime riches he reserved for them. Tertullian says that it is not incongruous for God to bestow riches, by which many works of justice and love are accomplished, just as he gave and promised other earthly goods in the Old Testament. It belongs to the Creator of heaven and earth to distribute and bestow these no less than heavenly goods (1).

He also disposes of objections drawn from the theft of the Israelites, which the Hebrews appear to have committed against the Egyptians at God’s command, and others drawn from an alleged contradiction among the commandments—for example, when he forbade them (2) [Col. 0243A] to make a likeness of anything in heaven, on earth, or in the waters, and at the same time commanded them to fashion the image of the bronze serpent and golden representations of the cherubim and seraphim upon the ark (3). Here he says that images are forbidden solely when made for the sake of idolatry.

Likewise, he says that the law of retaliation was given so that the commission of injury might be rooted out by fear that an equivalent requital would immediately follow, and so that permission to retaliate might serve as a prohibition against provocation.

The heretics mocked and despised those things in the Old Testament that seemed rather base, such as bloody sacrifices (4), the burdensome scruples of washings, and the selection of foods. But all these things were prescribed by God so that, with these legal disciplines confronting them everywhere, they might not for a single moment be free from regard for God . . . “to say nothing of their hidden significations—namely, those [Col. 0243B] of the spiritual and prophetic law, which was figurative in almost all its subjects” (5).

“If the Law,” he writes, “withholds something in respect of foods and pronounces unclean animals that were once blessed, understand this as a plan for exercising self-restraint, and recognize the bridles imposed upon that appetite which, though it had eaten the bread of angels, desired the cucumbers and melons of Egypt. Recognize at the same time the provision made against appetite’s companions—namely, lust and luxury. . . . Likewise, so that the passion for money, which is defended on the ground of the necessity of sustenance, might in part be extinguished, the ambition for costly foods was taken away. Finally, [Col. 0244A] this was done so that man might more readily be trained to fast for God. . . . Let no one criticize the burdens of sacrifices, observances, and the burdensome scruples of washings . . . but let him perceive that providential skill of God by which he wished to bind to his own religion, through duties of this kind, a people prone to idolatry and transgression. These were the very rites through which worldly superstition was practiced, and so he used them to call the people away from it (6).

“But even in the ordinary dealings of life and human intercourse, at home and abroad, down to the care of vessels, he made distinctions of every kind, so that, with these legal disciplines confronting them everywhere, they might not for a single moment be free from regard for God. . . . To support this benefit, not burden, of the Law, he appointed the prophets, who taught things worthy of God: to remove wickedness from the soul, to seek judgment, and the other things that prove the essence and [Col. 0244B] perfection of religion to consist in virtue and good works.”

He proceeds further in explaining this doctrine and proves that the Law prescribed love and the forgiveness of injuries, with vengeance reserved to God, which is necessary so that wicked men may be held in order (7). He adds that Christ made the prohibition of divorce conditional: it applies if someone dismisses his wife in order to marry another.

Finally, he lays down this rule concerning faith (8): “Nothing is to be believed rashly; and whatever is believed without recognition of its origin is believed rashly.” Lumper.

# Book One

## Subject

[Col. 0243]

[Col. 0243C] Since Tertullian had afterward recast his earlier short work *Against Marcion* with a fuller composition, and a certain brother who subsequently apostatized had then published it in an extremely corrupt form, he was compelled to correct it; and the occasion for revision persuaded him to add something further. Hence this work grew into five books, of which we here provide the subject matter of the first.

I. First, after an invective against Marcion of Pontus because he abolished marriage, mutilated the Gospels, and lost the God whom he had discovered by extinguishing the light of faith, Tertullian teaches that Marcion must now be classified as a heretic: because, abandoning what had existed before, he afterward chose for himself that which previously had not existed. He had maintained this more fully in his book *On Prescription Against* [Col. 0243D] *Heretics*.

II. Next, that Marcion introduced two gods: the Creator, that is, our God; and his own god, as well as that of Cerdo, his instructor—the former evil, the latter good.

III. But Christian truth has pronounced categorically that, unless God is one, he is not God, because he is the supremely great being, whom nothing can equal.

IV. Two supremely great beings cannot exist, even if each is bounded within distinct limits.

V. For if two supremely great beings are admitted, even more must also be admitted, as with Valentinus, who poured forth a whole swarm of divinity extending to the offspring of thirty aeons.

[Col. 0244C] VI. Accordingly, not only can two equal gods not be established, but neither can two unequal ones.

VII. Nor is Marcion supported by the name “God,” which is also permitted to others in the Scriptures, because for that very reason possession of supreme greatness does not belong to them.

VIII. Moreover, the heresy of the Marcionites is proved even from the fact that they make their God new, whereas the true God is eternal.

IX. This remains so even if they call him new only with respect to knowledge, because God could not have remained unknown or uncertain.

X. Rather, he was always known from the beginning, since even the pagan soul and conscience knew him.

XI. Consequently, since all things belong to God, if Marcion’s deity created nothing, the one whom Marcion sets up is not God.

[Col. 0244D] XII. Even if we could confess him to be a god, we would nevertheless have to argue that he existed without a cause, since he possessed no thing of his own, whereas a thing is the cause for something’s existence.

XIII. Nor is the world a work too unworthy of God; Tertullian proves this from the testimonies of the philosophers themselves.

XIV. Indeed, even the smallest animals can either help or harm. Nor does Marcion’s god reject the water of God the Creator, with which he washes his followers; or the oil with which he anoints them; or the bread with which, in the sacraments, he represents—that is, shows as present—his own body.

XV. Next he adds that Marcion’s god does not possess a [Col. 0245A] heaven and world of his own—a point discussed more fully below in book 5—both because no such substance had been discovered as late as the fifteenth year of the emperor Severus, in which the author indicates that he wrote this work, and because otherwise Marcion will be judged to assign nine gods.

XVI. Nor did Marcion’s god create only invisible things, as is likewise discussed more fully below in the aforesaid book 5; rather, visible and invisible things have the same author.

XVII. Furthermore, the single work of liberating man is insufficient for that god, since even a stern God made himself known through other works.

XVIII. Likewise, he cannot correctly be said to have been revealed when he was revealed neither by nature through his works nor by doctrine through proclamation.

XIX. Nor was he revealed even in Christ Jesus: both because Christ was revealed [Col. 0245B] more than 115 years before Marcion’s god, who appeared under Antoninus; and because Christ preceded that separation of the Law and the Gospel which Marcion was the first to devise in his *Antitheses*.

XX. It is useless for the opposing side to object that Marcion did not innovate the rule of faith but restored one that had previously been corrupted, appealing to the example of Paul, who reproved Peter. For in Peter he reproved only his conduct, not his faith in the Creator.

XXI. Faith in the Creator and in his Christ therefore always remained firm, not only under the apostles but also in the apostolic churches, among which Christ is shown to belong to no god other than the Creator.

XXII. Moreover, Marcion’s god cannot be called good by nature, since he did not come to the aid of fallen man from the beginning.

[Col. 0245C] XXIII. Nor can he be called reasonably good, because he chose to come to the aid of man who, according to Marcion, was alien to him.

XXIV. Nor is he perfectly good, because, according to Marcion, he saves the soul alone and not the flesh, although among Marcion’s followers the flesh is baptized, withdrawn from marriage, and suffers violence in confessing the divine name.

[Col. 0246A] XXV. Consequently, God must not be judged by goodness alone.

XXVI. Rather, judgment must also be attributed to him, so that he avenges and condemns sins.

XXVII. Otherwise sinners would have no fear.

XXVIII. Thus even baptism, the sacrament of faith, cannot stand. Baptism is the remission of sins, release from death, regeneration, and attainment of the Holy Spirit; finally, it seals and washes. These things can be conferred only by the one who created man from the beginning, bestowed a soul upon him, and condemned him to death because of sin.

XXIX. Lastly, he attacks Marcion’s heresy whereby Marcion wished only virgins and unmarried persons to be baptized: both because God blessed marriage and because, if there is no marriage, there will be no holiness either. Indeed, this would amount to suppressing the entire seed-stock of the human race.

[Col. 0246B] XXX. Finally, in a brief epilogue he prepares the reader for the following books. Pamelius.

### Chapter I

If anything has previously been done by us against Marcion, from this point onward let it be regarded as past.

[Note: [Col. 0245C] **If anything has previously been done by us against Marcion, from this point onward let it be regarded as past.** He most expressly disowns whatever he had composed against Marcion before these books. In the preface to the poems commonly inscribed under Tertullian’s name *Against Marcion* and usually passed off as works of Septimius, we have shown that it must by no means be supposed that this earlier work consisted of verse. Rigault.]

We undertake a new treatment of an old subject.

[Note: [Col. 0245D] **The first short work, as though hastily composed.** It was an initial and unfinished work, of the kind that Jerome, in his commentary on Obadiah, reports had also escaped from Origen, Quintilian, and even Cicero in certain passages of the books *To Herennius*: “If he could say this both of the books *To Herennius* and of the rhetorical works—which I consider nearly perfect—when comparing them with the skill of his old age, how much more freely may I profess that the one work belonged to youthful talent and the other to mature old age? In his books against Marcion, Septimius Tertullian also underwent the same experience; so did Origen in his *Commentary on the Song of Songs*, and Quintilian in the twelve books of his *Institutes of Oratory*.” Rigault.]

I had afterward recast my first short work, which had been produced as though in haste, into a fuller composition. This version too, before a sufficient number of copies had been made, I lost through the fraud of one who was then a brother but afterward an apostate.

[Note: [Col. 0245D] **Then a brother, afterward an apostate.** Marcion, who was a brother for as long as he was truly a Christian. It is clear from the preceding words that Tertullian had written against Marcion. Le Prieur.]

He had perhaps copied certain passages with extreme inaccuracy and released the work to the public.

[Note: [Col. 0246C] **Released it to the public.** That is, he sent it out among the people. So too in the *Apologeticum*, Tertullian used “the populations of the mountains” to mean the wild beasts inhabiting the mountains. Rigault.]

The necessity of correction arose. The occasion of revising it persuaded me to add something. Thus this present composition, now third instead of second, will henceforth be first instead of third. It necessarily provides this account of the history of its own publication, lest anyone [Note: [Col. 0245C] “Anyone at all,” Rhenanus] be confused by encountering its divergent forms in circulation.

[Note: [Col. 0246C] **Lest anyone be confused by encountering its divergent forms in circulation.** He would have had no reason to fear this in connection with any verses he might have written against Marcion, for they distinguish themselves very clearly from this kind of style. Rigault.]

[Col. 0246C] Pontus, which is called—[the source text breaks off here]

[Note: [Col. 0246D] **Pontus, which is called the Euxine, is denied by its nature.** We have emended the text thus, following the reading of the ancient manuscripts, which runs approximately: “Pontus which therefore Euximus.” Pithoeus had proposed: “Pontus which is called Euxine by the Greeks.” Nevertheless, the common reading can still be defended: “Pontus, therefore, which is called Euxine, is denied by its nature and mocked by its name.” Rigault.]

[Note: [Col. 0246D] **The Euxine is denied by its nature.** For it deceives by the falsehood of its surname, since, because of the character of the place and the savagery of its nature, it ought to be called **ἄξενος** (*axenos*, “inhospitable”). Rigault.—Since it should have been called “inhospitable,” whence Ovid:]

“Whom the Euxine Sea, false in its surname, contains.” LE PR.] “Euxine” [Note: [Col. 0245C] “The Pontus, therefore, which is Euxine,” Rhen.], is denied by its nature [Note: [Col. 0246C] “Nature” omitted, Rhen.] and mocked by its name. Moreover, do not judge the Pontus hospitable from its location: it has withdrawn so far from our more civilized seas, as though from a kind of shame at its own barbarity. The fiercest peoples inhabit it [Note: [Col. 0246D] “The fiercest peoples inhabit it.” Those peoples were the Sarmatians, Geloni, Massagetae, and the whole race of wagon-dwelling peoples [Col. 0247C], about whom and whose savagery histories shudder. LE PR.], if indeed dwelling in a wagon can be called habitation. Their abode is unsettled, their life uncivilized, their lust indiscriminate [Col. 0247A] and for the most part naked. Even when they conceal themselves, the quivers hanging from the wagon-yoke serve as warnings, lest anyone intrude rashly [Note: [Col. 0247C] “Lest anyone rashly,” Jun.; “so that they may be marked out by warnings, lest anyone,” Rhen.]. Thus they are not even ashamed of their weapons. [Note: [Col. 0247C] For they publicly display these signs of their shameful and exposed sexuality. RIG.] They consume at feasts the corpses of their parents, slaughtered together with their livestock. Those who have not died in such a way as to become edible have suffered an accursed death. Nor are the women softened by their sex into modesty: they do away with their breasts and perform their allotted labor with axes; they prefer soldiering to marriage. Even the climate is harsh. The day is never clear; [Note: [Col. 0247C] “The sun is never willing.” So the old copy reads. You might say that the sun scarcely deigns to look upon this region, so poorly does it shine there. RIG.] the sun is never willing [Note: [Col. 0247C] “Melting,” Wouwer; “free,” Fran.]; there is but one atmosphere—fog; the whole year is winter; every wind that blows is the North Wind. [Note: [Col. 0247D] “Liquids return through fires.” In that Pontic savagery, he says, every wind that blows is the North Wind. Consequently, all liquids congeal with frost and do not return except when fires are placed beneath them—that is, they are dissolved back into liquids. RIG.] Liquids return through fires; rivers are denied by ice; mountains are heaped higher by frost. Everything is numb, everything frozen: nothing there is warm except savagery—that savagery, namely, which has supplied the stage with tales of the sacrifices of the Taurians, the loves [Col. 0247B] of the Colchians, and the crosses of the Caucasus. Yet nothing in Pontus is so barbarous and grim [Note: [Col. 0247D] “As that Marcion was born there.” Although the things related about the Euxine Pontus and its neighboring peoples are hideous and horrible, nothing more hideous or horrible can be imagined than that Marcion was born there. LE PR.] as the fact that Marcion was born there: more repulsive than a Scythian, more unstable than a wagon-dweller, more inhuman than a Massagete, [Note: [Col. 0247D] “More daring than an Amazon.” The common text has *Amazonia*. It should be written as it stands in the copy, *Amazona*. He says *Amazonam*, just as he uses *Sirenarum* for *Sirenum* and *Synopae* for *Cynopes*. See the *Apologeticum*. RIG.] more daring than an Amazon; darker than cloud, colder than winter, more brittle than frost; more treacherous than the Danube, more precipitous than the Caucasus. And why not? In his hands the true Prometheus, Almighty God, is mangled by blasphemies [Note: [Col. 0247C] Others read “torn to pieces.”]. Indeed, Marcion is more troublesome even than the beasts of that barbarous land. For what beaver, castrator of its own flesh, is so much a castrator as the man who abolished marriage?
