What Pontic mouse is so voracious as the man who gnawed away the Gospels? Truly, Euxine, you have produced for philosophers a more commendable beast than you have for Christians. [Note: [Col. 0247D] “For that little dog Diogenes,” etc. That Cynic Diogenes was so called because of the freedom he assumed in censuring both men and even gods. Likewise in the *Apologeticum*, chapter 14: “The Roman Cynic Varro names three hundred Jupiters,” etc.—so that, namely, he might set a Roman against the Greek Diogenes. LE PR.] For that little dog [Note: [Col. 0247C] “That man,” Semler.] Diogenes desired to find a human being and carried a lamp around at midday; Marcion, after extinguishing the light of his faith, lost the God whom he had found. [Col. 0247C]

His disciples will not deny that his original [Note: [Col. 0248C] Others read “their” or “his.”] faith was shared with us, as his own writings [Col. 0248A] testify. From this it may already be established that he is a heretic, since, after deserting what he had formerly been, he later chose for himself what had not existed before. For what is introduced later will be reckoned heresy precisely to the degree that what was handed down before and from the beginning will be held to be truth. But another little work [Note: [Col. 0248C] “But another little work will sustain this position,” etc. Here he undoubtedly cites the book just mentioned, *On Prescriptions Against Heretics*, since in it he taught that heretics are to be refuted, without an examination of their doctrines, by the prescription of novelty. PAM.] will sustain this position against the heretics: even without reexamining their doctrines, they are to be refuted merely because, by the prescription arising from novelty, they are heretics. Yet an engagement must now be admitted to some extent, lest the summary procedure of prescription, if invoked everywhere, sometimes be attributed to lack of confidence. I shall first set out the adversary’s rule, so that no one may fail to see the ground upon which the principal question is to be fought.

## CHAPTER II

The man from Pontus presents two gods [Note: [Col. 0248C] “The man from Pontus presents two gods.” The author indicates the subject of this chapter in these words: concerning Marcion’s two gods, which is treated especially in these first and second books *Against Marcion*. On this matter see also the blessed Justin, *Apology* II. PAM.], as though they were the two Symplegades [Col. 0248B] of his shipwreck [Note: [Col. 0248D] “As though they were the two Symplegades of his shipwreck.” The Symplegades are two reefs—or, if you prefer, rocks—in the sea near the Thracian Bosporus. They are called the Cyanean Rocks by Apollonius Rhodius, *Argonautica*, book I, and the Cyanean Symplegades by Euripides in the *Medea*. LE PR.]: the one whom he could not deny, that is [Note: [Col. 0248C] “That is” omitted in Latin.], the Creator, namely our God; and the one whom he will not be able to prove, namely his own god. The unhappy man underwent the impulse of this presumption [Note: [Col. 0248D] “Underwent the impulse of this presumption.” So at the beginning of the book *On the Veiling of Virgins*: “Having myself undergone so personal a matter of my own opinion.” RIG.] from a simple maxim of the Lord’s pronouncement [Note: [Col. 0248C] Others read “foreannouncement.”], which applies those examples of the good and evil tree to human beings, not to gods: that neither does a good tree produce evil fruit, nor an evil tree good fruit (Matt. VIII, 18); that is, neither does a good mind or faith produce evil works, nor an evil one good works.

For, being weak—as many now are, and especially heretics—when confronted with the question of evil, “Whence comes evil?” [Note: [Col. 0248D] “Confronted with the question of evil, ‘Whence comes evil?’” That is, weak when confronted with the question of evil. That question is: “Whence comes evil?” RIG.], and his senses being blunted by the very enormity of his curiosity, he found the Creator declaring (Isa. LXV, 7) [Note: [Col. 0248C] Others read “foretelling.”], “I am he who fashions evils” [Note: [Col. 0248D] “I am he who fashions evils.” Vatican manuscript II reads “creates,” and a little later “creating” for “fashioning.” But the former reading occurs elsewhere in the author, not only in the book *On Flight in Persecution* but also in book II *Against Marcion*. PAM.]. To the extent that he had presumed from this and from other arguments—which persuade every perverse mind in this way—that the Creator himself was the author of evil, to that extent he interpreted the evil tree as the Creator, fashioning evil fruits, namely evils; and he presumed that there must be another god corresponding to the good tree and its good fruits. Thus, finding in Christ what seemed a different dispensation, one of sole and pure kindness, as though it were different from the Creator’s, he readily argued that a new and alien divinity had been revealed in his Christ; and from that little leaven he corrupted the whole mass of faith with heretical sourness [Note: [Col. 0249C] “Sharpness,” Semler; Pithaeus’s codex.] [Note: [Col. 0249D] “Corrupted the whole mass of faith with heretical sourness.” Literally, “deceived.” For there is a kind of perfidy in the badness of vinegar.]. He also had a certain Cerdo [Note: [Col. 0249D] “He also had a certain Cerdo.” Marcion, Cerdo’s disciple, further augmented his master’s doctrine, and thus became the best disciple and imitator of the worst master. LE PR.] as the instructor of this scandal; thus these blind men all the more readily supposed that they had discerned two gods. For they had not seen even one perfectly. To bleary eyes even a single lamp appears multiple. Accordingly, by defaming the one God whom he was compelled to acknowledge on account of evil, he destroyed him; while by bringing forward goodness, he constructed the other whom he was striving to invent. Through our answers themselves [Col. 0249B] we shall show under what headings he has arranged these natures.

## CHAPTER III

The principal dispute, therefore—and [Note: [Col. 0249C] “Is,” Jun.] consequently the whole dispute—concerns number: whether it is permissible to introduce two gods, perhaps by poetic and pictorial license [Note: [Col. 0249D] “Perhaps by poetic and pictorial license.” Since everything seems to be permitted to painters and poets, he indicates that Marcion wishes to use the same license in order to construct impiety against God. Nor does he mention painting here without reason; for, as we have noted elsewhere, Apelles and Hermogenes were painters by profession before they turned their minds to disturbing the Church. LE PR.], and now by a third, heretical license. But Christian truth has pronounced strictly: if God is not one, he does not exist; for we more fittingly believe that anything which is not as it ought to be does not exist.

To know that God must be one, inquire what God is, and you will find no other answer. Insofar as the human condition can define God, I give this definition, which the consciousness of all will also acknowledge: [Note: [Col. 0249D] “God is the supreme greatness.” A beautiful definition of God, insofar—to use the author’s preceding words—as the human condition can define God. Similarly, below in chapter 7 he says: “You will find this substance of God alone unborn, unmade, alone eternal, and the maker of the universe.” And above, in *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 7: “God is eternal, that is, unborn, greater and more exalted than all things, neither born nor made, without beginning, without end.” PAM.] God is the supreme greatness, established in eternity, unborn, unmade, without beginning, without end. For this condition must be assigned to eternity, which makes God the supreme greatness, since eternity itself is this in God, and so too are the other attributes; with the result that God is the supreme greatness in form, reason, strength, and power.

Since all agree on this—for no one will deny that God is something supremely great, unless he can, on the contrary, pronounce God to be something lowest and slight, thereby denying God through removing what belongs to God—what, then, will be the condition of the supreme greatness itself? Surely that nothing be made equal to it; that is, that there be no other supreme greatness. For if there were, it would be made equal to it; and if it were made equal to it, it would no longer be the supreme [Col. 0250A] greatness, since the condition—and, so to speak, the law—which permits nothing to be made equal to the supreme greatness would have been overthrown. Therefore, whatever is the supreme greatness must necessarily be unique, having no equal, lest it cease to be the supreme greatness. Therefore, it will exist in no other way than by that through which it possesses existence—that is [Note: [Col. 0249C] “And that,” Jun., Venet., Rig.], by being altogether unique.

Accordingly, since God is the supreme greatness, our truth rightly pronounced: if God is not one, he does not exist. We do not say, “If he is not one, he does not exist,” as though we doubted that God exists; rather, because we trust that he exists, we define him as being that which, if he is not that, he is not God [Note: [Col. 0249C] “The same,” Semler; “the same,” Fran.] [Note: [Col. 0249C] Semler inserts “and.”]—namely, the supreme greatness. Moreover, the supreme greatness must necessarily be unique. Therefore God also will be unique. He is not God except as the supreme greatness; nor is he the supreme greatness except as having no equal; nor does he have no equal [Col. 0250B] except by being unique.

Certainly, whatever other God you introduce, you will not be able to uphold him as God under any other form than by ascribing to him also the property of divinity: just as he is eternal, so too he is the supreme greatness. How, then, can two supreme greatnesses coexist, when it is the nature of the supreme greatness to have no equal? And to have no equal [Note: [Col. 0250C] “Since it does not,” Wouw.], since it belongs to one alone [Note: [Col. 0250C] Semler disregards “since.”], can in no way exist in two.

## CHAPTER IV

But someone will argue that two supreme greatnesses can coexist, distinct and separate within their respective boundaries, and he will certainly invoke this example: the kingdoms of the earth are so numerous and yet are supreme greatnesses in each of their respective regions. He will, of course, suppose [Note: [Col. 0250C] “Everywhere,” Seml.] that human things are to be compared with divine things. If, then, a place is granted to this argument, what prevents us from introducing—not merely a third and fourth god—but as many gods in number as there are kings of nations?

The subject is God, whose foremost property is that he admits comparison with no example. Nature itself will proclaim this, even if no Isaiah does, or God himself through Isaiah: [Note: [Col. 0250D] “To whom will you liken me?” Isaiah 40 reads somewhat differently: “To whom have you likened the Lord?” according to the Septuagint, or “God?” according to blessed Jerome’s version. Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book III, and after him Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book XIII, in Greek, report that the Sibyl learned from this passage to call God immeasurable and infinite; there he teaches that the things beautifully said by the philosophers were borrowed from the books of the prophets. PAM.] “To whom will you liken me?” (Isa. XL, 25). Will human things perhaps be compared with divine ones? They will not be so compared with God [Note: [Col. 0250C] “Our things,” Rhen.; “with our God,” Seml.]; for God is one thing, and the things of God another.

Finally, you who use the example of a king as though he were the supreme greatness, take care lest you already be unable to use it. For although a king is a supreme [Col. 0251A] greatness on his throne, as far as God, he is nevertheless beneath God; and when compared with God, he will immediately fall from the rank of supreme greatness, since that rank has been transferred [Note: [Col. 0251C] “The transfer,” all the others.] to God. If this is so, how can you employ as an example for comparison with God something which vanishes when brought into the comparison?

What, further, if even among kings the supreme greatness cannot appear in many forms, but is unique and singular—namely, in the man who, because of the supremacy of his greatness and the subjection of all lesser ranks, is acknowledged as king of kings, as though he were the summit of dominion? But even kings of another kind, who rule singly within a unified dominion, if they are brought from all sides together with their petty kingdoms, so to speak, for an examination intended to establish which of them excels in the resources and strength of his kingdom, the summit of greatness must necessarily be refined down to one [Col. 0251B], all the others being gradually squeezed out and excluded from the supreme rank of greatness by the outcome of the comparison. Thus, even if the supreme greatness appears manifold when dispersed, in its own powers, nature, and condition it is unique.

Accordingly, when two gods are compared as two kings and two supreme greatnesses, the unity of supreme greatness must necessarily yield to one of them, according to the verdict of the comparison. The one who stands supreme by his victory, his rival—another greatness, though not the supreme one—having been overcome, and who through his rival’s failure possesses a kind of solitude arising from the singularity of his own excellence, is unique. This inescapable chain of reasoning confines the conclusion to this: either it must be denied that God is the supreme greatness—which no wise person will tolerate—or that status must not be shared with any other.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0251C]

Or what principle has brought two supreme greatnesses together? First I shall demand: why not more, if two? For the substance of divinity ought to be believed richer if it were also compatible with numbers. [Note: [Col. 0251D] “Valentinus was more honorable and generous.” This alludes to Valentinus’s thirty divine aeons, concerning which the author writes at great length in his book *Against Valentinus*. He derives for them a new expression when he adds “like Aeneas’s sow,” alluding to the fecundity of a sow, which is sometimes reported to have borne as many as three hundred piglets. Marcus Varro writes in *On Agriculture*, book II, chapter 4, that this very ancient story relates that Aeneas’s sow at Lavinium bore thirty white piglets. Moreover, he rightly says: “For after one comes number”; and shortly afterward: “For two is already plurality, unity having been exceeded,” because unity is not a number but the principle of numbers. PAM.] Valentinus was more honorable and generous: once he had dared to conceive of two, Bythus [Note: [Col. 0251C] “Bythis,” Seml.; “Bythus,” Fran.] and Sige, he poured forth [Note: [Col. 0251D] “Then,” Latin, Semler.] a brood extending to thirty aeons [Note: [Col. 0251D] “A brood extending to thirty aeons, like Aeneas’s sow.” Thus we have emended what was commonly read, “like the Aeonian sow.” In Pithoeus’s codex [Col. 0252D] it is written *Aeoneiae*. It must certainly be read *Aeneiae*, for he alludes to Aeneas’s sow, which, as Virgil says:

> Found huge beneath the holm-oaks by the shore,  
> She lay, having borne a brood of thirty heads.

The same error occurs in Jerome’s words in his commentary *On the Epistle to the Galatians*: “Whom did the brood of Aeneas’s sow beget?” For the common text reads *Aeonia*. In manuscripts I have found *Enegia*, which means *Aeneia*. Juvenal, in Satire VI:

> And the same sow, more fertile than white Niobe.

RIG.], like Aeneas’s [Note: [Col. 0252C] “Aeonian,” Fran., Paris; *Aeoneiae*, Seml.] sow—a whole swarm of divinity.

Whatever principle does not allow several supreme greatnesses to be admitted, the same does not allow two, since two themselves are already several [Col. 0252A] after one; for after one comes number. The principle which could admit two could also admit several; for after [Note: [Col. 0252C] “Can,” Rhen.] two comes plurality, unity having already been exceeded. Finally, among us the force of this principle, by that very limit, does not permit belief in several gods, because it does not permit even two: it establishes one God by the rule that God must be that to whom nothing is equal, as the supreme greatness; and that to which nothing is equal must be unique.

Now, to what purpose or advantage would two supreme greatnesses, two equals, be assigned? What difference would their number make, since two equals do not differ from one? For that which is the same in two is one thing. Even if there were several equals, all of them would nevertheless be one and the same thing, since they differed in no respect [Note: [Col. 0252C] Seml. conjectures “no respect.”] from one another [Note: [Col. 0252C] “From themselves,” Paris.] insofar as they were equal. Moreover, if neither of the two differs from the other, since both are supreme greatnesses and both are gods [Note: [Col. 0252C] Others read “which.”], and neither excels [Col. 0252B] the other, they show no rationale for their number, since they possess no superiority. Yet the number of divinities ought to rest upon the highest rational ground, if only because even their worship would be rendered doubtful.

For behold: contemplating two gods, as equal as two supreme greatnesses, what should I do? If I worshiped both, I would fear that, through an excess of service, it might be judged superstition rather than religion; for, since the two are so equal and both are present in either one, I could conciliate both in one, thereby offering this very act as testimony [Note: [Col. 0252D] Perhaps “a testimony,” editions.] to their equality and unity, since I would venerate the one in the other, and in one would possess two. If I worshiped one of them, I would likewise reconsider, lest I appear to expose the vanity of a number that is superfluous because it makes no difference; that is, I would judge it safer to worship neither than to worship one with misgiving [Col. 0252C], or both in vain.

## CHAPTER VI

Thus far we still seem to be arguing as though Marcion established two equal gods. For while maintaining that the supreme greatness must be believed unique, and excluding equality from it, we have treated these gods as though they were two equals. Nevertheless, by teaching that they cannot be equal under the form of supreme greatness, we have sufficiently confirmed that there cannot be two.

Yet, since we know that Marcion establishes unequal gods—the one a judge, savage, mighty in war; the other gentle, placid, and only good and supremely good—let us examine this side equally: whether diversity, at least [Note: [Col. 0253C] Read “at least.”], can admit two when equality could not. Here too the same rule of supreme greatness will support us, since it vindicates the entire condition of divinity. For, meeting the adversary’s meaning directly and, as it were, seizing and detaining it by force of law, since he does not deny that the Creator is God, I most justly bar him from allowing any place for diversity between those whom, having confessed them equally as gods, he cannot make diverse. This is not because even extremely different human beings may not be included under the same designation, but because nothing may be called or believed to be God unless it is the supreme greatness.

Since, therefore, he is compelled to acknowledge as the supreme greatness the one whom he does not deny to be God, it cannot be admitted that he should ascribe to the supreme greatness any diminution by which it is subordinated to another supreme greatness; for if it is subordinated, it ceases to be supreme. But it is not possible for God to depart from his condition—that is, from supreme greatness. For even in that more powerful god the supreme greatness could be endangered if it can be depreciated in the Creator [Note: [Col. 0253D] “If it begins to be depreciated in the Creator.” He frequently uses the verb *capit* in this sense, like the Greek ἐνδέχεται (*endechetai*, “it is possible/admissible”). Here it has the same force as if you were to say: “If it is conceded, if it is granted, that the Creator may be depreciated.” Thus in book II: “because, if this were admissible by right.” RHEN.].

Thus, when two gods are pronounced to be two supreme greatnesses, necessarily neither is greater or lesser than the other, neither more exalted nor more abased than the other. Deny that he is God whom you call inferior; deny that he is the supreme greatness whom you believe lesser. But once you have confessed him to be God, you have confessed both to be two supreme greatnesses. You will take nothing away from the one or ascribe anything to the other. By acknowledging divinity, you have denied diversity.

## CHAPTER VII

In reply, you will attempt to unsettle [Note: [Col. 0253D] “Redirect,” Franeq.] the discussion by appealing to the name “God” [Col. 0253C], [Note: [Col. 0253D] “As common and permitted to others as well.” Here he plainly interprets himself, showing what he means by *passivum* when he says “and”—that is, “that is”—“permitted to others as well.” For *passivum* signifies for him something common and indiscriminate, from the adverb *passim* (“everywhere, indiscriminately”). Above, at the end of *On the Flesh of Christ*, he said: “another, common among the rest, ignoble”—that is, ordinary and obscure. RHEN.—In African councils, the bodies of martyrs were called *passiva*, that is, indiscriminate, τυχόντα (*tychonta*, “ordinary/chance specimens”). SEML.] claiming that it is common and permitted to others as well, because it is written (Ps. LXXXII, 1): “The God of gods stood in the assembly of gods; in their midst he will judge the gods” [Note: [Col. 0254C] “He judged,” Rhen.]. And again (ibid., v. 6): “I said: You are gods.” Yet, you will argue, possession of supreme greatness does not therefore belong to them merely because they are called gods, and neither, accordingly, does it belong to the Creator.

I shall answer even the fool who has failed to consider that the same objection may be turned equally against Marcion’s god: he too may be called a god without therefore being proved the supreme greatness, just as the Creator’s angels or human beings are not. If community of names prejudges conditions, how many worthless slaves swagger under the names of kings—Alexander, Darius, and Holofernes? [Note: [Col. 0254D] “Alexander, Darius, and Holofernes.” In Pithoeus’s codex the text reads *et Olofernae*, so that these are genitive-case names of slaves belonging to Alexander, Darius, and Holofernes. This reading appears to be Tertullian’s. He said *Olofernae*, just as *Cynopae* and *Syrenarum* in the *Apologeticum*. RIG.] Yet that does not detract from kings what they are. Indeed, even the idols of the nations are commonly called gods; but no one is a god merely because he is called a god.

Thus I defend supreme greatness in the Creator, not on the basis of the name “God,” nor its sound, nor the mark made by that name, but on the basis of the substance itself to which the name happens to belong. Finding this substance alone unborn, unmade, alone eternal and the maker of the universe, I both ascribe and vindicate supreme greatness not to its name but to its condition, not to its designation but to its essential state. And because the substance to which I ascribe it has already come to be called God, you suppose that I ascribe it to the name; whereas it is necessary for me to indicate by a name the substance to which I ascribe it—namely, the substance by which the one called God subsists and is accounted the supreme greatness from substance, not from name.

Finally, when Marcion vindicates this for his own god, he vindicates it according to condition, not according to the word. We therefore maintain that the supreme greatness which we ascribe to God by the law of substance, not by the chance of a name, must belong equally to the two who consist of that substance by virtue of which one is called God. For insofar as they are called gods—that is, supreme greatnesses—by the merit of a substance that is unborn and eternal, and for that reason great [Note: [Col. 0254D] Rhen. omits “and.”] and supreme, to that same extent one supreme greatness cannot be regarded as lesser and inferior to another supreme greatness.

If the felicity, sublimity, and integrity of the supreme greatness stand firm in Marcion’s god, they will stand equally firm in ours; if they do not stand firm in ours, neither will they stand firm in Marcion’s. Therefore, the two supreme greatnesses will be neither equal, because the rule of supreme greatness already established—which permits no comparison—prohibits it [Note: [Col. 0254D] “Once the rule has been established,” etc. Once that rule has been laid down, or that foundation cast, concerning which he has spoken in the three preceding chapters, there cannot be two gods, as Marcion of Pontus maintained. LE PR.]; nor unequal, because another rule of supreme greatness intervenes, admitting no diminution. You are trapped, Marcion, amid the tide of your own Pontus: the waves of truth engulf you from either side. You can establish gods neither equal nor unequal. For there are not two—so far as concerns the discussion of number properly speaking. Although the whole subject is a contest over two gods, we have for the present enclosed it within these lines; inside them we shall now engage with their individual properties.

## CHAPTER VIII

First, the Marcionites build their amazement upon haughtiness because they bring forward a new god, as though we were ashamed of the old God. Even boys are puffed up by new shoes; but once shod by the old schoolmaster [Note: [Col. 0254D] “Shod, their vainglory.” So in book III *Against Marcion*: “having put on as shoes the preparation of the Gospel of peace”; and in *On the Crown*: “shod with the equipment of the Gospel.” RIG.], their vainglory will soon be beaten out of them.

When, therefore, I hear of a new god in an old world and an old age, unknown and unheard of under the old God—a god whom, after so many ages in the past, no one knew, and who, ancient merely by virtue of that very ignorance, was revealed by a certain Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0255C] “Jesus Christ” in the accusative, others.], himself new despite his ancient names, and by no one before him—I give thanks for this boast of theirs, since with its powerful assistance I shall now prove that their profession of a new divinity is heresy. This will be the sort of novelty which also gave birth to gods among the pagans, each always under some new title of consecration. What god is new unless he is false? [Note: [Col. 0255C] “Not even Saturn,” etc. He demonstrates the falsity of gods from their novelty; he treated this matter in chapter 10 of the *Apologeticum*. [Col. 0255D] Accordingly, he says, Saturn by his sudden arrival naturally came to be called a celestial being. For the common people also call those whose ancestry is uncertain “sons of the earth.” I omit the fact that human beings were then still so uncultivated that they were stirred by the sight of any new man as though by something divine. Among the pagans, no commodity was more readily available than gods. Yet scarcely anyone was regarded as older than Saturn. Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII:

> First from ethereal Olympus Saturn came,  
> Fleeing Jove’s arms, an exile from his stolen realms.

LE PR.] Not even so great an antiquity as Saturn possesses today will prove him a god, because novelty once brought even him forward when it first consecrated him.

But living and genuine divinity is judged neither by novelty nor by antiquity, but by its own truth. Eternity has no time, for it is all time. What it produces, it cannot itself undergo. That which cannot be born has no age. If God is old, he will not exist; if he is new, he did not exist. Novelty testifies to a beginning; antiquity threatens an end. But God is as alien to beginning and end as he is to time, the arbiter and surveyor of beginning and end.

## CHAPTER IX

I know, of course, in what sense they boast of a new god: namely, new in being known. But I wished also to repel the very novelty of this knowledge [Note: [Col. 0255C] Perhaps “the novelty of knowledge.”], which strikes inexperienced minds, as well as novelty’s own natural attractiveness, and from this point onward to challenge them concerning an unknown god. For in opposing him as new in being known, they certainly demonstrate that he was unknown before being known.

Come, then, back to the lines and the starting position once more: persuade me that God could have been unknown. [Col. 0255C] [Note: [Col. 0255D] “I do indeed find,” etc. He alludes to the Apostle’s words in Acts XVII: “I found also an altar on which was written: ‘To an unknown God.’” Since this occurred at Athens, he rightly calls it Attic idolatry. Oecumenius, commenting on that passage, writes that the inscription was Greek, ἀγνώστῳ θεῷ (*agnōstō theō*, “to an unknown god”), and gives two explanations for it. The first is that, when a specter of Pan appeared near Parthenion to Athenians sent to the Lacedaemonians for aid against the Persians, and accused them of worshiping other gods while neglecting him, after winning the victory they erected not only a temple to Pan but also an altar to an unknown god, lest anything similar should happen afterward. The second is that, when they were suffering from a plague and the other gods, though invoked, brought no help, they understood that there was some God who was sending the plague and inscribed an altar “To the unknown god”; once this was done, the plague ceased. PAM. Jerome, in chapter II of his commentary on the *Epistle to Titus*, noted that the altar’s inscription was formulated thus: “To the gods of Asia, Europe, and Africa, to unknown and foreign gods.” LE PR.] I do indeed find altars prostituted to unknown gods; but that is Attic idolatry. [Note: [Col. 0256D] “Likewise, to uncertain gods; but that is Roman superstition.” Whenever they had felt an earth tremor or received a report of one, they ordered holidays for that event by an edict; but they refrained from proclaiming the god’s name, lest by naming one instead of another they bind the people to false religion. If anyone profaned those holidays and an expiatory sacrifice were required for the matter, he sacrificed a victim “whether to a god or to a goddess.” Aulus Gellius, book II, chapter 28. Tertullian himself cites Varro on this matter in book II *To the Nations*. RIG.] Likewise, I find altars to uncertain gods; but that is Roman superstition.

Moreover, uncertain gods are less known because less certain, and therefore unknown insofar as they are less certain. Which of these two titles shall we inscribe upon Marcion’s god? Both, I think: uncertain now and unknown in the past. For just as the known God, the Creator, made him unknown, so the certain God made him uncertain.

But I shall not wander farther in order to make my point. If God [Note: [Col. 0255C] “If” absent from Fran., Paris.] was unknown and lay concealed, some region of concealment overshadowed him—a region itself certainly new, unknown [Note: [Col. 0256C] “And” absent from Fran., Paris.], and likewise still uncertain; certainly some immeasurable region, and undoubtedly greater than the god whom it concealed. But I shall state my case briefly and pursue it most fully, prescribing [Note: [Col. 0256D] “Prescribing that [he will] make [it] fully equal.” “Prescribing to someone that there is one God” [the reading *cuinam* is uncertain]; that is, in forensic usage, replying to the opponents’ objections and refuting them. LE PR.] that God neither could have remained unknown, on account of his greatness, nor ought to have remained unknown, on account of his kindness—especially if, in both respects, he was more eminent than our Creator.

Yet because I observe that, in certain matters, the proof of every new and formerly unknown god must be challenged according to the pattern of the Creator, I must first establish that we do this rationally, so that I may employ the support of the principle already stated with greater firmness. Before all else, what sense does it make that you, who acknowledge God as Creator and confess that he was earlier in being known, should not understand that another god must be examined for you by the same methods through which you have already learned [Note: [Col. 0256C] “You have learned,” plural, Rhen.] to know God in the former? Every prior thing has furnished a standard in advance for what comes later.

Two gods are now proposed: one unknown, the other known. No question need be raised about the known one: it is established that he exists, because he would not have been known unless he existed. Concerning the unknown one the dispute presses: for he may also not exist, because, if he existed, he would have been known. Whatever is sought, therefore, remains uncertain so long as it is unknown; and so long as it is sought it is uncertain [Note: [Col. 0256C] “In uncertainty,” Rhen.]; and it may not exist so long as it is uncertain [Note: [Col. 0256C] “That,” i.e., the same reading.]. You have one God certain insofar as he is known, and another uncertain insofar as he is unknown.

If this is so, does it not seem to you to be defended by just reasoning that uncertain things should be tested according to the standard, pattern, and rule of certain things? Otherwise, if arguments drawn from uncertain things are applied to this case, which itself is still uncertain, the sequence of questions will become entangled through the examination of those equally uncertain arguments themselves, whose credibility is endangered by uncertainty; and the discussion will proceed into those interminable questions which the Apostle does not approve (1 Tim. I, 4).

If, however, the principles drawn from things certain, undoubted, and settled prejudge matters uncertain, doubtful, and unresolved, then certainly, where a diversity of condition is found, uncertain matters perhaps should not be challenged according to the pattern of certain ones, since the diversity of their principal condition frees them from the remaining demand for comparison. But when two gods are proposed, their principal condition is shared. For what God is [Note: [Col. 0257D] “For what is God?” Seml.], both are: unborn, unmade, eternal. This will be their principal condition. Let Marcion see to the other attributes, if he has arranged them in diversity; for they come later in the examination. Indeed, they will not even be admitted if the principal condition is established.

Moreover, it is established that both are gods, and thus that the condition of those under discussion is shared. When they are summoned under that condition for proof, if they are uncertain they must be challenged according to the pattern of those certain things with which they are judged to share the principal condition, so that they may likewise share in the manner of proof. Hence [Note: [Col. 0257D] “Accordingly I shall proceed most firmly.” I shall turn back upon them the arguments which they have directed against us. *Dirigere* means to proceed by law, or to bring suit and institute an action; thus Digest, book I, § *Si ego*, *If Part of an Inheritance Is Claimed*: “And let him also direct an action against the external possessor.” LE PR.] I shall accordingly maintain most firmly [Col. 0257B] that he is not God who is made uncertain today because he was unknown in the past; since, in the case of him whose existence is established, that existence is established by this very fact: that he was never unknown and therefore never uncertain.

## CHAPTER X
For from the beginning of things, their Creator was made known together with them, since they were brought forth precisely so that God might be known. Even if Moses, who came later, appears to have been the first to enshrine the God of the world in the temple of his writings, recognition of God is not therefore to be dated from the Pentateuch; for the whole tenor of Moses’ writing does not establish knowledge of the Creator for the first time, but recounts it from the beginning—from Paradise and Adam—not as something to be reckoned from Egypt and Moses. Indeed, the greater part [Note: [Col. 0257D] “The greater part of the human race.” That is, the consensus of the nations, the common consciousness. RIG.] of the human race, who do not even know the name of Moses, much less [Col. 0257C] his written document, nevertheless know the God of Moses, even though so great [Note: [Col. 0257D] *Tanta*, Semler.] a dominion of his is overshadowed by idolatry [Note: [Col. 0257D] *Idololatriae*, Rhenanus.]. Yet they speak of him separately, as though by his proper name, simply as “God,” and as “the God of gods”; and they say, “If God grants it,” “What pleases God,” and “I commend it to God.” See whether they know him whom they attest to be capable of all things. Nor do they owe this to any books of Moses. The soul is earlier than prophecy. For consciousness of God has been the soul’s endowment from the beginning; it is one and the same in Egyptians, Syrians, and people of Pontus. Souls call the God of the Jews “God.” [Note: [Col. 0258D] Semler inserts *et*.] Do not, barbarous heretic, place Abraham before the world. Even if the Creator had been the God of a single family, he would still not have been later than your god, since he was known even to the people of Pontus before him. Accept, therefore, the pattern from your predecessor: you who are uncertain, from him who is certain; you who are unknown, from him who is known. God will never be hidden; God will never be absent. He will always be understood, always heard; he will even be seen, in whatever way he wills. [Col. 0258A] God has witnesses: the entirety of what we are and that within which we exist. Thus he is proved to be both God and the one God, since he is not unknown, while another is still struggling to be proved.

## CHAPTER XI

“And rightly so,” they say; “for who is not better known to his own than to strangers?” No one. I hold you to this statement as well. For how can anything be foreign to God, to whom nothing would be foreign if he existed? For it belongs to the very nature of God that all things should be his and all things should pertain to him—unless he wished immediately to hear from us: “What, then, has he to do with strangers?” He will hear that more fully in its proper place. For the present, it is enough that no being is proved whose possessions furnish no proof of him. For just as the Creator is thereby both God and God beyond doubt, because all things are his and nothing is foreign to him, so the other is for that very reason not God, because all things are not his and are therefore [Col. 0258B] foreign to him. Indeed, if the universe belongs to the Creator, I no longer see any place for another god. All things are full and occupied by their own author. If some space lies vacant in created things for some divinity, it will clearly lie vacant for a false one. [Note: [Col. 0258D] *False*, Rhenanus, Junius.] Truth lies open to falsehood. Why does so great a host of idols not receive Marcion’s god somewhere among them?

Accordingly, on this point also I demand conformity to the pattern of the Creator: God ought to have been known from the works of some world, human being, and age belonging properly to himself. For even the world’s error assumed gods for this reason, gods whom it sometimes admits to have been human beings, because each of them appears to have provided something for the uses and conveniences of life. [Note: [Col. 0257D] “For even the world’s error,” etc. The author discussed this most extensively above, *Apology*, ch. 2, also demonstrating [Col. 0258D] the vanity of those reasons for which the world presumed beings to be gods—namely, because they had provided something for human benefit. PAM.] Thus, following the pattern of God, people believed that to establish or disclose something suitable and necessary for human affairs was divine. So thoroughly was authority for false divinity borrowed [Note: [Col. 0258D] Semler inserts *si*; Rhenanus reads *si false*.] [Col. 0258C] from the source from which that of the true divinity had first proceeded. Marcion’s god ought at least to have brought forth one little chickpea of his own, so that he might be proclaimed some new Triptolemus. [Note: [Col. 0258D] “At least one little chickpea,” etc. Vatican MS 2 reads *saltim*, in the old manner, but I was unwilling to alter it. He fittingly employs the metaphor of the chickpea because Triptolemus was the first to transmit the method of sowing. Hence the author’s words in the book *To Herennius*: “If Triptolemus, when he distributed seed to everyone.” PAM.]

Or else produce a reason worthy of God why he created nothing, if he exists; for he would have created something if he had existed. This follows from precisely that prior judgment by which it is evident that our God exists only because he created this entire universe. For once and for all this rule will stand: they cannot both confess that the Creator is God and fail to prove, according to the pattern of him whom they themselves and everyone else acknowledge as God, the being whom they likewise wish to be believed a god. Since no one doubts that the Creator is God for the very reason that he created this entire universe, by that same reason no one ought to believe that one who created nothing is also God, unless perhaps some explanation is produced. This explanation must necessarily be seen as twofold: either he was unwilling to create anything, or he was unable. [Col. 0258D] There is no third possibility. But inability is unworthy of God; I wish to inquire whether unwillingness is worthy of him.

Tell me, [Col. 0259A] Marcion: did your god wish to be known at any time whatsoever? Or [Note: [Col. 0259D] *Annon?*, Semler; *an*, Franek.] did he descend, preach, suffer, and rise again with some purpose other than to become known? And without doubt, if he became known, he willed it; for nothing would occur in relation to him unless he willed it. Why, then, did he take such pains to procure knowledge of himself that he was displayed in the disgrace of flesh—a disgrace all the greater if the flesh was false? [Note: [Col. 0259D] *False*, Rhenanus.] For it is more shameful if he also lied about the substance of his body, he who even accepted upon himself the Creator’s curse by being suspended from a tree. How much more honorably would he have prepared the way for knowledge of himself through some evidences of his own workmanship—especially since he had to become known in opposition to one by whom, from the beginning, he had not been known through works.

And what sort of arrangement is this: that the Creator, who according to the Marcionites did not know that another god existed above him and who even swore and affirmed that he alone existed (Isa. [Col. 0259B] 40:8), fortified knowledge of himself with such great works, although under the presumption that he was the only God he need not have taken such care over it; whereas the higher god, though knowing that the lower god was so well furnished, made no provision for the equipment by which he himself might be recognized? [Note: [Col. 0259D] “Made no provision for the equipment by which he might be recognized.” That is, an adornment or prerogative of creation through which he might be known by what was, as it were, his own apparatus and his own glory. LE PR.] For he ought to have created works still more distinguished and sublime [Note: [Col. 0259D] *Superiora*, Ciacconius.], so that, following the Creator’s pattern, he might be known as God from his works and, from works more honorable than the Creator’s, as greater and nobler than the Creator.

## CHAPTER XII

Besides, even if we could confess that he exists, we would have to argue that he exists without a cause. For one who possessed no thing would exist without a cause, because every thing is a cause for the existence of someone to whom that thing belongs. Now, insofar as nothing ought to exist without a cause—that is, without a thing—because [Col. 0259C] if it exists without a cause, it is just as though it did not exist, since it does not possess the thing that causes its existence, namely the thing itself [Note: [Col. 0259D] *Res ipsa*, Semler.]; to that same extent I shall believe it more worthy of God not to exist than to exist without a cause. For he exists without a cause who, because he possesses no thing, possesses no cause. But God ought not to exist without a cause, that is, without a thing belonging to him. Thus, whenever I show that he exists without a cause, supposing that he exists, I establish that he does not exist; for if he had existed, he certainly would not have existed without a cause.

So too I say that he seeks faith from humanity without cause, since humanity has customarily believed in a God whose form is established by the authority of his works [Note: [Col. 0259D] *Formatam*, Junius.], whereas he provided nothing of the kind through which humanity learned of God. For even if many believe in him, [Col. 0260A] they do not therefore believe on rational grounds, since they possess no pledge of his divinity—works worthy of God. Accordingly, by reason of this cessation and failure of works, he is closely allied both to shamelessness [Note: [Col. 0260D] Perhaps *imprudentiae*, “imprudence.” Editors.] and to malice: [Note: [Col. 0259D] “Allied to malice.” A participant in malice. Cicero uses that expression in this sense concerning Sulla: “Allied to this suspicion.” LE PR.] to shamelessness [Note: [Col. 0260D] The same.], because he seeks a faith not owed to him, having provided nothing by which that faith might be prepared; and to malice, because he has made many guilty of unbelief by providing nothing to support faith.

## CHAPTER XIII

When at this stage we expel a god whom no creation has marked out beforehand by its testimony—a condition as peculiarly proper to and worthy of God as the Creator’s—the utterly shameless Marcionites curl their noses [Note: [Col. 0259D] “The utterly shameless Marcionites curling their noses.” Mocking slyly and holding people up to ridicule with hooked nose. LE PR.] and turn to disparaging the Creator’s works. “A magnificent work indeed,” they say, “and worthy of God—the world! Is the Creator, then, by no means God?” Certainly he is God. “Then neither is the world unworthy of God.” For God made nothing unworthy of himself, even if he made the world for humanity and not for himself, and even if every work is inferior to its craftsman. And yet, if it is unworthy of God to have made something of a particular kind, how much more unworthy of God is it to have made absolutely nothing, not even something unworthy, by which he might have given grounds for hoping that he was the author of worthier things!

To say something, then, even about the supposed unworthiness of this world—whose very Greek name signifies adornment and ordered beauty, not filth [Note: [Col. 0259D] A well-known saying of Pythagoras. Hence also Aristotle’s statement in the book *On the World*: “You may fittingly call the universe itself κόσμος (*kosmos*), that is, a composite structure of things arranged harmoniously in an orderly system.” EDITORS, after PAM.]—those very professors of wisdom, from whose talents every heresy draws its life, declared its allegedly unworthy substances to be gods: Thales declared water a god; Heraclitus, fire; Anaximenes, air; Anaximander, all the heavenly bodies; Strato, heaven and earth; Zeno, air and ether; Plato, the stars, which in his discussion of the world he calls a fiery race of gods. Considering, [Col. 0260C] that is, the magnitude, force, power, dignity, beauty, assistance, reliability, and law of each of the elements—which work together in the generation, nourishment, dissolution, and renewal of all things—most natural philosophers were afraid to assign a beginning and an end to the world, [Note: [Col. 0260D] *Constare*, Semler.] lest its substances, so great as they are, should thereby be regarded as less divine. These are also worshiped by the Magi of the Persians [Note: [Col. 0260D] *Quos*, Semler.], the hierophants of the Egyptians, [Note: [Col. 0260D] “And the hierophants of the Egyptians.” They were called ἱεροφάνται (*hierophantai*) because they displayed or performed the sacred rites; they were a class of priests among the Egyptians. PAM.] and the gymnosophists of India. [Note: [Col. 0260D] “The gymnosophists of India.” In *Apology* 32 he had likewise spoken of the gymnosophists as Indians. Sidonius Apollinaris, *Letters* VIII.3, however, appears to maintain that the gymnosophists belonged to Ethiopia and the Brahmans to India: “Now, devoting yourself wholly to reading, travel in a sense even yourself to the gymnosophists of the Ethiopians and the Brahmans of the Indians.” Clement of Alexandria does not depart from that position in *Stromata* I: παρ᾽ Ἰνδοῖς ἀπὸ τῶν βραχμάνων, “among the Indians, from the Brahmans.” LE PR.]

Common popular superstition, too, which is shared by idolatry generally, when it is ashamed of the names and fables of ancient dead persons represented in its images, retreats to interpretations based on natural phenomena and veils its disgrace with ingenuity. It figures Jupiter as a fiery substance and his Juno as an airy one, according to the sound of their Greek names; likewise Vesta as fire, the Camenae as water, and the Great Mother as the earth—reaped of her seeds, plowed by arms, and watered by baths. So too Osiris, [Note: [Col. 0261B] *Osirin*, Paris, Franek.] who is always buried, sought alive, and found with rejoicing, is interpreted as signifying the reliable recurrence of crops, living elements, and the returning year; just as they philosophize that the lions of Mithras are mysteries of a dry and burning nature. [Note: [Col. 0261C] “Just as they philosophize that the lions of Mithras are mysteries of a dry and burning nature.” Images of lions were employed in the mysteries of Mithras, or the Sun. They were *sacramenta*, that is, signs or mysteries of the sun’s dry and burning nature. For the heat grows intense and springs and rivers dry up when the Sun is said to enter Leo; then, finally, the abduction of Ceres’ daughter is celebrated—that is, the harvest takes place. The scholiast on Aratus: Κόρην γὰρ εἶναι τοὺς καρποὺς λέγουσι, καὶ μητέρα τὴν γῆν· καὶ γὰρ παρ᾽ Αἰγυπτίοις κατὰ τὸν Ἐμφὶ μῆνα, ὅτε ἐν λέοντι γίνεται ὁ ἥλιος, ἡ τῆς Κόρης ἁρπαγὴ τελειοῦται. “For they say that the Maiden is the crops and the Mother is the earth. Indeed, among the Egyptians, in the month Emphi, when the sun is in Leo, the abduction of the Maiden is celebrated.” Germanicus, on Leo:

“When Phoebus’ more violent orbit reaches him,  
The summer, already kindled in Cancer, will then be doubled;  
Then the waters run thin, then the earth is most sorrowful,  
And the joyful plowman safely stores his dense-packed grain.”

EDITORS, FROM RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0261D] “They philosophize about Mithras.” There is scarcely anyone who does not know that Mithras is a god of the Persians, and indeed their foremost god. Hesychius: μίθρης ὁ πρῶτος ἐν Πέρσαις θεός, “Mithras, the foremost god among the Persians”; there he also says that Mithras is the Sun. He was portrayed with the face of a lion, the most ardent of animals, because, as St. Jerome teaches in Book I *Against Jovinian*, he was begotten from the heat of lust, in the manner of Erichthonius. Hence the expressions “burning nature” are also used here. LE PR.]

It is enough that substances higher in position or status have been more readily regarded as gods than as unworthy of God. I shall descend to lowly things. A single tiny flower from the hedges—I do not say from the meadows; a single little shell from any sea—I do not say the Red Sea; a single feather of a grouse—I say nothing of the peacock: will any of these declare to you that the Creator is a filthy craftsman? [Col. 0261B]

## CHAPTER XIV

But when you also ridicule the smaller animals, which the supreme Craftsman deliberately enlarged in ingenuity or strength—thus teaching that greatness is proved in smallness, just as power is proved in weakness, according to the Apostle (2 Cor. 12:9)—imitate, if you can, the structures of the bee, the storehouses of the ant, the webs of the spider, the threads of the silkworm. Endure, if you can, those very creatures of your bed and mat, the poisons of the blister beetle, the darts of the fly, and both the trumpet and the lance of the mosquito. What will the greater creatures be like, when things so small can either help or harm you, so that even among small things you may not despise the Creator?

Finally, turn your attention to yourself; consider the human being within and without. You will find pleasing [Col. 0262A] at least this work of our God, which that lord of yours, the “better god,” loved: for its sake he labored to descend from the third heaven into these paltry elements; for its sake he was even crucified in this little chamber belonging to the Creator. Yet to this very day he has not rejected the Creator’s water, with which he washes his own; nor the oil with which he anoints them; nor the mixture of honey and milk with which he feeds them as infants; nor the bread by which he presents his own body [Note: [Col. 0261D] “The bread by which he presents his own body.” Bellarmine explains as follows, against the Calvinists who misuse these words: “The verb *to represent* is ambiguous: for it signifies making some thing present, either in the thing itself or in some sign [Col. 0262C] or image. And, to omit the testimonies of Cicero and even of the holy Fathers, who frequently use this word to signify that some thing is exhibited as truly and properly present, Tertullian himself can furnish examples of both meanings. In Book IV *Against Marcion*, around the middle, he says, ‘Thus, now presenting him: “This is my Son,”’ etc. There he says that God the Father, who had once promised the Son, presented that same Son when he said on Mount Tabor, ‘This is my Son’; there he very plainly calls exhibiting something in the thing itself ‘representing.’ And in the book *Against Praxeas* he calls the Son the representative of the Father, because the Father is truly in the Son. But the same author, in his book *On Repentance*, distinguishes adultery committed in the act itself [Col. 0262D] from adultery represented in the mind through lust; there ‘to represent’ means to exhibit something not in the thing itself but in an image. Since, therefore, the word is ambiguous, it cannot in any way be rightly inferred that Tertullian is speaking of representation in a sign rather than in reality. Indeed, rather the contrary: because that which is exhibited in reality is said more properly to be represented than that which is exhibited only in a sign, it will more probably be inferred that Tertullian speaks of a representation by which the Lord’s body is exhibited in reality. Hence Peter Martyr, in his book *Against Gardiner*, objection 160, when treating this passage of Tertullian, admits that nothing certain can be concluded from this passage alone, but that Tertullian’s meaning must be sought from other passages (*On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, Book II, ch. 7).” And indeed the most learned cardinal cites several testimonies from our Author by which the doctrine of the real presence is confirmed in a remarkable manner. See especially *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 8. EDITORS.]; even in his own sacraments he is reduced to begging from the Creator.

But you, a disciple above the master and a servant above the lord, think more loftily than he does, destroying the things he desires. I wish to see whether you act at least in good faith, and whether you yourself do not crave the things you destroy. You oppose heaven, yet you seize the freedom of heaven for your dwellings. You despise the earth, though it is clearly the womb of your flesh, which is now hostile to you [Note: [Col. 0261C] *Inimice*, Semler.]; and you wrench all its marrow from it for food. You reject the sea—but only until you reach its provisions, which you regard as holier food. If I offer you a rose, you will not disdain the Creator. Hypocrite, prove yourself a Marcionite by self-starvation (*apokarterēsis*) [Note: [Col. 0262B] *Hypocritam! ut*, Semler; *hypocrita, muta*, Rhenanus.]—that is, one who repudiates the Creator; for this practice ought to have been pursued among you as martyrdom if the world displeased you. Into whatever material you are dissolved, you make use of the Creator’s substance. [Note: [Col. 0262D] “Prove yourself a Marcionite by self-starvation.” [Col. 0263D] Even if, from hatred of the Creator, you abstain from everything created and waste away after renouncing all the supports of life, nevertheless, into whatever material your limbs are dissolved, they will be resolved into one of the substances established by God the Creator. RIG.—According to Suidas, the Greeks use ἀποκαρτερεῖν (*apokarterein*) when someone ends his life either by starvation or by hanging; hence ἀποκαρτέρησις (*apokarterēsis*). The author also uses this term in the *Apology*, writing: “Lycurgus chose ἀποκαρτέρησιν (*apokarterēsin*) because the Spartans had amended his laws.” Moreover, he here calls Marcion a hypocrite because he destroys and despises the Creator’s things not in good faith or sincerely, but only in pretense. RHEN.] [Note: [Col. 0262C] *Substantia*, Semler.] How great is the obstinacy of your hardness! You depreciate the things in which you both live and die.

## CHAPTER XV

After this—or before it—when you have said that he too possesses his own creation, his own world, and his own heaven, [Col. 0263A] we shall indeed examine that third heaven if we come to the point of scrutinizing your apostle. Meanwhile, whatever that substance may be, it certainly ought to have appeared together with its own god. But as matters now stand, how is it that the Lord was revealed in the twelfth year of Tiberius Caesar, yet by the fifteenth year of the emperor Severus absolutely no substance had been discovered which, as necessarily surpassing the Creator’s paltry things, would have ceased to be hidden once its own lord and author was no longer hidden? [Note: [Col. 0263D] “That the Lord, in the twelfth year of Tiberius Caesar.” This passage is reckoned among Tertullian’s errors. We discussed it earlier. He evidently thought that Christ began his preaching in the twelfth year of Tiberius and suffered death three years later. LE PR.] And therefore, if that substance could not be manifested in this world, how did its Lord appear in this world? If this world contained its Lord, why could it not contain the substance—unless perhaps that substance was greater than its Lord?

The question now concerns place, and it pertains both to that higher world and to its God himself. For see: if he too possesses his own world beneath himself and above the Creator, he must have made it in a place, in the space that lay vacant between his own feet and the Creator’s head. Therefore God himself was also in a place and made the world in a place; and that place will now be greater than both God and the world. For whatever contains something is necessarily greater than that which it contains. We must also see [Note: [Col. 0264D] “Whether any leftover plots still lie vacant there.” *Subsiciva* or *subseciva* frequently occurs among writers on the regulation of boundaries. Agennius Urbicus: “When, however, an allotment was made within an allotted tract of land, the entire extent could not be assigned to the veterans within four boundaries. Something remained there which took its name from the line that cut it off: a *subsecivum*, or leftover plot.” RIG.] whether any leftover plots still lie vacant there [Note: [Col. 0263C] *Subcisiva*, Franek; *subscidiva, subsciva*, Rhenanus.], in which some third god [Note: [Col. 0263C] *Aliquis*, Paris.] might squeeze himself together with his own world. Therefore begin now to count gods. For the place too will be a god—not only because it is greater than God, but because it is unborn and unmade, and therefore eternal and equal to God, since God has always existed within it.

Next, if that god fashioned his world from some underlying matter—unborn, unmade, and coeval with God—just as Marcion believes concerning the Creator, you reduce this also to the majesty of the place that enclosed both god and matter: two gods. For matter too is God according to the defining form of divinity, since it is unborn, unmade, and eternal. Or if he fashioned the world from nothing, Marcion will be compelled to believe the same about the Creator, to whom he assigns matter as the substance of the world. Yet that other god too will have had to make his world from matter, since the same reasoning that was opposed to the Creator will also confront him as equally God. Thus, for the moment, count three gods of Marcion for me: Maker, Place, and Matter.

Likewise he locates the Creator in a place, necessarily judging him according to the same condition; and he subjects matter to him, necessarily regarding it as unborn and unmade and, on that account, eternal like the Lord. Furthermore, by ascribing evil to matter—an evil unborn as matter is unborn, unmade as it is unmade, and eternal as it is eternal—he has thereby made a fourth god. You therefore have three substances of divinity in the higher regions and four in the lower. When their respective Christs are added to these—the one who appeared under Tiberius and the other who is promised by the Creator—Marcion plainly suffers misrepresentation from those who presume that he introduces two gods, since he assigns nine, although unknowingly.

## CHAPTER XVI

Since, therefore, no other world appears, just as its God does not appear either, the consequence is that they divide the two classes of things, visible and invisible, between two divine authors, and claim the invisible things for their own god. But who could persuade himself—unless possessed by a heretical spirit—that invisible things belong to one who produced no visible things beforehand, rather than to the one who, by making visible things, also established confidence in the invisible, since it is far more reasonable to assent on the basis of some examples than on the basis of none? We shall also see to which author the Apostle (Col. 1:16) assigns the invisible things when we have examined him too.

For now, by means of generally accepted perceptions and sound arguments, we prepare confidence in the advocacy of the Scriptures that is to follow, [Note: [Col. 0264D] “The advocacy of the Scriptures.” *Advocatio* properly means the crowd of advocates and friends who stand beside someone in court. Here he uses it to mean a defense. So too in the book *On Patience*: “Thus both advocacy and laughter are promised to such people as consolation.” RHEN.] confirming that this diversity of visible and invisible things must so fully be assigned to the Creator [Note: [Col. 0264C] *Deo*, Wouwer manuscript; *a Deo creatori*, Rhenanus.], since his entire operation consists of diversities: corporeal and incorporeal, animate and inanimate, vocal and mute, mobile and stationary, generative and sterile, dry and moist [Note: [Col. 0264C] *Siccis*, Rhenanus.], hot and cold.

Diversity has likewise composed the human being himself, both in body and in sensation. Some limbs are strong, others weak; some honorable, others dishonorable; some paired, others single; some corresponding, others unequal. So too in sensation there is now joy, now distress; now love, now hatred; now anger, now gentleness. If this is so—if this whole created order has been harmoniously composed of things opposed to one another—then invisible things must belong with visible things and must not be assigned to any author other than the one to whom their opposites also belong. These oppositions mark the Creator himself as diverse [Note: [Col. 0264D] *Notant*, Pamelius.]: commanding what he had forbidden, forbidding what he had commanded, striking and healing. Why, in this one category alone, do they understand him as uniform, assigning him only visible things, both life and death, evils and peace (Sir. 11:14; Isa. 45:7)? And certainly, if those invisible things are greater than the visible creatures—which are themselves great in their proper sphere—it is likewise fitting that the greater things belong to him to whom the great things also belong; for neither great things, much less greater ones, can properly belong to one of whom not even small things appear.

## CHAPTER XVII

Pressed hard by these arguments, [Note: [Col. 0265D] “Pressed hard by these arguments, they burst out saying.” The Marcionites, evidently, who taunted God the Creator as the creator of worms, locusts, bedbugs, and so forth. Arnobius, Book II *Against the Nations*: “For it does not follow, if we deny that flies, beetles, bedbugs, small moths, weevils, and larger moths are the work of the omnipotent King….” But St. Jerome speaks with still greater clarity in the preface to his commentary on the *Epistle to Philemon*: “But if they do not think that small things belong to those to whom great things also belong, they ought, following Valentinus, Marcion, and Apelles, to introduce for me one creator of the ant, worms, mosquitoes, and locusts, and another of heaven, earth, sea, and angels. Or does it belong rather to the same power not to deny in smaller things the ingenuity you have exercised in greater things?” LE PR.] they burst out saying: “This single work is enough for our god: that he delivered the human being by his supreme and preeminent goodness, which is to be preferred to all the locusts.” O greater God, whose work, though so great, could be found nowhere except in the human being belonging to the lesser god!

In truth, you must first prove that he exists through the things by which God ought to be proved—through works—and only afterward through benefits. For the first question is whether he exists; then, what sort of being he is. The one will be discerned from works, the other from benefits. [Note: [Col. 0265C] *Dei dignoscitur*, Pamelius.] Besides, his existence is not established merely because he is said to have delivered humanity; rather, if his existence has been established, then it will also be said that he delivered humanity, so that whether he did deliver it may likewise be established. For he could both have existed and not have delivered it. How, then, will he also be believed to exist because he is said to have delivered humanity, when he could have existed without delivering it?

Now, having been led aside at this point from the question concerning the unknown God, [Note: [Col. 0265C] *Deducta*, Semler; *deductis*, Venetian edition; *deductus*, Gorze manuscript.] it has been sufficiently established both that he created nothing and that he ought to have created something so that he might be known from his works. For if he had existed, he ought to have been known—and certainly from the beginning of things, since it would not have been fitting for God to remain hidden. I must return to the origin of the question of the unknown God, so that I may also shake out its other branches. For the first question concerning one who subsequently brought himself to people’s knowledge must be: Why later, and not from the beginning of things? Since he was necessary to them as God—and, as the better God, all the more necessary—he certainly ought not to have remained hidden. For it cannot be said that there was neither material nor cause for making God known, since from the beginning humanity existed in the world—the humanity he now assists—and so did the Creator’s malice, against which he assists humanity as the good God. Therefore he either failed to recognize both the cause and the material [Col. 0266A] of his necessary revelation, or hesitated, or was unable, or was unwilling. All these alternatives are unworthy of God, especially of the supremely good God. But we shall also treat this subject fully elsewhere by reproaching the lateness of his revelation, just as here we provide only a demonstration of it.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Come, then: let him have advanced into people’s knowledge when he willed, when he was able, when the fated hour arrived. Perhaps the *anabibazon*—the ruling planet or rising sign—was obstructing him, [Note: [Col. 0265D] “Perhaps the *anabibazon* was obstructing him.” The chronocrator, that is, the planet or sign ascending in the horoscope at the hour of birth, as the astrologers teach—that most impious race of human beings, who put trappings upon the populace and deceive the simple with their inventions and falsehoods. LE PR.] or some malignant stars, or Saturn in quartile, or Mars in trine. For the Marcionites are very much astrologers [Note: [Col. 0266D] “For the Marcionites are very much astrologers.” They declared that they lived by the stars—that is, that their lives depended on the motion of the stars—although they refused to acknowledge the Creator of those stars. Here the name “mathematicians” does not condemn the whole of mathematics, but only that superstition which, though it is not a part of mathematics—I mean judicial astrology—wishes to be adopted among the branches of mathematical learning, something that cannot be done. Since the mathematical disciplines admit nothing without demonstration, they reject judicial astrology, for which—since it is a most pernicious error—there is no demonstration. He attacked judicial astrology elsewhere; see *On Idolatry*. LE PR.], and they do not blush even at deriving their life from the Creator’s own stars.

Here too we must consider the quality of the revelation: whether he became known in a manner worthy of God, so that it may be established whether he was truly made known, and consequently that the being whose revelation is shown to have been worthy of God may be believed to exist. For things worthy of God will prove him to be God. We maintain that God must first be known through nature and then recognized through teaching: through nature from his works, and through teaching from proclamations. But one who possesses no created order has no natural instruments available to him. Therefore he ought at least to have accomplished the revelation of himself through proclamations, especially since he had to be revealed in opposition to one who, through so many and such great works both of creation and proclamation, had nevertheless scarcely won human faith. [Note: [Col. 0266D] “Had filled human beings with faith.” So reads Ursinus’ copy. The common reading, which is also that of the Pithou manuscript, *hominem fide impleverat*, “had filled the human being with faith,” can nevertheless be retained. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0266C] *Hominem fide*, Pamelius.]

How, then, was he revealed? If through human conjecture, deny that God [Note: [Col. 0266C] Pamelius: *Est, si per humanam conjecturam negat Deum*; Semler: *negas, Deum*; perhaps *nego*, Editors.] can be known otherwise than through himself. This conclusion follows not only from an appeal to the Creator’s pattern, but also from the condition both of divine greatness and of human smallness, lest the human being appear greater than God by having somehow dragged into the public sphere of recognition, through his own powers, a god who did not spontaneously wish to become known. [Note: [Col. 0266C] Latinus inserts *modo*; Pamelius reads *qui non eum non*.] For, as the experience of every age shows, human smallness knows more readily how to fashion gods for itself than how to pursue the true God whom people already understand by nature.

Otherwise, if a human being is to devise a god in this way—as Romulus devised Consus, Tatius Cloacina, Hostilius Pavor, Metellus Alburnus, and someone before the present time Antinous—then the same will be permitted to others. We know Marcion as a shipmaster, not as a king or emperor.

## CHAPTER XIX

[Col. 0267A]

> “No,” the Marcionites say, “our God, although not from the beginning and although not through creation, was nevertheless revealed through himself in Christ Jesus.”

A separate book will also be devoted to Christ and to every aspect of his condition; for the subjects must be distinguished so that they may be examined more fully and systematically. Meanwhile, for the present stage it will suffice to meet the argument by showing, and indeed in a few words, that Christ Jesus was the agent of no God other than the Creator.

In the fifteenth year of Tiberius, Christ Jesus deigned to flow down from heaven as a saving spirit—the salvation of Marcion [Note: [Col. 0267C] Pamelius reads *salutis* (“of salvation”); Semler conjectures the same], who so willed it [Note: [Col. 0267C] Semler conjectures *valuit*, “was able”]. [Note: [Col. 0267D] In precisely what year of the elder Antoninus. What he said above, in *On the Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 30, simply as “approximately in the reign of Antoninus,” is explained here, since the text states in which year of Antoninus Marcion’s Christ began to be revealed. We said something there as though the heretic Marcion had first appeared under Antoninus the Philosopher, because it was under Anicetus. But because I later discovered that Anicetus occupied the Roman see for about six years before the death of Antoninus Pius, I am compelled to agree with the author here that Marcion began under the elder Antoninus, that is, Pius, as immediately follows; all the others borrowed from him either the name or the praenomen Antoninus. This is especially so because Eusebius writes, both in his *Chronicle* and in *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, ch. 13, that Polycarp came to Rome at the beginning of Anicetus’s pontificate, and likewise writes that Marcion encountered Polycarp there. PAM.] In precisely what year of the elder Antoninus that dog-day breeze [Note: [Col. 0267C] Junius reads *aula* (“court”) instead of *aura* (“breeze”)] exhaled from his native Pontus, I have not troubled to investigate. This much, however, is certain about him: he is an Antonine heretic, [Col. 0267B] impious under Pius. [Note: [Col. 0267D] But from Tiberius to Antoninus, the years, etc. [Col. 0268D] If the reading were “one hundred and five years,” it would come closer to historical truth, since that number is found between the fifteenth year of Tiberius, which he mentioned shortly before and from which he undoubtedly intended to begin his computation, and the time of Marcion. He is counting, as he adds, the intervening years between Christ and Marcion. PAM.] From Tiberius to Antoninus, moreover, there are approximately one hundred and fifteen and a half years, together with half a month: they place just that much time between Christ and Marcion.

Since, therefore, Marcion was the first to introduce this god under Antoninus, as we have proved, the matter is immediately clear, if you have any sense. The chronology establishes in advance that what first emerged under Antoninus had not emerged under Tiberius; that is, the god of the Antonine reign [Note: [Col. 0267C] Pamelius reads “of Antoninus, of the reign”] did not exist in the Tiberian reign, and accordingly was not revealed by Christ, since it is agreed that he was first [Note: [Col. 0267D] Semler and Oberthür read “for the first time”] proclaimed by Marcion.

To prove now that this is an established fact, I shall take the remaining evidence from our adversaries themselves. The separation of the Law and the Gospel is Marcion’s peculiar and principal work. His disciples will not be able to deny what they possess in their chief instrument, by which, in short, they are initiated and hardened [Note: [Col. 0267D] Semler and Oberthür read “are identified”] in this heresy. For these are Marcion’s *Antitheses*, that is, opposing contradictions, which attempt to set the Gospel at variance [Note: [Col. 0268C] Semler omits “of the Gospel”] with the Law, so that from the diversity of the propositions in the two Testaments they may also argue for a diversity of gods.

Therefore, since it is precisely that separation of the Law and the Gospel which insinuated the existence of one God of the Gospel in opposition to the God of the Law, it is evident [Col. 0268A] that before that separation the God who became known through the argument of separation was not known. Accordingly, he was not revealed by Christ, who existed before the separation, but was devised by Marcion, who instituted the separation against the harmony of Gospel and Law. From Christ’s appearance down to Marcion’s audacity, that harmony had assuredly been preserved unharmed and unshaken by the principle which maintained that no other God [Note: [Col. 0268C] The Paris edition reads “and God”] of both Law and Gospel existed besides the Creator, against whom the separation was launched so much later by the man from Pontus.

## CHAPTER XX

Against the clamorous objections of the opposing party, a defense of this very straightforward proof is also necessary on our part. For they say that Marcion did not so much introduce a novel rule by separating the Law and the Gospel as restore a rule that had previously been corrupted.

O Christ, most patient Lord, who endured the suppression of your preaching for so many years, until Marcion, of course, came to your aid! [Note: [Col. 0268C] Pamelius reads “of course, came to your aid”; “to you” is absent from Semler.]

For they also cite the fact that Peter himself and the others, the pillars of the apostolate, were rebuked by Paul (Gal. 2) for not walking with a straight step according to the truth of the Gospel. Yet this was the very Paul who, still inexperienced in grace and in fact anxious lest he had run or was running in vain (ibid.), was only then conferring for the first time with the apostles who preceded him.

Therefore, if in his fervor as one still a neophyte [Note: [Col. 0268D] Pamelius reads “still as”; Semler omits “still”] he judged that something in their conduct toward Judaism deserved rebuke—namely, indiscriminate association [Note: [Col. 0268D] “Indiscriminate association,” that is, promiscuous association. See ch. 7. SEML.]—although later by practice he himself would become all things to all people, so that he might gain all, being to the Jews as a Jew, and to those under the Law as though under [Note: [Col. 0268D] Semler and Oberthür read “in”] the Law (1 Cor. 9), you wish that rebuke, which concerned conduct alone and which would afterward be approved even by its own accuser, to be regarded as suspect [Note: [Col. 0268D] Rhenanus reads “undertaken”] of treachery in the preaching about God as well.

On the contrary, concerning unity of preaching, as we read above, they had joined right hands; and by the very distribution of their duties [Note: [Col. 0268D] “They had agreed upon fellowship in the Gospel.” *Condixerant* means “had agreed”; for *condicere* also means “to announce” and “to determine.” A little later we restore the reading, “Long ago proclaiming this very thing.” RHEN.], they had agreed upon fellowship in the Gospel.
