So too elsewhere (1 Cor. 15:11): [Note: [Col. 0268D] “Whether therefore it was I,” he says, “or they, so we preach.” The author translated literally as *praedicamus* (“we preach”) what in Greek is κηρύσσομεν (*kēryssomen*, “we proclaim”), as did Ambrose in his *Commentary*, blessed Augustine in *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, book II, ch. 2, the Syriac edition itself, and the more accurate Latin manuscript codices, instead of the reading in others, *praedicavimus* (“we preached”). The author also agrees with these below, in *Against Marcion*, book IV, ch. 4. PAM.] “Whether therefore it was I,” he says, “or they, so we preach.”

And even if he described certain false brethren as having slipped in, who wished to transfer the Galatians to another gospel (Gal. 1:7), he himself shows that this corruption of the Gospel was directed not toward transferring them to faith in another God and another Christ, but toward preserving [Note: [Col. 0269D] Others read “observing”] the discipline of the Law. He was, of course, rebuking those who championed circumcision and observed the seasons, days, months, and years of Jewish ceremonies (Gal. 4:10), which they ought already to have recognized as abolished under the Creator’s renewed dispensation. The Creator had long ago proclaimed this very thing [Note: [Col. 0269D] Semler and Oberthür omit “this very thing”] through his prophets, as through Isaiah (Isa. 43:19): “The old things have passed away,” he says; “behold the new things that I now perform”; and elsewhere (Jer. 31:32): “And I shall establish a covenant, not like the one I established with your fathers when I led them out of the land [Col. 0269B] of Egypt.”

So too through Jeremiah (Jer. 4:4): “Renew for yourselves a new renewal, and be circumcised to your God, and circumcise the foreskins of your heart.” Therefore, by now establishing this circumcision and this renewal, the Apostle was also dissuading them from those antiquated ceremonies which their own Founder had declared would one day cease, through Hosea (Hos. 2:11): “And I shall turn away all her delights, her feast days, her new moons, her sabbaths, and all her ceremonies.”

Likewise through Isaiah (Isa. 1:14): “Your new moons and sabbaths and great day I cannot endure; my soul hates your holidays and fasting and your feast days.” But if the Creator had already long ago rejected all these things, and the Apostle was pronouncing that they must now be rejected, the Apostle’s very pronouncement, being in agreement with the Creator’s decrees, proves [Col. 0269C] that the Apostle proclaimed no other God than the one whose decrees he desired now to be acknowledged. In this matter, he brands both the apostles and the brethren as false who transferred the Gospel of the Creator’s Christ away from the new order foretold by the Creator and back to the old order rejected by the Creator (Gal. 1:6ff.).

## CHAPTER XXI

Moreover, if in proclaiming what was supposedly a new God he wished to exclude the law of the old God, why does he lay down nothing at all concerning the new god, but only concerning the old Law, unless because, while faith in the Creator remained, only his Law had to be brought to an end? Thus that Psalm had also sung beforehand [Note: [Col. 0269D] Pamelius reads “had sung beforehand”]: “Let us break their bonds from us [Note: [Col. 0270D] Pamelius reads “their bonds from us”], and let us cast their yoke away from us” (Ps. 2:3)—because, of course, “the nations raged, and the peoples devised [Col. 0270A] vain things; the kings of the earth took their stand, and the magistrates assembled [Note: [Col. 0270D] Semler and Oberthür read “surrounded”] together against the Lord and against his Christ” (ibid. 1–2).

And assuredly, if another god were being proclaimed by Paul, there would have been no dispute over whether the Law should be observed, since it would not, of course, belong to the new lord who was hostile to the Law. The very novelty and difference of that god would have removed not merely the question of the old and alien Law but every mention of it. But the entire issue under dispute was that, although the same God of the Law was being proclaimed in Christ, his Law was being diminished. Faith, therefore, always remained fixed upon the Creator and his Christ, while conduct and discipline were unsettled.

[Note: [Col. 0269D] For some also disputed about eating food sacrificed to idols, etc. He alludes to the Apostle’s First Epistle to the Corinthians, in which he argues at length against disputes of this kind: about food sacrificed to idols in ch. 10, women’s veiling in ch. 11, marriages or divorces in ch. 7, and the hope of resurrection in ch. 15. PAM.]

For some also disputed about eating food sacrificed to idols, others about women’s veiling, others about marriage or divorce, and some even about the hope of resurrection; about God, no one disputed. For if [Note: [Col. 0270D] Semler omits “if”] this question too had been disputed, it would itself have been found in the Apostle’s writings—and all the more so, in proportion to its fundamental importance.

But if, after the apostles’ time, the truth suffered corruption concerning the rule of God, then the apostolic tradition had suffered nothing in its own time concerning the rule of God; and no other tradition of the apostles is to be acknowledged than that which is today set forth among the apostles’ own churches. Yet you will find no church of apostolic pedigree that does not profess Christianity in the Creator. Or, if those churches which date from the beginning have been corrupted, which ones will be sound? The Creator’s adversaries, no doubt. Produce, then, some one of your own churches that possesses apostolic doctrine, and you will have prevailed [Note: [Col. 0269D] “And you will have prevailed.” That is, “you will have proved your case.” RHEN. PAM.].

Therefore, since it is established in every way that from Christ down to Marcion no other god than the Creator existed in the rule of this sacrament, our proof is now sufficiently fortified: we have shown that knowledge of the heretics’ god began with the separation of the Gospel and the Law. Our earlier definition has also been substantiated: no god whom a human being has fashioned from his own conceptions is to be believed—unless, of course, that human being is a prophet, that is, one who does not speak from his own conceptions. If Marcion can be called one, that too will have to be proved.

There should have been no need to examine anything further, [Note: [Col. 0269D] “By this wedge of truth.” That is, by this argument, arranged like a wedge-shaped battle formation in defense of the truth. He used this metaphor drawn from military discipline in ch. 2 of *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*: “With what wedge-shaped formation must we meet them?” That type of battle line was invented by Philip of Macedon to break through even the most densely packed ranks of the enemy. By another name the wedge is called a phalanx, and in Greek ἔμβολος ἱππική (*embolos hippikē*, “cavalry wedge”) and στίφος (*stiphοs*, “compact body”). LE PR.] for every heresy is driven out by this wedge of truth, when Christ is shown to be the agent of no god other than the Creator.

## CHAPTER XXII

But how will Antichrist be utterly overthrown [Note: [Col. 0270D] Rhenanus reads “ventilated” or “exposed”] unless room is also given for refuting his other insinuations, by relaxing the defense based on preliminary objections? Let us therefore proceed from here to the very person of his God—or rather, to the shadow and phantom [Note: [Col. 0270D] “Or rather, to the shadow and phantom,” etc. He alludes to Marcion’s error that Christ became man as a phantom, against which he argued above in *On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. 5. PAM.], corresponding to his own Christ—and let him be tested by precisely that quality through which he is preferred to the Creator.

There will assuredly be definite rules for testing God’s goodness. But first I must find that goodness and lay hold of it, and only then bring it to the rules. For when I survey the course of time, it is nowhere to be found from the beginning of created substances and [Note: [Col. 0271D] Semler inserts *in* (“in”).] from the inception of the causes, together with which it ought to have been found, acting from that point onward upon what [Note: [Col. 0271D] Semler, Pamelius, and Oberthür read “whereby”] it had to act.

For death already existed, as did sin, the sting of death, and the Creator’s own supposed wickedness. Against these the goodness of another god ought to have come to the rescue, satisfying this first rule of divine goodness: if it wished to prove itself natural, it should have brought assistance immediately, as soon as the cause arose. For all things in God must be natural and unbegotten, so that they may be eternal in accordance with his condition, lest they be regarded as adventitious and foreign, and therefore temporal and alien to eternity.

Thus goodness too will be required to be perpetual and continuous [Note: [Col. 0271D] “And continuous” is absent from the Paris edition] in God. Stored up and ready in the treasury of his natural properties, it should have preceded its own causes and objects; and, if it did precede them, it should have taken up the very first one rather than disregarding and abandoning it.

In short, I shall ask no less here [Note: [Col. 0271D] Pamelius reads “here no less.”] why his goodness did not operate from the beginning than we asked concerning God himself why he was not revealed from the beginning. And why should I not? If he had existed, he would have had to be revealed through his goodness. [Note: [Col. 0271D] “It is not permissible for God to be unable to do anything.” The sense is: It is not permissible for God to lack the power to do anything, much less to be unable to exercise his natural properties. RHEN.] It is not permissible for God to be unable to do anything, much less to be unable to exercise his natural properties. If they are restrained from running their course, they will not be natural.

For in its own nature it knows no inactivity; hence it is judged by whether it acts [Note: [Col. 0271D] Pamelius reads “if it is acted upon”] and whether it does not appear meanwhile to have been unwilling to exercise goodness under the name of nature. For nature cannot refuse itself [Note: [Col. 0271D] Thus others read.]; it directs itself in such a way that, if it ceases, [Col. 0271C] it does not exist.

But in Marcion’s god goodness at one time ceased to operate. [Note: [Col. 0272D] The Paris edition and Rhenanus read “goodness’s operation.”] Therefore, the goodness that could at one time have ceased was not natural, because natural properties are not permitted to cease. And if it is not natural, it must no longer be believed eternal, nor equal to God, because it is not eternal insofar as it is not natural. Indeed, it gives no assurance of its own perpetuity, either by establishing it from the past or by promising it for the future. For it did not exist from the beginning, and without doubt it will not exist until the end. It can at some time cease to exist, just as at one time it did not exist.

Therefore, since it is established that in the beginning that God’s goodness ceased to act—for he did not liberate humanity from the beginning—and that it ceased through choice rather than weakness, the will that suppressed goodness will now be found to be the ultimate form of malignity. For what is so malignant as to be unwilling to help when you can? As to be tormented by another’s benefit [Note: [Col. 0272D] Rigault reads “to torment benefit”]? As to permit injury?

[Note: [Col. 0271D] “In short, the Creator’s entire indictment will be entered against him.” By *elogium* he means a name or title; and by *rescribere*, “to enter against,” what in the following book he will call *transcribere*, “to transfer”: “But even if you transfer the indictment of evil from the human being to the devil.” RIG.]

In short, the Creator’s entire indictment will be entered against the one who, by delaying his goodness, assisted the Creator’s cruelties. For when it lies in someone’s power to prevent something from happening, it is already charged to him when [Note: [Col. 0272D] Pamelius inserts “already”] it happens.

Humanity is condemned to death [Note: [Col. 0271D] “Humanity is condemned to death,” etc. A beautiful description of original sin, although he expresses the following in the plural—“and from that point sins advance (or *make progress*, as the Vatican manuscript z reads) together with punishments”—because many other sins also arise from it. He also says elegantly, “those who know not a single sod of paradise,” that is, those who have never entered the soil of paradise. PAM.] for tasting from one little tree, and from that point sins advance together with punishments, and now all perish who know not a single sod of paradise. And does some “better” God either not know this or tolerate it?

If [Note: [Col. 0272D] After “if,” supply “he tolerated it.” EDD.] he did so in order to be found better by contrast, in proportion as the Creator was regarded as worse, then in this design too he is sufficiently malicious: he wished the Creator to be burdened with the consequences of his permitted actions [Note: [Col. 0272D] Rhenanus reads “allowed him to be honored by his works”], and he kept the world in affliction.

What judgment will you pass on a physician of this kind, who nourishes a disease by delaying his assistance and prolongs the danger by postponing the remedy, so that he may cure it at a higher price or with greater fame? The same sentence must be pronounced upon Marcion’s god: he is a permitter of evil, a supporter of injury, a procurer of favor, and a betrayer of benevolence, because he did not display that benevolence to its cause immediately—as he certainly would have done if he were good by nature rather than by accession; if supremely good by innate character rather than by training; if God from eternity rather than from Tiberius—or rather, to speak more truthfully, [Note: [Col. 0272D] “From Cerdo and Marcion.” He joins the two because Marcion was Cerdo’s disciple. PAM.] from Cerdo and Marcion. Let that god now grant this much to Tiberius: that divine goodness was inaugurated upon earth under his reign.

## CHAPTER XXIII

[Note: [Col. 0272D] “I set out another rule against him.” I employ another argument against him and explain to him a rule of truth. LE PR.]

I set out another rule against him: just as all things in God must be natural, so they must also be rational. [Note: [Col. 0272D] Semler and Oberthür omit “must.”] I demand a reason for his goodness, because nothing else may be regarded as good unless it is rationally good, much less may goodness itself be found irrational. An evil in which some rational ground is present will more readily be taken for good than a good deserted by reason will escape being judged evil.

I deny that Marcion’s god possesses rational goodness, first of all for this very reason: it has gone forth for the salvation of a human being who belongs to another. I know what they will say: “On the contrary, this is the principal and perfect goodness, since without any obligation arising from familiarity it is voluntarily and freely poured out upon strangers, in accordance with that goodness by which we are commanded to love even our enemies, and those who on that account are already strangers.”

Since, therefore, he did not regard humanity from the beginning, although humanity was a stranger from the beginning, by his inaction he established in advance that he had nothing to do with a stranger. Moreover, the command to love the stranger [Col. 0273A] or enemy was preceded by the command to love one’s neighbor as oneself. [Note: [Col. 0273D] “The command to love one’s neighbor,” etc. He derives this partly from Matt. 5, “You have heard that it was said to those of old: You shall love your neighbor,” and partly, and more directly, from Lev. 19, to which Christ was alluding there. PAM.]

Even though this is from the Creator’s Law, you too will have to accept it as something not destroyed by Christ but rather built up by him. For in order that you may love your neighbor all the more, you are commanded to love your enemy and the stranger. The latter is an intensification of owed goodness, a demand for goodness not owed. But what is owed precedes what is not owed, because it is primary and more worthy than its attendant and companion, namely, what is not owed.

Therefore, since the first and primary rationale of goodness is that it be displayed toward what is one’s own as an act of justice, while the second is that it be displayed toward what belongs to another from the overflowing of righteousness beyond that of the scribes [Note: [Col. 0273D] “From the overflowing of righteousness beyond that of the scribes.” I see that *super* is used here in the sense of “more than,” as Suetonius did in his *Augustus*. Although this is not especially elegant, it is a form of novelty. LE PR.] and Pharisees, what sense does it make to attribute the second rationale to one who lacks the first—to one who has no human being of his own and is therefore himself deficient [Note: [Col. 0273C] Pamelius reads “of one who has”; Semler conjectures “deficient”]? Moreover, how did a goodness deficient because it possessed nothing of its own overflow upon what belonged to another?

[Col. 0273B] Produce [Note: [Col. 0273D] Semler adds *re-*; Pamelius reads “to produce”] the primary rationale, and then claim the one that follows. Nothing can be vindicated as rational without order; so far is reason itself from losing order in any matter.

Let us now suppose that the rationale of goodness begins at the second degree, that is, toward a stranger. Not even its second degree will stand rationally, since it is destroyed in another way. For goodness toward a stranger, even at the second degree, will be regarded as rational only if it operates without injury to the one whose property is involved. Whatever the form of goodness, justice first makes it rational. Thus at the primary degree it will be rational when displayed toward one’s own property, provided it is just; and likewise toward another’s property it will be able to appear rational, provided it is not unjust.

But what sort of goodness is established through an injury, and that on behalf of a stranger? Perhaps an injurious goodness might to some extent be regarded as rational on behalf of a member of one’s own household. But on behalf of a stranger, to whom even honorable goodness was not lawfully owed, by what reasoning will such unjust goodness be defended as rational?

For what is more unjust, more inequitable, and more dishonorable than to benefit another man’s slave in such a way that he is snatched from his master, claimed for someone else, and suborned against the person of his master—and, what is still more disgraceful, while he is yet in his master’s own house, still living from his master’s granaries and still trembling under his master’s lashes? Such a champion of liberty would be condemned even in the secular world [Note: [Col. 0273D] “Such a champion of liberty would be condemned even in the secular world.” An *assertor* is one who vindicates another’s freedom. LE PR.], much more a kidnapper [Note: [Col. 0273D] “Much more a kidnapper.” He contrasts the kidnapper with the champion of liberty. *Plagium*, from which *plagiator* derives, is the abduction and concealment of a free person or slave—either because, according to Suidas, it is committed πλαγίς (*plagis*, “obliquely”) or δολίως (*doliōs*, “deceitfully”), or, as Isidore says, from ἀπὸ τοῦ πλαγίου (*apo tou plagiou*, “from the oblique”). LE PR.].

Marcion’s god acts no differently when he breaks into another’s world and snatches the human being from God, the son from his father, the pupil from his educator, and the servant from his master, in order to make him impious toward God, irreligious toward his father, ungrateful toward his educator, and wicked toward his master.

I ask you: if rational goodness makes a person like this, what sort of person would irrational goodness make? I do not suppose [Note: [Col. 0274C] “Irrational.” The Paris edition reads *an* (“whether?”); Rhenanus and Oberthür read *at* (“but”)] it could make anyone more shameless than the man who is baptized for one god in another God’s water, stretches out his hands to one god beneath another God’s heaven [Note: [Col. 0274D] “Stretches out his hands to one god beneath another God’s heaven,” etc. Christians therefore stretched out their arms toward heaven when praying. RHEN.], prostrates himself before one God upon another God’s earth [Note: [Col. 0274D] “Prostrates himself before one God.” This was the practice of penitents. RHEN.], performs acts of thanksgiving to one God over another God’s bread [Note: [Col. 0274D] “Performs acts of thanksgiving to one God over another God’s bread.” Irenaeus spoke in the same sense: “But how will it be established for them that the bread over which thanks have been given is the body of their Lord, and the cup his blood, if they do not say that he is the very Son of the Maker of the world, that is, his Word?” RIG.—“Over another God’s bread, to one God,” etc. This refers to the sacrament of the Eucharist, in which it is certain that the bread does not remain but is changed into Christ’s body. PAM.], and from another God’s goods performs works in the name of almsgiving and love on account of a different god.

Who is this god so good that a human being is made evil by him? So gracious that he makes another god—and indeed the human being’s own Lord [Note: [Col. 0274C] Semler and Oberthür omit “his own”]—angry with him?

## CHAPTER XXIV

But God, just as he is eternal and rational, is also, I think, perfect in every respect: “For you shall be perfect, just as your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:48). [Col. 0274B] Produce, then, his perfect goodness as well.

That his goodness is imperfect is already sufficiently established, since it is found to be neither natural nor rational. It will now be exposed by another line of argument: it is not merely imperfect but defective, meager, and exhausted—smaller than the number of its own objects, though it is supposedly displayed toward all. For not all are saved, but fewer than the total number of both Jews and the Creator’s Christians.

Since the greater number perish, how is a goodness that remains inactive toward the greater part defended as perfect? It is something to a few and nothing to the many, yielding to perdition and sharing in ruin. But if the greater number will not be saved, it will no longer be goodness, but rather malignity, that is more perfect. For just as the operation of goodness is that which saves, so the operation of malignity is that which does not save. But that which does not save, insofar as it saves only a few, will be more complete in withholding assistance than [Col. 0274C] in giving it.

Nor can you refer to the Creator the failure of goodness toward all. Since you regard him as a judge, you may perhaps show that he must be understood as an administrator of goodness, not as its indiscriminate dispenser—which is what you claim for your god [Note: [Col. 0274D] “God” is absent from Semler.]. So completely do you prefer him to the Creator on account of this goodness alone; yet if he professes this goodness as both his only quality and his whole nature, it ought to have been lacking to no one.

But I no longer wish to argue that Marcion’s god is imperfect in goodness from the greater portion of those who perish. It is enough to show his goodness imperfect from the fact that even those whom he saves are found to possess an imperfect salvation: namely, they are saved only as far as the soul [Note: [Col. 0274D] “Namely, they are saved only as far as the soul, while they are lost in the flesh,” etc. This is what the author said above in *On the Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 51: “He affirms the resurrection of the soul alone but denies that of the body.” Against this heresy he argues at length in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*. As “division of salvation” is read here, so above, in *On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. 1: “Why do you divide Christ?” The statement below, “to rise in part,” has the same bearing. PAM.], while they are lost in the flesh, which according to him does not rise again.

Whence comes this division [Col. 0275A] of salvation, if not from the deficiency of goodness? For what is so characteristic [Note: [Col. 0275C] Semler and Oberthür read, “What belonged to perfect”; Latinus reads, “For what is so characteristic of perfect love”] of perfect goodness as to restore the entire human being to salvation—the whole human being condemned by the Creator and the whole human being enticed by the supremely good God?

As far as I know [Note: [Col. 0275C] Pamelius, Semler, and Oberthür read “But if now”], the flesh too is baptized among his followers [Note: [Col. 0275D] “The flesh too is baptized among his followers.” We read *tinguitur* here, in Tertullian’s manner, for *tingitur*. Similarly, above in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 8: “But the flesh too is washed,” etc. Virginity and widowhood, etc., are offered to God from the goods of the flesh; for this is what he adds here, “and the flesh is withdrawn from marriage.” At these and certain other passages we have noted that continence from marriage is confirmed—a practice which some today do not blush to attack—and likewise in *On the Veiling of Virgins* and *On the Dress of Women*, ch. 9. PAM.]; the flesh too is withdrawn from marriage; and the flesh too is savaged in confessing the Name.

But even if sins are charged to the flesh, the guilt of the soul precedes them, and the primacy of fault must rather be ascribed to the soul, which the flesh attends in the capacity of a servant. Indeed, flesh deprived of the soul sins no further. Thus in this respect too his goodness is unjust, and thereby also imperfect: it abandons to destruction the more innocent substance, which sins through obedience, not through free judgment.

Although his Christ did not assume the flesh’s reality, as your heresy has decided, he nevertheless deigned to assume its image. The very fact that he falsely represented it means that he must have owed it something. [Note: [Col. 0275C] Junius reads “had”; others, “I ought.”]

But what is a human being other than flesh? For the name “human being” was assigned by its author to the bodily, not the animate material: “And God made the human being,” he says (Gen. 2), “clay from the earth”—not the soul. For the soul came from the breath [Note: [Col. 0275D] “For the soul came from the breath.” It is a common etymology that *anima* (“soul”) is so named as though from ἄνεμος (*anemos*, “wind”). Tertullian may have had this in mind. LE PR.]: “And the human being became a living soul.” Who became so? Assuredly the one made from clay. “And God placed the human being whom he had formed in paradise”—the one he molded, not the one he breathed; the one who was flesh, not the one who was soul.

Accordingly, if this is so, with what face will you contend for the title of perfect goodness, when that goodness has failed not merely with respect to a particular part of the human being to be delivered, but with respect to the human being’s generic identity? If that grace is complete and that mercy substantial which brings salvation to the soul alone, this present life provides more, since in it we enjoy life as whole and complete persons.

Moreover, to rise in part will be to suffer a penalty, not to be liberated. It would also have belonged to perfect goodness that the human being, once liberated [Col. 0275C] into faith in the supremely good God, should immediately be removed from the dwelling and dominion of the savage god.

But even now, Marcionite, you suffer fevers; the pain of your flesh still produces for you the other thistles and thorns; and you remain exposed not only to the Creator’s thunderbolts, wars, plagues, and other blows, but also to his scorpions. In what respect do you suppose yourself liberated from the kingdom of one whose flies still trample upon you? If you have been rescued from the future, why not from the present also, so that you may be liberated perfectly [Note: [Col. 0275C] Semler adds “be”]?

Our condition [Col. 0276A] is different, since we stand before the Author, the Judge, and the offended ruler of our race. You put forward a God [Note: [Col. 0276C] “God” is absent from Franeker.] who is only good. Yet you cannot show him to be perfectly good [Note: [Col. 0276C] Rhenanus adds “God”] when you are not perfectly liberated by him.

## CHAPTER XXV

As regards the question of goodness, along these lines we have demonstrated that it is by no means commensurate with God, since it is neither unbegotten, nor rational, nor perfect, but rather dishonorable and unjust, and now unworthy even of the very name of goodness. For to precisely the degree that such goodness is compatible with God, it follows that the one commended even for such a kind of goodness is not God—and not merely for such a kind, but for it alone.

For it is now proper to examine this point as well: whether God should be characterized by goodness alone, while the other attendant qualities [Note: [Col. 0276D] “While the other attendant qualities, feelings,” etc. Here he presses Marcion and employs those terms adopted by Marcion’s disciples, such as calling God the Creator savage. LE PR.], feelings, and affections are denied. The Marcionites drive these away from their god and into the Creator; we, however, acknowledge them in the Creator as worthy of God. On this ground too we shall deny [Note: [Col. 0276C] Junius reads “we deny”] that he is God in whom all qualities worthy of God are not found.

If Marcion desired to give the title of God, under the name of Christ, to some deity from Epicurus’s school [Note: [Col. 0276D] “Some deity from Epicurus’s school.” Namely, as follows, one immovable and stupefied, and—as in ch. 26—utterly foolish. To the same point belongs the following statement about God: “he made trouble both for himself and for others, against Epicurus’s wishes.” PAM.], so that, because the blessed and incorruptible being causes trouble neither for itself nor for another—Marcion, ruminating upon this maxim, removed severity and judicial powers from him—then he ought either to have conceived a God wholly immovable and insensible; and what would such a God have to do with Christ, who caused trouble both for the Jews through his teaching and for himself through his suffering [Note: [Col. 0276C] Rhenanus reads “Jesus”]? Or else he ought also to have acknowledged the other emotions in him [Note: [Col. 0276C] Wouwer reads “he would have acknowledged”]; and then what would he have to do with Epicurus, who was necessary neither to himself nor to Christians?

For see: by the very fact that he who was previously at rest and had meanwhile taken no care through any work to make himself known, after so long an age developed a concern for human salvation—assuredly through an act of will—was he not then moved by a new will, so that he appears liable to other emotions as well?

And what will exists without the spur of desire? Concern too will accompany the will. Who will will [Note: [Col. 0276D] “Who will will what he does not desire?” etc. Rhenanus deleted this passage because it was not present in the Gorze codex. We restore it from the second Vatican manuscript because it contributes to the explanation. Whether one reads *concupivit* twice with those manuscripts or *concupiit* with the printed editions makes no difference. “Its proper functionaries” and “unwillingness,” which Rhenanus says he sets in opposition to will and applies to the human being, are Tertullianic expressions. PAM.] what he does not desire? For who will will something and desire it, yet not care about it?

Therefore, since he both willed and longed for human salvation, he made trouble both for himself and for others [Col. 0277A], against Epicurus’s wishes, with Marcion as his adviser [Note: [Col. 0277D] Others read “of Marcion”]. For he also established for himself an adversary—the very thing against which he willed, longed, and took care to act, whether sin or death; and above all the very arbiter of these things and lord of humanity, the Creator.

Moreover, nothing that will not be without an adversary can proceed without rivalry. In short, in willing, desiring, and taking care to liberate humanity, by this very fact he now rivals both the one from [Note: [Col. 0277D] Rhenanus and Oberthür read “with respect to”] whom he liberates it—since he is going to liberate it for himself in opposition to him—and the things from which he liberates it, since he is going to liberate it into other things. Accordingly, rivalry’s own functionaries must necessarily join it [Note: [Col. 0277D] Semler and Oberthür read “meet it”] against the objects of its rivalry: anger, discord, hatred, disdain, indignation, bile [Note: [Col. 0277D] Rhenanus reads “indignant bile”], unwillingness, and offense. If all these attend rivalry, while rivalry serves the liberation of humanity, and the liberation of humanity [Col. 0277B] is an operation of goodness, that goodness cannot exist without its endowments—that is, without the feelings and affections through which it is administered against the Creator—lest it be condemned as irrational on this ground also, because it lacks the feelings and affections properly owed to it. We shall defend these matters much more fully in the case of the Creator, in whom they are also made grounds for reproach.

## CHAPTER XXVI
But here it is enough to show that this god is utterly perverse in the very proclamation of his solitary goodness, by which they refuse to ascribe to him the sorts of emotions that they censure in the Creator. For if he neither feels rivalry, nor grows angry, nor condemns, nor punishes—as one who does not present himself as judge—I do not see how his system of discipline can stand, especially one supposedly more complete. For what sort of thing is it that he should establish precepts which he will not enforce? that he should forbid offenses [Col. 0277C] which he will not avenge, because he will not judge them? He is, of course, a stranger to every feeling of severity and punitive correction. Why, then, does he forbid the commission of something whose commission he does not punish? It would have been far more consistent not to forbid what he would not punish than not to punish what he had forbidden. Indeed, he plainly ought to have permitted it, since he would forbid it without cause, seeing that he would not [Note: [Col. 0277D] *Not* Semler; *not even* Junius.] punish it. For even then that which is forbidden without vengeance is tacitly permitted. And certainly he forbids the commission of nothing except what he does not wish to be done. He is therefore utterly senseless if he is not offended by the doing of what he does not wish to be done, since offense accompanies a frustrated will. Or, if he is offended, he ought to grow angry; if he grows angry, he ought to avenge. For vengeance is the fruit of anger, anger is owed to offense, and offense, as I have said, accompanies a frustrated will. But he does not avenge; therefore he is not offended. [Col. 0277D] But he is not offended; therefore his will is not injured when that is done which he did not wish to be done. And so the offense is committed in accordance with his will, because what does not injure his will is not done against his will. [Col. 0278A]

Or if this will be characteristic of divine power or goodness—to be unwilling, indeed, that something be done, and to forbid its being done, but nevertheless not to be moved if it is done—we reply that he who was unwilling has already been moved; and it is vain for one not to be moved by the deed when he had been moved to prevent its being done, since he did not wish it to be done: for by his unwillingness he forbade it. Did he not also judge? By being unwilling that it be done, and therefore forbidding it, he judged that it ought not to be done and pronounced that it ought to be forbidden. Therefore he too already judges. If it is unworthy of God to judge—or if it is worthy of God to judge only so far as he is merely unwilling and forbids, but does not also [Note: [Col. 0278D] *For* Paris.] punish the offense once committed—yet nothing is so unworthy of God as failing to enforce what he did not wish and had forbidden to be committed. First, because he owes vengeance to any sentence and law of his own, whatever it may be, in order to give it authority and make obedience necessary. [Col. 0278B] Second, because he must necessarily oppose what he did not wish to be committed and by his unwillingness forbade. But for God to spare evil is more unworthy than to punish it—and particularly for the best God, who cannot otherwise be fully good unless he is the adversary of evil, exercising his love of good through hatred of evil, and [Note: [Col. 0278D] *So that* Semler, Oberthür.] fulfilling his protection of good through the overthrow of evil.

## CHAPTER XXVII

But plainly he judges evil by being unwilling that it occur, and condemns it by forbidding it; yet he pardons it by not avenging it, and acquits it by not punishing it. O God who betrays truth and annuls his own sentence! [Note: [Col. 0277D] *An annuller of his own sentence.* *Circumscriptor* means “abrogator”; *circumscribere*, in the sense of “to circumvent and obliterate,” is a word frequent among jurists and reputable authors. Cicero, in *On Ends*: “Those opinions, then, which I have just set forth having been set aside.” RHENANUS.] He fears to condemn what he condemns; he fears to hate what he does not love; he allows the deed which he does not allow to be done; he prefers to show that he is unwilling rather than to prove it. This [Note: [Col. 0278D] *These* in other editions.] will be imaginary goodness [Note: [Col. 0278D] *Of goodness* Rhenanus.], a phantom discipline; [Note: [Col. 0278D] *And the precepts themselves are transfunctory.* He calls “transfunctory” what is perfunctory. Among jurists, however, something “perfunctory” is what is done with slight care and while attending to something else—when, evidently, we do not care that something be done well, but only that it be done. Hence the adverb “perfunctorily” is in frequent use among them. RHENANUS.] and the precepts themselves perfunctory, [Col. 0278C] the offenses free from concern.

Listen, sinners—and you who are not yet sinners, so that you may become so! A better God has been discovered, one who is neither offended nor angry nor vengeful, for whom no fire is kindled in Gehenna and no gnashing of teeth shudders in the outer darkness. He is merely good; in short, he forbids sinning, but only in writing. It is in your power, if you wish, to sign your obedience over to him, so that you may seem to have shown God honor; for he does not desire fear. Indeed, the Marcionites openly boast that they do not fear their god at all. “But an evil god,” they say, “will be feared, whereas a good one will be loved.” Fool, you call him “Lord” and deny that he is to be feared, though this name denotes power—and power that is also to be feared. Yet how will you love him unless you fear not loving him? Plainly he is not even your father, toward whom both love because of filial devotion and fear [Col. 0278D] because of authority would be fitting; nor is he your lawful master, whom you should love because of his kindness and fear because of his discipline. Thus, in fact, kidnappers are loved but not [Col. 0279A] feared. For dominion will not be feared unless it is just and lawful; but even an illegitimate dominion can be loved. It rests on enticement, not authority; and on flattery, not power. What, finally, is more flattering than not prosecuting offenses?

Come then, you who do not fear God because he is good: why do you not boil over into every kind of lust—the highest fruit of life, as far as I know, for all who do not fear God? Why do you not attend the customary pleasures of the raging circus, [Note: [Col. 0279D] *The pleasures of the raging circus.* Nearly all the ancients teach that frenzy and madness were attributed to the circus. Augustine, Book II, *On the Creed, to Catechumens*: “What delights one in the circus? To see the charioteers competing? the peoples panting in insanity and frenzy?” St. Jerome to Marcella: “Let the circus rave.” St. Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 27: περὶ τοὺς ἱππικοὺς καὶ τὰ θέατρα, καὶ τὰ στάδια, καὶ τὰ κυνογέσια τοσοῦτον μεμηνέναι, ὥστε ταῦτα ποιεῖσθαι βίον, “He was so mad about horse-races and spectacles, races and hunts, that he made his life consist in them.” The same Theologian also, *Poem* 3, in iambics. LE PRIEUR.] [Note: [Col. 0279C] *those raging around the circus* Rhenanus, Oberthür.], the savage amphitheater, [Note: [Col. 0279D] *The savage cavea.* *Cavea* is often used for the theater and amphitheater, as here. But St. Jerome expressed this passage excellently in the *Life of St. Hilarion*: “He took no delight in the frenzies of the circus, nor in the blood of the arena, nor in the wantonness of the theater.” You see that “arena” is used for *cavea*, whence in *Apology* 38 it is called “the atrocity of the arena.” LE PRIEUR.] and the wanton stage? [Note: [Col. 0279D] *The wanton stage.* Spectacles were forbidden to Christians because of their obscenity and shamelessness; the canons proclaim this everywhere. Tertullian himself, *Apology* 38: “We renounce your spectacles entirely”—at baptism, evidently. Hence St. Chrysostom, Oration 19, *To the People*, testifies that Christians ought not to be seen “on the stage and amid the antics of mimes,” ἐν σκηνῇ καὶ μίμων παιδιαῖς. LE PRIEUR.] Why, during persecutions, do you not immediately save your life by denial when the incense-box is offered? “God forbid,” you say, “God forbid!” Therefore you already fear the offense, and by fearing it you have proved that he who forbids the offense is to be feared. It would be another matter if, with the same perversity as your god, whom you do not fear, you obey him just as he forbids what he does not avenge. [Col. 0279B]

It is still more futile when, upon being asked, “What will happen to each sinner on that day?” they answer [Note: [Col. 0279C] *They will answer* in their Latin; *they answer* Semler. *Of their god* Rhenanus.] that he will be cast away, as though out of sight. Is not this too effected by judgment? For he is judged worthy of being cast away, and certainly by a judgment of condemnation—unless the sinner is cast away [Note: [Col. 0279C] *Unless into* Rhenanus, Oberthür.] for salvation, so that even this may befit the best God. And what will it mean to be cast away except to lose what he would have obtained had he not been cast away—that is, salvation? Therefore he would be cast away to the loss of salvation; and this cannot be decreed except by one who is angry, offended, and the prosecutor of the offense—that is, a judge.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

But what end awaits the man thus cast away? “He will be seized by the Creator’s fire,” they say. Does he possess no element of his own, provided even for this purpose, by which he might banish his sinners [Col. 0279C] without cruelty, rather than hand them over to the Creator? What, then, will the Creator do? I suppose he will prepare [Note: [Col. 0279D] *Has prepared* Semler, Junius.] for them a Gehenna richer in sulfur, precisely because they are his blasphemers—unless perhaps the jealous God will spare the deserters from his adversary [Note: [Col. 0280C] *Does he spare his adversary?* Paris, Frankfurt.].

O God perverse in every respect, irrational everywhere, futile in all things, and therefore no god at all! I see neither his status, nor his condition, nor his nature, nor any order belonging to him as coherent; [Col. 0280A] by now not even the sacrament of his faith itself. For to what purpose is baptism required even under him? If it is the remission of offenses, how will he appear to forgive offenses when he does not appear to retain them? For he would retain them if he judged. If it is release from death, how would he release from death one whom he did not bind over to death? For he would have bound him over if he had condemned him from the beginning. If it is the regeneration of the human being, how does one regenerate who did not first generate? Repetition does not belong to one by whom a thing was not done even once. If it is the attainment of the Holy Spirit, how will he bestow the spirit when he did not previously confer the soul? For [Note: [Col. 0280D] *The soul is, in a manner, to serve as a substitute for the spirit.* He calls it a substitute, as though placed beneath the spirit in order to sustain it, just as, with the opposite meaning, we speak of a “prefecture.” Thus he assigns substitution to the soul, so that we may understand that prefecture was given to the spirit. So too in the book *On the Soul*, he said that the *animus* was supplied to the *anima*. RIGAULT.] the soul is, in a manner, to serve as a substitute for the spirit.

He therefore seals a human being who was never unsealed under him; he washes a human being who was never unsealed under him; he washes a human being who was never defiled under him; [Col. 0280B] [Note: [Col. 0280D] *And in this he immerses the whole sacrament of salvation—the flesh.* Augustine, Book I, *On the Merits of Sins*, against Pelagius, chapter 24: “The Punic Christians,” he says, “most aptly call baptism itself nothing other than salvation.” RIGAULT.] and in this he immerses the whole sacrament of salvation—the flesh, which has no share in salvation. Not even a farmer will water land from which he will reap no fruit, unless he is as futile as Marcion’s god. Consequently, why does he impose so great a burden—or so great a glory—of holiness upon flesh that is utterly weak or unworthy? [Note: [Col. 0280C] *As Marcion’s god; consequently* with Semler, Oberthür.] What am I to say, moreover, about the futility of a discipline by which he sanctifies a holy substance? Why does he either [Note: [Col. 0280C] *Moreover* Semler.] burden one that is weak or adorn one that is unworthy? Why does he not reward with salvation that which he burdens or adorns? Why does he defraud it of the reward for its work, not repaying [Note: [Col. 0280C] *Rebuking* Rhenanus.] salvation to the flesh? Why does he allow even the honor of holiness to die in it?

## CHAPTER XXIX

Under him the flesh is not baptized unless it belongs to a virgin, a widow, an unmarried person, or one who has purchased baptism by divorce [Note: [Col. 0280D] *Divorce*, Junius.], [Col. 0280C] as though it had not been born from marriage even in the case of eunuchs. Without doubt this institution will rest upon the condemnation of marriage. Let us see whether it is just—not as though we intended to destroy the blessedness of holiness, like certain Nicolaitans, advocates of lust and luxury, but as people who have learned to recognize, pursue, and prefer holiness without condemning marriage: not as a good over an evil, but as a better thing over a good one. For we do not cast marriages away, [Note: [Col. 0280D] *But we lay marriages aside*, etc. The author certainly did not condemn marriages; rather, he commended holiness within them. But he rejected the obscenity already gaining strength under the pretext of marriage. LE PRIEUR.] but lay them aside; [Col. 0281A] nor do we impose holiness as a binding rule, but recommend it, preserving both the good and the better by pursuing each according to a person’s powers. Only then, indeed, do we expressly defend marriage, when it is attacked in a hostile fashion under the name of filthiness, for the destruction of the Creator, who accordingly blessed marriage because of the honorableness of the thing and for the increase of the human race, just as he blessed the whole creation for sound and good uses.

Foods will not, however, be condemned merely because, when sought out with excessive elaboration, they contribute to gluttony; nor [Note: [Col. 0281C] *Then* Rhenanus, Oberthür.] will clothing be accused merely because, when obtained at greater expense, it swells into ostentation. Likewise the institution of marriage must not be despised merely because, when indulged without restraint, it blazes into lust. There is a great difference between cause and fault, between an established condition and its excess. Thus it is not the institution of such a thing but its deviation that must be condemned, in accordance with the judgment of its Founder himself, to whom belong both “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1:28) and “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20:14), and “You shall not desire your neighbor’s wife” (Lev. 20:10)—he who punishes by death even incestuous [Note: [Col. 0281C] *Incestuous also* Junius.], sacrilegious, and monstrous madness of lust directed toward males and beasts.

But even if the impulse to marry is now being laid aside—a rule which among us the spiritual discipline, under the authority of the Paraclete, indeed defends, prescribing one marriage in the faith—it will belong to the same one to impose a limit who had once extended that limit. He who scattered will gather; he who planted the forest will cut it down; he who sowed the crop will reap it. He will say, “It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none” (1 Cor. 7:29), to whom the earlier saying also belonged, “Increase and multiply.” The end belongs to the same one [Col. 0281C] as the beginning. [Note: [Col. 0281C] *Yet the forest is not cut down as something deserving accusation.* By a comparison he teaches that marriages must not be condemned; and, as he was skilled in Roman law, he speaks of a forest meant for cutting, which is frequently mentioned in law, where every forest is divided into one meant for cutting and one not meant for cutting. The former is preserved in order to be cut; the latter is assigned to the grazing of livestock and is commonly called pasture. LE PRIEUR.]

Yet the forest is not cut down [Note: [Col. 0281C] *As* omitted by Semler, Oberthür.] as something deserving accusation, nor is the crop severed as something deserving condemnation, but as something obedient to its season. So too the institution of marriage admits the axe and sickle of holiness, not as though it were evil, but as though it had ripened for completion and had been reserved for holiness itself, to which, by being cut down, it grants even the possibility of existence [Note: [Col. 0281C] *May grant existence* Semler; *would grant existence* Rhenanus.]. From this [Col. 0282A] I shall now say that Marcion’s god, by rejecting marriage as an evil and a business of immodesty, acts against the very holiness which he seems to cultivate. For he uproots its material: if there are no marriages, there is no holiness. The testimony of abstinence becomes meaningless when permission is removed, since certain things are proved by their opposites. Just as “virtue is perfected in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9), so abstinence from marriage is recognized where the capacity to marry exists [Note: [Col. 0281C] *Distinguished* Rigault, Frankfurt.]. Who, finally, will be called abstinent when that from which one must abstain has been removed? What restraint of gluttony exists in famine? What repudiation of ambition in poverty? What bridling of lust in castration?

But as for wholly suppressing the sowing [Note: [Col. 0281C] *Seed* Junius.] of the human race [Note: [Col. 0282C] Semler deletes *in*.], I do not know whether this too is compatible with the best God. For how will he desire the salvation of a human being [Col. 0282B] whom he forbids to be born by taking away that from which he is born? How will he have anyone upon whom to set the seal of his goodness, when he does not allow him to exist? How does he love one whose origin he does not love? Perhaps he fears an excess of offspring, lest he be burdened with liberating more people, lest he make many heretics, lest he have Marcionites of more illustrious lineage born from Marcionites.

The cruelty of Pharaoh, the destroyer of newborn children, will not be more savage [Note: [Col. 0282C] *More humane* Semler, Oberthür; *more inhuman* in other editions.]. For Pharaoh takes away lives; this god does not give them. The former removes people from [Note: [Col. 0282C] *From* Semler, Pamelius.] life; the latter does not admit them into life. In respect of homicide there is no difference between the two: under both a human being is killed—under the one, after being born; under the other, when he is about to be born.

You would have been grateful, O heretical god, had you been favorably disposed toward the Creator’s arrangement, in that he joined male and female; for your own Marcion was certainly born from marriage. Enough, then, concerning Marcion’s god, whom both the definitions of the one Godhead and the conditions of his states [Note: [Col. 0282C] *State* Rhenanus, Oberthür.] confirm to have no existence at all [Note: [Col. 0282C] *Confirming* Rhenanus.]. But the course of the entire little work also proceeds toward this conclusion. Accordingly, if anyone thinks that we have done [Note: [Col. 0282C] *We shall seem to have done* Frankfurt.] too little in any respect, let him expect it to have been reserved for its proper time, as is also the examination of the Scriptures which Marcion uses.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0281]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0281D]

I. Since in the preceding book Tertullian determined that Marcion’s god is not God, because certain rules prescribe that there is one Godhead, in this book he defends the proposition that God the Creator is worthily God, since he is good, not evil.

II. He first sets forth an invective against the Marcionites, who by their curiosity [Col. 0282D] cause trouble for God, weighing God according to the judgment of their own understanding.

III. First of all, however, he teaches that the goodness of God the Creator is eternal,

IV. Especially from the making of the human being and the world, and from the law which he prescribed for the human being;

[Col. 0283A]

V. For the fall of the human being must be imputed not to God but to the human being’s free will;

VI. And indeed the goodness of God and the rational nature of the human being required that the human being be constituted with free will, since the reward either of good or of evil could not justly be paid to one who was found good or evil by necessity rather than by will;

VII. God’s dignity, faithfulness, and patience also required this very thing;

VIII. Thus the offense must be imputed entirely to the human being, whom God had created to live rightly;

IX. Nor must it therefore be imputed to God that the soul which sins is the breath of God, because the soul indeed possesses those lineaments of God insofar as it is immortal, free in its own choice, often foreknowing, and rational; [Col. 0283B] nevertheless, even in these respects it is only the image of God, not equal to the very power of divinity itself.

X. Nor, even if the fault were transferred to the devil as the instigator of the offense, should it therefore be directed against the Creator as the author of the devil, since the latter was made by God as an angel and made good—not as the devil, that is, the slanderer.

XI. Furthermore, if after the human being’s offense God was a judge and severe, this pertains not to malice but to justice;

XII. Since this justice has always acted in concert with goodness in God, it is wrong to reckon separately a good God and separately a just God;

XIII. Indeed, every work of justice serves the goodness of God, since fear of judgment contributes to good, not to evil;

XIV. Therefore, if God is ever read to create evils, this must be understood of the evils of punishment, not of guilt; [Col. 0283C]

XV. Accordingly, what appears to be severity is the justice, and thus the goodness, of God;

XVI. Nor should those things that attend justice be reproached in a judge, any more than a physician should be reproached for instruments that cut, cauterize, amputate, and constrict;

XVII. Finally, the entire order of God’s goodness is shown by his mercy toward those who err, his patience toward those who do not come to their senses, and his beneficence toward those who deserve it.

XVIII. Then, coming to Marcion’s *Antitheses*, he proves that the punishment of retaliation, the prohibition of unclean foods, and the burdens of sacrifices also pertain to the goodness of God;

XIX. And likewise each of the disciplines of the Law, so that they should not for a moment be free from regard for God;

XX. Indeed, even the plundering of silver which God commanded the Hebrews to carry out against the Egyptians; for the labor of six hundred thousand people over so many years, and the loss of the sons whom the Egyptians had drowned, were of greater value; [Col. 0283D]

XXI. Nor is there any contradiction in God’s forbidding work on the Sabbaths and commanding the ark to be carried around even on the Sabbath;

[Col. 0284A]

XXII. Nor do the bronze serpent or the golden images of Cherubim and Seraphim conflict with the law forbidding images, since they had causes far different from idolatry, concerning which, after forbidding an image to be made, he adds: “You shall not worship them or serve them.” For God’s institution of sacrifices was also rational, since it called people away from idols, although he subsequently rejected those sacrifices.

XXIII. Nor is it right to call God fickle because he sometimes rejects those whom he approved or at times approves those whom he would reject; for nothing is more fitting even for a good judge than both to reject and to choose according to present merits.

XXIV. Accordingly, Marcion wrongly interprets repentance in God, for even in its Greek sound—μετάνοια (*metanoia*)—the term “repentance” is composed not from confession of an offense but from a change of mind.

[Col. 0284B]

XXV. No less wrongly does he understand the saying, “Adam, where are you?” and that addressed to Cain, “Where is your brother?” Likewise the statement concerning Sodom and Gomorrah, “I shall go down and see,” etc.;

XXVI. Likewise God’s oath by himself and those words to Moses: “Let me be, and, angered with wrath, I shall scatter them.”

XXVII. Finally, the remaining instances of pettiness which the Marcionites charged against God are not so great as those which they themselves acknowledge in Christ, to whom those appearances of the Old Testament must be ascribed.

XXVIII. Lastly, against Marcion he constructs rival antitheses of his own, continuing to the end of the book. PAMELIUS.

## ARGUMENT

Whatever was made by God the Father and Creator, he teaches, was made with the greatest wisdom; therefore God the Creator is good, not evil.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0284C]

The occasion for revising this little work—what happened to it we stated in the preface to the first little book—has also afforded us this advantage: in reconsidering Marcion’s two gods, we could distinguish for each his own title and volume in accordance with the division of the subject matter, determining that the one god has no existence at all and defending the other as worthily God, since it pleased the man from Pontus to introduce the one and exclude the other. For he could not build falsehood without demolishing truth. He had necessarily to undermine one thing in order to construct what he wished. Thus does one build [Note: [Col. 0283D] *One who lacks material of his own.* Rhenanus says that here too he calls material *paratura*. Thus in *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 8: “I ought,” he says, “to refute them from their own material”; likewise in the preceding book, chapter 11: “He provided himself no material through recognition.” Latinius further notes similar passages from Book IV *Against Marcion*, near the beginning: “and all the material of the impious and sacrilegious Marcion”; and again in the same book, chapter 2: “He certainly possessed authentic material.” PAMELIUS.] who lacks material of his own.

It would, however, have been proper to dispute this point alone: that this god who is superimposed upon the Creator is no god at all. Once the false god had been driven away by certain rules prescribing that the Godhead is both one and perfect, nothing further ought to have been investigated concerning the true God. For the more certain it was that he existed, inasmuch as no other was established to exist, the more fitting it would have been that he should be accepted without controversy, whatever his character—worshiped rather than judged, and won over rather than reconsidered or even feared because of his severity. [Col. 0285A] For what more is necessary to a human being than concern for the true God, upon whom, so to speak, he had happened, because there was no other God?

## CHAPTER II

[Note: [Col. 0285D] *But now Almighty God is put to trouble*, etc. It is as though he wished to say that God is put to trouble by the rashness and audacity of the Marcionites, who fashioned for themselves another God distinct from the Almighty. LE PRIEUR.]

But now Almighty God, the Lord and Founder of the universe, is put to trouble—only, I suppose, because he has been known from the beginning; because he was never hidden; because he has always shone forth, even before Romulus himself, let alone before Tiberius. The only exception is that he has not been known by the heretics, who put him to trouble. For this reason they think another God must be presumed: because they can more readily criticize than deny the one whose existence is established, certain people weighing [Note: [Col. 0285C] *They weigh* Latinius, Junius.] God according to the judgment of their own understanding. It is just as though a blind man, or one [Note: [Col. 0285D] *With wavering eyes, to presume another sun.* Thus Book I: “To bleary eyes even a single lamp is manifold.” RIGAULT.] whose eyes are wavering, should therefore wish to presume another sun, milder [Col. 0285B] and more wholesome, because he does not see the one he sees.

There is one sun, O man, which regulates this world; and even when you do not think so, it is best and useful. Even when it is harsher and more hostile toward you, or even more foul and corrupted, it is nevertheless consistent with its own governing principle. If you are unable [Note: [Col. 0285C] *Were unable* in other editions.] to perceive that principle, you would certainly have been unable to endure the rays of any [Note: [Col. 0285C] *That* Semler, Oberthür.] other sun, had one existed—especially a greater one [Note: [Col. 0285C] *Greater rays* in other editions.]. For if you are blind toward [Note: [Col. 0285C] *Toward* absent in Rigault, Venice.] an inferior god, what would you be toward a higher one? Why do you not rather spare your weakness and refrain from stretching yourself into danger, since you possess a certain and undoubted God, sufficiently seen by this very fact: that your first perception was that he exists, although you know him only to the extent that he himself has willed?

Yet while acknowledging God, you do not deny him; while not knowing him, you reconsider him—indeed, you even accuse him as though you knew him. If you knew him, you would not accuse him; indeed, you would not even reconsider him. In giving him the name, you deny the substance of the name—that is, the greatness by which [Note: [Col. 0286C] *Of the greatness, which* Rhenanus, Venice, Pamelius.] he is called God—because you do not acknowledge it to be so great that, if a human being could know it in every respect, it would no longer be greatness.

Isaiah, already at that time [Note: [Col. 0286C] *He himself even then* Pamelius, Frankfurt; *he himself already* Rhenanus.], an apostle foreseeing heretical hearts, says: “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor? [Note: [Col. 0286C] *Who was his counselor?* Pamelius, Semler, Oberthür.] [Col. 0286A] Or whom did he consult? Or who showed him the way of understanding and knowledge?” (Isa. 40:13–14). With him the Apostle will agree: [Note: [Col. 0285D] *The Apostle will agree: O depth*, etc. The blessed Apostle agrees with Isaiah when he says in Romans II: “O depth,” etc.; in the Greek it is ὦ βάθος, “O depth.” LE PRIEUR.] “O depth of the riches and wisdom of God! How unsearchable are his judgments”—certainly those of God the Judge—“and how untraceable are his ways!”—certainly the ways of understanding and knowledge which no one showed him, unless perhaps these censors of divinity did so, who say: “God ought not to have acted thus,” and “He ought rather to have acted thus,” as though anyone knew the things within God except the Spirit of God.

But since they possess the spirit of the world and do not recognize God through wisdom within the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:21), they seem to themselves wiser in counsel than God. For just as the wisdom of the world is foolishness before God, so the wisdom of God is foolishness before the world. But we know that the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings, and the weakness of God stronger than human beings (1 Cor. 1:25). [Col. 0286B] And thus God is greatest precisely when he is petty to a human being; and best precisely when he is not good to a human being; and most truly one precisely when to a human being he is two or more.

But if from the beginning [Note: [Col. 0285D] *The natural human being. Ψυχικός*, “psychic” or “soulish.” And he immediately explains it: “not receiving the things of the Spirit.” RIGAULT.] the natural human being, not receiving the things of the Spirit (1 Cor. 2:14), considered God’s law foolishness, since he neglected to observe it, [Note: [Col. 0285D] *And therefore, since he did not have faith, even*, etc. He beautifully explains Luke 8: “For to him who has, it will be given; and from him who does not have, even what he thinks he has will be taken away.” Applying this by analogy to Adam, from whom, because he did not have faith, even what he appeared to have was taken away—namely, the grace of Paradise and intimacy with God, through which he would have known all things of God had he obeyed. Here he translated literally “what he appears to have,” corresponding to the Greek ὃ δοκεῖ ἔχειν. PAMELIUS.] and therefore, since he did not have faith, even what he appeared to possess was taken from him (Matt. 13:12; Luke 8:18)—the grace of Paradise and intimacy with God, through which he would have known all things of God had he obeyed—what wonder is it if, restored to his own material and banished to the workhouse of tilling the earth, [Note: [Col. 0286D] *In the very labor bent and sloping toward the earth.* Persius had said:

> O souls bent toward the earth and empty of heavenly things!

RIGAULT.] in that very labor bent and sloping toward the earth, he handed down to his whole race the spirit of the world which he had appropriated from that material, [Note: [Col. 0286D] *Merely natural and heretical.* Thus he makes some people “psychic,” others heretical, as also at the beginning of the book *On Monogamy*. And yet Adam himself, whom he calls “psychic,” he will shortly call a heretic. PAMELIUS.] a race merely natural and heretical, not receiving the things of God?

[Note: [Col. 0286D] *Or who will doubt that Adam’s very offense*, etc. This passage is also noteworthy because he derives the beginning of every heresy from Adam’s offense, inasmuch as, as follows, he committed it by choosing his own judgment rather than the divine judgment. In this he alludes to the definition of heresy discussed extensively above in *On Prescription*, chapter 6. I would therefore prefer the reading of the first edition, “he was still an unformed heretic,” in place of “he was altogether unformed,” which Rhenanus substituted from the Gorze manuscript, were the latter not also found in two Vatican manuscripts. PAMELIUS.]

Or who [Col. 0286C] will hesitate to pronounce Adam’s very offense a heresy, since he committed it by choosing his own judgment rather than the divine judgment? Except that Adam never said to his potter: “You fashioned me unwisely.” He confessed his deception; he did not conceal the woman who deceived him. He was an altogether unformed [Note: [Col. 0286C] Earlier editions read *still*.] heretic. He disobeyed; nevertheless, he did not blaspheme the Creator or criticize [Col. 0287A] his Maker, whom from his own beginning he had found good and [Note: [Col. 0287D] *And* absent in Rigault, Venice.] supremely good, even if perhaps he himself had made him a judge from that beginning.

## CHAPTER III

Therefore, as we enter upon an examination of the known God, if the question is under what condition he is known, we must begin from his works, which are prior to the human being. Thus his goodness, discovered immediately together with himself and thereafter established and laid down as a presumption, may furnish us with some means of understanding how the subsequent ordering of things came about. Moreover, Marcion’s disciples, upon recognizing the goodness of our God, can acknowledge it as worthy of God through the same grounds by which we showed the goodness of their god to be unworthy.

Now this very thing, which is the material for the knowledge of him, [Note: [Col. 0287D] Earlier editions read *very fact*.] he did not find in another’s possession, but made for himself from his own resources. The Creator’s first goodness, then, was that by which God was unwilling to remain hidden forever—that is, unwilling that there should be no being to whom God might be known. For what is so good as the knowledge and enjoyment of God? Even though it was not yet apparent that this was good, because as yet there was nothing to which it could appear, God nevertheless foreknew how good it would prove to be. And therefore [Note: [Col. 0287D] *He entrusted it to the sum of his own goodness.* *Entrusted* here means “stored away,” namely, to be brought forth in its own time. RIGAULT.] he entrusted it to the sum of his own goodness, which would bring forth the good destined to appear. That goodness was certainly neither sudden, nor accidental, nor awakened by provocation, as though it were to be dated only from the point at which it began to operate.

For if goodness itself established the beginning, then, at the point when it began to operate, it did not itself receive a beginning, since it made the beginning. Once the beginning had been made, the reckoning of times was also born from it, since the stars and heavenly lights were arranged to distinguish [Col. 0287C] and mark those times: “For they shall be,” he says, “for seasons, months, and years” (Gen. 1:14). Therefore the goodness which made time had no time before time, just as the goodness which established the beginning had no beginning before the beginning. Thus, lacking both an order of beginning and a measure of time, it will be reckoned as belonging to an immeasurable and indeterminable eternity. It cannot be regarded as sudden, accidental, or provoked, since there is nothing from which it could be so reckoned—that is, no form of time. Rather, it must be presumed [Note: [Col. 0287D] *And* omitted by Semler, Oberthür.] eternal, unbegotten together with God, and perpetual, and therefore worthy of God. From this point already it puts Marcion’s god’s goodness to shame—not merely because that goodness is later in its beginnings and times, but because it is later even than the Creator’s malice, if indeed malice could have been brought forth by goodness [Note: [Col. 0287D] *Could entrust* in other editions.].

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0288A]

Accordingly, since God’s own goodness had provided man for the purpose of knowing God, it added this also as its own proclamation: it first devised a dwelling for man, afterward a certain vast structure, and later one greater still, so that in the great, as though in the lesser, he might rehearse and be brought to perfection; and thus he might be advanced from God’s good—that is, from the great dwelling—to His best also—that is, to the greater dwelling. For the good work He employs also the best minister, His Word: [Note: [Col. 0287D] “My heart,” he says, “has uttered the best word.” In the same manner he cited the beginning of Psalm XLIV above, in *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 18, in place of what all the Hebrew, Greek, Chaldean, and Latin editions have: “good.” PAM.] “My heart,” he says (Ps. XLIV, 1), “has uttered [Note: [Col. 0288D] Others add “word.”] the best discourse.”

Let Marcion recognize here the first and best fruit, surely of the best tree. An utterly ignorant husbandman, indeed, has grafted a good tree onto a bad one; but the shoot [Note: [Col. 0287D] “The shoot of blasphemy,” etc. Thus Rhenanus correctly, instead of the earlier reading *sarculus* (“hoe”); for the word is understood as a shoot or branch, concerning which John XV, 6 is written, to which the author seems to allude: “It shall be cast outside like a branch, and shall wither.” [Col. 0288D] The expression *adspice ad summam* is genuinely Tertullian’s, in place of what is commonly said, *in summa* (“in sum”). The reading *fructificaverit* may be retained; or read with Vaticanus 1, *fructificavit*. PAM.] of blasphemy will not prevail: it will wither together with its cultivator, and thus the nature of the good tree will bear witness to itself.

Consider, in sum, what fruits the Word has produced: “And God said, ‘Let it be’; and it was made; and God saw that it was good” (Gen. I). It was not as though He did not know the good unless He saw it; rather, because it was good, He therefore looked upon it—honoring and authenticating it, and crediting the goodness of His works with the favor of His regard. So too He blessed the things that He made well, so that the whole God might be commended to you as good both in speaking and in acting. As yet the Word did not know how to curse, because He did not know how to do evil either. We shall examine the causes that also required this of God.

Meanwhile, the world consisted of every kind of good, sufficiently foreshowing how much good was being prepared for him for whom [Note: [Col. 0288D] Fran. adds “him.”] all this was being prepared. Who, finally, was worthy to inhabit God’s works except His own image and likeness? [Col. 0288C] Goodness produced that likeness also—and with still greater activity—not by an imperial command, but by a familiar hand, with a gracious word sent before it: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26). Goodness spoke; goodness fashioned man [Note: [Col. 0288D] “Man” is absent from Semler and Oberthür.] from clay, constructing out of a single material a substance of flesh endowed with so many qualities. Goodness breathed [Note: [Col. 0288D] Semler and Oberthür add “into.”] into him a soul—not a dead soul, but a living one. Goodness set him over all things, to enjoy and rule them and even to give them names (Gen. II, 7).

Goodness further added delights for man, so that, although he possessed the whole world, he might dwell in its lovelier regions, [Note: [Col. 0288D] “Transferred into paradise, even then from the world into the Church.” In the book *On Repentance*, he said that the Church existed “in one and another.” Here, therefore, he says that Adam and Eve were transferred into paradise, from the world into the Church, signifying that paradise had been assigned by God to the Church, and that the Church even then existed in those two persons. RIG.] transferred into paradise—even then, from the world into the Church.

The same goodness also provided a helper, so that nothing good might be lacking: “For it is not,” He says [Col. 0289A] (Gen. II, 18), “good for man to be alone.” [Note: [Col. 0289D] He knew that the female sex would benefit him through Mary, and thereafter through the Church. For the Virgin Mary bore Christ, the salvation of mankind. Hence the virgin Church also, the bride of Christ, bears Christians. RIG.] He knew that the female sex would benefit him through Mary, and thereafter through the Church.

But even the law that you accuse and twist into matters of controversy was bestowed by goodness, [Note: [Col. 0289D] “Taking thought for man, whereby he might adhere to God.” An excellent thought: that man belongs to God insofar as he adheres to the commandments laid down by God through the observance and worship of religion. RIG.] taking thought for man, whereby he might adhere to God, lest he should appear not so much free as cast off, equated with His other servants, the animals, which were released from God and free because they were disdained [Note: [Col. 0289D] Paris and Fran. read “high station.”]; but so that man alone might glory in the fact that he alone had been deemed worthy to receive a law from God, and so that, as a rational creature capable of understanding and knowledge, he might also be held within the bounds of rational liberty, subject to Him who had subjected all things to him (1 Cor. XV, 28).

Goodness likewise appended counsel for observing this law: “But on the day on which you eat, you shall surely die” (Gen. II, 17). For He most kindly disclosed the outcome of transgression, lest ignorance of the danger [Col. 0289B] should encourage negligence in obedience. Moreover, if there was first a reason for imposing the law, there followed also a reason for observing it: that a penalty should be assigned to transgression—a penalty which He nevertheless did not wish to occur, since He foretold it beforehand. Recognize, therefore, meanwhile and at least thus far, the goodness of our God: from His good works, His good blessings, His acts of indulgence, His providential arrangements, and His good and kindly laws and warnings [Note: [Col. 0289D] Semler and Oberthür read “forewarnings.”].

## CHAPTER V

From this point onward, then, to all the questions. [Note: [Col. 0289D] “O dogs, whom the Apostle drives outside,” etc. He alludes to Revelation XXII: “Outside are the dogs.” Accordingly, this passage also argues against Erasmus and certain others who dare to deny that the Apocalypse belongs to John the Apostle. Concerning this we said something above in the book *On Prescription*, and below in Book IV *Against Marcion* and in the *Scorpiace*. PAM.] O [Note: [Col. 0289D] Semler omits “O.”] dogs, whom the Apostle drives outside (Rev. XXII, 15), barking against [Note: [Col. 0289D] Fran. omits “against.”] the God of truth! These are the bones of your arguments that you gnaw upon.

If God is good, foreknows the future, and is able to avert evil, why did He permit man—and indeed His own image and likeness, or rather His own substance, in respect, of course, to the derivation of the soul—to fall away from obedience to the law into death, after being deceived by the devil? For if He was both good, so that He would not wish such a thing to happen; and foreknowing, so that He would not be unaware that it would happen; and powerful, so that He would be able to prevent it—then under no circumstances would that have occurred which could not occur under these three conditions of divine majesty. But if it did occur, the contrary conclusion is established: God must be believed neither good, nor foreknowing, nor powerful. For just as no such thing would have happened if God were of that character—that is, good, foreknowing, and powerful—so it happened for this reason: because God is not of that character.
