In reply to this, we must first defend in the Creator those attributes that are called into doubt: I mean goodness, foreknowledge, [Col. 0290A] and power. Nor shall I linger over this point, since even Christ’s own rule of determination leads the way (John X, 25): proofs must be undertaken from works. [Note: [Col. 0290D] “Proofs must be undertaken from works.” When he attributes this rule to Christ, he alludes to John X: “The works that I do in my Father’s name, these bear witness concerning me; and if you are unwilling to believe me, believe the works.” PAM.] [Note: [Col. 0289D] Semler and Oberthür read the singular, “proof.”]

The Creator’s works testify both to His goodness, by which they are good, as we have shown, and to His power, by which they are so great—and indeed made from nothing. For even if they were made from some matter, as certain people maintain, nevertheless in this very respect they were made from nothing, since they were not what they now are. Finally, even on that supposition they are great, because they are good; and even on that supposition God is powerful, because all things belong to Him—whence He is also almighty.

But what shall I say of His foreknowledge? It has as many witnesses as the prophets He made. Yet what special title can “foreknowledge” have in the Author of all things, who surely, by ordering all things, foreknew them, and by foreknowing them, ordered them—certainly including the transgression itself? For if He had not foreknown it, He would not have issued a warning against it under threat of death.

Accordingly, [Col. 0290B] if these faculties did exist in God—faculties in view of which no evil either could or ought to have happened to man—and yet it nevertheless happened, let us examine man’s condition also, lest it was rather through that condition that the event occurred which could not have occurred through God.

I find that man was established by God as free, possessed of his own choice and his own power; [Note: [Col. 0290D] “Of his own choice and his own power,” etc. Such was the madness of certain heretics that they denied that man had been created free. Such were Marcion and Valentinus. He will shortly prove that freedom remained even after sin. LE PR.] and I discern in him no image and likeness of God more especially than the form of such a condition. For he was not fashioned after the uniform God in face and bodily lineaments, which vary so greatly throughout the human race; rather, he was fashioned in that substance which he drew from God Himself—that is, the soul [Note: [Col. 0290D] Semler and Oberthür read the accusative, “soul.”], corresponding to the form of God [Note: [Col. 0290D] Semler and Pamelius read “pledging.”]—and he was marked by freedom and power of his own choice.

The law itself, then laid down by God, also confirmed this condition of his. For a law would not have been laid down for one who did not have it in his power to render the obedience owed to the law; nor, again, would the threat of death have been assigned to transgression if contempt for the law had not also been reckoned as belonging to man’s freedom of choice. So too in the Creator’s later laws you find Him setting before man good and evil, life and death (Deut. XXX, 15). Nor, otherwise, would the whole order of discipline have been arranged through commandments, with God calling man away, threatening him, and exhorting him [Note: [Col. 0290D] “And” is absent from Semler; Pamelius conjectures “or exhorting.”], unless man were free and voluntary both for obedience and for contempt. [Note: [Col. 0290D] Pamelius and the Venetian edition read “man” in the ablative.]

## CHAPTER VI

But since we are now understood from this to be constructing a case for man’s free power of choice, so that what happened to him must be reproached not to God but to man himself, you might now object that he ought not to have been established in this way if the freedom and power of choice were going to prove destructive. I shall therefore first defend the proposition that he ought to have been established in this way, so that I may commend all the more strongly both the fact that he was so established and that he was established worthily of God, once the superior reason that caused him to be so established has been demonstrated.

God’s goodness and His reason will support this arrangement also, since in our God they act in harmony in all things. For reason without goodness is not reason, nor is goodness without reason goodness—unless perhaps [Note: [Col. 0291D] “In the case of Marcion’s god,” etc. Marcion appeared ridiculous, since by denying to God the attributes with which he has just dealt, he makes God good by taking reason away from Him. LE PR.] in the case of Marcion’s god, who is irrationally good, as we have shown.

It was necessary that God should be known: this is surely good and rational. It was necessary that there should be something worthy to know God: what could be provided so worthy as [Note: [Col. 0291D] “The image and likeness of God,” etc. Here he interprets the image and likeness of God in which man was made very differently from his usual interpretation elsewhere, especially in *On Baptism*, chapter 5, where we annotated something concerning this matter, as also concerning how the soul is said there to be God’s breath. PAM.] God’s image and likeness? And this, without doubt, is both good and rational.

It was therefore necessary that God’s image [Col. 0291B] and likeness should be established with freedom of choice and power of its own, since precisely in these the image and likeness of God would be reckoned—namely, in freedom and power of choice. For this purpose there was adapted to man a substance suited to this condition: God’s breath, surely free and possessed of its own power.

Besides, what sense would it have made for man, possessing the entire world, not to reign first of all in possession of his own mind—lord of others, but slave of himself? You therefore have God’s goodness to recognize from the honor bestowed, and His reason from the arrangement. Let goodness alone now be taken into account: it granted so much to man, namely, freedom of choice. Let reason defend for itself another consideration in an institution of this kind.

For God alone is good by nature (Matt. XIX, 17). He who possesses what He is without a beginning possesses it not by institution but by nature. Man, however, who exists wholly by institution and has a beginning, received together with his beginning the form by which he was to exist. Thus he was disposed toward good not by nature, but by institution. His goodness was not his own, because he was disposed toward good not by nature but by institution, according to his good Institutor, who is, of course, the Creator of good things.

Therefore, so that man might now possess goodness as his own, emancipated to him by God, and so that goodness might now become man’s property and in some sense his nature, there was assigned to him by institution, like the official who holds the scales [Note: [Col. 0291C] Rhenanus and Oberthür read “as though by an official holding the scales.”] in the emancipation of the good by God, [Note: [Col. 0291D] “Like the official who holds the scales in the emancipation of the good by God.” The alienation of *res mancipi*—that is, property capable of being held and possessed by full legal title—was effected by bronze and scales. Accordingly, a scale-holder was employed as a kind of arbiter of the conveyance. Its formula is found in Boethius’ commentary on Cicero’s *Topics*. RIG.—“Like the official who holds the scales in the emancipation of the good by God.” This metaphor, which he employs from the law, is taken from emancipation, which was a fictitious sale and was effected by bronze and scales—that is, in the presence of five witnesses and a scale-holder. LE PR.] freedom and power of choice. This would bring it about that good, as something properly his own, [Col. 0292A] should thereafter be rendered voluntarily by man, since reason also required that goodness should be exercised voluntarily: that is, from freedom of choice, not favoring institution [Note: [Col. 0291C] Pamelius reads “of institution”; Wouwer reads “choice favoring institution”; [Col. 0291D] Semler conjectures “choice; for by favoring institution.”] nor serving it slavishly.

Only thus, indeed, would man stand as good: if he were found good in accordance with his institution, certainly, but now by his own will, as though from the property of nature. Similarly, against evil also—for God, of course, foresaw that as well—man would present himself [Note: [Col. 0292C] Semler and Oberthür add “as.”] all the stronger [Note: [Col. 0292C] Junius reads “press onward.”], since he was free and possessed of his own power. [Note: [Col. 0292D] “Because, if he lacked this right.” There is an extraordinary variety among the correctors: they substitute “received,” “desired,” “departed,” “underwent,” and “longed”; Rigaltius reads better, “lacked.” LE PR.] For if he lacked this right, so that he performed even the good not by will but by necessity, he would also be liable to appropriation by evil through the weakness of servitude, and equally a slave to evil as to good.

The whole freedom of choice was therefore granted to him in both directions, so that, as his own master, he might meet both alternatives steadfastly: by preserving the good voluntarily [Col. 0292B] and avoiding evil voluntarily. For there was another reason too: since man had been placed under God’s judgment, it was necessary to make that judgment just [Note: [Col. 0292D] “It was necessary to make that judgment just.” This passage too argues for the merits of works, as does what follows: “Otherwise neither the reward of good nor of evil,” etc. PAM.] on the basis of the merits of his own choice, which was free. Otherwise, neither the reward of good nor of evil would justly have been weighed out to one who had been found either good or evil by necessity, rather than by will.

For this purpose the law too was established, not excluding freedom but proving it, through obedience voluntarily rendered or transgression voluntarily committed. Thus freedom of choice lay open toward either outcome.

Therefore, if both God’s goodness and His reason are found to be involved in the freedom of choice granted to man, we must not omit the primary determination concerning goodness and reason—which must be established before the whole discussion—and then judge retrospectively from subsequent events that God ought not to have established man in this way because the outcome differed from what was fitting for God. Rather, after discerning that He ought to have established him in this way, we must preserve what has been discerned and investigate the remaining matters.

Otherwise, it is easy for those who immediately stumble upon man’s fall, before examining his condition, to refer what happened to his Author, because the Author’s reason has not been examined. Finally, both God’s goodness, perceived from the beginning of His works, will persuade us [Note: [Col. 0292D] “That no evil could have come from God,” etc. This also, and everything discussed in the preceding chapter and the two following chapters, argues against Calvin and others who are not ashamed to make God the author of evils. PAM.] that no evil could have come from God, and man’s freedom, when reconsidered, will show [Note: [Col. 0292D] Pamelius and Semler read “shows.”] that it is rather itself guilty of what it committed.

## CHAPTER VII

By this determination, all God’s attributes remain intact: the nature of His goodness, the reason of His ordering, and the fullness of His foreknowledge and power. Yet you must also require of God [Note: [Col. 0293D] Junius reads “you have.”] the highest constancy and the preeminent fidelity in every institution of His, so that you may cease asking whether anything could have happened against God’s will.

For once you maintain the constancy and fidelity of the good God—while recognizing that they must be vindicated in His rational institutions—you will not be surprised that God did not intervene against the things He did not wish to happen, so that He might preserve the things He did wish [Note: [Col. 0293D] Paris reads “did not wish.”]. For if He had once allowed man freedom and power of choice, and had allowed it worthily, as we have shown, He had surely allowed them to be used by the very authority of His institution. So far as depended upon Himself, however, He allowed them to be used according to Himself—that is, according to God, that is, for good; for who will permit anything against himself? But so far as depended upon man, He allowed them to be used according to the movements of freedom itself. For who does not grant to one whom he once allows to use something that he may use it according to his own inclination and choice?

It followed, therefore, that God should withdraw from the freedom once granted to man—that is, should restrain within Himself both His foreknowledge and His supreme power, [Note: [Col. 0293D] “Through which He could have intervened.” Among the Romans, the tribunes interposed against decrees of the senate when they obstructed them so that they should not be enacted. So too shortly afterward: “For if He had intervened.” RHEN.] through which He could have intervened to prevent man, once he had undertaken to use his freedom badly, from falling into danger. For if He had intervened, He would have annulled the freedom of choice that He had granted on rational and good grounds.

Finally, suppose that He had intervened; suppose that He had annulled freedom of choice by calling man back from the tree and by keeping the serpent, the deceiver, [Note: [Col. 0293D] “The serpent, the deceiver.” That is, one who circumvents or cheats. Juvenal, *Satire* XV, speaks of one “summoning a guardian of a ward to court … as a cheat.” For *circumscribere* also means “to circumvent.” RHEN.] from meeting the woman. Would not Marcion exclaim: [Note: [Col. 0293D] “O worthless lord,” etc. For Marcion made God irrationally good, as may be seen in chapter 6 of this book and elsewhere. LE PR.] “O worthless lord—unstable, unfaithful, annulling what He instituted! Why did He permit free choice if He intervenes? Why does He intervene if He permitted it?” Let him choose where he would mark God Himself with error: in the institution, or in its annulment.

Would God not then have appeared all the more deceived through lack of foreknowledge of the future, precisely when He obstructed it? And who would not say that He had granted something as though ignorant of how it would turn out? But even if He had foreknown that man would use His institution badly, what could be so worthy of God as the constancy and fidelity of His institutions, whatever their character?

It was for man to see to it if he failed to discharge well what he had received in good condition, so that man himself [Note: [Col. 0294D] Rigaltius and Latinus read “they themselves”; Pamelius and Semler omit “so that.”] might be guilty before the law that he had refused to obey, rather than that the Lawgiver Himself should defraud His own law by not permitting its prescription to be fulfilled.

If the Creator had opposed man’s free choice through the providence and power you demand, you would have delivered these most worthy arguments against Him. Now whisper to yourself, on the Creator’s behalf, about His constancy, patience, and fidelity, since He faithfully discharged His own institutions as both rational and good.

## CHAPTER VIII

For He had not brought man forth merely to live, without also bringing him forth to live rightly—that is, with regard for God and His law. Accordingly, He Himself had granted man simply to live by making him into a living soul; but He had entrusted to him the task of living rightly, after admonishing him to obey the law.

Thus He who now desires man to be restored to life, preferring the sinner’s repentance to his death (Ezek. XVIII, 23), proves that man was not instituted for death. Accordingly, just as God introduced man into a state of life, so man brought upon himself a state of death. And he did this neither through weakness nor through ignorance, lest anything should be imputed to his Author.

For although it was an angel who seduced him, the one who was seduced was nevertheless free and possessed of his own power; he was the image and likeness of God, stronger than an angel; and God’s breath was nobler than the material spirit from which the angels were constituted. “He makes,” Scripture says (Ps. CIII, 5), “spirits His angels” (Heb. I, 7), [Note: [Col. 0293D] “And His attendants a flame of fire.” It matters little whether this comes from the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter I, as Pamelius affirms, or from Psalm CIII. For although the Apostle calls it πυρὸς φλόγα, “a flame of fire,” he cites this from Psalm CIII, verse 5, where it reads, “and His ministers a burning fire.” In Greek it is πῦρ φλέγον, “burning fire.” In my judgment, the Vulgate version agrees better with the text in this passage than Tertullian’s version does. But whether one reads “a flame of fire” or “burning fire,” the sense is the same. That variation appears to have arisen from the Hebrew, which may correctly be translated “burning” or “flaming fire.” LE PR.] “and His attendants a flame of fire.”

For He would not have subjected the universe to man’s dominion if man were weak and not superior to the angels, to whom He subjected no such thing. Nor would He have imposed the weight of the law if the law were burdensome for one too feeble to bear it. Nor would He have prosecuted under sentence of death one whom He knew to be excusable on the ground of weakness [Note: [Col. 0294D] Pamelius, Semler, and Oberthür read “since.”]. Finally, He would not have made him weak by freedom and power of choice, but rather by the absence of those things.

Indeed, the same man, the same substance of soul, the same condition of Adam, and the same freedom and power of choice make him victorious today over the same devil, when that freedom is administered in accordance with obedience to God’s laws.

## CHAPTER IX

Nevertheless, you say, by whatever means it occurred, a substance derived from the Creator is found capable of sin, since God’s breath—that is, the soul—sinned in man. And the corruption of a portion cannot fail to be referred back to its original source [Note: [Col. 0294D] The Venetian edition and Rigaltius read “origin.”].

In reply to this, the character of the soul must be interpreted. First of all, it must be maintained [Note: [Col. 0294D] “What the Greek Scripture designated,” etc. The Greek word πνοή (*pnoē*, “breath”) was correctly noted in the margin by Rhenanus, for the author alludes to it here. It is the word read in Genesis II, not πνεῦμα (*pneuma*, “spirit”). Accordingly, the Latin translator also correctly rendered it “breath of life,” which the author relates to breathing, not “spirit.” PAM.] that the Greek Scripture designated it by calling it “breath” (*πνοή, pnoē*), not “spirit” (*πνεῦμα, pneuma*). For certain translators from the Greek, failing to reflect on the distinction or to attend to the proper meaning of the words, put “spirit” in place of “breath.” They thereby give heretics an opportunity to stain God’s Spirit with sin—that is, God Himself—and the question has now been usurped on that basis.

Understand, therefore, that the breath is less than the spirit [Note: [Col. 0295D] Semler and Oberthür read the accusative, “spirit.”], although it proceeds from the spirit: it is, as it were, a little breeze from it, but is nevertheless not the spirit. For a breeze too is thinner than the wind; although a breeze comes from the wind, the breeze is nevertheless not the wind.

[Note: [Col. 0295D] “It is also possible to call the breath an image of the spirit,” etc. Here too you see how he uses the word *capit*: that is, the breath also signifies an image of the spirit, or can be called an image of the spirit. RHEN.] It is also possible to call the breath an image of the spirit. For this is also why man is the image of God—that is, of the Spirit; for God is Spirit. The image of the Spirit, therefore, is the breath. [Note: [Col. 0295D] Pamelius and Semler delete “breath.”]

Moreover, an image will not be altogether equal to the reality. For it is one thing to exist according to the reality, and another to be the reality itself. Thus the breath also, since it is an image of the Spirit, cannot make the image equal to God [Note: [Col. 0295D] Ciacconius reads “be made equal.”] in such a way that, because the reality—that is, the Spirit, that is, God—is without sin, the breath too—that is, the image—ought therefore to have been incapable of committing sin. In this respect the image will be less than the reality, and the breath inferior to the Spirit. [Col. 0295B]

It certainly possesses those lineaments of God: insofar as the soul is immortal; insofar as it is free and possessed of its own choice; insofar as it often has foreknowledge; and insofar as it is rational and capable of understanding and knowledge. Yet even in these respects it is an image [Note: [Col. 0295D] Junius reads “as.”], and it does not extend to the full power of divinity. So neither does it extend to complete immunity from sin, because this belongs to God alone—that is, to the reality—and this alone is not permitted to the image.

For just as an image, although it expresses all the lineaments of the reality, nevertheless lacks its actual force [Note: [Col. 0295D] Semler conjectures “life.”], since it has no motion, so also the soul, as an image of the Spirit, was unable to express His power alone—that is, the blessedness [Note: [Col. 0295D] Pamelius conjectures “capacity.”] of not sinning. Otherwise it would not be a soul but the Spirit; nor would he who received the soul be man, but God.

Besides, not everything that belongs to God will therefore be regarded as God. You cannot demand that the breath should also be God—that is, empty of sin—merely because it is God’s breath. For if you blow into a flute, you do not thereby make the flute a human being, although you have blown into it from your own soul, just as God breathed from His own Spirit.

Finally, since Scripture plainly says (Gen. II, 7) that God breathed into man’s face, and that man became a living soul—not a life-giving spirit—it separated the soul from the condition of its Maker. For the work must necessarily be something other than the craftsman—that is, inferior to the craftsman. A vessel made by a potter will not itself be the potter. So too a breath made by the Spirit will not for that reason be the Spirit. By the very fact that it is a soul, it was called “breath.”

See also whether, from the condition of being breathed forth, it passed into some lesser quality. “Then,” you say, “you have conceded to the soul the weakness you denied above.” Certainly, when you require it to be equal to God—that is, immune from sin—I call it weak. But when it is compared with an angel, [Col. 0295D] I must maintain that the lord of the universe is stronger—he whom the angels now serve (Heb. I, 14), and who will even judge angels [Col. 0296A] (1 Cor. VI, 2), if he stands firm in God’s law, which at the beginning he refused to do.

God’s breath, therefore, was able to admit this very thing. It was able, but it ought not to have done so. It possessed the ability through the slightness of its substance, by which it was breath and not Spirit; but it had the obligation not to do so through its power of choice, by which it was free and not a slave. In addition, the warning not to sin, under threat of death, stood beside it, so that the slightness of its substance might be supported and the freedom of its decision governed.

Accordingly, the soul can no longer be seen to have sinned through that which is akin to God in it—namely, through the breath—but through that which was added to its substance, namely free choice: rationally bestowed by God, but exercised by man in whatever way he willed.

If this is so, God’s entire dispensation is now cleared of the reproach of evil. For freedom [Col. 0296B] of choice will not cast off its guilt upon Him by whom it was given, but upon him by whom it was not administered as it ought to have been.

What evil, finally, will you ascribe [Note: [Col. 0296D] The Venetian edition and Rigaltius read “assign”; Pamelius and Semler read “describe.”] to the Creator? If it is man’s sin, it will not belong to God, because it belongs to man. Nor must the person found to have forbidden and even condemned the sin be regarded as identical with its author. If death is the evil, death will bring reproach not upon Him who threatened it, but upon him who despised it, as its author. For by despising it he brought it about; it certainly would not have occurred if he had not despised it.

## CHAPTER X

But even if [Note: [Col. 0296D] Semler inserts “not”; Junius reads “now.”] you transfer the indictment of evil from man to the devil, [Note: [Col. 0296D] “Transfer the indictment of evil.” That is, attribute all the properties of evil to the devil; for this is Tertullian’s meaning of the expression. He used it thus in Book I *Against Marcion*. LE PR.] as the instigator of the sin, so that you may in this manner also direct the blame against the Creator as the devil’s author—He who makes angels spirits—the answer is this: what was made by God, namely the angel, will belong to Him who made it; but what was not made by God, namely the devil—that is, the slanderer—must necessarily have been made by the being himself, by slandering God, and indeed falsely.

His first falsehood was that God had forbidden them to eat from every tree; the second, that they supposedly would not die if they ate; the third, that God supposedly envied them divinity. Whence, then, came the malice of lying and deception against human beings, and of defamation against God? Certainly not from God, who also established the angel as good, in accordance with the form of His good works. Indeed, before he became the devil, he is represented as the wisest of all—unless wisdom is an evil.

And if you unfold Ezekiel’s prophecy (Ezek. XXVIII, 12), you will readily perceive that the angel was good by institution and corrupted by his own will. For under the person [Note: [Col. 0296D] Semler and Oberthür read “person.”] of the prince of Tyre, judgment is pronounced against the devil:

> And the word of the Lord came [Col. 0296D] to me, saying: Son of man, take up a lamentation over the prince of Tyre, and you shall say to him [Note: [Col. 0296D] Latinus adds “to him.”]: Thus says the Lord: You are the seal of likeness—

meaning, of course, that you had unsealed the integrity [Col. 0297A] of the image and likeness—

> full of wisdom [Note: [Col. 0297D] “Full of wisdom” is absent from Semler and the manuscripts, which do not contain “he says.” Yet nothing similar is found in the Septuagint version. Junius thinks it was inserted from the Hebrew or the Vulgate. Editors.], a crown of beauty—

this was said to him as the most eminent of the angels, an archangel, and the wisest of all—

> you were born amid the delights of the paradise of your God—

for it was there that God had made the angels, in the second formation of the figures of living beings—

> You were clothed with every precious stone: sardius, topaz, emerald, carbuncle, sapphire, jasper, lynx-stone, agate, amethyst, chrysolite, beryl, and onyx [Note: [Col. 0297D] Paris and Fran. read “onyx” with a variant spelling]; and with gold you filled your storehouses and your treasuries. From the day on which you were created, when I placed you with the cherub [Note: [Col. 0297D] Semler reads “cherubim,” against which stand the Hebrew reading, the Greek version of the Seventy, and finally the other editors, including Pamelius, Rigaltius, the Venetian edition, and Fran.; all support “cherub,” and the Vulgate favors it.] upon God’s holy mountain, you were in the midst of fiery stones. You were blameless in your days from the day on which you were created, until injuries were found in you. [Note: [Col. 0297D] “Until injuries were found in you.” The “injuries” are sins that injure the soul, for the Greek has ἀδικήματα (*adikēmata*, “wrongdoings”). In *On Patience*, chapter 7, he calls diminishing resources “injuries,” showing that through the casting away of riches, their losses too ought not to be counted as injuries. LE PR.] From the abundance of your commerce you filled your inner chambers and sinned,

and so forth.

It is manifest that these words pertain to the censure of the angel, [Col. 0297B] and not properly to that prince, because no human being was born in God’s paradise—not even Adam himself, who was instead transferred there. Nor was any human being placed with the cherub upon God’s holy mountain—that is, in the heavenly height from which the Lord also testifies that Satan fell. Nor did any human being dwell among the fiery stones, amid the sparkling rays of the burning stars, from which Satan was also cast down like lightning.

Rather, the author of sin himself was denounced under the person of the sinful man. Formerly he had indeed been blameless from the day of his creation, created by God for good, as by the good Creator of blameless creations; adorned with every angelic glory; and established with God, as a good being with the Good. But afterward he was transferred by his own act into evil.

“For from the time,” Scripture says, “when your injuries appeared”—reckoning to him those injuries by which, of course, he injured man, who was cast out from obedience to God [Note: [Col. 0298D] Latinus reads “chosen for obedience to God”; Rhenanus, “chosen from God.”]. And he sinned from the time when he sowed sin; and thus from that point onward he practiced the abundance of his commerce—that is, of his malice—namely the abundance of sins and designs. He too, no less than man, had been established with free choice, since he was a spirit. For God would not have ordered anything close to Himself without freedom of this kind.

Yet by condemning him beforehand, God testified that he had deviated from the form of his institution through his own lust for a malice conceived voluntarily. And by allotting a limited scope to his operations, God fulfilled the rational purpose of His goodness, with the same design that man [Note: [Col. 0297D] “By the same freedom of choice might crush the enemy,” etc. This passage maintains, against the heretics, that freedom was not altogether lost after Adam’s sin. LE PR.] might crush his enemy through the same freedom of choice by which he had fallen before him. Thus man would prove that the fault was his own and not God’s; would worthily recover salvation through victory; and the devil, defeated by the one whom he had previously overthrown, would be punished more bitterly. And God would be found all the more good, as He awaited man, who was now to return from this life to a more glorious paradise, with permission to pluck from the tree of life.

## CHAPTER XI
Thus, up to the time of man’s sin, God was from the beginning only good; thereafter he was also judge and severe and—what the Marcionites would have it—cruel. The woman is immediately condemned to give birth in pain and to serve her husband (Gen. 3:16); yet previously, without any sorrow, [Note: [Col. 0298D] Through the blessing for the increase of the race. This may be a Greek construction: “through the blessing according to the increase of the race she had heard only, ‘Increase and multiply.’” RHEN.] through the blessing for the increase of the race she had heard only, “Increase and multiply”; and she had been appointed as a help for the male, not for servitude. Immediately the earth too is cursed (Gen. 3:18), but previously it had been blessed. Immediately there are thorns and thistles, but previously grass, plants, and fruitful trees. [Col. 0298B] Immediately there is sweat and the labor of obtaining bread, but previously sustenance without toil from every tree and food free from anxiety. From then on man returns to the earth, whereas previously he came from the earth. From then on he goes to death, whereas previously he was destined for life. From then on [Note: [Col. 0298D] “From then on in hide garments.” He means garments of skin. RHEN.] he is clothed in garments of skin, whereas previously he was naked without embarrassment.

Thus God’s goodness is prior, according to nature; his severity is subsequent, according to its cause. The former is innate, the latter accidental; the former proper to him, the latter adapted to circumstances; the former brought forth from within, the latter called into use. For his nature ought not to have kept goodness inactive, nor ought the cause to have escaped severity through its being passed over. God furnished the one for himself, the other for the situation.

Now begin to accuse even the condition of a judge as akin to evil—you who dreamed of another God who is solely good because you cannot tolerate a judge, although we have shown that your god too is a judge. Or, if he is not a judge, he is certainly perverse [Col. 0298C] and ineffectual: the founder of a discipline that is not to be enforced, that is, not to be judged. Yet do you not condemn God as judge when you approve God as no judge? You will undoubtedly have to accuse justice itself, which produces the judge, or else even reckon it among the forms of wickedness—that is, enroll injustice among the titles of goodness. For justice is now evil if injustice is good. But since you are compelled to pronounce injustice one of the worst things, by the same constraint you are forced to rank justice among the best. For nothing opposed to evil is anything but good, just as nothing opposed to good is anything but evil. Therefore, to the same degree that injustice is evil, justice is good. And it must be regarded not merely as a form of goodness but as its safeguard, because unless goodness is governed by justice, so that it is just, it will not be goodness if it is unjust. For nothing unjust is good, while [Col. 0298D] everything just is good.

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0299A]

Thus, [Note: [Col. 0299D] “Thus, if the association and concord of goodness and justice cannot admit of their separation.” Latinius likewise judged that the customary reading, *separatione earum non potest carere* (“cannot be without their separation”), should be emended in this way. The Pithoean manuscript reads: *separationem eorum non potest carere*. Ursinus’ book exhibits Septimius’ style: “Thus, if the association and concord of goodness and justice cannot proceed with their separation, with what face,” etc. RIG.] if the association and concord of goodness and justice cannot admit of their separation, with what face will you establish the difference between two gods by separating them, reckoning one separately as the good god and the other separately as the just god? Goodness stands where justice also stands. Accordingly, from the beginning the Creator was as just as he was good, and both qualities came forth together. His goodness made the world; his justice proportioned it [Note: [Col. 0299D] “His justice proportioned it.” I would think that *moderata est* (“regulated it”) should be read. Although supported by no manuscripts, I would maintain this merely as a conjecture. LE PR.]; indeed, justice even then judged that the world should be made of good things, because it judged in accordance with goodness’s design.

It is the work of justice that a separation was pronounced between light and darkness, between day and night, between heaven and earth, between the upper and lower water, between the gathering of the sea and the mass of dry land, between the greater [Col. 0299B] and lesser lights, those of day and those of night, between male and female, between the tree of the knowledge of death and the tree of life, between the world and paradise, and between water-born and earth-born [Note: [Col. 0299D] “Between water-born and earth-born.” He delights in expressions derived according to Greek usage, as though he were saying ὑδρογενῆ and γηγενῆ τῶν ζώων, “water-born and earth-born animals.” LE PR.] animals. Just as goodness conceived all things, so justice distinguished them. This whole universe was disposed and ordered by judgment. Every location, configuration of the elements, effect, movement, condition, rising, and setting of each thing constitutes a judgment of the Creator. Do not imagine that he is to be defined as judge only from the moment evil began, and so obscure justice beneath the occasion of evil. By these considerations we show that justice came forth together with goodness, the author of all things, so that justice too must be regarded as innate and natural to God, not as something adventitious, since it is found in the Lord as the arbiter of his works.

## CHAPTER XIII

But when evil afterwards broke forth, and from then on [Col. 0299C] God’s goodness began to deal with an adversary, that same justice of God acquired yet another [Note: [Col. 0299D] “It acquired another function, now to direct goodness according to each person’s turning toward it.” That is, goodness was to be directed according as each person turned his mind toward the goodness of God. RIG.] function: now to direct goodness according to each person’s turning toward it, so that, once its unrestrained liberality was set aside [Note: [Col. 0300D] “Once its unrestrained liberality was set aside.” This is how the manuscripts read, and it may be explained without awkwardness in this sense: once the liberality of divine goodness—by which God is good even spontaneously—has been set aside, that divine goodness is now weighed according to each person’s merits. RIG.], by which God is also spontaneously good, it might be weighed according to each person’s merits, offered to the worthy, denied to the unworthy, withdrawn from the ungrateful, and, correspondingly, vindicated against all its enemies.

Thus this entire work of justice is the administration of goodness: in judging it condemns; in condemning it punishes; in your words, it acts cruelly—and thereby it surely advances good, not evil. Indeed, fear of judgment contributes to good, not to evil. For it was no longer enough that goodness should commend itself [Col. 0300A] by itself, since it was now struggling under an adversary. For although commendable in itself, it was not thereby also capable of being preserved, because it was now open to attack by the adversary, unless some power that inspired fear presided over it and compelled people, even against their will, both to pursue and to preserve the good. Otherwise, when so many enticements of evil were assailing the good, who would pursue what he could despise with impunity? Who would preserve what he could lose without danger? You read that the way of evil is broad and much more heavily traveled (Matt. 7:13): would not everyone slip into it [Note: [Col. 0299C] “Would not everyone enter it,” Pamel., Seml.] if there were nothing on it to fear? We shudder at the Creator’s terrifying threats and are scarcely torn away from evil; what if he threatened nothing?

Will you call that justice evil which does not favor evil? Will you deny that it is good when it provides for the good? [Note: [Col. 0299D] Rhen., Fran., and Lat. insert “not.” Jun.] Would you not want God to be [Note: [Col. 0300D] “Would you not want such a God as is fitting?” The Pithoean manuscript reads: “What sort of God ought you to want? What sort would you prefer to be expedient?” RIG.] such as is fitting [Note: [Col. 0299D] Lat. and Jun. read *vel* (“or”) for *velles* (“would you want”)]; [Col. 0300B] what sort would you prefer to be expedient? One under whom sins would rejoice? One whom the devil would mock? Would you judge that God good who could make man all the more evil by granting him security in sin? Who is the author of good unless he also exacts it? Accordingly, who is foreign to evil unless he is also its enemy? Who is its enemy unless he also attacks it? Who attacks it unless he also punishes it?

Thus God is wholly good when he is everything on behalf of the good. Thus, finally, he is omnipotent, because he has power both to help and to harm. It is something less merely to benefit, because such a being can do nothing other than benefit. With what confidence could I hope for good from one of that kind, if that alone is what he can do? How could I seek the reward of innocence if I did not also expect the recompense of guilt [Note: [Col. 0230C] Seml. and Rhen. read *speciem* (“appearance”), which makes no sense and is also contrary [Col. 0300D] to the manuscripts.]? I must distrust whether he will reward even the one side, since he was not competent to deal with both [Note: [Col. 0230D] Others read “reward.”].

To such a degree justice is also the fullness of divinity itself, [Col. 0300C] presenting God as perfect, both Father and Lord: Father in clemency, Lord in discipline; Father through gentle power, Lord through severe power; Father, to be loved with filial devotion; Lord, necessarily to be feared. He is to be loved because he prefers mercy to sacrifice (Hos. 6:6) and feared because he does not desire sin; loved because he prefers the sinner’s repentance to his death (Ezek. 33:11) and feared because he does not desire sinners who belong to him yet no longer repent. Therefore the Law defines both duties: “You shall love God,” and “You shall fear God.” It set the one before the obedient person, the other before the transgressor. [Note: [Col. 0300D] “The other before the transgressor.” By these words, *obsecutori* and *exorbitatori*, he denotes the compliant person and the rebel or offender. He uses the verb *exorbitare* in *Exhortation to Chastity*: “one who deviates from monogamy”; and in *Apology* 6: “If they have defected from nothing? If they have deviated in nothing?” Sidonius, letter 11, book VIII: “I fear that a man of this kind will deviate from the rules of the catholic faith.” Likewise Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*: “Nor does our present consul Posthumius deviate from your saving laws.” LE PR.]

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 0301A]

God meets you in every respect: the same God strikes, but also heals; puts to death, but also brings to life; humbles, but also exalts; creates evils, but also makes peace (Deut. 32:39). This enables me to answer the heretics on this point too. “For behold,” they say, “he confesses himself to be the creator of evils, saying: ‘I am he who creates evils’” (Isa. 45:7). Seizing upon the common use of a word that confounds two kinds of evil through its ambiguity—because both sins and punishments are called “evils”—they indiscriminately wish him to be understood as the creator of moral evils, so that he may be proclaimed the author of wickedness [Note: [Col. 0301C] Fran. adds “unjustly.”].

We, however, by applying the distinction between the two forms and separating the evils of sin [Note: [Col. 0301C] Seml. reads “sins … punishments.”] from the evils of punishment, the evils of guilt from the evils of penalty, assign [Note: [Col. 0301C] Seml., against all others, reads “defend.”] its own author to each part: the devil as author of the evils [Col. 0301B] of sin and guilt, but God the Creator as author of the evils of punishment and penalty. Thus the former part is assigned to wickedness, the latter to justice, which creates the penal evils [Note: [Col. 0301C] Paris reads “for one who creates.”] of judgment [Note: [Col. 0301C] Seml., Venet., Pamel., and Rig. read “judgments,” but we follow reason as our guide. EDD.] against the evils of sin [Note: [Col. 0301D] Others read “sins.”]. These, then, are the evils of which the Creator declares himself the author—those appropriate to a judge.

They are indeed evils to those upon whom they are repaid; in their own proper character, however, they are good, because they are just, because they defend the good, and because they are enemies of sins and, in this order, worthy of God. Or prove them unjust, so that you may prove that they are to be assigned to wickedness, that is, that they are the evils of injustice. For if they belong to justice, they will no longer be evils but goods—evils only to the evil, by whom, conversely, even good things are condemned as evils.

Maintain, then, that man, the voluntary contemner of divine law, unjustly received that which he refused [Note: [Col. 0302C] Paris, Rig., Fran., Pamel., and Venet. read “wished.”] to do without; that the wickedness of that age was unjustly struck first with floods [Col. 0301C] and afterwards with fires; and that utterly foul and superstitious Egypt, which moreover oppressed a people who were its guests, was unjustly struck with a tenfold chastisement. He hardens Pharaoh’s heart; but Pharaoh had deserved to be furnished for destruction, since he had already denied God, had already haughtily driven away God’s envoys so many times, and had already increased the people’s burden of labor. Finally, as an Egyptian he had long been guilty before God of pagan idolatry, worshipping the ibis and the crocodile [Col. 0302A] more readily [Note: [Col. 0301D] “Worshipping the ibis and the crocodile more readily.” It is well established that the Egyptians were formerly devoted to superstition beyond all other nations; this is also related in *Apology* 24. Indeed, they were so superstitious that in different places they appointed different gods for themselves: τὸν Ἄπιν ἐν Μέμφι … τὸν τράγον ἐν Μένδητι, τὸν κροκόδειλον ἐν τῇ Μύριδος λίμνῃ (Lucian, *On Astrology*): “They worship Apis in the city of Memphis … the he-goat in the city of Mendes, and the crocodile in Lake Myris.” Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus* III, ch. 2, after comparing women’s adornment with Egyptian temples, describes and amplifies the construction of the temples and the ornaments by which they are embellished. Yet if you enter, he says, it is not a god but a spectacle worthy of laughter that is displayed: οὐ γὰρ θεὸς ὁ ζητούμενος ἔνδον εὑρεθήσεται, ἐφ’ ὃν ἐσπεύσαμεν, αἴλουρος δὲ ἢ [Col. 0302D] κροκόδειλος, ἢ αὐτόχθων ὄφις, ἢ τι τοιοῦτον θηρίον: “For the god who is sought, toward whom we hastened, will not be found inside, but rather a cat, or a crocodile, or a native serpent, or some animal of that kind.” Likewise Diodorus Siculus, *Library*, book I: οἱ μὲν ναοὶ κάλλιστοι … ἔνδον δὲ ἢν ζητῇς τὸν θεόν, ἢ πίθηκός ἐστιν, ἢ ἶβις, ἢ τράγος, ἢ αἴλουρος: “The temples are indeed most beautiful … but if you seek the god within, it is either a monkey, an ibis, a he-goat, or a cat.” Philo Judaeus relates the same in his book *On the Decalogue*. I omit Cyril of Alexandria, *Homily on the Paschal Feasts*; Pomponius Mela, book I; and Juvenal, *Satire* 15. I add only that the ibis is a bird resembling a stork, which devours locusts and snakes, for which reason it is superstitiously worshipped by the Egyptians and held in the place of a divinity. Constantinus Manasses records innumerable such beasts in his *Annals*, and Heliodorus, book IX, writes that the Egyptians fashioned even the Nile itself into a god for themselves. LE PR.], than the living God. He assails [Note: [Col. 0302C] Venet. and Rig. read “expends”; Rhen. and Seml., “hinders.”] even his own people, but they were ungrateful. He also sent bears against children, but they were irreverent toward the prophet.

## CHAPTER XV

First, then, examine [Note: [Col. 0302C] Rhen. reads “despise.”] the justice of the judge. If its rationale stands firm, his severity will stand firm as well, and the means through which that severity runs its course will be reckoned to reason and justice. And, lest we linger over numerous examples, assert the other causes too before you condemn the sentences; excuse the sins before you reject the judgments. Do not censure the judge, but prove him to be an evil judge.

For even if [Note: [Col. 0302C] Seml. omits “if.”] he exacted the sins of the fathers from [Note: [Col. 0302C] Seml. reads “from” differently: *de*.] their sons, the people’s hardness had compelled remedies of this kind, so that at least, by taking thought for their descendants, they might obey the divine law. For who does not care more for [Col. 0302B] the salvation of his sons than for his own? But if the fathers’ blessing was also destined for their offspring without any merit of theirs as yet, why should the fathers’ guilt not likewise overflow to their sons? As with favor, so also with offense, so that both favor and offense might run through the entire race.

This is subject to what was afterwards to be decreed: that people would no longer say that the fathers had eaten a sour grape and the children’s teeth had been set on edge (Jer. 31:29); that is, the father would not bear the son’s sin, nor the son the father’s sin, but each would become answerable for his own sin. Thus, after the people’s hardness had been subdued by the hardness of the law, justice would now judge not a lineage but individual persons. Yet if you accept the Gospel of truth, you will recognize to whom the sentence that repays the fathers’ sins upon the sons applies: namely, to those who were of their own accord to pronounce this sentence upon themselves: “His blood be upon our heads and upon the heads of our children” (Matt. 27:25). [Col. 0302C] All this, therefore, God’s providence adjudged because it had already heard it.

## CHAPTER XVI

Severity, then, is also good because it is just, if the judge is good, that is, just. Likewise good are all the other things through which the good work of good severity proceeds—whether anger, jealousy, or fierceness. For all these are due to severity [Note: [Col. 0303D] Rig. reads “to severity.”], just as severity is due to justice. The insolence of an age that owes modesty will have to be punished [Note: [Col. 0303D] Jun. reads “had to be.”]. And so those things incidental [Note: [Col. 0303D] Venet. and Seml. read “accrue.”] to a judge cannot [Note: [Col. 0303D] Others read “could not.”] be reproached against the judge; they are themselves as free from blame as [Note: [Col. 0303D] Seml. omits “also.”] the judge is.

What if you were to say that there ought indeed to be a physician, but then accuse his instruments because they cut, cauterize, amputate, and constrict, although without the instruments of his art he could not be a physician? Accuse him, rather, of cutting badly, amputating at the wrong time, and cauterizing rashly; then censure his instruments too as evil means of service. It is precisely the same when you acknowledge God as judge but reject the emotions and dispositions through which he judges.

We learn about God from the prophets [Col. 0303B] and from Christ, not from philosophers or from Epicurus. We who believe that God acted even upon earth and assumed the lowliness of human condition for the sake of human salvation are far removed from the opinion of those who will not allow God to care about anything. From them a proposition of this sort has also reached the heretics: “If God grows angry, is jealous, is aroused, and is provoked, then he will also decay and consequently die.” Yet it is proper to Christians to believe even in a God who died and nevertheless lives for ever and ever.

Utter fools, who prejudge divine things from human ones [Note: [Col. 0303D] Paris and Fran. read “proclaim.”]: because passions of this kind are found in man, whose condition is subject to decay, they therefore suppose that in God too they have the same character. Distinguish the substances and assign to each its own dispositions, as different as the substances require, although they may appear [Col. 0303C] to share the same names. For the Scriptures also present a right hand and eyes—

[The supplied text appears to omit material here.]

[Note: [Col. 0303D] “That catholic and supreme goodness.” He uses *catholic goodness* in its proper sense, for goodness diffused throughout the whole world. He discusses this name more fully in *On the Prescription of Heretics*. PAM.]

—which the Marcionites refuse to acknowledge in the same God as remote from judicial emotions and pure in its own character: [Col. 0304C] the goodness that rains upon the good and the evil and makes its sun rise [Note: [Col. 0304D] Seml. conjectures “raining … making.”] upon the just and the unjust (Matt. 5:45), something no other God at all provides. For although Marcion dared to erase this testimony of Christ to the Creator from the Gospel, the world itself bears the inscription [Note: [Col. 0304D] “But the world itself bears the inscription.” That catholic and supreme goodness of God is inscribed upon the tablets of the world. RIG.], and it is read by every conscience. This very patience of the Creator will also serve for Marcion’s judgment [Note: [Col. 0304D] Paris reads “evidence.”]: that patience which awaits the sinner’s repentance rather than his death and prefers mercy to sacrifice (Hos. 6:6), averting the destruction already destined for the Ninevites, granting Hezekiah a span of life in response to his tears, and restoring the condition of his kingdom to Babylon’s tyrant after he had performed repentance [Note: [Col. 0304D] Seml. reads “through repentance.”].

I mean that mercy [Col. 0305A] which also granted Saul’s son, who was to die [Note: [Col. 0305D] “Which also granted Saul’s son, who was to die.” Here he speaks of Jonathan, whom the people delivered from the hands of his father Saul, as related in 1 Kings [1 Samuel] 14. By the words “and restored Israel itself as often as he judged it,” he alludes to Judges chapters 3, 4, 6, and 10. PAM.], to the people, freed from the doom of the vow; which freed David by pardon when he confessed his sins concerning the house of Uriah; and which restored Israel itself as often as he judged it, reviving it as often as he rebuked it.

Therefore, do not look only at the judge; turn also to the examples of the supremely good God. While noting when he takes vengeance [Note: [Col. 0305D] Paris and Fran. read “Note!”], consider when he grants indulgence. Set gentleness against austerity. When you have found both in the Creator, you will also find in him that quality on account of which you believe in another God.

Come, finally, to an examination of his teachings, disciplines, commandments, and counsels. You may perhaps say that these things are also determined by human laws. But before all the Lycurguses and Solons came Moses and God. Nothing later fails to receive from the beginnings. Nevertheless, my Creator did not learn from your god to prescribe [Col. 0305B] [Note: [Col. 0305D] Venet. and Rig. read “proscribe.”]: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not covet what belongs to another; honor your father and mother”; and, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

To these fundamental counsels of innocence, chastity, justice, and filial duty are also added humane prescriptions: slaves are released into freedom every seventh year (Lev. 25); at the same time the field is spared, with room yielded to the needy; even the muzzle is removed from the ox that treads out the grain, so that it may enjoy the fruit of its present labor. Thus humanity, first thoughtfully practiced toward animals, would the more readily be trained to afford relief to human beings.

## CHAPTER XVIII

But which benefits of the Law should I defend in preference to those that the heresy has coveted as grounds for attack—for example, the rule of retaliation, which requires eye [Col. 0305C] for eye, tooth for tooth, and bruise for bruise (Exod. 21:24)? It does not convey permission for injuries to be inflicted in return; rather, it provides for the complete restraint of violence. For to a people exceedingly hard and faithless toward God, it seemed too long a delay, or even incredible, to await from God the vengeance [Note: [Col. 0305D] *Defensam*, that is, vengeance or retribution. EDD.] that was afterwards to be proclaimed through the prophet: “Vengeance is mine, and I will avenge, says the Lord” (Deut. 32:35; Rom. 12:19). Meanwhile, the commission of an injury was to be rooted out through fear of an immediate equivalent response, and permission to retaliate was to serve as a prohibition against provocation. Thus cunning wickedness [Note: [Col. 0305D] Formerly *aestuata*, “inflamed,” was read.] would cease: by permitting the second injury, the first is deterred; and when the first is deterred, the second is not committed either. For [Note: [Col. 0305D] Jun. reads “because.”] in other respects too, fear of retaliation is more effective because the suffering has the same taste. Nothing is more bitter than to suffer precisely what you have done to others.

And if the Law removes certain foods and pronounces unclean animals that were once blessed, understand its design of training self-restraint and recognize the bridles placed upon that appetite which, while eating the bread of angels, desired the cucumbers and melons of the Egyptians. Recognize at the same time the provision made for [Note: [Col. 0305D] “For the companions of gluttony, namely lust and luxury.” The same idea occurs among the precepts of Dionysius Cato: “Do not indulge gluttony, which is the friend of the penis.” RIG.—“For the companions of gluttony, namely lust and luxury.” See here too that the author uses “gluttony” and “luxury” as they are understood today by scholastic doctors when they speak of the capital sins. Blessed Jerome spoke no differently somewhere: [Col. 0306D] “A belly inflamed with wine readily foams over into lust.” PAM.] the companions of gluttony, namely lust and luxury, which are generally cooled by chastising the belly. For “the people ate and drank and rose up to play” (Exod. 32:6).

Likewise, so that the passion for money might in part be extinguished [Note: [Col. 0306D] Formerly “restrained” was read.]—since it alleges the necessity of obtaining food—the ambition for costly foods was removed. Finally, [Col. 0306B] so that man might more readily be trained to fast for God, he was accustomed to few and [Note: [Col. 0306D] “Foods that are not splendid.” He calls those foods splendid in which some people glory, whether because of their rarity or their price. RHEN.] unsplendid foods and would feel no hunger for richer fare.

The Creator must certainly be censured because he withheld foods from his people rather than from the more ungrateful Marcionites! No one should censure [Note: [Col. 0306D] “The burdens of sacrifices.” In *On the Prescription of Heretics*, he aptly called these burdens of sacrifices and these troublesome scruples concerning works and offerings “the tediousness of Judaea.” RHEN.] the burdens of sacrifices either, or the troublesome scruples concerning works and offerings, as though God had desired such things specifically for himself, when he so plainly cries out: “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? And who has required these things at your hands?” (Isa. 1:11–12). Rather, let him perceive God’s purposeful care, by which he wished to bind a people prone to idolatry and transgression to his own religion through the kinds of rites by which the superstition of the age was practiced. He thereby called them away from that superstition, commanding that such things be done for himself as though he desired them, lest the people sin by performing them for idols.

## CHAPTER XIX

[Col. 0306C]

Even in the ordinary dealings of life and human conduct, at home and abroad, he made distinctions of every kind, extending as far as the care of vessels, so that, with these legal disciplines meeting them everywhere, they might not for a single [Note: [Col. 0306D] Seml. reads “for anyone”; Pamel., Fran., and Rhen., “for him”; Jun., “any moments.”] moment be free from regard for God. [Note: [Col. 0306D] “For what would make the man blessed?” The author uses *hominem* (“human being”) in the sense of *virum* (“man”), since the Greek, Latin, Hebrew, and Chaldaic words at the beginning of Psalm 1 all signify “man”; it is similarly used in the common speech of the French. The metaphor of hewing rough faith into shape through laborious duties is beautiful. PAM.] For what would make the man blessed other than that “his will is in the Law of the Lord, and on the Law of the Lord he will meditate day and night” (Ps. 1:2)?

That Law was promulgated not by the Author’s harshness but by the design of his supreme kindness, which subdued the people’s harshness instead and hewed their faith, still rough in obedience, into shape through laborious duties. I say nothing of the Law’s hidden meanings [Note: [Col. 0306D] Rig. and Venet. read “signifying.”], since it is spiritual [Col. 0307A] and prophetic, being figuratively expressed in almost all its subjects. For the present it is enough that, even in its simple sense, it bound man to God, so that no one ought to reject it except one who is displeased to serve God.

To support this benefit, not burden, of the Law, the same goodness of God also appointed the prophets, who taught things worthy of God: [Note: [Col. 0307C] “To remove wickedness from the soul.” He cites this from Isaiah chapter 1 according to the Septuagint, except that he omits—though the Hebrew, Chaldaic, and Latin editions also contain it—“to deliver one oppressed by injury.” Moreover, he adds “to love disputes”; but it should rather be “to set them straight” (as I correct it following an observation by the Englishman John Harris), for this expression is extremely frequent in the author. Perhaps it stands in place of “Come, and let us dispute,” for which Blessed Jerome has from the Hebrew: “and accuse me.” Chrysostom and Procopius explain this in their commentaries as meaning that one who has done a good work may boldly dispute with God, as the author also seems to understand it. If “with God” were added, it would be clearer. PAM.] “Remove wickedness from the soul; learn to do good; [Note: [Col. 0307D] ‘Seek out judgment’: after the right of each party has been investigated and fully examined. RIG.] seek out judgment; judge for the orphan and vindicate the widow; set disputes straight [Note: [Col. 0307C] Venet. reads “love.”]; [Note: [Col. 0307D] “To flee contact with the wicked.” The Pithoean manuscript and Rhenanus’ editions read *contactum* (“contact”), which certainly agrees better with the verb “flee.” Pamelius changed it, supposing in this way that he had brought it into conformity with the Greek words found at Isaiah 58, σύνδεσμον ἀδικίας, “bond of injustice.” But the text there is λῦε πάντα σύνδεσμον ἀδικίας, “loose every bond of injustice.” Septimius therefore intended something different. RIG.] flee [Note: [Col. 0307C] Perhaps “break.”] contact with the wicked [Note: [Col. 0307C] Pam. reads “contract.”]; [Note: [Col. 0307D] “To release the broken woman whole.” This is how the old manuscripts read. In Esdras, immediately after the words “vindicate the widow, judge for the orphan,” there follows: “Care for the broken and the weak.” But Isaiah said, ἀπόστελλε τεθραμμένους [Col. 0308D] ἐν ἀφέσει, “send away the broken in release.” All these passages are cited rather carelessly by Septimius. RIG.] release the broken woman [Note: [Col. 0307C] Pamel. and Seml. omit “as.”] whole; tear up the unjust document” (Isa. 58:1); “break your bread for the hungry, and bring into your house the one who has no shelter; if you see someone naked, cover him, and do not despise the members of your own family”; “restrain your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit” (Ps. 33:13); [Col. 0307B] “turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it”; “be angry and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5), that is, do not persist or rage in anger; “do not go into the council of the impious, nor stand in the way of sinners, nor sit in the seat of the pestilent” (Ps. 1:1).

But where, then, should one sit? See: “How good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132:1), meditating day and night on the Law of the Lord; because, certainly, “it is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man, and to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes” (Ps. 117:7–8). For what reward does man have with God? “He will be like a tree planted beside the outlets of waters, which will give its fruit in its season; its leaf will not fall, and everything whatsoever he does will prosper for him” (Ps. 1:3).

But the innocent and pure of heart, who has not taken [Col. 0307C] God’s name in vain and has not sworn [Note: [Col. 0307C] Others read “entered.”] deceitfully to his neighbor, “will receive blessing from the Lord and mercy from God his Savior” [Note: [Col. 0307C] Others read “his salvation.”] (Ps. 23:4). “For the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him and hope in [Col. 0308A] his mercy, [Note: [Col. 0308D] ‘To deliver their souls.’ This is how the Pithoean manuscript reads. RIG.] to deliver [Note: [Col. 0307C] Seml. reads “to determine”; Latin., “to free.”] their souls from death”—surely eternal death—“and to nourish them in famine” (Ps. 32:18)—surely the famine of eternal life. “For many are the afflictions of the righteous, and from them all the Lord will deliver them” (Ps. 33:19). “Honorable in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:15). “The Lord preserves all their bones [Note: [Col. 0308C] Seml. reads “their bones, and”]: not one of them will be broken. The Lord will redeem [Note: [Col. 0308C] Seml. reads “has redeemed.”] the souls of his servants” (Ps. 33:21–23).

We have adduced these few passages from the Creator’s many Scriptures, and I think nothing is now lacking [Note: [Col. 0308C] Pamel. and Seml. read “to be lacking.”] for testimony to the supremely good God, since both commandments and promises of goodness sufficiently attest him.

## CHAPTER XX

But indeed these cuttlefish [Note: [Col. 0308D] “But indeed these cuttlefish.” He elegantly and aptly compares the Marcionite heretics to cuttlefish. For as Pliny relates in book 9, chapter 29, cuttlefish are a kind of fish which, when they perceive that they are being caught, discharge ink—which serves them in place of blood—and hide themselves in the darkened water. In the same way, when the Marcionite heretics perceive that they are being exposed—that is, when they are accused and convicted of error—they spew the darkness of this blasphemy between themselves and their accuser like the ink of a cuttlefish. They thereby hinder and divert the one accusing them by alleging things that darken and obscure the Creator’s goodness. RHEN.] [Note: [Col. 0308C] Formerly “often” was read.]—a figure of that little sea creature which the Law likewise rejected as food—when they perceive themselves being exposed, spew forth from here a darkness of blasphemy and thereby scatter each person’s attention just when it has drawn close to the point, loudly alleging [Note: [Col. 0308C] Seml. reads “casting.”] and affirming things that may darken the Creator’s shining goodness. Yet we shall pursue their wickedness even through those mists and drag the devices of darkness into the light, especially those that charge the Creator with that fraud and theft of gold and silver which he commanded [Note: [Col. 0308C] Pamel. and Seml. read “commanded” in the neuter plural; Jun., feminine plural.] the Hebrews to perpetrate against the Egyptians.

Come now, most wretched heretic: I demand that you yourself act as arbiter. First investigate the case between the two nations, and then you will judge the author of the command. The Egyptians demand their gold and silver vessels back from the Hebrews; [Note: [Col. 0308D] “The Hebrews institute counterclaims.” Thus the emperor Alexander, law 1, chapter *Things Removed*: “For it is not fair that what you are established to owe should be paid before a response has been given to the counterclaim.” RIG.] the Hebrews institute counterclaims against them, alleging that, in the name of those same fathers and on the evidence of the same written record, wages for that laborious slavery ought also to be restored to them: for the bricks they had made and for the cities and villages they had built. [Col. 0308C] What judgment will you give, elector of the supremely good God? That the Hebrews ought to acknowledge fraud, or that the Egyptians ought to acknowledge a setoff? [Col. 0309A]

[Note: [Col. 0309D] “For they also say that the case was argued through envoys.” But Moses says so. RIG.] For they also say that the case was argued through envoys on both sides: the Egyptians demanding the vessels back and the Jews demanding their labor back; and at last the Egyptians renounced their claim to those vessels [Note: [Col. 0309D] “The Egyptians renounced their claim.” This seems to be ironic: namely, that the Egyptians justly renounced the Hebrews’ labor—that is, denied the wages owed for the labor. RHEN.] [Note: [Col. 0309D] Seml. and Pamel. read “and yet justice regarded these …”].

Today the Hebrews argue still more fully against the Marcionites, denying that any quantity of gold and silver, however great, was sufficient for the setoff if the labor of six hundred thousand people over so many years were valued at even a single coin per day for each. Which party’s claim, then, is greater: that of those demanding their vessels, or that of those inhabiting the villages and cities they had built? Was it therefore the grievance of the Egyptians, or [Note: [Col. 0309D] “Or the due of the Hebrews”—that which was owed to them and which they had earned, namely their wages. RHEN.] the due of the Hebrews?

Even if the Hebrews had merely retaliated against the Egyptians on the basis of the injuries done to them—free persons driven into a work prison—so that their shoulders alone, lacerated by the insulting savagery of the lash, were displayed before the Egyptians’ scribes at their judgment seats, would you not have pronounced that the Hebrews must receive satisfaction, not with a few [Col. 0309B] plates and cups, belonging of course everywhere to only a few rich men, but with the Egyptians’ entire wealth and the contributions of the whole population [Note: [Col. 0309D] Paris and Rhen. read “the Hebrew would have pronounced”; the Wouwer manuscript, “you would have pronounced the Hebrews”; Seml., “he would have pronounced for the Hebrews.”]?

Therefore, if the Hebrews’ case was good, good too was its cause—that is, the Creator’s command. He both made the Egyptians render compensation without knowing it and, in the short time available for their departure, settled his people’s account with some consolation afforded by a tacit settlement. Clearly, he ordered less to be exacted than was due: for the Egyptians ought also to have restored the Hebrews’ sons [Note: [Col. 0309D] Seml. omits “for.”].

## CHAPTER XXI
Thus in the other cases also you reproach him with contradictions in his commandments, as though he were changeable and unstable: he forbids work on the Sabbaths, yet commands the ark to be carried around for eight days—that is, even on the Sabbath—in the conquest of the city of Jericho. [Col. 0309C] For you do not examine the law of the Sabbath, which prohibits human works, not divine ones. For he says (Exod. 20:9–10): “Six days shall you labor and perform all your works, but the seventh day is a Sabbath [Note: [Col. 0309D] “Keep Sabbath,” Paris.] to the Lord your God; on it you shall perform no work.” What work? Surely your own. [Note: [Col. 0309D] “Surely your own”: Semler’s faulty correction.] For it follows that he excluded from the Sabbath those works which he had assigned to the six preceding days—your works, namely, that is, human and everyday works. But carrying the ark around can be regarded neither as an everyday work nor as a human one; it was both extraordinary and sacred, and, because it proceeded at that time from God’s own command, was certainly divine. I would also explain what this signified, were it not [Note: [Col. 0309D] “Unless it were too long,” Semler.] too lengthy a task to unfold all the Creator’s figurative arguments, which perhaps you do not even accept. But it is more effective if [Col. 0310A] you are refuted from things plain and absolute, by the simplicity of truth rather than by elaborate inquiry—as here too there is a definite distinction in the Sabbath’s prohibition of human works, not divine ones. Accordingly, the man who went to gather wood on the Sabbath was put to death, for he had performed his own work, which the law forbade. But those who carried the ark around on the Sabbaths did so with impunity, for they had administered not their own work but God’s, [Note: [Col. 0309D] “For—but God’s work,” Rigault, Venice.] in accordance, of course, with his own command.

## CHAPTER XXII

Likewise, when he forbids the making of a likeness of anything in heaven, on earth, or in the waters, he also discloses his reasons: namely, reasons restraining the substance of idolatry. [Note: [Col. 0310D] “Which restrain the substance,” Semler; Rhenanus: “which restrains the substance”; Ursinus’s codex. Semler conjectures *quasi* for *quae*. Rhenanus reads “restrain” for “restraining.”] For he adds: “You shall not worship them or serve them.” But the image of the bronze serpent, afterward commanded of Moses by the Lord, did not pertain to the category of idolatry, but to the healing of those who were being attacked by serpents. [Col. 0310B] And I pass over the symbolic meaning of the remedy. So too the golden Cherubim and Seraphim, fashioned as a representation upon the ark—certainly a simple ornament suited to its setting—had reasons far different from the condition of idolatry, on account of which likenesses are forbidden. They therefore do not appear to conflict with the law against forbidden likenesses, since they are not found in that condition of likeness on account of which likeness is forbidden.

We have already discussed the rational institution of sacrifices, which of course diverted toward God those acts of service formerly rendered to idols. If he afterward rejected them, saying (Isa. 1:11): “What need have I of the multitude of your sacrifices?” he intended precisely this to be understood: that he had not demanded them properly for himself. [Note: [Col. 0310D] “For I shall not drink,” he says, “the blood of bulls.” Here Tertullian departs from the reading of our Vulgate, in which Psalm 49 reads: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” But this is of no importance. God was indicating that he is appeased not by particular ceremonies or rites, but only by a sincere disposition of the heart. LE PRIEUR.] “For I shall not drink,” he says (Ps. 49:13), “the blood of bulls,” since elsewhere also he says (Isa. 40:28): “The eternal God will neither hunger nor thirst.” For even though he took notice of Abel’s offerings [Note: [Col. 0310D] Some read “you take notice.”], [Col. 0310C] and gladly smelled Noah’s burnt offerings [Note: [Col. 0310D] “Gladly” is absent from some copies.], what pleasure was there in the entrails of rams, or in the reek of burning victims? Rather, the sincere and God-fearing disposition of those offering what they possessed from God was accounted before God as nourishment and sweet fragrance, [Note: [Col. 0310D] “Of grace,” Junius, Semler.] for he demanded not the things that were done, but that for which they were done—namely, the honor of God.

If a client offers a wealthy man or king, who wants nothing, some gift, even of the most trifling kind, will the quantity and quality of the gift disgrace the wealthy man and king, or will the designation of the act of duty delight him? But if the client offers him gifts voluntarily, or even in accordance with the prescribed [Note: [Col. 0310D] “Prescribed,” Rigault, Venice; “or by prescribed order,” Latinus, Junius.] order of his rank, and observes the king’s solemnities, yet does so without faith, without a pure heart, and without complete obedience in all other matters as well, does it not follow that the king or [Col. 0311A] wealthy man should exclaim: “What need have I of the multitude of your gifts? I am full”; and: “My soul hates your solemnities, your feast days, [Note: [Col. 0311D] “And your Sabbaths my soul hates.” Not only the Jews are included in these words. Almost all other nations observed that day. Ovid sufficiently attests this concerning the Romans in Book I of *The Art of Love*:

> The seventh day, sacred to the Palestinian man, was observed as a festival.

And Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book I, chapter 7:

> The greater part of the Greeks—and Athens especially—  
> Perform rites for Saturn, which they repeatedly call the *Cronia*.

Since it was customary on those days to indulge one’s appetite, Sidonius Apollinaris, Book II, Letter 2, calls the luxury and banqueting of the Goths “Sabbath luxury.” Hence the Cynic Antisthenes calls a festival “an occasion for gluttony” (*ἑορτὴν γαστριμαργίας ἀφορμήν*); and in Isidore of Pelusium they call every festival a Sabbath (*σάββατον πᾶσαν ἑορτὴν καλοῦσιν*). LE PRIEUR.] and your Sabbaths”? [Note: [Col. 0311C] “My soul hates.” Semler omits “your.”] By saying “your,” he showed that his rejection of those things which he had prescribed should be performed was conditional and rational, because, by celebrating them according to their own desire and not according to the worship of God, [Note: [Col. 0311C] Some read “they celebrate for God.”] they had now made them their own rather than God’s.

## CHAPTER XXIII

If, moreover, you wish him to be understood as fickle [Note: [Col. 0311D] Others incorrectly read “of laws.”] even in his treatment of persons, because he sometimes rejects those whom he had approved, or as lacking foresight because he sometimes approves those whom he will later reject—as though he either condemned his past judgments or were ignorant of the future—nevertheless nothing is so fitting to one who is both good and a judge as to reject and choose according to present merits. Saul is chosen [Col. 0311B] [Note: [Col. 0311D] “Is selected,” Semler.], but before he has despised the prophet Samuel. Solomon is rejected, but only when he has been taken possession of by foreign women and enslaved to the idols of the Moabites and Sidonians.

What should the Creator have done to avoid criticism from the Marcionites? [Note: [Col. 0311D] “Should he have condemned beforehand those who were still acting well,” [Col. 0312D] etc.? This must certainly be read interrogatively, because he is speaking from the standpoint of the Marcionites. To this he aptly answers: “But it did not belong to a good God to condemn beforehand those who had not yet deserved it.” Correspondingly, should he not reject those who are sinning now because of their former good deeds? For foreknowledge of merits is not the cause of divine predestination, as Pelagius heretically supposed. To avoid excessive length, the reader may consult Sixtus of Siena, *Holy Library*, Book VI. PAMELIUS.] Should he have condemned beforehand those who were still acting well because of their future offenses? But it did not belong to a good God to condemn beforehand those who had not yet deserved it. Correspondingly, should he not reject those who are sinning now because of their former good deeds? But it did not belong to a just judge to pardon crimes after their former good deeds had already been annulled. [Note: [Col. 0311D] Others read “cut off.”]

Or what human being is without sin, so that God might always choose him [Note: [Col. 0311D] “Might have chosen,” Semler.] and never be able to reject him? Or, conversely, who is without some good work, so that God might always reject him and never be able to choose him?
