[Note: [Col. 0311D] “Select,” Semler.] Show yourself always good, and you will not be rejected; show yourself always evil, [Note: [Col. 0312C] Semler omits “always.”] and you will never be chosen. [Note: [Col. 0312C] “Is selected,” the same editor.] [Col. 0311C] But if the same person is each in turn at different times, God, both good and a judge, will settle his account in each respect. [Note: [Col. 0312D] “His account will be settled in each respect.” That is, satisfaction will be made to him in each, and in each he will receive his reward. RHENANUS.] God changes his sentences not through fickleness or lack of foresight, but by a most weighty and provident assessment dispenses according to the merits of each particular time.

## CHAPTER XXIV

Thus [Note: [Col. 0312D] “Thus also repentance,” etc. We supplied the missing word, without which the sense was badly impaired, and wrote “with him,” that is, with the Creator. RHENANUS.] you also misinterpret repentance in him, [Note: [Col. 0312D] “God,” Semler.] as though it likewise arose from changeability or lack of foresight, or indeed as though he now repented from recollection of a fault, [Col. 0312A] because he had said (1 Sam. 15:11): “I repent that I made Saul king.” You take it as established, of course, that repentance conveys a confession of some evil deed or error. Yet this is not always so. For a declaration of repentance also occurs in connection with good deeds, to the reproach and rebuke of one who has proved ungrateful for a benefit. So too it is then proclaimed by the Creator with reference to the honoring of Saul.

The Creator had not sinned when he took Saul up into the kingdom and increased him with the Holy Spirit, since Saul was still excellent: “There was none like him,” he says, “among the children of Israel.” He had chosen him most worthily. Nor had he been ignorant that events would turn out as they did, for no one will tolerate your ascribing lack of foresight to God when, since you do not deny that he is God, you acknowledge him also to be provident. Divinity is admittedly his proper attribute. Rather, as I have said, he was burdening Saul’s evil deed through his own declaration of repentance. [Col. 0312B] Since there was no fault in Saul’s selection, it follows that this repentance must be understood as reproachful rather than self-accusing.

“Look,” you say, “I perceive it to be self-accusing in the case of the Ninevites, when the Scripture of Jonah says (Jonah 3:10): ‘And the Lord repented of the evil which he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it.’” So too Jonah himself says to the Lord: [Note: [Col. 0312D] “God,” Semler.] “For this reason I hastened to flee to Tarshish, because I knew that you are merciful and compassionate, patient and abundant [Note: [Col. 0312D] “Of abundant,” Latinus.] in mercy, repenting of evils” (Jonah 4:2).

It is well, then, that he first placed the designation of a supremely good God: namely, one most patient toward the wicked, and most abundant [Note: [Col. 0312D] Others read “of most abundant.”] in mercy and compassion toward those who acknowledge and lament their sins, as the Ninevites did then. For if one who is such is supremely good, you will first have to concede concerning him that the conjunction of evil is incompatible [Col. 0312C] with such a one—that is, with one supremely good. And since [Note: [Col. 0312D] Semler and Junius insert “and.”] Marcion maintains that a good tree cannot also produce evil fruits (Matt. 7:18), yet Scripture has named “evil,” which the supremely good cannot contain, may there not be some interpretation by which even those “evils” can be understood which might have proceeded from one supremely good? There is indeed.

We say, then, that “evil” here signifies not something attributable to the Creator’s nature, as though he were evil, but something attributable to his authority [Col. 0313A] as judge. In accordance with this he declared (Isa. 45:7): “I am he who creates evils”; and: [Note: [Col. 0313D] “Behold, I send evils upon you,” etc. There are many passages of this kind in Scripture in which we read: “I shall bring evil,” or “evils,” upon them—for example, 1 Kings 9:4; 1 Kings 2:21; 2 Chronicles 7. PAMELIUS.] “Behold, I send evils upon you” (Jer. 18:11)—not sinful evils, but avenging ones. We have sufficiently cleared these of ill repute by showing them to be fitting for a judge. Although they are called “evils,” they are not condemned in a judge, nor do they show him to be an evil judge merely by bearing that name. In the same way, the “evil” here must be understood as one of those judicial evils and therefore as fitting for the judge.

For among the Greeks also “evils” are sometimes used for afflictions and injuries, not for acts of malice, [Note: [Col. 0313D] Formerly read “they use.”] as in this passage. Thus, if the Creator repented of this evil, it was the evil, of course, whereby the creature was to be rejected and punished with destruction. [Note: [Col. 0313D] Rhenanus: “on account of the offense”; Paris: *delitus*; others: “for destruction.”] Yet no criminal deed will be imputed to the Creator, who had worthily and deservedly [Col. 0313B] decreed that a most wicked city should be destroyed. Thus, what he had justly determined, without determining it wickedly, he had determined from justice, not from malice. Rather, he called the punishment itself “evil” because of the evil and painful nature [Note: [Col. 0313D] Semler inserts “and.”] of the suffering itself.

“Therefore,” you will say, “if you excuse the evil under the designation of justice, because he had justly determined destruction against the Ninevites, he is nevertheless blameworthy for repenting of justice, of which one certainly should not repent.” On the contrary, I say, God will never [Note: [Col. 0313D] Rhenanus reads “ever.”] repent of justice; it remains for us now to recognize what God’s repentance is. For although a human being repents, most often [Note: [Col. 0313D] “Most often from recollection of a fault.” *Plurimum* is adverbial, meaning “for the most part.” Terence in the *Phormio*: “I shall proceed home, where he is for the most part.” [Col. 0314D] Our author has spoken in this way above as well. The Latins likewise use *minimum* in this fashion. RHENANUS.] from recollection of a fault, and sometimes also from resentment at ingratitude for some good deed, it does not follow that God repents in the same manner. Insofar as God neither commits evil nor condemns good, there is no place with him for repentance over either good or evil.

The same Scripture [Col. 0313C] also establishes this for you when Samuel says to Saul (1 Sam. 15:28): “The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from your hand today, and will give it to your neighbor, one better than you; and Israel will be divided into two parts, and he will not turn back or repent, because he is not like a man, that he should repent.” This definition therefore establishes in every case a different form of divine repentance, one which must not be attributed, as human repentance is, either to lack of foresight or to the condemnation of any good or evil work.

What, then, will be the character of divine repentance? It is already clear, if you do not refer it to human conditions. It will be understood as nothing other than a simple alteration of a previous sentence, an alteration which can be admitted without condemnation of that sentence even in a human being, [Col. 0314A] much more in God, whose every sentence is free from fault. [Note: [Col. 0314D] “For even in its Greek sound,” etc. The word *μετάνοια* (*metanoia*), from which “repentance” is translated out of Greek, is derived from *μετανοεῖν* (*metanoein*), which signifies not confession of an offense but a change of mind, as is clear from Xenophon at the beginning of Book I of the *Education of Cyrus* and from other Greek writers. PAMELIUS.] For even in its Greek sound, the word for repentance is composed not from confession of a fault but from a change of mind; [Note: [Col. 0313D] Others read “prepared.”] and we have shown that this occurs in God as changing circumstances arise. [Note: [Col. 0313D] Venice and Rigault read “to be ruled”; the Pithou codex, “of a thing”; Pamelius and Franeker, “we have shown would occur.”]

## CHAPTER XXV

Now, to dispose of all such objections, I shall proceed to interpret and clear away the other instances of pettiness, weakness, and inconsistency—as you regard them. God calls out (Gen. 3): “Adam, where are you?” Was he, of course, ignorant of where Adam was? And when Adam alleges shame at his nakedness, God asks whether he had tasted from the tree: was he, of course, uncertain? On the contrary, he was neither uncertain of the deed nor ignorant of the place. Rather, it was fitting that the man who was hiding because of his consciousness of sin should be called forth and come out [Note: [Col. 0313D] “Betray,” Rigault, Venice.] into the Lord’s sight, not merely by the calling of his name [Col. 0314B] but with some rebuke, even then, of the deed.

For the words “Adam, where are you?” [Note: [Col. 0313D] Others read “Where are you, Adam?”] must not be read in a simple manner, that is, in an interrogative tone, but with emphasis and force, as an accusation: “Adam, where are you?”—that is, “You are in perdition”; that is, “You are no longer here.” Thus the utterance issues at once in rebuke and grief. Besides, he who holds the whole world in his hand as though it were a nest, whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is earth—could some portion of paradise really have escaped his eyes, so that Adam, wherever he was, would not have been seen by him before he was called forth, both while hiding and while taking the forbidden fruit? A wolf or petty thief does not escape the watchman of your vineyard or garden. I think that the more exalted sight of God cannot fail to observe anything below it. Fool, you who turn up your nose at so great an argument of divine majesty and [Col. 0314C] human instruction!

God was asking [Note: [Col. 0314D] “Asks,” Semler.] as though uncertain, so that [Note: [Col. 0314D] “So that” is absent from Pamelius.] by this means also, in testing [Note: [Col. 0314D] Rigault, Venice, and Semler read “condemning.”] man’s free will, he might give him opportunity, either for denial or confession, voluntarily to confess his offense and thereby lighten it, [Note: [Col. 0314D] Paris reads “reveal.”] just as he inquires of Cain where his brother is—as though he had not already heard Abel’s blood crying aloud from the earth. But this was so that Cain too might have the power, from that same faculty of free will, voluntarily to deny his offense and thereby aggravate it. In this way examples were established for us of confessing offenses rather than denying them, so that even then the evangelical teaching might be inaugurated (Matt. 12:37): “From your mouth you will be justified, [Note: [Col. 0314D] Rhenanus reads “justified together.”] and from your mouth you will be condemned.” [Note: [Col. 0314D] Others read “condemned together,” following the Vulgate.]

[Col. 0315A] For although Adam, because of the condition of the law, was consigned to death, hope remained safe for him, since the Lord said (Gen. 3:22): “Behold, Adam has become like one of us”—that is, with reference to man’s future selection for divinity. Finally, what follows? “And now, lest he at some time stretch out his hand and take from the tree of life, and live forever.” By interposing “and now,” an expression of the present time, he showed that he had imposed only a temporary and present postponement of life. Accordingly, he cursed neither Adam himself nor Eve, since they were candidates [Note: [Col. 0315D] “Candidates for restoration.” He calls the first parents “candidates for restoration” because they were to recover the happiness they had lost. Elsewhere he employs a similar expression when he speaks of “candidates for eternity.” *Candidates* were petitioners and seekers of public office at Rome; but there were also other “candidates” among the soldiers, who served as something like praetorians, *triarii*, or defenders of the emperor. Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXV: “While Julian was engaged amid the hazards of war, the candidates, whom terror had scattered, cried to him from every side that he should avoid the fleeing mass as though it were the collapse of a badly constructed roof.” LE PRIEUR.] for restoration, [Note: [Col. 0315D] “For restoration,” Rhenanus.] having been relieved through confession. Cain, however, he both cursed and, though Cain desired to pay for his offense by death, forbade for the time being to die, since Cain was burdened not only with the deed but also with its denial. [Note: [Col. 0315D] Franeker reads “by the example.”]

Such will be the “ignorance” of our God: it is simulated so that sinful man may not be ignorant of what he must do. [Col. 0315B] But when he descends to Sodom and Gomorrah, he says (Gen. 18:21): “I shall see whether they have acted entirely according to the outcry that has reached me; and if not, that I may know.” [Note: [Col. 0315D] Pamelius, Venice, and Semler read “consume.”] Here too, presumably, was he uncertain from ignorance and eager to learn? Or was this a necessary tone of declaration, expressing not a doubtful but a threatening sense under the guise of inquiry?

And if you also ridicule God’s descent, as though he could not otherwise have carried out judgment unless he descended, take care that you do not strike your own god equally. For he too descended in order to accomplish what he wished.

## CHAPTER XXVI

But God also swears. Perhaps by Marcion’s god? “No,” you say—what is much more absurd [Note: [Col. 0315D] Semler and Pamelius read, uncertainly, “many things—foolish, because.”]—“by himself.” What would you have wished [Note: [Col. 0315D] Semler reads “what would he have wished [that he]…?”] him to do [Note: [Col. 0315D] Pamelius and Paris read “to do.”], if there was no other god [Col. 0315C] within his consciousness, especially when in the very act of swearing [Note: [Col. 0316D] “Swearing,” Wouwer.] that there was absolutely no other besides himself? Do you therefore catch him perjuring himself, or swearing vainly? Yet he cannot be thought to have perjured himself, since, as you say, he did not know that another existed. For, swearing truly to what he knows, he committed no perjury. Nor does he swear vainly that there is no other God. He would have sworn vainly only if there had been no people who believed in other gods—then, indeed, the worshipers of images; now, the heretics as well.

He therefore swears by himself so that you may at least believe God when he swears that absolutely no other God exists. You too, Marcion, compelled God to do this, for even then you were foreseen. [Col. 0316A] Likewise, if he swears in promises or threats, compelling a faith that was difficult in those earliest times, nothing is unworthy of God if it brings about belief in God.

God was, you claim, sufficiently petty even then in his very ferocity, when, enraged against the people because of the consecration of the calf, he asks his servant Moses (Exod. 32:10): “Let me be, and, angered in wrath, [Note: [Col. 0316D] Rigault and Venice write “in wrath” in place of “angered in wrath.”] I shall destroy them and make you into a great nation.” From this you are accustomed to affirm that Moses was better than his God, because he entreated him—indeed, restrained his wrath. “You shall not do this,” he says, “or else destroy me together with them.”

You too must be pitied [Note: [Col. 0316D] Junius reads “you too must be pitied”; Rhenanus, “by pitying.”] along with the people, because you do not recognize that in the person of Moses Christ was prefigured as the intercessor before the Father and the one who offered his own life for the salvation of the people. But it is enough that the people was, in the immediate situation, granted to Moses personally. The Lord asked of himself what his servant needed to be able to request from his Lord. For this purpose he said to his servant, “Let me be, and I shall destroy them”: so that Moses, by requesting and offering himself, would not let him, and thus you might learn how much influence a faithful man and prophet has with God. [Note: [Col. 0316D] “And thus you might learn how much influence a faithful man,” etc. This passage is similarly interpreted to mean that the prayer of the saints has great weight with God by St. Jerome, on Ezekiel, chapter 28, in his treatment of Ezekiel 13, and in his letter to Gaudentius; and by Cyril of Alexandria, Book V *Against Julian*. “But if the Apostles and martyrs,” says St. Jerome against Vigilantius, where he adduces this same example of Moses, “while still established in the body can pray for others, at a time when they must still be anxious for themselves, how much more after their crowns, victories, and triumphs?” This passage therefore supports the prayers of the saints for us even after this life. We have treated these, as well as the invocation of the saints themselves, at length in our notes [Col. 0317D] on Letter 57 of St. Cyprian to Cornelius. PAMELIUS.]

## CHAPTER XXVII

Now, to dispose briefly of the remaining matters as well, whatever you still collect as petty, weak, and unworthy for the destruction of the Creator, I shall put forward one simple and certain explanation: God could not enter into dealings with human beings unless he assumed human sensations and affections, through which, by means of humility, he might temper the force of his majesty—a force certainly intolerable to human frailty. This humility was indeed unworthy of himself but necessary for man, [Col. 0316C] and thus already worthy of God, because nothing is so worthy of God as the salvation of man.

I would discuss this at greater length if I were dealing with pagans, although the contest with heretics does not stand on a very different footing. [Note: [Col. 0316D] Wouwer reads “nor with heretics by much”; Semler omits “different.”] Insofar as you yourselves have already believed that God sojourned [Note: [Col. 0316D] Rigault and Venice read “diversified himself.”] in visible form and in the rest of the ordering of the human condition, you will certainly not require prolonged persuasion that God conformed himself to humanity; rather, you are refuted from your own faith. For if God—and indeed a more exalted god—laid low the summit of his majesty in such humility that he subjected himself [Note: [Col. 0316D] Others read “was subjected.”] even to death, and to death on a cross, why do you not suppose that certain petty characteristics were also fitting for our God, though more tolerable than Jewish insults, crosses, and tombs? [Col. 0317A]

Or are these the petty characteristics which ought already to furnish a presumption that Christ, exposed to human sufferings, belongs to that God whose human characteristics you reproach? For we also profess that Christ always acted in the name of God the Father; that it was he who associated with men from the beginning; he who entered into dealings with the patriarchs and prophets—the Creator’s Son, his Word, whom the Creator made his Son by bringing him forth from himself, and whom [Note: [Col. 0317D] Pamelius and Semler read “so that.”] he thereafter placed over his entire dispensation and will. He made him a little lower than the angels, as it is written in David (Ps. 8:6). By this diminution the Father also appointed him for those things which you condemn as human, so that from the very beginning he was already learning to be what he was to become at the end: man. [Col. 0317B]

He is the one who descends; the one who questions; the one who asks; the one who swears. Moreover, [Note: [Col. 0317D] Semler inserts “because”; Junius reads “who.”] the common Gospel will also testify that the Father has been seen by no one, when Christ says (Matt. 11:27): “No one has known the Father except the Son.” For he himself had also declared in the Old Testament (Exod. 33:20): “No one shall see God and live,” thereby defining the Father as invisible. Under the Father’s authority and in his name, the one who was seen—the Son of God—was himself God.

But among us also Christ is understood in the person of Christ, [Note: [Col. 0317D] “But among us also Christ is understood in the person of Christ.” Thus the copies read. Septimius means: No man has seen God and lived—in the person of the Father, that is. Yet men have seen the Father in the Son, because the Son always acted in the name of God the Father. The Father and the Son, however, are one—that is, one God. Thus the Son himself was the God whom men saw. Thus we [Col. 0318D] Christians, unlike the Marcionites, receive or understand Christ as God in the person of Christ, because in this manner also he is our God. For Christ is also man. RIGAULT.] because in this manner also he is ours. Therefore, whatever attributes you demand as worthy of God will be found in the Father, who is invisible, inaccessible to encounter, [Note: [Col. 0317D] Others read “knowable.”] and tranquil—the philosophers’ God, so to speak. Whatever you condemn as unworthy will be assigned to the Son, who was seen, heard, and encountered, the Father’s agent [Col. 0317C] and minister, mingling in himself man and God: God in his mighty works, man in his petty characteristics, so that he conferred as much upon man as he detracted from God.

Indeed, the whole dishonor of my God in your eyes is the mystery of human salvation. God associated with man so that man might be taught to act divinely. God dealt with man as an equal so that man might be able to deal with God as an equal. God was found petty so that man might become supremely great. You who disdain such a God—I do not know whether you sincerely believe in a crucified God.

How great, then, is your perversity toward both aspects of the Creator! You designate him a judge, and reproach as savagery the severity of a judge proportionate to the merits of the cases. [Note: [Col. 0317D] Wouwer reads “of judgment.”] You demand a supremely good God, yet disparage as pettiness the gentleness proportionate to his goodness, when it lowers itself in its dealings to the capacity of human frailty. [Col. 0318A] Neither the great nor the modest pleases you; neither the judge nor the friend. What if the same characteristics are now [Note: [Col. 0318D] Semler and Pamelius read “not”; Latinus: “For what if?”; Wouwer: “What of the fact that now?”] found in your god as well? We have already shown in his own little book that he too is a judge; and because he is a judge, necessarily severe; and because severe, correspondingly [Note: [Col. 0318D] Latinus reads “of course.”] savage—if indeed he is savage.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

Now, concerning his petty characteristics, acts of malice, and other marks, I too shall construct against Marcion rival *Antitheses*. If my God was ignorant that there was another above him, your god was equally altogether unaware that there was another below him. For, as that obscure Heraclitus says, [Note: [Col. 0318D] “That obscure Heraclitus.” That philosopher so affected obscurity that he was consequently called “the obscure” or *σκοτεινός* (*skoteinos*). Even when death was imminent he retained that style of speech. For when he suffered from water under the skin and dropsy, he asked the physicians whether by the skill of their art they could produce drought from rain. Laertius reports this in Book IX. LE PRIEUR.] [Col. 0318B] “The way upward and downward is the same.” In short, if your god had not been ignorant, he would have confronted mine from the beginning.

Sin and death, the devil himself as the author of sin, and every evil which [Note: [Col. 0318D] Latinus, Junius, and Semler read “every evil whom.”] my God permitted to exist—your god likewise permitted them, since he permitted my God to permit them.

Our God changed his sentences. So did yours. For he who took notice of the human race so late changed the sentence by which he had not taken notice of it for so long an age.

Our God repented of something. So did yours. For by at last turning his attention to man’s salvation, he repented of his previous disregard, a repentance owed to an evil deed. Neglect of human salvation will indeed be accounted an evil deed, corrected in your god only through repentance.

Our God commanded fraud—but fraud involving gold and silver. Yet as a human being is more precious than gold and [Col. 0318C] silver, so your god is the greater defrauder, since he snatches man from his Lord and Maker.

Our God demands an eye for an eye. But yours, by forbidding retaliation, makes the injury more likely to be repeated. For who will not strike again when he has not been struck back?

Our God did not know [Note: [Col. 0318D] Semler and Pamelius read “does not know.”] what sort of men he was choosing? Then neither would yours have chosen Judas the traitor [Note: [Col. 0318D] Semler and Pamelius insert “not,” and punctuate after “yours”: “Neither would yours. He would not have chosen Judas…”] if he had foreknown him.

Thus you also say that the Creator lied somewhere. A far greater lie is found in your Christ, whose body was not real.

Did my God’s savagery destroy many? Your god also certainly consigns to destruction those whom he does not save.

Did my God [Note: [Col. 0318D] “My” is absent from Franeker.] command someone to be killed? Yours wished himself to be killed, being no less a murderer against himself [Col. 0319A] than against the man [Note: [Col. 0319B] Semler reads “in him.”] by whom he wished to be killed.

But I shall prove to Marcion that his god has killed many. For he made a murderer, who will certainly perish—unless, perhaps, the people committed no offense against Christ. But the ready power of truth prefers few words. Falsehood will require many.

## CHAPTER XXIX

Moreover, I would also have cut down Marcion’s *Antitheses* themselves at close quarters, had their destruction by a more elaborate treatment been required for the defense of the Creator as both good and a judge, in accordance with the examples fitting God in each respect, as we have shown. But if both aspects—goodness and justice—constitute the worthy fullness of an omnipotent divinity, I can meanwhile, by a shorter method, have blunted those *Antitheses* which eagerly attempt, from differences in dispositions, laws, or mighty works, to distinguish [Col. 0319B] and thus estrange Christ from the Creator—as the supremely good from the judge, the gentle from the fierce, and the saving from the destructive.

For they unite the two all the more by placing them within those differences which are fitting to God. Remove Marcion’s title [Note: [Col. 0319B] “Remove Marcion’s title.” That man of Pontus had written the *Antitheses*, or a book under this title. [Col. 0319C] Since our author now believes that he has sufficiently refuted them, he says that they should be removed when he writes that the title is to be removed. LE PRIEUR.] and the aim and purpose of the work itself, and it supplies [Note: [Col. 0319B] Semler reads “to supply”; perhaps “would supply.” “It supplies” is Rhenanus’s conjecture, afterward adopted by Pamelius, Rigault, Franeker, Paris, and Venice. Junius reads “it will supply.”] nothing other than a demonstration of one and the same God, supremely good and a judge, because these two attributes belong together in a single God. For the very effort in those examples to set Christ against the Creator points rather toward their unity. So completely was there one and the same substance in their divinities [Note: [Col. 0320B] Rhenanus conjectures “of divinity.”]—both good and severe, in the same examples and in similar arguments—that he wished to display his goodness in the same matters in which he had previously manifested severity.

Nor will a temporal difference be surprising, [Note: [Col. 0320B] Semler and Pamelius read “was.”] if God was afterward gentler because circumstances had been tamed, whereas formerly he was more austere because they were untamed. Thus, through the *Antitheses*, it can more readily be shown that the Creator’s order was reformed, reflected anew, and restored by Christ rather than abolished—especially since [Note: [Col. 0320B] Pamelius and Semler omit “since.”] you separate your god from every harsher movement, and therefore, of course, from rivalry with the Creator.

For if this is so, how do the *Antitheses* demonstrate that he rivaled every individual manifestation of the Creator? I shall therefore recognize through them, even in this respect, my God as jealous: by his own right, with good and rational rivalry, he took advance care to bring to maturity those things of his which were more luxuriant in their beginnings. [Note: [Col. 0319C] “Who took advance care to bring his more tree-like things in their beginnings to maturity by good and rational rivalry.” “Who took advance care of his more tree-like things” means “his more robust things.” That is, he did not plant mere shoots, but trees already grown—and indeed more fully tree-like, that is, already large—which produce fruit much earlier or more quickly than shoots. RIGAULT.—An elegant metaphor. *Arbustiores*—as Rhenanus correctly noted in the margin of his first edition—appears to be used for “more luxuriant” or “more vigorous,” the metaphor being taken from luxuriantly growing trees. Pliny also uses the verb *arbustare*. Otherwise one might suppose, though incorrectly, that the reading should be *austeriores*, “more austere.” He is comparing the maturity of the New Testament with the harsh immaturity of the Old. PAMELIUS.]

Even his world will recognize its Creator’s *Antitheses* in the opposition of its elements, though it is regulated with the highest reason. Therefore, most thoughtless Marcion, you should have presented one god of light and another of darkness, so that you might more readily persuade us that there is one god of goodness and another of severity. But the antithesis will belong to him whose antithesis is also present in the world.

# BOOK III

[Col. 0319]

## SUMMARY OF CONTENTS
[Col. 0319D] I. In preparing to write this third book against Marcion, **ON CHRIST**, he first lays down that Christ must be understood as belonging to no other God than the Creator: both because it was established in the preceding books that no God other than the Creator is to be believed in, and because a review of the apostolic and heretical churches proves that no discussion of another God or another Christ arose before the scandal caused by Marcion.

II. He then argues that Marcion’s Christ is suspect because he came so suddenly, before the Father bore witness concerning the Son—before the sender testified concerning the one sent.

III. Nor is it sufficient that he was supposedly going to prove himself the Son of God by demonstrations of miraculous powers: both because Christ himself shows that faith based on signs is rash, since such signs are very readily found even among false prophets, and because the Creator had already [Col. 0320D] worked miracles before him through his servants.

IV. But if Marcion’s Christ was revealed after the Creator in order to correct him, he ought to have been revealed not before but after the Creator’s Christ, so that he might correct him as well.

V. Now, since he is going to prove from the Scriptures that Christ belonged to the Creator, whose Scriptures were fulfilled by him, he begins by stating that his opponents must recognize two features of prophetic expression: one by which future events are sometimes announced as though they had already occurred, and another by which many things are foretold figuratively.

VI. Thus the Jewish error does not support the Marcionites’ case, on the grounds that the Jews killed the Creator’s Christ as though he were a stranger; for Scripture [Col. 0321A] had foretold that they would fail to recognize him—and this insofar as they regarded him as merely a man.

VII. Both groups, however, are refuted by the two advents of Christ, which the prophets indicated through his twofold condition; they could neither understand nor believe the first, which was more obscure and less honorable.

VIII. He next defends, against the Marcionites and the other authors of their errors—whom the apostle John pronounced antichrists—that Christ truly came in the flesh. Otherwise, among other things, the fruit of the Christian name, Christ’s death, and the resurrection would also have to be denied.

IX. Nor do the Creator’s angels support their position on the pretext that, when they dealt with Abraham and Lot, they acted in the phantasm of an apparent body, yet truly met with them and ate; for those angels were not destined to die for us.

[Col. 0321B] X. But if Christ spurned flesh as something unworthy, he ought also to have disdained its image, since resemblance follows the actual condition of a thing.

XI. And Marcion was wrong to assert that Christ had only an apparent corporeality so as not to be compelled to acknowledge his birth; for he could also have assigned him an apparent birth. Yet neither position can stand, since truth is more fitting for God than falsehood.

XII. Nor does it count against the Creator’s Christ that Isaiah writes that he was to be called Emmanuel, although he was not given that name; for it is enough that Christ was “God with us” in meaning, not in the sound of his name.

XIII. Nor do “the might of Damascus,” “the spoils of Samaria,” and “the king of the Assyrians,” which Isaiah applies [Col. 0321C] to Christ, portend that he would be a warrior; rather, they figuratively represent the eastern Magi presenting Christ in his infancy with gold and incense.

XIV. For elsewhere also—namely, in the Psalms and in John’s Apocalypse—weapons of war are figuratively ascribed to Christ.

XV. He next continues by arguing that the name “Christ” does not belong to Marcion’s Christ: both because it is the proper designation of one person alone, while the Creator’s Christ nevertheless possessed that name; and because one who had no body could not have been anointed, and therefore could in no way be called “Christ,” that is, “Anointed.”

XVI. Much less does the name Jesus belong to him—a Jesus whom the Jews do not await, and whose name belongs to the Creator’s Christ—because another God’s Christ ought to have nothing in common with the Creator’s Christ.

[Col. 0321D] XVII. He then cites, in almost the same words, the same testimonies of Scripture concerning Christ’s contemptible condition during his Passion that he cited above in the book *Against the Jews*.

XVIII. Likewise, from the Pentateuch, concerning his departure through the Passion of the cross.

XIX. Likewise, from the Psalms and the Prophets.

XX. Finally, he proves that the Creator’s Christ was truly the Christ because all the nations have turned to him [Col. 0322A] in accordance with David’s prediction—a prediction that cannot be understood as referring either to David himself or to his son Solomon.

XXI. For the calling not only of the Jews but also of the nations to the Creator’s Christ was foretold in numerous scriptural passages.

XXII. Indeed, it was prophesied that the apostles would be preachers not of another God but of the same God, and that both they themselves and all the faithful would suffer the same things as Christ.

XXIII. Yet because Marcion, together with the Jews, denied that Christ had come, he shows that their end—or destruction—which was foretold as something they would incur because of their impiety toward Christ, has already been fulfilled. This would have happened without cause if they suffered it on account of another God’s Christ, who had been driven to the cross by that God’s rivals, namely, the Creator’s powers; for the Creator could not have exacted vengeance unless the Christ was his own.

XXIV. Finally, taking occasion from Marcion’s claim that Judaea would be restored by his god, he refers the reader to **BOOK IV AGAINST MARCION**, concerning Abraham’s bosom, and to the **WORK ON THE HOPE OF THE FAITHFUL**, concerning the promised restoration of Judaea. Here too he treats at length the millenarians’ dream, concerning which there is a fuller discussion among the Author’s paradoxes. Tertullian is preparing to write against Marcion’s work, composed through the opposition of contrarieties and entitled *Antitheses*, which was designed to enforce a separation between the Law and the Gospel, whereby he divided two different Gods, one belonging to the Old Testament and the other to the New.

**Chapter I.** While first of all not denying the diversity of commandments and disciplines, he demonstrates that they belong to one and the same God, because God the Creator himself, through [Col. 0322C] his prophets, foretold that another and new law—namely, that of the Gospel—would arise in place of the Old, and an eternal covenant in place of a temporary one.

# CHAPTER I

Following the tracks of my former work, which, though lost, we persist in reconstructing, the orderly course of my argument now brings me to Christ—even if this treatment is superabundant after the completion of the defense of the one divine nature.

> **Note:** [Col. 0321D] “For the matter has been sufficiently prejudged.” In the preceding books it has been demonstrated plainly enough that Christ was sent by God the Creator, and was not a Christ belonging to another god than the Creator, as [Col. 0322D] Marcion dreamed. **LE PR.**

For the matter has been sufficiently prejudged: Christ must be understood as belonging to no other God than the Creator, since it has been established that no God other than the Creator is to be believed—the Creator whom Christ so emphatically preached. Thereafter, the apostles announced the Christ of no other God than the God whom Christ preached, that is, the Creator. Thus no mention of another God, and consequently none of another Christ, was ever discussed before the scandal caused by Marcion. [Col. 0322D]

This is most easily proved by a review of the apostolic and heretical churches: the corruption of the rule must plainly be assigned to the place where later origin is found—a point that I also incorporated into my first little book. But this present engagement, which is to examine [Note: “separately” in Semler and Pamel.] Christ as a separate matter, will also have this effect: while we prove that Christ belongs to the Creator, Marcion’s god will thereby be excluded as well.

Truth ought to employ all its powers,

> **Note:** [Col. 0322D] “Not as though it were struggling.” Truth struggles when it is either oppressed by falsehood or covered over with the appearance of truth. It also happens [Col. 0323D] not infrequently that speaking the truth is dangerous because of the violence and lack of self-control of certain people. Thucydides, *Histories* I, spoke in this sense when he said, ἀταλαίπωρος ἡ ζήτησις τῆς ἀληθείας, that is, “the investigation of truth is free from toil.” **LE PR. and EDD.**

not as though it were struggling. [Col. 0323A] In any case, it triumphs through the concise force of preliminary objections. But it has been decided that truth, eager for battle, should encounter its adversary everywhere—an adversary so far gone in frenzy that he more readily assumed the coming of a Christ who had never been announced than of the one who had always been proclaimed.

# CHAPTER II

From here, then, I proceed to the question

> **Note:** “I compare” in the Paris, Franeker, and Pamel editions.

whether he ought to have come so suddenly. First, because he was also his God’s Son; for the proper order was

> **Note:** “would have been” in Semler.

that the Father should declare the Son before the Son declared the Father, and that the Father should testify concerning the Son before the Son testified concerning the Father. Next, because he was also “sent,” in addition to bearing the name of Son.

> **Note:** “By which” in Semler and Pamel.

Accordingly, the authorization of the sender ought to have preceded as testimony on behalf of the one sent. For no one who comes on another’s authority himself defends that authority by his own assertion; rather, he expects himself to be defended [Col. 0323B] by that authority,

> **Note:** “the defense” in Semler; “by the defense” in Pamel.

with an advance declaration from the one who grants the authority preceding him. Otherwise, one will not acknowledge as Son someone whom the Father never named, nor believe that someone was sent whom no commissioning authority ever designated.

> **Note:** [Col. 0323D] “The commissioning authority designated.” The *mandator* is the person who entrusts something to be done; the *mandatarius* is the person who undertakes it. **RHEN.**

The Father would have named him, and the commissioning authority would have designated him, if he had been the Son and the one sent. Everything that has departed from the rule will be regarded with suspicion. The primary order of things does not permit the Father to be acknowledged after the Son, the commissioner after the commission, or Christ after God. In recognition, nothing precedes its own origin, because nothing precedes it in the ordering either.

Suddenly a Son, suddenly one sent, and suddenly a Christ? Yet I would suppose that nothing from God is sudden, because nothing from God is unordered. But if it was ordered, why was it not also proclaimed beforehand, so that it might be proved both ordered by its proclamation and divine by its ordering? Indeed, so great [Col. 0323C] an undertaking—one that was plainly being prepared for human salvation—would not have been sudden, if only because it was to achieve its benefit through faith. For insofar as it had to be believed in order to be beneficial, to that same extent it required preparation in order to be believed, built upon the foundations of ordering and proclamation. Once faith had been formed by this sequence, it could rightly both be commanded to the human being by God and be rendered to God by the human being; it was bound to believe on the basis of recognition, because it was capable of doing so, having learned what to believe from proclamation.

# CHAPTER III

You say that no such order was necessary, because he would immediately prove himself both Son, envoy, and God’s Christ by the realities themselves [Col. 0324A], through demonstrations of miraculous powers. But I shall deny that this form of testimony alone was appropriate to him, since he himself afterward invalidated it. For in declaring that many would come (Matthew 24:24),

> **Note:** [Col. 0323D] “For in declaring that many would come.” He paraphrastically cites Matthew 24: “Many false Christs will come,” etc. So also blessed Augustine, *Against Faustus* XIII.5: “You perform no miracles; although, even if you did, we would be on our guard, since the Lord instructs us [Col. 0324D] and says, ‘Many will arise,’” etc. And *Tractates on John* 14: “Pontius may perform a miracle, and Donatus may pray, and God may answer from heaven: first, they are either deceived or deceivers; finally, grant that they move mountains—if they do not have charity, they are nothing. But how could those who divided unity possess it?” Yet it is clear from *On the Soul* 57 and *Against Marcion* V.16 that the Author did not therefore think that the truth of signs and miraculous powers ever existed, or would ever exist, among heretics. **PAM.**

and that they would perform signs and produce great miracles, even leading the elect astray,

> **Note:** [Col. 0324D] “Even leading the elect astray.” Although I am not superstitious about variant readings, I would nevertheless judge that “the overthrow of the elect” should be read. **LE PR.**

yet nevertheless must not be accepted on that account, he showed that faith in signs and miracles is rash, since they are very readily found even among false Christs.

> **Note:** “Most readily found,” singular, in Franeker and Pamel.

Or what sense does it make if he wished himself to be proved, understood, and received on the very basis—I mean miraculous powers—on which he did not wish the others to be received, although they too were to come just as suddenly and had been proclaimed by no author? If

> **Note:** “But” in Semler and Pamel.

because he came before them and first authenticated demonstrations of power, he therefore seized faith as though it were a place in the public baths, anticipating and appropriating it before all later claimants, take care lest he himself be found in the position of those who came later. [Col. 0324B] For he is found to be later than the Creator, who had already been known beforehand and had accordingly worked miracles beforehand, and had explicitly

> **Note:** “By name” in Latinius.

declared that no others coming after him were to be believed.

Therefore, if coming first and speaking beforehand about later claimants closes the case for credibility,

> **Note:** [Col. 0324D] “Will elicit” in Latinius; “will elude” in others.

then he too will already stand condemned because he is recognized as later; and the authority to establish this rule concerning later claimants will belong to the Creator alone, who could not himself be later than anyone.

Now, since I am about to prove that the Creator formerly produced through his servants the same miracles that you claim as the sole basis for believing your Christ, and that at other times he appointed them to be produced through his own Christ, I may rightly lay down this further preliminary objection: Christ was all the less to be believed on the sole basis of miracles because these miracles, corresponding both to those of the Creator performed through his servants and to those promised for his Christ, could have been interpreted as belonging to no one other than the Creator. [Col. 0324C]

> **Note:** [Col. 0324D] For “corresponding,” Semler reads “for those corresponding,” and Pamel reads “the one corresponding.”

Even if other demonstrations were found in your Christ—new ones, of course—we would more readily believe that the new belonged to the same one to whom the old belonged than to one who possessed only new things, things in need of the proofs afforded by triumphant antiquity. Thus, on this ground too, he ought to have come after being proclaimed: both his own prophecies and his miraculous powers would then establish faith in him. This was especially necessary if he was to come in opposition to the Creator’s Christ, who was fortified by his own signs and prophets,

> **Note:** “Prophecies” in other editions.

so that, as a rival Christ, he might shine forth through every kind of distinction. But how could the Christ of a God who had never been proclaimed [Col. 0325A] himself be proclaimed? This, then, is what requires that neither your god nor your Christ be believed: God ought not to have remained unknown, and Christ ought to have been recognized through God.

# CHAPTER IV

He disdained, I suppose, to imitate the order of our God, as though it displeased him and were precisely what he intended to refute.

> **Note:** “And” in Latinius.

Being new, he wished to come in a new way: the Son before the declaration of the Father, and the envoy before the authority of the commissioner, so that he might introduce that most monstrous faith

> **Note:** “He himself” in Semler and Pamel.

by which it would be believed that Christ had come before it was known that he had existed.

I am also entitled to reconsider why he did not come after Christ. For when I see his lord patiently enduring for so great an age the most bitter Creator, who all the while was announcing his own Christ to humanity—whatever his reason for doing so—and postponing both his revelation and his intervention, I say that, for the same reason, he ought to have extended that patience to the Creator while the latter also carried out his plans in his own Christ. [Col. 0325B] Then, after every operation of the rival God and the rival Christ had been perfected and completed, he might at last have superimposed his own arrangements.

Otherwise, repentance for such great patience caused him not to persevere until the Creator’s course of events reached its end. Did he vainly endure the proclamation of a Christ whom he did not endure to be manifested? Or did he refrain from cutting the Creator off for so long without cause? What restrained him, or what disturbed him? Yet he failed in both respects: he was revealed so late after the Creator, but so precipitately before the Creator’s Christ. He ought long ago to have exposed the one, but not yet the other; he ought not to have endured the one raging for so long, yet ought not to have troubled the other while he was still at rest. [Col. 0325C] With respect to both, he fell away from the title of the Best God, being surely changeable and uncertain himself: lukewarm toward the Creator, hot against Christ, and ineffectual in both cases.

> **Note:** “In each case” in other editions.

For he no more restrained the Creator than he obstructed Christ. The Creator remains entirely what he is, and Christ will come just as he is described. Why did he come after the Creator, whom he was unable to correct? Why was he revealed before the Creator’s Christ, whom he could not recall?

Or, if he corrected the Creator, he was revealed after him so that the things requiring correction might come first. Therefore, if he was likewise going to correct the Creator’s Christ, he ought to have waited for him too, so as to become his later corrector just as he had become the Creator’s. It would be another matter if he himself were to come again after that Christ, so that in his first advent he came forth against the Creator, destroying his Law and [Col. 0325D] Prophets, but in the second he would come forth [Col. 0326A] against Christ, refuting his kingdom. Then, therefore, he would complete his orderly course; then perhaps he should be believed. But if his undertaking has already been completed from this point onward, he will therefore come in vain, since he will accomplish nothing.

# CHAPTER V

I offer these remarks as a preliminary skirmish,

> **Note:** “I have made a preliminary skirmish” in Rigault, Junius, and the Venice edition.

as though I were still at the first stage and still fighting from a distance. But now, as I prepare to fight from here at a fixed position and at close quarters,

> **Note:** [Col. 0325D] “To fight at a fixed position and at close quarters.” It is as though the preceding arguments had been conducted in the manner of a light skirmish; here he promises that he will fight more vigorously, so as to press his adversary under any wager. He therefore appeals to Scripture, which he turns against Marcion. **LE PR.**

I see that certain battle lines must first be drawn, according to which the combat is to be conducted—namely, the Creator’s Scriptures. Since I am going to prove from them that Christ belonged to the Creator, inasmuch as they were afterward

> **Note:** “After” in Junius.

fulfilled in his Christ, I must first set forth the form of their writing

> **Note:** [Col. 0325D] “The form of the Scriptures,” etc.: by explaining, clarifying, and commending it beforehand. **RIG.**

and, so to speak, its nature. Otherwise, if these matters are brought into controversy only when the Scriptures are being applied to the cases at issue, the defense of the Scriptures and that of the cases will become entangled [Col. 0326B] and dull the reader’s attention.

I therefore submit that our opponents must henceforth recognize two features of prophetic expression. The first is that future events are sometimes stated as though they had already occurred. For it befits the Divine Being to reckon as completed whatever he has decreed, since with him there is no difference of time: eternity itself directs before him one uniform condition of the times.

> **Note:** “Of time” in Semler and Pamel.

And it is especially characteristic of prophetic divination to present what it foresees, while foreseeing it, as something already seen and therefore already accomplished,

> **Note:** “As already” in Junius.

that is, as something certain to occur in every respect. Thus Isaiah says (Isaiah 50:6):

> “I gave my back to scourges, and my cheeks to blows with the palms; but I did not turn my face away from spittings.”

For whether, according to us, Christ was even then speaking about himself, or, according to the Jews, the prophet was speaking about himself, [Col. 0326C] he nevertheless described as already past something that had not yet happened.

The second form is that many things are figuratively foretold through riddles, allegories, and parables, and must be understood otherwise than they are written. For we also read that the mountains will drip sweetness (Joel 3:18); yet you are not thereby to expect concentrated grape syrup from stones

> **Note:** [Col. 0325D] “Concentrated grape syrup from stones, or boiled must from rocks,” etc. [Col. 0326D] These two terms mean the same thing, namely cooked must. The distinction is that *sapa* is must boiled down to half its original quantity, while *defrutum* is boiled down to one-third: so Marcus Varro. **LE PR.**

or boiled must from rocks. We hear, too, of a land flowing with milk and honey; yet you are not thereby to believe that you will ever gather cakes and Samian pastries from clods of earth.

> **Note:** [Col. 0326D] “Cakes and Samian pastries,” etc. Others read *psomias*, others *psomia*, from the Greek ψώμιον, “morsel” or “little piece of bread.” Those who read “Samian pastries,” I think, understand it as referring to Samian cakes, which were considered delicacies but bore the name of their inventor, who was called Samius. **LE PR.**

Nor did God’s mouth immediately promise to become a water-diviner and farmer when he said (Isaiah 41:19):

> “I will establish rivers in a thirsty region, and in the desert the cedar and box tree.”

Likewise, when proclaiming the conversion of the nations:

> “The beasts of the field, the sirens, and the daughters of sparrows will bless me” (Isaiah 43:20),

he is certainly not going to receive favorable omens from young swallows and little foxes, or from those monstrous and fabulous songstresses. [Col. 0326D]

Why should I say more about this class of expressions? [Col. 0327A] Even the apostle of the heretics (1 Corinthians 9:9),

> **Note:** “Of the Gentiles” in Latinius.

> **Note:** [Col. 0327D] “The apostle of the heretics.” He means the apostle Paul as edited and mutilated by Marcion. **PAMEL.**

interprets the Law’s indulgence in leaving the mouths of threshing oxen unmuzzled not as referring to oxen, but to us. He declares that the rock that accompanied the people and supplied them with drink was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). Accordingly, he teaches the Galatians (Galatians 4:22) that the two narratives concerning Abraham’s sons followed an allegorical course, and he suggests to the Ephesians (Ephesians 5:31) that what was proclaimed in the beginning concerning the man who would leave father and mother, and concerning the two who would become one flesh, is recognized by him as referring to Christ and the Church.

# CHAPTER VI

If these two characteristics of Jewish literature have meanwhile been sufficiently established, remember, reader, that they have been established, so that when we apply any such passage, the dispute will concern not the form of the Scripture but the substance of the case.

When, therefore, [Col. 0327B] heretical madness assumed that the Christ who had never been announced had come, it followed that it should contend that the Christ who had always been proclaimed had not yet come. Thus it was compelled to ally itself with the Jewish error and to construct its argument from it, as though the Jews, themselves certain that the one who came was someone else, had not only rejected him as a stranger but even killed him as an adversary—although they would undoubtedly have acknowledged him and attended upon him with every religious observance if he had been their own.

> **Note:** [Col. 0327D] Evidently that shipmaster had been protected not by Rhodian law but by Pontic law. He reproaches Marcion for his Pontic barbarism, as though Marcion had learned nothing except certain nautical ordinances, and those Pontic—that is, purely barbarous—rather than Rhodian. The Rhodians were admired by everyone for their care in civil law and their justice; but they also appear to have been highly skilled in maritime affairs and to have established most equitable laws concerning everything pertaining to navigation. Strabo records that for this reason they obtained dominion over the sea and flourished in friendship with the Romans. Not a few provisions of their maritime law concerning jettison, and perhaps also concerning the shipmaster’s action, were incorporated into the Pandects. **PAM.**

Evidently that shipmaster had been protected not by Rhodian law,

> **Note:** [Col. 0328D] “Not by Rhodian law,” etc. The laws of the Rhodians, who were highly skilled in maritime affairs, are mentioned in the Digest, under the Rhodian law concerning jettison. Tertullian says this to Marcion ironically. **LE PR.**

but by Pontic law, which forbade the Jews to err concerning their own Christ. Yet even if no such error had been foretold concerning them, the mere fact that human nature is liable to deception would surely have persuaded us that the Jews could have erred, since they were human beings. [Col. 0327C] One ought not immediately to draw a prejudicial conclusion from the judgment of people who could credibly have been mistaken.

Moreover, since it was also foretold that they would fail to recognize Christ, and would therefore kill him, the one whom they were foretold to treat in this way will consequently be the very one whom they failed to recognize and killed. If you demand proof of this, I shall not unfold the Scriptures that declare Christ capable of being killed and thus surely affirm that he could be unrecognized—for, unless he had been unrecognized, he plainly could not have suffered anything. Reserving those passages for the case concerning his sufferings, it will be sufficient for the present to apply those prophecies that prove in the meantime that Christ could be unrecognized. I shall do this briefly by showing that the Creator took away from the people every power of understanding.

He says [Col. 0328A] (Isaiah 29:14):

> “I will take away the wisdom of their wise men, and I will conceal the understanding of their prudent men.”

And again (Isaiah 6:10):

> “With your ears you will hear, and you will not hear; and with your eyes you will see, and you will not see. For the heart of this people has become dull; with their ears they have heard heavily, and they have closed their eyes, lest at any time they should hear with their ears, and see with their eyes, and comprehend with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them.”

For they had deserved this blunting

> **Note:** “Dulling” in Semler.

of their saving senses, because they loved God with their lips but stood far away from him in their heart.

Therefore, if Christ was being announced by the Creator—who “establishes the thunder,” “creates the spirit” (Amos 4:13),

> **Note:** “Encloses” in Pamel, Rigault, the Venice edition, and Semler; but Latinius prefers “creates,” a reading supported by the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin Vulgate texts of Scripture. **EDD.**

and announces his Christ to humanity, according to the prophet Amos;

> **Note:** “Announcing” in Semler.

and if the whole hope of the Jews—not to mention that of the Gentiles also—was appointed to await the revelation of Christ, [Col. 0328B] then without doubt

> **Note:** [Col. 0328D] Others read “much less” instead of “not to mention.”

 those who were shown to be destined neither to recognize nor to understand what was announced, because the powers of recognition

> **Note:** “Of recognition” omitted by Semler.

and understanding—wisdom and prudence—had been taken away, would fail to recognize that which was being announced, namely Christ. Their chief wise men, that is, the scribes, and their prudent men,

> **Note:** “Their” disregarded by Semler.

that is, the Pharisees, were destined to err concerning him. Likewise, the people would hear with their ears and not hear—surely, they would hear Christ teaching—and would see with their eyes and not see—surely, they would see Christ performing signs. This accords with what he says elsewhere (Isaiah 42:19):

> “And who is blind except my servants? And who is deaf except the one who rules them?”

Likewise, when he reproaches them through the same Isaiah (Isaiah 1:3):

> “I begot sons and exalted them, but they rejected me. The ox recognized its owner, and the ass its master’s manger; but Israel did not know me, and the people did not understand me.”

We, indeed, are certain that Christ always spoke in the Prophets—Christ being, of course, the Creator’s Spirit—as the prophet testifies [Col. 0328C]:

> **Note:** [Col. 0328D] “The spirit of his person is Christ the Lord.” I judge that this must certainly be read instead of “The person of our spirit is Christ the Lord.” For, first of all, the Author would otherwise depart too greatly from the Septuagint at Lamentations 4, where not only the Greek and Latin manuscripts read, “The spirit of our face”—that is, [Col. 0329D] “of our countenance,” or “before our face”—“is Christ the Lord,” but the same words are also cited with the same meaning by blessed Irenaeus, III.11; blessed Justin Martyr, *Second Apology to Antoninus Pius*; and Rufinus, *Commentary on the Creed*. Nor does the Hebrew edition dissent greatly from them, reading, “the spirit of our mouth,” while the Chaldean reads, “the breath of the spirit of life that is in our nostrils.” **PAM.**

> “The spirit of his person is Christ the Lord” (Lamentations 4:20).

From the beginning, acting as the Father’s representative, he was both heard and seen under the name of God. We know that even then it was his voice uttering against Israel reproaches concerning the offenses they were foretold to commit against him:

> **Note:** [Col. 0328D] Semler inserts “and” before “we know.”

> “You have forsaken the Lord and provoked the Holy One of Israel to anger” (Isaiah 1:4).

But if you prefer to refer every account of the Jews’ former ignorance not to Christ but rather to God himself—refusing to admit that even in former times the Creator’s Word and Spirit, that is, his Christ, was despised and unrecognized by them—you are still refuted in this way.

> **Note:** [Col. 0328D] Semler reads, “But if Israel did not,” instead of “But if not.” Since you do not deny that the Creator’s Christ is the Creator’s Son, Spirit, and substance [Col. 0329A], you must concede that those who did not recognize the Father could not have recognized the Son either, because he shares the same substance. If they did not understand the fullness of that substance, much less could they understand a portion of it—at least insofar as that portion shares in the fullness.

Once these matters have thus been considered, it is now apparent how the Jews both rejected and killed Christ:

> **Note:** [Col. 0329C] Franeker omits “both.” not because they understood him to be a foreign Christ, but because they failed to recognize him as their own. For how could they have understood as a stranger someone concerning whom nothing had ever been announced, when they could not understand the one concerning whom proclamation had always been made?

> **Note:** [Col. 0329C] Rhenanus reads “For neither” instead of “For.”

> **Note:** [Col. 0329D] “For that which is capable of being understood is also capable of not being understood.” We have often already pointed out this author’s use of the verb *capit*, “is capable of.” There is a very similar expression in the immediately preceding book: “The condition is also capable,” he says, “of being called an image of the Spirit.” **RHEN.**

For only that which possesses the substance of proclamation is capable of being understood or not understood, since it will also possess the material either of recognition or of error. But that which lacks such material does not admit of any outcome involving wisdom.

Accordingly, they did not turn away from

> **Note:** “Opposed” in other editions.

and persecute Christ [Col. 0329B] because he belonged to another God, but because they regarded him as merely a human being—one whom they considered a charlatan in his signs

> **Note:** [Col. 0329D] “A charlatan in his signs.” Rhenanus correctly noted in the margin: “That is, an impostor.” Pliny uses the word *planus* with the same meaning in Book XXXV, chapter 18, when speaking of the royal charlatan who was a favorite of Ptolemy. The word passed into the Latin vocabulary from the Greek πλάνος, “deceiver” or “impostor”; Eustathius, the interpreter of Homer, likewise uses it for certain impostors in his commentary on the *Odyssey*. **PAM.**

and a rival in his teachings. Thus they brought even the man himself to trial as one of their own—that is, as a Jew, but one who deviated from and destroyed Judaism—and punished him according to their own law. They plainly would not have judged one who was foreign to them. So far were they from appearing to have understood him as a foreign Christ that they did not even judge him, as a man, to be a foreigner.

# CHAPTER VII
Let the heretic now learn, by way of superfluity, together—if you please—with the Jew himself, the rationale of his errors: borrowing his guidance from the Jew in this argument, the blind led by the blind has fallen into the same pit. [Note: [Col. 0329C] *Led* (*deductus*), Pam., Fran., Paris.]

We say that the two conditions of Christ demonstrated by the Prophets prefigured the same number of his advents: one in humility—namely, the first—[Col. 0329C] when he was to be “led like a sheep to slaughter” (Isa. 53:7), and, “like a lamb before its shearer, voiceless,” not opening his mouth; [Note: [Col. 0330D] “Not even comely in appearance.” Understand this of the time of the Passion, because of the disfigurement that tortures and sufferings had impressed upon his sacred body. Nearly the same things, if I remember correctly, occur in Book I *Against the Jews*. LE PR.] not [Note: [Col. 0329D] *Os, ne*, Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] even comely in appearance. “For we proclaimed concerning him,” he says, “as a little child, as a root in thirsty ground; and there is neither form nor glory in him. And we saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty; but his appearance was dishonored, deficient in comparison with the sons of men; a man under scourges and knowing how to bear infirmity”; so that he was appointed [Col. 0330A] by the Father “as a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” (Isa. 8:14); “made by him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:6); declaring himself “a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21:6), “the disgrace of man and the nullity of the people.”

These indications of ignobility belong to the first advent, just as those of sublimity belong to the second, when he will no longer be a stone of stumbling or a rock of offense, but [Note: [Col. 0330D] “The chief cornerstone.” In Ephesians 2 Paul called the stone ἀκρογωνιαῖον, “cornerstone,” which the Psalmist had said had become ὡς κεφαλὴν γωνίας, “as the head of the corner.” This is a figure or allegory of Christ, rejected by the Jews. And yet there has recently been published at Angers, from the rubbish of some ancient library, the itinerary of the monk Antoninus, who claims to have seen that stone in the basilica of Zion. Some Syrian played this imposture upon the unlearned simplicity of an ignorant and excessively credulous man. RIG.] the chief cornerstone, taken up after his rejection and exalted to complete the temple—that is, the Church—and indeed that rock in Daniel (ch. 2), cut from the mountain, which will crush and shatter the image of the kingdoms of this age.

Of this second [Note: [Col. 0330C] *Second* omitted by Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] advent the same prophet says (Dan. 7:13): “And behold, one coming with the clouds of heaven like a son of man came as far as the Ancient of Days and stood in his presence; and those who stood by [Col. 0330B] brought him forward, and royal power was given to him, and all the nations of the earth according to their kinds, and every glory, were made subject to him; and his power is everlasting and shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be escaped.” Then, assuredly, he will possess both an honorable appearance and unfailing beauty beyond the sons of men. [Note: [Col. 0330D] “For,” he says, “timely in beauty.” This derives from the ambiguous meaning of the Greek word ὡραῖος (*hōraios*). The Vulgate has the better reading, “beautiful.” LE PR.] “For,” he says (Ps. 44:3), “you are timely in beauty beyond the sons of men; grace has been poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever. Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one, in your timeliness and your beauty.” Likewise, after the Father has “made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:6), he will crown him with glory and honor and subject all things [Note: [Col. 0330C] *Beneath* omitted by Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] beneath his feet.

Then, too, “those who pierced him will recognize him” (Zech. 12:10), and “they will beat their breasts, tribe by tribe,” [Col. 0330C] precisely because they did not formerly recognize him when he was established in the humility of the human condition. [Note: [Col. 0330C] *Established* omitted by Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] “And he is a man,” says Jeremiah (Jer. 17:9), “and who will recognize him?” For Isaiah also says (Isa. 53:8), “Who will recount his birth?”

Thus also in Zechariah (ch. 3), in the person of Jesus—indeed, in the mystery embodied by that very man [Note: [Col. 0330C] *That man himself* (*ipso*), Rhen., Seml., Oberth.]—Christ Jesus, the Father’s true high priest, is depicted in two conditions corresponding to his two advents. At first he is clothed in filthy garments, that is, in the indignity of passible and mortal flesh, [Col. 0331A] while the devil opposed him—the instigator, of course, of Judas the betrayer, not to mention also his tempter after his baptism. Then (Zech. 3:5), stripped of his former filth, he is adorned with a full-length robe, a mitre, and a clean turban: that is, with the glory and honor of the second advent.

For if I also offer an interpretation of the two goats presented during the fast (Lev. 16), [Note: [Col. 0331D] “For if also the two goats,” etc. The Author undoubtedly took this passage from the blessed martyr Justin’s *Against Trypho*. PAM.] do they not also symbolize both stages of Christ? They are equal and alike, because the same Lord appears in them, since he will not come in a different form, for he must be recognized by those who injured him. But one [Note: [Col. 0331D] “One indeed,” Seml., Pamel.] of them, wrapped in scarlet, cursed, spat upon, [Note: [Col. 0331D] *Spat upon* (*consputus*), Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] torn, and pierced by the people, was cast outside the city to destruction, marked by manifest tokens of the Lord’s Passion. [Col. 0331B] The other, however, offered for sins and given as food to the priests of the temple, signified the evidence of his second manifestation, in which, once all sins had been expiated, the priests of the spiritual temple—that is, the Church—would enjoy the Lord’s grace as though partaking of sacrificial flesh, while all others fasted from salvation.

Therefore, since the first advent was proclaimed both as very greatly obscured by figures and as cast down in every dishonor, whereas the second was proclaimed as both manifest and worthy of God, those who looked only toward the one they could easily understand and believe [Note: [Col. 0331D] *Would be able to* (*poterunt*), Paris.]—that is, the second, which is in honor and glory [Note: [Col. 0331D] “Which is in honor and glory” disregarded by Seml., Jun.]—were not unreasonably deceived concerning the more obscure and certainly more unworthy one, that is, the first. And thus to this very day they deny that their Christ has come, because he did not come in sublimity, while they remain ignorant that [Col. 0331C] he was also to come in humility.

## CHAPTER VIII

Let the heretic now cease borrowing poison from the Jew, as an asp does, so they say, from a viper; [Note: [Col. 0331D] *To borrow* (*mutuare*), others.] let him henceforth vomit out the venom of his own ingenuity by maintaining that Christ was a phantom.

Except that even this doctrine will have other authors: in a certain sense premature and abortive Marcionites, [Note: [Col. 0331D] “Premature and abortive,” etc. Other heretics, namely, preceded the Marcionites; they were, as it were, the abortive offspring and premature fruits of the heresy. In the book *On the Pallium*, the city of Utica is similarly called “prematurely Roman,” since it had adopted Roman dress before its time, before it had obtained the legal status of a colony. LE PR.] [Note: [Col. 0331D] *Abortive* (*aborsivos*), others.] whom the apostle John (1 John 4:2) pronounced antichrists because they denied that Christ had come in the flesh. Yet they did not do so in order to establish the claim of another god—for they would have been censured on that account [Note: [Col. 0332D] *Just* (*justo*), Par.] as well—but because they had rashly deemed it incredible that God should be flesh.

All the more, therefore, did Marcion the antichrist seize upon this presumption for himself, being, of course, better suited to rejecting Christ’s bodily substance, since he had represented Christ’s own god as neither the creator of the flesh [Col. 0331D] nor its raiser from the dead: a god supremely good, naturally, and in this respect [Note: [Col. 0332D] *And* added by Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] utterly unlike the falsehoods and deceptions of the Creator. Therefore, lest his Christ lie or deceive, [Col. 0332A] and perhaps thereby be assigned to the Creator, he was not what he appeared to be, and misrepresented what he was: flesh, yet not flesh; man, yet not man. By the same reasoning Christ was God, yet not God. Why, indeed, should he not have borne a phantom of God as well?

Am I to believe him concerning his inward substance when I have been deceived concerning his outward one? How will he be regarded as truthful in what is hidden when he has been found so deceptive in what is manifest? And how, by mingling the truth of the spirit with the deception of the flesh within his own person, does he unite what the Apostle denies can have fellowship (2 Cor. 6:14): light—that is, truth—and deception—that is, darkness?

Now, once Christ’s flesh is discovered to be a lie, it follows that everything performed through Christ’s flesh was performed as a lie: his encounters, contacts, companionship, and even his miracles. For if, by touching someone or by being touched by someone, he delivered that person [Col. 0332B] from an affliction, what was done bodily cannot be believed to have been done truly without the reality of his body itself. Nothing solid could be accomplished by what is insubstantial, nothing full by what is empty. An apparent condition, an apparent action; an imaginary worker, imaginary works.

Thus even the sufferings of his Christ will not deserve belief, for one who has not truly suffered has suffered nothing. A phantom, however, could not truly suffer. The whole work of God has therefore been overturned. The whole weight and fruit of the Christian name is overturned as well: the death of Christ is denied, though the Apostle insists upon it so emphatically—upon its truth, of course—establishing it as the supreme foundation of the gospel, of our salvation, and of his own preaching: “For I delivered to you first of all,” he says (1 Cor. 15:3–4), “that Christ died for our sins, and that he was buried, [Col. 0332C] and that he rose [Note: [Col. 0332D] *Rose* (*resurrexit*), Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] on the third day.”

Furthermore, if his flesh is denied, how is his death affirmed, when death is the peculiar suffering of flesh as it returns [Note: [Col. 0332D] *Returns* (*revertentis*), Lat.] through death to the earth from which it was taken, according to the law of its creator? But if death is denied by denying the flesh, neither will his resurrection be established. For by the same reasoning by which he did not die, he also did not rise, since he did not possess the substance of flesh, to which both death and resurrection belong (1 Cor. 15:13).

Consequently, if Christ’s resurrection is weakened, our own also is overthrown. For the resurrection for whose sake Christ came will have no force if Christ did not rise. [Note: [Col. 0332D] *Will have force* (*valebit*), Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] For just as those who said that there was no resurrection of the dead are refuted by the Apostle on the basis of Christ’s resurrection, so, if Christ’s resurrection does not stand, the resurrection of the dead [Col. 0332D] is also abolished. Thus [Note: [Col. 0332D] *And* added by Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] our faith is empty, the preaching of the apostles is empty, and they are even found to be false witnesses of God, because they testified that [Col. 0333A] he had raised Christ when he did not raise him; and we are still in our sins, while those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished—though, to be sure, they may rise again as phantoms, just as Christ did.

## CHAPTER IX

In this question you may suppose that the Creator’s angels should be set against us as an objection, on the ground that they too acted before Abraham and Lot in a phantom—namely, an apparent flesh—and nevertheless truly encountered them, ate, and carried out what they had been commanded to do.

First, you will not be admitted to the examples of the God whom you demolish. For the better and more perfect the god whom you introduce, the less appropriate are the examples of the Creator to him, since unless he is wholly different, he will not be better and more perfect at all.

Next, understand that not even this will be conceded to you: that [Col. 0333B] the angels’ flesh was apparent rather than of true and solid human substance. For if it was not difficult for him to display true sensations and actions in apparent flesh, it was much easier for him to give a true substance of flesh to true sensations and actions, especially because he is its own creator and craftsman.

Your god, however, since he produced no flesh whatsoever, may perhaps deservedly have introduced a phantom of that whose reality he had been unable to produce. My God, however, who fashioned flesh from clay in this condition—not yet from marital seed, and yet flesh nonetheless—could equally have constructed flesh for angels from any material whatever, since he also built the world out of nothing into so many bodies of such diverse kinds, and did so by his word.

And if your god at some time promises the true substance of angels to human beings—[Col. 0333C] “For they will be,” he says (Luke 20:36), “like the angels”—why should my God not also have fitted the angels with the true substance of human beings, taken from whatever source? [Note: [Col. 0333D] The second *from whatever source* omitted by Wouw., Pam., Par., Fran.] Since you will not answer me where the angelic substance in your system is taken from, it is enough for me to affirm what is fitting for God: namely, the reality of the thing that he presented to three witnesses, the senses—sight, touch, and hearing.
