It is more difficult for God to lie than to produce the reality of flesh from whatever source, [Note: [Col. 0333D] *From whatever source* only once in Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] even though that flesh was not born.

Moreover, to other heretics who maintain [Note: [Col. 0333D] “Moreover, to other heretics who maintain.” He is treating of Apelles, who, as is indicated in *On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. 6, appears to have asserted that not only Christ’s flesh but also that of the angels was made from the stars. PAM.] that the flesh of the angels, if it had truly been human, would have had to be born from flesh, we answer on a definite principle that it was both truly human and unborn: truly human because of the truthfulness of God, who is a stranger to falsehood and deception, [Col. 0334A] and because the angels could not have been treated in a human manner by human beings unless they possessed human substance; yet unborn because Christ alone was to be born into flesh from flesh, so that by his birth [Note: [Col. 0333D] *His* omitted by Par.] he might reform our birth, and thus also dissolve our death by his own death, rising again in the flesh in which he was born, so that in it he might also be capable of dying.

For this reason he himself, together with the angels, then appeared before Abraham in the reality of flesh, but flesh not yet born, because it was not yet destined to die; yet [Note: [Col. 0333D] *And* omitted by Par.] it was already learning to dwell among human beings. Still more, the angels, who were not appointed to die for us, ought not to have acquired their brief tenure of flesh through birth, since they were not going to put it off through death. Rather, it was taken from whatever source [Note: [Col. 0334D] *From whatever source* only once in Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] and relinquished in some manner altogether; nevertheless, they did not falsely represent it.

[Col. 0334B] If the Creator “makes his angels spirits and his ministers a blazing fire” (Ps. 103:4)—as truly spirits as fire—the same Creator also truly made them flesh. Let us now therefore recall, and declare to the heretics, that the promise of one day transforming human beings into angels belongs to the God who once formed angels into human beings.

## CHAPTER X

Therefore, since you have not been admitted to share in the Creator’s examples, because they are foreign to your god and have their own reasons, I should like you in turn to disclose the design of your god [Note: [Col. 0333D] “I should like you in turn to disclose the design of your god.” The sense itself compelled me to alter the reading here and substitute *of your god* (*tui*), so as to yield “his own Christ,” etc.; the old copies agree in their error. RHEN.] by which he presented his Christ without the reality of flesh.

If he despised flesh as earthly and, as you say, stuffed with filth, [Note: [Col. 0334D] *Stuffed* (*infarsam*), Jun.] why did he not similarly despise its likeness? For no image of a thing deserving contempt deserves respect: the likeness follows the condition of the thing. But how could he have dwelt [Col. 0334C] among human beings except through an image of human substance? Why, then, did he not rather do so through its reality, so that his dwelling among them might be real, if he had to dwell among them? How much more worthily would necessity have administered faith than a trick! [Note: [Col. 0333D] “Than a trick.” *Stropha* signifies deceit, cunning, and imposture; Greek στροφή (*strophē*). RHEN.]

You establish a sufficiently wretched god by the very fact that he could not present his Christ except in the likeness of an unworthy thing—and a foreign thing at that. For it will be appropriate to use certain unworthy things if [Note: [Col. 0334D] *If* omitted by Pam., Par., Fran.; *just as*, Rhen.] he uses ours, [Note: [Col. 0333D] “For it will sometimes be appropriate to use unworthy things if he uses ours.” So the Pithou manuscript reads. These words, however, seem to be spoken in Marcion’s person, from “You establish a sufficiently wretched god” as far as “seemed to have needed both an unworthy and a foreign thing.” “If God uses our members,” he says, “so that he can dwell among us, there are many things in our body unworthy of God, which it will nevertheless be appropriate for God to use if he wishes to use ours. But even if ours were worthy of God, it is nevertheless unfitting for God to use things belonging to another.” The preceding words, “But how could he have dwelt among human beings except through an image of human substance?” are spoken in Marcion’s person as well. Similar instances occur throughout Septimius’ disputations, and unless they are skillfully distinguished they throw the whole argument into confusion. RHEN.] just as it will be unfitting to use things belonging to another, even if they are worthy. Why did he not come in some other, more worthy substance, and above all in his own, lest he appear to have needed something both unworthy and foreign?

If my Creator encountered man through a bush and fire, and later through a cloud and a fiery mass, [Col. 0335A] and used the bodies of the elements in manifestations of himself, these examples sufficiently demonstrate the divine power: God did not need the provision either of false or even of true flesh.

Moreover, if we look to the precise point, no substance is worthy for God to put on. Whatever he puts on, he himself makes worthy—provided, however, that there is no falsehood. What sort of reasoning, then, is it that he should have regarded the reality of flesh as more disgraceful than a lie about flesh? On the contrary, he honored flesh by fashioning its likeness. How great a thing flesh must now be, when a phantom of it was necessary to the superior god!

## CHAPTER XI

Marcion adopted all these deceptions concerning Christ’s apparent corporeality [Note: [Col. 0335D] “Apparent corporeality in Christ.” Boethius, *On Faith*: “Even today there are those who deny that he bore our corporeality.” RIG.] with this purpose: that Christ’s birth [Col. 0335B] should not also be defended by the testimony of his human substance, and that Christ should not thereby be vindicated for the Creator, since he had been proclaimed as capable of birth and therefore as fleshly.

Here too the man from Pontus is utterly foolish, [Note: [Col. 0335D] *This* (*hoc*), Jun.] as though it would not more readily be believed that flesh in God was unborn than that it was false—especially since the Creator’s angels, who dwelt in true yet unborn flesh, had prepared the way for this belief.

Indeed, that Philumene more successfully persuaded Apelles and the other deserters from Marcion that Christ had carried flesh about with him in very truth, though flesh of no birth, since he had borrowed it from the elements. But if Marcion was afraid that belief in the flesh would also induce belief in Christ’s birth, then without doubt one who appeared to be a man would certainly be believed to have been born. For a certain woman had even cried out (Luke 11:27), “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked.” And [Col. 0335C] how were his mother and brothers said to be standing outside (Luke 8)? We shall examine these passages at their proper time.

Certainly, since he also proclaimed himself the Son of Man, he was confessing that he had been born. For the present I defer all these matters to the examination of the Gospel. Nevertheless, given what I established above—that one who appeared to be a man would necessarily be believed to have been born—Marcion vainly thought that belief in his birth could be erased by the device of imaginary flesh. For what advantage was gained by its not being real, if it was taken as real—both the flesh and the birth?

Or if you say, “Let human opinion see to itself,” you now honor your god with the title of deceiver, if he knew himself to be something other than what he had caused human beings to suppose. At that point you might also have assigned him an apparent birth, [Note: [Col. 0335D] “Assigned him an apparent birth.” As though he had truly been born, although in actual fact he had not. For that is what the word *apparent* means here, just as he had recently spoken of “apparent corporeality in Christ.” LE PR.] lest you also have stumbled into [Col. 0336A] this question. For even poor women sometimes imagine themselves pregnant when they are swollen either by a discharge of blood [Note: [Col. 0335D] “By a discharge of blood.” Thus in *On the Veiling of Virgins*: “Modesty is clothed everywhere, and the menses pay their dues.” RIG.] or by some illness.

And certainly he ought to have run through the entire drama of the phantom, [Note: [Col. 0335D] “He ought to have run through the drama of the phantom.” Thus he says “the drama of the phantom,” just as in *On Heresies* he says “the drama of error,” meaning what they call an act. The sense is: Marcion’s Christ ought to have served the drama completely and performed the story he had undertaken; if he bore apparent flesh, he also ought to have had an apparent birth, for in that way he would have run through the drama of the phantom. RHEN.] so that, after playing the role of that substance itself, he would not have omitted from the performance the origin of the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0335D] *Desultasset*, Seml.; *dealtasset*, Rhen.] Plainly, you refused the lie of a birth, for you produced the flesh itself as real. A real birth, naturally, would be most disgraceful for God.

Come now, make your concluding speech [Note: [Col. 0336D] “Come now, make your concluding speech.” You have this passage reproduced in almost the same words in *On the Flesh of Christ*, not very far from the beginning. RHEN.] against those most holy and venerable works of nature. Rail against the totality of what you are. Destroy the origin of flesh and soul. Call the womb a sewer, though it is the workshop for bringing forth so great a living creature—that is, man. Persecute the unclean and shameful torments of childbirth, and thereafter the filthy, anxious, and ridiculous outcomes of infancy itself. [Note: [Col. 0336D] “Ridiculous outcomes.” I once thought that *slippery* (*lubricos*) should be read, but the author is referring to what he says in the book just cited when speaking of a newborn infant: “he is mocked with caresses”; and shortly afterward, “reared amid mockeries,” etc. RHEN.]

Yet once you have destroyed [Col. 0336B] all these things in order to affirm them unworthy [Note: [Col. 0336D] *Worthy*, Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] of God, birth will not be more unworthy than death, infancy than the cross, nature than punishment, or condemnation than flesh. If Christ truly suffered these things, it was less for him to be born. [Note: [Col. 0336D] *Would have been* (*fuisset*), Seml., Pam.] If he suffered them falsely, as a phantom, he could also have been born falsely.

These are Marcion’s principal arguments by which he creates another Christ. I believe we have sufficiently demonstrated that they do not stand at all, since we show that the reality, rather than the falsehood, of the condition in which he presented his Christ is certainly more fitting for God. If it was real, it was flesh; if it was flesh, it was born. For the things this heresy attacks are confirmed when the things by which it attacks them are destroyed.

Accordingly, if he is held to be fleshly because he was born, and born because he was fleshly—because he was not a phantom—he must be recognized as the very one whom the Creator’s prophets proclaimed would come in the flesh and by [Col. 0336C] birth: namely, the Creator’s Christ.

## CHAPTER XII

Appeal now, as you are accustomed to do, to this comparison with Isaiah’s Christ, contending that it agrees with him in no respect. First, you say, Isaiah’s Christ (Isa. 7:14) was to be called Emmanuel; next, he was to take the might of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians. But the one who came was neither revealed under such a name nor performed any military exploit.

I, however, will admonish you to examine the connection between the two passages as well. For the interpretation of Emmanuel—“God with us”—is also appended, so that you may consider not only the sound of the name but also [Col. 0337A] its meaning. For the Hebrew sound, which is “Emmanuel,” belongs to its own nation. Its meaning, however, which is “God with us,” is made common to all through translation.

Ask, therefore, whether the expression “God with us”—which is Emmanuel—has been applied to Christ from the time that Christ shone forth. And I think you will not deny it, since you yourself also say that he is called “God-with-us,” that is, Emmanuel.

Or if you are so foolish that, because among your people he is called “God-with-us” rather than “Emmanuel,” you therefore refuse to admit that the one whose proper name was to be Emmanuel has come—as though “Emmanuel” were not also “God with us”—you will find that Hebrew Christians, and indeed even Marcionites, say “Emmanuel” when they wish to say “God-with-us.” Likewise, whatever sound any nation uses to say “God-with-us,” it will pronounce “Emmanuel,” preserving the meaning while dispensing with the sound.

[Col. 0337B] But if Emmanuel is “God-with-us,” and Christ is God with us, who is also in us—“For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ [Note: [Col. 0337C] *Christ* in the dative, Par., Fran.] have put on Christ”—then Christ is as properly indicated by the meaning of the name, which is “God-with-us,” as by the sound of the name, which is “Emmanuel.” And thus it is established that the one proclaimed as Emmanuel has already come, because that which Emmanuel signifies has come: namely, God-with-us.

## CHAPTER XIII

You are likewise led astray by the sound of names when you understand “the might of Damascus,” “the spoils of Samaria,” and “the king of the Assyrians” as though they foretold that the Creator’s Christ would be a warrior, failing to notice what Scripture places first (Isa. 8:4): [Col. 0337C] [Note: [Col. 0337C] *Promises* (*promittat*), Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] “For before he knows [Note: [Col. 0337C] “The child” added by Pam., Rig., Fran., Venet.; it was not in the manuscripts.] how to call father and mother, [Col. 0337C] [Note: [Col. 0337C] “For before the child knows how to call father,” etc. Here too the word *child* has been supplied, since all editions of Isaiah 8 contain it. PAM.] he will take the might of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians.”

You must first examine the indication of his age and ask whether it could present Christ even as a man, much less as a commander. An infant, of course, was going to summon troops to arms with his wailing and give the signals of war not with a trumpet but with a rattle; he was going to direct the enemy not from horseback, from a chariot, or from a wall, but from the neck or back of his nurse or bearer, [Col. 0338A] and so subdue Damascus and Samaria in place of her breasts.

It may be otherwise among the people of Pontus, where the infants of a barbarian [Note: [Col. 0337C] *Barbarous country* (*barbariae*), Venet., Pam., Rig.] nation burst into battle, first anointed, I suppose, in the sun, [Note: [Col. 0337C] *Throne* (*solium*), Jun.] [Note: [Col. 0337D] “First anointed, I suppose, in the sun.” He alludes to ἡλίωσις (*hēliōsis*), or exposure to the sun, whereby they were warmed after being anointed, so that their limbs might be dried and strengthened. Persius, Satire 4:

“Or if you idle about anointed and fix the sun upon your skin.” RIG.]

then armed with swaddling clothes and paid their stipend in butter—infants who know how to wield a lance before they know how to handle a platter. [Note: [Col. 0337D] “Who know how to wield a lance before they know how to handle a platter.” Since in ch. 1 of Book I *Against Marcion* the verb *lancinatur* occurs in the sense “is pricked,” at first glance *lancinare* seems to have the same meaning here, just as *lanceare* means “to pierce with lances.” But we think *lancire* is better understood here, because “paid their stipend in butter” precedes it, in the sense of “putting their hands to platters” (*lances*). Let the reader choose whichever he wishes. Meanwhile, this conjecture is supported by what follows, “to soldier before living,” and the Author is fond of expressions of this kind. PAM.]

But if nature nowhere permits this—[Note: [Col. 0337D] “If nature nowhere permits this, it follows that the declaration should be regarded as figurative.” He gave precisely this warning in the same words in the book *Against the Jews*. Augustine speaks similarly in Book XI of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*: “If in the words of God, or of any person taken up into the prophetic office, something is said that cannot be understood literally without absurdity, it must without doubt be taken figuratively for the sake of some signification.” Similar statements occur in Book III of *On Christian Doctrine*, ch. 15. RIG.] to serve as a soldier before beginning to live, or to take the might of Damascus before knowing the names “father” and “mother”—it follows that the declaration should be regarded as figurative.

“But,” he says, “nature does not permit a virgin to give birth either, and yet the prophet is believed.” [Note: [Col. 0338C] *The prophecy*, Fran.] And rightly so. For he prepared belief in the incredible event by stating the reason: it would occur as a sign. “Therefore,” he says (Isa. 7:14), “the Lord will give you a sign: behold, a virgin will conceive in her womb [Col. 0338B] and bear a son.” But a sign from God, unless it were some extraordinary marvel, would not have been worthy of so much notice. [Note: [Col. 0338D] “But a sign from God, unless it were some extraordinary marvel, would not have been worthy of so much notice.” Perhaps the truer reading is “would not have been a sign.” For thus he writes in the book *Against the Jews*: “But a sign from God, unless it were some extraordinary marvel, would not appear to be a sign.” Procopius on Isaiah: τὸ γὰρ σημεῖον, τερατίου τινὸς, καὶ παρηλλαγμένου τῆς τῶν ἀνθρώπων συνηθείας ἐστὶν ἐπίδειξις: “For a sign is evidence of something marvelous and exceeding customary human experience.” RIG. and EDD.] [Note: [Col. 0338C] *Now a sign*, Lat.]

Finally, even the Jews, whenever they dare to lie in order to cast us down, alleging that Scripture says not that a virgin but that a young woman would conceive [Note: [Col. 0338D] “But that a young woman would conceive.” The Jews’ fable or quibble—that the text should read “young woman,” not “virgin”—has now been exploded. See Blessed Jerome, Book I *Against Jovinian*. LE PR.] and give birth, are refuted on this very ground: an everyday occurrence—namely, the pregnancy and delivery of a young woman—could not appear to be any sign.

Therefore a virgin and mother, appointed as a sign, is rightly believed; [Note: [Col. 0338C] *Would be believed*, Par.] but not, in the same manner, an infant warrior. For here no rationale of a sign is involved. Once the sign has been assigned to the new birth, however, a different sequence is then proclaimed after the sign concerning the child: he is to eat honey and butter. This is certainly not given as a sign that he will not consent to wickedness, for this too belongs to infancy; [Note: [Col. 0338C] *To infancy* (*infantiae*), Wouw.] rather, it concerns his taking the might of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against [Col. 0338C] the king of the Assyrians.

Preserve the measure of his age and seek the meaning of the proclamation. Better still, restore to the Gospel of truth what you later removed from it, and the prophecy is understood precisely as its fulfillment is reported.

For [Note: [Col. 0338C] *But* (*autem*), Seml.] let those eastern Magi remain, bestowing gold and incense upon Christ when he was a newborn infant, and the child has taken the might of Damascus without battle or arms. [Col. 0339A] For apart from the fact that everyone knows that the might of the East—that is, its power and resources—has customarily abounded in gold and perfumes, the Creator [Note: [Col. 0339C] *Of the Creator* (*Creatoris*), Fran.] certainly identifies the might of other nations too with gold, as through Zechariah (Zech. 14:14): “And Judah will stretch out [Note: [Col. 0339C] *Display* (*praetendet*), Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] at Jerusalem and gather all the wealth of the surrounding peoples, gold and silver.”

David also speaks of that gift of gold: “And there will be given to him from the gold of Arabia”; and again: “The kings of Arabia and Saba will bring [Note: [Col. 0339C] *Offer*, Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] gifts to him.” [Note: [Col. 0339D] “They will bring gifts to him.” The Vulgate reads better there, “they will lead forward,” for the Greek is προσάξουσιν (*prosaxousin*). LE PR.]

For the East generally had Magi as kings, [Note: [Col. 0339C] *Kings* absent from Par.] [Note: [Col. 0339D] “For the East generally had Magi as kings.” By “kings” he means the rulers of some city or region, such as the king in Phaedrus’ fable before whom a physician who had formerly been a cobbler was mocked; many such kings likewise occur in the sacred writings. Septimius says that kings of this kind in various cities throughout the East were generally Magi, that is, men skilled in knowledge of the stars and heavenly bodies. Moreover, Porphyry teaches in his book περὶ ἀποχῆς (*On Abstinence*) that *Magi* is a Persian term, signifying τοὺς περὶ τὸ θεῖον σοφοὺς, καὶ τούτου θεράποντας, μέγα καὶ σεβάσμιον γένος, “those who are wise about the divine and serve it, a great and venerable race.” RIG.] and Damascus was formerly reckoned part of Arabia, before it had been transferred [Note: [Col. 0339D] *Was* (*erat*), Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] to Syrophoenicia when the Syrian territories were divided. Christ then took its might by receiving its insignia, namely, gold and perfumes.

The spoils of Samaria, however, were [Col. 0339B] the Magi themselves. After they recognized him, honored him with gifts, and worshiped him on bended knee as God and king, under the testimony of the star that indicated and guided them, they became the spoils of Samaria—that is, of idolatry—by believing in Christ. For he designated idolatry by the name of Samaria, since Samaria had become infamous through the idolatry by which it had then revolted from God under King Jeroboam.

Nor is it anything new for the Creator to use names figuratively, transferring them on the basis of comparable crimes. For he calls the rulers of the Jews “rulers of Sodom,” and the people themselves “the people of Gomorrah.” The same God says elsewhere (Ezek. 16:3), “Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite,” because of their similar impiety, though he had once even called them his own children: “I have begotten children and exalted them.”

Thus too [Col. 0339C] “Egypt” is sometimes understood in his writings as the whole world, under an indictment of superstition and accursedness. Thus also “Babylon,” in our John, is a figure of the city of Rome, [Note: [Col. 0339D] “Thus also Babylon, in our John, is a figure of the city of Rome.” It is a common slander that Rome is called Babylon. For that distinguished man and others understand this of ancient Rome, which can never be sufficiently condemned for its incredible worship of idols. Since the religion of Christ was established, what St. Prosper says in his poem *On the Ungrateful* ought to be said of Rome:

“What she does not possess by arms,  
she holds by religion.” LE PR.]

inasmuch as Rome is similarly great, proud in its dominion, and a conqueror of God’s saints.

By this usage, therefore, he also represented the Magi as despoiled under the designation “Samaritans,” because they had possessed idolatry in common with the Samaritans, as we have said.

As for “against the king of the Assyrians,” understand it as “against Herod,” [Col. 0340A] whom the Magi certainly opposed at that time by not reporting back to him concerning Christ, whom he was seeking to destroy.

## CHAPTER XIV
This interpretation of ours will be assisted when, although elsewhere you suppose Christ to be a warrior because of the names of certain weapons and words of that sort, you are convicted also by comparison with the remaining senses. “Gird,” says David (Ps. 44:4), “the sword [Note: [Col. 0340C] *Sword*, Fran.] upon your thigh.” But what do you read immediately before this concerning Christ? “Comely in beauty beyond the sons of men; grace has been poured upon your lips.” I laugh if, while girding someone with a sword for war, he was flattering him about the comeliness of his beauty and the grace of his lips. Likewise, when he next says, [Note: [Col. 0340C] Seml. prefixes *And*.] “Advance, prosper, and reign,” he adds, “For the sake of truth, gentleness, and justice.” For who will accomplish these things [Note: [Col. 0340C] Seml. neglects *these things*; cod. Wouw. has *those things*.] with a sword, [Col. 0340B] rather than what is contrary to gentleness and justice [Note: [Col. 0340D] Rhen., Seml., and Oberth. omit *to gentleness and justice*.]—deceit, harshness, and injustice, the proper business of battles, of course?

Let us therefore see whether that sword is another sort of sword, since its action is of another sort. For the apostle John also [Note: [Col. 0340D] “For John the apostle also, in the Apocalypse.” This passage likewise argues against those who deny that the apostle John was the author of the Apocalypse. On this, however, see more fully book IV, chapter 5, where he also reports that Marcion was in this error. PAM.] describes in the Apocalypse (Rev. 1:16) a sword proceeding from the mouth of God, double-edged and very sharp; this must be understood as the divine word (Eph. 6:17), double-edged through the two Testaments, the Law and the Gospel; sharp through wisdom; hostile to the devil; arming us against the spiritual enemies of wickedness and every lust; and even cutting us away from those dearest to us for God’s name.

But if you are unwilling to acknowledge John, you have Paul, the teacher common to us both, [Note: [Col. 0340D] “You have Paul, the teacher common to us both.” Marcion did not admit the Apocalypse of Blessed John, and therefore he introduces Saint Paul, whom Marcion did not reject, as the common teacher not merely of them both but also of everyone. That commendation of the holy Apostle should be added to the statements in chapter 16 of *On Prescription*, where he says that our faith owes obedience to the Apostle. LE PR.] who girds our loins with truth and the breastplate of justice, and shoes us with the preparation of the Gospel of peace, not war; who commands us [Col. 0340C] to take up the shield of faith, with which we may extinguish all the devil’s fiery darts; and the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which, he says, is the word of God. The Lord himself also came to send this sword upon the earth, not peace (Matt. 10:34). If he is your Christ, then he too is a warrior. If he is not a warrior when he threatens an allegorical sword, then the Creator’s Christ in the Psalm was likewise permitted, without martial circumstances, to be figuratively girded with the sword of God’s word [Note: [Col. 0340D] Seml. omits *of God*.]; and with him [Col. 0341A] the aforesaid comeliness and grace of the lips agree. He was already being girded with it upon his thigh in David’s time, since he was one day to send it upon the earth.

For this is what he means when he says, “Advance, prosper, and reign.” You will advance the word into all the earth, for the calling of all nations; you will prosper through the success of the faith by which you will receive them; and thereafter you will reign, because you have conquered death by resurrection. “And your right hand,” he says, “will lead you on wonderfully”: namely, the power of spiritual grace, by which the recognition of Christ is advanced. “Your arrows are sharp”: commandments flying everywhere [Note: [Col. 0341D] Others read *certainly*.], together with threats and [Note: [Col. 0341D] Seml. neglects *and*.] exposures [Note: [Col. 0341D] Fran. reads *threatening exposure*, or perhaps *piercing*, Seml. [Col. 0342D]], which prick and pierce every conscience. “Peoples will fall beneath you”—fall in adoration, of course.

Thus the Creator’s Christ is mighty in war and armed; thus even now he receives spoils, not from Samaria alone, [Col. 0341B] but from all nations. Recognize the spoils also as figurative, since you have learned that his weapons too are allegorical. Since the Lord speaks figuratively in this way and the Apostle writes figuratively, we do not rashly employ interpretations whose examples even our adversaries admit. And thus the Christ who came will belong to Isaiah precisely insofar as he was not a warrior, because Isaiah did not proclaim him as such.

## CHAPTER XV

Thus far concerning the question of the flesh and, through it, of the birth, and for the moment concerning the single name Emmanuel. But what will the opposing party answer concerning the other names, and first of all concerning *Christ*? If among you the name *Christ* is common, just as the name *God* is, so that, just as the Christ may suitably be called the Son of either God, so either Father may be called Lord, then reason will certainly [Col. 0341C] oppose this argument. For the name *God*, being as it were natural to divinity, may be shared by all to whom divinity is claimed, even by idols, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 8:5): “For there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth.” But the name *Christ*, arising not from nature but from a dispensation, becomes the property of him by whom that dispensation is found to have been arranged. Nor is it subject to being shared with another god, especially a rival god who possesses his own dispensation, to which he will also owe distinctive names.

For what sort of thing is this—that those who have devised the different dispensations of two gods admit a partnership of names amid the discord of their dispensations? No stronger proof of two rival gods could be established than if a diversity of names were also found in their dispensations. [Col. 0341D] For no condition of differences is marked except by the distinctive qualities [Col. 0342A] of appellations. If these should ever fail, then [Note: [Col. 0342D] *Now*, Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] the Greek catachresis (*κατάχρησις*, misuse) comes to the rescue by making improper use of what belongs to another. But in God, I think, nothing ought to fail, nor ought his dispensations to be furnished from another’s property.

Who is this god who claims even the names of his Son from the Creator? I do not say merely foreign names, but ancient and commonplace ones, which for that very reason would not befit a new and unknown god. How, finally, does he teach that a new patch must not be sewn onto the Old Testament [Note: [Col. 0341D] “A new patch must not be sewn onto the Old Testament.” He has the same statement in *On Prayer*, chapter 1. Here he understands *plagula* as patches, for *plagula* is counted among articles of clothing by our Turnebus. He means that a patch must not be sewn onto the New Testament as though onto a garment; for deformity will thereby result, such as Themistius explains in Oration 1: “He says that it is never fitting to stitch things indiscriminately together, just as beggars’ outer garments are woven together from patches both new-made and worn out” (*συρράπτειν πρὸς ἕκαστα λέγει μηδὲ ἐοικὸς εἶναι τῶν προσαιτούντων αἱ ἐφεστρίδες συμπεπλεγμέναι ἐκ ῥακίων νεουργῶν ἅμα καὶ ἐκτετριμμένων*). LE PR.], nor new wine entrusted to old wineskins [Note: [Col. 0342D] “Nor new wine entrusted to old wineskins.” In the cited passage of *On Prayer* the same statement occurs in the same words. A passage of Cassian, conference 14, chapter 24, is nearly similar: “For no one pours any noble ointment, the finest honey, or anything made of precious liquid into a foul and corrupted vessel.” LE PR.], when he himself is sewn up in and clothed with the old age of names? How does he sever the Gospel from the Law when he is clothed in the whole Law—namely, in the name *Christ*? Who prevented him, since he preached something different and came from elsewhere, from being called something different? Especially since he did not even assume the reality of a body precisely to avoid being believed to be the Creator’s Christ? [Col. 0342B]

Yet vainly did he refuse to appear to be the one whose name he wished to bear. Even if he had been truly embodied, he would have seemed less like the Creator’s Christ if he had not been so called. But now he rejected the substance whose name [Note: [Col. 0342D] Paris. and Fran. add *also*.] he accepted, even though the name would prove the substance. For if *Christ* means *anointed*, anointing is certainly an experience of the body. He who had no body could not possibly be anointed; he who could not possibly be anointed could in no way be called Christ. It is another matter if he aspired to the semblance of a name as well.

“But how,” he says, “could he have crept into the faith of the Jews except through a name customary and familiar among them?” You describe an inconsistent or deceitful god, pursuing a design either of distrust or of malice, in order to advance something by deception. The false prophets acted much more openly and straightforwardly when they came against the Creator in the name of their own god. But neither do I find that this design achieved its effect, since they would more readily have believed him either to be their own Christ or, rather, some impostor, than the Christ of another god, as the Gospel will prove.

## CHAPTER XVI

Now if he snatched the name *Christ* like a petty thief snatching a little basket, why did he also wish to be called Jesus, a name not so expectantly awaited among the Jews? For although we, having by God’s grace attained an understanding of his mysteries, also recognize that this name was appointed for Christ, it does not follow that the matter would have been known to the Jews, from whom wisdom had been taken away. Indeed, to the present day they await a Christ, not a Jesus; and they interpret Elijah, rather than Jesus, as the Christ. Therefore, he who came even under that name in which the Christ was not presumed could have come [Col. 0342D] under the one name that alone was presumed. [Col. 0343A]

But since he combined two names, the expected and the unexpected, both parts of his design are defeated. For if he was called *Christ* so that in the meantime he might creep in as though he were the Creator’s, *Jesus* gets in the way [Note: [Col. 0343C] *Creeps in*, Rhen., Seml., Oberth.], because Jesus was not expected in the Creator’s Christ. Or if he was called *Jesus* so that he might be regarded as belonging to another, *Christ* does not permit it, because no Christ was expected except the Creator’s. I do not know which of these can stand. Both, however, will stand in the Creator’s Christ, in whom Jesus also is found.

“How?” you ask. Here too, learn together with the Jews who share your error. When Hoshea the son of Nun was appointed as Moses’ successor, he was certainly transferred from his former name and [Note: [Col. 0343D] “He begins to be called Jesus.” He alludes to Matthew and Luke 1: “And you shall call his name Jesus,” with the interpretation of the name also added: “For he shall save his people from their sins.” This is what he says in the book *Against Praxeas*: “Jesus is his proper name, which was imposed by the angel.” PAM.] began to be called Jesus. “Certainly,” you say. We maintain first that this was a figure of what was to come. For Jesus Christ was to introduce the second people—that is, us, born in [Col. 0343B] the deserts of this age—into the land of promise flowing with milk and honey, that is, into the possession of eternal life, than which nothing is sweeter. And this was to come about not through Moses, that is, not through the discipline of the Law, but through Jesus, that is [Note: [Col. 0343C] Seml. omits *that is*.], through the grace of the Gospel, after we had been circumcised by a stone blade, that is, by Christ’s commandments [Note: [Col. 0343C] Rhen., Seml., and Oberth. omit *commandments*.]; for the Rock was Christ. Therefore that man, who was being prepared as an image of this mystery, was also inaugurated as a figure of the Lord’s name and surnamed Jesus.

Christ himself testified even then that this name was his own when he spoke to Moses. For who was speaking except the Creator’s Spirit, who is Christ? Thus, when he said by command to the people (Exod. 23:20), “Behold, I send my angel before your face, to guard you on the way and bring you into the land that I have prepared [Col. 0343C] for you. Attend to him and obey him; do not disobey him, for he will not overlook [Note: [Col. 0343C] *Will not spare*, Seml., Jun.] you, because my name is upon him,” he called him an angel because of the greatness of the mighty works he was to perform and because of the office of a prophet, namely one who announces the divine will; but he called him Jesus because of the mystery of his own future name. Again and again he confirmed his own name, which he himself had bestowed upon him, because he had commanded that from then onward he be called neither Angel nor Hoshea, but Jesus.

Therefore, if both names belong to the Creator’s Christ, so much the less does either belong to a Christ who is not the Creator’s, just as the remainder [Note: [Col. 0343D] Rhen., Seml., and Oberth. omit *not*.] of the order does not. [Col. 0344A] From this point onward, then, we must establish between us this firm and equitable preliminary rule, necessary to either side: it is settled that absolutely nothing should be common to the Christ of another god and the Creator’s Christ. For diversity must accordingly be defended by you, just as it must be opposed by us. You will not be able to prove that the Christ of another God came unless you demonstrate that he was far different from the Creator’s Christ; nor will we be able to claim him for the Creator unless we show him to be such as he is established by the Creator. We have now closed the issue concerning the names. I claim Christ for myself; I defend Jesus as mine.

## CHAPTER XVII

[Col. 0344B] Let us compare the remainder of his course with the Scriptures. Whatever that little body may have been, since it was borne and since it was seen—if it was inglorious, if undistinguished, if dishonorable [Note: [Col. 0343D] “If inglorious, if undistinguished, if dishonorable, he will be my Christ.” With a good and pious intention he consecrated the formula by which Cypris tracks down her Cupid:

> “If anyone has seen Love wandering at the crossroads,  
> he is my runaway slave.”

(*Εἴ τις ἐνὶ τριόδοισι πλανώμενον εἶδεν ἔρωτα,  
Δραπετίδας ἐμός ἐστιν.*)

RIG.—Let the Jewish Apollo believe it. EDD.]—he will be my Christ; for such was the appearance and aspect in which he was announced.

Isaiah is present again (Isa. 53:1–2): “We proclaimed,” he says, “before him; as a little child, as a root in thirsty ground. There is no form in him, nor glory; and we saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty, but his appearance was dishonored, deficient in comparison with all men.” So too, above, the Father’s voice to the Son says (Isa. 52:14), “Just as many will be appalled at you, [Note: [Col. 0343D] “Just as many will be appalled,” etc. I finally found this passage in Isaiah 52 according to the Septuagint—or, rather, according to the ancient Fathers—in chapter 53, which they begin at that place: “Behold, he shall understand,” etc. In interpreting that passage of the insults inflicted upon Christ in his passion, he imitates Blessed Justin Martyr, *Apology* 2. The Greek is *ἐκστήσονται*, which others render more properly as “they will be astonished” than the Author’s “they will be appalled”; and *ἀδοξήσει* is a single word corresponding to what is rendered here as “will be without glory.” PAM.] so will your form be without glory among men.”

For although in David (Ps. 44:3) he is “comely in beauty [Note: [Col. 0344D] “Comely in beauty.” Thus Septimius chose to express the Greek *ὡραῖος τῷ κάλλει*, which in the Vulgate version is “beautiful in form.” That an allegorical beauty must be understood is indicated by what is read in the same psalm: “Gird your sword upon your thigh.” For this sword is allegorical and refers to the word of Christ; the beauty is allegorical, and the weapons are allegorical. Jerome seems to have been rather undecided in mind when he touched upon these prophetic words in Epistle 140 to the virgin Principia. PAM.] beyond the sons of men,” this is in that allegorical [Col. 0344C] condition of spiritual grace, when he is girded with the sword [Note: [Col. 0344C] *Sword*, Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] of the word, which truly is his form, beauty, and glory. But in his condition capable of embodiment [Note: [Col. 0344D] “In a condition capable of embodiment.” The form in which Christ was to be embodied or incarnated. RIG.—Rather, as it seems to us, it means “in a formless condition.” EDD.]—[Note: [Col. 0344C] Jun. reads *in bodily form*; others, *in incorporeal form*.]—in the same prophet (Ps. 21:7), he is even “a worm and not a man, a disgrace of man [Note: [Col. 0344C] *Of man* is absent from Par.] and the nullity of the people.”

Nor do they announce his inner quality as being of that same kind. [Note: [Col. 0344C] Seml. reads *of the kind you announce*; Par. and cod. Wouw., *of this kind they announce* [Col. 0344D]; Rig., *he announces*.] For if the fullness of the Spirit rested upon him, I recognize the rod from the root of Jesse and its flower. He will be my Christ, upon whom, according to Isaiah (Isa. 11:2 [printed XC]), rested [Col. 0345A] “the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, the spirit of the fear of God.” For the diversity of spiritual teachings belonged to no human being except Christ: he was likened to a flower because of the grace of the Spirit, but reckoned from the stock of Jesse because he was to be traced from there through Mary. [Note: [Col. 0345C] *To be traced*, feminine, Rhen., Seml., Jun.]

I press you, however, concerning his purpose. If you grant him an intention of complete humility, patience, and tranquility, then by these qualities too he will be Isaiah’s Christ (Isa. 53:7): “A man under affliction, who knows how to bear weakness; who was led like a sheep to sacrifice and, like a lamb before its shearer, did not open his mouth”; who (Isa. 42:2) “neither contended nor cried out, nor was his voice heard outside”; who did not break the bruised reed—that is, the shattered faith of the Jews—and did not extinguish the burning flax—that is, [Col. 0345B] the momentary fervor of the nations—but instead made it into a lamp by the rising of his own light. He cannot [Note: [Col. 0345C] Rhen., Seml., Oberth., and Jun. have nothing between *extinguished* and *He cannot*.] be anyone other than the one who was foretold.

His activity must be reviewed according to the rule of the Scriptures, being divided, unless I am mistaken, into a twofold operation: preaching and power. But I shall arrange the treatment of both headings in such a way that, since it has been decided to examine Marcion’s own Gospel as well, we may defer the particular forms of his teachings and signs to that place, as though to the actual matter at hand. Here, however, let us complete in general terms the course we have begun, showing for the moment that Christ was announced as a preacher through Isaiah (Isa. 50:10): “For who among you,” he says, “fears God [Note: [Col. 0345C] Others read *the Lord*.] [Note: [Col. 0345D] “For who among you,” he says, “fears God?” Blessed Cyril likewise cites and interprets this passage of Isaiah 50 in his *Commentary on Isaiah*. From him the earlier part of this text is also supplied, since it was not found in the copy used by Blessed Jerome; nevertheless, it is established as genuine, since it is cited not only here but also in book IV, chapter 22, *Against Marcion*. PAM.] and will hear [Note: [Col. 0345C] *May hear*, Fran., Venet., Rig.] the voice of his Son?” He is likewise announced as a healer (Isa. 53): “For he,” it says, “has taken away our weaknesses and borne our infirmities.”

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 0345C]

Regarding his end, I think you plainly attempt to introduce a difference by denying that the passion of the cross was proclaimed for the Creator’s Christ, and by arguing further that it is not credible that the Creator exposed his Son to the kind of death upon which he himself had pronounced a curse: “Cursed,” he says (Deut. 21), “is everyone who hangs upon a tree.” But I defer the meaning of this curse to the treatment devoted exclusively to the proclamation of the cross, which is now [Note: [Col. 0345C] Lat. inserts *when*.] chiefly under inquiry, [Col. 0346A] because elsewhere too the proof supplied by events precedes the rationale.

I shall first instruct you from the figures. Assuredly this mystery above all had to be figured in the proclamation: the more incredible it was, the more it would become a stumbling block if proclaimed openly; and the more magnificent it was, the more it had to be veiled, so that the difficulty of understanding might seek the grace of God.

Thus, first of all, when Isaac was surrendered by his father as an offering and carried the wood for himself, he was already then marking out the end of Christ, who was surrendered by the Father as a victim and carried the wood of his own passion. Joseph too was fashioned as a figure of [Note: [Col. 0345C] Rhen., Seml., and Oberth. omit *of*.] Christ, not only—lest I delay our progress—because he suffered persecution from his brothers and was sold into Egypt [Note: [Col. 0345D] Seml. omits *and was sold into Egypt*.] on account of God’s grace, just as Christ was sold by the Jews, his brothers according to the flesh, by Judas [Note: [Col. 0346C] Rhen., Seml., and Oberth. omit *was sold, by Judas*.] when he was betrayed. For [Col. 0346B] he is also [Note: [Col. 0346C] Seml. omits *when he was betrayed. For he is also*.] blessed [Note: [Col. 0346C] Seml. openly inserts *by his father*; others omit it.] in these words (Deut. 33:17): “His beauty is that of a bull [Note: [Col. 0345D] “His beauty is that of a bull; his horns are the horns of a unicorn.” This very statement concerning Joseph, uttered by Moses in Deuteronomy 33, is interpreted of Christ not only by Justin Martyr, from whom the Author has taken these words almost verbatim, but also by Blessed Augustine, *Questions on Deuteronomy*, chapter 56, and by Rabanus in his commentary. PAM.]; his horns are the horns of a unicorn; with them he will winnow the nations together, as far as the ends of the earth.”

Certainly no one-horned rhinoceros was being appointed, nor a two-horned Minotaur. Rather, Christ was signified in him: a bull on account of both dispensations—fierce toward some as judge, gentle toward others as savior. His horns would be the extremities [Note: [Col. 0346C] *External parts*, Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] of the cross. For on the yard of a ship [Note: [Col. 0346C] Rhen., Seml., and Oberth. read *yard* and omit *of a ship*.], which forms part of a cross, the extremities are called horns. [Note: [Col. 0345D] “The extremities are called horns.” Thus in Virgil:

> “We turn the horns of the sail-clad yards.”

[Col. 0346D] LE PR.] The unicorn’s single horn, however, is the upright stake in the middle. [Note: [Col. 0346C] Cod. Wouwer. reads *the upright stake in the middle*, masculine.]

By this power of the cross [Note: [Col. 0346D] “By this power of the cross.” The histories of every age testify that the power of the Cross has always been very great. For the emperor Julian, although an apostate and an enemy of Christians, habitually fortified himself with the sign of the cross against apparitions and terrors of the night. Gregory Nazianzen reports this in Oration 1 *Against Julian*, and Corippus in book II, *On the Emperor Justin*:

> “He goes forth with his law, and armed his serene brow,  
> making the signs of the holy wood.”

Aldhelm, *On Virginity*, chapter 17, teaches that ancient Christians were commonly called both *Christ-worshipers* and *cross-worshipers* because of their supreme veneration of the cross. LE PR.], and horned in this fashion, he even now winnows all nations through faith, lifting them from earth into heaven; and then, through judgment, he will winnow them by casting them down from heaven to earth.

He will likewise be the bull elsewhere in the same Scripture, when Jacob, extending [Col. 0346C] a blessing [Note: [Col. 0346C] Rhen., Seml., and Oberth. omit *extending a blessing*.] to Simeon and Levi—that is [Note: [Col. 0346D] Fran. omits *that is*.], to the scribes and Pharisees, for their lineage is derived from them—interprets spiritually: “Simeon and Levi” (Gen. 49:6) “accomplished iniquity by their own sect,” namely, by which they persecuted Christ. “Let my soul not come into their council, and let my inward parts not recline in their assembly; because in their indignation they killed men”—that is, the prophets—“and in their desire they cut the sinews [Col. 0347A] of the bull”—that is, of Christ, whom they killed [Note: [Col. 0347D] Rhen., Seml., and Oberth. omit *killed*.] after the murder of the prophets, and raged savagely by fastening his sinews [Note: [Col. 0347D] Wouw. apparently prefers *into the sinews*.] with nails. Otherwise, it would be pointless if, after their homicides, he were reproaching them for the butchering of some ox.

And now consider Moses. Why, precisely at that time when Jesus was fighting against Amalek, did he pray seated with his hands outstretched [Note: [Col. 0347D] *Prays*, Rhen., Seml., Oberth.]—when amid such critical circumstances he should rather have commended his prayer with knees lowered [Note: [Col. 0347D] *Placed*, Fran.; others, *arranged*.], hands beating his breast, and face rolling upon the ground—unless because there, where [Note: [Col. 0347D] Rhen., Seml., and Oberth. add *is*.] the name of the Lord Jesus [Note: [Col. 0347D] Seml. omits *Jesus*.] was fighting, the posture of the cross was also necessary as a figure of the one who would one day fight against the devil, and through which Jesus was to carry off victory?

Again, after every representation of any created thing had been forbidden, why did the same Moses (Num. 21) set forth a bronze serpent placed upon wood, in the posture of one hanging, [Col. 0347B] as a saving spectacle for Israel [Note: [Col. 0347D] Rhen., Seml., and Oberth. omit *for Israel*.] at the time when they were being destroyed by serpents, unless because [Note: [Col. 0347D] Rhen. and Seml. omit “set forth? Or does everything else here” (reading uncertain).] here too he was presenting the power of the Lord’s cross? Through it the serpent, the devil, was publicly exposed, and for everyone wounded by spiritual snakes who nevertheless looked upon it and believed, healing from the bites of sins and consequent salvation [Note: [Col. 0347D] Seml. reads *healing*.] were proclaimed.

## CHAPTER XIX

Come now: if you have read in David (Ps. 95:10), “The Lord has reigned from the tree,” I await what you understand by it—unless perhaps you suppose that some Jewish king who dealt in timber is signified, and not Christ, who from the time of his passion upon the tree reigned after overcoming death. For even if death reigned from Adam until Christ, why should Christ not be said to have reigned from the tree, since by dying upon the tree of the cross he abolished [Col. 0347C] the reign of death?

Isaiah likewise says (Isa. 9:6), “For a child,” he says, “has been born to us, and a Son has been given to us.” [Note: [Col. 0347D] Seml. and Jun. omit *and a Son has been given to us*.] What would be new in this, if he were not speaking of the Son of God? [Note: [Col. 0348D] Seml. adds *and has been given to us*.] “His government was placed upon his shoulder.” What king at all bears the emblem of his power upon his shoulder, instead of a diadem upon his head, a scepter in his hand, [Col. 0348A] or some badge upon his own garment? Only the new king of the new ages, Christ Jesus, raised upon his shoulder both the power and the sublimity of his new glory—namely, the cross—so that, according to the preceding prophecy, the Lord might thereafter reign from the tree.

Jeremiah too (Jer. 11:19) intimates this tree to you, foretelling that the Jews would say, “Come, let us cast [Note: [Col. 0348D] *Let us lay upon*, Seml.; others, *let us cast*.] wood into his bread”—that is, into his body. For thus God revealed the matter even in your Gospel, calling bread his body. [Note: [Col. 0347D] “Calling bread his body.” That the reality of the Lord’s body in the Eucharist is confirmed by these words—in accordance with the words of the Evangelists and Blessed Paul, to which the Author alludes—has been noted not only by us . . . but even by the Magdeburg Centuriators themselves. At this passage they affirm that the body of Christ is truly and substantially distributed in the Eucharist; they err only when they cite this passage to prove that the bread remains together with the Lord’s body. We have refuted this . . . from the very fact that he says, “calling, or making, bread his body,” whereas otherwise he should have said “in the bread” or “under the bread.” Nor is this opposed by what is added here: “so that from this too you may now understand that he gave to bread the figure of his body” (for thus, from Vatican MS 2, we read *to bread* rather than *bread*, which pleases us more than Latinius’ conjecture, “gave to his body a figure by means of bread”), because . . . in a certain manner both the reality of Christ’s body and a figure are present in this sacrament. . . . Add to this that one may reasonably doubt whether the words “so that from this too you may now,” etc., are genuinely the Author’s, at least in their entirety, because above, in the book *Against the Jews*, they are read neither in the printed editions nor in the manuscript codices. PAM.]

Thus from this too you may now understand that he gave to bread [Note: [Col. 0348D] *Of bread*, Seml.] the figure of his body, whose body the prophet had formerly figured in bread, with the Lord himself afterward to interpret this mystery.

If you still seek the proclamation of the Lord’s cross, the twenty-first Psalm [Note: [Col. 0348D] “The twenty-first Psalm, containing the whole passion of Christ.” Blessed Justin similarly says against Trypho: “You say that this was not composed concerning Christ, being utterly blind and failing to understand that no one among your nation who was ever called King or Christ had his hands and feet pierced while alive, or died by this mystery—that is, was suspended upon a cross—except this Jesus alone.” On that occasion, accordingly, he interprets the entire twenty-first Psalm beautifully and at great length. PAM.], which contains the whole passion of Christ, can now sufficiently satisfy you. There he already sings of his own glory: “They pierced,” he says (Ps. 21:17), “my hands and my feet”—an atrocity belonging specifically [Note: [Col. 0348D] Seml. reads *particular atrocities*; Par., *specifically atrocities*.] to the cross. Again, when he implores the Father’s aid, he says, “Save me” (ibid. 22) “from the lion’s mouth”—that is, from death—“and my humiliation from the horns of the unicorns” [Note: [Col. 0348D] Fran. reads *unicorns*; *unicorns* is also read in the book *Against the Jews*.], namely, from the points of the cross, as we showed above.

Neither David himself nor any king of the Jews suffered this cross. You must not suppose that the passion of anyone other than him [Note: [Col. 0348D] Seml. omits *that the passion of anyone other than him was prophesied*.] was prophesied—the one who alone was crucified so conspicuously by the people.

Now even if heretical obstinacy rejects and mocks all these interpretations, I shall concede to it that no cross of Christ was signified [Note: [Col. 0348D] Rhen. reads *that I signify*; Seml. omits *spoils* and the remaining intervening material as though taken from the book *Against the Jews*.] by the Creator. Yet it will not thereby prove that the one crucified was another, unless perhaps it shows that this end of its Christ was proclaimed by its own god, so that a diversity of passions—and therefore of persons as well—may be maintained from a diversity of proclamations. Otherwise, even without its own Christ having been proclaimed, much less his cross, the prophecy of death alone is sufficient for my Christ. For because the manner of death was not disclosed, it could have occurred even through the cross. Only then would it have to be assigned to another, [Col. 0349A] if it had been proclaimed concerning another—unless, indeed, he is unwilling to admit that even the death of my Christ was prophesied. In that case he should be all the more ashamed if he announces that his own Christ died, though he denies that he was born, while denying that my Christ was mortal, though he confesses him capable of birth.

Moreover, I wish to demonstrate the death, burial, and resurrection of my Christ by a single saying of Isaiah (Isa. 57:2 [printed LVIII, 2]): “His burial was taken away from the midst.” For he would not have been buried unless he had died, nor would his burial have been taken away from the midst except through resurrection. Finally, he added (Isa. 53:12): “Therefore he himself will possess many as an inheritance and will divide the spoils of many.” Who else could this be but the one who was born, as we showed above? “Because his soul was delivered over to death.” For the cause of this favor is shown: namely, as compensation for the wrong of his death. At the same time it is shown that he would obtain these things on account of his death [Note: [Col. 0349D] Jun. rejects *would obtain these things on account of his death*.]—obtain them after death, certainly, through resurrection. [Note: [Col. 0349D] *Will obtain*, Seml.]

## CHAPTER XX
For the present it is enough to have followed thus far the sequence of these matters concerning Christ, so that, once he has been shown to be such as he was proclaimed, [Col. 0349B] he ought not to be regarded as anyone other than the one proclaimed in those terms. From this agreement between the events concerning him and the Creator’s Scriptures, credibility must now be restored—even by the prejudgment of the greater part—to those passages that, because they admit of differing interpretations, are either called into doubt or denied. We now build further upon this foundation by adducing corresponding passages from the Creator’s Scriptures concerning what had been foretold as destined to occur after Christ. For the dispensation would not be found fulfilled unless the one had come after whom it was to occur.

Behold all the nations emerging thereafter from the abyss of human error toward God the Creator and [Note: [Col. 0349D] “And” omitted by Semler.] toward God’s Christ; and, if you dare, deny that this was prophesied. But immediately the Father’s promise will confront you in the Psalms (Ps. 2:7) [Note: [Col. 0349D] “Confronts,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.]:

> You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of [Note: [Col. 0349D] Thus Franeker.] me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance, [Col. 0349C] and the ends of the earth as your possession.

You will no more be able to claim him as David’s son rather than Christ [Note: [Col. 0349D] “His,” Semler.], or that the ends of the earth were promised to David—who ruled within the single nation of the Jews—rather than to Christ, who has already taken the entire world by faith in his Gospel.

So too through Isaiah (Isa. 42:6–7):

> Behold, I have appointed you for the dispensation of my people [Note: [Col. 0349D] “My” rejected by Semler and Junius from the Septuagint.], as a light of the nations, to open the eyes of the blind—

that is, of those in error—

> to release those bound in chains—

that is, to free them from sins—

> and from the prison cell—

that is, from death—

> those sitting in darkness—

namely, the darkness of ignorance. If these things occur through Christ, they will not have been prophesied of anyone other than the one through whom they occur.

Again elsewhere (Isa. 55:4):

> Behold, I have appointed you as a witness among the nations, a leader and commander of the nations. Nations [Col. 0350A] that do not know you will call upon you, and peoples will take refuge with you.

You cannot interpret these words of David, because he prefaced them with:

> And I shall establish for you an everlasting covenant, the holy and faithful assurances of David.

Indeed, from this you ought all the more to understand Christ, reckoned as descended from David according to the flesh because of the registration of the Virgin Mary. For concerning this promise an oath is sworn to David in the Psalm (Ps. 132:11):

> From the fruit of your womb I shall set one upon your throne.

Whose womb is this? David’s own? Certainly not, for David was not going to give birth. Nor is it his wife’s, for Scripture would not have said, “From the fruit of your womb,” but rather, “From the fruit of your wife’s womb.” By speaking, therefore, of his own [Note: [Col. 0350D] “However,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.] womb, it remains that Scripture indicated someone from his line, the fruit of whose womb would be the flesh of Christ, which blossomed from Mary’s uterus. For this reason it named only “the fruit of the womb,” as belonging properly to the womb alone and not also to a man; and it traced that womb back to David as the founder of the line and father of the family. For because it could not ascribe the virgin’s womb to a husband [Note: [Col. 0350D] “That womb” was absent in Rhenanus.], it ascribed it to David, the father of her line.

Thus the new dispensation found today in Christ will be the one the Creator was then promising: [Col. 0350B] “the holy and faithful assurances of David,” now holy by its sacred character and faithful by virtue of the resurrection. For the prophet Nathan also, in the Second [Note: [Col. 0350D] “First,” Semler; “in the first,” Paris.] Book of Kingdoms, makes a declaration to David:

> To his seed, which shall come, he says, from his own womb (2 Sam. 7:12).  
> [Note: [Col. 0350D] “Your seed … your,” Franeker.]

If you were simply to expound this of Solomon, you would make me laugh. For it would appear that David gave birth to Solomon. Or is Christ indicated here too as David’s seed from that womb—namely Mary’s—which would be of David’s line? Indeed [Note: [Col. 0350D] “Because,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.], it was rather Christ who would build God’s temple, namely the holy human being in whom the Spirit of God would dwell as in a more excellent temple; and Christ was far more to be regarded as the Son of God than Solomon as the son of David. Finally, a throne forever and a kingdom forever are more applicable to Christ than to Solomon, who was plainly a temporal king. Moreover, [Note: [Col. 0350D] “And” omitted by Semler.] God’s mercy did not depart from [Col. 0350C] Christ; but God’s anger did come upon Solomon after his debauchery and idolatry. For Satan raised up against him [Note: [Col. 0350D] Franeker adds “that is.”] an Edomite enemy.

Since, therefore, none of these things applies to Solomon but all apply to Christ, the principle governing our interpretations will be certain, since the very outcome of events confirms that they were manifestly foretold of Christ; and thus in him will be found “the holy and faithful assurances of David.” God appointed him, not David, as a witness to the nations; him, not David, as leader and commander of the nations, for David commanded Israel alone. Today the nations that did not know Christ call upon him, and today peoples who formerly did not know him take refuge with Christ. What you see taking place cannot be called future.

## CHAPTER XXI

[Col. 0351A]

Nor can you maintain that objection of yours in order to distinguish two Christs—as though the Jewish Christ were destined by the Creator solely to gather back his people from dispersion, whereas your Christ had been bestowed by the supremely good God to liberate the entire human race—since, after all, the Creator’s Christians are found to be earlier than Marcion’s. From the time when all peoples were called into his kingdom, from the time when “God reigned from the tree,” there was as yet no Cerdo, much less Marcion.

But when you have been refuted regarding the calling of the nations, you next transform them into proselytes. You ask who from among the nations pass over to the Creator, although proselytes are named separately by the Prophet as people of a different and distinctive status:

> Behold, says Isaiah (Isa. 16:4), proselytes will come through me to you—

showing that the proselytes themselves [Col. 0351B] would also come to God through Christ. And [Note: [Col. 0351D] “So that,” Codex Wouwer.] the nations—that is, we ourselves—likewise had [Note: [Col. 0351D] “May have,” Semler.] their own designation, as those hoping in Christ:

> And in his name, he says (Isa. 42:4), the nations will hope.

But the proselytes whom you substitute in the proclamation concerning the nations are not accustomed to hope in Christ’s name, but in the ordinance of Moses, from whom their institution derives.

Besides, the summoning of the nations arose in the last days. Isaiah says in these very words (Isa. 2:2):

> And it shall be, he says, in the last days, that the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest—

that is, the loftiness of God—

> and the house of God above the highest mountains—

that is, Christ, God’s universal temple, in whom God is worshiped, established above all [Note: [Col. 0351D] Semler adds “for.”] eminences of virtues and powers—

> and all nations shall come to him; and many shall go and say: Come, let us ascend [Col. 0351C] the mountain of the Lord and the house of the God of Jacob; and he will proclaim his way to us, and we shall walk in it. For from Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.

This will be his way: the Gospel of a new law and a new word, now in Christ, not in Moses.

> And he shall judge among the nations—

that is, concerning their error—

> and shall convict a great people—

first and foremost the Jews themselves and the proselytes—

> and they shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their *sibynae* into sickles.  
> [Note: [Col. 0351D] “Their *sibynae* into sickles.” In Isaiah, according to the Septuagint version, the Greek reads καὶ τὰς ζιβύνας αὐτῶν εἰς δρέπανα, “and their *zibynae* into sickles.” According to [Col. 0352D] Tertullian, a ζιβύνη is a kind of hunting-spear. Suidas writes that it means ὁλοσίδηρον ἀκόντιον, that is, an entirely iron missile, and sometimes λόγχην or σπάθην, that is, a lance or sword. RHENANUS.]

That is, they will turn the contrivances of harmful minds, hostile tongues, and every kind of malice and blasphemy into pursuits of moderation and peace.

> And nation shall not take up sword against nation—

that is, the sword of discord—

> and they shall no longer learn to wage war—

that is, to carry hostilities through to completion. Thus here too you may learn that the Christ promised was powerful not in war but as a bringer of peace.

Either deny that these things were [Note: [Col. 0351D] “But,” another reading.] [Col. 0351D] prophesied, though they are seen before your eyes, or deny that they have been fulfilled, though they are read in Scripture. Or, if you deny neither, they will have been fulfilled in the one of whom they were prophesied. Consider further the very entry and onward course [Col. 0352A] of the calling among the nations, which in the last days are coming to God the Creator, not becoming proselytes, whose summoning belongs rather to the earliest days. [Note: [Col. 0351D] “Is” omitted by Semler; others read “the summoning is.”] For the apostles introduced this faith.

## CHAPTER XXII

You also have the work of the apostles foretold:

> How timely are the feet of those who proclaim good things!

—not war or evil. [Note: [Col. 0351D] “Evil,” singular, Semler.] The Psalm also responds (Ps. 19:4):

> Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their voices to the ends of the earth—

the voices, namely, of those carrying about the law that had gone forth from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, so that what was written might be fulfilled (Isa. 46:12–13):

> Those far from my righteousness have drawn near to my righteousness and truth.

When the apostles girded themselves for this undertaking, they renounced the elders, rulers, and priests [Col. 0352B] of the Jews. “Was it not especially,” you say [Note: [Col. 0352D] “You ask,” Junius.], “because they were preachers of another God?” On the contrary, [Note: [Col. 0352D] Franeker adds “he says.”] they were preachers of that very same God whose Scripture they were at that very moment fulfilling.

> Depart, depart, cries Isaiah (Isa. 52:11), go out from there and touch no unclean thing—

namely, blasphemy against Christ.

> Go out from the midst of it—

that is, of the synagogue—

> separate yourselves [Note: [Col. 0352D] “Be separated,” Franeker.], you who bear the Lord’s [Note: [Col. 0352D] “Of the Lord,” Semler.] vessels.

For by then, in accordance with what was written above (Isa. 52:10),

> the Lord had revealed his Holy One by his arm—

that is, Christ by his power—

> before the nations, so that all the nations and the ends of the earth might see the salvation that was from God.

Thus too, in departing from Judaism itself, when through the freedom of the Gospel they were exchanging the bonds and burdens of the Law, they were carrying out the Psalm (Ps. 2:3):

> Let us break their bonds apart and cast their yoke from us—

[Col. 0352C] certainly after

> the nations had raged and the peoples devised vain things; the kings of the earth took their stand, and the rulers assembled together against the Lord and against his Christ.

What did the apostles subsequently suffer? “Every injustice of persecution,” you say, “at the hands, of course, of the Creator’s people, because they were enemies of the one whom the apostles preached.” Did [Note: [Col. 0352D] “And those who,” Paris, Franeker; “and what,” Rhenanus.] the Creator—if he was Christ’s enemy—not only foretell that Christ’s apostles would suffer this, but even reproach people for it? For he would neither have foretold the dispensation of another God, whom, as you will have it, he did not know, nor would he have reproached conduct for which he himself had made provision.

> See how (Isa. 57:1) the righteous man perishes, and no one takes it to heart; righteous men are taken away, and no one notices. For the righteous man has been removed from the presence of injustice [Note: [Col. 0352D] “Justice,” another reading.].

Who is this, if not Christ?

> Come, they say (Wis. 2:12), [Col. 0352D] let us remove the righteous man, because he is useless to us.

Accordingly, by both placing before us and then adding the suffering of Christ himself, he likewise prophesied that Christ’s righteous ones would suffer the same things—both the apostles and thereafter all the faithful—marked [Col. 0353A] with that sign of which Ezekiel speaks (Ezek. 9:4):

> The Lord says to me: Pass through [Note: [Col. 0353D] Semler adds “in.”] the midst of the gate, into the midst [Note: [Col. 0353D] “The middle gate,” Franeker.] of Jerusalem, and place the sign [Note: [Col. 0353D] “Signs,” Semler.] Tau upon the foreheads of the men.

For the Greek letter Tau [Note: [Col. 0353D] “For the Greek letter Tau itself, and our own, etc.” Our fathers appear to have imitated this very practice when, at the beginning of the Canon in ancient missals, in the letter T where the words read, “Therefore, most merciful Father,” they commonly displayed a painted cross of Christ; in its place today the image of the cross itself has been introduced on the immediately preceding page. And indeed Blessed Jerome, imitating Tertullian almost word for word in his Commentary, says: “The final letter Tau has the likeness of the cross, which is drawn on the foreheads of Christians and marked by the frequent signing of the hand.” PAMELIUS.]—our T—is the form of the cross which he foretold would be upon our foreheads in the true and universal Jerusalem. There the twenty-first Psalm (Ps. 22:22), speaking in the person of Christ himself to the Father, sings that Christ’s brothers, namely God’s children, would render glory to God the Father:

> I shall declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the church I shall sing a hymn to you.

For because this was to be done today in his name and Spirit, he rightly foretold that he himself would do it. And a little later:

> From you comes my praise in the great church.

And in the sixty-seventh Psalm (Ps. 68:26):

> In the churches bless the Lord [Col. 0353B] God—

so that the prophecy of Malachi might likewise concur (Mal. 1:10–11):

> I take no pleasure in you, says the Lord, and I shall not accept your sacrifices; for from the rising of the sun to its setting my name has been glorified among the nations, and in every place a sacrifice is offered to my name, a pure sacrifice—

namely, the rendering of glory, blessing, praise, and hymns. Since all these things are found among you too—the sign upon the foreheads, the sacraments of the churches, and the purity of the sacrifices—you must now burst out and say that the Creator’s Spirit prophesied for your Christ.

## CHAPTER XXIII

Now, since together with the Jews you deny that their Christ has come, take note also of the fate which they were foretold to incur after Christ because of the impiety with which they [Col. 0353C] both [Note: [Col. 0353D] “And” omitted by Semler.] despised and killed him.

First, from the day when, according to Isaiah (Isa. 2:20),

> man cast away his objects of contempt in gold and silver, which they had made for worshiping vain things and owls [Note: [Col. 0353D] “Harmful things,” another reading.]—

that is, from the time when the human race, once the truth had been made clear through Christ, cast away its idols—see whether what follows was fulfilled:

> For the Lord Sabaoth removed from Judea and Jerusalem, among other things, both the prophet and the wise master-builder (Isa. 3:1–2)—

namely, the Holy Spirit, who builds the Church, that is, God’s temple, house, and city; for from that time God’s grace ceased among them.

And (Isa. 5:6)

> the clouds were commanded not to rain upon the vineyard of Sorech—

that is, the heavenly benefits were commanded not to come upon the house of Israel. For it had produced thorns, [Col. 0354A] with which it had crowned the Lord; and it had produced not righteousness but the outcry by which it had dragged [Note: [Col. 0353D] Junius conjectures “thrust.”] him to the cross. Thus, when the dews of spiritual gifts had been withdrawn [Note: [Col. 0353D] “The earlier things of the charism,” another reading; others, “the principles of the charisms.”], the Law and the Prophets lasted until John.

Then, since through their persistent fury the Lord’s name was blasphemed among the nations because of them, as it is written (Isa. 52:5),

> Because of you my name is blasphemed among the nations—

for the disrepute began with them—and during the intervening period from Tiberius to Vespasian [Note: [Col. 0354D] “And the intervening period from Tiberius,” etc. He names Vespasian because Jerusalem was devastated under him, as is better known from the Jewish histories of Josephus and Philo than to require fuller treatment. PAMELIUS.], they did not understand repentance [Note: [Col. 0354D] Junius: “Since they had neglected repentance”; Latinus: “of repentance”],

> their land was made desolate (Isa. 1:7), their cities burned with fire [Note: [Col. 0354D] “With fire” omitted by Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.]; foreigners devour their country in their very sight; the daughter of Zion has been left [Note: [Col. 0354D] “Has been” omitted by Semler; he adds “and.”] like a watchtower in a vineyard, or like a little hut in a cucumber field.  
> [Note: [Col. 0354D] “A little hut in a cucumber field.” *Casula* is the diminutive of *casa*, which in Greek is σκηνή, “tent.” LE PRIEUR.]

This occurred because Israel did not know the Lord and the people did not [Col. 0354B] understand him, but abandoned him and provoked the Holy One of Israel to indignation.

So too the conditional threat of the sword:

> If you are unwilling and will not listen to me, the sword will devour you (Isa. 1:20),

proved that he was Christ, through their refusal to hear whom they perished. He also, in the fifty-eighth Psalm, asks the Father for their dispersion (Ps. 59:11):

> Scatter them in your power.

And again through Isaiah, pleading for their burning, he says:

> Because of me these things have happened to you; in anguish you shall sleep.

This would be utterly pointless if they suffered these things not because of the one who had pronounced that they would suffer on his account, but because of another God’s Christ.

“But,” you say, “another God’s Christ was driven to the cross by the Creator’s forces and powers, as by rivals.” Yet behold, he is shown to have been defended by the Creator (Isa. 53:9):

> and the wicked were given for his burial—

namely, those who had asserted that he was stolen away—

> and the rich for his death—

namely, those who had both purchased his betrayal from Judas and purchased from the soldiers the false testimony that the corpse had been stolen.

Therefore, either these events did not befall the Jews because of him—but you are refuted by the agreement [Note: [Col. 0354D] Semler adds “and.”] of the meaning of the Scriptures with the outcome of events and the sequence of the times—or, if they did befall them because of him, the Creator could not have avenged anyone but his own Christ. He should instead have rewarded Judas if the Jews had destroyed his Lord’s adversary.

Certainly, if the Creator’s Christ, because of whom these things are foretold as destined to be suffered, has not yet come, then they will suffer them when he does come. And where then is the daughter of Zion that is to be abandoned, when today she does not exist? Where are the cities that are to be burned, when they already lie in ruins? Where is the dispersion [Col. 0355A] of the nation, when it is already banished from its land? Restore the condition of Judea in which the Creator’s Christ may find it, and then contend that another Christ has come.

But what sort of thing is this—that the Creator admitted through his own heaven the one whom he was going to put to death upon his own earth, after the more honorable and glorious region of his kingdom had been violated, his very court and citadel trampled underfoot? Or was this rather what he intended? Plainly, though a jealous God, he nevertheless prevailed. Be ashamed, you who believe in a defeated God. What will you hope for from one who was unable to protect himself? For either he was overpowered through weakness by the Creator’s powers and human beings, or through malice he endured it so as to fasten so great a crime upon them.

## CHAPTER XXIV

“On the contrary,” you say, “I hope from him for that which itself bears witness to the distinction: the kingdom of God, an eternal and heavenly possession.
