Your Christ, however, promises the Jews their former condition through the restoration of their land and, after the course of life is completed, refreshment in Abraham’s bosom in the underworld.”

What an excellent God—if, once appeased, he restores what he had also taken away in anger! O your God, who both strikes and heals, creates evils and makes peace! O God merciful even as far as the underworld! [Note: [Col. 0355C] “But concerning Abraham’s bosom.” He alludes to the book *On Paradise*, or rather to Book IV *Against Marcion*, chapter 34, where he discusses the passage in Luke 16 concerning Abraham’s bosom, in which Lazarus finds refreshment, and the underworld, [Col. 0355D] where torments are expressly described, showing that the underworld is one thing and Abraham’s bosom another. PAMELIUS.]

But Abraham’s bosom will be treated in its proper place. As for the restoration of Judea, which the Jews themselves hope for just as it is described because they are led by the names of places and regions: it would take too long to trace how its allegorical interpretation applies spiritually to Christ, the Church, and its condition and fruit. Moreover, [Note: [Col. 0355D] “Set out in another work that we entitle *On the Hope of the Faithful*.” This work of Tertullian was contained in the Codex Agobardinus, or at least in the exemplar from which Agobard had his own copy made. Even today the title appears among the twenty-four books included in its index. Jerome also mentions this work in his account of Papias of Hierapolis, in chapter 36 of his Commentary on Ezekiel, and in the preface to the eighteenth book on Isaiah. RIGAULT.] it has been set out in another work that we entitle *On the Hope of the Faithful*; and the matter would be superfluous in the present discussion, because the question concerns not an earthly but a heavenly promise.

[Col. 0355C] For we also confess that a kingdom has been promised to us on earth, but before heaven and in another condition: namely, after the resurrection, for a thousand years, [Note: [Col. 0355D] “In Jerusalem, a city of divine workmanship brought down from heaven.” Overly credulous of Jewish tales—which they called δευτερώσεις (*deuterōseis*, “secondary traditions”)—and deceived by certain words of Ezekiel and Isaiah wrongly understood, they hoped for a Jerusalem of gold and precious stones on earth. First Papias held this view; soon afterward Justin, who calls men rejoicing in that hope ὀρθογνώμονας κατὰ πάντα Χριστιανούς, “Christians entirely orthodox in judgment”; then Irenaeus, our own Septimius, Victorinus of Poetovio, Lactantius, [Col. 0356C] and others. Jerome, in that preface to Isaiah, says that Dionysius of Alexandria composed a book against Irenaeus and that the tale was elegantly ridiculed in it. Augustine, in Book XX of *The City [Col. 0356D] of God*, says the opinion would have been tolerable in some measure if it were believed that some spiritual delights would be granted to the saints through the Lord’s presence on that Sabbath—that is, in the seventh millennium of years. He even admits that he himself once held this opinion. RIGAULT.] in Jerusalem, a city of divine workmanship brought down from heaven. The Apostle designates this city as “our mother above” and, by declaring that our *politeuma*—that is, our civic citizenship—is in heaven, plainly assigns it to some heavenly city.

Ezekiel also knows this city (Ezek. 48), and the apostle John saw it (Rev. 21); and the utterance of the new prophecy, which is acknowledged among us, testifies to it, inasmuch as it foretold, as a sign, that even the image of the city would be presented to sight before its actual manifestation. [Note: [Col. 0356D] “Indeed, this was recently fulfilled during Severus’s eastern campaign,” namely against the Parthians. RIGAULT.—I have thus far been unable to find this prodigy among pagan or even ecclesiastical historians; I therefore leave it to the diligent reader to investigate whether anything of this sort occurred in Judea during the eastern campaign of the emperor Severus, to which the Author appears to refer. PAMELIUS.] Indeed, this was recently [Note: [Col. 0355C] “Recently” rejected by Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.] fulfilled during the eastern campaign. [Note: [Col. 0356D] “For it is established even by pagan witnesses.” Since this was reported among the prodigies, it is credible that the opinion of the Chiliasts or Millenarians was greatly strengthened by it. RIGAULT.] For it is established even by pagan witnesses that for forty days in Judea, in the morning hours, a city hung down from heaven; as the day advanced, the whole configuration of its walls gradually vanished, and at other times no city was visible nearby.

We say that God has provided this city to receive the saints at their resurrection and refresh them with an abundance of every good thing—spiritual, of course—as compensation for those things which in this world we have either despised or lost. Indeed, it is both just and worthy of God that his servants should rejoice in that very place where [Col. 0356B] they were afflicted in his name.

This is the rationale of the earthly kingdom. After its thousand years—within which period the resurrection of the saints is completed, as they rise earlier or later according to their merits—then, when the destruction of the world and the conflagration of judgment have been accomplished [Note: [Col. 0356D] “The conflagration having been committed.” Fire having been applied: namely, that final ἐκπύρωσις (*ekpyrōsis*, “cosmic conflagration”). RIGAULT.], we shall be changed “in an instant” into angelic substance, namely through that clothing-over with incorruption, and shall be transferred into the heavenly kingdom.

This kingdom is now being discussed as though it had not been foretold by the Creator, and as though it therefore proved Christ to belong to another God, by whom it was first and uniquely revealed. Learn now from what follows both that it was foretold by the Creator and that, even without such foretelling, it ought to be believed as belonging to the Creator.

What do you think when Abraham’s seed, after the first promise in which [Note: [Col. 0356C] “Which,” Semler.] it is promised a multitude like the sand, is also appointed to be like the stars? Are these not auspices of both an earthly and a heavenly dispensation? When Isaac blesses his son Jacob, saying (Gen. 27:28),

> May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the richness of the earth,

are these not examples of both kinds of bounty?

Indeed, the very structure of the blessing should be observed here. In Jacob, who is the figure of the later and more highly favored people—that is, of us—the first promise is the heavenly dew, and the second the richness of the earth. [Col. 0357A] For we are first invited to heavenly things when we are torn away from the world, and afterward are found also to obtain earthly things. And [Note: [Col. 0357C] “Your Gospel also contains.” He cites Marcion’s Gospel, which he preserved after corrupting it for his own purposes. I conjecture that it was Luke’s Gospel, upon which he had laid rash hands. See the comments on the final chapter of the following book. LE PRIEUR.] your Gospel also contains:

> Seek first the kingdom of God, and these things shall be added to you (Luke 12:31).

In Esau’s case, however, Isaac first promises the earthly blessing and then adds the heavenly:

> From the richness of the earth, he says (Gen. 27:39), shall be your dwelling, and from the dew of heaven.

For the dispensation of the Jews is represented in Esau: sons earlier in birth but later in affection. Having first been imbued through the Law with earthly goods, they are afterward led toward heavenly things by believing through the Gospel.

When Jacob dreams (Gen. 28) of a ladder fixed upon earth and reaching to heaven, with some angels ascending and others descending and the Lord leaning upon it from above, shall we perhaps interpret rashly if we say that by this ladder the way to heaven is shown, by which some arrive there and from which others fall away, and that this is determined by the Lord’s judgment? [Note: [Col. 0357C] “Judgment,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.]

But why, as soon as he awoke and was first shaken with dread at the place, did he turn to interpreting the dream? For after saying,

> How terrible is this place!

he continues:

> It is nothing other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.

For he had seen Christ the Lord, the temple of God and at the same time the gate through which heaven is entered. He certainly would not have named “the gate of heaven” if heaven were not entered under the Creator. But there is also a gate that receives and leads onward, a way already laid out by [Note: [Col. 0357C] Latinus: “A way laid out by Christ.”] Christ, of whom Amos says (Amos 9:6):

> He who builds his ascent into heaven—

plainly not for himself alone, but also for his people who will be with him. And:

> For you shall array them about yourself, he says (Isa. 49:18), like the adornment [Col. 0357C] of a bride.

Thus, as they press through him toward the heavenly kingdoms, the Spirit marvels and says (Isa. [Col. 0358A] 31:5; 60:8):

> They fly like kites. They fly like clouds and [Note: [Col. 0357C] Junius inserts: “Who are these who fly like clouds, and.”] like young doves toward me—

that is, as simply as doves. For according to the Apostle (1 Thess. 4:17),

> we shall be caught up in the clouds [Note: [Col. 0358C] “Clouds,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.] to meet the Lord—

that Son of Man, namely, who comes in the clouds according to Daniel (Dan. 7)—and so we shall always be with the Lord, both on earth and in heaven. Because some are ungrateful for both promises, he even calls the elements themselves as witnesses (Isa. 1:2):

[The transmitted Latin is syntactically uncertain at this point.]

> Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth.

For my part, even if Scripture did not so often extend its hand to me with the hope of heaven, I would regard it as a sufficient presumption in favor of this promise too that I already possess earthly grace. I would expect something from heaven as well, from the God of heaven. Just as he is God of earth, so I would believe that the Christ who promises higher things [Col. 0358B] belongs to the one who had also promised lower things; who [Note: [Col. 0358C] Franeker adds “also.”] had used lesser things as proofs of greater; who had perhaps reserved the proclamation of this previously unheard-of kingdom for Christ alone, so that earthly glory might be announced through servants, but heavenly glory through God himself.

Yet you infer from this too that he is another Christ, because he announces a new kingdom. First you must produce some example of his beneficence, lest I rightly doubt the trustworthiness of so great a promise as you say should be hoped for. Indeed, before all else, since you proclaim that he promises heavenly things, you must prove that he possesses a heaven. But as matters stand, you invite me to dinner without showing me the house; you claim a kingdom without displaying the royal palace. Is it because your Christ promises a heavenly kingdom without possessing a heaven [Note: [Col. 0357C] “Without possessing a heaven.” The passage should be joined in this manner: “Is it because your Christ promises a heavenly kingdom without possessing a heaven, just as he presented himself as a human being without possessing flesh?” RIGAULT.], just as he presented himself as a human being without possessing flesh? [Note: [Col. 0358C] “O empty phantom!” So he himself in Book IV: “He would have handled the reality of a solid body, not an empty phantom.” RIGAULT.] O empty [Note: [Col. 0358C] “Every,” Semler, Pamelius, Rhenanus, Oberthür.] phantom—a grand illusion even in its promise!

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0357]

## [ARGUMENT]

[Col. 0357D] Tertullian is about to write against Marcion’s work, composed as a series of opposing contradictions and consequently entitled *Antitheses*. It was designed to separate the Law from the Gospel, thereby dividing two different Gods, one belonging to the Old Testament and the other to the New.

**Chapter 1.** First, without denying the difference between the commandments and disciplines, he demonstrates that they belong to one and the same God. For God the Creator himself foretold through his prophets that another and new law—namely, the Gospel—would arise in place of the Old, and an eternal covenant in place of a temporal one.

[Col. 0358D] **Chapter 2.** Next, he lays down that not only Luke’s Gospel—which Marcion admitted in adulterated form, though without assigning it any title—but also the Gospels of the apostles John and Matthew and of Mark, an apostolic man, possess authority no less than Luke’s.

**Chapter 3.** Nor is it an obstacle that the apostle Paul rebukes the apostles in Galatians. For they were censured not for corrupting or interpolating the Gospel, but only for their conduct; indeed, the very arrangement of their Gospel had been perverted by false apostles.

**Chapter 4.** When, however, the title of the Gospel is disputed—Marcion claiming the Gospel as his own, while the Author affirms that it is an adulterated form of his own Gospel, namely Luke’s—authority is to be claimed for the one found to be earlier, and corruption charged against the later one. This is especially so since Marcion had for some time believed the catholic Church and only afterward defected into heresy.

**Chapter 5.** For Luke’s Gospel possesses authority from the apostolic churches, among which it is established that whatever is held sacred was handed down by the apostles; and the remaining Gospels—John’s, Matthew’s, and Mark’s—do so likewise. The same is true also of the Apocalypse, as is shown by tracing the succession of bishops back to its origin.

**Chapter 6.** Then, proceeding to his subject, the Author establishes that there is no difference between the Old and New Testaments from the very fact that our Christ fulfilled the Creator’s prophecies, realized his promises, [Col. 0359B] and supported his laws.

**Chapter 7.** He first confirms this from the latter part of Luke 4, concerning the demon expelled in the synagogue at Capernaum, because Marcion had erased Luke’s first three chapters and the beginning of the fourth as contrary to his position.

**Chapter 8.** From the same chapter, partly before and partly after the aforementioned narrative—for Marcion had also transposed it—concerning Christ’s teaching in the synagogue at Nazareth and other demons.

**Chapter 9.** Likewise, from Luke 5, concerning the calling of the apostles Simon and the sons of Zebedee, and the leper who was cleansed.

**Chapter 10.** From the same chapter, concerning the paralytic who was healed and the designation “Son of Man.”

**Chapter 11.** From the same chapter, concerning the tax collector summoned by the Lord, fasting, Christ as bridegroom, and the parable of the new and old wine.

**Chapter 12.** Next, from Luke 6, concerning the disciples who gathered ears of grain and the withered hand healed on the Sabbath.

**Chapter 13.** From the same chapter, concerning the ascent of the mountain and the prayer there by night, the apostles’ number of twelve, the change of Peter’s name, and the assembly of the nations around Christ.

**Chapter 14.** From the same chapter, concerning the Beatitudes, or the Lord’s sermon on the mountain.

**Chapter 15.** From the same chapter, concerning the various curses in which he called down “Woe” upon the Pharisees.

**Chapter 16.** From the same chapter, concerning the command to love both enemies and one’s neighbor.

**Chapter 17.** From the same chapter, concerning the prohibition of interest and other sayings of the Lord almost to the end of the chapter.

[Col. 0359D] **Chapter 18.** Also from Luke 7, concerning the centurion’s faith, the raising of the widow’s son, John the Baptist, and the sinful woman.

**Chapter 19.** Thereafter, from Luke 8, concerning the wealthy women who accompanied Christ, the Lord’s sayings to his disciples, and Christ’s mother and brothers.

**Chapter 20.** From the same chapter, concerning Christ’s miracles, by which he commanded the winds and sea, cast out a legion of demons, and healed a woman’s flow of blood.

**Chapter 21.** Likewise from Luke 9, concerning the disciples sent out to preach, the feeding of the people in the wilderness, Peter’s confession, “You are the Christ,” and the foretold persecution of the faithful.

[Col. 0360A] **Chapter 22.** From the same chapter, concerning Christ’s appearance with Moses and Elijah in the solitude of the mountain.

**Chapter 23.** From the same chapter, concerning the Lord’s sayings to the Pharisees, the love of little children, and his rebuke of the man who said, “I shall follow you wherever you go.”

**Chapter 24.** Further, from Luke 10, concerning the selection of the seventy disciples and the power given to them.

**Chapter 25.** From the same chapter, concerning the Lord’s prayer to the Father, his sayings to the disciples, and his answer to the teacher of the Law.

**Chapter 26.** Then, from Luke 11, concerning the Lord’s Prayer, other forms of prayer, and the parables relating to it; the expulsion of a deaf demon; and the exclamation of the woman from the crowd.

**Chapter 27.** From the same chapter, concerning the Pharisees who sought a sign and his other rebukes of them.

[Col. 0360B] **Chapter 28.** From Luke 12, concerning various sayings of the Lord to the disciples and the parable of the rich man who flattered himself over the yield of his fields.

**Chapter 29.** From the same chapter, concerning the command that the soul should not be anxious about food, nor the body about clothing; the girding of the loins; the blessed servants; the fire sent upon the earth; and other sayings of the Lord.

**Chapter 30.** Again, from Luke 13, concerning a healing performed on the Sabbath, parables, and other sayings of the Lord.

**Chapter 31.** Also from Luke 14, concerning what kind of people should be invited to a dinner or luncheon, and the dinner to which a man invited many.
c. 32. Likewise, from chapter XV of Luke, concerning the sheep and the drachma that were lost and found.

c. 33. Also from chapter XVI of Luke, concerning the two masters, [Col. 0360C] God and Mammon, and the Lord’s saying: “The Law and the Prophets were until John.”

c. 34. Concerning the prohibition of divorce, and consequently the approval of marriage, and concerning hell and Abraham’s bosom, from the same chapter.

c. 35. Next, from chapter XVII of Luke, concerning various sayings of the Lord, the healing of the ten lepers, and the Pharisees’ question concerning the kingdom of God.

c. 36. Likewise, from chapter XVIII of Luke, concerning the parables of the judge and of the Pharisee and the publican praying in the temple, the Lord’s words to the rich young man, and the healing of the blind man.

c. 37. Also from chapter XIX of Luke, concerning Zacchaeus and the parable of the servants who are judged according to the amount of money put out at interest.

c. 38. Likewise, from chapter XX of Luke, concerning various sayings of the Lord to the Pharisees, the chief priests, the Sadducees, [Col. 0360D] and the scribes.

c. 39. Furthermore, from chapter XXI of Luke, concerning those who are to come in the name of Christ, the signs of the final end, Christ’s teaching in the temple, and his withdrawal to the Mount of Olives.

c. 40. Likewise, from chapter XXII of Luke, concerning the day of Passover chosen for the Passion, Judas’s sale and betrayal of him, and the distribution of Christ’s body and blood.

c. 41. Concerning the curse pronounced upon him through whom the Son of Man would be betrayed, the betrayer’s kiss, and the Lord’s answer to the question whether he himself was the Christ, from the same chapter.

c. 42. Also from chapter XXIII of Luke, concerning the similar answer in Pilate’s residence, the trial before that same Pilate and before [Col. 0361A] Herod, the crucifixion, the signs at the Lord’s death, his expiration, and his burial.

CHAPTER XLIII. Finally, from chapter XXIV of Luke, concerning the women who came to the tomb with prepared spices, the resurrection after two days, Christ’s appearances to the women, the disciples, and the apostles, and the sending of the apostles to preach to all nations.

# CHAPTER I

We now summon every proposition [Note: [Col. 0361D] “And every preparation.” That is, all the material, the entire apparatus of arguments, as above. RHEN.] and the entire apparatus of the impious and sacrilegious Marcion to confront that very Gospel of his which, by interpolating it, he made his own. And to furnish it with credibility, he devised for it a sort of dowry: a work constructed from opposed contradictions and entitled *Antitheses* [Note: [Col. 0361D] “Entitled *Antitheses*.” This was Marcion’s book, in which he separated the Old Testament from the New and set them against one another. Here Tertullian also speaks of the interpolation of the Gospel, which we discuss elsewhere. Some think that Tertullian published a book [Col. 0362D] entitled *Antitheses*, and maintain that this passage must be explained with reference to it. That is foreign to the sense of this book and its discourse, for the *Antitheses* was Marcion’s book. LE PR.], designed to force a separation between the Law [Col. 0361B] and the Gospel, so that by dividing two Gods, correspondingly different, one belonging to one Instrument and the other to the other—or, as it is more customary [Note: [Col. 0361D] “In use,” Lat.] to say, one to each Testament—he might thereby also support belief in the Gospel according to the *Antitheses*.

I would have struck down these *Antitheses* as well in their own close engagement, that is, objection by objection, had it not been far more opportune to repel them within and together with the very Gospel for which they act as advocates. Yet it is so easy to meet them with a preliminary objection—and indeed [Note: [Col. 0361D] “For my part,” Seml.] to do so by accepting them, recognizing them as valid, and declaring that they support our position—that our own antitheses against Marcion should all the more make their author ashamed of his blindness.

I therefore acknowledge that one order ran its course under the Creator in the old dispensation and another under Christ in the new. I do not deny that the proofs given by the divine utterance, the precepts governing conduct, [Col. 0361C] and the disciplines of the Law differ, provided that the entire diversity belongs to one and the same God—namely, to him by whom it is established [Note: [Col. 0361D] Seml. adds “it.”] that it was arranged, just as it was also foretold.

Long ago Isaiah proclaimed (Isa. II, 3) that a law would go forth from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem—certainly another law and another word. Finally, he says: “He will judge among the nations and convict many peoples”; that is, not merely the single nation of the Jews, but the nations that, through the new law of the Gospel and the new word of the apostles, are judged and convicted among themselves of their former error as soon as they have believed. Thereafter they cut their swords into ploughshares and their *sibynae*, a kind of hunting spear, into pruning hooks; that is, they convert their formerly fierce and savage dispositions into upright understandings and into laborers who produce good fruit.

And again (Isa. LI, 4): “Hear me, [Col. 0361D] hear me, [Note: [Col. 0361D] Seml. adds “And.”] my people; and you kings, incline your ears [Col. 0362A] to me, because a law will go forth from me, and my judgment as a light to the nations.” By this judgment he had judged and decreed that the nations too were to be enlightened through the law and word of the Gospel. This will be the blameless law mentioned in David, which, being perfect, converts souls—certainly from idols to God. This will also be the word concerning which the same Isaiah says (Isa. X, 23): “For the Lord,” he says, “will make a shortened word upon the earth.” For the New Testament has been condensed [Note: [Col. 0362D] “And freed from the Law’s burdensome fringes.” He calls works “fringed” when they are numerous and keep people distracted by occupations, just as a fringed garment hinders one’s step. RHEN.] and freed [Note: [Col. 0362D] “And from the Law’s,” Seml.] from the Law’s burdensome fringes.

But why say more, when renewal is proclaimed by the Creator more manifestly and more clearly than daylight through the same prophet (Isa. XLIII, 18): “Do not remember the former things, and do not consider the things of old. The old things have passed away; new things are arising. Behold, I make new things, which will now arise”? The same God says through Jeremiah (Jer. IV, 3): “Break up for yourselves new ground, [Col. 0362B] and do not sow among thorns; and circumcise the foreskins [Note: [Col. 0362D] “Foreskin,” Seml.] of your hearts”; and elsewhere (Jer. XXXI, 31): “Behold, the days are coming [Note: [Col. 0362D] “Will come,” Seml.], says the Lord, and I will establish for the house of Jacob and the house of Judah a new testament—not according to the testament that I arranged for their fathers on the day when I took hold of their ordering, to lead them out of the land of Egypt.”

Thus he signifies that the former testament was temporary, since he shows it to be mutable, and also since he promises that the later one will be eternal. For through Isaiah he says (Isa. LV, 3): “Hear me, and you shall live, and I will arrange a testament for you,” adding: “The holy and faithful things of David,” in order to demonstrate [Note: [Col. 0362D] “In order that it might be demonstrated,” Par. Fran.] that this testament would run its course in Christ. He also foretold figuratively that this same Christ would be descended from David according to Mary’s register, in the rod that was to proceed from the root of Jesse.

Therefore, if the Creator said that other laws, other words, and new testamentary [Col. 0362C] dispensations would come to pass, and if he even appointed other and better forms of sacrificial service among the nations, as Malachi says (Mal. I, 10–11): “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord, and I will not receive your sacrifices from your hands, because from the rising of the sun to its setting my name has been glorified among the nations, and in every place a sacrifice is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice”—that is, simple prayer from a pure conscience—then every alteration arising from renewal must enter into diversity with the things whose alteration it is, and into opposition as a consequence of that diversity. For just as nothing has been altered unless it is different, so nothing is different unless it is opposed. Therefore, the opposition arising from diversity will also be attributed to the same one to whom belongs the alteration arising from renewal. He who arranged [Col. 0362D] the alteration also established the diversity; [Col. 0363A] he who proclaimed the renewal also foretold [Note: [Col. 0363D] “Declared,” Par. Jun.] the opposition.

Why do you interpret a difference between things as a separation between powers? Why do you distort the antitheses of examples against the Creator, when you can recognize them even in his own thoughts and affections? “I,” he says (Deut. XXXII, 39), “will strike, and I will heal”; “I,” he says (I Sam. II, 6), “will kill, and I will make alive”; he who, of course, “creates evil and makes peace” (Isa. XLV, 7). On this ground you are also accustomed to reproach him under the charge of changeability and inconsistency, as one who prohibits what he commands and commands what he prohibits [Note: [Col. 0363D] “May command . . . may prohibit,” Cod. Wouw.].

Why, then, did you not also reckon the antitheses among the natural works of the Creator who is always opposed to himself? Could you not at least have considered that even among the inhabitants of Pontus, unless I am mistaken, the world is constructed [Note: [Col. 0363D] “Built,” Seml.] from a diversity of substances competing with one another? [Col. 0363B] Accordingly, you should first have defined one God of light and another of darkness, so that you might then have been able to assert one God of the Law and another of the Gospel. Instead, it has already been established from manifest facts that the mysteries likewise possess the same form of antithesis as the works and designs of him whose works and designs are constituted through antitheses.

# CHAPTER II

You now have from us a ready answer to the *Antitheses* [Note: [Col. 0363D] “Antithesis,” another reading.]. I now pass to the demonstration that the Gospel—certainly not the Jewish Gospel, but the Pontic one—is at any rate adulterated, first laying out the order of the argument upon which we are entering.

We establish first of all that the authors of the Gospel Instrument are apostles, upon whom the duty of promulgating the Gospel was imposed by the Lord himself; and apostolic men as well [Note: [Col. 0363D] “And if apostolic men, nevertheless not alone,” etc. He says that the true Gospel was written only by apostles or apostolic men, in order to close the way against objections drawn from the corrupted copies of heretics, such as those of the Ebionites, Encratites, Nazarenes, Marcionites, etc. LE PR.], though not apostolic men alone, but together with apostles [Col. 0363C] and after apostles [Note: [Col. 0363D] “Apostolic men,” Jun.]. For the preaching of disciples might become suspect of ambition for glory if it were not supported by the authority of their masters—or rather by that of Christ, who [Note: [Col. 0364D] “Who,” feminine, Seml.] made the apostles their masters.

Accordingly, among the apostles John and Matthew instill the faith into us; among apostolic men Luke and Mark renew it, all beginning from the same rules with respect to the one God, the Creator, and his Christ, born of a virgin, the fulfillment of the Law and the Prophets. It does not matter if the arrangement of the narrative varies, provided that there is agreement concerning the chief article of the faith—an article concerning which there is no agreement with Marcion.

Marcion, by contrast, assigns no author to the Gospel—his own Gospel, that is—as though it had not been permissible for him also to fabricate a title for a work whose very body it was no sacrilege for him to overthrow. And I could already take my stand here, contending that a work ought not to be recognized when it does not raise its head openly, offers no firm assurance, and pledges no credibility through a complete title and the due declaration of its author. But [Col. 0364A] we prefer [Note: [Col. 0364D] “We preferred,” Seml.] to engage on every point, and we do not conceal what may be understood from our own Gospel.

For among the Gospel writers whom we possess, [Note: [Col. 0364D] Marcion seems to have chosen Luke as the one he would mutilate. You see clearly that the Gospel of blessed Luke was corrupted so that Marcion might twist it into support for his errors, cutting out many things, adding others, and defiling it with his own interpretation. LE PR.] Marcion seems to have chosen Luke as the one he would mutilate. Now Luke was not an apostle but an apostolic man, not a master but a disciple, and therefore inferior to his master; certainly he was later by as much as he was a follower of a later apostle—Paul, without doubt. Thus, even if Marcion had introduced the Gospel under Paul’s own name, the singularity of the Instrument, deprived of the support of its predecessors, would not suffice to establish its credibility. For the Gospel that Paul found, to which he gave his faith, and with which he soon strove to make his own preaching agree, would also be required.

Indeed, for this very reason he went up to Jerusalem (Gal. II, 1), to become acquainted and confer with the apostles, lest perhaps he had run in vain—that is, lest he should have believed otherwise than they did [Col. 0364B] and preached a different Gospel from theirs. Accordingly, when he had conferred with the authors and reached agreement concerning the rule of faith; they joined right hands and thereafter divided their preaching duties, so that they would preach among the Jews, while Paul would preach among the Jews and among the nations.

Therefore, if Paul himself, Luke’s enlightener, desired the authority of his predecessors [Note: [Col. 0364D] “Predecessor,” Par.] for his own faith and preaching, how much more must I require for Luke’s Gospel the authority that was necessary for the Gospel of his master? It would be otherwise if, in Marcion’s view, the mystery of the Christian religion began with Luke’s discipleship. But if it also ran its course before then, it certainly possessed an authentic apparatus by which it came down as far as Luke; and with the testimony of that apparatus supporting him, Luke too can be admitted.

# CHAPTER III

Marcion, however, having obtained Paul’s epistle to the Galatians, [Col. 0364C] which even censures the apostles themselves (Gal. II) for not walking with a straight step according to the truth of the Gospel and at the same time accuses certain false apostles of perverting the Gospel of Christ, strives to destroy the standing of those Gospels that are published as their own and under the names of apostles, or even of apostolic men, so that he may transfer to his own Gospel the credibility that he takes away from them.

Now even if Peter, John, and James, who were regarded as pillars, were censured, the reason is manifest. For they seemed to vary their fellowship out of respect for persons. And yet, since Paul himself became all things to all people so that he might gain everyone (1 Cor. IX, 19), Peter too could have had this same purpose when acting somewhat differently from what he taught.

Likewise, even if false apostles had slipped in, their character also was disclosed: they were defending circumcision [Col. 0364D] and Jewish observances [Note: [Col. 0364D] “Jewish observances.” As in Galatians IV: [Col. 0365D] “observing days and months and seasons and years.” This interpretation must therefore be noted against modern heretics, who do not shrink from adducing that passage against the observances of the Catholic Church, although the author expressly interprets them as Jewish observances—and does so not only here but also below, book V, chapter 4, where he treats this passage. PAM.] [Note: [Col. 0364D] “Pride,” Cod. Pithae.; Seml.]. Thus Paul was censuring them not for their preaching but for their conduct; and he would equally have censured them if they had erred in anything concerning God the Creator [Col. 0365A] or his Christ.

The individual points must therefore be distinguished. If Marcion complains that the apostles should be held suspect of transgression and dissimulation, even to the point of corrupting the Gospel, he is already accusing Christ by accusing those whom Christ chose. But if the apostles did transmit the Gospel intact and were censured only for inconsistency in their fellowship, while false apostles interpolated their truth and our compilations derive from those interpolations, which, then, will be that authentic Instrument of the apostles which suffered the adulterations? Which one enlightened Paul, and through him Luke?

Or if it was so utterly destroyed—obliterated as though by some deluge, by such a flood of falsifiers—then Marcion himself no longer possesses the true Gospel. Or if the Gospel possessed by Marcion alone is the true one, that is, the apostles’ Gospel, how does it agree with ours, [Col. 0365B] which is attributed not to the apostles but to Luke? Or if the Gospel Marcion uses is not immediately to be attributed to Luke merely because it agrees with ours—because ours, of course, has been adulterated even in its title—whereas in all other respects it belongs to the apostles, then ours too, which agrees with his, likewise belongs to the apostles, though it too has been adulterated in its title.

# CHAPTER IV

The rope of contention [Note: [Col. 0365D] Fran. omits “therefore.”] must therefore be pulled, with equal effort wavering to and fro. I say that mine is true; Marcion says that his is. I affirm that Marcion’s is adulterated; Marcion says the same of mine. Who will decide between us, unless it is the reckoning of time, which prescribes authority for the Gospel found to be earlier and prejudges as corrupted the Gospel proved [Note: [Col. 0365D] “Found,” another reading; Seml. conjectures that both words were absent.] to be later?

For insofar as falsehood is a corruption of truth, truth must necessarily precede falsehood. The thing itself will be prior to the injury done to it, and the material prior to the rivalry directed against it. Otherwise, how absurd it would be if, after we had proved ours the earlier and Marcion’s the later, ours should seem to have been false before it possessed any truth as material for its falsehood, while Marcion’s should be believed to have experienced rivalry from ours before it was even published! And finally, how absurd that the later should be regarded as the truer, after so many and such great works and testimonies of the Christian religion had already been published in the world—works that certainly could not have been published without the truth of the Gospel, that is, before the truth of the Gospel!

So far, then, as Luke’s Gospel is concerned, since the version shared between us and Marcion is disputed as to its truth, the Gospel according to us is so much older than Marcion that Marcion himself once believed it. For in the first fervor of his faith he even contributed money [Col. 0365D] to the catholic Church, which was soon afterward cast out along with him when he defected from our truth to his own heresy.

What now if the Marcionites deny [Col. 0366A] his original adherence to our faith, even against the evidence of his own letter? What if they do not even acknowledge the letter? They certainly not only admit that the *Antitheses* are Marcion’s but even display [Note: [Col. 0365D] “Bring forth,” Lat. Jun.] them prominently. From them I obtain sufficient proof.

For if the Gospel attributed to Luke among us—whether it is also so attributed among the Marcionites we shall see—is the very Gospel that Marcion censures through his *Antitheses* as having been interpolated by defenders of Judaism in order to incorporate it with the Law and the Prophets, so that they might thereby also attach Christ to them [Note: [Col. 0366D] “Fashion Christ from them,” Seml.], he certainly could not have censured anything except what he had already found. No one censures future things that he does not know will occur; correction does not precede the fault.

Marcion alone, and Marcion first, appeared as the corrector of a Gospel that had been overturned from the age of Tiberius down to that of Antoninus. Christ had waited for him so long, already regretting [Col. 0366B] that he had hastily sent the apostles ahead without Marcion’s protection! But heresy is an affair of human rashness, not of divine authority; it always “corrects” the Gospels by corrupting them. Even if Marcion were a disciple, nevertheless “the disciple is not above the master” (Matt. X, 24). Even if [Note: [Col. 0366D] Venice omits “if.”] Marcion were an apostle: “Whether it was I,” says Paul (1 Cor. XV, 11), “or they, so we preach.” Even if Marcion were a prophet: “The spirits of the prophets will be subject to the prophets” (1 Cor. XIV, 32), for they are spirits not of overthrow but of peace. Even if [Note: [Col. 0366D] Jun. omits “if.”] Marcion were an angel, he should more readily be declared anathema than an evangelist, because he preached a different Gospel (Gal. I, 8).

Accordingly, while he corrects, he confirms both: ours as the earlier, since he corrects what he found; and his as the later, since by constructing it out of the correction of ours he made it both his own and new.

# CHAPTER V

[Col. 0366C]

In sum, if it is established that what is earlier is truer, that what is from the beginning is earlier, and that what is from the apostles [Note: [Col. 0366D] Seml. omits “that.”] is from the beginning, it will equally be established that what was held sacred among the churches of the apostles is what was handed down by the apostles.

Let us see what milk the Corinthians drank from Paul; to what rule the Galatians were recalled [Note: [Col. 0366D] “Corrected,” another reading.]; what the Philippians, Thessalonians, and Ephesians read; and what the Romans nearby proclaim—the Romans to whom both Peter and Paul left the Gospel sealed with their own blood as well. [Note: [Col. 0366D] “We also have the churches reared by John.” He means churches that preserved the rules handed down by Saint John, just as he said above that the Corinthians drank milk from Paul. LE PR.] We also have the churches reared by John. For even if Marcion rejects his Apocalypse, the succession of bishops, traced back to its origin, will rest upon John as its founder. [Note: [Col. 0366D] “Thus the noble lineage of the others is also recognized.” That is, their stock, origin, and nobility. RIG.] Thus the noble lineage of the other churches is recognized as well.

I therefore say that among those churches—and now not only among the apostolic churches, but among all those that are joined to them in the fellowship of the mystery—the Gospel of Luke that we are presently defending has stood from the beginning of its publication. Marcion’s Gospel, by contrast, is not even known to most of them, and is known to none [Note: [Col. 0367D] Seml. omits “however.”] without being thereby [Note: [Col. 0367D] “By that same one,” Seml.] condemned.

It too, to be sure, has churches—but its own, as late as they are adulterous. If you sought their lineage, you would more readily find it apostatic than apostolic, with Marcion, of course, as their founder, or someone from Marcion’s swarm. Wasps too make honeycombs [Note: [Col. 0367D] “Wasps too make honeycombs.” Pliny relates that wasps make nests from mud in elevated places and produce their offspring in them. RIG.]; Marcionites too make churches.

The same authority of the apostolic churches will also support the other Gospels that we possess through them and in accordance with them: I mean those of John and Matthew, although the Gospel published by Mark is also affirmed to be Peter’s, whose interpreter Mark was; for they also customarily ascribe Luke’s compilation to Paul. What the disciples published may properly be regarded as belonging to their masters.

Marcion must therefore also be pressed to explain why, after passing over these Gospels, he fastened upon Luke [Col. 0367B] instead—as though these had not existed among the churches from the beginning, just as Luke’s did. Indeed, it is more credible that these existed from the very beginning, since they were earlier insofar as they were apostolic, and were dedicated together with the churches themselves.

But what sense would it make, if the apostles published nothing, for the disciples to have published instead, when they could not even have become disciples without any teaching from their masters? Since, therefore, it is established that these Gospels too existed among the churches, why did Marcion not touch them as well—either correcting them if they were adulterated, or acknowledging them if they were intact?

For it is also fitting that, [Note: [Col. 0367D] “If any were perverting the Gospel.” He touches upon the common artifices of heretics in corrupting copies of Scripture, especially those written by authors of great importance and authority. The Greek word μεταστρέψαι (*metastrepsai*) used by the Apostle in Galatians I, from whom Tertullian took these words, should be noted: it signifies not only “to turn,” but also “to corrupt” and “to draw into another meaning.” LE PR.] if any were perverting the Gospel, they would be more concerned to pervert the works whose authority they knew to be more widely accepted. They were therefore called false apostles precisely because they imitated the apostles falsely. To the same extent, therefore, that Marcion would have corrected the things requiring correction if they had been corrupted, he confirmed that the things he did not think needed correction had not been corrupted.

In fact, he corrected what he considered corrupted—but not even this with good reason, because it had not been corrupted. For if the apostolic Gospels ran their course intact [Note: [Col. 0367D] “Intactly,” Seml.] [Note: [Col. 0368D] “Ran their course,” Par. Rig. Venice], while Luke’s Gospel as we possess it agrees so fully with their rule that it remains with them among the churches, then it is established that Luke’s Gospel too ran its course intact down to Marcion’s sacrilege. Indeed, when Marcion laid hands upon it, it then became different from and hostile [Note: [Col. 0368D] Par. Fran. insert “from.”] to the apostolic Gospels.

I shall therefore give his disciples this advice: either let them, even at this late date, alter those Gospels also into the form of their own, so that it may seem to agree with the apostolic Gospels—for they reform it daily, in proportion as we [Col. 0368A] refute them daily—or let them be ashamed of their master, who is exposed everywhere: at one moment he hands over the truth of the Gospel through acknowledgment of it, and at another overthrows it through shamelessness.

We generally employ these concise arguments when we contend [Note: [Col. 0368D] “Concerning the Gospels,” Seml.] with heretics over the credibility of the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0368D] “We extricate ourselves,” Seml.]. These arguments defend both the order of time, which excludes the later falsifiers, and by the authority of the churches, which supports the tradition of the apostles: because truth must necessarily precede falsehood and must proceed from those by whom it was handed down.

# CHAPTER VI

But from this point we enter upon another stage. As we promised, we now call Marcion’s Gospel itself into court, intending by this means also to prove it adulterated. Certainly, the entire purpose for which he labored—even by preparing the way with the *Antitheses*—compels him to establish a diversity between the Old and New Testaments, and consequently to separate [Note: [Col. 0368D] “Being about to separate,” Par. Fran.; “who was to separate,” Jun.] his own Christ from the Creator, as the Christ of another God and as a stranger to the Law and the Prophets.

[Note: [Col. 0367D] “Certainly, for this reason he erased everything contrary to his position.” It is characteristic of all heretics [Col. 0368D] to eradicate from the Scriptures those things that are contrary to their position—and indeed from our Scriptures too. Thus they reject the two books of Maccabees because these support the prayers of the saints after this life and sacrifices for the dead; the Epistle of James and the Apocalypse because they support the merits of good works; and finally the Second Epistle of Peter because they perceive that their own heresies in these last times were foretold there. PAM.]

Certainly, for this reason he erased everything contrary to his position that agreed with the Creator, on the pretense that it had been interwoven by the Creator’s defenders, while preserving what suited his own position. These passages we shall confront; these we shall embrace, if they belong more to us. If they strike down Marcion’s presumption, it will then also be established that the other passages were erased through the same defect of heretical blindness by which these were preserved.

Such will be the purpose and method of our little work, subject, of course, to the condition agreed upon by both sides. Marcion has established that there is one Christ who, in the time of Tiberius, was revealed by a God previously unknown for the salvation of all nations, and another Christ who was appointed by God the Creator to restore the Jewish state and is to come at some future time. Between these he rends open a vast and absolute [Note: [Col. 0368D] “The difference between the just and the good.” That is, between the severe and the gentle, between the one who judges and the one who shows mercy, between the one who punishes and the one who spares, between the Creator and the Redeemer. RIG.] difference: as great as that between the just and the good, between the Law and the Gospel, and between Judaism and Christianity.

Hence also comes our preliminary rule, by which we firmly establish that Christ, if he belongs to another God, must have nothing in common with the Creator. Otherwise, he must be declared the Creator’s Christ if he administers the Creator’s dispensations, fulfills his prophecies, supports his laws, makes his promises present, restores his mighty works, re-establishes his judgments, or expresses his dispositions and distinctive qualities.

I ask you, reader, to remember this agreement and this preliminary rule everywhere, and begin to recognize whether the Christ before you is Marcion’s or the Creator’s.

# CHAPTER VII
In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius (Luke 3:1), he represents him [Note: [Col. 0369C] “God,” Par. Fran.] as having descended into Capernaum, a city of Galilee (Luke 4:31)—from the Creator’s heaven, of course, into which he had previously descended from his own. What order [Note: [Col. 0369C] “And what,” Seml.] was there, then, in his first being described as descending from his own heaven into the Creator’s? For why should I not also criticize those features that fail to satisfy the credibility of an orderly narrative—a credibility always lacking in falsehood? To be sure, let those points be regarded as stated once for all through the arguments we have already examined elsewhere: whether, in descending through the Creator’s domain—and indeed in opposition to the Creator himself—he could have been admitted by him and then dispatched from there to the earth, which likewise belonged to him.

For now, however, accepting that he descended, [Col. 0369B] I also demand the remaining sequence of his descent. Let it pass if somewhere it is written that he “appeared.” “To appear” conveys a sudden and unexpected coming into view, which at once strikes the eyes with something that has appeared without delay. But “to descend,” because it takes place [Note: [Col. 0369C] “goes,” Par. Fran.], is both visible and comes before the eyes; and, as an actual event, it also creates a sequence. It therefore compels one to ask in what form, with what equipment, by what force or measured motion, and even at what time of day or night he descended; furthermore, who saw him descending, who reported it, and who attested an event that would certainly not be readily believed even when someone attested it.

It is, finally, unworthy that Romulus should have had Proculus to affirm his ascent into heaven, while Christ—the Christ of God [Note: [Col. 0369C] “of God” is absent from Fran.]—should have found no herald of his descent from his own heaven, as though Romulus had not ascended by the same ladder of falsehood [Col. 0369C] by which this Christ descended.

But what did he have to do with Galilee, if he did not belong to the Creator, for whose entrance upon his preaching this region was appointed? Isaiah says (Isa. 9:1–2):

> [Note: [Col. 0369D] “Drink this first; do it quickly.” I believe the conjecture of the most distinguished Hugo Grotius concerning this interpretation of Isaiah’s words, in his annotations on the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 4, verse 14, to be correct. RIG.]  
> Drink this first [Note: [Col. 0369C] “Pass through,” Par. Rhen.], do it quickly, region of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, and the rest of you who [Note: [Col. 0370C] Rhen., from the Gorze manuscript, adds “inhabit the land.”] dwell by the sea, beside the Jordan [Note: [Col. 0370C] “and of the Jordan,” Seml.], Galilee of the nations: you people [Col. 0370A] who sit in darkness, see a great light; you who inhabit the land, sitting in the shadow of death, a light has risen upon you.

It is well, moreover, that Marcion’s God too is claimed as the illuminator of the nations; all the more, then, ought he to have descended from heaven—even if [Note: [Col. 0370C] “and (even if),” Jun.] he should certainly have descended into Pontus rather than into Galilee. But since both the place and the work of illumination correspond to the proclamation concerning Christ, we already begin to recognize him as the one who was prophesied. At his very first entrance he showed that he had come “not to abolish the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 5:17) [Note: [Col. 0369D] “Not to abolish the Law and the Prophets.” Irenaeus (Book IV, 13) says that Marcion read the opposite. SEML.], “but rather to fulfill them.” Marcion erased this as an addition. But he will deny in vain [Note: [Col. 0370C] “denied,” Seml.] that Christ said what he immediately did, at least in part. For he meanwhile fulfilled the prophecy concerning the place, going straight from heaven to the synagogue—in order, as the saying goes, to [Col. 0370B] **DO THE THING FOR WHICH WE CAME**.

Marcion, remove this too from the Gospel:

> I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt. 15:24);

and:

> It is not [Note: [Col. 0370C] Lat. inserts “good.”] right to take the children’s bread and give it to the dogs (Matt. 7:27),

lest Christ should evidently belong to Israel. Deeds suffice for me in place of sayings. Take away the words of my Christ; the facts will speak. See, he enters the synagogue—assuredly to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. See, he first offers the bread of his teaching to the Israelites—assuredly because he gives them preference as children. See, he does not yet distribute it to the others—assuredly because he passes them by as dogs. Yet to whom would he more readily have distributed it than to those who were strangers to the Creator, if he himself had not belonged first and foremost to the Creator?

And yet how could someone so sudden and so unknown have been admitted into the synagogue—someone whose tribe, people, household, and finally enrollment in the census [Col. 0370C] of Augustus were still known with certainty to no one? [Note: [Col. 0369D] “Finally, concerning the census of Augustus,” etc. What this census was, and to which census the statement should be referred, is the subject of considerable controversy. Baronius, in the *Apparatus to the Annals*, considers it the same census as the one mentioned by the Evangelist. This does not seem to me far from the truth. Casaubon, in his notes on Spartianus, explains it as a census ordinance, though I do not know on whose authority. I would more readily agree with Petavius, who writes that there were two censuses under Quirinius, if only that were certain. For if any room is granted for conjecture, I would offer my own conjectures with as much right as the learned Petavius. I would think that the ἀπογραφή (*apographē*, “registration”) conducted under Sentius Saturninus was the same as the [Col. 0370D] enrollment under Quirinius. I conjecture that Saturninus was the governor and Quirinius the procurator. Justin, indeed, designates him by this title in *Apology* II: ἐπὶ Κυρηνίου τοῦ ἡμέτερου ἐν Ἰουδαίᾳ πρώτου γενομένου ἐπιτρόπου, “under your Quirinius, when he first became procurator in Judaea.” Someone may object to me that this was insufficiently honorable after all the honors he had attained and the highest dignities he had discharged. But Augustus may have arranged it because of the greater confidence he had conceived in Quirinius’s ability; and thus Saturninus, in order in some fashion to favor the emperor’s will by complying with it, was governor in name only. For Eusebius, Book I, chapter 5, should be understood in this way: ἡγεμονεύοντος Κυρηνίου τῆς Συρίας, “while Quirinius was governing Syria.” In view of these considerations, I do not know whether anyone would dare pronounce Petavius correct when he holds that no procurators of Judaea existed at that time. LE PR.]

The Roman archives preserve that census as a most trustworthy witness of the Lord’s birth. They would certainly have remembered that he could not be admitted into the Holy of Holies unless they knew he had been circumcised. [Note: [Col. 0370D] “But even if the synagogue was entered indiscriminately.” That is, even by proselytes and Gentiles. Nor does Eusebius disapprove of laypeople ὁμιλεῖν (*homilein*, “speaking”) even in the Christian church, provided it is done τῇ τοῦ προεστῶτος ἐποπτείᾳ (*tē tou proestōtos epopteia*, “under the supervision of the presiding officer”). RIG.] But even if the synagogue was entered indiscriminately, one was nevertheless not admitted to teach unless he was thoroughly known, examined, and approved, having long before been commended for this very purpose—or [Col. 0371A] commended from elsewhere together with this commission.

Now everyone was astonished at his teaching, plainly “because,” it says, “his word was with authority” (Luke 4:32) [Note: [Col. 0371D] “Because his word was with authority.” That is, his word was powerful. Luke: ἐπὶ τοῖς λόγοις τῆς χάριτος, “at the words of grace.” RIG.], not because he taught against the Law and the Prophets. For divine speech certainly displayed both power and grace, building up rather than destroying the substance of the Law and the Prophets. Otherwise they would not have been astonished but horrified; they would not have marveled but would immediately have opposed [Note: [Col. 0371D] “become adversaries of,” alternative reading.] the destroyer of the Law and the Prophets—and above all, surely, the preacher of another god. For he could not have taught against the Law and the Prophets, and on that account against the Creator, without first making a declaration of a different and rival divinity.

Since, therefore, Scripture indicates no such thing, but only that the power and authority of his speech were the object of wonder, [Col. 0371B] it shows more readily that he taught in accordance with the Creator, because he did not deny him, than that he taught against the Creator, because Scripture did not indicate it. Thus either he must be recognized as belonging to the one in accordance with whom he taught, or he must be judged a traitor if he taught in accordance with the one against whom he had come.

In that same place a demonic spirit cries out (Luke 4:34):

> What have we to do with you, Jesus? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God.

Here I shall not reconsider whether this designation was also appropriate to one who ought not even to have been called Christ if he did not belong to the Creator. An account has already been demanded elsewhere concerning the names. But now I ask how the demon knew to call him this, when no proclamation concerning him had ever previously been issued by the unknown god, who had remained silent until that time. Nor could the demon testify that he was that god’s holy one, since this god was unknown even [Note: [Col. 0371D] “now unknown,” alternative reading.] to the demon’s own Creator.

[Col. 0371C] What deed characteristic of the new divinity had Christ yet performed by which he could be understood as the holy one of another god? Only this: he had entered the synagogue and had done nothing even in his discourse against the Creator. Therefore, just as the demon could in no way have recognized as Jesus and the Holy One of God someone whom it did not know, so it recognized the one whom it did know. For it remembered both that the prophet had proclaimed the Holy One of God and that Jesus was God’s name in the son of Nun. According to our Gospel, it had also received these words from the angel (Luke 1:35):

> Therefore that which will be born in you will be called holy, the Son of God, and you shall call his name Jesus.

And the demon certainly possessed some understanding—demon though it was—of the Lord’s dispensation, rather than of an alien dispensation not yet adequately known. For it began by saying, “What have we to do with you [Note: [Col. 0371D] Jun. adds “Jesus.”]?” It did not speak as though Jesus were a stranger [Note: [Col. 0371D] “not to a stranger, but to one with whom,” Jun.], since [Col. 0371D] the Creator’s spirits belong to him. Nor did it say, “What have you to do with us?” but “What have we to do with you?” It was lamenting itself and reproaching its own allotted fate. Seeing that fate already, it added, “Have you come to destroy us?” Thus thoroughly had it recognized Jesus as the Son of a judging, avenging, and—[Col. 0372A] so to speak—savage God, not of that supremely good god who does not know how to destroy or punish.

Why have we placed this passage first? To show that the Jesus recognized by the demon was no other [Note: [Col. 0371D] “and” omitted in another reading.], and that the Jesus attested by himself was no other than the Creator’s. “But,” you say, “Jesus rebuked him.” Certainly—as one who was malicious, insolent even in his confession, and [Note: [Col. 0372D] “as,” Seml.] offering wicked flattery, as though this were the highest glory of Christ: that he had come to destroy demons, rather than to save human beings. For he wished his disciples to glory, not in the subjugation of spirits, but [Note: [Col. 0371D] “In the white robe of salvation.” Understand “robe,” unless you prefer, [Col. 0372D] with Rhenanus, to take *candida* substantivally. This expression is commonly derived from the Romans, among whom candidates for public office wore a white robe and were therefore called *candidati*. LE PR.] in the white robe of salvation.

Or why did he rebuke him? If because he had lied altogether, then he was neither Jesus nor the Holy One of God at all. If because he had lied in part—because he had indeed regarded him as Jesus and the Holy One of God, but as belonging to the Creator—then Christ [Col. 0372B] most unjustly rebuked the demon for believing what it knew ought to be believed, and for not believing what it did not know ought to be believed [Note: [Col. 0372D] “judged,” Seml.]: namely, another Jesus and the holy one of another god. But if the rebuke has no more plausible basis than the one we propose, then the demon told no lie and was not rebuked for lying. For he was indeed Jesus, besides whom the demon could not have recognized another; and Jesus confirmed the one whom the demon had recognized, since he did not rebuke the demon for lying.

## CHAPTER VIII

According to prophecy, the Creator’s Christ was to be called a Nazarene; hence the Jews call us too Nazarenes [Note: [Col. 0372D] “Nazarenes,” Seml.] because of him. For we are those of whom it is said (Lam. 4:7):

> The Nazarenes were whiter than snow.

That is, those who had formerly been made sallow by the stains of transgression [Col. 0372C] and blackened by the darkness of ignorance.

The designation “Nazarene” was also to apply to Christ because of the hiding place of his infancy, to which he withdrew at Nazareth in order to avoid Archelaus, the son of Herod. I have not omitted this point because Marcion’s Christ ought to have renounced every connection even with places familiar to the Creator’s Christ. He had so many towns in Judaea available that had not been assigned [Note: [Col. 0372D] “made over,” Jun.] in this fashion to the Creator’s Christ through the Prophets. In any case, Christ will belong to the Prophets wherever he is found in accordance with the Prophets.

And yet even at Nazareth he is not recorded as having preached anything new, since he is reported to have been expelled for a different reason, on account of a single proverb (Luke 4:23). Noticing here for the first time that hands were laid upon him, I must now establish in advance something concerning his bodily substance: one who allowed himself to be touched—and indeed [Col. 0372D] with full violence, being detained, seized, and dragged all the way to the precipice—cannot be believed to have been a phantom. For even though he escaped through their midst, he had already first experienced their violence and was afterwards released, obviously because the disturbance subsided, as commonly happens, or because he broke through it. [Col. 0373A] Yet he did not evade them by means of a mist, which, had he been one, would have yielded to absolutely every touch.

> For nothing except body can touch or be touched.

[Note: [Col. 0373D] “For nothing except body can touch or be touched,” etc. He also cited this same statement in chapter 5 of *On the Soul*, in order to establish there that the soul is corporeal. It is found in Lucretius, *On the Nature of Things*, Book I, against whose delusions Lactantius argues in Book VII [Col. 0374D] of the *Divine Institutes*. LE PR.]

This is a saying worthy even of secular wisdom. In short, he himself soon afterwards touched others; laying upon them hands that could certainly be felt, he conferred the benefits of healing—benefits as real and as little imaginary as the hands through which he conferred them.

He himself, therefore, is the Christ of Isaiah as well, the restorer of health:

> He, it says, takes away our infirmities and bears our sicknesses (Isa. 53:4).

The Greeks are also accustomed to use “bear” in the sense of “take away.” For the present, the general promise is enough for me. Whatever Jesus heals, he is mine. We shall nevertheless come to the particular kinds of healing as well.

Moreover, liberation from demons [Col. 0373B] is itself a healing of health. Accordingly, evil spirits, as though following the pattern of the previous example, departed with testimony, crying out:

> You are the Son of God.

Let it be evident here too whose God. Yet in the same way they were rebuked and commanded to be silent. For Christ wished to be recognized as the Son of God by human beings, not by unclean spirits. This applies, at any rate, to that Christ to whom such conduct was appropriate, because he had sent before him those through whom he could be recognized, and who were certainly more worthy heralds. It belonged to the one who abounded in holy spirits to reject the proclamation of an unclean spirit.

But one who had never been announced—if he nevertheless wished to be recognized, and he had come in vain if he did not—would not have scorned testimony from an alien substance, whatever its character, since he had no testimony from his own and had descended into another’s domain. Moreover, precisely as the destroyer [Col. 0373C] of the Creator, he could have done nothing more useful than to be recognized and publicized by the Creator’s own spirits out of fear—except that Marcion denies that his god is feared. He maintains that the good god is not feared, but only the judge, with whom lie the grounds for fear: anger, savagery, judgments, vengeance, and condemnation.

Yet the demons were certainly yielding from fear. They were therefore confessing the Son of a God who was to be feared, though they would have had grounds not to yield if he were not to be feared. And he, driving them out by command and rebuke, rather than by persuasion as a good being, showed himself to be feared. Or did he perhaps rebuke them because he was feared, though he did not wish to be feared? And how did he wish them to depart, when they would not have done so except from fear? He therefore fell under the necessity of acting contrary to his own nature, although as a good being he could simply have spared them.

He also incurred another charge of betrayal: he permitted himself to be feared by the demons as though he were [Col. 0373D] the Creator’s Son, so that he no longer expelled demons by his own power, but through the Creator’s authority.

He goes out into the wilderness. This too is a region customary to the Creator. It was fitting that the Word should be seen there in a body where he had once acted in a cloud. The character of the place that had pleased the Law was also appropriate to the Gospel.

> Let the wilderness, therefore, receive joy.

Isaiah had promised this (Isa. 35:1).

When he was detained [Col. 0374A] by the crowds, he said (Luke 4:42):

> I must proclaim the kingdom of God to other cities also.

Had he already revealed his own god anywhere? I do not think he had, even by this point. But was he speaking about people who knew another god as well? I do not believe that either. Therefore, if neither had he disclosed another god, nor did they know any god besides the Creator, he was announcing the kingdom of the same God whom alone he knew to be known by those who were listening.

## CHAPTER IX

Among so many kinds of occupation, why did he turn specifically to fishing, so as to take Simon and the sons of Zebedee from that occupation into the apostolate? This cannot be regarded as a simple event, since an argument was to proceed from it when he said to Peter, who was alarmed at the abundant catch of fish (Luke 5:10):

> Do not be afraid; [Col. 0374B] from now on you will be catching human beings.

By this saying he suggested to them the understanding that a prophecy had been fulfilled: that he was the one who had declared through Jeremiah (Jer. 16:16):

> Behold, I shall send many fishermen, and they will fish for them—

human beings, that is. Finally, leaving their little boats behind, they followed him, understanding him to be the one who had begun to do what he had foretold.

It would be another matter if he had been eager to choose his men from the guild of boatmen because he was one day to have as his apostle Marcion, the shipmaster.

Against the *Antitheses* we have already laid the groundwork that the difference between the Law and the Gospel, as Marcion conceives it, does nothing to advance his case, since this difference too was ordained by the Creator and was finally proclaimed in the promise of a new law, a new word, and a New Testament. But because Marcion argues the point more elaborately before that wretched fellow of his—I know not [Col. 0374C] whom—his συνταλαίπωρος (*syntalaipōros*), that is, his “fellow-wretch,” and his συμμισούμενος (*symmisoumenos*), that is, his “fellow-object of hatred,” [Note: [Col. 0374D] “Before that certain fellow of his—I know not whom,” etc. Interpretations of the Greek words have slipped into the text from the margin. LE PR.] in connection with the cleansing of the leper, I shall not be reluctant to meet his argument and, first of all, to demonstrate the force of the figurative Law.

In the example of the leper, who was not to be touched but rather excluded from all association, the Law prohibited fellowship with a person stained by sins. The Apostle likewise forbids even taking food with such people (1 Cor. 5:11), for the marks of sins are shared, as though by contagion, if anyone associates himself with a sinner.

Accordingly, the Lord wished the Law to be understood more profoundly, as signifying spiritual realities through bodily ones. On this account he was not destroying the Law, but building it up even more in the way he wished it more appropriately to be recognized. He touched the leper. Although a human being could have been defiled by him, God certainly would not have been defiled, since he is incapable of contamination. No objection can therefore be raised [Col. 0374D] against him that he ought to have observed the Law and not touched an unclean person, since contact with an unclean person was not going to defile him.

I teach that this is more appropriate to my Christ by demonstrating that it is not appropriate to yours. For if he touched the leper as a rival of the Law, treating the Law’s command as nothing through contempt for defilement, how could one who had no body capable of being defiled have been defiled? A phantom [Col. 0375A] could not be defiled. Therefore, one who could not be defiled because he was a phantom will no longer be incapable of contamination by divine power, but by the emptiness of a phantom. Nor can he be thought to have despised defilement when he did not possess the material upon which it could act. Thus neither did he destroy the Law, since he escaped defilement because he was a phantom, not through a display of power.

Now if Elisha, a prophet of the Creator, healed only one leper, Naaman the Syrian, out of so many Israelite lepers (2 Kings 5:14), this does not establish a difference in Christ, as though Christ were better because, though an outsider, he cleansed [Note: [Col. 0375D] “cleanses,” Seml.] an Israelite leper whom his own lord had been unable to cleanse. The Syrian was more readily cleansed because the cleansing of the nations was signified [Note: [Col. 0375D] “signifies,” Seml.] in Christ, their light. They bristled with the seven stains of the chief sins: idolatry, [Col. 0375B] blasphemy, murder, adultery, sexual violation, false testimony, and fraud.

[Note: [Col. 0375D] “The seven stains of the chief sins.” Here you have a very different enumeration from the commonly transmitted list of the seven capital sins, since idolatry, blasphemy, murder, adultery, sexual violation, false testimony, and fraud are enumerated. Of these, idolatry and blasphemy can be referred to pride, murder to anger, adultery and sexual violation to lust, and false testimony and fraud to avarice; but envy, gluttony, [Col. 0376D] and sloth will still remain in addition. Cyprian also places three of those enumerated here—adultery, fraud, and murder—among mortal crimes in his book *On the Good of Patience*. Finally, the author of *On Modesty* numbers these same offenses among the graver and deadly, indeed mortal, sins, except that there he adds denial in place of false testimony and calls “fornication” what here, according to his custom, he calls sexual violation. PAM.]

For this reason Naaman washed seven times in the Jordan, as though under each individual heading, and also so that he might receive [Note: [Col. 0375D] “so many times,” Rig. Venet.] the expiation [Note: [Col. 0375D] “sing,” Rig. Venet.] of the entire week [Note: [Col. 0375D] Seml. inserts “and.”], because the power and fullness of a single washing was reserved for Christ alone, who was to perform on earth both an abridged word and, in the same way, an abridged washing.

Marcion also raises this objection: Elisha required material, used water, and used it seven times, whereas Christ, by his word alone and with that word used only once [Note: [Col. 0375D] “having discharged,” Seml.], immediately effected the cure. As though I would not dare to claim the word itself for the substance of the Creator! In every matter, the better claim to authorship belongs to the one who came first. It is plainly incredible that the Creator’s power should have effected by a word a remedy for a single affliction when by a word it once brought forth the immense mass of the world. From what, then, is [Col. 0375C] the Creator’s Christ more readily recognized than from the power of his word?

But he is supposedly another Christ because he acted differently from Elisha—because the master was more powerful than his servant. What are you maintaining, Marcion? That servants should perform deeds in precisely the same way as their masters? Do you not fear that it will turn to your disgrace if you deny that Christ belongs to the Creator because he was more powerful than the Creator’s servant? In comparison with Elisha’s littleness, he is recognized as greater—if, indeed, he is greater. For the cure is equal, although the method differs. What more did your Christ accomplish than my Elisha? Indeed, what great thing did the word of your Christ accomplish, when it accomplished what the Creator’s river had accomplished?

In accordance with these considerations, the remaining points are also answered. Insofar as the avoidance of human glory was concerned, he forbade the man to publicize it; but insofar as [Col. 0376A] the protection of the Law was concerned, he commanded its prescribed order to be fulfilled:

> Go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift that Moses commanded.

For he was still preserving the figurative proofs [Note: [Col. 0376D] “for example,” Seml.] of the prophesied [Note: [Col. 0376D] “prophet,” Seml.; “of the prophet,” Jun.] Law in their own images. These signified that a person who had once been a sinner, but was presently cleansed of stains by the word of God, ought to offer a gift to God at the temple—namely, prayer and thanksgiving in the Church through Christ Jesus, the universal priest of the Father.

He therefore added:

> That it may be a testimony to you.

Without doubt, this was the testimony by which he bore witness that he was not abolishing the Law but fulfilling it; and by which he bore witness that he himself was the one who had been announced as destined to take upon himself their diseases and sicknesses.

Marcion, the flatterer of his Christ, seeks to exclude this thoroughly [Note: [Col. 0376D] “entirely,” Par.] fitting and necessary interpretation of the testimony under the pretext of Christ’s gentleness [Col. 0376B] and mildness. “For,” he says, “being good, and knowing besides that everyone who had been freed from leprosy would perform the solemn requirements of the Law, he commanded it for that reason.”

What then? Did he persevere in goodness—that is, in permitting the Law—or did he not [Note: [Col. 0376D] “or not,” Seml.]? If he persevered in goodness, he will never [Note: [Col. 0376D] “nowhere,” Seml.] be the destroyer of the Law, nor will he be regarded as belonging to another god, since the destruction of the Law, through which he is claimed for another god, has ceased. But if he did not persevere in goodness when he later destroyed the Law, then he afterwards deposited false testimony among them through the healing of the leper; for he abandons goodness when he destroys the Law.

He is now evil when he overthrows the Law, if he was good when he permitted the Law. Yet by permitting obedience to the Law, he also confirmed that the Law was good, for no one allows obedience to an evil thing. Therefore, he is evil even on this account, if he [Col. 0376C] permitted obedience to an evil law; and on the other account he is worse, if he came as the destroyer of a good law.

Likewise, if he commanded the man to offer the gift because he knew that everyone freed from leprosy would do so, he could also have refrained from commanding what he knew would happen of its own accord. He therefore descended in vain as though he were going to destroy the Law, since he yielded to those who obeyed the Law. On the contrary, because he knew their customary practice, he ought rather to have acted beforehand to turn them away from it, if this was why he had come.

Why, then, did he [Note: [Col. 0376D] “therefore,” Seml.] not keep silent, so that the man might obey the Law solely by his own choice? For then Christ might, to some extent, appear to have granted this out of his own forbearance. But he also adds his own authority, intensified by the weight of the testimony. A testimony to what, then, if not to the vindicated Law?

Certainly it makes no difference how he confirmed the Law—whether as good, as superfluous, [Col. 0377A] as forbearing, or as inconsistent—provided that I drive you, Marcion, from your position. [Note: [Col. 0377D] “Drive you from your position.” That is: “I shall refute that objection of yours by which you say that the good god permitted the Law and the evil god took it away”; for this author argues here with great sharpness against these monstrous claims. LE PR.]

See: he commanded the Law to be fulfilled. In whatever manner he commanded it [Note: [Col. 0377D] “commands,” another reading.], in that same manner he could also have uttered beforehand the saying (Matt. 5:17):
