> I did not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it.

Why, then, did you erase from the Gospel something that remains intact? For you have confessed that, out of goodness, he did what you deny he said. It is therefore established that he said it, because he also did it—and that you erased [Note: [Col. 0377D] “Rooted out,” Seml.] the Lord’s utterance from the Gospel, rather than that our people inserted it.

[Note: [Col. 0377D] “Erased from the Gospel,” etc. This refers to the corruption throughout almost the whole Gospel of blessed Luke, including, among other passages, chapter 4, which is under discussion here. LE PR.]

## CHAPTER X
The paralytic also is healed (Luke 5), and indeed in an assembly, with the people looking on. “For the people,” says Isaiah (Isa. 35:2), “shall see the majesty of the Lord and the glory of God.” What majesty and what [Col. 0377B] glory? “Be strengthened, you feeble hands and loosened knees.” This will be paralysis. “Be strengthened, and do not fear.” He does not repeat “Be strengthened” idly, nor add “Do not fear” without purpose, because together with the restoration of the limbs he was also promising the recovery of strength: “Arise, and take up your pallet”; and courage of spirit, so that they should not fear those who were going to say, “Who can forgive sins except God alone?” You therefore now have both the prophecy of this particular healing fulfilled and the prophecy of the events that followed the healing.

Likewise recognize in the same prophet Christ as the forgiver of offenses: “For” [Note: Semler reads “How.”], he says (Isa. 53), “he shall forgive the offenses of many, and he himself bears away our offenses.” And also in the earlier passage [Note: “Earlier” (priore); another reading: “first” (primore).] (Isa. 1:18), in the person of the Lord himself: “Though your offenses be like rose-colored cloth, [Col. 0377C] I shall make them white as snow; and though they be like scarlet, I shall make them white as wool.” In the rose color he indicates the blood of the prophets; in the scarlet, the Lord’s blood, as being brighter.

Micah too speaks of the forgiveness of offenses (Mic. 7:18–19): “What God is like you, removing iniquities and passing over injustices in the remnant [Note: Another reading: “the remaining injustices.”] of your inheritance [Note: Semler inserts “and.”]? He has not retained his wrath as a testimony [Note: “He has not retained it as a testimony.” Here, as elsewhere, Tertullian follows the version of the Seventy Translators. Since they read the Hebrew word as *lahed*, where it ought to have been read *lehad*, they wrote here εἰς μαρτύριον (*as a testimony*), where they might more correctly have written εἰς αἰῶνα (*forever*).—EDD.], because he desired mercy. [Note: “Desired”; Semler reads “and merciful,” which neither makes sense [Col. 0378D] nor agrees with the Septuagint.] He will turn again [Note: Junius reads “He will turn his attention”; “He will return,” according to the Septuagint.] and have mercy on us. He will sink our offenses and plunge our sins into the depths of the sea.”

But even if nothing of this kind had been proclaimed concerning Christ, I would still have examples of this kindness in the Creator, promising me the Father’s dispositions in the Son as well. I see that the Ninevites obtained forgiveness of their crimes from the Creator—not to say, even then, from Christ, since from [Col. 0378A] the beginning he acted in the Father’s name. I read also that the prophet Nathan said to David, when he acknowledged his offense concerning Uriah (2 Sam. 12:13): “And the Lord has put away your offense, and you shall not die.” Likewise King Ahab (1 Kings 21), Jezebel’s husband, guilty of idolatry and of Naboth’s blood, obtained forgiveness on account of repentance; and Jonathan, Saul’s son, erased by entreaty the guilt of having broken the fast (1 Sam. 14). [Note: “Jonathan, Saul’s son, the broken fast,” etc. He calls a fast that has been violated “unsealed” or “broken” (*resignatum*), for Jonathan had given occasion for violating the fast when he put honey to his mouth.—LE PR.]

Why should I rehearse the case of the people themselves, so often restored by indulgence toward their offenses? They were restored, of course, by that God who (Ezek. 33:11) prefers mercy to sacrifice and the sinner’s repentance to his death. Your first task, therefore, is to deny that the Creator ever forgave offenses; the consequence [Note: Semler and Oberthür add “is.”] must then be that you show that he proclaimed nothing of this kind concerning his Christ. In that way you will prove this new kindness [Col. 0378B] of a new Christ—if, that is, you prove that it is neither matched by the Creator nor proclaimed by the Creator.

But whether forgiving sins can belong to one who is denied to retain them; whether absolving can belong to one to whom condemning does not also belong; and whether it is fitting for one to pardon against whom no offense has been committed—we have already engaged with these questions elsewhere [Note: “Already engaged elsewhere.” The passage is Book I, chapter 26.]; and we prefer [Note: The Venice edition and Oberthür read “we preferred.”] to recall them rather than reconsider them.

Concerning the Son of Man our preliminary objection is twofold: Christ could not lie by declaring himself the Son of Man if he was not truly such; nor can one be constituted the son of man who was not born of a human being, whether father or mother. Accordingly, we must determine of which human being he should be understood as the son—of his father or of his mother. If he is from God the Father, then certainly he is not [Note: Semler and Oberthür insert “is.”] from a man. If he is not also from a man as father, it remains that he is from a human mother. If from a human being, it is already evident [Col. 0378C] that he is from a virgin. For where no human [Note: Semler and Oberthür omit “human.”] father is assigned, neither will a husband be assigned to his mother; and where no husband is assigned, she is a virgin.

Otherwise there will now be two fathers, God and man, if the mother is not a virgin. For she will have a husband, so that she is not a virgin; and by having a husband she will create two fathers, God and man, for one who would be the son both of God and of man. Fables perhaps attribute a birth of this sort to Castor or Hercules. [Note: “Castor or Hercules”: both were sons of Jupiter—Castor by Leda, the wife of Tyndareus; Hercules by Alcmena, the wife of Amphitryon.—RHEN.]

If these distinctions hold—that is, if he is the son of a human being through his mother because he is not so through his father, and if he is from a virgin mother because he is not from a human father—then this will be Isaiah’s Christ, whom he proclaims that a virgin will conceive. On what grounds, therefore, you admit the Son of Man, Marcion, I cannot see. If he is the son of a human father, you deny that he is [Col. 0379A] the Son of God; if he is also the Son of God, you turn Christ into the Hercules of a fable; if he is the son only of a human mother, you concede my position; if he is not even the son of a human mother [Note: The Venice edition, Semler, and Oberthür read “father.”], then he is the son of no human being, and he who said that he was what he was not must necessarily have committed a falsehood.

Only one thing can relieve you in your straits: if you dare either to call your god, Christ’s father, a human being as well—which Valentinus did with the Aeon [Note: Another reading: “which he did not do concerning him.”]—or to deny that a virgin is human, something not even [Note: Semler and Oberthür read “nor.”] Valentinus did. [Note: “Which Valentinus did with the Aeon.” Tertullian seems to offer relief to Marcion, reduced to the greatest straits, and to supply him with an evasion, as though he held the same opinion as Valentinus, who said that Jesus, whom he also called Christ, was composed from the Aeons. But afterward Tertullian sharply casts him down from that position.—LE PR.]

What now, if Christ is designated by the very title “Son of Man” in Daniel? Will that not suffice [Note: Semler and Oberthür read “does that not suffice?”] as proof of the prophetic Christ? For when he calls himself by that designation which was proclaimed concerning the Creator’s Christ, he undoubtedly causes himself to be understood as the very one concerning whom it was proclaimed. A mere sharing of names [Note: Junius reads “a double sharing.”] might perhaps seem possible; and yet we maintain that he ought to have been called neither Christ nor Jesus, since we uphold a distinction of status.

But the designation “Son of Man,” insofar as it arises from a circumstance, is correspondingly unlikely to coincide merely in addition to the sharing of a name. For it arises from a circumstance peculiar [Note: Junius reads “peculiarly.”] to its bearer, especially when the same cause is present through which the sharing occurs. Thus, if Marcion’s Christ too were said to have been born of a human being, then he too would be capable of sharing the designation, and there would be two Sons of Man, just as there are two Christs and two Jesuses.

Therefore, since the designation properly belongs to the one in whom it has its cause, if it is claimed [Note: Semler inserts “and.”] for another, in whom there is a sharing of the name but not also of the designation, then even the sharing of the name becomes suspect in the person for whom the sharing of the designation is claimed without cause. [Col. 0379C] It follows that the one and same person must be believed to be he who is found more qualified to possess both the name and the designation, while the other is excluded because, lacking the cause, he has no share in the designation. Nor will anyone be more qualified to possess both than he who first received both the name of Christ and the designation Son of Man—namely, the Creator’s Jesus.

He it was who was seen by the king of Babylon in the furnace with his martyrs, a fourth figure “like a son of man” (Dan. 3). The same person was revealed plainly [Note: Semler and Oberthür read “likewise he himself.”] to Daniel himself (Dan. 7) as the Son of Man, coming with the clouds of heaven as judge, just as Scripture also shows.

I have said that this could have sufficed concerning the prophetic designation of the Son of Man. But Scripture supplies me with more—namely, through the interpretation of the Lord himself. For when the Jews, looking upon him merely as a man and not yet certain that he was also God, as also being the Son of God, reasonably argued that a man could not forgive offenses, but God alone could, why did he not answer them in accordance with their point concerning a man (Luke 5:24), [Note: The Venice edition and Rigault read “would he answer.”] saying that he had authority to forgive offenses, since in naming the Son of Man he would also be naming a man? The reason must be that he wished, by the very designation “Son of Man,” drawn from the document of Daniel, to strike back at them and show that he who forgave offenses was both God [Note: Another reading: “him.”] and man—namely, that sole Son of Man who, in Daniel’s prophecy, had obtained the authority to judge and therefore surely also to forgive offenses; for he who judges also acquits. Thus, once this stumbling block had been removed by the recollection of Scripture, [Col. 0380B] they might more easily recognize from the very forgiveness of sins that he was the Son of Man.

[Note: “Finally, nowhere up to this point had he declared,” etc. The Author is speaking only of Luke’s Gospel, according to which Christ first declared himself the Son of Man in this passage. For if we speak of all the Gospels, St. Matthew records before this miracle Christ’s saying, [Col. 0380D] “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head,” which is first repeated in Luke 9. Whether those words of Christ occurred before this miracle, as those who composed Gospel harmonies contend, or afterward, as the Author seems to indicate, I leave for others to dispute.—PAM.]

Finally, nowhere up to this point had he declared himself the Son of Man; he did so first in this passage, in which he first forgave sins—that is, in which he first judged, by acquitting. Whatever the opposing side may argue in response to this, consider [Note: Semler and Oberthür read “inspect.”] what kind of argument it is. For it must tend toward such madness that it both maintains that he is the Son of Man without making him a liar, and yet denies that he was born of a human being, lest it concede that he is the virgin’s son.

But since divine authority, the nature of things, and common wisdom do not admit [Note: Semler and Oberthür insert “into.”] this heretical insanity, here too there is occasion to interpose the briefest possible remark about the substance of the body against Marcion’s phantasms. If he was born of a human being, as the Son of Man, he is a body from a body. [Col. 0380C] Indeed, you might more easily find a human being born without a heart or a brain—such as Marcion himself—than without a body, as Marcion’s Christ is supposed to have been. Just so: inspect the heart or brain of that man from Pontus.

## CHAPTER XI

He brings forward the publican whom the Lord chose as an argument, as though he had been chosen by an opponent of the Law, one foreign to the Law and profane in relation to Judaism. [Note: “Foreign to the Law and profane in relation to Judaism,” etc. Above too he has more than once joined *extraneus* (“foreign”) with the genitive. Here he also said “profane in relation to Judaism,” meaning one rejected by the Jews as execrable.—RHEN.] He has forgotten even Peter, a man of the Law, who nevertheless was not merely chosen but also obtained testimony that his recognition had been granted by the Father (Matt. 16:17).

He had nowhere read that Christ was proclaimed as the light, hope, and expectation of the nations. Rather, Christ confirmed the Jews’ position by saying (Luke 5:31) that a physician is not necessary for the healthy but for those who are ill. For if he wished the Gentiles and publicans whom he was choosing to be understood as the sick, he was affirming that the Jews were healthy, since he denied that a physician was necessary for them. If this is so, he did wrong to descend for the destruction of the Law, as though to remedy an illness, when those who lived under it were healthy and did not need a physician.

Moreover, what sense does it make for him to have proposed the analogy of a physician without fulfilling it? For just as no one brings a physician to the healthy, so neither does one bring his own physician to persons so utterly [Note: Junius reads “insofar as.”] foreign to him as man is to Marcion’s god—man who has his own author and protector and ought rather to have Christ as physician from that author. This analogy establishes in advance that the physician is more properly supplied by the one to whom the sick belong.

And from where did [Col. 0381B] John suddenly appear in their midst? Suddenly Christ, and suddenly John! Everything that possesses its own complete order in the Creator’s dispensation appears in this way in Marcion’s. But more about John elsewhere; for [Note: Rigault and the Frankfurt edition omit “for.”] we must answer each of the points presently before us. For now I shall maintain this: I shall demonstrate that John accords with Christ, and Christ with John—John being, of course, a prophet of the Creator, and Christ being the Creator’s Christ. Thus the heretic may be ashamed that he has vainly frustrated John’s proper sequence.

For if John had performed no ministry whatsoever in accordance with Isaiah (Isa. 40:3), as the crier in the wilderness and preparer of the Lord’s ways through the proclamation and commendation of repentance; if he had not also baptized Christ himself among the others—then no one would have contrasted Christ’s disciples, who ate and drank, with the pattern of John’s disciples, [Col. 0381C] who fasted and prayed continually. For if any divergence existed between Christ and John and between the flock of each, there would be no demand for comparison, and the object of the challenge would be pointless. No one would be surprised or distressed if rival proclamations belonging to different deities also failed to agree with each other concerning their disciplines, since they had first failed to agree concerning the authorities from which those disciplines came.

So entirely did Christ belong to John, and John to Christ: both belonged to the Creator, and both were preachers and teachers arising from the Law and the Prophets. Otherwise Christ would also have rejected John’s discipline as belonging to another god, and would have defended his disciples as rightly walking in a different manner, since they had been initiated into a different and contrary divinity.

But as things stand, by humbly giving as his reason that the bridegroom’s sons could not fast so long as the bridegroom was with them, while promising that they would fast afterward, when the bridegroom had been taken away from them, he did not defend his disciples but rather excused them, as though they had not been reproached without reason. [Col. 0382A] Nor did he reject John’s discipline, but rather conceded it, assigning it to John’s time and reserving [Note: Junius reads “and.”] it for [Note: Rhenanus reads “of the time.”] his own time. Otherwise he would have rejected it and defended its rivals [Note: Semler and Oberthür read “reserving it, if not,” omitting the remaining words.], if the discipline that already existed had not been his own.

I hold fast to [Note: The Paris and Frankfurt editions read “And now I hold fast to.”] my Christ even under the name of bridegroom, concerning whom the Psalm says (Ps. 19:5–6): “He is like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber; his departure is from the summit of heaven, and his turning aside reaches even to its summit.” [Note: “And his turning aside,” etc. We have also read *devertere* and *deversari* above. A little later we have written: “This bride Christ also calls to himself through Solomon.”—RHEN.]

He also rejoices before the Father through Isaiah: “Let my soul exult,” he says (Isa. 61:10), “in the Lord, for he has clothed me with the garment of salvation and the tunic of gladness, like a bridegroom; he has placed a headdress upon me like a bride.” [Note: The Frankfurt edition, following the Septuagint, reads: “And like a bride he adorned me with adornment.”] For in himself [Note: Semler and Oberthür omit “for” (*enim*).] he also reckons the Church, concerning which the same Spirit says to him (Isa. 49:18): “And you shall put all of them around yourself like a bride’s adornment.” [Note: The Frankfurt edition reads “a bride.”]

[Col. 0382B] This bride Christ also [Note: Semler and Oberthür omit “also.”] summons to himself through Solomon by the calling of the Gentiles. For you have read (Song 4:8): “Come, bride, from Lebanon.” The mention of Mount Lebanon is elegantly introduced, for among the Greeks “Lebanon” is a term for frankincense; [Note: “Which is a term for frankincense among the Greeks.” In Theophrastus and Dioscorides it denotes frankincense and the frankincense-producing tree. In Dioscorides, Book I, chapter 38, φλοιὸς λιβάνου means “the bark of the frankincense tree.” Among the Hebrews too, frankincense is named from its whiteness, and Mount Lebanon is distinguished by its loftiest cedars.—LE PR.] for he will betroth the Church to himself out of idolatry.

Now deny that you are utterly insane, Marcion. Look: you attack even the law of your own god. He does not join marriages; he does not accept marriages already joined; he baptizes [Note: Semler and Oberthür read *tingit* for *tinguit*.] no one unless celibate or a eunuch; he reserves baptism until death or repudiation. Why, then, do you make his Christ a bridegroom? That title belongs to him who joined male and female, not to him who separated them.

You have also erred in that pronouncement of the Lord in which he seems to distinguish new things from old. You have been puffed up with old wineskins and had your brain knocked out by new wine; and thus you have sewn the patch of heretical novelty onto the old—that is, the earlier—Gospel. In what respect, [Note: The Venice edition reads *Inquo*.] I should like to learn, is the Creator different [Note: Some read “otherwise.”], when through Jeremiah (Jer. 4:3) he commands: “Renew for yourselves a new renewal,” does he not turn them away from old things? When he declares through Isaiah (Isa. 43:18–19), “The old things have passed away; behold the new things that I am making,” does he not turn them toward new things?

We established long ago that this appointed disposition of the former things, promised rather by the Creator, is manifested by Christ under the authority of one and the same God, to whom both the old and the new belong. For neither does he put new wine into old wineskins unless he has also possessed the old wineskins; nor does anyone put a new patch on an old garment unless he has also had the old garment. A person does not refrain from doing something, if it ought not to be done, unless he possesses the means from which he could do it, if it ought to be done.

Accordingly, [Note: Semler and Oberthür insert “and.”] if he directed the analogy to this purpose, to show that he was separating the newness of the Gospel from the oldness of the Law, he was showing that the Law from which he separated it was his own. The separation was not to be characterized as a separation of one’s own things from things belonging to others, because no one joins his own things to another’s in order afterward to be able to separate them from those other things. Separation presupposes the conjunction from which it is made. Thus the things [Note: Junius reads “And so also the things.”] that he separated he also showed to have been united in one, just as they would have remained had he not separated them.

Yet we concede this separation as one effected through reform, enlargement, and advancement, just as the fruit is separated from the seed although it is fruit arising from the seed. In the same way the Gospel is separated from the Law as it develops out of the Law: it is something other than the Law, but not foreign to it; different, but not contrary.

Nor is the form of Christ’s speech new. When he presents analogies and resolves questions, he comes from the seventy-seventh Psalm: “I shall open,” he says, “my mouth in a parable”—that is, in an analogy—“I shall utter problems”—that is, I shall expound questions. [Note: “I shall open my mouth in a parable.” That is: I shall shape my words to the capacity of human weakness. Concerning the parables of the ancient writers, Seneca says in Letter 59: “Those who spoke simply and for the sake of demonstrating a matter are full of parables, which I consider necessary—not for the same reason as poets do, but so that they may be supports for our weakness and may bring the learner and hearer into the immediate presence of the matter.” Cicero calls a parable a comparison. Quintilian, Book VIII: “In every parable, either the analogy comes first and the subject follows, or the subject comes first and the analogy follows.”—RIG.]

If you had wished to prove that a man belonged to another nation, you would surely have proved it from the distinctive character of his speech.

## CHAPTER XII

Concerning the Sabbath too, I first submit that this question could not have arisen [Note: Rigault and the Venice edition read “not even.”] unless Christ carried about with him the title “Lord [Note: Semler and Oberthür read “God.”] of the Sabbath.” [Note: “Unless Christ carried about the title Lord of the Sabbath,” etc. Here Tertullian alludes to Christ’s saying, “The Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath,” about which Epiphanius says: “At once,” he says, “the Savior confesses himself to be two things together, both Son of Man and Lord of the Sabbath, teaching that the Sabbath should not be regarded as foreign to his own creation.”—PAM.]

For there would have been no dispute over why he was destroying the Sabbath if he ought to destroy it. Moreover, he ought to destroy it if he belonged to another god, and no one would have been surprised that he did what was appropriate to him. They were therefore surprised because it was not appropriate for him to profess the Creator as God and yet attack his Sabbath.

And so that we may settle each of the initial points and not have to raise the same arguments everywhere against every argument of our opponent that relies on some new institution of Christ, the following definition will now stand: the reason why the newness of each institution was disputed was that up to this point nothing had been disclosed concerning a new divinity, just as nothing had been disputed concerning one. Nor can it be retorted that the very newness of each institution sufficiently demonstrated that Christ belonged to another divinity, since it has been established that the newness itself was proclaimed by the Creator and therefore should not be regarded as surprising in Christ.

Surely another god ought first to have been disclosed and his discipline introduced afterward, because God confers authority upon a discipline, not a discipline upon God—unless, of course, Marcion, so thoroughly perverse, learned his letters not through a teacher but his teacher through his letters.

[Col. 0384A] I direct the remainder of my argument concerning the Sabbath as follows. If Christ interfered with the Sabbath, he acted according to the Creator’s precedent. For during the siege of the city of Jericho, when the Ark of the Covenant was carried around its walls for seven [Note: Semler and Oberthür read “eight.”] days, including the Sabbath, the Creator, by his own command, destroyed the Sabbath through work—or so those suppose who hold the same opinion concerning Christ, unaware that neither Christ nor the Creator destroyed the Sabbath, as we shall soon explain.

And yet even then the Sabbath was shaken through Jesus, so that this too might be announced in advance concerning Christ—even if he persecuted the Jews’ most solemn day with hatred, as a Christ who did not belong to the Jews. By professing hatred of the Sabbath, too, he followed the Creator, as the Creator’s Christ, who exclaims through the mouth of Isaiah (Isa. 1:14): “My soul hates your new moons and Sabbaths.” But in whatever sense these words may have been spoken, we know [Col. 0384B] that in this case too a blunt challenge must nevertheless be applied.

I shall now debate the very subject matter in which Christ’s discipline seemed to destroy the Sabbath. The disciples had become hungry; on that day they had plucked ears of grain and rubbed them in their hands. [Note: Rigault, Semler, and the Venice and Oberthür editions read *efflixerant*; the Paris edition reads *effixerant*.] By preparing food they had broken the holiday. Christ excuses them and is charged with violating the Sabbath. The Pharisees accuse him; Marcion seizes upon the issue of the controversy (that I may frame some issue by means of the truth of my Lord): the written word and the intention [Note: *Scripti et voluntatis*: γραμμάτων καὶ διανοίας, “the letter and the intention.”—RIG.].

The letter is drawn from the Creator’s Scripture, while the ostensible defense is drawn from Christ’s intention, as though from the example of David entering the temple on the Sabbath and preparing food by boldly breaking the loaves of presentation, that is, the showbread. For David too remembered the privilege granted to the Sabbath from the beginning, when the day itself was first made known: I mean exemption from fasting. For although the Creator had forbidden manna to be gathered for two days, he permitted it only on the day of preparation, so that the previous day’s provision of food might free the holiday of the following Sabbath from fasting.

It is well, therefore, that the Lord also followed the same rationale in “destroying” the Sabbath, if they wish it to be called a destruction of the Sabbath [Note: Another reading: “of the day.”]. It is well that he also expressed the Creator’s disposition by honoring the Sabbath as a day not for fasting. Indeed, he would then truly have destroyed the Sabbath and the Creator himself if he had commanded the disciples to fast on the Sabbath, contrary to the established letter and intention of the Creator.

But because [Note: “He did not defend the disciples resolutely.” That is, not forcefully, in the sense in which Fabius Quintilian said in *Institutes*, Book V: “We should by now not even say that one bleats or neighs forcefully, unless we were supported by the judgment of antiquity.”—RIG.] he did not defend the disciples unconditionally but excuses them; because [Note: “He sets human necessity against it, as though pleading for them.” The excuse Christ presented to the people did not destroy the Sabbath. The necessity for food was too immediate for the time of gathering it to be postponed to another occasion. He therefore permitted it, yet did not abolish the Sabbath.—LE PR.] he sets human necessity against the charge as their advocate; [Col. 0385A] because he preserves as the higher honor of the Sabbath the duty not to cause sorrow rather than the duty to remain idle; because he places David and his companions on equal terms with his own disciples in both guilt and pardon; because he approves what the Creator allowed; and because, following the Creator’s example, [Note: Semler inserts “and.”] he himself is so good—for all these reasons, he is supposedly foreign to the Creator!

After this (Luke 6:7), the Pharisees watch to see whether he will perform healings on the Sabbath, so that they may accuse him—certainly as a destroyer of the Sabbath, not as one who professed a new god. Perhaps I shall press this one point everywhere: no other Christ had ever been proclaimed.

The Pharisees, however, were entirely mistaken [Note: Semler reads “will be mistaken.”] concerning the law of the Sabbath because they did not notice that it conditionally prescribed rest from works, limiting it to a particular class of works. For when it says concerning the Sabbath day (Exod. 20:10), “You shall not do any work of yours upon it,” [Note: “You shall not do any work of yours upon it.” Since we have been unable to find this anywhere in the Law of Moses, which he cites here, I suspect that it was once read at Exodus 31, where today the text reads: “Everyone who performs work upon it, that soul shall perish from the midst of his people”; or rather at Leviticus 23, where the following is found very frequently: “You shall perform no servile work upon it,” and, “Everyone who performs work upon it, that soul shall perish from the midst of his people”—especially since he cites this same passage above as well, in the book *Against the Jews*, chapter 4.—PAM. Perhaps Tertullian read *tuum* (“yours”) in place of *tu* (“you”), and the Greek σοῦ in place of σύ, at Exodus 20:10, in this form: “You shall not perform upon it any work OF YOURS”; οὐ ποιήσεις ἐν αὐτῇ πᾶν [Col. 0386D] ἔργον ΣΟΥ (“you shall not do upon it any work of yours”; σοῦ in place of σύ, as in the Septuagint).—EDD.] by saying “yours” it defined human work, which each person carries out through his own craft or business, not divine work.

The work of salvation and preservation, however, is not man’s but God’s peculiar work. Thus the Law says again (Exod. 12:16): “You shall not perform any work upon it except what shall be done for every soul”—that is, for the sake of delivering a soul. [Note: “Except what shall be done for every soul.” The Septuagint indeed reads πλὴν ὅσα ποιηθήσεται πάσῃ ψυχῇ, but it might be translated very well as “except those things, whatever they may be, that are done by every soul.” The Hebrew reading expressly signifies only those things that are eaten by every living creature, almost as our Vulgate translates it.—EDD.] For God’s work may also be done through a man for the salvation [Note: The Paris and Frankfurt editions read “in the salvation.”] of a soul, though it is nevertheless done by God. This is what Christ the man was about to do, because he was also God.

Therefore, wishing to lead them into this understanding of the Law through the restoration of the withered hand, he asks: “Is it lawful on the Sabbaths to do good or not—to deliver a soul or to destroy it?” By promising [Note: The Codex Wouwerianus reads “permitting.”] the work he was about to perform for a soul, he reminded them which works the Sabbath law prohibited—namely, human works—and which it commanded—namely, divine works, those performed for every soul. He was called Lord of the Sabbath because he was protecting the Sabbath as something belonging to himself.

Even if he had destroyed it, he would have done so rightly, as being all the more its lord because he had instituted it. But as its lord he did not destroy it at all. From this it can now be evident that not even when the Ark was carried around Jericho was the Sabbath destroyed by the Creator. For that too was God’s work, which he himself had commanded and which he had arranged for the sake of the souls of his own people, who were placed in the peril of war.

And if somewhere he professed hatred of Sabbaths by saying “your Sabbaths” (Isa. 1:13), he attributed to human beings [Note: The Venice edition reads “a human being.”] those Sabbaths—not to himself—which a people full of offenses celebrated without the fear of God, loving God with their lips [Col. 0386A] but not with their heart. He assigned a different status to his own Sabbaths—that is, to all that was conducted according to his discipline—which he afterward, through the same prophet (Isa. 58:13), declares to be true, delightful, and not to be profaned.

Thus Christ too did not abolish the Sabbath at all. He preserved its law both above in the case of the disciples, when he acted for the sake of the soul by granting hungry men the comfort of food, and now when he heals the withered hand. Everywhere by his deeds he presses the declaration (Matt. 5:17): “I did not come to dissolve the Law, but to fulfill it”; nor [Note: Semler reads “if.”] did Marcion silence him by removing these words.

For here too he fulfilled the Law: by interpreting its qualification, by illuminating the distinction between works, by doing those things that the Law excepts from the Sabbath rest, and by making still holier through his beneficence the Sabbath day itself, which had been holy from the beginning through the Father’s blessing. On that day, namely, [Col. 0386B] he supplied divine assistance—something an adversary [Note: The Frankfurt edition reads “for adversaries.”] would have furnished on other days, lest he adorn the Creator’s Sabbath or render to the Sabbath the works owed to it.

If on that day the prophet Elisha also restored the Shunammite woman’s dead son to life (2 Kings 4:23), you see, Pharisee—and you too, Marcion—that from long ago it belonged to the Creator to do good on the Sabbaths, to deliver a soul and not destroy it. Christ introduced nothing new that did not conform to the pattern, gentleness, mercy, and [Note: The Frankfurt edition reads “and.”] proclamation of the Creator.

For here too he embodies a prophecy of a particular healing. The loosened hands grow strong, just as the loosened knees did in the paralytic.

## CHAPTER XIII
Certainly he proclaims peace and every good thing to Zion and Jerusalem; certainly he ascends the mountain and spends the night there [Col. 0386C] in prayer, and surely he is heard by the Father. Unroll the prophets, then, and examine the whole sequence. “Ascend a high mountain,” says Isaiah (Isa. 40:9), “you who proclaim good news to Zion; raise your voice with strength, you who proclaim good news to Jerusalem.”

[Note: [Col. 0386D] “Ascend a high mountain,” says Isaiah, etc. St. Ambrose, *On Luke*, book V, chapter 6, interprets this prophecy of Isaiah 40 in the same way, as referring to Christ praying on the mountain. PAM.]

Still “with strength”: “They were astonished at his teaching, for he taught as one possessing power” (Luke 4:32). And again (Isa. 52:6): “Therefore my people shall know my name on that day.” What name, if not Christ’s? “For I am he who was speaking.”

[Note: [Col. 0386D] “I who speak,” Oberth.]

For at that time he himself was the one who spoke in the Prophets—the Word, the Son of the Creator: “I am present, when the hour has come, upon the mountains, as one proclaiming the report of peace, proclaiming good things.”

Likewise Nahum (Nah. 1:15), [Col. 0387A] one of the Twelve: “For behold, the swift feet upon the mountain of one proclaiming peace.”

[Note: [Col. 0386D] “Likewise Nahum, one of the Twelve,” etc.—namely, of the prophets. [Col. 0387D] For in Nahum 1 there is found the passage he cites: “For behold, the swift feet upon the mountain of those proclaiming peace,” except that the Septuagint reads ἐπὶ τὰ ὄρη, that is, “upon the mountains.” This is not surprising, since St. Jerome himself writes that here he differs from the Septuagint translators because even the chapters themselves are confused among them through variations of translation. PAM.]

Concerning the voice of nocturnal prayer to the Father, the Psalm is explicit (Ps. 21:2): “My God, I shall cry by day, and you will hear; and by night, and it shall not be in vain for me.” Elsewhere, concerning the same place and voice, the Psalm says (Ps. 3:4): “With my voice I cried aloud to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain.”

You have the representation of the name; you have the act—

[Note: [Col. 0387D] “Deed,” Ciaccon.]

—of the one proclaiming good news; you have the location, the mountain; the time, night; the sound of the voice; and the Father’s hearing.

[Note: [Col. 0387D] “Peace,” Rig., Venet.]

You have the Christ of the Prophets.

But why did he choose twelve apostles, and not some other number? Indeed, from this too I could interpret him as my Christ, proclaimed not only by the words of the Prophets but also by the symbolic evidence of events. For I discover prefigurations of this number in the Creator’s [Col. 0387B] Scriptures: the twelve springs of Elim (Num. 33); the twelve gems on Aaron’s priestly vestment (Exod. 28); and the twelve stones chosen by Joshua from the Jordan (Josh. 4) and deposited in the ark of the covenant. For the same number of apostles was being foreshadowed: like springs and rivers, they would water the world of the nations, formerly dry and barren of [the knowledge of God];

[Note: [Col. 0387D] The editors conjecture that “of God” has been omitted.]

as also through Isaiah (Isa. 43:20): “I shall set rivers in a waterless land”; like gems, they would illuminate the sacred vestment of the Church, which Christ, the Father’s high priest, puts on; and like stones, they would be solid in faith—those whom the true Jesus chose from the washing of the Jordan and received into the sanctuary of his covenant.

What comparable defense of the number is applicable to Marcion’s Christ? Nothing done by him can be regarded as merely incidental when it can be regarded [Col. 0387C] as having been done by my Christ with a definite purpose. The event will belong to the one in whose Scriptures its preparation is found.

He also changes Peter’s name from Simon, because the Creator likewise altered the names of Abraham, Sarah, and Hoshea, calling the latter Jesus—

[Note: [Col. 0387D] “Calling the latter Jesus.” This is the same as Joshua. EDD.]

—and adding syllables to the names of the former. But why “Peter”? If it was because of the strength of his faith, many names drawn from strong and solid substances would have been available to him. Or was it because Christ too is both rock and stone? For we also read (Isa. 8:14; 1 Pet. 2:8) that he was appointed “as a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.” I omit the rest. Thus he desired to share particularly with the dearest of his disciples a name drawn from his own figures—more properly, I think,

[Note: [Col. 0387D] “More nearly,” Rig., Venet., Seml.]

than from figures that were not his own.

A multitude comes together from Tyre and from other regions, even from across the sea. This—

[Note: [Col. 0387D] “These,” Ciaccon.]

—the Psalm had in view (Ps. 86:4): “And behold, the Philistines and Tyre, [Col. 0387D] and the people of the Ethiopians—these were there. [Col. 0388A] ‘Mother Zion,’ a man shall say; ‘and a man was made in her’” (because God was born as man), “and he built her by the Father’s will.” This is so that you may know that the Gentiles then assembled to him because God had been born as man and was going to build the Church by the Father’s will, even from foreigners.

Isaiah likewise says (Isa. 49:12): “Behold, these come from afar; these come from the north and the sea; and others from the land of the Persians.” Concerning them he says again (ibid. 18): “Lift up your eyes round about and see: they have all been gathered together.” And further below concerning them (ibid. 21): “You see—

[Note: [Col. 0387D] “Seeing,” Lat., Jun.]

—the unknown and the foreign; and you will say in your heart, ‘Who has begotten these for me? Moreover, who has brought these up for me? And where were these people of mine?’”

Is this not the Christ of the Prophets? And who will be the Christ of the Marcionites—if perversity is preferred—if he is not the Christ of the Prophets?

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 0388B]

I now come to his customary pronouncements, through which he presents the distinctive character of his teaching in what I might call Christ’s edict: “Blessed are the beggars” (for this is what the proper rendering of the Greek word requires), “because theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

[Note: [Col. 0387D] “Blessed are the beggars, for this is what the translation requires,” etc. The Greek at Luke 6 is πτωχοί, which properly means “beggars,” in accordance with the expression from Aristophanes’ *Plutus*, πτωχοῦ vita vivere, “to live a beggar’s life,” that is, the life of one who possesses nothing; whereas πένητος, that is, “of a poor person,” means to live sparingly and devote oneself to labor. Above, however, in *On Idolatry*, chapter 12, he translated it “happy are the needy.” PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0388D] “Of God,” Seml., Oberth.]

The very fact that he began with blessings belongs to the Creator, who, when he brought the whole universe forth, consecrated it with no utterance other than one of blessing.

[Note: [Col. 0388D] “With blessings,” Rig., Venet.]

“For my heart,” he says (Ps. 44:1), “has poured forth an excellent word.” This will be the excellent word—the word of blessing, namely—which is also recognized as inaugurating the New Testament after the example of the Old.

[Note: [Col. 0388D] “Of the Old,” Jun.]

What wonder is it, then,

[Note: [Col. 0388D] “Is” omitted by Seml.]

if he also began from the Creator’s own affections through such a pronouncement—the Creator who has always loved, consoled, defended, and vindicated beggars, the poor, the humble, widows, [Col. 0388C] and orphans? Thus you may believe that this kindness, supposedly Christ’s private possession, is a stream flowing from the Savior’s fountains.

In truth, amid so great an abundance of statements of this kind, I do not know where to turn. As though in a forest, a meadow, or a grove of fruit trees, the desired object must be gathered wherever one happens upon it.

The Psalm cries out (Ps. 81:3): “Judge for the orphan and the beggar, and treat the humble and the poor justly. Deliver the poor man, and rescue the beggar from the sinner’s hand.”

[Note: [Col. 0388D] “The Psalm cries out: Judge,” etc. This passage from Psalm 81 differs from the published Vulgate in reading “treat justly,” where all the others, following the Greek δικαιάσατε, have “justify.” PAM.]

Likewise Psalm 71: “He shall judge the beggars of the people in righteousness and shall save the children of the poor.” And in the following words, concerning Christ: “All nations shall serve him.” David, however, ruled over the single Jewish nation, lest anyone suppose that this was said of David merely because he too took in the humble and those afflicted by need.

[Col. 0388D] “For he shall deliver—

[Note: [Col. 0388D] “He delivered,” others.]

—the beggar from the ruler,” he says; [Col. 0389A] “he shall spare the beggar and the poor, and shall save the souls of the poor. From usury and injustice he shall redeem their souls, and their name shall be held in honor in his sight.”

[Note: [Col. 0389D] “Before him,” Fran.]

Likewise (Ps. 9:18): “Let sinners be turned back into hell—all nations that forget God—because the beggar shall not be forgotten forever; the endurance of the poor shall not perish forever.”

Likewise (Ps. 112:5): “Who is like our God, who dwells in the heights and looks upon the lowly in heaven and on earth? He raises the beggar from the earth and lifts the poor man from the dunghill, so that he may make him sit with the princes of the people”—surely in his kingdom.

So too, earlier in the *Books of Kingdoms*,

[Note: [Col. 0389D] *Basiliis*, that is, the Books of Kings, among which our author also numbers the first two, called Samuel by the Hebrews and consequently by Protestants. EDD.]

Hannah, Samuel’s mother, gives glory to God in the Spirit: “He,” she says (1 Sam. 2:8), “raises the poor man from the earth and the beggar, so that he may make him sit with the rulers of the people”—[Col. 0389B] surely in his kingdom—

[Note: [Col. 0389D] “Surely in his kingdom” omitted by Seml.]

“and upon thrones of glory”—surely royal thrones.

Through Isaiah, moreover (Isa. 3:13), how he inveighs against the oppressors of the needy! “But why do you set fire to my vineyard, and why is the plunder of the beggar in your houses? Why do you injure my people and shame the faces of beggars?” And again (Isa. 10:1): “Woe to those who write wickedness; for when they write, they write evil, evading the judgments of beggars and plundering the judgments of the poor among my people.”

He also demands those judgments for orphans and widows, so that they too, being needy, may receive consolation.

[Note: [Col. 0389D] “Of consolation,” Rig., Pamel., Venet.]

“Judge for the orphan and treat the widow justly” (Isa. 1:17),

[Note: [Col. 0389D] “And come, let us be reconciled, says the Lord.” He seems to have read διαλλάχθωμεν, for others translate “let us dispute,” [Col. 0390D] reading διαλεχθῶμεν. LE PR.]

“and come, let us be reconciled, says the Lord.”

To the one whose affection for every condition of lowliness is so great—that is, to the Creator—will also belong the kingdom promised by Christ; for those [Col. 0389C] to whom it is promised have long belonged to his affection. For even if you suppose that the Creator’s promises were earthly, whereas Christ’s were heavenly, it is well that, up to the present, heaven appears to belong to no other God than the one to whom the earth also belongs. It is also well that the Creator promised the lesser things, so that I may more easily trust him concerning the greater, rather than one who had never first established confidence in his generosity by lesser gifts.

“Blessed are those who hunger, because they shall be filled.”

[Note: [Col. 0389D] “They” omitted by Seml.]

I could have transferred this title to the preceding discussion, since those who hunger are none other than the poor and beggars, had not the Creator also specifically appointed this promise as a preparation for his own Gospel. For through Isaiah, concerning those whom he was going to summon from the end of the earth—surely the nations—he says: “Behold, they shall come swiftly and [Col. 0389D] lightly” (Isa. 5:26). “Swiftly,” because

[Note: [Col. 0389D] “Because,” Seml.]

they hasten at the end of the ages; “lightly,” because

[Note: [Col. 0389D] “Because,” Seml.]

they are without the burdens [Col. 0390A] of the former law. “They shall not hunger, nor shall they thirst”: therefore they shall be filled, something surely not promised except to those who hunger and thirst.

And again (Isa. 65:15): “Behold,” he says, “those who serve me shall be filled, but you shall hunger; behold, those who serve me shall drink, but you shall thirst.” We shall also see whether these antitheses are prepared in advance for Christ. For the present, the fact that he promises fullness to the hungry belongs to God the Creator.

“Blessed are those who weep, because they shall laugh.”

[Note: [Col. 0389D] “Who,” Venet.]

Run through Isaiah’s pronouncement (Isa. 65:13): “Behold, those who serve me shall exult in gladness—

[Note: [Col. 0390D] “Shall rejoice,” Oberth.]

—but you shall be confounded. Behold, those who serve me shall rejoice—

[Note: [Col. 0390D] “Shall exult in gladness,” Oberth.]

—but you shall cry out because of the pain of your heart.” Recognize these same antitheses in Christ. Certainly joy and exultation in gladness are promised to those who are in the opposite condition: [Col. 0390B] the sorrowful, the sad, and the distressed. Psalm 125 likewise says: “Those who sow,” it says, “in tears shall reap in exultation.”

[Note: [Col. 0390D] “In joy,” others.]

Laughter, moreover, accompanies those who exult and experience gladness, just as weeping accompanies those who mourn and suffer pain. Thus the Creator, when he foretold the occasions for laughter and weeping, had already said that those who weep would laugh.

Therefore, the one who began by consoling the poor, the humble, the hungry, and those who weep immediately sought to show himself to be the one whom he had revealed through Isaiah (Isa. 61:1): “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor.” “Blessed” (Luke 6) “are the beggars, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” “He sent me” (Isa. 61) “to heal those broken in heart.” “Blessed” (Luke) “are those who hunger, because they—

[Note: [Col. 0390D] “They” omitted by Seml.]

—shall be filled.” “To comfort” (Isaiah) “the afflicted.”

[Note: [Col. 0390D] “To comfort the afflicted.” *Advocare* means “to console” and “to act as advocate for the afflicted,” whom he calls below an *advocator*, “advocate.” RHEN.]

“Blessed” [Col. 0390C] (Luke) “are those who weep, because they shall laugh.” “To give” (Isaiah) “glory to the mourners of Zion, and—

[Note: [Col. 0390D] “And” omitted by Fran.]

—the joy of ointment in place of ashes, and the garment of glory in place of the spirit of weariness.”

If Christ, immediately upon his admission, carried out these things, then either he is himself the one who foretold that he would come for them; or, if the one who foretold them has not yet come, I must say—ridiculously, but necessarily—that perhaps he entrusted them to Marcion’s Christ.

“Blessed shall you be when men hate you, reproach you, and cast out your name as evil—

[Note: [Col. 0390D] “Bad,” Pamel.]

—because of the Son of Man.” By this declaration he undoubtedly exhorts them to endurance.

What less does the Creator say through Isaiah (Isa. 51:7)? “Do not fear disgrace from men, and do not be diminished by their contempt.” What disgrace? What contempt? That which was to come because of the Son of Man. Which Son of Man? The one who exists according to [Col. 0390D] the Creator. How shall we prove it? From the destruction foretold even against him, [Col. 0391A] as through Isaiah (Isa. 52:7) to the Jews, the authors of the hatred:

[Note: [Col. 0391D] “Of the hatred” omitted by Seml.]

“Because of you my name is blasphemed among the nations.” And elsewhere: “Sanctify—

[Note: [Col. 0391D] “Sanctify,” Latin codex.]

—the one who restricts his own soul, who is held in contempt by the nations, servants, and magistrates.”

For if hatred was foretold against that Son of Man who belongs to the Creator, while the Gospel testifies that the name “Christian,” which is of course derived from Christ, would be hated because of the Son of Man—that is, Christ—then it identifies as the cause of the hatred that Son of Man who belongs to the Creator and against whom hatred was foretold.

And surely, if those things had not yet come to pass, the hatred of the name that is occurring today could not have preceded the person who bears the name. For among us he is both sanctified and restricts his own soul, laying it down [Col. 0391B] for us; and he is held in contempt by the nations. The one who was born will himself be the Son of Man because of whom our name also is rejected.

## CHAPTER XV

“Accordingly,” he says (Luke 6), “their fathers used to do these things to the Prophets.” O shape-shifting Christ, now the destroyer and now the defender of the Prophets! He destroyed them as a rival by drawing away their disciples; he claimed them for himself as a friend by branding their persecutors.

Now, just as the defense of the Prophets would have been inappropriate—

[Note: [Col. 0391D] “Not” is absent in others.]

—for Marcion’s Christ, since he had come to destroy them, so the branding of their persecutors is appropriate for the Creator’s Christ, since he was fulfilling them in every respect. Or again, it belongs more properly to the Creator to reproach sons with their fathers’ offenses than to that god who does not punish even the personal offenses of each individual.

“But,” you say, “he was not immediately [Col. 0391C] defending the Prophets merely because he wished the iniquity of the Jews to be affirmed, since they had not treated even their own Prophets piously.” On the contrary, there was no iniquity here for which the Jews should have been reproached. They should rather have been praised and approved, if they prefigured the treatment of those whom the supremely good god was moved to destroy after so great a span of time.

But I think he is already no longer supremely good: he has already acquired some character along with the Creator,

[Note: [Col. 0391D] “He has already acquired some character along with the Creator.” He calls something *moratum* when it is endowed with certain characteristics such as those of the Creator—namely hatred, benevolence, anger, mercy, justice, and clemency. RIG.]

and is no longer entirely the god of Epicurus.

[Note: [Col. 0391D] “Nor entirely the god of Epicurus”: stupefied, inert, ἀλειτούργητος, “performing no service.” RIG.—The Epicureans maintained that God lives free from care, without any business or concern for human affairs; for this reason they rejected dreams, lest they impose business upon God. “The Epicurean,” says Tertullian in *On the Soul*, chapter 46, “judged dreams altogether vain, freeing the divinity from business.” Plutarch says in *On Tranquillity of Mind* that the Stoics were for a time more moderate: ἀπράγμονας εἴναι τοὺς σοφοὺς, ἐκκλίνειν γὰρ τὸ καθῆκον, “The wise are free from business, for they even avoid duty.” Seneca mentions both schools in *On the Happy Life*. LE PR.]

For behold, he changes over to a curse and reveals himself as one who knows how to take offense and become angry: for he says, “Woe.”

But a question arises for us concerning the character of this word, on the supposition that it is not so much a curse as an admonition. Yet what difference does the reason make, when even an admonition is not without the sting of a threat, [Col. 0392A] especially when it is made more bitter by “Woe”? Both admonition and threat belong to one who knows how to become angry. For no one will admonish, and no one will threaten someone not to do a thing, unless he will punish it when done; and no one will punish unless he knows how to become angry.

Others do acknowledge that the word is a curse, but they maintain that Christ pronounced “Woe” in this fashion not properly as an expression of his own judgment, but because “Woe” belongs to the Creator and he wished to set the Creator’s harshness over against them, so that he might commend his own forbearance in the preceding blessings.

[Note: [Col. 0392D] “Might commend his forbearance.” *Sufferentia* is a substantive used for patience, which he presently also interprets as kindness. RHEN.]

As though this did not properly belong to the Creator, who supplies both functions, both as good God and as judge! Since he had set kindness first in the blessings, he could also append severity in the curses, establishing the full range of both forms of discipline: both the blessing that must be pursued [Col. 0392B] and the curse that must be avoided. For he had also set them forth in this way (Deut. 30:19): “Behold, I have set before you blessing and curse.” This also foreshadowed the present arrangement of the Gospel.

Otherwise, what sort of god is he who, in order to suggest his own goodness, set against it the harshness of the Creator—

[Note: [Col. 0392D] “Of God” added by Seml.; “of the other God,” Rhen.]

? A weak commendation—

[Note: [Col. 0392D] “A weak commendation.” This passage, corrupted through the transposition of words, could be restored from the Gorze collation: “a weak commendation,” etc. RHEN.]

—is one that is supported by the destruction of another.

[Note: [Col. 0392D] “Of another” omitted by others.]

Yet—

[Note: [Col. 0392D] “Yet indeed,” Seml.]

by opposing the Creator’s harshness, he confirmed that the Creator must be feared. If he must be feared, surely he must be obeyed rather than disregarded; and now Marcion’s Christ begins to teach obedience to the Creator.

Then, if the “Woe” directed toward the rich belongs to the Creator, Christ therefore is not offended by the rich, but the Creator is; and Christ approves the causes of the rich—I mean pride, glory, worldly pursuits, and neglect of God—by which they deserve a “Woe” from [Col. 0392C] the Creator.

But how can it fail to belong to the same one to condemn the rich who above approved the beggars? Everyone condemns the opposite of what he has approved. Thus, if the curse against the rich is assigned to the Creator, the blessing of the beggars will be defended as belonging to the same; and now Christ’s entire work belongs to the Creator. If the blessing of the beggars is ascribed to Marcion’s god, the curse against the rich will likewise be imposed upon him; and he will now be the Creator’s equal, both good and judge. There will no longer be room for the distinction by which two gods are made; and once the distinction has been removed, it will remain to proclaim that there is one God, the Creator.

Therefore, if “Woe” is an utterance of cursing, or at least some sterner exclamation, and is directed by Christ against the rich, I must prove that the Creator likewise despises the rich, just as [Col. 0393A] I proved him the advocate of beggars, so that in this pronouncement too I may demonstrate that Christ belongs to the Creator.

The Creator did indeed—

[Note: [Col. 0393C] “Indeed” omitted by Pamel.]

—enrich Solomon (1 Kings 3), but this was because—

[Note: [Col. 0393C] “Who,” Jun.]

—when a choice was granted to him, he preferred to request the things that he knew were pleasing to God—wisdom—and had consequently deserved to obtain even the riches that he had not especially desired. And yet the granting of riches is not inconsistent with God, since by means of riches even the rich are assisted with consolation, and many works of righteousness and love are thereby administered.

But it is the vices that attach themselves to riches which are assigned to the Gospel’s “Woe to the rich”: “Because,” he says, “you have received your consolation,” surely from riches, from their glory and worldly fruits.

[Note: [Col. 0393D] “Because,” he says, “you have received your consolation”—that is, comfort. He is continuing the words of Luke 6, differing in that he translates the Greek word ἀπέχετε as “you have received,” both here and shortly afterward, whereas others have “you have had.” He apparently wished to explain the sense in which it means to receive something from another source, like revenue and income from fields. This is especially appropriate here, and the Vulgate translator renders it in the same way at Matthew 6: “They have received their reward.” The Syriac translator also renders it thus. The translator of Irenaeus, book III, chapter 14, renders it not very differently, though more suitably to the Greek word: “you receive.” PAM.]

Thus Moses says in Deuteronomy (Deut. 8:12): “Take care lest, when you have eaten and been filled, and [Col. 0393B] have built great houses, and your flocks and cattle have multiplied, and your silver and gold have increased, your heart be exalted and you forget the Lord your God.”

[Note: [Col. 0394D] “You have built great houses,” etc. The Greek manuscript requires “beautiful.” He has used “flocks” here for “sheep,” although the Greek reads προβάτων, and he ought to have translated it “sheep,” so that he could afterward add the multiplied cattle, or cloven-hoofed animals. LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0393C] “Have been multiplied,” Pamel.]

Likewise, when King Hezekiah was puffed up by his treasures and gloried in them rather than in God before those who had come from Persia, the Creator attacks him through Isaiah (Isa. 39:6): “Behold, the days are coming, and all the things in your house shall be taken away; and the things your fathers amassed shall be carried off to Babylon.”

So too, through Jeremiah (Jer. 9:22), he declares:

[Note: [Col. 0393C] “Declared,” Seml.]

“Let not the rich man glory in his riches”; and he who glories should, of course, glory in God. So too, through Isaiah (Isa. 3:15), he inveighs against the daughters of Zion, puffed up by adornment and abundance of riches. Elsewhere also (Isa. 5:14), he threatens the nobles and the proud: “Hell has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth, and the renowned and the great and the rich shall descend”—this will be Christ’s [Col. 0393C] “Woe” upon the rich—“and man shall be humbled,” surely the man exalted by riches, “and the man shall be dishonored,”

[Note: [Col. 0393C] “Shall be honored,” some.]

surely the man who was honorable on account of his possessions.

Concerning them he again says (Isa. 10:23): “Behold, the Lord of hosts shall confound the glorious with might, and the exalted shall be crushed, and the lofty shall fall by the sword.” Who are these more than the rich? For they have received—

[Note: [Col. 0393D] “Shall have received,” Pamel.]

—their consolation—that is, their glory, honor, and eminence arising from riches.

[Note: [Col. 0394D] “They have received their consolation,” namely. I think he has nothing else in view here than the words of the Gospel rebuking the rich and powerful: “Amen I say to you, they have received their reward.” LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0394C] “And riches,” Jun.]

Turning us away from these things, he also says in Psalm 48: “Do not be afraid when a man has become rich and when his glory abounds, because when he dies he shall not take everything with him, nor shall his glory descend with him.” Likewise in Psalm 61: “Do not desire riches; and if they shine, do not set [Col. 0394A] your heart upon them.”

[Note: [Col. 0394C] “You shall not desire … you shall not set,” Seml.]

Finally, the very word “Woe” was long ago directed through Amos against the rich who overflow with pleasures: “Woe—

[Note: [Col. 0394C] “For” added by Oberth.]

,” he says (Amos 6:4), “to those who sleep on ivory beds and luxuriate upon their couches; who eat kids from the flocks of goats and suckling calves from the herds of cattle, clapping their hands to the sound of instruments. They regarded these things as permanent and not as passing away; they drink strained wine and anoint themselves with the finest ointments.”

Therefore, even if I were to show merely that the Creator discouraged riches, without also showing that he condemned the rich beforehand by the very word Christ used, no one would doubt that Christ’s threat against the rich by means of “Woe” was added by the same one whose discouragement of its very subject matter—that is, riches—had preceded it. For a threat is an addition to discouragement.

[Note: [Col. 0394C] Venet. corruptly reads: “the communication chosen against the rich.”]

He presses the point: [Col. 0394B] “Woe also to those who are filled, because they shall hunger; and to those who laugh now, because they shall mourn.” These will correspond to the statements in the Creator’s Scriptures that were set above in opposition to the blessings: “Behold, those who serve me shall be filled, but you shall hunger” (Isa. 65:12)—surely because you have been filled. And: “Behold, those who serve me shall rejoice, but you shall be confounded”—surely because you who now laugh are going to weep.

For just as in the Psalm (Ps. 125:6), “Those who sow in tears shall reap in gladness,” so in the Gospel those who sow in laughter—that is, in gladness—

[Note: [Col. 0394C] “From gladness,” Rig., Venet.; “and gladness,” Rhen.]

—shall reap in tears. The Creator long ago set these things together; Christ renewed them merely by distinguishing them, not by changing them.

“Woe when men bless you: their fathers used to do the same things to the false prophets.” The Creator likewise denounces through Isaiah (Isa. 3:12) those who pursue human blessing and praise: “My people, those who call you blessed [Col. 0394C] deceive you and disturb the paths of your feet.” Elsewhere he also forbids trust in man altogether, and therefore trust in human praise, as through Jeremiah (Jer. 17:5): “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man.”

And in Psalm 117:

[Note: [Col. 0394C] “You shall not desire … you shall not set,” Seml.]

[Note: [Col. 0394C] “For” added by Oberth.]

“It is good to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in man.” And: “It is good to hope in the Lord rather than to hope in princes.” Thus the Creator rejected everything sought from man, much more a blessing.

For the Creator to reproach their fathers with having praised or blessed false prophets belongs to him just as much as to reproach them for having harassed and rejected the Prophets. Just as injuries to the Prophets would not have concerned [Col. 0395A] the God of the Prophets, so favors shown to false prophets would not have displeased him, unless he were the God of the Prophets.

## CHAPTER XVI

“But I say to you,” he says (Luke 6), “who hear”—showing that this had long ago been commanded by the Creator (4 Esdras 15:1): “Speak into the ears of those who hear.”

“Love your enemies, and bless those who hate you, and pray for those who slander you.”

[Note: [Col. 0395D] “And bless those who hate you,” etc. He seems to combine the Gospel’s words according to their sense; they occur in Luke 6: those who are enemies and hate, curse, and slander. LE PR.]

The Creator included all these things in a single declaration through Isaiah (Isa. 66:5): “Say, ‘You are our brothers,’ to those who hate you.” For if those who are enemies and who hate, curse, and slander must be called brothers, then surely the one who commanded that they be regarded as brothers also commanded that those who hate be blessed and that prayers be offered for slanderers.

[Note: [Col. 0395D] “Three,” Venet., corruptly.]

Plainly, Christ teaches a new patience—

[Note: [Col. 0395D] “Plainly, he teaches a new patience,” etc. This is written according to Marcion’s view, for I do not think these are Marcion’s own words. LE PR.]

—even restraining the repayment of injury permitted [Col. 0395B] by the Creator (Exod. 21:24), who required “an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.” Christ, by contrast, commands that the other cheek be offered in addition and that, over and above the tunic, the cloak also be surrendered.

[Note: [Col. 0395D] “An eye for an eye,” etc. The same words occur in *On the Pallium*, chapter 6. LE PR.]

Plainly, Christ must have added these things as supplements consistent with the Creator’s discipline. Accordingly, the question that must immediately be settled is whether the discipline of patience is proclaimed—

[Note: [Col. 0395D] “Proclaims,” Jun.]

—in the Creator’s Scriptures.

If through Zechariah he commanded (Zech. 7:10) that no one should remember his brother’s malice—and not even his neighbor’s, for he says again, “Let no one—

[Note: [Col. 0395D] “Let each,” Seml.]

—ponder the malice of his neighbor” (ibid. 8:17)—then the one who commanded forgetfulness much more emphatically commanded patience under injury. Moreover, when he says (Deut. 32:35), “Vengeance is mine, and I shall avenge,” he likewise teaches the patience that waits for vengeance.

Therefore,

[Note: [Col. 0395D] Oberth., following Seml., inserts “faith.”]

insofar as it is inconceivable that the same one should appear to require tooth for tooth and eye for eye in repayment of injury who prohibits not only repayment but also vengeance and even the remembering and reconsidering of injury, [Col. 0395C] to that same extent it is disclosed to us how he ordained eye for eye and tooth for tooth: not to permit a second injury by way of retaliation—which he had prohibited by forbidding vengeance—but to restrain the first injury, which he had prohibited by setting retaliation before it,

[Note: [Col. 0395D] “By retaliation set before it,” Seml.; “by an opposing retaliation,” Pamel.]

so that each person, considering the possibility of a second injury, might restrain himself from the first. For he knows that violence is more easily checked by the presentation of retaliation than by the promise of vengeance.

Both measures had to be established in view of the nature and faith of human beings: so that the one who believed God would await vengeance from God, while the one who trusted—

[Note: [Col. 0395D] “Who had confidence,” others.]

less [Col. 0396A] would fear the laws of retaliation.

The Lord of the Sabbath, the Law, and all the Father’s arrangements—Christ—both revealed this intention of the Law, which had suffered from lack of understanding, and made it intelligible by commanding that the other cheek also be offered. His purpose was all the more fully to extinguish the repayment of injury, which the Law too had sought to prevent through retaliation and which prophecy had certainly restrained explicitly, both by forbidding the remembrance of injury and by referring vengeance to God.

Thus, if Christ introduced anything, he did not destroy the Creator’s disciplines, since his command was not opposed to them but assisted them.

Finally, if we consider the very rationale for commanding patience, and indeed such full and perfect patience,

[Note: [Col. 0395D] “If I consider,” Pamel.]

it will not stand unless it belongs to the Creator, who promises vengeance and presents himself as judge. Otherwise, if the one who imposes upon me so great a burden of patience—not merely refraining from striking back but also offering the other cheek; not merely refraining from cursing in return but even blessing; and not merely refraining from withholding my tunic but conceding my cloak as well—is not going to defend me, [Col. 0396B] then he has commanded patience in vain, since he does not provide me with the reward of the command. By this I mean the fruit of patience, which is vengeance. He ought to have permitted it to me if he does not himself provide it; or, if he did not permit it to me, he ought himself to provide it—

[Note: [Col. 0396D] “Should provide it,” Pamel.]

—because it is also relevant to discipline that injury be avenged. For through fear of vengeance all iniquity is restrained. Otherwise, once unrestricted liberty is let loose everywhere, it will rule supreme, gouging out both eyes and knocking every tooth loose.

[Note: [Col. 0396D] “And knocking every tooth loose.” What is “roused” is virtually moved from its place. Thus he elegantly says that when a fist is driven into the jaw, every tooth is knocked loose. Nor is the wish of that wretched man who has been beaten in a brawl an idle one: that he may be allowed to return from it with a few teeth. Lucilius, *Satires* 9:

> I seize this Zephyrus’ snout and lips, and im—

[The supplied source breaks off here.]]

I seize the snout and lips of this Zephyrus, and strike—

I strike, and knock out all the opposing teeth, every one. RIG.]

—to set every tooth in motion [Note: [Col. 0396D] “Knock out,” Lat.] through confidence in impunity. But this is the conduct of a supremely good God, of one who is good and nothing more: to wrong patience, to throw open the door to violence, [Col. 0396C] not to defend the upright, and not to restrain the wicked.

“Give to everyone who asks you”—to the needy, of course; or all the more to the needy, if even to one who has abundance. Therefore, that no one may be in need, you have in Deuteronomy the Creator’s rule prepared for the giver [Note: [Col. 0396D] “Enjoined upon the giver,” Rig., Venet.; “prepared against the giver,” Pam.; “the giver enjoined,” Seml.]: “There shall be,” he says (Deut. 15:4), “no needy person among you, so that the Lord your God, in blessing, may bless you”—the giver, that is, who has brought it about that there is no needy person. And here there is something more, for he does not command that something be given only to one who asks. Rather, he says, “Let there be no needy person among you”; that is, take care beforehand [Note: [Col. 0396D] “Beyond,” Latin.] that there be none. How much more, then, does he establish that one must give to someone who asks, as also in the words that follow: “But if there is a needy person among your brothers, you shall not turn away your heart or close your hand against your needy brother [Note: [Col. 0396D] Seml. omits “your”]. Opening, you shall open your hand to him; lending, you shall lend him as much as he desires” [Note: [Col. 0396D] “Desires,” Oberth.]. [Col. 0397A] For a loan is not ordinarily given except to someone who asks. But more about lending later.

Now if anyone should wish to argue that the Creator indeed commanded giving to brothers, whereas Christ commanded giving to everyone who asks, so that this teaching is new and different: on the contrary, it will be one of those things through which the Creator’s law is present in Christ. For Christ commanded [Note: [Col. 0397D] “Commands,” Fran.] toward everyone nothing other than what the Creator commanded toward brothers. Although the goodness exercised toward strangers is greater, it is not prior to the goodness owed beforehand [Note: [Col. 0397D] “Would be owed,” Seml.] to those nearest us. For who, without loving those nearest him [Note: [Col. 0397D] Seml. and Oberth. omit “without loving those nearest him”], will be able to love strangers? But if goodness toward strangers is the second degree, while goodness toward those nearest us is the first, the second degree will belong to the same one to whom the first belongs—more readily than the second could belong to one in whom the first did not exist [Note: [Col. 0397D] “Does not exist,” Pamel.].

Thus, in accordance with the order of nature, the Creator first [Note: [Col. 0397D] “First” absent from Paris.] taught benevolence toward [Col. 0397B] those nearest us, intending afterward to extend it also [Note: [Col. 0397D] Pamel. omits “also”] to strangers; and, in accordance with the order of his dispensation, he taught it first toward the Jews, and afterward toward the whole human race as well. Accordingly, as long as the mystery was confined within Israel, he rightly commanded mercy toward brothers alone. But when he gave to Christ (Ps. 2:8) the nations [Note: [Col. 0397D] Paris and Rhen. add “as”] for his inheritance, and the ends of the earth for his possession, and what had been spoken through Hosea (Hos. 1–2) began to be fulfilled—“Not my people” became “my people,” and “she who had not obtained mercy” became “she who obtained mercy,” namely, the nation—from then onward Christ extended to everyone the law of his Father’s benevolence, excluding no one from compassion, just as he excluded no one from the calling. Thus, even if he taught something more, this too he received together with the inheritance of the nations.

“And just as you wish men to do to you, do likewise to them” (Luke 6). In this precept, of course, its other part is understood: “And just as you do not wish men to do to you, likewise do not do to them.” If a new God, formerly unknown and even now not yet fully revealed, gave this command—a God who had shaped me by no previous instruction through which I might first know what I ought to desire or not desire for myself, and so what I should do to others because I desired it for myself [Note: [Col. 0397D] Seml. and Oberth. insert “also.”], and what I should not do because I did not desire it for myself—then he has left my judgment unrestricted and has not bound me to consistency between will and deed, so that I should do to others what I desire for myself, and should not do to others what I do not desire for myself. For he did not define what I ought to desire or not desire for myself and others, so that I might conform the deed to the law of the will, and [Note: [Col. 0397D] “So that,” Jun.] might withhold from another what I desire another to provide for me—love, obedience, comfort, protection, and goods of that kind—and, likewise, might [Note: [Col. 0397D] “And,” Seml.] do to another what I do not wish another to do to me—violence, injury, insult, fraud, and evils of that kind.

Indeed, through this inconsistency between will and deed the gentiles act, for they have not yet been instructed by God [Note: [Col. 0398D] “By him,” Oberth., following Seml.]. For although good and evil are known by nature, God’s discipline is not; once it has become known, only then does consistency between will and deed proceed from faith, because conduct is governed by the fear of God. Accordingly, even though Marcion’s god [Note: [Col. 0398D] Latin inserts “even if”] has only now been revealed, once revealed he could not have issued so terse, obscure, and still-blind an abridgment of the precept under discussion—one more readily interpretable according to my own judgment—when he had laid down beforehand [Note: [Col. 0398D] “Restricted beforehand,” Seml., Oberth.] no distinctions for it.

But [Col. 0398B] my Creator, both [Note: [Col. 0398D] Oberth. omits the first “and.”] long ago and everywhere, commanded that the needy, the poor, orphans, and widows be protected, helped, and refreshed. Thus also through Isaiah (Isa. 58:7): “Break your bread for the hungry [Note: [Col. 0398D] Seml. omits “for the hungry”; Seml. adds “beggars”]; and bring into your house the beggars [Note: [Col. 0398D] Seml. omits “beggars”] who are without shelter; and if you see someone naked, clothe him.” Likewise through Ezekiel (Ezek. 18:7), concerning the righteous man: “He will give his bread to the hungry and clothe the naked.” Therefore, even then [Note: [Col. 0398D] “Now,” Paris.] he sufficiently taught me to do to others what I desire to be done to me. Likewise, by declaring, “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness,” he taught me not to do to others what I would not wish to be done to me. Therefore, the precept in the Gospel will belong to him who formerly both laid its foundation and distinguished its parts, and arranged it according to the rule of his own discipline. And he rightly compressed it now into an abridgment, since the Lord—that is, Christ—had also been foretold as one who would make “a shortened word upon the earth” (Isa. 10:23).

## CHAPTER XVII
