Here, when he now introduces the matter of lending (Luke 6)—“And if you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what credit is that to you?”—run through the words that follow in Ezekiel concerning the same righteous man: “He has not,” it says (Ezek. 18:8), “given his money at interest [Note: [Col. 0398D] *Foenore*, another reading.], and he will not take what is in excess” [Note: [Col. 0397D] That is, the surplus from a loan, which is usury. Take care not to suppose, with certain people, that only **τόκον τόκου** (*tokon tokou*), “interest upon interest,” or usury upon usury, is condemned; for all usury is prohibited here, both in the passages of Scripture that are cited and in Tertullian’s intention. Today, however, such a desire for usury has taken hold that people even exceed the interest formerly permitted by Roman laws. For although interest at one percent per month was lawful, and everyone was free [Col. 0398D] to stipulate for that rate (*l. si pro mutua, C. si cert. pet.*, and *l. lecta, D. de reb. cred.*), nevertheless, if anything above that rate had been paid, it was credited toward the principal. By Canon 17 of Nicaea, **ἡμιολίαν** (*hēmiolian*) is prohibited to clerics, that is, interest greater by half than the principal sum. Now, however, avarice is not restrained by these limits. Charles Dumoulin was not afraid to disguise so great a crime with his fabrications. St. Ambrose, [Col. 0399D] in his book *On Tobit* and elsewhere, St. Basil throughout his works, and St. Cyprian in his book *On the Lapsed*, inveigh against moneylenders of this kind. LE PR.].

That is, the surplus from the loan, which is usury. The first step, therefore, was to root out the profit [Col. 0399A] of lending, so that man might more easily be accustomed to surrendering the principal of the loan as well, if necessary, once he had learned to forgo its profit. For we say that this was the work of the Law as it prepared the way for the Gospel. By its earliest commandments, in which benevolence was still stammering, it gradually formed the faith of certain people toward the perfect splendor of Christian discipline. For immediately above it also says: “And he shall return [Note: [Col. 0399D] “You shall return,” Seml., Oberth.] the pledge”—obviously if the debtor is unable to pay; for if he were able to pay, would it be necessary for a man to write that the pledge must, of course, be restored to the payer [Note: [Col. 0399D] “To the one paying,” Pamel.]?

This is stated far more plainly in Deuteronomy (Deut. 24:12): “You shall not sleep upon his pledge; by returning, you shall return his cloak to him around sunset, and he shall sleep in his cloak.” Still more clearly, earlier (Deut. 15:2): “You shall remit every debt that your neighbor owes you, and you shall not [Col. 0399B] demand payment from your brother, because the remission of the Lord your God has been proclaimed.” Now, when he commands that a debt be remitted, obviously to someone unable to repay, this is even more [Note: [Col. 0399D] “For,” Pamel.]; and if the debtor is able to pay, yet he forbids demanding repayment, what else does he teach than that we should lend to one unable to repay, since he has already decreed loss upon the loan [Note: [Col. 0399D] “So great,” Pam., Venet., Seml.]?

[Note: [Col. 0399D] “And you shall be sons of God.” In the Greek text of blessed Luke it is **ὑψίστου** (*hypsistou*), “of the Most High”; here he translates it “of God.” It is not unusual in the Scriptures, however, for “Most High” to be translated in place of “God.” LE PR.]

“And you shall be sons of God.” Nothing could be more shameless, if he should make sons for himself [Note: [Col. 0399D] “He who did not permit us to make sons, by abolishing marriage”: namely, Marcion’s god. For so he says above: “See, you attack the law of your own god as well: he does not join marriages; he does not accept those already joined.” RIG.] who did not permit us to make sons, by abolishing marriage. How will he invite his people into a name that he has already erased? I cannot be the son of a eunuch, especially when I have as my Father the same one whom all things have. For the Creator of the universe is as truly the Father of all as he who created no substance is a eunuch.

Even if the Creator had not joined male and female, and even if he had not granted offspring to every kind of animal as well, I was his son before paradise, [Col. 0399C] before the transgression, before exile, before the two were one [Note: [Col. 0399D] “Before the two were one”: before God had said, “And the two shall be one flesh.” RIG.]. I was made his son anew immediately when he brought me forth with his hands and set me in motion with his own breath. He now calls me his son once again, begetting me no longer into soul but into spirit.

“Because he himself,” it says, “is kind toward the ungrateful and the wicked.” Well done, Marcion! Quite ingeniously you removed the rains and the suns from him, lest he appear to be the Creator. But who is this kind being who has not even been known until now? How is he kind, when no benefits from him have gone before [Note: [Col. 0399D] “Had gone before,” Pam.]? This is rather the kind of kindness displayed by him who had lent out suns and rains as the Creator, though he would receive no repayment from the human race: he who, despite such generosity with the elements, has until now endured men who render to idols rather than to him the debt of gratitude. He is truly kind in spiritual benefits as well; for “the utterances of the Lord are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Ps. 18:11). He, therefore, rebuked the ungrateful, since he deserved to find them grateful—the one whose sun [Note: [Col. 0399D] “Sun,” Pam.] and rains even you, ungrateful Marcion, have enjoyed. Your god, by contrast, could not yet complain of the ungrateful, since he had not prepared anyone to be grateful.

In commanding mercy as well, he says: “Be merciful, just as your Father [Note: [Col. 0400D] Seml. omits “your”] has had mercy on you.” This will correspond to: “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring into your house the beggars [Note: [Col. 0400D] Oberth. omits “beggars”] who are without shelter, and if you see someone naked, clothe him” (Isa. 58:7); and: “Judge for the orphan, and vindicate the widow” (Isa. 1:17). I recognize his ancient teaching, who prefers “mercy rather than sacrifice” (Hos. 6:6). Or if another has now commanded mercy because he too is merciful, why was he not merciful to me for so long an age?

“Do not judge, lest you be judged. Do not condemn, lest you be condemned. Forgive, and you shall be forgiven. Give, and it shall be given to you. They shall give a good measure, pressed down and overflowing, into your lap. With the same measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” (Luke 6). In my judgment, these words express recompense elicited in accordance with merits [Note: [Col. 0400D] “For merits,” another reading; “expresses,” Seml., Oberth.]. From whom, then, comes the recompense? If merely from men, then he teaches a human discipline and reward, and we shall obey men entirely. If it comes from the Creator, as judge and assessor of merits, then he directs our obedience toward him, with whom he establishes that recompense is to be sought or feared according as each person has judged, condemned, forgiven, or measured. If it comes from himself, then he too now judges—which Marcion denies.

Let the Marcionites therefore choose, lest it cost as much to depart from the rule of their master as [Note: [Col. 0400D] “As,” Pamel.] to maintain that Christ teaches obedience either to men or to the Creator. But the blind leads the blind into the pit. Some believe Marcion. Yet the disciple is not above the master. Apelles too [Note: [Col. 0400D] Oberth. omits “too.”], the corrector of Marcion after having been his disciple, ought to have remembered this.

[Note: [Col. 0400D] “Let him remove the beam from his own eye.” In St. Luke the word is **κάρφος** (*karphos*), that is, “straw,” commonly rendered “speck.” He marks the cunning of the heretics, who, like Aristarchuses, pass judgment on others although they themselves are the most culpable. They, as if bleary-eyed and with eyes smeared over, perceive their own faults poorly, while nevertheless being exceptionally keen in identifying even lighter errors in others. Against such people, and others highly pleased with themselves, one may turn the lines found in Plutarch, *On Tranquillity of Mind*:

> **Τί τὸ ἀλλότριον, ἄνθρωπε βασκανώτατε,  
> Κακὸν ὀξυδερκῶς τὸ δ᾽ ἴδιον παραβλέπεις;**

> Why, most malignant man, do you keenly discern another’s evil,  
> yet overlook your own?

LE PR.]

Let the heretic remove the beam from his own eye; then let him convict the speck, if he thinks there is one, in the Christian’s eye. Likewise, let a good tree not produce evil fruit, because neither does truth produce heresy; nor an evil tree good fruit, because neither does heresy produce truth. Thus Marcion produced nothing good from the evil treasury of Cerdo, nor Apelles from Marcion’s. For we shall interpret these sayings, which Christ allegorized concerning men, [Col. 0401A] far more fittingly against the heretics themselves than concerning two gods, according to Marcion’s stumbling block.

I think that I have not rashly maintained up to this point the line by which I determine that absolutely nowhere was another God revealed by Christ. I marvel that Marcion’s adulterating hand stood paralyzed [Note: [Col. 0401D] “At this act of adulteration,” Jun.] at this one passage alone [Note: [Col. 0401D] “I marvel that Marcion’s adulterating hand stood paralyzed.” He means the unheard-of crime by which Marcion corrupted blessed Luke’s Gospel, as we said above. LE PR.]—except that even robbers feel fear. No crime is without apprehension [Note: [Col. 0401D] “No crime is without apprehension.” One who fears is generally convicted of being conscious of a crime; for guilt weighs upon him as his companion, and:

> . . . Let this be your wall of bronze:  
> To be conscious of no wrong.

(Horace, *Epistles*, book I, epistle 1.) LE PR.], because none is without consciousness of itself.

Up to that time, therefore, the Jews knew no other God than the one besides whom they had thus far known no one; nor did they call any other “Lord” than the one whom alone they knew. If so, who will appear to have said, “Why do you call [Note: [Col. 0401D] “Do you call,” singular, Seml.] me ‘Lord, Lord’?” Was it the one who had never been called this, since he had nowhere yet been revealed? Or was it the one who had always been regarded as Lord because he had been known from the beginning—namely, [Col. 0401B] the God of the Jews?

Who likewise could have added, “And you do not do [Note: [Col. 0401D] “You do,” singular, Jun.] what I say”? Was it the one who was only then attempting to teach them, or the one who from the beginning had entrusted to them the utterances of both the Law and the Prophets, and who could therefore reproach them for disobedience even if he had never reproached them otherwise? Moreover, he who before Christ had proclaimed, “This people loves me with its lips, but their heart stands far from me” (Isa. 29:13), was surely charging them with an old stubbornness. Otherwise, how absurd that a new God, a new Christ, the illuminator of so new and so great a religion, should declare those people stubborn and disobedient whom he could never have put to the test!

## CHAPTER XVIII

Likewise, when the centurion’s faith is extolled (Luke 7), it is incredible that he should have professed that he had not found such faith even [Col. 0401C] in Israel if the faith of Israel did not pertain to him. Nor could it yet have pertained to him merely from that point onward, for it would have been too undeveloped to be tested or compared—not to say that it did not yet exist at all.

But why should he not have been permitted to use an example drawn from another’s faith? Because, if that were so, he would have said that such faith had never existed in Israel. By saying instead that such faith ought to have been found [Note: [Col. 0401D] “To find,” Seml.] in Israel, and by having come for the very purpose of finding it, he shows himself to be the God and Christ of Israel; nor would he have censured that faith unless he were its claimant and advocate. A rival, by contrast, would actually have preferred to find that faith in such a state, since he had come rather to weaken and destroy it, not to approve it.

He also raised the widow’s dead son—no new proof. The Creator’s prophets had performed this as well; how much more his Son? Indeed, up to that very moment the Lord Christ had introduced no other God, so that all who were there [Col. 0402A] gave glory to the Creator, saying: “A great prophet has arisen among us,” and “God has visited his people.” Which God? Obviously the God whose people they were and from whom the prophets came. But if they were glorifying the Creator, while Christ, though hearing and knowing it, did not correct them—and this precisely amid so great a proof, the raising of the dead, while they still honored the Creator—then beyond doubt either he was carrying about no other God than the one whom he permitted to be honored in his benefits and mighty works, or else what sense does it make that he should endure them in error for so long when he had come for the very purpose of healing their error?

But John takes offense [Note: [Col. 0402D] “But John takes offense,” etc. This is said according to Marcion’s absurd opinion, which one may learn from Epiphanius, *Against Marcion*. LE PR.] upon hearing of Christ’s mighty works, as though they were those of another. I, however, will first explain the reason for his offense, so that I may more easily dispose of the heretic’s stumbling block.

Now that the Lord himself—the Word and Spirit of the Father, the Lord of mighty works—was active and preaching on earth, it was necessary for the portion of the Holy Spirit which had operated in John, according to the form and measure of prophecy, to prepare the Lord’s ways [Note: [Col. 0402D] “To prepare the Lord’s ways.” Rhen. says that he used *praeparatum*, “that which has been prepared,” for *praeparatio*, “preparation,” just as he often uses *paratura*. Yet this too is a Tertullianic expression: *massalis summa*, “the integral total,” from a word derived from *massa*, “mass.” PAM.] now to depart from John, having, of course, been gathered back into the Lord as into its full and integral sum.

Accordingly, John, now an ordinary man and now one [Note: [Col. 0401D] Oberth. omits “now”] of the crowd, was indeed offended insofar as he was a man, but not because he hoped for or imagined another Christ. For neither could he have hoped for the same Christ [Note: [Col. 0402D] “Whence,” Pamel.] as one who taught or performed nothing new. No one will hesitate concerning someone whom he knows not to exist, and whom he therefore neither hopes for nor imagines. But John was certain that there was no God besides the Creator, both as a Jew and, still more certainly, as a prophet. Thus he hesitated, as it were, concerning one whom he knew to exist but did not know whether this was he.

With this concern, therefore, John too asks: “Are you,” he says, “the one who is coming, or do we await [Col. 0402C] [Note: [Col. 0402D] “Hope for,” Seml., Oberth.] another?” He is simply asking whether the one whom he awaited had himself come. “Are you the one who is coming?”—that is [Note: [Col. 0402D] “Or the one who is to come,” Oberth.], “Are you the one who is to come, or do we await another?”—that is, “Is the one we await someone else, if you are not the one whose coming we await?”

For, as everyone supposed from the similarity of the proofs, he hoped that a prophet might perhaps have been sent in the meantime, distinct from another—that is, from someone greater, namely the Lord himself, whose coming was awaited. Indeed, this was John’s stumbling: he doubted whether the very one whom they awaited had come, though they should have recognized him by the works that had been foretold. Thus the Lord informed John that he was to be recognized by those same works.

Since it is established that these works had been foretold of the Creator’s Christ, as we have shown in each individual case, it is sufficiently perverse to understand that a Christ [Note: [Col. 0402D] “Christ,” Pamel.] not belonging to the Creator proclaimed himself by the very means [Note: [Col. 0402D] “Proclaimed himself through them,” Seml.; “proclaimed himself through it,” Pamel.] through which he all the more compelled people to recognize the Creator’s Christ.

It is far more perverse if a Christ who is not John’s Christ also bears testimony to John, confirming him as a prophet—indeed, as more than a prophet, namely an angel—and even adduces what was written about him: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way.” He elegantly recalls the prophecy in relation to the preceding sense of John’s offense, so that, by confirming that John the forerunner had already come, he might remove the doubt expressed in John’s question: “Are you the one who is coming, or do we await another?” For, now that the forerunner had discharged his office and the Lord’s way had been prepared, he himself was to be understood as the one whom the forerunner had served.

John was indeed greater [Note: [Col. 0403D] “Than,” Pamel., Fran.; “greater than,” Rig., Venet.] than all born of women, yet he was not thereby made subject to him who was lesser in the kingdom of God—as if the kingdom in which some little one will be greater than John belonged to one God, while John, who is greater than all born of women, belonged to another. For whether he speaks of any “little one” because of humility, or of himself because he was held to be less than John—all, of course, running out into the wilderness to John rather than to Christ: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see?”—the whole matter equally suits the Creator: both that John, who belongs to him, is greater than those born of women, and that Christ, or any little one who will be greater than John in the kingdom, likewise belongs to the Creator; and that one who has not taken offense at Christ is greater than so great a prophet, since this offense then diminished John.

We have spoken about the remission of sins [Note: [Col. 0403D] “The remitted state of sins.” He uses *remissa* for *remissio*, “remission,” as does St. Cyprian in *On the Good of Patience* and Epistle XIV. From this, *Missa*, “Mass,” the term for the most holy sacrifice of the altar, is said to derive from a twofold dismissal. After the Gospel had been expounded, the deacon used to say two things: “If any catechumen remains, let him depart,” or “Let the catechumens depart”; and likewise at [Col. 0404D] the end, “Go, the dismissal has taken place.” From that twofold sending away or dismissal of the people and the catechumens, the Mass received its name. The initiates of the Calvinists execrate this word as if it were monstrous, although it is found in St. Ambrose. On this subject see Durantus’s extensive discussion *On Rites*. LE PR.].

The argument concerning that sinful woman will likewise serve to show that, when she fastened kisses upon the Lord’s feet, flooded them with tears, wiped them with her hair, and covered them with ointment, she touched the reality of a solid body, [Col. 0403C] not an empty phantom. It also shows that, in accordance with the Creator, the sinful woman’s repentance merited pardon, which he was accustomed to prefer to sacrifice. But even if the impulse to repentance had arisen from faith, then, having been justified through repentance arising from faith, she heard from him, “Your faith has saved you”—from the one who had proclaimed through Habakkuk (Hab. 2:4), “The righteous shall live [Note: [Col. 0403D] “Lives,” Seml., Oberth.] by his faith.”

## CHAPTER XIX

That wealthy women adhered to Christ and ministered to him from their possessions—including the wife of the king’s steward (Luke 8)—comes from prophecy. For he called them through Isaiah (Isa. 32:9): “Wealthy women, arise and hear my voice,” so as to show them first as disciples, then as workers and ministers: “Daughters, hear my words in hope. Remember the days of the year [Col. 0403D] with labor in hope.” For they ministered amid the labor with which they followed him, and on account of their hope.

Likewise, concerning parables, let it suffice to have proved once that this kind of discourse was promised by the Creator. But now that declaration of his to the people—“With the ear you shall hear, [Col. 0404A] and you shall not hear” (Isa. 6:10)—gave Christ occasion to repeat frequently: “He who has ears, let him hear.” It was not as though Christ, in opposition, permitted the hearing that the Creator had taken away; rather, the exhortation followed the threat: first, “With the ear you shall hear,” and then, “He who has ears, let him hear.” For those who had ears were not hearing of their own accord; he was showing that ears of the heart were necessary, those by which the Creator had said that they would not hear. Therefore, through Christ he adds: “Take heed how you hear—and do not hear,” that is, hearing with the ear but not with the heart. If you adapt a fitting meaning to the declaration in accordance with the intention of the one who was awakening them to hear, then even by saying, “Take heed how you hear,” he was threatening those who would not hear.

To be sure, he is called an exceedingly gentle God, because he neither judges nor grows angry. The sense that follows proves this as well: “To him who has, it shall be given; but from him who does not have, even what he thinks he has shall be taken away.” What shall be given? An increase of faith, or understanding, or salvation itself. What shall be taken away? Obviously what is to be given. By whom shall it be given and taken away? If it is taken away by the Creator, it will also [Note: [Col. 0404D] “Also” absent from Paris.] be given by him; if it is given by Marcion’s god, it will also be taken away by him. Yet under whatever description he threatens deprivation, he cannot belong to the God who does not know how to threaten because he does not know how to be angry.

I marvel, moreover, that he denies that a lamp is ordinarily hidden, when he himself had remained hidden for so long an age, though he was a greater and more necessary light; and that he promises that everything hidden will be brought into the open, when he continues even now to overshadow his own God—waiting, I suppose, for Marcion to be born.

We have come to the most steadfast argument of all who call the Lord’s birth into question. “He himself,” they say, “testifies that he was not born when he says, ‘Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?’” Thus heretics always either seize naked and simple expressions and drag them by conjecture wherever they wish, or, conversely, dissolve expressions that are conditional and reasoned into a condition of simplicity, as in this passage.

We, on the contrary, say first that it could not have been announced to him that his mother and brothers were standing outside seeking to see him if he had no mother and no brothers. The person making the announcement certainly knew them—either because they had been known previously, or because they were identified there and then when they desired to see him, or because they themselves sent the message.

To this first proposition of ours the opposite party customarily replies: “What if it was reported to him in order to test him?” But Scripture does not say this. Since it is accustomed to indicate when something was done as a test—“Behold, [Col. 0404D] an expert in the Law rose up to test him” (Luke 10); and concerning the consultation about tribute, “The Pharisees approached him, testing him” (Luke 20)—where it makes no mention of testing, it does not admit an interpretation based on testing.

And yet, for good measure, I demand the grounds for the test: for what purpose did they test him by naming [Col. 0405A] his mother and brothers? If it was to learn whether he had been born or not, when had there ever been a question about this that they needed to resolve through that test? Who, moreover, would doubt that a man had been born when he saw him as a man, heard him profess himself Son of Man, and—because of the appearance of every human quality—would hesitate to believe him God or Son of God? They more readily regarded him as a prophet, even if a great one, yet certainly as one who had been born.

Even if he had needed to be tested in an inquiry concerning his birth, any other argument would have suited the test better than mention of those persons whom even a man who had been born might not have. Tell me: Does every person born have a mother who survives him? Is every person born also provided with brothers? Is it not possible to have a father and sisters instead, or even no one at all?

[Note: [Col. 0405C] “But it is also established that censuses were conducted under Augustus, at that time in Judea, through Sentius Saturninus.” So the manuscript reads. And an annotation in the hand of P. Pithou, written beside Rhenanus’s text, explains the old reading thus: “‘Now,’ that is, when Christ was saying those things after the messengers announced that his mother and brothers were present.” Thus Septimius would be indicating censuses other than those he had learned from Luke 2 were conducted by Quirinius. RIG.—We discussed the census at chapter VII. That census, however, was conducted without any assessment of money or poll tax, but only so that the world might be registered and the names of citizens or subjects of the empire recorded. LE PR.]

But it is also established that censuses were conducted (Luke 2) under Augustus, at that time [Note: [Col. 0405C] “Then,” Jun.] [Col. 0405B] in Judea [Note: [Col. 0405C] “Into Judea,” Pam.] through Sentius Saturninus; in their records they could have investigated his lineage. Thus no rationale whatsoever for this supposed test is established.

But his mother and brothers truly were standing outside. It remains also [Note: [Col. 0405C] Seml. and Oberth. omit “also”] to examine the sense in which he declared, “Who is my mother or my brothers?” He did not say it simply, as if to deny his lineage and birth, but under the compulsion of the occasion and within a reasoned condition. For persons so close to him were standing outside while strangers within were intent upon his words; and, what is more, they were seeking to call him away from his solemn work. He was rightly indignant.

[Note: [Col. 0405D] He did not so much deny as disown them. Who today could tolerate someone speaking in this way? For even as Christ was dying, he nevertheless consoled Mary standing beside him; and after addressing her as “woman,” he immediately acknowledged her as his mother through the supremely honorable relation of a son and entrusted her to John. RIG.]

He did not so much deny [Note: [Col. 0405C] “Disown,” Pithou’s manuscript.] as disown them. Indeed, after first saying, “Who [Note: [Col. 0406C] “Who” (masculine), Seml.] is my mother, and who are my brothers?” he added, “except those who hear my words and do them?” [Note: [Col. 0405D] “He transferred the names of blood relationship to others.” That is, he metaphorically called those who heard and performed his words his brothers and mother. RIG.] He transferred the names of blood relationship to others, whom he judged nearer to him by faith. [Col. 0405C] No one, however, transfers anything except from someone who possesses what is transferred. Therefore, if he made those who were not his mother and [Note: [Col. 0405D] “He made those who were not his brothers.” He made those who were not his own blood into his own blood; that is, by employing the figure [Col. 0406C] of blood relationship or brotherhood, he demonstrated his affection toward those who heard and performed his words. “He made them his brothers,” that is, he called them so, figuratively and allegorically. RIG.] brothers into such, how did he deny those who were?

[Note: [Col. 0406C] Wouw. inserts “by reason”] It was, of course, under a condition of merit, not through denial of their original relationship. In himself he was teaching that whoever preferred father, mother, or brothers to the word of God was not worthy (Matt. 10:27) to be his disciple. On the contrary, by this [Col. 0406A] he all the more acknowledged his mother and brothers, because he refused to recognize them. By adopting others, he confirmed the existence of those whom he denied because of offense; he substituted the others not as truer relatives, but as worthier ones. In short, there is nothing remarkable in preferring faith to blood relationship if one had no blood relationship.

## CHAPTER XX

Who, then, is this who commands even the winds and the sea (Luke 8)? A new master and possessor of the elements, no doubt, now that the Creator has been subdued and excluded? It is not so. Rather, the substances recognized their own author, since they had been accustomed to obey even his servants.

Examine Exodus (Exod. 14), Marcion. Look at the Red Sea, broader than all the lakes of Judea, and at Moses’ rod commanding it: split entirely to its depths and held fixed in an equal marvel of separation on both sides, it allowed the people to pass through its interior pathway on dry foot; and then, at the command of the same rod, as nature returned, it overwhelmed the Egyptian army through the reunion of the waves. For this work even the south winds rendered service.

[Note: [Col. 0406D] Read also “the lots of the family to be divided.” So the manuscript has it. This may be explained as follows: “Read,” he says, “the history of the Jordan, and you will know that its sword stood in the way of the family whose lot was to be divided: it opposed the crossing of the children of Israel like the edge of a huge sword; it opposed the crossing of the family whose lot was to be divided; and yet its force and current stood still while the prophets crossed. The prophets bearing the Ark of the Covenant, and with them the children of Israel, crossed on dry foot.” Evidently the word “read” corresponds to the preceding “examine.” Accordingly, just as he said above, “Examine Exodus,” so here too he appears to have said, “Read also the lots of the family to be divided”—the history of which, of course, is contained in Joshua 3 and 4. RIG.]

Read also (Josh. 3–4) of the lots of the family to be divided, and of its passage across—

[Note: [Col. 0406D] “The Jordan was a sword.” Thus the Tiber was called *Serra*, “Saw,” in the arcane language of sacred rites, according to Servius on these verses of Virgil:

> . . . I am he whom you see, with full-flowing stream,  
> Confining my banks and cutting through the fertile fields,

[Col. 0407D]

Blue Tiber. RIG.] that the Jordan was a sword, whose force and downward course Joshua had plainly taught to stand still while the prophets crossed. What answer is there to this? If he is your Christ, he will not be more powerful than the servants of the Creator.

But I would have used only these examples, had not the prophecy of this maritime expedition also preceded Christ. For when he crosses the sea, the Psalm is fulfilled: “The Lord,” it says, “is upon many waters” (Ps. 28:3). When he scatters the waves of the strait, Habakkuk is fulfilled: “Scattering [Note: [Col. 0406C] ‘You will scatter,’ Pam.] the waters,” it says, “along the way” (Hab. 3:9). When the sea is crushed by his threats, Nahum likewise is accomplished: “Threatening the sea,” it says, “and drying it up” (Nah. 1:4)—the sea, of course, together with the winds by which it was being disturbed. From what do you wish me to establish my claim to Christ: from examples, or from the Creator’s prophets?

Come now, you who suppose that a military and armed warrior was foretold—not figuratively or allegorically—as one who would spiritually wage a spiritual war against spiritual enemies, with spiritual soldiery and spiritual weapons: when you find in one man a multitude of demons professing itself to be a legion, a spiritual legion of course, learn that Christ too must be understood as a conqueror of spiritual enemies, spiritually armed and spiritually warlike; and thus as the very one who was also to fight against a legion of demons. Accordingly, the Psalm may be seen to have pronounced concerning this war as well: “The Lord is strong, the Lord is mighty in battle” (Ps. 23:8). [Note: [Col. 0407D] Others read “combat.”] For when he had fought against the final enemy, death, he triumphed by the trophy of the cross.

[Note: [Col. 0407D] But whose God’s Son did the legion testify Jesus to be? As though pursuing another point, he follows up the words: “What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?” and there, of course, “pardon of the abyss,” that is, pardon from the abyss, just as above, chapter XII, “pardon from the fast.” PAM.]

But whose God’s Son did the legion testify Jesus to be? [Note: [Col. 0407D] “Did the legion testify,” Seml., Oberth.] Without doubt, the Son of the God whose torments and abyss they knew and feared. For they cannot be thought still to have been unaware that the power of a new and unknown God was at work on earth, since it is unlikely that the Creator was unaware of it. For even if he had once been ignorant of another God above himself, he would certainly by now have discovered one acting beneath his own heaven. And what the Lord had discovered would already have become known to his whole household in the same world and within the same circuit of heaven in which the foreign Divinity was dwelling. Therefore, to the extent that the Creator and his substances would have known that Divinity, had it existed, to that same extent—because there was no such Divinity—the demons knew no other Christ than the Christ of their own God. They do not ask [Note: [Col. 0407D] “For they would ask,” Wouw.] from another what they remembered they must ask from the Creator: namely, exemption from the Creator’s abyss. In fact, they obtained it. On what merit? Because they had lied? Because they had made him the son of a savage God? And what kind of being would he be who aided liars and tolerated those who defamed him?

But because they had not lied, because they had recognized the God of the abyss and their own God, he likewise confirmed himself to be the one whom the demons had recognized [Note: [Col. 0407D] “Recognized,” Pam.]: Jesus, the judge and the Son of the avenging God.

Here is something also concerning those pettinesses and weaknesses of the Creator in Christ. For I too wish to ascribe ignorance to him. Allow me to do so against the heretic. He is touched by a woman suffering from a flow of blood, [Note: [Col. 0407D] “By a woman suffering from a flow of blood.” Thus Jerome, Epistle 131 to Raffinus, spoke of “a woman flowing with blood,” and in Epistle 128 to Fabiola: “If one of the priests has a discharge of semen.” RIG.] and he did not know by whom. “Who touched me?” he says. Even when the disciples offer excuses, he persists in the language of ignorance: “Someone touched me”; and he affirms this from the evidence: “For I perceived power going out from me.” What does the heretic say? Did he know the person? And why did he speak as though ignorant? Surely to elicit a confession, to test her fear. So too Adam had once been sought as though God were ignorant: “Adam, where are you?” You now have both the Creator excused together with Christ, and Christ made equal to the Creator.

But you will also claim that this was because he was [Note: [Col. 0408D] “By which,” Jun.] an adversary of the law: because the law [Note: [Col. 0407D] “Excludes from contact with a bleeding woman,” etc. This alludes to the statement near the end of Leviticus 15: “This is the law,” etc., “of a woman bleeding,” that is, as blessed Jerome puts it, “who continually flows with blood.” In its place the Septuagint is now incorrectly read: καὶ ὁ γονορρυὴς, that is, “the man with a seminal discharge”; but καὶ τῇ αἱμορροούσῃ, that is, “and for the woman with a flow of blood,” must be repeated. For that chapter did not treat of a woman with a seminal discharge, but of a man with a seminal discharge and a woman bleeding for many days outside the time of her menstruation. PAM.] excludes one from contact with a bleeding woman, he was therefore eager not merely to admit her touch but even to grant her health. O God, beneficent not by nature but from rivalry! Yet if we find that the woman’s faith deserved this, since he says, “Your faith has saved you,” who are you to interpret as hostility to the law [Note: [Col. 0408D] “Hostility to the law,” etc. Here he takes *aemulatio* to mean opposition to the law; for shortly before he says “adversary of the law,” and near the end of this chapter, “rival of the law,” in the same way that Pliny called Carthage “the rival of Rome,” book XV, chapter 18. PAM.] an act which the Lord himself shows to have been performed as a reward for faith?

“But,” you say, “this constituted the woman’s faith: that she had scorned the law.” And to whom is it credible that a woman, as yet conscious of no God and initiated into no new law [Note: [Col. 0408D] “Into no law,” Wouw.’s codex.], would violate the law to which she was still subject? By what faith, then, did she violate it? Believing in which God? Despising which? The Creator? Certainly, she touched him in faith. If it was faith in the Creator—a faith that knew no other God—how did she violate his law? For if she violated it, she did so just as truly as she acted from faith in the Creator. How can both propositions agree: that she violated the law, and that she violated it from the very faith on account of which she ought not to have violated it?

I shall explain. First, this was her faith: that she trusted her God to prefer mercy to sacrifice itself; that she was certain this God was at work in Christ; and that she therefore touched him not as a holy man, nor as a prophet whom she knew to be capable of contamination because of his human substance, but as God himself, whom she presumed no uncleanness could pollute. Accordingly, she did not rashly interpret the law for herself as signifying that things capable of contamination were contaminated—not God, whom she trusted to be present in Christ. But she also reflected that the law specified the regular and customary flow of menstrual or childbirth blood, which proceeds from the operation of nature, not one arising from a disorder of health. Her own flow, however, abounded from a disorder of health, for which she knew that not a temporal limit but the aid of divine mercy was necessary. Thus she may be seen [Note: [Col. 0408D] “May be seen” omitted by Seml.] not to have violated the law, but to have drawn a distinction. This was the faith that had also bestowed understanding. “Unless you believe,” he says, “you will not understand” (Isa. 7). By approving the faith of that woman, who believed in the Creator alone, Christ showed himself to be the God to whom the faith he approved was directed.

Nor shall I omit the fact that, when his garment was touched—a garment worn, of course, upon a body, not upon a phantom—the body too was thereby demonstrated. I do not say this as though we were already reopening that question, but because it concurs with the present issue. For if his body was not real, a phantom certainly could not be contaminated, being an empty thing. He who cannot be contaminated because of the emptiness of his substance—how could he have wished to be? As a rival of the law, he was lying, since he was not truly polluted.

## CHAPTER XXI

He sends the disciples to preach the kingdom of God (Luke 9). Did he even here disclose whose kingdom it was? He forbids them to carry anything for food or clothing on the road. Who would have commanded this, except the one who both feeds the ravens [Note: [Col. 0409C] “Fed,” Oberth.] and clothes the flowers of the field, and who had already granted even the threshing ox freedom of the mouth (Deut. 25:4), [Note: [Col. 0409D] “For the privilege of taking food from its work.” He says that the threshing ox was “removed from its work” by the same formula of exemption by which the legal writers spoke of property “removed from the husband’s goods.” RIG.] for the privilege of taking [Note: [Col. 0409D] “Taking,” Wouw.’s codex.] food from its work—because “the worker is worthy of his wages”? Let Marcion delete these words, provided their sense remains intact.

But when he commands them to shake the dust from their feet against those by whom they had not been received, and orders this to be done as a testimony, no one gives testimony concerning something not destined for judgment. He who orders inhumanity to be entered into evidence threatens judgment.

That no new god had been established by Christ was also made plain by the opinion of everyone: some affirmed to Herod that Jesus Christ was John, others Elijah, and others one of the ancient prophets. Whichever of these he might have been, he certainly had not been raised for the purpose of preaching another god after his resurrection.

He feeds the people in the wilderness, in accordance, of course, with the former manner. [Note: [Col. 0409D] “In accordance, of course, with the former manner”: namely, that of the Old Instrument or Testament. Thus in the book *On Baptism*: “We are anointed with blessed anointing in accordance with the former discipline,” that is, the Jewish discipline. RIG.] Or if his majesty is not the same, it is therefore already inferior to the Creator’s; for the Creator sustained not for a single day but for forty years, not five thousand or thereabouts but six hundred thousand people, not from the inferior materials of bread and fish but from heavenly manna. [Note: [Col. 0409D] “But sustained six hundred thousand people.” That is, he continued, prolonged, and extended the tenure of life and strength for six hundred thousand people. RIG.] So fully, however, was it that same majesty that he willed, in accordance with the former example, that the scantiness of the food should not merely suffice but even overflow. For so too, in the time of famine under Elijah, the small and last provisions of the widow of Zarephath had abounded, through the prophet’s blessing, throughout the entire period of famine (1 Kings 17).

You have the Third Book [Note: [Col. 0409D] “The third,” Fran., Jun.] of Kings. If you also unfold the Fourth [Note: [Col. 0409D] “The fourth,” Fran., Jun.; “And if you turn again to the third,” Wouw.], you will find this whole course of Christ’s action surrounding that man of God who, when twenty [Note: [Col. 0409D] “Ten,” Seml., from certain Greek copies and from Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, book VI.] barley loaves had been offered to him, commanded them to be distributed among the people. His servant, likewise comparing the multitude with the meagerness of the food, answered: [Note: [Col. 0409D] “What, then, am I to give this in the sight of a hundred men?” The exemplar reads: “What, then, am I to give this, the sight of a hundred men?” I think it should be written: “What, then, am I to give this very thing within sight of a hundred men?” RIG.] “What, then, am I to give this [Note: [Col. 0409D] “I,” Paris, Fran.] in the sight [Note: [Col. 0410C] “For the viewing of,” Seml.] of a hundred [Note: [Col. 0410D] Pam. adds “thousand.”] men?” “Give it,” he says, “and they will eat, for thus [Note: [Col. 0410D] “This,” Oberth.] says the Lord.” And they ate and left [Note: [Col. 0410D] “They will eat and leave,” Seml.; “they will eat and leave, and they ate and left,” Jun.; thus the Septuagint.] remnants, according to the word of the Lord. O Christ, ancient even amid new things!

Peter, therefore, had seen these things, had compared them with the former things, and had recalled not only the deeds accomplished in the past but also those already at that time prophesying the future. When the Lord asked who he seemed to them to be, Peter answered for everyone: [Note: [Col. 0410D] “You are the Christ,” etc. Because of that confession, blessed Peter is the foundation and the rock upon which the Church of God stands: ἐπὶ τῇ πέτρᾳ ταύτῃ τῆς ἀσφαλοῦς πίστεως οἰκοδομήσω μου τὴν ἐκκλησίαν, “Upon this rock of secure faith I shall build my Church,” as St. Epiphanius has it, *Heresy* 59. LE PR.] “You are the Christ.” He cannot have understood him to be any Christ [Note: [Col. 0410D] “He cannot have understood him to be a new Christ,” Latinus.] other than the one whom he knew from the Scriptures and whom he was now recognizing in his deeds.

Christ himself confirms this, still remaining patient, or rather even imposing silence. For if Peter could confess him to be none other than the Creator’s Christ, while Christ commanded him not to tell anyone this, then surely he did not wish what Peter had understood to be made public. “No,” you say, “because Peter had understood incorrectly, and Christ did not wish a falsehood to be disseminated.” But Christ declared another reason for the silence: “Because the Son of Man must suffer many things, and be rejected by the elders and scribes and chief priests, [Note: [Col. 0410D] “Elders and scribes and priests.” He preferred to retain *presbyteris* rather than its common translation, “older men.” As for “priests,” that is not particularly admirable, although the Greek is ἀρχιερέων, which the Vulgate renders “chief priests.” LE PR.] and be killed, and rise after the third day.” Since these very things too were foretold concerning the Creator’s Christ, as we shall establish in their proper places, he thus also showed himself to be the one concerning whom they were foretold. Certainly, even if they had not been foretold, the reason he gave for imposing silence would demonstrate not Peter’s error [Note: [Col. 0410D] Paris and Fran. add “but.”] but the necessity of undergoing the sufferings.

“Whoever,” he says, “wishes to save his life will lose it; and whoever loses it for my sake will save it.” Certainly, it was the Son of Man who uttered this sentence. Look, then, with the king of Babylon into his burning furnace (Dan. 3), and there you will find one “like the Son of Man”—for he was not yet truly the Son of Man, since he had not yet been born from man—even then determining these outcomes. He saves the lives of the three brothers who had agreed to lose them for God; but he destroyed the lives of the Chaldeans, which they had preferred to save through idolatry. What new doctrine is this, when its proofs are ancient?

Moreover, prophecies had already run their course concerning martyrdoms—both that they would occur and that they would receive their reward from God. “See,” says Isaiah, “how the righteous man perishes, and no one takes it to heart; and righteous men are taken away, and no one considers it” (Isa. 57:1). When does this occur more than in the persecution of his saints? [Note: [Col. 0411C] “Certainly not an ordinary doctrine, nor one common under the law of nature.” These words can refer to nothing other than the question, “What new doctrine is this?”—certainly not an ordinary doctrine, that is, nor one common under the law of nature, etc. RIG.] Certainly this doctrine is not ordinary, nor common under the law of nature, but distinguished and militant on behalf of faith: in it, the one who loses his life for God preserves it. Thus here also you may nevertheless recognize the Judge, [Note: [Col. 0411C] “Recognize,” Pam.] who will repay an evil gain of the soul with its destruction, and a good loss of the soul with its salvation. [Note: [Col. 0411C] “Repays,” Paris, Fran.]

But he also presents to me a jealous God, [Note: [Col. 0411C] “To me” absent from Paris.] returning evil for evil: “Whoever,” he says, “is ashamed [Note: [Col. 0411C] “Ashamed of me,” Seml., Oberth.] of me, of him [Note: [Col. 0411C] “Of that person,” Franeq.] I too will be ashamed.” Yet the grounds for shame are not applicable to any Christ except mine, whose whole course is the more shameful, [Note: [Col. 0411C] “Whose course is the more shameful.” He means the course of his birth and upbringing. RIG.] since it lies open even to the insults of the heretics as they plead, with all the bitterness they can muster, the entire foulness of birth and upbringing and even the indignity of the flesh itself. [Note: [Col. 0411C] “Of the flesh itself.” That is, of passible and mortal flesh, which certainly seemed unworthy of God. Thus *Against the Jews*: “First he was clothed in filthy garments,” that is, “in the indignity of passible and mortal flesh.” Or understand “indignity” as εἶδος οὐκ ἄξιον τυραννίδος, “an appearance unworthy of sovereignty.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0411C] Seml. conjectures “of those very things.”] [Note: [Col. 0411C] “Of those pleading,” Wouw.’s manuscripts.]

Otherwise, how will that Christ be liable to shame who does not admit it? He was not coagulated in a womb—which, though a virgin’s, was nevertheless a woman’s; nor, though without semen, from a woman’s fluid according to the law of corporeal substance; [Note: [Col. 0411D] “From a woman’s fluid.” In *On the Flesh of Christ* he spoke of “foul clots of fluid and blood.” RIG.] he was not flesh before taking shape; he was not called a “beast” after acquiring a form; [Note: [Col. 0411D] “Not called a beast after acquiring a form.” Julius Firmicus uses the same word in book VII, chapter 1: “The beast, cut limb by limb within the mother’s viscera, will be brought forth by the physicians.” RIG.] he was not brought to completion through the torment of ten [Note: [Col. 0412C] “Nine,” Fran.] months; [Note: [Col. 0411D] “Not brought to completion through the torment of ten months.” Thus the exemplars read. If they have preserved the author’s text intact for us, Septimius will have said that birth is brought to completion as long as the fetus is being perfected in the womb, according to the course of human birth over a period of ten months, just as in the *Apologeticum* he said that conception is brought to completion while the blood is still being developed into a human being. Otherwise, Latinius’s conjecture, “brought to completion through the torment of ten months,” would seem by no means contemptible. For an infant’s position in the womb is such that it seems to be tortured, entirely bent and contracted. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0412C] “Brought to completion,” Fran.] he was not, through a sudden convulsion of labor pains, poured down to the earth through the sewer of the body together with the filth of so long a period; [Note: [Col. 0412C] “Together with the filth of so long a period,” etc. The book *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 4, has almost the same words: “Beginning with the birth itself, which you hate, declaim against it; come now, speak of the filth of the genital organs in the womb, the foul clots of substances, fluids, and blood, and of flesh to be nourished from the same mire for nine months.” By “mire” he means what Hippocrates says in *On the Nature of the Child*, no. 136: Τὰ γὰρ καταμήνια οὐ χωρέει, ὁκόταν γυνὴ λάβῃ πρὸς ἑαυτήν, ἢν μέλλῃ τὸ παιδίον ὑγιαίνειν, “The menses do not flow in a woman carrying in the womb, if the child is to be healthy.” In this passage there is an admirable description of human origin and an image of its weakness, which I remember reading in almost the same form in Pliny, who immediately exclaims: “From these beginnings arises the mind of an executioner,” etc. If the book were at hand, I would transcribe the entire passage. LE PR.] nor did he immediately inaugurate the light with tears and with the first wound severing what held him; [Note: [Col. 0412D] “Inaugurated the light with tears,” etc. He begins life amid miseries, namely with wailing; he lives that same life amid labors; and, to complete his evils, must undergo death. LE PR.] nor was he thoroughly washed; nor treated with salt and honey; nor, through swaddling-cloths, initiated already into the wrapping of burial; [Note: [Col. 0412C] “Into the wrapping,” Wouw.’s codex.] nor thereafter rolled amid impurities between embraces, troublesome to the breasts, long an infant, scarcely a boy, slowly [Note: [Col. 0412C] “More slowly,” Seml., Oberth.] a man. Instead, he was set down from heaven, fully grown at once, complete at once, immediately Christ—spirit and power, and nothing but God.

Moreover, because he was not real, since he was not what he appeared to be, neither was he an object of shame because of the curse of the cross; he lacked its reality because he lacked a body. He could not, therefore, have said: “Whoever is ashamed of me.” [Note: [Col. 0412C] “Of me,” Pam., Fran.] It was our Christ who had to make this pronouncement: “Made by the Father a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:6); “a worm and not a man; the disgrace of mankind and the contempt of the people” (Ps. 21:6)—inasmuch as he so willed it that “by his bruise we might be healed” (Isa. 53:5), and that our salvation might rest upon his dishonor.

And rightly did he lay himself down for his own human being, for his own image and likeness, not another’s, [Note: [Col. 0412C] Seml. adds “then.”] so that, since man had not been ashamed when adoring stone and wood, he might with the same steadfastness remain unashamed of Christ and, for the shamelessness of idolatry, make satisfaction to God through the shamelessness of faith. [Note: [Col. 0412D] “For the shamelessness of idolatry, make satisfaction to God through the shamelessness of faith.” It was the shamelessness of idolatry when one was not ashamed to adore stones and pieces of wood; the shamelessness of faith is when one is in no way ashamed to believe that God was born and crucified. RIG.] Which of these things belongs to your Christ, Marcion, to furnish grounds for shame? Certainly you ought to be ashamed that you fabricated him yourself.

## CHAPTER XXII

Indeed, you ought especially to have been ashamed of this too: that you permit him to be seen with Moses and Elijah in the seclusion of the mountain, though he had come as their destroyer. This, of course, is what that voice from heaven wished to be understood to mean: “This is my beloved Son; hear him”—that is, no longer Moses and Elijah.

Then the voice alone would have sufficed, without the display of Moses and Elijah. For by determining whom they should hear, it would have forbidden them to hear any others whatsoever. Or did it perhaps permit Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the others whom it did not display to be heard, if it forbade those whom it did display? Even if their presence was necessary, they certainly ought not to have been shown conversing with him, which is a sign of familiarity; nor sharing in his splendor, which is an example of favor and grace; but amid some kind of filth, which would be evidence of their destruction—or rather in the Creator’s darkness, which he had been sent to disperse. They ought also to have been far removed from Christ’s splendor, since he was going to separate their very words and writings from his Gospel. Is this how [Note: [Col. 0413D] “Thus,” Rig., Venet.] he demonstrates that they are strangers—by having them with him? Is this how he teaches that they must be abandoned—by joining them to himself? Is this how he destroys them—by building them up out of his own rays?

What would their own Christ have done? According to the logic of perversity, I suppose, he would have revealed them as the sort of men Marcion’s Christ ought to have revealed—or else would have revealed with himself anyone at all other than his own prophets. But what could be more characteristic of the Creator’s Christ than to display his own heralds with himself; to be seen with those by whom he had been seen in revelations; to speak with those who had spoken of him; to share his glory with those by whom he had been called the Lord of glory; and to be with his chief men, [Note: [Col. 0413D] “With his chief men.” Vatican manuscript I reads, “with his princes.” But the former has more of the flavor of Tertullian’s African style. The author calls them this because Moses and Elijah were the foremost of the ancient prophets, long before those whom we call the greater prophets. PAM.] one of whom had once formed the people and the other would one day reform them, the one the inaugurator of the Old Testament and the other the consummator of the New?

Peter, therefore, rightly recognized the fellowship of his own Christ in Christ’s inseparability from them, and offered the counsel: “It is good for us to be here.” Good indeed, where Moses and Elijah were! And: “Let us make three tabernacles here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah”—but he did not know what he was saying. How did he not know? Was it through a simple error, or according to the principle [Note: [Col. 0413D] “Which we defend in the cause of the new prophecy: that ecstasy—that is, madness—is compatible with grace.” He seems to have done this in the books *On Ecstasy*, which Jerome mentions. RIG.] which [Note: [Col. 0413D] “According to which,” Jun.] we defend in the cause of the New Prophecy: that ecstasy, that is, loss of reason, is compatible with grace? For when a man is established in the Spirit—especially when he beholds the glory of God or when God speaks through him—he must necessarily fall away from his ordinary consciousness, since he is overshadowed by divine power. This is a question between us and the “psychics.” [Note: [Col. 0413D] “Concerning which there is a question between us and the psychics.” This is the first of all references made by the author to the psychics; from this it is clear that this book was written by the author at the beginning of the heresy. RIG.]

Meanwhile, it is easy to establish Peter’s loss of reason. For how could he have recognized Moses and Elijah except in the Spirit? The people could not have possessed images, statues, or likenesses of them, since the law prohibited them. It was because he had seen them in the Spirit; and thus, being established in the Spirit rather than in his senses, he could not know what he had said.

But if he “did not know” in the sense that he was mistaken because he thought Christ belonged to them, then it is already established that, when Peter was questioned above by Christ concerning who they thought he was, he had spoken of the Creator’s Christ in saying, “You are the Christ.” For if he had then recognized him as the Christ of another God, he would not have been mistaken here. But if he erred here for the same reason that he erred above, it is therefore certain that down to that very day no new divinity had been revealed by Christ, and that Peter had not erred down to that point, since Christ had so far revealed nothing of that kind. Christ must be reckoned as belonging to no one other than the Creator for as long as he exhibited the Creator’s whole established order, as he also did here.

He takes three of the disciples as witnesses of the future vision and voice; this too belongs to the Creator: “By three witnesses,” he says, “every word shall stand” (Deut. 19:15). He withdraws to a mountain; I recognize the pattern of the place. For the Creator had also initiated the former people at a mountain, both by his vision and by his voice. The New Testament had to be sealed upon the same height upon which the Old had been inscribed, and also beneath the same enclosure of the cloud—which no one doubted had been gathered from the Creator’s atmosphere—unless Marcion’s Christ had brought clouds of his own down to that place because he had also broken a path through the Creator’s heaven, or had similarly made borrowed use of the Creator’s cloud.

Accordingly, the cloud was not mute even now. Instead, a voice rose from heaven, the Father’s renewed testimony concerning the Son and the words already found in the second Psalm: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” Of him he also says through Isaiah: “Whoever fears God, let him hear the voice of his Son” (Isa. 50:10). Thus, when he now presents him with the words, “This is my Son,” the implied addition is surely, “whom I promised.” [Note: [Col. 0414D] “He promised,” Oberth.] For if he once promised him and afterward says, “This is he,” it belongs to the one who presents what was promised to employ the language of demonstration—the one who once made the promise—and not to one to whom the answer might be given: “And who are you yourself to say, ‘This is my Son,’ when you no more announced him beforehand than you revealed yourself and what you previously were?” [Note: [Col. 0414D] “Was,” Pam.]

“Hear him,” therefore: the one whom from the beginning he had declared must be heard under the title of “prophet,” since the people were going to regard him as a prophet. “A prophet,” says Moses, [Note: [Col. 0414D] “A prophet,” says Moses. He cites this Scripture very differently from the text now found in the Septuagint, but rather according to the citation in Acts 3 and 8. This is not surprising, since the same thing is repeated twice in other words in Deuteronomy 18. The author’s wording, “will raise up for you,” agreeing with the apostle Peter, approaches more closely to the former passage, except that the word “for you” occurs there; while from the latter passage he took the remaining words. PAM.] “God will raise up for you from among your sons”—according, of course, to fleshly descent [Note: [Col. 0414D] “Meaning,” Paris, Fran.]—“one like me; you shall hear [Note: [Col. 0414D] “You shall have heard,” Pam.] him. But every person who does not hear him shall be exterminated from his people” (Deut. 18:15). So too Isaiah: “Who among you fears God? Let him obey the voice of his Son” (Isa. 50:10)—a voice that the Father himself was also going to commend. For he confirms [Note: [Col. 0415D] “For he confirms,” it says, “the words of his Son,” etc. Again, the author renders the words of Isaiah 44, “of his Son,” where the Greek has παιδός σου, for which others read “of his servant.” Consequently, this passage was very difficult to locate, especially since blessed Jerome translates from the Hebrew, “raising up the word.” PAM.] [Note: [Col. 0415D] Pam. adds “it says.”] the words of his Son by saying, of course: “This is my beloved Son; hear him,” he says. [Note: [Col. 0415D] “He says” omitted by Pam.]

Therefore, even if the act of hearing was transferred from Moses and Elijah to Christ, [Note: [Col. 0415D] “To Christ,” Wouw.’s codex.] it was not transferred as though from another god or to another Christ, but from the Creator to his Christ, in accordance with the passing away of the Old Testament and the succession of the New. “Neither an envoy,” says Isaiah, “nor a messenger, but the Lord himself [Note: [Col. 0415D] “God himself,” Seml., Oberth.] saved them [Note: [Col. 0415D] “Will save them,” Oberth.]” (Isa. 63:9), himself now preaching and fulfilling the Law and the prophets.

The Father, therefore, handed over the new disciples to the Son, after first displaying Moses and Elijah with him in the privilege of splendor, and then dismissing them as though their office and honor had now been discharged. This very thing was thereby confirmed against Marcion: that Christ’s splendor too was shared with Moses and Elijah.

We also possess the entire form of this vision in Habakkuk, where the Spirit speaks at times in the person of the apostles: “Lord, I heard your report and was afraid” (Hab. 3:2). What report more than that heavenly voice: “This is my beloved Son; hear him”? “I considered your works [Note: [Col. 0415D] “Your work,” others.], and fell away in mind.” When [Note: [Col. 0415D] “How much,” Paris; “by which,” Fran.] more than when, after seeing his splendor, Peter did not know what he was saying? “In the midst of two living beings you shall be known”—Moses and Elijah. Zechariah too saw them figuratively as two olive trees and two olive branches (Zech. 4:3, 14). For these are the ones of whom it was said to him: “The two sons of richness stand beside the Lord of the whole earth.”

And again the same Habakkuk says: “Power covered the heavens” (Hab. 3:3)—surely by that cloud. “And his brightness shall be like the light”—surely the light by which even his clothing shone.

And if we recall the promise made to Moses, we shall find it fulfilled here. For when Moses desired the sight of the Lord, saying, “If, therefore, I have found favor before you, manifest yourself to me, so that I may knowingly see you,” he desired that sight in which God was to act as man, as the prophet knew. Otherwise, he had already heard: “No man shall see my face [Note: [Col. 0415D] “Me” absent from Rig., Venet.] and live” (Exod. 33). “And this word,” he says, “which you have spoken, I will perform for you.” And Moses again: “Show me your glory.” And the Lord similarly speaks of the future: “I shall pass before you in my glory,” and the rest. And at the end: “Then you shall see my posterior parts”—not his loins or calves, but the glory Moses had desired, which was to be revealed in later times.

In that glory he promises that he will become visible to Moses face to face, [Note: [Col. 0416D] “He had promised,” Seml.] saying also to Aaron: “If there is a prophet among you, I shall be known to him in a vision and speak to him in a vision—not as to Moses; mouth to mouth I shall speak to him [Note: [Col. 0416D] “To him” omitted by Seml.] in a form”—surely the form of a human being, which he was going to bear—“and not in a riddle” (Num. 12:6). [Note: [Col. 0416D] Oberth. inserts “And.”]

For although [Note: [Col. 0416D] “Marcion did not wish him to be shown conversing with the Lord.” He had deleted from the Gospel of blessed Luke the words “conversing with him”; but here Marcion is nevertheless pressed by Exodus 34, in which the same thing is reported. LE PR.] Marcion did not wish Moses to be shown conversing with the Lord, but merely standing, nevertheless even while standing he stood mouth to mouth and face to face with him—“with him,” it says, not outside him—in his very glory, much less merely in his sight. Moses departed from Christ illuminated by this glory in no other way than he was accustomed to depart from the Creator, striking [Note: [Col. 0416D] “To strike,” Pam.] the eyes of the children of Israel then, just as he now strikes the blinded eyes of Marcion, who failed to see that this argument too works against him.

I take upon myself the person of Israel.

## CHAPTER XXIII
Let Marcion’s Christ stand forth and cry out: “O unbelieving generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I endure you?” [Note: [Col. 0416D] “How long shall I endure you?” omitted by Semler.] He should immediately hear from me: “Whoever you are, you newcomer (ἐπερχόμενε, *eperchomene*), first declare who you are, whence you come, and what right you have over us. Up to this point, everything about you belongs to the Creator. [Note: [Col. 0416D] “You are,” Oberthür.] Certainly, if you come from him and act on his behalf, we accept the rebuke. But if you come from another, I should like you to say what of your own you have ever entrusted to us, which we ought to have believed, so that you may reproach us for unbelief—you who have never even revealed yourself to us. How long ago did you begin to deal with us, that you should complain about the length of time? In what circumstances have you endured us, that you should charge us against your patience? You have only just come like Aesop’s ass from the well, and already [Col. 0416C] you are shouting.”

I still assume the person of the disciples against whom he sprang: “O unbelieving nation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I endure you?” I would certainly, and with perfect justice, have beaten back his outburst in this manner: “Whoever you are, you newcomer (ἐπερχόμενε, *eperchomene*), first declare who you are, whence you come, and what right you have over us. Up to this point, I think, you belong to the Creator, and therefore we have followed you, recognizing in you everything that is his. But if you come from him, we accept the rebuke. If, however, you act on behalf of another, I beg you, say what you have ever entrusted to us—at least anything of your own—which we ought already to have believed, so that you may reproach us for unbelief, when even now you do not reveal your author. And how long ago did you begin to deal with us, that you should also hold the length of time against us? In what circumstances have you endured us, that you should boast of your patience as well? Aesop’s ass has only just appeared here from the [Col. 0416D] well, and already it is shouting.”

Who would not [Col. 0417A] thus have beaten back the injustice of the rebuke, if he had believed Christ to belong to one who did not yet have the right to complain? Except that neither would Christ have assailed them if he had not long dwelt among them in the Law, in the prophets, in mighty works, and in acts of kindness, and had always found them unbelieving.

But look: Christ loves little children, teaching that those who always wish to be greater ought to be like them. The Creator, however, sent bears against children, avenging the prophet Elisha for the insults he had suffered from them (2 Kings 2). A thoroughly shameless antithesis, since it sets together such different things: little children and older children—an age still innocent, and one already capable of judgment, which could insult, not to say blaspheme. [Note: [Col. 0417C] “Since,” Paris and Franeker editions.] Insofar, then, as God is just, he did not spare even impious children, requiring honor to be shown to the greater age, and surely still more by the lesser. Insofar as he is good, he so loves little children [Col. 0417B] that in Egypt he showed favor to the midwives who protected the Hebrew children endangered by Pharaoh’s edict. Thus this affection of Christ, too, is shared with the Creator.

Now Marcion’s God, who abhors marriage [Note: [Col. 0417C] “Opposes,” Rigault, Venetian edition.], how can he be regarded as a lover of little children, [Note: [Col. 0417D] Marriage is the entire cause of these children. The author uses “entire cause” for “the principal cause”; for the blessed Augustine noted in more than one place the three goods of marriage—fidelity, sacrament, and offspring—while most people in fact contract marriage chiefly for the sake of children. For, as Nonius says, “the whole,” which is regarded as the greater part, may sometimes be taken as not meaning the entirety. The author indicates this in express words when, shortly afterward, he adds: “He also promised by his blessing the very fruit of marriage, the first of which is infancy.” PAM.] when marriage is the entire cause of their existence? He who hates the seed must necessarily execrate its fruit as well. Indeed, he must be judged crueler than the Egyptian king: for Pharaoh did not allow infants to be brought up; this god does not even allow them to be born, taking life away from them even during their ten months in the womb. How much more credible it is that affection for little children should be attributed to him who, by blessing marriage for the propagation of the human race, also promised by his blessing the very fruit of marriage, the first of which is infancy.

At Elijah’s request the Creator reproduces the plague of fire in the case of that “false prophet” (2 Kings 1). [Col. 0417C] I recognize the severity of the Judge; on the other side, I recognize the gentleness of Christ rebuking [Note: [Col. 0417C] “Reproving,” Wouwer manuscript.] the disciples when they intended the same punishment against that Samaritan village. Let the heretic recognize that this gentleness of Christ was promised by that same most severe Judge: “He will not contend,” he says (Isa. 42:2), “nor will his voice be heard in the street. A bruised reed he will not break, and smoking flax he will not extinguish.” Such a one, surely, was much less likely to burn human beings. [Note: [Col. 0417D] “For even then, in his approach to Elijah, he was not in the fire.” This alludes to the history of Elijah in 1 Kings 19. His words, “For even then, in his approach to Elijah,” mean that even in the Old Testament God was gentle, merciful, and placable. Procopius: ὅτι δὲ οὐ πῦρ πῦρ ὁ τῆς παλαίας θεὸς, Ἡλίας διδάσκεται, καὶ δι’ αὐτοῦ πάντες ἡμεῖς· ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ αὐρὰ λεπτή, δι’ αὐρᾶς δὲ λέγεται παρεῖναι λεπτῆς. “That the God of the Old Testament is not fire, Elijah is taught, and through him all of us; but neither is he a gentle breeze, though he is said to be present by means of a gentle breeze.” [The repeated Greek πῦρ is an evident textual duplication.] See [Col. 0418D] the remarks on the book *On Patience*. RIG.] For even then, in his approach to Elijah (1 Kings 19:12), the Lord was “not [Col. 0418A] in the fire,” but in a gentle spirit.

But why does this most humane God reject the man who offers himself to him as so inseparable a companion? If it was because he had said proudly or hypocritically, “I will follow you wherever you go,” then, in judging pride or hypocrisy worthy of rejection, he acted as a judge. And surely he condemned the man whom he rejected, since he would not attain [Note: [Col. 0418C] “Follow,” Semler.] salvation. For just as he calls to salvation one whom he does not reject, or even one whom he calls of his own accord, so he condemns to destruction the man whom he rejects.

But when he answers the one who pleaded the need to bury his father, “Let the dead bury their dead; but you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God,” he plainly confirmed both laws of the Creator: the law concerning the priesthood in Leviticus, which forbids priests to attend even the final rites of their parents: “The priest,” he says (Lev. [Col. 0418B] 21:1), “shall not go in to any dead person, and he shall not defile himself for his parent” [Note: [Col. 0418C] “Father,” Oberthür.]; and the law concerning a vow in Numbers (Num. 6:6–7). For there too, among other things, he commands that one who has vowed himself to God shall not go in to any dead person—not even to his father, mother, or brother. I think that he intended for both a vow and the priesthood the man whom he had instructed to preach the kingdom of God. Or, if this is not so, he must be pronounced thoroughly impious for commanding sons to despise their parents’ burial when no provision of the law intervened.

Moreover, when he forbids that third man, who was preparing first to bid farewell to his own people, to look back, he follows the rule of the Creator. The Creator had also refused to allow those whom he delivered from Sodom to do this.

## CHAPTER XXIV

[Col. 0418C] He also chose another seventy apostles in addition to the twelve (Luke 10). For why were there twelve, corresponding to the same number of springs at Elim, unless there were also seventy, corresponding to the same number of palm trees? Difference of circumstances has produced most of the *Antitheses*, not difference of powers. But one who failed to consider the difference of circumstances readily supposed it to be a difference of power.

The Creator brought the children of Israel out of [Note: [Col. 0418C] “From,” Semler.] Egypt, loading them not only with the spoils of gold and silver vessels and clothing, [Note: [Col. 0418D] “In addition to burdens of dough.” So it reads in the copy. Here, therefore, *praeter* functions adverbially and means “in addition.” By “burdens of dough” he means a mass of flour bound together by the sprinkling of water. Exodus 12:34: ἀνέλαβε δὲ ὁ λαὸς τὸ σταῖς αὐτῶν, “and the people took up their dough.” Hesychius: Σταῖς, φύραμα ἀλεύρου πυροῦ, “*stais*: a kneaded mass of wheat flour.” An old glossary: σταῖς, “fat.” Likewise, φύραμα, “mass, dough”; so too, against the Valentinians: “he hid it in the kneading-troughs of the dough until the whole was leavened.” The Vulgate version of Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians 5: “that you may be a new dough, as you are unleavened.” RIG.] but also with burdens of dough packed upon them. [Note: [Col. 0418D] “Packed upon them.” Exodus: τὰ φυράματα αὐτῶν ἐνδεδεμένα ἐν τοῖς ἱματίοις αὐτῶν, “their kneaded masses bound up in their garments.” RIG.] Christ, [Note: [Col. 0418D] “Christ, however, prescribed that the disciples should not carry even a staff,” etc. I would read with Pamelius, “not even a bag,” for this reading agrees exactly with the Gospel of the blessed Luke. LE PR.] [Col. 0419A] however, prescribed that the disciples should not carry even a staff [Note: [Col. 0419D] “Bag,” Franeker edition.] on their journey. For the former were advancing into the wilderness, while the latter were being sent into cities. Consider the difference of circumstances, and you will understand that the power is one and the same: it arranged its people’s equipment according to scarcity or abundance, curtailing what would be plentiful throughout the cities just as it had furnished [Note: [Col. 0419D] “Restricted,” notes Rhenanus.] what would be needed throughout the wilderness.

[Note: [Col. 0419D] “He also forbade them to carry sandals.” Do not understand this to mean that Christ the Lord wanted his disciples to walk with bare feet, but only that they should not provide themselves with sandals to use when those already on their feet had worn out. For the same one who, in accordance with the Old Testament, preserved the Israelites so safe and unharmed for forty years that neither their clothes nor their sandals wore out, could in the New Testament give his own people the same confidence and security. The context itself requires this meaning. LE PR.] He also forbade them to carry sandals. For he himself was the one under whom the people did not wear out their sandals even during all those years in the wilderness.

“You shall greet no one,” he says, “along the way.” [Note: [Col. 0419D] “On the way,” Oberthür.] O Christ, destroyer of the Prophets, from whom he received this command also! When Elisha sent his servant Gehazi along the road, I think, to raise the Shunammite woman’s son from death, he instructed him as follows (2 Kings 4:29): “Gird your loins, take my staff in your hand, and go. Whoever meets you on the road, do not bless him”—that is, do not greet him—“and whoever blesses you, do not answer him”—that is, do not return his greeting. For what blessing occurs between people on the road except the mutual greeting exchanged when they meet?

So too, the Lord’s command that they should speak peace to whatever house they entered [Note: [Col. 0419D] Others read: “that they should speak peace to whatever house.”] follows the same example. For Elisha also gave this command: when he came in to the Shunammite woman, he was to say to her, “Peace to your husband; peace to your son.” [Note: [Col. 0419D] “Your” omitted by Semler.] These will rather be our *Antitheses*: those which compare Christ, not those which separate him.

“The laborer is worthy [Note: [Col. 0419D] “Is” omitted by Oberthür.] of his wages”: who is more likely to have pronounced this than God the Judge? For the very act of declaring the laborer worthy of his wages is an act of judgment. No recompense has ever been determined without judgment.

And now here too the Creator’s law is ratified, which judges even [Col. 0419C] working oxen worthy laborers of their wages: “You shall not muzzle,” he says (Deut. 25:4), “the ox that treads out the grain.” Who is so generous toward human beings except one who is generous even toward cattle? But if Christ also pronounces laborers worthy of wages, he has vindicated that commandment of the Creator concerning the removal of the Egyptians’ gold and silver vessels.
