For those who had labored in the Egyptians’ country estates and cities were surely laborers worthy of their wages: they were instructed [Note: [Col. 0420D] “Prompted,” Pamelius.] not to commit fraud, but to obtain compensation for wages which they could not otherwise exact from their masters.

He also confirmed that the kingdom of God was neither new nor unheard-of [Col. 0420A] when he commanded them to announce that it had drawn near. For something that was once far away can be said to have drawn near. But if it had never existed previously, before it drew near, neither could something that had never been far away be said to have drawn near. Everything new and unknown is sudden. Everything sudden, when it is announced, then assumes appearance for the first time and first acquires a point in time. Otherwise, it could not have been delayed in the past, as long as it was not being announced, nor could it have drawn near from the point when its announcement began.

He further adds [Note: [Col. 0420D] Others read “says”; another reading, “decrees.”] that they should say to those who had not received them: “Nevertheless, know that the kingdom of God has drawn near.” If he does not command this also by way of threat, his command is utterly pointless. For what would it matter to them that the kingdom was drawing near, unless it was drawing near with [Col. 0420B] judgment—namely, for the salvation of those who had received its announcement? How so? If a threat cannot exist without its execution, you have God as executioner in the threatener, and as judge in both capacities.

Thus he also commands them to shake off the dust against them as testimony, [Note: [Col. 0419D] “And the clinging soil of their land.” The copy reads: “Thus he also commands the dust both to be shaken off against them as a testimony to him; and also the land’s heart.” He seems to have said “the clinging soil of their land” to explain what Luke intended to convey by the word “dust.” RIG.] and even the soil of their land that clung to them, to say nothing of any remaining fellowship. [Note: [Col. 0420D] “Adhering soil,” Paris edition; “abhorrent soil,” Franeker edition; “rough soil,” Junius.] For if inhumanity and inhospitality are to receive no vengeance from him, why does he send testimony in advance, which surely portends threats?

Furthermore, since the Creator also forbids the Ammonites and Moabites to be received into the assembly in Deuteronomy (Deut. 23:3), [Note: [Col. 0420D] “He forbids the Ammonites and Moabites to be received into the Church.” Septimius adapts the term “Church” to Jewish times. RIG.] because they had inhumanely and inhospitably withheld provisions from the people departing Egypt, it will therefore be evident that the prohibition of fellowship passed from there into Christ; [Note: [Col. 0420D] “Prohibition of fellowship.” Thus in the book *On Monogamy*: “But they exclude that woman from fellowship.” RIG.—“Prohibition of fellowship.” This can be explained with reference to the Church’s interdicts. Tertullian, a diligent observer of forensic formulas and legal terminology, employed this phrase. Among the jurists an interdict is something pronounced temporarily by a judge; and the glosses say, διαλεγόμενον δύο ἀμφισβητούντων περὶ νομῆς, “a determination between two persons disputing over possession.” Thus an interdict of the Church is temporary separation from the common assembly of the faithful until one who is ἀκοινώνητος, “excluded from communion,” has made satisfaction for his offenses. *Interdictum* means, as it were, *interim dictum*, “something pronounced for the meantime,” as in Cicero, *Letters to Friends* VII.32: “Let us, [Col. 0421D] I beg you, defend our possession of urbanity by every kind of interdict.” The emperor Justinian, however, maintains that it is so called as though “pronounced between two parties.” LE PR.] here he has [Col. 0420C] the formula: “He who despises you despises me.” The Creator said the same thing to Moses (Num. 14:27): “They have not despised you, but me.” For Moses was as much an apostle as the Apostles were prophets. The authority of the two offices must be made equal, since there is one and the same Lord of Apostles and Prophets.

Who, now, will give power to tread upon serpents and scorpions? The Lord of all animals, or a god who does not own even one lizard? [Note: [Col. 0420D] “Lizard” omitted by Semler.] It is fortunate that through Isaiah (Isa. 11:8) the Creator promised this power to little children [Note: [Col. 0420D] “Very young children,” Oberthür.]: to put their hands into the holes of asps and into the den of the offspring of asps, and yet [Col. 0421A] suffer no injury at all.

And we surely know—without prejudice to the literal sense of Scripture, for even the beasts themselves will be unable to harm where there is faith—that scorpions and serpents figuratively portend spiritual forces of wickedness. Their prince himself, in the Creator’s writings, is designated by the name of the serpent, the dragon, and every most monstrous beast. The Creator granted this power first to his Christ, as Psalm 90 says to him (Ps. 90:13): “You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon”; and as Isaiah also says (Isa. 27:1): “On that day the Lord God will bring his holy, great, and mighty sword”—that is, his Christ—“against that dragon, the great and twisting serpent, and on that day he will kill him.”

But the same Isaiah also says (Isa. 35:8): “It shall be called a clean way and a holy way, and nothing unclean shall pass along it, nor shall there be an unclean way there; but those who have been scattered shall walk upon it, and they shall not go astray. There shall no longer be a lion there, nor shall any of the worst beasts come up upon it or be found there.” [Col. 0421B] Since the way signifies the faith by which we shall come to God, he promised even then to that same way—that is, to the faith—this dispensation [Note: [Col. 0421D] “Removal,” Pamelius; “summoning,” Paris edition.] and subjection of the beasts.

Finally, you will find that the times of the promise also agree, if you read what precedes (Isa. 35:3): “Be strengthened, hands that hang down and knees that are feeble. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear. Then the lame man shall leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute shall be clear.” Therefore, when he manifested the benefits of healing, he also subjected scorpions and serpents to his holy ones: he, namely, who had first received this power from the Father so that he might confer it upon others also, and who bestowed it in accordance with the order of the proclamation.

## CHAPTER XXV

[Col. 0421C]

Who will be invoked as Lord of heaven if he has not first been shown to be its Maker? For he says: “I give thanks and make confession, Lord of heaven, because you have revealed to little children the things that were hidden from the wise and prudent.” What are these things? Whose are they? By whom were they hidden, and by whom revealed?

If they were hidden and revealed by Marcion’s god, who had introduced absolutely nothing beforehand in which anything could have been hidden—no prophecies, no parables, no visions, no indications in things, words, or names, obscured by allegories and figures or by the clouds of riddles—but had hidden his own greatness itself, which he was just then revealing through Christ, he had acted quite unjustly. For what offense had the wise and prudent committed, that God should be hidden from them? Their wisdom and prudence had not sufficed for knowing him, [Col. 0421D] because he himself had provided no path through any proclamation of his works, or any footprints by which the wise and prudent might be led.

And even if they had in some respect [Col. 0422A] sinned against the unknown God—suppose him then [Note: [Col. 0422D] “Now,” Semler.] to have been known—they still ought not to have found him jealous, since he is presented as unlike the Creator. Therefore, if he had neither provided materials from which he might conceal something, nor had guilty persons from whom he might conceal it, nor ought to have concealed it even if he had had such persons, then he will not be its revealer either, since he was not its concealer. Thus neither is he Lord of heaven nor Christ’s Father; rather, he is the one to whom all these things properly belong.

For the Creator both concealed, having first supplied the instrument of prophetic obscurity, whose understanding faith would deserve—“For unless you believe,” he says (Isa. 7:9), “you will not understand”—and had as guilty persons [Col. 0422B] the wise and prudent, who did not seek the intelligible God from so many and such great works of his, or who philosophized wrongly about him and furnished their cleverness to heretics. Finally, he is jealous. Indeed, long ago he proclaimed through Isaiah the very thing over which Christ rejoices (Isa. 29:14): “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will hide the prudence of the prudent.”

Likewise elsewhere (Isa. 45:3) he signifies both that he has concealed and that he has revealed: “I will give them hidden treasures; I will open invisible things to them.” And again (Isa. 44:25): “Who else will scatter the signs of ventriloquists [Note: [Col. 0421D] “The signs of ventriloquists.” The author translates the Greek ἐγγαστριμύθων, and does so not only here, but wherever the blessed Jerome translates it as “Pythons.” According to the lexicons of Cyril and Hesychius, they were so called because they pretended to have gods in their bellies and therefore spoke from the belly; hence women possessed by a Python were more common than men. PAM.], and divinations from the heart, turning the wise backward and making foolish their thoughts?”

Moreover, if he also designated his Christ as the illuminator of the nations (Isa. 42:6), “I have appointed you as a light of the nations”—whom we understand under the name of “little children,” since formerly they were small in understanding and infants in lack of prudence, and now are also lowly through the humility of faith—then we shall surely find it easier to believe that the same one also revealed to little children through Christ who had formerly concealed and had promised revelation through Christ.

[Col. 0422C; the supplied source is textually corrupt at this transition, and the translation follows its apparent sense.] Or if Marcion’s god disclosed things that had formerly been hidden by the Creator from the wise and prudent, then he acted on the Creator’s business, explaining the Creator’s affairs. “But,” you say, “he did so to destroy them, by exposing them.” Then he ought to have exposed them to those from whom the Creator had hidden them. For if he acted out of kindness, recognition ought to have been granted to those from whom it had been denied, not to little children, from whom the Creator had withheld nothing. And yet, even now, I think, we prove that Christ is found to build up rather than destroy the Law and the Prophets.

[Note: [Col. 0422D] “He says that all things were delivered to him by the Father.” He proceeds again with the words of the Gospel. Yet what the author adds here—that the Creator delivered all things to the Son as to one who was not inferior to himself—also argues against the Arians and certain modern Arianizers. The blessed Hilary and Augustine likewise interpret this passage in the same way in various places. PAM.] He says that all things were delivered to him by the Father. You may believe it if Christ belongs to the Creator, to whom all things belong: the Creator delivered all things, which he made through him—that is, through his Word [Col. 0422D]—to the Son, who was not inferior to himself.

But if he is that newcomer, ἐπερχόμενος (*eperchomenos*), what are the “all things” that were delivered to him by the Father? Are they the Creator’s things? Then the things that the Father delivered to the Son are good, and the Creator, all of whose things are good, is now good; [Col. 0423A] and the other is now not good, for he invaded another’s goods in order to deliver them to his Son, while teaching people to abstain from what belongs to another. Certainly he is utterly destitute, since he had nothing with which to enrich his Son except another’s property.

Or, if nothing belonging to the Creator was delivered to him by the Father, how does he claim for himself the Creator’s human being? Or, if the human being alone was delivered to him, a human being is not “all things.” Scripture, however, declares that all things were delivered to the Son.

But even if you interpret “all things” as the races of humanity—that is, all nations—it is the Creator who delivered these also to the Son: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. 2:8). Or, if Marcion’s god himself has some things of his own, all of which he might deliver to the Son together with the Creator’s human being, show me any one thing [Note: [Col. 0423D] “Anyone,” Pamelius.] out of them all, as proof and example. Otherwise I have as much reason [Col. 0423B] not to believe that all things belong to one of whose property I see nothing, as I have reason to believe that even the things I do not see belong to the one to whom belong all the things I do see.

“But no one knows who the Father is except the Son, or who the Son is except the Father, and anyone to whom the Son has revealed him” (Matt. 11:27). [Note: [Col. 0423D] “And anyone to whom the Son has revealed him” omitted by Semler, who then writes by repetition: “For no one knows the Father except the Son, or the Son except the Father, and anyone to whom the Son has revealed him.”] And thus Christ proclaimed an unknown God.

[Note: [Col. 0423D] “For other heretics too are supported by this.” These were evidently those who, because of the frequent revelations expressed in Scripture, confused the Father with the Son and asserted that they were the same; Praxeas fell into impious delusions of this kind. LE PR.] For other heretics too are supported by this, arguing that the Creator was known to everyone: to Israel through familiarity, and to the nations through nature. Yet how does he himself testify that he was not known even to Israel: “But Israel did not know me, and my people did not understand me” (Isa. 1:3)? Nor to the nations: “For behold,” he says, “there is no one even among the nations” (Isa. 65:5). For this reason he also reckoned them as a drop from a bucket and left Sion like a watchtower in a vineyard (Isa. 1:8; 40:15).

Consider, therefore, whether this is not a confirmation [Col. 0423C] of the prophetic utterance that reproaches humanity’s ignorance of God, which continued until the Son. For this reason he also added that the Father is known by the one to whom the Son reveals him, since he was the one announced as appointed by the Father to be the illumination of the nations (Isa. 42), which certainly had to be enlightened concerning God, and of Israel also, surely through a fuller recognition of God.

Thus arguments that can properly apply to the Creator will not advance belief in another god; only those that cannot properly apply [Note: [Col. 0423D] “Do not properly apply,” Pamelius.] to the Creator will be able to advance belief in another god.

If you also examine what follows—“Blessed are the eyes that see what you see; for I tell you that the prophets did not see what you [Note: [Col. 0423D] “You” absent from the Franeker edition.] see”—these words descend from the preceding sense: to such a degree had no one known God as was fitting, since not even the prophets had seen the things that were being seen under Christ. For if Christ were not mine, [Col. 0423D] he would not have introduced mention of the prophets in this passage. For what wonder would it be if they had not seen the affairs of an unknown god who was revealed so many ages later?

And what blessedness would have belonged to those who then saw things which others [Col. 0424A] had rightly been unable to see, if they had not obtained the realization of things that those others had never proclaimed? The point is rather that [Note: [Col. 0424D] Pamelius adds “who.”] those who might have seen the works of their own God, which they had also proclaimed, nevertheless had not seen them. [Note: [Col. 0424D] Junius proposes “these” in place of “who.”] But this will be the blessedness of the others: they saw the things that the former had only proclaimed.

Finally, we shall show—and have already shown—that the things seen in Christ were the things that had been proclaimed, yet had remained hidden even from the prophets themselves, so that they might also be hidden from the wise and prudent of the age.

In the Gospel of truth, a teacher of the Law approached the Lord and said: “What must I do to obtain eternal life?” In the heretic’s Gospel merely “life” is written, without mention of “eternal,” so that the teacher may appear to have inquired about that long life [Note: [Col. 0424D] Oberthür adds “eternal.”] which is promised in the Law by the Creator, and so that the Lord may therefore appear to have given him an answer according to the Law: [Col. 0424B] [Note: [Col. 0424D] “Gave,” Semler.] “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength,” because he was asking about the life promised by the Law.

But surely the teacher of the Law knew how he could obtain the life prescribed by the Law, and so would not have asked about something whose rules he himself taught. Rather, since even the dead were now being raised by Christ, and since the examples of restored life had awakened him to hope for eternal life, he inquired about obtaining eternal life in order to learn whether that higher hope required some additional observance. [Note: [Col. 0424D] “Of hope,” Rhenanus.]

Accordingly, the Lord, showing both that he himself was not another and that he was introducing no new commandment other than what is fundamentally effective for all salvation and for both kinds of life, confronts him with the very head of the Law: the command to love the Lord his God in every respect.

Finally, if the man inquired about long life, and Christ answered concerning that life which is with the Creator, [Col. 0424C] not concerning the eternal life which is with Marcion’s god, how does he obtain eternal life? Surely not in the same way as long life. For corresponding to the difference in rewards, a difference in works must also be believed to exist. Therefore a Marcionite will not obtain eternal life through love of your god, in the way that a lover of the Creator obtains long life.

But what sense does it make that the one who promises eternal life should not be loved still more, if the one who promises long life must be loved? Therefore both kinds of life will belong to the same God, since the discipline by which each life must be sought is the same. What the Creator teaches is also what Christ requires in order that he may grant the reward: namely, the love of God. [Note: [Col. 0424D] The Wouwer manuscript reads “the command to love God.”] Here too there intervenes that rule by which greater things ought more readily to be believed of the one with whom lesser things precede than of one for whom no lesser things have prepared any confidence concerning the greater.

Let him now consider whether our people added the word “eternal.” [Col. 0424D] This is enough for me: that this Christ, the inviter to eternal rather than merely long life, when consulted about the long life which he was destroying, did not exhort the man instead to the eternal life which he was introducing.

[Col. 0425A] What, I ask you, would the Creator’s Christ have done if one who had built the man up to love the Creator did not belong to the Creator? I suppose he would have denied that the Creator ought to be loved.

## CHAPTER XXVI
When in a certain place (Luke 11) he had prayed to that higher Father—lifting sufficiently shameless and reckless eyes toward the Creator’s heaven, by whom, harsh and cruel as he was, he might have been struck down by hail and lightning, just as he too might have been crucified by him at Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0425D] “Crucified” (*suffigi*), Paris.]—one of his disciples approached him and said: “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John also taught his disciples”; [Note: [Col. 0425D] “Also” is absent from Paris.] evidently because he supposed that a different God must be prayed to in a different way. Whoever has presumed [Note: [Col. 0425D] *Praesumpserit* in Wouwer’s codex.] this must first prove that another God had been revealed by Christ. For no one would have wished to learn how to pray before he had learned whom he was to pray to. Therefore, if [Col. 0425B] he had learned this, prove it. If thus far you prove it nowhere, know that he requested a form of prayer addressed to the Creator, to whom John’s disciples also prayed.

But because John had introduced a certain new order of prayer, Christ’s disciple quite reasonably presumed that he should request the same [Note: [Col. 0426D] *Expostulandum*, Semler.] from Christ, so that they too, according to the particular institution of their own master, might pray not to another God but to God in another way. Likewise, Christ would not have imparted knowledge of prayer to the disciple before imparting knowledge of God himself. Thus he too taught prayer directed to the one whom the disciple had known up to that point. Finally, examine which God the meanings of the prayer indicate.

[Note: [Col. 0425D] “Whom shall I call Father?” The Author rightly gives this alone, because although the Greek is now read, πατὴρ ἡμῶν ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς, “Our Father who is in the heavens,” and similarly in Syriac, nevertheless in the Latin codices at Luke 11 nothing more than “Father” is read. I suspect that the Greek phrase was added from the Gospel of Matthew 6, according to which it is read in *On Prayer*, chapter 2: “Our Father who art in heaven.” PAM.]

Whom shall I call Father? Him who did not make me at all, from whom I derive no origin? Or him who begot me by making and forming me? From whom shall I ask for the Holy Spirit? [Note: [Col. 0425D] “The Holy Spirit.” Gregory of Nyssa has this in place of “Hallowed be thy name.” SEMLER.] From him by whom not even the spirit of the world [Col. 0425C] is supplied? Or from him by whom even the angels are made spirits, and whose Spirit at the beginning was borne over the waters? Shall I desire the kingdom of one to come whom I have never heard called the King of Glory? Or the kingdom of him in whose hand are even the hearts of kings?

[Note: [Col. 0426D] “Who will give me my daily bread?” Christ clearly forbids us to be anxious about tomorrow, for our life is unstable. Thus the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 9, explains it. That bread, moreover, is Christ, as he himself says. But when he said “daily bread,” he signified the need human beings have of his aid, and also warned that life is lived one day at a time, ζωὴν εἶναι ἐφήμερον, “that life is for a day.” LE PRIEUR.]

Who will give me my daily bread: one who does not create even millet for me, or one who also furnished his people daily with the bread of angels from heaven? Who will forgive my sins: one who, by not judging them, does not retain them, or one who, if he has not forgiven them, will retain them for judgment?

[Note: [Col. 0426D] “Who will not allow us to be led into temptation?” The sense [Col. 0427D] is that we pray God not to permit us to succumb to temptation. LE PRIEUR.]

Who will not allow us to be led into temptation: one whom the tempter need not fear, or one who from the beginning condemned the angelic tempter beforehand? According to this sequence, anyone who supplicates another God rather than the Creator does not pray to that god but defames him.

Likewise, from whom shall I ask, that I may receive? With whom shall I seek, that I may find? At whose door shall I knock, that it may [Col. 0425D] be opened to me? Who has anything to give the petitioner except the one to whom all things belong and to whom I myself, the petitioner, also belong? But what have I [Col. 0426A] lost with that god, that I should seek it with him and find it? If wisdom and prudence, the Creator concealed them; therefore I shall seek them with him. If salvation and life, these too are with the Creator. Nothing will be sought elsewhere in order to be found except where it lay hidden in order to appear. Thus I shall knock nowhere else than at the place from which I was dismissed [Note: [Col. 0426D] “Driven away,” Paris.].

Finally, if receiving, finding, and being admitted are the fruits of labor and persistence for the one who asked, sought, and knocked, understand that these things are commanded and promised by the Creator. For that supremely good god, coming of his own accord to bestow benefits upon a human being who was not his own, would have imposed neither labor nor persistence upon him. Indeed, he would no longer be supremely good if he did not give spontaneously to one who did not ask, grant finding to one who did not seek, and open to one who did not knock.

The Creator, however, could impose these things through Christ, so that, because by sinning [Col. 0426B] the human being had offended his God, he should labor, and through persistence in asking receive, through seeking find, and through knocking enter. So too the preceding parable makes the man who asks for bread at night a friend, not a stranger; and one who knocks at a friend’s door, not at that of someone unknown. Moreover, even if he has caused offense, a human being belongs more properly to the Creator than to Marcion’s god. Therefore he knocks at the door of one upon whom he had a claim, whose door he knew, whom he knew to have bread, and who was already lying down with the little children whose birth he had willed.

Even the fact that the knocking occurs late belongs to the Creator’s time. The late hour belongs to him to whom the age and the age’s setting also belong. No one, however, would have knocked late upon a new god who had only just begun to dawn. It is the Creator who long ago had closed the door to the nations, while it had long been knocked upon by the Jews; [Note: [Col. 0426D] *Cluserit*, Venice.] it is he too who rises and gives—even if now not because the man is his friend, yet [Col. 0426C] not as though he were a stranger, but, as he says, because he is troublesome. Yet a recently arrived god could not so quickly have found anyone troublesome.

Acknowledge, therefore, the Father whom you also call the Creator. It is he who knows what his children ask for. For he both gave manna from heaven to those asking for bread and sent quails to those desiring flesh—not a serpent for a fish, nor a scorpion for an egg. Yet it will belong to the one to refrain from giving evil in place of good to whom both belong. Marcion’s god, by contrast, possessing no scorpion, could not have said that he would not give something he did not possess; but the Creator, though possessing a scorpion too, does not give one. Accordingly, he will also give the Holy Spirit with whom there is also an unholy spirit.

When he had cast out a deaf demon—so that in this kind of healing too he might correspond to Isaiah (Isa. 29:3)—he was said to cast out demons by Beelzebul. “If I,” he said, [Col. 0426D] “cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out?” What did he indicate by this more than that he cast them out by the same one [Col. 0427A] by whom their sons also did—that is, by the power of the Creator?

For if you think it must be understood thus: “If I cast out demons by Beelzebul, [Note: [Col. 0427D] “If I cast out demons by Beelzebul.” Although *Beelbebul* is read in Saints Mark and Luke, the etymology of the word nevertheless requires *Beelzebub*, that is, “prince of flies.” For if you read *Beelzebul*, it will either be a name without any meaning, or one with a better meaning than would be appropriate. For *zebul* means “dwelling,” and sometimes “heaven.” LE PRIEUR.] by whom do your sons cast them out?” [Note: [Col. 0427D] “I cast out demons” is omitted by Oberthür.]—as though he were reproaching them for casting demons out by Beelzebul—the preceding thought will oppose you: that Satan cannot be divided against himself. Therefore, they too did not cast them out by Beelzebul, but, as we have said, by the power of the Creator. To make this understood, he adds: “But if I cast out demons by the finger of God, has the kingdom of God therefore drawn near upon you?”

For when Pharaoh employed those magicians against Moses, with whom he was entering into conflict, they called the Creator’s power “the finger of God” (Exod. 8): “This is the finger of God”—a phrase that [Note: [Col. 0427D] *Quo*, Latinus.] also signified something small, yet exceedingly powerful. [Note: [Col. 0427D] *Significarent*, Paris and Franeker.] Showing this same thing, Christ—the commemorator, not the obliterator, of ancient things, evidently his own—called God’s power “the finger of God,” meaning the power of no other god [Col. 0427B] than the one in whose dispensation it had been so called. Therefore, the kingdom of that same God had drawn near whose power [Note: [Col. 0427D] “Whose power was also called the finger.” That elegant interpretation of “the finger of God” as God’s strength and power is employed by everyone. When Pharaoh’s magicians were unable to produce gnats, they attributed this to God’s finger or power, which was hindering them. LE PRIEUR.] was called his finger.

He therefore rightly applied to the parable of that armed strong man, whom another stronger than he overpowered, the prince of the demons, whom above he had called Beelzebul and Satan, indicating that he was overpowered by the finger of God—not that the Creator was subdued by another god. Otherwise, how would the Creator’s kingdom still stand within its own boundaries, laws, and functions, when Marcion’s stronger god might have been thought to have conquered him, even while the world remained intact, unless even Marcionites still died according to the Creator’s law, sinking back into the earth and often being taught even by a scorpion that the Creator had not been conquered?

A woman from the crowd cried out, [Note: [Col. 0427D] “Cries out,” Pamelius.] “Blessed is the womb that bore him, and the breasts that nursed him.” And [Col. 0427C] the Lord replied: “Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and do it.” For previously too he had similarly set aside his mother or brothers when he preferred hearers and obeyers of God. Indeed, neither was his mother standing near him here. Thus he had not denied her previously either, since [Note: [Col. 0428D] “Neither,” Junius.] even when he hears this again, he again transfers the blessedness from his mother’s womb and breasts to his disciples—a blessedness he would not have transferred from her if he had no mother.

## CHAPTER XXVII

Elsewhere I prefer to clear the Creator of the charges for which the Marcionites criticize him. Here it is enough if the same things are found in Christ. [Col. 0428A] See, he too is inconsistent and inconstant, capricious, teaching one thing and doing another: he commands that something be given to everyone who asks, yet he himself does not give a sign to those asking for one. For so long an age he hid his light from humanity, yet he denies that a lamp ought to be concealed; rather, he declares that it must be placed upon a lampstand so that it may shine for everyone. He forbids returning a curse—much more, surely, uttering a curse—yet he heaps woes upon the Pharisees and the teachers of the law. Whose Christ is so like my God, unless he is his own Christ?

We have often already established [Note: [Col. 0428D] *Finximus*, Pamelius.] that he could in no way have been characterized as a destroyer of the law if he had proclaimed another God. Therefore, when the Pharisee who had invited [Note: [Col. 0428D] *Vocaret*, Paris, Rigault, Venice.] him to dine was then considering within himself why Jesus had not first washed before reclining at table according to the law, was it because Jesus represented the God of the law? Jesus, moreover, interpreted the law for him, saying that they cleansed the outsides of the cup and dish, [Col. 0428B] but that their own insides were full of plunder and iniquity. He thereby indicated that the cleanliness of vessels was to be understood before God as the cleanliness of human beings, because the Pharisee too had been reflecting within himself about the man, not about an unwashed cup.

“You wash,” he therefore said, “the outsides of the cup,” that is, the flesh, “but you do not cleanse your insides,” that is, the soul, adding: “Did not he who made the outsides,” that is, the flesh, “also make the insides,” that is, the soul? By this statement he plainly demonstrated that the cleanliness of both the outward and inward human being belongs to the same God, because both belong to him—the God who prefers mercy not merely to a human being’s washing, but even to sacrifice (Hos. 6:6). For he adds:

[Note: [Col. 0427D] “Give what you have as alms,” etc. The Author rightly translates “what you have,” as does the Syriac interpreter: this is the meaning of the Greek τὰ ἐνόντα, “the things within,” as though he were saying, in Theophylact’s words, “not what you have seized, but what is your own.” The Vulgate translator had precisely this in view when rendering it “what remains,” namely, what remains beyond plunder and iniquity. Once this sense has been explained, there is no need to read *datis*, “when these things have been given,” instead of *date*, “give,” with Erasmus and Cajetan. Meanwhile, Blessed Cyprian, book 3 *Against Quirinus*, chapter 1, reads neither form; nor does Blessed Ambrose in his *Commentary*, or Blessed Augustine in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 75. Since, however, the Vulgate version also admits the same sense, as we have said, one must repeat here what we have said more than once: Isidore Clarius’s correction, “from the things available to you,” is too free, as though the alternative reading could not possibly be tolerated. PAM.]

“Give what you have as alms, and all things will be clean for you.” Even if another god could also have commanded mercy, nevertheless he could not have done so before he was known. Furthermore, it is apparent here too that they [Col. 0428C] were rebuked not concerning their God, but concerning the discipline of the one by whom both the cleanliness of vessels had been figuratively commanded and works of mercy explicitly enjoined.

So too he reproaches them for tithing garden herbs while passing over the calling [Note: [Col. 0428D] “Calling.” He appears to have read κλῆσιν, “calling,” in place of κρίσιν, “judgment”; or rather to have taken it from Marcion’s Gospel—which denied that judgment belonged to the good God—as an acknowledged point. JUNIUS.] and love of God. The calling and love of which God, except the one to whom they offered rue and mint also, in accordance with the Law’s rule concerning tithes? For the whole point of the reproach was that they attended to small matters for the very one to whom they did not render the greater obligations, though he said (Deut. 6:5): “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart [Note: [Col. 0428D] “Your” is omitted by Semler.] and with [Col. 0429A] all your soul and with all your strength, who called you out of Egypt.”

Otherwise, the time itself would not have permitted Christ to demand so premature—indeed, so immature—a love for a new and recently arrived god, not to say one who had not yet been openly revealed. When he also censures those who seek the foremost seats and the honor of greetings, he administers the Creator’s teaching, who calls such rulers of Sodom *archons* (Isa. 1:23), who also forbids trust in rulers, and indeed pronounces utterly wretched the human being who places his hope in a human being (Ps. 117:8–9).

But if someone seeks preeminence in order to glory in the services of others, then because the Creator forbade such services of hope and trust in a human being (Jer. 17:5), that same Creator also [Note: [Col. 0429D] “Also” is absent from Paris.] rebuked those who seek positions of preeminence.

He inveighs also against the teachers of the law themselves because they burdened others with unbearable burdens [Col. 0429B] which they themselves did not dare to touch even with a finger. He was not disparaging the burdens of the Law as one who detested it; for how could he detest it when he was at that very moment accusing them of neglecting the weightier matters of the Law—almsgiving, the calling and love of God—things that were not burdensome at all, much less the tithing of rue [Note: [Col. 0429D] “And” is absent from Paris.] and the cleansing of dishes? Otherwise, he should rather have judged them excusable if they could not bear unbearable things.

But what burdens does he censure? Those which they themselves heaped up on their own authority, teaching commandments and doctrines of human beings for the sake of their own advantage (Isa. 5:23), joining house to house so that they might seize what belonged to their neighbors, oppressing the people, loving gifts, pursuing recompense, plundering the judgments due to the poor, so that the widow became their spoil and the orphan their prey. Concerning these [Col. 0429C] the same Isaiah says (Isa. 28:14): “Woe to those who are powerful in Jerusalem,” [Note: [Col. 0429D] “Israel,” Oberthür.] and again (Isa. 3:3): “Those who make demands upon you are your masters.” Who more than the teachers of the law? If they displeased Christ also, they displeased him as his own servants.

[Note: [Col. 0429D] “For they were teachers of another’s law.” Here and frequently elsewhere, the teachers of the Law, those learned in the Law, and the Pharisees are called οἱ νομικοί, “the lawyers,” in Greek. LE PRIEUR.]

For he would not have attacked teachers of another’s law at all. Why, moreover, do they also hear “woe” because they built monuments to the prophets whom their fathers had killed? They would instead have deserved praise, because by this work of piety they testified that they did not consent to their fathers’ deeds—unless he was a jealous God of the kind the Marcionites charge him with being, exacting the sins of the fathers from their children down to the fourth generation.

What key, moreover, did the teachers of the law possess except the interpretation of the law? They themselves did not approach its understanding, because they did not believe: “For unless you believe, you will not understand.” Nor did they admit others, [Col. 0429D] since, of course, they taught [Note: [Col. 0429D] “Were teaching,” Semler.] instead the commandments and doctrines of human beings. Therefore, should the one who rebuked them because they neither entered themselves nor granted entrance to others be regarded as a detractor from the law, or as its supporter? If a detractor, then those who barred access to the law ought also to have pleased him; if a supporter, then he is no longer an opponent of the law.

But he heaped up all these things to cast a shadow upon the Creator as cruel, since those who sinned against him would incur woe. Yet who would not fear all the more to provoke a cruel God by defecting [Note: [Col. 0429D] “Despising,” in some copies.] from him? Therefore, he taught all the more that favor must be won from the one whom he represented as an object of fear. Such was necessarily the Christ of the Creator.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

The hypocrisy of the Pharisees therefore rightly displeased him: [Note: [Col. 0430D] That is, loving God with their lips but not with their heart. They followed the letter that kills, not the life-giving spirit of the Law; for they did not possess the key—that is, the interpretation of the Law, as he has just said. While they superstitiously observed certain outward matters, they neglected what was foremost. LE PRIEUR.] they loved God with their lips, not with their heart. “Beware,” he said to his disciples (Luke 12), “of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy”—not the proclamation of the Creator. The Son hates those who are rebellious against the Father; he does not wish his own followers to behave like that toward him—not toward some other god, against whom hypocrisy would have been committed, with the Pharisees’ example serving as something the disciples must avoid. [Col. 0430B] Thus he forbids [Note: [Col. 0429D] “Presents,” in other copies.] the Pharisees’ example: he was forbidding such conduct toward the one against whom the Pharisees committed it.

Accordingly, since he had censured their hypocrisy, which concealed the hidden things of the heart and covered over the secrets of unbelief with superficial observances—hypocrisy which, though possessing the key of knowledge, [Note: [Col. 0430D] Pamelius inserts “in.”] neither entered itself nor allowed others to enter—he therefore adds: “But there is nothing covered that will not be revealed, and nothing hidden that will not become known.” No one, therefore, should suppose that he intended the revelation and recognition of a God previously unknown and hidden, since he also includes the things they whispered or discussed among themselves—namely, what they said about him: “This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebul”—which would be brought into the open and come to be on human lips through the proclamation of the Gospel.

Then, [Note: [Col. 0430D] “Thereafter,” Pamelius.] turning to the disciples, he said: [Col. 0430C] “But I say to you, my friends, [Note: [Col. 0430D] “My” is absent from other copies.] do not be terrified by those who can only kill you and after this have no further power over you.” Isaiah had prophesied of them (Isa. 57:1): “See how the righteous man is taken away, and no one takes notice.” “But I shall show you whom you should fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna”—plainly signifying [Note: [Col. 0430D] “Signifying” is omitted by Semler.] the Creator. “Accordingly, I say to you, fear him.”

At this point it would be enough for me that, when he commands someone to be feared, he forbids that person to be offended; when he forbids him to be offended, he commands that his favor be won; and the one who commands these things belongs to the very God whose interests he serves by seeing that he is feared, not offended, and won over. But I can also draw evidence from what follows: “For I say to you: Everyone who confesses me before human beings, I shall confess in him before God.”

Those who make their confession in Christ will have to be killed before [Col. 0430D] human beings, and after being killed they will of course suffer nothing further from them. These, [Note: [Col. 0430D] “This one,” Rigault and Venice.] therefore, will be the persons whom he warned above not to fear being merely killed. Thus he first declares that death is not to be feared so that he may add that confession must be maintained [Col. 0431A] [Note: [Col. 0431D] “Endured,” Oberthür.]: “And everyone who denies me before human beings will be denied before God”—plainly by the one who would have confessed the person confessing him. For if he confesses the confessor, he himself is also the one who will deny the denier.

Furthermore, if the confessor is the one who has nothing to fear after being killed, the denier will be the one who has something to fear even after death. Accordingly, since what must be feared after death—namely, the punishment of Gehenna—belongs to the Creator, the denier too belongs to the Creator. But if both the denier and the confessor—the one who after being killed will suffer nothing from a human being but will certainly suffer from God if he denies—belong to the Creator, then Christ too belongs to the Creator, because he shows that those who deny him ought to fear the Creator’s Gehenna.

After discouraging denial, therefore, there follows a warning that blasphemy too must be feared:

[Note: [Col. 0431D] “Whoever speaks against the Son of Man,” etc. Although the Author does not express it, he nevertheless understands “whoever speaks blasphemy,” in place of the wording others have, “whoever blasphemes,” as is clear both from the Greek and Syriac and from the following words: “His Holy Spirit must not be blasphemed.” PAM.]

“Whoever speaks against the Son of Man will be forgiven; [Col. 0431B] but whoever [Note: [Col. 0431D] “But whoever,” Pamelius.] speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.” If forgiving and retaining sin already indicate God as judge, then the Holy Spirit who must not be blasphemed will belong to that God [Note: [Col. 0431D] “Whose,” Semler.] who, of course, will not forgive the blasphemy—just as above Christ must not be denied because that God will kill even in Gehenna.

But if Christ also turns blasphemy away from the Creator, I do not know how he came as his adversary. Or if by these declarations too he casts a shadow upon the Creator’s severity—because he will not forgive blasphemy and will kill even in Gehenna—it remains that the Spirit of that different god may be blasphemed with impunity, and his Christ denied, and that it makes no difference whether he is worshiped or despised; and just as no punishment follows contempt, so no reward is to be hoped for from worship.

When they are brought [Note: [Col. 0431D] “Produced,” in other copies.] before the authorities, he forbids them to think beforehand, when questioned, about their answer: [Col. 0431C] “For the Holy Spirit,” he says, “will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.” [Note: [Col. 0431D] “What you are to say,” in other copies.] If an example of this kind belongs to the Creator, the command too will belong to the one whose example preceded it. Balaam the prophet, in Numbers (Num. 22), was summoned by King Balak to curse Israel, with whom the king was going to war, and was at once filled with the Spirit. He pronounced not the curse for which he had come, but the blessing that the Spirit suggested to him at that very hour, having first declared before the royal messengers [Note: [Col. 0432D] “Of the king,” Semler.], and shortly afterward before the king himself, that he would pronounce what God had put into his mouth. These are the new teachings of the new Christ, which the servants of the Creator inaugurated long ago.

Here, plainly, is a different example in Moses and Christ. [Note: [Col. 0432D] Moses intervenes of his own accord between brothers who are quarreling. He calls those “brothers” who were of the same stock of Israel; a little later he takes the word in its proper sense. He also rendered in the single word *injuriosum*, “the wrongdoer,” what in the Greek of Exodus 2 is ἀδικοῦντι, “the one who was doing wrong”; and, remarkably, he rendered as *magistrum*, “master,” what in Greek is ἄρχοντα, for which everywhere else, and properly, he uses “ruler.” PAM.] Moses intervenes of his own accord between brothers who are quarreling [Note: [Col. 0432D] Rhenanus places “and” before this.], and rebukes the wrongdoer: “Why do you strike your neighbor?” But the man rejects him: “Who appointed you master or judge over us?” Christ, however, when asked by someone to mediate between him and his brother [Col. 0432A] concerning the division of an inheritance [Note: [Col. 0432D] “Concerning” is omitted by Venice.], refused his assistance, even in so worthy a cause. Thus my Moses is now better than your Christ, striving for peace between brothers and intervening against wrongdoing.

But of course he is the Christ of the supremely good and non-judging God: “Who,” he says, “appointed me judge over you?” He could find no other plea of excuse, lest he fail to use the very one by which a wicked man and impious brother had rebuffed the champion of uprightness and piety. In short, by using it he approved the wicked statement, and by declining to establish peace between brothers he approved the wicked deed. Or did he perhaps take it amiss that Moses had been driven away by this statement, and therefore, in the parallel case of brothers in dispute, wish to put them to shame by recalling the same statement? Precisely so. For it was he himself who had then been in Moses and had heard such things—namely, the Spirit of the Creator.

I think we have already established sufficiently elsewhere that the glory of riches is condemned by our God, who casts potentates themselves down from the throne and raises the poor from the dunghill (Ps. 112:13). From him, therefore, will also come the parable of the rich man flattering himself over the yield of his fields, to whom God says: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul back; then whose will the things you have prepared be?” [Note: [Col. 0432D] “For whom,” Latinus.] Thus, indeed, the king who boasted among the Persians about the treasuries and storehouses of his pleasures was reproved through Isaiah (Isa. 39).

## CHAPTER XXIX
Who would not wish us to take no thought for the soul’s food and the body’s clothing, except the one who had already provided these things for humankind [Col. 0432C] and, by thereafter supplying them, rightly forbids anxiety about them as though it rivaled his generosity—the one who furnished the very substance of the soul, which is more valuable than food, and fashioned the material of the body itself, which is more valuable than a tunic; whose ravens neither sow nor reap nor gather into storehouses, and yet are fed by him; whose lilies and grass neither weave nor spin, and yet are clothed by him; and in comparison with whose flowers even Solomon, most glorious though he was, was not more splendidly arrayed? Besides, nothing is so incoherent as that one should provide, while another commands people to feel secure [Note: [Col. 0432D] “Unconcerned,” Oberthür.] about his provision [Note: [Col. 0432D] *De praestantia.* Here *praestantia* means the same as *praestatio*, “provision” or “supply.” SEMLER.]—and that other, moreover, his detractor. Finally, if, as a detractor of the Creator, he does not wish people to concern themselves with such trifles, over which neither ravens nor lilies labor, because they are naturally beneath his notice owing to their worthlessness, the truth will become apparent shortly. Meanwhile, why does he accuse them of having little faith [Col. 0433A]—that is, little faith in whom? Is it the faith which they could not yet exhibit perfectly toward God, since they were only then learning about him under a veil [Note: [Col. 0433D] “Revealed,” Lat.], or the faith which under this very title they owed to the Creator, namely, that they should believe that he freely supplies these things to the human race and therefore should not [Note: [Col. 0433D] “Not,” Latinius.] be anxious about them?

For when he adds, “For the nations of the world seek after these things”—because, of course, they do not believe in God, the founder and provider [Note: [Col. 0433D] “Approver,” Semler.] of all things—he did not wish his hearers to be like the Gentiles, and so rebuked them for little faith in the same God in relation to whom he censured the Gentiles for unbelief [Note: [Col. 0433D] “Unbelievers,” Semler.]. Moreover, when he also adds, “But the Father knows that you need these things,” I shall first ask which father Christ wishes to be understood. If he indicates their Creator, he also confirms that he is good, since he knows [Note: [Col. 0433D] “May know,” codex Wouwer.] what his children need. But if he means another God, how does that God know that food and clothing are necessary for man [Col. 0433B], when he has supplied neither? For if he had known, he would have supplied them. But if he knows what things are necessary for man and nevertheless did not supply them, he failed to supply them either through malice or through weakness. Yet by declaring that these things are necessary for man, he has surely confirmed that they are good, for nothing evil is necessary. And he will no longer be a disparager of the Creator’s works and indulgences; thus I have settled the point I deferred above.

Moreover, if another both foresaw and supplies the things which he knows to be necessary for man, how does he himself promise them [Note: [Col. 0433D] “Promises,” Pamelius.]? Is he good at another’s expense? “For seek,” he says, “the kingdom of God, and these things will be added to you.” Surely by him. But if by him, what sort of person is he who will supply another’s property? If they are supplied by the Creator, to whom they also belong, who is this that promises another’s property? If these things are to be added [Note: [Col. 0433D] “Are added,” Oberthür.] to the kingdom, as goods to be bestowed in the second rank, the second rank belongs to him to whom the first also belongs [Col. 0433C]; the food and clothing belong to him whose kingdom it is. Thus the whole promise belongs to the Creator.

The coherence of parables and the correspondence of similitudes hold only if they refer [Note: [Col. 0433D] “To” is absent from Rigault and the Venetian edition.] to no other than the one whom they resemble in every respect [Note: [Col. 0434D] “Have come as equals,” another reading.]. We are servants [Note: [Col. 0434D] *Id* absent from Rigault and the Venetian edition.], for we have God as our Lord. We must gird up our loins, that is, be unencumbered by the hindrances of a trailing and entangled manner of life; likewise, we must have our lamps burning, that is, minds kindled by faith and shining with works of truth; and so await the Lord, that is, Christ. Returning from where? If from a wedding, he belongs to the Creator, to whom marriage belongs. If he does not belong to the Creator, not even Marcion himself would have gone to a wedding if invited, since he regards [Note: [Col. 0434D] “Fears,” Latinius.] his God as one who detests marriage. The parable therefore fails in the person of the Lord unless he is one to whom marriage is appropriate.

In the following parable too, the man is seriously mistaken who assigns to the person of the Creator that thief whose hour, if the householder knew it, he would not allow his house to be broken into [Col. 0434A] [Note: [Col. 0434D] “Dug out,” Paris edition.]. For how can the Creator be regarded as a thief when he is Lord of the whole man? No one steals or breaks into what is his own; rather, the thief is the one who descends upon another’s property and alienates man from his Lord. Moreover, since he shows us that the thief is the devil [Note: [Col. 0434D] “Will have shown,” another reading.], whose hour, even in the beginning, if man had known it, he would never have been broken into by him, he therefore commands us to be ready, because “at an hour when we do not suppose, the Son of Man will come”—not because he himself is the thief, but because he is the judge, namely, of those who have not prepared themselves or guarded against the thief. Therefore, if he himself is the Son of Man, I apprehend him as judge, and in the judge I uphold the Creator.

But if in this passage he presents the Creator’s Christ under the name “Son of Man” in order to foreshadow as a thief the one whose time of coming we do not know, you have it written above [Col. 0434B] that no one is a thief of his own property. There remains also this consideration: insofar as he impresses upon us that the Creator is to be feared, to that same extent, by advancing the Creator’s cause, he belongs to the Creator.

Accordingly, when Peter asked whether he had spoken the parable for them or also for everyone, he set forth for them and for all who would preside over the churches the analogy of stewards [Note: [Col. 0433D] The analogy of stewards. *Actor* means “agent” or “manager.” SEMLER.]. The one among them who treats his fellow servants well in the Lord’s absence [Note: [Col. 0433D] “The one among them who treats his fellow servants well in the Lord’s absence,” etc. Here the Author has translated in a general sense “treats well,” in place of Luke’s τοῦ διδόναι ἐν καιρῷ τὸ σιτομέτριον, that is, as the common Latin translator renders it [Col. 0434D], “that he may give them their measure of wheat at the proper time.” Although this applies to every kind of food, Clarius has nevertheless emended it much too freely here also to “allowance.” He ought therefore to have called it his own translation rather than an emendation of the common translator. PAMELIUS.] will, when the Lord returns, be placed over all his goods. But the one who acts otherwise will, when the Lord returns on a day he did not expect and at an hour he did not know—that Lord being, of course, the Son of Man, the Creator’s Christ, not a thief but a judge—be separated, and his portion will be assigned with the unbelievers.

Accordingly, either here too he confronts us with the Lord as judge and instructs us in submission to him; or, if he confronts us with the supremely good God, he now affirms that this God too is a judge, however unwilling the heretic may be. For they try to soften the meaning of this passage [Col. 0434C] when it is claimed for his God, as if it were an act of serenity and gentleness merely to separate a man and assign his portion with the unbelievers—as though the man had not been summoned so that, being returned to his own condition, this very thing should be done by a judicial sentence. Folly! What will be the fate of those separated? Will it not be the loss of salvation, since they will be separated from those who obtain salvation? What [Note: [Col. 0434D] “What thing,” Pamelius.] then will be the condition of the unbelievers? Will it not be damnation? Or, if the separated and unbelieving suffer nothing, then conversely the retained and faithful will equally obtain nothing. But if the retained and faithful obtain salvation, the separated and unbelieving must conversely lose it. This will be a judgment; and he who threatens it belongs to the Creator.

Whom else am I to understand as the one who beats servants with few or many stripes, and who demands from them in proportion to what he entrusted to them, except God the requiter? Whom is it fitting [Note: [Col. 0434D] “Teaches,” François and Pamelius.] for me to obey except the rewarder? [Col. 0435A] Your Christ proclaims, “I came to cast fire upon the earth”—that supremely good one, lord of no Gehenna, who shortly before had restrained his disciples from calling down fire upon a most inhospitable village. When did this Christ burn Sodom and Gomorrah with a fiery storm? When was it sung, “Fire will go [Note: [Col. 0435C] “Proceed,” Pamelius.] before him and burn up his enemies” (Ps. XCIII, 3)? When did he also threaten through Hosea, “I will send fire upon the cities of Judah” (Hos. VIII, 14) [Note: [Col. 0435C] “Judaea,” Semler.]? Or through Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0435C] Read “Jeremiah,” Junius; the explicit words occur at Jeremiah XV, 14.], “A fire has blazed forth from my indignation” (Isa. XXX, 27)?

Let him not lie. If he is not the one who also sent forth his voice from the burning bush, let him see [Note: [Col. 0435D] “You see,” Semler.] what fire he insists must be understood [Note: [Col. 0435D] “You insist,” Pamelius.]. Even if it is a figure, by the very fact that he takes from my element the imagery for his meaning, he is mine, since he uses what is mine. The likeness of fire will belong to him to whom its reality also belongs.

He himself will better interpret the nature of this fire [Col. 0435B] by adding, “Do you suppose that I came to send peace upon the earth? No, I tell you, but division.” [Note: [Col. 0435D] “A sword,” indeed, is what was written—in Marcion’s Gospel, that is, Luke’s Gospel adulterated by Marcion. Tertullian says at the beginning of this book that he appeals to this kind of Gospel in order to convict Marcion of madness from that very text. RIGAULT.] “A sword” indeed is what was written; [Note: [Col. 0435D] But Marcion emends it. For Luke said διαμερισμόν, “division.” RIGAULT.] but Marcion emends it [Note: [Col. 0435D] As though division were not also the work of a sword. It was in this sense that Matthew used μάχαιρον, “sword,” for what Luke called διαμερισμόν, “division,” so that Marcion’s emendation of Luke is now pointless. Epiphanius, however, does not mention it. RIGAULT.], as though division were not also the work of a sword. Therefore, the one who denied that he brought peace also threatens the fire of overthrow. As the battle is, so is the conflagration; as the sword is, so is the flame—neither being consistent with such a Lord.

Finally, he says: “Father will be divided against son, and son against father; mother against daughter, and daughter against mother; mother-in-law against daughter-in-law, and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.” If the prophet’s trumpet sounded this conflict between relatives in these very words, I fear that Micah (Mic. VII, 6) may have proclaimed Marcion’s Christ. And for this reason he called them hypocrites: they knew how to discern the appearance of heaven and earth, but did not recognize [Col. 0435C] that time—the time, namely, in which he was fulfilling everything that had been foretold concerning them and teaching nothing different, and therefore ought to have been recognized. Besides, who could know the times of one who possessed no evidence by which he could be identified?

Rightly, too, does he reproach them for not judging what is just of themselves. Long ago he commanded this through Zechariah (Zech. VIII, 16): “Judge a just and peace-making judgment.” Through Jeremiah (Jer. XXII, 3): “Execute judgment and justice.” Through Isaiah (Isa. I, 17; V, 6): “Judge for the orphan and vindicate the widow”; he also charged the vineyard of Sorech [Col. 0436A] with having produced not judgment but an outcry. He, therefore, who had taught them to act according to a commandment was also demanding that they act according to their own judgment. He who had sown the commandment was also pressing for its abundant fruit.

And indeed, how absurd it would be for the one who was destroying the just God as judge to command people to judge justly! For they also interpret the judge who sends a man to prison and does not release him until even the last farthing has been paid as a figure of the Creator, for the purpose of disparaging him. I must answer this on the same footing: as often as the Creator’s severity is adduced, so often Christ belongs to him whose obedience he compels by fear.

## CHAPTER XXX

How did he settle once again the question concerning a cure performed on the Sabbath? [Note: [Col. 0435D] “Does not every one of you on the Sabbaths loose his ass,” etc. Epiphanius did not press this point—in which alone the Author differs from the others by reading “on the Sabbaths” instead of “on the Sabbath”—but rather, in Refutation 39, the words of Christ that follow: “But this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan bound.” From this he proves that Christ belongs to the same God to whom Abraham belongs. This is all the more so because, as he continues in Refutation 40, Marcion had also excised the statement near the end of this chapter of Luke, “When you see Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and all the prophets in the kingdom of God,” reading only, “When you see all the righteous in the kingdom of God.” Thus what the Author omitted, Epiphanius particularly presses. *Against Marcion.* PAMELIUS.] “Does not every one of you on the Sabbaths loose [Col. 0436B] his ass or his ox from the manger and lead it to water?” Therefore, by acting in accordance with the terms of the Law, he confirmed the Law rather than abolished it—the Law that commands no work to be done except what is done for every living being [Note: [Col. 0436D] “No work to be done except what is done for every living being.” We have already observed that the translation of the Septuagint followed by Tertullian can be understood in another way, one more consistent with the idiom of the Greek language and the meaning of the Hebrew text. See Chapter 12 of this book. EDITORS.], and how much more for a human being!

I insist that the coherence of the parables be recognized everywhere [Note: [Col. 0436C] “Recognize,” Latinius.]. “The kingdom of God,” he says, “is like a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his garden.” Who is to be understood in the person of the man? Surely Christ, because although he is Marcion’s Christ, he is called the Son of Man—the one who received from the Father the seed of the kingdom, namely, the word of the Gospel, and sowed it in his garden, surely in the world, or suppose, for the present, in man. But since he said “in his own garden,” while neither the world nor man belongs to him but to the Creator, the one who sowed in his own property is therefore shown to be none other than [Note: [Col. 0436C] “Nor” omitted by Pamelius.] the Creator.

Or if, in order to escape this snare, they transfer the person of the man [Col. 0436C] from Christ to a human being who receives the seed of the kingdom and sows it in the garden of his own heart, the subject matter itself will still suit no one but the Creator. For how can the kingdom of the most gentle God be signified by a seed [Note: [Col. 0436C] “Be signified by a seed” is absent from Pamelius, but is present in the Wouwer codex.] which is followed even by the heat of judgment with its tearful harshness [Note: [Col. 0436D] “The judgment of heat and tearful severities follow,” codex Wouwer.]?

As for the next similitude, I certainly fear that perhaps it portends the kingdom of another God. For he compared it to leaven, not to unleavened bread, which is more familiar to the Creator. This conjecture too is fitting for those who beg for arguments. Accordingly, I too shall repel vanity with vanity [Col. 0437A], saying that fermentation also suits the Creator’s kingdom, because after it comes the oven or furnace of Gehenna.

How often does he still show himself to be judge, and in the judge the Creator! How often, surely, has he cast people out, and condemned them by rejecting them! As here too: “When the householder [Note: [Col. 0437D] “Head of the household,” Pamelius.] rises,” he says. Rises to what, unless to what Isaiah said (Isa. II, 19): “When he rises to shatter the earth”? “And shuts the door”—surely for the exclusion of the wicked. When they knock, he will answer them, “I do not know where you are from.” And when they in turn recount that they ate and drank in his presence and that he taught in their streets, he will add, “Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” Where? Outside, of course, where they will be after being excluded by him and the door shut. Therefore punishment will come from the one by whom exclusion is effected as punishment, when they see the righteous entering the kingdom of God while they themselves [Col. 0437B] are kept outside.

Kept outside by whom? If by the Creator, who then will be inside, receiving the righteous into the kingdom? The good God. What business, then, has the Creator there, detaining outside for punishment those whom his adversary has excluded, when instead he ought to receive them himself, all the more to spite his adversary? Yet the one who will exclude the wicked must either know that the Creator will detain them for punishment, or not know it. Therefore, either they will be detained against his will, in which case he is inferior to the one who detains them and yields to him unwillingly; or, if he wills it to happen so, he himself has judged that it ought to be done so, and he will be no better than the Creator, since he himself is the author of the Creator’s ill repute.

Since these claims cannot stand on any rational basis—that one God is believed to punish and another to deliver—both judgment and kingdom will belong to one God; and since both belong to one, the one who also judges belongs to the Creator.

## CHAPTER XXXI

[Col. 0437C] What sort of people does he command to be invited to luncheon or dinner? Those whom he had indicated through Isaiah (Isa. LVIII, 7): [Note: [Col. 0437D] “Break your bread for the hungry, and the beggars,” etc. “Beggars,” where the Vulgate has “the needy,” or πτωχούς, “the poor.” PAMELIUS.] “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the beggars and those without a roof into your house”—those, namely, who cannot repay the service of this humanity. If Christ forbids such repayment to be sought, while promising it in the resurrection, this is the pattern of the Creator, who is not pleased with those who love gifts and pursue repayment.

Consider [Note: [Col. 0437D] “I consider,” Pamelius.] also to which side the parable of the host is more applicable: “A certain man made a dinner and invited many.” Surely the preparation of the dinner represents the fullness of eternal life. I say first that strangers and those connected by no legal bond are not ordinarily invited to dinner; household members and friends certainly are invited more readily. It therefore belongs to the Creator to have invited those who belonged to the one who invited them—through Adam insofar as they were human beings, and [Col. 0437D] through the Fathers insofar as they were Jews. It does not belong to one to whom they belonged neither by nature nor by privilege.

Next, if the one who prepared the dinner sends to the guests, then on this ground too the dinner belongs to the Creator, who sent to remind the guests—those already invited beforehand through the Fathers, but now reminded through the prophets. It does not belong to one who sent no one to remind them and had done nothing beforehand to invite them, but who himself descended [Col. 0438A] suddenly: no sooner becoming known than inviting, no sooner inviting than compelling people to the banquet, making the hour of dining the same as the hour of invitation.

The invited guests excuse themselves. If the invitation came from another God, they do so deservedly, because they were invited suddenly. If not deservedly, then they were not invited suddenly. But if they were not invited suddenly, then they were invited by the Creator, by whom they had been invited long ago. For it was his invitation they had originally declined when they said to Aaron (Exod. XXXII, 1), “Make us gods to go before us,” and from that time onward (Isa. VI, 10), “Hearing with the ear and not hearing”—namely, the call of God. Most appositely to this parable he says through Jeremiah (Jer. XI, 40): “Hear my voice, and I will be your Lord and you will be my people; and you shall walk in all my ways, whatever I command you.” Behold God’s invitation. “And they did not hear,” he says [Col. 0438B], “and did not incline their ear.” Behold the people’s refusal. “But they departed after the things their evil heart desired.” “I bought a field, I purchased oxen, and I married a wife.”

And he further presses the point (Jer. VII, 24): “And I sent to you all my servants the prophets.” Here the Holy Spirit will be the one who reminds the guests, by day and before dawn. “And my people did not hear and did not incline their ears, but hardened their neck.” When this was reported to the householder, he became angry—well indeed that he became angry, for Marcion denies that his God is moved; by this too, then, he is mine—and commanded that a selection be made from the squares and streets of the city.

Let us see whether this is in the same sense as what he says again through Jeremiah (Jer. II, 31): “Have I become a wilderness to the house of Israel, or a land abandoned without cultivation?” That is: “Do I not have people whom I may choose, or a place from which [Col. 0438C] I may choose them?” “Because my people said, ‘We will not come to you.’” Accordingly, he sent to summon others, still from the same city.

Then, since there was still room, he commanded that people be gathered even from the roads and hedges—that is, us, now from the foreign nations—through that rivalry of which he speaks in Deuteronomy (Deut. XXXII, 20): “I will turn my face away from them and show what will happen to them in the last days,” that is, that others will possess their place; “because they are a perverse generation, children in whom there is no faith. They have provoked me to jealousy by what is no god and have provoked me to anger with their idols; and I will provoke them to jealousy by what is no nation; by a foolish nation I will provoke them to anger.” This refers, of course, to us, whose hope [Note: [Col. 0438D] “Appearance,” Latinius.] the Jews bear. [Note: [Col. 0437D] Concerning this dinner the Lord denies that they will taste it. This interpretation teaches that the Jews were rejected because of their obstinacy, while Christians were called to the dinner—or, as he explains it, to the fullness of heavenly life. LE PRIEUR.] The Lord denies that they will taste of that dinner. Zion was abandoned (Isa. I, 8) like a watchtower in a vineyard and a hut in a cucumber field, after she [Col. 0438D] had also refused the last invitation in Christ [Note: [Col. 0438D] “Christ,” accusative, Pamelius, François, Rigault, Paris edition.].

What feature of this sequence, when reviewed according to the Creator’s arrangements and prophecies, can suit one who possesses neither the sequence nor any arrangement harmonizing with the parable, but performed the whole work all at once? Or what will be his first call, and what his reminder in a second action? Some must first make excuses, and afterward others must have assembled. [Col. 0439A] But as matters now stand, he came to invite both groups simultaneously—those from the city and those from the hedges—contrary to the parable’s model. Nor can he now judge as disdainful those whom he never invited before and whom he is only now approaching.

Or if he judges that in the future they will despise the invitation, then he likewise foreshadows as future the selection of Gentiles in their place. Certainly he will come a second time for this purpose, to preach to the Gentiles! Yet if he is to come, I think it will not be to invite the guests still, but to seat them at the feast.

Meanwhile, you who interpret the invitation to this dinner [Note: [Col. 0439D] “To” is absent, Chacón would have it so.] as an invitation to a heavenly banquet of spiritual fullness and delight, remember that the earthly promises [Note: [Col. 0439D] Earthly promises of wine, oil, and grain, such as occur very frequently in the Old Testament. LE PRIEUR.] of wine, oil, grain, and the city itself are likewise interpreted spiritually by the Creator.

## CHAPTER XXXII

[Col. 0439B] Who searches for the lost sheep and the lost drachma? Is it not the one who lost them? And who lost them? Is it not the one who possessed them? Who, moreover, possessed them? Is it not the one to whom they belonged? If, therefore, man is the property of no one other than the Creator, he possessed man because man belonged to him. He who possessed him lost him. He who lost him sought him. He who sought him found him. He who found him rejoiced.

Thus the argument of both parables is inapplicable to one to whom neither the sheep nor the drachma—that is, man—belongs. For he did not lose because he did not possess; nor did he seek because he did not lose; nor did he find because he did not seek; nor did he rejoice because he did not find. Indeed [Note: [Col. 0439D] Rejoicing over a sinner’s repentance belongs to him. I do not see why Pamelius tortures himself so greatly in explaining this passage. For when he says from the Gospel context that the rejoicing belongs to the angels, and that therefore what was said of the angels is here attributed to God, he should take careful heed not to disrupt and divide the sequence of the discourse. For its order and meaning are straightforward: rejoicing over a sinner’s repentance belongs to the one who said—namely God—“I prefer the sinner’s repentance to his death.” LE PRIEUR.], rejoicing over the repentance of a sinner—that is, over the recovery of one who was lost—belongs to the one who long ago declared that he preferred the sinner’s repentance to his death.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

[Col. 0439C]

He himself makes clear which two masters he says cannot be served, because one must necessarily be offended and the other defended: he sets forth God and Mammon. Then, if you have no interpreter to tell you what he means by Mammon [Note: [Col. 0440D] What he means by Mammon: what the Punic speakers call *mammon* is called *lucrum*, “gain,” in Latin. Augustine, Sermon XXXV *On the Words of the Lord*. RIGAULT.], you can learn from Christ himself. For in accordance with the example of that servant who, when removed from his stewardship, provides relief for his master’s debtors by reducing [Note: [Col. 0439D] “He reduced,” Pamelius.] their promissory notes so that they may in turn support him, Christ admonishes us to secure for ourselves the assistance of worldly friendships. “And I,” he says, “tell you: make friends for yourselves from the Mammon of injustice”—that is, from money, the very thing with which that servant was dealing. For we all know that money is the author and ruler of the injustice of the whole age.

Seeing that the Pharisees’ greed was enslaved to money, he launched this saying like a javelin [Note: [Col. 0440D] “He launched this saying like a javelin”: he hurled it as a missile. The manuscripts variously spell the noun *amentum*, *admentum*, and *ammentum*. It derives from the Greek ἄμμα, “knot” or “fastening.” RIGAULT.—That is, he hurled it, sent it forth: the verb *amentare*, “to launch,” derives from *amentum*, meaning a strap. RHENANUS.]: “You cannot serve [Col. 0439D] God and Mammon.” Finally, the money-loving Pharisees mocked him because they understood, of course, that “Mammon” meant money [Col. 0440A]—lest anyone suppose that by Mammon the Creator is meant, and that Christ was recalling them from service to the Creator.

What then? Learn rather from this that Christ revealed one God. For he named two masters: God and Mammon, the Creator and money. “You cannot serve God”—surely the God whom they appeared to serve—“and Mammon,” to whom they were more truly devoted. But if he were presenting himself as the representative of another God, he would have disclosed not two masters but three. For the Creator too is Lord because he is God—indeed, more truly lord than Mammon, and more deserving of obedience because he is more truly lord. Why, then, after calling Mammon a master and coupling it with God, would he have kept silent about their true Lord, namely, the Creator? Or did he, by keeping silent about him, concede that the Creator ought to be served, since he denied only [Col. 0440B] that his own God and Mammon could both be served?

Thus, when he presents one God while intending to name the Creator—if he himself belonged to another—he has in fact named the Creator, whom he did not set forth as Lord alongside another God. And so this statement too will become clear: “If you have not proved faithful in unjust Mammon, who will entrust to you what is true?” He means unjust money, of course, not the Creator, whom even Marcion makes just. “And if you have not been found faithful in what is another’s, who will give you what is mine [Note: [Col. 0440D] “You are mine; who,” Semler.]?” What is unjust ought indeed to be alien to God’s servants. But how [Note: [Col. 0440D] “In another way,” Rhenanus.] was the Creator alien to the Pharisees, when he was the proper God of the Jewish nation?

If, therefore, these statements do not apply to the Creator but to Mammon, “who will entrust to you what is truer, and who will give you what is mine?” cannot have been spoken by one God about the grace of another [Col. 0440C].
