It would have appeared to have been spoken in that way only if, by censuring them for unfaithfulness toward the Creator rather than toward Mammon, he had made, through mention of the Creator, a distinction involving another God—one who would not entrust his own truth to those unfaithful to the Creator. How, then, can he be regarded as belonging to another God if that other God is not introduced precisely so that he may be distinguished from the God under discussion by you?

Moreover, if the Pharisees, by justifying themselves before men, placed their hope of reward in man, he rebuked them in the same sense as the prophet Jeremiah (Jer. XVII, 5): [Note: [Col. 0440D] “Wretched is the man who places his hope,” etc. He should have said “cursed,” for the Greek is ἐπικατάρατος, “accursed.” LE PRIEUR.] “Wretched is the man who places his hope in man.” If he also adds, “But God knows your hearts,” he was recalling the power of that God who declared himself to be a lamp searching the kidneys and hearts. If he touches upon pride—“What is exalted among men is hateful to God”—he sets Isaiah before their eyes (Isa. II, 12): “For the day [Col. 0440D] of the Lord Sabaoth is against everyone who is insolent and proud, against everyone lofty and exalted; and they shall be humbled.”

I can now infer [Col. 0441A] why Marcion’s God remained hidden for so long an age. He was waiting, I suppose, until he had learned all these things from the Creator. He therefore continued learning until the time of John, and from then onward came forth to announce the kingdom of God, saying: [Note: [Col. 0441D] “The Law and the Prophets until John,” etc. The Author very frequently cited this passage against Marcion in this very book, because Marcion cited it on his own behalf. But Tertullian elegantly deduces that John’s advent too was foretold by the Creator, both here and elsewhere. What of the fact that Epiphanius, in Refutation 43, proves from it that the Creator God and the God of Christ are the same, since Christ names the Law and the Prophets, attributes no injustice to them, and thereby bears testimony to the same God? Epiphanius, moreover, translates “from that time” more clearly, for Luke’s Greek is ἀπὸ τότε, “from then,” whereas the Author more obscurely has [Col. 0442D] “from which time.” PAMELIUS.] “The Law and the Prophets were until John; from that time the kingdom of God is announced.”

This is as though we too did not recognize that John was established as a kind of boundary between the old and the new, at whom Judaism would cease and from whom Christianity would begin—not, however, so that the cessation of the Law and the Prophets and the inauguration of the Gospel, in which is the kingdom of God, namely Christ himself, were effected by a different power. For we have proved that the Creator foretold both that the old things would pass away and that new things would succeed them (Isa. XLIII, 19). If John is also shown to be the forerunner and preparer of the Lord’s ways—the Lord who would bring in the Gospel [Col. 0441B] and proclaim the kingdom of God—and if, from the very fact that John came, this will be the Christ who was to follow John as his forerunner; and if the old things ceased and the new began with John standing between them, it will be no wonder that the kingdom of God, which exists by the Creator’s arrangement, should be proved from some other source [Note: [Col. 0441D] “Whence,” Pamelius; “from whatever source,” Latinius.] rather than from the setting of the Law and the Prophets at John and the kingdom’s rising thereafter.

Let heaven and earth, then, pass away sooner—as also the Law and the Prophets—than one apex of the Lord’s words. “For the word,” says Isaiah (Isa. XL, 8), “of our God abides forever.” For since in Isaiah Christ himself—the Word, that is, and Spirit of the Creator—had already at that time proclaimed John as “the voice of one crying in the wilderness” to prepare the way of the Lord, and had foretold that he would come for this purpose, that from then onward the order of the Law and the Prophets should cease through fulfillment [Col. 0441C], not through destruction, and that the kingdom of God should be announced by Christ, he therefore added that the elements would pass away more readily than his words. In this way he also confirmed that what he had said concerning John had not passed away.

## CHAPTER XXXIV
“But Christ forbids divorce, saying: ‘Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery; whoever marries a woman dismissed by her husband is likewise an adulterer.’ Thus, in this way too, he forbids divorce by making marriage to a repudiated woman unlawful. Moses, however, permits repudiation in Deuteronomy (Deut. 24:1): ‘If anyone takes a wife and lives with her, and it happens that she finds no favor with him because some indecent matter has been found in her, [Col. 0442A] he shall write a bill of repudiation, place it in her hand, and dismiss her from his house.’ Do you see the difference between the Law and the Gospel, between Moses and Christ?”

Certainly. For you have not also accepted that Gospel (Matt. 19:8) which belongs to the same truth and the same Christ, in which, while forbidding divorce, he resolves the very question concerning it: “Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, commanded that a bill of repudiation be given; but from the beginning it was not so,” because, of course, he who had made male and female had said, “The two shall become one flesh” [Note: [Col. 0441D] “Into one flesh,” Fran.]; “therefore, shall man separate what God has joined?” [Note: [Col. 0441D] “Man does not separate,” Fran.] By this answer he both safeguarded Moses’ ordinance as his own and restored the Creator’s institution as the Creator’s Christ.

But since you must be refuted from those things which you have accepted, I shall meet you on that ground, as though he were my Christ. Did not he himself, while forbidding [Col. 0442B] divorce and yet presenting [Note: [Col. 0441D] “Attesting,” Lat.] as Father the one who joined male and female, excuse rather than destroy Moses’ ordinance? But suppose this Christ is yours, teaching what is contrary to Moses and the Creator, on condition that, if I do not show that he teaches nothing contrary, he shall be mine.

For I say that on this occasion he made the prohibition of divorce conditional: namely, if someone dismisses his wife in order to marry another. “Whoever dismisses,” he says, “his wife and marries another has committed adultery; and whoever marries a woman dismissed by her husband is likewise an adulterer”—surely for the same reason [Note: [Col. 0442D] Oberth. adds “dismissed.”] that she may not be dismissed, namely, so that another may be married. For one who marries a woman unlawfully dismissed, treating her as though she were no longer married, is an adulterer. The marriage remains in force because it was not properly dissolved. To marry while a marriage remains in force is adultery. Thus, if he conditionally forbade the dismissal of a wife, he did not forbid it altogether; [Col. 0442C] [Note: [Col. 0442D] “And what he did not forbid altogether, he permitted. It is otherwise where the cause ceases.” The exemplar reads: “He permitted altogether. Another cause submitted ceases.” From the traces of this reading, we think that the passage should be emended as follows: “And what he did not forbid altogether, he permitted in other cases, where the cause for which he prohibited it ceases.” RIG.] and what he did not forbid altogether, he permitted in other cases, where the cause for which he prohibited it ceases.

Neither, therefore, does he teach what is contrary to Moses, whose commandment he preserves in a certain case—I do not yet say confirms. Or, if you deny that Christ permits divorce under any circumstances, why do you dissolve marriages, neither joining male and female nor admitting those joined elsewhere to the sacrament of baptism and the Eucharist unless they have conspired together [Note: [Col. 0442D] Against the fruit of marriage. What he called “the fruit of wedlock” in chapter 23 means the procreation of children. We have discussed these matters elsewhere. LE PR.] against the fruit of marriage, as though against the Creator himself?

Certainly, what will [Note: [Col. 0442D] “Will do,” Wouwer codex.] a husband among you do if his wife has committed adultery? Will he keep her? Yet you know [Note: [Col. 0442D] Rhen. omits “you know.”] that even your apostle does not permit the members of Christ to be joined to a prostitute. Christ, therefore, is also the defender [Note: [Col. 0442D] The justice of divorce. Here he appears to favor the opinion of those who maintain that, even if divorce were evil in itself, nevertheless, once it was permitted through Moses, it became just and lawful. But if what follows is carefully examined, it becomes clear that it was permitted only “if an indecent matter has been found in the woman.” This is also supported by the prophecy of Malachi 2, which he soon cites according to the Septuagint: “You shall not dismiss the wife of your youth.” To this may be added what the prophet continues there: “But if, hating her, you dismiss her, says the Lord God of Israel, impiety will cover your thoughts.” PAM.] of the justice of divorce.

From this point onward [Col. 0443A] Moses is confirmed by him, since Moses forbids repudiation on the same ground as Christ, unless an indecent matter has been found in the woman. For in the Gospel of Matthew as well (Matt. 5:32), he says: “Whoever dismisses his wife, except on the ground of adultery, causes her to commit adultery”; and thus [Note: [Col. 0443D] Seml. omits “thus”; “likewise thus,” Par., Fran.] the man who marries a woman dismissed by her husband is also accounted an adulterer.

Apart, however, from the ground of adultery, not even the Creator separates what he himself has joined, since the same Moses elsewhere ordains (Deut. 22:28) that the man who [Note: [Col. 0443D] Who had brought about marriage through forcible intercourse. He means violence or violation, in which either the adulterer or the unchaste man “uses force against the female” (*biázetai tēn thēleian*, βιάζεται τὴν θηλεῖαν). LE PR.] brought about marriage through forcible intercourse could never dismiss his wife. If a marriage compelled by violence is to remain in force, how much more one entered voluntarily by agreement? So too by the authority of prophecy [Note: [Col. 0443D] “Of the prophet,” Lat.] (Mal. 2:15): “Do not dismiss the wife of your youth.”

You therefore have Christ spontaneously following [Col. 0443B] the Creator’s footsteps everywhere, both in permitting repudiation and in forbidding it. You also have him as the guardian of marriage in whichever direction you please: he does not wish marriages to be separated, and therefore forbids repudiation; nor does he wish them to be maintained with a stain, and therefore permits divorce in that case. Be ashamed that you do not join those whom even your Christ has joined. Be ashamed also that you separate them without the ground upon which even your Christ wished them to be separated.

I must now also show from what source the Lord derived this pronouncement and to what end he directed it. It will thereby be more fully established that, by the proposition concerning repudiation introduced at this point, he was not aiming to destroy Moses. For it was not introduced abruptly, since it has its root in the same mention of John.

John had rebuked Herod for having taken, contrary to the Law, the wife of his deceased brother, who had a daughter by her. [Col. 0443C] The Law permitted—indeed, commanded—this in no other case (Deut. 25) [Note: [Col. 0444D] Than if the brother died childless. In Greek this is *ápais* (ἄπαις), “childless.” LE PR.] than when a brother had died childless, so that offspring might be raised up for him by his brother and from his own stock. John had therefore been cast into prison and was later killed by that same Herod [Note: [Col. 0443D] Oberth. omits “Herod.”].

Accordingly, once mention had been made of John, the Lord—certainly following out the consequence of John’s fate—hurled against Herod figures of unlawful marriages and adultery [Note: [Col. 0443D] “A figure,” Pam.; “flashes,” Ciaccon.]. He pronounced even the man who married a woman dismissed by her husband an adulterer, thereby weighing down Herod’s impiety all the more, since Herod had married a woman dismissed by her husband no less by death than by repudiation. He had done so although his brother had a daughter by her, and therefore unlawfully on that ground alone; he acted at the prompting of lust, not of the Law, and for that reason had also killed the prophet who defended the Law.

My discussion of this point will also assist me with [Note: [Col. 0443D] Seml. inserts “with.”] the following argument concerning the rich man suffering in the underworld and the poor man resting in Abraham’s bosom. For that account too, so far as the surface of Scripture is concerned, is introduced abruptly; but so far as the intention of its meaning is concerned, it is itself connected with the mention of John’s mistreatment and with the stigmatizing [Note: [Col. 0443D] “Stigmatized,” Pam.] of the ill-deserving Herod [Note: [Col. 0444D] “Married,” Par.; “provoked,” Jun.]. It depicts the fate of each: Herod’s torments and John’s refreshment. Thus Herod might already hear: [Note: [Col. 0444D] “They have Moses and the Prophets there.” The author added “there” for greater emphasis—namely, in the synagogue of the Jews—for it is not read in the Greek, Syriac, or Latin, nor in Epiphanius, who in *Refutation* 46 likewise turns this passage against Marcion, the opponent of Moses and the Prophets. PAM.] “They have Moses and the Prophets there; let them hear them.”

But Marcion forces the passage in another direction. He holds, namely, [Note: [Col. 0444D] Oberth. inserts “that.”] that both forms of the Creator’s recompense—whether torment or refreshment—are appointed in the underworld [Col. 0444B] for those who have obeyed the Law and the Prophets, but assigns [Note: [Col. 0444D] “May assign,” Seml.] a heavenly bosom and harbor to his Christ and his god.

We shall answer him, with this very Scripture refuting his blindness, for it distinguishes Abraham’s bosom, in which the poor man rests, from the underworld [Note: [Col. 0444D] “To the underworld,” Oberth.]. The underworld is one thing, as I understand it, and Abraham’s bosom another. [Note: [Col. 0444D] For he says that a great depth, a *chásma* (χάσμα), lies between those regions; others have called it chaos. RIG.] For he says that a great depth lies between [Note: [Col. 0444D] “Between,” Seml.] those regions and prevents passage in either direction. Nor would the rich man have lifted up his eyes, and that from far away, unless he were looking upward, across the immense distance between height and depth.

It is therefore apparent to every knowledgeable person who has ever heard of the Elysian regions that there is a definite locality called Abraham’s bosom, intended to receive the souls of his children, including those from the nations. For he is the father of many nations, which are to be enrolled in Abraham’s line [Col. 0444C] through the same faith by which Abraham believed God, while under neither the yoke of the Law nor the sign of circumcision.

That region, therefore—I mean Abraham’s bosom—although not heavenly, is nevertheless higher than the underworld. It will in the meantime provide refreshment for the souls of the righteous, until the consummation of all things brings the resurrection of all to completion with the fullness of their reward. Then the heavenly promise that Marcion claims for his own [Note: [Col. 0444D] Ciaccon. adds “Christ.”] will appear, as though it had not been proclaimed by the Creator.

For this promise Christ builds his ascent into heaven, according to Amos (Amos 9:6)—for his own, of course—where the eternal place is, concerning which Isaiah says (Isa. 33:14): “Who will announce to you the eternal place?” Who, indeed, but Christ, “walking in righteousness, speaking the straight way, hating injustice and iniquity”? If, then, an eternal place is promised and an ascent into heaven is built by the Creator, who also promises that Abraham’s offspring will be like the stars of heaven—surely on account of the heavenly promise—then, without prejudice to that promise, [Note: [Col. 0445D] Why it may not be called Abraham’s bosom. We have already encountered this verb frequently above. The meaning here is: “Why can it not be called Abraham’s bosom, a temple,” etc. So too in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*: “the Holy Land, Paradise, which may also be called the land of the fathers.” RHEN.] why may not some temporary receptacle for the souls of the faithful be called Abraham’s bosom? There the image of the future is already outlined, and [Note: [Col. 0446D] A certain white robe of expectation for both judgments. “White robe” signifies hope and expectation. It was the clothing of candidates, as we noted above. RHEN.] a certain white-robed expectation [Note: [Col. 0445D] “And,” Lat.] of each judgment is held out in prospect.

It also admonishes you heretics, while you are alive, to hear Moses and the Prophets, who proclaim one God, the Creator, and one Christ who is his, and who declare that both judgments—of punishment and of eternal salvation—are vested in the one God, who kills and makes alive.

“But,” he says, “our God’s admonition from heaven did not command Moses and the Prophets to be heard, but Christ: ‘Hear him.’” Quite rightly. For by then the apostles had already heard Moses and the Prophets sufficiently: they had followed Christ by believing Moses and the Prophets. Peter could not have begun [Note: [Col. 0445D] “Could not have begun, Peter,” Ciaccon.] to say, “You are the Christ,” before he had heard and believed Moses and the Prophets, by whom alone Christ was as yet being announced.

Their faith, therefore, had deserved to be confirmed also by a heavenly voice commanding them to hear the one whom they had accordingly acknowledged: the one “evangelizing peace, evangelizing good things,” announcing the eternal place and building for them his ascent into heaven (Isa. 52:7; 33:14; Amos 9:6).

In the underworld, however, it was said of those people, [Col. 0445C] “They have Moses and the Prophets there; let them hear them” (Luke 16:29), who did not believe—or who did not fully believe—that after death the punishments of pride in riches and vaunting in pleasures had been announced by Moses and the Prophets, and decreed by that God who (Ps. 113:6) casts rulers down from their thrones and raises the needy from dunghills [Note: [Col. 0445D] “Dungheaps,” Pam.]. Thus, since the difference between the two pronouncements is appropriate to the Creator, no separation between deities is to be established, but only between the subjects themselves.

## CHAPTER XXXV

Turning in the same passage to his disciples (Luke 17), he pronounces woe upon the author of scandals: it would have been better [Note: [Col. 0445D] “Would have been,” Par.] for him if he had not been born, or if, with a millstone tied around his neck, he had been cast into the deep, than if he had scandalized one of those little ones—his disciples, of course. [Col. 0445D] Consider what punishment he threatens that man [Note: [Col. 0445D] “That man,” Lat.]. For no other will avenge the scandal given to his disciples.

Recognize him, therefore, as Judge as well, pronouncing this out of that same feeling of care for his own with which the Creator had previously said [Col. 0446A] (Zech. 2:8): “Whoever touches you touches, as it were, the pupil of my eye.”

The same sentiment belongs to the same God: he commands that a sinning brother be rebuked. Whoever does not do so has surely sinned, whether because in hatred he wishes his brother to persist in sin, or because, through partiality, he spares him. He has Leviticus (Lev. 19:17): “You shall not hate your brother in your heart; with rebuke you shall rebuke [Note: [Col. 0445D] “You shall not rebuke,” Sem.; “it is not absent,” Pam.] your neighbor”—and surely your brother as well—“and you shall not incur sin because of him.”

Nor is it surprising if he teaches in this way, since he forbids you to disregard even your brother’s livestock if you find them straying on the road (Exod. 23:4), instead requiring you to bring them back to your brother [Note: [Col. 0446D] Oberth. omits “your”]; much less may you disregard your brother himself and fail to restore him to himself.

He also commands you to grant forgiveness to a brother who sins against you, even seven times. Too little, certainly. For there is more with the Creator, who sets no limit, declaring without qualification (Lev. 19:18): [Col. 0446B] “Do not remember your brother’s malice.” Nor [Note: [Col. 0446D] “Do not,” Venet.] does he command that you grant forgiveness only to one who asks for it, but also to one who does not ask. For he does not wish you merely to pardon the offense, but to forget it.

It will be our part to understand how much interpretation the law concerning lepers (Lev. 13–14) requires with regard to the manifestations of the disease itself and the high priest’s inspection of them. Marcion’s part is to object to the Law’s tediousness, so that here too he may affirm that Christ was its rival: one who anticipated the Law’s solemn rites even in the healing of the ten lepers (Luke 17), whom, after merely commanding them to go and show themselves to the priests, he cleansed on the way, now without a touch and without a word, by silent power and sheer will.

This is as though, once Christ has been proclaimed as the healer of illnesses and diseases and proved by his effects, it were necessary to reopen the question because of the particular manner of his healings; or as though the Creator in Christ must be measured against the Law whenever he accomplished something in a manner different from that prescribed by the Law. Yet the Lord naturally works in one manner [Col. 0446C] through himself or through the Son, and in another through his servants the prophets, who were proofs of his very great [Note: [Col. 0446D] “Especially,” Rig.] strength and power. Since his own works are brighter and more powerful, it is proper that they should differ from works performed through deputies. But matters of this kind have already been discussed elsewhere, in the preceding example.

Now even if he had declared beforehand that there were many lepers in Israel in the days of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian (Luke 4:27), the number will certainly [Note: [Col. 0446D] Seml. adds “also.”] not establish a difference between the gods, to the destruction of the Creator who healed one and the exaltation of the god who cleansed ten. For who could doubt that more could have been healed by the one who had healed a single man than by the one who healed ten but had never previously healed even one?

Rather, by this pronouncement above all [Col. 0446D] he strikes at Israel’s distrust or pride: although there were many lepers there and a prophet was available—even after a proof of divine power had been given—no one had hastened to the God who worked through the prophets.

Therefore, [Col. 0447A] because he himself was the authentic high priest of God the Father, he inspected them according to the mystery of the Law, which signified that Christ is the true judge and remover of human stains. Yet he also commanded what belonged to the Law’s public observance: “Go, show yourselves to the priests.” Why, if he was going to cleanse them beforehand? Was it as a mocker of the Law, so that, after healing them on their way, he might show that the Law, together with its priests, amounted to nothing? Let anyone to whom Christ seems so conceited judge that for himself. More worthy interpretations, and ones more just to faith, must be given.

He therefore healed them because, having been ordered in accordance with the Law to go to the priests, they had obeyed. For it is not credible that observers of the Law should have earned healing from the Law’s destroyer. But why did he give no such command to the former leper? Because Elisha gave no such command to Naaman the Syrian either; yet Elisha did not for that reason cease to belong to the Creator.

I have answered sufficiently; but one who believes also understands something more profound. Learn, then, the reasons. The event took place in the region of Samaria, from which, at least, one of the lepers came. Samaria had broken away from Israel in the schism involving the ten [Note: [Col. 0447D] “Nine,” Oberth.] tribes, which Jeroboam, after they had been torn away through the prophet Ahijah, had settled in Samaria (1 Kings 11 and 16).

Moreover, the Samaritans had always taken pride in their mountains and the wells of their ancestors, as did the Samaritan woman in the Gospel of John (John 4), in her conversation with the Lord at the well: “Surely [Note: [Col. 0447D] “Not,” Seml.] you are not greater,” and so forth; and again: “Our ancestors worshiped on this mountain, and you say that one must worship at Jerusalem.”

Accordingly, he who had also said through Amos [Note: [Col. 0447D] “Isaiah,” Rhen.] (Amos 6:1), “Woe to those [Note: [Col. 0447D] Who trusted in Mount Samaria. He touched above on the history of that schism, in which Jeroboam separated ten tribes from the others and led them to Samaria, where he was made king. The remaining two, namely Judah and Benjamin, remained under Rehoboam. This is recounted in 1 Kings. LE PR.] who trust [Note: [Col. 0447D] “Who are trusting,” Venet.] in Mount Samaria,” now, deeming Samaria itself worthy of restoration as well, deliberately commands them to show themselves to the priests—surely those who existed nowhere except where the Temple was. He thus subjects the Samaritan to the Jew, because the salvation of both the Israelite and the Samaritan [Note: [Col. 0447D] “Samaritan woman,” Venet.] comes from the Jews.

For the whole promise to the tribe of Judah was Christ, so that they might know that in Jerusalem were both the priests and the Temple, and the mother-source of religion, and the fountain—not the well—of salvation. And therefore, when he saw that they had acknowledged that the Law must be discharged at Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0447D] “They had acknowledged the Law,” Seml.], he healed them, since they were now to be justified by faith without the Law’s order.

Hence also, when he marveled at that one man out of the ten—the Samaritan alone [Note: [Col. 0448D] “Alone,” Wouwer.] released from obligation, mindful of divine grace—he did not command him to offer the gift prescribed by the Law. For he had already offered enough by giving glory to God, since the Lord also wished the Law to be interpreted in this way.

And yet to which God did the Samaritan give thanks, when not even the Israelite had yet learned of another God? To what other God than the one to whom all those previously healed by Christ had given thanks? Therefore he hears, “Your faith has saved you,” [Col. 0448A] because he had understood that he ought to make a true offering to Almighty God—namely, thanksgiving—at God’s true Temple and before his true high priest, Christ.

Nor can the Pharisees be thought to have questioned the Lord about the kingdom of some other God—asking when it would come—so long as no other God had been revealed by Christ. Neither can Christ be thought to have answered concerning any kingdom other than the one about which he was being questioned.

“The kingdom of God,” he says, “does not come with observation; nor do they say, ‘Behold, here,’ or ‘Behold, there.’ For behold, the kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:20–21). Who would not interpret “within you” as meaning “in your hand, within your power, if you hear and perform God’s commandment”?

But if God’s kingdom consists in his commandment, then set Moses over against it, [Note: [Col. 0448D] According to our antitheses. Marcion had compiled *Antitheses* in which he opposed the Law of Moses to the Gospel. Tertullian opposed other antitheses to them, in which he reconciled the old Law with the new. LE PR.] according to our antitheses, and the pronouncement is one and the same. “The commandment,” he says (Deut. 30:11–14), “is not too high, nor is it far from you. It is not in heaven, so that you should say, ‘Who will ascend [Note: [Col. 0448D] “Ascends,” Seml.] into heaven and bring [Note: [Col. 0448D] “Brings,” Oberth.] it down to us, so that, when we have heard it, we may perform it?’ Nor is it beyond the sea, so that you should say, ‘Who will cross the sea and take it for us, so that, when we have heard it, we may perform it?’ The word is near you, in your mouth, in your heart, and in your hands, that you may perform it.” This will be the meaning of: “Not here, nor there; for behold, the kingdom of God is within you.”

And lest heretical audacity argue that the Lord was answering them about the Creator’s kingdom, concerning which he was being questioned, and not about his own, what follows stands in its way. For when he says that the Son of Man must first suffer many things and be rejected before his coming, in which the kingdom will also be substantially revealed, he shows that the kingdom about which he had answered was his own—the kingdom that awaited his sufferings and rejection.

Moreover, since being rejected implies afterward being recognized, received, and exalted, he took [Note: [Col. 0448D] “Excerpted,” another reading.] even the word “rejected” itself from the passage in which both revelations of him were sung by David under the riddle of the stone (Ps. 118:22): the first dishonored, the second honored. “The stone,” he says, “which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This was done by the Lord.”

For it would be meaningless if we believed that God had foretold the dishonor or glory of just anyone, rather than [Note: [Col. 0448D] “Rather than that,” Seml.] thereby foreshadowing the same person whom he had also foreshadowed under the figures of the stone, the rock, and the mountain (Isa. 8:14) [Note: [Col. 0448D] “Had foreshadowed,” Oberth.].

But if he is speaking of his own coming, why does the good, gentle, and mild God compare it to the grim and dreadful days of Noah and Lot? Why does he admonish them to remember Lot’s wife, who did not despise the Creator’s command without punishment, unless he comes with judgment [Col. 0448D] to vindicate his own commandments? Even if he vindicates them as the Creator did, even if he judges me, he ought not to have fashioned my conduct through the Creator’s examples while destroying the Creator, lest it appear to be the Creator who fashions my conduct.

But if here too he is speaking not of his own coming, but of the Jewish Christ’s, let us wait even now to see whether he ever foretells anything about his own; meanwhile, let us believe him to be the one whom he proclaims everywhere.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

For when he also commands perseverance and urgency in prayer (Luke 18), he sets forth the parable of the judge who was compelled to hear the widow by the urgency and persistence of her appeals. He therefore shows that God the Judge must be prayed to, not himself—if he himself is not the Judge. But he added that God would execute vengeance for his elect. If, therefore, he will himself be the Judge, he is also the Avenger. Thus he proved the Creator to be the better God, since he shows him as the avenger of his elect, who cry to him day and night.

And yet, when he introduces the Creator’s Temple [Col. 0449B] and describes two men worshiping with different dispositions—the Pharisee in pride and the tax collector in humility—and therefore says that the one went down rejected and the other justified (Luke 18), he is teaching by what discipline one must pray. Here too he consequently appoints as the object of prayer the one from whom they would receive the corresponding outcome of that discipline of prayer: either the rejection of pride or the justification of humility.

In Christ’s teaching I find neither temple, worshipers, nor judgment belonging to another God, but only those of the Creator. [Note: [Col. 0449D] He commands that the Creator be worshiped in humility, etc. He seems to me to allude to Christ’s saying: “Everyone who humbles himself will be raised, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled”; or to the other saying in Mary’s canticle: “He has cast the powerful down from their seat” (for this is what it means to destroy) “and has exalted” (or raised) “the humble.” PAM.] He commands the Creator to be worshiped in humility, as the one who raises the humble; not in pride, as the destroyer of the proud. What other being does he show me must be worshiped? By what discipline? With what hope? No one, I think.

For we have also proved that the prayer he taught is appropriate to the Creator. It would be another matter if, as the best God, good without prompting, he did not also wish to be worshiped. But “who is best,” [Col. 0449C] he says, “except the one God?” He did not mean that, out of two gods, he had shown one to be best, but that the one and only God is best, who is uniquely best because he alone is God.

And he is certainly best who rains upon the just and unjust and causes his sun to rise upon the good and evil, sustaining, nourishing, and helping even the Marcionites.

Finally, when a certain man asked him, “Best Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?” he demanded to know whether he knew—that is, practiced—the Creator’s commandments, in order to testify that everlasting life is acquired through the Creator’s commandments.

When the man affirmed that he had observed all the principal commandments from his youth, Christ said: “One thing is lacking to you. Sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.”

Come now, Marcion, and all his fellow-wretches [Col. 0449D] and fellow-objects-of-pity among the heretics: what will you dare to say? [Col. 0450A] Did Christ annul the preceding commandments—not to kill, not to commit adultery, not to steal, not to bear false witness, and to love father and mother? Or did he both preserve those commandments and add what was lacking? Yet even this command to make gifts to the needy is diffused everywhere throughout the Law and the Prophets, so that this most boastful observer of the commandments might be exposed as one who held money far dearer.

This declaration in the Gospel therefore also remains secure (Matt. 5:17): “I did not come to dissolve the Law and the Prophets, but rather to fulfill them.” At the same time he freed all the other points from doubt, making clear that the name of God and of the Best, eternal life, treasure in heaven, and Christ himself all belong to one and the same being; for by supplementing his commandments, Christ both preserved and enlarged them.

He must also be recognized here in accordance with Micah, who says (Mic. 6:8): [Col. 0450B] “Has a man announced to you what is good, or what the Lord requires from you, other than to execute judgment, love mercy, and be ready to follow the Lord your God?”

Christ is indeed the man announcing what is good: knowledge of the Law—“You know,” he says, “the commandments”; the execution of judgment—“Sell,” he says, “what you possess”; the love [Note: [Col. 0449D] “Love,” Seml.] of mercy—“And give,” he says, “to the needy”; readiness to go [Note: [Col. 0449D] “If you are ready, he says, to go,” Oberth.] with God [Note: [Col. 0450D] “With the Lord,” Seml.]—“And come,” he says, “follow me.”

From the beginning the Jewish nation had been so carefully distinguished into tribes, peoples, families, and households that scarcely anyone’s lineage could have been unknown, [Note: [Col. 0449D] Or from the recent Augustan census-records, perhaps still extant at that time. “At that time” means when the blind man said, “Jesus, son of David.” “Extant” refers to the census registers; for, as we noted above, censuses appear to have been conducted more than once under Augustus. Septimius himself, in the book *Against the Jews*, seems uncertain whether Christ was entered in the census immediately upon his birth. RIG.] or perhaps from the recent Augustan census-records, which were still extant at that time.

Yet Marcion’s Jesus, who appeared to be a man, could not have been doubted to have been born; for precisely because he had not been born, he could have had no publicly recorded identification of his lineage. [Note: [Col. 0450D] But he had to be reckoned as some one individual among those, etc. *Unus aliqui* is used for *aliquis*, as at the beginning of the following book, *unus aliqui discipulus*, “some one disciple.” The meaning is: “He will be a son of the earth, or just anyone from the crowd, one of the many,” what the Greeks call *ek tou pollou dēmou, kai tōn pollōn heis tōn tychontōn* (ἐκ τοῦ πολλοῦ δὴμὸυ, καὶ τῶν πολλῶν εἐς τῶν τυχόντῶν), “one chance individual from the common people and the multitude.” RHEN.] Rather, he would have had to be reckoned as some one individual among those who were regarded as obscure for one reason or another.

When, therefore, the blind man heard him passing by, why did he cry out, “Jesus, son of David, have mercy on me,” unless Jesus was commonly reckoned, and not without reason, to be the son of David—that is, a member of David’s family—through his mother and brothers, who had once certainly been announced to Jesus by people personally acquainted with them?

But those walking ahead rebuked the blind man and told him to be silent. Quite rightly, because he was shouting—not because he was lying about the son of David. Otherwise, show that those who rebuked him knew that Jesus was not the son of David, so that we may believe that this was why they enjoined silence upon the blind man.

But even if you were to prove it, it would more readily be presumed [Note: [Col. 0450D] “Would presume,” Rhen.] that they were ignorant than that the Lord could have tolerated a false proclamation about himself. Yet the Lord is patient, though not one who confirms error; indeed, he is the revealer of the Creator. Thus he would not first have dispelled the cloud over that man’s blindness without dispelling his error about himself. [Col. 0450D] On the contrary, lest you bring his patience into disrepute, [Col. 0451A] or [Note: [Col. 0451D] “Lest,” Ciaccon.] attribute to him any reason for dissimulation, or deny that he is the son of David, he most plainly confirmed the blind man’s proclamation, both by rewarding him with healing and by bearing testimony to his faith. “Your faith,” he says, “has saved you.” What would you have the blind man believed? That Jesus had descended from another [Note: [Col. 0451D] “That,” Oberth.] God to overthrow [Note: [Col. 0451D] “To the love of,” Seml.] the Creator? To destroy the Law and the Prophets? That he was not the one destined to come from the root of Jesse and the fruit of David’s loins (Ps. 132:11), who was also to reward the blind? But I do not think that there were yet blind men at that time of the same sort as Marcion, so that this could have been that blind man’s faith when he believed at the cry, “Jesus, son of David.” He who both knew himself to be this and wished to be known [Note: [Col. 0451D] “Known by all,” Oberth.; “known by men,” another reading; “by all” is absent from Par.] by everyone granted outward sight as well to the man’s faith—a faith that already saw better and possessed the true light—[Col. 0451B] so that we too might learn both the rule and the reward of faith. Whoever wishes to see Jesus must believe that he is the son of David through the virgin’s census-record. Whoever does not so believe will not hear from him, “Your faith has saved you.” He will thus remain blind, falling into the antithesis, while the antithesis itself also falls. For so the blind are accustomed to lead the blind.

“For if on one occasion (2 Sam. 5), when David was recovering Zion, the blind resisted him and gave offense by preventing his admission”—thereby prefiguring the likewise blind people who would one day refuse admission to Christ, the son of David—“Christ therefore, conversely, assisted a blind man so that by this he might show that he was not the son of David; and, because of their difference in disposition, he was kind to the blind whom David had ordered to be struck. And why did he say that he had granted this on account of faith—and false faith at that?” On the contrary, the son of David answers this objection too: the antithesis must be beaten back on its own ground. [Col. 0451C] For those who had offended David were blind, whereas now a man of the same flesh [Note: [Col. 0451D] “Disfigured,” Par., Fran.] had presented himself as a suppliant to the son of David. Therefore the son of David, placated because the man had in some sense made satisfaction to him, restored his sight, together with testimony to the faith by which he had believed this very thing: that he must entreat the son of David. And yet I think it was men’s audacity that had offended David, not their physical infirmity.

## CHAPTER XXXVII
And so (Luke 19) salvation also comes to the house of Zacchaeus. By what merit? Had he too perhaps believed that Christ had come from Marcion? On the contrary, that cry of the blind man was still in everyone’s ears: “Have mercy on me, Jesus, son of David”; and all the people were rendering praises to God—not Marcion’s god, but David’s. Indeed, although Zacchaeus was perhaps a foreigner, he had nevertheless been inspired with some knowledge of the Scriptures through intercourse with the Jews. More than that [Note: Rhenanus inserts “if”], and though you do not know it, [Col. 0451D] he had fulfilled the commandments of Isaiah (Isa. 58:7). [Col. 0452A] “Break,” he says, “your bread for the hungry, and bring those who have no shelter into your house.” This was precisely what he was then doing, receiving the Lord into his house and feeding him. “And if you see one naked, clothe him.” This was precisely what he was promising to do, offering half his substance for every work of mercy; [Note: [Col. 0451D] “Undoing the bonds of oppressive contracts.” The word *obnexus* is compounded from *nexus*, a term very commonly used by the jurists. Hence Papinian’s expression in *Digest*, *Familiae erciscundae*, law *Si pater familias*, “the bond of a pledge”; and Ulpian’s, in law *Si non saltem*, § *Adeo*, title *De condictione indebiti*, “the bond of a sale.” Hence also Cicero, *Pro Murena*, says “to bind by a bond,” and Tacitus, book III, “released from the bonds of the law.” To the same subject belong the “law of bond” and the law concerning “money placed under obligation by bond”—that is, by a particular kind of civil obligation through which, as Budé says, a person’s body, no less than a pledge, was subjected to a bond. PAM.] undoing the bonds of oppressive contracts [Note: Semler reads “of those liable”], releasing the afflicted into freedom, and canceling every unjust written obligation, when he said: “And if I have extorted anything from anyone by false accusation, I restore it fourfold.” Accordingly the Lord says: “Today salvation has come to this house.” He thereby testified that the things commanded by the Creator’s prophet were salutary.

But when he says, “For the Son of Man came to save what was lost” [Note: Others read “what had perished”], I shall no longer press the point that he came to save what had been lost, which had belonged to the one to whom it was lost and whose lost thing [Col. 0452B] he had come to save; instead, I direct the argument to another stage of the question. There is no doubt that a human being is under discussion. Since a human being consists of two substances, body and soul, we must ask in which kind of substance he appears to have been lost. If in the body, then the body had been lost, but the soul had not. The Son of Man saves what had been lost; the flesh, therefore, also possesses salvation. If the soul too had been lost, the soul’s perdition is destined for salvation, while the flesh, which had not been lost, is already safe. If the whole human being had been lost in both substances, the whole human being must necessarily be saved; and thus the doctrine of the heretics who deny the salvation of the flesh is overthrown. Christ is now also confirmed as the Creator’s Christ, since in accordance with the Creator he promised the salvation [Note: “salvation” is absent from Rigault] of the whole human being.

The parable of the servants also, who are judged according to the accounting of the lord’s money put out at interest, [Col. 0452C] shows that God is a judge, even in respect of severity: he not only gives honor, but also takes away what someone appears to have possessed. Or if here too Marcion represents the Creator as harsh, taking up what he did not lay down and reaping what he did not sow, here too that very one instructs me whose money he teaches me to put out at interest.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

Christ knew whence the baptism of John came (Luke 20); why, then, did he ask as though he did not know? He knew that the Pharisees would not answer him; why, then, did he ask in vain? Was it so that he might judge them from their own mouths—or from their hearts? Refer these matters, therefore, both to the vindication of the Creator and to the comparison with Christ; and now consider what would have followed if the Pharisees had given any answer to the question. Suppose they had answered that John’s baptism was of human origin: they would immediately have been crushed with stones. Some Marcion would then arise [Col. 0452D] [Note: “Some Marcion would arise”—that is, if one should emerge, originate, or rise up. For so Asconius Pedianus interprets this verb in Cicero. RHEN.] [Note: Semler reads “some Marcion”; the Venetian edition, “someone belonging to Marcion”] against Marcion, [Col. 0453A] who would say: “O most excellent God! O God so different from the Creator’s examples! Knowing that men would rush headlong, he himself placed them upon the precipice [Note: The manuscript reads *praerupium*.].” For this is also how the Creator is treated in the discussion of the law concerning the tree.

But John’s baptism was from heaven. “And why,” Christ says, “did you not believe him?” Therefore he who had wished John to be believed, and who was about to rebuke them because they had not believed, belonged to the one whose sacrament John administered. Certainly, when they refused to disclose what they thought, he himself in turn opposed them: “Neither do I tell you by what power I do these things.” He returns evil for evil [Note: Pamelius reads “he returned evil for evil”].

“Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” What things, then, will be God’s? Those which resemble Caesar’s denarius—namely, God’s image and likeness. He therefore commands that the human being be rendered to the Creator, in whose image and likeness, and in whose name and material, [Col. 0453B] he was stamped. Let Marcion’s god seek a coin for himself. Christ commands that the human denarius be rendered to its own Caesar, not to another’s—[Note: Except that he who has no denarius of his own must necessarily do so. Septimius means: Let Marcion’s god, who has no denarius of his own, seek a coin for himself. Let him seek another’s human being, since he has none of his own—inasmuch as he created none. RIG.] except, of course, that one who has no denarius of his own must necessarily do so.

It is a just and proper rule that in every question the meaning of the answer must pertain to the subject of the inquiry. Otherwise, to answer one thing when asked another is the act of a madman. So much the more must that be far removed from Christ which is not even becoming in a human being. The Sadducees, deniers of the resurrection, having a question about it, had put before the Lord a case from the Law concerning a woman who, after seven brothers had died in succession, had married them in accordance with the legal commandment: whose wife was she to be reckoned at the resurrection? This was the subject of the question; this was the substance of their inquiry. Christ [Col. 0453C] must necessarily have answered this. He feared no one, so that he should appear either to have evaded their questions or, on the occasion of them, to have covertly indicated something that at other times he did not teach openly.

He therefore answered: “The children of this age marry.” You see how directly this pertains to the issue. Since the question concerned the coming age, in which he was about to declare [Note: Others spell *definiturus* as *diffiniturus*.] that no one marries, he first laid down that marriage does take place here, where death also exists; but those whom God has deemed worthy of possessing that age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, because they will no longer die, since they are [Note: Semler reads “become”] like the angels, having become children of God and of the resurrection.

Since, therefore, the meaning of an answer must be directed to nothing other than the subject of the question, if the subject of the question is resolved by this meaning of the answer, [Col. 0454A] the Lord’s answer means nothing [Note: Others add “with respect to”] other than that by which the question is resolved. You have both the periods in which marriage is permitted and denied—not from a question concerning marriage in its own right, but from the question of the resurrection. You also have confirmation of the resurrection itself and the whole subject about which [Note: [Col. 0453D] “The Sadducees, deniers of the resurrection.” Epiphanius (*Haer.* 14) says: *ἠθετήσαν μὲν γὰρ οὗτοι νεκρῶν τὴν ἀνάστασιν, ὁμοῖα Σαμαρείταις φρονοῦντες*—“For these men denied the resurrection of the dead, holding the same opinions as the Samaritans.” Nor did they reject only the resurrection, but also the immortality of the soul, as Josephus testifies, *Jewish Antiquities*, book XVIII. Blessed Jerome, *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, teaches that the heresies both of the Sadducees and of the Samaritans were propagated by Dositheus: “I pass over,” he says, “the heretics of Judaism, who before the coming of Christ destroyed the Law that had been handed down: that Dositheus, the leader of the Samaritans, rejected the prophets; that the Sadducees, springing from his root, denied even the resurrection of the flesh.” They were called Sadducees after Sadok, a disciple of Antigonus; Antigonus had been a disciple of Simeon the Just, as is related in *Pirke Avot*, chapter 1. LE PR.] the Sadducees were asking. They were not asking about another God, nor inquiring about the law of marriage considered by itself.

But if you make Christ answer matters about which he was not consulted, you deny that he was able to answer those about which he was questioned—having evidently been outwitted by the wisdom of the Sadducees. Now, beyond what is required, and after establishing this rule, I shall reconsider the related arguments. For, having seized upon the wording of Scripture, they ran its words together in their reading as follows: “But those whom God has deemed worthy of that age.” They join “of that age” to “God,” [Col. 0454B] so as to create another God belonging to that age. Yet it ought to be read: “But those whom God has deemed worthy”—with a division made here after “God,” so that “of that age” belongs to what follows; that is, those whom God has deemed worthy of possessing that age and the resurrection. For the inquiry concerned not God, but the condition of that age: whose wife she would be in that age after the resurrection.

Thus they also overturn the answer concerning marriage itself: “The children of this age marry and are given in marriage,” they say, refers to the Creator’s people, whose God permits marriage; but those whom the God of that age—that is, another god—has deemed worthy of the resurrection do not marry even here, because they are not children of this age. Yet when he was consulted about marriage in that age, not in this one, he denied the marriages about which he was being consulted. And so those who had grasped the very force of the wording, the utterance, and its divisions [Col. 0454C] understood nothing other than what pertained to the subject of the inquiry. Indeed, the scribes said, “Master, you have spoken well.” For he had confirmed the resurrection by setting forth its form against the opinion of the Sadducees. Finally, he did not reject the testimony of those who understood him to have answered in that way.

But if the scribes considered Christ to be the son of David, while David himself calls him Lord, what relevance has this to Christ? [Note: [Col. 0454D] “Not David, but the error of the scribes.” Lest matters be treated confusedly, it must be noted that there were two kinds of scribes. Some were *γραμματεῖς τοῦ νόμου*, “scribes of the Law,” and others *γραμματεῖς λαοῦ*, “scribes of the people.” The scribes of the people were clerks or public recorders; they were not, however, heretics, although it is certain that there were other scribes who were heretics. See Scaliger in the *Elenchus*. LE PR.] He was not refuting David, but the error of the scribes; rather, David was securing honor for Christ, whom he affirmed to be the Lord Christ [Note: “Christ” is absent from the Paris and Frankfurt editions] rather than merely the son of David—a thing that would not be fitting for one who destroyed the Creator.

But from our side, how fitting [Col. 0455A] is the interpretation! For he who had once been invoked by that blind man as the son of David—something he had then left unanswered, since the scribes were not present—now deliberately brought the matter forward of his own accord in their presence, so that he might show himself, whom the blind man in accordance with the scribes’ teaching had proclaimed only as David’s son, also to be David’s Lord. Thus he rewarded the blind man’s faith, by which the man had believed him to be the son of David, while striking at the tradition [Note: Others read “the public exposure”] of the scribes, by which they did not know him also as Lord. Whatever pertained to the glory of the Creator’s Christ [Note: Junius omits “of Christ”] would thus [Note: The Venetian edition reads “if”] be maintained by none other than the Creator’s Christ.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

It has long been established (Luke 21), concerning the ownership of the names, that it belongs to him [Note: Rigault and others insert “It has long been established concerning the ownership of the names that it belongs to him” after “him,” from the manuscript of Wouwer], who first announced his Christ among humankind and gave him the additional name Jesus. [Col. 0455B] The shamelessness of one who says that many will come in his name will therefore also be established, since it is not his name if he is not the Creator’s Christ and Jesus, to whom ownership of the names belongs. More than this: he forbids the reception of those whose equal he himself is, since he too has likewise come in another’s name. If the name was not his, it was not for him to forewarn the disciples against a false claim to the name; it was he who, through ownership of the name, possessed its truth. Those men will finally come, saying, “I am Christ.” You will receive them, since you received one just like them. For he too came in his own name.

What now of the fact that the Lord of the names himself, the Creator’s Christ and [Note: Oberthür omits “Christ and”] Jesus, will also come? Will you reject him? How inequitable, how unjust, and how unworthy of the most excellent God it would be for you not to receive the one coming in his own name, when you received another [Note: Paris reads “a stranger”] in his name!

Let us also see [Col. 0455C] what signs he assigns to the times: wars, I suppose, kingdom against kingdom and nation against nation, pestilence, famines, earthquakes, terrors, and portents from heaven—all of which are fitting for a severe and cruel God [Note: The Venetian edition reads “is fitting”]. When he also adds [Note: Others read “says”] that these things must take place, what does he show himself to be: the destroyer or the approver of the Creator? He confirms that the Creator’s arrangements must be fulfilled, whereas, if they were not his own, as the most excellent God he would have abolished such grim [Note: Junius reads “so” (*tam*)] and cruel things rather than established them.

Before these things, moreover, he foretells that persecutions and sufferings will come upon them—certainly for martyrdom and salvation. Hear what was foretold in Zechariah (Zech. 9:15): “The Lord Almighty,” he says, “will protect them; [Col. 0456A] and they will consume them and stone them with sling-stones, and they will drink their blood like wine and fill the bowls as though they were bowls of the altar [Note: Frankfurt reads “as bowls for the altar”]; and the Lord will save them on that day like sheep, his people, because [Note: Semler reads “who”] holy stones roll about.”

And lest you think that these things are foretold of the sufferings that awaited them from foreigners under the heading of so many wars, look to the particulars. No one, in a prediction of wars to be waged with regular weapons, lists stoning, which is more characteristic of popular gatherings and an unarmed riot. No one measures such rivers of blood in war by the capacity of bowls or equates them with the bloodshed of a single altar [Note: Pamelius reads *cruentatione*]. No one calls those men sheep who fall in war while armed and themselves [Note: Junius reads “and” (*et*)] contending with the same ferocity; rather, the term applies to those who, surrendering themselves in their proper character and patience, and sacrificing themselves rather than avenging themselves, [Col. 0456B] are slaughtered. Finally, [Note: [Col. 0455D] “Because holy stones roll about.” These words from Zechariah are also cited according to the Septuagint edition: “they roll about,” *κυλίονται ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς*, “they roll upon the earth.” RIG.] “because [Note: Semler reads “who”] holy stones,” he says, “roll about”—not because [Note: Paris and Frankfurt read “not but that”] soldiers fight.

For they are also stones and foundations upon which we are built: “built,” according to Paul (Eph. 2:21), “upon the foundation of the apostles,” who, as holy stones exposed to the blows of all, rolled about. Therefore here too the very one who forbids them to consider beforehand what they ought to answer before tribunals is he who suggested to Balaam [Note: Oberthür reads “Balae”] what he had not considered—indeed, the opposite of what he had considered (Num. 22)—and who, when Moses pleaded the slowness of his tongue, promised him a mouth. He also demonstrated through Isaiah (Isa. 44:5) that very wisdom which no one could resist: “This one will say, ‘I belong to God,’ and will cry out in the name of Jacob, and another will inscribe himself [Note: Others read “will inscribe”] with the name of Israel.” For what is wiser and more irrefutable than the simple and forthright confession made in [Col. 0456C] the name of a martyr who prevails with God? [Note: [Col. 0455D] This is the interpretation of “Israel.” Concerning the meaning of this word, Saint Jerome (*Questions on Genesis*) proves at length that “Israel” properly means the same as “a prince of God” or “one directed by God”: “As for the interpretation,” he says, “given in the *Book of Names*, that Israel means ‘a man seeing God’ or ‘a mind seeing God,’ though worn smooth by the speech of almost everyone, it appears to me to have been interpreted not so much truthfully as forcibly.” The question therefore remains whether “prince of God” or “one directed by God” ought rather to be accepted as the interpretation. Jerome himself, however, indirectly resolves this question when he says: “We are guided more by the authority of Scripture and of the angel, or God, who called him Israel, than by any secular eloquence.” Yet God himself, or the angel, interpreted the name Israel in neither of the ways Jerome mentioned, but—as our Tertullian most excellently puts it—as “one who prevails with God”: “Your name,” he says, “shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel; for if you have been strong against God, how much more will you prevail against men?” EDD.]—which is the interpretation of Israel.

Nor is it surprising that he restrained [Note: Others read “forbade”] forethought, since he himself received from the Father the timely supply of what he was to say: “The Lord gives me” (Isa. 50:4) “the tongue of instruction, so that I may know when I ought to bring forth a word”—unless Marcion introduces a Christ who is not subject to the Father.

Nor ought I again to demonstrate that persecutions by one’s neighbors and blasphemy arising from hatred of the name had been foretold. “But through endurance,” he says, “you will save your own selves”—the endurance, of course, of which the Psalm says (Ps. 9:19): “The endurance of the righteous will not perish [Note: Semler reads “shall perish”] forever.” For elsewhere also it says (Ps. 115:5): “Honorable is the death of the righteous”—honorable, without doubt, [Col. 0457A] because of their endurance. Zechariah also says (Zech. 6:14): “The crown, moreover, will belong to those who have endured.”

But do not venture to argue that the apostles were harassed by the Jews because they were heralds of another God. Remember that the prophets too suffered the same things at the hands of the Jews, yet were not apostles of any God other than the Creator.

After indicating the time of the destruction, when Jerusalem had begun to be surrounded by armies, he next recounts the signs of the final end: portents in the sun, moon, and stars, and distress upon the earth among nations stupefied, as though by the sound of a surging sea, in expectation of the evils threatening the world. That even the powers of the heavens are to be shaken, hear Joel (Joel 2:30): “And I will give portents in heaven and on earth: blood, fire, and vapor of smoke. The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great [Col. 0457B] and glorious day of the Lord comes” [Note: Rigault and the Venetian edition read “will come”].

You also have Habakkuk (Hab. 3:9): “The earth will be torn apart by rivers; the peoples will see you and travail; you will scatter [Note: Rhenanus and Semler read “scattering”] the waters by your stride [Note: The Venetian edition reads “strides”]. The deep gave forth its voice; the height of its fear was raised. The sun and moon stood still in their station; they will go into the light of your flashing [Note: Franequer reads “flashings”; others, “encirclements”], into the splendor; lightning is your shield. In your threatening [reading *comminatione* for the apparent OCR *communicatione*], you will diminish the earth, and in your indignation you will cast down the nations.”

The pronouncements of the Lord and those of the prophets, I suppose, agree concerning the shakings of the world and the inhabited earth, of the elements and the nations. What does the Lord say after these things? “And then [Note: [Col. 0458D] ‘They will see the Son of Man coming.’ Here he proves the second advent of Christ against Marcion from innumerable passages. LE PR.] they will see the Son of Man coming from heaven with very great power. But when these things take place, you will stand erect and lift up your heads, because your redemption will draw near” [Note: Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “will draw near”]. This will be, of course, in the time of the kingdom, to which the parable itself [Col. 0457C] will have been appended [Note: Rhenanus, Semler, and Pamelius read “will be appended”]. “So also, when you see all these things taking place, know that the kingdom of God has drawn near.”

This will be the great and glorious day of the Lord: the coming from heaven of the Son of Man according to Daniel (Dan. 7:3): “Behold, one coming with the clouds of heaven like a son of man,” and so forth. “And royal power was given to him”—the power that in the parable he had gone away to request, leaving with his servants money to be put out at interest [Note: Latinus reads the plural, “which they were to put out at interest”]. And all the nations were given to him, as the Father had promised him in the Psalm (Ps. 2:8): “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance.” And all glory serves him; and his power is eternal and will not be taken away, and his kingdom will not be corrupted—because in it they will neither die nor marry, but will be like the angels.

Of the same advent of the Son of Man and its fruit [Note: Paris and Frankfurt read “fruits”], Habakkuk says (Hab. 3:13): “You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones”—those, of course, who, having been redeemed [Note: Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read the singular, “the redeemed one”], will stand erect and lift up [Col. 0458A] their heads in the time of the kingdom.

Therefore, since these things belonging to the promises agree in the same way as those belonging to the shakings, you will be unable, given the concord between the prophetic and the Lord’s pronouncements, to insert any distinction here, as though you might refer the shakings to the Creator, the God of cruelty, although the most excellent God ought neither to permit them, much less await them, while assigning the promises to the most excellent God—promises which the Creator would not have prophesied if he were ignorant of that god. Or, if the Creator prophesied his own promises, which do not differ from Christ’s promises, he will be equal to the most excellent God in generosity; nor will your Christ appear to promise any more than my Son of Man.

You will find that the actual course of the Gospel text, from the disciples’ question to the parable of the fig tree, so adheres throughout its connected meaning to the Son of Man [Col. 0458B] that both grim and joyful things, both shakings and promises, converge upon him, and you cannot separate either part from him. For since the advent of one Son of Man has been placed between two outcomes—the shakings and the promises—both the sufferings of the nations and the hopes of the saints must necessarily belong to one Son of Man. For he [Note: Pamelius, Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “who”] has been placed in the middle in such a way as to be common to both outcomes: concluding the one by his advent—that is, the sufferings of the nations—and beginning the other—that is, the hopes of the saints.

Thus, whether you concede that the coming of the Son of Man is the coming of my Christ, in order to attribute to him the impending evils that precede his advent, you will also be compelled to ascribe to him the good things that arise from his advent; or whether you prefer it to be the coming of your Christ, in order to ascribe to him the good things that arise from his advent [Col. 0458C] [Note: Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür omit “or whether you prefer it to be the coming of your Christ, in order to ascribe to him the good things that arise from his advent”], you will also be compelled to attribute to him the evils that precede his advent. For the evils cohere with the advent of the Son of Man by preceding it just as the good things do by following it.

Ask, therefore, which of the two Christs you establish in the person of the one Son of Man, to whom [Note: Pamelius, Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “than whom”] both arrangements are referred. Either you have granted that the Creator is most excellent, or [Note: Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür add “that”] your god is harsh by nature.

Finally, consider the illustration in the parable itself: “Look at the fig tree and all the trees. When they have produced fruit, people understand that summer is approaching. So also you, when you see these things taking place, know that the kingdom of God is near.” For if the fruiting of small trees supplies a sign of summertime by preceding it, in the same way the world’s convulsions also [Note: Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür omit “and” (*et*)] foreshadow the kingdom as a sign by preceding it. Every sign, however, belongs to the one to whom belongs [Note: The manuscript of Wouwer reads “and”] the thing of which it is a sign. And a sign is imposed upon every thing [Col. 0459A] by the one to whom that thing belongs. Thus, if the convulsions are signs of the kingdom, just as fruiting trees are signs of summer, then the kingdom also belongs to the Creator, to whom [Note: Latinus reads “whose”] are assigned the convulsions that are signs of the kingdom.

The most excellent God had declared beforehand that these things—so cruel, so dreadful, and certainly foretold by the Prophets and the Law—must take place. To that extent he was not destroying the Law and the Prophets, since he confirms that what they foretold must be fulfilled. He further insists that heaven and earth will not pass away until all things are accomplished. What “all things” are these? If they are things belonging to the Creator [Note: Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “are done”], the elements will rightly endure until their Lord’s order has been fully discharged. If they are things belonging to the most excellent God, I do not know whether heaven and earth will endure until the things appointed by their rival are fulfilled. If the Creator permits this, he is not a jealous God.

Come now, let earth and heaven pass away, for thus their Lord has appointed, [Col. 0459B] while his Word remains forever; for thus Isaiah also foretold (Isa. 40:8).

The disciples are also admonished lest at any time their hearts be weighed down with gluttony and [Note: [Col. 0459C] “Drunkenness and worldly cares.” The same two things that are forbidden here to the disciples are forbidden to clerics—both presbyters and even bishops—later in Apostolic Canons 6 and 80, canon 6 of the Council of Carthage, and law *Generaliter* 52, *Codex*, title *De clericis et episcopis*. Earlier, however, this appears in Apostolic Canons 41 and 24, by which clerics of every order are forbidden *εἰς καπηλεῖον εἰσιέναι*, “to enter a tavern.” All these provisions are found everywhere among the ancients against the intemperance and luxury of clerics. Read the letter of Blessed Bernard to Fulco, who was later made Archdeacon of Langres. LE PR.] drunkenness and worldly cares, and that sudden day come upon them like a snare—upon those, certainly, who had forgotten God through satiety and preoccupation with the world. The admonition will belong to Moses (Deut. 32:15). Thus the one who formerly introduced this warning is precisely the one who will deliver them from the snare of that day.

There were other places in Jerusalem in which he could teach, and there were places outside Jerusalem to which he could withdraw; nevertheless, during the day he taught in the temple, as one who had foretold through Hosea (Hos. 12:4): “They found me in my temple, and there the matter was disputed with them.” At night, however, he withdrew to the *elaeon* [Note: *Elaeon* means the olive grove, from the Greek word *ἔλαιον*, “olive.” EDD.]; for Zechariah had indicated it thus (Zech. 14:4): “And his feet will stand upon the Mount of Olives.”

There were [Col. 0459C] also hours appropriate for his audience. They had to assemble at daybreak because, after saying through Isaiah (Isa. 50:4), “The Lord gives me the tongue of instruction,” he added [Note: “he added” is absent from the Paris edition]: “He has applied my ear in the morning to listen.” [Col. 0460A] If this is what it means to dissolve the prophecies, what will it mean to fulfill them?

## CHAPTER XL
Accordingly (Luke XXII), he also knows when it was necessary for him to suffer, whose passion the Law prefigures. For from among all the Jewish festivals he chose [Note: [Col. 0459C] “And” in Rhen., Seml., Obert.] the day of Passover [Note: [Col. 0459C] “He may have chosen” in Venet.; “he observed” in Rhen., Seml., Oberth.]. For with reference to this mystery Moses had declared (Lev. XXIII): “It is the Lord’s Passover.” He therefore also reveals his own desire: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.” O destroyer of the Law, who had desired even to observe the Passover! Was it perhaps Jewish mutton that delighted him? Or was he himself the one who (Isa. LIII), since he was to be led like a sheep to slaughter, and like a sheep before its shearer was not to open his mouth, desired to fulfill the figure of his saving blood?

He could also have been betrayed by any outsider, lest I should say [Note: [Col. 0460C] “They might say” is not in the Wouwer manuscript; “lest I should say, in this also,” Jun.] that in this also [Col. 0460B] the Psalm (Ps. XL, 10) was fulfilled: “He who eats bread with me will lift up his heel against me.” He could also have been betrayed without a reward; for how much effort on the betrayer’s part was needed against one who openly gave offense to the people and could not so much have been betrayed as simply seized? But this would have suited some other Christ, not the one who was fulfilling the prophecies. For it is written (Amos II, 6): “Because they sold [Note: [Col. 0460C] ‘They sold,’ elsewhere.] the righteous man.” Moreover, Jeremiah (Jer. XXXII) foretells both the amount and the subsequent disposal of the payment—when Judas repented, it was returned and used to purchase the potter’s field—as is related in the Gospel of Matthew (Matt. XXVII): “And they received thirty pieces of silver [Note: [Col. 0460C] ‘Thirty silver coins,’ elsewhere.], the price of him who was valued, or honored, and they gave them [Note: [Col. 0460C] ‘Those,’ Paris, Fran.] for the potter’s field.”

Thus, after professing that with desire he had desired to eat the Passover as his own—for it would be unworthy of God to desire something belonging to another—[Col. 0460C] he took bread, distributed it to his disciples, and made it his body by saying, “This is my body” [Note: [Col. 0460C] “His own body,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth.], [Note: [Col. 0459D] “That is, the figure of my body.” These words are not to be understood as the Calvinists wish—whom Rigaltius favored excessively both here and elsewhere—but as their context requires them to be understood and as the polemical theologians explained them, among whom the most learned cardinals Perron and Bellarmine hold first place. It will suffice to cite the latter:

“A third passage follows from Book IV *Against Marcion*, where we read as follows: ‘He took bread, distributed it to his disciples, and made it his body by saying, “This is my body”; that is, “the figure of my body.” But it would not have been a figure unless there were a true body.’

“I answer: the earlier words of this [Col. 0460C] testimony, which all the sacramentarians place in their front line as a kind of Achilles, support us most strongly; the later words do no harm to our case. For the statement, ‘He took bread and made it his body by saying, “This is my body,”’ plainly indicates a real [Col. 0460D] change of the bread into Christ’s body. The statement, ‘That is, the figure of my body,’ does not mean—as the sacramentarians believe—that the Eucharistic bread is a figure of the Lord’s body, but that what was formerly a figure in the Old Testament has now been changed into the reality of the body. For ‘the figure of my body’ is connected not with the immediately preceding expression ‘my body,’ but with the pronoun ‘this,’ so that the sense is: ‘He took bread and made it his body, saying: “This”—that is, the bread which was formerly a figure of my body—“is now my body.”’ Here the pronoun ‘this’ points to bread, not bread that remains unchanged, but bread that is changed, as we said above.

“That this is so is proved, first, from the words that follow: ‘But it would not have been a figure unless there were a true body.’ For if by ‘figure’ he meant the Eucharist, he would not say ‘it would not have been,’ but ‘it would not be.’ He is therefore speaking of a figure in the Old Testament, which undoubtedly would not have been a true figure unless a true body corresponded to it.

“Second, the same is evident from the words that follow a little below: [Col. 0461C] ‘Why,’ he says, ‘does he call the bread his body, rather than the melon which Marcion had in place of a heart? Marcion did not understand that this was an ancient figure of the body of Christ, who says through Jeremiah: “Come, let us cast wood upon his bread”—that is, the cross upon his body. Thus the illuminator of antiquities sufficiently disclosed what he had then intended the bread to signify, by calling the bread his body.’ Here Tertullian says that Christ called the bread his body rather than a melon or some other food in order to fulfill Jeremiah’s figure, in which the name ‘bread’ signified Christ’s body. Christ therefore did not institute a figure of his body in the Eucharist, as our opponents wish, but fulfilled the [Col. 0461D] ancient figure by making his body out of bread.

“Third, this is evident from other words that follow, where, in explaining Jacob’s prophecy (Gen. XLIX), ‘He shall wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape,’ he says: ‘By the robe he indicated the flesh, and by the wine the blood. Thus even now he consecrated his blood in wine, he who then prefigured wine in blood.’ Here IT MUST BE NOTED that, just as in Jeremiah bread signified the body because the Lord’s body is the food of the faithful, as we said above, so in the patriarch Jacob wine signifies the Lord’s blood because the Lord’s blood is the drink of the faithful. But Christ, in order to explain these figures or prophecies, delivered to us his body under the species of bread and his blood under the species of wine. And certainly, if he had not in reality given his true body and blood, he would not properly have explained or fulfilled the prophecies. For, as Tertullian says, Jeremiah foretold the true body by bread, and Jacob the true blood by wine. Tertullian’s words, ‘He who then prefigured wine in blood’ [Col. 0462C], refer to Jacob’s words, ‘his cloak in the blood of the grape.’ For he means that by the blood of the grape wine is understood, while by wine the Lord’s blood is understood, as he himself explains when he says that the robe indicates the flesh, and the wine the blood.

“Fourth and finally, the same is evident from the course of the entire book. For his purpose was to show that Christ did not destroy the Old Testament in the Gospel, but fulfilled it. Tertullian therefore reviews many of Christ’s works and shows that in all of them Christ took care to fulfill the figures of the Law. Thus in this passage also he does not introduce a figure instituted in the New Testament, but only the fulfillment [Col. 0462D] of ancient figures.”

Thus far Bellarmine (*On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, book II, ch. 7). EDD.]

—that is, “the figure of my body.” But it would not have been a figure unless there were a true body. An empty thing, however—something that is a phantom—could not receive a figure. Or if he fashioned bread as his body precisely because he lacked the reality of a body, then he ought to have handed over bread on our behalf. It would have suited Marcion’s illusion if bread had been crucified.
