But why [Note: [Col. 0462D] “He calls the bread his body.” This is a distinguished passage concerning the reality of Christ’s body; add to it chapter 10 of the book *Against the Jews*: “Christ calls the bread his body”; chapter 2 of *On Prayer*, etc. Justin Martyr has a lucid testimony on this matter (*Apology* I). I do not cite others here. LE PR.] does he call the bread his body rather than the melon which Marcion had in place of a heart? Marcion did not understand that this was the ancient figure of the body of Christ, who says through Jeremiah (Jer. XI, 19): “They devised a plan against me, saying, ‘Come, let us cast wood upon his bread’”—that is, the cross upon his body. Thus the illuminator of antiquities sufficiently disclosed what he had then intended the bread to signify, by calling the bread his body.

Likewise, when in mentioning the cup he established the covenant sealed by his blood, he confirmed the substance of the body. [Col. 0461B] For there can be no blood belonging to any body unless that body is flesh. Even if some non-fleshly quality of body is advanced against us, it certainly will not possess blood unless it is fleshly. Thus the proof of the body is established from the testimony of the flesh, and the proof of the flesh from the testimony of the blood.

And so that you may also recognize in wine the ancient figure of the blood, Isaiah will be at hand (Isa. LXIII, 1): “Who,” he says, “is this who comes from Edom? The redness of his garments is from Bozrah. [Note: [Col. 0462D] “The redness of his garments is from Bozrah.” Either Tyrian or Carthaginian purple is meant, or we must explain “Bozrah” as redness; for the Hebrew means an unripe grape, and *Boser* should be read instead of *Bosor*. LE PR.] Thus beautiful in his wine-stained robe, with strength? Why are your garments red, and your clothing like that of one coming from a fully trodden winepress floor?” [Note: [Col. 0461C] “But,” Paris.]

For the prophetic Spirit, as though already contemplating the Lord coming to his passion, clothed, of course, in flesh so that he might suffer in it, signifies the bloodied condition of the flesh by the redness of the garments, [Col. 0462A] flesh trodden down and pressed out by the force of the passion as though on [Note: [Col. 0461C] “On,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] a winepress floor; for from there people descend stained, as it were, with blood from the redness of the wine.

Genesis speaks much more plainly in the blessing of Judah. Since the lineage of Christ’s flesh was to proceed from Judah’s tribe, Genesis was already then portraying Christ in Judah [Note: [Col. 0462C] “Turning aside,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth.; “portraying,” Franeq.]. “He shall wash,” it says (Gen. XLIX, 11), “his robe in wine, and his garment in the blood of the grape”—the robe and garment indicating the flesh, and the wine the blood. Thus even now he consecrated his blood in wine, he who then prefigured wine in blood.

## CHAPTER XLI

“Woe,” he says, “to him through whom the Son of Man is betrayed.” It is therefore now established that “Woe” must be understood as an exclamation of imprecation and threat, and attributed to one who is angry and offended—[Col. 0462B] unless Judas was going to incur so great a crime with impunity. But if with impunity, “Woe” is meaningless. If not with impunity, then he was certainly to be punished by the one against whom he committed the crime of betrayal.

Moreover, if Christ knowingly allowed a man whom he himself had chosen for his company to fall into so great a crime, do not now raise again against the Creator your objections concerning Adam, since they can also be turned back against your own god: either he was ignorant, since in his providence he did not prevent the man from sinning; or, if he was ignorant, he was unable to prevent him; or, if he both knew and was able, he was unwilling. He must therefore be judged malicious for allowing his own man to perish through sin. I advise you, then, to recognize the Creator in this instance as well, rather than make your “best god” equal to him contrary to your own doctrine.

For by consigning Peter, who had spoken somewhat presumptuously, [Col. 0463A] to denial, he also reveals to you a jealous God. [Note: [Col. 0462D] “For Peter too had spoken somewhat presumptuously.” In these very few words the author expressed Christ’s conversation concerning the foretold denial of St. Peter, which he treats at greater length in the book *On Flight in Persecution*, omitting what intervenes in Luke. PAM.]

He also had to be betrayed with a kiss [Note: [Col. 0463D] “He also had to be betrayed with a kiss.” Epiphanius, *Refutation* 66, also proves the reality of Christ’s body from these words of Luke, to which our author alludes: “And Judas drew near to kiss him.” In *Refutation* 67 he adds that Marcion also excised from what follows what Peter did when he struck and cut off the high priest’s servant’s ear, and, so far as appears, the entire account of Peter’s denial, since our author also omitted it here. PAM.], namely as the prophetic Christ, and therefore as the son of the one who was loved by the people with their lips (Isa. XXIX).

When brought before the council, he is asked whether he himself is the Christ. Concerning which Christ would the Jews have asked, unless their own? Why, then, did he not reveal to them even then that he was another? “So that he could suffer,” you say. That is, so that your supremely good god might plunge men who were still ignorant into crime. Yet even if he had told them, he would still have suffered. “For if I tell you,” he says, “you will not believe” [Note: [Col. 0463D] “You do believe,” Rhen., Seml., Ober.]. Since they would not believe, they would have persisted in killing him. And why would he not all the more certainly have suffered if he had revealed himself as belonging to another god and, for that very reason, as the Creator’s adversary?

Would he therefore not have suffered? He refrained from showing himself as another even then; but since [uncertain reading; the Latin is textually corrupt here] they wished to extort a confession from his own mouth, although they would not believe him even if he confessed—men who ought to have recognized him from his works fulfilling the Scriptures—[Col. 0463B] it was fitting for him to conceal himself, since recognition was already owed to him of their own accord.

Yet even then he stretched out his hand to them: “From now on,” he says, “the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.” For he was suggesting that he was the Son of Man from Daniel’s prophecy (Dan. VII), and the one seated at God’s right hand from David’s Psalm (Ps. CIX). Thus, enlightened by this saying and by comparison with Scripture as to whom he wished himself to be understood to be, they say: “Then are you the Son of God?” Of which God, except the only one they knew? Of which God, except the one whom they remembered saying to his Son in the Psalm, “Sit at my right hand”?

But he replied: “You say that I am” [Note: [Col. 0463D] “As though not I,” Jun.]. Yet he confirmed that he was what they had said when they questioned him again. But how will you prove that they spoke interrogatively and not affirmatively: “Then you are the Son of God”? Since he had indirectly shown through the Scriptures that he was to be understood as the Son of God, they may have meant: “Then you are the Son of God, which you are unwilling to say openly.” In the same way, [Note: [Col. 0463D] “And so,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] his reply, “You say it,” was also affirmative. Indeed, such was the force of his declaration that they persisted in the conclusion conveyed by it.

## CHAPTER XLII

For when they brought [Note: [Col. 0463D] “Produced,” elsewhere.] him before Pilate (Luke XXIII), they began to accuse him of calling himself a king—Christ, without doubt, the Son of God, who was to sit at God’s right hand. Otherwise they would have charged him under another title, uncertain whether he had called himself the Son of God, unless [Note: [Col. 0464D] “If,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] he had pronounced “You say it” in such a way as to affirm that he was what they said.

Likewise, when Pilate asked, “Are you the Christ?” he answered correspondingly, “You say it,” lest they seem to have given a fuller response because they feared the governing authority.

The Lord, then, was placed on trial. “And he set his people in judgment.” “The Lord himself came [Note: [Col. 0464D] “Will come,” Fran.] into judgment with the elders and rulers of the people,” according to Isaiah (Isa. III, 13). From that point onward he fulfilled everything written concerning his passion.

“There the nations raged, and the peoples devised vain things” (Ps. II, 1). “The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers were gathered together as one against the Lord and against his Christ”: the nations were the Romans who were with Pilate; the peoples, the tribes of Israel; the kings, represented in Herod; the rulers, in the chief priests.

For when he was sent by Pilate to Herod as though a gift, he also vindicated the reliability of Hosea’s words; for Hosea had prophesied concerning Christ (Hos. X, [Col. 0464B] 6): “And they shall lead him bound as a gift to the king.” Herod, indeed, was delighted to see Jesus, but heard not a single word from him. “For like a lamb before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII, 7), because the Lord had given him the tongue of instruction, so that he might know how he ought to utter a word (Isa. L, 4). This, namely, was the tongue which he then proved to be fastened to his throat in the Psalm (Ps. XXI), by not speaking.

And Barabbas, though utterly guilty, is granted life as though he were good; but Christ, though utterly righteous, is demanded for death as though he were a murderer. Two criminals are also crucified around him, so that he might, of course, “be reckoned among the lawless.” [Note: [Col. 0464D] “But two criminals are also crucified around him.” In Luke the Greek is κακοῦργοι (*kakourgoi*, “criminals”), which he correctly translates as *scelesti*, “criminals.” That rendering corresponds more closely to Isaiah LIII, which he cites here, as though repeating what is found in Luke XXII: “And he was reckoned among the lawless”; in the Evangelist’s Greek, μετὰ τῶν ἀνόμων (*meta tōn anomōn*, “among the lawless”). PAM.]

Marcion entirely removed the account that his clothing [Note: [Col. 0464D] “His” inserted by Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] was divided among the soldiers [Note: [Col. 0464D] “Partly” added in Latin editions.], partly being allotted by lot, because he had regard to the prophecy of the Psalm (Ps. XXI, 19): “They divided my garments among themselves, and cast lots for my clothing.” Remove the cross itself, then! Yet the same Psalm does not remain silent about it: “They pierced my hands and my feet” [Note: [Col. 0464D] “My” omitted in Rhen., Seml., Ober.].

His entire end is read there: “Dogs surrounded me; the assembly of evildoers encircled me. All who watched me mocked me with their noses. They spoke with their lips and shook their heads. He trusted in God; let God deliver him.” Since you already possess the testimony of the garments as plunder belonging to your falsehood [Note: [Col. 0464D] “You possess,” Rhen., Latin editions.], the whole Psalm constitutes Christ’s garments.

And behold, even the elements are shaken. For it was their Lord who was suffering. Otherwise, if it were the adversary who had been injured, heaven would have blossomed with lights; the sun would rather have exulted with its rays; the day would rather have stood still, gladly watching Marcion’s Christ hanging upon the gibbet. These arguments too would have belonged to my case even if they had not been foretold.

“I shall clothe the heavens in darkness,” says Isaiah (Isa. L, 3). This will be the day of which Amos also speaks (Amos VIII, 9): “And on that day, says the Lord, the sun shall set at noon”—you have here also the indication of the sixth hour—“and he shall darken the earth.”

The temple veil too was torn, when the angel broke forth and abandoned the daughter of Zion (Isa. I, 8), “like a watchman’s hut in a vineyard and like a shelter in a cucumber field.”

O how thoroughly he persevered in presenting Christ himself even through the thirtieth Psalm! He cries aloud to the Father so that, even as he dies, he might fulfill the prophets with his final utterance. Having said this, he expired.

Who expired? Was it the spirit itself, or the flesh breathing out the spirit? But the spirit could not breathe out itself. The one who breathes out is one thing; that which is breathed out is another. If the spirit is breathed out, it must necessarily be breathed out by another. But if there had been only spirit, it would have been said to depart rather than to breathe out its spirit. Who, then, breathes out the spirit except the flesh, which breathes while it possesses the spirit and, when it loses it, thus breathes it out?

Finally, if there was no flesh [Note: [Col. 0465D] “Had been,” elsewhere; one of the two readings is omitted in Rhen., Seml., Oberth.], but only a phantom of flesh, and the phantom was spirit, then the spirit breathed out itself and departed in breathing itself out. Without doubt, the phantom departed when the spirit that constituted the phantom departed; and the phantom appeared nowhere together with the spirit. Did nothing, then, remain upon the wood? Did nothing hang there even after the spirit was breathed out? Was nothing requested from Pilate? Was nothing taken down from the gibbet? Was nothing wrapped in linen? Was nothing laid in a new tomb?

Yet it was not nothing. What, then, was it? If it was the phantom, then Christ was still within it. If Christ had departed, then he had taken away the phantom. It remains for heretical shamelessness to say that a phantom of the phantom remained there.

But Joseph too knew that it was a body [Note: [Col. 0465D] “If,” elsewhere.], which he handled with complete devotion—that Joseph who had not agreed with the Jews in their crime: “Blessed is the man who has not gone away in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of plagues [Note: [Col. 0465D] ‘Pestilence,’ elsewhere.].” For the one who would bury the Lord also had to be prophesied and, already then, deservedly blessed.

## CHAPTER XLIII

Thus [Note: [Col. 0465D] “If,” elsewhere; Jun. deletes one of the two readings.] prophecy does not overlook the service of those women either (Luke XXIV), who came to the tomb before daylight with spices prepared. For Hosea says concerning this (Hos. VI, 1): “So that they may seek my face, they shall keep watch for me before daylight, saying: ‘Let us go and return to the Lord, because he himself has seized us and will heal us; he has struck us and will have mercy upon us; he will heal us after two days; on the third day we shall rise.’”

For who would not believe that these words revolved in the thoughts of those women, between their grief at the present abandonment, by which they imagined themselves struck by the Lord, and their hope in his resurrection, by which they rightly supposed that they themselves would be restored?

Since the body was not found, “his burial had been taken away from their midst,” according to Isaiah (Isa. LVII, 2). Two angels also appeared there. He was accustomed to employ approximately that number of attendants at his side, since the Word of God is established upon two witnesses. [Note: [Col. 0465D] “So many *laterenses*.” *Laterenses* are attendants or bodyguards, because they enclose one’s side. RHEN.]

Isaiah also foresaw the women returning from the tomb and from that vision of angels (Isa. XXVII, 11): “Women,” he says, “coming from the vision, come”—that is, to announce the Lord’s resurrection. [Note: [Col. 0465D] “The women returning from the tomb.” Here too he shows that the Evangelist agrees with Isaiah XVII: “Women coming from the vision have come.” Here we omit what was formerly read in the first position, “Come,” [Col. 0466D] because it is not read more than once either in the Septuagint, now or formerly, or in St. Jerome, Cyril, Procopius in his *Commentary*, Origen on Matthew, or Rufinus on the Creed among the works of St. Cyprian. PAM.]

It is well, moreover, that the disciples’ unbelief persisted, so that our defense might remain intact to the very end: Jesus Christ presented himself to his disciples as no other than the one who had been prophesied.

For when two of them were traveling and the Lord joined them, without appearing to be who he was, and even feigning ignorance of what had happened, they say: “But we were hoping that he was the redeemer of Israel”—certainly their own Christ, that is, the Creator’s. To such an extent had he not presented himself to them as another. Otherwise, they would not have thought him the Creator’s Christ; and when he was thought to be the Creator’s, he would not have tolerated this opinion concerning himself if he were not the one he was thought to be [Note: [Col. 0465D] “Is thought,” Rig., Venet., Seml.]. Or else he himself will be the author of error and a violator of truth, contrary to the title of the “best god.”

Nor did he show himself to them after the resurrection as anyone other than the one whom [Note: [Col. 0466D] “Which,” Paris, Fran.] they said they had thought him to be. He did, indeed, rebuke them: “O foolish and slow of heart, in failing to believe all the things he spoke to you!” The fact that he had spoken them proves that he belonged not to another god, but to the same God [Note: [Col. 0466D] “And less concerning God,” Seml.; “and a hand concerning God,” Rhen.].

The angels likewise said to the women: “Remember what he spoke to you in Galilee, saying that the Son of Man must [Note: [Col. 0466D] ‘Would have to,’ Wouwer manuscript.] be betrayed and crucified, and rise on the third day.” And why did it have to happen, unless because it had been so written by God the Creator?

He therefore rebuked [Note: [Col. 0466D] “Reproved,” elsewhere, following Seml.] them as men scandalized only by the passion and doubtful about the resurrection announced to them by the women—circumstances through which they had failed to believe that he was the one they had thought him to be. Thus, because he wished them to believe that he was precisely what they had thought, he confirmed that he was the one they had thought him to be: namely, the Creator’s Christ, the redeemer of Israel.

What, moreover, could be clearer concerning the reality of his body? When they hesitated lest he be a phantom—or rather, when they believed him to be a phantom—he said: “Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in [Col. 0466D] your hearts? See my hands and feet, because it is I myself; for a spirit does not have bones, as you see that I have” [Col. 0467A] [Note: [Col. 0467A] “As you see me having,” Rhen., Seml., Obert.].

Marcion, I believe, deliberately refused to erase from his Gospel certain things that contradict him, so that, on the basis of those things which he could have erased but did not, it might either be denied that he erased those which he did erase [Note: [Col. 0468A] “Not,” Seml.], or said that he erased them with good reason. He spares only those passages which he can subvert by interpretation just as effectively as by deletion.

Thus he wishes the statement, “A spirit does not have bones, as you see that I have,” to be referred to the spirit in this way: “as you see that I have”—that is, as you see that I, like the spirit, do not have bones. But what rationale is there for this contortion? He could have said plainly: “Because a spirit does not have bones, as you see that I do not have.”

Why, moreover, does he offer for their inspection his hands and feet—limbs composed of bones—if he had no bones? Why does he add: [Col. 0468A] “And know that it is I,” namely the one whom they had previously known as bodily? Or, if he was entirely a phantom, why did he rebuke them for believing him to be a phantom? Indeed, while they still did not believe, he asked for food precisely in order to show that he even had teeth.

We have fulfilled our undertaking, I think. We have presented Jesus Christ—in the prophets’ teachings, judgments, dispositions, meanings, mighty works, sufferings, and even resurrection—as no other than the Creator’s Christ. Indeed, when he sent the apostles to preach to all nations, he commanded that their sound should go out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the earth, thereby fulfilling the Psalm.

I pity you, Marcion: you have labored in vain. For Christ Jesus in your Gospel is mine. [Note: [Col. 0467B] “For Christ Jesus in your Gospel is mine.” That Marcion corrupted and falsified the Gospel is proved both by this passage and by the final chapter of the preceding book—“And your Gospel,” etc.—and also by chapter 29 of this book. St. Epiphanius testifies that Tertullian possessed that corrupted manuscript of Marcion. [Col. 0468B] No one who reads this book can doubt that it was Luke’s Gospel that had been corrupted, for this becomes manifest everywhere. Verse 25 of St. Luke XXIV is also quoted in corrupt form: “O foolish Galatians,” etc. For that wording is quoted not from the received Gospel, but from Marcion’s Gospel. LE PR.]

# BOOK V

[Col. 0467]

## SYNOPSIS

[Col. 0467B]

—Just as in the preceding book Tertullian used the Gospel of St. Luke, which Marcion had appropriated for himself, so now, from Paul’s Epistles—which Marcion had mutilated and arranged in a different order as a volume published under his own title, *The Apostolic Book*, with the exception of those to Timothy and Titus and the Epistle to the Hebrews—Tertullian proves that the Apostle proclaims no God other than the Creator.

**Chapter I.** First, he makes this evident even from the fact that no authority is established for the apostle Paul except from the Creator’s Old Testament Scriptures and the Acts of the Apostles, which Marcion rejected.

**Chapter II.** Next, through both the argument and the Apostle’s words, from chapter I of the Epistle to the Galatians.

**Chapter III.** Likewise from chapters II and III of the same Epistle.

**Chapter IV.** Also from chapters IV, V, and VI of the same Epistle.

**Chapter V.** Next, through the Apostle’s words, from chapter I of the First Epistle to the Corinthians.

**Chapter VI.** Also from chapters II and III of the same Epistle.

[Col. 0467D]

**Chapter VII.** Likewise from chapters IV, V, VI, VII, VIII, IX, and X of the same Epistle.

**Chapter VIII.** Likewise chapters XI, XII, XIII, and XIV.

**Chapter IX.** From the first part of chapter XV as well.

**Chapter X.** And from the second part of the same chapter XV.

**Chapter XI.** Again, through the Apostle’s words, from chapters I, II, and III of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians.

**Chapter XII.** Likewise from chapters V, VII, XI, XII, and XIII.

**Chapter XIII.** Furthermore, through the Apostle’s words, from chapters I, II, III, V, VI, and VII of the Epistle to the Romans.

[Col. 0468B]

**Chapter XIV.** Also from chapters VIII, X, XI, XII, XIII, and XVI of the same Epistle.

**Chapter XV.** No less through the Apostle’s words from the Epistle [Col. 0468C] to the Thessalonians.

**Chapter XVI.** And from the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians.

**Chapter XVII.** Next, through the Apostle’s words, from chapters I and II of the Epistle to the Laodiceans—or to the Ephesians.

**Chapter XVIII.** Also from chapters III, IV, V, and VI of the same Epistle.

**Chapter XIX.** Finally, through the Apostle’s words from the Epistle to the Colossians.

**Chapter XX.** From the Epistle to the Philippians.

**Chapter XXI.** Lastly, from the Epistle to Philemon. PAMELIUS.

## CHAPTER I
Nothing is without an origin, except God alone. Just as origin necessarily takes precedence in establishing the condition of all things, so it must also take precedence in their examination, so that their condition may be established [Col. 0468D]. For you cannot discern what sort of thing something is unless, once you have learned whence it comes, you are certain that it exists. [Note: [Col. 0467D] “Once” (*cum*) omitted by Junius.]

And therefore, having been brought by the order of this little work to the present subject, I too demand from Marcion the origin of the apostle Paul—as some new disciple, a hearer of no one else, who meanwhile believes nothing except that nothing is to be believed rashly. For whatever is believed without acknowledgment of its origin is believed rashly. I am all the more justified in reducing this inquiry to a matter of careful concern, since the man affirmed to me as an apostle is one whom [Note: [Col. 0467D] “In the register of the apostles.” Here *album* means a catalogue [Col. 0468D] of the apostles; for among the jurists an *album* [Col. 0469D] is a register, or a section containing the names of the decurions, whence elsewhere *proscriptio*, in *Herennius* 10, Digest, *De decurionibus et filiis*. In much the same sense Dionysius, book LV, called the roll of senators λεύκωμα τῶν βουλευόντων, “the register of those serving in the senate,” and Suetonius spoke of the register of cithara-players in *Nero*, chap. 20. LE PR.] I do not find in the register of the apostles [Col. 0469A] in the Gospel.

Then, on hearing afterward that he was chosen by the Lord when the latter was already at rest in heaven, I take this as a kind of lack of foresight, if Christ did not know beforehand that Paul would be necessary to him, but only after the office of apostleship had already been organized and dispatched upon its work decided, as an afterthought rather than by forethought, that he should be added—by necessity, so to speak, rather than by choice.

Therefore, shipmaster of Pontus, if you have never received stolen or illicit goods [Note: [Col. 0469D] “Into your light vessels.” An *acatus*, either ἄκατος or ἀκάτιον, is a kind of vessel propelled by sails rather than oars. LE PR.] into your light vessels; if you have never diverted or adulterated any cargo at all, then, as one presumably still more cautious and trustworthy in matters concerning God, I should like you to disclose to us under what bill of lading you received the apostle Paul. Who stamped him with the mark of his title? Who consigned him to you? Who placed him aboard, so that you may produce him with confidence? Otherwise he may be shown to belong to the one who has produced all [Col. 0469B] the documentary evidence of his apostleship.

“He himself,” you say, “professed himself to be an apostle” (Gal. 1:1), and indeed “not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ.” [Note: [Col. 0469D] Certainly anyone can make a declaration concerning himself. Tertullian is speaking of the declaration made before the public records. For we “profess” when we voluntarily declare something publicly and before the records, as when we declare merchandise so that the state may not be defrauded in the payment of duty. Hence in the Pandects Marcian calls merchandise upon which no duty has been paid *merces improfessas*, “undeclared goods.” The ancients likewise registered before the public records children born to them; this provided both certain and ready proof of age if any doubt of this kind should arise. In this sense Seneca elegantly speaks of “declaring a debt,” something candidates and defendants were compelled to do, *De Beneficiis*, book VI. Livy speaks of “declaring grain,” book IV, decade 1, where the commonly printed copies incorrectly read “by compelling them to confess the grain.” RHEN.]

Certainly anyone can make a declaration concerning himself. But his declaration is authenticated by another’s authority: one person writes it, another subscribes it, another seals it, and another enters it into the public records. No one is both his own declarant and his own witness. Besides this, you have surely read (Luke 21:8) that many will come saying, “I am Christ.” If there is one who falsely claims to be Christ, how much more readily might someone proclaim himself an apostle of Christ?

I am still acting in the character of a disciple and inquirer, so that from this point I may both blunt your faith, since you have no means of proving its source, and put your impudence to shame, since you lay claim to him but do not accept the source from which you could substantiate your claim. Let Christ be another’s [Col. 0469C], let the Apostle be another’s, provided that they cannot be proved except from the documentary record of the Creator. [Note: [Col. 0469D] “Thus … thus,” according to others.] For [Note: [Col. 0469D] “Not,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.] Genesis long ago also promised Paul to me.

For among those figures and prophetic blessings concerning his sons, Jacob, when he had turned to Benjamin, said (Gen. 49:27): “Benjamin is a ravening wolf; in the morning he will still devour, and in the evening he will give food.” For he foresaw that Paul would arise from the tribe of Benjamin: a ravening wolf, devouring in the morning—that is, in his early years devastating the Lord’s flock as a persecutor of the churches—and afterward giving food in the evening—that is, as his life was already declining, nourishing Christ’s sheep as the teacher of the nations. [Note: [Col. 0470D] “When he had said,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.]

Likewise, Saul’s initial savagery in persecuting David, followed by his repentance [Col. 0470A] and satisfaction toward the man who returned good for evil, foreshadowed nothing other than Paul in Saul, according to their tribe, and Jesus in David, according to the Virgin’s lineage.

If these mysteries of the figures displease you, at least the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 9) have handed down to me this account of Paul, which you too must not deny. From that source I demonstrate that the persecutor became an apostle, “not from men nor through a man”; from that source I am also led to believe him; from that source I exclude you from defending him. Nor do I fear your saying, “Then you deny the apostle Paul?” I do not blaspheme the man whom I defend. I deny him in order to compel you to prove him. I deny him in order to establish that he is mine.

Either, if you look to our faith, accept the things that establish it; or, if you appeal to your own, produce the things that lay its foundation. Either prove that what you believe exists, or, if you do not prove it, how [Col. 0470B] do you believe? Or what sort of believer are you, opposing the very source by which alone what you believe is proved to exist?

You now have the Apostle from my possessions, just as you have Christ: the Apostle is as much mine as Christ is. [Note: [Col. 0470D] “Here too we shall fight within the same lines.” He gladly refers proverbially to “lines,” as in “back to the lines” and “to draw lines beforehand.” RHEN.] Here too we shall fight within the same lines. At the very outset we shall invoke the preliminary objection that an apostle who is denied to belong to the Creator—and indeed is brought forward against the Creator—must teach nothing, understand nothing, and will nothing in accordance with the Creator; and, above all, that he must proclaim another God with a firmness equal to that with which he broke away from the Creator’s law.

For it is not plausible that, while turning people away from Judaism, he would not at the same time show them toward faith in which God he was turning them, since no one could pass away from the Creator without knowing to whom he had to pass. If Christ had already revealed another God, the Apostle’s testimony would necessarily follow [Col. 0470C], both so that he might not be regarded as the apostle of a God other than the one Christ had revealed, and because the one who had already been revealed by Christ could not lawfully be concealed by the Apostle. But if Christ had revealed nothing of this sort concerning God, then it was all the more necessary that he be revealed by the Apostle, since by then he could not be revealed by another; and such a god would undoubtedly not be worthy of belief if he had not been revealed even by the Apostle.

We have laid this foundation so that from this point onward we may declare that we shall likewise prove that the Apostle circulated no other God, just as we have proved that Christ did not—proving it, of course, from Paul’s own epistles. The fact that these have likewise been mutilated even in their number will already have to be prejudged from the established character of the heretic’s Gospel.

## CHAPTER II

[Note: [Col. 0470D] “The principal epistle against Judaism,” etc. This had crept from the margin into the text; we have restored it to the [Col. 0471D] margin, both here and everywhere below. It is, in fact, the title of this chapter: “The Epistle to the Galatians,” to which we have added “from the chapter.” Yet the phrase “the principal epistle against Judaism” bears against modern heretics, who pervert the meaning of the Apostle’s words and do not hesitate to cite the words of this epistle, chapter 4, not against Judaism but against the Church’s observances of feast days. PAMEL.]

We too acknowledge that the epistle which instructs the Galatians is the principal epistle against Judaism (Gal. 1) [Col. 0471A]. For we embrace that entire abolition of the old law as a dispensation proceeding from the Creator himself, just as we have already discussed often in the course of this work with regard to the renewal foretold by the prophets of our God.

For if the Creator promised that the old things would cease, evidently because new things were to arise, while Christ, when he marked the time of this distinction—“The Law and the Prophets were until John”—set in John the boundary between the two orders, so that from that point the old things ended and the new began, then necessarily the Apostle, under Christ revealed after John, invalidates the old things but confirms the new. In this way he advances the faith of no God other than the Creator, with whom the passing away of the old things had also been foretold.

Therefore both the destruction of the Law and the building up of the Gospel support my position [Col. 0471B] in this epistle as well. They concern that presumption of the Galatians by which they presumed that Christ, as belonging to the Creator, must be believed in while the Creator’s law remained intact—for it would still have seemed incredible that a law should be abolished by its own author.

But if they had heard of an altogether different God from the Apostle, they would of course have known of their own accord that they must withdraw from the law of the God whom they had abandoned when they followed another. For who would wait any longer to be taught that he ought to follow a new discipline after he had received a new God? Rather, because the same divinity that had always been known in the Law was proclaimed in the Gospel, but the discipline was not the same, the entire issue in dispute was whether the Creator’s law ought to be excluded by the Creator’s Gospel in the Creator’s Christ. Take away this issue, and the question becomes pointless.

If the question were pointless, and everyone already recognized of his own accord [Col. 0471C] that through faith in another God he must depart from the Creator’s order, the Apostle would have had no subject matter for teaching so emphatically what faith itself would spontaneously have dictated.

Therefore the whole intention of this epistle teaches nothing other than that departure from the Law [Note: [Col. 0471D] “Cessation,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür; *dicessionem*, Pamelius.] which proceeds from the Creator’s dispensation, as we shall further demonstrate. Likewise, if he brings forward no mention of any new God—something he would have done nowhere more appropriately than in this subject, so as to set forth, in the single and wholly sufficient definition of a new divinity, the reason for dismissing the Law—it is evident in what sense he writes:

“I marvel that you are so quickly being transferred from him who called you into grace, to another gospel”: another in manner of life, not in religion; in discipline, not in divinity. For the Gospel of Christ ought to call them away from the Law to grace, not away from [Col. 0471D] the Creator to another God. No one had moved them away from the Creator, so that they might seem to be transferred to another Gospel precisely while being transferred to the Creator.

Moreover, by adding that there was in fact no other Gospel, he confirms as belonging to the Creator the Gospel whose existence he defends. For [Col. 0472A] the Creator too promises a Gospel, saying through Isaiah (Isa. 40:9): “Ascend the high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion; lift up your voice in your strength, you who bring good news to Jerusalem.” Likewise, in the person of the apostles (Isa. 52:7): “How timely are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things”—surely proclaiming them to the nations as well, since he also says (Isa. 42:4), “In his name the nations will hope,” that is, in Christ’s, to whom he says, “I have appointed you as a light to the nations.”

Suppose [Note: [Col. 0471D] Perhaps *esto*, “suppose,” should be read.] there is also a Gospel of the new God you desire, and that this was the one defended by the Apostle. There are now, then, two Gospels belonging to two Gods, and the Apostle will have lied when he said that there was no other at all, since there is another. He could have defended his Gospel by demonstrating its distinct character, rather than by defining it as the one Gospel.

But perhaps [Col. 0472B], to escape from this difficulty, you will say that this is why [Note: [Col. 0471D] “Here I see,” Latinius.] he added: “Even if an angel from heaven should proclaim a different gospel, let him be accursed”—because he knew that the Creator too would proclaim a gospel. Once again, then, you entangle yourself. For this is precisely what binds you fast. To affirm two Gospels is not the act of one who has already denied that there is another.

Yet the meaning is clear from his placing his own person first: “But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should proclaim a different gospel.” For this was said by way of example. Otherwise, if he himself was not going to proclaim a different gospel, then surely neither was an angel. Thus he named an angel in order to show that men were all the less to be believed when neither an angel nor an apostle was to be believed. He was not referring the angel to the Creator’s Gospel.

From there, as he runs through the course of his conversion from persecutor to apostle, he confirms the text of the Acts [Note: [Col. 0472D] “Of Acts” omitted by Junius.] of the Apostles, in which [Col. 0472C] the very subject of this epistle is also recognized: certain persons had intervened [Note: [Col. 0472D] “Certain persons had intervened,” etc. That is, certain persons had come between and opposed them. RHEN.] who said that circumcision was necessary and that the law of Moses must be observed. The apostles were then consulted about this question, and by the authority of the Spirit reported that burdens must not be imposed upon men which their fathers themselves had been unable to bear.

Now if the Acts of the Apostles agree with Paul in this matter as well, the reason why you reject them is already apparent: namely, because they preach no God other than the Creator and no Christ belonging to any other than the Creator, since even the promise of the Holy Spirit cannot be proved to have been fulfilled from any source other than the documentary record of Acts.

It is surely not plausible that Acts should agree with the Apostle in one respect, when they set forth his history in accordance with his own testimony, yet disagree in another when they announce the Creator’s divinity in Christ; for Paul did indeed follow the apostles’ preaching in every respect [Col. 0472D], since he received from them the rule for teaching the abolition of the Law. [Note: [Col. 0472D] “As though Paul had not followed the apostles’ preaching in every respect,” Pamelius.]

## CHAPTER III

Finally, he writes (Gal. 2–3) that after fourteen years he went up to Jerusalem to obtain the support of Peter and the other [Col. 0473A] apostles, so that he might compare with them the rule of his Gospel, lest for so many years he had run, or was still running, in vain—that is, if in any respect he was proclaiming the Gospel outside their rule. To such an extent had he desired [Note: [Col. 0473D] “He desired,” Latinius.] to be approved and confirmed by them.

But if at any time you wish [Note: [Col. 0473D] “But if those whom you sometimes wish,” Latinius.] the apostles to be understood [Note: [Col. 0473D] “To be understood,” Latinius.] as more closely allied with Judaism, since [Note: [Col. 0473D] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür add “however.”] he says that not even [Note: [Col. 0473D] “Not even” omitted by Latinius.] Titus was circumcised, he now begins to show that the question of circumcision alone, arising from their continuing defense of the Law, was agitated by those whom for this reason he calls false and intruding [Note: [Col. 0474D] “Introduced,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.] brothers. They were pressing for the establishment of nothing other than the continuance of the Law, undoubtedly from an unimpaired faith in the Creator, and were thus perverting the Gospel—not by an interpolation of Scripture [Note: [Col. 0473D] “Interpolation of Scripture.” An interpolator, or corrupter, is a heretic who distorts, truncates, diminishes, or adds to Holy Scripture. LE PR.] through which they might fashion Christ as belonging to the Creator, but by retaining [Col. 0473B] the old discipline so that they might not exclude the Creator’s law.

“Therefore,” he says, “because of the intruding false brothers who slipped in to spy upon our liberty, which we have in Christ, so that they might reduce us to slavery, we did not yield in submission even for an hour.”

Let us attend both to the meaning itself and to its cause, and the corruption of the text will become apparent. He first says: “But not even Titus, who was with me, although he was a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised”; then he adds, “because of the intruding false brothers,” and the rest. He plainly begins to give the reason for an action contrary to the preceding statement, showing why he did it—an action he would neither have done nor explained if the circumstance for which he did it had not occurred.

Finally, I should like you to say: if those false brothers had slipped in to spy upon their liberty, would they have yielded in submission? I think not. Therefore they did yield [Col. 0473C], because there were persons [Note: [Col. 0474D] “Would they not have yielded in submission? I think they would. Therefore they had yielded, because there were persons,” the Wouwer manuscript.] on whose account they had to yield. For this was appropriate to an immature faith still hesitating over observance of the Law, when the Apostle himself was uncertain whether he had run, or was running, in vain.

The false brothers who were spying upon Christian liberty therefore had to be frustrated, lest they carry it off into the slavery of Judaism before Paul knew that he had not run in vain, before his predecessors gave him the right hand of fellowship, and before, on their authorization, he undertook [Note: [Col. 0474D] “Discharged,” Latinius.] the duty of preaching among the nations.

He therefore necessarily yielded for a time. This is consistent with his reason for circumcising Timothy and bringing men with shaven heads into the temple, events recorded in Acts (Acts 16; 21). They are so true that they agree with the Apostle when he declares (1 Cor. 9:20) that he became a Jew to the Jews in order to gain the Jews, and behaved as one under the Law on account of [Col. 0473D] those who were under the Law. Thus too, on account of those intruding men [Note: [Col. 0474D] “Those introduced men,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.], he finally became all things to all people [Col. 0474A], so that he might gain them all.

If they demand that these matters too be understood from this passage, no one will doubt [Note: [Col. 0474D] “No one will doubt,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.] that Paul was a preacher of that God and Christ whose law, though excluding it, he nevertheless admitted temporarily as circumstances required—a law which would have had to be cast off immediately if he had brought forward a new God.

It is therefore fitting that Peter, James, and John gave Paul the right hand of fellowship and made an agreement concerning the distribution of their duties: Paul was to go to the nations, and they to the circumcision, provided only that they remembered the poor. This too was in accordance with the law of the Creator, who sustains the poor and needy, as was proved in our examination of your Gospel.

Thus it is established that the question concerned the Law alone, since the dispute reveals what it was appropriate to preserve from the Law. [Note: [Col. 0473D] “But he rebuked Peter for not walking with a straight foot.” In the Greek the word is ὀρθοποδοῦντα, “walking straight.” Nevertheless, concerning that rebuke one should note what Eusebius has in his *History*, book [Col. 0474D], chap. 12, where, on the authority of St. Clement, he says that this Cephas was someone other than blessed Peter: ἕνά φησί γεγονέναι τῶν ἑβδομήκοντα μαθητῶν, ὁμώνυμον Πέτρῳ τυχόντα τῷ ἀποστόλῳ, “He says that this man was one of the seventy disciples who happened to bear the same name as the apostle Peter.” LE PR.]

But he rebuked Peter because he was not walking with a straight foot according to the truth of the Gospel. Certainly he rebuked him; yet for no other reason than his inconsistency in eating, since he varied his practice according to the identity of those present, fearing those who were of the circumcision. He did not rebuke him for any perversion concerning the divinity, on account of which he would also have resisted others to their faces, since he did not spare Peter himself over the lesser matter of an ambiguous manner of life. But how do the Marcionites want this to be believed?

For the rest, let the Apostle proceed in denying that a man is justified by works of the Law, but rather by faith—yet by faith in the same God to whom the Law also belongs. For he would not have labored to distinguish faith from the Law if a difference in the divinity itself, had it existed, would automatically have distinguished them. Rightly, then, he did not rebuild the things he had destroyed.

The Law, however, had to be destroyed from the time when John’s voice cried out in the wilderness (Luke 3): “Prepare the ways of the Lord,” so that ravines might be filled, hills and mountains lowered, and crooked and rough places made straight and level—that is, [Col. 0474C] the difficulties of the Law changed into the facilities of the Gospel.

He also remembered that the time spoken of in the Psalm had now come (Ps. 2): “Let us break their bonds away from us and cast off their yoke from us.” This was from the time when “the nations raged, the peoples meditated vain things, the kings of the earth took their stand, and the rulers gathered together as one against the Lord and against his Christ,” so that man might now be justified by the liberty of faith, not by the slavery of the Law: “Because the righteous man lives by faith” (Heb. 10:38).

And if the prophet Habakkuk foretold this (Hab. 2:4), you have the Apostle confirming the Prophets, just as Christ did. Faith, therefore, in which the righteous man will live belongs to the same God whose is the Law by which the worker is not justified.

Likewise, if there is a curse in the Law but a blessing in faith, you find both set forth by the Creator: “Behold,” he says (Deut. 11:26), “I have set before [Col. 0474D] you a curse and a blessing.” Marcion cannot claim the distinction for himself. Although it is a distinction between things, it is not therefore a distinction between authors [Col. 0475A], since both things are set forth by one author.

Why Christ became a curse for us is evident from the Apostle’s own teaching, as is how strongly this supports our side—that is, in accordance with faith in the Creator. For because the Creator pronounced, “Cursed is everyone who is suspended on a tree,” Christ will not therefore appear to belong to another God and for that reason already to have been cursed by the Creator at that time in the Law. And how could the Creator have cursed him beforehand if he did not know him?

Why should it not be more fitting for the Creator to have surrendered his own Son to his own curse than for that god of yours to have subjected his son to the Creator’s curse—and indeed on behalf of a man who belonged to another? Finally, if this seems savage in the Creator’s treatment of his Son, it is equally savage in your god. But if it is rational in your god, it is equally so in mine—and more so in mine.

For it would more readily be believed that the one who had once set both a curse and a blessing before man had provided a blessing for man through Christ’s curse [Col. 0475B] than that a god who, according to you, had never declared either should have done so.

“We have therefore received the spiritual blessing through faith,” he says—the faith by which, according to the Creator, the righteous man will live. This, then, is what I say: faith belongs to the God to whom the established form of grace through faith belongs.

But when he also adds, “For you are all sons of faith,” what heretical industry erased above becomes evident [Note: [Col. 0475D] Namely, what heretical industry erased above: the mention of Abraham. Tertullian indicates that Marcion erased several preceding verses both at the beginning of this chapter and before the words already quoted. He repeats this in the following chapter, and not only concerning the mention of Abraham but also concerning the statement, “Nevertheless, he does not reject or add to a human covenant.” PAMEL.]: namely, the mention of Abraham, in connection with which the Apostle affirms that through faith we are sons of Abraham, and in accordance with which mention he here too described us as sons of faith.

Otherwise, how are we sons of faith? And of whose faith, if not Abraham’s? For if Abraham believed God and it was reckoned [Note: [Col. 0475D] “Is reckoned,” Latinius.] to him as righteousness, and he thereby deserved to be called the father of many nations, while we [Col. 0475C], moreover, by believing God, are justified in the same way as Abraham and likewise attain life, just as the righteous man lives by faith, it follows that above he pronounced us sons of Abraham in his capacity as the father of faith, and here sons of the faith through which Abraham had been promised as the father of the nations.

By the very fact that he was calling faith back from circumcision, was he not seeking to establish as Abraham’s sons those who believed while preserving the integrity of their flesh, just as Abraham had believed? Finally, the faith of one God cannot be admitted according to the pattern established by another God, so as to reckon believers righteous, cause the righteous to live, and call the nations sons of faith. All this belongs to the God [Note: [Col. 0475D] “His” is absent from the Paris manuscript.] with whom it is already known beforehand under the same mention of Abraham, since Marcion is refuted by the very meaning of the passage.

## CHAPTER IV
Source/review notes: The corrupt apparatus readings Ortaneorum and ortam eorum remain semantically uncertain and are retained verbatim.

“Further,” he says (Gal. III, IV, V, and VI), “I speak in human [Col. 0475D] terms: while we were children, we were placed under the elements of the world, to serve them.” Yet this is [Col. 0476A] not spoken in merely human terms, for it is not an illustration but the truth. For what child—child, of course, in understanding, as the nations are—is not subject to the elements of the world, which he regards as God [variant: “receives,” al.]? What he does [variant: “was,” Jun.], however, is that although he had spoken in human terms, nevertheless no one rejects or adds provisions to a human covenant. For by the example of an enduring human covenant he was defending the divine one.

“The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He did not say, ‘and to seeds,’ as though referring to many, but ‘and to your seed,’ as referring to one, who is Christ.” Let Marcion’s sponge blush—except that it is superfluous for me to reconsider what he removed, since he is more powerfully refuted from what he preserved.

“But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son”: assuredly that God who is also the God of the very times of which the age consists; who also ordered [Col. 0476B] the signs of the times—the suns, moons, constellations, and stars; and who both appointed and foretold the revelation of his Son for the end of the times (Isa. II, 2): “In the last days the mountain of the Lord will be manifest”; and, according to Joel (Joel II, 28): “In the last days I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh.” It belonged to him to wait for the time to be fulfilled, to whom the end of time belonged just as its beginning did.

But that idle god, responsible neither for any work nor for any proclamation, and therefore for no time either—what did he ever do to bring about the fulfillment of time, or even [variant: “or now,” Lat.; Col. 0476D] to endure the time that had to be fulfilled? If nothing, it is quite pointless that he should have waited upon the Creator’s times, thereby serving the Creator.

For what purpose did he send his Son? “To redeem those who were under the law”: that is, to make (Isa. XL, 4) [Col. 0476C] “crooked things into a straight way, and rough places into gentle ways” [variants: “the crooked way,” Fran.; “smooth ways,” Jun.], according to Isaiah; so that old things might pass away and new things arise: “A new law from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. II, 3); and “so that we might receive adoption as sons”—we, assuredly, the nations, who were not sons. For “he too will be a light of the nations,” and “in his name the nations will hope.”

> **Note [Cols. 0475D–0476D].** Thus, to make it certain that we are sons of God. This is how he explains the Apostle’s words: “Now because you are sons of God.” The reading of all the Latin witnesses, which add “of God,” is confirmed; this phrase is lacking among the Greeks, according to the consistent reading of the Greek Fathers. Conversely, the Author reads “our hearts,” in accordance with the Greek ἡμῶν (*hēmōn*, “our”), with Blessed Ambrose and Jerome in his Commentary likewise agreeing, whereas others read “your hearts.” Moreover, Rhenanus rightly understands “is” there when the Author says, “whose grace.” —PAM.

Thus, to make it certain that we are sons of God, “he sent his Spirit into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father.’” For he says (Joel II, 28): “In the last days I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh.” Whose grace is this, unless it is his whose promise of grace it also was? Who is the Father, unless he who is also the Maker?

After such riches, therefore, there was to be no return to the weak and beggarly elements. Among the Romans too, moreover, the first letters are commonly called “elements.” He was not, therefore, seeking to turn them away from the God of the cosmic elements [Col. 0476D] by disparaging those elements. Even though he had said above, “If, then, you serve those who by nature are not gods,” he was censuring [variant: “censures,” Rhen. Seml. Oberth.] the error [Col. 0477A] of physical—that is, natural—superstition, which regards the elements as God; yet even so he was not reproaching the God of the elements.

But he himself makes clear which “elements” he wishes to be understood: namely, the first letters of the law. “You observe days, and months, and seasons, and years, and Sabbaths, I suppose, and pure suppers, and fasts, and great days.”

> **Note [Col. 0477C].** “Pure suppers. Days of Preparation. ἐν τῇ ἔκτῃ τῶν ἡμερῶν” (“on the sixth day of the days”). Irenaeus interprets it thus, book I, chapter 10. Glosses: “pure supper,” προσάββατον (*prosabbaton*, “the day before the Sabbath”). —RIG.

For it was necessary to cease from these also, just as from circumcision, by the decrees of the Creator, who says through Isaiah as well (Isa. I, 14): “Your new moons and Sabbaths and great day I will not endure; my soul hates your fast, festivals, and ceremonies”; and through Amos (Amos V, 21): “I hate and reject your ceremonies, and I will not smell [variant: “be adored,” Rhen. Seml. Oberth.] in your assemblies.” Likewise through Hosea (Hos. II, 11): “I will turn away all her joys, her ceremonies, her Sabbaths, her new moons, and all her assemblies.”

[Col. 0477B] “He abolished what he himself had instituted,” you say? He, more properly than anyone else. Or [variant: “But,” Par.], if someone else abolished them, then that other supported the Creator’s judgment by taking away the things the Creator too had condemned. But the question why the Creator annulled his own laws does not belong to this passage. It is enough that we have proved he would annul them, so that it may be established that the Apostle determined nothing against the Creator, since the removal [variant: “abolition,” al.] of the law itself comes from the Creator.

But [variant: “And,” Par.] just as thieves commonly let something fall from their booty as evidence, so I believe Marcion left behind the final reference to Abraham—the one above all that ought to have been removed—even if he partly altered [variant: “swept away,” Lat.; Col. 0478C] it:

“For Abraham had two children, one by the slave woman and the other by the free woman. But the one [Col. 0477C] by the slave woman was born according to the flesh; the one by the free woman, through [Col. 0478A] the promise. These things are allegorical,” that is, they portend something else. “For these are the two covenants,” or two manifestations, as we find it interpreted: one from Mount Sinai, giving birth into slavery in the synagogue of the Jews according to the law; the other [variant readings: alium, Rhen. Seml. Obert.; alterum, Lat.] “above every principality,” giving birth to power, dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come. This is our mother, into whom we have promised the holy Church. Therefore he adds: “Consequently, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman.”

He plainly showed that the noble freedom of Christianity possesses an allegorical mystery in Abraham’s son born of the free woman, just as the legal servitude of Judaism does in the son of the slave woman; and thus that both dispensations belong to that God in whose writings we find [Col. 0478B] the delineation [“delineation,” Pam.; variant: “declension,” Jun.] of both dispensations.

When he says, “With the freedom by which Christ set us free,” does he not establish as the manumitter the one who had been Lord?

> **Note [Cols. 0477C–0478D].** “For not even Galba manumitted another man’s slaves.” This is certainly how the manuscripts read, and nothing should be changed. Marcion’s heresy was to say that Christ was not the Son of God the Creator, and that the God of the Old Testament, or Law, was one God, while the God of the New Testament, or Gospel, was another. The God of the Law was the Creator, fierce and savage; the God of the Gospel, however, had created nothing and was only good and exceedingly indulgent, having freed us through his Christ from the yoke of that savage and tyrannical God. Tertullian refutes this doctrine with many arguments, among them the fact that Paul, in the Epistle to the Galatians, calls Christ our manumitter. Not even Marcion rejected that Epistle. From this it necessarily follows that we were once in servitude under God the Creator, and that Christ is the Son of that God the Creator, since no one can be called or be a manumitter unless he was Lord, nor can anyone be a freedman unless he served in lawful servitude under the one who manumits him.

> We, therefore, as the same Epistle teaches, were for a time servants under the Law of the Old Testament; afterward, however, we were freed from that servitude to the Law by Christ’s beneficence, and are no longer under the Law but under the Gospel. Accordingly, Tertullian argues thus: if we acknowledge Christ as the manumitter, we must necessarily acknowledge that this same Christ belongs to that Creator whose Law it was from which we have been released, having obtained freedom. For unless Christ belonged to the Creator, he would not lawfully have freed us from the servitude in which we served under the Creator, beneath the harshness of his law. We served under the Creator; therefore the manumitter had to come from the Creator. For one who manumits another man’s slaves accomplishes nothing.

> Here, in his customary fashion, Tertullian sprinkles in a little wit. “For,” he says, “not even Galba manumitted another man’s slaves, though he was more likely to release free men.” He had read in Suetonius Tranquillus—an author familiar to him and cited by him more than once—that Nero’s death afforded such public rejoicing that the common people ran throughout the city wearing the caps of freedmen, as though delivered from the grim yoke of slavery. Galba, Nero’s successor, began his reign under the following auspices: as though preparing to conduct a manumission, he mounted the tribunal and, after setting before himself very many images of people condemned and killed by Nero, began to lament the condition of the times; while in that posture or action, he was acclaimed Emperor by the bystanders. Tertullian therefore says that not even Galba, in that state of affairs, manumitted another man’s slaves. He adds, “though he was more likely to release free men”—that is, to restore liberty to Roman citizens who had endured shameful slavery under Nero. —RIG.

“For not even Galba manumitted another man’s slaves, though he was more likely to release free men” [variant: “not Galba,” omitting “even,” Jun.]. Freedom, therefore, will be granted by him under whom there had been the servitude of the law. And rightly so.

> **Note [Col. 0478D].** “It was not fitting for those who had been manumitted to be bound again to the yoke of slavery.” These words are taken from chapter V of Galatians according to all editions. Moreover, he correctly translates the Greek ἐνέχεσθαι (*enechesthai*) as “to be bound.” In the words “he persisted in erasing circumcision itself, the mark of servitude,” he alludes to what follows in the same passage: “Behold, I Paul say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing,” and so forth through verse 6. Epiphanius, in his third refutation of Marcion from the Epistle to the Galatians, cites the intervening words: “And I testify again that every circumcised man is a debtor to fulfill the whole law.” —PAMELIUS.

It was not fitting for those who had been manumitted to be bound again to the yoke of slavery—that is, of the law—now that the Psalm (Ps. II) had been fulfilled: “Let us burst their bonds and cast their yoke away from us,” after the rulers had gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ.

Thus, for those released from servitude, he persisted in erasing the very mark of servitude [Col. 0478C], circumcision, on the authority, of course, of the prophetic proclamation [Col. 0479A], remembering what was said through Jeremiah (Jer. IV, 4): “And circumcise the foreskins [variant: “foreskin,” al.] of your heart.” Moses too says (Deut. X, 16): “You shall circumcise your hardness of heart”—that is, not the flesh.

Finally, if he came from another god and was excluding circumcision, why does he also deny that uncircumcision has any value in Christ, just as circumcision does not? For he ought to have preferred circumcision’s rival, which he was attacking, if he came from a god who was the rival of circumcision. But because circumcision and uncircumcision alike were assigned to the one God, both were therefore without effect in Christ because of the preeminence of faith: that faith of which it was written (Isa. XLII, 4), “And in his name the nations will believe”; that faith which, by saying it is perfected through love, he thereby also shows to belong to the Creator.

For whether [Col. 0479B] he means love toward God, this too belongs to the Creator (Deut. VI): “You shall love God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength”; or love toward one’s neighbor: “and your neighbor as yourself”—this too belongs to the Creator.

“The one who troubles you will bear judgment.” From what God? From the supremely good one? But he does not judge. From the Creator? But neither will he condemn an advocate of circumcision. Yet if there is no other who judges except the Creator, then the defenders of the law will now be condemned only by the one who himself ordained that it should cease.

What if he also confirms the law in the respect in which he ought? “For the whole law,” he says, “has been fulfilled among you” [“among” omitted in Fran.]: “‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’” Or, if he wishes “has been fulfilled” to be understood as meaning that it is no longer to be fulfilled, then he does not wish me to love my neighbor as myself, since this too would have ceased along with the law. But one must persevere [Col. 0479C] in this commandment forever.

Therefore even by its adversary the Creator’s law was approved. It obtained from him not a diminution but an abridgment, its sum being reduced to a single commandment. Yet this too is more fitting for no one than for its Author. Indeed, when he says, “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ,” if this cannot be done unless one loves one’s neighbor [variant: “a neighbor for oneself” (sibi), Rhen. Seml. Oberth.] as oneself, it is evident that “You shall love your neighbor [variant: “the neighbor to you” (tibi), Rhen. Seml. Oberth.] as yourself,” which is heard in “Bear one another’s burdens,” is the law of Christ, which is the Creator’s law. Thus Christ belongs to the Creator, since the Creator’s law is Christ’s law.

“You are mistaken; God is not mocked.” Yet Marcion’s god can indeed be mocked, since he knows neither how to become angry nor how to take vengeance. “Whatever a man has sown [variant: “will have sown” (severit), Rhen. Seml. Ober.], that he will also reap.” Therefore [Col. 0479D] he holds out a God of retribution and judgment. “Let us not grow weary in doing good”; and: “While we have time, let us [Col. 0480A] do good.” Deny that the Creator commanded people to do good, and then a different doctrine may belong to a different divinity. But if he proclaims retribution, both the harvest of corruption and the harvest of life will come from the same God. “In its own time we shall reap,” because Ecclesiastes too [variant: “Ecclesiasticus,” Rhen. Seml. Oberth.] says (Eccl. III, 17): “There will be a time for every matter.”

Moreover, “the world has been crucified to me,” a servant of the Creator—but not the God of the world; “and I to the world”—but not to the God of the world. By “the world” he meant its manner of life, in relation to which, by renouncing it, we are mutually transformed and die to one another; he calls the persecutors of Christ “the world.”

But when he adds that he “bears the marks of Christ in his body” (bodily marks, assuredly, are appropriate), he has thereby professed Christ’s flesh to be no longer imaginary but true and solid, for he displays its bodily marks.

> **Note [Cols. 0479D–0480D].** “That he bears the marks of Christ in his body,” and so forth. From the fact that, to prove Christ’s true and solid flesh, he adds that he displays its bodily marks, the Author appears to take “marks” not as mere brands of the kind with which slaves were marked by their masters so that they could be recognized as belonging to them, but as wounds such as Christ too bore bodily in himself—as though he were saying that he had suffered the same afflictions as Christ. In this, however, his reading differs: he read “of Christ,” where others have “of the Lord Jesus.” —PAM.

# CHAPTER V

[Col. 0480B]

The preliminary treatment of the preceding Epistle led me not to reconsider its salutation, since I was certain it could be reconsidered elsewhere: namely, the common and identical salutation in all the Epistles. It does not, of course, prescribe “health” to those to whom he writes, but “grace and peace.”

I will not ask what a destroyer of Judaism has to do with a still-Jewish custom; for even today the Jews greet one another in the name of peace, and formerly in the Scriptures they saluted in the same way. But I understand him to have defended, by performing his office, the Creator’s proclamation (Isa. LII): “How timely are the feet of those who proclaim good things, who proclaim peace!” For as a proclaimer of good things—that is, of God’s grace—he knew that grace should be placed before peace.

In announcing these things as coming “from God our Father and the Lord Jesus,” he uses common names, names also compatible with our mystery. I do not think it can be discerned which [variant: “why,” Fran.] God the Father and which Lord Jesus is being proclaimed except from their attributes [Col. 0480C]—which claimant they fit better.

First, I lay it down as a rule that no other should be acknowledged as Father and Lord than the Creator and Founder both of man and of the universe. Further, the name “Lord” accrues to the Father also because of his power, a name that the Son too receives through the Father.

Next, grace and peace belong not only to him by whom they were proclaimed, but to him who had been offended. For there can be no grace except where there has been offense, nor peace except where there has been war. Both the people, through transgression of discipline, and the whole human race, through disregard of nature, had sinned and rebelled against the Creator. But Marcion’s god, both because [variant: qua, Latin.] he was unknown, could not be offended, and because [variant: qua, Latin.] he does not know how to become angry. [Col. 0480D] What grace, then, can come from one who was not offended? What peace from one against whom no rebellion had occurred?

> **Note [Cols. 0480D–0482D].** He says that the cross of Christ is foolishness to those who are perishing, but power, and so forth. Here too the Author differs from the Apostle, perhaps following Marcion. For in Marcion’s text there is first: “The word of the cross of Christ”; then, “to those who perish, but to us who are being saved”; and it does not contain “and wisdom.” When the Author then adds from the Apostle, “I will render understanding void,” the Greek is ἀθετήσω (*athetēsō*, “I will set aside”), for which the Vulgate translator, and Epiphanius as well, has “I will reject.” Epiphanius likewise hurls this against Marcion in his first refutation, from the Epistle to the Corinthians. —PAM.

He says that “the cross of Christ is foolishness to those who are perishing,” [Col. 0481A] but “the power and wisdom of God” to those who will obtain salvation. To show whence this came, he adds [variant: “something,” Rhen. Seml. Oberth.]: “For it is written: ‘I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and render the understanding of the prudent void.’”

If these words belong to the Creator, and those matters [“those matters” omitted in Rhen. Seml. Ober.] concerning the cross were reckoned as foolishness [variant: “he reckons them foolishness,” Pam.], then both the cross and, through the cross, Christ will belong to the Creator, by whom that which concerns the cross was foretold. Or if the Creator, as a rival, therefore took away wisdom so that the cross of Christ—his adversary’s Christ, of course—might be reckoned foolishness, how could the Creator have pronounced anything concerning the cross of a Christ who was not his, when he did not know him at the time he made the proclamation?

Moreover, why is it that, under the supremely good Lord of lavish mercy, some receive salvation because they believe the cross to be the power and wisdom of God, while others receive destruction [Col. 0481B] because Christ’s cross is reckoned foolishness by them, unless the Creator had punished some offense committed by both the people and the human race with the loss of wisdom and understanding?

What follows will confirm this, when he says: “Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?” And when he here adds the reason: “Because the world, in the wisdom of God, did not understand God [variant: “the Lord,” Rhen. Seml. Oberth.] through wisdom, God deemed it good, through the foolishness of proclamation, to save those who believe.”

> **Note [Col. 0482D].** “God deemed it good.” Thus he translates the Greek εὐδόκησεν ὁ θεὸς (*eudokēsen ho theos*, “God was well pleased”). For just as authors say “to account it good,” and “to regard it as fair and good,” so he said “to deem it good.” —RHEN.

But first I shall discuss “the world,” since the most subtle heretics interpret “the world” here, most emphatically, as “the Lord of the world.” We, however, understand it as the human being who is in the world, in accordance with the ordinary form of human speech, by which we very often put the container for what is contained. “The Circus shouted,” “the Forum spoke,” and “the Basilica roared”—that is, the people who were conducting affairs in those places.

[Col. 0481C] Therefore, because man—not the God of the world—did not know God through wisdom, though he ought to have known him—the Jew through the wisdom of the Scriptures, and every nation through the wisdom of his works—the same God, who had not been acknowledged [variant: adagnitus, al.] in his own wisdom, consequently resolved to strike back at human wisdom by means of foolishness, saving all who believed in the foolish proclamation of the cross.

“For Jews desire signs,” although they ought already to have been certain about God; “and Greeks seek wisdom”—their own wisdom, of course, not God’s wisdom, which they set forth. But if a new God were being proclaimed, what offense had the Jews committed by desiring signs through which they might believe? Or the Greeks by pursuing wisdom in which they might more readily believe?

Thus the requital itself against Jews and Greeks confirms that God is both jealous and judge, since by a retribution marked by rivalry and judgment he made foolish [Col. 0481D] the wisdom of the world. But if both the grounds of the argument and the Scriptures brought to bear belong to the same God, then when the Apostle discusses the God who was not understood, he assuredly teaches that the Creator is to be understood.

Likewise, [Col. 0482A] when he proclaims Christ as “a stumbling block to the Jews,” he seals the Creator’s prophecy concerning him, spoken through Isaiah (Isa. XXVIII, 15): “Behold, I have laid in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.” “The rock, moreover, was Christ”—even Marcion preserves this.

“What is foolish in God” and wiser than men, if not the cross and death of Christ? “What is weak in God” and stronger than man, if not the birth and flesh of God? But if Christ was neither born of a virgin nor constructed of flesh, and therefore did not truly suffer either the cross or death, there is [variant: “there was,” Rhen. Seml. Oberth.] nothing foolish or weak in him.

Nor, then, did “God choose the foolish things of the world to confound wisdom” [variant reading: sapientia (“wisdom”), Par.]; nor did “God choose the weak things of the world to confound the strong”; nor “the dishonorable, the least, and the contemptible things—the things that are not,” that is, that do not truly exist, “to confound the things that are,” that is, that truly [Col. 0482B] exist.

For nothing ordained by God [“is” omitted in some copies] is truly insignificant, ignoble, or contemptible, but only what is ordained by man. [Col. 0482B] Yet in the Creator’s dispensation even the old ordinances [variant: “true things,” Lat.] may be reckoned foolish, weak, dishonorable, paltry, and contemptible. What is more foolish or weaker than God’s demand for bloody sacrifices and smoke-reeking burnt offerings? What is weaker than the purification of little vessels and beds [variant: “platters,” Ciaccon. Jun.]? What is more dishonorable than a further disfigurement of flesh already causing shame? What is so lowly as the pronouncement of retaliation? What is so contemptible as the restriction of foods? Every heretic, so far as I know, ridicules the whole Old Testament.

“For God chose the foolish things of the world to confound wisdom” [variant reading: sapientia (“wisdom”), Par.]. Marcion’s god did nothing of the kind, because he does not even display rivalry by refuting contraries with contraries, [Col. 0482C] “so that no flesh may boast”; so that, “as it is written, ‘Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.’” In which Lord? Assuredly in the one who commanded this—unless the Creator commanded him to boast in Marcion’s god [variant: “the god” (Deum), Rhen. Seml. Ober.].

# CHAPTER VI

Thus, through all these statements (1 Cor. II and III), he shows which God’s wisdom he speaks “among the perfect”: namely, the wisdom of him who took away the wisdom of the wise and rendered void the understanding of the prudent; who made foolish the wisdom of the world, choosing its foolish things and appointing them for salvation.

He says that this wisdom had been hidden: it had been present in foolish, paltry, and dishonorable things and had also lain concealed beneath figures, allegories, and riddles, afterward to be revealed in Christ, whom the Creator appointed as a light of the nations when he promised through the voice of Isaiah [Col. 0482D] that he would uncover invisible and hidden treasures.

For that the god who performed absolutely no work in which he might be thought to have hidden anything should have hidden something is [Col. 0483A] quite incredible. If he himself existed, he could not have remained hidden, much less any mysteries belonging to him.

But both the Creator himself and his mysteries were known: they were, of course, openly enacted among Israel, but obscured as to their meanings. In these the wisdom of God lay hidden among the perfect, to be declared in its proper time, although it had been determined in God’s purpose before the ages.

Whose ages, unless the Creator’s? For if the ages too are constructed from times, while times are joined together from days, months, and years, and days, months, and years are marked by the Creator’s suns, moons, and stars, which were appointed by him for this purpose—“For they shall be,” he says (Gen. I), “for signs of months and years”—it is evident that the ages too belong to the Creator, and that everything said to have been determined before the ages belongs to no other than him to whom the ages themselves belong.

> **Note [Col. 0483D].** “For they shall be,” he says, “for signs of months and years.” That is, the motions of moon and sun distinguish days, years, ages, and times. Those who enlist this passage from Genesis I in defense of astrology misuse it; this interpretation argues against them. —LE PR.

Or let Marcion prove [Col. 0483B] the ages of his own god: let him also show the world itself in which ages may be reckoned, a vessel, as it were, of the times; and let him show some signs or their origin [variants: Ortaneorum, Rhen.
