Seml. Obert.; notas eorum (“their marks”), Wouw.; ortam eorum, Jun.; the readings Ortaneorum and ortam eorum are uncertain]. If he demonstrates nothing, I return to make this further point.

Why, moreover, did he determine our glory before the Creator’s ages? He could have been thought to have determined it before the ages if he had revealed it when the age was introduced. But since he does so only after almost all the Creator’s ages have already been prolonged [variant: “extended,” al.], he determined it “before the ages” in vain, rather than “within the ages,” when he was going to reveal it almost after the ages. For eagerness in determining something does not belong to one who delayed revealing it.

Both are fitting for the Creator, however: both to have determined it before the ages and to have revealed it at the end of the ages, because throughout the intervening span of the ages he [Col. 0483C] ministered beforehand [variant: “foreshadowed,” Jun.] in figures, riddles, and allegories what he both determined and revealed.

But because he adds concerning our glory that “none of the rulers of this age knew it—for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory”—the heretic argues that the rulers of this age fastened to the cross the Lord, that is, the Christ of another God, so that this accusation too may rebound [variant: “be redirected,” Rhen. Seml. Oberth.] upon the Creator.

Yet for one to whom we have shown [variant: “shall have shown,” Rhen. Seml. Ober.] above the ways in which our glory must be assigned to the Creator, it should have been established beforehand that this glory, since it had been hidden with the Creator, was rightly unknown even to all the Creator’s powers and authorities [variant: “all men,” Rig. Venet.]. For servants are not permitted to know their masters’ counsels—still less those apostate angels and the prince of transgression himself, the devil, whom I would all the more insist were alienated, through their fault, from all knowledge of the Creator’s dispensations.

But now it is not even appropriate for me to interpret [Col. 0483D] “the rulers of this age” as the Creator’s powers and authorities, because the Apostle ascribes ignorance to them. Yet [Col. 0484A] according to our Gospel (Matt. IV), the devil too recognized Jesus during the temptation; and according to the commonly held canonical record (Luke IV, 34), the unclean spirit knew that he was the Holy One of God, that he was called Jesus, and that he had come for their destruction.

> **Note [Col. 0484D].** “According to our Gospel”: this distinguishes it from Marcion’s corrupted codex. These things are related in Matthew IV. A little later comes: “For it is written in my text that Satan entered Judas.” That passage is from Luke XXII, which Marcion had cut out of “my” text. —LE PR.

Even the parable of the strong armed man, whom another stronger man overcame and whose goods he seized (Luke XI), if in Marcion’s reading it is understood of the Creator, means that the Creator could no longer have remained ignorant of the God of glory, since he was overcome by him; nor could he have fastened to the cross one against whom he had no power.

It remains, according to my position, credible that the Creator’s powers and authorities, though they knew the God of glory, crucified their own Christ, since through desperation and an excess of malice even the most wicked servants do not hesitate to kill their masters. For it is written [Col. 0484B] in my text (Luke XXII, 3) that Satan entered Judas.

According to Marcion, however, the Apostle does not permit ignorance of the Lord of glory to be ascribed in this passage to the Creator’s powers, because he plainly does not intend “the rulers of this age” to mean those powers. If he does not appear to have spoken of spiritual rulers, then he spoke of secular rulers: assuredly of the people that held primacy—not among the nations—and of that people’s own rulers—King Herod, Pilate as well, and the Roman magistracy by which the higher principality of this age presided.

Thus, when the opposing party’s arguments are demolished, our interpretations are built up. But do you still wish our glory to belong to your god, and to have been hidden with him? Then why do God and the Apostle still rely on [variant: “use,” Lat.] the same instrument? [Col. 0484C] What has he to do everywhere with the sayings of the Prophets?

“For who has known the mind of the Lord? And who has been his counselor?” That is Isaiah (Isa. XL, 13). What has he to do even with the examples belonging to our God? For when he declares himself a wise architect, we find that the Creator, through Isaiah (Isa. III, 2), indicated by this phrase one who makes divine discipline manifest: “For I will remove [variant: “also remove,” Par.],” he says, “from Judaea, among other things, the wise architect.”

Was not [variant reading: “not” (Non), al.] Paul himself then destined to be removed from Judaea—that is, from Judaism—for the building up of Christianity, since he would lay the one foundation, which is Christ? For concerning this foundation too the Creator says through the same prophet (Isa. XXVIII, 15): “Behold,” he says, “I lay in the foundations of Zion a precious and honorable stone, and whoever believes in it will not be confounded.”

Unless, indeed [si (“if”) omitted in Par.], God was professing himself an architect of an earthly work, [Col. 0484D] so that he was not signifying his own Christ, who was to become the foundation of those who believe in him. Upon that foundation, according as each person builds [Col. 0485A] a worthy or unworthy doctrine, if his work is tested by fire and if his reward is repaid to him through fire, that fire belongs to the Creator, because your superstructure is judged [variant: “indicated,” Par. Fran.] through fire—assuredly the superstructure raised upon [“upon” inserted in Rhen. Seml. Oberth.] his own foundation, that is, upon his own Christ.

> **Note [Col. 0485D].** “If his reward is repaid to him through fire.” Almost everyone explains this passage of the Apostle as referring to the fire of Purgatory; among them Francis Turrianus, S.J., discusses it most extensively in his *Defense of the Apostolic Canons*. —LE PR.

“Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” If man—his substance, workmanship, image, likeness, flesh through earth, and soul through the Creator’s breath—belongs to the Creator, then Marcion’s god dwells wholly [variant: “your,” Par. Fran.] in another’s property [variant: “Marcion,” Par. Fran.], if we are not the Creator’s temple [variant: “if we are the Creator’s temple,” Rhen. Seml. Oberth.].

“If anyone destroys God’s temple, he will be destroyed”—assuredly by the God of the temple. In holding out an avenger, he will be holding out [variant: “you will be holding out,” Rhen. Seml. Ober.] the Creator.

“Become fools, that you may be wise.” Why? “For the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God.” Before what God? Even if nothing in our preceding interpretations [variant: “up to this interpretation,” Par. Fran.] has decided this point beforehand, it is well that [Col. 0485B] here too he supports it: “For it is written, ‘He catches the wise in their wickedness.’” And again: “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile.”

For it will have been established by us as a general rule that he could not have used any saying belonging to the God whom he was bound to destroy, unless he were teaching on behalf of that God.

“Therefore,” he says, “let no one boast in man.” This too accords with the Creator’s discipline (Jer. XVII, 5): “Wretched is the man who places his hope in man”; and (Ps. CXVII): “It is good to trust in God rather than to trust in man” [variant: “men,” Rhen. Seml. Oberth.]. So too with boasting (1 Cor. IV, X).

# CHAPTER VII
And he himself will illuminate the hidden things of darkness—assuredly through Christ, since he promised Christ [Note: [Col. 0485D] “Christ” in the Venetian edition; “of Christ” in Wouwer’s codex] as an illumination (Isa. 42:6); he also declared himself to be the lamp [Col. 0485C] that searches hearts and reins (Ps. 7:10). From him, too, will come praise for each person, since from him, as judge, comes praise’s opposite as well.

“Surely,” you say [Note: [Col. 0486D] “he says” in another edition], “here at least he interprets ‘the god of this world’ as the god of the world when he says: ‘We have been made a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings.’ For if by ‘world’ he had meant the human beings of the world, he would not subsequently also have named human beings.” On the contrary: precisely so that you would not argue in this way, the providence of the Holy Spirit demonstrated what he had meant [Note: [Col. 0486D] “how he had spoken” in Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür] by “We have been made a spectacle to the world”: namely, to the angels who minister to the world and to the human beings to whom they minister. Evidently a man of such constancy—not to mention the Holy Spirit—was afraid to name the God of the world openly, especially when writing to the children whom he had begotten in the Gospel, although he could not be seen to preach against him unless he did so explicitly!

[Col. 0485D] I do not maintain that it was according to the Creator’s law that [Col. 0486A] the man who had his father’s wife was found displeasing; the discipline followed may have been that of common and public religion. But when Paul condemns him to be handed over to Satan, he is the herald of the condemning God. Let him see also how Paul said, “for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord,” since he passed judgment both on the destruction of the flesh and on the salvation of the spirit; and, in ordering evil to be removed from their midst, he recalled a most frequently repeated sentence of the Creator.

“Purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new batch of dough, as you are unleavened.” The unleavened loaves, then, were figures of us in the Creator’s dispensation. So too, “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.” Why is Christ the Passover, unless the Passover was a figure of Christ through the likeness of the saving blood and of Christ as the sacrificial animal? Why does he clothe us and Christ with images drawn from the Creator’s solemn rites [Note: [Col. 0486D] “imbues” in Rhenanus and the Venetian edition], if those images were not ours?

Moreover, in turning us away [Col. 0486B] from fornication, he makes manifest the resurrection of the flesh. “The body,” he says, “is not for fornication, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body”—as a temple is for God, and God for the temple. Will the temple, then, perish for God, and God for the temple? Yet you see: “He who raised the Lord will also raise us”; he will raise us in the body as well, because the body is for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. And it is well that he adds: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” What will the heretic say? That the members of Christ will not rise, because they are no longer ours?

[Note: [Col. 0485D] “For we were bought at a great price.” [Col. 0486D] To prove against Marcion that Christ assumed true flesh, he says that we were redeemed either at a great price or at no price: at no price, if he was merely a phantom; at a great price, if he bore our sins in his own body. LE PR.]

“For we were bought at a great price” [Note: [Col. 0486D] “at a price” omitted by Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür]. Indeed, at no price at all if Christ was a phantom and possessed no bodily substance that he could pay out for our bodies. Therefore [Note: [Col. 0486D] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür add “and”] Christ possessed something with which to redeem us; and if at some great price he redeemed these bodies, in which that same fornication must not be committed [Note: [Col. 0486D] “admitted,” Ciacconius], [Col. 0486C] since they are now Christ’s members rather than ours, he will surely preserve for himself what he purchased at great cost. How, then, shall we now honor God? How shall we bear God in a body destined to perish?

Next comes the dispute concerning marriage, which Marcion prohibits more uncompromisingly than the Apostle. For although the Apostle prefers the good of continence, he nevertheless permits marriage both to be contracted and to be exercised, and advises that it should be preserved rather than dissolved. Christ, to be sure, forbids divorce (Matt. 5 and 19), whereas Moses permits it. Marcion, by entirely removing sexual intercourse from believers—for his catechumens may look to themselves—and ordering the repudiation of a woman married previously [Note: [Col. 0486D] “marriage,” Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür; “those married,” Junius], follows whose judgment, Moses’ or Christ’s? Yet Christ’s Apostle also, when he commands a woman not to leave her husband, or, if she has left, to remain unmarried or be reconciled [Col. 0486D] to her husband, both permits divorce, since he did not prohibit it altogether, [Col. 0487A] and confirms marriage, since he first forbade its dissolution and, if it should happen to have been dissolved, wished it to be restored.

But what causes does he give for continence? “Because the time has been shortened.” I had supposed it was because there is another God in Christ! And yet from the one from whom the shortening of time comes will also come whatever accords with that shortening of time. No one makes provision for another’s time. You affirm your God to be a very little God, Marcion, since the Creator’s time constrains him in some respect.

Certainly, in laying down the rule that one must marry “only in the Lord,” lest any believer contract marriage with a pagan, he upholds the Creator’s law, which everywhere prohibits marriages with foreigners. “But even if there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth,” it is evident how he said this: not as though those who are so called truly exist [Note: [Col. 0487D] “because,” another reading; Semler adds “but because they exist”; François reads “but because it exists”], when in fact they do not. For he began with idols, intending to discuss things sacrificed to idols: [Col. 0487B] “We know that an idol is nothing.” Yet even Marcion does not deny that the Creator is God. Therefore the Apostle cannot be thought to have placed the Creator among those who are called gods and yet do not exist, since, even if they did exist, nevertheless for us there would be “one God, the Father, from whom are all things” [Note: [Col. 0487D] “from whom are all things” is read by Semler in the Venetian edition].

“From whom are all things” for us—unless he is the one to whom all things belong? What are these “all things”? You have them in what precedes: “All things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come.” Thus he makes the Creator God of all things, since from him come the world, life, and death, which cannot belong to another god. Therefore Christ too, among all things, comes from him.

In teaching that everyone ought to live by his own labor [Note: [Col. 0487D] “Teaching everyone to live by his own labor.” Here, by various examples, he proves that everyone ought to procure his livelihood by his own labor. Thus the blessed Apostle once said that his hands had supplied the things he needed. Those who serve the Gospel ought to live from it. LE PR.], he had offered enough preliminary examples from soldiers, shepherds, and farmers; but he lacked divine authority. He therefore [Col. 0487C] sets against the ungrateful [Note: [Col. 0488D] “gratuitously,” Junius] the Creator’s law—the law he was supposedly destroying—for his own god had no such law. “You shall not muzzle,” he says, “an ox while it is threshing”; and he adds: “Does the Lord have concern for oxen?” Is he even [Note: [Col. 0488D] “concerning,” Pamelius] kindly to oxen for the sake of human beings? “For it was written for our sake,” he says. He thus proved both that the law is allegorical in accordance with our interpretation and that it supports those who live from the Gospel; and for this reason he proved that the evangelists belong to no other god than the one whose law provided for them when it said, “For it was written for our sake” [Note: [Col. 0488D] “for” omitted by François]. But he did not wish to use the law’s authority, because he preferred to labor without payment. He referred this to his own glory, which he said no one would nullify, not to the destruction of the law, whose provision he proved another would use.

But look: blind Marcion also stumbles against the rock from which our fathers [Col. 0487D] drank in the wilderness. For if that rock was Christ, it was surely the Creator’s Christ, since the people too belonged to the Creator. As a figure of what [Note: [Col. 0488D] “A figure of an alien sacrament.” This may be explained as “a figure of him who is alien to the sacrament.” For *extraneus* is customarily construed with the genitive, as above in *Against Marcion*, book II: “Who is alien to evil, unless he is also its enemy?” RHEN.] alien sacrament does he interpret it? Or was it so that he might teach this very thing: that the ancient events were figurative of Christ, who must therefore be reckoned as belonging to them?

[Col. 0488A] For when he is about to recount the remainder of the people’s fate, he premises: “These things were made examples for us.” Tell me: were examples for human beings belonging to another, hitherto unknown god made by the Creator? Or does one god borrow examples from another—and indeed from a rival? Does he terrify me on his own behalf by means of the one from whom he transfers my faith? Will his adversary make me better for him? Now, if I commit the same sins as the people, am I to suffer the same things, or not? If not the same, then in vain he sets before me as objects of fear things that I shall not suffer. But from whom shall I suffer what I am to suffer? If from the Creator, of what kind are the punishments that it belongs to him to inflict? And how will it make sense that a jealous God should punish his rival’s sinner rather than, conversely, cherish him? If from that other god—yet he does not know how to punish. Thus this entire proposition of the Apostle stands on no rational basis unless it belongs to the Creator’s discipline.

Finally, [Col. 0488B] in his conclusion he corresponds to his preface: “But these things, just as they happened to them, were written to admonish us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.” O Creator, already both foreknowing and admonishing Christians who belong to another god!

I pass over some matters when they are parallel to those already discussed, and sometimes dispose of them briefly. A great argument for another god, indeed: the permission of every kind of food, contrary to the law—as if we ourselves did not also confess that the law’s burdens have been remitted, but remitted by the one who imposed them and promised renewal. Thus he who took foods away also restored them, as he had granted them from the beginning. Besides, if some other god had been the destroyer of our God, there would have been nothing he would have prohibited his own people more strongly than living from his adversary’s resources. (2 Cor. 11:14.)

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0488C] “The head of the man is Christ.” Which Christ—the one who is not the man’s author? For “head” is used to denote authority, and authority will belong to none other than the author. Of what man, then, is he the head? Surely of the man about whom he adds: “For the man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image of God.” Therefore, if he is the image of the Creator—for it was the Creator who, looking upon Christ, his Word, as the man who was to come, said, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness”—how can I have as my head someone other than the one whose image I am? Since I am the image of the Creator, there is no place in me for another head.

But why must a woman have authority over her head? If it is because she was made from the man and for the man according to the Creator’s institution, then here too the Apostle upheld his discipline, since he explains the grounds of that discipline from the Creator’s institution.

[Col. 0488D] He also adds, “because of the angels.” Which angels—that is, whose? If the Creator’s apostate angels, reasonably so: that the face which caused them to stumble should bear a certain mark in the guise of humility and in the concealment of its beauty. But [Col. 0489A] if because of the angels of the other god, what does she fear, if even the Marcionites themselves do not lust after women?

We have already frequently shown that heresies are placed by the Apostle among evils as an evil, and that those “approved” are to be understood as those who avoid heresies as an evil. Likewise, with regard to the sacrament of the bread and the cup, we have already proved in the Gospel (Luke 22) the reality of the Lord’s body and blood [Note: [Col. 0489D] “We have proved the reality of the Lord’s body and blood.” Namely in the preceding book; this was done against Marcion’s perverse opinion that Christ’s flesh was phantasmal. LE PR.], against Marcion’s phantom. And that every mention of judgment properly belongs to the Creator, as the judging God, has been treated throughout almost the whole work.

I now speak of spiritual gifts: these too were promised with reference to Christ by the Creator, under that most just preliminary rule, as I judge it, according to which the fulfillment should be believed to belong to none other than the one whose promise has been proved. Isaiah declared (Isa. 11:1): “A rod will go forth from the root of Jesse” [Note: [Col. 0489D] Pamelius adds “from the rod”], “and a flower will rise from the root; [Col. 0489B] the Spirit of the Lord will rest upon him.” He then enumerates its forms: “the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, and the spirit of knowledge and religion; the spirit of the fear of God will fill him.”

For under the figure of the flower he showed that Christ would arise from a rod sprung from the root of Jesse—that is, from a virgin of the lineage of David, son of Jesse—and that in this Christ the whole substance of the Spirit would abide. This was not as though it would subsequently come upon him, since he had always been the Spirit of God, even before the flesh; lest from this you argue that the prophecy pertains to that Christ who, merely as a man descended solely from the stock of David, would afterward obtain the spirit of his god. Rather, from the time when he flowered in flesh taken from the line of David, the whole operation of spiritual grace was to rest upon him, and was to cease and come to an end as regards [Col. 0489C] the Jews. The event itself bears witness to this, since from that time nothing of the Creator’s Spirit has breathed among them, after the wise and prudent master-builder, counselor, and prophet was taken away from Judaea (Isa. 3:2); so that this is the meaning of “The Law and the Prophets were until John” (Luke 16:16).

Now learn how he also declared that the gifts would come after Christ had been received into heaven: “He ascended on high,” that is, into heaven; “he led captivity captive,” that is, death or human servitude; “he gave gifts” [Note: [Col. 0489D] “he gave things given,” Pamelius] “to the sons of men,” that is, the free gifts that we call *charismata*. With elegance he said “to the sons of men,” not indiscriminately “to men,” thereby showing us to be sons of men—that is, truly men—the sons, namely, of the Apostles. “For in the Gospel,” he says, “I begot you.” And (Gal. 4:19): “My children, whom I am again bringing to birth.”

There is also that promise of the Spirit made without qualification [Col. 0489D] through Joel (Joel 2): “In the last days [Note: [Col. 0489D] ‘times,’ Semler] I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and their sons and daughters will prophesy; and upon my male and female servants I will pour out of my Spirit.” And assuredly, if the Creator promised the grace of the Spirit for [Col. 0490A] the last days, while Christ, the dispenser of spiritual gifts, appeared in the last days—as the Apostle says (Gal. 4:4), “But when the time was fulfilled, God sent his Son,” and again (1 Cor. 7:29), “Because the time has now been shortened”—it is evident from the preaching concerning the final times that this grace of the Spirit belongs to the Christ of the preacher who foretold it.

Compare, then, the Apostle’s several kinds with Isaiah’s (Isa. 11). “To one,” he says, “is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom”; Isaiah immediately likewise placed the spirit of wisdom. “To another, a word of knowledge”: this will be the word of understanding and counsel. “To another, faith in the same Spirit”: this will be the spirit of religion and the fear of God. “To another, the gift of healings; to another, of mighty works”: this will be the spirit of might. “To another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, interpretation [Col. 0490B] of tongues”: this will be the spirit of knowledge. You see the Apostle agreeing with the Prophet both in making the distribution of the one Spirit and in explaining spirituality [Note: [Col. 0489D] “speciality,” Venetian edition].

I can say that the very man who likened the unity of various *charismata*, through the many and diverse members of our body, to an articulated whole is thereby shown to acknowledge the same Lord of both the human body and the Holy Spirit. He did not will that any rank [Note: [Col. 0489D] “ranks,” Rhenanus] of the *charismata* should exist in the body of the Spirit which he had not also assigned in the human body. He also instructed the Apostle concerning love, which must be preferred to all *charismata*, by that chief commandment which Christ too approved: “You shall love the Lord with all your heart, and all your strength, and all your soul, and your neighbor [Note: [Col. 0490D] “your neighbor,” François] as yourself” [Note: [Col. 0490D] “self” omitted by Oberthür].

And although it was written in the law, he recalls that the Creator would speak “in other tongues and with other lips”; by this recollection he confirms the gift of tongues, and here too he cannot be thought to have confirmed an alien gift by the Creator’s proclamation.

Likewise, in prescribing silence for women in the church, so that they should not speak, at least for the purpose of learning [Note: [Col. 0490D] “teaching,” Rhenanus; “speaking,” Pamelius] [Note: [Col. 0490D] “glory,” Semler], while elsewhere he has already shown that they too possess the right of prophesying, since he imposes a veil even on a woman who prophesies, he takes from the law his authority for a woman’s subjection—a law which, as I have said once for all, he should not have acknowledged except for the purpose of destroying it.

But now, so that we may leave spiritual gifts behind, the facts themselves will have to prove which of us rashly claims them for his own God, and whether [Note: [Col. 0490D] “because,” Paris and François; “from,” Rhenanus] the following objection can be made against our side: that although the Creator promised these things for his own Christ, who has not yet been revealed, as destined for the Jews alone, they will have [Col. 0490D] their operations in their own time, in their own Christ, and among their own people.

[Note: [Col. 0490D] Let Marcion, then, produce the gifts of his god. Let him bring forward his own prophecies concerning his god, provided that those prophets were moved by the Spirit of God; then I will certainly obey them. LE PR.]

Let Marcion, then, produce the gifts of his god: some prophets who spoke not from human understanding but from the Spirit of God, who both foretold future events [Col. 0491A] and exposed the secrets of the heart. Let him publish some psalm, some vision, some prayer—provided it is spiritual, in ecstasy, that is, in madness—if an interpretation of tongues has accompanied it. Let him prove to me that even [Note: [Col. 0491D] “even to me,” Pamelius] a woman among his own people has prophesied—one, namely, of those more holy women of his, a woman who speaks great things [Note: [Col. 0491D] “I shall regard as great,” Venetian edition].

[Note: [Col. 0491D] “One of those more holy women of his.” Perhaps he indicates Maximilla, a follower of Montanus; although I would not rashly deny that he is here censuring many women, such as Helena of Simon Magus, Philumena of Apelles, Marcellina of Carpocrates, and that woman of Marcion himself whom he had sent to Rome to prepare a house for him. LE PR.]

If all these things are more readily produced by me, and if they assuredly agree with the Creator’s rules, arrangements, and disciplines, then without doubt both Christ, the Spirit, and the Apostle belong to my God. Whoever wishes to demand it has my declaration.

## CHAPTER IX

Meanwhile the Marcionite will produce nothing of this kind [Note: [Col. 0491D] “of such a kind,” Venetian edition] (1 Cor. 15), since he is afraid even now [Note: [Col. 0491D] “even,” Latin edition] to declare whose Christ has the better claim still not to have been revealed [Note: [Col. 0491D] “whose, exactly,” Latin edition]. Just as mine is to be awaited because he was proclaimed from the beginning, so his is not to be awaited precisely because he was not from the beginning. We do better not to believe in a Christ still to come than the heretic does to believe in none at all.

[Note: [Col. 0491D] How some at that time denied the resurrection of the dead. He means the Sadducees, whom we discussed at sufficient length above. LE PR.]

We must first examine how some people at that time denied the resurrection of the dead. Assuredly, they did so in the same way as people do now, since it is always the resurrection of the flesh that is denied. Many of the philosophers, however, claiming that the soul is divine, promise its preservation; and the common people themselves honor the departed on the assumption that their souls continue to exist. Bodies, on the other hand, whether immediately consumed by fire or by beasts, or even buried with the greatest care, plainly are nevertheless destroyed by time. If, therefore, the Apostle refutes those who deny the resurrection of the flesh, he certainly maintains against them the very thing they denied: namely, the resurrection of the flesh. [Col. 0491C] There you have the answer in brief. What follows is now added for completeness.

For the very expression “resurrection of the dead” requires us to defend the proper meanings of the words. Nothing is “dead” [Note: [Col. 0491D] “of the dead,” Paris; Semler accordingly omits “by the word”] in the proper sense of the word except that which has lost the soul by whose power it lived. It is the body that loses the soul and, by losing it, becomes dead; thus the term “dead” properly applies to the body. Further, if resurrection is the resurrection of the dead, and the dead is nothing other than the body, the resurrection will be that of the body.

Likewise, the term *resurrection* claims for itself no other thing than that which has fallen. For something that has never fallen at all but has always lain there may be said to rise; but to rise again belongs only to something that has fallen. Because it rises again after having fallen, it is said to “re-surge.” For the syllable *re-* is always used to denote repetition. We therefore say that the body falls into the earth through death, as the fact itself also bears witness, according to God’s law; for it was said to the body (Gen. 3:19): “Earth you are, and into the earth you will go.” Thus what comes from the earth will go into the earth. It is this that departs, which will go into the earth [Note: [Col. 0492D] “What goes into the earth falls; it departs,” Ciacconius]; it is this that rises again, which falls.

“Because through a man came death, and through a man resurrection.” Here Christ’s body is shown to me in the name “man,” for a man consists of a body, as we have already often taught. And if “in Christ we are all made alive” just as we are put to death in Adam, then, since [Note: [Col. 0492D] “in what manner,” Latin edition] we are put to death bodily in Adam, it is necessary that we likewise be made alive bodily in Christ. Otherwise [Col. 0492B] the parallel does not hold, unless the being-made-alive in Christ corresponds in the same substance to the being-put-to-death in Adam.

But he has inserted something further concerning Christ, which must not be omitted because of the present dispute. For the resurrection of the flesh will be proved all the more strongly, the more I show that Christ belongs to the God with whom the resurrection of the flesh is an article of belief. When he says, “For he must reign until he puts his enemies beneath his feet,” he thereby already proclaims a God who avenges, and consequently the very God who promised this to Christ (Ps. 109): “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet”; “The Lord will send forth the rod of your power from Zion, and he will rule” [Note: [Col. 0492D] “you will rule,” François; “and rule,” another reading] “in the midst of your enemies”; “with you,” and the rest [Note: [Col. 0492D] “and the rest” omitted by Semler].

But it is necessary for me to defend as belonging to my position [Col. 0492C] those Scriptures which [Note: [Col. 0491D] The Jews endeavor to wrest from us—namely, the rabbis, who, to defend their obstinacy, endeavor to snatch that passage from our hands, explaining “he will rule in the midst of your enemies” as referring to Hezekiah. LE PR.] the Jews also endeavor to wrest from us. They say, indeed, that this Psalm (Ps. 109) was sung concerning Hezekiah, because he sat at the right hand of the Temple and God turned away and destroyed his enemies (2 Kings 19). Consequently, they say that “Before the morning star, from the womb I begot you” also applies to Hezekiah [Note: [Col. 0492D] “And to Hezekiah’s birth.” The blessed Epiphanius rightly refutes this against the Ebionites, *Heresy* 30, proving from Scripture that Hezekiah had been born eleven years before Isaiah foretold, in chapter 7, “Behold, a virgin will conceive.” It was enough for the blessed Justin to say that Hezekiah was not born from a virgin. PAM.], and to [Note: [Col. 0492D] “before,” Pithou’s codex] Hezekiah’s birth.

[Note: [Col. 0492D] “We publish the Gospels,” etc. Here he declares that Marcion rejected both the first three chapters of Luke’s Gospel and the whole Gospel of Matthew, since Tertullian wishes to adduce evidence from Luke 2 and Matthew 4, which the blessed Justin likewise cites a little earlier. PAM.]

We set forth the Gospels, concerning whose credibility we surely ought by now, in so extensive a work, [Note: [Col. 0492D] “In so extensive a work we ought to have confirmed them.” “Them” means, of course, the Jews. RIG.] to have convinced these men; they declare that the Lord’s birth occurred at night. Thus “before the morning star” is fulfilled both by the star through which he was made known to the Magi and by the angel’s testimony, for the angel announced to the shepherds at night that Christ had just then been born; and also by the place of birth, since people arrive at an inn for the night. Perhaps it was also mystically arranged that Christ should be born at night, since he was to be the light of truth amid the darkness of ignorance.

Nor would God have said, “I begot you,” unless he spoke to a child who was his son [Note: [Col. 0493C] “true,” Ciacconius, approved by Junius]. For even though he says of the whole people (Isa. 1), “I begot sons,” he did not add, “from the womb.” Why, moreover, did he add “from the womb”—so pointlessly, as though anyone could doubt that a human being was born from a womb—unless he wished it to be understood with more precise attention as referring to Christ: “From the womb I begot you,” that is, from the womb alone, without a man’s seed, [Note: [Col. 0493C] “Assigning the flesh from the womb to the Spirit.” In that Psalm the Holy Spirit applied the words “from the womb” to signify the flesh. RIG.] the Spirit assigning the flesh from the womb?

This too follows here [Note: [Col. 0493C] “This follows from the passage itself,” Oberthür]: “You are a priest forever.” Yet Hezekiah was neither a priest nor, even if he had been one, a priest forever. “According to the order,” he says, “of Melchizedek.” What has [Col. 0493B] Hezekiah to do with Melchizedek, priest of the Most High, and indeed uncircumcised, who blessed the already circumcised Abraham after receiving from him the offering of tithes?

But the order of Melchizedek will apply to Christ, since Christ is the proper and lawful high priest of God, the chief priest of the uncircumcised priesthood, then established among the nations, by whom he was to be received more readily. When at last he comes, he will deem the circumcision, and the race of Abraham which will one day acknowledge him, worthy of acceptance and blessing [Note: [Col. 0493C] Semler adds “and”].

There is also another Psalm (Ps. 71), beginning thus: “O God, give your judgment to the king,” that is, to Christ who is to reign; “and your righteousness to the king’s son,” that is, to the people of Christ. For those who are reborn in him are his sons. But [Note: [Col. 0494C] “thus inserted,” Latin edition, Semler, and Oberthür] this Psalm too will be said to have been sung for Solomon. Yet could not those details which apply to Christ alone teach [Col. 0493C] that all the other details too pertain not to Solomon but to Christ?

“He will descend,” it says, “like rain upon a fleece, and like drops dripping upon the earth,” describing his gentle and imperceptible descent [Col. 0494A] from heaven into the flesh. But even if Solomon descended from somewhere, he did not descend like rain, because he did not descend from heaven. I shall, however, present the more straightforward statements. “He will rule,” it says, “from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth.” This was given to Christ alone. Solomon, by contrast, ruled over the single and small territory of Judaea. “All kings will worship him”—whom would they all worship, if not Christ? “And all nations will serve him”—whom would they all serve, if not Christ? “His name will endure forever”—whose name is eternal, if not Christ’s? “His name will remain before the sun,” for before the sun was the Word of God, that is, Christ. “And all nations will be blessed in him”; no nation is blessed in Solomon, but every nation is blessed in Christ.

What if this Psalm now also demonstrates that he is God [Note: [Col. 0494C] “my God,” Rhenanus with the Venetian edition]? “And they will call him blessed, because blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who alone performs wonders. Blessed is the name of his glory, and the whole earth will be filled with his glory.” By contrast, Solomon—I dare say it—even lost the glory he had possessed in God, after being drawn by a woman all the way into idolatry.

Accordingly, since this statement too is placed in the middle of the Psalm, “His enemies will lick the dust,” being of course subjected beneath his feet, it pertains to the point on account of which I both introduced this Psalm and defended it as belonging to my position. Thus I have confirmed that the one who will obtain [Note: [Col. 0494C] “the one who is to obtain,” Pamelius] both the glory of the kingdom and the subjection of his enemies, according to the Creator’s arrangement, must be believed to be none other than the Creator’s Christ.

## CHAPTER X

Let us now return to the resurrection. Elsewhere, indeed, in a volume devoted to the subject [Note: [Col. 0493C] “In a volume devoted to the subject.” This is the book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*. SEML.], we have given a sufficient account of it in opposition to all the heretics; but neither shall we neglect it here, for the sake [Col. 0494C] of those who do not know that little work.

“What,” he says, “will those do [Note: [Col. 0493C] “Who are baptized for the dead.” I know that some explain this not of the baptism of a living person on behalf of a dead person, but of the cleansing of the body from the defilements it has contracted through contact with a corpse. LE PR.] who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise?” (1 Cor. 15).

[Note: [Col. 0493D] Let that institution answer for itself. Perhaps the Kalends of February will correspond to it: “they would make petitions for the dead.” This is the reading of Ursinus’s copy. Yet I do not believe that Tertullian’s text was of this form. For to the Apostle’s question, “What will those do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise?” it would have been an absurd response: “The Kalends of February would make petitions for the dead.” That institution which Septimius believed to have existed among certain people in the age of the Apostles—being baptized for the dead—would not thereby be assisted in any way. Indeed, the Apostle’s question presupposes that the dead do not rise. And so, to one saying that the dead do not rise, who would have responded so foolishly that the Kalends of February would make petitions for the dead? For dead people who do not rise, the February rites (*februa*) would have been as absurd and useless as baptism.

Let us therefore see what Septimius meant. He cites the Apostle’s words: “What will those do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise?” He thinks these words signify that it had then been instituted among certain people that they should be baptized on behalf of the dead. He then says: “Let that institution answer for itself, whether it rests upon any rational basis.” And immediately he compares with it a pagan custom: “The Kalends of February,” he says, “correspond to it and may be compared with it: making petitions for the dead”—*τῷ εὔχεσθαι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν*, “with praying on behalf of the dead”—that is, with that rite or institution, namely being baptized or making petitions on behalf of the dead. For the *februa* too are celebrated for beloved dead relatives; hence the name given to the month of February and to the Kalends of February. Ovid:

> The month of February has its vows for the god Dis.

Likewise:

> After the worship of the gods above, in the neighboring month of February,  
> Numa gives funeral offerings to the ancestral spirits of his kin.

The manuscript of Dijon preserved this reading, “they will answer: making petitions for the dead”; so too did the manuscripts used by Rhenanus. RIG.]

Let that institution answer for itself. Perhaps the Kalends of February will correspond to it: [Note: [Col. 0494D] “Making petitions for the dead.” “Making petitions for the dead” appears to me to be the same as “requesting *februa*,” concerning which Ovid says in *Fasti*, book II:

> I myself saw the flamen’s wife requesting *februa*,
Source/review notes: The source phrase “non substantium capere regnum Dei” is grammatically corrupt; the draft should mark rather than resolve this inherited uncertainty.

A pine branch was given to one asking for the *februa*. That is, to request the sacred *februa*, or expiation, on behalf of the dead, whether because of a killing or because funeral rites had been omitted. LE PR.] to petition on behalf of the dead [Col. 0495A] [Note: [Col. 0495D] “They should petition,” Wouw.]. Do not, therefore, immediately identify the Apostle as the new author or confirmer of that practice, on the grounds that he would thereby establish the resurrection of the flesh all the more firmly, since those who were vainly baptized on behalf of the dead did this from faith in the resurrection. Elsewhere (Eph. IV.5) we have him defining one baptism [Note: [Col. 0495D] “Defining,” another reading.]. Therefore, to be immersed on behalf of the dead is to be immersed on behalf of bodies, for we have shown that it is the body that is dead. What will those do who are baptized on behalf of bodies, if bodies do not rise? And so rightly do we establish this stage of the argument, since the Apostle likewise introduced the second discussion concerning the body.

But some will say: “How will the dead rise? And with what body will they come?” For once the resurrection that was denied had been defended, it followed that the quality of the body—which was not apparent—should be reconsidered. But on that matter it is appropriate to engage with others [Col. 0495B]. Marcion, however, since he does not admit the resurrection of the flesh at all and promises salvation to the soul alone, raises a question not of quality but of substance. Moreover, this is most clearly refuted by what the Apostle discusses concerning the quality of the body because of those who say, “How will the dead rise? And with what body will they come?” (for he has already proclaimed that the body will rise) [Note: [Col. 0495D] Pam. inserts this; Ciaccon. reads “therefore”]: the discussion concerns the quality of the body.

Finally, if he sets forth examples of a grain of wheat, or of some such thing, or of things to which God gives a body as he wills; if he says that each kind of seed has its own body, and [Note: [Col. 0496D] “As,” Seml.] that the flesh of human beings is one kind, that of cattle and birds another; and that there are celestial and terrestrial bodies; and that the glory of the sun is one, that of the moon another, and that of the stars another—does he not indicate a fleshly and bodily [Col. 0495C] resurrection, which he commends by fleshly and bodily examples? Does he not also guarantee it from that God from whom the examples themselves come?

“So also,” he says, “is the resurrection.” How so? Just as a grain is sown as a body, so it rises as a body. Indeed, he called the dissolution of the body into the earth a sowing, because it is sown in corruption and rises in honor and power. The order that belongs to it in dissolution belongs to it here also in the resurrection of the body, namely, as with the grain. But if you remove from the resurrection the body that you granted to dissolution, wherein will the difference of outcomes consist?

Likewise, although it is sown an animate body, it rises a spiritual body. And even if the soul or the spirit possesses some body of its own, so that “animate body” could be understood as signifying the soul, and “spiritual body” the spirit, he does not therefore say that in the resurrection the soul [Col. 0495D] will become [Note: [Col. 0496D] “Will become,” feminine form, Ober.] spirit, but that the body—which, by being born together with the soul and living through the soul, begins to be called animate—will become spiritual when it rises through the Spirit into eternity. Finally, if it is not the soul but the flesh that is sown in corruption when it is dissolved into the earth, then the “animate body” will not be the soul but the flesh, which was the animate body. For from animate it becomes spiritual, just as he also [Col. 0496A] says below: “The spiritual is not first.”

To this end he also lays the groundwork from Christ himself: “The first man Adam was made into a living soul; the last Adam into a life-giving spirit,” [Note: [Col. 0495D] “Although the most foolish heretic.” This is Marcion, who is celebrated here with this encomium, just as in St. Jerome Vigilantius, Jovinian, and others are painted in their true colors [Col. 0496D] when they are adorned with such titles. LE PR.] although the most foolish heretic refused to let the text stand thus. For he substituted “the last Lord” for “the last Adam”—evidently fearing that, if he had “the Lord” as the last Adam also, we would maintain that Christ in the last Adam belonged to the same one to whom the first Adam belonged. But the falsification shines through. For why “the first Adam,” unless there is also a “last Adam”? Nothing stands in an order with something else unless the items are corresponding, and belong to the same name, substance, or author. For although among different things one may be first and another last, they must nevertheless belong to one author. But if the author too is different, the thing may indeed itself be called “last”; yet that which the other author introduced [Col. 0496B] is “first,” whereas it is “last” only if it corresponds to the first. But it does not correspond to the first, because it does not belong to the same author.

In the same manner he will also be refuted by the human being’s humanity. “The first man,” he says, “is from the earth, earthly; the second, the Lord from heaven.” Why “second,” if he is not a man, as the first was? Or was the first perhaps also “Lord,” if the second is? But it is enough that the Gospel presents Christ as Son of Man and as man; and under the name Adam the heretic will be unable to deny him. What follows also presses him hard. For when the Apostle says, “As is the one from the earth”—that is, the man—“such also are the earthly”—human beings, of course—then also, “As is the one from heaven”—a man—“such also are those from heaven”—human beings. For he could not have opposed heavenly non-human beings to earthly human beings, if he wished more carefully to distinguish their condition and hope while retaining a common designation. [Col. 0496C] He calls human beings earthly and heavenly with respect to condition and hope, yet on a corresponding basis: they are assigned, according to their final outcome, either to Adam or to Christ.

And therefore he now turns to an exhortation toward heavenly hope: “Just as we have borne,” he says, “the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly.” He is not referring this to any substance of the resurrection, but to the discipline of the present time. For he says, “Let us bear,” not “We shall bear”: by way of command, not promise. He wishes us to walk as he himself walked, and to depart from the image of the earthly—that is, of the old man—which is fleshly conduct.

Finally, what does he add? “For this I say, brothers: flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God”—namely, the works of flesh and blood, from which, when writing also to the Galatians (Gal. V.19–21), he excluded the kingdom of God. Elsewhere too he is accustomed to put the substance for the works of the substance, as when he says, “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.” For when will we be able to please God, unless while we are in this flesh? There is, I think, no other time for action. But if, though established in the flesh, we flee the works of the flesh, [Note: [Col. 0496D] “Then we shall not be in the flesh.” If throughout the course of this life we avoid the works of the flesh, or sins, we shall not [Col. 0497D] therefore be said to have been “in the flesh.” For it is not the substance of the flesh that is denied the kingdom of God, but sin. LE PR.] then we shall not be “in the flesh,” although we are not outside the substance of flesh, but are outside [Col. 0497A] its guilt.

But if, under the name “flesh,” we are instructed to interpret the works and not the substance of the flesh, then it is to the works of the flesh, not the substance of the flesh, that the kingdom of God is denied under the name of flesh [Note: [Col. 0497D] “Flesh” omitted here by Seml.]. For that in which an evil deed is done is not condemned, but the deed that is done. To administer poison is a crime; yet the cup in which it is administered is not guilty. So too the body is the vessel of fleshly works, but the soul is what mixes in it the poison of some evil deed.

How [Note: [Col. 0497D] Obert. adds “is it.”] can it be that, if the soul, as author of the works of the flesh, will merit the kingdom of God [Note: [Col. 0497D] through expiation of the things it committed in the body—these words may, not unreasonably, be understood of a purification undergone after death, indeed an exact and diligent one. LE PR.], through expiation of the things it committed in the body, the body, which was merely its servant, should remain under condemnation? Once the poisoner has been acquitted, will the cup be punished?

And yet we are not, of course, claiming the kingdom of God for the flesh, but the resurrection of its substance, as a kind of doorway through which the kingdom is entered. Resurrection is one thing; the kingdom another. First comes the resurrection, and then the kingdom. We therefore say that the flesh rises, but that it attains the kingdom after being changed. “For the dead will rise incorrupt”—namely, those who had been corrupted when their bodies fell apart into destruction. “And we shall be changed, in an atom, in the momentary movement of an eye. For this corruptible thing”—the Apostle was, of course, speaking while holding his own flesh—“must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing immortality,” so that the substance may indeed be made fit for the kingdom of God. For we shall be like the angels. This will be the transformation of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0497D] Seml. adds “but.”] after it has been raised. Or, if there will be none, how will it put on incorruption and immortality?

Therefore, when it has become something other through transformation, it will then attain the kingdom of God: no longer flesh and blood, but whatever body God shall have given it. And therefore the Apostle rightly says, “Flesh [Col. 0497C] and blood shall not attain the kingdom of God,” assigning this to the transformation that follows upon the resurrection.

But if at that time the saying written in the Creator’s scriptures will come to pass—“Where, O death, is your victory,” or [Note: [Col. 0497D] “Where,” another reading.] “your contest? Where, O death, is your sting?”—and this saying belongs to the Creator, spoken through the prophet, then the reality too, that is, the kingdom in which the saying will come to pass, will belong to him whose saying it is. Nor does he give thanks to any other God for having granted us the winning of victory—victory, of course, over death—than to him from whom he received the word that taunts and triumphs over death (II Cor. I, III, and IV).

## CHAPTER XI

If “God” has become a common designation through the fault of human error, insofar as many gods are said and believed to exist in the world, nevertheless “the blessed God and Father of our Lord [Col. 0497D] Jesus Christ” will be understood as none other than the Creator, who both blessed all things—you have Genesis [Col. 0498A] (Gen. I)—and is blessed by all things—you have Daniel (Dan. III).

Likewise, if “Father” can be said without qualification, it can be applied to no God more fittingly than to the Creator; nevertheless the same one will be “the Father of mercies,” who is called merciful, compassionate, and most abundant in mercy. You have this in Jonah (Jon. III–IV), together with the very example of the mercy that he bestowed upon the Ninevites when they entreated him; he was readily moved by Hezekiah’s tears (IV Kings XX), forgave the blood of Naboth when Ahab, Jezebel’s husband, entreated him (III Kings XXI), and immediately pardoned David when he acknowledged his offense (II Kings XII), evidently preferring the sinner’s repentance to his death, from the disposition of mercy, of course (Hos. VI). If Marcion’s God has produced or proclaimed anything of this kind, I shall acknowledge him as the Father of mercies.

But if Marcion ascribes this title to him from the time when he was revealed, as though he became Father of mercies from the time when he undertook to liberate the human race, we, on the contrary, deny him from the very time at which he is said to have been revealed. He cannot, therefore, ascribe anything to one whom he reveals only at the moment when he ascribes something else [Note: [Col. 0498D] “Something,” Pam.] to him. For if it had first been established that he existed, something could then be ascribed to him. What is ascribed is an accident; but accidents are preceded by the manifestation of the thing itself to which they happen. This is especially so when that which is ascribed already belongs to another: the one who has not previously been revealed will be denied to exist all the more strongly, since the very attribute by which his existence is affirmed belongs to one who has already been revealed.

Thus the New Testament also will belong to none other than the one who promised it beforehand; even if not its letter, at least its spirit—this will constitute its newness. Finally, the same one who had engraved the letter upon stone tablets had also proclaimed concerning the Spirit (Joel III.28): “I shall pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh.” And if “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life,” both belong to him who said (Deut. XXXII.39): “I shall kill, and I shall make alive; I shall strike, and I shall heal.” Long ago we asserted [Note: [Col. 0498D] “We assert,” Seml.] the twofold power of the Creator, both as judge and as good [Note: [Col. 0497D] “Of the letter that kills through the Law.” These are Paul’s words in II Corinthians III.6: “The letter kills; the Spirit gives life.” He calls the Mosaic laws “the letter,” and the Gospel “the Spirit.” The Mosaic Law, having been abrogated through the Gospel, is now nothing but a letter, something bodily presented for our eyes to read. And for as long as it stood, it furnished something bodily. For when violated it brought death; when observed, the reward of some bodily or earthly happiness. But the words of Christ contained in the Gospel are spirit and life. For they offer to guilty persons who repent mercy and pardon for offenses, and eternal life; these are heavenly, not earthly. RIG.—“Of the letter that kills.” Menander:

> A law observed is nothing but a law;  
> But one not observed is both law and executioner.

Concerning the letter of Moses, Chrysostom says: “If the law catches a murderer, it puts him to death. And why do I say a murderer? The law caught a man gathering sticks on the Sabbath and stoned him.” RIG.], through the letter that kills by means of the Law, and through the Spirit that gives life by means of the Gospel. Things which, though different, were already accounted under one God cannot make two gods.

He also recalls the veil of Moses, with which he covered his face, unendurable to the sight of the children of Israel. If he does this in order to maintain the greater splendor of the New Testament, which remains in glory, over that of the old, which was destined to be abolished, this agrees with my faith too, which places the Gospel above the Law. And see whether it does not agree even more with mine. For something can be placed above only where that over which it is placed also exists.

But when he says, [Col. 0498D] “The perceptions of the world were dulled,” he certainly does not mean the Creator’s perceptions, but those of the people who are in the world. For he speaks of Israel [Note: [Col. 0498D] “Israel,” Ober.]: [Col. 0499A] “To this very day the same veil is upon their heart.” He shows that the veil upon Moses’ face was a figure of the veil upon the people’s heart, because even now Moses is not clearly perceived among them by the heart, just as at that time he was not perceived by the face.

What, then, is still veiled in Moses that pertains to Paul, if the Creator’s Christ proclaimed by Moses has not yet come? How are the hearts of the Jews already identified as still covered and veiled, when the things proclaimed by Moses—that is, the things concerning Christ, in whom they ought to understand Moses—have not yet been presented? What concern is it of the apostle of another Christ if the Jews did not understand the mysteries of their own God, unless the veil over their heart pertained to their blindness, by which they had failed to perceive the Christ of Moses?

Finally, what follows—“But when one turns to God, the veil will be removed”—he says properly of the Jew, with whom the veil of Moses is found: when he passes over to faith in Christ, he understands that Moses proclaimed Christ. Otherwise, how will the Creator’s veil be removed in the Christ of another God, whose mysteries the Creator could not have veiled—unknown things belonging, of course, to an unknown God?

He therefore says that we, now with unveiled face—the face of the heart, of course, which is veiled in the Jews—beholding Christ, are transformed into the same image from glory (that glory by which Moses too was transformed by the glory of the Lord) to glory. Thus, by setting forth Moses’ bodily illumination from his encounter with the Lord, and the bodily veil because of the people’s weakness, and by introducing in addition spiritual splendor in Christ, “as from the Lord,” he says, “of spirits” [Note: [Col. 0499D] “From the Lord, the Spirit,” another reading.], he testifies that the whole dispensation of Moses was a figure of Christ, unrecognized among the Jews but recognized among us.

We know that certain expressions can admit ambiguity because of the sound of their pronunciation or the manner of their punctuation, when a double sense intervenes. Marcion seized upon this by reading it thus: “Among whom [Note: [Col. 0500D] “The god of this age.” He designates the evil demon, because “the gods of the nations are demons,” as it is written in the Psalm and in the Apostle: “whose god is their belly.” LE PR.] the god of this age”—so that, by presenting the Creator as the God of this age, he might suggest another God of another age. We, on the contrary, say it must be punctuated thus: “Among whom God”; then: “has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age.” “Among whom” means among the unbelieving Jews, among whom the Gospel is still veiled for some beneath the veil of Moses.

For God had threatened those who loved him with their lips but whose heart stood far away from him (Isa. XXIX.13): “With your ear you will hear, and you will not hear; with your eyes you will see, so that you will not see” (Isa. VI.10); and, “Unless you believe, neither will you understand” (Isa. VII.9); and, “I shall take away the wisdom of the wise, and render void the prudence of the prudent” (Isa. XXIX.14). Yet he certainly was not threatening these things [Col. 0499D] in order to conceal the Gospel of an unknown God.

Thus it must be understood that it is not [Note: [Col. 0499D] “Even if,” Venet.] “the God of this age,” but God who blinds the heart of “the unbelievers [Col. 0500A] of this age,” because they did not of their own accord recognize his Christ from the Scriptures. Having dealt thus far with the passage because its punctuation is ambiguous, lest it profit the adversary, and content with the victory, I could indeed [Note: [Col. 0499D] “And no further,” Lat.] have passed over this dispute entirely with a simpler answer.

It will, of course, be ready to hand [Note: [Col. 0500D] “Of course” omitted by Venet.] to interpret the devil as the lord of this age, who said, as reported by the prophet (Isa. XIV.14): “I shall be like the Most High; I shall set my throne in the clouds.” Likewise, all the superstition of this age has been enslaved to him, who blinds the hearts of unbelievers—and first among them, the apostate Marcion.

Finally, he did not see the concluding clause of the passage confronting him: “Because God, who said that light should shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts for the illumination of the knowledge of himself in the person of Christ.” Who [Note: [Col. 0500D] Seml. adds “thus.”] said, [Col. 0500B] “Let there be light”? And concerning the illumination of the world, who said to Christ (Isa. XLII.6), “I have appointed you as a light of the nations”—those sitting, of course, in darkness and in the shadow of death? The Spirit answers him in the Psalm, from foreknowledge of the future (Ps. IV.7): “The light of your countenance, O Lord,” he says, “has been marked upon us.” But the *persona*—the person or countenance—of God is Christ the Lord. Hence the Apostle also said above: “Who is,” he says, “the image of God.”

Therefore, if Christ is the person of the Creator who said, “Let there be light,” then Christ, the Apostles, the Gospel, the veil, Moses, and the whole sequence—according to the testimony of the concluding clause—belong to the Creator, the God of this age, certainly not to him who never said, “Let there be light.”

Here I pass over also a passage from another Epistle, which in our copies is entitled “To the Ephesians,” [Note: [Col. 0500D] but in the heretics’ copies, “To the Laodiceans.” From this Epistle he also adduces testimonies against the Marcionites in chapter XVII below, where the passage about the nations remembering, etc., is also explained, but in very different words, more consistent with the Apostle. PAM.] but in the heretics’ copies “To the Laodiceans.” For he says (Eph. II.12) that the nations should remember that at that time, when they were without Christ, alienated from Israel, without citizenship, covenants, or hope of the promise, they were also without God [Note: [Col. 0500D] “Without the Lord,” Ober.]—in the world, of course, even if the reference is to the Creator.

Therefore, if he said that the nations were without God, but their god is the devil, not the Creator, it is apparent that “the lord of this age” must be understood as the one whom the nations accepted as God, not the Creator whom they do not know.

But how can the treasure in our earthen vessels be held not to belong to the same one to whom the vessels themselves belong? For if it is to the glory of God that so great a treasure is held in earthen vessels, and the earthen vessels belong to the Creator, then the glory also belongs to the Creator, whose vessels savor of the surpassing greatness of God’s power, as does the power itself. For they were entrusted to earthen vessels precisely so that its surpassing greatness might be proved. Otherwise it will no longer be the glory of another God, nor therefore [Col. 0500D] his power, but rather his disgrace and weakness, since earthen vessels—and foreign ones at that—have contained his surpassing greatness.

But if these are the earthen vessels in which he says that we suffer so much, in which we also carry about the mortification of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0501D] “Of God,” Seml.], then God is sufficiently ungrateful and unjust if he is not also going to raise this substance [Note: [Col. 0501D] “Is” omitted by Ober.] in which so much is endured for faith in him, in which the death of Christ is carried about, and in which the surpassing greatness of his power is consecrated.

But indeed he sets forth this purpose: “So that the life of Christ also may be manifested in our body,” just as his death also is carried about in the body. Of what life of Christ, then, does he speak? Of the life by which we now live in him? And how is it that in what follows he exhorts us not toward things visible or temporal, but toward things invisible and eternal—that is, not toward things present, but future? But if he speaks of Christ’s future life and says that it will appear in the body, he has plainly proclaimed the resurrection of the flesh.

He says that our outer human being [Col. 0501B] is being corrupted, not as though by eternal destruction after death, but by the labors and hardships of which he had spoken before, adding: “And we shall not fail.” For when he also says that our inner human being is being renewed day by day, he demonstrates both things here: the corruption of the body from the affliction of trials, and the renewal of the mind from contemplation of the promises.

## CHAPTER XII

“Our earthly [Note: [Col. 0501D] “What he touched upon in the First Epistle.” He is speaking of I Corinthians. Rhenanus notes that *strinxit* is used for *perstrinxit*, that is, “indicated in passing” or “touched upon lightly.” PAM.] dwelling” (II Cor. V, VI, VII, XI, XII, and XIII) [Note: [Col. 0501D] Perhaps “our earthly dwelling,” following Pam.]: he does not say that we have an eternal house, not made by hand, in heaven [Note: [Col. 0501D] “Heaven,” Seml.], because the one made by the Creator’s hand perishes, being wholly dissolved after death.

For he is reconsidering these matters in order to console us for fear of death and sorrow over the dissolution itself, and he does so still more plainly through what follows, when he adds that we groan in this tabernacle of the earthly body, desiring to be clothed over [Note: [Col. 0501D] “To clothe over,” Ober.] with what is from heaven, “provided that, even after being stripped, we shall not be found [Note: [Col. 0502D] “May not be found,” Fran.] naked”—that is, we shall receive again that of which we were stripped, namely, the body.

And again: “For we who are in this tabernacle of the body groan because we are burdened, not wishing to be unclothed but to be clothed over.” Here he expressed [Note: [Col. 0501D] “What he touched upon in the First Epistle.” He is speaking of I Corinthians. Rhenanus notes that *strinxit* is used for *perstrinxit*, that is, “indicated in passing” or “touched upon lightly.” PAM.] what he touched upon in the First Epistle: “The dead will rise incorrupt”—those who have already died—“and we shall be changed”—those whom God finds still in the flesh.

For the former will rise incorrupt, having, of course, received back the body, and indeed a whole body, so that in this respect also they may be incorrupt. The latter, because the very last moment of time is already at hand, and because of the merit of their sufferings under Antichrist, will receive an abridgment of death; but they will attain it after being changed [Note: [Col. 0502D] Lat. reads “of death; changed, they may attain”], being clothed over with what is from heaven rather than stripped of the body.

Thus, if [Col. 0501D] these will put that heavenly garment over the body, the dead too will certainly receive a body over which they themselves may put on incorruption from heaven, since of them also he says: “This corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal [Col. 0502A] thing immortality.” They put it on when they have received back the body; these others put it on over the body, because they have not lost the body.

And therefore he did not say without purpose, “Not wishing to be stripped of the body, but to be clothed over”—that is, not wishing to experience death, but to be overtaken by life—“so that this mortal thing may be swallowed up by life,” when it is snatched from death through being clothed over with transformation.

Therefore, because [Note: [Col. 0502D] “Therefore, he who,” another reading; “and therefore,” Ciaccon.] he shows this to be better, so that we may not be grieved if perhaps death comes first, he says that we have from God the pledge of the Spirit, as though pledged to the same hope of being clothed over; and that we are absent from the Lord so long as we are in the flesh, and for that reason ought to judge it better to be absent from the body and to be with the Lord, so that we may also welcome death willingly.

And indeed, he says that we must all be manifested before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what he committed through the body, [Col. 0502B] whether good or evil. For if the recompense of merits takes place only then, how will some already be accounted as being with God? Moreover, by naming both a judgment seat and the settlement of good and evil works, he reveals a judge who pronounces both kinds of sentence, and confirms the presentation of all bodies. For what was committed in the body cannot be punished [Note: [Col. 0502D] “Judged,” Venet.; but Lat. reads “punished.”] apart from the body. For God would be unjust if anyone were not punished or assisted through that by which he acted.

[Note: [Col. 0501D] “If, then, there is any new creation in Christ.” In Tertullian’s usage, *conditio* is taken to mean “creation,” Greek *κτίσις*. He also agrees with the Old Latin translator in rendering “if any,” where Isidore, more clearly but, like Erasmus, too freely, has “if anyone.” PAM.] “If, then, there is any new creation in Christ, the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new”: Isaiah’s prophecy has been fulfilled (Isa. XLIII.19).

If he also commands that we cleanse ourselves from the defilement of flesh and blood—[the transmitted phrase *non substantium capere regnum Dei*, “not of substances to receive the kingdom of God,” is corrupt and materially uncertain; Note: [Col. 0502D] All the others read *substantiam*, “substance,” which yields no sense.]—if he also intends to present the Church to Christ as a holy virgin, certainly as bride to bridegroom—the image cannot [Col. 0502C] be joined to an enemy of the reality’s truth.

If he also calls the false apostles deceitful workers, disguisers of themselves, he accuses them of hypocrisy in their conduct, not of adulterating the proclamation. Thus the dispute concerned discipline, not divinity.

If Satan disguises himself as an angel of light, this cannot be directed against the Creator. For the Creator is God, not an angel; Satan would have been said to disguise himself as the God of light, not as an angel, if he did not mean that Satan whom both we and Marcion know to be an angel.

In the matter of paradise his own pen is proof against every difficulty he suffers. Here I might perhaps wonder whether a God who possesses no earthly arrangement of his own could have a paradise of his own—unless, perhaps, he also used the Creator’s paradise by permission, just as he did the world. And yet there is in Elijah an example [Col. 0502D] of a man being taken up into the Creator’s heaven (IV Kings II).

But I shall wonder still more that the supremely good Lord, alien to striking and cruelty, applied to his Apostle an angel of Satan—not even his own, but the Creator’s—to buffet him, and, though entreated by him three times, [Col. 0503A] did not grant his request.

Marcion’s god, therefore, also corrects in accordance with the Creator, who opposes the exalted, as one who casts rulers down from their throne. Or is he perhaps the very one who also gave Satan power over Job’s body, so that power might be proved in weakness?

Why does the chastiser of the Galatians still retain the form of the Law, laying down beforehand that every word shall be established by three witnesses? Why does the preacher of the most gentle God threaten that he will not spare sinners? Indeed, he affirms that the Lord gave him authority even to act more severely when present. Deny now, heretic, that your God is to be feared, when his Apostle was feared.

## CHAPTER XIII
When the little work is nearing completion, the points that recur must now be reconsidered briefly; but some things that have occurred more often must be passed over. [Col. 0503B] I am weary of still contending over the Law, since I have so often [Note: [Col. 0503D] *Contending*, *as often as*, Semler.] proved that its cessation [Note: [Col. 0503D] *Withdrawal*, Franeker edition.] furnishes no argument for a different God, seeing that it was proclaimed in Christ and promised anew in relation to Christ by the Creator, even though the Apostle himself [Note: [Col. 0503D] *Even though the Epistle itself*, Latin edition.] appears in many places to exclude the Law (Rom. I, II, III, V, VI, VII). But we have also already shown repeatedly that God is presented by the Apostle as judge, as avenger in his capacity as judge, and as Creator in his capacity as avenger.

Accordingly, when he says here, “For I am not ashamed of the Gospel; for it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew and to the Greek, because in it the righteousness of God is revealed, from faith to faith,” he undoubtedly assigns both the Gospel and salvation to the just God, not to the good God—if I may put it that way, according to the heretic’s distinction—who transfers people from faith in the Law to faith in the Gospel: from faith, of course, in his own [Col. 0503C] Law to faith in his own Gospel. For he also says that wrath [Note: [Col. 0503D] Franeker adds *of God*.] is revealed from heaven against the impiety and injustice of men who hold the truth in injustice. [Note: [Col. 0503D] *Who may hold*, Oberthür.] Whose God’s wrath is it? The Creator’s, of course. Therefore the truth also belongs to him whose wrath it is, since that wrath is to be revealed in vindication of the truth.

Moreover, by adding, “But we know that the judgment of God is according to truth,” he both established the wrath from which judgment comes on behalf of the truth, and once again confirmed the truth as belonging to the same God whose wrath he established by establishing his judgment. It would be otherwise if the wrathful Creator were avenging the truth of another God that had been suppressed in injustice.

[Note: [Col. 0503D] What enormous gaps Marcion made, especially in this Epistle! Tertullian indicates that he is treating only those passages that Marcion did not see fit to erase, although he removed whatever he wished. Consequently, he adduces very few passages from this exceedingly long Epistle, as does also blessed Epiphanius. To the same point belong the words he has in the following chapter: “Here too I leap over a very extensive section,” etc. PAM.]

How enormous the gaps are that Marcion made, especially in this Epistle, by removing whatever he wished, will become evident from the completeness of our own Scriptural corpus. For my purposes it is enough to take up the passages he did not see fit to erase, regarding them as instances of his negligence and blindness.

[Col. 0503D] For if God will judge the secrets of men—both of those who sinned under the Law and of those who sinned without the Law, because even these, though ignorant of the Law, naturally do the things that belong to the Law—[Col. 0504A] then surely the God who judges will be the one to whom both the Law and nature itself belong, since nature serves in place of the Law for those ignorant of the Law. [Note: [Col. 0503D] *Being ignorant, naturally*, Ciacconius.]

But how will he judge? “According to the Gospel,” he says, “through Christ.” Therefore both the Gospel and Christ belong to him to whom the Law and nature belong, since the Law and nature will be vindicated through the Gospel and through Christ, by that judgment of God which, as stated above, is “according to truth.” Therefore, just as wrath is revealed from heaven in defense of that truth only by the God of wrath, so too the sense here, cohering with the preceding one in which the Creator’s judgment is proclaimed, cannot be referred to another God who neither judges nor grows angry. It must instead be referred to him to whom these things—by which I mean judgment and wrath—belong; [Note: [Col. 0504D] *While* absent in the Paris edition.] [Note: [Col. 0504D] *Wrath*, Semler.] and therefore those things through which these actions are to be carried out—the Gospel and Christ—must likewise belong to him.

For this reason the Apostle inveighs against transgressors of the Law who teach that one must not steal and yet steal themselves. He does so as a man of [Col. 0504B] the God of the Law, not as one assailing the Creator himself in such terms because, while forbidding theft, the Creator allegedly ordered the Egyptians to be defrauded of their gold and silver, just as the other objections are turned back against him. Evidently the Apostle was afraid to revile openly the God from whom he was not afraid to defect!
