Indeed, he had attacked the Jews so thoroughly that he pressed upon them the prophetic rebuke: “Because of you the name of God is blasphemed.” How perverse it would therefore be for him himself to blaspheme the God whose being blasphemed is the reason for which he reproaches the wicked!

He also prefers circumcision of the heart to uncircumcision. In the presence of the God [Note: [Col. 0504D] Franeker adds *for*.] of the Law, circumcision is made of the heart, not the flesh; in spirit, not in letter. But if this is Jeremiah’s circumcision (Jer. IV, 4), “And you shall circumcise the foreskin of your heart,” as it is also that of Moses (Deut. X, 16), [Note: [Col. 0504D] *Moses*, Pamelius.] “You shall circumcise your hardness of heart,” then the spirit [Col. 0504C] that circumcises the heart will belong to the same God whose letter cuts the flesh; and the Jews who are Jews inwardly will belong to the same God whose Jew is a Jew outwardly. For the Apostle would not even have wished to use the name “Jew” if he had not been a servant of the Jews’ God.

Then there was the Law; now there is the righteousness of God through faith in Christ. What is the nature of this distinction? Did your god serve the Creator’s dispensation, granting time to him and to his Law? Or did the former dispensation belong to him to whom the present one also belongs? The Law belongs to him to whom faith belongs. Christ marks a distinction between dispensations, not between gods.

[Note: [Col. 0504D] He admonishes those justified by faith, etc., to have peace with God. In these words at the beginning of chapter V, after omitting the whole of chapter IV of the Epistle to the Romans, the Author reads ἔχομεν, “we have,” in place of what others read as ἔχωμεν, “let us have.” PAM.]

He admonishes those justified by faith in Christ, not by the Law, to have peace with God. With which God? With the one whose enemies we never were, or with the one whose Law and nature we rebelled against? For if peace is properly made with him against whom there was war, then we shall also be justified before him, and Christ will belong to him by faith in whom we shall be justified, since it is proper that those who were once his enemies should be restored to peace with him.

“But the Law,” [Col. 0504D] he says, “entered in alongside, so that the offense might abound.” Why? “So that grace,” he says, “might superabound.” Whose God’s grace is this, if not that of the God whose Law it is? Unless, perhaps, the Creator inserted [Note: [Col. 0504D] *Inserted the Law*. That is, says Rhenanus, he interjected, interposed, introduced, or put it into the middle; for here this is the meaning of *intercalare*. Macrobius mentions this word and also discusses at length the principle of intercalation. Julius Caesar established that one day should be intercalated, that is, inserted, every fourth year; hence Pliny calls the bissextile year “intercalary,” and Livy called a month “intercalary.” The Greeks call it ἐμβόλιμον and ἐμβολιμαῖον, “intercalated.” PAM.] the Law [Note: [Col. 0504D] *The Law* is absent in Rhenanus.] [Col. 0505A] precisely in order to transact the business of another god’s grace—and indeed that of a rival god, not to say an unknown one—so that, just as sin had reigned under the Creator unto death, grace too might reign through righteousness unto life through Jesus Christ, the Creator’s adversary!

For this purpose, then, the Creator’s Law had shut up all things under offense, reduced the whole world to guilt, and stopped every mouth, so that no one might boast through the Law, in order that grace might be reserved for the glory of Christ—not the Creator’s Christ, but Marcion’s. Here too I can lay a foundation concerning the substance of Christ, in anticipation of the question that follows. For he says that we have died to the Law. [Note: [Col. 0505D] *For he says that we have died to the Law.* This too is spoken from Marcion’s point of view and derives from his corrupted text, since Marcion had rendered it “we have died to the Law,” where the Apostle says “we have died to sin,” at the beginning of Romans VI. But Tertullian rightly refutes him from the words that follow, where he adds that Christ rose from the dead. PAM.] Therefore, it is through the body of Christ. [Note: [Col. 0505D] *To the Law through the body of Christ. Therefore*, Ciacconius.] It may, however, be contended that a “body” is not necessarily flesh. But whatever the substance may be, when the Apostle names the body of the one whom he goes on to say rose from the dead, [Col. 0505B] no other body can be understood than the body of flesh, against which the law of death was pronounced.

See, moreover, how he bears testimony to the Law and excuses it from being the cause of the offense. “What, then, shall we say? Is the Law sin? Far from it!” Blush, Marcion! “Far from it!” The Apostle abominates the accusation against the Law. “But I did not know the offense except through the Law.” O supreme commendation of the Law, through which it became clear that the offense had been hidden! [Note: [Col. 0505D] *It was permitted*, Semler and Oberthür.] [Note: [Col. 0505D] *Hidden*, Ciacconius.] Therefore it was not the Law that deceived, but sin, through the opportunity afforded by the commandment. Why do you impute to the God of the Law what the Apostle does not dare impute to his Law?

Indeed, he heaps praise upon it: “The Law is holy, and its commandment is just and good.” If he venerates the Creator’s Law in this manner, I do not know how he can destroy the Creator himself. Who can distinguish two gods, one just and the other good, when the God whose commandment [Col. 0505C] is both good and just must be believed to be both? And if he also confirms that the Law is spiritual, then surely it is also prophetic, and surely also figurative. From this too, therefore, I must establish that Christ was proclaimed figuratively in the Law, which is why he could not be recognized by all the Jews.

## CHAPTER XIV

*(Rom. VIII, X, XI, XII, XIII, XIV)*

If the Father sent him “in the likeness of sinful flesh,” the flesh that appeared in him is not for that reason to be called a phantom. For above, the Apostle ascribed sin to the flesh, made it the law of sin dwelling in his members and opposing the law of his understanding. The Son was therefore sent in the likeness of sinful flesh so that he might redeem sinful flesh by means of a like substance—that is, a fleshly one—which would be similar to sinful flesh [Col. 0506A] although it was not itself sinful. For this too will be the power of God: to accomplish salvation in an equal substance. It would be no great thing if the Spirit of God healed flesh; the great thing is if flesh like sinful flesh heals it, being flesh but not sinful.

Thus the likeness will pertain to the designation “sin,” not to any falsity of substance. For he would not have added “sinful” if he had wished a likeness of substance to be understood in such a way as to deny its reality. He would merely have written “flesh,” without also adding “sinful.” But since he constructed the phrase in this way, “sinful flesh,” [Note: [Col. 0505D] *He constructed it in this way*, Semler; *he set both beneath*, Latin edition.] he both confirmed the substance—that is, flesh—and referred the likeness to the defect of the substance—that is, to sin.

Suppose now that the likeness is said to be a likeness of substance: the reality of the substance will not for that reason be denied. Why, then, is something real also like? Because it is indeed real, but not from seed; like in condition, but [Note: [Col. 0505D] *And*, Latin edition.] [Col. 0506B] real in origin, and not unlike in reality. [Note: [Col. 0505D] *Real from likeness*, Latin edition.] Besides, there is no likeness between contrary things. Spirit would not be called a likeness of flesh, because neither could flesh receive the likeness of spirit. It would instead be called a phantom if it appeared to be what it was not. A likeness, however, is spoken of when a thing is what it appears to be; for it exists, since it is the equal of another.

[Note: [Col. 0506D] *But a phantom.* Tertullian discussed this at greater length above against Marcion, who attributed to Christ phantasmal flesh and a phantom, not a real body. LE PR.]

But a phantom, [Note: [Col. 0506D] *But* neglected by others.] because [Note: [Col. 0506D] *Because*, other editions.] it is only an apparition of this kind, is not a likeness. [Note: [Col. 0506D] For *only this*, the Latin edition proposes *an apparition*.]

Here too, moreover, the Apostle himself explains how he does not wish us to be “in the flesh” although we are in the flesh: namely, so that we may not be engaged in [Note: [Col. 0506D] *From*, Semler.] the works of the flesh. He thereby shows that it was in this sense that he wrote (1 Cor. XV, 50), “Flesh and blood cannot attain the kingdom of God.” He was not condemning the substance but its works; and since we can refrain from these while still situated in the flesh, they will pertain not to the guilt of the substance but to our manner of life. [Col. 0506C]

Likewise, if “the body is dead because of the offense”—so fully is death the death not of the soul but of the body—“but the spirit is life because of righteousness,” then life because of righteousness will surely come to that to which death came because of the offense, namely, the body. For nothing is restored to someone unless he has lost something else; and so the resurrection of the dead will be a resurrection of bodies.

For he also [Note: [Col. 0506D] Pamelius omits *also*.] adds: “He who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies.” Thus he has both confirmed the resurrection of the flesh—apart from which no other “body” can be spoken of, nor any other thing understood as “mortal”—and proved Christ’s bodily substance. For our mortal bodies will be given life in the same way as he too was raised, and not otherwise in the same way [Col. 0507A] except because [Note: [Col. 0507D] *Which*, Junius.] he was raised in a body.

Here too I leap over a very extensive section cut away from Scripture; but I seize upon the Apostle’s testimony concerning Israel, that “they have zeal for God”—for their own God, surely—“but not according to knowledge.” “For being ignorant of God,” he says, “and seeking to establish their own righteousness, they did not subject themselves to the righteousness of God. For Christ is the end of the Law unto righteousness [Note: [Col. 0507D] *Righteousness*, Semler and Oberthür.] for everyone who believes.”

Here will be the heretic’s argument: the Jews were allegedly ignorant of a higher God, against whom they established their own righteousness—that is, the righteousness of their own Law—by not receiving Christ as the end of the Law. Why, then, does the Apostle also bear witness to their zeal for their own God, if he does not reproach them for ignorance concerning that same God? They were indeed moved by zeal for God, but not according to knowledge: they were ignorant of him, of course, insofar as they were ignorant of the consummation of his dispensations in [Col. 0507B] Christ, who was to establish an end for the Law, [Note: [Col. 0507D] *Who was to establish*, Rigault; *I shall establish*, Venetian edition.] and in this way they defended their own righteousness against him.

Indeed, the Creator himself testifies to their ignorance concerning himself (Isa. I, 3): “Israel did not recognize me, and my people did not understand me.” He also testifies that they preferred to establish their own righteousness, “teaching as doctrines the commandments of men” (Isa. XXIX, 13), and likewise that they “assembled together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. II, 2), evidently out of ignorance.

Nothing, therefore, can be interpreted as referring to another God when it properly applies to the Creator. Otherwise, the Apostle would also have undeservedly censured the Jews for ignorance concerning an unknown god. For how had they sinned if they established the righteousness of their own God against one whom they did not know?

Indeed, he exclaims: [Note: [Col. 0507D] “O depth of riches.” Ὢ βάθος, “O depth,” for which the Vulgate has “O height.” LE PR.] “O depth of the riches and wisdom of God, and how unsearchable [Note: [Col. 0507D] *Unsearchable.* Since the Greek has ἀνεξιχνίαστοι, that is, “not traceable,” many rightly judge that one should read *unsearchable*, that is, “which cannot be searched out.” LE PR.] [Col. 0507C] are his ways!” From where comes this outburst? Evidently from his recollection of the Scriptures which he had reviewed above, and from his contemplation of the mysteries he had discussed above concerning faith in Christ as coming from the Law.

If Marcion deliberately did not [Note: [Col. 0507D] Pamelius omits *not*, but it is present in the Codex Wouwerianus.] erase these words, why does his apostle exclaim while contemplating no riches belonging to a god as poor and destitute as one who created nothing, foretold nothing, and in short possessed nothing, since he descended into the property of another? Yet the Creator had long ago promised resources and riches that were then hidden but have now been disclosed (Isa. XLV, 3): “And I will give them hidden treasures; I will open invisible things to them.” From this, therefore, came the exclamation: “O depth of the riches and wisdom of God!”—the God whose treasures were now being laid open. That comes from Isaiah, [Note: [Col. 0507D] *Were laid open from Isaiah, so that*, Latin edition.] and what follows comes from the written corpus of the same prophet (Isa. XL, 13): “For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been [Col. 0507D] his counselor? Who has given to him, and it shall be repaid to him?” You who have removed so much from the Scriptures, why did you preserve these words, as though they too did not belong to the Creator?

Let us, to be sure, examine the precepts of the new god. “Hating evil,” he says, “and cleaving to good.” It is apparently otherwise with the Creator: “Remove evil from among you,” and (Ps. XXXIII, 14), “Turn away from evil and do good.” “Affectionate toward one another in brotherly love.” This is surely not identical with, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself”! “Rejoicing in hope”—in God, of course: “For it is good to hope in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0507D] *In the Lord*, Oberthür.] rather than to hope in rulers” (Ps. CXVII). “Enduring tribulation”: “For the Lord will hear you in the day of tribulation” (Ps. XIX, 1). There you have the Psalm.

“Bless, and do not curse.” Who will teach this except the one who created all things by blessings? “Not thinking lofty thoughts, but associating with the humble, [Note: [Col. 0508D] *Pursuing*, Venetian edition.] lest you be wise in your own estimation”; for through Isaiah they hear, “Woe to them” (Isa. V, 21). “Repay no one evil for evil”; and (Lev. XIX, 18), “You shall not remember your brother’s malice.” [Col. 0508B] [Note: [Col. 0508D] *You shall not remember*, Junius.] “Neither avenge yourselves: for vengeance is mine, [Deut. XXXII, 35] and I will avenge, says the Lord.” “Have peace with all [Note: [Col. 0508D] Semler omits *all*.] people.” Thus even the legal principle of retaliation did not permit repayment of injury; rather, by fear of repayment, it restrained the initiation of injury.

Rightly, therefore, the Apostle summed up the Creator’s whole discipline in the Creator’s chief commandment: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” If this fulfillment of the Law comes from the Law itself, I no longer know who the God of the Law may be—I fear it may be Marcion’s god! But if Christ’s Gospel is fulfilled by this commandment, while Christ is not [Note: [Col. 0508D] *And*, Latin edition.] the Creator’s, what are we now arguing about? Did Christ say, or did he not say, “I did not come to dissolve the Law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. V, 17)? The man from Pontus labored in vain to deny this saying. [Note: [Col. 0508D] *The man from Pontus labored.* Rhenanus very well conjectured that *Ponticus*, “the man from Pontus,” should be read in place of *Pontus*; that is, Marcion, who originated in Pontus. LE PR.] If the Gospel did not fulfill the Law, behold, the Law has fulfilled the Gospel.

It is well, moreover, that in the conclusion he also threatens the tribunal of Christ—of Christ as judge and avenger, and therefore as the Creator’s—at any rate establishing that the one whom he declares must be feared is to be won over, even if he were preaching another.

## CHAPTER XV

Nor will it be irksome to attend to the shorter Epistles: there is flavor even in a few words.

The Jews had killed their own prophets. I can say: What concern is that of the apostle of another God, and indeed of the supremely good God, who is said not even to condemn the sins of his own people and who himself, by destroying those same prophets, in a certain sense puts them to death? For what evil [Note: [Col. 0508D] Semler omits *for*.] did Israel commit against him if it killed those whom he too rejected, if he had previously pronounced a hostile sentence against them? Israel did, however, sin against their own God. It was he [Note: [Col. 0508D] Semler adds *and*.] who reproached them for the iniquity, [Col. 0508D] to whom the injured party belonged—certainly anyone other than the injured party’s adversary.

Nor would the Apostle have burdened them by also charging them with the murder of the Lord, saying that they “killed both the Lord [Col. 0509A] and their own prophets”—although “their own” is an addition made by the heretic. For what would be so bitter in the fact that they killed Christ, the preacher of another God, when they had butchered the prophets of their own God? The force of the aggravation, however, lies in their having killed both the Lord and his servants. Finally, if they killed the Christ of one God and the prophets of another, the Apostle equated the acts of impiety; he did not aggravate them. But they ought not to have been equated. Therefore the charge could not have been aggravated unless both offenses, under their respective descriptions, had been committed against the same Lord. Christ and the prophets therefore belong to the same God.

You would recognize what holiness he calls the will of God from the contrary things he prohibits. He says, “To abstain [Note: [Col. 0509D] Oberthür, following Semler, adds *for*.] from fornication,” not from marriage. “That each person should know how to treat his own vessel with honor.” How? By not treating it “in lust, as the Gentiles do”; but even among the Gentiles lust [Col. 0509B] is attributed not to marriage but to extraordinary, unnatural, and monstrous practices.

Holiness is also contrary to the shame and uncleanness [Note: [Col. 0509D] “Holiness is contrary to the shame of lust,” etc. Those who read *luxury* do not adequately agree with the text, and wrongly fasten upon Tertullian the charge of having held a poor view of marriage; for the particle “not,” which follows, removes every doubt. LE PR.] [Note: [Col. 0509D] Rhenanus reads: *Monstrous. Luxury is also contrary to shame and uncleanness; it does not …*.] of lust. Such holiness does not exclude marriage but lust; it treats our vessel with the honor of marriage.

I would discuss this passage while preserving the preeminence of the other—that is, fuller—holiness, preferring continence and virginity to marriage, [Note: [Col. 0509D] *Preferring continence and virginity to marriage.* Let the heretics who assail vows of virginity and continence attend to this passage and to many others in this writer, in *On the Apparel of Women*, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, and Book I *To His Wife*. LE PR.] but not to marriage as though it were prohibited. For I am refuting destroyers of the God of marriage, not followers of chastity.

He says that those who remain until the coming [Note: [Col. 0509D] *At the coming*, Semler.] of Christ, together with those dead in Christ who will rise first, will be caught up in the clouds into the air [Note: [Col. 0509D] *Air*, Oberthür.] to meet the Lord. I recognize that, since these things had already been foreseen at that time, the heavenly substances marvel through Isaiah at Jerusalem herself, which is above (Gal. IV, 26), and declare (Isa. [Col. 0509C] LX, 8): “Who are these who fly here like clouds, like doves with their young, toward me?”

If Christ prepared this ascent for us, he will be the Christ of whom Hosea [Note: [Col. 0509D] Junius proposes *Amos*, and rightly.] says (Amos IX, 6): “He who builds his ascent into the heavens”—surely for himself and his own people. From whom, then, shall I now expect it, except from the one from whom I heard these things?

Whose spirit does he prohibit from being quenched? And whose prophecies does he forbid to be treated as nothing? According to Marcion, surely not the Creator’s Spirit or the Creator’s prophecies. For by destroying them he has already quenched them and reduced them to nothing; and he cannot prohibit people from doing what he himself has done, treating them as nothing.

Marcion is therefore under obligation to exhibit today in his own church the spirit of his god, which must not be quenched, and prophecies which must not be regarded as nothing. If he has exhibited what he thinks answers to this description, let him know [Note: [Col. 0510D] *Let you know*, Venetian edition.] that we shall challenge whatever it is to conform to the pattern of spiritual [Col. 0509D] and prophetic grace and power: [Col. 0510A] it must foretell the future, reveal the secrets of the heart, and explain mysteries. Since he has produced and proved nothing of this kind, we shall bring forward both the Creator’s Spirit and the Creator’s prophecies, while preaching in accordance with the Creator himself.

It will thus be established which things the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0510D] *The Apostle*, Pamelius.] was speaking about: namely, those things that were to be present in the church of his God—the God who, because he exists, also has his Spirit [Note: [Col. 0510D] *To them*, Semler, incorrectly.] at work and his promise being fulfilled.

Come now, you who deny the salvation of the flesh and, whenever “body” is mentioned in a passage of this sort, interpret it as some other thing unknown to me rather than as the substance of the flesh: how did the Apostle distinguish all three by definite names as distinct substances, yet include them all in a single prayer for salvation, wishing that “our spirit and body and soul may be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord and Savior Christ”? [Col. 0510B]

For he named both soul and body as two things and as different things. Although the soul too has a body of some sort, of a quality proper to itself, as does the spirit, nevertheless, when body and soul are named distinctly, the soul possesses its own proper designation and does not require the shared designation “body.” That designation is left for the flesh, which, because it is not named by its proper term, must necessarily make use of the common term. Indeed, after spirit and soul, I see no other substance in a human being to which the designation “body” may be applied except the flesh. He understands flesh under the name of the body as often as flesh is not explicitly named—and much more so here, where that which is called “body” is designated by its own name.

## CHAPTER XVI

*(On the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians)*

We are compelled to repeat certain things over and over [Col. 0510C] so that we may confirm the points connected with them. Here too we say that the Apostle presents the Lord as the requiter of both kinds of merit: either the Creator or—what Marcion would reject—one equal to the Creator. With him [Note: [Col. 0510D] “It is just that affliction be repaid to those who afflict us.” This is how he renders 2 Thessalonians I. In Greek: ἂν ἀποδοῦναι τοῖς θλίβουσιν ἡμᾶς, “to repay those who afflict us.” PAM.] it is just that affliction be repaid to those who afflict us, and rest to us who are afflicted, “at the revelation of the Lord Jesus, coming from heaven with the angels of his power and in a flame of fire.”

But by deleting “flame” and “fire,” [Note: [Col. 0510D] *But by deleting “flame” and “fire.”* From this alone it is evident that what blessed Epiphanius writes against Marcion is true: that he himself treats nothing from this Epistle, because Marcion had already perverted it excessively. PAM.] the heretic extinguished them, lest he should, of course, make Christ belong to our God. The futility of the erasure nevertheless shines through.

For when the Apostle writes that the Lord will come to exact vengeance upon those who do not know God and those who do not obey the Gospel—people whom he says will pay a penalty, [Note: [Col. 0510D] *A penalty, whom he says*, Latin edition.] namely, eternal destruction from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his might—it follows that he should introduce the flame of fire, since the Lord is coming to punish. Thus, even in this passage and against Marcion’s will, Christ belongs to the God who burns, [Col. 0510D] [Col. 0511A] [Note: [Col. 0511C] Pamelius omits *is*.] and in the other respect he belongs to the Creator, because he takes vengeance even upon those who do not know the Lord—that is, the Gentiles.

For the Apostle separately listed those who do not obey the Gospel, whether sinful Christians or Jews. Now to exact penalties from Gentiles who perhaps do not know the Gospel is not characteristic of Marcion’s god, who is naturally unknown, revealed nowhere except in the Gospel, and incapable of being known by everyone. Knowledge of the Creator, however, is owed even by nature: he is to be understood from his works, and from that point a fuller knowledge of him is to be sought. It therefore belongs to the Creator to punish even those ignorant of God, since it is not permissible for him to be unknown. [Note: [Col. 0511C] *To be ignorant*, Pamelius.]

The very words he uses—“From the face of the Lord and from the glory of his might”—are Isaiah’s words (Isa. II, 19), and for this very reason they savor of the same Lord “rising up to crush the earth.”

Who, moreover, is [Note: [Col. 0511D] *The man of offense.* He immediately explains sufficiently who the man of offense is: namely, Antichrist. By that name he calls the Marcionites, who appear to have perpetrated the same things that were foretold concerning Antichrist. LE PR.] “the man of offense, the son of perdition,” [Col. 0511B] who must be revealed before the Lord’s coming, “exalting himself above everything called God and every object of religion,” taking his seat [Note: [Col. 0511C] *Obtaining*, other editions.] in the temple of God and boasting that he himself is God?

According to us, he is Antichrist, as the old and new prophecies teach; so too the apostle John, who says that antichrists have already gone out into the world (1 John IV, 1–2), spirits who are forerunners of Antichrist, denying that Christ came in the flesh and dissolving Jesus—that is, dissolving him in relation to God the Creator. According to Marcion, however, I do not know whether he may be [Note: [Col. 0511C] *Unless he is the Christ*, Codex Wouwerianus; *whether he may be the Christ*, Semler.] the Creator’s Christ, since according to Marcion he has not yet [Note: [Col. 0511C] Pamelius omits *for*.] come.

Whichever of the two he is, [Note: [Col. 0511C] Franeker omits *is*.] I ask why he comes “with all power and signs and lying wonders.” “For this reason,” he says: “because they did not receive love of the truth so that they might be saved; and for this reason there will be [Note: [Col. 0511C] *He will give*, Latin edition.] for them an impulse of deception, so that [Col. 0511C] all who did not believe the truth but consented to injustice may be judged.”

Therefore, if he is [Note: [Col. 0511D] *And*, Pamelius.] Antichrist according to the Creator [Note: [Col. 0512C] *According to us, and God*, Codex Wouwerianus.], then God will be the Creator who sends him to drive into error those who did not believe the truth so that they might be saved. Both truth and salvation will belong to the same God who takes vengeance by sending error—that is, to the Creator, to whom this very jealousy appropriately belongs: to deceive by error those whom he did not win through truth.

But if he is not Antichrist according to us, then according to Marcion he is the Creator’s Christ. And how can it be fitting that, to avenge his own truth, Marcion’s god should subject Christ to the Creator? [Note: [Col. 0512C] *The Creator’s*, Codex Wouwerianus.]

But even if [Note: [Col. 0512C] Pamelius omits *if*.] Marcion agrees that the passage concerns Antichrist, I would similarly ask: [Col. 0512A] how is it that Antichrist needs Satan, an angel of the Creator, and is killed by him, while having the function of carrying out the operation of deception on the Creator’s behalf?

In sum, if it is beyond doubt that the angel, the truth, and salvation belong to the same God to whom wrath, jealousy, and the sending of deception against despisers and deserters also belong—even against those who are ignorant, so that Marcion must now retreat from his position and concede that God is also jealous—which God will more deservedly be angry?

I think it is the one who, from the beginning of things, prepared nature [Note: [Col. 0512C] *Of nature*, Codex Wouwerianus.] through works, benefits, plagues, proclamations, [Note: [Col. 0512C] *Of proclamations*, Pamelius.] and witnesses so that he might be recognized, and yet was not recognized. Or is it the one who was brought forward a single time through one solitary [Note: [Col. 0512C] *United*, Codex Wouwerianus.] instrument of the Gospel—an instrument itself uncertain and not openly proclaiming another God?

Thus, to the one to whom vengeance appropriately belongs, the grounds of vengeance will also belong: by which I mean the Gospel, truth, and salvation. [Col. 0512B] Moreover, the command that anyone who wishes to eat must work belongs to the discipline of the God who commanded that the ox treading out grain be left unmuzzled.

## CHAPTER XVII
By the truth of the Church, we possess this Epistle as sent to the Ephesians (*On the Epistle to the Ephesians*, I and II), not to the Laodiceans. [Note: [Col. 0511D] “Not to the Laodiceans.” Those certainly err who think that the Epistle which Tertullian here seems, on Marcion’s authority, to indicate was written to the Laodiceans; for the passages quoted are found in chapter IV of the Epistle to the Ephesians. [Col. 0512D] The error arose from a rather inaccurate interpretation of Colossians IV, where τὴν ἐκ Λαοδικείας occurs; for they translated it “the one which is addressed to the Laodiceans,” when it should have been translated “the one which is from the city of Laodicea.” The epistle circulated today appears apocryphal and spurious. Blessed Jerome speaks of that Epistle to the Laodiceans as false and deserving rejection; and some think that it is the First Epistle to Timothy, which was written at Laodicea. Marcion, however, had entitled “To the Laodiceans” the Epistle which for us is “To the Ephesians.” LE PR.] But Marcion at one time took delight in tampering with its title, as though in this matter too he were an exceptionally diligent investigator. Yet nothing depends upon titles, since, in writing to certain persons, the Apostle wrote to everyone; at any rate, he proclaims that God in Christ to whom the things proclaimed properly belong.

To whom, then, will it belong, according to the good pleasure which he purposed in the mystery of his will, for the dispensation of the fulfillment of the times—to “recapitulate” (if I may put it so, in accordance with the force of the Greek word), that is, to bring back to their beginning, or to review from [Col. 0512C] the beginning, all things in Christ, both those in heaven and those on earth—unless to him to whom all things have belonged from the beginning, including the beginning itself, from whom come both the times and the fulfillments of the times [Note: [Col. 0512D] Junius inserts “and.”], as well as the dispensation on account of which all things are reviewed from the beginning in Christ?

But what beginning—that is, what point of origin—belongs to another god, who has no work at all? What times can there be without a beginning? What fulfillment without times? What dispensation without a fulfillment? Finally, what did he do on earth long ago, so that some lengthy dispensation involving the fulfillment of times might be reckoned to him, for the purpose of reviewing all things in Christ, including those in heaven? Nor shall we suppose that the things which [Col. 0513A] exist in heaven were done by one being other than him by whom, as everyone agrees, the things on earth were done. But if all these things cannot be assigned from the beginning to anyone other than the Creator, who will believe that they are reviewed by another in another Christ, rather than by their own author and in his own Christ?

If they belong to the Creator, they must necessarily be different from a different god. If different, they are surely contrary. How, then, can contrary things be reviewed in him by whom they are ultimately destroyed? For the words which follow also declare which Christ he means, when he says, “That we should be to the praise of his glory, we who [Note: [Col. 0513D] “Have hoped beforehand in Christ”: a literal rendering of the Greek προηλπικότας, “those who have hoped beforehand.” LE PR.] have hoped beforehand in Christ.” For who could have “hoped beforehand,” that is, have hoped in God before he came, except the Jews, to whom Christ was announced beforehand from the beginning? The one who was announced beforehand, therefore, was also the one hoped for beforehand.

Indeed, he applies this to himself—that is, to the Jews—in such a way as to draw a distinction when he turns [Col. 0513B] to the nations: “In whom you also, after you had heard the word of truth, the Gospel, in whom you believed and were sealed with his Holy Spirit of promise.” Whose promise? The one made through Joel (*Joel* II): “In the last days I shall pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh”—that is, upon the nations also. Thus both the Spirit and the Gospel will belong to that Christ who was hoped for beforehand because he had been proclaimed beforehand.

Moreover, the “Father of glory” is he whose Christ is sung in the Psalm as the King of Glory ascending (*Ps.* XXIII, 10): “Who is this King of Glory? The Lord of hosts, he is the King of Glory.” From him the spirit of wisdom is sought, with whom these several forms of spiritual gift are also enumerated among the seven spirits through Isaiah (*Isa.* XI). He will give enlightened eyes of the heart who also enriched the outward eyes with light, and to whom the blindness of the people is displeasing (*Isa.* XLII, 19): [Col. 0513C] “And who is blind but my servants?” And: “The servants of God have been blinded.”

With him also are “the riches of the inheritance among the saints,” for he promised that inheritance through the calling of the nations (*Ps.* II, 8): “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance.” He worked his power in Christ by raising him from the dead, seating him at his right hand, and subjecting all things to him—the same one who also said (*Ps.* CIX): “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.” For elsewhere too the Spirit says to the Father concerning the Son (*Ps.* VIII, 7): “You have subjected all things beneath his feet.”

If, from these statements which are recognized as belonging to the Creator, another god and another Christ are inferred, let us now look for the Creator. Clearly, I think, we find him when the Apostle says that they were dead in the offenses in which they had walked, according to the age of this world, according to [Col. 0513D] “the prince of the power of this air” [Note: [Col. 0513D] Semler and Oberthür omit “of this.”], who works in the children of unbelief. But even here Marcion cannot interpret “the world” as “the god of the world.” A created thing is not identical with its creator, something made with its maker, or the world with God.

Nor will he who is the prince of the power of the ages be called the prince of the power of the air. For the ruler [Col. 0514A] of higher things is never designated from the lower, even though the lower things too are assigned to him. Nor can he be regarded as the agent of unbelief, since he himself rather suffers unbelief at the hands of Jews and nations. It is enough, therefore, that these descriptions do not fall upon the Creator. But if there is also someone to whom they are more applicable [Note: [Col. 0513D] Pamelius: “it is applicable.”], the Apostle certainly knew this better.

Who is he? Without doubt, the one who sets the children of unbelief in opposition to the Creator himself, having gained possession of this air, just as the prophet reports him as saying [Note: [Col. 0513D] Pamelius also reads: “puts him forward as saying.”] (*Isa.* XIV, 14): “I shall set my throne in the clouds; I shall be like the Most High.” This will be the devil, whom elsewhere also—if indeed they wish the Apostle to be read in that way—we shall recognize as “the god of this age.” For in this way he has filled the whole age with the lie of his divinity. Had he not existed, these statements could indeed have been understood as referring to the Creator.

Moreover, although the Apostle had lived within Judaism [Note: [Col. 0513D] Latinius adds “had.”], it does not follow, merely because [Col. 0514B] he inserted the words concerning the offenses “in which we too all once lived,” that the Creator must be understood as the lord of offenses and the prince of this air. Rather, while in Judaism, he had been one of the children of unbelief, having the devil as his operator when he persecuted the Church and the Creator’s Christ.

“For this reason,” he says, “we too were children of wrath—but by nature.” This was lest, because the Creator called the Jews his children, the heretic should argue [Note: [Col. 0514D] Junius adds “this.”] that the Creator is the lord of wrath. For when he says, “We were by nature children of wrath,” whereas the Jews are not the Creator’s children by nature but by the adoption of their fathers, he referred the “children of wrath” to nature, not to the Creator. To sum up, he adds, “Just as the rest also”—who certainly are not children of God. It is apparent that he ascribes offenses, the desires of the flesh, unbelief, and wrath to the common nature of all human beings [Note: [Col. 0514D] Pamelius: “to be ascribed.”], although the devil has laid hold of nature [Note: [Col. 0514D] “Although the devil has laid hold of nature.” Thus Dionysius Cato said in his *Distichs* that the miser “lays hold of the form of a denarius.” RIG.], [Col. 0514C] which he himself has now corrupted by introducing the seed of offense.

“We are,” he says, “his workmanship, created in Christ.” To make is one thing, to create another. Yet he assigned both to one and the same being. A human being, moreover, is the Creator’s workmanship. Therefore the same one created him in Christ who also made him. With respect to substance, he made him; with respect to grace, he created him.

Examine also the connected words: “Remember that you were formerly nations in the flesh, [Note: [Col. 0514D] Oberthür inserts “who.”] called the uncircumcision by what is called the circumcision in the flesh, made by hand; that you were at that time without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to their covenants and promise, having no hope and without God in the world.” Without which God, and without which Christ, were the nations? Surely the one to whom belonged the commonwealth of Israel, the covenants, and the promise.

“But now,” he says, “in Christ, [Col. 0514D] you who were far away have been brought near by his blood.” From whom had they formerly been far away? From those whom he named above: from the Creator’s Christ, from the commonwealth of Israel, from the covenants, from the hope of the promise, and from God himself. If these things are so, then the nations are now brought near in Christ to those from whom they had once been far away.

But if in Christ we have been brought near to the commonwealth of Israel, which consists in the religion of God the Creator, and to the covenants, the promise, and the God of Israel himself, it is quite ridiculous to suppose that the Christ of another god brought us from afar to the Creator. The Apostle remembered that the calling of the nations, who were to be called from afar, had been proclaimed thus (*Isa.* XLVI, 12): “Those who were far from me have drawn near to my righteousness.” For the Creator’s righteousness, no less than his peace, was announced in Christ, as we have often already shown.

Accordingly, “he himself,” the Apostle says, “is our peace, who made the two one”—namely, the Jewish people and the Gentile people, what was near and what was far—“by dissolving in his flesh the intervening wall of hostility.” But Marcion removed the word “his,” so as to assign the flesh to the hostility, as though it were hostile through carnal vice, rather than hostile to Christ. As I have said elsewhere, so too here: [Note: [Col. 0515D] “Not Marrucinian, but Pontic.” The Marrucini were peoples neighboring the Ferentani and Vestini in Italy outside Latium, and therefore barbarians and uncultivated; hence *Marrucinus* means ἀμαθής καὶ ἀναίθητος, “ignorant and senseless,” since the name was customarily used as an insult against stupid people. I would think that “cliff-dwellers” means almost the same as “Marrucinians”; Tertullian uses that word twice in chapter 4 of *On the Pallium*. Juvenal, Satire 2, says:

> The rustic crowd, their plows laid aside, would listen to Montanus.

LE PR.] [Col. 0515B] Not Marrucinian, but Pontic man: above you confessed his blood, but here you deny his flesh.

If he made the law of commandments void in its ordinances, he certainly did so by fulfilling the law. For “You shall not commit adultery” is now without further function when it is said, “You shall not even look with lust”; and “You shall not kill” is without further function when it is said, “You shall not even curse.” You cannot turn the law’s helper into its adversary.

“He created the two in himself”: the same one who had made them was also creating them, in accordance with what was said above: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ.” He made them “into one new human being, making peace.” If truly new, then truly a human being also, not an apparition; new, moreover, and born in a new way from a virgin, by the Spirit of God, “that he might reconcile both to God”—and to that God whom both races, Jewish and Gentile [Note: [Col. 0515D] Pamelius: “the Gentile people.”], had offended—“in one body,” he says, “when he had slain the hostility in it through the cross.”

Thus here too the flesh is a body in Christ, one which could suffer [Col. 0515C] the cross. When he had therefore announced peace to those who were near and to those who were far, and both together had obtained access to the Father, “we are no longer strangers or sojourners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household”—surely of that God from whom we showed above that we had been alienated and situated far away.

“You have been built upon the foundation of the apostles.” The heretic removed the words “and the prophets,” forgetting that the Lord appointed in the Church prophets as well as apostles. He was afraid, naturally, that [Note: [Col. 0515D] Rhenanus: “whether perhaps.”] our building in Christ might be established upon the foundations of the ancient prophets also, although the Apostle himself never ceases everywhere to build us up from the prophets. For where did he obtain the expression that Christ is “the chief cornerstone,” except from the signification of the Psalm (*Ps.* CXVII): “The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the chief cornerstone”? As for [Col. 0515D] the hands of a mutilating heretic, I am not surprised if he removes syllables, since he very often steals away whole pages. [Note: [Col. 0515D] Pamelius: “steals away.”]

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 0516A]

(*On the Epistle to the Ephesians*, III–VI.) The Apostle says that grace was given to him, the last of all, to enlighten everyone concerning “the dispensation of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things.” The heretic snatched away the preposition “in” and caused the passage to be read thus: “Hidden from the ages from the God who created all things.” But the falsehood leaps out. For the Apostle continues: “So that through the Church the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places.”

Whose principalities and powers does he mean? If the Creator’s, how can it be that the other god wished to display his wisdom to the Creator’s principalities and powers, but not to the Creator himself, when not even the powers could have learned anything without their own prince? Or, if he did not name God here because the prince himself is implicitly included among them, then he must also have declared that the mystery was hidden from the principalities and powers of him who created all things, likewise including God himself among them.

But if he says that it was hidden from them, he ought to have said that it was manifested to him. Therefore it was not hidden from God, but “in God, the Creator of all things”; it was hidden, however, from his principalities and powers (*Isa.* XL, 13): “For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” [Note: [Col. 0516D] “Here the heretic was caught.” This refers to Marcion; the passage requires no explanation from me. LE PR.]

Caught here, the heretic perhaps altered the text so as to say that his god wished to make the dispensation of his mystery known to his own powers and principalities, although the God who created all things had been ignorant of it. And how was it appropriate to allege the ignorance of an alien creator, separated from him by a long interval, when even the members of the higher god’s own household did not know it?

Nevertheless, it was also destined to become known to the Creator. Was it not surely known to him that the mystery was to be revealed beneath [Col. 0516C] heaven [Note: [Col. 0516D] Oberthür, following Semler, adds “and.”], on his earth? From this, therefore, what we established above is confirmed. For if the Creator was one day to learn that hidden mystery of the higher god, and if Scripture read, “Hidden from the God who created all things,” the Apostle ought to have continued thus: “So that the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to them”—then also to the powers and principalities of whichever god would learn it together with the Creator. It is therefore evident that something has been removed, since even in this form the text remains secure for its own truth.

Now I too wish to weave a controversy for you out of the Apostle’s allegories. What novel [Note: [Col. 0516D] Junius: “new”; the Vatican manuscript: “which we know that he had in the prophets.”] forms would he have had in the prophets? “He led captivity captive,” he says. With what weapons? In what battles? From the devastation of what nation? From the overthrow of what city? What women, what children, or what petty kings did the victor bind in chains?

For when Christ is sung in David (*Ps.* XLIV, 4) as girded with a sword upon his thigh, or in Isaiah (*Isa.* VIII) as taking the spoils of Samaria and the might of Damascus, you portray him as a genuine [Col. 0517A] and visible warrior. Now therefore recognize that his armor and warfare are spiritual, if you have now learned that the captivity is spiritual, so that you may recognize this captivity also as his; or recognize it because the Apostle took mention of this captivity from the prophets, from whom he also took his commandments:

“Putting away falsehood, let each one speak truth to his neighbor.” [Note: [Col. 0517C] Semler omits “his.”] And, “Be angry, and do not sin”—the very words in which the Psalm (*Ps.* IV, 5) expressed its meaning. “Let not the sun go down upon your anger.” “Have no fellowship with the works of darkness.” “For with the righteous you will be righteous, and with the perverse you will act perversely” (*Ps.* XVII, 27). And: “Remove the evil person from your midst” (*1 Cor.* V, 13). And: “Come out from among them, and do not touch what is unclean” (*2 Cor.* VI, 17). “Separate yourselves, you who carry the vessels [Col. 0517B] of the Lord” (*Isa.* LII, 11).

So too the command not to “be drunk with wine, in which is disgrace” [Note: [Col. 0517C] Rigaltius; the Venetian edition incorrectly reads “disgraceful.”], comes from the passage where those who made the saints drunk are rebuked: “You gave my saints wine to drink” (*Amos* II, 12)—the wine which Aaron the priest and his sons were forbidden to drink when they approached the holy things (*Deut.* XXII [reference as printed]). And to teach people to sing to God in psalms and hymns belongs to him who knew that those who drank wine accompanied by drums and harps were rebuked by God (*Isa.* XI, 12 [reference as printed]).

Thus, when I find someone’s commandments, the seeds of his commandments, or their enlargements, I recognize his apostle. But from where does he confirm that women ought to be subject to their husbands? “Because,” he says, “the man is the head of the woman.” Tell me, Marcion: does your god establish the authority of his law from the Creator’s work? This by now is clearly too little, since he also derives from it the constitution of his own Christ and his own Church: “Just as Christ is the head [Col. 0517C] of the Church.”

Likewise, when he says, “He who loves his wife [Note: [Col. 0517C] Oberthür omits “his.”] loves his own flesh, just as Christ loves the Church.” You see your Christ and your Church compared with the Creator’s work. How much honor is bestowed upon the flesh under the name of the Church! “No one,” he says, “hates his own flesh”—except, plainly, Marcion alone—“but he nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church.” But you alone hate it, taking resurrection away from it. You will also have to hate the Church, since it is loved in the same way by Christ.

But Christ loved the flesh as he loved the Church. No one will fail also to love the image of the bride; indeed, he will preserve, honor, and crown it. The likeness shares in the honor of the reality. Must I now labor to prove that the God of the man and of Christ, of the woman and of the Church, of flesh and of spirit, is the same, when the Apostle himself applies—and indeed expounds—the Creator’s declaration: “For this reason [Note: [Col. 0517C] Semler: “this.”] a man shall leave his father and mother, and the two shall become one flesh” [Note: [Col. 0518C] Oberthür: “in one flesh.”]? “This mystery is great.”

Amid all this, it is enough that the Creator’s mysteries are great in the Apostle’s estimation, though insignificant among the heretics.

[Note: [Col. 0517D] “But I speak,” he says, “with reference to Christ and the Church.” These are Paul’s words to the Ephesians, chapter V, where he treats of conjugal love and says that marriage is a mystery, and indeed a great one; but immediately he adds, ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω εἰς Χριστὸν καὶ εἰς τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν, “But I speak with reference to Christ and the Church.” “This mystery,” he says, “is great; but I speak with reference to Christ and the Church.” He indicates that the union of man and woman is a great mystery because it signifies and figures something great, extending to Christ and the Church. The Apostle exhorts spouses to love one another with that love, namely, by which one is made from two, so that both are one flesh and one soul. He says that this love is a figure and mystery—or type, image, and mirror—of Christ’s love toward the Church, which ought to cleave and be joined to her bridegroom in such a way that one is made from two and both are one; and therefore she should live and be governed while animated by no spirit other than Christ’s, so that Christ lives in her and she in Christ.

The Apostle therefore treats two matters. He shows that the marriage of man and woman was instituted by God so that one might be made from two; therefore a human being ought not to separate what God has joined, nor ought there to be divorce between spouses, for if one spouse divorces the other, one of them separates things which have been joined by God. This is Paul’s first point.

He then adds that harmony between spouses ought to be holy and chaste, since Christ takes from it an example, mystery, and likeness of his own love toward the Church, such as the love of a bridegroom toward his bride ought to be; and this love ought to be repaid according to the same example of love, such as that of a bride toward her bridegroom. Paul says that this comparison is a great mystery. This should certainly teach the shepherds τῆς καλλίστης ζώων ἀγέλης ἀνθρώπων, “of the noblest flock of living creatures, human beings,” to impress it again and again upon the minds of the faithful. RIG.]

“But I speak,” he says, “with reference to Christ and the Church.” The mystery receives an interpretation, not a separation. He shows that the figure of the mystery had been provided beforehand by him to whom the mystery itself certainly belonged.

[Col. 0518B] What does Marcion think? The Creator could not have provided figures beforehand for an unknown god, especially since that god was his adversary. But if he was known, the higher god ought not to have borrowed anything from the lower, especially for the purpose of destroying it.

Let children also obey their parents. For even if Marcion removed the words, “For this is the first commandment with a promise,” the Law says (*Exod.* XX): “Honor your father and mother.” And: “Parents, bring up your children in the discipline and correction of the Lord.” For you have also heard it said to the ancients: “You shall recount these things in the ears of your children, and your children likewise in the ears [Note: [Col. 0518C] Pamelius: “into the ears.”] of their children.” Why now give me two gods, if there is one discipline? And if there are two, I shall follow the one who taught first.

But if our struggle is against “world-rulers,” oh, how many creator gods there now are! Why should I not also insist that a single “world-ruler” ought to have been named if the Creator was meant, since the powers mentioned beforehand would have belonged to him? Moreover, since above the Apostle commands us to put on the armor in which we may stand against the machinations of the devil, he has already shown that the things he adds after the devil—the powers and world-rulers of this darkness—belong to the devil, as we too assign them to the devil.

Or, if the devil is the Creator, who will be the devil under the Creator? Are there two devils, just as [Note: [Col. 0518C] Semler: “if.”] there are two gods, and powers and [Note: [Col. 0518D] “Against the world-rulers.” The Vulgate has “rulers of the world”; but since Tertullian preserves the etymology, not without a certain scrupulousness, he thus translates the Greek κοσμοκράτορας, “world-rulers.” [Col. 0519D] It signifies a demon; and by those “world-rulers,” he presently means “spiritual forces of wickedness,” translating πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας. LE PR.] world-rulers in the plural?

[Col. 0519A] But how can the Creator be at once both the devil and God, when the devil is not both God and devil in the same respect? Either both are gods, if both [Note: [Col. 0519C] Oberthür omits “both.”] are now devils; or else the one who is God here is not the devil, just as the devil is not God.

I ask from what act of denunciation the very term “devil,” or “slanderer,” can apply to the Creator. Perhaps he denounced some intention of the higher god, since he himself suffered denunciation from the archangel—and a lying denunciation at that. For he had not forbidden the taste of that little tree to prevent them from becoming gods, but to prevent them from dying through transgression.

Nor did “spiritual forces of wickedness” signify the Creator merely because the Apostle added “in the heavens.” For the Apostle also knew that spiritual wickedness had been committed in the heavens by the angels who stumbled because of the daughters of human beings (*Gen.* VI).

And what sense would it make [Note: [Col. 0519D] Oberthür: “made.”] for him to censure the Creator through ambiguities and I know not what riddles, when, although already placed in chains because of his freedom in preaching, he surely afforded the Church an example of constancy in manifesting the mystery through the opening of his mouth—the constancy that he there instructed it to request from God?

## CHAPTER XIX

(*On the Epistle to the Colossians*.) In my prescription against all heresies, I am accustomed to establish a concise argument from the testimony of chronology, claiming priority for our rule over every later heresy. The Apostle will now prove this too when he says: “Concerning the hope laid up in heaven, which you heard in the word of the truth of the Gospel, which has come to you, just as it has throughout the whole world.” For if even then the Gospel tradition had flowed everywhere, how much more has it done so now!

Moreover, if what flowed everywhere is ours rather than that of any heresy—much less that of Marcion in the age of Antoninus [Note: [Col. 0519D] Rigaltius: “Antonian.”]—then ours will be the apostolic tradition. But even when Marcion’s tradition has filled the whole world, it will not even then be able to defend itself as apostolic. For even so it will be established that the apostolic tradition is the one which first filled the world—with the Gospel, namely, of that God who also sang these words concerning its proclamations (*Ps.* XVIII, 4): “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

He calls Christ “the image of the invisible God.” But we too call the Father of Christ invisible, knowing that the Son was always seen in former times—if anyone was seen in the name of God—as the Father’s image. Thus Marcion must not tear apart, on this ground also, a distinction between a visible and an invisible god, since from of old the declaration of our God has been (*Exod.* [Col. 0520A] XXXIII, 20): “No one will see God [Note: [Col. 0519D] Rhenanus: “the Lord.”] and live.”

If Christ is not “the firstborn of creation,” as the Creator’s Word through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made; if in him all things were not created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers; if all things were not created through him and in him—for these statements ought to have displeased Marcion—the Apostle surely would not have stated so unreservedly: “And he is before all.”

For how is he before all persons if he is not before all things? How is he before all things if he is not [Note: [Col. 0519D] “The firstborn of creation”: that is, the firstborn of all things formed and created by God. RIG.] the firstborn of creation, if he is not the Creator’s Word? From what will it be proved that he existed before everyone, when he appeared after everything? Who knows that someone existed earlier when he did not know that he existed at all?

Likewise, how did it please God that all fullness should dwell in him? First, what is [Col. 0520B] this fullness, unless it consists of those things which Marcion removed—the things created in Christ, in heaven and on earth, angels and human beings; unless it consists of those invisible and visible things, of thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers?

Or if our pseudo-apostles and Judaizing evangelists inserted these things on their own authority, and assigned them to the fullness of Marcion’s god, who created nothing, then what sense does it make for the Creator’s rival and destroyer to have wished the Creator’s fullness to dwell in his own Christ?

Finally, to whom does he “reconcile all things in himself, making peace through the blood of his cross,” unless to the one whom all those things [Note: [Col. 0520D] Oberthür: “all things.”] had offended, against whom they had rebelled through transgression, and to whom they had most recently belonged? For they could be conciliated to a stranger; but they could be reconciled to no one except their own master.

Thus he also restores us, who were once “alienated and enemies in mind through evil [Col. 0520C] works,” to favor with the Creator, against whom we had committed offense by worshiping the creation in opposition to the Creator.

Whenever, moreover, he says that the Church is the body of Christ—as here he says that he “fills up what remains of the afflictions of Christ in his flesh, for his body, which is the Church”—you must not on that account transfer every mention of “body” away from the substance of the flesh. For above he also says that we were reconciled “in his body through death”—surely in that body in which he could die through the flesh. He died not through the Church, but certainly for the Church, exchanging one “body” for another: the carnal for the spiritual.

But when he warns [Note: [Col. 0519D] One must beware of subtle argumentation and philosophy. Tertullian cited this passage of the Apostle in more than one place, though in a different form; for in *On Prescription*, chapter 7, he spoke of this philosophical vanity, and elsewhere he calls philosophers the patriarchs of the heretics. What that philosophy was would be doubtful if the Fathers did not indicate the Peripatetic philosophy, which, although it gained strength among Catholics through corrupt custom, nevertheless supplied the Carpocratians and the Gnostics with weapons for disturbing the truth. Saint Ambrose in *On Duties*, and Origen against Celsus, show that the sect founded upon Epicurus’s doctrine was more pernicious.

Moreover, during the reign of Philip Augustus, when a council was convened against the heresy of Amalric, Rigordus testifies in his *Deeds of Philip Augustus* that Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, only recently brought into Gaul from Greece, was burned. And, as something to be noted in favor of the Peripatetics, I remember reading in Alexander Neckam’s work *On the Nature of Things* that learned men at that time held the opinion that they freely declared that Antichrist alone [Col. 0521D] could understand Aristotle’s books, which he would use to refute those who were to dispute against him. LE PR.] against subtle argumentation, philosophy, and [Note: [Col. 0520D] Pamelius: “and.”] empty deception, which is [Note: [Col. 0520D] Par.: “arises.”] “according to [Col. 0521A] the elements of the world,” he does not mean according to heaven or earth, but according to secular learning; and “according to tradition,” namely, the tradition of human subtle reasoners and philosophers.

It would indeed take too long, and belong to another work, to show that by this declaration all heresies are condemned, since they are all constructed from the resources of subtle argumentation and the rules of philosophy. But let Marcion recognize the principal boundary of his faith as coming from the school of Epicurus: he introduces a sluggish Lord so that he may say that the Lord is not to be feared; he places matter alongside God the Creator, borrowing from the portico of the Stoics; and he denies the resurrection of the flesh, on which likewise no philosophy agrees.

Our truth is so far removed from their inventions that it fears to provoke the wrath of God, trusts that he brought forth all things from nothing, promises that he will restore the selfsame flesh, and is not ashamed that Christ [Col. 0521B] was born from the womb of a virgin, although philosophers, heretics, and pagans themselves laugh. For God chose the foolish things of the world (*1 Cor.* I) to confound the wise—without doubt that God who, in view of this arrangement of his, had threatened beforehand that he would destroy the wisdom of the wise.

With this simplicity of truth, which is contrary to subtle argumentation and philosophy, we can entertain no perverse belief. Finally, if God gives us life together with Christ by forgiving our offenses, we cannot believe that offenses are forgiven by one against whom they were never committed, since he was formerly unknown.

Come now, when he says, “Let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a feast day, a new moon, or Sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come, but the body is Christ’s,” what do you think, Marcion? We are no longer reopening the question of the Law, except to note that here too he teaches how it has been set aside: namely, by being transferred from shadow to body—that is, from figures to the reality, which is Christ.

Therefore both the shadow and the body belong to the same one; that is, both his Law [Note: [Col. 0521D] Pamelius: “light.”] and his Christ. Assign the Law to one [Note: [Col. 0521D] Semler adds “God.”] and Christ to another god, if you can separate a shadow from the body whose shadow it is. Christ plainly belongs to the Law, if he is the body belonging to its shadow.

If, moreover, he censures certain people who, on the basis of angelic visions, were saying that one must abstain from foods—“Do not touch, do not taste”—and who wished to walk in humility of mind while not holding fast to the head, he does not on that account strike at the Law and Moses as though Moses had established the prohibition of certain foods on the basis of angelic superstition. For it is established that Moses received the Law from God.

Finally, he assigned this discipline “according to the commandments,” he says, “and doctrines of human beings,” to those who did not hold fast to the head [Col. 0521D]—that is, to Christ himself, in whom all things are reviewed and recalled to their beginning, including matters indifferent in respect of foods.

As for the remaining commandments, since they are the same, let it suffice that elsewhere we have already shown how they flowed from the Creator. When he proclaimed that the old things would pass away and that he would make all things new, and also commanded (*Jer.* IV, 3), “Break up for yourselves a new fallow ground,” he was already then teaching people to put off the old human being and put on the new (*On the Epistle to the Philippians*).

## CHAPTER XX
When he enumerates the variety in preaching—how some, encouraged by confidence arising from his bonds, proclaimed the word more boldly; others through envy and contention; some, indeed, from esteem for the word [Note: [Col. 0521D] “Good esteem,” Lat.]; most from love; some from rivalry; and still others from hostility preached Christ—this surely would have been the place to censure the preaching itself for a diversity of doctrine that produced so great a diversity even of dispositions. Yet, since he presents only the motives of their dispositions as diverse, and not the rules of the mysteries, he confirms that there is nevertheless one Christ and one God of Christ, whatever the purpose [Col. 0522B] with which he is preached. And therefore he says: “It matters nothing to me whether Christ is proclaimed from pretext or in truth,” because it was one and the same Christ who was proclaimed, whether from pretext or from the truth of faith. For he referred the mention of truth to the faithfulness of the preaching, not to the rule itself: the rule was indeed one, but the faith of some of the preachers was true—that is, sincere—while that of others was overly sophisticated.

Since this is so, it is evident that the Christ who was preached was the one who had always been proclaimed. For if another Christ, far removed from the Apostle’s, had been introduced, the novelty of the matter would have created a doctrinal difference. Nor would there have been lacking those who would nevertheless have interpreted the evangelical preaching as referring to the Creator’s Christ, since even today, in every place, those who hold our doctrine are more numerous than those who hold the heretical one. Therefore neither here [Note: [Col. 0521D] *So that not*, Pam.; *because neither*, Lat.; *indeed neither*, others.] would the Apostle have remained silent [Col. 0522C] about identifying and rebuking the difference. Thus, since the difference is not even censured, the novelty is not established.

The Marcionites plainly suppose that the Apostle supports them here also concerning the substance of Christ, namely, that the flesh in Christ was a phantom, when he says that, being constituted in the form of God, [Note: [Col. 0521D] “He did not consider equality with God a robbery.” If Christ’s body had been phantasmal, none [Col. 0522D] of these things would have happened to him, nor would he have undergone death. This passage proves the point at length and departs slightly from the Vulgate, for *pariari* means “to be equal,” Greek εἶναι ἴσα (“to be equal”); and “he emptied himself,” that is, “he cast himself down,” Greek ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσε, “he made himself empty.” LE PR.] he did not consider equality with God a robbery, but emptied himself, taking the form—not the reality—of a servant; being in the likeness of a human being, but not actually human; and being found in the figure of a human being, but not in human substance, that is, not in flesh—as though figure, likeness, and form did not also belong to substance.

It is well, however, that elsewhere he also calls Christ “the image of the invisible God.” Is Christ, then, not truly God here also, because he places him in the form of God? Equally, Christ will not truly be a human being if, when constituted in the form of a human being, he was not truly human. For in both cases reality must necessarily [Col. 0522D] be excluded if form, likeness, and figure [Note: [Col. 0522D] *Cura*, Venet., erroneously.] are claimed for a phantom. But if, in the form and image in which the Son of the Father was proclaimed truly to be God [Note: [Col. 0522D] *Was prejudged*, Ober.], he was likewise, in the form and image of a human being, in which he is the Son of Man, found truly to be a human being—for the Apostle used “found” deliberately, meaning [Col. 0523A] “most certainly a human being,” since whatever is found is established as existing—so too he was found to be God through power, just as he was found to be human through flesh. For the Apostle would not have declared him subject to death if he had not been constituted in a mortal substance.

Still stronger is what he added: “Even the death of the cross.” For he would not have intensified [Note: [Col. 0523B] *Would have intensified*, Lat.] the horror of the death by extolling the virtue of submission [Note: [Col. 0523B] *Collection*, Rhen.], if he had known that submission to be imaginary in a phantom, which had mocked death rather than experienced it, and had not exercised virtue in suffering but merely played a game.

The things that he had formerly counted as gain, and which he also enumerates above—the glory of the flesh, the mark of circumcision, descent as a Hebrew from Hebrews, the title of the tribe of Benjamin, and the distinction of Pharisaic purity—he now counts as loss to himself: not God, but the dullness of the Jews. He regards these things as dung in comparison with the knowledge of Christ, not in comparison with the rejection [Col. 0523B] of God the Creator, having righteousness no longer his own, which comes from the Law, but that which comes through him, namely Christ, from God.

“Therefore,” you say, “by this distinction the Law was not from Christ’s God.” Subtle enough. Then receive an even subtler answer. For when he says, “Not that which comes from the Law, but that which comes through him,” he would not have said “through him” of anyone other than him whose Law it was.

“Our citizenship,” he says, “is in heaven.” I recognize the Creator’s ancient promise to Abraham (Gen. XXII, 17): “And I will make your seed like the stars in heaven.” Therefore also “star differs from star in glory.”

But if Christ, coming from heaven, will transform [Col. 0524A] the body of our humiliation so that it conforms to the body of his glory, then this body of ours, which is humiliated in sufferings and cast down [Note: [Col. 0523B] *In* deleted by Ciacc.] to the earth under the very law of death, will rise again. For how will he transform it [Note: [Col. 0523B] *Transformed*, Venet.; *will have transformed*, Rig.; *will be transformed*, Pam.] if it will not exist? Or, if this was said [Note: [Col. 0523C] “Those who are found in the flesh at the coming of God will have to be reckoned.” Rather, “to be changed,” which he will presently call “to be transformed.” RIG.] of those who, being found in the flesh at God’s coming, will have to be reckoned [Note: [Col. 0524B] *To be changed*, others; *to be caressed*, Lat.], [Note: [Col. 0523D] What will those who rise first do? In a similar construction Paul said, “What will those do who are baptized [Col. 0524C] for the dead?” RIG.] what will those who rise first do? Will they have nothing from which they may be transformed? Yet, he says, “Together with them we shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord.” If we are taken up with them, then surely we shall also be transformed with them.

## CHAPTER XXI

*(On the Epistle to Philemon.)* This Epistle alone profited from its brevity, so as to escape Marcion’s falsifying hands. Yet I wonder, since he accepted a letter written [Col. 0524B] to one individual, why he rejected the two addressed to Timothy and the one to Titus, which were composed concerning the ordering of the Church. He wished, I suppose, to tamper even with the number of the Epistles.

Remember, reader, that we have also proved from the Apostle the matters treated earlier; and if any matters had been deferred to this work, [Note: [Col. 0524C] *Expunxerimus*: that is, “we have discharged what was owed and fulfilled it.” Thus in the preceding Book IV: “And if we are reminded,” he says, “of the promise to Moses, it will be found discharged here.” RHEN.] we have discharged them. Thus you should neither regard as superfluous the repetition here by which we have confirmed our former hope, nor consider suspicious the postponement there by which we have brought these present occasions to light. If [Note: [Col. 0524B] *But*, Fran.] you inspect the entire little work, you will judge that there is neither redundancy here nor lack of confidence there.

[Col. 0523]

# THE BOOK OF QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN AGAINST THE VALENTINIANS

## Preface

[Col. 0523D] Tertullian (*On Prescription*, chap. 30) and Theodoret (*On Heretical Fables*, Book I) affirm that the heresy of Valentinus broke forth under Antoninus Pius, who assumed the imperial power in the year 138. Valentinus was a native of Phrebonis, on the maritime coast of Egypt, a follower of Platonic philosophy, imbued with the arts and inventions of the Greeks and—as his followers boasted (in Origen, *Dialogue Against Marcion*)—a hearer of Theodas, a disciple of the Apostle Paul. Massuet (*Dissertation* [Col. 0524D] *on Irenaeus*, no. 7) judges that Valentinus was born in the year of Christ 85 and died in 158.

Valentinus is said to have written several psalms, as well as letters cited by Clement of Alexandria in Books II and III of the *Stromata*. One of those letters is entitled *To Agathopous, the Antiochene Deacon*, as Grabe and Cave suppose. Valentinus also published homilies and a work entitled Πόθεν τὰ κακά, that is, *Whence Come Evils?* Fragments of this work survive in the aforementioned Clement, Book VI, and in [Col. 0525A] Epiphanius, Heresy XXXI. No one except the author of the final nine chapters of the book *On Prescription* reports that he wrote a gospel of his own. He defected from the Catholic Church because he was unable to obtain the episcopate for which he burned with desire, as Tertullian relates against the same Valentinus in chapter IV.

After leaving Alexandria, Valentinus came to Rome during the episcopate of Hyginus and remained there until that of Anicetus. Besides St. Irenaeus, Tertullian, Epiphanius, and Theodoret, Massuet (*ibid.*, in the same Dissertation), Natalis Alexander (*Ecclesiastical History*, Century II, chap. 2, art. 6), Beausobre (*History of the Manichaeans*, part II, Book V), Semler (*First Volume of Baumgarten’s Polemics*), Walch (*History of Heresy*, vol. I), and Ittig (*Dissertation* [Col. 0525B] *on the Heresiarchs*, sect. II, chap. 5, and the same author’s dissertation appended to sect. II, chap. 5) write at greater length about the Valentinians; and, more recently, Matter (*History of Gnosticism*, vol. II).

Although the fabulous heresy of Valentinus appears utterly absurd from its mere description, there were nevertheless some who considered Valentinus himself orthodox, such as the Abbé Faydit, who published a *Clarification of the Doctrine of the Early Centuries*. Beausobre likewise inserted much into his *History of the Manichaeans* to polish and improve Valentinus’s system (Lumper, *Critical Theological History of the Life, Writings, and Doctrine of the Holy Fathers*, part III, sect. IV, chap. 3, preliminary dissertation, art. 1).

Moreover, it is more certain than certainty itself that Tertullian, while composing his book against the Valentinians, had before his eyes the ancient and commonly circulated Latin translation of St. Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, [Col. 0525C] *Books Against Heresies*. That translation, preserved down to our own time, is known to have been published either while Irenaeus himself was still alive or shortly after his death. Whoever compares the Latin Irenaeus with Tertullian will readily discover that the latter follows the former’s footsteps so closely, adheres so closely to his very words, figures of speech, and order, that he seems to have set himself the single task of condensing the same material into fewer words. He often preserves the same language, though he intermingles, according to his custom, biting remarks expressed with a certain impudence characteristic of an African temperament. Compare Irenaeus, Book I, chap. 11, no. 3, with Tertullian, chap. 23, and Irenaeus, no. 5, with Tertullian, chap. 25, etc. See Massuet, Dissertation II on Irenaeus’s books, no. 55, pp. 89–90.

We have taken care diligently to collect the many similar passages scattered here and there [Col. 0525D] and to place them in the notes, so that the reader may compare them more easily. Nor, unless I am mistaken, will it now remain doubtful to anyone that Irenaeus preceded Tertullian. Johann Salomo Semler was therefore wrong to call these matters into question and reject the books [Col. 0526A] as spurious—a man who, if anyone ever was, seems truly to have been born to cast down nearly all the monuments of venerable antiquity from their authority on his own authority. For in his *Historical Introduction to Baumgarten’s Polemics* (vol. II, p. 131), in his *Discourse on Avoiding Troublesome Sacred Zeal in Correcting Certain Opinions of Irenaeus and Tertullian* (Halle edition, 1772), and in the *Dissertation on the Variable and Uncertain Character of These Books* appended to the Halle edition of Tertullian (vol. V, pp. 245–290, Halle-Magdeburg edition, 1828), he attempted to diminish the credibility of Irenaeus and to bring his books under suspicion of νοθεία (*spuriousness*).
