The celebrated Walch, theologian of Göttingen, undertook their defense in the *New Commentaries of the Royal Society of Sciences of Göttingen* (vol. V, part 100, [Col. 0526B] years 1774–1775; Lumper, work cited, chap. II, art. 1, p. 218). THE EDITORS.

[Col. 0526B] Moreover, that this book against the Valentinians belongs to Tertullian is established even from the fact that in chapter XVI he expressly mentions the book *Against Hermogenes*, which is known to be his. And indeed clear witnesses that he wrote against the Valentinians are the blessed Optatus of Milevis, Book I *Against Parmenian the Donatist*, and Vincent of Lérins, in his book *On the Profane Novelty of Heresies*. A manuscript was also seen long ago by Trithemius and Politian, and it was among the first works edited by Rhenanus, who illustrated it first with scholia and then with annotations, with such care as he displayed nowhere else.

Nevertheless, the reader will easily gather that this latest recension of ours is not to be despised, from the annotations that we have added for still greater illumination, drawing upon St. Irenaeus, Book I, chapter 1 and several [Col. 0526C] following chapters—both the Greek text preserved in Epiphanius and the Latin text in its various versions—as well as three Vatican manuscript copies; and from the clearer Argument, and indeed the Catalogue of the Aeons and the diagram of their respective positions. PAMELIUS.

A more suitable occasion will certainly present itself for a fuller discussion of the immense medley of ΓΝΩΣΕΩΣ (*gnōseōs*, “of knowledge/gnosis”) in general, and of the difficult Valentinian theme in particular, when we come to discuss Irenaeus’s most excellent books *Against Heresies*. For us, therefore, according to our custom and modest capacity, let it suffice to have offered these few remarks in advance by way of preface, and to add a few items drawn from various sources, whether Pamelius or Massuet. By these, before we approach this book—admittedly obscure and almost impenetrable to understanding—the [Col. 0526D] reader may be furnished with preliminary illumination both by an interpretation of the names of Valentinus’s Aeons and by an ordered scheme of the gnosis constructed according to his hypothesis. THE EDITORS.

## NAMES OF VALENTINUS’S AEONS AND GODS—OR RATHER OF CRIMES THAN DIVINITIES—AND OF OTHER THINGS PERTAINING TO THE SAME SYSTEM

*(From the edition of Pamelius.)*

[Col. 0525]

[Col. 0525D] Concerning these names, Tertullian speaks as follows below, in chapter 6:

> For some of them, he says, no Greek interpretation readily occurs; in others, the grammatical genders do not correspond to their sex; and for still others the Greek form is more familiar. Accordingly, we shall for the most part give the Greek; the meanings will be supplied in the margins of the pages. Nor will the Greek forms be lacking even for the Latin names, but will be marked above the lines.

[Col. 0527] Thus far Tertullian. Since, however, neither Rhenanus nor I found this done in the manuscript codices, it seemed advantageous, for greater understanding, to place this Catalogue of Names at the beginning. I have now both enlarged it and arranged it in the proper order, adding, for the sake of fuller explanation, the numbers of the chapters in which the individual names are discussed. I have also indicated which forms are used here or elsewhere by Tertullian, which by the Latin Irenaeus in Book I *Against Heresies*, chapter I, and which, finally, by the Greek Epiphanius in Heresy XXXI or by his Latin translator. Several names have also been corrected from these sources. PAMELIUS.

## NAMES OF THE THIRTY AEONS

## NAMES OF THE REALMS IN WHICH THE INDIVIDUAL AEONS ARE STATIONED, CHAPTERS XXIII, XXIV, XXV

## NAMES OF THE CREATURES FASHIONED BY THE DEMIURGE AND ACHAMOTH, CHAPTERS XX, XXII, XXV

## GNOSTIC SCHEME DRAWN FROM THE FABLES OF VALENTINUS AND HIS DISCIPLES

[Col. 0533]

## Synopsis

[Col. 0535]

[Col. 0535A] Intending to write against the Valentinian heretics, Tertullian postpones direct engagement and declares that he will merely recount their errors—or rather, their fables—with ridicule.

First, he relates that the Valentinians, certainly the most numerous association among the heretics, take greater care over nothing than concealing what they preach. Chapter I.

Next, since they called Catholics “simple,” he teaches that simplicity is approved by the Scriptures. Chapter II.

However much they hide themselves in the meantime—whereas truth, by contrast, feels no shame—ordinary Christians nevertheless know all their fables and genealogies, which the Apostle condemns as endless. Consequently, merely to display them is to destroy them. Chapter III.

The origin of the Valentinians from Valentinus is also well known, [Col. 0535B] although Ptolemy, Heracleon, Secundus, Marcus the Magician, and Theotinus departed from him. Thus Valentinus is now found nowhere, and yet there are Valentinians named after him, while only a certain Axionicus at Antioch preserved his rules in their entirety. Chapter IV.

Meanwhile, Tertullian declares that his dispute is with the original authorities and that he does not rely upon fabricated materials, since contemporaries of the heresiarch himself—Justin Martyr, Miltiades, Irenaeus, and a certain Proculus—disclosed and reported them in most fully documented volumes. Chapter V.

Then, in words quoted partly at the beginning of this Summary and partly beneath it below, he promises only an exposition of their secret doctrine and indicates the method he has decided to employ. Chapter VI.

He begins with the first Ogdoad of the Valentinian Aeons, or [Col. 0535C] the double Tetrad, in which Nous (*Mind*) and Truth were born from Bythos (*Depth*) and Sige (*Silence*); Nous and Truth produced Word and Life, and from these came Human Being and Church. Chapter VII.

Then, from that second Tetrad, Word and Life poured forth a Decad of Aeons together, while Human Being and Church produced the number twelve, so that the Pleroma, or Fullness, of the thirtyfold divinity was thus completed. Chapter VIII.

Then, when all fecundity had failed, Sophia, the final Aeon, was restrained by Horos (*Limit*) so that she would not dissolve; and, from the violence of her passion, without any act of conjugal union, she brought forth an aborted offspring, Enthymesis (*Thought*), which was exposed. Chapter IX.

Meanwhile, at the entreaty of the whole kindred, Sophia was restored to her consort Theletos, but Enthymesis was banished outside the Pleroma. Chapter X.

Therefore, lest any such disturbance recur, [Col. 0535D] that Nous produced a new pair: Christ and the Holy Spirit. Chapter XI.

Then, from all the Aeons together, there was fashioned Jesus, the perfect fruit of the Pleroma, whom they also call Soter (*Savior*), Christ, and Word; and the angels were fashioned as his attendants. Chapter XII.

And thus far, says the author in jest, extends the first scene of the tragedy; now comes another performance in tragic buskins outside the Pleroma. Chapter XIII.

For Enthymesis—now bearing the new and interpretable name [Col. 0536A] Achamoth—was expelled into that void of Epicurus. Although she had already been given form by Christ, who had been sent down from above together with the Holy Spirit, she nevertheless could not reach the light of the Pleroma. Excluded by Horos, who guarded its outermost boundary, she was afflicted by grief, fear, consternation, and ignorance. Chapter XIV.

From these, they say, matter—which the Pythagoreans, Stoics, and Plato himself hold to be ungenerated—and the very elements derived their origin. Chapter XV.

She then turned to prayer; and when the Paraclete, Soter Jesus, was sent to her, she was again strengthened and cleansed of all the injuries of passion. From that conversion she produced the corporeal realities of the psychic order. Chapter XVI.

Thereafter, out of joy arising from the contemplation of Soter and of the angelic lights that had come with him, she produced the spiritual realities; and thus the trinity of kinds came into being. Chapter XVII.

Then from psychic substance was produced the Demiurge, this God of ours, king of all things. Chapter XVIII.

They are not, however, in agreement among themselves about this matter. Chapter XIX.

Next, the Demiurge, stationed outside the boundaries of the Pleroma, fashioned this world from psychic and material substances, but from incorporeal substances he fashioned the sevenfold stage of the heavens. Chapter XX.

Amid these matters Tertullian occasionally inserts the various names of Achamoth, or the second Sophia. Chapter XXI.

Indeed, they even make the devil a work of the Demiurge, calling him the Munditenens (*World-Holder*). Chapter XXII.

Then, after inserting an account of the position of the individual powers, he adds fire, fanned into all these bodies and elements. Chapter XXIII.

After this, the Demiurge set his hands to the human being and created flesh for him, not from the mud of the earth, but from that philosophical matter. Chapter XXIV.

When the Demiurge then imparted a soul to him from his own breath, spiritual seed was likewise channeled into him by Achamoth; this they called the Church. Chapter XXV.

From this Tertullian describes the three kinds of human beings, or the trinity within the human being, and the end allotted to each. Chapter XXVI.

They also teach that the Demiurge sent forth Christ, his natural Son, through the Virgin, though he was not produced from the Virgin; and that Soter descended upon him in the form of a dove and remained impassible in Christ, while the psychic Christ suffered. Chapter XXVII.

The better souls, too, were selected for the prophets, priests, and kings. Chapter XXVIII.

They establish three kinds of human beings: the choic or earthly, the psychic, and the spiritual. Chapter XXIX.

For the spiritual—whom they boast themselves to be—works are unnecessary, though they are necessary for us, insofar as we are psychics, that is, animal human beings. In this way they also evade the necessity of martyrdom. Chapter XXX.

And indeed, at the consummation the reward is allotted in such a way that Achamoth is transferred from the middle story into the Pleroma, where Soter, that composite bridegroom, receives her; while the Demiurge is transferred from his celestial Hebdomad into the empty place formerly occupied by his mother. Chapter XXXI.

The human race, however, will proceed to the following ends: souls of the choic and material class will perish; the souls of righteous psychics—that is, our souls—will be sent into the dwelling places of that intermediate region; and finally the souls of the spiritual—that is, of the Valentinians themselves—will be conducted into the palace of the Pleroma and taken as brides by the angels. Chapter XXXII.

Ptolemy’s revisers differ from Valentinus on this point: they assign two consorts to Bythos, Thought and Will, with Truth arising from Thought and Only-Begotten from Will. Chapter XXXIII.

There are also others who either assign no sex to Bythos or make him a hermaphrodite. Chapter XXXIV.

There is likewise someone who maintains that Bythos holds not the first but the last position, coming after the first Ogdoad, which was itself derived from a Tetrad, though under different names. Chapter XXXV.

[Col. 0538A] Some teach that from the father Bythos and the mother Ennoea (*Thought*) that entire Ogdoad was delivered in a single birth. Chapter XXXVI.

Likewise, another makes Monotes (*Singularity*) and Henotes (*Unity*) the first parents, from whom came Monas (*Monad*) and Henosis (*Union*), and from these the remaining Aeons. Chapter XXXVII.

Finally there is the more humane Secundus, who divides the two Tetrads into right and left, light and darkness, but holds that the defecting power, namely Achamoth, was not derived from any of the Aeons. Chapter XXXVIII.

Lastly, there is still greater disagreement about Jesus himself. Valentinus maintains that he was fashioned from the little blossoms of all the Aeons; others from only the ten or only the twelve; others from Christ and the Holy Spirit alone; and still others from some different source. Thus the doctrines of the Valentinians have now grown wild into whole forests [Col. 0538B] of Gnostics. Chapter XXXIX.

## CHAPTER I
[Note: [Col. 0537B] At the very beginning of this chapter we encounter some of Tertullian’s most intricate words, if ever there were any—words still thickly scattered with obscurity, although illuminated by frequent commentaries from the most learned men and emended through innumerable [Col. 0537C] attempts at variant readings. For our part, we have striven, as best we could, to mend and restore the text by comparing the recensions of the editions of Rhenanus, Scaliger, Pamelius, Casaubon, Petavius, Salmasius, Rigaltius, Priorius, Junius, Latinius, Franeker, Paris, Venice, Halle, and Würzburg. We have also used two corrections inserted by the distinguished scholars Lobeck and Séguier de Saint-Brisson—the former in his celebrated *Aglaophamus*, vol. I, book I, § V, and the latter in a recent work known to rather few scholars, entitled *Essay on Polytheism*, vol. II, p. 105 ff.

But, setting aside—or at least postponing until later—an investigation of the text we have presented, and excluding the excessive bulk of a laborious commentary, we have thought it best to proceed as quickly as possible to a brief exposition of the clearer and sounder meaning of Septimius in this preface. We consider it to be as follows:

“The Valentinians—whose association must plainly be the largest among the heretics, both because it has retained very many doctrines of the faith it renounced, because it readily inclines toward popular fables, and because it is not deterred by a harsher discipline—care about nothing more than concealing what they preach, if indeed those who conceal can be said to preach, or to be preaching at all. For among them the anxious duty of guarding a secret must rightly be regarded as the function, or the indication, of an unhealthy conscience. The disgracefulness of their morals is proclaimed while religion is either asserted or preserved by them, whether it is disclosed or kept silent. For even in those Eleusinian rites—which are themselves a heresy derived from the fountain of Attic superstition—what the *epoptai*, or initiated participants in the rites, keep silent is something shameful. For that reason they torment and almost kill those approaching the entrance—that is, those coming to them or learning from them—by circumlocutions and trials. Thus they spend longer initiating than sealing, and consume more time in preparing than in completing the initiation, since even before the gates they prescribe a five-year period to test those who desire to become *epoptai*. Their purpose is to build up an enormous reputation through the protracted suspense of secret knowledge, and thus to appear to display in the hidden [Col. 0538B] rites as much majesty and *semnotēs* (σεμνότητα, solemn dignity) as the desire they have first constructed, elevating the mind to expect great things. Then follows the law and duty of silence, for what is discovered slowly is guarded attentively. Yet the entire divinity hidden in the innermost sanctuaries, all the curtains fastened to the leaves of the doors, this whole seal of secrecy impressed upon the tongue, ends in obscenity; and once so wearisomely prolonged an initiation has been completed, nothing but a foul image of the male member is revealed—shameful to tell. But by putting forward the venerable name of nature and alleging that the arrangement of shameful myths contains empty allegorical inventions, under the patronage of a forced and foolish figure it obscures, diminishes, and repudiates the sacrilege, and excuses the manifest reproach of a false and foul fabrication by means of such counterfeit images.”

Having expounded these matters *paraphrastikōs* (παραφραστικῶς, by paraphrase), no small task might appear to lie before us: namely, to comment on those words of Tertullian one by one, either by defending the genuine authority of the text that we have ventured to publish after so many emendations, or by comparing this preface with other testimonies on the same subject and extracting from them many pieces of evidence useful for explaining ancient religions. From this could easily arise a vast dissertation upon the discipline of the Eleusinian mysteries—a subject worn threadbare again and again, although even now covered with dense [Col. 0538D] darkness—which it is better to omit, since it has been almost exhausted by many others far superior in learning. We shall cast some light upon only two or three points in this preface, while taking care to append here and there annotations from various scholars’ notes.

If you wish these matters to be treated more fully and systematically, consult Warburton, *The Divine Legation of Moses*, book II, section IV; Michael Maier, *Symbols of the Golden Table*, book III, and *On Hieroglyphics*, book IV; Plessing, *Memnonium*, vol. II; Barthélemy, *Anacharsis*, vol. V; Payne Knight, *Inquiry into the Symbolic Language*, in the *Classical Journal*, vol. XXVI; Ouvaroff, *Essay on the Mysteries of Eleusis*; Lobeck, *Aglaophamus, or On the Sources of the Greeks’ Mystical Theology*, book I; Sainte-Croix, *Historical and Critical Researches on the Mysteries of Paganism*, second edition by de Sacy, vol. I, sections 3, 4, and 5; Villoison, *On the Threefold Theology*; Séguier de Saint-Brisson, *Essay on Pantheism*, vol. II, p. 3.

As for Tertullian’s text, some have emended it by reliance upon a comparison of manuscripts, and others by trusting, with greater or lesser safety, in their own ingenuity: Scaliger, *Emendation of Chronology*, book V, p. 393; Salmasius on Spartianus’ *Hadrian*, p. 33 ff.; Casaubon on Athenaeus VI, chap. 15; Wouwer on Petronius, chap. 17; Petavius on Themistius, p. 414; Guther, *On Pontifical Law* I, chap. 25; Croius, *Specimen of Observations*, p. 15, in Grabe’s Irenaeus; Fr. IV, p. 695 ff.; Panelius, *On Cistophori*, p. 84; Petit on the *Attic Laws*, p. 99; Van Dale, *Dissertation on Contests*, p. 608; Lobeck, *Aglaophamus*, vol. I, p. 32 ff.; Séguier de Saint-Brisson, work cited, pp. 105–109. EDD.]

The Valentinians—[Note: [Col. 0537B] Croius in Grabe and the Franeker edition read “the association of Valentinus.”] plainly the largest association among the heretics, because [Note: [Col. 0538B] Oberthür alone reads “who,” perhaps through a printer’s error.] it consists chiefly of apostates from the truth, readily inclines toward fables, and is not deterred by discipline [Col. 0539A]—[Note: [Col. 0539B] “They care about nothing more than concealing what they preach.” From the outset Tertullian follows the blessed Irenaeus, who has the following in the preface to book I:

Ἡ γὰρ πλάνη καθ᾽ αὑτὴν μὲν οὐκ ἐπιδείκνυται, ἵνα μὴ γυμνωθεῖσα γένηται κατάφωρος· πιθάνῳ δὲ περιβλήματι πανούργως κοσμουμένη, καὶ αὐτῆς τῆς ἀληθείας ἀληθεστέραν ἑαυτὴν παρέχειν φαίνεσθαι διὰ τῆς ἔξωθεν φαντασίας τοῖς ἀπειροτέροις.

“For error does not display itself in its own character, lest, when stripped bare, it should become plainly detectable; but, being cunningly adorned with a persuasive covering, it presents itself—ridiculous though it is even to say so—as apparently truer than the truth itself, so as to deceive the less experienced by its outward appearance.”

The old translation—which, as some have thought, is so ancient that it may perhaps have lain before Tertullian’s own eyes—will henceforth be cited in preference to others throughout the course of these notes. Compare *Apology* VII, above, vol. I, p. 6. [Note: [Col. 0540A] Junius reads “the person about to approach”; Salmasius, “at the entrance.”] [Note: [Col. 0539D] “They first torment the person approaching the entrance.” Namely, by *sklēragōgia* (σκληραγωγία, austere training): a harsher diet, silence, sleeping on the ground, chastity, and other such practices of stricter discipline. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0540A] Wechel, Pamelius, and Séguier place punctuation after “torment.”]

They spend longer initiating than sealing. [Note: [Col. 0540A] Rigaltius reads “the tongue”; Junius, “than whom.”] [Note: [Col. 0540A] Séguier reads “than unsealing”; Salmasius, “than sealing the mouth.”] [Note: [Col. 0539D] “They spend longer initiating than sealing.” That is, πλείονα χρόνον μύουσιν ἢ τελοῦσι, “they spend more time preparing than teaching and completing.” *Consignare*, “to seal,” means ἐπισφραγίζεσθαι, “to affix a seal,” or τέλος ἐπιθεῖναι, “to put on the finishing touch.” Thus σφράγις, “seal,” and τελείωσις, “completion,” are used of Baptism; see Segaar on Clement, *Who Is the Rich Man That Is Saved?*, p. 380. To seal or mark with Baptism is the same as τελειοῦν, “to perfect”; see Milles on Cyril, *Catecheses* II, p. 35, and, concerning the mysteries themselves, Clement, *Exhortation*, p. 94. LOBECK.—Those who had been initiated, μεμυημένοι, and those who had been sealed, σφραγισθέντες, were called *consignati*. Philo, *On Monarchy*; Irenaeus, book I, chap. 24; Prudentius, [Col. 0540B] *Martyrdom of St. Romanus*; Arnobius, book III. LE PR.]

Even before the gates [Note: [Col. 0540A] Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür, Wechel, and Pamelius read “and before the gates”; Scaliger, Rigaltius, the Paris edition, Casaubon, Wouwer, and Lobeck read “the *epoptai*.” Séguier very well corrected this to “before the gates.” Petavius, in his work on Themistius, reads “at the gates … they train.”] [Note: [Col. 0540B] “Before the gates.” Scaliger was the first who ventured, despite the silence of the manuscripts, to thrust *epoptai* into this text. Casaubon on Athenaeus VI, chap. 15, and Wouwer on Petronius, chap. 17, approved Scaliger’s emendation. Rigaltius followed it straightaway, and from him it was transmitted here and there to the other editions. But the very learned Petavius rejected Scaliger’s invention, using, in addition to the silence of the manuscripts, this further argument: novices could and did undergo training, but *epoptai*—those who had reached the final grade of initiation—neither did nor could. There were five grades, though others distinguish them by different names. Olympiodorus, on the *Phaedo*, chap. XIII, writes:

Ἐν τοῖς ἱεροῖς ἡγοῦντο οἱ μὲν καθάρσεις πάνδημοι, εἶτα ἐπὶ ταύταις αἱ ἀπορρητότεραι, μετὰ ταύτας συστάσεις, καὶ ἐπὶ ταύταις μυήσεις, ἐν τέλει δ᾽ ἐποπτεῖαι.

“In the sacred rites, first came the purifications open to all; after these, the more secret purifications; after these, introductions; after these, initiations; and finally, the highest visions.”

Similarly, Theon of Smyrna counts five, although he distinguishes them in a different order and under different names: καθαρμός, “purification”; τελετή, “initiation”; ἐποπτεία, “highest vision”; τέλος τῆς ἐποπτείας, “completion of the highest vision,” or consummation of initiation; and finally the supreme [Col. 0540C] good, or perfection of life. EDD.] they prescribe a five-year period, [Note: [Col. 0540C] “They prescribe a five-year period.” From this arose a famous controversy among scholars disputing how long the preparation for receiving the Eleusinian rites continued: whether five years, one year, or fewer. There have been those who vigorously assailed Tertullian’s assertion that a five-year period was prescribed, among them Petavius and, most recently, Lobeck in the *Aglaophamus*. It is worth touching here, at least in passing, upon their principal arguments.

1. The words of Herodotus, book VIII, chap. 45, are cited against him. Herodotus introduces a certain Dicaeus discussing the celebration of the Eleusinian rites with King Demaratus and saying, among other things:

Τὴν ἑορτὴν ταύτην ἀγουσι Ἀθηναῖοι ἀνὰ πάντα ἔτεα τῇ Μητρὶ καὶ τῇ Κόρῃ καὶ αὐτέων τε βουλόμενος τῶν ἄλλων Ἑλλήνων μυεῖται.

“The Athenians celebrate this festival every year for the Mother and the Maiden, and whoever wishes, whether one of themselves or of the other Greeks, is initiated.”

But what if an evident scribal error occurs there? For if Herodotus had wished to say that the rites were celebrated and revealed annually, he would surely have written ἀνὰ πᾶν ἔτος, “every year.” It is therefore intrinsically certain that πάντα, “all,” should there be read as πέντε, “five”—a reading that supports our Septimius’ position remarkably well.

2. But Socrates openly states that the mysteries were revealed every year: καὶ τὰ μυστήρια ἔτι καὶ νῦν καθ᾽ ἕκαστον ἐνιαυτὸν δείκνυμεν, “and even now we display the mysteries every year.” Yet what if this last word means either that the Great Mysteries themselves had to recur every year, or only the Lesser Mysteries, or merely that instructions were to be given annually to the candidates, or finally that during the Thesmophoria sacred to Ceres τὰ ἀπόρρητα, “the secret things,” were to be revealed? Certainly nothing definite follows from it.

3. Nor should certain examples from a later age, which establish that the ancient five-year law was sometimes disregarded, properly be opposed to our Tertullian. We know that this unfortunately happened when Demetrius Poliorcetes besieged Athens; when Philip, king of Macedon and father of Perseus, sought to establish tyranny over it; when Sulla captured the city; when Antony the triumvir was there; and when Augustus was preparing to triumph over the whole world after the battle of Actium. The more numerous the testimonies to the law’s violation, the more clearly its own authority and unavoidable recognition would shine forth. Compare Otfried Müller, *Göttingische Gelehrte Anzeigen*, January 1830; Séguier, vol. II, pp. 110–115.

4. Against the objections of Lobeck stand very many other testimonies supporting the five-year period. One would have to cite the words of the *Etymologicum Magnum* under ἱεροποιοί, “sacred officials”; Pollux, book VIII, chap. 107; Theophrastus in the third *Character*, Ἀδολέσχης, “the Garrulous Man”; Theon of Smyrna; and Artemidorus, concerning whom see above and, more fully, Séguier, work cited, pp. 115–120. EDD.] [Note: [Col. 0540A] Latinius reads “they instruct.”] in order to build up a reputation through the suspense of knowledge. And thus they may appear to display as much majesty [Col. 0541A] as the desire they have first constructed.

Then follows the duty of silence: what is discovered slowly is guarded attentively. Yet the entire divinity in [Col. 0542A] the inner sanctuaries, all [Note: [Col. 0541A] Rigaltius and Lobeck read “the whole.”] the curtains [Note: [Col. 0541A] Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür, Lobeck, the Paris edition, Latinius, Junius, and Petavius read “sighs.” Croius in Junius reads *suspicia*, that is, θεωρίαι, “visions.”] [Note: [Col. 0541B] “All the curtains of the gates.” Although all the copies we have seen agree, we have nevertheless ventured to write *siparia*, “curtains,” in place of *suspiria*, “sighs.” *Siparia* are the curtains used by actors on the dramatic stage, according to Festus. I shall say more about this word below, when explaining the passage in chap. 13: “but beyond the curtain is another piece of tragic posturing.” The priests of Eleusinian Ceres used to cover the gates of the inner sanctuary with many curtains. Tertullian is speaking here of the drawing of these curtains across them. RHEN.] of the gates, [Note: [Col. 0541A] Rigaltius, the Paris edition, and Lobeck read “of the *epoptai*.” Rhenanus, Junius, Wechel, Pamelius, Semler, Oberthür, and Séguier read “of the gates.”] the whole seal upon the tongue—an image of the male member [Note: [Col. 0542A] Junius reads “of the male member, μορίου γυναικείου, ‘of the female part’”; Séguier, “of a woman’s member.”] is revealed.

[Note: [Col. 0541B] “An image … is revealed.” Christian apologists always regarded it as established and thoroughly ascertained that the secret assemblies of the mysteries had been convened from the beginning, and retained thereafter, for the sake of gluttony and fornication. Yet the modern scholars who have most curiously investigated the Eleusinian rites have preferred to torment, pull, and exhaust their ingenuity in remarkable ways so as to discover in those mysteries certain hidden seeds of the highest and most honorable doctrine.

Thus Michael Maier wishes the precepts of Hermetic art to have been concealed there, *Symbols of the Golden Table*, book III, p. 105, and *On Hieroglyphics*, book IV, p. 183. Warburton contends that the *epoptai* plainly learned that the gods had originally been human beings, *The Divine Legation of Moses*, section IV, p. 210; after him, Villoison, *On the Threefold Theology*, p. 48; Meiners, *Miscellaneous Writings*, vol. III, p. 299; Barthélemy, *Anacharsis*, vol. V, p. 68. Plessing asserts that only abstruse Pythagorean and Platonic doctrines were concealed there, in *Memnon*, vol. II, p. 91. The impious Boulanger, with the stale arrogance that he alone had discovered the whole of remote antiquity, boasts—with Voltaire applauding so slight a knowledge of ancient disciplines—that those teachings contain nothing but certain floods, cycles, and calendars: *Antiquity Unveiled*, book III, chap. 5.

Still more audacious—or more insane, a head incurable even by three Anticyras—was Dupuis, who thought it established that the ancient mysteries of the nations concealed teachings far loftier and purer than all the teachings of the Christian religion: *Origin of All Cults*, part I, vol. IV, p. 369. Another herald of shameful secrets, Payne Knight, discovered in them an intellectual and, as it were, transcendental knowledge of the nature of God: *Inquiry into the Symbolic Language*, in the *Classical Journal*, vol. XXII, p. 4. The very learned Heeren does not directly oppose him; in his cursory investigation he seems to have been deluded by certain supposedly true physical and symbolic conceptions of the gods: *Ideas on Politics*, vol. III, p. 90. This view must also have pleased Creuzer, the great father of myths and patcher-together of symbolic clouds. According to de Sacy in his notes on Sainte-Croix, work cited, vol. I, p. 448—and de Sacy himself is not far removed from the same opinion—Creuzer wished the mysteries to concern at once the primordial constitution of things and an ancient cosmogony; the ascetic discipline of souls and the training of morals; the precepts and praises of agriculture; the one eternal God; and the final end both of humanity and of the world.

Finally, Ouvaroff joined these in a special treatise entitled *Essay on the Mysteries of Eleusis*. Entering, not without praise, the academic arena from the Hyperborean region, he too wished a kind of summary of the Primitive Revelation of the Patriarchs, together with certain venerable prophecies about fallen humanity and its restoration, to have been safely entrusted to the Eleusinian discipline. These are the principal modern fabrications concerning the Eleusinian secrets.

But if one wishes to return to the ancients, their opinions vary so much that one must remain in uncertainty. I would not wish to deny that several of them—Pindar, Plato, Cicero, and Epictetus—received the Eleusinian rites of Ceres with great praises and commended them to posterity. Nor could anyone easily be brought to believe that so many and such distinguished men, conspicuous for nobility of mind and character no less than for intellectual excellence, mistook shameful things for honorable ones through blind delusion and deliberately conspired in unanimous collusion to foster that error. Consequently, there is some reason to suppose that, at least up to a certain period, the rites of Ceres were to some extent pious from their beginning.

Why, then, did all the most holy Fathers without exception, and especially the earliest Apologists, cry out with one voice against the unspeakable mysteries and think it right to vie with one another in assailing that religion in their writings? Justin, Athenagoras, and Tatian indeed affirm that nothing but Jupiter’s incest was displayed at Eleusis. Clement of Alexandria inveighs against the rites sharply and with the full force of his spirit. He reproaches Jupiter’s intercourse with Ceres and her daughter; unfolds the secrets of the mystic chests, poppies, parsley, and the rest of the rubbish; shudders as he reports that among the symbols of Themis a representation of the κτένος γυναικείου, “woman’s comb” (with an obscene implication), was carried in the phallic procession; and finally rebukes the hierophants and torchbearers. He judges that those who venerate a wretchedly dismembered boy, a wailing little woman, and the shameful parts of the body should be numbered among atheists. See St. Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation*, pp. 19, 30.

Arnobius, *Against the Nations*, book V, p. 176, ed. Maire, advances the same charges no less vehemently; as do Augustine, *Mixed Questions from the Old and New Testaments*, p. 100 D, in the appendix to vol. III, p. 11, Benedictine edition; Chrysostom, *Discourse on St. Babylas against Julian*, vol. II, p. 558; Asterius, *Encomium on the Holy Martyrs*, *Supplement to the Library of the Fathers* II, 193, compare vol. XVIII, ed. Combefis; Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, book III, § 11, vol. II, p. 1093.

Consider, then, who the witnesses standing on either side are: on the one side the wise men, poets, and legislators of the nations; on the other, the Fathers, Doctors, and Pontiffs of the Church. Nor, in order to settle the dispute between them more easily, can you perhaps tell yourself that two periods of Eleusinian history must be distinguished: one blackened by hoary antiquity, in which the rites were observed with pious worship, and another foul with the recent dregs of superstition and deservedly chastised by the Fathers. Nor does the final refuge of a wavering mind remain: to think privately that the Fathers, carried away by harsher contempt for the nations’ rites and more fervent anger, overstepped the bounds of fair criticism.

For pagan witnesses are not lacking—either from the ancient period or from the Christian era and contemporary with the Fathers—from whom it becomes known that the same rites were infamous in every age. In Caecilius’ play *Titthe*, fragment 1, one reads: “By the mysteries he dishonorably made her pregnant through violation.” Plautus, *Aulularia*, prologue 36: “He violated her during the vigil of Ceres.” That prostitutes were frequently present at these rites is clear from Alciphron, fragmentary letter IV. In Athenaeus XIII, 591 F, a certain Themistius is punished with death because he ὕβρισε τοῖς ἐλευσινοῖς, “violated a Rhodian female lyre-player during the Eleusinian rites.” Dinarchus, *Against Demosthenes*, p. 93. Plutarch reports reproaches of this kind, *Table Talk* II, 2, 73: ἐν Ἐλευσῖνι μετὰ τὰ μυστήρια τῆς πανηγύρεως ἀκμαζούσης, “at Eleusis, after the mysteries, when the festal gathering was at its height.” Compare *On Isis and Osiris*, § 36. Nor did Lucian restrain his sarcasm on this subject, as may be seen in *Alexander, or the False Lover*, § 39, vol. V of the works, pp. 99–100, Bipont edition. Compare Diodorus Siculus, book I, § 22; Plotinus, *Enneads* III, book VII, chap. 9.

We therefore have defendants who confess. Despite the encomia of other witnesses who praise the rites, it must justly be decided that even the wise among the pagan superstitions lacked a sense of honor; indeed, that the moderns were more foolish still when, though guided by the torch of tradition and the light of the Gospel, they admired these foul works of darkness and attempted to weave foolish symbols and empty fables into them so that they might inspire less horror. We must therefore stand by Tertullian’s bitter and deservedly witty gibe against the Eleusinian rites: “The entire divinity in the inner sanctuaries, all the curtains of the gates, the whole seal upon the tongue—an image used in the phallic procession is revealed.” EDD.]

But an allegorical arrangement, putting forward the venerable name of nature, obscures the sacrilege under the patronage [Note: [Col. 0543C] “Under the patronage of a forced figure”: namely, of an allegory in which that obscenity signifies the nature of things. RIG.] of a forced figure, and excuses the reproach of falsehood [Note: [Col. 0543B] Séguier reads “of a lewd image”; Pamelius, “with false images.”] by means of images. [Note: [Col. 0543D] “And excuses the reproach of falsehood by means of images.” The presiding officials of the Eleusinian rites approach that image of the male member in the posture of worshipers, as though approaching a divinity. They are therefore liable to the charge of falsehood, since they worship one thing with their eyes and another in their minds. For they say that they worship not the image itself, but the Nature of things expressed by that image. This is to excuse the charge of falsehood by means of images—to wash away a lie with a lie, one falsehood with another. For what else is an image but a falsehood? RIG.]

Accordingly, the heretics whom we now have in view, [Note: [Col. 0543D] “Accordingly, the heretics whom we now have in view,” etc. These words are connected with what follows thus: “Accordingly, the Valentinians, the heretics whom we now have in view, have made Eleusinian procurings out of holy names and titles,” etc. RIG.] fashioning the emptiest and most shameful fabrications in the form of holy names, titles, and arguments of the true religion, have—for credulous charity’s sake, [Note: [Col. 0543D] “Credulous charity”: namely, that of the brethren or faithful. “Credulous” or “compliant” charity, as Virgil says, “compliant Nymphs” and “compliant Napaeae”; or rather that credulous charity which “bears all things, believes all things,” 1 Corinthians 13. RIG.] and taking advantage of the abundance of divine material, [Note: [Col. 0543D] “Taking advantage of the abundance of divine material.” He means the abundance—or, as he likes to call it, the breadth—of the Holy Scriptures. In this sense he says in *On the Shows*: “Yet divine Scripture is always broadly distributed, wherever discipline is also fortified according to the meaning of the matter at hand.” And in *On Prescription*: “And certainly divine literature is the more productive for the resources of every subject.” RIG.] since many things may arise out of many—[Note: [Col. 0543B] Rigaltius suspects *succidere*, “be cut down,” in place of *succedere*, “arise.”] made Valentinian panderings out of the Eleusinian rites, [Note: [Col. 0543B] Rigaltius reads “the Valentinian Eleusinian rites”; Priorius prefers it. Junius conjectures “Eleusinian or Valentinian.”] things holy because of their great silence and heavenly solely because of their taciturnity.

If you ask in good faith, with contracted face and raised eyebrow they say, “It is profound.” [Note: [Col. 0544C] “They say, ‘It is profound.’” Irenaeus attests that the Valentinians did not possess such candor as to communicate their monstrous trifles readily to everyone. They taught those who had something to pay. For he writes: “It seems fitting to me that they do not wish to teach these things openly to everyone, but only to those able to pay large fees for such mysteries. For they no longer speak like those to whom the Lord said: ‘Freely you have received; freely give.’ Instead they impart isolated, monstrous, and profound mysteries, sought out with great labor, to the credulous.” RHEN.]

If you test them subtly, they affirm the common faith through double-tongued ambiguities. [Note: [Col. 0544C] “They affirm the common faith.” Irenaeus: “Speaking things similar to ours, but understanding dissimilar things.” RIG.] If you hint that you know, they deny whatever they recognize. [Note: [Col. 0544D] “They deny whatever they recognize”: that is, whatever they recognize that you know about their mysteries. RIG.] If you contend with them at close quarters, [Note: [Col. 0543B] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “certainly.”] they shatter your simplicity with their own blows. [Note: [Col. 0543B] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “your fixed simplicity”; Rigaltius and the Paris edition, with a distinguishing comma, “your foolish simplicity.”] [Note: [Col. 0544D] “They shatter your simplicity with their own blows.” Tertullian uses the noun *caedes*, “striking/slaughter,” and the verb *caedere*, “to strike,” in the same sense when he says in the book he wrote *To the Martyrs*, chap. 2: “You are not struck by the cries of the shows, by the cruelty or frenzy or immodesty of those celebrating them.” St. Jerome, imitating Tertullian in the *Life of Hilarion the Hermit*, said “the striking of the hand”: “Angry with himself, therefore, and beating his breast with his fists, as though he could drive thoughts out by the striking of his hand.” PAM.]

They do not entrust their teaching even to their own disciples [Col. 0543B] before they have made them their own. They possess an art by which they first persuade [Note: [Col. 0543B] The Paris edition reads “they persuade.”] and then instruct. Truth, however, persuades by teaching; it does not teach by persuasion.

## CHAPTER II

[Note: [Col. 0544D] See the final note on this book, col. 594.]

And so we are marked among them as “simple,” as though we were merely that and not also wise—as though wisdom were immediately compelled [Col. 0544A] [Note: [Col. 0543B] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “is compelled.”] to depart from simplicity, although the Lord joins the two together: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matthew 10:10).

Or if we are foolish because we are simple, are they therefore not simple because they are wise? Yet those who are not simple are the most harmful, just as those who are not wise are the most foolish. And yet I would rather be classed on that side under the better fault, if perhaps [Note: [Col. 0544B] Junius prefers: “I would prefer that, on that side, the better person should assume the fault, if perhaps.”] it is better to know too little than to know what is worse—to err rather than to deceive.

Moreover, the face of God looks upon [Note: [Col. 0544B] Semler and Oberthür read “awaits.”] those who seek him in simplicity (Wisdom 1), [Note: [Col. 0544B] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “of seeking.”] as Sophia herself teaches—[Note: [Col. 0544B] Others read “wisdom itself”; others prefer the Greek name.] not Valentinus’ Sophia, but Solomon’s.

Next, infants consecrated Christ’s testimony with their blood. [Note: [Col. 0544D] “Infants consecrated Christ’s testimony with their blood.” Augustine spoke in precisely the same sense in book X of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chap. XXIII: “That tender age too possesses the great weight of testimony, for it was the first to deserve to shed its blood for Christ.” PAM.] Shall I call those who cry aloud for the cross “children”? Yet they were neither children nor infants—that is, they were not simple.

The Apostle also commands us to become children again according to [Col. 0544B] God (1 Corinthians 14:20), so that, being infants in malice through simplicity, we may thus at last be wise in our understanding; [Note: [Col. 0544D] “Thus at last wise in our understanding; at the same time I have placed [the words] in the order of the wisdom that flows from simplicity.” We have emended this passage, most corrupt in every edition, from the Pithou manuscript. He says: “The Apostle also commands us to become children again according to God, so that, being infants in malice, at the same time I have placed [the words] in the order of the wisdom that flows from simplicity.” The manuscript reads *manandi* (“of flowing”), erroneously. RIG.] at the same time I have placed [the words] [Note: [Col. 0544B] The Franeker and Paris editions read: “let us be in the order of divine wisdom.”] in the order of the wisdom that flows from simplicity. [Note: [Col. 0544B] The Franeker and Paris editions and Junius retain “by loving”; Semler prefers “by flowing”; he says *minandi* is a verb used of those who drive beasts of burden.]

In short, the dove is accustomed to reveal Christ, whereas the serpent is accustomed to tempt him. From the beginning the former was the herald of divine peace; from the beginning the latter was the plunderer of the divine image. Thus simplicity by itself will more readily be able both to recognize and to reveal God; prudence by itself will rather shake and betray him.

## CHAPTER III

Let the serpent, then, hide himself as much as he can, and twist all his prudence through the winding paths of hiding places. Let him dwell in the depths, be thrust down into darkness, unwind his length through crooked passages, and advance tortuously, never appearing whole at once—a beast that flees the light.

The house of our dove [Note: [Col. 0545C] Semler and Oberthür omit “also.”] also is simple, always in elevated, open places and toward the light. The form [Note: [Col. 0545C] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “the image.”] of the Holy Spirit loves the East, [Note: [Col. 0545C] “The East, a figure of Christ.” In Holy Scripture Christ is often understood by the word “East,” as in Zechariah: “Behold, I shall bring forth my servant, the East”; and a little later in the same prophet: “Behold the man whose name is East.” He is called East because in his days righteousness arose. From this you have the ancient Christians’ custom of praying while turned toward the east, which we still observe. RHEN.] [Note: [Col. 0545C] Semler and Oberthür read “the East, a figure of Christ.”] the figure of Christ.

Truth is ashamed of nothing except being concealed. For the person concerned will not be ashamed to lend his ears to it and to recognize as God the one whom nature has already commended to him, whom he perceives daily in all his works, and who is less known for this reason alone: that he did not regard him as one, named him among a multitude, [Col. 0545B] [Note: [Col. 0545C] Junius reads “named him among multitudes.”] and worshiped him in others.

Otherwise, to recommend still another crowd in addition to their multitude, to remove faith from a familiar sovereignty to an unknown one, to turn it away from what is manifest toward what is hidden, is to make faith stumble on the threshold. Now if he is also initiated into the whole fable, will he not be given something like what you heard from your nurse in infancy amid the troubles of sleep—the towers of Lamia [Note: [Col. 0545D] “The towers of Lamia and the combs of the Sun?” Children’s tales at Carthage in Tertullian’s time. Below we have written “so many offspring,” and a little later “and yet we simple people know everything,” from the Gorze collation. “We” means the orthodox. RIG.] and the combs of the Sun?

But if someone comes to the faith with a different conscience and immediately finds so many names of Aeons, so many marriages, so many offspring, [Note: [Col. 0545C] The first edition of Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “so many pairs.”] so many departures, so many events, successes and misfortunes belonging to a scattered and dismembered divinity, will he hesitate to declare on the spot [Note: [Col. 0545D] “That these are fables and interminable genealogies.” Irenaeus at the beginning of his book against the Valentinians: “Inasmuch as certain persons, rejecting the truth, introduce false words and endless genealogies,” etc. The Greek in Epiphanius is γενεαλογίας ματαίας, “vain genealogies.” The Apostle had said γενεαλογίας ἀπεράντους, “endless genealogies,” 1 Timothy 1. RIG.] that these are the fables and interminable genealogies which the Apostle’s Spirit twice condemned in anticipation even then, when the seeds of heresy were already sprouting?

They are therefore deservedly called “not simple,” deservedly “merely prudent”: people who neither readily bring such things forward nor openly defend them, and who do not even teach fully all those whom they instruct. This is certainly cunning if the things are shameful, but inhuman if they are honorable.

And yet we simple people [Note: [Col. 0546C] The first edition of Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “we all.”] know everything. Finally, we have armed this first wedge for the encounter, as the revealer and indicator of their entire conscience, and we take this as an omen of our first victory: because, when something is hidden at such great expense, merely to expose it is also to destroy it.

## CHAPTER IV
We know, I say, very well their origin too, and we know [Note: [Col. 0546C] “And” omitted in the Venetian edition] why we call them Valentinians, although they may appear not to be so. For they departed from their founder, but their origin is by no means erased; and if they happen to change, [Col. 0546B] the very change is evidence of it.

Valentinus had hoped for the episcopate, because he was capable in both intellect and eloquence. But, indignant that another had obtained the office by the privileged claim of martyrdom, he broke away from the Church of the authentic rule [Note: [Col. 0545D] “He broke away from the Church of the authentic rule.” Pithoeus had noted that he would have preferred: “He broke out from the authentic rule of the Church.” RIG.]. As minds excited by ambition for precedence are accustomed to be inflamed with the presumption of revenge, he turned to the overthrow of the truth; and, having found the seed of a certain ancient opinion [Note: [Col. 0546C] “Having found the seed of a certain ancient opinion, he marked out a path for Colarbasus.” Latinius judged that the passage should be emended in this way, whereas it had previously read: “By a serpentine action he marked out a path for the seed of a certain opinion.” The authority of the ancient manuscripts makes me all the more doubtful that this reading should be rejected, as do the things Septimius said above about the serpent: “Let it dwell deep; let it be thrust into darkness; let it unwind its succession through winding passages; let it proceed tortuously,” etc. For this “serpentine action” corresponds aptly to those words. Finally, [Col. 0546D] Irenaeus and Epiphanius—and indeed the author of the *Catalogue of Heretics* himself—judged Colarbasus to be later than Ptolemy and Secundus. RIG.], marked out the path for Colarbasus [Note: [Col. 0546C] Rhenanus and Semler read “having found a serpentine path”; Latinius, “for the seed, by a serpentine action”].

Ptolemy afterward paved that path by distinguishing the names and numbers of the Aeons into personal substances, though substances defined as existing outside God; Valentinus had enclosed them within the very fullness of divinity as thoughts, affections, and movements. From there Heracleon also drew certain bypaths, as did Secundus and Marcus the magician [Note: [Col. 0546D] **Marcus the magician.** On him see the most learned preliminary dissertations of Dom Massuet prefixed to the works of Irenaeus, Dissertation I, article 11, § VI, p. 50. He sets out in concise form almost the same things that Rhenanus gives here: Irenaeus relates that Marcus, the corrector of his master Valentinus, was highly skilled in magical imposture, through which he seduced many men and no small number of women. Those converted to him regarded him as supremely learned and perfect, and as possessing the greatest power from the invisible *Logoi*. Yet he accomplished all this through the tricks of Anaxilaus and magical deception, being a true forerunner of Antichrist.

From the same author we shall present one or two examples of this utterly depraved man’s tricks. Having mixed wine for a chalice, he pretended to give thanks—that is, to *eucharistein* (εὐχαριστεῖν), what we now call consecrating—and after a lengthy invocation he caused it to appear purple and red, [Col. 0547B] so that the simpler people might think that blood had dripped by divine power into his chalice, and therefore all might desire to taste from that cup and thus become participants in heavenly grace.

Another kind of imposture: he presented a woman with a mixed chalice and ordered her to give thanks. Then, bringing out a larger vessel, he poured the smaller chalice—which had been made a Eucharist—into it, to the great amazement of the spectators, since the larger vessel was not only filled but even overflowed.

Furthermore, he had an attendant demon, what ordinary people today call a familiar spirit. He ensnared women, especially those of respectable birth and [Col. 0547C] wealth, making them prophetesses with these words: “Receive from me a bridegroom, take him, and be taken in him. Behold, grace has descended upon you; open your mouth and prophesy.”

He also mocked the chastity of many women. At any rate, it is established that in Asia he secretly carried off the wife of a certain deacon, a woman of uncommon beauty. When she returned after a long time, she declared that Marcus had corrupted her not only in mind but also in body, and she spent the remainder of her life in perpetual public confession.

Hence a certain holy man cited by Irenaeus rebuked this deceiver in words of this kind: “Marcus, maker of idols and observer of portents, expert in astrology and the magical art, through which you confirm doctrines of error by displaying signs to those whom you seduce—operations of apostate power which your father Satan furnishes to you through the angelic power Azazel, having you as the forerunner of wickedness opposed to God.”

This Marcus boasted that he had adapted the mysteries of numbers to Valentinus’ dreams. As for Theotimus, however, I have found no mention in [Col. 0547D] any author I have seen thus far. Perhaps one should read “Tatian”; for concerning him Tertullian wrote above, in *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 52 (*Heresy* XX), that he was wholly in agreement with Valentinus. MASSUET.] [Note: [Col. 0546C] Others wrongly read “Marcus the Great”; Rigault, the earlier Venetian edition].

Theotimus labored extensively over the images of the Law. Thus Valentinus himself is now nowhere to be found, and yet [Col. 0547A] there are Valentinians, who exist through Valentinus. Axionicus alone, at Antioch to this very day [Note: [Col. 0547B] “Arionicus” in the Vatican manuscript, according to Junius], consoles the memory of Valentinus by preserving his rules intact [Note: [Col. 0547B] “Regularly,” Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür].

Otherwise [Note: [Col. 0547D] “Only so much persuasion is permitted to this heresy.” Irenaeus: “By persuasive conduct they entice simpler persons, under the guise of good men, into a manner of inquiry.” And shortly afterward: “Subtly adorned with a persuasive covering.” RIG.], this heresy is permitted to commend itself only as much as it is customary for a prostitute (*lupa*, literally “she-wolf”) to make up her appearance every day [Note: [Col. 0548B] “To surpass,” Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür]. Why not, when they identify their own “spiritual seed” in every individual in this way? If they construct anything new, they immediately call their presumption a “revelation,” and their cleverness a “charism”; they acknowledge not unity but diversity. We therefore foresee that, once their customary dissimulation has been set aside, many will divide over particular points and will even say in good faith [Note: [Col. 0548B] Unless I am mistaken, “being about to say” is the reading of the first edition. Editors]: “This is not so”; “I understand this differently”; and “I do not acknowledge this.” [Col. 0548A] For the face of their rules is continually renewed through variation; it even has the colors of their states of ignorance.

## CHAPTER V

My boundary will be the archetypes of the principal teachers [Note: [Col. 0547D] **My boundary will be the archetypes of the principal teachers.** He says that he will direct his pen against the origins themselves and the authentic writings of the principal teachers, and that he sets these as boundaries beyond which he does not wish to proceed. “Archetypal teachers” are the leading and more ancient teachers. Atilius Fortunatianus says in his *Art*: “Read the ancients,” that is, as Lucilius says, “the archetypes from which all these things arose.” Martial spoke of “archetypal friends.” RIG.], not the affected leaders of ordinary disciples [Note: [Col. 0547D] **Ordinary disciples:** that is, common ones. RIG.].

Nor will it be said on every side that we ourselves fabricated the subject matter which so many men already—distinguished for holiness and excellence, not merely our predecessors but contemporaries of the heresiarchs themselves—both exposed and refuted in most learned volumes: Justin the philosopher and martyr [Note: [Col. 0547D] **Justin the philosopher and martyr.** He alludes, I think, to Justin’s book against all heresies, which he mentions—Jerome says in the *Catalogue* [Col. 0548B] *of Ecclesiastical Writers*—in the *Apology* he presented to Antoninus Pius, in these words: “We have, moreover, composed a book against sects and heresies.” PAM.]; Miltiades, the sophist of the churches [Note: [Col. 0548B] **Miltiades, the sophist of the churches.** He wrote against Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla; against the Gentiles; against the Jews; and he offered an *Apology for the Christians* to the Caesars Commodus and Severus. Jerome is the authority. Tertullian calls him “the sophist of the churches” not as an insult, but because he possessed great ability in disputing about all kinds of subjects and passages of Sacred Scripture. For that is what “sophist” meant among the ancients. Jerome, [Col. 0548C] in the letter to Antonius *On Modesty*, says: “Against the sophists of the age and the wise men of the world, Peter and James, fishermen, are sent.” Such a sophist of the churches was once that Anglo-Saxon priest Bede, of whom so many monuments survive in every branch of learning, sacred as well as secular, although he was more devoted to sacred learning. RHEN.]; Irenaeus, the most diligent investigator of every doctrine [Note: [Col. 0548C] **Irenaeus, the most diligent investigator of every doctrine.** Among the many highly valuable pieces of evidence we have received from this little work of Tertullian against the Valentinians, especially worthy of mention is this testimony concerning our great bishop, doctor, and martyr, the most blessed Irenaeus. Septimius—himself still more inquisitive, or at least equally studious—judges him to have been a true contemporary of the heresiarchs, distinguished for holiness and excellence, the author of most learned volumes, and the most diligent investigator of every doctrine. Septimius is surely worthy to judge so great a defender of the truth, to extol him with praises, and to commend him to the coming age.

[Col. 0548D] Hence no one can adequately wonder whence certain recent authors eager for novelty derived such audacity that, despising the gray antiquity of so many centuries, overthrowing the majesty of so many encomia succeeding one another, and suppressing the voice of so many witnesses cited by Tertullian, one or two men scarcely known even by name dared to say that Irenaeus’ works against all the heresies—works that can never be sufficiently praised, studied, and embraced—did not exist at all before Tertullian.

Furthermore, this monstrous opinion is claimed as his own proper right by Johann Salomo Semler, who extracted and twisted arguments from this very book of Septimius against the Valentinians in order to strip Dom Irenaeus of all credibility and authority. To refute these arguments thoroughly, nothing seemed better to us than to arrange for Irenaeus’ own genuine words to be placed beside the text of Septimius, proceeding on equal footing and in parallel columns for comparison. From this it will become more certain than certainty itself, and it will be impossible for anyone to be deceived, that when Tertullian wrote his little work he had before him not merely the authentic works of the most holy martyr, not merely works composed in the original Greek, but also works already rendered in a Latin translation.

To make this shine forth more clearly, we shall bring to light in distinctive type every word of Irenaeus’ old translation which Tertullian either used or alluded to. Indeed, even the other words not so similar to Septimius’ text will serve our purpose, since they establish that Tertullian used many authors whom he praises—namely Justin the philosopher, Miltiades the sophist of the churches, and his own Proculus—in the manner of one who collects and makes others’ material his own: at one point elucidating or explaining Irenaeus; at another subtracting something from his fullness; elsewhere slightly changing certain things here and there; yet never allowing anyone to deny that Irenaeus was, as he himself testifies, his predecessor and guide, or that he had before his eyes precisely the same works that we possess.

For a fundamental demonstration of the matter, one should consult C. W. Franz Walch, *Commentary on the Authenticity of the Books of Irenaeus*, in *New Commentaries of the Royal Society of Göttingen* V, 2, 3 ff., against J. Sal. Semler’s *Historical Introduction to Baumgarten’s Polemics*, the prologue *On Avoiding Troublesome Sacred Zeal in Correcting Certain Opinions of Irenaeus and Tertullian*, and the final dissertation *On the Varied and Uncertain Character of Tertullian’s Books*. EDD.]; and [Col. 0549A] our own Proculus [Note: [Col. 0549D] **Our own Proculus, the glory of virginal old age and Christian eloquence.** Pacianus, to Sympronianus, *On the Name Catholic*: “Those very more prominent Phrygians who falsely claim that they were inspired by Leucius boast that they were instructed by Proculus.” RIG.], the glory of virginal old age and Christian eloquence. I would wish to follow these men in every work of faith, just as in this one.

Or, if there are no heresies at all, so that those who drive them away may be believed to have invented them, then the Apostle, who proclaimed them, will be lying (1 Cor. 11:19). But if they do exist, they will be none other than those which are examined. No one is said to be so idle with his pen that, though he has subject matter ready at hand, he invents it.

## CHAPTER VI

Accordingly, in this little book [Note: [Col. 0549B] “Because,” Venetian edition], in which we promise only an exposition of that mystery [Note: [Col. 0549B] Franciscus: “we promise an exposition of that mystery alone”; Rhenanus: “first setting forth only”], lest anyone be overwhelmed by darkness because of names so foreign, forced, compounded, and ambiguous [Note: [Col. 0549B] The Venetian edition corruptly reads “heat.” Oberthür, Semler], I shall first explain how we intend to use them. For in some cases no translation from the Greek occurs which would provide a correspondingly convenient form of the name; in some, the grammatical genders do not correspond to their sex; and in some, the Greek designation is better known.

We shall therefore use Greek forms for the most part. Their meanings will be supplied at the margins of the pages [Note: [Col. 0549D] **Their meanings will be supplied at the margins of the pages.** Of the marginal and interlinear notes Tertullian indicates here, no manuscript, however ancient, has preserved any trace. EDD.]. Nor, indeed, will Greek forms be absent where Latin ones are used, but they will be marked above the lines, so that this may serve as the sign of personal names, because of the ambiguity of words that also bear another meaning [Note: [Col. 0549B] Others read the singular “ambiguity”].

Although I have deferred the contest, professing for the present to provide only a narrative, nevertheless, wherever some disgrace deserves to be branded, there will be no assault that pierces through in this mere sampling [Note: [Col. 0549B] Venetian: “perfunctory.” Pamelius, [Col. 0550B] Franciscus, and the Paris edition: “There will be no assault through perfunctory deliberation.” Junius, from a manuscript: “through transfixing deliberation”]. [Col. 0550A] [Note: [Col. 0549D] **The assault will not consist of a transfixing taste of battle.** That is: we shall indeed brand and take a taste, but we shall not pierce through. Branding pricks; assault pierces through. Here, therefore, there will be no assault involving transfixion in the branding or tasting. So the ancient manuscripts read, and what follows shows the reading to be entirely correct: “I shall display wounds, but not inflict them.” It is as though he said: “I shall prick, not stab through.” RIG.].

Reader, reckon it a practice-skirmish before the battle [Note: [Col. 0550C] **Reckon it a practice-skirmish before the battle, reader.** So the ancient books read. Nevertheless, one should read “for the contest.” He alludes to gladiators’ preliminary exercises, which were conducted with practice-staves. For a practice-skirmish before battle is a preliminary exercise. Thus he says: “Reader, reckon this practice-skirmish before the battle as preparation for the contest and the true combat.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0550B] Paris reads “hardly a battle”; others “whether a battle,” and others “or a battle”]. I shall display wounds but not inflict them. If laughter too occurs somewhere, justice will be done to the subject matter itself: many things are so unworthy of serious refutation that they must not be honored with gravity [Note: [Col. 0550B] Junius reads “adorned”]. Wit is properly employed against vanity. It also befits truth to laugh, because truth rejoices, and to jest about its rivals, because truth is secure. One must certainly take care that its laughter is not itself laughed at, should it prove unworthy. But wherever laughter is deserved, it is a duty. Finally, I shall begin in this way.

## CHAPTER VII

Ennius, the first of all Roman poets, simply declared that the heavens were “the highest upper rooms,” naming them from the breadth of their extent [Note: [Col. 0550B] Rhenanus and Semler read “from a broad extent”], or perhaps because he had read in Homer of Jupiter feasting there.

But it is astonishing how many upper realms above upper realms, [Col. 0550B] and how many heights above heights [Note: [Col. 0550C] **Heights above heights.** Irenaeus: “In invisible and ineffable heights.” RIG.], the heretics have hung, raised, and spread out as a dwelling for each one’s god. Even for our Creator the upper rooms of Ennius [Note: [Col. 0550C] **Upper rooms.** *Coenacula* are the upper stories of a house. Vitruvius, *Architecture*, book II, says: “Since, with the Roman population having increased to an astonishing degree, it had become necessary to live in upper stories—for previously, when the spaciousness of the city permitted it, buildings had only one floor—they resorted to greater heights of buildings and a crowded multiplication of houses.” RHEN.] have been arranged in the form of little apartments, with one gallery built above another and allotted to each god by as many staircases as there have been heresies.

The universe has become a tenement house. You would think it Felicula’s apartment block [Note: [Col. 0550D] **You would think it Felicula’s apartment block.** Buildings not joined to their neighbors by shared walls are called *insulae*. This, then, was some remarkable tenement containing a great many stories, perhaps named “Felicula” after its owner Felix. He himself occupied the top floor of his Felicula. In Arrian’s *Discourses of Epictetus*, “Felicio” is the name of a slave. RIG.—**Felicula’s apartment block.** We have written it thus because the manuscripts agree. By metaphor, large houses entirely surrounded by a public road are also called *insulae*. These commonly have merchants’ shops along every side. I suspect that some building of this kind was famous at Rome, or certainly at Carthage. It was evidently called “Felicula” after Felix, the owner of the block, unless one prefers to derive the name from its abundance of wares for sale. RHEN.] [Note: [Col. 0550B] “Felicula” is absent from Semler and Oberthür], so many are the stories of the heavens—though I do not know where [Note: [Col. 0550D] **Though I do not know where.** These words are found in the ancient manuscripts, but are no more acceptable for that reason. RIG.]. For there the God of the Valentinians inhabits the highest roof tiles.

In respect of substance they call him ΑἸΩΝ ΤΈΛΕΙΟΝ (*Aiōn Teleion*, “Perfect Aeon”), but personally [Col. 0551A] ΠΡΟΑΡΧΉΝ and ΤῊΝ ἈΡΧΉΝ (*Proarchēn* and *tēn Archēn*, “Pre-beginning” and “the Beginning”) [Note: [Col. 0551C] **ΠΡΟΑΡΧΉΝ and ΤῊΝ ἈΡΧΉΝ.** Pithoeus’ old manuscript has the corrupt forms ΑΠΡΟΑΡΧΩ ΠΡΑΡΡΧΗΝ, and also “Bythion.” From the traces of that writing it seems one should read ΠΡΟΠΆΤΟΡΑ and ΠΡΟΑΡΧΉΝ (*Propatora* and *Proarchēn*, “Forefather” and “Pre-beginning”), and also “Bythos.” Irenaeus: “They call him both Proarchē and Propator and Bythos.” The Greek preserved in Epiphanius has only Προπάτορα καὶ Βυθὸν, “Forefather and Depth.” RIG.], and also Bython (“Depth”) [Note: [Col. 0551C] **Also Bython.** The Greeks call a depth βυθός. Yet it was unsuitable for the supreme God of the Valentinians, who dwells not in the depths but on high and upon the highest roof tiles of the heavenly upper rooms—as Tertullian writes in jest—to have his name from the deep. Irenaeus calls him “Bythos”; Tertullian, “Bythion.” RHEN.] [Note: [Col. 0551B] “Bythion,” Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür], a name scarcely suitable for one who inhabits the heights.

They define him as unbegotten, immeasurable, infinite, invisible, and eternal—as though they immediately proved that he exists if they define him as being such as we know he ought to be, so that [Note: [Col. 0551B] “So that” is absent from Rhenanus and others] he may thus also be said to have existed before all things. But I demand that he exist [Note: [Col. 0551C] **But I demand that he exist.** That is, “I also contend against them on this point: that God existed before all things”—something which they themselves nevertheless deny when they assign God a coeternal companion, Ennoea or Sige. RIG.]. Nor do I censure anything more in an account of this kind [Note: [Col. 0551C] **In an account of this kind:** namely, in this fable of the Aeons. RIG.] than the fact that those said to have existed before all things are found only after all things—and indeed not on their own [the Latin is elliptical] [Note: [Col. 0551C] **And not, indeed, by their own testimony. Let Bythos, therefore, exist.** Rhenanus wrote this, whereas the previous reading was the corrupt: “And indeed not persuaded. Therefore Bythos,” etc. RIG.].

Let this Bythos, then, exist throughout infinite ages in the past, in the greatest and loftiest repose, in the fullest leisure, with a placid and, so to speak, stupefied divinity of the kind prescribed by Epicurus. Yet, although they wish him to be alone, they give him a second person within and alongside himself: Ennoea (“Thought”), whom they additionally name Charis (“Grace”) and Sige (“Silence”).

And perhaps in that highly commended repose they go so far as to admonish him [Col. 0551B] [Note: [Col. 0551B] Rhenanus, Pamelius, and others read “move him”] at last to bring forth from himself the beginning of things. He deposits this, in place of seed, in his Sige’s genital womb, as it were [Note: [Col. 0551B] Rhenanus and others read “as though in the genital parts”]. She receives it at once, becomes pregnant, and gives birth—as was fitting for Sige—in silence. What she bears is Nus (*Nous*, “Mind”), most like the Father and equal to him in all things. In short, he alone is sufficient to comprehend that immeasurable and incomprehensible greatness of the Father.

Thus he too is called Father, the Beginning of all things, and properly Monogenes (“Only-begotten”). Yet not properly, since he is not acknowledged as the only offspring [Note: [Col. 0551B] Franciscus reads “born”]. For a female, Veritas (“Truth”), came forth with him [Note: [Col. 0551B] Rhenanus and others read “to whom the name Truth”; Junius, “to whom also the name”; others omit “to whom” and “name”]. If he is Monogenes because he was the first-born, how much more fittingly would he be called Protogenes (“First-begotten”)!

Thus Bythos and Sige, Nus and Veritas, are maintained as the first four-horse team [Note: [Col. 0551D] **The first four-horse team.** He alludes to the four factions of charioteers. RIG.] of the Valentinian faction, the matrix and origin of them all. For there, as soon as Nus undertakes [Note: [Col. 0552B] Pamelius and Semler read “received”] the duty of his own emanation, he too emits from himself Sermo (“Word,” Logos) and Vita (“Life,” Zoe)—and if Life did not previously exist, then certainly it did not exist even in Bythos. And what a state of affairs it is, that there should have been no life in God!

But this offspring too, emitted as the beginning of the universe and the formation [Note: [Col. 0552B] Rhenanus, Pamelius, the earlier Paris edition, the Venetian edition, Semler, and all editions read the corrupt “of the formed”; Junius, “form.” The most learned Grabe and Dom Massuet correctly emended this to “formation” in Irenaeus, book I, chapter 1] of the entire Pleroma (“Fullness”), produces fruit: it begets Homo (“Humanity”) and Ecclesia (“Church”). You now have the Ogdoad, a double Tetrad [Note: [Col. 0551D] **From pairings of males and females.** Irenaeus expresses it differently but with the same meaning: “For each of them consists of male and female.” Epiphanius: ἀρρενόθηλυς, “male-female.” RIG.], formed from pairings [Note: [Col. 0552B] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “unions”] of males and [Col. 0552B] females: the chambers, so to speak, of the primordial Aeons; the fraternal marriages of the Valentinian gods; the whole census of heretical holiness and majesty. I do not know whether it is a crowd of crimes or divinities; it is certainly the source of the remaining fecundity.

[Note: [Col. 0551D] Beginning with this seventh chapter, Semler instituted his comparison between Irenaeus and Tertullian. Following the same path after him, we print both texts together within a single view; and to Irenaeus’ Greek original we add the old Latin translation, so that the true and certain character of Tertullian’s work may become evident. Then, in obedience to what was said above, we shall take care that all similar words or clauses are diligently printed in italics and brought more openly to notice.

“They say, then, that in the invisible and unnameable heights there exists a certain Perfect Aeon who existed before all things. Him they also call … Forefather and Depth.… He is incomprehensible and invisible, eternal and unbegotten, and has existed in profound silence and repose throughout infinite ages of time. Thought coexists with him, whom they also name Grace and Silence. At some point this Depth conceived the intention of emitting from himself a beginning of all things; and, like seed, he deposited this emanation which he had conceived the intention of emitting, as though in a womb, in the Silence coexisting with him. Having received this seed and become pregnant, she gave birth to Mind, who was like and equal to the one who had emitted him and alone capable of containing the greatness of the Father.

“They also call this Mind Only-begotten, Father, and Beginning of all things; and Truth was emitted together with him. This is the first and primordial Pythagorean Tetrad, which they also call the root of all things. For there are Depth and Silence, then Mind and Truth.

“This Only-begotten, perceiving the purpose for which he had been emitted, himself emitted Word and Life, the father of all things that would exist after him and the beginning and formation of the entire Pleroma. From Word and Life, Humanity and Church were emitted as a pair. This is [Col. 0552D] the primordial Ogdoad, the root and substance of all things,” etc.

**Old translation.**—“They say that in the invisible and ineffable heights there is a certain Perfect Aeon who existed before all things. Him they also call Proarchē, Propator, and Bythos. They say that he is invisible and incapable of being contained by anything. Since he was contained by nothing and was invisible, eternal, and unbegotten, he existed in silence and profound repose throughout immeasurable ages.

“With him also existed Ennoea, whom they also call Charis and Sige. At some point this Bythos wished to emit from himself the beginning of all things; and he willed that this emanation be sent forth like seed and deposited it as though in the womb of Sige, who existed with him. She received this seed, became pregnant, and generated Nus, like and equal to the one who had emitted him and alone capable of containing the greatness of the Father.

“They call this Nus Only-begotten, [Col. 0553B] Father, and Beginning of all things. Truth was emitted together with him, and this is the first and first-begotten Pythagorean Quaternity, which they also call the root of all things. For there are Bythos and Sige, then Nus and Aletheia.

“This Only-begotten, perceiving the purposes for which he had been brought forth, himself emitted Logos and Zoe, the father of all who would exist after him and the beginning and formation of the entire Pleroma. From Logos and Zoe were emitted, as a pair, Humanity and [Col. 0553C] Church; and this is the first-begotten Octonary, the root and substance of all things.” EDD.]

## CHAPTER VIII

Behold, then, the second Tetrad: Word and Life, Humanity and Church. Because it had sprouted for the Father’s glory, these too, exulting in this number [Note: [Col. 0552B] Rhenanus, Junius, and Semler read “for this number”], wish to offer the Father something of their own of the same kind. They bubble forth other offspring, likewise marital, [Col. 0553A] through the coupling of the two sexes. On the one side, Word and Life pour forth a Decad of Aeons together; on the other, Humanity and Church produce two more than that, equaling their parents, because they themselves, two together with those ten, make as many as they themselves begot.

I now give the names of those whom I called the Decad: Bythos (“Depth”) and Mixis (“Mixture”); Ageratos (“Unaging”) and Henosis (“Union”); Autophyes (“Self-produced”) [Note: [Col. 0553B] Rhenanus and Semler omit “Ageratos and Henosis; Autophyes”] and Hedone (“Pleasure”); Acinetos (“Immovable”) and Syncrasis (“Commingling”); Monogenes (“Only-begotten”) and Macaria (“Blessedness”).

By contrast, the following will constitute the number twelve: Paracletus (“Advocate”) and Pistis (“Faith”); Patricos (“Paternal”) and Elpis (“Hope”); Metricos (“Maternal”) and Agape (“Love”); Ainus (reading uncertain; the parallel Greek has Aeinous, “Eternal Mind”) and Synesis (“Understanding”); Ecclesiasticus (“Ecclesiastical”) and Macariotes (“Blessedness”); Theletus (“Willed”) and Sophia (“Wisdom”).

I am compelled here to present a comparable example of what these names deserve. In the schools [Note: [Col. 0553B] The old editions and manuscripts read the uncertain *isclis*. Rhenanus’ conjecture “in the schools” was adopted by Franciscus; others read “in the suns.” Junius retains *iselis*] of Carthage [Note: [Col. 0553C] **In the schools of Carthage.** The ancient manuscripts read *in isclis*. This is perhaps an African word. RIG.] there was once an utterly frigid [Col. 0553B] [Note: [Col. 0553B] Rhenanus and Semler read “most rigid”] Latin rhetor named Phosphorus [Note: [Col. 0553B] Junius prefers “Phosphorius,” and afterward “of Phosphorius”].
