While declaiming as a brave man, he said: “I come to you, excellent citizens, from battle, with my victory, with your good fortune, enlarged, glorious, fortunate, greatest, triumphant!” And the students immediately cried [Note: [Col. 0553C] **The household of Phosphorus.** That is, the followers of that Carthaginian rhetor; and a little later, “the household of Ptolemy.” For *familia* here means familiars, like the Greek οἰκεῖοι ἑταῖροι, “intimate companions.” LE PR.]: “The household of Phosphorus—Φεῦ (*Pheu!*—‘Bravo!’)” [Note: [Col. 0554B] Rhenanus reads the corrupt *Phosphorifae* and suspected *Phosphoricae*].

[Note: [Col. 0553C] **Φεῦ.** They acclaim *Pheu!* It is here the cry of students offering congratulations and praise and standing amazed at such eloquence in their teacher, as the same commentator notes. Among the Greeks φεῦ is the cry not only of one grieving but also of one expressing wonder. Here, moreover, Tertullian alludes to the words of Irenaeus, book I, chapter 5: “Iou, iou! Pheu, pheu! For one must speak tragically concerning this fabrication of names.” Epiphanius illustrates this by adding the following paraphrase: “Holy Irenaeus too, mocking them for the things stated above, introduced that tragic cry, ‘Iou, iou! Pheu, pheu!’ For one may truly utter this tragic cry over such a calamity—the calamity of those who described these ridiculous fabrications of names, and of the man who, with such audacity and entirely without shame, imposed a name upon his lie.” Feuardent establishes from Aristophanes’ *Birds* and Sophocles’ *Ajax* that Irenaeus should be read in this way—and, in my judgment, Epiphanius as well, in both Greek and Latin. PAMELIUS.]

You have heard Fortunata, Hedone, Acinetus, and Theletus; now acclaim: “The household of Ptolemy—Φεῦ (*Pheu!*—‘Bravo!’)” [Note: [Col. 0554B] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read the corrupt *Ptolomaeifae*].

This will be that mysterious Pleroma, the fullness of a thirtyfold divinity. Let us see what privileges belong to these numbers—four, eight [Note: [Col. 0554B] Junius suspects that “and ten” should be added], and twelve. Meanwhile, at thirty the whole fertility comes to an end: the force, capacity, and generative lust of the Aeons have been castrated. As though so many clusters of shoulders did not still remain, along with no other [Note: [Col. 0554B] Junius suggests “and a thousand other”] names from the nursery! Why, indeed, are not fifty or a hundred begotten? Why are not Stercolae (“excrement-cleaners”) and Syntrophi (“foster-companions”) also named [Col. 0554B]?

[Note: [Col. 0553D] **Why are Stercolae and Syntrophi not also named?** What precedes sufficiently indicates that these words should be understood with reference to the nursery—that is, to attendants upon cradles and to the fellow-nurslings and playmates of children. I had thought of the guardians of the domestic enclosure, whom the Greeks call ἑρκῖται (*herkitai*, “guardians of the enclosure”), comparable to Jupiter Hercius and the Lares Hercii; nor did the conjecture συνερκείους (*synerkeious*, “those sharing an enclosure”), proposed by a most learned man, displease me. But all these conjectures depart too far from the traces of the ancient text, which must be followed as closely as possible, even at the risk of contamination.

[Col. 0554B] The old books read: *Stercejae et Syntrophi*. Others have *Sterceae*; two Vatican manuscripts, *Stercojae*. This last comes nearest to the truth. Copyists’ hands frequently make such an error as writing *j* for *l*: *Stercojae* for *Stercolae*. Septimius is plainly joking and asks the inventors of the Aeons—who imagined various chambers throughout those many stories and couplings of the sexes—how it comes about that all fertility is contained within the number thirty, as though numerous other names from the nursery did not remain. “Why,” he asks, “are Stercolae and Syntrophi not also named?” By *Stercolae* he means nurses who clean or move cradles, formed in the same way as *Stercolus*, the deity presiding over the manuring of fields. RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0554B] Others read *stercoiae*, whence Rhenanus’ *sterceiae* or *sterceae*, or *sterciae*. Junius approves all these readings.]

[Note: [Col. 0554C] **Are named.** We wish to append here in full, as above, the passages of Irenaeus that agree with this chapter of Tertullian, and to place them before the diligent reader for comparison; he will have little difficulty in pointing out which author preceded the other.

Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book I, chapter 1, no. 2, § 2:

“These Aeons, having been emitted for the glory of the Father and themselves wishing to glorify the Father from what was their own, emitted emanations in pairs. Word and Life, after Humanity and Church had been emitted, brought forth ten further Aeons, whose names they say are these: Bythios and Mixis; Ageratos and Henosis; Autophyes and Hedone and Macaria [the supplied Greek is defective here and omits part of the list]. These are the ten Aeons whom they say were emitted from Word and Life. Humanity himself, together with Church, emitted twelve Aeons, upon whom they bestow these names: Paracletus and Pistis; Patricos and Elpis; Metricos and Agape; Aeinous and Synesis; Ecclesiasticus and Macariotes; Theletus and Sophia.

“§ 3. These are the thirty Aeons of their error; this is, according to them, the invisible and spiritual Pleroma, divided into three parts: an Ogdoad, a Decad, and a Duodecad,” etc.

**Old translation.**—“§ 2. These Aeons, having been emitted for the glory of the Father and themselves wishing to glorify the Father from what was their own, emitted emanations in pairs. Logos and Zoe, after Humanity and Church had been emitted, brought forth ten other Aeons whose names they say are these: Bythius and Mixis; Ageratos and Henosis; Autophyes and Hedone; Acinetos and Syncrasis; Monogenes and Macaria. These are the ten Aeons whom they say were emitted from Logos and Zoe. Anthropos himself, together with Church, emitted twelve Aeons, upon whom they bestow these names: Paracletus and Pistis; Patricos and Elpis; Metricos [Col. 0555B] and Agape; Aenos and Synesis; Ecclesiasticus and Macariotes; Theletus and Sophia.

[Col. 0555C] “§ 3. These are the thirty Aeons of their error, who are silent and unrecognized; this, according to them, is the invisible and spiritual Pleroma, divided into three parts: an Octonary, a Decad, and a Duodecad,” etc. EDD.]

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0555A]

But this too is favoritism: that this Nous alone, out of all of them, enjoys knowledge of the immeasurable Father, rejoicing and exulting while the others, of course, grieve [Note: [Col. 0555B] “Deserving” in Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür]. Indeed, Nous [Note: [Col. 0555B] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür add “and”], so far as it lay in him, had both wished and attempted to communicate to the others also what he knew—how great and how incomprehensible the Father was. But Mother Silence intervened, she, namely, [Note: [Col. 0555C] Who also commands her own heretics to keep silent: namely, the Valentinians, whose holy enticements are attended by profound silence, whose heavenly mysteries consist in taciturnity alone, as he said above. RIG.] who also commands her own heretics to keep silent. And although they say that this was done at the Father’s bidding, [Note: [Col. 0555C] “Who wished them all to be kindled with desire for himself.” Septimius has rendered the Greek of Irenaeus preserved in Epiphanius: “because he wished to bring them all to a conception and a longing to seek the aforesaid Forefather of theirs” (διὰ τὸ θελεῖν πάντας αὐτοὺς εἰς ἔννοιαν καὶ πόθον ζητήσεως τοῦ προειρημένου προπάτορος αὐτῶν ἀγαγεῖν). The Latin, however, says something different: “But Silence restrained him by the Father’s will, because he did not wish to bring all these to an understanding and desire for the search for their Father.” The same.] who wished them all to be kindled with desire for himself.

And so, while they torment themselves inwardly, while they burn with a silent longing to know the Father, a crime almost occurs. For among those twelve Aeons whom Man and Church had produced [Note: [Col. 0555B] “Had produced,” according to the same witnesses], the youngest Aeon—let the solecism answer for itself—whose name is Wisdom (Sophia), [Col. 0555B] through her lack of self-restraint, [Note: [Col. 0555C] “Without union with her consort Philetus.” Irenaeus: “Without the embrace of her consort Theletus.” The same.—I myself would prefer to retain *Philetus* rather than *Theletus*. It better suits the sense, for he intends it to signify something erotic. LE PR.] without the company [Note: [Col. 0555B] “Of her own,” Paris; “without,” others; “or without her consort,” Latin] of her consort Philetus [Note: [Col. 0555B] “Satiety,” Rhenanus, from the Gorze manuscript], bursts forth to investigate the Father. She contracts a kind of fault that had indeed begun [Col. 0556A] among those others around Nous, but had flowed down into this Aeon—that is, [Note: [Col. 0555B] Or “into Sophia,” Rhenanus and others] into Sophia—just as faults originating [Note: [Col. 0555B] “Attempted,” Junius, from the Vatican manuscript] elsewhere in a body commonly breathe their destruction into another member.

Yet beneath the pretext [Note: [Col. 0555B] “Pretext,” Paris] of love for the Father, rivalry with Nous—who alone rejoiced in the Father—was gaining the upper hand. But when Sophia, striving after impossibilities, had failed [Note: [Col. 0555B] Junius conjectures “was in vain”] and was overcome by the difficulty, [Note: [Col. 0555D] “And is stretched out by affection.” Irenaeus: “As she was always stretching forward to his further pursuit.” In these words either some error lies concealed, so that one should read “toward his sweetness” rather than “toward his pursuit,” for Epiphanius has “by his sweetness” (τῆς ὑπὸ γλυκύτητος αὐτοῦ); or else “pursuit” was used for a further attempt, or rather for the affection mentioned immediately before. Both expressions are barbarous, to be sure, but they come from a man who, as he himself says, dwelt among the Celts and was frequently drawn into barbarous speech. The Greek is certainly easier: “and her affection for him, always being moved farther forward by his sweetness” (καὶ τὴν πρὸς αὐτὸν στοργὴν ἐκεινόμενον ἀεὶ ἐπὶ τὸ πρόσθεν ὑπὸ τῆς γλυκύτητος αὐτοῦ). RIG.] and was stretched out by affection, she came within a little of being swallowed up by the force of the sweetness [Note: [Col. 0556B] Others, after Junius, read “sloth”] and the exertion, and [Note: [Col. 0555D] “Dissolved into the remaining substance,” so that whatever substance remained to her would be dissolved. Irenaeus: “She would have been swallowed up and dissolved into the universal substance.” RIG.] dissolved into the remaining substance. Nor would she otherwise have ceased except by perishing, had she not by good fortune encountered Horos [Note: [Col. 0556B] Rhenanus places a comma here, and the Paris and Frankfurt editions enclose certain words—“…guardian…”—in parentheses. Junius, however, reads: “had encountered a certain Horos (and this is the power, the foundation, the guardian outside that universe), whom,” etc.], it too being a certain Power—the foundation and external guardian of that universe—whom they also call Cross, [Note: [Col. 0556B] “And whom,” Rhenanus and others] Redeemer, and Liberator.

Thus Sophia was delivered from danger and, after being persuaded only with difficulty, abandoned [Note: [Col. 0556B] “After being turned away,” Rhenanus; Junius thinks this reading closer to Irenaeus] [Col. 0556B] the investigation of the Father and came to rest; and she cast off [Note: [Col. 0555D] “She laid aside the whole Enthymesis.” That is, “deposited.” Irenaeus: “She laid aside her former intention together with the passion that had befallen her.” RIG.] the whole Enthymesis—that is, her impulse—together with the Passion that had additionally befallen her.

[Note: [Col. 0555D] Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book I, chapter 2, § 1.—“They say, then, that their Forefather is known only to the Only-Begotten who came into being from him, that is, to Nous; but that to all the rest he is invisible and incomprehensible. According to them, Nous alone took delight in beholding the Father and exulted in contemplating his immeasurable greatness. He intended to communicate to the remaining Aeons also the greatness of the Father—how great and extensive he was, and how he was without beginning, uncontainable, and impossible to comprehend by sight. But Silence restrained him, by the Father’s will, because he wished to bring them all to a conception and longing to seek the aforesaid Forefather of theirs. And the remaining Aeons likewise, in a quiet fashion, yearned to see the emitter of their seed and to investigate the root that is without beginning.

“§ 2. But the last and youngest Aeon of the Dodecad emitted by Man and Church—that is, Sophia—advanced very far and suffered a passion without conjunction with her yokefellow Theletus. It had begun among those around Nous and Truth but came down upon this Aeon who had gone astray: ostensibly from love, but in fact from audacity, because she had not shared in the perfect Father as Nous also had. The passion was a search for the Father, for, as they say, she wished [Col. 0556D] to comprehend his greatness. Then she was unable to do so, because she had undertaken an impossible task and had come into a very great struggle,” etc. “Always stretching forward, she would finally have been swallowed up by his sweetness and dissolved into the whole substance, had she not encountered the Power that sustains all things and guards them outside the ineffable Greatness. This Power they also call Horos,” etc. “And having scarcely returned to herself … she laid aside her former Enthymesis, together with the Passion that subsequently arose from that overwhelming astonishment.”

**Old Translation.—§ 1.** They say that their Forefather is known only to the one born from him, the Only-Begotten, that is, Nous; but that to all the rest he is invisible and incomprehensible. Nous alone, according to them, delighted in seeing the Father, and exulted as he considered his immeasurable greatness; and he thought of sharing with the remaining Aeons also the greatness of the Father—how great he was, how he was without beginning, incapable of being contained, and impossible to comprehend by sight. Silence, however, restrained him by the Father’s will, because he wished [Col. 0557B] to bring all these to an understanding and desire for the search for their Father. And all the remaining Aeons somehow silently desired to see the emitter of their seed and to contemplate the root that is without beginning.

[Col. 0557C] **§ 2.** But the last and youngest Aeon of the Dodecad emitted by Man and Church—that is, Sophia—leapt very far forward and suffered a passion without the embrace of her consort Theletus. This passion had indeed begun among those who are around Nous and Truth, but it flowed down into this Aeon—that is, Sophia—when she changed course, ostensibly under the occasion of love, but actually from recklessness, because she had not shared in the perfect Father in the way Nous had. The Passion was the search for the Father; for, as they say, she wished to comprehend his greatness. Then, since she could not, because she was attempting an impossible thing, she was placed in great agony on account of the greatness of his depth, the unsearchable quality of the Father, and the love that she bore toward him; and as she stretched always toward what lay ahead, she would finally perhaps have been swallowed up by his sweetness and dissolved into the universal substance, had she not encountered the Power that strengthens all things and guards them outside the ineffable Greatness. This Power they call Horos. Restrained and strengthened by it, and having scarcely returned to herself and now come to believe that the Father is incomprehensible, she laid aside her former intention, together with the Passion that had arisen from that astonished wonder. EDD.] [Note: [Col. 0556B] Others read “laid aside.”]

## CHAPTER X

But some have dreamed up a different conclusion and restoration for Sophia. After her fruitless attempts and the collapse of her hope, she was disfigured, I suppose, by pallor, emaciation, and neglect of her appearance, as one who grieved no less because the Father had been denied her than because he had been lost. Then, from that grief, she conceived by herself alone, without any marital agency, and gave birth to a female. Are you astonished? Even the hen has received the lot of giving birth from herself. But [Note: [Col. 0557D] “But they also say that vultures are only females.” So reads the old manuscript. Those who insert “give birth” fail to grasp the sharpness of Tertullian’s diction. RIG.] they also say that vultures are only females—and nevertheless she is a mother without a male [Note: [Col. 0557B] “Mothers,” Junius].

At first [Note: [Col. 0557D] “At first, indeed, she was grieved because the generation was incomplete.” Irenaeus has the same words: “At first, indeed, she was grieved because the generation was incomplete.” It is therefore evident that Tertullian had the Latin Irenaeus in his hands. But elsewhere again there are indications persuading us that he also saw the Greek preserved in Epiphanius. RIG.] she was grieved because her offspring was incomplete; finally she feared that its end too was imminent; she was perplexed about the explanation of the disaster and concerned with concealing it. Remedies were nowhere to be found. Where [Note: [Col. 0557D] “Where now are the tragedies and comedies?” For in them infants born from shameful and clandestine embraces are said to have been exposed. But this one, being “unpaired” (ἄζυγος), had given birth from herself. RIG.] now are the tragedies and comedies from which she might borrow a pattern for exposing what had been born without shame [Col. 0557B] [Note: [Col. 0557B] “Around shame,” Rhenanus and Semler]?

While matters are in this evil condition, she looks upward and turns toward the Father; but when she had struggled in vain and [Note: [Col. 0557B] “As,” Junius] her strength was failing her, she collapsed [Note: [Col. 0557B] “She proceeds,” Rhenanus and others] into prayer. Her whole kinship also [Col. 0558A] makes supplication for her, [Note: [Col. 0557D] “Especially Nous.” The Latin Irenaeus does not have this; [Col. 0558B] the Greek reads: “The remaining Aeons also joined her supplication, and especially Nous” (συνδεηθῆναι δὲ αὐτῆ καὶ τοῖς λοιποῖς αἰῶνας· μάλιστα δὲ τὸν νοῦν). But from this the Latin must be emended: “Together with her the remaining Aeons also prayed, but especially Nous. From this, they say, matter first had its beginning,” etc. The common reading is: “Together with her the remaining Aeons also prayed; but especially from this, they say,” etc. RIG.] especially Nous—why not? He was the cause of so great an evil.

Yet none of Sophia’s sufferings proved empty [Note: [Col. 0557B] Junius conjectures “could”]; all her afflictions become productive. For that very struggle then issued in the origin of Matter: ignorance, terror [Note: [Col. 0558B] Junius places “and terror” earlier, after “fear”], and grief become substances. Then at last the Father is moved. Through the Only-Begotten Nous he emits [Note: [Col. 0558B] “Through the Only-Begotten Nous he emits for these purposes.” Rhenanus and others; Junius incorrectly reads “sends before”] the Horos whom we mentioned above, in his own image, [Note: [Col. 0558C] “Female-male.” Irenaeus: “A female male.” Such a compound is rather harsh in Latin, though elegant in Greek; it is as if he said “male-female”: *arrhenothēlys* (ἀῤῥενοθῆλυς) signifies this in Greek. Thus Cicero calls certain figurines “Hermeracles” and “Hermerathenas,” book I of the *Letters to Atticus*. LE PR.] female-male [Note: [Col. 0558B] *Foeminamare*, Paris, Frankfurt, Rigault], since they vary thus regarding the Father’s sex.

They further add that Horos is also called Metagogeus—that is, Conductor—and Horothetes. By his agency, they proclaim, Sophia was restrained from unlawful acts, cleansed of evils, thereafter strengthened, restored to her consort, and herself remained within the register of the Pleroma. Her Enthymesis, [Note: [Col. 0558C] “Enthymesis.” Irenaeus: “Desire together with Passion.” LE PR.] however, together with that appendage, Passion, [Note: [Col. 0558C] “And that appendage, Passion.” Septimius has this from the Latin Irenaeus. RIG.] was banished and crucified by Horos, [Col. 0558B] and [Note: [Col. 0558C] “Made outside the Aeon” is read in the old manuscripts. Nevertheless, one must write “made outside it,” for these are the very words of the Latin Irenaeus; and the Greek reads “having come to be outside it” (ἐκτὸς αὐτοῦ γενομένην). RIG.] made outside it [Note: [Col. 0558B] “The Aeon,” Rhenanus, Semler]—evil, as they say, cast outside. Yet she was a spiritual substance, like a certain natural impulse of an Aeon, [Note: [Col. 0558C] “Of an Aeon.” In the preceding chapters Tertullian could not be compared with Irenaeus without openly showing himself not merely as an imitator, but as one who reads and publishes what he has read. The same fact will shine more brightly than the noonday sun, again and again, from the words of Irenaeus quoted below. Several things especially in the present chapter would require no preliminary comment at all to strike eyes closed even by blind unbelief, and to serve as proof that the very works of Irenaeus we possess were the source from which Septimius did not hesitate to drink deeply. The following points are particularly worthy of notice:

1. Tertullian falls into the very same errors as the translator and uses the very same expressions. Thus each read *telos* (τέλος, “end”) for *teleiōs* (τελείως, “completely”) and translated it as “end.”

2. Near the close of this chapter each has the same words verbatim: “like a certain natural impulse of an Aeon, but formless and without appearance”—or, in accordance with his characteristically greater boldness, Tertullian has “without visible form,” etc.

3. The best editions of Tertullian and Irenaeus have literally the same words a little above, near the beginning of the same chapter: “At first indeed she was grieved because the generation was incomplete; she feared.” Depending solely upon Rhenanus’s imperfect edition, Semler did not hesitate to omit these last words. The rest, however, which refute him no less than these, he was obliged to print and even to admit that here and there the passages are altogether alike.

This entire chapter of Irenaeus must therefore be appended here in full: Book I, chapter 1, § 3.—“Some of them tell in mythical fashion how Sophia’s Passion and return occurred. Having attempted an impossible and incomprehensible undertaking, she gave birth to a formless substance, such as her female nature was capable of bearing. When she contemplated it, she was at first grieved because the offspring was incomplete; then she feared that it might not even possess existence completely; next she was distraught and perplexed, seeking the cause and a means of concealing what had come into being. Having become immersed in these passions, she underwent a conversion and attempted to return upward to the Father. After venturing so far, she grew weak and became the Father’s suppliant. The remaining Aeons [Col. 0559C] joined in her supplication, and especially Nous. From this, they say, the substance of matter had its first beginning: from ignorance, grief, fear, and astonishment.

“§ 4. The Father then, through the Only-Begotten, emits the aforementioned Horos for these purposes, in his own image,” etc. “For they wish the Father sometimes to exist in conjunction with Silence, but at other times to be above both male and female. They call this Horos Joint-Redeemer, Liberator, Boundary-Maker, and Conductor. Through this Horos, they say, Sophia was cleansed and restored to her conjunction. For when her Enthymesis, together with the Passion that had arisen, was separated from her, Sophia herself remained within the Pleroma; but her Enthymesis, together with the Passion, was bounded off, deprived, and made to exist outside it by Horos. It was indeed a spiritual substance, possessing a certain natural impulse of an Aeon, but formless and without appearance because it had comprehended nothing. For this reason they call it a weak and female fruit,” etc.

**Old Translation.—§ 3.** But some of them relate Sophia’s Passion and return in the manner of [Col. 0559D] a fable: that, having attempted an impossible and incomprehensible undertaking, she gave birth to a formless substance, such as her female nature was capable of bearing. When she fixed her attention upon it, she was at first grieved because the generation was incomplete; afterward she feared that this very thing might have an end; next she became terrified and *aporiated*, that is, confused, seeking the cause and how she might conceal what had been born. Having fallen into these passions, she underwent a return and attempted to return to the Father; after daring this for some time, she nevertheless failed and became the Father’s suppliant. Together with her the remaining Aeons also prayed, and especially Nous. From this, they say, the substance of matter first had its beginning: from ignorance, weariness, fear, and astonishment.

**§ 4.** For these purposes the Father sends forth through the Only-Begotten the aforementioned Horos in his own image, without a consort, [Col. 0560B] a female male. For they wish the Father sometimes to exist with his consort Silence, but at other times as both male and female. They call this Horos Cross, Redeemer, Liberator, Boundary-Maker, and Conductor. Through this Horos, they say, Sophia was cleansed and strengthened and restored to her consort. For when her intention, together with its appendage Passion, had been separated from her, Sophia herself remained within the Pleroma; but her desire, together with Passion, was separated and crucified by Horos and made outside it. It was indeed a spiritual substance, like a certain natural impulse of an Aeon, but formless and without appearance, because it had apprehended nothing. For this reason they call its fruit weak and female. EDD.], [Col. 0559A] but formless and without visible form, [Note: [Col. 0560C] “Without visible form.” Irenaeus: “Without appearance,” ἀνείδεον. RIG.] insofar as it had apprehended nothing; and therefore it was pronounced a weak and female fruit.

## CHAPTER XI

Thus, after Enthymesis had been banished and her mother Sophia restored to her consort, that same Only-Begotten, that same Nous—clearly idle as regards care and consideration for the Father—once more, for the purpose of [Note: [Col. 0560C] “Consolidating affairs and fortifying the Pleroma.” Here the Greek words of Irenaeus, “for the consolidation and stabilization of the Pleroma” (εἰς πῆξιν καὶ στηριγμὶν τοῦ πληρώματος), are reproduced, though they do not appear in the Latin. RIG.] consolidating affairs, fortifying the Pleroma, and now fixing it securely lest any such disturbance strike [Note: [Col. 0559A] “Occur,” Frankfurt, Paris] it again, produces a new pair: Christ and the Holy Spirit—a most shameful pair of two males. Or else the Holy Spirit will be female, and the male is wounded by the female [Note: [Col. 0560C] “And the male is wounded by the female”: the male is offended by his female, who has been furnished with power and function equal to his own. What follows suggests this. RIG.].

One divine function is assigned to them: to provide for the harmonious ordering [Note: [Col. 0559B] Pamelius would substitute “completion”; Latinus defends “harmonious ordering”] of the Aeons. And from sharing this function there immediately arise two schools and two chairs, a kind of inauguration of Valentinus’s doctrine as something to be divided. [Col. 0560A] Christ’s task was [Note: [Col. 0559B] “For Christ’s task was to teach the Aeons,” Junius; so too Irenaeus: “he taught”] to initiate the Aeons into the nature of conjunctions—do you see what a thoroughly [Note: [Col. 0559B] “Pious thing,” Frankfurt, Paris] respectable business this is?—to impart a conception of the Unbegotten, and to make them capable of generating within themselves the knowledge of the Father: namely, that he cannot be contained or comprehended and cannot, finally, be possessed by sight or hearing, except through the Only-Begotten.

[Note: [Col. 0560C] “And yet I shall tolerate the fact that they thus learn to know the Father, lest they should know him; I shall rather censure that perversity of doctrine.” Rhenanus ultimately published the text in this form and persuaded Pamelius that it was correct. Nevertheless, I would prefer the old reading to be restored, changing only *discebant* (“they were learning”) for *discebunt* (“they will learn”). It ran thus: “And yet I shall tolerate the fact that they thus learned to know the Father, lest we too should know that all the more. I shall censure the perversity of the doctrine,” etc.

Concerning the knowledge of God the Father, the Valentinians taught as follows: “That he cannot be contained or comprehended; that he cannot, finally, be possessed by sight or hearing, except through the Only-Begotten.” This doctrine was already consonant with the catholic and authentic rule. Tertullian therefore says that he will gladly tolerate the fact that they thus learned to know the Father, “lest we too should know that all the more”—that is, lest we Catholics should learn this better, namely, to know the Father, since today above all we ought to know concerning God that he can least of all be comprehended by human intellects. Then follows: “I shall censure the perversity of the doctrine, because they were taught,” etc. For they were now corrupting sound doctrine by a faithless consequence. RIG.]

And yet I shall tolerate the fact that they thus learn [Note: [Col. 0560A] “Depart,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür] to know the Father, lest they should know him [Note: [Col. 0560A] “Lest we should know that all the more,” Rhenanus, Semler; “that perversity of the doctrine,” Rigault; “that greater perversity of the doctrine,” Frankfurt, Paris; Junius, from the manuscripts: “I shall rather censure this, the perversity of the doctrine: that they are taught”]. I shall rather censure this perversity of doctrine: that they were taught that the Father’s incomprehensibility was the cause of their perpetuity, while his comprehensibility was the principle of their generation and formation.

By this arrangement, I think, it is suggested that it is advantageous [Note: [Col. 0560B] “To experience,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür] for God not to be apprehended; for his unapprehensibility is the [Col. 0561A] cause of perpetuity, whereas his apprehensibility is the cause not of perpetuity but of the nativity and formation of beings that stand in need of perpetuity. They make the Son, however, the Father’s comprehensible element. How he is comprehended, the Christ who was then emitted taught them. The Holy Spirit’s particular task was that all, having been made equal in their devotion to doctrine, [Note: [Col. 0561C] “Might know how to offer thanksgiving.” Irenaeus: “He taught them all to give thanks,” εὐχαριστεῖν ἐδίδαξε. RIG.] might know how to offer thanksgiving and be initiated into true rest.

[Note: [Col. 0561C] Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book I, chapter 1, § 5.—“After she had been separated outside the Pleroma of the Aeons and her mother restored to her own conjunction, the Only-Begotten again emitted another conjunction, in accordance with the Father’s providence, so that none of the Aeons might suffer in the same manner as she had: Christ and the Holy Spirit, for the consolidation and stabilization of the Pleroma. Through them the Aeons were perfected. For Christ taught them the nature of conjunction, making them capable of knowing the comprehension of the Unbegotten; and he proclaimed among them the knowledge of the Father: that he is uncontainable and incomprehensible, and that he cannot be either seen or heard, but is known only through [Col. 0561D] the Only-Begotten. The cause of eternal continuance for the rest is the Father’s original incomprehensibility; but the cause of his generation and formation is his comprehensible element, to which he is equal. The Christ who had just been emitted produced these things among them.

“§ 6. The one Holy Spirit, having made them all equal, taught them to give thanks and led them into true rest.”

**Old Translation.—§ 5.** After she had been separated outside the Pleroma of the Aeons and her mother restored to her own conjunction, the Only-Begotten again emitted another conjunction, in accordance with the Father’s providence: Christ and the Holy Spirit, by whom, they say, the Aeons were perfected. For Christ taught them the nature of conjunction, making them sufficient or capable when they knew the comprehension of the Unbegotten. He also declared among them the knowledge of the Father: that he is incapable of being contained and incomprehensible, and that he can neither be seen nor heard except through the Only-Begotten alone. The cause of eternal continuance for them all was the Father’s incomprehensible element; [Col. 0562C] but the cause of generation and formation was his comprehensible element, which indeed is the Son. The Christ who had then been emitted accomplished these things among them.

**§ 6.** The Holy Spirit, however, having made them all equal, taught them to give thanks and brought them into true rest. EDD.]

## CHAPTER XII

Accordingly, all are made equal in form and wisdom [Note: [Col. 0561B] “Disposition,” Frankfurt; Irenaeus has “disposition,” γνώμη], each having been made what every one of them is: none is something different, [Note: [Col. 0562C] “Because all are others.” We have printed this and what follows as it stands in Pithou’s manuscript. “All are others, not something different”—that is, all are Words, all Men, all Phileti, all Silences, all Lives. Thus the first is Philetus, the second another Philetus, the third another Philetus, and so with the rest. For in this way all are others and therefore not something different. RIG.] because all are the others. They are poured back into Nouses, [Note: [Col. 0561B] *Noas*, Irenaeus and the Old Translator; *Nun*, Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür; Νοῦς, Junius; Νοῦν, Paris, which adds “Words”] into Words [Note: [Col. 0561B] “Words” omitted by Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür], into Men [Note: [Col. 0561B] “All into Men,” Rhenanus and the same editors], into Phileti [Note: [Col. 0561B] “Into Christs,” Frankfurt; Irenaeus does not have this]. Likewise [Note: [Col. 0561B] “And who,” Rhenanus and others] the females are poured back into Silences [Note: [Col. 0561B] “Into Truths,” Frankfurt], Lives, Churches, and Fortunate Ones [Note: [Col. 0561B] “Into Spirits,” Frankfurt. Nothing of this kind appears in either the Greek or Latin Irenaeus]—so that Ovid would have destroyed his *Metamorphoses* had he known of a greater one today.

Thereafter they were restored, established, and brought into rest from the truth [Note: [Col. 0561B] Perhaps “from diversity,” as later “because of diversity”; “to perfection,” Old Translator, Semler; τελέως, “completely”]. With the great fruit of joy, they sing hymns together to the Father. He himself was overflowing with gladness, naturally enough, since his sons and grandsons sang well. Why should he not overflow with every delight, [Note: [Col. 0562C] “The Pleroma having been delivered.” For the Aeons had disturbed the Pleroma and were about to cause trouble for Bythos. But now that the Aeons had been ordered, composed, and instructed through Christ and the Holy Spirit, the Pleroma was in no further danger. The purpose for which he had come had evidently been accomplished: affairs had been consolidated and the Pleroma fortified and strengthened, lest any similar disturbance recur. RHEN.] now that the Pleroma had been delivered? What shipmaster [Col. 0562A] does not rejoice even disgracefully? [Note: [Col. 0562D] “We see daily the revelries of sailors.” From this passage one sees that Tertullian dwelt near the sea, as one living in the territory of Carthage. RHEN.] We see daily the wanton rejoicings of sailors.

And so, just as sailors always exult when contributing [Note: [Col. 0562D] “Toward a common contribution.” *Symbola* signifies a collection, namely whenever each person contributes something to a common fund. Hence *asymbolus*, one who contributes nothing to the common fund. RHEN.] to a common fund [Note: [Col. 0562B] “Cymbal,” Paris, incorrectly, as is evident from Irenaeus; Junius], so too something of this kind happens among the Aeons. Now all are one even in form, much more in disposition; and their new brothers [Note: [Col. 0562B] “New” is absent from Semler] and teachers, Christ and the Holy Spirit, agree with them. Each contributes to the common stock whatever was flourishing [Note: [Col. 0562B] Latinus has “of each one”; Junius prefers “to each one,” or else transposes the words thus: “Whatever was best and most beautiful was flourishing; each contributes…”] in him as best and most beautiful.

In vain, I think. For if they were all one through the aforementioned equalization, there was no point in the common contribution, which normally depends upon diversity. All contributed the one good, which they all were. Perhaps the question concerned its degree, or the form of the equalization itself. Therefore, from the money thus contributed, [Note: [Col. 0562D] “From the contributed money.” What is read in the old manuscripts, “allocated money,” is sufficiently shown to be corrupt by Irenaeus when he says: “Each contributing what he possessed in himself as best and most flourishing, they made a collection.” RIG.] as they call it, [Note: [Col. 0562B] “Allocation,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür; “contributed,” others; “allocated,” old manuscript] they assemble, for the Father’s honor and glory, the most beautiful star of the Pleroma and its perfect fruit: Jesus. They surname him Savior, Christ, and Word, patronymically [Note: [Col. 0562B] Greek πατρωνυμικῶς, “patronymically,” Irenaeus], and also “All Things,” since he was constructed by plucking something from all.

He is Aesop’s Jackdaw, [Note: [Col. 0562D] “Aesop’s Jackdaw.” A fable about it survives among those attributed to Aesop, whence arose the Greek proverb “Aesopic jackdaw” (Αἰσωπείος κολοιὸς), customarily applied to those who display other people’s things as their own. RHEN.] Hesiod’s Pandora, Accius’s Medley [Note: [Col. 0562B] Junius orders the words thus: “Hesiod’s Pandora, Aesop’s jackdaw, the tragedian’s medley,” so that both Aesop the fabulist and Aesop the actor are meant], Nestor’s Lamentation, Ptolemy’s Miscellany. [Col. 0563A] How much more fitting [Note: [Col. 0563B] “Indeed, more fitting,” others] it would have been for him to be called *Pankarpon* (“All-Fruit”), after certain Attic compositions, [Note: [Col. 0563C] “How much more fitting it would have been to be called *Pankarpon*, after certain Attic wits.” We have so printed it, following traces in Pithou’s manuscript: “after certain sacrificial Attic wits.” These words are indeed corrupt, but from them we finally elicit the true reading: “after certain Attic compositions.” By “Attic compositions” he means Greek books, whose titles, conceived with such ostentatious playfulness, were deservedly ridiculed in Pliny’s preface to Vespasian. RIG.] by authors so idle in devising names!

[Note: [Col. 0563C] “*Pankarpon*.” The old manuscript has *Pancapipannirapiam*. Septimius perhaps wrote ΠΑΓΚΑΡΠΟΝ, Η ΤΟ ΠΑΝ, “All-Fruit, or The All.” For Aulus Gellius, in the final chapter of book XX, as that passage is written in an excellent manuscript of the Royal Library, records that these titles also occurred among “Attic compositions”: “There is also one called *Meadow*. There is likewise one called *Pankarpon*. There is one called *The All* (ΤΟ ΠΑΝ). There are also many,” etc. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0563B] This passage is astonishingly corrupt: “after certain sacrificial compositions, Pancapipan Nirapion,” Rhenanus, Semler; “to be called Carpram from Attic compositions,” Frankfurt, Paris. Junius restores it thus: “Ptolemy the music-lover’s miscellany; how much more fitting it would have been for him to be called *Pancarpi*, a *pancarpia*, from Attic histories, by such,” etc.]

Moreover, to embellish so great a figurine from outside as well, [Note: [Col. 0563B] “Had embellished,” Semler] they emit angels as his attendants—a matching kind. If they match one another, this may be so; but if they are of one substance with the Savior—for I found the statement ambiguous—what eminence will he possess among attendants equal to himself?

[Note: [Col. 0563D] Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book I, chapter 1, § 6.—“Thus, they say, the Aeons were made equal in form and disposition, all becoming Nouses, all Words, all Men, and all Christs; and likewise all the females becoming Truths, Lives, Spirits, and Churches. All things, having been established upon this basis and brought completely to rest, hymned the Forefather with great joy, while he shared in abundant gladness. In return for this benefit, with one purpose and disposition, the whole Pleroma of the Aeons consenting together with Christ and the Spirit, and their Father affixing his approval, each of the Aeons brought together and contributed whatever he possessed within himself as most beautiful and flourishing. Having fittingly woven these things together and harmoniously united them, they emitted, for the honor and glory of Bythos, the most perfect beauty and star of the Pleroma, the perfect fruit, Jesus, who was also called Savior, Christ, and Word patronymically, and ‘All Things,’ because he came from all. Together with him they also emitted angels of the same kind as his bodyguard, for their own honor,” etc.

**Old Translation.—§ 6.** And thus, they say, the Aeons were made alike in form and disposition: all were made Nouses and Words, all Men, and all Christs. Likewise, all the females were made Truths and Lives, Spirits and Churches. When all things had been strengthened in this condition and had come completely to rest, they learned to hymn the Forefather with great joy, while he shared in great exultation. [Col. 0564D] In return for this benefit, with one will and disposition, the entire Pleroma of the Aeons, with Christ and the Spirit consenting and their Father jointly affixing his approval, made a collection, each Aeon contributing what he possessed within himself as best and most flourishing. Fittingly assembling these things and carefully joining them into one, they emitted, for the honor and glory of Bythos, a certain most perfect beauty and star of the Pleroma, the perfect fruit Jesus, whom they also call Savior, Christ, and Word patronymically, and “All Things,” because he came from all. Together with him they also emitted angels of the same kind as his attendants, for their own honor. EDD.]

## CHAPTER XIII

This order therefore contains the first procession of Aeons who are simultaneously born, marry, and beget; Sophia’s most perilous fall arising from desire for the Father; Horos’s most timely assistance; the expulsion of Enthymesis and the Passion joined to it; the schooling given by Christ and the Holy Spirit; the protective [Col. 0563B] reformation of the Aeons; the peacock-like adornment of the Savior; and the posting before him of angels comparable to him. [Note: [Col. 0564D] “The posting before him of comparable angels.” He calls the angels the Savior’s *antistates*: attendants standing before him, or presenting themselves to him to perform ministries. They are “comparable” because their kind could be compared with the Savior’s substance. RIG.]

“As for what remains,” you say, “farewell and applaud.” No; rather, I say, hear what remains—and hiss it off the stage. These events, however, are said to have run their course within the assembly of the Pleroma: the tragedy’s first scene. The buskin-strutting of the next act lies beyond the curtains—I mean outside the Pleroma. And yet, if such things happen beneath the Father’s bosom, within the enclosure of Horos the guardian, what will they be like outside, now in the open, where God was not?

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 0564A]

For when Enthymesis—or henceforth Achamoth [Note: [Col. 0564D] “Achamoth, under this one untranslatable name.” More audacious than Tertullian—or perhaps more skilled in Hebrew—are recent translators of the Fathers who derived this word’s origin from Hebrew sources. Feuardent, as learned men consider correct, derives it from *Hokhmah*, “Wisdom,” whose root was *ḥakham*, “wise.” *Achamoth* is either the same noun used in the plural for emphasis (ἔμφασις), of which you have an example at Proverbs 1:20. Moreover, because Tertullian, otherwise most learned, stumbles over this foreign gloss, one must by no means agree with Semler, who infers from it that in Tertullian’s time Valentinian doctrine had not yet been accurately investigated by Christians, and therefore—an argument Semler pursues hand and foot—that the antiquity of the books of Saint Irenaeus must be doubted. Everyone sees how tasteless such an argument is, hanging upon a mere point: namely, a little Hebrew word, from a language which, it is agreed, had not yet been separated from barbarous idioms, had not received citizenship among Romans and Greeks, and was not thoroughly cultivated and known “inside and skin,” especially by Fathers of the Latin Church, until a late date. EDD.]—for henceforth she is designated by this single untranslatable [Note: [Col. 0563C] “Translatable,” Frankfurt] name—was expelled, together with the fault of her inseparable Passion, into regions alien to the light, which belongs to the Pleroma, into that void and emptiness of Epicurus, she was pitiable even with respect to her location. Certainly she had no form or appearance, being, of course, a defective and abortive offspring [Note: [Col. 0563C] Junius punctuates this passage thus: “she is pitiable even with respect to her location, certainly; nor did that defective and abortive offspring have form or appearance”].

While this is her condition, Christ bends down from above [Note: [Col. 0564B] “Christ is brought down from above,” Junius], and through Horos is brought downward so that he may give form to the abortion from his own powers—but form of substance alone, not also of knowledge. Yet meanwhile she is left with a certain small endowment [Note: [Col. 0564B] “She is left with a certain small endowment: a repeated fragrance,” etc., Junius; meanwhile “fragrance” is the uncorrected reading of Latinus]: the fragrance of incorruptibility, by which, becoming aware of her fall, she might be prepared for the desire for better things. Having performed this merciful act, not without the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, Christ returns [Col. 0564B] to the Pleroma.

It is customary for names also to arise from acts of beneficence. *Enthymesis* came from her activity; whence *Achamoth* comes is still under investigation; *Sophia* flows from the Father [Note: [Col. 0564B] “From the mother,” Rhenanus, Semler]; *Holy Spirit* comes from the angel with [Note: [Col. 0564B] “With” omitted by the manuscripts] Christ [Note: [Col. 0564C] “Of Christ,” Frankfurt], by whom, once she had been abandoned, she immediately experienced [Note: [Col. 0564C] “She immediately experienced within herself,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür] desire.

Accordingly, she too leapt forward to seek his light. But if she had not known him at all, since he had worked invisibly, how was she seeking his light, unknown to her, together with him himself? Nevertheless she attempted it and perhaps would have apprehended him, [Col. 0565A] had not the same Horos who had come so opportunely to her mother now encountered the daughter so inopportunely [Note: [Col. 0565B] “So that he even shouted ‘Jao!’ at her.” Eusebius, at the end of book IV of the *Demonstration of the Gospel*, interprets Ἰαώ as “salvation” and “Jesus”; Chrysostom, on Matthew, chapter 1: “The name Jesus in the language of the Hebrews means Savior” (τὸ Ἰησοὺς ὅνομα τῇ τῶν ἑβραίων φωνῆ σωτὴρ λέγεται); Cyril: “The Hebrews called salvation *Jao*” (Ἰαὼ τὴν σωτηρίαν ἑβραῖοι ἔλεγον). That the name was known even to pagans is indicated by the verse of Apollo of Claros:]

“Consider that Iao is the supreme god of all.” RIG.], so that he even cried out to her, “JAO!”—as though [Note: [Col. 0565C] “Make way, Romans!” Porters used to shout this to the people, so that each person might take care lest they inadvertently strike anyone with their load. RHEN.] “Make way, Romans!”—[Note: [Col. 0565C] Or, “The protection of Caesar!” Perhaps, says Tertullian, that unknown word means this: when Horos, the guardian of the Pleroma, saw Enthymesis rushing in with such recklessness while seeking the light she had lost, and when no other remedy remained in this extreme danger, he cried out, “The protection of Caesar!”—which is customarily invoked only in a dire emergency. RHEN.] or “The protection of Caesar!” [Note: [Col. 0565C] Hence *Jao* is found in the Scriptures. Does he mean the sacred Scriptures? I do not sufficiently remember in which ones, unless this is a corruption [Col. 0565D] of the name *Jova* or *Jehova*. Certainly, some most holy name seems to be meant, whose majesty restrained Achamoth as she burst forth too violently. As for what is read in Irenaeus, “Horos, restraining her lest the adversary rush in, said *Jao*,” I am mistaken unless this means: “Restraining her lest she press farther forward”—κωλύοντα αὐτὴν τῆς εἰς τοὔμπροσθεν ὁρμῆς, “preventing her forward impulse.” RIG.] Hence *Jao* is found in the Scriptures.

Thus repelled and prevented from proceeding, and unable to fly over the Cross—that is, Horos—because she had received no training [Note: [Col. 0565D] “Because she had received no training in Catullus’ *Laureolus*.” This is a Tertullianic expression: *exercitata laureolum*, “trained in the *Laureolus*.” Yet, Rhenanus says, the poet Naevius is reported to have written a play entitled *Laureolus*, as well as *Leo in Prison*. After him Catullus the mime-writer—Laberius too was such a writer—composed two mimes, one of which was called *The Apparition*, the other *Laureolus*. Juvenal mentions both in Satire 8, in these verses:

> Your resources exhausted, Damasippus, you hired out your voice  
> To the stage-curtain, so that you might perform the noisy *Apparition* of Catullus.  
> Though swift, Lentulus also played *Laureolus* well,  
> Deserving, in my judgment, of a real cross. . . .

[Col. 0566A] Thus Laberius, according to Gellius, entitled one mime *The Basket*, another *Alexandria*, and another *The Fuller*. In the mime *Laureolus*, therefore, a judge was represented as being put upon a cross, and this was fictitiously enacted before the people. But Domitian ordered a certain man convicted and condemned for a capital crime actually to be fastened to a cross and afterward torn apart by a bear, thereby presenting the people with the spectacle of a real event. On this deed there survives a very elegant epigram in Martial, Book I, approximately as follows:

> As Prometheus, bound upon a Scythian rock,  
> Fed the tireless bird upon his living breast,  
> So Laureolus offered his naked breast to a Calydonian bear,  
> Hanging upon no counterfeit cross.  
>   
> His mangled limbs still lived, though streaming blood,  
> And nowhere in his whole body was a body left.  
> He had, after all, paid the penalty for murdering his father,  
> Or, guilty man, had pierced his master’s throat with a sword;  
> Or in madness had stripped temples of their hidden gold,  
> Or, Rome, had set savage flames beneath you.  
> The criminal surpassed the crimes of ancient legend:  
> In him what had been fiction became punishment.

[Col. 0566C] Suetonius mentions the performance of the mime *Laureolus* at Rome in his *Gaius Caligula*, calling it the “Laureate Mime,” for so some manuscripts read: “And when, in the *Laureate Mime*,” he says, “in which the actor, throwing himself from a ruin—or rather crawling out from beneath a ruin—vomited blood, so many understudies competed to give a display of their skill that the stage overflowed with gore.”

Josephus, in Book XIX of the *Antiquities*, when describing the death of Gaius Caligula, virtually explains the plot of the mime *Laureolus* when he says: “In that spectacle, indeed, two omens occurred to him. For a mime was introduced in which it was enacted that a judge, after being detected, was crucified. And a pantomime danced the story of Cinyras, in which both Cinyras himself and his daughter Myrrha appeared to be killed, while blood was shed by mimetic art both around the crucified judge and around Cinyras and Myrrha.”

Tertullian, who was extremely learned in all antiquity, therefore means this: Enthymesis had not been trained upon the stage in performing the play that the mime-writer Catullus entitled *Laureolus*, in which a judge was represented upon a cross. Otherwise, if she had possessed the stage-actors’ skill in representing a condemned governor upon a cross, she might perhaps have flown over the Cross—that is, Horos. PAM.] in Catullus’ *Laureolus*, she was abandoned to that Passion of hers in a many-stranded and entangled snare [Col. 0566A] [Note: [Col. 0565A] “In a threefold, manifold entanglement,” Fran.; “so that, abandoned to that passion of hers in a manifold race-course,” Jun.], and began to be afflicted by every variety of it: by grief, because she had not accomplished what she had begun; by fear, lest she be deprived of life as she had been of light [Note: [Col. 0566A] Jun. adds “then by consternation”]; then by consternation and ignorance.

Nor was it with her as with her mother. Her mother was an Aeon, but this one, in accordance with her inferior condition, fared worse. Yet another wave also arose—[Note: [Col. 0566A] Fran. adds “namely,” which Jun. deletes.] namely, her conversion toward Christ, by whom she had been brought to life and adapted for this very conversion. [Note: [Col. 0566D] “Adapted.” Tertullian compressed the whole of Irenaeus’ chapter 3 into only the briefest epitome in his own chapter 13. In this chapter 14 he follows Irenaeus more fully and closely; indeed, in his usual jeering and joking manner, he adds certain things, while at his pleasure he divides, transfers, or omits others. Yet he plainly shows—as even Semler himself previously acknowledged—that he had the Greek text of Irenaeus before his eyes.

Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, ch. 4, § 1.—“They say that the Enthymesis of the higher Sophia, whom they also call Achamoth, after being separated from the Pleroma together with the passion, was necessarily cast out into shadows and the regions of emptiness; for she came to be outside the light and the Pleroma, formless and shapeless, like an abortion, because she had apprehended nothing. They say that Christ, taking pity on her and extending himself through the Cross, formed her by his own power with the formation that pertains only to substance, but not with that which pertains to knowledge. After doing this, he ran back, withdrawing his power, and left her, so that, becoming conscious of the passion surrounding her because of her separation from the Pleroma, she might desire the superior things, since she possessed a certain fragrance of incorruptibility left in her by Christ and the Holy Spirit. Accordingly, she is called by both names: Sophia, patronymically—for her father is named Sophia—and Holy Spirit, from the Spirit associated with Christ.

“After she had been formed and had become intelligent, but was immediately emptied of the Word who had invisibly been present with her—that is, of Christ—she rushed off in search of the light that had left her, but was unable to apprehend it because Horos prevented her. And here Horos, preventing her forward impulse, said ‘Jao.’ Hence, they declare, the name *Jao* originated.

“Since she could not pass through Horos, because she was entangled with the passion, and since she had been left outside alone, she succumbed to every part of the passion, which was manifold and multifarious. She suffered grief because she had not apprehended the light; fear [Col. 0567C] lest, just as the light had abandoned her, life also should fail her; and, in addition to these, bewilderment. All these were accompanied by ignorance. Unlike her mother, the first Sophia and Aeon, she did not experience a mere alteration through the passions, but an opposition. Yet another disposition also befell her: conversion toward the one who had given her life,” etc.

The old translation.—§ 1. “They say that the Enthymesis of that higher Sophia, whom they also call Achamoth, after being separated from the higher Pleroma together with the passion, necessarily boiled away in the shadowy regions of emptiness; for she came to be outside the light and outside the Pleroma, formless and without shape, like an abortion, because she apprehended nothing. But the higher Christ, taking pity on her and extending himself through the Cross, formed by his own power a form that pertained only to substance, but not to recognition. After accomplishing these things, he returned, withdrawing his power, and left her so that, perceiving the passion affecting her through her separation from the Pleroma, she might desire those things that were better, possessing within herself a certain fragrance [Col. 0567D] of immortality left there by Christ and the Holy Spirit.

“Therefore she herself is called by two names: Sophia, in a paternal sense—for her father is called Sophia—and Holy Spirit, from the Spirit associated with Christ. After she had been formed and made capable of perception, but was immediately emptied of the Word who had been invisibly present with her, that is, Christ, she went out in search of the light that had abandoned her, but could not apprehend it, because she was restrained by Horos. And thus Horos, restraining her lest she rush farther forward, said ‘Jao’; hence, they say, the name *Jao* arose.

“And since she could not pass through Horos, because she had become entangled with the passion, and had been left outside alone, she succumbed to every part of the passion, which was manifold and various. She suffered sorrow because she had not apprehended it; fear lest, just as the light had abandoned her, life should also abandon her; and, beyond these, consternation—all in ignorance. And unlike her mother, the first Sophia and Aeon, she did not experience a change through the passions, but an opposition. Beyond these, there befell her another affection: conversion toward the one who had given her life.” EDD.]

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 0567A]

Come now: let the Pythagoreans learn, let the Stoics acknowledge, and Plato himself as well, whence matter—[Note: [Col. 0567A] “Matter” in the accusative, Rhen. Seml.] which they maintain is unbegotten—derived both its origin and its substance for this whole fabric of the world, something that not even that Mercury Trismegistus, the teacher of all natural philosophers, contrived to discover.

You have heard of Conversion, another kind of Passion. From this, they say, the entire soul of this world [Note: [Col. 0567A] “Of this kind,” Rhen. and a few others against the remaining witnesses.] was constituted, including the soul of the Demiurge himself, that is, of our God. You have heard of grief and fear; from these the other things took their beginning. For from her tears [Col. 0568A] the entire nature of the waters flowed.

Here one must consider what outlet it took and with how many kinds of tears she caused a flood. She had false drops and bitter ones, sweet and hot and cold ones, as well as [Note: [Col. 0568A] “Bituminous and iron-bearing.” Irenaeus ridicules these follies and says it is credible that, in such great consternation, Achamoth not only wept but also sweated. Thus salty waters flowed from her tears, but fresh waters from her sweat. Indeed, he says that, with her bladder loosened by excessive fear, she urinated acidic, bituminous waters, and so forth. RIG.] bituminous, iron-bearing, sulphurous, and certainly poisonous ones. Thus from her came the sweat of Nonacris, which killed Alexander, and from her flowed the water of the Lyncestians, which makes people drunk, [Note: [Col. 0568A] “And from her Salmacis discharged itself, which makes males effeminate.” This is the entirely authentic reading of the ancient exemplar. For the verb “makes” precedes and must be understood as repeated here: “The spring of the Lyncestians makes people drunk; Salmacis makes males effeminate.” RIG.—“And from her Salmacis discharged itself, which makes males effeminate.” Yet it was because of this effect, Rhenanus says, that Ovid calls it obscene in these verses, *Metamorphoses* XV:

> And, more wonderful still, some waters have the power  
> To alter not only bodies but even minds.  
> Who has not heard of the obscene water of Salmacis,  
> Or of the Ethiopian lakes? Whoever drinks from them  
> [Col. 0568C] Either goes mad or, weighed down, falls into a wondrous sleep.

Seneca explains the cause of this phenomenon: “It has,” he says, “a power similar to wine, but more violent. For just as drunkenness, until it dries away, is madness and, through excessive heaviness, sinks into sleep, so the sulphurous potency of this water possesses a certain sharper poison derived from its noxious air, which either drives the mind to madness or overwhelms it with sleep.”

But Marcus Vitruvius, in Book II of his *Architecture*, explains why Salmacis is said to make those who drink from it effeminate and shameless—which Tertullian here calls “making males effeminate.” “That spring,” he says, speaking of Salmacis, “is falsely believed to infect those who drink from it with venereal disease. But it will not be irksome to explain why this belief has spread throughout the world by false report. For the claim that this water makes men effeminate and shameless cannot be true; rather, the power of this spring is crystal-clear and its flavor excellent.

“When Melas and Arevanias led a joint colony from Argos and Troezen to that place, they drove out the barbarian Carians and Leleges. These, driven into the mountains, gathered together, made raids from there, and cruelly devastated the colonists by brigandage. Later one of the colonists, because of the excellence of the water, furnished a tavern near the spring with every provision for the sake of profit, and by operating it attracted the barbarians. Thus, coming down one by one and assembling socially, they were changed from their hard and savage way of life and were voluntarily brought back to Greek customs and refinement. Therefore that water acquired its reputation not through the disgrace of an impure disease, but because the minds of the barbarians were softened by the charm of civilized life.” Thus Vitruvius.

Meanwhile, the material added from Ovid and Seneca about sulphurous waters that overwhelm people with madness or sleep pertains not to Salmacis but to certain Ethiopian lakes. PAM.] and from her Salmacis discharged itself, which makes males effeminate. [Note: [Col. 0568A] “Makes effeminate,” Par.; “makes effeminate,” Fran.; “grows effeminate,” Rh. Sem.]

[Note: [Col. 0568D] “Achamoth whimpered forth the rains of heaven, and we in our cisterns,” etc. The spiritual Achamoth herself wept the rains of heaven, while we strive to contain in our cisterns—that is, in our flesh, which is assuredly mud and earth—not only our own griefs but even those of others. Every day there is so much cause for everyone to weep; yet we do not weep, but discourage others from weeping. RIG.] Achamoth whimpered forth [Note: [Col. 0568D] “Whimpered forth.” Festus writes, Rhenanus says, that *pipiatio* in the language of the Oscans is the cry of one weeping. Thus Achamoth *whimpered forth* the rains of heaven, that is, emitted them by whimpering and weeping. The verb is coined from the sound of people crying, *pi, pi*. Similarly, the Author says in his book *On Monogamy*, “whimpering infants.” PAM.] the rains of heaven; and we take care to preserve even other people’s griefs and [Col. 0569A] tears in our cisterns!

Accordingly, the bodily elements were derived from consternation and terror. Yet, amid such encompassing loneliness, [Note: [Col. 0569C] “In so great a survey of abandonment.” Or more correctly, “within so great an enclosure of abandonment”? He is playing with antitheses, and just before this said, “amid such encompassing loneliness.” RIG.] within so great an enclosure [Note: [Col. 0569B] “Survey,” Rhen. Seml. Oberth.; “surveyed,” Fr.] of abandonment, she would meanwhile laugh whenever she recalled seeing Christ, and from that joyful laughter the light [Note: [Col. 0569B] “From that laughter of joy the light,” Jun.; “from the same joy, by her laughter, the light,” Rhen. Seml.] shone forth.

Whose providential kindness was it, and what sort of kindness, that compelled her to laugh precisely so that we should not remain forever in darkness? And do not be astonished that her joy radiated so splendid an element upon the world, when her sorrow also poured forth [Note: [Col. 0569B] “Was lacking” in the manuscripts; Rig. conjectures “poured forth.”] so necessary an instrument upon the age. O laughter that gives light! O weeping that gives water!

Yet by now she could have employed a remedy against the horror of that place. For she would have dispelled all its darkness whenever she wished to laugh, even without being compelled to summon [Note: [Col. 0569C] “Summon.” The farther Tertullian advances in his description of the *gnosis*, the more freely and with looser reins he ranges, and the more impudently he assails Valentinus’ divinations. Yet in his joking he does not abandon Irenaeus as his guide. Irenaeus, as befits a judge denouncing so many follies, sometimes lays aside his severe brow and wittily ridicules the new deluge that Sophia’s tears and sweat introduced into the world. A few individual passages should therefore be compared.

Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, ch. 4, § 2.—“They say that this became the constitution and substance of the matter from which this world is composed. For from the conversion the entire soul of the world and of the Demiurge received its origin; while from fear and sorrow the remaining things took their beginning. From her tears came the whole liquid substance; from her laughter, the luminous substance; and from sorrow and consternation, the bodily elements of the world. For sometimes, as they say, she wept and grieved because she had been left alone in darkness and emptiness; but at other times, when she came to think of the light that had left her, she relaxed and laughed,” etc.

The old translation.—§ 2. “They say that this assemblage and substance was the matter from which this world is composed. For from the conversion the entire soul of the world and of the Demiurge received its genesis; but from fear and sorrow the remaining things took their beginning. For from her tears [Col. 0570C] came the entire moist substance; from her laughter, the luminous substance; and from sorrow and terror, the bodily elements of the world. For sometimes she wept and was sorrowful, as they say, because she had been left alone in darkness and the void; but sometimes, when she came to think of the light that had left her, she relaxed and laughed,” etc. EDD.] [Note: [Col. 0569B] “Entreat,” Rhen. Seml. Oberth.] those who had deserted her.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0569B]

For she too, after her mother’s fashion, turns to prayers. But Christ, who was by now weary of traveling outside the Pleroma again, appointed [Note: [Col. 0569B] Jun. rejects “again.”] the Paraclete as his deputy [Note: [Col. 0569B] “Appoints,” Rhen. Seml.; “while appointing,” Jun.] and sent the Savior to her—this will be Jesus—the Father of all the Aeons having bestowed upon him supreme power [Note: [Col. 0570C] “Power.” Grabe, Dom Massuet, and Semler observed that Tertullian understood Irenaeus’ words in this passage less accurately, as though supreme power over all things, even the Aeons, had been given to Jesus the Paraclete, rather than given by the Aeons. EDD.], with all of them being subjected to him [Note: [Col. 0569B] Massuet more correctly reads “to him” in the singular.] [Col. 0570A] so that, according to the Apostle, all things might be created in him—[Note: [Col. 0569B] “Might be joined in covenant,” Rhen. Seml.; “might be created” is better, from the Greek κτισθῇ.] [Note: [Col. 0569B] “And sends him to her,” Jun.] together with an official staff and a retinue of angels of his own age; [Note: [Col. 0570C] “With an official staff.” Among jurists, *officium* is the actual body of persons who attend upon a magistrate; hence, in the same authors, “to resign one’s staff” and “to hand over to the staff.” Tertullian uses it here in this sense. RHEN.] you might even suppose that he came with twelve fasces. [Note: [Col. 0570D] “You might even suppose that he came with twelve fasces.” The handwritten exemplars incorrectly read “torches.” We have restored “fasces,” for Roman consuls proceeded with pomp of this kind. Twelve fasces and the same number of axes, together with their lictors, were assigned to Lucius Junius Brutus and Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus, the first consuls after the expulsion of the kings. They were arranged, however, so that they were in the possession of only one consul at a time, who for this reason was called the senior consul. RHEN.]

Then at last Achamoth, shaken by his ceremonious arrival, immediately drew a veil over herself, performing the primary duty of reverence and modesty. Next she gazed upon him and upon his [Note: [Col. 0570D] “Fruit-bearing equipment.” Irenaeus has “with all his fruitfulness,” σὺν ὅλῃ τῇ καρποφορίᾳ αὐτοῦ. Tertullian’s wording stains Achamoth with the reproach of wantonness. RIG.] fruit-bearing [Note: [Col. 0569C] Thus Fran. and Par.; “having gazed upon him and his fruit-bearing equipment,” Jun. and Rig.] equipment. With such strength as she had conceived from them, she ran to meet him, crying, “Lord, hail!” (*Κύριε, χαῖρε*).

At this point, I suppose, he receives her and strengthens her, and now gives her form [Note: [Col. 0570B] “Strengthens and strengthens.” Rhen. and others read “gives form,” more correctly from Irenaeus’ μορφῶσαι κατὰ τὴν μόρφωσιν, “to form according to the formation.”] through knowledge [Note: [Col. 0570B] “Her through knowledge,” Jun.], and cleanses her of all the outrages of the Passion. He did not separate them for destruction [Note: [Col. 0570D] “The outrages of the Passion, separated for destruction.” Irenaeus: “He effected the healing of her passions by separating them from her.” What Septimius calls “separating for destruction,” the Latin Irenaeus had called “exterminating”; the Greek has ἀφανισθῆναι, “to be annihilated.” RIG.] with the same neglectfulness that had occurred in her mother’s misfortunes. Rather, the defects had become established through practice and powerful through use. [Note: [Col. 0570D] “Powerful.” In the same sense, in *On the Soul*, speaking of the vine, he said, “It winds around more powerfully,” that is, more strongly and with greater force. RIG.] He compacted them together, and, once they had thus been solidified into a mass, fixed [Note: [Col. 0570B] “Fashioned,” Lat.] them apart as a bodily preparation of matter, [Note: [Col. 0570B] Tertullian incorrectly read εἰς σῶμα, “into a body,” in Irenaeus instead of εἰς ἀσώματον, “into something incorporeal”; he should have written “an incorporeal preparation.”] [Col. 0570B] transforming them from incorporeal passion and implanting an aptitude and nature [Note: [Col. 0570B] Jun. punctuates this passage as follows: “and thus—transforming it into a bodily preparation from incorporeal passion, with an implanted aptitude.” Latinus’ conjectures “fashioned separately” and “implanted cheerfulness,” [Col. 0570C] approved by Jun., are not acceptable.] by which they might presently attain rival equivalences of corporeal forms.

Thus a twofold condition of substances was established: the worst substance from the defects, and a passible substance from conversion. This will be the matter that brought us into conflict with Hermogenes and the others who presume [Col. 0571A] that God made all things from matter, not from nothing. [Note: [Col. 0571B] “Presume.” Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, ch. 4, § 5.—“. . . They say that she turned in supplication toward the light that had left her, that is, toward Christ. He, having ascended into the Pleroma, was himself evidently reluctant to descend a second time, but sent the Paraclete to her, that is, the [Col. 0571C] Savior, after the Father had bestowed all power upon him and subjected everything to his authority, with the Aeons likewise contributing, so that in him all things might be created, visible and invisible, Thrones, Divinities, Dominions. He was sent to her together with the angels of his own age.

“They say that Achamoth, revering him, first put on a veil out of modesty; but afterward, seeing him with all his fruitfulness, ran to him, receiving strength from his manifestation. And he formed her with the formation that pertains to knowledge and effected the healing of her evils, separating them from her but not neglecting them; for they could not be annihilated, as those of the former Sophia had been, because they were now habitual and powerful. Rather, after separating them, he mixed and solidified them apart, and transformed them from incorporeal passion into incorporeal matter. Then he implanted in them such aptitude and nature that they could enter into compounds and bodies, so that two substances might come into being: the base substance of the passions and the passible substance of conversion. For this reason, they say, the Savior potentially performed the work of creation,” etc.

The old translation.—§ 5. “When, therefore, the Mother had traversed [Col. 0571D] every passion . . . she turned in supplication toward the light that had abandoned her, that is, Christ, they say. He returned to the Pleroma and, as may be understood, was himself reluctant to descend a second time. He therefore sent the Paraclete to her, that is, the Savior, the Father furnishing him with all power and delivering all things under his authority, and the Aeons likewise doing so, so that in him all things might be created, visible and invisible, Thrones, Divinities, Dominions. He is sent to her with the angels of his own age.

“They say that Achamoth, revering him, first put on a covering out of reverence; then, when she saw him with all his fruitfulness, she ran to him, having received strength from the sight of him. And he formed her with the formation that pertains to recognition, and effected the healing of her passions, separating them from her and not neglecting them. For it was not possible for them to be destroyed, as those of the former Sophia had been, because they were now established and capable. Rather, separating them apart, he mixed and coagulated them, and transferred them from [Col. 0572B] incorporeal passion into incorporeal matter. And thus he produced in them an aptitude and nature by which they might enter into aggregates and bodies, so that two substances might come into being: one evil, from the passions; the other passible, from conversion. For this reason, they say, the Savior performed the work of creation potentially.” EDD.]

## CHAPTER XVII

From this point Achamoth, finally freed from all evils, now advances and becomes fruitful in greater works. Heated by joy at so great a success following her misfortune, and at the same time, so to speak, leavened by the very sight of the angelic lights—I am ashamed to say it, but there is no other way to express it—[Note: [Col. 0572B] “In a certain sense she lusted inwardly toward them.” Thus Rhenanus edited it. But the ancient exemplars read “she builds beneath.” From this a truer emendation would seem to be: “And in a certain sense she herself began to rut toward them.” RIG.] in a certain sense she lusted inwardly toward them [Note: [Col. 0571B] “She builds beneath,” Seml.; “she lay with,” Par.; “she lusted,” Fran.; “she lusted within herself,” Lat., Jun., Rhen.; “she began to rut,” Rig.], and immediately swelled with a spiritual conception [Note: [Col. 0571B] “Spiritual,” Rhen. Seml.], after the very image that the force of her joyful and joyfully itching concentration had absorbed and impressed deep within her.

At last she gave birth; and from that point there came to be a trinity of kinds [Note: [Col. 0571B] Jun. prefers “a trinity of kind.”], arising from a trinity of causes: one material, from the Passion; another psychic, from [Col. 0572A] Conversion; and a third spiritual, from imagination. [Note: [Col. 0572C] “Imagination.” Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, ch. 4, § 5.—“They teach that Achamoth, after being freed from passion and conceiving through joy the vision of the lights accompanying him—that is, of the angels who were with him—and becoming pregnant with them, bore fruits according to their image, a spiritual offspring made according to the likeness,” etc.

Chapter 5, § 1.—“According to them, therefore, when these three already existed—the one from passion, which was matter; the one from conversion, which was the psychic substance; and the one she brought forth, that is, the spiritual—she then turned to forming them.”

The old translation.—Chapter 4, § 5. “They teach that Achamoth, after being placed outside passion, conceived from rejoicing the vision of the lights that were with him, that is, of the angels who were with him; and, delighted at the sight of them, bore fruits according to his image, a spiritual offspring made according to the likeness [Col. 0572D] of the Savior’s attendants.”

Chapter 5, § 1. “According to them, therefore, when these three subsisted, one was from expression [probably a corrupt reading for ‘passion’], which was matter; another from conversion, which was psychic; and another was what she had brought forth, which is spiritual. She then turned to forming them.” EDD.]

## CHAPTER XVIII

By the authority conferred by these three children, [Note: [Col. 0572D] That is, of three children. Much is said throughout the constitutions of the ancient emperors about the *right of three children*. The ancient interpreter—that is, the commentator on the Theodosian Code whose work survives in mutilated form—teaches, in the chapter on lawful heirs in Book V, that a mother possesses the right of three children if, being freeborn, she has delivered three living children, or, if a freedwoman, four. This privilege was also sometimes granted through imperial favor to persons who had produced no children. The emperor Trajan granted the right of three children to Suetonius Tranquillus, who had experienced an unhappy marriage, though Trajan was accustomed to do this very rarely and never to exceed the number that he had told the most illustrious Senate would suffice for himself. Moreover, the right of three children was of great importance for entering upon inheritances. RHEN.] she became more practiced [Note: [Col. 0571B] Jun. suggests that “more thoroughly trained” could be read.] in conducting affairs, and resolved to give form to each kind.

The spiritual kind, however, she could not touch in this way, since she herself was spiritual.
