For beings nearly equal and consubstantial could not exercise power over one another, because their common nature prevented it. With this in mind, she turned her attention exclusively to the psychic kind [Note: [Col. 0572B] “If one,” Rhen. Seml.; Jun. suggests “her hand toward the psychic kind.”], bringing forth the Savior’s teachings.

And first—a thing that must be spoken, read, and heard with a great shudder at its blasphemy—she fashions [Note: [Col. 0572B] “Our God is still being fashioned,” Rhen. Seml.] this God of ours and of everyone else except the heretics: Father, Demiurge, and King of all things that come after him. [Note: [Col. 0572B] “God the Demiurge,” Rhen. Seml.]

For all things came from him—[Note: [Col. 0572B] “For from him, if . . .” Seml. omitted “all things,” perhaps through a printer’s error.] if indeed they came from him and not rather from Achamoth herself. Unaware of anything originating from her hidden influence, he was moved toward every operation by her from outside, like a puppet [Note: [Col. 0573C] “By an isolated impulse from outside.” The old books do indeed read this, but falsely. One must certainly read “by a puppeteer’s impulse.” Thus in *On the Soul*: “By a puppeteer’s movement agitating the surface from within.” The old glosses explain *puppets* as Νευρόσπαστοι, “things moved by strings.” Marcus Aurelius, at the beginning of Book VII, said σιγιλλάρια νευροσπαστούμενα, “little figures moved by strings.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0573B] “Like a puppet,” Jun.] pulled by strings.

Finally, because of this ambiguity concerning the agents responsible for the works, they compounded for him the name *Metropator* (“Mother-Father”), while distinguishing his other titles according to the conditions and positions of his works. Thus, with respect to the psychic substances, which they assign to the right, they call him Father; with respect to the material substances, [Note: [Col. 0573B] “Maternal,” Rhen. Seml.; perhaps “material,” Jun.] which they assign to the left, they name him Demiurge; but with respect to the totality [Note: [Col. 0573C] “Totality.” In this chapter, as in both the preceding and the following chapters, Tertullian returns to a restrained and serious style of argument, temporarily renouncing his jokes. He not only reproduces with exactness the description of the *gnosis* given by Irenaeus, recasting it in his own diction and distinctive manner of writing, but also develops it clearly and expounds it more fully.

Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, ch. 5, § 1.—“. . . But they teach that she was unable to form the spiritual substance, because it was consubstantial with her. She therefore turned to the formation of the psychic substance that had come into being from her conversion, and brought forth the teachings received from the Savior. And first, they say, she formed [Col. 0573D] from the psychic substance the Father and King of all things consubstantial with him. . . . They say that the things after him were formed by him, though he was moved secretly and without his knowledge by the Mother; hence they call him *Metropator* . . . and they call him Demiurge and Father: Father of the things on the right, that is, of the psychic things; Demiurge of the things on the left, that is, of the material things; and King of them all.”

The old translation.—§ 1. “But they teach that she could not form the spiritual substance, because it was of the same substance as herself. Let us note the term ὁμοούσιον, ‘consubstantial,’ which Tertullian rendered in a novel and forceful manner by writing *consubstantiva*. Turning instead to the formation of that substance which had arisen from her conversion, namely the psychic substance, she also brought forth the teachings received from the Savior. And first, they say, she formed from the psychic substance God the Father and Savior and King of all things of the same substance as himself. . . . They say that the things after him were formed by him, though he was secretly moved by his Mother, without knowing it; hence they call him *Metropator* . . . and Demiurge and Father. They call him Father of the things on the right, that is, of the psychic things; but Demiurge of those on the left, that is, of the material things, and [Col. 0574C] King of all.” EDD.] of them all, they call him King.

## CHAPTER XIX

But not even the proper application of the names corresponds to the proper attribution of the works from which all those names arise. She ought to have been called all these things, since she was the one by whom the works were being performed—except that by now they were not performed even by her.

For although they say that Achamoth devised images in honor [Col. 0573B] of the Aeons, they again divert authorship of this to the Savior, who supposedly worked through her. Thus he caused her herself to serve as the image of the invisible and unknown Father—unknown, of course, and invisible to the Demiurge—while the Demiurge himself represented the Son, Nous, and the archangels, the Demiurge’s work, represented the remaining Aeons.

When I hear of three such images, do you not now wish me to laugh at the images painted by their utterly perverse artist? Achamoth, a female, the image of the Father? And the Demiurge ignorant of his mother, much more of the Father? [Note: [Col. 0573B] Jun. places “much more of the Father” in brackets.] Nous the image of one who is ignorant of the Father? And servant-angels likenesses of their masters?

[Note: [Col. 0574C] “This is to paint a mule from an ass.” He uses “to paint a mule from an ass” as a proverb: that is, to reproduce one set of absurdities after the pattern of similar absurdities, or to fabricate new lies from old lies. For he adds, “and to copy Ptolemy from Valentinus.” Valentinus first devised these monstrous follies; Ptolemy added something of his own, varying somewhat from his author. Thus the name “ass” appropriately belongs to Valentinus, the author of this heresy, and “mule” to his disciple Ptolemy. A mule is born from an ass and a mare in the twelfth month, says Pliny, Book VIII. RHEN.] This is to paint a mule from an ass, and to copy Ptolemy from Valentinus. [Note: [Col. 0574C] “Valentinus.” Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, ch. 5, § 2.—“For they say that this Enthymesis, wishing to make all things in honor of the Aeons, made images of them—or rather that the Savior made them through her. He preserved her herself as an image of the invisible Father, unknown to the Demiurge; the Demiurge as an image of the Only-begotten Son; and the archangels and angels produced by the Demiurge as images of the remaining Aeons.”

The old translation.—§ 2. “For they say that this Enthymesis, wishing to make all things in honor of the Aeons, made images of them—or rather that the Savior did so through her. He preserved her herself in the image of the invisible Father, unknown to the Demiurge; the Demiurge in the image of the Only-begotten Son; and, as images of the remaining Aeons, those angels and archangels who were made by him.” EDD.]

## CHAPTER XX
Therefore the Demiurge, stationed outside the boundaries of the Pleroma, founded a new province in the ignominious desolation of eternal exile—this world—after clearing away the confusion and distinguishing the diversity of that twofold substance,

> **Note [Col. 0574D]:** On the mass of psychic and material things. We have emended the text thus, although the old books consistently read *destrusae*. He calls it a “mass” of psychic and material things—what Irenaeus calls “the two confused substances,” those of the material and the psychic. **RIG.**

from the mass

> **Note [Col. 0573B]:** *Detrusae*, Paris; *destrusae*, Rhenanus, Semler.

of psychic and material things. From incorporeal things he constructs bodies: heavy and light, rising and sinking, heavenly and earthly. Then he bounds the sevenfold stage of the heavens above with his own throne [Col. 0574B]; hence also the Sabbath was so named,

> **Note [Col. 0573C]:** “Is.” Others have “They have.” Junius: “And he was called Sabbath.”

from the hebdomad of his seat; and the mother Achamoth is called the Ogdoad, after the pattern of the first-born Ogdoad.

> **Note [Col. 0574B]:** *Primogenitalis*, François; *primigenium*, Paris.
>
> **Note [Col. 0574D]:** They regard the heavens as *noeroi*. The Latin Irenaeus has “intellectual”; the Greek, νοητούς (*noētous*, intelligible). **RIG.**

They regard the heavens as *noeroi* (“intelligible”),

> **Note [Col. 0574B]:** *Noetos*, Rhenanus, Semler.

and sometimes make them angels, just as they do the Demiurge himself; likewise Paradise, the fourth archangel, since

> **Note [Col. 0574B]:** Others read “in what manner.”

they also fasten it above the third heaven, and say that Adam, while dwelling there

> **Note [Col. 0574B]:** Others read “having taken lodging there.”

among little clouds

> **Note [Col. 0574C]:** Junius reads “nut trees.”

and shrubs, received something from its power.

> **Note [Col. 0574D]:** Ptolemy remembered well enough. Ptolemy, a follower of Valentinus, appears to have invented this claim about Paradise as the fourth archangel stretched above the third heaven. By “children’s sayings” he means childish tales customarily recited to children by nurses or old women. **RHEN.**

Ptolemy [Col. 0575A] remembered well enough the children’s tales that apples grow in the sea and fish upon trees; and so he presumed that there were nut groves in the heavens as well.

> **Note [Col. 0575B]:** “Nut groves.” A *nucetum* is a place planted with nut trees, from *nux* (“nut”), as *lauretum* from *laurus* (“laurel”) and *quercetum* from *quercus* (“oak”). **RHEN.**

The Demiurge works in ignorance, and therefore perhaps does not know

> **Note [Col. 0575B]:** “And therefore perhaps does not know.” This is a joke at the expense of the Demiurge, whom the Valentinians fabulously represent as thinking that he made everything by himself, although Achamoth had made it. For they say that he made heaven without knowing heaven, fashioned man without knowing man, displayed earth without knowing earth, and likewise in everything remained ignorant of the forms of the things he made; that he was even ignorant of the Mother herself and thought himself to be the whole of reality. **RHEN.**

that trees ought to be established only on earth. The Mother, of course, knew. Why did she not advise him, when she was also administering the execution of his work? But why, while building so lofty a pinnacle for her son through those works which—before the inventions of the Valentinians—attest him as Father, God, and King, she did not wish those works also to be known as her own, I shall ask later.

> **Note [Col. 0575C]:** “I shall ask.” Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 1.5.2:
>
> “They say, then, that he became Father and God, being the maker of everything outside the Pleroma, both psychic and material. For, after separating the two substances that had been confused and embodying what was incorporeal, he created both heavenly and earthly things and became the Demiurge of material and psychic things, of right and left, of light and heavy, of things borne upward and things borne downward. For he constructed seven heavens, above which they say the Demiurge exists. For this reason they call him the Hebdomad, and the Mother Achamoth the Ogdoad, since she preserves the number of the primordial and first Ogdoad of the Pleroma. They say that the seven heavens are not intelligible beings, but suppose them to be angels, and the Demiurge himself likewise to be an angel resembling God. Similarly, they say that Paradise, existing above the third heaven, is a fourth angel, and that Adam, while dwelling in it, received something from it.”
>
> Old translation—§ 2: “Accordingly, they say that he became Father and God of the things outside the Pleroma, as maker of all things both psychic and material; and that, after distinguishing those two essences previously confused and changing incorporeal things into corporeal ones, he founded both heavenly and terrestrial things and became the fabricator of material and psychic things, of right and left, of light and heavy, of things flying upward and sinking downward. They also say that he made seven heavens, above which the Demiurge exists. And for this reason they call him the Hebdomad, but the Mother Achamoth the Ogdoad, preserving the number of the first-born and primary Ogdoad of the Pleroma. But the seven heavens, which they say are intellectual, they also hand down as angels; and the Demiurge himself as an angel, though like God. Likewise, they say that Paradise, existing above the third heaven, is by power the fourth archangel, and that Adam, while dwelling in it, received something from it.” **EDD.**

## CHAPTER XXI

Meanwhile it must be held that Sophia is also surnamed Earth and Mother—as though “Mother Earth”—and, what should make you laugh still more, even the Holy Spirit. Thus they have conferred every honor upon that female—her beard too, I suppose, not to mention the rest.

Otherwise, the Demiurge had so little mastery of things [Col. 0575B],

> **Note [Col. 0576B]:** Namely, because by his origin among psychic beings he was too weak to apprehend spiritual things. Above, Tertullian noted the Valentinians’ dreadful blasphemy in calling the Demiurge a being of psychic substance. Now, ridiculing the foolish consequences of their doctrine, he says that from that psychic substance, by the circumstance of weakness, the Demiurge derived something weak; and that his weakness consisted in approaching spiritual things—that is, that he was too weak to approach them, unable and incapable of doing so. Irenaeus said in Greek: διὰ τοῦτο ἀτονώτερον αὐτὸν ὑπάρχοντα πρὸς τὸ γινώσκειν τινὰ πνευματικά, “for this reason he was too feeble to know any spiritual things.” From this, the barbarous Latin text would seem to require: “And because of this, being inferior, he failed to discern the things that are spiritual.” **RIG.**

namely, being too weak by his origin among psychic beings to apprehend spiritual things,

> **Note [Col. 0575B]:** Semler: one must certainly read “by his origin among psychic beings.”

that, thinking himself alone, he proclaimed: “I am God, and apart from me there is none” (Isa. 45:6). Yet he certainly knew that he had not existed before. He therefore understood both that he had been made and that someone—whoever it might be—was the maker of the thing made. How, then, did he seem to himself to be alone, even if he was not certain, but at least suspicious, that there was some maker?

> **Note [Col. 0576C]:** “Maker.” Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 1.5.2, 4:
>
> “They also call this Mother Ogdoad, Sophia, and Earth … and Holy Spirit. … And because he was thus too feeble to know any spiritual things, he supposed himself alone to be God and said through the prophets: ‘I am God, and besides me there is none.’”
>
> “This Mother they call Ogdoad, Sophia, Earth … and the Holy Spirit. … And because he was thus superior, he failed to discern the things that are spiritual, thought himself alone to be God, and said through the prophets: ‘I am God, and besides me there is none.’”
>
> Our author gradually glides from jesting into lashing *Gnosis*. Contrary to Semler’s opinion, what he adds to Irenaeus for the sake of refutation is neither wretched nor are the remarks with which he ridicules this empty and shameful philosophy tasteless. For the Gnostics had reached such madness that they offered the foulest worship to a female and conferred every honor upon her—“her beard too, I suppose,” says Septimius, “not to mention the rest.” **EDD.**

## CHAPTER XXII

Among them, the disgrace attached to the devil is more tolerable, perhaps because a more sordid origin is capable of bearing it. For he is assigned to the wickedness of that grief, from which they trace the births of angels, demons, and all spiritual powers of evil. Yet they also affirm that the devil is a work of the Demiurge; they call him the “world-ruler” (*kosmokratōr*),

> **Note [Col. 0576B]:** Irenaeus has *cosmocrator*, “world-ruler.”

and maintain that, being spiritual by nature, he knows the things above better than does the Demiurge, who is psychic. He deserves precedence from them, since all heresies are administered on his behalf [Col. 0576B].

> **Note [Col. 0576D]:** “Are administered.” Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 1.5.4:
>
> “From grief, they teach, came the spiritual powers of wickedness; from this the Devil derived his origin—whom they also call the World-Ruler—as did the demons, the angels, and the entire spiritual substance of wickedness. … The World-Ruler knows the things above him because he is a spirit of wickedness; but the Demiurge, since he is psychic …”
>
> Old translation—§ 4: “From sorrow, moreover, they teach that the spiritual powers of evil were made. From this the Devil also had his origin—whom they call the Cosmocrator—as did the demons and the whole spiritual substance of evil … and that the Cosmocrator understands the things above him because he is spiritual wickedness, whereas the Demiurge is ignorant because he is psychic.”

## CHAPTER XXIII

[Col. 0577A]

They place the citadels of the individual powers within the following boundaries. At the very summit of the heights presides the thirtyfold Pleroma, with Horos marking its outermost line. Below it Achamoth occupies the middle region, trampling upon her son; for beneath her is the Demiurge in his Hebdomad, and lower still the devil, in this world shared with us, constituted of the same elements and embodied together with us. As stated above, this world arose from Sophia’s most useful misfortunes. Without them it would not even possess air—the space in which breath moves back and forth, the delicate garment of all bodies, the revealer

> **Note [Col. 0577C]:** Semler reads “judge.”

of all colors, the instrument of the seasons—had Sophia’s sadness not strained out even this; just as her fear strained out psychic beings, and her conversion the Demiurge himself. Into all these elements and bodies fire was fanned. Since they have not yet disclosed its original passion in Sophia, I shall meanwhile argue that it was shaken out of her by her little agitations. For one may readily believe that amid such great torments she even ran a fever.

> **Note [Col. 0577C]:** “Ran a fever.” Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 1.5.4:
>
> “Their Mother dwells in the supercelestial place, that is, in the middle region; the Demiurge in the supercelestial place, that is, in the Hebdomad; and the World-Ruler in the world that is on our level.”
>
> Old translation—§ 4: “Their Mother dwells in the place that is celestial, that is, in the middle region; the Demiurge in the place that is in heaven, that is, in the Hebdomad; but the Cosmocrator in the world that is on our level.” **EDD.**

## CHAPTER XXIV

What fabrications about God—or gods!—when their fabrications about man are of this sort. For when the Demiurge had labored to produce the world,

> **Note [Col. 0577C]:** Junius reads “therefore.”

he set his hands to man; yet, they say, he did not take his substance from this dry earth, which alone we know,

> **Note [Col. 0577C]:** “As though it had not, even if dry afterward.” In his book *On Baptism*, Tertullian explains the work of fashioning man thus: “Earth was suitable as the material; yet it was not workable unless moistened and juicy—the residual moisture left before the fourth day, when the waters were separated into their station, having tempered it into clay.” **RIG.**

as though, even if dry afterward, it had not nevertheless already dried at that time, after the waters had first been separated, with mud remaining;

> **Note [Col. 0577C]:** The Latin edition reads *tantum quod*, “only just.”

rather, he took it from the invisible body of that matter—the “philosophical” matter, of course—from its fluid and fusible part. Where that came from I cannot estimate, because it exists nowhere [Col. 0578A]. For if fluidity and fusibility are qualities of liquid, and every liquid flowed from Sophia’s tears, it follows that we must believe the clay consisted of Sophia’s mucus and rheum, which are accordingly the dregs of tears, just as mud is the sediment of water.

Thus the Demiurge fashions man and animates him from his own breath. He will accordingly be both *choic*—earthly—and psychic, made in image and likeness: a fourfold thing. The image is to be reckoned *choic*, that is, material, although the Demiurge is not made of matter;

> **Note [Col. 0577C]:** Semler reads “materially.”

the likeness, however, is psychic, for the Demiurge is psychic too. There you have two. Meanwhile, they say that afterward a fleshly surface was woven over the *choic* man, and that this is the “coat of skin,”

> **Note [Col. 0577D]:** “Coat of skin.” Saint Jerome, refuting the errors of John of Jerusalem, charges him with interpreting the coats of skin as human bodies, with which, supposedly, our first parents covered their nakedness and immediately became liable to guilt. **LE PR.**

subject to sensation.

> **Note [Col. 0577D]:** “Sensation.” Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 1.5.5:
>
> “After creating the world, the Demiurge also made the *choic* man—not from this dry earth, but by taking from the invisible substance, from the diffused and fluid part of matter—and, they determine, breathed the psychic element into him. This is the one made according to image and likeness. … Later, they say, the leather tunic was placed around him; by this they mean the perceptible little body of flesh.”
>
> Old translation: “When, therefore, he had fabricated the world, he also made the *choic* man, not from this dry earth but by taking from the invisible substance and from diffusible and [Col. 0578C] fluid matter; and into this one, they determine, he breathed the psychic element. This is the one made according to image and likeness. … Afterward, they say, the leathern tunic—his bodily substance—was placed around him; by this they mean perceptible flesh.” **EDD.**

## CHAPTER XXV

[Col. 0578B]

Within Achamoth, from the substance of Mother Sophia,

> **Note [Col. 0578C]:** “From the substance of Mother Sophia.” This tends toward the error concerning the soul; Tertullian reviews and explains this doctrine more fully in *On the Soul*, chapter 11. **LE PR.**

there was a certain private store of spiritual seed; Achamoth had secretly deposited it in her son, the Demiurge, without even his knowing it. Observe the ingenuity of this clandestine providence.

> **Note [Col. 0578C]:** “For this purpose she had deposited and concealed it.” Irenaeus reveals the same thing in these words: “As for the offspring of their Mother, Achamoth, which she generated according to the contemplation of the angels surrounding the Savior, they say that, being spiritual and of the same substance as its Mother, it too was unknown to the Demiurge and was secretly deposited in him without his knowledge, so that through him it might be sown into the soul that came from him and into this material body; and, carried as in a womb and increased within these, it might be made ready to receive the perfect Reason.” **RHEN.**

For this purpose she had deposited and concealed it: when the Demiurge presently imparted a soul from his own breath to Adam, the spiritual seed would simultaneously be conducted into the *choic* man as though through a channel;

> **Note [Col. 0578C]:** Pamelius, Semler, and Oberthür add “the soul.” Junius conjectures “by means of the soul.”

and, thus conceived in the material body as in a womb,

> **Note [Col. 0578D]:** “Conceived in the material body as in a womb.” Irenaeus: “carried as in a womb,” κυοφορηθέν (*kyophorēthen*). **RIG.**

and grown to maturity there, it would eventually be found fit to receive the perfect Word.

> **Note [Col. 0578D]:** “Eventually to receive the perfect Word.” Irenaeus: “for the reception of perfect Reason.” **RIG.**

Thus, when the Demiurge committed

> **Note [Col. 0578C]:** Junius reads “had committed.”

the transmitted shoot of his own soul to Adam, the spiritual man lay hidden, inserted with the breath

> **Note [Col. 0578C]:** Semler adds “Jesus”; Junius reads “his.”

and simultaneously clothed with the body, because the Demiurge knew the Mother’s seed no more than he knew the Mother herself.

> **Note [Col. 0578D]:** “The spiritual man lay hidden.” Irenaeus says: “Thus, as they say, the spiritual man sown together with his breath by Sophia escaped the Demiurge’s notice, through ineffable power and providence.” This last point is what Tertullian presently expresses: “Observe,” he says, “the ingenuity of this clandestine providence.” **RHEN.**

This seed they call the Church, the mirror

> **Note [Col. 0579B]:** “Mirror of the Church above.” Irenaeus: “A copy of the higher Church.” **RIG.**

of the Church above,

> **Note [Col. 0579B]:** Irenaeus reads “copy.”

and the lineage of the spiritual man. Accordingly, they assign the spiritual man to Achamoth, just as the psychic man is assigned to the Demiurge; the *choic* man to the substance of the *archē* (“beginning”); and the flesh to matter.

> **Note [Col. 0579B]:** Junius reads: “the *choic* man, by substance fleshly, from matter.”

There you have a new Geryon—that is, one fourfold rather than three-bodied.

> **Note [Col. 0579B]:** “Geryon.” Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 1.5.6:
>
> “As for the offspring of their Mother Achamoth, which she … brought forth as spiritual and consubstantial with its Mother, they say that the Demiurge was ignorant of it too, and that it was secretly deposited in him without his knowledge, so that through him it might be sown into the soul that came from him and into this material body, be carried in these as in a womb and increased there, and become ready to receive the Perfect. Thus, as they say, the spiritual man sown together with his breath by Sophia escaped the Demiurge’s notice through ineffable providence. For just as he was ignorant of the Mother, so also of her seed, which they likewise call the Church, the antitype of the Church above. And they claim that this is the man within them, so that they possess the soul from the Demiurge, the body from the dust, the fleshly part from matter …”
>
> Old translation—§ 6: “As for the offspring of their Mother Achamoth, which she generated as spiritual and of the same substance as its Mother, they say that the Demiurge was ignorant of it too, and that it was secretly deposited in him without his knowledge, so that through him it might be sown into the soul that came from him and into this material body, and, carried in these as in a womb and increased, be made ready to receive perfect Reason. Thus, as they say [Col. 0579D], the spiritual man, sown together with his breath by Sophia, escaped the Demiurge’s notice through ineffable power and providence. For just as he was ignorant of his Mother, so also of her seed, which they likewise call the Church, the copy of the higher Church. They maintain that this is the man within themselves, so that they possess the soul from the Demiurge, the body from clay, the fleshly element from matter, and the spiritual man from Mother Achamoth.” **EDD.**

## CHAPTER XXVI

Thus they also apportion a separate end to each kind. To the material—that is, the fleshly—which they also call the left, they assign certain destruction. To the psychic, which they also call the right, they assign an uncertain outcome, since it wavers between material and spiritual and owes allegiance to whichever side it chiefly favors. The spiritual, however, was sent out to be matched with the psychic [Col. 0579B], so that it might be educated together with it and trained in modes of life.

> **Note [Col. 0579D]:** “And educated together with it and trained in modes of life.” Irenaeus: “So that, joined with it, it might be formed, being educated together with it in conduct.” This passage declares very plainly that the Latin text of Irenaeus now in our hands is precisely that which Septimius saw. **RIG.**
>
> **Note [Col. 0579B]:** Rhenanus reads “could.”

For the psychic element required instruction even through sensible things. The provision of the world was planned for this purpose; and for this purpose the psychic Savior was manifested in the world—namely, for the salvation of the psychic element.

> **Note [Col. 0579B]:** Junius, Semler, and Oberthür read “they cast out the psychic.”

In a still more monstrous composite, they maintain that he put on the first-fruits

> **Note [Col. 0579D]:** “First-fruits of those substances he put on.” The Pithoean codex corruptly reads “you may foresee” and “to have begrudged.” Tertullian says *proficias*, corresponding to Irenaeus’ “first-fruits,” ἀπαρχάς (*aparchas*). The old glosses have: “*proficiae*: ἀκροθίνια, αἱ τῶν θυμάτων ἀπαρχαί,” “choice offerings, the first-fruits of sacrifices.” Festus: “*Proficium*, the portion cut off.” **RIG.**
>
> **Note [Col. 0579B]:** François and Paris read “providences”; Ciacconius, “first-fruits”; Pamelius, ἀπαρχίας, ἀκροθίνια (“first-fruits, choice offerings”).

of those substances whose totality he was to restore to salvation: he received the spiritual from Achamoth, while the psychic was the Christ whom he afterward put on from the Demiurge;

> **Note [Col. 0579B]:** Junius reads: “which … he had put on.”

the bodily element, however, constructed from psychic substance by a marvelous and ineffable ingenuity of Reason,

> **Note [Col. 0580B]:** Pamelius reads the feminine form “constructed.”

conferred upon him, for the sake of the dispensation,

> **Note [Col. 0580B]:** “For the sake” is absent from François and Paris; Semler and Oberthür read “for the sake.” Junius conjectures “perhaps, moreover, by way of …”

a power

> **Note [Col. 0580B]:** Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür, Pamelius, and Rigault read “by a power”; Semler proposed “carried around,” or “conferred upon him for the sake of the dispensation.”

by which he would be exposed, unwillingly,

> **Note [Col. 0580B]:** “Unwillingly”: even against his will. **RIG.**

to encounter, sight, touch,

> **Note [Col. 0580B]:** Semler reads “contract.”

and death.

> **Note [Col. 0580B]:** “Death”: suffering and death. Thus Tertullian rendered Irenaeus’ “passible.” **RIG.**
>
> **Note [Col. 0579D]:** “Conferred.” The Pithoean codex reads *in contulisse*. Hence I think it should be emended to “carried around,” corresponding to Irenaeus’ “a body placed around him.” **RIG.**

They say that there was nothing material in him, because matter is foreign to salvation—as though he had been necessary for anyone other than those needing salvation. And all this serves to estrange the condition of our flesh from Christ and thereby cast it out even from the hope of salvation.

> **Note [Col. 0580B]:** Up to this point Tertullian has followed closely behind Irenaeus. From here he proceeds more freely, omitting many things, wrapping some into the following chapters, and adding much that completes the outline of the Gnostics described by Irenaeus. He thus represents for us excellent material from the now-lost writings against the Valentinians by Justin the Philosopher and Miltiades the Sophist of the Churches, which Tertullian had before his eyes. Moreover, as Semler admits, it is clearer than the sun that in this chapter 26 Tertullian rendered more briefly what stood more fully in the Greek. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 1.6.1:
>
> “Since there are three elements, they say that the material, which they also call the left, necessarily perishes, since it is incapable of receiving any breath of incorruption; but the psychic, which they also call the right, since it is midway between the spiritual and material, proceeds toward whichever side it inclines; while the spiritual was sent forth so that, joined here to the psychic, it might be formed, being educated together with it in conduct. … For the psychic element needed instruction through things both psychic and sensible. For their sake, they say, the world was constructed; and for this purpose the Savior came to the psychic element—which is also endowed with free choice—so that he might save it. For they say that he assumed the first-fruits of those whom he was going to save: the spiritual from Achamoth; from the Demiurge he put on the psychic Christ; and from the dispensation he was clothed with a body having psychic substance, but constructed with ineffable skill so as to become visible, tangible, and passible. They say that he assumed nothing material at all, for matter is incapable of salvation.”
>
> Chapter 7, § 2: “There are also those who say that the Demiurge emitted a Christ as his own son, but a psychic one, and spoke of him through the prophets. This is the one who passed through Mary as water passes through a pipe. At the baptism, the Savior who came from all the constituents of the Pleroma descended upon him in the form of a dove. In him was also the spiritual seed from Achamoth. Thus, they say, our Lord was composed of these four, preserving the type of the primordial and first Tetrad: of the spiritual element, which came from Achamoth; of the psychic, which came from the Demiurge; of that from the dispensation, which had been constructed by ineffable skill; and of the Savior, which was the dove that descended upon him.”
>
> [Col. 0581B] Old translation—Chapter 6, § 1: “Since, therefore, there are three, they say that the one—the material, which they also call the left—necessarily perishes, since it cannot receive any breath of incorruption; but the psychic—which they also call the right—since it stands midway between the spiritual and material, is carried wherever it inclines; while the spiritual was sent forth so that, joined here to the psychic, it might be formed, being educated together with it in conduct. For the psychic element needed sensible disciplines. For this reason, they say, the world was fabricated, and the Savior came for the psychic element, because it is under its own control, in order to save it. They say that he assumed the first-fruits of those whom he was going to save: the spiritual from Achamoth; from the Demiurge he put on the Psychic—that is, the animal—Christ; and from the dispensation he was surrounded with a body possessing psychic substance, yet prepared by ineffable art so as to become visible, palpable, and passible. But he assumed nothing material at all, for the material is incapable of salvation.
>
> “Chapter 7, § 2: There are also those who say that he emitted Christ, his own son, but a psychic one, and spoke concerning him through the prophets. This is the one who passed through Mary as water passes through a tube; and at the baptism the Savior, who was from all the constituents of the Pleroma, descended upon him in the form [Col. 0581D] of a dove. In him was also that spiritual seed which comes from Achamoth. Thus they say that our Lord was composed of these four, preserving the type of the first-born and first quaternity: of the spiritual, which came from Achamoth; of the psychic, which came from the Demiurge; of that from the dispensation, which was made by ineffable art; and of the Savior, which was that dove that descended upon him.” **EDD.**

## CHAPTER XXVII

[Col. 0581A]

I now return to Christ. Into him some insert Jesus with the same license with which they stuff the spiritual seed into the psychic element along with the breath—contriving some sort of stuffed beings, both their men and their gods.

> **Note [Col. 0581D]:** “Into whom they insert Jesus with such license.” Receiving no assistance from the manuscripts, we have written “into whom,” etc. Furthermore, the Valentinians insert as Savior into the Demiurge’s psychic Christ that Jesus who consists of the finest contributions from all the Aeons, thus making a stuffed Christ; and in the same way they cram the spiritual seed into the psychic element. **RHEN.**

For the Demiurge, they say, has his own Christ, his natural son.

> **Note [Col. 0581B]:** Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “also.”

He was, in short, emitted by the Demiurge as a psychic being and proclaimed through the prophets. He was placed within the questions concerning prepositions: that is, he was brought forth *through* a virgin, not *from* a virgin, because, having been conveyed into the virgin, he emerged by a mode of transit rather than generation—through her, not from her; she served not as his mother but as his route.

Upon this Christ, therefore, at the sacrament of baptism, the Savior descended in the likeness of a dove.

> **Note [Col. 0581D]:** “The Savior then descended at the sacrament of baptism.” The old manuscript does not have *Soterem* (“Savior”) but *Jem*, corrupted from an older exemplar in which was written *IHM* or *Ihm*, which regularly signifies Jesus in manuscripts. Nor should anything else be read here, although Irenaeus wrote “Savior.” **RHEN.**
>
> **Note [Col. 0581B]:** The manuscripts read *Jen* or *lem*; Paris reads “Jesus.”

And in Christ there was also a seasoning of spiritual seed from Achamoth, evidently to keep the rest of the stuffing from spoiling. For, according to the figure of the principal Tetrad, they cram him with four substances: the spiritual substance from Achamoth, the psychic from the Demiurge, the bodily substance of ineffable construction,

> **Note [Col. 0581B]:** Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read *ine enarrativa*; Pamelius, François, and Paris, *Jesuaciana* (“Jesuan”).

and the soteric—that is, the dove-like—substance.

The Savior remained in Christ, impassible, inviolable,

> **Note [Col. 0581B]:** Junius, following Irenaeus, thinks “invisible” should be read.

and ungraspable. Consequently, when they came to seize him,

> **Note [Col. 0582B]:** Junius reads “when they were coming.”

he departed from him at the judicial examination before Pilate. Likewise, the Mother’s seed did not admit injuries, being equally unsusceptible of subjection and unknown even to the Demiurge himself. But the psychic and fleshly Christ suffered, as an outline

> **Note [Col. 0582B]:** Junius reads “delineation.”

of the higher Christ, who, to form Achamoth with the substantial rather than the cognitive form, had leaned upon the Cross—that is, Horos.

> **Note [Col. 0582B]:** “But the psychic and fleshly Christ suffers.” Irenaeus clearly explains this proposition: “According to them,” he writes, “the psychic Christ suffered, together with that which had been fashioned from the dispensation, in a mystery, so that through him the Mother might display the type of the higher Christ, of him who was stretched upon the Cross and formed Achamoth with the formation according to substance.” Therefore understand “as an outline” to mean “as a delineation of the higher Christ”—that is, as a type or example. **RHEN.**

Thus they force everything into images—being, plainly, themselves imaginary Christians.

> **Note [Col. 0582C]:** “Thus they force everything into images.” Irenaeus: “For they say all these are copies of those things.” The Greek has τύπους (*typous*, “types”). **RIG.**
>
> **Note [Col. 0582C]:** “Christians.” Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 1.7.2:
>
> “This one remained impassible—for it was not possible for him to suffer, since he was ungraspable and invisible—and therefore, when he was brought before Pilate, the Spirit of Christ that had been deposited in him was taken away. Nor, they say, did the seed from the Mother suffer, for it too was impassible, being spiritual and invisible even to the Demiurge himself. According to them, therefore, it was the psychic Christ who suffered … so that through him the Mother might display the type of the Christ above, of him who was stretched upon the Cross and formed Achamoth with the formation according to substance. For they say that all these things are types of those.”
>
> Old translation: “And this one remained impassible—for it was not possible that he should suffer, since he was incomprehensible and invisible; and for this reason, when he was being dragged before Pilate, the Spirit of Christ that had been deposited in him was taken away. Nor, they say, did that seed which came from the Mother suffer, for it too was impassible, as being spiritual and invisible even to the Demiurge himself. According to these people, however, the psychic Christ suffered … so that through him the Mother might display the type of the higher Christ, of him who was stretched upon the Cross and formed Achamoth with the formation according to substance. For they say that all these things are copies of those.” **EDD.**

## CHAPTER XXVIII

Meanwhile, the Demiurge still knows nothing of any of this, although he himself declaims something through the prophets without understanding even this work of his own—for they divide the prophetic advocacy

> **Note [Col. 0582D]:** “Advocacy in Achamoth.” What this word, repeated so often even to the point of tedium, means is not entirely clear. It is conjectured to derive from the Hebrew word for “wisdom,” and thus for a while it has been turned into “Achamoth.” **LE PR.**
>
> **Note [Col. 0582B]:** Junius reads “proclamation.”

among Achamoth, the seed, and the Demiurge. But when he learned of the Savior’s advent, he hurried joyfully to meet him

> **Note [Col. 0582D]:** “He hurried joyfully to meet him with all his powers.” Irenaeus had expressed it very obscurely: “And it resulted in joy for him with all his power.” **RIG.**
>
> **Note [Col. 0582B]:** Others read “went to meet.”

with all his powers, as the centurion of the Gospel. Enlightened by him concerning everything [Col. 0583A], he also learns from him his own hope: that he will succeed to the Mother’s place. Thus, from that time onward secure, he continues the administration

> **Note [Col. 0583B]:** “Administration of this world”: τὴν κατὰ τὸν κόσμον οἰκονομίαν, “the dispensation relating to the world.” Thus by “administration” here he means what he called “dispensation” above. **RIG.**

of this world for as long as necessary, especially for the sake of protecting the Church.

> **Note [Col. 0583C]:** “Continues.” Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 1.7.3:
>
> “Those souls … were loved by the Demiurge more than the others, although he did not know the cause but supposed them to be such from himself. Consequently, they say, he assigned them as prophets, priests, and kings; and they explain that many things were spoken through the prophets by this seed. … They then divide the prophecies, maintaining that one thing was spoken by the Mother, another by the seed, and another by the Demiurge.
>
> “§ 4. The Demiurge … continued in this way until the coming of the Lord. When the Savior came, they say, he learned everything from him and gladly joined him with all his power; and he is the centurion in the Gospel. … He will continue the dispensation relating to the world until the proper time, especially because of his care for the Church, and also because he knows the reward prepared for him: that he will proceed into the Mother’s place.”
>
> Old translation—§ 3: “Those souls … they say were more beloved by the Demiurge, though he did not know the cause but thought them to be such from himself. Therefore, they say, he also distributed them among prophets, priests, and kings; and they explain that many things concerning this seed were spoken through the prophets, since it was of a higher nature. They also say that the Mother spoke many things concerning the higher realities, both through him and through the souls made by him. Thereafter they divide the prophecies, teaching that one thing was spoken by the Mother, another by the seed, and another by the Demiurge. …
>
> “§ 4. The Demiurge … thus preserved his ignorance until the Savior’s advent. But when the Savior came, they say, he learned everything from him, and it resulted in joy for him with all his power; and he is that centurion in the Gospel. … He will complete the creation of the world that is under him until the time that is proper, especially because of his diligence and care for the Church and because he knows the reward prepared for him: that he will pass into the Mother’s place.” **EDD.**

## CHAPTER XXIX

I shall now gather together, from its scattered presentation, what they teach concerning the ordering of the whole human race, so as to bring the matter to a conclusion. Having initially professed a threefold nature, yet one united

> **Note [Col. 0583B]:** Others read “united.”

in Adam, they then divide it according to the particular properties of the races, having found an occasion for such a distinction in Adam’s posterity, which is likewise divided into three by differences of character. Cain, Abel, and Seth, as it were the fountains of the human race, they turn into a corresponding number of proofs of nature and essence.

The *choic* element, degenerate with respect to salvation,

> **Note [Col. 0584B]:** “The *choic* element, degenerate with respect to salvation.” Just as we call someone “degenerate” who is not nobly born, so Tertullian calls that “degenerate with respect to salvation” which has not been generated for salvation. **RHEN.**
>
> **Note [Col. 0584C]:** “Degenerate with respect to salvation.” Irenaeus: “It passes into corruption.” **RIG.**

they trace to Cain. The psychic, released to a hope lying midway,

> **Note [Col. 0584C]:** “Released to a hope lying midway.” That is, entrusted to its own liberty and choice. By “intermediate hope” he means what he called above an “uncertain outcome.” Meanwhile, however, he also alludes to the middle region, where the Valentinians said that the souls of the righteous find refreshment. “Released”: liberated. Thus Tertullian himself writes in *Against Marcion* IV, “released from the torment of ten months,” that is, liberated. **RIG.**
>
> **Note [Col. 0583B]:** Junius reads *delibratum*.

they connect with Abel. The spiritual, prejudged for certain salvation, they deposit in Seth.

Thus they also distinguish the souls themselves by a twofold property—as good and evil: according to the *choic* condition from Cain, the psychic from Abel,

> **Note [Col. 0583B]:** Junius adds “and.”

and the spiritual from Seth. By way of what supervenes they now add not a nature but a favor: what Achamoth pours from above

> **Note [Col. 0583B]:** Junius reads “by which Achamoth concerning …”

into good souls—that is, those enrolled in the psychic class.

> **Note [Col. 0584C]:** “Pours down upon good souls.” Irenaeus: “Achamoth sows the spiritual elements.” **RIG.**

For the *choic* race—that is, evil souls—can never receive saving things. They have declared its nature immutable and incapable of reformation.

That grain of spiritual seed, therefore, though small and slight when sown, grows and advances through its education—which is faith—

> **Note [Col. 0584C]:** “But through its education—which is faith,” etc. Thus below Tertullian uses the thing emitted for the act of emission, a usage also common in Tacitus and Livy. **RHEN.**

as we said above; and the souls thereby so surpass the others that the Demiurge, still ignorant at the time, held them in great esteem. From their register,

> **Note [Col. 0584C]:** “From their register.” A *laterculum* is the name of a book containing the records of all ranks, both military and civil. In it stood the chief of the notaries. **RHEN.**

therefore, he customarily chose both kings and priests. Even now, if these souls attain a full and perfect knowledge of those dirges,

> **Note [Col. 0584B]:** Semler conjectures “nymphs.”

then, made spiritual by their natural kinship with the spiritual condition, they will obtain certain salvation—indeed, salvation owed to them in every respect.

> **Note [Col. 0584D]:** “Owed.” Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 1.7.5:
>
> “They posit three races of men: spiritual, *choic*, and psychic, as were Cain, Abel, and Seth; and from these they demonstrate the three natures, no longer according to the individual but according to race. The *choic* proceeds into corruption; but the psychic, if it chooses the better things, is refreshed in the place of the middle region. … The spiritual elements which Achamoth sows, from that time until now, are educated in righteous souls,” etc.
>
> “Again subdividing the souls themselves, they say that some are good by nature and others evil by nature. … Those evil by nature can never receive that seed.”
>
> Chapter 6, § 2: “For just as it is impossible for the *choic* element to participate in salvation …”
>
> Old translation—Chapter 7, § 5: “They say that there are three races of men: spiritual, *choic*, and psychic, as were Cain, Abel, and Seth, so as to demonstrate from them the three natures, no longer according to each individual but according to race. The *choic* passes into corruption; but the psychic, if it chooses the better things, is refreshed in the place of the middle region. … Achamoth, however, sows the spiritual elements from that time until now [Col. 0585B], on account of which the souls will be educated here. …
>
> “Again subdividing the souls themselves, they say that some are evil by nature … but those naturally wicked never receive that seed.
>
> “Chapter 6, § 2: … For just as it is impossible for the *choic* element to receive salvation …”
>
> In this chapter Tertullian, as he himself says, has gathered many things from their scattered presentation; and, as is his custom, he inserts much and arranges it according to his own pleasure. Through these remarks and those that follow, *gnōsis* (γνῶσις, “knowledge”) is examined in a remarkable fashion within its own domestic organization and practical mode of conduct. See these matters lucidly explained by Dr. Massuet in his dissertation on Saint Irenaeus, Dissertation 1, article 1, no. 74 ff., p. 46. **EDD.**

## CHAPTER XXX

[Col. 0585A]

Therefore they consider no works necessary for themselves, nor do they observe any duties of discipline; [Note: [Col. 0585C] They also evade the necessity of martyrdom. Tertullian was so devoted to martyrdom, and strives everywhere to persuade everyone that it must not be fled from, but must be borne courageously and steadfastly by a Christian, that even pious men deemed him worthy of a black mark here, because he asserted its necessity with more fervor than caution. Hence those commendations of martyrdom in more than one passage, and his abhorrence of flight during persecution. RHEN.] they also evade the necessity of martyrdom by whatever interpretation they please. For they say that this rule was laid down for the psychic seed: that we must labor to obtain by the support of conduct the salvation which we do not possess by privilege of condition. For to us belongs the enrollment [Note: [Col. 0585B] “In Scripture,” Seml., Pam.] of this seed [Note: [Col. 0585C] *The enrollment of this seed.* That is, as I said above, because we have been enrolled in the psychic census. Thus “the enrollment of this seed” is the rule laid down for the psychic seed. [Col. 0585D] RHEN.], since we are of imperfect essence, because we are assigned to the loves of Philetus—and certainly to miscarriage—which is what their mother was. [The reading and syntax are uncertain.] But woe indeed to us if in anything we overstep the yoke of discipline; if we grow sluggish in works of holiness and righteousness; [Note: [Col. 0585D] *If we have to confess elsewhere, I know not where,* etc. He discusses this question more fully in the *Scorpiace*. RHEN.] if we should choose to confess elsewhere—I know not where—and not under the authorities of this age, before the tribunals of governors. [Note: [Col. 0585B] “Governor,” Fran., Rig.] But they, by contrast, may claim their noble birth both on account of the unrestrained character of their lives [Note: [Col. 0585D] *But they, on account of the unrestrained character of their lives.* Irenaeus says: “In whatever deeds they may be found.” By the “unrestrained character of life” he means a life passed without restraint and according to lust.—He calls the disorderly and licentious freedom of their life the “unrestrained character of life”; Irenaeus states that the Valentinians were notorious for it. RHEN.] and their zeal for transgressions, [Col. 0585B] [Note: [Col. 0585D] *Zeal for transgressions.* Through lust inclined to wrongdoing. He employs “zeal” here in the sense in which we noted immediately above that it was employed by Irenaeus. RIG.—*And zeal for transgressions.* By “zeal for transgressions” he means an inclination and eagerness to transgress or sin. RHEN.] while their Achamoth flatters her own, since she herself advanced through transgression. [Note: [Col. 0585B] “By failing,” Seml.; “by flattering,” Par.] For they also say that, in honor of the higher marriages, their sacrament [Note: [Col. 0585D] *The sacrament of the higher marriages.* The mystery of those ineffable and unnamable syzygies above. Iren. RHEN.] must always be rehearsed and celebrated by cleaving to a companion, that is, a woman; otherwise anyone who has sojourned in the world without loving a woman and joining himself to her is degenerate and no legitimate child of truth. [Col. 0586A] And what will the eunuchs whom we see among them do?

## CHAPTER XXXI

There remains the consummation and the distribution of the reward. When Achamoth has pressed the whole harvest of her seed [Note: [Col. 0585B] “Achamoth suddenly [pressed] the whole mass,” Seml.], and then begun to gather it into the granary—or when, after being brought to the mills and ground into flour, she has hidden it in the kneading-troughs [Note: [Col. 0585B] “Of salvation,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] until the whole has been leavened [Note: [Col. 0585B] “Gathered together,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth.]—then the consummation will press upon them.

Thus, first of all, Achamoth herself is transferred from the region of the middle, from the second story, to the highest, and restored to the Pleroma. Immediately that composite [*compactitius*] Soter receives her [Note: [Col. 0586B] *That composite Soter.* Rhenanus thus emended what is read in the ancient copies as *comparcinus*. Septimius calls the Soter “composite,” whose peacock-like adornment he described above. Irenaeus had said: “She receives her bridegroom, the Savior, who [Col. 0586C] was made from all.” Our author will say shortly afterward: “constructed from the blossoms of all the Aeons.” RIG.]—her bridegroom, of course: the two become a new married pair. [Col. 0586B] And [Note: [Col. 0586B] “It will become new.” Here Pam., Rhen., Seml.; “they will become,” pref. Jun.; “and this.”] this will be the bridegroom and bride in the Scriptures, and the Pleroma will be the bridal chamber.

You would suppose [Note: [Col. 0586C] *You would suppose that, where one migrates from place to place, the Julian laws also intervene, as does the dinner.* I think one should read *coenam* (“dinner”) instead of *Cainam*, but an explanation is needed. The whole fable of the Valentinian Aeons is occupied with recommending love affairs, as is readily shown by the terms “copulations,” “conjugations,” “marriages,” and “joinings” that occur everywhere in this work—not to mention other expressions which Septimius, provoked by indignation, uttered almost at the cost of modesty. Their nonsense ran as follows: their higher Pleroma was thronged with syzygies; Achamoth herself, the daughter of Sophia, was at last transferred from the middle story to the highest and restored to the Pleroma, where she was immediately received into the embraces of the bridegroom whom they call Soter, so that a marriage might be formed between Soter and Sophia. This, they claimed, is what we read in the sacred Scriptures as “the Bridegroom and the Bride”; and by “Pleroma” nothing else is meant than the bridal chamber and wedding. Septimius therefore jokes here, though always with a mind hostile to weddings. “You would suppose,” he says, “that, where one migrates from place to place, the Julian laws also intervene”—laws that do not permit anyone to remain unmarried—and consequently that, for all who migrate from here to heaven, a spouse will be as readily available as an arrival-dinner for guests. RIG.] that, where one migrates from place to place, the Julian laws also intervene, [Note: [Col. 0586D] *The Julian laws also.* He means the laws concerning adultery and illicit intercourse, and concerning public and private violence; see the Code, book 9, titles 9 and 12. Observe meanwhile that in these titles “adultery” and “illicit intercourse” are used indiscriminately, although adultery is committed with a married woman, and illicit intercourse with a widow or maiden. LE PR.] as does a dinner. [Note: [Col. 0586D] *As does Caina.* “I do not know,” says Rhenanus, “whether he means the law of Gaius Pompeius Strabo, by which he gave the old inhabitants north of the Po the Latin right enjoyed by the other Latin colonies, enabling them to seek magistracies and acquire Roman citizenship. Achamoth, moreover, [Col. 0587C] in passing from the outer and lower story situated beneath the Pleroma into the Pleroma itself, certainly needed some privilege that would make her eligible for the higher and more dignified place. Otherwise she had reason to fear the penalty of the *Lex Visellia*, concerning which see the Code, book 9, title *Ad Legem Viselliam*.” PAM.] [Note: [Col. 0586B] “Caina,” Pam., Seml., Oberth.; *canulciam*, Jun.; three manuscripts and the Vatican manuscript, *caniam*.]

Then the Demiurge will move from the subcelestial Hebdomad [Note: [Col. 0586B] “Celestial,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth., Jun.] into the regions above, [Col. 0587A] into his mother’s now-vacant upper chamber, knowing her now, though not seeing her. [Note: [Col. 0587C] *Knowing her now, though not seeing her.* He said above that the Demiurge was guided and impelled by his mother Achamoth in every operation, like a *νευρόσπαστον*—a puppet moved by another’s strings—because he perceived nothing of her; that is, he did not know that he was being moved by his mother, but thought that everything was being done by himself. After being transferred into his mother’s upper chamber, however, he now knows that whatever he had done was done by his mother through him. Septimius therefore mocks the foolish Valentinian doctrine: “For if that was how matters stood,” he says, “he would have preferred always to remain ignorant.” RIG.] For if that was how matters stood, he would have preferred always to remain ignorant. [Note: [Col. 0587B] “Than if it will always be so,” Jun.] [Note: [Col. 0587C] *He would have preferred.* Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, ch. 7, §1: “But when all the seed has been perfected, they say that Achamoth, their mother, will pass from the place of the middle, enter within the Pleroma, and receive her bridegroom, the Soter who was made from all, so that a syzygy may arise between Soter and Sophia Achamoth; and that this is the bridegroom and bride, while the bridal chamber is the entire Pleroma.” Ch. 5, §4, near the end: “The Demiurge, however, dwells in the subcelestial place, that is, in the Hebdomad.” Ch. 7, §1: “The Demiurge himself passes into the place of his mother Sophia, that is, into the middle.”

The old translation.—Ch. 7, §1: “But when the whole seed has been perfected, they say that Achamoth, their mother, passes from the place of the middle and enters within the Pleroma and receives her bridegroom, the Savior, who was made from all, so that a syzygy may arise between the Savior and Sophia, who is Achamoth; and that this is the bridegroom and bride, while the bridal chamber is the entire Pleroma.” Ch. 5, §4: “The Demiurge, however, dwells in the place that is in heaven, that is, in the Hebdomad.” [Col. 0588C] Ch. 7, §1: “The Demiurge himself passes into the place of his mother Sophia, that is, into the middle.” EDD.]

## CHAPTER XXXII

The human race, however, will reach this outcome [Note: [Col. 0588C] *In this outcome.* So the old copy reads, that is, “into this outcome.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0587B] “These,” Jun.]: those bearing the earthly and material mark will pass into total destruction [Note: [Col. 0587B] “Into” is absent from Rhen., Seml., Oberth., Jun.] [Note: [Col. 0587B] “About to perish,” Jun.], because all flesh is grass, and the soul is mortal among them [Note: [Col. 0587B] “Animals,” Venet., erroneously.], except the soul that has found salvation through faith. The souls of the righteous—that is, our souls—will be sent to the Demiurge in the receptacles of the middle. We give thanks; we shall be content to be reckoned with our God, to whom the ascent leads. [Note: [Col. 0587B] “Where there is an enrollment,” Seml., Rhen., Pam., Oberth.]

Nothing psychic is admitted into the palace of the Pleroma, except Valentinus’ spiritual swarm. There, accordingly, the human beings themselves—that is, their inner selves—are first stripped. To be stripped, [Col. 0587B] moreover, is to put off the souls with which they seemed to be clothed; and they will return to their Demiurge the souls that they turn away from him. [Note: [Col. 0587B] “Had turned away,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] The spirits themselves will then become wholly intellectual, subject neither to confinement nor to sight, and thus will be received invisibly into the Pleroma—surreptitiously, if this is so.

What next? They will be distributed among the angels who attend the Soter. As sons, do you suppose? No. As attendants, then? [Col. 0588A] Not even that. As images? [Note: [Col. 0588C] *Would that it were even this.* That is, would that they were merely images of wickedness for those angels, and not wickedness itself. RIG.] Would that it were even this. Into what, then—if it is not shameful to say it? Into brides. Then those angels will applaud one another over their marriages, like men who have carried off the Sabine women. [Note: [Col. 0588B] “Praise,” Seml., Rhen., Oberth.; “will applaud the abducted women by right of marriage,” Pam., Fran., Par.]

This will be the reward of the Spirituals, this the prize of believing. Such tales are useful, so that Marcus or Gaius—bearded in this flesh [Note: [Col. 0588B] “In this flesh,” Jun.; for “bearded” perhaps “barbarian,” Sem.] and all that [Note: [Col. 0588B] “This soul,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth.; “with this soul,” Jun.]; a stern husband, father, grandfather, and great-grandfather; certainly, what is enough, a male—may in the bridal chamber of the Pleroma, by an angel—I have already said it by falling silent—perhaps give birth to some Onesimus-Aeon. [Note: [Col. 0588B] “Symphony,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] [Note: [Col. 0588C] *And perhaps give birth to some Onesimus-Aeon.* He alludes to Philemon’s Onesimus, whom Paul begot in chains, as he himself writes to Philemon—but by a plainly heavenly birth, namely, making him a Christian from a Gentile and an upright man from a fugitive. “We expect,” Septimius says mockingly, “that you, who are Marcus or Gaius, certainly—and that is enough—a male, will give birth amid those unspeakable bonds or embraces of the Valentinian angels.” But what will you give birth to? Some Pauline Onesimus, of course? No: some monstrous spawn of Satan. This is what he means. RIG.]

For the proper celebration of these nuptials, in place of torch and bridal veil, [Note: [Col. 0588C] *Then, I suppose, that hidden fire will burst forth.* Irenaeus: “After these things have thus occurred, the fire hidden in the world”—*ἐμφωλεῦον τῷ κόσμῳ πῦρ*, “the fire lurking in the world”—“blazing up and seizing all matter, consumes it; and, being itself consumed along with it, passes into nonexistence.” RIG.] then, I suppose, that hidden fire will burst forth; and after devastating the whole substance, it too, when everything has been reduced to ashes, will come to an end in nothingness; [Note: [Col. 0588D] *And there will be no tale any longer.* These final events, he says, will all occur in reality. It will not be a tale. RIG.] and there will be no tale any longer.

But indeed I am rash, to have betrayed so great a sacrament even in mocking it. I must fear that Achamoth, who did not wish even her son to know her, may rage; that Philetus may become angry; that Fortune may grow bitter. Yet I am a man of the Demiurge; I have to turn aside to that place where, after death, there is absolutely no marrying or giving in marriage; [Note: [Col. 0588D] *There is absolutely no marrying or giving in marriage.* With a single word he expressed both: *οὔτε γαμοῦσιν, οὐ γαμίσκονται*, “they neither marry nor are given in marriage.” Mark 12 and Luke 20. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0588B] “There is no marrying,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth., Pam.] where one is clothed over rather than stripped; [Note: [Col. 0588B] “Could,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] where, even if I am stripped of my sex, I am assigned among the angels—not made an angel, nor a female angel. [Note: [Col. 0588D] *I am assigned among the angels; not an angel, nor a female angel.* That is, I become like the angels and am no longer reckoned male or female. The dead will rise, each with his or her own sex, but the functions of sex will no longer exist, because there will no longer be either birth or death. Augustine, on Psalm 26, at the words from Ecclesiasticus, “Wait for the Lord; act manfully”: “Therefore one who has lost endurance has become effeminate; he has lost vigor. Let men dare this; let women dare it, because in the one man are both man and woman. Such a person in Christ is neither male nor female.” RIG.] [Col. 0589A] No one will do anything to me, whom even then they will find male. [Note: [Col. 0589C] *No one will do anything to me.* Thus in *To Scapula*: “We have no master except God alone. He is before you and cannot be hidden, but you can do nothing to him.” Psalm 55: “I will not fear what man may do to me. I will not fear what flesh may do to me.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0589C] *They will find.* Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, ch. 7, §1: “The souls of the righteous will themselves rest in the place of the middle. For nothing psychic enters within the Pleroma. When these things have thus occurred, they teach that the fire lurking in the world, flashing out and kindling, will work upon all matter, be consumed together with it, and pass into nonexistence.”

“The souls of the righteous will themselves also find refreshment in the place of the middle. For nothing psychic passes into the Pleroma. When these things have thus occurred, the fire hidden in the world, blazing up and seizing all matter, consumes it; and, being itself consumed along with it, passes into nonexistence.”—These words were not very successfully rendered by the old translator. They should therefore be translated with Billius: “When these events have taken place in this manner, they then teach that the fire which lies hidden in the world will shine forth and be kindled and, after destroying all matter, will itself also be consumed along with it and reduced to nothing.” Tertullian has here added many highly witty remarks corresponding to Irenaeus, ch. 7, §1, or the end of that chapter. EDD.]

## CHAPTER XXXIII

Finally, as a kind of concluding flourish after so great a fable, I shall bring forward also those doctrines which—lest they disrupt the order and scatter the reader’s attention by their insertion—I preferred to postpone until this point, though they have been recommended in various different forms by Ptolemy’s revisers.

For pupils from his own school arose above their master, who assigned a double conjugal pair to their Bythos: Thought and Will. For a single Thought, by which he could have produced nothing, was not enough; with two, production was very easy. [Note: [Col. 0589B] “Produced very easily,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] The first conjugal pair was Only-Begotten and Truth: Truth, the female, in the image of Thought; Only-Begotten, the male, in the image [Col. 0589B] of Will. For the power of Will, as that which gives effect to Thought, possesses the status of the male. [Note: [Col. 0589B] “And” is absent from Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] [Note: [Col. 0589B] “As indeed,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] [Note: [Col. 0589D] *Status.* Tertullian has passed over a great many things and omitted everything that made up Irenaeus, chapters 8, 9, 10, and 11. How successfully, as he intended, he took care that nothing should disrupt the order, I should like you to see and judge at your pleasure. Irenaeus, book II, ch. 12, §1: “Ptolemy and those with him, being even more expert than their own teacher in these matters … devised and bestowed upon God, whom they call Bythos, two spouses, which he also called dispositions: Thought and Will. For first, he says, he thought of producing, and then he willed it. Therefore, from these two dispositions … the production of Only-Begotten and Truth took place as a conjugal pair; they came forth as certain types and images of the Father’s two dispositions … the male became the image of ungenerated Thought, and the female of Will; Will, therefore, became the power of Thought.”

The old translation.—“Those around Ptolemy, being more knowledgeable, say that Bythos has two spouses, which they also call dispositions, Ennoea and Thelesis. For first he conceived in his mind the production of something, as they say, and afterward willed it. Therefore, by these two affections … the emission of Monogenes and Aletheia occurred as a conjugal pair. They say that these came forth as types and images of the Father’s two affections … the male is the image of adventitious Will, but the female of innate Ennoea, since Will became, as it were, the power of Ennoea.” EDD.]

## CHAPTER XXXIV

Others, more modest, recalling the honor due to divinity and wishing to remove from him even the disgrace of a single marriage, preferred to assign no sex to Bythos. And [Note: [Col. 0589B] “So that,” al.] perhaps [Col. 0590A] they pronounce *hoc Deum* (“this God,” with a neuter demonstrative), not *hic Deus* (“this God,” with a masculine demonstrative). [Note: [Col. 0590B] “Lord,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] Others, on the contrary, call it both male and female, lest Fenestella, the commentator on the *Annals*, suppose that a Hermaphrodite existed only among the people of Luna. [Note: [Col. 0590C] *Only among the people of Luna.* He means the ancient Etruscan town from which Luna marble takes its name. LE PR.]

## CHAPTER XXXV

There are some who do not defend Bythos’ primacy, but his posteriority. They place the Ogdoad before everything, itself derived from a Tetrad, though under [Note: [Col. 0590B] “And” is absent from Pam., Fran.] different names. First they establish Proarche; second, Anennoeton; third, Arrheton; [Note: [Col. 0590B] “Archeton,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] fourth, Aoraton. From Proarche, therefore, they say that Arche proceeded in the first and fifth place; from Anennoeton, Acatalepton in the second and sixth place; from Arrheton [Note: [Col. 0590B] “Arceton,” Seml.] Anonomaston in the third and seventh place; and from the Invisible, Agenneton in the fourth and eighth place. [Col. 0590B]

What principle orders this—so that the several beings are born in two places apiece, and places so widely separated—I would rather remain ignorant of than learn. For what soundness can things possess when they are produced so perversely? [Note: [Col. 0590C] *Are produced.* Irenaeus, ch. 11. In this chapter Tertullian now returns to the end of Irenaeus, ch. 11, namely: “Others among them, again, have called the first and primordial Ogdoad by these names: first Proarche, then Anennoeton, third Arrheton, and fourth Aoraton. From the first, Proarche, Arche was produced in the first and fifth place; from Anennoeton, Acatalepton in the second and sixth place; from Arrheton, Anonomaston in the third and seventh place; and from Aoraton, Agenneton.”

The old translation.—“Others among them, again, have named the first and primordial octonation by these names: first Proarche, then Anennaeton, third Arrheton, and fourth Aoraton. From the first, Proarche, Arche was emitted in the first and fifth place; from Anennoeton, Acatalepton in the second and sixth place; from Arrheton, Anonomaston in the third and seventh place; and from Aoraton, Agenneton in the fourth and eighth place.” EDD.]

## CHAPTER XXXVI

How much better are those who, having removed this whole wearisome business from the way, maintained that no Aeon was constructed from another by steps that were truly Gemonian, [Note: [Col. 0590D] *Steps that were truly Gemonian.* The names “Gemonian Steps” and “Gemonian Stairs” are very well known among philologists. It was a place on the Aventine Hill notorious for the punishment of criminals. LE PR.] but rather that—as they say—once the starting signal had been given, this eightfold team was brought forth all at once from the Father and [Col. 0591A] his Ennoea. [Note: [Col. 0591B] “And from the Father,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth. Semler nevertheless notes that one should certainly read “Father.”]

They bear their names, finally, from his own activity. When, they say, he thought of producing, in this respect he was called Father. When he produced, since he produced true things, in this respect he was called Truth. When he wished himself to be recognized, in this respect he was declared Man. When he produced those whom he had forethought, then he was named Church. Man uttered Word, and this is the firstborn Son; and Life was joined to Word, and the first Ogdoad was completed. But this weariness is no [Note: [Col. 0591B] “No” is absent from Pam., Fran., Par.] small thing. [Note: [Col. 0591B] *Small thing.* Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, ch. 12, §2: “They declare, as though he himself had acted as midwife, that the first Ogdoad was not produced by descent, one Aeon from another, but that the production of the six Aeons was brought forth simultaneously and all at once by the Forefather and his Ennoea.… For that which the Forefather thought to produce was called Father; [Col. 0591C] because that which he produced was truth, it was named Truth; when, therefore, he wished to reveal himself, this was called Man; and those whom he had previously conceived, when he produced them, were called Church. And Man uttered the Word; this is the firstborn Son. Life follows the Word, and thus the first Ogdoad was completed.”

The old translation.—“Those regarded as more prudent among them say that the first octonation was not emitted by degrees, one Aeon from another, but that the emission of the Aeons was brought forth simultaneously and as a unity by the Forefather and his Ennoea; and they affirm that he himself acted as midwife.… When the Forefather thought of emitting something, this was called Father; but when the things he emitted were true, this was called Aletheia. When, therefore, he wished to display himself, this was called Anthropos. Those whom he had forethought, after he emitted them, were called Ecclesia. Anthropos spoke Logos; this is the firstborn Son. Zoe follows Logos, and thus the first octonation was completed.” EDD.]

## CHAPTER XXXVII

Receive now the other conceptions of Ennius’ Curruca, [Note: [Col. 0591C] *Receive the other conceptions.* Latinius thought it should be emended to “Receive other huge, merchant-vessel-like things.” A *cercurus*, he says, is the name of a very large Asian ship. Festus indeed handed down this information. But this is far too feeble in comparison with the stupidity and madness of the Valentinian whom Tertullian is ridiculing. The wholly consistent reading of the old copies, however, is: “Receive other Circurianian conceptions.” From this we conjecture that our author wrote: “Receive the other conceptions of Ennius’ Curruca, a more distinguished teacher among them,” etc. *Curruca* was the name of a certain foolish mimic actor, as we learn from the ancient commentator on this verse from Juvenal’s sixth Satire:

> Now, Curruca, you are pleased with yourself, and from her lips  
> You drink the tears—

where some fool is clearly being portrayed. Ennius, it seems, was the first to introduce this Curruca as a character well suited to ridiculous performances. Hence Tertullian here called one of the leading Valentinians—who uttered his ravings as though they were pontifical pronouncements, with words contrived for the occasion—“Ennius’ Curruca.” Jerome, imitating Tertullian, said in the second book *Against Rufinus*: “You translate a scholion of Didymus in which, with fruitless labor, he attempts to defend another man’s work, claiming that Origen indeed spoke correctly, but that we, simple men and Ennius’ Currucae, cannot understand either his wisdom or yours, who translated him.” For this is also how the corrupt reading there, “Ennius’ tame creatures,” should be emended. Moreover, our conjecture may also appear to be confirmed by the fact that Irenaeus, attacking this Valentinian whom Septimius calls Curruca, played upon the words for melon, gourd, and cucumber. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0591B] “Circurian,” Seml., Oberth.; “Ennian Cicuria,” Pam., Fran., Jun.; “Lyncurian,” Rhen.; “merchant-vessel-like,” Lat.] a more distinguished teacher among them, [Note: [Col. 0592C] *A more distinguished teacher among them.* Irenaeus: “Another certain man, who is also a celebrated teacher among them, reaching upward to greater sublimity and, as it were, to greater knowledge.” RIG.] who, on his pontifical authority, [Note: [Col. 0591B] “From,” Pam., Fran., Par.] issued the following decree.

“Before all things,” he says, “there is Proarche, inconceivable, ineffable, and unnamable, [Note: [Col. 0591B] “And unnamable” is absent from Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] which [Note: [Col. 0592C] *I call Monotes.* He fabricates words peculiar to himself; he subsequently explains this word as *Solitas*, “Solitariness.” LE PR.] I call Monotes.” [Col. 0592A] With it there was another power, which I also call Henotes. Monotes and Henotes—that is, Solitariness and Oneness—being one, produced without producing the intellectual, unbegotten, invisible Beginning of all things, which the discourse called Monad. [Note: [Col. 0592B] “Monad” is absent from the copies of Rhen.] With it is a power of the same substance, which he calls Union. These powers, therefore—Solitariness, Singularity, Oneness, [Note: [Col. 0592B] “Singularity, Oneness” are absent from Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] and Union—propagated the remaining productions of the Aeons.

O what a difference! Let Union and Oneness, Singularity and its own Solitariness, [Note: [Col. 0592B] “And its own, and accustomed,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] change places: whichever [Note: [Col. 0592B] “And whichever,” Pam.] you designate, it is one and the same. [Note: [Col. 0592C] *Whichever you designate.* That is, whichever of them you name—Union, Oneness, Singularity, or Solitariness—you say nothing other than “one.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0592C] *It is one.* Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book I, ch. 11, §3: “… Before all things there is a Proarche, beyond prior conception, ineffable and unnamable, which I designate Monotes. With this Monotes coexists a power which I also name Henotes. This Henotes and Monotes, being one, produced without producing the intellectual, unbegotten, and invisible Beginning of all things, which the discourse calls Monad. With this Monad coexists a power consubstantial with it, which I also name the One. These powers—Monotes and Henotes, Monad and the One—produced the remaining productions of the Aeons.”

The old translation.—“Before all there is Proarche, Proanennoetos (surpassing every thought), and unnamable, which I also call Henotes. With this Henotes, moreover, coexists Monotes. This Henotes and Monotes, being one, emitted, although they emitted nothing, the Beginning of all things, Noeton and Agenneton and Aoraton, which the discourse calls Monad.
