With this Monad is a power of the same substance as it, which I also call Hen. These powers, therefore—that is, Monotes and Henotes, Monad and Hen—emitted the remaining emissions of the Aeons.”]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

Secundus is now more humane, because more concise. He divides the Ogdoad into two Tetrads, right and left, light and darkness. His only qualification is that he does not derive that power which leapt away and fell short from any one of the [Col. 0592B] thirty [Note: [Col. 0592B] “Thirty” is absent from Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] Aeons, but from the fruits proceeding from their substance. [Note: [Col. 0592D] “Proceed.” Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, ch. 11, §2: “Secundus says that the first Ogdoad consists of a right-hand Tetrad and a left-hand Tetrad, handing down that they are called respectively light and darkness; but he says that the power which separated and fell short did not come from the thirty Aeons, but…”

The old translation.—“Secundus, however, handed down the first Ogdoad as follows, saying that there is a right-hand quaternion and a left-hand quaternion, light and darkness; and he says that the power which departed and was deprived did not come from the thirty Aeons, but from their fruits.”] [Note: [Col. 0592B] “Proceed from the substance,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth.]

## CHAPTER XXXIX

[Col. 0593A]

Concerning the Lord Jesus himself [Note: [Col. 0593A] “Ien,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth.], how great a diversity rends them apart! [Note: [Col. 0593B] *From the blossoms of all the Aeons.* Observe here the supreme blasphemy of these utterly impious men. They declare that Jesus, our Savior and champion, was generated from the whole of their Pleroma, from all the Aeons.]

O head incurable even by the hellebore of three Anticyras! LE PR.] Some construct him from the flowerings of all the Aeons; others maintain that he consisted solely of the ten whom Word and Life brought forth—hence also the buds (*oculi*) of Word and Life converged in him. These [Note: [Col. 0593A] “Flowerings.” “That one,” Pam.] derive him rather from the twelve [Note: [Col. 0593A] “Christ,” Rhen. Seml. Oberth.], from the offspring of Man and Church; and for that reason, they say, he was proclaimed the Son of Man [Note: [Col. 0593A] “From the ancestor,” Rhen. Seml. Pam. Obert.]. Others say that he was fashioned by Christ and the Holy Spirit, who had been provided for the stabilization [Col. 0594A] of the universe [Note: [Col. 0594A] “For its conversion,” Rhen. Seml. Oberth.], and thus rightly [Note: [Col. 0594A] “And in himself,” Rhen. Seml. Oberth.; “and to be,” Jun.] became heir to the paternal designation. There are some who have conceived the expression “Son of Man” differently, although [Note: [Col. 0594A] “Since,” Jun.] they have ventured to call the Father himself “Man” because of a great mystery contained in the name.

[Note: [Col. 0593B] “They have ventured.” Chapter 12, § 4. “There is also much contention among them concerning the Savior. For some say that he came into being from all of them; others say that he was emitted from only the ten Aeons derived from Word and Life, preserving the ancestral names. Others say that he came from the twelve Aeons generated from Man and Life [sic; the context requires ‘Church’], and that for this reason he is acknowledged as the Son of Man, as though he were the offspring [Col. 0593C] of Man. Others say that he was brought into being by Christ and the Holy Spirit for the support of the Pleroma, and that for this reason he is called Christ, preserving the Father’s . . . designation. Still others . . . some of their rhapsodists say that the Forefather . . . is called Man; and that this is the great and hidden mystery: that the power which is above all things and encompasses all things is called Man.”

Old Translation.—“There is also much contention among them concerning the Savior. For some say that he was generated from all. Therefore he is called Good Pleasure, because the entire Pleroma thought it good to glorify the Father through him. Others say that he was emitted solely from the ten Aeons who derive from Logos and Zoe; and for this reason he is called Logos and Zoe, preserving the names of his parents. Others say that he came from the twelve Aeons who were produced from Anthropos and Ecclesia; and for this reason he is called the Son, as though born afterward from Anthropos. Others say that he was made by Christ and the Holy Spirit for the establishment of the Pleroma, and that for this reason he is called Christ, [Col. 0593D] preserving his Father’s . . . designation. Others again say that the Forefather of all is himself called Anthropos, and that this is the great and hidden mystery: that the power which is above all things and contains all things is called Anthropos.” EDD.]

What more, then, can you expect of his faith in God, with whom you are now being placed on an equal footing? Such inventive notions grow rank among them from the overflowing abundance of the maternal seed. And thus the doctrines of the Valentinians, flourishing into wild growth [Note: [Col. 0594A] “Growing insolent,” Rhen. Seml. Obert. Pam.], have now matured into forests of Gnostics.

[Note: [Col. 0593D] **Conclusion.**—Thus far, then, it is clearer than the sun that throughout the whole course of his little book Tertullian followed closely in Irenaeus’ footsteps. He did indeed either omit much, expand it, or wrap it in different words; yet by many clear indications he disclosed that he had set before himself no earlier, more distinguished, or more diligent guide. As we have seen, he had obtained for himself and drawn from abundantly not only Irenaeus’ Greek work but also its old Latin translation. Hence Semler’s insane paradoxes concerning the uncertain character and origin of the books of Irenaeus and Tertullian collapse utterly.

Nor does Semler’s frequent accusation against the ancient Apologists rest upon any firmer foundation: namely, that they were ignorant of the true teaching [Col. 0594A] of the Gnostics and corrupted their sound opinions and indications of a more perfect knowledge so that they might be ridiculed more easily. These and similar charges he repeatedly levels and amplifies, as though with particular zeal, against our Irenaeus and his faithful interpreter Septimius. But from where, pray, do you possess those Gnostic teachings and opinions, except from Irenaeus and Tertullian? If you insist that they were ignorant of them, how much more certain it is that we too are ignorant of them! They, after all, were contemporaries of the heretics, mingled with them, and dealt with them at close quarters in preaching and controversy; whereas we have been placed in the last ages and are far more remote from them in doctrines, dispositions, the whole manner of life, and customs. Therefore let all Gnostics—whether ancient and dead or revived and more recent—lie prostrate, and lie forever, pierced through by the invincible weapons of Irenaeus and Tertullian.

For no one fails to see how closely connected are, on the one hand, the decaying ravings of ancient *Gnosis* (Γνῶσις) and, on the other, the more recent experiments of the new “science,” especially the arguments of audacious initiates, mythicists, and symbolists springing up everywhere in the schools of Germany. Hence their anger against Irenaeus and Tertullian alike, but greatest of all against Irenaeus, who, in addition to these offenses, incurred enormous charges against himself when he exalted the Roman see with such great praise and celebrated it with such exceptional proclamations as the Queen of the Catholic Church [Col. 0594C] and Advocate of mankind. Be that as it may, the arguments of the Fathers have not yet faded from the minds—or the anger—of modern thinkers; and even now from those Fathers we must take up the weapons by which these ranks of enemies, covered in clouds and dust, may be routed and put to flight. They have dreamed up a new ordering of divine and human realities, stuffed with fables and allegories, “forcing everything,” as Septimius says most aptly, “into images”—themselves plainly imaginary Christians. EDD. CAP. II, col. 544.

Recent investigators of Gnostic matters have regarded it as altogether established and certain that, in this and the other chapters of his little book, Tertullian frequently alluded to the books of Valentinus himself, and that he manifestly had in his hands and before his eyes Valentinus’ principal volume, entitled *Sophia*. [Col. 0594D] Moreover, this other father of *Gnosis* (Γνῶσις) published a great many works, some fragments of which survive scattered throughout Clement of Alexandria’s *Stromata*: namely, certain fragments of Valentinus’ letters in book I, pp. 975 and 409, and III, p. 450; then a scrap of his homilies in *Stromata*, book IV, p. 641; and finally a detached fragment from his treatise *On Friends*, p. 509. In addition, the most distinguished Grabe collated and corrected a short dissertation *On the Origin of Evil* from two manuscripts of the Bodleian Library, nos. 2040 and 2584, in *Spicilegium Haereticum of the Second Century*, p. 55. All these texts are found republished in the appendix to the five books of Irenaeus *Against Heresies*, pp. 352ff., ed. D. Massuet, Paris, 1710.

Indeed, the celebrated volume *On Sophia* would not even now be entirely lost, if any credit is due to Woide, an English philologist of the last century. Among the manuscripts collected by Dr. Askew, he found one composed of parchment leaves, in quarto format, written in Greek uncial letters of extreme antiquity, but composed throughout in the Egyptian language of the Copts. It bore no title at its beginning, but at the end of its second part displayed these words: “The Second Volume of the Faithful Sophia.” Woide became persuaded that this was Valentinus’ book, to which Tertullian sometimes alludes, since he saw that the codex contained thirteen penitential psalms of Sophia, thirteen songs in praise of Christ as Sophia’s redeemer, and certain conversations of Christ with the disciples and the women of the Gospels.

Yet in these very annotations Woide supplied grounds for doubting whether these texts were rightly or wrongly attributed to Valentinus. For it is by no means probable that Valentinus composed his greatest work in the Egyptian language, and not a few of the passages that Woide extracted and translated have the character of a translation of this work. Nothing in fact clearly points either to Valentinus or to his following; indeed, certain features wholly foreign to Valentinus oppose Woide’s opinion—namely, Barbelo, Jaldabaoth, twelve saviors, and [Col. 0596A] other teachings concerning the dignity of the Apostles and the origin of souls. Furthermore, psalms or songs would wrongly be attributed to the book *On Sophia*; how much more, then, the discourses of Christ, which show more clearly that these materials were taken from the apocryphal *Gospel according to the Egyptians*. Nor is this conclusion weakened by the title *The Faithful Sophia*, from which one may infer only that the book treats a Gnostic subject.

To the same subject should likewise be referred another codex described by Woide. It was written in the same Egyptian language, in the Sahidic dialect, consisted of seventy-six quarto leaves, and was divided into two parts. The former is entitled *Book of Gnosis* (Γνώσεως liber); the latter, *Book of the Great Logos according to the Mystery* (liber Magni Λόγου κατὰ Μυστήριον). The very celebrated traveler Bruce brought it from the East to England. Any investigator of antiquity who would undertake the task of publishing this book would satisfy the desires of scholars to no small degree. Cf. Matter, *Hist. du Gnostic.*, vol. II, pp. 106–107. EDD.]

# [Col. 0595] THE BOOK OF QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIANUS AGAINST THE JEWS. (C, G, S)\*

## SUMMARY

[Col. 0595B]

—After a disputation was held between a Christian and a Jewish proselyte—Tertullian apparently speaking of himself in the third person—he takes up again in writing what could not be elucidated fully enough because of the clamor of the spectators shouting together. He argues against the Jews with the most solid reasoning and from the foundations of Sacred Scripture. This was written while the Church still enjoyed peace, before the British war, at the time when the Moors were being besieged by the Romans.

First, he vindicates the grace of God for the Gentiles also, proving that they can be admitted to God’s law. Chapter I.

For the primordial law, the matrix of all the commandments, was given to Adam and Eve in Paradise; and before the written law of Moses came the righteousness of natural law in Noah and Abraham, and even the priesthood in Melchizedek. Chapter II.

The circumcision of the flesh was indeed given to Abraham for a time, but as a sign by which Israel would be distinguished in the last age, when, according to its deserts, it would be forbidden to enter the holy city. Now, however, spiritual circumcision is for the salvation of the obedient people. Chapter III.

The observance of the Sabbath was likewise temporary, a figure of the eternal Sabbath. For it is established by the examples of Joshua the son of Nun and the Maccabees that the Sabbath was observed perpetually neither by the aforementioned patriarchs before the law of Moses nor by everyone after that law. Chapter IV.

What is more, it is evident from Malachi and the Psalms that the very sacrifices of earthly offerings made by Abel and Cain and prescribed in Leviticus were predictions of spiritual sacrifices. Chapter V.

And thus it may be concluded from the foregoing that a new law was to come. The question must therefore be asked whether the legislator of the new law is still awaited or has already come. Chapter VI.

That he has come is shown first from the prophecies concerning his kingdom over the Gentiles and the eternity of that kingdom. Chapter VII.

Next, from the times of the birth of Christ the Leader, of his Passion, [Col. 0596B] and of the destruction of Jerusalem, as foretold by Daniel. Chapter VIII.

Further, from the various predictions by which Christ’s birth was announced by the prophets. Chapter IX.

Likewise, from the things foretold concerning Christ’s Passion on the cross and from its figures. Chapter X.

Again, from the prediction of Jerusalem’s destruction, not only by Daniel but also by the prophet Ezekiel. Chapter XI.

In addition, from a repetition of certain passages of Sacred Scripture concerning the conversion of the Gentiles to Christ. Chapter XII.

[Col. 0596C] Finally, by adducing other scriptural passages from which it is proved that he has already come. Chapter XIII.

Lastly, the Jews are convicted from the very abundance of their error: from Christ’s second advent in sublimity after that first advent in humility. They were deceived concerning the first advent because he did not come in sublimity, since they did not understand that he was to come in humility. Chapter XIV.

Moreover, no one can doubt that both works are by the same author, not only because in the third book *Against Marcion* Tertullian repeats in almost the same words, though somewhat more expansively, what he treats more briefly here, but also because the blessed Cyprian, in the first two books of his *Testimonies to Quirinus against the Jews*, imitated this book so closely [Col. 0596D] that he excerpted many passages from it; Julianus Pomerius did the same in his three books *Against the Jews*. Certainly Eusebius, in his *Chronicle*, expressly recounts Tertullian’s opinion concerning Christ’s birth from this book; Pomerius transcribed it into his first book, and the blessed Jerome transcribed a considerable part of Chapter IX into his commentary on Daniel. Vincent of Lérins, Abbot Trithemius, and Politian likewise explicitly mentioned this work before Rhenanus committed it to the press.

Rhenanus also published a second, more carefully corrected edition from the Gorze codex, adding several scholia. Yet because the work was absent from Leland’s British codex and therefore was not collated by Gelenius, it had not yet recovered its original form. Accordingly, we too had to labor over its restoration. For this purpose we were aided by one Vatican manuscript of this book, two copies of the third book *Against Marcion*, the aforementioned commentary of the blessed Jerome, and several passages observed in both works by Latinius, as may be seen from our annotations. PAMELIUS.

# CHAPTER I

Recently [Note: [Col. 0597D] But where and when? Who was that Christian? SEML.] it happened that a disputation was held between a Christian [Note: [Col. 0597D] “And a Jewish proselyte.” This word occurs frequently in Scripture. Among the Jews it signifies a foreigner or newcomer who, though not himself a Jew, has come over from the Gentiles to their law. LE PR.] and a Jewish proselyte. Taking turns, as though pulling upon a contentious rope [Note: [Col. 0597D] “Upon a contentious rope.” He used the proverbial expression “taking turns upon a contentious rope”: each of them drew the day out into evening. So too in the book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*: “Now,” he says, “to draw out upon the contentious rope whether destruction claims a human being in this direction or that.” RHEN.], they both drew out the day into evening. Since certain supporters [Note: [Col. 0597C] “Supporters” is absent from Pam., Oberth., and Seml.] of each side were also shouting them down [Note: [Col. 0597C] Lat. reads: “with certain spectators”—*spectantibus* for Rhenanus’ *spectatoribus*—“amid a kind of cloud of hissing and quarrels.”], the truth was obscured by a kind of cloud.

I therefore resolved [Note: [Col. 0597D] That is, “I resolved.” SEML.] to examine more carefully what could not be elucidated fully enough amid the concerted noise of the disputation [Col. 0597B], and to settle the questions thus reconsidered by means of a written treatment [Note: [Col. 0597C] “By written treatments,” Oberth. Seml.]. The occasion for defending the Gentiles’ claim [Note: [Col. 0597C] “Claim” is absent from Jun.] to divine grace also possessed this advantage: a man from the Gentiles, and not a Jew descended from the stock of the Israelites, had undertaken to claim God’s law for himself [Note: [Col. 0597D] “To claim for himself.” The Vatican codex has *vendicare* rather than *vindicare*; the meaning is the same. For *vindicare*, which derives from *vindiciae*, means to assert one’s claim to a disputed matter. PAM.]. This fact alone is enough [Note: [Col. 0597C] “Is,” Oberth. Seml.] to establish that the Gentiles can be admitted to God’s law, so that Israel may no longer boast that the Gentiles are reckoned “like a drop from a bucket” or “dust from the threshing floor” (Isa. 40:15).

Besides, we have God himself as a competent promisor and faithful guarantor. He promised Abraham that in his seed all the nations of the earth would be blessed (Gen. 22:18), and that from Rebecca’s womb two peoples and two nations would come forth (Gen. 25:23): namely, of course, the Jews—that is, Israel—and the Gentiles—that is, ourselves. Each, therefore, is called both [Note: [Col. 0597C] “Both” is absent from Pam. and Par.] a people and a nation [Col. 0597C], so that no one may dare to defend for himself a privilege of grace merely from the designation of a name. For God ordained that two peoples and two nations should come forth from the womb of one woman. He did not distinguish grace [Note: [Col. 0597D] “Nor did he distinguish grace.” The Fulda Codex reads, “Nor did grace distinguish,” which is more correct. RIG.] by their designation, but by the order of their birth: the one who would come forth from the womb first was to be subjected to the younger—that is, to the one who came afterward.

For thus God spoke to Rebecca, saying: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly; one people shall overcome the other, and the elder shall serve the younger” (ibid.). Accordingly, although the people or nation of the Jews is earlier in time and greater through the grace of having first been deemed worthy under the law, our people is younger in the chronology of the ages [Note: [Col. 0597C] The words “in the chronology of the ages” are understood of Rebecca and the two peoples. Lat. and Rig. delete this parenthesis as though it arose from a gloss. Jun., however, thinks it has been transposed here from what follows; Seml. places it after “earlier and greater.” Obert.: “In the chronology of the ages it is understood, from Rebecca and the two peoples, that this is possible.” This passage is hyperbatonic or corrupt and could not be remedied from the manuscript. PAM.], since it obtained knowledge of divine mercy only in the final period of the age. Without doubt, therefore, according to the declaration [Note: [Col. 0598C] “Saying,” Rhen.] of the divine utterance, the earlier and [Note: [Col. 0598C] “And” is absent from Pam. and Obert.] greater people—that is, the Jewish people—must serve the younger; and the younger people—that is, the Christian people—must overcome the elder.

For according to the records of the divine Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0598C] “Of the divine Scriptures” is absent from Pam., Rhen., and Obert. Pam. uses “records” for “Sacred Scriptures.”], the greater [Note: [Col. 0598C] “Greater” is absent from Pam. and Rhen.] people of the Jews [Col. 0598B]—that is, the more ancient people—abandoned God, served idols, and, forsaking the divine, devoted itself to images. The people said to Aaron: “Make us gods who shall go before us” (Exod. 32:23). When gold from the women’s necklaces and the men’s rings [Note: [Col. 0597D] “And the men’s rings.” Similarly, the blessed Ambrose, Epistle 56 to Romulus: “Aaron, therefore, being compelled, asks for their rings and the women’s earrings.” Since this is read neither in the Greek text now current nor in the Latin edition of the blessed Jerome, the Septuagint’s edition must in certain places have differed from the one now extant. This is confirmed by the words that the Author cites presently. PAM.] had been melted in the fire [Note: [Col. 0598C] Jun. deletes “gold.”], and a calf’s head came forth for them, all Israel abandoned God and gave honor to this fabrication, saying: “These are the gods [Note: [Col. 0598C] “Gods,” Obert. Seml.] who brought us out of the land of Egypt.”

Thus also, in later times, when kings ruled over them, they worshiped Jeroboam’s golden calves and sacred groves [Note: [Col. 0598D] “And when they worshiped Jeroboam’s golden calves,” etc. He attacks Jewish superstition and idolatry, to which that nation was especially prone. The particular figure noted here is King Jeroboam I. After he had been made king, he feared that if the Israelites returned to Jerusalem for the sacred rites, they would become dissatisfied with the separation they had then effected. So, to provide them with something to worship among themselves, he set up golden calves, one in Dan and the other in Bethel; he added sacrificing priests and forbade the Israelites from thereafter going to Jerusalem. The account is found at 1 Kings 12 [Vulgate: 3 Kings 12]. LE PR.], and enslaved themselves to Baal. Hence the record of the divine Scriptures proves that they were always marked out as guilty of the crime of idolatry [Note: [Col. 0598C] Others read: “they were thought.”].

Our younger people, however—that is, the people who came later—abandoned the idols it had previously served and turned to the same God from whom Israel, as we recalled above [Col. 0598C], had departed. Thus the younger—that is, later—people overcame the elder people when it obtained the grace of divine favor, from which Israel was rejected.

# CHAPTER II

[Col. 0599A]

Let us therefore advance a step and define the substance of the question itself within precise boundaries [Note: [Col. 0599C] “Bring to an end,” Jun., from Pam.’s manuscript.]. Why should it be believed that God—the creator of the universe, governor of the entire world, fashioner of humanity, and planter of all nations—gave the law through Moses to one people, and be said not to have bestowed it upon all nations? For if he had not given it to all, he would by no means have permitted proselytes from the Gentiles to gain access to it.

Rather, as befits the goodness and equity of God, since he is the fashioner of the human race, he gave the same law to all nations. He commanded it to be observed at particular and appointed times—when he wished, through whom he wished, and in the manner he wished. For at the beginning of the world he gave Adam and Eve themselves a law: they were not to eat from the fruit of the tree planted in [Col. 0599B] the middle of Paradise; and if they acted contrary to it, they would surely die (Gen. 2:7). That law would have sufficed for them, had it been kept.

For in this law given to Adam we recognize all the commandments contained within it that afterward sprouted forth when given through Moses. These are: [Note: [Col. 0599D] “You shall love the Lord your God,” etc., “and your neighbor as yourself.” He imitates a Hellenism and the Greek expression πλησίον σου, “your neighbor,” as is customary with him when citing Scripture. LE PR.] “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deut. 6:5); “You shall love your neighbor [Note: [Col. 0599C] “Your neighbor,” manuscripts and Pam.] as yourself” (Lev. 19:18); “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness. Honor your father and your mother” (Exod. 20:12–17); and “You shall not covet what belongs to another” (Deut. 5:16–21).

The primordial law given to Adam and Eve in Paradise is therefore, as it were, the matrix of all God’s commandments. Indeed, if they had loved the Lord their God, they would not have acted against his commandment. If they had loved their neighbor—that is, themselves [Col. 0599C]—they would not have believed the serpent’s persuasion; and thus they would not have committed murder against themselves by falling away from immortality through acting against God’s commandment. They would also have abstained from theft, had they not secretly tasted the fruit of the tree (Gen. 3:6), or attempted to hide from the sight of the Lord their God beneath a tree (ibid. 8). Nor would they have made themselves accomplices of the devil in his false assertion by believing him when he said that they would become like God [Col. 0600A] (ibid. 8). And thus they would not have offended God as their Father, who had fashioned them from the clay of the earth as though from a mother’s womb. If they had not coveted what belonged to another [Note: [Col. 0599C] “Did not covet,” Seml.], they would not have tasted the forbidden fruit.

Thus, in this general and primordial law of God, which God ordained to be observed in relation to the fruit of the tree, we recognize that all the commandments of the later law were individually contained. When issued at their appointed times, they germinated. For it belongs to the same one to teach the law more fully afterward who had earlier sent the commandment before it; just as it belongs to the one to instruct afterward who had earlier undertaken to form righteous people. What wonder is it if he who instituted the discipline also enlarges it [Note: [Col. 0599D] Irenaeus and others are accustomed to frame the matter in this way. SEML.]? If he who began it also perfected it [Note: [Col. 0599C] “Perfects,” Pam.; “advances,” Rhen. Obert.]?

Indeed, before the law of Moses was written [Note: [Col. 0599D] “Indeed, before the law of Moses was written,” etc. Thus the same author in the book *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 6: “Will you therefore seek the law of God, although you possess that law common to all in the public domain of the world, on the tablets of nature, to which the Apostle also customarily appeals?” Pertinent to this may be Cicero’s statement in the *For Milo*: “For this law,” he says, “was not written but born with us; we did not learn, receive, or read it, but seized, imbibed, and drew it from nature itself. We were not taught it but made for it, not instructed in it but imbued with it.” Robert Cedalia, in the *Shalshelet*, testifies that the precepts of the law were given to Adam and inscribed upon his breast: [text absent]. Origen does not differ from him in the *Philocalia*, in these words: “Besides these, the law is said to be that which, in accordance with the common conceptions, has been implanted in the soul and which, as Scripture terms it, is a word inscribed upon the heart, commanding what must be done and forbidding what must not be done” (παρὰ δὲ ταῦτα λέγεται νόμος ὁ κατὰ τὰς κοινὰς ἐννοίας ἐνεσπαρμένος τῇ ψυχῇ, καὶ ὡς ὀνομάζει ἡ γραφή, ἐγγεγραμμένος τῇ καρδίᾳ λόγος, προστακτικὸς μὲν τῶν ποιητέων, ἀπαγορευτικὸς δὲ τῶν οὐ ποιητέων). [Col. 0600D] Moreover, the natural law is said to be implanted within the soul and, as Scripture calls it, inscribed upon the hearts, commanding what must be done and forbidding what must not be done. LE PR.], I maintain that there was an unwritten law, understood naturally and kept by the fathers.

For how was Noah found righteous (Gen. 6:9; Sir. 44:17), if the righteousness of natural law did not precede him? How was Abraham accounted a friend of God (Isa. 41:8; Jas. 2:23), if it was not because of the equity and righteousness of natural law? How was Melchizedek called a priest of the Most High God (Gen. 14:18), if, before the priesthood of the Levitical law, there were not Levites who offered sacrifices to God? For it was only after the patriarchs named above that the law was given to Moses, when they had departed from Egypt, following an interval and span of many ages. Indeed, the law was given 430 years after Abraham [Note: [Col. 0600D] “The law was given 430 years after Abraham.” The meaning of this passage is not that this law was given to Abraham. For if anyone contends that the law of circumcision is under discussion here, chronology altogether opposes him, since only 391 years are counted from the Flood to the institution of circumcision. If he understands Abraham’s calling, he is even farther from the truth, since only 367 years elapsed between the Flood and that calling. Another law, therefore, is mentioned in this passage. Which law is meant is taught by Gen. 15:13; Exod. 12:40; Acts 7:6; and Gal. 3:17, where these 430 years are specified. They are counted from the first promise made to Abraham (Gen. 12:3). For in that same year the people of Israel were delivered from Egypt and received the law. Compare Estius, Cornelius a Lapide, Fromondus, *Complete Course of Sacred Scripture*, and, before them, Augustine, St. Thomas, etc. EDD.].

From this we understand that God’s law existed even before Moses: not only on Horeb or Sinai and in the wilderness, but more anciently [Note: [Col. 0600C] “More anciently; first,” Obert. Seml.—“First, but more anciently” is absent from Pam.]—first in Paradise, afterward among the patriarchs, and then reconstituted for the Jews at appointed times [Col. 0600C]. We should therefore no longer regard the law of Moses as though it were the primary law, but as a subsequent law, which God at a definite time also presented to the Gentiles, reconstituted for the better as promised through the prophets, and foretold would come [Note: [Col. 0600C] “Would come,” feminine, Rhen. Obert.]. Thus, just as the law was given through Moses at a definite time, it should be believed to have been observed and kept only for a time. Nor should we take away this authority of God, who, according to the circumstances of the times, reconstitutes the commandments of the law [Col. 0601A] for humanity’s salvation [Note: [Col. 0601B] “In salvation,” Seml.].

Indeed, whoever contends that the Sabbath must still be observed as though it were a remedy of salvation, and that circumcision on the eighth day must be practiced because of the threat of death, must show that in former times righteous men kept the Sabbath or were circumcised and thereby became friends of God. For if circumcision purifies a human being, why, when God made Adam uncircumcised, did he not circumcise him—either then or after Adam sinned—if circumcision purifies? Certainly, when he placed him uncircumcised in Paradise, he appointed him cultivator of Paradise.

Therefore, since God established Adam as neither circumcised nor Sabbath-observant, he consequently also praised Adam’s offspring Abel, who offered sacrifices to him while uncircumcised and not observing the Sabbath. God accepted what Abel offered in simplicity of heart, but rejected the sacrifice of his brother [Note: [Col. 0601B] “His” is absent from Seml. and Obert.; in Pam. it is placed after “Cain.”] Cain [Col. 0601B], who did not offer rightly and did not divide rightly (Gen. 4).

God likewise delivered Noah from the Flood although he was uncircumcised and did not observe the Sabbath (Gen. 6ff.). He also translated the most righteous Enoch from this world, although Enoch was neither circumcised nor Sabbath-observant (Gen. 5:22). Enoch, who has not yet tasted death, thereby showed us already, as a candidate for eternity [Col. 0602A], that we too can please God without bearing the burden of the law of Moses.

Melchizedek too, the priest of the Most High God (Gen. 14:18), was chosen for God’s priesthood though uncircumcised and not observing the Sabbath. Lot, Abraham’s brother, likewise proves [Note: [Col. 0601B] “And the approved Lot,” Pam. Rhen. Obert.] that, because of the merits of his righteousness [Note: [Col. 0601B] “His” is absent from Pam., Fran., Rig., and Venet.], he was delivered from the burning of the Sodomites without observance of the law.

# CHAPTER III

“But Abraham,” he says [Note: [Col. 0602B] “You say,” Obert. Rhen.], “was circumcised.” Yet he pleased God before he was circumcised, and nevertheless did not observe the Sabbath. For he had received circumcision, but a circumcision intended as a sign of that particular time, not as a privileged means of salvation.

Indeed, the patriarchs who followed were uncircumcised, such as Melchizedek, who [Note: [Col. 0601B] “Melchizedek offered bread and wine to Abraham himself as Abraham returned from battle.” The passage is Gen. 14, [Col. 0601C] and in the Latin Vulgate it is extremely intricate, since the offering of bread and wine is left ambiguous: was it made to God or to Abraham? Here, however, Tertullian states with complete clarity that Melchizedek offered bread and wine to Abraham as he returned from battle. It would follow that the verb “to offer” in this passage has no reference to sacrifice. For who could tolerate the idea that Melchizedek, priest of the Most High, was sacrificing to Abraham?

Our own Septimius, moreover, in Book V *Against Marcion*, shows that Melchizedek performed a priestly act when he blessed Abraham and received tithes from him. Yet that priest of the Most High, since he was also king of Salem, likewise performed an act most fitting to royal magnificence. Going out to meet Abraham as he led his army back from battle after brave and successful exploits, he received him and his victorious forces with bread and wine—that is, with everything necessary to restore bodies wearied by war.

And indeed the Greek translation of the seventy elders contradicts this interpretation: “And Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought out bread and wine; and he was priest of [Col. 0601D] God Most High; and he blessed,” etc. (Καὶ Μελχισεδὲκ βασιλεὺς Σάλημ ἐξήνεκε ἄρτον καὶ οἶνον· ἦν δὲ ἱερεὺς τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ ὑψίστου· καὶ εὐλόγησε, etc.). Josephus puts it excellently: “This Melchizedek provided gifts of hospitality for Abraham’s army and furnished a great abundance of provisions” (Ἐχορήγησε δὲ οὗτος ὁ Μελχισεδέκης τῷ Ἀβράμου στρατῷ ξένια, καὶ πολλὴν ἀφθονίαν τῶν ἐπιτηδείων παρέσχε).

Nevertheless, the most ancient and holy Fathers handed down a far different interpretation of this event: namely, that by the sacrifice of bread and wine Melchizedek expressed the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood, and prefigured the sacrament of the Lord that was to come much later. These are Jerome’s words in his *Epistle to Demetrias*; Chrysostom, Augustine, and others wrote in agreement with them. RIG.

—I do not know what Rigaltius finds so intricate here. Some assert that this offering was made to God, among them the blessed Jerome in Epistle 17 to Marcella, where he at least says that the king of Salem, as a type of Christ, offered bread and wine and inaugurated the Christian mystery in the Savior’s blood and body. Others say it was made to Abraham; among these too is the blessed Jerome, in Epistle 126 to Evagrius, where he recounts that entire history. In it, however, one must observe that Genesis states that the king offered Abraham tithes from everything [Col. 0602B], although the blessed Jerome, in the passage mentioned, asserts that he offered tithes only from the spoils of the enemy.

All the ancients teach that this event signified the Eucharist. In addition to those cited by Rigaltius, I add Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* VI. Melchizedek is said to have been a king because among various nations the kings themselves were priests and sacrificers. This is absolutely certain concerning the Romans; and Virgil, referring to that custom, says in *Aeneid* III: …]

“King Anius, at once king of men and priest of Phoebus.” [LE PR.] To Abraham himself, already circumcised [Note: [Col. 0602B] “Uncircumcised,” Jun.] and returning from battle, [he], though himself uncircumcised, offered bread and [Col. 0602B] wine (ibid.). But Moses’ son too, he says, would then [Note: [Col. 0602B] “When,” Seml.] have been strangled by the angel if Zipporah his mother had not circumcised the infant’s foreskin with a stone (Exod. 4:24–25). From this, he says, [Note: [Col. 0602B] “There is the greatest danger from circumcision,” Pam., Seml.] there is the greatest danger if anyone does not circumcise the foreskin of his flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0602C] And therefore, if circumcision brought salvation. Some maintain that circumcision was given as a sign of Baptism; here, however, the Author asserts this with a certain qualification. Original sin was indeed remitted in circumcision, but not through circumcision as through baptism, because at that time this occurred by virtue of the covenant initiated by God with the Jews. In this Tertullian follows the Apostle in Romans 4. LE PR.—Le Prieur is perhaps mistaken in asserting that Tertullian shared the opinion of those who attribute the saving effects of baptism to circumcision, although with a certain qualification, as he himself says. For anyone who reads this third chapter attentively will see that the Author thought rather that this Jewish rite contributed nothing to salvation, since he says that circumcision was given by God as a sign, not for salvation; a little earlier he had said: “He [Abraham] had received circumcision as a sign . . . not as a privilege of salvation.” The same opinion was embraced by all ecclesiastical writers who flourished before Augustine. For the bishop of Hippo was the first of all to affirm that original sin was erased by circumcision. That holy Doctor was followed by Gregory the Great (*Morals on Job*, book IV, ch. 3), St. Fulgentius, the Venerable Bede, St. Bernard (passim), Innocent III, and not a few theologians. St. John Chrysostom (*Homilies on Genesis* 39), St. Epiphanius (*Heresies* 30), St. Jerome (book I *On the Epistle to the Galatians*), St. John Damascene (*On the Orthodox Faith*, book IV, ch. 25), and other theologians of no lesser reputation and by no means negligible in number adopted the contrary opinion. It may be added that, even if circumcision erased [Col. 0603D] original sin, other equally efficacious rites were nevertheless available, for example, the faith of the parents and sacrifices; otherwise the salvation of all females, and also of males who did not survive to the eighth day, would have been impossible. EDD.]

And therefore [Note: [Col. 0602B] “But indeed,” Cod. Fuld., Rig.], if circumcision brought [Col. 0603A] salvation in every respect [Note: [Col. 0603C] “Brings,” Pam., Rhen.], Moses himself would not have omitted to circumcise his son on the eighth day, since it is evident that Zipporah was compelled by the angel to do it during the journey. Let us therefore consider that the compulsory circumcision of one infant could not have laid down a rule for the whole people and, as it were, established the law of this commandment. For because God foresaw that he was going to give this circumcision to the people of Israel as a sign, not for salvation, he therefore caused the son of Moses, their future leader, to be circumcised, so that when he began through Moses to give the people the commandment of circumcision, the people would not reject it, seeing that this precedent had already been enacted upon the leader’s son [Note: [Col. 0603C] “The judge’s son,” Rhen., Obert.].

For circumcision was to be given, but as a sign, by which Israel was to be recognized in the last time, when in accordance with its own deserts it would be forbidden to enter the holy city, [Col. 0603B] through the words of the prophets, who say: “Your land is desolate; your cities have been burned with fire; foreigners devour your territory in your sight, and it is desolate and overthrown by foreign peoples; the daughter of Zion will be left like a shelter in a vineyard, like a watchman’s hut in a cucumber field, and like a city under siege” (Isa. 1:7–8). And therefore the prophet’s following statement reproaches them, saying: “I begot and exalted sons, but they despised me” (ibid., 2) [Note: [Col. 0603C] “Rejected me,” Cod. Fuld.]. And again: “Even if you stretch out your hands, I will turn my face away from you; and even if you multiply your prayers, I will not hear you, for your hands are full of blood” (ibid., 15). And again: “Woe, sinful nation, people full of sins, wicked children! You have forsaken God and have driven [Note: [Col. 0603D] “Provoked,” Cod. Fuld.] the Holy One of Israel to indignation” (ibid., 4).

This, then, was God’s providential purpose [Col. 0603C] in giving circumcision to Israel as a sign by which it could be recognized when the time came in which, because of the deserts stated above, it would be forbidden admission into Jerusalem. Because this was going to happen, it was announced; and because we see that it has happened, we acknowledge it. Thus, just as fleshly circumcision, which was temporary, was bestowed as a sign upon a disobedient people, so spiritual circumcision was given for the salvation of an obedient people, as the prophet Jeremiah says: “Renew for yourselves a newness [Note: [Col. 0603D] “A newness” is absent from Cod. Fuld.], and do not sow among thorns. Be circumcised to God, and circumcise the foreskin of your heart” (Jer. 4:3–4).

And elsewhere he says: “For behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will establish with the house of Judah and the house of Jacob a new covenant, [Col. 0604A] not like the one I formerly gave to their fathers on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt.” From this we understand that it was announced both that the former circumcision, given at that time, would cease, and that a new law would come forth, unlike the one he had formerly given to the fathers, just as Isaiah foretold when he said that in the last days the mountain of the Lord and the house of God would be made manifest above the summits of the mountains: “And it will be exalted,” he says, “above the hills; all nations will come upon it, and many will walk and say: ‘Come, let us ascend the mountain of the Lord and the house of the God of Jacob’” (Isa. 2:2–3)—not the house of Esau, the elder son [Note: [Col. 0603D] “People,” Obert., Seml.], but that of Jacob, the younger, that is, of our people, whose mountain is Christ, shown in Daniel as cut out without the hands of those cutting it and as filling the whole earth (Dan. 2:34, 37).

Finally, Isaiah announces in the following words that the new law too would come forth from this house of the God [Col. 0604B] of Jacob, saying: “For from Zion the law will go forth [Note: [Col. 0603D] “Will be,” Fran.], and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem; and he will judge among the nations” (Isa. 2:3–4), that is, among us who have been called from the nations. “And they will beat,” he says, “their swords into ploughs and their spears into sickles; nation will no longer take up the sword against nation, and they will no longer learn [Note: [Col. 0604C] “Be said,” Obert., Seml.] to wage war” (ibid.).

Are those who observe these things, having been instructed by the new law while the old law has been obliterated, therefore understood to be any other people than ourselves, when the very practice demonstrates the future abolition of that old law [Note: [Col. 0604C] The question mark is absent from Seml. and Obert.]? For the old law avenged itself with the retribution of the sword, exacted an eye for an eye (Exod. 21:24; Lev. 24:20; Deut. 19:21), and repaid vengeance for injury. The new law [Note: [Col. 0604D] “Law” is absent from Rhen. and Obert.], however, signified clemency and transformed the former prosecution of war against rivals of the law and against the enemy [Note: [Col. 0603D] “And the prosecution of the enemy.” “*Exsecutio*,” says Rhenanus, “is used for *persecutio*”; so too in book I *Against Marcion*: “What, finally, is more flattering than not to prosecute offenses?”—that is, not to pursue them. And in the same work, a little earlier, “the prosecution of evil”; and afterward, “the prosecutor of an offense,” that is, a judge. PAM.] [Col. 0604C] [Note: [Col. 0604D] “Both war and the former things, and rivals, and the enemy by prosecution,” Cod. Fuld.] into peaceful activities [Note: [Col. 0604D] “Activities among peaceful things,” Cod. Divion.] of ploughing and cultivating the earth. Therefore, just as we showed above that the old law and fleshly circumcision were announced as destined to cease, so the observance of the new law and of spiritual circumcision has shone forth in duties of peace.

“For a people,” he says, “whom I did not know has served me; at the hearing of the ear it obeyed me” (Ps. 17:29), the prophets announced. What people, moreover, was ignorant of God except ours, we who formerly did not know God? And who heard at the hearing of the ear except us, who abandoned idols and turned to God? For Israel, which had been known to God and exalted by him in Egypt, [Note: [Col. 0603D] And carried through the Erythraean Sea, etc. Many debate whether the Erythraean or Red Sea differs in color from the neighboring sea or any other. Some think that it does, and devise such reasons as they can: namely, because of the abundance of coral clinging to the bottom; because of the proximity of red earth, with which the shores are filled, which is absorbed by the flowing waters and stains those waters with its own color. I omit other causes no less plausible than these, and consider the Erythraean Sea to be of the same color as other seas. I adduce a passage from Quintus Curtius, book VIII: “It received its name from King Erythrus”—he is speaking of the Erythraean or Red Sea—“because of which the ignorant believe that its waters are red.” And in book X, right at the beginning: “They had believed the inhabitants about the other things, among them that the Red Sea [Col. 0605D] was so called, not from the color of its waves, as most believed, but from King Erythrus.” LE PR.—Following Pliny, as he usually does, who calls the sea which we term Red the Erythraean Sea (book VI, ch. 23), as does Dionysius in *On the Situation of the World*. PAM.] and carried through the Erythraean Sea [Col. 0605A] (Exod. 14:22), fed with manna in the wilderness (Exod. 16:13ff.), brought over forty years into a likeness of eternity, neither defiled by human passions nor nourished by the food of this world, but fed with manna, the bread of angels (Ps. 77), and sufficiently indebted to God for his benefits, forgot its Lord and God, saying to Aaron: “Make us gods who will go before us; for that Moses who brought us out of the land of Egypt has abandoned us, and we do not know what has happened to him” (Exod. 32:1). And therefore we, who formerly were not God’s people, have become his people by receiving the new law stated above [Note: [Col. 0605C] Rhen. and Obert. add “and”] and the new circumcision foretold earlier.

## CHAPTER IV

It follows, then, that just as the abolition of fleshly circumcision [Col. 0605B] [Note: [Col. 0605D] “The abolition of the old law, canceled at its appointed time, is demonstrated.” I follow Rhenanus’ interpretation, who considers “canceled” to be equivalent to “fulfilled.” The old law was indeed canceled when the new one supervened. The metaphor may perhaps have been taken from ancient moneylenders, who, when debts recorded upon wax tablets or daybooks had been discharged, canceled them by reversing the stylus. LE PR.] and of the old law is demonstrated to have been canceled at its appointed time, so too the observance of the Sabbath must be demonstrated to have been temporary [Note: [Col. 0606C] “Temporal,” Rhen., Obert.].

For the Jews say that from the beginning God sanctified the seventh day by resting on it from all the works that he had made, and that Moses therefore also said to the people: “Remember the day of the Sabbaths; sanctify it. You shall do no servile work on it” (Exod. 20:8), except what pertains to life. From this we understand instead that we must always keep Sabbath from every servile work, and not only on every seventh day, but throughout all time. And for this reason we must inquire which Sabbath God wished us to observe. For the Scriptures indicate both an eternal Sabbath and a temporal Sabbath. The prophet Isaiah says: “My soul hates your Sabbaths.” [Col. 0605C] And elsewhere he says: “You have profaned my Sabbaths” (Ezek. 22:8). From this we recognize that the temporal Sabbath is human, while the eternal Sabbath is regarded as divine. Concerning the latter he proclaims through Isaiah: “And it will be,” he says, “month after month, day after day, and Sabbath after Sabbath, and all flesh will come to worship in Jerusalem, says the Lord” (Isa. 66:23).

We understand this to have been fulfilled in the time of Christ, when all flesh—that is, every nation—came to Jerusalem to worship God the Father through Jesus Christ his Son, as was foretold through the prophet: [Col. 0606A] “Behold, proselytes will go through me to you” (Isa. 52 [Note: [Col. 0605D] “Behold, proselytes will go through me to you.” He cites the same Scripture in book III *Against Marcion* and explains it a little more fully, expressly ascribing it to Isaiah. Some have noted that it is found in Isaiah according to the Seventy translators (ch. 52), but thus far I have not found it there. PAM.—Tertullian perhaps had in mind Isaiah 55:5: “Nations that did not know you will run to you [Col. 0606D] because of the Lord”; or perhaps chapter 60. EDD.].

Thus, therefore, before this temporal Sabbath, the eternal Sabbath had been foreshown and foretold, just as spiritual circumcision had been foreshown before fleshly circumcision. Finally, let them show, as we said at the outset, that Adam kept the Sabbath; or that Abel, when he offered a holy victim to God, pleased him through the religious observance of the Sabbath; or that Enoch, when he was translated, was an observer of the Sabbath; or that Noah, who built the ark because of the immeasurable flood, observed the Sabbath; or that Abraham offered his son Isaac while observing the Sabbath; or that Melchizedek received the law of the Sabbath in his priesthood.

But the Jews will say that, once this commandment was given through Moses, it had thereafter to be observed. It is therefore evident that the commandment was not eternal or [Col. 0606B] spiritual, but temporal, and would at some point cease. Indeed, this solemn observance is so far from having to be celebrated by resting on the Sabbath—that is, on the seventh day—that Joshua son of Nun, at the time when he was overthrowing the city of Jericho, said that he had received a command from God to instruct the people that the priests should carry the ark of God’s covenant around the city for seven days, and that, after the circuit of the seventh day had thus been completed, the walls of the city would fall of their own accord (Josh. 6:4ff.). This is what happened; and when the period of the seventh day was finished, the walls of the city fell, just as had been foretold.

From this it is clearly shown that the Sabbath day fell within the number of those seven days: for seven days, from whatever day they take their beginning, must necessarily include the Sabbath day. On that day not only did the priests labor, but the city was also made spoil by the entire people of Israel [Col. 0606C] at the edge of the sword. Nor is there any doubt that they performed servile work when, by God’s command, they carried off the spoils of war.

For in the [Note: [Col. 0606D] Time of the Maccabees. Since he cites the history of the Maccabees here in a matter of faith, there is no doubt that he recognized it as canonical Scripture. Nor is it surprising that those books are not contained in the Hebrew canon, since they were written more than a century after the canon published by Ezra. For at least 180 years intervened between Cyrus’ successor Darius, under whom Ezra flourished, and Antiochus Epiphanes, under whom the Maccabees flourished. PAM.] time of the Maccabees they acted valiantly by fighting on the Sabbaths [Note: [Col. 0606D] “And the foreign enemies.” “The Greek translators of the Bible,” says St. Jerome (*On Isaiah*, ch. 2), “translated *allophýlous* (ἀλλοφύλους, ‘foreigners’) for *Philistiim*, which is the nation now called Palestine.” This is also confirmed in the Latin edition of the Septuagint by the title of Psalm 55. Here, however, Tertullian applies it to the Greeks against whom the Maccabees fought, because the Greek word signifies foreigners in general. PAM.] and conquered their foreign enemies, and by fighting on the Sabbaths restored their ancestral law to its former condition of life. Nor do I think they were defending any other law than the one in which they remembered that a prescription concerning the Sabbath day had been laid down. From this it is evident that commandments of this kind had force [Col. 0607A] for a limited time and for the necessity of the immediate occasion [Note: [Col. 0607C] “Gained force,” Pam., Rhen., Obert.], and that God had not previously given them a law of this kind [Note: [Col. 0607C] The same witnesses read “so that . . . he had given”] to be observed for all time.

## CHAPTER V

Thus we also show that sacrifices consisting of earthly offerings and spiritual sacrifices were foretold [Note: [Col. 0608C] “Previously stated,” the same witnesses.]. And indeed, from the beginning, the earthly sacrifices of the elder son—that is, Israel—were foreshown in Cain, while the different sacrifices of the younger son, Abel—that is, of our people—were demonstrated. For Cain, the elder by birth, offered gifts to God from the produce of the earth, while the younger son Abel offered from the produce of his sheep. God looked favorably upon Abel and his gifts, but he did not look favorably upon Cain and his gifts.

And God said to Cain: “Why has your face fallen? Surely, if you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, [Col. 0607B] you have sinned? Be still: for your turning is toward him, and he will rule over you.” Then Cain said to his brother Abel: “Let us go into the field.” He went there with him and killed him. Then God said to Cain: “Where is your brother Abel?” And he said: “I do not know. Am I my brother’s keeper?” And God said to him: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth. Therefore cursed is the earth that opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood. Groaning and trembling you will be upon the earth.” And Cain said to the Lord: “My offense is greater than can be forgiven me; and today you will cast me away from the face of the earth, and I will be hidden from your face; and I will be groaning and trembling upon the earth, and everyone who finds me will kill me” (Gen. 4).

From this, therefore, we perceive that the two kinds of sacrifices belonging to the two peoples were foreshown even then, from the beginning. [Col. 0607C]

[Note: [Col. 0607D] “Finally, when the priestly law was being written through Moses in Leviticus.” Even from this passage it is evident that the Author sometimes suffered a lapse of memory when citing passages of Scripture, since this commandment is nowhere found in Leviticus, but in Deuteronomy 12. The same applies to what he said above in ch. 3: “And therefore the prophet’s following statement,” etc., although that Scripture precedes the one cited earlier rather than follows it; and below: “And elsewhere he says,” although it is contained in the same chapter. It is sufficient to have noted this once against certain pedants who refuse to admit an *hamártēma mnēmonikón* (ἀμάρτημα μνημονικόν), “an error of memory,” in the Fathers. PAM.—“In Leviticus.” Latinius thinks these words originated from a gloss, for they are found in Deuteronomy. SEML.]

Finally, when the priestly law was being written through Moses in Leviticus, we find it prescribed to the people of Israel that sacrifices should be offered to God nowhere except in the land of promise, which the Lord God was going to give to the people of Israel and their brethren, so that, once Israel had been brought in, sacrifices and burnt offerings would be celebrated there, both for sins and for souls, and nowhere else except in the holy land [Note: [Col. 0608C] “The holy land,” Ven.] (Deut. 12).

Why, then, does the Spirit afterward proclaim through the prophets that sacrifices would be offered to God in every land or in every place? Thus he says [Col. 0608A] through Malachi [Note: [Col. 0607D] “Angel.” *Malachias* means “angel” or “messenger.” What he adds, “one of the twelve prophets,” must be understood of the Minor Prophets. EDD.], one of the twelve prophets: “I will not receive a sacrifice from your hands, because from the rising of the sun to its setting my name has been glorified among all nations, says the Lord Almighty. And in every place pure sacrifices are offered to my name” (Mal. 1:10–11).

Likewise David says in the Psalms: “Bring to God, kindreds of the nations” (Ps. 96:7)—assuredly because the preaching of the apostles was destined to go out into all the earth (Ps. 18:5). “Bring glory and honor to God; bring to God sacrifices for his name. Take up victims and enter his courts” (Ps. 96:8).

For [Note: [Col. 0607D] “That sacrifice must be offered to God not with earthly sacrifices but with spiritual ones.” Hence these words in the *Apologeticum*: “I offer a rich and greater victim, which he himself commanded: prayer proceeding from chaste flesh, an innocent soul, and the Holy Spirit,” etc. And in the little book *To Scapula*: “We sacrifice as God commanded, with pure prayer.” And in the book *On Prayer*, where he speaks of the prayers accompanying the sacrifices in which the body of the Lord is received. And in the book *On Fasting*: “This will be a late station, which, fasting until evening, sacrifices a richer prayer to God.” It must, however, be observed that these statements of Tertullian do not agree in every respect with what is read in Irenaeus, book IV, chs. 33 and 34. RIG.] we read as follows that sacrifice must be offered to God not with earthly sacrifices but with spiritual ones, as it is written: “A contrite and humbled heart is a victim to God” (Ps. 50:19). And elsewhere: “Sacrifice [Col. 0608B] to God a sacrifice of praise, and render your vows to the Most High” (Ps. 49:14). Thus, therefore, spiritual sacrifices of praise are indicated, and a contrite heart is shown to be a sacrifice acceptable to God.

Accordingly, just as fleshly sacrifices are understood to have been rejected—of which Isaiah too speaks, saying, “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? says the Lord” (Isa. 1:11)—so spiritual sacrifices are proclaimed acceptable, as the prophets announce.

[Note: [Col. 0608D] “For even if you bring me fine flour,” he says. *Simila* or *similago* is flour made from ordinary wheat. The Hebrew *simila* is Greek *semídalis* (σεμίδαλις). In the Latin translation “sacrifice” occurs in this passage, although the word *simila*, “fine flour,” is used elsewhere, namely in Genesis 18 and Leviticus 2. LE PR.]

“For even if you bring me fine flour,” he says, “a vain offering, it is an abomination to me” (ibid.). And he further says: “Your burnt offerings and sacrifices, and the fat of goats, and the blood of bulls, I do not desire; not even if you come to appear before me. For who has required these things from your hands?” (ibid., 12). Concerning spiritual sacrifices, however, he adds: “And in every place pure sacrifices will be offered [Col. 0608C] to my name, says the Lord.”

## CHAPTER VI

Therefore, since it is evident that both a temporal Sabbath has been shown and an eternal Sabbath foretold; that fleshly circumcision has been foretold and spiritual circumcision indicated beforehand; that both a temporal law and an eternal law have been announced; and that fleshly sacrifices and spiritual sacrifices have been foreshown—it follows that, after all these commandments had earlier been given in a fleshly manner to the people of Israel, a time should supervene in which the commandments of the ancient law and the old ceremonies would cease, and the promise of the new [Col. 0609A] law, the recognition of spiritual sacrifices, and the promise of the New Covenant would supervene, as light from on high shone upon us who sat in darkness and were held in the shadow of death [Note: [Col. 0609C] Rhen. and Obert. add “light would arise”] (Luke 1:78–79).

Accordingly, since we have said that a new law was foretold by the prophets, and one not like [Note: [Col. 0609C] “It, and not such,” Rhen., Seml.; “and it not such,” Obert.] that which had already been given to their fathers at the time when he brought them [Note: [Col. 0609C] “Brought forth from the land of Egypt,” for “brought out.” It is surprising, however, by what line of reasoning he argues against the Jews, in order to demonstrate the end of the Mosaic law and the [Col. 0609D] advent of the Gospel law, which contains the truth of which the old law was the figure, confined as it was to certain ceremonies or rites and to outward worship; for the new law, without despising those rites, requires something more perfect and draws the spirit toward the contemplation and love of God. LE PR.] out of the land of Egypt, we must show and prove both that the old law has ceased and that the promised new law is now in operation.

And first of all, indeed, it must be asked whether there is still awaited a legislator of the new law, an heir of the New Covenant, a priest of the new sacrifices, a purifier by the new circumcision, and an observer of the eternal Sabbath, [Note: [Col. 0609D] “Who would restrain the old law.” That is, abolish it, so as to introduce the new. LE PR.] who would restrain the old law, establish the New Covenant, offer new sacrifices, suppress the ancient ceremonies, restrain the old circumcision together with its Sabbath, and announce a new kingdom that will not be corrupted. For it must also be asked whether [Note: [Col. 0609C] “Here indeed,” Rhen., Obert.; “here, I say, of the new,” Paris.] the legislator of the new law, the observer of the spiritual Sabbath, the high priest of eternal sacrifices, and the eternal ruler of the eternal kingdom has already come [Note: [Col. 0609C] “Whether or not,” Rhen., Obert.], or not.

And if he has already come, he must be served; if he has not yet come, he must be awaited—provided that it is evident that at his advent the commandments of the old [Note: [Col. 0609C] “When the former,” the same witnesses; “to restrain,” Fran., Paris.] law must be suppressed and the beginnings of the new law must come into operation. And first of all it must be established that the ancient law and the prophets could not have ceased unless he had come who was announced through that same law and those same prophets as the one who was to come.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0609C] Let us therefore take our position [Note: [Col. 0609C] “At this stage,” the same witness.] on this question: whether the Christ who was announced as coming [Note: [Col. 0610C] “Whether the Christ who is to come has already come,” the same witnesses.] has already come, or whether he is still expected to come. In order that this very matter may be proved, we must also inquire into the times when [Col. 0610A] the prophets announced that Christ would come, so that if we recognize that he came within those times, we may believe without doubt that he is the very one whom the prophets celebrated as destined to come, and in whom we—that is, the nations—were announced as destined to believe. And when it has been established that he came, we may assuredly also believe that the new law was given by him, and not deny that the New Covenant was established for us in him and through him.

For we know that not even the Jews deny that Christ will come, since they extend their hope toward his advent. Nor need this point be investigated at greater length, since all the prophets of old foretold him [Note: [Col. 0610C] “Foretold,” Fran.], as Isaiah says:

[Note: [Col. 0609D] “Thus says the Lord God to my Christ.” On this erroneous reading, although it had already become established long ago, see our annotations on Cyprian, book I, *Testimonies Against the Jews*, ch. 21, note 60. PAM.]

“Thus says the Lord God to my Christ [Note: [Col. 0610C] “To my anointed, Cyrus,” is the true reading; but many Latin writers read it thus. Seml.], the Lord, whose right hand I have held, that the nations may hear him: I will shatter the strength of kings; I will open gates before him, and cities will not be closed [Col. 0610B] to him” (Isa. 45:1–2).

We see that this very thing has been fulfilled.

[Note: [Col. 0609D] “For whose right hand does the Father hold?” Without doubt he alludes to the preceding passage of Scripture, as he does also in the words “whom all the nations have heard.” PAM.]

For whose right hand does God the Father hold except that of Christ his Son, whom all nations have heard—that is, in whom all nations have believed—and whose preachers, the apostles, are shown in the psalms of David: “Their sound,” he says, “has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 18:5)?

In whom else have all the nations believed except in Christ, who has already come? In whom else have the other nations believed?

[Note: [Col. 0609D] “Parthians, Medes, Elamites.” In demonstrating that even at that time all nations had believed in Christ, the Author first uses the words of Scripture concerning those who, after hearing the apostles speak in their respective languages at the feast of Pentecost, were converted to Christ. There the Parthians, Medes, and Elamites—not “Aelamites,” that is, Persians, so named from Elam son of Shem, according to Josephus (*Antiquities*, book I, ch. 7)—appear deliberately to have been joined together [Col. 0610D] because they were neighbors of one another. Moreover, the Author’s opinion is confirmed by St. Sophronius (*Catalogue of Illustrious Greek Men*, among Jerome’s works), who says that St. Thomas the Apostle preached Christ’s Gospel to the Parthians, Medes, and Persians, as well as to the Carmanians, Hyrcanians, Bactrians, Magi, and finally the Indians, among whom he suffered martyrdom in the city of Calamina. PAM.]

“Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and those who inhabit Mesopotamia, [Note: [Col. 0610D] “Armenia.” This province is indeed not mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles; but that the faith of Christ flourished among them even then is evident from the fact that not very long afterward the Armenians, formerly allies of the Romans, declared war on the tyrant Maximus for the sake of the Christian faith and religion, from which he was attempting to draw them away into idolatry. Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, ch. 28, is witness to this. PAM.—Augustine likewise attests it against the epistle of Mani. Augustine has “Africa”; we have “Libya.” SEML.] Armenia, Phrygia, Cappadocia; those inhabiting Pontus, Asia, and Pamphylia; those dwelling in Egypt and inhabiting the region of Africa beyond Cyrene; Romans [Note: [Col. 0610C] “Rome,” Obert., Seml.] and residents; and then Jews in Jerusalem” (Acts 2:9–10), and [Col. 0610C] the other nations besides: including now [Note: [Col. 0610C] “Also,” the same witnesses.] the various tribes of the Gaetuli, the many territories of the Moors, all the boundaries of the Spains, the diverse nations of the Gauls, the regions of the Britons inaccessible to the Romans but subject to Christ, and those of the Sarmatians, [Col. 0611A] the Dacians, the Germans [Note: [Col. 0611D] Irenaeus too names the Germans; on what grounds is uncertain. SEML.], the Scythians, and many further nations, provinces, and many islands unknown to us and which we are less able to enumerate.

In all these places the name of Christ, who has already come, reigns, since before him the gates of all cities have been opened and none are closed to him; before him iron bars have been shattered and bronze gates opened [Note: [Col. 0611C] “Broken,” Jun.] (Isa. 45:1–2). Although these things are also to be understood spiritually, in that the hearts of individuals, besieged by the devil in various ways, have been unlocked by faith in Christ, they have nevertheless plainly been fulfilled, since in all these places a people bearing Christ’s name dwells [Note: [Col. 0611C] “A Christian people dwells,” Paris.].

For who could have reigned over all [Note: [Col. 0611C] Rhen. and Obert. add “nations”] except Christ, the Son of God, who was announced as destined to reign over all nations [Note: [Col. 0611C] “Nations” is absent from Rhen. and Obert.] forever (Ps. [Col. 0611B] 46:2, 9; 85:9; Isa. 2:4; 49:6)?

For although Solomon reigned, he reigned only within the boundaries of Judah: the boundaries of his kingdom are marked from Beersheba to Dan.

[Note: [Col. 0611D] “The boundaries of his kingdom are marked.” In 1 Kings 4:21 we read: “Solomon, moreover, had under his dominion all the kingdoms from the River to the land of the Philistines and as far as the land of Egypt.” And in 2 Chronicles 9:26: “He [Solomon] also exercised authority over all the kings from the River Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and as far as the boundaries of Egypt.” Perhaps the Author read the boundaries of Solomon’s empire in 1 Kings 4:25, which reads: “And Judah and Israel lived without any fear, each man beneath his vine and beneath his fig tree, from Dan to Beersheba, all the days of Solomon.” EDD.]

Although Darius reigned over the Babylonians and Parthians, [Note: [Col. 0611C] “He did not have authority any farther; he did not have authority beyond the boundaries of his kingdom,” Rhen., Obert.] he did not have authority over all nations. If Pharaoh reigned over the Egyptians—or whoever succeeded him in the inheritance of the kingdom—his royal dominion was confined only to that place. Likewise Nebuchadnezzar, together with his subordinate kings, had the boundaries of his kingdom from India to Ethiopia. Likewise Alexander the Macedonian never held all Asia and the other regions after he had conquered them. Likewise the Germans are still not permitted to cross their own [Note: [Col. 0611C] “Their own” is absent from Rhen. and Obert.] frontiers. The Britons [Note: [Col. 0611C] “The Britains . . . are enclosed,” Rhen., Obert.] are enclosed within the circuit of their ocean. The nation of the Moors and the barbarous tribes of the Gaetuli are blockaded by the Romans, lest they cross the boundaries of their own territories [Note: [Col. 0612C] “Religions,” Rhen.]. [Col. 0611C]

What shall I say of the Romans, who defend their empire with the garrisons of their legions and cannot extend the strength of their kingdom beyond those nations? But Christ’s kingdom and name extend everywhere, are believed everywhere, are worshiped by all the nations enumerated above; [Col. 0612A] everywhere he reigns, everywhere he is adored, and he is bestowed equally upon everyone everywhere. With him a king enjoys no greater favor; no barbarian has lesser joy [Note: [Col. 0612C] “Authority,” Obert., Seml.]; no one’s deserts are distinguished according to rank or birth. He is equal to all, king to all, judge to all, and God and Lord to all. Nor should you doubt what we assert [Note: [Col. 0612C] “You assert,” Rhen.], since we see it happening.

## CHAPTER VIII
Accordingly, the times of the foretold and future birth of Christ, of his passion, and of the destruction of the city of Jerusalem—that is, its devastation—must be investigated. For Daniel says that both the holy city and the sanctuary are to be destroyed together with the leader who is to come, and that the pinnacle is to be destroyed unto annihilation. Accordingly, the times of the coming of Christ the leader must be investigated. These we shall examine in Daniel; and when they have been calculated, we shall prove that he has come, both from the times prescribed, from the corresponding signs, and from his works [Col. 0612B]. These things we prove [Note: [Col. 0612C] “Works” in Par.] from the events that followed, which were announced as destined to occur after his advent, so that we may believe all things both fulfilled and foreseen [Note: [Col. 0612C] “Thus we shall prove” in Jun. [Col. 0612C] Rhen. adds “and.” [Col. 0612C] “Perceived” in Rhen.].

Thus, therefore, Daniel prophesied concerning him in such a way as to show both when and at what time he would liberate the nations, and that after the passion of Christ this city was to be destroyed. For he speaks as follows:

> In the first year under Darius, son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, who reigned over the kingdom of the Chaldeans, I, Daniel, understood from the books the number of the years. And while I was still speaking in prayer, behold, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, came flying and touched me, as it were at the hour of the evening sacrifice; and he made me understand, and spoke [Col. 0612C] with me, and said: “Daniel, I have now come forth to imbue you with understanding. At the beginning of your supplication [Note: [Col. 0612C] “Observation” in Rhen. and Oberth.] the word went forth. And I have come to announce it to you, because you are a man of desires; therefore consider the word and understand the vision.”

[Note: [Col. 0611D] “Seventy weeks have been shortened concerning your people,” etc. This is a celebrated passage against the Jews for proving the advent of the Messiah. The passage occurs in Daniel 9 and is commonly adduced for this purpose by theologians. Another passage conforming to this one is from Genesis 49; that is, the famous prophecy of the patriarch Jacob: [Col. 0612D] “The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a leader from his thigh, until he who is to be sent comes.” In the Hebrew codices it reads, “until Shiloh comes.” But Shiloh is the Messiah—a point not difficult to demonstrate against the Jews, since the ancient Jews attest it. The three Chaldean paraphrases also—those of Onkelos, Jonathan, and the Jerusalem paraphrase—have “King Messiah” in place of “Shiloh.” Likewise, in the very ancient and highly authoritative book called *Bereshith Rabbah*, [text absent in the supplied source]; that is, “Shiloh is the King Messiah.” Among more recent writers, Rabbi Solomon, Rabbi Kimchi, and Rabbi Bechai hold the same view. Hence contemporary Jews are readily convicted from this passage of their folly and stubborn impiety. In the Greek text, however, it reads: Οὐκ ἐκλείψει ἐξ Ἰούδα ἕως ἂν ἔλθῃ ᾧ ἀπόκειται, “A ruler shall not fail from Judah until he comes for whom it is reserved”; that is, as St. Epiphanius interprets it, “for whom it is reserved that he should be Christ.” This occurs, of course, in his treatment of the heresy of the Herodians, who were so called because they professed that Herod was Christ. LE PR.]

> Seventy weeks have been shortened concerning your people [Col. 0613A] and concerning the holy city, until transgression grows old, sins are sealed, acts of injustice are expiated, and eternal righteousness is introduced; so that [Note: [Col. 0613C] The same witnesses read “and so that.”] vision and prophet may be sealed, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed. And you shall know, perceive, and understand that from the going forth of the word to restore and rebuild Jerusalem until Christ the leader there shall be seven and a half weeks, and seventy-two and a half weeks; and it shall return and be built in joy and with an enclosing rampart, and the times shall be renewed. And after these seventy-two weeks the anointing shall be destroyed and shall be no more; and the city and the sanctuary he shall destroy together with the leader who is coming, and they shall be cut down as in a flood, until the end of the war, which shall be cut short unto annihilation. And he shall confirm the covenant among [Note: [Col. 0613C] “Among” is absent from Fran.] many. For one week and half a week my sacrifice [Col. 0613B] and libation shall be taken away; and in the sanctuary there shall be the abomination of desolation, and until the end of the time a consummation shall be imposed upon this devastation.

Let us therefore attend to the limit: how truly he foretold [Note: [Col. 0613C] Rhen. and Oberth. read “in the word which he spoke.”] that seventy weeks were to come, during which, if they received him, the city would be built in breadth and length and the times would be renewed. But God, foreseeing what was to happen—that they would not merely refuse to receive him, but would even persecute him and hand him over to death—summed the matter up again and said that within sixty-two weeks he would be born and the Holy of Holies would be anointed; but when the seven and a half weeks were fulfilled, he would have to suffer, and the city would be destroyed after one and a half weeks, namely at the time [Note: [Col. 0613C] Pam. omits “time.”] when the seven and a half weeks had been completed. For he speaks as follows:

> And the city [Col. 0613C] and the sanctuary shall be destroyed together with the leader who is to come; and they shall be cut down as in a flood, and he shall destroy the pinnacle unto annihilation.

[Note: [Col. 0613C] “How, then, do we show that Christ came within the seventieth and a half week?” The author of the *Questions from the Old Testament*, appended to volume IV of the works [Col. 0613D] of Augustine, says: “From the time of the first year of Darius, king of the Persians, until the birth and passion of the Lord and the destruction of Jerusalem, which was accomplished by Vespasian, ruler of the Roman Empire, the seventy weeks were fulfilled. These amount to 490 years; and this calculation through the reigns and successions of the empire is manifest, just as it is found calculated by Tertullian in the book he wrote *Against the Jews*. Lest it should redound to his injury, because he calculated correctly, we have omitted it. And who could doubt this number, when approximately three hundred years are now found to have elapsed beyond it?” From these words it is inferred that the age of this writer was somewhat earlier than Augustine’s. RIG.]
