How, then, do we show [Note: [Col. 0613C] Others have “shall we show.”] that Christ came within the sixty-two and a half weeks? We shall count from the first year of Darius, since [Note: [Col. 0613C] The Dijon codex and Jerome on Daniel 9 have “because.”] [Col. 0614A] at that very time the vision itself was shown to Daniel. For he says:

> And understand, and reckon unto the completion [Note: [Col. 0613C] Rhen. and Oberth. have “from the going forth.” The Dijon codex reads, “From the prophecy of this word, therefore, from the first,” etc. [Col. 0614C] “From the prophecy of this word, therefore, from the first,” etc., in the Dijon codex. “From the prophecy” is also read in Jerome.] of the word by which I answer [Note: [Col. 0614C] The same witnesses read “to answer.”] these things to you.

We must therefore calculate from the first year of Darius, when Daniel saw this vision. Let us therefore see how [Note: [Col. 0614C] Fran. reads “that.”] the years are fulfilled up to the advent of Christ.

Darius reigned for nineteen years; Artaxerxes reigned for forty years; then King Ochus, who was also Cyrus, reigned for twenty-four years; Argus [Note: [Col. 0613D] “Argus, for one year.” Eusebius calls this man Arses, and Sulpicius calls him Arse; yet they assign him either four or three years, while they assign Darius only six. PAM.] for one year; another Darius, who was also named Melas, for twenty-two years; Alexander the Macedonian for twelve years.

[Note: [Col. 0613D] “Alexander the Macedonian, for twelve years.” This must undoubtedly be read thus on the authority of Blessed Jerome (*On Daniel*, chapter 2), [Col. 0614C] Berossus, Sulpicius Severus (*Sacred History*, book II), and the *Glossa Ordinaria*, rather than the “ten” previously printed both here and in Pomoerius. These figures can be reconciled with the mere six years given by Eusebius, because Eusebius assigns forty years to the successor, Ptolemy Lagus—who here, and in Josephus, *Antiquities*, book XII, chapter 1, is called SOTER—whereas the author assigns him only thirty-five, so that they differ by only one year overall. PAM.]

Then, after Alexander—who had ruled over the Medes and Persians, whom he had reconquered [Note: [Col. 0614C] Jerome and Jun. read “conquered.”], and had established his kingdom at Alexandria, which at that time he also called by his own name—Soter afterward [Note: [Col. 0614C] “Afterward” is absent from Ven.] reigned there in Alexandria for thirty-five years. Philadelphus succeeded him and reigned [Col. 0614B] for thirty-nine years [Note: [Col. 0614D] “He reigned for thirty-nine years.” Jerome reads: “Philadelphus succeeded him, reigning for thirty-eight years.” RIG.]. Euergetes succeeded him for twenty-five years; then Philopator for seventeen years; after him Epiphanes for twenty-four years; likewise another Euergetes for twenty-nine years, Soter for thirty-eight years, Ptolemy for thirty-eight years, and Cleopatra for twenty years and six months.

Cleopatra also reigned jointly with Augustus for thirteen years, and after Cleopatra Augustus reigned for another forty-three years. For all the years of Augustus’s rule amounted to fifty-six. We see, moreover, that in the forty-first year of Augustus’s rule [Note: [Col. 0614D] “We see, moreover, that in the forty-first year of Augustus.” This passage is cited in Eusebius’s *Chronicle* and examined in Joseph Scaliger’s *Annotation* at number 2015. Irenaeus, book [omitted], chapter 25: “Around the first-and-fortieth year of Augustus’s rule.” RIG.], during which [Note: [Col. 0614C] Jerome reads “who.”] he ruled after Cleopatra’s death, Christ was born. And this same Augustus survived for fifteen years after Christ was born.

[Note: [Col. 0614D] “And the remaining span of years up to the day of Christ’s birth shall be....” The Fulda manuscript reads: “Up to the day of Christ’s birth, the forty-first year; after Cleopatra’s death, the twenty-eighth year of Augustus: the total is 437 years and five months at the time of the birth.” Jerome, however, reads more correctly: “And the remaining span of years up to the day of Christ’s birth, in the forty-first year of Augustus after [Col. 0615C] Cleopatra’s death, shall be 437 years and five months,” etc. RIG.]

And the remaining span of years up to the day of Christ’s birth shall be forty-one years. The total is therefore 437 years and six months. Thus the sixty-two and a half weeks are fulfilled, which amount to 437 years [Col. 0614C] and six months, up to the day of Christ’s birth. And eternal righteousness was manifested, and the Holy of Holies—that is, Christ—was anointed; and vision and prophecy were sealed, and sins were forgiven, which through faith in Christ’s name are remitted [Note: [Col. 0614C] Rhen. reads “granted.”] to all who believe in him.

What, then, does his statement that vision and prophecy [Col. 0615A] are sealed mean [Note: [Col. 0615C] Rhen. and Oberth. read “the prophet.”], since all the prophets announced concerning him that he was to come and would have to suffer? Therefore, since prophecy was fulfilled through his advent, for this reason he said that vision and prophecy were sealed: because he is himself the seal of all the prophets, fulfilling everything that the prophets of old had announced concerning him.

For after [Note: [Col. 0615C] “For” is absent from Rhen. and Oberth.] the advent of Christ and his passion, there is now neither vision nor a prophet [Note: [Col. 0615C] Others read “nor is there prophecy.”] to announce that Christ is to come. Finally, if this is not so, let the Jews produce any writings of prophets subsequent to Christ, or visible miracles of angels such as the patriarchs of old saw up to the advent of Christ—who has now come, and by whose coming vision and prophecy have been sealed, that is, established.

And rightly does the Evangelist say [Col. 0615B]:

> The Law and the Prophets were until John the Baptist (Matt. 11:13).

For when Christ was baptized—that is, when he sanctified the waters in his baptism [Note: [Col. 0615C] “Sanctifying the waters in his baptism.” A similar statement occurs in Blessed Cyprian’s sermon *On the Baptism of Christ*: “Christ came to baptism, not because he needed washing, since there was no sin in him, but so that perennial authority might be given to the sacrament.” These passages should be noted against Calvin and others who deny that water is necessary in baptism. Another such passage is Blessed Cyprian’s second letter to Donatus; the reader may consult our annotations on it, number 8. PAM.]—all the fullness of the spiritual gifts of former times came to an end in Christ, as he sealed the vision and all the prophecies that he fulfilled by his advent. Hence he says with complete assurance that his advent seals vision and prophecy.

Accordingly, having shown both the number of years and that the period of sixty-two and a half weeks had been fulfilled, and that Christ then came—that is, was born—let us see [Note: [Col. 0615C] Seml. adds “in what.”] in what event the other seven and a half weeks, which were subdivided when they were cut off from the preceding weeks, were fulfilled.

After Augustus, who survived for fifteen years following Christ’s birth, Tiberius Caesar succeeded him and held the empire for twenty-two years, seven months [Col. 0615C], and twenty days [Note: [Col. 0616C] Rhen., following Jerome, reads “twenty-eight.”]. In the fifteenth year [Col. 0616A] of his reign Christ suffered, being approximately thirty years old when he suffered.

Likewise Gaius Caesar, also called Caligula, reigned for three years, eight months, and thirteen days [Note: [Col. 0615D] “Thirteen days.” No one is unaware that Claudius reigned after Caligula. Rhen. and Oberth. therefore restore his reign here as follows: “Tiberius Claudius, for thirteen years, seven months, and twenty days”; although we do not read this either in Jerome or in Pomoerius. Indeed, it ought to be omitted, so that the author’s reckoning of only fifty-two years and seven months may stand, as Pamelius says. He immediately adds: “It can therefore be seen even from this that he—Tertullian—was not very attentive to history, perhaps imitating in this respect Matthew the Evangelist, who in the book of Christ’s genealogy omitted three generations, so that, according to Blessed Jerome’s interpretation, he might not exceed three groups of fourteen. Meanwhile, the number of years agrees sufficiently with Clement of Alexandria.” EDD.]; Nero Caesar for nine years, nine months, and thirteen days; Galba for seven months [Note: [Col. 0616C] Jerome reads “twenty-nine days.”] and six days; Otho for three months and five days; Vitellius for eight months and ten days [Note: [Col. 0616C] Jerome reads “twenty-eight days.”].

In the first year of his reign Vespasian defeated the Jews; and the total comes to fifty-two years and six months. For he reigned for nine years [Note: [Col. 0616C] The same witnesses read “eleven years.”]. And thus, by the day of their conquest, the Jews had fulfilled the seventy weeks foretold by Daniel.

Therefore, when these periods too had been completed and the Jews defeated, libations and sacrifices afterward ceased there, since from that time onward they could no longer be celebrated there. For the anointing there was also destroyed after the passion of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0615D] “For it had been foretold that the anointing there would be destroyed.” Ἐνδελεχισμόν: “the continual sacrifice.” Jerome on Daniel 8. Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book VII, chapter 8: τὸν ἐνδελεχισμὸν καλούμενον ἀνδρῶν ἀπορίᾳ διαλελοιπέναι τῷ Θεῷ, “the offering called the continual sacrifice had ceased to be offered to God for lack of men.” PAM.]

For it had been foretold that the anointing there would be destroyed [Col. 0616B], just as it was prophesied in the Psalms:

> They destroyed my hands and feet (Ps. 21:17).

The suffering involved in this destruction was completed within the period of the seventy weeks, under Tiberius Caesar, when Rubellius Geminus and Fufius Geminus were consuls [Note: [Col. 0615D] “Rubellius Geminus and Rufinus Geminus.” Rhenanus had printed it thus [Col. 0616C] in his second edition; the first and third editions read “Rufinus Geminus.” The spelling of these names varies in the ancient books: the Sicilian *Fasti* have “Rufus and Rubellinus”; the Capitoline *Fasti*, “Rubellius and Fufius,” as does Tacitus; Sulpicius Severus has “Rubellius”; others, “Rubellio.” Some have “the two Gemini.” The Sicilian *Fasti* have “Geminus and Geminus,” and immediately afterward, “Rufus and Rubellinus.” This gave rise to the error of those who thought that Rufus and Rubellinus had been appointed substitute consuls for the two Gemini, although this means nothing other than “the two Gemini,” that is, Gaius Rubellius Geminus and Gaius Fufius Geminus. Thus Tacitus states it most clearly at the beginning of book V: “When Rubellius and Fufius were consuls”; and each of these, of course, had the cognomen Geminus. RIG.], in the month of March, at the time of Passover, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April,

[Note: [Col. 0616D] “On the first day of Unleavened Bread.” I have not yet been able to agree with Pamelius, who thinks that this passage can prove the practice of our Church whereby the body of Christ the Lord is consecrated in the Eucharist with unleavened bread. Granted that Moses commanded in Exodus 12 that everyone should use unleavened bread on those days, does that therefore prove the Church’s custom? Many think that leavened bread was formerly used in the sacred rites. On this subject there is an elegant treatise by Father Jacques Sirmond, of blessed memory (*μακαρίτου*). Demetrius Chomatenus, Archbishop of Bulgaria, formerly maintained this in his *Response to the Bishop of Dyrrachium*, saying: λατινικῶν ἀζύμων οὐδεὶς οὐδαμοῦ κανὼν μέμνηται, “No canon anywhere has ever mentioned the unleavened bread used by the Latins.” Nevertheless, St. Cyprian says in the book *On the Lord’s Supper*: “This unleavened bread, true and sincere food in outward form and sacrament, sanctifies us by touch, illuminates us by faith, and [Col. 0617C] conforms us to Christ by truth”—if indeed this book is by Blessed Cyprian. LE PR.—“On the eighth day before the Kalends of April.” From this, first of all, the opinion of those Fathers is confirmed who write that Christ suffered on the same day—namely, the eighth day before the Kalends of April—on which the annunciation was made to the Blessed Virgin. Secondly, it confirms the consistent interpretation given by all Latin writers of the three Evangelists—Matthew 26, Mark 14, and Luke 22—namely that, on the fourteenth day of the moon, the first day of Unleavened Bread having already begun in the evening, Christ celebrated the Passover [Col. 0617D] with his disciples. PAM.]

on the first day of Unleavened Bread, on which Moses had commanded that they slaughter the lamb toward evening. Accordingly, the whole synagogue of the children of Israel killed him, saying to Pilate when he wished to release him:

> His blood be upon us and upon our children (Matt. 27:25);

and:

> If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend (John 19:12),

so that everything written concerning him might be fulfilled.

## CHAPTER IX.

Let us therefore begin to prove that Christ’s nativity was announced by the prophets. [Col. 0616C] Thus Isaiah says:

> Hear, house [Col. 0617A] of David: [Note: [Col. 0617D] “No small contest for you.” The passage of Isaiah is chapter 7; but for this Latin interpretation to agree with the Greek and also with the text of the Vulgate, it must be read: “Is a contest with men a small thing for you?” and then there should follow: “Because God presents a contest”; that is, because you contend even against God, you are troublesome even to God. Symmachus said: “Is it not enough for you to cause trouble to men? For you are troublesome even to my God.” The Septuagint has: καὶ πῶς κυρίῳ παρέχετε ἀγῶνα, “And how do you present a contest to the Lord?” The author of the translation followed by Septimius and Cyprian seems to have read in the Greek: καὶ πῶς κύριος παρέχεται ἀγῶνα, “And how does the Lord present a contest?” RIG.] It is no small contest for you with men, because God presents a contest. Therefore God himself will give you a sign: [Note: [Col. 0617D] “Behold, a virgin shall conceive.” In the corrupted Greek version it is νεᾶνις, “young woman,” not παρθένος, “virgin,” as in the version of the Seventy. In the Hebrew there is some distinction, concerning which see St. Jerome in *Hebrew Questions*. LE PR.—Tertullian consistently reads it thus everywhere, both a little below and in the cited passage, and also in the book *On the Flesh of Christ*. We have therefore added “in her womb,” especially since it is also read in both passages cited immediately below from St. Cyprian. We discuss this more fully in our notes there on Epistle 6, no. 16, and in the book *Against the Jews*. PAM.] Behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel, which is interpreted: God with us. He shall eat butter and honey. For before the infant knows how to call father or mother, he shall receive the might of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians. (Isa. 7:13–16)

And so the Jews say: “Let us challenge this proclamation of Isaiah and make a comparison, to see whether the Christ who has now come fits, first, the name that Isaiah proclaimed and, secondly, the distinguishing marks that he announced concerning him. Isaiah indeed proclaims that he must be called Emmanuel, and thereafter that he will take the might of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians. But,” they say, “this man who came [Col. 0617B] was neither brought forth under such a name nor engaged in warfare.”

We, on the contrary, have thought that they should be admonished to examine the connected statements of this chapter as well. For the interpretation of “Emmanuel”—“God with us”—is also appended, so that you may consider not merely the sound of the name [Note: [Col. 0617C] “Expect,” Rhen., Oberth.], but also its meaning. For its Hebrew sound, which is *Emmanuel*, belongs to its own nation; but its meaning, which is “God with us,” is made common to all through translation. [Note: [Col. 0618C] “But its meaning, which is ‘God with us,’ etc.” According to Semler, these words are written in the margin of the Paterniacensis codex, but in such a way that they appeared to belong in the text. Semler nevertheless struck them out, although he found them in Pam., Rhen., and Rigalt. EDD.]

I ask, [Note: [Col. 0617C] “Therefore,” Seml.] then, whether this expression, “God with us,” which is *Emmanuel*, has been current in reference to Christ from the time when Christ shone forth. And I think you will by no means deny it. For those from Judaism who believe in Christ, whenever they wish to say “Emmanuel” after coming to believe in him, signify that God is with us. And [Col. 0617C] thus it is established that the one who was proclaimed as Emmanuel has already come, because what “Emmanuel” signifies has come—that is, “God with us.”

They are likewise misled by the sound of the name [Col. 0618A] when they understand “the might of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians” as though these words foretold Christ as a warrior, failing to notice what Scripture places first:

> For before the boy knows how to call father or mother, he shall receive the might of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians.

You must first examine [Note: [Col. 0618C] “For. Let us examine,” Jun.] the indication of his age: could this age present Christ even as a grown man, much less as a commander? The infant, of course, would summon men to arms by wailing and give the signal for battle not with a trumpet [Note: [Col. 0618D] “But with a rattle.” A *crepitacillum*, “little rattle,” is one of children’s toys; it is a diminutive form derived from *crepitaculum*, just as *specillum* is derived from *speculum*. He aptly uses the diminutive when speaking of a tiny infant. RHEN.], but with a baby-rattle; he would mark out the enemy not from horseback or from a wall, but from the back or neck of his nurse and bearer; and thus he would subdue Damascus and Samaria in place of breasts. It would be another matter if among you infants burst forth into battle—after first being anointed, I suppose, at the sun [Col. 0618B] [Note: [Col. 0618C] “At the seat,” Jun., Seml., Oberth.] [Note: [Col. 0618D] “At the sun.” *Solium* (“seat” or “bath”) is more pleasing to Semler, who interprets it as πυέλος, “a vessel in which people were anointed while seated.” EDD.], then armed with swaddling clothes and paid their wages in butter—infants who know how to wield a lance before they know how to lacerate. [Note: [Col. 0618D] “To wield a lance before they know how to lacerate.” Infants made irritable by teething lacerate breasts while sucking. RIG.]

But indeed, if nature nowhere permits this—[Note: [Col. 0618D] “To serve as a soldier before making a man.” Before puberty one is scarcely ever described as a soldier; and nature makes a man when it shows him to be mature. Tertullian expresses the same thought in book III *Against Marcion* as follows: “Nature nowhere permits this: to serve as a soldier before living.” For life makes the infant a man. RIG.] to serve as a soldier before becoming a man, to receive the might of Damascus before knowing one’s father—it follows that the declaration must be understood figuratively.

“But,” they say, “nature does not allow a virgin to give birth either, and yet the prophet must be believed.” Quite rightly. For he laid the foundation for belief in an incredible event by saying that it would be a sign:

> Therefore, he says, a sign shall be given to you: Behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son.

But a sign from God would not have appeared to be a sign unless it had been some extraordinary novelty. [Note: [Col. 0618D] “Finally, if at any time, in order to cast some people down.” More briefly and readily in *Against Marcion* III: “Finally, even the Jews, if at any time they dare to lie in order to cast us down, saying that it was not a virgin,” etc. RIG.] Finally, if at any time you are eager to draw some people away from this divine proclamation, or to turn aside individual simple folk, you dare to lie, claiming that Scripture says not that a virgin but that a young woman would conceive and give birth. Here too you are refuted, because an everyday occurrence—the pregnancy [Col. 0619A] and childbirth of a young woman—could not appear to be any sign at all.

A virgin mother, therefore, is rightly believed to have been set before us as a sign, but not likewise an infant warrior. For the rationale of the sign does not apply here also [Note: [Col. 0619C] “Not likewise? And here,” Rhen., Oberth.]; [Note: [Col. 0619C] “Applies. But the same.”] rather, once the sign of the new birth has been recorded, a different sequence concerning the infant is thereafter set forth: he is to eat honey and butter. Nor, certainly, is this a sign [Note: [Col. 0619C] “And this certainly is a sign of infancy,” Par. For *utique*, Pam. reads *utrique*. “Nor certainly is this a sign; it is infancy,” Oberth., Seml.], for this too belongs to infancy. But that he would receive the might of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians—this is the wondrous sign.

Observe the measure of his age and seek the meaning of the proclamation; rather, yield to the truth which you refuse to believe. Then the prophecy is understood just as clearly as it is declared fulfilled. [Note: [Col. 0619C] *Renuntiatur expuncta*, “is declared fulfilled”—that is, fulfilled by the event. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0619C] “The prophecy was declared, just as it is believed to have been fulfilled,” Oberth., Rhen. “Then … when,” Jun.]

The infant Christ received the might of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria. Let those eastern Magi, then, await him, [Note: [Col. 0619D] “Let those Eastern Magi await him.” *Maneant*, “let them await,” as in Terence’s *Phormio*, where he says *mansurus patrem*, “about to await his father.” PAM.] presenting the newly born Christ [Note: [Col. 0619D] “Presenting the newly born Christ with gold and incense.” I have preferred this reading to all others as the one most consistent with the author’s thought, and as one employed by him also in book III *Against Marcion*: “Let those Eastern Magi,” he says, “await him, presenting the newly born Christ in his infancy with gold and incense.” RIG.] with gold and incense [Note: [Col. 0619C] “As king,” Pam., Rhen., Oberth.] [Col. 0619B] [Note: [Col. 0620C] “And myrrh,” the same editors.], and the infant will have received [Note: [Col. 0620C] “Received,” the same editors.] the might of Damascus without battle or weapons.

For besides the universally known fact that the might of the East—that is, its resources [Note: [Col. 0620C] “That is, its resources” is absent from the Wouw codex.]—has customarily abounded in gold and perfumes, it is certain [Note: [Col. 0620C] “It is certainly the Creator’s,” Pam., Rhen., Oberth. *Creatoris*, “of the Creator,” in Fran., seems to have arisen from *certe est*, “it is certain.” Seml.], even from the divine Scriptures, that gold also constitutes the might of other nations, as he says through Zechariah:

> And Judah shall stretch toward Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0620C] “Israel stretched forward,” Rhen., Oberth.], and shall gather all the strength of the surrounding peoples, gold and silver. (Zech. 14:14)

For David also spoke of this gift of gold:

> And there shall be given to him from the gold of Arabia. (Ps. 71:15)

And again:

> The kings of the Arabs and of Sheba shall bring him gifts. (Ibid., 10)

[Note: [Col. 0619D] “For the East also generally had Magi as kings.” It cannot be inferred from this passage that the Persian kings were Magi, but rather that they generally had Magi; for since they were instructed in the teachings of the Magi, they retained something from them. Those called Magi among the Persians were the tutors of kings, as Cicero testifies [Col. 0620C] in book III *On the Nature of the Gods*, and Apuleius in the *Apology*; and according to the same Apuleius, *Magus* is the same as “priest” in the Persian language. [Col. 0620D] LE PR.]

For the East also generally had Magi as kings, and Damascus was formerly reckoned part of Arabia, before it was transferred to Syrophoenicia when the Syrian regions were distinguished. Christ then received its might [Col. 0619C] by receiving its insignia, namely gold and perfumes.

The spoils of Samaria, moreover, were the Magi themselves. After recognizing him, honoring him with gifts, and worshiping him on bended knee as Lord [Note: [Col. 0620C] “God,” Fran.] and king, under the testimony of the star as indicator and guide [Note: [Col. 0620C] “Of the star that judged and indicated,” Rhen., Oberth.], they were made the spoils of Samaria—that is, of idolatry—by coming to believe in Christ. For he designated idolatry by the name “Samaria,” since Samaria was infamous for the idolatry by which it had then revolted from God under King Jeroboam.

[Note: [Col. 0620D] “For neither is this new to the divine Scriptures.” In book III *Against Marcion*: “For neither is it new for the Creator to employ a metaphor figuratively.” RIG.]

For neither is it new to the divine Scriptures to use the transference of names figuratively, by comparing crimes. Thus he calls your rulers “rulers of Sodom” (Isa. 1:10), and calls your people “the people of Gomorrah” (ibid.), although those cities had long since been destroyed. Elsewhere, too, he says through the prophet to the people Israel:

> Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite. (Ezek. 16:3)

They had not been born from the stock of those peoples, but were so named because of similar impiety—although through the prophet Isaiah he had at another time called them his own sons:

> I have begotten sons and exalted them. (Isa. 1:2)

[Col. 0620B]

[Note: [Col. 0620D] “Thus Egypt too is sometimes understood as the whole world.” He perhaps alludes to Isaiah chapter 19, in which, although most statements concern Egypt, some are nevertheless interpreted not only by the ancients but also by the Jews as referring to the world enveloped in Egyptian darkness, and specifically the statement concerning the Church dispersed throughout the whole world: “On that day there shall be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt.” PAM.]

Thus “Egypt” too (Isa. 19:1) is sometimes understood in his writings as the whole world, under the designation of superstition and a curse.

[Note: [Col. 0620D] “Thus Babylon too.” The marginal annotation *Babylon Rome* should be struck out. It was undoubtedly added by enemies of the Roman Church, since those who are not ashamed to twist this passage against it fail to see that it concerns not the Church but the city of Rome, and Rome at the time when, as the vanquisher of the saints, it was stirring up persecution against Christians through its high priests—that is, the pontiffs of its idols. PAM.]

Thus “Babylon” too (Rev. 17:5), in our John, is a figure of the city of Rome, which is correspondingly great, proud in its dominion, and a vanquisher of the saints. In this way, therefore, he also gave the Magi the designation “Samaritans”; and they were despoiled of what they had shared with the Samaritans—idolatry, as we have said.

“Against the king of the Assyrians” means against the devil, who thinks that he reigns for this purpose: to cast the saints down from the religion of God.

This interpretation of ours will also be assisted by the fact that elsewhere the Scriptures designate Christ as a warrior because of the names of certain weapons and words of this kind. But the Jews will be refuted [Col. 0620C] by comparison with the remaining senses. David says:

> Gird your sword upon your thigh. (Ps. 44:4)

But what do you read immediately before this concerning [Col. 0621A] Christ [Note: [Col. 0621C] Oberth. and Seml. add Ὡραῖος τῷ κάλλει, “Beautiful in comeliness.”]?

> Comely in beauty above the sons of men; grace has been poured upon your lips. (Ibid., 3)

It would be exceedingly absurd if, while girding someone with a sword for war, he flattered him concerning the comeliness of his beauty and the grace of his lips. Continuing about him, he said:

> Advance, prosper, and reign. [Note: [Col. 0621C] “And prosper, hasten and reign,” Fran. “And prosper and reign,” Jun.] (Ibid., 5)

And he added:

> Because of your gentleness and justice. (Ibid.)

[Note: [Col. 0621C] “For who will work with the sword and not practice things contrary to gentleness and justice?” Tertullian’s writings scarcely permit military service to Christians. In chapter 3 of *On Patience*, he says that the Lord’s patience was wounded in Malchus, and that the Lord thereby cursed the works of the sword for the future. Likewise in *On the Crown*, he says that the sword was not necessary even for the Lord’s defense. And generally, in *On Idolatry*: “How,” he asks, “will he serve as a soldier even in peacetime without the sword that the Lord took away?” RIG.—The author everywhere forbids military service to all Christians, as was observed before me. St. Jerome writes to Gerontia: “At that time it was said to warriors, ‘Gird your sword upon your thigh, most mighty one’; now Peter hears, ‘Put your sword into its sheath.’” Yet although many Christians and many martyrs were commanders of armies, that fact is nevertheless condemned by this most ancient teacher and also by others. In the letter that Emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote from Germany to the Senate on behalf of the Christians, he says that warfare was forbidden to them: διὰ τὸ ἐχθρὸν εἶναι τὸ τοιοῦτο αὐτοῖς, διὰ τὸν θεόν, ὃν φοροῦσι κατὰ συνείδησιν, “because such a thing was opposed to them on account of the God whom they bear within according to conscience.” This letter is found in Justin Martyr after *Apology* II. I can offer no other explanation than that military service at that time was for the most part bound up with pagan rites and impieties and was a workshop of crimes. The martyrs and Christians who distinguished themselves under arms, however, emerged uncontaminated by that mire. [Col. 0622C] LE PR.]

For who will work with the sword [Note: [Col. 0621C] “Who will gird on the sword?” Rhen., Oberth.] and not practice things contrary to gentleness and justice—that is, deceit, harshness, and injustice, the proper business of warfare?

Let us therefore see whether that sword is another sword, whose operation is also another: [Note: [Col. 0622C] “That is, the divine word of God.” In the passage very frequently cited, he inserts the actual text of the Apocalypse of the apostle [Col. 0622D] John, to which he alludes here (Rev. 1). In accordance with it, omitting *ut* as superfluous, we also read: “two-edged through the two Testaments.” LE PR.] namely, the divine word of God, two-edged [Note: [Col. 0621C] “It,” Jun.] [Note: [Col. 0621C] Rhen. and Oberth. add “as.”] (Heb. 4:12) through the two Testaments, the old law and the new law, sharpened by the equity of its wisdom and repaying each person according to his deed.

It was therefore permissible [Note: [Col. 0621C] “It is pleasing,” the same editors.] [Col. 0621B] for the Christ of God in the Psalms to be figuratively girded with the sword of God’s word, without reference to warfare. The aforesaid comeliness together with the grace of his lips appropriately belongs to him. He was then being girded upon his thigh in David when he was announced as destined to come to earth by the decree of God the Father:

> And the greatness of your right hand, he says, shall lead you forth (Ps. 44:5),

that is, the power of spiritual grace, through which the knowledge of Christ is led forth.

> Your arrows, he says, are sharp (ibid., 6),

meaning, certainly, the flying [Note: [Col. 0621C] “Everywhere,” the same editors.] precepts of God, threatening the arraignment of every person’s heart [Note: [Col. 0622D] “The arraignment of the heart.” This signifies the force of spiritual grace, which pierces the conscience of every believer with the arrows of the divine precepts. RIG.], pricking and piercing every conscience. [Note: [Col. 0621C] “Both of the one pricking and of the one piercing,” Rhen.] [Note: [Col. 0621C] “The conscience. For the peoples,” Rhen., Oberth.]

> Peoples shall fall beneath you,

certainly by worshiping you.

Thus Christ is mighty in war and armed; thus he shall receive [Note: [Col. 0621C] “Shall take,” Pam., Rhen., Oberth.] the spoils not only of Samaria but of all nations. Recognize [Col. 0621C] the figurative spoils of the one whose allegorical weapons you have learned. [Col. 0622A] And thus the Christ [Note: [Col. 0622C] Jun. adds “was.”] who came was so far from being [Note: [Col. 0622C] “Insofar as,” Lat.] a warrior, precisely because he was not proclaimed as such by Isaiah.

“But,” they say, “if the Christ who is believed to be coming is not called Jesus [Note: [Col. 0622C] “Is,” Oberth., Seml. “Nor indeed is he believed by the Jews to be Jesus,” Seml.], why is the one who came called Jesus Christ?”

Both names will be established in the Christ of God, in whom the name Jesus is also found. Learn the manner of your error. When Auses son of Nave was appointed Moses’ successor, he was certainly transferred [Note: [Col. 0622C] “The manner, when … Auses son of Nare was appointed, he was certainly transferred,” Oberth., Seml.] from his former name and began to be called Jesus. [Note: [Col. 0622D] “And began to be called Jesus.” Thus from the manuscripts.… He alludes to what is found in Num. 13:17: “And Moses called Osee, the son of Nun, Josue.” … St. Augustine translated this from the Greek version in book XVI *Against Faustus*, chapter 19: “And Moses surnamed Ausen, son of Nave, Jesus.” PAM.]

“Certainly,” you say. [Note: [Col. 0622C] “You say, this,” Oberth.]

We declare that this was first a figure of the one to come. For Jesus Christ was going to lead a second people—namely us, the nations who formerly dwelt in the wilderness of the world [Note: [Col. 0622C] “In the world, in the wilderness,” Oberth., Seml. “In the wilderness-world,” Par.]—into the land of promise, flowing with milk and honey, that is, into possession of eternal life [Note: [Col. 0622C] “Of the promise,” Seml.], than which nothing [Col. 0622B] is sweeter. And this [Note: [Col. 0622C] “Into which,” Rhen., Oberth. “Which,” Wouw codex.] was to come about not through Moses—that is, not through the discipline of the law—but through Jesus, that is, through the grace of the new law, after we had been circumcised by a blade of stone, that is, by Christ’s precepts. For Christ is the rock (1 Cor. 10:4), proclaimed in many manners and figures.

Therefore the man who was being prepared as an image of this mystery was also inaugurated with a figure of the Lord’s name, so that he might be called Jesus. For the one who spoke to Moses was himself the Son of God, who was also always seen. [Note: [Col. 0622D] “Who was also always seen.” This too appears to belong among Tertullian’s errors, as though he held the same view as the Arian Maximinus—that the Son of God had always been seen by men—against whom St. Augustine argues at length in book III, chapter 26. Moreover, what follows, “For no one has ever seen God the Father and lived,” occurs in entirely the same way in the book *Against Praxeas*. PAM.] For no one has ever seen God the Father and lived (Exod. 33:20). It is therefore established that the Son of God himself spoke to Moses and said to the people:

> [Note: [Col. 0622D] “Behold, I send an angel.” We have added “I” from the manuscripts, [Col. 0623D] here and later, for it is read in most Greek, Hebrew, and Latin codices. PAM.] Behold, I send my angel before your face—that is, before the people—to guard you on the way and lead you [Col. 0622C] into the land which I have prepared for you. Attend to him, [Col. 0623A] and hear him, and do not disobey him; for he has not concealed you, because my name is upon him. (Exod. 23:20–21)

For Jesus, not Moses, was to lead the people into the land of promise. He did indeed call him an angel, because of the greatness of the mighty works that he was to perform—the mighty works performed by Jesus Nave, which you yourselves read—and because of [Note: [Col. 0623C] “Because of” is absent from Pam., Rhen., and Oberth.] the office of a prophet, namely one who announces the divine will.

Thus the Spirit through the prophet also calls John, the forerunner of Christ, an angel who was to come, saying in the person of the Father:

> Behold, I send my angel before your face [Note: [Col. 0623D] “Behold, I send my angel before your face.” In the prophet Malachi it is “before my face,” πρὸ προσώπου μου. But the same is read both in the prophet and in the Evangelists. LE PR.]—that is, before Christ—who shall prepare your way before you. (Mal. 3:1)

Nor is it new for the Holy Spirit to call those whom God has set over the ministry of his power “angels.” For the same [Note: [Col. 0623C] “He says,” Seml. “For, he says,” Pam., Oberth.] John was called not only the angel of Christ [Col. 0623B] but also a lamp shining before Christ. David proclaims:

> For I have prepared a lamp for my Christ. (Ps. 131:17)

Therefore Christ himself, coming to fulfill the prophets, says to the Jews:

> He was, he says, a burning and shining lamp. (John 5:35)

For he not only prepared his ways in the wilderness (John 1:23), but, by pointing out the Lamb of God (ibid., 29), he also illuminated the minds of men through his proclamation, so that they might understand him to be the lamb whom Moses had announced [Note: [Col. 0623C] “Had named,” Pam., Rhen.] would suffer (Exod. 12).

So too Jesus, because of the future mystery of his name—for he confirmed as his own the name that he himself had given him, since he had commanded him thereafter to be called not “angel” or “Ausen,” but “Jesus.” Thus, therefore, both names fit the Christ of God, so that he might also be called Jesus.

And because the virgin from whom Christ had to be born was to derive her lineage from David’s seed, as we recalled above, the prophet Isaiah says plainly in the following words:

> And there shall be born, he says, a rod from the root of Jesse—which is Mary—and a flower shall ascend from his root. And upon him [Note: [Col. 0623C] “From the root. Shall ascend upon him,” Rhen., Oberth.] shall rest the Spirit of God: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might [Note: [Col. 0623C] “Truth,” Par.], the spirit of knowledge and piety; the spirit of the fear of God shall fill him. (Isa. 11:1–2)

For the totality [Col. 0624A] of spiritual gifts belonged to no human being except Christ, who was indeed likened to a flower because of grace [Note: [Col. 0623D] “Except to Christ, flourishing indeed because of glory, because of grace,” [Col. 0624C] Oberth., Seml.], but reckoned from the stock of Jesse [Note: [Col. 0623D] “Namely, to be reckoned thence through Mary.” Shortly afterward: “Just as Mary was registered in the Roman census.” He mentions this census in many places; I therefore refer the reader to our notes on chapter 7 of book IV *Against Marcion*. I remark in passing that there is no small difficulty in explaining that registration: whether it took place under Sentius Saturninus or under Quirinius, as St. Luke has it, or whether a double census was undertaken, as some assert. LE PR.], namely through Mary, who was to be reckoned from that stock. For Mary was from the native town of Bethlehem and the house of David, as she was registered in the Roman census (Luke 2:1 ff.); from her Christ was born.

I further ask: since it was proclaimed by the prophets that he would come from Jesse’s lineage and [Note: [Col. 0623D] “All humility and patience.” In chapter 3 of *On Patience*, he has almost the same: “But when about to depart, he wished to be feasted upon the delight of patience.” Not long before, he had called Patience the mother [Col. 0624D] of mercy. In this sense St. Chrysostom says in Homily 4 *To the People*: Εἰ βούλει τρυφᾶν, καὶ ἀνέσεως ἀπολαύειν, καὶ ἡδονῆς, μὴ ζήτει ἡδονήν, μήτε ἄνεσιν, ἀλλὰ ζήτει ψυχὴν ὑπομονῆς γέμουσαν, “If you wish to enjoy delights, relaxation, and pleasure, do not seek pleasure or ease, but seek a soul full of patience.” LE PR.] would display all humility, patience, and tranquility, has he come? Thus the man who is shown to be such will himself be the Christ who has come.

For concerning him the prophet says:

> A man placed under affliction and knowing how to bear weakness (Isa. 53:4), who was led like a sheep to slaughter and, like a lamb before its shearer, did not open his mouth. (Ibid., 7)

If he neither contended nor [Col. 0624B] cried out, nor was his voice heard outside; [Note: [Col. 0624D] “Who the bruised reed.” In chapter 3 of *On Patience*, he says nearly the same: “He did not break the battered reed.” Here it is “bruised,” there “battered,” which is the same, just as in the prophet Isaiah 42 it is συγκεθλασμένον, “crushed,” and in Matthew 12 συντετριμμένον, “broken.” Here I shall use St. Hilary’s explanation: in commenting upon this passage of Matthew, he understands by the battered reed the Gentiles, who were indeed not broken by God but preserved for salvation. LE PR.] if he did not break the bruised reed—that is, Israel’s battered [Note: [Col. 0624C] “That is, battered” is absent from Rhen. and Oberth.] faith; if he did not extinguish the burning flax—that is, the momentary ardor of the nations (Isa. 42:2–3)—but rather caused it to shine more brightly [Note: [Col. 0624D] “By the rising of his light.” In accordance with: “The people who walked in darkness saw a great light,” a passage he used earlier.] through the rising of his own light, he can be no other than the one who was proclaimed. [Note: [Col. 0624C] “Was being foretold,” Pam.]

The conduct of the Christ who has come must therefore be examined according to the rule of the Scriptures. For, unless I am mistaken, we read that he was distinguished by a twofold activity: proclamation and miraculous power. I shall arrange the discussion under both headings. [Note: [Col. 0624C] “Thus arranged for the people,” Rhen., Oberth. “Thus arranged under a heading,” Jun.] Let us therefore examine in detail the sequence we have begun, showing that Christ was announced as a preacher, as through Isaiah:

> Cry aloud, he says, with strength, and do not spare; raise your voice like a trumpet, and announce to my people their crimes and to the house of Jacob [Col. 0624C] their sins. They seek me from day to day and desire to know my ways, as though they were a people who had practiced righteousness and had not abandoned the judgment of God (Isa. 58:1–2),

and the rest.

Isaiah also says that he would perform mighty works by the Father:

> Behold, our God renders judgment; he himself shall come and save us. Then the weak shall be healed, the eyes of the blind shall see, the ears of the deaf shall hear, the lame man shall leap like a deer, and the tongues of the mute shall be loosened (Isa. 35:4–6),

[Col. 0625A] and the other deeds that not even you deny Christ performed, since you said that you did not stone him because of the works, but because he performed them on the Sabbaths (John 5:18).

[Note: [Col. 0625C] Semler thought that he had found in chapter 9 of this book his first reason for asserting that this work is not Tertullian’s, but merely a compilation made by an inept man from the books *Against Marcion*. Semler attempts to support his conjecture solely by comparing this book *Against the Jews* with book III *Against Marcion*. By this mode of hairsplitting, however, the treatise is certainly taken away from Tertullian in vain. Besides St. Jerome, the author of the *Questions Drawn from Scripture* published under Augustine’s name, and Vincent of Lérins, all learned men down to the innovating Semler attributed it to the same author. And how could the book *Against the Jews* be a compilation from book III *Against Marcion* if the former was earlier than, or at least contemporary with, the books *Against Marcion*? Finally, I do not see how it is a paradox or anything resembling a monstrosity if the same author employed the same arguments and formulas of speech in different works written against people of different sects, when those works were by no means different in respect to their subject and the matter under discussion. EDD., from LUMPER. [Col. 0625D]]

## CHAPTER X

You do indeed raise doubts about the manner of his Passion, denying that the suffering of the cross was proclaimed concerning Christ, and further arguing that one must not believe that God exposed his Son to that kind of death, because he himself said:

> Cursed is every man who hangs upon wood. (Deut. 21:23)

But an examination of the circumstances must precede the interpretation of this curse. For he says in Deuteronomy:

> If there is in anyone an offense such that he is under a judgment of death, and he dies, you shall hang him upon wood. But you shall surely bury [Col. 0625B] him on that same day, because everyone who has been suspended upon wood is cursed by God; and you shall not defile the land that the Lord your God will give you as an inheritance. (Ibid., 22–23)

He did not, therefore, curse Christ in respect to this suffering. Rather, he made a distinction: the person who had incurred a judgment of death for some offense, died, and was suspended upon wood—this person would be cursed by God, because [Note: [Col. 0625C] “Who,” Rhen., Oberth.] he was suspended upon wood for what his offenses deserved.

Christ, by contrast, spoke no deceit with his mouth (Isa. 53:9) [Note: [Col. 0625D] “And displayed all righteousness and humility.” He most excellently extols the voluntary abasement of Christ the Lord, from which even to Christ himself is attributed the greatness of condescension and abasement, μέγεθος συγκαταβάσεως καὶ ταπεινώσεως, in the prologue to the Council in Trullo. Gregory Thaumaturgus attributes to God himself ταπείνωσιν ἄκα[.....]ν, “supreme humility” [uncertain reading]. LE PR.], and displayed all righteousness and humility. As we recalled above that it had been foretold concerning him, he was exposed to this kind of death not for what he himself deserved, but so that those things foretold by the prophets as destined to befall him through you might be fulfilled. Thus in the Psalms the Spirit of Christ was already singing:

> [Col. 0625C] They repaid me evil for good (Ps. 34:12); [Col. 0626A]

and:

> What I had not stolen, I then repaid (Ps. 68:5);

> They destroyed [Note: [Col. 0625D] “They destroyed my hands.” From Psalm 21, where this version differs from the Hebrew. For in the Hebrew it is “like a lion,” whereas it ought to be [Hebrew text missing in the supplied source], that is, “they dug,” [Col. 0626C] a fact noted long ago by the Masorah. Thus the mouths of the Jews are stopped, since they are reluctant to allow these words to be understood of the Lord’s Passion. What possible meaning could there be if “like a lion” were written, unless we resort to Rabbi David Kimchi’s interpretation of a lion pursuing prey? Anyone who reads such trifles, unless he is completely made of iron and has an expression more severe than a Stoic’s, will be unable to restrain his laughter. Better, therefore, is the Greek version, followed by the Vulgate: ὤρυξαν, “they dug.” Meanwhile I note that Justin Martyr, near the middle of *Apology* II, most appropriately applies and explains this passage with reference to the Lord’s Passion. LE PR.] my hands and feet (Ps. 21:17);

> They put gall in my drink, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink (Ps. 68:23);

and:

> They cast a lot upon my garment. (Ps. 21:19)

So too the other things you were going to commit against him were foretold.

Although he suffered all these things himself, [Note: [Col. 0625C] “Those things,” others.] he did not suffer because of any evil deed of his own, but so that the Scriptures from the mouths of the prophets might be fulfilled (Matt. 26:56).

The mystery of his Passion certainly had to be represented figuratively in the proclamations. The more incredible it was, the more it would have become a stumbling block if it were proclaimed openly; and the more magnificent it was, the more it had to be veiled, so that the difficulty of understanding might seek the grace of God.

Thus, first of all, Isaac, when he was led as a victim by his father and himself carried the wood (Gen. 22:6), already at that time denoted Christ’s end: surrendered as a sacrifice by his Father and carrying the wood of his own Passion.

Joseph likewise prefigured Christ—even in this alone, so that I may not delay the course of my argument—because he suffered persecution from his brothers and was sold into Egypt (Gen. 37:28) on account of God’s grace, just as Christ was sold because of Israel by his brothers when Judas betrayed him.

[Note: [Col. 0626D] “For Joseph too is blessed in these words.” We have omitted “by his father.” For this is not his father’s blessing upon Joseph, but Moses’ blessing in Deuteronomy 33, by which he blessed Joseph’s tribes. Moreover, he translated *ventilabit*, “shall winnow,” for κερατιεῖ, which the Latin translator of the Seventy renders more literally as *cornu petet*, “shall strike with the horn.” PAM.]

For Joseph too is blessed in these words:

> His beauty is that of a bull; his horns are the horns of a unicorn; with them he shall winnow the nations together, even to the ends of the earth. (Deut. 33:17)

Surely no unicorn-rhinoceros [Note: [Col. 0626D] “Unicorn-rhinoceros.” Pliny says this about it in *Natural History*, book VIII, chapter 20: “At the same games—namely, those of Pompey the Great—there was also a rhinoceros with a single horn upon its nose, such as has often been seen. This other animal is born an enemy of the elephant; its length is equal, its legs much shorter, and its color boxwood-yellow.” I have thought it proper to cite this author against the opinion of those who think that a rhinoceros with a single horn has never existed in nature, since several remarkable horns of such animals exist in the royal treasury at Saint-Denis near Paris. PAM.] or two-horned Minotaur was being foretold. Rather, Christ was signified in him: a bull because of his twofold dispensation—fierce toward some as judge, gentle toward others as savior. [Note: [Col. 0626D] “Whose horns were the outermost parts of the cross.” He is speaking here of figures, indeed even of the image, of the cross. From the manuscripts in part, both here and in book III *Against Marcion*, and in part from the printed editions, we have corrected the text to “the outermost or extreme parts of the cross.” PAM.] His horns were to be the outermost parts of the cross; [Col. 0626C] for even [Note: [Col. 0626D] “On the yard of a ship the extremities are called horns.” [Col. 0627C] This is most clearly indicated by the verse of Persius:

We turn the horns of the sail-clad yardarms about. Servius on *Aeneid* V: “Horns: the extremities of the yardarms.” RIG.] On a ship’s yardarm, which forms part of a cross, the extremities are called “horns.” [Note: [Col. 0627B] Semler adds *hujus* (“of this”).] But the unicorn is the central stake of the upright. [Note: [Col. 0627C] “But the unicorn is the central stake of the upright.” This is how Pamelius edited the text. Rhenanus had printed, “But the unicorn is a stake in the central upright.” And thus it is written in the Dijon manuscript. But these words make no good sense. Those who inspected the Fulda manuscript attest that they read there, “But the unicorn is the stake secured in the middle.” This offers some appearance of truth: the “horns” would be the extremities of the cross, or of the crossbeam, to which the hands were nailed or bound; while the unicorn would be the stake secured in the middle, or the upright, which in Book I *To the Nations* is called the projecting seat. RIG.] Finally, by this power of the cross, and horned in this manner, he even now winnows all nations through faith, carrying them from earth into heaven; and then, through judgment, he will winnow them by casting them down from heaven to earth. [Note: [Col. 0627B] “Descending,” Oehler? [Obert.] and Semler.]

He will likewise be the bull elsewhere in the same Scripture, when Jacob, in extending his blessing to Simeon and Levi, prophesies concerning the scribes and Pharisees; for their lineage is traced from them. It is interpreted spiritually thus: [Note: [Col. 0627C] “Simeon and Levi accomplished iniquity from their own sect.” He translated literally the Greek ἐξ αἱρέσεως αὐτῶν (“from their own choice/sect”), in place of what the Latin edition of the Septuagint renders “of their own purpose.” PAM.] “Simeon and Levi accomplished iniquity from their own sect,” namely, the sect by which they persecuted Christ. “Let my soul not enter into their council, and let my inward parts not recline in their assembly; [Note: [Col. 0627B] “My viscera,” Obert. and Rhen.] because in their indignation they slew men”—that is, the prophets—“and in their desire they hamstrung the bull” [Col. 0627B] (Gen. 49:6), that is, Christ, whom they killed after the murder of the prophets, and savagely pierced his sinews by driving in nails. Otherwise it would be pointless if, after the homicide they had already committed, he were reproaching them for the butchery of some ox. [Note: [Col. 0627B] Others read “and not to those very men,” Rhen. and Obert.]

Again, why did Moses, precisely at the time when Joshua was fighting against Amalek, pray seated with his hands outstretched (Exod. 17:11)? [Note: [Col. 0627D] “He prayed with outstretched hands.” Ursinus’s exemplar had this reading. What follows demonstrates that it is the truest reading: “For those who would fight against the devil, the posture of the cross was also necessary.” Likewise in the book *On Prayer*: “When we pray, we spread out our hands in a form patterned upon the Lord’s Passion.” RIG.] In circumstances so alarming, surely he ought rather to have commended his prayer with knees bent, hands beating [Col. 0628A] his breast, and face rolled upon the ground—[Note: [Col. 0627D] “With his face rolled upon the ground.” In the Dijon manuscript one reads *voluntate* (“by the will”). Hence I am led to think that the truest reading is the one preserved by the exemplars in Book III *Against Marcion*: “with his face rolling upon the ground.” Thus in the *Apology*: “But we, parched by fasting, rolling in sackcloth and ashes.” RIG.]—unless it was because, there where the name of Joshua/Jesus was fighting, the posture of the cross was also necessary for those who would one day fight against the devil, since through the cross Jesus was to win the victory.

Again, after Moses had forbidden the likeness of every created thing, why did he set up a bronze serpent placed upon wood, in the posture of one hanging, as a saving spectacle for Israel, at the time when they were being destroyed by serpents after their idolatry (Num. 21:9), unless because in this he was foreshadowing the Lord’s cross, by which the serpent, the devil, is made manifest [Note: [Col. 0628B] “Was represented,” Obert. and Semler.], and salvation was obtained for everyone wounded by serpents of that kind—that is, by his angels—when he turned away from the sinfulness of transgressions toward the mysteries of Christ’s cross? For whoever then looked upon it was freed from the serpents’ bite.

Come now: if [Col. 0628B] you have read in the prophet, in the Psalms, “God has reigned from the tree” (Ps. 95:10), [Note: [Col. 0627D] “The Lord has reigned from the tree.” Thus from the manuscripts and printed editions; below, “will reign,” for that is read in Greek and Latin. Likewise the phrase “from the tree” is rightly added by the author both here and again in chapter 13, as well as in Book III *Against Marcion*: not only in the Roman edition, from which that Paschal verse is sung in the Church, but also in the Gallican edition, at least according to the more correct Latin manuscripts, among them the Donatian manuscript of the Bible, which Erasmus calls “golden” because of its golden capital letters. Other ancient writers read the same phrase, specifically, among the Greeks, Justin Martyr against Trypho; and among the Latins, the author of the book *On Mount Sinai and Zion* among the works of blessed Cyprian, Arnobius on the Psalms, and Theodulf (bishop of Orléans—or rather Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers) in his poem on the Passion, in these words:

> Fulfilled are the things that David sang  
> in faithful song, saying:  
> “Among the nations  
> God has reigned from the tree.”

The manuscript at this place reads “God,” but we have retained “the Lord.” So far am I from being able to agree with Jacques Lefèvre (*Commentary on the Fivefold Psalter*), who thinks that the phrase was added merely as a paraphrase through someone’s private devotion; on the contrary, I consider it the genuine reading, especially since he himself acknowledges that reading in the old edition of the Psalter [Col. 0628D] prior to the age of blessed Jerome. Nor is it an objection that it is not read in the Hebrew manuscripts, since it could have been expunged by the Jews, as were many other things, as the Most Reverend William Lindanus, bishop of Roermond, discusses more fully. PAM.—Pamelius omitted several testimonies of no slight authority, which we have thought it useful to list here. It is therefore established that the following held the same opinion: Augustine (*Expositions on the Psalms*), St. Leo the Great (*Sermon IV on the Lord’s Passion*), St. Gregory the Great (*On Ezekiel*, Book I, Homily VI; *On 1 Kings* V), Cassiodorus (*On the Psalms*), St. Peter Damian (*Dialogue between a Jew and a Christian*), and St. Bernard (*Sermon I on the Resurrection*). The same reading is also found in the ancient Italic version published first by Blessed Cardinal Joseph Tommasi and afterward by Dom Pierre Sabatier, a Benedictine monk of the Congregation of St. Maur; and in the very ancient Psalters of St. Germanus, bishop of Paris, and of the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres. EDD.]

I await what you understand by this, lest perhaps you think that some timber-merchant king is meant rather than Christ, who has reigned from the time of Christ’s Passion onward, death having been overcome. [Note: [Col. 0628B] “Christ” is omitted by the Latin manuscript, or “of the tree” is substituted.]

Accordingly Isaiah too says: “For a child has been born to us, and a son has been given to us” (Isa. 9:6). What would be remarkable, unless he is speaking of the Son of God, in saying: “A son has been born to us, whose dominion [Note: [Col. 0628B] Semler adds “beginning.”] has been placed upon his shoulder” (ibid.)? What king at all carries the emblem of his power upon his shoulder, rather than a diadem upon his head, a scepter in his hand, or sometimes a distinctive mark upon his own garment? [Note: [Col. 0629D] “Having employed some novel distinction,” Rhen. and Obert.] But Christ Jesus alone, the new King of the ages, carried upon his shoulder both his new glory [Note: [Col. 0629D] “A new glory,” the same editors.] and his power and exaltation—the cross, that is—so that, in accordance with the preceding [Note: [Col. 0629D] “Earlier,” the same editors.] prophecy, the Lord might thereafter reign from the tree.

For concerning this tree God also intimates through Jeremiah what you would say: “Come, let us put wood into his bread, and destroy him from the land of the living, and his name shall no longer be remembered” (Jer. 11:19). Wood, of course, was put into his body. For this is how Christ disclosed it, calling his body bread, [Note: [Col. 0629D] “Calling his body bread.” He appears to allude to those words of the Evangelists and blessed Paul: “Jesus took bread,” etc., and said: “Take and eat; this is my body.” Thus this marginal annotation, “he calls his body bread,” would be truer than the one that has crept in from I know not whom, “the body into bread.” PAM.] whose body the prophet formerly represented under the figure of bread. [Note: [Col. 0629D] “Whose body the prophet formerly represented under the figure of bread.” In the book *On Prayer*: “Then also because his body is reckoned in the bread.” The same passage of Jeremiah is treated somewhat more explicitly in Book III *Against Marcion*. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0629D] “Announced,” Obert. and Semler.]

If you still seek a proclamation of the Lord’s cross, the twenty-first Psalm can now sufficiently satisfy you, since it contains the whole Passion of Christ, who already then sang of his glory: “They pierced,” he says, “my hands and my feet” (Ps. 21:17). This is the distinctive cruelty of the cross. And again, when he implored the Father’s help: “Save me,” he says, “from the lion’s mouth”—that is, surely, from death—“and my humility from the horns of unicorns” (Ps. 21:22), namely, [Col. 0629B] from the points of the cross, as we showed above. [Note: [Col. 0629D] “From the points of the cross.” By “points” he means what he called “horns” above. RIG.] Neither David himself nor any king of the Jews suffered this cross, lest you think that the passion of anyone other than him who alone was so conspicuously crucified by the people was being prophesied.

Now, even if the hardness of your heart rejects and mocks all these interpretations, we have proved that the prophesied death of Christ can suffice, so that, from the fact that the character of the death was not specified, [Col. 0629C] [Note: [Col. 0629D] “Specified—what kind of death,” Rhen. and Obert.] it may be understood to have occurred through the cross, and that the suffering of the cross was to be attributed to no other than the one whose death was proclaimed.

For I wish to demonstrate his death, Passion, and burial with a single utterance of Isaiah: “Because of the crimes,” he says, “of my people he was led to death, and I shall give the wicked for his burial, and the rich for his death; because he committed no crime, nor was deceit found in his mouth, and God willed to deliver his soul from death” (Isa. 53:8–10), etc. [Note: [Col. 0629D] “And God willed to deliver,” etc. He rendered this paraphrastically from what follows; for first the Septuagint has in Greek and Latin: “And the Lord wills to cleanse him from the wound”; and shortly afterward, “and the Lord wills to place the suffering of his soul into his hands.” He therefore interprets the wound and the suffering as death. PAM.] He also says further: “His burial was taken away from the midst” (ibid.). For he was not buried unless he was dead, nor was his burial taken away from the midst [Col. 0630A] [Note: [Col. 0629D] “From the midst. In what way unless,” etc., Obert. and Semler.] except through his resurrection. [Note: [Col. 0630D] “His” is absent from Pam., Rhen., and Obert.]

Finally he adds: “Therefore he himself shall have many as an inheritance, and shall divide the spoils of many” (Isa. 53:12). Who else could this be but the one who was born, as we showed above, because his soul was handed over to death? For once the cause of his favor was shown—namely, as repayment for the injury of death—it was shown at the same time that he would obtain these things because of his death, and thus, after death, would attain resurrection. [Note: [Col. 0630D] Obert. and Semler add “through.”]

For what occurred during his Passion, when midday was darkened, the prophet Amos announces, saying: “And it shall be on that day,” says the Lord, “that the sun will set at midday, and the day of light will grow dark over the earth; and I shall turn your feast days into mourning and all your songs into lamentation; and I shall put [Col. 0630B] sackcloth upon your loins and baldness upon every head; and I shall make it like the mourning for a beloved one, [Note: [Col. 0630D] “For a sinful one,” Obert. and Semler.] and those who are with him like a day of mourning” (Amos 8:9–10). [Note: [Col. 0630D] “The sun will set at midday.” He touches upon the prophecy of Amos, chapter 9; he also mentioned this darkening in chapter 21 of the *Apology*, speaking of the death of Christ the Lord: “At that same moment, the day, though the sun was marking the middle of its course, was withdrawn. An eclipse, certainly,” etc. We once used this testimony, under the name of Eusebius of Rome, in our observations, to prove to the Pre-Adamites that an eclipse—that is, an obscuration of the sun—occurred throughout the whole world. LE PR.]

Moses also prophesied at the beginning of the first month that you would do this, when the whole multitude of the children of Israel was to sacrifice the lamb at evening; [Note: [Col. 0630D] “Would sacrifice,” Pam., Rhen., and Obert.] and he foretold that you would eat the solemn observance of that day—that is, the Passover of unleavened bread—with bitterness; and he added that it was “the Lord’s Passover” (Exod. 12), that is, Christ’s Passion. This too was fulfilled in such a manner that you killed Christ on the first day of Unleavened Bread (Matt. 26), and, so that the prophecies might be fulfilled, the day hastened to bring on evening—that is, to produce darkness—which occurred at midday. [Note: [Col. 0630D] “Will prophesy,” Semler.] And thus God turned your feast days into mourning and your songs [Col. 0630C] into lamentation. For after Christ’s Passion, captivity and dispersion also befell you, as had been foretold through the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XI

For on account of these deserts of yours Ezekiel announces your future disaster—not only the disaster in this age, which has already occurred, but also that on the day of retribution, which will follow. From that disaster no one will be delivered unless he has been sealed by the Passion of Christ, whom you reject. For thus it is written:

“And the Lord said to me: ‘Son of man, have you seen what the elders of Israel are doing, each one [Col. 0631A] of them in darkness, each in his hidden chamber? For they have said: “The Lord does not see us; the Lord has abandoned the earth.”’ And he said to me: ‘Turn again, and you will see still greater crimes that these men commit.’ And he brought me to the threshold of the door of the Lord’s house that faces north, and behold, women were sitting there [Note: [Col. 0631D] “And mourning for Tammuz.” So it also stands in Greek, for which the standard Latin translator from the Hebrew renders “Adonis.” He appears, however, to have read the phrase twice, although in the Greek exemplars today it occurs only once. Then, both here and shortly afterward, where one reads, “Is it a small thing” (or, as he says presently, “a slight thing,” Greek μὴ μικρά) “for the house of Judah,” since the Greek reads “house,” I preferred to follow the manuscript reading. PAM.] and mourning for Tammuz. And the Lord said to me: ‘Son of man, have you seen? Is it a small thing for the house of Judah to commit the crimes they have committed? Yet you will see still greater inclinations on their part.’ And he brought me into the inner sanctuary of the Lord’s house, and behold, at the thresholds of the Lord’s temple, midway between the porch and the altar, there were about twenty-five [Note: [Col. 0631D] “Five” is absent from Rhen. and Obert.] men. They had turned their backs toward the Lord’s temple and their faces toward the east; these men were worshiping the sun. And he said to me: ‘Do you see, son of man? [Col. 0631B] Is it a slight thing for the house of Judah to commit the crimes they have committed here? [Note: [Col. 0631D] “These men,” Rhen. and Obert.] For they have filled up their impieties, and behold, they are as though jeering. I shall act in my indignation; my eye shall not spare, nor shall I have mercy. They will cry into my ears with a loud voice, and I shall not hear them, nor shall I have mercy’” (Ezek. 8:12–18).

[Note: [Col. 0631D] “And he cried into my ears.” This is indeed a continuation of the prophet Ezekiel’s words, but the beginning of chapter 9. Moreover, the author more correctly translates πέλυξ as “double axe”; but the Greek today does not contain “of dispersion,” but rather what the Latin Septuagint translator renders “of extermination,” and Jerome, translating from the Hebrew, “of slaughter.” PAM.]

“And he cried into my ears with a loud voice, saying: ‘The vengeance upon this city has drawn near, and each man had the instruments of extermination in his hand.’ And behold, six men were coming by the way of the upper gate, which faced north, and each man’s double axe of dispersion was in his hand. And one man in their midst was clothed in a full-length robe, with a sapphire belt upon his loins. And they entered and stood near the bronze altar; and the glory of the God of Israel rose from the cherubim upon which it had been, [Note: [Col. 0631D] “They had been,” the same editors.] [Col. 0631C] into the open court of the house.” [Note: [Col. 0631D] “Into the open court of the house.” *Subdival* stands for *subdivale*; it is the same as *subdivum*. For the glosses give *subdivum* as ὑπαίθριον (“open to the sky”) and *subdival* as αἴθριον (“open court”), while those Greek words signify the same thing, namely, something bright and open. The *subdivum* of a house is the open space outside the roof. Hesychius says, αἴθρον ὑπὸ τὸν ἀέρα ποιμανεῖ (“in the open air he will pasture beneath the sky” [wording uncertain]). LE PR.]

“And he called the man who was clothed in the full-length robe, who had the belt upon his loins, and the Lord said to him: [Note: [Col. 0632D] ‘Pass through the midst of Jerusalem.’ He also cites this scriptural passage concerning the sign Tau below, in Book III *Against Marcion*. LE PR.] ‘Pass through the midst of Jerusalem and write the sign Tau upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over all the crimes being committed in their midst.’ And to the others, within hearing, he said: ‘Go after him into the city and cut them down; do not let your eyes spare, and have no pity on old man or virgin; kill all the little children and women, so that they may be utterly destroyed. But do not approach any upon whom is the sign Tau. And begin from my holy places’” (Ezek. 9:1–6).

[Col. 0632A] The mystery of this sign was proclaimed in various ways: in it life was being prepared in advance for human beings, yet the Jews would not believe in it. [Note: [Col. 0632D] “As Moses foretold in Exodus.” Since the words of Scripture he cites occur not in Exodus but in Deuteronomy 28, Tertullian’s memory has failed him here too, unless, against the authority of all the manuscripts, we should read “in Deuteronomy.” LE PR.] Thus Moses foretold in Exodus, saying: “You will be cast out of the land into which you are entering, and among those nations you will have no rest. There will be no firm standing for the sole of your foot; and God will give you a weary heart, a wasting soul, and failing eyes, so that they do not see; and your life will hang upon wood before your eyes, and you will not believe your life” (Deut. 28:64–65).

Therefore, since the prophecy was fulfilled through his advent—that is, through the birth we mentioned above—and through the Passion we have clearly declared, for that reason Daniel also said that vision and prophet were to be sealed, because Christ is the seal of all the prophets, fulfilling everything that had formerly been announced concerning him. For after his advent and his Passion there is now neither vision nor prophet. Hence he says with the utmost firmness that his advent seals vision and prophecy.

Accordingly, by showing both the number of years and the completed period of sixty-two and one-half weeks, we have proved that Christ then came—that is, was born; and within the seven and one-half weeks [Note: [Col. 0632D] “And seven and one-half weeks”—namely, the period. This reading is necessary, not “and four,” as the text was most corruptly read; this is more than sufficiently clear above in chapter 8, and not only once. PAM.] that are separated off after the cutting-off of the former weeks, we have shown that Christ suffered. Thus, when the seventy weeks had been completed, the city was destroyed, and sacrifice and anointing thereafter ceased.

For the present it is sufficient that our exposition of Christ has proceeded thus far, proving him to be such as he was announced to be, also from this agreement of the Scriptures, which [Note: [Col. 0632D] “Which,” Pam., Rhen., and Obert.] we have set forth against the Jews on the basis of the judgment of the greater part. For they cannot call into doubt or deny the texts we produce; so that from this too they cannot deny that later events correspond to the divine Scriptures, since the things foretold as future after Christ are recognized as fulfilled. For the divine arrangement would not have been found carried out [Note: [Col. 0632D] “For the divine arrangement would not have been found carried out” is absent from Semler and Obert.] unless he had come after whom the things announced were to be carried out—the same things that are proved to have been completed. [Note: [Col. 0632D] “Have been,” Obert. and Semler.]

## CHAPTER XII

Look upon all the nations, thereafter emerging from the abyss of human error toward the Lord God, the Creator, [Note: [Col. 0631D] “It,” the same editors.] [Col. 0633A] and toward his Christ, who is God; [Note: [Col. 0633D] “And toward his Christ, who is God.” Thus from the frequently cited Book III *Against Marcion*, in place of which the text previously had only “and his Christ.” Moreover, whether Christ was God will provide an occasion for fuller treatment, either there or elsewhere, against certain sectarians of our own age who are not afraid to deny it. PAM.] [Note: [Col. 0633C] “God” is absent from Semler and Obert.] and, if you dare, deny that the prophet spoke truly. Immediately the Father’s promise confronts you in the Psalms, saying: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. 2:7–8).

You will not be able to call him the son of David rather than the Christ, nor to say that the ends of the earth were promised to David—who reigned within Judea alone—rather than to Christ, who has already taken the whole world by faith in his Gospel. As he says through Isaiah: “Behold, I have given you as a covenant for my people, as a light to the nations, to open the eyes of the blind”—that is, of those in error—“to release the bound from their chains,” that is, to free them from transgressions, “and those sitting in darkness”—namely, the darkness of ignorance—“from the prison-house,” that is, from death (Isa. 42:6–7). If these things come about through Christ, they will not have been prophesied concerning any other than the one through whom [Note: [Col. 0633D] “Anyone,” Semler.] we see them accomplished.

## CHAPTER XIII
Therefore, since the children of Israel affirm that we are in error by accepting Christ, who has already come, let us establish against them from the Scriptures themselves that the Christ who was proclaimed has already come—even though we have already proved, from the chronology proclaimed by Daniel, that the Christ who was announced has come. For he had to be born in Bethlehem of Judah; thus it is written in the prophet:

> And you, Bethlehem, are not least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come forth a ruler who shall shepherd my people Israel (Mic. 5:1).

[Note: [Col. 0633D] “And you, Bethlehem, are not least.” Thus from the manuscript and the Greek sources of Blessed Matthew, in place of “of Judah”; likewise “shall shepherd” instead of “shall rule,” for in Greek it is ποιμανεῖ, “shall shepherd.” Although the Old Latin translator renders it “shall rule,” both there and in the final chapter of John the same author uses the same word as here; it is therefore evident that in antiquity the Fathers understood “to shepherd” in the sense of “to rule.” This is worth noting against those who wish all governing authority to be removed from the Church. What follows, moreover, appears to contain a hyperbaton. Whether a little later one reads “foreigners,” as in the printed editions, or “outsiders,” as in the manuscript, the sense is the same; for above he translated it as “aliens.” PAM.]

But if the one who was announced as the ruler destined to proceed from the tribe of Judah and from Bethlehem has not yet been born—for he must proceed from the tribe of Judah and from Bethlehem—yet we observe that today no one of the stock of Israel remains in the city of Bethlehem, and furthermore that it has been forbidden for any Jew to reside within the boundaries of that region, so that this too might be fulfilled through the prophet:

> Your land is desolate; your cities have been burned with fire—

that is, what happened to them in time of war—

> foreigners will devour your territory before your eyes, and it will be desolate and overthrown by alien peoples (Isa. 1:7).

And elsewhere it is said through the prophet:

> You will see the king in splendor—

that is, Christ performing mighty works in the glory of God the Father—

> and your eyes will see the land from afar (Isa. 33:17).

This has been permitted to you in accordance with your deserts after the conquest of Jerusalem: being forbidden to enter your land, you may see it only with your eyes from afar.

> Your soul, he says, will meditate upon fear (ibid., 18),

namely at the time when they suffered their own destruction. How, then, will a ruler be born from Judea, and how will he proceed from Bethlehem, as the divine books of the prophets announce, when to this very day no one at all of Israel has been left there from whose lineage Christ could be born?

For if, according to the Jews, he has not yet come, when he begins to come, from where will he be anointed?

[Note: [Col. 0634C] “Christ. According to the Jews … begins.” Thus Oberthür and Semler.—“Could be born? Christ, according to,” etc., Latinus.]

[Note: [Col. 0634D] “For the Law commanded,” etc. I do not know to what passage he is alluding, unless perhaps to Deuteronomy 28, and, in his customary paraphrastic manner, he extracted this statement from several verses; or perhaps he used another edition, whether Aquila’s or Theodotion’s. In that case, “commanded” would have to be understood as “foretold.” PAM.]

For the Law commanded that in captivity it was not permissible to prepare the anointing oil of royalty. But if there is now no anointing among them either, as Daniel prophesied—for he says:

> The anointing shall be destroyed (Dan. 9:27)—

then there is now no anointing there, because there is no temple either, in which was kept the horn from which kings were anointed.

[Note: [Col. 0634C] Semler does not add “no,” omitting “either” as well.]

[Note: [Col. 0634D] “Nor the temple in which was the horn.” He alludes to 1 Kings 1:39: “And Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the tabernacle and anointed Solomon”; from this it is inferred that it had been kept in the temple. PAM.]

If, therefore, there is no anointing, from where will the ruler who is to be born in Bethlehem be anointed? Or how will he proceed from Bethlehem, when there is no one at all of the stock of Israel in Bethlehem?

[Note: [Col. 0634D] Others read “seed.”]

Let us therefore show once again that, according to the prophets, Christ has already come, has suffered, has already been received into heaven, and will come from there in accordance with the proclamations of the prophets.
