For we read in Daniel that after his advent that very city was destined to be destroyed, and we recognize that this is what happened. Scripture says:

> Thus both the city and the sanctuary shall be destroyed together with the ruler (ibid.),

undoubtedly the one who was to proceed from Bethlehem and from the tribe of Judah. Hence it is also manifest that the city was to be destroyed at the same time as its ruler was destined to suffer in it, according to the writings of the prophets, who say:

> I stretched out my hands all day long to a defiant people who contradict me, who walk in a way that is not good, but after their own sins (Isa. 65:2).

[Note: [Col. 0634D] “According to the writings of the prophets.” Again he adduces Scriptures in which it was foretold—as Blessed Cyprian writes in imitation of this passage, book II *Against the Jews*, chapter 20—that the Jews would fasten him to the cross. PAM.]

And in the Psalms he says:

> They pierced my hands and feet; they counted all my bones. But they themselves gazed upon me and saw me;

and:

> In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink (Ps. 21:17–18; 68:22).

David did not suffer these things, such that he might rightly be thought to have spoken them about himself, but Christ, who was crucified, did.

[Note: [Col. 0635D] “But Christ, who was crucified.” That barbarous nation of the Jews demanded by the violent force of their votes that Christ the Lord be delivered to the cross, as in chapter 21 of the *Apology*. On this subject Cyril of Alexandria says in Homily IV, *On the Paschal Feast*: σταυρῷ προσηλώκασιν οἱ πάντολμοι τῶν Ἰουδαίων λαοί, καὶ πᾶν εἶδος ἐπενεγκόντες κακίας τε ὁμοῦ καὶ ἀτιμίας, θανάτῳ παραδεδώκασιν: “The utterly audacious people of the Jews fastened him to the cross and, after subjecting him to every kind both of wickedness and of dishonor, delivered him over to death.” LE PR.]

Hands and feet, moreover, are not pierced except in the case of one who is suspended from wood. Hence David himself also used to say that the Lord would reign from the wood (Ps. 95:10); for elsewhere too the prophet proclaims the fruit of this wood, saying:

> The earth has yielded its blessings (Ps. 66:7).

That earth, assuredly, was the virgin earth, not yet watered by rains nor made fruitful by showers, from which the first man was then fashioned, and from which Christ has now been born according to the flesh from a virgin.

[Note: [Col. 0636D] “That virgin earth.” Irenaeus also speaks thus: γῆ παρθένος, “virgin earth.” SEML.]

And:

> The tree, he says, has brought forth its fruit (Joel 2:22).

Not that tree in paradise which brought death to the first-formed human beings, but the wood of Christ’s passion, from which the life hanging there was not believed by you (Deut. 28:66).

For this wood was then present in mystery when Moses sweetened the bitter water, from which the people who were dying of thirst in the wilderness drank and revived (Exod. 15:23–26). So too we, who have been drawn out of the calamities of the present age in which we dwelt, and who were dying of thirst—that is, deprived of the drink of the divine word—have drunk the water of baptism sweetened by the wood of Christ’s passion, or the water which consists in faith in him, and have revived.

[Note: [Col. 0635D] Oberthür and Semler read: “given the divine word to drink.”]

From this faith Israel fell away, according to Jeremiah, who says:

> Send and inquire very diligently whether such things have been done. Will nations change their gods? Yet those are not gods. But my people have exchanged their glory for that from which they will derive no benefit. Heaven was appalled at this (Jer. 2:10–12).

And how and when was it appalled? Undoubtedly when Christ suffered:

> And it shuddered, he says, exceedingly, and the sun was darkened at midday (Amos 8:9).

And when did it shudder exceedingly, if not at Christ’s passion, when the earth too trembled, the veil of the temple was torn, and the tombs were broken open (Matt. 27:51)?

> For my people have committed these two evils: they have abandoned me, he says, the fountain of the water of life, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that will not be able to hold water (Jer. 2:13).

Undoubtedly, by not accepting Christ, the fountain of the water of life, they began to possess broken cisterns—that is, synagogues scattered among the nations—in which the Holy Spirit no longer dwells as he formerly dwelt in the temple before the advent of Christ, who is the true temple of God.

For the prophet Isaiah had also said that they would suffer this thirst for the divine Spirit:

> Behold, those who serve me will eat, but you will hunger; those who serve me will drink, but you will thirst, and from affliction of spirit you will howl. For you will leave your name for my chosen ones to use as a designation, but the Lord will put you to death. Yet for those who serve me a new name will be given, which will be blessed upon the earth (Isa. 65:13–16).

[Note: [Col. 0635D] The same editors read “unto affliction.”]

The mystery of this wood is further celebrated, as we read, in the Books of Kings. For when the sons of the prophets were cutting wood with axes beside the river Jordan, the iron flew off and sank in the river. Then, when the prophet Elisha arrived, the sons of the prophets asked him to retrieve from the river the iron that had sunk. Elisha took a piece of wood and threw it into the place where the iron had sunk; immediately the iron floated, while the wood sank, and the sons of the prophets recovered it (2 Kings 6:4–7). From this they understood that the spirit of Elijah had been manifested in him.

[Note: [Col. 0636D] Others read “into which.”]

What could be more manifest than the mystery of this wood? The hardness of this age, sunk in the depths of error, is delivered in baptism by the wood of Christ—that is, by his passion—so that what had once been lost through the tree in Adam might be restored through the wood of Christ.

We, therefore, who have succeeded to the place of the prophets, endure today in this age the things that the prophets always suffered on account of divine religion. For they stoned some, drove others into exile, and delivered still more to be put to death—something they cannot deny.

[Note: [Col. 0636D] Wouwer reads: “We, assuredly.”]

Isaac, the son of Abraham, himself also carried this wood for his own sacrifice when God had commanded that he be made an offering (Gen. 22:6). But because these things were mysteries reserved for fulfillment in the times of Christ, Isaac was spared together with the wood, while a ram caught by its horns in a thicket was offered; and Christ in his own time carried the wood upon his shoulders, fastened to the horns of the cross, with a crown of thorns encircling his head.

For he had to be made a sacrifice for all nations, he who was:

> led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth (Isa. 53:7).

For when Pilate questioned him, he said nothing (John 19:9):

> For in his humiliation his judgment was taken away. But who shall recount his generation (Isa. 53:8)?

[Note: [Col. 0636D] “But who shall recount his generation?” There is no doubt that this is how it must be read, in accordance with all editions of Isaiah, and not “recounted,” especially since Blessed Cyprian also reads it thus in book II *Against the Jews*, chapter 15, and Tertullian below in book III *Against Marcion*. PAM.]

For absolutely no human being was privy to Christ’s generation at his conception, when the Virgin Mary was found pregnant by the word of God.

> And because his life would be taken away from the earth (ibid.).

For after his resurrection from the dead, which took place on the third day, heaven received him, in accordance with the prophecy delivered by Hosea in this form:

> Before dawn they will arise to me, saying: Let us go and return to the Lord God, for he himself will rescue and deliver us; after two days, on the third day (Hos. 6:1–3)—

[Note: [Col. 0636D] “After two days, on the third day.” We have corrected the punctuation in accordance with the Vulgate reading, although all the printed editions begin another phrase with the words “After two days,” as though Christ had been received into heaven on the third day, rather than after the completion of forty days following his resurrection (Acts 1:3, 9). We were moved to make this correction by the author’s meaning, since he employs this prophecy of Hosea to demonstrate that Christ’s resurrection occurred three days after his death. EDD.]

—that is, his glorious resurrection from the earth into heaven, when heaven received him, whence the Spirit himself had also come to the Virgin. Neither his birth nor his passion was recognized by the Jews.

Therefore, since the Jews still maintain that their Christ—whom we have proved in so many ways to have come—has not yet come, let the Jews recognize the fate that it was foretold they would suffer after Christ’s advent because of the impiety with which they both despised and killed him.

[Note: [Col. 0637C] “Their” is absent from Rhenanus and Oehler.]

[Note: [Col. 0637D] “It was foretold that they would suffer because of their impiety.” The author uses this epithet more than once; for in chapter 3 of *On the Shows* he says: “For if at that time he called the few Jews an assembly of the impious,” etc. Blessed Augustine also uses the characterization “impious” for the Jews in Epistle 54. Blessed John Chrysostom attributes ἀσέβειαν, “impiety,” to them in Oration II against them, and παράνομον πολιτείαν, “a lawless manner of life.” Nearly all the ancient Fathers do likewise, as does the Council in Trullo, canon 1, where it speaks of Nestorius: καὶ τὴν Ἰουδαϊκὴν ἀνανεοῦντος δυσσέβειαν, “and renewing Jewish impiety.” LE PR.]

First, from the day when, according to Isaiah’s saying:

> A man cast away his abominations of gold and silver, which they had made for the worship of vain things and owls (Isa. 2:20)—

that is, from the time when the nations, namely we ourselves, cast away our idols after the truth had been made clear through Christ—

[Note: [Col. 0637C] Oberthür and Semler read: “our hearts having been enlightened through the truth of Christ”; the Fulda manuscript reads “our hearts having been enlightened.”]

let the Jews observe that what follows was also fulfilled.

[Note: [Col. 0637C] Oberthür and Semler punctuate: “the idols. Let the Jews observe,” etc.]

For the Lord Sabaoth removed from the Jews and from Jerusalem, among other things:

> the wise architect (Isa. 3:1, 3),

who builds the Church, the temple of God, the holy city, and the house of the Lord. For from that time the grace of God ceased among them.

[Note: [Col. 0637D] “For from that time the grace of God ceased among them.” The Jews, once God’s beloved people, fell from grace because of the stubborn impiety and cruelty that they exercised against the Redeemer of the whole world. In chapter 18 of the *Apology* they are called by this author “God’s household nation.” Christians, however, were grafted and inoculated into this wild tree. LE PR.]

And the clouds were commanded not to rain upon the vineyard of Sorek (Isa. 5:6)—that is, the heavenly benefits were commanded not to come upon the house of Israel. For it had produced thorns (ibid., 4), with which it crowned Christ; and not righteousness but an outcry (ibid., 7), by which it extorted his condemnation to the cross. Thus, when the former gifts of grace had been withdrawn, the Law and the Prophets lasted until John (Luke 16:16), and the pool of Bethesda (John 5:2), which until Christ’s advent had healed Israel’s infirmities, thereafter ceased from its benefits, when, through the persistence of their fury, the Lord’s name was blasphemed because of them, as it is written:

> Because of you the name of God is blasphemed among the nations (Isa. 52:5; Ezek. 36:20).

[Note: [Col. 0637C] Junius reads “Bethesda.”]

[Note: [Col. 0637C] Oberthür and Semler read “good health.”]

[Note: [Col. 0637C] Junius punctuates: “from its benefits. Thereafter.”]

[Note: [Col. 0637C] “From” is absent from Rhenanus and Oberthür.]

For the defamation began with them, and the intervening period extended from Tiberius to Vespasian.

[Note: [Col. 0638C] “For the defamation began with them.” So too in book I *To the Nations*, chapter 14, where he likewise says of the Jews: “For what other race is the seedbed of the slanders against us?” RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0638C] Latinus reads “began.”]

When they had committed these things and had failed to understand that Christ was to be found in the time of their visitation, their land was made desolate and their cities burned with fire, while strangers devoured their territory before their eyes:

> The daughter of Zion was left like a watchtower in a vineyard or like a hut in a cucumber field (Isa. 1:7–8).

For Israel did not know the Lord, and the people did not understand him, but rather abandoned him and provoked the Holy One of Israel to indignation (ibid., 3–4).

Thus also the conditional threat of the sword—

> If you are unwilling and do not obey, the sword will devour you (ibid., 20)—

proved that Christ was the one through their refusal to hear whom they perished.

[Note: [Col. 0638C] Rhenanus and Oberthür read “Likewise.”]

[Note: [Col. 0638C] Oberthür and Semler read: “will devour you. From this we prove that Christ was the sword.”]

In the Psalm he also asks the Father for their dispersion, saying:

> Scatter them by your power (Ps. 58:12).

[Note: [Col. 0638D] “He asks for their dispersion,” etc. No one doubts that they were scattered because of the abomination of the punishment and disgrace that they inflicted upon Christ the Lord. They were not only scattered and wandering but also hated by all, to such an extent that the council cited above, canon 11, forbids the following: “Let no cleric or layman eat unleavened bread among the Jews, associate with them, summon them in illness, receive medicine from them, or bathe with them in a bathhouse. If anyone presumes to do this, if he is a cleric, let him be deposed; if a layman, deprived of communion.” LE PR.]

And again through Isaiah he prays for their burning:

> Because of me, he says, these things have happened to you; you shall lie down in anguish (Isa. 50:11).

Therefore, since it is proclaimed that the Jews would suffer these things because of Christ, and since we find that they have suffered them and see that they remain in dispersion, it is manifest that these things happened to the Jews because of Christ, the meaning of the Scriptures agreeing with the outcome of events and the sequence of times.

[Note: [Col. 0638C] Junius reads “sequence.”]

Or, if Christ has not yet come—the one because of whom it was proclaimed that they would suffer these things—then they will suffer them when he comes. And where then is the daughter of Zion to be abandoned, when she does not exist today? Where are the cities to be burned, when they already lie burned in heaps of rubble? Where is the nation to be dispersed, when it is already in exile? Restore the condition of Judea that Christ is to find, and then contend that another Christ is coming.

## CHAPTER XIV

Now learn, from the superabundance of your error, the course of Christ’s leadership. We say that two conditions of Christ were shown by the prophets, marking beforehand the same number of his advents: one in humility, namely the first, when he was destined to be:

> led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer, voiceless, so he did not open his mouth (Isa. 53:7),

without even comeliness of appearance:

> For we proclaim concerning him, he says, that he is like a little child, like a root in thirsty ground; and there was in him neither form nor glory. And we saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty, but his appearance was dishonored, deficient in comparison with the sons of men—a man under affliction, knowing how to bear infirmity (ibid., 2–4).

[Note: [Col. 0638C] The same editors read “marked beforehand.”]

[Note: [Col. 0638D] “And like a lamb before its shearer.” The ancients employed this manner of speaking with remarkable effect—“sheep,” “beast,” “lamb”—when speaking of Christ’s betrayal. The Council in Trullo, canon 1, says: ὁ θεὸς θυόμενος, “God being sacrificed.” LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0639D] “Without even comeliness of appearance.” This is what he said in *On Patience*: “And moreover he is an object of reproach against himself.” RIG.—Rigaltius understands these words in such a way that he believes them to mean the same as the statement in *On Patience*: “And moreover he is an object of reproach against himself.” But in my judgment, in that passage understand those words as referring to Christ’s silence, which was imputed to him as a fault, as though he were a man of little dignity and distinction who did not dare to speak; or, if you prefer, as referring to his face, covered and bruised with blood and blows. LE PR.]

Thus he was appointed by the Father as a stone of stumbling (Isa. 8:14), and, having been made by him a little lower than the angels (Ps. 8:6), he declares himself to be a worm and not a man, the reproach of mankind and the rejection of the people (Ps. 21:7).

These tokens of lowliness belong to the first advent, just as those of exaltation belong to the second. When that advent occurs, he will no longer be a stone of stumbling or a rock of offense, but the chief cornerstone, taken up after his rejection and exalted to consummation (Isa. 28:16); and indeed that stone in Daniel, cut from the mountain, which will crush and grind to pieces the image of the kingdoms of this age (Dan. 2:34ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0639D] “Just as those of exaltation belong to the second.” The second advent of Christ must not be judged in the same way as the first. In the first he assumed the form of a servant and, everywhere taking upon himself human weakness, was exposed to injuries and torments of every kind. In the second, however, he reveals himself as the Son of God and, by the excellence of his glory, raises up from contempt the humbler condition beneath which he was once overwhelmed. LE PR.]

Concerning this second advent the same Daniel said:

> And behold, one coming with the clouds of heaven like a son of man came as far as the Ancient of Days and stood in his sight. And those who stood by brought him forward; and royal authority was given to him, and all the nations of the earth according to their peoples, and every glory, will serve him. His authority is eternal and will not be taken away, and his kingdom will not be corrupted (Dan. 7:13–14).

[Note: [Col. 0639C] Semler and Oehler read “of the same.”]

[Note: [Col. 0639C] Franeker reads “led him away.”]

Then, assuredly, he will possess an honorable appearance and unfailing beauty beyond the sons of men:

> For you are distinguished in beauty beyond the sons of men. Grace has been poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever. Gird your sword around your thigh, O mighty one, in your splendor and beauty (Ps. 44:3–5).

For the Father, after making him a little lower than the angels, subsequently crowned him with glory and honor and subjected all things beneath his feet (Ps. 8:6–8; Heb. 2:7).

Then they will recognize the one whom they pierced, and the tribes will beat their breasts, tribe by tribe (Zech. 12:10; John 19:37), precisely because they did not recognize him previously, when he was placed in the humility of the human condition. Jeremiah says:

> And he is a man, and who will recognize him? (Jer. 17:7, according to the Septuagint).

[Note: [Col. 0639C] “And” is absent from Semler and Oehler.]

For Isaiah too says:

> Who shall recount his generation?

Thus also in Zechariah 12, in his own person—indeed, even in the mystery of his very name—the true high priest of the Father, Christ Jesus, is portrayed in a twofold condition corresponding to his two advents.

[Note: [Col. 0639C] Semler and Oehler insert “he says.”]

[Note: [Col. 0639C] The same editors read “most true.”]

[Note: [Col. 0639D] “Jesus” is absent from Semler and Oehler.]

At the first he is clothed in filthy garments—that is, in the indignity of passible and mortal flesh—while the devil opposes him, namely as the instigator of Judas the betrayer, who had also tempted him after his baptism. Then, stripped of his former filth, he is adorned with a long robe, a mitre, and a clean turban, signifying the second advent, because he is shown to have obtained glory and honor.

[Note: [Col. 0640C] The same editors read “filth.”]

[Note: [Col. 0640C] The same editors read “a clean turban.”]

Nor will you be able to call him the son of Jehozadak, who was never adorned with any filthy garment but was always adorned in priestly vestments (Zech. 6:11), nor was he ever deprived of the priestly office.

[Note: [Col. 0640C] The same editors read “Joseph.”]

Rather, this Jesus is Christ, the high priest of God the Father, who at his first advent came in human form and capable of suffering, in humility extending even to the passion. He himself was also made in every respect an offering for us all; and after his resurrection he was clothed in the long robe and named the priest forever (Ps. 109:4; Heb. 5:6) of God the Father.

Thus too I shall interpret the two goats that were offered at the fast (Lev. 16). Do not those two also show both stages of the Christ who has already come? They were equal and similar, because of the same appearance of the Lord, who will not come in a different form, since he must be recognized by those who also injured him.

[Note: [Col. 0640C] The same editors read “because he must be recognized.”]

One of them, however, was wrapped in scarlet, accursed, spat upon, maltreated, pierced, and cast out by the people beyond the city to destruction, marked by the manifest emblems of Christ’s passion.

[Note: [Col. 0640C] Semler reads “marked by emblems.”]

For Christ was clothed in a scarlet garment, spat upon, afflicted with every insult, and crucified outside the city.

[Note: [Col. 0640D] “Who was clothed in a scarlet garment.” The scarlet garment is the same as a purple or blood-colored garment, dyed with the grain of the kermes insect; that color is also the color of slaughter. Hence, to demonstrate Christ’s most bitter punishment, he calls the garment both blood-spattered and scarlet. In chapter 4 of *On the Pallium*, this color is called “Galatian red,” because that insect is produced in the greatest abundance in Galatia. LE PR.]

The other, however, was offered for sins and given solely to the priests of the temple for food. It signified the marks of the second manifestation, in which the priests of the spiritual temple—that is, the Church—having been cleansed from all sins, would enjoy, as it were, a certain distribution of the Lord’s grace, while all others fasted from salvation.

[Note: [Col. 0640D] Franeker reads “having been cleansed”; others read “to those having been cleansed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0640D] “The priests of the spiritual temple, that is, the Church.” He calls Christians “churches”; having been cleansed from all sins through Christ, they are priests of the spiritual temple. RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0640D] “As though by a distribution of the Lord’s gracious bounty.” He signifies the Eucharist, given to the churches—that is, to the Christian faithful—as a distribution and as food. RIG.—*Visceratio*, as Rhenanus noted in the margin, was a distribution of meat customarily made either at a solemn sacrifice or at the funeral of some distinguished person. PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0641B] “While all others fasted from salvation”—namely the pagans and unbelievers. RIG.]

Therefore, since the first advent was proclaimed as being both obscured by numerous figures and cast down in every deformity, whereas the second was proclaimed as manifest and worthy of God, they looked only to the advent that they could readily both understand and believe—that is, the second, which is attended by honor and glory. Thus it is not without reason that they were deceived concerning the less worthy, or certainly the more obscure advent—that is, the first.

[Note: [Col. 0641B] “And in every deformity.” Rhenanus remarks, both here and below in book III *Against Marcion*, that he uses “deformity” in the sense of ugliness, just as a little earlier he used “comely” in the sense of beautiful. Above, however, when he said in *To Scapula*, “How many honorable men,” I noted there that “honorable men” means men held in honor. PAM.]

And so to this very day they deny that their Christ has come, because he did not come in exaltation, while they are unaware that he was first to come in humility.

For the present, it is enough to have traced the course of Christ thus far in these matters, whereby he is proved to have been such as he was announced to be. From this agreement of the divine Scriptures we may now understand that the things proclaimed as destined to occur after Christ should also be believed to have been fulfilled according to the divine arrangement. For if the one after whose coming they were to be fulfilled had not come, the things proclaimed as destined to occur at his advent could in no way have happened.

[Note: [Col. 0641B] Semler and Oberthür read “would have come.”]

Therefore, if you see all the nations emerging thereafter from the depths of human error toward God the Creator and his Christ, you do not dare deny that it was prophesied.

[Note: [Col. 0641B] Semler and Oehler add “which.”]

For even if you denied it, the Father’s promise in the Psalms would immediately confront you, as we have already stated beforehand:

> You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession (Ps. 2:7–8).

Nor will you be able, with respect to this proclamation, to claim Solomon, David’s son, rather than to declare Christ the Son of God; nor to claim that the ends of the earth were promised to David’s son, who reigned only within Judea, rather than to Christ, the Son of God, who has already illuminated the whole world with the rays of his gospel.

[Note: [Col. 0642B] “Declare” is absent from other editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0642B] “Who has already illuminated the whole world,” etc. Although at his first advent he appeared in a contemptible condition, he will nevertheless appear as king at his second; and all kings, sovereigns, and emperors will worship the cross, which had been a mark of disgrace. For he is the King of kings and Lord of lords; and elsewhere: “Let all nations worship him,” etc. Just as it had been foretold that he would come, so too that he would reign. If, therefore, as he proves against the Jews—and as is most certain to all Christians—he has come, so that the prophecy of the prophets may be fulfilled, he also reigns over the whole world. LE PR.]

Finally, an eternal throne belongs more properly to Christ, the Son of God, than to Solomon, a temporal king who reigned over Israel alone. For today the nations that did not know Christ invoke him, and today the peoples that formerly did not know him flee for refuge to Christ. You cannot contend that something is still future when you see it taking place. Either deny that these things were prophesied, though they are seen before your eyes; or deny that they have been fulfilled, though they are read in Scripture. Or, if you deny neither, they will have been fulfilled in the one concerning whom they were prophesied.

[Col. 0641]

# THE BOOK OF QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN, *ON THE SOUL* (C)

## [SUMMARY]

[Col. 0641D] Tertullian had written, as he himself says, a book against Hermogenes on the provenance or origin of the soul. That book, now lost, is mentioned, insofar as can be determined, in the following section. In the present treatise, however, the Author—by now a Montanist—contends against the philosophers concerning the condition of the soul and the remaining questions pertaining to it; nevertheless, Tertullian himself has interspersed false principles and introduced various errors.

**I.** First of all, he teaches that the immortality of the soul must be learned not from Socrates but from God.

**II.** For although many things are suggested by nature, or were even drawn from the prophets, the philosophers nevertheless handed down many falsehoods mingled with truths.

**III.** If only no heresy existed, there would be no need at all to enter into conflict with the philosophers, the patriarchs of the heretics; nor would it then be necessary to demolish those things by which heretics are captivated by philosophy, or to repel those things by which the faithful are shaken by heresy. [Col. 0642D]

**IV.** Then, approaching his subject, he first declares against Plato that the soul was born and made, since it came from the breath of God.

**V.** He states that several philosophers also asserted the soul to be a body, although Aristotle and Plato deprived it of corporeality.

**VI.** Following that paradox here as well, the Author refutes rather frivolously the arguments by which the Platonists maintained that the soul is incorporeal.

**VII.** Indeed, he improperly attempts to prove the corporeality of the soul from the Gospel.

[Col. 0643A] **VIII.** He responds in turn to other arguments of the Platonists.

**IX.** What is more, he does not shrink from assigning a form even to the immortal soul, and one of an airy and luminous color.

**X.** He next teaches, more correctly, that soul and spirit are one, as are living and breathing; and, on the basis of what pertains to the state of faith, he defines the soul as simple, in accordance with Plato.

**XI.** Yet the soul is called “spirit” in such a way that it is neither the Spirit of God—which Hermogenes appeared to believe—nor endowed with some indefinable “spiritual seed” of the Valentinians.

**XII.** Likewise, the mind is not separated from the soul, since it is nothing other than the soul’s impulse or equipment by which it understands. He maintains this against Anaxagoras and Aristotle, the former of whom denied that the mind could be mingled, and the latter that it could be affected. [Col. 0643B]

**XIII.** He also proves this from the fact that preeminence is attributed to the soul and not to the mind; moreover, God always addresses the soul, not the mind.

**XIV.** When the soul is divided into parts by Plato or others, different powers, efficacies, and operations are to be understood, as Aristotle too indicated concerning some of them, since he himself, together with most others, recognized the soul’s unity.

**XV.** Meanwhile, Christians too recognize with Plato and Aristotle the *hegemonikon* (ἡγεμονικόν)—that is, the supreme faculty of understanding in the soul—contrary to the opinions of Asclepiades and Dicaearchus; and they locate it in the innermost chamber of the heart.

**XVI.** It likewise belongs to the faith that Plato divides the soul into the rational and irrational; yet in such a way that the rational is attributed to its original nature, while the irrational is attributed to transgression. Nevertheless, he does not approve the division of the irrational faculty into the irascible and the concupiscible, since both are also applicable to Christ and to a rational soul. [Col. 0643C]

**XVII.** Plato and the Academics are also rejected in this respect: they declare the sensory activity of the five senses to be irrational. For it is not permissible to call those senses into doubt, lest their trustworthiness in Christ also become a matter for deliberation.

**XVIII.** Nor should the heretics be heard who, just as Plato did with his Ideas, make intellectual things the truths themselves, but sensory things mere images of truth. Rather, the soul perceives bodily things through the body just as it understands incorporeal things through the mind—yet in such a way that it also perceives when it understands. [Col. 0643D]

**XIX.** Thus understanding is always present in the soul, just as the soul’s other natural properties are.

**XX.** Although the soul is uniform, it is nevertheless multiform in the production of dispositions, according to the condition of climate and soil, the character of occupation and concern, the occurrence of circumstances, the freedom of accidents, and even the health of the body—to say nothing of the necessity of fate, which he treated under its own heading.

**XXI.** Accordingly, contrary to the opinion of the Valentinians, the soul was also capable of change through the power of free choice, as he had already demonstrated against Marcion and Hermogenes.

[Col. 0644A] **XXII.** The soul is therefore defined as born from the breath of God; immortal; corporeal—behold, once again the Author’s paradox; endowed with form; simple in substance; capable of suffering in its own right; proceeding in various ways; free in choice; subject to accidents; mutable through its dispositions; rational; sovereign; and divinatory.

**XXIII.** When the question then arises as to where the soul comes from, certain heretics incorrectly assert that it descends from heaven and will undoubtedly return there; the purveyor of all these notions is Plato.

**XXIV.** He therefore destroys a further argument of Plato: that acts of learning are acts of recollection—that is, that souls coming from heaven forget the things among which they formerly existed, and subsequently, from the visible things here, recollect those same things.

**XXV.** He next argues against the Stoics, and at times against Plato himself, who introduce the soul into the body after birth, as a result of the impact of cold air or of the first breath. [Col. 0644B]

**XXVI.** He attacks their opinion, also on the basis of the Christian Scriptures.

**XXVII.** At the same time, he determines that both substances—that of the soul and that of the body—are conceived, formed, and perfected.

### XXVIII

Furthermore, he attacks Plato’s rash falsehood, derived from Pythagoras, concerning **metempsychosis** (μετεμψύχωσις), that is, the recurrence of souls in a revolving cycle through the alternating replacement of the dead by the living.

### XXIX

For even if the dead are made from the living, it does not therefore follow that the living are made from the dead.

### XXX

Next, if the living always come from the dead, the number of human beings must always have been one and the same; whereas, on the contrary, we find that the human race has gradually increased beyond measure.

[Col. 0644C]

### XXXI

Even if this were so, individual souls would have to return into individual bodies—with the same age, the same training, dispositions, and skills, and from every nation, sex, and rank; yet Pythagoras himself did not admit this.

### XXXII

Empedocles, however, raved still more wildly, for he introduced **metensomatosis** (μετενσωμάτωσις), making beasts return from human beings and human beings from beasts.

### XXXIII

Nor, indeed, can this doctrine be defended under the name of judgment; for judgment is nullified if crimes are punished in no other way, or if no other reward is given to the good, than restoration into animal bodies.

### XXXIV

The similar opinion of Simon the Samaritan heretic concerning his Helena is struck down by the same rebuttal. He claimed that she had passed successively through one female form after another, [Col. 0644D] and that she had even been the woman most ruinous to Priam.

### XXXV

Much more does this apply to Carpocrates’ reincorporation of souls, by which he maintained that a soul is recalled into bodies as many times as it has failed to make full satisfaction for its offenses. He also interpreted Elijah’s return, though vainly, in support of his own position.

### XXXVI

Returning from this point to his former subject, he teaches that the sex of the soul and that of the body arise together.

### XXXVII

Moreover, the entire formation of a human being is regulated by some power ministering to the divine will—namely, by some angel—and soul and body grow and advance together: the soul in intelligence and perception, the body in size and physical condition.

### XXXVIII

Puberty likewise arises simultaneously in the soul and in the body, through the prompting of the senses. The craving for food, too, is in the soul, but because of the body’s necessity, not as a property of the soul itself—lest anyone should therefore believe it mortal.

[Col. 0645A]

### XXXIX

Likewise, scarcely any soul is without a demon—at least among the gentiles—until they are born in Christ.

### XL

For so long as the soul remains in association with the flesh in Adam, it is regarded as unclean; and both soul and flesh are said to be sinful.

### XLI

Thus evil is not merely superimposed upon the soul by the arrival of an evil spirit, but is also present from its origin. Its prior good is thereby obscured until the soul is re-formed through its second birth from water and through the heavenly power of the Holy Spirit. At that birth it is received by the Holy Spirit, just as at its former birth it was received by the profane spirit.

### XLII

Yet the consideration of death also concerns us—contrary to Epicurus’ opinion—for in death the soul reaches its consummation.

[Col. 0645B]

### XLIII

Accordingly, sleep is also the mirror of death. He proves, both by other arguments and by the sacred Scriptures, that sleep is not supernatural but natural.

### XLIV

For the story written about Hermotimus—that he was without his soul during sleep—is a fabrication, devised so that sleep might be believed to be, not the soul’s inactivity, but its withdrawal.

### XLV

Dreams and the incidents of sleep must also be discussed, insofar as they differ from ecstasy. Dreams show that the soul is perpetually active, which is a ground for its immortality. Yet in dreams we shall no more be condemned for a vision of sexual violation than we shall be crowned for martyrdom.

### XLVI

Many examples prove that dreams are not altogether empty, as Epicurus judged; and there have been various interpreters and advocates of this position.

[Col. 0645C]

### XLVII

The Christian view, however, is that dreams are very often cast into us by demons, even when they are sometimes true; but that any dreams which are honorable, holy, prophetic, revelatory, edifying, or vocational must be assigned to God. The soul also fashions some dreams for itself from its concentration upon surrounding circumstances. Finally, the remaining phenomena must be distinguished from ecstasy.

### XLVIII

Thus Plato evaluates dreams more according to conjecture than according to any consistent principle, supposing them to be more reliable at the close of night, at certain seasons of the year, according to one’s posture in sleep, according to distinctions among foods, or through abstinence from them.

### XLIX

Indeed, infants and nursing children also dream. And since dreams also come from God, no nation is now foreign to God, while the Gospel flashes forth to all the boundaries of the world.

### L

Now, as regards death, the end appointed by nature is a debt owed by the whole human race, however much Epicurus denies it, and however much the heretic Menander denies that it applies to those initiated by his baptism. Among his followers, there is not even a law requiring one to die for God; for even Enoch and Elijah are destined to die, and John has already died.

[Col. 0645D; Col. 0646A]

### LI

The work of death is the separation of body and soul, however much certain philosophers believed that, after death, some souls remain attached to their bodies.

### LII

Every death, whether ordinary or extraordinary, derives not from nature but from fault—and not even the fault itself is natural.

### LIII

Furthermore, the soul departs; it does not fail as the body’s instruments gradually dissolve. As death approaches, its vision is already clearer, as though it were emerging from sleep. It then exults or trembles according as it perceives, from the face of the angel who summons souls, the preparation of its own lodging-place.

[Col. 0646B]

### LIV

There are various philosophical opinions concerning the place to which souls are conducted. Among these philosophers, the Stoics place the souls of the wise in heavenly dwellings and all others in the underworld. Christians locate this underworld, not in the bosom of the earth, as Plato does, but in its innermost depths.

### LV

He states as his own opinion—though it is not accepted by the Church—that only the souls of martyrs migrate to Abraham’s bosom, or paradise, concerning which he published a book, while all other souls go to the underworld.

### LVI

Yet those opinions are empty according to which souls were thought to be detained on earth until they had received their proper burial rites, or according to which those overtaken by an untimely death wander here until the remainder of their allotted lifetime has been completed.

### LVII

Nor, indeed, do souls return here from the underworld either at the command of demons through magic—several forms of which he enumerates—or at their own discretion.

[Col. 0646C]

### LVIII

Yet there, while they await the body, the souls of the innocent rejoice, while those of the guilty suffer pain and punishment—even for thoughts alone, which divine judgment pursues. This is especially so because the Gospel teaches that even slight offenses must be paid for there, down to the last farthing.

# CHAPTER I

**Note [Col. 0645D]:** In Agobard’s manuscript this book is repeatedly entitled *On the Origin of the Soul* (*De censu Animae*), but incorrectly. For, as is evident from the beginning of the present work, that was the title of another book composed by our Septimius against Hermogenes, in order to show what the soul ought to be considered as deriving from. In that work he had argued against the heretic only this point: that the soul consists of God’s breath, not, as Hermogenes said, of a substratum of matter. That little book is now lost. Here he treats the soul’s condition and the remaining questions concerning it, in opposition to the philosophers. We have therefore retained the general title *On the Soul*, now universally accepted in the printed editions. **RIG.**

Having engaged Hermogenes solely concerning the origin of the soul, insofar as he presumed that it had been constituted from a substratum of matter rather than from the breath of God, I now turn to the remaining questions, in which I shall appear to contend chiefly with the philosophers.

Even in Socrates’ prison there was a skirmish concerning the condition of the soul.

**Note [Col. 0646D]:** “I do not know whether this was the first occasion, or whether it was at an opportune time, masters.” He addresses the masters—that is, the philosophers: “I do not know,” he says, “whether this was the first occasion, masters, or whether it was at an opportune time that there was a skirmish concerning the condition of the soul in Socrates’ prison, although the place makes no difference,” etc. The passage should therefore be written and punctuated as follows: “Even in Socrates’ prison there was a skirmish concerning the condition of the soul. I do not know whether this was the first occasion or whether it was at an opportune time, masters, although the place makes no difference.” **RIG.**

I do not know whether this was the first occasion, or whether it was at an opportune time, masters—

**Note [Col. 0645D]:** Rigault punctuates: “at an opportune time, masters.”

—even though the place makes no difference. [Col. 0646D] For what clear judgment could Socrates’ soul then possess,

**Note [Col. 0646D]:** “Socrates’ soul then.” He alludes to Plato’s *Phaedo*, in which is recounted the discussion that Socrates, as he was about to die after drinking the hemlock, held concerning the immortality of the rational soul. **LE PR.**

[Col. 0647A] now that the sacred ship had returned, now that the hemlock-draughts of his condemnation had been exhausted,

**Note [Col. 0647C]:** “Now that the hemlock-draughts of his condemnation had been exhausted.” He does not mean simply the hemlock, which was not ground for Socrates until sunset, but “the hemlock-draughts of his condemnation,” which the Eleven had announced to him at sunrise. For after his friends had subsequently been admitted, that celebrated discourse concerning the soul began. “Now that the hemlock-draughts of his condemnation had been exhausted” means that the sentence condemning him had already been heard—as though Socrates had begun to drink death from that very moment, since the judges are also considered to have deprived him of life by imprisonment from the moment when they pronounced the sentence of death. **RIG.**

with death already present—his soul assuredly dismayed into some movement, if that movement accorded with nature, or driven out of itself, if it did not accord with nature?

For although it was calm and tranquil, and although neither the weeping of his wife, soon to be a widow, nor the sight of his children, thereafter to be orphans, had bent it according to the law of natural affection, nevertheless it was moved at least in this: that it should not be moved. Its very steadfastness was shaken in resistance to the shock of instability.

And what else would any man unjustly condemned think about except consolation for the injustice—much more a philosopher, that creature of glory, for whom the injustice was not to be consoled but rather mocked? Indeed, after his sentence, when his wife met him and cried out in womanly fashion, “You have been condemned unjustly, Socrates,” he had already answered her by way of congratulation: “Would you have preferred me to be condemned justly?”

[Col. 0647B] There is nothing astonishing if, even in prison, as he eagerly sought to break the ribboned palms of Anytus and Meletus—

**Note [Col. 0647C]:** The Paris edition reads *indiscatas*; the Latin edition, *lemniscatas*; Junius suggests *miniclatas* or *numiculatas*.

—with death itself before him, he maintained the immortality of the soul by a necessary presumption intended to frustrate the injustice.

**Note [Col. 0647C]:** The Paris edition reads “maintaining” (*vindicans*); others, “maintaining the soul immortal.” The Latin edition restored “he maintains” (*vindicat*).

**Note [Col. 0647D]:** “Thus all Socrates’ wisdom at that time.” I think the sense of Plato’s words in the *Phaedo* is rendered here:

> Εἰ μὲν τυγχάνει ἀληθῆ ὄντα ἃ ἐγὼ λέγω, καλῶς δὴ ἔχει τὸ πεισθῆναι· εἰ δὲ μηδέν ἐστι τελευτήσαντι, ἀλλ’ οὖν τοῦτόν γε τὸν χρόνον τὸν πρὸ τοῦ θανάτου ἧττον τοῖς παροῦσι τὰ ἡδὴς ἔσομαι ὀδυρόμενος· ἡ δὲ ἄγνοιά μοι αὕτη οὐ συνδιατελεῖ, κακὸν γὰρ ἂν ἦν, ἀλλ’ ὀλίγον ὕστερον ἀπολεῖται.

> If what I say is true, it is well that I have believed it. But if nothing remains after death, nevertheless during this time before death I shall be less burdensome to those present through my lamentation. This ignorance of mine will not last with me—for that would be an evil—but will perish a little later.

**LE PR.**

Thus all Socrates’ wisdom at that time had arisen deliberately from a calculated equanimity, not from confidence in truth ascertained. For to whom is truth ascertained without God? To whom is God known without Christ? To whom is Christ known with certainty without the Holy Spirit? To whom is the Holy Spirit imparted without the sacrament of faith?

Certainly Socrates was more readily driven by a different spirit. For they say that a demon had adhered to him from childhood—a truly most wicked tutor, even though poets and philosophers rank demons after the gods and together with the gods. For there had not yet appeared [Col. 0647C] the proofs of Christian power,

**Note [Col. 0647D]:** “Which alone exposes that most destructive power.” Christians alone denounce demons, drive them away, compel them to depart, and cast them out of human beings—by adjuration, of course, whence comes the word “to exorcize,” which was known even to pagan authors on civil law. Christians performed this office, not through frauds or impostures, but by the power of Christ’s name, with which every Christian was endowed, as Septimius testifies in the *Apology*: “When commanded by any Christian whatsoever to speak, that spirit will confess himself to be a demon as truly as elsewhere he falsely declares himself to be a god.” From what Sulpicius Severus relates concerning Martin, we learn that the office of exorcist remained customary and common among Christians even in his century: Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, ordered Martin, as a test of the man, to serve as an exorcist. “He did not refuse that ordination,” Sulpicius says, “lest he appear to have despised it as too humble.” **RIG.**

which alone exposes that most destructive force—never a good one—the artificer of ancient error and the seducer from all truth.

**Note [Col. 0647C]:** The Paris edition adds “of the old man.” Junius reads: “never good to man, the artificer of ancient error,” etc.

**Note [Col. 0648D]:** “Alone exposes.” Irenaeus reports that this same power had also been granted to the Jews even in his own time, I believe because of their familiar knowledge of the true God: “And for this reason,” he says, “the Jews even now put demons to flight by this very invocation.” **RIG.**

But if Socrates was therefore considered the wisest of men, even according to the testimony of the Pythian demon—who was, of course, promoting the business of his confederate—how much worthier and more steadfast is the affirmation of Christian wisdom, before whose breath the whole force of demons yields?

This wisdom, from the school of heaven, is freer to deny the gods of this age. It does not betray its own cause by ordering that a cock be repaid to Aesculapius;

**Note [Col. 0648D]:** “It does not betray its own cause by ordering that a cock be repaid to Aesculapius.” Socrates had taught that the gods commonly worshiped did not exist, and yet, when dying, he said that he owed a cock to Aesculapius. Septimius therefore says that he betrayed his cause, because he departed from the tenor of his own teaching. **RIG.**

nor does it introduce new demons, but expels the old; nor does it corrupt the young, but forms them in every good exercise of modesty. Therefore, for the name of truth, it endures the unjust sentence not merely of one city but of the whole world—a truth hated all the more bitterly because it is all the fuller. Thus it does not swallow death from a cup while assuming a demeanor of cheerfulness, but drains it from the cross and the fire that burns men alive, through every device of cruelty.

Meanwhile, in this darker prison of the world, among its own Cebeses and its own Phaedos, if anything concerning the soul must be examined, Christian wisdom directs it according to the rules of God. Certainly it will find no better revealer of the soul than its Author. Let it learn from God

**Note [Col. 0648C]:** Semler reads: “Let it learn the Author from God.”

what it has from God;

**Note [Col. 0648C]:** Semler and Oberthür read “what it has from God”; the Venetian codex and Wouwer read “what you may learn from God.”

or let it learn from no other, if not from God. For who will reveal what God has concealed? Inquiry must be made from the same source from which it is also safest to remain ignorant. It is better not to know through God, because he has not revealed it, than to know through man, because man himself has presumed it.

# CHAPTER II

We shall certainly not deny that philosophers have sometimes thought in agreement with us; even its being found is testimony to truth.

**Note [Col. 0648C]:** The Venetian edition and Rigault read “its outcome” (*eventus*).

Sometimes, amid a storm, when the tracks of sky and sea are confused, some harbor is encountered through a fortunate error. Sometimes, even in darkness, certain entrances and exits are discovered through blind good fortune. Many things are also suggested by nature, as though from that common consciousness with which God has deigned to endow the soul.

Philosophy seized upon this [Col. 0649A] and inflated it for the glory of its own art. Through devotion to eloquence—[it is not surprising if I have called it so]—it became skilled in constructing anything whatever, and in persuading more by speaking than by teaching. It imposes forms upon things, now equating them, now treating them as distinct;

**Note [Col. 0649C]:** “Now it individualizes.” It separates things and assigns them properties of their own. **RIG.**

it prejudges uncertainties on the basis of certainties; it appeals to examples, as though all things were comparable;

**Note [Col. 0649C]:** “It determines all things beforehand.” By predetermined definitions it comprehends all things. **RIG.**

it determines all things beforehand, although properties differ even among similar things;

**Note [Col. 0649C]:** François reads: “as though all things were comparable, it determines properties according to ages.”

it reserves nothing for divine freedom; it turns its own opinions into laws of nature. I could tolerate this if philosophy itself were natural, and if, as mistress of nature, it were proved such through participation in the common condition of nature.

Indeed, it seemed to itself to have drawn even from writings which they regard as sacred, because antiquity considered many authors to be gods, not merely divinized men: for example, the Egyptian Mercury, with whom Plato was especially familiar; and Silenus the Phrygian, to whom, when the shepherds brought him, [Col. 0649B] Midas surrendered his enormous ears.

**Note [Col. 0649C]:** “To whom, when the shepherds brought him, Midas surrendered his enormous ears.” Silenus the philosopher had taken possession of his mind through his ears. The well-known saying of Zeno to Craterus is relevant: “I can be held by the ears, not by the cloak.”

> Λαβὴ φιλοσόφων ἐπιδέξιος ἡ διὰ τῶν ὤτων.

> The skillful hold upon philosophers is that which is taken through the ears.

“He surrendered his ears” is said in the same sense as the earlier statement that Adam did not yet owe his ears to Eve. **RIG.**

Another example is Hermotimus, to whom the people of Clazomenae granted a temple after his death.

**Note [Col. 0649D]:** “Hermotimus, to whom the people of Clazomenae,” etc. Pliny, book VII, chapter 52, calls him Hermotimus of Clazomenae. Plutarch, however, retained the name Hermodorus in his book *On the Daemon of Socrates*, where he says that it is false that the soul of Hermodorus of Clazomenae was accustomed to leave his body, wander through many places for days and nights, and then return to the body. The city of Clazomenae, which was in Ionia, was formerly called Gryna, and there was a temple of Apollo there, exceedingly famous for its oracle; hence “Grynaean Apollo.” **LE PR.**

**Note [Col. 0650C]:** The Paris edition reads “Hermippus.”

Other examples are Orpheus,

**Note [Col. 0649D]:** “Orpheus.” Orpheus is renowned; the Greeks regard him as the son of Oeagrus and Calliope:

> Ὀρφεῦ Καλλιόπης τε καὶ Οἰάγρου φίλε κοῦρε.

> Orpheus, dear son of Calliope and Oeagrus.

Apollonius Rhodius likewise says in book I of the *Argonautica*:

> … Τὸν ῥά ποτ’ αὐτὴ  
> Καλλιόπη θρήικι φατίζεται εὐνηθεῖσα  
> Οἰάγρῳ.

> … whom Calliope herself, it is said, once bore after sharing the bed of Thracian Oeagrus.

I very much doubt whether he is the same Orpheus whose little works we possess. **LE PR.**

and Musaeus.

**Note [Col. 0650C]:** “Musaeus.” Meursius discusses this Musaeus extensively in book II of his *Ancient Readings*, and lists many persons in this connection. He was the son of Eumolpus and a disciple of Orpheus. He flourished at Athens and had Linus at Thebes as his contemporary (*σύγχρονον*). **LE PR.**

Another is Pherecydes, the teacher of Pythagoras.

**Note [Col. 0650C]:** “Pherecydes, the teacher of Pythagoras.” Iamblichus, in his book *On the Life of Pythagoras*, relates a remarkable testimony to Pythagoras’ gratitude toward Pherecydes. When Pherecydes was suffering from *phthiriasis*, or the disease of lice, Pythagoras sailed from Italy to the island of Delos to care for him and remained with him until, after his death, he had performed the funeral rites. [Col. 0650D] **LE PR.**

But what if the philosophers also made incursions into those writings which among us are condemned by the acknowledgment that they are apocryphal? Certainly nothing must be accepted which does not accord with the genuine prophetic preparation, already produced in that very age, since we remember both the false prophets and, much earlier,

**Note [Col. 0650D]:** “Apostate spirits.” He means the angels who fell from heaven upon the daughters of men, as he himself says in book I, chapter 11, *On the Dress of Women*. Irenaeus, book I, chapter 2, spoke of “spiritual forces of wickedness” and of angels who transgressed and became apostates. **RIG.**

the apostate spirits, who furnished the whole appearance of the world with the cunning of such inventions.

Finally, even if it is credible that every investigator of wisdom, by reason of his inquisitive occupation, approached the Prophets themselves, you will nevertheless find more disagreement than agreement among the philosophers, since even in their agreement their disagreement is detected. For every true doctrine which accords with the Prophets they either recommend as coming from some other source or manipulate toward some other end, inflicting the greatest injury upon truth by making it appear either to be assisted by falsehoods or to serve as their advocate.

This, then, will have brought us and the philosophers into conflict, especially on this subject: sometimes they clothe shared opinions in arguments peculiar to themselves, which in some places oppose our rule; at other times they fortify opinions peculiar to themselves with arguments shared by us, which in some places agree with their rule. [Col. 0650A]

**Note [Col. 0650D]:** “So that truth is almost shut out by philosophy.” It is as though human vision and acuteness bewitched truth and our contrived reasonings drove it away, just as spirits are expelled by magical poisons; or else the presumption of one’s own reasoning is a poison for destroying truth. **LAC.**

Thus truth is almost shut out by philosophy through philosophy’s sorceries against it. On both grounds, therefore, this hostile association presses us to defend truth: we must free shared opinions from the philosophers’ arguments and separate shared arguments from their opinions, recalling the questions

**Note [Col. 0650C]:** The Paris edition reads “the question.”

to the writings of God. We plainly except those statements which may be adopted as simple testimony without the snare of some prejudgment; for necessary testimony can sometimes come even from rivals, provided it does not benefit the rivals’ cause.

I am not unaware how vast a forest this subject presents among the philosophers, in proportion also to the number of its commentators: how many varieties of opinions, how many wrestling-grounds of theories, how many offshoots of questions, how many entanglements of proposed solutions.

But I have also examined medicine, which, as they say, is philosophy’s sister.

**Note [Col. 0650D]:** “I have examined medicine, which, as they say, is philosophy’s sister.” The leading physicians treated this inquiry concerning the soul as belonging to their own field of investigation; the Author cites some of them in this work. For although consideration of the soul properly belongs to philosophers, physicians claim it by right of the kinship between medicine and philosophy. Many writers cite Aristotle, Plato, and Galen as saying that philosophy and medicine are sisters, the one preserving the mind and the other the body. John of Alexandria certainly said this in his commentaries on the book *On Heresies*. But among more ancient authors, I find that Democritus wrote it in a letter to Hippocrates. **LAC.**

Medicine also claims this business for itself, since the account of the soul seems more closely to concern medicine through its care of the body. Hence it very often contradicts its sister, because it supposes that it knows the soul better by handling it, as it were, directly in its own dwelling-place. But let the rivalry between the two professions look to itself.

Philosophy had freedom of invention, and medicine the necessity imposed by its art, for extending their inquiries concerning the soul. Uncertainties are investigated at length; presumptions are debated at still greater length. [Col. 0650C; Col. 0651A] The greater the difficulty of proof, the greater the labor of persuasion.

Thus, with good reason,

**Note [Col. 0651C]:** “That obscure Heraclitus.” Rather similarly, St. Jerome at the beginning of book I *Against Jovinian* calls Heraclitus *σκοτεινόν*, “obscure,” whom sweating philosophers scarcely understand. According to Laertius, Heraclitus deliberately wrote his book *On Nature* rather obscurely, so that only the learned might read it. Hence a certain Crates, when bringing that book to the Greeks, said that there was need of some Delian swimmer who would not be drowned in it. **PAM.**

that obscure Heraclitus, observing still vaster darkness among those who examine the soul, became so weary of the questions that he declared he had been entirely unable to find the boundaries of the soul, though he had entered upon every path.

A Christian, however, needs only a few things for knowledge of this subject; for certainty is always found among few things, and he is not permitted to seek more than it is permitted to find, since the Apostle forbids endless questions. Furthermore, one is permitted to find no more than what is learned from God; and what is learned from God is the whole.

# CHAPTER III

And would that it had not been necessary for heresies to exist, so that all who are approved might become manifest (1 Cor. 11:19); then we should have had no need whatever to contend with the philosophers concerning the soul as well—those patriarchs, so to speak, of the heretics. [Col. 0651B]

**Note [Col. 0651D]:** “For even by the Apostle,” etc. He cites no particular passage here, but alludes to Colossians 2: “Let no one despoil you,” or “shake you, through philosophy.” **PAM.**

For even at that time the Apostle foresaw philosophy as a shock to truth.

**Note [Col. 0651C]:** Semler reads “was foreseen.”

Having experienced at Athens that city of tongues, and having sampled all the traders there in wisdom and eloquence, he there conceived that admonitory edict. Accordingly, the account of the soul too—through philosophized doctrines of men mixing water with wine.

Some deny that the soul is immortal; others affirm that it is more than immortal.

**Note [Col. 0651D]:** “Some deny that the soul is immortal; others affirm that it is more than immortal.” Such were the Valentinians, Sadducees, Epicurus, Democritus, and others. The latter words designate the Priscillianists, who said that souls were of the same substance as God, and the Gnostics, who claimed that souls were coeternal with God. Epiphanius, *Heresy* 66, testifies that the Manichaeans, disciples of the Gnostics, babbled the same thing. **LE PR.**

Some dispute about its substance, others about its form, others about each aspect of its arrangement. Some derive its condition from one source; others carry its destination elsewhere, according as they have been persuaded by Plato’s prestige, Zeno’s force,

**Note [Col. 0652C]:** Junius reads “severity.”

Aristotle’s tenor, Epicurus’ insensibility, Heraclitus’ gloom, or Empedocles’ madness. [Col. 0651C]

Divine doctrine was at fault, I suppose, for arising from Judaea rather than Greece. Christ too was mistaken in sending fishermen to preach before he sent sophists.

If, therefore, anything of this kind darkens the bright and pure [Col. 0652A] air of truth with the fumes of philosophy, Christians must clear it of clouds, both by striking down the original—that is, philosophical—arguments and by opposing to them heavenly—that is, the Lord’s—definitions. Thus both those teachings by which gentiles are captivated by philosophy may be destroyed, and those by which the faithful are shaken by heresy may be blunted.

One controversy has already been decided against Hermogenes, as we said in the preface: we maintain that the soul comes from the breath of God, not from matter. There, too, we were fortified by the undarkenable rule of the divine determination:

> “And God,” it says, “breathed the breath of life into the face of the man, and the man became a living soul”—

assuredly from the breath of God. Nothing further concerning this point must be reconsidered. It has its own title and its own heretic. From this point I shall introduce the beginning of the remaining questions.

# CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0652B] After the definition of the soul’s origin, the question of its condition follows. For since we have professed that the soul comes from the breath of God, it follows that we must assign it a beginning.

**Note [Col. 0652C]:** Pamelius reads “we should assign.”

**Note [Col. 0651D]:** “Plato excludes this.” That is, the soul’s beginning. For in the *Phaedrus*, while discussing the immortality of the soul, he says—according to Cicero’s translation in *Tusculan Disputations* I and *Republic* VI: “If among all things there is one soul which moves itself, and is thus the beginning of motion for itself, it certainly was not born and is eternal. For that which arose from elsewhere would not be a beginning.” **PAM.**

Plato excludes this, since he holds that the soul is unborn and unmade. We, however, teach that it is both born and made, on the basis that it has an appointed beginning. We have not immediately fallen into error by saying both, because “born” is plainly one thing and “made” another, since the former properly applies to living creatures. Yet distinctions, while possessing their own places and times, sometimes also share one another’s modes of being acted upon.

**Note [Col. 0652C]:** “It is therefore permissible to say that a created thing is generated, in the sense of being brought into existence.” *Capit* means “it is permitted,” “it is lawful.” By the soul’s *factura*, “making,” he means what elsewhere he would call “creation.” **RIG.**

It is therefore permissible to say that a created thing is generated, in the sense of being brought into existence, since everything that in any manner receives existence is generated. For even the maker himself can be called the parent of what he has made; Plato too uses the word in this way.

Therefore, so far as concerns our faith that the soul was made or born, the philosopher’s opinion has been driven away by the authority of prophecy as well. [Col. 0652C]

# CHAPTER V

Let him summon some Eubulus,

**Note [Col. 0652D]:** “Some Eubulus.” Eubulus of Alexandria was a Pyrrhonist, as Laertius testifies in his account of Timon, concerning whom he writes:

> Εὐφράνορος δὲ διήκουσεν Εὔβουλος Ἀλεξανδρεύς.

> Eubulus of Alexandria was a pupil of Euphranor.

But the *Suda* writes otherwise:

> Εὔβουλος Κήττιος Ἀθηναῖος, υἱὸς Εὐφράνορος.

> Eubulus, an Athenian of Cettus, son of Euphranor.

The Author here gathers, by gradation, the classes of philosophers who held the soul to be incorporeal. **LAC.**

and Critolaus,

**Note [Col. 0652D]:** “Critolaus.” Critolaus of Phaselis was a pupil of Lyco and a Peripatetic, as will be stated in this same chapter. I do not think that Tertullian is referring here to two different men named Critolaus, as we shall soon see, but to only one, who thought the soul incorporeal like a point, as Marsilio Ficino confirms. Cicero mentions Critolaus and Xenocrates in book V of the *Tusculan Disputations*, where he cites their testimonies concerning virtue. **LAC.**

and Xenocrates,

**Note [Col. 0652D]:** “Xenocrates.” He was Plato’s disciple, according to Laertius. Cicero gives his opinion concerning the soul in book I of the *Tusculan Disputations*: “Xenocrates denied that the mind had a shape or anything like a body, but said that it was number, whose power, as Pythagoras had previously believed, was supreme in nature”; and in book IV of the *Academica*: “Or, as Xenocrates says, is the mind without any body?” Aristotle, *On the Soul* I.2 and I.4, mentions this doctrine. [Col. 0653D] **LAC.**

and, in this matter, Plato’s friend Aristotle. [Col. 0653A] Perhaps their case for removing corporeality from the soul would be strengthened if they had not looked at others who, on the contrary—and in greater numbers—maintain that the soul is a body.

I do not mean only those who fashion it from manifest bodily substances: Hipparchus and Heraclitus from fire; Hippo and Thales from water; Empedocles and Critias from blood; Epicurus from atoms, if even atoms produce corporeal masses from their conjunction;

**Note [Col. 0653D]:** “If even atoms produce corporeal masses from their conjunction.” Quintilian, *Institutes* X, called atoms “figures.” **RIG.**

or Critolaus and his Peripatetics from some fifth substance or other—if that too is a body, since it contains bodies. I also invoke the Stoics. By declaring that the soul is spirit, they come close to us, given the near relation between breath and spirit; nevertheless, they will readily establish that the soul is a body.

Thus Zeno, defining the soul as an implanted spirit, argues in this manner:

> That whose departure causes the living creature to die is a body. But when the implanted spirit departs, the living creature dies. Therefore the implanted spirit is a body. But the implanted spirit is the soul. Therefore the soul is a body.

[Col. 0653B]

Cleanthes also maintains that not only the bodily features but also the soul’s characteristics correspond by resemblance from parents to children, as is evident in the reflection of their characters, dispositions, and emotions. The soul, moreover, receives the body’s likeness and unlikeness. Therefore the soul is subject to likeness or unlikeness, which is bodily.

Likewise, the experiences of corporeal and incorporeal things cannot be shared with one another. Yet the soul suffers together with the body: when the body is injured by blows, wounds, or ulcers, the soul shares its pain. The body also suffers with the soul: when the soul is afflicted by anxiety, anguish, or love, the body becomes ill together with it,

**Note [Col. 0653C]:** The Latin edition reads *coagrescit*.

namely, through loss of vigor; and it bears witness to the soul’s shame and fear by blushing and growing pale. Therefore the soul is a body, because it shares in bodily experiences. [Col. 0653C]

Chrysippus also extends his hand in support, establishing that corporeal things cannot possibly be abandoned by incorporeal things, because neither can corporeal things be touched by them.

**Note [Col. 0653D]:** “Hence Lucretius.” Lucretius, the follower of Epicurus, in book I of *On the Nature of Things*, following his master’s example, proves that those things which reach the senses—such as odors, heat, cold, and voices—are corporeal. Lactantius, chapter VI of *On the Workmanship of God*, says that he raved, and argues against him in book VII of the *Divine Institutes*. **LE PR.**

Hence Lucretius says:

> For nothing except body can touch or be touched.

But when the soul abandons the body, the body is affected by death. Therefore the soul is a body, since, were it not corporeal, it would not abandon the body.

# CHAPTER VI
The Platonists confuse these matters by subtlety rather than truth. Every body, they say, must be either animate [Col. 0654A] or inanimate. If it is inanimate, it will be moved from without; but if animate, from within. The soul, however, will be moved neither from within, since it is not inanimate, nor from without, since it is itself rather what moves the body. Accordingly, it does not appear to be a body, since it is not moved from some quarter according to the form proper to corporeal things. [Note: [Col. 0653D] “According to the form proper to corporeal things.” That is, according to the law or nature of corporeal [Col. 0654D] things. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0654D] “From some quarter.” That is, under some directing agency. RIG.]

In reply to this, we shall first express our astonishment at the incongruity of a definition that appeals to categories which do not apply to the soul. [Note: [Col. 0654D] “For the soul cannot,” etc. Septimius posits a middle term between contradictory propositions, though this is hardly consistent with Aristotelian doctrine. For the Platonists do not seem to me to argue badly on this point: “Every body,” etc. RIG.] For the soul cannot be called either an animate or an inanimate body, since it is itself that makes the body animate if it is present, or inanimate if it is absent from it. Therefore, that which produces a condition cannot itself be that condition, so as to be called animate or inanimate. For “soul” is the name of its own substance. But if that which is soul does not admit of being called an animate or inanimate body, how [Col. 0654B] will it be brought under the form of animate and inanimate bodies?

Next, if it is characteristic of a body to be moved from without by something else—and we showed above that the soul is moved by another when it prophesies and [Note: [Col. 0653C] “The soul is moved by another, when it prophesies, when [Col. 0653D] it raves”—assuredly from without by another, etc. JUN.] when it raves, assuredly from without, since it is moved by another—I may rightly recognize as a body that which, according to the proposed example, is moved from without by another. Indeed, if being moved by another is characteristic of a body, how much more is moving another? The soul, however, moves the body, and its exertions become visible externally. For it is from the soul that the feet are impelled to walk, the hands to touch, the eyes to see, and the tongue to speak, as though by the motion of a figurine whose surface is actuated from within. [Note: [Col. 0654D] “By the motion of a figurine.” What would follow if we read *singulari motu*, “by an individual motion,” as though by a private motion? But if we retain *sigillario*, we shall understand an inward or automatic motion, produced by a certain artifice and organic power. It is well known that *sigillaria* were statuettes and small images of the gods; hence Arnobius, book VI: “Indeed, you consider the statuettes themselves to be gods.” LE PR.] Whence does an incorporeal soul possess this power? [Note: [Col. 0654C] *Visio* (“vision”): Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] How can an empty thing propel solid things?

But how, they ask, do the corporeal and [Col. 0654C] intellectual senses appear to be divided in the human being? They say that the qualities of corporeal things, such as earth [Note: [Col. 0654C] *Terra* (“earth”): Paris.] and fire, are reported by corporeal senses such as touch and sight; [Note: [Col. 0654D] *Tactui . . . visui* (“to touch . . . to sight”): Rhen. and others.] whereas incorporeal things, such as benevolence or malice, are apprehended by the intellectual senses. Accordingly, it is established that the soul is incorporeal, since its qualities are comprehended not by corporeal but by intellectual senses.

Certainly—if I do not overthrow this stage of the definition. For observe: I show that incorporeal things are subject to corporeal senses—sound to hearing, color to sight, odor to smell. Following their example, the soul too comes into contact with the body, lest you say that such things are reported through the corporeal [Col. 0655A] senses [Note: [Col. 0655C] *Censum* (“classification”): Paris.] precisely because they come into contact with corporeal things. Therefore, if it is established that incorporeal things also are apprehended by corporeal senses, why should not the soul, which is corporeal, be reported by incorporeal senses? The definition is certainly overthrown.

Among their more notable arguments will also be the claim that every body, in their judgment, is nourished by corporeal things, whereas the soul, being incorporeal, is nourished by incorporeal things, namely by the pursuits of wisdom. But this stage too will not stand, since [Note: [Col. 0655C] “Soranus, most learned in methodical medicine.” This was Soranus of Ephesus, as the Suda teaches, the son of Menander and Phoebe, *ἰατρεύσας ἐπὶ Τραϊανοῦ καὶ Ἀδριανοῦ βασιλέων*, “who practiced medicine under the emperors Trajan and Hadrian.” He composed many volumes, which the Suda cites; fragments also survive today, formerly published by Adrianus Turnebus. To these add the *Introduction to Medical Treatment*, transmitted with the minor works of Pliny, Oribasius, and Apuleius. It is established that there were two men named Soranus, the elder and the younger, and that both wrote on the ailments of women. Everyone admits that the fragments of Soranus the physician addressed to Cleopatra are spurious. Since these touch upon indecent subjects, they were expounded by Scioppius, a diligent investigator of sexual matters. [Col. 0655D] LE PR.] Soranus, the most learned authority on methodical medicine, replies that the soul is nourished by corporeal things as well; [Note: [Col. 0655D] “Indeed, when it is failing, it is very often sustained by food.” Horace:

> Let support at once be brought to the collapsing stomach.

RIG.] indeed, when it is failing, it is very often sustained by food. And why should it not be, since, when food is withdrawn, the soul wholly slips away from the body?

Thus Soranus himself, who commented most fully on the soul in four volumes and examined all the opinions of the philosophers, vindicates the corporeal substance [Col. 0655B] of the soul, even though he deprived it of immortality. For it is not given to everyone to believe what belongs to Christians. Therefore, just as Soranus himself demonstrates from facts that the soul is nourished by corporeal things, let the philosopher likewise show that it is fed by incorporeal things. Yet no one has ever poured the honeyed water of Plato’s eloquence into a person wavering at the soul’s departure, or [Note: [Col. 0655D] “Inserted crumbs from Aristotle’s minute discourse.” By “crumbs” and “minute discourse” he means *λεπτολογία* (*leptologia*), a subtle and concise style of writing such as Aristotle’s. Irenaeus, book II, where he had said against the Valentinians: “They also attempt to introduce into the Faith minute discourse and subtlety concerning questions, although this is Aristotelian.” Hence our own Septimius too, above in *On the Prescription of Heretics*: “Wretched Aristotle, who established Dialectic for them, an artisan of building up and tearing down, Protean in his opinions,” etc. The old glosses have: *λεπτότης ἐπὶ πράγματος*, “subtlety concerning a matter.” RIG.] inserted crumbs from Aristotle’s minute discourse.

And what will all those many souls of mountain-dwellers and barbarians do [Note: [Col. 0655D] “Of barbarians, mountain-dwellers, and boors.” Pithoeus approved this reading from a verse of Lucilius:

> The squalid, uncultivated mouths of boors and mountain-dwellers.

[Col. 0656C] But the manuscript of Agobard reads “of barbarians.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0655C] *Baronum* (“of boors”): Rig., Venice.], who lack the nourishment of wisdom, yet, though uneducated, abound in practical intelligence and continue to live without academies, Attic porticoes, or the prisons of Socrates—in short, though fasting from philosophy? [Note: [Col. 0655C] “From philosophy”: the same editions.] The nourishment supplied by studies benefits not the soul’s substance itself but its training, since it makes the soul not fatter [Col. 0656A] but more cultivated.
