It is well, moreover, that the Stoics affirm even the arts to be corporeal. Thus the soul is corporeal on this ground also, if it is believed to be nourished by the arts. But the immense concentration of philosophy is often accustomed not even to notice what lies before its feet: [Note: [Col. 0656C] “Thus Thales into the well.” Laertius: *εἰς βόθρον*, “into a pit.” RIG.] thus Thales fell into the well. It is also accustomed, when it fails to understand its own opinions, to suspect a disorder of health: [Note: [Col. 0656C] “Thus Chrysippus to hellebore.” Lucian: *ἑαυτὸν ἐλλεβορίζει*, “he treats himself with hellebore.” RIG.] thus Chrysippus resorted to hellebore.

Something of this sort, I think, happened to philosophy when it denied that two bodies could occupy one place, having lost sight and recollection of pregnant women, who daily carry within the compass of a single womb not merely individual bodies, but sometimes two and three. [Note: [Col. 0655C] “Two bodies in one place”: Rig.] [Note: [Col. 0656C] *Alienata*: Jun.; *alienate*: Rhen.] [Note: [Col. 0656C] *Terrena* (“earthly”): Paris.] [Note: [Col. 0656C] *Praeferunt* (“carry before them”): Paris.] [Note: [Col. 0656C] “There is even found in the civil law a certain Greek woman who gave birth to five at once.” I do not think Septimius derived this from Julius Paulus, since the latter reports a numerically different delivery in book III, *Si pars hereditatis petatur*—namely, that in the Peloponnese a woman gave birth to quadruplets five times. In mentioning this number, Paulus differs from Pliny. For in book VII of the *Natural History* we read: “There is also found in the Peloponnese a woman who gave birth to quintuplets four times.” I would by no means affirm that this was taken from Aristotle, although he said: *ἀνὰ πέντε γὰρ ἔτεκε, καὶ τὰ [Col. 0656D] πολλὰ αὐτῶν ἐξετράφη*, “for she bore five at a time, and most of them were reared.” For he does not mention the Peloponnese. Strabo too, in book XV, recounts the matter differently from the same Aristotle, and Aulus Gellius differently again in book X. Finally, Aristotle himself, in the book cited above, records that he had spoken elsewhere about the same matter, though that passage is not extant today. Gaius, book I *On Fideicommissaries*, as cited in book III *On Doubtful Matters*, and Julian, book XXXVI *On Discharges*, relate precisely the same thing about an Alexandrian woman as our Septimius relates here about a Greek woman. RIG.]

There is even found [Note: [Col. 0656D] “In the civil law.” In the books of the jurists, which even the ancient grammarians customarily cite in this fashion. The author of Question 115 says: “For it is written as an established rule in a certain little book of law that a woman once bore five children.” RIG.] in the civil law a certain Greek woman who gave birth to a quintuplet of children: the mother of all at once, the multiple parent of a single offspring, the numerous childbearer of a single womb, [Note: [Col. 0656D] “The numerous childbearer of a single womb, who, crowded with so many bodies—almost, I would say, with a populace.” Thus Manilius, *Astronomica* I, said of the triplet Horatii: “The birth was an entire battle line.”—For the manuscripts attest that this is how the passage should be read. RIG.] [Col. 0656B] who, crowded with so many bodies—almost, I would say, with a populace—was herself the sixth body. The whole creation [Note: [Col. 0656D] “The whole creation.” Everything established and created by God. RIG.] will testify that bodies destined to proceed from bodies are already there in that from which they proceed. That which is from another must necessarily be second; moreover, nothing is from another except while it is being begotten; but then there are two. [Note: [Col. 0656C] “But then it is absent”: Rig.]

## CHAPTER VII

As far as the philosophers are concerned, this is enough. As far as our own people are concerned, there is evidence in abundance, since for them the corporeality of the soul will shine forth in the Gospel itself. In the underworld, the soul of a certain man grieves; it is punished in flame and tormented in its tongue, and it begs for the comfort of dew from the finger of a happier soul.

Do you consider the fate of the rejoicing poor man [Note: [Col. 0656D] “Do you consider it an image?” A parable. RIG.] [Col. 0657A] and the sorrowing rich man to be an image? And why is the name of Lazarus given there, if the event is not real? [Note: [Col. 0657C] “And why the name of Lazarus?” The manuscript of Agobard reads “Eleazar.” Moreover, from the same argument based on the story of Lazarus, Irenaeus seems to share Septimius’s opinion concerning a certain corporeal condition of the soul, book II, chapters LXII and LXIII. Yet Septimius alone is castigated. I suppose this is because his more eloquent style made him conspicuous. RIG.—The error is wrongly attributed here to Irenaeus by which Tertullian imagines that souls retain a certain bodily outline, shadowy senses, and airy colors. Irenaeus intended only that certain distinctive marks and a certain order surviving the body remain in human minds, even when dwelling in heaven, by which human souls are distinguished from other spirits, namely angels. This is precisely what Irenaeus calls “the character of the body” and “the figure of the human being.” Dom Massuet treats these matters more fully at the cited passage and especially in his third dissertation, article XI. EDD.] But even if it must be believed to be an image, it will be testimony to the truth. For if the soul had no body, an image of the soul could not assume the image of a body; nor would Scripture falsely speak of corporeal members if they did not exist.

What, moreover, is that which is transferred to the underworld after its separation from the body? What is detained there? What is reserved for the Day of Judgment? To what did Christ too descend in dying? To the souls of the Patriarchs, I suppose. But why, if the soul is nothing beneath the earth? For it is nothing if it is not a body. [Note: [Col. 0657D] “For the soul is nothing if it is not a body.” Augustine observes: “Finally, Tertullian believed that the soul was a body for no other reason than that he could not conceive it as incorporeal; and therefore he feared that it would be nothing if it were not a body,” etc. Book X of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, near the end. RIG.] For incorporeality is free from every kind of custody, immune from punishment and refreshment. That through which it is punished or refreshed will be a body. I shall give a fuller account of this in the proper place.

Therefore, if the soul receives in advance any torment or comfort [Col. 0657B] [Note: [Col. 0657C] *Praecepit* (“received beforehand”): Rig., Venice.] in the prison or lodging place of the underworld, in the fire or in Abraham’s bosom, the corporeality of the soul will have been proved. For incorporeality suffers nothing, since it possesses nothing through which [Note: [Col. 0657C] *Per* (“through”) omitted in Venice.] it can suffer; or, if it does possess such a thing, that thing will be a body. For insofar as everything corporeal is capable of suffering, so everything capable of suffering is corporeal.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Note: [Col. 0657D] “It would otherwise be rash and absurd to remove something from the category of corporeal things merely because it does not correspond to the other corporeal examples, wherever the particular differences among properties are found.” It is remarkable that after these words Augustine nevertheless becomes severely angry with our Septimius: “For indeed,” he says, “because he is acute, he is sometimes overcome by the truth when it becomes visible, contrary to his own opinion. For what truer statement could he have made than what he says in a certain passage: ‘Everything corporeal is capable of suffering’? He ought therefore to have changed the opinion according to which he had said a little earlier that even God is a body. For I do not think he was so foolish as to believe even the divine nature capable of suffering.” Septimius assuredly intended that both souls and God himself were bodies, but bodies of their own kind—that is, bodies possessing their own properties according to their particular distinction. By this he clearly indicated that he understood bodies of such a kind as would in no respect impair either the dignity of the soul or the divine majesty. Accordingly, the divine nature is not for that reason capable of suffering, although the nature of the soul is for that reason capable of suffering. For the soul possesses a body of its own kind through which it suffers; God too possesses a body of his own kind—that is, a divine body—and therefore one exempt from suffering. RIG.]

It would otherwise be rash and absurd to remove something from the category of corporeal things merely because it does not correspond to the other corporeal examples, wherever the particular differences among properties are found through which the magnificence of the Creator is marked by the diversity of those same works—so that they are as distinct as they are equal, as friendly as they are rival. Indeed, the philosophers themselves agree that all things consist of opposites, [Col. 0657C] [Note: [Col. 0658D] “According to the friendship and strife of Empedocles.” The verses of Empedocles on this matter read:

> At one time all things come together into one through Love,  
> At another, each is borne apart through the hatred of Strife.

RIG.] according to the Friendship and Strife of Empedocles.

[Col. 0658A] Thus, therefore, even if corporeal things stand in opposition to incorporeal things, corporeal things themselves also differ from one another, so that difference enlarges the number of their species without changing their genus: they are corporeal, yet numerous to the glory of God [Note: [Col. 0657C] “In the glory of God”: Rhen.], because varied; varied because diverse; some having one mode of perceiving qualities and others another; some having one kind of nourishment and others another; some invisible and others visible; some heavy and others light.

For they also say that the soul must be pronounced incorporeal for this reason: once it has departed, the bodies of the dead become heavier, although they ought to become lighter through being relieved of the weight of one body, if the soul is a body. “What then,” Soranus asks, “if they deny that the sea is a body because a ship becomes motionless and heavy when it is outside the sea?” How much more powerful, then, must the soul’s body be, since it carries about with the lightest mobility a body that afterward has such weight?

Furthermore, the [Note: [Col. 0658C] *Etsi invisibilis* (“even if invisible”): Rhen., Seml., Oberth., Jun. prefer “Even if the soul is invisible”; but “according to its condition.”] soul is invisible [Col. 0658B] both according to the condition of its own body, according to the property of its substance, and according to the nature of those to whom it has fallen to be invisible. The owl’s eyes do not know the sun; eagles endure it so fully that they judge the nobility of their offspring by the boldness of their pupils. Otherwise, they will not rear the chick that turns away from the sun’s ray, regarding it as degenerate. Thus something is invisible to one being but not to another, without being incorporeal on that account, merely because the power of sight [Note: [Col. 0658C] *Visus* (“sight”): Jun.] is not equal in all.

The sun is certainly a body, since it is fire; yet the eagle acknowledges it while the owl denies it, though the owl does not thereby prejudice the eagle’s judgment. Similarly, the body of the soul may perhaps be invisible to the flesh but visible to the spirit. Thus John, having been placed in the Spirit of God, sees the souls of the martyrs (Rev. VI, 20).

[Col. 0658C]

When [Note: [Col. 0658D] “When we assert that the soul has a body.” From the absurd supposition in the preceding chapters concerning the corporeality of the soul, he is drawn into another absurdity: everything comes linked like rings in a chain toward the advancement of a single assertion. He next attempts to prove that the soul possesses a corporeal shape. RIG.] we assert that the soul has a body of its own quality [Note: [Col. 0658D] “Of its own quality and kind.” Pliny, although not the best teacher in these matters, after saying of God, “He is wholly sensation, wholly sight, wholly hearing, wholly soul, wholly mind,” added, “wholly his own.” RIG.] [Col. 0659A] and of its own kind, [Note: [Col. 0659C] “A body of its own kind.” He speaks similarly in the book *On the Flesh of Christ*. RIG.] this condition of its particular nature has already furnished a preliminary judgment regarding the other attributes of corporeity: [Note: [Col. 0659C] “Has furnished a preliminary judgment regarding the other attributes of corporeity.” He often uses the verb *praejudico* in its proper sense, meaning “to render a preliminary judgment” or “to indicate beforehand.” The meaning of this clause is: the condition of corporeal particularity will already be a certain evident indication for judging the other attributes of corporeity. LAC.] either those attributes are present in that which we show to be a body, yet are themselves also of their own kind in keeping with the body’s particular nature; [Note: [Col. 0659C] “By which we may show it to be a body”: Rhen., Pam., and others.] or, even if they are absent, it belongs to the particular nature of the soul’s body that the attributes present in other bodies are absent from it.

Yet we shall consistently profess that all the more customary attributes which belong universally and necessarily to corporeity are also present in the soul: shape, boundary, and that threefold extension—[Note: [Col. 0659C] *Distentivum*: V.C., Wouw.; *distinctivum* or *distantivum*: Lat.; the Agobard manuscript has “the dimensions of length, breadth, and height.”] I mean length, breadth, and height—by which the philosophers measure bodies.

What now, if we also grant the soul a shape, [Note: [Col. 0659C] “What now, if we also grant the soul a shape?” Irenaeus, book II: “The figure of the human being”; and “The character of the body [Col. 0659D] to which it is adapted.” LAC.] despite Plato’s objections, as though the soul’s immortality would thereby be endangered? [Note: [Col. 0659D] “Despite Plato’s objections.” Clement of Alexandria cites Plato’s words in book V of the *Stromata*. In the *Timaeus* too he says that its substance is simple but its faculties manifold, and that it is like a scraped tablet, as Aristotle taught, especially in the work in which he agrees most closely with Plato, *On Divine Wisdom According to the Egyptians*, book II, chapter III; see also Alcinous in the *Institutes of Plato*. LAC.]

For he affirms that everything possessing shape is composite and constructed; that everything composite and [Col. 0659B] constructed is dissoluble; but that the soul is immortal, and therefore indissoluble because immortal, and shapeless because [Note: [Col. 0659C] “Because immortal—because indissoluble”: Rhen. and others.] indissoluble. Yet he himself makes it composite and constructed if it possesses shape, while in another fashion he gives it shape through intellectual forms: beautiful through justice and the disciplines of philosophy, but deformed through the contrary arts.

We, however, also inscribe corporeal lines upon it, not only by inference from our confidence in its corporeality, but also through revelation grounded in the certainty of grace. [Note: [Col. 0659D] “From the certainty of grace.” By “certainty of grace” he means a grace whose existence is most certainly established. Today there is among us a sister who has obtained gifts of revelation. Tertullian seems to speak of a sister or private person, whereas Priscilla was a public figure, since she assumed the priesthood and the office of teaching, as stated in the book *On Prescription*. Moreover, the revelation of hearts and the healing of diseases suggest that these things did not occur through the disorder of melancholy. She converses with angels, and sometimes even with the Lord; she both sees and hears mysteries, [Note: [Col. 0660D] “She both sees and hears mysteries.” Parables, enigmas, figures, mysteries—the sort of things shown or suggested through dreams by which God’s will is signified or disclosed. Thus, in the book *On Fasting*, he called the skill in interpreting dreams granted by God to Daniel “the knowledge of mysteries.” And in book I *Against Marcion*: “Lions are mysteries of a dry and burning nature,” that is, signs or figures.—“She sees and hears mysteries.” Mysteries. During his rapture Paul heard *ἀῤῥητα ῥηματα*, “inexpressible words.” Irenaeus renders this in Latin as “unutterable sayings,” book V, chapter VII. RIG.] she discerns the hearts of certain people, [Note: [Col. 0660D] “She discerns the hearts of certain people.” Such were those perfect persons in Irenaeus, at the passage cited above, who “bring the hidden things of human beings into the open for their benefit”: *τὰ κρύφια τῶν ἀνθρώπων εἰς φανερὸν ἄγοντες ἐπὶ τῷ συμφέροντι*. These words are found in Eusebius, book V, chapter 7. RIG.] and she provides remedies to those who desire them. [Note: [Col. 0660C] “Receives”: Paris.]

Moreover, according as the Scriptures are read, Psalms are sung, addresses are delivered, [Note: [Col. 0660D] “Addresses are delivered.” In the *Apology* he himself says: “We assemble for the commemoration of the divine writings, if the character of the present times compels us either to give forewarning or to reconsider anything,” etc. RIG.] or petitions are offered, material is supplied from these to her visions. We had perhaps been discussing something about the soul while this sister was in the spirit. After the solemn rites had concluded and the congregation had been dismissed, following her customary practice she reported to us what she had seen—for these things are most carefully recorded, so that they may also be tested.

“Among other things,” she said, “the soul was shown to me corporeally. It appeared as a spirit, but not of an insubstantial and empty quality; rather, it even promised that it could be grasped: tender, luminous, of an airy color, [Note: [Col. 0660C] “Of an ethereal color”: Paris; Junius prefers “of an airy color.”] and in every respect of human form.” [Col. 0660B]

This was the vision; [Note: [Col. 0660C] Rhen. delete “This was the vision”; Pam.: “This is the vision.”] God is the witness, and the Apostle is a competent guarantor of gifts that would exist in the Church. Yet you would not believe [Note: [Col. 0660C] Pam. reads *nisi* (“unless”) for *nec si* (“not even if”).] even if the fact itself persuaded you of every particular! [Note: [Col. 0660C] Pam. inserts *ne* (“not”) before *credas* (“believe”).] If, then, the soul is a body, it is doubtless among those things that we professed above. Accordingly, the property of color too adheres to every body. What other color, therefore, would you assign to the soul than airy and luminous?

Not that its substance is itself air, although this was the opinion of Aenesidemus and Anaximenes, and, I believe, of Heraclitus according to some; nor that it is light, although this pleased Heraclides of Pontus. For the substance of thunderstones is not fiery merely because they flash with a gleaming redness; nor is the material of beryls watery merely because they shimmer with a filtered brilliance. [Col. 0661A] How many other things color associates that nature separates!

But since everything fine and translucent resembles air, such will be the soul, inasmuch as it is a breath and an offshoot of spirit. Indeed, because of the very fineness of its subtlety, belief in its corporeality is endangered.

Likewise, from your own present understanding conceive that no shape other than human is to be assigned to the human soul, and indeed the shape of the body that each soul bore about. For the present, let contemplation of the beginning lead us to this understanding. Consider again: when God breathed the breath of life into the human being’s face and the human being became a living soul, that whole breath was assuredly transmitted immediately through the face into the inner parts and diffused throughout every space of the body. At the same time, condensed by the divine breathing, it was impressed with every internal line of the body that it had filled, and, as it were, congealed in a mold.

Thus the corporeity [Col. 0661B] of the soul was solidified by condensation, and its shape was formed by impression. This will be the inner human being, another than the outer, yet doubly one. The inner human being too possesses his own eyes and ears, with which Paul ought to have heard and seen the Lord; [Note: [Col. 0661C] “With which the people ought to have heard and seen the Lord.” The Agobard manuscript has: “With which the people two ought to h. and s. the L.” The reading from Fulvio Orsini’s manuscript must certainly be adopted: “With which Paul ought to have heard and seen the Lord.” For he is alluding to Paul’s rapture, which Paul himself mentions in 2 Corinthians, chapter III, where he says that he was caught up into paradise, [Col. 0661D] but did not know *εἴτε ἐν σώματι εἴτε ἐκτὸς τοῦ σώματος*, “whether in the body or outside the body.” Augustine refutes the opinion of Septimius at the passage cited above: “See,” he says, “with what ears and eyes Paul ought to have heard and seen God—those with which the soul functions in dreams. Yet if someone were to see Tertullian himself in a dream, Tertullian would never say that he had been seen by, and had conversed with, someone whom he himself had not seen in return,” etc. This passage, as commonly read, suffers from the same corruption as Septimius’s. For “people” is read there twice where “Paul” should be read. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0661C] “Paul”: V.C., Wouw.] he possesses the other limbs as well, which he employs both in thought and in dreams. [Note: [Col. 0661C] “In dreams”: Rhen., Seml., Oberth., Pam.]

Thus the rich man in the underworld has a tongue, the poor man a finger, and Abraham a bosom. Through these outlines the souls of the martyrs beneath the altar are also understood. For the soul, created together with and conformed to the body from the beginning in Adam, produced the seed not only of the whole substance but also of this condition. [Note: [Col. 0662C] “Produces”: Pam.]

## CHAPTER X
It belongs to the rule of faith to define the soul as simple, according to Plato—that is, uniform, at least as regards its substance. [Col. 0661C] Let the arts and disciplines, and the heresies as well, look to their own concerns. For some maintain that another natural substance, spirit, is inherent in it, as though [Note: [Col. 0661D] living, which comes from the soul, were one thing, and breathing, which is effected by the spirit, another. The argument drawn from respiration carried great weight with the philosophers: by this means they distinguished the soul from the spirit, or else said that the soul was nothing other than spirit or wind. *Anima* (“soul”), as though from ἄνεμος (*anemos*, “wind”), according to Isidore, *Origins*, book 11. The Fathers were not similarly pleased by that argument, but regarded it as frivolous. LE PR.] living, which comes from the soul, were one thing, and breathing, [Col. 0662A] which is effected by the spirit, another; for, they say, both are not present in all animals. Most animals merely live and do not also breathe, because they lack the organs of respiration, the lungs and arteries.

But what sort of procedure is it, in an examination of the human soul, to look to arguments drawn from a gnat and an ant? For the craftsman God has adapted the vital organs proper to every animal according to the constitution of its particular kind, so that no inference is to be drawn from them. A human being, because he is furnished with lungs and arteries, will not on that account breathe from one source and live from another; nor will an ant, because it lacks members of this sort, on that account be denied to breathe, as though it merely lived. To whom, indeed, has so much of God’s work lain open that he has presumed to declare that any creature lacks these things?

[Note: [Col. 0661D] That Herophilus, physician or butcher. Anatomy, which was both celebrated and highly esteemed among the pagans, was regarded with the greatest hatred by the ancient Christians. [Col. 0662C] It is nevertheless clear that Herophilus is here called a butcher because he dissected living human beings. Claudius Galen, *On the Opinions*, book VIII, and *Anatomical Procedures*, book II, teaches that Erasistratus, Diocles, and Herophilus were accustomed to do this. In the century just past, the learned Vesalius, a man highly skilled in anatomy, repented of having anatomically cut apart a living man, for this does not savor of Christianity. LE PR.]

That Herophilus, physician or butcher, who cut open six hundred persons in order to investigate nature, who hated the human being in order to know him—I do not know whether he clearly [Col. 0662B] explored all his internal parts, since death itself altered what had been alive, and not a simple death, [Note: [Col. 0662D] but one that went astray amid the very techniques of dissection. And so that Herophilus butchered even living persons. RIG.] but one that went astray amid the very techniques of dissection.

The philosophers have reported as certain that gnats, ants, and moths lack lungs and arteries. Tell me, most inquisitive investigator: do they have eyes for seeing? Yet they both proceed where they wish and avoid or seek what they recognize by seeing. Point out their eyes; mark their pupils. Moths also eat: show their jaws [Note: [Col. 0662C] Others read the singular, “jaw.”], bring forth their molars. Gnats also make a sound, [Note: [Col. 0662D] not blind in their ears even in darkness. Even in darkness they distinguish ears, for they are especially troublesome to the ears. Those savage trumpets seek these above all with their sting. RIG.] not blind in their ears even in darkness. [Note: [Col. 0662D] Both the trumpet and the lance. Thus reads the Agobard manuscript. Previously *hianceam* was read, a thoroughly corrupt reading. The gnat’s mouth is both trumpet and lance. Pliny, XI.2: “With what subtlety did she attach the wings and arrange the very long shanks of the legs? Where did she kindle that greedy thirst for blood, and human blood above all? And with what ingenuity did she furnish the weapon for piercing the hide with a point, so that it might be at once sharpened for piercing and hollow like a pipe for sucking?” RIG.] Show me the mouth that is both its trumpet and its lance.

Every animal, though no larger than a point, must necessarily be nourished by something; exhibit the members for transmitting, digesting, and discharging its food. What, then, shall we say? If life is sustained through these organs, they will certainly be present in all things that live, even if [Col. 0662C] they are not seen, even if they are not apprehended because of their minuteness. You should believe this all the more if [Note: [Col. 0662D] you reflect upon God as being as great a craftsman in the smallest things as in the greatest. Thus it was fitting to refer to the Author of Nature what Pliny attributes only to Nature: “Nowhere,” he says, “is the craftsmanship of Nature more remarkable. For in large bodies, or at least in larger ones, the workshop was easy, since the material was compliant. But in things so small and nearly nothing—what design! What power! What inextricable perfection!” RIG.] you reflect upon God as being as great a craftsman in the smallest things as in the greatest.

But if you do not think God’s ingenuity capable of encompassing such tiny bodies, [Col. 0663A] even so you should acknowledge his magnificence, in that he has equipped minute animals to live nevertheless without the necessary members, preserving sight without eyes, eating without little teeth, and digestion without intestinal passages—just as some creatures also advance without feet: snakes by a flowing impetus, worms by a rising effort, and [Note: [Col. 0663D] slugs. A slug is a naked snail. LE PR.] slugs by a foaming crawl.

Why, then, should you not also think that breathing occurs without the bellows of lungs and without the tubes of arteries?—unless you wish to embrace as a weighty argument the claim that spirit is added to the human soul because there are creatures that lack spirit, and that those creatures lack spirit because they have not been furnished with organs of respiration. You suppose that something can live without spirit, but do not think it can breathe without lungs? What, I ask you, is breathing? It is, I suppose, to emit breath from oneself. What is not [Col. 0663B] living? It is, I suppose, not to emit breath from oneself. This is how I must answer if breathing is not the same thing as living. But not emitting breath belongs to a dead thing; therefore emitting breath belongs to a living thing. Yet emitting breath also belongs to a breathing thing; therefore breathing belongs to a living thing.

If both activities could have proceeded without the soul, then breathing would not have belonged to the soul, but only living. Yet living is breathing, and breathing is living. Therefore all of this—both breathing and living—belongs to that to which living belongs, namely, the soul. Finally, if you separate spirit and soul, [Note: [Col. 0663C] Rhenanus reads “nature” for “spirit.”] separate their operations as well. Let both perform something independently: the soul by itself, the spirit by itself. Let the soul live without the spirit; let the spirit breathe without the soul. Let one depart from the body and the other remain; let death and life come together. For if soul and spirit are two things, they can be divided, so that through their division—one departing and the other remaining—a conjunction [Col. 0663C] of death and life may occur. But this will in no way occur. Therefore things that cannot be divided will not be two; yet they could have been divided if they had been two.

But perhaps two things may also be conjoined. Yet they will not be [Note: [Col. 0663C] “Things which could be divided if they had been. But perhaps two things may also be conjoined. Yet they will not be,” omitted by Pamelius following Gelenius. “They could not be divided, and they would have existed; but perhaps two things may be conjoined,” etc., Gagnaeus.] conjoined if living is one thing and breathing another. Their operations distinguish their substances. How much more firmly, then, should you believe them to be one [Col. 0664A], since you admit no separation between them: that the soul itself is spirit, because breathing belongs to the same thing to which living belongs!

What if you wished to maintain that the day was one thing and the light that came upon the day another, when the day itself is light? There will, of course, be other kinds of light, such as that supplied by fires. There will likewise be other kinds of spirit, such as that which comes from God and that which comes from the devil. Thus, when soul and spirit are under discussion, the soul itself will be spirit, just as the day itself is light. For a thing is itself that through which it is what it is.

## CHAPTER XI

But the argument of the present question compels me to call the soul “spirit,” because breathing is ascribed to another substance. Since we claim this act for the soul, which we acknowledge as uniform and simple, we must call it spirit under a particular qualification: not as the name of its state, but [Col. 0664B] of its activity; not as the designation of its substance, but of its operation—because it breathes, [Note: [Col. 0663D] not because it is properly spirit. That is, not because spirit is independently and in itself a peculiar thing distinct from the soul. Tertullian may conveniently and more gently be softened in this way. Yet I shall not be excessively indignant if you detect a paradox here, as though Tertullian denied that the soul is properly spirit because, if it were spirit, it would not be a body. LAC.] not because it is properly spirit. For blowing also is breathing. Thus the soul, which we defend as properly a breath because of its distinctive nature, we now declare to be spirit out of necessity.

Against Hermogenes, however, who contends that it derives from matter, not from the breath of God, we defend it properly as breath. For he, [Note: [Col. 0663D] contrary to the authority of Scripture itself, changes “breath” into “spirit.” Others followed Hermogenes both in the translation and in the opinion, whom Augustine notes in *The City of God*, XIII.25. There he observes against them and Hermogenes that Scripture has not πνεῦμα (*pneuma*, “spirit”) but πνοήν (*pnoēn*, “breath”), thereby excluding their interpretation concerning the Holy Spirit rather than the soul. LAC.] contrary to the authority of Scripture itself, changes “breath” into “spirit,” [Note: [Col. 0663D] so that, since it is incredible. Hermogenes did not do this to detract from the authority of the Old Scripture, which other heretics of his age attacked; for he himself did not deny the authority of the book of Genesis. Rather, he interpreted that “spirit” as the Holy Spirit, supposing that the soul was already in the human being, so that from this he might argue that the soul’s origin was not from God but from matter. Thus Philastrius, book [Col. 0664C] L. LAC.] so that, since it is incredible that God’s Spirit should fall into sin and soon afterward into judgment, the soul may be believed to derive from matter rather than from God’s Spirit.

For this reason we defend it there too as breath, not spirit, in accordance with Scripture and with the distinction among spirits; [Note: [Col. 0664D] and here we pronounce it spirit against their will. *Ingratis* means “unwilling.” Above he said, “we declare it out of necessity.” RIG.] and here we pronounce it spirit against their will, because breathing and blowing have a common character. There the question concerns substance; for breathing [Col. 0664C] is an activity of substance.

No more need be said on this subject, except on account of the heretics who foist upon the soul some sort of spiritual seed, bestowed by the hidden generosity of their mother Sophia without the Creator’s knowledge, although Scripture, being more conscious of its own God the Creator, [Note: [Col. 0664C] “with greater consciousness,” Agobard manuscript.] has proclaimed nothing beyond [Note: [Col. 0664D] God’s breathing the breath of life into the face of the human being. He alludes to Genesis 2, cited above in chapter 3 and in *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 31: “And God breathed the breath of life into the face of the human being, and the human being became a living soul.” In both places he interprets “the breath of life” as the soul; we showed above, in *On Baptism*, chapter 5, that this explanation is true. It has seemed appropriate to add to these the statement of Theodoret in the *Epitome of Divine Doctrines*: “By the term ‘breath’ we do not understand any portion of the divine essence, according to the madness of Cerdo and Marcion; rather, the nature of the soul is denoted by it, because the soul is a rational and intellectual spirit.” Prudentius agrees with him in the *Hamartigenia*, as does blessed Irenaeus before Tertullian, book V, chapter 7. Philastrius therefore wrongly lists among heresies the teaching that the soul is God’s breath. It sufficiently declares the differences between spirit and soul through the passages that follow, God himself pronouncing (Isa. 57:16): [Note: [Col. 0665C] “The Spirit proceeded from me.” Above, in *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 32, when citing this Scripture, Isaiah 57, he makes no distinction between spirit and spirit; indeed, he says that by it is understood the spirit from which even the winds were constituted. Here, however, he takes “spirit” for the Holy Spirit and “breath” for the soul, imitating Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, V.12, almost word for word, through his citation not only of this but also of the following Scriptures. PAM.] “The Spirit proceeded from me, and every breath I made.” For the soul is the breath made from the Spirit. And again (Isa. 42:5): “He who gave breath to the people upon the earth, and spirit to those who tread upon it.” [Note: [Col. 0665C] “He who gave breath to the people upon the earth, and spirit to those who tread upon it,” etc. Here too he imitates [Col. 0665D] blessed Irenaeus, at the place cited above, almost word for word. PAM.]

For first comes soul, that is, breath, for the people walking upon the earth—that is, acting carnally in the flesh—and afterward spirit for those who tread upon the earth, that is, subdue the works of the flesh. For the Apostle too says (1 Cor. 15:46): “What is spiritual is not first, but what is animate; afterward comes what is spiritual.”

For even though Adam immediately prophesied that great mystery concerning Christ and the Church (Eph. 5:30–31): “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; for this reason [Col. 0665B] a man shall leave father and mother and shall cleave to his wife, [Note: [Col. 0665C] “woman,” Agobard manuscript.] and the two shall become one flesh,” he underwent the accession of the Spirit: for ecstasy fell upon him, the power of the Holy Spirit that produces prophecy.

An evil spirit too is an adventitious thing. Thus afterward the Spirit of God changed Saul into another man, that is, into a prophet, when it was said (1 Sam. 10:11): “What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?” Just so, an evil spirit afterward changed him into another man, namely, an apostate. Judas also, after being counted for some time among the chosen, even to the office of keeping the money-box—and though already a thief, nevertheless [Note: [Col. 0665C] “at last,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.] not yet a betrayer—was afterward entered by the devil.

Therefore, if neither God’s Spirit nor the devil’s spirit is conferred upon the soul by birth, it is evident that the soul exists by itself before the coming of either spirit. If by itself, then it is simple and uniform as regards its substance, and [Col. 0666A] thus breathes from no source other than the condition of its own substance.

## CHAPTER XII

Accordingly, by *animus*, [Note: [Col. 0665D] or “mind,” which is νοῦς (*nous*) among the Greeks. Since *animus*, as Tertullian rightly says here, is called νοῦς among the Greeks, while *anima* is ψυχή (*psychē*), I cannot agree—as I note in passing—with those who give Aristotle’s books περὶ τῆς ψυχῆς (*peri tēs psychēs*) the title *On the Mind* rather than *On the Soul*, as is customary. PAM.] or “mind”—νοῦς (*nous*) among the Greeks—we understand nothing other than an innate and implanted faculty of the soul, naturally proper to it, by which it acts and understands. Possessing this faculty within itself, the soul moves itself from itself and within itself, and thus seems to be moved by it as though by another substance, as those maintain [Note: [Col. 0665D] who also determine the mind to be the mover of the universe. He seems to be indicating Thales, who, according to Aristotle (*On the Soul*, book I, chapter 5), said that the entire universe was animate and that its soul was God. Likewise Zeno, who—as the Author himself says in the *Apology*, chapter 21—determined that the maker of the universe was both called God and the mind of Jupiter. Nor did Pythagoras disagree with them, for according to Lactantius (book I, chapter 5), he called God a mind that passes through and is diffused throughout every part of the world and all nature, from which all living creatures that are born receive life. Aristotle indeed recounts similar opinions of Thales, Anaxagoras, Diogenes, Heraclitus, and Alcmaeon (*On the Soul*, book I, chapter 2). PAM.] who also determine the mind to be the mover of the universe: [Note: [Col. 0666C] that god of Socrates. What Plato wrote about God according to the opinion of Socrates is attributed to Socrates not only by the Author but also by blessed Justin (*Apology* III). Yet in the *Timaeus* Plato also regards the soul of Jupiter as diffused throughout the whole world. He declared this same being, the father and craftsman [Col. 0666D] of the universe, difficult to discover, as blessed Augustine likewise reports in the cited *City of God*, XIII.17. To the same point belongs the Author’s statement above, *Apology*, chapter 47: “The Platonists place God within the world, so that, after the example of a helmsman, he remains within that which he governs.” Nor does Plato’s expression “soul of the world” present an obstacle, because it is certain that in Plato νοῦς (*nous*, “mind”) and ψυχή (*psychē*, “soul”) are frequently taken as the same. PAM.] that god of Socrates, that Monogenes (“Only-Begotten”) of Valentinus, born from the father Bythus (“Depth”) and the mother Sige (“Silence”). [Note: [Col. 0665C] “and the mother ἔννοια (*ennoia*, ‘thought’),” François and Pamelius; εἰρήνη (*eirēnē*, “peace”), Paris edition; others, ἠρεμία (*ēremia*, “stillness”).] [Note: [Col. 0665C] “Quam,” Rigault and the Venice edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0666D] Although Anaxagoras’ opinion is confused. Anaxagoras of Clazomenae was a follower of Thales of Miletus, and said that God was an infinite mind which is moved by itself, and that the divine mind was the maker of all things. LE PR.] Although Anaxagoras’ opinion is confused: after imagining mind as the beginning of all things and [Note: [Col. 0666D] suspending the oscillation of the universe upon its axis. On this expression, see above, *On the Pallium*, chapter 1, at the words “into the oscillation of a suspended impetus.” PAM.] suspending the oscillation of the universe upon its axis, while [Col. 0666B] affirming it to be pure, simple, and unmixed, he by this very designation above all separates it from any mixture with the soul; yet elsewhere he assigns that same mind to the soul. [Note: [Col. 0666D] Aristotle noted this as well. He doubtless alludes to Aristotle, *On the Soul*, book I, chapter 2, where he sets forth Anaxagoras’ opinion in almost the same words. PAM.]

Aristotle noted this as well, though I do not know whether he was more prepared to fill out his own views than to empty those of others. [Note: [Col. 0666C] Others read “condemn.”] Indeed, while postponing a definition of mind, he himself provisionally pronounced that there was another kind of mind, the divine one. But by subsequently indicating that it was impassible, he himself removed it from association with the soul.

For since it is agreed that the soul is capable of undergoing those things that fall to its lot, it will either undergo them through and together with the mind, if it is conjoined with the mind—in which case the mind cannot be introduced as impassible—or, if the soul does not undergo them through or together with the mind, it will not be conjoined with one with which it undergoes nothing and which itself undergoes nothing. [Note: [Col. 0666C] “with which it undergoes nothing and for which it undergoes nothing,” François; “with which it undergoes nothing and through which it undergoes nothing,” Junius.]

Moreover, if the soul undergoes nothing through and together with the mind, then neither will it perceive, understand, or be moved through the mind, as they maintain. [Col. 0667A] [Note: [Col. 0667C] For Aristotle also makes the senses passions, etc. Aristotle has this same point in *On the Soul*, chapter 5: “Sensation therefore occurs,” he says, “when something is moved and affected; for sensation itself seems to be a kind of alteration.” If this is true, says the Author, then, since the soul undergoes none of these things without the mind, the mind is therefore already passible, contrary to Aristotle’s opinion. PAM.]

For Aristotle also makes sensations passions. Why should he not? To perceive is to undergo, because to undergo is to perceive. Accordingly, to understand is also to perceive, and to be moved is to perceive; thus the whole is undergoing. Yet we see that the soul experiences none of these things without their also being attributed to the mind, because it is transformed through and together with the mind. Therefore the mind is now both miscible, contrary to Anaxagoras, and passible, contrary to Aristotle.

But [Note: [Col. 0667D] if a distinction is admitted. Let the arguments of those who say that mind and soul are separate and different now be presented. Lactantius has and sets out these arguments in *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 18. LE PR.] if a distinction is admitted, so that mind and soul are two things in substance, then passion, sensation, every act of discernment, activity, and motion will belong to one of them, while idleness, rest, stupor, and hence complete purposelessness will belong to the other; and either the mind or the soul will be idle. But if it is agreed that all these things are attributed to both, then the two will be one, and Democritus will prevail by abolishing the difference. The question will then be how [Col. 0667B] the two are one: by the fusion of two substances, or by the disposition of one.

We, however, say that the mind is conjoined with the soul, not as another substance, [Note: [Col. 0667C] “of the substance,” François.] but as a function of the substance.

## CHAPTER XIII

It remains, in this connection, to determine where the primacy lies—that is, which [Note: [Col. 0667C] “what,” Rigault and the Venice edition.] presides over which—so that whichever is shown to possess primacy may be the substantial mass, while that over which the substantial mass presides may be regarded as the substance’s natural function.

Indeed, who will not assign the whole supremacy to the soul, when the entire human being is designated by its name? [Note: [Col. 0667D] “How many souls I feed,” says the rich man. This is taken from Plautus’ *Pluto*, or from some other comic poet. In adding “to yield up the soul,” however, he seems to imitate Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book I, where he says: “Our people commonly show that *anima* is also called *animus*; for we say *agere animam*, ‘to yield up the soul.’ The word *animus* itself is derived from *anima*.” PAM.] “How many souls I feed,” says the rich man—not “minds.” The helmsman hopes that souls, not minds, will be saved. The peasant at his work and the soldier in battle affirm that they stake their soul, not their mind. Which is named in these dangers or wishes [Col. 0667C]—the mind or the soul? And what are the dying said to yield up—the mind or the soul?

Finally, the philosophers themselves and the physicians themselves, although intending to discuss the mind as well, have nevertheless each inscribed the face of the work and the title-page of the subject [Col. 0668A] “On the Soul.” But so that you may also learn from God, [Note: [Col. 0667D] God always addresses the soul. He alludes to the very frequent passages in the books of Leviticus and Numbers, and elsewhere, concerning the soul that has sinned, and similar passages. Likewise to Psalm 34: “Say to my soul: I am your salvation.” PAM.] God always addresses the soul; he calls and summons the soul, so that it may direct its mind toward him. [Note: [Col. 0667D] Christ came to save it. The remaining Scriptures that he cites here are sufficiently well known: Luke 2, Matthew 10, and John 10. The statement “he forbids it to be valued more highly” is a paraphrastic rendering of Luke 14, where the Christian is commanded to hate his own soul—that is, not to value it more highly than God. PAM.] Christ came to save it; he threatens to destroy it in Gehenna; he forbids it to be valued more highly; and the good shepherd himself lays it down for his sheep.

You have the primacy of the soul; you have in it also the unity of substance, and may understand that the mind is its instrument, not its protector.

## CHAPTER XIV

Moreover, the soul is singular and simple, and wholly derived from itself. It is no more capable of being constructed from another source than it is divisible in itself, because it is not dissoluble either. For if it is constructed, it is also dissoluble; if dissoluble, then no longer immortal. Therefore, because it is not mortal, it is neither dissoluble nor divisible. For to [Col. 0668B] divide is also to dissolve, and to dissolve is to die.

Yet it is divided [Note: [Col. 0667C] “is divided,” Pamelius and Semler.] into parts: [Note: [Col. 0668C] It will, however, be divided into parts. The Author explains himself shortly afterward when he says: “Things of this sort, however, will be regarded not so much as parts of the soul as its powers, capabilities, and operations.” Hence Nyssenus, *Philosophy*, IV.8: “They divide the soul,” he says, “into powers, or kinds, [Col. 0668D] or parts.” PAM.] now into two by Plato, now three by Zeno, now five and six by Panaetius, [Note: [Col. 0668D] into seven by Soranus. The four books *On the Soul* composed by Soranus, which the Author cited above, are lost. I can therefore determine nothing certain about his opinion; indeed, only blind conjectures can be made. Perhaps, just as Panaetius added τὸ ἡγεμονικόν (*to hēgemonikon*, “the ruling faculty”) to the division into the five senses, according to Nemesius, Soranus, as a physician, added τὴν σπερματικήν (*tēn spermatikēn*, “the generative faculty”). But I do not yet affirm this slight suspicion, even though Junius applauded it. Seneca, moreover, distinguished only seven parts, thereby dissenting from his fellow Stoics, chapter 92. LAC.] into seven by Soranus, even into eight according to Chrysippus, even into nine [Note: [Col. 0668D] according to Apollophanes. Is this the physician mentioned by Pliny, book XXII, chapter 11; or the philosopher who wrote on physics, according to Diogenes Laertius; or even the Apollophanes who accompanied blessed Dionysius in Egypt and, while in the city of Hierapolis, observed with him the darkening of the sun when Christ the Lord suffered, concerning whom blessed Dionysius writes in his letter to Polycarp? LE PR.] according to Apollophanes, but into ten among certain Stoics, and into two more according to Posidonius. For, having begun from two designations—the principal faculty, which they call ἡγεμονικόν (*hēgemonikon*, “ruling”), and the rational faculty, which they call λογικόν (*logikon*, “rational”)—he then proceeded to twelve. [Note: [Col. 0668C] “seventeen,” Paris edition; “ten,” Junius.] Thus they divide the soul into [Note: [Col. 0668C] “Thus other,” Venice edition.] different kinds, one classification arising from another.

Things of this sort, however, will be regarded not so much as parts of the soul as its powers, capabilities, and operations, just as Aristotle too judged concerning some of them. For they are not members of the soul’s substance, but faculties: the faculty of motion, of action, of thought, and whatever other distinctions of this kind [Col. 0668C] they make. Such too are those five best-known senses: sight, hearing, taste, touch, and smell.

Although they have assigned fixed dwelling places in the body to each of these, [Note: [Col. 0668D] this distribution of the soul will not on that account pertain to divisions of the soul. This is precisely how the manuscript reads. Nor should we be troubled by the repetition of the word [Col. 0669B] “soul.” Although its powers, capabilities, and faculties are distributed into fixed parts of the body, the soul itself nevertheless fills the entire body and is not thereby cut into parts. Thus this distribution of the soul, whether into fixed or individual parts of the body, will not pertain to divisions of the soul itself. RIG.] this distribution [Col. 0669A] of the soul will not on that account pertain to divisions of the soul, since not even the body itself is divided into its members in the manner in which these men wish the soul to be divided. On the contrary, one body is produced from the multitude of its members, so that the very division is a conjunction instead.

Consider the most astonishing work of Archimedes’ ingenuity—[Note: [Col. 0669C] the hydraulic organ. The inventor of this instrument was Ctesibius of Alexandria; Archimedes, however, rendered it completely finished and perfected it. See Hero’s *Pneumatics*. There were also other celebrated machines of Archimedes—the mirror and the sphere—concerning all of which writers speak everywhere. LE PR.] I mean the hydraulic organ: so many members, so many parts, so many joints, so many paths for voices, so many contractions of sounds, so many interchanges of musical modes, so many ranks of pipes—and all will constitute a single structure. In the same way, the breath that gasps there under the pressure of the water is not divided into parts merely because it is administered through parts; it is solid in substance but divided in operation.

This example is not far removed from Strato, Aenesidemus, and Heraclitus. For they too maintain the unity of the soul, which is poured throughout [Note: [Col. 0669B] “diffused,” Pamelius, Semler, Oberthür.] the entire body and [Col. 0669B] is itself present everywhere; like breath in a reed-pipe passing through its hollows, so it flashes forth in various ways through the sensory organs, not so much cut apart as distributed.

The physicians, together with the philosophers, [Note: [Col. 0669B] “then the philosophers,” Pamelius.] may consider by what names all these are called, into what divisions derived from itself each is confined, [Note: [Col. 0669B] “are derived,” Pamelius, Semler, Rhenanus, Oberthür.] and into what stations within the body they are separately assigned. Only a few points will concern us.

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 0670A]

First of all, whether there is in the soul some highest vital and cognitive faculty, which they call the *hēgemonikon* (ἡγεμονικόν), that is, the ruling faculty: if this is denied, the whole constitution of the soul is endangered. Indeed, those who deny a ruling faculty first judged the soul itself to be nothing.

[Note: [Col. 0670B] “Something” (*aliquid*), Venetian edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0669C] A certain Dicaearchus of Messene. Dicaearchus, Cicero says (*Tusculan Disputations*, book 1), in the discourse which he sets out in three books as having been conducted at Corinth by learned men engaged in debate, makes many persons speak in the first book; in the other two he introduces a certain Pherecrates, an aged Phthiotian whom he says was descended from Deucalion, arguing that mind is absolutely nothing, that the whole word is an empty name, that living beings and animate beings are so called to no purpose, and that neither a mind nor a soul exists in a human being or an animal. And shortly afterward Cicero indicates in the same place that this was indeed Dicaearchus’ own opinion: “What am I to say of Dicaearchus, who says that mind is absolutely nothing?” Suidas also attests that this man was a Messenian and a disciple of Aristotle. Plutarch and Quintilian cite his *Music*; Gellius, his *Pythagoras*; Athenaeus, several books; St Jerome, book 2 *Against Jovinian*, a description of Greece taken from his books on antiquities; and Cicero elsewhere, finally, a book on divination and dreams. PAM.]

A certain Dicaearchus of Messene, and among the physicians Andreas and Asclepiades, abolished the ruling faculty in this way: they wished the senses themselves to reside in the soul, whose ruling faculty is thereby vindicated. Asclepiades even presses the argument that many animals, after those bodily parts in which the ruling faculty is chiefly believed to reside have been removed, nevertheless both remain alive for some time and retain awareness: flies, wasps, and locusts, if you cut off their heads; goats, tortoises, and eels, if you remove their hearts. [Col. 0670B] Therefore, he says, there is no ruling faculty; for if there were, once it and its attendants had been lost, the soul’s vigor would not persist.

[Note: [Col. 0670B] “Certain persons” (*aliqui*), Junius.]

[Note: [Col. 0669D] “Once it and its attendants had been lost.” That is, once that ruling faculty and its attendants—namely, the head and heart—had been lost. “Its attendants”: as though with its entire household, retinue, and train. RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0670B] Rigault reads: “Once it had been lost together with its seats.”]

But a greater number of philosophers opposed Dicaearchus—Plato, Strato, Epicurus, Democritus, Empedocles, Socrates, and Aristotle—and the physicians Herophilus, Erasistratus, Diocles, Hippocrates, and Soranus himself opposed Andreas and Asclepiades.

[Note: [Col. 0669D] Against Andreas. The physician Andreas is frequently cited by Pliny, not only among the names of the authors from whom he drew much material, but also in book XXII, chapter 23, and book XXXII, chapter 5. In certain copies, however, *Andrias* is incorrectly read for *Andreas*; for his book *On Plants* is also cited by Dioscorides and Galen. PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0670B] And Asclepiades. Besides attesting, among the names of his authorities, that he drew much material from Asclepiades, the physician of Prusa, Pliny treats him specifically in book XXVI, chapter 3. Certain writings of his are also cited by Aëtius and Galen, although Galen mentions two men of that name. A little later the Author ridicules him in these words: “So that Asclepiades, confuted even by these men, may go looking for his goats bleating without hearts and chase away his flies flying without heads.” He tacitly signifies the absurdity of one who wished, from their example, to deprive even a human being of the ruling faculty. The Author mentions Asclepiades again below, chapter 25. Apuleius also relates much about the same Asclepiades in book IV of *The Golden Ass*. PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0670C] Erasistratus. In the place cited above, Pliny ranks Erasistratus fifth among physicians, before Herophilus and Asclepiades. Likewise, in book XIV, chapter 7, he writes that Erasistratus lived in the 450th year of the City of Rome, and he mentions his school in book XX, chapter 9. Finally, in book XXIX, chapter 2, he makes him a disciple of Chrysippus, born of Aristotle’s daughter, who, after curing King Antiochus, was rewarded with one hundred talents by Ptolemy, the king’s son. Suidas also mentions this event, and Galen cites several of Erasistratus’ books in the work already cited. The Author cites him again in chapter 25. PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0670D] Diocles. Diocles of Carystus, a physician second only to Hippocrates in age and reputation, is celebrated by Pliny in book XXVI, chapter 2. He is also cited by Pliny in book XX, chapters 3 and 5, and in book XXI, as well as in the catalogue of physicians whose works he used; likewise by Galen, Plutarch, the scholiast on Nicander, Athenaeus, and Paul of Aegina. PAM.]

And now there are more Christians than all of them, who are guided by God regarding both points: that there is a ruling faculty in the soul and that it is consecrated in a definite recess of the body.

[Note: [Col. 0670D] “Who are guided by God regarding both points.” So reads the Agobard manuscript. “And now,” he says, “there are more Christians than all the philosophers and physicians,” Christians who, when investigating what judgment should be made regarding both points—that is, regarding that ruling faculty of the soul and the place and position of that faculty—are guided by God and learn from the sacred pages. Thus the ancient Christians, even when disputing with pagans, adduced the authority of Holy Scripture. The pagans rejected divine utterances unless they were proved by human, that is, purely philosophical, arguments. In this blindness Galen inveighs against Archigenes with the following prohibition: “He will not listen to unproved laws” (*nomous anapodeiktous*, νόμους ἀναποδείκτους), “such as those who have reached the school of Moses and Christ commonly employ” (*Mōyseōs kai Christou diatribēn aphigmenoi*, Μωυσέως καὶ Χριστοῦ διατριβὴν ἀφιγμένοι). These are Galen’s words in the second book *On Differences of the Pulse*. RIG.]

[Col. 0671A]

[Note: [Col. 0671B] “Are led” (*deducimur*), Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür, and Pamelius; “we infer” (*deducimus*), Junius.]

[Note: [Col. 0671C] The ruling faculty in the soul. Jerome to Fabiola, letter 128: “The question is where the soul’s ruling faculty resides. Plato places it in the brain; Christ shows that it is in the heart: ‘Blessed are the pure in heart,’” etc. RIG.]

For if we read that God is the searcher and inspector of the heart (Wisdom 1; Proverbs 24); if his prophet is also approved by exposing the heart’s hidden things (Psalm 138); if God himself anticipates the thoughts of the heart among the people (Matthew 9): “Why do you think evil things in your hearts?”; if David too says (Psalm 50), “Create a clean heart in me, O God”; and Paul says (Romans 10) that belief unto righteousness takes place in the heart; and John says (1 John 3) that each person is reproved by his own heart; if, finally, whoever has looked upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery in his heart (Matthew 5)—then both points are simultaneously made clear: that there is in the soul a ruling faculty upon which the divine intention bears, namely the cognitive and vital power—for whatever understands is alive—and that this faculty is contained in that treasury of the body toward which God looks.

[Note: [Col. 0671B] So reads the Paris edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0671B] “Which” (*quod*), Pamelius and Rhenanus.]

You are therefore not to suppose that this ruling faculty is agitated from without, according to Heraclitus; nor wafted throughout the entire body, according to Moschion; nor enclosed in the head, according to Plato; nor seated chiefly at the crown of the head, according to Xenocrates; nor lying in the brain, according to Hippocrates; nor around the base of the brain, as Herophilus held; nor in its little membranes, as Strato and Erasistratus held; nor in the middle of the eyebrows, as Strato the Natural Philosopher held; nor throughout the whole breastplate of the chest, as Epicurus held. Rather, it is where the Egyptians also assigned it, and where those who seemed to be recorders of divine matters placed it, as does that verse of Orpheus or Empedocles:

> For in man the blood surrounding the heart is sensation.

[Note: [Col. 0671C] Junius reads: “in its membrane.”]

[Note: [Col. 0671C] Strato the Natural Philosopher. This also comes from Plutarch. He is called Strato “the Natural Philosopher” both to distinguish him from the preceding Strato the physician and because, according to Suidas, he devoted himself to the study of nature more than others. Suidas makes him a native of Lampsacus, a son of Theophrastus, and reports that he wrote many books. PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0671C] “Nor throughout the whole breastplate of the chest.” The corresponding Greek in Plutarch reads: *en holō tō thōraki* (ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ θώρακι), “in the whole chest.” PAM.]

[Col. 0672A]

[Note: [Col. 0672B] “And where” (*et quod*), Rhenanus, Pamelius, and Semler.]

[Note: [Col. 0671C] “Assigned.” The Author appears here to take *renuntiare* in the sense of “attribute,” the same meaning which he discusses more fully below in *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 1. PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0672B] “To it” (*ei*), Pamelius, Rhenanus, Semler, and two manuscripts of Wouwer.]

[Note: [Col. 0671D] Recorders of divine matters. He seems to mean Hermes Trismegistus, Anebo, and Amabo, whom Plotinus, Iamblichus, and Plato himself generally followed. PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0670D] “Who are guided by God regarding both points.” So reads the Agobard manuscript. “And now,” he says, “there are more Christians than all the philosophers and physicians,” Christians who, when investigating what judgment should be made regarding both points—that is, regarding that ruling faculty of the soul and the place and position of that faculty—are guided by God and learn from the sacred pages. Thus the ancient Christians, even when disputing with pagans, adduced the authority of Holy Scripture. The pagans rejected divine utterances unless they were proved by human, that is, purely philosophical, arguments. In this blindness Galen inveighs against Archigenes with the following prohibition: “He will not listen to unproved laws” (*nomous anapodeiktous*, νόμους ἀναποδείκτους), “such as those who have reached the school of Moses and Christ commonly employ” (*Mōyseōs kai Christou diatribēn aphigmenoi*, Μωυσέως καὶ Χριστοῦ διατριβὴν ἀφιγμένοι). These are Galen’s words in the second book *On Differences of the Pulse*. RIG.]

Protagoras, Apollodorus, and Chrysippus likewise hold these views; so that Asclepiades, confuted even by these men, may go looking for his goats bleating without hearts and chase away his flies flying without heads; and so that everyone may now know that those who have prejudged the organization of the human soul from the condition of animals are themselves living without heart and brain instead.

[Note: [Col. 0671D] Protagoras. Although Diogenes Laërtius mentions Protagoras, the philosopher of Abdera and pupil of Democritus, nevertheless, because no book *On the Soul* is listed among his works, and because the Author here appears once again to oppose other physicians to Asclepiades, I think that *Praxagoras* should be read. Yet I was unwilling to alter the text without the aid of a manuscript. Certainly the physician Praxagoras is celebrated by Pliny in the third place in the aforementioned book XXVI, chapter 2, etc. PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0672C] Likewise Apollodorus. Here too, although Diogenes Laërtius lists Apollodorus of Athens, an Epicurean philosopher, I nevertheless think that the Author is speaking instead of another Apollodorus, one of those physicians whom Pliny discusses in book XX, chapter 4. PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0672C] And Chrysippus. Here too I think that the Author is speaking of the physician Chrysippus rather than the philosopher mentioned above in chapter 5, for that physician is frequently cited by Pliny. PAM.]

## CHAPTER XVI

There is also a point relevant to the conclusion, namely that Plato divides the soul in two, into the rational and the irrational.

[Note: [Col. 0672B] “Faith” (*fidem*), Pamelius and Semler.]

[Note: [Col. 0672C] “That Plato divides the soul in two,” etc. Similarly he said above, chapter 14: “It is divided into parts, but now into two by Plato.” Plato has this in dialogue 4 of the *Republic*: “It is therefore not unreasonable,” he says, “that these two parts are distinct and different from one another, so that we call the part by which the soul reasons [since it governs reason like a kindly and attentive mother, showing the right path of life] the rational part of the soul; but the part by which it loves, hungers, thirsts, and is affected as though distraught by other desires, the irrational part.” PAM.]

We too indeed applaud this definition, but not in such a way that both parts are attributed to nature. For the rational must be believed natural, since it was implanted in the soul from the beginning by a rational Author. For what would not be rational if God produced it by his command, much less that which he sent forth specifically by his own breath?

The irrational, however, must be understood as later, since it occurred through the serpent’s prompting—the very commission of their transgression—and thereafter took root and grew together with the soul, [Col. 0672B] so as by now to assume the likeness of a natural quality, because it occurred immediately at the beginning of nature.

[Note: [Col. 0672C] “The very thing” (*ipsum*), Pamelius, Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür.]

[Note: [Col. 0672D] “So as by now to assume the likeness of a natural quality.” Through the corruption and deformation of nature. This passage supports original sin. The Author deliberately said “after the likeness of a natural quality,” because neither corruption nor original sin is itself our nature, substance, or form, as Illyricus thought, but is something that has happened to nature. For, as Tertullian very properly intimates, if sin were our substance or nature, since every substance was created by God, it would follow that sin was created by God alone and implanted in Adam and his descendants. LAC.]

[Note: [Col. 0672D] “It occurred at the beginning.” As the illustrious Bossuet observes (*Defense of Tradition and the Holy Fathers*, vol. II, book VIII, chapter XXIX, p. 148), in Tertullian’s expression *primordium* one must understand not only a beginning in temporal sequence but also a beginning in principle and origin. By this is understood that immense change in our body and soul which occurred at the beginning and origin of the human race and which St Augustine undertook to defend against the Pelagians. Nor can the “in whom” of the Epistle to the Romans be better explained, nor can the fact that we all sinned in Adam be more expressly stated, than by saying that Adam’s sin passed into our nature. Tertullian acknowledges the natural consequence of this principle when he admits that even the infants of the faithful are born impure. Therefore Christ said: “Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven.” Thus every soul is reckoned in Adam until it is reckoned anew in Christ: impure for as long as it is not reckoned anew. Now, to be reckoned in Adam is not merely to be in misery and punishment, but also under curse, condemnation, perdition, and sin. He therefore adds: every soul is sinful because it is impure, and it remains impure until regenerated through baptism. This sacrament does not remove death or the root of concupiscence. Therefore, if baptism removes a stain from the soul, it surely removes the stain of sin, which, according to Tertullian, the soul contracted through its union with the flesh, owing to the disorderly concupiscence by which the flesh lusts against the spirit and which makes the flesh sinful before it can even exist. Behold the entire theology of original sin most clearly expounded! Behold the first sin transmitted into the nature of all human beings! Behold its propagation through the concupiscence of the flesh! Behold its remission in baptism! What more can be added? LUMP.]

But since Plato describes only the rational as present in the soul of God himself, if we also ascribe the irrational to the nature which our soul received from God, the irrational will equally belong to God as something natural, because God is the author of nature.

[Col. 0673A]

[Note: [Col. 0673C] “If we should ascribe” (*adscripserimus*), Pamelius, Rhenanus, and Semler.]

But the implantation of sin came from the devil, and every sin is irrational; therefore the irrational came from the devil, from whom sin also came. It is foreign to God, to whom the irrational is alien. Consequently, the difference between these two derives from the remoteness of their authors.

Accordingly, when Plato, reserving the rational for God alone, subdivides two kinds from the rational—the irascible, which they call *thymikon* (θυμικόν), and the appetitive, which they call *epithymētikon* (ἐπιθυμητικόν)—so that the former is common to us and lions, the latter to us and flies, while the rational is common to us and God, I see that I must reconsider this point as well because of what is found in Christ.

For behold, this entire triad is also present in the Lord: the rational, by which he teaches, discusses, and lays out the paths of salvation; the irascible, by which he inveighs against the scribes and Pharisees; and the appetitive, by which he desires to eat the Passover with his disciples.

[Col. 0673B]

[Note: [Col. 0674C] This entire triad. That is, the threefold function of the reasoning, angry, and desiring soul is indicated in the Gospel: the rational and teaching function in Matthew 7 and 12; the indignant or angry function in Matthew 23; and the desiring or appetitive function in Luke 22. LAC.]

[Note: [Col. 0673C] “By which” (*quae*), François and Pamelius.]

Therefore, among us the irascible and appetitive faculties are not always to be reckoned as proceeding from the irrational, since we are certain that in the Lord they operated rationally.

[Note: [Col. 0674C] “In the Lord” (*Domino*), Pamelius and François.]

God will be indignant rationally—that is, against those who deserve it—and God will rationally desire things worthy of himself. For he will both be indignant at evil and, for good, desire salvation.

[Note: [Col. 0674D] “God will be indignant rationally.” If this is understood hypothetically, in the manner in which Scripture speaks—so that God’s indignation is taken for God’s vengeance—nothing prevents its attribution to God. Elsewhere, however, we have noted that it must be numbered among Tertullian’s paradoxes that he appears to attribute anger properly so called to God. PAM.]

The Apostle too grants us desire (1 Timothy 3:1): “If anyone desires the episcopate, he desires a good work”; and by calling it a good work he shows the desire to be rational. He also permits indignation; why should he not, when he himself entertained it?

[Note: [Col. 0674D] “I wish they would even cut themselves off.” Paul directs this against the Jews in Galatians, chapter 5: “I wish,” he says, “that those who recall you to circumcision and the other Mosaic observances would not merely be circumcised but cut themselves off as well”: *ophelon kai apokopsontai* (ὄφελον καὶ ἀποκόψονται). Chrysostom: *mē peritemnesthōsan monon, alla kai perikoptesthōsan* (μὴ περιτεμνέσθωσαν μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ περικοπτέσθωσαν), “Let them not only be circumcised, but also be cut off.” And in Primasius of Hadrumetum: “Let them not only be circumcised but also be cut off, if the removal of the member is advantageous.” RIG.]

“I wish,” he says (Galatians 5:12), “that those who unsettle you would even cut themselves off!” Indignation which proceeds from zeal for discipline is rational.

[Col. 0673C]

But when he says (Ephesians 2:3), “We were once by nature children of wrath,” he stigmatizes the irrational irascible faculty, which does not derive from that nature which is from God, but from the nature introduced by the devil. The devil himself is called the lord of his own order (Matthew 6:24): “You cannot serve two lords”; and he is also given the name father (John 8:44): “You are of your father the devil.” Do not be afraid, then, to ascribe to him possession of another nature, a later and adulterous one, since you read that he is the sower of darnel over the crop (Matthew 13) and the nocturnal corrupter of the wheat-field.

[Col. 0674A]

## CHAPTER XVII

We must also encounter the question concerning those five senses which we learn in our first lessons, since from this subject too some support is furnished to the heretics. These senses are sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch.

The Academics condemn their reliability rather harshly; according to some, Heraclitus, Diocles, and Empedocles do so as well; and Plato certainly does in the *Timaeus*, where he declares sense-perception irrational and entangled with opinion.

[Col. 0674B]

[Note: [Col. 0674C] “Declares” (*pronuntiat*), Pamelius and Rhenanus.]

Thus sight is charged with falsehood because it asserts, contrary to our knowledge of their straightness, that oars in water are bent or broken; because it persuades us that a square tower is round when seen from a distance; because it misrepresents a perfectly uniform portico as narrower at its far end; and because it joins the heaven, suspended at so great a height, to the sea. Hearing is likewise accused of deception: as when we suppose a rumbling to be in the sky although it is a wagon; or, when thunder is gathering, confidently believe the sound comes from a wagon.

Smell and taste are similarly impeached, since the same perfumes and the same wines decline in value when used again. Touch is similarly criticized, since the same pavements are judged rougher by the hands but smoother by the feet; and in the baths, the same pool of hot water is reported first to be extremely hot and afterward perfectly temperate.

[Col. 0674C]

“To such a degree,” they say, “are we also deceived by the senses when we change our judgments.”

[Note: [Col. 0674D] The Stoics are more moderate. The Stoics declare that the senses are truthful, but that some impressions are true and others false, as Plutarch observes in book IV, chapter 9, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*. Epicurus asserted that every impression and all the senses are true, but that some opinions are true and others are not. In Clement of Alexandria the senses are *epibathra tēs epistēmēs* (ἐπίβαθρα τῆς ἐπιστήμης), “stepping-stones of knowledge.” LE PR.]

The Stoics are more moderate and do not burden every sense, or any sense at all times, with the charge of falsehood. The Epicureans more resolutely defend an equal and perpetual truth in all the senses, though by a different route: it is not the sense, they say, that lies, but opinion; for sense undergoes an impression but does not form an opinion, whereas the soul forms an opinion.

[Col. 0675A]

[Note: [Col. 0675C] Junius deletes “for”; Rigault and the Venetian edition do not add it.]

They have severed opinion from sensation and sensation from the soul. Yet whence comes opinion, if not from sensation? Indeed, unless sight has perceived the tower as round, no opinion of roundness will arise. And whence comes sensation, if not from the soul? Indeed, a body lacking a soul will also lack sensation. Thus sensation comes from the soul, opinion from sensation, and the soul is the whole.

But it will be most properly proposed that there is assuredly something which causes a thing to be reported by the senses otherwise than it exists in reality. Moreover, if something which does not exist in reality can be reported, why can it not likewise be reported through something which does not reside in the senses, but in those conditions which intervene on their own account? And so it will be possible to identify those conditions.

[Note: [Col. 0675D] For example, an oar bent in water. If an oar immersed in water sometimes appears broken, or a square tower appears round, this should not be attributed to a defect and error in the senses, but to the understanding. For sensation is a faculty devoid of reasoning, and therefore that appearance cannot deceive it; yet the same does not hold true of the understanding. The understanding participates in reason; and when it becomes aware that sensation has occurred, it does not proceed farther to examine it but renders a hasty judgment. Consequently, every error must be attributed to it, since it does not weigh the matters which belong to its own function. LE PR.]

For example, water is the cause of an oar’s appearing bent or broken in water. Indeed, outside the water the oar appears intact to sight. The delicacy of that substance, through which a mirror-like effect is produced from light, according as it is struck or moved, likewise distorts the straight line when it reflects the image.

[Col. 0675B]

Again, the conditions of distance in an open space compel the tower’s shape to deceive us: for the uniformity of the surrounding air, clothing the angles with equal light, effaces their lines. Similarly, the uniformity of a portico sharpens to a point at its far end, because the visual ray, crowded into a confined space, grows thinner precisely where it is prolonged.
