Likewise, the sky is joined to the sea where vision is exhausted; for as long as sight retains its force, it keeps them separate.

What else deceives hearing but the similarity of sounds? And if perfume afterward breathes less fragrance, wine tastes less strongly, and the pool feels less hot, in almost every case the first impression possesses the whole force.

[Note: [Col. 0675C] “The whole” (*totum*), Junius.]

As for the rough and the smooth, the hands and feet rightly disagree, since the former are delicate members and the latter calloused.

[Col. 0675C]

Thus, in this manner, no deception of the senses will be without a cause. But if causes deceive the senses, and opinions through the senses, falsehood must no longer be located either in the senses, which follow the causes, or in opinions, which are directed by the senses that follow those causes.

The insane see one person in another: Orestes sees his mother in his sister, Ajax sees Ulysses in a herd of cattle, while Athamas and Agave see wild beasts in their children. Will you reproach their eyes for this falsehood, or their madness?

Those who are jaundiced through an excess of bile find everything bitter. Will you therefore reproach their taste for betrayal, or their state of health?

[Note: [Col. 0675D] Those who are jaundiced through an excess of bile. George of Baetica also treated this passage against the Arians in his discussion of the Wisdom of God: “They behold nothing in it of the most unalloyed beauty,” he says, “just as no vision of truth exists for inflamed eyes, since their sight reports otherwise than accords with the reality of things. So too, if the excessive bitterness of his own bile has corrupted someone’s proper sense of taste, then, should he taste sweet honey, he slanders the honey’s sweetness as bitter, failing to recognize the defect of his own bitterness.” LE PR.]

[Col. 0676A]

All the senses, therefore, are overthrown or circumvented only temporarily, so that they lack the inherent property of falsehood. Indeed, the verdict of falsehood must no longer be assigned even to the causes themselves. For if these things occur according to reason, reason does not deserve to be called falsehood. What must occur in this way is not a lie.

Accordingly, if the causes themselves are freed from reproach, how much more are the senses, before which the causes now proceed free of blame! Indeed, truth, reliability, and integrity must be vindicated for the senses chiefly on this ground: that they report nothing other than what that rational condition commanded which causes a thing to be reported by the senses otherwise than it exists in reality.

What are you doing, most shameless Academy? You overthrow the whole condition of life; you disturb the entire order of nature; you blind the providence of God himself, who, for understanding, inhabiting, administering, and enjoying all his works, would in that case have placed over them deceitful and lying masters—the senses.

[Note: [Col. 0675D] “Most shameless Academic,” Pamelius and Rhenanus.]

[Col. 0676B]

Is not the entire creation supplied to us through them? Did not the world also receive through them its secondary equipment: so many arts, talents, studies, occupations, duties, commercial exchanges, remedies, plans, comforts, and every provision, refinement, and ornament of life? They have seasoned the entire savor of life, since through these senses man alone among all creatures is recognized as a rational animal, capable of understanding—and capable even of the Academy itself.

But Plato, to avoid affixing any attestation to the senses, therefore denies in the *Phaedrus*, speaking in the person of Socrates, that he can know himself, as the Delphic inscription admonishes; and in the *Theaetetus* he deprives himself both of knowing and of perceiving. In the *Phaedrus* he postpones the judgment of truth until after death, making it posthumous; yet, although not yet dead, he was philosophizing.

[Note: [Col. 0676D] “And in the *Phaedrus* he postpones it until after death.” I could not find the precise words in Plato’s *Phaedrus*, but the reference seems to me to concern his philosophical account there of souls which, after this life, are deemed worthy to contemplate in the supracelestial place that which truly exists, or truth itself, and which, after beholding the things that truly exist, return again to the inner region of heaven; all of them, indeed, are held by an intense desire to see where the plain of truth may be. PAM.—“And in the *Phaedrus*.” I am very nearly persuaded that *Phaedo* should be read, as in the following chapter, where he adduces the testimony. Observe also the words “he postpones it until after death.” For Socrates, being about to die, composed the *Phaedo* and philosophized after taking the poison. LE PR.]

[Col. 0676C]

We may not, we may not call these senses into doubt, lest their reliability in Christ too be called into question.

[Note: [Col. 0676C] Pamelius and Rhenanus write “We may not” only once.]

[Note: [Col. 0676D] “Be weighed,” Junius.]

Otherwise it might perhaps be said that he falsely saw Satan hurled down from heaven (Luke 10:18), or falsely heard the Father’s voice testifying about him (Matthew 3:17); or that he was deceived when he touched Peter’s mother-in-law (Matthew 8:15); or that he afterward perceived a different fragrance in the ointment which he accepted for his burial, and afterward a different taste in the wine which he consecrated in memory of his blood. For in this way Marcion too preferred to believe him a phantom, disdaining the reality of the whole body in him.

[Col. 0677A]

Yet not even in his Apostles was nature made the object of mockery. Both sight and hearing were trustworthy on the mountain (Matthew 17); the taste of that wine at the wedding in Galilee was trustworthy, although it had previously been water (John 2); and thereafter the touch of believing Thomas was trustworthy (John 20).

[Note: [Col. 0677D] The taste of that wine was trustworthy, although it had previously been water. Away, then, with that trifler Nicephorus, who speaks of Christ’s first miracle in such a way that someone might consider it the fraud of an illusionist: “Wine sprang from unseen clusters,” he says—*ex adēlōn botryōn oinos epēgazeto* (ἐξ ἀδήλων βοτρύων οἶνος ἐπηγάζετο). No: it sprang “from lowly water-jars”—*ex atimōn hydriōn* (ἐξ ἀτίμων ὑδριῶν). RIG.]

Recite John’s testimony: “What we have seen,” he says (1 John 1:1), “what we have heard, we have seen with our eyes, and our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life.” The testimony is certainly false if the natural sense of eyes, ears, and hands lies.

[Note: [Col. 0677D] “What we have seen,” he says, “what we have heard.” The Author perhaps cites this passage somewhat differently, so as to preserve the order of the senses of sight and hearing, and more clearly than it is read in Greek, Latin, or Syriac; namely: “What we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked upon.” PAM.]

## CHAPTER XVIII

I turn to the province of intellectual things: how Plato, after separating it from bodily things, recommended it to the heretics, having attained recognition before death.

[Col. 0677B]

For he says in the *Phaedo*:

> What, then, of the possession of wisdom itself? Will the body be an impediment, or not, if anyone takes it as a partner in the inquiry? I mean something like this: do sight and hearing possess any truth for human beings, or not? Do not even the poets continually mutter these things to us—that we neither hear anything certain nor see anything certain?

[Note: [Col. 0677C] “*Phaedrus*,” Paris and other editions.]

He was evidently also mindful of Epicharmus the comic poet:

[Note: [Col. 0677D] “The mind sees, the mind hears,” etc. Many agree that this is a verse of Epicharmus; it is nevertheless found in Plutarch’s short work *On Fortune*, but without the author’s name:]

Καὶ νοῦς ὁρῇ, καὶ ἀκούει, τὰ δ’ ἄλλα κωφὰ καὶ τυφλά (“It is the mind that sees and hears; all else is deaf and blind”). LE PR.] The mind sees, the mind hears; everything else is deaf and blind. And so, once again, he says that the man who is wise chiefly by means of his mind possesses the highest wisdom: he neither sets sight before himself nor draws any such sense into the mind, but, in his reflection, employs the pure mind itself to apprehend whatever is pure in things, withdrawing as far as possible from the eyes and ears and, so to speak, from the entire body, because it disturbs the soul and, whenever it associates with it, does not permit the soul to possess truth and wisdom. [Note: [Col. 0678C] “Withdrawing” (segressus); Rhenanus reads “having departed” (egressus).] We therefore see another apparatus being advanced in opposition to the bodily senses as being far more suitable—namely, the powers of the soul, which exercise the understanding of that truth [Note: [Col. 0678C] “Whose objects are not present.” The Author intimates why [Col. 0678D] Plato asserted the Ideas, of which he speaks presently. Nor is this far removed from Aristotle’s view, who in Books I and II of the *Metaphysics* states that Plato associated with Cratylus and was imbued with the opinion of Heraclitus, who maintained that everything falling under the senses is in flux and that no knowledge of such things could exist. Plato therefore established Ideas, which, since they always remain in the same condition, would provide stability for definitions and sciences. Aristotle himself dismisses this reasoning as futile, just as he ridicules the doctrine of Ideas in *Ethics* I, chapter 6. LAC.] whose objects are not present or subject to the bodily senses, but are far removed from common awareness, in secrecy, in the higher realms, and with God himself.

For Plato holds [Note: [Col. 0678D] “That there are certain invisible substances,” etc. Very many of the Fathers accept the Ideas. Those who reject them, however, reject them as they were understood by the Gnostics and the followers of Valentinus. These heretics appear to follow Plato in many matters, although I have also read the Ideas condemned by many Fathers in the sense taught by Aristotle: namely, that Plato admitted certain Ideas as separate universal natures, through participation in which individual things were produced. In this Aristotle either perpetrates or suffers an imposture, for this cannot be elicited from the Platonic writings. LE PR.] that there are certain invisible, incorporeal, supramundane, divine, and eternal substances, which he calls Ideas—that is, forms, exemplars, and causes of these natural things that are manifest and subject to the bodily senses. Those Ideas, he says, are the truths, while these things are their images. Do the heretical seeds of the Gnostics and Valentinians now begin to shine through? For from this source they seize upon the distinction between the bodily senses and the intellectual powers, and they even adapt to it the parable of the ten virgins (Matt. 25): the five foolish virgins are supposed to represent the bodily senses—foolish, of course, because they are easily deceived—whereas the wise virgins are supposed to express the mark of the intellectual powers, namely wisdom, because they attain that secret, heavenly truth established within the Pleroma—the mysteries of the heretical Ideas. For this is what their Aeons and genealogies are.

Thus they also divide sense-perception: intellectual perception belongs to their spiritual seed, while sensory perception belongs to the animal seed, because the latter can in no way apprehend spiritual things. Invisible things belong to the former; visible, lowly, and temporal things, which are encountered by sense and consist in images, belong to the latter. For these reasons, therefore, we have laid down beforehand that the mind is nothing other than something supplied and constituted by the soul, and that the spirit is nothing foreign, but simply what the soul itself is through breath. Any later addition, however, must be attributed to what either God or the devil subsequently breathes into it.

And now, regarding the distinction between sensory and intellectual things, we admit no distinction other than the diversity of the objects themselves: bodily and spiritual, visible and invisible, openly disclosed and secret. The former are assigned to sense and the latter to understanding, yet both are allotted to the service of the soul, which perceives bodily things through the body just as it understands incorporeal things through the mind—with the qualification that it also perceives while it understands. For is not perceiving also understanding, and is not understanding [Col. 0679A] [Note: [Col. 0679C] Wouwer inserts “not.”] also perceiving? Or [Note: [Col. 0679C] Rhenanus and Pamelius read “But.”] what will perception be except the understanding of the thing perceived? What will understanding be except the perception of the thing understood? Why these instruments of torture for tormenting simplicity and suspending truth? Who will produce for me a perception that does not understand what it perceives, or an understanding that does not perceive what it understands, so as to prove that either can exist without [Note: [Col. 0679C] From the Codex Agobardinus.] the other?

If bodily things are perceived while incorporeal things are understood, it is the classes of objects that are different, not the dwelling places of perception and understanding—that is, not the soul and the mind. After all, by what are bodily things perceived? If by the mind, then the mind is already sensory and not merely intellectual; for while it understands, it perceives, since if it does not perceive, neither does it understand. But if bodily things are perceived by the soul, then the power of the soul is already intellectual and not merely sensory; for while it perceives, it understands, since if it does not understand, neither does it perceive.

Likewise, by what are incorporeal things understood? If by the mind, where will the soul be? If by the soul, where will the mind be? Things that are distinct ought to be absent from one another when they perform their respective functions. You might indeed suppose that the mind is absent from the soul whenever we are so occupied in mind that we do not know that we have seen or heard something, [Note: [Col. 0679C] “Because the mind was elsewhere.” Pertinent in part is this passage of Blessed Gregory of Nyssa, *Philosophy*, Book IV, chapter 3: “Or when the mind attends to other things: for example, when someone has resolved to meet a friend and, just as he is about to address him, passes him by because his mind is distracted by other things. This is not an error of sight, but of understanding.” PAM.] because the mind was elsewhere. So much so, however, would I contend that the soul itself neither saw nor heard, because it was elsewhere together with its own power—that is, the mind. For when a man loses his mind, it is the soul that loses its mind: the mind is not then wandering away, but suffers together with the soul.

[Note: [Col. 0679D] “The fall, however, belongs principally to the soul.” These words appear to be adduced from the opinion of those who distinguished the mind from the soul, as also are the words, “when the soul has departed,” etc. Yet he adapts that argument to his own opinion in the words that follow: “But since it follows,” etc. PAM.—“The fall belongs principally to the soul.” He is not speaking from the opinion of those who distinguished the mind entirely from the soul, as Pamelius supposed, but from his own position against them. For they said that, while the soul remained intact, the mind and intellect could perish and fall; Tertullian, however, maintains that the mind follows the soul, and that when the soul perishes and falls, as the more fundamental entity, then the mind also collapses, since it rests upon the soul. LAC.] The fall, however, belongs principally to the soul. This is confirmed by the fact that, when the soul has departed, the mind is likewise no longer found in the man: thus the mind follows the soul everywhere and does not remain behind even at the end. But since the mind follows the soul and is attached to it, the understanding is likewise attached to the soul: the mind follows the soul, and the understanding is attached to the mind.

Let understanding now be superior to perception and the superior knower of mysteries, if you will. Provided that it too, like perception, is a proper power of the soul, it makes no difference to me—except when understanding is preferred to perception for the very purpose of treating it as more separate in proportion as it is declared superior. Then, after refuting the distinction, I must also blunt the claim of superiority, since it would ultimately lead [Note: [Col. 0679C] Semler and Pamelius read “which would also lead.”] to belief in a superior God. [Note: [Col. 0679D] “Belief in a superior God.” He strikes at the Marcionites and other Gnostics, who invented several gods and preferred one to another—the good god to the evil. He treats these matters extensively, however, in the books against Marcion. LAC.] [Note: [Col. 0680C] “But concerning God, on his own field, when dealing with the heretics.” He appears [Col. 0680D] to indicate his books against Marcion, which he was already contemplating and which are included below. For the first and second books deal especially with God. PAM.] But we shall contend with the heretics concerning God on the field proper to that subject. Our present title concerns the soul, and this is the place for showing that understanding must not be insidiously preferred.

For even if the things apprehended by understanding, such as spiritual things, are superior to those apprehended by sense, such as bodily things, the superiority will belong to the objects—namely, the higher things over the lower—not to understanding over sense. [Note: [Col. 0680D] “For how can understanding be preferred to sense?” Tertullian, relying artfully upon the confidence of his genius, is accustomed, in order to persuade us of what is right, to bend toward the contrary and oblique side, as those who straighten a crooked rod twist it in the opposite direction. Thus here he appears to equate sense with understanding against those who unduly debased the former and exalted the latter. Yet although, when the faculties are compared in themselves with one another, understanding excels sense, when they are referred to their first root and origin, as he has done in this chapter, neither excels: for the source and original dwelling place of both is the same thing—namely, the soul—not the soul and mind as different things, as his opponents had supposed. The proofs Tertullian adds may also be referred to this point, so that the dependence of understanding upon the senses may be an argument for the unity of their principle and root, and consequently for the equality of their origin. LAC.] For how can understanding be preferred to sense, when it is instructed by sense in the knowledge of truths? If truths are apprehended through images—that is, if invisible things are known through visible things—since the Apostle also writes to us (Rom. 1:20), “For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are seen when understood through the things that have been made”; and since Plato says for the heretics, “The face of hidden things is the things that appear,” and “This world must in every respect be a kind of image of some other world” [Note: [Col. 0680C] Francius adds “that which for itself”; Pamelius reads “that which for itself.”]—then understanding evidently employs sense as its guide, author, and primary foundation, and cannot attain truths without it. How, then, will it be superior to that through which it exists, which it needs, and to which it owes everything it apprehends?

Thus both points are established: understanding must neither be preferred to sense—for whatever is established through something else is inferior to that thing itself—nor separated from sense; for whatever exists through something else exists together with it.

## CHAPTER XIX

Nor should we pass over those who deprive the soul of understanding even for a brief period. For in this way they prepare the road for subsequently introducing understanding into the soul, just as they also introduce [Note: [Col. 0680C] Junius deletes “also.”] [Col. 0680C] the mind, from which, of course, understanding proceeds. [Note: [Col. 0680C] Francius reads: “so that the soul, namely.”] They maintain that infancy consists of the soul alone, by which it merely lives, without at the same time possessing intelligence, because not everything that lives is intelligent. Trees, after all, live without being intelligent, according to Aristotle and anyone else who attributes animal substance [Note: [Col. 0680D] “Animal substance.” He uses “animal substance” for the animal or vegetative power. PAM.] universally—a thing which, according to us, is the private possession of the human being, not merely as a work of God, as all other things are, but as the breath of God, which this alone is. We say that it is born [Note: [Col. 0681C] “With all its equipment.” As though “with everything fitted out and supplied,” “with all its endowment,” “with all that belongs to it.” For so he writes above. Augustine, in Book II of *Questions on Exodus*, question 47, indicates that these expressions bore this meaning particularly among Africans: “The Greek,” he says, “has ἀποσκευήν (‘equipment’), where the Latin translator rendered *substantia* (‘substance’), which our writers sometimes translate as *census* (‘endowment’), just as we have now chosen to say *instructus* (‘equipment’).” Accordingly, the passage in our Septimius’s *Apology* should also be read thus: “In dress, food, equipment, property, and finally even speech, you have renounced your ancestors.” RIG.] with all its equipment.

And if we are referred to trees, we shall embrace the example. For even while they are not yet saplings, but still merely stems and even now only shoots, there arises together with them from the planting holes the distinctive power of their soul. For a time, however, it is delayed, consolidating and maturing together with its own strength until age completes [Note: [Col. 0681C] Semler and Oberthür omit “and maturing together.”] [Note: [Col. 0681C] Pamelius and Rhenanus read “fully completes.”] the condition in which its nature performs its function. Otherwise, from where do branches immediately begin to be grafted upon them, leaves to be formed, buds to swell, little flowers to be adorned, and juices to be seasoned, unless the entire equipment of their kind lies at rest within them and, as it advances through their parts, grows larger? Therefore they derive intelligence from the same source from which they derive life, possessing from their own infancy the distinctive properties both of living and of understanding.

For I see even a vine that is still tender and immature, yet already understands its work and desires to cling to something upon which it may lean [Note: [Col. 0681C] Pamelius and Rhenanus read *innixa*, with the same sense.] and fasten itself so as to grow. Indeed, without waiting for instruction from the farmer, without a reed, [Note: [Col. 0681D] “Without a forked support” (*cervus*). Rigaltius preferred to preserve the word *cervus* rather than substitute *cornus* (“cornel tree”) or *ornus* (“ash tree”). For the subject here is vine-props, not trees friendly to the vine, such as the ash and cornel. *Cervi* are forked sticks shaped like the letter V, from their resemblance to the antlers of a stag, as Marcus Varro teaches in Book IV. LE PR.] without a forked support [Note: [Col. 0681C] Pamelius and Francius read “cornel”; others, “ash.”], if it touches anything, it will spontaneously coil around it—and indeed more vigorously according to its own disposition than according to your direction: it hastens to make itself secure.

I also see ivies, however young you please, immediately striving upward and, with no one leading them, hanging aloft, because they would rather advance over walls as a woven woodland than be trampled on the ground—choosing an injury voluntarily. Conversely, see how those [Note: [Col. 0681D] “For which it goes badly with a building.” Similarly, in *On the Pallium*: “It goes well from heaven.” RIG.] for which a building is harmful withdraw from it as they grow! How they flee! [Note: [Col. 0681C] Rhenanus, Pamelius, and Semler read “a refuge.”] You would perceive that the branches [Note: [Col. 0681C] Another reading is “for the branches”; Junius reads “directed.”] are directed elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0682C] The Paris edition reads the singular “directed.”], and from their separation from the wall you would understand the animation of the tree. [Note: [Col. 0681D] “It is content with smallness.” The Codex Agobardinus reads: “Self-restraint is small...” RIG.] It is content [Note: [Col. 0682C] Pamelius, Rhenanus, and Semler read “content with its own.”] with the smallness it learned from the beginning as a most provident plant, [Col. 0681C] fearing [Note: [Col. 0682C] Pamelius, Rhenanus, and Semler read “of one fearing.”] even collapse.

Why should I not argue for these forms of wisdom and knowledge in trees? Let them live, as the philosophers wish; let them understand, as the philosophers do not wish. Let even the infancy of a piece of wood possess understanding [Note: [Col. 0682C] Pamelius and Rhenanus read “Let them also understand the infancy of a piece of wood.”]—how much more the infancy of a human being, whose soul, like a kind of shoot drawn into propagation from the stock of Adam and entrusted to the female’s generative furrows with all its equipment, will bud forth in understanding as well as in sense?

I am lying if the infant, as soon as [Note: [Col. 0682C] “It greeted life with a wail.” Pliny treats these sufficiently unhappy beginnings and first conditions of human beings in the preface to Book VII. LE PR.] it greeted life with a wail, did not by that very act testify that it perceived and understood that it had been born, simultaneously inaugurating all the senses there: sight by light, hearing by sound, taste by moisture, smell by air, and touch by earth. Thus that first cry is forced out by the first impulses both of the senses and of understanding. More than this: [Note: [Col. 0682D] “From its foresight of a tearful life.” What is more deserving of tears than that life which begins in wretched wailing, pain, hunger, thirst, and a thousand other hardships; which is spent amid the same and still greater hardships; and which has death as its end? LE PR.] some interpret that plaintive cry as an omen of the hardships foreseen in a tearful life, so that the infant must be regarded as possessing foreknowledge from the very entrance of birth, much less merely understanding. [Note: [Col. 0682C] Pamelius, Rhenanus, and Semler insert “not indeed.”]

Thereafter it tests its mother by scent, examines its nurse by scent, and recognizes its attendant by scent, fleeing unfamiliar breasts, rejecting unknown beds, and seeking no one except through familiarity. From where does it derive its judgment of novelty and habit if it possesses no intelligence? From where its capacity to be offended and soothed if it possesses no understanding? It would be sufficiently astonishing if infancy were naturally ensouled (*animosa*) while lacking a mind (*animus*), and naturally affectionate while lacking understanding. Yet Christ, by drawing praise from the mouths of nursing infants and little children, did not declare either childhood or infancy dull-witted: the former (Matt. 21), coming forward with its acclaim, was able to offer testimony to him; the latter (Matt. 2), slaughtered for his sake, certainly felt the violence.

## CHAPTER XX

Here, therefore, we also conclude that all the soul’s natural properties, as substantial attributes of it, are present within the soul itself and proceed and develop together with it from the moment the soul itself takes its origin. So too says [Note: [Col. 0682D] “Seneca, often one of ours.” Because he frequently thinks in accordance with Christians. RIG.—“Seneca, often one of ours.” That is, one who agrees with us on many points. I would not dare affirm that letters of Seneca to Blessed Paul, and likewise of Blessed Paul to Seneca, ever existed, although Saint Jerome testifies to it; for if any such letters existed, they were spurious. Nor should anyone object that Saint Jerome, a man of refined judgment, could not easily have been deceived. For when he calls Seneca a man of the most abstemious life, who does not recognize that he was deceived? LE PR.] Seneca, often one of ours: “[Note: [Col. 0682D] “The seeds of all arts and stages of life are implanted in us, and God, the teacher, brings forth our natural capacities from their concealment.” These words are from Seneca, *On Benefits*, Book IV, chapter 6. LE PR.] The seeds of all arts and stages of life are implanted in us, and God, the teacher, brings forth our natural capacities from their concealment.” He brings them forth, of course, from seeds implanted and hidden throughout infancy, which are seeds of understanding also; for from them our natural capacities are produced.

Moreover, just as [Note: [Col. 0683C] Pamelius and others read “and” instead of “just as.”] the seeds of crops have one form for each kind, while their developments vary—some emerge in an unimpaired condition, some yield even better results, and some degenerate according to the condition of the climate and soil, the character of the labor and care, the course of the seasons, and the license of accidents—so we may regard the soul as uniform in seed but multiform in fruit. For here too locality makes a difference. [Note: [Col. 0683D] “It is reported that dull and brutish people are born at Thebes.” He means Thebes in Boeotia. Indeed, this is so proverbial that some think the Boeotians were named from their grossness of intellect, and the expressions “a Boeotian pig,” “a Boeotian ear,” and—more directly relevant here—“a Boeotian intellect” passed into proverbs. Erasmus discusses these at length in his *Adages*; he also thinks it derives from the fact that in the German and British languages we call dull and brutish people *Bot*, that is, Boeotians. PAM.] It is reported that dull and brutish people are born at Thebes; [Note: [Col. 0683D] “At Athens, those most acute in wisdom and speech.” Relevant here is the statement of Cicero in his speech *For Flaccus*: “The Athenians are present, from whom civilization, learning, religion, agriculture, rights, and laws are thought to have arisen and been distributed throughout every land.” Likewise, in Plato’s *Protagoras*, Athens is called the prytaneum of wisdom. Finally, in the first dialogue of *The Laws*, Plato calls it a city devoted to eloquence and abundant discourse. PAM.] at Athens, those most acute in wisdom and speech. In the district of Colytus children speak a month earlier, their tongues precocious. Plato, accordingly, asserts in the *Timaeus* that when Minerva founded that city, she considered nothing other than the nature of the region, which promised minds of that kind. Hence he himself, in *The Laws*, directs Megillus and Clinias to procure a suitable site for the city they are to found.

Empedocles, however, located the cause of an acute or obtuse disposition in the quality of the blood, while deriving its perfection and development from teaching and discipline. Yet the distinctive traits of nations have now become common knowledge. The comic poets ridicule the Phrygians as timid; Sallust lashes the vain Moors and the ferocious Dalmatians; even the Apostle (Titus 1:12) brands the Cretans as liars. [Note: [Col. 0683D] “The Cretans as liars.” The Cretans had a bad reputation for lying. The scholiast on Callimachus’s *Hymn to Zeus*, from which passage the blessed Apostle cites the words in Titus 1, says: παροιμία ἐστὶ τὸ κρητίζειν ἐπὶ τοῦ ψεύδεσθαι, ἀπὸ Ἰδομενέως τοῦ κρητὸς ῥηθεῖσα· ὃς λαχὼν μερίσαι τοῖς Ἕλλησιν τὰ λάφυρα Ἰλίου, τὰ κρείττω ἑαυτῷ περιεποιήσατο—“‘To Cretanize’ is a proverbial expression for lying, said with reference to the Cretan Idomeneus, who, when it fell to him to distribute the spoils of Troy among the Greeks, reserved the better things for himself.” “To Cretanize”—that is, to lie—became proverbial; it arose from Idomeneus, a native of Crete, who, when he was to divide the spoils of Troy among the Greeks, reserved the better things for himself. LE PR.]

Perhaps something is also contributed by the body and its health: corpulence impedes wisdom, thinness assists it; paralysis dissipates the mind, consumption preserves it. How much more must those things be regarded as accidents which, apart from [Note: [Col. 0683C] Pamelius, Semler, and Oberthür read “in relation to.”] bodily condition and health, either sharpen or dull the mind! Teaching, discipline, the arts, experience, occupations, and studies sharpen it; ignorance, idleness, sloth, lusts, inexperience, leisure, and vices dull it. Above all these stand, if there are any others also, the ruling powers.

And indeed, according to us, the Lord God and the rival devil rule; according to common opinion, providence [Note: [Col. 0683C] Pamelius, Semler, and Rhenanus read “both providence and.”], fate and necessity, fortune [Note: [Col. 0683C] Rigaltius and the Venetian edition read “of fortune.”], and freedom of choice. For the philosophers distinguish these things, while we have already promised under its own title to discuss them according to the faith.

It is apparent how many things have variously disposed the one nature of the soul so that they are commonly attributed to nature, although they are not species but fortunes of one nature and substance—that nature, namely, which God bestowed upon Adam and made the matrix of all. And they will indeed be fortunes, not species, of one substance, because this moral diversity, as great as it is now, did not exist to the same extent in Adam himself, the founder of the race. For all these things would have had to exist in him as in the fountainhead of nature and to have flowed from him in all their diversity, if the diversity had belonged to nature itself.

## CHAPTER XXI

Therefore, if the nature of the soul was uniform from the beginning in Adam, before so many different dispositions arose, it is not made multiform [Note: [Col. 0684C] Rhenanus and Pamelius add “because it is uniform.”] by those many dispositions. Nor, then, is it [Note: [Col. 0684C] Rigaltius and the Venetian edition read “nor in what respect”; the Codex Agobardinus reads “nor fourfold.”] threefold, so that the Valentinian [Note: [Col. 0684D] “The Valentinian trinity.” This is a trinity of the human being, not of God; for those heretics made the human being spiritual, animal or fleshly, and earthly or material. LE PR.] trinity may still be demolished—a trinity which is itself not recognized in Adam.

For what was spiritual in him? If it was because he prophesied that great mystery concerning Christ and the Church (Gen. 2): “This is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh; she shall be called woman. Therefore a man shall leave father and mother and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh”—this came upon him afterward, [Note: [Col. 0684D] “When God cast madness upon him.” Above: “He underwent the accident of spirit, for ecstasy fell upon him—the power of the Holy Spirit, which produces prophecy.” RIG.—“He cast madness upon him.” This comes from the Septuagint translators, who have ἔκστασιν (“ecstasy”) at Genesis 2. Thus the Author himself in chapter 11 called Adam’s sleep an ecstasy, and he means nothing else by “madness.” LAC.] when God cast madness upon him, the spiritual power in which prophecy consists.

If evil also appeared in him through the commission of transgression, this too must not be accounted natural, since he committed it at the serpent’s instigation (Gen. 3); it was no more natural than it was material, because we have already excluded the claim that it derived from matter. Therefore, if neither the spiritual nor what is called the material was properly present in him—for the material would have been present if the seed of evil [Note: [Col. 0684C] Semler and Oberthür read “even if.”] had come from matter—it remains that only one thing was in him, namely what is reckoned animal and natural; and this we maintain was simple and uniform in condition.

It plainly remains to ask whether that which is called natural should be believed capable of change. For the same people deny that nature is convertible, so that they may fix their trinity within the respective properties of its members: because a good tree does not bear bad fruit, nor a bad tree good fruit; and no one gathers figs from thorns or grapes from brambles. If this is so, therefore, God will be unable to raise up children of Abraham from stones (Matt. 3), or to make the offspring of vipers produce fruits of repentance; and the Apostle was mistaken when he wrote (Eph. 5), “You too were once darkness”; and (Eph. 2), “We too were once by nature children of wrath”; and (1 Cor. 6), “Such also were you, but you have been washed.”

But the holy sayings will never disagree. For a bad tree will not produce good fruit (Luke 6) if it is not grafted; and a good tree will produce bad fruit if it is not cultivated. Stones will become children of Abraham if they are formed in the faith of Abraham; and the offspring of vipers will produce the fruit of repentance if they spit out the poisons of wickedness. This will be the power of divine grace, which is certainly more powerful than nature and has within us, subject to itself, the free power of choice called αὐτεξούσιον (*autexousion*, “self-determination”). Since this power is itself both natural and mutable, in whatever direction it is turned, nature is converted. [Note: [Col. 0685C] Rhenanus and Semler add “and.”] [Note: [Col. 0685C] “That τὸ αὐτεξούσιον is present within us.” Thus free choice is named among the Fathers and Philosophers. Nazianzen calls the human being τῷ αὐτεξουσίῳ τιμηθείς, “honored with free choice.” LAC.]

We have already shown both Marcion and Hermogenes that τὸ αὐτεξούσιον (*to autexousion*, “the power of self-determination”) is naturally present within us. What, then, [Note: [Col. 0685C] Semler and Rhenanus omit “also.”] if the condition of nature must also be defined in such a way that a twofold classification is established: of things born and unborn, made and unmade? Accordingly, whatever is established as born and made will possess a nature capable of alteration, for it will be able both to be reborn and to be remade. But the unborn and unmade will remain immovable. Since this belongs to God alone—as alone unborn and unmade, and for that reason immortal and unchangeable—it is settled that the nature of all other things, as born and made, is convertible and mutable. Thus, even if a trinity were to be ascribed to the soul, it would be attributed to a change arising from accident, not to the constitution of nature.

## CHAPTER XXII

Hermogenes has already heard from us the soul’s other natural properties, together with the defense and proof of them by which the soul is known to derive from God rather than from matter. Here they will only be named, lest they appear to have been omitted. For we assigned to the soul freedom of choice, as we wrote above, and dominion over things, [Note: [Col. 0685D] “And divination.” That is, natural divination, whether through dreams or other premonitions. Carneades argued against divination with many lines of reasoning. Tertullian, however, chiefly points to spontaneous impulses of the mind, which are evident to everyone: namely, when the mind, as though foreknowing future evil or good, is affected by grief or joy before the bodily senses detect it through certain signs. For, as Seneca says:

> A savage storm looms within the mind,  
> When calm waters swell though there is no wind.

He skillfully describes this mode of foreboding in the *Thyestes*, before Atreus’s deadly banquet. Thus the breast leaps and tears flow against one’s will, because a secret spur and warning arouses them within. LAC.] and sometimes divination, apart from that which comes through God’s grace [Col. 0686A] from [Note: [Col. 0685C] Perhaps “and” should be read instead of “from.” The editors.] prophecy.

And so I shall now withdraw from this reconsideration of its arrangement [Note: [Col. 0685D] “That I may complete its order.” That is, finish and perfect it, as is his custom in *Apology*, chapter 3, and very frequently elsewhere. LAC.] so that I may complete the account of its order. We define the soul as born from the breath of God; [Note: [Col. 0685D] “Immortal.” Although he does not treat this expressly, since at that time it lay outside controversy, it is nevertheless frequently mentioned in this book: namely, in chapters 2, [Col. 0686C] 3, 6, 9, and 14, and below in chapters 24, 38, 45, 51, 53, and 54. PAM.] immortal; [Note: [Col. 0686C] “Corporeal.” Although the assertion that the soul is corporeal belongs among his paradoxes, he treated it extensively above in chapters 5, 6, 7, and 8. PAM.] corporeal; [Note: [Col. 0686D] “Endowed with form.” That it is endowed with form is another paradox, which you will also find treated above in chapter 9. PAM.] endowed with form; simple in substance; capable of suffering in its own right [Note: [Col. 0685C] Rigaltius and the Venetian edition read “wise.”]; developing in various ways; free in choice; [Note: [Col. 0686D] “Subject to accidents.” He alludes to the soul’s gradual progress in wisdom. PAM.] subject to accidents [Note: [Col. 0686C] Francius reads the singular, “to an accident.”]; mutable through its dispositions; rational; ruling; divining; and propagated from one soul. It follows now that we consider how it is propagated from one—that is, whence, when, and by what means it is derived.

## CHAPTER XXIII

Some believe that they have descended from heaven, with as much conviction as they confidently promise that they will return there. Thus Saturninus, the disciple of the Simonian Menander, introduced the doctrine that the human being was made by angels. He asserted that at first their work, futile, feeble, and unstable, writhed on the earth like a worm because it lacked the strength to stand; that afterward, through the mercy of the supreme power, in whose image—though an image not fully perceived—it had rashly been constructed, it received a little spark of life, which awakened and raised it, endowed it with firmer vitality, and after life’s departure would carry it back to its original matrix.

Carpocrates likewise claims so much for himself from the higher realms that his disciples equate their own souls even with Christ, much less with the Apostles, and prefer them whenever they please. They suppose these souls were similarly conceived from a sublime power that despises the ruling powers of the world.

Apelles reports that souls were enticed by earthly foods from their supercelestial abodes by the fiery angel who is the God of Israel [Note: [Col. 0686C] Pamelius and Rhenanus read “of the Israelites.”] and our God, and that he thereafter fashioned sinful flesh around them.

Valentinus’s swarm fastens the seed of Sophia upon the soul, [Note: [Col. 0686D] “Through which they recognize the stories and Milesian tales.” More celebrated fables are called “Milesian,” either from the vanity of the Milesians because of Apollo’s oracle, on which see Strabo, *Geography*, Book XIV, or from Milesian roses, which were highly prized. LE PR.] through which they recognize the stories and [Note: [Col. 0686C] Perhaps “equally,” or “and those,” according to Latinius.] Milesian tales of their Aeons from the images of visible things.

I sincerely grieve [Note: [Col. 0686D] “That Plato became the provider of condiments for all heretics.” The Author often slanders ancient philosophy as though it were the storehouse and fountain of heresies, as in chapter 7 of *The Prescription*. Hence, in chapter 8 of *Against Hermogenes*, he calls the philosophers the patriarchs of the heretics. From this one doctrine concerning the origin of souls, Giovanni Battista Crispo, Book II, question 1, observes which heresies Plato shaped: for the Menandrians, Saturninians, Enthusiasts, Carpocratians, Valentinians, Apellites, Seleucians, Messalians, Avicenna, and Ramon Llull appear to have been deceived by Plato’s teaching concerning the origin of souls. LAC.] that Plato became the provider of condiments for all heretics.

For his too is the statement in the *Phaedo* that souls departing from here go there, and from there come here; likewise, in the *Timaeus*, that the offspring of God [Note: [Col. 0687C] Pamelius and Rhenanus read “sprouts” (*germina*).], having been entrusted with the generation of mortals, received the immortal beginning of the soul and congealed a mortal body around it; and then, that this world is the image of some other world. In order to commend all these things to belief [Note: [Col. 0687C] The Paris edition reads “he commends.”], he devised a new argument: [Note: [Col. 0687C] “And that the soul formerly associated with God in the higher realms.” I could find nothing else in Plato’s *Timaeus* pertinent here except the statement that, after the supreme God and Craftsman had established the universe, he divided the souls into a number equal to that of the stars, assigned each one to a particular star, placed them as though upon a vehicle, showed them the nature of the universe, and expounded the laws of fate to them; and that the first origin would be ordained alike for all, but that the souls, once sown into the instruments appropriate to each at their proper times—namely, bodies—were required to produce the living creature most devoted to divine worship. Since nowhere in that book does he say that the soul rehearses here, from the exemplars, the things that it formerly knew, I think this refers rather to the *Phaedo*, which he also mentioned shortly before and in which both teachings may be found. PAM.] namely, that the soul had formerly lived with God in the higher realms in communion with the Ideas; that it then crossed over from there to here; and that here it rehearses, from their exemplars, the things it knew before: μαθήσεις ἀναμνήσεις—that is, “acts of learning are acts of recollection.” [Note: [Col. 0687D] “That is, acts of learning are acts of recollection.” This passage was undoubtedly taken from Plato’s *Phaedo*, not from the *Timaeus*. For there Cebes says: “But according also to that doctrine, Socrates, if it is true, which you are frequently accustomed to advance, ὅτι ἡμῖν ἡ μάθησις οὐκ ἄλλο τι ἢ ἀνάμνησις τυγχάνει οὖσα”—that is, if we translate literally with Tertullian, “that for us learning is nothing other than recollection,” for which Plato’s translator rendered, “that learning is nothing other for us than remembering.” “According to this,” he continues, “it is necessary that at some former time we learned the things we now recollect. But this could not occur unless our soul existed somewhere before it entered this form.” Soon afterward Simmias acknowledges the same thing there, and not merely Cebes but Socrates himself endeavors to confirm this paradox by many arguments. The Author, however, refutes it admirably in the next chapter. PAM.]

For souls coming from there to here, he says, forget the things among which they previously existed and then, once instructed by these visible things, remember them. Since, therefore, Plato employs an argument of this kind to insinuate the doctrines that the heretics borrow from him, I shall have sufficiently beaten back the heretics if I demolish Plato’s argument.

## CHAPTER XXIV
First, I shall not concede that the soul is capable of forgetfulness, because Plato has granted it such divinity that it is made equal to God. He makes it unbegotten—a point which alone I could have marshaled as evidence of complete divinity. He adds that it is immortal, incorruptible, incorporeal—because he believed God also to be such—invisible, incapable of being represented, uniform, sovereign, rational, and intellectual. What more could he have asserted of the soul if he had called it God?

We, however, who attach nothing to God as an appendage, by this very fact assess the soul as far beneath God: we acknowledge that it was born and is therefore of a more diluted divinity and a more meager felicity; that it is breath, not spirit; and that, even if it is immortal, as belonging to divinity, it is [Col. 0687C] nevertheless capable of suffering, as belonging to birth. Hence it was capable of deviation from the beginning, and consequently also liable to forgetfulness. Enough has been said about this in the controversy with [Col. 0688A] Hermogenes.

[Note: [Col. 0688C] **Enough has been said about this in the controversy with Hermogenes.** He alludes to the book *On the Origin of the Soul against Hermogenes*, fragments of which survive. PAM.]

Moreover, a soul that might deservedly be regarded as God through the complete equality of all its attributes will be subject to no passion, and thus not to forgetfulness either, since forgetfulness is as great an injury as the glory of that to which it does injury—namely, memory. Plato himself called memory the preservation of sense-perceptions and intellectual conceptions, and Cicero proclaimed it the treasury of every branch of learning.

[Note: [Col. 0687C] “God” added here by Fran.]

[Note: [Col. 0688C] “Of memory”: Jun.]

[Note: [Col. 0688D] **Cicero proclaimed it the treasury of every branch of learning.** In Book I of *On the Orator* he calls memory “the treasury of all things.” See also Cassiodorus, *Variae* V, epistle 22, and *On the Soul*, chapter 12. LAC.]

The question will no longer be whether so divine a soul could have lost its memory, but whether, after losing it, it can recover it again. For if it has forgotten what it ought not to have forgotten, I do not know whether it is capable of recollecting it. Thus both capacities will suit my soul, but not Plato’s.

At the second stage I shall object: you make the soul naturally possessed of those Ideas, do you not? “Indeed, naturally,” you say. No one, therefore, will concede that a natural knowledge of natural arts can perish. [Col. 0688B] Knowledge of studies may perish; knowledge of teachings and disciplines may perish; perhaps even talents and dispositions may perish. These appear to belong to nature, but they do not, because, as we stated beforehand, they are constituted by accidents according to places, forms of education, bodily constitutions and states of health, ruling powers, and freedoms of choice. But knowledge of natural things does not fail even in beasts.

Certainly a lion will forget its ferocity once forestalled by training in gentleness, and, with the full display of its mane, will become the pet of some Queen Berenice, licking the blemishes from her cheeks with its tongue: its habits will forsake the beast, but its knowledge of natural things will remain.

[Note: [Col. 0688D] **With the full display of its mane.** That is, with all its ornament. Perhaps he is alluding to the celestial sign of Leo, at whose tail are seven stars which astrologers call Berenice’s locks or hair. LAC.—**With the full display of its mane.** The pet of Berenice. We have noted more than once that the Author uses *suggestus* for ornament. Aelian, *On Animals* V.39, relates that a lion trained to gentleness became the pet of a certain Queen Berenice. He says “a certain” both in accordance with his usual manner of speaking and because there were several queens of that name. PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0688C] “Trumpets” (*tubarum*): Fran.]

It will not forget its natural food, its natural remedies, or its natural fears. Even if the queen offers it fish and cakes, it will desire meat; [Col. 0688C] even if she compounds an antidote for it when it is sick, the lion will seek an ape; and even if no hunting spear withstands it, it will nevertheless fear a cock.

[Note: [Col. 0688D] **If she compounds an antidote for it when it is sick.** He alludes to the words of Pliny, Book VII, chapter 40: “It experiences only the sickness of loss of appetite, in which it is treated by affront, through the wantonness of apes tied to it driving it into a rage.” PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0688D] **It will nevertheless fear a cock.** This too is from Pliny in the same place: “And yet,” he says, “this animal, of such a kind and so savage, is terrified by wheels spun round, by empty chariots, by the crests of barnyard fowl, and still more by their crowing.” PAM.]

[Col. 0689A] Likewise, in the human being—perhaps the most forgetful of all creatures—the knowledge of natural things alone will persist unerased, precisely because it alone is natural: one always remembers that in hunger one must eat, in thirst one must drink, that one must see with the eyes, hear with the ears, smell with the nostrils, taste with the mouth, and touch with the hand. These, surely, are the senses which philosophy depreciates by giving preference to intellectual things. Therefore, if the natural knowledge of sensible things remains, how does the knowledge of intellectual things, which is regarded as superior, perish?

Whence, then, comes that power of forgetfulness which precedes recollection? “From the great length of time,” he says.

[Note: [Col. 0689D] **From the great length of time, he says.** He alludes to those words of Plato in the *Phaedo*: “Is it not recollection, especially when this happens to someone concerning things which, because of the passage of time and because he has not seen them for a long while…?” The Author rendered this “from the great length of time.” But the Author beautifully refutes even this on the ground that Plato called the soul unbegotten and therefore eternal, without any beginning in time. PAM.]

That is most improvidently said. For a quantity of time will have no bearing upon a thing said to be unbegotten and therefore believed, above all, to be eternal. For what is eternal, precisely because it is also unbegotten, admits neither a beginning nor an end of time and suffers no measure of time. That for which there is no measure of time is neither subject to time through any change nor exposed to that force arising from a great length of time. [Col. 0689B]

[Note: [Col. 0689C] “Of time” (*temporis*): Pam., Rhen.]

[Note: [Col. 0689C] “Nor is the force the same through a great length of time”: Pam., Rhen.; “in the multitude”: Lat.]

If time is the cause of forgetfulness, why does memory fail from the moment when the soul is introduced into the body, as though only from that point onward did the soul endure time, although it unquestionably existed before the body and certainly did not exist without time? Once it has entered the body, does it forget immediately or some time later? If immediately, what great length of time can there be when time has not yet begun to be reckoned? Infancy, presumably. If some time later, then during that interval before the time of forgetfulness the soul will still act with memory. And what sort of thing is it that it should later forget and later still recollect once again?

At whatever time forgetfulness assails it, how great a measure of time will even this be regarded as? The whole course of life, I think, will not be enough [Col. 0689C] to overthrow the memory of so great an age before the body.

[Note: [Col. 0689D] “To turn” rather than “to overturn”: Pam., Rhen., Seml., Oberth.]

But Plato shifts the cause once more to the body—as though it were credible that a created substance could extinguish the power of an uncreated one. Yet bodies have great and numerous differences according to nation, size, condition, age, and health. Are differences in forgetfulness therefore also to be posited?

[Note: [Col. 0690C] “Forgetfulness” in the singular: Venet., incorrectly.]

But forgetfulness is uniform; therefore multiform corporeality will not be the cause of a uniform result.

Again, many proofs, as Plato himself bears witness, have established the soul’s power of divination—proofs which we have already set before Hermogenes. [Col. 0690A] Indeed, there is no human being who does not sometimes feel that his own soul is prescient, foretelling either an omen, a danger, or a joy. If the body does not obstruct divination, I think it will not hinder memory either. Certainly, in the very same body souls both forget and recollect.

If some property of the body induces forgetfulness, how will it admit forgetfulness’s contrary, recollection? For recollection after forgetfulness is itself a revived memory. Why does that which opposes the first memory not also resist the second?

[Note: [Col. 0690C] “Resist” (*refragetur*): Rhen., Pam.]

Finally, who ought to recollect more readily than little children, since their souls are more recent, not yet submerged in domestic and public cares, and devoted solely to those studies whose learning is supposed to constitute recollection? Indeed, why do we not all recollect equally, since we all forget equally, but philosophers alone do so? [Col. 0690B] Not even all of them do.

[Note: [Col. 0690C] “Not even they” (*nec ii*): Lat.]

Plato alone, it seems, in so great a forest of nations and so broad a meadow of sages, both forgot and recollected the Ideas.

[Note: [Col. 0689D] **Both forgot and recollected the Ideas.** The passage concerns Plato, who first brought dreams about the Ideas into the light, writing on that subject the dialogue entitled *Parmenides* and introducing extremely frequent mention of them elsewhere, as we have also noted above. PAM.]

Therefore, if this principal argument is in no way sound, the whole theory to which it was applied is overthrown along with it: namely, that souls should be believed unbegotten, to have lived in the heavens, to have been conscious there of divine things, to have been brought down from there, and to have recollected them here—plainly furnishing opportunities for the heretics.

## CHAPTER XXV

Now I shall return to the subject from which this digression arose, so that I may explain how souls issue in abundance from a single soul, when and where they are received, and by what principle. With respect to this question, it makes no difference whether it comes from a philosopher, a heretic, or the common people. For professors of the truth, [Col. 0690C] there is no difference among its adversaries, especially those as audacious as, first, the men who presume that the soul is not conceived in the womb, nor compacted and produced together with the molding of the flesh, but is impressed upon the infant from outside only after the child has been delivered and is not yet alive.

[Note: [Col. 0690D] **The soul is not conceived in the womb, etc.** Tertullian attributes this opinion to the Stoics; but Aëtius adds Diogenes and Herophilus, and even Empedocles, in his book *On the History of Philosophy*. LAC.]

[Note: [Col. 0690D] “And” added by Pam., Rhen.]

[Note: [Col. 0690D] **Is impressed upon it from outside.** Lucretius, Book III, presents the opinion of the Stoics, whom Tertullian presently adduces in support of this tenet:

> But if perhaps you think that, introduced from without,  
> The soul is accustomed to permeate our limbs.

They used the term “is impressed” or “is introduced” so as not to say that the soul is born; Lactantius, Book III, chapter 18. LAC.]

They hold, moreover, that the seed separated through intercourse in the female organs, and quickened by natural movement, thickens into the substance of the flesh alone; and that, once it has been brought forth, still smoking from the furnace of the womb and relaxed by heat, it is struck by the chill of the air just as glowing iron is when plunged into cold water, and so seizes the vital force and produces vocal sound.

[Note: [Col. 0690D] **And produces vocal sound.** Some thought that the soul, cast down from its celestial dwelling, then began to inhabit the earthly body, and that the infant was consequently forced to suffer pain and cry, as Alexander of Aphrodisias reports in *Problems* 64 while answering the question, “Why do infants cry as soon as they are born?” His solution is this: “Because their sensation and nature are, as it were, in a foreign land. For they pass from the warm and soft body of the womb itself into the cold air. Perhaps, however, they are also frightened by the light—not, as some say, because the soul, exiled from the celestial regions, inhabits an earthly body and infants are therefore forced to cry.” Soranus of Ephesus, *Introduction* 17, assigns a similar cause to an infant’s crying. LAC.]

[Col. 0691A] This is the view of the Stoics together with Aenesidemus, and sometimes of Plato himself, when he likewise says that the soul, otherwise alien and exiled from the womb, is brought in with the newborn infant’s first inhalation, just as it is led out with its final exhalation.

[Note: [Col. 0691C] “Is led” (*duci*): Fran.]

We shall see whether he fabricated this opinion.

[Note: [Col. 0691C] Rig. proposes that the text means “whether the opinion has fixed it.”]

Not even among physicians was Hicesius lacking—a traitor both to nature and to his own art.

[Note: [Col. 0691D] **Hicesius, a traitor both to nature and to his own art.** The physician Hicesius denied that the soul was conceived in the womb and said that it was impressed from outside upon the infant, not yet alive, only after the child had been delivered—namely, with its first inhalation. Septimius calls him a traitor to nature and to his own art: to nature, because pregnant women affirm that the fetus lives in the womb already endowed with a soul; and to his art, because the physicians themselves, whenever it is necessary to extract a child from the womb by a violent delivery, do not ordinarily dismember its limbs [Col. 0692C] before they have killed it—since it is already living and endowed with a soul. RIG.]

They were ashamed, I suppose, to establish something which women would recognize. Yet how much more shameful [Col. 0692D] the outcome—to be refuted by women rather than approved by them!

[Note: [Col. 0692D] **A more shameful outcome.** He calls an outcome “more shameful” when it occasions greater embarrassment and shame. RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0691C] “More strongly confirmed” (*roboratior*): Pam., Rhen.]

For in this matter no teacher, judge, or witness is so competent as the sex itself. Answer, mothers, pregnant women, and women who have given birth; let barren women and men be silent. The truth of your nature is being investigated; the credibility of your experience is being summoned as witness. Do you perceive in the fetus some vitality distinct from your own, causing your groin to throb, your sides to quiver, the entire circuit of the belly to be struck, and the position of the burden to shift everywhere? [Col. 0691B]

[Note: [Col. 0692D] **The entire circuit of the belly.** Jerome uses the same meaning in his epistle to Principia: “The interior members of the Church are wrapped up, and the entire circuit of the womb is covered”—that is, the whole womb, the whole belly. RIG.]

Are these movements your joys and your firm assurance that you may thus trust the infant both to be alive and to be playing? If its restlessness ceases, do you not first fear for it? Does it not already hear within you when it is startled by a new sound? Do you not desire various foods for its sake and likewise reject them for its sake? Do you not share illnesses with it in turn?

[Note: [Col. 0691C] “And” omitted by others.]

[Note: [Col. 0691C] “Vanities” rather than “varieties”: Rhen., Pam., Rig.]

Indeed it does so to such an extent that, from your bruises, by which it too is marked inwardly upon the corresponding limbs, it takes to itself the injuries of its mother.

[Note: [Col. 0691C] “To such an extent” omitted by Lat.; “therefore” omitted by Rhen., Pam.]

If bruising and redness are a condition of the blood, there will be no blood without a soul. If health is an accession of the soul, there will be no health without a soul. If nourishment, hunger, growth, decline, fear, movement, and handling are activities of the soul, whoever performs these activities is alive.

[Note: [Col. 0691C] “Every” (*omnis*): Fran.]

[Col. 0691C] Finally, whoever ceases to perform them ceases to live. And finally, children are also born dead; how could they be, unless they had also been alive? And how could they be dead unless they had first been alive?

Indeed, while still in the womb the infant is sometimes slain by a necessary cruelty, when, lying crosswise at the outlet, it prevents delivery—destined to kill its mother unless it dies. [Col. 0692A] Accordingly, among the physicians’ instruments there is one by which the hidden passages are first forced open, with a twisting mechanism; then there is a ring-shaped knife by which the limbs within are severed under anxious judgment; then a blunt hook by which the whole victim is dragged out in a violent delivery.

[Note: [Col. 0692C] “Instruments” (*organa*): Fran.]

[Note: [Col. 0692C] “A knife-bearing ring” (*anulo cultrato*): Rhen., Pam.]

[Note: [Col. 0692C] “Animal” (*pecus*): Fran., Pam.; likewise, “is drawn out.”]

There is also a bronze spike by which the actual killing is performed in a blind act of violence. They call it the *embryospháktēs* (ἐμβρυοσφάκτην), “embryo-slayer,” from its function in infanticide—an instrument, surely, for destroying a living infant.

[Note: [Col. 0692C] Ἐμβρυονέκτην: Lat.; ἐμβρυορέκτην: Fran.; ἐμβρυοπακτην: others; ἐμβρυοσέκτην: Codex Agobardinus.]

Hippocrates possessed such an instrument, as did Asclepiades, Erasistratus, Herophilus—who dissected even adults—and even Soranus himself, though gentler than the others. They were certain that the conceived fetus was a living creature, and so pitied this most unhappy infancy in such a way that it should first be killed, lest it be torn apart alive.

Hicesius too, I believe, did not doubt the necessity of this crime, although he superimposed the soul upon children only after birth, as a result of the cold air’s impact, because the Greek word for soul was itself supposed to correspond to cooling. [Col. 0692B]

[Note: [Col. 0692C] “Corresponding” (*respondens*): Rhen., Pam.]

Are barbarian and Roman peoples, then, endowed with souls in some different way because they have given the soul a name other than *psychē* (ψυχή)? And how many nations live beneath the most burning part of the heavens, their very complexion baked by it? Whence do they receive a soul, since they experience no chill of air?

I pass over the heat of bedrooms and all the arrangements for warmth required there by women in labor, for whom exposure to a draft is especially dangerous. A fetus slips forth almost in the baths themselves, and its wailing is heard immediately. But if the chill of the air is the treasury of the soul, no one ought to be born outside Germany, the Alps, and Mount Argaeus.

[Note: [Col. 0692D] **The Alps and Mount Argaeus.** He joins Argaeus, or the Argaean mountains in Cappadocia, with the Alps because this mountain, like the Alps, is covered with perpetual snow. LE PR.]

And yet populations are more numerous in the eastern and southern climates, and their intellects more acute than those of all the Sarmatians, who are benumbed even in mind. [Col. 0692C] For minds also would emerge more intelligent from cold regions if souls originated from little chills: with the substance would come its power.

With these foundations thus laid, we may also call to mind those who, after their mother’s womb had been cut open, drew breath alive—certain Libers and Scipios. [Col. 0693A]

[Note: [Col. 0692D] **Certain Libers and Scipios.** The elder Scipio Africanus was born after the womb of his mother Pomponia had been cut open. Liber too is said in the fable to have been cut out after being conceived from Jupiter’s seed, although some explain the statement as referring to a Roman clan or family named Liber. Everyone thinks the Caesars were likewise named from the cutting open of the mother’s womb, although Pliny says that before the family of the Caesars there was a Claudius Caesar prior to the Samnite War. Those born after the mother’s womb had been cut open, like Scipio, were also called *Caesones*. LE PR.]

But if someone, like Plato, likewise does not think that two souls can come together in one being, just as neither can two bodies, I would have shown him not only two souls gathered together, just as bodies are in a multiple pregnancy, but many other beings joined to a soul as well: demons, for example—not merely one, as in Socrates himself, but seven spirits, as in Magdalene, and a legionary number, as in the Gerasene. Thus one soul may all the more readily be joined to another soul because of their community of substance, when evil spirits can be joined to it despite the difference of their nature.

[Note: [Col. 0693D] **As Plato likewise does not think, etc.** Plato affirmed that each body contains one single, simple soul and did not admit two souls simultaneously in the same human being. Tertullian attributed the latter position above to Chrysippus. LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0693C] “Should be reckoned” (*censeretur*): Seml., Rhen., Oberth., Codex Ursini.]

Yet in the sixth book of the *Laws*, when warning that one must take care lest a corruption of the seed arising from some baseness in intercourse attach a stain to the body and soul, I do not know whether Plato forgot his former opinion or this present one.

[Note: [Col. 0693C] “Former” in the singular: Rhen., Pam.]

For he shows that the soul is conveyed through the seed, which he warns must be cared for, rather than through the newborn’s first inhalation. [Col. 0693B]

Why, I ask you, do we also resemble our parents in soul with respect to our dispositions, according to the testimony of Cleanthes, if we are not produced from the soul’s seed? And why did the ancient astrologers arrange a person’s nativity from the beginning of conception, if the soul also does not exist from that point—the soul to which equally belongs whatever may pertain to its condition?

[Note: [Col. 0693C] “Condition” (*status*): Codex Wouw.]

## CHAPTER XXVI

But all the inconsistency of human opinion extends only as far as the boundaries established by God. I shall now gather my step within our own lines, so that what I answered to philosophers and physicians I may prove to a Christian.

[Note: [Col. 0693D] **But all the inconsistency of human opinion extends only as far as the boundaries established by God.** As though he were saying: “But let human opinions concerning the soul have remained inconsistent, uncertain, and inconstant only until the divine testimonies.” RIG.]

Build your faith, brother, upon your own foundation.

[Note: [Col. 0693D] **Build your faith, brother, upon your own foundation.** He now addresses a Christian, whose foundation he calls Sacred Scripture; he supplies him with the testimony of Sacred Scripture as a foundation. RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0693C] “Let me build” (*aedificem*): Pam., Rhen., Gagnae.]

Look upon the living wombs of the most holy women: not merely were infants already breathing within them, but they were also prophesying.

[Note: [Col. 0693D] **Look upon the living wombs.** Galen too draws an argument from the same proof, though within his own boundaries, confirming from pagan examples that the fetus is alive in the womb, in the book he wrote entitled *Whether What Is in the Womb Is a Living Creature*. LAC.]

[Col. 0693C] Behold, the womb of Rebecca is disturbed (Gen. 25), though birth is still far off and there has been no impact of air.

[Note: [Col. 0693D] **Behold the womb of Rebecca.** He treats at length the history in Genesis 25 concerning Rebecca and her two sons, both while they were in the womb and during birth; unless they had already been endowed with souls, they could not have begun those struggles. PAM.]

Behold, twin fetuses riot in their mother’s recesses, though the two peoples are nowhere yet to be seen. Perhaps this was the monstrous impudence of infancy, contending before it lived, high-spirited before it possessed a soul—if it had merely disturbed its mother by leaping. [Col. 0694A] But when the birth passage is opened, their number is observed, and the prophecy is recognized, I think that not merely the infants’ souls but their very struggles are now established.

The one who had been first to be born was held back by the one whom he had forestalled, though that second child had not yet fully emerged and only his hand had been born. And if the first drank in his soul with his first inhalation, in the Platonic manner, or seized it from the chill of the air in Stoic fashion, what of the other, who was still awaited, was still being held within, and yet was already holding the one outside?

[Note: [Col. 0694D] **Drank in his soul with his first inhalation, in the Platonic manner.** Others read “carried.” He alludes to the statements in the preceding chapter, where he charged Plato with holding that the soul is first drawn in through breathing. LAC.]

[Note: [Col. 0694C] “Breathing” (*spiratione*): Pam., Rhen.]

[Note: [Col. 0694D] **Or seized it from the chill of the air in Stoic fashion.** Here too he recalls what he attributed to the Stoics in the preceding chapter: that after birth a child seizes the soul when struck by the chill of the air. LAC.]

Not yet breathing, I suppose, he had seized his brother’s heel; still warm with his mother’s heat, he desired to emerge first. O infant, at once rivalrous, strong, and already contentious! I believe it was because he was alive.

Look also at the single conceptions in Luke 1—indeed, ones still more portentous: that of a barren woman and that of a virgin. By this very fact they might have produced imperfect offspring because of nature’s overthrow, since the one was insensible to seed and the other untouched. [Col. 0694B]

[Note: [Col. 0694D] **Look also at the singular conceptions.** Here likewise are the conceptions of John the Baptist and Christ, and the mutual movements of the infants while still in the womb, concerning whom Luke speaks in chapter 1. PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0694C] “Seed” in the genitive: Pam., Fran.]

If ever there were reason for it, those improperly conceived ought to have been born without souls; but they too live, each in his own womb. Elizabeth exults: John had stirred her from within. Mary glorifies the Lord: Christ had impelled her from within. The mothers recognize one another’s fetuses, having themselves been mutually recognized by those who were surely alive—who were not only souls but also spirits.

Thus you also read the voice of God to Jeremiah (Jer. 1): “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you.”

[Note: [Col. 0694D] **Thus also to Jeremiah, etc.** To prove the same matter he adduces the testimony of the prophet Jeremiah from chapter 1, comparing it with the frequently cited passage in Genesis 1. PAM.]

If God forms a person in the womb, he also breathes into him according to the pattern of the beginning (Gen. 1): “And God formed the human being and breathed into him the breath of life.” God, moreover, would not have known the human being in the womb unless he were whole. “And before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you.” Did he sanctify a body still dead? Certainly not, for God is the God of the living, not of the dead (Matt. 22). [Col. 0694C]

[Note: [Col. 0694C] The editions suggest that “perhaps” (*forte*) should be read as “if” (*si*).]

## CHAPTER XXVII

How, then, is a living creature conceived? Are the two substances, body and soul, formed together, or does one precede the other? We say, rather, that both are conceived, formed, and perfected simultaneously, just as they are also brought forth, and that no intervening moment occurs in conception by which an order of position might be assigned. [Col. 0695A]

[Note: [Col. 0694D] **Both are conceived, formed, and perfected simultaneously, etc.** Here, and more fully in chapter 36, Tertullian unfolds his paradox, which he had suggested above in chapters 9 and 22, concerning the propagation of souls together with the seed by transmission from Adam. Rufinus forces Lactantius into the same opinion, though Rufinus himself remains doubtful. His position is summarized from Jerome, *Apology against Rufinus* II. LAC.]

[Note: [Col. 0695C] **And no intervening moment occurs in conception, etc.** That is, in conception no order of existence can be established between soul and body, nor can it be affirmed whether the soul existed first or not, whether it takes the first or second place, whether it precedes the body or follows it. Tertullian himself says in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*: “Flesh and soul come into being simultaneously, without a calculation of time; they are blended in the fetus and are born at the same age.” RIG.]

Reconsider first things from last things. If death is determined to be nothing other than the separation of body and soul, life, the opposite of death, will be defined as nothing other than the conjunction of body and soul.

[Note: [Col. 0695D] **If death is determined to be nothing else.** This argument does not establish that souls are sown together with the body, but only that they are conjoined with it—something that can occur through creation. Tertullian treats this argument again in chapter 42. LAC.]

If separation happens simultaneously to both substances through death, the corresponding form of conjunction must have prescribed that life likewise comes simultaneously to both substances.

Furthermore, we acknowledge life from conception because we claim the soul from conception.

[Note: [Col. 0695D] **We acknowledge life from conception because we claim the soul, etc.** Pamelius comments that this is utterly false, because according to the opinion of physicists and physicians a male is not endowed with a soul until the fortieth day, and a female not until the eightieth. Yet Tertullian is not so far wrong that many have not believed his view to be true, since they did not believe nature so slow and sluggish in bestowing the benefit of life. LAC.—The opinion of Tertullian has been embraced, after St. Basil and Congiamila, by most recent writers, among them P. J. C. D. Breyne, in the work entitled *Essay on Moral Theology Considered in Its Relations with Physiology and Medicine*. EDD.]

For life begins at the point at which the soul does. Those things, therefore, which are separated together in death are compacted together into life.

[Note: [Col. 0695C] “Then” is absent from Par.]

If, then, we grant primacy to one and second place to the other, the times of their seeds must also be distinguished according to their ordered status: when will the seed of the body be implanted, [Col. 0695B] and when that of the soul? Indeed, if the times of the seeds are divided, their materials too will be regarded as different because of that distance in time.

For although we shall acknowledge two kinds of seed, bodily and psychic, we nevertheless maintain that they are undivided, and in this sense contemporaneous and belonging to the same moment.

Let us not, therefore, be ashamed of an interpretation demanded by necessity. Nature is to be revered, not blushed at. Lust, not the institution itself, has defiled sexual intercourse.

[Note: [Col. 0695D] **Lust, not the institution itself, has defiled sexual intercourse.** Septimius does not always remain faithful to this position, although it is entirely true.
