Accordingly, in his hatred of marriage he sometimes seems to betray it. Theano, the wife of Pythagoras, used to say that a woman who had intercourse with a man, provided he was her own husband, was pure immediately afterward; but if he belonged to another, she would never be pure. RIG.—**Lust, not the institution itself, has defiled sexual intercourse.** A most beautiful passage concerning the state of marriage blessed before God, which is treated more fully near the end of Book I *Against Marcion*. PAM.]

Excess, not the state itself, is immodest. For the state is blessed before God (Gen. 1): “Increase and multiply.” But excess is accursed: adulteries, debaucheries, and brothels.

Accordingly, in this solemn function of the sexes which joins male and female—in ordinary intercourse, I mean—we know that both soul and flesh act together: the soul through desire, the flesh through performance; the soul through impulse, the flesh through action. Therefore, by the single impulse of both, when the whole human being has been shaken, the seed of the whole human being foams forth, having moisture from the bodily substance and heat from the psychic substance. [Col. 0695C–0696A]

[Note: [Col. 0696C] **The seed of the whole human being foams forth.** This metaphor, derived from foam, is not uncommon among philosophers and physicians. Aristotle, *Generation of Animals* II.2: οἷον δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀφρὸς γίνεται παχύτερος καὶ λευκός, “just as foam also becomes thicker and white.” According to Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers* V.3, Pythagoras said: ἀφρὸν χρηστοτάτου τοῦ αἵματος, “that it is the foam of the most serviceable blood.” I omit Galen, *On the Usefulness of the Parts* XIV.9. LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0695C] “Foams forth into seed”: Fran., Pam.]

And if the Greek name for soul is a word denoting cold, why does the body grow cold when the soul has been removed?

[Note: [Col. 0696D] **The Greek name for soul is a word denoting cold.** Tertullian evidently derives the Greek word ψυχή, “soul,” from ψῦχος, which means “cold” in Latin. EDD.]

Finally—though I risk modesty here more than proof—in that final heat of pleasure in which the generative fluid is expelled, do we not feel something from the soul also departing, so that we languish and lose vigor, with a diminution of our light?

[Note: [Col. 0696D] **In that final heat of pleasure.** Augustine, *City of God* XIV.16: “At the very moment when its culmination is reached, nearly all acuteness and, as it were, wakefulness of thought is overwhelmed.” RIG.]

This, accordingly, will be the psychic seed, arising from the soul’s distillation, just as that bodily fluid is seed arising from the purification of the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0696D] **From the soul’s distillation.** The same appears to be the opinion of Epicurus, which we transcribed a little above. Tertullian seems to agree with those who thought that seed is drawn from every part of a living being. St. Macarius likewise holds this regarding bodily components, as did some of the ancient philosophers. LAC.]

The examples furnished by the beginning are entirely trustworthy. In Adam the flesh came from clay: what else is clay but a rich liquid? From this will come the generative fluid. The soul came from God’s breath: what else is God’s breath but the vapor of spirit? From this will come that which we breathe out through that fluid.

Thus, when at the beginning two diverse and separate things, clay and breath, had combined to form one human being, both substances, now mingled in one, also mixed their respective seeds and thereafter transmitted the pattern for propagating the race. Consequently, the two, although diverse, now flow out united and together; and, being implanted together in their own furrow and field, they together cause a human being to sprout from both substances. In that human being, in turn, his own seed is present according to kind, just as has been prescribed for every condition capable of generation. [Col. 0696B]

Thus this whole abundance of souls proceeds from one human being, while nature observes God’s decree: “Increase and multiply.”

[Note: [Col. 0696C] “Proceeds” is absent from Par.]

For even in the very preface to this single work of creation (Gen. 1), “Let us make the human being,” all posterity was announced in the plural: “And let them have dominion over the fish of the sea.” No wonder: the promise of the harvest is contained within the seed. [Col. 0696C]

## CHAPTER XXVIII

[Col. 0697A]

What, then, is that ancient saying remembered by Plato concerning the reciprocal passage of souls: that those departing from here go there, and again return here and live, and thereafter depart from life, and that the living are again produced from the dead?

[Note: [Col. 0697C] “What is that ancient saying now remembered by Plato?” Thus Socrates speaks in Plato’s *Phaedo*: “There is, then, an ancient saying which we remember, that souls arriving there come from here, and that they return here again and are born from the dead,” etc. RIG.]

Was it Pythagorean, as they maintain—or even divine, as Albinus thinks—or perhaps derived from the Egyptian Mercury?

[Note: [Col. 0697C] Some read “a certain one.” PAM. RHEN.]

[Note: [Col. 0697C] “As Albinus thinks.” A short introductory work by Albinus the Platonist on Plato’s dialogues is extant in the Royal Library. Cassiodorus Senator also records that, before the pagan invasion, he possessed Albinus’s book on music in his library at Rome. RIG.]

But no saying is divine except that of the one God—the saying with which the prophets, the apostles, and Christ himself thundered. Moses is far more ancient even than Saturn, by about nine hundred years, to say nothing of Saturn’s great-grandsons; and certainly he is far more divine, for he set out the course of the human race from the beginning of the world, birth by birth, with names and dates, sufficiently proving the divinity of his work by the prophetic character of his utterance.

[Note: [Col. 0697D] “Moses is far more ancient even than Saturn, by about nine hundred years.” Anyone who considers what Tertullian says in *Apologeticum*, chapter 19, will not be surprised that here he calls Moses about nine hundred years older than Saturn; for there he says that Moses preceded the fall of Priam by about a thousand years. As I long ago replied to a letter on this subject from François Baudouin, jurisconsult, on the testimony of Eusebius, Bede, and Hermannus Contractus, we read that Saturn reigned only 150 years before Aeneas’s arrival in Italy. If, therefore, Moses preceded the fall of Priam by a thousand years, he was certainly about nine hundred years older than Saturn. I know that some others hold a different opinion; but we have noted in the *Apologeticum* that our author took this from Josephus. PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0697C] Some read “all the way through.” JUN.]

But if the Samian [Col. 0697B] sophist was Plato’s authority for the doctrine that souls repeatedly return in a revolving cycle, through the alternating replacement of the dead by the living and the living by the dead, then that Pythagoras—though otherwise a good man—nevertheless, in order to establish this doctrine, resorted not merely to a shameful but also to a reckless lie.

[Note: [Col. 0697D] “But if the Samian sophist.” “Samian” is an epithet of Pythagoras, from the island of Samos, where he became renowned; he carried the Italic discipline into the other Greece. Perhaps the author calls him a sophist not out of contempt, since immediately afterward he speaks of him honorably and calls him good. For the name “sophist” was not always used in a bad sense, but sometimes to signify a man of outstanding intellect and consummate wisdom. Accordingly, Isocrates writes that Solon was the first of all men to be called a sophist. LAC.]

Learn the facts, if you do not know them, and believe with us. He feigns death and hides underground, condemning himself to remain there patiently for seven years. Meanwhile, from his mother—the sole accomplice and agent in the deception—he learns the facts concerning those who died afterward, which he will report in order to gain credibility. When he thinks that he has sufficiently altered his corpulence into all the ghastliness of a long-dead man, he emerges from the sanctuary of his deception as though restored from the underworld. Who would not believe that a man had returned to life whom he had believed dead—especially upon hearing from him facts concerning persons who had subsequently died, which he would not appear capable of learning except in the underworld? This, then, [Col. 0697C] is how the saying that the living are produced from the dead became ancient.

But what if it were also recent? Truth has no need of antiquity, nor does falsehood avoid novelty. [Col. 0698A] I plainly possess a falsehood ennobled by age. Why should it not be false, when even its testimony proceeds from a falsehood? How am I to believe that Pythagoras is not lying, when he lies in order to make me believe? How will he persuade me that before he was Pythagoras he had successively been Aethalides, Euphorbus, Pyrrhus the fisherman, and Hermotimus, so as to persuade me that the living are produced from the dead, when he perjured himself yet again in claiming to be Pythagoras? For the more credible it would have been that he himself returned to life from himself only once rather than becoming one different person after another so many times, the more culpably did he deceive in the harder claims, since he had lied in the easier ones.

[Note: [Col. 0697C] “Ephaclides” in the Paris manuscript and others.]

[Note: [Col. 0698C] “Hermippus.” PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0698C] PAM. omits “only once.”]

But he recognized the shield of Euphorbus, which had long ago been dedicated at Delphi; he declared that it was his and proved it by markings generally unknown.

[Note: [Col. 0698D] “But the shield of Euphorbus.” Besides Diogenes and Lactantius, Iamblichus and Philostratus also mention this, as does our author frequently: chapter 31, where he refutes it; chapter 34; and chapter 1 of *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*. Maximus of Tyre gave a particularly full account of this fable in Discourse 28. LAC.]

Look back at his underground chamber—and believe, if you can.

[Note: [Col. 0698D] “And believe, if you can.” That is: “If you can bring yourself to believe it, believe.” By an elegant omission he has suppressed the second verb. RIG.]

For a man who devised such a trick, injuring his good health and defrauding his life—[Col. 0698B] tortured underground for seven years by hunger, inactivity, and darkness—a man to whom the open sky was worth so much aversion: what recklessness would he not have embraced? What inquiry would he not have attempted in order to discover the identifying mark on that shield? What if he found it in some comparatively obscure historical work? What if he caught some lingering breath of a tradition whose transmission had already failed? What if he learned it from the temple attendant by secretly purchasing an inspection? We know that magic can also investigate hidden things through *catabolic* spirits, attendant spirits, and Pythonic spirits.

[Note: [Col. 0698D] “Through catabolic spirits.” The very learned Turnebus taught me in his *Adversaria* that “catabolic” spirits are sinister and infamous demons that overthrow fanatics and dash them to the ground. LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0698D] “And attendant spirits.” Demons that accompany certain persons continually. Simon Magus had such a one. LE PR.—“And Pythonic spirits.” Pythons, or ventriloquists (*engastrimythoi*, ἐγγαστριμύθους), possessed by a demon. LE PR.]

Did not Pherecydes, Pythagoras’s teacher, perhaps practice divination by these arts—not to say that he dreamed? What if the same demon was in him that also performed the deeds of bloodshed in Euphorbus? Finally, since he had proved himself to be Euphorbus from the evidence of the shield, why did he not likewise recognize any one of his Trojan comrades-in-arms? [Col. 0698C] For they too would already have returned to life, if the living were produced from the dead.

## CHAPTER XXIX

It is established that the dead are produced from the living; it does not therefore [Col. 0699A] follow that the living are also produced from the dead.

[Note: [Col. 0698D] “It is established that the dead are produced from the living.” In this chapter he argues against Plato in the *Phaedo*, whose inference Tertullian here rejects. Plato argued that the dead are produced from the living, and therefore that the living are also produced from the dead, according to the philosophers’ rule that one contrary arises from another. Our author refutes this rule, when taken universally, by evident examples. LAC.]

For in the beginning the living came first; consequently, from the beginning the dead came afterward, and from no other source than the living. The former had a source from which they might more properly arise, provided it was not from the dead; the latter had no other source from which they could more properly be derived except the living. Therefore, if at the beginning the living did not arise from the dead, why should they do so afterward? Had that original source, whatever it may be, failed? Or had it repented of its method? And how is that method preserved among the dead? Because at the beginning the dead arose from the living, does it not follow rather that they must always arise from the living? For the original pattern should either have continued on both sides or have changed on both sides. If afterward the living had to arise from the dead, then likewise the dead would have had to cease arising from the living. If fidelity to the original institution need not be maintained equally, then it is not invariably true that contraries are restored from contraries in alternation.

For we too shall set against them [Col. 0699B] the contrary pairs of born and unborn, sight and blindness, youth and old age, wisdom and folly. Yet the unborn does not therefore proceed from the born merely because one contrary arises from another; nor does sight return from blindness merely because blindness supervenes upon sight; nor does youth revive again from old age merely because old age withers out of youth; nor is folly blunted anew out of wisdom merely because wisdom is sharpened out of folly. Albinus too, fearing these objections for his Plato’s sake, subtly seeks to distinguish different kinds of contraries—as though these examples were not placed among contraries just as absolutely as those which he interprets in support of his master’s doctrine, namely life and death. Yet life is not restored from death merely because death is brought forth from life.

## CHAPTER XXX

[Col. 0699C] But what shall we answer concerning the remaining points? First, if the living arose from the dead just as the dead arise from the living, the total number of all people would always have remained one and the same: namely, that number which first entered life. For the living preceded the dead; afterward came the dead from the living, and again the living from the dead. And since this would always occur from the same persons, the same number would always arise from the same persons: no more and no fewer would have departed than returned.

[Note: [Col. 0699C] Others read “would have returned.”]

Yet we find, even in the records of human antiquity, that the human race gradually increased, while [Col. 0700A] indigenous peoples, wanderers, exiles, or all manner of celebrated peoples occupied new lands: the Scythians, Parthian territory; the Amyclaeans, the Peloponnese; the Athenians, Asia; the Phrygians, Italy; and the Phoenicians, Africa; and while formal migrations, which they call colonies (*apoikiai*, ἀποικίαι), disgorged swarms of a people into other territories for the deliberate purpose of relieving overpopulation.

[Note: [Col. 0699D] “While indigenous peoples, wanderers, exiles, or all manner of celebrated peoples occupied lands.” We know that indigenous peoples are called *autochthones* (αὐτόχθονας) and *enchōrioi* (ἐγχωρίους). We also know that in ancient books *ab origine* is not infrequently written where *aborigines* certainly ought to have been written; and some accordingly read *aborigines* here from Ursinus’s manuscript, nor do we deny that this can be read. But since the reading found in that most ancient Agobardine manuscript, *ab origine*—that is, “from primeval generation” (*apo archaiogonias*, ἀπὸ ἀρχαιογονίας)—can be accepted and readily explained, we do not think that anything more recondite should be sought. RIG.—“While indigenous peoples.” He contrasts indigenous peoples with wanderers; he therefore does not mean the ancient peoples of Italy called Latins, but those whom the Greeks call *autochōroi* (αὐτόχωροι), *proterogeneis* (προτερογενεῖς), or *enchōrioi* (ἐγχώριοι), as Ambrose uses the word in his *Hexameron*: namely, the earliest ancestors, inhabitants of cities, and natives, who were called *aborigines* as though they had no foreign origin. On these see Thucydides, book I, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book I. LAC.]

[Note: [Col. 0699C] Wouwer reads “Parthian territory”; Ursinus’s manuscript, “Parthia.”]

[Note: [Col. 0699C] Wouwer reads “Amadae”; Junius, “Semenidae.”]

[Note: [Col. 0700D] “Formal migrations.” The dispatching of colonies, but formal ones—that is, those undertaken in accordance with a solemn procedure, either by a public law or at an emperor’s command—not colonies formed fortuitously, by chance or through the desire of the victors, without other authority or the requisite rite. LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0699D] PAM. and RHEN. read *metoikiai* (μετοικίαι), “migrations.”]

For the indigenous peoples still remain in their own territories, while elsewhere they have lent out their nationality at interest and increased it. Certainly the world itself lies open before us, more cultivated and better equipped every day than formerly. Everything is now accessible, everything known, everything engaged in commerce. Most delightful estates have erased the wildernesses once notorious; cultivated fields have subdued the forests; flocks have put wild beasts to flight; sandy wastes are sown, rocks are planted, marshes are drained. There are now cities as numerous as once there were not even [Col. 0700B] huts.

[Note: [Col. 0700C] PAM. and RHEN. omit “now.”]

No longer do islands inspire dread or cliffs terror. Everywhere are houses, everywhere people, everywhere civil communities, everywhere life. The supreme testimony to humanity’s abundance is this: we are a burden to the world; the elements scarcely suffice for us; our necessities grow more constricting, and there are complaints among all, because nature can no longer sustain us. In truth, plagues, famines, wars, and the engulfing of cities must be regarded as remedies, like the pruning of an overgrown human race. And yet, even when axes of this kind cut down at one stroke a very great multitude of mortals, never has the world once stood aghast at their restoration bringing the living back from the dead after a thousand years.

[Note: [Col. 0700D] “Bringing the living back from the dead after a thousand years.” Manilius had this in view in *Astronomica* I when he said:

> Or whether nature, dissolved into indivisible  
> First principles, remains destined to return to the same state  
> After a thousand years.  
>
> RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0700D] “After a thousand years.” He alludes to the thousand-year journey that Plato describes after this life in dialogue X of the *Republic* and in the *Phaedrus*. Since our author here refutes these accounts as fables, it is remarkable that he afterward fell into the paradox of the Millenarians. PAM.]

For this too—the equal magnitude of loss and restoration—would have produced a perceptible effect if the living arose from the dead. Why, moreover, should the living arise from the dead after a thousand years, and not immediately? [Col. 0700C] For unless what is expended were immediately replaced, it would be in danger of being wholly consumed, depletion overtaking restoration; because this provision of life could not have equaled a millennium in duration, being of course far shorter, and therefore more liable to be extinguished before it could be rekindled. Accordingly, something that would have perished in this way if the living arose from the dead—since it has not perished—does not permit us to believe that the living arise from the dead.

[Note: [Col. 0700D] PAM. and RHEN. read “what has been expended.”]

## CHAPTER XXXI

Now if the living arise from the dead, each individual must arise from an individual. The souls of individual bodies would therefore have had to return individually [Col. 0701A] into individual bodies. But if two, three, and as many as five are taken up together in a single womb, the living will not arise from the dead, because they do not arise one by one from individuals. Yet in this very manner the pattern of the beginning is preserved in its singularity, since even now several souls are brought forth from one.

[Note: [Col. 0701C] “The pattern of the beginning is preserved in its singularity.” Thus reads the Agobardine manuscript: “Indeed,” he says, “the true pattern of humanity’s beginning is preserved in its singularity, since even now several are generated from one individual human being.” In this way the singular character of humanity’s beginning is preserved, since even now several souls are brought forth from one. RIG.]

Again, since souls depart at various ages, why do they all return at the same age? For all begin their formation in infancy.

[Note: [Col. 0701C] PAM. and RHEN. add, “At what age does the infant return?” Junius prefers the Latin reading, “it returns.”]

What sort of arrangement is it that one who died an old man should return as an infant? If the soul grows younger outside the body by a retrograde course of age, how much more fitting would it be for it to return more advanced in age after a thousand years! It should at least be of the same age as at its death, so that it might take up again the span of life that it had left behind.

But even if the same souls were always returning, though they did not also bring back the same bodily forms, they ought at least to bring back with them [Col. 0701B] the former characteristics of their dispositions, pursuits, and affections. For they would groundlessly be regarded as the same if they lacked the features by which their identity could be proved.

“How do you know,” you ask, “whether this does not in fact occur secretly, but the interval of a thousand years destroys the ability to recognize them, because those who return are unknown to you?”

[Note: [Col. 0701C] PAM. and RHEN. read, “Because both here and there they are unknown.”]

But I know that it does not occur, since you set Pythagoras and Euphorbus before me. For Euphorbus plainly possessed a military and warlike soul, as is sufficiently established even by the glory of the dedicated shields; Pythagoras, by contrast, was so sedentary and unwarlike that, avoiding the wars then raging in Greece, he preferred the peace of Italy. He was devoted to geometry, astrology, and music, and was alien to the pursuits and disposition of Euphorbus.

Moreover, that Pyrrhus was occupied in deceiving fish; Pythagoras, by contrast, would not even eat them, [Col. 0701C] since he abstained from animals.

[Note: [Col. 0701C] “But that Pyrrhus.” Pyrrhus, whom Pythagoras falsely claimed that he had formerly been, was a Delian fisherman. LAC.]

[Note: [Col. 0701C] “Pythagoras, by contrast, would not even eat them.” Elsewhere our author gives the reason why Pythagoras abstained from animals, *Apologeticum*, chapter 48: “Lest someone should happen to serve up beef taken from one of his own great-grandfathers.” Relevant here also is the statement of the blessed Jerome, *Against Jovinianus*, book II: “And I shall prove that we do not follow the doctrine of Empedocles and Pythagoras, who, because of metempsychosis (*metempsychōsis*, μετεμψύχωσιν), think that nothing which moves and lives should be eaten.” Lactantius, book III, chapter 19, interprets this more mildly. PAM.]

Aethalides and [Col. 0702A] Hermotimus, however, had even included beans among ordinary foods; but Pythagoras taught his disciples that they must not even pass through a bean field.

[Note: [Col. 0701C] “Ephafides” in the Paris manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0701D] “Even included beans among ordinary foods.” What is better known than Pythagoras’s precept, *kyamōn apechou* (κυάμων ἀπέχου), “abstain from beans”? Iamblichus writes that this was forbidden for many reasons—some religious, some natural, and some concerning the soul—on which the authorities are full. LAC.]

[Note: [Col. 0701D] “That they must not even pass through a bean field.” Iamblichus, chapter 31, writes that Pythagoras’s precept, *kyamōn mē thinganein* (κυάμων μὴ θιγγάνειν), “beans must not be touched,” was observed even at the risk of life. He tells how certain disciples of Pythagoras, while fleeing the soldiers of the tyrant Dionysius, happened upon a bean field. Remembering the decree and refusing to violate it, they stopped, not daring to cross the field, and chose instead to be slaughtered and buried. Myllias alone was captured and brought before the tyrant, where he gave no lesser demonstration of courage. When Dionysius asked why his companions had preferred death to trampling beans, he replied: “They stopped so that they would not trample the beans; I, for my part, shall choose death rather than explain to you why we refuse to trample beans.” Suidas likewise writes that when Pythagoras’s enemies pursued him after setting fire to his house, he stopped upon reaching a field planted with beans and was killed. LAC.]

How, then, are the same souls recovered, when they will not be proved the same in dispositions, practices, or even diet?

And now, out of so large a census of Greece, only four souls are identified. But why, in any event, only from the census of Greece? Why do transmigrations of souls (*metempsychōseis*, μετεμψυχώσεις) and reincorporations (*metensōmatōseis*, μετενσωματώσεις) not occur daily from every nation, every age and rank, and indeed every sex? Why does Pythagoras alone recognize that he has been one person after another, and not I too? Or if this is a privilege of philosophers—and specifically Greek philosophers, as though Scythians and Indians did not also philosophize—why does Epicurus not remember that he formerly was someone else, nor Chrysippus, nor Zeno, nor even Plato himself, whom perhaps [Col. 0702B] we might have believed to be Nestor because of the honeyed sweetness of his eloquence?

[Note: [Col. 0701C] “And” added by Semler.]

## CHAPTER XXXII

But Empedocles, because he had raved that he was a god, therefore, I suppose, disdained to remember that he had been one of the heroes.

[Note: [Col. 0702C] “Empedocles, because he had raved that he was a god.” Together with the historians I marvel at the man’s madness and stupidity. For the following verse of Empedocles is cited here:

> Χαίρετ᾽· ἐγὼ δὲ ὑμῖν θεὸς ἄμβροτος, οὐκέτι θνητός·  
> Greetings! For to you I am an immortal god, no longer a mortal man.  
>
> LE PR.]

“I have been a shrub and a fish,” he says. Why not rather a melon, since he was so tasteless, and a chameleon, since he was so puffed up?

[Note: [Col. 0702D] “I have been a shrub and a fish.” Empedocles himself accordingly says, in Athenaeus, book VIII, and in Laertius:

> Ἤδη γάρ ποτ᾽ ἐγὼ γενόμην κούρη τε κόρος τε,  
> Θάμνος τ᾽ οἰωνός τε, καὶ εἰν ἁλὶ ἔλλοπος ἰχθύς.  
>
> For once already I became both girl and boy,  
> A shrub, a bird, and in the sea a darting fish.
>
> We think that the hitherto badly corrupted translation of Calcidius should be restored as follows:
>
> > For long ago I lived as boy and solid tree,  
> > A bird, a creature from the waves, and then a milk-white maiden.
>
> In the latter verse, however, Cyril, book VIII *Against Julian*, seems to have read:
>
> > καὶ εἰν ἁλὶ φαίδιμος ἰχθύς  
> > and in the sea a shining fish.
>
> LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0702D] “And a chameleon, since he was so puffed up.” Many of the ancients noted Empedocles’s arrogance and “tragic vanity” (*tragikon typhon*, τραγικὸν τῦφον). LE PR.]

Clearly, like a fish, lest he putrefy through some more respectable kind of burial, he preferred to be roasted by hurling himself into Etna. And from that point let reincorporation have ended in his case, like a summer dinner after the roast.

[Note: [Col. 0702C] Wouwer reads “be exposed”; Pamel and Rhenanus, “consider the condition.”]

Accordingly, we must likewise contend here against the still more monstrous presumption that rotates beasts out of human beings and human beings out of beasts. Let the shrubs look to themselves. It will be permissible to deal with the matter in passing, [Col. 0702C] lest we be compelled to provoke more laughter than instruction.

[Note: [Col. 0702D] “It will be permissible to deal with the matter in passing.” That is: it will suffice to touch upon it incidentally. For these claims are so ridiculous that merely pointing them out in passing is enough to refute them. We have therefore emended the common reading, “It will be permissible—and sorrel too.” The Agobardine manuscript reads, “It will be permissible and seized.” RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0702C] Variant readings: “sorrels,” PAM. RHEN.; “seized,” Paris manuscript; “twice exalted,” Latin manuscript; “and burrs,” JUN.]

We say that the [Col. 0703A] human soul can in no way be transferred into beasts, even if, according to the philosophers, it were reckoned as deriving from elemental substances. For whether the soul is fire, water, blood, breath, air, or light, we must consider the animals that are contrary to each individual kind. Contrary to fire are those that are cold: snakes, spotted lizards, and salamanders; and indeed all creatures produced from the element opposed to fire, namely water. Correspondingly contrary to water, of course, are those creatures that are dry and without moisture: locusts, papiunculi [a kind of small creature; reading uncertain], and chameleons, which in fact delight in arid conditions.

[Note: [Col. 0703D] Junius reads “of water.”]

Likewise contrary to blood are creatures that lack its purple color: snails, little worms, and the greater part of the fishes. Contrary to breath are those that do not appear to breathe, lacking lungs and arteries: gnats, ants, moths, and tiny creatures of this kind. Likewise contrary to air [Col. 0703B] are creatures that always live underground or underwater and do without inhaling it—you will know the realities better than their names.

[Note: [Col. 0703D] The Paris manuscript, Gelenius, and Junius read “I should know.”]

Likewise contrary to light are creatures that are entirely blind or have eyes only for darkness: moles, bats, and owls.

[Note: [Col. 0703D] “Bats.” Latin *vesperugines*, that is, bats. They received their name from Lucifer, or the evening star (*vesperugo*), the planet Venus, because they are commonly believed not to leave their caves before that star appears. LE PR.]

I offer these examples by way of substances that are visible and manifest. But if I could grasp Epicurus’s atoms, see Pythagoras’s numbers, encounter Plato’s Ideas, and apprehend Aristotle’s entelechies, perhaps I would find animals to set in opposition to these kinds as well under the category of contrariety.

For I maintain that, from whichever of the aforesaid substances the human soul were constituted, it could not be reconstituted in animals so contrary to each particular substance and confer upon them their origin by its transference. It ought rather to be excluded and rejected by them than admitted and received; [Col. 0703C] by reason of this first contrariety, which produces the diversity of substantial condition, and then by reason of all the remaining contrarieties that follow in due order from each creature’s nature.

For the human soul has also been allotted different habitations, food, equipment, senses, affections, acts of intercourse, offspring, and likewise dispositions; then works, joys, distresses, faults, desires, pleasures, states of health, and remedies; and, finally, its own modes of life and manners of death.

[Note: [Col. 0703D] “How, then, will that soul,” etc. From the diversity of foods he demonstrates that transformations and transmigrations of souls cannot occur. LE PR.]

How, then, will that soul which clung to the earth, fearless neither of heights nor of depths, liable to fatigue even from climbing stairs and to strangulation even from being submerged in swimming pools—how will it afterward assault the air [Col. 0704A] in an eagle or plunge into the sea in an eel?

Likewise, how will a soul reared on generous, delicate, and carefully prepared foods chew—not merely straw, but thorns, the rustic bitterness of leaves, and the vermin of dung heaps, or even the poisons of worms, if it has passed into a goat or a quail? Indeed, how will it chew carrion—even human flesh—in a bear or lion, though surely mindful of itself?

[Note: [Col. 0703D] François reads “of water.”]

[Note: [Col. 0703D] “It will chew even poisons.” Perhaps this is because Pliny, book X, chapter 23, writes: “Quails are nourished on poison.” LE PR.]

In the same way you may reduce all the other cases to incongruity, so that we need not delay over arguing each individually.

Whatever the size or dimensions of the human soul, what will it do in animals far larger or far smaller? For every body must be completely filled by its soul, and every soul must be completely enclosed by its body. How, then, will a human soul fill an elephant? Or how, in turn, will it be enclosed within [Col. 0704B] a gnat?

[Note: [Col. 0704D] “How, then, will a human soul fill an elephant?” He argues against reincorporation from the inequality and incompatibility of bodies. For how can what was an elephant become a gnat? LE PR.]

If it is stretched or contracted to such a degree, it will certainly be endangered.

[Note: [Col. 0704D] PAM. and RHEN. read “were stretched or contracted.”]

And therefore I add: if the soul is by no means capable of a transference of this kind into animals—animals corresponding neither to the dimensions of its body nor to the other laws of its nature—will it then perhaps be transformed in accordance with the characteristics of those species and their manner of life, which is contrary to human life, itself becoming contrary to the human soul through transformation?

Yet if it admits transformation and loses what it was, it will not be what it was; and if it is not what it was, reincorporation is dissolved, since it plainly cannot be attributed to a soul which, if it is transformed, will no longer exist as that soul. For reincorporation will be said to belong to whatever undergoes it while remaining in its own condition. Therefore, if the soul can neither be changed, lest it cease to be itself, nor remain in its condition, because that condition cannot admit contraries, I still seek some [Col. 0704C] credible cause for a transference of this kind.

For although certain human beings are compared to beasts because of the qualities of their morals, dispositions, and affections—for God too says, “Man has been made like irrational cattle”—rapacious persons will not therefore become kites, nor filthy persons dogs, nor savage persons panthers, nor good persons sheep, nor talkative persons swallows, nor chaste persons doves.

[Note: [Col. 0704D] “Man has been made like irrational cattle.” The Greek is *hōmoiōthē* (ὡμοιώθη), “was made like.” Our translator rendered *tois anoētois* (τοῖς ἀνοήτοις) more literally as “foolish,” whereas the author has “irrational.” PAM.]

It is not as though the same substance of soul everywhere repeats its own nature in the characteristic traits of animals.

[Note: [Col. 0704D] “As though the same substance of soul.” Whether Plato maintained substantial reincorporation or only a moral reincorporation is disputed. Most Platonists defend him as having meant only a moral one; but Crispus, Division III, book I—who should certainly be consulted—attempts to establish the contrary with many arguments. Yet although he condemns Plato, he defends Pythagoras. LAC.]

Substance is one thing, and the nature of a substance another. For the substance of each thing is peculiar to it, whereas a nature can be shared. Take an example. [Col. 0705A] Stone and iron are substances; the hardness of stone and iron is a nature of their substance. Hardness is shared, but the substances differ. The softness of wool and the softness of a feather make their natural properties equal; they do not make their substances equal.

Thus, too, if a man is called a savage or a good beast, he does not therefore possess the same soul as a beast. For it is precisely when a likeness of nature is noted that a dissimilarity of substance is perceived. By the very fact that you judge a human being similar to a beast, you acknowledge that the soul is not the same: in calling it similar, you deny that it is the very same thing.

[Note: [Col. 0705C] PAM. adds “similar again.”]

This is also the meaning of the divine declaration, which equates man with cattle in nature, not in substance. Otherwise, God would not have characterized man in this way if he knew him to be a beast in substance.

## CHAPTER XXXIII
Even when this doctrine is defended under the name of judgment [Note: [Col. 0705C] Under the name of judgment. Plato is repeatedly censured for asserting in the *Timaeus* that souls are thrust into the bodies of animals according to their good or evil deserts. LAC.], [Col. 0705B] namely, that human souls obtain different kinds of animals according to their life and deserts—each to be slaughtered in animals destined for killing, subdued in beasts of service, wearied in working animals, and defiled in unclean ones; and likewise to be honored, cherished, tended, and desired in the most beautiful, excellent, useful, and delicate animals—here too I shall say: If they are changed, the very souls that earned their deserts will not themselves be brought to account. The rationale of judgment will be nullified if the consciousness of deserts is lost; but consciousness of deserts will be lost if the condition of souls has been altered; and the condition of souls is altered if they have not remained the same. Equally, if they have [Note: [Col. 0705C] *Not* inserted by Wouwer.] remained the same for judgment—as even the Egyptian Mercury knew, when he said that the soul, after departing from the body, is not poured back into the soul of the universe, but remains individually determined, so that, as he says, it may render to the Father an account of the things it did [Col. 0705C] in the body—I wish, assuredly, to review the justice, gravity, majesty, and dignity of divine judgment, and to ask whether human judgment does not preside from a loftier tribunal, being richer in the honor accorded to both kinds of sentence, punishments and rewards, more severe in avenging and more generous in bestowing.

What do you suppose the soul of a murderer will become? Some animal, [Col. 0706A] I imagine, destined for slaughter and the meat-market, so that it may likewise have its throat cut because it too cut throats; likewise be flayed because it too stripped others; likewise be set out as food because it too cast to beasts those [Note: [Col. 0705C] “Defiled the mouth,” Pamelius, Rhenanus.] whom it slaughtered in woods and trackless places [Note: [Col. 0705D] “Because it too cast to beasts those whom it slaughtered in woods and trackless places.” The common reading was: “Because it too infected beasts with those whom it slaughtered obliquely in woods and fields.” Ursinus’s manuscript reads: “Because it too cast to beasts those whom.” Agobard’s copy: “Because it too made for beasts those whom it slaughtered in woods and trackless places.” “Let it likewise,” he says, “be set out as food, because it too made food for beasts of those whom it slaughtered in the woods.” RIG.]. If it is judged in this way, will not that soul carry away more comfort than punishment? It finds a funeral amid the most costly cooks [Note: [Col. 0705C] “Cooks,” Paris, Rigault, Venice.]; it is buried with Apician and gluttons’ seasonings; it is brought onto Ciceronian tables; it is carried out on the most splendid Sullan platters; it undergoes a banquet as its funeral rites [Note: [Col. 0705D] “It undergoes a banquet as its funeral rites”: it is brought to a banquet, not a tomb; it is expended upon a dinner, not a funeral. RIG.]; it is devoured by its equals rather than by kites and wolves, so that, buried in a human body and returned to its own kind, it may seem to have risen again—exulting over human judgments, if it has experienced them.

For [Col. 0706B] human judgments tear a murderer apart, while still alive—indeed, not even allowing him to die easily—with various, specially selected beasts, even beasts trained [Note: [Col. 0706C] “And now,” Rigault, Venice.] contrary to nature [Note: [Col. 0705D] “Even beasts trained contrary to nature.” Namely, in the school of beasts, that is, the circus or amphitheater. RIG.], the delay of his end being carefully arranged to complete his punishment [Note: [Col. 0705D] “Indeed, not even allowing him to die easily.” Agobard’s manuscript: “Indeed, easily not even allowing him to die.” In many passages in Septimius, *facile* means “often.” RIG.]. But even if his soul escapes before [Note: [Col. 0705D] “But even if his soul escapes before the final sword.” That is, if by chance the soul departs from the body amid the mauling of the beasts before it is driven out by the final sword, etc. This, therefore, was the murderer’s punishment. He was thrown to beasts to be mangled; yet the delay of punishment was so arranged that, after the beasts had tired from their prolonged butchery, he was finally stabbed, the sword being driven into his throat and genitals, and even through his ribs into his vital organs. But if it happened that he died after being mangled by the savagery of the beasts, it was nevertheless customary to pierce the dead man’s throat, groin, and ribs with a sword, so that, by compensation and reenactment of his own crime, the guilty body might also be struck with the steel with which he had struck his fellow citizens. RIG.] the final sword, lest his body too should have escaped the steel, compensation for his own crime is nevertheless exacted by stabbing his throat and belly [Note: [Col. 0706C] “Both pierced,” Pamelius, Rhenanus; “both having been pierced,” Wouwer.] and transfixing his ribs. Then he is given to the fire, so that even his burial may be punished [Note: [Col. 0706D] “So that even his burial may be punished”—that is, with a fiery burial. He called the punishment of fire the supreme punishment in the book *To the Martyrs*. RIG.]; indeed, no other course is permitted. Nor, however, is such care taken over the pyre [Note: [Col. 0706D] “Nor, however, is so much care taken over the pyre.” Bodies scorched on the malignant pyre are left behind. RIG.] as to keep other beasts from finding the remains [Note: [Col. 0706D] “That other beasts may find the remains”: dogs, wolves, etc. RIG.]. Certainly, neither are the bones spared [Note: [Col. 0706D] “Certainly neither are the bones spared, nor are the ashes shown indulgence: they must be punished with nakedness.” This too was a punishment peculiar to murderers. For otherwise even the bodies of those condemned to be burned could be requested, namely so that their bones and ashes might be collected and entrusted to burial, as Ulpian says in the book *On the Corpses of the Punished*. RIG.], nor are the ashes shown indulgence: they must be punished with nakedness.

So great among human beings is the vengeance exacted for murder—so great as the very nature that is being avenged. Who would not prefer the justice of this world, which the Apostle not without reason testifies is armed with the sword (Rom. 13), and which is religious precisely when it rages on behalf of a human being [Col. 0706C]? If we also consider the recompense for other crimes—the crosses, burnings alive, sacks, hooks, and cliffs—to whom would it not be advantageous to undergo sentence under Pythagoras and Empedocles? For even those who deserve punishment by labor and servitude will surely be reincorporated in asses and mules. How greatly [Col. 0707A] will they congratulate themselves on millstones and water-lifting wheels [Note: [Col. 0707C] “Water-lifting wheels.” Draft animals, mules, and asses employed in turning these machines would congratulate themselves on their condition if ever they happened to be changed into human beings, for they would no longer sweat at turning these wheels. Vitruvius describes them: they were devices that drew up and discharged water by means of buckets and certain vessels. LE PR.], if they remember the mines, workhouses, public works, and prisons themselves, even when idle!

Likewise, concerning those who, through upright conduct, have commended their lives to the Judge, I look for rewards but instead find punishments. Is it, indeed, a great recompense for the good to be restored to just any animals? Homer remembers that he was a peacock [Note: [Col. 0707C] “Homer remembers that he was a peacock, as Ennius dreamed.” Those words of Ennius in which he said that Homer was changed into a peacock have perished. There were, I think, two dreams of Ennius about which authors wrote. I should think the following lines from Persius, Satire 6, pertain to the matter:

> The heart of Ennius commands this, after he snored himself awake  
> as the Maeonian, fifth in descent from the Pythagorean peacock.

LE PR.], as Ennius dreamed; but I would not believe poets even when they are awake. Granted that the peacock is exceedingly beautiful and adorned with whatever color it might wish; still, its feathers [Note: [Col. 0707C] “Feathers,” Rigault, Venice.] are silent, and its voice displeases—and poets desire nothing more than to sing. Homer was therefore condemned, not honored, in becoming a peacock. Regarded as the father of the liberal disciplines, he will take greater pleasure in the recompense of this world, preferring the ornaments of his fame to those of a tail [Note: [Col. 0707C] “Joys,” Rhenanus, Semler; “may rejoice,” Pamelius, Franeker.].

Come now: let poets pass into peacocks or [Col. 0707B] swans, if indeed the swan possesses a graceful voice. What animal will you put upon the just man Aeacus [Note: [Col. 0707C] “From the place,” Paris; “cast down,” Latinus; “in jest,” Pamelius, Franeker.]? What beast upon the virtuous woman Dido? What bird will patience obtain, what cattle holiness, what fish innocence? All animals serve humanity; all are subjected, all enslaved. If the virtuous person is to become any one of them, he is diminished [Note: [Col. 0707C] “Is diminished,” Pamelius, Rhenanus, Rigault, Venice, Semler, Oberthür.]. Is that the place for the man to whom, in return for the merits of his life, portraits, statues, inscriptions, public honors, and privileges are repaid? For whom the senate and the people offer their votes as a sacrifice?

O divine judgments after death, more deceitful [Note: [Col. 0707C] “More beggarly,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.] than human judgments—contemptible in their punishments and repellent in their favors—which neither the worst need fear nor the best desire; toward which [Note: [Col. 0708C] “And toward which,” Franeker.] the wicked rather than the holy will hasten: the former so as to escape the justice of this world more quickly, the latter so as to receive it later! Admirably, philosophers, do you teach; advantageously do you advise: lighter punishments or [Col. 0708A] rewards after death! Yet if any judgment awaits souls, it ought to be believed more severe in settling the account of life than in its administration, because nothing is more complete than what comes last, and nothing more complete than what is divine. God, therefore, will judge more fully [Note: [Col. 0707D] “God, therefore, will judge more fully because he judges last.” Namely, in the last and supreme judgment. RIG.] because he judges last, by an eternal sentence both of punishment and of refreshment, with souls returning not into beasts but into their own bodies—and this only once, on that day which the Father alone knows—so that the earnestness of faith may be tested by suspenseful expectation: always watching for the day because it is always ignorant of it; fearing daily what it daily hopes for.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

To [Note: [Col. 0708C] *Ad*, Pamelius, Rhenanus.] the present day, indeed, no doctrine of madness of this kind has broken forth under a heretical name, one that refashions human souls into beasts. But we necessarily [Col. 0708B] introduced and excluded this form as well, because it coheres with the foregoing doctrines, so that Homer might likewise be beaten back in his peacock just as Euphorbus was in Pythagoras; and thus, once this metempsychosis or *metensomatosis*—transmigration into another body—had also been repelled, that other doctrine which supplied the heretics with something might in turn be struck down.

For Simon the Samaritan, the would-be purchaser of the Holy Spirit in the Acts of the Apostles, after being condemned by the Spirit himself to perish with his money [Note: [Col. 0708C] *In* omitted by Franeker.], wept in vain [Note: [Col. 0707D] “Wept in vain.” That is, repented in vain. For Luke reports in the Acts of the Apostles that this Samaritan Simon, certainly moved to repentance for his sacrilegious speech, entreated Peter and the other apostles in these words: “Pray to the Lord for me, that none of these things which you have spoken against me may happen.” Luke relates nothing further about Simon. Septimius says that he wept in vain. This may also be understood to mean that he is said to have wept in vain because, after coming to the Christian faith and professing, as is likely, that he renounced the magical arts and repented of his former frauds, he nevertheless later returned faithlessly to the same deceits and impostures. RIG.]. Turning to the assault upon truth, as though to console himself by revenge, and supported also by the powers of his art, he redeemed with the same money, for the display of some supposed power, a certain Tyrian woman named Helen from a place of public lust [Note: [Col. 0708C] “A certain Tyrian woman named Helen from a place of public lust.” Irenaeus, book I, chapter 20, called her a prostitute. RIG.—“A certain Tyrian woman named Helen.” Both here and in the following chapter we have retained *Helenē* or *Helena*, both because Simon the Magician said that she was that same Helen of Troy and because she is so named by the blessed martyr Justin in *Apology* II, and after him by Eusebius in the Greek *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 12 or 13; by the blessed Jerome, *Letter to Ctesiphon against the Pelagians*; Epiphanius, *Heresy* 21, more than once; Theodoret, *Heretical Fables*, book I; and John of Damascus, *On Heresies*. The manuscripts of Irenaeus vary, although more read *Selene*, as do also the blessed Augustine in *On Heresies*, Rufinus in his translation of Eusebius, Cyril in one place, and, before all of them, Pope Clement in the *Recognitions*, where he wishes her to have been named from the moon, which is called σελήνη (*selēnē*) in Greek. It is therefore likely that she was called by both names. PAM.], obtaining for himself a reward worthy of himself in place of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0708D] “A reward worthy of himself.” So too Agobard’s copy reads. Yet I think the better reading would be *mercem*, “merchandise.” Simon, he says, purchased that Helen as merchandise worthy of himself with the same money with which he had wished to purchase the Holy Spirit. RIG.].

He fashioned himself as the supreme Father [Note: [Col. 0708C] “Fashions,” Rhenanus, Semler.], but her as his own first projected Thought [Note: [Col. 0708D] “But her as his own first projected Thought.” The blessed martyr Justin speaks more clearly: “a certain first Mind or Intelligence”; Irenaeus: “the conception of his mind, the mother of all, through whom at the beginning he conceived in his mind the making of angels and archangels.” Likewise, the phrase “she, having attained the object of this purpose,” etc., supports Irenaeus’s meaning. PAM.], by which he had conceived the plan of creating angels and archangels. [Col. 0709A] Having attained the object of this purpose, she had leapt forth from the Father and bounded down into the lower regions; and there, anticipating the Father’s purpose, she had generated the angelic powers, which were ignorant of the Father and were the makers of this world. Through envy [Note: [Col. 0709C] “By them through envy,” Latinus; “by them likewise in spirit,” Pamelius, Semler.] she was detained by them [Note: [Col. 0709D] “But through envy she was detained by them.” Irenaeus: “She was detained by them out of envy, because they did not wish to be thought the offspring of someone else.” From this it is perfectly clear that the readings found in the common editions and even in ancient manuscripts are corrupt: “By them likewise she was detained in spirit,” and “By them the soul was not detained in like manner.” RIG.], lest, if she departed, they should be seen to be another’s offspring. For that reason she was subjected to every indignity, so degraded that she was nowhere permitted to depart, and fell even into human form, as though to be restrained by bonds of flesh. Thus, for many ages, she was rolled through one female guise after another. She had even been that Helen who was utterly ruinous to Priam, and afterward to the eyes of Stesichorus [Note: [Col. 0709D] “And afterward to the eyes of Stesichorus.” That story is related by many writers. For when he had been deprived of his sight because of his invectives against Helen, he testified in a poem he called a palinode that what he had said about her was false, and immediately recovered his sight. LE PR.]: she had blinded him because of his poem’s abuse, and afterward restored his sight because of the reparation made by his praise. Accordingly, as she migrated from body to body, she had, as her final degradation [Note: [Col. 0709C] “Finally, from adornment,” Wouwer manuscript.], stood for sale under the title of Helen, now cheaper still.

[Col. 0709B] She, therefore, was the lost sheep for whom the supreme Father—that is, Simon—had descended [Note: [Col. 0710C] “Descends,” Rigault, Venice.]. After first recovering her and carrying her back—I do not know whether upon his shoulders or between her thighs [Note: [Col. 0709D] “I do not know whether upon his shoulders or between her thighs.” Septimius’s style alludes to the parable of the Good Shepherd, punning upon Helen the prostitute. RIG.]—he then turned his attention to the salvation of human beings, as though they were to be liberated by vengeance from those angelic powers. To deceive them, he too conformed himself in like fashion; and, falsely presenting himself to human beings as a man, he played the Son in Judaea but the Father in Samaria.

O Helen, afflicted alike among poets and heretics—then infamous for adultery, now for prostitution! Except that she is rescued more gloriously from Troy than from the brothel: from Troy by a thousand ships, but from the brothel perhaps for less than a thousand denarii. Blush, Simon: you were slower in seeking her and less steadfast in bringing her back. But Menelaus immediately pursues her when lost, immediately reclaims her when taken away, and wrests her back by a ten-year [Col. 0709C] war, neither concealing himself, nor deceiving, nor quibbling. I fear that he was more truly her father, since he labored more watchfully, boldly, and persistently to recover Helen.

## CHAPTER XXXV

But metempsychosis did not construct this fable for you alone. Carpocrates too makes use of it, being likewise a magician [Note: [Col. 0709D] “Likewise a magician.” In one phrase he states what Irenaeus says at greater length about Carpocrates and his disciples, followed by Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapter 7) and Epiphanius: “For,” he says, “they practice magical arts and incantations, as well as love potions, χαροτήσια [*charotēsia*, that is, aphrodisiacs, as Eusebius’s translators render it], *paredroi* [that is, assistants], *oneiropompoi* [that is, senders of dreams], and other malign practices—or, as Epiphanius’s translator has it, magical deceptions.” “Likewise a fornicator.” The Author adds this because, according to Irenaeus, Marcellina, who came to Rome under Anicetus and belonged to this school, led many to destruction. Epiphanius repeats this, adding that they live in luxury and customarily do everything for bodily pleasure, to such a degree that Eusebius imputes especially to his Gnostic disciples the suspicion which the pagans had conceived on their account concerning all Christians—of promiscuous sexual acts and infanticide following an illicit union. Tertullian defended himself at great length against these charges above, in the *Apologeticum*. PAM.], [Col. 0710A] and likewise a fornicator, though possessing less of a Helen—why not? [Note: [Col. 0710D] “Likewise a fornicator, though possessing less of a Helen”—although he was a fornicator, he nevertheless did not have a Helen. RIG.—“Though possessing less of a Helen.” Although a fornicator, he nevertheless did not equal Helen, who, through the shamefulness of her life, was the cause of Troy’s destruction and the death brought by many calamities. LE PR.] For, in order to establish the complete overthrow of every divine and human rule, he asserted that souls are reincorporated. He maintained that this life is assigned to no one unless all the deeds that condemn it have been discharged, because nothing is regarded as evil by nature but only by opinion. Metempsychosis must therefore necessarily threaten if, in every first passage through this life, satisfaction is not made for all unlawful deeds. Crimes, evidently, are the appointed dues of life. Otherwise the soul must be summoned back as many times as it has rendered too little, remaining in arrears for its offenses until it pays the last farthing (Matt. 5), repeatedly cast into the prison of the body.

For he adapts to this the Lord’s entire allegory, which shines clearly under definite interpretations. First, it should indeed be [Col. 0710B] understood simply: for a pagan person too is our adversary, walking with us along the same road of our common life. Otherwise we would have had to depart from the world (1 Cor. 5), if it were not lawful for us to associate with them. The Lord therefore commands you to show goodwill toward such a person (Luke 6): “Love your enemies,” he says, “and pray for those who curse you,” lest, provoked by some injury arising from commercial dealings, he drag you before his judge and, once handed over to custody, you be confined until the entire debt has been paid.

Then, if the reference to the adversary is transferred to the devil by reason of the accompanying observance, you are warned to enter with him too into that agreement which is reckoned to arise from the covenant of faith. For you have covenanted to renounce him, his pomp, and his angels. This is what has been agreed between you. The friendship in question will consist in observing the pledge [Note: [Col. 0710C] “The observance,” Pamelius, Rhenanus.], so that afterward [Col. 0710C] you take back nothing of his from among those things which you renounced and returned to him, lest he accuse you before God the Judge as a defrauder and transgressor of the covenant—just as elsewhere we read that he is the accuser of the saints (Rev. 12:10), and as the very name “devil” [Note: [Col. 0710C] “Devil” omitted by Rigault, Venice.] means “informer”—and the Judge hand you over to the angel who executes the sentence, and that angel commit you to the infernal prison, from which you will not be released until even your slight offense [Col. 0711A] has been paid for by the delay of the resurrection [Note: [Col. 0710D] “Until even a slight offense has been paid for by the delay of the resurrection.” That is, in the interval before we rise again—not because the postponement of the resurrection by itself is the expiation and purgation of venial faults, but because in purgatory we are cleansed by various punishments after this life and before we rise again. Moreover, Pamelius noted that this interpretation of Tertullian supports the purgation of souls after this life from all lesser offenses, and therefore purgatory, adding other testimonies from St. Cyprian. LAC.].

What is more fitting than these meanings? What is truer than these interpretations? But, according to Carpocrates, if the soul is indebted for every crime, who must be understood as its enemy and adversary? I suppose it is the better mind, which drove it toward some degree of innocence, so that it must be forced again and again into a body until it is found guilty of no good life whatsoever. This is to recognize a good tree from evil fruits [Note: [Col. 0711C] “This is to recognize a good tree from evil fruits.” It is irony, by which he ridicules Carpocrates’ interpretation. Likewise, the word “I hope,” which follows, is understood in the sense of “I fear,” as more than once above—as though he feared that he might be unable to answer the arguments proposed. PAM.]; that is, to recognize the doctrine of truth from the worst possible precepts.

I fear that heretics of this kind will also seize upon Elijah’s example, on the ground that he was so represented in John [Note: [Col. 0711C] “So” omitted by Rigault, Venice.] that the Lord’s declaration might support metempsychosis [Note: [Col. 0712C] “That they may support the forerunner,” Rigault, Venice.] (Matt. 17): “Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him.” And elsewhere (Matt. 11): “And if you are willing to hear it, this is Elijah who is to come.” Were [Col. 0711B] the Jews, therefore, asking John from a Pythagorean belief (John 1), “Are you Elijah?” and not from the divine proclamation (Mal. 4), “And behold, I shall send you Elijah the Tishbite”?

But their metempsychosis is the recall of a soul that had long ago undergone death and is introduced anew into another body. Elijah, however, will come not after departing from life [Note: [Col. 0711D] “Elijah, however, not after departing,” etc. Irenaeus, book V, chapter 7, in his discussion of paradise in Eden, relates that this teaching about Elijah had been received from presbyters who were disciples of the Apostles: that he was translated into the paradise prepared for righteous people, into which the Apostle Paul too was carried and heard words inexpressible to us at present; that Elijah will remain there until the consummation of the age and meanwhile be preserved incorrupt. RIG.], but after being translated. He is not to be restored to a body from which he was not removed (2 Kings 2), but restored to the world from which he was translated; not by a restoration to life after absence, but by the completion of his prophecy. He will be the same person himself, bearing both his own name and his own humanity.

But how, then, is John Elijah [Note: [Col. 0711D] “But how, then, is John Elijah?” The blessed Augustine interprets these passages of Scripture in precisely the same way (*Tractate XIV on John*, chapter 1, and *On the Trinity*, book V, chapter 14). He does not, however, read in either place the phrase “before the people,” which is therefore peculiar to our Author. In the latter passage he also interprets “the spirit of Elijah” by comparison with “the spirit of Moses,” just as this Author does, who says in a single phrase that Moses’ spirit was transferred, because it is said to have been taken from Moses and given to the seventy elders. PAM.]? You have the angel’s words (Luke 1): “And he,” it says, “will go before the people in the power and spirit of Elijah”—not in Elijah’s soul or flesh. For those substances belong individually to each human being. Spirit [Col. 0711C] and power, however, are conferred from without by God’s grace. [Col. 0712A] They can thus also be transferred to another by God’s will, as was done formerly with the spirit of Moses.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

We have, I think, digressed into these questions from the point to which we must now return. We had established that the soul is sown in and from the human being himself [Note: [Col. 0711D] “We had established that the soul is sown in and from the human being himself,” etc. Tertullian established this paradox of his in chapters 25, 26, and 27, where he asserted that the soul is propagated in the womb together with the flesh, and that all souls are derived through the seed from Adam’s stock—a point which he presses again in this chapter. LAC.], and that from the beginning there is one seed, just as there is also one stock from which the entire lineage of the flesh springs. We did so, of course, because of the rival opinions of philosophers and heretics [Note: [Col. 0712C] “Because of the rival opinions of philosophers and heretics.” In chapter 23, before declaring his own opinion on the propagation of souls, he reviewed the various opinions of heretics concerning the soul’s origin, which rivaled the philosophical doctrines—especially the Platonic ones—that granted souls a heavenly origin. There he showed that Valentinus, Saturninus, Carpocrates, and Apelles were Plato’s rivals and disciples. LAC.], and because of that lethargic old discourse of Plato [Note: [Col. 0712C] “That lethargic old discourse of Plato.” He does not call Plato’s discourse “lethargic” because Plato said that acts of learning are acts of recollection, as though they proceeded from a lethargic sleep. Rather, he alludes to the ancient discourse in Plato about the reciprocal circulation of souls, concerning which chapter 28 says: “What, then, is that old discourse now found in Plato’s memory?” etc. He plays wittily upon the word, to show that this old discourse is a mere dream, without any brains, and is just as lethargic as it is old. Arnobius too used *veternosum* in the sense of “old” in book I. LAC.].

We now construct from that point the sequence of the discussions that follow. The soul, being sown in the womb together with the flesh, receives its sex together with the flesh, so that neither substance by itself is regarded as the cause of sex. For if the conceptions of the two substances admitted some interval between them, so that either the flesh or the soul was sown first, it would then be possible to ascribe the distinctive character of sex to one substance rather than the other by reason of that temporal interval between the two seeds: either the flesh would imprint sex upon the soul, or the soul upon the flesh. Apelles—not the painter, but the heretic—is relevant here [Note: [Col. 0712D] “Apelles—not the painter, but the heretic.” Ἀφέλλης (*Aphellēs*), in Latin *Apelles* and *Apella*. Horace: “Let the circumcised Jew Apella believe it.” He, perhaps, was circumcised because he was a Jew; but *Apella* is the Greek Ἀπέλλα (*Apella*).]—[the sentence continues beyond this excerpt].

Apelles placed male and female souls before their bodies, as he learned from Philumena, and therefore made the flesh, as the later substance, receive its sex from the soul. Those who introduce the soul into the flesh after birth likewise make the soul, which comes to flesh already formed, receive from the flesh a prior determination of male or female sex. But the undivided seeds of both substances and their united outpouring undergo a common outcome of sex, according to whatever lines that mysterious principle of nature may draw [Note: [Col. 0712D] “According to whatever lines it may draw.” Since he had mentioned a painter shortly before, he also borrowed this proverbial expression from painters. PAM.]. Here too the archetypal form bears witness, since the male is fashioned first in time: Adam was first; the woman somewhat later, for Eve came afterward. Thus for a long while [Col. 0713A] the flesh is unformed, like the flesh taken from Adam’s side; yet it is already animate, because they acknowledge that portion of Adam also to have been animate [Note: [Col. 0713B] *Animate*, Pamelius, Rhenanus; *a soul*, Agobard’s manuscript.]. [Note: [Col. 0713B] “Moreover, God’s breath would have animated the woman herself.” Augustine appears to answer this passage in book I of *On the Soul*, when he says: “Those who assert the propagation of souls think that they fortify their position most invincibly from this fact: although Scripture says that God took a rib from the man’s side and built it into a woman, it does not add that he breathed the breath of life into her face; the reason, they say, is that she had already been animated from the man.” For this the Author said, “she too was already animate.” Augustine replies, however, that this does nothing to support their position: “For,” he says, “if it had been written, ‘He breathed [Col. 0713C] the breath of life into the woman’s face,’ it would not even then follow that the soul was not propagated from parents, unless the same thing were also found written concerning a son. But since the matter is left unspoken, it is neither denied nor affirmed.” PAM.]

Moreover, God’s breath would have given life to the woman herself as well, if the soul, like the flesh, had not been transmitted into the woman from Adam’s stock [Note: [Col. 0712D–0713C] Moreover, God’s breath would have given life to the woman herself as well, if she had not derived from Adam a transmitted stock of soul as well as of flesh. But if Scripture had said, “He breathed the breath of life into the woman’s face,” it would not even then follow that the soul was not propagated from parents, unless the same thing were also found written concerning a son. Since it is left unspoken, however, it is neither denied nor affirmed. PAM.].

## CHAPTER XXXVII
But surely some power, serving the divine will, regulates the whole preparation by which a human being is sown, built up, and fashioned in the womb. [Note: [Col. 0713C] **“Some power, serving the divine will, regulates it.”** What this power is he explains shortly afterward, when he says: “We believe that the angels are God’s functionaries” (that is, in the phraseology of the jurists, God’s ministers). This passage therefore serves to confirm the Catholic doctrine concerning the particular angels assigned to each human being. On these there is an elegant statement by blessed Jerome on Matthew 18, “Their angels always behold the face of my Father”: “Great,” he says, “is the dignity of souls, since each one has, from the beginning of its birth, an angel assigned to guard it.” On the same subject there is Question 30 in Justin Martyr’s *Questions and Responses*; and the same thing is affirmed by blessed Hilary on Psalm 133, Basil on Psalm 48 and elsewhere, and Augustine in *Soliloquies*, ch. 27. To the same point belongs the fact that, among the works of blessed Cyprian, in the prologue to the work *On the Cardinal Works of Christ*, the angels are called “the ministers of our salvation,” and that Rufinus, in his *Exposition of the Creed*, writes that from the beginning certain powers of the heavenly virtues were appointed, by whom the mortal race should be governed and administered. See also Origen, Homily 13 or 35 on Luke, and Homily 11 on Numbers. PAM.]—by whatever method that power has been allotted to carry out the process.

Reflecting upon this, Roman superstition even fashioned the goddess Alemona [Note: [Col. 0713D] **“Roman superstition even fashioned the goddess Alemona.”** On Alemona see Giraldi, *On the Gods of the Gentiles*. Concerning the other three—as Turnebus too noted before me, *Adversaria*, book XVIII, ch. 34—Gellius writes as follows: “Two Fates were named by the Latins: one, from birth in the ninth month, was called Nona; the other, from delivery in the tenth month, Decima. A third was added, called Parca, as though *Parta*, with *t* changed to *c*.” Here the author calls her Partula because she governs childbirth. On Lucina, moreover, he speaks more fully below in ch. 39. PAM.], charged with nourishing the fetus in the womb; and Nona and Decima, named after the more anxious months; and Partula, who governs childbirth; and Lucina, who brings the child forth into the light. We believe the angels to be divine functionaries.

The fetus in the womb is therefore a human being from the moment when its form is complete. [Col. 0714A] [Note: [Col. 0713D] **“For the law of Moses also then holds one guilty of miscarriage,” etc.** That law is found in Exodus 21 according to the Septuagint. The decree there is that, if anyone strikes a pregnant woman, then, if the child has not been formed, he shall be guilty and condemned according to the will of that woman’s husband, with whom he shall settle the dispute; but if the child has been formed—that is, animated—he shall give life for life, for he shall be guilty of homicide. According to some, *aborsus* is said of miscarriage in the first months of pregnancy, but *abortus* when childbirth is imminent. LE PR.] For the law of Moses (Exod. 21:22) also holds one guilty of miscarriage [Note: [Col. 0713B] *Oborsus*, Fran.] liable to retaliation only when the case already concerns a human being, [Note: [Col. 0714B] **“When the case already concerns a human being.”** That is, when the designation and title “human being” applies. Once the fetus is formed, παιδίου ἐξεικονισμένου (*paidiou exeikonismenou*, “the child having been fully fashioned”), it must now be regarded as a human being. For, as Jerome says to Algasia, Question 4: “It is not reckoned a human being until the confused elements receive their own shapes and limbs.” RIG.] when the condition of life and death is already assigned to it, and when it is already entered upon the rolls of fate, even though, while still living in its mother, [Note: [Col. 0713B] “And thus still,” with Jun.] it shares her lot to a very great extent. [Note: [Col. 0714C] **“Even though, while still living in its mother, it shares her lot to a very great extent.”** He takes this from the teaching of the Law, which says that an unborn child is a portion of the woman, or of her entrails. Law 1, *On the Inspection of a Pregnant Woman*. RIG.]

I shall also say something about the periods of the soul’s birth, so that I may follow the sequence through. A lawful birth occurs approximately at the beginning of the tenth month. [Note: [Col. 0714C] **“A lawful birth occurs approximately at the beginning of the tenth month.”** Although the ninth month is nowadays assigned to childbirth, this nevertheless agrees with the rules of the ancients, who fixed the tenth month. Our Turnebus says that this is because the months of the ancients were shorter, being lunar, whereas ours are adjusted to the movement of the sun and are therefore longer. Among the jurists, birth in the tenth month is held lawful. A grandson or granddaughter by a deceased son may also be instituted as heir, provided that the child is born in the tenth month after the father’s death, from the law *Gallus* 29, Digest, *On Children*, or *On the Institution of Posthumous Heirs*, final section, Code, *On Posthumous Children*. After ten months this cannot be done, from law 6, *On Those Who Are Their Own Heirs*. Angelius, however, wrote that the emperor Hadrian decreed a birth in the eleventh month to be lawful. LE PR.]

Those who reason from numbers honor the number ten as the parent of all the numbers following from it [Note: [Col. 0714D] **“The decurial number.”** *Decurialis* is used in a novel sense by the author for the number ten. Relevant here is Athenagoras’ statement (*Oration for the Christians*) that, according to the Pythagoreans, the number ten is the greatest: it is also quaternary and embraces both arithmetical number and the ratio of musical harmony or concord. For it contains every kind of counting, is the source and beginning of numbers, and consists of one, two, three, and four. PAM.] [Note: [Col. 0714B] *Parentum* (“of parents”), Pam., Rhen., Seml.], and consequently as the perfecter of human birth. [Note: [Col. 0714D] **“I, rather, shall argue from God.”** Ingeniously indeed, but he refutes superstitions by superstitions. RIG.] I, rather, shall derive this measure of time from God: let the ten months inaugurate a human being by reference to the Decalogue, so that we are born according to the same number of time by which we are reborn according to the number of commandments.

But even in the seventh month birth is complete [Note: [Col. 0714B] *Nativitatis* (“of birth”), Rig., Ven.] [Note: [Col. 0714D] **“But even in the seventh month.”** A seven-month birth is so fully lawful that it benefits the mother, since it is regarded as full-term under the law *Septimo*, Digest, *On the Status of Property*. Some think that the reason why an eight-month birth does not have the same effect must be attributed to the power of the number seven; but blessed Ambrose’s Letter 39 to Horontianus should be consulted. Hippocrates, *Epidemics*, book II, section 3, counts 280 days for a viable birth. LE PR.], [Col. 0715A] more readily than in the eighth. Here I recognize the honor of the Sabbath: so that in the month corresponding to the day on which God’s creation was dedicated, [Note: [Col. 0715C] *Quoto* (“corresponding to which”), Fran.] [Note: [Col. 0715C] *Est* omitted, Seml.] the image of God may sometimes be brought forth. [Note: [Col. 0715C] *Toto* (“the whole”), Fran.] Birth has been permitted to hasten and to coincide so fittingly with the hebdomad—under the auspices of resurrection, rest, and the kingdom. Therefore the *ogdoad* (ὀγδοάς, “group of eight”) does not create us: for then there will be no marriages. [Note: [Col. 0715C] **“The ogdoad does not create us.”** He alludes to the eighth month, in which births are generally not viable. He also alludes to the eighth day, when, after the week has elapsed, the day of the Sun returns—a day which we rightly call the Lord’s Day because of our Lord’s resurrection, and on which the day of the last judgment, and therefore of our resurrection, is also to occur. Then, however, as Matthew affirms, there will no longer be any marriages for us. RIG.]

We have long since established the partnership of flesh and soul from the coalescence [Note: [Col. 0715C] *Congregatione* (“coming together”), Codex Agobardinus.] of the very seeds up to the perfection of the formed being. In the same way we now defend that partnership from birth onward [Note: [Col. 0715C] *Et nativitatem* (“and birth”), Codex Agobardinus.], chiefly because flesh and soul grow together, though by different [Note: [Col. 0715C] *Divisa* (“separate”), Rig., Ven.] processes in accordance with the condition of their kinds: the flesh in size, the soul in capacity; the flesh in configuration, the soul in perception. Yet it must be denied that the soul grows in substance, lest it also be said to diminish in substance and thus be believed capable of perishing.
