[Note: [Col. 0715D] **“It must be denied that the soul grows in substance, lest it also be said to diminish in substance and thus be believed capable of perishing.”** Augustine: “He was evidently afraid that it would perish by diminishing if it grew, yet was not afraid that it would perish by becoming rarified as it grew.” But since Septimius said that the soul does not grow in substance, and therefore neither diminishes nor perishes, he seems to have guarded sufficiently against its perishing by becoming rarified, since substance does not become rarified, just as substance does not diminish; rather, the soul manifests its powers in proportion to the body’s size and brings forth its distinctive possessions. Finally, he attributes a body to the soul, but a body of its own kind—that is, one appropriate to the soul, to which, since it is immortal, growth or perishing in substance is inappropriate. But enough on these matters, of which one day will make us possessors and certain—the day that will present us immortal before God. RIG.]

[Col. 0715B] Rather, its power, in which its natural endowments are implanted and preserved, is gradually developed together with the flesh, while the measure of its substance, with which it was breathed in from the beginning, remains intact.

Imagine a definite weight of gold or silver, still an unworked mass. [Note: [Col. 0716C] **“Imagine a definite weight of gold or silver.”** Augustine writes as follows concerning this passage: “Who would believe that a man with such a mind could have been so eloquent? But these things should be feared, not mocked; for he would never have been driven to this if he had been able to conceive of something that exists and yet is not a body. But what could be more absurd than to think that a mass of some metal can grow in one part while being hammered unless it diminishes in another? Or that it can increase in breadth unless it is reduced in thickness? Or that any body, while the quantity of its nature remains unchanged, can grow in every direction unless it becomes rarified?” etc. (*On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book X, final chapter). PAM.] Its configuration is compact, and for the time being smaller than what it will become; yet within the limit of its measure it contains everything that belongs to the nature of gold or silver. Then, when the mass is spread into a sheet, it becomes larger than it was at first through the extension of a fixed weight, not through addition—by being stretched, not increased. Yet even in this way it is increased while it is stretched, for it may increase in configuration although it cannot increase in substance.

Then the very brilliance [Note: [Col. 0716C] *Exsplendor*, Rig., Ven.] of the gold or silver is also brought forth [Note: [Col. 0716C] *Perhibetur* (“is reported”), others, less suitably.]—a brilliance that had indeed been present in the mass, though more obscurely, and was nevertheless not nonexistent. Then one configuration after another is added, according to the material’s pliability and the direction in which the craftsman draws it, [Note: [Col. 0716C] *Aget* (“will work”), Par.; others, less suitably, *auget* (“increases”), Jun.] contributing nothing to its measure [Col. 0715C] except form. The soul’s increments must likewise be understood as developmental, not substantial. [Note: [Col. 0716C] *Provocativa* (“evocative”), all witnesses except Jun.]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

[Col. 0716A]

Although we have already laid the groundwork for the proposition that all the soul’s natural attributes [Note: [Col. 0716C] **“The soul’s natural attributes.”** Its distinctive possessions, namely, as above. RIG.]—those pertaining to perception and understanding—are present in the soul’s substance itself and belong to the soul’s innate estate, but emerge gradually through the periods of life and develop in different ways through contingent circumstances, according to skills, education, places, and ruling powers, nevertheless, in relation to the partnership of flesh and soul now under discussion, we say that the soul’s puberty also coincides with the flesh’s. Both arise together, the one through the prompting of the senses and the other through the development of the bodily members, at about the fourteenth year—not because Asclepiades begins to reckon wisdom from that point, nor because the civil laws from that age onward adapt a person to the management of affairs, [Note: [Col. 0716D] **“Nor because the civil laws,” etc.** Under the civil laws, a minor below puberty could not administer his own affairs or make a will. The age of puberty is defined in law 1, *From What Age*, §1, Digest, *Who May Make Wills*. LE PR.] but because this principle too derives from the beginning.

For if Adam and Eve, through the knowledge of good and evil, became conscious of covering their private parts, then at the age when we become conscious of that same thing we profess the knowledge of good and evil. From those years onward [Col. 0716B] each sex becomes fuller and more clothed; desire employs the eyes as its arbiters, shares in the common desire, [Note: [Col. 0716D] **“Reaches a common agreement.”** Now through a shared desire for embrace and intercourse. RIG.] understands what those things are, [Note: [Col. 0716D] **“And understands what those things are.”** Now each sex understands what those things are which they are constituted to do and undergo. The words denoting the acts of each sex are omitted. With a similar aposiopesis he veils an obscene word near the end of the book *Against the Valentinians*. RIG.] and girds its extremities with itching, after the fashion of the contagion of the fig tree; [Note: [Col. 0716C] **“Girds its extremities with itching, after the fashion of the contagion of the fig tree.”** He means the pubic region and the other areas of the human body covered by a garment of fig-leaf loincloths, περιζωμάτων (*perizōmatōn*). It is as though our first parents, Adam and Eve, had itched to the very tips of their nails when they plucked leaves from the fig tree, and thereafter the infection had contaminated the whole tree—the infection, namely, of that whitish juice or fluid which we see dripping from a broken fig tree. Thus in the book *On Modesty*: “He had readily seen something attractive and desired it, looking downward and retaining the itching from the fig leaves.” RIG.] it leads the human being out of the paradise of integrity, and from then on becomes scabby with the other faults as well, and with forms of transgression that are not natural, since they now arise not from nature’s ordinance but from vice. [Note: [Col. 0716C] *Delinquenti* (“to the transgressor”), Jun.]

Strictly speaking, however, there is only one natural desire: solely the desire for food, which God also bestowed at the beginning: “From every tree,” he says (Gen. 3), “you shall eat.” He also extended it beyond measure to the second generation after the flood (Gen. 9 [printed text: Gen. 2]): “Behold, I have given you everything for food, like the green plants”—providing not so much for the soul as for the flesh, though for the sake of the soul. [Note: [Col. 0716C] *Prospectum* (“provision”), Pam., Rhen.]

For we must remove the opportunity for the disputant who, because the soul appears to desire food, wishes to infer from this too that it is mortal, since it is sustained by food, then languishes when food is withheld, and finally dies when food is entirely withdrawn. It must, however, be asked not only who desires food, but also for whom he desires it; and whether for himself, but also why, when, and to what extent. One thing is desired by nature, [Note: [Col. 0717C] “It is one thing to be desired by nature,” Fran., Gagn.] another by necessity; one according to its own proper condition, another for the sake of something else.

The soul will therefore desire food for itself, certainly, because of necessity, but for the flesh by reason of the flesh’s natural property. For the flesh is the soul’s house, and the soul is the flesh’s tenant. The tenant will therefore desire, by reason of and under the necessity of that name, whatever benefits the house throughout the whole period of his tenancy—not so that he himself may be built up, nor so that he himself may be fortified, [Note: [Col. 0717C] *Gloriandus* (“glorified”), Fran.] nor so that he himself may be propped up, but only so that he may be contained, because he cannot otherwise be contained unless the house is kept standing.

Otherwise, when the house has fallen apart, the soul will be able to depart unharmed despite the loss of supports that were proper to the house, since it possesses its own foundations and the nourishment of its own condition: immortality, rationality, sentience, intelligence, and freedom of choice.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

All these things, bestowed upon the soul at birth, are now likewise overshadowed and corrupted by the same being who envied them at the beginning, so that they are neither perceived spontaneously nor administered as they ought to be. For to what human being will an evil spirit not attach itself, lurking to catch souls [Note: [Col. 0717C] *Animae* (“of the soul”), Jun.] even from the very gateway of birth, or by what invitation will it not be summoned—[Col. 0718A] by that whole superstition surrounding childbirth? [Note: [Col. 0717C] **“By that whole superstition surrounding childbirth.”** Saint Augustine describes that superstition and the absurdity of the pagans in *The City of God*, book IV, ch. 21. For during childbirth they invoked innumerable gods and goddesses: Lucina, Ops, the god Vaticanus, the goddess Cunina, Rumina, Adeona, Abeona, the god Statilius, Volumnus, the goddess Volumna, and others concerning whom I intend to remain silent here. LE PR.]

Thus all are born with idolatry as their midwife, while their parents, themselves still wreathed with the womb’s fillets prepared before the idols, proclaim their offspring as candidates for the demons; while in childbirth cries are raised to Lucina and Diana; [Note: [Col. 0717D] **“While in childbirth cries are raised to Lucina and Diana.”** Lucina was so called, as the author said above in ch. 37, because she “brings forth into the light.” Relevant here is what Saint Augustine says in *The City of God*, book IV, ch. 12: “Lucina, who is invoked by women in labor”; and that line of Terence in the *Andria*: “Juno Lucina, bring aid.” For Cicero, if Vives is to be believed, writes somewhere that both Juno and Diana were called Lucina—a point supported by the conjunction “and” placed between them here. PAM.] while for the whole week a table is set before Juno; [Note: [Col. 0717D] **“While for the whole week a table is set before Juno,”** etc. Tibullus, on the Juno of birth:

> *Natalis Juno, sanctos cape thuris acervos.*
>
> “Juno of Birth, receive the sacred heaps of incense.”

It therefore appears that, just as a table was customarily set before a person’s *genius*, so too one was set before that person’s Juno. For just as, according to the author’s next statement, *genii* were assigned to everyone, so too were Junos—contrary to the opinion of some who wish to assign *genii* to men and Junos to women. Our position is certainly supported by this statement of Pliny, book X: “Since individuals make just as many gods out of themselves by adopting *genii* and Junos for themselves”; and by this statement of Seneca somewhere: “For they assigned to each person both a *genius* and a Juno.” PAM.] while on the final day the Fates who write destiny are summoned; [Note: [Col. 0717C] *Scribundo*, Jun.] while even the infant’s first placement [Note: [Col. 0717C] *Constitutione* (“placement”), Jun.] upon the ground is consecrated to the goddess Statina. [Note: [Col. 0718C] **“Is consecrated to the goddess Statina.”** He mentions her in book II of *To the Nations*: “Statina for setting the infant upright.” They also had a god Statilinus for children learning to stand, whom Augustine mentions in *The City of God*, book IV, ch. 21. In Nonius, from Varro, we read of Statilinus and Statanus as guardian gods of childhood. RIG.]

Who thereafter does not either devote his child’s whole head to guilt, [Note: [Col. 0718C] **“Either devotes his child’s whole head to guilt.”** That is, to idolatry. RIG.] or reserve some lock of hair, or shave it all with a razor, [Note: [Col. 0718C] *Totum* (“the whole”), Jun.] or bind it by sacrifice, or seal it with a sacred rite, in accordance with a national, ancestral, public, or private dedication? [Note: [Col. 0718D] **“In accordance with a national dedication.”** He says “national dedication” just as Tacitus says “national custom” in *Annals*, book VI. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0718C] **“Devotes his child’s whole head to guilt, or reserves some lock of hair.”** This was a vow customarily performed at the Apaturia. The Apaturia lasted three days: on the first day a banquet was prepared; on the second, after the rites had been performed, the boy was led to the altar; on the third, they entered him upon the roll of citizens. Consult Herodotus in the *Life of Homer*. Here “reserves a lock” signifies nothing other than the ancient rite by which boys’ hair was cut. LE PR.]

Thus the demonic spirit found Socrates while he was still a boy. Thus *genii* are assigned to everyone, for that is a name for demons. Accordingly, scarcely any birth is pure—certainly no pagan birth.

Hence the Apostle too says that holy children are born when either spouse has been sanctified, both by the prerogative of the seed [Note: [Col. 0718C] *Procreativa* (“procreative”), Codex Agobardinus.] and by the discipline of their upbringing: “Otherwise,” he says (1 Cor. 7:14), “they would be born unclean.” His intention was that the children of believers should nevertheless be understood as designated for holiness, and thereby also for salvation, [Note: [Col. 0718D] **“His intention was that the children of believers should nevertheless be understood as designated for holiness, and thereby also for salvation.”** He intended children of this sort in the book *On Baptism*, when he says that delay in baptism is more advantageous, especially, however, in the case of little children. For he adds: “Why does an innocent age hasten to the forgiveness of sins?” RIG.—Jerome appears to have taken from this passage what he cited from the books *On Monogamy* in his letter to Paulinus; there, however, instead of “designated,” he says “candidates for the faith, polluted by no stains of idolatry.” RIG.] so that through this pledge [Note: [Col. 0718C] *Pignora* (“pledges”), Seml.] of hope he might defend the marriages that he had judged should be maintained. [Note: [Col. 0718C] *Patrocinarentur* (“might defend”), Seml.]

Otherwise, he had remembered the Lord’s declaration (John 3): “Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of God”—that is, he will not be holy. [Note: [Col. 0718D] **“He will not be holy.”** That is, he will not be a Christian. For Christians are brethren, believers, saints. The Apostle calls “saints” those who are not outside, or beyond the Church. He opposes the saints to the nations, the pagans. George of Baetica, in his book *On Faith and God*: “They came through an approved manner of life and through the sealing of the Holy Spirit himself.” RIG.]

## CHAPTER XL

[Col. 0719A]

Thus every soul is reckoned in Adam (Rom. 5) until it is reckoned anew in Christ; it remains unclean until it is so reckoned anew. It is sinful because it is unclean, receiving disgrace from its partnership with the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0719D] **“Receiving disgrace from its partnership with the flesh.”** Since Tertullian immediately says that the flesh is not infamous in its own right, one may doubt whether he genuinely attributes the soul’s disgrace solely to its association with the flesh because of mere origin, or because the soul possesses in the flesh an instrument for sinning, as he shortly afterward proves. Otherwise, according to Tertullian, the soul itself draws original guilt into itself from Adam, since, as he absurdly claims, it is propagated from the stock of Adam—a point noted by the Master of the Sentences, book II, distinction 31. LAC.]

For although the flesh is sinful—the flesh according to which we are forbidden to walk, whose works are condemned, which lusts against the spirit, and on account of which people are branded as carnal [Note: [Col. 0719C] “With infamy” added, Seml.]—the flesh is nevertheless not infamous in its own right. For it has no wisdom or perception of its own with which to persuade or command sin. How could it, since it is an instrument of service? And its service is not like that of a slave or a lesser friend—terms for living beings—[Note: [Col. 0719D] **“Not like that of a slave or a lesser friend.”** He calls one a “lesser friend” when he humbly courts and pays deference to a far more powerful friend. Horace used *amiculum* (“little friend”) in his Epistle to Scaeva. In the same passage he uses “greater men” for more powerful friends:

> And you know by what method it is fitting to deal with greater men.

That is, with friends, says Porphyrio; but in common usage we say “greater men.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0719C] *Animalis nomine* (“under the name of a living being”), Seml.] but like that of a cup or some other body of that sort, not a soul.

For a cup too is an instrument serving the thirsty person; yet unless the thirsty person applies the cup to himself, the cup will render no service. Thus there is no property of the human being in the earthy element considered by itself; nor is the flesh “the human being,” as though the soul were one power and the flesh another person. Rather, the flesh is a thing of an entirely different substance and condition, yet assigned to the soul as equipment and as an instrument for the duties [Note: [Col. 0719C] *Officina* (“workshop”), Seml.] of life.

The flesh, therefore, is rebuked in the Scriptures because the soul does nothing without the flesh in carrying out lust, gluttony, drunkenness, cruelty, idolatry, and the other carnal things—carnal not in their perceptions but in their effects. Indeed, even sinful intentions, apart from their effects, are regularly imputed to the soul. [Note: [Col. 0720C] **“Indeed, even sinful intentions,” etc.** This does nothing to show that original sin is imputed to the soul, because, says the Apostle in Romans 7, “It is no longer I who perform it, but the sin that dwells in me,” that is, in my flesh. PAM.] “Whoever has looked at a woman [Note: [Col. 0719C] “Woman” omitted, Par.; others read “in order to lust.”] with lust has already committed adultery in his heart.”

But what can the flesh do without the soul, likewise, in the performance of goodness, justice, endurance, and chastity? What sense is there in refusing to credit the flesh with good achievements of its own, while fastening crimes upon it? Yet the thing through which the sin is committed is brought to trial so that the one by whom the sin is committed may be burdened, even through the accusation [Note: [Col. 0719C] *Accusatione* (“in the accusation”), Jun.] of its servant. Greater odium falls upon the governor [Col. 0720A] when his officials are prosecuted. [Note: [Col. 0720C] **“When his officials are prosecuted.”** That is, officeholders. Augustine on Psalm 21: “Who is this other bishop from the party of Donatus?” The official body replied: “We recognize no one but Aurelius the Catholic.” RIG.] The one who gives the command is punished more severely when not even the one who obeys it is excused.

## CHAPTER XLI

The soul’s evil, therefore, apart from what is built upon it through the arrival of an evil spirit, precedes that arrival through the defect of its origin; it is, in a certain sense, natural. [Note: [Col. 0720D] **“In a certain sense, natural.”** He distinguishes what is “natural in a certain sense,” so called from the corruption of nature, from what is properly natural. He still acknowledges remnants of the latter—namely, of that good which was originally primary in the soul before the human fall, and which, in the now-corrupted human being, is not so much extinguished as overshadowed. PAM.] For, as we have said, the corruption of nature is another nature, possessing its own god and father—namely, the very author of corruption.

Yet there is also present within the soul its good: that primary, divine, genuine good which is natural in the proper sense. For what comes from God is not so much extinguished as overshadowed. [Note: [Col. 0720D] **“For what comes from God is not so much extinguished,” etc.** He takes a fine metaphor from light, for God made the soul luminous, as above in ch. 9. Observe in passing that Tertullian was unwilling to say that free choice was extinguished in the human being after sin, as our recent heretics particularly wish it to be regarded as not merely diminished but destroyed. LAC.] It can be overshadowed because it is not God; it cannot be extinguished because it comes from God.

Accordingly, just as light obstructed by some obstacle remains but does not appear, if the obstacle’s density is great enough, [Note: [Col. 0720C] *Via* (“way”) added, Codex Agobardinus.] so also the good in the soul, oppressed by evil, according to evil’s degree either remains altogether inactive, its light concealed, [Note: [Col. 0720C] *Occulta* (“concealed”), Fran.] or shines wherever it is permitted, when it finds freedom. Thus there are some very wicked and some very good people, and yet there is one kind of soul in them all. Thus there is something good even in the worst and something bad even in the best.

For God alone is without sin, and the only human being without sin is Christ, [Note: [Col. 0720D] **“The only human being without sin.”** By nature, namely; for the blessed Virgin too was without sin, but by the gift of grace, not by what was due to nature. EDD.] because Christ is also God. Thus the soul’s divinity also bursts forth in presentiments, [Note: [Col. 0720C] *Praesentia* (“present things”), Ven.] by virtue of that prior good, and its consciousness of God comes forth in testimony: “God is good!” “God sees,” and “I entrust it to God.”

For this reason no soul is without guilt, because none is without a seed of good. Accordingly, when it comes to faith, reformed by a second birth from water and power from above, [Note: [Col. 0720C] “And” inserted, Jun.] the curtain of its former corruption having been removed, it beholds all its light. It is also received by the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0720C] just as at its former birth it was received by a profane spirit. [Note: [Col. 0720C] *Profanos* (“profane spirits”), Jun.]

The flesh follows the soul as it marries the Spirit, like property transferred as a dowry; and now it is no longer the soul’s servant but the Spirit’s. O blessed marriage, if it admits no adultery!

## CHAPTER XLII

[Col. 0721A]

It remains now to discuss death, so that the subject may end there [Note: [Col. 0721C] **“So that the subject may end there.”** That is, so that this discourse on the soul may end there. RIG.] where the soul itself completes its account. [Note: [Col. 0721D] **“Where the soul itself completes its account.”** Where the soul, departing from the body, counts each one of its deeds performed in the body and collects their total, as though it were a sum of money composed from many accounts. RIG.]

Epicurus, however, following a sufficiently common opinion, denied that death concerns us. “For what is dissolved,” he says, “lacks sensation and is nothing to us.” Yet what is dissolved and lacks sensation is not death itself but the human being who undergoes it. But Epicurus has assigned passivity to the thing to which the action belongs. And if it belongs to the human being to undergo death, which dissolves the body and destroys sensation, how absurd it is to say that so great a force does not concern the human being!

Seneca is much more strained: “After death,” he says, “all things come to an end, even death itself.” If this is so, death will now concern itself as well; if it too comes to an end, it concerns the human being all the more, since, while bringing everything in him to an end, death itself also comes to an end in him.

“Death is nothing to us”: therefore life too is nothing to us. For if that by which we are dissolved lies outside us, then that by which we are put together also lies outside us. If the loss of sensation is nothing to us, neither is the acquisition of sensation anything to [Col. 0721B] us. But let the one who also destroys the soul destroy death as well. [Note: [Col. 0721C] *Si et* (“if also”), Jun.]

We, however, shall treat death as a posthumous life and [Note: [Col. 0721C] An uncertain and apparently corrupt variant is reported: *Interimat, quia et anima in nobis ut depositum habitat, et ut*, Pam.; *A nobis ut depositum avita, et*, Codex Agobardinus.] as another province of the soul; [Note: [Col. 0721D] **“We, as concerning a posthumous life and another province of the soul.”** Septimius speaks with great elegance: “we,” namely Christians, treat death as though treating a posthumous life. For we know that eternal life remains, and that one passes to it from death. It therefore comes after death. RIG.] and we ourselves pertain to death, if death pertains to us. [Note: [Col. 0721C] *Pertinet* (“concerns”) omitted, Rig., Ven.] Finally, sleep, death’s mirror, is no foreign subject either.

## CHAPTER XLIII
Let us first discuss sleep; afterward, how the soul passes through death.

[Note: [Col. 0721D] Sleep is certainly not contrary to nature, as some philosophers maintain. Here he proves from the various doctrines of the philosophers that sleep accords with nature. There are, however, various opinions about the cause of sleep. See Galen in *History of Philosophy* and Plutarch, books 24 and 25 of *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*. LE PR.]

Sleep is certainly not contrary to nature, as some philosophers maintain, although they assign it to causes that seem to be regarded as contrary to nature. The Stoics affirm that sleep is a relaxation of sensory vigor; the Epicureans, a diminution of the animal spirit;

[Note: [Col. 0721D] Anaxagoras, together with Xenophanes, calls it weariness. Plutarch, book 5, chapter 25 of *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*: “Anaxagoras thinks that sleep occurs in the bodily functions; for it is an affection not of the [Col. 0722C] soul but of the body, while death is [Col. 0722D] the soul’s separation. Leucippus holds that sleep belongs to the body alone; and when, because of the fineness of its particles, more than the proper amount of animate heat is discharged, death thereby comes upon the body. These are affections of the body, not of the soul. Empedocles holds that death is the separation of the fiery nature from those elements from which the human being was compounded; and therefore death is common to soul and body, while sleep occurs through a separation of the fiery nature.” Aristotle refutes this opinion in his book *On Sleep and Waking*, chapter 3. LAC.]

Anaxagoras, together with Xenophanes, calls it weariness; Empedocles and Parmenides, cooling;

[Note: [Col. 0722D] Strato calls it a separation of the associated spirit, etc. Plutarch does not mention these men; but their opinion appears akin to that of Epicurus and to the one Plutarch attributes to Empedocles—namely, that sleep occurs through a separation of the fiery nature. Plutarch nevertheless mentions others, such as Alcmaeon and Diogenes. LAC.]

Strato [Col. 0721C] calls it a separation of the associated spirit; Democritus, a deficiency of spirit; Aristotle, a languishing of the heat surrounding the heart. I presume that I have never slept in such a way as to recognize any of these things in myself.

For sleep must not be believed to be [Col. 0722A] weariness; it is, rather, the opposite of weariness, which it removes. Indeed, a person is refreshed by sleep more than he is fatigued by it. Moreover, sleep does not always arise from fatigue; and yet, when it does arise from fatigue, the fatigue is then no longer present.

Nor shall I admit either cooling or any languishing of the heat, since bodies grow so warm in sleep that the processing of food would not readily proceed during sleep—with heat hastening it and cold retarding it—if sleep made us cold. More than this, even perspiration

[Note: [Col. 0722C] “More than this: even perspiration,” Rigault, Venetian edition.]

is an indication of active digestion. Finally, we speak of “digesting,” which is an operation of heat, not of cold.

Likewise, the soul’s immortality does not permit us to believe in a diminution of the animal spirit, a deficiency of spirit, or a separation of the associated spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0722D] The soul perishes if it is diminished. Some have said that the associated spirit is the soul; consequently, if that spirit is diminished, the soul will be diminished, and would therefore be mortal. LAC.]

The soul perishes if it is diminished.

It remains, perhaps, for us to define sleep with the Stoics as a relaxation of sensory vigor, because it provides rest for the body alone, not for the soul also. For the soul, as something always in motion [Col. 0722B] and always active, never gives way

[Note: [Col. 0722C] “Succeeds to,” Rhenanus, Pamelius.]

to rest, which is plainly foreign to the condition of immortality. For nothing immortal admits an end to its activity, whereas sleep is an end to activity. Finally, rest, as an end to activity, indulges only the body, to which mortality belongs.

Whoever, therefore, doubts that sleep is natural has, to be sure, the dialecticians, who call into doubt the entire distinction between natural and contrary-to-natural things. From them he may learn that the things he has thought to be outside nature can be claimed for nature, from which they received precisely such a condition that they appear to be regarded as outside it; and thus either everything is nature or nothing is nature.

Among us, however, heed may be given to what contemplation of God suggests—God being the author of all the things under inquiry. For we believe

[Note: [Col. 0722D] If nature is anything, it is some rational work, etc. Lactantius, [Col. 0723C] *Divine Institutes*, book 2, chapter 9, testifies in the following words that this is Seneca’s opinion: “Better, therefore, is Seneca, the most acute of all the Stoics, who saw that nature is nothing other than God. Shall we therefore, he says, not praise God, for whom virtue is natural? For he did not learn it from anyone. [Col. 0723D] Indeed, we shall praise him; for although it is natural to him, he gave it to himself, since God himself is nature.” Since it is not unusual for Tertullian to cite Seneca, I would readily think that he received this from Seneca; and I would judge the same concerning Lactantius. It was evidently taken from chapter 7 of book IV of *On Benefits*: “For what else is nature but God and divine reason?” LE PR.]

that, if nature is anything, it is some rational work of God. Moreover, reason precedes sleep, which is so fitting, so useful, [Col. 0722C] so necessary that no soul can sustain itself without it: it refreshes bodies, restores strength, confirms

[Note: [Col. 0722C] “Prolongs,” or “extends,” Latin edition.]

health, pacifies activity, and heals toil. To allow its lawful enjoyment, the day gives way and the night imposes its law, even removing the color of things. [Col. 0723A]

But if sleep is life-giving, healthful, and helpful, nothing of this sort is irrational, and nothing is unnatural.

[Note: [Col. 0723C] “Nothing unnatural” is absent from the Paris edition and others.]

Thus physicians also relegate everything opposed to life, health, and aid beyond the bounds of nature. For by judging the conditions that rival sleep—delirium and cardiac disease—to be contrary to nature, they have already pronounced sleep natural. Even when they characterize sleep in lethargy as unnatural, they answer to natural sleep’s testimony when it exists in its proper measure. For every nature is destroyed either by deprivation or by excess, but is preserved by the propriety of due measure. Thus something will be natural in its normal condition, although it can be made unnatural by deficiency or excess.

What if you also remove eating and drinking from the allotments of nature? For in these too there is much preparation

[Note: [Col. 0723C] “Provision,” Pamelius, Rhenanus, Semler.]

for sleep. Certainly, the human being was imbued with these things from the beginning of his nature. [Col. 0723B] If you learn from God—

[Note: [Col. 0723D] If you learn from God—that is, from the sacred writings among the Jews or Christians. LE PR.]

Adam, the fountainhead of the human race, drank deeply of slumber before he thirsted for rest; he slept before he labored—indeed, before he even ate, and indeed before he even spoke—so that people may see in sleep a natural token more primordial than all other natural things.

From this we are led also to recognize that even then he displayed an image of death. For if Adam furnished a figure of Christ—

[Note: [Col. 0723C] “Prefigured,” Pamelius, Rhenanus, Semler.]

Adam’s sleep was the death of Christ, who was to sleep in death, so that from the wound in his side the Church, the true mother of the living, might likewise be prefigured. Therefore sleep, so healthful and so rational, is also fashioned as a representation of the death that is now public and common to all.

For God, who in other respects also undertook nothing in his ordering without models, willed—

[Note: [Col. 0723D] More fully than by a Platonic paradigm. This again comes from Plato’s *Phaedo*, where Socrates, through examples of contraries succeeding one another, proves that life will succeed death. RIG.—Pamelius admits that he does not know to what Platonic paradigm Tertullian alludes. Junius, no more learned but shrewdly diverting the matter elsewhere, says that “more fully than by a Platonic paradigm” was expressed by inversion—that is, more fully than Plato did by any mathematical demonstration or paradigm. I am surprised that they did not attain the more straightforward and obvious sense concerning Platonic ideas. [Col. 0724C] They were misled by a less common word. Yet even the divine Justin, in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*, called τὸ ἑκάστου τῶν γινομένων παράδειγμα, “the paradigm of each individual thing that is created.” Similarly, St. Dionysius, *On the Divine Names*, chapter 5, calls the same things [Col. 0724D] τῶν ὄντων παραδείγματα, “paradigms of existing things.” The same Dionysius cites Clement the philosopher, whom I think to have been St. Clement of Rome, who also called them παραδείγματα, “paradigms.” Consequently, Tertullian’s meaning is that God undertakes nothing without models, and this not in the Platonic sense, but more fully and perfectly than Plato supposed: God undertakes all things according to his own ideas and models. That Plato also compared sleep and waking to life and death in the *Phaedo* is of little relevance to the present matter. LAC.]

more fully than by a Platonic paradigm—to enact with us daily the outlines especially of the human beginning and end, [Col. 0723C] extending a hand to faith so that it might more easily be assisted through images and parables of things just as of words.

He therefore presents to you a body overcome by the friendly force of slumber, laid low by the gentle necessity of rest, motionless in its position, just as it lay before life and as it will lie [Col. 0724A] after life, as a testimony to its fashioning and burial, awaiting the soul as though it had not yet been bestowed and as though it had already been taken away.

But the soul too undergoes this in such a way that it seems to act elsewhere, learning its future absence through the concealment of its presence. Yet meanwhile it dreams and does not rest; it is not altogether idle, nor does it subject its immortal nature as a slave to sleep.

[Note: [Col. 0723C] “Of slumber,” Pamelius, Rhenanus, Semler.]

It proves itself always in motion: it travels over land and sea, conducts business, is agitated, labors, plays, grieves, rejoices, and pursues lawful and unlawful things. It shows both that it can do very much even without the body and that it is furnished with limbs of its own, but nevertheless has need of the body once again in order to set it in motion.

Thus, when the body has awakened and been restored to its functions, it affirms to you the resurrection of the dead. This will be both sleep’s natural rationale and its rational nature. Even through an image of death you are initiated into faith, rehearse hope, learn to die and to live, and learn to be awake while you sleep.

## CHAPTER XLIV

Next, concerning Hermotimus. As they say, he was deprived of his soul in sleep, because it departed from his body as though taking advantage of an opportunity afforded by the man’s coming idleness. His wife betrayed this. His enemies found him asleep and cremated him as though he were dead. When the soul returned too late, it imputed the murder, I suppose, to itself. The citizens of Clazomenae console Hermotimus with a temple. No woman enters it, because of the disgrace attached to his wife.

To what purpose is this story? It must not be allowed that, because [Col. 0724C]

[Note: [Col. 0724C] “So that, because it is not,” Pamelius, Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.]

the common people readily suppose that sleep

[Note: [Col. 0724C] “Succession,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.]

is a separation of the soul,

[Note: [Col. 0724C] “A dream,” Paris, Rigault, Venetian edition.]

credulity should also be encouraged by this argument concerning Hermotimus. It had been a somewhat deeper kind [Col. 0724C] of sleep, such as is presumed in the case of nightmare,

[Note: [Col. 0724D] Or a medical condition, which Soranus sets against it, excluding nightmare. For he used to say that it was an assault of epilepsy. Caelius Aurelianus, in the section *On Nightmare*: “The aforesaid condition is an assault of epilepsy. For in the books on causes, which Soranus called *Aetiologoumenoi*, he explained most fully that it is neither a god, a demigod, nor Cupid.” RIG.]

or it was a medical condition, as Soranus objects, excluding nightmare; or it was some defect of the kind that also cast Epimenides into legend as one who slept

[Note: [Col. 0724D] Nearly fifty years. Junius suspects that “sixty” should be read, evidently because a round number would be more appropriate. “For,” he says, “everyone agrees on fifty-seven years.” [Col. 0725C] Yet I find a remarkable discrepancy concerning the years of Epimenides’ sleep. For although Pliny and Laertius record that Epimenides slept [Col. 0725D] fifty-seven years, Plutarch, in *Whether an Old Man Should Engage in Public Affairs*, assigns him only fifty years. Varro confirms this number given by Tertullian and Plutarch, and Sabellicus embraces it in book VII, chapter 4. Others reduce the period still further and assign only forty years, as Pausanias does in the *Attica*. Others, such as Eudemus, gave forty-seven; others seventy-seven; and Apuleius two, in the *Florida*. But whatever the number of years may be, Laertius gives the story of Epimenides more fully in book I. LAC.]

for nearly fifty

[Note: [Col. 0724C] “Sixty,” Junius.]

years. But Suetonius says that Nero [Col. 0725A]

[Note: [Col. 0725D] But Suetonius says that Nero, etc. This is found in Suetonius’s *Life of Nero*, chapter 46, where Nero is said, after his mother’s murder, never previously to have been accustomed to dream. Below, in chapter 49, he is also called a late dreamer in the same sense. LE PR.—The words of Suetonius in *Nero*, chapter 46, are these: “In addition, he was terrified by manifest portents in dreams and auspices of every kind, old as well as new, although he had never previously been accustomed to dream.” PAM.]

and Theopompus says that Thrasymedes

[Note: [Col. 0725D] And Theopompus says that Thrasymedes. Junius thinks that this Thrasymedes was the son of Nestor; but what [Col. 0726C] need is there for conjecture when Plutarch clearly writes who he was in his book *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*? LAC.]

never dreamed—except perhaps Nero, at the very end of his life, after his terrors.

What if Hermotimus too was like this, so that the idleness of a soul doing nothing in dreams was believed

[Note: [Col. 0725C] “He believed,” as in the Latin edition.]

to be a separation? You may conjecture anything more readily than grant the soul this license to flee without death,

[Note: [Col. 0726C] And indeed continuously, according to a prescribed form—as though by some solemn rite and according to the formula of some decree. RIG.]

and that continuously, according to a prescribed form.

[Note: [Col. 0725C] “Of one continuous thing,” Latin edition.]

For if something of the kind were said to happen once, like an eclipse of the sun

[Note: [Col. 0725C] “To the sun,” Junius.]

or moon, and likewise of the soul, I certainly might be persuaded that it had occurred by divine agency. For it would be fitting that a person should either be admonished or terrified by God, as though by a swift flash of lightning,

[Note: [Col. 0725C] “To shine,” Latin edition.]

through the stroke of a momentary death—if it were not more immediately plausible that it was a dream, although it ought rather to have happened to one awake; if, indeed, it ought not rather to be believed a dream.

[Note: [Col. 0726C] “If it ought not rather to be believed a dream” omitted by Rigault and the Venetian edition.]

## CHAPTER XLV

[Col. 0725B]

At this point we are obliged also to set forth the Christian position concerning dreams, as incidents

[Note: [Col. 0726C] “Accents,” Rhenanus, Semler.]

of sleep and as no slight agitations of the soul, which we have declared to be busy and always active because of the perpetuity of its motion—the rationale of its divinity and immortality.

Accordingly, when rest comes to bodies, for which it is a peculiar solace, the soul, being without this alien solace, does not rest; and if it lacks the agency of bodily limbs, it employs its own. Imagine

[Note: [Col. 0726C] “Observe,” Fran.]

a gladiator without weapons or a charioteer without chariots, gesticulating every posture and exertion of his craft. There is fighting and competing, but the agitation is empty. Nevertheless, the things that do not appear actually to occur still appear to occur: in action they do occur, but in result

[Note: [Col. 0726C] “In feeling,” Junius.]

they do not.

This force [Col. 0725C]

[Note: [Col. 0726D] We call ecstasy a departure from sense, etc. This is the distinction between sleep and ecstasy: through sleep the functions of mind and sensation are bound, so that the soul’s vegetative powers are then freer and stronger; in ecstasy, however, the opposite occurs, for the nutritive and sensory activities are impeded, while the functions of the mind are then especially vigorous. Finally, sensation and ecstasy agree in this: in both, the senses grow torpid—or, rather, are bound. As far as Tertullian is concerned, he sometimes takes “ecstasy” in an unfavorable sense and said that it was a kind of madness, as in the book *On Ecstasy*, which he wrote against the Church; there, following Montanus’s position, he took away freedom and the cognition belonging to prophecy itself. Above, however, in chapter 21, he explained madness in ecstasy in a sounder sense. LAC.]

we call *ecstasy* (*ecstasis*), a departure from sense and a likeness of madness. Thus also in the beginning sleep was inaugurated together with ecstasy (Gen. II): “And God sent an ecstasy upon Adam, and he fell asleep.” For sleep came upon the body for rest; ecstasy came upon the soul in opposition to rest. From that point onward there was already the established form, mixing sleep with ecstasy, and nature proceeded from the form. [Col. 0726A]

Finally, in dreams we are delighted, saddened, and terrified—with what feeling, anxiety, and susceptibility to suffering! Yet we would be moved by nothing at all, namely by empty images, if we dreamed while in possession of ourselves. Finally, good deeds are unrewarded in dreams and offenses go unpunished; for we shall no more be condemned because of a vision of fornication than crowned because of one of martyrdom.

“And how,” you ask, “does the soul remember dreams, if it is not permitted to be in possession of itself?” This will be a property of this madness, because it does not arise from the corruption of good health but from the rational order of nature. For it does not banish the mind but summons it away. It is one thing to shatter, another to move; one thing to overthrow, another to agitate.

Accordingly, the fact that memory remains available is evidence of the mind’s soundness; the fact that soundness [Col. 0726B] of mind, with memory preserved, nevertheless stands stupefied is a kind of madness. Therefore we are said not to be insane but to dream.

[Note: [Col. 0726D] Therefore even prudent people dream, if ever we are prudent. Therefore, he says, even we prudent people dream—if, nevertheless, we can ever be called prudent, since it is our characteristic to err and stumble. RIG.]

Therefore even prudent people dream, if ever we are prudent; for although our wisdom may be overshadowed, it is not extinguished. Except that even wisdom itself may then seem to be idle; while ecstasy also operates from its own peculiar power, so as to bring before us images of wisdom just as it does images of error.

## CHAPTER XLVI
Behold, once again we are compelled to set forth our view even concerning the examination of the dreams by which the soul is tossed about. And when shall we arrive at death? Here too I would say: when God grants it; there can be no long delay in what is bound to happen.

Epicurus judged dreams altogether vain, freeing the divinity from all business, dissolving the order of things, and scattering everything into passivity, so that all things are exposed to chance [Col. 0726C] and are fortuitous. But if that is so, then some chance event will also prove true, since truth alone cannot be exempted from the chance to which all things are subject.

Homer assigned two gates to dreams: the horn gate of truth and the ivory gate of deception. For, they say, one can see through horn, whereas [Col. 0727A] ivory is opaque.

[Note: [Col. 0727B] **Aristotle, assigning the greater part to falsehood.** Aristotle considers dreams for the most part false, though not always. LE PR.]

Aristotle, assigning the greater part to falsehood, nevertheless acknowledges some truth.

[Note: [Col. 0727B] *Balaridem* Pam. Rhen. Seml.]

[Note: [Col. 0727B] **The Telmessians, etc.** Those people of Caria reject no dreams as empty, but interpret them. LE PR.]

The Telmessians dismiss no dreams as empty, but blame the weakness of the interpretation. Yet who is so alien to human experience that he has not at some time perceived some trustworthy vision? By touching briefly upon a few of the more notable ones, I shall put Epicurus to shame.

Herodotus relates that Astyages, ruler of the Medes, dreamed that the bladder of his still-virgin daughter Mandane produced a flood that inundated Asia; and likewise, a year after her marriage, that a vine sprang from those same parts and spread over all Asia. Charon of Lampsacus, who preceded Herodotus, also reports this. Those who interpreted her son as the meaning of so great an event were not deceived, since Cyrus both submerged and overmastered Asia.

[Note: [Col. 0727B] **Philip the Macedonian, not yet a father.** Plutarch: [Col. 0727C] ὑστέρῳ χρόνῳ μετὰ τὸν γάμον, “at a later time after the marriage.” RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0727C] **He had seen that he sealed his wife’s generative part.** Plutarch: “He saw in a dream that he himself was placing a seal upon his wife’s womb”: Εἶδεν ὄναρ αὐτὸν ἐπιβάλλοντα σφραγῖδα τῇ γαστρὶ τῆς γυναικός, “He saw in a dream that he himself was placing a seal upon his wife’s womb.” RIG. and EDD.]

Philip the Macedonian, not yet a father, dreamed that he had sealed with a ring the generative part of his wife Olympias [Col. 0727B]; the device upon it was a lion.

[Note: [Col. 0727C] **He had believed that offspring was precluded.** That is, that his wife’s womb would be barren. RIG.]

He had believed that offspring was precluded,

[Note: [Col. 0727C] **I suppose because the lion becomes a father only once.** A false popular opinion became widespread that the lion gives birth only once, and to only one cub. This fable nevertheless had Herodotus as its advocate: ἅπαξ ἐν τῷ βίῳ, he says, τίκτει ἕν, “once in its life it gives birth to one.” But Aristotle ridicules it as μῦθος ληρώδης, “a foolish tale,” in Book III. Indeed, Homer describes a lion περὶ οἷσι τεκέεσσιν, “among its offspring,” and ἄγων ἐν ὕπῃ νήπια, “leading its young in the thicket.” Nor could I readily say that our Septimius here shared the popular belief, or that a Carthaginian was ignorant of facts very well known to Gaetulian and Numidian hunters. But when Septimius says that a lion is a father only once, we must understand it as meaning with a single female—unless someone prefers to think that so severe a censor of marriage approved even of monogamous lions. But with Alexander not yet a father, how could a lion’s becoming a father only once signify that offspring was precluded, since even a lion cannot become a father once unless offspring has been brought forth and the womb has already been opened? Let us therefore say that Alexander’s inference was that his wife would not give birth, because the animal whose form he had seen in his dream was believed to produce offspring only once. Lions, however, are rare, and therefore the lion gives birth rarely. What happens rarely is popularly said to happen only once in a lifetime. Asconius observes that “once” is close to “almost never”; and in that sense Lucilius wrote that Crassus—the grandfather of the Crassus killed among the Parthians—laughed once in his life. Pliny renders this without qualification as “never laughed.” RIG.—**I suppose because the lion becomes a father only once.** Certain writers attest that this belief had spread among the common people: that a lioness tears open her own womb with her claws in giving birth. Aristotle, however, taught that this is false. Aelian, Book IV, chapter 23, says that the lioness gives birth five times: first to five cubs, then four, then three, afterward two, and finally one. LE PR.]

I suppose because the lion becomes a father only once.

[Note: [Col. 0728B] **Aristodemus or Aristophon.** Rather, neither, if we believe Plutarch, but Aristander, a seer and interpreter of dreams, very famous in the age of Alexander, whose volume *On Portents* is also cited by Pliny. RIG.—**Aristodemus or Aristophon.** The latter was a comic poet, the former a mythographer. LE PR.]

Aristodemus or Aristophon, interpreting the dream—

[Note: [Col. 0728C] **Rather, that nothing empty is sealed.** Plutarch: οὐδὲν γὰρ ἀποσφραγίζεσθαι τῶν κενῶν, “for nothing empty is sealed.” RIG.]

or rather, that nothing empty is sealed—

[Note: [Col. 0728C] **A son of great force.** Plutarch: παῖδα δυσμενιδῆ καὶ λέοντος παῖδα τὴν φύσιν, “a formidable child, and a child lion-like in nature.” RIG.]

declared that a son was portended, and one of the greatest force.

[Note: [Col. 0728C] **Those who know Alexander.** That is, those acquainted with the history of Alexander. It circulated everywhere, variously written by various persons and interwoven with generally very foolish fables. Of this sort is the manuscript volume identified long ago by Casaubon which falsely bears the name of Callisthenes. RIG.]

Those who know Alexander recognize the lion on the ring: Ephorus records the story. [Col. 0728A]

A certain woman of Himera also dreamed of Dionysius’ tyranny over Sicily: Heraclides reported it. And Laodice, before she had yet given birth to Seleucus, foresaw his rule over Asia: Euphorion made the account public. I also learn from Strabo that Mithridates gained possession of Pontus as the result of a dream.

[Note: [Col. 0728C] **And that the Illyrian Baraliris ruled from the Molossians as far as Macedonia because of a dream.** This is precisely the reading of the Agobardine manuscript, through the increasingly easy slippage of scribes from *Bardiem* or *Bardirem* at first, next to *Biradirem* and *Baralirem*. From this flowed the reading *Balaridem* found in the printed editions. Five copies of Frontinus’ *Stratagems* consistently present *ab Ardie Illyrio*, which means “by Bardies,” and comes very close to the truth, Bardylis. The Greeks appear to have preserved the correct form of this name, Βάρδυλιν, “Bardylis.” Hence Cicero has *Bargulus* for *Bardylis*, according to the very certain conjecture of that exceptionally upright and learned man Henri de Valois. Bardylis the Illyrian, who rose from brigandage to become commander or prince of the Illyrians and Molossians, was checked by Philip when he also attacked the Macedonians, and was confined within the borders of the Illyrians. The source is Diodorus, cited by our Valois. RIG.]

And from Callisthenes I learn that Baraliris the Illyrian ruled from the Molossians as far as Macedonia as the result of a dream.

[Note: [Col. 0727B] *Praelium* (“battle”) Pam. Rhen. Seml. Oberth.]

The Romans too knew dreams of this truthful kind. Marcus Tullius knew from a dream the future restorer of the empire, while he was still a boy and a private person, known only as Julius Octavius and personally unknown to Cicero himself; he already recognized in him both Augustus and the one who would lay civil convulsions to rest.

[Note: [Col. 0728D] **It is preserved in Vitellius’ memoirs.** Suetonius cites certain details concerning the Vitellian family from a little book by Q. Eulogius, addressed to Q. Vitellius, Augustus’ quaestor. RIG.]

It is preserved in Vitellius’ memoirs.

Nor will this class of dreams predict only the highest powers, but also dangers and deaths. Thus, when Caesar was ill during the battle at Philippi against the rebel forces of Brutus and Cassius, he nevertheless escaped another, greater danger by abandoning his tent because of Artorius’ vision.

[Note: [Col. 0728B] *Verum* Pam. Rhen. Seml. Oberth.]

Thus too the daughter of Polycrates of Samos foresaw his crucifixion through his being anointed by the sun

[Note: [Col. 0728D] **Through his being anointed by the sun.** Herodotus explains this in Book III, writing that the daughter of Polycrates saw in a dream her father raised aloft in the air and anointed by the sun, by which she foresaw that he would be put upon a cross and dried out by the sun’s heat. PAM.]

and washed by Jupiter.

[Note: [Col. 0728D] **And washed by Jupiter.** This is what Herodotus writes in the same place that she dreamed: that her father was washed by Jupiter—that is, drenched by rains and showers, which the pagans attributed to Jupiter. PAM.]

Honors and talents too are revealed in sleep; remedies are provided, thefts disclosed [Col. 0729A], and treasures bestowed. Indeed, Cicero’s nurse, while he was still a very small child, had already beheld his future distinction.

[Note: [Col. 0729B] *Suam* Par. and others.]

[Note: [Col. 0729B] **The swan from Socrates’ bosom, etc.** Laertius relates this in his *Life of Plato*: Socrates is said to have dreamed that he held a young swan between his knees, which immediately spread its wings and flew away, uttering a delightful cry; and that on the following day Plato was commended to him, whereupon Socrates said that this was the very swan. PAM.]

The swan from Socrates’ bosom, charming humanity, is his disciple Plato. Cleonymus the boxer

[Note: [Col. 0729B] **Cleonymus the boxer.** See Homer. *Pyctes*, “boxer,” is a familiar word. PAM.]

is cured by Achilles in a dream. When a golden crown had disappeared from Athena’s citadel, Sophocles the tragedian recovered it through a dream. Neoptolemus the tragic actor, at Rhoeteum near Troy, was warned in dreams by Ajax himself and freed Ajax’s tomb from collapse; and when he cleared away the decrepit mass of stones, he returned rich in gold.

[Note: [Col. 0729B] *Erithraeum* Par. and others; *Rhaetum* Jun.]

[Note: [Col. 0729B] **At Rhoeteum near Troy, Ajax’s tomb.** With Leopardus, *Emendations*, Book III, chapters 15 and 16, I restored this passage from the former reading “at Erythraeum.” For Pliny confirms it in these words, Book V, chapter 30: “Outside the gulf,” he says, “are the Rhoetean shores, inhabited by the towns Rhoeteum and Dardanium.” And shortly afterward: “In Sigeum there was also Aeantion, founded by the Rhodians; on the other promontory is the tomb of Ajax.” PAM.]

How many commentators and guarantors there are for this subject! Artemon, Antiphon, Strato, Philochorus, Epicharmus, Serapion, Cratippus, Dionysius of Rhodes, Hermippus—the entire literature of the age.

[Note: [Col. 0729C] **Artemon, Antiphon, etc.** Pliny, Book XXVIII, chapter 1, appears to have copied certain things from Artemon the physician. Artemon of Clazomenae is also cited by the Suda and Aelian.—**Antiphon.** The Suda says of him: Antiphon the Athenian interpreter—or diviner, as the Suda elsewhere calls such a person—wrote on the interpretation of dreams.—**Strato.** Laertius attests that this man, namely Strato of Lampsacus, wrote *On Sleep* and *On Dreams*.—**Philochorus.** This man too, an Athenian seer and diviner, wrote in part four books *On Divination*; and divination was also practiced through dreams. The Author speaks of him again shortly afterward: “with Philochorus the Athenian.”—**Epicharmus.** You have certain poems of Epicharmus. Laertius, however, also relates that he wrote commentaries *On Nature* and *On Medicine*. It is therefore likely that in these he also wrote something about dreams. They may be consulted at Rome in the Vatican Library. Certainly the Author says shortly afterward: “Moreover, Epicharmus raised dreams even to the highest pinnacle among forms of divination.”—**Serapion.** Pliny noted that he took certain things from one Serapion for Book II, and again for Book IV, where he calls him an Antiochene. There were, however, other men named Serapion.—**Cratippus.** Cratippus, a Peripatetic philosopher, wrote books on divination and dreams.—**Dionysius of Rhodes.** The Suda notes that Dionysius, son of Musonius, was called a Rhodian by some; he was a historian and priest of the temple of the Sun.—**Hermippus.** The Author speaks of him shortly afterward. The Suda relates that he was a disciple of Philo of Byblos, lived under the emperor Hadrian, and wrote many works. PAM.]

I shall laugh only, perhaps, at the man [Col. 0730A] who thought he could persuade us that

[Note: [Col. 0729D] **Saturn dreamed before everyone else.** Because melancholic persons—whom for this reason they call πολυονείρους, “much-dreaming,” on account of the intensity of their mental power—are occupied by many kinds of visions. According to Aristotle, *On Divination through Dreams*, chapter 2. LAC.]

Saturn dreamed before everyone else—

[Note: [Col. 0729B] *Somniavit* (“dreamed”) Jun.]

unless Aristotle too lived before everyone else. Forgive my laughter.

Moreover, Epicharmus, together with Philochorus the Athenian, even raised dreams to the highest pinnacle among forms of divination. For the world has also been furnished with oracles of this kind: that of Amphiaraus at Oropus,

[Note: [Col. 0729D] **Of Amphiaraus at Oropus.** With Leopardus we read *Oropum* in place of *Horopum*, because Oropus, a town on the border of Boeotia, is mentioned by Pliny, Book IV, chapter 7. He also mentions Amphiaraus, who died near Thebes one generation before the Trojan War, and whose son Tiburtus was said to have been inaugurated beside three holm oaks in the territory of Tibur, which were older than Tiburtus himself. PAM.]

that of Amphilochus at Mallus,

[Note: [Col. 0730B] **Of Amphilochus at Mallus.** With the same Leopardus we read *Amphilochi* in place of *Ampliloci*, for Clement of Alexandria also celebrates the oracle of Amphilochus, as does Justin Martyr in his *Second Apology*. The Author implicitly means Mallus, a nearby town of Cilicia mentioned by Pliny in Book V, chapter 27. PAM.]

that of Sarpedon in the Troad,

[Note: [Col. 0730B] **Of Sarpedon in the Troad.** Pliny writes as follows about this, Book XIII, [Col. 0730C] chapter 13: “Furthermore, Mucianus, three times consul, reported that while governor of Lycia he had read, in a temple, a document written at the time of Sarpedon’s departure from Troy.” On his oracle, however, see Philostratus, *Heroicus*. PAM.]

that of Trophonius in Boeotia,

[Note: [Col. 0730C] **Of Trophonius in Boeotia.** In Book XXXIV Pliny praises a work of Eutychrates, a statue of Trophonius at the oracle, concerning which he speaks more fully in Book XIII, chapter 2: “In Boeotia, at the shrine of the god Trophonius, beside the river Orchomenus, there are two springs, one of which brings memory and the other forgetfulness, and from them the divine powers were discovered.” From this arose the proverb, “To prophesy in Trophonius’ cave,” about which Erasmus writes at length in the *Adages*. Plutarch also referred to this oracle in his book *On the Decline of Oracles*, cited by Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book V, chapter 8. Nowhere in those parts is an oracle now found except at Lebadeia in Boeotia. PAM.]

that of Mopsus in Cilicia,

[Note: [Col. 0730C] **Of Mopsus in Cilicia.** I do not know why Rigaltius retained “Sicily,” since the reading appears to be “Cilicia.” For Pomponius Mela mentions a certain seer Mopsus, who founded the city of Phaselis on the borders of Pamphylia. LE PR.]

that of Hermonia in Macedonia,

[Note: [Col. 0730D] **Of Hermonia in Macedonia.** The Suda says of the oracle of Hermione: “Hermione is a town in the Peloponnese, a sanctuary of Ceres and Proserpina.” It is therefore likely that oracles were customarily pronounced there. PAM.]

and that of Pasiphaë in Laconia.

[Note: [Col. 0730D] **Of Pasiphaë in Laconia.** This must certainly be read in place of *Pasiphaeae*, as Leopardus correctly noted in *Emendations*, Book VIII, chapter 4. Cicero, *On Divination*, Book I, and Plutarch, in the *Life of Agis and Cleomenes*, agree. “Those who governed the Lacedaemonians,” Cicero says—hence the Author adds “in Laconia”—“not content with their waking deliberations, lay down to sleep in the temple of Pasiphaë, which is in the countryside near the city, because they regarded dreams as true oracles.” Pausanias also agrees with Plutarch at the end of his *Laconica*, writing: “At Thalamae”—which Stephanus says was a city of Messenia—“there was an oracle and temple of Jupiter, in which those practicing divination foresaw the future; and in that part of the temple which is beneath the open sky there were bronze statues erected, one of Pasiphaë”—for thus he too should correctly be restored in place of “Paphia”—“and another of the Sun.” Nor is this surprising, since Pasiphaë, wife of Minos, king of Crete, was the daughter of the Sun. PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0730B] *Pasipheae* Par.]

Hermippus of Berytus will set forth all the rest—with their origins, rites, and reports, together with the whole subsequent history of dreams—in the fullest possible manner in five volumes.

[Note: [Col. 0730B] *Berytensis* Jun. Ven.; the Agobardine manuscript has *Beriensis*; Wouwer’s manuscript, *Bergensis*; Ursinus’ manuscript likewise.]

[Col. 0731A]

[Note: [Col. 0731D] **But the Stoics too prefer to think that God, etc.** As the Epicureans above rejected everything because they removed divine providence from consideration, so the Stoics, conversely, believed in dreams because they exalted divine providence itself. Cicero, *On the Divination of the Gods*, Book I, and Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, Book V, chapter 1, confirm this Stoic religious regard for dreams. LAC.]

But the Stoics too prefer to think that God, in his supreme providence for the instruction of humanity, implanted dreams in us among the other aids supplied by the divinatory arts and disciplines, as a distinctive comfort in the form of a natural oracle.

This much was necessary for us too to confirm the credibility of dreams and to interpret them in this manner.

[Note: [Col. 0731C] *Aliter* Fran. Pam.]

[Note: [Col. 0731D] **For concerning the other oracles too, etc.** From this it is evident that Tertullian intended above to recount only those oracles that answered sleepers through dreams. Eusebius, Clement, and Lactantius enumerate many other oracles belonging to another kind of prophecy. LAC.]

For as to the other oracles, at which no one falls asleep, what else shall we pronounce than that their system is demonic—the work of those spirits which either already inhabited those very human beings at that time, or

[Note: [Col. 0731C] *Ad* added by Fran. Pam.]

appropriated their memories for every scene in their own malicious drama? In this form too they counterfeit divinity, and with the same contrivance deceive even through the benefits of remedies, warnings, and predictions—benefits which do greater harm by helping, since through the things by which they help they lead people away [Col. 0731B] from seeking the true divinity, by insinuating a false one.

And indeed this power is not confined or circumscribed by the boundaries of shrines. It is wandering, swiftly flying, and meanwhile at liberty. Therefore no one need doubt that houses too lie open to demons, and that they beset people with images not only in sanctuaries but also in bedrooms.

## CHAPTER XLVII

We therefore determine that dreams are very largely inflicted by demons, even though at times they are true and favorable, yet courting and captivating for the purpose of which we have spoken;

[Note: [Col. 0731D] **How much more the vain.** That is, false dreams, although the words might be referred to the vanity of superstitions practiced by those who rather diligently use dreams to arrange for future events. LAC.]

how much more those that are vain, deceptive, confused, mocking, and impure. Nor is it surprising if the images belong to the same beings to whom the realities belong.

Those dreams, however, will be assigned to God—which correspond to his grace—since he promised the grace of the Holy Spirit to all flesh, and promised that his male and female servants would dream just as they would prophesy [Col. 0731C]: dreams that are honorable, holy, prophetic, revelatory, edifying, and invitational. The bounty of such things is accustomed to drip down even upon the profane, since God distributes his rains and suns equally to the just and the unjust. Thus even Nebuchadnezzar dreams by divine agency.

[Note: [Col. 0731D] **And almost the greater part of humanity learns of God from visions.** Through visions and dreams they are called [Col. 0732D] to the Christian faith. RIG.]

And almost the greater part of humanity learns of God from visions.

Therefore, just as God’s favor extends even to the pagans, so the Evil One’s temptation extends even to the saints. He does not desist from them even by day, so that he may steal upon them while they sleep by whatever means he can, if he cannot do so while they are awake.

A third class will consist of the dreams which the soul itself appears to induce in itself through its concentration upon surrounding circumstances. But since dreaming does not lie within our choice—for Epicharmus too holds this view—how will the soul itself be the cause of any vision? Should this class, then, be left to the natural order, preserving the principle that the soul undergoes its own experiences even in ecstasy?

But those things that appear to occur neither from God, nor from a demon, nor from the soul,

[Note: [Col. 0731C] *Cum* Rhen. Seml.; *quam* Pam.; *qua* in the old Wouwer manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0731D] *Occidere* Par. and others.]

and which lie beyond conjecture, beyond interpretation, and beyond the capacity for explanation, will properly be set apart for ecstasy itself and its own principle.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

They maintain that more certain and more refined dreams occur toward the end of the night [Col. 0732B], as though the vigor of souls were already rising again as sleep grew prolonged.

As to the seasons of the year, the soul is said to be more tranquil in spring,

[Note: [Col. 0732D] **More tranquil in spring.** Almost all writers relate that in springtime the soul becomes more tranquil and is occupied by more peaceful dreams. LE PR.]

because summer relaxes souls, winter in some fashion hardens them, and autumn—otherwise a season that puts health to the test—dissolves them with the wine-laden juices of fruits.

Likewise they distinguish according to one’s position in sleep: provided that one lies neither on one’s back nor upon the right side,

[Note: [Col. 0732D] **Provided one lies neither on one’s back nor upon the right side.** Philosophers observed that sleep comes more readily to those who lie upon the right side. Hence Aristotle, section 6, problem 5, asks why sleep comes more quickly when we lie upon the right side of the body. Sleeping flat upon the back is also less healthy, since serious illnesses arise from that position. LE PR.]

lest, when the internal organs are pressed backward, as though their chambers had been overturned,

[Note: [Col. 0731D] *Repulsis localis* in the Agobardine manuscript.]

the seat of the senses should float,

[Note: [Col. 0732D] **The seat of the senses.** He means the region around the heart, περικάρδιον, and the blood surrounding the heart, discussed above. RIG.]

or the mind be constricted by pressure upon the liver.

[Note: [Col. 0732D] **Or be constricted by pressure upon the liver.** So the manuscript reads. He uses *compressam*, “compressed,” for *compressionem*, “compression,” just as *remissam*, “relaxed,” may stand for *remissionem*, “relaxation.” RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0732C] Others incorrectly read *sagina*, “fattening.”]

But I think these things have been ingeniously conjectured rather than firmly proved, even though Plato was the one who conjectured them; and perhaps they occur by chance. Otherwise dreams will be under our control, if they can be directed.

For the rule that presumption in one case and superstition in another now prescribes for dreams regarding the selection or rejection of foods

[Note: [Col. 0732C] *Decurandis* Rig. Ven., that is, “regarding them as of no concern”; others read *decorandis*.]

must be examined. Superstition does so when fasting is enjoined upon those who are about to sleep at oracles, so as to induce ritual purity.

[Note: [Col. 0732D] **Fasting is enjoined upon those who are about to sleep at oracles.** The pagans sometimes also sought to please their demons by fasts, and these were appointed or imposed upon those consulting oracles. LE PR.]

Presumption does so when the Pythagoreans reject beans on this ground as well, as a heavy food that causes flatulence.

And yet those three brothers together with Daniel, content with legumes alone so that they would not be defiled by the royal dishes, obtained from God—besides all their other wisdom—the grace especially associated with dreams: both the ability to receive them and the ability to expound them.

When fasting, however [Col. 0733A]—unless I alone experience this—I dream so much that I do not perceive that I have dreamed.

[Note: [Col. 0732D] *Jejunus* (“when fasting”) Jun.]

“Then sobriety contributes nothing to this matter,” you say? On the contrary, it contributes the more to this matter in proportion as it contributes to everything. If it contributes even to superstition, much more does it contribute to religion.

For demons too demand sobriety from their dreamers, so as to promote their counterfeit divinity, because they know that it is familiar to God.

[Note: [Col. 0733C] *Norant* (“they knew”) Par.]

[Note: [Col. 0733C] **Because Daniel too again kept a station for three weeks.** I am surprised that Pamelius—otherwise a diligent and very learned man—expresses surprise at what the Author here affirms concerning Daniel’s fast for three weeks, since he asserts that no mention of it occurs anywhere in Daniel, although it is found very clearly in Daniel, chapter 10: “In those days I, Daniel, was mourning for the days of three weeks. I ate no desirable bread, and flesh and wine did not enter my mouth; neither was I anointed with oil, until the days of three weeks were completed.” LAC.]

For Daniel too (Dan. 10), during a renewed observance of three weeks, dried himself out by his diet;

[Note: [Col. 0733D] **He dried himself out by his diet.** This signifies *xerophagia* (ξηροφαγία, “dry eating”), which in the book *On Fasting* he calls “a dry diet” and “dry foods,” with the food deprived of every kind of meat, every broth, and all juicier fruits. Daniel himself says: “I ate no desirable bread.” RIG.]

but he did this to draw God by acts of humility, not to equip the soul that was about to dream with perception and wisdom, as though it were not going to act in ecstasy. Thus sobriety will not serve to remove ecstasy, but to commend the ecstasy itself, so that it may take place in God.

## CHAPTER XLIX

[Col. 0733B] Those who suppose that infants do not dream, although all the soul’s functions are discharged in life according to the measure of their age, should observe their jolts,

[Note: [Col. 0733C] *Successus* Rig. Ven.]

their nods, and their smiles during sleep, so that they may understand from the fact itself that the movements of the dreaming soul readily break through to the surface because of the tenderness of the flesh.

But as for the report that the Atlantes, a Libyan people, pass the night in dreamless sleep,

[Note: [Col. 0733D] **The Atlantes, a Libyan people, in dreamless sleep, etc.** Pliny, Book V, chapter 8: “The Atlantes, a Libyan people, have degenerated from human customs. They see no dreams such as the rest of mortals see.” Herodotus: λέγονται δὲ οὐδὲ ἐνύπνια ὁρᾶν, “they are said not even to see dreams,” etc. RIG.]

the nature of the soul is certainly being censured by it. Either the report deceived Herodotus, being sometimes slanderous toward barbarians, or a great force of demons of this kind dominates that region.

For if Aristotle also notes a certain hero of Sardinia who deprived those sleeping in his shrine of visions, this too will lie within the caprice of demons: to remove dreams as well as to introduce them. Thus arose the notable cases of Nero, who began dreaming only late, and of Thrasymedes. [Col. 0733C]

But we also derive dreams from God. Why, then, would the Atlantes receive no dreams from God either, since no nation is now foreign to God,

[Note: [Col. 0733D] **No nation is now foreign to God.** See concerning this the book *Against the Jews*, chapter 7, where, after enumerating various nations, he concludes as follows: “But Christ’s kingdom and name extends everywhere, is believed everywhere, is worshiped by all nations … reigns everywhere, is adored everywhere, and is bestowed equally upon all everywhere.” The Author’s statement in the following chapter bears on the same point: “since, on the contrary, all nations are now ascending the mountain of the Lord and the house of the God of Jacob.” PAM.—“For Christ is also among the barbarians,” Tertullian, *On the Crown*. RIG.]

when the Gospel flashes throughout all the earth and to the ends of the world? Did the report therefore deceive Aristotle too, or is the explanation still that of the demons, so long as no part of the soul’s nature

[Note: [Col. 0734C] Pam. Rhen. Seml. omit *animae abest a*.]

is believed to be exempt from dreams?

## CHAPTER L

Enough concerning the mirror of death, that is, sleep; and also concerning the activities of sleep, that is, dreams. Now we turn to the origin of this departure, that is, to the order of death, since even death is not without questions, although it is the end of all questions.

According to the common judgment of the entire human race, we pronounce death a debt owed to nature. The voice of God stipulated this (Gen. 3); everything that is born has pledged it. From this point onward, therefore, let Epicurus’ stupefaction be confounded, when he denies that this debt concerns us. Still more, let the madness of the heretic

[Note: [Col. 0734C] *Magi* (“the magician”) Rhen. Pam. Seml.]

Menander the Samaritan be spat upon, when he says that death not only does not concern his followers, but will not even reach them. For this purpose, of course, he claims that he was sent by the supreme and secret Power: that those who put on his baptism may become immortal, incorruptible, and immediately possessed of resurrection.

We have indeed read of many marvelous kinds of water. But either the wine-like spring of the Lyncestians makes people drunk,

[Note: [Col. 0734D] **The spring of the Lyncestians makes people drunk.** He means the celebrated Macedonian spring, for the Lyncestians are a people of Macedonia. The force of this water is said to be so great that it induces a sleep deeper than wine does. Seneca, *Natural Questions*, Book III, chapter 23; Pliny, Book II, chapter 103; Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book I. Athenaeus, from Theopompus, *Deipnosophists*, Book II, reports that similar water existed near the river Erganes. LE PR.]

or the demonic spring at Colophon drives them mad,

[Note: [Col. 0734D] **The spring at Colophon drives them mad.** Colophon is a well-known town in Ionia, once made illustrious by the oracle of Clarian Apollo, which delivered its responses in a grove where that celebrated spring was located. LE PR.]

or the poisonous water of Nonacris in Arcadia befell Alexander.

[Note: [Col. 0734D] **The water of Nonacris, etc., befell Alexander.** Nonacris is a part or region of Arcadia where water is found that shatters every vessel; certain writers say that Alexander was killed by drinking it. LE PR.]

There was also a healing pool in Judaea before Christ (John 5).

[Note: [Col. 0734D] **A healing pool before Christ.** The Pool of Bethesda. PAM.]

The poet indeed related that the Stygian marshes wash away mortality.

[Note: [Col. 0734D] **The Stygian marshes indeed.** Take careful heed not to understand here the Stygian pool at Nonacris, but only the marsh of the underworld from which Cocytus and Phlegethon arise, as those relate who profess themselves expert in the topography of the underworld. LE PR.]

Yet Thetis nevertheless mourned her son. Even if Menander plunges a person into the Styx, one will nevertheless have to die in order to reach the Styx, [Col. 0734C] for it is said to be in the underworld.

What and where, then, is this blessedness of waters, which neither John the Baptist administered beforehand nor Christ himself pointed out to his disciples?

[Col. 0735A]

[Note: [Col. 0735B] **What is this bath of Menander?** He means Menander the heretic, the Samaritan magician and disciple of Simon Magus, whom in this very book he calls “the Simoniacal Menander.” LE PR.—**What is this bath of Menander? Magical, I believe.** In the Agobardine manuscript the reading is “comic,” as though Septimius were alluding to Menander the writer of stories or comedies and for that reason had given this impostor’s baptism the name of the fabulous Styx, and indeed called it a bath—but a comic one. Nevertheless, we judge this reading false. For the preceding words indicate, and the following words plainly confirm, that Septimius was thinking only of Menander the Samaritan.
