To that Menander, infamous for magical arts and for that reason called above “the Simoniacal Menander,” a “magical bath” is well suited, like the bronze cauldron said to have belonged to the sorceress Medea. For among the other mad ravings of his heretical frenzy, he also promised that the bodies of those washed in his baptism or bath would become immortal. Hence our Septimius, after speaking of the magical bath made famous by the poets’ fables, added: “Nor will anyone grant magic such power that it may abolish death or plant life anew after the manner of a vine, with age renewed. For not even Medea was able to do this to a human being, although she was able to do it to a ram.” Thus, rejecting the reading of the Agobardine manuscript, we recognize and follow Septimius’ own text as preserved in Ursinus’ book: “What is this bath of Menander? Magical, I believe.” RIG.]

What is this bath of Menander? Magical, I believe.

[Note: [Col. 0735B] *Comicum* (“comic”) Rhen. Pam. Semler. Oberth.]

But why is it so little frequented and so secret, so that very few bathe in it? Such great rarity would make me suspicious of a sacrament alleged to be perfectly secure and safe, under which there is no law requiring one to die even for God himself;

[Note: [Col. 0735C] **Under which there is no law requiring one to die even for God himself.** He intimates that Alexander was one of those who opposed martyrdom, against whom he argues in the *Scorpiace against the Gnostics*. The story of the sorceress Medea is known to everyone. He adds, “although she was able to do it to a ram,” because of the golden fleece stolen by her. PAM.]

since, on the contrary, all nations are now ascending the mountain of the Lord and the house of the God of Jacob, who demands death even through martyrdom—the death which he also required of his own Christ.

Nor will anyone grant magic such power that it may abolish death or plant life anew after the manner of a vine, with age renewed. For not even Medea was able to do this to a human being, although she was able to do it to a ram.

Enoch was translated (Gen. 5), and Elijah likewise (2 Kings 2), and their deaths were not found—because they were deferred, of course. Nevertheless, they are being preserved to die (Rev. 11),

[Note: [Col. 0735D] **Enoch was translated.** These words expressly oppose the Judaizing Ibn Ezra, who understands “the Lord translated him” (Gen. 5) as referring to death. On the contrary, Philo the Jew, Book I *On the Life of the Wise*; Irenaeus, Book I, chapter 5, and Book IV, chapter 30; Jerome, *Against the Pelagians*, Book III; and all the Fathers agree with the Author. Indeed, so does the apostle Paul himself, Heb. 11: “By faith,” he says, “Enoch was translated so that he should not see death.” PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0735D] **They are being preserved to die.** He alludes to Revelation, chapter 11. Hence it is evident that the opinion both of the Author and of the blessed Jerome, Letter 148 to Marcella, and Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book VII, and *On the Merits of Sins*, chapter 3—that they are being preserved to die—is truer than either the opinion of Procopius, who thinks that they were endowed with immortality, or Gregory Nazianzen’s doubtful opinion on the matter. PAM.]

so that they may extinguish Antichrist with their own blood. [Col. 0735B]

John too died, although there had vainly been a hope that he would remain until the Lord’s coming (John 21). [Col. 0736A] For heresies commonly leap upon examples drawn from us, taking from them the weapons with which they fight.

Finally, here is the short proof:

[Note: [Col. 0736B] **Where are those whom Menander himself sprinkled, etc.?** *To sprinkle* and *to immerse* are both terms of baptism. Immersion and pouring or sprinkling, where the faith of giver and recipient is complete, equally belong to Christian baptism: the former according to regular order, for believers in good health; the latter from necessity, for believers afflicted by illness and thus “clinical” or bedridden. On these matters there is Cyprian’s distinguished letter to Magnus, and above all this judgment of that most holy martyr must be noted: “In the saving sacraments, when necessity compels and God grants his indulgence, the divine abridgments bestow the whole benefit upon believers.” It should also be noted that in baptism people were customarily both sprinkled and immersed. From these words of Tertullian it may be observed that there was a twofold rite in baptism: sprinkling and immersion. Sprinkling signified the washing away of sins; immersion signified death and burial, as of those who died and were buried together with Christ. RIG.]

Where are those whom Menander himself sprinkled? Those whom he plunged into his Styx? Let those everlasting apostles come and stand before us.

[Note: [Col. 0736C] **Let those everlasting apostles come.** That is, those whom Menander baptized and rendered immortal by plunging them into that Styx of his. RIG.]

Let my Thomas see them, hear them, handle them, and believe.

[Note: [Col. 0736C] **Let my Thomas see them, hear them, handle them, and believe.** He here calls any truly Christian but prudent person “his Thomas”: one who does not credulously trust the impostor Menander, since the incredulity of the apostle Thomas is needed against the illusions of this heretic and magician. “I shall cherish,” he says, “and he shall be my Thomas, the Christian who does not believe in the immortality conferred by Menander’s Styx until he has first investigated it diligently by sight, hearing, and touch.” [Col. 0736D] RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0735B] *Credidit* (“believed”) Par. Ven. Rig.]

## CHAPTER LI
But the work of death lies between: the separation of body and soul. Yet certain persons [Note: [Col. 0736B] *Quidam* (“certain persons”) Pam. Rhen. Seml. Oberth.] who have not been taught by God defend the soul’s immortality feebly, and therefore beg arguments wherever they can, wishing it to be believed that even after death certain souls remain attached to their bodies. To this end Plato too, although he dispatches such souls as he chooses immediately to heaven, nevertheless in the *Republic* presents the corpse of a certain unburied man [Note: [Col. 0736D] “Nevertheless in the *Republic* presents the corpse of a certain unburied man.” The passage occurs in the *Republic*, book X: “But I shall not,” he says, “tell you the tale of Alcinous, but that of a brave man, Er the Egyptian, a Pamphylian by birth. Once, after he had been killed in battle, when on the tenth day the dead, now exposed, were being taken up, his body was recovered sound and intact. When he had been carried home and was to be buried on the twelfth day, he was placed upon the pyre and came back to life.” See also, concerning the same man, Valerius Maximus, book I, ch. 8, and Macrobius, *On the Dream of Scipio*. PAM.], preserved for a long time without any decay [Col. 0736B], supposedly on account of the soul’s indivisibility. To the same end Democritus [Note: [Col. 0736D] “To the same end Democritus.” The Author perhaps infers that Democritus held the opinion that souls remain attached to bodies after death from the fact that, as Pliny testifies, book VII, ch. 55, he wished human bodies to be preserved because he promised that they would live again. The Author admirably refutes his argument on this matter, drawn from the growth of hair and nails in graves, by adducing natural causes. PAM.] points to the growth of nails and hair [Col. 0737A] in graves over a certain period.

Moreover, the keen quality of the air may have preserved that body. What if the air was drier and the soil more saline? What if the substance of the body itself was more desiccated? What if the manner of death had already discharged beforehand the materials of corruption? Nails, moreover, since they are the beginnings [Note: [Col. 0737C] *Exodia* Jun.] of the sinews, rightly appear to have advanced farther when the sinews are extended by dissolution, and to be pushed outward daily as the flesh recedes. Hair likewise has its nourishment from the brain, whose enclosed protection enables it to endure for some time. Indeed, even among the living [Note: [Col. 0737C] “According to the abundance of the brain.” From the moisture of the brain it happens that hairs arise and perish very rapidly. LE PR.] the hair either grows luxuriantly or falls away according to the abundance of the brain. You have the physicians as authorities.

Nor does some small portion of the soul settle in the body, itself destined eventually to depart when time has abolished the entire stage-setting of the body. For this too is among the opinions of certain persons. [Col. 0737B] For that reason they say that the body must not be committed to the funeral flames, out of consideration for the soul’s remnant. But there is another rationale for this act of piety: it does not flatter the soul’s remains, but recoils from cruelty even on the body’s account, since surely the body too, being human, does not deserve to be expended in a punitive destruction.

Furthermore, the soul, being indivisible because it is immortal, requires death also to be believed indivisible—not as though death happened indivisibly to the soul because the soul is immortal, but because it is indivisible. Death, however, will be divided if the soul is divided, with, of course, a remnant of the soul destined eventually to die [Note: [Col. 0737C] *Moriturae* (“destined to die,” feminine) Fran.]. Thus a portion of death will remain with a portion of the soul.

I am not unaware that there is some trace of this opinion. I learned it from my own experience. I know of a certain woman [Note: [Col. 0737C] “A native daughter of the Church.” That is, a Christian born of Christian parents. Thus Pliny, book XIV, ch. 2, says that grapes peculiar and native to Italy are nobler than the others that had arrived from Chios or Thasos. So too Septimius in the *Apologeticum*: “the native populace of the seven [Col. 0737D] hills”; and in book I of *On the Dress of Women*: “Gold is native among the barbarians.” RIG.], a native daughter of the Church, who died in the fullness of beauty and youth after a single, brief marriage. When she had fallen asleep in peace, while her burial was still being delayed [Col. 0737C] and she was meanwhile being arranged by the presbyter’s prayer [Note: [Col. 0737D] “She was being arranged during the presbyter’s prayer.” This also serves to establish the antiquity of prayer for the dead; the reader may see similar passages in *On Prayer*, ch. 1, and *On the Soldier’s Crown*, ch. 3. Here he is certainly speaking specifically of the presbyter’s prayer—that is, according to Tertullian’s usage, the sacrifice at the burial of the dead. For the words “at the first breath [or posture] of the prayer” and “when peace had again been concluded” are recognized as pertaining more to sacrifice than to prayer, especially since he adds that the dead woman shaped her hands into the posture of supplication—a posture presbyters customarily employ in sacrifice more than in other prayer. PAM.], at the first breath [Note: [Col. 0737C] *Aditum* (“approach”) Wouw.; *habitum* (“posture”) Fran. Pam.] of the prayer she moved her hands away from her sides and shaped them into the posture of supplication [Note: [Col. 0737D] “She moved her hands away from her sides and shaped them into the posture of supplication.” That is, extended in the form of a cross, which he often indicates to have been the posture of a Christian at prayer; even today no few representations of this sort are found in the subterranean monuments of the ancient Christians at Rome. RIG.]; [Col. 0738A] and, when peace had again been concluded, she returned them to their former position. [Note: [Col. 0738C] “And, when peace had again been concluded, she returned them to their former position.” That is, after the kiss of peace, which was the seal and conclusion of prayer, as he himself says near the end of the book *On Prayer*. He specifically called the kisses mutually exchanged “peace concluded”—namely, exchanged among the Brethren or Faithful who had taken part in the duty of arranging the dead woman. Here *condere* means “to give mutually,” just as *condicere* means “to say mutually.” RIG.]

There is also another report [Note: [Col. 0738C] *Illa* (“that”) Codex Agobardinus.] among our people: [Note: [Col. 0738D] “In a cemetery.” Concerning Christian cemeteries—which, as we said above in *On the Testimony of the Soul*, ch. 4, were formerly constructed outside the gate—see our annotations on Blessed Cyprian, epistle 68 to Stephen. Whether anything of this sort is also reported among the pagans I leave to the curious reader to investigate. PAM.] in a cemetery, as one body was being placed beside another, it moved aside [Note: [Col. 0738C] *Accessu* (“by approaching”) Codex Agobardinus.] and yielded space to it. If anything of this kind is also reported among the pagans, God can everywhere display signs of his power: for the consolation of his own and as testimony to outsiders. For I would sooner believe that this was done by God than by any remains of the soul. If those had been present, they would have moved other limbs too; and even if only the hands, they would not have moved them specifically for prayer. That other body also would not merely have yielded to a brother but would at other times, by changing its position, have afforded relief to itself. [Note: [Col. 0738D] “Would have afforded relief to itself.” With a similar phrase the Author said in *To Scapula*, ch. 4: “We afford relief to the needy,” that is, we bring them refreshment. PAM.]

Certainly, from whatever source [Note: [Col. 0738C] *Unde tantum* Rhen. Pam. Seml.] these things arise, they must be reckoned as signs and portents rather than allowed to establish a law of nature. If death is not total once and for all, it is not death; if any portion of the soul has remained, that is life. Death can no more be mingled with life [Col. 0738B] than night with day.

## CHAPTER LII

Therefore, setting aside the question of things fated and fortuitous, human sentiment has divided this work of death—the separation of flesh and soul—[Note: [Col. 0738D] “Setting aside the question of things fated.” He does not wish to make this discussion of the soul too lengthy; but whether the limit of death comes by fate or by chance, he passes over that question and proceeds to divide death into ordinary and extraordinary. LAC.] into two forms, ordinary and extraordinary. It assigns every peaceful death to the ordinary form, as natural, but judges every violent end extraordinary, as contrary to nature.

We, however, who know the origins of humanity, confidently determine that death followed man not from nature but from fault—a fault that was itself not natural. Yet the name of nature is readily appropriated by things that appear to have adhered to us accidentally from birth. For if man had been constituted expressly for death, then at last death would be ascribed to nature. But the law itself proves that he was not [Col. 0738C] constituted for death, since it suspended death upon a conditional threat and subjected the event of death to the human will. [Note: [Col. 0738D] “Subjecting the event of death to the human will.” This passage again supports man’s free will, which shortly afterward he calls, in a rather novel expression, “the power of what is offered,” because by his will man can accept the life or death offered to him by God. PAM.] In short, if he had not sinned [Col. 0739A], he would certainly not have died. Thus that which occurs through the will, by virtue of the power of what is offered, and not through necessity, by authority of the original constitution, will not be [Note: [Col. 0739C] *Erat* (“was”) Pam. Rhen. Seml.] nature.

Accordingly, although the forms of death are various, just as the condition of their causes is manifold, we say that none is so gentle as not to be brought about by force. [Note: [Col. 0739D] “As not to be brought about by force.” Philosophers have disputed whether death is natural to man. Although Tertullian appears to say that every death is violent, he says this because death now always happens from some contrary affection. Yet he does not thereby deny that death in itself accords with nature, although it cannot altogether be called properly natural, since nature does not intend corruption. LAC.] The very agency that effects death, though simple, is force. What else is it that tears apart and sunders so great a partnership of soul and flesh, so great a union, from conception onward, of these sister substances?

For even if someone breathes out his spirit from joy, as Chilon the Spartan did while embracing his son who had won at Olympia [Note: [Col. 0739D] “For even if someone breathes out his spirit from joy, as Chilon.” The Author took this, as he did many other things, from Pliny, book VII, ch. 32, where he says: “Indeed, all Greece attended the funeral of Chilon the Lacedaemonian, who expired from joy when his son won at Olympia.” The same writer says in ch. 53 that this happened not only to him but also to Sophocles and to Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, on receiving news of a tragic victory. PAM.]; or from glory, as Clidemus the Athenian did when he was crowned with gold by actors because of his excellence [Note: [Col. 0739D] “Even if from glory, as Clidemus the Athenian.” Athenaeus and Plutarch, in his *Aristides*, cite writings of a certain Clidemus. Whether he is the same man I do not know, for I have been unable to find this example of death in another author. PAM.]; or in a dream, as Plato did; or from laughter, as Publius Crassus did—even then death is all the more violent because it rages through favorable circumstances [Col. 0739B], because it expels the soul through pleasures and brings death precisely when life is more delightful: amid exultation, honor, repose, and pleasure.

There is force even against ships when, far from the rocks of Caphareus [Note: [Col. 0739D] “Far from the rocks of Caphareus,” etc. Propertius, book III, elegy 7, speaks of them as follows, alluding, as does the Author, to the Greek fleet, which was terribly afflicted near the promontory of Euboea facing the Hellespont:

> The Capharean rocks shattered the triumphant ships  
> when shipwrecked Greece was ensnared by a vast deceit. PAM.],

with no tempests attacking them, no towering waves battering them, the breeze caressing, their course gliding smoothly, their company rejoicing, they are suddenly struck by an internal blow and sink amid complete security. Likewise, even the events of a peaceful death are shipwrecks of life. It makes no difference whether the vessel of the body departs intact or broken apart, when the soul’s voyage is overturned.

## CHAPTER LIII

But where the soul, naked and expelled, next turns aside we shall undoubtedly pursue in due order. First, however, we shall complete what belongs to this place, lest, because we have declared the various forms [Col. 0739C] of death, someone expect us to provide the reasons for each one. These are better left to physicians, the proper judges of all lethal things or causes and of bodily conditions themselves.

Still, in order to protect the soul’s immortality at this point also, I shall interweave into the discussion [Col. 0740A] of death something about that kind of departure in which the soul slips away little by little and particle by particle. For, sustaining the appearance of failure, it is led away while it seems to be consumed, and from the gradual measure of its departure it furnishes a conjecture of annihilation.

The whole explanation, however, lies in the body and in its departure from the body. For whatever particular departure death may be, it is unquestionably the destruction either of vital materials, regions, or channels: materials, such as bile or blood; regions, such as the heart or liver; channels, such as veins or arteries. Therefore, while these are being ravaged in the body, each by the cause peculiar to its injury, even to the final destruction and severance [Note: [Col. 0739C] *Recussionem* (“striking back”) Pam. Rhen. Seml.] of the vital—that is, natural—boundaries, positions, and functions, the soul also, as its instruments, dwellings, and spaces gradually collapse, is necessarily compelled to migrate little by little [Col. 0740B], and is reduced to an image of diminution.

It is no different from the way in which even the charioteer himself is presumed to have failed when the exhaustion of his horses has denied him their strength: this judgment concerns the plight of the helpless man, not the true condition of what he undergoes. In just the same way the animate spirit, the charioteer of the body, fails on account of its failing vehicle, not on its own account: it withdraws from its work, not from its vigor; grows weak in activity, not in condition; exhausts its stability, not its substance, because it ceases to appear, not because it ceases to exist.

So too every rapid death—such as the reaping of necks, opening so great a gateway at once [Note: [Col. 0739C] *Ac* added by Rig. Ven.]; or the force of a collapse crushing all the vital parts at once [Note: [Col. 0740D] “As the force of a collapse crushing all the vital parts at once.” The Author most carefully notes three kinds of death: one from an external cause, such as decapitation; another from an internal cause, such as apoplexy; and a third from both, such as a collapse crushing the body, by which its internal organs are consequently corrupted. LAC.]; or apoplexy, an internal collapse—allows the soul no delay and does not torment its departure by dividing it into moments. [Note: [Col. 0740D] “So too every rapid death.” Here he treats the question of the quality of death. For philosophers—especially those, like the Stoics, who with Tertullian made the soul corporeal—thought the manner of death highly relevant to the soul’s immortality or duration after death: whether, for example, someone was crushed by a collapse, overwhelmed by water, or snatched away by another kind of sudden death. Servius on *Aeneid* I, “Aeneas groaned”: not because of death, but because of the manner of death. For according to Homer it is grievous to perish by shipwreck, because the soul is fiery and seems to be extinguished in the sea. LAC.] [Note: [Col. 0739D] *Ut ruinae* Rhen. Pam. Seml. Oberth.; *ut ruma* Codex [Col. 0740C] Agobardinus; *aut ruinae* Rig. Ven., book of Ursinus.] [Note: [Col. 0740C] *Vitalia* is absent from Par. and others.]

But where death is prolonged, the soul departs in the same measure as it is deserted. [Col. 0740C] Yet it is not cut into pieces in this manner but drawn out; and while it is being drawn out, it causes its last portion to appear. Not every part is immediately severed merely because it comes last; nor, because it is small, is it therefore immediately destined to perish. [Note: [Col. 0740C] *Ipsa* is absent from Par. and others.] [Col. 0741A] Its proper end follows the sequence; what is intermediate is drawn toward the extremities, and the remnants, adhering to the whole, are awaited by it and do not abandon it. Thus I would venture to say that the final portion of the whole is the whole: although it is smaller and later, it belongs to that whole.

Hence, indeed, it frequently happens that at the very moment of separation the soul acts more powerfully, with a more intent gaze and extraordinary loquacity. Already established in freedom as upon a higher platform, it announces, through the superfluous remnant that still lingers in the body, the things it sees, the things it hears, and the things it is beginning to know. For if [Note: [Col. 0741C] “This body, according to the Platonic opinion,” etc. Rufinus objected to Saint Jerome that in his commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians he had called the body the soul’s prison. Jerome replied that he had spoken according to the opinion of Origen, who in this as in many things imitated Plato. Origen readily adopted this view, as did those who thought that souls had been thrust into bodies by the supreme God because of sins. LAC.] this body is, according to the Platonic opinion, a prison, but according to the apostolic opinion (1 Cor. 3:16) a temple of God when it is in Christ, nevertheless in the meantime it confines the soul within its enclosure, obscures it, and sullies it through union with the flesh. Hence the light it has of things is dimmer, as though [Note: [Col. 0741C] “Through a horn window.” He imitates Plato, who [Col. 0741D] likewise called the flesh a horn window in the *Charmides*. Both allude to the gates of horn and ivory belonging to dreams in Homer. LAC.] through a horn window.

[Col. 0741B] Without doubt, when by the force of death it is pressed out from its union with the flesh and purified by that very pressure, it breaks out from behind the obstructing body into the open. Immediately, in the clear, pure light proper to it, it recognizes itself in the liberation of its substance and, through freedom itself, recovers its sense of the divine—as one emerging from sleep passes from images to realities. Then it announces what it sees; then it exults or trembles according as it perceives the preparation of its lodging, from the immediate countenance of its own angel, [Note: [Col. 0741D] “From the immediate countenance of its own angel,” etc. He thinks that an angel appears to each person at the end of life, just as above he indicated that an angel accompanies a person at the beginning and from birth; and he notes the conducting angel concerning whom Chrysostom speaks in homily 29 on Matthew 8 and in the homily on Lazarus at Luke 16. LAC.] the summoner of souls, the poets’ Mercury.

## CHAPTER LIV

Where, then, the soul is conducted we shall now explain. Nearly all the philosophers who, in whatever manner they choose, nevertheless [Note: [Col. 0741C] *Tantum* (“only”) Rhen. Seml.; *tanquam* (“as though”) Pam.] maintain the soul’s immortality—Pythagoras [Col. 0741C], Empedocles, Plato, and those who grant it some period from its departure until the conflagration of the universe, such as the Stoics [Note: [Col. 0741D] “And those who grant it some period.” Nearly all philosophers affirm the rational soul’s incorruptibility; but the Stoics, although they believe that the soul remains after death, nevertheless hold it to be corruptible. Hence Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I: “The Stoics grant us the use of life as though we were crows: they say souls will endure for a long time, but deny that they will endure forever.” LE PR., with the editors’ corrections.]—place only their own souls, that is, the souls of the wise, in the upper abodes.

[Col. 0742A] Plato, indeed, does not grant this indiscriminately [Note: [Col. 0741D] “Plato, indeed, does not grant this indiscriminately.” You have this paradox of Plato partly in the *Phaedo*, partly in the *Phaedrus*, and finally in the *Timaeus*, where he teaches—as the Author also repeats in the following chapter—that wise souls are raised into the ether together with boys. Although the Author interprets it otherwise, Marsilio prefers to refer it to those who had combined instruction in philosophy with the education of boys. PAM.] to the souls of philosophers, but to those who have embellished philosophy, to be sure, with the love of boys. So great a privilege does impurity possess even among philosophers. Accordingly, in his system wise souls are raised into the ether; according to Arius, into the air [Note: [Col. 0742C] “According to Arius, into the air.” He repeats the same point in the following chapter. Everyone knows how air differs from ether: namely, air is one of the four elements [Col. 0742D], according to the doctrines of the ancients, while ether is generally taken to mean heaven. Let the diligent reader determine who this Arius was. PAM., with annotations. EDD.]; according to the Stoics, beneath the moon. [Note: [Col. 0742C] “According to the Stoics, beneath the moon.” On this again in the following chapter. Besides the fact that Cicero appears to follow their opinion (*Tusculan Disputations* I), Lucan embraced it in these verses:

> The space extending between the earth and the moon’s courses  
> is inhabited by demigod shades, whom fiery virtue,  
> innocent and patient in life, has made inhabitants of the lowest ether  
> and gathered as spirits into eternal spheres. PAM.]

I wonder, however, why they prostrate the souls of the foolish near the earth when they affirm that those souls are to be taught by the wise, who dwell much higher. Where will the school district be, with their lodgings separated by so great a distance? By what means will the female pupils meet with their female teachers [Note: [Col. 0741C] *Discipula ad magistras convertentur* (“the pupil will be turned toward the teachers”) in the Codex Agobardinus, corruptly.], when they are mutually absent by so great an interval? [Note: [Col. 0741C] *Alvo* Jun.] And what use or fruit will they derive from instruction after death, when they are on the very point of perishing in the conflagration? The remaining souls they cast down to the underworld.

Plato describes it in the *Phaedo* as a kind of bosom [Col. 0742B] of the earth, into which all the defilements of worldly filth flow and there settle and exhale, thickening and crowding the air there—an air set apart—with a kind of muddy vapor from their impurities.

## CHAPTER LV

We do not believe the underworld to be a mere cavity, nor some open-air sewer of the world, but a vast space in a hollow of the earth, a depth concealed in its very entrails. For we read that Christ [Note: [Col. 0741C] *Christo* (“for Christ”) Rig. Ven., corruptly.] spent the three days of his death in the heart of the earth (Matt. 12)—that is, in its innermost and interior recess, hidden within the earth itself and enclosed inside it [Note: [Col. 0742C] *Cavato* (“hollowed out”) Pam. Rhen. Seml.], with still lower abysses built beneath it.

Therefore, if Christ, though God, died because he was also man, according to the Scriptures and was buried according to [Col. 0742C] the same Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0742C] *Secus* (“otherwise”) Rig. Ven.], he also fulfilled this law [Note: [Col. 0742C] *Huic* (“to this”) Rig. Ven.], undergoing in the underworld the form of human death. Nor did he ascend into the higher reaches of heaven before descending into the lower regions of the earth [Note: [Col. 0742D] “He descended into the lower regions of the earth.” Here, besides the scriptural passages cited there—as do Blessed Jerome, Irenaeus, and Ambrose—he adduces Ephesians 4: “Now that he ascended”—to which the Author adds for explanation, “into the higher reaches of heaven”—“what does it mean except that he first descended into the lower parts of the earth?” Irenaeus and the present text have “into the lower regions of the earth.” He does not appear to have read the word μέρη (*parts*), which today [Col. 0743B] is read in all the Greek manuscripts and, by translation, in the Latin ones.

The following scriptural testimonies are also commonly adduced in confirmation of this argument: Zechariah 9; Ecclesiasticus 24; Acts 2; Hosea 13; and finally that passage of Jeremiah which Justin Martyr, *Against Trypho*, says the Jews excised: “The Lord God remembered his dead from Israel, who had fallen asleep in the land of the mound—or of burial—and he descended to them to preach the Gospel and to announce to them by joyful tidings his salvation.” Since Irenaeus cites this same text in the passage just mentioned, one must certainly read there “in the land of burial” instead of “of stipulation.”

Feuardentius cites the following patristic testimonies in his notes on Irenaeus: Thaddaeus in Eusebius, book I, final chapter; Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, ch. 4; [Col. 0743C] Ignatius, *Epistle to the Trallians*; Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* II and VI; Origen, on Romans 5; Basil, on Psalm 48; Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration on Easter*; Epiphanius, *Heresies* 64 and 77, and the *Ancoratus*; and finally Arnobius, on Psalms 15, 87, and 137. To these, besides Irenaeus, Cyprian, and Jerome in the cited passages, add another passage of Blessed Jerome on Hosea 13; Nazianzen, *Theological Oration* III; Augustine, epistle 57 to Dardanus and epistle 99 to Evodius; Gregory of Nyssa, *Oration II on the Resurrection*; Fortunatus, *Hymn on Easter*, which is wrongly ascribed to Lactantius; Lactantius himself, book IV, ch. 19; and Germanus of Constantinople, *On the Cross of Christ*.

What of the fact that Augustine likewise affirms this when he treats the fifth article of the Creed in book IV of *On the Creed for Catechumens*, ch. 6? Blessed Cyril of Jerusalem too, in Catechesis IV, expressly inserts between the mention of burial and that of resurrection—as we also do—the clause, “He descended into the underworld.” Indeed, giving the same reason as the Author, that he might also liberate the righteous, he adds with a certain indignation: “For why should he wish those who were alive to enjoy grace, although some of them were not holy, while those who had long been shut up with Adam should not obtain freedom?” etc.

To avoid undue length, let us add only that, in confirmation, he also adduces Matthew 11: “Are you he who is to come?” They themselves, meanwhile, appear rather to have joined this article with the preceding one, “And he was buried.” Hence Rufinus too, in his exposition of the Creed, says that the force of the phrase appears to be the same as that of the statement that he was buried. Farewell, then, to Erasmus and his *Catecheses*, where he does not shrink from doubting whether Thomas Aquinas was the first to add this clause to the Apostles’ Creed—especially since the Author plainly joins these three statements: he died according to the Scriptures, was buried, and descended into the lower regions of the earth. PAM. See also what we have annotated against Rigault in ch. 13 of the book *On Idolatry*. EDD.], in order that there he might make the Patriarchs and [Col. 0743A] Prophets (Eph. 4) possessors of himself.

You are therefore to believe [Note: [Col. 0743B] *Habens* (“having”) Rig. Ven.] that the region [Note: [Col. 0743B] *Originem* (“origin”) Par.] of the underworld is subterranean, and you are to elbow aside those [Note: [Col. 0743B] *Quia* (“because”) Par.] who, quite arrogantly, do not think [Note: [Col. 0743B] *Putent* (“should think”) Pam. Rhen. Seml. Oberth.] the souls of the faithful worthy of the underworld—servants above their Lord and disciples above their Master—who disdain, perhaps, to receive in Abraham’s bosom the consolation of awaiting the resurrection. [Note: [Col. 0743D] “In Abraham’s bosom the consolation of awaiting the resurrection.” These passages can receive a reasonably suitable interpretation if we say that the Author holds that souls do not yet enjoy the perfect blessedness of heaven, but await the fuller blessedness that follows the resurrection of the body. PAM.] [Note: [Col. 0744B] *Capere* (“receive”) Gelen. Rig. Ven.]

“But,” they say, “Christ went to the underworld precisely so that we would not go there. Otherwise, what difference is there between pagans and Christians if the prison for the dead is the same?” [Note: [Col. 0744B] “But, they say, Christ went to the underworld precisely so that we would not go there.” That argument, which he silently raises against himself, is approved neither by the Author nor by us; otherwise it would follow that whoever had once become a Christian could not deserve the underworld.]

How, then, will the soul breathe forth into heaven [Note: [Col. 0744B] “How, then, will the soul breathe forth into heaven?” These are the words of one refuting the opinion of those who think that the souls of the faithful breathe forth into heaven immediately upon departure. Christ, he says, has not yet come to act as judge; he still sits at the Father’s right hand; the trumpet has not yet given the signal; the earth does not yet burn; and so forth. Augustine on Psalm 36: “After this brief life you will not yet be where the saints will be,” etc. RIG.—Yet, conversely, this does nothing for the Author’s paradox either. For nothing prevents Christ from still sitting at the Father’s right hand while nevertheless receiving some into heaven. For in 1 Peter 3 it is written of Christ: “Who is at God’s right hand, swallowing up death so that we might be made heirs of eternal life, having gone into heaven.” But if we are heirs and coheirs with Christ, we shall be glorified together with him and therefore received into heaven. Otherwise the Apostle would surely say in vain at Galatians 2: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.” PAM.], while Christ still sits there at the Father’s right hand; while God’s command through the archangel’s trumpet has not yet been heard [Col. 0744A] [Note: [Col. 0744C] “While God’s command through the Archangel’s trumpet has not yet been heard.” Since it is agreed that these words pertain to the time of the resurrection of bodies, this too supports the sound interpretation mentioned shortly before. PAM.]; while those whom the Lord’s advent finds in the world have not yet been caught up [Note: [Col. 0744B] *Raptis* (“caught up”) Pam. Rhen. Seml.] to meet him in the air, together with those who died in Christ and will rise first?

Heaven is open to no one while the earth still remains intact—not to say closed. For the kingdoms of heaven will be unsealed when the world’s course has been completed.

“But our sleeping place is in the ether, with Plato’s boys [Note: [Col. 0744B] *Puerariis* (“boy-lovers”) Rig. Ven.] [Note: [Col. 0744C] “In the ether, with Plato’s boys.” He said above that Plato did not indiscriminately grant this to the souls of philosophers, but to those who had embellished philosophy, to be sure, with the love of boys. RIG.—These words are again spoken ironically in the person of philosophers and others. PAM.]; or in the air, with Arius; or around the moon, with the Stoics’ Endymions [Note: [Col. 0744D] “Or around the moon, with the Stoics’ Endymions.” Mocking the Stoics, he calls their souls “Endymions,” because that poetic Endymion, a sleeper for a very long time, is said to have been loved by the Moon, since, according to Pliny, book II, ch. 7, he was the first to discover many things pertaining to the moon’s course. PAM.]!”

“No,” you say, “in paradise, to which even then the Patriarchs and Prophets, appendages of the Lord’s resurrection, migrated from the underworld.” [Note: [Col. 0744D] “In paradise, to which even then the Patriarchs.” Neither is this established. According to the Church’s rule, we believe that the Patriarchs and Prophets, appendages of the Lord’s resurrection—that is, those who rose with him—migrated from the underworld into heaven, not into paradise according to certain persons, nor into an Abraham’s bosom of the kind the Author imagines. Otherwise the statement of Psalm 67 would not be true: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive”; the Apostle, explaining this in Ephesians 4, interprets “on high” as “above all the heavens.” PAM.]

Then how is it that, when the region of paradise lying beneath the altar [Note: [Col. 0744D] “The region of paradise lying beneath the altar.” In favor of Tertullian’s [Col. 0745C] opinion, it would seem that by “altar” one must understand [Col. 0745D] the earth stained with martyrs’ blood like an altar. RIG.—Here he interprets the altar mentioned in Revelation 6 as paradise, in which he appears to place martyrs alone, granting the rest only Abraham’s bosom. We, however, together with Blessed Cyprian, epistle 52 to Antonianus, assign heaven to the martyrs and a place of purgatory to the rest. PAM.] was revealed to John in the Spirit, [Col. 0745A] it showed him no other souls within it except those of martyrs? How is it that [Note: [Col. 0745D] “Perpetua, the most courageous martyr.” Perpetua suffered martyrdom for the faith of Christ in Africa with Felicitas under the emperor Severus. Saint Augustine admired the courage of both, and Baronius cites him in the *Roman Martyrology*. It is admitted that Tertullian lived under Severus; thus, by calling them “most blessed martyrs,” he proves false those who write that they suffered under Gallienus. LE PR.] Perpetua, that most courageous martyr, on the day before her passion, saw in her revelation of paradise only her fellow martyrs there? It was because the sword that guards paradise yields to none except those who have died [Note: [Col. 0745C] *Decesserit* (“has died”) Venet. Rig.; *Caedit, n. q. in Ch. decesserint* Pam. Fran.] in Christ, not in Adam.

A new death for God, an extraordinary death for Christ, is received in a different and private lodging. Recognize, then, the difference in death between pagan and believer. If you fall for God, as the Paraclete admonishes—not in soft fevers and little beds but in martyrdoms—if you take up your cross and follow the Lord, as he himself commanded (Matt. 10), your blood is the whole key to paradise. You also have our little book *On Paradise* [Note: [Col. 0745D] “You also have our little book *On Paradise*.” The Agobardine manuscript contained this little book *On Paradise* before it fell into destructive hands. RIG.], in which we established that every soul is sequestered in the underworld until the day of the Lord.

## CHAPTER LVI

[Col. 0745B]

A dispute now arises whether this too occurs immediately upon departure; whether some reason meanwhile detains certain souls here; or whether souls already received into the underworld may afterward intervene again, either at their own discretion or by command—for none of these opinions lacks advocates.

It has been believed that the unburied are not taken down to the underworld before they receive their funeral rites, as with Homer’s Patroclus [Note: [Col. 0745D] “As with Homer’s Patroclus.” The passage to which he alludes is found in *Iliad* 23:

> Bury me with all speed, that I may pass through Hades’ gates;  
> far off the souls, the phantoms of the toil-worn dead, keep me away. PAM.], who in a dream demanded a funeral from Achilles, since otherwise he could not approach the gates of the underworld, because the souls of the buried kept him far away.

We know, however, apart from poetic laws, the calculated purpose of Homeric piety as well. For he devoted all the greater care to burial inasmuch as he also denounced delay in it as injurious to souls. At the same time, his purpose was that no one, by keeping the deceased at home, should himself pine away [Col. 0745C] any longer with him [Note: [Col. 0746D] “Nourished in grief by the enormity of the consolation.” We mourn the one taken away, and yet it pleases us to preserve, gaze upon, embrace, and kiss the remains of the departed. Thus we nourish grief with the consolation of the remains; thus we nourish consolation with grief. A cruel and monstrous consolation, which cannot exist except through grief. Fulgentius, *Mythologies* I: “For he had done something by which mourning might acquire daily renewals, not something in which mourning might find consolation.” Yet it must be admitted that there is a certain pleasure in that mourning, of the kind Achilles expresses as he embraces the dead Patroclus in a dream: [source breaks off here]]

“. . . For a little while longer, embracing one another,

Let us take our fill of grievous lamentation.” RIG.]

—a monstrous consolation nourished by grief. Thus he constructs the complaints of the unburied soul with both purposes in view: that, through urgency concerning the funeral, both respect for bodies may be preserved and the grief [Note: [Col. 0745C] “Memory,” Rhen. Rig. Seml. Ven. Agobardine codex.] of the affections may be moderated.

Yet how vain it is that the soul should await the body’s due rites, as though it carried something of them down to the underworld! Much more vain still, if delay [Col. 0746A] in burial is to be reckoned [Note: [Col. 0745C] “Is reckoned,” others.] an injury to the soul, when it ought to embrace it as a favor. For surely a soul that did not wish to die would prefer to be dragged down to the underworld later. [Note: [Col. 0745C] “Would have preferred,” Seml.] It will love the impious heir through whom it is still sustained by the light of day. Or, if being thrust beneath the earth later is certainly some injury, and the ground of the injury is delay in burial, how unjust it is that the soul should be affected by an injury for which delay in burial will not be imputed [Note: [Col. 0745C] “Is imputed,” Par. Jun.] to it, since that matter plainly belongs to its next of kin.

They also say that those overtaken by an untimely death wander about here [Note: [Col. 0746C] *Isti hic*, Jun. Lat.] until the remainder [Note: [Col. 0746D] “Until the remainder is completed.” He has very elegantly transferred this jurists’ term to the residue of life that is lacking in those overtaken by an untimely death. For in Paulus, law *Qui nominibus*, Digest, *De administratione et periculo tutorum*, *reliquatio* means what remains after the accounts have been deducted. PAM.] of the span of life that they would then have lived out, had they not died prematurely, has been completed. [Note: [Col. 0746C] “Of the age which, when,” Pam. Rhen.]

But either times are fixed for each person—and I will not believe that fixed times can be snatched away—or, if they are indeed fixed yet are curtailed by God’s will or by some power, they are curtailed to no purpose [Col. 0746B] if those persons now endure them as though already completed; [Note: [Col. 0746C] “Are endured,” Rig. Ven.] or, if the times are not fixed, there will be no remainder of times that were never fixed.

I shall add this as well. Suppose, for example, that an infant has died beneath the fountains of its mother’s breasts; suppose now a beardless boy; suppose one whose beard is just beginning to grow, who nevertheless would have lived eighty years. What sense does it make that his soul should pass here after death the years that were snatched from him? For it cannot acquire age without a body, because ages do their work through bodies. Our own people, moreover, should also reflect that at the resurrection souls will receive the same bodies in which they departed. Accordingly, the same bodily conditions [Note: [Col. 0746D] “And the same ages that produce the bodily conditions.” Take care not to think [Col. 0747D] that Tertullian meant infants; rather, he says that the remainder of one’s age will then emerge in completed form. Thus he seems in no way to differ from theologians who affirm that human beings will rise at the same age at which Christ rose. Those who were blind, lame, or disabled will assume the integrity owed to the body, and will then be in the state they would have possessed if nature had remained incorrupt and whole. LE PR.] and the same ages that produce those bodily conditions must therefore be expected.

How, then, can the soul of an infant pass here the years snatched from it, so that at eighty years of age it may rise in the body of a one-month-old? Or, if those periods that had been assigned must be completed here, will the soul likewise pass through here, together with them, the course of life assigned here to the periods that fell to its lot [Note: [Col. 0746C] “Which,” Ven.]—so that from infancy it may also study, being allotted to boyhood; serve as a soldier from adolescence, being summoned to youth [Note: [Col. 0746C] “Youth,” Rhen. Pam.]; give its vote from youth, being weighted with old age; exact interest, work a field, sail, litigate, marry, labor, undergo illnesses; and experience whatever sorrows and joys awaited it along with those times? But how will these things be passed through without a body—a life without life? “But the periods will be empty, to be completed merely by their passage.” What, then, prevents them from being completed in the underworld, where there is likewise no use for them?

Thus we say that every soul, at whatever age it departed, remains in that age until the day when that perfect state is promised, adjusted to the measure of angelic fullness. Accordingly, neither [Note: [Col. 0747C] “Neither” is absent from Pam. Fran.] will those whom they suppose to have been violently torn away be regarded as exiles from the underworld, especially through the atrociousness [Note: [Col. 0747C] “By a particular atrocity,” Rig. Ven. Gagn.] of their punishments—I mean the cross, the axe, the sword, and the wild beast; nor indeed are those deaths violent which justice, the avenger of violence, decrees.

“And therefore,” you will say, “all wicked souls are banished from the underworld.” I therefore compel you to establish one of two alternatives: either the underworld is good, or it is bad. If you prefer that it be bad, then the worst souls ought to be cast down there at once. If it is good, why do you meanwhile judge immature and unmarried souls, pure and innocent by reason of their age, not worthy of the underworld? [Note: [Col. 0747C] “Do you judge them unworthy of the underworld?” Jun. Rig. Ven.]

## CHAPTER LVII

Either it is best to be detained here, according to the doctrine concerning the *aōroi*; [Note: [Col. 0747D] “According to the *aōroi*, etc.” Those who perish by an untimely death are called *aōroi* (ἄωροι); *biaiothanatoi* are those who die violently. But these *biaiothanatoi* maintained that this kind of death was best. LE PR.] or it is worst, according to the doctrine concerning the *biaiothanatoi*—to use now the very terms sounded forth by magic, the originator of these opinions: [Note: [Col. 0747D] “Ostanes and Typhon, etc.” Ostanes was a distinguished magician, concerning whom see Minucius in the *Octavius*; Pliny, book XXX, chapter 1; Augustine, book VI *On Baptism Against the Donatists*, final chapter: “Yet Ostanes, chief of the magicians, both denies that the form of the true God can be seen and says that true angels stand beside His throne.” Favorinus reports that among the Persians magicians were once called *Hostanae*. Typhon was another magician, celebrated, like the rest, for his infamy; concerning him see Herodotus in *Euterpe* and Synesius, book I, *On Providence*. LE PR.] Ostanes, [Note: [Col. 0747C] *Ostanes*, Par. and others.] Typhon, Dardanus, Damigeron, Nectabis, and Berenice. [Note: [Col. 0748D] “And Dardanus and Damigeron, etc.” Here he lists the most renowned practitioners of magic. Many authors mention Dardanus: Clement of Alexandria in the *Protrepticus*; Eusebius, book II, *Preparation*; Arnobius, book I; Apuleius in the *Apology*. From him the magical art was called “Dardanian.” By magical art he was accustomed to empty storehouses and draw the grain into his own granaries. Arnobius mentions Damigeron in book I.—Nectabis is perhaps Nectanebus, king of Egypt.—As for Berenice, I do not know whether this was a man or a woman; for I do not believe it was the Berenice who was the mother of Ptolemy Philadelphus. LE PR.]

It is now a matter of public literature [Note: [Col. 0747C] “Writing,” Rig. Ven.] that magic promises to summon from their dwelling in the underworld even souls lulled to sleep at their proper age, even those severed from life by an honorable death, even those discharged by prompt burial, and to display them to sight. What, then, shall we call magic? What nearly everyone calls it: deceit. But Christians alone understand the rationale of the deceit [Note: [Col. 0748D] “Does not escape Christians alone”: it is known to Christians alone. RIG.], for we know the spiritual forces of wickedness—not through a conscience allied with them, but through knowledge hostile to them—and we deal with them not by inviting their operation but by conquering their dominion. Magic is the protean plague of the human mind, [Note: [Col. 0748D] “The artificer of all error, etc.” Magic was therefore infamous and once prohibited to Christians with such severity because [Col. 0749D] it is the mother of idolatry, which was formerly the principal crime. LE PR.] the artificer of all error, the science that ravages salvation and the soul alike, [Note: [Col. 0747D] “Ravager.” So also Fran. Pam.] that is, a second idolatry. In magic demons similarly pretend to be dead persons, just as in idolatry they pretend to be gods. Why not, since the gods too are dead?

And so the *aōroi* and *biaiothanatoi* are indeed invoked, on the ground for belief that it seems credible that those souls in particular should serve violence and injury whose savage and untimely end wrenched them away by violence—as though in repayment for the wrong. But demons operate under their guise, especially those demons who were in them at the time when they were still alive and who drove them to such deaths. [Note: [Col. 0748C] “Had driven,” Pam. Rhen.] For we have already suggested that almost no human being is without a demon; and it is also known to many that the operations of demons produce untimely and atrocious deaths, which people attribute to hostile attacks.

Unless I am mistaken, we prove this deceit as well—the wicked spirit lurking beneath the identities of the dead—from actual events. For during exorcisms it sometimes asserts that it is some person from among the relatives of those present, [Note: [Col. 0748C] “His,” Pam. Rhen.; “their,” Rig. Ven. Wouw. codex.] sometimes a gladiator or beast-fighter, just as elsewhere it claims to be a god. It is concerned with nothing more than suppressing the very truth we proclaim, lest we readily believe that all souls are conducted to the underworld, and so that it may disturb faith in judgment and resurrection. And yet that demon, after attempting to deceive the bystanders, is overcome by the pressure of divine grace and unwillingly confesses what is true.

So too, in that other kind of magic which is believed to wrench souls already at rest from the underworld and display them to sight, no other power of deceit is at work. Certainly an apparition is produced, and [Note: [Col. 0748C] The second “because” is redundant, Jun.; “and it produces,” Wouw.] a body is fabricated. Nor is it a great thing for one who finds it very easy to blind the mind’s inner sight to deceive the outer eyes. After all, Pharaoh and the Egyptians saw bodily forms—the dragons produced by the magical rods—but for Moses [Note: [Col. 0748C] “Of Moses,” Rig.; *Mosis*, Semler.] truth devoured falsehood (Exod. VII). Simon certainly produced [Note: [Col. 0748C] “Produced” is absent from Rig. Ven.] many things against the Apostles, and so did Elymas the magician (Acts XIII); but the stroke of blindness was no illusion. What novelty is there in an unclean spirit’s rivalry with truth?

Behold, today such presumption in their art exalts the heretics of that same Simon that they even undertake to move the souls of the prophets from the underworld. And I believe they can do so by falsehood; for neither was it any less possible for the pythonic spirit at that time [Note: [Col. 0748C] “Produced” is absent from Rig. Ven.] [Note: [Col. 0749D] “It was no less possible to counterfeit the soul of Samuel.” The question is not insignificant: did the pythoness truly display Samuel, or rather a demon that deceived Saul by trickery and illusions? Some maintain the former; the latter is affirmed, together with Septimius, by Justin Martyr in his response to question 52 of the *Questions of Christians*, who says that it happened through the operation of a demon that bewitched the eyes of the spectators: μετὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν τοῦ δαίμονος, τοῦ τὰς ὄψεις φαντάσαντος τῶν ὁρώντων, “through the operation of the demon, which presented an apparition to the sight of those looking on.” Augustine takes this view in more than one place, as do others. Nevertheless, the majority of writers who think that Samuel’s true soul appeared have prevailed. The Augustine cited above also seems more inclined toward this interpretation in chapter XV of *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*. See chapter XLVI of Ecclesiasticus and weigh its words. I also remember reading an autograph manuscript treatise by Guillaume Postel in which this episode is discussed at length. LE PR.] to counterfeit the soul of Samuel (1 Reg. XXVIII), when Saul consulted the dead after consulting God.

Far be it from us, moreover, to believe that the soul of any saint—much less of a prophet—was drawn forth by a demon. We have been taught that Satan himself (2 Cor. XI; 2 Thess. II) is transformed into an angel of light, much more easily therefore into a man of light; that at the end he will even assert himself to be God [Note: [Col. 0749C] “At the end,” Fuld. Ursin.; “a sign,” Wouw.; Seml. disregards either reading.] and produce still more portentous signs, to overthrow, if possible, the elect (Matt. XXIV). Did he perhaps hesitate at that time to assert that he was a prophet of God—and to Saul, moreover, in whom he himself was already dwelling? Do not suppose that one spirit managed the apparition and another vouched for it. It was the same spirit, both in the false prophetess and in the apostate, readily lying about what it had caused to be believed. Through that spirit Saul’s treasure was in the same place as his heart—where, namely, God was not. And therefore he saw through the one by whom he believed that he would see, because through the one by whom he saw, he also believed.

If nocturnal visions are also raised as an objection, because the dead have often been seen in them and not without purpose—for the Nasamonians [Note: [Col. 0749D] “Nasamonians.” Pliny (book V, chapter 5) places the Nasamonians on the shore of the Syrtis. The Greeks called them *Mesammones* from the character of their location, because they were situated amid the sands. PAM.] remain overnight at their ancestors’ tombs in order to obtain private oracles, as Heraclides, Nymphodorus, or Herodotus writes; and the Celts spend the night at the tombs of brave men for the same reason, as Nicander affirms—we experience the dead no more truly in dreams than we do the living. Rather, the dead, the living, and [Col. 0749C] everything else that is seen are experienced on the same principle. For they are not true because they are seen, but because they are fulfilled. The credibility of dreams is declared by their outcome, not by their appearance.

That no passage out of the underworld lies open to any soul has been sufficiently established by the Lord in that account of the poor man at rest and the rich man groaning (Luke XVI), where, in the person of Abraham, He declares that a messenger reporting on the conditions of the underworld cannot be sent away from there—though this might have been permitted on that occasion so that Moses and the Prophets might be believed.

But even if the power of God recalled certain souls into bodies as demonstrations of His sovereign right, the same credibility will not therefore be shared by the audacity of magicians, the deceit of dreams, and the license of poets. On the contrary, in the examples of resurrection, when the power of God restores souls to bodies—whether through the Prophets, through Christ, or through the Apostles—the solid, tangible, and fully substantial truth has established beforehand that this is the form of truth, so that you may judge every incorporeal display of the dead to be an illusion.

## CHAPTER LVIII

“Are all souls, then, in the underworld?” you ask. Whether you wish it or not, both punishments and consolations are already there. You have the poor man and the rich man. And because I deferred something or other to this part, I shall now appropriately discharge it at the conclusion.

[Note: [Col. 0750D] “For why should you not suppose that the soul, etc.?” Count among Tertullian’s errors and paradoxes his teaching that souls do not enter heaven until the day of judgment but remain in the underworld. Hence in chapter LV he said: “Disdaining, perhaps, to receive in Abraham’s bosom the consolation of awaiting the resurrection.” Yet Tertullian shares that view with many others in whom there can be no heresy, since the Church had defined nothing. For I do not think they denied the glory of the beatific vision, or that the saints would enjoy complete blessedness only after the resurrection. Those persons, and Tertullian with them, should be treated more leniently, since perhaps they did not deny that souls see the glory of God. LE PR.]

For why should you not suppose that the soul is both punished and cherished in the underworld meanwhile, as it awaits either judgment, in a kind of preliminary enjoyment and anticipation of it?

“Because,” you say, “the proceedings of the divine judgment must be preserved intact, [Note: [Col. 0750C] All insert *in* except Wouw.] without any foretaste of the sentence; and because the restoration of the flesh must also be awaited, since it shared in the deeds and their rewards.”

What, then, will happen during this interval? Shall we sleep? But souls do not sleep even in living persons. Sleep belongs to bodies, as does death itself together with its mirror, sleep. Or do you want nothing to take place there, whither the whole of humanity is drawn, where every hope is held in reserve? Do you suppose that judgment is tasted in advance, or that it is begun? That it is hastily precipitated, or administered beforehand?

Indeed, how grossly unjust it would be even in the underworld if the guilty are still well off there and the innocent are not yet! [Note: [Col. 0750D] “What? Do you wish there to be an adjournment after death?” He speaks elegantly by asking, “What? Do you wish there to be an adjournment after death?” In the practice of the courts, a defendant is said to be *ampliatus*, “adjourned,” when no verdict is pronounced concerning him, but because of the confused and uncertain opinions of the judges his case is deferred to another time or tribunal. RIG.] What? Do you wish there to be an adjournment [Note: [Col. 0750C] “Anything further,” Fran. Pam.] after death, trifling amid confused hope and uncertain expectation, rather than already shuddering at the review of one’s life and the ordering of judgment?

Must the soul always await the body in order to suffer or rejoice? Is it not sufficient of itself for either kind of experience? How often, while the body is unharmed, is the soul alone tormented by bitterness, anger, or weariness—often from a cause unknown even to itself! How often, likewise, when the body is afflicted, does the soul seek out a secret joy for itself and withdraw from its body’s unwelcome companionship at that moment! I am lying if [Col. 0751A] the soul is not accustomed by itself even to glory and rejoice in the body’s very torments.

[Note: [Col. 0751B] “Look to the soul of Mucius”: Mucius Scaevola. LE PR.] Look to the soul of Mucius when he releases his right hand into the flames. Look [Note: [Col. 0751B] “To that of Zeno.” This is Zeno of Elea, who, when asserting before Dionysius that contempt for death could be attained through philosophy, was tortured by him with savage torments and proved the truth of his answer by his steadfastness. LE PR.] to that of Zeno when the tortures of Dionysius pass it by. The bites of wild beasts are ornaments of youth, as [Note: [Col. 0751B] “In Cyrus, the scars of the bear.” Xenophon reports in book I that Cyrus the Younger encountered a bear while hunting and, after receiving wounds from it, killed it. LE PR.] the scars of the bear were in Cyrus. Thus the soul knows how both to suffer and to rejoice without the flesh, even in the underworld; for while the flesh is unharmed, it suffers if it wishes, and while the flesh is injured, it rejoices if it wishes. If it does this by its own choice in life, how much more by God’s judgment after death!

Nor does the soul share every deed with the flesh’s assistance. For divine judgment examines even thoughts alone and bare intentions (Matt. V): “Whoever has looked with lust has already committed adultery in his heart.” Therefore [Note: [Col. 0751B] Some add “even,” Par. Gelen. Jun.] it is most fitting on this account that the soul, even without awaiting the flesh, should be punished for what it committed without the flesh’s participation. So too, because of pious and benevolent thoughts in which it had no need of the flesh, it will be refreshed without the flesh.

What now if, even in carnal acts, it is the soul that comes first—the soul that conceives, arranges, commands, and impels? And if it is sometimes unwilling, it nevertheless first considers what it is going to do through the body. Conscience, after all, will never come after the deed. Thus it also accords with this order that the soul should first pay the recompenses that are first owed to it.

In sum, since we understand that prison which the Gospel presents to mean the underworld, and interpret payment of the last farthing as the discharge there, during the delay of the resurrection, of every minor offense, [Note: [Col. 0752B] “We interpret it as something to be discharged there during the delay of the resurrection.” What else is it than the punishment of purgatory if souls are purified during the delay of the resurrection and wash away every minor offense? LE PR.] [Note: [Col. 0751B] “We understand—we interpret,” Rhen. Pam.] no one will doubt that the soul pays something in the underworld, while the fullness of the resurrection through the flesh is preserved.

The Paraclete too has very frequently affirmed this, if anyone accepts his discourses in recognition of the promised spiritual gifts. Having contended, as I think, from the doctrine of faith against every human opinion concerning the soul, we have satisfied at least a just and necessary curiosity. [Note: [Col. 0752B] “We shall have satisfied,” Wouw. codex.] An excessive and idle curiosity, however, will always remain as far from learning as it chooses to extend its inquiries.

[Col. 0751]

# QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN  
## ON THE FLESH OF CHRIST (C)

### Summary

Intending to discuss the reality of Christ’s flesh, Tertullian first indicates the occasion for the work: those who were disturbing faith in the resurrection were also tearing Christ’s flesh apart with their questions. Chapter I.

Then, coming to his subject, he argues against Marcion, who removed the account of Christ’s birth from the Gospel, and proves Christ’s nativity by an appeal to apostolic tradition. Chapter II.

He then shows that it was neither impossible nor unsuitable for God. Chapter III.

Nor unworthy of God, nor foolish. Chapter IV.

Therefore Christ was not crucified and did not die in an apparition, but truly—however much Marcion also denied this—and He was also truly born. Chapter V.

Next, against Apelles, he argues that Christ did not borrow His flesh from the stars and the substances of the higher world. Chapter VI.

He interposes that Christ’s saying, “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” does nothing to support them. Chapter VII.

[Col. 0752C] He adds that, according to the Apelleians, their fiery angel also established the heavenly things out of repentance for his offense; and consequently, if Christ’s flesh was constructed from the stars, it was sinful flesh. Chapter VIII.

Indeed, all the signs of true flesh were present in Christ. Chapter IX.

Again, against certain others, he argues that Christ’s flesh was not “psychic.” Chapter X.

Nor was it merely “carnal.” Chapter XI.

Christ also came, not so that the soul might know itself, but to save it. Chapter XII.

There were likewise different substances in Christ: flesh and soul. Chapter XIII.

Christ alone, moreover, was the bringer of salvation, not an angel. Chapter XIV.

Against Valentinus, he proceeds to show that Christ’s flesh was not spiritual. Chapter XV.

Likewise, against a certain Alexander, he shows that Christ’s flesh was not sinful and, even if it did not come from seed, was nevertheless real. Chapter XVI.

He incidentally proves from the Scriptures that Christ was to be born of a virgin. Chapter XVII.

It was also not fitting for the Son of God to be born of human seed, lest, if He were wholly the son of man according to Ebion’s opinion, He should not be believed to be the Son of God. Chapter XVIII.

Nor does the passage adulterated by Valentinus favor him: “He was born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of a man, but of God.” Chapter XIX.

Moreover, against the same persons, he demonstrates very extensively from the Scriptures that Christ was born not merely through the Virgin but from the Virgin. Chapters XX and XXI.

Accordingly, in all these matters the prophetic saying of Simeon concerning Christ is fulfilled: “Behold, this one is appointed as a sign [Col. 0753B] that will be contradicted.” Chapters XXII and XXIII.

And all those heretics were branded and foretold in the Scriptures. Chapter XXIV.

Finally, repeating by way of epilogue what he has proved in this book, he makes the transition to the following book, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*. Chapter XXV.

Moreover, besides the fact that Tertullian cites the book just mentioned, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, below in book V *Against Marcion*, mention is also made there of the subject and title of this work. “For this reason,” he says in chapter II, “we too prefaced it with a volume *On the Flesh of Christ*, in which we prove it to be solid against the supposed nativity of an apparition and vindicate it as human against the peculiar property alleged of its nature.” And again: “Therefore, as far as the heretics are concerned, we have demonstrated with what wedge we must oppose them; and opposition has already been offered under its own title as well, *On the Flesh of the Lord Against Heresies*, especially in preparation for this question.”

Besides the fact that Abbot Trithemius and Politianus once saw a manuscript of this book, as is shown by passages frequently cited, Rhenanus first published it from the Hirsau and Payerne manuscripts with scholia; later, after collating the Gorze codex, he corrected it and furnished it with annotations. Meanwhile, because it was lacking in the British codex of Laelandi and had not been examined by Gelonius, it was worthwhile [Col. 0754A] to compare it with three Vatican manuscripts. From these we have restored a good many passages and have also added a new summary and our own annotations. PAM.

He demonstrates that Christ assumed human flesh, against four heretics—Marcion, Apelles, Valentinus, and Basilides—or rather, he writes against four heresies: first, that of the Marcionites; second, that of Apelles; third and fourth, those of the Valentinians. VENET.

## CHAPTER I

Those who seek to unsettle the faith in the resurrection—a faith that, before these kinsmen of the Sadducees, had unquestionably remained firm [Note: [Col. 0753D] “Those close to the Sadducees.” He means the heretics Marcion, Apelles, and Valentinus, who followed the heresy of the Sadducees after a long interval. Or he calls any heretics holding wrong opinions about the soul “close to the Sadducees.” There is a controversy over whether the Sadducees were named from the Hebrew for “just,” as St. Jerome seems to believe, or from Sadoc, the founder of the heresy, who flourished under Alexander the Great. Thus Rabbi Abraham in the *Historical Kabbalah* and Elijah Levita in the *Tishbi*. LE PR.]—so that they may deny that this hope extends to the flesh as well, naturally also tear Christ’s flesh apart with their questions. They claim either that it did not exist at all or that it was in some fashion other than human, lest, if it is established that it was human, a precedent be established against them that the flesh must by all means rise again, since it rose again in Christ. [Note: [Col. 0753C] “Christ,” Paris, Rhen. Pam.]

[Note: [Col. 0753D] “Firm.” He calls the faith *morata*, meaning stable, firm, and unshaken. PAM.]  
[Note: [Col. 0753C] Rig. and Venet. add “those.”]

Therefore, from the very point at which they destroy the hopes of the flesh, our own defenses [Note: [Col. 0753C] “Our own” is absent from Rig. and Venet.] must be prepared. Let us examine the Lord’s bodily substance, for there is certainty regarding His spiritual substance. The truth of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0753C] “Flesh,” Seml. Rig. Ven.] is in question, and its quality is reconsidered [Note: [Col. 0753D] “Are reconsidered,” Seml.]: [Note: [Col. 0753D] “Reconsidered.” Besides using *retractare* in the sense of *tractare*, “to treat,” elsewhere, the author also employs it more than once in this book. PAM.] whether it existed, whence it came, and what kind it was. [Note: [Col. 0753D] “Its declaration.” Magistrates are *renuntiati* when elected; a friendship is *renuntiata* when dissolved. Here *renuntiatio* means demonstration and definition. RHEN.] Its declaration will provide the rule for our resurrection.

To deny Christ’s flesh, Marcion also denied His nativity; or, to deny His nativity, he also denied His flesh—[Note: [Col. 0754D] “Namely, lest they should bear reciprocal testimony to one another.” This is an *asyndeton*, for he habitually omits connective particles, a practice that sometimes brings obscurity to his discourse, as we have noted before. RHEN.] namely, lest nativity and flesh should bear reciprocal testimony to one another and correspond: [Note: [Col. 0753D] Wouw. deletes “and correspond”; “and” is absent from Par.; “bear witness [Col. 0754C] and” is absent from Ursinus’s book.] for there is no nativity without flesh, nor flesh without nativity.

As though, with the same heretical license, he could not either have admitted the flesh and denied the nativity, as did Apelles, his disciple and later deserter; or have confessed [Note: [Col. 0754C] “Also” is absent from Rig.] both the flesh and the nativity but interpreted them differently, [Note: [Col. 0754C] “Those things,” Seml. Rhen.] as did Valentinus, his fellow disciple and fellow deserter! But one who introduced an imaginary flesh of Christ could equally have fabricated His nativity as an apparition, [Note: [Col. 0754C] “Apparitions of the nativity,” Pam. Rhen.] so that the Virgin’s conception, pregnancy, [Note: [Col. 0754D] “Pregnancy.” He uses *praegnatus* in the form of a fourth-declension noun to mean impregnation, delighting in words with this termination. RHEN.] and delivery, and thereafter the entire course of the infant Himself, might be regarded as τὸ δοκεῖν, “mere appearance.” [Note: [Col. 0754D] Jun. prefers τῷ.] [Note: [Col. 0754D] “Might be regarded,” Pam. Rhen.]

[Note: [Col. 0754D] ΤΟ ΔΟΚΕΙΝ. This is a synecdochic expression. The preposition κατά is understood: κατὰ τὸ δοκεῖν, that is, “according to appearance”—so that it appeared to be so, although in reality it was not. RHEN.—Jerome, book II *Against the Pelagians*: “The weakness of the flesh rejoiced in God as its inhabitant, and yet could not exceed the measure of its own frailty, so that He might be believed to be the Son of Man, truly the Son of God, not merely τὸ δοκεῖν according to the ancient heretics.” RIG.]

They would have deceived the same eyes and the same senses that the appearance of flesh deluded.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0755A]

Certainly the nativity is announced by Gabriel—but what has Marcion to do with that angel of the Creator? Christ is introduced as conceived in the Virgin’s womb [Note: [Col. 0755C] “And in the Virgin’s womb,” Pam. Par. Fran.]—but what has Marcion to do with Isaiah, the Creator’s prophet? [Note: [Col. 0755C] “Prophet” omitted by Seml.; “with the Creator’s essence,” Paris. Fran. Pam.] One who suddenly brought Christ down from heaven hates delays.

“Remove from here,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0755C] “You remove,” Seml.] “Caesar’s ever-troublesome censuses, the cramped lodgings, the filthy swaddling-cloths, and the hard manger. Let the multitude of angels see to itself, honoring its Lord by night. Let the shepherds keep watch over their livestock instead. And let the Magi not be wearied by a long journey; I grant them their gold. Let Herod too be a better man, so that Jeremiah may not boast. But neither let the infant be circumcised, lest He suffer pain; nor be carried to the Temple, lest He burden His parents [Note: [Col. 0755C] “His parent,” Fran.] with the expense of an offering; [Note: [Col. 0755C] “Obligation,” Rhen., Agobardine codex.] nor be handed into Simeon’s arms, [Note: [Col. 0755C] “Of Simeon,” Pam.] lest He thereby grieve the old man who is about to die. And let that aged woman too be silent, lest she bewitch the child.”

[Note: [Col. 0755C] “Remove from here, he says.” Rhenanus correctly noted that these words are presented in the person of Marcion and continue as far as “by these counsels, I think”; for Marcion cut out from the Gospel of Luke—the only Gospel he acknowledged—those opening chapters in which these events are contained, as is soon discussed more fully in book IV *Against Marcion*. All these words, moreover, are spoken ironically. PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0755D] “Let the multitude of angels see to itself.” This is wittily said in irony because nighttime is suitable for deception, as though even the angels could have been deceived. The event mentioned comes from the beginning of Luke’s Gospel narrative. RHEN.]

[Note: [Col. 0755D] “So that Jeremiah may not boast.” It is as though he were saying: let Herod not kill the children in Bethlehem, lest Jeremiah—or Micah—boast of his prophecy, also cited in Matthew II, as though it had now been fulfilled. The following words, “lest she bewitch the child,” are likewise ironic; for bewitching belongs to the class of incantation. PAM., with corrections by the editors.]

By these counsels, I think, Marcion dared to erase all the original documentary records of Christ, so that His flesh might not be proved. [Note: [Col. 0755C] Rhen. Pam. add “and.”]

By what authority, I ask you? [Note: [Col. 0755C] The Agobardine codex adds “Produce your authority.”] If you are a prophet, foretell something. If an apostle, preach publicly. If apostolic, [Note: [Col. 0756C] “If apostolic”: if you have imbibed the Apostles’ discipline and teaching. LE PR.] agree with the Apostles. If you are merely [Note: [Col. 0755C] “Merely,” Fran. Pam.] a Christian, believe what has been handed down. [Note: [Col. 0756D] “Believe what has been handed down.” A splendid passage against those who, though they are neither Apostles nor apostolic, nevertheless perpetually dispute about the faith from the Scriptures, when tradition ought to be sufficient for them. This is treated at great length in *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 3. PAM.]

If you are none of these, I should rightly tell you: die. For you are already dead, since you are not a Christian, because you do not believe what has been handed down—the very thing that makes Christians. [Note: [Col. 0756C] “Believed,” Rig. Pam. Par. Fran.] And you are all the more dead, the more you are not [Note: [Col. 0756C] “You are, who do not,” Rhen.] a Christian: you who once were one, but fell away, [Note: [Col. 0756C] “Because,” Wouw., Ursinus’s book.] by rescinding what you formerly believed. [Note: [Col. 0756D] “You who once were one, but fell away.” This passage should also be noted against those who are not ashamed to call heretics Christians, although the author does not wish those who have rescinded what they formerly believed and—just as he says below of Marcion himself—withdrawn from the Church and the faith to be called by that name. Pertinent too is the statement below in chapter 15: “Heretics, by believing, do not believe.” On Marcion’s withdrawal from the faith and the Church, see *On Prescriptions*, chapter 30. PAM.] [Note: [Col. 0756D] “By rescinding what you formerly believed”: by abrogating it, that is.
