The word is taken from legal usage, for it is employed in various formulas, as in wills: “concerning the rescission of wills,” that is, dissolving and invalidating that compact. LE PR.]

You yourself admit this in a certain letter; your followers do not deny it, and ours prove it. Therefore, in rescinding what you believed, it was as one who no longer believed that you rescinded it; yet it does not follow that, because you ceased to believe, you were right to rescind it. And by rescinding what you believed, you prove that, before you rescinded it, what you believed had been otherwise. Since it was otherwise, it had been handed down in that form. Moreover, what had been handed down was true, since it had been handed down by those whose office it was to hand it down. Therefore, by rescinding what had been handed down, you rescinded what was true. You did so without any right.

[Note: [Col. 0755D] “By what authority, I ask you?” He rightly adds below: “But we have already employed such prescriptive arguments more fully elsewhere against all heresies,” plainly alluding to the book bearing that title which he soon cites, especially chapters 20, 21, 31, 32, 35, and 36. PAM.]

But we have already employed such prescriptive arguments more fully elsewhere against all heresies. [Note: [Col. 0756C] “May we be,” Ven.] After those arguments, we now examine the matter again by way of superabundance, desiring to know the reason why [Note: [Col. 0756C] “Because,” Ven.] you did not think that Christ was born.

## CHAPTER III
It is necessary, insofar as you think that this was permitted by your own judgment, that you regarded birth either as impossible or as unfitting for God. [Col. 0756B] But nothing is impossible for God except what he does not will. Let us therefore consider whether he willed [Note: [Col. 0756C] “Did not will,” Seml., Rig., Ven.] to be born—for if he willed it, he both could be [Note: [Col. 0756C] “And could be” omitted by Rhen., Seml.] and was born. I shall take the shortest route. For if God had been unwilling to be born, for whatever reason, he would not have allowed himself to appear human either. For who, seeing a human being, would deny that he had been born? Thus, what he did not wish to be, he would not have wished even to appear to be at all [Note: [Col. 0756C] “To a human being,” Agobardine manuscript.]. Even the mere supposition of anything displeasing is rejected. For it makes no difference whether something exists or does not exist if, although it does not exist, it is presumed to exist. There is certainly this difference [Note: [Col. 0756C] “This” absent from Rig., Ven.]: what truly does not exist does not suffer falsely [Note: [Col. 0756C] “What is false,” Pam., Rhen.].

“But,” you say, “his own consciousness was enough for him. Let human beings see to it if they thought him born because they saw him as a human being.” How much more worthily, then, and how much more consistently would he have endured human estimation if he had truly been born, [Col. 0757A] since even without being born he was going to incur that same estimation, to the injury of his own consciousness! [Note: [Col. 0757D] “Which you reckon as confidence.” He had said: “But, you say, his own consciousness was enough for him.” For Marcion’s excuse was that it made no difference whether God appeared to be human, provided that he truly was not, because, with his own consciousness intact, he could confidently and steadfastly endure the estimation by which he was judged to be human, although this appeared unfitting and unworthy of God. So Marcion asserted, and added that God counted this false opinion as an occasion for confidence—that is, God judged it sufficient to endure the false and unworthy report with courage and confidence. LAC.]—an estimation which you reckon as an occasion for confidence, so that, although unborn, he endured being regarded as born, contrary to his own consciousness. Explain what was so important that Christ, knowing [Note: [Col. 0757C] “Explain, so that knowingly,” Rhen., Seml.] what he was, should present himself as what he was not [Note: [Col. 0757C] “Was,” Rhen., Pam.]. You cannot say: “[Note: [Col. 0757C] Rig., Ven. insert “not.”] If he had been born and had truly put on humanity, he would have ceased to be God, losing what he was while assuming [Note: [Col. 0757C] “Becoming,” Rig., Ven.] what he was not.” For God faces no danger to his own state.

“But this is why,” you say, “I deny that God was truly changed into a human being, so as both to be born and to be embodied in flesh [Note: [Col. 0757C] “To operate,” Rig., Ven.]: because one who is without end must also be immutable. For to be changed into something else is the end of what one was before; change, therefore, is not compatible [Note: [Col. 0757C] Rig., Ven. add “with him.”] with one for whom an end is not compatible.” Certainly, the nature of mutable things is governed by this law: they do not remain in that element of themselves which is changed, and thus, by not remaining, they perish [Note: [Col. 0757C] “They become subject,” Rig., Ven.] when through change they lose what they were. But nothing is equal to God: his nature stands apart from the condition of all things. If, therefore, things that differ from God [Note: [Col. 0757C] Ursinus’ manuscript inserts “or.”] lose what they were when they are changed, where will the difference between divinity and other things lie, unless the contrary holds true [Note: [Col. 0757C] “Contains,” Pam., Par., Fran.]—that is, unless God can both be changed into all things and continue to be what he is? Otherwise, he will be equal to those things which, once changed, lose what they were; and God is surely not unequal [Note: [Col. 0757C] “Equal,” Rhen., Seml., Pam.] to them in every respect if he is not unequal even in the outcome of change.

You have sometimes read and believed that the Creator’s angels were changed into human form, and that they bore such bodily reality that Abraham washed their feet, Lot was rescued from the Sodomites by their hands, [Col. 0757C] and an angel who wrestled with a man, exerting the whole weight of his body, desired to be released by the one [Note: [Col. 0757C] “So greatly,” Rig., Ven., Seml., Rhen.] who held him. What, therefore, was permitted to angels inferior to God—namely, that, although changed into human corporeality, they nevertheless remained angels—you deny to the more powerful God [Note: [Col. 0757D] “You will deny,” Rig., Ven., Par.], as though Christ could not put on true humanity and yet continue to be God. Or did those angels too appear as phantoms [Note: [Col. 0757D] Singular “phantom,” Sem., Pam.] of flesh? But you will not dare to say this. For if the Creator’s angels are such in your view, just as Christ also is, Christ will belong to that God [Note: [Col. 0757D] “Of the same substance,” Pam.] whose angels [Note: [Col. 0757D] Pam. repeats “angels.”] are such as Christ is.

If you had not deliberately rejected some Scriptures that resist your opinion and corrupted others, John’s Gospel would have confounded you on this point [Note: [Col. 0758C] “You from this point,” Pam., Rhen.], when it proclaims that the Spirit, gliding down [Note: [Col. 0758C] “Descending,” Rig., Ven.] in the body of a dove, settled [Note: [Col. 0758C] “Descended,” Pam., Vatican manuscript.] upon the Lord. Although that Spirit was what he was, he was as truly a dove as he was Spirit [Note: [Col. 0757D] “He was as truly a dove as he was Spirit.” In this interpretation of the passage, the author of *On the Christian Struggle*—among the works of Blessed Augustine—chapter 22, agrees with Tertullian. But Augustine himself thinks otherwise in Letter 102 to Evodius and in *On the Trinity*, chapter 5; the blessed Ambrose, *On the Sacraments* I.5, and Chrysostom, Homily 12 on Matthew, also agree with Augustine, drawing this conclusion from the expressions “like a dove” and “in the form of a dove.”], nor had he destroyed his own substance by assuming a foreign substance.

But you ask where the dove’s body is now that the Spirit has returned to heaven. Likewise, the bodies of the angels [Note: [Col. 0758C] “Of the angels also,” Rhen., Seml.] were withdrawn by the same principle by which they had been produced. If [Col. 0758B] you had seen them when they were brought forth from nothing, you would have known what happened when they were withdrawn into nothing. If their beginning was not visible, neither was their end. Nevertheless, the body possessed solidity at the moment [Note: [Col. 0758C] “At whatever moment,” Rig., Ven.] when it was seen as a body. What is written cannot have failed to exist.

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore, if you do not reject embodiment as either impossible or dangerous for God, it remains for you to reject and accuse it as unworthy. Beginning, indeed, with birth itself [Note: [Col. 0758C] Pam. adds “held in hatred.”], go on now, declaim about the filthiness of the generative elements in the womb [Note: [Col. 0758D] “Go on now, declaim about the filthiness of the generative elements in the womb.” Similar words occur in the third book *Against Marcion*: “Go on now, declaim against the most holy and venerable works of nature.” RIG.]: the foul clots of fluid and blood, the flesh that must be nourished for nine months from the same mire. Describe the womb swelling from day to day [Note: [Col. 0758C] “From day to day” omitted by Rig., Ven.], heavy, distressed, secure not even in sleep [Note: [Col. 0758C] “Bound, wholly,” Pam., Seml.; “wholly straining,” Ursinus’ manuscript, Wouwer manuscript; “wholly without sound,” Agobardine manuscript.], uncertain amid the cravings of nausea [Note: [Col. 0758D] “The cravings of nausea and appetite.” He calls all inclinations and appetites “cravings.” LAC.] and appetite. [Col. 0758C] Rail now even against the modesty of the woman in labor, whether to be honored because of its danger [Note: [Col. 0758C] “Whether to be honored because of its danger” omitted by Seml.] or reverenced because it is natural. You surely recoil also from the infant poured forth with its accompanying obstructions and covered in filth. You disdain [Note: [Col. 0758D] “You will disdain,” Pam., Seml.] the fact that it is straightened in swaddling cloths [Note: [Col. 0758D] Others read “carried.”], shaped by bindings [Note: [Col. 0758D] “Anointings,” Rig., Ven., Seml., Rhen.], and made sport of with caresses.

[Col. 0759A] This reverence [Note: [Col. 0759D] “This reverence for nature.” He means the reverence owed to nature. The sense is: what you ought to have revered, you despise. So too in Book III *Against Marcion*: “The most holy,” he says, “and venerable works of nature.” RHEN.] for nature [Note: [Col. 0759C] “Hunting,” Rhen., Seml.], [Note: [Col. 0759C] Pam., Rhen. insert “O.”] Marcion, you despise—and how were you born? You hate a human being at birth; and how do you love anyone? You certainly did not love yourself when you withdrew from the Church and the faith of Christ. But see to it yourself whether you displease yourself, or whether you were born in some other way [Note: [Col. 0759C] “You were born in some other way,” Pam.; “born in some other way. And,” Rhen.].

Christ, at any rate, loved that human being clotted amid uncleanness in the womb, brought forth through the private parts, nourished amid humiliations. For his sake he descended; for his sake he preached; for his sake he cast himself down in every humility, even to death, and death on a cross (Philippians 2). He surely loved the one whom he redeemed at great [Note: [Col. 0759C] Pam., Vatican manuscript 3, add “price.”] cost. If Christ belongs to the Creator [Note: [Col. 0759C] “If the Creator is his,” Pam., Rhen.], he rightly loved his own; if he belongs to another God, he loved him all the more, since he redeemed what belonged to another. Therefore, together with humanity, he also loved its birth and its flesh. Nothing can be loved [Col. 0759B] apart from that through which it is what it is. [Note: [Col. 0759C] Pam., Rhen. add “or.”] Remove birth and produce a human being; take away flesh and present the one whom God redeemed. If these things constitute the human being whom God redeemed, then you make shameful for him those very things that he redeemed, and unworthy those things which he would not have redeemed unless he had loved them.

Having refashioned birth [Note: [Col. 0759C] “He refashions birth from death,” Rig., Ven.] by heavenly regeneration, he restores the flesh from every affliction: he cleanses it when leprous, illuminates it when blind [Note: [Col. 0759C] Others read “reilluminates.”], makes it whole when paralyzed, purifies it when possessed by a demon [Note: [Col. 0759C] “Captures,” Rig., Ven.], and raises it when dead—and is he ashamed to be born into it [Note: [Col. 0759C] Others: “And shall we be ashamed of it?”]?

If he had truly wished to come forth from a she-wolf, a sow, or a cow, and, clothed in the body of a wild or domestic animal, to preach the kingdom of heaven, your judgment, I suppose, would prescribe against him: “This is shameful for God and unworthy of God’s Son, and anyone who believes thus is therefore foolish [Note: [Col. 0759C] “Because,” Rig., Ven.].” Let it certainly be foolish, if [Note: [Col. 0759C] “If” absent from Rig., Ven.] we judge God according to our own understanding. But look around you, Marcion—if, that is, you have not deleted the passage—at 1 Corinthians 1:27: “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” [Note: [Col. 0759C] “Wisdom,” Rig., Ven.; “the wisdom,” Pam., Fran.].

What are these foolish things? A human being’s conversion to the worship [Note: [Col. 0759D] Others: “Human beings’ conversion to the worship of the true God.”] of the true God? The rejection of error? The discipline of justice, chastity, patience, [Col. 0760A] mercy, and innocence? None of these things, certainly, is foolish. Ask, therefore, what things he spoke about; and if you presume that you have discovered them, it will not be so [Note: [Col. 0760C] “Now,” Pam., Rhen.] foolish as [Note: [Col. 0760C] “As” absent from Pam., Rhen.] believing in a God who was born—and born indeed of a virgin, and indeed made flesh—who rolled through those indignities of nature. Let someone say that these things are not foolish and that the things God chose to challenge worldly wisdom were something else. Yet worldly wisdom more readily believes that Jupiter became a bull or a swan than, in Marcion’s system, that Christ became truly human.

## CHAPTER V

There are certainly other things just as foolish, pertaining to the humiliations and sufferings of God; or let them call [Note: [Col. 0760C] “Let me call,” Rhen., Seml.] a crucified God wisdom. Remove [Note: [Col. 0760C] “You remove,” Rhen., Seml.] this [Note: [Col. 0760C] “These things,” Pam., Paris, Fran.] also, Marcion—indeed, remove this above all. For what is more unworthy [Col. 0760B] of God? What is more shameful: to be born or to die? To bear flesh or a cross? To be circumcised or fastened to the cross? To be reared or buried? To be laid in a manger or enclosed in a tomb? You will be wiser if you do not believe these things either. But you will not be wise unless you become a fool [Note: [Col. 0760C] Rig., Ven. insert “in.”] to the world by believing God’s foolish things.

Or did you refrain from excising Christ’s sufferings for the reason that, as a phantom, he was exempt from feeling [Note: [Col. 0760C] “With respect to the perception,” Rhen., Seml.] them? We said above that he could equally have undergone the empty mockeries of an imaginary [Note: [Col. 0760C] “Imaginary and,” Pam., Seml.; “an imaginary thing belonging to imaginary,” Rhen.] birth and infancy. But now answer here [Note: [Col. 0760C] “From here,” Rig., Ven.], you murderer of the truth [Note: [Col. 0759D] “Murderer of the truth.” No one doubts that heretics were formerly branded with harsher language. Our author does so more than once; for in Book I *Against Marcion* he paints that heretic in his true colors and declares him more hideous than every savagery found in his homeland. In a not dissimilar sense, St. Ignatius, in the Letter to the Trallians, calls heretics κακὰς παραθυάδας, “an impious offshoot.” St. Prosper, in his poem *On the Ungrateful*, says of Pelagius:

> The British serpent vomited forth with pestilential speech.

Everyone knows that Blessed Jerome pursued heretics sharply. LE PR.]. Was God not truly crucified? Was he not truly dead, just as [Note: [Col. 0760C] “And,” Seml.] he was truly crucified [Note: [Col. 0760D] “Was he not truly dead, as he was truly crucified?” Christ’s birth is proved from his death. He chose an infamous death and a spectacle full of disgrace so that the truth might be acknowledged by everyone, no one might doubt his real death, and no one might call the resurrection into question. I refrain from citing the Fathers; I mention only St. Ignatius, Letter to the Trallians, where he treats this subject at length. LE PR.]? Was he not truly raised, precisely because he was truly dead?

Was Paul therefore falsely resolved to know among us only Jesus [Note: [Col. 0760C] “Jesus” absent from Rhen., Seml.] crucified? Did he falsely thrust burial upon us? [Col. 0760C] Did he falsely insist upon the resurrection? Then our faith too is false, and everything we hope for from Christ is a phantom [Note: [Col. 0760D] “Will be,” Rig., Ven.]. Most criminal of men, you excuse the killers of God [Note: [Col. 0760D] “You excuse the killers of God.” Marcion, whom Tertullian presses vehemently, proclaimed that Christ had not truly been human but only apparently so, and that he had assumed nothing from humanity. Therefore, if it were certain that he did not take the substance of our flesh and was not a true human being, he certainly would not truly have died; and by that impious and poisonous doctrine Marcion would thus excuse the Jewish executioners. LE PR.]. For Christ suffered nothing from them if he suffered nothing truly. Spare the sole hope of the whole [Col. 0761A] world.

Why [Note: [Col. 0761C] “Who,” Pam., Rhen.] do you destroy the necessary disgrace [Note: [Col. 0761C] “Glory,” Pam., Rhen.] of faith [Note: [Col. 0761D] “Why do you destroy the necessary disgrace of faith?” This may also be said to those who, contrary to the tradition of Tertullian and all the ancient writers, imagine Christ as exceedingly beautiful in stature and countenance. This is unquestionably how the text must be read, and not, as commonly, “glory.” For this is what he undertakes to prove against Marcion: all these things—God being born, God being crucified, God dying, God being buried—which are judged shameful, foolish, and absurd according to human understanding, and which Marcion rejected as unworthy of God, were all chosen by God so that worldly wisdom might be confounded. Septimius therefore says that what we consider disgraces are not disgraces before God, but are in fact necessary to the Christian faith. “Why,” he says, “do you destroy the disgrace necessary to faith?” Georgius Boeticus, in *On Faith*: “You see how beautiful and becoming is the mystery of our salvation. Insofar as he is the Son, he is shown to have been made lesser. Why, therefore, do you reproach as obscuring his divinity what he carries out for its adornment?” RIG.]? Whatever is unworthy of God is advantageous to me. I am saved if I am not ashamed of my Lord. “Whoever is ashamed of me [Note: [Col. 0761C] “Me,” Pam.],” he says, “of him [Note: [Col. 0761C] “Him,” Pam., Fran.] shall I also be ashamed.” Otherwise, I find no grounds for shame that would prove me commendably shameless through contempt for embarrassment and happily foolish.

The Son of God was born: I am not ashamed, because it is shameful. And the Son of God died: it is wholly credible, because it is absurd. And, having been buried, he rose again: it is certain, because it is impossible. But how will these things be true of him if he himself was not real—if he did not truly possess in himself that which could be fastened to the cross, die, be buried, and be raised: namely, flesh suffused with blood, constructed with bones, interwoven with sinews, [Col. 0761B] entwined with veins, which knows how to be born and to die? Human flesh [Note: [Col. 0761C] Accusative “human,” Pam., Rhen.], without doubt, since it was born [Note: [Col. 0761C] Accusative “born,” Pam., Rhen.] of a human being; and therefore [Note: [Col. 0761C] “Because,” Rhen., Seml.] it will be [Note: [Col. 0761C] “Is,” Seml., Pam.] mortal in Christ, because Christ [Note: [Col. 0761C] “Because Christ” absent from Rhen., Seml.] is a human being and the Son of Man.

Or why is Christ a human being and the Son of Man if he has nothing human and nothing derived from a human being? Unless, perhaps [Note: [Col. 0761C] “If” absent from Rig., Ven.], a human being is something other than flesh, or human flesh comes from somewhere other than a human being; or Mary is something [Note: [Col. 0761C] Pam., Fran., Par. add “is.”] other than human; or Marcion’s god is human [Note: [Col. 0761D] “Or Marcion’s god is human”—that is, an imaginary and false human being. For he will presently explain it himself: [Col. 0762D] “So that he bore flesh hard without bones, solid without muscles, bloody without blood, clothed without a tunic, hungry without hunger, speaking without a tongue—so that his speech was a phantom to the ears through the semblance of a voice.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0761C] “Or human” omitted by Pam., Rhen.; [Col. 0762C] “God, Marcion,” Pam.; “In short, Marcion,” Fran.; “Hardly,” Ursinus’ manuscript; “Or Marcion’s god,” Rhen., Seml.].

Otherwise, Christ would not be called human without flesh, nor Son of Man without some human parent—just as he would not be called God without the Spirit of God, nor Son of God without God as Father. Thus the origin derived from each substance displayed him as both human and God: on the one side born, on the other unborn; on the one side fleshly, on the other spiritual; on the one side weak, on the other supremely powerful; [Col. 0761C] on the one side dying, on the other living. This [Note: [Col. 0762C] “By which,” Jun.] distinctive character of the two conditions, divine and human, was certainly reckoned according to the equal reality of both [Note: [Col. 0762C] “Both” absent from Rhen., Pam.; Pam. adds “of each.”] natures, [Col. 0762A] with equal faith in both spirit and flesh [Note: [Col. 0762C] “By faith, spirit and flesh,” manuscripts of Ursinus and Dijon, Seml.]. His mighty works proved the Spirit of God; his sufferings proved human flesh. If the mighty works did not occur without spirit, likewise [Note: [Col. 0762C] “Equally,” Rig., Ven.] neither did the sufferings occur without flesh. If the flesh together with its sufferings was fictitious, then the spirit together with its mighty works was also false.

Why do you divide Christ in half by a lie? [Note: [Col. 0762D] “Why do you divide Christ in half by a lie? He is wholly truth.” Ignatius, Letter to the Trallians: Ἐγὼ δὲ οὐ τῳ δοκεῖν ἔχω τὰς ἐλπίδας ἐπὶ τῷ ὑπὲρ ἐμοῦ ἀποθανόντι, ἀλλὰ τῷ ὄντι· ἀληθείας γὰρ ἀλλότριον τὸ ψεῦδος: “I, however, do not place my hope in the one who died for me merely in appearance, but in reality; for every lie is alien to the truth”—that is, to Christ. LAC.] He was wholly truth. Believe it: he preferred to be born rather than to lie in any [Note: [Col. 0762C] Pam., Par., Fran. add “of himself.”] part—and indeed to lie about himself—so that he might bear flesh hard without bones, solid without muscles, bloody without blood, clothed without a tunic [Note: [Col. 0762D] “Without a tunic.” By the term “tunic” he means the skin. RHEN.], hungry without hunger, eating without teeth, speaking without a tongue; so that his speech was a phantom to the ears through the semblance of a voice.

He was therefore a phantom even after the resurrection, when he offered his hands and feet for his disciples’ inspection [Col. 0762B] [Note: [Col. 0762C] “Offers,” Rhen., Seml.]: “Look,” he says [Note: [Col. 0762C] “Saying,” Pam., Rhen., Seml.], “that it is I, because a spirit does not have bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24)—without doubt, hands and feet and bones, which a spirit does not have but flesh does.

How do you interpret this utterance, Marcion, when [Note: [Col. 0762C] “Because,” Rhen., Ven.] you introduce Jesus as coming from a god who is supremely good, simple, and only benevolent? Look: he cheats, deceives, and circumvents everyone’s eyes, everyone’s senses, and everyone’s approaches and touches. Therefore, you ought no longer to have brought Christ down from heaven, but from some troupe of itinerant performers; nor as a God beyond man, but as a man who was a magician; nor as the high priest of salvation, but as a producer of spectacle; nor as one who raises the dead, but as one who summons the living away [Note: [Col. 0762D] “But one who summons the living away.” One who summons the living away from life to death, from right faith to heresy, from God to Satan. RIG.—“One who summons the living away.” Understand “one who cheats and deceives”; and he plays not ineptly upon the word, since the souls of the dead are said to be summoned. LAC.]. Except that, even if he was a magician, he was born.

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0762C] But certain disciples [Note: [Col. 0762C] “What now,” Rhen., Paris.] of that man from Pontus [Note: [Col. 0762D] “But certain disciples of that man from Pontus.” He means Marcion’s disciples, among whom Apelles was the leader. Marcion is called “the man from Pontus,” just as at the beginning of Book I *Against Marcion* he is called “the Pontic mouse”; for he was a native of Sinope in Pontus. LE PR.], compelled to be wiser than their teacher, concede that Christ’s flesh was real, [Col. 0763A] yet without prejudicing their rejection of his birth. “Let him have had flesh,” they say, “provided only [Note: [Col. 0763C] “The Lord,” Agobardine manuscript, Pithou.] that it was unborn.”

We have therefore come [Note: [Col. 0763C] “We have obeyed,” Agobardine manuscript, Pithou, Rhen., Jun.; “let us produce,” others.], as the saying goes, from the limekiln into the charcoal furnace—from Marcion to Apelles. After Apelles had fallen away from Marcion’s discipline into a woman in the flesh [Note: [Col. 0763C] “Slipped through a woman,” Rhen., Seml.], and thereafter [Note: [Col. 0763C] “And” absent from Rig.] had been spiritually overthrown by the virgin Philumene [Note: [Col. 0763D] “Overthrown spiritually by the virgin Philumene”—that is, seduced by the demon that took possession of that infamous prostitute. LE PR.], he received from her the doctrine he proclaimed [Note: [Col. 0763C] “Proclaiming,” Pam., Rhen.; “he proclaims it as received from him,” Wouwer manuscript.]: that Christ’s body was solid but without birth.

To that angel [Note: [Col. 0763C] “As an angel,” Wouwer manuscript, Pam., Rhen.] of Philumene [Note: [Col. 0763C] “A certain one,” Latin edition; “of that man,” Pam., Fran.; “of Philumene” absent from the Wouwer manuscript; “Philomene,” others.], indeed, the Apostle will reply in the very words with which he foretold even him at that time, saying (Galatians 1:8): “Even if an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel different from what we preached to you, let him be accursed.” But we shall resist the further arguments [Note: [Col. 0763C] “Who,” Pam., Rhen.] they advance [Note: [Col. 0763C] “We have resisted,” Rhen.].

They confess [Col. 0763B] [Note: [Col. 0763D] “Of one confessing,” Pam.] that Christ truly had a body. From what did its material come, if not from the same kind of substance in which it appeared? From what came the body, if the body was not flesh? From what came the flesh, if it was not born? For what comes into being by birth would have to be born.

“He borrowed his flesh,” they say, “from the stars and from the substances of the higher world.” And, of course, they argue that a body without birth should not be considered remarkable, since among us too angels were able to advance into flesh [Note: [Col. 0763D] “In flesh,” Rig., Ven.] without any agency of the womb. We acknowledge that this is indeed what has been related. Yet what sort of thing is it that a faith belonging to one rule should borrow the documentary authority for its arguments from the very faith it attacks [Note: [Col. 0764C] “Should be changed,” Rig., Ven.]? What has Apelles to do with Moses, when he rejects the God of Moses [Note: [Col. 0764C] “Moses, who rejects the God of Moses,” Seml.]? If his God is another, let his affairs also be different.

But [Note: [Col. 0764C] “And,” Rhen., Seml.] let all heretics use the Scriptures of the one whose world they also use: this too will serve as testimony [Note: [Col. 0764C] “This too as testimony of him,” Agobardine manuscript.] against them at the judgment, because they construct their blasphemies from his own examples. It is easy for the truth to prevail even without advancing any such preliminary objection against them. [Col. 0764A]

Therefore, I would like those who set forth the angels as an example for Christ’s flesh—saying that it was flesh, although unborn [Note: [Col. 0764C] “Fleshly, of course,” Pam., Rhen.]—to compare the reasons for which both Christ and [Note: [Col. 0764C] Pam., Rhen. add “the.”] the angels entered into flesh [Note: [Col. 0764C] “In flesh,” Rig., Ven.; “came,” Pam., Fran., Par.; “went forth,” Rhen., Seml.]. No angel ever descended in order to be crucified, to experience death, or to be raised from death [Note: [Col. 0764C] “To be brought to life,” Rig., Ven.]. If the angels never had any such reason for becoming embodied, you have the reason why they received flesh without being born. They had not come to die; therefore neither had they come to be born.

Christ, however, was sent to die and therefore also necessarily had to be born, so that he could die [Note: [Col. 0763D] “Christ, sent to die, also necessarily had to be born so that he could die.” Marius Victorinus was not yet properly a Christian when he wrote thus in Book I of his commentary on Cicero’s *Rhetoric*: “Among human beings, necessity has only as much force as it possesses according to human opinion; otherwise, according to the Christians’ opinion, this is not a necessary argument: ‘If she gave birth, she had intercourse with a man’; nor, again, is this one: ‘If he was born, he will die.’ For among them it is manifest that he was born without a man and did not die.” On the contrary, we confess that our Lord, whom we know to have been truly born, also truly died, and we declare that he also truly rose again. RIG.]. For nothing normally dies except what is born. Birth and mortality stand in reciprocal debt to each other. The manner of dying is the reason for being born [Note: [Col. 0764D] “The manner of dying is the reason for being born.” After saying that there was a reciprocal debt between life and death, he now says that the form is the cause of birth. The “form” of the loan is thus like a certain formal quality in a loan, inhering in it. Tertullian’s meaning, therefore, is this: we die by compact and condition, so that only because we have been born are we bound by this law of death, as though the condition of death were the final cause of birth; for we are not born except under the condition of dying, and the contract of life was made under this condition. So Seneca, *Remedies for Fortune*. LAC.].

If [Col. 0764B] Christ died because of that which dies, and what dies is also what is born, it followed [Note: [Col. 0764C] Rhen., Seml. add “however”; likewise Pam., Fran., Par.]—indeed, it had to precede—that he should likewise be born because of that which is born, since he was going to die because of that very thing which dies because [Note: [Col. 0764C] Rhen., Pam. add “that which.”] it is born. It was not fitting that he should remain unborn in respect of that for which it was fitting that he should die.

“But surely [Note: [Col. 0764C] “But,” Seml.] the Lord himself also appeared to Abraham among those angels [Note: [Col. 0764C] “Those angels,” Rig.] at that time, in flesh but without birth” [Note: [Col. 0764D] “But surely the Lord himself also appeared to Abraham among those angels at that time.” This interpretation, which seems to have arisen from the reading of Genesis 3, “He saw three and worshiped one,” is not approved by Blessed Augustine; the reader should therefore consult *On the Trinity* II.17. Moreover, following Vatican manuscript 3, we again read *atquin* rather than *atqui*. PAM.]. Certainly—because the reason was correspondingly different.

But you do not accept this, because you do not accept that Christ who even then was learning, in the guise of flesh, to address, deliver, and judge the human race—flesh not yet born because it was not yet to die, unless his birth and mortality were first announced. Therefore, let them prove that those angels [Col. 0764C] received [Note: [Col. 0764C] “Flesh,” Rig., Ven.] the substance of their flesh from the stars [Note: [Col. 0764C] “Desired,” Rig., Ven.; [Col. 0764D] “The substance of their flesh” absent from Rig., Ven.]. If they do not prove it—because neither is it written—then neither will Christ’s flesh have come from there, since they apply the example of the angels to it.

It is agreed that the angels did not bear flesh proper to themselves [Col. 0765A] [Note: [Col. 0765D] “It is agreed that the angels did not bear flesh proper to themselves.” That is, they were not altogether and properly fleshly as we are, nor heavy with bodily weight. Above, he calls what belongs to the angels “proper”—namely, proper to themselves—not what is superior to flesh. For he immediately indicates, and elsewhere teaches, that those angels displayed real flesh, though flesh assumed and not proper and natural to them; Augustine and Bernard, when sometimes cited on this matter, are uncertain. LAC.], since they were natures [Note: [Col. 0765C] “For example,” Pam., Rhen.; “a nature,” Rhen., Seml.; “from a nature,” Agobardine manuscript; “of a nature,” Pam., Paris.] of spiritual substance—or, if of some bodily substance, nevertheless of their own kind—yet capable of being transfigured temporarily into human flesh, so that [Note: [Col. 0765C] “So that” omitted by Rig., Ven.] they could be seen and associate with human beings [Note: [Col. 0765C] “Could,” Rig., Ven.].

Therefore, since it has not been related from where they took their flesh, it remains for our understanding not to doubt that this is proper to angelic power: to assume a body for itself from no material. “How much more certain it is,” you say, “that it came from some material!” But nothing concerning that is established, because Scripture does not disclose it. Besides, those who [Note: [Col. 0765C] “Because,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth.] are able to make themselves what they are not by nature—why should they not also be able to make themselves from no substance [Note: [Col. 0765C] “A substance,” Rhen., Seml., Oberth.]? If they become what they are not, why should they not become it from what does not exist? But what does not exist, when it comes to exist, is from nothing.

For this reason it is neither asked nor shown [Col. 0765B] what afterward became of their bodies [Note: [Col. 0765D] “What afterward became of their bodies.” This is thoroughly idiomatic Latin; that is, where they ended up. The preposition *de* is understood. So Cicero, *Against Verres*: “What will become of you? Where will you flee?” Plautus: “What became of the money I gave?” Again Cicero, *For Cluentius*: “What is,” etc. RHEN.]. What came from nothing became nothing. Those who could change themselves into flesh can change nothing itself into flesh. It is a greater thing to alter a nature than to produce material.

But even [Note: [Col. 0765C] “And” absent from Rhen., Pam.] if the angels had necessarily [Note: [Col. 0765C] “Had,” Rig., Ven.] assumed flesh from material, it is surely more credible that it came from earthly material than from any class of heavenly substances, since it proved to be so earthly in quality that it was nourished on earthly food. Suppose now [Note: [Col. 0765C] “Suppose” omitted by Rhen., Seml.; [Col. 0766C] Rhen. adds “if.”] that flesh of stellar origin was similarly [Note: [Col. 0766C] “In the same manner,” Rhen.] nourished on earthly food although it was not earthly, just as earthly flesh was nourished on heavenly food although it was not heavenly—for we read that manna was given to the people for food: “A human being,” he says (Psalm 77), “ate the bread of angels.” Nevertheless, the once-for-all distinct condition of the Lord’s [Col. 0765C] flesh is not invalidated by the reason belonging to a different dispensation. Because he was to become truly human even to the point of death, he had to put on that flesh [Note: [Col. 0766C] “That” omitted by Rhen., Seml.] to which death belongs; [Col. 0766A] and birth precedes that flesh to which death belongs.

## CHAPTER VII
But whenever the birth is disputed, all who reject it because it prejudges the reality of Christ’s flesh wish to deny that God himself was born, on the ground that he said (Matt. 12:48): “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” Let Apelles, therefore, also hear [Note: [Col. 0765D] What answer we have already given to Marcion. He doubtless means Books IV *Against Marcion*, for there too he explains this passage in nearly the same words, though somewhat fewer; they will be cited a little below. [Col. 0766C] Hence it is also evident that this book and the following one were written at almost the same time as the first four books *Against Marcion*; only after these had been completed was the fifth book against the same man composed. PAM.] what answer we have already given to Marcion in that little work in which [Note: [Col. 0766D] We appealed to his own Gospel. Tertullian sometimes uses Marcion’s Gospel against Marcion himself: he turns it back against him, evidently, so that he may press him by any possible wager. Marcion rejected the other three Gospels and in many places refused Luke’s Gospel; he devised a fifth, suited and conformed to his own folly. This is the work in question. LE PR.] we appealed to [Note: [Col. 0766C] *To* omitted by Pam., Rhen.] his own Gospel—namely, that the context of this pronouncement must be considered.

First, no one would ever have announced to him that his mother and brothers were standing outside [Note: [Col. 0766C] *Standing*, Codex Agobardinus.] unless he were certain [Note: [Col. 0766C] Rig., Ven. add *and*.] that he had a mother and brothers, and that these were the very persons whom he was then announcing, either known previously or identified there and then [Note: [Col. 0766C] Others read *found*.]. The heresies have, admittedly, removed this from the Gospel [Col. 0766B] because those who marveled at his teaching said that they knew very well his reputed father Joseph the carpenter, his mother Mary, and his brothers and sisters. “But they announced a mother and brothers whom he did not have in order to test him.” [Note: [Col. 0766C] Fran. reads *they announced*.] Scripture certainly does not say this, although elsewhere it does not remain silent when something was done to test him: “Behold,” it says (Matt. 22), “a teacher of the Law arose, testing him.” And elsewhere (Matt. 19): “And the Pharisees came to him, testing him.” Nothing prevented it from being indicated here too that the act was done as a test. [Note: [Col. 0766D] I do not accept what is outside Scripture. Among the forty articles drawn up by the heretics in the preceding century, there is one in which they profess to believe or teach nothing unless it is found in the sacred books—their purpose, of course, being to expel the traditions of the Church. LE PR.—Lest anyone twist this passage against ecclesiastical traditions, let him remember that the Author taught in *On the Soldier’s Crown*, ch. 3, that even unwritten tradition must be accepted. PAM.] I do not accept what you introduce on your own authority from outside Scripture.

Next, there must be subject matter for the test. What did they think they were testing in him? Surely whether he had been born or not; for if his answer denied this, then this is what the tester’s announcement sought to catch. But no test aimed at discovering something about which the tester is in doubt proceeds so abruptly that it is not preceded by a question which, by raising the doubt, gives rise to the test. Moreover, if Christ’s birth was nowhere being debated, why do you argue that through this test they wished to inquire into something they had never made a subject of controversy?

To this we add [Note: [Col. 0767C] Pam., Fran., Par. read *we added*.]: even if he were to be tested about his birth, he would certainly not be tested in this manner, by the announcement of persons who might not have existed even if Christ had been born. We are all born, yet not all of us have either brothers or a mother. A man may still have a father rather than a mother, and maternal uncles rather than brothers. Thus this is no suitable test of birth, since birth could be established without naming either a mother or brothers.

It is plainly more likely that, since they were certain he had a mother and brothers, they tested his divinity rather than his birth: whether, while occupied inside, he knew what was outside, when they assailed him with a lie [Note: [Col. 0767C] Rhen., Seml. read *rather*.] concerning the presence [Note: [Col. 0767C] Rig., Ven. add *announced*.] of persons who were not actually present [Note: [Col. 0767C] Rig., Ven. read *in the presence*.]. Except that, even if [Note: [Col. 0767C] Thus Codex Agobardinus.] the ingenuity of the test had been free from this objection [Note: [Col. 0767C] Par. reads *had been effective*.], it might have happened that he knew those whom they announced to be standing outside [Note: [Col. 0767D] He knew them to be absent. The question concerns Christ’s mother and relatives, whom those slanderers said that he had scorned or neglected. Here, however, Tertullian proves from Blessed Luke that he was never insulting toward his parents but always compliant and subject to them. LE PR.] to be absent through some already known necessity of health [Note: [Col. 0767C] Rig., Ven. read *because of health*.], business, or travel. No one conducts a test in a manner by which he knows he may bring the shame of the test back upon himself.

Since, therefore, there was no suitable subject matter for a test, the straightforwardness of the messenger [Note: [Col. 0767C] Rig., Ven. read *of the announcement*.] is vindicated: his mother and brothers had truly arrived. But let Apelles also learn the reason for the answer that denied his mother and brothers at that moment. The Lord’s brothers had not believed [Note: [Col. 0767C] Pam., Fran., Par.: erroneous spelling of *believed*.] in him, as is also contained in the Gospel published before Marcion’s. Nor is his mother shown [Col. 0767C] to have attached herself to him [Note: [Col. 0767D] Nor is his mother shown to have attached herself to him. This may be understood of constant attendance at Christ’s discourses, which Martha and Mary regularly frequented. Furthermore, what follows—their unbelief—must be referred to the Lord’s brothers, not to Mary. PAM.—Or it must be said that here, as sometimes elsewhere, good Tertullian nodded. For did she not indeed remain attached to Christ her Son—she who followed him, suffering with him, as far as the cross; and who, after he had ascended into heaven, remained with the Apostles in the upper room and persevered in prayer, awaiting the Father’s promise, which she too had heard from his own mouth? Yet we demonstrate each of these points without difficulty from John’s Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles. EDD.], whereas Martha and Mary [Note: [Col. 0767D] Rig., Ven., Rhen., Seml. read *other Marthas and Marys*.] are repeatedly found elsewhere in association with him.

Indeed, in this very passage their unbelief is apparent: while he [Note: [Col. 0768C] Codex Agobardinus reads *these*.] was teaching the way of life, while he was preaching God’s kingdom, while he was engaged in healing diseases and infirmities, strangers were intent upon him, yet [Note: [Col. 0768C] Jun. reads *then*.] his nearest relatives were absent. At last they arrive and remain outside; they do not enter, evidently taking no account of what was being done within. Nor do they wait, at least, as though they were bringing something more necessary [Note: [Col. 0768D] “As though they were bringing something necessary,” etc. He used *necessary* to mean *more necessary*. RHEN.] than what he was especially doing at the time. Instead they interrupt him still further and wish him to be recalled from so great a work.

I ask you, Apelles—or you, Marcion—if, perhaps, while playing a board game [Note: [Col. 0768D] “If, perhaps, while playing a board game.” He means a gaming board, or a board for the game of brigands, on which men played with dice and counters. Those who explain *tabula* as a dice-box are perhaps less correct. For the *fritillus* is a little vessel into which dice or cubes are thrown and shaken; because of its oblong shape it is called a *pyrgus* (πύργος, “tower”). Thus in Horace, “to throw the knucklebones into the tower.” Martial calls this vessel a “little tower.” LE PR.], or arguing about actors or charioteers, you were called away by such a message, would you not have said: “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?” While Christ was preaching and demonstrating God, fulfilling the Law and the Prophets, and dispersing the darkness of so many preceding ages, did he make an unworthy use of this saying when he employed it to strike at the unbelief of those standing outside, or to shake off the importunity of those recalling him from his work?

Besides, to deny his birth, another [Col. 0768B] place, time, and order of discourse would have been necessary [Note: [Col. 0768C] *Necessary* absent from Codex Agobardinus, Rig., Ven.; Codex Ursinianus reads *more necessary*.], not a saying that could [Note: [Col. 0768C] Pam., Rhen. read *can*.] be uttered even by one who had both a mother and brothers, since indignation does not deny relatives but rebukes them [Note: [Col. 0768C] Rig., Ven., on Cujacius’s authority at the chapter *Ex litteris*, Book III of the *Decretals*, read: “denies relatives—not ‘does not deny,’ but rebukes.”]. Indeed, he preferred others and showed the ground of their preference—namely, hearing the word [Note: [Col. 0768D] Namely, hearing the word. *Audientia* is a Latin word, which Cicero also used in *On Old Age*: “And it very often wins itself a hearing,” etc. LE PR.]—thus demonstrating under what condition he denied his mother and brothers. By the same principle by which he adopted as his own those who adhered to him, he disowned those who stood apart from him.

Christ is also accustomed to fulfill what he teaches others. What sort of thing would it have been, then, if, while teaching that a mother or brothers should not be esteemed as highly as God’s word, he himself, the Word of God, abandoned that word when his mother and brotherhood were announced? He therefore denied his relatives in the manner in which he taught that they must be denied for God’s work.

But in another sense, the separated mother [Note: [Col. 0768C] Pam. reads *the joined mother*.] is a figure of the synagogue, and the unbelieving brothers [Col. 0768C] are a figure of the Jews. In them Israel was outside; but the new disciples inside—hearing, believing, and clinging to Christ—were outlining [Note: [Col. 0768C] Jun. reads *delineating*.] the Church, which, after rejecting fleshly lineage, he called his preferable mother and worthier brotherhood [Note: [Col. 0768C] Rhen., Seml. read *they call*; Fran., Par. *he calls*; [Col. 0768D] Pam. *you call*.]. Finally, in the same sense he also answered that exclamation, not denying his mother’s womb and breasts, but designating as more blessed those who hear God’s word.

## CHAPTER VIII

The interpretation, according to the truth of the complete and uncorrupted Gospel, of these passages alone—the ones with which Marcion and Apelles consider themselves especially well equipped [Note: [Col. 0769C] Rhen., Pam. read *consider themselves*.]—should have sufficed to prove Christ’s human flesh by defending his birth.

But since these Apelleans [Note: [Col. 0769C] Codex Agobardinus, Rig., Ven. read *Apelleiaci*; Codex Ursinianus *Apelliaci*; Codex Pithoeanus *Apelliaciani*; Codex Divionensis *appellationi*; Rhen. *Apellaciani*.] especially allege the disgrace of the flesh—which, they maintain, was constructed for the seduced souls by that fiery ruler of evil [Note: [Col. 0769C] Pam. erroneously reads *association*.], and was therefore unworthy of Christ, so that a substance drawn from the stars was consequently appropriate for him—I must strike them back with their own stock of material [Note: [Col. 0769C] *Stock of material.* He calls that which supplies material a *paratura*. RHENAN.].

They name a certain illustrious angel [Col. 0769B] who established this world and, after establishing it, mingled repentance with it [Note: [Col. 0769C] Pam., Rhen. read *admitted*.]. We have treated this in its proper place, for we have a little work against them [Note: [Col. 0769C] Namely, a little work *Against the Apelleans*, a book that no longer survives. SEML.—Whether this book ought to be entitled *Against Apelles* or *Against the Apelleans* caused me to doubt for some time, because Vincent of Lérins numbers Apelles among the other heretics against whom Tertullian wrote. This also made us hesitate as to whether the Author had composed several little works against Apelles himself and his disciples. But since, although he mentions Apelles so often and no one else, he nevertheless makes no mention of any book against him except in this passage, it seems credible to me both that he wrote only one and that it was entitled *Against the Apelleans*—especially since Blessed Cyprian also calls Apelles’s disciples “Apelleans,” Epistle 73, to Jubaianus.

Tertullian’s words are admittedly rather obscure; but this is what he means: the principal argument of the book against the Apelleans was whether that fiery angel, ruler of evil—who, according to them, had both established this world and constructed flesh for the seduced souls—although he possessed Christ’s spirit, will, and power for those works, had done anything worthy of repentance. For they said, as is read in *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, ch. 31, that he mingled repentance with the lower world because he had not made it as perfectly [Col. 0770C] as the higher world had been established. This very point the Author meanwhile turns elegantly against them where, speaking of striking them back with their own stock of material, he says. . . .

On the souls seduced by that fiery god, an angel according to Apelles, see *On the Soul*, ch. 23. On the world established by him, *On the Prescription*, chs. 34 and 51. Likewise, on human flesh constructed by him, see further *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 5. Finally, the Author of this book argued at length against Apelles concerning Christ’s flesh—not created by that angel, but constructed from the heavenly stars—in ch. 6 and in Book III *Against Marcion*. Epiphanius agrees on all these points, except that he calls him the lower god whom the Author calls the fiery angel. Blessed Augustine, *Heresies* 23, Isidore in his book *Against Marcion*, our Rabanus, Blessed Honorius, and Gratian in the *Catalogue of Heretics* likewise recognize him.

What is peculiar to the Author is what has already been said about the creating angel’s repentance, as is also their interpretation of the figure of the wandering sheep (Luke 15) as referring to that angel—as though there had been joy in heaven among God’s angels over that one sinner converted to repentance. The Author preferred instead to interpret it of fallen humanity, sought again through Christ, as did all the other ancients. PAM.]—asking whether one who possessed Christ’s spirit, will, and power for those works had done anything worthy of repentance, since they also interpret the angel through the figure of the wandering sheep.

On the testimony, therefore, of its creator’s repentance, the world will be a sin, since all repentance is a confession of sin [Note: [Col. 0770D] All repentance is a confession of sin. The Lutheran definition, “Repentance is a new life,” is therefore insufficient. PAM.], because repentance has no place except where there is sin. If the world is a sin because it is a body and has members, then heaven likewise will be a sin, and the heavenly things together with heaven. If the heavenly things [Note: [Col. 0769C] “Together with heaven. If the heavenly things” is absent from Codex Agobardinus, Rigalt., Ven.], then whatever has been conceived and brought forth from them must be the bad fruit produced by a bad tree (Matt. 7).

Christ’s flesh, therefore, constructed from heavenly things, consisted [Note: [Col. 0769C] Rig., Ven. read *consists*.] of the elements of sin; it was sinful by virtue of its sinful origin [Note: [Col. 0770C] Par., Lugdun. read *meaning*.], and will now be equal [Note: [Col. 0770C] Rig., Ven. read *a part*.] in substance to that flesh of ours which, because it is sinful, they disdain to assign to Christ [Note: [Col. 0770C] Pam., Rhen. read “Christ disdains to put on.”]. Thus, if there is no difference in disgrace, either those who are displeased with our material must devise for Christ another material of purer quality, or they must acknowledge [Note: [Col. 0770C] Pam., Rhen. read *recognize*.] that same material, than which even heavenly material could not be better.

We certainly read (1 Cor. 15): “The first man was from the clay of the earth; the second man from heaven.” This does not, however, refer to a difference in material. It merely contrasts the heavenly substance derived from the Spirit in the second man, that is, Christ, with the originally earthly substance of the first man’s flesh, that is, Adam’s. And to such an extent does it refer the heavenly man to the Spirit, not to the flesh [Col. 0770B], that those whom it compares with him in this way are clearly made heavenly in this earthly flesh—namely, through the Spirit.

But if Christ were heavenly according to the flesh also, those who are not [Note: [Col. 0770C] *Not* absent from Rig., Ven.] heavenly according to the flesh would not be compared [Note: [Col. 0770C] Rig., Ven. read *would be compared*.] with him. If, therefore, those who become heavenly, as Christ also [Note: [Col. 0770C] Pam., Rhen. read *is*.] is, bear an earthly substance of flesh, this too confirms that Christ himself was heavenly in earthly flesh, just as those are [Note: [Col. 0770C] Rig., Ven. add *they*.] who are made equal to him.

## CHAPTER IX

We further maintain that nothing received from something else, so as to become something other than that from which it was received, is so completely [Col. 0771A] other [Note: [Col. 0771B] *Other* omitted by Seml.; Pam., Rhen. prefix *completely*.] that it does not disclose [Note: [Col. 0771B] Jun. reads *because it discloses*; Seml. *that it should disclose*; Rhen., Pam. *to which it does not disclose*.] whence it was received. No material is without testimony to its origin, even if it is changed into a new property.

Certainly this very body of ours, which was fashioned from clay—a truth transmitted even [Note: [Col. 0771B] Lat. reads *as now*.] into the myths of the nations [Note: [Col. 0771C] Into the myths of the nations. The myth of Prometheus. He alludes to the son of Iapetus, who first formed human beings from mud. On this, Juvenal, Satire 13; Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book 1; Horace, *Odes*, Book 1. LE PR.]—confesses both elements of its origin [Note: [Col. 0771B] Rig., Ven., Seml. read *the origin of both elements*.]: in the flesh, what is earthly [Note: [Col. 0771B] Rig., Ven., Pam., Rhen., Seml. read *earth*.]; in the blood, what is watery [Note: [Col. 0771B] Thus Codex Ursinianus, Wouw.; Rig., Ven. read *water*; Pam., Rhen., Seml. *aquatic*.]. For [Note: [Col. 0771C] *For* omitted by Rhen., Pam., Seml.], although the form of the quality is different—this is what it means for one thing to become another from something else—nevertheless, what is blood but reddened fluid? What is flesh but earth transformed into its own shapes [Note: [Col. 0772B] Others read *earth in its own shape*.]?

Consider the individual qualities: the muscles like clods [Note: [Col. 0771C] The muscles like clods. He compares muscles excellently with clods, for just as clods are neither so solid as stones nor so loose as powdered earth, so muscle is intermediate between a ligament, which is hard, and a nerve, which is softer, as Galen explains in Book 1 of *On the Use of the Parts* and Vesalius in Book 2 of *On the Fabric of the Human Body*. Otherwise the muscles, which are the organs of voluntary motion, could not suitably move the human body. LAC.]; the bones like rocks; even around the nipples certain little stones [Note: [Col. 0771C] Even around the nipples certain little stones. On feeling a nipple, Septimius perceived that his hand was filled with the rather hard little clusters of glands. Thus in Book II *To the Nations* he said, “the breasts turn stony.” RIG.]. Observe the tenacious junctions of the sinews [Note: [Col. 0771D] The tenacious junctions of the sinews. He indicates the *syndesmata*, or very solid ligaments of the human body, which some call nerves, though not in the strict sense. On these, see Galen, Book 3 of *On Affected Places*. LAC.], like the extensions of roots; the branching courses of the veins, like the windings of streams; the fine hairs like mosses; the hair of the head like turf; and the very treasures of the marrow in their hidden recess [Col. 0771B], like the mines of the flesh.

All these signs of earthly origin were also present in Christ. These [Note: [Col. 0772B] Rig., Ven. read *and*.] are the things that concealed the Son of God, who was considered a mere man for no other reason than that he was formed from the human substance of the body [Note: [Col. 0772B] Rig., Ven. read “existing from human substance”; Codex Pithoeanus “from human substance.”]. Or produce something heavenly in him, begged from the Great Bear, the Pleiades, and the Hyades [Note: [Col. 0771D] From the Great Bear, the Pleiades, and the Hyades. He names those stars near Ursa Minor which reproduce the figure of a wagon and are called the *Septemtriones*, either from the shape of yoked oxen, which are called *triones*, as though *teriones*, or from seven triangles, because they represent three triangles. The *Vergiliae*, also called the Pleiades, are seven stars before the knees of Taurus, though one is hidden. They appear at the beginning of spring, whence they are called *Vergiliae*. The *Suculae*, or Hyades, rise at the same time and are likewise seven stars on the forehead of Taurus. LE PR.] [Col. 0772A]. For the things we have enumerated are so clearly evidence of earthly flesh that they are evidence of our own flesh.

But I detect nothing new, nothing foreign. Indeed, men were astonished solely at Christ’s words and deeds, his teaching and power [Note: [Col. 0772B] Rig., Ven. read *Christ the man*.]. Had the flesh in him been novel, that too would have been remarked upon as a miracle [Note: [Col. 0772B] Rig., Ven. add *however*.]. But the condition of earthly flesh is not miraculous: this was the very flesh that made his other deeds marvelous. When they said, “Where did this man obtain this teaching and these signs?” these were also the words of people who despised his appearance.

Thus his was not even a body of human comeliness [Note: [Col. 0771D] Thus his was not even a body of human comeliness. So in the book *Against the Jews*: “not even comely in appearance.” These words confirm what we noted above, in connection with the book *On Patience*, about a coin seen at Rome in the possession of Laelius Pasqualinus and afterward of Cardinal Altemps. Gregory of Elvira—or whoever else was the author of the book *On Faith*—renders Isaiah’s words thus: “There is no beauty in him, nor honor of form; and we saw him, and he had neither beauty nor splendor, but his appearance was without honor.” RIG.], much less a body of heavenly radiance. Even if the Prophets among us were silent [Note: [Col. 0772B] Rhen., Seml. read *you*.] about his undistinguished appearance, the sufferings and insults themselves speak: the sufferings indeed proved his flesh human; [Note: [Col. 0772C] But the insult proved it uncomely. Rigalt. at ch. 5 of this book thinks Christ was deformed, and several others likewise misuse this passage. The memory of the Lord’s Passion could silence them, if they noticed that Tertullian says this about the period of his sufferings. For many arguments prove that he was beautiful. I omit the paintings executed by Blessed Luke. Saint Jerome, Epistle 140 to Principia: “For unless there had been in his face and eyes something star-like, the Apostles would never have followed him immediately, nor would those who came to seize him have fallen down.” Blessed Chrysostom, Homily 28 on Matthew: “For just as he was marvelous in performing signs, so he is said to have been most gracious in appearance.” Bonaventure in the *Mirror* cites words of Augustine to this effect. The deformity he contracted during his sufferings is excellently explained by Blessed Bernard in his treatise *On the Passion*. LE PR.] the insults proved it uncomely [Note: [Col. 0772B] *Proved* omitted by Rig., Ven.].

Would anyone ever have dared to graze with the very tip of a fingernail [Note: [Col. 0772D] Would anyone have dared to graze with the very tip of a fingernail a novel body? That is, a body of some extraordinary beauty or heavenly radiance. Augustine on Psalm 127: “And unless they had thought him ugly, they would not have attacked him, beaten him with scourges, crowned him with thorns, or dishonored him with spittle.” A marvelous beauty would have disarmed the torturers and obtained release even without a word.] a novel body, or to defile its face with spittle, unless it deserved it [Note: [Col. 0772D] To defile its face with spittle, unless it deserved it? Who would not shudder at the boldness of the expression? Christ’s face deserving to be spat upon! Worthy to be defiled by missiles of spittle! Forgive us, Christ. As suppliants we kiss this deformity of yours. And may it profit us to have said that what our debts made deserving is ours. RIG.]?

Why do you call the flesh heavenly when you have no grounds from which to understand it as heavenly? Why deny that it was earthly, when you have grounds from which to recognize it as earthly? He hungered under the devil’s testing, thirsted beside the Samaritan woman, wept over Lazarus, and trembled [Note: [Col. 0772C] Rhen., Pam. read *weeps over Lazarus, trembles*.] at death. “For the flesh,” he says, “is weak.” Finally [Note: [Col. 0773D] Codex Agobardinus reads *finally he shed*.], he shed blood. These, I suppose, are heavenly signs.

But how, I ask [Note: [Col. 0773D] Codex Agobardinus reads *you ask*.], could it have been despised and made to suffer, as I have also said, if anything of heavenly nobility had shone forth in that flesh? From this, therefore, we prove that there was nothing heavenly in it, precisely so that it could be despised and made to suffer.

## CHAPTER X

I turn to others who are equally wise in their own estimation [Note: [Col. 0773D] Codex Agobardinus, Rhen., Seml., Oberth. read *custom*.]. They affirm that Christ’s flesh was animate, because the soul became flesh and consequently the flesh became soul; and just as the flesh was ensouled, so the soul was fleshly.

Here too, therefore, I ask for their reasons. If Christ took a soul into himself in order to save the soul, because it could not be saved except through him while it was in him, I do not see why he made it into animate flesh by putting on flesh, as though he could not otherwise save the soul unless it were made fleshly. For since he renders our souls saved not merely when they are not fleshly but even when they are separated from [Note: [Col. 0773D] Rhen., Seml., Oberth. read *in*.] the flesh, how much more could he have brought to salvation the soul he himself assumed even without making it fleshly!

Likewise, since they assume [Note: [Col. 0773D] Rhen., Seml., Oberth. read *he assumes*.] that Christ came forth for the sake of liberating not our flesh but our soul alone [Note: [Col. 0773D] Not our flesh but our soul alone. The Agobardine manuscript extends this far. Henceforth the discussion will proceed only with the manuscripts of Ursinus and Pithoeus. RIG.], first, how absurd it is that, when he was going to liberate the soul alone, he should have made it into the very kind of body he was not going to liberate! Next, if he had undertaken to liberate our souls through the soul he bore, he ought also to have borne our kind of soul—that is, one of the same form as ours, whatever the form of our soul may be in its hidden state, yet certainly not fleshly. Otherwise, he did not liberate our soul if the one he possessed was fleshly; for ours is not fleshly.

Moreover, if he did not liberate ours because he liberated a fleshly soul [Note: [Col. 0773D] “Because he liberated a fleshly soul” absent from Rhen.], this has no relevance to us [Note: [Col. 0773D] Rhen. adds *It is not fleshly*.], because he did not liberate our soul. Nor was that soul in need of liberation, since it was not ours—namely, because it was fleshly; for it was not in danger if it was not ours—that is, not fleshly. Yet it is established that that soul was liberated. Therefore it was not fleshly; and it was ours, if it [Note: [Col. 0773D] Others insert *not*.] was the soul that required liberation, because [Note: [Col. 0773D] Others read *in what manner*.] it was in danger.

Therefore, if the soul in Christ was not fleshly, neither could the flesh have been animate in the sense they allege.

## CHAPTER XI

But let us confront another of their arguments, asking why Christ, by assuming animate flesh, is thought to have possessed a fleshly soul. For God, they say [Note: [Col. 0773D] Rhen. reads *he says*.], desired [Note: [Col. 0773D] Rig. reads *bore*.] to display the soul visibly to human beings by making it a body. Previously it had been invisible [Col. 0774A], by nature a nothing, unable even to see itself because of the obstruction of this flesh, so that it was even debated whether the soul was born or not and whether it was mortal or not [Note: [Col. 0774D] “Whether it was mortal or not” is absent from the Vatican manuscripts and the first edition of Rhen.; Jun. also rejects it.]. Accordingly, the soul was made a body in Christ so that we might see it being born, dying, and—what is more—rising again.

But what kind of procedure was this: that through flesh the soul should be demonstrated either to itself or to us, when through flesh it could not be recognized; that it should be revealed in this way, by becoming the very thing to which it was hidden—that is, flesh? It received darkness, evidently, so that it might be able to shine [Note: [Col. 0774D] Pam., Rhen., Seml. read *may be able*.].

In any case, let us first reconsider [Note: [Col. 0774D] Rhen., Seml., Oberth. read *for this purpose*.] whether the soul had to be revealed in this manner, or whether they allege that it was previously invisible altogether: whether because it was incorporeal or because it possessed some kind of body of its own. And yet, when they call it invisible, they establish that it is corporeal, possessing something that is invisible. For if it possesses nothing invisible, how can it be called invisible? Indeed, it cannot even exist unless [Note: [Col. 0774D] Others read *nothing*.] it possesses that by which it exists. Since it exists, however, it must necessarily possess something by which it exists. If it possesses [Note: [Col. 0774D] *Possesses* absent from Rhen., Seml.] something by which it exists, this will be its body. Everything that exists is a body of its own kind; nothing is incorporeal except what does not exist.

Since the soul therefore possesses an invisible body, the one who had undertaken to make it visible would surely more fittingly have made visible that body of it which was regarded as invisible. For neither falsehood nor weakness is compatible with God: falsehood, if he showed the soul as something other than what it was; weakness, if he was unable to show what it was. No one wishing to display a man puts a helmet or mask on him. Yet this is what was done to the soul if, after being transformed [Note: [Col. 0774D] Pam., Rhen., Seml. read *having been transformed*.] in flesh [Note: [Col. 0774D] Others read *into flesh*.], it put on [Note: [Col. 0774D] Pam. reads *you put on*.] a foreign exterior.

But even if the soul is judged incorporeal, so that by some abstruse force of reasoning the soul is indeed something, yet whatever the soul is, it is not a body, it was no more impossible for God—and would have accorded more suitably with his purpose—to display it in some new bodily form than in this common form belonging to everyone and already known as something different [Note: [Col. 0774D] “Different.” He used *alterius* for *alius*, that is, “of another kind.” RHENAN.]. Otherwise, he would have desired without cause to make the soul visible from invisible, merely exposing it to those same questions through the interposition of human flesh over it [Note: [Col. 0774D] *Over it* absent from Codex Pithoeanus.].

But Christ could not be seen among human beings except as a human being. Restore to Christ, then, his good faith: since he wished to walk as a human being, he also displayed a soul of human condition—not by making it fleshly, but by clothing it with flesh.

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0775A]

Let the soul now be shown through the flesh, if it is established that it had in some way to be shown [Note: [Col. 0775C] “In what way,” Rhen. Seml.], that is [Note: [Col. 0775D] Unknown to itself and to us. He indicates why the Valentinians said that the soul had to be shown, as though it were unknown: it is equally unknown and in need of being shown. LAC.], unknown to itself and to us. Yet this distinction is empty, as though we existed separately from the soul, [Note: [Col. 0775D] Since the soul is the whole of what we are. It was a doctrine of the Platonists and Pythagoreans that the soul alone is the human being. Thus Plato in the *Alcibiades*, where he proves that the body is not the human being but belongs to the human being, while external things do not belong to the human being but to fortune. Against him Johannes Crispus discusses this question in Book IX of *On the Philosophers of the Gentiles*. Adrianus Sasbout Delphius also refutes that point, in Homily 3 on Genesis, in accordance with Plato’s position. LAC.] when the soul is the whole of what we are. Indeed, without a soul we are nothing, bearing not even the name of a human being, but that of a corpse. [Note: [Col. 0775D] If, therefore, we do not know the soul, it does not know itself. This is true, for the intellective power is in the soul, and the soul cannot be perceived otherwise than by the intellect; material sensation does not attain to a spiritual thing. Hence, if [Col. 0776D] we do not know the soul, neither does the soul know itself. LAC.] If, therefore, we do not know the soul, it does not know itself. Accordingly [Note: [Col. 0775C] “Thus,” Seml.], it remains only to examine whether the soul was here [Note: [Col. 0775C] “Here” is absent from Rhen. Seml.] ignorant of itself, so that it might in some way [Note: [Col. 0775C] “In what way,” Rhen. Seml.] be made known.

I think that the soul’s nature is sentient. Indeed, nothing animate is without sensation, and nothing sentient is without a soul. To put it more emphatically [Note: [Col. 0775C] “More precisely,” Rhen.], sensation is the soul of the soul. Therefore, since the soul enables all things to perceive, and itself perceives even the sensations of all things, [Note: [Col. 0776D] Much more their qualities. By “qualities” he means not what philosophers strictly call mere accidents, but the properties of things, even their essential properties—namely, of what sort and what they are—as he says later of the soul: “If it does not know its own quality.” LAC.] much more their qualities, [Col. 0775B] how [Note: [Col. 0775C] “For whom,” Pam. Fran.] is it likely that it did not from the beginning possess perception of itself? How could it know what is sometimes necessary for it by the necessity of natural things [Note: [Col. 0775D] “By natural necessity,” Pam. Fran. Par.], if it does not know its own quality, for which something is necessary? This indeed may be recognized in every soul: I mean self-knowledge, without which no soul could have governed itself [Note: [Col. 0776C] “By itself,” Fran. Par. Pam.].

But I think all the more that the human being, the sole rational animal, received a soul capable of reason, which makes him [Note: [Col. 0776C] “Which may make him,” Rhen. Seml.] a rational animal because it is itself rational in the first place. Moreover, how can that which makes a human being a rational animal be rational if it does not know its own reason, being ignorant of itself? But so far is it from being ignorant that it knows its author, its judge, and its own condition. Though it has learned nothing yet about God, it names God; though it has yet admitted nothing about his judgment, [Col. 0775C] it says that it commends itself to God [Note: [Col. 0776C] “It has learned,” Rhen. Seml.; “it says,” Ven.]. Though it hears nothing more than that there is no hope after death, [Note: [Col. 0776D] It invokes both good and evil upon every deceased person. To assail the dead with insults was considered cruel and inhuman; hence the familiar sign of respect for the dead, S. T. T. L. (*Sit tibi terra levis*, “May the earth lie lightly upon you”). To wish the earth heavy upon someone was a kind of curse. LE PR.] it invokes both good and evil upon every deceased person. These matters are pursued more fully in the little book we wrote *On the Testimony of the Soul*.

Otherwise, if the soul had been ignorant of itself from the beginning, it ought to have learned nothing from Christ except what sort of thing it was. As matters stand, however, it learns [Note: [Col. 0776C] “Learned,” Rhen. Seml.] from Christ not its own form but salvation. For this reason [Col. 0776A] the Son of God descended and took upon himself a soul—not so that the soul might know itself in Christ, but so that it might know Christ within itself; for it is not by ignorance of itself that its salvation is endangered, but by ignorance of the Word of God. “The Life,” he says (1 John 1:2), “was manifested”—not the soul, and so forth. “I came,” he says (Luke 9:56), “to save the soul”; he did not say, “to show it.”

We were presumably ignorant that the soul, although invisible, is born and dies, unless it were exhibited corporeally. We were certainly ignorant that it would rise again with the flesh. This will be what Christ manifested. Yet he manifested even this in himself no differently than in some Lazarus, whose flesh was not animate in the sense of being made of soul, just as his soul was not fleshly. What more, then, became known to us concerning the previously unknown constitution of the soul? What was invisible in it that required visibility through the flesh?

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0776B]

The soul was made flesh so that the soul might be shown. Was the flesh, then, also made soul so that the flesh might be manifested? If flesh is soul, it is no longer soul but flesh. If soul is flesh, it is no longer flesh but soul. [Note: [Col. 0776D] Where, then, is the flesh, etc.? Tertullian’s sole purpose is to show that in Christ the flesh and the soul were substances of different kinds. LE PR.] Where, then, are flesh and soul, if one has been made the other? Indeed, if neither remains what it is while each becomes the other, it is surely most perverse that, when we name flesh, we should understand soul, and when we signify soul, we should interpret it as flesh. Everything will be in danger of being understood otherwise than it is, and of losing what it is while being understood otherwise, if it is named otherwise than it is. Faithfulness in names safeguards the properties of things.

Even when qualities are changed, things take possession of new names. For example, baked clay receives [Col. 0776C] the name “pottery”; it does not share the name [Note: [Col. 0776C] “With” is absent from Pam. Rig.] of its former kind, because it no longer shares the kind itself. Accordingly, Christ’s soul, if made flesh, cannot fail both to be what it was made and not to be what it had been, since it was made something else. And because we have employed a closely relevant example, we shall use it more fully. Pottery made from clay is certainly one body and has one name—the name, that is, of one body. Nor can it [Note: [Col. 0776D] “Pottery” added by Pam. Rhen.] also be called clay, [Col. 0777A] because what it was, it is not; and what it is not simply [Note: [Col. 0777C] “It is not, and does not adhere; and the soul,” Pam. Rhen.] does not attach to it.

Therefore, if the soul is made flesh, it has one form and is consolidated into one thing: the whole is, of course [Note: [Col. 0777C] “But,” Pam. Rhen.], a single [Note: [Col. 0777C] “Secure,” Pam. Rhen.] and undifferentiated substance. In Christ, however, we find soul and flesh expressed by their plain and unqualified names—that is [Note: [Col. 0777D] Soul as soul, and flesh as flesh. Here he strives for simplicity in order to avoid ambiguity. LE PR.], soul as soul and flesh as flesh; nowhere do we find soul called flesh or flesh called soul, although they ought to have been so named if they had so existed. Indeed, each substance is separately declared by him to be itself [Note: [Col. 0777C] “Declared under,” Pam. Rhen.], plainly [Note: [Col. 0777C] “Everywhere,” Cod. Wouw.] because of the distinction between the two qualities: the soul separately and the flesh separately. “Why [Note: [Col. 0777C] “And” added by Lat.] is my soul distressed,” he says (Matt. 26:38), “even unto death?” And (John 6) [Note: [Col. 0777D] “The bread that I shall give for the salvation of the world.” The objection of certain people is frivolous when they say that the blood was poured out *ἀντὶ πλείστων* (“for many”), not *ἀντὶ πάντων* (“for all”), if this passage is considered. He translates it “for the salvation of the world,” though he should have said “for the life of the world.” LE PR.]: “The bread that I shall give for the salvation of the world is my flesh.”

Moreover, if the soul had been flesh, there would have been one thing in [Col. 0777B] Christ: a fleshly soul or animate flesh. But when he distinguishes the kinds—flesh and soul—he shows two things; if two, then no longer one; if not one, then neither a fleshly soul nor animate flesh, for soul-flesh or flesh-soul is one thing. Unless, indeed, he also bore separately another soul besides the one that was flesh, and carried about another flesh besides the one that was soul. But if there was one flesh and one soul—the latter sorrowful unto death and the former bread for the salvation of the world—the number of two substances is preserved, substances differing according to their respective kinds, and excluding the single kind of a fleshly soul.

## CHAPTER XIV
