But Christ, they say, bore an angel. For what reason? The same reason for which he bore a human being. Then the cause for Christ’s bearing a human being is also the same: the salvation of the human being was the cause, [Col. 0777C] namely, the restoration of what had perished. The human being had perished; the human being had to be restored. [Note: [Col. 0777D] There is no such causal reason for his bearing an angel. That is: there was no reason why he should bear an angel. It must be observed that a hypostatic union, if it is to restore a nature, must occur in that same nature. Irenaeus suggests this reasoning in Book III, chapter 20. LAC.] For Christ to bear an angel there was no such causal reason. For although perdition is also assigned to the angels, in the fire prepared for the devil and his angels, [Note: [Col. 0777D] Nevertheless, restoration was never promised to them. Here he anticipates the Origenists and the more recent demonists, who promise that the demons will someday be restored and have said that Christ suffered for the demons. Hence, although in the preceding words the term “eternal” is absent in connection with their fire, he supplies it here, since restoration was never promised to them. Damascene gives the reasons why the angels are not to be restored in Book II of *On the Orthodox Faith*, chapters 3 and 4; St. Thomas, Part I, question 63, article 2. The theological reason is that what death is to human beings, the fall is to angels; and just as all hope of repentance is taken from human beings after death, so it is taken from angels after the fall. Hence Lactantius, Book VII, chapter 26. LAC.] nevertheless, restoration was never promised to them. Christ received no command from the Father concerning the salvation of angels. [Note: [Col. 0778D] What the Father neither promised nor commanded, Christ could not administer. It is as though he said: Christ had to administer what the Father promised and commanded, so that you may see Christ’s obedience commended. Relevant to this, Clement of Alexandria, Book I of the *Paedagogus*, chapter 12, says that commandments are like divine characters through which power is, as it were, infused for accomplishing something: *χαρακτηρίζεται τὰς* [Col. 0779D] *ἐντολὰς αὐτὰς, τελεῖν δύνασθαι*—“God impresses the commandments themselves as characters, so that we may be able to fulfill them.” LAC.] What the Father neither promised nor commanded, Christ could not [Col. 0778A] administer.

For what purpose, then, did he also bear an angel, unless as a powerful attendant with whom he might accomplish the salvation of the human being? For was the Son of God incapable of liberating by himself the human being who had been cast down by one solitary serpent? Then there is no longer one God or one savior, if there are two makers of salvation, each of course needing the other. Or was it so that he might liberate the human being through an angel? Why, then, did he himself descend to accomplish what he was going to effect through an angel? If through an angel, why was he himself involved? If through himself, why an angel?

He was indeed called the Angel of Great Counsel, that is, its messenger—a title of office, not of nature. For he was going to announce to the world the Father’s great design, namely, concerning the restoration of the human being. Yet he is not therefore to be understood as an angel such as some [Note: [Col. 0777C] “Some” is absent from Par.] Gabriel or Michael. For the son is also sent by the lord of the vineyard to [Col. 0778B] the tenants, just as the servants were, to ask for its fruits. But the son will not therefore be counted as one of the servants merely because he succeeded to the servants’ office. I would more readily call the Son himself, if need be, an angel—that is, the Father’s messenger—than place an angel within the Son.

But since it was declared concerning the Son himself (Ps. 8), “You made him a little [Note: [Col. 0777C] “By a little,” Rhen. Seml.] lower than the angels,” how will he appear to have put on an angel when he was thus lowered beneath the angels by becoming [Note: [Col. 0777D] “By being,” Rig. Ven.] a human being, insofar as he is flesh and soul and the Son of Man? Insofar [Note: [Col. 0778C] “Because,” Rhen. Seml.] as he is the Spirit of God and the power of the Most High (Luke 1), he cannot be regarded as lower than the angels, since he is God and the Son of God. Therefore, to the same extent that he was made lower than the angels by bearing a human being, he did not bear [Note: [Col. 0778C] “Not yet,” Pam. Seml.] an angel.

This opinion might suit Ebion, who maintains that Jesus was a mere man, born only from the seed of David—that is, not [Note: [Col. 0778C] “Born, not likewise,” Pam. Fran.; “not the same,” Seml.] [Col. 0778C] also the Son of God—though plainly somewhat [Note: [Col. 0778C] “In some manner” added by Lat.] more glorious than the prophets, so that an angel [Note: [Col. 0778C] “Among some” added by Fran. Pam.; “angel” [accusative], Rhen. Seml.] might be said [Note: [Col. 0778C] “Might proclaim,” Rhen. Seml.] to have been in him, just as in some Zechariah. Except that Christ never said [Note: [Col. 0778C] “By” omitted by Rhen. Seml.] (Zech. 1), “And the angel who spoke within me said to me”; nor did he use that daily formula of all the prophets, “Thus says the Lord.” For the Lord himself was present, declaring on his own [Note: [Col. 0778D] “And,” Pam. Fran.] authority (cf. Isa. 1), “But I say [Col. 0779A] to you.” What more is needed? Hear Isaiah still crying out (Isa. 63): “Neither an angel nor an envoy, but the Lord himself saved them.”

## CHAPTER XV

Valentinus too was permitted, by the privilege of heresy, to invent a spiritual flesh for Christ. Anyone who refused to believe it human could fashion it into whatever he pleased. For—as was said against them all—if it was not human and not derived from a human being, I do not see from what substance Christ himself [Note: [Col. 0779C] “Himself” is absent from Par.] declared himself [Note: [Col. 0779C] “Himself” is absent from Rhen. Seml.] a human being and the Son of Man (John 8:40): “But now you wish to kill a man who has spoken the truth to you”; and (Luke 6:5), “The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.” Isaiah also says of him (Isa. 53:3): “A man under affliction, and knowing how to bear weakness”; and Jeremiah (Jer. 17): “And he is a man, and who will know [Note: [Col. 0779C] “Has known,” Rhen. Seml.] him?” And Daniel (Dan. 7): “And upon the clouds, as it were, the Son of Man.” The apostle Paul also says (1 Tim. 2), “The mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.” Likewise Peter in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 2): “Jesus of Nazareth, [Note: [Col. 0779D] A man appointed for you by God. The Vulgate has “approved.” The difference arose from Greek copies: some have *ἀποδεδεγμένον*, which the Vulgate renders “approved,” while others have *ἀποδεδειγμένον*, [Col. 0779D] meaning “declared,” “presented,” or “demonstrated”—or, as Tertullian renders it, “appointed.” LAC.] a man appointed for you by God”—certainly a human being.

These statements alone ought to have sufficed, by way of a preliminary rule, as testimony that his flesh was human, taken from a human being, and not spiritual—just as it was neither psychical, nor sidereal, nor imaginary—if heresies could have existed without the studied artifice of controversy. For, as I read in a certain author belonging to Valentinus’s faction [Note: [Col. 0779C] “Nation,” Rig. Ven.; “reason,” Rhen.], they think, first, that an earthly and human [Note: [Col. 0779D] “And human” omitted by Rhen. Seml.] substance was not formed for Christ, lest the Lord should be found inferior to the angels, who did not consist [Note: [Col. 0780C] “May not have consisted,” Rhen.] of earthly flesh; and then, that flesh like ours ought to be born in the same way—not from the Spirit or from God, but from the will of a man. [Note: [Col. 0779D] And why not from corruption? These are the subtleties of the Valentinians that this Alexander had compiled. The question was later revived in the East—namely, whether Christ’s flesh was corruptible or incorruptible—as Count Reginus noted in his letter to Fulgentius, which Ferrandus the Deacon mentions in his *Paraeneticus*. LAC.] And why was it born not from corruption but from incorruption? And why, just as his flesh rose and was taken back into heaven, is ours, which is equal to his, not likewise taken up immediately? Or why was his flesh, equal to ours, not likewise dissolved into the earth?

The Gentiles too will ponder [Note: [Col. 0780C] “And” omitted by Rhen. Seml.; “used to ponder,” Pam. Rhen.] such questions: “Was the Son of God, then, emptied to such a degree of humiliation?” And, “If he rose as an example of our hope, why has nothing of the kind been demonstrated concerning us?” [Col. 0780A] The Gentiles ask such things appropriately—but so, appropriately, do the heretics. For what difference is there between them, except that the Gentiles believe by not believing, while the heretics do not believe by believing? They read, after all (Ps. 8), “You made him a little lower than the angels,” and deny the inferior substance of Christ, who declares himself not a man but a worm (Ps. 21), and who (Isa. 53) “had neither form nor beauty,” but whose “form was without honor, despised [Note: [Col. 0780C] “Defective,” Fran. Pam.] beneath all human beings; a man under affliction and knowing how to bear weakness.” They acknowledge a human being mingled with God, yet deny the human being. They believe he died, yet contend that what died was born from incorruption—as though corruption were something other than death.

“But our flesh too ought to rise immediately.” Wait: Christ has not yet subdued his enemies, so that he may triumph over those enemies together with his friends. [Col. 0780B]

## CHAPTER XVI

Furthermore, through his appetite for argument, in accordance with the heretical cast of his mind, Alexander created an opening for himself, alleging that we affirm that Christ put on flesh of earthly derivation precisely so that he might nullify sinful flesh in himself. Even if we did say this, we would defend our position by some line of reasoning, provided that we avoided the enormous madness he imputed to us—as though we believed that Christ’s very flesh was sinful and was nullified in him. For we remember that it sits at the Father’s right hand in heaven, and proclaim that it will come from there, borne upon the elevation of the Father’s glory. Therefore, just as we cannot [Note: [Col. 0780C] “Could not,” Jun.] call it nullified, neither can we call it sinful; nor was that in which there was no deceit nullified.

[Note: [Col. 0779D] But we maintain. This entire chapter is an apology for the Christians against Alexander’s slanders, since he imputed to them the belief that Christ had possessed sinful [Col. 0780D] flesh. I am surprised that Baronius, under the year of Christ 209, did not understand this chapter, for he attributed to this Alexander a heresy entirely different from the one he held. Rebuking Alexander, he exclaims: “Impiously—what wickedness!—he said that Christ’s flesh had been infected with sin by its origin.” Alexander did not say this; rather, he said that we Catholics said it, in which he was egregiously lying. For this very reason, so that he might not say Christ’s flesh had been infected with sin, he invented a spiritual flesh for him. Nothing else can be gathered from Tertullian. He therefore does two things in this chapter: first, he clears the Catholics of this imposture; second, he explains how Christ’s flesh, although it was indeed ours, was nevertheless not sinful. Accordingly, the chapter title in the old edition, which is obscure and may have deceived Baronius, will be clearer thus: “A Reply on Behalf of the Catholics: That Christ’s True Flesh Was Not Sinful.” LAC., as noted by the EDD.]

But we maintain that what was nullified in Christ was not sinful [Col. 0780C] flesh but the sin of the flesh—not its material but its nature, not its substance but its guilt—in accordance with the Apostle’s authoritative declaration (Rom. 8:3): “He nullified sin in the flesh.” For elsewhere too (ibid.) he says that Christ was “in the likeness of sinful flesh.” This does not mean that he received merely a likeness of flesh, as though it were an image of a body and not its reality. Rather, he wishes us to understand a likeness to sinful flesh: Christ’s flesh, itself not sinful, was equal to the flesh whose [Col. 0781A] sin it was—equal in Adam’s kind, not in Adam’s fault. Hence we also confirm that Christ possessed the flesh whose nature is sinful in a human being, and that sin was thus nullified in that flesh, because in Christ it was possessed without sin, although in a human being it had not been possessed without sin.

For it would have served neither Christ’s purpose in nullifying the sin of the flesh nor his glory if he had not nullified it in the flesh in which the nature of sin existed. What greatness would there have been if, in a better and different flesh—that is, one of a nature not sinful—he had redeemed its blemish [Note: [Col. 0781C] “Bond,” Jun.]?

“Therefore,” you say, “if he put on our flesh, Christ’s flesh was sinful.” Do not force into narrow bounds a meaning that can be explained. For in putting on our flesh, he made it his own; and by making it his own, he made it not sinful. Furthermore—as must be said against all who think that our flesh was not in Christ [Col. 0781B] because it did not come from a man’s seed—let them remember that Adam himself was made in this flesh without a man’s seed. Just as earth was changed into this flesh without a man’s seed, so the Word of God could pass without coagulation into the material of the same flesh.

## CHAPTER XVII

But let us dismiss Alexander, together with the syllogisms he twists about in his arguments, [Note: [Col. 0781D] Together with Valentinus’s psalms. They are mentioned again below in chapter 20: “We too shall have psalms to support this form—not, indeed, those of the apostate, heretical, and Platonic Valentinus,” etc. From the later passage, however, it appears that Valentinus, together with the Nicolaitans and Gnostics—to whom Philastrius attributes this error—did not acknowledge the Psalms of David. Paul of Samosata later imitated them, according to Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chapter 24. He abolished the psalms that were sung concerning the Lord Jesus, as though they were modern and recently invented; but on the days of Easter he ordered women to sing psalms composed by himself in the midst of the church, so that anyone who heard them shuddered. These words have been introduced here so that our modern male and female singers, who perform the psalms of the Marotics rather than those of Christ—and do so with such bellowing that their hearers’ spirits shudder—may recognize whose example they imitate. PAM.] as well as Valentinus’s psalms, which with great impudence he inserts as though they were the work of some competent authority. Let us now direct the encounter toward a single line of engagement: whether Christ received his flesh from the virgin, so that it may be established as human especially in this way, if he drew its substance from a human womb. Although it has already become clear [Note: [Col. 0781C] “It was permissible,” Rhen. Seml.] from his designation as a human being, from the condition of his quality, from the meaning of the discussion, and from [Col. 0781C] the outcome of his suffering, that it was human.

Before all else, however, we must commend the rationale that determined that the Son of God should be born of a virgin. The inaugurator of a new birth had to be born in a new manner—the birth of which the Lord was foretold by Isaiah as about to give a sign. What [Note: [Col. 0781C] “What kind of,” Rig.] is that sign? “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son” (Isa. 7). The virgin therefore conceived and bore Emmanuel, “God with us.” This is the new birth: a human being is born in God, [Col. 0782A] in which human being God was born, [Note: [Col. 0782D] Taking on flesh of the ancient seed without the ancient seed. For although Christ assumed flesh deformed by the stain of sin, he did not put on that deformity; he did not assume sin. Indeed, by that assumption he received it cleansed from its ancient defilements. LE PR.] taking on flesh of the ancient seed without the ancient seed, so that he might reform it by a new seed—that is, spiritually—after excluding and cleansing away the defilements of antiquity.

But this entire novelty, as also in all other things, is patterned after an ancient figure, the Lord being born through a rational dispensation [Note: [Col. 0781C] “Human being” added by Fran. Par. Pam.] involving a virgin. The earth was still a virgin, not yet pressed by labor and not yet subjected to sowing. From it, we have learned [Note: [Col. 0781C] “We learn,” Rhen. Pam. Seml.] that a human being was made by God into a living soul. Therefore, if the first Adam is said to have come from the earth [Note: [Col. 0781C] “Thus” inserted by Par.], it is fitting that the following—or last—Adam, as the Apostle called him, was likewise brought forth by God from earth, that is, from flesh not yet [Note: [Col. 0781D] “Not,” Rhen. Seml.] opened to generation, as a life-giving spirit.

And yet, lest I fail to exploit the argumentative force of the name Adam [Note: [Col. 0782D] Lest I fail to exploit the argumentative force of the name Adam. That is: lest I allow the opportunity of arguing from the name Adam to slip away. By *incursus* he means the force of an argument. RIG.], why was Christ called Adam by the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0782C] “Christ to the same,” Rhen. Seml.; “Christ in place of ‘whence Adam,’” Pam.] [Note: [Col. 0782C] “Apostles,” Lat.] if the manhood belonging to him was not of earthly derivation? [Col. 0782B]

Here too the rationale provides a defense: God recovered by a rival operation his own image and likeness, which had been captured by the devil. For while Eve was still a virgin, the word that constructed death had slipped into her [Note: [Col. 0782D] For while Eve was still a virgin, etc. Eve is here compared with the Most Blessed Virgin. Such antitheses are not unusual among the Fathers: St. Bernard said that Eve was transformed into Mary. Sergius of Hierapolis, speaking of the Virgin’s nativity, said that she was the *ἀνάκλησιν τῆς Ἔυας*, “restoration of Eve.” I shall say no more about a sufficiently familiar matter. LE PR.]; likewise, the Word of God that constructed life had to be introduced into a virgin, so that what had gone [Note: [Col. 0782C] “Might have gone,” Fran. Rig. Ven.] to perdition through that sex might be restored to salvation through the same sex. Eve believed the serpent; Mary believed Gabriel. The transgression that the former committed by believing, the latter erased by believing.

“But [Note: [Col. 0782C] “And” added by Rhen. Seml.] Eve did not then conceive anything in her womb from the devil’s word.” On the contrary, she did conceive. For from that time onward, so that she might bear children as an outcast and bear them in pains, the devil’s word served as seed within her. Indeed, she brought forth the devil, the fratricide. Mary, by contrast, gave birth to the one who would one day save his fleshly brother Israel, his own slayer. God therefore conveyed his Word, the good brother, into the womb, so that he might erase [Note: [Col. 0782D] “Restore,” Rhen.] the memory of the evil brother. Christ had to come forth for the salvation of the human being by the route through which the human being, now condemned, had entered. [Col. 0782C]

## CHAPTER XVIII

Now, to answer more simply, it was not fitting [Col. 0783A] for the Son of God to be born from human seed, lest, if [Note: [Col. 0783C] “Unless,” Rhen.] he were wholly the Son of Man, he should not also be the Son of God and should possess nothing greater than Solomon [Note: [Col. 0783D] And should possess nothing greater than Solomon. He artfully refutes Ebion’s heresy—that Christ was not the Son of God—from Matthew 12: “Behold, something greater than Jonah is here,” and “Behold, something greater than Solomon is here.” He reverses the order, as does Irenaeus, Book III, chapter 29: “For if he were Joseph’s son, how could he possess anything greater than Solomon or anything greater than Jonah?” LAC.], or greater than Jonah, and thus should have to be believed according to Ebion’s opinion.

Therefore, since the Son of God already derived from the Father’s divine seed [Note: [Col. 0783D] God’s seed. Theologians gladly embrace this expression to support their explanation of why the procession of the Holy Spirit is not filiation, whereas the procession of the Word is. They say, namely, that the Word proceeded from the seed of God but the Holy Spirit did not. What is this seed of God? They answer: an intelligible species, or God’s knowledge of himself. But let the Scholastics see to this. Tertullian did not explain it individually, but spoke more generally: “That is, from the Spirit of God.” LAC.]—that is, from the Spirit—so that he might also be [Note: [Col. 0783C] “Also” omitted by Pam. Rhen.] the Son of Man, only his flesh [Note: [Col. 0783C] “That alone which,” Rhen. Seml.] had to be taken from human flesh, without a man’s seed. A man’s seed [Note: [Col. 0783C] “The seed of a man,” Rhen. Seml.] was superfluous for one who possessed the seed of God. Accordingly, just as, before being born of the virgin, he could have God as Father without having a human mother [Note: [Col. 0783C] “Mother” omitted by Rhen.], so also, when he was born of the virgin, he could have a human mother [Note: [Col. 0783C] “Human” omitted by Rhen.] without a human father. Thus, finally, there is a human being together with God, since human flesh is together with the Spirit of God: flesh without seed, from a human being; Spirit with seed, from God.

[Note: [Col. 0783D] Therefore, if there was a rational dispensation, etc. He says this because the Valentinians maintained that Christ the Lord was brought forth through the Virgin and came forth into the world, yet received nothing from her. They are likewise refuted by Origen, Dialogue II, *On Christ the Man*; Irenaeus, Book III, *Against the Valentinians*; Euthymius, Part II of the *Panoply*; and others cited by Canisius, Book III, *On the Mother of God*, chapter 16. LAC.]

Therefore, if there was a rational dispensation for bringing forth the Son [Col. 0783B] of God from the virgin, why did he not receive from the virgin the body that he brought forth from the virgin? “Because what he took from God is something else. For,” they say, “the Word was made flesh” (John 1). This expression bears witness to what was made flesh, yet it is not thereby endangered—as though what was made flesh were immediately something other than the Word. If the Word was made flesh from flesh, or if it was made from the seed itself [Note: [Col. 0783C] “From itself,” Pam. Rig.], let Scripture say so. Since Scripture says only that it was made, and not also from what it was made, it consequently suggests that it was made from something else, not from the seed itself [Note: [Col. 0784C] “From itself,” Par. Rig. Ven.]. If it was not made from the seed itself [Note: [Col. 0784C] “From itself,” Par. Rig. Ven.] but from something else, then infer from this what it is more fitting to believe the Word was made flesh from, unless from the flesh in which it was also made.

Or consider that the Lord himself pronounced, sententiously and definitively (John 3): “What is born in flesh [Col. 0783C] is flesh,” because it was born from flesh. But if he spoke only about a human being and not also about himself, then plainly deny that Christ was a human being, and in that way maintain that this did not apply to him. Yet he adds (ibid.): “And what is born from the Spirit is spirit,” because God is Spirit and he was born from God. This certainly applies to him all the more, [Col. 0784A] even if it also applies to those who believe in him. If, therefore, the latter statement applies to him, why not the former as well? For you cannot divide the text so that the latter applies to him while the former applies to all other human beings, since you do not deny Christ’s two substances, flesh and Spirit.

Furthermore, if he possessed flesh as well as Spirit, then when he makes a declaration concerning the condition of the two substances that he himself also bears, he cannot appear to have determined something concerning his own Spirit but not his own flesh. Thus, since he himself is from the Spirit of God, and the Spirit is God, he himself is God [Note: [Col. 0784C] “And God” is absent from Rhen. Par. Fran. Pam.] born from God; and since he is from human flesh, he is a human being generated in flesh.

## CHAPTER XIX

What, then, does this mean: “Who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God” [Note: [Col. 0784C] “Who was born,” Pam. Rhen.]? I shall rather use this very passage myself, [Note: [Col. 0784D] When I have overthrown its adulterators, etc. The “adulterators” are *κάπηλοι* or *καπηλεύοντες λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ*—“peddlers who adulterate the word of God.” Or he calls the heretics adulterators of Scripture because they corrupted it with the worst interpretations. LE PR.—*Obduxero*, etc.: “I have routed” or “destroyed,” as he uses the term in chapter 46 of the *Apology* and in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*. He often calls those who grossly misused this passage from John to support the Valentinian fantasy “adulterators,” not because they corrupted the wording itself. LAC.] once I have overthrown its adulterators. For they contend that it is written thus: “Who was born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God,” as though it referred to those previously described as believing in his name, so as to show that there exists [Note: [Col. 0784D] That secret seed. He alludes to the Valentinian fantasy concerning the psychical and spiritual seed, which, according to their doctrine, was introduced into the elect by the Demiurge and Achamoth, as he himself relates in chapter 25 of *Against the Valentinians*. They wished the phrase “of God” to signify this seed. Others, however, read “his seed.” LAC.] that [Note: [Col. 0784C] “His,” Rhen. Seml.] secret seed of the elect and the spiritual [Note: [Col. 0784C] “Spiritual,” Par. Fran. Pam.], which they claim for themselves.

But how can it be so, when all who believe in the Lord’s name are born, under the common law of the human race, from blood and from the will of the flesh and of a man—even Valentinus himself? It is so distinctly and individually stated because it was written concerning the Lord: “And he was born of God.” Rightly so, because Christ is the Word of God, and with the Word of God is the Spirit, and in the Spirit of God is power, and Christ is whatever belongs to God. But insofar as he is flesh, he was born neither of blood nor of the will of the flesh and of a man, because the Word was made flesh by God’s will.

For the formal account [Note: [Col. 0784C] “Negation,” Pam. Rhen. Seml.] of our manner of birth pertains to the flesh, not to the Word, because it was the flesh that had to be born in this manner, not the Word. But when he denies that he was born even from the will of the flesh, why did he not also deny that he was born from the substance of the flesh? For by denying that he was born of blood, he did not reject the substance of the flesh, but the material of the seed, which is known to be the heat of the blood, transformed by foaming into a coagulum of the woman’s blood. For in the coagulum used in cheese there is the active power of the substance that it congeals by treating it—that is, of milk.

We therefore understand that what is denied is the Lord’s birth from sexual union, which is what “the will of a man and of the flesh” signifies, not participation in the womb. And why did he press so emphatically and repeatedly that he was born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh or of a man, unless his was the sort of flesh that no one would doubt to have been born from sexual union? Moreover, by denying birth from sexual union, he did not deny birth from flesh; indeed, he confirmed it, because he did not deny birth from flesh in the same way that he denied birth from sexual union.

I ask you: if the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0785C] “Son,” Fran. Par. Pam. Rhen.] of God descended into the womb without intending to receive flesh from the womb, why did he descend into the womb? Spiritual flesh could have been made outside it far more simply than it could be made within the womb yet outside the womb [Note: [Col. 0785C] “Outside the womb” is absent from Fran. Pam.]. Without cause he introduced himself into a place from which he brought nothing out. But he did not descend into the womb without cause; therefore, he received something from it. For if he received nothing from it, he descended into it without cause—especially if he was to become flesh of a quality that did not belong to the womb, namely, spiritual flesh.

## CHAPTER XX
What sort of perversity is yours, that you seek to remove the very syllable *ex* (“from”), where it is employed as a preposition, and prefer to use another expression which, in this connection, is not found in the Holy Scriptures? You say that he was born *through* a virgin, not *from* a virgin; and *in* the womb, not *from* the womb. For the angel also said to Joseph in a dream: “For that which has been born in her,” he says (Matt. 1), “is of the Holy Spirit”; he did not say “from her.” Yet surely, even if he had said “from her,” he had already said “in her”; for that which was from her was in her. [Col. 0785C] Thus, when he says “in her,” it amounts to the same thing and agrees with “from her,” because that which was in her was from her.

But happily the same Matthew, tracing the Lord’s origin from [Col. 0786A] Abraham down to Mary, says: “Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Christ is born.” Paul too silences these grammarians: “God,” he says (Gal. 4:4), “sent his Son, made from a woman.” Does he perhaps say “through a woman,” or “in a woman” [Note: [Col. 0785C] “Woman,” Pamelius, Rhenanus]? Indeed, this is still more emphatic, because he says “made” [Note: [Col. 0785C] “Rather” omitted by Semler] rather than “born”; for he could more simply have stated “born.” By saying “made,” however, he both confirmed that “the Word was made flesh” and affirmed the reality of the flesh made from the virgin [Note: [Col. 0785C] “Made,” Pamelius, Venice].

The Psalms too will support us on this point—not, to be sure, those of Valentinus, the apostate, heretic, and [Note: [Col. 0785C] “And” absent from the Paris edition] Platonist, but those of the most holy and universally accepted prophet David. Among us he sings of Christ, through whom Christ himself sang concerning himself. Receive Christ, and hear the Lord speaking with God the Father [Note: [Col. 0785C] “Receive also David speaking to the Lord,” Rhenanus; “receive Christ and [Col. 0786C] David speaking to the Lord,” Junius] [Note: [Col. 0786C] “Speaking eloquently,” Rhenanus, Semler] (Ps. 21): [Col. 0786B] “For you are he who tore me from my mother’s womb”: there is one statement. “And my hope from my mother’s breasts; upon you I was cast from the womb”: there is another. “And from my mother’s womb you are my God”: there is another [Note: [Col. 0786C] “Otherwise,” Rhenanus, Semler].

Now let us contend over the meanings themselves. “You tore me” [Note: [Col. 0786C] “Me” omitted by Rhenanus, Pamelius], he says, “from the womb.” What is torn away except that which adheres, which is fixed and joined to the thing from which it must be torn in order to be removed? If he did not adhere to the womb, how was he torn away? If the one torn away did adhere, how could he have adhered unless, [Note: [Col. 0785C] “While he is from the womb.” That is, while he belongs to the womb as though a part and portion of it. Rigault] while being from the womb, he was attached through that umbilical cord, as though by a shoot extending from his own membrane [Note: [Col. 0785C] “Through that umbilical cord.” By “umbilical cord” he means the junction of veins and arteries, insofar as their fibers come together and unite at the navel. Rigault.—The umbilical cord is that vein which hangs down into the womb and touches it; that cord is also called the *tradux*, because through it nourishment is conveyed to the fetus. Le Prieur] [Note: [Col. 0785D] “As though by a shoot extending from his own membrane.” By “membrane” he means what Hippocrates or Polybius calls ὑμένα, τὸν περιέχοντα τὴν γονήν, “the membrane enclosing the offspring.” Galen says that by these words the fetal envelope, called χύριον [materially uncertain reading], is described; in Hesychius, Κάλυμμα· τὸ συγγενόμενον ἐκ τῆς κοιλίας, “a covering: that which is generated from the womb.” The Latins called it the *secundinae*, the afterbirth. In these are veins through which, as through conduits, blood is conveyed to the fetus’s navel; and therefore Septimius says that the cord which he calls umbilical is a conduit of the membrane. Servius, on *Georgics* III, notes that *folliculus* means the womb: “‘In the genital field,’” he says, “means in the female membrane, which they call the womb,” as Pliny also teaches. For it was formerly called *folliculus*. Rigault], and joined [Note: [Col. 0786C] “Joined,” feminine form, Rhenanus] to the source in the womb [Note: [Col. 0785D] “Joined to the source in the womb.” I restore the reading of the old manuscripts: “joined to the source in the womb.” The fetus, he says, is called a portion of the mother’s viscera and is understood to be from the womb through that umbilical cord joined [Col. 0786C] to the source in the womb. For the veins and arteries through which blood and vital spirit are carried from the mother to the fetus arise from the veins and arteries of the uterus or womb, whose extremities open into the inner region of the womb. In no other way does communication take place between fetus and mother. [Col. 0786D] These are Galen’s words in his book *On the Formation of the Fetus*: ἡ δὲ ἀρχὴ τῆς γενέσεως τῶν ἀγγείων τούτων ἐστὶν ἐκ τῶν κατὰ τὰς μήτρας ἀρτηριῶν καὶ φλεβῶν, ὧν εἰς τὴν ἐντὸς χώραν τῆς μήτρας ἀναστόμωται τὰ πέρατα· καὶ διὰ τούτων μόνον ἡ κοινωνία τοῖς κυομένοις ἐστὶ πρὸς τὰς κυούσας: “The origin of the formation of these vessels is from the arteries and veins around the womb, whose ends open into the inner region of the womb; and through these alone do the unborn have communication with those who carry them.” Rigault] [Note: [Col. 0786D] “To the source in the womb.” He does not mean the womb’s own origin, but the origin which the umbilical cord takes from the womb. Rigault].

Even when something foreign is glued to another foreign thing, it becomes so incorporated into its flesh and viscera that, when it is torn away, it carries with it something from the body from which it is torn, [Note: [Col. 0786D] “As though some remnant of a ruptured unity.” Septimius speaks well here: “when something foreign is glued to another foreign thing.” For as regards the fetus, physicians deny that it belongs to the mother or womb in such a way that the two coalesce in some part of themselves into a unity. Ψαύει δὲ μήτρας, ἄνευ συμφύσεως, “It touches the womb, but without organic union,” says Galen concerning the fetus. Rigault] as though it were some remnant [Col. 0786C] of a ruptured unity and the offshoot [Note: [Col. 0786D] “And the offshoot of their mutual conjunction.” Thus it is read in Pithou’s manuscript. He uses *produx* in the same way as *tradux* above. He therefore calls the unity produced by mutual conjunction the offshoot of that conjunction. Rigault] [Note: [Col. 0786C] “Conduit,” François and Paris; *traducem*, Pamelius; *producem*, Rhenanus, Semler] of their mutual conjunction.

Moreover, what breasts does he call his mother’s? Without doubt, those from which he drank. Let midwives, [Col. 0787A] physicians, and natural philosophers answer concerning the nature of breasts: do they ordinarily flow in any other way than through the genital activity of the womb, when the veins extending [Note: [Col. 0787C] “Opening,” Latinus; “hanging,” Pamelius, Rhenanus] from it draw off into the breast that cesspool of infernal [Note: [Col. 0787C] “Infernal,” the Wouw manuscript; “internal,” Pamelius, François, Paris] blood [Note: [Col. 0787C] Pamelius and Rhenanus add “into the breast”], and by that very transfer refine it into the more agreeable substance of milk [Note: [Col. 0787C] “Broader,” Rhenanus, Lemnius]? Hence it is that during the period of nursing the monthly flow of blood ceases.

But if the Word became flesh from himself, and not through participation in the womb—if the womb did nothing, performed no function [Note: [Col. 0787C] “Was joined to nothing,” Rhenanus, Semler], and underwent nothing—how did it pour its fountain into the breasts, which it does not alter unless it possesses that fountain? Yet it could not possess blood to supply milk unless it possessed the causes of that blood itself, namely the tearing away of its own flesh.

What was novel in Christ’s birth from a virgin is plain: namely, this alone, that he was born from a virgin, in accordance with the account we have set forth; [Col. 0787B] and that our regeneration might be virginal, spiritually sanctified from every defilement through Christ, who was himself a virgin even carnally, because born from a virgin’s flesh.

## CHAPTER XXI

If, therefore, they contend that the novelty required this—that just as the Word of God did not become flesh from a man’s seed, so neither did he become flesh from a virgin’s flesh—why should the entire novelty not instead be that the flesh, though not born [Note: [Col. 0787C] Pamelius and Rhenanus insert “from”] of seed [Note: [Col. 0787C] Latinus deletes “born”], nevertheless proceeded from flesh? Let them approach [Note: [Col. 0787C] “Let me approach,” Rigault, Venice] still closer [Note: [Col. 0787C] “More commonly,” Rhenanus and the Pithou manuscript] to the encounter. “Behold,” he says, “a virgin shall conceive in the womb.” Conceive what? Surely the Word of God, not a man’s seed [Note: [Col. 0787C] “Seed,” ablative, Rhenanus]; certainly so that she might bear a son. For he says: “And she shall bear a son.” Therefore, just as the conceiving was hers, so what she bore was hers, even though what she conceived did not originate from her.

Conversely, if the Word became flesh from himself, then he conceived himself [Col. 0787C] and bore himself, and the prophecy becomes meaningless. For the virgin neither conceived nor bore if whatever [Note: [Col. 0787D] “What,” Pithou’s manuscript] she bore from her conception of the Word was not her own flesh. Will this declaration of the prophet alone be annulled? Or also that of the angel, who announced the virgin’s conception and delivery? Or indeed every passage of Scripture that calls her Christ’s mother? For how was she his mother, unless he was in her womb? Yet he took nothing from her womb that would make her the mother of the one who was in it. This title is not owed on account of foreign flesh [Note: [Col. 0788C] “To foreign flesh,” Latinus]. The womb is not called a mother’s unless the flesh is the daughter of the womb. But it is not the daughter of the womb if it was born from itself.

Elizabeth, therefore, must also fall silent [Note: [Col. 0788C] “Would have been silent,” Rhenanus, Semler], though she carried the prophet [Note: [Col. 0788C] “Proclaiming,” Rhenanus], the infant already conscious of his Lord, and was herself moreover filled with the Holy Spirit. For she says without cause (Luke 1): “And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me” [Note: [Col. 0788C] “Should come to me,” Rhenanus, Semler]?—if Mary was carrying Jesus in her womb not as a son but as a guest. How does she say, “Blessed [Note: [Col. 0788C] “Happy,” Rhenanus, Semler] is the fruit of your womb”? What sort of fruit of the womb is this which did not sprout from the womb, which did not take root in the womb, which does not belong to her whose womb it is? And who, assuredly, is the fruit of the womb? Christ.

Is it because he himself is [Col. 0788B] the flower from the branch sprung [Note: [Col. 0788C] “Cast forth,” Rhenanus, Rigault, Semler, Venice] from the root of Jesse? The root of Jesse, moreover, is the line of David; the branch from the root is Mary, descended from David; the flower from the branch is Mary’s son, who is called Jesus Christ: he will himself also be the fruit. For the flower is fruit, because through the flower and from the flower every fruit is developed into fruit. What then? Do they deny to the fruit its flower, to the flower its branch, and to the branch its root, so that the root may not, through the branch, claim as its own [Note: [Col. 0788C] “Its own” absent from Rhenanus] the property of that which comes from the branch—the flower and the fruit? For every stage in a lineage is reckoned back from the last to the first, so that they may now know that Christ’s flesh belongs not only to Mary, but also through Mary to David, and through David to Jesse. For this reason [Note: [Col. 0788C] “Belongs to God,” Paris, Rhenanus] God swears to David that he will grant him this fruit from his loins—that is, from the posterity of his flesh—to sit upon his throne. If from David’s loins, how much [Col. 0788C] more from Mary’s loins, on whose account he was in David’s loins!

[Note: [Col. 0787D] “From Mary’s loins.” Here he takes “loins” to mean “womb”; for what is said in Psalm 131, “Of the fruit of your womb I shall place upon your throne,” Peter interprets in Acts 2 as “of the fruit of his loin.” Where the latter has τῆς ὀσφύος, “of the loin,” the former has τῆς κοιλίας, “of the womb.” Yet the expression “of the fruit of the womb” is not without mystery and is contrasted with “loins,” as Irenaeus acutely observes in book III, chapter 27. La Cerda]

## CHAPTER XXII

Let them therefore erase also [Note: [Col. 0787D] “The testimonies of demons.” Pamelius doubts what these testimonies of demons are, since in the Gospel the demons cried out “Son of God” or “Jesus of Nazareth,” never “Son of David.” What if the reading should be “of the blind”? But I alter nothing. To find a way out of the difficulty, Pamelius charges Tertullian with forgetfulness, supposing that he attributed to the demons the words of the Canaanite woman in Matthew 15, “Have mercy on me, Son of David,” because her daughter was demon-possessed. I do not greatly trouble myself over the matter. Since the demons actually cried out “Son of God,” [Col. 0788D] Tertullian could have changed “Son of God” into “Son of David.” Yet, foolish though I may be, I do not refer this to testimonies found in Scripture but to the many found elsewhere, such as that statement of Augustine in *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, book I, chapter 15: “What of the fact that those empty eulogists and covert detractors of the Christian religion do not dare to blaspheme Christ because certain of their philosophers, as Porphyry of Sicily disclosed in his books, consulted their gods as to what answer they should give concerning Christ, and those gods were compelled by their own oracles to praise Christ? Nor is this surprising, since we read in the Gospel that demons confessed him.” For these very gods of the Gentiles were demons, and they praised Christ. Cyprian also indicates the same confession in *On the Vanity of Idols*. And if you wish to embellish this page with many such examples, consult Plutarch, *Why the Oracles Became Silent*. La Cerda] the testimonies of demons proclaiming Jesus the Son of David. But they will not be able to erase the testimonies of the apostles [Note: [Col. 0788D] “Were not able,” Rhenanus, Semler], if those of demons are unworthy [Col. 0789A].

First and foremost, Matthew himself, the most faithful expositor of the Gospel as a companion of the Lord, began as he did for no other reason than to make us acquainted with Christ’s carnal origin: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.” Since the line of descent flows from these sources of origin, and its order is brought down step by step to Christ’s birth [Note: [Col. 0789C] “From Christ’s birth,” Rhenanus], what else is being traced but the very flesh of Abraham and David, propagating its own stock through each successive person down to the virgin and bringing Christ into her—or rather, Christ himself being brought forth [Note: [Col. 0789C] “Produced,” Pamelius, François, Paris] from the virgin?

Paul also, as both disciple and teacher and witness of the same Gospel, and as the apostle of that [Note: [Col. 0789D] “Because,” others] very same [Note: [Col. 0789D] “Same” absent from Rhenanus, Semler] Christ, confirms that Christ was from David’s seed according to the flesh—surely according to Christ’s own flesh. Therefore Christ’s flesh is from David’s seed. But it is from David’s seed according to Mary’s flesh; therefore it is from Mary’s flesh, since it is from David’s seed. Whichever way you twist the statement, either that which is from David’s seed is from Mary’s flesh, or that which is from Mary’s flesh is from David’s seed.

The same apostle ends this entire controversy by defining Christ himself as Abraham’s seed. If Abraham’s, then surely much more David’s, as the more recent ancestor. For, when rehearsing the promise that the nations would be blessed in Abraham’s name—“And in your seed all nations shall be blessed”—he says: “He did not say, ‘And to seeds,’ as referring to many, but ‘to your seed’” [Note: [Col. 0789D] “To the seed,” François, Pamelius], as referring to one, “which is Christ.” We who read and believe these things—what quality of flesh ought we, and can we, acknowledge in Christ? Surely none other than Abraham’s, since Christ is Abraham’s seed; none other than [Col. 0789C] Jesse’s, since Christ is the flower from Jesse’s root; none other than David’s, since Christ is the fruit from David’s loins; none other than Mary’s, since Christ is from Mary’s womb. And, going still farther back, none other than Adam’s, since Christ is the second Adam. It follows, therefore, either that they must contend that those men possessed spiritual flesh, so that the same condition of substance might be transmitted to Christ, or they must concede that Christ’s flesh was not spiritual, since it is not derived from a spiritual stock.

## CHAPTER XXIII

But we recognize the fulfillment of Simeon’s prophetic declaration, pronounced [Col. 0790A] over the Lord while he was still a newborn infant (Luke 2): “Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign which [Note: [Col. 0789D] “To whom,” Pamelius, François] shall be contradicted.” For the sign is Christ’s birth, according to Isaiah: “Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and shall bear a son.” We therefore recognize as the contradicted sign the conception and delivery of the Virgin Mary. Concerning it these Academics say: “She gave birth and did not give birth; she was a virgin and not a virgin”—as though, even if such language had to be used, it would not be more fittingly used by us.

For she gave birth because she did so from her own flesh; and she did not give birth from a man’s [Note: [Col. 0789D] “Male,” Rhenanus, Semler] seed. She was a virgin with respect to a man; [Note: [Col. 0789D] “Not a virgin with respect to delivery.” This is a very grave error. Tertullian falsely said that she was not a virgin with respect to delivery, as he extensively teaches here. Canon III of the Lateran Council under Martin I decreed that the Most Blessed Virgin gave birth without corruption. Le Prieur] she was not a virgin with respect to delivery. Yet not in such a way that she therefore both gave birth and [Note: [Col. 0789D] “Therefore,” Paris, Rhenanus; Pithou’s manuscript reads: “Yet not therefore did she give birth, because [Col. 0790C] she did not give birth from her own flesh, and…”] did not give birth, and [Note: [Col. 0790C] Pithou deletes “did not give birth and”] was therefore both a virgin and not a virgin, because she was not a mother from her own viscera [Col. 0790B].

But with us there is nothing doubtful, nothing twisted into an equivocal defense. Light is light, and darkness darkness; “Yes” is “Yes,” and “No” is “No.” Whatever is more than this is from evil [Note: [Col. 0790D] “Is” absent from Rhenanus, Semler]. She who gave birth gave birth. And if she conceived as a virgin, in her delivery she entered wedlock [Note: [Col. 0790D] Paris and the Ursinus manuscript add “did not”], by the very law of the opened body [Note: [Col. 0789D] “By the very law of the opened body.” He presently recites the law: “Every male that opens the womb,” etc. Rigault]; in this it made no difference whether the same organ of her sex [Note: [Col. 0789D] “That same organ of her sex.” He means the womb. Thus it is read in Ursinus’s book. Rigault] was unsealed [Note: [Col. 0790D] “That is,” Rhenanus, Pamelius] by the force of a male entering or of a male emerging [Note: [Col. 0790D] “Was unsealed,” Pamelius, Rhenanus].

This, finally, is the womb on account of which it is also written concerning others: “Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord.” Who is truly holy but the Son of God [Note: [Col. 0790D] “Of the Holy One,” others]? Who properly opened the womb but he who opened what was closed? In all other cases, marriage opens it. Therefore it was opened all the more because it had been closed all the more. Surely she must be called not a virgin rather than a virgin, since by a certain leap she became a mother before becoming [Col. 0790C] a wife.

And why should this be discussed any further, since for this reason the apostle declared that the Son of God was brought forth not from a virgin but from a woman, because he recognized the nuptial experience of an opened womb? We do indeed read [Note: [Col. 0790D] “In Ezekiel,” etc. Since nowhere in the prophet Ezekiel is there any mention of the words “The cow gave birth and did not give birth,” interpreters rightly doubt how this passage should be explained. Pamelius and others think it refers to what occurs in Job 21: “The cow gave birth and was not deprived of her offspring.” Although these words are not found in Ezekiel’s prophecy, they may have perished, though they were still extant in Tertullian’s time. Or this may have been a certain Ezekiel, a Jewish tragedian, rather than the prophet whose oracle we possess. Le Prieur] in Ezekiel of that cow which gave birth and did not give birth. But take care lest the Holy Spirit, already foreseeing you at that time [Note: [Col. 0790D] “Us now,” Rhenanus, Semler], marked you by this saying as those who would dispute over Mary’s womb. Otherwise, contrary to his own simplicity, he would have spoken doubtfully, although Isaiah says (Isa. 6): “She shall conceive and shall bear.”

## CHAPTER XXIV

For what Isaiah hurls as a taunt against the heretics [Col. 0791A] themselves, especially in Isaiah 5—“Woe to those who make sweet bitter and darkness light”—marks precisely those who do not preserve even these terms in the clear light of their proper meanings: so that the soul is no other thing than what is so called, the flesh no other thing than what is seen [Note: [Col. 0791B] “Is other than what is seen,” Pamelius], and God no other than he who is proclaimed.

Thus, also foreseeing Marcion, he says (Isa. 45): “I am God, and there is no other apart from me.” And when elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0791B] “In” absent from Rhenanus, Semler] [Note: [Col. 0791C] “At other times,” François, Pamelius] he says the same thing in the same manner—“Before me there was no God”—he strikes at those genealogies of Valentinian Aeons, whatever they may be. And the statement, “He was born not from blood, nor from the will of the flesh or of man, but from God” (John 1), answered Ebion. Likewise: “Even if an angel from heaven [Note: [Col. 0791C] “From the heavens,” Rhenanus, Semler] should preach to you a gospel other than ours, let him be anathema” (Gal. 1), directs its thread [Note: [Col. 0791C] “Son,” Pamelius, Rhenanus] against the possessed Apelleian virgin [Col. 0791B] Philumene.

Certainly, “He who denies that Christ has come in the flesh is antichrist” (1 John 4). By pronouncing “flesh” nakedly, absolutely, and by the simple name of its nature, he strikes all who dispute about it. So too, by defining Christ himself as one, he smites those devisers of a multiform Christ [Note: [Col. 0791C] “Multiform Christs,” François], who make one person Christ and another Jesus; one who slipped away from the midst of the crowds and another who was detained; one who, in the mountain’s solitude and the cloud’s enclosure, shone gloriously before three witnesses, and another who was exposed to suffering before the rest and was without distinction; one who was magnanimous and another who trembled; finally, [Col. 0792A] one who suffered and another who was raised. By this means they also assert that he was raised in a different flesh.

But happily the same one who suffered will come from heaven; the same one who was raised will appear to all. “And those who pierced him shall see and recognize him” (Zech. 11; John 19)—surely the very flesh against which they raged, without which he could neither be himself nor be recognized. Thus let those also be put to shame who affirm that the flesh sits in heaven devoid of sensation, like a sheath after Christ has been drawn from it; or those who affirm flesh and soul in equal measure, or only the soul, but no longer the flesh.

## CHAPTER XXV

But enough thus far concerning the present subject. For I now consider the proof concerning the flesh in Christ—both that it was born from the virgin and that it was human—to have been established [Col. 0792B]. The discussion of this point alone could have sufficed, [Note: [Col. 0792B] Rhenanus and Semler insert “but”] without an encounter with the several opposing opinions; yet we challenged them as well, superabundantly, through their own arguments and through the Scriptures they employ, so that, by proving what Christ’s flesh was and whence it came, and what it was not, we might have settled the question against them all [Note: [Col. 0792B] “Might have proclaimed,” Paris; “might have guarded against,” Rigault, Leopold, Venice].

But in order that the resurrection of our flesh—which must be defended in another treatise—may form the conclusion [Note: [Col. 0792C] “Conclusion,” nominative, Rhenanus, Semler] to this common preface [Note: [Col. 0792C] “Our” absent from Rhenanus, Semler], it will here receive its preliminary foundation [Note: [Col. 0791C] “But in order that the resurrection of our flesh may form the conclusion to this common preface.” This conclusion corresponds to the words read in the preface to the present work: “Those who endeavor to disturb faith in the resurrection naturally also rend Christ’s flesh with their questions.” Rigault], since it is now manifest what it was that rose [Note: [Col. 0792C] “Should have risen,” Rhenanus, Semler] in Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0792C] (d) “Since it is now manifest.” “Being” is understood, as in the Greek δήλου ὄντος, “it being manifest.” Rhenanus]

[Col. 0791]

# QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN  
## ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE FLESH (C)

## SUMMARY

—Preparing to write on the resurrection of the flesh, the author first teaches that it was not unknown even to the secular world, and especially to Platonists and Pythagoreans. Chapter I.

Although the heretics do not acknowledge it, any more than the Sadducees do, they are nevertheless refuted both by the preceding book, *On the Flesh of Christ*, and, concerning God as the author of the flesh and Christ as the redeemer of the flesh, by the books written *Against Marcion*. For they do not deny the resurrection of the soul, with the sole exception of Lucanus; against him the author defended the soul’s immortality in the book *On the Soul*. Chapter II.

Accordingly, the heretics ought not to follow the common people’s ignorance in denying it. Chapter III.

[Col. 0792D] Nor does the indignity of the flesh, which they allege, stand in the way. Chapter IV.

First, because it was made by God. Chapter V.

Likewise, because it was fashioned by God’s hand. Chapter VI.

Because clay has already been refashioned and transformed into flesh. Chapter VII.

Because among Christians the flesh is washed, anointed, signed, overshadowed by the laying on of hands, and fed with the body and blood of Christ; and finally, after the soul’s struggles, fasts, virginity, and widowhood, it dies for faith in Christ’s name. Chapter VIII.

Because Christ loved the flesh, though weak and sinful. Chapter IX.

[Col. 0793A] Finally, because the flesh is honored in the Scriptures. Chapter X.

Nor does the resurrection of the flesh exceed God’s power. Chapter XI.

For examples of divine power are found in the alternations of day and night, winter and summer, spring and autumn. Chapter XII.

There is also the phoenix, the bird of the East, which renews itself by conducting its own funeral. Chapter XIII.

Moreover, an adequate ground for restoring the flesh is found in God’s judgment, which rewards good and punishes evil. Chapter XIV.

For since soul and flesh share partnership in their works, they must also share the recompense either of punishment or of grace. Chapter XV.

Although the flesh is called the vessel of the soul, [Col. 0793B] it does not follow that it does not also share in the soul’s merits. Chapter XVI.

Indeed, since the soul’s deeds are performed through the flesh, it is not sufficient for the soul to be comforted or tormented without the flesh for works done by means of the flesh. Chapter XVII.

Next, God’s decree is displayed before everyone: the resurrection of the dead. Chapter XVIII.

Some wrongly twist this into a figurative meaning. Chapter XIX.

For the prophets did not proclaim everything through figures: first, because if everything is a figure, what will remain as the reality of which these things are figures? Second, because all the more notable prophecies were fulfilled in Christ himself more clearly than daylight—truly, not figuratively. Chapter XX.

There are also so many divine instruments attesting bodily [Col. 0793C] resurrection so openly that they admit no suspicion of figurative meaning. Chapter XXI.

Finally, attention must be paid to those Scriptures which do not permit the belief that the resurrection has either already occurred or takes place immediately upon departure from this life. Chapter XXII.

Although the apostle says to the Colossians that we have been spiritually raised, he nevertheless does not deny that we shall also rise bodily. Chapter XXIII.

For in his own epistles to the Thessalonians he openly confirms the resurrection. Chapter XXIV.

Likewise, in John’s Apocalypse the very times of the resurrection are indicated. Chapter XXV.

What then? Bodily resurrection may also be vindicated with the support of figurative prophetic language. Chapter XXVI.

[Col. 0793D] This is done under the names both of land and of garments. Chapter XXVII.

Indeed, the resurrection was prophesied not only through words but also through things and deeds. Chapter XXVIII.

Finally, Ezekiel’s determination concerning it is exceedingly plain. Chapter XXIX.

And it is such that it cannot be understood figuratively or allegorically. Chapter XXX.

It is also proved by other manifest testimonies of the prophets. Chapter XXXI.

These are of such a kind that even the resurrection of unburied bodies is proclaimed in them. Chapter XXXII.

Moreover, in the Gospels the Lord did not pronounce everything in parables. Chapter XXXIII.

Indeed, in every mention of the resurrection the Lord properly signifies the bodily nature [Col. 0794A] of the flesh; and the whole human being whom the devil wholly struck down is to be raised by God. Chapter XXXIV.

Both body and soul are distinctly presented as destined either for Gehenna or for eternal life. Chapter XXXV.

Hence the Sadducees’ doctrine is turned completely upside down. Chapter XXXVI.

Although Christ does say that the flesh profits nothing, the sense must be determined from the subject matter of the statement. Chapter XXXVII.

Especially since, by raising the dead in deed as well, he signified the future resurrection. Chapter XXXVIII.

The documentary accounts of the Acts of the Apostles also testify to the resurrection. Chapter XXXIX.

Accordingly, the heresies wrongly interpret for their own purposes, in their customary fashion, the “inner” and “outer” human being, as though by “corruption” the apostle meant the decay of the outer flesh. Chapter XL.

They likewise misinterpret the statement concerning the house of our tabernacle which is dissolved. Chapter XLI.

But corpses are merely changed, not devoured by death, since the skeletons of the most ancient giants still survive, as the author has also said elsewhere. Chapter XLII.

Nor does absence from the body support their case, because the apostle adds that each person must receive through the body according to what he has done, whether good or evil. Chapter XLIII.

Likewise, because he says that the life of Jesus is to be manifested in the body. Chapter XLIV.

In another manifestation of blindness, they also stumble over the old and new [Col. 0794C] human being. Chapter XLV.

Similarly, when the same apostle appears to condemn the flesh, he condemns the works of the flesh. Chapter XLVI.

For he promises salvation to the flesh. Chapter XLVII.

Finally, in 1 Corinthians 15 the resurrection of the flesh is most plainly confirmed by him. Chapter XLVIII.

Indeed, from the preceding discussion one learns in what condition he disinherited flesh and blood from God’s kingdom—namely, as the works of the flesh. Chapter XLIX.

Indeed, even setting aside interpretations of this sort, the very substances of flesh and blood, understood just as they are, may be vindicated for the resurrection. Chapter L.

The same point may also be proved through Christ, who carried flesh and blood with him into heaven. Chapter LI.

And indeed the apostle argues that the dead will return in the same body. Chapter LII.

For the “animate body” cannot be understood as the soul, but as the flesh. Chapter LIII.

Nor, as he touched upon above, is the flesh itself devoured by life, but that which is mortal in it. Chapter LIV.

Furthermore, the transformation of the flesh is one thing; its destruction is another. Chapter LV.

Otherwise it would be absurd for one substance—namely the flesh—to perform the work, and another—namely the soul—to receive payment of the reward. Chapter LVI.

The resurrection must also be believed to be complete, as the Scriptures affirm. Chapter LVII.

Thus both flesh and soul will undergo the sentence of salvation or punishment. Chapter LVIII.

[Col. 0795A] In the age to come the constitution of the human being will not differ in substance. Chapter LIX.

The human being will also rise with sex and members preserved, even though these are free from their customary functions necessary to life. Chapter LX.

This is especially so since certain functions of those members—by which we praise God and prophesy—will remain; even in this life those who fast abstain from food, while voluntary eunuchs and virgins wedded to Christ withdraw their sex from procreation. Chapter LXI.

Finally, we shall become not angels, but like God’s angels. Chapter LXII.

Therefore the conclusion is that the flesh will rise—indeed, all of it; indeed, the selfsame flesh; indeed, the whole of it. Chapter LXIII.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0795B]

[Note: [Col. 0795C] “The confidence of Christians,” etc. That the resurrection afforded great hope and [Col. 0795D] confidence to all Christians in the early days of the Church, and that this was also demonstrated by blessed Paul, is evident. St. Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* XVIII: ῥίζα τῆς ἀγαθοεργίας ἡ τῆς ἀναστάσεως ἐλπίς, “The hope of the resurrection is the root of every good work”; and St. Epiphanius in the *Ancoratus*: πάντος σώφρονος λογισμοῦ κρηπίς, “the foundation of every sound thought.” The Gentiles therefore considered nothing more urgent than overthrowing that confidence and foundation. Le Prieur]

The confidence of Christians is the resurrection of the dead. By believing it [Note: [Col. 0795C] “It,” Pamelius], we are believers. Truth compels belief in it. God reveals the truth; but the common people ridicule it, supposing that nothing survives after death. Yet [Note: [Col. 0795D] “They perform rites for the dead, and indeed with most lavish observance.” This refers to pagans. But book VIII, chapter 27, of the holy Augustine’s *City of God* shows that in his time Christians in certain places also practiced such customs. They brought their feasts to the memorial shrines of the martyrs, prayed and presented food for them to eat, or else distributed some of it to the needy. “This,” he says, “is not done by the better Christians, and in most regions no such custom exists.” Rigault] they perform rites for the dead, and indeed with the most lavish observance, adapting the food to their customs and its seasons; thus, though they deny [Note: [Col. 0795C] “He denies,” Rhenanus] that the dead perceive anything, they presume that they desire food [Note: [Col. 0795C] “Even,” Pamelius, Rhenanus, Semler] [Note: [Col. 0795C] “He presumes,” Rhenanus].

But I shall laugh at the common people still more [Note: [Col. 0795C] “I laugh,” others], since they first burn those very dead with the utmost savagery and afterward feed them with the utmost gluttony, both winning their favor and offending them with the same fires. O piety that makes sport of cruelty! When it burns offerings for the cremated dead, does it sacrifice or [Note: [Col. 0795C] “Whom,” others] insult?

[Note: [Col. 0795D] “When it burns offerings for the cremated.” That is, when it sacrifices to the dead. He uses words which display the custom in a more ridiculous light. Rigault]

Certainly, even the wise sometimes join their opinion [Note: [Col. 0795C] “Their” absent from Rhenanus] to that of the common people. The doctrine that there is nothing after death belongs to the school of Epicurus. [Note: [Col. 0796C] Seneca too says: “Everything ends after death, even death itself.” He has already noted this in the book *On the Soul*; likewise in the *Troades*, chorus XI: “After death there is nothing, and death itself is nothing.” Rigault] Seneca too says that everything [Col. 0795C] ends after death, even death itself.

It is enough, however, that no lesser philosophy belongs to Pythagoras and Empedocles. The Platonists too, on the contrary, loudly proclaim the soul immortal [Note: [Col. 0795C] “And” absent from Rhenanus]; indeed, coming still nearer, they even affirm that it can return into bodies [Col. 0796A], though not into the same bodies and not into human bodies alone, so that Euphorbus is reported to have passed into Pythagoras and Homer into a peacock. Certainly they pronounced the soul’s return to be bodily; it was more tolerable that they should alter [Note: [Col. 0796C] “Leave unaltered,” others] its condition than deny it.

[Note: [Col. 0796D] “At least knocking upon truth, although not entering it.” Latinus approved this reading. But it seems preferable to retain the common reading, “knocking upon salvation.” For it both suits Septimius’s style and is confirmed by the authority of the old manuscripts. The Platonists, defenders of the immortality of souls, knocked at salvation’s door, but because they were ignorant of the quality and manner of immortality, they did not enter into truth. Rigault]

They at least knocked upon truth [Note: [Col. 0796C] “Salvation,” Rhenanus, Pamelius], even though they did not enter [Note: [Col. 0796C] “Add to,” Rhenanus, Semler] into it. Thus the secular world is not ignorant of the resurrection of the dead, even when it errs concerning it.

## CHAPTER II
[Note: [Col. 0796D] “But if there is also some sect with God.” That is, among the Jews or Christians—that is, in the sacred Scriptures. So in the book *On the Testimony of the Soul*: “And although Christians alone know him, or whatever sect belongs to the Lord.” RIG.] But if there is also some sect with God that is more closely allied to the Epicureans than to the prophets, we shall learn what the Sadducees hear from Christ. For it was reserved for Christ to lay bare all that had previously been hidden, to set doubtful matters straight, to complete what had been anticipated, and to present anew what had been foretold—in particular, to prove the resurrection of the dead, not only through himself [Col. 0796B] but also in himself.

Now, however, [Note: [Col. 0796D] Against other Sadducees. These are mentioned frequently. The Sadducees denied the resurrection and immortality of the soul and were a Jewish sect; here Marcion, Apelles, Valentinus, Basilides, Saturninus, and others are indicated as different Sadducees. LE PR.] we are preparing ourselves against other Sadducees, who share their opinion. Thus they acknowledge only half a resurrection, namely, that of the soul alone, having rejected the flesh just as they rejected the Lord of the flesh himself. Indeed, none begrudge salvation to bodily substance except heretics who profess another divinity. For this reason they were also compelled to arrange Christ differently, lest he be regarded as the creator of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0796C] The Wouwer and Ursinus manuscripts read “be regarded as belonging to the Creator.”]; and they first went astray concerning his very flesh: either by contending, with Marcion and Basilides, that it possessed no reality, or, according to the heresies of Valentinus and Apelles, that it possessed a quality peculiar to itself. It follows accordingly that they exclude from salvation the substance whose fellowship with Christ [Note: [Col. 0796C] “Fellowship with Christ” is absent from Rhenanus.] they deny, being sure [Note: [Col. 0796C] “Surely,” Rigault and Venice.] that the flesh would be furnished with the supreme presumption in favor of resurrection if flesh had already risen [Col. 0796C] [Note: [Col. 0796C] “Had risen,” Rhenanus and Semler.] in Christ.

For this reason we previously issued the treatise *On the Flesh of Christ*, in which we prove that it is both substantial, against the emptiness of a phantom [Note: [Col. 0796C] “Nativity,” Franecker and Pamelius.], [Note: [Col. 0796D] “And we vindicate it as human against,” etc.—that is, in the book *On the Flesh of Christ* [Col. 0797D], in which he proved against Marcion that Christ’s flesh was real. Apelles and Valentinus acknowledged real flesh, but not human flesh: they fabricated a flesh that was astral, heavenly, or animate. LE PR.] and human, against the peculiarity ascribed to its quality; [Col. 0797A] its constitution [Note: [Col. 0797C] Others read “publication.”] entitled Christ both “man” and “Son of Man.” For by proving him fleshly and bodily, we likewise [Note: [Col. 0797D] “We likewise overcome.” *Obducere* means “to prevail over,” as shortly afterward, “then overcome concerning God” (for so we have punctuated it, as the sense requires), meaning “convicted.” RHEN.] overcome them through the preliminary rule that no other God is to be believed besides the Creator, since we show Christ—in whom God is recognized—to be such [Note: [Col. 0797C] Venice reads the neuter “such.”] as the Creator promised.

Once they have been overcome concerning God, the author of the flesh, and concerning Christ, the redeemer of the flesh, they will then also be convicted concerning the resurrection of the flesh. Appropriately so, of course [Note: [Col. 0797C] Rhenanus and Pamelius add again: “concerning God, the author of the flesh, and concerning Christ, the redeemer of the flesh.”]. And this is approximately the method by which, we say, the dispute with heretics must be undertaken. For proper order always demands that one proceed from first principles, so that agreement may first be reached concerning the one by whom the matter under inquiry is said to have been ordained.

Indeed, heretics, conscious of their weakness, never conduct their argument in an orderly fashion. For they know how much difficulty they have in introducing another divinity [Col. 0797B] in opposition to [Note: [Col. 0797D] “The God of the world, known naturally.” This conviction has adhered so firmly to the minds of all people that the Athenians burned a book by a certain sophist Pythagoras because it began with the question, “Does God exist?” Similarly, when the founder of the University of Cambridge was once passing through that place and heard theologians debating whether God exists, he regretted having founded that university, in which a matter clear by natural knowledge was still being doubted. LE PR.] the God of the world, who is naturally known to everyone from the testimony of his works, who is certainly prior in the mysteries and more manifest in the proclamations. Under the pretext that a more urgent question must be investigated before all others—namely, human salvation itself—they begin with questions concerning the resurrection, because the resurrection of the flesh is harder to believe than the unity of the Godhead. Thus, after stripping the argument of the strength supplied by its proper order and burdening it instead with objections that depreciate the flesh, they gradually [Note: [Col. 0797C] Franecker and Pamelius insert “toward.”] dispose the mind toward another divinity by shaking and altering its very hope.

For anyone who has been cast down or displaced from the level of the hope he had received from the Creator is thereafter easily turned even to suspect, of his own accord, an author of another hope [Note: [Col. 0797C] “Beyond,” Pamelius and Franecker.]. A diversity of gods is insinuated through a diversity of promises. Thus we see many caught in the net when they are refuted concerning the resurrection of the flesh before they are refuted concerning the unity of the Godhead.

So far as the heretics are concerned, therefore, we have demonstrated what wedge we must use against them [Note: [Col. 0797C] “What course we must run,” Rhenanus and Semler.]; and the encounter has already taken place [Note: [Col. 0797C] “Even,” Rhenanus and Semler.] under its own appropriate title: concerning the one God and his Christ, against Marcion; and concerning the Lord’s flesh, also against the four heresies. This was done especially to prepare the ground for the present question, [Col. 0798A] so that I might now arrange the discussion solely concerning the resurrection of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0797D] “So that it may thus have to be arranged,” Pamelius and Franecker.] as though it were uncertain among us, while it is nonetheless certain [Note: [Col. 0798C] Franecker and Pamelius read: “as though these matters were also uncertain among us.”] with the Creator.

For there are many who are uninstructed, and very many who are doubtful and simple in their faith; there are more whom it will be necessary to instruct, direct, and fortify, because on this flank too the unity of the Godhead will be defended. For just as that unity is shaken when the resurrection of the flesh is denied, so it is established when the resurrection is vindicated.

The salvation of the soul, however, I believe requires no reconsideration. Almost all heretics, however [Note: [Col. 0798C] “In what manner,” Rhenanus.] they may wish [Note: [Col. 0798C] “They wish,” Rhenanus and Pamelius.] to conceive it, nevertheless do not deny it. Let some solitary Lucanus look to himself, for he spares not even this substance: dissolving it in accordance with Aristotle, he substitutes something else for it, as though some third thing [Note: [Col. 0798C] “As though it were a third thing” is absent from Rhenanus.] were to rise again—neither soul nor flesh, that is, not a human being, [Note: [Col. 0798D] “But perhaps a bear, since he is Lucanian.” He ridicules the Marcionite heretic Lucanus. For “bear” is a Lucanian word, that is, a word from the province of Lucania, now called Basilicata. LE PR.—This is an allusion to the name of the people (*lykos*, λυκὸς, “wolf”). RHEN.] but perhaps a bear, since he is Lucanian [Note: [Col. 0798C] “As though,” Rhenanus and Semler.].

He too has from us [Col. 0798B] a most comprehensive treatise concerning every condition of the soul. In it we defend above all the soul’s immortality, while recognizing [Note: [Col. 0798D] “The dissolution of the flesh alone.” That is, death. RIG.] the dissolution of the flesh alone and now especially asserting [Note: [Col. 0798D] “And its restoration.” That is, resurrection. RIG.] its restoration. We have brought the subject matter into orderly form, although elsewhere, when occasioned by particular issues, we touched briefly upon [Note: [Col. 0798C] “Discussed,” Franecker and Pamelius.] certain points and postponed them. For just as it is customary to anticipate certain matters, so it is necessary to postpone them, provided that what has been anticipated is completed in its proper body and what has been deferred is presented under its proper title.

## CHAPTER III

It is indeed possible to reason about divine matters even [Note: [Col. 0798D] “From common conceptions.” Common conceptions are *koinai ennoiai* (κοίνοι ἔννοαι), or notions approved by the perception and agreement of almost everyone. LE PR.] from [Note: [Col. 0798C] “From” is omitted by Rhenanus and Semler.] common conceptions—but as testimony to truth, not as assistance to falsehood; only when a conception accords with the divine ordering, not when it opposes it. Some things are known even by nature, such as the immortality of the soul among most people and our God among everyone.

[Note: [Col. 0798D] “I shall therefore also use the opinion of some Plato.” This must undoubtedly be understood of every rational soul, for it is of that soul that Plato speaks both in the *Phaedo* and elsewhere whenever he declares the soul immortal. PAM.] [Col. 0798C] I shall therefore use the opinion of some Plato who declares: “Every soul is immortal.” I shall also use the consciousness of the people, who invoke “the God of gods.” I shall use the other common conceptions too, which proclaim God as judge: “God sees”; and, “I commend it to God.”

But when they say, “What is dead is dead”; and, “Live while [Note: [Col. 0798C] “While one must live,” the Pithoean manuscript and Rhenanus.] you live”; and, “After death all things come to an end—even death itself,” then I shall remember both that God has reckoned the heart of the common people as ashes [Col. 0799A] and that the wisdom of the world itself has been declared foolishness.

Then, if [Note: [Col. 0799C] “And” is absent from Rhenanus and Semler.] a heretic should take refuge in the vices of the crowd or the cleverness of the world, I shall say: “Depart from the pagan, heretic!” Even though all of you who fabricate God [Note: [Col. 0799C] Others read “flee from God.”] are one, nevertheless, because you do this in Christ’s name and regard yourself as a Christian, you are different from the pagan. Give him back his own conceptions, since he is not instructed from yours either. Why lean upon a blind guide, if you can see [Note: [Col. 0799C] “If you seem to see,” Rhenanus and Semler.]?
