Why are you clothed by a naked man, if you have put on Christ? Why do you use another’s shield, if you have been armed by the Apostle? Let him instead learn from you to confess the resurrection of the flesh, rather than you learning from him to deny it. For even if [Note: [Col. 0799C] “Even” is absent from Franecker and Pamelius.] Christians were obliged to deny it, it would be enough for them to be instructed from their own knowledge, not from the ignorance of the crowd.

Accordingly, anyone who denies what Christians confess will not be a Christian, and [Col. 0799B] he will deny it with the arguments used by one who is not a Christian [Note: [Col. 0799C] Others read “which non-Christians use.”]. Finally, take away [Note: [Col. 0799C] “You take away,” Rhenanus and Semler.] from the heretics the opinions they share with pagans [Note: [Col. 0799C] “Whatever pagans think,” Rhenanus and Junius.]; make them present [Note: [Col. 0799C] “Construct,” Latinius.] their questions from the Scriptures alone, and they will be unable to stand.

For common conceptions are commended by their very simplicity, by the mutual sympathy of their judgments [Note: [Col. 0799C] “Mutual sympathy of judgments”: namely, among those who share a common interest through a common opinion. Conversely, in the book *On the Veiling of Virgins* [Col. 0799D], he begins by saying that his own opinions have now become a matter of personal concern to him. RIG.], and by the familiarity of their opinions. They are consequently considered more trustworthy because the things they affirm are plain, open, and known to everyone.

## CHAPTER IV

Heretics therefore begin from this point at once and from it lay their foundation; they then build into their argument those considerations by which they know minds are easily captured, drawing upon the favorable agreement of common conceptions.

[Note: [Col. 0799D] “Would you hear anything else first,” etc. The heretics against whom Tertullian is arguing said that our flesh was evil because it had been made by an evil god. So too did the pagans: according to Epiphanius in the *Anchored One*, the Epicureans and other philosophers launched many attacks upon our flesh and generation, as is evident from Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* III, and Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God* III. LAC.] Would you hear anything else sooner or more often from a heretic than from a pagan? [Note: [Col. 0799C] “As” is absent from Rhenanus.] Do you not immediately and everywhere hear abuse of the flesh—of its origin, its material, its fall [Note: [Col. 0799C] Others read “cause.”], and its every end? It is unclean from the beginning, from the dregs of the earth; more unclean thereafter, from the mire of its own seed [Col. 0799C]; [Note: [Col. 0799D] “Paltry,” on account of nakedness, because an infant comes forth not with a natural covering, as other animals do, but naked and trembling. Sidonius discusses this excellently in Book VII, Epistle 4, and Lactantius in *On the Workmanship of God* III.5. LAC.] paltry, weak, guilty, burdensome, [Col. 0800A] troublesome; and, [Note: [Col. 0799D] “After the whole catalogue of its ignobility.” That is, its enumeration. *Elogium* may be used in both a favorable and an unfavorable sense. Thus below: “Religion, exposed to public hatred and a hostile indictment.” RHEN.] after the entire catalogue of its ignobility [Note: [Col. 0800C] “Illogium,” Junius.], destined to fall back into the earth from which it sprang [Note: [Col. 0800C] “Earthly,” Junius.], to receive the name “corpse,” and [Note: [Col. 0799D] “Destined to perish even from this name.” After the corruption of our corpse, no appointed name remains by which the matter that had constituted a human body may be designated. [Col. 0800C] He calls this the death of the word, for a corpse passes away into earth or into other animals. LAC.] thereafter to perish even from that name into no name at all, [Note: [Col. 0800C] “Into the death now of every word.” The dead cease to be whatever they were called while alive and are now nothing. Pliny, *Natural History* XI, where he treats the nature of earth. RIG.] into the death of every designation?

Do you therefore wish, wise man, to persuade yourself [Note: [Col. 0800C] “To be persuaded,” Junius and Rhenanus.] that this flesh, though snatched from your sight, touch, and memory, will one day recover itself—whole from corruption, solid from dissolution, full from emptiness, indeed something from nothing at all? And this despite the fires and waters, the bellies of beasts, the crops of birds, the stomachs [Note: [Col. 0800C] “Castings,” Semler.] of fish, [Note: [Col. 0800D] “And even the peculiar appetite of the times themselves.” He alludes to the gluttonous cruelty and cruel appetite of Vedius Pollio, who plunged condemned slaves into ponds of lampreys—not only so that he could watch an entire person torn apart at once, as Pliny reports, but also so that he could eat human flesh in the fish, as Tertullian teaches in *On the Pallium*: “I likewise plunge the knife,” he says, “into the cruelty with which Vedius Pollio exposed slaves to the attacks of lampreys. A novel cruelty indeed! Delighting in an earthly beast that had small teeth and no claws or horns, he decided to turn fish into wild beasts—fish, of course, that were to be cooked immediately, so that he himself might taste in their entrails something of his servants’ bodies.” Thus there. He therefore says here not without reason, “and even their own peculiar appetite giving back”—supply, “what it had devoured of human flesh.”] and the peculiar appetite even of the times themselves [Note: [Col. 0800C] “Of the times” is absent from Rhenanus.] having to give it back?

But will precisely the same flesh that perished be hoped for, so that the lame, the one-eyed, the blind, the leprous, and the paralytic may return, making it disagreeable to have returned to their former condition? Or will they return whole, only to fear suffering such things again? [Col. 0800B] What then of the flesh’s attendant consequences? Will all its necessities return as well—especially food and drink, the lungs having to swim, the bowels to boil, the private parts to know no shame, and all the members to labor? Again ulcers and wounds, fever and gout [Note: [Col. 0800C] “And gout” is absent from Rhenanus.], and death to be desired once more [Note: [Col. 0800C] Others read “desired again.”]? Surely these will be the aspirations of recovered flesh: to desire once more to escape from it.

We, to be sure, express these things somewhat more decently out of regard for literary propriety. Yet how much filthy speech from both pagans and heretics may be encountered in their disputes! [Note: [Col. 0800C] “How much filthy speech their disputes permit,” Rhenanus and Pamelius.]

## CHAPTER V

Since, therefore, all the uninstructed still reason from common conceptions, while the doubtful and simple are disturbed anew by those same conceptions, and since everywhere this is the first [Note: [Col. 0800C] “First of all,” Rhenanus.] [Col. 0800C] battering ram directed against us, by which the condition of the flesh is assaulted, it is necessary that we first fortify the condition of the flesh. [Col. 0801A] You must repel reproach with praise [Note: [Col. 0801C] “Reproach having been driven away by praise,” Rhenanus and the Pithoean manuscript.]. Thus the heretics provoke us to employ rhetoric [Note: [Col. 0801D] “Thus they make us employ rhetoric.” The ancient Fathers were very reluctant to divert the streams of philosophy and eloquence that their modesty restrained. Simon Magus (*Recognitions of Blessed Clement* II), Julian, and Porphyry, as cited by Eusebius, therefore charged Christians with ignorance of philosophy and eloquence. The charge’s falsity is demonstrated by the Fathers’ most elegant and eloquent volumes, for, compelled by heretics, they poured forth full streams. LAC.] as well as philosophy.

Even if that futile and paltry little body [Note: [Col. 0801D] “That little body, which they finally call evil.” I think the author has Marcion’s heresy in view, since, by saying that the body was created by an evil god and from evil matter, he indirectly concluded that the body itself was also evil. The Manichaeans later followed that error more openly. PAM.]—which they do not shrink from calling evil—had been the work of angels, [Note: [Col. 0801D] “As Menander and Marcus maintain.” That angels created the world, and consequently human flesh as well, was a heresy Menander shared with his teacher Simon Magus, as may be seen above in *Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 46. PAM.] as Menander and Marcus maintain; or even if it had been the construction of some fiery being, likewise an angel, as Apelles teaches—the patronage of a secondary divinity would suffice to confer dignity upon the flesh. We recognize angels as coming after God.

Indeed, whoever the supreme god of each heretic may be, I could reasonably derive the dignity of the flesh from him too, since the will to produce it would have been present in him. For surely he would have prevented the making of something which he knew would be made, had he not wished it to be made. Thus even according to them the flesh is likewise a thing belonging to God. No work fails to belong to the one who permitted it to exist.

It is well, however, [Col. 0801B] that most doctrines, even the harsher ones, concede to our God the entire fashioning of the human being. You know sufficiently how great he is, since you have believed him to be the only God. Let the flesh now begin to please you, since its craftsman is so great.

“But the world too,” you say, “is God’s work, and nevertheless the fashion of this world passes away, as the Apostle also testifies (1 Cor. 7). Nor will the world’s restoration be prejudged [Note: [Col. 0801C] “Is prejudged,” Rhenanus.] merely because it is God’s work. And if the universe cannot be re-formed after its passing, what hope is there for one of its parts?”

Certainly—if the part is placed on the same level as the universe. But we appeal to the difference between them. First, all things were made by God’s Word, and without him nothing was made. The flesh too came into being by God’s word, for the sake of its form, lest anything should exist without the Word, since he first said, “Let us make man.” But it was fashioned additionally by his hand, for the sake of its preeminence, lest it be equated with the universe. [Col. 0801C] “And God fashioned man,” Scripture says.

There was undoubtedly a substantial reason for the difference, namely, the respective condition of the things made. For the things being made were lesser than the one for whom they were being made: indeed, they were being made for man, to whom they were soon assigned by God. Rightly, therefore, [Note: [Col. 0801D] “As servants, by command and authority.” Tertullian speaks acutely here, as though God, even then in the creation of things, were inaugurating or furnishing those very things for service under human authority. They were made by command; man, by contrast, since he was to become their lord, was made not by an imperative but in the image of God, who commands, and was made supreme by the Lord himself. For according to certain Fathers, man’s status as God’s image consisted in his dominion over all things. Isidore of Pelusium, Book III, Epistle 95. LAC.] as servants, by command and authority, all things had proceeded from the power of a mere spoken summons [Note: [Col. 0801C] “Vocal,” Pamelius and Rhenanus.]. By contrast, man, as their lord, was constructed by God himself precisely so that he could be lord, since he was made by the Lord. [Col. 0802A]

But remember that “man” properly designates the flesh, which first took possession of the name “man”: “And God fashioned man, mud from the earth.” He was already “man” while still mud. “And he breathed into his face the breath of life; and man”—that is, the mud—“became a living soul.” “And God placed the man whom he had fashioned in paradise.” Thus, first the fashioned object was “man,” and afterward the whole composite was “man.”

I have commended this point so that you may know that absolutely everything provided and promised by God to man is owed not to the soul alone but also to the flesh—if not by its participation in the human kind, then certainly by the privilege of the human name.

## CHAPTER VI

I shall therefore pursue my argument—if only I can vindicate for the flesh as much as the one who made it conferred upon it. Even then it could glory that its littleness, the mud, [Col. 0802B] came into the hands of God, whatever those hands may be; it was sufficiently blessed if it had merely been touched.

For what if, without any further workmanship, the fashioned object had immediately been completed by God’s touch? So great was the business being conducted through the construction of this material! Thus it is honored as many times as it experiences God’s hands: while it is touched, while portions are taken from it, while it is drawn out, while it is shaped.

Consider God wholly occupied and devoted [Note: [Col. 0801D] “Dedicated,” Rhenanus and Semler.] to it—with hand, mind, work, counsel, wisdom, providence, and especially with that affection which traced its contours [Note: [Col. 0802C] “Kept tracing,” Pamelius and Franecker; “befitted,” Rhenanus; “dictated,” others.]. For whatever form the mud was taking, Christ was being contemplated as the man who was to come, since he too was to be mud; and the Word as the flesh he was to become, since he too was then to be earth [text and punctuation uncertain] [Note: [Col. 0802D] “Christ was in view as the man who would be, because both mud and flesh; the Word, because also earth at that time.” These words seem clearer with the punctuation found in the Pithoean manuscript: “Christ was in view as the man who would be, because both mud and flesh; the Word, because also earth at that time.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0802C] “The Word, flesh,” Franecker and Pamelius.].

For thus ran the Father’s preliminary address to the Son: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” And God made man. That which he fashioned, of course, [Col. 0802C] he made in God’s image; that is, in the image of Christ. For the Word too is God, who, being constituted in the form of God, [Note: [Col. 0802D] “Did not consider it robbery to be made equal to God.” “The divinity of God and Lord—that is, of Father and Son—is equal,” says Gregory of Elvira in *On the Faith*; he then adds: “For the will of God and of any other, yet not God, cannot be equal.” RIG.] did not consider equality with God a robbery [Note: [Col. 0802C] “Equal,” Rhenanus; “equal things,” Gelenius; “to be equal,” others.].

Thus that mud, even then putting on the image of Christ who was to come in the flesh, was not merely God’s work but also his pledge. What purpose does it now serve, in order to darken the flesh’s origin, to bandy about the name “earth” [Note: [Col. 0802D] “Adam: man, or earthborn, or native, or red earth,” says Blessed Jerome in *On Hebrew Names*. EDD.] [Col. 0803A] as though it denoted an element filthy and prostrate? Even if some other material had been suitable for forming [Note: [Col. 0803C] “Hammering out,” Rhenanus.] man, it would still have been necessary to consider the eminence of the craftsman, who would have judged that material worthy by choosing it [Note: [Col. 0803C] Others add “in.”] and would have made it worthy by handling it.

The hands of Phidias, [Note: [Col. 0803C] “The Olympian Jupiter from ivory,” etc. Pliny, Book 34, chapter 8: “An almost countless multitude of artists,” he says, “won fame through smaller statues and images. Before them all, however, was Phidias the Athenian, who made the Olympian Jupiter, indeed from ivory, but also produced statues from bronze.” RHEN.] which fashioned the Olympian Jupiter from ivory, are adored [Note: [Col. 0803C] “It is fashioned and adored,” Pamelius and Rhenanus.]. It is no longer regarded as the tooth of an animal—and a particularly stupid animal at that—but as the supreme deity of the age, not because an elephant supplied it but because Phidias was so great.

Would the living and true God not have cleansed any baseness of material through his workmanship and cured it of every weakness? Or are we to conclude that man fashioned God more honorably than God fashioned man?

Now, even if the mud is a stumbling block, the flesh is already something else. I now have flesh in my grasp, not earth—even though the flesh too hears, “You are earth, and into earth you will go.” Its origin is recalled; its substance is not revoked. [Col. 0803B] It has been granted to become something nobler than its origin [Note: [Col. 0803C] The Pithoean manuscript inserts “in.”] and more fortunate through transformation. Gold too is earth, because it comes from earth; but only until it becomes gold. Once it is gold, it is an entirely different material, more splendid and noble, derived from a humbler [Note: [Col. 0803C] “More fading,” Rhenanus and Junius.] matrix.

[Note: [Col. 0803D] “Thus it was permissible for God too to refine the gold of the flesh, its material hammered free from what you consider the filth of mud.” One is said to be *excusatus* when placed outside the jurisdiction of a law, burden, or accusation—that is, when he has shown that his circumstances do not require him to be oppressed by some burden or accusation or to be assessed or held by some law. Thus “we excuse the mouth from food” means that we abstain, and “they excuse our neck from so great a yoke.” So too here the material of flesh would seem “excused” from the filth of mud, as though free of muddy filth; and in *On the Veiling of Virgins*, “the flower of virginity excuses human lust,” that is, refuses the stains of human lust. Nevertheless, we believe our Septimius had another meaning in mind. He says that both gold and flesh come from earth, but that both, perfected by the craftsman’s hands, pass from a humbler matrix into a far different, more splendid, and nobler material, so that they are no longer called earth but gold and flesh. Therefore, just as the craftsman was permitted to hammer gold from earth and so purify the material from the violence of its ore that at last [Col. 0804C] it advances to the most perfect excellence, so too the supreme craftsman of all, God, was permitted to hammer the gold of our flesh from mud, bake and refine it in the furnaces of divine powers, and assign it to the class of the noblest material, with that former class of earth or mud [Col. 0804D] hammered free from filth. He used *census* for material, of whatever class it may be reckoned. By *excusatum*, moreover, he meant “hammered out,” from *cudere* and *excudere*, from which come *cusare* and *excusare*, just as from *quatere*, *jacere*, and *premere* we form *quassare*, *jactare*, and *pressare*, and thence *quassatum*, *jactatum*, and *pressatum*, where elsewhere one finds *quassum*, *jactum*, and *pressum*. RIG.] Thus God too was permitted to refine the flesh’s gold, its material hammered free from what you consider the filth of mud.

## CHAPTER VII

But [Note: [Col. 0803C] Others add “lest.”] perhaps the dignity of the flesh may seem more diluted because the divine hand did not properly handle the flesh itself as it handled the mud. Yet since it handled the mud for the purpose that flesh might subsequently come from mud, it was surely conducting the business of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0803C] “For the flesh,” Rhenanus.].

But I would still have you learn when and how [Note: [Col. 0803C] “How and when,” Rhenanus.] the flesh blossomed [Note: [Col. 0803C] Others read “flowed.”] from the mud. [Note: [Col. 0804D] “For those coats of skins which Adam and Eve put on after being stripped of paradise were not, as some maintain, themselves the transformation of the mud into flesh.” He attacks the opinion of the Valentinians, who said that the human being created by God possessed the rank of spiritual substance, but that after he was expelled from the region of paradise a fleshly surface was woven over him, as Tertullian says in *Against the Valentinians*. Or, as Irenaeus said against them, he was clothed in a “leathern tunic,” *dermatinon chitōna* (δερμάτινον χιτῶνα). They called the flesh subject to sensation “this perceptible little flesh,” *touto de to aisthēton sarkion einai legousi* (τοῦτο δὲ τὸ αἰσθητόν σαρκίον εἶναι λέγουσι), as Irenaeus says in Epiphanius. RIG.] For those coats of skins which Adam [Col. 0804A] and Eve put on after being stripped of paradise were not, as some maintain, themselves the transformation of mud into flesh [Note: [Col. 0804C] “Leathern,” Semler and Pamelius.]. Some time earlier Adam had already recognized in the woman the flesh [Note: [Col. 0804C] “Of the woman,” Rhenanus and Semler.] propagated from his own substance [Note: [Col. 0804C] “As flesh,” Rhenanus and Semler.] [Note: [Col. 0804C] “Had known,” Franecker.]: “This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh.” Moreover, the portion taken from the male was completed in the woman with flesh; it should, I suppose, have been completed with mud if Adam were still mud.

The mud, therefore, was obliterated and swallowed up into flesh. When? When the human being became a living soul through God’s breath, which was evidently a vapor [Note: [Col. 0804C] “Vaporous,” Rhenanus.] suitable [Note: [Col. 0804C] Rhenanus and the Pithoean manuscript insert “also.”] for baking, as it were, the mud into another quality—into flesh, just as clay is baked into pottery. In the same way, a potter may, by the measured breath of fire, reconstitute clay into a stronger material and form [Note: [Col. 0804C] “Contract,” Rhenanus and Semler.] from one thing another form, more suitable than the former and now possessing its own kind and name.

For although it is written (Rom. 9), [Col. 0804B] “Will the clay say [Note: [Col. 0804C] “Does the clay say,” others.] to the potter?”—that is, will man say to God?—and although the Apostle speaks of “earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7), nevertheless man is clay because he was previously mud, and flesh is pottery because it was formed from mud through [Note: [Col. 0804C] “Through” is absent from Rigault and Venice.] the vapor of the divine breath. [Note: [Col. 0804D] “The flesh, which the coats of skins—that is, the skins laid over it—subsequently clothed.” Thus Septimius considers the coats of skins to have been literal skins, not, as the Valentinians held, the flesh itself. RIG.] The coats of skins—that is, the skins laid over it—subsequently clothed that flesh.

So true is this that, if you remove the skin, you have laid the flesh bare. Thus what today becomes a covering removed from the body was its garment when first laid over it. Hence the Apostle too, by calling circumcision “the stripping off of the flesh,” confirmed [Note: [Col. 0804C] “Affirmed,” Rhenanus and Semler.] that the skin was a tunic.

Since these things are so, you possess both mud made glorious by God’s hand and flesh made more glorious by God’s breath. By that breath the flesh at once laid aside the rudiments of mud and received the adornments of the soul.

You are not more attentive than God: you do not mount Scythian and Indian gems and the gleaming pearls of the Red [Col. 0805A] Sea in lead, bronze, or iron, [Note: [Col. 0805C] “Nor even encircle them with silver.” Rhenanus correctly conjectured this reading. He interprets *oblaquees* as “surround, encompass, enclose,” deriving the word from *lacus*; similarly, the following *descrobes* means “you insert,” from *scrobs*, “a pit.” The old reading *ferroginis* for *ferruginis* in the English and Vatican manuscripts should also be noted. PAM.] nor even encircle them with silver, but set them in the choicest and most elaborately worked gold. Likewise, for every most precious wine and ointment, you first ensure the suitability of its vessel [Note: [Col. 0805C] “Likewise, for wines” is not read in the Pithoean manuscript or Rhenanus.]. Similarly, you match the dignity of the sheath to swords of perfectly tempered iron [Note: [Col. 0805D] “A sword of perfectly tempered iron.” We emended this from the Pithoean manuscript; previously the reading was “of visibly tempered iron.” By “perfectly tempered iron” he means iron of perfect excellence, whose edge is pure—not only outstanding in the natural quality of its vein but also in its manufacture and in the nobility of the water into which it is repeatedly plunged while glowing. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0805C] “Visible,” Franecker; “perfectly,” Rhenanus.] [Note: [Col. 0805C] “Iron,” Rhenanus.].

Yet is God supposed to have entrusted the shadow of his soul, the breath of his spirit, the working of his mouth, to some utterly worthless hilt [Note: [Col. 0805D] “Entrusted it to some hilt.” He calls the body the soul’s *capulum*, that is, its receptacle. RHEN.], and by placing it unworthily to have thereby condemned it? But did he merely place it there—or did he not rather implant and intermingle it with the flesh in so intimate a union that it may be considered uncertain whether the flesh carries the soul about or the soul the flesh, whether the flesh appears to the soul or the soul to the flesh [Note: [Col. 0805C] “Obeys,” Rhenanus and Semler.]?

Yet it must rather be believed that the soul is borne upon and rules the flesh, since it is nearer to God [Note: [Col. 0805C] “Even if,” Pamelius and Franecker.]. This too redounds to the flesh’s glory: it both contains the soul, which is nearest to God, [Col. 0805B] and makes the flesh itself a participant in the soul’s dominion.

For what use of nature, what fruit of the world, what savor of the elements does the soul not feed upon through the flesh? And why should it not, since through the flesh it is supported [Note: [Col. 0805C] “Is supported,” Rhenanus.] by every instrument of sensation—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch? Through the flesh it is sprinkled with divine power, accomplishing everything through speech, even when speech is silently conceived beforehand. For speech too comes through an organ of the flesh; arts are through the flesh; studies and intellectual abilities through the flesh; works, business, and duties through the flesh. Thus indeed [Note: [Col. 0805D] “The soul’s entire living belongs to the flesh.” This is most truly said while the soul is united to the body, because it performs nothing except through the organs of the flesh. Indeed, intellection itself, which is, as it were, the soul’s peculiar possession, does not occur without dependence upon material species and images. LAC.] the soul’s entire living belongs to the flesh, [Note: [Col. 0805D] “So that the soul’s not living is nothing other than,” etc. This statement of the author is also true in that sense. For unless the soul acts through bodily ministries, it does nothing and is, as it were, [Col. 0806C] dead. Accordingly, when the material organs of the flesh are impeded, the soul becomes sluggish and unable to act. For this law or compact was established while flesh and soul are united: the soul can accomplish nothing without the flesh’s assistance. Moreover, by the soul’s “living” and “life,” Tertullian here understands the soul’s animation of the body and the life it causes in the body by that animation [Col. 0806D]. LAC.] so that for the soul not to live is nothing other than to depart from the flesh. [Col. 0805C] Likewise, even the actual dying belongs to the flesh, to which living also belongs.

Furthermore, if all things are subjected to the soul through the flesh, they must be subjected to the flesh as well [Note: [Col. 0805C] “Are subjected,” Rigault, Venice, and Semler. Perhaps “it must be subjected.” EDD.], since it is necessary that you use them through it [Note: [Col. 0806C] Pamelius, Rigault, and Venice add “since you use it.”]. Thus, although the flesh is reckoned the soul’s minister and servant, [Col. 0806A] it is found to be its partner and coheir. If it shares in temporal things, why not also in eternal things?

## CHAPTER VIII
And these points I have advanced, as it were, from the common pattern of the human condition in support of [Note: [Col. 0806C] “Supports,” Rhenanus, Semler.] the flesh. Let us now also consider, from the distinctive pattern of the Christian name, how great a prerogative this substance—frivolous and filthy though it is—possesses with God. Indeed, it might have sufficed for it that no soul whatsoever can attain salvation unless it has believed while it is [Note: [Col. 0806C] “Is” omitted by others.] in the flesh: so true is it that the flesh is the hinge of salvation. In short, [Note: [Col. 0806C] “Concerning which,” Rhenanus.] when the soul is enlisted for God, it is the flesh itself that makes it possible for the soul to be enlisted. Thus [Note: [Col. 0806C] “But also,” Rhenanus, Pamelius.] the flesh is washed so that the soul may be cleansed of stains; the flesh is anointed so that the soul may be consecrated; the flesh is signed so that the soul too may be fortified; the flesh is overshadowed by the laying on of hands [Col. 0806B] so that the soul too may be illuminated by the Spirit; the flesh feeds upon the body and blood of Christ so that the soul too may be fattened upon God. [Note: [Col. 0806D] “The flesh is washed, the flesh is anointed, the flesh is signed,” etc. In this passage he has reviewed briefly, but most aptly set forth, Baptism, Anointing, the Sign of the Cross, the Laying on of Hands, and the Eucharist. Rigaltius.] Therefore those whom their works unite cannot be separated in their reward.

For even the sacrifices pleasing to God—I mean the soul’s struggles: fasts, late and dry meals, and [Note: [Col. 0806D] “The filth that attends this observance.” Elsewhere he spoke of the horror of ashes and the roughness of sackcloth. To these they also added the following expressions from Lucilius: filthiness, lack of bathing, lack of washing, and neglect. Rigaltius.] the filth that attends this observance—the flesh supplies at the cost of its own discomfort. [Note: [Col. 0806C] “Is supplied,” Rhenanus.] Virginity too, and widowhood, and [Note: [Col. 0806D] “Modest concealment within the privacy of marriage.” He means the intimacies of marriage themselves, which in book II *To His Wife* he says are, among the saints, the duties of sex and ought to be conducted modestly and temperately, with due regard for the necessity itself, as though under the eyes of God. Rigaltius.] modest reserve within the privacy of marriage, and acquaintance with it only once, are offered to God from the good things of the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0806C] *Adolantur*, Rhenanus, Semler.]

Come now: what do you think of the flesh when, [Note: [Col. 0806D] “For faithfulness to the name.” We have noted more than once that Tertullian and blessed Cyprian commonly use “the name” for “the Christian name.” So also in chapter 40, “because of punishments for the name”; the expressions are characteristically Tertullianic. Pamelius.] dragged out into public for its faithfulness to the Name and exposed to public hatred, it enters the contest; when it is wasted away in prisons, in that most hideous banishment from daylight, amid deprivation of the world, [Col. 0806C] squalor, stench, and an insulting diet; not even free to sleep, since it is chained even to its beds and mangled upon its very pallets; when now, in full daylight too, [Note: [Col. 0806D] “It is torn by every contrivance of tortures.” He touches upon the fertile and ingenious cruelty of tyrants in devising [Col. 0807D] punishments. On those varied and unheard-of penalties, Eusebius should be consulted. Le Prieur.] it is torn by every contrivance of torture; when [Col. 0807A] at last it is expended in punishments, striving to repay Christ in kind by dying for him—and often by the very same cross, to say nothing of still more atrocious inventions of punishment? Is it not then most blessed and most glorious, [Note: [Col. 0807D] “Which is able to obey so great a debt before Christ the Lord.” This is how the copies read, and I do not think anything should be changed, although Ciacconius preferred *pariare*, “to balance the account.” A debtor obeys a creditor who calls upon him when he makes satisfaction. The one who exacts commands; the one who renders what he promised obeys. Rigaltius.] since it can obey so great a debt before Christ the Lord, [Note: [Col. 0807C] “Be equal,” Latinus; “balance the account,” Ciacconius.] so that this alone remains its debt to him: that it has ceased to owe him—bound all the more precisely because [Note: [Col. 0807C] “In that,” Pamelius, François.] it has been discharged?

## CHAPTER IX

Therefore, to retrace the flesh which God fashioned with his own hands in the image of God, which he animated from his own breath in the likeness of his own vitality, which he placed over his whole creation to inhabit, enjoy, and rule it, which he clothed with his mysteries and disciplines; whose purity he loves, whose chastisements he approves, whose sufferings he values for himself—shall this flesh, belonging to God in so many ways, not rise again? [Col. 0807B] Far be it, far be it [Note: [Col. 0807C] “Far be it” only once, Rhenanus.] that God should abandon to eternal destruction the work of his hands, the object of his creative care, the sheath of his breath, [Note: [Col. 0807D] “The queen of his creation.” By “creation” he means the act of creating. For God created the human being as king of everything on earth and in the sea. Rigaltius.] the queen of his creation, the heir of his liberality, [Note: [Col. 0807D] “The priest of his religion”: one who offers praise and thanks to God. Rigaltius.] the priest of his religion, the soldier of his testimony, [Note: [Col. 0807D] “The sister of his Christ,” because it is akin and of one stock with the flesh of Christ—not as most of those heretics against whom the author contends supposed, namely, that Christ’s flesh was of a different nature, whether phantom-like, celestial, animal, or spiritual. Their heresies were discussed in the preceding book. Lac.] the sister of his Christ!

We know God to be good; [Note: [Col. 0807D] “We learn that he alone is supremely good from his Christ,” etc. God has been recognized as supremely good through works [Col. 0808D] of grace. This is also said against the Marcionites, who distinguished two gods, an evil creator-god and a good god, and said that the latter was the God to whom Christ belonged and whose goodness was made known through Christ. Lac.] from his Christ we learn that he alone is supremely good. [Note: [Col. 0807C] “His” absent from Rhenanus, Semler.] He who commands love, after love of himself, toward one’s neighbor, will himself also do what he has commanded: he will love the flesh, which is his neighbor in so many ways. Though it is weak (Matt. 26:41), strength is perfected in weakness (2 Cor. 12:9); though feeble, none desire a physician except those who are ill (Matt. 22 [sic]); though dishonorable, [Note: [Col. 0808D] “But upon the more dishonorable we bestow greater honor.” When it is necessary to name such parts, we are accustomed first to express respect. Rigaltius.] upon the more dishonorable we bestow greater honor (2 Cor. 12 [sic]); though lost, “I came,” he says, [Col. 0807C] “to save what was lost” (Luke 5 [sic]); though sinful, “I prefer,” he says, “the salvation of the sinner to his death” (Ezek. 18); though condemned, “I,” he says, “will strike and I will heal” (Deut. 32).

Why do you reproach the flesh with those conditions which await God, which hope in God, which are honored by him, and which he assists? I would venture to say that, had these things not befallen the flesh, [Col. 0808A] goodness, grace, mercy, and every beneficent power of God would have had no occupation. [Note: [Col. 0807C] “Would have been vacant,” others.]

## CHAPTER X

You retain the Scriptures by which the flesh is darkened; retain also those by which it is made illustrious. You read when [Note: [Col. 0807C] “When,” Rhenanus.] the flesh is cast down: direct your eyes also to when [Note: [Col. 0807D] “When,” Rhenanus.] the flesh is raised up. [Note: [Col. 0808C] “Revealed,” others.] “All flesh is grass” (Isa. 41 [sic]); Isaiah did not pronounce this [Note: [Col. 0808C] “This” absent from Pamelius, François.] alone, but also: [Note: [Col. 0808D] “All flesh shall see the salvation of God.” Below, chapter 59, these same Scriptures are cited in almost the same words. It is read according to the Septuagint in place of what blessed Jerome translates simply as “and all flesh together shall see”; Leo de Castro, on Isaiah, shows elegantly that both readings come to the same thing. Le Prieur.] “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (*ibid.*).

In Genesis, God is marked as saying (Gen. 6): “My Spirit shall not remain in these people, because they are flesh”; but he is also heard through Joel (Joel 2): “I shall pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh.” Nor should you recognize the Apostle from only one manner of writing, in which he frequently goads the flesh. For although he denies that anything good dwells in his flesh; although he affirms that those who are in the flesh cannot [Col. 0808B] please God, because it lusts against the spirit; and if he makes any other statements of this sort, so that not the substance of the flesh but its conduct is dishonored—we shall indeed say elsewhere that nothing ought properly to be reproached against the flesh except as a rebuke to the soul, which subjects [Note: [Col. 0808C] “Submits,” others.] the flesh to itself as its servant. Yet meanwhile [Note: [Col. 0808D] “Paul is also in those writings”; that is, Paul’s voice is also heard in those testimonies of Scripture. Rigaltius.] Paul is also in those writings when he bears the marks of Christ in his body; when he forbids [Note: [Col. 0808C] Rhenanus and Semler add “the body.”] our body, as God’s temple, to be defiled; when he makes our bodies members of Christ; when he admonishes us to bear and magnify God in our body.

Accordingly, if the disgraces of the flesh exclude its resurrection, why should its dignities not rather introduce it? For it is more consonant with God to restore to salvation what he has at times rejected than to surrender to destruction what he has also [Col. 0808C] at some time [Note: [Col. 0808C] “At some time” lacking in Rhenanus.] approved.

## CHAPTER XI

Thus far concerning the commendation of the flesh against its enemies, who are nevertheless its greatest friends. For no one lives more carnally than those who deny the resurrection of the flesh. By denying its [Note: [Col. 0808C] “Its” lacking in Rhenanus, Semler.] punishment, they also despise its discipline. Of them the [Note: [Col. 0808D] “The Paraclete through the prophetess,” etc. He calls the spirit of Montanus the Paraclete, to which the author had already adhered when he wrote this treatise. Prisca, elsewhere [Col. 0809C] Priscilla, whom the author mentions *Against Praxeas* and in the book *On Fasts*, was a prophetess of Montanus. Lac.] Paraclete also spoke lucidly through [Col. 0809A] the prophetess Prisca: “They are flesh, and they hate the flesh.”

If so great an authority fortifies the flesh—an authority able to plead so powerfully for its claim to salvation—must we not also review God’s own might, power, and freedom of action: whether he is great enough to be able to rebuild and restore the tabernacle of the flesh after it has fallen apart, been devoured, and been carried away [Note: [Col. 0809C] “Removed,” Junius.] in any conceivable manner? And has he promulgated any examples of this sovereign right of his [Note: [Col. 0809D] “In the public record of nature”: in nature’s public tablets. The author himself, in *On the Crown*: “Do you therefore seek God’s law? You have this common law in the public record of the world, in the natural tablets, to which the Apostle too is accustomed to appeal.” Rigaltius.] in the public record of nature, [Note: [Col. 0809C] “Had promulgated,” Rhenanus; “may promulgate,” others.] lest there be any who perhaps [Note: [Col. 0809D] “Lest some perhaps still do not know how to know God.” The Pithoean manuscript reads “thirst.” This form of expression is familiar to Septimius. Those who do not yet know God thirst to know him, and therefore do not know him. So too: “Nevertheless, they thirst for an interpretation of his very simplicity.” Rigaltius.] still do not know [Note: [Col. 0809C] “Thirst,” Rhenanus, Semler; “know,” Pamelius, François.] how to know God, who must be believed in according to no other rule than that he be believed able to do all things?

Certainly, among the philosophers you have those who maintain that this world is unbegotten and unmade; [Note: [Col. 0809D] “Among the philosophers you have those who say that this world is unbegotten.” The saying “Nothing comes from nothing” is commonplace; from it Aristotle, *Physics* I and *On the Heavens*, thinks that the world has existed and will exist eternally. But if one attends to the true and genuine explanation of that principle, God said: “I am who I am”; it must therefore be inferred that all things flowed forth from that existing God and that the world was created. Some think Aristotle later reconsidered this opinion. Le Prieur.] but far better is the position that almost all the heresies, admitting that the world was born and made, ascribe its creation to our God. Therefore trust [Note: [Col. 0809C] “He will trust,” Rigaltius, Venice.] that he brought forth this whole universe from nothing, [Col. 0809B] and you know God by trusting that God possesses such power.

For some, too weak to believe this first point, prefer to hold that the universe was brought into being by him out of an underlying matter [Note: [Col. 0809C] “Of the whole,” Wouwer manuscript.]—according to the philosophers. [Note: [Col. 0809D] Plato, as Athanasius attests in *On the Incarnation of the Word*, at the beginning, and Epiphanius, [Col. 0810C] *Heresy* 6, said that God fashioned the world from pre-existent and unmade matter. Yet Marsilio Ficino, [Col. 0810D] in his compendium of Plato’s *Timaeus*, chapters 9 and following, attempts to excuse him from this error and claims that Plato meant only that matter was made by God more immediately than other things. Lac.] But even if this were held to be true, since he would nevertheless be said to have brought forth, through the reformation of matter, substances entirely different and forms entirely different from what the matter itself had been, I would defend no less that he brought them forth from nothing, if he brought forth things that had not existed at all.

[Note: [Col. 0810D] “For what difference does it make,” etc. The author does not say this dogmatically, since he does not dare despise the settled laws of philosophy approved by the Fathers—as, on the matter under discussion, Gregory, homily 20 on Ezekiel. Lac.] For what difference does it make whether something is brought forth from nothing or from something, provided that what did not exist comes to be? For even not to have existed is to have been nothing. Conversely, to have existed is not to have been nothing. Now, even if there is a difference, both alternatives nevertheless support me. For whether God fashioned all things out of nothing, he will also be able to produce out of nothing the flesh reduced [Col. 0809C] to nothing; [Note: [Col. 0809C] “Produced,” Pamelius, Rhenanus.] or whether he formed [Note: [Col. 0810C] “Moderated,” Rhenanus, Semler.] other things out of matter, he will also be able to summon the flesh out of whatever else it has been absorbed into.

[Note: [Col. 0810D] “And surely one who made it is competent to remake it.” The Manichaeans, Cerdonians, and Marcionites denied that re-creation or resurrection, although creating from nothing seems far more difficult than remaking. Le Prieur.] And surely one who made it is competent to remake it. How much greater a thing it is to have made than to have remade, [Col. 0810A] to have given a beginning than to have restored it! Thus you should believe that the restoration of the flesh is easier than its original formation.

## CHAPTER XII

Look now also at the actual examples of divine power. Day dies into night and is buried everywhere in darkness; [Note: [Col. 0810D] “The glory of the world is laid in mourning.” He means the sun, which Orpheus calls κόσμου τὸ περίδρομον ὄμμα, “the roaming eye of the world,” and Proclus of Lycia in hymn 1 calls ἀλλὰ Θεῶν ἄριστε, πυριστεφὲς, ὄλβιε δαῖμον, “but you, best of gods, fire-crowned, blessed divinity.” Le Prieur.] the glory of the world is laid in mourning; every substance is blackened; all things grow squalid, silent, and numb; everywhere there is a cessation of business. [Note: [Col. 0810C] The Pithoean manuscript adds “a repose of things.”] Thus the lost light is mourned; and yet, once again, with its splendor, its endowment, and its sun, that same light—undiminished, whole, and complete—revives for the entire world, killing its own death, the night; tearing open its own tomb, the darkness; becoming its own heir, until night too revives with its own equipment.

For the rays of the stars are rekindled, which the morning blaze had extinguished; the absent constellations are brought back, [Col. 0810B] which the temporal division had removed; the mirrors of the moon are adorned anew, [Note: [Col. 0810C] “Are given back,” Rhenanus.] which the monthly reckoning had worn away; winters and summers revolve again, [Note: [Col. 0810C] Rhenanus and Semler insert “and.”] springtimes and autumns, with their powers, characteristics, and fruits. Indeed, the earth too is instructed by heaven to clothe the trees after their stripping, to color the flowers anew, to spread the grasses again, to bring forth the same seeds that have been consumed, and not to bring them forth before they have been consumed.

A wondrous order! The plunderer becomes the preserver: that she may restore, she takes away; that she may keep, she destroys; that she may make whole, she damages; that she may even increase, she first consumes. For she restores things richer and more cultivated than those she annihilated—truly, destruction at interest, injury at usury, damage at a profit. Let me say it once for all: the whole creation is recurrent. Whatever you encounter has existed before; whatever you lose, there is nothing that does not exist again. [Col. 0810C] All things return to their condition once they have departed; all things begin once they have ceased. They are therefore ended so that they may come to be; nothing wholly perishes except unto salvation.

Thus this entire [Note: [Col. 0810D] “This revolving order of things.” From the perpetual alternation of things, their continual flux and revolution, he demonstrates the resurrection. Indeed, from that sequence of natural things the wiser philosophers had an inkling of it, such as Plato in the *Timaeus* and *Phaedo*, and Seneca, Epistle 35: “The death which we so greatly fear and accuse interrupts life; it does not take it away. One will come again who will restore these days to the light.” The same in Epistles 40, 92, and 102, and *To Marcia*, [Col. 0811D] chapter 26. Le Prieur.] revolving order of things is a testimony to the resurrection of the dead. [Col. 0811A] God prescribed it through works before he did through writings; he proclaimed it through powers before he did through words. He sent nature ahead to be your teacher, intending afterward to send prophecy, so that, as nature’s pupil, you might believe prophecy more readily; so that, when you hear, you might immediately admit what you have already seen everywhere [Note: [Col. 0811C] “Certainly,” François.]; and so that you might not doubt that God also raises the flesh, since you know him [Note: [Col. 0811C] “Who,” Rhenanus, Junius.] to be the restorer of all things.

And surely, if all things rise again for the human being, for whom they were provided—and moreover not for the human being apart from the flesh—how can the flesh itself perish completely, when it is for the flesh and for its sake that nothing perishes?

## CHAPTER XIII

If the universe insufficiently prefigures the resurrection; if creation signifies nothing of the sort, because its individual elements are said not so much to die as to cease and are thought not to be reanimated but [Col. 0811B] re-formed, then accept the fullest [Note: [Col. 0811C] “Clearest,” others.] and firmest specimen of this hope. For it is an animate creature, subject both to life and to death. I mean that bird peculiar to the East, famous for its uniqueness and extraordinary in its succession: [Note: [Col. 0811D] “Which willingly performs its own funeral and renews itself.” Clement, *To the Corinthians*, relates it thus: when the phoenix senses that it is near death, it constructs for itself from frankincense, myrrh, and other aromatics of this sort a σηκόν, “enclosure” (Pliny: “nest”); soon afterward the bird, laid within it, dies. From the dead flesh there is born first, as it were, a little worm, which then becomes a fledgling. In this, he says, an image of the resurrection is given us by God. Rigaltius.] it willingly performs its own funeral and renews itself, departing and succeeding itself through an end that is also a birth; once again a phoenix where now there was none; once again itself, which no longer existed; another and yet the same.

What could be more explicit and more significant for this cause? Or what other matter possesses such a proof? God speaks even in his Scriptures: [Note: [Col. 0811D] “‘For he shall flourish,’ he says, ‘like the phoenix.’” ὡς φοῖνιξ means “like a palm tree,” Ps. 12 [sic]. The author was deceived by the ambiguity of the Greek word. Semler.—Septimius is accustomed thus to interpret Scripture very broadly for his purpose. Accordingly, here he wished the ambiguous word *phoenix*, which may denote either bird or tree, to be understood of the phoenix bird, and he adapted the verb “shall flourish” to the resurrection. Rigaltius.] “For he shall flourish,” [Note: [Col. 0811C] “You shall flourish,” Rhenanus; “he shall flower forth,” others.] he says (Ps. 91:13), “like the phoenix”—that is, out of death, out of burial—[Note: [Col. 0811D] “So that you may believe that the substance of the body can be exacted even from fires.” These are indications that, in his account of the phoenix, Tertullian followed reports handed down in different forms by different authors, selecting those which he saw [Col. 0812C] as most useful to his argument. Clement’s epistle had related that the phoenix was reborn from its decomposing, not its cremated, flesh. Therefore, to confirm the restoration of bodies even in that kind of death in which hope of restoration seemed especially extinguished, he turned [Col. 0812D] to those who had written that a new phoenix was restored from the ashes of the one cremated. “So that you may believe,” he says, “that the substance of the body can be exacted even from fires.” He joins this to the cited verse of the Psalm, as though the psalmist had in mind the story of the cremated phoenix. Rigaltius.] so that you may believe that the substance of the body can be exacted even from fires. The Lord pronounced that we are worth more than many sparrows: if we are not also worth more than phoenixes, that is nothing great. But [Note: [Col. 0811C] “Indeed,” Junius.] are human beings to perish once for all, [Col. 0811C] while the birds of Arabia are secure in their resurrection?

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 0812A]

With such outlines of divine powers before us—God operating through parables no less than speaking through them—let us now come also to his actual edicts and decrees, for it is by these that we are chiefly arranging this division of our subject matter. We began with the dignity of the flesh: whether, after it has fallen apart, salvation belongs to it. We then proceeded to the power of God: whether it is great enough and accustomed to confer salvation upon a thing that has fallen apart. Now, if we have established both, I would have you inquire also into the cause: whether there is any cause worthy enough to vindicate the resurrection of the flesh as necessary, and indeed as in every way owed by reason. For there remains the objection that, although the flesh is capable of being restored and although the divinity is competent to restore it, [Note: [Col. 0811C] “And,” Rhenanus, and so Junius.] a cause for the restoration must nevertheless take precedence.

Accept, then, the cause, you who learn concerning [Note: [Col. 0811C] “Because, I think,” Junius.] God that he is [Note: [Col. 0812D] “As supremely good as he is just.” He strikes at the Marcionites, who did not unite justice and goodness in one God but, dividing the divine substance into two gods, called one good, the other evil and just. Theodoret reported this error of Marcion, together with its arguments, in book V *On the Divine Decrees*. Lac.] as supremely good [Col. 0812B] as he is just: supremely good from his own nature, just on account of ours. For if the human being had not sinned, he would have known God solely as supremely good, from the property of his nature; but now he also experiences him as just, from the necessity of the case [Note: [Col. 0812C] François and Pamelius add “his own.”]—yet supremely good even in this very fact, while also just. For in displaying justice by assisting the good and punishing the evil, he furnishes both verdicts for the good: on the one side avenging this good, on the other rewarding that good. [Note: [Col. 0812D] “But you will learn more fully in the controversy with Marcion.” He refers the reader to the books he wrote against Marcion. Rhenanus.] But in the controversy with Marcion you will learn more fully whether this constitutes the whole nature of God.

Meanwhile, such is our God: rightly a judge, because Lord; rightly Lord, because author; rightly author, because God. Hence that nameless god of the heretics is rightly not a judge, since he is not God; [Note: [Col. 0812C] “Lord,” the Ursinus and Wouwer manuscripts.] rightly not Lord, since he is not the author. I no longer know whether he is God, [Note: [Col. 0812D] “I no longer know whether he is God,” etc. The sense appears to be: “I do not know whether the god of the heretics is God, since he is not the author, although the true God—that is, our God—is known to be the author; nor is he Lord, although he ought to be if he were the author.” Rhenanus.] seeing that he is neither author, as God is, nor Lord, as the author is. [Note: [Col. 0812C] “As Lord … as author” absent from the Ursinus and Wouwer manuscripts.]

Therefore, if it is most fitting for [Note: [Col. 0812C] Wouwer inserts “concerning.”] God and Lord and [Note: [Col. 0812C] Rhenanus inserts “not.”] author to ordain judgment for the human being on this very question—whether he has taken care to acknowledge and observe [Col. 0813A] [Note: [Col. 0813C] “Should take care,” Rhenanus, Semler.] his Lord and author, [Note: [Col. 0812C] “And his author” absent from the Wouwer manuscript.] or not—then surely [Note: [Col. 0813C] “Accordingly,” Semler, Rhenanus; “this also,” Pamelius.] the resurrection will discharge the judgment. This will be the whole cause—or rather, the necessity—of the resurrection: [Note: [Col. 0813D] Namely, the ordaining of judgment, which is most fitting for God. Thus it must be read, since “to ordain judgment for the human being” precedes, and below: “Finally, this will be the rationale of the judgment ordained for the final end.” Rhenanus.] namely, the ordaining of judgment, which is most fitting for God. In considering its arrangement, determine whether divine adjudication presides over both substances of the human being that must be judged—the soul as well as the flesh. For whatever is fittingly judged is also appropriately raised.

We say, first, that God’s judgment must be believed full and perfect, as now the final judgment and thereafter perpetual; that it is also just in this respect, since it is deficient in nothing; and also worthy of God in this respect, since, after so great a measure of his patience, it is full and perfect. Consequently, [Note: [Col. 0813C] Pamelius and François add “perfect.”] the fullness and perfection of judgment can consist only in the presentation of the whole human being. The whole human being, moreover, comes forth from the union [Col. 0813B] of both substances, [Note: [Col. 0813C] “Assembly,” Rhenanus.] and must therefore be presented in both, since it is the whole who must be judged. Unless whole, surely the human being will not have lived. As he lived, therefore, so must he be judged, since he must be judged concerning the life he lived. For life is the cause of judgment and must be accounted for through as many substances as those through which it was lived.

## CHAPTER XV

Come now: let our adversaries sever the interweaving of flesh and soul first in the conduct of life, so that they may then dare to sever it also in the recompense of life. [Note: [Col. 0813D] “Let them deny the partnership of works,” etc. The reasoning of this chapter is derived from what is good, equitable, and fitting, and all who wrote on the resurrection of the flesh after Tertullian employed it. Lac.] Let them deny the partnership of deeds, [Note: [Col. 0813D] “Works,” others.] so that they may justly be able to deny the reward as well. Let the flesh have no share in the verdict if it had no share in the cause. Let the soul alone be recalled if it alone departs. [Note: [Col. 0813D] “It alone departs.” He does not take “depart” to mean “perish altogether,” for the immortal soul persists, but “depart from this life,” which depends upon the ministries of the flesh. Lac.]

Yet the soul no more departs alone than it alone completed the course from which it departs—[Col. 0813C] I mean this life. Indeed, so far is the soul [Note: [Col. 0813D] “Alone,” Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür.] from passing through life alone that we do not even exclude thoughts, though solitary and though not brought to realization [Note: [Col. 0814C] “Disposition,” Rhenanus.] through the flesh, from fellowship with the flesh. For whatever the soul does in the heart is done in the flesh, with the flesh, and through the flesh. This particular part of the flesh—the soul’s citadel—even the Lord censures on account of wicked thoughts: “Why do you think evil things in your hearts?” (Matt. 9); and: “Whoever has looked upon a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery in his heart” (Matt. 5). Thus even a thought without deed and [Col. 0814A] without accomplishment is an act of the flesh.

But even if the ruling faculty of the senses, which is called the *hegemonikon* (ἡγεμονικόν, “governing faculty”), has its appointed seat in the brain, or in the central division between the eyebrows, or wherever [Note: [Col. 0814C] “Wherever” only once, Rhenanus, Semler.] philosophers please, the flesh will be the whole thinking-place of the soul. [Note: [Col. 0813D] “The flesh will be the whole thinking-place of the soul.” Tertullian calls *cogitatorium* the place in the body, or the part of the body, where the soul thinks. Rigaltius.] The soul is never without the flesh for as long as it is in the flesh. It does nothing apart from that without which it does not exist.

Inquire further whether thoughts too are administered [Note: [Col. 0814C] “Are administered,” Rhenanus, Semler.] through the flesh, seeing that through the flesh they are discerned externally. Let the soul turn something over within itself: the countenance produces an indication. [Note: [Col. 0814D] “Judgment,” Rhenanus, Semler.] The face is the mirror of every intention. [Note: [Col. 0814D] “The face is the mirror of every intention.” The affections of the mind are commonly observable in the countenance, so that sadness, cheerfulness, love, hatred, and other emotions are readily judged from the face; hence the grammarians derived *vultus* (“countenance”) from *velle* (“to will”). Cicero himself also said in *Against Piso*: “The eyes, eyebrows, forehead—in short, the whole countenance—are a kind of silent speech of the mind.” Le Prieur.] Let them deny partnership in deeds to that whose partnership in thoughts they cannot deny.

They themselves enumerate the transgressions of the flesh: therefore, as a sinner, it will be liable to punishment. We, however, also set against these the virtues of the flesh: therefore, as one that has done well, it will also be entitled to reward. [Col. 0814B] And although it is the soul that acts and impels toward everything, obedience belongs to the flesh. It is impermissible to believe God either an unjust judge or an ineffectual one: unjust, if he bars the partner in good works from rewards; ineffectual, if he exempts the partner in evil works from punishments—since human adjudication is considered more perfect precisely insofar as it also calls the assistants in every deed to account, neither sparing them nor begrudging them the right to share with its authors in the fruit either of punishment or of favor.

## CHAPTER XVI
But when we assign command to the soul and obedience to the flesh, care must be taken lest they overturn even this by another argument, wishing to place the flesh in the soul’s service, but not as a servant, so that they may not thereby be compelled to acknowledge it as a partner. [Note: [Col. 0814D] *Ne et* in Rhen. and Seml.] For they will say that servants and [Col. 0814C] partners possess the discretion to serve and to associate themselves, and the power of their own will in either direction—being, of course, themselves human beings—and that they therefore share merit with the authors of deeds, to whom they voluntarily lend their assistance. [Note: [Col. 0814D] *Accommodarint* in Rhen. and Seml.] But the flesh, knowing nothing and perceiving nothing by itself, possessing of itself neither willing nor unwilling, instead attends upon the soul in the capacity of a vessel—as an instrument, not as a servant. [Note: [Col. 0814D] “Instead attends upon it in the capacity of a vessel.” *Apparere* means to minister, serve, and attend upon, and, as Asconius teaches, it is used of an inferior toward a superior; hence the attendants called *viatores*, who stand ready for judges and await their commands and gestures. RHEN.] Accordingly, judgment presides over the soul alone, concerning how it has used the vessel of the flesh; the vessel itself, however, is not liable to sentence, because neither is a cup [Col. 0815A] condemned if someone has mixed poison in it, nor is [Note: [Col. 0815C] “Nor is the sword sentenced to the beasts.” Everyone knows that among the Romans condemnation *to the beasts*—that is, to fight with wild animals—was customary, as was condemnation to the mines, the quarries, or the islands. LE PR.] a sword sentenced to the beasts if someone has used it to commit robbery.

The flesh, then, is now innocent [Note: [Col. 0815C] *Ea* omitted in Pam. and Fran.] insofar as those evil services will not be charged to it; and nothing prevents it from being saved under the title of innocence. For although its good services are not charged to it either, just as its evil ones are not, [Note: [Col. 0815C] *Bona opera* in Rhen. and Seml.] [Note: [Col. 0815C] *Mala* in Rhen. and Seml.] it is nevertheless more fitting for divine kindness to deliver the innocent: for it owes this to those who do good; but it belongs to supreme goodness to offer even what is not owed. [Note: [Col. 0815C] “For he is beneficent and supremely good. He owes”: Rhen. and Seml.] [Note: [Col. 0815C] *Deberetur* in Rhen. and Seml.]

And yet I ask whether you would condemn any less than their kisses a cup—not merely a poisoned cup [Note: [Col. 0815D] “Into which some death has belched”: into which someone, seized by the swiftness of the poison, breathed out his soul with a belch while drinking. RIG.] into which some death has belched, [Note: [Col. 0815C] *Ructaret* in Rhen.] but one tainted by the breath of a *fictrix* [uncertain: perhaps “tribade” or “prostitute”], an archigallus, a gladiator, or an executioner? [Note: [Col. 0815D] “But of a *fictrix* or an archigallus.” Perhaps one should read *frictricis*; Tertullian would thus have been speaking of cups from which those shameful women called *frictrices*, or eunuchs, drank while kissing them. LE PR.—“Of a *fictrix* or an archigallus.” The archigalli are the chiefs of the Galli, or castrated priests, according to Julius Firmicus: “Venus in the tenth place from the horoscope produces eunuchs and archigalli.” This class of persons, moreover, is usually hated as ill-omened; and because of those who keep such persons as their favorites, it is also regarded as shameful and disgraceful. RHEN.] [Note: [Col. 0815C] *Fictricis* in Rhen. and Seml.; *fascinatricis* in the book of Ursinus and the codex of Wouwer.] [Note: [Col. 0815C] *Thracis vel galli* conjectured by Ciacconius; *archithreys vel archigalli* by Canterus.] We are also accustomed to dash away a cup clouded by our own filth, or one not mixed to our liking, so that we may be all the angrier with the boy. [Col. 0815B] And who would not banish from his entire house—much more from his bedroom, and much more from its office beneath his head—a sword drunk with acts of robbery, [Note: [Col. 0815C] *Vel* in Rhen. and Seml.] [Note: [Col. 0815D] “From its office beneath his head”: from serving as a pillow. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0816C] *Relegarit* in Pam., Fran., Rig., and Ven.] naturally supposing that he would dream of nothing but mockeries [*inludia*; uncertain reading] of souls pressing upon and disturbing the bedfellow of their blood? [Note: [Col. 0816C] *Invidia* in Rhen. and the codex of Pithoeus; Rig. conjectures *invidiam*.] [Note: [Col. 0815D] “The bedfellow of their blood.” It is as though one lies upon the blood of the slain when one places beneath one’s pillow a sword stained with their blood. RIG.]

Yet a cup conscious of having served well, and commended for diligence in its service, will also be decorated with the wreaths of its drinker, [Note: [Col. 0816C] *De* omitted in Rhen.] or honored with a sprinkling of flowers; [Note: [Col. 0816C] *Inorabitur* in Seml., Rig., and Ven.; *ornabitur* in Rhen.; *coronabitur* in others.] and a sword honorably bloodied in war—both a better kind of killer [Note: [Col. 0816C] “And a better killer.” He calls a sword bloodied in war a killer, but a better one, so that one may infer that a sword bloodied in robbery is a worse killer. He therefore says that the former is better, yet still a killer. For he did not wish Christians to wage wars. RIG.]—will repay its praise by consecration. It is therefore possible to fix a sentence even upon vessels and instruments, [Note: [Col. 0816C] Rhen. and Seml. add *ne*.] [Note: [Col. 0816D] “To fix a sentence”: that is, to affirm fearlessly and steadfastly. RIG.] so that they too may share in the merits of their owners and authors. Thus I have answered this argument as well, although the difference between the things leaves the example without force.

For every vessel or instrument comes from elsewhere into use, being made of material wholly foreign [Col. 0815C] to the substance of the human being; but the flesh, sown together with the soul from the beginning [Col. 0816A] in the womb, formed together with it and born together with it, is also mingled with it in every operation. [Note: [Col. 0816C] *Consita* in Rhen. and Seml.] For although the Apostle calls it a vessel, which he commands to be treated with honor, [Note: [Col. 0816C] *Tractare* in Rhen. and Seml.] the same flesh is nevertheless called by the same Apostle the “outer man”: namely, that clay upon which the title “man” was first inscribed—not “cup,” “sword,” or any other “vessel.” It is called a vessel by reason of its capacity, by which it receives and contains the soul; but it is called man by reason of its community of nature with the soul, which renders it not an instrument in operations, but a servant. Thus the servant too will be subject to judgment, even though it understands nothing of itself, [Note: [Col. 0816C] *Ut* in Rhen. and Seml.] because it is a portion of that which understands, not a piece of equipment.

The Apostle also knows this: although the flesh does nothing by itself that is not attributed to the soul, he nevertheless judges the flesh sinful, lest, because it appears to be driven by the soul, it be believed exempt from judgment. [Col. 0816B] So too, when he enjoins upon the flesh certain works deserving praise—“Glorify,” he says, “and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 15)—he is certain that these endeavors also are performed by the soul; yet he commands them to the flesh as well, because he also promises it their fruit. [Note: [Col. 0816C] “He says, and” absent from Rhen.; Junius has “that man says.”] [Note: [Col. 0816C] *Repromittunt* in Rhen. and Seml.] Otherwise neither would reproach have been appropriate against one foreign to the guilt, nor exhortation toward one foreign to the glory. Both reproach and exhortation would be pointless with respect to the flesh if the reward sought in the resurrection were also absent.

## CHAPTER XVII

Any rather simple supporter of our position will suppose that the flesh must be presented again for judgment for this reason also: that otherwise the soul, being incorporeal, cannot experience the suffering of torment or refreshment. This, indeed, is what the common people suppose. [Note: [Col. 0816D] “Because otherwise the soul cannot experience the suffering of torment,” etc. Thus even in ancient times this argument caused difficulty—how spirits could be tormented by corporeal fire—so that it was no slight matter even for Tertullian, and drove him especially toward his paradox concerning the corporeality of the soul. Augustine too seems to have hesitated somewhat, or at least not to have completely refuted, on account of the same argument, the proposition that demons are corporeal; although the position was eventually established that spirits could be tormented by that fire. Augustine, *City of God*, book 21, chapter 10. LAC.]

We, however, profess here too that the soul is corporeal, [Note: [Col. 0816D] “We profess here too that the soul is corporeal.” On this blemish of Tertullian, see St. Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 89, addressed to Quodvultdeus, and St. Thomas, *Against the Gentiles* II, chapter 86. LAC.] [Col. 0816C] and prove it in its own volume: it possesses [Col. 0817A] its own kind of substance and solidity, through which it is capable both of perceiving and of suffering. For the example of Lazarus has proved [Note: [Col. 0817C] “For souls are even now tormented.” Here the Author corrected himself, for in chapter 48 of the *Apology* and chapter 4 of *The Testimony of the Soul* he had said that souls in hell could in no way be tormented without the flesh. Here he has now openly come to his senses, as also in the final chapter of the book *On the Soul*. LAC.] that souls are even now tormented and comforted in the regions below, although naked and still exiled from the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0817C] “And comforted in the regions below.” He alludes to the request of the rich miser, when he asked Lazarus for a drop of water; Lazarus was being comforted in Abraham’s bosom. From this arose another paradox of Tertullian, who thought that the souls of the saints are comforted in Abraham’s bosom, or paradise, or beneath the altar, and rejoice until the day of judgment. On this, see *On the Soul*, chapters 7, 9, 55, 56, and 58. LAC.] [Note: [Col. 0817C] *Probabit* in Rhen. and Seml.]

I have therefore allowed the adversary to say: [Note: [Col. 0817D] “I have therefore allowed the adversary to say.” We have thus emended the text from the codices of Ursinus and Pithoeus. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0817C] *Dedim* in Pam. and Fran.] “Therefore the soul, which possesses a corporeality of its own, will by itself suffice for the capacity of suffering and sensation, so that it has no need for the restoration of the flesh.”

On the contrary, it will need it to this extent: not because it cannot perceive anything without the flesh, but because it must also perceive together with the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0817C] *Quia* in Rhen. and Seml.] [Note: [Col. 0817C] *Quia* in Rhen. and Seml.] For insofar as it is sufficient by itself for action, it is sufficient also for suffering. Yet it is less sufficient by itself for action. For by itself it possesses only the ability to think, desire, and determine; to complete the deed, however, it awaits the flesh’s assistance. Thus, likewise, [Col. 0817B] for suffering it demands partnership with the flesh, so that it may suffer through the flesh as fully as it was unable to act fully without it.

And therefore, concerning those things for which it is sufficient by itself—desire, thought, and will—it meanwhile pays their penalty. But if these were sufficient for the fullness of merit, so that deeds too were not required, the soul would suffice entirely for the completion of judgment, being judged for those things in performing which it alone had sufficed. Since, however, deeds too are bound to merit, and deeds are administered through the flesh, the soul’s being comforted or tormented without the flesh is no longer sufficient for the works of the flesh as well—even if the soul has a body, [Note: [Col. 0817D] “Even if it has a body.” This error of Tertullian can be excused if the multitude of those who fell into it in those times carries any weight. I shall nevertheless add one testimony only, lest I become too lengthy, from Clement of Alexandria in the *Epitome*, Greek edition of Sylburgius: καὶ οἱ ἄγγελοι σώματά εἰσιν, ὁρῶνται γοῦν· ἀλλὰ καὶ ψυχὴ σῶμα, “The angels are bodies, for they are seen; and the soul too is a body.” Since this passage also mentions angels, I note that Tertullian held the same opinion about angels and maintained this paradox in *Against Marcion*, book 3, chapter 9, and *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapters 3 and 6, where he teaches that angels assumed real bodies. St. Basil also seems to hold this opinion in *On the Holy Spirit to Amphilochius*, chapter 16. Lactantius likewise, *Institutes*, book 2, chapter 15, where he says that angels are subtle spirits. Add Cassian, *Conference* 7, chapter 13, and John of Thessalonica in the Seventh Synod. Blessed Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 59, seems to hesitate—as St. Bernard later did in Homily 5 on the *Song of Songs*—over whether spirits themselves possess natural bodies as human beings possess theirs. But when they are called πῦρ φλέγον, “burning fire,” in Psalm 103, Augustine says concerning that passage that this is said not properly but metaphorically: namely, that by these words the angels, God’s ministers, fervent in spirit, are signified. Blessed John Chrysostom agrees with this interpretation in his treatment of Isaiah 6: τὸ ταχὺ, τὸ κοῦφον, τὸ δραστήριον ἡμῖν διὰ τῶν στοιχείων ἐνδεικνύμενος, “indicating to us through these elements their swiftness, lightness, and energetic activity.” Theodoret has almost the same on that same Psalm 103. LE PR.] even if it has members, which accordingly are not sufficient for it to perceive fully, just as they are not sufficient for it to act perfectly. [Note: [Col. 0817C] “Fully, just as” is absent from Rhen.]

For this reason, in whatever manner it acted, in that same manner [Col. 0818A] it suffers in the regions below, tasting judgment first, just as it first introduced the offense; yet it awaits the flesh, so that through it the soul may also make recompense for the deeds whose conceptions it entrusted to the flesh. Finally, this will be the rationale of the judgment appointed for the final end: that through the presentation of the flesh the whole divine judgment may be completed. Otherwise, what souls even now reap in the regions below would not have been deferred until the end, if it were appointed for souls alone. [Note: [Col. 0817C] *Decerpuntur* in Rhen. and Seml.]

## CHAPTER XVIII

Thus far I have dealt with preliminary constructions designed to fortify the meaning of all the Scriptures that promise the return of the flesh. Since so many authoritative grounds of just advocacy provide for it—by which I mean the honors belonging to the substance itself, then the powers of God, then examples of those powers, then the principles of judgment and its necessities—the Scriptures must surely be understood [Col. 0818B] in accordance with the prior determinations of so many authorities, not according to the inventions of heretics that arise from unbelief alone: namely, because it is held incredible that a substance withdrawn by destruction should be restored, not because the substance itself is undeserving of it, or because it is impossible for God, or because it is unfit for judgment. [Note: [Col. 0817C] *Tota auctoritate si* in Rhen.] [Note: [Col. 0817C] *Rationis judicii et necessitatis* in Fran.] [Note: [Col. 0818C] *Et* in Rhen. and Seml.] [Note: [Col. 0818C] Rhen. conjectures *inremeabile*.] [Note: [Col. 0818C] *Inhabitabile* in Rhen.]

It would plainly be incredible if it had not been proclaimed by God—except that, even if God had not proclaimed it, it ought to have been presumed of itself, so that its not having been proclaimed would be because it had already been determined by so many authorities. [Note: [Col. 0818C] *Aut plane* in Rhen.] [Note: [Col. 0818C] *Praejudicatum* in Rhen.] But since it also resounds in divine utterances, it is so far from being understood otherwise than those considerations demand by which it is proved even without divine utterances. [Note: [Col. 0818C] *Personat* in Rhen., Pam., and Seml.] [Note: [Col. 0818C] *Persuadeatur* in Rhen. and Seml.]

Let us therefore first see under what title [Note: [Col. 0818C] *Quoniam* in Ven.] [Note: [Col. 0818C] *Stylo* in Rhen. and Seml.] this hope has been posted publicly. [Col. 0818C] One edict of God, I think, hangs before everyone: [Note: [Col. 0818D] “One edict of God, I think, hangs before everyone.” It hangs on an affixed tablet, from which it may conveniently be read at ground level. Thus Ausonius, *Panegyric*: “If I should order these letters of yours to be hung like an edict upon all pillars and porticoes, from which they may be read at ground level,” etc. Thus he calls the creed of the Christian faith an edict; and above he said, “under what title this hope has been posted publicly,” alluding to the edicts of praetors or Caesars, which were customarily written and displayed upon the *album*, that is, a tablet. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0818D] “An edict of God hangs before everyone.” I add nothing to the explanation of [Col. 0819D] Rigault except that the learned Cujacius has taught me that the *album* was a clean and polished tablet or sheet, not a tablet marked with white letters, as Theophilus believed. Against anyone convicted of damaging that sheet or tablet, even when it was made of some other material, there lay a pecuniary or popular action. Moreover, he was also punished by extraordinary proceedings under the penalty of the Cornelian Law concerning forgery. Gather this from law *Si quis id quod*, Digest, *De Jurisdictione*, and the penultimate law of the Digest, *Lex Cornelia de falsis*. LE PR.] [Col. 0819A] **the resurrection of the dead**. Two words: plain, definite, polished clean.

I shall address the words themselves and examine them, to determine to which substance they bind themselves. When I hear that resurrection threatens—or awaits—a human being, I must ask what part of him has been allotted the fate of falling.
