For nothing will await resurrection except that which has first fallen. Anyone who does not know that the flesh falls through death can likewise be ignorant that it stands through life. Nature pronounces God’s sentence: “Earth you are, and into earth you shall go.” Even one who has not heard it sees it. [Note: [Col. 0819C] *Audit* in Rhen. and Seml.] No death is anything other than the collapse of the members. [Note: [Col. 0819C] *Est* absent from Rhen. and Seml.]

The Lord also expressed this fate of the body when clothed in that very substance: “Destroy,” he says (John 11), “this temple, and I will raise it again in three days.” For he showed that what belongs to that which is destroyed, dashed down, and lies fallen is also to be raised and resurrected, [Note: [Col. 0819C] *Cum* absent from Par.] [Note: [Col. 0819C] *Cujus* in Rhen., Rig., Ven., and Seml.] [Note: [Col. 0819C] *Revelari* in Ven.] although he also carried about a soul trembling even unto death, but not falling through death. [Note: [Col. 0819C] *Circumferat* in Rhen. and Par.] For Scripture had said, “He spoke concerning his body.” [Col. 0819B]

Indeed, it is so completely the flesh that is overthrown by death that it is thereafter called a *cadaver* from *cadere*, “to fall.” [Note: [Col. 0819C] *Enuntietur* in Par. and Jun.] The soul, however, does not fall even in terminology, because it does not collapse in condition. Rather, it is the soul that brings collapse upon the body when it is breathed out, just as it is the soul that will raise the body from the earth when it enters it. That which raised it by entering cannot fall. That which dashes it down by departing cannot collapse. [Note: [Col. 0819C] “That which raised it by entering cannot fall. It cannot” omitted in Rig. and Ven.] [Note: [Col. 0819D] *Eligit* in Rhen. and Seml.]

I shall state it more closely: the soul does not even fall asleep with the body, nor is it prostrated when the flesh is. For it is active and tossed about in dreams; but it would be at rest if it lay fallen, and it would lie fallen if it had fallen. [Note: [Col. 0819D] *Sedenim* in Rhen. and Seml.] [Note: [Col. 0820C] “And it would lie fallen if it had fallen” absent from Rhen. and Seml.] Thus it does not fall into the reality of death, since it does not collapse even into its image. [Note: [Col. 0820C] *Veritate* in Rhen. and Seml.] [Note: [Col. 0820C] *Imagine* in Rhen. and Seml.]

Now examine the following word, “dead,” in the same way, to determine upon which substance it rests. In this matter, however, let us grant that mortality is sometimes assigned to the soul by heretics: [Note: [Col. 0819D] “Mortality is assigned to the soul by heretics,” etc. Those who substitute “immortality” give no consideration at all to the matter under discussion. For I think Tertullian is identifying those heretics who arose in Arabia in the time of Origen, who said that souls were corrupted and perished together with bodies and that the bodies would return to life together with those same souls. Eusebius relates this in *Ecclesiastical History*, book 6, chapter 30. LE PR.] so that, if the mortal soul is to obtain resurrection, this establishes in advance that the no less mortal flesh will also share in resurrection. But now the proper sense of the word must be vindicated for the lot that belongs to it. [Col. 0820A]

Since resurrection, by the very fact itself, belongs to a thing that falls—that is, to the flesh—the same thing will also be present in the designation “dead,” because the resurrection belonging to a thing that falls is called “the resurrection of the dead.” We also learn this through Abraham, the father of faith and a man intimate with God. For when he asked the sons of Heth for a place in which to bury Sarah, he said: “Give me, therefore, a possession for a tomb among you, and I shall bury my dead” (Gen. 23)—that is, her flesh. [Note: [Col. 0820C] *Heth* in Rhen. and Seml., with the same meaning.] [Note: [Col. 0820C] *Mortuum meum* in Rig. and Ven.] For he would not have desired a place in which to bury the soul, even if the soul were believed mortal and even if it deserved to be called dead. But if the body is the dead thing, the resurrection will belong to bodies when it is called “the resurrection of the dead.”

## CHAPTER XIX

Accordingly, this examination of the title and of the proclamation itself, which certainly defends the faithful meaning of the words, must contribute to this end: if the opposing party introduces confusion under the pretext of figures and riddles, all the clearer passages should prevail, and the more certain should prescribe the interpretation of the uncertain. [Note: [Col. 0820C] *Illic* in Fran.] [Note: [Col. 0820C] *Qua* in Rhen., Seml., and Oberth.] [Col. 0820B]

For certain people, having seized upon the very customary form of prophetic speech—which is often, though not always, allegorical and figurative—distort even the plainly announced resurrection of the dead into an imaginary meaning. They assert that death itself must likewise be understood spiritually: that the real death is not this one that lies before us, the separation of flesh and soul, but ignorance of God, through which a human being, dead to God, has lain in error no less than in a tomb.

Consequently, they contend that the resurrection is that by which someone, having entered into the truth, is reanimated and restored to life for God, the death of ignorance having been dispelled, and bursts forth as though from the tomb of the old man. [Note: [Col. 0820D] “They contend that the resurrection is that.” These are trifles and sophistries employed by Hymenaeus and Philetus and by those heretics who asserted that death itself must be understood spiritually. They abused the Apostle’s words in Romans 6: “Do you not know, brothers, that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead,” etc. He refutes this in the next chapter. Those heretics, I mean Hymenaeus and Philetus, who had departed from the truth and affirmed, as the blessed Apostle testifies in 2 Timothy 2, that the resurrection had already occurred, called the procreation of children “resurrection.” LE PR.] [Note: [Col. 0820C] *Addita* in Rhen. and Seml.] They argue this because the Lord also likened the scribes and Pharisees to whitewashed tombs. [Note: [Col. 0820C] “Whitewashed” absent from Rig. and Ven.]

Hence, therefore, those who have obtained resurrection through faith are with the Lord once they have put him on in baptism. [Col. 0820C] [Note: [Col. 0820D] *Cum baptisma* in Rhen.; Junius has *cum eam baptismate vel baptismo*.] Indeed, by this very device they have often been accustomed to deceive our people in discussions, as though they too admitted the resurrection of the flesh. “Woe,” they say, “to him who has not risen in this flesh,” lest they be struck down at once if they openly deny the resurrection. [Col. 0821A] Silently, however, according to their own understanding, they mean this: “Woe to him who, while still in the flesh, has not come to know the heretical mysteries.” [Note: [Col. 0821D] “Has come to know the heretical mysteries.” Since heretics love darkness more than light, they employ a secret and obscure tradition, fearing that, if they reveal their shamefulness, their inventions will vanish into smoke. But whoever has once exposed those mysteries trusts that he has gained the victory; for to have exposed heresies is to have defeated them. Tertullian teaches this in chapter 3 of the book *Against the Valentinians*. LE PR.] For this is resurrection among them.

Moreover, many who contend that resurrection occurs when the soul departs interpret “to leave the tomb” as “to escape from the world,” because the world is the habitation of the dead—that is, of those ignorant of God. Or they understand it as escaping from the body itself, because the body, like a tomb, confines the soul and detains it in the death of worldly life. [Note: [Col. 0821C] *Detinebat* in Par.]

## CHAPTER XX

On account of conjectures of this kind, therefore, I shall repel their first preliminary assumption, by which they maintain that the Prophets proclaimed everything through images. For if that were so, even the images themselves could not have been distinguished, unless realities too had been proclaimed, from which the images might be delineated. [Col. 0821B] [Note: [Col. 0821C] *Delinearentur* in Jun.] Indeed, if everything consists of figures, of what will those things be figures? How will you hold up a mirror if there is nowhere any face?

Thus, not everything consists of images, but there are also realities; not everything consists of shadows, but there are also bodies. This is so true that all the more notable things concerning the Lord himself were proclaimed more clearly than daylight. For the virgin both conceived in her womb—not figuratively—and gave birth to Emmanuel, God with us, Jesus—not obliquely. [Note: [Col. 0821C] “Lord” in Rhen. and Seml.] Yet he was to receive the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria obliquely (Isa. 8:4), but was manifestly to come in judgment with the elders and rulers of the people (Isa. 3:14). [Note: [Col. 0821C] “Princes” in Rhen. and Seml.]

For “the nations raged” (Ps. 2) in the person of Pilate, and “the peoples devised vain things” in the person of Israel. “The kings of the earth stood up”—Herod—and “the rulers assembled together”—Annas and Caiaphas—“against the Lord and against his Christ.” He also (Isa. 53) “was led like a sheep to slaughter,” [Note: [Col. 0821C] “Victim” in Fran.] and “like a lamb before its shearer”—namely Herod—he was voiceless, and thus “he did not open his mouth”; [Note: [Col. 0821C] Others add *se*, “itself.”] he placed his back before the scourges, [Col. 0822A] his cheeks before blows, and did not turn his face away from the missiles of spittle. [Note: [Col. 0821C] *In* in others.] [Note: [Col. 0821D] “From the foulness of spittle” in the codex of Pithoeus, Pam., and Fran.; “from the stains of spittle” in Jun.; “from the foulness of spit” in the Paris edition.] He was also “reckoned among the lawless”; his hands and feet were pierced (Ps. 21); he endured the casting of lots for his garment, bitter drinks, and the nodding heads of those who mocked him; and he was valued by the traitor at thirty pieces of silver (Zech. 11:12).

What figures are there here in Isaiah? What images in David? What riddles in Jeremiah, [Note: [Col. 0821D] “In Jeremiah.” Here Jeremiah is certainly put for Zechariah, for none of Jeremiah’s words are cited in what precedes; instead, mention is made of the thirty pieces of silver, concerning which Zechariah speaks. The blessed evangelist Matthew, whose feast we celebrate today, used the same freedom. EDD.] when not even his miracles were foretold through parables? Or were the eyes of the blind not opened (Isa. 35:6), and did the tongue of the mute not become clear? Were withered hands and feeble knees not restored, and did the lame not leap like a deer? [Note: [Col. 0822C] *Clodi* in Fran.]

Although we ourselves are also accustomed to interpret these things spiritually, according to an analogy with the soul’s faults that the Lord has healed, [Note: [Col. 0821D] “Although we are also accustomed to interpret these things spiritually.” Paul interpreted it thus in Hebrews 12, alluding to the passage of Isaiah, chapter 53: “Therefore, the hands that hang down,” etc. There he employs, not without reason, the metaphor of the stadium, which the Apostle frequently uses; and Faber discusses it learnedly in his work on athletic contests. For he is not speaking—indeed, he is not even alluding—to weakness arising from disease, but to weakness from struggle and weariness, exhorting us to do what vigorous contestants did, who, however fatigued, persisted bravely and fearlessly. LAC.] [Note: [Col. 0822C] *Et ipsi* in Fran. and Rig.; *ipsi* is absent from Seml.] [Note: [Col. 0822D] “The soul’s faults,” ψυχικῶν (*psychikōn*). RIG.] nevertheless, since they were also fulfilled carnally, they show that the Prophets proclaimed both kinds of fulfillment. This remains subject to the qualification that many of their utterances can be defended as bare and simple, pure of every cloud of allegory. [Col. 0822B] [Note: [Col. 0822C] *Quo* in Rig. and Ven.] [Note: [Col. 0822C] *Possunt* in Rhen. and Seml.]

Thus it is when the destructions of nations and cities resound (Isa. 13): of Tyre, Egypt, Babylon, Idumaea, and the Carthaginian ships; [Note: [Col. 0822D] “Thus it is when the destructions of nations,” etc. He undoubtedly means Isaiah, where the destructions—or fatal ends—of Tyre are foretold in chapter 23, of Egypt in chapter 20, of Babylon in chapter 13, of Idumaea in chapter 21, and of the Carthaginian ships. I read this in the English codex in place of *Carthaginensium*, in the aforementioned chapter 23, where according to the Septuagint one reads πλοῖα καρχηδόνος, that is, “ships of Carthage,” in place of what the Hebrew has as “ships of Tarshish,” that is, “of the sea,” according to blessed Jerome. The Septuagint also customarily renders this word as “sea,” except in this chapter alone, and there not only once but three times. PAM.] and thus it is when they fully recount the plagues or pardons of Israel itself, its captivities and restorations, and the outcome of its final dispersion. Who will interpret these things rather than acknowledge them? The events are contained in the writings, just as the writings are read in the events. [Note: [Col. 0822C] *Ligantur* in Pam., Fran., Rig., and Ven.] Thus the form of prophetic speech is not always allegorical, nor allegorical in everything, but only sometimes and in certain things.

## CHAPTER XXI

“If, then, it is allegorical sometimes and in certain things,” you say, “why may it not also be understood spiritually in the edict concerning the resurrection?” Because a very great body of reasoning intervenes.

First, what will they do with so many other divine documents that testify so openly to a bodily resurrection [Col. 0822C] that they admit no suspicion of figurative meaning? [Note: [Col. 0822C] *Ac talia* in Fran. and Pam.; *tot alia* in Rhen. and Seml.] [Note: [Col. 0822D] “That they admit no suspicion of figurative meaning,” etc. He means “suspicion” as he earlier spoke of a “cloud of allegory.” For suspicion concerns things hidden, obscure, and mystical. Thus George of Baetica, in his book *On Faith*: “Furthermore, if you do not understand from the many expressions set forth above, observe at least from what follows that all suspicions of an impious interpretation have been excluded.” RIG.] [Col. 0823A]

Surely it is equitable, as we also prescribed above, that the uncertain should be prejudged from the certain, and the obscure from the manifest, lest amid disagreement between the certain and the uncertain, the manifest and the obscure, faith be dissipated, truth be endangered, and the divinity itself be branded inconsistent. [Note: [Col. 0823C] “Faith be dissipated, truth be endangered,” etc. If the predictions concerning the resurrection were accepted in discordant senses, so that the conspicuous and explicit testimonies that speak openly of the resurrection of bodies did not compel the more obscure passages to be interpreted concerning bodily resurrection, but these ambiguous passages were instead distorted to refer only to a resurrection of souls, the following absurdities plainly result: God would be regarded as inconsistent, since in the manifest passages he had predicted a bodily resurrection, but in others a resurrection of souls only, as the adversaries maintained. Truth would therefore also be endangered, for since the prophecies would have been contradictory, people would risk error by assenting to a false prophecy; and faith would be dissipated, for all trust would rightly be denied to one who made such predictions. LAC.]

Then there is the fact that it is not credible that that article of the mystery to which the whole faith is committed and upon which the whole discipline exerts itself should appear to have been announced ambiguously and set forth obscurely. [Note: [Col. 0823C] *Tunc* in Rhen. and Seml.] [Note: [Col. 0823D] “That article of the mystery”: that is, the principal doctrine of the Christian faith, the resurrection of the flesh.] [Note: [Col. 0823C] *Annuata* in Rhen. and Seml.; *annuta* or *annutata* in Jun.] For unless the hope of resurrection plainly revealed the peril and reward, it would persuade no one to embrace a religion of this kind, especially one exposed to public hatred and a hostile indictment. No work is certain when its reward is uncertain. No fear is justified when the peril is doubtful. Both reward and peril depend upon the outcome of the resurrection.

[Col. 0823B] Moreover, if prophecy has so openly hurled forth God’s temporal, local, and personal decrees and judgments against cities, nations, and kings, how can it be that his eternal and universal arrangements for the whole human race fled from their own light? [Note: [Col. 0823C] *Sed* absent from Seml.] [Note: [Col. 0823C] *Aperta* in Pam. and Rhen.] [Note: [Col. 0823C] *Humanum* in others.] [Note: [Col. 0823C] *Quae* absent from Rig. and Ven.] The greater they were, the clearer they ought to have been, so that they might be believed to be greater. And I think that neither envy, deceit, inconsistency, nor pandering can be ascribed to God—the faults by which the promulgation of the decrees of the great is commonly mocked. [Note: [Col. 0823D] “By which the promulgation of the decrees of the great is commonly mocked.” “Of the great” means the more powerful, magistrates, and authorities. RIG.]

## CHAPTER XXII
After this, we must also consider those Scriptures which do not allow the resurrection—according to these “psychic” men, not to call them “spiritual”—either to be presumed to have occurred already here, in the knowledge of the truth, or to be claimed immediately upon departure from life.

[Note: [Col. 0823D] “According to these psychic men.” He preferred here to call the Valentinians “psychic” rather than “spiritual”; for although they interpreted the passages of Scripture concerning the resurrection spiritually [Col. 0824C], they are nevertheless called “psychic” here because they distorted the scriptural passages so as to refer only to the resurrection of souls. LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0824C] “Already here, in the knowledge of the truth,” etc. Since the heretics said that death was ignorance, as is clear from chapter 19, it followed that knowledge of the truth would be resurrection. Thus they said that the resurrection took place here, in this life and age [Col. 0824D], when someone attained knowledge of the truth—to which, as Paul said, God desires all people to come. LAC.]

For since the times of our entire hope have been fixed by the sacred pen, and it is not permissible to place that hope before the advent of Christ—toward which, I believe, our prayers sigh, toward the setting of this age, toward the passage of the world also into the great day of the Lord, the day of wrath and recompense, the final and hidden day, known to none but the Father, yet marked beforehand by signs and wonders, by convulsions of the elements, and by conflicts among the nations—I would unfold the prophecies, had the Lord himself remained silent. The prophets, indeed, were the Lord’s voice; but it carries greater weight that he seals them with his own mouth.

[Note: [Col. 0823C] Others read *aeque*; both words are absent from Semler and Rhenanus.]

[Note: [Col. 0823C] Rhenanus and Semler read “at the advent.”]

[Note: [Col. 0824D] “Our prayers sigh.” The position toward the Gentiles is therefore one thing, and that toward Christians another. For in the *Apology* he says to the Gentiles, “We pray for the postponement of the end,” meaning the end of the age. And in the book *On Prayer*: “How did certain people ask for a kind of prolongation for the age, when the kingdom of God, whose coming we pray for, tends toward the consummation of the age?” RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0823C] “Toward” is absent from Rhenanus and Semler.]

[Note: [Col. 0824C] “But” is absent from Rhenanus and Semler.]

[Note: [Col. 0824C] “Than” is absent from the Pithou manuscript, Rigault, and Venice.]

When questioned by his disciples as to when the events would occur which his remarks about the fate of the temple had meanwhile disclosed, he sets out the sequence of the times: first those belonging to the Jews, as far as the destruction of Jerusalem; then those common to all, as far as the consummation of the age. For after declaring, “And then Jerusalem will be trampled by the nations until the times of the nations are fulfilled”—that is, of the nations to be chosen by God and gathered together with the remnant of Israel—he thereafter proclaims to the whole world and age, in accordance with Joel and Daniel and the whole council of the prophets, the signs destined to appear in the sun, moon, and stars; the constriction of nations accompanied by bewilderment; the roaring of the sea; and the agitation of people growing cold with fear and with expectation of the things threatening the inhabited earth. “For,” he says (Matt. XXI), “the powers of the heavens will be shaken; and then they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with very great power and glory. But when these things begin to happen, you will rise up and lift up your heads, because your redemption has drawn near.”

[Note: [Col. 0824D] “When questioned by his disciples.” Because the following material is supplied by Luke the Evangelist alone, we merely noted Luke 21 in the margin; and concerning the Evangelist’s words we therefore refer the reader to Book IV *Against Marcion*, where this chapter 21 is explained more fully. PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0824C] Rhenanus and Semler read the singular, “had disclosed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0824C] Ursinus’s book reads “arranges.”]

[Note: [Col. 0824C] Others read “consummation.”]

[Note: [Col. 0824C] Francius and Pamelius read “to be bound.”]

[Note: [Col. 0824C] Paris reads “the remnant.”]

[Note: [Col. 0824D] “According to Joel and Daniel.” The passage from Joel, chapter 2, is cited below at the place indicated, as is also that from Daniel, chapter 7. It is clear from the words cited in both places—both concerning wonders in heaven and concerning the Son of Man coming in the clouds—that the Author is also alluding to Daniel here. PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0824C] Others read “the bruising.”]

[Note: [Col. 0824C] Others read “growing thoroughly cold”; others, “wasting away.”]

[Note: [Col. 0825C] The Wouwer manuscript reads “you will rise out.”]

[Note: [Col. 0825C] Rhenanus and Semler read “will have drawn near.”]

And yet he said that it was drawing near, not that it was already present; and “when these things begin to happen,” not “when they have happened.” For when they have happened, then our redemption will be present; until then it is said to be drawing near, meanwhile raising and arousing our spirits toward the now imminent fruit of hope. To this is also appended the parable of trees growing tender into the stalk of the blossom, and thereafter into the blossom itself, the forerunner of fruit: “So also you, when you see all these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near. Therefore keep watch at all times, that you may be deemed worthy to escape all these things and to stand before the Son of Man”—assuredly through the resurrection, after everything has previously been accomplished.

Thus, although it puts forth shoots in the knowledge of the mystery, it blossoms and bears fruit at the manifestation of the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0825C] Rhenanus reads “had borne fruit”; others, “bears fruit.”]

Who, then, has so prematurely and harshly roused the Lord—who is still at the right hand of God—to shatter the earth according to Isaiah, though the earth, I think, is still intact? Who has already subjected Christ’s enemies beneath his feet, according to David, as though he were swifter than the Father, while the entire assembly of the populace is still shouting, “The Christians to the lion”? Who has beheld Jesus descending from heaven in the same form in which the apostles saw him ascend, according to the angels’ decree? To this day no tribe has beaten its breast before another tribe, acknowledging him whom they pierced. No one has yet received Elijah; no one has yet fled Antichrist; no one has yet mourned Babylon’s fall. And is there already someone who has risen again—other than a heretic?

[Note: [Col. 0825D] “While the entire assembly of the populace is still shouting,” etc. That is, the whole people, the entire circus. And in the book *On the Spectacles*, “the divisions of the populace,” that is, the people distinguished according to each person’s condition and status. Juvenal: “They kill anyone at all by popular acclaim.” RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0825C] Rhenanus and Semler read “shouting in protest.”]

[Note: [Col. 0825D] “The Christians to the lion.” The Gentiles of old pursued Christians with implacable hatred and consigned them to the beasts, to the lions. Christians, as a hated nation, were subjected to that punishment. In the *Martyrdom of Polycarp*, Eusebius reports the cry, “A lion for Polycarp” (*tō Polykarpō leonta*, τῷ Πολυκάρπῳ λέοντα). See Cyprian, Epistle 55. LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0825D] “No one has yet fled Antichrist,” etc. The former statement is not found in express words in the Apocalypse, but is sufficiently implied in chapter 12, where the woman—that is, the Church—is said to have fled into the wilderness from the face of the dragon, and especially in chapter 18 [Col. 0826D], where the people are commanded to depart from Babylon, and where it is further written: “And the kings of the earth will weep and lament over her.” For that reason we noted only this passage in the margin. PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0825C] “And” is absent from Rhenanus and Semler.]

[Note: [Col. 0825C] Others read “has risen.”]

He has indeed already come forth from the tomb of the body, though he is even now subject to fevers and ulcers; he has already trampled his enemies, though he must even now wrestle against the world’s rulers. And of course he already reigns, though he must even now render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s.

[Note: [Col. 0826D] “He has indeed already come forth from the tomb of the body.” This is irony concerning Christ, by which—in my opinion—he ridicules the belief of those heretics who acknowledged that Christ had indeed risen, but remained mortal. At the same time he tacitly alludes both to Ephesians 6, “Our wrestling is against the rulers of the world,” or, as he himself translates it, “the powers of the world”—the Greek being *kosmokratoras* (κοσμοκράτορας)—and to Matthew 22, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s.” PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0826D] “Even now subject to fevers and ulcers.” The sense is this: because the heretics babbled that the resurrection had already occurred through spiritual life and through a kind of withdrawal and separation from the body, which they called a tomb, when the soul asserted and freed itself from the body’s laws and, as it were, its weight—for they were not speaking merely of departure from the body, which occurs through natural death—the Author cleverly and ironically says: Very well, let the awakened heretic come forth from the tomb of the body; but how is he still subject to fevers and ulcers, which prove that he bears the body’s burden? LAC.]

## CHAPTER XXIII

The Apostle, writing to the Colossians (Col. I, 29), does indeed teach that we were once dead, estranged and hostile to the Lord in our understanding, while we lived in the most wicked works; and then that we were buried with Christ in baptism and raised together with him through faith in the effective power of God, who raised him from the dead: “And when you were dead in your transgressions and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made you alive with him, forgiving you all transgressions.” And again: “If you died with Christ to the elements of the world, why do you pass judgment as though living in the world?”

[Note: [Col. 0825C] The editors conjecture the singular, “understanding.”]

[Note: [Col. 0825C] Others read “raised.”]

[Note: [Col. 0825C] Others read “uncircumcision.”]

[Note: [Col. 0825C] Francius and Pamelius read “as indeed”; Junius, “why as.”]

But while he thus makes us spiritually dead, yet acknowledges that at some time we shall also die bodily; and therefore, while likewise reckoning us spiritually raised, he equally does not deny that we shall also rise bodily. Finally, he says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, sitting at God’s right hand; set your mind on the things above, not on those below.” Thus he shows that it is in mind that we rise, since as yet it is by the mind alone that we can reach heavenly things. We would neither seek nor set our minds upon them if we already possessed them.

[Note: [Col. 0825D] Venice reads “we shall seek.”]

He also adds: “For you are dead”—that is, to transgressions, not to yourselves—“and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” What is hidden, therefore, has not yet been grasped.

[Note: [Col. 0826C] Semler and Rhenanus read “to us.”]

[Note: [Col. 0826C] Paris reads “our.”]

So too John: “And,” he says, “it has not yet been manifested what we shall be. We know that, if he manifests himself, we shall be like him.” So far are we from already being what we do not know—for surely, if we already were it, we would know. Thus during this interval there is a contemplation of hope through faith, not its manifestation or possession, but its expectation.

[Note: [Col. 0826C] Rhenanus and Semler read “manifest.”]

[Note: [Col. 0826C] Rhenanus and Semler read “we are.”]

[Note: [Col. 0826C] Others read “has been manifested.”]

[Note: [Col. 0826C] Rhenanus and Semler read “like him.”]

[Note: [Col. 0826C] Rhenanus and Semler read “presentation.”]

Concerning this hope and expectation Paul says to the Galatians (Gal. V): “For through the Spirit, by faith, we await the hope of righteousness.” He does not say, “We possess it.” By “righteousness” he means God’s righteousness arising from the judgment in which we shall be judged regarding our reward.

[Note: [Col. 0826C] Rhenanus and Semler read “it will be judged.”]

While he himself remains in suspense toward this, he writes to the Philippians (Phil. III): “If by any means,” he says, “I may arrive at the rising again which is from the dead—not that I have already received it, or have already been perfected.” Yet he had certainly believed and had come to know all the mysteries—he, the vessel of election and teacher of the nations. Nevertheless he adds: “But I pursue, if I may grasp that for which I have been grasped by Christ.” More emphatically still: “I do not consider myself, brothers, to have grasped it. One thing, however: forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue according to the goal, toward the prize of the calling to account, through which I might arrive”—assuredly at the rising again from the dead, but at its own proper time, as he says to the Galatians (Gal. VI): “Let us not grow weary in doing good, for in its own time we shall reap.”

[Note: [Col. 0827D] “He had come to know all the mysteries.” He calls “mysteries” everything pertaining to the true or Christian faith. Above he said “knowledge of the truth,” and shortly below he will say “knowledge of the mystery.” RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0827C] Others add “in what way.”]

[Note: [Col. 0827D] “Toward the prize of the calling to account.” Thus Septimius read the Apostle as *epi to brabeion tēs anenklēseōs* (ἐπὶ τὸ βραβεῖον τῆς ἀνεγκλήσεως), not as we read today, *tēs anō klēseōs* (τῆς ἄνω κλήσεως), “of the upward calling.” RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0827C] Pamelius, Francius, Rigault, and Venice read “we shall reap.”]

So also concerning Onesiphorus he says to Timothy (II Tim. I): “May the Lord grant him to find mercy on that day.” And Timothy himself he commands (I Tim. VI) to keep the commandment unstained and irreproachable until the appearing of the Lord Jesus Christ, “which in his own times the blessed and only Ruler, the King of kings and Lord of lords, will reveal”—speaking of God.

Concerning these times Peter also says in Acts (Acts III): “Repent, therefore, and return to soundness, that your transgressions may be blotted out, so that times of refreshing may come upon you from the presence of God, and that he may send the Christ appointed beforehand for you, whom heaven must receive until the times of the manifestation of all things which God spoke by the mouth of the holy prophets.”

[Note: [Col. 0827C] Rhenanus and Semler read “for us.”]

## CHAPTER XXIV

Learn what these times are together with the Thessalonians. For we read (I Thess. I): “How you turned from idols to serve the living and true God and to await from heaven his Son, Jesus, whom he raised from the dead.”

[Note: [Col. 0827C] “These” is absent from Rhenanus and Semler.]

[Note: [Col. 0827C] Rhenanus and Semler read “from.”]

And again (I Thess. II): “For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of exultation, if not you also before our Lord Jesus Christ at his advent?”

[Note: [Col. 0827C] Others read “as also”; Semler, “which also.”]

Likewise (I Thess. II): “Before our God and Father, at the advent of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints.”

[Note: [Col. 0827C] Rhenanus and Semler read the accusative, “the advent.”]

While teaching that their falling asleep should occasion less grief, he at the same time explains the times of the resurrection, saying (I Thess. III and IV): “For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him through Jesus those who have fallen asleep. For this we say to you in the word of the Lord: that we who are alive, who remain until the advent of our Lord, will not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself, at the command, at the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven, and the dead in Christ will rise first; then we who are alive, who together with them will be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air; and so we shall always be with the Lord.”

[Note: [Col. 0827C] Others read “to be pitied.”]

[Note: [Col. 0827C] Rhenanus and Semler read “God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0828C] Francius reads “the Lord.”]

What voice of the archangel, what trumpet of God, has already been heard—unless perhaps in the chambers of the heretics? For even if the evangelical word may be called the trumpet of God, which has already summoned them, still they must either already be bodily dead in order to have risen—and then how are they alive?—or have been caught up into the clouds—and then how are they here? Truly most wretched, as the Apostle declared, they will be found to have hoped in this life alone, and are to be excluded because they seize beforehand what is promised after it, having missed the truth no less than Phygelus and Hermogenes.

[Note: [Col. 0828C] Others read “has summoned.”]

[Note: [Col. 0828C] Rhenanus, Semler, Rigault, and Venice read “by excluding.”]

Therefore the majesty of the Holy Spirit, discerning opinions of this sort, warns in the very Epistle to the Thessalonians (I Thess. V): “But concerning the times and the intervals of times, brothers, there is no need to write to you; for you yourselves know most certainly that the day of the Lord will come just like a thief in the night. When they say, ‘Peace, and all things are secure,’ then sudden destruction will press upon them.”

[Note: [Col. 0828C] Semler conjectures “first.”]

And in the Second Epistle, with fuller solicitude for the same people (II Thess. II): “But I beseech you, brothers, by the advent of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering to him, that you not be quickly shaken in mind or disturbed, either by a spirit, or by a word”—that is, of false prophets—“or by a letter”—that is, of false apostles—“as though from us, as if the day of the Lord were imminent. Let no one deceive you in any way: for unless the apostasy comes first”—that is, the apostasy of this empire—“and the man of transgression is revealed, that is, Antichrist, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or religion, so that he sits in God’s temple, declaring himself to be God. Do you not remember that, when I was with you, I told you these things? And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of iniquity is already at work; only let him who now holds continue to hold, until he is removed from the midst.”

[Note: [Col. 0828C] “But” is absent from Rhenanus and Semler.]

[Note: [Col. 0828C] Rhenanus and Semler read “false apostles.”]

[Note: [Col. 0828C] Rhenanus and Semler read “false prophets.”]

[Note: [Col. 0828C] Venice reads “is at hand.”]

[Note: [Col. 0827D] “For unless the apostasy comes first”—namely, the apostasy of this empire. Paul’s statement in the First Epistle to the Corinthians VII is: “The time that remains has been shortened” (*ho kairos synestalmenos to loipon estin*, ὁ καιρὸς συνεσταλμένος τὸ λοιπὸν ἐστιν). From this Tertullian translated his expression, “The time has been gathered in.” Nor does Peter mean anything else when, in his later epistle, he affirms that the day of the Lord—which will make present to the saints the joys promised them—is not delayed.

But the interpretation of this admonition held the minds of some among the Christian common people of Thessalonica in such uncertainty that, as though already wearied by waiting, they began to call their hopes empty, to despair of the Lord’s advent, and thus to lend an ear to impostures urging them toward apostasy. Who would not marvel that people formed by the discourses of the Apostle himself as he administered the divine commandments should prove so frivolous as not to retain what they had properly understood?

Paul therefore comes to the aid of those dangerously troubled and asks that they not allow their faith to be undermined by rash fickleness, but remember what he had discussed with them in person concerning the end of the age and the day of the final judgment. That day of the Lord would not be present until first the departure occurred, and immediately thereafter the man of sin, the man of perdition, was made manifest. The Apostle therefore says that they had no reason to be shaken as though deceived by false promises, for two things would precede it: the apostasy and that man of sin.

That Paul had spoken at length about these two matters when he came to Thessalonica can be inferred from his rebuking them as forgetful and insufficiently retentive. He then mentions darkly and in riddles the matters he had treated more openly among them. “For,” he says, “the mystery of iniquity is already at work; only let him who now holds continue to hold, until he is removed from the midst.”

He had said above that the advent of the Lord’s kingdom had been ordered in such a way that first the apostasy must precede it, and then the man of sin. He says that the mystery of iniquity was already bringing this man of sin into operation even then, indicating impostors, false brothers, and perverse Christians, who were furtively and secretly proceeding to choke the apostolic seed with sterile wild oats and ill-fated darnel. These were indeed the cradle of Antichrist, already creeping in behind the apostles’ footsteps, but destined not to ravage openly until the apostasy had first occurred.

“Only let him who holds continue to hold, until he departs from the midst.” The Apostle surely would not have wrapped these matters up so carefully unless he meant something whose more explicit declaration might have harmed either himself or even the Thessalonian church. He therefore sought darkness a second and a third time. For after saying that the day of the Lord would not come unless the apostasy came first, he added, “You know what restrains.” Finally he poured yet more obscurity over it: *monon ho katechōn arti, heōs ek mesou genētai* (μόνον ὃ κατέχων ἄρτι, ἕως ἐκ μέσου γένηται), which the old translator, so far as he was able, plunged into still darker concealment: “Only let him who holds continue to hold, until he is removed from the midst.”

These things may indeed have remained unknown to those from whom it was conducive to Christian peace that they be concealed. I would by no means believe, however, that they were obscure to the Thessalonians, with whom the Apostle had personally discussed the matter. Nor were they obscure to the Christians immediately succeeding the apostolic tradition, from whom Tertullian appears to have received the interpretation which, in his book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, he inserts among the Apostle’s words in the clearest light at last.

He reports the very words showing that the day of the Lord was not imminent and would not come “unless the apostasy comes first.” “Of this empire, of course,” he says, plainly signifying the Roman Empire, “and the man of transgression is revealed, that is, Antichrist, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or religion, so that he sits in God’s temple, declaring himself to be God. Do you not remember that, when I was with you, I told you these things? And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of iniquity is already at work; only let him who now holds continue to hold, until he is removed from the midst. Who but the Roman state, whose departure, when it has been dispersed among ten kings, will bring Antichrist upon us, and then the lawless one will be revealed?”

We observe that the interpretation of so great a man, one so close to the times of the apostles, was confirmed as most appropriate to the matter under discussion by the common agreement of all later writers except Augustine and Theodoret. Augustine, indeed, in Book XX of *The City of God*, admits that he is altogether ignorant of what the Apostle meant. Yet immediately afterward he adds, in the clearest terms, the “suspicion,” as he calls it, of those who believed that Paul had been unwilling to write it openly lest he incur the accusation that he wished evil upon the Roman Empire, which was expected to be eternal.

Chrysostom certainly judged this suspicion—or rather opinion—so consonant with the truth that, neglecting the other interpretations, he handed down this one alone to his church as entirely certain, praising the counsel of the most holy Apostle in avoiding hatreds which he would have incurred not only without any benefit to the Christian cause, but at the greatest danger to it. For had the letter once been intercepted, and the prophecy of an apostasy destructive to the Roman Empire discovered, who would not immediately have crushed the Apostle himself as leader and standard-bearer, and indeed all the faithful as accomplices in a most criminal conspiracy?

As for Theodoret, I marvel that, after rejecting so suitable an interpretation, he follows one utterly insipid: namely, that the words “you know what restrains” and “only let him who holds continue to hold” signify the decrees of God forbidding Antichrist’s assault until the Gospel has been preached throughout the whole world. For what prevented this from being written in the plainest possible terms? Why did it have to be so heavily shadowed by such studied obscurity?

Let us therefore be content with our Tertullian, to whose opinion Augustine himself finally appears to yield. “Yet,” he says, “the Apostle’s statement, ‘Only let him who now holds continue to hold,’ is not unreasonably believed to have been spoken of the Roman Empire itself, as though it said: ‘Only let him who now rules continue to rule until he is removed from the midst,’ that is, taken away from the midst.” Jerome explained this opinion so accurately and copiously in his *Epistle to the Philippians* and Question XI *To Algasia* that he left no room for doubt. RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0829A] Francius and Pamelius read “because.”]

[Note: [Col. 0829A] Rhenanus reads “who.”]

[Note: [Col. 0829A] Rhenanus and Semler read “holds.”]

[Note: [Col. 0830C] “Only let him who now holds continue to hold.” Lampridius relates that, by a similar riddle, a prophet promised Alexander Severus the imperial power: “The imperial power awaits you—the power which holds imperial power.” From this, he says, it was understood that Alexander would become ruler of the Roman Empire; for where is imperial power except among the Romans—the power which holds imperial power? RIG.]

Who is it but the Roman state, whose departure, when dispersed among ten kings, will bring Antichrist upon us? “And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of his mouth and nullify by his appearing; his advent is according to the operation of Satan, with every power and signs and lying wonders, and with every deception of unrighteousness for those who perish.”

[Note: [Col. 0830A] Rhenanus and Semler read “of Antichrist.”]

[Note: [Col. 0830C] “By the appearing of his advent.” As though translating *epiphaneia* [the printed Greek, *ἐπιφπνεία*, is evidently corrupt]. For he often describes Satan as the Lord’s rival. RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0830D] “His advent.” That is, Antichrist’s. RIG.]

## CHAPTER XXV

In the Apocalypse of John, too, the sequence of the times is set forth—a sequence which even the souls of the martyrs beneath the altar, as they demand vengeance and judgment, have learned to await: first, the world must drink its plagues from the angels’ bowls; that prostituted city must receive its deserved end from the ten kings; and the beast, Antichrist, together with his false prophet, must wage war against the Church of God. Then, after the devil has meanwhile been confined in the abyss, the privilege of the first resurrection is to be dispensed from the thrones; and afterward, once the fire has also been given, the verdict of the universal resurrection is to be adjudged from the books.

[Note: [Col. 0830D] “In the Apocalypse of John.” He indicates chapter 20. From this very many took occasion to embrace the opinion of the Chiliasts, or Millenarians. They believed that the righteous would remain upon the earth for a thousand years, so as to receive a hundredfold return for what they had abandoned for Christ, as the Lord had promised. There were very many heretics of this kind in antiquity, among whom Cerinthus was conspicuous. Tertullian nevertheless differs from him, although he appears to have imbibed the Chiliasts’ error. He shared this with certain ancient Fathers—I mean Papias, bishop of Hierapolis, and blessed Justin in his *Dialogue Against Trypho*. Eusebius teaches what authority Justin possessed, Book IV of the *History*, chapter 17: *houtōsi de spoudēs einai axioi kai tois palaiois edokoun hoi tandros logoi, hōs ton Eirēnion apomnēmoneuein autou phōnas* (οὑτωσὶ δὲ σπουδῆς εἶναι ἄξιοι καὶ τοῖς παλαιοῖς ἐδόκουν οἱ τἀνδρὸς λόγοι, ὡς τὸν Εἰρήνιον ἀπομνημονεύειν αὐτοῦ φωνάς): “The writings of this man Justin were considered so worthy of attention by the ancients that Irenaeus quotes his words.” After Tertullian, others followed the error; Tertullian himself, however, is excused by blessed Augustine in chapter 7 of Book XX of *The City of God*. LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0830A] “John” is absent from Rhenanus and Semler.]

[Note: [Col. 0831D] “Together with his false prophet.” I would say that Satan is meant, were it not immediately to follow, “and then, after the devil has meanwhile been confined in the abyss.” It remains, therefore, for us to say that the one meant is the lawless agent who presides over Antichristian fury in the age. RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0831C] Rhenanus and Semler read “bound.”]

[Note: [Col. 0831D] “From the thrones.” From the thrones in Apocalypse XX. RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0831C] Pamelius and Francius read “to the fire.”]

[Note: [Col. 0831D] “From the books”: *tōn gegrammenōn en tois bibliois* (τῶν γεγραμμένων ἐν τοῖς βιβλίοις), “of the things written in the books.” Ibid. RIG.]

Since, therefore, the Scriptures mark out both the condition of the final times and place the whole fruit of Christian hope at the *exodium*—the conclusion—of the age, it is evident either that everything whatsoever promised to us by God is then fulfilled, in which case what the heretics claim to possess already here is void; or, if the knowledge of the mystery is also a resurrection, that resurrection which is proclaimed for the end is certainly still believed intact. It follows that, by the very fact that the present resurrection is claimed as spiritual, the other is prejudged to be bodily. For if no resurrection were proclaimed for that time, this present resurrection alone, and as solely spiritual, would rightly be claimed. But since a resurrection is also declared for the final time, it is recognized as bodily, because a spiritual resurrection is not proclaimed for that time as well.

[Note: [Col. 0831D] “They place the whole fruit of Christian hope at the *exodium* of the age.” That is, at the end of the age. “*Exodium*: departure, end,” say the ancient glosses; Greek *exodion* (ἐξόδιον), “funeral rites.” Lucilius:

> First will come an ending worthy of him, and then the *exodium*.

Juvenal, Satire III:

> …and at last he returns to the stage for the familiar  
> *Exodium*….

According to an ancient interpreter, the *exodiarius* among the ancients entered at the end of the games, and the laughter of this spectacle wiped away whatever tears and sadness the tragic emotions had produced. Septimius therefore cleverly called the end of the age an *exodium*. For then the time will be present when, for faithful Christians, the sadness of all their labors and afflictions will be turned into joy of the kind Septimius describes near the end of his book *On the Spectacles*. RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0831C] Pamelius and Rhenanus read “beginning.”]

[Note: [Col. 0831C] Rhenanus and Semler read “but.”]

[Note: [Col. 0832D] “Knowledge of the mystery”: knowledge of the truth of the Christian faith. RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0831C] “Is” is absent from Rhenanus and Semler.]

[Note: [Col. 0831C] Rhenanus reads “because.”]

[Note: [Col. 0831C] Rigault and Venice read “is claimed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0831C] Rhenanus and Semler read “is brought forth.”]

For why would a resurrection of the same kind—that is, a spiritual one—be proclaimed a second time, when it ought either to be accomplished now, without any distinction of times, or then, at the complete closure of the times? Thus it is all the more fitting for us also to defend a spiritual resurrection from the entrance of faith, since we acknowledge its fullness at the departure of the age.

[Note: [Col. 0831C] Paris reads “closure”; “of the times” is absent.]

[Note: [Col. 0832C] Francius reads “at the departure.”]

## CHAPTER XXVI
[Col. 0831C] I shall make one further reply to the earlier contention concerning allegorical Scriptures: we too are entitled to vindicate the resurrection of the body by appealing to the figurative language of the prophets. For behold, at the beginning the divine sentence [Note: [Col. 0832C] “In” is absent from Rhenanus and Semler.], in declaring man to be earth—“Earth you are, and into earth you shall go”—plainly did so with reference to the substance [Col. 0832A] of the flesh, which had been taken from the earth and, as we have shown, had previously been called “man.” It thus gives me a rule for interpreting with reference to the flesh whatever God decrees against the earth in wrath or for it in grace. For the earth itself is not properly liable to his judgment, since it has committed neither good nor evil. It was indeed cursed because it [Note: [Col. 0832C] “Which,” Rhenanus, Semler.] drank in blood (Gen. 4); but even this was a figure of murderous flesh. For although the earth is capable of being benefited or harmed, that [Note: [Col. 0832C] “That” is absent from Rhenanus and Semler.] too is for man’s sake, so that he may be benefited or harmed through what happens to the place in which he has his standing. [Note: [Col. 0832D] **What happens to the place in which he has his standing.** He calls the earth a *consistorium*, from *consistere*, “to stand,” because man stands upon it. Otherwise, we call *consistorium* the place in which cases are heard. RHEN.] All the more, therefore, will he himself bear the consequences of what even the earth suffers on his account. Accordingly, when God threatens the earth, I shall say that he is threatening the flesh instead; and when he promises something to the earth, I shall understand him to be promising it to the flesh instead. Thus in David (Ps. 96): “The Lord has reigned; let the earth [Col. 0832B] rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0832C] “Rejoiced,” Rhenanus, Semler.]—that is, the flesh of the saints, to which the fruit of God’s reign pertains. He then adds: “It saw, and the earth was shaken; the mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord”—plainly, the flesh of the profane; and: “For they shall see him whom [Note: [Col. 0832C] “Him who,” Franeker; “him whom,” Junius.] they pierced” (Zech. 12:10). Indeed, if both statements are thought to have been uttered simply about the element of earth [Note: [Col. 0832C] “Earth,” Franeker, Rigault, Venice.], how will it be consistent for it both to be shaken and melted before the face of the Lord whose reign above made it rejoice?

Likewise in Isaiah: “You shall eat the good things of the earth.” These will be understood as the good things of the flesh, which await it when it has been refashioned and made angel-like in the kingdom of God, and when it is to obtain those things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2). Otherwise, it is quite pointless for God to invite obedience by offering the fruits of the field and the foods of this life, [Note: [Col. 0832D] **Which, once creation had been assigned to man, he shares even with the religious and the blasphemous.** Seneca treated this passage exceptionally well in *On Benefits*, book IV, chapter 28: “God gave certain things universally to the human race, from which no one is excluded,” etc. RIG.] which [Col. 0832C] he shares even with the religious and the blasphemous, once creation had been assigned to man, “raining upon the good and the evil, and sending [Note: [Col. 0832C] “Sending,” Rhenanus, Semler.] his sun upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5). Faith will certainly be fortunate if it is to obtain [Note: [Col. 0832C] “They are,” Rhenanus, Rigault, Venice.] things which the enemies of God and Christ not only use but even abuse, worshipping [Note: [Col. 0832D] **Worshipping creation itself.** The world created by God. RIG.] creation itself [Col. 0833A] against its Creator. Will you reckon bulbs and truffles among the good things of the earth [Note: [Col. 0833C] “Earth,” Rhenanus, Semler.], when the Lord declares that man will not live even by bread?

Thus the Jews, by hoping only for earthly things, lose the heavenly, since they are ignorant both of the bread promised from heaven and of [Note: [Col. 0833C] **The oil of the divine anointing, etc.** He enumerates the delights of the Church, namely three sacraments: the Eucharist, Extreme Unction, and Baptism. He enumerates the same in book I *Against Marcion*, chapter 14: “But up to the present he has rejected neither the water with which he washes his people, nor the oil with which he anoints them, nor the bread with which he represents his own body.” He has used “the soul-strengthening” for “receiving strength,” a passive meaning for an active one, as he sometimes does. [Col. 0833D] LAC.] the oil of the divine anointing, the water of the Spirit, and the wine [Note: [Col. 0833C] “The wine of the Spirit and the water,” Venice, Rigault, the Pithou manuscript. “The water of the Spirit and” is absent from Franeker.] that strengthens the soul, from the vine of Christ.

Likewise, they regard the holy land itself, properly speaking Jewish soil, as instead to be interpreted of the Lord’s flesh, which for that reason is also holy land in all who have put on Christ: truly holy [Note: [Col. 0833D] **Through the indwelling of the Holy Spirit.** An *incolatus* is a city of which one is not a citizen but a resident. Modestinus, law 34, Digest, *De muneribus et honoribus*: “Residence indeed establishes one as an inhabitant”; law 3, Code, *De incolis*. But, as Alciatus says in *On the Meaning of Words*, “An *incola* is properly one who, after having been a newcomer, comes to dwell in some city with the intention of remaining there permanently and of maintaining the sum of his affairs there.” Christ was therefore rightly the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit; for the Spirit established in him a perpetual domicile, never interrupted, in a full stream. LAC.] through the indwelling of the Holy Spirit; truly flowing with milk and honey, through the sweetness of that hope; truly Judaea, through intimacy with God: “for he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, but he who is one inwardly.” Thus the same flesh is also the temple of God [Note: [Col. 0833C] “Of God” is absent from Rhenanus and Semler.] and Jerusalem, hearing from [Col. 0833B] Isaiah (Isa. 51): “Rise, rise, Jerusalem; put on [Note: [Col. 0833C] “Put on,” Rhenanus, Semler.] the strength of your arm; rise as at the beginning of the day” [Note: [Col. 0833C] “Of the day” is absent from Rhenanus and Semler.]—plainly, in that integrity [Note: [Col. 0833C] “In which,” Rhenanus, Semler.] which existed before the transgression’s offense. For how could exhortations and appeals of this kind apply [Note: [Col. 0834C] “Will apply,” Pamelius, Rhenanus.] to that Jerusalem which killed the prophets, stoned those sent to it, and finally crucified its own Lord? Nor indeed is salvation promised to any land whatever [Note: [Col. 0834C] “Land” is absent from Rigault and Venice.], since it must pass away together with the condition of the whole world.

Further, if anyone should venture to argue that the holy land is Paradise instead, let him grasp that it is also [Note: [Col. 0834C] “Even,” Pamelius, Franeker.] called the land of the fathers, namely Adam and Eve. Accordingly, restoration to Paradise will likewise be seen to have been promised to the flesh, which received the lot of dwelling in it and guarding it, so that man may be recalled there [Col. 0833C] in the same condition in which he was expelled [Note: [Col. 0834C] “Driven out,” others.] from it.

## CHAPTER XXVII

[Col. 0834A]

We can also allegorize the mention of garments in the Scriptures with reference to the hope of the flesh, because the Apocalypse of John also says (Rev. 3 and 14): “These are,” it says, [Note: [Col. 0833D] **Who have not defiled their garments.** Scripture combines different passages, as it sometimes does; or rather, it alludes to different passages, from whose words it composes a third statement, explaining the words of one passage through the words of another. LAC.] “those who have not defiled their garments with women”—plainly signifying virgins and those who have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdoms of heaven. Accordingly, they shall be in white garments, that is, in the brightness of [Note: [Col. 0833D] **Unmarried flesh.** “Virginal,” the Pithou manuscript; *innube* [“unmarried”]. RIG.] unmarried flesh. In the Gospel too, the wedding garment can be recognized as the holiness of the flesh.

Accordingly, when Isaiah teaches what kind of fast the Lord has chosen, he adds concerning the reward of goodness: [Note: [Col. 0833D] **Then, he says, your early light shall break forth.** [Col. 0834C] The Author renders Isaiah 58 as “early,” where others have “morning.” The Greek word πρώϊμον means “early” or “premature.” He then reads ἱμάτια, that is, “garments,” where present-day Greek manuscripts and some ancient ones have ἰάματα, that is, “healings.” There are two readings of this passage even among the Greeks, for agreement with Tertullian is found not only in Blessed Cyprian, *On Almsgiving and Works*, near the beginning, and *On the Lord’s Prayer*, near the end, and Blessed Augustine, sermon 172, but also in Chrysostom, homily 55 on Matthew 16. For more on this, see Leo Castrius on Isaiah, where he also shows that even those who read otherwise interpret this passage of the resurrection. PAM.] “Then,” he says (Isa. 58), “your early light shall break forth, and your garments shall rise swiftly.” He certainly did not mean an undergarment of silk [Note: [Col. 0834C] “I shall write beneath,” Rhenanus; “silken undergarment,” Junius.] or a cloak, but intended the flesh to be understood; he foretold the rising of the flesh destined to rise again from the setting of death. [Col. 0834B] Thus an allegorical defense of bodily resurrection is also available to us.

For when we read (Isa. 26), “My people, enter your storerooms for a little while, until my wrath has passed,” the storerooms will be the tombs in which those who, at the end of the age, under the final wrath, have departed through the violence of Antichrist will have to rest briefly. Or why did he use the term “storerooms” rather than that of some place of reception, unless because [Note: [Col. 0834D] **In storerooms salted flesh is kept.** These rooms, which he here calls *cellae promae*, he will shortly call *cellaria*. Sulpicius Severus uses this word in book II of the *Sacred History*, where he speaks of the bishops summoned to Ariminum: “The Emperor had ordered that provisions and storerooms be supplied to all of them.” RIG.] in storerooms salted flesh is preserved and laid aside for use, to be brought out from there at its proper time? In like manner, bodies treated with the spices of burial are set apart in mausoleums and monuments, to come forth from there when the Lord commands.

Since it is fitting to understand it in this way—for what shelters of [Col. 0834C] storerooms will preserve us from the wrath of God?—the very words “until the wrath has passed,” the wrath that will destroy Antichrist, show that after the wrath the flesh will come forth [Col. 0835A] from the tomb [Note: [Col. 0835C] “From the tombs,” Franeker.] into which it had been placed before the wrath. For nothing is brought out of storerooms except what has been put into them; and after Antichrist has been eradicated, the resurrection will take place.

[Note: [Col. 0834D] **Of storerooms.** A *cellarium* is properly a place in which table provisions, or surplus necessities for sustenance, are gathered. But a distinction relevant to Tertullian’s point has been observed between a *promptuarium* and a *cellarium*: things intended for only a few days are stored in the latter, but things intended for a long time in the former. Tertullian therefore indicated by the term *cellarium* that death would not last long. St Gregory the Great mentions the word *cellarium* in book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 28: “The monk who was in charge of the storeroom [Col. 0835C] did indeed hear the words of Benedict’s command, [Col. 0835D] but delayed carrying them out.” PAM.]

## CHAPTER XXVIII

We know, moreover, that the resurrection is proclaimed by the prophets not only through words but also through objects—both represented and enacted. When Moses puts his hand into his bosom and brings it out as though dead, [Note: [Col. 0835D] **And brings it out as though dead.** This account is related in Exodus 4, where there appears only ἐγένηθη ἡ χεὶρ αὐτοῦ λεπρῶσα, “and his hand became leprous.” But below, in chapter 55, he explains the matter more clearly: “Moses’ hand,” he says, “is changed, and indeed becomes bloodless, after the likeness of something dead,” etc. Here, then, he calls it dead by a certain resemblance, not in reality. St Jerome uses the same testimony against John of Jerusalem to prove the resurrection: “Moses’ hand was changed to the whiteness of snow and afterward restored to its former color; amid both changes it remained the same hand.” LE PR.] and then puts it in again [Note: [Col. 0835D] **And then puts it in again.** What he has just called “putting it into his bosom.” LE PR.] and displays it alive, does this not portend what is to happen to the whole man? For the threefold power of God was indicated [Note: [Col. 0835C] “Was denoted,” Paris.] by those three signs in their proper order: first, it would subdue for man the serpent, the devil, formidable though he is; next, it would draw [Note: [Col. 0835C] “Would be going to draw,” Rigault, Venice.] the flesh back from the bosom of death; and thus [Col. 0835B] it would exact [Note: [Col. 0835C] “Would seek out,” Junius.] an account of all blood in judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0835D] **Concerning which, in the same prophet.** Namely Moses, tacitly indicating that he is the author both of Exodus and Genesis, from which he cites these testimonies, and therefore of the whole Pentateuch as well. Certainly this is evident regarding Exodus and Deuteronomy from the words of Scripture in Exodus 24 and Deuteronomy 31; and Philo, in *On the World*, and Josephus somewhere, assert it of the entire work. PAM.]

Concerning this, God says in the same prophet [Note: [Col. 0835C] *Prophetem*, Pamelius; *propheta*, Venice, incorrectly.] (Gen. 9): “For I shall also require your blood from all beasts, and from the hand of man, and from the hand of his brother I shall require it.” Now nothing is required unless it is demanded back; nothing is demanded back unless it will also be restored. And certainly that which is demanded back and required in the name of vengeance will be restored. For that which will have no existence at all cannot be avenged. But it will exist when it is restored, so that it may be avenged. Accordingly, whatever is foretold concerning blood is directed toward the flesh, without which there will be no blood. The flesh will be raised so that the blood may be avenged.

There are also certain statements uttered in such a way that, although they lack the cloud of allegory, they nevertheless thirst for an interpretation of their own plain meaning. [Note: [Col. 0836C] **Such as that passage in Isaiah, etc.** The words Tertullian reports from Isaiah are not found verbatim—αὐτολέξει—anywhere in the entire prophecy; yet they can be gathered from those passages in which God displays his power by showing that he can cast the people into the straits of death and recall them from death. They are found more clearly in 1 Kings 2: “The Lord puts to death and gives life”; and in the Psalm. Isaiah 38, however, reads: “You will chastise me and give me life.” LE PR.] Such is the passage in Isaiah: “I shall kill and [Col. 0835C] give life.” Certainly, after he has killed, he will give life. Therefore, killing through death, he will give life through resurrection. It is the flesh that is killed [Note: [Col. 0835C] “He has killed,” Rhenanus.] through death; therefore, it is likewise the flesh that will be given life through resurrection. Certainly, if to kill is to take the soul away from the flesh, then to give life, [Col. 0836A] its opposite, is to restore the soul to the flesh. The flesh must rise again, since the soul taken from it through killing must be restored to it through vivification.

## CHAPTER XXIX

Therefore, if allegorical Scriptures, the arguments of enacted signs, and plain declarations all shed light upon [Note: [Col. 0835C] “Shed light upon,” others.] the resurrection of the flesh, although without naming that substance itself, how much less ought those passages which determine this particular form [Note: [Col. 0836C] “Hope,” Pamelius, Rhenanus.] in the bodily substances themselves by expressly mentioning them to be called into question! Take Ezekiel (Ezek. 37):

> “And,” he says, “the hand of the Lord came upon me, and the Lord carried me out in the Spirit and set me in the midst of the plain; it was filled with bones. And he led me all around them, and behold, they were very numerous upon the face of the plain, and behold, exceedingly dry. And he said to [Col. 0836B] me: ‘Son of man, shall these bones live?’ And I said: ‘Adonai, Lord, you know.’ And he said to me: ‘Prophesy to these bones and say: Dry bones, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord Adonai to these bones: Behold, I bring spirit into you, and you shall live; and I shall put spirit into you and restore flesh upon you [Note: [Col. 0836C] “Into you,” Rhenanus, Semler.] and clothe you with [Note: [Col. 0836C] “Upon you,” Rhenanus, Semler.] skin, and put spirit within you, and you shall live [Note: [Col. 0836C] From “and I shall put spirit into you” through “and you shall live” is absent from Venice.], and you shall know that I am the Lord.’
>
> “And I prophesied according to the command; and behold, there was a sound while I prophesied, and behold, a movement; and the bones came together, bone to bone. And I saw, and behold, sinews upon the bones; and flesh came up, and skins [Note: [Col. 0836C] “Fleshes,” Rhenanus, the Pithou manuscript.] were drawn around them, but there was no spirit within them. And he said to me: ‘Prophesy to the spirit, son of man; prophesy and say to the spirit: Thus says the Lord Adonai: Come, O spirit, from the four winds, and breathe upon these slain, and let them live.’
>
> “And I prophesied [Col. 0836C] to the spirit as he commanded me; and the spirit entered into them, and they lived and stood [Note: [Col. 0836C] “They stood,” Rhenanus, Semler.] upon their feet, an exceedingly great host. [Note: [Col. 0836D] **Upon their feet, an exceedingly great host.** The expression is in the nominative case, not the ablative. In Greek: καὶ ἔστησαν ἐπὶ τῶν ποδῶν αὐτῶν καὶ συναγωγὴ πολλὴ σφόδρα, “and they stood upon their feet, and were an exceedingly great assembly.” The Vulgate has: “And they stood upon their feet, an army exceedingly great.” By *valentia*, “host,” Tertullian means the great might of gathered forces and an assembled army, following the translation of Aquila and Theodotion, which has δύναμις μεγάλη, “a great force.” LAC.]
>
> “And he said to me: ‘Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel. They say: Our bones have dried up, and our hope has perished; we have been torn away [Col. 0837A] among them. Therefore prophesy to them: Behold, I open your tombs and shall bring you up from your tombs, my people; and I shall lead you into the land of Israel. And you shall know that I am the Lord, when I have opened [Note: [Col. 0837C] “I opened,” Rhenanus.] your tombs and brought you out of your tombs, my people. And I shall give you [Note: [Col. 0837C] “Put into you,” others.] spirit, and you shall live and rest in your land; and you shall know that I, the Lord, have spoken and accomplished it, says the Lord.’”

## CHAPTER XXX

I know how they also shake this proclamation into an allegorical interpretation. Because, by saying, “These bones are the whole house of Israel,” [Note: [Col. 0837C] “Israel is,” in Rhenanus and Semler; “is Israel,” in Pamelius.] God made these bones an image of Israel [Note: [Col. 0837C] “For Israel,” Semler; “of Israel,” the Pithou manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0837D] **Made them an image of Israel.** The passage here in question is, in my judgment, most excellently explained by Tertullian as referring to the resurrection of the dead; nor do I find attractive the interpretation that the Author refutes, which is that of almost all more recent writers. By like reasoning, Blessed Jerome, on Ezekiel 37, proves the resurrection of the dead from the fact that the restoration of the Jewish people is promised and is supported by the resurrection; for if there were no resurrection, the promise would be empty, since no one can prove anything certain by things that do not exist. See the passage. LE PR.] and [Note: [Col. 0837C] “But,” Rhenanus, Semler.] transferred them from their own proper condition, they claim that this proclamation of resurrection is figurative, not literal. For they say that the condition of the Jews was represented as in some fashion dead, dried up, and scattered over the plain of the world. Accordingly, the image of resurrection is allegorized as applying to that condition, because it is to be gathered together again and fitted bone to bone—that is, tribe to tribe and people to people—and clothed again as a body with the flesh of its resources [Note: [Col. 0837C] “The capacity of the flesh,” Rhenanus, Semler.] and the sinews of its kingdom. In this way it is to be led out of the tomb—that is, from the most sorrowful and hideous dwellings of captivity—and, under the name of refreshment, breathe again, and thereafter live in its own land, Judaea.

And what after this? They will undoubtedly die. And what after death? No resurrection, I suppose, if this is not itself the resurrection revealed to Ezekiel. But the resurrection is proclaimed elsewhere too; therefore this will also be a resurrection, and they rashly convert it into a description of Jewish affairs. Or, if that resurrection which we defend is a different one, it makes no difference to me, provided that there is both a resurrection of bodies and a resurrection of Jewish affairs. Finally, by the very fact that the restoration of the Jewish condition is represented by the re-embodiment and reanimation [Note: [Col. 0837D] **Re-embodiment and reanimation.** It is ἀναψύχωσις, “revivification”; those who write *readunatione*, “reunion,” wrongly correct it. LE PR.] of the bones, it is also proved that this will happen to the bones themselves. For a figure could not be constructed from bones if precisely this were not also going to happen to the bones.

[Note: [Col. 0837D] **For even if it is a fabrication of truth.** He means to indicate an example—or rather a metaphor or likeness—which is employed to fashion or represent the truth. LE PR.]

For even if it is a representation of truth in an image, the image itself exists in the truth of its own reality. It must first exist for itself [Col. 0838A] before it can be configured to something else. A likeness cannot properly be made from emptiness; a parable cannot be drawn from nothing. Thus one will also have to believe in the stated restoration of flesh and breath to the bones, from which may be expressed the alleged restoration of Jewish affairs.

But it is more reverent to defend the truth by the authority [Note: [Col. 0838C] “By the authority and simplicity of its truth,” Paris.] of its own plain meaning, as the sense of the divine declaration demands. For if this vision concerned Jewish affairs, immediately after the condition of the bones had been revealed it would have added, “These bones are the whole house of Israel,” and then the rest. But when, after the bones have been displayed, God mentions what they say against their own hope [Note: [Col. 0838C] “Who,” Franeker.]—Israel not yet having been named—and tests the prophet’s faith: “Son of man, shall these bones live?” so that he too answers, “Lord, you know,” God certainly would not have tested the prophet’s faith concerning something that would not happen, of which Israel had never heard, and which ought not to be believed.

But because the resurrection of the dead was indeed being proclaimed, while Israel, dissenting in its unbelief, was scandalized by it, and, looking upon [Note: [Col. 0838D] **The condition of a burial grown old.** Elegantly said of a late and prolonged delay in burial, just as things with a prolonged and long-lasting life grow old; similarly in chapter 32: “how like a coffin, how like a tomb, how like the old age of some resting and hidden burial.” LAC.] the condition of burial grown old, despaired of resurrection—or rather, did not direct its mind toward it but toward its surrounding circumstances—therefore God first prepared both the prophet, as though [Note: [Col. 0838C] “As though,” Rigault, Venice.] he too were doubtful, for constancy in proclamation by revealing the order of resurrection, and commanded the people to believe what he had revealed to the prophet. He said that they themselves, who did not believe that they would rise, were the bones destined to rise. Finally, in the conclusion he says: “And you shall know that I, the Lord, have spoken and accomplished it”—that is, he will certainly accomplish what he had spoken. Otherwise, he would not accomplish [Col. 0838C] what he had spoken if he were to accomplish something different.

## CHAPTER XXXI

Certainly, if the people too had been murmuring allegorically about their bones having dried up and their hope having been lost, complaining of what resulted [Note: [Col. 0838C] “Arousal,” Rhenanus, Semler.] from their dispersion, then God might deservedly be thought [Note: [Col. 0838C] “Is thought,” others.] to have consoled [Note: [Col. 0838D] **A figurative despair.** For by a figurative proverb they explained their extreme calamity, saying, “Our bones have dried up”; and God consoles them in the same manner, through that prophecy and the vision of the dry bones. LAC.] a figurative despair with a figurative promise.

[Note: [Col. 0838D] **But since the injury of dispersion, etc.** The Author seems to have thought that Ezekiel delivered this oracle before that calamity of the Israelite people. This appears false, since Ezekiel’s prophecy came after the captivity. But Tertullian can be understood as meaning, not that he wished to place it entirely before the captivity, but before the complete dispersion and most bitter oppression [Col. 0839D] of Israel. Yet the Author does not cling too tightly to this opinion, since he immediately confirms his interpretation by another route when he says, “Although, even if Israel was then grieving under some conflict involving present circumstances,” etc. For when Ezekiel prophesied, this dispersion had already occurred. Thus Jerome says that, through the parable of resurrection, the restoration of Israel is prophesied—Israel being captive in Babylon at that time. Epiphanius, in *Lives of the Prophets*, records that Ezekiel prophesied in captivity. LAC.]

But since the injury of dispersion had not yet befallen the people, while the hope of resurrection had very often collapsed among them, and the manifest destruction of bodies was undermining confidence in the resurrection [reading contextually restored from uncertain text], so too God was rebuilding the faith which the people were destroying. Although, even if Israel was then grieving [Note: [Col. 0839C] “Was clinging,” Rhenanus, Semler.] under some conflict involving present circumstances, [Note: [Col. 0839D] **It would not for that reason have to be understood as a parable, etc.** He proves that this restoration of the Israelites was not so much a revelation by which God wished to restore them as it was a testimony to the resurrection. LE PR.] the intention of the revelation would not for that reason have to be understood as a parable, but as testimony to the resurrection, so as to raise them toward that hope—namely, of eternal salvation and the more necessary restoration—and turn them away from concern for present circumstances.

For this purpose the other prophets [Note: [Col. 0839C] “Prophets,” Venice.] also say: “You shall come forth from your tombs like calves released from their bonds, and you shall trample your enemies” (Mal. 4:3). And again: “Your heart shall rejoice, and your bones shall spring up like grass” [Note: [Col. 0839C] “Swiftly,” Rhenanus, the Pithou manuscript.] (Isa. 66), because grass too is restored from the dissolution and decay of its seed.
