In sum, if it is contended that the image of the rising bones properly concerns the condition of Israel, why is the same hope announced not only to Israel but also to all nations—the hope both of remains being re-embodied and reanimated, and of the dead being raised [Note: [Col. 0839C] “Raised,” Rhenanus, Semler.] from their tombs? For it was said concerning all (Isa. 26): [Note: [Col. 0839D] **The dead shall live.** In Greek it is “shall rise,” ἀναστήσονται. Isaiah 26, according to the Septuagint. LE PR.] “The dead shall live, and those in the tombs shall rise; for the dew that comes from you is healing for their bones.”

Likewise elsewhere (Isa. 66): “All flesh shall come to worship in my sight, says the Lord.” When? When the condition of this world has begun to pass away. For above it says: “As the new heaven and the new earth which I make stand in my sight, says the Lord, so shall your seed stand.” Then, therefore, what he adds will be fulfilled: “And they shall go forth”—certainly from their tombs—“and shall see the limbs of those who have acted impiously, because their worm shall not die and their fire shall not be extinguished, and they shall be a spectacle to all flesh”—namely, to all flesh which, having been raised and having come forth from the tombs, will worship the Lord for this grace.

## CHAPTER XXXII

But lest it appear that the resurrection is proclaimed only of those bodies which are committed to tombs, you have it written (Rev. 3): [Note: [Col. 0839D] **And I shall command the fish, etc.** Revelation 20, although it seems to be a different passage; but the ancients sometimes cite certain things from Scripture which nevertheless are not extant. LE PR.] “And I shall command the fish [Col. 0840A] of the sea, and they shall belch forth the bones that have been consumed; and I shall join [Note: [Col. 0839C] “They shall join,” Rhenanus.] joint to joint and bone to bone.”

“Therefore,” you say, “the fish will also be raised, as will the other beasts and [Note: [Col. 0840D] **And flesh-eating birds.** Σαρκοβόροι, “flesh-eating,” birds. It was the heretics’ objection that those who had been torn apart by beasts and birds could not rise. Tertullian refutes them here. LE PR.] flesh-eating birds, so that they may vomit back [Note: [Col. 0839C] “May vomit,” Rhenanus, Semler.] those whom they ate—because in Moses too you read that blood will be required from all beasts?” Certainly not. But beasts and fish are named for the restoration [Note: [Col. 0839D] “In the restoration,” Pamelius, Franeker.] of flesh and blood, so that the resurrection even of devoured bodies may be expressed all the more strongly, since an accounting is proclaimed even from the devourers themselves.

I also consider Jonah an adequate proof of this divine power, since he emerges [Note: [Col. 0840C] “Is vomited forth,” Latinus.] from the belly of the fish incorrupt in both substances, flesh and soul. And surely, over three days, the entrails of the sea-monster would have been just as capable [Note: [Col. 0840C] “As,” or “as though,” Rhenanus.] of digesting the flesh as any coffin, tomb, or long duration [Col. 0840B] of a resting and concealed burial.

[Note: [Col. 0840D] **Without prejudice to the fact that beasts, savage toward the Christian name, etc.** These words, spoken by Tertullian with some irony, indicate this interpretation of the heretics concerning the passage in Genesis 9 which the Author recently mentioned and had adduced in chapter 28 to prove the resurrection as well. But he immediately proceeded to turn the heretics’ escape back against them. LAC.]

This is without prejudice to the fact that “beasts” [Note: [Col. 0840C] “Savage beasts,” Rhenanus, Semler.]—men exceptionally savage toward the Christian name—or even the angels of wickedness themselves were represented figuratively, and from them blood will be exacted by the payment of vengeance.

Who, then, is more disposed to learn than to presume; more diligent in believing than in disputing; more reverent toward divine wisdom than wanton with his own opinions? Hearing that God has ordained something for flesh, skins, sinews, and bones, will he devise some other meaning for them, as though what is proclaimed concerning these substances were not ordained for man? Either nothing is ordained for man—not the generosity of the kingdom, not the severity of judgment, not resurrection, whatever it may be—or, if it is ordained for man, it must necessarily be ordained for those substances [Col. 0840C] of which the man for whom it is ordained is constructed.

I also ask these exceedingly subtle transformers of bones, flesh, sinews, and tombs [Note: [Col. 0840D] **Why, whenever something is declared concerning the soul, etc.** He asks the heretics to explain why they interpret statements in Scripture about bodily resurrection as referring to the soul, yet are entirely unwilling to let statements about the soul extend to the body. LAC.] why, whenever something is declared concerning the soul, they interpret the soul as nothing other than the soul and do not transform [Note: [Col. 0840C] “Pierce,” Rhenanus, Rigault, Semler, Venice.] it into an argument for some other thing; yet whenever something is proclaimed concerning some bodily substance, they assert that it is anything whatever rather than what is named.

[Col. 0841A] [Note: [Col. 0841D] **If bodily things are parables.** If, among the heretics, the things foretold concerning the body are parables, and they interpret them figuratively and parabolically, why do they not also extend to the body the things said concerning the resurrection of the soul? LAC.] If bodily things are parables, then so are things pertaining to the soul; if things pertaining to the soul are not parables, neither are bodily things. For man is body just as much as he is soul, so that one kind cannot admit enigmas while the other excludes them.

## CHAPTER XXXIII
Enough on the prophetic instrument; I now appeal to the Gospels. Here too I shall first meet that same cunning of theirs, whereby they contend that the Lord likewise uttered everything in parables, because it is written: “Jesus spoke all these things in parables, and without a parable he did not speak to them”—that is, [Note: [Col. 0841C] “To” added by Rig.] to the Jews. For the disciples also say, “Why do you speak in parables?” And the Lord replies: “For this reason I speak to them in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not hear,” in accordance with [Col. 0841B] Isaiah. But if he spoke to the Jews in parables, then he did not speak so to everyone; if not to everyone in parables [Note: [Col. 0841C] “Then not to everyone; if not to everyone in parables” is absent from Ven.], then neither did he always speak in parables, nor is everything a parable, but only certain things, when addressed to certain persons—to certain persons, namely the Jews, though sometimes plainly to the disciples as well.

But consider how Scripture reports it: “He also spoke a parable to them.” Therefore he also spoke what was not a parable, since it would not have been noted when he spoke a parable if he always spoke in that manner. And yet you will find no parable [Note: [Col. 0841C] “Parable” is absent from Par.] that is not either explained by him himself, as that of the sower in its application to the ministry of the word; or elucidated beforehand by the Evangelist as commentator, as that of the arrogant judge and the importunate widow, concerning perseverance in prayer; or readily open to inference, as that of the fig tree granted a reprieve in hope, as an image of Jewish unfruitfulness.

But if even the parables do not obscure [Col. 0841C] [Note: [Col. 0841C] “Adumbrate,” Rhen., Seml.] the light of the Gospel, far less can propositions and definitions, whose nature is explicit, mean something other than what they say. Now it is by definitions and propositions that the Lord declares either the judgment, the kingdom of God, or the resurrection: [Note: [Col. 0841D] “It will be more tolerable for Tyre,” etc., Matt. 11. The Greek word ἀνεκτότερον, “more tolerable,” as the Author translates it, also means “more lenient,” as in the Vulgate edition. PAM.] “It will be more tolerable,” he says (Matt. 11), “for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment”; and (Matt. 10), [Col. 0842A] “Tell them that the kingdom of God has drawn near”; and (Luke 14), “You will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.”

If these are unqualified names [Note: [Col. 0841C] “Absolutely,” Rhen., Seml.] of things—that is, of the judgment, the kingdom of God, and the resurrection—so that none of them can be compressed into a parable, neither should those things be forced into parables [Note: [Col. 0841D] “Which are declared concerning the experience of the resurrection.” Just as in the book *On the Veiling of Virgins* he speaks of the “experience of marriage,” so here he speaks of the “experience of the resurrection,” signifying that manifestly divine force to be brought upon bodies through the return of their souls to them. RIG.] which are declared concerning the ordering [Note: [Col. 0842C] “Dispensation,” Rig.], accomplishment, and experience of the kingdom, judgment, and resurrection. They should therefore be maintained [Note: [Col. 0842C] “Will be maintained,” Pam., Rhen.] as bodily realities intended for bodies—that is, [Note: [Col. 0841D] Not spiritual, because not figurative. Conversely, things are figurative when they are spoken of the body in such a way that they must be understood of the spirit. “The words that I speak,” says Christ, “are spirit and life”; they are therefore figurative: they mean something other than what they sound like. The lineaments of Christ, the image of Christ, holiness, righteousness, truth. Paul, [Col. 0842A] 1 Corinthians 15: “As we have borne the image of the earthly, let us bear the image of the heavenly.” RIG.] not spiritual realities, because they are not figurative.

[Note: [Col. 0842D] “For this reason we also established beforehand that both the body of the soul,” etc. In chapter 16 the Author established beforehand that both soul and body are liable either to punishment or to reward; and in chapter 17, because, according to his own position, the soul was corporeal and possessed a body of its own kind, he also proved that it can be tormented without the flesh in hell. Therefore he speaks here of both the body of the soul and that of the flesh, because he also assigned a body to the soul. LAC.] For this reason we also established beforehand [Note: [Col. 0842C] “Touched upon beforehand,” Rhen.] that both the body of the soul and that of the flesh are liable to recompenses apportioned for their joint activity, lest the corporeality of the soul, by providing an occasion for figurative interpretations, exclude the corporeality of the flesh, since both must be believed to share in the kingdom, the judgment, and the resurrection. [Col. 0842B] We now proceed to demonstrate that, in every mention of the resurrection, the Lord signifies the corporeality of the flesh in the proper sense, without prejudice to that of the soul [Note: [Col. 0842D] “Without prejudice to that of the soul.” That is, with the corporeality of the soul left unshaken. For he wishes the things declared concerning the resurrection to be referred to the corporeality of the flesh, yet not in consequence to deny that the soul has its own particular body. But he immediately reveals this position to be paradoxical when he adds, “which itself few have accepted”—namely, the corporeality of the soul. LAC.], which itself few have accepted.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

First of all, when he says that he came for this purpose, to save what had perished, what do you say [Note: [Col. 0842C] “Do you say,” Rhen., Seml.] had perished? The human being, without doubt. The whole human being, or only a part? Certainly the whole. For the transgression that caused humanity’s perdition was committed both at the soul’s instigation, through desire, and by the flesh’s act, through tasting; [Note: [Col. 0842D] “Branded the whole human being with the official record of transgression,” etc. An *elogium* is the public and lawful declaration of a crime and sentence, sometimes made by the voice [Col. 0843D] of a herald, and sometimes written as a title upon a tablet. LAC.] it branded the whole human being with the official record of transgression, and consequently filled the whole with liability to perdition. Therefore the whole one who perished will be saved, since the whole perished [Note: [Col. 0842C] “Perishes,” Rhen., Rig., Ven., Seml.] by sinning [Col. 0842C] [Note: [Col. 0842C] “The whole” added by Pam., Fran.]—unless perhaps that sheep too is lost without its body and brought back without its body. For if its flesh also, together with its soul—which constitutes the whole animal—is carried back upon the shoulders of the good shepherd, it is surely an illustration of the restoration of the human being in both substances.

Or how unworthy of God it would be to restore half a human being to salvation! It would be almost [Col. 0843A] to do less, since even [Note: [Col. 0843D] “The full pardon of secular rulers is always insisted upon,” etc. That age began commonly to use this word in this sense. Thus below: “If divine indulgence did not dry every shower of tears.” RHEN.] secular rulers always lay claim to the prerogative of full pardon. The devil would be understood to be stronger in injuring a human being, since he crushes the whole; God would be declared weaker, since he does not raise up the whole. Yet the Apostle also teaches (Rom. 5) that where sin abounded, there grace superabounded.

Moreover, how will one be regarded as saved who can also be called lost—lost, namely, in the flesh, though saved in the soul—unless the soul too must now be included in what was lost, so that it can be made safe? For that which was lost will need to be saved. We accept, however, the immortality of the soul, so that when it is lost it is believed to pass not into annihilation but into punishment—that is, into Gehenna. And if this is so, salvation will no longer concern the soul, since by its own nature it is safe through immortality, but rather the flesh, which all agree is perishable.

Or if [Col. 0843B] the soul also is perishable—that is, not immortal—just as the flesh is, then that pattern of salvation must equally benefit the flesh also, since it is likewise mortal and perishable, because [Note: [Col. 0843C] “By which,” Fran.] the Lord will save that which perishes. [Note: [Col. 0843D] “I do not now wish to draw the matter out with a contentious rope.” A proverbial expression for arguments that are both lengthy and highly intricate. RHEN.] I do not now wish to draw the matter out with a contentious rope, debating whether perdition lays claim to the human being on this side or on that [Note: [Col. 0843C] “Claims,” Rig., Ven.], since salvation, being destined for both sides, is equally distributed between the two substances.

For see: from whichever substance you assume the human being to have perished, he did not perish in the other. He will therefore already be safe in that in which he did not perish, and will nevertheless be made safe in that in which he did perish. You have the restoration of the whole human being, since whatever part of him perishes the Lord will save, and whatever part does not perish he certainly will not cause to perish. Who will any longer doubt [Note: [Col. 0843C] “Doubted,” Pam., Fran.] the security of both substances, when one [Note: [Col. 0843C] “Either one,” Rhen.] will obtain salvation [Col. 0843C] and the other will not lose it?

And yet the Lord expresses the meaning of the matter still further, saying: “I came not to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me.” What will, I ask you? “That I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but should raise it up on the last day.” What had Christ received from the Father except that which he had also put on? The human being, without doubt—the interwoven fabric of flesh and soul. He will therefore allow neither of the things he received to perish; indeed, not anything belonging to either of them; indeed, not even a small part. [Col. 0844A]

[Note: [Col. 0843D] “But if the flesh is a small thing,” etc. Here he alludes to these heretics’ contempt for our flesh, which they despised as cheap, trifling, and devoid of all dignity, as was sufficiently indicated above. For even if it were so that the flesh was as cheap and insignificant as these heretics reproachfully claim, it would still have to be raised. The works performed through the service of the flesh are not so insignificant that God should neglect them; and for that reason the flesh must be raised for God’s judgment, as Athenagoras argues [Col. 0844D] in *On the Resurrection*. LAC.] But if the flesh is a small thing, then he will not lose even the flesh, because he will lose not even a small thing; nor anything at all, because not anything at all [Note: [Col. 0843C] “Because not anything at all” is absent from Rhen., Seml.]. Yet if he will not also raise the flesh on the last day, he will allow to perish not a small portion of the human being, but, I would say, in view of so great a part, almost the whole.

He presses the point further: [Note: [Col. 0844D] “This is the Father’s will.” This is “the will”; John 6:40: τοῦτο δὲ ἐστι τὸ θέλημα, “and this is the will.” RIG.] “This [Note: [Col. 0843D] “This thing,” Rhen., Seml.] is the Father’s will: that everyone who sees [Note: [Col. 0844C] “Looks upon,” Rhen., Seml.] the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him on the last day.” He establishes the fullness of the resurrection, for he apportions to each substance, according to its respective function, its own [Note: [Col. 0844C] “Former,” Par.] reward of salvation: to the flesh, through which the Son [Note: [Col. 0844C] “Of Man” added by Rhen.] was seen, and to the soul, through which he was believed.

“Therefore,” you will say, “the reality promised will belong to those by whom Christ was seen.” Let it plainly be so, provided that the same [Col. 0844B] hope has flowed from them to us as well. For if the works of flesh and soul were fruitful at that time for those who saw and therefore believed, much more are they so for us. “For more blessed,” he says, “are those who have not seen [Note: [Col. 0844C] “Do not see,” Rhen., Seml.] and yet believe.” Even if the resurrection of the flesh were denied to the former, it would certainly have belonged to those who are more blessed. For how are they blessed if they are to perish in part?

## CHAPTER XXXV

He also commands that we should rather fear [Note: [Col. 0844D] “Who can kill body and soul,” etc. Here and near the end of the chapter he rendered another meaning of the Greek word ἀπολέσαι, translating it as “to kill,” whereas in the preceding chapter he gave it another meaning, namely “to destroy” or “lose,” together with the Vulgate translator, when he says of the soul that, when lost, it is believed to pass into Gehenna. PAM.] him who can kill body and soul in Gehenna—that is, the Lord alone—and not those who kill the body but can do no harm to the soul—that is, human authorities. Thus the soul’s natural immortality is acknowledged here, since it cannot be killed by human beings, as is also the mortality of the flesh, since it can be killed; and thus the resurrection [Col. 0844C] of the dead is likewise shown to belong to the flesh, which could not be killed in Gehenna unless it had been raised.

[Note: [Col. 0844D] “But since even here a captious question is raised about the interpretation of ‘body,’” etc. He points to the heretics’ evasion by which, in order to elude that Gospel authority, they dragged the word “body” into a foreign and absurd meaning through novel quibbles and sophistical inventions. St. Jerome, *Against John of Jerusalem*, addressed to Pammachius, severely censures in him the ridiculous use of the word “body” to deny that our flesh will rise. LAC.] But since even here a captious question is raised about the interpretation of “body,” I shall understand the human body to be nothing other than this entire structure of flesh, of whatever kinds of materials it is fashioned and diversified [Note: [Col. 0844C] “May be diversified,” Ven., erroneously.]: that which is seen [Note: [Col. 0844D] “That which is seen” is absent from Ven.], that which is touched, and finally that which is killed by human beings. So too I shall recognize the body of a wall as nothing other than mortar, stones, and bricks. [Col. 0845A] If anyone introduces some hidden body, let him show, reveal, and prove that it too is what is killed by a human being, and then the statement will concern that body.

Likewise, if “body” is set in opposition [Note: [Col. 0845D] “He sets in opposition,” Pam., Fran.] to “soul,” their cunning will be idle. For when both are presented—body and soul—as being killed in Gehenna, the body is distinguished from the soul, and we are left to understand “body” as that which is readily apparent: namely, the flesh. Just as it will be killed [Note: [Col. 0845D] “Is killed,” Rig., Ven.] in Gehenna if it has not chosen rather to fear being killed by God, so it will also be brought to life for eternal life if it has chosen rather to be slain by human beings.

Accordingly, if anyone takes the killing of flesh and soul in Gehenna to mean the destruction and termination of both substances—not their punishment, as though they were to be consumed rather than chastised—let him remember that the fire of Gehenna is proclaimed eternal, for eternal punishment. From this let him recognize the eternity of that killing, on account of which it must be feared more than human killing, [Col. 0845B] since the latter is temporal. He will then also believe the substances to be eternal whose killing in punishment is eternal.

Certainly, since after the resurrection the body together with the soul is to be killed by God [Note: [Col. 0845D] “By God” omitted by Rhen., Seml.] in Gehenna, both points will be sufficiently established: the resurrection of the flesh and the eternal killing. Otherwise it would be utterly absurd if the flesh were raised only to be killed in Gehenna so that it might cease to exist, when it would have suffered the same thing by not being raised. It would, apparently, be restored for this purpose: that it might not exist, although nonexistence had already befallen it.

Supporting us in the same hope, he also adds [Note: [Col. 0845D] “Added,” Rig., Ven.] the example of the sparrows: not one [Note: [Col. 0845D] “The other,” all editions except Jun.] of two falls to the ground without God’s will. Thus you may believe that the flesh too, which has fallen into the earth, can likewise rise again through the will of the same God. For even if this is not permitted to sparrows, we rank above many sparrows [Col. 0845C] precisely because, though we fall, we rise again.

Moreover, by affirming [Note: [Col. 0845D] “He affirms,” Rig., Ven.] that all the hairs of their heads have been numbered [Note: [Col. 0845D] “Counted out,” Rig., Ven.], he surely promises that they will be preserved. For what reason would he have brought into a reckoning things that were to perish, unless because this is the meaning of: “Of all that the Father has given me, I will lose nothing” (John 6)—that is, not even a hair, just as not an eye or a tooth?

Besides, whence will come weeping and gnashing of teeth in Gehenna unless from eyes and [Note: [Col. 0845D] “From” added by Rhen., Seml.] teeth? The body too, of course, has been killed in Gehenna and thrust into the outer darkness—torments particularly suited to the eyes—if anyone has come to the wedding clothed in works of insufficient worth. He is immediately to be bound by hands [Col. 0846A] and feet, as one who has risen with the body. Thus reclining in the kingdom of God, sitting upon the thrones [Note: [Col. 0845D] “Twelve” added by Fran.] of Christ, standing then at his right [Note: [Col. 0846D] “Then at his right,” Rig., Ven.] or left hand, and eating from the tree of life are all most trustworthy indications of a bodily ordering.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

Let us now see whether, in crushing the Sadducees’ subtlety, he has not established our position all the more. The occasion of the question, I think, was the destruction of belief in the resurrection. For the Sadducees [Note: [Col. 0845D] “For the Sadducees admit the salvation neither of the soul,” etc. More than once in this work and elsewhere I have noted concerning those heretics that they denied the immortality of the soul and the resurrection of bodies. LE PR.] admit salvation neither of the soul nor of the flesh. They therefore adapted to their problem an argument drawn from precisely that aspect under which faith in the resurrection is most severely shaken [Note: [Col. 0846D] “From precisely that source from which hope in the resurrection is most severely shaken,” Paris.]: [Note: [Col. 0845D] “Namely, under the pretext of the flesh.” Because legitimate arguments for proving their inventions were lacking, the Sadducees put forward fictitious ones. They asked Christ concerning the wife of seven husbands, whose wife she would be at the resurrection—a question not merely frivolous but ridiculous. LE PR.] namely, under the pretext of the flesh, asking whether it would marry after the resurrection. They used the case of the woman who had married seven [Col. 0846B] brothers, where it would be uncertain to which of them she would be restored.

Now preserve the meaning both of the question and of the answer, and the controversy has been met. For if the Sadducees rejected the resurrection, while the Lord [Note: [Col. 0845D] “Confirmed it.” It might perhaps be no bad reading to have “confirms”; this would please me more, for it speaks more pointedly and forcefully. LE PR.] confirmed it [Note: [Col. 0846D] “Confirms,” Rhen., Seml.], rebuking them as ignorant of the Scriptures—namely, those that proclaimed the resurrection—and as unbelieving in the power of God, which was surely adequate to raise the dead; and if he finally added, “But concerning the fact that [Note: [Col. 0846D] “How,” Rhen., Seml.] the dead rise” [Note: [Col. 0846D] I would read “rise” or “will rise.” LE PR.], then, without doubt, by confirming the very thing that was denied—namely, the resurrection of the dead, who are alive before God [Note: [Col. 0846D] “The Lord,” Rhen., Seml.]—he also confirmed that it is of the same kind as that which was being denied: namely, a resurrection of both human substances.

Nor, because he denied that they would marry then, did he thereby show that they would not rise [Note: [Col. 0846D] “Will deny … will show,” Rhen., Seml.]. On the contrary, he called them “children of the resurrection” [Col. 0846C] [Note: [Col. 0846D] “Calls,” Rhen., Seml.], since through it they will in a sense be born, after which they will not marry. Rather, once raised, they will be like the angels: [Note: [Col. 0846D] “Insofar as they will not marry, because they will not die.” After the resurrection there will be no use for marriage. Since marriages were instituted solely for the propagation of the human race, when that necessity of dying ceases, that form of propagation also ceases. LE PR.] insofar as they will not marry, because they will not die, but insofar as they will pass into an angelic condition through that clothing of incorruptibility, through the transformation of a substance that nevertheless has been raised.

Besides, the question whether we would marry or die again would never have arisen unless the restoration of precisely that substance which properly performs the functions both of dying and of marrying—that is, the flesh—were being called into doubt. You therefore have the Lord confirming against the Jewish heretics what is now denied among [Note: [Col. 0846D] “The Sadducees of the Christians.” Just as the Sadducees were heretics among the Jews, so he calls the Christian heretics of his own time “the Sadducees of the Christians.” LE PR.] the Sadducees of the Christians: a solid resurrection.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

[Col. 0847A]

Thus, even if [Note: [Col. 0847C] “Although,” Rhen.] he says that the flesh profits nothing, the meaning must be determined from the subject matter of the saying. [Note: [Col. 0847C] “For because they considered his discourse harsh and intolerable, as though he had actually ordained that they should eat his flesh.” Theodorus of Heraclea excellently softens all the harshness of this saying: Σκληρὸς ἦν ἀληθῶς ὁ λόγος ἐνομιζόμενος σαρκοφάγους τινὰς καὶ αἱμοβόρους τοὺς ἀκούοντας ἀποτελεῖν· τοῖς δὲ πνευματικῶς τὰ πνευματικὰ ἐκλαμβάνουσιν, οὐδὲν ἐφαίνετο σκληρόν, ἀλλὰ ῥήματα εὐσεβείας ὑπάρχοντα, τὴν αἰώνιον αὐτοῖς πρυτανεύοντα ζωήν: “The saying was truly harsh when it was thought to turn its hearers into people who ate flesh and drank blood; but to those who received spiritual things spiritually, nothing in it appeared harsh. Rather, its words were words of piety, procuring eternal life for them.” See Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book IV, chapter 15. RIG.] For because they considered his discourse harsh and intolerable, as though he had actually ordained that they should eat his flesh, he first said, in order to assign the basis of salvation to the spirit [Note: [Col. 0847C] “In the spirit,” Pam., Fran.]: “It is the Spirit who gives life”; and thus he added: [Note: [Col. 0847D] “The flesh profits nothing.” So too her maternal kinship would have profited Mary nothing unless she had borne Christ more blessedly in her heart than in her flesh. Augustine, *On Holy Virginity*. RIG.] “The flesh profits nothing” [Note: [Col. 0847C] “But” inserted by Rhen., Seml.]—for giving life, that is.

He also explains what he wishes “spirit” to mean: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and are life.” So too above: “He who hears my words and believes in him who sent me has eternal life, and will not come into judgment, but will pass [Note: [Col. 0847C] “Passes,” some editions; “has passed,” others; “will pass,” others.] from death to life” (John 5–6).

Thus, by establishing that the word gives life, because the word is spirit and life, he also called that same word his flesh, because [Col. 0847B] the Word had also been made flesh. Accordingly, it must be sought as the cause of life, [Note: [Col. 0847D] “And devoured by hearing.” This unusual metaphor is derived from the fact that, since Christ is the Word of God and his flesh is bread, he is said to be devoured by hearing just as bread is devoured by the mouth. LE PR.] devoured by hearing, ruminated upon by the understanding, and digested by faith [Note: [Col. 0847C] “Directed,” Rhen.]. For shortly before this he had also declared his flesh to be heavenly bread, everywhere pressing upon them, through the allegory of necessary nourishment [Note: [Col. 0847C] “Peoples,” Rig., Ven.], the memory of the fathers who had preferred the bread and meat of the Egyptians to the divine calling.

Therefore, turning to their thoughts, because he perceived that they were about to disperse [Note: [Col. 0848C] Variant spelling in Rhen., Seml.], he said: “The flesh profits nothing.” What has this to do with destroying the resurrection of the flesh? As though something might not exist which, although it profits nothing, may nevertheless itself be profited by something else! The Spirit profits, for it gives life. The flesh profits nothing, for it is put to death. Thus he has arranged [Note: [Col. 0848C] “Illuminated,” Lat.] the proposition concerning both substances in greater accordance with our position. For by showing what profits and what does not profit, he equally illuminated [Col. 0847C] what profits what: namely, that the Spirit gives life to the flesh that has been put to death.

“For the hour will come,” he says, “when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.” [Col. 0848A] What is dead but the flesh? What is God’s voice but the word? And what is the word but spirit? He is deservedly going to raise the flesh, because that is what he himself became; to raise it from the death that he himself suffered, and from the tomb into which he himself was carried.

Finally, when he says, “Do not marvel that the hour will come in which all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God and will come forth: those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment,” no one will any longer be able to interpret the dead who are in the tombs as anything other than bodies and flesh, because the tombs themselves are nothing other than lodging places for corpses.

For even those “old human beings”—that is, those dead through ignorance of God—whom the heretics argue should be understood as the tombs, are expressly proclaimed as persons who will come forth from the tombs to judgment. Otherwise, how will tombs come forth from [Col. 0848B] tombs?

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

After the Lord’s sayings, what are we to believe his deeds mean—his raising the dead from their biers and tombs? To what purpose was this? If it was for a mere display of power or for the present favor of restoring life, it was no very great thing for him to raise persons who would die again [Note: [Col. 0848C] “To be raised,” Rhen., Seml.].

But indeed, [Note: [Col. 0847D] “If rather to place the faith of the future resurrection in safekeeping.” *Sequestrare* means to deposit something with a custodian so that it may be secure. Hence the jurists’ expression “property placed in sequestration.” Explain the phrase, therefore, as meaning “to place faith in the future [Col. 0848C] resurrection in safekeeping”—that is, so to speak, to certify it and secure it in safety. This word also occurs above, unless I am mistaken. Moreover, when he says shortly afterward, “lest he seem to have presented the proofs in one form but deposited the reality in another,” he explains what he previously meant by “placing the faith in safekeeping.” RHEN.—We must not depart from Rhenanus’s interpretation. I add only that a *sequester* is a person with whom several parties deposit the same disputed object; Digest 50.16.209. Yet the observation of the grammarians who derive the word from *sequi*, “to follow,” appears pointless in this legal text. In Basil it is called μεσογενήτης, “an intermediary,” and the objects are the disputed property. LE PR.] if it was rather to place faith in the future resurrection in safekeeping, then by the form of its own evidence that resurrection is prescribed as bodily. Nor shall I tolerate those who say that the resurrection, though destined at that time for the soul alone, was anticipated [Note: [Col. 0848C] “Had preceded,” Rig., Ven.] in the flesh as well because the resurrection of an invisible soul could not otherwise have been shown except through the raising of a visible [Note: [Col. 0848C] “Invisible,” Rig., Ven.] substance. [Col. 0848C]

They know God badly who do not think that he can do what they themselves do not think possible; and yet they know that he could have done so, if [Note: [Col. 0848D] “They know John’s instrument.” Among the masters of law, *instruments* are public documents by which proof is furnished in the absence of the persons concerned. Likewise John’s Gospel is called an “instrument,” because it hands down, proves, and teaches the mysteries of religion; for *instrumentum* is derived from *instruere*, “to instruct”—Digest, *On Production of Documents*, “The Banker,” § “He Shall Produce.” It is customary for Tertullian to call Sacred Scripture an “instrument,” as in chapter 2 of *On the Flesh of Christ*: “So many original instruments”; and several times in this book, in the following book, and elsewhere. LE PR.] they know John’s instrument. For he who submitted to sight the souls of the martyrs still resting alone beneath the altar could certainly also have presented those souls rising without flesh to the eyes. [Col. 0849A]

But I prefer to believe that God cannot deceive—that deception alone is a weakness in him—lest he seem to have presented the proofs in one form but arranged the reality in another; indeed, lest, if he was unable to provide an example of resurrection without flesh, he should be even less able to display the fullness of the example in the same substance. No example, however, is greater than that of which it is the example. Yet it would be greater [Note: [Col. 0849C] “Would have been,” Wouwer manuscript.] if souls were to be raised together with bodies [Note: [Col. 0849C] “Were raised,” Wouwer manuscript.] as evidence of a resurrection without bodies, so that the salvation of the whole human being supported the case for the salvation of half—whereas the nature of examples would instead require that which would be regarded as the lesser thing—I mean the resurrection of the soul alone—as a foretaste of the flesh that would also [Note: [Col. 0849C] “Also” is absent from Fran.] rise in its own time.

And so [Note: [Col. 0849C] “For this reason,” Wouwer manuscript.], according to our assessment of the truth [Note: [Col. 0849C] “True,” Ven.; [Col. 0849D] “Opinion,” Fran., Pam.], those examples [Col. 0849B] of dead persons raised by the Lord did indeed commend the resurrection both of flesh and of soul, lest this gift be denied to either substance. Yet those examples displayed something less—for they were raised not to glory and incorruptibility, but to another death—than Christ displayed.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

The apostolic instruments also testify to the resurrection. For the Apostles had no other task, at least among Israel, than [Note: [Col. 0849D] “Unsealing the Old Testament and sealing the New.” An excellent metaphor indicating that the Apostles explained the Old Testament and confirmed the New. For a testament is opened by breaking its seal and is established by sealing it. The labor of apostolic preaching was therefore the exposition of the Old Testament and the confirmation of the New. LAC.] to unseal the Old Testament and to seal the New—or rather, by then, to proclaim God in Christ. Thus they introduced [Note: [Col. 0850C] “Had introduced,” Rhen.] nothing new about the resurrection either, except that they also proclaimed it [Col. 0849C] to the glory of Christ. In all other respects it had already been received in a simple and familiar faith, [Note: [Col. 0849D] “Without any question about its character.” That is, without any controversy over what kind it would be—namely, whether of the body or of the soul. For the dispute with the Sadducees did not concern which resurrection was to occur, that of the soul or that of the flesh, as the Author argues against the heretics, but the reality of resurrection, which the Sadducees denied absolutely and entirely. LAC.] without any question about its character, with the Sadducees alone opposing it. So much easier was it for the resurrection of the dead to be denied altogether than to be understood in a different sense.

You have Paul, before the chief priests and under the tribune, professing his faith among Sadducees and Pharisees: “Men and brothers,” he says, “I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees; it is concerning the hope and the resurrection that I am now judged before you.” He certainly means the resurrection common to them all, lest, because he now appeared to be a transgressor of the law, he should be thought to agree with the Sadducees concerning the chief article of the entire faith—that is, the resurrection. Thus he certainly confirmed the faith of the resurrection according to the Pharisees, which he did not wish [Col. 0850A] to appear to abolish, rejecting the Sadducees who denied it.

Similarly, before Agrippa he says that he puts forward nothing beyond what the prophets had proclaimed. Therefore he preserved the resurrection too in the form in which the prophets had proclaimed it. For when he recalled that the resurrection of the dead was written of in Moses, he knew it to be bodily—the resurrection in which, namely, the blood of a human being will have to be required. Thus he preached it in the form in which the Pharisees had accepted it, the Lord himself had defended it, and the Sadducees, lest they believe it even in that form, had wished it not to exist at all.

Nor had the Athenians understood Paul to be presenting any other kind of resurrection. In fact, they ridiculed it; they certainly would not have ridiculed him if they had heard from him of the restoration of the soul alone, for they would have accepted an assumption commonly held in their native philosophy. [Col. 0850B]

But when the proclamation of the resurrection—previously unheard of—shook the nations by its very novelty, and an unbelief commensurate with so great a reality began to put faith to the torture with questions [Note: [Col. 0850C] “To extort faith,” Rhen., Seml.], then the Apostle too [Note: [Col. 0849D] “Throughout almost the entire instrument.” He means the Epistles of blessed Paul, as Rhenanus testifies, in which powerful proofs of the resurrection are offered. You see that in this chapter he calls Scripture an “instrument” more than once. LE PR.] took care throughout almost the entire instrument to strengthen faith in this hope, showing that it exists, that it has not yet been accomplished, that it is bodily—which was the principal question—and, what was additionally doubted, that it is bodily in no other manner.

## CHAPTER XL
There is nothing surprising, however, if arguments are also seized upon from the Apostle’s own body of writings, since heresies must exist; and they could not exist unless Scripture were also capable of being wrongly understood. Thus heresies, having seized upon [Note: [Col. 0850C] Rhenanus reads “having arisen” (*natae*) for “having seized upon” (*nactae*).] the two men presented by the Apostle—the inner man, that is, the soul, [Col. 0850C] and the outer man, that is, the flesh—have assigned salvation to the soul, that is, to the inner man, but destruction to the flesh, that is, to the outer man, because it is written to the Corinthians: “For even if our outer man is corrupted, yet the inner man is renewed from [Note: [Col. 0850C] “From” omitted by Rigault and the Venice edition.] day to day.”

Yet neither is the soul by itself a man, since it was subsequently inserted into the formed being already called “man”; nor is the flesh without the soul a man, since after the soul’s departure it is designated a corpse. Thus the word “man” is, as it were, the clasp joining the two interwoven substances: under that designation they cannot exist except [Note: [Col. 0850D] “Except” is absent from Rhenanus.] in union.

[Note: [Col. 0850D] “Moreover, the Apostle [means] the inner man,” etc. The Apostle uses “inner man” and “outer man” in different senses in Romans VII and II Corinthians IV. There the outer man is concupiscence, while the inner man is love and spirit—that is, the man who desires and the man renewed in spirit. Here, however, the outer man is the bodily man himself insofar as he is visible, tangible, and, finally, perceptible and capable of suffering, and can receive injuries from without; the inner man is the man insofar as he consists of the invisible mind, which bears the body’s afflictions bravely and nobly. LAC.]

Moreover, by the “inner man” the Apostle prefers us to understand [Note: [Col. 0850D] “Not so much the soul as the mind and intelligence,” etc. [Col. 0851D] Philosophers either observe or assume a distinction between *anima* and *animus*. For *animus* is understood as the mind, namely insofar as it performs intellectual functions; *anima*, however, insofar as it gives life to the body and manages the operations of the senses and the functions of the limbs. The latter is understood as the nature and substance of the thing, the former as its excellent disposition. LAC.] not [Col. 0851A] so much the soul as the mind and intelligence—that is, not the substance itself, but the substance’s disposition. For when he writes to the Ephesians that Christ dwells “into the inner man,” [Note: [Col. 0851D] “Christ dwells into the inner man.” Here too he has reproduced the Greek, *εἰς τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον* (“into the inner man”), joining this phrase to what follows, whereas all other editions, including the Syriac, join it to what precedes. PAM.] he surely means that the Lord is to be brought into the inmost [Note: [Col. 0851D] “To be brought into the inmost.” A word commonly frequent in that age. *Intimare* means “to make inward.” RHEN.] affections [Note: [Col. 0851C] “Initiated,” Rigault and the Venice edition.]. He therefore added (Eph. III), “Through faith,” and “In your hearts,” and “In love,” presenting faith and love not as constituent substances of the soul, but as its conceptions. By saying “in your hearts,” however—and hearts are constituent substances of the flesh—he has already assigned to the flesh that very inner man whom he located in the heart.

Now examine how he declared that the outer man is corrupted, but that the inner man is renewed from [Note: [Col. 0851C] “From” is absent from Rhenanus, Rigault, the Venice edition, and Semler.] day to day. You must not affirm that this corruption is the corruption of the flesh which it will suffer when it passes away forever from the day of death onward. Rather, it is the corruption which, during the course of this life, before death and right up [Col. 0851B] to death, the flesh will undergo through harassments and pressures, torments and punishments, for the sake of the Name. For the inner man likewise will surely have to be renewed here through the prompting of the Spirit, advancing in faith and discipline from [Note: [Col. 0851C] “From” is absent from Rhenanus, Rigault, the Venice edition, and Semler.] day to day—not there, that is, not after the resurrection, where we shall certainly not be renewed from [Note: [Col. 0851C] “From” is absent from Rhenanus, Rigault, the Venice edition, and Semler.] day to day, but once and for all to perfection.

Learn this from what follows: “For that which is present,” he says (II Cor. VI), “the temporal and light burden of our affliction, [Note: [Col. 0851D] “Through excess unto excess.” So it is read in the manuscripts. He has rendered Paul’s Greek, *καθ’ ὑπερβολὴν εἰς ὑπερβολήν* (“according to excess unto excess”). So below, “we were burdened beyond measure, beyond our strength,” which Paul expressed as *καθ’ ὑπερβολὴν* [Col. 0852D] *ὑπὲρ δύναμιν* (“exceedingly beyond our strength”). RIG.] through excess unto excess, [Note: [Col. 0851C] “Unto excess” omitted by Rhenanus, Semler, and Pamelius.] will produce in [Note: [Col. 0851C] “To be produced,” in Rhenanus and Semler.] us an eternal weight of glory, while we look not at the things that are seen,” that is, sufferings, “but at the things that are not seen,” that is, rewards; “for the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal.” [Note: [Col. 0851C] “Are” is absent from Rigault and the Venice edition.]

For he declares that the pressures and injuries by which [Col. 0851C] the outer man is corrupted should be despised because they are light and temporal, preferring instead the weight of eternal and invisible rewards and of glory, as compensation for the hardships through which the flesh is corrupted by suffering here. So entirely is this not the corruption which they ascribe to the outer man as the flesh’s everlasting destruction, in order to exclude the resurrection.

Likewise elsewhere he says (Rom. VIII): “Provided that [Note: [Col. 0852D] “We suffer together, so that we may also be glorified together.” Here too he properly translates the Greek words *εἴπερ*, “provided that,” and *συνδοξασθῶμεν*, “we may be glorified together.” Likewise *λογίζομαι*, “I reckon.” “To suffer together” is understood as “to suffer jointly,” and therefore the word *compassio* (“shared suffering”), which the Author uses shortly afterward, must be understood in the same way. PAM.] we suffer together, so that we may also be glorified together; [Col. 0852A] for I reckon that the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which is to be revealed in us.” Here too he shows that the hardships are less than their rewards. Moreover, if it is through the flesh that we suffer together—and it belongs properly to the flesh to be corrupted by sufferings—then to that same flesh will also belong what is promised in return for shared suffering.

And so fully does he assign the property of enduring pressure to the flesh [Note: [Col. 0852D] “So that above too he says” (namely Paul): “When we came,” etc. By “above,” the Author means again the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, whose passages are principally treated in this chapter; for this text is found in II Corinthians. Unless perhaps someone prefers to suppose that he follows Marcion’s ordering, observed in the books against Marcion, since Marcion places the Epistle to the Romans—from which he had produced the immediately preceding testimony—after the Epistles to the Corinthians. PAM.] that above too he says [Note: [Col. 0851C] “Says,” Rhenanus and Semler.]: “But when we came into Macedonia, our flesh had no relief.” Then, to assign shared suffering [Note: [Col. 0851D] Rhenanus and Semler add “and.”] to the soul as well, he says (II Cor. VII): [Note: [Col. 0852D] “Afflicted in all things,” he says. This too is word for word from the Greek: *ἀλλ’ ἐν παντὶ θλιβόμενοι* (“but afflicted in every way”). PAM.] “Afflicted in all things: conflicts without,” which were, of course, assaulting the flesh; “fear within,” which was, of course, distressing the soul.

Thus, even if the outer man is corrupted, he will be understood [Note: [Col. 0852C] “Would be understood,” Rhenanus and Semler.] to be corrupted not by losing the resurrection, but by enduring harassment. And this does not occur without the inner man. Thus it will belong to both [Col. 0852B] to be glorified together, just as it belongs to both to suffer together. In accordance with their partnership in hardships, their partnership [Note: [Col. 0852C] Rhenanus and Semler read “also.”] in rewards must likewise follow.

## CHAPTER XLI

He continues to pursue the same argument, preferring recompenses to afflictions. “For we know,” he says (II Cor. V), “that even if our earthly house of this [Note: [Col. 0852C] “Our,” Rhenanus and Semler.] tabernacle is dissolved, we have a house not made by hands, eternal in heaven”; that is, through the dissolution of our flesh by sufferings, [Note: [Col. 0852C] Rhenanus adds “that.”] we shall obtain a dwelling in heaven. He was mindful of the Gospel’s declaration [Note: [Col. 0852C] *Diffinitionis*, Rhenanus and Semler.] (Matt. V): “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

Yet he did not deny the restoration of the flesh merely because he set the reward as compensation over against it, since compensation is owed to the very thing to which dissolution is assigned [Note: [Col. 0852C] “Reckoned,” Rhenanus and Semler.], namely, the flesh. But because he had called the flesh a “house,” he elegantly chose to use the word “house” also in comparing the reward, promising to the very house which will be dissolved through suffering a better house through the resurrection. For the Lord too promises many mansions, as though they were houses, with the Father (John XIV).

Although it [Note: [Col. 0852D] “Nor,” Rigault and the Venice edition.] may also be understood of the dwelling place of the world, [Note: [Col. 0852D] “Although it may also be understood of the dwelling place [Col. 0853C] of the world,” etc. He signifies the human body by two metaphors, that of a dwelling and that of a garment: a dwelling in this life, and a garment of glory in the next. Even the pagan Seneca seems to acknowledge both—the first in Epistle 120, the second in Epistle 92. LE PR.] whose dissolution is followed by the promise of an eternal abode in heaven, the statements that follow, which plainly concern the flesh, show that the preceding statements wholly [Note: [Col. 0853C] “Not,” Rhenanus, Semler, and Pamelius.] concern the flesh.

For the Apostle makes a distinction when he adds: “For in this too we groan, [Note: [Col. 0853C] “In this we groan,” Pamelius and Franeker.] desiring to be clothed over with our dwelling which is from heaven, provided that when clothed [Note: [Col. 0853C] “Unclothed,” Semler.] we are not found naked”; that is, we wish to be clothed over with the heavenly power of eternity before we are stripped of the flesh. For the privilege of this grace awaits those who will be found in the flesh at the coming of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0853D] “Will be found in the flesh.” Here he speaks of the Lord’s second coming, at which the Judge of all will weigh and examine sins. Those who are found in the flesh—that is, alive—will present themselves before the Lord together with that same flesh; those who are not found in the flesh will assume the flesh, for he will be the Judge of the living and the dead. He explains this in Question 109. Blessed Justin: *οὐ πάντες κοιμηθησόμεθα. κρινεῖ οὖν ζῶντας μὲν τοὺς τότε ζῶντας, νεκροὺς δὲ τοὺς ἀνισταμένους ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν.* “We shall not all sleep. He will therefore judge as the living those who are then alive, and as the dead those who rise from the dead.” LE PR.] and who, because of the hardships of Antichrist’s times, will deserve—through the shortcut of having death canceled by transformation—to join those who are rising, just as he writes to the Thessalonians (I Thess. IV): “For this we say to you in the word of the Lord: we who are alive, who remain until [Col. 0853B] the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself, at the command and the voice of the Archangel [Note: [Col. 0853C] “Angel,” Rhenanus and Semler.] and at the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven; and the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we, together with them, shall at once [Note: [Col. 0853C] “At once” is absent from Rhenanus and Semler.] be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord [Note: [Col. 0853C] “Christ,” Rhenanus and Semler.] in the air; and so we shall always be with the Lord.”

## CHAPTER XLII

He presents [Note: [Col. 0853C] “Presented,” Pamelius and Franeker.] their transformation to the Corinthians (I Cor. XV), saying: “We shall indeed all rise, but we shall not all be transformed, in an atom, in the momentary movement of an eye, at the last trumpet”—that is, only those, of course, who are found in the flesh. “And the dead,” he says, “will rise first, and [Note: [Col. 0853C] Rhenanus and Semler do not have “first, and.”] we shall be transformed.”

Once you have first taken account of this arrangement, [Note: [Col. 0854C] “Position,” Rhenanus and Semler.] therefore, you will refer the remainder back to the preceding sense. For when he adds, “For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal [Col. 0853C] must put on immortality,” this will be that dwelling from heaven with which, groaning in this flesh, we desire to be clothed over [Note: [Col. 0854C] “To be clothed over,” Pamelius and Franeker.]—surely over the flesh in [Col. 0854A] which we shall be found. For he says that we who are [Note: [Col. 0854C] “May be,” Rhenanus and Semler.] in the tabernacle are burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed, but rather to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life—that is, while it is transformed [Note: [Col. 0854C] Others read “while we transform.”] by putting on what comes from heaven.

For who, while in the flesh, would not desire to put on immortality and continue in life, cheating death by a transformation in its place, so that he need not experience the lower regions, which will exact payment down to the last farthing? The one who is to obtain transformation after the resurrection, by contrast, has already experienced the lower regions.

From this point, then, we establish that the flesh will in every respect [Note: [Col. 0854C] “In every respect indeed,” Rhenanus and Semler.] rise, and that it [Note: [Col. 0854C] “That flesh,” Pamelius and Franeker.], when the transformation supervenes, will assume an angelic condition. Otherwise, if only in those who are found in the flesh must the mortal be transformed so that it may be swallowed up by [Col. 0854B] life—that is, so that the flesh may be swallowed up by that heavenly and eternal over-garment—then those found dead will not obtain life, since they have already been deprived of life’s material and, so to speak, food, namely the flesh. Or else they too must necessarily receive it, so that in them also what is mortal may be swallowed up by life, if they are to obtain life.

“But in the dead,” you say, “this mortal thing will already have been swallowed up.” Certainly not in all of them. For how many men may be found to have died only the day before, their corpses so fresh that nothing in [Note: [Col. 0854C] “In” is absent from Rhenanus and Semler.] them could be seen to have been swallowed up! For surely by “swallowed up” you mean nothing other than overtaken, abolished, taken away from every sense—something which has ceased by every means to appear. Yet even the most ancient corpses of giants cannot be shown to have been swallowed up, since their frameworks still survive. We have already spoken about this elsewhere.

But quite recently in [Col. 0854C] this city, when the foundations of the Odeum [Note: [Col. 0854C] Rhenanus reads *Hodie* (“today”); others *dei*; the Wouwer manuscript *eo die* (“on that day”).] were being laid and the sacrilegious disturbance of so many ancient tombs took place, [Note: [Col. 0854C] “When the foundations of the Odeum.” There were various *odea* at Rome—that is, places to which spectators from the theater sometimes withdrew if rain came on, for there were colonnades there. Poems were also recited in these places, and grain offered for sale [Col. 0854C] was customarily displayed there. [Col. 0854D] Cases concerning grain were also conducted there. Thus Pollux, book VIII: *τὰς δὲ ἐπὶ τῷ σίτῳ δίκας ἐν τῷ ὠδείῳ ἐδίκαζον· σῖτος δέ ἐστιν αἱ ὀφειλόμενοι τροφαί.* “Cases concerning food were adjudicated in the Odeum; and ‘food’ means any sustenance owed.” LE PR.] [Note: [Col. 0854D] “The sacrilegious disturbance of ancient tombs,” etc. When the foundations of the Odeum were being laid—for a new Odeum had been built at Carthage, about which he is perhaps speaking here—countless bones, not yet decayed or consumed, were dug up, including those of giants, which were monstrous. This was indeed akin to sacrilege, for the crime of violating a tomb is sacrilege, and the action against its violator carries infamy. Nor is it surprising that Tertullian, highly experienced in law, did not forget this; we have remarked on it elsewhere. LE PR.] the people recoiled in horror at bones nearly five hundred years old [Note: [Col. 0854D] “Nearly five hundred years old.” Who will give credence to Jerome Cardan, who reports that his father’s body, because of various exercises and a precise regimen of life, remained intact for twenty years? LE PR.] which were still moist, and at hair that still gave off its odor. [Note: [Col. 0854D] “And hair that still gave off its odor.” The same Cardan recorded in writing, in *Various Matters*, VIII, chapter 4, that the body of Cicero’s daughter Tullia [Col. 0855D] was found in the time of Sixtus IV without having suffered any deterioration. Indeed, the hair upon it appeared interwoven with a golden net; the passage of more than 1,500 years had had no effect upon the hair or upon the whole body. LE PR.]

[Col. 0855A] [Note: [Col. 0855D] It is established that not only bones endure, but also teeth. Plato in the *Phaedo*: *ἔνια δὲ μέρη τοῦ σώματος, καὶ ἐὰν σαπῇ, ὀστᾶ τε καὶ νεῦρα καὶ τὰ τοιαῦτα πάντα ὅμως, ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, ἀθάνατά ἐστιν.* “Some parts of the body, even if it decays—bones, sinews, and all such things—are nevertheless, so to speak, immortal.” RIG.] It is established that not only bones endure, but teeth too remain incorrupt; they are preserved like seeds of the body that is to bear fruit in the resurrection.

Finally, even if at that time what is mortal is found to have been swallowed up in all the dead, it will certainly have been swallowed up by death, certainly by the passage of time, certainly through age. But will it have been swallowed up by [Note: [Col. 0855C] “From,” Rhenanus and Semler.] life, by the over-garment, by the accession of immortality? Moreover, by saying that what is mortal will be swallowed up by these things, [Note: [Col. 0855C] “Because by these,” Rhenanus and Semler.] he has denied that it will be swallowed up by the others. And surely it is fitting that this should be accomplished and bestowed by divine powers, not by natural laws.

Therefore, since what is mortal must be swallowed up by life, it must necessarily be produced in every case so that it may be swallowed up, and swallowed up so that it may be transformed. If you say that a fire must be kindled, you cannot affirm that the material by which it is kindled is necessary in one case but not in another.

So too when he reinforces the point: “Provided that, once unclothed, we are not found naked” [Note: [Col. 0855C] “We shall be found naked,” Rhenanus and the Venice edition.], he is speaking, of course, about those who will not be found alive or in the flesh on the day of the Lord. He has called those whom he previously described as unclothed “naked” for no other reason than that he wished them to be understood as clothed again with the same substance of which they had been stripped. For they will be found naked because the flesh has been laid aside, or partly torn apart or worn away; this too can be called nakedness. Then [Note: [Col. 0855C] Pamelius and Franeker add “and.”] they will receive it back, so that, reclothed with the flesh, they may also be clothed over with immortality. For being clothed over cannot apply unless one is already clothed.

## CHAPTER XLIII

Accordingly, when he says: “Therefore, [Note: [Col. 0855D] ‘Always confident.’ He translated the Greek *θαρροῦντες* (‘being confident’). LE PR.] always confident and knowing that, while [Note: [Col. 0855D] ‘We remain in the body, we are absent from the Lord.’ He also explains the Greek *ἐκδημοῦντες* (‘being away from home’). LE PR.] we remain in the body, we are absent [Note: [Col. 0855C] ‘May be absent,’ Rhenanus and Semler.] from the Lord—for we walk by faith, not by sight,” it is clear that this too does not serve to disparage the flesh, as though it separated us from the Lord. For here the exhortation is directed toward scorning this life, since we are absent from the Lord as long as we live, walking by faith, not by sight—that is, by hope, not by reality.

He therefore adds: “But being confident, and considering it better [Note: [Col. 0855C] “Saying,” Rhenanus and Semler.] rather to be absent from the body and to be present with the Lord”—that is, so that we may walk by sight rather than by faith, by reality rather than by hope. You see how here too [Note: [Col. 0855C] “Here too,” Pamelius and Franeker.] he relates contempt for bodies to the excellence of martyrdom. For no one who has become absent from the body is immediately present with the Lord except by the prerogative of martyrdom, since he is to lodge in paradise, [Note: [Col. 0855D] “In paradise, of course,” Rhenanus and Semler.] not in the lower regions. [Note: [Col. 0856C] Others read *diversurus*.]

[Note: [Col. 0855D] “But had the Apostle run out of words?” Theophylact prudently observed that the Apostle avoided the terms “death” and “life,” calling death “presence with the Lord,” or “remaining with him,” but calling life “absence” [Col. 0856D] and “being away from home.” LAC.] But had the Apostle run out of words to signify departure from the body? Or does he speak in this unusual way for a reason? For since he wished to signify a temporary absence from the body, he said that we are away from home in relation to it, because one who is away from home will also return to his dwelling.

Hence he also says to everyone: “And therefore [Note: [Col. 0856C] Rhenanus and Semler delete “And therefore.”] we strive,” he says (II Cor. V), “whether absent or present, to be pleasing to God. [Note: [Col. 0856C] “To please him,” Paris and Franeker.] For we must all be manifested before the judgment seat [Note: [Col. 0856C] “Before the judgment seat,” Pamelius and Franeker.] of Christ Jesus.” If all of us, then the whole of us; [Col. 0856B] if the whole of us, then both our inner and outer parts—that is, both souls and bodies: [Note: [Col. 0856D] “So that each one,” he says, “may receive.” The Vulgate has: “that each one may receive the things proper to the body.” The loss of a single letter alone produced the variant reading. The Vulgate reads *ἴδια τοῦ σώματος* (“the things proper to the body”), but Tertullian *διὰ τοῦ σώματος* (“through the body”); it is so read in Greek manuscripts and is followed by the Syriac, Theophylact, and Oecumenius. In Tertullian, the English manuscript had “the past things of the body.” LAC.] “So that each one,” he says, “may receive [Note: [Col. 0856C] Franeker, Rigault, and the Venice edition add “the things.”] through the body according to what he has done, whether good or evil.”

I ask, then, how do you read this? For he has constructed it obscurely through hyperbaton: [Note: [Col. 0856D] “For he has constructed it obscurely through hyperbaton.” The grammatical figure of hyperbaton occurs when a word is transposed, as though the sentence had become confused and obstructed. A word placed farther away produces hyperbaton, as would happen if “through the body” were connected with the verb “has done.” LAC.] does it refer to the things that must be received through the body, or to the things that were done through the body? But if it means the things that must be received through the body, then the resurrection is undoubtedly bodily; and if it means the things done through the body, [Note: [Col. 0856D] “They must certainly be repaid through the body.” That is, expiated or rewarded. Theodoret gives a similar explanation, inferring the resurrection with Tertullian. LAC.] then they must certainly be repaid through the body through which they were also done. Thus this entire discussion of the Apostle from its beginning, woven to a conclusion of such a kind as demonstrates the resurrection of the flesh, must be understood according to those things that accord with its conclusion.

## CHAPTER XLIV

[Col. 0856C] For if you look back still further, to the point from which mention of the outer and inner man was introduced, will you not find both the dignity and the hope of the flesh intact? For while [Note: [Col. 0856C] “When,” Rhenanus and Semler.] he speaks of the light which God has made to shine in our hearts, for the illumination of the knowledge of his glory in the person of Christ, he says that we possess this treasure in earthen vessels—that is, in the flesh. Is it to be destroyed because it is earthen, in accordance with its origin in [Note: [Col. 0856D] Pamelius and Franeker add “from.”] clay, or will it [Col. 0857A] be exalted because [Note: [Col. 0857D] “The repository of the divine treasure.” He calls the flesh the repository of the divine treasure, not without allusion to ancient rites and to a common expression among philosophers. For they called the flesh a tomb, as I have already shown from Plato, and Tertullian himself called it a coffin and a tomb. Yet treasures were formerly deposited in tombs—a fact better known than almost anything else. The flesh, therefore, is such a tomb that it encloses the divine treasure together with the soul. Moreover, a *conditorium* is a tomb. Petronius Arbiter: “She even followed the deceased into the tomb and began to guard him after he had been placed in the underground chamber, according to the Greek custom.” LAC.] it is the repository of the divine treasure?

Indeed, if that true light itself, which is in the person of Christ, contains life within itself, and that life is entrusted together with the light to the flesh, will the flesh to which life is entrusted perish? Certainly—if the treasure itself is also to perish. For things destined to perish are entrusted to things destined to perish, just as new wine is entrusted to old wineskins.

Likewise, when he adds: “Always carrying about the mortification of Christ Jesus in our body,” what kind of thing is this which, after being God’s temple, can now also be called Christ’s tomb? Why, moreover, do we carry the Lord’s mortification about in the body? “So that the life [Note: [Col. 0857C] Pamelius and Franeker add “of Jesus.”],” he says, “may also be manifested.” Where? “In the body.” [Note: [Col. 0857C] Pamelius and Franeker add “our.”] In what sort of body? “In a mortal one.” Therefore in the flesh—certainly mortal according to guilt, but also capable of life according to grace.

See how great that grace is: that in the flesh the life of Christ should be manifested. [Col. 0857B] Will the eternal, perpetual, incorruptible life of Christ—which is now also the life of God—be manifested in something foreign to salvation, [Note: [Col. 0857C] “To salvation,” Rhenanus and Semler.] in a substance destined for everlasting dissolution? Or at what time will the Lord’s life be manifested in our body? Will it be the life which [Note: [Col. 0857C] “By which,” Rhenanus and Semler.] he lived until his Passion, which was manifested not only among the Jews but has now also been disclosed to all nations? Rather, he signifies the life which broke apart the adamantine gates of death and the bronze bars of the lower regions, and which from that time onward is also ours.

Therefore, “it will be manifested in the body.” When? After death. How? When we rise in the body, just as Christ did. For lest anyone argue that the life of Jesus is now manifested in our body through the discipline of holiness, patience, righteousness, and wisdom, in which the Lord’s life flourished, the Apostle’s most provident intention insists: “For if we who live are delivered over to death because of Jesus, so that his life may be manifested in our mortal body,” he says that this will take place in our body after we have died. [Note: [Col. 0857C] “And so,” Pamelius and Franeker.] But if it will occur then, how can it occur unless the body has been raised?

Accordingly, also in the conclusion he says: [Col. 0858A] “Knowing that he who raised Jesus will also raise us with him, because he has already risen [Note: [Col. 0857C] “Has risen,” Rhenanus and Semler.] from the dead.” Is this not because “with him” has the sense “just like him”? But if just like him, then certainly not without the flesh.

## CHAPTER XLV

But again, with another sort of blindness, they stumble upon two men—the old and the new—because the Apostle admonishes us (Eph. IV) to put off the old man, [Note: [Col. 0857D] “Who is corrupted through the concupiscence of deception.” What he translates here with “through,” he renders below with “according to,” which better expresses the Greek word *κατά*. Meanwhile, the expression “the concupiscence of deception,” in the singular, is peculiar to the Author and, after him, to Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book XII, whereas all other editions of Ephesians IV, Syriac and Greek as well as Latin, read it in the plural. Yet we certainly read, according to three Vatican manuscripts, “to be renewed in the spirit of perception,” instead of “in the perception of the spirit”: first, because blessed Cyprian also so reads it in book III, *To Quirinus*, chapter 2; and secondly, because the Greek is *τῷ πνεύματι τοῦ νοῦς* (“in the spirit of the mind”), which the Latin translator rendered “in the spirit of the mind.” PAM.] “who is corrupted through the concupiscence of deception,” but to “be renewed in the spirit of perception and put on the new man, who according to God was created in righteousness and the holiness of truth.” By distinguishing here too according to two substances, they assign oldness to the flesh and newness to the soul, and maintain everlasting corruption for the old man, that is, for the flesh.

Yet if this is understood according to substances, neither is the soul the new [Col. 0858B] man merely because it came later, nor is the flesh the old man merely because it came first. For how very little time there was between God’s hand and his breath! I would dare say that even if the soul were much earlier than the flesh, the flesh, by the very fact that it waited to be filled with the soul, made itself prior. For every completion and perfection, [Note: [Col. 0858D] “Even if last in order.” It should be written *postumat*, not *posthumat*, both here and above in the book *Against the Valentinians*, chapter 55, and in the *Scorpiace Against the Gnostics*, as is evident from ancient monumental inscriptions cited by Aldus in his *Orthography*. William Canter likewise observed this in *New Readings*, book II, chapter 10, adding that *postumus* is derived not from one born after his father was buried, as Rhenanus and most suppose, but from the adverb *post*, just as *extumus* comes from *extra* and *citumus* from *citra*. It can therefore refer indifferently both to one who comes in the last place and to one born after his father’s death, as Cujacius too states somewhere. PAM.] even if last in order, nevertheless anticipates [Note: [Col. 0858C] “Nevertheless” is disregarded by Rhenanus and Semler.] in effect. That is more truly first without which the prior things cannot exist.

If the flesh is the old man, when did it become so? From the beginning? Yet Adam was wholly new, and no one becomes old from something new. Moreover, ever since the blessing of procreation, flesh and soul come into being simultaneously, without any reckoning of time; and the things which are also sown together [Note: [Col. 0858C] Pamelius and Franeker read “formed.”] in the womb—as we taught in our commentary on the soul—make these two men contemporaneous in conception and coeval [Note: [Col. 0858C] “Of equal age,” Pamelius, Paris, and Rigault.] in birth, [Note: [Col. 0858D] “They make them contemporaneous in conception and coeval in birth.” He coined these unusual verbs because *contemporaneus* and *coaetaneus* are Latin words. But he claims more license for himself than is proper. LE PR.] although they are indeed of two substances, but not also of two ages. [Col. 0858C] Thus they produce one man, since neither is prior.

It is more immediate and natural to say that we are wholly either old or new; for we do not know how we could be one of them only in part. But the Apostle plainly identifies the old man: “Put off,” [Note: [Col. 0858C] “Putting off,” Pamelius and Franeker; “putting off,” Junius.] he says, “the old man according to your former manner of life,” [Col. 0859A] not according to the old age of some substance. For he does not command us to put off the flesh, but those things which elsewhere too he shows to be fleshly, accusing works, not bodies. Concerning these he also adds here:

“Putting away falsehood, speak the truth, each one to his neighbor, because we are members of one another. Be angry, but do not sin. Let not the sun go down upon your anger. Nor give place to the devil. [Note: [Col. 0859D] “Place to the devil,” Rhenanus and Semler.] Let the one who used to steal [Note: [Col. 0859D] “Who steals,” Rhenanus and Semler.] steal no longer, but rather let him labor, working with his hands, so that he may have something to share with one in need. Let no foul speech proceed from your mouth, but only such as is best for the building up of faith, so that it may bestow grace upon those who hear. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you have been sealed for the day of redemption. Let all bitterness and wrath and clamor and blasphemy and indignation [Col. 0859B] [Note: [Col. 0859D] Rhenanus and Semler do not have “and indignation.”] be removed from you, together with all malice. But be kind to one another, merciful, forgiving one another, just as God also forgave you in Christ.”

Therefore, those who consider the flesh to be the old man—why do they not hasten their own death, so that, once the old man has been put off, they may fulfill the Apostle’s commands? For we, who have believed that the whole faith must be administered in the flesh—indeed, also through the flesh, to which belong the mouth for uttering every excellent word, the tongue for refraining from blasphemy, the heart for refraining from indignation, and the hands for working and giving—maintain that both the oldness and the newness of man pertain to a moral, not a substantial, distinction.

And thus we likewise acknowledge that the man who was old according to his former manner of life is the same man who is said to be corrupted according to [Col. 0859C] the concupiscence of deception, just as he is old according to his former manner of life—not according to the flesh through everlasting destruction. On the contrary, the man remains safe in his flesh and remains the same man, since what he has put off is a corrupt mode of conduct, not bodily substance.

## CHAPTER XLVI
You will recognize the Apostle as such everywhere: condemning the works of the flesh in such a way that he seems to condemn the flesh, yet taking care, by the indication supplied by other or connected passages, that no one should think so. For when he also says (Rom. VIII) that those who are in the flesh [Note: [Col. 0859D] “Are” (sint), Rhen. Seml.] cannot please God, he immediately recalls the statement from a perverse interpretation to its full meaning by adding: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit.” For by denying that those who were manifestly in the flesh were in the flesh, he showed that they were not in the works of the flesh; and thus [Note: [Col. 0859D] “Thus” omitted by Rig. Ven.] that those, finally, who could not please God [Col. 0859D] were not those who were in the flesh, but those who lived carnally; [Col. 0860A] whereas those pleased God who, though situated in the flesh, walked according to the spirit.

And again he says: “The body indeed is dead, but [Note: [Col. 0859D] “Because of transgression.” This word is very often used by this author for sin; for where the Apostle says “sin,” he calls it “transgression.” LE PR.] because of transgression,” just as the spirit is life because of righteousness. But by opposing life to the death established in the flesh, he undoubtedly also promised life there by reason of righteousness, where he had determined death by reason of transgression. Otherwise he opposed life to death in vain, if life is not to be present where death itself is—the death to which he opposed it—so that death might, of course, be expelled from the body. Moreover, if life expels death from the body, it cannot accomplish this unless it penetrates there [Note: [Col. 0859D] “That” (illud), Pam. Rhen. Seml.; “those” (illae), cod. Wouw.] where that which it expels is present.

And why do I argue more intricately, when the Apostle speaks more plainly? “For if,” he says, “the Spirit of him who raised Jesus dwells in you, he who raised Jesus from the dead will also raise” [Note: [Col. 0860D] “Will give life to,” Pam. Fran.] “your mortal bodies, because of his Spirit dwelling in you.” [Col. 0860B] Thus, even if someone presumes the soul to be the mortal body, since he cannot deny the flesh as well, he is compelled to acknowledge the resurrection of the flesh also, in accordance with their participation in the same condition.
