Learn still further from what follows that the works of the flesh are condemned, not the flesh itself: “Therefore, brethren,” he says, “we are debtors, not to the flesh, so that [Note: [Col. 0860D] “For living, if,” Rhen.; “for living according to the flesh. If,” Jun.] we should live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you are going to die; but if by the spirit you put to death the actions of the flesh, you will live.”

Moreover, to answer each point individually: if salvation is promised to those who are situated in the flesh but nevertheless conduct themselves according to the spirit, then it is no longer the flesh that opposes salvation, but the operation of the flesh. Once the operation of the flesh—which is the cause of death—has been excluded, the flesh is thereby shown to be safe, because it lacks the cause of death. “For the law,” [Col. 0860C] he says, “of the Spirit of life [Note: [Col. 0859D] ‘In Christ Jesus has manumitted me.’ We were all slaves and delivered into Satan’s ownership, but the law of Christ shook the yoke [Col. 0860D] of servitude from our necks. Here he uses the term *manumission*, customary among jurists, who recognize three kinds of manumission: by census, by the vindicta, and by testament. By those three methods Christ manumitted us. LE PR.] in Christ Jesus has manumitted me from the law of transgression and death”—certainly the law which he had said before dwelt in our members [Note: [Col. 0860D] “Your,” Rhen. Seml.]. Therefore, our members will no longer be held by the law of death, because neither will they be held by the law of transgression, from which they have been manumitted.

“For what was powerless in the law, in that it was weakened through the flesh, God, by sending his Son in the likeness of the flesh of transgression, and through transgression” [Note: [Col. 0860D] “The flesh,” Rhen. Seml.] “condemned transgression in the flesh”—not the flesh in transgression; for a house will not be condemned together with its inhabitant. Indeed, he said that sin dwells in our body. Once transgression is condemned, however, the flesh is acquitted, just as, while transgression remains uncondemned, the flesh is bound by the law of death and transgression.

Thus too he called [Note: [Col. 0860D] “Even if,” Rhen. Seml.] the mind of the flesh death, and thereafter also hostility toward God, but not the flesh itself. “To what, then,” you will say, “is the mind of the flesh to be attributed, if not to the substance itself?” Certainly—if you prove [Col. 0860D] that the flesh understands anything of itself. But if there is no understanding without the soul, understand that the mind of the flesh must be referred [Col. 0861A] to the soul, although it is sometimes attributed [Note: [Col. 0861C] “Must be attributed,” Rhen. Jun.] to the flesh because [Note: [Col. 0861C] Rhen. Seml. add “on account of the flesh to it.”] it is exercised through the flesh. And for that reason he says that transgression dwells in the flesh, because the soul, by which [Note: [Col. 0861C] “Of the soul,” Rhen. Seml.; *abest a qua* (“by which” absent).] transgression is introduced, is the flesh’s tenant. The flesh is indeed mortified, but not in its own name; rather, in the name of transgression.

For elsewhere too he says: “Why, even now, as though living in the world, do you submit to decrees?” He was not writing to the dead, but to those who ought to cease living in a worldly manner.

## CHAPTER XLVII

For this will be worldly life, [Note: [Col. 0861D] “In which the old man.” Some formerly thought that the old man was the body, and the new man the soul; but that interpretation is inadmissible. For in Rom. VI the Apostle understands by the old man nothing other than one’s former life in sins, and by the new man that reformation which was effected by Christ when he washed away our crimes with his blood, so that, once that old man had been rendered void, he might establish us in true liberty. LE PR.] in which [Note: [Col. 0861C] “Which,” Rhen. Seml.] he said that the old man had been crucified with Christ—not corporeality, but moral character [Note: [Col. 0861C] “Mortality,” Pam. Fran. Rig. Ven.]. Otherwise, if we do not understand it thus, our corporeality has not been crucified, nor has our flesh undergone the cross of Christ. Rather, as [Col. 0861B] he added, “so that [Note: [Col. 0861D] ‘The body of transgression may be rendered void.’ We have already commented upon this last word. The Vulgate version has: ‘that the body of sin may be destroyed.’ Tertullian seems to me to have translated the sense of the Greek word καταργηθῇ (*katargēthē*, ‘may be rendered inoperative’) more exactly. LE PR.] the body of transgression may be rendered void”: through the amendment of life, not through the destruction of substance. So too he says, “So that henceforth we may not serve transgression,” and so that, having died together [Note: [Col. 0861C] Rhen. Seml. insert “in.”] with Christ in this manner, we may believe that we shall also live together [Note: [Col. 0861C] “We shall live together,” Pam. Fran.] with him.

“For thus,” he says, “reckon yourselves indeed dead.” To what? To the flesh? No, but to transgression. Therefore, they will remain alive to the flesh, “but living to God in Christ Jesus”—through the flesh, of course, to which they will not be dead; dead, namely, [Note: [Col. 0861C] “Namely” absent from Rhen. Seml.] to transgression, not to the flesh.

For he presses the point still further: “Therefore, do not let transgression reign in your mortal body, so that you obey it and present your members as weapons of unrighteousness to transgression; but present yourselves to God as living from the dead”—not merely as living, but as living from the dead—“and your members as weapons of righteousness.” And again: “Just as you presented [Col. 0861C] [Note: [Col. 0861D] ‘Your members as servants of uncleanness.’ In his customary manner he renders the Greek word δοῦλα (*doula*, ‘slaves’). Blessed Jerome used *famulantia* (‘serving’) in his work to Pammachius against John of Jerusalem. LE PR.] your members as servants of uncleanness and lawlessness [Note: [Col. 0861C] “Lawlessness,” others.] unto lawlessness, so now present your members as servants of righteousness unto sanctification [Note: [Col. 0861C] “Sacrifice,” Rhen. Seml.]. For when you were slaves of transgression, you were free from righteousness. What fruit, then, did you have from those things of which you are now ashamed? For their end [Note: [Col. 0862C] “Therefore,” Rhen. Seml.] is death. But now,” [Col. 0862A] “having been freed from transgression and made servants of God, you have your fruit unto sanctification [Note: [Col. 0862C] “Sacrifice,” Rhen. Seml. Ven.], and the end, eternal life. [Note: [Col. 0862D] ‘For the wages of transgression is death, but the donative of God,’ etc. A *stipendium* was the pay of soldiers serving in the army; a *donativum*, however, was a gift customarily bestowed upon soldiers by the emperor. Accordingly, just as he had used the military term *stipendium* in rendering blessed Paul, so, while aptly maintaining the same metaphor, he employed this term. LE PR.] For the wages of transgression is death, but the donative of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

Thus, throughout this entire [Note: [Col. 0862C] “Gate,” others.] sequence of meanings, by severing our members from unrighteousness and transgression, joining them to righteousness and holiness, and transferring those same members from the wages of death to the donative of eternal life, he assuredly promises the recompense of salvation to the flesh. No proper discipline of holiness and righteousness could have been imposed upon it at all unless the reward of that discipline also belonged to it. Nor would baptism itself be entrusted to it if, through regeneration, it were not also inaugurated for restoration, as the Apostle likewise insists: “Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ [Col. 0862B] Jesus [Note: [Col. 0862C] “Jesus” omitted by Rhen. Seml.] were baptized into his death? Therefore, we were buried together with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead, we too might walk in newness of life.”

And lest you suppose that this was said only of the present life, which must be lived [Note: [Col. 0862C] “Walked,” Pam. Par. Fran.] in newness through faith and baptism, he most providently adds: “For if we have been planted together [Note: [Col. 0862C] “Sown together,” Pam. Par. Fran.] in the likeness of Christ’s death, so shall we also be in the likeness of his resurrection.” [Note: [Col. 0862D] For through a likeness we die in baptism. We are baptized for the dead. We are immersed as though undergoing death. We emerge as those returning to life. RIG.—Lest the heretics reply that we shall rise in the same manner with Christ as we died with him—namely, that because we died with Christ only mystically and figuratively in baptism, we shall likewise rise only mystically and spiritually, not truly—Tertullian observes that type and mystery are present only in our death, not in the resurrection, for we shall truly rise. LAC.] For through a likeness we die in baptism, but through reality we rise [Note: [Col. 0862C] “We shall rise,” Pam. Fran.] in the flesh, just as Christ also did: “So that, just as offense reigned in death, grace likewise may reign through righteousness unto everlasting life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

How could it be so [Note: [Col. 0862C] “This,” Rhen. Seml.] unless equally in the flesh? For where there is death, there too is life after death, because life was formerly there where death afterward came. For if the reign of death [Col. 0862C] effects nothing but the dissolution of the flesh, then life, as the contrary of death, must correspondingly effect the contrary, namely, the reintegration of the flesh. Thus, just as death had swallowed it by prevailing, so, once the mortal has been swallowed by immortality, death may hear: [Note: [Col. 0862D] ‘Where, O death, is your sting?’ Thus he reads in chapters 51 [Col. 0863D] and 53, substituting ‘contention’ for ‘victory,’ which the Vulgate has; for in some Greek copies it gives νῖκος (*nikos*), or νίκη (*nikē*), that is, ‘victory’; in others νεῖκος (*neikos*), that is, ‘quarrel, altercation, strife,’ or δίκη (*dikē*), that is, ‘a forensic case, right, judgment, and penalty’: the term is plainly forensic. LAC.] “Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O death, is your contention?”

For thus grace too will superabound [Col. 0863A] [Note: [Col. 0863C] “Superabounded,” Rhen. Seml.] there where lawlessness also abounded [Note: [Col. 0863C] “Will abound,” Pam. Fran.]. Thus too power will be perfected in weakness, [Note: [Col. 0863D] ‘Saving what perished.’ Ezek. XXXIV has: ‘I will seek what had perished, bring back what had been cast away, bind up what had been broken, strengthen what had been weak, and preserve what was fat and strong.’ [Col. 0864D] LAC.] saving what perished [Note: [Col. 0863C] “Will be,” Rhen. Seml.], giving life to what is dead, healing what has been struck, treating what has languished, redeeming what has been snatched away, freeing what has been enslaved, recalling what has been led astray, and raising what has been dashed down—and indeed raising it from earth to heaven, where the Philippians too learn from the Apostle that our citizenship lies: “From there also we await Jesus Christ our Deliverer, who will transform [Note: [Col. 0863C] “Transformed,” Rhen.] the body of our humility to be conformed to the body of his glory”—undoubtedly after the resurrection, because Christ himself was not glorified before his passion.

These will be our bodies, which he beseeches the Romans to present as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing [Note: [Col. 0863C] “Propitiatory,” Rhen. Seml.] to God. How [Col. 0863B] can the sacrifice be living if the bodies are to perish? How can it be holy if they are profane? How can it be pleasing [Note: [Col. 0863D] “Pleasing,” plural, Rhen. Seml.] if they are condemned?

Come now: what he writes to the Thessalonians is, I should think, so clear that it might have been written by the sun’s own ray. How will these light-shunners receive the Scriptures? “May the God of peace himself sanctify you wholly.” That is not enough, but [Note: [Col. 0863D] “Which,” Rhen. Seml.] he continues: “And may your entire body, soul, and spirit be preserved blameless at the presence of the Lord.” You have the whole substance of the human being destined for salvation, and at no other time than at the advent of the Lord, which is the key to the resurrection.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

“But flesh and blood,” you say, “cannot possess the kingdom of God by inheritance.” We know that this too is written; but we have deliberately postponed it until now, so that what our adversaries [Col. 0863C] set up against us in the very first line of battle we might overthrow in the final engagement, after all the questions that serve, as it were, as its auxiliaries had first been cast down.

But even now let them expect [Note: [Col. 0863D] “Seek,” Rhen. Seml.] the preceding passages to be reviewed, so that this statement’s own origin may determine its meaning. [Note: [Col. 0863D] Rhen. Seml. insert “that.”] I take it that the Apostle, [Note: [Col. 0864D] ‘Having arranged for the Corinthians every distinction of ecclesiastical discipline.’ He did this in the preceding chapters of chapter XV, upon which Tertullian is now dwelling; for Paul had given many instructions concerning ecclesiastical discipline. LAC.] after arranging for the Corinthians every distinction of ecclesiastical discipline, had brought the sum both of his Gospel and of their faith to its conclusion in the committal of the Lord’s death and resurrection, [Note: [Col. 0864D] ‘So that he might derive the rule of our hope from that on which it was established.’ He derived it from Christ’s resurrection, since it was established from that. At chapter I of *On the Flesh of Christ* we supplied several observations [Col. 0865D] to show the strength of Saint Paul’s inference from Christ’s resurrection. LAC.] so that he might derive the rule of our hope from that on which it was established.

Accordingly he adds (I Cor. XV): [Col. 0864A] “But if Christ is preached as having risen [Note: [Col. 0863D] “Has risen,” Rhen. Seml.] from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? If there is none, neither has Christ risen. But if [Note: [Col. 0863D] “But” absent from Rhen. Seml.] Christ has not risen [Note: [Col. 0863D] “Has not risen,” Rhen. Seml.], our preaching is empty [Note: [Col. 0864C] Pam. adds: “and your faith is empty”]; for we shall be found [Note: [Col. 0864C] “But we are found,” Pam. Fran.] false witnesses of God, because we testified [Note: [Col. 0864C] “We may have said,” Rhen. Seml.; Pam. Fran. add “against God.”] that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise. For if the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen. If Christ has not risen, your faith is vain, because you are still in your offenses; and those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished.”

Through these words, what matter does he appear to be preparing us to believe? “The resurrection,” you say, “of the dead, which was being denied.” Surely he wishes it to be believed on the basis of the Lord’s resurrection as an example? “Certainly,” you say. Now, is an example formed from dissimilarity or from likeness? [Col. 0864B] “From likeness, of course,” you say.

But how did Christ rise? In the flesh, did he not? Without doubt: if you hear that he died and was buried according to the Scriptures in no other respect than in the flesh, you likewise concede that he was raised in the flesh. For that very thing which fell in death [Note: [Col. 0864C] “Into death,” Pam. Fran.], which lay in burial, also rose—not so much Christ in the flesh as the flesh in Christ.

Therefore, if we shall rise according to Christ’s example, who rose in the flesh, we shall no longer rise according to Christ’s example if we ourselves do not also rise in the flesh. “For through a man,” he says, “came death, and through a man resurrection”: thus indeed distinguishing the authors—Adam as author of death, Christ of resurrection—while establishing the resurrection as belonging to the same substance as that to which death belonged, by comparing the respective authors under the name “man.” For “just as in Adam [Col. 0864C] all die, so also in Christ all will be given life”: they will be given life in the flesh in Christ, just as in Adam they die in the flesh [Note: [Col. 0864D] “All,” Fran.].

“But each in his own order”—clearly because each is also in his own body. For order is nothing other than the disposer of merits [Note: [Col. 0864D] The Pithoean codex reads: “For order will be arranged under the name of merits arranged”; Rig. thinks *dispositor horum* (“the arranger of these”) should be read for *dispositorum*.]. And since merits are ascribed to the body also, the order of bodies must likewise be arranged, so that there may be an order of merits.

But if some are also baptized [Note: [Col. 0864D] “Indeed,” Rhen.] for the dead, we shall see whether this is reasonable. Certainly, he maintains that they instituted this practice on the supposition that others believed a vicarious baptism [Col. 0865A] [Note: [Col. 0865C] “That” absent from Pam. Par. Fran.] [Note: [Col. 0865D] ‘Vicarious baptism.’ Fabius likewise used the expression ‘vicarious death,’ *Declamation* 19. RIG.] would benefit even the flesh toward the hope of resurrection. Unless that resurrection were bodily, it would not otherwise [Note: [Col. 0865D] “Not unless otherwise,” Rhen. Seml.; “not otherwise,” thus Pam. Paris. Fran.; “not otherwise” in cod. Wouw.] be bound here by bodily baptism.

“Why are they themselves also baptized,” he says, “if the bodies that are baptized do not rise?” [Note: [Col. 0865D] “Who,” Rhen. Seml.] For the soul is sanctified not by washing, but by its response. “Why do we too,” he says, “stand in danger every hour?” Through the flesh, of course. “I die daily”—through the dangers of the flesh, of course, through which he also fought with beasts at Ephesus: namely, [Note: [Col. 0865D] ‘The beasts of the Asian affliction.’ Whether by these beasts he understands the uprising at Ephesus stirred up by Demetrius the silversmith, I could not readily say; yet, with the leave of more learned men, I would say that he certainly fought with beasts, but that battle occurred at Ephesus after this epistle, which he wrote at Ephesus, had been written. [Col. 0866D] LE PR.] the beasts of the Asian affliction, concerning which he says in the second epistle to the same people: “For we do not wish you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning our affliction in Asia, that we were exceedingly weighed down [Note: [Col. 0865D] “Weighed down,” others.] beyond our strength, so that we despaired even of life.”

Unless I am mistaken, he recounts all these things so that, being unwilling that the struggle of the flesh should be believed vain, he would have the resurrection of the flesh believed without doubt. [Col. 0865B] For the struggle of that which will have no resurrection must be regarded as vain.

“But someone will say: How will the dead rise? And with what body will they come?” Here he now discusses the qualities of bodies: whether the very same bodies or others are to be resumed. But since a question of this sort is treated subsequently, it will suffice for the present that the resurrection is defined as bodily from this fact also, since the quality of bodies is under inquiry.

## CHAPTER XLIX

We have now come to the flesh and blood that truly constitute the whole question: under what condition the Apostle disinherited those [Note: [Col. 0865D] “As though,” Pam. Fran.] substances from the kingdom of God. This too must be learned from the preceding statements.

“The first man is from the earth, earthy”—that is, made of mud, that is, Adam; “the second man is from heaven”—that is, the Word of God, that is, Christ. [Col. 0865C] Yet he is not otherwise a man, although from heaven, except because he too is flesh and soul, which is what man is, what Adam is. For above also he was called [Note: [Col. 0865D] “Even if,” Rhen. Seml.] the last Adam [Note: [Col. 0865D] “Will say,” Rhen. Seml.], deriving the shared name from participation in the same substance; for Adam’s flesh was no more from seed than Christ’s.

“Therefore, as the earthy one is, such also are the earthy; and as the heavenly one is, such also are the heavenly.” Are they such in substance? Or first in discipline, and afterward also in dignity, which discipline has secured? Yet the earthy and heavenly will in no way be distinguished in substance, since they have once been called men by the Apostle.

For although Christ alone is truly heavenly—indeed, above heaven—he is nevertheless man insofar as he is flesh and soul, and in no respect is he distinguished by this condition of his substances from the earthy quality. [Col. 0866A] Consequently, those who are heavenly according to him are understood to have been called heavenly not by reason of their present substance, but by reason of their future glory. For previously also, where this distinction flowed from a difference of dignity, it was shown that the glory of celestial bodies is one thing, that of terrestrial bodies another, that of the sun another, that of the moon another, and that of the stars another; for star differs from star in glory, but not in substance.

Finally, after first setting forth the difference of dignity—both that which must be pursued now in the same substance and that which must be attained then—he also adds an exhortation, so that here we may pursue Christ’s condition through discipline, and there attain his summit through glory: “Just as we have borne the image of the earthy, let us also bear the image of the above-heavenly.”

For we have borne the image of the earthy through fellowship in transgression, through partnership in death, and through exile from paradise. For [Col. 0866B] although [Note: [Col. 0865D] “Although also,” Pam. Par.] the image of Adam is borne here in the flesh [Note: [Col. 0866C] “Is thus thought,” Rhen. Seml.], we are nevertheless not admonished to cast off [Note: [Col. 0866D] “Lay down,” Pam. Par. Fran.] the flesh. If not the flesh, then it is our conduct, so that correspondingly we may also bear within ourselves the image of the heavenly one—not being gods [Note: [Col. 0866D] “Gods” (*dii*) is perhaps better. Editors.], nor yet established in heaven, but [Note: [Col. 0866D] ‘Walking according to the lineaments of Christ.’ Imitating the conduct which Christ maintained in the flesh. Bernard, sermon on Psalm XC. From this, of course, Christ is to be recognized above all others: by holiness, righteousness, and truth. Thus, in book II *Against Marcion*, the soul is said to possess the lines of God insofar as it is immortal, free and possessed of its own choice, often foreknowing, and capable of understanding and knowledge. RIG.] walking according to the lineaments of Christ in holiness, righteousness, and truth.

Indeed, he directs this whole matter so fully toward discipline that he says the image of Christ must be borne here, in this flesh and in this time of discipline. For in saying, in the imperative mode, “Let us bear,” he speaks to this present time, in which a human being has no other substance than flesh and soul. Or if [Note: [Col. 0866D] “Or even if,” Rhen. Seml.] this faith looks to some other, that is, heavenly substance, it has nevertheless been promised to this present substance, which is commanded to labor toward it.

Since, therefore, he places the image both of the earthy and of the heavenly in conduct—the former [Col. 0866C] to be renounced [Note: [Col. 0866D] “To be borne,” Rhen. Seml.], but the latter to be pursued—and then adds [Note: [Col. 0866D] “Adds,” Rhen. Seml.], “Now this I say,” that is, “because of those things which [Note: [Col. 0866D] “Which? Which,” Rhen.] I said above” (for the conjunction completes the sense by referring back to the preceding statements), “that flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God by inheritance,” he commands that “flesh and blood” be understood as nothing other than the aforesaid image of the earthy.

If that image is reckoned as belonging to the old conduct, and the old conduct does not receive [Note: [Col. 0866D] “May not receive,” Rhen. Seml.] the kingdom of God, then flesh and blood, in not receiving the kingdom of God, are accordingly reduced to the old conduct [Note: [Col. 0866D] “Of truth,” Rhen. Seml.].

This holds, of course, if the Apostle never used substance for works, and does not do so here either. But if he denied that persons still situated in the flesh were [Col. 0867A] in the flesh, because he denied that they were in the works of the flesh, you must overthrow its mode of life, not its substance: not the substance, but those works of the substance which estrange it from the kingdom of God.

After making these works manifest to the Galatians also, he professes that he warns and has warned them (Gal. V) that those who do [Note: [Col. 0867C] “May do,” Rhen. Seml.] such things will not [Note: [Col. 0867C] “May not,” Rhen. Seml.] obtain the kingdom of God by inheritance. They do not, of course, bear the image of the heavenly one as they have borne [Note: [Col. 0867C] “Had borne,” Rhen. Seml.] that of the earthy; and therefore, on account of the old conduct, they are to be reckoned [Note: [Col. 0867C] “Considered,” others.] as nothing other than flesh and blood.

For even if the Apostle had suddenly broken out into this declaration, that flesh and blood must be driven from the kingdom of God, without any preparatory construction of the preceding sense, would we not accordingly interpret these two substances as the old man, devoted to flesh and blood—that is, to eating and drinking—whose part it is to say against faith in the resurrection: [Col. 0867B] “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die”? For by inserting this also, the Apostle censured flesh and blood on account of their fruits, eating and drinking.

## CHAPTER L

But even [Note: [Col. 0867C] “Even” omitted by Fran.] if we set aside interpretations of this sort, which censure the works of flesh and blood, [Note: [Col. 0867D] ‘The substances themselves also, understood as nothing other than what they are,’ etc. By another path he meets the heretics, in order to prove that nothing can be established from the passage which they prize for refuting the defenders of the resurrection of the flesh. For even if flesh and blood were taken strictly and rigidly by Paul, and not for the works of carnal people, faith in the bodily resurrection nevertheless cannot be broken. Irenaeus likewise meets the heretics with a twofold answer to the same passage. LAC.] it will still be permissible to vindicate for the resurrection the substances themselves, understood as nothing other than what they are. For it is not the resurrection that is directly denied [Note: [Col. 0867C] “Denied,” Pam. Fran.] to flesh and blood, but the kingdom of God, which follows upon resurrection; [Note: [Col. 0867D] ‘There is also a resurrection unto judgment.’ We have enclosed this clause in parentheses to make the sense clearer. In it he alludes to John VI: ‘And those who have done good will go forth into the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil into the resurrection of judgment.’ PAM.] (there is also a resurrection unto judgment). Indeed, the general resurrection of the flesh is even confirmed when a particular resurrection is excepted. For when it is declared into which condition it does not rise, it is implied into which condition it does rise.

And thus, since the work of the substance, not its kind, [Col. 0867C] undergoes the distinction of resurrection according to merits, it is also apparent from this that flesh and blood are barred from the kingdom of God under the designation of guilt, not of substance. Yet under the designation of their form [Note: [Col. 0867D] ‘Yet under the designation of their form.’ He has just taken *form* in the same sense as *substance*. The meaning is: although because of guilt they do not rise to the glorious resurrection and life, nevertheless by reason of their substance they will at least rise to judgment. LAC.] they rise unto judgment, because they do not rise into the kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 0868D] ‘I shall say still more.’ He acts more liberally and grants the heretics not only that the Apostle speaks of the substances themselves, taking the expression ‘flesh and blood’ strictly, but also that it is impossible for flesh and blood to inherit the kingdom of God. LAC.] I shall say still more: “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God by inheritance.” [Col. 0868A] Quite rightly—when alone and by themselves—so that he might show that the spirit is still necessary for them: “For it is the Spirit who gives life unto the kingdom of God; the flesh profits nothing.” Yet something else can profit it [Note: [Col. 0867D] “Them,” Pam. Fran.], namely the spirit, and, through the spirit, the works of the spirit also.

Accordingly, all flesh and blood rise equally [Note: [Col. 0867D] “From that by which,” Rhen. Seml.] in their own quality. But those whose lot it is [Note: [Col. 0868C] “Is” absent from Rhen. Seml.] to enter the kingdom of God will have to put on [Note: [Col. 0868C] “Bring in,” Rhen. Seml.] the power of incorruptibility and immortality, without which they cannot enter the kingdom of God, before they can attain it.

Quite rightly, therefore, flesh and blood, as we have said, fail to receive the kingdom of God when alone. But since this corruptible thing—that is, the flesh—is to be swallowed by incorruptibility, and this mortal thing—that is, the blood—by immortality, after the resurrection through transformation, quite rightly flesh [Col. 0868B] and blood, if not [Note: [Col. 0868C] “Not” absent from Rhen. Seml.] transformed and swallowed up, cannot possess the kingdom of God by inheritance [Note: [Col. 0868C] “As an inheritance,” Rhen. Seml. Ven.], though this does not mean [Note: [Col. 0868C] “Not” absent from Paris.] that they are not [Note: [Col. 0868C] “Not” absent from Rhen. Seml.] raised.

There are some who wish “flesh and blood” [Note: [Col. 0868D] ‘There are some who understand flesh and blood as Judaism,’ etc. The first interpretation was that, although flesh and blood do not rise to the resurrection of life, they nevertheless rise to judgment. The second is this: that Judaism is understood under the name of flesh and blood, just as the expression is taken by the Apostle in Gal. I. PAM.] to be understood as Judaism, on account of circumcision. It too is alien to the kingdom of God, because it too is assigned to antiquity, and because it is marked by this title elsewhere also by the Apostle, who, after the Son of God had been revealed in him so that he might evangelize him among the nations, immediately [Note: [Col. 0868D] ‘Did not refer the matter to flesh and blood.’ The author expressed the Greek προσανεθέμην (*prosanethemēn*) more exactly in this way than others did by translating it ‘I did not acquiesce.’ Moreover, the author rightly interprets Judaism as flesh and blood, as though he were saying that he referred neither to the Jews nor to his predecessors, the apostles. Thus there is no need to labor at refuting the calumny that he called the apostles flesh and blood. PAM.] did not refer the matter to flesh and blood (Gal. I), that is, to circumcision, that is, to Judaism, as he writes to the Galatians.

## CHAPTER LI
But what we have reserved for the conclusion will now stand for all, and will serve even to convict the Apostle himself [Note: [Col. 0868C] *In* is omitted by Seml.] of truly the greatest lack of reflection, if, as some maintain, he so abruptly, “with his eyes shut,” as the saying goes, without distinction [Col. 0868C] and without qualification, indiscriminately excluded all flesh and blood from the kingdom of God [Note: [Col. 0868D] *Excluded* (*extrusit*); Rhen. reads *built up* (*extruxit*).], and therefore also from the very palace of heaven—although Jesus still sits there at the Father’s right hand, man though also God, the last Adam though also the primordial Word, flesh and blood though purer [Col. 0869A] than ours [Note: [Col. 0869C] “Flesh and blood, though purer than ours.” Relevant here is what the scholastic doctors teach: that Christ was conceived from the most pure blood of the Blessed Virgin Mary. PAM.]; nevertheless the same both in substance and in form as when he ascended, and destined to descend in that same condition, as the angels affirm, so that he may, of course, be recognized by those who wounded him. [Note: [Col. 0869C] “So that he may, of course, be recognized by those who wounded him.” [Col. 0869D] Above, ch. 26, and *On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. 44, has “pierced.” Christ, therefore, is to be recognized by those who wounded him through the marks of those same wounds: Christ still preserves his wounds. St Epiphanius explained it thus in his sermon *On the Ascension*. LAC.] [Note: [Col. 0869C] *Recognized* (*agnoscendus*); Rhen. reads *to be recognized* in the plural (*agnoscendi*).]

He who is called the mediator between God and human beings (1 Tim. 2), from the deposit entrusted to him by both parties, preserves within himself the deposit of the flesh as well, as a pledge of the entire final sum. For just as he left with us the pledge of the Spirit (2 Cor. 5), so too he received from us the pledge of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0869D] “So too he received from us the pledge of the flesh.” This denotes a kind of exchange and commerce between us and God, between heaven and earth: our flesh, which was not in heaven, was to be exchanged for the Spirit of God, who was not on earth, so that flesh might thus be in heaven and the Spirit on earth. Christ, as a divine broker, negotiated and completed this commerce by pledges deposited on both sides: when he ascended into heaven, he both sent the Spirit down to us and introduced our flesh into heaven. LAC.], and carried into heaven the security for the entire sum that is one day to be brought there. Be confident [Note: [Col. 0869C] *Confident* in the masculine plural (*securi*); Pam., Fran., Par., and Ven. read the feminine plural (*securae*).], flesh and blood: in Christ you have taken possession of both heaven and the kingdom of God. [Note: [Col. 0869D] “You have taken possession of both heaven and the kingdom in Christ.” He said that flesh “takes possession” in this commercial exchange because equality of right and justice is not maintained. The Spirit surpasses flesh and heavenly things surpass earthly things; and because an extraordinary gift will be given in return for something unequal and paltry, it seems an appropriation [Col. 0870C] rather than an exchange. LAC.] Or, if those who have denied heaven to you deny that you are in Christ, let them also deny that Christ is in heaven.

Thus he says that corruption will not inherit incorruption [Note: [Col. 0869C] Rhen. and Seml. insert *in*.] [Col. 0869B]—not so that you should suppose flesh and blood to be corruption, since they are rather liable to corruption through death (for it is death that not merely corrupts flesh and blood but even consumes them); rather, since he had declared that the works of flesh and blood cannot attain the kingdom of God, in order to emphasize this still further he also deprived corruption itself—that is, death, toward which the works of flesh and blood advance—of the inheritance of incorruption. For a little later he expressed, in a manner of speaking, the death of death itself, saying (1 Cor. 15): “Death has been swallowed up in conflict.” [Note: [Col. 0869C] Rhen. and Seml. read *in conflict* (*contentione*) rather than *into conflict* (*in contentionem*).] “Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O death, is your conflict?” [Note: [Col. 0869C] Rhen. and Seml. read *power* (*potentia*) rather than *conflict* (*contentio*).] Now the sting of death is sin: this will be corruption. The strength of sin, moreover, is the law—undoubtedly that other law which he says has been established in his members, warring [Col. 0869C] against the law of his mind, namely the very force that drives one to sin against one’s will. [Note: [Col. 0870C] “Which he has established in his members.” That is, he says that it has been constituted and firmly established, so that it inheres radically unless the grace of Christ roots it out. LE PR.] For above as well [Note: [Col. 0869C] Seml. reads *even if* (*etsi*).] he says that the last [Col. 0870A] enemy, death, is to be abolished. In this sense corruption will not attain the inheritance [Note: [Col. 0869C] *The inheritance* is absent from Seml.] of incorruption [Note: [Col. 0869C] Seml. reads *attains* rather than *will attain*.]; that is, death will not persist. [Note: [Col. 0870C] Rhen. and Seml. read *persisted*.]

When and how will it fail? When, “in an indivisible instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet, the dead will also rise incorrupt.” Who are these, except those who were previously corrupted—that is, bodies, that is, flesh and blood? “And we shall be changed.” [Note: [Col. 0870C] Rhen. and Seml. read *we are changed*.] From what condition, except that in which we shall be found? “For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.” What is mortal except the flesh? What is corruptible except the blood? And lest you suppose that the Apostle means something else, he makes provision for you and labors to make you understand that this is spoken of the flesh: when he says “this corruptible” [Note: [Col. 0870C] Pam. and Fran. add *something*.] and “this mortal,” he says it while grasping his very skin. [Note: [Col. 0870C] “And ‘this mortal,’ he says while grasping his very skin.” [Col. 0870D] “Is this not the utterance of one who, as it were, touches his own body and feels it with his finger?” says Rufinus in his *Exposition of the Creed*. It should also be noted in passing that, according to the same author, the Church of Aquileia added “of this” to the article of the Creed in which we confess the resurrection of the flesh, so that by pronouncing “the resurrection of this flesh” people might be made more certain that the very flesh in which they bore themselves would rise again. RIG.] Certainly he could not have uttered “this” [Col. 0870B] except of something lying before him, something present. It is a word of bodily demonstration.

Moreover, the corruptible is one thing and corruption another [Note: [Col. 0870C] Rhen. and Seml. add *will be*.]; the mortal is one thing and mortality another. For what undergoes an effect is one thing, and what causes it to be undergone another. Thus those things that undergo corruption and mortality—namely flesh and blood—must necessarily undergo incorruption and immortality as well. [Note: [Col. 0870C] Fran. and Ven. read *mortality* rather than *immortality*.]

## CHAPTER LII

Let us now see [Note: [Col. 0870C] Rhen. and Seml. read *we see*.] in what body he argues that the dead will come. [Note: [Col. 0870D] “Let us now see in what body they will come.” From this chapter onward he attacks chiefly the Valentinians, who conceded the resurrection not of this flesh but of another, as is evident from the book *On Prescription*. Others too had come to the same opinion because of the arguments set out in ch. 13 concerning corpses devoured by wild beasts and consumed by fire; it seemed to them that a body dispersed in so many ways could not return as the very same body. In what follows he adequately answers and dissolves this objection. Nyssenus does so from the analogy of the seed, which the Author examines and supports from St Paul in this chapter. LAG.] And it is well that he immediately broke out into an explanation, as though someone had asked precisely such a question. “Fool,” he says, “what you sow is not made alive [Note: [Col. 0870C] Rhen. reads *is it not*; Wouw.’s manuscript perhaps likewise.] unless it has died.” [Note: [Col. 0870C] Fran. and Ven. read *will be made alive*.] From the example of the seed, therefore, let it now be established that no flesh other than that which will have died is made alive; and the subsequent statements will thus become clear, for nothing may be understood contrary to the governing principle [Col. 0871A] of the example.

Nor, because [Note: [Col. 0871C] Pam., Ven., Fran., and Rig. read *ne quia*; Rhen. and Seml. read *qua*.] what follows is, “And what you sow, you do not sow the body that is to be,” should you therefore suppose that a body other than the one sown by dying will rise again; otherwise you have departed from the example. For when wheat has been sown and dissolved in the earth, barley never springs forth, but the same kind of grain, of the same nature, quality, [Note: [Col. 0871C] Pam. and Fran. read *in the same quality*.] and form. Indeed, from where would it come, if not from that very thing? Even the corruption is that very thing, since it belongs to that very thing. Does he not also indicate how it is that the body which is to be is not sown, [Note: [Col. 0871C] Pam., Fran., Rig., and Ven. read *is sown* rather than *is to be sown*.] when he says: “But a bare grain, perhaps of wheat, or [Note: [Col. 0871D] Rhen. and Seml. read *or* (*vel*) rather than *or* (*aut*).] of some such kind; but God gives it a body as he wills”? Surely he gives it to the grain which, Paul says, is sown bare. “Surely,” you say. Therefore that to which God is to give a body is preserved. But how is it preserved if it is nowhere, if it does not rise, if that very thing does not rise? It is not preserved. And if it is not preserved, it cannot receive a body from God. But it is certainly preserved in every respect.

Why, then, will God give it a body as he wills, when it already possesses its own bare body, unless so that it may rise no longer bare? What is built over the body will therefore be an addition; [Note: [Col. 0871D] Pam. and Fran. read *something added* (*addititium*).] that over which it is built is not destroyed, [Note: [Col. 0871D] Pam. and Rhen. read *is destroyed*.] but enlarged. What is enlarged is preserved. For only the grain is sown, without the garment of its husk, without the base of the ear, without the protection of the beard, without the proud stature of the stalk; but it rises enriched with abundance, constructed into a fabric, arranged in order, fortified with adornment, and clothed on every side. These constitute for it the other body given by God, into which it is changed not by abolition but by enlargement. And “to each of the seeds he has assigned its own body” [Note: [Col. 0871D] “Its own body.” The Latin translator renders the Greek word ἴδιον more accurately as *proprium*, “its own,” unless one says that *suum* means the same thing. LE PR.] [Col. 0871C]—not “its own” in the sense of its former body, so that at that time what it acquires outwardly from God may also be its own.

Adhere, therefore, to the example, and preserve its reflection in relation to the flesh, believing that the same flesh which was sown will bear fruit: the very same, though fuller; [Note: [Col. 0871D] Rhen. and Seml. read *it is fuller*.] not another, though returning in another condition. [Note: [Col. 0871D] Pam. and Par. incorrectly read *showing reverence* (*reverentem*).] For it too will receive provision and adornment [Note: [Col. 0871D] “And it too will receive provision and adornment.” *Suggestus* here is an ensemble or ornament. LE PR.], of whatever kind God wills to lay upon it according to its merits. Undoubtedly the statement “not all flesh is the same flesh” tends to this point [Note: [Col. 0871D] Rhen. and Seml. read *tended*.]: not to denying a shared substance but to differentiating privilege; it reduces the body to a distinction of honor, not of kind.

To this end he also adds figurative examples drawn from animals and the elements. “One flesh belongs to human beings,” that is, to God’s servant, who is truly human; [Col. 0872A] “another to beasts of burden,” that is, to the pagan, of whom the Prophet also says: “Man has been made like irrational beasts of burden”; [Note: [Col. 0871D] “Another to a beast of burden.” Beasts of burden are animals subdued for carrying on their backs, such as horses, mules, and asses, which for this reason are called *dossuaria jumenta*, back-bearing beasts of burden, by Varro. Elephants and camels, as well as cattle, sheep, goats, and every kind of herd animal, are also included under this name “beast of burden.” [Col. 0872D] LE PR.] “another flesh belongs to birds,” [Note: [Col. 0872C] Rhen. and Seml. read *flying creatures*.] that is, to martyrs who strive toward the heights; “another, moreover, to fish,” [Note: [Col. 0872C] *Moreover* is absent from Rhen. and Seml.] that is, to those for whom the water of baptism suffices. [Note: [Col. 0872D] “For whom the water of baptism suffices.” This passage also supports baptism with water, which certain people do not shrink from attacking; but it is treated more fully in *On Baptism*, ch. 1. PAM.]

In the same way he combines arguments drawn from bodies above the heavens. [Note: [Col. 0872C] Rhen. and Seml. read: *It is appropriate to argue*.] “One is the glory of the sun,” that is, of Christ; “another of the moon,” that is, of the Church; “another of the stars,” that is, of Abraham’s seed; “for star differs from star in glory”; “there are earthly and heavenly bodies,” namely the Jew and the Christian. [Note: [Col. 0872D] “Earthly and heavenly bodies—the Jew,” etc. The Jew is signified by “earth,” but the Christian by “heaven,” because God promised only earthly things to the Jews, whereas he promised heaven to Christians. LE PR.] Otherwise, if the statements are not figurative, he has quite pointlessly set [Note: [Col. 0872D] Pam. and Fran. read *set in opposition*.] the flesh of mules and kites and the bodies of the heavenly lights alongside human bodies, although they have no relevance to a comparison of their condition, just as they have none to the attainment of resurrection.

Finally, when by these examples he had established a difference of glory, not of substance, he says [Col. 0872B]: “So too is the resurrection of the dead.” How so? [Note: [Col. 0872D] Rhen. and Seml. read *because*.] Not differing in any other respect, but in glory alone. For once again he refers the resurrection back to the same substance and looks again to the grain: “It is sown,” he says, “in corruption; it rises in incorruption. It is sown in dishonor; it rises in glory. It is sown in weakness; it rises in power. An animate body is sown; a spiritual body rises.” Certainly nothing other than what is sown rises; nothing other than what is dissolved in the ground is sown; and nothing other than the flesh is dissolved in the ground. For God’s sentence struck the flesh (Gen. 3): “Earth you are, and into the earth you will go,” because it had also been taken from the earth.

From this the Apostle derived his statement that it is sown when it is returned to the earth, since the earth is also the custodian of seeds, in which they are deposited [Col. 0872C] and from which they are reclaimed. For this reason he stamps the point with a second seal, [Note: [Col. 0872D] Rhen. and Seml. read *seals*.] impressing upon it the words, “For so it is written,” [Note: [Col. 0872D] Others read *just as*.] lest you suppose “to be sown” to be anything other than “you will go into the earth from which you were taken,” or suppose that it refers to anything other than the flesh: “for so it is written.”

## CHAPTER LIII

They argue, however, that the “animate body” means the soul, so that they may divert the resurrection in question away from the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0872D] Par. and Rhen. read: “so that they may divert *it* away from the flesh.”] Yet since it is established and fixed that the body which was sown is the one that will rise, they will be summoned to produce the reality itself. Let them show that the soul is sown [Col. 0873A] after death—that is, that it is dead, struck down into the ground, cast apart, and dissolved, although no such fate was decreed for it by God. Let them exhibit its corruption, dishonor, and weakness, so that it may also be the soul itself that rises [Note: [Col. 0873C] Rhen. and Seml. read *rises together*.] into incorruption, glory, and power.

But in Lazarus, the preeminent example of resurrection, it was the flesh that lay in weakness; the flesh that nearly rotted away in dishonor; the flesh that meanwhile stank in corruption. [Note: [Col. 0873D] “But in Lazarus,” etc. Here he speaks of a different Lazarus from the one mentioned above in ch. 17, namely the man of John 11. What our translator renders *instita*, “bands,” the Author calls linen bonds. The Greek is κειρίας. Furthermore, *comparet* below means “is manifested.” PAM.] And yet Lazarus as flesh rose again, together indeed with the soul, but with a soul that was uncorrupted: no one had bound it with linen bands; no one had placed it in the tomb; no one had perceived it already beginning to stink; no one had seen it sown for four days. The flesh of everyone today undergoes [Note: [Col. 0873C] Fran. and Ven. read *undergoes*.] the entire condition and entire end of Lazarus, but no one’s soul does. Therefore the entity in which the Apostle’s pen is manifest, and of which it is clear that he speaks, will be both the animate body when it is sown and the spiritual body when [Col. 0873B] it is raised.

To make you understand it in this way, [Note: [Col. 0873C] Pam. and Fran. read *that he may understand*.] he extends his hand still further and, again on the authority of the same Scripture, retraces how the first man Adam was made “into a living soul.” [Note: [Col. 0873C] Pam. and Fran. read *a living soul* with a different Latin adjective.] If Adam is the first man, while the flesh is man before the soul, then undoubtedly the flesh was made into a living soul. [Note: [Col. 0873C] *Living* is absent from Rig. and Ven.; Pam. and Fran. use a different form for “living.” *Was made* is absent from Par. and Pam.] Moreover, since it was made into a soul [Note: [Col. 0873C] Seml. reads *inanimate*.] while it was already a body, it was certainly made an animate body. [Note: [Col. 0873C] Rhen. and Seml. insert *into*.] What do they want it to be called, other than that which it was made through the soul—other than that which did not exist before the soul, and which will not exist after the soul except when it rises? [Note: [Col. 0873D] “Other than that which did not exist before the soul?” There was formerly a controversy in the churches, as Nyssenus testifies in *On the Making of Man*, ch. 28, over whether the soul existed before the body or whether our body and flesh existed before the soul. The Origenists maintained the former; others, against them, gave precedence to the flesh over the soul because of its iniquity. Nyssenus fully attacks both positions: the former in ch. 28, against Origen; the latter in ch. 29, where he attempts to prove philosophically this most true opinion of Tertullian and considers this view true concerning the formation of all human beings in [Col. 0874D] the womb: neither a vegetative body nor thereafter a sentient or animate body precedes the infusion of the rational soul, as philosophers commonly claim when they suppose that an embryo first lives by the vegetative life of plants and then by a sentient life before the advent of the rational soul. Nyssenus instead thinks that the rational soul is present from the beginning of every animation of the fetus and before its organization, and that the soul itself effects this organization for itself. See the words of Nyssenus. LAC.]

For when the soul has been received back, it again becomes an animate body, so that it may become spiritual; for nothing rises unless it previously existed. Thus, on the same ground on which it is appropriate to call the flesh an animate body, it is in no way appropriate to call the soul one. For the flesh existed as a body before it was an animate body. Once animated, it was afterward made [Col. 0873C] an animate body. The soul, however, although itself a body, still cannot be called or become an animate body, because it is not itself an animated body but rather a body that animates: it cannot become what it makes. [Note: [Col. 0873D] Seml. reads *made*.] For that which is an accident to another makes that other animate; but since it is not an accident to itself, how will it make itself animate? [Note: [Col. 0874D] “For that which is an accident to another.” He does not take *accident* in the strict sense, but in a broader sense that is also appropriate to substantial forms—that is, as something “adjoining,” a term that philosophers do not deny to substantial realities. Or perhaps the Author wrote *accidens*, “an accident”; or *accidens* may mean the same as “contingent,” because this or that form falls to matter. LAC.]

Therefore, just as the flesh becomes an animate body by receiving the soul, so afterward it becomes spiritual by putting on the Spirit. [Note: [Col. 0874C] *Before* is absent from Rhen. and Seml.] [Col. 0874A] In arranging this order, the Apostle rightly distinguishes it in Adam and Christ as well, as in the representative heads of that very distinction. And when he calls Christ the last Adam, recognize from this that he has directed the entire force of his teaching toward the resurrection of the flesh, not of the soul. For if the first man Adam was flesh, not soul, since he was finally made into a living soul [Note: [Col. 0874C] Others incorrectly read: “Why should not she who was made into a soul?”]; and if the last Adam, Christ, is Adam precisely because he is man, and man precisely because he is flesh rather than because he is soul; then he accordingly adds: “Not first that which is spiritual, but that which is animate; afterward that which is spiritual,” with reference to both Adams.

Does it appear to you [Note: [Col. 0874C] Rhen. and Ven. read *And what*.] that he distinguishes the animate body and the spiritual body in the same flesh, whose distinction he had laid down beforehand in the two Adams—that is, in the two men? From what [Note: [Col. 0874C] Pam., Par., and Fran. read *from both*.] substance do Christ and Adam stand in mutual relation [Col. 0874B]? From flesh, of course, although also from soul; but both are called “man” from the name of the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0874C] Paris., Fran., and Pam. read: “Of course from both flesh and soul; but from the flesh … they are … man.” Jun. reads: “Of course from flesh and from soul (but from the flesh—are—man), from the latter.”] For the flesh is the first “man.” From it they could also enter into an order, so that one might be reckoned the first and the other the last man—that is, Adam. Different things, however, cannot be placed in an order, at least with respect to substance, although perhaps they can with respect to place, time, or condition. Here, however, they are called first and last with respect to the substance of the flesh; just as, again, “the first man is from the earth, and the second from heaven,” because although the second is from heaven according to the Spirit, he is man according to the flesh.

Accordingly, since order is applicable to the flesh in both Adams but not to the soul—so that the first man was distinguished as made into a living soul and the last as made into a life-giving Spirit [Note: [Col. 0874C] Fran. and Pam. add *Adam*.]—their distinction likewise established in advance a distinction in the flesh, so that it is of the flesh that it was said: “Not first that which is spiritual, but that which is animate; [Col. 0874C] afterward that which is spiritual.” The same flesh must accordingly be understood both above and here: it is sown as an animate body and rises as a spiritual body, because “not first that which is spiritual, but that which is animate”; because the first Adam was made into a soul, the last Adam into a Spirit. The whole discussion concerns man; the whole concerns flesh whenever it concerns man.

What, then, shall we say? Does the flesh not even now possess the Spirit through faith, [Col. 0875A] so that we must ask how it is said to be sown an animate body? Certainly the flesh has received the Spirit here too, [Note: [Col. 0875C] Seml. incorrectly repeats: “Through faith, so that we must ask how the animate body is said to be sown. Certainly the flesh has received the Spirit here too.”] but only as a pledge; of the soul, however, it has received not a pledge but the fullness. Accordingly, for this reason too the flesh has been called an animate body under the name of the greater substance within which it is sown; and likewise, through the fullness of the Spirit, it is destined to be spiritual in addition when it is raised. What wonder is it if it has been named more from that with which it is filled than from that with which it is merely sprinkled? [Note: [Col. 0875C] Rhen. and Seml. read *scattered*.]

## CHAPTER LIV

Thus questions very frequently arise from the particular usages of terms, just as they do from shared uses of words. For because the Apostle also has the statement, “So that the mortal may be swallowed up by life”—meaning the flesh—they seize upon “swallowing up” as signifying destruction, namely the destruction of the flesh, [Col. 0875B] as though we were not also said to swallow bile and pain, that is, to hide and cover them [Note: [Col. 0875C] Rhen. reads *cover over*.] and contain them within ourselves.

Finally, since it is also written, “This mortal must put on immortality,” it is shown how the mortal is swallowed up by life: while clothed with immortality it is hidden, covered, and contained within, rather than consumed and lost. “Then death too,” you say, “will be preserved when it has been swallowed up.” Therefore distinguish the common use of words according to their meanings, and you will understand completely. [Note: [Col. 0875D] “You will understand completely.” Cyprian, Epistle 28: “Completely and with discipline.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0875D] Rhen., Seml., and Venet. read *you understand*.]

For death is one thing and the mortal another. Death, therefore, will be swallowed up in one way, and the mortal in another. Death is not capable of receiving immortality, but the mortal is capable of it. Indeed, it is written that “this mortal must put on immortality.” How, then, does it receive it? By being swallowed up by life. How is it swallowed up by life? By being received, [Col. 0875C] incorporated, and enclosed within life itself. [Note: [Col. 0875D] “Enclosed within life itself.” He takes *to enclose* in the sense in which, in the book *On Repentance*, he said that certain people neglect “to enclose repentance.” His meaning, then, is that the mortal is enclosed within life; in Spanish it may be expressed, *engastose en la vida*, “set into life.” LAC.]

Death, however, is rightly swallowed up into destruction [Note: [Col. 0875D] Rhen. and Seml. read *in destruction*.], because it too swallows up to that same end. “Death,” he says, “swallowed up by growing strong,” and for that reason “it has been swallowed up in conflict.” [Note: [Col. 0875D] “‘Death,’ he says, ‘swallowed up by growing strong.’” I do not know what passage of Scripture the Author has in view, unless perhaps he means Rom. 5: “Death passed upon all people,” as Pamelius thinks. I believe that *invadendo*, “by invading,” should be read rather than *invalescendo*, “by growing strong.” [Col. 0876D] LAC.] “Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O death, is your conflict?” [Note: [Col. 0876D] “Where, O death, is your sting?” He has the same statement in ch. 47, where, as here, he writes, “Where, O death, is your conflict?” The Vulgate translator, however, better renders the Greek νίκη or νῖκος as “victory.” LE PR.] Accordingly, life too, as death’s rival, will by conflict swallow up unto salvation what death had swallowed up by conflict [Note: [Col. 0875D] Rhen. incorrectly adds *your*.] unto destruction.

## CHAPTER LV

Although, therefore, by proving that the flesh will rise, [Col. 0876A] we prove by that very fact that no other flesh will rise than the flesh now at issue, [Note: [Col. 0876D] “We prove that no other flesh will rise,” etc. Here he presses the Valentinians; they denied only the resurrection of this flesh, but not that of another. LE PR.] nevertheless the individual questions, and their causes, demand their own particular engagements [Note: [Col. 0875D] Others read *whomsoever* (*quosque*) instead of *also* (*quoque*).], even though they have already been cut down from another direction. We shall therefore interpret more fully both the force and the rationale of the change, which commonly supplies the presumption that another flesh will rise—as though to be changed meant wholly to cease to be and to perish from one’s former condition.

Change, however, must be distinguished from every conception of destruction. [Note: [Col. 0876D] “Change, however, must be distinguished,” etc. The Marcionites trifled with the claim that to be changed is the same as to perish, and that the flesh we possess will therefore not enjoy the glory of the resurrection, since it must be changed, as the Apostle teaches. [Col. 0877D] LE PR.] Change is one thing, destruction another. Yet they would not be different if the flesh were to be changed in such a way as to perish. It will perish through being changed if that very flesh which is presented in the resurrection does not remain within the change. [Note: [Col. 0875D] Rhen. and Seml. read *into the change*.] For just as it perishes if it does not rise, so too, even if it does rise but is withdrawn into a change, it likewise perishes. For it will equally not exist, [Col. 0876B] just as [Note: [Col. 0875D] *Just as* is absent from Rhen. and Seml.] if it had not risen. And how absurd it is if it rises in order not to exist! It could simply have failed to rise and failed to exist, since it had already begun not to exist.

Change and destruction—things wholly different and certainly different in their operations—will not be confused. [Note: [Col. 0876C] Franc. reads *only*.] The latter destroys; the former changes. Therefore, just as what has been destroyed has not been changed, so what has been changed has not been destroyed. For to have perished is wholly to cease being what one was; to have been changed is to exist otherwise. But [Note: [Col. 0876C] Rhen. and Seml. insert *but*.] while a thing exists otherwise, it can still be that very same thing, for that which does not perish retains existence. It has undergone change, not destruction.

Indeed, something can be changed and nonetheless remain the same thing. Thus the whole human being in this age remains the very same in substance, yet is changed in manifold ways—in appearance, bodily bulk, health, condition, [Col. 0876C] rank, age, occupation, business, craft, resources, residence, laws, and morals—and nevertheless loses nothing of being human. [Note: [Col. 0876C] Seml. reads *admits nothing of the human being*.] Nor does one so become another [Note: [Col. 0876C] Fran. and Pam. read *another thing*.] [Note: [Col. 0876D] Others read *becomes*.] as to cease being the same; indeed, one does not become another person at all [Note: [Col. 0876D] Rhen. and Seml. read *becomes*.], but something different.

Divine proofs also attest this form of change. Moses’ hand is changed, and indeed into the likeness of something dead: bloodless, white, [Note: [Col. 0876D] Fran. reads *and white*; Seml., *whitened*.] and cold. But when its heat is restored and its color returns, it is the same flesh and blood. The face of the same man is afterward changed with a brightness that cannot be gazed upon. [Note: [Col. 0876D] Paris. and Fran. read *with a brightness that can be gazed upon*.] But he was still Moses, [Note: [Col. 0876D] Venet. reads *they were*.] even though he could not be looked upon. So too Stephen had already put on the summit of angelic glory, yet no other knees gave way [Col. 0877A] beneath the stoning. [Note: [Col. 0877C] Paris. and Fran. read *during the stoning*.]

The Lord also, in the mountain retreat, had changed even his garments with light, but had preserved features recognizable to Peter. [Note: [Col. 0877D] “But features recognizable to Peter.” Christ’s transfiguration was the pattern of our resurrection; therefore each person will preserve the features and form by which that person can be recognized. Justin gives the reasons for this in Question 60. LAC.] There too Moses and Elijah had taught that the same bodily condition persists even in glory: the one in the image of flesh not yet recovered, and the other in the reality of flesh not yet deceased. [Note: [Col. 0877D] “The one in the image of flesh not yet recovered.” This opinion of Tertullian is approved by St Thomas in his commentary on Matthew and *Summa Theologiae*, III, q. 45, art. 3, ad 2; Lyra on Matt. 17; and Abulensis, Questions 54 and 55. Nevertheless, the more numerous testimonies of the Fathers and interpreters suggest that Moses too appeared in the reality of his own flesh, having risen from the dead for that occasion. Epiphanius approves this opinion on the authority of Proclus and Methodius; Augustine, *On the Miracles of Scripture*, bk. III, ch. 10; Jerome on Matt. 17. [Col. 0878D] LAC.]

Instructed by this example, Paul too says: “He will transfigure [Note: [Col. 0877C] Venet. reads *has transfigured*.] the body of our humiliation so as to conform it to the body of his glory.” But if you maintain [Note: [Col. 0877C] Rhen. and Seml. read *even if*.] that transfiguration and conversion involve the passing away of any substance, [Note: [Col. 0878D] “The passing away of substance.” Here the Author calls *passing away* what earlier in this chapter he repeatedly called *destruction*, just as we customarily call death a passing. This is confirmed by what he adds: “Therefore Saul too, when converted into another man, departed from his body.” PAM.] then Saul too, when converted into another man, departed from his body, [Note: [Col. 0877C] Rig. and Venet. delete *his*.] and Satan himself, when transfigured into an angel of light, loses his own quality. I think not. Thus, with a view to the event [Note: [Col. 0877C] Others read *in the event*.] of the resurrection, it will be possible to be changed, converted, and re-formed while the substance is preserved.

## CHAPTER LVI

For how absurd, how truly unjust [Note: [Col. 0877C] Others incorrectly read *pagan*.], and how unworthy of God in either respect, that one substance should perform the work and another be paid the reward [Note: [Col. 0877D] Rhen. and Seml. read *reward* in the accusative]: that this flesh should be torn apart through martyrdoms but another crowned; and conversely, that this flesh should wallow in filth but another be condemned! Is it not better to draw all faith away from the hope of resurrection once and for all than to make sport of God’s gravity and justice? It would be to raise Marcion instead of Valentinus!

For it is not credible that the mind, memory, or conscience of the present-day human being will be abolished by that changing garment of immortality and incorruption—an abolition that would, of course, empty the benefit [Col. 0877C] and fruit of the resurrection and the character of God’s judgment in either outcome. If I do not remember that I am the person who earned the reward, how shall I give glory to God? How shall I sing him a new song, if I do not know that I am the person who owes gratitude to God? [Note: [Col. 0878C] Rhen. and Seml. delete *to God*.]

Why, moreover, is the change of the flesh alone made an exception, and not simultaneously that of the soul, which has governed the flesh in everything? What sense does it make that [Note: [Col. 0878C] *That* is absent from Rhen.] the same soul which passed through the entire course of life in this flesh, which learned God [Col. 0878A] in this flesh, put on Christ, and sowed the hope of salvation, should reap its fruit in some other flesh, I know not what? Indeed, that would be a most highly favored flesh, for which life would cost nothing. But if the soul too will not be changed, there is no resurrection of the soul either; for the soul itself will not be believed to have risen unless a different soul has risen.

## CHAPTER LVII
Hence comes that familiar subtlety of unbelief: “If,” they say, “the very same substance is restored with its own shape, outline, and qualities, then it is restored also with all its remaining distinctive marks; and thus the blind, the lame, the paralytic, and whatever deformity marked a person at death will return in the same condition.”

[Note: [Col. 0878C] Others read: *illae vulgaris in argutiae*.]

[Note: [Col. 0878C] “Even if all the rest.”]

[Note: [Col. 0878D] “Whatever deformity marked a person at death.” The word *insignis* is sometimes used for “deformed,” just as the Greek ἐπίσημος (*epísēmos*, “marked, conspicuous”) is. LE PR.]

What then? Even if it were so, would you disdain to obtain so great a grace from God, whatever your condition? For even now, when you admit the salvation of the soul alone, do you not ascribe that same salvation to half-men? [Col. 0878B]

[Note: [Col. 0878C] Rhenanus and Semler read *eadem*.]

What is it to believe in the resurrection, if not to believe it complete? For if the flesh is restored from dissolution, much more will it be recalled from mutilation.

[Note: [Col. 0878C] All editions except Junius read *vexatione* (“affliction”) instead of *vitiatione* (“mutilation”).]

The greater cases settle the lesser. Is not the severing or blunting of any limb the death of that limb? If universal death is annulled by resurrection, why not partial death?

[Note: [Col. 0878D] “If we are transformed into glory, how much more into soundness.” This will be the transformation of bodies in the resurrection: they will rise not in the condition in which they died, but in that in which the first parent existed before he touched the forbidden fruit. LE PR.]

If we are transformed into glory, how much more into soundness! Bodily mutilation is accidental; integrity is proper to the body: in integrity we are born. Even if we are injured in the womb, the injury is already something suffered by a human being.

[Note: [Col. 0878D] Rhenanus, Rigault, and the Venetian edition read *vexemur* (“are afflicted”).]

The kind exists before the accident. As life is conferred by God, so it is conferred again. As we receive it, so we receive it back. We are restored to nature, not to injury. We revive as what we are born, not as what we are harmed into. If God does not raise us whole, he does not raise the dead. [Col. 0878C] For what dead person is whole, even if he dies whole? Who is sound when lifeless? What body is uninjured when slain, cold, pallid, rigid, a corpse?

[Note: [Col. 0878D] “When is a man weaker than when he is so altogether?” That is, when he is wholly weak. RIG.]

When is a man weaker than when he is so altogether? When is he more completely paralysed than when he is motionless? Thus to raise the dead is nothing other than to make them whole, lest they should remain dead in that part in which they have not risen.

God is capable of restoring what he made. [Col. 0879A] He has already sufficiently pledged—indeed, displayed—both this power and this generosity of his in Christ, showing himself not merely the raiser of the flesh but also its restorer to wholeness. Accordingly, the Apostle too says: “And the dead shall rise incorrupt” (1 Cor. 15). How could they do so unless whole, when they had previously been corrupted both by bodily infirmity and by the decay of burial?

[Note: [Col. 0879D] “Both by bodily infirmity,” etc. The theologians agree that human beings will rise entire and whole; for although they died mutilated, that mutilation will be repaired. Thus Augustine, *The City of God*, book XXII, chapters 19 and 20: “Nor, if certain members were amputated and taken from the martyrs, will they be without those members in the resurrection of the dead, since it was said to them: ‘Not a hair of your head shall perish.’” Moreover, Basil of Seleucia infers the resurrection of the whole human being from the restoration of one human limb, in Oration 14, on the lame man sitting at the Beautiful Gate, where he says against the Jews: ἀναστάσεως ἀνδριάντα τὸν χωλὸν ἐχάλκευσε, γλώτταις ψευδομέναις ἀληθεύοντας ἀντεστράτευε πόδας: “In the lame man he fashioned a bronze statue of the resurrection, and against lying tongues he marshalled truthful feet.” LE PR.]

For when, above, he set forth both propositions—that “this corruptible must put on incorruption” and “this mortal must put on immortality”—he was not repeating the same thought, but assigning a distinction. By apportioning immortality to the annulment of death and incorruption to the obliteration of decay, he adapted the one to resurrection and the other to restoration. I think, moreover, that to the Thessalonians he also promised the integrity of the whole substance. [Col. 0879B]

Therefore bodily defects will not be feared in the world to come either. Integrity, whether preserved or restored, will be incapable of losing anything, since even whatever it had lost is restored to it.

[Note: [Col. 0879C] Rhenanus and Semler read *admittere* (“admit”) instead of *amittere* (“lose”).]

For when you object that the flesh will still undergo the same sufferings if it is said that the same flesh will rise, you rashly defend nature against its Lord and impiously uphold law against grace—as though the Lord God had no right both to alter nature and to save apart from its law.

[Note: [Col. 0879C] Rhenanus and Semler read *ad hoc* (“for this”) instead of *adhuc* (“still”).]

[Note: [Col. 0879C] “God” is omitted by Rhenanus and Semler.]

How, then, do we read: “Things impossible with men are possible with God” (Matt. 19), and: “God chose the foolish things of the world, that he might confound the wisdom of the world” (1 Cor. 1)?

[Note: [Col. 0879C] Rhenanus and Semler read *quo* instead of *quomodo*.]

[Note: [Col. 0879C] “Are” is omitted by Rhenanus and Semler.]

I ask you: if you transform your slave by granting him freedom, will it follow—because the same flesh and soul remain which had formerly been exposed to lashes, fetters, and brands—that they must therefore suffer the same things? [Col. 0879C]

[Note: [Col. 0879C] François reads *illos*; Pamelius, *illas*.]

I think not. On the contrary, he is honoured by the splendour of a white garment, the distinction of a gold ring, and the name, tribe, and table of his patron.

[Note: [Col. 0879D] “The distinction of a gold ring.” This was a prerogative of equestrian rank; yet it became so debased that not only did freedmen elevated to that equestrian grade assume such rings, but the practice gradually descended even to the lowest common people. LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0880D] “The name, tribe, and table of his patron,” etc. Slaves called their masters “heroes” and “lords,” while freedmen called them “patrons”; and when they were manumitted, they prefixed the patron’s third name to their own two names. Those who were granted freedom also used to be enrolled in the urban tribes and to sit at their patrons’ tables, something they did not venture to do until they had been manumitted. LE PR.]

Allow God this power too: through the force of that transformation to reform the condition, not the nature, both removing its liabilities to suffering and conferring safeguards upon it.

[Note: [Col. 0879C] Rigault and the Venetian edition read “of that transformation” in the reverse word order.]

Thus the flesh will indeed remain even after the resurrection—capable of suffering insofar as it is itself and the same flesh; yet incapable of suffering insofar as it has been manumitted by the Lord precisely for this purpose, so that it may no longer be able to suffer. [Col. 0880A]

## CHAPTER LVIII

“Everlasting joy,” says Isaiah, “shall be upon their head” (Isa. 35).

[Note: [Col. 0880C] The Venetian edition reads *Jucunditas*.] Nothing is everlasting except after the resurrection. “Pain and sorrow and sighing,” he says, “have fled from them.” Similarly, the angel says to John: “And God shall wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Rev. 17). Certainly from the same eyes that had formerly wept and that could still have wept, had not divine mercy dried up every shower of tears. And again: “For God shall wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more” (Rev. 11). Therefore corruption too shall be no more, being likewise driven away [Col. 0880B] through incorruption, just as death is driven away through immortality.

[Note: [Col. 0880C] “Death” is absent from Rhenanus.]

If pain, sorrow, sighing, and death itself arise from injuries to both soul and flesh, how will they be removed unless their causes cease—that is, the injuries of flesh and soul? Where are adverse accidents in the presence of God, or hostile assaults in the presence of Christ? Where are demonic attacks in the presence of the Holy Spirit, when the devil himself and his angels have already been plunged into the flames?

[Note: [Col. 0880C] Rhenanus and Semler read “the Lord” instead of “God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0880C] Rigault and the Venetian edition read *daemoniaci* (“demonic”).]

Where is necessity, or what is called fortune or fate? What wound is there for the risen after pardon? What wrath for the reconciled after grace? What infirmity after power? What weakness after salvation?

The garments and shoes of the children of Israel remained unworn and unsoiled during those forty years; even in their bodies, justice checked the readily occurring growth of nails and hair at the measure of fitness and dignity, lest even excessive growth should be reckoned as corruption. [Col. 0880C]

[Note: [Col. 0880D] “That the garments and shoes of the children of Israel,” etc. Why, he asks, were the garments of the Israelite people not worn out during forty years in the desert, unless so that they might appear incorrupt and be believed immune from decay, God so arranging it? I discussed this miracle in my observations on the *Prae-Adamitae*, under the name of Eusebius Romanus, against the perverse opinion of Peyrère, who mocks the miracles of Scripture with both wickedness and madness. LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0880C] Rhenanus and Semler read the singular *corruptela*.]

The Babylonian fires did not damage the tiaras or *sarabara* of the three brothers, although these were foreign to the Jews.

[Note: [Col. 0880D] “Neither tiaras nor *sarabara*.” *Tiaras* is a Persian word, just as *saraba* is perhaps Chaldaic. On this see *On the Pallium*, chapter 4. LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0880C] Rigault and the Venetian edition read *sarabara*; others *saraboeas*; Rhenanus *sarabas*; others *saraballa*.]

[Note: [Col. 0880C] Rigault and the Venetian edition read the singular *aliena*.]

Jonah was swallowed by the sea-monster, in whose belly shipwrecks were digested, yet three days later he was vomited out unharmed. Enoch and Elijah, even today, have not yet discharged the debt of resurrection, because neither have they discharged that of death; nevertheless, having been removed from the world and thereby already made candidates for eternity, they are learning the flesh’s immunity from every defect, every loss, and every injury and outrage. [Col. 0881A]
