[Note: [Col. 0881C] The Codex Pithoeanus, Rigault, and the Venetian edition read *emunitatem*.]

To what faith do these examples affix their testimony, unless to the faith by which we must believe that they are proofs of the integrity to come? For, on the Apostle’s authority, the things that were written were figures of us, so that we might believe the Lord superior to every law governing bodies, and certainly the preserver above all of the flesh, whose very garments and shoes he also protected.

[Note: [Col. 0881C] Rhenanus adds “and.”]

[Note: [Col. 0881C] Semler reads *calceamenta*.]

## CHAPTER LIX

“But,” you say, “the age to come belongs to a different and eternal order; therefore that different order cannot possess the non-eternal substance of this age.” Certainly—if man existed for the sake of the future order, and not the order for the sake of man. But the Apostle, writing, “Whether the world, or life, or death, or things to come, or things present—all are yours” (1 Cor. 3:22), appoints the same persons heirs even of the things to come. [Col. 0881B]

Isaiah grants you nothing when he says, “All flesh is grass,” and elsewhere, “And all flesh shall see the salvation of the Lord” (Isa. 40:5–6).

[Note: [Col. 0881C] Pamelius, François, Rigault, and the Venetian edition read “of God.”]

He distinguished destinies, not substances. For who does not place God’s judgment in a twofold sentence, one of salvation and one of punishment? Therefore all flesh destined for fire is grass; and all flesh appointed for salvation shall see the salvation of the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0881C] Pamelius, François, Rigault, and the Venetian edition read “of God.”]

I know that I did not commit adulteries with one flesh and am not now striving after continence with another.

[Note: [Col. 0881D] “I know that I did not commit adulteries with one flesh,” etc. If the Author is speaking of himself, he appears not to have preserved continence in his youth before marriage. But since we indicated above, in book I *To His Wife*, that he was continent within marriage itself, and since he was so great a lover of continence that on that account he subsequently adhered to Montanus, he seems rather to be speaking generally of any human being under the person of himself. PAM.]

If anyone goes about carrying two sets of sexual organs, he can now remove the grass of the unclean flesh and reserve for himself only that flesh which is to see the Lord’s salvation. [Col. 0881C]

[Note: [Col. 0881C] Pamelius, François, Rigault, and the Venetian edition read “of God.”]

But since the same Prophet also presents the nations as at one time reckoned like dust and spittle, and at another as destined to hope and believe in the name and arm of the Lord, are we mistaken about the nations too? Are some nations destined to believe, and others reckoned as dust, because their substances differ?

Yet Christ, within the ocean and from this very heaven that hangs over us, shone forth as the true light for the nations; and the Valentinians themselves learned here how to go astray. [Col. 0882A]

[Note: [Col. 0881D] “Yet Christ within the ocean, and from this heaven that hangs over us.” The Valentinians also raved that beyond this circuit of the earth there were other human beings, of a different substance, whom they called “true,” *teletoi*, *abaskantoi*, and *akinētoi*—that is, “perfect,” “unenvied,” and “immovable.” For they said that our people were not true human beings, whom the Demiurge reckoned as a drop from a bucket, dust from the threshing floor, and locusts. Our Septimius discusses this more openly in *Scorpiace*. I do not think that these ravings are connected with what is read in the First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians about worlds situated beyond the ocean, which he calls ἀπεράντους (*aperántous*, “boundless”). That statement probably escaped this apostolic man through ignorance of geography rather than through a desire to affirm any doctrine. RIG.—Christ was of the same nature as we are; for he did not, as the heretics imagined, draw his flesh from heaven or from a world beyond the bounds of the Ocean. LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0882C] Rhenanus and Semler read *incumbat*.]

[Note: [Col. 0882C] Pamelius, François, and the Paris edition read *effulsit*.]

Nor will the constitution of the believing nations in flesh and soul be other than that of the unbelieving nations. Therefore, just as he distinguished the same nations not by kind but by lot, so too he divided the fleshes—which in those nations are of one substance—not by matter but by recompense.

## CHAPTER LX

But now, to aggravate the controversy still further, they argue from the functions of the members, with particular reference to this same flesh. They say either that the members themselves must continue in their operations and fruits, since they are assigned to the same bodily mass; or, because it is agreed that the functions of the members will cease, they also eradicate the bodily mass itself. Its continuance, they say, surely cannot be believed without members, since members cannot be believed to exist without functions.

[Note: [Col. 0882C] Rhenanus and Semler read *exaggerant* (“they aggravate”).]

“What use will there now be,” they say, “for this cavern of the mouth, this rank of teeth, this descent of the throat, this crossroads of the stomach, this abyss of the belly, and this long, intricate system of intestines, when there will be no place for food and drink? [Col. 0882B]

[Note: [Col. 0882D] “The crossroads of the stomach.” He calls the stomach’s gathering-place and receptacle a “crossroads,” because everything edible introduced through the mouth comes together there. The metaphor is taken from roads that meet and converge; grammarians accordingly derive *compitum* from this. RHEN.]

“What will those members receive, work upon, pass downward, separate, digest, and expel? What use will there be for the hands themselves, the feet, and every working limb, when even concern for sustenance will cease? What use for the kidneys, accomplices in the production of seed; for the remaining organs of generation in either sex; for the receptacles of conception; and for the fountains of the breasts, when intercourse, childbirth, and child-rearing have ceased?

[Note: [Col. 0882C] Rigault and the Venetian edition read *desessuro*; Rhenanus and Semler, *discessuro*.]

“Finally, what use will there be for the whole body, when the whole body will plainly be idle?”

Against these arguments we have already laid the foundation that the orders of the future and the present must not be brought into collision, since a transformation will intervene. We now build further upon it: these functions of the members remain only as long as the necessities of this life, until life itself is transferred from temporality into eternity, just as the animal body is transferred into the spiritual when “this mortal puts on immortality and this corruptible puts on incorruption” (1 Cor. 15). [Col. 0882C]

When life itself is then freed from necessities, the members too will be freed from their functions; but they will not therefore be unnecessary. For although they are released from functions, they are retained for judgments, so that each may receive through the body according to what he has done (2 Cor. 5).

[Note: [Col. 0882D] “But they are retained for judgments.” The Author very often relies upon this argument to support the resurrection, particularly in chapter 14. Although the Fathers place great and deserved confidence in it, Athenagoras, who pursues it more fully, assigned it somewhat less weight. He offers three arguments to prove the resurrection, but somewhat diminished the force of this one concerning the necessity of divine judgment. Yet his second argument, drawn from human nature itself, has far less strength; nor does his first, drawn from the end for which God created man, possess greater weight, although I consider it by no means ineffective. PAM.]

For God’s tribunal requires a whole human being; yet without his members a human being cannot be whole, because he consists of their substances, not merely their functions. [Col. 0883A]

[Note: [Col. 0883C] The Codex Wouwerianus, Rigault, and the Venetian edition read *liquet*.]

Unless, perhaps, you would assert that a ship is whole without keel, prow, stern, and the integrity of its entire structure. And yet we have often seen a ship shattered by a storm or dissolved by decay become the same ship again once all its parts were restored and repaired, even glorying in the designation “restored.”

[Note: [Col. 0883D] “And yet a ship shattered by a storm.” Alfenus likewise held that, if a ship had been repaired so often that no plank remained the same because every one had been replaced, it was nevertheless to be considered the same ship. Law *Proponebatur*, *De judiciis*. Thus the Athenians, at the time when they mixed the hemlock for Socrates, said that the ship customarily sent to Delos every year was the very ship in which Theseus had carried their ancestors to Crete. “This is the ship, as the Athenians say” (τοῦτο ἐστι τὸ πλοῖον, ὡς φᾶσιν Ἀθηναῖοι), etc., says the Platonist Phaedo. RIG.]

Are we troubled by God’s craftsmanship, will, and right? Suppose, then, that a rich and generous master, satisfying his affection or his glory by the restoration of a ship alone, has wished to carry the restoration only thus far. Will you therefore deny that it needs its former structure because that structure will henceforth be idle, when the mere preservation of the ship without operation is appropriate to it?

[Note: [Col. 0883C] Rhenanus reads *tunc* (“then”) instead of *tu* (“you”).]

It is therefore enough to learn only this: whether the Lord, in destining man for salvation, has destined the flesh also; whether he wills the same flesh to exist again. You must not argue from the future idleness of its members that it cannot exist again. [Col. 0883B]

[Note: [Col. 0883C] Rhenanus and Semler read *et* (“and”) instead of *ex* (“from”).]

For a thing may exist again and nevertheless be idle; but it cannot be said to be idle unless it exists. Yet if it exists, it may also not be idle; for nothing will be idle in the presence of God.

## CHAPTER LXI

“But, man, you received a mouth for eating and drinking.” Why not rather for speaking, so that you might differ from the other animals? Why not rather for proclaiming God, so that you might also preside among human beings? In short, Adam pronounced names for the animals before he plucked from the tree; he also prophesied before he ate.

“But you received teeth to gnaw meat from the market.” [Col. 0883C]

[Note: [Col. 0883D] “But you received teeth to gnaw meat from the market.” Like that Maenius of Horace: “The ruin, storm, and abyss of the meat-market.” RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0883C] The English manuscript and Pamelius read *coornandum*.]

Why not rather to furnish a crown for every opening and gape of your mouth? Why not rather to regulate the beats of the tongue and mark the articulations of the voice by their impact?

[Note: [Col. 0883C] François and Pamelius read *temporandos*.]

Hear and observe even the toothless, so that you may regard the array of teeth as serving also for the adornment of the mouth. [Col. 0884A]

[Note: [Col. 0883C] “Even the toothless” is omitted by Semler.]

[Note: [Col. 0883C] Rigault, the Venetian edition, and Semler read *honorem*.]

The lower parts of man and woman have openings—surely, you say, so that lusts may flow through them. Why not rather so that the boiled residue of drink may be strained through them?

[Note: [Col. 0884C] Rhenanus and Semler read *defluxura* (“what is to flow down”) instead of *defruta* (“boiled-down liquids”).]

[Note: [Col. 0883D] “So that the boiled residue of drink may be strained through them.” Junius greatly approves the reading of the first edition, *qua defluxura colentur*, and wonders that the alternative reading was admitted. Yet *defruta* is more expressive, for digested drink is strained through the lower passages. *Defrutum* is boiled wine, so called from boiling down, as Palladius says—to one half, according to Pliny; or, according to Nonius, they called it *defrutum* if by boiling they reduced two portions to one third. LAC.]

Within women there is also a place where seed may be collected. Or is it rather a place where burdens of blood may be discharged, since the more sluggish sex is unable to disperse it?

[Note: [Col. 0884C] Pamelius and François add *in*.]

These functions of the members must indeed be mentioned, since our opponents, choosing whatever functions they please, of whatever organs they please, and in whatever manner they please, mockingly bark them out with the deliberate aim of shaming the resurrection. They fail to consider that the very causes of necessity will then become idle: hunger for food, thirst for drink, procreation through intercourse, and sustenance through labour.

[Note: [Col. 0884C] Pamelius, Rhenanus, and Semler transpose the phrases to read: “and in whatever manner they please, and of whatever organs they please.”]

[Note: [Col. 0884D] “These functions of the members must indeed be mentioned.” Jerome played with astonishing freedom upon functions of this kind in the first book *Against Jovinian*. RIG.]

For once death is removed, neither the supports of sustenance for preserving life nor the heavy apparatus of procreation will burden the members. Besides, even today it is possible for the intestines and sexual organs to be idle. Moses and Elijah completed forty days of fasting and were nourished by God alone. [Col. 0884B] Even then this saying was being inaugurated: “Man shall not live by bread, but by the word of God.” Behold outlines of the power to come.

We too, so far as we can, excuse the mouth from food; we even withdraw our sex from intercourse. How many voluntary eunuchs are there? How many virgins married to Christ? How many sterile persons of either sex, constructed with fruitless generative organs?

[Note: [Col. 0884C] “For” is absent from Pamelius, the Paris edition, and François; Rhenanus and Semler read, “for even if already here.”]

For if, already here, the functions and advantages of the members may be idle through a temporary idleness appropriate to a temporal order, and yet the human being is no less whole, then likewise, with the human being preserved—and indeed preserved more fully in the eternal order—we shall all the more have no need of those things which we have already grown accustomed not to need here.

## CHAPTER LXII

[Col. 0884C] But the Lord’s declaration puts an end to this dispute. “They shall be,” he says, “like angels” (Matt. 22).

[Note: [Col. 0884D] “They shall be, he says, like angels.” He touched upon this passage in chapter 36. Here, however, this argument may be attached to those preceding, as though increasing their force. He had said that in this life people are excused from carnal intercourse, and therefore live a heavenly life like the angels, as Bernard says in Sermon 2 *To the Brothers*, and Cyprian in *On the Singularity of Clerics*. Therefore in the other life too human beings will be able to conduct themselves in the manner of angels, as Christ confirms and defines: “They shall be like angels.” LAC.]

If they are like angels by not marrying, because they also do not die, then surely they are likewise so by not succumbing to any similar necessity of bodily existence. [Col. 0885A]

[Note: [Col. 0884D] “Succumbing to a similar necessity.” Above he used the same verb, *succidere*, in the sense of *succumbere*. As regards the meaning of the sentence, Aeneas of Gaza expresses it elegantly in the *Theophrastus*. LAC.]

For angels also were once like human beings, eating, drinking, and extending their feet for washing: they had put on a human appearance while their own inward substance remained intact. Therefore, if angels, when made like human beings, undertook fleshly activities while remaining in the same spiritual substance, why may not human beings, when made like angels, enter upon a spiritual order while remaining in the same substance of flesh? Under their angelic clothing they will no more be subject to the customary functions of flesh than the angels under their human clothing were then subject to the customary functions of spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0885D] “They undertook fleshly activities.” Indeed, some affirm that even after the resurrection angels will sometimes undertake fleshly activities by assuming human form and functions, and that they will accompany human beings in the customary actions of human limbs: using the mouth to praise God, as I noted in the preceding chapter, and the feet to form choruses and perform the most chaste and solemn dances as a sign of exultation. So affirm Salas, volume I, on *Prima Secundae*, question 5, article 5, disputation 4, and Aegidius, book IV, question 22, articles 4 and 6. LAC.]

[Note: [Col. 0885C] Pamelius, the Paris edition, and François read *spiritibus*.]

Nor will human beings therefore fail to remain in the flesh merely because they do not remain in the customary functions of the flesh, since the angels did not fail to remain in the spirit merely because they did not remain in the customary functions of the spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0885C] “In” is absent from Rhenanus and Semler.]

[Note: [Col. 0885C] The Paris edition and François read “flesh” instead of “spirit.”]

Finally, he did not say, “They shall be angels,” lest he deny that they are human beings; but “like angels,” so that he might preserve them as human beings. [Col. 0885B] He did not take away the substance to which he attributed the likeness.

## CHAPTER LXIII

The flesh, therefore, shall rise: all of it, the very same flesh, and the whole of it.

[Note: [Col. 0885D] “The flesh, therefore, shall rise.” By recapitulation he concludes the argument and leaves it ἀνατίρρητον (*anatírrhēton*, “indisputable”): the flesh, both of the blessed and of the reprobate, will one day rise, and the same flesh—not another—will rise. LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0885C] Semler reads “rises.”]

Wherever it is, it is held on deposit with God through Jesus Christ, the most faithful trustee between God and human beings. He will restore God to man and man to God, spirit to flesh and flesh to spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0886D] “Trustee between God and human beings.” That is, mediator—μεσίτης (*mesítēs*)—for a trustee is placed midway between plaintiff and defendant in order to compose and settle the dispute. Law *Ab executore*, *Quorum appellationes*. LE PR.]

He has already joined the two in covenant within himself; he has matched bride to bridegroom and bridegroom to bride. For even if anyone should contend that the soul is the bride, the flesh will accompany the soul at least in the name of her dowry. The soul will not be a prostitute, to be received naked by the bridegroom: she has her document, her adornment, her own servant—the flesh—which will accompany her as her foster-sister.

[Note: [Col. 0885C–D] Rhenanus and Semler read *collatanea*; Pamelius, François, and the Paris edition read *collectaneam*.]

But the flesh is the bride, for in Christ Jesus it contracted the Spirit as its bridegroom by blood. [Col. 0885C]

[Note: [Col. 0886C] “Spirit” is absent from Pamelius, the Paris edition, and François.]

[Note: [Col. 0886C] Rhenanus and Semler read *passa* (“suffered”) instead of *pacta* (“contracted”).]

What you suppose to be its destruction, understand to be its withdrawal. The soul is not the only thing laid aside; the flesh too has meanwhile its own places of withdrawal—in waters, in fires, in birds, in beasts.

[Note: [Col. 0886C] Pamelius, the Paris edition, and François read “its own recesses.”]

When it appears to be dissolved into these, it is as though poured into vessels. Even if the vessels themselves perish, when it has flowed out of them too, it is absorbed through circuitous routes into its matrix, the earth, so that from the earth Adam may once more be presented, [Col. 0886A] destined to hear from the Lord: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us”—then truly master of the evil which he has escaped and of the good which he has attained.

[Note: [Col. 0886C] Rhenanus and Semler read “may be presented” rather than “presented again.”]

Why, soul, do you envy the flesh? No one is so near to you, no one whom after the Lord you ought to love so much; no one is more your brother than the flesh, which is born together with you even in God. You should rather have entreated resurrection for her, since it was through you, perhaps, that she sinned.

[Note: [Col. 0886D] “Why, soul, do you envy the flesh?” Here he addresses chiefly the Marcionites and Valentinians, who thought and spoke so badly of the flesh that it was as though their soul were affected by jealousy and envy of another. Hence he also adds: “But it is no wonder if you have hated her whose author you also rejected.” For Marcion rejected and hated God the Creator. LAC.]

But it is no wonder if you have hated her whose author you also rejected, and whose existence in Christ you have habitually either denied or altered.

[Note: [Col. 0886D] “Whose author you also rejected.” The Marcionites and others rejected God the Creator with such bitter hatred that they sometimes abstained from foods in detestation of the Creator’s works. LAC.]

In the same manner you corrupt, either by your pen or by your interpretation, the Word of God himself who became flesh, while also introducing the mysteries of the apocrypha—fables of blasphemy.

But God Almighty, pouring out his most provident grace against these devices of unbelief and perversity, has in these last days poured out from his Spirit upon all flesh, upon his servants and handmaids (Joel 2:28–29). He has both revived the struggling faith in the resurrection of the flesh and purified the ancient Scriptures from every obscurity of ambiguity by manifest lights of words and meanings. [Col. 0886B]

For because there had to be heresies, so that all the approved might be made manifest (1 Cor. 11:19), while those heresies could not have dared to arise without certain occasions in the Scriptures, the ancient Scriptures accordingly appear to have supplied them with certain materials—though the heresies can indeed be refuted by those very same writings.

[Note: [Col. 0886C] “Them” is absent from Semler and Oberthür.]

But because the Holy Spirit ought not to be restrained from overflowing also with utterances of such a kind as would scatter no seeds for the cunning devices of heretics, but would even tear up their old sods, he has therefore now dispelled all former ambiguities—and whatever things they choose to call parables—through the open and transparent proclamation of the whole mystery, by means of the new prophecy pouring forth from the Paraclete.

[Note: [Col. 0886D] The Paris edition and François read *necdum* (“not yet”) instead of *nec* (“not”).]

If you drink from his springs, you will be able to thirst for no doctrine; no fever of questions will burn you. By drinking in the resurrection of the flesh everywhere, you will be refreshed.

## Second Series  
## MORAL WORKS WRITTEN AFTER THE AUTHOR’S EMBRACE OF MONTANISM

*On the Veiling of Virgins. On the Exhortation to Chastity. On Monogamy. On Fasts. On Modesty. On the Pallium.*

[Col. 0887]

# THE BOOK OF QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIANUS ON THE VEILING OF VIRGINS (C)

## Preface

[Col. 0887] Among all Tertullian’s Montanist works there is scarcely any in which he employs greater force to defend the Montanists’ discipline against the charge of novelty than the treatise *On the Veiling of Virgins*. Hence it is rightly believed to have been composed near the beginning of the period he spent among the Montanists. [Col. 0887A]

The very learned Rémi Ceillier indeed considers *On the Veiling of Virgins* to be the latest of all his books, because Tertullian cites it in no other work, not even in *On the Crown*, where the subject itself, treated in chapter 14, appears to have required such a citation. But this conjecture proves nothing, because *On the Crown* was composed before *On the Veiling of Virgins*, while we do not perceive that Tertullian had any occasion to cite the latter work in his other writings.

However these matters may stand, it is at least evident that this little work was written during the schism, since it all too openly bears the character of Montanus. For presently, in chapter 1, he says: “Righteousness was at first in its rudimentary stages; thereafter, through the Law and the Prophets, it advanced into infancy; thereafter, through the Gospel, it grew fervent into youth; now, through the Paraclete, it is being ordered into maturity.” [Col. 0887B]

Tertullian was given the occasion to write this little book by the custom of certain churches, both in the West and in many other parts of Greece or the East, of veiling virgins in church, whereas in the African church most Christian virgins went about with uncovered heads. [Col. 0888A] Therefore, in this book, against the custom of his own country, where married women alone were veiled, he shows that custom cannot prescribe against truth. According to the observation of the distinguished Dupin, this is indeed true when dogma is in question, but not when the matter is one of discipline of little importance. LUMP.

## ARGUMENT

Tertullian, having, as it appears, been assailed with abuse and harassed as a heretic because of a certain dispute with the Greeks about the veiling of virgins, begins by inveighing against his assailants, who boasted of custom, and declares that custom cannot prescribe against truth.

He then asserts that the custom of veiling virgins is better; that it is not condemned in Holy Scripture but, on the contrary, commended by the Apostle, confirmed by the discipline of the Church, supported [Col. 0888B] by many examples of saints, and ratified by the dangers incurred by unveiled virgins themselves. EDD.

## CHAPTER ONE

Having now suffered a controversy directed particularly against my opinion, I shall demonstrate in Latin also that our virgins ought to be veiled, from the time when—

[Note: [Col. 0887B] “Having now suffered a controversy directed particularly against my opinion.” In a certain dispute against the Greeks, when he had perhaps asserted rather vehemently that virgins too ought to be veiled, he appears to have been assailed by Greek abuse and harassed as a heretic. RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0887B] “I shall demonstrate in Latin also.” The commentators agree that Tertullian had previously written another treatment of this subject in Greek. LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0888B] “The transition of age.” That is, when they have passed beyond the years of childhood. On this subject there is that passage of Virgil, *Eclogue* 4, in praise of Pollio:

From this point, when mature age has made you a man.

That is, when you have grown into a man and are *in your prime* (ἐν ἀκμῇ); Synesius writes, “having now enrolled yourself among men” (ἤδη εἰς ἄνδρας ἀγγειλάμενος). LE PR.]

once they have passed the transition-point of their age. Truth demands this, and against truth no one can prescribe—

[Note: [Col. 0888B] **No one can prescribe.** Lacerda has adduced many passages to explain the verb *praescribere* as meaning “to raise an objection” or “to produce exceptions,” in accordance with juristic usage. Here, in my judgment, it means simply that nothing can detract from the truth by any argument whatsoever, and nothing can diminish its splendor or majesty. LE PR.]

[Col. 0889A] neither length of time, nor the patronage of persons, nor the privilege of regions. For it is generally from one of these that custom, having taken its origin in some ignorance or simplicity, is strengthened into usage by succession and is then asserted against the truth. But our Lord—

[Note: [Col. 0889D] **Christ called himself the truth.** Christ himself testified in countless passages, which I omit, that he is the truth. Hence I have often wondered that certain men who display the arrogance of the Pharisees should have descended to such impiety as to say that Christ lied, or at least spoke equivocally, eight times in chapter VIII of the Gospel of blessed John. But this is neither the place nor the time to lament that overthrow of Christian morals and discipline. LE PR.]

Christ called himself the truth, not custom. If Christ is eternal and prior to all things, truth is likewise an eternal and ancient reality. Let those, therefore, for whom it is new consider that, in itself, it is old. It is not so much novelty as truth that refutes heresy. Whatever savors of opposition to the truth will be heresy, even if it is an ancient custom.

For the rest, it is through his own fault that anyone remains ignorant of something. What is unknown ought to have been sought out, just as what is recognized ought to be received. The rule of faith, indeed, is altogether one, alone immovable and incapable of reformation: namely, the belief in one almighty God, the Creator of the world, and in his Son Jesus Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, crucified [Col. 0889B] under Pontius Pilate, raised from the dead on the third—

[Note: [Col. 0889C] *On the third* [*tertio*], Paris edition.]

day, received into heaven, now sitting at the right hand of the Father, and destined to come to judge the living and the dead, with the resurrection of the flesh as well.

While this law of faith remains, the other matters of—

[Note: [Col. 0889D] **Discipline and conduct.** Severe discipline is always understood by the term *conduct* (*conversatio*). In Theodoret it is called ἄσκησις, “ascetic discipline.” St. Jerome, book I *Against Jovinian*: “We are armed with the same manner of life with which Christ was armed.” LE PR.]

discipline and conduct admit the novelty of correction, as the grace of God works and advances even to the end. For how could it be that, while the devil is always at work and daily adds to the contrivances of iniquity, the work of God should either have ceased or stopped advancing? It was precisely for this reason that the Lord sent the Paraclete: because human weakness could not grasp everything at once, discipline was gradually to be directed, ordered, and brought to perfection by that vicar of the Lord, the Holy Spirit.

“I still have many things,” he says, “to tell you, but [Col. 0889C] you cannot yet bear them. When that Spirit of truth comes, he will lead you into all truth and will announce to you the things that are to come” (John 16:12). But [Col. 0890A] he had also previously declared this concerning the Spirit’s work. What, then, is the administration of the Paraclete except this: that discipline is directed, the Scriptures are revealed, understanding is reformed, and progress is made toward better things?

Nothing exists without its proper age, and all things await their time. Finally, Ecclesiastes says: “There is a time for every matter” (Eccles. 3:17). Look at creation itself, advancing gradually toward fruit. First there is the grain; from the grain a shoot arises, and from the shoot a sapling struggles forth. Then its branches and foliage gain strength, and the full form implied by the name “tree” unfolds. From there comes the swelling of the bud—

[Note: [Col. 0889D] **From there comes the swelling of the bud.** A *swelling* (*tumor*) is anything that is conceived; but *germen* and *gemma*—“shoot” and “bud”—are the same in this instance. LE PR.]

and the flower is released from the bud, and from the flower the fruit opens. It too is for a while crude and unformed; gradually advancing through its proper age, it is trained into gentleness of flavor.

[Note: [Col. 0889D] **It is trained into gentleness of flavor.** For in fruit that is still crude and unripe there is, as it were, a wild savagery of juice and flavor; but it is trained into gentleness [Col. 0890D] as it is gradually ripened to maturity. RIG.]

So too righteousness—for the God of righteousness and of creation is the same—was first in its rudimentary stage, when nature feared God. Then, through the Law and the Prophets, it advanced into childhood. Then, through the Gospel, it surged into youth. Now, through the [Col. 0890B] Paraclete, it is being ordered into maturity. He alone must be called and revered as the teacher appointed by Christ. For he does not speak on his own—

[Note: [Col. 0889C] “He will speak,” Rhen., Seml., Leop.]

but speaks what is commanded by Christ. He alone is the guide who goes before us, because he alone comes after Christ. Those who have received him place truth before custom. Those who have heard him prophesying—not long ago, but right down to the present—

[Note: [Col. 0889C] Thus Rig., on the authority of the manuscripts of Wouwer and Ursinus. The Dijon manuscript, Rhen., and others read: “right down, not long ago” (*usque non olim*). But Rig. plausibly conjectured that the words “not long ago” were added for the sake of explaining the phrase, and that only the words “right down to the present” (*usque nunc*) should be retained.]

cover their virgins.

## CHAPTER II

But for the moment I do not wish to ascribe this practice to truth—

[Note: [Col. 0890C] “Of truth,” Seml.]

Let it be custom for the time being, so that I may oppose custom with custom. Throughout Greece and certain barbarian regions associated with it—

[Note: [Col. 0890D] **Throughout Greece and certain barbarian regions associated with it.** By the “barbarian regions of Greece” he means certain regions outside Greece but adjoining it, with which the Greeks had dealings or wars. Horace:

> Greece, clashing with barbarism in a protracted war.

**Throughout Greece and certain barbarian regions associated with it.** I think that certain cities or regions of Greece are meant, although others believe that he indicates cities neighboring Greece and adjacent nations. LE PR.]

a great many churches conceal their virgins. This institution is also found somewhere beneath this very sky, lest anyone ascribe that custom merely to Greek or barbarian heathenism. But I have cited those churches [Col. 0890C] which the apostles themselves or apostolic men—

[Note: [Col. 0890D] **Apostolic men.** By “apostolic men” understand the leading figures of the Christian religion, who were either instructed and trained by the apostles or performed deeds worthy of apostolic teaching. It seems rather inappropriate to explain the expression as referring only to bishops or solely to the supreme pontiff, since it is also attributed to Constantine the Great in many passages, as in Theodoret, book I, chapter 25: τὰς ἀποστολικὰς φροντίδας ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ περιέφερεν, “he constantly bore apostolic concerns in his soul”; and elsewhere. LE PR.]

founded, and, I think, before certain others.

[Note: [Col. 0890D] **And, I think, before certain others.** He spares the names of those who, although later than the apostles and apostolic men, were said to have given authority to the custom that virgins should by no means be veiled. RIG.]

Those churches, therefore, possess the same authority of custom; they can oppose to these later churches both earlier times and earlier predecessors. What shall we observe? What shall we choose?

[Note: [Col. 0891C] “Shall we choose” [*deligimus*], Seml.]

We cannot reject a custom that we cannot condemn, since it is not foreign to us, because it belongs not to outsiders but to those with whom we share the right of peace and the name of brotherhood. We and they have one faith, one God, the same Christ, the same hope, and the same sacraments of the washing.

[Note: [Col. 0891C] **Let me say it once: we are one Church.** In his book *On the Unity of the Church*, blessed Cyprian likewise adduces Scripture to prove this same point, as well as many other passages; we refer the reader to that book. Both authors interpret the text as meaning one body, one Church. PAM.]

Let me say it once: we are one Church. Thus whatever belongs to our people belongs to us. Otherwise, you divide the body.

Yet here—

[Note: [Col. 0891C] “So here, as in all things,” Seml.]

as in all matters characterized by differing institutions—

[Note: [Col. 0891C] *Institutus*, wrongly in Fran.]

and by doubt and uncertainty, an examination ought to have been undertaken to determine which of two such divergent customs was more consistent with God’s discipline. Certainly that custom should be chosen which encloses virgins—

[Note: [Col. 0891D] **Which encloses virgins.** With a veil. RIG.]

and keeps them known to God alone. For besides the fact that they must seek glory from God, not from human beings—

[Note: [Col. 0891C] “Besides” [*praeterea*], Seml.]

they must even blush at their own good. You would embarrass a virgin more by praising than by reproaching her, because the brow of sin is harder, having been taught shamelessness by sin itself and in sin itself.

For no one would have approved that custom which denies the existence of virgins by exhibiting them, except certain persons—

[Note: [Col. 0891C] “Certain women of the same kind,” Seml.]

of the same character as the virgins themselves. For the sort of eyes that will wish to see a virgin are the sort possessed by the virgin who wishes to be seen. The same kinds of eyes—

[Note: [Col. 0892C] “Of the same eyes,” Seml.]

desire one another.

[Note: [Col. 0891D] **It belongs to the same lust to be seen and to see.** For this reason Jerome, speaking of this subject to Eustochium, says: “No gaze is safe.” It is as though he said that neither seeing nor being seen is safe. And Ambrose, book I of *On Duties*, chapter 18, says: “Let a woman neither wish to see men nor to be seen.” These precepts are intended to make a virgin understand how precious virginal modesty is. For that reason a virgin is called by Cyprian, in *On the Dress of Virgins*, a “candidate for modesty,” as though this were her sole pursuit; and Manilius, book III:

> It is always too little merely to love; they will wish to be seen to love as well.

LAC.]

It belongs to the same lust to be seen and to see. It is as fitting for a holy man to blush if he has seen a virgin as for a holy virgin to blush if she has been seen by a man.

## CHAPTER III

But those most holy predecessors were unwilling even to discriminate between the customs. Nevertheless, among [Col. 0891C] us, until very recently, both customs were tolerated. The matter was left to individual choice, so that each woman might choose either to be covered or to be exposed, just as she might choose to marry; for marriage itself is neither compelled nor prohibited. Truth was content—

[Note: [Col. 0892C] Some previously read *paucis* wrongly; read *pacisci cum*, “to make terms with.”]

to make terms with custom, so that silently, under the name of custom, it might enjoy its own rights at least in part.

But since recognition of the truth had begun to advance, so that through permission for both practices the superiority of the better part might become evident, that adversary of good things—and much more of good institutions—

[Note: [Col. 0891D] **That adversary of good things, and much more of institutions.** That is: but especially of good institutions and good disciplines. RIG.]

immediately did his work. The virgins of men canvass men against the virgins of God, their foreheads wholly bare and their rash audacity aroused.

[Note: [Col. 0892C] “Into audacity rashly,” Seml.]

And virgins are put on display who can request something from men—to say nothing of such a deed as this: that their rivals, all the freer in proportion as they are handmaids of Christ alone, should be surrendered to them.

“We are scandalized,” they say, “because some women walk differently from others”; and they prefer to be scandalized rather than challenged to do better. A scandal, unless I am mistaken, is an example not of a good thing but of an evil one, which builds a person up toward sin. Good things scandalize no one except an evil mind. If modesty, shamefastness, and disdain for glory—which seeks to please God alone—are good, let those who are scandalized by such goodness acknowledge their own evil.

What if the incontinent were also to say that they were scandalized by the continent? Must continence be revoked? And lest women married many times be scandalized, must monogamy be rejected?

[Note: [Col. 0891D] **And lest women married many times be scandalized.** This is certainly how the text must be read, not as it is found written and printed everywhere: “And lest many be scandalized by us.” RIG.]

Why do they not complain instead that the insolence and shamelessness of ostentatious virginity are a scandal to them?

[Note: [Col. 0892C] **Of ostentatious virginity.** He censures the ostentatious virgin as one who lives not for herself but for the public and for spectators, as Seneca puts it near the end of letter 94. For, he says, it is characteristic of vice, not virtue, to be displayed and stared at. [Col. 0892D] Thus ostentatious virginity is wholly vicious. LAC.]

On account of heads of this kind, then—heads put on display in the marketplace—are holy virgins to be dragged into the church, blushing because they are recognized in public, trembling because they are uncovered, summoned—

[Note: [Col. 0892D] **Trembling because they are uncovered.** Fear befits virgins, who ought to tremble at every cast of an eye; but when they are stripped bare, the Author says, they are terrified as though summoned to rape. In this discipline, as in other matters, the ancient Church was then illustrious. LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0892C] “Summoned” [*arcessitae*], others; Jun.]

as though to rape? For they are no less unwilling to suffer this.

[Note: [Col. 0892D] **For they are no less unwilling to suffer this.** “This” means to be exposed publicly and to have the head uncovered. But I prefer the reading of certain copies, “For they are no less willing to suffer even this,” so that “this” refers to rape, which is the more immediate reference. RIG.]

Every public exposure of a good virgin is an experience of rape. And yet to suffer violence in the flesh is the lesser thing, because it comes from the function of nature. But when the spirit itself is violated in a virgin, once her veil has been removed she has learned to lose what the veil had been guarding.

O sacrilegious hands—

[Note: [Col. 0892D] **O sacrilegious hands!** These virgins had put on a form of dress consecrated to God, and to touch it was the greatest sacrilege. Dionysius Exiguus, in the *Life of Pachomius*, says that this habit was consecrated and that Pachomius, on receiving him, consecrated him with the monastic habit. And Jerome writes to Marcella: “Having put on a fuller tunic, she suddenly consecrated herself to the Lord.” LAC.]

that could strip away a form of dress consecrated to God!

[Note: [Col. 0893C] **A form of dress consecrated to God.** Some of the virgins had placed a veil upon their heads, while others had remained with their heads free and uncovered. Tertullian calls the latter “virgins of men” and the former “virgins of God.” But the virgins with uncovered heads, offended by that distinction marking veiled virginity, lodged a complaint about scandal and demanded that virgins be forbidden to wear a veil, lest the veiled women should wear something that made the unveiled women objects of unfavorable comparison. Perhaps the bishop had granted the request. Tertullian became indignant with him as with a sacrilegious person. “What worse thing,” he says, “would any persecutor have done? You have stripped the girl bare from the head, and now she is no longer a virgin in her own possession as a whole.” RIG.]

What worse thing—

[Note: [Col. 0893C] “Worse” [*prius*], Fran., Rig., Seml.]

would any persecutor have done, if he had learned that the virgin had chosen this for herself? You have stripped the girl bare from the head—

[Note: [Col. 0893D] **You have stripped the girl bare from the head.** He is indignant, as though about to add, “down to her lowest ankles.” RIG.]

and now she is no longer wholly a virgin in her own possession: she has been made another person.

[Note: [Col. 0893D] **And now she is no longer wholly a virgin in her own possession.** For she blushes throughout her entire body, as though deprived of her virginity by the wanton eyes of the spectators. RIG.]

Rise up, therefore, Truth; rise up and, as it were, burst forth from your patience. I do not want you to defend any custom, for now even that custom—

[Note: [Col. 0893C] Seml. adds “custom.”]

under which you used to enjoy your own rights is being erased.

[Note: [Col. 0893C] “Is being conquered,” Seml., Leop.]

Show that you are the one who veils virgins.

[Note: [Col. 0893C] Thus Wouwer and Rigalt, and better, in Seml.’s judgment; Seml. reads “who veils” in the singular.]

Interpret your own Scriptures, which custom does not know. For if it had known them, it would never have existed.

## CHAPTER IV

But because it is also customary to argue from the Scriptures against the truth, the objection is immediately raised against us that the Apostle made no mention of virgins when he laid down the rule concerning the veil, but named women only. If he had wished virgins also to be covered, he would have pronounced on virgins by name—

[Note: [Col. 0893C] “By name,” Jun.]

along with women, just as, our opponent says, in the passage where he treats of marriage he also declares what is to be observed concerning virgins. Accordingly, virgins are not contained within the law of veiling the head, since they are not named in that law; indeed, from this they are shown to be unveiled—

[Note: [Col. 0893C] Fran. adds “not,” but Jun. removes the negation. Seml.: “by this they are veiled.”]

because those who are not even named are not commanded.

But we turn the same argument back upon them. For he who knew how elsewhere to mention both classes—

[Note: [Col. 0894C] “He knew how to mention others,” the manuscript of Wouwer and Rig.]

I mean virgin and woman, that is, non-virgin—for the sake of making a distinction, shows, in those passages in which he does not name the virgin and makes no distinction, that they share the same condition. Otherwise he could have established a difference here too between virgin and woman, just as elsewhere [Col. 0893C] he says: “The woman and the virgin are divided.”

Therefore, by not dividing those whom he did not divide, he rendered them mutually inclusive.

[Note: [Col. 0893D] **He rendered them mutually inclusive** (*inalteravit*). I think this is correct, although the manuscripts have *in altera iniit*. *Inalteravit* means that he put one within the other, joined them, and merged them, so that both are now one and mutually contain each other. A little later he himself says: “He did not separate her from the woman, and by not separating her he joined her to the one from whom he did not separate her.” RIG.

**He rendered them mutually inclusive.** The Author uses this in the sense of “did not alter.” Likewise elsewhere he uses *incriminari* in the sense of “not to accuse.” PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0894C] Fran.: *In altera ivit*; others: *iniit*.]

Yet the fact that woman and virgin are divided in that other passage [Col. 0894A] will not support the same division here as well, as certain people wish.

[Note: [Col. 0894C] “Certain” [*quidem*], Fran.]

For how many things said elsewhere have no force in a place where they were not said, unless the same ground exists there as elsewhere, so that a single statement may suffice? But the reason for the distinction between virgin and woman there is entirely separate from the present case.

“The woman and the virgin are divided,” he says (1 Cor. 7:32). Why? Because the unmarried woman—that is, the virgin—thinks about the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in both body and spirit. But the married woman—that is, the non-virgin—thinks about how she may please her husband. This is the interpretation of that distinction. It has no place in the present chapter, in which nothing is pronounced either about marriage or about the mind and thought of woman and virgin—

[Note: [Col. 0894C] **Of woman and virgin.** They commonly distinguish the terms so that a *woman* is properly one who has married and has children, while a *virgin* is intact and truly uncorrupted. Jerome speaks according to this distinction when expounding the passage of Hosea, “I will betroth you to myself,” and so forth. Yet this distinction is so far from being invariable that a virgin is, rather, also understood under the designation “woman,” as Tertullian says here and will prove below, and so forth. LAC.]

[Note: [Col. 0894C] “Womanly,” Seml.]

but about covering the head. Since the Holy Spirit wished there to be no difference in this matter, by the single designation “woman” [Col. 0894B] he intended the virgin also to be understood. By not naming her separately—

[Note: [Col. 0894D] **By naming her separately.** Take note of this expression, which overturns the grammarians’ distinction between proper and common nouns. For here Tertullian uses “to name properly” of the noun that they call common or appellative. RIG.]

he did not separate her from the woman; and by not separating her, he joined her to the one from whom he did not separate her.

Is it something new, then, to use a principal term while nevertheless understanding the remaining classes within that term, where there is no necessity to distinguish the whole category item by item? A natural economy of expression is both pleasing and necessary, since a prolix discourse—

[Note: [Col. 0894D] **A prolix discourse.** That is, diffuse. You may also find this word in the books *Against Marcion*, and likewise in *On the Dress of Women*: “But to occupy the other parts of the body with the elaborate follies of pomp and luxury.” RHEN.]

is burdensome and futile. Thus we are content with general terms that comprise within themselves the meaning of particular terms.

Let us proceed, then, to the term itself. “Female” (*foemina*) is the natural designation; “woman” (*mulier*) is the general form of the natural designation.

[Note: [Col. 0894D] **The natural designation, etc.** That “woman” is a general designation even among the jurists is clear from Ulpian, in the law beginning *Quaeritur*, *Digest*, *On the Aedilician Edict*, where even one who has not known a man is called a woman. PAM.]

The general term includes the particular as well: virgin, married woman, widow, and however many additional designations of age there may be. The particular, therefore, is subordinated to the general, because the general is prior; the subsequent to the antecedent—

[Note: [Col. 0894C] Thus the manuscript of Wouwer; Paris and Venice read *subcessivum*.]

and the partial to the universal. It is understood—

[Note: [Col. 0894C] “Will be understood,” Seml.]

within that to which it is subordinated, and is signified within it because it is contained within it. Thus neither hand nor foot nor any limb requires separate mention when the body has been named. If you say “the world,” heaven will be there also, together with the things within it—the sun, moon, constellations, stars, earth, and seas, the entire inventory of the elements. You have named everything when you have named that which consists of everything. So too, by naming “woman,” he named whatever belongs to woman.

## CHAPTER V

But since they use the designation “woman” in such a way that they do not think it applicable to anyone except her who has experienced a man, we must prove that the proper scope of this designation pertains to the sex itself, not to a particular status within the sex, and that virgins too are commonly included under it.

[Note: [Col. 0895D] **That virgins too are commonly included.** They are comprehended under the common designation “woman.” RIG.]

When this second kind of human being was made by God [Col. 0895B] as a help for the man (Gen. 2:18), that female was immediately called “woman,” while she was still blessed, still worthy of paradise, and still a virgin.

[Note: [Col. 0895D] **While she was still blessed, etc.** Tertullian proves his position in this way; Ambrose, in *On the Institution of a Virgin*, chapter 5, insisted upon the same point: “Finally, virginity first received this designation, namely the designation ‘woman.’ For when God had taken one of Adam’s ribs and filled up the flesh in its place, he built it, Scripture says, into a woman. Certainly she had not yet known a man, and yet she was already called a woman.” LAC.]

“She shall be called woman,” he says (Gen. 2:23). You therefore have a designation that, I will not merely say, is shared with the virgin, but is properly hers, since it was the virgin who received it at the beginning.

But certain ingenious persons wish the words “she shall be called woman” to have been spoken about the future, as though she would become a woman when she surrendered her virginity, because Scripture also adds: “Therefore—

[Note: [Col. 0895C] Others add “it adds.”]

a man shall leave father and mother and shall be joined fast to his woman, and the two shall be in one flesh.”

[Note: [Col. 0895D] **He shall be joined fast to his woman.** He translated literally from the Greek, καὶ προσκολληθήσεται τῇ γυναικὶ αὐτοῦ, “and he shall be joined fast to his woman,” using a compound derived from κόλλη, which means “glue.” PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0895C] “Into one flesh,” Fran.]

Let them first show where this clever subtlety of theirs resides. If she was called “woman” with reference to the future, what designation did she receive in the meantime? For she could not have existed without a designation for her present condition. Besides, what sense does it make for her to be designated by the name by which she would be called in the future, while receiving no designation at all in the present?

Adam assigned names to all the animals, and to none—

[Note: [Col. 0896C] “No one,” wrongly in the Venice edition.]

on the basis of a future condition, but according to its present formation. Whatever condition each was to serve, it was called what God had intended from the beginning. What, then, was she called at that time?

In fact, whenever she is named in Scripture, she is called “woman” before she is married, and never “virgin” while she is a virgin. At that time this alone was her designation, and no statement had yet been made—

[Note: [Col. 0895D] **It was spoken prophetically.** For prophets are accustomed to speak of future things as though they were present. The expression that follows, “according to the prophetic mode,” has the same meaning; likewise, “let no one interpret the designation as belonging to the prophecy.” RHEN.]

in the prophetic mode. For when Scripture relates that the two were naked, Adam and his woman—

[Note: [Col. 0895D] **That the two were naked, Adam, etc.** The words of the common Latin interpreter in Genesis chapter 2 are: “Now each of them was naked, namely Adam and his wife.” But Tertullian is consistent in his translation, for where the Greek has γυνή he always renders it “woman,” unlike the interpreter, who renders it now “woman,” now “wife.” LAC.]

this does not have the character of a statement about the future, as though Scripture called her “his woman” in anticipation of her becoming his wife. Rather, even while unmarried she was his woman, since she came from his substance: “This,” he says, “is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh; she shall be called woman.”

[Note: [Col. 0896D] **Flesh from my flesh; she shall be called woman.** Here he omitted the Greek word αὕτη, “this woman,” and therefore joined the two clauses without punctuation, although the Greek and Latin read differently: “This woman shall be called.” PAM.]

Hence, through the unspoken consciousness of nature, the soul’s own divinity brought it into ordinary speech, though human beings were unaware of it—just as we shall elsewhere be able to show that many other things are customarily done and said from Scripture—so that we call our wives “women.” Although we do speak certain things improperly, even the Greeks, who more commonly use the term for “woman” to mean “wife,” have other terms proper to a wife.

[Note: [Col. 0896D] **They have other terms proper to a wife.** Pertinent here above all is the fact that in Plato, book IX, a wife is called γυνὴ γαμετή, “a wedded woman,” as likewise in Xenophon’s *Oeconomicus*. Then there are these synonyms: σύγγαμος, “spouse”; ἄλοχος, “bedfellow”; ἄκοιτις, “consort”; and παράκοιτις, “one who lies beside.” PAM.]

But I prefer to ascribe this usage to the testimony of Scripture. For where two are made into one flesh [Col. 0896B] through the bond of marriage—

[Note: [Col. 0896D] **The bond of marriage.** In the poet, Dido calls it the nuptial bond:

> That I would wish to unite myself to anyone in the bond of marriage,

*Aeneid*, book IV. Gregory of Nyssa, *On Virginity*, chapter 3, calls marriage ἄρκυα, “nets,” and describes it as ἀφύκτοις πάγαις ἐγκρατηθῆναι, that is, “to be caught in inescapable snares.” LE PR.]

she who is flesh from flesh and bone from bones is called, according to her origin, his woman; from his substance she begins to be reckoned as having become his wife. Thus “woman” is not by nature the designation of a wife—

[Note: [Col. 0896C] “Thus ‘woman’ is by nature the designation of a wife, and ‘wife’ by condition,” Latin edition.]

but “wife” is by condition the designation of a woman. Finally, someone can be called a woman without being a wife, but a wife cannot be called someone who is not a woman, because neither can she be one.

Once, therefore, the designation of the new female—namely “woman”—had been established, and what had come first had been explained, that is, once the designation had been assigned, Scripture then turned to the prophetic mode and said: “Because of this woman a man shall leave father and mother.” The designation is so completely separate from the prophecy, just as it is also separate from the person herself, that he certainly did not speak about Eve herself, but about those future females whom he had designated in the womb of the female race. Otherwise, Adam was not going to leave father and mother, whom he did not have, because of Eve.

Therefore the prophetic statement does not pertain to Eve, because it does not pertain to Adam either. It was a prediction concerning the condition of husbands, who were to leave their parents on account of a woman. This could not apply to Eve, because it could not apply to Adam. If this is so, it is evident that she was not called “woman” on account of a future condition that did not pertain to her.

In addition, he himself gave the reason for this designation. For after he had said, “She shall be called [Col. 0897A] woman,” he added—

[Note: [Col. 0897C] Rig., following Wouwer, inserted the word from a manuscript; Seml. deleted it after Rhen.]

“because she was taken from her own man”—

[Note: [Col. 0897C] Jun. inserts “he says.”]

while he too was still a virgin. But we shall also discuss the designation “man” in its proper place.

Let no one, therefore, interpret as belonging to the prophecy a designation derived from another meaning, especially since it is evident where she received a designation referring to the future: namely, where she is called Eve by a personal designation, because the natural designation had preceded it. For if Eve is the mother of the living, there she is indeed named from the future; there she is indeed announced as a wife and not a virgin. This will be the designation of one who is to marry, since a mother comes from one who has married.

Thus it is also demonstrated here that she was not then called “woman” with reference to the future, since she was subsequently to receive a designation belonging to her future condition. Enough has been said in answer to this part.

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0897B] Let us now see whether the Apostle too observes—

[Note: [Col. 0897C] “Observes,” Seml.]

the pattern of this designation in accordance with Genesis, assigning it to the sex by calling the Virgin Mary a “woman,” just as Genesis calls Eve a woman.

[Note: [Col. 0897C] **Calling the Virgin Mary a woman.** Since he adduces only two passages for this, one from Luke 1 and the other from Galatians 4, one may add John 2: “Woman, what have I to do with you?” Likewise John 19:26: “Woman, behold your son.” PAM.]

For in writing to the Galatians he says: “God sent his Son, made from a woman” (Gal. 4:4).

[Note: [Col. 0897D] **Made from a woman.** To Pamelius’s references add these words of Ulpian, *Digest*, *On the Aedilician Edict*: “It is certain that what is bequeathed to women is also owed to virgins.” LAC.]

It is, of course, agreed that she was a virgin, although Ebion resists this. I recognize that the angel Gabriel was sent to a virgin; but when he blesses her, he ranks her among women, not among virgins: “Blessed are you among women” (Luke 1:28).

[Note: [Col. 0897D] **Blessed are you among women.** This rendering is more explicit than the Vulgate’s “among women” (*in mulieribus*), although blessed Jerome’s translator also has “among” in the same chapter, in Elizabeth’s blessing. PAM.]

The angel too knew that even a virgin is called a woman. But someone has fancied that he ingeniously answered both these passages as follows: since Mary was betrothed, she was therefore called a woman by both the angel and the Apostle, for a betrothed woman is in a certain sense married. Yet there is sufficient difference between “in a certain sense” and the reality, at least in the present passage; elsewhere, indeed, it may properly be understood in that way. Here, however, they called Mary a woman not as though she were already married, but simply as a female—even if she had not been betrothed—since she had been so called from the beginning. For that from which the pattern descends must establish the precedent.

As regards the present chapter, if a betrothed woman is here equated with a married woman, so that Mary was called a woman not because she was female but because she was married, then Christ was not born of a virgin, because he was born of a betrothed woman who, by that designation, had ceased to be a virgin. But if he was born of a virgin, although of one who was betrothed yet remained intact, acknowledge that even a virgin, even an intact virgin, is called a woman.

Here certainly nothing can appear to have been said prophetically, as though the Apostle, by saying “made from a woman,” had named her a future woman, that is, a married woman. For he could not have meant the woman she would become afterward, from whom Christ was not to be born—that is, a woman who had experienced a man—but the woman who then existed, who was a virgin and was called a woman by virtue of the proper scope of this designation, according to the pattern established at the beginning—a scope vindicated for the virgin [Col. 0898B] and thus for the whole class of women.

[Note: [Col. 0898C] Seml. reads “after.”]

[Note: [Col. 0897D] **And thus vindicated for the whole class of women.** That is, claimed and established for them. RIG.]

## CHAPTER VII
Let us now turn [Note: [Col. 0898C] “Let us turn,” Semler.] to reviewing the actual arguments by which the Apostle teaches that a woman ought to be veiled, and ask whether the same arguments [Note: [Col. 0898C] “The same argument,” Semler.] also apply to virgins. Thus, from this consideration too, the shared application of the term [Note: [Col. 0898C] “By the term,” Semler.] [Note: [Col. 0898C] “Sharing,” Semler.] to virgins and non-virgins may be established, since the same reasons for veiling are found in both classes.

If the man is the head of the woman, he is surely also the head of the virgin, from whom comes the woman who has married—unless, that is, a virgin is some monstrous third kind, with a head of her own. If it is disgraceful for a woman to be shaved or shorn (1 Cor. 11:5), it is surely so for a virgin as well. Accordingly, let the age that emulates God see to it [Note: [Col. 0897D] “The age that emulates God.” He means the Christian age. For “emulator” and “to emulate” are generally taken by the Author in a favorable sense, meaning “imitator” and “to imitate.” PAM.—“Emulator of God.” The Author here condemns the custom of the pagans, who cut the hair of girls, and therefore calls the pagan age an emulator of God: that is, because God had permitted young men to have their hair cut, they wished women also to have theirs cut. No one doubts, however, that girls ought to be unshorn and young men shorn. Canon 17 of the Council of Gangra seems to me worthy of attention; its words are: εἴ τις γυναικῶν διὰ νομιζομένην ἄσκησιν ἀποκείροιτο τὰς κόμας, ἃς ἔδωκεν ὁ θεὸς εἰς ὑπόμνησιν τῆς ὑποταγῆς, ὡς ἀναλύουσα τὸ πρόσταγμα τῆς ὑποταγῆς, ἀνάθεμα ἔστω: “If any woman, thinking thereby to adopt a stricter discipline, cuts off the hair that God gave as a reminder of subjection, as though dissolving the ordinance of subjection, let her be anathema.” This is repeated in *Decretum*, distinction 30, *Quaecumque*. The pursuit of ornaments in women was, of course, condemned, as was every kind of cosmetic artifice: *De consecratione*, distinction 5, *Fucare*, and 33, question 5, *Mulier*. LE PR.] if it so falsely claims that cut hair is becoming to a virgin [Col. 0898C] [Note: [Col. 0898D] “If it so falsely claims that cut hair is becoming to a virgin.” All editions read thus, as does the Dijon manuscript. But the sense of the words is difficult unless they are explained in this way: “Let the age see to it,” he says, “if it lies so greatly in favor of propriety”—that is, if it so perversely favors what is becoming as to assert falsely that cut hair is becoming to a virgin, when it is instead a dishonor. Latinius sought another sense by removing one letter: *Si ita virgini caesum capillum decori metitur*, “If it thus measures cut hair for a virgin by the standard of propriety”; the sense would then be: “Let the age see to it if it assigns to cut hair in a virgin the same measure of propriety as to long hair in a boy.” This conjecture is not displeasing. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0898C] *Metitur*, “measures,” Latinius; Rigault also approves.] just as it is permitted to a boy [Note: [Col. 0898D] “Just as it is also permitted to a boy.” Latinius writes *promissum*, “granted”; but there is no need, since each word has the same meaning. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0898C] *Promissum*, “granted,” Latinius.]. Therefore, one for whom it is equally unbecoming to be shaved or shorn is equally required to be covered.

If the woman is the glory [Col. 0899A] of the man, how much more is the virgin, who is also a glory to herself! If woman is from man and for man, that rib of Adam was first a virgin. If a woman must have authority upon her head [Note: [Col. 0899C] “If a woman must have authority upon her head.” [Col. 0899D] That is, the sign of the authority to which God subjected woman. The sign of that authority is the covering of the head. RIG.], much more justly must a virgin have it, since the matter under discussion pertains to her.

For if it is “because of the angels” (1 Cor. 11:8, 10)—namely, those whom we read to have fallen from God and heaven through lust for women [Note: [Col. 0899D] “Because of the angels.” This again pertains to Tertullian’s error, of which he has made mention above in the books *On Idolatry*, *On the Apparel of Women*, and *On the Dress of Women*. St Ambrose, however, interprets the angels as bishops, in accordance with the Apocalypse of St John the Apostle. PAM.]—who can presume that angels such as these desired bodies already defiled and the leavings of human lust, rather than having burned with passion for virgins, whose bloom refuses even human lust? [Note: [Col. 0899D] “Whose bloom refuses even human lust.” That is, “rejects”; just as elsewhere he says “to expose a garment” for “to take it off.” A virgin refuses lust when she rejoices in the bloom of her virginity and does not wish it to be plucked, like that untouched and inviolate flower of Catullus:

> Unknown to the flock, bruised by no plough,  
> Which no slender fingernail has yet plucked and deflowered, etc.

Tertullian says that it is credible that the angels burned for such girls rather than for bodies already defiled. RIG.]

For Scripture also presents the matter in this way: “And it came to pass,” it says, “when men began to become numerous upon the earth, and daughters were born to them, that the sons of God, seeing that the daughters of men were beautiful, took wives for themselves from among all [Col. 0899B] whom they chose.” Here the Greek term for women has the sense of “wives,” because marriage is being mentioned. When, therefore, it says “the daughters of men,” it plainly indicates virgins who were still reckoned as belonging to their parents. Married women, after all, are named after their husbands; Scripture could instead have said “the wives of men.” Likewise, it does not call the angels adulterers but husbands, since they took the unmarried daughters of men, whom it had said above had been born. Thus too, by saying above that they had been born, it signified virgins. [Note: [Col. 0899C] “Signifying.” “Born above”: but here François Junius and Rigault restore the whole passage thus: “When, therefore, it says ‘the daughters of men,’ likewise it names the angels not adulterers but husbands, since they took the unmarried daughters of men, whom it had said above were born; thus too, by saying above that they were born, it signified virgins. But here, married to angels …”] But here, once married to angels, they became something else—I know not what—than those who were born, and thereafter married.

Therefore so dangerous a face, which hurled stumbling blocks all the way to heaven, must be overshadowed [Note: [Col. 0899D] “Therefore it must be overshadowed,” etc. That is, veiled. For the unveiled face of a virgin [Col. 0900C] could offer beauty as an occasion of sin; for this reason Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, book III, chapter 2, calls beauty μοιχικὸν κάλλος, “beauty that incites adultery.” LE PR.], so that, when she stands before God—to whom she is answerable for the banishment of the angels—she may also blush before the other angels, and may restrain that wicked former freedom of her head, which must now no longer be presented even to the eyes of men [Col. 0899C].

But even if those angels had desired women already defiled, women should all the more have been veiled because of the angels, inasmuch as the angels could all the more have sinned because of virgins. Moreover, if the Apostle adds the precedent of nature [Note: [Col. 0900D] “The Apostle adds the precedent of nature.” Let no inattentive person suppose that Septimius contradicts St Paul. For although abundant hair is, as it were, a natural ornament of woman, nevertheless—even if women are shorn (although, as we have shown elsewhere, there was a contrary custom)—women must always be veiled after their hair has been cut, so that the veil takes the place of the hair. This is customarily done among nuns even in our own times. LE PR.], namely, that an abundance of hair is a woman’s honor, because her hair is given as a covering [Col. 0900A], surely this is preeminently the distinction of virgins. Their very arrangement of the hair [Note: [Col. 0900C] “Wherefore,” Semler.] [Note: [Col. 0900C] “Itself,” the manuscripts, Wouwer and Rigault.] is properly of such a kind that, gathered up upon the crown, it covers the very citadel of the head with a circuit of tresses.

## CHAPTER VIII

The opposites of all these considerations assuredly have the effect that a man must not veil his head: namely, because he has not naturally acquired an ambitious profusion of hair; because it is not disgraceful for him to be shaved or shorn; because the angels did not go astray on his account; because he is the glory and image of God; and because Christ is his head (1 Cor. 11:2, 7).

Accordingly, since the Apostle discusses man and woman—why she ought to be veiled, but he ought not—it is apparent why he also remained silent about the virgin: namely, because by the same reasoning he allowed the virgin to be understood under “woman” [Note: [Col. 0900C] “Woman,” Semler.] by which he also did not name the boy, since the boy was to be reckoned under “man” [Col. 0900B]. He encompassed the entire order of each sex under their proper terms, “woman” and “man.”

Thus Adam, even [Note: [Col. 0900C] Semler deletes “even.”] while still sexually intact, is called “man” in Genesis: “She shall be called woman,” he says, “because she was taken from her man” (Gen. 2:23). Thus Adam was a man before marital intercourse, just as Eve was a woman. On both sides the Apostle has pronounced sufficiently upon the entire class of each sex, both briefly and fully, by so comprehensive a definition: “Every woman,” he says (1 Cor. 11:5). What is “every” unless every kind, every rank, every condition, every dignity, every age? For “every” denotes a whole, complete and lacking no part of itself. A virgin, moreover, is a part of woman.

Likewise, concerning a man’s not being veiled, he says, “Every man” (1 Cor. 11:4). [Col. 0900C] See: two distinct terms, “man” and “woman,” and “every” applies to each. There are two laws corresponding to one another: on the one side, veiling; on the other, uncovering. Therefore, if, because “every man” was said, the term “man” is common even to one who is not yet a man—an unbearded male [Note: [Col. 0900D] “An unbearded male.” I have seen it observed by others, before we applied our hand to these brief annotations, that *investis* means “prepubescent,” and *vesticeps* “pubescent.” Lucretius, book V, should perhaps be understood in that sense:

> To become pubescent with the soft garment of puberty.]—then, since the term is common according to nature, the law of not being veiled is also common to him who, according to discipline, is a virgin among males [Col. 0901A]. Why, then, should it not likewise have been settled beforehand that every virgin woman is included under the term “woman” by sharing the name, so that she is also included by sharing the law? [Note: [Col. 0901C] “Why should it not have been settled beforehand,” etc. He continues in that manner of arguing which he employs throughout this work: the term “woman” is used indiscriminately of a virgin and of one joined to a husband. LE PR.]

If a virgin is not a woman, neither is an unbearded boy a man. If a virgin is not covered because she is not a woman, let the unbearded boy be covered because he is not a man. Let the same allowance be made for the same virginity. Just as female virgins are not compelled to be veiled, so boys should not be commanded to be unveiled.

Why do we acknowledge the Apostle’s definition as absolute on one side [Note: [Col. 0901C] “The Apostle’s definition on one side.” Why does the heretic adhere to one part of that command rather than the other? For when Paul wrote “every woman,” he included females of every kind, condition, and age. LE PR.] [Note: [Col. 0901C] *Diffinitionem*, Semler.] with regard to every man, without reconsidering [Note: [Col. 0901C] *Detractamus*, Semler.] why he did not also name the boy, yet on the other side violate the equally absolute definition concerning every woman? “If anyone,” he says, “is contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God” (1 Cor. 11:16). He shows that there had been some dispute [Col. 0901B] concerning this class; to extinguish it he employed a complete brevity: not naming the virgin, to show that there was no room for doubt about her being veiled, and naming “every woman,” when he might have named the virgin. The Corinthians themselves understood it in this way. Indeed, to this day the Corinthians veil their virgins; by approving what they learned, they show what the Apostles taught [Note: [Col. 0901C] “They approve,” Semler.].

## CHAPTER IX

Let us now see whether, just as we have shown that the arguments from nature and causation also apply to a virgin, the prescriptions of ecclesiastical discipline concerning a woman likewise extend [Note: [Col. 0901C] *Spectant*, “extend,” Semler and Leopold; Junius perhaps reads *speciant*, “refer.”] to a virgin.

A woman is not permitted to speak [Col. 0902A] in church (1 Cor. 14:34; 1 Tim. 2:12), nor to teach, baptize, [Note: [Col. 0901C] “A woman is not permitted to speak in church.” It was accepted in Roman custom that women should not exercise public offices—not because they lack judgment, but lest they involve themselves in masculine duties contrary to the modesty proper to their sex. For that reason the Church too judged that they should be excluded [Col. 0901D] from masculine functions. For the decree of the Apostle contains the words: “I do not permit women to speak in church.” Since this expression is general, it embraces every masculine function, including priestly ones. A woman is not permitted to speak in church—that is, neither to inquire nor to dispute, for these are masculine functions and are granted only to men. Nor may she teach, baptize, or offer, since these are indeed the duties of a priest, president, or overseer of a church. The Author of the *Questions from the Old Testament*, question 45, volume IV of the works of Augustine, says that it is absurd to assert that it was granted to woman that she, like man, should be the image of God by right of dominion: “For how can it be said of woman that she is the image of God, when it is agreed that she is subject to the dominion of man and possesses no authority? For she can neither teach, nor be a witness, nor give a pledge, nor judge; much less can she command!” In short, public and masculine functions are not permitted to a woman, and priestly functions much less. RIG.] nor to offer, [Note: [Col. 0901D] “Nor to offer.” Following Rhenanus, Pamelius explains this [Col. 0902C] as “to sacrifice,” which I would scarcely admit. For what is meant by an interpretation according to which a woman is not permitted to celebrate Mass? Who ever permitted it? “To offer” should be understood of vows and prayers. LE PR.] nor to claim for herself a share in any masculine function, much less [Note: [Col. 0902C] Semler reads *ne duo sacerdotalis officii*; the reading is uncertain.] in priestly office. Let us ask whether any of these things is permitted to a virgin.

If it is not permitted to a virgin [Note: [Col. 0902C] “But if it is not permitted to a virgin,” Semler.], but in every matter she is subjected under the same condition, and the necessity of humility is assigned to her together with woman, whence shall this one thing be permitted to her which is not permitted to any female? What prerogative against her own condition does she deserve merely because she is a virgin and has resolved to sanctify her flesh? [Note: [Col. 0902C] “To sanctify her flesh.” Below: “to consecrate nature itself.” These words are found in Isidore, but are most absurdly twisted into another sense in book II of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. RIG.]

Is an exemption from the veil therefore granted her, so that she may enter the church as a conspicuous and distinguished person and display the honor of sanctity in the freedom of her head? [Note: [Col. 0902C] “So that she may display the honor of sanctity in the freedom of her head?” Those who sought human glory from virginity repeatedly claimed that the exemption from the veil had rightly been granted to them and that a prerogative granted to sanctity ought not to bring them disadvantage or resentment.
