For in this way, they said, being conspicuous and distinguished by that honor when they entered the church, they would encourage [Col. 0902D] the others toward the same work of sanctifying the flesh. But Tertullian contends that such an honor is inappropriate for them. He refutes it by proposing other, indeed greater, honors, but ones even more inappropriate for a virgin: “She could,” he says, “have been honored more worthily by some prerogative of masculine rank or office.” It is evident from what precedes that these words are spoken in mockery: “A woman is not permitted to claim for herself a share in any masculine function, much less in priestly office.” Likewise from what follows: “Thus nothing by way of position has been permitted to a virgin as an honor, nor anything by way of insignia.”—“That she may display the honor of sanctity.” Isidore reads: “the honor of a sanctified body.” RIG.] She could have been honored more worthily by some prerogative of masculine rank or office.

Indeed, I know that somewhere a virgin less than twenty years old [Col. 0902B] was placed in the order of widowhood. [Note: [Col. 0902D] “Placed in widowhood.” Namely, by the bishop; he says “in widowhood” just as one says “in the diaconate.” From this it is gathered that at that time there was in the Christian Church an order or dignity of widows. Thus, in book I *To His Wife*, he does not permit a widow to be chosen into the order unless she has been the wife of one man. Later the Councils of Orange I and Epaon resolved that no widows at all should be ordained. RIG.] If the bishop owed her some relief, he could surely have provided it in another way while preserving respect for discipline, lest such a prodigy—not to say a monstrosity—should now be marked out in the Church: a virgin widow, made all the more portentous because, precisely as a widow, she does not cover her head. She denies herself in both respects: both as a virgin who is reckoned a widow and as a widow who is called a virgin. Yet she sits there uncovered [Note: [Col. 0902C] “Covered,” Semler; Latinius perhaps reads *non texta*, “not covered.”] by the same authority by which she is a virgin.

For that seat, women are sometimes chosen only after sixty years of age (1 Tim. 5:9), and not merely women who have had one husband—that is, married women—but also mothers, and indeed women who have reared children. Thus, equipped by experience of every affection [Col. 0903A], they may readily know how to aid others with both counsel and consolation, and may also have passed through all those things by which a woman can be tested. Thus nothing by way of position has been permitted to a virgin as an honor.

## CHAPTER X

Nor, similarly, has anything been permitted by way of insignia. Besides, it is quite inhuman if women, though in every respect subject to men, display an honor-bearing mark of their virginity by which [Note: [Col. 0903C] “As though,” Venice.] they are admired, gazed upon, and magnified by the brethren, while men—so many virgins, so many voluntary eunuchs—walk about with their good unseen, carrying nothing that would also make them illustrious.

They too will therefore have to claim certain insignia for themselves: either the feathers of the Garamantes, or the headbands of the barbarians, [Note: [Col. 0903C] Perhaps *ut*, “so that,” Junius.] [Note: [Col. 0903C] “The headbands of the barbarians.” In the ancient manuscripts and Rhenanus’ editions, *Scrobulos* or *Strubulos*. It should be read, as Salmasius advised, *Stropulos*. The ancient Latins called ribbons and bands *strupi*. The word is Greek, στρόφος and στρόφιον. From it come *stropi* and *stropiola*, or *strophiola* and *stropuli*. RIG.—“Stropuli.” I adhere to Rigault’s interpretation; add that *crobylos* could be read. The commentator on Thucydides, book I, says: κρώβυλος δ’ ἔστιν εἶδος πλέγματος τῶν τριχῶν ἀπὸ ἑτέρων εἰς ὀξὺ ἀπολῆγον, “A *crobylus* is a form of hair braided from either side and terminating in a point.” The *crobylus* was worn by men, the *corymbus* by women, and the *scorpius* by boys. LE PR.] [Note: [Col. 0903C] *Scropulos*, François; *strobulos*, Paris; Salmasius and Rigault read *stropulos*.], or the cicadas of the Athenians, [Note: [Col. 0903D] “The cicadas of the Athenians.” The Athenians, called τεττιγοφόροι, “cicada-wearers,” fastened their braided hair with a clasp shaped like a cicada. RIG.] or the twisted locks [Col. 0903B] of the Germans, [Note: [Col. 0903D] “The twisted locks of the Germans.” Their hair was twisted into a knot. Tacitus, *On the Customs of the Germans*: “It is a distinction of the nation to sweep the hair sideways and bind it in a knot.” RIG.] or the tattoos of the Britons; [Note: [Col. 0903D] “The tattoos of the Britons.” Herodian, book III, relates that the bodies of the Britons were punctured with various figures. Hence Claudian writes:

> And on the bloodless forms he reads the figures  
> marked by iron, as the painted man lies dying. RIG.]

or else the opposite should be done, and they should remain hidden in church with veiled heads.

We are certain that the Holy Spirit could more fittingly have endorsed some such thing for males, if he had endorsed it for women. For, besides the authority of their sex, males ought rather to have been honored in the name of continence itself: the more avid and ardent their sex is toward women, the more laborious their continence is because of its greater passion, and therefore the worthier of every display—if virginity derives its dignity from display.

Does not continence, moreover, take precedence over virginity, whether that of widowers or of those who by mutual consent have now renounced their common degradation? [Note: [Col. 0904C] “Their common degradation.” This belongs among Tertullian’s blemishes. He burned with so great a love of virginity and continence that in this passage—and below, chapter 2—he calls the lawful intercourse of husband and wife by that name. As an antidote, however, it may serve that in *On Modesty* he calls it “the intercourse of blessing.” PAM.] For virginity consists in grace, but continence in virtue. Not to desire what you have grown accustomed to desiring is a mighty contest. But what you have never known the pleasure of desiring [Col. 0903C], you will readily refrain from desiring, since you have no adversary—the desire for that pleasure. [Note: [Col. 0904D] “The enjoyment of desiring you have never known.” Those who explain this otherwise than of forbidden desire waste their oil and labor. It cannot be said of children, even though the children born of love are called “the rewards of Venus” by Anna, Dido’s sister, in the Latin poet, and δῶρ’ Ἀφροδίτης, “gifts of Aphrodite,” in Homer. LE PR.]

How, therefore, would God not more fittingly have endorsed some such distinction for men as an honor, either because the male is more akin to him—namely, as his image—or because he labors more? But if nothing is granted to the male [Col. 0904A], much less is it granted to the female.

## CHAPTER XI

But we shall now dispose of by an answer the point that we omitted above because of the discussion that followed, lest we break its coherence.

When we took our position upon the Apostle’s absolute definition—that “every woman” must be understood as including every age (1 Cor. 11:5)—it was open to reply on the other side that a virgin must therefore be covered from birth and from the first designation of her age. But this is not so. Rather, she must be covered from the time when she begins to understand herself, to enter the register of her own nature, to depart from the status of a virgin [Note: [Col. 0903C] “Virgin qualities,” François.], and to undergo that new experience which belongs to another age.

For Adam and Eve, the founders of the race (Gen. 2), went naked as long as they lacked understanding. But when they tasted of the tree of knowledge, the first thing they perceived was that they had cause to be ashamed. Each therefore [Note: [Col. 0904C] *Ita*, “thus,” Semler.] marked the understanding of his or her sex by a covering. Yet even if she must be veiled because of the angels, the law of the veil will undoubtedly begin to operate from that age at which the daughters of men could provoke desire for themselves and become capable of marriage. [Note: [Col. 0904D] “Become capable of marriage.” This expression frequently occurs in Tertullian concerning a virgin who is now mature and marriageable. Petronius, *Satyricon*: “at years eager for sexual experience.” LAC.]

For a virgin ceases to be such from the moment when she is capable of not being one. And therefore [Note: [Col. 0904D] “Among Israel.” Pamelius asks where this is written in the sacred Scriptures; Junius observes that it does not derive from the law of God, but only from Jewish custom founded upon natural law and with reference to what is said in Deuteronomy 22. LAC.] among Israel it is unlawful to give a girl to a man unless her maturity has been attested by blood: before this indication she is an unripe thing. Therefore, if she is a virgin only so long as she is unripe, she ceases to be regarded as a virgin when she is mature [Note: [Col. 0904C] “By nature,” Paris.], and is brought under the law as one who is no longer a virgin, just as she is brought under marriage.

Betrothed women, indeed, have the example of Rebecca (Gen. 24:64). While she was being conducted, still unknown, to a bridegroom still unknown to her, as soon as she recognized him as the man whom she had seen [Col. 0904C] [Note: [Col. 0904C] “Observed,” Rhenanus.] from afar, she did not await a struggle of right hands, [Note: [Col. 0904D] “She did not await a struggle of right hands.” That is, she did not wait. RIG.] an encounter of kisses, or an exchange [Note: [Col. 0904C] “Communion,” François.] of greeting. Instead, confessing what she felt—that is, that in spirit she was married—she denied herself to be a virgin by veiling herself there and then. O woman already formed by the discipline of Christ! For she showed that marriage, like fornication, is effected even by sight and intention. Except that some still veil Rebecca. [Note: [Col. 0905C] “Some still veil Rebecca.” That is, some still veil betrothed virgins, but by no means the others. Tertullian, however, contends that the others too must be veiled. RIG.]

As for the others—that is, those who are not betrothed—let the parents’ postponement, arising from poverty [Note: [Col. 0905B] Most editions read *viderint*, “let them see to it.”] [Note: [Col. 0905C] “From poverty.” That is, from slender means or fortune. For, as the satirist says:

> Those whose virtues are obstructed by straitened means at home  
> do not easily rise.

Poorer girls of this sort also find husbands with greater difficulty. RHEN.] or excessive scrupulousness, [Note: [Col. 0905D] “Or excessive scrupulousness.” That is, from the fastidiousness of parents whom no one pleases. RHEN.] see to that; and let the vow of continence itself see to it as well. [Note: [Col. 0905D] “The vow of continence.” This passage should be noted most carefully. Here an author of the greatest antiquity mentions the vow of continence, which believers were already accustomed to make at that time. LAC.] None of this concerns age as it runs through its own stages and pays the dues belonging to maturity. Another mother in secret—nature—and another father in concealment—time—have married their daughter according to their own laws.

Look at that virgin of yours, already married: married in soul by expectation and in flesh by transformation, [Note: [Col. 0905B] “Expectation, transformation,” Semler; Rigault reads *ex spectatione*, “by reason of expectation.”] for whom you are preparing a second husband. [Note: [Col. 0905D] “Look at that virgin of yours, already married.” “That virgin of yours,” he says, “is already married: married in soul by the expectation of a husband, married in flesh by the transformation of puberty.” She is married in flesh and soul, just as “in face and shoulders she is like a god.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0905D] “For whom you are preparing a second husband.” The sense is: your virgin, whom you still consider a virgin, has ceased to be one because of her age—not indeed corrupted by a man, but changed by age. Consequently, the husband to whom you give her will be her second. RHEN.] Her voice has already changed, her limbs are fully developed, her private parts are clothed everywhere, HIL [Gl. 11.5, 3.14.10, 5.12] [Note: [Col. 0905D] “And modesty is clothed everywhere.” Tertullian himself says in *On the Soul*: “The sex is more fully clothed.” RIG.] and the monthly periods pay their tribute. [Note: [Col. 0905D] “And the monthly periods pay their tribute.” So the Fulvio Orsini manuscript reads. But the Dijon manuscript and Rhenanus’ editions read “defend.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0905B] “Defend,” Semler. “Pay”: this conjecture of Ciacconius is confirmed as probable by the authority of the manuscript, according to Rigault.] Yet you deny that she is a woman whom you say undergoes the experiences of women [Col. 0905B]!

If intercourse with a man makes a woman, let them not be covered until after the actual consummation of marriage. Yet even among the pagans women are led to their husbands veiled. If, however, they are veiled at betrothal because they have been united to a male in both body and spirit by a kiss and the joining of right hands—through which they first unsealed the modesty of the spirit [Note: [Col. 0905C] “In spirit,” Semler.]—and by the mutual pledge of conscience through which they covenanted the whole experience of shame, [Note: [Col. 0906C] “Through which they covenanted the whole experience of shame.” He came close to saying: “They covenanted the entire shamelessness of the degradation of marriage!” RIG.] how much more will time veil them? Without time they cannot become betrothed, and, when time presses upon them, they cease to be virgins even without betrothal.

Even the pagans observe the authority of time, so as to render to each age its rights according to the law of nature. For they send females to conduct legal business from the age of twelve, but a male two years later [Col. 0906A], determining puberty by years, not by betrothal or marriage. A female is called *materfamilias*, “mother of a household,” though a virgin, and a male *paterfamilias*, “father of a household,” though still unbearded. We, however, do not observe even the things of nature [Note: [Col. 0906B] “According to natural principles,” Venice.], as though the God of nature were other than our God.

## CHAPTER XII

Acknowledge her as a woman; acknowledge her also as married, from the testimonies of both body and spirit which she undergoes in both conscience and flesh. These are the first tablets recording her natural betrothal and marriage. Place a veil upon her outwardly, since she has an inward covering. Let the upper parts also be covered in one whose lower parts are not naked.

Do you wish to know the authority possessed by age? Place side by side a girl prematurely violated but dressed as a woman, and one who, though advanced in maturity, remains in virginity and retains her own mode of dress: the former will more easily be denied to be a woman than the latter will be believed to be a virgin. So great is the credibility of age that it cannot even be obstructed by clothing [Col. 0906B].

What of the fact that these virgins of ours also acknowledge by their dress the change of age, and, as soon as they understand themselves to be women, are led out of the class of virgins? [Note: [Col. 0906B] “What of the fact that they already,” Junius.] [Note: [Col. 0906C] “Are led out of the virgins.” They lead themselves out of the register of virgins. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0906B] “Are led out,” others.] Beginning with the head itself, they lay aside what they formerly were: they alter their hair [Note: [Col. 0906C] “They alter their hair.” I would not venture to affirm that this means the same as twisting the hair. For when I read in *On the Dress of Women*, book II, chapter 6, “to alter heads with saffron,” it recalls the care the ancients devoted to changing and dyeing the hair. Herodian says of Antoninus: κόμας τε τῇ κεφαλῇ ἐπετίθετο ξανθάς, “he even placed blond hair upon his head”; and Clement of Alexandria says, τρίχας ξανθὰς ποιοῦν, “making the hair blond.” Capitolinus says in *Verus*: “He is indeed said to have taken such care over the blondness of his hair,” etc. So strong was the fashion for blond hair that St Jerome warns Laeta: “Do not dye your hair red.” LE PR.], insert tresses with a more wanton hairpin, and, by parting their hair from the forehead, openly profess their womanhood.

They now seek from the mirror advice about their beauty, soften a more unyielding face by washing it, perhaps adulterate it with some cosmetic, toss a mantle over themselves, furnish themselves with shoes of many forms, and carry more equipment to the baths. [Note: [Col. 0906D] “They carry more equipment to the baths.” Clement, *Paedagogus* III.5: τὰ τε ἀργυρώματα μεθ’ ὧν ἐμπομπεύουσιν ἀπειροκάλως ἐν τοῖς βαλανείοις προτιθέασι, “They display in the baths, with vulgar ostentation, the silver articles with which they make their procession.” RIG.]

Why pursue each detail? They alone, by the conspicuousness of their attire, carry their entire womanhood about with them. [Note: [Col. 0906D] “They alone, by the conspicuousness of their attire, carry their entire womanhood about with them.” This is precisely how the Dijon manuscript reads, and I do not doubt that such was Tertullian’s own wording. “These virgins of ours,” he says—that is, Christian virgins—“also acknowledge by their dress the change of age; and as soon as they feel puberty rising within them, they understand that they are now women and have departed from the class of virgins. Accordingly, beginning with the head itself, they lay aside virginal dress, alter their hair, insert tresses with a more wanton hairpin, and, by parting their hair from the forehead, openly profess their womanhood.” He then concludes: “Indeed, virgins alone, by the conspicuousness of their attire, carry their entire womanhood about with them.” For they go about with uncovered heads, the principal part of conspicuous feminine attire, which women are accustomed to govern. Thus they display more conspicuous womanhood than women themselves. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0906B] *Solemnem*, “customary,” François and Paris; *solae enim*, “for they alone,” Latinius and Junius; *sola enim manifesta paratura*, “for by conspicuous attire alone,” Ciacconius; *solae*, “they alone,” in the Dijon manuscript, [Col. 0906C] which Rigault prefers.] Yet by the mere nakedness of the head they wish to play the virgin, [Note: [Col. 0907C] “But they wish to play the virgin.” They wish to be regarded as virgins. Useless and shameless seems to me the labor of those who immediately explain *devirginari*, “to be deprived of virginity,” as its contrary and thrust forward a thousand obscenities merely to hunt for that little glory by which they may be thought learned. I therefore leave it to investigators of sexual matters and ancient impurity. *Devirginare* is διαπαρθενεύειν, “to diminish, to dishonor,” as the glosses teach—an interpretation wholly irrelevant and most unfitting to this passage. But I do violence to you, modesty! LE PR.] denying by one article of dress [Note: [Col. 0907D] “By one article of dress.” Namely, the uncovered head. RIG.] what they profess by their entire equipment.

## CHAPTER XIII

If they misuse clothing because of men, [Note: [Col. 0907D] “If they misuse clothing because of men.” This entire passage should be read and punctuated as follows: “If they misuse clothing because of men, let them fulfill it in this respect also; and, as they veil their heads among the pagans, let them certainly hide in church the virginity that they conceal outside the church. They fear strangers; let them also respect their brethren. Or else let them consistently dare to be seen as virgins in the streets, just as they dare in the churches.” Christian virgins, although bareheaded in church, nevertheless went about among the pagans and in the streets with their heads veiled. They said that they “misused clothing”—that is, that they walked about in clothing not properly their own—lest, if they wore their virginal dress, the pagans should desire them more ardently. Tertullian praises their prudence, but further requires them to fulfill that dress, which was not their own, even when they attended church—namely, because of the brethren, who are also men. RIG.] let them fulfill that clothing in this respect also, by veiling their heads among the pagans. At least in church let them hide the virginity that they conceal outside the church. They fear strangers; let them also respect their brethren. Or else let them consistently dare to be seen as virgins in the streets, just as they dare in the churches. I shall praise their resolution if they also market some portion of their virginity among the pagans. [Note: [Col. 0907D] “If they also market some portion of their virginity among the pagans.” If only they possess enough constancy in their virginity to dare to set forth examples of it from which the pagans may take something to imitate. RIG.]

Their nature is the same outside as inside; their rule of life among men and before the Lord is established by the same freedom. Why, then, do they hide away their good outside but publish it in church [Col. 0907B]? I demand a reason: is it so that they may please their brethren, or so that they may please God himself?

If God himself, he is as capable of seeing what is done in secret as he is just in rewarding what is done for himself alone. Accordingly, he commands us not to trumpet any of the things that will earn a reward with him, nor to obtain compensation for them from men.

Now if we are forbidden to perform even the gift of a single *victoriatus*, [Note: [Col. 0908C] “A single *victoriatus*.” A kind of coin introduced from Illyricum, which circulated as merchandise; concerning it, see Pliny, book XXXIII, chapter 3. LE PR.] or any act of almsgiving whatever, with the left hand aware of it [Note: [Col. 0908C] “With the left hand aware.” The reading of the ancient manuscripts should be restored as follows: *sinistra conscientia*, “with left-hand awareness.” He said *sinistra conscientia* for *sinistra conscia*, just as in the book *On the Pallium* he says “priestly equipment” in place of “the equipment of a priest.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0907C] *Sinistra conscientia*, “with left-hand awareness,” Semler.] (Matt. 6), how much darkness ought we to spread around ourselves when we offer so great an offering to God—our very body and our very spirit—when we consecrate that very nature itself? [Note: [Col. 0908C] “When we consecrate that very nature itself.” The Dijon manuscript reads: “When we consecrate nature to him himself.” I would prefer: “When we consecrate nature itself to him.” RIG.]

Therefore, because this cannot be regarded as done for God—since God does not wish it to be done in this way—it follows that it is done for the sake of men. It is thus illicit from the outset, as being lustful for glory. For glory is illicit for those whose probation consists in every humiliation. [Note: [Col. 0907C] “In every humility,” Rhenanus.] And if the virtue of continence is conferred by God, “Why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7). But if you have not received it, what do you possess that was not given to you? By this very fact, moreover, it is established that it was not given to you by God: you do not render it to God alone. Let us therefore see whether that which is human is firm and genuine.

## CHAPTER XIV
It is reported that, when this question was first raised, a certain woman once said [Note: [Col. 0908C] Wouwer’s manuscript and Rigault read *a certain woman*; the others, *a certain man*]: “And how shall we encourage the others [Note: [Col. 0908C] To such a work. Understand the undertaking of sanctifying the flesh and consecrating virginity. So too “the undertaking of almsgiving” and “the undertaking [Col. 0908D] of fasting.” RIG.] to such a work?” That is to say, they will make us blessed if they become more numerous, and not God’s grace or each person’s merits. Do virgins adorn or commend the Church to God, or does the Church adorn or commend virgins to God? She has therefore confessed that glory [Note: [Col. 0908C] The same witnesses read *she confessed*; the others, *he confessed*.] is the motive.

Moreover [Note: [Col. 0908D] Where there is glory, there is solicitation. These words show that in that age virgins were indeed consecrated to God, but were neither veiled nor enclosed. RIG.], where there is glory, there is solicitation; where there is solicitation, there is compulsion; where there is compulsion, there is necessity; where there is necessity, there is weakness. Deservedly, therefore, while they do not cover their heads so that they may be solicited for glory’s sake, [Note: [Col. 0908D] They are compelled to conceal their wombs. He says *wombs*, as legal authors customarily say “wombs made pregnant through intercourse with a man.” Thus, “to conceal their wombs” means to conceal their pregnancies. RIG.] they are compelled to conceal their wombs after weakness has brought them to ruin. For rivalry, not religion, produces them; sometimes even [Note: [Col. 0908D] Their belly itself is their god. Here, in the ordinary sense, he has used *belly* for gluttony. RIG.] their belly itself is their god, [Note: [Col. 0908D] Because the brotherhood readily receives a virgin. I have referred this to the charity by which Christian brethren gladly received virgins; for the preceding words about the belly lead me to this interpretation: “Sometimes the belly produces them,” that is, gluttony does so, because they see the brethren supplying food to virgins. LAC.] because the brotherhood readily receives a virgin.

They do not merely fall, however, but also draw after themselves a long rope of sins. [Note: [Col. 0908D] Brought forward into the midst and their good publicly proclaimed. These things were customarily done when a virgin made a religious profession. Before a large assembly of the Church, a virgin of such a purpose was brought into the midst before the presiding officer or superior, and by him the virgin’s good was publicly proclaimed—namely, her good resolution to consecrate [Col. 0909C] her virginity. Thereafter the brethren, that is, the Church, heaped every honor and charitable service upon her. RIG.] For once they have been brought forward into the midst, exalted by the public proclamation of their good, and heaped with every honor and charitable service by the brethren, since it does not remain hidden when some offense [Note: [Col. 0909C] Latinius conjectures: “provided it remains hidden where some offense has been committed.”] has been committed, they contemplate a disgrace as great as the honor they formerly possessed.

If an uncovered head is ascribed to virginity, then, should any virgin fall from the grace of virginity, she keeps her head uncovered so that she may not be exposed; and she now goes about in a dress belonging to another state, namely [Note: [Col. 0909C] That is, the dress which virginity claims for itself; she nevertheless remains in that dress, one now belonging to another state at least, lest the change expose her. Although all these words are found in the ancient copies, they seem to me out of place and perhaps introduced from some interpretation written in the book’s margin. RIG.] the dress which virginity claims for itself. She nevertheless remains in that dress, one now belonging to another state at least, lest the change expose her. Conscious of their now unquestionable womanhood [Note: [Col. 0909C] Rigault reads “conscious of their now unquestionable womanhood”; the first edition of Rhenanus, “with the consciousness of womanhood now unquestionably,” etc.], they dare approach God with uncovered head.

But God, the jealous God and Lord, who said, [Note: [Col. 0909D] “Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed.” He follows the Greek copies, *apokalyphthēsetai* (ἀποκαλυφθήσεται), “will be revealed.” There are nevertheless also Latin manuscript copies of the Vulgate edition which read thus: “may be revealed.” PAM.] “Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed” (Matt. 10:26), brings most of them into public view as well. For they will not confess unless they are betrayed by the cries of their own infants. And will you not regard many more women as suspect of numerous crimes [Col. 0909B] as well?

I shall say it, though unwillingly: [Note: [Col. 0909D] A woman hardly becomes one only once if she does not fear becoming one. It is scarcely possible for a woman who sins once, and who after that first offense does not fear becoming a woman, to sin only once—especially one who, although she has now become a woman, can falsely claim to be a virgin before God, that is, in the Church. I have restored the negation, which had dropped out even from the ancient copies. RIG.] a woman hardly becomes one only once if she does not fear becoming one [Note: [Col. 0909C] Rhenanus reads: “who fears becoming one.”], and if, after becoming one, she can falsely claim to be a virgin before God. Again, what will she dare concerning her own womb, lest she be exposed as a mother too! God knows [Note: [Col. 0910C] Rhenanus substituted *how many* for *that*.] that infants have before now both come to full development and been brought intact to birth, although assailed for some time by their mothers. Virgins of this sort always conceive with the greatest ease and give birth with the greatest success—and to children exceedingly like their fathers.

[Note: [Col. 0909D] A virginity compelled and unwilling commits these outrages. The Dijon codex reads *invited*, which appears to correspond to “solicitation.” He calls the virginity of those whom rivalry, not religion, produced and solicited to this undertaking of dedicating and consecrating virginity to God both compelled and invited. They poorly preserve what they undertook from zeal for human glory, not from love of holiness.] A virginity compelled and unwilling [Note: [Col. 0910C] Not *invited*, as Rhenanus and the Dijon codex read.] commits these outrages. The very desire not to remain hidden is unchaste: it admits something that does not belong to a virgin—the desire to please, and certainly to please men as well. However sincerely she may strive with a good intention, she must necessarily be endangered by making herself public, while she is struck by the uncertain eyes of many, tickled by the fingers of those pointing her out, excessively loved, and [Note: [Col. 0909D] While she grows warm amid constant embraces and kisses. This is what the brotherhood did. For Christians once greeted one another with a kiss. And earlier he said: “the brotherhood readily receives virgins”; reception, moreover, is accomplished through an embrace. RHEN.—“She grows warm amid constant kisses.” Clement speaks of this kiss in book III of the *Paedagogus*, chapter 11: “There is also another unholy kiss, full of poison, which feigns holiness” (*esti de kai allo anagnon philēma plēres iou, hagiosynēn hypokrinomenon*, ἔστι δὲ καὶ ἄλλο ἄναγνον φίλημα πλήρες ἰοῦ, ἁγιοσύνην ὑποκρινόμενον). And shortly afterward: “Kisses often inject the poison of licentiousness” (*philēmata de pollakis eniēsin ion akolasias*, φιλήματα δὲ πολλάκις ἐνίησιν ἰὸν ἀκολασίας). Yet a kiss, if not given with such an intention, must be religious. RIG.] grows warm amid constant embraces and kisses. Thus her brow is hardened, thus her shame is worn away, thus it is dissolved; thus she learns now to desire to please in another way.

## CHAPTER XV

But true, complete, and pure virginity fears nothing more than itself. It does not wish to endure even the eyes of women; it has eyes of another kind itself. It takes refuge in a covering for the head, as though in a helmet, as though in a shield, to protect its good against the blows of temptations, against the missiles of scandals, against suspicions, whispers, rivalry, and [Note: [Col. 0910D] Envious malice itself. As is also clear from what follows, the author takes *livor* to mean hatred, and shortly afterward *lividum* to mean envious. So too blessed Cyprian, who wrote a book *On Jealousy and Envy*, and blessed Jerome, who cites that book in his commentary on Galatians 5. PAM.] envious malice itself.

For there is something to be feared even among the pagans, [Note: [Col. 0910D] Which they call the evil eye. The ancients believed that envy—which the author, as we have said, calls *livor*—possessed great power to harm, since they considered it malevolent and poisonous through mere intention and through its very breath and contagion, and believed that it gravely injured those to whom it wished evil. The author therefore rightly says that the pagans called this the *evil eye* (*fascinum*), and he relates it to the devil’s hatred. Accordingly, after the manner of those who employed various remedies against the evil eye, especially for children, he proposes a head covering for virgins. PAM.] which they call the evil eye—the more disastrous consequence of extraordinary praise and glory. Sometimes we interpret this as the devil: for hatred of the good belongs to him. Sometimes we assign it to God: for the judgment of pride belongs to him, who raises the humble and brings down the exalted.

Thus the holier virgin will fear, even under the name of the evil eye, the adversary on the one side and God on the other: the former’s envious disposition and the latter’s judicial [Note: [Col. 0910C] The Venetian edition incorrectly reads “of the censors.”] light. And she will rejoice to be known to herself alone and to God. But even if she becomes known to someone, she shows wisdom if she has blocked the approach [Note: [Col. 0910D] “To block the approach” means to forestall and anticipate. LAC.] of temptations. For who will dare press his eyes upon a closed face, an unresponsive face, a face which I might call sorrowful? Every evil thought will be broken by its very severity. She who conceals the virgin even denies that she is a woman.

## CHAPTER XVI

In these considerations consists the defense of our opinion according to Scripture, according to nature, and according to discipline. Scripture establishes the law, nature bears corroborating witness, discipline demands it. Which of these does customary opinion support [Col. 0910C], or what plausible appearance does the contrary position possess? Scripture belongs to God, nature belongs to God, discipline belongs to God. [Col. 0911A] Whatever is contrary to these does not belong to God.

If Scripture is uncertain, nature is manifest, and in view of nature’s testimony Scripture cannot be uncertain. If nature is doubted, discipline shows what is more pleasing to God. Nothing is dearer to him than humility, nothing more acceptable than modesty, nothing more hateful [Note: [Col. 0911C] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “more laborious.”] than glory and the desire to please human beings. Therefore, let that which you find pleasing to God be Scripture, nature, and discipline for you, since you are commanded to examine everything and pursue whatever is better (1 Thess. 5:21).

It remains for us also to turn to the women themselves, so that they may receive these teachings more willingly. I implore you, virgin—whether I should call you mother, sister, or daughter [Note: [Col. 0911C] According to the designations of age. He intimates that Christian women were once called sisters by the brethren, that is, by Christians who held no ecclesiastical rank, but daughters by the fathers, that is, by bishops and presbyters. Hence it is evident that the designations “fathers” and “brothers,” and likewise “daughters” and “sisters,” are not new in the Church. PAM.], according to the designations of age: veil your head. If you are a mother, veil it for the sake of your sons; if a sister, for the sake of your brothers; if a daughter, for the sake of your fathers. Every age is endangered in you.

Put on [Col. 0911B] [Note: [Col. 0911C] Rhenanus reads “lead around.”] the armor of modesty; lead around yourself the rampart of shame; build a wall for your sex, one that neither sends forth your eyes [Note: [Col. 0911C] “Sends forth the eyes.” The verb belongs to the terminology of the circus, and the metaphor is taken from it. Thus Statius, *Silvae*, book I:

> Scarcely had the day been sent forth, and already the favorable omens were at hand.

Bernartius went astonishingly astray here in understanding “the day sent forth” to mean evening, since it undoubtedly denotes the morning, as Casperius rightly observes against him. Thus Claudian, *Panegyric on Manlius*:

> Whatever the sun bathes when its rising has been sent forth.

Nor should the following verse of Virgil be understood otherwise:

> And Neptune perceived that winter had been sent forth.

LAC.] nor admits those of strangers. Fully assume the dress of a woman, so that you may preserve the state of a virgin. Make an outward representation of something that is inward, so that you may exhibit the truth to God alone—although you do not falsely represent yourself as married, [Note: [Col. 0911D] For you have married Christ. He praises above all the dress of the monastic life; from this it is plainly inferred that this manner of life flourished in the Church before this author’s time. Cyprian, moreover, wrote an entire book *On the Dress of Virgins*. See Ambrose, epistle 81. LAC.] for you have married Christ. To him you have delivered your flesh; to him you have betrothed your maturity. Walk according to the will of your bridegroom. It is Christ who commands even the betrothed and married women of others [Note: [Col. 0911C] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “married women.”] to be veiled—and certainly his own all the more.

## CHAPTER XVII

But we also admonish you who have entered into marriage concerning the other form of chastity: do not [Note: [Col. 0911C] Semler reads “nor.”] fall away from the discipline of the veil [Col. 0911C], not even for a moment, so that, because you cannot cast it aside, you do not destroy it in another way, going about neither covered nor bare. [Col. 0912A]

For with caps and woolen bands [Note: [Col. 0911D] A *mitra* is a woman’s ornament for the head, or a crown bound with bands and ribbons; those woolen bands were called *lanae* or *phylla*. LE PR.] some women do not veil the head but merely bind it, covered indeed at the forehead, but bare [Note: [Col. 0911C] The Venetian edition reads “laid bare again.”] where the head properly is. Others, covered only as far as the crown of the head with small pieces of linen which, I suppose, are kept slight lest they weigh upon the head, and which do not descend as far as the ears—I pity them, if their hearing is so weak that they cannot hear through a covering.

Let them know that the whole head constitutes the woman [Note: [Col. 0912C] Junius reads “to a woman.”]. Its boundaries and limits extend as far as the place where the garment begins. As much space as her loosened hair can occupy is the territory of the veil, so that the neck too must be encompassed. For the necks themselves are what ought to be subjected, and it is on their account that a sign of authority must be borne upon the head (1 Cor. 11:10): the veil is their yoke.

The pagan women of Arabia [Col. 0912B] will judge you, for they cover not merely the head, but [Note: [Col. 0911D] The face also in such a way. Jerome to Eustochium, epistle 22: “With the face covered, they leave scarcely one eye free for seeing.” They are far stricter than the women of Chalcis, of whom Plutarch says in the *Greek Questions*: “They themselves transacted whatever business they needed before judges and magistrates, drawing aside one side of the veil from the face” (*autai di’ hautōn epratton hotou deētheien para dikastais kai archousin, apagousai thateron meros tou prosōpou tēs kalyptras*, αὐταὶ δι’ αὑτῶν ἔπραττον ὅτου δεηθεῖεν παρὰ δικασταῖς καὶ ἄρχουσιν, ἀπάγουσαι θάτερον μέρος τοῦ προσώπου τῆς καλύπτρας). RIG.] the entire face as well, in such a way that, leaving one eye free, they are content to enjoy half the light rather than prostitute their entire face. A certain Roman queen therefore called them most unhappy, [Note: [Col. 0912C] Because they can fall in love more readily than be loved. With one eye left free, they are of course permitted to see what they desire, and indeed to see more keenly, since their entire power of sight has been concentrated and gathered into one eye. For this reason Dio Chrysostom judged that even the girls of Tarsus, although their whole faces were veiled, should not be trusted, since they were permitted to hear things that might arouse lust—and indeed to hear them more attentively, because the mind, with its eyes denied, transfers to the ears its entire power of forming images. [Col. 0912D] “Accordingly they see more keenly with one eye, like geometers” (*toigaroun oxyteron blepousin heni tōn ophthalmōn, hōsper hoi geōmetrai*, τοιγάρουν ὀξύτερον βλέπουσι ἑνὶ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν, ὥσπερ οἱ γεωμέτραι). The verse of Persius to the same effect is well known:

> Just as if one were directing a red line with one eye.

RIG.] because they can love more than they can be loved, although they are happy in being exempt from another kind of unhappiness [Note: [Col. 0912C] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “happiness.”], and indeed the more frequent kind, since women can more often be loved than fall in love.

[Note: [Col. 0912D] And indeed the modesty of pagan discipline is purer and, so to speak, more barbarous. The meaning is: “But the discipline of that pagan modesty is altogether rustic, unmannered, uncivilized—pure barbarism.” These words are spoken ironically. RIG.] And indeed the modesty of pagan discipline is purer and, so to speak, more barbarous. For us, the Lord has marked out the dimensions of the veil even through revelations. An angel, appearing in a dream to one of our sisters, seemed to strike her neck as though applauding it, saying: [Note: [Col. 0912D] “An elegant neck,” he says, “and deservedly bare.” A grave admonition, and not unworthy of an angel, if we consider it carefully enough. He addresses a Christian woman: “An elegant neck,” he says, “which Christ wished to redeem at so great a price. And deservedly bare,” since Christ removed from it the yoke of most dreadful slavery. But it is good that you be veiled from the head down to the loins, lest you lie bare and exposed to sin. Once mastered by sin, you may become Satan’s slave, and thereafter the freedom of the neck won for you by so great an emancipator may be of no benefit, since through your own fault you will fall back into eternal service under the harshest tyranny. RIG.] “An elegant neck,” he said, “and deservedly [Col. 0912C] bare! It is good that you be veiled from the head down to the loins [Note: [Col. 0912C] Junius reads “unveiled.”], [Col. 0913A] lest this freedom of your neck be of no benefit to you either.” And certainly what he said to one woman, he said to all.

But what great chastisement will those women also deserve who remain uncovered during the singing of psalms, or during any mention whatever of God! Do even those who [Note: [Col. 0913A] Pamelius omits “who.”], in prayer itself, very frequently [Note: [Col. 0913B] A fringe or tuft, very frequently. Here *very easily* must be understood as *very frequently*, as above: “because women can more often be loved than fall in love,” that is, more often, for the most part. RIG.] place a fringe, a tuft, or some thread or other upon the crown of the head and suppose themselves covered rightly measure [Note: [Col. 0913A] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “misrepresent.”] their head at such a value? [Note: [Col. 0913A] Rigault proposes “will they deserve.”]

Other women, [Note: [Col. 0913B] For whom, plainly, a palm is larger than every fringe and thread. Those who allowed themselves to be persuaded that *palm* here meant anything other than the hand have strayed far from sound reasoning. He identifies three degrees of shamelessness among virgins who came to church without a veil. This is the third: those who, during prayer itself or any mention whatever of God, placed upon their head not a fringe, tuft, thread, or some similar thing, but a hand. Although it was larger than all the fringes and threads used by the others, they still could not be said to be covered even in this way, and they abused their head no less than the others. RIG.] for whom, plainly, a palm is larger than every fringe and thread, abuse their head no less—like a certain beast rather than a bird [Note: [Col. 0914B] Pliny, book V: “The ostrich-camels are very large and almost of the class of beasts.” RIG.], though winged, with a small head, an elongated neck, and the rest of its body carried high on its legs. They say that when it needs to hide, it thrusts only its whole head deep into a thicket, leaving the rest of itself in the open. Thus, while it feels safe in regard to its head, it is naked where it is larger, and [Note: [Col. 0914B] It is captured whole, together with its head. The same Pliny, book IX: “The nature of mullets is ridiculed because, when frightened, they hide their heads and believe their whole bodies concealed; their wantonness is equally incautious,” etc. RIG.] is captured whole, together with its head. Such too will be these women, who are covered less than is useful.

Therefore, they must go about at every time and in every place mindful of the law, prepared and equipped for every mention of God. For if he is in the heart, he will also be recognized upon the head of women. To those who read these words in good peace, preferring truth [Note: [Col. 0914A] Rhenanus, Pamelius, Semler, and Oberthür read “utility.”] to custom, may peace and grace abound from our Lord Jesus, together with Septimius Tertullian, whose little work this is.

[Col. 0913]

# THE BOOK OF QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN, *ON THE EXHORTATION TO CHASTITY* (C)

[Note: [Col. 0913D] *On the Exhortation to Chastity.* Tertullian gave this work the title *On the Exhortation to Chastity*, in the same form as the titles we read in the catalogue of the works contained in the very ancient Codex Agobardinus: *On Scorpiace*, *On the Prescription of Heretics*; and in Cyprian, *On the Exhortation to Martyrdom*. These should be understood as though they had been framed thus: *Exhortation to Chastity*, *Scorpiace*, *Prescription against Heretics*, *Exhortation to Martyrdom*. Thus in book I of *On Modesty*, he said “on the exhortation of acts of sanctity” [Col. 0914D] for “exhortation to acts of sanctity.” This edition of the present book has been supplemented, restored, and corrected in so many places that it should now be regarded as a new one. Of all Tertullian’s writings, this had received the worst treatment. RIG.]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0913C]

—This treatise was written by Tertullian as a Montanist. In it he dissuades a certain widowed brother from a second marriage, which at one point he expressly permits and asserts was not forbidden by Saint Paul, while at another he condemns it and represents it as adultery. EDD.

## CHAPTER I

I do not doubt, brother, that after sending your wife ahead in peace [Note: [Col. 0913C] Rigault and Renet read “into peace.”], you have turned to composing your mind and are thinking [Col. 0914C] about the outcome of your solitary state [Note: [Col. 0914D] About the outcome of your solitary state—that is, about what will happen to you, now that you live alone and have survived your wife. RIG.], and therefore certainly need counsel [Note: [Col. 0913C] Rhenanus and Semler read “to digest counsel”; Franeker and Paris, “to direct counsel.”].

Although in a matter of this kind everyone ought to confer with his own faith and take account of its strength, nevertheless, because in this particular case the necessity of the flesh prompts [Note: [Col. 0913C] Junius reads “admonishes.”] reflection and, in nearly every instance [Note: [Col. 0913C] Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür, and Pamelius read “to seek.”], resists faith within the same conscience [Note: [Col. 0914C] Rhenanus, Semler, Oberthür, and Pamelius add “which.”], faith needs counsel from outside, as though it were an advocate [Note: [Col. 0914C] Rhenanus, Pamelius, Semler, and Oberthür read “counsel as an advocate.”] against the necessities [Note: [Col. 0914C] Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür read “necessity.”] of the flesh.

That necessity can indeed very easily [Note: [Col. 0914C] Rhenanus, Pamelius, Semler, and Oberthür omit “very easily.”] be circumscribed, if God’s will rather than his indulgence is considered. [Col. 0915A] No one gains merit by making use of indulgence, but by obeying the will. God’s will is our sanctification. For he wills that we, his image, also become his likeness [Note: [Col. 0915C] Junius reads “in the likeness.”], so that we may be holy just as he himself is holy.

He distributes this good—I mean sanctification—into several forms [Note: [Col. 0915C] Rigault and the Venetian edition read “I distribute.”], so that we may be found in one of them. The first form is virginity from birth. The second is virginity from the second birth, that is [Note: [Col. 0915C] “From the second birth, that is” is absent from Rhenanus, Semler, Pamelius, and Oberthür.], from the washing of baptism. This either purifies within marriage by mutual agreement or, by personal choice, perseveres in widowhood. The third rank remaining is monogamy [Note: [Col. 0915C] Rhenanus reads “of monogamy.”], when, after one marriage has been ended, [Note: [Col. 0915] Thereafter the sex is renounced. “Sex is devoured by the virgin,” says Jerome to Principia, epistle 3. RIG.] the sexual life is thereafter renounced.

The happiness of the first virginity [Note: [Col. 0915C] Junius reads “of the first virginity.” The Wouwer codex reads: “The first happiness belongs to the first virginity—the second belongs to virginity’s virtue—the remaining form, namely, of not marrying thereafter—besides virtue, is also the praise of modesty,” etc.] is not to know at all [Note: [Col. 0915C] “At all” is absent from Rhenanus.] that from which you will later desire to be freed. The second [Note: [Col. 0915C] Rhenanus and Semler read “The second belongs to virginity.”] is the achievement of virtue: to despise that whose power you know very well. The remaining form—namely, to refrain from marriage after a marriage has been dissolved by death—is, besides praise for virtue [Note: [Col. 0915C] Rhenanus and Semler read “virtues.”], also [Note: [Col. 0915C] Rigault reads “For it is the praise of modesty.”] the praise of modesty. For it is modesty not to desire what has been taken away—and taken away [Col. 0915B] by the Lord God, without whose will neither does a leaf fall from a tree nor a sparrow worth a single penny fall to the ground.

## CHAPTER II

How modest, then, is that declaration: “The Lord gave; the Lord has taken away” (Job 1:21); “As it seemed good to the Lord, so it was done.” Accordingly, if we restore marriages that have been taken away, we are undoubtedly striving against God’s will, desiring to possess again what he did not wish us to possess. For if he had wished it, he would not have taken it away—unless we also interpret this as God’s will, as though he wished us again to possess what he had already ceased to wish [Note: [Col. 0915C] Others read “as though he wished it in us again”; the Wouwer codex, “in us, which God had already ceased to wish.”].

It does not belong to good and solid faith to refer everything to God’s will in this way, and for each person thus to flatter himself by saying that nothing happens without his nod [Note: [Col. 0915D] Others read “command.”], so that we fail to understand that something also lies within ourselves [Col. 0915C]. Otherwise every sin will be excused if we maintain [Note: [Col. 0915D] Rhenanus and Semler read “if we continue.”] that nothing occurs within us apart from God’s will; and this definition [Note: [Col. 0915D] Rhenanus and Semler read: “But there the definition destroys it”; the Wouwer codex has an uncertain reading, “but for you the definition.”] will proceed to the destruction of the whole system of discipline, and even of God himself, if he either brings forth from his own will those things which he does not will [Note: [Col. 0915D] Rigault and the Venetian edition read “may bring forth.”], or if there is nothing that God does not will.

But how [Note: [Col. 0915D] Rigault and the Venetian edition read “when.”] does he forbid certain things and [Col. 0916A] even threaten eternal punishment for them? Certainly [Note: [Col. 0916C] Semler and Leopold read “certainly also.”] he does not will the things he forbids, by which he is also offended; just as he commands and accepts the things he wills [Note: [Col. 0916C] Rigault, Paris, and Venice read: “Just as, conversely, he both commands and makes acceptable,” etc.], and settles the account with the reward of eternity.

Therefore, since from his precepts we have learned both what he wills and what he does not will, the will and choice [Note: [Col. 0916C] Pamelius omits “and choice.”] to choose one or the other nevertheless belong to us, as it is written: “Behold, I have set before you good and evil” (Ecclus. 15:18), for you have tasted from the tree of knowledge. Accordingly, we ought not to refer to God’s will what has been placed at the disposal of our own [Note: [Col. 0916C] Rhenanus and Semler read “of ourselves.”] choice [Note: [Col. 0916C] Rhenanus and Semler read “within God’s will.”], since he himself wishes us also to will what he wishes [Note: [Col. 0916C] Semler reads: “We, whom he himself wills, must also will.”]—he who does not will evil. Thus the will is ours when we will evil against the will of God, who wills the good.

Moreover, if you ask whence comes that will by which we will something contrary to God’s will, I shall say [Note: [Col. 0916C] Rhenanus and Semler read: “God’s will, so to speak.”]: from ourselves. And not without reason, for you must necessarily correspond to your own seed. Indeed, that founder both of the race and of sin, [Col. 0916B] Adam, willed the thing by which he sinned. For the devil did not impose upon him [Note: [Col. 0916C] Rhenanus and Semler read “his.”] the will to sin; he merely supplied material to his will. God’s will, on the other hand, had come to him in the form of a command to obey [Note: [Col. 0916C] The Wouwer codex and Leopold read “obedience.”].

Likewise, if you do not obey God, who established you with free power by setting a command before you, then by the freedom of your will you willingly incline toward that which God [Note: [Col. 0916C] Rhenanus and Semler read: “willingly allows you to incline toward what God”; Franeker, Paris, and Pamelius: “willingly you incline toward that which.”] does not will; and yet you suppose yourself to have been overthrown by the devil. Although he wills you to will something that God does not will, he does not thereby make you will it. For not even then did he compel those first-formed human beings [Note: [Col. 0916C] Semler reads “unwilling.”] to the will to sin. Indeed, they were neither unwilling nor ignorant of what God did not will; for clearly God did not wish it to happen, since he appointed death as the penalty once it was committed.

Thus the devil’s single work is to test [Note: [Col. 0916C] Rhenanus and Semler read “to moderate.”] what is within you—whether you are willing. But once you have willed, it follows that he subjects you to himself [Note: [Col. 0916C] Franeker, Venice, and Rigault read “that he also subordinates you to himself.”], not because he produced the will within you, but because he obtained an opportunity [Note: [Col. 0916D] Rhenanus and Semler read “possession.”] from your will. Therefore, [Col. 0916C] since willing alone is [Note: [Col. 0916D] Rhenanus and Semler read “will be.”] within us, and since in this our disposition toward God is tested [Note: [Col. 0916D] The same witnesses read “may be tested.”]—whether we will those things that accord [Note: [Col. 0916D] The same witnesses read “are consonant.”] with his will—

## CHAPTER III
Deeply [Note: [Col. 0916D] “By you” (*A te*) in the printed editions, MSS., Wouwer, Paris.] and firmly, I say, one must reflect upon God’s pleasure—[Col. 0917A] what he wills even in secret. For what he wills openly [Note: [Col. 0917C] “For openly” (*Enim manifesto*), Rhenanus, Semler.] we all know; and one must examine precisely how those very things are openly willed. For although [Note: [Col. 0917C] “For if” (*Nam si*), ibid.] certain things seem to savor of God’s will because they are permitted by God, not everything that is permitted proceeds immediately from the pure and entire will of him who permits it. [Note: [Col. 0917D] It is by indulgence that anything is permitted. He is evidently distorting the Apostle’s passage, 1 Cor. 7: “But I say this by way of indulgence, not by way of command.” He does the same in *On Monogamy*, ch. 3. LE PR.] Whatever is permitted is so by indulgence. Although indulgence is not without an act of will, nevertheless, because it has some cause in the person [Note: [Col. 0917C] “In the place” (*In loco*), ibid.] to whom it is granted, it proceeds as though from an unwilling will: the will has admitted a cause for itself, and that cause constrains it. Consider the nature of a will whose cause lies in someone else. A second kind [Note: [Col. 0917C] “A second kind,” Rhenanus, Semler.] of will must likewise be considered—one that is not [Note: [Col. 0917C] “Not” is absent from the same editions.] pure. God wills us to do certain things pleasing to him, [Note: [Col. 0917C] “God wills us to do certain pleasing things,” Rhenanus, Semler.] in which indulgence does not provide support [Note: [Col. 0917C] “Indulgence operates,” the same editions.], but discipline rules. Yet if he has placed other things before these [Note: [Col. 0917C] “Sets these before,” the same editions.]—things which he assuredly wills more—[Col. 0917B] can there be any doubt that we must pursue [Note: [Col. 0917C] “Must be assessed,” the same editions.] the things he prefers? For the things he wills less, because [Note: [Col. 0917C] “Who wills other things more,” the same editions.] he wills other things more, are likewise [Note: [Col. 0917C] “Consequently must be regarded,” the same editions.] to be regarded as though he did not will them. [Note: [Col. 0917D] Semler omits “as though he alone.”] For by showing [Note: [Col. 0917D] “I show,” Semler; “by showing,” Pamelius, Wouwer.] what he wills more, he has effaced the lesser will by the greater. And insofar as he has set both before your knowledge, he has thereby determined that you must pursue what he has declared [Note: [Col. 0917D] “Prepared you,” Semler.] himself to will more. Therefore, if he declared it so that [Note: [Col. 0917D] Wouwer corrects the whole passage from a manuscript thus: “It has some cause in the person to whom—Consider how great that will is—it must be considered as not belonging to a pure will. God wills us to do things pleasing to himself, in which—Yet if also other things—he wills more. Nor is it doubtful that we must assess the things he wills, since the things he wills less, because he wills others more, must be regarded just as though he did not will them. For by showing.”] you might pursue what he wills more, then unquestionably, unless you do so, your inclination is contrary to his will, because it is contrary to his stronger will; and you offend him more than you earn his favor [Note: [Col. 0917D] Rhenanus and Semler place punctuation after *promereris* (“earn favor”). They then read what follows continuously with [Col. 0918C] “And by rejecting in part.”]: you do what he wills, certainly, but reject what he prefers. In part you sin; and in the part in which you do not sin, nevertheless you earn no favor. Moreover, to refuse to earn favor is itself to sin. Therefore, if a second marriage derives from that will of God which is called [Col. 0917C] indulgence [Note: [Col. 0918C] “Is compelled,” Rhenanus, Semler.], we shall deny [Note: [Col. 0918C] “We denied,” the same editions.] that this is a pure will [Note: [Col. 0918C] “Will” is absent from Rhenanus.], since indulgence is its cause. If it derives from that will before which another, stronger will is set—the will that continence should be more eagerly desired—we shall have learned that the weaker is annulled [Note: [Col. 0918C] “Divided,” Rhenanus.] by the stronger.

I have briefly outlined these points so that I may now run through the Apostle’s statements. First of all, I shall not appear irreligious [Col. 0918A] if I observe what he himself professes: that he introduced the whole indulgence concerning marriage from his own judgment—that is, from human understanding—not from a divine ordinance. For when he laid down concerning widows and [Note: [Col. 0918C] “And” is absent from Rhenanus.] the unmarried that they should marry if they cannot exercise self-control, because it is better to marry than to burn, he turned to [Note: [Col. 0918C] “Another,” Rhenanus, Semler, Pamelius.] the other category and said: “But to the married I give notice—not I, indeed, but the Lord” (1 Cor. 7:10). Thus, by transferring [Note: [Col. 0918C] “Outside reason,” Rhenanus, Semler.] the speaking person from himself to the Lord, he showed that what he had said above—“It is better to marry [Note: [Col. 0918C] The impersonal *nubi*, Rhenanus, Paris.] than to burn”—had been pronounced not in the Lord’s person but in his own. Although this statement concerns those whom the faith finds unmarried [Note: [Col. 0918C] “Married,” Rhenanus.] or widowed, [Note: [Col. 0918D] “Widows,” Rhenanus, Semler; the words from “by the faith” are absent from the same editions.] nevertheless, because [Note: [Col. 0918D] “Who,” Pamelius, Rhenanus, Semler.] everyone embraces it as a license to [Note: [Col. 0918D] “To” is absent from the same editions.] marry, I should like to examine [Note: [Col. 0918D] “Reconsider,” Rigault.] what sort of good it shows to be better than [Col. 0918B] punishment. [Note: [Col. 0917D] What kind of good does he show to be better than punishment? It is entirely certain that in those early times virginity was valued more highly, and that marriages, if compared with it, appeared to be a kind of evil, though in reality they were not. Apart from the praiseworthy continence of that age, the basis of this opinion was the Apostle’s passage, “It is better to marry than to burn.” Those ancients explained it as though Paul had said that it was better to lack one eye than two. Blessed Jerome himself, who had sharpened his pen against Jovinian because, among his other delusions, he assigned equal merit to virginity [Col. 0919D] and marriage, sometimes appears to follow this author’s opinion. Yet in his letter on monogamy to Ageruchia he admits that second and even third marriages, if necessary, were conceded by the Apostle to the incontinent. LE PR.]

That cannot appear good except in comparison with what is worst, so that marriage is good only because burning is worse. A thing is good as such [Note: [Col. 0918D] “If it possesses this name in itself,” Rhenanus, Pamelius, Semler.] if it continues to possess the name without comparison—not merely with an evil, but even with another good—so that, even if it is compared with another good and overshadowed [Note: [Col. 0918D] “Is compared and overshadowed by it,” Wouwer’s codex.] by that other, it nevertheless retains the name of good. But if it is compelled to be called good by comparison with evil [Note: [Col. 0918D] “By comparison with evil,” Semler, Rhenanus.], it is not so much a good as a lower species of evil, which, because it is obscured by a greater evil, is forced to assume the name of good. [Note: [Col. 0918D] The same editions read: “is forced, and remove the expression of comparison.”] Remove, then, the condition of comparison, so that you do not say, “It is better to marry than to burn,” and I ask whether you would dare to say simply, “It is better to marry,” without adding what it is better than. Therefore, what is not “better” is surely not “good” either, because you have taken away and removed the condition of comparison which, [Col. 0918C] by making it “better,” compels it to be regarded [Note: [Col. 0918D] “Thus good, thus compels one to regard it,” the same editions.] as good.

“It is better to marry than to burn” must be understood in the same way [Note: [Col. 0918D] “As if,” the same editions.] as “It is better to lack one eye than two.” Yet if you leave the comparison aside, possessing one eye will not be better [Note: [Col. 0918D] “Nor good,” the same editions.], because it is not good. Let no one, therefore, seize upon this passage as a defense, [Col. 0919A] for it properly concerns the unmarried and widows [Note: [Col. 0919D] “The married and widows,” Rhenanus, Semler.], for whom no union has yet been counted. Even so, I have shown that they too must understand [Note: [Col. 0919D] “Must count.”] the condition attached to the permission.

## CHAPTER IV

As for a second marriage, however, we know perfectly well that the Apostle pronounced: “Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife; but if you marry, you do not sin.” Yet he likewise introduces the tenor of this statement as his own counsel, not as a divine command. There is a great difference between God’s command and a man’s counsel. “I have,” he says, “no command from the Lord; but I give counsel, as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be trustworthy.” Moreover, neither in the Gospel nor in Paul’s own epistles will you find remarriage permitted by God’s command. From this [Col. 0919B] it is confirmed that one marriage must be maintained, because what is not found to have been permitted by the Lord is merely pardoned.

Add that this very intervention of human counsel, as though it had already reflected upon its own excess, immediately checks and recalls itself when he adds: “Nevertheless, such people will have affliction of the flesh”; when he says that he is sparing them; when he adds that the time has been drawn short [Note: [Col. 0919D] “Is in a shortened state,” Rhenanus, Semler, Pamelius.], in which even those who have marriages ought to behave as though they had none; and when he compares the anxieties of the married and the unmarried. [Note: [Col. 0919D] The words “and of the unmarried” are absent there.] For by teaching through these statements why it is not expedient to marry, he discourages what he had permitted above. And this concerns a first marriage; how much more a second? [Note: [Col. 0919D] “But when he exhorts us to follow his own example.” This passage also supports the continence of the blessed Apostle Paul from marriage. PAMELIUS.]

But when he exhorts us to his own example, he plainly shows what he wills us to be—namely, continent—and equally declares what he does not will us to be, [Col. 0919C] namely, incontinent. [Note: [Col. 0919D] These final words are absent from Rhenanus and Semler.] Thus, when he wills one thing, even he does not permit what he does not will either voluntarily or in truth. For if he willed it, he would not have permitted it; indeed, he would have commanded it.

[Note: [Col. 0920D] “But behold, once again he says that a woman may marry after her husband’s death.” Here the author still proceeds with sufficient moderation: he does not absolutely prohibit second marriage, but proves monogamy happier. Hence blessed Jerome too admits that, in these words, the Apostle concedes second and third marriages in the Lord. PAMELIUS.]

But behold, once again he says (1 Cor. 7) that, after her husband’s death, a woman may marry whomever she wishes, provided that it is in the Lord. “But she will be happier,” he says, “if she remains as she is, according to my counsel. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.” We see two counsels: the one above, by which he grants permission to marry, and the later one, by which he enjoins the continence that abstains from marriage. [Note: [Col. 0919D] “Introduces,” according to others.] Which, then, you ask, shall we follow? Look and read. When he grants permission, he alleges the counsel of a prudent man. When he enjoins continence, he affirms the counsel of the Holy Spirit. Follow the admonition that has divinity as its advocate.

[Col. 0920A] The faithful, certainly, also possess the Spirit of God, but not all the faithful are Apostles. Therefore, after the man who had called himself trustworthy [Note: [Col. 0919D] “Because he had called him trustworthy,” Rhenanus, Pamelius, Semler.] subsequently added that he possessed the Spirit of God—a fact no one would doubt even concerning an ordinary believer—he said this so as to restore to himself the dignity of an Apostle. For the Apostles possess the Holy Spirit in a distinctive manner: in works of prophecy, in the efficacy of miracles, and in demonstrations of tongues, [Note: [Col. 0919D] “And demonstrations of a tongue.”] not [Note: [Col. 0919D] Rhenanus adds “as though.”] partially, as others do. Thus he caused the authority of the Holy Spirit to attach to [Note: [Col. 0920D] “By authority to it,” Rhenanus, Semler.] the position which he wished us more especially to obey; and it became no longer the counsel of the divine Spirit but, in keeping with his majesty, a command.

## CHAPTER V

The very origin of the human race supports the establishment [Note: [Col. 0920D] “I shall establish,” Pamelius, Rhenanus, Semler.] of the law of marrying once, bearing witness to what God [Col. 0920B] established in the beginning [Note: [Col. 0920D] “From the beginning,” the same editions.] as a pattern to be followed [Note: [Col. 0920D] “To be reviewed,” others.] by posterity.

For when he had fashioned [Note: [Col. 0920D] Others write “molded as a potter” (*figulasset*).] the man and had foreseen that he needed a corresponding companion, he borrowed one of his ribs and fashioned one woman for him. Certainly neither the craftsman nor the material had failed: there were more ribs in Adam and tireless hands in God, but there were not to be more wives in God’s sight. Accordingly, Adam, the man of God, and Eve, the woman of God, fulfilled one marriage with each other. [Note: [Col. 0920D] “Fulfilled one marriage as a pattern for the people of God, etc.,” Rigault.] From the authority of their origin and God’s first will, they established a pattern for the people of God. Finally, “The two,” he says, “will become one flesh”—not three or four. Otherwise there would no longer be one flesh, nor two in one flesh. They will then [Note: [Col. 0920D] “There will no longer be one flesh; they will then be so, if the union, etc.,” Junius.] be two in one flesh if union and fusion into unity occur once. But if this occurs again [Col. 0920C] or repeatedly, it has ceased to be a unity: there will not be two in one flesh, but plainly one rib [Note: [Col. 0920D] “Flesh,” Semler, Rhenanus.] distributed among several.

Since the Apostle interprets the words “the two will become one flesh” as referring to the Church and Christ, according to the spiritual marriage of the Church and Christ—for there is one Christ and one Church belonging to him—we must recognize that the law [Note: [Col. 0920D] “Law” is absent from Pamelius, Rhenanus, Semler.] of one marriage has been doubled and intensified for us, both according to the foundation of the race and according to the mystery of Christ. In both respects we are registered under one marriage: carnally in Adam and spiritually in Christ. The rule of monogamy is one for our two births. Whoever departs from monogamy degenerates in both. A plurality of marriages began with a man under a curse. Lamech, the first to be married to two women, made three into one flesh.

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0921A]

“But,” you say, “even the blessed [Note: [Col. 0921C] “But even the blessed Patriarchs,” he says. In *To the Martyrs*: “Blessed martyrs designated among the nourishment of the flesh.” You also have this usage in Book IV of the *Life of Blessed Martin*: [Col. 0921D] “And the urn of the blessed martyr Fortunatus.” LE PR.] Patriarchs mingled marriage not merely with several wives but even with concubines.” Therefore shall it also be permissible for us [Note: [Col. 0921D] “To marry without numerical limit.” Elsewhere he said, “To make manifold use of marriages.” RIGAULT.] to marry without limit? Certainly it will be permissible [Note: [Col. 0921D] “If the types—the mysteries of some future reality—still remain.” Thus the exemplar reads, and Jerome reads no differently in his letter to Gerontia on monogamy. He calls types or figures “mysteries of future things,” sacred signs sent beforehand by God as signs of some future reality. RIGAULT.] if types still remain as mysteries of some future reality for your marriages to represent; or if there is still room for that declaration, “Increase and multiply”—that is, if another declaration has not yet supervened: “The time has now been drawn short; it remains that even those who have wives should behave as though they had none.” For by enjoining continence and restraining sexual intercourse, the seedbed of the race, he abolished [Note: [Col. 0921C] “Allows to become obsolete,” Pamelius, Rhenanus, Semler.] that command to increase and multiply.

In my judgment, both declarations and both arrangements belong to one and the same God. At the beginning he released the seed of the race, loosening the reins of marriage until the world should be filled, [Col. 0921B] until the material for the new discipline should mature. But now, at the end of the ages, he has restrained what he had released and recalled what he had granted—not without reason for the extension at the beginning and the pruning [Note: [Col. 0921C] “Renewed digging,” the same editions.] at the end. Beginnings are always given latitude; ends are drawn tight. [Note: [Col. 0921C] “Ends are drawn tight” is absent from the Venetian edition.] A person plants a forest and allows it to grow for the very purpose of cutting it down at the proper time. The forest will be the old dispensation, which is assigned to the new Gospel, in which also (Matt. 21) the axe has been laid at the root of the tree. Thus too, “an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth” has grown old since “let no one repay evil for evil” (Rom. 12:17) grew young. I think that even among human enactments and decrees, later provisions [Note: [Col. 0921C] “Subsequent,” Rhenanus, Semler, Leopolde.] prevail over earlier ones.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0921C]

Why, then, should we not instead recognize among the earlier examples [Col. 0922A] those that agree with the later ones [Note: [Col. 0921C] “Subsequent ones,” Rhenanus.] and transmit from antiquity to the new order both discipline and pattern? For behold, in the old law I observe that permission to marry repeatedly was curtailed. It was provided in Leviticus: “My priests shall not marry more than once” (Lev. 21:14). [Note: [Col. 0921D] I can say that anything which is not once is “more.” For “once,” as Asconius notes in his commentary on the second *Against Verres*, has the same sense when, he says, Lucilius writes that Crassus laughed once in his life and Cicero that Verres was terrified once in his life. RIGAULT.] I can say that anything which is not once is “more.” What is not one is a number. Indeed, number begins after one. Everything that occurs once, however, is one.

But the fullness of the law, in this matter as in the rest, was being reserved for Christ. [Note: [Col. 0921C] “For Christ alone,” Frankfurt, Paris, Gelenius; “in Christ,” Semler.] Accordingly, among us it is prescribed more fully and completely [Note: [Col. 0921C] “More structurally,” Rhenanus, Semler; “more strictly,” Frankfurt, Latin edition.] that those selected [Note: [Col. 0921C] Thus Rigault; Rhenanus’s edition: “whom he may select”; the Frankfurt edition: “whom it is lawful to select”; Wouwer’s codex: “whom it is proper to select into holy orders.” Leopolde conjectures that one should perhaps read: “whom they select into the priestly order.”] for the priestly order must be men of one marriage (Titus 1:6). I even remember some twice-married men being removed from office. But you will say, “Then it is permissible for the others, since he singles out those [Note: [Col. 0921C] Rhenanus: “It is permitted, since he does not single out those for whom it is not permitted—vain”; Pamelius: “It is permitted, since he singled out those for whom it is not permitted”; Paris has an abbreviated variant.] for whom it is not.” We shall be foolish [Col. 0922B] if we suppose that what is not lawful for priests is lawful for laypeople. Are not we laypeople also priests? It is written: “He has also made us a kingdom and priests to his God and Father” (Rev. 1:6).

The Church’s authority established the distinction between the order and the people, and the honor was sanctified through the order’s assembly. Accordingly, [Note: [Col. 0922C] “Accordingly,” Rhenanus; “sanctified; therefore, where,” Wouwer’s codex; “accordingly, where,” Frankfurt, Paris, Venetian edition; “by God,” Pamelius, Semler; “sanctified. Accordingly,” Leopolde.] [Note: [Col. 0921D] “Where there is no assembly of the ecclesiastical order.” In *On Baptism* he said that this order consists of bishops, presbyters, and deacons: accordingly, deacons are placed in the third degree of priesthood, presbyters in the second, [Col. 0922C] and bishops at the summit as chiefs of all. Hence bishops are also called high priests, and simply priests. Presbyters, however, are second priests, or, as in Sidonius, [Col. 0922D] prelates in the second order. Finally, laypeople—whether called commoners or the people—are all the others in the Church who are not yet supported by any dignity, as Optatus of Milevis says in Book I; in Book II he also subjects ministers to deacons. “The Church,” he says, “has its definite members: bishops, presbyters, deacons, ministers, and the multitude of the faithful.” The one who presided over both the multitude and the assembly was called by the general term “president,” “presiding officer,” or “one set over them”—Greek *ho proestōs* (ὁ προεστώς). RIGAULT.] where there is no assembly of the ecclesiastical order, you both offer and baptize, and you are a priest for yourself alone. [Note: [Col. 0922D] “You both offer and baptize, and you are a priest for yourself alone.” The Agobard exemplar reads exactly thus. These words appear obscure to those who do not observe what Tertullian usually signifies by the verb “to offer” and by the terms “offerings,” “prayers,” “sacrifices,” and, finally, “sacraments.” All these matters may be gathered from the *Index of Glosses*. RIGAULT.] Yet where there are three, there is a church, even though they are laypeople. For each person lives [Note: [Col. 0922C] “By his faith,” Rhenanus, Pamelius, Semler.] by his own faith, and there is no partiality with God, because it is not the hearers of the law who are justified [Note: [Col. 0922D] “Will be justified,” Rhenanus, Pamelius.] by God but its doers, as the Apostle also says (Rom. 2:11, 13).

Therefore, if you possess a priest’s right within yourself when necessity requires it, you must also possess a priest’s discipline when it is necessary to possess a priest’s right.
