[Note: [Col. 0922D] “You, a twice-married man, baptize!” Those who had married twice were not admitted by the Church to the priesthood; nor does the Church allow those who have “taken a widow” (*chēran labōn*, χήραν λαβών; the printed Greek, χήραν λαβίον, is corrupt) to preside, this same author says in Book I of *To His Wife*, ch. 7. LE PR.] [Col. 0922C] Do you, a twice-married man, baptize? Do you, a twice-married man, offer? [Note: [Col. 0922C] “Will you baptize? Will you offer?” Wouwer’s codex.] How much more capital an offense is it for a twice-married layman to act as a priest, [Note: [Col. 0922C] The first edition of Rhenanus is corrupt here; Frankfurt and Pamelius offer other readings.] [Col. 0923A] when even a priest, upon becoming twice married, is deprived of performing the priestly office! [Note: [Col. 0923C] The first edition of Rhenanus read: “to the priest it is said that by this act he is admitted to communion” (for which the Latin edition substituted “is excommunicated”) “from priestly action”; Pamelius read: “who by that act is admitted to communion with priestly action.”]

“But,” you say, “allowance is made for necessity.” No necessity is excused when it is capable of not existing. Take care, then, not to be found twice married, and you will not expose yourself to the necessity of administering [Note: [Col. 0923C] “Those administering under necessity,” Frankfurt.] what is not lawful for a twice-married man. God wills [Note: [Col. 0923C] “Willed,” Rhenanus, Pamelius.] all of us to be so ordered that we may everywhere be fit to perform his sacraments. [Note: [Col. 0923C] “To obey his ordinance,” others; “to obey his ordinances,” Pamelius.] One God, one faith, and one discipline. [Note: [Col. 0923C] Thus Rigault edited the passage; the others either omitted it or preserved nothing sound.] Indeed, unless laypeople too observe the qualifications by which presbyters are selected, how will there be presbyters, since presbyters are selected from the laity? Therefore, we must contend [Note: [Col. 0923C] “Endure,” Rhenanus, Frankfurt, Paris; “prefer,” Pamelius, Frankfurt; “bring forward,” Wouwer’s codex.] that the layman is commanded beforehand to abstain from a second marriage [Note: [Col. 0923C] “Retain,” Pamelius, Semler; “restrain,” Wouwer’s codex.], since no one can become a presbyter except a layman who [Note: [Col. 0923C] “Who” is absent from Semler.] has been the husband of one wife. [Note: [Col. 0923C] “Has married once,” Rhenanus, Semler, Pamelius.]

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0923B] Let it now be lawful to marry again, if everything lawful is good. The same Apostle cries out: “All things are lawful, but not all things are beneficial” [Note: [Col. 0923D] “For salvation,” Rhenanus, Pamelius, Semler.] (1 Cor. 6:12). I ask you: can what is not beneficial be called good? If even things that do not conduce to salvation are lawful, then things that are not good are also lawful. What, however, should you desire more: that which is good because [Note: [Col. 0924C] “Therefore,” Rhenanus, Pamelius.] it is lawful, or that which is good because [Note: [Col. 0924C] “Therefore,” Rhenanus, Pamelius.] it is beneficial? I consider the distance between license and salvation [Note: [Col. 0924C] “Utility,” Venetian edition; the others read “salvation.”] to be great.

One does not say of a good thing, [Note: [Col. 0924C] “You do not prevail, namely,” Rhenanus.] “It is lawful,” because a good thing does not wait to be permitted but to be embraced. What is permitted is something whose goodness is in doubt—something that could also be forbidden, were there not some prior cause for permitting it. A second marriage is permitted because of the danger of incontinence; for unless permission to do some thing that is not good lay before us, there would be no circumstance in which it could be proved [Col. 0923C] who obeyed the divine will and who obeyed his own power, [Note: [Col. 0923D] “Which of us pursues the presence of utility.” Perhaps *praestantiam* (“superior advantage”), a word he uses elsewhere when he means what is more advantageous. RIGAULT.] which of us pursued the immediate advantage [Note: [Col. 0924C] Perhaps “superior advantage,” Rigault.], and which embraced the opportunity furnished by license.

License is frequently a trial of discipline, because discipline is proved through trial, and trial operates through license. Thus it comes about that all things are lawful but not all are expedient: the person to whom permission is given is tested, and he is judged [Note: [Col. 0924C] Wouwer’s manuscript: “the one to whom it is permitted is also conquered.”] while being tested through the permission.

[Note: [Col. 0923D] It was lawful even for the Apostles to marry and take wives about with them. They had them as sisters, as Clement of Alexandria teaches in *Stromata* III. Hence the effort of the Lutherans, who attempt to establish clerical marriage from Tertullian, vanishes into smoke. After the Magdeburg Centuriators, Callistus, a distinguished Lutheran, undertook to defend this position and published a very large book on clerical marriage. Yet Socrates and Sozomen fall into error when they say that the Council of Nicaea left marriage free to clerics. How false this is appears from its third canon: *Apēgoreusen katholou hē megalē Synodos mēte episkopō, mēte presbyterō, mēte diakonō, mēte holōs tini tōn en klērō exeinai syneisakton echein; plēn ei mē ara mētera ē adelphēn, ē theian, ē ha mona prosōpa pasan hypopsian diapephygen* (ἀπηγόρευσεν καθόλου ἡ μεγάλη Σύνοδος μήτε ἐπισκόπῳ, μήτε πρεσβυτέρῳ, μήτε διακόνῳ, μήτε ὅλως τινὶ τῶν ἐν κλήρῳ ἐξεῖναι συνείσακτον ἔχειν· πλὴν εἰ μὴ ἄρα μητέρα ἢ ἀδελφήν, ἢ θείαν, ἢ ἃ μόνα πρόσωπα πᾶσαν ὑποψίαν διαπέφευγεν): “The great Synod absolutely forbade any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all belonging to the clergy to keep a woman brought into his household, except perhaps a mother, sister, aunt, or only such persons as are beyond every suspicion.” You have the same in canon 3 of the Council of Carthage and, from civil law, in the law *Sacris*, canon 45, *Concerning Bishops and Clerics*. LE PR.]

It was lawful even for the Apostles to marry and take wives about with them (1 Cor. 6:12); it was also lawful to live from the Gospel. But the one who did not use this right as an opportunity calls us to follow his example, teaching that the test lies precisely where permission has laid the groundwork for an experiment in abstinence. [Note: [Col. 0924C] “Laid the groundwork for abstinence,” Junius; “will have laid the groundwork,” Wouwer’s codex.]

## CHAPTER IX

If we interpret his meaning thoroughly, a second marriage will have to be called nothing other than a species of fornication. For when he says that husbands have this concern—how they may please themselves—he assuredly does not mean in respect of character, for he would not censure a good concern. Rather, he wishes them to be understood as concerned with dress, adornment, and every effort of beauty calculated to arouse [Note: [Col. 0924C] “Contrive,” Semler, Venetian edition.] enticements. But since pleasing by beauty and adornment belongs to the character of carnal desire, which is also the cause of fornication, does a second marriage not seem to you akin to fornication, since I find in it the features that belong to fornication?

The Lord himself says: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed fornication with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28). But he who looks upon her in order to marry her—has he done less [Note: [Col. 0924D] “Has he done less or more?” The exemplar reads, “has done less more.” Perhaps the particle *an* (“or”) coalesced with the following word through similarity of sound: *minus an plus fecit*.] or more? [Note: [Col. 0924C] “Has done less completely,” Frankfurt, Paris; “has done something less equal,” Rhenanus.] What if he has actually married her? He would not have done so unless he had desired her with a view to marrying her and had looked upon her with a view to desiring her—unless, perhaps, a wife can be married whom you have neither seen nor desired. [Note: [Col. 0924C] “Even if you have not seen her, at least you will have desired her when you begin to marry her,” Rhenanus, Paris, and others.]

There is certainly a great difference whether a married or unmarried man desires another woman. [Note: [Col. 0924C] “A husband who is not desiring out of jealousy,” Frankfurt, Paris; “certainly a husband is far removed from jealousy,” Pamelius.] [Col. 0924C] Every woman is “another woman” even to an unmarried man [Note: [Col. 0924C] “A woman has a jealous husband,” Pamelius, Paris, Frankfurt.] so long as she belongs to another; and yet she becomes a wife through no other act than that by which she also becomes an adulteress. The laws appear to distinguish marriage from fornication through a difference in lawfulness, not through the nature [Col. 0925A] of the act itself. Otherwise, what act [Note: [Col. 0925C] “What” is absent from Pamelius, Rhenanus, Semler.] is equally present for all men and women [Note: [Col. 0925C] “The same thing imposes; for it is also marriage,” Frankfurt, Paris, Pamelius.] in marriage and fornication? The union of the flesh, of course, whose desire the Lord [Note: [Col. 0925C] “Certainly we must contend that its desire,” Pamelius.] equated with fornication.

“Then,” you say, “you are now destroying even first—that is, single—marriages.” Not without reason, since they too consist of the same act as fornication. Therefore it is best for a man not to touch a woman; and therefore the preeminent sanctity of virginity, because it lacks affinity with fornication. And if these arguments can be advanced in favor of continence even against first and single marriages, how much more decisively will they prejudge the case for rejecting a second marriage! [Note: [Col. 0925C] “Will be foreseen,” Rhenanus, Pamelius.]

Be grateful if God has granted you permission to marry once; you will be grateful, however, if you do not suppose that he has granted you permission a second time. Otherwise you abuse indulgence when you use it without moderation. “Moderation” (*modestia*) is understood from “measure” (*modus*). [Col. 0925B] Is it not enough for you to have fallen, by marrying, from that highest degree of immaculate [Note: [Col. 0925C] Rhenanus joined the words; he conjectured “pure”; Pamelius and Paris, “unmarried.”] virginity to the second degree? [Note: [Col. 0925C] “To have sinned,” Rhenanus, Pamelius.] Must you still tumble down to the third, the fourth, and perhaps to still more, after failing to remain continent at the second station? For if he hesitated to provoke people toward second marriages, he certainly did not intend to prohibit a greater number! Let us marry every day, then, and let us be found marrying at the last day, like Sodom and Gomorrah—the day on which that “Woe to those who are pregnant” will be fulfilled, [Note: [Col. 0925C] Rigault supplied this word.] that is, against the married and incontinent; for wombs, breasts, and infants arise from marriage. And when will there be an end of marrying? [Note: [Col. 0925D] “I believe, after the end of living.” Jerome read thus in his letter to Gerontia, not as in the commonly printed editions, “after the end”—with “of living” understood. “Let us neigh,” he says, “after every woman, and, following the example of Sodom and Gomorrah, let us be found on the last day selling and buying, marrying and giving in marriage, so that the end of marriage comes only when life reaches its limit.” RIGAULT.] I believe, after the end of living.

## CHAPTER X

Let us renounce carnal things, so that at last we may turn again to spiritual things. [Note: [Col. 0925C] “May bear fruit,” Rigault.] Seize the opportunity—even if it is not the most desirable one, nevertheless a suitable one—of having no one to whom you must pay the marital debt and no one by whom it must be paid to you. You have ceased to be a debtor. O happy man! You have released your debtor; endure the loss. [Note: [Col. 0925D] “A similar loss,” Rhenanus, Pamelius.] What if you experience as profit what we have called a loss? For through continence you will trade for a great wealth of sanctity; through economy in the flesh you will acquire the spirit. [Note: [Col. 0925D] “Of the subservient flesh,” Frankfurt, Paris; “for the raging flesh,” Junius.]

Let us consider our own consciousness—how different a person a man feels himself to be when, perhaps, he abstains from his own woman: his inclination becomes spiritual. If [Col. 0926A] he offers prayer to the Lord, he is close to heaven. If he applies himself to the Scriptures, he is wholly present there. If he sings a psalm, he is pleasing to himself. If he adjures a demon, he has confidence in himself.

[Note: [Col. 0925D] For this reason the Apostle added a temporary purification for the sake of making prayers acceptable. He means a religious truce from marital relations. Juvenal’s statement in the sixth satire testifies that something of this kind also existed [Col. 0926D] among the Gentiles:

> He begs forgiveness whenever his wife does not abstain  
> From intercourse on sacred days that must be observed.

RIGAULT.]

For this reason the Apostle added a temporary purification for the sake of making prayers acceptable, so that we might know that what is beneficial for a time [Note: [Col. 0925D] “He recommended prayer for purification, alleging as the reason what he had permitted for a time,” Pamelius, Paris, Frankfurt.] must always be practiced by us, so that it may always be beneficial. Daily [Note: [Col. 0926C] Wouwer’s codex: “Daily—indeed, if at every moment.” Rigault: “Daily—at every moment.” Others: “If daily, at every moment.”]—indeed, at every moment—prayer is necessary for human beings; therefore continence too is necessary, once prayer is necessary.

Prayer proceeds from the conscience. If the conscience blushes, [Note: [Col. 0926C] Wouwer’s codex: “If the conscience blushes.” Rigault: “Of a blushing conscience.”] prayer blushes. The spirit conducts prayer to God. If the spirit is guilty in its own judgment because of a blushing conscience, how will it dare to conduct prayer from that conscience, [Note: [Col. 0926C] Agobard’s codex: “to conduct prayer from another matter.” Rigault alone reports the words from “from which” to “minister.”] when its holy minister is himself put to shame by the conscience’s shame? For there is a prophetic declaration of the Old Testament: [Col. 0926B] “You shall be holy, because God is holy” (Lev. 11:44–45; 19:2; 1 Pet. 1:16); and again: “With the holy you will be made holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent, and with the chosen you will be chosen” (Ps. 18:26).

For we must enter into the Lord’s discipline in a worthy manner, not according to the flesh’s burning desires. [Note: [Col. 0926C] Rhenanus and others preserve a corrupt reading: “so that a fruit worthy of God, not according to the flesh’s…” Rigault: “burning desires”; Paris perhaps: “filthy desires”; Junius likewise offers a conjecture.] For thus the Apostle too says that to be inclined according to the flesh is death, but to be inclined according to the spirit [Note: [Col. 0926D] “Is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.” After these words, a somewhat longer passage is found in a very ancient exemplar. It appears to have been rejected because of its excessive praises of that Montanist Prisca, whose words are also cited. Nevertheless, we reproduce it here, so that we may marvel all the more that so great a man could have been deceived even by such things. RIGAULT. [Col. 0927D] Rigault found the following inserted in his manuscript, and August Neander does not doubt that Tertullian himself wrote it: “Likewise, through the holy prophetess Prisca it is proclaimed as gospel that the holy minister should know how to minister holiness. ‘For purifying things are in harmony,’ she says, ‘and they see visions; and those who turn their faces downward also hear voices—manifest voices, as salutary as they are mysterious.’”] is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. If this defilement [Note: [Col. 0926D] “Dulling,” Frankfurt, Paris, Pamelius.] turns away the Holy Spirit even when the activity of the flesh is exercised within a single marriage, how much more when it is exercised in a second marriage?

## CHAPTER XI

For the shame is twofold, because in a second marriage two wives stand around the same husband: one in spirit, the other in the flesh. For you will not be able to hate the former wife, toward whom you preserve an even more religious [Note: [Col. 0926D] “Dearer,” Junius; “more illustrious,” Frankfurt, Paris.] affection now that she has been received by the Lord—for whose spirit you pray, and for whom you render annual offerings.

Will you therefore stand before the Lord with as many wives as you commemorate in prayer? Will you offer for two? Will you commend [Note: [Col. 0926D] “Commemorate,” Frankfurt, Paris.] those two through a priest ordained on the basis of monogamy, or even consecrated on the basis of virginity, surrounded by virgins and persons married only once? And will your sacrifice [Col. 0927A] ascend with an unashamed countenance? And among the other desires of a well-disposed mind, will you ask for chastity for yourself and your wife?

## CHAPTER XII
I know with what excuses we give a respectable appearance to the insatiable desire of the flesh: we plead the necessities of assistance—a household to administer, a family to govern, money-boxes and keys to guard, wool-work to assign, provisions to procure, and domestic cares to be attended to [Note: [Col. 0927C] “To be shared,” Rig.]. As if, indeed, only married men’s households prospered! The households of the unmarried, the possessions of eunuchs, and the fortunes of soldiers or travelers without wives have all perished, apparently. Are we not soldiers too—and soldiers under a discipline all the greater in proportion to the greatness of our Commander? Are we not also travelers in this world? Why, Christian, have you arranged your life so that you cannot do without a wife?

Now, however, a partner in domestic burdens is said to be necessary. Then have some spiritual wife: take one from among the widows, beautiful in faith, endowed with poverty, and distinguished by age. You will have made an excellent marriage. To have even several such wives is pleasing to God. Yet Christians give thought to posterity, though for them there is no tomorrow. Will a servant of God desire heirs when he has disinherited himself from the world? And is this why a man should marry again, if he has no children from his former marriage? His first concern, then, will be to wish to live longer, although the Apostle himself hastens toward the Lord! No doubt he will be entirely unencumbered in persecutions, utterly steadfast in martyrdoms, exceedingly ready in acts of fellowship, and thoroughly restrained in acquiring possessions. Finally, he will die free from anxiety, having perhaps left children who will perform funeral rites for him.

[Col. 0927C] Are marriages of this kind contracted, then, out of concern for the commonwealth as well, lest cities fail if offspring are not reared; lest laws, legal rights, and commerce collapse; lest temples be abandoned; and lest there be no one to shout: “THE CHRISTIANS TO THE BEASTS!” [Note: [Col. 0927C] “A lion for the Christians,” Rig.]? For this is what those who seek children desire to hear.

Even this may suffice as counsel in favor of widowhood, especially among us: the troublesome burden of children, whom human beings are compelled by law to rear—for every wise person would never willingly have desired children. What, then, will you do if you knowingly impregnate your new [Note: [Col. 0927C] “If unwillingly, a wife,” Ciaccon.; “if you are unwilling, if a wife,” Paris, Pam.] wife? Will you dissolve the conception with drugs [Note: [Col. 0927C] “You will dissolve it with a drug,” Fran., Par.]? I think it is no more lawful for us to kill one being born than one already born.

But perhaps, while your wife is pregnant, you will dare to ask God for a remedy to so grave an anxiety [Note: [Col. 0927D] “Will you dare to ask God amid such anxiety,” etc. I have read this passage, though with the wording altered slightly: “Will you dare amid such anxiety to ask for what you refused when it lay in your own power?” This is what Aristides says *On Concord, to the Rhodians*: ἄτοπον τοῖς θεοῖς ἐνοχλεῖν, αὐτοῖς δὲ μὴ βούλεσθαι πράττειν ἃ ἡμῖν εἶναι δοκεῖ τοῖς θεοῖς αὐτοῖς [text materially uncertain]. “It is ridiculous to weary the gods, yet to be unwilling oneself to do those things which the gods themselves know to lie within our power.” [Col. 0928D] Thus Demosthenes rebukes the Greeks in *Philippic III*: they behaved like those who watch hail about to fall and wish themselves safe from it, though no one makes any effort to avert it. Le Pr.]—something which you refused when it lay within your own power [Note: [Col. 0927C] “In such solitude,” Rhen.]?

Some woman believed to be barren, I suppose, will be chosen, or at least one of more advanced and colder age. A sufficiently prudent plan—and, above all, a faithful one! For we have believed that no woman is barren, if God wills otherwise, nor any old woman incapable of giving birth. Indeed, this may happen all the more readily if someone, through presumption upon such foresight of his own, provokes God’s jealousy. We know, in fact, a certain one of the brethren who, because of his daughter, sought a barren wife in a second marriage, and became a father a second time just as surely as he became a husband a second time.

## CHAPTER XIII

To this exhortation of mine [Note: [Col. 0927C] “Contention,” Fran., Par., Pam.], dearly beloved brother, there are also added secular examples [Note: [Col. 0928D] There are also added secular examples. Porphyry reports that even among those who sacrificed sheep and oxen, chastity was held in the highest esteem: ἀγνήν τε ταύτην κομιζόντα τὴν ἱερὸν ὅσιον καὶ θεοῖς κεχαρισμένην [text materially uncertain], “bringing this sacred chastity, holy and pleasing to the gods.” Rig.]. These have often been set forth even as testimony for us, whenever something good and pleasing to God is recognized even by outsiders and is given the weight of their testimony.

Indeed, monogamy is held in such supreme honor among the pagans that, when virgins are lawfully married, a woman who has had only one husband is employed as the *pronuba* [matron of honor] [Note: [Col. 0928D] A once-married *pronuba*. According to Donatus, the *pronuba*, on the wife’s side, presided over and attended the ceremonies preceding a marriage, just as the *auspex*, whom the Author also mentions here, did on the husband’s side. He was so called because the *auspicia* were named as though *avispicia*: he used to take omens for marriages from the flight of birds. Pam.]. And if she is employed for the sake of the omen, it is certainly regarded as a good omen. Likewise, in certain solemn rites and offices, precedence is given to the woman who has had only one husband. Certainly, a priest’s wife (*flaminica*) must be once-married, and this is also the law governing the priest (*flamen*). For since, in the first place, even the chief pontiff himself is not permitted to marry again, this is assuredly a distinction conferred upon monogamy.

[Col. 0928C] But when Satan imitates God’s mysteries, it is a challenge to us—indeed, a cause for shame—if we are sluggish in offering God the continence that some render to the devil, now by virginity, now by perpetual widowhood [Note: [Col. 0928C] “Who excel, now by virginity, now by widowhood, emasculate,” Fran.]. We know the virgins of Vesta; those of Juno in an Achaean town; those of Apollo at Ephesus; and those of Minerva in certain places. We also know continent men [Note: [Col. 0928C] “But since Satan is merely God’s ape, this is a challenge to us for attaining perfection … because to the devil … we know the virgins of Vesta at Rome, of Juno in Achaia, of Apollo at Delphi, and of Minerva and Diana everywhere. We know continent men,” Cod. Wouw.], including, indeed, the priests of that Egyptian bull. We know women devoted to African Ceres, for whom they even voluntarily renounce marriage and grow old, thereafter turning away from contact with males [Note: [Col. 0929B] “Thereafter with contact removed,” Fran., Par.], even from the kisses of their sons.

Thus the devil, after sensuality, has also devised a chastity that destroys [Note: [Col. 0929B] “The splendor of chastity,” Fran., Par.], so that the Christian who has refused the chastity that preserves may be all the more guilty.

Certain secular women, too, will serve as testimony for us, having won renown through their unyielding devotion to single marriage: Dido, for example [Note: [Col. 0929B] “Some Dido,” Rig.], who, though an exile on foreign soil, where she ought eagerly to have desired marriage to a king, nevertheless preferred, rather than experience a second marriage, to be burned instead of wed [Note: [Col. 0929B] She preferred, contrariwise, to burn rather than marry. By the contrary fire, that is, she extinguished the fire of love. Rig.]; or Lucretia, who, although only once and by force, and against her will, endured another man [Note: [Col. 0929B] “So that,” Fran., Par., and Rhen.], washed the defiled flesh with her own blood [Note: [Col. 0929B] Defiled flesh—for her mind had remained undefiled by adultery. Accordingly, that saying of a certain ancient declaimer was splendidly and most truthfully expressed: “There were two, and one committed adultery.” Augustine, however, admirably diminishes the glory of this deed as empty, human, and by no means Christian, saying that there is nothing in it deserving such extravagant praise. “Lucretia, having been violated,” he says, “killed the chaste Lucretia. Why do you praise so highly the murderess of an innocent and chaste woman?” Rig.] so that she might not live after she was no longer, in her own judgment, the wife of only one man [Note: [Col. 0929B] “Defiled,” Rhen.; “certainly,” Rhen., Seml., Pam.].

You may find more examples among our own people by searching more carefully [Note: [Col. 0930B] You may find more examples among our own people by searching more carefully. We reproduce the entire sentence here as it stands in the Agobardine manuscript. Rig.], and examples all the more excellent inasmuch as it is easier to live in chastity than to die for it—that is, to unite that good with the soul rather than to be separated from it by ceasing to live [Note: [Col. 0930B] “Than for the soul to be separated from evil by living,” Jun.; “for that good to be implanted, rather than separated from one while living,” Lat.; “than to be separated by not living. How many men and women,” Cod. Wouw.; “than for the soul to be separated by living,” Fran., Par.].

How many men and women, therefore, are ranked in the ecclesiastical orders on account of continence—those who preferred to marry God, who restored the honor of their flesh, and who dedicated themselves as children of that coming age, killing within themselves the desire of lust and that whole thing which could not be admitted within paradise? From this it must be presumed that those who wish to be received into paradise must at last cease from that by which paradise remained untouched.

[Col. 0929]

# QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN: ON MONOGAMY

[Note: [Col. 0929D] In this book, and likewise in those that follow, he openly defends Montanus’s doctrine. He believed that the day of the Lord was imminent and wished the faithful to be as fully prepared as possible for martyrdoms. He therefore thought that Christians should be stripped of all the bonds of a more humane life, which tended to make their spirits more sluggish in facing dangers. Such are wives and children and the manifold cares arising from them. This counsel might perhaps otherwise have been excusable; but since he did not hesitate to advance it by distorting the words both of God and of the Apostle—from which many gave themselves excessive reassurance—it was rightly censured and condemned by the Church. Rig.]

## BOOK (C)

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0929B]

Throughout this work he calls Montanus the Paraclete [Col. 0929C] and denies that he is a heretic, although he himself follows the sect of the Cataphrygians. He claims, however, to hold a middle course between those who reject marriage and others who introduce repeated marriages in plurality. He accordingly defends monogamy and teaches that this discipline is not new, but ancient and proper to Christians.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0930B]

[Col. 0930C] Heretics abolish marriages [Note: [Col. 0929D] Heretics abolish marriages. Here he designates only the Marcionites, who condemned marriage. Le Pr.]; the “psychic” Christians thrust them upon us [Note: [Col. 0929C] “Natural philosophers,” Rhen.] [Note: [Col. 0929D] The “psychic” Christians thrust them upon us. He appears to wish to hold a middle course between the Marcionites, who condemned marriage, and the Psychics, who permitted repeated marriages. There is no doubt, however, that by “Psychics” he means the orthodox, among whose number he testifies that he himself once belonged in *Against Praxeas*, ch. 1: “We indeed were later separated from the Psychics by our recognition and defense of the Paraclete.” He called them “Psychics,” that is, natural or merely animate persons, because after becoming a follower of Montanus he called himself “spiritual”; but “the psychic man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God,” as the Apostle has it in 1 Corinthians 2: ψυχικὸς δὲ ἄνθρωπος οὐ δέχεται τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ θεοῦ, “But the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God.” Rig.]. The former do not marry even once; the latter marry more than once.

What are you doing, law of the Creator? Amid eunuchs alien to you [Note: [Col. 0930D] Amid eunuchs alien to you. That is, amid heretics who abolish marriages. Heretics are alien and foreign to Catholics. He calls the haters of marriage eunuchs. Rig.] and your own charioteers [Note: [Col. 0930D] “And your charioteers.” It should read *et perorigas tuos*. In Varro, *On Agriculture*, book II, where he discusses the mating of mares, anyone who admits them to the male is called a *peroriga*. Thus, with great wit, he calls the Psychics—who, as he says, thrust marriages upon people and as it were induce an itch—*perorigas*, or *praurigas*, or *prurigas*. He says “your own” while addressing the law, for even Septimius did not regard the Psychics, who were also Catholics, as alien to it. Rig.—“Your urgers.” If one reads *urigas*, as though from “burning,” meaning those who stir up an itch, what aid will come from Pamelius’s conjectures about charioteers in the Roman Circus? Le Pr.] you complain just as much about obedience from within your household as about rejection by outsiders; accordingly, those who abuse you injure you just as do those who make no use of you.

But neither is continence of the former kind to be praised, because it is heretical, nor is license of the latter kind to be defended, because it is psychic. The one blasphemes; the other indulges in excess. The one destroys the God of marriage; the other throws marriage into confusion.

Among us, however, whom recognition [Note: [Col. 0931D] “Recognition” is absent from Rhen. and Fran.] of spiritual gifts rightly causes to be called spiritual, continence is as religious as permission is modest, since both accord with the Creator. Continence honors the law of marriage; permission moderates it. The former is not compelled; the latter is governed. The former possesses freedom of choice; the latter has a limit. We acknowledge one marriage, just as we acknowledge one God. The law of marriage receives greater honor where it also possesses modesty.

Yet because the Psychics do not receive the Spirit, the things of the Spirit do not please them. Thus, while the things of the Spirit do not please them, the things of the flesh will please them, [Col. 0931B] as things opposed to the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0931D] “Opposed to the Spirit’s,” Rhen.]. “The flesh,” he says, “desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17). What, however, will the flesh desire except what most belongs to the flesh? For this reason, even at the beginning it became alien to the Spirit: “My Spirit,” he says, “shall not remain in these human beings forever, because they are flesh” (Gen. 6:3).

## CHAPTER II

They therefore reproach the discipline of monogamy as heresy [Note: [Col. 0931D] “Reproach,” Rhen.]. Nor are they compelled to deny the Paraclete for any reason more than because they suppose him to be the founder of a new discipline—one exceedingly harsh [Note: [Col. 0931D] “Most dreadful,” Rhen.] to them. Consequently, we must first take our stand on this point in [Note: [Col. 0931D] “That,” Rhen.] a general examination: whether it is possible that the Paraclete taught anything of such a kind that it could either be reckoned new in opposition to catholic tradition, or burdensome in opposition to the Lord’s light burden [Col. 0931C] [Note: [Col. 0932D] “Of the Lord” is absent from Rhen. and Par.].

On both points, however, the Lord himself pronounced judgment. For when he said, “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot yet bear them. When the Holy Spirit comes, he will lead you into all truth” (John 16:12), he surely gave sufficient advance notice that the Spirit would do things which might be thought both new, because they had never previously been disclosed, and somewhat burdensome, since this was why they had not been disclosed.

“Then,” you say, “by this argument anything whatever that is new and burdensome could be ascribed to the Paraclete, even if it came from an adversarial spirit.” Certainly not. For an adversarial spirit would become evident from the divergence of its proclamation [Note: [Col. 0932D] “Becomes evident,” Leop.], first corrupting the rule of faith and then corrupting the order of discipline. For the corruption of that which occupies the first rank must come first—that is, the corruption of faith, which precedes [Col. 0931D] discipline. A person must first be a heretic concerning God, and only afterward concerning conduct.

The Paraclete, however, having many things to teach which the Lord deferred to him, will, in accordance with that prior definition, first bear witness to Christ himself as we believe him to be, together with the entire ordering of God the Creator; he will glorify Christ himself and bring Christ himself to remembrance. Once recognized by this principal rule, he will thus reveal those many matters belonging to disciplines, the integrity of his proclamation providing assurance for them: although new, because they are only now revealed; although burdensome, because even now they are not borne. Yet they belong to no other Christ than the one who said that he had many other things to be taught by the Paraclete, things no less burdensome to these people than they were to those who could not yet bear them at that time.

## CHAPTER III

Whether monogamy is burdensome may still be considered by the shameless weakness of the flesh. For the present, let it be established whether it is new. Indeed, we go further and say that even if the Paraclete today had prescribed complete and absolute virginity or continence, so as not to permit the heat of the flesh to spend itself even in a single marriage, he would still appear to introduce nothing new. For the Lord himself opened the kingdoms of heaven to eunuchs (Matt. 19:12), [Note: [Col. 0931D] “Being himself also a eunuch.” Although that term, by which Christ the Lord is designated, agrees poorly with his extraordinary integrity, no one doubts that he was a virgin [Col. 0932D] and born of a virgin. Le Pr.] being himself also a eunuch; and the Apostle, looking toward him and therefore likewise castrated, prefers continence.

“But,” you say, “with the right to marry preserved.” Certainly preserved; and we shall see for how long. Nevertheless, it is already abolished on that side on which continence is preferred. “It is good,” he says, “for a man not to touch a woman” (1 Cor. 7:1). Therefore, it is evil to touch one. [Note: [Col. 0932D] For nothing is contrary to good except evil. Here he treats at somewhat greater length what he touched upon in the preceding book, ch. 3. From both passages the blessed Jerome transcribed nearly the very words in book I *Against Jovinian*. In his *Apology to Pammachius* he shows how they may be understood without condemning first marriages. Pam.] For nothing is contrary to good except evil.

Accordingly, it remains that even those who have wives should be as though they had none; all the more, those who have none ought not to acquire them. He also gives the reasons why he offers this counsel: the unmarried think about God, whereas the married think about how each may please his spouse in marriage (1 Cor. 7:32).

I can also maintain that what is permitted is not purely good. For what is purely good is not permitted as an indulgence; it is lawful of itself. Permission has a cause, sometimes even one of necessity [Note: [Col. 0932D] “Necessity,” Seml.]. Indeed, in the present instance it is not the will of the one granting permission that people marry. For he wills something else: “I wish,” he says, “that all of you were as I am” (1 Cor. 7:7). And when he shows that something is better [Note: [Col. 0932D] “That something is better, certainly,” Seml.], what does he thereby confirm that he wills, if not what he had already declared to be better? Thus, if he permits something other than what he willed, granting it not from willingness but from necessity, he shows that what he reluctantly conceded is not purely good.

Indeed, when he says, “It is better to marry than to burn,” what kind of good must that be understood to be which is better than a punishment? How can it appear better except in comparison with something worst? That is good [Col. 0933A] which possesses this name in itself, without comparison—not merely with evil, but even with some other good—so that, even if it is overshadowed by comparison with another [Note: [Col. 0933D] “Another,” Seml.] good, it nevertheless retains the name of good. But if something is forced to be called good through comparison with evil, it is not so much good as a lesser kind of evil which, obscured by a greater evil, is driven into receiving the name of good.

Remove, then, the condition, so that you do not say, “It is better to marry than to burn,” and I ask whether you dare say simply, “It is better to marry,” without adding what it is better than. It is therefore no longer “better”; and since it is not better, neither is it good once the condition has been removed—the condition which, by making it better than something else, forces it thus to be regarded as good. It is better to lose one eye than two. Yet if you withdraw from comparison between both evils [Note: [Col. 0934D] “Evils” omitted by Seml.], it will not be better to have one eye, because neither is it good.

What if, then, he grants every indulgence for marrying on his own authority—that is, from human judgment—because of the necessity we have mentioned, since “it is better to marry than to burn”? Indeed, when he turns to the other case and says, “To the married, however, I give this command—not I, but the Lord,” he shows that what he had said above did not possess the Lord’s authority, but rested upon human judgment. Yet when he redirects their minds toward continence—“I wish, however, that all of you were so; and I think,” he says, “that I too have the Spirit of God”—it is as though he were revoking by the Holy Spirit’s authority whatever he had granted out of necessity.

John too, when he warns that we ought to walk just as the Lord walked, plainly warns us to walk also according to holiness of the flesh. “And everyone,” he says, “who has this hope in him makes himself chaste, just as he himself is chaste” (1 John [Col. 0933C] 3:3) [Note: [Col. 0933D] “Makes himself chaste, just as he himself is chaste.” From John’s Epistle, 3, he translates more freely than is proper, rendering ἁγνίζει ἑαυτόν as “makes himself chaste,” and ἁγνός as “chaste”; for the meaning is “pure” and “clean.” Le Pr.]. For elsewhere too: “Be holy, just as he was holy” (1 John 2:3), namely, in the flesh. He would not have said this of the spirit, because the spirit is recognized as holy of itself and does not await an admonition to holiness, which belongs to it by its own nature. The flesh, however, is taught holiness—a holiness which was also present in Christ.

Therefore, if all these things efface the permission to marry—both when the condition of that permission is examined and when the preference for continence is imposed—why could not the same Spirit, coming after the Apostles to lead discipline into all truth, through the stages of the times (in accordance with the saying of Ecclesiastes, “There is a time for everything”), now place the final clasp upon the flesh, no longer indirectly calling it away from marriage, but openly doing so [Note: [Col. 0933D] “Especially since the time has now been shortened.” In precisely this sense the blessed Jerome writes in his letter to Gerontia: “What is that to us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come?” Le Pr.], especially since the time has now been shortened, about 160 years having elapsed since then?

Would you not reconsider the matter within yourself? “This discipline is ancient, already foreshown at that time in the Lord’s flesh and will, and thereafter in both the counsels and examples of his Apostles. Long ago we were destined for this holiness. The Paraclete introduces nothing new. What he gave warning of, he now defines; what he tolerated, he now demands.” And if you now reflect upon these things, you will readily persuade yourself that it was far more fitting for the Paraclete to proclaim single marriage—he who could have proclaimed no marriage at all—and that he should all the more be believed to have moderated what he might fittingly have abolished, if you understand what Christ wills. In this too [Note: [Col. 0933D] You ought to recognize the Paraclete as an advocate. He plays upon the meaning of the word παράκλητος, which signifies “advocate,” but the Author’s application is ridiculous. Pam.] you ought to recognize the Paraclete as an advocate, because he excuses your weakness from total continence.

## CHAPTER IV

Let mention of the Paraclete now withdraw, as though he were an authority belonging only to some of us. Let us unroll the shared documents of the earlier Scriptures. Our very point is demonstrated from them: that the discipline of monogamy is neither new nor foreign but, rather, both ancient and proper to Christians, so that you may regard the Paraclete as its restorer rather than its founder.

As far as antiquity is concerned, what pattern can be produced more ancient than the very origin of the human race? God fashioned one woman for the male, taking one of his ribs, though certainly he had several. In the preface to this very work he also said: “It is not good for the man to be alone; let us make a helper for him.” He would have said “helpers” if he had destined him for several wives. He also added a law concerning the future. For it was said prophetically: “And the two shall become one flesh” (Gen. 2:18, 24)—not three or more. Otherwise, they would no longer be two if there were more.

The law stood firm. Indeed, the union of marriage endured in the founders of the race right to the end—not because there were no other women, but because they did not exist for this very purpose: that the firstfruits of the race should not be defiled by double marriage. Otherwise, had God willed it, they could have existed. Adam certainly could have taken a wife from the number of his daughters, having Eve no less from his own bones and flesh, if this could have been done piously.

But when the first crime, homicide, was inaugurated in fratricide, no crime was so worthy of second place as two marriages. [Note: [Col. 0934D] For it makes no difference whether a man had two wives one after the other, or both together made two. Indeed, because it makes a very great difference, an edict of the praetor marks with infamy the man who has contracted two betrothals or two marriages at the same time. Rig.] For it makes no difference whether a man had two wives one after the other or had two together: the number is the same, whether the persons joined are together or separated.

Although God’s institution was once violated by Lamech, it thereafter remained firm until the end of that race. No second Lamech appears as the husband of two women. [Note: [Col. 0934D] Scripture denies what it does not record. When I first read these words, though only in passing and superficially, they seemed rather harsh in an author who had defended tradition so strongly. But there he was orthodox; here he has strayed from the truth. Le Pr.] Scripture denies what it does not record. Other iniquities provoked the Flood and, whatever they were, were punished once [Col. 0934D]; yet not seventy-seven times, which was what two marriages deserved.

Moreover, the re-formation of the second human race is reckoned through monogamy as its mother. Again there are two in a single marriage. Monogamy is recognized even among the animals, lest even beasts should be born from adultery. “From all the beasts,” he says, “from every kind of flesh, you shall bring two into the ark so that they may live with you: male and female. Of the winged creatures according to their kind, and of all the creeping things of the earth according to their kind, two of every kind shall enter with you: male and female.” By the same pattern, he commands that the groups of seven be selected in pairs, male and female, one male and one female. What more shall I say? Even unclean birds were not permitted to enter with two females.

## CHAPTER V

So much for the testimony of the beginnings, the advocacy of our origin, and the prescriptive authority of the divine institution. This is assuredly a law, not a mere memorial. For if it was established thus from the beginning, we find ourselves directed back to the beginning by Christ. Thus, in the question concerning divorce, when he says that it was permitted by Moses because of their hardness but had not been so from the beginning, he undoubtedly recalls the indivisibility of marriage to its beginning. Therefore, the two whom God joined from the beginning into one flesh, man shall not separate today (Gen. 2:24).

The Apostle too says, writing to the Ephesians, that God purposed in himself, for the dispensation of the fullness of the times, to bring all things back to the head—that is, back to the beginning—in Christ, the things above the heavens and the things upon the earth, in him (Eph. 1:9–10).

Thus the Lord also assumed for himself the two Greek letters, the first and the last, as figures of the beginning and the end converging in himself. Just as α rolls onward to ω and ω in turn folds back to α (Rev. 1:8; 22:13), so he showed that in himself are both the course of the beginning toward the end and the return of the end to the beginning. Thus every dispensation, ending in him through whom it began—namely, through the Word of God, who became flesh—likewise ends just as it began.

And to such an extent are all things recalled [Note: [Col. 0935D] “Were recalled,” Rhen.] to the beginning in Christ that faith has returned from circumcision to the integrity of the flesh, as it was from the beginning; the freedom of foods and abstinence from blood alone have returned, as they were from the beginning; the indivisibility of marriage has returned, as it was from the beginning; divorce has been restrained, since it did not exist from the beginning; and, finally, the whole human being is recalled to paradise, where he was from the beginning. Why, then, should Christ not restore Adam there as at least a monogamist, when he cannot present him as wholly unblemished as when he was sent from there?

As far as the restoration of the beginning is concerned, therefore, the principle of both your dispensation and your hope requires of you what existed from the beginning, according to the beginning which is reckoned for you in Adam and reckoned anew in Noah. Choose in which of them you reckon your beginning: in both, the rule of monogamy claims you for itself.

But if the beginning passes onward to the end, as α to ω, and the end passes back to the beginning, as ω to α, and our origin is thus transferred into Christ—from the natural to the spiritual, because the spiritual does not come first, but the natural, and afterward the spiritual—then let us see whether you owe this same obligation to this second origin also, and whether it is fitting for you to exist in the same form as the last Adam and the first. For the last Adam, that is, Christ, was entirely unmarried, as the first Adam also was before his exile.

Yet, by the example of his own flesh, the more perfect Adam—that is, Christ, more perfect in this respect also because more inviolate—makes a concession to the weakness of your flesh. If you are willing, he meets you in the flesh as a eunuch; but if you are not equal to that, he meets you in the spirit as a monogamist, having one bride, the Church, according to the figure of Adam and Eve. The Apostle interprets this as that great mystery concerning Christ and the Church, showing that fleshly monogamy corresponded to the spiritual.

You see, therefore, how, even when renewing your origin in Christ, you cannot establish it without a profession of monogamy—unless you are in the flesh what he is in the spirit, although you ought equally to have been what he was in the flesh.

But let us seek still other founders of our origin. For certain people are not pleased with monogamous parents—Adam and Noah, and perhaps not even Christ. They appeal instead to Abraham, although forbidden to acknowledge any father other than God. Let Abraham now be our father, then; and let Paul be so too: “In the gospel,” he says, “I begot you” (1 Cor. 4:16).

Show yourself also to be Abraham’s son. For your descent from him is not indiscriminate [Note: [Col. 0935D] Indiscriminate descent, etc. Rhenanus says that he calls “indiscriminate descent” an unlimited, wandering, unrestricted, and permissive—or licentious—descent. Pam.]. There is a definite time at which he is your father. For if we are reckoned Abraham’s children by faith, as the Apostle teaches when he says to the Galatians, “You know, surely, that those who are of faith are the children of Abraham” (Gal. 3:7), when did Abraham believe God and have it reckoned to him as righteousness? While still, I think, in monogamy, because he was not yet under circumcision.

But if he was afterward changed in both respects—into double marriage through concubinage with the slave-woman, and into circumcision through the seal of the covenant—you cannot acknowledge him as father except at the time when he believed God, since you are his child according to faith, not according to the flesh. Or if you follow the later Abraham as your father—that is, the twice-married Abraham—accept him also as circumcised. If you reject the circumcised Abraham, you must likewise reject the twice-married one. You cannot combine his two dispensations, which differ from each other in two corresponding ways. He began to be twice-married together with circumcision, and was monogamous together with uncircumcision.

Do you accept double marriage? Admit circumcision too. Do you defend uncircumcision? You are bound to monogamy as well. So fully are you the son of the monogamous Abraham, just as you are of the uncircumcised Abraham, that if you are circumcised, you are no longer a son, because you will not be a son by faith but by the seal of the faith that was justified in uncircumcision. You have the Apostle; learn together with the Galatians.

Accordingly, even if you bring double marriage upon yourself, you are not the son of that Abraham whose faith came first during monogamy. For although he was afterward called the father of many nations, these were the nations whose members, through the faith that preceded his double marriage, were accounted Abraham’s children. Let what followed take care of itself.

Figures are one thing, forms another; images are one thing, definitions another. Images pass away when fulfilled; definitions remain to be fulfilled. Images prophesy; definitions govern. What Abraham’s double marriage foreshadows, the same Apostle teaches, as interpreter of both Testaments, just as he determines that our seed was called in Isaac.

If you belong to the free woman and pertain to Isaac, he certainly maintained one marriage. These, then, are the persons, I think, among whom I am reckoned. The rest I do not know.

If you look about for examples from those others—some David forcing marriages upon himself even through bloodshed, some Solomon rich even in wives—you have been commanded to follow better examples. You have Joseph, the husband of one wife, and by this title, I dare say, better than his father. You have Moses, the one admitted close to God’s counsel. You have Aaron, the chief priest. [Note: [Col. 0937D] A second Moses. He means Joshua the son of Nun, concerning whose marriages Scripture relates nothing. Accordingly, nothing can be inferred from him either for or against marriage, whether first or second. Nevertheless, Jerome follows Septimius in book I *Against Jovinian*: “Show me,” he says, “that Joshua the son of Nun had either a wife or children.” Rig.] The second Moses too, of the second people—the one who led our figure [Col. 0937B] into God’s promise, and in whom the Lord’s name was first inaugurated—was not twice married.

## CHAPTER VII
After the ancient examples of the original persons, let us likewise pass to the ancient documents of the legal Scriptures, so that we may review in order [Note: [Col. 0937D] “Of all our equipment.” He means the Scriptures of both Instruments, or Testaments. RIG.] all our equipment. And since certain people sometimes say that they have nothing to do with the Law—which Christ did not abolish but fulfilled—while at other times they seize upon whatever parts of the Law they please, we too plainly say that the Law has passed away in such a manner that its burdens, which, according to the judgment of the apostles, not even the Fathers were willing to bear, have been remitted; but those provisions that concern righteousness not only remain preserved but have even been enlarged, so that our righteousness may, of course, exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees [Col. 0937C]. If righteousness, then chastity as well.

If, therefore, because the Law commands a man to take in marriage the wife of his brother who has died childless, in order to raise up offspring for his brother, and because this can happen repeatedly to a single person, as in that cunning question of the Sadducees, they consequently think that repeated marriages of other kinds are also permitted, they must first understand the rationale of that commandment. They will then know that, since its rationale has now ceased, it belongs among those provisions of the Law that have been annulled.

It was necessary to succeed to the marriage of a brother who had died childless. First, because that ancient blessing still had to run its course: “Increase and abound” (Gen. I, 28). Next, because the offenses of fathers were still exacted from their children. Third, because eunuchs and the sterile were regarded as dishonorable [Col. 0937D]. Accordingly, lest those who had died childless—not through any fault of nature, but because death had overtaken them—should on that account be judged accursed [Col. 0938A], a substitute and, as it were, posthumous offspring was procured for them from their own stock.

But when the end of the ages annulled “Increase and abound,” with the apostle declaring (I Cor. VII, 29), “It remains that even those who have wives should be as though they had none, because the time has been shortened”; and when “The sour grape eaten by the fathers has ceased to set the children’s teeth on edge, for each person shall die in his own offense” (Jer. XXXI, 29); and when eunuchs not only ceased to bear disgrace but even merited grace, being invited into the kingdoms of heaven—then, once the law of succeeding to a brother’s marriage had been buried, its contrary, the rule of not succeeding to a brother’s marriage, took its place. And thus, as we said before [Note: [Col. 0937D] “As we say beforehand,” Venetian edition.], a provision that has ceased to be valid because its rationale has ceased cannot furnish an argument for another matter [Col. 0938B].

Therefore, after her husband has died, a wife will not marry—for, if she does marry, she will of course marry a brother. For we are all brothers, and she who intends to marry must marry “in the Lord,” that is, not a gentile but a brother, because the ancient Law also forbids marriage with foreigners. But since Leviticus also provides, “Whoever takes his brother’s wife—it is uncleanness, a shameful thing—shall die childless” [Note: [Col. 0938D] “They shall die,” Frankfort and Venetian editions.] (Lev. XX, 31), there can be no doubt that, while he is forbidden to marry again, she too is forbidden, since she may marry none but a brother.

How this will agree with the apostle and with the Law, which he does not oppose altogether, will be shown when we come to his epistle. Meanwhile, so far as the Law is concerned, its arguments favor us more. Indeed, the same Law forbids priests to marry again (Lev. XXXI, 14). [Note: [Col. 0937D] “A priest’s daughter also,” etc. Blessed Jerome puts it more clearly: “A priest’s widow is commanded to remain in her father’s house and not to know a second marriage.” But [Col. 0938D] the Author follows the words of Scripture in Lev. XXII. PAM.] It also commands a priest’s daughter [Col. 0938C], if widowed or divorced and without offspring, to return to her father’s house and be sustained from his bread. It says “if she has no offspring” not so that, if she does have offspring, she may marry again—for how much less will she marry if she has children!—but so that, if she has a son, she may be supported by him rather than by her father, and the son may thereby fulfill God’s commandment, “Honor father and mother” (Lev. XXXI, 13).

But Jesus, the high and great priest of the Father, clothing us with what is his own—for “those who are baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III, 27)—[Note: [Col. 0938D] “He made us priests to God his Father.” On the meaning of this passage and the words that follow, see the preceding book, chap. 7. PAM.] made us priests to God his Father, according to John (Apoc. I, 6). For he also calls back that young man who was hastening to his father’s funeral precisely to show that we are called by him to be priests, whom the Law forbade to attend the burial of their parents: [Note: [Col. 0938D] “Over any dead soul,” he says. Here too he compares the evangelical law with the Law of Moses, because the high priest is forbidden to bury his father, Lev. XXI. Therefore, in the Author as well, one must understand the description given of Jesus shortly before: “high priest,” or “great priest”; otherwise other priests were permitted to approach the body of a father, mother, brother, and virgin sister, as is stated at the beginning [Col. 0939D] of the same chapter. Hence blessed Jerome likewise cites this of the high priest in Epistle 25, on the death of Blaesilla, to Paula. PAM.] “The priest shall not approach any dead soul, and he shall not defile himself even for his father or his mother” [Col. 0938D] (Lev. XXII, 13).

Must we, then, observe this prohibition too [Col. 0939A]? Certainly not. For our one Father, God, lives, as does our mother, the Church; nor are we ourselves dead, since we live to God; nor do we bury the dead, because they too live in Christ. Yet we are certainly priests called by Christ, and therefore debtors to monogamy under the ancient Law of God, which at that time prefigured us in its priests.

## CHAPTER VIII

Now, turning to the law that is properly our own, that is, the Gospel, by what examples are we received! When we come to its pronouncements, behold, immediately, as though upon the threshold, two [Note: [Col. 0939D] “Two,” another reading.] presiding figures of Christian holiness meet us: monogamy and continence—the one chaste in Zechariah the priest, the other inviolate in John the Forerunner; the one propitiating God, the other proclaiming Christ; the one wholly representing the priest, the other presenting more [Col. 0939B] than a prophet [Note: [Col. 0939D] “Prophesying,” Rhenanus.], namely, the man who not only proclaimed Christ or pointed him out face to face, but even baptized him. For what flesh could more worthily initiate (that is, baptize) the Lord’s body [Note: [Col. 0939D] *initiarit*, Leopold, against all editions.] than flesh of the same kind as that which conceived and bore it?

[Note: [Col. 0939D] “And Christ indeed was brought forth by a virgin who was to marry once after giving birth.” Jerome contradicted Helvidius when the latter asserted this opinion of Tertullian: “Of Tertullian,” he says, “I say nothing more than that he was not a man of the Church.” By these words he indicates that Septimius wrote certain things by no means consonant with Catholic teaching. RIG.] And Christ indeed was brought forth by a virgin who was to marry once after giving birth, so that both titles of holiness might be entered to Christ’s account through a mother who was both virgin and once-married.

But when the infant is presented in the temple, who takes him into his hands? Who is the first to recognize him in the Spirit? A righteous and circumspect man, and certainly [Note: [Col. 0939D] “Each,” others.] not twice-married, lest Christ immediately be proclaimed more worthily [Note: [Col. 0940D] “More unworthily,” Frankfort and Oberthür.] by a woman—an aged widow, once-married and dedicated to the temple, who sufficiently prefigured in her own person what sort of women ought to cling to the spiritual temple, that is, the Church.

The infant Lord, having experienced such witnesses [Col. 0939C], had no others when grown. Peter alone I find to have been married, through the mention of his mother-in-law; I presume him once-married, on account of the Church built upon him, which was to establish every rank of its order from among the once-married. Since I do not find the others to have been husbands, I must understand them either as eunuchs or as continent.

For even if among the Greeks women and wives are designated by a common word, as a convenient matter of usage—although there is, in fact, a word proper to wives—we will not therefore interpret Paul as though he were showing that the apostles had wives. If he had been discussing marriages—which he does later, where he could more appropriately have named some apostle as an example—he might rightly seem to say [Col. 0939D], “Do we not have the right to take wives about with us [Col. 0940A], as do the other apostles and Cephas?” (I Cor. IX). But when he adds statements showing his abstinence from material support, saying, “Do we not have the right to eat and drink?” he does not indicate wives who were taken about by the apostles—for those who have no wives nevertheless have the right to eat and drink—but simply women who, under the same arrangement as those who accompanied the Lord, ministered to them.

Again, if Christ reproves the scribes and Pharisees who sit in Moses’ chair but do not do what they teach, how could he place upon his own chair [Note: [Col. 0940D] “Had placed,” Frankfort.] men who remembered to prescribe holiness of the flesh rather than also to practice it, when he had impressed [Note: [Col. 0940D] “Might impress,” Frankfort.] and taught by every means that it must both be taught and practiced: first by his own example, then [Note: [Col. 0940D] “Thereafter,” Latin edition.] by his other arguments [Col. 0940B]? He says that the kingdom of heaven belongs to children (Matt. XVIII, 3; XXIX, 14); he makes others into children after marriage, as their fellows; he summons us to the simplicity of the dove (Matt. XXIX, 16), a bird not only innocent but also chaste, [Note: [Col. 0939D] “One male knows one female.” He perhaps takes this from Pliny, book X, chap. 34, but careful historians [Col. 0940D] of nature attest that it is false. LE PR.] since one male knows only one female. He denies that the Samaritan woman’s man is her husband, [Note: [Col. 0940D] “So as to show that a husband multiplied in number is an adulterer.” This belongs to the heresy of Montanus; hence he also twists Christ’s words to the Samaritan woman in John IV so that they refer to second marriages, although Christ is speaking of the man who was attached to her not in marriage but in fornication, as blessed Augustine and the Greek commentaries interpret it. Although blessed Jerome said something similar in book I *Against Jovinian*, he later interprets it in his *Apology to Pammachius* as referring not to second—or indeed sixth—marriages, but to prostitution. PAM.] so as to show that a husband multiplied in number is an adulterer (John IV, 17). In the revelation of his glory, out of all the saints and prophets, he prefers to have Moses and Elijah with him, the one once-married, the other a eunuch! For Elijah was none other than John, who came in the power and spirit of Elijah.

And though he was “a gluttonous man and a drinker,” one who frequented luncheons and dinners with publicans and sinners (Matt. X; Luke XV, 13, 19), he dines on only one occasion at a single wedding, although there were surely many people marrying. For he wished to celebrate weddings as many times as he wished them to occur [Col. 0940C].

## CHAPTER IX

But let these arguments be judged forced conjectures, unless they are also supported by the pronouncements the Lord uttered in his reconsideration of divorce, which, though once permitted, he now forbids: first, because “from the beginning it was not so,” just as there was no plurality of marriage; then, because “what God has joined, man shall not separate” (Matt. XIX, 6, 8)—that is, lest man act against the Lord. For he alone who joined will also separate; but he will separate not through the hardness of divorce, which he reproaches and restrains, but through the obligation of death. Indeed, not one of two sparrows falls to the ground apart from the Father’s will (Matt. X, 29).

Therefore, if man is not to separate by divorce those whom God [Col. 0940D] has joined, it is equally consistent [Col. 0941A] that man should not join by marriage those whom God has separated by death. For in joining what has been separated he would likewise act against God’s will, just as if he had separated what was joined. So much for not destroying God’s will and for restoring the form of the beginning.

Furthermore, another rationale concurs—or rather, not another, but the very one that established the form of the beginning and moved God’s will to forbid divorce: “Because whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of adultery, causes her to commit adultery”; and, “He who marries a woman dismissed by her husband certainly commits adultery” (Matt. X, 22). For if a divorced woman cannot lawfully marry [Note: [Col. 0941D] “Cannot even lawfully marry,” Frankfort. Rigault: *non abest*, Paris.], and if she commits some such act without the name of marriage, how does she incur the charge of adultery, since adultery is an offense committed within marriage? God has judged differently from men: he pronounces the admission of another man, whether through marriage [Col. 0941B] or promiscuously, to be adultery altogether [Note: [Col. 0941D] “By God” is added by Rhenanus, Pamelius, Semler, and Leopold; omitted by Rigault and the Venetian edition.].

Let us therefore see what marriage is before God, and thus we shall likewise recognize what adultery is. Marriage exists when God joins two into one flesh, or, finding them joined in that same flesh, seals the union. [Note: [Col. 0941D] “Adultery is,” etc. Here too he includes fornication under the name of adultery, like the Greeks, who understand it under the name *μοιχείας* (*moicheias*, “adultery”). LE PR.] Adultery exists when, after two have in any manner been separated, another—indeed, an alien—flesh is mingled with one of them, of which it cannot be said, “This is flesh of my flesh and bone of my bones” (Gen. II, 23). For this was done and pronounced once; as at the beginning, so also now, it cannot apply to another flesh.

You will therefore say in vain that God does not wish a divorced woman to be joined to another man while her husband is alive, as though he wished it when the husband was dead. For if she is not bound to him when he is dead, then neither is she bound to him while he lives. Whether divorce or death dissolves the marriage [Col. 0941C], she will not be bound to the man from whom that by which she was bound has been severed. Thus it makes no difference [Note: [Col. 0941D] “To whom, then, will she be bound? It makes no difference to God whether the husband is living,” etc., Semler and Oberthür. Rhenanus: “It makes no difference at all whether”; Leopold: *an*.] whether she marries while her husband is alive or dead. For she sins not against him but against herself. “Every offense a person commits is outside the body; but one who commits adultery sins against his own body” (I Cor. VI, 18).

Now, as we established above, the one who commits adultery is he who mingles another flesh with himself over and above that former flesh which God either joined in the two persons or found already joined. Therefore he abolished divorce, which did not exist from the beginning, in order to safeguard what did exist from the beginning: the perseverance of two in one flesh, so that neither necessity nor occasion might introduce a third embodiment in flesh. He permits divorce for the sole cause in which the very thing being guarded against may already have occurred.

So completely was divorce absent from the beginning [Note: [Col. 0941D] “As among the Romans.” Servius Sulpicius, says Rhenanus in the book he composed *On Dowries*, wrote that legal guarantees concerning a wife’s property were first deemed necessary when Spurius Carvilius, surnamed Ruga, a nobleman, divorced his wife because, owing to a bodily defect, children could not be begotten from her. In the 523rd year from the founding of the City, when Marcus Atilius and Publius Valerius were consuls. PAM.] that among the Romans this kind of hardness is recorded as having been committed only after the six-hundredth year [Col. 0942A] from the founding of the City. But they commit adultery even without divorcing; [Note: [Col. 0942D] “As for us, even if we divorce, we shall not be permitted even to marry.” “Us,” that is, the Paracletans. For at the beginning of book I *To His Wife*, he indicates that among the Psychics another marriage after divorce was permitted. RIG.] as for us, even if we divorce, we shall not be permitted even to marry.

## CHAPTER X

I already see that from here we are being summoned to the apostle. To perceive his meaning more easily, it must first be impressed all the more insistently that women are all the more bound to a deceased husband, so that they may not admit another man.

Let us reflect that divorce either arises from discord or produces discord, whereas death occurs by the law of God, not through a human offense, and that it is a debt owed by all, even by the unmarried. Therefore, if a divorced woman, who through discord, anger, hatred, and the causes of these—injury, insult, or any grievance whatever—has been separated in both soul and body, remains bound to an enemy, not to call him a husband, how much more will the woman who, by neither her own fault nor her husband’s, but by the operation of the Lord’s law, has not been separated from marriage but merely left behind, still belong to him even when dead, since she owes concord to him even in death [Col. 0942B]!

She did not hear divorce pronounced by him; she did not depart from him; she did not write him a bill of divorce; she remains with him; she retains the man whom she did not wish to lose. [Note: [Col. 0942D] “She has with her the license of the mind, which represents to a person through imaginary enjoyment all the things he does not possess.” How licentiously Septimius speaks here!—even if the duties he describes in the second book *To His Wife* are meant. RIG.] She has with her the license of the mind, which represents to a person through imaginary enjoyment all the things he does not possess.

Finally, I ask the woman herself: “Tell me, sister, did you send your husband ahead in peace?” What will she answer? “In discord,” perhaps? Then she is bound all the more to the man with whom she has a case before God. She who remains bound has not departed. [Note: [Col. 0942D] “But in peace.” This answers what preceded: “In discord?” RIG.] “But in peace.” Then she must necessarily persevere in that peace with the man whom she can no longer divorce; nor could she have married another even if she had been able to divorce him [Col. 0942C].

Indeed, she also prays for his soul, asks refreshment for him in the meantime [Note: [Col. 0942D] “Let her ask, let her offer,” Paris; “for she asks,” Rhenanus and Semler.], asks fellowship with him in the first resurrection, and makes an offering on the anniversaries of his falling asleep. For if she does not do these things, she has truly divorced him, so far as lies within her; and that all the more unjustly, insofar as she did it in the only way she could because she could not do it otherwise; and all the more unworthily, insofar as it is now more unworthy, if because he did not deserve it. [Note: [Col. 0942D] Franciscus Junius emends this corrupt passage as follows: “all the more unjustly, because she could not; and all the more unworthily, because he did not deserve it.”]

Or shall we perhaps be nothing after death? According to some Epicurus, and not according to Christ? But if we believe in the resurrection of the dead, we shall surely remain bound to those with whom we are to rise, each required to render an account concerning the other. If, however, in that age “they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but will be equal to angels” (Matt. XXII, 30), one will not therefore cease to be bound to spouses [Col. 0943A] who have died merely because marriage will not be restored. On the contrary, we shall be bound all the more, because we are destined for a better condition: rising again into spiritual fellowship and recognizing both ourselves and those who are ours.

Otherwise, how shall we sing thanks to God forever if the sense and memory of this debt do not remain in us—if our substance is reconstituted, but not our consciousness? Therefore, when we are with God, we shall be together, since all of us are with the one God—even though the reward varies, even though there are many dwellings with the same Father (John XIV, 2)—as workers receiving the one denarius of the same reward, that is, eternal life. In that life God will be even less likely to separate those whom he has joined than he is in this lesser life to permit their separation.

Since these things are so, how will a woman be available to another man when she remains occupied by her own even in the future? We are speaking to both sexes, although the discourse is addressed to one [Col. 0943B], because one rule governs both. Will she have one man in the spirit, another in the flesh? This will be adultery: one woman’s consciousness directed toward two men. If one has been separated from the flesh but remains in the heart [Note: [Col. 0943C] “They remain,” Frankfort.], there—where even thought, without intercourse of the flesh, first completes adultery [Note: [Col. 0943C] “Is completed,” Rhenanus.] through desire, [Note: [Col. 0943D] “And marriage through the will,” etc. This confirms the common opinion of the Fathers and jurists that even without carnal intercourse it is the will, or consent, that constitutes marriage. Thus the marriage of the Blessed Virgin and Joseph is also confirmed in Augustine, book I *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chap. 11; and blessed Chrysostom, homily 32 of the *Imperfect Work*, and blessed Ambrose, *On the Institution of Virgins*, chap. 16, expressly affirm it as well. Yet what the Author asserted before does not follow from it. PAM.] and marriage through the will—he is still her husband, [Note: [Col. 0943D] “Possessing that very thing through which he became a husband, namely the mind.” For, as the jurists say, consent, not intercourse, makes a marriage. RIG.] possessing that very thing through which he became a husband, namely the mind. If another man also dwells therein, that will be a crime. The former, moreover, has not been excluded merely because he has departed [Note: [Col. 0943D] “Withdrawn,” Rhenanus and Semler.] from the baser commerce of the flesh. He is a more honorable husband now that he has been made purer.

## CHAPTER XI

So, in order that you may marry “in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0944C] “In God,” Rhenanus, Semler, and Oberthür.] according to the Law and the apostle—if indeed you care even about this—what sort of woman are you, requesting such a marriage [Col. 0943C] from those who are not permitted to have it: from a once-married bishop, [Note: [Col. 0943D] “From presbyters and deacons of the same sacrament.” That is, once-married. LE PR.] from presbyters and deacons bound by the same sacrament, and from widows whose way of life you have rejected in your own case?

[Note: [Col. 0944D] “And they, plainly, will give husbands and wives just as they give morsels”—that is, to everyone who asks. As though the saying “Give to everyone who asks you” had also been spoken about marriage, although in the book *On Baptism* he says that it has its own heading pertaining to almsgiving. Thus, with decorous words, he enfolds an indecent meaning, just as we read in the Proverbs of Solomon: “Such is the way of an adulterous woman: she eats and wipes her mouth.” LE PR.] And they, plainly, will give husbands and wives just as they give morsels. For this, among them, is the meaning of “You shall give to everyone who asks you.” And they will join you in the virgin Church, the one bride of the one Christ. And you will pray for your husbands, the new and the old. Choose to which of them you will present yourself as an adulteress. To both, I think.

But if you were wise, you would be silent concerning the dead husband. Let your silence be a bill of divorce written to him with another man’s [Note: [Col. 0944D] “Another man’s bridal property.” The Greeks call bridal goods brought by the woman in addition to the stipulated dowry *ἐξωπρόικα* (*exōproika*) and *παράφερνα* (*parapherna*). LE PR.] bridal property. In this way you will earn a new husband, if you forget the old one. You ought rather to please the man for whose sake you preferred not to please God [Col. 0944A].

The Psychics maintain that the apostle either approved these things or gave them no consideration at all when he wrote: “A woman is bound for as long as her husband lives; but if he has died, she is free: let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (I Cor.
