VII, 39). From this passage they defend the license of a second marriage—indeed, of any number, if a second is allowed; for that which has once ceased to be singular is subject to every number.

But the sense in which the apostle wrote will become clear if it is first established that he did not write in the sense employed by the Psychics. This will be established if one recalls the matters inconsistent with this interpretation in his teaching, his will, and Paul’s own personal discipline. For if he permits second marriages [Note: [Col. 0944C] “Admits,” another reading.], which did not exist from the beginning, how does he affirm that all things are gathered up again from the beginning [Col. 0944B] in Christ? If he wishes us to repeat marriages, how does he maintain that our offspring in Isaac derives from a once-married father? How does he arrange the entire order of the Church from among the once-married, unless this discipline first governs the laity, from whom the order of the Church is recruited? How, while people are still in marriage, does he call them away from the fruit of marriage, declaring that time has been shortened, if he summons those released from marriage by death back into marriage?

If these things are inconsistent with the passage under discussion, it will be established, as we said, that he did not write it in the sense employed by the Psychics. For it is easier that this one passage should have some rationale consonant with the others than that the apostle should appear to have taught mutually contradictory things. We shall be able to recognize that rationale in the subject matter itself.

What subject matter led the apostle [Col. 0944C] to write such things? The novice condition of a new Church only just coming into being—a Church that he was, of course, nourishing with milk, not yet with the solid food of stronger doctrine (I Cor. III). So great was that infancy of faith that they still did not know what they ought to do concerning the necessities of the flesh and sex. We understand the particular forms of their uncertainty from his replies, when he says: “Now concerning the matters about which you wrote: it is good for a man not to touch a woman; [Note: [Col. 0944D] “But because of fornications.” He translated literally the Greek *διὰ δὲ τὰς πορνείας* (*dia de tas porneias*, “but because of fornications”); in this the Author was also imitated by blessed Jerome three or four times in book I *Against Jovinian*. PAM.] but because of fornications, let each man have his own wife” (I Cor. VII). He shows that there were people whom faith had found already married, but who feared that from then on they might not be permitted to make use of their marriage because they had come to believe in the holy flesh of Christ.

And yet he grants this by way of permission [Col. 0945A], not command—that is, indulgently, not by prescribing that it be done. Rather, he preferred all people to be what he himself was. Likewise, in replying concerning divorce, he shows that some had been considering that matter too, especially because they thought they ought not to remain in marriages with gentiles after coming to faith.

They also asked for counsel concerning virgins—for there was no commandment of the Lord—that it was good for a person to remain as he was, that is, as faith had found him. “Are you bound [Note: [Col. 0945C] “For,” Rhenanus and Semler.] to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you take a wife, you have not sinned,” because for a man released from a wife before coming to faith, a wife taken after coming to faith will not be counted as a second wife: she is his first after faith. For even our life itself is reckoned from faith.

But here he says that he is sparing those who, because of the constraints of the times, refuse the impediments to marriage; otherwise distress of the flesh would follow them [Col. 0945B]. Rather, they should be concerned about meriting the Lord’s favor rather than about a husband [Note: [Col. 0945C] “Bringing forth,” Frankfort.]. And [Note: [Col. 0945C] “And” is absent from the Frankfort edition.] thus he retracts what he permitted.

Accordingly, in the very same chapter in which he determines that each person ought to remain in the calling in which he was called, he adds: “A woman is bound for as long as her husband lives; but if he has fallen asleep, she is free; let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (I Cor. VII, 39). From this too [Note: [Col. 0945C] “This,” Rhenanus.] he shows that the woman must be understood as one who was herself found already released from a husband, just as the man was released from a wife—the release having occurred through death, of course, not through divorce, because he would not permit divorced persons to marry, contrary to the preceding commandment [Col. 0945C].

Thus, if the woman marries, she will not sin [Col. 0946A], because this man will not be counted as a second husband either, since [Note: [Col. 0945C] “Who,” Rigault and Venetian edition.] he is her first from the time of faith. That this is so is shown by the fact that he added, “Only in the Lord,” because he was dealing with a woman who had had a gentile husband and, after losing him, had come to faith, lest she presume that even after faith she could marry a gentile—although the Psychics do not care about this either [Note: [Col. 0946C] “Lest” is absent from Rhenanus.].

[Note: [Col. 0945C] “Let us know plainly that it does not so read in the authentic Greek.” Since every document of both the Old and New Scripture was subsequently translated into the Latin language, the water of the fountain should be believed much purer than that of the streams, as Jerome says *Against Helvidius*. Accordingly, in the book *On the Prescription of Heretics*, he appeals to the apostolic churches, among which, he says, the authentic letters of the apostles are read aloud, sounding their voice and presenting their countenance. But Gregory of Nyssa long ago observed, in Oration II *On the Lord’s Resurrection*, that not all editions of that authentic Greek were entirely accurate. For he says that *ἐν τοῖς ἀκριβεστέροις ἀντιγράφοις* (*en tois akribesterois antigraphois*, “in the more accurate copies”) the Gospel [Col. 0945D] of Mark does not continue beyond the words *ἐφοβοῦντο γάρ* (*ephobounto gar*, “for they were afraid”). No such copy is yet known to survive today, except for a manuscript preserved in the royal library and written in rather large letters, where, after *ἐφοβοῦντο γάρ*, a sign marking the end is appended. Immediately afterward, in the same scribe’s hand, it is said that in certain books the following is found: *Πάντα δὲ παρηγγελμένα τοῖς περὶ τὸν Πέτρον συντόμως ἐξήγγειλον. Μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα καὶ αὐτὸς οἷς ἀπὸ ἀνατολῆς καὶ ἄχρι δύσεως ἐξαπέστειλεν δι’ αὐτῶν τὸ ἱερὸν καὶ ἄφθαρτον κήρυγμα τῆς ἀϊδίου σωτηρίας* (“And all that had been commanded they briefly reported to those around Peter. After these things, Jesus himself also sent out through them, from east even to west, the sacred and incorruptible proclamation of eternal salvation”). Then another note by the scribe says that in some manuscripts, after *ἐφοβοῦντο γάρ*, there also follows *Ἀναστὰς δὲ πρωῒ* (*Anastas de prōi*, “Now, having risen early”) and the rest found in the commonly printed editions. RIG.]

Let us know plainly that it does not so read in the authentic Greek. [Note: [Col. 0945D] “In the authentic Greek”—in the Greek truth, in the Greek original. Jerome, Preface to the Gospels. Augustine, book II *On Christian Doctrine*, chap. 13: “There is no doubt that, if anything wavers amid the variations of the Latin copies, the books of the New Testament ought to yield to the Greek, especially those found among the more learned and diligent churches.” And in book II, chap. 6, *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, where [Col. 0946C] he cites an emended Latin codex and an emended Greek codex of Paul’s epistles, he calls the latter “authentic,” meaning more worthy of authority, whether among Greek or Latin copies. Nor did Augustine shrink from examining several manuscripts, as he himself testifies on Psalm LXVII: “Several Latin manuscripts,” he says, “and especially the Greek, have the verses divided in this manner”; and shortly afterward: “This division, confirmed by the agreement of many manuscripts, and those of greater authority, must undoubtedly be preferred,” etc. The same author on that Psalm: “Not all manuscripts contain this repetition, and the more careful ones mark it beforehand with an appended asterisk.” RIG.] It passed into use [Note: [Col. 0946C] “By the transposition of two syllables.” In that “authentic” text of his he seems to have read *ἐὰν κοιμᾷ δέ* (*ean koima de*), “but if he sleeps,” “if he is dead”—the husband, that is, before the wife was called to faith. By a transposition of two syllables, *ἐὰν κοιμᾷ δέ* supposedly became *ἐὰν κοιμηθῇ* (*ean koimēthēi*), “if he shall have fallen asleep,” “if he shall have died.” “This also has the force of a future,” says Septimius, as though the apostle’s meaning extended even to the case in which the husband happened to die after the wife had received the faith, and as though in that case too the wife were permitted to marry another man. Yet in those extremely ancient parchments that learned men long ago praised from the most ample library of the illustrious Puteanus, it is written most explicitly: *ἐὰν δὲ κοιμήθη ὁ ἀνὴρ αὐτῆς* (*ean de koimēthē ho anēr autēs*), which is also rendered there in Latin, “But if her husband has received his falling asleep.” This form of expression certainly seems to signify a Christian husband more than a gentile one. RIG.] through either the cunning or the innocent transposition of two syllables [Note: [Col. 0946C] “Emergence,” Semler.]: “If her husband shall have fallen asleep” [Note: [Col. 0946C] Rhenanus and Semler insert “however.”], as though it referred to the future and therefore seemed to concern a woman who had lost her husband after already coming to faith.

If this were indeed so, a license extended without limit would give her a husband as many times as one was lost, without any modesty in marrying—even the sort of modesty customary among gentiles. Yet even if it did refer to the future—“If anyone’s husband shall have died” [Col. 0946B]—the future would apply just as much to a woman whose husband was going to die before she came to faith. Take whichever reading you please [Note: [Col. 0946C] “Although,” Semler and Pamelius.], provided you do not overturn the rest.

For since the following pronouncements also correspond: “Were you called as a slave? Do not concern yourself”; [Note: [Col. 0945D] “Were you called uncircumcised?”—“in uncircumcision,” *ἐν ἀκροβυστίᾳ* (*en akrobystia*). RIG.] “Were you called uncircumcised? Do not be circumcised”; “Were you called circumcised? [Note: [Col. 0946D] “Do not draw it over”—the foreskin, that is. Juvenal, Satire 6, used the expression “to draw over foreskins.” RIG.] Do not draw it over”; and since these are matched by, “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife,” it is sufficiently clear that these statements concern people who, in their new and recent calling, were consulting him about the conditions in which faith had found them.

This, then, will be the interpretation of that passage, to be tested as to whether it agrees with the time and the occasion; with both the preceding examples and arguments [Col. 0946C] and the subsequent pronouncements and meanings [Col. 0947A]; and above all, with the apostle’s own counsel and personal rule. For nothing must be guarded more carefully than that a person not be found inconsistent with himself [Note: [Col. 0947C] “A person” is absent from Semler.].

## CHAPTER XII
Listen also to their most subtle counterargument. “So fully,” they say, “did the Apostle permit remarriage that he bound only those who are in the clergy to the yoke of monogamy; for what he prescribes for certain persons he does not prescribe for all.” Does it follow, then, that what he commands everyone he does not prescribe for bishops alone, if what he prescribes for bishops he does not also command everyone? Or is it prescribed to everyone because it is prescribed also to bishops, and to bishops because it is prescribed also to everyone? For whence come the bishops and clergy? Is it not from among everyone? If not everyone is bound to monogamy, [Col. 0947B] whence are monogamists to be found for the clergy? Or will some separate order of monogamists have to be established, from which selection for the clergy may be made?

But when we are exalted and puffed up against the clergy, then we are all one; then we are all priests, because “he made us priests to God and his Father” (Rev. 1:6; 5:10). When, however, we are summoned to equality in priestly discipline, [Note: [Col. 0947D] “We lay aside our mitres and are unequal.” Thus we have emended the text from Ursinus’s manuscript. He therefore says: “When we laypeople are summoned to equality in priestly discipline, we lay aside the priestly character and now say that laypeople are one thing and priests another.” RIG.] we lay aside our mitres and are unequal. [Note: [Col. 0947C] Thus Rigalt from Ursinus’s manuscript; Rhenanus: “equal”; others: “parts”; Wouwer’s codex: “unequal.”]

The discussion concerned ecclesiastical orders [Note: [Col. 0947C] “Orders” was absent from the Dijon Codex. Rigalt.]: what sort of persons ought to be ordained. [Note: [Col. 0947D] “It was therefore necessary that the pattern of the common discipline should be displayed upon its own front.” He elegantly calls the bishops, presbyters, and deacons the “front” of the Church. It was necessary, he says, that the pattern—that is, the tablets—of the entire ecclesiastical discipline should be displayed and hung upon the front of the Christian Church, so that an edict might thus precede which everyone would follow. For thus it is read in the ancient Dijon Codex: “an edict destined, as it were, to serve as a precept for everyone.” RIG.] It was therefore necessary that the complete pattern [Note: [Col. 0947D] “The pattern of the common discipline.” He means the common law addressed to laypeople as well as priests, τύπον τοῦ ποιμνίου, “a pattern of the flock” (1 Pet. 5). RIG.] of the common discipline should be displayed upon its own front, destined, as it were, to serve as an edict for everyone by way of precept, [Note: [Col. 0947C] Rigalt and the Venetian edition: “by way of precedence”; Rhenanus, Semler, Leopold, and Oberthür: “by way of impression.”] [Note: [Col. 0947D] “So that the people might know all the more that they must observe that order which produced their leaders.” He means the order of monogamists, [Col. 0948D] from which the leaders are chosen. Thus he wished the whole people to be monogamists. RIG.] so that the people might know all the more that they must observe that order which produced their leaders, and so that even the office itself might not flatter itself into some license, as though by privilege of rank. [Note: [Col. 0947D] Rigalt: “sound.”] [Note: [Col. 0948C] Semler, Oberthür, and Wouwer’s codex: “might flatter itself.”]

[Col. 0947C] The Holy Spirit foresaw that certain persons would say, “Everything is permitted to bishops,” just as that bishop of yours at Uthina did not even fear the Scantinian law. [Note: [Col. 0948D] “That bishop of yours at Uthina did not even fear the Scantinian law.” Uthina is a town in Africa, a Roman colony. The church of Uthina, however, did not acknowledge, as it seems, Montanus’s new prophecy. He charges the bishop with illicit sexual intercourse when he says that he did not even fear the Scantinian law. Publius Scantinius enacted a law under which pederasts were subjected to severe punishment. RHEN.] For how many twice-married men preside among you, certainly insulting the Apostle and assuredly not blushing when these words are read under their authority! [Note: [Col. 0948C] Rigalt: “because.”] [Note: [Col. 0948C] Rhenanus: “from a second marriage.”]

Come now, you who suppose that an exception concerning [Col. 0948A] monogamy was made for bishops: withdraw also from the remaining titles of discipline which are ascribed to bishops together with monogamy. Do not be blameless, sober, well behaved, hospitable, or able to teach; indeed, be devoted to wine, ready with your hand to strike, quarrelsome, [Note: [Col. 0948C] Rhenanus: “quarrels.”] a lover of money, one who does not govern his household or care for the discipline of his children, and one who does not even pursue a good reputation among outsiders (1 Tim. 3:2ff.). For if bishops have a law of their own concerning monogamy, then the other requirements which must accompany monogamy will likewise have been written for bishops. But for laypeople, to whom monogamy does not apply, the other requirements also are irrelevant. You have escaped, Psychic, if you wish, the bonds of the whole discipline. Maintain resolutely that whatever has been commanded to certain persons is not commanded to everyone; or, if the other requirements are indeed common [Col. 0948B] to all, while monogamy alone has been imposed on bishops, are they alone to be declared Christians—the men upon whom the whole discipline has been conferred?

## CHAPTER XIII

Writing also to Timothy, [Note: [Col. 0948D] “He wishes younger women to marry.” The author twists this passage toward his own purpose so much that one can scarcely grasp what he means. The interpretations of the ancients likewise vary; among them the most satisfactory is that of Epiphanius against the Montanists: in the earlier passage, when Paul says, “Avoid younger widows,” etc., he is speaking of those who have made a promise but do not stand by it, incurring condemnation because they have nullified their first pledge; afterward, however, in the words “I therefore wish younger widows to marry,” he speaks of those whom he permits, because of weakness, to pass to a second marriage. PAM.] he wishes younger women to marry, bear children, and manage households (1 Tim. 5:14). He addresses women of the sort he marked out above: younger widows who, having been found in widowhood and having pursued it for some time, [Note: [Col. 0948C] Rhenanus: “affected it.”] afterward, when they have lived wantonly against Christ, wish to marry, incurring condemnation because they have broken their first pledge—that pledge, namely, which, having been found in widowhood and having professed it, they do not persevere in keeping. For this reason he wishes them to marry: so that they may not afterward break the first pledge of widowhood they have undertaken—not so that they may marry as often as, after widowhood has been tried, [Note: [Col. 0948D] Rhenanus: “is to be tried.”] or rather even wantonly enjoyed, [Col. 0948C] they have refused to persevere in it.

We also read him writing to the Romans: “The woman who is under a husband is bound to her husband while he lives; but if he dies, she is released from the law of her husband. Accordingly, then, while her husband lives she will be considered an adulteress if she is joined to another man. But if her husband dies, she is freed from the law, so that she is not an adulteress if she becomes another man’s wife” [Col. 0949A] (Rom. 7:2–3). But consider also what follows, so that this meaning which flatters you may vanish: “Therefore, my brothers,” he says, “you also were put to death to the law through the body of Christ, so that you might belong to another, namely to him who rose from the dead, in order that we might bear fruit for God. For when we were in the flesh, the passions of sins, which were aroused through the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death. But now we have been released from the law, having died to that in which we were held, so that we may serve God in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter.”

Therefore, if he commands us to be put to death to the law through the body of Christ—that is, the Church, which consists in the Spirit’s newness, not in the letter’s oldness, that is, the law—then, by removing you from the law, which does not prevent a wife whose husband has died from becoming another man’s wife, he brings you under the opposite condition: that, [Col. 0949B] having lost your husband, you are not to marry. And to the same degree that you would not be reckoned an adulteress for becoming another man’s wife after your husband’s death, if you were still obliged to conduct yourself under the law, so by the difference of your condition he adjudges you guilty of adultery if you marry another after your husband’s death. For you have now been put to death to the law: something cannot be lawful for you after you have withdrawn from that law under which it was lawful for you.

## CHAPTER XIV

Now even if the Apostle had unconditionally permitted a believer who had lost a marriage partner to marry, he would have acted in the same way as in those other matters which, contrary to the form of his own rule, he carried out because of the circumstances of the times: circumcising Timothy because of false brethren who had been brought in, [Note: [Col. 0949D] Rhenanus: “brought in.”] and bringing certain men who had shaved themselves into the temple because of Jewish observance (Acts 16:3; 21:24)—the very man [Col. 0949C] who chastises the Galatians for wishing to conduct themselves under the law. But circumstances required [Note: [Col. 0949D] Others: “required” in the singular.] him to become all things to all people, so that he might gain them all, laboring to give birth to them until Christ should be formed in them, and warming the little ones in faith like a nurse (1 Cor. 9:20; Gal. 4:19), teaching certain things by permission, not by command—for it is one thing to grant indulgence, another to give an order. In the same way, he permitted for a time the license to marry anew because of the weakness of the flesh, just as Moses permitted divorce because of hardness of heart (Deut. 24:1).

Here too, therefore, we shall supply what completes this line of thought. If Christ abolished what Moses prescribed because “from the beginning it was not so” (Matt. 19:8), and Christ will not on that account be considered to have come from another power, why should the Paraclete not also have abolished what Paul allowed? For [Col. 0949D] a second marriage likewise did not exist from the beginning; nor, on that account, ought the Paraclete to be held suspect as though he were an alien spirit, provided only that what is subsequently introduced [Note: [Col. 0949D] Others: “subsequently declared.”] is worthy of God and Christ. If [Note: [Col. 0949D] Semler and Oberthür: “But if.”] it was worthy of God and Christ to restrain hardness of heart when its time had run its course, why should it not be still worthier [Col. 0950A] of God and Christ to shake off weakness of the flesh now that time has been drawn nearer to its consummation?

If it is right that a marriage not be dissolved, surely it is also honorable that it not be repeated. Indeed, in the secular world both are counted part of good discipline: the one under the name of concord, the other under that of chastity. Hardness of heart reigned until Christ; let weakness of the flesh likewise have reigned until the Paraclete. The new law abolished divorce; it had something to abolish. The new prophecy abolishes second marriage, which is no less a divorce from the first. Yet hardness of heart yielded to Christ more readily than weakness of the flesh does. The latter defends itself by Paul more than the former did by Moses; nevertheless, it defends him when it seizes upon him as granting indulgence, but rejects him when he lays down precepts. It evades his weightier pronouncements and abiding intentions; it does not permit us to render to this Apostle [Col. 0950B] what he prefers.

And how long will this most shameless weakness persist in assailing what is better? Its time lasted until the Paraclete should begin his work; to him were deferred by the Lord those things which could not then be borne, [Note: [Col. 0950D] Rhenanus: “were prolonged.”] [Note: [Col. 0950D] François: “to bear.”] things which it now befits no one to be unable to bear, because he through whom the ability to bear is given is not absent. How long shall we plead the flesh as our excuse because the Lord said, “The flesh is weak” (Matt. 26:41)? But he first said, “The Spirit is willing,” so that the Spirit might conquer the flesh and what is weak might yield to the stronger.

For he also says, “He who can receive it, let him receive it” (Matt. 19:12); that is, he who cannot, let him depart. That rich man too departed because he had not received the command to distribute his property to the needy, and he was dismissed by the Lord to the judgment of his own choice (Matt. 19:16–22). Nor on that account will hardness be imputed [Col. 0950C] to Christ because of the fault of each person’s free choice. [Note: [Col. 0950D] Rhenanus: “servitude.”] “Behold,” he says, “I have set before you good and evil” (Deut. 30:15; Sir. 15:17); choose what is good. If you cannot, it is because you will not—[Note: [Col. 0949D] For he shows that you can if you will, because he has set both before your choice. This passage argues for continence so strongly that it seems to be placed within our own power, provided that we have recourse to God. St. Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages* II.29: “The burden of continence will be light if it is Christ’s; it will be Christ’s if faith is present, which obtains from God when he commands whatever he has commanded.” LE PR.] for he shows that you can if you will, because he has set both before your choice—you must depart from him whose will you do not perform.

## CHAPTER XV

What, then, is our hardness here, if we renounce those who do not perform the will of God? What heresy is there if we judge second marriages to be unlawful, alongside adultery? For what is adultery but an unlawful marriage? The Apostle censures those who forbade marriage altogether and who also prohibited foods which God created (1 Tim. 4:3). But we no more abolish marriages by refusing second marriages [Col. 0950D] than we condemn foods by fasting more frequently. It is one thing to abolish, another to moderate; one thing to impose a law against marrying, another [Note: [Col. 0950D] Rhenanus repeats “is.”] to establish a limit on marrying.

Certainly, those who reproach us with hardness or heresy in this matter, [Note: [Col. 0950D] Others add “suppose.”] if they cherish the weakness of the flesh so much [Col. 0951A] that they think it must repeatedly be supported in marrying, why do they neither support it in another matter nor cherish it with pardon when it has been overcome by torments into denial? Surely that weakness is more entitled to excuse which fell in battle than that which fell in the bedroom; which succumbed on the rack rather than on the bed; which yielded in the matter of faith rather than to lust; which was conquered while groaning rather than while willing. Yet the former they drive from communion because it did not endure to the end, while the latter they receive as though it too had endured to the end. Set forth what each failed to endure to the end, and you will find the cause of the one who could not endure cruelty more honorable than that of the one who could not endure chastity. And yet weakness of the flesh does not excuse even a bloody apostasy, much less an unchaste one.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0951B] I laugh, however, when weakness of the flesh is pleaded as an objection, when it ought rather to be called the greatest strength. To marry again is a matter of vigor; to rise again to the works of the flesh from the repose of continence requires robust loins. Such weakness is sufficient for a third and a fourth and perhaps even a seventh marriage, since it becomes stronger as often as it becomes weaker. It will by then have as its authority not the Apostle, but some Hermogenes, a man accustomed to take more women than to paint them. For “matter” abounds in him, from which he also presumes the soul to be derived; much less, therefore, does he possess the Spirit from God. He is no longer even “psychic,” because his soul is not from the breath of God.

What if someone pleads poverty, thereby openly confessing that his flesh is prostituted, since he marries for the sake of maintenance, forgetful that one must take no thought (Matt. 6:25) for food and clothing? He has God, who feeds even the ravens and clothes even the flowers. [Col. 0951C] What if he alleges the loneliness of his household? As though one woman provided a crowd for a man who is close to departing! He surely has widows whom he is permitted to take in. He is allowed to have not one wife of this kind but even [Note: [Col. 0951C] Rhenanus: “now.”] several.

What if someone is concerned about posterity with the same disposition with which Lot’s wife turned her eyes back, so that [Col. 0952A] he repeats marriage because he had no children from the first? A Christian, forsooth, disinherited from the entire world, will seek heirs! He has brothers; he has the Church as his mother. It is another matter [Note: [Col. 0951C] “If they believe that even under Christ matters are conducted according to the Julian laws.” He undoubtedly had regard to the Julian laws, [Col. 0951D] which contained penalties for celibacy and childlessness. Augustus increased these, as Dio attests in Book LV; hence the Julian law was called the law of escheat. For since celibates received nothing from wills except from their nearest relatives, while the childless received only half, a legacy made to a celibate was called “lapsed” unless he produced a child within one hundred days. Sozomen carefully notes this in Book I of his *Ecclesiastical History*: νόμος ἦν Ῥωμαίοις παλαιὸς, ἀπὸ εἴκοσι καὶ πέντε ἐτῶν τῶν ἴσων ἀξιοῦσθαι κωλύων τοῖς ἀγάμοις, “There was an ancient law among the Romans which prevented unmarried persons over twenty-five years of age from being accorded equal rights.” Plutarch also refers to those penalties in *Dialogue on Love*: Ῥωμαίων πολλοὶ γαμοῦσι, γεννῶσιν, καὶ οὐκ ἵνα κληρονόμους ἔχωσιν, ἀλλ᾽ ἵνα κληρονομεῖν δύνωνται, “Many Romans marry and beget children, not so that they may have heirs, but so that they themselves may be able to inherit.” Hence Juvenal introduces an adulterer who mutters these words to the husband:

> . . . Because of me you will be named heir.  
> You receive every legacy, and also the pleasant windfall.

[Col. 0952C] For “to receive the whole,” which is at issue here, is ἴσων ἀξιοῦσθαι, “to be accorded equal rights,” which is the same as becoming heir to the whole estate and entering upon the entire inheritance. As I have said, this did not happen in the case of celibates, for their legacies lapsed and went to the imperial treasury. Book VI, *On Common and Pupillary Substitution*. Yet on account of Christians—ἴσων ἀξιοῦσθαι παρθενίαν καὶ ἀπαιδίαν διὰ θεὸν ἀσκοῦντας, “that those who practice virginity and childlessness for God’s sake might be accorded equal rights”—Constantine later abolished the penalties for celibacy. Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, and Sozomen, Book I. LE PR.] if they believe that even under Christ matters are conducted according to the Julian laws and suppose [Note: [Col. 0951C] Rhenanus: “judge.”] that celibates and the childless cannot receive the whole under God’s testament.

Let such persons, then, continue marrying right to the end, so that amid this confusion of the flesh, as in Sodom and Gomorrah and in the days of the flood, they may be overtaken by that final departure of the age. Let them add a third saying (1 Cor. 15:32): “Let us eat and drink and marry, for tomorrow we shall die,” without reflecting that the “woe” pronounced upon the pregnant and nursing will be fulfilled far more grievously and bitterly in the convulsion of the whole world than it was in the devastation of one small part of Judaea. Let them gather from their repeated marriages fruits well suited to the last times: [Col. 0952B] flowing breasts, heaving wombs, and infants mewling. [Note: [Col. 0952D] “Infants mewling.” *Pipiare* in the Oscan language means “to wail”; from it comes *pipilare*, which Catullus uses of the chirping of a sparrow. LE PR.] [Note: [Col. 0951C] François and Junius: “mewling.”] Let them bear children for Antichrist, upon whom [Note: [Col. 0952C] Rhenanus and Semler: “in whom.”] he may vent his lustful savagery. He will bring them executioners as midwives.

## CHAPTER XVII

They will plainly have something to plead before Christ: that splendid privilege, the utter weakness of the flesh. But this will now be judged [Note: [Col. 0952C] Rhenanus: “so”; Junius: “then.”] neither by Isaac, our monogamous father; nor by any John, Christ’s eunuch; nor by Judith daughter of Merari; nor by so many other examples of holy persons. [Note: [Col. 0952D] “Pagans are commonly appointed as judges.” This alludes to the trials of Christians conducted before pagan tribunals. It will be nothing new, he says, for Christians to be arraigned before the tribunals of pagans. And so he attempts to prove his monogamy even by the judgment of pagans—that is, by those examples so often inculcated: those of Lucretia, the wife of the Flamen, the Vestal Virgins, and others of that kind. I believe he did so because he perceived that most believers of his age were persuaded by such examples. RIG.] Pagans are commonly appointed as judges.

The queen of Carthage will arise and pass judgment against Christian women: though a refugee, on foreign soil, and at that very moment the founder of so great a city, when she ought willingly to have desired marriage to a king, yet, lest she experience a second marriage, she preferred instead [Col. 0952C] to be burned rather than to marry. Beside her will sit that Roman matron who, though she experienced another man by nocturnal violence, nevertheless washed away the stain upon her flesh with her own blood, so that she might vindicate monogamy upon herself. [Note: [Col. 0952C] François: “by herself.”] There have also been women who preferred to die for their husbands rather than to marry after their husbands’ deaths.

Certainly, monogamy and widowhood are conspicuous even among the idols. No one places a crown upon Fortuna Muliebris except a woman who has had one husband; [Col. 0953A] nor upon Mother Matuta. [Note: [Col. 0953A] “Mother Matuta.” She is Ino by another name and is numbered among the sea-goddesses. Ovid, *Fasti* VI:

> You will be called Leucothoe by the Greeks, Matuta by our people.

[Col. 0954A] She is indeed distinguished by various names. LE PR.] [Note: [Col. 0954A] “The chief pontiff and the Flaminica.” In *Exhortation to Chastity* he said “the Flamen and the Flaminica.” LE PR.] The *Pontifex Maximus* and the Flaminica marry only once. The priestesses of Ceres, even while their husbands are living and consenting, become widows through an amicable separation.

There are also those who may judge us regarding complete continence: the virgins of Vesta, of Achaean Juno, of Scythian Diana, and of Pythian Apollo. Even the priests of that Egyptian bull will judge the weakness of Christians in the matter of continence. Blush, flesh that has put on Christ! Let it suffice you to marry once, for which you were made from the beginning and to which you are recalled at the end. [Note: [Col. 0953A] Rhenanus and Junius: “to which you are also recalled at the end.”] [Col. 0954A] Return to the first Adam, if you cannot return to the last. Once he tasted of the tree; once he desired; once he covered his shame; once he blushed before God; once he hid his blush; once he was exiled from the paradise of holiness; once thereafter he married. If you were in him, you have your pattern; if you have passed into Christ, you ought to be better. Produce [Note: [Col. 0954A] Rhenanus adds “yourself”; Junius, “you.”] a third Adam—and let him too be twice married—and then you will be able to be what you cannot be between the two.

[Col. 0953]

# QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN: ON FASTING

[Note: [Col. 0953C] In the editions of Gelenius, Semler, and others, this book is entitled *On Fasting, Against the Psychics*.] (C)

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0953B]

The orthodox, whom he here calls “Psychics,” rejected Montanus’s teachings concerning fasts. Having therefore become a follower of Montanus, he defends the Montanist fasts, xerophagies, and stations.

## CHAPTER I

I would be surprised if these Psychics [Note: [Col. 0953C] François adds “these.”] were strained only by the luxury through which they marry repeatedly, and were not also torn apart by the gluttony [Note: [Col. 0953D] “Torn apart by gluttony”: “burst.” RIG.] through which they hate fasts. [Note: [Col. 0953C] Rhenanus and Leopold: “were held”; Semler and Leopold: “were led”; Ursinus’s codex: “were loosened.”] For lust without gluttony would surely be regarded as a monster, since these two are so united and fused together that, if they could ever have been separated, the genitals themselves would not in the first place be attached to the belly. Look at the body: it is a single region.

Indeed, [Note: [Col. 0953D] “According to the arrangement of the members is the order of the vices.” Hence Jerome’s statement in Letter 147 to Amasis: “According to the order of the members is the order of the vices.” RIG.] according to the arrangement of the members is the order of the vices: first the belly, and immediately thereafter lust lies beneath the fattening. Sexual heat passes through [Col. 0953C] voracity.

I therefore recognize [Note: [Col. 0953D] “Animal faith”: psychic faith. RIG. (See above, note (a). EDD.] the animal [Note: [Col. 0953C] Ψυχικήν, “psychic.”] faith by its devotion to the flesh, of which it wholly consists, inclined equally to many meals and many marriages. Thus it deservedly accuses the spiritual discipline, its rival in substance, in [Col. 0954B] this kind of continence also, since that discipline puts a bridle upon gluttony by sometimes admitting no food, or only late or dry food, just as it puts a bridle upon lust through a single marriage.

I am now weary of engaging with such persons; I am ashamed even [Note: [Col. 0954C] Semler rejects “with.”] to dispute with those whose very defense is shameless. For how am I to defend chastity and sobriety without censuring their opponents? I shall name only once what these people are: [Note: [Col. 0953D] “The outer and inner sausages of the Psychics.” He rightly prefaced this with respect for his hearers’ ears. For the inner sausage is packed with the gluttonous stuffing of meat, like some gourmand’s abdomen; the outer is [Col. 0954D] shamelessly distended like a belly, like that Horatian god made from a fig-tree trunk:

> And the red stake projecting from his obscene groin.

RIG.] the outer and inner sausages of the Psychics.

These people quarrel with the Paraclete; [Note: [Col. 0954D] “For this reason the new prophecies are rejected.” Thus, at the beginning of his book against Praxeas, he complains that Praxeas expelled prophecy from Rome. The Montanists also called the Catholics προφητοφόντας, “slayers of prophets” (or “murderers of prophets,” EDD.), as can be learned from the fragments of Apollonius of Hierapolis preserved in Nicephorus, Book IV, chapter 5. RIG.] for this reason the new prophecies [Note: [Col. 0954C] Semler: “prophetic things.”] are rejected—not because Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla proclaim another God; not because they dissolve Jesus Christ (1 John 4:3); not because they overthrow any rule of faith or hope; but plainly because they teach people to fast more often than to marry.

Concerning the measure of [Col. 0954C] marrying, we have already published our defense of monogamy. Now, concerning the chastisement of diet, comes the second—or rather the first—[Note: [Col. 0954C] Semler and Leopold: “of the second, or rather the first.”] contest of continence.

[Note: [Col. 0954D] “They accuse us because we observe fasts peculiar to ourselves”: peculiar, that is, to the Montanists or followers of the Paraclete, by command of the new discipline. RIG.—Ἴδια, “not customary among others.” [Col. 0955B] SEML.—“They accuse us because we observe fasts peculiar to ourselves.” It must not be thought that all xerophagies are condemned here, but only those observed under Montanus’s superstitious discipline. Canon 50 of the Council of Laodicea has: δεῖ πᾶσαν τὴν τεσσαρακοστὴν νηστεύειν ξηροφαγοῦντας, “One ought to fast throughout the whole Lent while practicing xerophagy.” This, however, does not agree with what Tertullian says below in [Col. 0955C] chapter 15. LE PR.] They accuse us because we observe fasts peculiar to ourselves; because we generally prolong our stations [Col. 0955A] until evening; because we also observe xerophagies, drying our food by excluding all flesh, every kind of gravy, and all especially moist fruits, so that [Note: [Col. 0955B] Rhenanus: “and not.”] we neither eat nor drink anything with a vinous quality; and because we also abstain from bathing, which accords with a dry diet.

They therefore reject the novelty, concerning whose unlawfulness they lay down a preliminary objection: it must either be judged a heresy, if it is a human presumption, or pronounced a false prophecy, if it is a spiritual ordinance. Thus, from whichever side, we who proclaim differently are to hear an anathema (Gal. 1:8). [Note: [Col. 0955B] Thus Semler.]

## CHAPTER II
For as regards fasts, they set against us the fixed days appointed by God, as when in Leviticus the Lord commands Moses that the tenth day of the seventh month is the Day of Atonement, saying: “It shall be a holy day for you, and you shall afflict your souls”; [Col. 0955B] and “every soul that has not been afflicted on that day shall be cut off from his people” (Lev. 16:29).

> **Note [Col. 0955C].** Certainly they suppose that in the Gospel those days were designated for fasting on which the Bridegroom was taken away, and that these alone are now the lawful days for fasting. “In the Gospel,” that is, today, among Christians. So think, namely, the Catholics, whom he calls the “Psychics.” Yet in his book *On Prayer* he expressed the view that on the day of the Passion there is a common and, as it were, public observance of fasting—as though among Catholics, apart from the day of the Passion, or apart from those days on which the Bridegroom was taken away, there were no lawful days for fasting, nor any common or public observance of fasting, but, as he will soon say, one practiced freely at each person’s discretion. And yet the testimony of Jerome in his *Epistle to Marcella* ought to carry the greatest authority: that the Catholic Church, by apostolic tradition, fasts one Lent (*Quadragesima*) each year at the appropriate season. For who would listen to someone saying that those days on which the Bridegroom was taken away—Good Friday and Saturday, a period of forty-eight hours—constituted that one Lent? Or would it be more truthful to say that the ancient Christians, formed by divine [Col. 0955D] and apostolic institutions, called their fasts “Lent” after Christ’s forty-day fast, so as to signify that they were not Jewish but Christian, and that the punctilious observances of the Jewish law—pure meals, great days, and sabbath fasts—had been abolished by the benefit of Christian liberty?

> Accordingly, mindful of the liberty obtained through the Lord’s Passion, which had occurred on the day of Preparation, they consecrated the day of Preparation to fasting, so that on that day there might be what Septimius calls in his book *On Prayer* “a common and, as it were, public observance of fasting.” Soon afterward, in their desire to manifest the grief conceived from the Lord’s Passion, they extended this kind of fast into Saturday. They nevertheless continued to observe other fasts useful for commending their prayers, though these varied according to each person’s discretion; above all, however, they remained free from the yoke of that sabbath rite. Indeed, lest they appear to Judaize in any respect, they did not call the fast of the Christian day of Preparation, or of the Pascha of the Crucifixion (*πάσχα σταυρωσίμου*), and of the following Saturday either “the Preparation” or “the Sabbath,” but “Lent”; so that it might now be a Christian [Col. 0956B] fast—not a sacrament of the Preparation or the Sabbath, but of that Lent which Christ had completed by an altogether divine fast.

> Certainly, in this sense, what Catholics in Tertullian’s age said—that those days on which the Bridegroom was taken away were days designated for fasting, while at other times one should fast differently, by discretion rather than command, according to each person’s circumstances and reasons; and that the apostles had observed the same rule, imposing no other yoke of fixed fasts to be undertaken by everyone in common—will be confirmed by Jerome’s statement in his letter to Marcella that the Catholic Church, by apostolic tradition, fasts one Lent each year at the appropriate season. For whatever Christians fasted—which Irenaeus, as quoted by Eusebius in *History* V, relates was observed with such variety and diversity that some believed they should fast for one day, others for two, others for more, while still others prolonged their own day of fasting for forty hours, day and night—whatever, I say, and in whatever manner they fasted, they professed that they were fasting Lent. Socrates too, in the fifth book of his *History*, says that this seemed remarkable to him. He certainly would have had less cause for wonder had he remembered that this was the apostles’ intention: once the Jewish sabbaths had been effaced, Christians were to name the fasts that they offered to their Lord—such little things in return for such great things—after the duration of the Lord’s fast, so that those who were less capable [Col. 0956D] of attaining it in actual practice might at least honor it in remembrance. Thus some, by a fast of one day, others of two, and others of several days, alike honored Christ’s Lent while nevertheless maintaining peace among themselves. For this is what Irenaeus says: *ἡ διαφωνία τῆς νηστείας τὴν εὔνοιαν τῆς πίστεως συνίστησι*—“Difference in fasting commends concord in faith.” RIG., following the editions.

Certainly, in [Col. 0956A] the Gospel they suppose that those days were designated for fasting on which the Bridegroom was taken away, and that these alone are now the lawful days for Christian fasts, once the ancient observances of the Law and the Prophets have been abolished. For when it suits them, they acknowledge the meaning of “the Law and the Prophets were until John” (Luke 16:16). Accordingly, thereafter fasting is to be undertaken without distinction, [variant: “differently,” Rig., Venetian ed.] at one’s discretion, not by command of the new discipline, according to each person’s circumstances and reasons.

> **Note [Col. 0956D].** “The apostles too observed this.” Namely, the days mentioned above on which the Bridegroom was taken away. For he repeatedly presses this reasoning in this very work, where he says that the day of Preparation, dedicated to fasting, was continued by the Catholics into Saturday: fasting was never obligatory except at the Pascha, according to the reasoning transmitted elsewhere. On this subject a passage of Augustine’s *Epistle to Casulanus* should be noted: he says that he sees fasting commanded in the evangelical and apostolic writings, but that the commands of the Lord or of the apostles do not define on which days one ought not to fast and on which one ought. RIG.

Thus the apostles too observed this rule, imposing no other yoke of fixed fasts to be undertaken by everyone in common (Acts 15:10); nor, consequently, of stations, which themselves indeed had their own days—Wednesday and Friday [variant: “have,” Semler]—

> **Note [Col. 0956D].** “The apostles too observed this.” Namely, the days mentioned above on which the Bridegroom was taken away. For he repeatedly presses this reasoning in this very work, where he says that the day of Preparation, dedicated to fasting, was continued by the Catholics into Saturday: fasting was never obligatory except at the Pascha, according to the reasoning transmitted elsewhere. On this subject a passage of Augustine’s *Epistle to Casulanus* should be noted: he says that he sees fasting commanded in the evangelical and apostolic writings, but that the commands of the Lord or of the apostles do not define on which days one ought not to fast and on which one ought. RIG.

yet were practiced at large [variant: *passim*, “everywhere,” in Wouwer’s manuscript; that is the older form],

> **Note [Col. 0956D].** “Yet they are practiced at large.” That is, here and there and at each person’s discretion. RIG.

and neither under the law of a command nor beyond the close of the day, since prayers too are generally concluded at the ninth hour, after Peter’s example as related in Acts (Acts 3:8).

As for xerophagies, [Col. 0956B] they regard the term as a new name for an affected observance and something very close to pagan superstition. Such are the purificatory rites that cleanse Apis, Isis, and the Great Mother through the exclusion of specified foods. For faith, being free in Christ, owes no abstinence from particular foods even to the Jewish law, since the Apostle has once for all admitted it to the entire meat market. He denounces those who, just as they forbid marriage, command abstention from foods created by God; and thus, they say, we were already marked out at that time as those who in the last days would depart from the faith, giving heed to the seductive spirits of the world and to the teachings of liars, having their conscience branded with a hot iron (1 Tim. 4:1). With what fires, I ask you? I suppose with those by which we so often conduct weddings and cook our dinners every day.

Likewise they say that we too are struck by what was said to the Galatians (Gal. 4:10), as observers of days and months and years. Meanwhile they also hurl at us Isaiah’s declaration: “The Lord has not chosen such a fast” (Isa. 58:4–5)—that is, not abstinence from food, but the works of justice that he adds afterward. They say too that the Lord himself in the Gospel gave a concise answer to every [Col. 0957B] scruple concerning diet [variant: “of diet,” Semler]: a person is not defiled [text: *communicari*; variants: *coinquinari*, Semler and Leopold] by what is put into the mouth, but by what proceeds from the mouth (Mark 7:15). He himself ate and drank, even to the point of being reproached: “Behold, a gluttonous man and a drinker” (Matt. 11:19). Likewise, they say, the Apostle teaches that food does not commend us to God: we do not abound if we eat, nor are we deficient if we do not eat (1 Cor. 8:8).

By these and similar arguments they now subtly aim at enabling everyone more inclined toward his belly to regard as superfluous and not particularly necessary the observances connected with food withheld, reduced, or delayed—

> **Note [Col. 0957D].** Withheld or reduced: food withheld by fasting, reduced by xerophagy, and delayed because of the stations, which, since they were prolonged, customarily postponed food. LE PR.

[variants: “postponed,” Semler; “brought,” Junius; “reduced,” Junius].

> **Note [Col. 0957D].** “The observances of delayed food.” “Delayed” means postponed. Thus below in this little work: “They sigh for the authority of a star that delays.” RIG.

They evidently set before God [variant: “setting before,” Junius; “God” absent in Semler] the works of justice and innocence.

> **Note [Col. 0957D].** “And we know what sort of suasoriae are composed in favor of fleshly comforts.” He means: We know the sort of declamations our Psychics are accustomed to deliver in recommending fleshly comforts. Among rhetoricians two classes of themes are treated: *suasoriae* and *controversiae*. The *suasoriae*, being regarded as lighter exercises requiring less judgment, are assigned to boys as elementary exercises in speaking. The *controversiae*, or judicial speeches, are assigned to those of more mature ability. RIG.

And we know what sort of *suasoriae* are composed in favor of fleshly comforts, since [variant: “how,” Semler] it is easy to say: “It is necessary that I believe with my whole heart, love God and my neighbor [Col. 0957C] [variant: “as myself,” Semler]; for on these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets—not on the emptiness of my lungs and intestines.”

## CHAPTER III

Accordingly, we must first affirm that which is in danger of being covertly undermined: how much this emptiness avails before God, and, before everything else, whence arose the very principle of meriting God’s favor in this manner.

> **Note [Col. 0958D].** “For the necessity of the observance will then be acknowledged when the authority of its principle has become evident.” In his book *On the Crown*, Tertullian himself prescribed the rule by which a custom or observance is to be approved: namely, that a custom must be honored when it is found consonant with reason, and that the rationale of Christian observances becomes stronger when they are also defended by nature, which is the first discipline of all. Here, however, he appeals only to the authority of reason. RIG.

For the necessity of the observance will then be acknowledged when the authority of its principle, which must be traced from the beginning, has become evident.

[Col. 0958A] Adam had received from God the law that he was not to taste of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and that he would die if he tasted it. But then, after the spiritual ecstasy in which he had prophesied that great mystery concerning Christ and the Church, he himself reverted to the psychical state [variant: “was overthrown,” Junius]. No longer comprehending the things of the Spirit, he yielded more readily to his belly than to God, consented to food rather than to the commandment, and sold salvation for gluttony. In short, he ate and perished; otherwise he would have been saved if he had preferred to fast from that one little tree [Semler also reads “had preferred”].

> **Note [Col. 0958D].** “If he had preferred to fast from that one little tree.” What sort of fast was that, seeing that God had permitted Adam to eat from every tree, excepting only one little tree? In truth, Adam was destroyed not by gluttony but by desire for a premature divinity. RIG.

Thus from this point psychical faith may recognize its own seed, deriving from it its appetite for fleshly things and its rejection of spiritual things.

I therefore hold that from the beginning gluttony has been a murderer, destined to be punished with torments and penalties on the Day of Judgment, even if God had commanded no fasts. Nevertheless, by showing me whence Adam had been slain, he who had revealed the offense had left me to understand its remedies: of my own accord, in whatever ways and at whatever times I could, I was to regard food as poison and take hunger as its antidote. Through hunger I was to purge away the cause of death transmitted from the beginning [variant: “the fall,” Semler] into me together with the whole race. I was certain that this was God’s will, since he had willed the contrary not to be done, and sufficiently confident that concern for self-restraint would please him from whom I had learned that the fault of self-indulgence was condemned.

Moreover, since he himself commands fasting and specifically calls the soul afflicted by restrictions of food a sacrifice (Ps. 50:18), who will now doubt that this was the rationale of every mortification concerning diet: that through food again being forbidden and the commandment being observed, the primal sin might now be expiated, so that a human being might make satisfaction to God through the same material that had occasioned his offense, [Col. 0958C] that is, through the prohibition of food; and thus rekindle salvation by abstinence, in a manner corresponding to that in which he had extinguished it by overfeeding, now despising many lawful foods in compensation for the one unlawful food?

## CHAPTER IV

This principle was preserved in the providence of God, who regulates [variant: “governs,” Semler] everything according to its proper seasons. Let no one, therefore, argue contrariwise in order to overthrow our proposition: “Why, then, did God not immediately establish some restriction of diet? Why did he, rather, even enlarge the permission?”

For in the beginning he had indeed assigned to humankind only the produce of plants and trees [Col. 0959A]: “Behold, I have given you every seed-bearing plant that sows seed upon the earth, and every tree that has within itself the fruit of seed fit for sowing; it shall be food for you” (Gen. 1:29 [printed here as Gen. 9:29]). But afterward, when he had enumerated to Noah the subjection of all the beasts of the earth, the birds of heaven, the creatures moving upon the earth, the fish of the sea, and every living creature [variant: “creeping creature,” Semler], he said: “They shall be food for you; as I gave you all the green plants, so have I given you them all. But you shall not eat flesh with the blood of its life” (Gen. 9:2). For by the very fact that he excludes from consumption [Semler adds “removes”] only that flesh whose life is not poured out through its blood, it is manifest that he permitted the use [variant: “consumption,” Junius] of every other kind of flesh.

To this we reply that it was not fitting for a human being to be burdened at that point with any law of abstinence, when he had just proved incapable of enduring so slight a prohibition as that of a single fruit. He was therefore to be relaxed and strengthened by liberty itself. Likewise, [variant: “and,” Semler and Leopold] after the flood, in the restoration of the human race, it was enough for the time being to impose the single law of abstinence from blood while permitting [variant: “by permission,” Semler] the use [Junius thinks “consumption” had perhaps dropped out] of everything else. For the Lord had already displayed judgment through the flood; he had also issued a further threat through the demand for blood from the hand of a brother and from the hand of a beast (Gen. 9:5).

> **Note [Col. 0959D].** “From the hand of a beast, every…” Thus Junius and Leopold.

Therefore, in administering beforehand all that was necessary for the justice of judgment, he released the material of liberty, preparing discipline by indulgence: permitting all things so that he might remove certain things; intending to demand more if he had entrusted more; and intending to command abstinence after he had first granted indulgence [variant: “permitted,” Semler]. Thus, all the more, as we have said, the primal sin would be expiated by the practice of greater abstinence amid the occasion of greater license.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0959C]

Finally, when a people belonging to God’s household had begun to be chosen for God, and the restoration of humankind could be given its initial formation, then all laws and disciplines were imposed, including those that curtailed diet by removing certain foods as unclean, so that humanity might someday endure fasts more readily through having practiced perpetual abstinence in certain matters.

> **Note [Col. 0959D].** “For the first people,” etc. The Jewish people are called the “first people,” in distinction from the second, that of the Gentiles. Here, however, the words that we have therefore enclosed in parentheses—“its Lord appeared,” or rather “appeared to them”—seem altogether superfluous. PAM.

For the first people had recarved within itself the crime of the first human being—

> **Note [Col. 0959D].** “Had recarved the crime of the first human being.” Augustine on Psalm 6: “For when we are converted—that is, by the transformation of our former life—we recarve the spirit.” Rufinus on the same Psalm: “When we are converted—that is, when through the transformation of our former life we are recarved.” RIG.

—being found more inclined toward its belly than toward God. When its Lord, by the strong hand and uplifted arm of God, had rescued it from the harshness of Egyptian bondage [variant: “the rescued lord,” Semler; “its Lord appeared,” Junius; Wouwer’s manuscript adds “and”; Pamelius conjectures “to them” and uses parentheses], and it had been destined for a land flowing with milk [Col. 0960A] and honey, it was immediately scandalized by the sight of the abundant wilderness. Sighing over the loss of Egyptian plenty, it murmured against Moses and Aaron: “Would that we had died, struck by the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat over the pots of meat and ate bread to the full! Why [variant: “Because,” others] have you brought us out into these deserts, to kill this whole congregation with hunger?” (Ex. 16:2).

Through the same preference for its belly, it was later to lament those same leaders, who acted as God’s arbiters, provoking them with its craving for meat and its recollection of Egypt’s abundance: “Who will give us meat to eat [variant: “Who will feed us,” Junius; “will give us to eat,” Leopold]? We remember the fish that we ate freely in Egypt, and the cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic. But now our soul is dry; our eyes see nothing except [variant: “without,” Semler] manna” (Num. 11:4).

Thus even those angelic loaves of xerophagy [Col. 0960B] displeased them [variants: “in the possession of,” Francis; “bread,” Wouwer’s manuscript].

> **Note [Cols. 0959D–0960D].** “The angelic loaves of xerophagy.” Far unlike those provisions supplied for the stuffing of dry-fare athletes and fattened human beings. RIG.

They preferred to smell of garlic and onion rather than of heaven. Therefore, from people so ungrateful, all the more agreeable and palatable foods were withdrawn, at once to punish gluttony and train self-restraint, so that the former might be condemned and the latter instructed.

## CHAPTER VI

Now, if we have rashly referred the rationale of diet restricted by God, and to be restricted by us for God’s sake, back to the experiences of the beginning, let us consult the common consciousness. Nature herself will declare what sort of persons she customarily presents us as being before food and drink, while our saliva is still untouched—at least in conducting those affairs of the senses [variant: “by sense,” Gelenius] in which divine things are treated: how much more powerful in mind and how much more lively in heart than when that whole dwelling of the inner person, packed with food, flooded with wine, [Col. 0960C] and heated by excrement already being digested [variant: “seething,” others], becomes a preliminary workshop for latrines—

> **Note [Col. 0960D].** “A preliminary workshop.” Blessed Jerome also imitated this: “What kind of fast,” he says, “or what kind of refreshment after a fast is it? We distend ourselves with the previous day’s feasts, and our throat becomes a workshop—or rather a preliminary workshop—for latrines.” He too cites the Scriptures quoted here: Exodus 31, Deuteronomy 33 and 8, and Isaiah 6; except that there too the reading should be “God,” which in Greek is *θεόν*, and that the author uses his own expression *salvificatorie* for “saving.” PAM.

—in which, plainly, nothing remains nearer at hand than to think in the direction of lust. “The people ate and drank and rose up to play” (Ex. 32:6). Understand the modesty of Holy Scripture: it would not have censured the play unless it had been indecent.

Besides, how few will remember religion when the places of memory are occupied and the faculties of wisdom obstructed? No one will remember God as he ought, as is fitting, and as is useful, at the time—

> **Note [Cols. 0960D–0961D].** “At the time when it is customary for a person to fall away from himself.” For through drunkenness wisdom dies for a time. RIG.

—when it is customary for a person to fall away from himself. Food [Col. 0961A] either kills or wounds every discipline.

I am lying if the Lord himself, when reproaching Israel for forgetting him, does not attribute [variant: “reckon,” Semler] the cause to fullness: “The beloved grew fat and stout and broad; and he abandoned God who made him and withdrew from the Lord his Savior” (Deut. 32:15). Finally, in the same Deuteronomy, when commanding that precaution be taken against the same cause, he says: “Lest, when you have eaten and drunk and built excellent houses, and your sheep and cattle have multiplied, and your silver and gold, your heart be exalted and you forget the Lord your God” (Deut. 8:12).

He placed before the corrupting influence of riches the monstrousness of voracity, which riches themselves procure. Through them, of course, the people’s heart had grown fat, so that it could not see with its eyes, hear with its ears, or understand with its heart, obstructed by the fat that God specifically removed from consumption, thereby unteaching humanity to pursue fattening.

By contrast, in whom was the heart found to be uplifted [variant: “carried upward,” Francis] rather than fattened? The man who maintained a continuous fast for forty days and as many nights, beyond the capacity of human nature, while spiritual faith supplied the strength. He saw the glory of God with his eyes, heard the voice of God with his ears, and understood with his heart the law of God, who was already teaching at that time that a person lives not by bread alone but by every word of God (Luke 4:4). Meanwhile the fatter people were unable steadfastly to contemplate even Moses himself being fed by God and his abstinence being fattened by God’s name [variant: “divine power,” Wouwer’s manuscript and Leopold].

Deservedly, therefore, the Lord later showed himself in the flesh to Moses as a companion in his fasts, and no less to Elijah. For Elijah too, by the very fact that he first called down a famine, had already dedicated himself sufficiently to fasting: “As the Lord lives,” he said, “before whose sight I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain in these years” (3 Kings 17).

Then, fleeing from Jezebel’s threat, after a single portion of food and drink that he had found when awakened by an angel, he too, for forty days and nights, with empty stomach and dry mouth, reached Mount Horeb. There, when he had turned aside into a cave [variant: “into the cave,” Junius], with what intimate fellowship from God was he received! “What are you doing here, Elijah?” (3 Kings 19:9). That voice was far friendlier than “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3:9). For the latter threatened a man who had eaten; the former caressed [variant: “the fasting man,” Venetian ed.] one who had fasted. So great is the privilege of restricted diet that it gives God to a human being as his tent-companion—truly, like with like. For if the eternal God does not hunger (Isa. 1:11), as he testifies through Isaiah, then the time when a human being is made equal to God will be [Col. 0961D] when he lives without food.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0962A]

> **Note [Col. 0961D].** “We have therefore now proceeded.” He has shown what intemperance produces, so that he may demonstrate the effects of fasting, which he pursues here through various examples. LE PR.

We have therefore now proceeded to examples, in order to review the effective powers [variant: “power,” Venetian ed.] of the usefulness of this [variant: “that very,” Semler] observance, which even reconciles an angry God to humankind.

Israel had sinned; but when it was gathered by Samuel at the drawing of water at Mizpah [variant: “Mizpah,” Semler; “but” absent in Francis], it immediately washed away the sin by fasting, with the result that it simultaneously escaped [variant: “routed,” Semler] the danger of battle. At the very time when Samuel was offering the burnt offering (1 Kings 7:9), we hear that God’s clemency was procured by nothing more than the people’s abstinence.

And the Philistines were moving into battle [conjectures: “so that the Philistines moved into battle,” Junius; Leopold conjectures *admovedbantur*]; then at last [variant: “in that very place,” Francis] the Lord thundered with a mighty voice over the Philistines, and they were thrown into confusion and fell before Israel. The men of Israel went forth from Mizpah and pursued the Philistines, and as far as Beth-car the unfed struck down the well-fed, and the unarmed [Col. 0962B] the armed. Such will be the strength of those who fast for God: heaven fights on behalf of such people. Here you have the pattern of protection necessary also for spiritual wars.

Likewise, when Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, after already capturing many cities, directed blasphemies and threats against Israel through Rabshakeh (4 Kings 18–19), what but this diverted him from his purpose toward Ethiopia? Then what but King Hezekiah’s humiliation destroyed one hundred and eighty thousand of his army through an angel? For when the enemy’s cruelty had been reported, the king tore his garment, put on sackcloth, and ordered the elders of the priests to approach God through Isaiah in the same dress, prayer of course being accompanied by fasting. For there is no time for food in danger,

> **Note [Col. 0962D].** “Nor any display of fullness in sackcloth.” He calls it a display of fullness because gladness arises from fullness, and from gladness concern for more luxurious adornment; this is incompatible with the horror of ashes and the roughness of sackcloth. RIG.

nor any display of fullness in sackcloth. Abstinence always follows grief, just as overfeeding attends gladness.

Through this attendant of grief—abstinence—even that sinful city Nineveh was delivered from the destruction proclaimed against it. For repentance for its crimes had sufficiently commended it to God when it had fulfilled a three-day fast, even starving the cattle, with whom God was not angry (Jonah 3). Sodom and Gomorrah too would have escaped if they had fasted.

Ahab also recognizes this remedy when, after his transgression, idolatry, and the murder of Naboth—whom Jezebel had killed because of the vineyard—Elijah reproached him: “How have you killed and taken possession of the inheritance? In the place where [variant: “in which place,” Semler] the dogs licked Naboth’s blood, they shall lick yours as well” (3 Kings 21:19). He humbled himself, put sackcloth upon his body, fasted, and slept in sackcloth. Then the word of the Lord came to Elijah: “Have you seen how Ahab has shown reverence [Col. 0962D] before my face? Because he has shown reverence, I shall not bring the affliction in his days, but in the days of his son [Col. 0963A] I shall bring it” (ibid., 29)—for the son was not going to fast.

Thus fasting is an act of reverence toward God. Through it Hannah too, Elkanah’s petitioning wife, previously barren, easily obtained from God that her stomach, emptied of food, should be filled with a son—and indeed a prophet.

But fasts will merit from God not only a change in nature, the averting of dangers, or the obliteration of sins, but also the recognition of mysteries.

> **Note [Col. 0963D].** “Recognition of mysteries.” Thus he calls skill in interpreting sacred figures and images—those, namely, that are divinely presented in dreams. “Mysteries,” therefore, are dreams sent by God. RIG.

Look at Daniel’s example. Concerning the king of Babylon’s dream, all the sophists are thrown into confusion.

> **Note [Col. 0963D].** “All the sophists are thrown into confusion.” He calls those “sophists” whom elsewhere he calls sages, interpreters of dreams, and conjecturers. RIG.

They deny outright [variant: “further,” Junius] that it can be known by human excellence.

> **Note [Col. 0963D].** “They deny outright that it can be known by human excellence.” That is, they deny that an interpretation of the royal dreams can be furnished by human ability. RIG.

Daniel alone, trusting in God and knowing what would avail to merit God’s favor, asks for a period of three days. He fasts with his brotherhood, and so, once his prayers have been commended, he is instructed in every detail of both the sequence and meaning [Col. 0963B] of the dream. The tyrant’s sophists are spared, God is glorified, and Daniel is honored.

Later too, in the first year of King Darius, he was to obtain no lesser favor from God, when, after reconsidering the times foretold by Jeremiah, he set his face toward God in fasting, sackcloth, and ashes.

> **Note [Col. 0963D].** “He set his face toward God.” He turned toward God. RIG.

For the angel sent to him immediately declared that this was the reason for the divine favor: “I have come,” he said, “to show you how deserving of mercy you are”—

> **Note [Col. 0963D].** “How deserving of mercy you are.” How great a grace of compassion you have obtained. RIG.

—namely, through fasting. If he was deserving of mercy from God, he had been terrible to the lions in the pit, where indeed an angel provided a meal for him after he had fasted six days.

## CHAPTER VIII

We also set forth the remaining examples [variant: “We have set forth the ancient examples; now to the new,” Latin translation; “also now to the new,” Junius], for we are now hastening to the new testimonies.

At the threshold of the Gospel (Luke 2:37), [Col. 0963C] Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, who both recognized the infant Lord and proclaimed many things about him to those awaiting the redemption of Israel, is further honored by the testimony of her fasts after the distinguished title of her long widowhood following a single marriage. She shows by what observances one ought to remain in attendance upon the Church, and that Christ is understood by none more than by those who marry once and fast often.

Soon afterward the Lord himself dedicated his baptism—and in his own baptism that of all people—by fasting, though he possessed the power to make loaves from stones and perhaps even to make the Jordan flow with wine, had he truly been a glutton and a drinker. Rather, to the reproach of the old human being, he was initiating the new human being by the power of disdaining food, so that when the devil sought once more to tempt humanity through food, he might display the new human being to him as stronger through complete hunger.

From that point he established in advance a law that fasts were to be completed without sadness. Why should that which is salutary be sad? He also taught that fiercer demons must be fought by fasting. For what wonder is it if [variant: “by,” added by Semler] the unclean spirit is driven out by the same operation through which the Holy Spirit is brought in?

Finally, in order that the favor of the Holy Spirit, together with the further gift of prophecy, might hasten to Cornelius the centurion even before he was baptized, we read that his fasts were heard. I think, moreover, that in Second Corinthians the Apostle too, among his labors, dangers, and hardships, after hunger and thirst, enumerates his many fasts as well (2 Cor. 11:27).

## CHAPTER IX
[Col. 0964B] This principal form of disciplining one’s diet can now also establish a presumption concerning the lesser practices of abstinence, according as they too are useful or necessary in their measure. For the exclusion of certain foods is a partial fast. Let us therefore examine the novelty or futility of xerophagies—that is, dry diets—to see whether in these too there is not a practice of religious discipline as ancient as it is effective.

I return to Daniel and his companions, who preferred a diet of vegetables and a drink of water to the royal dishes and wine-jars, and thereby became more handsome—so that no one need fear even for his little body’s appearance—and, moreover, spiritually cultivated. For God gave the young men knowledge and understanding in every branch of learning, and to Daniel understanding in every utterance, in dreams, and in all wisdom (Dan. 1:17), by which he might also know this very thing: by what means an understanding of mysteries could be obtained from God.

Finally, in the third year of Cyrus, king of the Persians, when he had fallen into reflection upon a vision, he adopted another form of humiliation:

> “In those days I, Daniel, was mourning for three weeks. I ate no pleasant bread; neither flesh nor wine entered my mouth; I did not anoint myself with oil, until the three weeks were completed.”

When they had elapsed, an angel was sent and addressed him as follows:

> “Daniel, you are a pitiable man; do not be afraid, because from the first day on which you applied your soul to reflection and humiliation before God, your word was heard, and I came in response to your word.”

[Col. 0965A] Thus the wretched condition and humiliation of xerophagies dispel fear, turn God’s ears toward us, and make us masters of hidden things.

I return also to Elijah. Although ravens had been accustomed to satisfy him with bread and meat, why afterward, near Beersheba in Judaea, when he had been awakened from sleep, did that angel undoubtedly offer him only bread and water? Had the ravens failed, which might have fed him more generously? Or would it have been difficult for the angel to seize some servant from a royal banquet somewhere, together with a fully furnished dish, and transfer him to Elijah, just as a reapers’ meal was supplied to the hungry Daniel in the lions’ den? Rather, it was necessary to establish an example teaching that in a time of distress, persecution, or any sort of exigency, one must live by xerophagies.

With such a diet David gave expression to his confession: he ate ashes as though they were bread—that is, bread dry and foul as ashes—and mixed his drink with weeping, plainly in place of wine (Ps. 101:10). For abstinence from wine also has its claims to distinction: it both vowed Samuel to God and consecrated Aaron. For Samuel’s mother said:

> “He shall drink neither wine nor intoxicating drink” (1 Reg. 1:15);

for such was also the manner in which she herself prayed to God. And the Lord said to Aaron:

> “You shall drink neither wine nor strong drink, you and your sons after you, whenever you enter the tabernacle or go up to the altar, and you shall not die.”

So truly will those die who minister in the Church without sobriety. In the same way he reproaches Israel shortly afterward:

> “And you gave my consecrated ones wine to drink.”

This restriction of drink, moreover, is a part of xerophagy. Yet wherever abstinence from wine is either required by God or vowed by a human being, there we should understand that restriction of food is also implied, setting the pattern for the drink: as the food, so the drink. It is not likely that anyone would sacrifice half his appetite to God, sober in his water but drunken in his food.

Whether the Apostle too knew xerophagies—he who had undergone greater things, thirst and hunger and many fasts, and who rejected drunken bouts and revelries—the case of his disciple Timothy is sufficient proof. On account of Timothy’s stomach and frequent infirmities, he advised him to use a little wine, from which Timothy had abstained not by institutional rule but by devotion—although habit would have been better for his stomach. [Col. 0966A] By the very fact that he discouraged abstinence from wine under the compulsion of necessity, he commended it as worthy of God (cf. Lev. 10:9; Amos [sic] 15:13; 2 Cor. 11:27; Rom. 13:13; 1 Tim. 5:23).

> **Note [Col. 0964D].** “And to them.” From Semler.
