> **Note [Col. 0964D].** “The novelty or futility of xerophagies.” Abstinence from wine and meat is condemned unless it is undertaken for the sake of continence: Apostolic Canons 51 and 53. —LE PR.

> **Note [Col. 0964D].** “So that no one need fear even for his little body’s appearance.” Thus in Book II *To His Wife*: “Will you escape notice when you sign your bed and your little body?” At this point, then, we should note that Septimius everywhere speaks in the Stoic manner, using diminutives such as “little body,” “little bed,” “little tree,” “little woman,” “little dog,” “little movements,” and “little portions,” and other expressions of this kind, just as the Stoics use σωμάτιον (*little body*), οὐσίδιον (*little property/substance*), ἀξιωμάτιον (*little proposition*), ἀγρίδιον (*little field*), πραγμάτιον (*little affair*), λεξίδιον (*little expression*), δουλάριον (*little slave*), ὀνάριον (*little donkey*), ἀργυρωματίδια (*little pieces of silverware*), ὁπλάρια (*little weapons*), and other such Epictetan terms. —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 0964D].** “Who.” Semler.

> **Note [Col. 0965C].** “Certain for him,” Semler; “for him,” Wouwer manuscript.

> **Note [Col. 0965C].** “For Daniel in the sacred text”; in Latin, “Daniel,” Semler; “in the pit,” Leopold.

> **Note [Col. 0965C].** As Rigault; “you and your son,” Leopold.

> **Note [Col. 0965C].** “Soberly,” Franeker edition.

> **Note [Col. 0965D].** “This restriction of drink, moreover, is a part of xerophagy.” Septimius says that, by thus restricting the form of drink, dry food too is signified. —RIG.

## CHAPTER X

They likewise denounce our stations—our appointed fasts—as unworthy, and some of them, because they are continued into the evening, under the charge of novelty. They say that this duty too should be undertaken voluntarily and not prolonged beyond the ninth hour, following, of course, their own custom. But as regards the question of their being imposed, I shall answer once for all the relevant cases. For the moment, concerning the particular issue belonging to this form of observance—that is, the measure of its duration—we must first demand of them whence they derive this new rule which they prescribe for terminating stations.

If it is because Peter and those with him are said to have entered the temple for prayer at the ninth hour, who will prove to me that they were observing a station on that day, so that the ninth hour may be interpreted as the conclusion and discharge of the station? Indeed, you would more readily find that Peter went up to the upper parts at the sixth hour to pray because it was time to take food, so that the sixth hour might all the more be fixed as the conclusion of this duty, which he seemed about to complete after prayer.

Moreover, since in the same narrative of Luke the third hour is also shown as an hour of prayer, when those who had been initiated by the Holy Spirit were regarded as drunk; and the sixth, when Peter went up to the upper parts; and the ninth, when they entered the temple—why should we not understand that, while the unrestricted liberty of praying always, everywhere, and at every time remains entirely intact, these three hours nevertheless had greater solemnity in divine prayers, since they are especially distinguished in human affairs, divide the day, mark off its business, and are publicly sounded?

Daniel’s example also recommends this interpretation, for he prayed three times a day—plainly by setting apart certain hours, and none other than those which were distinguished and afterward apostolic: the third, sixth, and ninth. Accordingly, I shall say that Peter, following the ancient custom, observed the ninth hour, praying for the third time in the duty of the final prayer.

I say this because of those who think they are acting according to Peter’s rule, though they do not understand it; not as though we rejected the ninth hour, at which we most often complete our stations on Wednesday and Friday, but because, in the case of observances kept by tradition, we ought all the more to provide a worthy rationale in proportion as they lack the authority of Scripture, until they are either confirmed or corrected by some heavenly gift.

> “And if there is anything you do not understand, the Lord will reveal it to you” (Phil. 3:15).

Therefore, after setting aside the Paraclete, the confirmer of all these things and guide of all truth, I ask whether among you a less worthy rationale is advanced for observing the ninth hour, so that this same rationale may be attributed even to Peter, if he was then observing a station. For it is derived from the Lord’s departure. Although that departure ought always to be commemorated without distinction of hours, we are nevertheless then more deeply bound to him, in accordance with the very designation “station”; for soldiers too, although never forgetful of their military oath, are more especially obedient when on station-duty.

Accordingly, the discipline of abstinence must be observed until that hour at which the world, darkened from the sixth hour onward, performed its mournful office for the Lord at his death, so that we too may then return to gladness when the world also recovered its brightness.

If this savors more strongly of Christian religion because it more fully celebrates Christ’s glory, I can equally establish from the same sequence of events the fixed point of a late station: namely, that we should fast until evening, awaiting the time of the Lord’s burial, when Joseph carried away the body he had requested and laid it in the tomb. Hence it is even irreligious to refresh the servants’ flesh before the master’s.

But I would concede this only in response to the challenge of their arguments, repelling conjectures with conjectures—though, I think, with more trustworthy ones. Let us see whether antiquity too affords us any such support.

In Exodus, did not that posture of Moses, as he fought against Amalek with prayers and persevered until sunset, constitute a late station? Do we suppose that Joshua son of Nun ate lunch on that day when, as he fought the Amorites, he commanded even the elements to keep station?

> “The sun stood still in Gibeon, and the moon in Aijalon. The sun and moon stood still at the command, until the people took vengeance upon their enemies; and the sun stood still in the middle of heaven and did not proceed toward its setting and the end of a single day.”

No such day existed before or afterward—plainly one so prolonged—“that,” Scripture says, “God should listen to a human being,” one, to be sure, equal to the sun in remaining so long at his duty, his station even longer than a late one.

Certainly Saul too, when engaged in battle, expressly imposed this duty (1 Reg. 14:24):

> “Cursed is the man who eats bread before evening, until I take vengeance upon my enemy.”

None of all his people tasted, and the whole land did not eat. God, moreover, granted such authority to the edict of that station that Jonathan, Saul’s son, although unaware that the fast had been fixed to last into the evening, was immediately convicted by lot of an offense because he had tasted honey; and only with difficulty was he delivered from danger through the people’s entreaty, for he had become guilty of appetite, however innocent.

Daniel too, in the first year of King Darius, while fasting in sackcloth and ashes and making confession to God, says:

> “And while I was still speaking in prayer, behold, the man whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, flying swiftly, drew near to me at about the hour of the evening sacrifice.”

This will be a late station, which, fasting until evening, sacrifices to God a richer prayer.

> **Note [Col. 0965D].** “Likewise our stations, as unworthy.” The author’s meaning proves that one should read “as imposed,” as also a little later: “But as regards the question of imposition.” He says that the Psychics accuse our stations as being imposed and prolonged into the evening. They contend that this duty ought not to be imposed but undertaken at one’s discretion, and that stations should not be prolonged into the evening but terminated at the ninth hour. —RIG.

> **Note [Cols. 0965D–0966D].** “Our stations as unworthy,” etc. He has spoken elsewhere about stations. A station differs from a fast, although Pamelius does not think so. It was a religious observance whereby Christians who were to attend the synaxis prolonged their fasting until the ninth hour. For in former times fasting was of two kinds: one ended only in the evening, such as the Lenten fast; the other was extended only until the ninth hour, such as the fast of Wednesday and Friday. Here, however, he attacks the Montanists, not the Catholics, as Pamelius wrongly asserted. —LE PR.

> **Note [Col. 0966C].** “Will prove,” Semler; “may prove,” Junius.

> **Note [Col. 0966D].** “The sixth hour of the day may be fixed as the conclusion of this duty.” That is, may be fixed or determined beforehand. —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 0966C].** “That one must pray,” Semler.

> **Note [Col. 0966D].** “Which are publicly sounded.” Therefore, in Septimius’s age only these three more distinguished hours were publicly sounded, a signal being given by trumpet or bell. We learn from Varro’s fifth book *On the Latin Language* that among the ancient Romans too the same divisions of the day were customarily announced, an attendant, whenever it seemed proper to the praetor, proclaiming to the people that it was the third hour, then noon, and the ninth hour. —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 0966C].** “Of other hours,” Semler.

> **Note [Col. 0967D].** “Which,” Junius.

> **Note [Col. 0967D].** “To refresh the flesh.” That is, to rest. —RIG.

## CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0968B] I believe, however, that all these things are unknown to those who take offense at our practices, or are perhaps known only from reading and not from attentive consideration. This accords with the greater mass of the unlearned among, of course, that most glorious multitude of the Psychics.

For this reason we have proceeded through each separate form—fasts, xerophagies, and stations—so that, as we review the preparation furnished by both Testaments and show how greatly the duties of refusing, reducing, or delaying food are beneficial, we may blunt those who disparage these practices as useless. Likewise, by showing at the same time the rank they have always held within religious discipline, we may refute those who denounce them as novel: for what has always existed is not new, and what is useful is not empty.

There is also this consideration before us: some of these duties, having been commanded by God to a human being, established a law; others, having been offered by a human being to God, fulfilled a vow. Yet even a vow, when accepted by God, creates a law for the future through the authority of the one who accepted it; for by approving what had been done, he thereby commanded that it should be done thereafter.

Here, accordingly, the controversy of the opposing side is introduced under another form when they say: “It is either false prophecy, if a spiritual voice established these solemn observances, or heresy, if human presumption devised them.” Yet in censuring the very form through which the ancient observances too ran their course, and in turning back upon us arguments that opponents of the ancient observances might have raised against them, they will be obliged either to reject those ancient observances too or certainly to accept these current ones—especially since the latter, whoever their institutor may be, whether spiritual or merely faithful, tend toward the same God as the ancient observances.

For both heresy and false prophecy will undoubtedly be judged by a difference of divinity among all of us who are champions of the one God, the Creator, and of his Christ. I therefore defend this side without distinction, offering them whichever position they wish to take.

“It is the spirit of the devil,” you say, O Psychic. How, then, does it impose duties belonging to our God and require them to be offered to none other than our God? Either contend that the devil cooperates with our God, or let Satan be regarded as the Paraclete.

But you affirm that it is a human Antichrist; for in John heretics are called by this name. How, then, did whoever he is arrange in our Christ these duties toward our Lord, when Antichrists too have come forth against our Christ in relation to God? On which side, therefore, do you think the spirit is confirmed among us: when it commands, or when it approves what our God has both always commanded and always approved?

Yet once again you plant boundary-stakes for God, in discipline just as in grace, in solemn observances just as in spiritual gifts—as though his duties had ceased just as his benefits had, and so you deny that he still imposes obligations because here too “the Law and the Prophets were until John.” It remains for you to abolish him altogether, since as far as lies in you he is so wholly inactive.

> **Note [Col. 0967D].** “Those who take offense at our practices”—that is, plainly, at the Montanist institutions of the Paraclete. —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 0967D].** “Those who disparage these things as useless”—that is, as unprofitable and of no value. —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 0968D].** “Sanctions,” Latin edition.

> **Note [Col. 0968D].** “Hence,” Semler.

> **Note [Col. 0968D].** “And,” added by Semler.

> **Note [Col. 0968D].** “Will have been able,” Semler.

> **Note [Col. 0968D].** The Latin edition reads: “would have been able … ought to have.”

> **Note [Col. 0968D].** “Expressly,” Semler; “clearly,” Franeker edition.

> **Note [Col. 0968D].** “Especially” is absent from Wouwer’s codex.

> **Note [Cols. 0968D–0969B].** “Tend toward the same God.” That is, they agree with the same God and should be understood as being spoken concerning the same God. Thus Baeticus said concerning God: “It is vain to give commandments by which human beings should live, while he himself, now that he has deigned to become human, has run his course without observing the commandments.” That is, he accomplished what had been ordained and foretold concerning him. —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 0969B].** “Toward God” deleted by the Latin edition.

> **Note [Col. 0969C].** “You plant boundary-stakes for God.” Authors who treat the regulation of boundaries teach that in some regions stakes were set up as boundary markers—of holm oak, olive, juniper, and so forth, including pitch-coated stakes of holm oak. —RIG.

## CHAPTER XII

For already in this kind of observance too, “made rich and filled, you reign” [Col. 0970A] (1 Cor. 4:8), accusing yourselves of no sins to be worn away by fasts, needing no knowledge of revelations to be wrested forth through xerophagies, and fearing no battles of your own to be dispersed by stations.

Even if the Paraclete had fallen silent after John, we ourselves ought especially for this purpose to have become prophets to ourselves. I no longer mean merely for appeasing God’s anger, or obtaining his protection or grace, but for fortifying ourselves beforehand against the condition of the last times, by imposing every form of ταπεινοφρόνησις (*humble self-abasement*). For prison must be learned beforehand; hunger and thirst must be practiced; endurance of both starvation and a straitened diet must be acquired, so that a Christian may enter prison in the same condition in which he would have emerged from it.

He will not be going there to suffer punishment, but discipline; not the world’s torments, but his own duties. Thus he will go forth from confinement to the contest all the more confidently, already worn away, having nothing left of the flesh, so that the tortures too may have no material upon which to work; armed only in dry skin, hardened like horn against the claws; having already sent ahead the sap of his blood, as though it were the soul’s baggage, while the soul itself now hastens onward, having through frequent fasting already learned to know death close at hand.

It is plainly your practice to furnish taverns in prisons for martyrs whose constancy is uncertain, lest they miss their customary fare, grow weary of life, or be scandalized by the new discipline of abstinence—a discipline which not even that former martyr of yours, Pristinus, no Christian, had touched. For a while, taking advantage of lax custody, you stuffed him with every bath as though it were better than baptism, every retreat of luxury as though it were more private than the Church, and every enticement of this life as though it were worthier than eternal life. By these things, I suppose, you so bound him not to wish to die, and finally, on the very day of his trial, so enervated him—having first medicated him in broad daylight with spiced wine as though with an antidote—that, when merely tickled by a few claws, for that was all his drunkenness perceived, he could no longer answer the governor when asked which Lord he confessed.

And thus, already wrenched away from this confession, having nothing but hiccups and belches, he defecated in the very act of his denial.

That is why those who preach the discipline of sobriety are false prophets; that is why those who observe it are heretics! Why, then, do you hesitate to believe in Apicius as the Paraclete whom you deny in Montanus?

You lay down as a prior objection that the solemn observances belonging to this faith were established by the Scriptures or by the tradition of the elders, and that nothing further is to be added to its practice, because innovation is unlawful. Stand your ground at that position, if you can.

> **Note [Col. 0969C].** “Going forth from confinement to the contest, worn away.” *Abusus* means almost consumed and exhausted by long use. If the manuscript evidence afforded any help, I would prefer *obesus*, in the sense in which an ancient poet cited by Gellius used *obesus* for “thin and slender.” —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 0969C].** “Hardened like horn against the claws.” Claws were instruments of torture. At first, as the name suggests, they were claws cut from animals; later they were iron implements made in their shape. With these they scraped—or, as some said, “wrote upon” or “engraved”—the victims’ sides. Septimius therefore says that skin made dry and horny by fasting would be more resistant to such tortures. —RIG.

> **Note [Cols. 0969C–0969D].** “Having already sent ahead the sap of his blood.” That is, having sent it ahead to God, to whom he himself is already hastening in his entirety. Thus elsewhere he spoke of a “wife sent ahead” and “children sent ahead,” meaning those who had already departed from this world. —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 0969D].** “As though it were the soul’s baggage.” He uses “baggage” in the military sense. A Christian emaciated by many fasts has already sent this part of himself—his blood—to the Lord as his baggage, vessels, and equipment. How severe this Paraclete-inspired teacher is with those exceedingly austere fasts! Yet I marvel that in bloodless and horny tissues there is so much wit, charm, and elegance. —RIG.

> **Note [Cols. 0969D–0970C].** “It is plainly your practice to furnish taverns in prisons for martyrs whose constancy is uncertain.” At the beginning of the book *Against the Valentinians*, he says that the love of the brethren is readily given; and in the book *Against Praxeas*, that the greater part of believers are always simple and uneducated. Here, therefore, he seems to reproach people of this kind for the offices of most generous charity bestowed upon that impostor Peregrinus, who was eventually recognized and expelled from Christian communion, as Lucian relates. Septimius also mentions him among pagan examples in the book *To the Martyrs*. —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 0970C].** “To furnish taverns.” Lucian: συνεκάθευδον μετ’ αὐτοῦ, διαφθείροντες τοὺς δεσμοφύλακας, εἶτα δεῖπνα ποικίλα εἰσεκομίζετο—“They slept there with him, bribing the prison guards; then varied dinners were brought in.”

> **Note [Col. 0970C].** “Martyrs whose constancy is uncertain”—those whose faith had been less thoroughly tested and not sufficiently proved.

> **Note [Col. 0970C].** “Lest they miss their customary fare”—lest they long for what was customary and familiar to them; so that they might live more luxuriously in prison than at home.

> **Note [Cols. 0970C–0970D].** “Lest they be scandalized by the new discipline of abstinence, which not even that former martyr of yours, Pristinus, no Christian, had touched.” We think one should read “your former one”—that is, one who was once yours—just as at the beginning of the book *Against Praxeas* he said “a former teacher.” Many details in Lucian’s account of Peregrinus fit the history Septimius narrates here. Lucian reports that for a time this man was famous and highly esteemed among the Christians; that because of discourses about Christ which he delivered throughout the cities of Syria, he was arrested and thrown into prison; that there he was cared for with the greatest diligence by the Christians’ charity and zeal, with dinners of every kind brought in; and that he was soon released from prison through the governor’s clemency. Later, after being expelled from Christian fellowship for certain offenses, he traveled through various cities, philosophizing with some renown. Finally at Athens, driven mad by a craving for fame, he summoned a crowd, delivered a lengthy speech on contempt for death, leapt into a blazing pyre, and was seen no more. Septimius says that this martyr, whatever his character, was a Psychic—that is, a Catholic—but not a Christian, because under torture he had denied Christ. Lucian writes that his Peregrinus was cast into prison because he revered Christ, τὸν μέγαν ἐκεῖνον ἄνθρωπον ἐν Παλαιστίνῃ ἀνασκολοπισθέντα—“that great man who was crucified in Palestine”; that the Christians immediately hurried to him as brothers and provided every kind of consolation; and indeed that, after bribing the guards, they remained with him and spent the night in the prison. —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 0971C].** “Taking advantage of lax custody.” Lucian: διαφθείραντες τοὺς δεσμοφύλακας—“bribing the prison guards.” —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 0971C].** “Taking advantage of,” Wouwer codex.

> **Note [Col. 0971C].** “Stuffed,” Semler.

> **Note [Col. 0971C].** “Bound over,” Semler.

> **Note [Cols. 0971C–0971D].** “Having first medicated him with spiced wine as though with an antidote.” He was stupefied with myrrh-flavored wine and fortified in advance by the myrrh. In the account of the martyrdom of Fructuosus, Augurius, and Eulogius, we read that a spiced drink was offered to them by the charity of the brethren. When advised to take the mixed drink, they replied that it was not yet the hour for breaking the fast. It was then the fourth hour of the day, and a Wednesday; on that weekday they were observing their customary station even in prison. But why did that brotherly charity offer them the spiced drink on Wednesday, when the martyrs were not led out until Friday, unless they thought they were to be led out on that very Wednesday? Moreover, those who, at the very onset of martyrdom, took such care of their bodies that they would feel neither suffering nor torture seem to have made a mockery of martyrdom. For what steadfastness or glory belongs to a person stupefied into insensibility by intoxication from a medicated drink? —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 0971D].** “So that, when merely tickled by a few claws, for this was all his drunkenness perceived.” He had been so stupefied that he experienced the application of the claws as though it were the hand of someone tickling him. —RIG.

> **Note [Cols. 0971D–0972C].** “And thus, already wrenched away from this confession”—namely, because he did not answer the governor when questioned. Lucian does not report that his Peregrinus was tortured; on the contrary, he says that he was released. —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 0971C].** “Having arisen,” Semler.

> **Note [Cols. 0972C–0972D].** “Having nothing but hiccups and belches, he defecated in the very act of his denial.” With a decorous word he signifies a foul act. For this Pristinus, stuffed with excessive wine and food, denied Christ when torture was applied, and in the very act of denial, amid hiccups and belches, his perfidious bowels having been loosened, he did what Lucius did in the Milesian tale when he drove the executioners away from his donkey—or what the dying emperor Claudius did, speaking through the part by which, as Seneca says, he spoke more readily. But how did he deny Christ if in his drunkenness he could produce nothing but hiccups and belches? He appears to have denied Christ because through drunkenness he deprived himself of the consciousness of martyrdom and the glory of a splendid confession. —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 0971C].** “Departed,” Junius.

## CHAPTER XIII

For behold, I now bring a countercharge against you. Apart from Easter, you fast outside those days on which the Bridegroom was taken away; you introduce the half-fasts of stations; and at times you live on mere bread and water, as each person sees fit. Finally, you reply that these things are to be done voluntarily, not by command.

You have therefore abandoned your position and gone beyond tradition, since you perform observances that have not been established. What sense does it make for you to allow to your own discretion what you do not grant to God’s command? Shall human will be permitted more than divine power?

I remember that I am free in relation to the world, not to God. With me, voluntarily performing a duty for the Lord stands on the same footing as his imposing it: I owe him not only obedience but courtship; the former I render at his command, the latter at my own discretion.

It is well, moreover, that bishops too are accustomed to command fasts for the whole people. I do not mean deliberately for the purpose of gathering contributions, as is your means of profit, but sometimes because of some cause for ecclesiastical concern. Accordingly, if at a human edict all of you together practice ταπεινοφρόνησις (*humble self-abasement*), how do you censure among us the very unity of fasts, xerophagies, and stations? Unless perhaps by our assemblies we are violating senatorial decrees and imperial mandates directed against associations.

When the Holy Spirit preached in whatever lands and through whatever persons he chose, he foresaw impending ecclesiastical trials or worldly scourges and, as Paraclete—that is, Advocate—commanded the remedies furnished by such duties for the purpose of entreating the Judge. Suppose for the moment that this was done merely to train us in the discipline of sobriety and abstinence: because we receive him, we necessarily observe what he then established.

Look at the Jewish calendars, and you will find nothing novel: whatever practices have been commanded to the fathers, all subsequent posterity preserves by hereditary religious observance.

In addition, throughout the regions of Greece, councils drawn from all the churches are held in designated places. Through these, all the more important matters are dealt with in common, and the very representation of the entire Christian name is celebrated with great reverence. And how worthy a thing this is: with faith presiding, to assemble from every direction unto Christ!

> “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 102 [sic]).

You hardly know how to sing this except when dining with a great many others. Those assemblies, however, first performed their work through stations and fasts; they know how to grieve with those who grieve, and only then to rejoice together with those who rejoice.

If we too, in different provinces yet mutually represented in the Spirit, perform these solemn observances for which the word then present provided authority, that is the law of the sacrament.

> **Note [Col. 0972D].** “For behold, I now bring a countercharge against you”—as though by a counter-action. —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 0972D].** “At times living on mere bread.” That is, on plain and unmixed bread, drying their food of all meat and every sauce, as he himself says in this book. —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 0971C].** “And you,” Semler.

> **Note [Col. 0972C].** “Are,” Semler.

> **Note [Col. 0972C].** “Thus,” Semler.

> **Note [Col. 0972D].** “Throughout the regions of Greece”—through the various provinces of Greece, in which various councils were convened. Others read “those Greek regions,” perhaps not badly. —LE PR.

> **Note [Col. 0972C].** “Commands,” Franeker edition.

> **Note [Col. 0972C].** “Those,” Franeker edition.

> **Note [Col. 0972C].** “If,” Junius.

> **Note [Col. 0972C].** “I am,” Franeker edition.

> **Note [Col. 0973B].** “That is the law of the sacrament.” It is a law of Christian communion that whatever belongs to any of our people belongs to us; otherwise, you divide the body. For so he says in the book *On the Veiling of Virgins*, where there are also other splendid remarks concerning the harmony of the parts of the Christian body. —RIG.

## CHAPTER XIV
Observing, therefore, these times, and days and months and years, [Note: [Col. 0973B] *We are Galatianizing.* We are behaving madly like the Galatians. Thus, from the deceitful character of the Cilicians, the comic poet Pherecrates formed the verb ἐγκιλικίζειν (*engkilikizein*, “to act the Cilician”), to signify the frauds and impostures of the pagan gods: ἀείποθ’ ἡμῶν ἐγκιλικίζουσ’ οἱ θεοί, “the gods are always imposing upon and mocking us in Cilician fashion.” *We are Galatianizing*: we are behaving foolishly in Galatian fashion; we are Judaizing like the Galatians. RIG.] we are Galatianizing. Certainly, this is so if we are observers of Jewish ceremonies and legal festivals; for it is those that the Apostle teaches us to abandon, restraining the persistence of the Old Testament, which has been [Note: [Col. 0973B] “They persist, though buried,” added by Semler.] buried in Christ, and establishing that of the New. But if there is now a new order in Christ, there ought also to be new solemn observances; or, if the Apostle has utterly erased every religious observance of times, days, months, and years, why do we celebrate Passover in an annual cycle in the first month? Why, from that point, do we pass through fifty days in unbroken rejoicing? [Note: [Col. 0973C] Why do we dedicate the fourth and sixth days of the week to stations, and the Preparation Day to fasts? Tertullian says that, once the solemn observances of the Old Testament had been buried, Christians established new laws and new solemn observances in Christ, and, after the Mosaic fasts had been abolished, instituted Christian stations and fasts. To the stations, indeed, the fourth and sixth weekdays of every week were dedicated, with the exception of the sixth weekday that was the παρασκευὴ τοῦ πάσχα (*paraskeuē tou pascha*, “Preparation Day of Passover”)—that is, of the authentic week in which Passover, or Passover Day, fell: the Paschal Sabbath, the day on which Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church, was taken away. For fasts were prescribed on that day, and these were continued into the Sabbath not only by the Paracletists but also by the Psychics. Here, however, Tertullian observes that the Sabbath must be fasted at Passover—that is, the Sabbath of the week in which the day [Col. 0973D] of Passover, or of the Lord’s Passion, fell, which is the νήστιμος ἡμέρα (*nēstimos hēmera*, “fasting day”); the other Sabbaths must never be fasted, lest we appear to Judaize or Galatianize. He adds: “For us, certainly, every day is celebrated even by its commonly established consecration.” Consistent with these words are the following from Jerome, *Epistle* 151: “For us who believe in the risen Christ, there is one continuous and eternal festival, and we ought not to suppose that some days are festive and others not.” This is evidently because of the freedom obtained through Christ, which has removed from our necks the yoke of Mosaic ceremonies and legal solemn observances. Hence we understand, says our Septimius in *Against the Jews*, chapter IV, that we ought all the more always to keep Sabbath from every servile work, and not merely on every seventh day, but throughout all time. In short, one who is wise concerning evangelical freedom and abstains from every servile work—that is, from Jewish observances and ceremonies—keeps all time as Sabbath, that is, sanctifies it. RIG.] Why do we dedicate the fourth and sixth days of the week to stations [Note: [Col. 0973D] “The fourth and sixth days of the week,” etc. This passage is decidedly difficult, for the Preparation Day is the sixth day of the week. Its meaning, however, appears to be this: stations were held on the fourth and sixth weekdays; but on the fourth weekday the fast could be broken at the ninth hour, whence it was called a half-fast; whereas on the sixth weekday Tertullian calls it a fast until the ninth hour. I believe, however, that Pamelius missed the point when he wrote that the Preparation Day was unusually called the Sabbath. LE PR.], and the Preparation Day to fasts?—although you also sometimes prolong your fast through the Sabbath, which [Col. 0973B] must never be fasted except at Passover, according to the reason given elsewhere. [Note: [Col. 0974C] “And the Preparation Day to fasts?” He calls by way of excellence “the Preparation Day” what the Jews called the “Preparation Day of Passover.” John chapter XIX: παρασκευὴ τοῦ πάσχα (*paraskeuē tou pascha*), as though the holiness of the Paschal Sabbath ennobled its preceding Sabbath. But because Christ had been seized by the Jews and crucified on that sixth weekday, or Preparation Day, the Christian Church in Tertullian’s age had dedicated every sixth weekday to stations or half-fasts. This day, however, returned annually before Passover Day, and the Church made it more notable by prescribing the sorrow of a full fast, because of the grief occasioned by the Bridegroom’s removal. Tertullian therefore calls this most solemn Preparation Day, in an emphatic manner of expression, “the Preparation Day,” now no longer Jewish but Christian, while leaving to the other παρασκευαί (*paraskeuai*, “preparation days”) the generic designation. It is thus perfectly clear that in Tertullian’s age the Psychics—as he called the Romans—and also the Paracletists or Montanists dedicated the fourth and sixth weekdays of every week to stations, which were half-fasts, and the Preparation Day—that is, the sixth weekday of the Greater [Col. 0974D] or Authentic Week—to fasts. The Paracletists were more austere in this respect than the Romans, because they offered God two weeks of xerophagy each year, although not the whole weeks, since Sabbaths and Sundays were excluded. He does not say “the Preparation Day of Passover,” so as to indicate that the two weeks of xerophagy immediately preceded Passover; and yet the very subject cries aloud that this was indeed his meaning, for immediately afterward he speaks of Passover Day. LE PR.] For us, certainly, [Col. 0974A] every day is celebrated even by its commonly established consecration. The Apostle’s rationale, therefore, involves no failure to distinguish, since he distinguishes the new from the old. But here, too, your inconsistency will be laughed at, since you reproach us with the pattern of antiquated practices in the very matter in which you accuse the [Note: [Col. 0973B] *Qua*, Semler.] cause of novelty.

## CHAPTER XV

He also censures those who were commanding [Note: [Col. 0973B] *Would command*, Semler.] abstinence from foods, but he does so through the providence of the Holy Spirit, [Note: [Col. 0974B] *Holy*, Semler.] already condemning beforehand the heretics who would prescribe perpetual abstinence in order to destroy and despise the Creator’s works. Such persons I may find among Marcion’s followers, among Tatian’s, and among those of Jupiter—the present-day heretic descended from Pythagoras—but not among the Paraclete’s followers. [Note: [Col. 0974D] “For how slight is our prohibition of foods?” etc. Here he establishes two weeks of xerophagy—that is, fourteen days—not fourteen weeks, as Pamelius thought; for he would not have spoken these words in minimizing so brief a period: “For how slight is it?” etc. LE PR.] For how slight is our prohibition of foods? [Note: [Col. 0974D] “Two weeks of xerophagy in the year.” Jerome to Marcella, speaking of Montanus’s followers: “They observe three Lents in a year.” Such are mortal minds once they have departed from the rule. Thus, by Jerome’s time, the disciples had surpassed the master and added a third week to the two weeks of Montanist xerophagy. But we think they likewise called weeks “Lents,” just as Jerome said: “We fast one Lent throughout the year, according to the tradition of the Apostles, at the season appropriate to us.” RIG.] We offer God two weeks of xerophagy in the year, and not even the whole of them, since Sabbaths and Sundays are of course excepted. We abstain from things that we do not reject, but merely postpone.

Yet when writing to the Romans, the Apostle now pricks you, the detractors [Note: [Col. 0974B] *Reconsiderers*, Semler.] of this duty: “Do not,” he says, “destroy God’s work on account of food.” What work? That of which he says: “It is good not to eat meat or drink wine. For he who serves in these matters is acceptable and pleasing to our God. One man believes that all things may be eaten; but another, being weak, eats vegetables. Let him who eats not nullify [Note: [Col. 0975C] *Disparage*, Semler.] him who does not eat. Who are you [Note: [Col. 0975C] *Who*, Semler.] to judge another’s servant? Both he who eats and he who does not eat give thanks to God” (Rom. XIV, 2 ff.). But since he forbids controversy when the matter rests on human discretion, how much more when it rests on divine authority! Thus he knew how to censure certain disciplinarians and prohibitors of food—those who abstained out of disgust, not those who abstained as a duty—whereas he approved those who abstained in honor of, not in insult to, the Creator.

And if he has handed you the keys of the meat-market, permitting all things to be eaten in order to establish the exception concerning meat sacrificed to idols, he has nevertheless not enclosed God’s kingdom within the [Col. 0975B] meat-market. “For,” he says, “the kingdom of God is not eating or drinking,” and, “Food does not commend us to God”—lest you suppose this to have been said about dry fare, rather than about rich and carefully prepared food. Indeed, by adding, “Neither, if we eat, shall we abound; nor, if we do not eat, shall we be deficient,” [Note: [Col. 0975C] *Have abounded*, Paris.] he is speaking more loudly against you, who suppose that you abound if you eat and are deficient if you do not, and therefore disparage these practices.

How unworthily, too, you interpret the Lord according to your own appetite because he ate and drank openly! Yet I think he also fasted, [Note: [Col. 0975D] *Had fasted*, Semler.] he who pronounced blessed not the satiated but those who hunger and thirst; who declared his food to be not what the disciples had supposed, but the completion of his Father’s work; who taught men to labor for the food that endures to eternal life; and who, even in the customary prayer, commanded that bread be requested, [Col. 0975C] not Attalic riches. [Note: [Col. 0975D] *He rejects riches*, Semler.]

So too Isaiah did not deny that God had chosen a fast, but enumerated the kind he had not chosen. “For on the days,” he says (Isa. LVIII, 3), “of your fasts, your pleasures [Note: [Col. 0975D] *Your voluntary acts*, Franeker.] are found, and you shake down all those subject to you; or you fast for insults and quarrels and strike with fists. I did not choose such a fast.” But the kind he then added, by adding it he did not abolish fasting but confirmed it. For even though he prefers works of justice, he nevertheless does not prefer them without sacrifice, which is a soul afflicted by fasts.

## CHAPTER XVI

That God, certainly, was pleased neither by a people incapable of restraining its gluttony, nor by a priest, nor by a prophet. The memorials of lust still remain, where the people most greedy for flesh were buried after devouring quails to the point of bilious sickness. [Note: [Col. 0975D] *Octygometra*, Semler.] [Note: [Col. 0975D] *Seasoning them*, another reading; *belching them up*, Pamelius.] The aged Eli is struck down before the doors of the temple; his sons fall in battle; his daughter-in-law dies in childbirth. For this was the blow from God deserved by that shameless household, which defrauded the fleshly sacrifices. [Note: [Col. 0975D] “Shemaiah, a man of God.” In the Third Book of Kings the name of this prophet is not transmitted; Josephus calls him Jadon, Epiphanius Joam. RIG.]

Shemaiah, the man of God, after he had prophesied the outcome of the idolatry introduced by King Jeroboam—after the king’s hand had withered and was immediately restored, [Note: [Col. 0975D] “After the altar was poured out.” For the ashes of the demolished altar were poured out and scattered: ῥήγνυται, καὶ ἐκχυθήσεται ἡ πιότης ἐπ’ αὐτοῦ, “it shall be rent, and the fatness upon it shall be poured out” (II Kings XII, 3). RIG.] and after the altar was poured out [Note: [Col. 0976C] *Split apart*, another reading.]—was invited by the king, in consequence of these signs, to accept his amends, but flatly declined. For God had forbidden him to touch any food there at all. Yet soon afterward, rashly taking food at the bidding of another old man who falsely claimed a prophecy, according to the word of God spoken there [Col. 0976B] over the table, he was not buried in his fathers’ tomb: he was struck down when a lion met him on the road, and, buried among strangers, paid the penalty for having abandoned his fast.

These will be examples both for the people and for bishops, even spiritual ones, if they admit any lack of restraint in gluttony. Nor did the admonition cease even in the underworld, where banquets are tormented in the rich man, whereas fasts are refreshed in the poor man—both having Moses and the Prophets as their teachers (Luke XVI, 29).

For Joel also cried out (Joel I, 14): “Sanctify a fast, and proclaim a religious service,” [Note: [Col. 0976C] “Sanctify a fast and prayer,” and nothing further, Semler.] already foreseeing even then that other apostles and prophets would sanctify a fast and proclaim duties of service to God. Hence those who flatter their gods by adorning idols and decorating altars, [Note: [Col. 0976D] “And by adorning them in this matter,” Semler.] and by saluting them [Note: [Col. 0976D] “They flatter them by saluting them. Ursinus’s book reads: ‘By decorating altars and flattering the gods by saluting them at each several hour.’” RIG.] at every hour, [Note: [Col. 0976D] *The gods*, added by the manuscript of Wouwer.] are said to perform a service of propitiation.

But the pagans also recognize every form of ταπεινοφρόνησις (*tapeinophrosynē*, “self-abasement”). When the sky is unyielding and the year grows parched, barefoot processions are proclaimed; the magistrates lay aside their purple robes, turn their fasces backward, prescribe the prayer, and renew the sacrifice. Among certain colonies, moreover, in an annual rite, men covered with sackcloth [Note: [Col. 0976D] “And sprinkled with ashes.” The appearance of defendants, upon whom ashes were sometimes sprinkled to make them more pitiable, is extensively described here. Apuleius, book VII: “Drawing the ash-covered woman with both hands.” This is especially common in Sacred Scripture. LE PR.] and sprinkled with ashes present a supplicating fast before their idols; baths and [Note: [Col. 0976D] *Tabernacles.* Shops. RIG.] shops [Note: [Col. 0976D] *Shops.*] are closed until the ninth hour. There is only one public fire, at the altars, and not even water in the dishes. I believe it to be a Ninevite cessation from business. [Note: [Col. 0976D] *Ninevite*, Junius. “I believe it to be Ninevite justice,” another reading; [Col. 0977C] incorrectly, as Junius thinks.]

Certainly the Jewish fast is celebrated everywhere, when, abandoning their temples, they send up their prayer to heaven along every shore, wherever they may be in the open. And although by the garb and [Col. 0977A] appearance of mourning they bring dishonor upon their religious duty, they nevertheless make a show of fidelity to abstinence and sigh for the authoritative arrival [Note: [Col. 0977C] “They sigh for the authoritative arrival of the delaying star.” He means the star that Plautus calls *Vesperugo*, Ennius *Vesper*, and Virgil *Hesperus*. By “authority,” moreover, he means presence. For although famished, they did not dare touch any food before the appearance of the Evening Star. [Col. 0977D] RIG.] of the delaying star. [Note: [Col. 0977D] “Delaying.” Lingering. Tarrying. Thus Plautus’s Sosia complains that the Sun has fallen asleep drunk. RIG.]

But it is well that, while hurling blasphemies at our xerophagies, you equate them with the sacred abstinence of Isis and Cybele. [Note: [Col. 0977D] “You equate them with the sacred abstinence of Isis and Cybele.” *Casto*, τῇ ἁγνείᾳ (*tē hagneia*, “with the ritual purity”). Above he said *castimonia*, “chastity.” What Latin speakers call *in casto Cereris esse*, “to be under the ritual abstinence of Ceres,” a certain Greek author in Suidas called τὰς Μητρῳακὰς καστείας ἀγεύειν, “to observe the abstinences of the Mother’s rites.” Varro said “with Greek *castus*,” meaning “according to the Greek rite.” RIG.] I accept the comparison as testimony. From this it will be established that our practice is divine, since the devil, the rival of divine things, imitates it. Falsehood is constructed from truth; superstition is built from religion. Hence you are more irreligious in proportion as the pagan is more ready. He, after all, sacrifices his appetite to an idol; you refuse to sacrifice yours to God. For your belly is your god, your lung is the temple, your paunch the altar, your cook the priest, the aroma the Holy Spirit, your seasonings the charisms, and your belching prophecy.

## CHAPTER XVII

[Note: [Col. 0977D] “You are old, if we wish to speak the truth.” Catholics gloried chiefly against the Montanists in being adherents of the ancient discipline and in not admitting new rites or new fasts. Septimius, therefore, after he had already defected to Montanus, addresses a Catholic and mocks that Catholic antiquity. “You are old,” he says; “we certainly admit this, and you look back to those ancient things—but only to present us from them with some Esau, a hunter of wild beasts,” [Col. 0978C] etc. RIG.]

You are old, if we wish to speak the truth—you [Col. 0977B] who indulge your appetite so greatly and deservedly boast yourself the earlier. I always recognize in you the taste of Esau, hunter of wild beasts: so diligently do you seek thrushes everywhere; so do you come in from the field of your utterly lax discipline; so does your spirit fail if I offer you a dish of lentils reddened with must syrup. You will immediately sell all your claims to primacy. [Note: [Col. 0978C] “You will immediately sell all your claims to primacy.” He means the primacy of his discipline, which preceded the discipline of Montanus in time; hence he said above, “and deservedly boast yourself the earlier.” RIG.]

Among you, *agapē* boils in cooking pots, [Note: [Col. 0978D] “*Agapē* boils in cooking pots.” Paul, book XVIII, *On Instruction*: “There is little difference between cooking pots and the bronze vessel that hangs above the hearth: in the latter water is heated for drinking, while in the former a relish is cooked.” The commentator on Juvenal, at Satire XI, interprets cooking pots as *bascaudae*, that is, vessels in which cups were washed; I would not assert that this is perfectly said. For it is the vessel that the Romans called a *miliarium*. LE PR.] faith grows warm in kitchens, and hope lies in serving dishes. But greater than these [Note: [Col. 0977C] *This*, Venetian edition.] is *agapē* (1 Cor. XIII, 13), through which your young men sleep with the sisters. Lust and luxury [Note: [Col. 0978C] *Are*, added by Semler.] are, of course, appendages of gluttony. The Apostle also knew this association, for after first saying, “Not in drunkenness or revelry,” he added, “nor in beds and lusts” (Rom. XIII, 14).

It contributes to the eulogy of your gluttony that [Note: [Col. 0978D] “Among you a double honor is allotted to those who preside, assigned to two parts.” By “two parts” he means the belly and the genitals—that is, gluttony and lust. Thus he says that among the Psychics bishops are indeed shown double honor, but not as brothers and overseers, as the Apostle commanded, but as men powerful in appetite and virility. RIG.] among you a double honor is allotted to those who preside, assigned to two [Col. 0978A] parts—although the Apostle bestowed double honor upon them as both brothers and overseers. Who among you is holier unless he gives feasts more frequently, provides more lavish fare, and is better furnished with cups? Deservedly do you, men of soul and flesh alone, reject spiritual things. If the prophets were pleasing to such persons, they would not be mine.

Why, then, do you not consistently proclaim: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (1 Cor. XV, 32)? Just as we do not hesitate openly to command: “Let us fast, brothers and sisters, lest perhaps we die tomorrow.” Let us openly defend our disciplines. We are certain that those who are in the flesh cannot please God—not, of course, in the substance of the flesh, but in its care, affection, operation, and will.

Leanness does not displease us; for God did not distribute flesh by weight, any more than he gave the Spirit by measure. Perhaps a thinner flesh will more easily enter through the narrow gate of salvation; a lighter flesh will rise again more quickly; a drier flesh will endure longer in the grave. Let wrestlers and Olympic boxers be fattened: bodily ambition is fitting for those to whom physical strength is necessary. And yet they too grow strong through xerophagies. But ours are other powers and other kinds of strength, just as ours are other contests; for our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against the powers of the world, [Note: [Col. 0978C] *Powerful beings*, Latin edition.] against spiritual forces of wickedness. Against these we must take our stand, not strong in flesh and blood but in faith and spirit. Otherwise, a fatter [Note: [Col. 0978C] *One who fattens*, Semler.] Christian will perhaps be more useful to bears and lions than to God—except that even against the beasts he will have to train himself in leanness.

[Col. 0979]

# QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN, *ON MODESTY* (C)

## [SUMMARY]

[Col. 0979A] I. Having fallen into heresy through his love of chastity, Tertullian pursues in this book Montanus’s error concerning the refusal to readmit penitents, at least adulterers and fornicators. After first praising chastity, he briefly indicates that this is the very subject of the book—admitting that formerly, namely when he wrote the book *On Repentance*, he held a different opinion—especially since adultery and fornication occupy the summit of crimes.

II. First, setting Scriptures against Scriptures, he endeavors to gather from them that some sins are remissible and others irremissible.

III. Yet the repentance appropriate to certain sins is not therefore to be utterly neglected.

IV. Then, after teaching that under the names of adultery and fornication he includes every sin of lust,

[Col. 0979B] V. he shows from Scripture that adultery is comparable to idolatry and murder.

VI. Although examples of pardon for adulterers exist in the Old Testament, examples of judgment are also found; and the rationale of the New Testament is different.

VII. He next discusses at length the parables of the lost sheep and the lost drachma.

VIII–IX. Likewise the parable of the two sons.

X. For repentance applies even to pagans.

XI. He then describes the Lord’s deeds performed for sinners.

XII. Certainly fornication is forbidden by the Apostles together with idolatry and murder.

XIII–XIV. Furthermore, he examines the pardon granted by the Apostle to the Corinthian fornicator.

XV–XVI. He adduces passages against fornicators from both the Second and the First [Col. 0979C] Epistles to the Corinthians.

XVII. Likewise similar statements from the other epistles of the apostle Paul.

XVIII. Also such passages, both from Paul and from the Old Testament, as deprive adulterers of ecclesiastical communion.

XIX. Similar passages also from the apostle John, both the Apocalypse and his Epistle.

XX. He then adduces certain Scriptures from the Epistle to the Hebrews—formerly, in his opinion, attributed to Barnabas—and from Leviticus, although in vain for his purpose.

XXI. And although he does not deny that the Apostles possessed the power to remit sins, and consequently that the Church does also, he vainly claims this power for his own spiritual Church.

XXII. Finally, he argues against the pardon for crimes and the peace that certain martyrs granted to adulterers while denying them to those who had denied the faith. PAM.

## CHAPTER I

Modesty is the flower of morals, the honor of bodies, the adornment of the sexes, the integrity of blood, the fidelity of lineage, the foundation of holiness, and the anticipatory judgment of every good disposition. Although it is rare, not easily perfected, and scarcely ever permanent, it will nevertheless [Note: [Col. 0979C] “It will remain for some time in the world.” He had in mind the opening of Juvenal’s satire:

> I believe that Modesty remained on earth  
> while Saturn was king and was long seen there, etc.

RIG.] remain for some time in the world, if nature has laid its foundation, discipline has commended it, and censure has restrained it. [Col. 0980B] For every good of the soul is either born, taught, or compelled.

But since evils prevail all the more, as is characteristic of the last times, good qualities are now not even permitted to be born, so corrupted are their seeds; nor to be taught, so abandoned are their studies; nor to be compelled, so disarmed are the laws. In short, the virtue with which we begin has now fallen so completely out of use that modesty is believed to consist not in the renunciation but in the moderation of lusts, and a man is considered sufficiently chaste [Note: [Col. 0979C] “Who has been less chaste.” Fulvius Ursinus thought it should read, “who has not been excessively unchaste.” Certainly the easier reading would have been, “who has been excessively unchaste.” RIG.] if he has been less unchaste.

But let the modesty of the world [Note: [Col. 0979C] “But let the modesty of the world see to itself.” You have an extensive treatment of this in book I *To His Wife*, the book *On the Exhortation to Chastity*, and the book *On Monogamy*. PAM.] see to itself along with the world itself: with its own natural disposition if it was born, with its own study if it was taught, and with its own servitude if it was compelled. Indeed, it would have been still more unfortunate even if it had remained, because it would have been fruitless, since it would not have acted before God. I would rather have no good at all than a vain good. [Note: [Col. 0980C] “I would rather have no good,” etc. Here he calls “vain” what shortly before he called “fruitless.” His calling the modesty of the world “good” tells against those who make all the works of unbelievers sins. PAM.] What benefit is there in something’s existing, if its existence is of no benefit?

[Col. 0980C] The standing of our own goods is now being challenged; [Note: [Col. 0979C] *Is submerged*, Oberthür, Semler.] the principle of Christian modesty is being shaken. Christian modesty draws everything from heaven: nature through the washing of regeneration, discipline through the instrument of preaching, and censure through judgments drawn from both Testaments; and, when compelled, it is made more steadfast by fear of eternal fire and aspiration toward the kingdom.

Against this could I not have pretended not to notice? [Note: [Col. 0980C] *Now could I not*, Paris.] I hear that an edict has even been posted, and indeed a peremptory one. [Note: [Col. 0980C] “I hear that an edict has even been posted.” If there was an actual formula for the edict, I believe that it consisted only of these words: “The bishop of bishops decrees: I remit the sins both of adultery and fornication for those who have completed repentance.” The preceding words, “the supreme pontiff,” were evidently added by Septimius so that, by these characterizations, he might charge with ambition and pride the Catholic bishop whose clergy’s hostility and insults drove him to defect to the doctrine of Montanus, as Jerome attests. Thus above, when mocking a certain distinguished teacher among the Valentinians, he says: “From his pontifical authority he decided as follows.” RIG.]

[Col. 0981A] The “Supreme Pontiff,” that is, [Note: [Col. 0981C] “The Supreme Pontiff,” etc. Septimius’s wording is sound and worthy of note, because even when already established in heresy and writing against the Church, he calls the Roman Pontiff “Bishop of Bishops,” and below, in chapter 13, “the good shepherd” and “blessed Pope,” and in chapter 21, “apostolic,” as we also noted above when discussing the authority of the Supreme Pontiff in connection with *On Prescriptions*, chapter 36. . . . Here, moreover, . . . we shall add that the Roman See was adorned by Emperor Flavius Constantine not only with privileges but also with the imperial scepter and diadem, and indeed with the City and very extensive territories in Italy, as is clear from Constantine’s edict of donation published by Blessed Isidore, which survives today in the volumes of the Councils. Its authenticity is also evident—although many wrongly call it into doubt, including some who wish to be regarded as Catholics—from both the Roman Council under Pope Sylvester, canon I, and the Second Council of Nicaea, the seventh general council. There, in confirmation of images used in the primitive Church, the images of Saints Peter and Paul shown to Constantine by Sylvester are cited from the acts of the same donation. . . . For if part of the acts is cited, the trustworthiness of the remaining matters contained in them is also proved. To the same point belong what Blessed Gregory of Tours, *History*, book II; Bede, in his *Chronicles* at the year of the world 4288; Pope Adrian, *Epistle to Constantine and Irene*; Nicephorus, book VII, chapter 33; and Blessed Thomas, part III of his *Summa*, question 6, argument 4, report—undoubtedly drawing from the same acts—concerning the healing of Constantine’s leprosy. The same applies to what, in addition to those already named, the said two synods; Damasus, in Liberius’s *Pontifical*, acts, chapter 6; Nicephorus, book VII, chapter 35, and book VIII, chapters 3 and 54; Marianus Scotus, in his *Chronicle*; and Blessed Thomas in the passage already cited write concerning Constantine’s baptism by Blessed Pope Sylvester, since these things are contained in the same Acts. . . . What of the fact that Ammianus [Col. 0982B] Marcellinus, book XXVII, describes already in the time of Damasus the same splendor of the Roman Pontiffs as those Acts describe; and Laonicus Chalcocondyles . . . in his book *On the Deeds of the Turks* . . .; furthermore, Suo, book IV, *On the Dignity [Col. 0982C] and Privileges of the Roman Church* . . .; Gratian, distinction 46, chapter *Constantinus*, and 12, question 1, chapter *Futuram*; . . . Balsamon on Photius’s *Nomocanon*, title VIII, *On Parishes*; . . . Vincent of Beauvais, book XIII of his *History*, chapters 54, 55, and 56. . . . Whatever, therefore, other historians report concerning the munificence toward the Roman See of Justinian, Theodoric, king of the Lombards, Pepin, Charlemagne, Otto, Rudolf of Habsburg, and other emperors, must likewise be understood as the restitution of the city of Rome, Ravenna, and other Italian cities that had, it appears, been occupied and seized by Julian the Apostate, the Arians, and the exarchs of Ravenna. PAM.], the Bishop of Bishops, issues an edict: “I remit the sins both of adultery and fornication for those who have completed repentance.” [Note: [Col. 0982C] “Bishop of Bishops.” Thus Rufinus says that James the Just was appointed bishop of the Apostles; in Eusebius, *History* II, chapter 1, Clement had called him ἐπίσκοπον Ἱεροσολύμων (*episkopon Hierosolymōn*, “bishop of Jerusalem”). The well-known passage of Cyprian concerning a “bishop of bishops” is in the preface to the Council of Carthage. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0982C] “I remit the sins both of adultery and fornication,” etc. Since the Author disparages this edict so greatly, it is clear that he is astonishingly mistaken, if only from the apostle John, Apocalypse II, 20–22, where concerning Jezebel, who taught people to fornicate . . . it is said: “And I gave her time to repent. . . . And those who commit adultery with her will be in the greatest tribulation unless they repent of their works.” The Author himself, while still a Catholic, stated this expressly . . . in *On Repentance*, chapter 8; and after him Blessed Pacian, epistle I to Sympronian the Novatian. To the same point belongs what Blessed Cyprian says in his *Epistle to Antonianus*. PAM.]

O edict upon which the words “A good deed!” cannot be inscribed! [Note: [Col. 0982D] “A good deed.” Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book III, chapter 12, explains this phrase by saying that the ancients customarily prefaced edicts with “A good deed” for the sake of a favorable omen, from this line of Plautus in the *Poenulus*:

> May it turn out well that he should obey my edicts.

PAM.]

And where will this liberality be posted? In that very place, I suppose, at the very doors of lust, beneath the very titles of lust. Such repentance must be proclaimed where the sin itself is practiced; pardon must be read there, so that one may enter with hope of it.

But this is read in the Church, and pronounced in the Church—and she is a virgin? Far, far from the Bride of Christ be such a proclamation! She who is true, modest, and holy will be free even from stains upon her ears. She has no one to whom she might make this promise; and if she did have such persons, she would not promise it. For even God’s earthly temple could sooner be called by the Lord a “den of robbers” [Col. 0981B] (Matt. XXI, 13) than a den of adulterers and fornicators.

This work, therefore, too, will bear the title *Against the Psychics*, [Note: [Col. 0982D] “This work, therefore, too, will bear the title *Against the Psychics*.” Since he indicates here that he had published another book under the title *Against the Psychics*, it is evident that this work was written later than the preceding book, to which he undoubtedly alludes here. PAM.] and it will also oppose the fellowship I formerly shared with them in this opinion, so that they may all the more cast it against me as evidence of fickleness. The repudiation of a fellowship is never proof of wrongdoing, as though it were not easier to err with the many, when truth is loved among the few.

[Col. 0982A] Yet beneficial fickleness will no more dishonor me than harmful fickleness honored me. [Note: [Col. 0982D] “Yet beneficial fickleness will no more dishonor me [Col. 0983D] than harmful fickleness honored me.” Just as no fickleness that brings calamities and losses with it is glorious for anyone, so no fickleness from which an immense and honorable benefit follows is disgraceful to anyone. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0981B] *Useless*, Rhenanus, Oberthür.] I do not blush for an error from which I am free, because I rejoice in being free from it, because I recognize that I am better and more chaste. No one who makes progress is ashamed.

Knowledge also has its stages of life in Christ, through which the Apostle himself passed. “When I was a child,” he says, “I spoke as a child, I understood as a child; but when I became a man, I put away the things that belonged to childhood” (1 Cor. XIII, 11). To such an extent did he depart from his former opinions, and he did not sin on that account, because he had become a zealous champion not of the traditions of his fathers (Gal. I, 14), but of Christian traditions; he even wished that those who urged the retention of circumcision would cut themselves off (Gal. V, 11–12).

And would that these men too were cut off—men who mutilate the pure and true integrity [Col. 0982B] of the flesh, cutting away not the outermost surface but the innermost image of modesty itself when they promise pardon to adulterers and fornicators against the principal discipline of the Christian name. Even the world bears such witness to that discipline that, whenever it can, it strives to punish it in our women by defilements [Col. 0983A] of the flesh rather than by tortures, wishing to tear away that which they esteem above life itself.

But now this glory is being extinguished, and indeed by those who ought all the more steadfastly to have subscribed no pardon to such stains, inasmuch as, whenever they wish, they marry [Note: [Col. 0983D] *May marry*, Oberthür, Semler.] precisely so that they may not be compelled to fall into adultery and fornication: “for it is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. VII, 9). Evidently, incontinence is necessary for the sake of continence; fire will be extinguished by fires!

Why, then, do they afterward pardon in the name of repentance the crimes for which they have prescribed remedies through the right of multiple marriages? For the remedies will be meaningless when the crimes are pardoned, and the crimes will remain if the remedies are meaningless. Thus in both respects they make sport of vigilance and negligence: most vainly guarding against offenses that they pardon, and most foolishly pardoning offenses against which they have guarded; [Col. 0983B] whereas there should either be no guarding against an offense where it is pardoned, or no pardon where it is guarded against. For they guard against it as though unwilling that any such thing should be committed, yet pardon it as though willing that it should be committed; whereas, if they are unwilling that it be committed, they ought not to pardon it, and if they are willing to pardon it, they ought not to guard against it.

Adultery and fornication will not, after all, be reckoned both among minor and [Note: [Col. 0983D] “Among the greatest sins,” etc. Minor sins are those easily pardoned by God; the greatest are those pardoned with difficulty, such as adultery. LE PR.] among the greatest [Note: [Col. 0983D] *Intermediate*, Junius.] sins, so that both measures may apply: the vigilance that guards against them and the confidence that pardons them. But since these are sins that occupy the summit of crimes, they cannot both be pardoned as though minor and guarded against as though the greatest.

Among us, however, the greatest or supreme sins are guarded against in this further way: we are not permitted even to know a second marriage after faith, although marriage and dowry contracts perhaps distinguish such unions from the deed of adultery and fornication. And therefore, while most harshly defaming [Col. 0983C] us because of the Paraclete’s extraordinary strictness of discipline, we keep the twice-married outside; we set the very same boundary at the threshold for adulterers and fornicators as well. They will pour out tears fasting from the hope of peace, [Note: [Col. 0983D] “Tears fasting from peace.” Without hope of peace. Thus, “fasting from philosophy”; “with the rest fasting from salvation.” RIG.] and will receive nothing further from the Church than the public disclosure of their disgrace.

## CHAPTER II
But, they say, God is good and most excellent, merciful and compassionate (Ps. 111:4), and abundant in mercy (Joel 2:13), which he sets before every sacrifice (1 Sam. 15:22; Hos. 6:6; Matt. 9:13; 12:7); [Col. 0983D] he does not value the death of the sinner so highly as repentance (Ezek. 18:23, 32; 33:11), being the Savior [Note: [Col. 0984D] *Salutificator* (“Savior”) Fran.] of all men, and especially of the faithful (1 Tim. 4:10). Accordingly, the children of God too must be merciful and peaceable (Matt. 5:9, 7), forgiving one another, just as Christ forgave us (Col. 3:13); not judging, lest we be judged (Matt. 7:1). For it is before his own Lord that each man [Col. 0984A] stands or falls: who are you to judge another’s servant? (Rom. 14:4). Forgive, and you will be forgiven (Luke 6:37).

[Note: [Col. 0984D] “Such and so many are their futile arguments.” Thus Rhenanus edited the text. But with what face could Septimius call “futile” things drawn from the sacred pages, even if, as he himself believed, they had been twisted into perverse arguments? I would therefore prefer what Pamelius produced from the English manuscript: *sparsilia* (“scattered sayings”). Pithoeus had also noted that *sparsilia* was the reading in the Reims manuscript. RIG.]

Such and so many are their futile arguments, by which they both flatter God and pander to themselves, enervating discipline rather than strengthening it. With how many equally weighty contrary texts can we strike back—texts which both press upon us the severity of God and summon up our steadfastness? For although God is good by nature, he is nevertheless also just (Ps. 7:12). As the occasion requires, he knows not only how to heal but also how to strike (Deut. 32:39); he makes peace, but also creates evils (Isa. 45:7); he prefers repentance (Ezek. 18:23, 32), yet he also commands Jeremiah not to intercede for a sinful people:

> “For even if they fast,” he says, “I will not hear their supplication”;

and again:

> “And as for you, do not pray for this people, and do not petition for them in prayer and [Col. 0984B] supplication, because I will not hear them when they call upon me in the time of their affliction” (Jer. 7:16; 11:14; 14:11–12).

And still earlier, the same God who gives mercy precedence over sacrifice says:

> “And as for you, do not pray for this people,”

and:

> “Do not ask that they obtain mercy,”

and:

> “Do not approach me on their behalf, because I certainly will not hear those who ask for mercy” (ibid.)—

those, assuredly, who weep and fast in repentance and offer their affliction to God. For God is jealous (Exod. 20:5; 34:14),

[Note: [Col. 0984D] “And who is not mocked by the nose.” In this way he rendered Paul’s expression in Gal. 6, *οὐ μυκτηρίζεται* (“is not mocked”). Hesychius: *Μυκτηρίζῃ, χλευάζῃ, καταγελᾷ ὑπὸ τοῦ μυζὴν τοῖς μυκτῆροις*—“You mock: you jeer, you ridicule; from making a contemptuous sound with the nostrils.” RIG.]

and one who is not mocked by a wrinkling of the nose (Gal. 6:7)—that is, by flattering his goodness. And although he is patient (Ps. 7:12), nevertheless through Isaiah he threatens an end to patience:

> “I have kept silent; surely I will not always keep silent and endure? I have been still like a woman in labor; I will arise and cause them to wither” (Isa. 42:14–15).

For fire will go [Col. 0984C] before his face and consume his enemies (Ps. 96:3), and he kills not only the body but also souls in Gehenna (Matt. 10:28).

Moreover, the Lord himself shows how he threatens those who judge:

> “For with whatever judgment you have judged, judgment will be passed upon you” (Matt. 7:2).

Thus he did not prohibit judging, but taught how to judge. Hence the Apostle too passes judgment—and indeed in a case of fornication—that such a man must be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh (1 Cor. 5:5). He also reproaches them because disputes among brethren were not being judged before the saints (1 Cor. 6:1 [Col. 0984D] ff.). For he adds:

> “Why should I judge those who are outside?” (1 Cor. 5:12).

You forgive, moreover, so that you may be forgiven by God (Luke 6:37). The offenses that are wiped away are those which someone has committed against a brother, not against God. Indeed, in prayer we profess that we will forgive our debtors (Matt. 6:12).

But it is unfitting to continue stretching a contentious rope of this kind, drawn alternately [Col. 0985A] in opposite directions from the authority of the Scriptures, so that some texts appear to tighten the reins of discipline and others to loosen them, as though the Scriptures were uncertain, and as though some texts laid down the aid of repentance through leniency while others denied it through severity.

[Note: [Col. 0985C] “And” is absent from Rhen., Oberth., Pam.]

Rather, the authority of Scripture will remain within its own limits without mutual contradiction, provided that

[Note: [Col. 0985C] “If” is absent from Rhen., Oberth.]

the aid of repentance is defined by its own conditions, without indiscriminate concession, and that the grounds for repentance themselves are first distinguished, without a confused statement.

[Note: [Col. 0985C] *Praepositione* (“preposition”) Oberth., Seml.]

We stipulate that offenses are the ground of repentance. We divide these into two outcomes: some will be remissible, others irremissible; just as no one doubts that some deserve correction and others condemnation. Every offense is canceled either by pardon or by punishment: by pardon as a result of correction, by punishment as a result of condemnation. Concerning this distinction we have already set out certain opposing passages of Scripture, some retaining and others [Col. 0985B] remitting offenses.

But John too will teach us:

> “If anyone knows that his brother is committing an offense not unto death, he shall ask, and life will be given to him” (1 John 5:16),

because he does not sin unto death: this offense will be remissible.

> “There is an offense unto death; I do not say that anyone should ask concerning that” (ibid.):

this offense will be irremissible. Thus, where there is a condition or rationale for petition, there too is one for remission; where there is none for petition, there likewise is none for remission.

According to this distinction among offenses, the condition of repentance is likewise differentiated. One kind will be capable of obtaining pardon—namely, in the case of a remissible offense; another will be wholly incapable of obtaining it—namely, in the case of an irremissible offense. It remains, therefore, to examine specifically the status of adultery and fornication, and into which class of offenses they must be placed.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0985C]

But first I shall dispose of a response brought forward from the opposing side against that kind of repentance which we are now especially

[Note: [Col. 0985C] “We define as lacking pardon.” In *On Repentance*, [Col. 0985D] chap. 4, when he was still a Catholic, he did not hold this position: “Therefore, for all offenses,” he says, “whether committed in spirit, deed, or will, the same one who appointed punishment through judgment also promised pardon through repentance.” For through repentance remission is granted for all sins, however grave, as the holy Fathers teach against the Novatians. LE PR.]

defining as lacking pardon. For if, they say, any repentance lacks pardon, then you ought not to undertake it at all. Nothing, after all, should be done in vain. But repentance will be undertaken in vain if it lacks pardon.

[Note: [Col. 0985D] “But every repentance must be undertaken.” It seems that one should read: “But with every repentance it must be undertaken.” RIG.]

Yet every repentance [Col. 0986A] must be undertaken. Therefore, let every repentance obtain pardon, lest it be undertaken in vain; for it should not be undertaken if it is undertaken in vain. But it will be undertaken in vain if it lacks pardon. They certainly

[Note: [Col. 0985C] “If it lacks pardon, deservedly indeed,” Wouwer’s manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0985C] “Indeed” is absent from Rhen., Seml., Oberth.]

make this objection with reason, since they have appropriated into their own power the fruit of this repentance also—that is, pardon. For as far as they are concerned, from whom human peace is obtained,

[Note: [Col. 0986C] Ciacconius adds: “it is undertaken in vain.”]

it is undertaken in vain; but as far as we are concerned, who remember that the Lord alone forgives offenses—

[Note: [Col. 0985D] “Who remember that the Lord alone forgives offenses.” He alludes to Mark 2:7: “Who can forgive sins except God alone?” On this matter, however, he speaks more fully below. PAM.]

and mortal offenses at that—it will certainly not be undertaken in vain. For when repentance is referred to the Lord and prostrated before him, it will by that very fact work all the more toward pardon, because it implores it from God alone;

[Note: [Col. 0985D] “Because it implores it from God alone,” etc. Against this point . . . more fully below as well, chap. 21. Here we shall say only that the Author appears to have held the same view which blessed Cyprian attributes to Novatian (*Epistle* 52, to Antonianus). And therefore he could be answered in Cyprian’s own words: “O mockery devised to frustrate the brotherhood! O unstable deception of the wretched who lament! O ineffectual [Col. 0986C] and empty tradition of a heretical institution! To exhort men to the repentance of satisfaction, [Col. 0986D] and then to withdraw the medicine from that satisfaction! To say to a brother: ‘Mourn, shed tears, groan by day and night, and labor frequently and abundantly to wash away and cleanse your offense; yet outside the Church, after all this, you will die. Do whatever belongs to peace, but you will receive none of the peace you seek.’” For here he sets forth public acts of repentance, the same as those in *On Repentance*, chap. 9; and yet he wishes pardon to be implored from God alone, while refusing communion with the Church. Indeed, pardon is very uncertain, and therefore—however much he denies it—repentance is futile, if anyone must await pardon from God alone. PAM.]

because it does not believe that human peace suffices for its offense; because it prefers to blush before the Church rather than to enter into communion with it. For the penitent stands before her doors, admonishes others by the example of his disgrace, calls the tears [Col. 0986B] of the brethren also to his aid, and returns having certainly gained more—

[Note: [Col. 0986C] *Plusque* (“and more”) Pam.]

compassion, that is,

[Note: [Col. 0986C] “And having gained it through prayers, he elicits compassion.” Lat.]

than communion. And if he does not reap peace here, he sows it with the Lord; he does not lose the fruit, but prepares it. He will not be without reward, if he has not been remiss in duty. Thus neither is repentance of this kind futile, nor discipline of this kind harsh. Both honor God: the former, by flattering itself in nothing, will more readily obtain his favor; the latter, by assuming nothing for itself, will give more complete assistance.

## CHAPTER IV

We can therefore, now that the distinction concerning repentance has been entrusted to its proper terms, return to the classification of the offenses themselves and ask whether they are such as may obtain pardon from everyone. First, usage requires that we employ the terms “adultery” and “fornication”;

[Note: [Col. 0986D] “The faith too has a familiarity with certain names.” Here by “faith” he means what elsewhere he calls the Christian sect, philosophy, discipline, or religion. Above he said: “Knowledge too has its own ages in Christ.” RIG.]
