the faith too has a familiarity with certain [Col. 0986C] names, and so throughout every work we observe established usage.

But if I should say “adultery” or “debauchery,”

[Note: [Col. 0986D] “If I should say adultery or debauchery,” etc. He taught the same thing concerning adultery in *On Monogamy*, chap. 9, and concerning debauchery in *On Exhortation to Chastity*, chap. 9. He frequently uses the latter term not only for adultery but also for fornication. . . . I would prefer, however, to read: “Every murder within the wood is robbery,” instead of “outside”; but I was unwilling to alter anything in the text. PAM.]

the verdict will be one and the same: pollution of the flesh. For it makes no difference whether a man assaults another man’s married woman or a widow, provided that she is not his own woman;

[Note: [Col. 0986C] Ciacconius deletes the words from “another man’s” through “woman.”]

just as it makes no difference in respect of place whether chastity is slaughtered in bedrooms or in carriages.

[Note: [Col. 0986C] “Towers” Lat., Rig., Ciacc.]

Every killing outside the forest is [Col. 0987A] robbery; so too, wherever or with whatever woman, a man who engages in sexual relations otherwise than in marriage adulterates and violates himself.

For this reason, among us even clandestine unions—that is, those not first professed before the Church—

[Note: [Col. 0987C] “Not first professed before the Church.” The faithful who were to be married were presented to the Church through the presbyters, so that their marriage might be blessed by the common prayers. This is what he means at the end of Book II of *To His Wife*, when he says: “How could we ever suffice to recount the happiness of that marriage which the Church arranges and the offering confirms?” By interpreting clandestine unions as those “not first professed before the Church,” he remarkably confirms the decree of the Council of Trent concerning the invalidity of such unions, since he adds concerning them: “They run the risk of being judged on a level with adultery and fornication. Nor, once formed, are they to evade the charge under the pretext of marriage.” PAM., Session 24, *On the Sacrament of Matrimony*, chap. 1. RIG.]

run the risk of being judged on a level with adultery and fornication. Nor, once formed,

[Note: [Col. 0987C] “It will run the risk, lest from there” Lat.]

are they to evade the charge under the pretext of marriage.

The remaining impious frenzies of lust,

[Note: [Col. 0987D] “The remaining impious frenzies of lust,” etc. He elegantly distinguishes between removing someone from the threshold of the Church and removing him from every shelter of the Church; as though he means that fornicators and adulterers were admitted to the Church’s threshold, among the penitents, as in the preceding chapter—although in vain, if the Church cannot grant pardon, as he wrongly asserted—whereas those guilty of such monstrous acts were not admitted even there, but were entirely excluded. This also confirms the antiquity of ecclesiastical excommunication; concerning which see above . . . *Apology*, chap. 39, and frequently elsewhere. It is again alluded to below in chap. 7, in the words: “For such an act he was put outside the flock,” and, “He is expelled from the Church.” See more in chap. 14. PAM.]

committed against bodies and sexes beyond the laws of nature, we exclude not merely from the Church’s threshold, but from every shelter of the Church, because they are not offenses but monstrosities.

## CHAPTER V

What degree of wickedness, then, adultery—which is also a matter of fornication—must be judged to possess according to the nature of its act is shown at once by the foremost law of God.

[Note: [Col. 0988C] “The foremost law of God is at hand.” The first law of God was delivered through Moses, the second through Christ. Elsewhere, in *Against the Jews*, he says that God’s first or primordial law was given to Adam and Eve at the beginning of the world. We may therefore interpret the phrase more suitably as: “The foremost law of God is at hand”; that is, before everything else the law of God presents itself. RIG.]

For after the superstition of foreign gods had been forbidden, [Col. 0987B] and the making of their idols; after reverence for the Sabbath had been commended; after religion toward parents, second only to that toward God, had been commanded—no other commandment was placed next in establishing and safeguarding

[Note: [Col. 0988D] “In establishing and admonishing such headings.” In this work of Septimius we feel our way as if with our hands, deprived of the light of ancient manuscripts. “In establishing and fortifying such headings” would certainly seem more suitable. For shortly afterward there follows: “And so he fortified this integrity also.” By “headings” he means the clauses of the divine law; above he likewise spoke of “headings of condemnation.” RIG.]

such headings than:

> “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20:14).

For after spiritual chastity and holiness, bodily integrity came next. And so he fortified this integrity also by immediately prohibiting its enemy, adultery. Understand now the character of an offense whose prohibition he placed directly after that of idolatry.

[Note: [Col. 0987C] “Idolatry” Pam., Rhen., Oberth., Leop.]

Nothing in the second position is far removed from the first; nothing is so close to the first as the second. That which is made second from the first is, in a certain sense, itself first. Accordingly, adultery is akin to idolatry; for idolatry too, which was often charged against the people under the name of adultery and fornication [Col. 0987C] (Jer. 3:1 ff.; Ezek. 16:15 ff.), will also be joined with it in lot, just as in sequence; it will also be linked with it in condemnation, just as in arrangement.

Moreover, after setting first, [Col. 0988A]

> “You shall not commit adultery,”

he adds:

> “You shall not kill.”

He has surely burdened adultery with greater gravity by placing it before murder. Thus, on the opening front of the most holy law, among the foremost headings of the heavenly edict, marked by the proscription of the principal offenses,

[Note: [Col. 0987C] *Signatam* (“marked,” feminine accusative). On the passage, Oberth., Seml.]

you may discern from its position its degree, from its order its status, and from its proximity the desert of each. Even evil has its own rank, because it is placed at the summit or in the midst of the worst evils.

I behold a kind of procession and elevated throne for adultery: on this side the leadership of the idolatry that precedes it, on that side the escort of the murder that follows it. It has undoubtedly taken its worthy seat between the two loftiest pinnacles of crime and, through the midst of them, has filled what was as though an empty place with an authority of guilt equal to theirs.

Who will tear it—enclosed by such flanks and supported all around by such [Col. 0988B] ribs—from the body of the offenses joined to it, from the bond of its neighboring crimes, from the embrace of its kindred wicked deeds, so as to separate it alone for the fruit of repentance? Will not idolatry on one side and murder on the other hold it fast? And if they had any voice,

[Note: [Col. 0988C] “Force” Ciacc.]

would they not protest: “This wedge is ours, this joining is ours”? “We take our boundary from idolatry; through its distinction we are joined; we are united to adultery as it rises prominently between us.

[Note: [Col. 0988C] “We flatter it” Pam., Rhen., Oberth.]

Divine Scripture has incorporated us into one body; the very letters are our glue, and adultery itself can no longer exist without us.

“I, Idolatry, certainly very often furnish occasion for adultery. My groves and my mountains know it, and the living waters, and the temples themselves in the cities: they know how greatly we labor to overthrow chastity.

[Note: [Col. 0988C] *Procurem* (“I procure”) Ciacc.]

“I too, Murder, sometimes labor on behalf of adultery. To omit the tragedies, [Col. 0988C]

[Note: [Col. 0988D] “Poisoners know it today; magicians know it.” You will scarcely be able to distinguish magicians from poisoners, for poisoners or sorcerers were formerly confused with magicians, Chaldeans, astrologers, and Thessalians, who injured others by potions and evil arts and sometimes even took life through their incantations. Apuleius, in his *Apology*: “She cried out before many hearers that she was my lover, and I a magician and poisoner.” LE PR.]

poisoners know it today, and magicians know it:

[Note: [Col. 0988C] “Because” Fran., and in what follows.]

they know how many illicit liaisons I avenge,

[Note: [Col. 0988D] “How many rivalries I defend.” For many lovers defend their beloved women against rivals by murder, their rivals being killed by various kinds of death. RIG.]

how many rivalries I defend, how many guards, informers, and accomplices I remove. [Col. 0989A] Midwives too know how many adulterously conceived children are slaughtered.

“Even among Christians, adultery does not exist without us: idolatry is present wherever an unclean spirit is involved; murder is present wherever a human being, when defiled, is killed.”

Therefore, either the aids of repentance will not be suitable for those offenses, or they will also be suitable for us. Either we hold adultery fast, or we follow it. These realities themselves speak. If realities lack a voice, the idolater appears, the murderer appears, and between them the adulterer also appears. Alike they sit performing the duty of repentance; alike they bristle in sackcloth and ashes; they groan with the same breath, petition with the same prayers, entreat upon the same knees, and invoke the same mother.

[Note: [Col. 0989D] “What are you doing, most indulgent and humane discipline?” Elsewhere he similarly speaks of “the open field of the most lax discipline.” In the opposite sense Augustine says in *On Faith and Works*: “the ancient and robust custom.” RIG.]

What are you doing, most indulgent and humane discipline? Either you will have to be this same thing for all of them—for blessed are the peacemakers (Matt. 5:9)—or, if not for all, you must be [Col. 0989B] ours.

[Note: [Col. 0989D] “You condemn the idolater and murderer once for all.” He himself says below: “Neither to idolatry nor to bloodshed is peace restored by the churches.” RIG.—Here the author slanders the orthodox, as though they did not admit the idolater and murderer to repentance. PAM.]

You condemn the idolater and murderer once for all, but remove the adulterer from their midst as an exception—the successor of idolatry, the predecessor of murder, and the colleague of both? This is partiality: you have abandoned the more pitiable acts of repentance.

## CHAPTER VI

Certainly, if you show by what supporting examples and heavenly precepts you open wide the door of repentance to adultery alone, and in adultery to fornication also, our contest will now be fought on this line. Nevertheless, I must prescribe a rule for you: do not reach your hand toward the old things; do not look back.

For the old things have passed away, according to Isaiah (Isa. 43:18–19), and there is now a new renewal, according to Jeremiah (Jer. 4:3); and, forgetting what lies behind, we stretch forward toward what lies ahead, [Col. 0989C] according to the Apostle (Phil. 3:13); and the Law and the Prophets lasted until John, according to the Lord (Matt. 11:13). For although we have just now begun from the Law in demonstrating the character of adultery, we rightly began from that aspect of the Law which Christ did not abolish but fulfilled (Matt. 5:17).

The burdens of the Law lasted until John, not its remedies; the yokes of works were cast off, not those of discipline. Freedom in Christ has done no injury to innocence. The entire law of piety, holiness, humanity, truth, chastity, justice, mercy, benevolence, and sexual purity remains. Blessed is the man who will meditate upon that law day and night (Ps. 1:1). Concerning it the same David says again:

> “The law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls; the ordinances of the Lord are right, delighting hearts; the commandment of the Lord shines from afar, enlightening the eyes” [Col. 0989D] (Ps. 18:8 ff.).

So too the Apostle:

> “Therefore the law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy and excellent” [Col. 0990A] (Rom. 7:12)—

certainly including:

> “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20:14).

And earlier:

> “Do we therefore nullify the Law through faith? By no means; rather, we establish the Law” (Rom. 3:31),

namely, in those matters which are forbidden even now by the New Testament, under an even more comprehensive command. In place of:

> “You shall not commit adultery,”

there is:

> “Whoever looks with lust has already committed adultery in his heart” (Matt. 5:27–28);

and in place of:

> “You shall not kill,”

there is:

> “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ will be liable to Gehenna” (ibid. 5:22).

Ask whether the law against adultery remains intact, when a prohibition even against lust has been added to it.

Moreover, if any examples applaud you from the folds of your garment, they will not be opposed to this discipline which we defend. For the Law was built up in vain, condemning the very origins of offenses—that is, desires and acts of will—no less than deeds, if pardon will be granted to adultery today merely because [Col. 0990B] it was also once

[Note: [Col. 0989D] “Some” Pam., Rhen., Oberth.]

granted. Why is it now restrained by the advantage of a more complete discipline, unless perhaps so that it may be indulged through your greater pandering?

You will therefore grant pardon to idolatry and every kind of apostasy, because we find that the people themselves, though so often guilty

[Note: [Col. 0989D] “The people themselves, so often guilty,” etc. [Col. 0990D] However much the author may attempt to evade the point, blessed Cyprian, blessed Pacian, and blessed Jerome certainly employ these very examples . . . to confirm against the Novatians the repentance available for every sin, however grave; and so does the Author himself, using the examples of Ahab and David in Book V of *Against Marcion*, chap. 11. PAM.]

of these things, were so often restored in times past (Judg. 3 ff.). You will also grant communion to the murderer, because Ahab wiped away Naboth’s blood by supplication (1 Kings 21:29), while David cleansed through confession the killing of Uriah and the adultery which was its cause (2 Sam. 12:13).

[Note: [Col. 0990D] “Since adultery was its cause” Rhen., Pam., Oberth., Leop.]

You will now grant pardon even to acts of incest because of Lot (Gen. 19:33, 35); to fornications involving incest because of Judah (Gen. 38:18); to shameful marriages arising from prostitution because of Hosea (Hos. 1:2–3); and to marriages not merely repeated, but contracted with several women at once, because of our patriarchs (Gen. 16:3–4; 29–30). [Col. 0990C]

For it is surely fitting that grace should now likewise be equalized in relation to all things formerly indulged, if pardon for adultery is claimed from some ancient example.

We too, certainly, possess examples from the same antiquity in support of our position—examples not merely of judgment not being remitted, but of judgment being made immediately present

[Note: [Col. 0990D] “Judgment being made immediately present.” Here *repraesentati* is understood to mean “brought into the present.” PAM.]

against fornication (Gen. 19:24, 28). Surely it is enough that so great a number—twenty-four thousand of the people who fornicated with the daughters of Moab—fell by a single plague (Num. 25:1 ff.).

But I prefer, for the glory of Christ, to derive discipline from Christ. Let former times, if the Psychics wish, even have possessed license for every kind of sexual impurity;

[Note: [Col. 0990D] “Let former times have possessed,” etc. Here too he slanders the orthodox. PAM.]

let the flesh have sported before Christ—or rather, let it have perished before it was sought out by its Lord. It was not yet worthy of the gift of salvation, not yet fit for the duty of holiness. It was still accounted as being in Adam together with his fault, readily desiring what [Col. 0990D] it had seen to be attractive, looking down toward lower things, and retaining the irritation from the fig leaves. [Col. 0991A]

[Note: [Col. 0991C] “The poison of lust clung everywhere, and the discharged impurities were unfit to be washed away.” From the broken fig leaves there arises, as it were, the poison of sexual irritation. Septimius intimates that the first human beings, Adam and Eve, became inflamed by this irritation immediately after tasting the fruit of the forbidden tree and, upon perceiving their nakedness, plucked fig leaves to cover it; that these leaves adhered to their private parts and thereafter produced milky impurities, stains of lust, which could not be washed away before Christ came, because the waters themselves had not yet washed them, not yet having been medicated by Christ’s baptism. Thus they were not yet capable of washing away impurities of this kind. RIG.—The phrase “and milky impurities” is thoroughly obscure, indeed corrupt. PAM.—“And the discharged impurities were unfit to be washed away.” This is the reading of the ancient manuscripts which Ursinus saw. Previously it was read, “and the cast lots, not having, fit.” Hence even Ursinus’s manuscripts might perhaps be emended thus: “and milky impurities.” For Septimius alludes to the moisture that exudes from fig leaves or, as he will soon say, from the foliage of wantonness. RIG.]

The poison of lust clung everywhere, and the discharged

[Note: [Col. 0991C] “Milked” or “milky” Pam. and others.]

impurities were unfit to be washed away,

[Note: [Col. 0991C] “Not having” Wouwer’s manuscript.]

because not even the waters themselves had yet washed them.

But when the Word of God descended into flesh not opened even by marriage,

[Note: [Col. 0991D] “Flesh not opened even by marriage.” Tertullian’s expression is elegant: “flesh not opened even by marriage,” referring to the virgin flesh of the blessed Mary, although she was married; and “flesh not even to be opened by marriage,” referring to the virgin flesh of Christ. He contrasts the deeds of Christ with those of Eve. PAM.]

and the Word was made flesh (John 1:14)—flesh not even to be opened by marriage; flesh that would approach the tree not of incontinence but of endurance; that would taste from it not something sweet but something bitter;

[Note: [Col. 0991C] Junius deletes “something.”]

that would proceed not to the lower regions but to heaven; that would be girded not with the foliage of wantonness but with the flowers of holiness; that would impart its purity to the waters—

[Note: [Col. 0992C] “That would entrust its purity to the waters.” This is the same as what he said somewhere above in *On Baptism*: that Christ sanctified the waters by his baptism. There he also treats at length of the material of baptism, pure water.]

from then onward, whatever flesh in Christ casts off its remaining former impurities becomes something different: it now emerges new, not from the depths of seed, not from the dung of desire, but from pure water and a clean Spirit.

Why, then, do you excuse that flesh on the basis of its former condition? [Col. 0991B] It was not

[Note: [Col. 0992C] “Not the body of Christ,” etc. This is part of the slander. [Col. 0992D] PAM.]

called the body of Christ, the members of Christ, or the temple of God (1 Cor. 12:27; 6:15, 19; 2 Cor. 6:16) when it obtained pardon for adultery.

Accordingly, if from the point at which it changed its condition, was baptized into Christ and put on Christ (Gal. 3:27), and was redeemed at a great price (1 Cor. 6:20)—namely, by the blood of the Lord and the Lamb (1 Pet. 1:19)—you possess any example, precept, rule, or pronouncement of fornication and adultery either having been or being entitled to be indulged, then you also have from us a definition of the period from which the age relevant to the question is to be reckoned.

## CHAPTER VII
You may begin with the parables, where the lost sheep is sought by the Lord and carried back upon his shoulders (Luke 15:4ff.). Let the very images on your cups come forward,

> **Note [Col. 0992D]: “The images on your cups.”** The same point is made below, chapter 10: “the shepherd whom you depict on the cup,” etc. From this it is inferred that at that time cups were customarily decorated with figures from the histories of the New Testament—confirming the use of images in the Church—and were also made of glass, for this is what makes them “easy to break” (chapter 10). This is also what is cited in our Latin liturgies concerning the blessed Zephyrinus, the Roman pontiff of that age, from Damasus, Walafrid, and Rudolph of Tongeren: that he decreed that all the Church’s vessels should be of glass. Martinus Polonus adds: “or of tin.” Nevertheless, it is clear that not much later silver and gold vessels were also in use, from the Passion of the blessed Lawrence in the blessed Ambrose (*On Duties*, II.18)—Lawrence suffered about one month before the blessed Cyprian—and likewise from Optatus of Milevis (*Against Parmenian*, I). Moreover, he repeatedly uses the word “livestock” for “sheep.” **PAM.**  
> By “images” he means figures which in Scripture signify the use and rite of cups [Col. 0993D]. I think what Pamelius adduces from pontifical decrees concerning glass, tin, gold, and silver cups has no relevance to this passage. **LE PR.**

[Col. 0991C] if in them, at least, an interpretation of that sheep will shine through: whether it promises restoration to a Christian sinner or to a gentile sinner. For we lay it down as a preliminary rule, from the discipline of nature, from the law governing ear and tongue, and from soundness of mind, that responses are always made to the matters that provoke them—that is, [Col. 0992A] to the provocations themselves.

The provocation, I think, was that the Pharisees murmured indignantly because the Lord admitted gentile tax collectors and sinners and shared food with them (Matt. 9:11). In response to this, to whom else are we to believe that the Lord likened the restoration of the lost sheep

> **Note [Col. 0991C]: “We are to believe.”** Thus nearly all printed editions. Rhenanus and Pamelius read: “When he had represented the restoration [Col. 0992C], to whom else is it to be referred?”

than to the lost gentile who was under discussion—not to a Christian, since as yet there was no such person? Or what sense would it make for the Lord, like one who quibbles in answering, to pass over the present case which he ought to refute and occupy himself with a future one?

“But the sheep is properly a Christian; the Lord’s flock is the people of the Church; and Christ is the good shepherd” (John 10:11, 14ff.). “Therefore the Christian must be understood in the sheep”

> **Note [Col. 0992C]: “Man,” Wouwer manuscript.**  
> **Note [Col. 0992C]: “Must not be understood,” Gelenius, Pamelius.**

“who has wandered from the Church’s flock.”

Then you would have the Lord answer nothing to the Pharisees’ murmuring, but answer your presumption instead. Yet you will have to maintain that presumption in such a way as to deny that what you think applies to a Christian is applicable to a gentile.

Tell me: is not the whole human race one flock of God? Is not the same God both Lord and shepherd of all nations? Who is more lost from God than a gentile so long as he wanders? Who is more sought by God than a gentile when he is recalled by Christ? Indeed, this order comes first in gentiles, since Christians are made from gentiles in no other way than by first being lost, then sought by God, and carried back by Christ. This order must therefore be maintained as well: we should interpret such a thing of those in whom it occurs first.

But you, I suppose, would wish

> **Note [Col. 0992C]: “Would wish,” Rhenanus, Oberthür, Leopold.**

him to make the sheep lost not from the flock, but from a chest or cupboard.

Likewise, even though he calls the remaining number of the gentiles righteous, he does not thereby show them to be Christians [Col. 0992C] while dealing with the Jews and especially reproaching them because they were indignant at the gentiles’ hope (Matt. 21:43). Rather, to express against the Pharisees’ envy his grace and goodwill even toward a single gentile, he placed the salvation of one sinner [Col. 0993A] through repentance before theirs through righteousness. Or were the Jews not “righteous”—persons who had no need of repentance—since they possessed the rudders of discipline and the instruments of fear, the Law and the Prophets? He therefore placed them in the parable, not indeed as they were, but as they ought to have been, so that they might be put to greater shame when they heard that repentance was necessary for others but not for themselves.

Accordingly, in the parable of the drachma—

> **Note [Col. 0993D]: The word “parable” is absent from Rhenanus and Oberthür.**

because it was prompted by the same subject, we likewise interpret the drachma

> **Note [Col. 0993D]: “Drachma” is absent from Rhenanus and Oberthür.**

as the gentile: even though it was lost in a house, as though in the Church; even though it was found by the light of a lamp, as though by God’s word. Yet this entire world is the one common house of all, in which God’s grace shines more brightly upon the gentile, who is found in darkness, than upon the Christian, who is already in God’s light.

Finally, one kind of error is ascribed to both the sheep and the drachma. For [Col. 0993B] if they were already being fashioned as figures of the Christian sinner, their repeated loss and restoration after the loss of faith would have been indicated.

I shall now step down briefly from this position, so that by stepping down I may commend it all the more, once I have also blocked the presumption of the opposing side in the following way. I concede that the Christian who has now become a sinner is foreshadowed in both parables; he is nevertheless not on that account to be affirmed as one who may be restored through repentance after the crime of adultery or fornication. For although he is said to have been lost, the kind of loss will still have to be reconsidered, because the sheep was lost not by dying but by wandering, and the drachma not by perishing but by lying hidden. Thus even something that remains intact may be said to have been lost.

The believer, therefore, is also lost when he has slipped away

> **Note [Col. 0993D]: “Into a spectacle,” etc.** On these four kinds of spectacle, see the notes on the book *On the Spectacles*. On arts of curiosity employed in the service of another’s idolatry, see *On Idolatry*, chapters 4–9; on equivocal commerce, the same work; and on a word of blasphemy, when someone swears by idols, chapters 20 and 29. It would, however, be astonishing if the author, in the vehemence of his spirit, classed blasphemy among remissible offenses, since below, in chapters 9 and again 13, he places it among the irremissible. We have therefore necessarily omitted the words “or blasphemy.” **PAM.**

into a spectacle of chariot-racing frenzy, gladiatorial bloodshed, theatrical obscenity, or athletic vanity; into games; into [Col. 0993C] banquets of secular solemnity; or when he has applied certain curious arts in an office or service belonging to another’s idolatry; or has stumbled into a word of equivocal denial

> **Note [Col. 0993D]: “Commerce,” Junius.**

or blasphemy. For some such reason he has been put outside the flock; or perhaps he himself has broken away through anger, arrogance, jealousy, or—as often happens—resentment of correction. He ought to be sought and recalled. What can be recovered will not perish, unless

> **Note [Col. 0993D]: “Will not be able [to be recovered], if he remains outside,” Rigault, Paris edition.**

it remains outside.

You will interpret the parable well if you recall a sinner who is still alive. But the adulterer and fornicator—who has not [Col. 0994A] pronounced him dead immediately upon the commission of the act? With what effrontery will you restore a dead man to the flock on the authority of a parable that recalls no dead sheep?

Finally, if you remember the prophets, when shepherds are rebuked, the following, I think, is the voice of Ezekiel:

> “Shepherds, behold, you consume the milk and clothe yourselves with the wool. What is strong you have killed; what is weak you have not tended; what is broken you have not bound up; what is driven away you have not brought back; what is lost you have not sought” (Ezek. 34:2–3).

Does he also reproach them concerning what is dead because they failed to take care to restore even that to the flock? He plainly charges them with having caused the sheep to perish and be eaten by the beasts of the field. Nor can sheep perish unto death or be eaten if they are left behind only so that, though not lost unto death or eaten, they may be recovered.

Likewise, according to the example of the drachma, even within God’s house, the Church, there may be [Col. 0994B] certain offenses moderate in degree and weight, like the drachma itself. While hidden there, they are soon found there as well, and are immediately settled there with the joy of amendment. Adultery and fornication, however, are not a drachma but a talent.

> **Note [Col. 0993D]: “Not a drachma but a talent.”** Even if it were a talent, the author fails to notice the other parable, that of the king who forgave his servant ten thousand talents (Matt. 18).

To search these out, what is needed is not the light from the point of a lamp,

> **Note [Col. 0994D]: Latinius deletes “light.”**

but

> **Note [Col. 0993D]: “The spear of the whole sun.”** That is, its ray. He attributes a spear to the sun [Col. 0994D] to set it against the lamp’s point, which Julius Pollux calls a *σκεῦος στρατιωτικόν* (*skeuos stratiōtikon*), “military implement.” **RIG.**  
> What follows pertains not to repentant sinners but to those who do not repent—unless perhaps he is speaking of his own Montanist Church. **PAM.**

the spear of the whole sun.

> **Note [Col. 0994D]: “Lanceo,” Pum.**

As soon as the offense appears, the person is immediately expelled from the Church. He neither remains there nor brings joy to the Church that found him, but grief; nor does he summon the neighboring churches to congratulations, but the nearest brotherhoods to sorrow.

Thus, when even this interpretation of ours is brought into conflict with theirs, the arguments from both the sheep and the drachma will pertain all the more to the gentile, because they cannot apply to a Christian guilty of that offense for whose sake the opposing side is compelled to apply them to a Christian.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0994C]

Many interpreters of the parables are deceived by the same outcome that very frequently occurs

> **Note [Col. 0994D]: “In bringing out the sheen in purple garments.”** That is, illuminating them. Thus Pliny says of the sun: “It gives sight to the other stars.” The radiance or brilliance of purple itself is called “light.” Quintilian, *Institutes* VIII: “A stripe and pieces of purple inserted in their proper place will bring light.” Horace, *Art of Poetry*:  
>   
> “One or two purple patches, gleaming far and wide.”  
>   
> Arrian, *Epictetus* I.2: *Ἐγὼ δὲ πορφύρα εἶναι βούλομαι, τὸ ὀλίγον ἐκεῖνο, καὶ στίλπνον, καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις αἴτιον τοῦ εὐπρεπῆ φαίνεσθαι καὶ καλά*—“But I wish to be the purple: that small and shining part which causes the rest to appear handsome and beautiful.”

in bringing out the sheen in purple garments. You may think that you have correctly blended the gradations of the colors and believe that their mutual comparisons have enlivened them;

> **Note [Col. 0994D]: “Loved them,” François.**

but as soon as both fabrics have been finished and their colors brought fully into view, the contrast, once exposed, will disgorge every error.

> **Note [Col. 0994D]: “The contrast, once exposed, will disgorge every error.”** It will show that the gradations of the colors were badly blended. He says that the wool “disgorges” the colors it absorbed. **RIG.**

Some people wander in the same darkness concerning the parable of the two sons (Luke 15:11ff.):

> **Note [Col. 0994D]: “Concerning the parable of the two sons.”** In this case the author himself surely strays from the true light into darkness even more. Consequently, that elegant metaphor applies more aptly to him—as it does to all heretics—than to the orthodox, especially since he himself cited this parable in support of repentance in *On Repentance*, chapter 8, and *On Patience*, chapter 12; as did the blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, Letter 8 to Demophilus; the blessed Jerome, Letter 46 to Damasus; Ambrose, *On Repentance* I.3; and Augustine, *Questions on the Gospels* I.33. **EDITORS, from PAM.**

because certain figures are for the moment similar in color, [Col. 0995A] they stray from the true light of the comparison that the parable’s subject has set before them. For they locate two peoples in the two sons:

> **Note [Col. 0995C]: “They locate two peoples in the two sons,” etc.** I have thus far seen none of the ancients who expressly interpret the two sons as the elder Jewish people and the younger Christian people. There is therefore no reason for us to defend that opinion [Col. 0995D], but rather the one that understands the righteous and sinners. **PAM.**

the elder being the Jewish people and the younger the Christian. They cannot, after all, arrange for the younger son to represent the Christian sinner who is to receive pardon unless they have made the elder represent the Jew.

But if I show that the Jew fails to correspond to the elder son, it will consequently follow

> **Note [Col. 0995C]: “It will follow,” Semler, Leopold.**

that the Christian cannot be admitted as the figure of the younger son either. For although the Jew may be called both “son” and “elder,” because he was earlier in adoption (Rom. 9:4; source reads 9:29), and although he envies the Christian’s reconciliation with God the Father—the point that the opposing side especially seizes upon—the Jew cannot say to the Father:

> “Behold, for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your commandment” (Luke [Col. 0995B] 15:29).

For when is the Jew not a transgressor of the Law, hearing with his ear yet not hearing, hating him who rebukes in the gates,

> **Note [Col. 0995D]: “Hating him who rebukes in the gates.”** He twists this also against the “Psychics,” who fled in persecution or bought themselves off by paying money to extortioners. Thus in *On Flight*: “When you give money, you surely wished not to be betrayed. Yet if you were not betrayed, you were liable to be exposed. Therefore, when by refusing to be betrayed you wish not to be exposed, in your refusal you have denied what you were—the thing you did not wish to be exposed as being.” **RIG.**

and scorning

> **Note [Col. 0995C]: “You scorn,” Wouwer manuscript, Leopold.**

the holy word? Nor, similarly, can the Father’s words to the Jew be:

> “You are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (Luke 15:31).

For the Jews are pronounced apostate sons: indeed begotten and raised on high, but those who did not take account of the Lord, who forsook the Lord, and provoked the Holy One of Israel to anger (Isa. 1:2, 4).

We shall say, to be sure, that everything has been granted to the Jew,

> **Note [Col. 0995D]: “From whom every more agreeable created thing has been snatched away from his throat.”** By “created thing” he means every item of food created and constituted by God. **RIG.**

from whose throat even every more agreeable created thing has been snatched away, much less the very land of the paternal promise. Indeed, the Jew today, no less than the younger son, begs in a foreign country after squandering God’s substance, still serving its rulers—that is, the rulers of this age.

Let Christians therefore [Col. 0995C] seek another brother of their own; the parable has not admitted the Jew. [Col. 0996A] They would have compared the Christian with the elder son and the Jew with the younger far more suitably, according to the comparison of faith, if the order of the two peoples signified from Rebecca’s womb (Gen. 25:22ff.) allowed the reversal—except that the conclusion too would resist it. For it will be fitting for the Christian to rejoice, not grieve, over the Jew’s restoration, since our entire hope is joined with the remaining expectation of Israel (Rom. 11).

Thus, although some details support their interpretation, the equivalence of the examples is destroyed by other, contrary details. And even

> **Note [Col. 0995D]: “Even if everything could correspond to the mirror.”** By “mirror” he means image, example, or parable. Thus in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*: “Serve the example, therefore, and preserve its mirror for the flesh.” **RIG.**

if everything could correspond to the mirror, there remains one principal danger in interpretation: that the successful correspondences may be blended toward some destination other than that prescribed by the subject of each parable.

For we remember that actors too,

> **Note [Col. 0995D]: “Actors adapt allegorical gestures to songs.”** Thus there is no longer need for the herald who in ancient times, while a pantomime danced, announced to the people [Col. 0996C] of Carthage what the dancer wished to be understood. Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine* II.25. And the parables occurring in Holy Scripture are allegories and allegorical arguments. Augustine, on Psalm 103: “Take care, however, that when ‘allegory’ is mentioned you do not suppose that I have said something about a pantomime,” etc. **RIG.**

when they adapt allegorical gestures [Col. 0996B] to songs, most appropriately express a story, scene, and character

> **Note [Col. 0996C]: “A story, scene, and character.”** On these, see extensively *On the Spectacles*, chapters 10 and 17. **PAM.**

altogether different from the present one. But let that extraordinary contrivance look to itself.

> **Note [Col. 0996C]: “But let that extraordinary contrivance look to itself.”** He likes to use *ingenium* for a device or contrivance. Here, however, he calls the actor’s contrivance “extraordinary” because it is wholly unfitting for a Christian, being outside the order of Christian discipline [Col. 0996D]. Hence he adds: “For it has nothing to do with Andromache”—that is, nothing to do with Christ, nothing with the Christian Church. **RIG.**

For it has nothing to do with Andromache.

Thus the heretics too—

> **Note [Col. 0996D]: “Thus the heretics too.”** Not only the Psychics. **RIG.**

assign the same parables wherever they please,

> **Note [Col. 0996C]: “Drag,” Latinius, Neander.**

and most appropriately hatch them out where they ought not.

> **Note [Col. 0996D]: “Where they ought not, they most appropriately hatch them out.”** This too is a fine observation about the interpretation of Scripture among heretics released from the rule of truth, a matter treated more fully in *On Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 17. There is irony in the words “most appropriately hatch them out.” Why most appropriately? Because, etc. The passage must certainly be punctuated in this way. And indeed *excludunt*—a metaphor taken from hens or birds, which are said to hatch their young—is used for “unfold,” “expound,” or “interpret”…. Yet he seems to me to be arguing against the heretics Marcus and Colorbasus, who constructed their god from numbers and, among other things—as Irenaeus testifies, I.13—from the lost drachma and the sheep. **PAM.**

Why “most appropriately”? Because from the outset, according to the occasions of the parables, they fashioned the very subject matter of their doctrines. Released from the rule of truth,

> **Note [Col. 0996D]: “Released, of course, from the rule of truth,” etc.** Here he censures all heretics together with the Psychics, not merely the Colorbasians, who constructed their god from numbers, as Pamelius thinks. **LE PR.**

they had leisure,

> **Note [Col. 0996C]: “It was empty,” Pamelius, Rhenanus, Oberthür, Leopold.**

of course, to seek out and put together the things whose parables they appear to be.

## CHAPTER IX

We, however, because we do not invent subject matter from parables but interpret parables from their subject matter, do not labor greatly to force every detail into the exposition, provided that we guard against all contradictions. Why are there a hundred [Col. 0996C] sheep (Luke 15:4)? And why ten drachmas? [Col. 0997A] And what are those brooms (ibid. 8)? It was necessary for one who wished to express how exceedingly welcome the salvation of one sinner is to God to name some numerical quantity, from which he might describe one as lost. It was necessary that the circumstances of the woman searching for the drachma in her house be furnished with the aid of both broom and lamp.

Curiosities of this kind make some things suspect and, through the subtlety of forced expositions, often lead away from the truth. Some details, however, have simply been placed there to construct, arrange, and weave the parable, so that it may be brought to the point for which the example is provided.

The two sons certainly refer to the same point as the drachma and the sheep. Since they are connected with those parables, they have the same cause: namely, the same murmuring of the Pharisees against the Lord’s association with gentiles. [Col. 0997B] Or, if anyone doubts that the tax collectors in Judea were gentiles—Judea having long since been seized

> **Note [Col. 0997D]: “Judea having been seized.”** Seized by the hand of Pompey; see Josephus, *Antiquities* XIV.8 and *Jewish War* I.5, and Hegesippus, *On the Destruction of Jerusalem* I.14, 17. **PAM.**

by the hand of Pompey and Lucullus—let him read Deuteronomy: “There shall be no one paying tribute from among the children of Israel” (Deut. 23:19).

Nor would the name of tax collectors have been so accursed in the Lord’s eyes

> **Note [Col. 0997D]: “Nor would the name of tax collectors have been so accursed.”** Septimius curses the sinews of war; in *On the Crown* he stripped the Christian soldier of his military belt. **RIG.**

unless it referred to foreigners selling passage through heaven, earth, and sea, which belonged to him. Moreover, when he joins “sinners” to tax collectors (Luke 15:2), he does not immediately show them to be Jews, although some may have been. Rather, by placing them together he distinguished two classes of gentiles: some sinners by profession—that is, tax collectors—and others sinners by nature—that is, those who were not tax collectors. Otherwise, the Lord would not have been censured for sharing food with Jews,

> **Note [Col. 0998D]: “Nor would he have been censured for sharing food with Jews,” etc.** Here too the author is mistaken, because the Lord was censured when he permitted himself to be touched by the sinful woman (Luke 7), although she too was Jewish, not a gentile. **PAM.**

but with gentiles, whose table Jewish discipline rejects.

Concerning the prodigal son, we must first consider what is more conducive to salvation. [Col. 0997C] For an equation of examples must not be admitted, however perfectly it may correspond to the image, if it is exceedingly harmful to salvation. We see the whole condition of salvation, established in the maintenance of discipline, overturned by the interpretation promoted by the opposing side.

For if the Christian is the man who, after receiving from God the Father his substance—namely baptism, the Holy Spirit, and thereafter the hope of eternity—wanders far from the Father and squanders it by living as a gentile; if, stripped of the goods of the mind, he also hands over his service to the ruler of the world—to whom else but the devil?—and is appointed by him to tend swine, that is, to minister to unclean spirits; and if he then comes to his senses and returns to the Father, then by this parable it will be not merely adulterers and fornicators, but idolaters, blasphemers, deniers, and every class of apostates who make satisfaction to the Father. And in this way, most truly,

> **Note [Col. 0997D]: “Most truly” is absent from Rigault.**

the whole [Col. 0997D] substance of the sacrament is all the more completely destroyed.

> **Note [Col. 0998D]: “The whole substance of the sacrament is destroyed.”** Baptism is meant. **PAM.**

For who will fear to squander what he will afterward be able to recover? Who will take care to preserve forever what he cannot lose forever? Security from punishment is itself an inducement to sin.

The apostate, therefore, will recover his former robe, the clothing [Col. 0998A] of the Holy Spirit; and again the ring, the seal of baptism; and Christ will again be slaughtered for him (Luke 15:22–23). He will recline there upon that couch from which those unworthily clothed are customarily taken by the torturers and cast into darkness (Matt. 22:12–13), much more those who have been stripped bare.

It is therefore a stronger point that the sequence of the prodigal son is not even suitably applicable to a Christian. But if the son’s image does not completely correspond to the Jew either, the interpretation will simply be governed by the Lord’s purpose.

The Lord had surely come to save what had been lost, as a physician more necessary to the sick than to the healthy (Matt. 18:11; 9:12; Luke 19:10; 5:31). This he both represented in parables and proclaimed in sayings. Who among human beings is lost? Who fails in health, except the one who does not know God? Who is safe and sound, except the one who knows God? This parable too will signify these two brotherly kinds within the human race.

Consider whether the gentile possesses in God the Father a patrimony of wisdom and natural knowledge of God. Through this the Apostle also remarks that, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom (1 Cor. 1:21)—a wisdom it had, of course, received from God. The gentile therefore squandered this when, in his conduct, he went far away from the Lord amid the errors, enticements, and desires of the world. There, driven by hunger for the truth, he handed himself over to the ruler of this age. That ruler appointed him over the swine—to feed that livestock so familiar to the demons—where he himself had no share in life-giving food, while at the same time he saw others, engaged in divine service, abounding in heavenly bread.

He remembers God the Father, returns after making satisfaction, and receives his former robe: namely, the condition Adam lost through transgression. He then receives the ring for the first time, with which, when questioned, he seals [Col. 0998C] the covenant of faith. Thereafter he feeds upon the richness of the Lord’s body—that is, the Eucharist.

This will be the prodigal son: one who was never thrifty before, who was prodigal from the outset because he was not a Christian from the outset. It was this man, returning from the world to the Father’s embrace in the persons of tax collectors and sinners, whom the Pharisees mourned. The elder brother’s envy was therefore adapted to this point alone: not because the Jews were innocent and obedient to God, but because they envied salvation to the nations, though certainly they ought always to have remained with the Father.

And the Jew certainly groans at the Christian’s first calling, not at his second restoration. The former shines even upon the gentiles; the latter, however, which is transacted within the churches, is unknown even to the Jews.

I think I have produced interpretations better adapted to the subject matter of the parables, the correspondence of the facts, [Col. 0998D] and the protection of discipline.

But if the opposing side is eager to make the sheep, the drachma, and the son’s dissipation figures of the Christian sinner, so that by repentance they may pardon adultery and fornication, then either pardon must likewise be granted to all the other capital offenses, [Col. 0999A] or adultery and fornication, which are their equals, must likewise be maintained as unpardonable.

More importantly, nothing may be inferred beyond the matter under discussion. Indeed, if it were permissible to transfer the parables elsewhere, we would direct their hope toward martyrdom instead. Martyrdom alone will be able to restore the son after his entire substance has been squandered; will proclaim with joy the drachma found among everything else, though even in dung; and will carry the fugitive sheep back to the flock upon the Lord’s own shoulders through every rough and precipitous place.

But we prefer, if it may be, to understand less in the Scriptures rather than to understand against them. Accordingly, we must preserve the Lord’s meaning and command. Transgression in interpretation is no lighter than transgression in conduct.

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 0999B]

Now that the obstacle to explaining these parables as referring to the gentile has therefore been removed, and once the necessity has been discerned or accepted of interpreting them in no other way than the subject under discussion requires, they contend that the proclamation of repentance does not apply even to gentiles. Their offenses, they say, are not answerable to repentance, since they must be imputed to ignorance, which nature alone makes culpable before God. Nor, they say, can people understand remedies when they do not understand the dangers themselves. The rationale of repentance exists only where sin is committed knowingly and voluntarily, where both guilt and grace are understood. The man who knows both what he has lost and what he will recover if he sacrifices repentance to God—who surely offers it to sons more than to strangers—is the one who should mourn and roll in the dust.

Did Jonah, then (Jonah 3:4), for that reason think repentance unnecessary for the gentile Ninevites when he quibbled over [Col. 0999C] his duty of preaching?

> **Note [Col. 0999C]: “Did not,” Pamelius; “for,” Oberthür, Semler.**

Or rather, foreseeing God’s mercy poured out even upon strangers and fearing that it would nullify his proclamation, did he not nearly perish as a prophet on account of a profane city not yet possessing God and still sinning in ignorance? Except that he underwent a figure of the Lord’s Passion, which was to redeem repentant gentiles as well (Luke 13:29–30).

It is well that John too, while preparing the Lord’s ways, was a herald of repentance no less to soldiers and tax collectors than to the sons of Abraham (Luke 3:13ff.). [Col. 1000A] The Lord himself presumed that Sidon and Tyre would have repented if they had seen the evidences of his mighty works (Matt. 11:21).

Indeed, I shall contend that repentance applies more to natural sinners than to voluntary ones. For one who has not yet used it will better deserve its fruit than one who has already abused it; and first remedies will be more effective than remedies worn out through use.

No doubt the Lord is more kindly to the ungrateful than to the ignorant, and more quickly merciful to those who have already been rejected than to those not yet tested! Thus he is supposedly not more angered by insults to his clemency than he is ready to show favor, and does not more gladly bestow that clemency upon strangers than he has lost it among his sons—even though he adopted the nations precisely while the Jews made sport of his patience.

> **Note [Col. 0999D]: “The Jews make sport of his patience.”** That is, patience so often injured by offenses so often repeated. Thus canon 3 of the Council of Elvira, concerning *flamines* who committed adultery after repentance: “It was resolved that communion should no longer be given to them, lest they appear to have made sport of the Lord’s communion”; and canon 47: “If, after being restored, he again commits adultery, it was resolved that God should no longer be mocked through the communion of peace.” **RIG.**

But this is what the Psychics desire: that God, the just judge, should prefer the repentance rather than the death of the sinner who preferred death to repentance. [Col. 1000B] If that is so, we earn merit by sinning.

Go on, then, tightrope-walker of modesty and chastity and of every holiness concerning sex! You advance along the most slender thread of discipline of this kind, with your steps suspended above the byways of truth, balancing the flesh by the spirit, governing the soul by faith, and restraining the eye by fear. Why, then, are you wholly fixed upon the rope? Go forward, certainly, if you can and if you wish, while you are so secure and as though standing on solid ground. For if some wavering of the flesh, distraction of the mind, or wandering of the eye knocks you from your course, God is good: he holds open his bosom to his own, not to gentiles. A second repentance will receive you;

> **Note [Col. 0999D]: “You will again become a Christian from being an adulterer.”** As though one who fell into adultery after baptism had ceased to be a Christian. **RIG.**

from an adulterer you will again become a Christian.

So much for you, my most benevolent interpreter of God. But I would yield to you if the writing of *The Shepherd*, which alone loves adulterers, had deserved to be inscribed among the divine documents; if it were not judged apocryphal and false by every council of the churches, including [Col. 1000C] your own—being itself adulterous and therefore the patroness of its companions;

> **Note [Col. 0999D]: “By which you are initiated in other respects too.”** By that apocryphal and false writing of *The Shepherd*, of course, rather than by writings that are unquestioned and universally received. **RIG.**

and by which you are initiated elsewhere too.

If perhaps that shepherd depicted upon your cup will patronize that writing, he too is

> **Note [Col. 0999D]: “A panderer of the Christian sacrament.”** That is, of the Eucharist. **RIG.**

a panderer of the Christian sacrament. He is deservedly both an idol of drunkenness and a gadfly inciting the adultery that will follow the cup—

> **Note [Col. 0999D]: “And a gadfly inciting the adultery that will follow the cup.”** The text should read *asilum*, for it signifies *οἶστρον* (*oistron*), “gadfly, frenzy.”  
>   
> “…which bears the Roman name *asilus*,  
> while the Greeks have translated it by calling it *oestrus*.”  
>   
> Pliny XI.16: “Sometimes larger bees are born at the outer edges of the honeycombs, and these drive away the others. This affliction is called *oestrus*.” Again: “It has been decided to call it *asilus* or *tabanus*; its sting is in its mouth. Animals struck by it are driven as though into madness.” From this the word was transferred to sexual frenzies. Hesychius: *οἶστρος, ἐρεθισμός, ὁ λεγόμενος μῦα· μανία ἀφροδισίων, κύρωσις, ἔκκαυσις*—“gadfly; irritation; the so-called fly; sexual madness, excitation, inflammation.” Septimius therefore calls Catholics who condemn dry fasts and restore the Church to repentant adulterers “Psychics”; and he calls the Shepherd depicted on their cup an idol of drunkenness and a gadfly of lust, because, their bodies being well tended, they are supposedly struck as by frenzy and rush into adultery and every kind of wantonness, invited by the flattering confidence that repentance may be obtained. How bitter are these insults against Catholics! **RIG.**

from which you would drink nothing more gladly than the sheep of second repentance.

> **Note [Col. 1000D]: “The sheep of second repentance.”** That is, the lustful sheep, the adulterous sheep: the hope of obtaining pardon even for adultery committed after baptism. **RIG.**

But I drink from the writings of that Shepherd who cannot be broken. John immediately presents him to me together with the washing and duty of repentance, saying:

> “Produce fruits worthy [Col. 1001A] of repentance, and do not say, ‘We have Abraham as our father’”

—lest, of course, they should once again derive inducements to sin from the favor enjoyed by their fathers—

> “for God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. 3:8–9).

Thus it follows for us too

> **Note [Col. 1001D]: “So that those who sin up to this point.”** “Up to this point” means “now no longer.” **RIG.**

that those who sin only up to this point must produce worthy fruit of repentance. For what ripens from repentance except the accomplishment of amendment?

But even if pardon is instead the fruit of repentance, pardon too cannot exist without the cessation of sin. Thus the cessation of sin is the root of pardon, so that pardon may be the fruit of repentance.

## CHAPTER XI

Thereafter, as regards the Gospel, the question of the parables has now been examined. But if by his deeds the Lord also performed some such act on behalf of sinners—[Col. 1001B] as when he permitted the sinful woman even to touch his body, while she washed his feet with tears, wiped them with her hair, and with ointment inaugurated his burial (Luke 7:37ff.); or when he revealed even who he was, something he did not readily disclose to anyone, to the Samaritan woman now in her sixth marriage—not an adulteress, but a prostitute (John 4:7ff.)—nothing from this assists our adversaries, even if he had already granted Christians pardon of their offenses.

For now we say: this is permitted to the Lord alone; today the power of pardon belongs to him. Yet concerning those times when he acted on earth, we determine that it establishes no precedent against us if pardon was granted to sinners, even Jewish ones.

For Christian discipline is reckoned from the renewal of the Testament and, as we stated beforehand, from the redemption of the flesh—that is, from the Lord’s Passion. Before [Col. 1001C] the order of faith was discovered, no one was perfect; before Christ was taken back into heaven, no one was a Christian; before the Holy Spirit was manifested from heaven as the one who determines that discipline, no one was holy.

## CHAPTER XII
Therefore, those who received another Paraclete in the apostles and through the apostles—a Paraclete whom they did not recognize more fully even in the Prophets—now no longer possess him even in the apostles. Come now, let them show, at least from the apostolic record, that stains with which the flesh is bespattered after baptism can be washed away by repentance.

> **Note [Col. 1001C].** *Propius* in Rhenanus, Oberthür, and Leopold.

> **Note [Col. 1001D].** “Or let them teach it from the apostolic record.” It does not follow: “From the Acts of the Apostles—which he calls the apostolic record—it is not taught that stains with which the flesh is bespattered after baptism are washed away by repentance; therefore sins committed after baptism are not erased by repentance,” since this is sufficiently established by other Scriptures. —PAM.

> **Note [Col. 1001D].** “The flesh bespattered after baptism.” Here he has used *respersae* for “sprinkled and stained anew,” namely with fresh filth after the washing. —RIG.

In the apostles too we recognize the form of the old law in its demonstration of how grave adultery is, lest perhaps it be regarded as less serious under the newness of the disciplines than under the old. When the Gospel first thundered forth and shook the old order, so that the question whether the law was to be retained was debated, the apostles issued this first rule, on the authority of the Holy Spirit, to those who had already begun to be chosen from among the nations:

> “It has seemed good,” they say, “to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose no further burden upon you than those things from which it is necessary to abstain: from sacrifices, from fornication, and from blood. By guarding yourselves from these things you do well” (Acts 15:28 ff.), the Holy Spirit bearing you along.

> **Note [Col. 1001D].** “From sacrifices, from fornication, and from blood.” Irenaeus preserves the same order: “They must be instructed to abstain from the vanities of idols, and from fornication, and from blood, and not to do to others whatever they do not wish to be done to themselves.” A little later, in place of “the vanities of idols,” he says “things sacrificed to idols.” These two words, *eidōlothyton kai haima* (εἰδωλόθυτον καὶ αἷμα), “an idol-sacrifice and blood,” received various interpretations and even disturbed the ancient manuscripts of Acts through ambiguity of readings. But what is read here and in Irenaeus is perfectly clear concerning these three principal defilements (*alisgēmata*, ἀλισγήματα): those “of idols, fornication, and blood” (*eidōlōn, porneias, haimatos*, εἰδώλων, πορνείας, αἵματος). —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 1001C].** “Forbidding” (*vetante*) in Wouwer’s manuscript.

> **Note [Col. 1002D].** It is sufficient that here too the place belonging to adultery and fornication has been preserved. But Luke himself did not preserve it. For in Acts 15, after first saying, “of idols and of fornication and of blood” (*tōn eidōlōn kai tēs porneias kai tou haimatos*, τῶν εἰδώλων καὶ τῆς πορνείας καὶ τοῦ αἵματος), he afterward prescribed them as “things sacrificed to idols, and blood, and fornication” (*eidōlothytōn kai haimatos kai porneias*, εἰδωλοθύτων καὶ αἵματος καὶ πορνείας). Accordingly, Septimius’s argument from the order or position of the words is quite frivolous, as is the vain conjecture of those who think that the words should be connected thus: “For the Holy Spirit it is sufficient that here too the place belonging to adultery and fornication has been preserved.” Irenaeus contradicts this, nor did it ever occur to our Septimius. —RIG.

It is sufficient that here too the place of honor belonging to adultery and fornication has been preserved between idolatry and murder; for we shall understand the prohibition of blood to refer much more especially to human blood.

> **Note [Col. 1002C].** “The Holy Spirit: it is sufficient,” Junius.

What sort of crimes, then, do the apostles intend these to be, which alone they select from the former law for observance, and which alone they prescribe as things from which it is absolutely necessary to abstain? Not that they permit the others, but because they set forth these alone as plainly incapable of remission, while, for the sake of the Gentiles, they made the remaining burdens of the law remissible. Why, then, do they free our neck from so great a yoke, unless they mean always to impose upon them these concise summaries of discipline?

> **Note [Col. 1002C].** “Upon him” (*illi*) in Rigault and Venice.

Why do they loosen so many bonds, unless they mean to bind us perpetually to the more indispensable ones? They released us from many things so that we might be bound to observe the more perilous. The matter was settled by compensation: we gained many concessions so that we might render certain obligations. But a compensation is not revocable—

> **Note [Col. 1002D].** “And it will be revoked by the same things.” Something is missing which cannot be restored except with the aid of a manuscript. Or certainly one should write: “Unless, finally, it is revoked by repetition—repetition, that is, of adultery, bloodshed, and idolatry.” —RIG.

—and it will be revoked by those same things: namely, by a repetition of adultery, bloodshed, and idolatry. For the whole law will then be resumed if the condition of pardon is dissolved. But the Holy Spirit did not make a trivial covenant with us; indeed, he made it voluntarily and is therefore all the more to be honored. No one dissolves his compact except an ungrateful person. He will neither take back what he released nor release what he retained. The settled state of the New Testament is forever unchangeable, and surely the recital of that decree and that decision will last until the end of the age. He has sufficiently denied pardon for the things whose observance he chose; he claimed for punishment what he did not similarly concede. Hence it is that peace is restored by the churches neither to idolatry nor to bloodshed. We may not, I think, believe that the apostles fell away from this determination of their own; or, if some can believe it, they will have to prove it.

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 1003A]

We are, to be sure, well acquainted with their suspicions here too. For they actually suppose that the apostle Paul, in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians (2 Cor. 2:5–11), granted pardon to the same fornicator whom in the First Epistle he pronounced must be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh (1 Cor. 5:3 ff.), the impious man who had inherited his father’s marriage-bed;

> **Note [Col. 1003D].** “Granted pardon to the same fornicator,” etc. You will observe, of course, that in 1 Corinthians 5 the man who had polluted himself with incest is called a fornicator. Hence Tertullian afterward calls him a defiler of his father’s bed, and thus uses “fornication” and “incest” indiscriminately. —LE PR.

and they suppose that he afterward reversed his very pen, writing:

> “But if anyone has caused sorrow, he has not caused sorrow to me, but in part—lest I burden all of you. For such a person this rebuke inflicted by many is sufficient; so that, on the contrary, you ought rather to forgive and encourage him, lest such a person perhaps be swallowed up by more abundant sorrow. Therefore I ask you to confirm your love toward him. For this purpose I also wrote, that I might know the proof of you, whether you obey me in everything. But if you forgive anyone, I also forgive him. For if I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven it in the person of Christ, lest we be defrauded by Satan, since we are not ignorant of his devices” (2 Cor. 2:5–11).

> **Note [Col. 1003D].** *Quasive* in Rhenanus and Oberthür; *quasi vel* in Leopold.

What here is understood concerning the fornicator, the defiler of his father’s bed, the Christian who surpassed the shamelessness of the Gentiles, when surely Paul would have absolved by a specific pardon the man whom he had condemned in a specific wrath?

> **Note [Col. 1003D].** “The shameless Gentile,” Paris.

He shows mercy more obscurely than he expresses indignation; he is clearer in severity than in leniency. Yet anger more readily takes an indirect course than indulgence does; sorrowful matters are kept waiting more often than joyful ones. It was, of course, a matter of some slight indulgence! If it were being considered now, when even the greatest concessions are not usually granted without public declaration, still less would it be granted without any indication.

You, at any rate, when bringing the adulterer’s repentance into the church in order to entreat the brotherhood, prostrate him in the midst, before the widows and the presbyters, clothed in sackcloth and covered with ashes, arranged as a spectacle of disgrace and horror, clutching at everyone’s garments, licking everyone’s footprints, clasping everyone’s knees.

> **Note [Col. 1003D].** “Clothed in sackcloth and covered with ashes.” In the penitents’ squalor of sackcloth and ashes. —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 1003D].** “Prostrating,” in Pamelius, Oberthür, and Semler.

And for the sake of that man’s final fate, with every enticement to mercy that you can muster, you deliver your public address, good shepherd and blessed pope; and in the parable of the sheep you seek your goats. You make sure that your sheep does not again leap from the flock—as though from then onward something could be permitted that was not permitted even once—and you fill the rest with fear at the very moment when you grant indulgence.

> **Note [Col. 1003D].** “The blessed pope delivers a public address.” In this very ancient author the title *pope* occurs, and so does “blessed,” as in chapter 30 of *On Prescription*, where he calls Eleutherius blessed; he was also Roman pontiff and martyr. —LE PR.

> **Note [Col. 1004D].** La Cerda deletes “your sheep.”

Yet would the apostle have so carelessly forgiven criminal lust burdened with the further guilt of incest that he did not require from the man even that garb appointed for repentance which you ought to have learned from the apostle himself, nor threaten anything concerning the future, nor address him at all concerning his subsequent conduct?

> **Note [Col. 1003D].** “The garb appointed for repentance.” That is, appointed by the consent of the nations, dedicated, and regarded as most appropriate to the grief of penitents or defendants; or else the garb assigned and bequeathed to the penitent, as though by a sentence expressed in these words: “Whoever, being an adulterer or fornicator, asks that the Church’s peace be restored to him, let him be sentenced, in mourning and squalor, in sackcloth and ashes, to clasp the knees of the brethren.” Otherwise, the reading *legitimum* (“legitimate”), which I see proposed, would not displease me. —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 1004D].** “Legitimate” (*legitimum*) in Leopold, from Wouwer’s manuscript.

Indeed, he even begs them of his own accord to confirm their love toward him, as one offering satisfaction rather than granting forgiveness. And yet I hear of love, not communion. So too he writes to the Thessalonians:

> “But if anyone does not obey our word through this letter, mark that man and do not associate with him, that he may be ashamed; do not regard him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother” (2 Thess. 3:14).

> **Note [Col. 1004D].** “Beyond” (*ultra*) in Oberthür and Semler.

Thus he could have said that only love, and not communion, was granted even to the fornicator. But not even love was granted to the incestuous man, whom he had commanded, of course, to be removed from their midst—and therefore all the more from their affections.

But was Paul afraid that they might be defrauded by Satan through the loss of the very person whom he himself had cast out to Satan? Or that the man whom he had condemned to the destruction of the flesh might be swallowed up by an abundance of grief? At this point they interpret the destruction of the flesh as the work of repentance: the flesh is said to make satisfaction to God by being worn away with fasts, filth, every form of neglect, and deliberate ill-treatment. From this they argue that the fornicator—or rather, that incestuous man—was delivered by the apostle to Satan not for ruin but for correction, as one who would afterward obtain pardon because of the destruction, that is, the affliction, of his flesh, and therefore did obtain it.

Certainly, the same apostle delivered Hymenaeus and Alexander to Satan so that they might be corrected and cease blaspheming, as he writes to his Timothy (1 Tim. 1:20). But he also says that there was given to him a stake, an angel of Satan, to buffet him lest he exalt himself (2 Cor. 12:7).

> **Note [Col. 1004D].** “But he also says that there was given to him a stake, an angel of Satan.” Someone may wonder, not without reason, that Tertullian, after rendering Paul’s *skolops* (σκόλοψ), “thorn,” in Latin as *sudis*, “stake,” immediately inclines toward the opinion of those who suppose that these words signify pain in the ear or the head. —RIG.

If they also bring this forward so that we may understand those delivered by him to Satan as delivered for correction rather than for destruction, what similarity is there between blasphemy and incest, on the one hand, and, on the other, a soul untouched by these things—a soul exalted by nothing other than the highest holiness and complete innocence—which in the apostle was perhaps restrained by blows, through pain in the ear or the head, as they say? Incest and blasphemy, however, deserved to deliver the whole persons themselves into the possession of Satan, not merely to his angel.

There is also a difference in this very point—and indeed it is highly pertinent to this issue—that we read that those men were delivered by the apostle to Satan, whereas an angel of Satan was given to the apostle. Finally, when Paul entreats the Lord, what does he hear?

> “Let my grace be sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9).

Those delivered to Satan cannot hear this.

But if the crime of Hymenaeus and Alexander—namely blasphemy—is unforgivable both in this age and in the age to come, the apostle surely would not, contrary to the Lord’s determination, have delivered to Satan under hope of pardon men who had already sunk from faith into blasphemy.

> **Note [Col. 1005D].** “Contrary to the Lord’s determination.” That is, contrary to the Lord’s sentence and decision. For in Septimius, *determinare* means to judge, pronounce, or define by judgment. —RIG.

Hence he also pronounced them shipwrecked concerning the faith, as no longer possessing the consolation of the Church’s ship; for pardon is denied to those who have crashed from faith into blasphemy. Gentiles and heretics, however, emerge from blasphemy every day.

But even if he said, “I delivered them to Satan so that they might receive the discipline of not blaspheming,” he was speaking about the others, who, through those men’s delivery to Satan—that is, their expulsion from the Church—were to be taught that they must not blaspheme. In the same way, therefore, he delivered the incestuous fornicator to Satan not for correction but for destruction, since by sinning worse than the Gentiles he had already passed over to Satan, so that the others might learn not to fornicate.

Finally, he says “for the destruction of the flesh,” not “for its torment.” He condemns the very substance through which the man had fallen away, which had already perished from that point onward through the loss of baptism:

> **Note [Col. 1005D].** “Through the loss of baptism.” A person is said to have lost baptism when, after the washing, he has fallen into the crime of idolatry, adultery, or murder. Conversely, in canon 38 of the Council of Elvira, one who after receiving baptism has been guilty of none of these crimes is said to “have his washing intact.” —RIG.

> “So that the spirit,” he says, “may be saved in the day of the Lord” (1 Cor. 5:5).

Here too it must be asked whether the spirit of the man himself will be saved. Will a spirit polluted by so great a crime, then, be saved because the flesh has been destroyed, so that it may be saved in punishment? The opposing interpretation, therefore, will assign punishment without the flesh, if we thereby lose the resurrection of the flesh.

> **Note [Col. 1005D].** “The opposing interpretation, therefore, will assign punishment without the flesh; thus we lose the resurrection of the flesh.” There were those who said that Paul’s words, “To deliver him to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord,” were to be understood as follows: the flesh of that criminal whom Paul delivered to Satan perished after being tortured by various torments, so that, having thus been punished in the flesh, his spirit might be saved in the day of the Lord. This interpretation, however, was contrary to that of Septimius, who did not concede that even in this way the spirit would be saved. He therefore says that the opinion opposed to his own assigns to that criminal the punishment of being without flesh—that is, that his flesh would not rise. From this there follows the utterly absurd consequence that there would be no resurrection of that flesh. “Thus,” he says, “we lose the resurrection of the flesh.” I see this reading produced from Ursinus’s manuscripts. Hence it becomes likely that the preceding words too—which otherwise I would certainly suspect had been incorrectly transmitted to us—stand in the same manuscripts just as they are printed here. —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 1005C].** “Interpretation.” Thus Leopold, from Wouwer’s manuscript.

It remains, therefore, that by “spirit” he meant the spirit that belongs to the Church, which must be kept safe—that is, intact—in the day of the Lord from the contagion of impurities by the expulsion of the incestuous fornicator. For he adds:

> “Do you not know that a little leaven makes the whole lump lose its savor?” (1 Cor. 5:6).

And yet incestuous fornication was not a little but a great leaven.

## CHAPTER XIV

Having thus examined these intervening matters, I return to the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, in order to prove that this statement of the apostle too—“For such a man this rebuke inflicted by many is sufficient” (2 Cor. 2:6)—does not apply to the person of the fornicator. For if he had pronounced that the man must be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, he had surely condemned rather than rebuked him. It was therefore another person for whom he wished rebuke to suffice, since the fornicator had received from his sentence not rebuke but condemnation.

I submit this very matter to you for consideration: whether there were not others in the First Epistle who caused the apostle sorrow by behaving disorderly, and who were in turn made sorrowful by him when they received rebuke according to the meaning of the Second Epistle—some one of whom could have obtained pardon in that epistle.

Let us observe, moreover, that the whole First Epistle was written, so to speak, not with ink but with gall: swelling, indignant, disdainful, threatening, reproachful, and directed in each particular matter against certain persons as though they were the contractors responsible for those offenses.

> **Note [Col. 1006D].** “And in each particular matter.” That is, in connection with specific crimes. —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 1006D].** “Against certain persons as though they were the contractors responsible for them.” He calls conspicuous criminals “contractors,” as though they had brazenly purchased the right to commit crimes, with Satan—the great wholesaler and dealer in every form of wickedness—awarding the contract. —RIG.

For schisms, rivalries, dissensions, presumptions, arrogance, and contentions had demanded such treatment: that they should be burdened with reproach, beaten down by correction, have their pride filed away, and be frightened by severity.

And what a goad to humility is reproach!

> **Note [Col. 1006D].** “And what a goad to humility is reproach?” What a goad is humility humbled into reproach? That is, so humbled and abased that it makes his adversaries objects of reproach. —RIG.

> “I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, lest anyone say that I baptized in my own name” (1 Cor. 1:14–15).

> “For I determined to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:2).

> “And I think God has selected us apostles as the last of all, like men condemned to fight beasts, because we have become a spectacle to this world, to angels, and to human beings; and we have become the refuse of this world, the offscouring of all” (1 Cor. 4:9, 13).

> **Note [Col. 1006D].** “Like men condemned to fight beasts.” *Bestiarii* are slaves condemned to the beasts. Gloss: *bestiarius*, *thēriomachos* (θηριομάχος), “beast-fighter.” He uses the same word in chapter 9 of the *Apology*. —LE PR.

And:

> “Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Christ Jesus our Lord?” (1 Cor. 9:1).

Against what sort of haughtiness was he compelled to declare:

> “But to me it is a very small thing that I should be examined by you or by a human day of judgment; for I am not conscious of anything against myself” (1 Cor. 4:3–4);

> **Note [Col. 1006C].** “See from what sort,” La Cerda.

and:

> “No one shall make my glory empty” (1 Cor. 9:15).

> “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6:3).

But how open is the freedom of his rebuke, how exposed the edge of his spiritual sword!
