> “Already you are enriched; already you are satisfied; already you reign” (1 Cor. 4:8).

And:

> “If anyone thinks that he knows, he does not yet know how he ought to know” (1 Cor. 8:2).

Is he not then striking someone in the face as well?

> “For who,” he says, “distinguishes you? And what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

Does he not also strike those others directly in the mouth?

> “But some, in their conscience, still eat it as something sacrificed to an idol. And by thus sinning, striking the weak consciences of the brethren, they will sin against Christ.”

Then he even names names:

> “Or do we not have authority to eat and drink, and to take women about with us, as do the other apostles, the Lord’s brothers, and Cephas?” (1 Cor. 9:4–5).

And:

> “If others share in this authority over you, do not we all the more?” (1 Cor. 9:12).

Likewise he pierces particular individuals with his pen:

> “Therefore let him who thinks that he stands take care lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10:12);

and:

> “If anyone appears contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:16).

With such a concluding clause woven out of a curse—

> “If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be anathema. *Maranatha* (‘Our Lord, come!’)” (1 Cor. 16:22)—

he surely struck someone.

But I shall take my stand especially where the apostle burns most fiercely, where the fornicator himself also caused trouble for others:

> “As though I were not coming to you, some have become puffed up. But I shall come to you soon, if the Lord permits, and I shall learn not the speech of those who are puffed up, but their power. For the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power. And what do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in a spirit of gentleness?” (1 Cor. 4:18–21).

For what lay beneath this?

> “Fornication is actually reported among you, and such fornication as is not found even among the Gentiles: that someone has his father’s wife. And you are puffed up and have not rather mourned, so that the man who committed such a deed might be removed from your midst!” (1 Cor. 5:1–2).

For whom were they to mourn? Surely for one dead. To whom were they to mourn? Surely to the Lord. In what manner was he to be removed from their midst? Surely not by being placed outside the Church; for they would not ask from God something that lay within the presiding officer’s duty. Rather, through death—this death being both common to all and proper to the flesh itself—his very flesh, which was already a corpse, already a sheath wasting away in irrecoverable impurity, ought to be removed more fully from the Church.

> **Note [Col. 1007D].** “How he might be removed,” Pamelius.—“To the Lord, that in what manner,” La Cerda and Leopold.

> **Note [Col. 1007D].** “Placed outside the Church.” This means nothing other than excommunication, or “divine censure,” as the same author says in chapter 39 of the *Apology*: that is, when certain persons, because of their crimes, are wholly forbidden the communion of the brethren. Concerning this censure, in Act III of the Council of Chalcedon, in the council’s letter to Dioscorus, it is written: *keleuei hē theosebeia hymōn tois epitimiois tois ekklēsiastikois chrēsōmetha kat’ autou* (κελεύει ἡ θεοσέβεια ὑμῶν τοῖς ἐπιτιμίοις τοῖς ἐκκλησιαστικοῖς χρησώμεθα κατ’ αὐτοῦ), “Your piety demands that we employ an ecclesiastical penalty against him.” —LE PR.

> **Note [Col. 1007D].** “Of his own flesh, which was already a corpse, already a sheath wasting away in irrecoverable impurity.” He describes the body as though it were the sheath of a most worthless soul, thoroughly polluted by the foul filth of crimes. —RIG.—“Wasting away in irrecoverable impurity.” He calls that impurity irrecoverable from which nothing can be recovered: impurity, namely, curable by no art. Thus below, where he speaks of the curable impurity of leprosy, he uses the terms “recovery” and “restoration.” —RIG.

> **Note [Col. 1007D].** Others read “a captive” (*captivum*).—La Cerda reads “that which was corruptible.”

And therefore, in the manner in which he could meanwhile be removed, Paul judged that such a person must be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh. For the curse followed the flesh that was being cast out to the devil, so that it might be discharged from service under the sacrament of blessing, never to return to the camp of the Church.

We therefore see in this passage the apostle’s severity divided between a certain puffed-up man and a certain incestuous man, armed against the one with a rod and against the other with a sentence: with the rod that he threatened, and the sentence that he executed; the former still flashing, the latter immediately striking like lightning; by the one he rebuked, by the other he condemned.

> **Note [Col. 1007D].** “Which” (*qua*) in Oberthür and Semler.

And it is certain that from that time the man merely rebuked trembled beneath the threat of the rod, whereas the condemned man perished beneath the immediate infliction of punishment: the former, fearing the blow, immediately withdrew; the latter paid the penalty.

When the letters of the same apostle to the Corinthians mention pardon a second time, pardon is indeed granted—but it is uncertain to whom, because neither the person nor the cause is specified.

> **Note [Col. 1008D].** “Let it be” (*sit*) in Rigault and Leopold.

I shall compare the matter with the relevant meanings. If the incestuous man is put forward, the puffed-up man will also be found there. Certainly the account of the matter is sufficient: the puffed-up man was rebuked, whereas the incestuous man was condemned. The puffed-up man is forgiven, but as one rebuked; the incestuous man does not appear to have been forgiven, since he was condemned.

> **Note [Col. 1008D].** “The reasoning of the matter,” Pamelius; “relation,” Gelenius.

If pardon was granted to the man whose being swallowed up by excessive sorrow was feared, it was the man merely rebuked who was still in danger of being swallowed up, failing beneath the threat and grieving beneath the rebuke. But the condemned man, condemned by both guilt and sentence, was already reckoned as swallowed up; he was no longer to grieve, but to suffer what he could have grieved over before suffering it.

> **Note [Col. 1008D].** “By grief,” Gelenius.

If he was forgiven so that “we might not be defrauded by Satan,” the loss being guarded against was surely in something that had not yet perished. No precaution is taken concerning what is already past, but concerning what is still safe. The condemned man, however—delivered, indeed, into Satan’s possession—had already then perished from the Church when he committed such a deed, much more when he was also cast out by the Church herself. How could Paul fear suffering the loss of one whom he had already lost after he had been seized away, and whom, once condemned, he could no longer possess?

Finally, what will it be fitting for a judge to pardon: that which he has settled by final pronouncement, or that which he has left pending by an interlocutory ruling? And this is especially true of a judge who is not accustomed to rebuild what he has destroyed, lest he be regarded as a transgressor.

Come now: even if the First Epistle had not saddened so many persons; if it had rebuked no one and terrified no one; if it had struck only the incestuous man; if it had cast no one else into fear on account of his case and had not thrown the puffed-up man into consternation—would you not more reasonably suspect, and more faithfully argue, that there was at that time some entirely different person among the Corinthians involved in the same affair, so that, having been rebuked, terrified, and now wounded by grief, he afterward received pardon because the limited measure of his offense permitted it, rather than interpret that pardon as referring to the incestuous fornicator?

You ought to have read this—even if not in the epistle itself, at least in the apostle’s own character—impressed more clearly by his sense of shame than by his pen.

> **Note [Col. 1008D].** “In the apostle’s own character.” He has used *secta* for “conduct.” Thus Justinian, near the end of the title *On Legacies*, where he treats disgraceful legacies, says: “The character of my times does not permit testamentary dispositions of this kind to stand.” Thus by “the apostle’s character” he means what he shortly afterward calls the apostle’s nature and purpose, the form and rule of his teachings. So above: “from the pattern of Peter.” —RIG.

Otherwise you would stain Paul, the apostle of Christ, teacher of the nations in faith and truth, vessel of election, founder of churches, censor of disciplines, with such fickleness that either he rashly condemned one whom he was soon to absolve, or rashly absolved one whom he had not rashly condemned—even if it had been merely for the fornication of ordinary unchastity, much more for incestuous marriage, impious lust, and parricidal desire. He does not even compare that desire with the nations, lest it be attributed to customary practice; he had judged it while absent, lest the defendant gain an interval of delay; and he had condemned it after invoking even the power of the Lord, lest it appear to be a human sentence.

He therefore made sport of his own spirit, of the angel of the Church, and of the power of the Lord if he rescinded what he had pronounced in accordance with their counsel.

> **Note [Col. 1009D].** “Of the angel of the Church.” As though an angel presided over the congregations of the Church—unless one prefers to refer it to the bishop of Corinth, using the same phrase in which the blessed apostle John writes to the angels of the seven churches in Revelation 2 and 3. —PAM.

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 1009B]

Even if you take the following passages of that epistle as extending the apostle’s denunciation, they too will not be reconcilable with the erasure of the incest, lest here also the apostle be put to shame by the inconsistency of his later sentiments.

For what sense would it make that, immediately after granting an incestuous fornicator the right of return to ecclesiastical peace, he should at once press upon them the rejection of impurities, the cutting away of stains, and the encouragement of holiness, as though he had decreed nothing contrary to these principles shortly before?

Consider, finally, whether it belongs to the same man to say:

> “Therefore, having this ministry according as we have obtained mercy, we do not lose heart, but renounce the hidden things of disgrace” (2 Cor. 4:1–2),

when he had revoked the condemnation of a deed that was not merely disgraceful but openly criminal;

> **Note [Col. 1009D].** “Had condemned beforehand,” La Cerda.

> **Note [Col. 1010D].** “Had revoked the condemnation” (*dedamnaverit*): had rescinded the sentence of condemnation. Below he will say “had restored,” that is, had reincorporated the man into the Church. —RIG.

whether it belongs to the same man to excuse any act of unchastity when, among the titles of his labors, after distress and oppression, after fasts and vigils, he also proclaimed chastity (2 Cor. 6:5 ff.);

> **Note [Col. 1009D].** The word “is” (*sit*) is absent from the Paris edition.

whether it belongs to the same man to receive every reprobate into communion when he writes:

> “For what fellowship has righteousness with iniquity? What communion has light with darkness? What concord has Christ with Belial? Or what portion has the faithful with the faithless? Or what agreement has the temple of God with idols?” (2 Cor. 6:14–16).

Will he not consistently have to hear: “And how do you separate the things that you joined above by restoring the incestuous man?” For when that man is reincorporated into the Church, righteousness is joined in fellowship with iniquity, darkness communes with light, Belial accords with Christ, and the faithless shares the sacraments with the faithful. And let the idols look to themselves: the very defiler of God’s temple enters God’s temple.

For here too he says:

> “For you are the temple of the living God; for he says, ‘I shall dwell in you and walk among you, and I shall be their God, and they shall be my people. Therefore depart from their midst, be separate, and do not touch what is unclean’” (2 Cor. 6:16–17).

You unfold this passage too, O Apostle, at the very moment when you yourself extend your hand to so great a whirlpool of impurities; and you add still further:

> “Therefore, beloved, having this promise, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting chastity in the fear of God” (2 Cor. 7:1).

> **Note [Col. 1010D].** “Of faith” in Gelenius.

I ask you: had the man who drives such principles into our minds recalled some fornicator into the Church? Or does he write them precisely so that he may not now appear to you to have recalled one?

These passages ought both to prescribe the interpretation of what precedes and to prejudge what follows. For near the end of the epistle he says:

> “Lest, when I come again, my God humble me, and I mourn many of those who sinned before and did not repent of the impurity, fornication, and vileness that they committed” (2 Cor. 12:21).

He surely does not determine that those whom he was going to find in the Church should be received if they had entered upon repentance, but that they should be shunned and, without doubt, expelled, so that they might forfeit their repentance.

> **Note [Col. 1010D].** “So that they might forfeit their repentance.” Without any hope that the Church would ever be restored to them: such as those tears, fasting from peace, of which he spoke above, which would bring back from the Church’s bosom nothing more than the public disclosure of disgrace. —RIG.

Besides, it is not appropriate to claim that he revealed anything here about communion, since above he had denied communion between light and darkness and fellowship between righteousness and iniquity.

But all these people are ignorant of the apostle when they understand anything contrary to the nature and purpose of the man himself, contrary to the form and rule of his teaching: a teacher, even by his own example, of all holiness; an execrator and purifier of all impurity; and everywhere such a man that one would sooner presume him to have restored the Church to an incestuous man than to some offender whose guilt was more ordinarily human.

> **Note [Col. 1010D].** “To some offender whose guilt was more ordinarily human.” That is, whose sin might appear to have been committed through human frailty. —RIG.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 1010C]

It is therefore necessary that the Apostle still be shown to them—a man whom I shall defend in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians as being such as I have known him in all his letters. In the First Epistle too, the first thing he did was to consecrate the temple of God: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Lord dwells in you?” (I Cor. 3:16). And, to safeguard and purify the temple, he wrote a law for its sacristan: “If anyone defiles the temple of God, God will destroy him; for the temple of God is holy, which you are” (ibid. 17). Come now: whom has he ever restored to God after he was utterly defiled—that is, delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh—when he therefore added beneath it: “Let no one deceive himself” (ibid. 18), that is, let no one presume that one defiled can be restored to God once again? Likewise, when elsewhere—indeed, before all else—he denies that adulterers and fornicators [Col. 1010D], the effeminate, and men who lie with men will obtain the kingdom, he prefaced it with: “Do not [Note: [Col. 1010D] “Nor,” Rhen., Oberth., Leop.] be deceived” [Col. 1011A] (I Cor. 6:9–10), namely, by supposing that they will obtain it. But those from whom the kingdom is taken away are certainly not permitted the life that exists within the kingdom.

He presses the point as well: “And such indeed you were; but you have been washed, but you have been sanctified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (ibid. 11). The more he makes those offenses antecedent to the reception of the washing, the more he establishes them as unpardonable after the washing, since it is not permissible to be washed a second time.

Recognize Paul also in what follows, an immovable pillar of discipline: “Foods are for the belly, and the belly for foods; but God will bring both it and them to an end; the body, however, is not for fornication, but for God” (ibid. 13). “Let us make man,” God says, “in our image and likeness”; and “God made man in the image and likeness of God he made him” (Gen. 1:26–27). “The Lord is for the body” (I Cor. 6:13); for “the Word became [Col. 1011B] flesh” (John 1:14). “But God both raised the Lord and will raise us through his power” (I Cor. 6:14), namely because of the body’s union with him. And therefore: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” (ibid. 15), because Christ also is God’s temple: “Destroy this temple, and I will raise it up in three days” (John 2:19). “Shall I take away the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body? ‘For the two,’ it says, ‘will be one flesh.’ But he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit. Flee fornication” (I Cor. 6:15–18).

If it can be revoked by pardon, why should I flee it, since I may become an adulterer again? I shall have gained nothing if I flee it; I shall become one body with the person to whom I shall be joined through intercourse. “Every offense that a man commits is outside the body; but he who fornicates sins against his own body” (ibid. [Col. 1011C] 18). And lest you seize upon this saying as a license for fornication, as though you would sin against something that is your own rather than the Lord’s, he takes you away from yourself and attaches you to Christ, just as he had determined: “And you are not your own,” immediately adding: “For you were bought with a price,” namely, the Lord’s blood; “glorify and bear the Lord in your body” (ibid. 19–20).

Consider whether the man who commands this has pardoned one who dishonored the Lord and cast him out of his own body—and by incest, at that. If you wish to drink in the Apostle’s whole teaching, so as to understand with how mighty an axe of judgment he cuts down, uproots, and clears away the entire forest of lusts, permitting nothing from the fallen stock [Note: [Col. 1011D] “Remaining stock,” Obert., Seml.] to sprout, behold him desiring souls to fast even from the lawful fruit of nature—I mean the fruit of marriage. “Now concerning the matters about which you wrote: it is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of fornication, [Col. 1011D] let each man have his own wife; let the husband render what is due to his wife, and the wife to her husband” (I Cor. 7:1 ff.).

Who does not know that he reluctantly loosened the clasp of this “good,” in order to forestall fornication? If he has granted, or does grant, indulgence to anyone for fornication, he has certainly undermined the purpose of his remedy; and henceforth he will be held responsible for bridling marriages with continence, if fornication—the reason for which they are permitted—is not to be feared; for what is pardoned will not be [Col. 1012A] feared. And yet he declares that he has granted the use of marriage as an indulgence, not commanded it, for he wishes everyone to cleave to himself (ibid. 7). If even lawful things are granted as indulgences, who can hope that unlawful ones will be?

To the unmarried and widows also he says that it is good to persevere after his example; but if they should fail, they should marry, because it is better [Note: [Col. 1011D] “It is preferable,” Lat.] to marry than to burn (ibid. 8–9). With which fires, I ask, is it worse to burn: those of desire, or those of punishment? Yet if fornication possesses pardon, its desire does not burn; but it is more characteristic of the Apostle to provide against the fires of punishment. But if it is punishment that burns, then fornication has no pardon, since punishment awaits it.

Meanwhile, in prohibiting divorce, he provides instead either perseverance in widowhood or the reconciliation of peace, according to the Lord’s command against adultery, because “he who dismisses his wife except on account of adultery causes [Col. 1012B] her to commit adultery; and he who marries a woman dismissed by her husband commits adultery” (Matt. 5:32). How many remedies the Holy Spirit institutes to prevent the renewed commission of that which he does not will to be pardoned anew!

Again, if he says everywhere that it is best for a man to remain as he is: “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release,” lest you give adultery a place. “Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife,” so that you may preserve your opportunity. “But even if you marry a wife, you do not sin; and if a virgin marries, she does not sin; nevertheless, such persons will have affliction of the flesh” (I Cor. 7:26–28). Here too he permits by way of forbearance. Moreover, he establishes that “the time has been shortened,” so that “those who have wives should be as though they had none” (ibid. 29); for “the fashion of this world is passing away” (ibid. 31), since it now no longer demands: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1:28).

Thus he wishes us to live free of anxiety, because the unmarried [Col. 1012C] care for the things of the Lord, how they may please God, while the married think about the things of the world, how they may please a spouse (I Cor. 7:32–34). Thus he declares that the man who preserves his virgin does better than the man who gives her in marriage (ibid. 40); thus too he judges happier the woman who, after losing her husband and entering the faith, [Note: [Col. 1011D] “Entering the faith.” Tertullian adopts Montanist views, thus condemning the marriage of a woman who became a widow after entering the faith. That this is the author’s meaning is clear from the books *On the Exhortation to Chastity* and *On Monogamy*. EDD., from PAM.] has cherished the opportunity of widowhood; thus [Note: [Col. 1012D] “If,” Oberth., Seml.] he commends all these counsels of continence as divine: “I think,” he says, “that I too have the Spirit of God” (ibid.).

Who is this most audacious champion of all immodesty, this altogether faithful advocate of adulterers, fornicators, and the incestuous, who has undertaken this case against the Holy Spirit in order to honor them, so that he may recite false testimony concerning his Apostle? Paul granted no such indulgence, for he strives to erase the whole necessity of the flesh even under honorable titles. He grants indulgence, certainly, not to adulteries but to marriages; [Col. 1012D] he spares, certainly, matrimony, not debauchery; he attempts not even to pardon nature, lest he flatter guilt; he labors to restrain the intercourse of blessing, lest the intercourse of curse be excused. This alone remained for him: to purify the flesh at least from filth, for from stains he cannot purify it.

But this is the usual practice of the perverse, the ignorant, and heretics—and now of all the *psychici* as well—to seize upon the occasion of some ambiguous chapter and arm themselves against [Col. 1013A] an army of pronouncements drawn from the entire body of Scripture.

## CHAPTER XVII

Summon him to the apostolic battle-line; examine his Epistles. All of them take the field for modesty, chastity, and holiness; all hurl their weapons against the business of luxury, wantonness, and lust. What, finally, does he write to the Thessalonians? “For our exhortation was not from deceit, nor from uncleanness” (I Thess. 2:3); and: “This is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication; that each one know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the lust of desire, like the nations that do not know God” (I Thess. 4:3–5).

What do the Galatians read? “The works of the flesh are manifest.” [Col. 1013B] What are they? [Note: [Col. 1013D] He placed fornication first. Here he weighs the gravity of fornication and proves it to be the greatest offense from the Apostle. By this testimony, certainly, those are convicted who exempt it from sin in order to indulge their disease and vice. Given any opportunity, he attempts to prove this with a manifold and windy circumlocution—not only laymen, but even bishops, though it is shameful to say so. Modesty bids that no one be identified here. LE PR.] “First of all,” he placed fornication, uncleanness, and wantonness, “of which I forewarn you, as I forewarned you before, that those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God as an inheritance” (Gal. 5:19).

What, moreover, do the Romans learn more emphatically than not to abandon the Lord after faith? “What, then, shall we say? Shall we persevere [Note: [Col. 1013D] “Shall we endure,” Gelen.] in transgression, so that grace may abound? Far be it! We who have died to transgression, how shall we still live in it? Or do you not know that those of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ rose from the dead, we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been buried with [Note: [Col. 1013D] “United with,” Rhen., Oberth., Leop.] the likeness of his death, we shall also share in his resurrection, knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him. But if we have died with [Col. 1013C] Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him, knowing that Christ, raised from the dead, no longer dies; death no longer has dominion over him. For in that he died to transgression, he died once; but in that he lives, he lives to God. So also reckon yourselves dead indeed to transgression, but alive to God through Christ Jesus” (Rom. 6:1–11).

Therefore, since Christ died once, no one who has died [Note: [Col. 1014D] “After” absent from Seml.] after Christ to transgression—and especially to so grave a transgression—can come to life again in it; or, if fornication and adultery can be committed anew, Christ too will be able to die anew.

The Apostle presses on, forbidding transgression to reign in our mortal body (ibid. 12), whose weakness of flesh he knew. “For just as you presented your members as servants to uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so now present them as servants to righteousness unto [Col. 1013D] sanctification” (ibid. 13). For although he denied that good dwelt in his flesh (Rom. 7:18), that was according to the law of the letter under which he had been; according to the law of the Spirit, however, to which he attaches us, he liberates us from the weakness of the flesh: “For the law,” he says, “of the Spirit of life has set you free from the [Col. 1014A] law of transgression and death” (Rom. 8:2).

Although he may seem in part to be arguing from Judaism, he nevertheless directs toward us the integrity and fullness of the disciplines, for our sake who were laboring under the law through the flesh: God sent his Son in the likeness of the flesh of transgression, and on account of transgression condemned transgression in the flesh; “so that,” he says, “the right requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. For those who walk according to the flesh mind the things of the flesh; and those who walk according to the Spirit, the things of the Spirit” (ibid. 3–5).

Moreover, he affirmed that the mind of the flesh is death (ibid. 6). Then he called it enmity even toward God, and said that those who are in the flesh—that is, in the mind of the flesh—cannot please God (ibid. 7). And: “If you live according to the flesh,” he says, “you are going to die” [Col. 1014B] (ibid. 13). What do we understand by the mind of the flesh and the life of the flesh, if not whatever it is shameful to pronounce? For the Apostle would have named the other things of the flesh.

Likewise, when reminding the Ephesians of their former state, he admonishes them concerning the future: “Among whom we too once conducted ourselves, carrying out the desires and pleasures of the flesh” (Eph. 2:3). Finally, censuring those who had denied what they were—Christians, that is—because they had delivered themselves over to the practice of every uncleanness, he says: “But you did not so learn Christ” (Eph. 4:20). And again he says: “Let him who used to steal steal no longer” (ibid. 26–28). So too, let him who used to commit adultery commit adultery no longer; and let him who used to fornicate fornicate no longer. He would have added these also if he had been accustomed to extend pardon to such persons, or had wished it to be extended at all—he who, unwilling to be defiled even by a word, says: “Let no [Col. 1014C] foul speech proceed from your mouth” (ibid. 29).

Likewise: “But let fornication and all uncleanness not even be named among you, as becomes saints”—so far is it from being excused—“knowing this, that no fornicator or unclean person has the kingdom of God. Let no one deceive you with empty words. Because of this the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief” (Eph. 5:3–5). Who deceives with empty words, if not one who publicly preaches that adultery is pardonable? He does not see that the Apostle has even dug away its foundations by restraining drunkenness and revelry, as here too: “And do not become drunk with wine, wherein is debauchery” (ibid. 18).

He also shows the Colossians which members they are to mortify upon earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and foul speech (Col. 3:5). Now set against so many and such great pronouncements that single passage to which you cling: [Col. 1014D] [Note: [Col. 1014D] “The few are overshadowed by the many, the doubtful by the certain, the obscure by the manifest.” They are darkened and hidden, so that the few, compared with the many; the doubtful, compared with the certain; and the obscure, compared with the manifest, are no longer visible at all. LE PR.] “The few are overshadowed by the many, the doubtful by the certain, the obscure by the manifest.” Even if it were certain that the Apostle had granted fornication to that Corinthian, it would be another case in which, for reasons belonging to the time, he once acted against his own rule [Col. 1015A] [Note: [Col. 1015D] “For reasons belonging to the time,” etc. He wrongly asserts that, if we admit pardon was granted to the Corinthian, it was done for reasons belonging to the time, as was Timothy’s circumcision; for the two matters have nothing in common. PAM.]. He circumcised Timothy alone, and yet abolished circumcision.

## CHAPTER XVIII

“But these things,” he says, “will pertain to the prohibition of all immodesty [Note: [Col. 1015D] “And the adjudication of all modesty.” A praetor *addicit*—“adjudicates”—when he orders that something belong to someone as his property. RIG.] and to the adjudication of all modesty, while nevertheless leaving room for pardon. Pardon is not immediately denied if offenses are condemned, since the time for pardon may coincide with the condemnation that excludes it.”

It followed that the *psychici* would think this too; and therefore we have reserved for this place those testimonies that even from antiquity were directed expressly toward denying ecclesiastical communion in cases of this kind. For Solomon too, in the Proverbs, which we call *Paroemiae*, speaks specifically of an adulterer who can nowhere be expiated: “But the adulterer,” he says, “through deficiency of understanding acquires the destruction of his soul; [Col. 1015B] he sustains pains and dishonors. His disgrace will not be abolished forever. For indignation full of jealousy will not spare a man on the day of judgment” (Prov. 6:32–36).

If you suppose this was said of a pagan, you have certainly already heard with regard to the faithful, [Note: [Col. 1015D] “In vain.” Latinius conjectures “through Isaiah,” very plausibly, unless the reading “in vain” is confirmed by the authority of ancient manuscripts, so that it means “vainly, fruitlessly.” RIG.] in vain [Note: [Col. 1015C] “Through Isaiah,” Lat., Leop.; “through the cause,” Oberth., Seml.]: “Depart from their midst and be separated, and do not touch what is unclean” (II Cor. 6:17).

You immediately have in the Psalms the blessed man who has not gone into the council of the ungodly, has not stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the seat of pestilence (Ps. 1:1). His voice afterward is also: “I have not sat with the assembly of vanity, and I will not enter with those who act wickedly” [Note: [Col. 1015D] “This concerns the church of evildoers.” He twists the cited words of the Psalm against his own *psychici*. Under this guise he cloaked his secession from the Church. RIG.]—this concerns the church of evildoers—“and I will not sit with the ungodly”; and, “I will wash my hands with the innocent and encircle your altar, Lord” (Ps. 30:4–5), [Note: [Col. 1015D] “So that he alone might be many.” Once again he lashes the Catholics [Col. 1016D] and consoles himself for his schism, as though, surrounded by his own innocence, he alone were in God’s sight the equivalent of many. In this sense he said elsewhere, more than once, that the Church exists in one or two persons. Thus, although accompanied by few, or even alone, he would nevertheless encircle the Lord’s altar as much as if there were many. So too, in Theodoret, Liberius, Bishop of Rome, says in his dispute with the emperor Constantius: οὐ διὰ τὸ εἶναί με μόνον ὁ τῆς πίστεως ἐλαττοῦται λόγος, “The cause of the faith is not diminished because I am alone.” RIG.] so that he alone might be many [Note: [Col. 1015C] “And several similar,” Jun.; namely, “sayings,” Leop.], since “with the holy you will be holy [Col. 1015C], and with the elect you will be elect, and with the perverse you will be perverse” (Ps. 17:26).

And elsewhere: “But to the sinner the Lord says: Why do you expound my statutes and take up my covenant in your mouth? If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and with adulterers you placed your portion” (Ps. 49:16 ff.).

Instructed by this, therefore, the Apostle too says: “I wrote to you in the Epistle not to associate with fornicators—not, certainly, with the fornicators of this world,” and the rest: “otherwise you would have had to leave the world. But now I write to you: if anyone among you is named a brother and is a fornicator, or an idolater” [Col. 1016A]—for what is so closely joined?—“or a defrauder”—for what is so nearly related?—and the rest, “with such persons not even to take food,” much less the Eucharist. A little [Note: [Col. 1015D] “The medicinal Eucharist, namely,” Fran.] leaven, certainly, ruins the taste of the whole lump (I Cor. 5:9 ff.).

Likewise, to Timothy: “Lay hands hastily on no one, nor share in the offenses of others” (I Tim. 5:22). Likewise, to the Ephesians: “Therefore do not become their partners; for you were once darkness” (Eph. 5:7–8). And more insistently still: “Do not share in the fruitless works of darkness; rather, even convict them, since the things done by them in secret are shameful even to declare” (ibid. 11). What is more shameful than acts of immodesty?

Moreover, if he commands the Thessalonians to withdraw even from a brother who walks idly (II Thess. 3:6), how much more from a fornicator? For these are the carefully considered provisions [Note: [Col. 1015D] “Counsels,” Obert., Leop.] of Christ, who loves the Church [Col. 1016B] and delivered himself for her, that he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word, that he might present to himself a glorious Church, having neither spot nor wrinkle—certainly, after the washing—but holy and without reproach (Eph. 5:25–27): thereafter, namely, [Note: [Col. 1016D] “Without the wrinkle of old age.” This too is directed against the Catholics, who opposed their own antiquity to the novelty of Montanus, as we observed above. Septimius therefore acknowledges that they were earlier and more ancient, but reproaches them with the wrinkles of old age. RIG.] without the wrinkle of old age [Note: [Col. 1015D] “Vanity,” Lat.; “truth,” Fran.], as a virgin; without the stain of fornication, as a bride; without the disgrace of vileness, as one cleansed.

What [Note: [Col. 1015D] “But,” Ven.] if you should undertake to answer here too that communion is indeed taken away from sinners—especially those polluted in the flesh—but is presently to be restored, namely, on the ground of repentance, in accordance with that mercy of God by which he prefers the sinner’s repentance to his death (Ezek. 33:11)? For this foundation of your opinion must be battered down everywhere.

We therefore say: if it had accorded with divine mercy that a manifestation [Note: [Col. 1016C] Thus Lat. emends the text: “if it had thus been fitting for restoration to be granted even to his own.”] of itself should be granted even to those who have fallen after faith [Col. 1016C], then [Note: [Col. 1016D] “Or,” Lat.] the Apostle would have said: “Do not share in the works of darkness, unless they have repented”; and, “With such persons do not even take food, unless they have first wiped clean the sandals of the brethren by rolling at their feet”; and, “He who defiles the temple of God, God will destroy, unless he has shaken from his head in the Church the ashes of every hearth.” For he ought similarly to have qualified what he had condemned, since [Note: [Col. 1016D] “Where,” Oberth., Seml., Leop.] he would have condemned it only [Note: [Col. 1016D] “Only” absent from Ven.] conditionally, if he had condemned it with temporal and conditional, rather than perpetual, severity.

But since in all his Epistles he forbids the admission [Col. 1017A] of such a person after faith and drives one already admitted away from communion, without hope of any condition or term, he supports our position more strongly, showing that the repentance the Lord prefers to the sinner’s death is that which occurs before faith and before baptism—the sinner being washed only once through the grace of Christ, who died once for our sins.

For the Apostle establishes this even in his own person. When he affirms that Christ came for this purpose, to save sinners, of whom he himself had been the first, what does he add? “And I obtained mercy because, being ignorant, I acted in unbelief” (I Tim. 1:16). Thus that mercy of God which prefers the sinner’s repentance to his death concerns those who are still ignorant and still unbelieving, for whose deliverance Christ came—not those who have already known God and [Col. 1017B] learned the sacrament of faith.

But if God’s mercy applies to those still ignorant and unbelieving, then repentance too invites mercy to itself—while preserving that form of repentance after faith which, for lighter offenses, may obtain pardon from the bishop, but for greater and unpardonable offenses from God alone.

## CHAPTER XIX

But how long shall we speak of Paul, when even John seems somehow to applaud the opposing side? It is alleged that in the Apocalypse he manifestly assigned the aid of repentance to fornication, where the Spirit commands the angel of the Thyatirans that he has this against him: that he tolerates the woman [Note: [Col. 1017C] “The woman Jezebel,” Paris.] Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess and teaches and seduces my servants to fornicate and to eat things sacrificed to idols. “And I granted her a space of time [Col. 1017C] to enter upon repentance, but she does not wish to enter upon it” concerning fornication. “Behold, I shall cast her onto a bed, and her adulterers with her into the greatest affliction, unless they repent of her works” (Apoc. 2:20–22).

It is well, however, that this accords with the Apostles and the rules both of faith and discipline. “For whether I,” he says, “or they, so we preach” (II Cor. 15:11). The whole sacrament, therefore, depends upon believing that John granted nothing Paul denied. Whoever observes this equality of the Holy Spirit will be led by the Spirit himself into John’s meanings.

For he was introducing covertly into the Church a heretical woman who had undertaken to teach what she had learned from the Nicolaitans, and was covertly introducing her into [Col. 1018A] the Church; with good reason he urged her to repentance. For who doubts that a heretic deceived by instruction, who afterward recognizes his fall and expiates it by repentance, both obtains pardon and [Note: [Col. 1017D] “Is restored to the Church.” A person is said to be restored to the Church when the Church is restored to him—that is, communion in ecclesiastical peace. RIG.] is restored to the Church?

Hence among us the heretic, being equal to a pagan—indeed, worse than a pagan—is admitted only when [Note: [Col. 1017D] “Through the baptism of truth.” Although he rightly asserts that a heretic deceived by instruction obtains pardon after recognizing his fall and expiating it through repentance, he nevertheless adds “purified through the baptism of truth,” and thus . . . he followed the error of those who thought that heretics coming to the Church had to be baptized. PAM.] purified through the baptism of truth from both persons [Note: [Col. 1017D] “Purified from both persons.” For pagans baptized by heretics were regarded as pagans—that is, as something worse than pagans because of the heretics. Therefore, if they asked to be received into the orthodox Church, they were baptized anew, so that they might be purified from both persons: the former pagan and the superimposed heretic. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1017C] “Name,” Jun., Lat.].

Or, if you are certain that this woman, after living in the faith, afterward lapsed into heresy, so that you may claim pardon through repentance for her not as a heretic but as a faithful woman who sinned [Note: [Col. 1017D] “He may claim,” Seml., Oberth.], then [Note: [Col. 1017D] “Let her indeed repent, but so as to bring her adultery to an end.” Let her repent in such a way that she ceases from adultery; for, as he said above, cessation of the offense is the root of pardon. Septimius, however, says that pardon for this offense must be hoped for from God, not from the Church, just as with idolatry and murder. He maintains this so rigorously that, once that adulterer has been cast outside the Church, the other faithful may receive discipline against committing adultery. For thus he interprets the Apostle’s words. RIG.] let her indeed repent, but so as to bring her adultery to an end; she is not, however, to obtain restoration as well. For this will be the repentance that we too acknowledge to be due all the more, though we reserve the matter of pardon to God.

Finally, that same Apocalypse in its later passages [Col. 1018B] decreed that the shameless and fornicators, like the cowardly, unbelieving, murderers, sorcerers, and idolaters—[Note: [Col. 1018D] “Who have been such a thing while in the faith.” That is, those who committed such a sin after baptism. RIG.] those who have been such a thing while in the faith [Note: [Col. 1018C] “Has been,” Fran.]—should enter the lake of fire, without any conditional form of condemnation. For it cannot appear to be speaking about pagans when it has declared concerning the faithful: “Those who overcome will possess these things by inheritance [Note: [Col. 1018D] “This inheritance,” Paris.], and I shall be their God, and they shall be sons to me”; and then added: “But for the cowardly, unbelieving, [Note: [Col. 1018D] “The shameless.” The author uses *propudiosos* to translate the Greek ἐβδελυγμένοις, for which the Vulgate translator has “the accursed”; and he cautiously omitted “sinners and liars,” because not much later he again acknowledges certain pardonable sins, including lying either from embarrassment or necessity. PAM.] shameless, fornicators, murderers, sorcerers, and idolaters, their portion is in the lake of fire and sulfur, which is the second death” (Apoc. 21:7–8).

Likewise again: “Blessed are those who act according to the commandments, so that they may have authority over the tree of life and may enter through the gates into the holy city. Outside are the dog, the sorcerer, the fornicator, and the murderer” (Apoc. 22:14–15)—certainly those who do not act according to the commandments; for it belongs to those who were inside [Col. 1018C] to be cast outside. Moreover, the preceding question was: “What have I to do with judging those who are outside?” (I Cor. 5:12).

They immediately seize upon John’s Epistle as well. It is said: “The blood of his Son cleanses us from every offense” (I John 1:7). Therefore we shall sin always and in every manner, if he always cleanses us from every offense; or, if not always, then not after faith either; and if not from every offense, then not from fornication either.

But where did he begin? He had previously declared that God is light and that there is no darkness in him, and that we lie if we say we have communion with him while walking in darkness [Col. 1019A]. “But if,” he says, “we walk in the light, we shall have communion with him, and the blood of Jesus Christ our Lord cleanses us from every offense” (ibid. 5 ff.). Do we therefore sin while walking in the light, and shall we be cleansed while sinning in the light? By no means. For he who sins is not in the light but in darkness.

Hence he also shows how we shall be cleansed from offense while walking in the light, in which an offense cannot be committed: so clearly does he say that we are cleansed, not insofar as we sin, but insofar as we do not sin. For while walking in the light and not sharing in darkness, we shall live as persons cleansed—not by laying aside an offense, but by not admitting one. For this is the power of the Lord’s blood: after it has cleansed people from offense and thereafter established them in the light, it thereafter keeps them clean, provided that they persevere in walking in the light.

“But he adds,” you say [Col. 1019B]: “If we say that we have no offense, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our offenses, he is faithful and just to forgive them to us and to cleanse us from every unrighteousness” (ibid. 8–9). Does he say “from uncleanness”? Or if so, then also from idolatry. But the meaning is otherwise.

For behold, once again: “If we say,” he says, “that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us” (ibid. 10). More emphatically still: “Little children, I have written these things to you so that you may not sin; and if you do sin, we have as advocate before God the Father Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for our offenses” (I John 2:1–2).

“According to these words,” you say, “it will be established both that we sin and that we possess pardon.” What, then, will happen when, as I proceed, I find something different? For he denies that we sin at all and treats this point at great [Col. 1019C] length, so as to grant nothing of the kind. He sets forth that offenses were erased once by Christ and would have no pardon afterward; in this [Note: [Col. 1019D] “Which,” Seml., Oberth.] sense he entrusts us to the admonition of chastity:

“Everyone,” he says, “who has this hope purifies himself, because he too is pure. Everyone who commits an offense also commits iniquity, and offense is iniquity. And you know that he was manifested in order to take away offenses”—those, certainly, which were committed up to that point, since he adds: “Everyone who remains in him does not sin; everyone who sins has neither seen nor known him. Little children, let no one deceive you. Everyone who practices righteousness is righteous, just as he is righteous. He who commits an offense is from the devil, because the devil sins from the beginning. For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might dissolve the works of the devil.”

And indeed he dissolved them, liberating man through the washing and canceling [Col. 1019D] the written bond of death. “And therefore everyone who is born of God does not commit an offense, because the seed of God remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he has been born of God. In this the sons of God and the sons of the devil are manifest” (I John 3:3–10). In what respect, unless the former do not sin from the time they were born of God, while the latter sin because they are from the devil, just as though they had never been born of God?

[Col. 1020A] But if he says, “He who is not righteous is not from God,” and likewise he who is not chaste, how will one who has ceased to be from God become so again? It follows, therefore, that we must say John contradicted himself: in the first chapter of his Epistle (1:8), indeed, denying that we are without offense, but now laying down the rule that we are not to sin at all; and there, indeed, soothing us with one statement concerning pardon, but here strictly denying that those who have sinned are sons of God.

Far be it! For neither have we ourselves fallen away from the distinction between offenses from which we digressed. Here too John commended that distinction: there are certain offenses of daily incursion to which we are all exposed. For to whom does it not happen either to become unjustly angry, and beyond sunset; or even to strike someone; or readily to curse; or to swear rashly; or to break the faith of an agreement; or to lie from embarrassment or necessity? [Col. 1020B] [Note: [Col. 1019D] “In business, in duties, in trade.” From this it is clear that even those early Christians were human beings—namely, liable to these more human failings. RIG.] In business, in duties, in trade, in food, in sight, and in hearing, how greatly are we tempted, so that if there were no pardon for these things, salvation would belong to no one! For these, therefore, there will be pardon through Christ, the Father’s intercessor.

But there are also offenses opposed to these, as being more serious and deadly, which cannot receive pardon: murder, idolatry, fraud, denial, blasphemy, and certainly adultery and fornication, as well as any other violation of God’s temple. [Note: [Col. 1019D] “For these Christ will no longer be an intercessor.” Augustine’s opinion was more humane, in the book *On Faith and Works* [Col. 1020D]: “But those who suppose,” he says, and so forth, “make compensation by alms” [the reading is uncertain]; nevertheless, they should not doubt that three sins are mortal and require excommunication until they are healed by a humbler repentance: immodesty, idolatry, and murder. RIG.] For these Christ will no longer be an intercessor. One who has been born of God will not commit them at all, since he will cease to be a son of God if he commits them.

Thus John’s account of the difference will remain coherent, as he establishes [Note: [Col. 1019D] “John . . . establishing,” Wouw.’s manuscript.] the distinction between offenses, at one moment affirming and at another denying that the sons of God sin. For he was looking ahead [Col. 1020C] to the conclusion of his letter and preparing these meanings for it, since at the end he was to say more explicitly:

“If anyone knows that his brother is committing an offense not unto death, he shall ask, and the Lord will give life to him who sins not unto death. There is an offense unto death; I do not say that anyone should ask concerning it” (I John 5:16).

He himself also remembered that Jeremiah had been forbidden by God to intercede for a people committing mortal offenses (Jer. 7:16; 11:14; 14:11). “Every unrighteousness is an offense, and there is an offense unto death. But we know that everyone who is born of God does not sin” (I John 5:17–18)—that is, does not commit the offense that is unto death.

Thus nothing now remains except either to deny that adultery and fornication are mortal offenses, or to confess that they are unpardonable, since it is not permitted even to pray for them.

## CHAPTER XX

[Col. 1020D]

The discipline of the Apostles, therefore, properly instructs and determines, as its chief concern, the safeguarding of all holiness toward the temple of God, and everywhere roots out of the Church every sacrilege against chastity [Note: [Col. 1020D] “Unchastity” in Latinius], without any mention of restoration. [Col. 1021A] Yet, by way of superabundance [Note: [Col. 1021C] “Superfluously” in Latinius], I wish also to add the testimony of one of the Apostles’ companions [Note: [Col. 1021C] “Of one of the Apostles’ companions.” As though Peter and Paul were Apostles so far above the others that the rest should be regarded as their companions and disciples. Thus Barnabas himself, though an Apostle, is called “apostolic” by Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book II, [Col. 1021D] καὶ συνεργὸς τοῦ Παύλου, “and Paul’s fellow-worker”; and in book V, συρκηρύξας τῷ Ἀποστόλῳ, “having preached together with the Apostle.” Jerome too, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, says that the words “Paul, an apostle, not from men nor through a man” may appear to have been spoken indirectly against Peter and the others, because the Gospel was not handed down to Paul by the Apostles, but by Jesus Christ himself, who had also chosen them as Apostles. RIG.], testimony well suited to confirm, by a closely related authority, the discipline of his teachers.

For there is also the title of Barnabas attached to the Epistle to the Hebrews, a man of sufficiently great authority [Note: [Col. 1021C] “For the authority of the man” in François], since Paul placed him beside himself in the observance of abstinence: “Or is it only I and Barnabas who do not have this right not to work?” (1 Cor. 9:6). [Note: [Col. 1022C] “This” is absent from the Paris edition.] And certainly the Epistle of Barnabas is more widely accepted among the churches [Note: [Col. 1021D] “And certainly the Epistle of Barnabas is more widely accepted among the churches.” This opinion of Tertullian concerning the Epistle to the Hebrews is reported by Jerome in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Paul. Jerome himself, however, says under Barnabas that Barnabas wrote an epistle pertaining to the edification of the Church, but that it was reckoned among the apocryphal writings. It is likewise numbered by Eusebius ἐν τοῖς νόθοις, “among the spurious writings.” Yet Clement of Alexandria cites it as the authentic work of Barnabas, and Origen, in book I *Against Celsus*, calls it catholic. We have seen it in Greek, almost complete, in the possession of the most learned Jacques Sirmond, together with an ancient Latin translation. The whole work consists of the same arguments that our Septimius uses in his book *Against the Jews* and in the third book *Against Marcion*. RIG.—Our Hugo Menard, moreover, discovered this epistle among the manuscript codices of the monastery of Corbie and was the first to publish it. EDD.] than that apocryphal *Shepherd* of adulterers. [Note: [Col. 1022D] “That apocryphal *Shepherd* of adulterers.” He calls the psychics adulterers, for they had accepted the book of the *Shepherd*, mentioned above.]

Accordingly, when he warns the disciples to leave behind all elementary matters, to press on instead toward perfection, and not again to lay foundations of repentance from dead works, he says:

> For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, have tasted the heavenly gift, have shared in the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the sweet word of God, if, as the age is now [Col. 1021B] declining, they fall away, to be brought back again to repentance, since they crucify the Son of God afresh in themselves and expose him to disgrace. For land that repeatedly drinks in the moisture falling upon it and produces vegetation suitable for those on whose account it is cultivated receives God’s blessing; but if it produces thorns, it is rejected and near to a curse, and its end is burning. (Heb. 6:4–8)

[Note: [Col. 1022C] “Renewed” in Latinius.]

The man who learned this from the Apostles and taught it together with the Apostles knew that the Apostles had never promised a second repentance to an adulterer and fornicator. [Note: [Col. 1022D] “Never to an adulterer and fornicator,” etc. The Author wrongly interprets the passage just cited (Heb. 6) as referring to a second repentance. Other ancient writers understand it as referring to the repetition of baptism, particularly blessed Ambrose, *On Repentance*, chapter 2, and in his commentary . . . ; and Epiphanius (*Heresies*, 59). Chrysostom, together with the other Greeks who follow him, supports this interpretation when he explains in the same way the passage in Hebrews 10: “After we have received knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains . . .” Certainly the Latin phrases “those who have once been enlightened” and “to be renewed again,” and the Greek words φωτισθέντας ἀνακαινίζειν, “to renew those who have been enlightened,” favor this interpretation, for the ancients regularly use them of the baptized. PAM.] For he interpreted the Law exceedingly well and was already preserving its figures in the reality itself.

Finally, provision was made for this form of discipline in the law concerning the leper:

> But if the discoloration breaks out upon the skin and covers the whole skin from head to foot, as far as the eye can see, and the priest, upon seeing it, pronounces him clean because it has turned white, he is clean. But on whatever day living color is seen in such a condition, he is defiled. (Lev. 13:12–13)

[Col. 1021C] For he intended us to understand that the person who has been changed from the former condition of the flesh into the whiteness of faith—which is regarded as a blemish and stain in the world—and has been wholly renewed is clean, since he is no longer variegated, no longer speckled with a mixture of the old and the new. [Col. 1022A] But if, after its abolition, anything of that former condition comes to life again, and there appears once more in his flesh what had been reckoned dead to sin, he is to be judged unclean and may no longer be purified by the priest. Thus adultery recurring from the former condition and staining the unity of the new color from which it had been excluded is an impurity that cannot be cleansed.

Likewise concerning a house: if stains and hollows in its walls had been reported to the priest, before he entered to inspect it he commands that everything be removed from the house, so that the things belonging to the house will not thereby become unclean. Then, after entering, if the priest found greenish or reddish hollows whose appearance lay beneath the ordinary surface of the wall, [Col. 1022B] he was to go out through the doorway and quarantine that house for seven days. Then, returning on the seventh day, if he observed that the affected area had spread upon the walls, he was to order the stones in which the leprosy had been found to be pulled out and cast outside the city into an unclean place; other stones, polished and solid, were to be taken and put in place of the former ones, and the house was to be coated with fresh plaster (Lev. 14:34–42).

For when we come to Christ, the supreme priest of the Father, all hindrances must first be removed from the house of our human being during the period of the week, so that the house remaining—the flesh and the soul—may be clean. And when the Word of God has entered it and found stains of redness and greenness, the deadly and bloodstained dispositions must immediately be pulled out and cast outside. For the Apocalypse also mounted Death upon a green horse, and a warrior upon a red one (Rev. 6:4, 8). [Col. 1022C] In place of these it lays beneath polished stones, fitted into the structure and strong—stones of the kind from which children of Abraham are made [Note: [Col. 1022D] “Such as are made into Abraham’s.” Either “children” must be understood mentally or the word must be supplied in the text, for he alludes to the saying: “God is able from these stones to raise up children of Abraham” (Matt. 3:9). RIG.]—so that the human being may thus be serviceable to God.

But if, after recovery and reconstruction, [Col. 1023A] [Note: [Col. 1023C] “After recovery and reconstruction.” Thus he uses “recovery” here for healing and cure, just as above he called uncleanness “irrecoverable.” RIG.] the priest again notices in the same house something derived from the former causes [Note: [Col. 1023C] “Hollows” in Latinius] and stains, [Note: [Col. 1023C] “Something derived from the former causes and stains.” Latinius advised that *cavis*, “hollows,” should be written. Not without reason, for above we read “stains and hollows.” Nevertheless, it has seemed best to retain *caussis*, “causes,” because Septimius frequently uses this word to signify corruptions and faults. Thus above, what he had called “causes” he explains as schisms, rivalries, dissensions, presumptions, and so forth. RIG.] he pronounced it unclean and ordered its timbers, stones, and entire structure to be taken down and cast into an unclean place (Lev. 14:43–45).

This will be the human being, flesh and soul, who, after baptism and the entry of the priests, has been reconstructed, but then takes up again the roughness and stains of the flesh and is cast outside the city into an unclean place—delivered, that is, to Satan for the destruction of the flesh (1 Cor. 5:4–5)—and is no longer rebuilt in the Church after his ruin.

So too concerning intercourse with a female slave who had been reserved for a man but had not yet been redeemed or freed: “Provision shall be made for her,” he says, “and she shall not die” (Lev. 19:20), because she who was being reserved for the man had not yet been manumitted. For the flesh, not yet manumitted by Christ, for whom it was being reserved, was defiled with impunity; but once manumitted it no longer has pardon. [Note: [Col. 1023C] “Once manumitted it no longer has pardon.” Yet here too the Author does not rightly conclude that adultery receives no pardon after manumission, because that reserved female slave was betrothed to another man—a circumstance that would not apply if she had merely been manumitted. Thus the passage contributes nothing to the Author’s purpose. PAM.]

## CHAPTER XXI

If the Apostles knew these things better, they certainly took greater care over them. But now I shall descend even to this level, separating [Note: [Col. 1023D] *Excernens*, “separating,” for *discernens*, “distinguishing.” PAM.] the Apostles’ teaching from their power.

Discipline governs the human being; power designates him; power is one thing apart, but the Spirit is God. [Note: [Col. 1023D] “Discipline governs the human being; power designates him; power is one thing apart, but the Spirit is God.” No one will deny that these words are corrupt. Yet who can confidently promise anything certain without the authority of ancient manuscripts? It will nevertheless be of some help to have attempted a provisional restoration. Both sense and wording appear to return if we read: “Discipline governs the human being; power designates him. Apart from that, what is power? The Spirit. And the Spirit? God.” RIG.—Latinius emends this passage as follows: “Power designates; but again, what is power? Spirit. But the Spirit is God” (John 4:24). EDD.—Power designates the human being, identifies him, marks him out as exceptional, χαρακτηρίζει, “characterizes him.” Thus the power given to Peter designates Peter’s person, so that the power pertained to Peter’s person alone. This, indeed, is what Tertullian says. But most, or rather virtually all, of the Fathers thought otherwise. [Col. 1024C] RIG.]

What, then, did he teach? That one must not participate in the works of darkness (Eph. 5:11). Observe what he commands. But who had the power to forgive sins? This belongs to him alone. [Note: [Col. 1024C] “This belongs to him alone”: that is, to God, or to the Spirit. RIG.] “For who forgives sins except God alone?” (Mark 2:7)—and certainly mortal sins committed against him and against his temple. For those that make a person guilty against you, you are commanded, in the person of Peter, to forgive even seventy-seven times [Col. 1024A] (Matt. 18:22).

[Note: [Col. 1024C] “For who forgives sins except God alone?” In the first place, this was not Christ’s assertion but that of the Pharisees (Mark 2:7; Luke 5:21). Next, Christ declares that this power was communicated even to himself as a human being, when he adds: “But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins,” etc. And indeed he communicated the same authority to the Apostles in Matthew 18:18, and especially in John 20:23: “Whose sins you forgive,” he says, “are forgiven them, and whose you retain are retained.” Conquered by this truth, the Author—although he deliberately omits that scriptural passage because it contradicts him—nevertheless cannot deny that the blessed Apostles themselves granted something of this sort . . . But he distorts the matter by adding that they did so not by discipline but by power, although . . . he admits that this power was granted to his own Montanist church. PAM.]

Accordingly, even if it were established that the blessed Apostles themselves granted some such indulgence [Note: [Col. 1023C] “If it had been granted even to the blessed Apostles . . .” in the Paris edition], where pardon was properly God’s to give and not a human being’s, they would have done so not by discipline but by power. For they also raised the dead, something God alone does; they restored the infirm, something no one but Christ does; indeed, they also inflicted plagues, something Christ declined to do. For it was not fitting for him to rage who had come to suffer. Ananias and Elymas were struck down—Ananias with death, Elymas with blindness (Acts 5:5; 13:11)—so that by this very fact it might be proved [Note: [Col. 1024C] “He himself might be proved” in the Paris edition] that Christ could have done these things as well. So too the prophets had forgiven murder and, along with it, adultery to those who repented, because they had also provided demonstrations of severity.

Produce for me, therefore, even now, O apostolic one, prophetic examples, [Note: [Col. 1024D] “Produce for me, therefore, even now, O apostolic one.” He calls him “apostolic” in the same form in which he called him above “the supreme pontiff,” “bishop of bishops,” “the good shepherd,” and “the blessed pope.” RIG.—Since he is undoubtedly speaking of the Roman Pontiff, the Author confirms even from this the authority of the Roman Church, because he calls its head “apostolic,” as the successor of the Apostles, just as he does more explicitly in book IV of his *Poems Against Marcion*, chapter 8. That title has moreover remained in use to the present day. PAM.] and I shall acknowledge your divine character; [Note: [Col. 1024D] “And I shall acknowledge your divine character”: that is, “I shall acknowledge that you have been designated by divine strength and power.” RIG.] claim for yourself the power to forgive sins of this kind. But if you have been allotted only the duties of discipline, not to preside by sovereign command but to serve in ministry, who or how great are you that you should grant indulgence—you who, presenting neither prophet nor Apostle, lack the power to which the granting of indulgence belongs?

“But,” you say, “the Church possesses the power to forgive sin.” I acknowledge and arrange this claim more fully than you do, for I possess the Paraclete himself speaking in the new prophets: “The Church can forgive sin, but I shall not do so, lest others also sin.”

“What if a pseudo-prophetic spirit made that declaration?” [Note: [Col. 1024D] “What if a pseudo-prophetic spirit made that declaration?” [Col. 1025C] These are the words of the catholic, whom he calls a psychic. RIG.] Yet it would have been more characteristic of a subverter both to recommend himself for his clemency and to dispose others toward sinfulness. Or if that spirit also wished to affect such conduct in accordance with the Spirit of truth, then the Spirit of truth is indeed able to grant pardon to fornicators, but is unwilling to do so at the cost of harm to the many.

I now ask, on the basis of your own position, whence you usurp this right for the Church. Is it because the Lord said to Peter, “Upon this rock I shall build my Church; I have given you the keys of the kingdom of heaven,” or, “Whatever you bind or loose on earth will be bound or loosed in heaven” (Matt. 16:18–19)? Do you therefore presume that the power of binding and loosing has been transmitted even to you—that is, to every church akin to Peter, such as yours? [Note: [Col. 1025C] “And that the power of binding and loosing has been transmitted even to you.” Greater trust should be placed in the Author when he was still a catholic than now, when he is a heretic and writes expressly against the Church, especially in this chapter. Therefore, as an antidote, those passages of the Author will suffice in which he admits more than once that the Church was built upon Peter—not merely “in him,” that is, “through him,” as he slanderously claims here—namely, *On the Prescription of Heretics*, chapter 22, and book IV *Against Marcion*; or, even after he had fallen into heresy, *On Monogamy*, chapter 8 . . . And indeed, that statement was not addressed personally to blessed Peter alone, but was also transmitted to his successors and thus to the Roman Church, as may be seen there from the Fathers. PAM.] [Note: [Col. 1025C] “To every church akin to Peter.” That is, one able to trace its origin to Peter. But other churches too, although they can produce no Apostle or apostolic man as their founder, are nevertheless regarded as no less apostolic if they agree in the same faith, by reason of the kinship of their doctrine. So the Author himself says in *On the Prescription of Heretics*. RIG.]

You overturn and alter the Lord’s manifest intention, which conferred this personally upon Peter: “Upon you,” he says, “I shall build my Church”; and, “I shall give you the keys,” not the Church; and, “Whatever you loose or bind,” not “whatever they loose or bind”? [Note: [Col. 1025D] “Altering the Lord’s manifest intention, which conferred this personally upon Peter: ‘Upon you,’ he says, ‘I shall build my Church.’” Septimius does not correctly cite Christ’s words, which occur at Matthew 16:18. Chrysostom’s observations on them, however, are exceedingly wise. RIG.]

For the outcome itself teaches this. The Church was built upon him—that is, through him. [Col. 1025B] He himself first put the key to use. [Note: [Col. 1025D] “He himself first put the key to use.” He was the first to insert the key into the lock; he began to use the key granted by God. So in *On Fasting*: “Where the restoration of the human being could now be inaugurated.” RIG.] See which key: “Men of Israel, commit to your ears what I say: Jesus the Nazarene, a man appointed for you by God” (Acts 2:22), and what follows. He, finally, was the first to unlock through Christ’s baptism the entrance to the heavenly kingdom, by which former sins that were bound are loosed, while those that have not been loosed are bound, according to true salvation. He bound Ananias with the bond of death and released the man disabled in his feet from the defect of his health (Acts 3:7).

So too, in that dispute over whether the Law was to be observed, Peter, inspired by the Spirit, was the first of all to speak in advance concerning the calling of the nations:

> And now, why do you put the Lord to the test by imposing upon the brothers a yoke that neither we nor our fathers were able to bear? But we believe that through the grace of Jesus we shall obtain salvation, just as they will. (Acts 15:10–11)

[Col. 1026A] This judgment both loosed those provisions of the Law that were set aside and bound those that were retained. Thus the power of binding and loosing bestowed upon Peter has no application to the capital sins of believers. For if the Lord had commanded him to forgive even a brother who sinned against him seventy-seven times (Matt. 18:22), he certainly would not afterward have commanded him to bind—that is, to retain—anything, except perhaps those offenses someone committed against the Lord rather than against a brother. For it is established beforehand that sins against God are not to be forgiven, since those committed against a human being are pardoned.

What, then, does this have to do with the Church—and specifically with your church, O psychic? For, in accordance with Peter’s person, this power will belong to spiritual persons [Note: [Col. 1025D] “This power will belong to spiritual persons”: to adherents of the Paraclete, whom he opposes to the psychics. RIG.], whether Apostle or prophet. For the Church itself, properly and principally, is the Spirit [Note: [Col. 1025D] “Principally, he himself is the Spirit, in whom is the Trinity.” This is the Spirit that he attributes to Montanus; and Pamelius thinks—not without amazement at such madness—that by the Trinity he means [Col. 1026C] Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla. LE PR.] in whom is the Trinity of the one divinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. [Note: [Col. 1026C] “The Spirit, in whom is the Trinity of the one divinity.” He appears to have added these words as a reproach against the Roman Pontiff, as though the latter agreed with Praxeas concerning the Trinity. Thus in *Against Praxeas*: “Praxeas managed two of the devil’s affairs at Rome: he drove out prophecy and brought in heresy; he put the Paraclete to flight and crucified the Father.” RIG.]

[Col. 1026B] He gathers that Church which the Lord located in three persons. And thus, from that point onward, every number of persons who agree in this faith is reckoned a Church [Note: [Col. 1025C] Others read “of the Church”] by reason of its founder and consecrator. Therefore the Church will indeed forgive sins—but the Church that is Spirit, through a spiritual person, not the church that is a number of bishops. [Note: [Col. 1026C] “Not the church that is a number of bishops.” “The Church,” he says, “will forgive sins, but the Church that is Spirit”—that is, the Church that glories in the Spirit, who is God and who alone can forgive sins—not the church that prevails by the number of its bishops. He contrasts the small size of his Paraclete-inspired or Montanist church with the multitude of Catholics. Thus he says in *On Fasting*: “the greater strength of the ignorant, among, of course, the most glorious multitude of the psychics.” [Col. 1026D] RIG.] For the right and decision belong to the Lord, not to the servant; to God himself, not to the priest.

## CHAPTER XXII

But now you pour out this power even upon your martyrs. As soon as anyone, by agreement, puts on bonds that are still soft, under the novel title of imprisonment, adulterers immediately surround him and fornicators immediately approach him. [Note: [Col. 1026D] “As soon as anyone, by agreement, puts on bonds that are still soft.” He notes the devices of certain psychics who, by prior arrangement, surrendered themselves to prison and put on bonds so that, through the reputation of a martyrdom already begun, they might deceive simple believers—men or women who perhaps had been expelled from the Church for fornication—when these came repeatedly to prison out of affection to comfort the martyr; and so that they might send them back to the Church, stained with fresh marks of lust, bearing letters of peace and communion. What sort of letters of peace could come from scoundrels of this kind, who were themselves in danger of losing their own peace? Septimius says these things about Catholics under the name of psychics, but he was by then hostile to Catholic authority. RIG.—From what follows, “He gathers that Church which the Lord located in three persons, and accordingly the Church is not a number of bishops,” I think I can infer that the Author descended even to such madness as to understand by the three in whom the Church consists Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla. PAM.] [Note: [Col. 1026C] “Confession” in Latinius, Neander, and Leopold.]

[Col. 1027A] Already petitions resound about him; already the tears of every stained person form a pool around him. No one pays more eagerly for access to the prison than those who have lost the Church. [Note: [Col. 1027C] “No one pays more eagerly for access to the prison than those who have lost the Church.” Latinius preferred “access to the Church,” so that the phrase would be understood of entry into the Church. Those who have been expelled from the Church are said to have “lost the Church,” or “access to the Church”; conversely, those to whom the rights of peace or ecclesiastical communion are restored are said to be “restored to the Church.” [Col. 1027D] RIG.]

Men and women are violated in the darkness, plainly amid conditions familiar to acts of lust, and they seek peace from those whose own peace is in peril. [Note: [Col. 1027D] “Men and women are violated in the darkness.” What the pagans once hurled against Christians was no more atrocious than these accusations that Septimius levels against his psychics. RIG.]

Others take refuge in the mines and return from there as communicants, although another martyrdom is now necessary because of their new sins committed after their martyrdom. [Note: [Col. 1027D] “Others take refuge in the mines.” Others, he says, who had been expelled for adultery or fornication, bribed the pagan overseers of the mines and took refuge there, pretending that they had been dragged off to them for the name of Christ. From there they soon returned to the peace of ecclesiastical communion, as though they had tasted martyrdom. But they returned from a place where another martyrdom had already become necessary, namely because of the offenses they contracted, in a by no means trivial form of denial, while conducting their illicit bargain at the mines through fraud. What a martyr! Living in the world among pagans, a suppliant to the condemned—namely, to the enemies of God and Christ—beholden to the adulterer and fornicator, that is, to worshipers of idols or even to persons who were themselves actual adulterers and fornicators, from whom he nevertheless purchases his own peace with the Church! [Col. 1028C] RIG.]

For who upon earth and in the flesh is without fault? What martyr, while an inhabitant of the world, does not supplicate with coins and remain beholden to the physician and the moneylender? [Note: [Col. 1028C] “A suppliant with denarii, beholden to the physician and the moneylender.” I have offered this conjecture, which I value only as highly as comparison with the manuscripts will show it deserves. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1027C] “With gifts” in Latinius.]

Suppose now that he is beneath the sword, his head already poised; [Note: [Col. 1028C] “Suppose now beneath the sword.” As though he said: “Let us grant that the men discussed above are true and undoubted martyrs.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1027C] “Over the head” in Latinius.] suppose his body is already stretched upon the cross; suppose the lion has already been granted against him at the stake; [Note: [Col. 1028D] “The lion has already been granted.” That is, after the circus crowd has shouted for a lion against the Christians. Thus in *On the Spectacles*: “There daily lions are demanded against us.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1027C] “To the lion” in Latinius.] suppose he is already bound to the axle and the fire prepared.
