[Note: [Col. 1028C] “Bound fast” in Semler and Oberthür.] In the very security and possession of martyrdom itself, I ask: who permits a human being to forgive what must be reserved for God—acts that God has condemned without excuse, and that not even the Apostles, themselves martyrs, so far as I know, judged pardonable? For Paul had already fought with beasts at Ephesus (1 Cor. 15:32) when he decreed destruction for the incestuous man (1 Cor. 5:3 ff.).

Let it suffice for the martyr to have purged his own sins. [Note: [Col. 1028D] “Let it suffice for the martyr,” etc. Either he is speaking of martyrs who were baptized by their martyrdom, or he means the complete purification from sins that both he himself, more than once above, and blessed Cyprian, Letter 52 to Antonianus, attribute to martyrs alone, so that nothing remains to be purified after this life. PAM.] It is the act of an ungrateful or arrogant man to scatter among others as well what he obtained as a great gift. Who pays for another person’s death by his own, except the Son of God alone? For even during his Passion he delivered the robber (Luke 23:43). He had come for this very purpose: that, himself pure of sin and entirely holy, he might die for sinners. [Note: [Col. 1028C] “Obey” in Semler and Oberthür.]

Accordingly, you who imitate him by forgiving sins, if you yourself have committed no sin, then by all means suffer for me. But if you are a sinner, how will the oil of your lamp [Col. 1027C] be able to suffice for both you and me?

I have even now a means of proving Christ. [Note: [Col. 1028D] “I have now a means of proving Christ.” That is: “I now have a means of proving that Christ forgives sins, but not the martyr.” RIG.] If Christ is in the martyr for the purpose of enabling the martyr to absolve adulterers and fornicators, let him reveal the hidden things of the heart so that he may grant sins in this way—and then he is Christ. For this was how the Lord Jesus Christ demonstrated his power:

> Why do you think evil things in your hearts? For which is easier: to say to the paralytic, “Your sins are forgiven you,” or, “Rise and walk”? Therefore, that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, I say to you, paralytic: “Rise and walk.” (Matt. 9:4 ff.)

[Col. 1028A] If the Lord took such care to prove his power that he exposed men’s thoughts and then commanded healing, lest people fail to believe that he could forgive sins, I am not permitted to believe in that same power in anyone without the same proofs.

Yet when you demand pardon from a martyr for adulterers and fornicators, you yourself admit that crimes of this kind can be washed away only by the offender’s own martyrdom, though you presume upon another person’s. If that is so, martyrdom will now be another baptism. “For I have,” he says, “another baptism” (Luke 12:50). Hence water and blood flowed from the wound in the Lord’s side, providing the material for both washings (John 19:34). Therefore I ought also to deliver another person by the first washing, if I can do so by the second.

We must press the argument home against you. [Note: [Col. 1028D] “We must press it into the bosom.” Into the bosom of the psychics, to confound their obstinacy. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1028C] “I shall press it all the way” in Latinius.] Whatever authority, whatever rationale restores ecclesiastical peace to the adulterer and fornicator must likewise come to the aid of the penitent murderer and idolater—and certainly of the denier, especially one whom cruelty caused to fall after he had struggled against tortures in the battle of confession.

Otherwise it is unworthy of God and of his mercy—which prefers the sinner’s repentance to his death—that those who fell through copulation should return to the Church more readily than those who fell through combat. The indignity compels us to speak. Will you recall defiled bodies rather than bloodied ones? Which repentance is more pitiable: that which casts down flesh that was titillated, or flesh that was torn? Which pardon is more just in every case: that implored by the voluntary sinner, or that implored by the involuntary one?

No one is compelled to deny Christ willingly; no one fornicates unwillingly. There is no force driving a person to lust except lust itself; it does not know how to be compelled to do what it desires. But what engines of the executioner and what varieties of punishment compel denial! [Note: [Col. 1028D] “But what great things compel denial,” etc. What is this? To make fornication greater than idolatry? πορνεία, “fornication,” is certainly a grave and deadly sin; but [Col. 1029A] idolatry is the gravest, on account of which there were so many punishments and so many established rites of repentance in the ancient Church. LE PR.]

Who denied Christ more completely: the man who lost him while being tortured, or the man who lost him while taking pleasure? The man who grieved as he lost him, or the man who played as he lost him? Yet those scars, engraved in Christian combat, are surely objects of reproach to Christ [Note: [Col. 1029A] “Objects of reproach to Christ”: casting reproach upon Christ. Thus in *On Flight*: “I prefer to cast reproach upon him by perishing in accordance with his will.” We discussed this above. RIG.], because they desired to conquer; and they are nevertheless glorious, because it was only through failure to conquer that they yielded. Even the devil himself still sighs over them, with his own misfortune, yet a chaste one; with repentance that mourns but does not blush, they come to the Lord for pardon.

Yet pardon is granted a second time to those who denied Christ sacrilegiously; [Note: [Col. 1029A] “Pardon is granted a second time to those who denied in a particularly personal fashion.” Let embarrassment yield to truth, and let us be permitted to change our judgment, if it cannot be denied that the authentic text read: *Denuo dimittitur eis qui peculiariter negaverunt*. The clause that follows proves this. The African plays upon the ambiguity of the word and hurls a dart against the psychics, like the one above where he reproached them with their bulging outer wineskins, swollen by luxury, and their approval of repeated marriages: “Pardon is granted a second time,” he says, “to those who denied in a peculiarly personal fashion.” It is as though he said: “The psychics favor men well furnished with vessels and private property, when they grant repentance to adulterers who misuse their own vessel and property and thereby deny Christ whenever they make their members, which belonged to Christ, members of a prostitute. Those who sport with their own private property, contrary to the pledge given to Christ, deny Christ ‘peculiarly’—with their own *peculium*.” RIG.] for them alone is the flesh weak. [Note: [Col. 1030A] “For them alone is the flesh weak”: for the lustful, adulterers, and fornicators. He condemns the discipline of the psychics, who, of the three deadly sins—idolatry or denial, murder, and adultery—restored the Church only to adulterers, although it would appear more fittingly restored to idolaters or deniers who repented after idolatry or denial had been wrung from them by the violence of torture. The latter had sinned only under compulsion from the harshness of torture, whereas adulterers and fornicators sinned of their own accord, spontaneously, through lust and pleasure. RIG.] Yet no flesh is so strong as the flesh that crushes the spirit.

[Col. 1029]

# THE BOOK OF QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN, *ON THE CLOAK* (C)

[Note: [Col. 1029D] *On the Cloak*. The distinguished Salmasius, in his most accurate edition based upon the authority of ancient manuscripts, presented many excellent observations on this subject, indeed observations that illuminate the entire little work. We follow that edition almost everywhere here. RIG.]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 1029C]

Learned scholars agree that this little work is a defense of the cloak, sprinkled with satirical wit, and delivered before the Carthaginians. For when he was reproached by his fellow citizens because he had exchanged the toga for the cloak—that is, because he had enlisted in Christ’s army—he answered them with this satirical defense. He was unwilling to let the charge of inconstancy adhere to him, and argued that changes of roles had always occurred throughout the whole world from the time of its foundation.

## CHAPTER ONE
Source/review notes: The supplied source itself ends in the middle of the final note after the first line quoted from Martial; the draft explicitly marks this inherited truncation with an ellipsis.

Always foremost in Africa, [Note: [Col. 1029D] **Always foremost in Africa.** Since throughout this entire little work Tertullian intends to discuss the various changes undergone by the whole world, by cities, and by other things, and even the change in the Carthaginians’ own dress and constitution (*πολιτεία*, *politeia*), he nevertheless declares at the very outset of this work that, so far as preeminence is concerned, they have changed nothing. SALM.] men of Carthage, [Note: [Col. 1029D] **Always foremost in Africa.** No one doubts that supremacy in Africa belonged solely to the Carthaginians. Apuleius spoke in this sense in *Florida*, book III, chapter 1, and repeats it twice—a point that others might perhaps have observed. MERC.], noble through antiquity and fortunate through novelty, I rejoice that the times are so prosperous for you that you have leisure and inclination [Col. 1030C] to censure [Note: [Col. 1029D] **To censure dress.** Tertullian uses *denotare* in the sense of “to mark” or “to criticize.” RHEN.] a mode of dress. Such is the leisure afforded by peace and the grain supply [Note: [Col. 1029C] “Both the grain supply and leisure,” Salmasius.]: all is well under both the government and the heavens. Yet you too once dressed differently. You had tunics, and indeed ones renowned [Note: [Col. 1029D] **For the care bestowed upon the weft.** He commends those tunics for the care bestowed upon the weft, because they were plainly woven studiously and diligently. By “weft” he may perhaps mean the whole fabric. [Col. 1030D] SALM.] for the care bestowed upon their weft, for the harmony [Note: [Col. 1030D] **For the harmony of their brilliance.** That is, because the gradations of their colors were well joined and matched. He himself interprets this quite explicitly in the book *On Modesty*. “Brilliance” is said of purple. Pliny, book IX, where he discusses purple: “It illuminates the whole garment”; and in Trebellius Pollio: “Cloaks of true brilliance.” By *concilium*, however, understand “harmonization” or “reconciliation.” RIG.] of their brilliance [Note: [Col. 1029C] *Consilio*, Rhen., Franeq., Paris.], and for their moderation of proportion: neither extravagantly extending below the calves, nor immodestly ending above the knees, neither scanty [Note: [Col. 1030D] **Nor scanty at the arms.** What Salmasius observed from the old books is entirely correct: *parae* must be read, so that *parus* is used, just as *rarus* is. RIG.—Salmasius thinks that the adverb *parum* arose from this adjective, just as *nimium* arose from *nimis*. LEOP.] [Note: [Col. 1030C] *Parcae*, Fran., Par.; *pare*, Rhen.] at the arms nor tight at the hands; nor was there any desire to divide [Note: [Col. 1030D] **Nor was there any desire to divide the folds with a belt.** So the old books read. That is: in former times the Carthaginians neither desired nor cared to divide the folds of their garment. LEOP.] the folds with a belt [Note: [Col. 1030C] *Dividente expedita*, Rhen.; *expeditum*, Salm.]. Blessed in their squared symmetry, [Note: [Col. 1030D] **Blessed in their squared correctness, they stood upon the men.** He speaks of the “correctness” of the tunics in the same sense in which, in *Against Hermogenes*, he speaks of the correctness of a movement inclining to neither side. LEOP.—By “correctness” he means *τὴν συμμετρίαν*, “symmetry.” SALM.] they rested upon the men. [Col. 1031A] The cloak [Note: [Col. 1031C] *Pallii* in the manuscript codices.], an outer garment [Note: [Col. 1031C] “But with a dividing and squared border on the men, externally,” Fran., etc.] and itself quadrangular, was thrown back from both sides, drawn closely around the neck [Note: [Col. 1031C] *Circumstructus*, Fran., Par.] and, held in the bite of a clasp, [Note: [Col. 1031C] **In the bite of a clasp.** *In fibulae morsu* means “by means of the clasp’s bite.” Thus the Greeks use *ἐν ξίφει* for *διὰ ξίφους*, “by the sword.” SALM.] rested upon the shoulders. [Note: [Col. 1031C] **Rested upon the shoulders.** This refers to the ordinary Greek-style cloak, fastened on the shoulders with a clasp and covering both shoulders. SALM.] Today a garment resembling it is the priestly dress of Aesculapius, now your own. [Note: [Col. 1031C] **Of Aesculapius, now your own.** For previously he belonged only to the people of Pergamum. RIG.] Thus too the neighboring sister city [Note: [Col. 1031C] **Sister city.** Utica, which Strabo records as the second colony of the Tyrians. RHEN.] used to dress, as did any other Tyre that might exist [Note: [Col. 1031C] **Any other Tyre that might exist.** That is, if another Tyre lies in some region of Africa. He means Hadrumetum, another Tyre besides Utica and itself a colony of Tyre. EDD.] elsewhere in Africa.

But when the urn of worldly fortunes changed its verdict and God favored the Romans, [Note: [Col. 1031C] **God favored the Romans.** For some time the issue wavered between the two peoples, Roman and Carthaginian, and there was a period in which, amid their varying fortunes, each was suspended between uncertain hope and fear. [Col. 1031D] MERC.] your sister city hastened to change of her own accord, so that, even before Scipio landed, she might greet him by her dress [Note: [Col. 1031C] *Salutasset*, Venet., Salm.], precociously Roman [Note: [Col. 1031D] **Precociously Roman.** By her premature and overhasty assumption of Roman dress. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1032C] *Romana*, Fran.] as she was. [Note: [Col. 1031D] **Precocious.** Although, during the Second Punic War, she had been unsuccessfully attacked by the other Scipio—the grandfather of the man who destroyed Carthage—and could not be taken, she voluntarily submitted herself to Roman rule while African power still stood. MERC.] But in your case, after the benefit conferred by an injury—when you were released from old age rather than deprived of eminence [Note: [Col. 1032C] *Fastidium*, Rhen.]—after all the obscenities of Gracchus and the violent mockeries of Lepidus, after Pompey’s three altars and Caesar’s long delays, when Statilius Taurus erected your walls [Col. 1031B] and Sentius Saturninus recited the solemn formula, [Note: [Col. 1031D] **Recited the solemn formula.** That is, he pronounced the ceremonial words for inaugurating the colony. RIG.] then, when concord proved pleasing, the toga was offered to you.

Ah! How far it traveled—from the Pelasgians to the Lydians, from the Lydians to the Romans—so that, leaving the shoulders of a loftier people, it might embrace the Carthaginians! Since then, suspending a longer tunic with the cincture serving as judge, you support the ample mass of your now-rounded cloak [Note: [Col. 1031D] **Of the now-rounded cloak.** You exchanged your square cloak for a circular or rounded cloak, that is, the Roman toga. Salmasius cited as a particularly apt witness to this interpretation an ancient commentator on Persius, who says that the toga is “a plain cloak of rounded shape, with a fuller and billowing fold.” RIG.] by a layered gathering. [Note: [Col. 1032C] **By a layered gathering.** With the boss of the toga formed from several layers, or constructed by manifold layering. RIG.] And whatever else condition, rank, or season [Note: [Col. 1032C] **Season.** The season of the year. RIG.—Because, of course, one dresses differently in peace and in war, and differently in winter and summer. SALM.] may put upon you, you nevertheless universally censure the cloak that is yours, though you have forgotten it.

Indeed, in view of an earlier example, I am not surprised. For even the ram—not the one that Laberius calls “curved-horned, woolly, and head-dragging” [Note: [Col. 1032C] “Both butchering and head-dragging,” Leop.], but the machine consisting of beams [Note: [Col. 1032C] **Whose military function is to break walls.** Whose service is the breaking of walls. RIG.] whose military function is to break walls—though no one had ever yet set it swinging, is attributed to that Carthage,

[Col. 1032A]  
Most fierce in the pursuits of war.  
(Virgil, *Aeneid*, book I, 18.)

She was the first of all to arm its pendulous impact [Note: [Col. 1032C] **Pendulous impact.** The swinging, *αἰώρα* (*aiōra*), of a machine balanced for a blow and an assault. Athenaeus Mechanicus thus describes an invention devised by a certain Pephasmenus of Tyre against the people of Gades: *Ἱστὸν στήσας, καὶ ἄλλον ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ πλάγιον ἀρτήσας παραπλησίως ταῖς τῶν ζυγῶν φάλαγξιν, ἔτυπτε τὸ τεῖχος ἕλκων ἐξ ἀντισπάστου τὸ πλάγιον.* “Having erected a mast and suspended another beam crosswise from it, in the manner of the arms of balances, he began to strike the wall, alternately drawing back and advancing that transverse beam.” RIG.—That is: “After he had erected a mast and suspended from it another transverse beam, like the arms of balances, he began to strike the wall, now drawing back that transverse beam, now driving it forward.” EDD.] [Note: [Col. 1032C] **Carthage was the first of all, etc.** The machine called the ram was a Punic invention; they devised it during the siege of Gades. Rigault’s subsequent remarks about the swinging motion were taken from Salmasius. LE PR.], devising the force of an engine that avenged the feeble [Note: [Col. 1032C] “From bile,” Salm.] head of an animal. Yet when her homeland’s final days arrived and the ram, now Roman, [Note: [Col. 1032D] **The ram, now Roman.** It had formerly belonged to the Carthaginians. He used the same sense above: “Aesculapius, now your own,” who had, of course, previously belonged to the people of Pergamum and to the Romans. SALM.] dared assault the walls that once were its own, the Carthaginians were immediately astonished at it as something novel, an alien contrivance: [Note: [Col. 1032D] **An alien contrivance:** *διὰ τὸ ξένον τοῦ μηχανήματος*, “because of the unfamiliarity of the machine.” RIG.—That is, because the type of machine was unfamiliar. EDD.]

So greatly can the distant passage of time change things.  
(*Aeneid*, book III, verse 415.)

Thus, in short, even the cloak is no longer recognized.

## CHAPTER II

Let the matter now be approached from another quarter, so that anything Punic among Romans may neither blush nor grieve. Certainly, changing one’s appearance is a customary function of [Col. 1032B] all nature. Even this world upon which we rest performs that same function from time to time. Let Anaximander answer for it if he thinks there are several worlds; and let anyone else answer if, somewhere among the Meropians, like Silenus, he babbles into the ears of Midas—ears well suited, assuredly, to rather tall tales. But even if there is some world which Plato judges this one to be the image of, that world too must necessarily undergo change in the same manner. For if it is a world, it will consist of diverse substances and functions after the pattern of what this present world is; indeed, it would not be a world if it did not behave correspondingly as a world. Diverse things come together into one; through change, they become different. In short, successive alternations reconcile the discord of diversity. Thus every world will exist by changing, [Note: [Col. 1032D] **Thus every world will exist by changing.** That is, if the world did not change, it would not exist, for it is composed and compacted from diverse substances. SALM.] being both embodied through diversity and tempered through alternation.

Certainly our present lodging-place, [Note: [Col. 1032D] **Certainly our present lodging-place.** This world upon which we rest, in which we lodge. SALM.] as is obvious even to eyes closed altogether [Col. 1033A] in Homeric fashion, is wholly changeable in form. Day and night alternate. The sun varies with its annual stations, the moon with its monthly modulations. The stars’ ordered confusion [Note: [Col. 1033C] **The stars’ ordered confusion.** He will be his own best interpreter in the book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*: “The clusters of stars are kindled again, and the vanished constellations, which temporal distinction had withdrawn, are brought back.” RIG.] at one time casts something down and at another raises it again. [Note: [Col. 1033C] **At one time casts something down, at another, etc.** The author meant nothing other than the rising and setting of the stars, which are said to be cast down and to fall when they set, and to be raised again when they rise. SALM.] The vault of heaven is now splendid beneath a clear sky, [Note: [Col. 1033C] **Splendid beneath a clear sky.** *Subdivum*, Greek *ὑπαίθριον*, means “serene” or “clear.” RIG.] now filthy with cloud: either rains pour down, or whatever projectiles come with the rains; then comes a drizzle, [Note: [Col. 1033C] **Drizzle.** When water repeatedly falls from heaven drop by drop. The glosses: *Substillat*, *στραγγουριᾷ*, “it dribbles.” RIG.] and afterward clear weather again.

So too the sea has a notorious reliability [Note: [Col. 1033B] Perhaps *maris*, “of the sea,” in the sense in which the sea is called unreliable. Edd.], since, with the breezes likewise changing, it is blameless in calm weather, [Note: [Col. 1033C] **Blameless in calm weather.** Blameless because of its tranquillity, calm, so that no one can justly complain of it. RIG.] temperate amid lulls, [Note: [Col. 1033D] **Moderate amid light airs.** Agitated by winds, now violent, now gentler. RIG.—Are *flustra* here contrasted with a moderate sea? Not at all, for *flustra* signify a calm at sea. SALM.] and suddenly disturbed by mountainous waves. [Note: [Col. 1033D] **Disturbed by mountainous waves.** It is disturbed by “tenth waves.” Tertullian himself uses this passive-like form below: “He is banished from paradise,” and “When the slough has been cast off, he unfolds new,” that is, “is unfolded.” SALM.]

Likewise, if you examine the earth, which loves to clothe itself according to the season, you will come close to denying that it is the same earth when, remembering it green, you behold it yellow, and soon afterward you will laugh to see it white-haired. What other one of its ornaments does not change from one state into another? The shoulders of mountains change by running down, [Note: [Col. 1033D] **The shoulders of mountains by running down.** When rocks broken loose by the force of torrents roll down from the shoulders of mountains into the depths. SALM.] [Col. 1033B] the veins of springs by playing false, [Note: [Col. 1033D] **The veins of springs by playing false.** Springs are said to play false when they cease to provide their supply and enter the hollows of the earth; for then they deceive, frustrate, and defraud the surrounding inhabitants. SALM.] [Note: [Col. 1033B] *Ebullando*, Par., Rhen.] and the courses of rivers by being choked with earth. [Note: [Col. 1033D] **The courses of rivers by being choked with earth.** Through a river’s alluvium its channel is filled with silt or soil, so that, once the channel is occupied, the river is compelled to turn aside and make a new course for itself. Thus *obhumatio* means alluvium, *πρόσχωσις* (*proschōsis*). SALM.] [Note: [Col. 1033B] *Obumbrando*, Franeq., Rhen.]

The whole world too once changed when it was covered by all the waters. Even now seashells and trumpet-shells sojourn upon mountains, eager to prove to Plato that even the heights once floated. But the world, swimming forth again, changed once more in form [Note: [Col. 1033B] *Infirma*, Rhen.; *infima*, others.]: different, yet the same. Even now it changes its appearance locally when [Col. 1034A] its configuration is injured: when Delos is no longer counted among the islands; when sandy Samos [Note: [Col. 1033B] Rhene, Pam.: Stephen mentions a small island neighboring Delos whose name was Rhene.] [Note: [Col. 1034C] **Samos.** According to Pliny, this island suddenly emerged from the sea. PAM.] appears; and when—if he is not lying [Note: [Col. 1034C] **He.** Namely Plato, who writes in the *Timaeus* of an immense island submerged in the Atlantic Sea. Tertullian discusses at greater length the destruction of these and other islands, and Sicily as an island severed from the continent, in the *Apology* (chapter 40, cols. 480–481), where he uses almost the same words. I understand the name of the deformity with which that tract invested—or, as the Vatican codex reads, imbued—the sea by its sundering to be Rhegium, since in Greek the name signifies “broken apart” (from *ῥήγνυμι*, “to break”). The strait between Sicily and Italy was so called because, although they had previously been joined, the intervening space was overwhelmed by waters and split through its narrowness, as Isidore, *Etymologies*, book IV, under the word “Sicily,” cites from Sallust, borrowing from Servius. PAM. and EDD.] [Note: [Col. 1033C] “And if he is not lying,” Fran.; “and if the Sibyl is not lying,” [Col. 1034B] Seml., Ven., Rig., Leop.]—an island equal in size to Libya or Asia is sought in the Atlantic; [Note: [Col. 1034B] *Aeon*, Fran., Pam., Leop.] [Note: [Col. 1034B] “Is now sought,” Fran., Leop.; *nunc* for the following *cum*.] when the side of Italy that once existed there, broken by the Adriatic and Tyrrhenian seas and intercepted midway, leaves Sicily as its remnant; when that whole region of severance, driving back the contentious meeting of the seas through narrow passages [Note: [Col. 1034B] *Angustiis*, Fran.] [Note: [Col. 1034D] **Narrow passages**, that is, “straits.” He uses the neuter adjective substantivally, like the Greek *στενά*. RIG.], imbues the sea [Note: [Col. 1034B] *Induit*, Pam., Leop.] with a novel deformity, [Note: [Col. 1034D] **A novel deformity.** That is, *novum vitium*. So below he uses *endormidis solocem* for *endormidem solocem*. RIG.] whereby it does not spit out shipwrecks but devours them.

The mainland too suffers from heaven or from itself. Look toward Palestine, where the river Jordan is the arbiter of boundaries: an immense wasteland, a bereaved region, and a field laboring in vain. Yet formerly there were cities, throngs of people, and that field alone was spoken of; [Note: [Col. 1034B] “The field exists too,” Fran.] [Note: [Col. 1034D] **Was alone spoken of.** That field, which is now barren because it produces nothing, was once on everyone’s lips because of its fertility, and scarcely anything else was discussed. RIG.] then, since God is judge [Note: [Col. 1034B] *Esset*, Fran.], impiety earned rains of fire. Sodom existed only until then, [Col. 1034B] and Gomorrah exists no longer; ash covers everything, and the neighboring sea [Note: [Col. 1034D] **The neighboring sea.** That is, the nearby sea called the Dead Sea. RIG.] lives a death together with the soil. [Note: [Col. 1034D] **Lives a death.** We believe this reading to be genuine, although the *Poem on Sodom* reads: “Nor does the sea live where there is that death of the quiet sea.” That sea is still seen and lives, but is called dead; accordingly it lives not a life but a death. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1034B] *Bibit*, Fran.; *mortuum ivit*, Salm.]

By a cloud of this kind Etruria too had Volsinii burned [Note: [Col. 1034C] Fran. adds “ancient.”]—which gives Campania all the more reason to hope concerning its own mountains, after Pompeii was snatched away. [Note: [Col. 1034D] **Pompeii.** It is well enough known to everyone that this city, buried beneath the ashes of Vesuvius, was finally raised from its ruins almost in our own time. EDD.] But may that be averted. Would that Asia too might now be secure from the ravening of its soil! Would that Africa had fed its chasm but once and, at the cost of a single army-camp, [Note: [Col. 1034D] **At the cost of a single army-camp.** There can be no doubt that this must be understood of Cambyses’ army, covered and buried beneath immense heaps of sand in the Libyan Syrtes. Plutarch, *Alexander*. SALM.] been appeased! [Col. 1035A]

Many other losses of this kind have changed the world’s appearance [Note: [Col. 1035C] *Novavere*, Fran.] and altered its configuration. How greatly wars too have been permitted to do would lead us onward into grief [Note: [Col. 1035C] “Have been permitted. But it is irksome to recount grievous things,” Fran., Leop.], no less than would recounting the successive changes of kingdoms. How often have those too changed [Note: [Col. 1035C] *Mutaverint*, Leop.], beginning as far back as Ninus, offspring of Belus—if, that is, Ninus was the first to reign, [Note: [Col. 1035C] *Regnavit*, Fran.; *regnare*, Salm.] as the profane learning of earlier authorities supposes! [Note: [Col. 1035C] **As the profane learning of earlier authorities supposes.** We once discussed Ninus, from whom the origin of the Assyrians must be traced, in our observations against *Praeadam*. Diodorus speaks of him in book II: *πρῶτος τῶν εἰς ἱστορίαν καὶ μνήμην παραδεδομένων, Νῖνος ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἀσσυρίων*—“the first of all those handed down to history and memory was Ninus, king of the Assyrians.” LE PR.] Among you, your pen does not generally venture farther back. The records of the ages may perhaps open with the Assyrians; but we who regularly read the divine writings possess knowledge extending from the very birth of the world.

But now I prefer happier things, since happy things also change. In short, whatever the sea has washed away, heaven has burned up, earth has swallowed, or the sword has mown down, returns compensated by a converse transformation. [Note: [Col. 1035C] **Compensated by a converse transformation.** Here *versura* does not mean interest or usury, as is commonly and incorrectly interpreted, but *τὸ ἀντίστροφον* or *ἡ ἀντιστροφή*, what the Greeks call a reciprocal reversal. SALM.—That is, compensation is made by another transformation. EDD.] For originally the earth, empty over a wider expanse [Note: [Col. 1035C] “Over a wider expanse,” Fran.] and vacant of human beings, belonged exclusively to any people that had occupied any part of it. Thus humanity began to cultivate [Col. 1035B] everything—if only you understand the population as crowded together in one place and absent from another [Note: [Col. 1035C] “To color … conveying,” Ven.] [Note: [Col. 1035C] “Considering everything, if the home,” Fran.; “to cultivate everything for itself, the home,” Leop.]—to weed and clear away scrub, [Note: [Col. 1035D] **To clear away scrub.** *Rustum* or *ruscus* means brambles and thorns; hence *ruscare* or *rustare*, “to clear scrub”; and hence also the *rustariae falces*, pruning hooks designed for removing thorns, in Varro, *On Agriculture*, book I. Thus in the *Apology*: “With the axes of your edicts you clear and cut down,” chapter 4, col. 286. RIG.] so that from there, as though from shoots and offshoots, peoples might be planted from peoples and cities from cities throughout every part of the world.

Swarms of overflowing nations flew abroad. The Scythians pour over into Persia; Phoenicia disgorges into Africa; Phrygians give birth to the Romans; Chaldaean stock is brought into Egypt; afterward, when it is led out from there, it becomes the Jewish nation. Thus too the descendants of Hercules, issuing equally from Temenus, occupy the Peloponnese. [Note: [Col. 1036C] “They are brought forth equally from Temenus by occupying the Peloponnese,” Leop.] Thus the Ionians, companions of Neleus, [Col. 1036A] furnish Asia with new cities. Thus the Corinthians, together with Archias, fortify Syracuse.

But antiquity is now an empty matter when the course of our own age [Note: [Col. 1035D] **The course of our own age.** Our own century, as its years run on. RIG.] lies before our eyes. How greatly this age has reshaped the world! How many cities the threefold power [Note: [Col. 1035D] **Threefold power.** That is, three emperors or Augusti, whom he names immediately: Severus the father, and his sons Antoninus and Geta. RIG.] of the present empire has founded, enlarged, or restored, with God favoring so many Augusti united as one! How many assessment rolls have been transcribed! How many peoples driven back [Note: [Col. 1035D] **How many peoples driven back.** Florus: “He drove back the Carthaginians by sea.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1036C] *Repurgati*, Salm.; *propaginati*, Fran.]! How many orders made illustrious! How many barbarians shut out! Truly the world is the most highly cultivated estate of this empire: every aconite of hostility, every cactus, [Note: [Col. 1035D] **Cactus.** Pliny, book XXI, chapter 16, describes the cactus as having a thorny leaf; and the ancient Glosses say, *Cactum, ἀκάνθας εἶδος*, “cactus, a kind of thorn.” Hesychius: *Κάκτος ἄκανθα, ὑφ’ ἧς ἐὰν πληγῇ νεβρὸς ἀχρεῖα ἔχει τὰ ὀστᾶ εἰς αὐλούς*—“The cactus is a thorn; if a fawn is struck by it, its bones become useless for making flutes.” RIG.] and every bramble of treacherous familiarity has been rooted out, and the whole is cultivated and pleasant, [Note: [Col. 1036C] **Cultivated and pleasant.** He uses *concultum* where elsewhere he would simply say *cultum*, “cultivated”; it is the opposite of “uncultivated.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1036C] “Planted and pleasant,” Fran.; *consultus et amoenus*, codex.] surpassing the orchard of Alcinous and the rose garden of Midas. [Note: [Col. 1036C] **The orchard of Alcinous.** The orchards of King Alcinous on the island of Corcyra are celebrated by Pliny, book XIX, chapter 4. Homer too mentions them in book VII of the *Odyssey*, whose words are quoted by Justin Martyr, *Against the Nations*. PAM.]

## CHAPTER III

Since, then, you praise a changing world, why do you censure a human being? Even animals change their appearance in place of clothing. [Col. 1036B] The peacock’s plumage is itself a garment—and indeed one fit to be kept under lock and key; [Note: [Col. 1036C] **A garment kept under lock and key.** That is, precious and guarded with particular care. Thus Apuleius, book XI: “A chorus resplendent in snow-white and carefully guarded attire”; and Sextus Empiricus: *τίμιον καὶ κατάκλειστον*, “precious and kept under lock.” Hesychius: *Κατάκλειστοι, ἐν Κορίνθῳ ἑταῖραί τινες*, “the *katakleistoi* were certain courtesans in Corinth”—women, namely, who were scarcely ever seen in public, like that woman of Catullus:

> To be guarded more carefully than dark grapes.

RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1036C] *Cataclitis*, Fran., Leop.] indeed, more deeply dyed than any shellfish purple [Note: [Col. 1036D] **More deeply dyed than any shellfish purple.** Purple is called “deep” when it shines more purely and richly. For its greatest excellence is the color of pressed and clotted blood, blackish when viewed directly, yet gleaming when viewed at an angle. Pliny, IX, 38. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1036C] “More depressed,” Fran.] where its neck blooms; [Note: [Col. 1036D] **Where its neck blooms.** “To bloom” is said of purple. Tertullian himself writes in the book *On Idolatry*: “What sort of purple would bloom from his shoulders.” RIG.] more gilded than any gold border [Note: [Col. 1036D] **Than any gold border.** The *patagium*, from which garments were called *patagiatae*, is nothing other than a golden stripe sewn to the upper part of a tunic. In common usage it was called a *patagium* on matrons and a *clavus* on men. LE PR.] where its back gleams; and looser than any trailing robe [Note: [Col. 1036D] **Looser than any trailing robe.** A tragic costume; hence women in tragedies too were dressed loosely and freely. LAC.—It was so called from the Greek verb *σύρω*, “to trail,” because it flowed down the back and dragged upon the ground behind the ankles. EDD.] where its tail lies spread. It is multicolored, differently colored, changeably colored—never the same, always different; and if it is always the same precisely when it is different, then it must change as often as it must move.

The serpent too deserves mention, though after the peacock, for it also changes what has fallen to its lot: its skin and its age. Indeed, when it has become conscious of old age, it compresses itself into a narrow space [Note: [Col. 1036D] **Compresses itself into a narrow space.** Tertullian himself, in *To the Martyrs*: “Regulus, compressed into a kind of chest.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1036C] “Itself into a narrow place,” Fran.; “itself into narrow spaces,” Leop.] and enters a hole; immediately scraped clean from the very threshold, it leaves its slough there and emerges unfolded anew. [Note: [Col. 1037B] “Unfolds itself anew,” Leop.; *nomis explicat*, Seml.; “unfolds itself as something new,” Pam.] [Col. 1037A] Together with its scales, its years too are cast off. [Note: [Col. 1037C] **Its years too are cast off.** They are left behind together with the slough. Just above, *explicat* was read for *explicatur*, “is unfolded.” EDD.] [Note: [Col. 1037B] *Recursantur*, others; *recurantur*, others.]

The hyena, if you observe it, changes sex annually: it alternates between male and female. I say nothing of the stag, because it too, master of its own age, feeds upon a serpent and grows weak from the poison into youth.

There is also a quadruped, slow-moving, wild, lowly, and rough. Do you suppose I mean Pacuvius’ tortoise? I do not. The little beast too receives, along with others, [Note: [Col. 1037C] **Along with others.** *Allis* is used for *aliis*, a usage also found in Catullus. RIG.] a line of verse—quite an ordinary one, but with a grand name. When you hear “chameleon” without prior acquaintance with it, you will already fear something even greater than a lion; but when you find it in a vineyard, usually entirely beneath a vine leaf, you will at once laugh at the audacity and Greek pretension of its name. [Note: [Col. 1037C] **The audacity and Greek pretension of its name.** What lies beyond audacity except shamelessness? Thus, to say something surpassing even shamelessness, he says “Greekness.” There is the familiar verse of Martial:

> But they are Greeks, to whom nothing is denied.

And Juvenal:

> And whatever lying Greece  
> Dares to put into history.

RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1037C] **Greek pretension of its name.** So it is read in the Dijon codex.] [Note: [Col. 1037B] “And already the Greeks,” Rhen.; “distinction,” Salm.] For its body does not even contain fluid, although creatures much smaller than it plainly do. [Note: [Col. 1037C] **Although creatures much smaller than it plainly do.** So the old books read, except that they write *licet* for *liquet*, and I see no reason why anything else should have been changed. He says that the chameleon’s body has no fluid, whereas much smaller insects generally plainly do—that is, much smaller creatures are not without fluid. *Liquet succo* is used impersonally, as in reports of prodigies: “it rains milk,” “it rains blood,” and so forth. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1037B] “Which may be much smaller,” Fran.]

The chameleon, [Col. 1037B] [Note: [Col. 1037B] Salmasius inserts *si*, “if.”] a mere skin, nevertheless lives. [Note: [Col. 1037D] **The chameleon, a mere skin, nevertheless lives.** Although it is nothing other than a little skin, it nevertheless lives. RIG.] Its little head springs directly from its back, for it has no neck; it is therefore difficult for it to turn around, but it surveys its surroundings with roving little eyes—or rather, points of light—which whirl about. Sluggish and weary, it scarcely raises itself from the ground; it undertakes its gait in a stupor and moves forward, displaying a step more than completing it. Always fasting, of course, yet never exhausted [Note: [Col. 1037B] “Never weary,” Paris.], it feeds by yawning, ruminates by puffing itself up like a bellows, [Note: [Col. 1037D] **Puffing itself up like a bellows.** Inflated in the manner of a bellows. RIG.] [Col. 1038A] and takes its food from the wind.

Yet the chameleon too can change completely while remaining no other creature. [Note: [Col. 1038B] “Completely, and nothing else,” Fran.] For although it possesses one color as its own, it is suffused with the color of whatever comes near it. This alone has been granted to the chameleon—that which is commonly called “playing with one’s own skin.” [Note: [Col. 1037D] **Playing with one’s own skin.** Martial, against a certain Cerdo, so ostentatiously foolish that from the money he earned by patching hides he furnished gladiators to the people:

> You are drunk, for you would never do this sober, …

So that you might play, Cerdo, with your own hide.

**RIG.**] “To play with one’s own hide.” Much had to be said,

[Note: [Col. 1037D] “So that the way might first be prepared for arriving at man.” Many things had to be set forth beforehand so that man might be reached. **RIG.**—“Much had to be said.” This is a Graecism, or an imitation of the construction used with the verbal adjectives in *-teos, -tea, -teon*; for example, πολλὰ πράκτεον ἐστι (*polla prakteon esti*), that is, “many things must be done”—word for word, “much is to be done.” **EDD.**]

so that the way might first be prepared for arriving at man. At whatever beginning you take him, he certainly stood naked and unclothed before his potter. Only afterward did he obtain wisdom, seized prematurely when it was not yet permitted to him.

[Note: [Col. 1038C] “Not yet permitted.” For Adam, by choosing to taste the forbidden fruit, attempted to seize prematurely a wisdom which he was not yet permitted to possess. **EDD.**]

There, hastening to cover what in his new body was still not subject to shame, he temporarily girded himself with fig leaves. Then, when he was banished

[Note: [Col. 1038C] “Banished.” That is, *is banished*, is expelled from the place of his origin—namely, paradise. **EDD.**]

from the place of his origin, he was given to the world clad in skins, as though condemned to the mines.

[Note: [Col. 1038C] “To the world, as though to the mines.” As a slave is condemned to the mines, so the first parent was condemned to thorns and thistles. **EDD.**]

But these are mysteries, and not for everyone to know. I believe that by now we may turn to your own account—

[Note: [Col. 1038C] “What the Egyptians relate and Alexander sets out.” This concerns Alexander Polyhistor, whom the *Suda* reports to have been a Milesian, captured in war, employed as a tutor in the household of Cornelius Lentulus, and subsequently manumitted and called by the name Cornelius. He wrote a very great many works, from which he acquired the surname Polyhistor. He appears frequently among the authors cited by Pliny in the books of the *Natural History*. The books *On Phrygian Affairs* and *On Egyptian Affairs, to His Mother* seem indeed to have been his; from the latter derive the statements about Mercury which Septimius records here. From it also derive the statements in Athenagoras’s *Apology*, Cyprian’s *On Idols*, Minucius’s *Octavius*, and Augustine’s *City of God*, book VIII, chapters 5 and 27, and book XII, chapter 10. They attribute these works to Alexander the Great of Macedon, son of Philip, perhaps deceived by the title *Alexander, On Egyptian Affairs, to His Mother*, which they immediately took to mean Olympias. Tertullian was therefore more discerning than they. **RIG.**]

what the Egyptians relate, Alexander sets out, and his mother [Col. 1038B]

[Note: [Col. 1038B] “The African,” **Fran.**—“He abounds in sheep.”]

reads: in the age of Osiris,

[Note: [Col. 1038D] “In the age of Osiris, when Ammon came to him from Libya.” In his section on Aries, Hyginus, citing Leo, who wrote on Egyptian affairs, reports that Ammon came from Africa to Liber. Liber, however, among the Egyptians—see the book *On the Crown*. **RIG.**]

when Ammon came to him from Libya,

[Note: [Col. 1038D] “When Ammon came to him from Libya.” Here *facit* means *facessit*: “makes a journey,” “sets out.” Thus in the book *On Patience*: “One does not *facit* to another,” that is, does not admit him. **RIG.**]

rich in sheep. Finally, since they believe that Mercury himself,

[Note: [Col. 1038B] “They themselves,” **Leop.**]

perhaps delighted by the softness of a ram he had touched, skinned

[Note: [Col. 1038B] *Deglubasse*, **Leop.**]

a little sheep; and while experimenting with it, following the lead suggested by the pliability of the material,

[Note: [Col. 1038D] “What the pliability of the material suggested.” That is, the ductility of the pliant material into threads. **RIG.**]

he drew out a thread by continued pulling, after the fashion of the primitive rope

[Note: [Col. 1038B] “He drew out,” **Fran.**]

which he had fashioned as a band of linden-bark, and [they suppose] that the thread thus emerged,

[Note: [Col. 1038D] “Which he had fashioned as a band of linden-bark.” The ancients twisted their ropes from *philyra*, that is, from the inner membrane of the linden tree cut into strips. *Tenus philyrae* means a ribbon, noose, or bond made from *philyra*. *Tenus* and *taenia* are Greek words. Hesychius: Τέναι· ζῶναι, “*tenai*: belts.” Likewise: Τέναι· ζῶναι, στέφανοι, δεσμοί, διαδήματα, “*tenai*: belts, wreaths, bonds, diadems.” Likewise: Τέννος, ὑφάντος ἐλαῖνος ἐρίῳ πεπλεγμένος, “*tennos*: a woven olive band intertwined with wool.” **RIG.**]



[Note: [Col. 1038B] “After the fashion of the primitive rope, which he had bound with a slender strip of linden-bark, he wove,” old editions.]

[Col. 1039A] But you preferred to assign the entire management of wool-working and the construction of looms to Minerva, although Arachne possessed the more industrious workshop. From that point came the material—and I do not mean the sheep of Miletus, Selge,

[Note: [Col. 1039B] “Salge,” **Fran.**]

and Altinum, or whatever stock at Tarentum or in Baetica is renowned for being colored by nature. Rather, even shrubs provide clothing, and flaxen plants, after their greenness, are whitened like snow by washing. Nor was it enough to fasten and stitch together a tunic unless clothing could also be fished from the sea:

[Note: [Col. 1039C] “Nor was it enough to fasten together a tunic unless clothing could also be fished.” Pliny has a splendid expression of indignation to this effect: “What,” he asks, “has the sea to do with clothing? If our belly has so great a partnership with it, why should our back? It would be too little unless, besides feeding upon perils, we were also clothed in them,” etc., book IX, chapter 35. Yet he says nothing about that mossy woolliness of shellfish. **RIG.**]

for there are fleeces from the sea as well,

[Note: [Col. 1039C] “Fleeces from the sea as well.” The Greeks call sea-wool πίννινον or πιννικὸν ἔριον (*pinninon* or *pinnikòn erion*, “pinna-wool”). **RIG.**]

with which the broader

[Note: [Col. 1039C] “Broader shellfish,” πλατύτεραι (*platyterai*), better adapted for applause; from this was also formed the barking name “Planti.” **RIG.**]

[Note: [Col. 1039B] “More luxurious,” **Fran.**]

shellfish grow hairy with mossy wool. Nor, plainly, is the silkworm hidden from view: it is a kind of little worm which, by liquefying itself through the air, stretches out a dwelling more fittingly than spiders according to the observers of the hours [*horoscopis*; the text is materially uncertain]; then it devours it, and presently returns it from its belly.

[Note: [Col. 1039B] “At some time,” **Fran.**]

[Note: [Col. 1039B] “From an empty belly,” **Salm.**, likewise **Fran.**]

Accordingly, if you kill it, you will unwind threads that are already alive.

[Note: [Col. 1039D] “Accordingly, if you kill it.” Salmasius’s reading seems preferable: “Accordingly, if you kill it, once it has spun its thread, you will unwind the warp.” That is, if you kill that little creature before it has discharged its thread, you will afterward unwind from the bottom of its belly the warp with which it is filled. **LE PR.**]

[Note: [Col. 1039B] “With thread,” **Fran.**; “once it has spun its thread, you will unwind the warp,” **Salm.**]

So great a provision of materials was followed by the ingenuity of the clothing trade. At first, since necessity took precedence, [Col. 1039B] it clothed man; afterward, when ambition succeeded necessity, it also adorned him—indeed, inflated him. It promulgated various forms of garments. Some of these are worn according to individual nations and are not shared by others; but some are commonly useful to all, as is this cloak, the *pallium*. Even if it is especially Greek, its word now belongs to Latium: it entered together with the garment itself. Indeed, even that same Cato who believed that Greeks should be kept outside the city,

[Note: [Col. 1039D] “Kept outside the city.” He expelled them from the city. **RIG.**]

after he had learned their literature and language in his old age, exposed one shoulder in the period when he exercised judicial office

[Note: [Col. 1039D] “In the period of his judicial office.” That is, his praetorship. **RIG.**]

[Note: [Col. 1039D] “With one shoulder exposed.” In the Gabine manner of girding the toga. **LE PR.**]

and favored the Greeks no less by adopting the dress of the *pallium*. [Col. 1040A]

What, then, if Romanity is salvation for everyone, yet you nevertheless go over to the Greeks by dishonorable means?

[Note: [Col. 1039D] “What, then, if Romanity is salvation for everyone,” etc. Before Salmasius, this passage was wrapped in the thickest darkness. We follow him as he goes before us with his torch lit. Tertullian addresses his fellow Carthaginians: If it is useful and glorious for all peoples to embrace Roman customs, why do you now go over to the Greeks through pursuits that are utterly dishonorable and useless? Or, if you do not do so, from what nation has the wrestling school—which is accustomed to hand over an exhausted body to old age and to labor in vain—invaded your provinces, which are better trained and equipped by nature rather for subduing the soil? From what nation, unless from Greece, did that muddy anointing, dusty rolling, and dry fattening come to us? **RIG.**]

[Note: [Col. 1040B] “You are thoroughly Greek,” **Fran.**; “you are Greeks,” others.]

Or, if that is not so, from what nation have the practices of the wrestling school come into better-trained provinces, which nature fitted rather for wrestling with the soil—practices which age badly

[Note: [Col. 1040C] “Age badly.” There are two interpretations here. Either the practices of the wrestling school are said to be aging badly among the Carthaginians because, when they had nearly fallen into disuse, Severus revived them; or they are said to age badly because boxers rarely grow old. **LE PR.**]

and labor to no purpose—along with the muddy anointing, rolling in dust, and dry fattening?

[Note: [Col. 1040C] “Dry fattening.” The great scholar errs in interpreting *arida saginatio* as ξηραλοιφή (*xēraloiphē*, “dry anointing”), since it is ξηροφαγία (*xērophagia*, “a dry diet”), which was peculiar to athletes. **SALM.**]

Whence comes it that among certain Numidians

[Note: [Col. 1040C] “Among certain Numidians.” He calls the Carthaginians Numidians to some extent, since they are neighbors of the Numidians. **RIG.**]

some even wear horsehair,

[Note: [Col. 1040C] “Even wear horsehair.” They had a mane of horsehair upon their helmets. **RIG.**]

while the razor shaves close to the skin and only the crown is spared the blade?

[Note: [Col. 1040C] “The razor close to the skin, and only the crown spared the blade.” The beard is shaved close to the skin with a sharper shave, while only the head is left unshorn. He uses “crown” for “head.” **RIG.**]

Whence, among shaggy and bristling men, comes resin so rapacious from the buttocks,

[Note: [Col. 1040D] “Resin so rapacious from the armpit.” Hence the *alipilarius*, who removed the hair of the armpits with resin and pitch-plaster. For *alipila* was resin with which the armpits were depilated. **SALM.**]

and tweezers so thievish at the chin?

[Note: [Col. 1040D] “Tweezers so thievish at the chin”—snatching, stealing, and plucking away the hairs. **RIG.**]

It is a marvel that these things are done without the *pallium*. This whole business belongs to its Asia. What have you, Libya and Europe, to do with the fastidious cleanliness of the exercise ground,

[Note: [Col. 1040D] “The fastidious cleanliness of the exercise ground.” Athletes and wrestlers exercised naked in covered tracks and colonnades; consequently, they took the greatest care over the body and its cleanliness. **RIG.**]

when you do not know how to clothe such practices? For what sort of thing is it, in truth, to be depilated in the Greek manner

[Note: [Col. 1040B] “To be flayed,” **Fran.**]

rather than dressed in it? [Col. 1040B]

## CHAPTER IV

A change of dress comes close to being blameworthy only if it changes not custom but nature.

[Note: [Col. 1040D] “To change one’s dress.” This is equivalent to saying that a change of dress becomes a disgrace only under this condition. Yet one garment is not a disgrace to another garment; it is a disgrace to the person. **SALM.**]

[Note: [Col. 1040B] “A disgrace of attire,” **Fran.**; “close to blame,” **Saml.**]

There is a considerable difference between deference to an age and religious obligation. Let custom keep faith with time, and nature with God.

[Note: [Col. 1040D] “Let custom keep faith with time.” Salmasius splendidly restored this passage in conformity with Tertullian’s meaning and hand. Certainly custom ought to keep faith with time, since custom itself is nothing other than long-standing usage through time. Thus one who changes custom despises only time. But nature owes fidelity to God, namely, to its author; for God created nature, and the majesty of the divine hands is impressed upon it. Man himself is the foremost part of nature. Human nature itself therefore owes fidelity to God its creator. If it breaks faith, if it violates or defrauds its own nature by the effeminization of its male character, or by any other falsification, then it is truly guilty against nature and the divine majesty. **RIG.**]

[Note: [Col. 1040B] “Religious obligation to God,” old editions.]

[Col. 1041A] Thus the hero of Larissa shook nature by changing himself into a maiden: he who had been nourished on the marrow of wild beasts—which was also the origin of the name he acquired,

[Note: [Col. 1041C] “Which was also the origin of the name he acquired.” From this he adopted and secured his name. **RIG.**]

since his lips had abstained from tasting breasts; he who had been educated in a craggy school by a rude, forest-dwelling,

[Note: [Col. 1041C] “With the crag-dweller and forest-dweller.” *Rupex* is not derived from *rupes*, “rocks,” for its first syllable is short, but from the Greek ῥύπαξ (*rhypax*), “uncultivated”; so too *petrones* derives from *petrae*. **SALM.**]

monstrous instructor.

[Note: [Col. 1041D] “A monstrous instructor.” That is, a monstrous preceptor or teacher. He means Chiron, the Centaur composed of horse and man. **RIG.**]

You may tolerate it if, as a boy, he yielded to his mother’s anxiety; but certainly once he was a little stage-player,

[Note: [Col. 1041D] “A little stage-woman.” In the glossaries, *histriculus* and *hirticulus*: δασύπρωκτος (*dasuprōktos*), “hairy-buttocked.” **RIG.**]

[Note: [Col. 1041C] *Ustriculas*, **Fran.**]

once he had secretly performed the man’s part for someone,

[Note: [Col. 1041D] “Performed secretly.” *Clanculum*, “secretly.” **RIG.**]

[Note: [Col. 1041C] “Secretly for someone,” **Fran.**]

he still submitted to trailing a woman’s robe,

[Note: [Col. 1041D] “To trail a woman’s robe.” That is, to wear a more flowing robe. **SALM.**]

arranging his hair, painting his skin, consulting a mirror, fondling his neck, and even feminizing his ear by piercing it—as the round image

[Note: [Col. 1041D] “The round image,” στρογγύλη (*strongylē*): a statue whose face and torso are represented in relief upon a shield. From this comes the expression which even our common people use, *La trogne d’un tel*, “So-and-so’s mug.” **RIG.**]

[Note: [Col. 1041C] “Statue,” **Fran.**]

at Sigeum preserves it. Of course, afterward he became a soldier, for necessity restored his sex. The signal for battle had sounded, and the weapons were not far away. “Iron itself,” he says, “attracts the man.” But if he had continued to be a girl even after that stimulus, he might also have married.

Behold, [Col. 1041B] then, a transformation—a double monstrosity indeed: from man to woman, and presently from woman to man, when neither should the truth have been denied nor the deception confessed. Both changes of dress were evil: one was against nature, the other against safety.

Lust transformed a man by dress even more disgracefully than did any maternal fear—although he is worshiped by you who ought rather to be ashamed of him: that club-and-arrow-bearing wearer of hides, who offset the entire lot implied by his epithet with feminine attire. So much was permitted to the secret dalliance of Lydia that Hercules was prostituted in Omphale, and Omphale in Hercules. Where was Diomedes, and where his blood-soaked mangers? Where was Busiris and his funeral-pyre altars? Where was Geryon, three yet one? His club would have preferred still to stink of their brains when it was drenched in perfumes.

The ancient blood of the Hydra [Col. 1042A] and the Centaurs was now being removed from his arrows with the pumice stone used for the mirror,

[Note: [Col. 1041D] “Was being removed with the pumice stone used for the mirror.” I know that mirrors were commonly made in antiquity from silver and bronze, and that these could properly be rubbed and polished with pumice; but I do not see what resemblance there is between a mirror and arrows. **SALM.**]

while extravagance mocked him, so that after piercing monsters they might perhaps sew a garland. Not even the shoulders of a modest woman, or of some virago, could have entered beneath the hide of so great a beast unless they had long been softened, robbed of strength, and thoroughly hardened—

[Note: [Col. 1041C] “Perfumed,” **Fran.**]

something I hope was accomplished in Omphale’s case with balsam or fenugreek perfume. I believe the mane too submitted to the comb. Lest the lion’s hard roughness

[Note: [Col. 1041D] “The lion’s hard roughness.” Σκίρρία, σκληρότης (*skirria, sklērotēs*), the hardness of the lion’s hide, which was never softened but grew dry and bristling through being worn untreated. **RIG.**]

[Note: [Col. 1041C] *Stiria*, **Fran.**; *ciria*, **Seml.**]

should chafe the enervated neck, its gaping mouth was stuffed with hair, and the molars were outlined amid the sidelocks.

[Note: [Col. 1041D] “The molars outlined amid the sidelocks.” *Antiae* are locks of hair διὰ τῶν κροτάφων κρεμάμεναι, “hanging down along the temples,” or, as another glossary has it, τρίχες μεταξὺ τῶν κεράτων τῶν βοῶν, “hairs between the horns of cattle.” I learned from Salmasius that some locks, τὰς ὑπὲρ τὸ μέτωπον, “those above the forehead,” were called *capronae*; others, ἐπὶ πλαγίου, “at the side,” were called *antiae*, *remulsae*, and, by Apuleius, *antependulae*; and still others were grown κατόπιν, “behind.” **LE PR.**]

[Note: [Col. 1042C] “The molars outlined amid the sidelocks,” **Fran.**]

The entire insulted face would have roared if it could. Nemea, at least—if there was any guardian spirit of that place—groaned, for then it looked about and realized that it had lost its lion. What Hercules must have looked like in Omphale’s silk, Omphale herself—portrayed in the harlot Hercules—has already depicted.

But Cleomachus [Col. 1042B] the boxer, who had entered the lists before the Tirynthian,

[Note: [Col. 1042C] “Before the Tirynthian.” Hercules was certainly the founder of gymnastic contests, but he boxed and wrestled by strength, not by skill. Hence the ancients praised his bodily powers and native strength in contests, not his technique. **SALM.**]

after flowing away from masculinity at Olympia in an incredible transformation,

[Note: [Col. 1042C] “Had flowed away from masculinity.” He means that the boxer had dissolved into the softness of feminine passivity, was drenched with perfume, and wore flowing clothes. **RIG.**]

beaten within the skin and beyond it, was now fit to be crowned among the fullers of Novius and deservedly commemorated by Lentulus the mime-writer in his *Men of Catina*. Just as he filled the marks left by the boxing thongs with bracelets,

[Note: [Col. 1042D] “He filled the marks left by the boxing thongs with bracelets.” In place of the boxing thongs, he put bracelets upon his arms. **RIG.**]

[Note: [Col. 1042C] “The tops,” **Fran.**]

[Note: [Col. 1042C] “With diseased ornaments,” **Fran.**]

so too he cast off the coarse texture of the training cloak in exchange for some ensemble of translucent fabric.

[Note: [Col. 1042D] “The coarse texture of the training cloak.” A coarse *endromis*, woven, that is, from rough, thick thread. **RIG.**]

[Note: [Col. 1042D] “An ensemble of translucent fabric.” *Multicia* is also the name for any soft, delicate, and translucent garments such as women usually wear. Juvenal sufficiently indicates this:

> . . . But what  
> Will others not do, when you put on translucent robes,  
> Creticus?

And in Satire VI:

> Showing moist translucent cloth in its suspicious creases.

**RIG.**]

[Note: [Col. 1042C] “Built up,” **Fran.**]

Physcon and Sardanapalus must be passed over in silence: had they not been notorious for their lusts, no one would otherwise know that they were kings. They must be passed over lest they in turn mutter something about certain of your Caesars, who were equally shameful—lest perhaps canine constancy have been commissioned to point out a Caesar more unclean than Physcon and more effeminate than Sardanapalus, and indeed a second Nero.

[Note: [Col. 1042D] “A second Nero.” Domitian, who is called a portion of Nero in the *Apology*, col. 293. *Subnero*, like Cicero’s *Submarius*, book X, letter 1. **RIG.**—“A second Nero.” That is, one who came very close to Nero. Domitian was called the Nero of his age. Thus Tullius, letter 1, book X, *To Atticus*, said *Sumbarius* of a man who equaled Marius in cruelty. **LE PR.**]

Nor is the force of empty glory any less ardent in changing clothing, [Col. 1043A] even when manhood remains intact. Every passion is heat; but when it is fanned into affectation, its blaze is already the fire of glory. You therefore have, sweltering from this fuel, the great king who was less than his glory. He had conquered the Median nation and was conquered by Median dress. Removing the cuirass of his triumph,

[Note: [Col. 1043C] “Removing the cuirass of his triumph, he descended into captive trousers.” By taking off the cuirass in which he had triumphed, he descended from that eminence and almost subjected himself when he put on the captive *sarabara*. These are the garments of the barbarians whom he had defeated and slain in battle. **LE PR.**]

he descended into captive trousers.

[Note: [Col. 1043C] “He descended into captive trousers.” Are not those interpreters ridiculous who want Alexander to have died in his own breeches? For so they understood the verb *decessit*, as though he had died in his *sarabara*. **SALM.**—“Into captive *sarabara*.” I would think that *saraballa* ought to be read here, for Daniel III has *saraballim*, meaning cloaks or mantles. **LE PR.**]

He stripped bare the breast engraved with the imprints of armor-scales by covering it with translucent cloth; and, while it was still panting from the labor of war, he gently cooled it as the silk fanned it. The Macedonian was not sufficiently swollen in spirit unless a still more inflated garment had cast him down.

Except that, I think, philosophers themselves also affect something of the sort. I hear, indeed, of philosophy being practiced in purple. If a philosopher may wear purple, why not also the gilded woman’s shoe?

[Note: [Col. 1043C] “Why not also the gilded woman’s shoe?” Tertullian himself, in *On Idolatry*, p. 108: “The slipper and the gilded woman’s shoe are daily covered with gold.” **RIG.**—The *baxa* was a kind of gilded woman’s footwear. **SALM.**]

[Note: [Col. 1043B] “A Tyrian shoe,” **Fran.**]

Unless Tyrian footwear is gilded, it is hardly Greek at all. [Col. 1043B] Someone will say—

[Note: [Col. 1043C] “Unless gold is becoming to those who are hardly Greek,” **Fran.**]

yet did not another philosopher walk about both clad in silk and bronze-shod in sandals? Fittingly indeed: so that he might make some tinkling sound to accompany his Bacchic garments, he walked as though with a cymbal.

But if the Diogenes of that place had then barked from his jar, he would have borne the whole Empedocles—not merely his mud-stained feet, as the admirers of Platonic dew know—into the inner sanctuaries of the sewer goddesses,

[Note: [Col. 1043D] “Into the inner sanctuaries of the sewer goddesses.” Into the sewers, over which the Cloacinae preside—as many Cloacinae, therefore, as there are sewers. Pliny, however, asserts that Venus Cloacina was named not from the sewers over which she presided but from *cluere*, that is, “to purify.” For this reason the African author said *Cloacinae*, in the plural, rather than *Cloacina*. **SALM.**]

so that he who had raved that he was a heavenly being might, as a god, greet first his sisters,

[Note: [Col. 1043D] “First his sisters.” Very appropriately, indeed, he gave that stinking god Empedocles the most stinking sewer goddesses as sisters. **RIG.**]

and then human beings.

[Note: [Col. 1044B] “Goddesses,” **Fran.**]

Such forms of dress, then, as effect a departure from nature and modesty deserve to be fixed with the eye, pointed out with the finger,

[Note: [Col. 1043D] “Pointed out with the finger.” This is the same as indicating and marking someone with an outstretched finger. **SALM.**]

and betrayed by a nod. Certainly, if anyone trails a delicate robe over the ground with Menandrian looseness, let the comic poet beside him be heard saying, “What sort of cloak is this madman ruining?”

[Col. 1044A] Yet the general prevalence of the practice now presents, to the extent that the furrowed brow [*episcynium*] of censorial severity has long since relaxed its denunciation, freedmen in equestrian dress,

[Note: [Col. 1043D] “With the furrowed brow relaxed.” With the eyebrow less tightly drawn and contracted, and less severe in its denunciation and rebuke. **RIG.**]

half-scorched slaves in the clothing of free men,

[Note: [Col. 1043D] “Half-scorched slaves in the clothing of free men.” You may see men who are still *mastigiae*, marked by the welts of the lashes with which they were seared, clothed in “liberal” garments—that is, in the clothing of free men. **RIG.** [Col. 1044C] ὁ μαστιγίας or στιγματίας (*ho mastigias* or *stigmatias*), “the scourged or branded man”; *stigmaticus* in Tullius, *stigmosus* in Pliny. **LE PR.**]

surrendered foreigners in the dress of the freeborn, rustics in city dress, buffoons in the clothes of the forum, and civilians in military dress. The undertaker, the pimp, and the trainer of gladiators dress like you.

Turn also to the women, and you have before your eyes what Caecina Severus gravely impressed upon the senate: matrons appearing in public without the *stola*. Indeed, under the decrees of Lentulus the augur,

[Note: [Col. 1044C] “Under the decrees of Lentulus the augur.” Gnaeus Lentulus the augur was consul first with Publius Lentulus and again with Marcus Crassus in the time of Augustus. No mention of the decree made under him concerning the dress of matrons occurs in Seneca or Suetonius, who spoke of him. **MERC.**]

a woman who had thus divested herself of her rank incurred the same penalty as for sexual disgrace:

[Note: [Col. 1044C] “The same penalty as for sexual disgrace.” So shameful a divestment of rank incurred the same penalty as adultery or fornication. **RIG.**]

for, since forms of dress are the signs and guardians of dignity and obstacles to the practice of procuring, certain women had deliberately ceased to use them. But now, by procuring themselves so that they may be approached more readily, they have renounced the *stola*, the *supparum*, the little crested headpiece, and the wig,

[Note: [Col. 1044C] “The *stola*, the *supparum*, the little crested headpiece, and the wig,” etc. Turnebus reads “little shoe,” but the common reading is more pleasing. For according to Festus, *crepitulum* signifies an ornament of the head which makes a rattling sound when the head moves. Turnebus says that *caliendrum* signifies a covering for the head, from the Greek καγγανον (*kanganon*); it is also used by Arnobius in book VI *Against the Nations*. **PAM.**]

and now even the litters [Col. 1044B] and chairs in which, even in public, they were kept as though at home and in privacy. But one man extinguishes his own eyes; another kindles eyes that are not his.

Look at the she-wolves who are marketplaces for common lusts—even the procuresses and sorceresses themselves.

[Note: [Col. 1044D] “Even the procuresses and sorceresses themselves.” He joins the *fictrix* to the she-wolf, the procuress to the prostitute. A *fictrix* is a dissembler, one who fashions wax images for the winning of love or for destruction: a witch and procuress. **RIG.**]

And although it is better to avert one’s eyes from such disgraceful exhibitions of chastity murdered in public, nevertheless look, even with your gaze raised above them,

[Note: [Col. 1044D] “Even with your gaze raised above them.” That is, with the eyes looking sideways. **RIG.**]

and you will now see matrons. When the attendant of the latrines makes silk flutter, consoles with necklaces a neck more unclean than its place,

[Note: [Col. 1044D] “Consoles with necklaces a neck more unclean than its place.” With the shamelessness of the most absurd luxury, she consoles her neck, condemned to the wretched service of cleaning a latrine. **RIG.**]

thrusts hands privy to every shameful part into bracelets which even matrons would have been reckless to assume from the gifts awarded to brave men, and puts a clean, perhaps even a red patrician, shoe upon an unclean leg—

[Note: [Col. 1044D] “Upon an unclean leg a clean,” etc. Since Roman shoes covered part of the leg, they were high boots; hence Ovid, *Art of Love*, book III:

> Let an ugly foot always be concealed in snow-white leather.

Of red shoes, some were boots, others hooked shoes. Those who had held magistracies wore red shoes; soldiers wore hobnailed shoes; everyone else wore boots and shoes of ὠμοβύρσινος (*ōmobyrsinos*), “raw hide.” **LE PR.**]

why do you not look at those people, or [Col. 1045A] likewise at those forms of dress which falsely claim a religious sanction for their novelty? Thus persons are initiated into the rites of Ceres because of clothing entirely white, and because of the distinguishing headband and the privilege of the ceremonial cap;

[Note: [Col. 1045C] “Because of the distinguishing headband and the privilege of the ceremonial cap.” The headband and ceremonial cap were the marks or privileges of matrons—specifically, matrons initiated into the rites of Ceres. The cap should be understood as white. **RIG.**]

because of a different association with gloomy clothing

[Note: [Col. 1045C] “Gloomy clothing.” Black clothing. **RIG.**]

and a forbidding fleece above the head,

[Note: [Col. 1045C] “A forbidding fleece above the head.” A grim one: Bellona, or Minerva, shod and wearing a helmet of dark form. Tertullian himself, *On the Testimony of the Soul*, p. 82. **RIG.**]

minds are put to flight in Bellona’s temple;

[Note: [Col. 1045C] “Minds are put to flight in Bellona’s temple.” The fanatic loses his mind when seized by frenzy in Bellona’s shrine. A Bellonarian is ὁ θεοφορούμενος (*ho theophoroumenos*), “one possessed by a god.” **RIG.**—The common reading is “they flee to the hills of Bellona.” Even before the first appearance of our edition of Tertullian, we knew that Augustine, in the acts concerning Caecilian’s acquittal, mentioned a hill of Bellona near Carthage, to which certain persons withdrew during the persecution. But since no one has yet shown either that there were several hills of Bellona or that the Bellonarians were driven into the hills of Bellona—and since, on the contrary, the most ancient authors have reported that they were called Bellonarians because fanatics were seized by violent frenzy in Bellona’s sanctuary—we readily allowed ourselves to be persuaded that the common reading could in no way be defended here and that the text must therefore read: “minds are put to flight in Bellona’s temple.” In Bellona’s temple, namely, minds are put to flight: the minds of those from whom mind and reason are taken away by frenzy. Minds are said to be put to flight in the same way as reason is said to flee, or minds to wander, become alienated, be moved, hurled headlong, or agitated—and, in the opposite sense, to return. Salmasius approves “minds are put to flight,” corresponding to the Greek construction ἐξιστάναι φρενός (*existanai phrenos*), “to drive out of one’s mind.” Septimius said “minds are put to flight” just as at col. 1034 he said, “Campania was taken away from Pompey.” **LE PR.**]

[Note: [Col. 1045B] “Hills,” **Fran.**]

the ostentation of a broader purple stripe

[Note: [Col. 1045D] “The ostentation of a broader purple stripe.” A broader strip of purple surrounds and clothes Saturn. **RIG.**]

and the overlay of Galatian red commend Saturn;

[Note: [Col. 1045D] “Galatian red.” Scarlet. Pliny: “The red berry of Galatia is cochineal.” **RIG.**]

and this very *pallium*, arranged with rather affected precision and made Greek by its sandal,

[Note: [Col. 1045D] “Made Greek by its sandal.” “Greekified by the sandal” means “wearing a Greek sandal.” **RIG.**]

[Note: [Col. 1045B] “Chalked in the Greek manner,” **Fran.**]

flatters Aesculapius. How much more, then, should you arraign it and press it upon the eyes, if—though now guilty only of simple and unaffected superstition—it were nevertheless guilty of superstition?

But when it first clothes that wisdom which rejects the most empty superstitions, then most certainly the *pallium* is a more majestic garment than every hide and robe, and, above all priestly conical caps

[Note: [Col. 1045B] “Conical caps and titles,” **Seml.**]

and ritual headdresses, a priestly array.

[Note: [Col. 1045D] “A priestly elevation.” Priestly adornment. Thus Persius, Satire I:

> See how we now teach heroic sentiments  
> To men accustomed to chatter trifles in Greek—

that is, “heroes,” or “heroic sentiments.” **RIG.**]

Lower your eyes, I advise you; [Col. 1045B] revere the dress which, for the present, proclaims your renunciation of your one error.

## CHAPTER V
Yet, you say, such a change—from toga to pallium? What then, if it were from diadem and sceptre? Did Anacharsis make a different change when he preferred philosophy to the throne of Scythia? There are no outward signs for one who has passed to something better [Note: [Col. 1045B] *Transgressus*, Fran.]; this is the one thing this garb provides. Even before that, its simple ease of putting on [Note: [Col. 1046C] *Ad simplicem captatelam.* Salmasius thus restored the text from traces of the old reading—that is, “the simple convenience of taking up and putting on.” Tertullian did not wish to say *capturam*, for that relates to plunder; nor *captionem*, for that relates to fraud; nor *captum*, for that relates to intellect. Therefore, on the same pattern by which he elsewhere says *peccatelam*, *monelam*, and *fovelam*, and by which ordinary speech likewise says *tutelam*, *cautelam*, and *loquelam*, he preferred to say *captatelam*. RIG.] [Col. 1046A] [Note: [Col. 1045C] *Spectatilam*, Fran.] entails no trouble. Indeed, there is no need even for the craftsman who on the preceding day shapes the folds from the beginning, then draws them out into strips [Note: [Col. 1046C] *Deducat in talias.* Into folds and pleats, as though into cuttings. Writers on agriculture called cuttings *taleae* and *taleolae*. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1046B] *Tilias*, Fran.], and consigns the whole contrivance of the gathered boss to forceps as its guardians; who then, at dawn, first gathers the tunic with a belt—though it would have been better to weave it to a more restrained size [Note: [Col. 1046B] *Moderatiorem*, Seml.]—then inspects the boss again and reshapes anything that has strayed out of line, lets one part hang down on the left, but draws back from the shoulders the sweep from which the fold arises, since the panels are already running short, excludes the right arm and heaps it still further toward the left [Note: [Col. 1046C] *And, leaving the right arm free, heaps it still further toward the left.* Among the ancient Romans the hands were kept within the garment or toga; afterward, however, the toga came to be thrown beneath the right arm, leaving the hand free. Septimius is speaking here of the latter arrangement. The philosophers of Greece wore the pallium in this way. LE PR.], together with another equal panel reserved for the back [Note: [Col. 1046D] *Reserved for the back.* Dedicated and kept for the purpose of adorning the back also. RIG.], and thus clothes the man with a burden.

Finally, I shall question your own conscience: when dressed in the toga, do you feel yourself clothed first, or burdened? If you deny it, I shall follow you home and see what you hasten to do immediately upon crossing the threshold. Surely the removal of no other garment [Col. 1046B] is greeted with such delight as that of the toga. We say nothing of shoes, the toga’s peculiar instrument of torture [Note: [Col. 1046D] *Shoes, the toga’s peculiar instrument of torture.* For shoes were put on together with the toga. Thus, wearing shoes that fettered their feet, they carried the toga as a burden. RIG.], a most unclean protection for the feet—and indeed a deceptive one. For who would not find it better to have bare feet stiff with cold or heat than feet fettered in shoes [Note: [Col. 1046B] *Hook-footed*, Fran.]? The Venetian shoemakers have devised a mighty safeguard for walking [Note: [Col. 1046D] *The Venetian shoemakers have devised.* Formerly the corrupt reading was *Veneriae*; it is, however, *Venetian shoemakers’ workshops*, in which Venetian hides were prepared for making shoes. For just as the Venetian territory possessed a great abundance of cattle, so it also had hides for shoes. LE PR.]: effeminate boots.

But nothing is more convenient than the pallium, even when doubled, since, when it is put on, dressing nowhere entails the delay of Crates [Note: [Col. 1046C] *More n. v. componitur*, Fran.]. Indeed, its entire construction [Note: [Col. 1046D] *Its entire construction, etc.* With a single cast around the body, the philosopher’s pallium confines and surrounds the body while leaving it free and unencumbered. LE PR.] consists in covering one loosely [Note: [Col. 1046D] *To cover loosely.* With ostentation discarded, by a single cast around the body. RIG.]. This it does with a single cast, one that is assuredly nowhere unkind, and so covers every part of the man at once. Veiling the shoulder, it leaves it exposed or encloses it; in either case it clings to the shoulder. It props up nothing, constricts nothing, and is not troubled about the reliability of its panels.
