It readily arranges itself and is readily restored; even when it is taken off [Note: [Col. 1047B] *Put away*, Fran.], it is not entrusted to any cross for the next day [Note: [Col. 1047C] *It is not entrusted to any cross for the next day.* This is the same as what he said above: it is not consigned to forceps as its guardians. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1047B] *To a block*, Fran.]. If there is an under-tunic beneath it [Note: [Col. 1047C] *Above it*, Fran.], it is spared the torture of a belt. If any footwear is put on, it is an entirely clean affair; alternatively, the feet are bare—and certainly more manly than when shod.

So much for the pallium for the moment, in answer to all that you reproached under its name in the assembly [Note: [Col. 1047C] *All that you reproached under its name in the assembly.* All that you reproached me with in the assembly on account of the pallium. Plautus used *incomitiare* in the *Curculio* and opposed it to *inforare*, in an obscene sense. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1048B] *Stirred up*, Fran.]. Now it also issues a challenge concerning occupation [Note: [Col. 1047C] *Now it also issues a challenge concerning occupation.* From this point the pallium speaks—or rather, the philosopher in the pallium. RIG.].

“I owe nothing,” it says, “to the forum, the Campus, or the senate-house. I keep watch over no official duty, preoccupy no speaker’s platform, haunt no governor’s residence; I do not sniff about the market channels [Note: [Col. 1047C] *I do not sniff about the channels.* The first edition of Rhenanus reads, *I do not worship the channels*. Salmasius correctly emended it to *sniff about*. According to Festus, they were called ‘channels of the forum’ because people gathered around the forum’s channels. This, however, concerns the marketplace where merchandise is bought and sold. RIG.]; I do not worship the railings [Note: [Col. 1047C] *I do not worship the railings.* This may be a sound reading; nevertheless, I wonder whether one might equally read *I do not assail them*. For advocates, when undertaking a case and presenting themselves before the judges, are said to ‘assail the railings.’ LE PR.]. I do not wear down the benches, confound the laws, bellow out lawsuits, sit in judgment, or serve as a soldier. I have withdrawn from the people. My sole occupation is with myself [Note: [Col. 1047D] *My sole occupation is with myself.* I am wholly occupied in avoiding sin. I have enough business attending to myself. Thus that student of Epictetan wisdom knew that he must guard against himself as against an enemy and a plotter: ἐνὶ τε λόγῳ, ὡς ἐχθρὸν ἑαυτὸν παραφυλάσσει, καὶ ἐπίβουλον, ‘in a word, he watches himself as an enemy and a conspirator.’ RIG.], unless it be that I care for nothing but freedom from care.

“You will enjoy a better life more in retirement than in public display—but you will brand it idle [Note: [Col. 1048B] *But idle and infamous*, Fran.]. ‘One must live, of course, for country, empire, and commonwealth.’ Such was once the maxim: ‘No one is born for another who is to die for himself.’ Yet certainly, when the discussion reaches Epicurus and Zeno [Note: [Col. 1047D] *Certainly, when the discussion reaches Epicurus, etc.* The attentive reader must remember that these words are spoken by the pallium of Crates—that is, by a Cynic, not a Christian. SALM.], you call those sages who were masters of an entire doctrine of repose, and who consecrated it under the title of the highest and sole pleasure.

“Nevertheless, perhaps I too shall be permitted to render some slight service to the public. From any boundary-stone or altar [Note: [Col. 1047D] *From any boundary-stone or altar.* The speaker in the pallium here is plainly a philosopher, not a Christian. For I do not think that any Christian at that time could have been induced to mount an altar in order to deliver a speech, since Christians detested altars and sacrifices and, in those days, blew upon them in contempt as they passed. RIG.] I am accustomed to prescribe remedies for morals, remedies that will confer sound health upon public affairs, cities, and empires more successfully than your services do. Indeed, if I proceed to sharp weapons against you [Note: [Col. 1047D] *If I proceed to sharp weapons.* If I proceed to fight you with sharp and decisive weapons, not with practice weapons that are blunt. Ovid [Col. 1048C]: ‘Now put away the blunt swords; let the fight be with sharp ones.’ SALM.], the toga has done more harm to the commonwealth than cuirasses have.

“Yet I flatter no vices, spare no lethargies and no scab. I apply the cautery to the ambition by which Marcus Tullius bought a round citrus-wood tabletop for five hundred thousand sesterces, and by which Asinius Gallus paid twice as much for a table of the same Mauretanian wood. Ah, at what great fortunes they valued stains in wood! I cauterize likewise the ambition by which Sulla had dishes made weighing a hundred pounds. Indeed, I fear this scale may be too small, since Drusillanus, a slave of Claudius, constructed a first-course dish weighing five hundred pounds [Note: [Col. 1048C] *A first-course dish weighing five hundred pounds.* A dish made of five hundred pounds of silver. Tertullian calls what Pliny calls a dish here a *promulsis*. How many scholars today insist that *promulsis* means the course before dinner, or an appetizer! But all antiquity always used this word for a vessel or dish. RIG.], perhaps necessary for the tables just mentioned; and if a workshop was built for it [Col. 1048B], a dining room ought also to have been built.

“I plunge the scalpel equally into that cruelty by which Vedius Pollio threw his slaves to be attacked by lampreys [Note: [Col. 1048C] *Delighting, of course, in a novel cruelty.* Seneca censures this cruelty and at the same time tells the story in *On Anger* III, chapter 40. One of the slaves had broken a crystal vessel; Vedius ordered him seized, and he was not even to die an ordinary death: he was ordered to be thrown to the lampreys kept in an enormous fishpond. Who would not suppose that he did this from luxurious indulgence? It was cruelty, etc. Pliny IX.23. RIG.]. Delighting, of course, in a novel cruelty, he was pleased to gather beasts from among fishes—terrestrial beasts, toothless, clawless, and hornless [Note: [Col. 1048C] *Terrestrial beasts.* Pliny calls those fish terrestrial which live in caves containing water. The scholar who judged that Septimius used these words in the nominative plural conjectured entirely correctly; the following words must accordingly be read: ‘toothless, clawless, and hornless.’ Pliny XII.23: ‘as though the beasts of the earth were insufficient for this purpose, and because in another class he could not watch an entire man likewise being torn apart.’ RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1048D] *He chose to collect wild beasts from among fish, etc.* To confine them in fishpond preserves; Pliny: ‘which an enormous fishpond contained.’ RIG.]—certainly to be cooked immediately, so that in their entrails he himself might taste something of his slaves’ bodies.

“I shall cut away the gluttony by which Hortensius the orator was the first to bring himself to kill a peacock for food; by which Ausidius Lurco was the first to corrupt animals’ bodies through fattening and, by forced foods [Note: [Col. 1048D] *By forced foods.* So the old books read: *by forced foods*, that is, by putting before them as fodder things that the nature of the animals would by no means seek. RIG.], advanced them toward an artificial flavor; by which Asinius Celer paid six thousand sesterces for the dish of a single mullet [Note: [Col. 1048D] *The dish of a single mullet.* Those versed in ancient coinage know that individual *sestertia* equal a thousand sestertii; but scarcely two people know that when *sestertii* is used, *nummi* is understood, while when *sestertia* is used, *pondo* is understood. Thus one *sestertium pondo* was worth two and a half pounds of silver, just as one *sestertius as* was worth two and a half asses, and likewise a *sestertius pes* and similar expressions; but the sestertius coin afterward began to be exchanged for four asses, though formerly it was exchanged for only two and a half. SALM.] [Col. 1049A]; by which Aesop the actor confiscated a hundred-thousand-sesterce dish out of birds equally costly—every one of them songbirds or talking birds [Note: [Col. 1049B] *Out of songbirds or talking birds.* Birds vocal either with some kind of song or with human speech. Pliny. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1049B] *He confiscated a hundred-thousand-sesterce dish.* Among his confiscated property he had one hundred thousand, which he could pay for that dish. [Col. 1049C] RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1049B] *Six hundred thousand*, Fran.]. After such a delicacy, Aesop’s son was capable of hungering at still greater expense: for he swallowed a pearl, precious even by its very name, lest, I suppose, he should have dined more beggarly than his father.

“I pass over the Neros, Apiciuses, and Rufuses. I shall administer a purgative to the impurity of Scaurus, the gambling of Curius, and the drunkenness of Antony. And remember meanwhile that these were merely a few among many toga-wearers [Note: [Col. 1049C] *And remember meanwhile that these, etc.* The text must certainly be read as Rhenanus printed it: ‘And remember meanwhile that these were merely a few among many toga-wearers. What men like these will one find under the pallium? Not easily. Who will draw out and discharge these suppurations of the state unless speech clothed in the pallium?’ RIG.]. What men like these will one find under the pallium? Not easily will anyone draw out and discharge these suppurations of the state [Note: [Col. 1049B] *Evaporate*, Fran.] unless speech is clothed in the pallium.”

## CHAPTER VI

“You have persuaded me,” it says, “by speech, the wisest medicine. Yet even if eloquence remains silent, whether withdrawn through speechlessness or restrained through modesty—for even a tongueless philosophy is content with its life—the garb itself [Col. 1049B] makes itself heard. Thus, indeed, a philosopher is heard merely by being seen. At my approach I suffuse vices with shame. Who, on seeing his rival, does not suffer? Who can bear with his eyes the man whom he cannot bear in his thoughts? Great is the benefit of the pallium: at the very thought of it, wicked morals at least blush.

“Let philosophy now see what profit it brings, for it is not alone with me. I also possess other arts useful to the public. From my cloth are clothed the first instructor in letters, the first trainer of the voice [Note: [Col. 1049C] *The first trainer of the voice.* They understand ‘trainer of the voice’ as a vocal teacher, incorrectly; for I cannot believe that in those first rudiments of letters a boy in former times studied under a vocal teacher, unless some wished to become tragic or comic singers. SALM.] [Note: [Col. 1050B] *Untangler*, Venet.], the first reckoner upon sand [Note: [Col. 1050B] *The first reckoner upon sand.* He means the arithmetician who demonstrated various combinations of numbers to his pupils upon a counting-board sprinkled with dust. RIG.], the grammarian, rhetorician, sophist, physician, poet, the man who plays music, the man who interprets the stars [Note: [Col. 1050B] *The man who interprets the stars.* An interpreter of the stars, Book I of *On the Dress of Women*. RIG.], and the man who observes the flight of birds. Every liberal branch of learning is covered by my four corners.

“Certainly, Roman knights come first; yet gladiatorial trainers [Note: [Col. 1050C] *Accendones.* So the old books read. By *accendones* he means trainers who inflame gladiators for combat. Thus Laberius called those who covet another’s property *appetones*; on the same pattern Varro said *comedones*, and Ammianus Marcellinus *reposcones*. But why should Septimius not have called parasites *accedones*, since they are accustomed to come even when uninvited? For they are also called followers and buffoons. SALM.] and every disgrace of the sword are paraded in the toga. This, presumably, will be the indignity: to pass from toga to pallium.” But that is what the pallium says.

For my own part, I now bring it into fellowship even with the divine sect and discipline. Rejoice, pallium, and [Col. 1050B] exult! A better philosophy has now deemed you worthy, from the time you began to clothe the Christian.

# APPENDICES TO THE AUTHENTIC WORKS OF QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN

## First Appendix

# [Col. 1049] POEMS ATTRIBUTED TO TERTULLIAN

[Col. 1049D] Among scholars it is still universally accepted, with no one dissenting, that the poems which Pamelius judged should be inserted into the volume of Tertullian’s works are spurious and wrongly bear Tertullian’s name. Thus, says Lumper, the five books against Marcion composed in verse are not Tertullian’s.

1. Their style sufficiently proves them unworthy of a man of such outstanding genius: so often guilty of violated prosody, so often unequal to its subject matter, so often blunt when drawing weapons against the enemy.

2. In Book I *Against Marcion*, chapter 1, Tertullian himself states in his preface that he prepared his work against that heresiarch a second [Col. 1050D] and a third time, and that he then annulled it by a fuller composition. Certainly it was annulled in the same genre of discourse in which it had first been hurriedly written. Since, therefore, the work against Marcion by which Tertullian annulled the earlier composition is a disputation, not a poem, it follows that the earlier work too was a hastily written disputation, not poetic lucubration.

3. These verses were ascribed to Tertullian by Fabricius on the authority of a single, admittedly unknown and obscure manuscript.

4. None of the ancient writers numbered Tertullian among the ancient poets.

5. The author of these books openly contradicts Tertullian. For in *On the Soul*, chapter 57, Tertullian maintains that it was not Samuel himself but a phantom that had been raised by the Pythoness through evil arts. “Far be it from us,” he says, “to believe that the soul of any holy man, much less of a prophet, was drawn forth by a demon, since we have been taught that Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light, much more into a man of light, and will even affirm himself to be God,” etc. But the author of Book III of the poems against Marcion states the contrary in these verses:

> Wondrous Samuel, who first received the command  
> To anoint kings, to bestow chrism, and reveal men as anointed ones;  
> So praiseworthily did he act throughout the span of life  
> That even after death he retained prophetic rights.

In *On the Prescription of Heretics*, chapter 32, when describing the succession of Saint Peter’s successors in the Roman See, Tertullian teaches that Clement succeeded Peter immediately. But the author of Book III of the poems against Marcion states the contrary in these verses:

> [Col. 1051B] In this chair, in which Peter himself had sat,  
> Great Rome ordered Linus to be placed and sit first;  
> After him Cletus himself received the flock of the fold.  
> By lot Anacletus was appointed his successor,  
> And Clement follows him . . . . . . .

Who could believe that Tertullian was so forgetful of himself that he made statements so contrary and mutually contradictory? It is, moreover, uncertain who the author of that poem was. Nevertheless, this poem against Marcion deserves commendation for certain points, both historical and doctrinal. First, it affirms the eternity of the Word and the twofold nature in Christ Jesus; cites the Apocalypse under the name of John the disciple; relates that Jesus Christ suffered on the same day and in the same place in which Adam fell; attributes the name “Holy Spirit” to Jesus Christ; considers Hermas, surnamed the Shepherd, to have been the brother of Pope Pius; and finally holds that Ezra, filled with the divine Spirit and assisted by his own memory alone, dictated anew the lost books of the Prophets and restored them to the canon of Holy Scripture.

[Col. 1051C] The poems *On the Judgment of the Lord*, *On Genesis*, and *On Sodom* have likewise been falsely attributed to Tertullian. For it must not be believed that so great a man ever had Muses so hostile to him, as Rigault elegantly says. The poem *On Jonah and Nineveh*, which Margarinus de la Bigne published from the manuscript of the most distinguished P. Pithou at the end of volume VIII of the *Library of the Fathers*, must be placed in the same category. Finally, the poem *To a Senator*, which is read among Cyprian’s works in volume III and which Allix considers to have been composed before the age of Constantine, is wholly denied to Tertullian by learned men. As for Gennadius’s book *On Definitions of Faith and Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, formerly attributed to Tertullian, no scholar today assigns it to him, since many things are found there that postdate the third century and are not compatible with him.

On the spurious works of Tertullian, consult Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, second century; Dom Rémy Ceillier, *History of Ecclesiastical Writings*; Dupin, *Ecclesiastical Library*, vol. I, p. 252; Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. III, Life of Tertullian, art. 14; P. Allix, *Dissertation on the Life and Writings of Tertullian*, X.31; Walch, *Patristic Library*, chap. 4, §46; chap. 7, §70. In the dissertation just mentioned, P. Allix says that the poem *On the Judgment* is by Verecundus, an African bishop who flourished around the middle of the sixth century. The same scholar suspects that the books against Marcion were written after the time of Jerome.

Tertullian’s poetic works have appeared many times: namely, together with several Christian poets, in Georg Fabricius, *Works of the Ancient Christian Poets*, Basel, 1564; Michael Maittaire, *Works and Fragments of the Ancient Latin Poets*, London, 1715; in the Pesaro collection of all Latin poems, Pesaro, 1766, vol. V, pp. 1–16. The poem *On Jonah and Nineveh*, with corrections by François Juret, appears in the *Library of the Fathers*, vol. VIII, and at Leipzig, 1681, octavo, at the end of the Daum edition of Paulinus of Périgueux, 1681. Finally, Andreas Rivinus edited all Tertullian’s poetic works and, after Pamelius, Junius, and Barthius, added brief notes: Gotha, 1651. These poems did not appear important enough for us to furnish them with extensive commentaries; it was therefore sufficient to publish the annotations of Pamelius, slight and insubstantial though they are. EDD.

[Col. 1051]

# FIVE BOOKS AGAINST MARCION (C, G, S)

## TO THE READER

[Col. 1051D] It had been decided to omit the poems against Marcion that follow, not only because they appear scarcely worthy of Tertullian, but especially because Septimius himself testifies that they are by no means Tertullian’s. That they are plainly unworthy of a man of such excellent genius is sufficiently indicated by their style: so often guilty of violated prosody, so often unequal to its subject matter, so often blunt and inept when drawing weapons against the enemy.

Finally, at the beginning of his disputations against Marcion—from which I see that arguments for defending these verses are being drawn—Tertullian himself expressly states in his preface that he revised his work a second and a third time. He does not, however, relate that any of those revisions was poetic; indeed, he indicates that none was poetic when he says that he afterward annulled his first little work, which had been composed as though in haste, by a fuller composition. For if he had preluded against Marcion in verse, that work could indeed have been called hurried and preliminary; but if what he afterward annulled by a fuller composition was poetry, it ought to have been annulled by fuller poetry, not by a rhetorical dissertation or a dialectical [Col. 1052D] disputation. For if the genres of writing differed, the treatments of the same subject would have remained distinct: the poet would have played his part, the dialectician his, and the rhetorician his.

What he had published in Greek concerning the veiling of virgins, the crown, and spectacles he afterward published in Latin. He did not, however, annul the Greek works by the Latin ones, but added Latin works to the Greek. If he had wished to annul the Greek works, he would surely have revised and reshaped those earlier ones through later Greek works as well. Thus, whatever writing of his against Marcion he annulled was a disputation, not a poem. He annulled a hurried and insufficiently finished disputation through a later and fuller disputation, and submerged the meagerness of the earlier beneath the abundance of the later.

Let this suffice concerning the first and second products—unless it may also be useful to add that, when publishing the third, Septimius judged it necessary to preface it with an account of those three versions, lest the diversity of the work, found in scattered circulation, confuse anyone. Those words certainly confirm what we said above: namely, that none of the three revisions against Marcion was [Col. 1053A] poetic. For if any had been, it surely ought to have been excepted from the character of the others, since the difference in style would have protected it from all confusion.

One must also observe that Septimius says he annulled that first product; he does not complain that it had been made public. It is therefore no longer credible that anything of it survived except what he himself transferred into the fuller second version. But if we believe that he transferred poetic material, we must also admit that the poet was so thoroughly dismembered that none of his limbs can now be found. Indeed, if anything poetic is observed in those celebrated disputations—such as, perhaps, the description of Pontus that follows the preface—no trace of it appears anywhere in the five books of poems.

Lastly, to remove every doubt: if Septimius’s first product poured forth verses against [Col. 1053B] Marcion, then, when he annulled it, he himself destroyed his verses, and we seek them in vain. The third version, moreover, shows that the second was not poetic, since Septimius declares that the third was composed by correcting and enlarging the second.

We therefore conclude as follows: these verses, whatever their quality, were inscribed with Tertullian’s name by Fabricius, who was induced to do so solely by the authority of some manuscript or other. Experts in such matters know how slight and frivolous that authority must be considered, especially since Fabricius produced no sufficiently competent witness acquainted with that manuscript, while the ancient copies of this most diligently studied author that passed through their hands disclosed nothing poetic. Nor did any ancient writer number Tertullian among the Christian poets.

Nevertheless, although these poems have been badly combed by an uneven versifier, we do not despise them so greatly as to deny that there is anything good in them. Indeed, we affirm that in very many places they can usefully be compared and collated with Septimius’s works against Marcion. We therefore permit them to appear here as appendices. But because we do not know their author with certainty, we give them the name “Anonymous.” VENETIAN EDITOR.

# BOOK I: ON THE ONE GOD

[Col. 1053]

## [NOTE]

Pamelius added this phrase to the title as a kind of brief synopsis, just as he did for the first book *Against Marcion*. He alone annotated this entire poem and judged that these metrical works should not be denied to Tertullian. EDD.

## SYNOPSIS OF BOOK I, FROM TERTULLIAN HIMSELF, AT THE BEGINNING OF BOOK V

[Col. 1053C]

> The first book will recount in order the enemy’s words,  
> Which the mad renegade unlawfully contrived and uttered;  
> Then too the hope of the flesh and Christ’s victory,  
> And a brief description of the forms of false paths.

Georg Fabricius, who was the first to publish these five books among the Christian works of the ancient ecclesiastical poets, considers them—and on this point I do not disagree with him—to be the books mentioned by Tertullian at the beginning of Book I *Against Marcion* in these words:

“If we have previously composed anything **AGAINST MARCION**, let it henceforth fend for itself. We undertake a new work from an old one. I had afterward annulled my first little work, composed as though in haste, by a fuller composition. Before this second version had been adequately supplied with copies, I lost it through the fraud of a man who was then a brother and afterward an apostate; he happened to have transcribed certain portions with the utmost corruption and exhibited them to an audience.”

Together with Fabricius, I acknowledge that this statement is entirely true of the present work. Fabricius complains that there were almost as many errors as words and as many blemishes as verses. He adds that, although he removed very many errors from traces of the ancient text—you see that he possessed a manuscript communicated to him by Johann Herold—nevertheless, he says, “the reader will see from what remains how much still requires [Col. 1054C] correction.” The reader will perceive from our annotations that we too have attempted something in this regard; and we would have done somewhat more if any manuscript had been at hand.

The same scholar adds:

> “The subject itself shows this work of Tertullian to be unfinished. For, following his own impetus until time should permit correction, he did many things contrary to metrical rules. Some of these are excused by the circumstances of time; some can be excused as grammatical figures; and some must be attributed to the author’s haste, since he intended to bring his work, as though merely outlined, back to the anvil, as the saying goes. Such features include his willingness to employ caesura, his shortening of the ablative of the first declension, and his indulgence in unusual elisions. These poems are therefore presented not for imitation, but for recognition, because of the devotion—singular and weighty in this man—and the effort he devoted to sacred matters for the instruction of all posterity.”

Thus far Fabricius. If anyone wishes to know more precisely the licenses of the ancient Christian poets, and therefore of our author, let him read the Venerable Bede’s book *On the Metrical Art*. PAM.

# CHAPTER I

> The profound impiety of the Evil One [Note: [Col. 1053D] *The profound impiety of the Evil One, a mind envious of life, etc.* We have entitled this chapter: “On the Devil’s First Seduction of Man, and Then His Seduction into Idolatry”; for in Tertullian’s manner the poet calls the devil “the Evil One.” A little later we corrected *to be able to see* in place of *to seem*.], a mind envious of life,  
> After it captured deluded humankind with empty hope,  
> [Col. 1055A] Stripped them bare by persuading them wickedly to believe its falsehood—  
> Yet not with impunity; for immediately, as one guilty of the deed  
> And the reckless author of so great a crime,  
> He received his deserved curses. Then, still more insane,  
> Advancing further, a most desperate enemy,  
> He flooded human minds, now plunged in darkness.  
> Teaching them, forgetful of the Lord, to abandon certain hope,  
> To follow empty idols [Note: [Col. 1055C] *To follow empty idols, etc.* According to Bede in *On the Metrical Art*, the middle syllable of *idolum* is always short. Ecclesiastical poets, perhaps yielding to popular usage, employed it thus; consequently, the changes made by some scholars in several passages of Prudentius, Sedulius, and Arator in order to lengthen it run contrary to the trustworthiness of the ancient reading.], and fashion for themselves a throng of gods;  
> To follow lots, auguries, and the false names of stars;  
> To constrain the nativities of those being born [Note: [Col. 1055C] *To constrain the nativities of those being born, etc.* This is directed against astrologers who attempt to bind the *geneses* of those being born—that is, their births—to fixed outcomes. You have many passages on them above.],  
> To believe they could see through inspection of entrails and await events to come.  
> The dreadful magical audacity of the renegades [Note: [Col. 1055C] *Of renegades, etc.* Similarly below, chapter 6:  
>   
> “The dreadful renegade assigns savage gifts of death.”  
>   
> He uses *refuga* for a deserter, as does Prudentius in the *Peristephanon*. Again, at the beginning of Book II, “as the renegades breathe”; chapter 4, “the monstrous trophy of renegades”; and Book V, “which the mad renegade,” etc., “uttered.”],  
> Led them to admire a fabricated mass and despise life [Note: [Col. 1055D] *Led by audacity, etc.* Not otherwise a little later, “plunged by criminal madness”; and in the next chapter, “wisdom beneath veiled words”; likewise “by endurance of punishment”; finally, chapter 7, “full of magical madness,” and chapter 9, “with his own part abandoned,” etc.; “he did it by wisdom and art,” and “clothes him in his own glory”—and very frequently throughout these five books. In these instances he shortens ablatives in *-a*, which the ancients ordinarily lengthen, following the custom of Christian poets, as Bede relates in *On the Metrical Art*.],  
> And drove them headlong, plunged in criminal madness,  
> Rejoicing in blood, to threaten savage murders;  
> [Col. 1055B] Then to love, in another’s body, the wounding of flesh;  
> And, burning too, captivated by heated sweetness,  
> To transgress the covenants of nature and defile clean bodies,  
> Polluting the male sex with an unspeakable embrace;  
> To mingle feminine practices with the illicit pollution [Note: [Col. 1055D] *Pollution, etc.* He uses the same word below, Book IX, chapter 4: “the populace full of pollution,” for a polluted thing, or filth and disgrace.]  
> Of the common herd; and to regard chaste wombs, dedicated to offspring,  
> As instruments for obscene intercourse in the service of lust.  
>   
> Advancing in this way through times past, he accomplished such deeds  
> Through the hiding places of the soul, while the seps-serpent’s venom flowed [Note: [Col. 1055D] *While the seps-serpent’s venom flowed, etc.* The *seps*, says Epiphanius, *Heresies* 36, is a four-footed reptile resembling a newt. Its bite is regarded as causing no injury, but when its spittle is discharged into food or drink it immediately brings death upon those who consume it. Hence the comparison with the serpent-devil is most apt: through the eating of the forbidden tree he infected humankind with venom. Yet the following expression—“not because human beings might blame,” etc.—is obscure unless “the devil” is understood as the object of *blame*.].  
> It was not because human beings might blame him—for they followed willingly:  
> He persuaded through deceit; man accomplished it through freedom.

# CHAPTER II

> While the faithless one continually breathes out these things through the ages [Note: [Col. 1056C] *While the faithless one continually breathes out these things through the ages, etc.* We have given this chapter the title “On Christ, Redeemer of Fallen Man.” *Breathes out* is used here in the sense of infecting and corrupting with one’s breath. Yet the passage is defective down to the verse “A throng of prophets,” together with what follows. It is as though the author intended to say: Although the enemy of the human race hoped that he would retain forever among humankind the path of crime, he was first obstructed by the prophets’ words; and although he nevertheless continued to attempt secretly what he did not dare publicly, Christ the Redeemer came.],  
> [Col. 1055C] And implants his design in deluded hearts;  
> [Col. 1056A] Hoping—alas!—that he, the fool, possesses the path of crime,  
> Ignorant of what sentence awaits the deed.  
>   
> A throng of prophets, wisdom beneath veiled words,  
> Speaking with a foretelling voice from God’s Spirit [Note: [Col. 1056D] *From God’s Spirit, etc.* Not only here but frequently afterward in the books of poems, he shortens the letter *u* at the ends of verses. Such is the following in Book II, chapter 5: “and poured forth a pledge from his own Spirit,” and “life from the Spirit”; and Book IV, chapter 2: “no place confines within a circuit.” Bede observes that other Christian poets employed something similar. Of the same kind is the shortening of final *e* in the word *publice*, and of *i* a little later in “Son of God.” Yet the now-antiquated phrase “to curse the Lord” belongs to Tertullian’s diction, both here and below in chapter 6. Likewise, *fashioner* is presently used for one who bestowed form, as also below, chapter 4:  
>   
> “And he who fashioned living flesh by his breath.”  
>   
> And somewhere above.],  
> Caused him not to dare curse the Lord openly and plainly,  
> Though in his secret cunning he hoped he could remain hidden.  
>   
> At last the light of the soul is held captive in flesh;  
> The hope of the desperate strives, stronger than the enemy:  
> The Fashioner himself, himself the Renewer of the body;  
> The true Glory of the Father, Son of God, sole Author;  
> Judge and Lord, he comes, the glorious King of the world,  
> Ready to grant pardon to the oppressed and release the bound.  
> Through friendship with him as aid and endurance of punishment,  
> Both God and renewed man are mingled into one [Note: [Col. 1056D] *Both God and renewed man are mingled into one, etc.* The true doctrine concerning Christ’s incarnation and his two natures, divine and human, is found above in the book *Against Praxeas*, chapter 27.].  
>   
> A holy virgin gives birth; a new door of life has opened [Note: [Col. 1055C] *Is opened*, Pam., Obert.].  
> [Col. 1056B] The prophets’ words are proved fulfilled by deeds.  
> Priests leave the temples; guided also by a star,  
> They marvel at the Lord and distinguish so extraordinary a birth.  
>   
> Waters are turned into wine, a memorable sight;  
> Sight is restored to the blind, and at his command trembling  
> Demons are expelled; they cry out and confess Christ.  
> Limbs already wasting away are all healed by a word;  
> Now the lame man walks, the deaf man immediately hears hope,  
> The maimed extends his right hand, and the mute speaks mighty things.  
> At his command the sea grows calm and the winds fall still.  
> All things recognize the Lord; the enemy is confounded,  
> And now the savage foe, defeated in triumph, submits to hostile arms.

# CHAPTER III

> [Col. 1056C] When he sees all things recovered that he himself had seized [Note: [Col. 1056D] *When he sees all things recovered that he himself had seized, etc.* We have entitled this chapter: “On the Devil’s Sprinkling Abroad of Heresies.”]

[Col. 1057A] …of calamity unto destruction; the flesh, already submerged, rising again [Note: [Col. 1057C] “The flesh, already submerged, rise again,” etc. This pertains to the ceremonies of baptism, which were discussed more fully above, [Col. 1057D] in the book *On Baptism*; likewise “the peoples are sealed” pertains to the sacrament of confirmation, also discussed there, chapter 8, and in *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 40.],

And humanity, death defeated, be raised into heaven,

And the peoples be sealed by the outpouring of the holy pledge—

A work of wondrous power, and deeds hateful to him;

When he hears that the final punishments in the gulf of flames

Have been prepared by the Lord for him eternally, together with darkness,

By God’s irrevocable sentence—stripped bare, disarmed,

Condemned, conquered, destined to perish in everlasting death,

Already guilty and certain that he has no pardon—

At once he dared the ultimate wickedness [Note: [Col. 1057D] “Dared the ultimate wickedness,” etc. The shortening of the final syllable in *nefas* is peculiar to Tertullian, both here and in chapter 5:

> To lie—a wickedness—or falsely to call himself a man.

Something similar occurs at the beginning of the following chapter in *duos esse patres* (“that there are two fathers”); Bede noted a comparable shortening of final *i* in words from Prudentius, Sedulius, and Fortunatus. Moreover, just below we corrected *Aggressus pravi, pravos docet esse magistros* (“The assailant of the depraved teaches them to be depraved masters”) in place of *decet*.], scattering everywhere

In their ears a word dreadful and not to be uttered aloud.

Assailing men cast out from God’s people, wandering without light,

Found to be mindless and pursuing earthly things,

The assailant of the depraved teaches them to be depraved masters.

## CHAPTER IV

To these he proclaims that there are two fathers and divided kingdoms [Note: [Col. 1057D] “To these he proclaims that there are two fathers and divided kingdoms,” etc. We have entitled this chapter “On the Heresies of Marcion,” since he proclaims to them that there are two fathers—that is, Gods; that the Lord is the cause of evil; he denies that there is judgment for the guilty, against which there is below the book *On the Judgment of God*; he denies that the flesh can rise; and finally [Col. 1058C] he teaches that Christ’s body was fictitious, made under a semblance. All these matters are treated generally and more fully in the aforementioned *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 51, heresy 17, and individually throughout the five books *Against Marcion*. Further, a little below we corrected *falsum sine nomine numen* (“a false divinity without a name”) in place of *nomen*.];

[Col. 1057B] That the Lord who founded the world is the cause of evil—

He who fashioned flesh and made it live by his breath,

Who gave the Law and spoke through the voice of the prophets.

He denies that this one is good, although he admits that he is just:

Cruel, harsh, one whose savage delight is war,

Dreadful in judgment, softened by no prayers.

He urges that there is another, never known to anyone,

Who exists nowhere, a false divinity without a name,

Who established nothing and uttered no commandments.

This one, he says, is good, for he judges no one,

But distributes life to all alike and begrudges it to none.

He denies that there is judgment for the guilty, and carries about

For the wretched a bloody poison, sweet and mixed with honey.

He denies that the flesh can rise, though he himself

Caused its ruin and wickedly stripped it after despising it.

[Col. 1057C] Therefore he is accursed and suffers grief without end,

Always hostile to it, because with manifold wounds he strives

To drive out its life and the salvation from which he himself fell.

And in this matter also he would deceive mankind: that Christ

Came suddenly to earth, but was joined by no union of flesh,

Being instead spirit in form and a body fashioned beneath a semblance,

So that what does not exist might appear to exist.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 1058A]

Does he therefore teach that it befits God to sport in darkness with those he has persuaded [Note: [Col. 1058D] “Does it therefore befit God to sport in darkness with those he has persuaded,” etc. We give this chapter the title “Refutation of the Heresy Concerning Christ’s Fictitious Body.” The author treated this argument more fully above in *On the Flesh of Christ*. Here we corrected *quae sancto in corpore versans* (“all the things which, while living in a holy body”) in place of *versis*. We also read “sent by the true God, the Father,” etc., in place of the transmitted “but by God,” especially since both Tertullian and other Christian poets customarily shorten final *o*, even in adjectives.],

To lie—a wickedness—or falsely to call himself a man?

He is carried, walks, is clothed, duly rests,

Is handled, suffers, is suspended, and is buried.

While dwelling in a holy body, he accomplished in the proper sense

Everything belonging to humanity—sent by the Father, the true God

Who created all things—seeking his own, not another’s.

He was known by his very work to peoples who had long hoped for him,

And was thoroughly known to the world through the prophets’ voice.

Yet now, at the manifest threshold of death,

They seek a wandering, unknown Lord and abandon the known one.

Their faith is false, their God false, their reward void [Note: [Col. 1058D] “Their reward void,” etc. This pertains to the reward of works, discussed more than once above; in the lines that follow he alludes to chapter 15 of the First Epistle to the Corinthians.],

Their resurrection false, their conquest of death false,

Their martyrdoms empty, and even the name of Christ vain.

[Col. 1058B] By teaching that he came like a magical mist,

In their madness they confess that the doer of the deed was a liar:

That he suffered nothing, and that the people were fashioned without guilt.

Is God truthful in this way? Are these the honors rendered to the Lord?

Alas, wretched men, destroyed to no purpose by a thankless death,

Who, with a blind guide, fell headlong into a hidden pit [Note: [Col. 1058D] Fabricius correctly interprets *in fossa ruistis* as “you fell into a dug-out place,” amid hidden thorns.].

And just as one rich through the gift of treasure in a dream

Exults and holds it in his hands, deluded by an empty hope,

So, deceived, you hope for the empty shadow of a gift.

## CHAPTER VI

[Note: [Col. 1058D] “Ah! the wasting maw,” etc. We have entitled this chapter “Against the Heresy Concerning God as the Author of Evils,” against which see above, book II *Against Marcion*. We necessarily corrected *tabidi* (“wasting”) in place of *tacidi*, especially because the former is an epithet of the dragon.]

Ah! the wasting maw and death-bearing prey of the dragon!

In place of peace you savagely hope for flattering murders.

You dare to blame the God who created such great things;

Upon whose earth, with excessive loving-kindness poured forth,

You rush about unmindful, abundantly praising his gifts,

[Col. 1058C] Rejecting the maker himself while approving what he made—

The craftsman of the world, whose work you yourselves are [Note: [Col. 1057C] *Cujusne*. Obert.]?

He who granted you, though small, great honors,

Sowed the crops, and subjected all animals to you;

Who makes the seasons of the year fruitful in their appointed months;

Who bestowed sweetnesses, varied drinks, rich foods and fragrances,

Pleasant flowers and the welcome shade of groves;

[Col. 1059A] Who granted wondrous juices to flourishing herbs,

Pours out springs and rivers in sweet waters,

Adorns heaven with stars, and illuminates the whole world—

The sole immeasurable Lord, both just and good,

Known from his work, though seen and known by no one.

Although foolish nations, covered by error [Note: [Col. 1059C] *Copertae* in place of *coopertae* (“covered”), as also below in book II, chapter 1: “With the spear-point covered”; and book V, chapter 9: “Covered by wave and strait.” He also uses this figure in the perfect tense in book III, chapter 4:

> He covered the desire for sin by a violent death.],

And flourishing in wealth, praise him under another’s name,

They nevertheless recognize the Maker and fear to blame him.

Nor does anyone but you alone—the new gateway of Gehenna—

Ungratefully choose to curse your own Lord.

Through Marcion, with Cerdo as his teacher [Note: [Col. 1059C] “With Cerdo as his teacher,” etc. On the heresies of Cerdo, Marcion’s teacher, see the aforementioned *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 51, heresy 16.],

A terrible apostate assigned you these savage gifts of death;

Nor did it occur to you that, after seducing you away from Christ’s name,

He bore you down to the depths in Marcion’s name.

Tell me: among the many things, what single thing displeases you?

[Col. 1059B] Or what has God made that should not be extolled with praise?

Is it perhaps that, through his overly abundant patience,

He permits you, though unworthy, to behold the pleasant light?

You read what is true, but teach it mutilated as false;

You approve that what comes afterward and is still to be was done before.

Or what difference is there in believing your incredible doctrine?

## CHAPTER VII

Nor is it strange that the cunning one captured you while unarmed [Note: [Col. 1059C] “Nor is it strange that the cunning one captured you while unarmed,” etc. We corrected *Nec mirum* (“Nor is it strange”) in place of *nimirum*. It is worth noting that he calls heresy [Col. 1059D] an “incorrigible crime,” since daily experience teaches us that this is entirely true of those who have once become heretics.],

Persuading you that there are two fathers who are Gods—though condemned by one—

He who in the beginning had seduced everyone.

Afterward he distributed among many the plague that flowed

From manifold wounds, and the incorrigible crime.

He persuaded unspeakable men, filled with every madness of magic [Note: [Col. 1059D] “Unspeakable men, filled with every madness of magic,” etc. He alludes to Simon Magus. On his claim to be the supreme Power, see the aforementioned *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 46, heresy 1; and concerning Helena, his prostitute, see *On the Soul*, chapter 34. On his flight, see Hegesippus, *On the Destruction of Jerusalem*, book II, chapter 2, and blessed Maximus’s sermon on Saints Peter and Paul.],

To call himself the supreme Power [Note: [Col. 1059C] *Pervasit*. Pamelius, Obert.];

[Col. 1059C] To practice deception with a prostitute, traverse wickedness, and fly.

[Col. 1060A] For Valentinus has a mad God [Note: [Col. 1059D] “For Valentinus,” etc. Concerning him, see the aforementioned book, chapter 49, heresy 12, and the complete book *Against the Valentinians.], and assigns to eternity

Thirty heavens and a father called the Depth.

He taught that one should be baptized twice, the body being conveyed through flame [Note: [Col. 1059D] “He taught that one should be baptized twice, the body being conveyed through flame,” etc. He means certain heretics who baptized twice, once in water and once in fire; yet I have found no mention of them elsewhere, except that Philastrius, though still rather obscurely, appears in his book *On Heresies* to attribute to the Herminians and Seleucians the teaching that baptism should be performed not in water but in fire, under the pretext of John the Baptist’s words, Matthew 3: “He will baptize you in spirit and fire.” [Col. 1060C] We have substituted the Tertullianic form *tingui* for *tingi*.].

Basilides commanded belief in as many gods [Note: [Col. 1060C] “Basilides commanded belief in as many gods,” etc. Epiphanius treats this heresy of Basilides at length in Heresy 31, where he enumerates by name 365 gods, as many as there are days in the year. We also said something about it above in the aforementioned *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 46, heresy 4. What the author adds—“and, finally, as many worlds”—is peculiar to him.]

As the year has days—and, finally, as many worlds.

Marcus, arguing subtly by means of numbers [Note: [Col. 1060C] “Marcus, arguing subtly by means of numbers,” etc. *Marcus* must certainly be corrected here in place of *Marcion*, for neither statement is written of Marcion, but of Marcus’s heresy [Col. 1060D], constructed from the Greek alphabet, in which he argued by numbers up to 888. . . . On the magical tricks he employed in offering the chalice, see *Against the Valentinians*, chapter 4. Moreover, the author’s statement that the chalice is offered also serves to confirm the Christian sacrifice.],

Taught that through magic the chaste form should be violated,

That the chalice should be offered and changed into blood by prayers.

He persuaded Ebion that Christ was born from human seed [Note: [Col. 1060D] “He persuaded Ebion that Christ was born from human seed,” etc. On this heresy of Ebion, see above, *On the Flesh of Christ*, the whole of chapter 18; and on his having proposed the Law together with the Gospel, see the aforementioned *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 48, heresy 11.],

And taught him to be circumcised and devote himself to the Law,

Forsaking the fountains and taking up again the elements of the Law.

I do not wish to prolong the final outrage in words,

Or to relate every cause or every name.

It is enough, through a few examples, to mark the many cruelties,

The unspeakable men and savage instruments of the dragon,

[Col. 1060B] Through whom those who have now uttered so great a crime without witness

Continually labor to blame the Maker of the world.

## CHAPTER VIII

But draw back your foot [Note: [Col. 1060D] “But draw back your foot,” etc. We necessarily corrected *Revocate* (“draw back”) in place of *revocare*, and *dum spatium datur* (“while an opportunity is given”) in place of *detur*. Then the conjunction *vero* is used with a short final syllable in “Believe in the true Father, truly”; and in “because he believed beforehand,” *credere* is used in the sense of “to entrust.” The reading “finally, the enclosed” appears corrupt. We emended *poenamque merentes* (“deserving punishment”) in place of *merentem*, because *populos* (“peoples”) precedes.] from the savage robber’s cave,

While an opportunity is given, and God—ever patient in loving-kindness—

Forgives the wretched all deeds committed through error.

Believe indeed in the true Father, who founded the world,

Who sent the true Lord to restore the fallen

Who were unequal to the Law and submerged in the gulf of sin,

And to bring the salvation promised long ago through the prophets.

He who gave the commandments also forgives sins.

He rightly requires something here, because he entrusted it beforehand;

Or the Lord grants lavishly, as though paying debts to servants.

Finally, as for the peoples shut in and deserving punishment,

[Col. 1060C] Once the indictment is erased [Note: [Col. 1060C] *Delecto*. Obert.] he himself commands that all be washed [Note: [Col. 1060D] “Once the indictment is erased, he himself commands that all be washed,” etc. Fabricius observed, not unreasonably, that the author here uses *elogium* for the definite establishment of some matter, if the old reading *Deleto elogio* is retained. But since in the passages cited above—*Apology*, chapter 2, and elsewhere, so far as I recall—the author always uses this word unfavorably for the heading of an accusation, we thought that *Deleto elogio* (“once the indictment is erased”) should instead be read, just as in *To Scapula*, chapter 4, he says *scisso elogio* (“the indictment torn up”), alluding to the Apostle’s words in Colossians 2: “Erasing the handwriting of the offense that stood against us.”].

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 1061A]

Therefore the whole human being believes, and the whole is washed.

He abstains, or truly suffers wounds for the Name;

The true human being rises, and death, truly conquered, will be silent.

But the soul, only one part of the human being, will not receive the palm

While leaving behind its own part—the flesh that labored beside it [Note: [Col. 1061C] “Will receive the palm,” etc. This serves [Col. 1062C] to confirm reward according to the merits of works, as do “rewards are repaid,” “the equitable payer of reward,” “through merit alone,” and finally “after merited,” etc., “honors.” Moreover, the following verses appear corrupt:

> Nor unlawfully to wish to blame the Lord by teaching  
> That he should raise—or whom?—the soul, as though it had suffered ruin, etc.

Likewise this verse:

> To see what it had once been, when turned to dust.

Here the passage seems mutilated.].

Having contended in the arena, the two together deserve it in union.

It is a great wickedness for two to bear the weight in chains,

One of whom is rich and the other destitute,

And for the wretched one to be despised while rewards are repaid to the fortunate.

The just God does not do this—the equitable payer of reward,

Good and rich, whom we believe capable of all things,

Gracious toward the ungrateful, his will full of compassion.

Rather, to the one in whom mortal need is greater,

So that it may become equal, the rich one, preferred above its companion,

[Col. 1061B] Will freely bestow whatever it lacks: thus we are commanded to believe.

Nor unlawfully to wish to blame the Lord by teaching

That he should raise—or whom?—the soul, as though it had suffered ruin,

And free it from death, while the living soul retained

An abundance gained solely through merit, because it acted bravely;

While the flesh, which always shared the common labor,

Should be abandoned to the earth and become death’s perpetual prey.

Did the human soul, then, please God through courageous deeds?

By itself it could in no way have pleased him without the flesh.

It bore chains and punishments; the flesh carried bonds upon its limbs;

It despised death, yet by death abandoned the flesh.

[Col. 1061C] The soul suffered in giving birth; the flesh was cut off from life by a wound.

[Col. 1062A] The former seeks rest; the latter, poured into the dust by the sword,

Was abandoned to fish, birds, putrefaction, and ashes.

Unhappy, it is broken and mangled; scattered, it dissolves.

Did it not deserve to rise? For what could it alone have committed

When lifeless? What envious cause of life

Hinders or forbids the flesh from receiving God’s gifts

And living forever united with its companion?

To see what it had once been, when turned to dust?

After its deserts, let it be restored and bear to God the honors of praise,

Not ignorant of itself—once frail, mortal, and sick—

So that, after its struggles, living power may show what it can accomplish:

For he who is good and mighty begrudges life to no one.

Was this flesh death’s captive, and will this bound thing perish,

Which the Lord fashioned with wondrous wisdom and skill?

By his wondrous power he himself raises it;

The leader himself recalls it, and clothes it with his glory.

[Col. 1062B] Therefore God’s craftsmanship and wisdom fitted together the body

Which he desires to be made for these purposes; does his power lack the means to restore it?

No cause can resist holy loving-kindness,

Lest the cause of evil be greater than supreme power;

So that humanity, now saved by God’s gift, may know—

Once mortal, but now clothed in inviolable and immense light,

Alive and whole in body—

God, immeasurable in power and everlasting in loving-kindness,

Through Christ the King, through whom the way of light has been opened;

And now, in new light and filled with both gifts,

Joyful amid the delightful fruits of the living paradise,

May praise him forever, rich in the heavenly court.

# BOOK II: ON THE HARMONY OF THE OLD AND NEW LAW

[Col. 1061]

## SUMMARY OF BOOK II, ALSO BY THE AUTHOR HIMSELF

Then the following book, joined to the first, teaches the mysteries of the Law

And what the one God handed down in the new covenant.

### NOTE

By these rather obscure words the author indicates that this book was written on the concord of the Old and New Law; we have therefore recently added that description to the title. We have also corrected *Deus* (“God”) in place of *divis* (“divinities”): first, because the author more than once lengthens the first syllable of the word *Deus* in these books; second, because the ancients were not accustomed to call any beings *divi*; and finally, because “one God” serves the present argument against Marcion’s many Gods. PAMELIUS.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1061D]

After faith was shattered by apostates breathing out the enemy [Note: [Col. 1061D] “After faith was shattered by apostates breathing out [Col. 1062D] the enemy,” etc. We emended *emersit pestis operta* (“the hidden plague emerged”) [Col. 1063C] in place of *pectis*, which seemed to have crept in through a typographical error. Likewise, a little below:

> Unexpectedly killing the unwary by the final death,

in place of “The unexpected thing denying.” Moreover, the phrase “that he might charge his own wicked deeds to God” is Tertullianic [Col. 1063D], as are *suasos* for *persuasos* (“those persuaded”), “fasten them to punishments,” and shortly afterward “set the Lord’s words against one another.”],

[Col. 1062D] And, massed together with deceits, the hidden plague emerged

Of its own accord: a lying mind that despised the Divine Majesty

[Col. 1063A] Inflicted wounds and, growing pale upon its deceitful path,

Mingled its impious words with the sayings of the saints

And sowed wretched darnel among the good seed.

Then, wishing the whole cause of the fall to be established—

Namely, that it might the more swiftly charge its own wicked deeds to God

And be able to fasten those it had persuaded to punishments—

It covered falsehoods with truths and transformed harsh things into gentle ones;

And, with the spear-point concealed by rosy garlands,

Unexpectedly killed the unwary by the final death.

It is the supreme wickedness that men cut off and sunk

By madness so deep should divide into parts the Divine Majesty

That must be feared without end; that they should follow Christ’s sublime deeds

With false praise, yet blame the deeds that came before—

God’s innumerable miracles, never seen [Note: [Col. 1063D] “God’s innumerable miracles, never seen,” etc. We joined to this verse:

> Nor heard before, nor contained in any heart,

and placed after it:

> So rashly to fashion an unlawful crime in words,

because there he alludes to Isaiah 64 and 1 Corinthians 2: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart.” Hence we also corrected *contentaque* (“contained”) in place of *contemptaque*; likewise, shortly afterward, *quia corde gravatis* (“because their hearts are weighed down”) in place of *gravati*. Moreover, an error seems to underlie this verse as well:

> Dull, they think things borne by the Spirit worthy of animals;

or the passage is mutilated and cannot be remedied without a manuscript codex.],

Nor heard before, nor contained in any heart.

[Col. 1063B] So rashly to fashion an unlawful crime in words:

That the two Testaments sound against one another;

To set the Lord’s words against the prophets;

To seek to prove that their meaning is utterly different;

To drag down the whole cause of the Law [Note: [Col. 1064C] “And does not read.” Obert.] and make it infamous;

And to reject the former lives of the holy fathers,

Whom God drew into friendship and toward his gifts.

A work without a beginning is accepted in its smaller part:

Though four come from one, and from the four comes one,

Only one pleases them, and they reject the remaining three parts;

And in many matters they lay claim to Paul as their authority.

From Paul himself, moreover, their madness raged against the final words:

Whatever he said concerning the ancient covenant

Appears harsh to them, deservedly, because their hearts are weighed down.

The apostolic weight, the grace of the resplendent word,

[Col. 1063C] Brings light before the mind, yet they cannot see;

Dull, they think things borne by the Spirit worthy only of animals.

## CHAPTER II

But you who have not yet, under the guidance of a false Divinity,

Become wholly reprobate in mind and penetrated death’s inner depths:

[Col. 1064A] Learn that from the fountain flows an everlasting river [Note: [Col. 1063D] “From the fountain flows an everlasting river,” [Col. 1064C] etc. Bede testifies that Christian poets commonly lengthen final *e* when two consonants follow in the next word; for example, both this author here and more than once afterward, Juvencus, book IV, “Behold the scribes,” and Prudentius in the *Cathemerinon*, “by a wondrous slaughter.” He alludes to the twice-six apostles, whose sound went out into all the earth and into the world’s four winds—that is, to the ends of the earth—as Psalm 18 reads. We corrected *Sordes diluere* (“to wash away filth”) in place of *sordide*. Here he unusually uses “dead destinies” for dead human beings, and shortly afterward we corrected *Electaque fide* (“received by chosen faith”) in place of *electoque*.],

Which grace nourishes, with twice-six fruits;

It goes out into the earth and the world’s four winds;

Into so many parts flows the fountain’s one color and flavor.

So too the Church flows forth through the apostolic word,

From Christ’s womb, filled with all the Father’s glory,

To wash away filth and revive the dead.

One Gospel, fourfold in number, was spread among the nations

And received with chosen faith; the bountiful teacher

Paul hands it down pure and without fault.

Apart from this, he forbade the holy Galatians to depart—

Those whom false brothers persuaded to be circumcised

And taught to follow the elements, abandoning their new freedom,

And to serve the old shadow of things to come.

These were the reasons Paul had for writing to the Galatians,

[Col. 1064B] Not so that they should receive a small part of the Gospel

As though it were the entire body, abandoning the greater part.

Indeed, the Gospel is not the words of a book, but Christ himself,

Sent into the world—if you are willing to see—

Who came from the Father, alone bearing good tidings

Attested beforehand; his immense glory fulfills them,

Showing by his work how great the world’s Creator is.

His faithful followers—Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John—

Wrote down his deeds together with his sayings,

Speaking pure words, not foreign ones,

Made holy by God’s Spirit, with so great a teacher present.

## CHAPTER III

Here the Paschal lamb, the sacrificial victim, is suspended upon the wood [Note: [Col. 1064D] “Here the Paschal lamb, the sacrificial victim, is suspended upon the wood,” etc. He alludes to 1 Corinthians 5: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed”; and “who was to be life and God” refers to what follows, “promised,” after which comes the archaic form *illectaverat*, and soon afterward the penultimate syllable of *poteritis* is lengthened in poetic fashion.].

Writing his decrees to Corinth, Paul declares that this Passover

Was slain, and was to be life and God,

[Col. 1064C] Promised to the fathers, whom he had attracted before.

Perceive what power can do, and what the image of Passover can do;

Thus you will be able to see what the true Passover is.

Lest the faithful father and prophet [Note: [Col. 1064D] “Lest the faithful father and prophet,” etc. He means Abraham, to whom (Genesis 22), in place of his son Isaac as the sacrifice,

> A lamb caught by its head among thorns is shown,

as also in what follows:

> That through its death, once atonement had been made,  
> It might serve as a sign,

[Col. 1065D] referring to Exodus 12, where the doorposts and many thresholds are commanded to be marked with the blood of the Paschal lamb. In place of “many” I would prefer to read “mute,” but I have changed nothing. To these he adds the Passover celebrated in Joshua 5. A little afterward we corrected “or by its blood it erases death” in place of “grieves.”], to whom the pledge and heir

Was dear—the son whom God had perhaps granted him—

Should sacrifice him to God, he was rightly tested in his love:

A great ordeal. In place of holy blood, blood is supplied;

A lamb caught by its head among thorns is shown

As a holy victim to God. So that through its death, once atonement had been made,

It might serve as a sign and pledge of the ravaged nation,

The doorposts and many thresholds are marked with blood—

A mighty aid: its flesh, a witness, is believed to be food.

Jesus crossed the Jordan, took possession of the land,

And, according to the Law, instituted Passover, rejoicing and sacrificing the lamb.

The remaining great kings and holy prophets as well,

Not ignorant of the promises of certain salvation

And, filled with awe, unwilling to transgress the immense Law,

Celebrated Passover in due order—the great reality to come,

Beheld in a mirror through an image of supreme power.

Finally, if with swift mind you retrace the beginnings,

[Col. 1065B] You will find something exceedingly deadly after the impious words:

Alas, credulous man, easily stripped of the covering of life!

So that humanity might be clothed with skins, a lamb is suspended;

Either it slays sins, or by its blood erases death,

Or covers the naked, or warms a wound with its fleece [Note: [Col. 1065D] “Or warms a wound with its fleece,” etc. Here, by poetic license, the final *o* of *suo* is shortened, as it frequently is afterward in these books; concerning the same usage in other Christian poets, see Bede. We also emended *ut pro peccatis* (“so that, offered for sins”) in place of *aut*, so that the preceding “Is not the blood of a beast” becomes a question, with *non* understood in the Tertullianic manner as *nonne* (“is it not?”). Moreover, he also proves from John 1 that Christ is the Lamb [Col. 1066D].].

Is the blood of a beast worth more than human blood,

So that, offered for sins, it may put an end to wrath—

Or for that of a multitude, as though the lamb were more precious?

A mighty aid, the safeguard of so great a salvation:

Could the victim offered be a sufficient price for the redeemed? [Note: [Col. 1065D] “Salvation.” Pamelius, Venetian edition.]

But almighty God, creator of heaven and earth,

Immeasurable, living, perfect, everlasting in light,

Is not appeased by these things, nor does he rejoice in the blood of cattle.

Let every beast be slaughtered, let every flock burn away upon the altars,

So that a single animal might gain pardon or atone for sin:

[Col. 1065C] By no means did the wise but defiled image of the Lord—

Foul flesh—obtain honors at so paltry a price.

Rather, hope and the faith promised long ago to mortals

Accomplished this and bore it: an image of the great design,

Forethought by the Father and prepared in abundant loving-kindness—

That Christ would come to earth and become human.

When John saw him—the first to inaugurate baptism,

Companion of the prophets and also a mighty apostle,

The sure forerunner sent forth and faithful witness,

August in life and distinguished by sublime praise—

He finally showed to those seeking the Passover of God, the true Lamb,

That he had come: the one who by his own blood would discharge

The penalties of the deed and the sins of many;

Good for the reprobate, dear for the worthless—the one;

Human in body and God in life, slaughtered like a lamb,

[Col. 1065D] That he might receive us and pour out himself for us.

[Col. 1066A] Thus it pleased the Lord to despoil proud death;

Thus pitiable humanity could hope for salvation.

Paul proclaims that this Lamb was sacrificed as our Passover.

The sublime Lord does not suffer a likeness in form

To an unfeeling beast; that is not why he is called a lamb.

Rather, it is because his renewed fleece clothes these bodies,

Providing a covering for many while he himself never fails.

## CHAPTER IV

Thus the Lord, by the Father’s power, clothes in his own light

Those whom he redeemed by death—a light always present in him [Note: [Col. 1066D] “Thus the Lord, by the Father’s power,” etc. “To gain possession of the flock” and “strong to rescue” are Tertullianic; thus we read *eripere* with the final *e* lengthened, where one might expect *eriperet*. Likewise “a virgin drawn aside by the dragon”; and not much afterward, “without the debt of death,” which we corrected in place of “the due [feminine]”; likewise “the footprints of death” in place of “death.” Again, “he extends his hand,” etc., and “to touch the wood” belong to the author’s style.].

Therefore the shepherd who lost his sheep seeks it himself.

Prepared to tread upon the oak, the thorns, and the grapes,

Or to overcome the wolf’s fury and gain possession of the flock,

Strong to rescue, freely scorning its teeth,

[Col. 1066B] He offers himself, a lion covered in a sheep’s skin,

Deceiving it by his appearance, about to seize its jaws by his blood.

Thus Christ seeks everywhere for Adam, captured by violence,

Walking himself along the path by which death accomplished the fall,

Surveying all the memorials of the ancient men,

Examining each one, himself the single fulfillment of every pattern;

Beginning from the womb to expel hostile death,

Traversing every age in silent wisdom together with the flesh’s seed,

Conceived in the womb, taking on what was owed,

Prepared to cleanse all and restore to the Maker the many

Whom the one man had scattered.

And because a man, frightfully plunged into an evil pit,

Had fallen, and a virgin drawn aside by the dragon had persuaded him,

It pleased his design to abandon the heavenly covering.

The tree exposed them as naked; black death compelled them.

[Col. 1066C] From the same substance, restored by a similar design,

Now renewed, returns the flower of flesh and the guest of peace:

Flesh from the betrothed virgin, not born from human seed,

Joined to its own Maker, without the debt of death.

An angel bears these commands of the Father through the bright stars,

So that the tidings may be believed on the angelic report:

So that virgin may pay what virgin owes, and flesh what flesh owes.

Entering through such means, the immense little child,

The older boy and youthful man, follows the footprints of death.

Afterward, when the rightful age of manly strength was complete—

The age accustomed gradually to decay along with its companion life,

To change in appearance into ugly wrinkles and enfeebled limbs

As the veins were emptied of blood—

He halted, not allowing the condition of his flesh to grow old,

At the age when Adam recklessly extended his hand to touch the tree.

[Col. 1066D] On the same day and in the same place where glorious Adam fell [Note: [Col. 1066D] “On the day and in the place where glorious Adam fell,” etc. Thus we emended the text in place of “dearest.” What he says here he shortly repeats more clearly in these words:

> [Col. 1067D] The place is Golgotha, once the Calvary of the head, etc.  
> Here our ancestors taught that a great bone was found;  
> Here, we have received, the first human being was buried, etc.

This is also found in blessed Cyprian’s treatise *On the Resurrection of Christ*; see there the similar passages from the ancients in our notes, no. 3. It is peculiar to this author that he writes that Christ suffered on the same day on which Adam fell.],

[Col. 1067A] When that same day returned in the revolving years,

The mighty athlete entered the contest in the arena of the tree.

He extended his hands, pursued punishment instead of praise,

And conquered death, because he voluntarily left death.

He stripped off the spoils of flesh and the debt of death;

And, once the ruler of the world had been conquered, affixed to the tree

The serpent’s spoil—a mighty trophy taken from the apostates.

As a sign of this Moses had suspended a serpent,

So that all who had been struck by the many serpents

Might look upon the modeled and transfixed dragon.

Afterward, when he came to the secret waters of the underworld,

Victorious, he disclosed his captive by his light

And fulfilled the Father’s command with his power standing by;

He himself willingly took up again the body he had abandoned.

This had been the cause of death; it became the same road of salvation.

[Col. 1067B] That one was a messenger of deceit, but this one a messenger of peace;

A bride killed her husband, but a bride gave birth to the lion;

A virgin harmed a man, but a man born of a virgin conquered.

As an image of this, when the body had been lulled to sleep,

A woman, the husband’s rib, was taken from his side.

Upon awakening he called her flesh of his flesh

And bones from his bones, speaking with prophetic understanding.

Wondrous is the faith; rightly Paul is its most certain authority,

For he teaches that Christ from heaven is the second Adam.

Truth itself shines, employing its own patterns;

It does not desire to display vigorous strides with borrowed things:

That is the work of a pauper, one lacking power of his own.

The great Paul taught these learned mysteries,

Clearly seeing that in Christ is your glory, O Church [Note: [Col. 1067D] “Clearly seeing that in Christ is your glory, O Church,” etc. This verse is corrupt, and I could not remedy it because manuscripts were lacking. Meanwhile, the first syllable of *Ecclesia* is shortened, as is peculiar to the author both above in book I, chapter 6, “The Church flows forth through the word,” here, and shortly afterward:

> This is the true mother of the living people, the Church,

and below in book III, chapter 7:

> That Christ is the head, whose members are the Church.

I suspect an error also underlies “the woman was blood.”].

[Col. 1067C] From his side, while his lifeless body hung high upon the tree,

Blood and water flowed.

The woman was blood; the water was the new gift of the washing.

This is the true mother of the living people, the Church:

Flesh from Christ’s new flesh, and bone from his bones [Note: [Col. 1067C] “Bones.” Venetian edition.].

The place is Golgotha, once the Calvary of the head [Note: [Col. 1068D] “The place is Golgotha,” etc. Here the middle syllable of this word is lengthened, whereas in the *Hymn on the Lord’s Passover*, attributed to Cyprian, it is shortened:

> There is a place which we perceive to be at the center of the whole world;  
> The Jews in their ancestral tongue call it Golgotha.

So too in Juvencus, book IV: “Where the countryside bears the name Golgotha.” Shortly afterward we emended “to be raised by the power of the dripping water” in place of “to raise.”];

Thus the ancestral tongue first named it.

Here is the earth’s center; here is the sign of victory.

Here our ancestors taught that a great bone was found [Note: [Col. 1067D] “Of the ancient one.” Obert.];

Here, we have received, the first human being was buried.

[Col. 1068A] Here Christ suffers; the earth is soaked with holy blood,

So that the dust of ancient Adam, mingled with Christ’s blood,

May be raised by the power of the dripping water [Note: [Col. 1068C] “To raise.” Obert.].

This is the one sheep whom the shepherd determined, on the Sabbath,

To draw alive from the pit of the underworld [Note: [Col. 1068D] “Or, on the Sabbath, called the whole lifeless man back alive,” etc. It is peculiar to this author that he intimates that the raising of Lazarus (John 11) took place on the Sabbath; for it is clear from what follows—“As the holy day began,” etc.—that he is speaking of Lazarus.].

For this reason on the Sabbaths he healed the prematurely dead limbs

Of all flesh; or, by giving sight, perfected the eyes

Of the man blind from birth—eyes which he had not previously given;

Or, on the Sabbath, called the whole lifeless man back alive

From the tomb, with the people present.

He is himself the Maker of the new and the good Restorer of the old,

Either supplying what was lacking or restoring what had been lost.

By this he taught that, as the holy day began, he would be able

To accomplish these things fully, according to the covenant, for those who hoped in him.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 1068B] What? If the flesh dies and no hope of salvation is given [Note: [Col. 1068D] “What? If the flesh dies and no hope of salvation is given,” etc. We emended *Quid?* (“What?”) in place of *quod*, and *salutis* (“of salvation”) in place of *saluti*. “To heal,” etc., is Tertullianic. “Will the Lord’s power not be able,” etc., has the sense “Surely it will be able.”],

What reason did Christ have to fashion himself as a human being,

To heal human beings, or to care for the flesh?

Powerful corruption can dissolve the body into decay:

Will the Lord’s power not be able to restore what has been dissolved?

Those who believe that their bodies—not the Lord’s own—are dissolved in destruction

Do not believe the Lord, who wills to raise his own submerged bodies.

They say either that he is unwilling to bestow the good or that the Mighty One cannot,

Unaware of how great a crime they suckle,

Daring to set feeble arguments above death.

In the grain a tree lies hidden; and unless the grain, buried in the earth,

Decays, it does not yield the fruits that adorn the tree.

Now liquid waters are hardened; beneath the creaking frost

They become rocks, and will remain so forever unless a mighty power

[Col. 1068C] Dissolves them by bringing in a gently breathing warmth.

Within the slender body of the little vine lies hidden a mighty cluster;

If you seek it, it is not there; when God wills, it is seen to exist.

The leaves on trees, the rose on thorns, the shoots in the fields

Die and disappear, and once again rise alive.

God restores these things before man’s eyes after bringing them back,

For whose sake the bountiful First One richly made all things.

All things fall naked; he clothes each in its own body:

Why should he not likewise recall man alone to himself,

Upon whom he lavished such honors and whom he made above all things?

[Col. 1069A] Therefore flesh and blood are denied to be worthy of God’s kingdom [Note: [Col. 1069B] *Therefore flesh and blood are denied to be worthy of God’s kingdom*, etc. He gives an excellent interpretation of the Apostle’s words, 1 Cor. 15: “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God”; this is discussed more fully above, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chs. 46, 49, and 51. We have presently corrected *Carnali sermone putent*, deriving *putent* from *putere*, “to be putrid,” in place of *putant*; and a little later, once again, *et debito mortis*, in place of *debita*. Likewise *humanum*—that is, the human race—[Col. 1070B] *rursus debere renasci*, in place of *humano*.],

As though Paul had been speaking specifically about the flesh.

He indeed taught great things, but empty hearts

Stink with carnal discourse; for by the name

Of blood and flesh he meant deeds belonging to the former state,

Calling to mind the words of the great heavenly Master,

Who gave those begotten of himself through water his own name as an honor,

And poured out the pledge of his own Spirit,

So that those who had been redeemed by his power

Might also, when renewed, receive the honor of his name.

Therefore, because he denied the heavenly kingdom to peoples

Not yet reborn from his own font, covered in their ancient stains

And liable to death through the old cause,

Saying that the human race must be born again—

[Col. 1069B] “What is born of flesh is flesh; what is born of the Spirit is life”—

[Col. 1070A] And because glory, transforming the new shoots of the ancient root,

Declared that the washed body should no longer be called “flesh,”

Paul follows this teaching; in this sense he spoke concerning flesh.

Finally, he said that this frail condition, this mortal form,

Must be clothed over with a garment [Note: [Col. 1070B] Finally he said: “The flesh must be clothed over,” etc. Concerning this passage of the Apostle, 2 Cor. 5, see also the book cited above, more fully, chs. 41, 42, and 43; likewise concerning the words “in an atom, in the momentary movement of an eye,” in the same place. By “red wax,” moreover, he means reddish wax, according to his custom, and uses *glutitam* in the sense of *deglutitam*, “swallowed up.”].

Not that another body is given, but that the former body, defenseless,

Is wholly surrounded on every side by the far-reaching kingdom of God.

“In the moment of an eye’s glance it will be changed,” he says,

As the surface of red wax is overspread by a green plant

And changes its own color beneath the shining sun.

Thus the same flesh, receiving splendor from glory,

Will rejoice forever in gladness and will be free from death,

Crying aloud that the cruel enemy of the body has been conquered:

“Death has been swallowed up; Christ is the mighty victory,”
