His father—whom those in error suppose to have been the primordial god—did not know that Jupiter was being concealed on the island of Crete. The son likewise—whom they believe to be the more powerful god—did not know that the father he had driven away lay hidden in Italy. If he was in heaven, why did he not see what was happening in Italy? Italy is not some corner of the earth. Indeed, if he had been a god, nothing ought to have been hidden from him.

That he nevertheless remained hidden there, and that the Italians called him [Col. 1116C] Saturn, has been plainly established: from his concealment the western Latin tongue has been called *Latina* down to the present day, as their own authority Virgil also records: [Note: [Col. 1115D]

> . . . and that it was called Latium

]

[Col. 1116D] “He preferred it, since he had lain safely hidden upon these shores.” *Aeneid*, book VIII, vv. 322–323.]

Therefore he is said to have been born on earth, since he both fears being driven from his kingdom by him, and seeks to kill him as a rival, and does not know that he has been secretly taken away and is in hiding. Afterward the son-god pursues his father and seeks—one may believe it—to kill an immortal though himself immortal; he is deceived by the intervening sea and does not know that his father has fled. And while these things were being done between two gods on earth, heaven was deserted. No one administered the rains, no one thundered, no one governed the vast mass of the world. Nor can they say [Col. 1116D] that their deeds and wars took place in heaven, for these things happened on Mount Olympus in Greece. But Olympus is not called heaven [Note: [Col. 1116D] *Olympum*. Perhaps *Olympus*. SUAR.], for heaven is heaven.

Which of their deeds, then, shall we discuss first? Their birth, concealment, ignorance, parricide, adulteries, and obscene acts—[Col. 1117A] things committed not by God but by the filthiest and most savage of men, who, if they lived in our times, would be answerable as defendants under every law, laws far more just and severe than their deeds. He drove his father out by force of arms: the Falcidian and Sempronian law would bind the parricide in a sack with wild beasts. He violated his sisters: the Papinian law would punish the outrage with every penalty upon each member of his body. He invaded the marriages of others: the Julian law would punish its adulterer with death. He defiled freeborn boys: the Cornelian law would condemn, by unprecedented punishments, the sacrilegious perpetrator of an unprecedented sexual act who had transgressed the covenant.

Here too he is shown to have possessed no divinity, for he was a man: his father’s flight escaped his notice. Divine honor was assigned by men to such a man, so abominable a king, so obscene and cruel. Yet since he was born on earth and grew to maturity through successive stages [Col. 1117B] of life—the period in which he committed all these evils—and is not now upon earth, what can he be thought but dead? Or does foolish error suppose that wings grew upon him in old age, by which he flew to heaven? But men bereft of sense can believe even this, if indeed they believe [Col. 1118A] that he became a swan in order to beget the Castors; an eagle in order to defile Ganymede; a bull in order to violate Europa; gold in order to violate Danaë; a horse in order to beget Pirithous; a he-goat in order to beget “Egyppa” [Note: [Col. 1117B] *Egyppam*. Perhaps Aegipan. SUAR.] from a she-goat; and a satyr in order to overpower Antiope.

Those who look upon these adulteries—to which sinners are prone—readily believe them for this reason: that they may borrow from a fictitious god an authorization for wrongdoing and every kind of filthiness. But do they notice how incorrigible are the rest of his deeds, deeds that can be believed and are true, and which they say he performed without transformation? By Semele he begets Liber; by Latona, Apollo and Diana; by Maia, Mercury; by Alcmena, Hercules. But I do not wish to record his other debaucheries, which they themselves acknowledge, lest filthiness already buried be revived once more in people’s ears. I have mentioned only these few [Col. 1118B], whom deluded men likewise believe to be gods—born, that is, of an incestuous father, adulterous and supposititious—and they have confounded the living, eternal God of everlasting divinity [Note: [Col. 1117B] “Of everlasting divinity.” Perhaps “Son” is missing. SUAR. [Col. 1118B] Rather, nothing appears to be missing. EDD.], who foreknows the future and is boundless, with such abominable crimes.

## Third Appendix [Col. 1117]

### FRAGMENTS AND BRIEF NOTICES OF THE GREEK WORKS, WITH ANNOTATIONS BY JACOBUS PAMELIUS. (C)

### FRAGMENTS OF THE GREEK *APOLOGETICUS AGAINST THE GENTILES ON BEHALF OF THE CHRISTIANS*, from Eusebius of Caesarea, with three translations

### SHORT PREFACE TO THE GREEK FRAGMENTS OF THE *APOLOGETICUS*

[Col. 1117C] Eusebius and Nicephorus expressly affirm that Tertullian’s *Apologeticus against the Gentiles*—as Rufinus translated its title paraphrastically—or *On Behalf of the Christians*—as Christophorsonus in Eusebius and Langius in Nicephorus translated it word for word from the Greek—was composed in Latin but translated into Greek. Whether this was done by the author himself or by someone else is not sufficiently [Note: [Col. 1117C] Perhaps “clear” is to be supplied. EDD.] established, although the former opinion is favored by the fact [Col. 1118C] that he also composed certain other books in both Latin and Greek. I have therefore considered it worthwhile to publish the Greek fragments separately and, for greater comprehension, to accompany them with three translations: for Eusebius, those of his two translators, Rufinus and Christophorsonus; and for Nicephorus—who copied these passages from Eusebius word for word—that of Langius. PAM.

### I. From chapter 11 of the *Apologeticus*, according to Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, book III) and Nicephorus (book III, chapter 17)

[Col. 1117]

[Col. 1117D] Yet we have found that even the investigation of us has been forbidden. For Pliny the Younger, while governor of the province, condemned certain Christians and expelled others from Asia; but, disturbed by their multitude, he was at a loss as to what should be done about it. He therefore reported the matter to Emperor Trajan, saying that, apart from their refusal to worship idols, he had found nothing impious among them. He also reported [Col. 1118D] this: that the Christians rose at dawn and sang hymns to Christ as to God; and that, in order to preserve their discipline, they were forbidden to murder, commit adultery, defraud, deceive, and do similar things. In reply Trajan wrote that the race of Christians was not to be sought out, but that when brought before the authorities it was to be punished.

[Note: [Col. 1117] The translations of Rufinus, Christophorsonus, and Langius are printed in parallel in Migne.]

#### RUFINUS

[Col. 1117D]

The weight of persecutions from without, however, pressed upon the Church, and such immense companies of martyrs were being slaughtered daily that Pliny the Younger, who was then administering the province, was moved by the multitude of those killed and reported to the emperor that countless thousands of people [Col. 1119] were being slain every day, among whom absolutely no criminal act was found to have been committed, nor anything done contrary to human laws, except this alone: that before dawn they sang hymns to someone called Christ as God. Adulteries, however, and other crimes of this sort were regarded among them as unlawful and were completely prohibited; in all other respects they acted in accordance with the common laws. In response Trajan then decreed by the authority of his rescript that Christians were not indeed to be sought out, but that any who nevertheless came before the authorities were to be punished. By this decree the blaze of persecution was thought to have been quelled to some extent.

#### CHRISTOPHORSONUS

[Col. 1117D]

Yet we have found that even the investigation of us has been forbidden. For Pliny the Younger, while governing the province, condemned certain Christians and deprived others of their rank; but at length, disturbed by their very multitude and not knowing what he should do thereafter, he consulted Emperor Trajan, [Col. 1119] alleging that, apart from their obstinate refusal to sacrifice, he had found nothing criminal among them. He also disclosed this: that the Christians rose and assembled very early in the morning and praised Christ in hymns as God; and that, to preserve their discipline, they prohibited murder, adultery, fraud, breach of trust, and other crimes. In response Trajan wrote that Christians were not to be investigated, but that those brought forward were to be punished.

#### LANGIUS

[Col. 1118D]

Yet we have found that even the investigation of us has been forbidden. For Pliny the Younger, while governing the province, condemned certain Christians and deprived others of their rank; but, disturbed by their very multitude and uncertain what he should do thereafter, he consulted Emperor Trajan, alleging [Col. 1120] that, apart from their obstinate refusal to sacrifice, he had discovered nothing else concerning their rites except meetings before dawn to sing to Christ as to God, and prohibitions against murder, adultery, fraud, breach of trust, and other things, for the preservation of discipline. Trajan then wrote that people of this kind were not indeed to be investigated, but that those brought forward ought to be punished.

### II. From chapter V of the *Apologeticus*, according to Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, book II) and Nicephorus (book II, chapter 8)

[Col. 1119]

[Col. 1119A] But let us discuss the origin of laws of this kind as well. It was an ancient decree that no god should be consecrated by an emperor before being approved by the senate. Marcus Aemilius acted in this way concerning a certain idol of Alburnus. And this fact supports our case: among you divinity is bestowed by human approval. Unless a god pleases a man, he will not be a god; thus, according to this principle, man must be gracious [Col. 1120A] toward God.

Tiberius, therefore—during whose reign the Christian name entered the world—when this doctrine was reported to him from Palestine, where it first began, communicated it to the senate, making it clear to them that he approved the doctrine. But the senate rejected it because it had not itself examined and approved it. He remained firm in his judgment and threatened the accusers of Christians with death.

[Note: [Col. 1119] The translations of Rufinus, Christophorsonus, and Langius are printed in parallel in Migne.]

#### RUFINUS

[Col. 1119A]

To reconsider something of the origin of laws of this kind: there was an ancient decree that no god should be consecrated by the emperor unless approved by the senate, as Marcus Aemilius did concerning his god Alburnus. This too supports our case, because among you divinity is weighed according to human judgment. Unless God pleases man, he will not be a god. Man must now be gracious toward God.

Tiberius, therefore, in whose time the Christian name entered the world, when the events from Syrian Palestine which had revealed the truth of that divinity there were reported to him, referred the matter to the senate with the prerogative of his own favorable vote. The senate rejected it because it had not itself approved it. Caesar remained firm in his judgment and threatened danger to the accusers of Christians.

#### CHRISTOPHORSONUS

[Col. 1119A]

To reconsider the origin of laws of this kind: there was an ancient decree that no god should be consecrated by the emperor unless approved by the senate, as Marcus Aemilius did concerning his god Alburnus. This too supports our case, because among you divinity is weighed according to human judgment. Unless a god pleases man, he will not be a god. Man must now be gracious toward God.

Tiberius, therefore, in whose time the Christian name entered the world, when the truth of that divinity—which had been revealed there—was reported to him from Syrian Palestine, referred the matter to the senate with the prerogative of his own favorable vote. The senate rejected it because it had not itself approved it. Caesar remained firm in his judgment and threatened danger to the accusers of Christians.

#### LANGIUS

[Col. 1120A]

To reconsider something of the origin of laws of this kind: there was an ancient decree that no god should be consecrated by the emperor unless approved by the senate. Tiberius, therefore, in whose time the Christian name entered the world, when the truth of this doctrine was reported to him from Palestine—for it had taken its first beginnings there—referred the matter to the senate with the prerogative of his own favorable vote. The senate rejected it because it had not itself approved it. Caesar remained firm in his judgment and threatened the accusers of Christians with death.

[Col. 1119]

[Col. 1119B] Domitian too once attempted the same action as Nero, being a portion of Nero’s cruelty. But, I think, because he possessed some [Col. 1120B] understanding, he stopped very quickly and recalled those whom he had banished.

#### RUFINUS

[Col. 1122]

[Col. 1121]

[Col. 1121A] Thus likewise, in regard to the pleasures of the spectacles, their condition has been disgraced by those who recognize by nature that all the things from which spectacles are constructed belong to God, [Col. 1122A] but are deficient in knowledge. [Col. 1121A] You have this same subject treated most fully by the author himself in the book composed in Latin, *On the Spectacles*. [Col. 1121]

### MENTION OF THE BOOK *ON BAPTISM*, FROM THE BOOK OF THE SAME TITLE (chapter 15)

[Col. 1121]

[Col. 1121B] But what rule ought properly to be observed concerning heretics is a matter someone might worthily reconsider, for the present work was published for us. Heretics, however, have no fellowship in our discipline, since the very deprivation of communion proves them to be outsiders. I ought not to recognize among them what has been commanded to me, because we and they do not have the same God, nor one Christ—that is, the same Christ. Consequently there is not one baptism either, because it is not the same. Since they do not possess it rightly, they undoubtedly do not possess it at all; what is not possessed cannot be counted. Thus they cannot receive it either, because they do not possess it. But we have already set out this subject more fully in Greek.

#### [NOTE]

[Col. 1121B] These words also recall the principal subject matter of the Greek work *On Baptism*. Since, moreover, we promised to discuss here what Tertullian’s opinion was concerning the baptism of heretics, we certainly cannot deny that he held the same view as Blessed Cyprian. Perhaps, therefore, someone might say that this little book was suppressed when the opinion of certain African bishops was reconsidered by the Council of Nicaea.

Nor should it be surprising that Tertullian embraced that paradox, since the council under Agrippinus, bishop of Carthage, which Blessed Cyprian mentions in Epistle 71 to [Col. 1122B] Quintus, appears to have been held at almost the same time. That council also drew both him and the contemporary African bishops into this opinion. Cyprian appears to indicate this sufficiently in Epistle 70 to Januarius, when he says that the opinion had long before been established by their predecessors; and more expressly in Epistle 73 to Jubaianus, where he says that many years had passed since numerous bishops under Agrippinus had made this decree.

Yet approximately fifty years intervened between the time when Tertullian, before falling into any heresy, composed the book *On Baptism*, and the first African council of seventy-two bishops concerning the baptism of heretics, which was held in the year of the Lord 255. This is demonstrated more fully in the author’s Life.

## Fourth Appendix [Col. 1121]

### FRAGMENTS, MENTIONS, AND BRIEF NOTICES OF THE LOST WORKS OF QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIANUS. (C, S)

### I. BRIEF NOTICES FROM BLESSED JEROME OF THE BOOK *TO A PHILOSOPHER-FRIEND, ON THE TROUBLES OF MARRIAGE*

[Col. 1121C] At the beginning of this little book I stated in advance that I would say either nothing at all or very little about the Troubles of Marriage, and I now repeat the same warning. If you wish to know how many troubles beset a virgin who is free and how many a wife who is bound, read Tertullian writing *To a Philosopher-Friend*, and the other little books *On Virginity*, and Blessed Cyprian’s excellent volume, and the works composed on this subject in verse and prose by Pope Damasus, and the little works which our Ambrose recently wrote to his sister (*Epistle 28, to Eustochium*).

[Col. 1122C] This is not the place to describe the troubles of marriage and to exult, as though amid rhetorical commonplaces, in rhetorical discourse. I believe that I treated the subject more fully against Helvidius and completed it in the book I wrote to Eustochium. Tertullian, certainly, played with this subject while he was still a young man; and my teacher Gregory of Nazianzus, discussing Virginity and Marriage, expounded it in Greek verse (*Against Jovinian*, book I).

#### [NOTE]

[Col. 1123A] Thus far Blessed Jerome, whose complete periods we have reproduced, both to avoid presenting anything in mutilated form and to enable the reader to understand which of the ancients wrote on Virginity, a subject so greatly disputed today. For this reason I greatly wish that this little work of the author still survived, whether composed in prose or—more probably, as the verb “played” appears to indicate—in verse.

Accordingly I find even less acceptable the judgment of a certain learned man who thought this was the same book as the one entitled *Exhortation to Chastity*. For apart from the fact that he is said to have written the former as a young man, whereas the latter is known to have been written near the end of his life, the latter does not deal expressly with the troubles of marriage.

Nor do I approve the opinion of those who maintain that two different books [Col. 1124A] of Tertullian appear to be meant in the passages cited, since Blessed Jerome indicates in express words that both were entitled *On the Troubles of Marriage*. Yet whether Blessed Jerome also attributes to Tertullian the other little books *On Virginity* that he mentions might perhaps have been doubtful according to the earlier editions of Jerome, if the reading were: “read Tertullian’s *To a Philosopher-Friend*, and other little books *On Virginity*.” Certainly the two books *To His Wife* and the aforementioned *Exhortation to Chastity* have almost the same subject, and the book *On the Veiling of Virgins* treats nothing else. The reader will find in our index many additional passages in Tertullian concerning virginity, continence, and the preservation of chastity.

### II. MENTION AND FRAGMENT OF THE BOOK *ON FATE*, FROM TERTULLIAN’S BOOK *ON THE SOUL* (chapter 20) AND FULGENTIUS PLACIADES, *ON ANCIENT EXPRESSIONS*

[Col. 1123]

[Col. 1123B] Powers, to be sure, exercise dominion. According to us, there are the Lord God and his rival, the devil; according to common opinion, there are also Providence, [Col. 1124B] Fate, necessity, fortune, and freedom of choice. For the philosophers distinguish these things, and we already know that they must be discussed according to faith under their own title.

#### [NOTE]

[Col. 1123B] Thus far the author. Since no work of his survives in which he treats those four subjects, he appears to me quite plainly to allude to his book entitled *On Fate*, since it is evident from the following citation by Fulgentius Placiades—long ago printed with the *Mythologies* of Hyginus—that Tertullian composed such a book:

> “For Tertullian too says as follows in the book he wrote *On Fate*: ‘Return this man, first enslaved to the problem of fate’”—under the word *problema*, in the book *On Ancient Expressions*. [Col. 1124B]

Blessed Jerome, moreover, in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, relates that a little book *On Fate*, or *Against the Astrologers*, once circulated under the name of Minucius Felix. Yet although that work too is by an eloquent man, its style does not appear to agree with that of his dialogue *Octavius*. Perhaps it is the very book that we here attribute to Tertullian, since Jerome elsewhere calls him not merely eloquent but most eloquent.

### III. CITATION OF QUESTIONS *ON CLEAN AND UNCLEAN ANIMALS*, FROM BLESSED JEROME’S EPISTLE 125 TO DAMASUS

[Col. 1123]

[Col. 1123B] Among other questions, Damasus asks, as question III:

> “If God made all things very good (Gen. I), why did he give Noah instructions concerning clean and unclean animals (Gen. VIII), since nothing unclean can be [Col. 1123C] good? And in the New Testament, after the vision shown to Peter, when he said, ‘Far be it from me, Lord, for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth,’ a voice from heaven answered, ‘What God has cleansed, do not call common’ (Acts X).”

Blessed Jerome writes that he answered all but two short questions—namely, this one and the one discussed in the following fragment:

> “Not,” he says, “because I could not have answered those as well, but because they have been treated in the Latin language by most eloquent [Col. 1124C] men, our Tertullian and Novatian; and if we wished to introduce new material, a more extensive discussion would be required, etc. For Origen too discussed clean and unclean animals at considerable length in his work on Leviticus.”

#### [NOTE]

[Col. 1123C] Whether this refers to a particular book bearing that title—which nevertheless seems more probable—or to Tertullian’s discussion of the matter in a few lines in book II, chapter 18, *Against Marcion*, we leave to the reader’s judgment. Here we shall merely present the substance of his answer in these words:

> “And if the law detracts something from foods and pronounces unclean animals that were once blessed, understand this as a plan for exercising continence and as restraints imposed, etc.” [Col. 1124C]

Although this same point is presented in the book *On Jewish Foods*, but in very different words, it is evident from that fact—and from the remaining style of the entire book—that the work is not Tertullian’s but rather Novatian’s, since Blessed Jerome appears to allude to him in the words already quoted. The subject is treated there at greater length.

### IV. CITATION OF QUESTIONS *ON CIRCUMCISION*, FROM THE SAME PASSAGE OF BLESSED JEROME

[Col. 1123]

[Col. 1123D] Concerning Damasus’s penultimate question—

> “Why did Abraham receive circumcision as the sign of his faith?” (Gen. XVII)—

Blessed Jerome answers in the words already cited that he omitted this question together with the preceding one [Col. 1124D] because it had been treated in the Latin language by our Tertullian and Novatian. He adds that Origen also discussed Circumcision splendidly in the fourth *volume of his commentaries* (*ἐξηγήσεων τόμῳ*) on Romans.

#### [NOTE]

[Col. 1123D] It is not as certain that Tertullian wrote a distinct book *On Circumcision* as it is in Novatian’s case, to whom Blessed Jerome expressly assigns a book entitled *On Circumcision* in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*. Yet a very extensive treatment can also be seen in our author, volume I, *Against the Jews*, chapter 3.

There is indeed in volume IV—now volume IX—of the works of Blessed Jerome a book *On True Circumcision*, which Erasmus conjectures to be Tertullian’s. But apart from the fact that its style does not correspond, the contrary is proved both by the scriptural passages cited there according to Blessed Jerome’s version and by its mention of the Manichaeans. Consequently it cannot be attributed to Novatian either, but should rather—as a certain highly learned man judged—be attributed to Paulinus.

### V. MENTION OF THE BOOK *ON THE VESTMENTS OF AARON*, FROM BLESSED JEROME’S EPISTLE 128 TO FABIOLA, *ON THE PRIESTLY VESTMENT*

[Col. 1123]

[Col. 1123D] A book *On the Vestments [Col. 1124D] of Aaron* is listed in the catalogue of Septimius Tertullian, but to this day [Col. 1125A] I have not found it. If it has been found among you because of the renown of the City, I ask that you not compare my drop with his river. [Col. 1126A] For I am to be judged not by the talents of great men but by my own powers.

#### [NOTE]

[Col. 1125A] Aaron’s eight vestments are enumerated from Exodus chapter XXVIII and explained at great length by Blessed Jerome in the aforementioned Epistle *On the Priestly Vestment*. Four of them—namely, the linen breeches, linen tunic, belt, and turban—were also common to the priests; [Col. 1126A] the others were proper to the high priests: the ankle-length violet tunic with bells, the shoulder-piece or ephod, the breastpiece, and the gold plate. We therefore refer the reader there.

### VI. BRIEF NOTICE OF THE BOOK *ON THE TRINITY*

[Col. 1125]

[Col. 1125A] Blessed Jerome says in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> Novatian wrote a large volume *On the Trinity*, as though an epitome (*ἐπιτομήν*) [Col. 1126A] of Tertullian’s work; many, not knowing this, consider it Cyprian’s.

#### [NOTE]

[Col. 1125A] These words of Blessed Jerome reasonably create doubt as to whether Tertullian wrote another work *On the Trinity* besides his book *Against Praxeas*. For an epitome (*ἐπιτομή*) is an abridgment of a larger work, whereas Novatian’s book *On the Trinity*, being a large volume, as Jerome himself testifies, is much longer than the book *Against Praxeas*. Thus, if Blessed Jerome’s manuscripts are not corrupt, it will be necessary to acknowledge that Tertullian composed another [Col. 1125B] book *On the Trinity*.

But if we read *ἐπίτασιν* (“amplification”)—which may perhaps have been Jerome’s reading—Novatian’s book will be regarded as an expansion of the argument treated by Tertullian in his book *Against Praxeas*. The same judgment must be made if we read *μίμησιν*, that is, “imitation,” since Novatian imitates Tertullian at times.

We, therefore, since we are reluctant to alter [Col. 1126A] the reading of ancient authors without manuscript evidence, have preferred to place a book *On the Trinity* among Tertullian’s lost works. This is especially warranted because, although Novatian treats the same argument more extensively concerning God the Father and God the Son, Tertullian in turn treats more extensively, in *Against Praxeas and the Monarchians*, the distinction of the Son from the Father, whom they made one and the same—as Sabellius did later, against whom Novatian argues more briefly. Furthermore, [Col. 1126B] the Holy Spirit is treated there more extensively and more correctly, since Novatian has only a single chapter on him. Thus, strictly speaking, Novatian’s book cannot be called an *epitome*, because it is a larger work; nor an *amplification*, because in certain matters it is more concise; nor an *imitation*, because it does not imitate Tertullian in every respect.

### VII. SUBJECT AND FRAGMENTS OF THE BOOK *ON THE ORIGIN OF THE SOUL, AGAINST HERMOGENES*, from the book *On the Soul*, chapters 1, 3, 22, and 24

[Col. 1125]

[Col. 1125B] Tertullian says:

> Having confronted Hermogenes solely concerning the origin of the soul, insofar as he presumed that it was constituted from the prompting of matter rather than from the breath of God, I now turn to the remaining questions, in which I shall appear chiefly to be contending with the philosophers.

[Col. 1125C]

> One encounter against Hermogenes has already been decided, as we stated at the outset, because we vindicate the soul as derived from the breath of God, not from matter; there too we were fortified by the unclouded rule of the divine determination: “And God,” it says, “breathed the breath of life into the face of man, and man became a living soul” (Gen. II; 1 Cor. XV)—a soul derived, surely, from the breath of God. Nothing further need be reconsidered concerning this matter; it has its own title and its own heretic.

> But against Hermogenes, who maintains that it—the soul, namely—is derived from matter and not from the breath of God, we defend the term “breath” (*flatus*) in its proper sense. For, contrary to the authority of Scripture itself, he changes “breath” into “Spirit,” so that—because it is incredible that the Spirit of God should fall into sin and soon afterward into judgment—the soul might be believed to derive from matter [Col. 1126B] rather than from the Spirit of God. For this reason we there defend it as “breath,” not “spirit,” according to Scripture and according to the distinction between spirits; but here, despite our opponents, we pronounce it “spirit,” according to the nature of breathing and blowing. There the question concerns substance, for breathing [Col. 1126C] is an act of a substance.

> Hermogenes has already heard from us about the soul’s other natural properties, together with their defense and proof, through which it is recognized as akin to God rather than to matter.

> We, however, who attach nothing to it, by this very fact weigh the soul as far inferior to God, because we acknowledge that it was born and therefore possesses a more diluted divinity and a feebler felicity: it is breath, not Spirit. Although immortal—insofar as this belongs to divinity—it is nevertheless capable of suffering, insofar as this belongs to birth; and thus it was capable of deviation from the beginning and, consequently, liable also to forgetfulness. Enough concerning this matter with Hermogenes.

#### [NOTE]

[Col. 1125D] In these five passages the author first indicates the title and subject: *On the Origin of the Soul, against Hermogenes*. That *census* here means “origin” is evident not only from the first passage but also from the fact that the work refuted the heresy of Hermogenes, by which he maintained that the soul’s origin lay not in the breath of God but in matter. In precisely the same way he said that the world was made not from nothing but from matter coeternal with God—a heresy against which the author argued above in the book *Against Hermogenes*.

He also adduces two scriptural passages by which he indicates that he proved the soul to be God’s breath: Genesis II and 1 Corinthians XV. In these passages Hermogenes, to make them appear favorable to his heresy, rendered “spirit of life” where others rendered “breath,” contrary to the authority of Scripture, since the Greek reads *πνοήν* (*pnoēn*, “breath”). Most interpreters prefer—as Blessed Augustine also testifies in *The City of God*, book XIII, chapter 24—to translate this as “breath,” [Col. 1126D] “inspiration,” “breathing,” or “soul,” rather than “spirit.” In the third passage cited here, the author indicates that in the aforementioned book he undertook to defend the term “breath” rather than “spirit.”

Meanwhile, although Tertullian in another sense also acknowledges the soul to be “spirit,” from “breathing,” in the book *On the Soul*, he does not agree in every respect with the Catholic position. Catholics properly call the soul a spirit, though not the Holy Spirit, and therefore also translate *πνοήν* as “spirit” in the said passage of Genesis and elsewhere. But regarding this paradox of his, we have referred the reader to our Prolegomena. . . .

He next intimates that, closer to his intended subject, he treated the soul’s other natural properties against Hermogenes, in order to prove that the soul is akin to God rather than to matter. Finally, perhaps because someone might compare the soul with God, he writes that in the said book he defended the soul as far inferior to God: because it was born, [Col. 1127A] because it is capable of suffering and deviation, and consequently liable also to forgetfulness. Thus nearly the argument of the entire book, and what might be called certain fragments of it [Col. 1128A], may be seen here repeated in the author’s very own words.

### VIII. CITATION OF THE BOOK *AGAINST THE APELLETIANS*, FROM THE BOOK *ON THE FLESH OF CHRIST* (chapter 8)

[Col. 1127]

[Col. 1127A] But since these Apelletians in particular also plead the disgrace of the flesh—which, they maintain, was fastened by that fiery ruler of evil upon souls he had enticed, and was therefore unworthy of Christ, so that a substance drawn from the stars was appropriate for him—I must strike them down with their own equipment.

They name a certain illustrious angel who established this world and, after establishing it, admitted repentance. We have treated this matter in its proper place. For we have a little book against them, examining whether one who possessed the spirit, will, and power of Christ for those works had done anything deserving repentance, since they also interpret the angel [Col. 1127B] as the figure of the wandering sheep.

Therefore, on the testimony of its maker’s repentance, the world will be a sin, since all repentance is a confession of sin, because [Col. 1128A] it has no place except where there is sin. If the world is a sin because it is a body and its members are sin, then heaven too, and the heavenly things together with heaven, will likewise be sin. If the heavenly things are sin, then whatever has been conceived and brought forth from them must be the evil fruit of an evil tree.

Christ’s flesh, therefore, if constructed from heavenly things, consisted of the elements of sin; it was sinful, derived from a sinful origin, and will be equal in substance to that flesh—that is, ours—which Christ disdains to assume because it is sinful. Thus, if there is no difference in respect of disgrace, those who are displeased with our material must either devise for Christ some other material of a purer character, or [Col. 1128B] acknowledge this material of ours, than which even heavenly material could not have been better.

#### [NOTE]

[Col. 1127B] Whether this book ought to be entitled *Against Apelles* or *Against the Apelleians* caused me to hesitate for some time, because Vincent of Lérins, among the other heretics against whom Tertullian wrote, enumerates Apelles; consequently, we also wondered whether the author had composed several treatises against Apelles himself and his disciples. But since, although Apelles is mentioned so many times and no one else is, Tertullian nevertheless makes no mention of any book against him except in this passage, it seems credible to me both that he composed only one and that it was entitled *Against the Apelleians*. This is especially so because blessed Cyprian also calls the disciples of Apelles “Apelleians,” Epistle 73, *To Jubaianus*.

Now the words of Tertullian already cited are indeed rather obscure, but their meaning is this: the principal subject of the book *Against the Apelleians* [Col. 1127C] was whether that fiery angel, the ruler of evil, who had both fashioned this world (according to them) and constructed flesh for the souls he had enticed—although for this purpose he had possessed the spirit, will, and power of Christ—had done anything worthy of repentance. For they used to say, as may be read in the book *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, ch. 51, Heresy 19: “He mingled repentance with the lower world, because he had not made it as perfect as the higher world had been fashioned.” Meanwhile, Tertullian turns this very point elegantly against them when he speaks of “refuting them from their own equipment.” What he means by calling this angel “the ruler of evil” is explained by Epiphanius, Heresy 44, according to the opinion of Apelles: “But he proved not to be good, and the things made by him were not well made, but were created by him in accordance with his own evil mind.”

On the souls enticed by that fiery god or angel according to Apelles, see above, vol. III, *On the Soul*, chs. 23 and 36, where the author adds, as a consequence, that Apelles held male and female souls to have existed before [Col. 1127D] bodies. On the world fashioned by him, see *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chs. 34 and 51, Heresy 19. On human flesh consequently constructed by that same being, see ch. 8 of *On the Flesh of Christ*, from which these words are taken, and *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 5. Finally, concerning the flesh of Christ—not created by that angel but constructed from the heavenly stars—the author argues at length against Apelles in ch. 6 of the said book *On the Flesh of Christ*. Epiphanius agrees on all these points, except that he calls the being whom the author terms a fiery angel the “lower god”; this angel is, however, also acknowledged by blessed Augustine, [Col. 1128B] *Heresies* 23; blessed Isidore, *Against Marcion*; our Rabanus; blessed Honorius; and Gratian, in their catalogues of heretics.

Peculiar to our author is what has already been said about the repentance of the creator-angel, as is also the claim that they interpreted the figure of the wandering sheep (Luke 15) as referring to him—as though there had been joy in heaven among the angels of God over that one sinner converted to repentance. The author, by contrast, preferred to interpret it as referring to fallen humanity, sought out again through Christ, as did all the other ancients. Thus far concerning the points that contribute to understanding this fragment.

Since, however, we promised to present here a complete history of Apelles and his heresies, we shall do so in as few words as possible. Apelles, therefore, was a disciple of Marcion. To use the author’s words from the said book *On the Prescription* [Col. 1128C] *Against Heretics*, chs. 6, 30, and 51: having fallen into involvement with a woman, and having deserted Marcionite continence—which Marcion merely pretended to observe—he withdrew from his master’s sight to Alexandria. There he stumbled upon another woman, the virgin Philumene, who afterward became an enormous prostitute. Led astray by her signs and prodigies, he published a book which he entitled *The Manifestations of Philumene*, whom he followed as though she were a prophetess.

Indeed, the author calls him not merely a deserter but also a corrector of Marcion and a disciple above his master, *Against Marcion*, book IV, ch. 17. This was not only because, as we said there, he posited one higher God and called the other “Lord,” but made him an angel; it was also because of the other heresies listed a little earlier, which he introduced as novelties after being seduced by Philumene. He differed in no respect from Marcion in rejecting the God of Moses, the Law, and the prophets, as is stated in *On the Prescription*, ch. 51. He taught the salvation of souls alone and denied the resurrection of the flesh, which the author therefore attacks in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*; likewise, he used only the Apostle, and even that was Marcion’s version—that is, not the complete text. On most of these matters one may also consult Epiphanius, Theodoret, and John of Damascus.

But this detail is peculiar to our author: “He has, moreover, his own books, which he entitled *Syllogisms*, in which he attempts to prove that not everything Moses wrote about God is true, but that it is false.” Consequently, nothing else concerning these matters presents itself for annotation. I shall add only this: it is not surprising that the author wrote against the Apelleians, since in the frequently cited *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, ch. 30, he reports that distinct pupils and successors of Apelles were still surviving.

## X. SUBJECT OF THE BOOK *ON PARADISE*, FROM *ON THE SOUL* (CH. 55)

[Col. 1127]

[Col. 1127D] “But our dwelling is in the ether,” etc. “No,” you say, “it is in paradise, to which even then the patriarchs and prophets, [Col. 1128D] appendages of the Lord’s resurrection, migrated from the lower regions. And how is it that the region of paradise, [Col. 1129A] revealed to John in the spirit and lying beneath the altar, shows no other souls with it except those of the martyrs? How is it that Perpetua, that most valiant martyr, on the day before her passion, in a revelation of paradise, saw there only her fellow martyrs? Is it not because the sword that guards paradise yields to none except those who have died in Christ? [The text is apparently corrupt here; conjecturally:] A new death for God, extraordinary for Christ, is received in another, private lodging. Recognize, therefore, the difference [Col. 1130A] between a pagan and a believer in death. If you fall for God,” etc., “not amid mild fevers and upon little beds, but in martyrdoms; if you take up your cross and follow the Lord, as he himself commanded, your blood is the complete key to paradise. You also have our treatise *On Paradise*, in which we establish that every soul is kept apart in the lower regions until the day of the Lord.”

### [NOTE]

[Col. 1129A] Thus far the author; but he must be understood in a sounder sense, as we have noted more fully among the Paradoxes in the Prolegomena, where we shall answer all his arguments. It must be noted here that the author composed this book not only on the earthly paradise in which Adam was created, and to which Enoch and Elijah are said to have been translated, but also—and principally by design—on the spiritual paradise into which the apostle Paul is said to have been caught up in 2 [Col. 1129B] Cor. 12. Yet in this he disagrees with the other Fathers, who call that paradise heavenly—blessed Ambrose does so expressly in his commentary on that passage—whereas our author does not distinguish it from Abraham’s bosom, although he admits that the latter is higher than the lower regions. But on this also, see the Paradoxes in the Prolegomena.

He expressly acknowledges the earthly paradise when speaking of Adam in *Against the Jews*, ch. 2; *On Patience*, ch. 5; *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 26; and *Against Marcion*, book II, chs. 2 and 10. Again, in *Against the Valentinians*, ch. 20, mocking the Valentinian Ptolemy because he dreamed that Paradise was a fourth archangel, he jokes as follows:

> “For they place this being above the third heaven as well, from whose power Adam supposedly drew while lodging there amid little clouds and little trees. Ptolemy remembered children’s sayings well enough: that apples grow in the sea and fish upon trees; in the same way he presumed there to be walnut groves in the heavens. The Demiurge works in ignorance, and therefore perhaps he does not know that trees ought to be established on the earth alone!”

Most openly of all, however, he acknowledges it in this very volume, in the poem *On the Judgment* [Col. 1129C] *of the Lord*, ch. 8, and in *Genesis*, chs. 2 and 3.

Blessed Irenaeus had already acknowledged the same paradise in *Against Heresies*, book III, ch. 55, and more openly in book V, ch. 5, where he says that the presbyters who were disciples of the Apostles taught that Enoch and Elijah had been translated into the paradise where the first man was placed, concerning which Scripture says (Gen. 2): “And God planted a Paradise in Eden toward the East, and placed the man there.”

Blessed Justin Martyr also agrees in *Apology* I, where he writes that Homer, in imitation of the paradise described by Moses, invented the garden of Alcinous. Likewise, Theophilus in book II *To Autolycus*, Novatian in *On the Trinity*, and Lactantius in the poem *On the Phoenix*, alluding to the quoted words of Scripture, report that paradise was situated in the East. Finally, Epiphanius, in the *Anchored One*, *Against the Origenists*, and the *Letter to John, Bishop of Jerusalem*, translated into Latin by blessed Jerome, argues at very great length from Scripture (Gen. 2 and 3) against Origen, who transferred paradise from the earthly realm to the heavens. He proves the same from those four rivers flowing out of paradise, whose water he writes that he himself had drunk; and he maintains that in the Apostle’s words at 2 Cor. 12 the third heaven is one thing and paradise another.

Blessed Augustine, in *On Heresies*, attributes the same heresy to the Seleucians and Herminians. Blessed Jerome also, somewhere in his *Commentary on Daniel*, commands all their ravings to fall silent. As for where paradise is located, I consider it superfluous to recount here the various opinions of different writers, since blessed Augustine writes in *Against Pelagius and Coelestius*, book II, ch. 23, that this belongs among questions that lie outside the faith.

## SUBJECT OF THE BOOK *ON THE HOPE OF THE FAITHFUL*, FROM *AGAINST MARCION*, BOOK III, FINAL CHAPTER; BLESSED JEROME ON EZEKIEL 36 AND ELSEWHERE; AND GENNADIUS

[Col. 1129]

[Col. 1129C] Tertullian says:

> Concerning the restoration of Judaea, which the Jews themselves also hope for just as it is described, being led by the names of places and regions: it would take too long to trace how the allegorical interpretation applies to Christ and the Church, and to its condition and fruit; and this has been set out in another work, which we entitle *On the Hope of the Faithful*. In the present work it would also be superfluous for the additional reason that the question concerns not an earthly but a heavenly promise. For we also confess that a kingdom upon earth has been promised to us, [Col. 1129D] but before heaven and in another condition—namely, after the resurrection, for a thousand years (Rev. 20 and 21), in Jerusalem, a city of divine workmanship brought down from heaven. The Apostle also designates this as our mother above (Gal. 4); and by declaring that our πολίτευμα (*politeuma*), that is, our citizenship, is in heaven (Phil. 3), he assigns it to some city—surely a heavenly one. Ezekiel also knew this city (Ezek. 48), and the Apostle John saw it (Rev. 21).

Blessed Jerome says:

> For we do not, according to Jewish fables—which they call δευτερώσεις (*deuterōseis*, “repetitions” or “secondary traditions”)—expect a jeweled and golden Jerusalem from heaven; nor shall we again suffer the injury of circumcision, offer sacrifices of bulls and rams, or sleep in Sabbath idleness. Yet many of our own writers promise this, especially Tertullian’s book entitled *On the Hope of the Faithful*, the seventh volume of Lactantius’ *Institutions*, the frequent expositions of Victorinus, bishop of Poetovio, and, recently, our Severus in the *Dialogue* to which he gave the name *Gallus*. And, to name the Greeks and join the first with the last: Irenaeus and Apollinaris.

The same Jerome says in the preface to book XVIII on Isaiah, alluding to the same book:

> Nor am I unaware how great a diversity of opinions there is among men, etc., concerning the promises of future things and the manner in which John’s Apocalypse ought to be understood. If we accept it according to the letter, we must Judaize; if we expound it spiritually, as it was written, we shall appear to contradict the opinions of many ancients: among the Latins, Tertullian, Victorinus, and Lactantius; among the Greeks—to pass over the others—I shall mention only Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons. Against him Dionysius, that most eloquent man and bishop of the church of Alexandria, wrote an elegant book, ridiculing the fable of the thousand years, a golden and jeweled Jerusalem upon earth, the restoration of the Temple, the blood of sacrificial victims, Sabbath idleness, the injury of circumcision, marriages, childbirth, the upbringing of children, the pleasures of banquets, and the enslavement of all nations; and, again, wars, armies, triumphs, the slaughter of the defeated, and the death of the sinner at a hundred years of age. [Col. 1131A] Apollinaris answered him in two volumes.

The same Jerome says in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> Papias is said to have published a Jewish δευτέρωσις (*deuterōsis*, “repetition” or “secondary tradition”) concerning the thousand years. Irenaeus, Apollinaris, and the others followed him who say that after the resurrection the Lord will reign in the flesh among the saints. Tertullian, too, in the book *On the Hope of the Faithful*, Victorinus of Poetovio, and Lactantius are led by this opinion.

Gennadius says in *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, among the works of blessed Augustine, alluding to the same book:

> In the divine [Col. 1132A] promises we expect nothing earthly or transitory, as the Melitanians hope; not the union of marriage, as Cerinthus and Marcus rave; not anything pertaining to food or drink, as Irenaeus, Tertullian, and Lactantius assent to Papias, their authority; nor do we hope that after the resurrection Christ’s kingdom will exist upon earth for a thousand years and that the saints will reign with him amid pleasures, as Nepos taught, who invented a first resurrection of the just and a second resurrection of the wicked.

### [NOTE]

[Col. 1131A] Thus far the several testimonies concerning the subject of the book *On the Hope of the Faithful*. We added the last chiefly because it attributes to each author his own paradoxes, whereas blessed Jerome at first sight appears to fasten them upon everyone collectively. Yet, out of reverence, Jerome calls them “opinions,” not heresies or errors; in this Gennadius also imitated him.

But so that we may not be more prolix here concerning the opinions of others, or concerning the answer to all the arguments that Tertullian cites from Scripture in this passage, let the reader consult our Prolegomena among the Paradoxes. Here we shall say only that Tertullian’s opinion appears to us milder than the others, namely, the view about which blessed Augustine writes in *The City of God*, book XX, ch. 7:

> This opinion would indeed be tolerable if it were believed that certain spiritual delights would be granted to the saints in that Sabbath—that is, during the thousand years—through the Lord’s presence. “For we ourselves,” he says, “once held this opinion.”

Thus, what Gennadius attributes to the Melitanians—that they hoped for an earthly kingdom of Christ—applies to Tertullian, who described it in *On the Hope of the Faithful*, more properly than does what Gennadius imputes to him concerning food and drink. Perhaps this was why the author, above others, commends Melito in those books written for Montanus whose fragments follow, according to the passage that will be cited there from blessed Jerome. For, in the passage mentioned, he indicates in these words that this paradox also belonged to Montanus:

> This, etc., is also attested by the utterance of the New Prophecy, which is held among us to belong to the faith, inasmuch as it foretold that even an image of the city would appear to human sight as a sign before the city itself was manifested.

The author’s words that chiefly confirm what I have said are those cited above:

> Concerning the restoration of Judaea, how the allegorical interpretation applies to Christ and the Church, and to its condition and fruit—it would take too long to trace, etc.

For if the interpretation is allegorical, it is therefore not literal; and consequently one would wrongly impute to him—as applies more properly to Cerinthus and the Dimœrites, according to Epiphanius—the restoration of the Temple, the blood of sacrificial victims, Sabbath idleness, and the injury of circumcision.

The words he adds shortly afterward in the same passage tend to the same conclusion:

> We say that this city—namely, Jerusalem brought down from heaven—has been provided by God to receive the saints at their resurrection and to refresh them with the abundance of all goods, which are of course spiritual, in compensation for those things that in this age we either despised or lost.

For if it is an abundance of spiritual goods, it is therefore not an abundance of the temporal goods of which others dream. Meanwhile, he agrees with the others in this point, although erroneously: he confesses that a kingdom has indeed been promised to us upon earth, but before heaven.

## MENTION OF THE SIX BOOKS *ON ECSTASY*, FROM BLESSED JEROME’S *CATALOGUE OF ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS* AND NICEPHORUS, *ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY*, BOOK IV, CHS. 22 AND 34

[Col. 1131]

[Col. 1131C] Blessed Jerome says of Tertullian—and Nicephorus uses precisely the same words:

> Although he had remained a presbyter of the Church until middle age, he afterward fell into the doctrine of Montanus because of the envy and insults of the clergy of the Roman Church. In many books he mentions the New Prophecy; but he composed especially against the Church the volumes *On Modesty*, *On Flight in Persecution*, [Col. 1132C] *On Fasts*, *On Monogamy*, and six books *On Ecstasy*.

The same author says:

> Tertullian, having published six volumes against the Church, which he wrote περὶ Ἐκστάσεως (*peri Ekstaseōs*, “On Ecstasy”), etc.

The same Jerome says in his notice on Melito:

> Praising Melito’s elegant and declamatory genius, Tertullian, in the seven books *Against the Church, for Montanus*, says that many of our people considered him a prophet.

### [NOTE]

[Col. 1131C] Thus far Jerome. From the latter passage it appears [Col. 1131D] that these books were composed in Greek rather than Latin, as we shall explain more fully in the following fragment.

But, to keep our promises, we have thought it proper to add briefly what “ecstasy” means to the author and to other ancient ecclesiastical writers. A general definition is found in *On the Soul*, ch. 45:

> We call ecstasy a departure from the senses and something resembling madness. Thus at the beginning sleep was also inaugurated with ecstasy: “And God sent an ecstasy upon Adam” (Gen. 2:21), “and he fell asleep.” For sleep came upon the body for repose, while ecstasy came upon the soul in opposition to repose; and from that point onward the pattern combines sleep with ecstasy.

And a little later:

> This will be the distinctive quality of this madness: it does not arise from the corruption of good health, but from the order of nature; for it does not destroy the mind, but calls it away. To shake is one thing, to move another; to overturn is one thing, to agitate another. Therefore, the fact that memory remains available indicates soundness of mind; and when soundness of mind, with memory preserved, is nevertheless stupefied, it is a kind of madness. Hence we are said not to rave but to dream; hence also we remain rational, if we ever are so. For our understanding, although it is overshadowed, [Col. 1132C] is nevertheless not extinguished, except that it may itself appear to be inactive at the time. Ecstasy, moreover, also produces this effect from its own peculiar nature: it introduces images of wisdom into us just as it does images of error.

Briefer, however, and more consistent with the author’s purpose is the definition found in ch. 2 of the same book, where he speaks of Adam:

> An ecstasy fell upon him: the power of the Holy Spirit, the agent of prophecy.

And in ch. 21:

> God sent madness upon him, the spiritual power in which prophecy consists.

Yet the former kind of ecstasy could in some fashion be acknowledged in Adam, but not this latter kind, since it appears designed to confirm the enthusiasms of Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla. Their own disciples admitted that these persons customarily spoke in ecstasy and as though mad; and after his middle age Tertullian himself was among those disciples.

To this belongs the following statement concerning Prisca or Maximilla in *On the Soul*, ch. 9:

> There is today among us a sister who has obtained gifts of revelations, which she experiences in the church, amid the Lord’s solemn rites, through ecstasy in the spirit.

This, indeed, is what he means in *Against Marcion*, book IV, ch. 22, [Col. 1133A] where he explains the words about Peter in Luke 9, “But not knowing what he was saying”:

> How was he not knowing? Was it through a simple error, or through irrationality—“irrationality” being the sense in which he also said in *Against Praxeas*, ch. 15, that Peter, John, and James did not experience the vision of God without irrationality and madness—which we defend in the cause of the New Prophecy, namely, that ecstasy, that is, madness, belongs to grace? For when a person is placed in the Spirit, especially when he beholds the glory of God or when God speaks through him, he must necessarily fall away from the senses, being overshadowed, of course, by divine power. Concerning this there is a dispute between us and the Psychics.

Here—as more fully in *On Fasts, Against the Psychics*—by “Psychics” he means Catholics, and he alludes to these six books *On Ecstasy*, which it is certain that he wrote against the Church.

But Epiphanius argues admirably against the Montanists in Heresy 48. After proving from the Scriptures that true prophets spoke under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit with constant reason and understanding, sound in mind and body, he comes to the prophecy of Montanus and proves from Montanus’ own words that he prophesied neither with a stable mind nor with mental understanding.

The same point appears to be served by blessed Jerome’s annotation in *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*: instead of “ecstasy,” that is, a departure of the mind, the Hebrew has [Hebrew term missing in the supplied text], which Aquila translated καταφοράν (*kataphoran*, “deep sleep”) and Symmachus κάρον (*karon*), that is, a heavy and profound sleep. Finally, the text continues: “And he slept.” The same word is also used of Jonah’s snoring sleep.

Yet Peter’s words, “not knowing what he was saying,” do nothing to support the insane prophecy of Montanus. Others prefer to understand them as referring to unconsidered speech, such as people customarily use when mentally overwhelmed, because Mark adds: “For they were terrified by fear.” And this is certain: Peter prophesied nothing there.

Moreover, the author also attempts to twist a passage of the Apostle, 1 Cor. 14, into confirmation of the same New Prophecy, with these words in *Against Marcion*, ch. 8:

> Let him produce some psalm, some vision, some prayer—provided it is spiritual—in ecstasy, that is, in madness, if an interpretation of the tongue has been added. Let him also prove to me that a woman among them has prophesied, one of those holier females of theirs, a speaker of great things.

But besides the fact that the phrase “in ecstasy” is not found there in the Apostle, the same passage says: “And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets.” From the Apostle’s immediately following words blessed Jerome refutes Montanus, and consequently Tertullian, in the prologue to his *Commentary on Habakkuk*:

> It is a prophet’s vision; and, against the perverse doctrine of Montanus, the prophet understands what he sees. He does not speak as a madman, nor, after the manner of raving women, utter sound without understanding. Hence the Apostle also commands that, if something is revealed to another while others are prophesying, [Col. 1134B] those who were speaking first should be silent.

From this it is understood that when someone voluntarily falls silent and gives another an opportunity to speak, he can both speak and remain silent when he wishes. But one who speaks in ecstasy—that is, involuntarily—has it within his power neither to remain silent nor to speak.

The same point is made by Jerome in the prologue to the prophet Nahum:

> For he does not speak in ἐκστάσει (*ekstasei*, “ecstasy”), as Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla rave; rather, what he prophesies is the book of a vision belonging to one who understands everything he says.

## NOTES ON THE BOOK *AGAINST APOLLONIUS*, FROM BLESSED JEROME’S *CATALOGUE* AND NICEPHORUS

[Col. 1133]

[Col. 1133B] In the passages cited above concerning Tertullian, they say:

> He composed especially against the Church the volumes *On Ecstasy*, six books, and a seventh, *Against Apollonius*.

Blessed Jerome says:

> Apollonius, a most eloquent man, [Col. 1133C] wrote against Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla a distinguished and lengthy volume, in which he asserts that Montanus and the insane prophetesses perished by hanging, and many other things. Among these, he relates the following concerning Priscilla and Maximilla: “If they deny that these women accepted gifts, let them confess that those who do accept them are not prophets; and I shall prove this by a thousand witnesses. But prophets are also proved by other fruits. Tell me: does a prophet dye his hair? Does he smear his eyes with antimony? Is a prophet [Col. 1134B] adorned with clothing and jewels? Does a prophet play at tables and dice? Does a prophet receive interest? Let them answer whether it is permissible to do this or not. It is my task to prove”—for so I read, instead of “to approve”—“what they did.”

> In the same book he says that it was the fortieth year, down to the time when he was writing the book, since the heresy of the Cataphrygians had its beginning. Tertullian, having published six volumes against the Church, which he wrote περὶ ἐκτάσεως (*peri ektaseōs*, “On Ecstasy”), composed a seventh specifically *Against Apollonius*, in which he attempts to defend everything that Apollonius censures. Apollonius flourished under the emperors Commodus and Severus.

### [NOTE]

[Col. 1133C] For two reasons I am persuaded that this book *Against Apollonius*, together with the six preceding books, was published not only in Latin but first in Greek. First, Apollonius was Greek and wrote in Greek, being a different man from the Roman senator whom blessed Jerome mentions subsequently; secondly, Jerome gives the title [Col. 1133D] in Greek, περὶ ἐκστάσεως (*peri ekstaseōs*, “On Ecstasy”). In the preceding fragments, however, he did not wish to add that they had been written against the Church.

Moreover, since blessed Jerome asserts that Tertullian attempted to defend everything Apollonius censured, we find it entirely true that blessed Augustine wrote of him in *On Heresies, to Quodvultdeus*: Tertullian passed over to the Cataphrygians whom he had formerly demolished. For above all, in *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, ch. 52, Heresy 21, he expressly calls heretics

> those who are called “according to the Phrygians,” etc., who said that the Holy Spirit had indeed been in the Apostles, but not the Paraclete; and that the Paraclete said more through Montanus than Christ set forth in the Gospel—and not merely more, [Col. 1134C] but also better and greater things.

Against the coloring of hair and staining of the eyes with antimony, which he nevertheless appears to have defended in these prophetesses, he argues expressly in *On Women’s Dress*, ch. 4, and more openly in *On the Adornment of Women*, ch. 5. There he attacks those

> who smear their eyes with soot,

reproaching God the craftsman whom [Col. 1134D] they correct; and in ch. 6 he attacks

> those who turn their hair saffron-colored, making an ill omen for themselves with their flaming head and bringing destruction upon the brain.

Against adornment with clothing and jewels, which he also tolerated in those women, he argues both there and in *On the Pallium*, ch. 4, and throughout the book *On Women’s Dress*, particularly on jewels in ch. 6.

The game of tables and dice, which he does not condemn here, as though treating another subject, he tacitly censures in prophets or teachers in *On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. 7, in these words:

> I ask you, Apelles—or you, Marcion—if perhaps, while playing at tables, etc., you were called away by such a messenger, etc.

Finally, in *Against Marcion*, book IV, ch. 17, he treats at great length of interest on loans, forbidden by Christ at Luke 6, although Montanus accepted it.

## MENTION OF SEVERAL LOST WORKS, FROM THE SAME PASSAGES OF BLESSED JEROME AND NICEPHORUS, AND FROM VINCENT

[Col. 1133]

[Col. 1133D] Blessed Jerome says of Tertullian:

> He is reported to have lived to an extremely advanced age and to have composed many minor works that are no longer extant.

Nicephorus says:

> But many others also contended for our faith in an altogether Christian spirit and fought against heresies. They committed to writing the received condition and customs [Col. 1135A] of the Church, and other things that they had received from their predecessors either in writing or without writing, and left a great many books to posterity. Gaius and Tertullian are deservedly numbered among them, for they certainly published very many [Col. 1136A] and very excellent writings, which it is not part of the present purpose to enumerate individually. He wrote, however, *On Modesty*, etc., and several others.

### [NOTE]

[Col. 1135A] Thus far those authors. And indeed, would that the *Index of Septimius Tertullian*, mentioned above in the fragment of the book *On the Garments of Aaron*, were extant! There is no doubt that it would mention many more of his writings.

Whether he wrote additional works against heretics once caused me to hesitate because of what Vincent of Lérins writes of him:

> The Marcions, Apelleses, Praxeases, Hermogeneses, Jews, pagans, Gnostics, and the others know how he overthrew their blasphemies by means of the many great masses of his volumes, as though with thunderbolts.

But when I noticed that the Valentinians and Quintilla were omitted there, together with twenty-five others whose catalogue he recounts in *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, [Col. 1135B] from ch. 45 to the end, as well as those against whom he wrote the latter part of *On the Soul*—Simon the Samaritan, Carpocrates, Menander, and others—I became persuaded that no work of this kind is now missing.

Therefore, I also consider the text of blessed Optatus of Milevis, *Against Parmenianus*, book I, corrupt where it reads:

> Marcion, Praxeas, Sabellius, and the others were in their own times defeated by Victorinus of Poetovio, Zephyrinus of Rome, Tertullian of Carthage down to the Cataphrygians, and by [Col. 1136A] other defenders of the Catholic Church.

For Sabellius began his heresy much later, in the interval between the Novatians and the Donatists, as is manifest even from the age of Dionysius of Alexandria, the first to write against Sabellius. He was a contemporary of blessed Cyprian, but younger. Accordingly, either some other heretic must be supplied in Sabellius’ place, or Optatus’ words must certainly be corrected to “Praxeas, a Sabellian,” because Sabellius partly revived that heresy when he contended that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were a single οὐσία (*ousia*, “essence”) and hypostasis of the divinity.

For the rest, to say something also concerning those books wrongly attributed to Tertullian by Erasmus in volume IX of the works of blessed Jerome: we explained above, among the fragments under *Question on Circumcision*, why the book *On True Circumcision* cannot be attributed to him. Still less does the style of the book *To a Sick Friend* resemble his; moreover, Scripture is cited there according to blessed Jerome’s edition. Finally, Tertullian is nowhere said to have written any dialogue.

## [Col. 1135] FRAGMENT: IN WHAT RESPECT TERTULLIAN THE MONTANIST DIFFERED FROM THE PSYCHICS

[Col. 1135B] The author of the book entitled *The Predestined*, book I, which concerns heresies, no. 26, reports the following verbatim:

> Holy Soter, pope of the City, and Apollonius, bishop of the Ephesians, wrote a book against them—the Montanists or Cataphrygians. Against these men Tertullian, [Col. 1135C] a presbyter of Carthage, wrote. Although he wrote everything well, excellently, and incomparably, he made himself blameworthy in this point alone: he defended Montanus, arguing against Soter, the aforesaid pope of the City, and asserting that the reports concerning the blood of an infant were false; that they confessed the Trinity in the unity of the Godhead, granted repentance to the fallen, shared the same mysteries, and observed one Passover with us. “We differ only in this,” he says: “we do not accept second marriages, and we do not reject Montanus’ prophecy concerning the future judgment.” Some object against Tertullian that he derived the soul by transmission—that is, that he said a soul is generated from a soul just as a body is generated from bodies—which the Catholic faith vehemently abhors.

The words of Tertullian that we have just transcribed are not found in his extant works. From this [Col. 1136C] it may be concluded, with Döllinger (*Origins of Christianity*, vol. I, ch. 27, trans. L. Boré), that they were excerpted from some long-lost Montanist work of our author.

Yet anyone, without being prompted, can readily see that Tertullian was not a contemporary opponent of Pope Soter, nor, as some have asserted, were the Tertullianists condemned by that holy pope, since it is clearly established that Tertullian embraced the heresy of Montanus nearly thirty years after Soter’s death.—ED.

## Fifth Appendix. [Col. 1135] NOTES ON TERTULLIAN’S BOOKS *ON BAPTISM* AND *ON REPENTANCE*, BY THE REVEREND FATHER DOM CORBINIAN THOMAS, A BENEDICTINE MONK OF THE CONGREGATION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT IN BAVARIA

## NOTICE

[Col. 1135D]

Dom Corbinian Thomas was born at Augsburg in 1694 and assumed the monastic habit in the imperial monastery of Elchingen in 1715.

For many years he taught the mathematical disciplines at the University of Salzburg, enjoying a great reputation for learning. [Col. 1136D] Afterward, having been appointed professor of sacred theology, he won for himself the admiration of all, as he had before. While laboring diligently in the discharge of these duties, he nevertheless published many most elegant and learned works of various kinds. Their catalogue is presented by Dom Ziegelbauer in his *History of the Literary Affairs of the Order of St. Benedict*, vol. II, p. 220; vol. IV, pp. 265, 304, 311. See also the *General Library of Writers of the Order of St. Benedict*, vol. III, p. 134.

Nor was our Thomas content with these achievements; for, observing, as he himself says, “that this reading [of the holy Fathers] would be supremely profitable and delightful, especially for clerics, throughout every stage of life,” he undertook Tertullian and published the books *On the Prescriptions*, *On Baptism*, and *On Repentance* (Salzburg, 1752, 1755). But “just as [Note: [Col. 1137B] Preface to the books *On Baptism* and *On Repentance*.] the African style of that same author [Tertullian] is sometimes covered and obscured, as it were, by the ashes of that scorched Carthage—although even those who criticize him admit that they themselves are sometimes wonderfully captivated by him—so most of his statements rightly demand that light be shed upon them. This is all the more true because [Col. 1137B] this author is extremely ancient, and is one of the Latin writers whom posterity has reclaimed for itself almost entire from that most remote age. From him the discipline of those times, especially in the African churches—which owed their original foundation to the Roman Church and had therefore first received that discipline from it—has come down to our knowledge; and this matter must certainly be regarded as being of no small importance in dogmatic theology.”

Hence there are the very numerous annotations with which Dom Thomas adorned these three books of Tertullian. We were obliged to relegate them to the end of this second volume, since [Col. 1138A] they reached our hands too late for each to be inserted in its proper place. Should anyone perhaps complain that these notes “seek out every minute detail as though with a little probe,” Dom Thomas replies that he “wrote these things not for the learned, but for those who are to be taught”; and he adds that “even much slighter matters can sometimes cause sufficient difficulty.” We have nevertheless omitted a few minor notes here and there for the sake of brevity; but, consulting both the reader’s profit and his pleasure, we have retained the interpolated dissertation concerning Baptism and Repentance. We have also arranged, as best we could, for the two other dissertations, on the use and authority of Tertullian—which are merely shorter and scantier and sometimes stray beyond their subject—to be recast into the preface.

Why, moreover, our Thomas chose specifically to publish and annotate the books *On Baptism* and *On Repentance*, we learn from Thomas himself in the aforementioned preface:

[Col. 1138B] “I wished, therefore,” he says, “to place this author in the hands of students, both so that they might perceive somewhat more accurately what the practice of the sacraments of Baptism and Repentance—sacraments supremely necessary for salvation—was in the primitive Church and then in its second century, when the traditions were still recent and could be least open to suspicion; and so that they might learn not to pass hurriedly and overhastily over the writings of the ancient Fathers, but to dwell upon them a little longer, though without utterly dying over one and the same author. In this way due esteem will accrue to those writings, and immense profit and pleasure to the students themselves.” —EDS.

## TABLE OF CONTENTS OF THE BOOK *ON BAPTISM*

[Col. 1137]

[Col. 1137C] Chapter I. He explains the usefulness and occasion of this work.

II. Unbelievers take offense at the simplicity of Baptism and the magnitude of its effect, though these should instead be objects of admiration to them.

III. He demonstrates that already at the beginning of the world the element of water was endowed with a singular power and efficacy for imparting life.

IV. He shows that the element of water, above the others, was suitable to be employed for the sanctification of the soul.

V. He teaches that Christians have a far greater right than pagans to locate in water the power of expiating sins.

VI. He teaches that, once cleansed in water through Baptism, we are prepared for the greater gifts of the Holy Spirit.

VII. On the anointing customarily administered after Baptism.

VIII. On the imposition of hands after Baptism and its meaning.

IX. Baptism is foreshadowed by various figures in the Old Testament and confirmed in the New.

[Col. 1138C] X. How does Christ’s Baptism differ from the baptism of John?

XI. Christ did not baptize personally, but nevertheless baptized through the Apostles.

XII. Whether the Apostles themselves were washed, and with what baptism?

XIII. On the necessity of Baptism imposed upon all human beings.

XIV. How is that statement of St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 1:17 to be understood: “Christ did not send me to baptize,” etc.?

XV. There is one Baptism of water, and consequently it cannot be repeated.

XVI. On the baptism of blood.

XVII. On the ordinary and extraordinary minister of Baptism.

XVIII. On the subject of Baptism.

XIX. On the time for conferring Baptism.

XX. On the preparation necessary for Baptism.

## Notes on Chapter I

[Col. 1137D] **Our water.** Ordinary and elemental water, of course—the sort encountered everywhere in our daily use and most easily procured for Baptism, which is so necessary for our salvation.

**Because.** I am almost inclined to prefer *which*, referring, that is, to the water.

**From transgressions.** Not only from original sin—for this is one and the same in everyone [Col. 1138D]—but also from personal sins, as below, Chapter V.

**Of blindness.** For just as blindness is a kind of death of the bodily eye, depriving it of all its vigor and, as it were, its life, so, conversely, through Baptism sight is restored to the eye of the soul, which had been blinded through sin, [Col. 1139A] and it is flooded with the new light of grace. Thus the Apostle’s statement in Ephesians 5:8 can truly be said of the baptized: “You were once darkness, but now you are LIGHT in the Lord.” From this one may readily understand the saying of Clement of Alexandria, Book I of the *Paedagogue*, chapter 6:

> Βαπτιζόμενοι φωτιζόμεθα, φωτιζόμενοι υἱοποιούμεθα, υἱοποιούμενοι τελειούμεθα, τελειούμενοι ἀπαθανατιζόμεθα,

that is:

> Being baptized, we are illuminated; being illuminated, we are adopted as children; being adopted, we are perfected; being perfected, we are made immortal.

And shortly afterward he calls Baptism φώτισμα, “illumination,” through which we behold that holy and saving light—that is, through which we perceive what is divine. But perhaps more concerning this elsewhere.

**We are delivered.** And he therefore called this Sacrament “happy,” because it makes us happy in this way.

**A digest.** It is used substantivally here, as the jurists speak of the *Old Digest* and the *New Digest*. So too our Author, in Book IV *Against Marcion*, chapter 3, calls the Scriptures *Digesta*, because in them the doctrine of our faith is distributed and arranged in due order.

[Col. 1139B] **Especially.** Or “to the highest degree,” as in Cicero’s *For Cluentius* and elsewhere.

**Are formed.** In the sense of “are informed,” or imbued with a fuller knowledge of the mysteries of the faith.

**They carry.** He speaks of those who are still untutored in the faith and cannot give reasons why they believe, and who are ignorant of the sources from which faith itself flows and of the channels of tradition through which the truths to be believed have come down to us. Thus, having been nourished in that faith from earliest childhood, they adhere to it simply through inexperience, or through lack of fuller knowledge: it is an untested faith—not yet sufficiently examined—yet a probable one, that is, approved by others, namely their teachers, and in reality worthy of approval by all.

**There.** At Carthage in Africa, of course, where Tertullian was residing when he wrote these things.

**The Cainite heresy.** Concerning this utterly shameful heresy, see our Tertullian, *On the Prescriptions*, chapters XXXIII and XLVII. St. Augustine, [Col. 1139C] in his book *On Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeus, heresy 15, reports that these Cainites, or Caians, among their other errors, abolished all efficacy of baptism.

**Most venomous.** The most virulent reptile is called *vipera* in Latin, as though *vivipara*, “bearing living young,” because, unlike other serpents, it brings forth not eggs but living offspring; or, as Martinius says in his *Lexicon*, because it loves thorn-brakes, *vepreta*—for the ancients are said to have used *vipre* for *vepre*; or because it gives birth violently, its offspring, as though weary of so laborious a delivery, gnawing through its mother’s womb with what seems the height of impiety. Thus Pierius, Book XIII, under the heading *On the Viper*, testifies that the Egyptian priests represented sons conspiring against their mother by the hieroglyph of a viper. Some among the Greeks likewise maintain that the viper is called ἔχιδνα for this reason: παρὰ τὸ ἔχειν ἐν ἑαυτῇ τὴν γονὴν ἄχρι θανάτου, “because it retains its offspring within itself until its own death.” Experience, however, as Theophrastus already observed long ago, contradicts this excessive credulity of the ancients. Moreover, some—not without reason—punctuate that passage as follows: “the viper, most venomous through her doctrine,” etc. Finally, whom he designates by the name “viper” he reveals plainly and by her own [Col. 1139D] name shortly below.

**Snatched away.** Seized, or snatched over to herself and to her most pestilential heresy.

**Nature.** The nature of vipers, that is.

**Generally.** Others read “wild,” which Junius rightly dislikes. Accordingly, *generally* must be retained here in the sense of “for the most part.”

**Asps.** Ἀσπίς, ἴδος properly means “shield” in Greek.
