From this the scholiast on Aristophanes thinks that a certain species of serpent was called “asp” διὰ τὸ εἰς κύκλους πολλοὺς ἑλισσόμενον, “because it is accustomed to coil itself into many circles,” and by this coiling assumes a circular shape such as shields commonly had at that time. How great the power of an asp’s venom is may be demonstrated by this fact alone, related by Kircher in *Mundus Subterraneus*, Book IX, section I, chapter 3, concerning one of his companions:

> When he struck an asp sitting in a tree, the creature poisoned the man who struck it by its breath alone, rendering him [Col. 1140A] immobile for three full years by a kind of paralysis; and afterward he died from it, since no remedy could match such venom.

Thus Kircher. Suetonius, in *Augustus*, chapter 17, likewise records that Cleopatra died from the bite of an asp which she herself placed upon her breast, when the remedies of the Psylli were no longer of any avail. It is therefore unsurprising that Deuteronomy 32:33 speaks of “the incurable venom of asps,” and that Psalm 13:3 says generally of the impious: “They dealt deceitfully with their tongues; the venom of asps is beneath their lips.” Concerning the insuperable potency of this venom, see what our most reverend Calmet writes on Psalm 90:13, and Bochart in the *Hierozoicon*, Part II, Book III, chapters 5 and 14.

**Basilisks.** The basilisk-serpent, called Βασιλίσκος in Greek, is said to have received that name because it gleams with a white spot upon its forehead, like a royal diadem; or because, although extremely small, it nevertheless surpasses even the largest of the other serpents in the fierceness of its venom, and is accustomed to kill a person—unless he flees—by its breath alone, or even by its gaze if it sees the person first. This was the common [Col. 1140B] belief of the ancients, as may be seen in Aelian, *On the Nature of Animals*, Book II, chapters 5 and 7, and likewise in Pliny, *Natural History*, Book VIII, chapter 21. Through Jeremiah 8:17, certainly, God threatens the Jews with what amounts to the greatest possible plague: “Behold, I shall send among you”—what the Vulgate renders as “basilisk-serpents,” but the Septuagint as ὄφεις θανατοῦντας, “death-dealing serpents”—“against which there is no enchantment,” or against which no magical incantation is effective.

They say that it is hatched from the egg of a cock already one year old. Basilisks are in fact exhibited in certain museums, as I myself have seen more than once: two-footed and winged, distinguished by a serpentine tail, and not very unlike the form of a cock, except that they are featherless. Others, however, affirm that they are rays belonging to one of the smaller species and are customarily fashioned into that shape by artful fraud. It is certain, at any rate, that the ancient writers—Pliny, Aelian, Solinus, and others—class them not among birds but among true serpents. Finally, the more distinguished physicians [Col. 1140C] and philosophers of our own age do not hesitate to consign basilisks—and especially accounts of their birth—to the realm of fables.

**They frequent.** For they are said to make their lairs in sandy deserts, rocky mountains, and especially in the ruins of ancient buildings.

**We are born.** Among the Sibylline Oracles there circulates a certain acrostic poem, consisting of twenty-seven verses, attributed to the Erythraean Sibyl—or, as others prefer, the Cumaean Sibyl—whose beginning is this: ΙΧΘΥΣ.

Since ἰχθύς means “fish” in Greek, certain ancient Fathers called Christ the Ἰχθύς, “Fish.” “In this name,” says St. Augustine in Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 23, “Christ is mystically understood, because in the abyss of this mortality, as in the depth of the waters, he was able to remain alive—that is, without sin.”

Although these oracles were highly esteemed by the ancient Fathers—Justin Martyr, Theophilus of Antioch, Athenagoras, Clement of Alexandria, Eusebius, Lactantius, and others—and were hurled against the pagans like mighty weapons, [Col. 1140D] nevertheless even the pagans themselves were persuaded that those Sibylline acrostics were wholly spurious. This was true not only of Celsus, as cited by Origen in Book V *Against Celsus*, but also of Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, Book IV, chapter 70, who relied in this matter upon the authority of Terentius Varro. Indeed, the far more common opinion among critics now holds that they were composed long after the Sibyls, around A.D. 130 under the reign of Hadrian, by some Christian wishing to commend our Religion to the pagans, and that they were issued under the falsely assumed name of the Sibyl. That even the apostolic age was not without pious frauds of this sort is evident from Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 7, and other sources. St. Augustine, in the same Book XVIII, chapter 45, appeared to express some doubt concerning them, saying: “Unless perhaps someone should say that Christians invented concerning Christ those prophecies which are produced under the name of the Sibyl or of others,” etc. He has similar remarks in chapter 47.

But you will object: could this acrostic, already praised by Cicero in Book II *On Divination* before the birth of Christ, be attributed [Col. 1141A] to a Christian? I reply: Tullius was indeed acquainted with a poem of this kind under the name of the Sibyl, but certainly not with the poem which so clearly refers to Christ. It was another poem, obscurely predicting that some king or other would rule the Romans—a prediction which, in the opinion of many, was to be fulfilled in Julius Caesar, who was secretly seeking the title of King. “A report had already spread,” says Suetonius in *Julius Caesar*, chapter 79, “that Lucius Cotta, one of the Board of Fifteen, intended to propose that, since it was contained in the books of fate”—namely the Sibylline books, whose custody and consultation are known to have been entrusted to a single college of fifteen men—“that the Parthians could not be defeated except by a king, Caesar should be called King.” Suetonius confirms the same point still more clearly immediately afterward, in chapter 80. Yet Tullius found it incredible that this very poem had been composed by some Sibyl under divine inspiration: “This,” he says, “is the work of a writer, not of one in a frenzy; of one employing diligence, not madness.” For my own part, I would more readily believe it to have been the work of some flatterer seeking to ingratiate himself with Caesar. Nor was the acrostic form of poetry unknown at that time, since it had already been frequently employed by Ennius, who was more than sixty years older than Cicero, [Col. 1141B] and was praised by Tullius himself in the same passage.

“But what then?” you ask. “Are we to believe that the ancient Fathers brought forward those spurious oracles against the Jews and pagans to persuade them of the true Messiah’s advent—or, more accurately, mocked them by means of those oracles?” I answer that this was done in good faith and not ineptly, especially against the pagans: not, of course, in order to confer authority upon oracles of this sort, but to employ, as what we call an *argumentum ad hominem*, the authority which those oracles already possessed among the pagans. Finally, those earliest Fathers of the Church, intent solely upon propagating the true Religion by whatever means they could, had no leisure to evaluate writings of this sort by critical examination. Hence they are known frequently to have used the books of Hystaspes and Hermes Trismegistus, the *Acts of Pilate*, and certain Gospels now judged apocryphal by everyone. Why, then, should we be surprised that Tertullian also alludes to that acrostic of some supposed Sibyl and calls us “little fishes,” imitators of our Ἰχθύς, “Fish,” [Col. 1141C] as it were of Christ the great Fish? Following his example, we receive Baptism and are born in its waters into the spiritual life of the soul. Moreover, anyone wishing to learn more about the Sibyls will find it in Dupin, *Bibliothèque nouvelle*, vol. I, p. 28 of my edition, etc.; Cave, *De Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis*, under “Sibylla”; Basnage, at the fourth year before Christ; Isaac Vossius; Blondel; Marckius; Crasset; and many others.

**We are saved.** By persevering in the faith which we received and professed through Baptism; for “he who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matthew 24:13).

**Quintilla.** An otherwise obscure woman, had not men permitted themselves to be smeared with her venom and with her very name—being called, for shame, “Quintillians.” Moreover, St. Epiphanius, *Heresy* 49, enrolls this Quintilla in the company of Priscilla and Maximilla, the prophetesses of Montanus. Basnage, however, in the *Politico-Ecclesiastical Annals* at A.D. 200, no. 5, carefully distinguishes two women of the same name. He places the former, a follower of Montanus and teacher of the Pepuzians, in Phrygia in Asia, [Col. 1141D] but the Quintilla of our Tertullian in Africa alone, as an adherent of the Cainite heresy, as he had already noted above.

**Most monstrous.** For she was the leader among a company of men and had already been compared above to a viper, an asp, and a basilisk.

**She had the right.** St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 14:34ff. takes this right away from women universally, strictly imposing silence upon this talkative sex, which was likely to cause excessive disturbance in the sacred assemblies of the faithful: “Let women keep silence in the church; for they are not permitted to speak, but are to be subject to their husbands,” etc. Thus he does not permit them the office of teaching even sound doctrine—that is, doctrine otherwise free from corruption. See below, Chapter XVII, near the end. It is clear from this passage, moreover, that when Tertullian wrote these things he was not yet among the Montanists, among whom women were permitted, even with public applause, to prophesy openly and to teach men themselves—an indignity!—as we demonstrated in Critical Question [Col. 1142A] V, prefixed by us to Tertullian’s book *On the Prescriptions*.

**Taking away.** Withdrawing Baptism, without which no one can become a Christian.

## Notes on Chapter II

**It is evident.** This statement expresses astonishment at the perversity of the heretics and must therefore be taken θαυμαστικῶς, “as an exclamation of wonder”: namely, that they labor to fashion weapons against us from the very elements of our Faith.

**May harden**, that is, render obstinate and refractory.

**In the act**, or in the action itself and the outward work.

**In the effect.** The interior and spiritual effect, namely Sacramental Grace, which exceeds every power and comprehension of nature as a whole.

**Is promised again.** Simply for “is promised,” just as our Author commonly uses *retractare* for *tractare* and other such compounds in place of their simple forms.

**In water.** Others think it should read “into water”; but what prevents us from retaining “in water”? Tertullian is speaking of baptism by immersion, commonly practiced at that time not only in the African [Col. 1142C] Churches but almost everywhere. In it those being baptized were not merely placed into the water, but were customarily lowered into it with their whole body. But we shall discuss this baptism elsewhere.

**Dipped.** Our Author consistently uses “to dip” for the Greek “to baptize.”

**Rises again.** For the sudden immersion and emergence from the waters of Baptism brings the body not the cleanliness ordinarily produced by baths, but brings the soul a far greater cleanliness.

**For that reason**, in the sense of “therefore.”

**Of eternity.** Or of eternal salvation, into which we are initiated through Baptism.

**Solemn rites.** According to Festus, an ancient grammarian, a “sacred solemnity” was something customarily performed at fixed times and years—hence also “anniversaries,” as things especially to be celebrated whenever the year comes around—principally on behalf of the people and at public expense, such as the Agonalia, Carmentalia, Quirinalia, and so forth.

[Col. 1142C] **Mysteries.** The ancients called secluded sacred rites *sacra seclusa*, and the Greeks called them Μυστήρια, “mysteries” or “hidden things.” An *arcanum*, moreover, was a particular kind of sacred rite which, according once again to Festus, was performed by the Augurs and was so far removed from common knowledge that it was not even divulged in writing, but was celebrated from the memory of their successors. Such were the rites celebrated with the common people excluded, such as the Nyctelia mentioned by St. Augustine in Book VI of *The City of God*, chapter 9; likewise the Samothracian rites of the Cabeiri, or “powerful gods,” concerning whom our Author writes in the *Apology*, chapter 7; the Eleusinian rites in Attica; and others, which because of their obscenity were called ἄῤῥητα, “unspeakable.” Among these deserve to be numbered the rites performed among the Romans for the Good Goddess. Among the mysteries were also the Mithraic rites, concerning which our Author writes in the final chapter of *The Soldier’s Crown*, and we in *On the Prescriptions*, chapter XI, note h, and below, Chapter V. Here, however, Tertullian chiefly means those sacred rites into which the celebrants had to be initiated by certain ablutions, such as those of the god Aesymnetes, concerning which Pausanias writes in the *Achaica*, chapter 226 [probably 26; reading uncertain], and others mentioned here and there.

**Display.** A *suggestus* is properly a somewhat elevated place constructed from a heap of many things, or by placing some things on top of others. Hence the Latins eventually called any elevated place a *suggestum*, [Col. 1142D] such as the one in the Campus Martius from which the magistrates addressed public assemblies. Indeed, a speech of that kind itself was also called a *suggestio*, concerning which Vopiscus, chapter 19, writes: “We refer to you, Conscript Fathers, the recommendation of the pontiffs.”

It is also used generally for “equipment” or “display,” as in our Author’s *On the Spectacles*, chapter 7: “The display of the circus games is somewhat more pompous, since what properly bears the name ‘procession’ precedes them,” etc. And in the same work, chapter 12: “We shall interpret the same concerning ceremonial equipment, which must be accounted part of the display of the honors themselves,” etc. Likewise, in *On Idolatry*, chapter 18: “Now, indeed, we must examine the mere display and ceremonial equipment of office,” etc. Thus the gold and silver images of the Caesars, affixed one above another upon a spear and carried before the legions, were also called *suggestus*, as again in our Author’s *Apology Against the Pagans*, chapter 16: “All those conspicuous displays of images are the pendants of crosses.”

It is also used for women’s adornment in clothing, as in *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 12: “Only those who openly parade their finery carry their whole womanhood about with them [Col. 1143A] . . . denying by a single garment what they profess by their entire display.” And in *On the Apparel of Women*, chapter 2: “You should know that you must reject not only the display of contrived and elaborated lust,” etc. In a more particular sense, however, it is applied to an adornment of the head and to hair arranged in curling locks, as in Statius, *Silvae*, Book I:

> . . . Behold from afar the glory of her lofty brow,  
> And the structure of her hair.

It is sometimes also taken to mean “provision” or “supply,” as again in Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 16: “If he who made it is himself the author of evil, matter is plainly his accomplice through the supply of its substance.”

**They build up.** He indicates here especially the enormous luxury of games, garments, banquets, and so forth, which was customarily employed in certain pagan rites.

**Power.** These are indeed attributes of God which especially commend one another, since so great a simplicity of divine works shines forth within infinite Power, and infinite Power within so great a simplicity. [Col. 1143B] The Author of nature takes the shortest route and does not use a great apparatus of instruments; he does nothing in vain, does not multiply entities without necessity, and so forth, but confines his Power to the fewest possible means. Indeed, those very things which seem to have been created merely for the adornment of the universe nevertheless possess their own simplicity; nor does God employ more ornament even in his own works than is necessary to attain the end established by Supreme Wisdom.

Yet nearly everything happens in the opposite manner in human affairs; for the very absence of simplicity and the great apparatus of instruments betray the weakness of human power. The larger the house that is to be built, the greater the accumulation of material and the greater the number of workmen required. Yet this entire fabric of the world was created from nothing by its Architect, without another’s assistance, without tumultuous exertion, through a single “Let it be.” Nature perfects gold by silent and extremely simple processes; Art, amid all its attempts, has perhaps been able to produce genuine gold [Col. 1143C]—to say nothing of diamonds and the like—only with difficulty and rarely, or rather never. Mechanical art provides remarkable assistance to what are called motive powers, but only through multiplied pulleys and other laborious machines, and with correspondingly greater slowness in achieving success. How many medicines are required to overcome the obstinacy of a more serious disease? How many diseases are there which no medical skill can conquer?

Yet Christ—to mention only these few examples—restored to health the leper with two little words, “I will; be cleansed” (Matthew 8:3); the daughter of the Canaanite woman with a single “Let it be” (Matthew 9:25 [reference apparently corrupt]); the man blind from birth merely by anointing him with clay and washing him in the pool of Siloam (John 9); Peter’s mother-in-law suffering from fever (Matthew 8:15) and two blind men (Matthew 20:34) by touch alone; and the centurion’s paralytic servant even while absent (Matthew 8:13). Indeed, he restored to life itself the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter, who was completely dead, merely by taking the girl’s hand (Mark 5:41ff.): all through means, that is, which were utterly disproportionate to their effects.

**Death.** For who is ever recorded as having raised the dead by human power and by pouring [Col. 1143D] a bath over them? Yet to raise the soul, through Baptism in ordinary, simple water encountered everywhere, from the death of sin to the life of grace is a much simpler act and one requiring power greater than all human weakness.

**It is not believed.** For we human beings are accustomed to admire things which surpass our comprehension; therefore, we ought to believe these things all the more, the more Divinity shines forth in them and the more remote they are from human power and the human mode of acting.

**He does not believe.** There is therefore a twofold wonder. One arises from faith, when we do not in fact doubt the existence or properties of a thing, and so forth, but nevertheless wish inwardly to know and understand how that thing is constituted or its causes, though they surpass our comprehension, and are unable to do so; hence we can only admire it. In this sense wonder—as Aristotle says somewhere—is the daughter of ignorance.

The other kind is without faith, when we are astonished that someone else believes or proclaims something which surpasses our own faith, [Col. 1144A] because we refuse to conform that faith to the authority of another—indeed, to the authority of GOD himself.

**Empty**, that is, devoid of content; for unbelief is accustomed to measure everything by the senses. Accordingly, things which appear outwardly simple it supposes to be simple inwardly as well.

**Impossible.** The unbeliever does not believe that things which are said to be inwardly magnificent, or to produce great effects, can occur, since they cannot be apprehended by the senses. For, as the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 2:14, “the natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of GOD, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them.” Such people therefore judge from the senses alone, but with little sense.

**With God.** This plainly alludes to Christ’s saying in Matthew 19:26:

> παρὰ ἀνθρώποις τοῦτο ἀδύνατόν ἐστι, παρὰ δὲ Θεῷ πάντα δυνατά ἐστι,

which our Vulgate renders word for word:

> With men—that is, in human opinion—this, namely to be saved or to attain eternal salvation, is impossible; but with GOD all things are possible.

Perhaps, however, Tertullian read *extremely difficult* in his manuscript, in the sense in which Cicero translated the passage from Plato’s *Timaeus*, ἀδύνατον Θεῶν παισὶν ἀπιστεῖν, [Col. 1144B] as: “It is difficult not to place faith in those born of the gods”—that is, in the children of the gods. And certainly we are accustomed to call things that are extremely difficult, or very difficult, “impossible” morally, or in human estimation. What immediately follows makes this meaning of Tertullian clear.

**Passing over it**, that is, considering it incidentally and, as it were, in passing.

**By opposites**, or contrary things.

**Cause**, that is, causal being, or, if we speak in the manner of the Scholastics, causative power. It may also be taken as the cause or reason why something is or exists—that is, as its principle or origin. The same mode of expression occurs in our Author’s *On the Spectacles*, chapter 12: “Whatever is administered under the name of an office must necessarily share also in the stains of that from which it has its causes.” Yet what prevents us from taking “cause” here as the state and condition of a thing? Cicero also used the word in this sense in *On Ends*: “Those who have been put to death are in the same condition as [Col. 1144C] before they were born.” Likewise, in *On Duties*, he says: “When he was being killed by being kept awake, his condition was better than if he had remained at home as an aged captive,” etc.

**Is called forth**, or is brought into effect and, as it were, summoned from a state of possibility into actual existence. The meaning, therefore, is that every work receives its state and condition from that which produces it, and consequently that the efficacy of Baptism must be measured not from its outward apparatus but from the Wisdom and Power of GOD operating inwardly and spiritually.

## Notes on Chapter III

**To be re-formed.** We are said to be re-formed through water when in Baptism we recover the form of divine grace which had previously been lost through sin.

**Why.** In place of “for what reason,” as in Ovid’s epistle of Oenone to Paris:

> . . . Why do you entrust seed to sand?

**Authority.** A certain excellence and, as it were, inherent dignity.

**Must be demanded.** To some this entire sentence seems tangled, and they therefore judge that, with Junius, it should be read: “. . . we discuss being re-formed by water; what office, then, etc., has it deserved? Its authority, I suppose,” etc. [Col. 1144D] But what need is there to punctuate it thus? Or why should we not instead understand the words “I suppose” ironically, in the sense of “naturally,” so that the meaning is: as though GOD could do nothing which exceeded the powers and claims of water or of any other creature?

**From the beginning**, namely, of the world itself.

**Display**, that is, adornment, or its unfolding into distinct species. On *suggestus*, see the preceding chapter, col. 1142D.

**Unfinished.** Or still crude and formless.

**With God.** In the sense of “in GOD’s presence,” or as resting in GOD’s power and will—namely, whatever he wished to make from each thing. In almost the same sense our same Author says in *On Patience*, chapter 1: “What is supremely good belongs supremely to GOD, nor does anyone distribute it except the one who possesses it, as he deems each person worthy.”

**They rested.** As though still inert and endowed with no faculty of action.

**He says.** Moses, namely, in Genesis 1:1.

**Invisible.** The Hebrew [word omitted in the supplied text] is [Col. 1145A] rendered *empty* in the Vulgate, κένωμα, “emptiness,” by Aquila, ἀργόν, “idle and inert,” by Symmachus, and κενόν, “empty,” by Theodotion. The Septuagint, however, translates it as ἀόρατος, “unseen” or “invisible,” because it was still enveloped in utter darkness. In the same way our Vulgate renders a certain passage of Wisdom 11:18: “He created the world from INVISIBLE matter,” where the Greek has ἐξ ἀμόρφου ὕλης, “from FORMLESS matter.”

**Uncomposed.** The Hebrew word [omitted in the supplied text] is rendered *void* by our Vulgate, οὐθέν, “nothing,” by Aquila and Theodotion, ἀδιάκριτον, “undifferentiated” or “confused,” by Symmachus, and ἀκατασκεύαστος, “unprepared, unworked, UNCOMPOSED,” or “confused,” by the Septuagint.

**The abyss.** The Hebrew [word omitted in the supplied text] is rendered ἄβυσσος, “abyss,” by all the Greek translators. As Eustathius interprets this name, it means an immeasurable body of water possessing infinite depth, or lacking a bottom; or, as Cornelius a Lapide explains it, the mass of waters which at that time covered the whole earth; and finally, according to our most reverend Calmet, it is the watery matter still commingled with earth, or mud.

**The Spirit of God.** But what is this [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], the SPIRIT OF GOD? [Col. 1145B] This considerable difficulty has chiefly produced three opinions.

The first holds that it must here be understood as wind, or air moving more violently over the waters. This is the opinion of Severianus, Bishop of Gabala, a writer of the fourth century, whom Theodoret explains more fully in Question VIII on Genesis:

> I should consider it more correct that he here calls the air “spirit”; for, after saying that GOD created HEAVEN—namely the Empyrean, named from FIRE, which in Greek is πῦρ—and EARTH, and after mentioning the Waters under the name ABYSS, he necessarily made mention of the AIR, etc.

Nor is this opinion rejected by Saints Basil, Ambrose, Augustine, and others. It is well established that the Hebrews, whose language lacks superlatives, often employ, among other devices for expressing them, a noun qualified by the proper name of GOD. Thus Genesis 35:5 says: “The TERROR OF GOD”—that is, the greatest terror, sent, as it were, by GOD himself—“fell upon them all.” [Col. 1145C] Similarly, Psalm 35:7 has: “Your righteousness is LIKE THE MOUNTAINS OF GOD,” that is, the highest mountains. And Psalm 79:11: “Its shadow covered the mountains, and its branches the CEDARS OF GOD,” namely, the loftiest and tallest cedars. In addition, Isaiah 40:7 uses the same words as Moses in Genesis 1:2: “The grass has withered because the SPIRIT OF THE LORD blew upon it”; and this plainly must be understood of the wind.

The second opinion is held by many who, according to St. Augustine in the unfinished *Literal Commentary on Genesis*, chapter 4, understand by that spirit “the LIVING CREATURE by which the whole visible world and all corporeal things are contained and moved,” etc.; or, as St. John Chrysostom affirms in Homily III on Genesis, that “a certain efficacious and LIFE-GIVING OPERATION was present in the waters”—that is, a fecundity secretly impressed upon them for generating living creatures, namely fish and birds, Genesis 1:21—“and that it was not simply still and motionless water, but water that moved and possessed a certain LIFE-GIVING POWER.”

The third opinion interprets this of the HOLY SPIRIT; toward it [Col. 1145D] I am impelled by the far greater number of the holy Fathers. “It is more true,” says St. Basil, *Homily II on the Hexaemeron*, “and has been approved by our predecessors, that that spirit was called the HOLY SPIRIT OF GOD,” etc. And St. Ambrose, Book I of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 8, says: “We, agreeing with the judgment of the saints and the faithful, understand the Holy Spirit,” etc. St. Jerome likewise affirms, in *Hebrew Traditions on Genesis*, that this is said not of the spirit of the world, but of the Holy Spirit, who is also called the Vivifier of all things from the beginning. And he confirms the very same thing in the *Letter to Oceanus*, saying: “The unformed and invisible matter was being oppressed by the vastness of the abysses and by shapeless darkness; the Spirit of GOD alone was borne over the waters after the manner of a charioteer, and was bringing the nascent world to birth under the figure of Baptism.” But what of St. Augustine? Here too, in Book XIII of the *Confessions*, chapter 3, he excellently discloses his thought: “I now grasped,” he says, “the FATHER in the name of God, who made these things”—heaven and earth—“and the SON in the name of the Beginning, in whom he made these things; and, seeking the TRINITY, I sought it in [Col. 1146A] the words of his Scriptures; and behold, your SPIRIT was borne over the waters,” etc. Hence it is not surprising that, on the basis of so great a consensus of the Fathers, the Church too adopted this opinion in the Blessing of the Baptismal Font, singing as follows: “O GOD, whose Spirit was borne over the waters amid the very beginnings of the world, so that even then the nature of water might conceive the power of sanctification,” etc.

But what prevents us from combining these three opinions, as it were, into one? Let us therefore say that by the SPIRIT OF GOD is understood, first of all, wind or elemental air; that this air, set in motion by a singular power of GOD, flowed through the waters and was, as it were, incorporated into them, and thus rendered them fertile for the generation of living things; and that the Holy Spirit, invisibly concealed beneath this air, in some fashion initiated those same waters into the power of one day sanctifying the soul through Baptism.

**Was borne.** The Hebrew expression that the Septuagint renders by ἐπεφέρετο, “was borne over,” is said to possess a somewhat more arcane significance among the Hebrews. Indeed, St. Basil, in the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 1, adducing the testimony of a certain Syrian interpreter [Col. 1146B]—commonly believed to have been St. Ephrem, Basil’s distinguished friend—speaks as follows: “That expression ἐπεφέρετο, ‘WAS BORNE OVER,’ he says”—that is, the Syrian—“is interpreted as συνέθαλπε, ‘WARMED AND CHERISHED,’ by analogy with ἐζωογόνει, ‘ANIMATED,’ after the likeness of ἐπωαζούσης ὄρνιθος, ‘A HEN BROODING OVER HER EGGS,’ and imparting a certain vital power τοῖς ὑποθαλπομένοις, ‘TO THE THINGS BEING WARMED BENEATH HER,’ namely, those eggs.” Diodorus of Tarsus agrees, discussing the aforesaid passage of Genesis as follows: “For the Hebrew expression [Hebrew word absent in the supplied text], corresponding to the word ἐπεφέρετο, is intended to signify that, just as a hen broods over her eggs, gently touching them with her wings as though to animate them, so too the Spirit was borne over the waters, imbuing them with vital warmth.” St. Jerome confirms this very point in the *Letter to Oceanus* and in the book *Hebrew Traditions*, as does St. Ambrose, Book I of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 8; this may be seen more fully in Noël Alexandre, vol. I, First Age of the World, Dissertation I, Article 2, Proposition 2. Finally, St. Augustine explains it still more subtly in *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 4: “Just as the craftsman’s [Col. 1146C] will is borne over the wood,” etc., “or even over the members of his own body, which he moves in order to work.” And St. Thomas, Augustine’s faithful follower, likewise interprets it thus in Part I, question 66, article 1.

**Substance.** Supply the omitted verb “is.”

***Dignationem***, in place of *dignitatem*.

**Seat.** Thus Tertullian anticipated those Fathers mentioned above with the words “The Spirit of God,” and no less clearly suggests the same opinion in Book IV *Against Marcion*, chapter 26—although, if we wish to speak the truth, he does so with little consistency. For in the book *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 32, discussing Amos 4:13—in the wording of the Septuagint—στερεῶν βροντὴν, “who makes thunder firm,” καὶ κτίζων πνεῦμα, “and creates spirit,” etc., he argues as follows: “He shows that spirit to have been created which was assigned to the created earth, which was borne over the waters, the balancer, breather, and animator of the universe—not, as some suppose, that the SPIRIT OF GOD himself is meant, for the waters would not have been capable of sustaining their Lord—but he speaks of that spirit of which the winds also consist,” etc. [Col. 1146D] Either, therefore, he wrote this forgetful of his former opinion, or, to gratify his Montanus—for by then, alas, he had already surrendered himself entirely to him—who is reported by some to have sacrilegiously vaunted himself as the Holy Spirit, and indeed is greeted by Tertullian himself with the title “Paraclete” in *On Monogamy*, chapter 1, he perhaps struck out his former opinion.

**Liquid.** The liquid element of air.

**Always.** That is, from the very beginning of its creation.

**Joyful.** It is opposed to the gloomy abyss.

**Simple.** Of a substance uniform throughout.

**Placed beneath.** So that upon it the Holy Spirit might be carried over the waters after the manner of a charioteer, as St. Jerome explains in Letter 83 to Oceanus. See above.

**Modulating.** *To modulate* means to arrange a thing harmoniously according to a fixed mode, or according to a more elegant pattern and measure. Hence the waters are here called “modulating,” because [Col. 1147A] from them, as though they were themselves assigning form and furnishing the prescribed patterns for each species of things, this universe was arranged and coordinated.

**Was established by God.** Others read *a DEO* instead of *DEO*. Yet there is no reason entirely to condemn the ordinary reading. For *DEO* may be understood, according to Greek idiom, as “through GOD,” while *constitit* may mean “stood firmly,” or, rather, “was constituted.”

**Separated in the midst**, that is, separated in the middle by this very firmament. For thus the sacred text says in Genesis 1:6–7: “Let there be a firmament IN THE MIDST OF THE WATERS, AND LET THERE BE A DIVISION”; or, as our Vulgate has it, “let it divide the waters from the waters. And GOD made the firmament and divided the waters,” etc. Genesis 1:6–7.

**Might suspend**, namely, in the center of the universe; for there GOD “suspended the mass of the earth with three fingers.” Isaiah 40:12.

**Adaptable**, tractable or suitable for receiving figures of this kind. [Col. 1147B]

**Moist**, in place of *succulent*, as Varro likewise says in Book II, chapter 11: “Freshly shorn wool was called *succida* from the sweat of the sheep.”

**Into mud.** By Greek idiom, *limo* stands for “into mud,” into which the earth had been softened by the water remaining upon it.

**Or grace.** As Cicero says in Book II, Letter 3 to Quintus: “The other things of this kind in our affairs are full of dignity and grace,” that is, of charm.

**Natures.** *Ingenium* is also said of inanimate things, at least improperly, to mean a force innate or internally generated within them, which elsewhere we are also accustomed to call their disposition. I suspect, however, that *ingenita*, “innate qualities,” should be read instead of *ingenia*, “natures.”

**Instrument**, for almost infinitely many uses and effects.

**To appear** (*parere*), in place of *apparere*, as our Author likewise says in *On the Shows*, chapter 8: “Before these, three altars appear for three gods.” See also Book I *Against Marcion*, chapter 15, and elsewhere.

[Col. 1147C] **Eternal.** From the context I strongly suspect that *terrenam*, “earthly,” should be read. Yet I think *aeternam*, “eternal,” can be tolerated, so that the meaning would be: “upon whose command, as it were, eternal life depends,” etc., since water acquired the power of sanctifying, in a certain fashion, even at the very beginning of its existence, as was said above and will be explained more fully in part in the following chapter. Moreover, that water is a symbol of eternal life was foreshown by Christ himself to the Samaritan woman in John 4:10 and following, especially verse 14, when he said: “The water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.”

**In the heavenly**, that is, through something heavenly—namely, the Sacrament of Baptism—as a means supremely necessary for our salvation, which we finally attain in heaven.

## Notes on Chapter IV

**By its very condition**, that is, through that initial power of sanctifying which it possessed within itself after receiving it soon after its creation. [Col. 1147D]

**Over the waters.** See the notes “Spirit” and “was borne” on the preceding chapter.

**About to reform.** Ibid., note “To be reformed.”

**Borrowed.** Thus also in Exodus 3:2 Mount Horeb, on which the Lord appeared to Moses in a flame of fire from the midst of the bush, acquired a certain singular sanctity from the presence of GOD. GOD therefore said to him: “Remove the footwear from your feet, for the place on which you stand is HOLY GROUND.” Ibid., verse 5. A similar example occurs in Joshua 3:5, and several others elsewhere.

**May seize.** May acquire, as though drawing it to itself by a certain force.

**Easy to enter and settle in.** This is a Hellenism; for a Greek would say εἰσδῦναι καὶ ἐγκαθέζεσθαι πρόχειρον, whereas a Latin would say, “easily penetrating and settling within.”

**Subtlety.** He seems to employ a certain corporeal analogy adapted to the senses, drawn from particular oils [Col. 1148A] and dyes that penetrate even the most solid substances. But how a spiritual substance or quality is received in a corporeal subject is indeed much more difficult for philosophers to explain.

**Conceived**, perhaps in place of *began*; or the sense is: “it conceived the power of sanctifying,” that is, received it into itself.

**In that respect in which**, that is, insofar as it is indeed the genus, etc.

**In the species** (*in specie*). Perhaps *in speciem*, “into the species,” should be read.

**May be washed away.** Some codices have *deluatur*; for the ancients used *deluere* for “to wash away,” and in Festus they said *deluvium* instead of *diluvium*.

**In the Tiber.** At Rome, namely, which he designates by the Tiber, the river flowing through that city. Tertullian assumes, as a wholly undoubted fact, that Peter was at Rome and suffered there together with Paul—not only in this passage but also elsewhere. Thus in Book IV *Against Marcion*, chapter 5, he says: “We see also what the Romans close at hand proclaim, to whom Peter and Paul left the Gospel sealed with [Col. 1148B] their blood.” Parallel to this are the words he has in *On Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 36: “The Church of the Romans likewise declares that Clement was ordained by Peter.” Where could this have occurred but at Rome? For Clement was Roman by birth, and did not leave Rome until, already Bishop of the Romans, he was driven into exile by Trajan. Again, in *Scorpiace*, chapter 15, he speaks as follows: “Nero was the first to stain the rising faith with blood at Rome. Then Peter is girded by another when he is bound to the cross; then Paul obtains the birthright of Roman citizenship when he is reborn there through the nobility of martyrdom.” Thus, by the beginning of the third century, this tradition had already become firmly established in the Carthaginian Church and, indeed, throughout Africa at large, although no one—not even any of the heretics whom Tertullian had so sharply and everywhere assailed—dared to attempt to overthrow it.

Nor was Carthage so isolated from the Romans that events of some distinction that had recently occurred could be conveyed back and forth only belatedly and by uncertain rumor. [Col. 1148C] For an entire colony of Roman citizens had been transferred there by Julius Caesar; Africa itself had been committed by his successor Augustus to the authority of the Senate, and was thereafter administered as a Roman province by annual proconsuls; and it was constantly frequented by ships from Italy because grain was exported almost daily—for it is exceedingly well known from Tacitus, Book III of the *Histories*, chapter 48, and from very many writers of Roman history, both Greek and Latin, that Africa was called the granary of Italy in those days—as well as for the sake of other merchandise. I therefore ask and adjure: on whose authority would not only Carthage, but all Africa, have allowed so great and so persistent a falsehood to be smeared upon it? Or how could it have been so negligent in investigating the truth itself more carefully, when innumerable opportunities existed, that not even Tertullian—elsewhere by no means sparing of insults against the Roman Church, especially after he had fled as an impious deserter to his Montanus—would have torn the lying mask from that tradition? Surely he would not have failed to charge the Roman clergy [Col. 1148D] with this imposture, had he ever been led even to suspect it. Or would not the proconsuls themselves—and foremost among them Clodius Macer, who, according to Tacitus, *Histories* I, chapter 7, governed Africa during Nero’s final years, or those who succeeded him, Vipsanius Apronianus, Vigellius Saturninus, and others, and especially Scapula, the persecutor of the African Church, to whom Tertullian had written so spiritedly on behalf of the Christians—have hesitated, once its falsity was detected, to uproot a tradition so glorious to the Christians and so powerful in confirming them in their faith? And then, if Peter died elsewhere, is he alone among the Apostles to be believed to have suffered martyrdom in so obscure a place that not even a rumor of it reached Tertullian, or anyone else before or after him, whether living at Carthage, at Rome, or anywhere whatsoever? Or, finally, is the Roman Church alone of such unknown origin that, although the first founders of almost all the other churches, even far more obscure ones, are identified from [Col. 1149A] at least probable knowledge, all antiquity was deceived in assigning the origin of the Roman Church?

Accordingly, this tradition of the Carthaginian Church did not arise there rashly or through crafty fabrication. Rather, it was transmitted to posterity by all those who had seen Peter at Rome, had heard him preaching, and had been eyewitnesses to his martyrdom; and it must be believed beyond doubt to have been brought to Carthage, and thence to the other African churches, together with the Gospel that those churches had received from the Roman Church, as St. Augustine testifies in Letter 162. It was so firmly established throughout all the churches everywhere in the world that it could never thereafter have wavered against the testimony of so many witnesses and public monuments, stones, churches, and so forth.

You see, therefore, that even this testimony of Tertullian alone—to say nothing now of the wholly unanimous agreement of the other most ancient Fathers, some of whom were also contemporaries of Peter himself—is sufficient to trace this tradition back to its very sources and to break the audacity of the sectarians [Col. 1149B], by which they now drag into controversy a fact so manifest that no other heretic or schismatic before the sixteenth century of the Church ever dared to contradict it in the least. Our modern men alone are evidently so keen-nosed—or rather, so snub-nosed—that they now begin to scent what none of the ancients could smell out. And if it pleased me to argue against such men at greater length, or if doing so were worthwhile, I would bring forward in a long array even those who, though most alien from our sacred rites, otherwise enjoy the greatest authority among them: Pearson, Grotius, Ussher, Chamier, Blondel, Pierre du Moulin, and others, by whose names alone the few others of recent birth could easily be overwhelmed. For now it is enough to have adduced even two of them, Samuel Basnage and William Cave. The former, although in his *Political-Ecclesiastical Annals*, at the year 42, no. 8, he obstinately denies that Peter was Bishop of Rome, nevertheless, at A.D. 64, no. 9, unwaveringly affirms that he was at Rome in these [Col. 1149C] words: “There has never been any tradition surrounded by a greater number of witnesses; thus Peter’s coming to the City cannot be doubted without overturning all the monuments of history.” The latter, in *Ecclesiastical Writers: Literary History*, p. 5, says: “That Peter was at Rome and held a see there for some time, we confidently affirm together with the whole assembly of antiquity.” Then, after producing witnesses beyond all exception and drawn from the remotest antiquity, and after citing St. Ignatius of Antioch, a disciple of St. Peter himself, Papias of Hierapolis, Irenaeus, a disciple of St. Polycarp the Apostolic Man, Dionysius of Corinth, Tertullian, Gaius the Roman presbyter, and Origen, he proceeds as follows: “After so many venerable names and such illustrious monuments of earliest antiquity, who will call into doubt a fact handed down so clearly and consistently? Surely, if so dense a cloud of witnesses and so harmonious a judgment of the ancients may be plucked apart according to the whim of any individual intellect, the memory of the first centuries will be utterly done away with, and no one will be permitted to know anything beyond [Col. 1149D] his own age.” So it is that certain of our heterodox opponents, while everywhere thrusting their own judgments forward as truth, and while scraping together from every quarter so many insulting fables against our religion—some of which they themselves also invent—demand that immediate credence be given to them, although even the whole of antiquity is insufficient to obtain credence from them in return. But since we have thus far been carried almost wholly beyond the limits of our undertaking, anyone who desires still more will find it abundantly in our Calmet’s special dissertation on St. Peter’s Roman journey.

**Philip**, who is more commonly believed to have been not the Apostle, but one of the first seven deacons elected in Acts 6:5.

**Fortuitous**, that is, presented by chance.

**Repaid.** This statement certainly has the flavor of irony. Moreover, Tertullian does not here intend to make the Baptism conferred by Peter entirely equal to John’s Baptism, which had been only a preliminary [Col. 1150A] figure and, as it were, a forerunner of the former—for below, in chapter 10, he establishes a manifest and more than single difference between the two. He wished only to confirm that every kind of water diffused throughout our world, since it is entirely the same as that primordial water, has now likewise been adapted by the Holy Spirit to confer salvation upon human beings, in whatever manner this may finally occur. Yet it certainly must not be denied that our Baptism, being a sacrament instituted by Christ himself, possessed a far more efficacious power than John’s Baptism, which did not of itself confer the remission of sins, but merely aroused people to acts of repentance through which that remission was effected. On this subject our interpreters and theologians may be consulted throughout, and we shall confirm it more fully in its proper place.

**Prerogative.** That is, sharing, as though by transfusion, in that privilege and in the character of that primitive water.

**Sacrament of sanctification**, or that hidden and spiritual [Col. 1150B] power of sanctifying the soul.

**God having been invoked.** This invocation is made in the blessing of the baptismal font. From this passage alone it can be sufficiently gathered that this rite was already employed in Tertullian’s time and probably descended from the Apostles themselves.

**Is over the waters**, that is, is above the waters and, as it were, floats upon them.

**Imbibe.** Whether this power is truly real and physical, impressed upon the waters by the Holy Spirit and physically causing baptismal grace, or merely moral, is vigorously disputed by the Scholastics in their treatises on Baptism.

**For a simple act**—the accusative *ad simplicem actum* in place of the dative *simplici actui*—namely, the act of washing.

**In place of filth**, that is, as a counterpart to filth, or in the stead of filth.

**In the spirit**, or in the soul; for sin is committed by the will alone and leaves in the soul a spiritual stain, which the Scholastics commonly call habitual sin.

**Liability.** The flesh or body certainly contracts no guilt properly so called, nor does that tinder by which the flesh [Col. 1150C] lusts against the spirit—Galatians 5:17—possess the character of sin except in an improper sense. Yet because, as they again say in the schools, actions belong to concrete subjects, and consequently it is not the soul alone but the whole human being—as the concrete subject consisting of body and soul—that sins in the flesh and through the flesh, the liability both to guilt and to punishment is in some fashion extended to the body or flesh itself, namely because of the soul’s intimate union with the body. Thus it is not the body by itself and for its own sake that is punished, but the soul in the body and through the body, and therefore the whole human being who sinned.

**Because of its ministry.** The things said above are therefore chiefly true of carnal sins, or of those accomplished by the flesh, however it may finally cooperate.

**Because by medicinal waters**, that is, by waters imbued with medicinal power, such as natural hot springs and mineral waters. Elsewhere, though more rarely, *medicatus* is also used to mean “poisoned,” as Suetonius relates that the emperor Claudius was removed from the living by a poisoned mushroom, and Silius, Book VI, sings of missiles treated with poison.

**Intervention.** He alludes to the Sheep Pool, concerning [Col. 1150D] which see John 5 and our Author more explicitly in the following chapter.

**Is washed clean**, namely, from that guilt which it incurred through the body and through corporeal and sensible pleasures.

**Is cleansed.** That is, from the stain it contracted in the soul intimately joined to it.

## Notes on Chapter V

**Of spiritual things**, that is, devoid of all understanding, etc., and discerning only carnal things. Perhaps this sentence might be punctuated as follows: “alien to all understanding, they supply the power, or virtue, of spiritual things with the same efficacy,” etc.

**Supply**, or attribute.

**Empty**, that is, vacant and destitute of every power of this kind.

**Are initiated.** *To initiate*, a verb used especially of sacred rites, means to consecrate, to imbue with sacred things, or rather to render suitable for them. “There were,” says Casaubon on Athenaeus, Book VI, chapter 15, “certain stages to be observed in participation in the mysteries. The first [Col. 1151A] of all was ἡ κάθαρσις, ‘purification’”—namely, a purification to be performed by certain washings—“then followed the lesser mysteries, by which they were instructed and prepared for the greater; the final act was that of the Greater Mysteries and what was called ἐποπτεία,” namely, the viewing of certain secret sacred objects, to which the initiated were not admitted until a full year had elapsed, as Plutarch relates in his book *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*.

What has been said thus far is admirably confirmed by Clement of Alexandria, who argues as follows in Book V of the *Stromata*: “Not without reason, therefore, in the mysteries practiced among the Greeks, τὰ καθάρσια, ‘purifications’ or ‘lustrations,’ hold the first place, just as among the barbarians τὸ λοῦτρον, ‘the washing.’ After these come μικρὰ μυστήρια, ‘the Lesser Mysteries,’ which possess a certain foundation of instruction and προπαρασκευῆς, ‘preparation’ or ‘initiation,’ for the things to come,” etc. And in Book VII of the *Stromata* he says that before the transmission of the mysteries or sacraments, καθαρμούς τινας προσάγειν τοῖς μυεῖσθαι μέλλουσιν ἀξιοῦσιν, “they consider it necessary to apply certain expiations or purifications [Col. 1151B] to those who are to be initiated into the mysteries,” etc. Cicero, moreover, in Book II of *On the Laws*, says that those mysteries are called *initia*, “initiations.” Indeed, even among us Christians it is commonly said that someone is “initiated into Holy Orders,” and the first tonsure is called a kind of initiation into them.

**Of some Isis.** Io, daughter of Inachus, after giving birth to Epaphus, her son by Jupiter, was changed into a cow through the agency of the jealous Juno. After recovering her human form, she married Apis, king of the Egyptians, under the new name of Isis, and, because of the very great benefits she bestowed upon that nation, was after her death enrolled by the Egyptians among the gods together with her husband. Some believe that this thoroughly fabulous goddess—because *Isis* in the Cimbrian language means “IS, IS”—represented the infinite WISDOM OF GOD, who says of herself in Proverbs 8:14: “Counsel and equity ARE mine, prudence IS mine, strength IS mine.” Plutarch, in his book *On Osiris and Isis*, certainly records that the following inscription was once found in a temple of Isis:

[Col. 1151C] Ἐγώ εἰμι πᾶν τὸ γεγονὸς καὶ ὂν καὶ ἐσόμενον.

“I am ALL that WAS, that IS, and that SHALL BE.”

Others believe that beneath the figure of Isis lies the Earth, the Moon, the Dog-Star—because the Nile was accustomed to inundate Egypt at the rising of this star—Ceres, Minerva, or some other goddess. Certain writers cited by the most illustrious and learned Huet, Bishop of Avranches, in *Demonstration of the Gospel*, Proposition IV, chapter 10, no. 1, disregarding all distinction of sex, entirely confuse her with Osiris, Astarte, Saturn, Cybele, and others. And what of the fact that the same Huet contends that, among the idolatrous Egyptians, Moses was transformed into Osiris, his wife Zipporah—and indeed also his sister Miriam—into Isis?

Moreover, whoever this Isis may have been, it is nevertheless established that sacrifices were once offered to Isis not only by the Romans and many other peoples, but even by the Suebi, as Tacitus reports in *On the Customs of the Germans*. Her idol was brought from Egypt to the Black Sea and thence carried upstream by the Danube [Col. 1151D] to that region. You will find more in Plutarch’s book *On Isis*, Pitiscus’s *Lexicon*, Natale Conti’s *Mythology*, Book VIII, chapter 18, Dempster’s *Roman Antiquities*, Book II, chapter 22, and others.

As regards the rites of Isis, moreover, they are said to have been exceedingly secret, to have been performed only at night, and to have been customarily conducted by women alone. Herodotus, in *Euterpe*, Book II, testifies that the priests of Isis were accustomed to wash in cold water daily, three times by day and twice by night; and Lucian, in *On the Syrian Goddess*, relates that a jar of water was customarily carried in procession among her mysteries. Juvenal too, in Satire 6, sings of a woman of this kind, a priestess of Isis:

> Breaking the winter ice, she will descend into the river,  
> Three times in the morning Tiber she will immerse herself,  
> And wash her fearful head in the very whirlpools . . .

And shortly afterward:

> . . . If radiant Io commands,  
> From Meroë she will carry waters to sprinkle in the shrine  
> Of Isis, which rises close beside the ancient sheepfold. [Col. 1152A]

**Of Mithras.** “Those who transmit the initiations—or mysteries—of Mithras,” says St. Justin Martyr in the *Dialogue with Trypho*, “record that he was born from a rock, and they call the place in which those who believe in him are said to be initiated a Cave.” Hence, on a certain ancient marble, Rosinus, in his *Additions to Dempster’s Roman Antiquities*, Book II, chapter 8, read:

> TO THE GOD, THE SUN, MITHRAS, FLAVIUS SEPTIMIUS ZOSIMUS, U.P., PRIEST OF THE GOD BRONTON AND OF HECATE, ESTABLISHED THIS CAVE.

These Mithraic rites, which were customarily conducted in hidden caves, were peculiar to the Persians. By the name of Mithras, as Macrobius testifies in Book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 17, they worshiped the Sun and were accustomed to sacrifice to him, amid the harmonious singing of hymns, a bull drawn by its horns from a cavern. The idol therefore had a lion’s face and a tiara, wore Persian dress, and with both hands gripped the horns of a struggling bull, as we learn from Statius, Book I [Col. 1152B] of the *Thebaid*, where he writes:

> . . . whether you prefer to be called the rosy Titan,  
> According to the rite of the Achaemenian nation, or fruitful Osiris,  
> Or Mithras, who beneath the rocks of the Persian cave  
> Twists the horns reluctant to follow.

Tertullian testifies concerning the washings customarily employed in initiations into this deity in the final chapter of *On the Soldier’s Crown* and in *On Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 40, where we offer more in note g.

Moreover, the monuments of the ancients everywhere testify that washings of this kind generally preceded the sacrifices of the gentiles. Thus Hesiod:

> Never pour ruddy wine to Jupiter or the gods above  
> Before you have washed your hands in the pure water of a river.

Thucydides too should be heard; in Book II of the *Peloponnesian War* he speaks as follows: “They also used the spring Callirrhoë in matters of the greatest importance, and even now, from ancient times onward, its water is customarily used before weddings and in other sacred rites.” Pausanias likewise, in Book I of the *Eliaca*, chapter 164, testifies as follows concerning [Col. 1152C] the same matter: “Neither the Sixteen Women”—these were placed in charge of the rites and games of Juno in Elis—“nor the magistrates of the Eleans undertake any part of their office before they have purified themselves with a special pig and with water drawn from the spring Piera.” Timarchides, cited by Natale Conti in Book I of the *Mythology*, chapter 4, indeed records that a certain Asterius was struck by lightning and killed because he had touched the altar of Jupiter with impure—that is, unwashed—hands. And what of the requirement that prayers could be offered to the gods only after washings of this kind had first been performed? Among the Romans, when a sacrifice was to be made—as Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book VIII of *Roman Antiquities*, chapter 71, is an ample witness—“after their hands had been washed and the victims purified with clean water,” etc., “AFTERWARD THEY PRAYED, and only then did they order the attendants to slaughter them.” Lactantius, Book V of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 20, wittily ridicules such people: “Defiled,” he says, “by every crime, they come to pray and imagine that they have sacrificed piously if they have washed their skin—as though any rivers could wash away the lusts enclosed within the breast, or any seas could purify them.”

But see the origin of this superstitious rite, and [Col. 1152D] read everywhere how those wicked spirits are all too truly apes of the Divine SPIRIT! “When the demons heard this washing proclaimed through the Prophet,” says St. Justin Martyr in *Apology II*, speaking of our Baptism, “they brought it about that those who were about to enter their shrines and approach them,” etc., “should purify themselves by sprinkling with water; indeed, through their prompting and agency they arrange that those who go out should even wash their whole bodies before coming to the temples in which they are stationed.” Moreover, that part of a temple in which those about to sacrifice washed or cleansed themselves—see the preceding chapter, note “Into the species”—was properly called the *delubrum*, a term whose meaning was afterward extended to the temple itself. Others, however, explain the etymology of that word differently.

**Carry forth.** It is established from Ovid, Book IV of the *Fasti*, and Lucan, Book I of the *Civil War*, that this was customarily done with the Mother of the gods. The Greeks—and, following them, our Author in *On the Shows*, chapter 8—called her μεγάλην Μητέρα, “the Great Mother”; the Phrygians called her Rhea and Cybele; the Assyrians, according to Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, chapter 23, Adergatis; the Egyptians, according to Servius on *Aeneid* VIII, Isis; the Africans, in St. Augustine’s *City of God* II, chapter 4, the Heavenly Goddess; and the Germans, in Tacitus, *Histories* VII, chapter 20, Hertha [a parenthetical form is absent in the supplied text]. [Col. 1153A] She was thus carried to the river Almo. A distinguished parallel passage occurs in Tacitus, *Annals* XV, chapter 44: “Juno was propitiated by the matrons, first on the Capitol and afterward by the nearest sea. From there water was drawn, with which the temple and the image of the goddess were sprinkled.”

Moreover, *to carry forth* here appears to mean carrying idols out of the temple and, after first washing them in water, carrying them around through the streets and squares of the city in public supplications or processions, of which the gentiles had many and which still exist in Asia.

**Country houses.** *Villae*, as though *vehillae*, were originally the name for certain huts in the countryside, built only of turf or some other material dictated by necessity, for conveying and storing produce there, and for receiving farmers at night, together with shepherds and their flocks, and so forth. Later, when they had become the settled dwellings of country people [Col. 1153B], they were built somewhat more substantially; finally, they also became retreats of the nobility for pleasure and summer residence, and thereafter were customarily inaugurated all the more solemnly with lustral sacrifices and sprinklings of that kind.

To this category also belonged the festival of the Parilia, customarily celebrated in April in honor of the god Pales, concerning which Ovid, *Fasti* IV, verse 735, writes:

> At early twilight let the shepherd purify the well-fed sheep;  
> First let him sprinkle them with water, etc.

For this purpose that rustic and fitting formula preserved in Cato, *On Agriculture*, chapter 141, was used to invoke the rustic god: “May you forbid, ward off, and avert visible and invisible diseases, barrenness and devastation, calamities and inclement weather,” etc. Indeed, the shepherds themselves also had to be purified with fire and water; concerning them Ovid writes in the same place, verse 725:

> Surely I leapt three times across the flames arranged in a row,  
> And the laurel branch scattered glistening drops of water.

[Col. 1153C] But what prevents us from also referring to this category those Ambarvalian sprinklings during which the Ambarval victim was led around the fields, as though “going around the plowed lands,” etc.?

**Houses.** I adduce just one passage for this purpose, Theocritus, Idyll 24, where the seer Tiresias orders the house of Amphitryon to be expiated because of the serpents that Hercules, gripping them in both hands in his cradle, had strangled:

> Καθαρῷ δὲ πυρώσατε δῶμα θεείῳ  
> Πρῶτον· ἔπειτα δ᾽ ἅλεσσι μεμιγμένον (ὡς νενόμισται)  
> Θαλλῷ ἐπιῤῥαίνειν ἐστεμμένον ἀβλαβὲς ὕδωρ.

> First fumigate the house with pure sulfur; then, as custom ordains, sprinkle garlanded, harmless water mixed with salt, using a leafy branch.

**Temples.** Another distinguished testimony concerning the purification of temples occurs in Tacitus, Book IV, chapter 53. When the temple of Capitoline Jupiter, destroyed by the soldiers of Vitellius, was to be restored by the emperor Vespasian, the Vestal Virgins, together with boys and girls whose fathers and mothers were still living, washed the entire site with water drawn from streams, springs, and rivers, so that it might be dedicated with solemn rite, etc. This rite, however, was far more ancient, being traced back to King Numa himself. Plutarch says in his [Col. 1153D] *Life* that Numa assigned to the Virgins of Vesta, as sacred water, the spring that irrigated the place—namely, the field in which he was accustomed to meet with the nymph Egeria—so that, drawing from it, they might purify and sprinkle the sacred building.

**Cities.** There were also the sacred Amburbalia, when the city and its sacred boundary were purified, as in Lucan, *Pharsalia* I, verse 593:

> Then he orders the entire city to be encircled by its fearful citizens,  
> And its walls to be solemnized with a festal purification.  
> The sacred pontiffs encircle the long boundary  
> Along its outermost limits, etc.

This purification was performed every year in February; for Numa dedicated this second month, as Macrobius says in Book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 13, “to the god Februus, who is believed to possess power over purifications; and it was necessary that the state be purified”—which the ancients called *februari*—“during that month, so that it might render the due rites to the divine Shades.”

[Col. 1154A] **Sprinkling.** Junius thinks *aspargine* should be read. But what need is there for this change? More polished Latin authors say *asperginem*, as Virgil does in *Aeneid* III:

> . . . The rocks foam with salt spray.

I do indeed find *asparginem* used by Callistratus in Law 4 of the Digest, title *On the Rhodian Law of Jettison*, but with another meaning, namely, for damage contracted by an object from water, especially rainwater—although some do not fail to read *aspergine* there also.

**At the Apollinarian games.** When Hannibal was in Italy, these games were first celebrated by decree of the Senate, on the instruction of the verses of the seer Marcius, then perhaps newly discovered, as is established from Livy, Book XXV, chapter 12, and Macrobius, Book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 17. Here, however, our Author has in view rather that most celebrated Egyptian rite performed for Horus at Buto, on the island of Chemmis—for Herodotus testifies in *Euterpe* that Apollo was designated among them by this name—or the games consecrated by the Dorians to Triopian Apollo, concerning which the same Herodotus speaks in *Clio*.

[Col. 1154B] **At the Pelusian games.** Pelusium, now Damietta, is situated at the easternmost mouth of the Nile. It was once a noble city, reportedly founded by Peleus, Achilles’ father, after he had been ordered to purify himself in a nearby lake because he had killed his brother Phocus, and had thereby recovered his sanity from the Furies by whom he was tormented on account of that murder. There, in honor of Diana—who in the language of the Egyptians, and hence the city itself under another name, was called Bubastis—games once very famous were held annually, as Herodotus again recounts at length in *Euterpe*, ch. 49. I am nevertheless aware that our Vulgate translator, at Ezek. 30:16–17, distinguishes Bubastis from Pelusium: “Like a woman in labor, (Sin) PELUSIUM shall be in pain; the young men of (Phibeseth) BUBASTIS shall fall by the sword.”

**They are dipped.** These games, without doubt, like all others of their kind, were accompanied by sacrifices, preceded, of course, by washings and purifications.

**They presume.** Just as philosophers who once enjoyed no small [Col. 1154C] authority—and especially Thales of Miletus among them—believed that the generation of all things proceeded from Water as its first principle, so perjurers, already nearly dead, as it were, because the vengeance of the angry gods threatened them everywhere and at every moment, imagined that through washings of this kind—which, as they falsely believed, expiated those crimes—they obtained a kind of immunity from punishment, returned to a new life and its security, and were, as it were, regenerated. Since, therefore, perjury was extremely common among the Greeks, before the games they were particularly anxious to propitiate the gods beforehand by washings of this kind, lest they should disgracefully succumb during the games, as though these constituted a public punishment for their perjuries.

**He purified himself.** Many examples of this practice survive, especially among the Greeks. Thus, in Herodotus, bk. I, ch. 7, Adrastus, guilty of fratricide, was purified by Croesus, king of the Lydians. They also relate that Apollo and Diana, after Python had been slain, came to Aegialea to purify themselves, as Pausanias records in *Corinth*, ch. 51. The same Pausanias, bk. I, ch. 74, relates: “Before Orestes had washed away through expiations the stain of his mother’s blood, none of the Troezenians was willing to receive him beneath his roof,” etc. But, if we believe Virgil, this [Col. 1154D] rite was already practiced among the Trojans; for Aeneas thus speaks to Anchises, *Aeneid* II, v. 717:

> You, father, take the sacred objects in your hand, and our ancestral Penates.  
> For me, departing from so great a war and from recent slaughter,  
> It would be sacrilege to touch them until in a living stream  
> I have washed myself . . .

And Seneca, *Hercules Furens*, Act IV, Scene I, v. 918:

> . . . Son, first purify your hands,  
> Dripping with bloody and hostile slaughter.

Ovid, indeed, himself mocks this custom of the gentiles in *Fasti* II:

> Ah, all too credulous are you who think that grievous crimes of blood  
> Can be removed by river-water.

Yet it is established that at that time, under the name of expiations and purifications, nothing but washings performed with water were ordinarily understood.

[Col. 1155A] A singular example, moreover, appears in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, bk. V, ch. 58. When, by decree of the Senate, the conspirators had been publicly and lawfully put to death at Rome, a further decree of the Senate was then enacted that the entire city should be purified, because necessity had compelled it to become responsible for the killing of citizens: for it was unlawful to approach the sacred rites and sacrifice victims before the deed had been expiated and the pollution removed by purifications.

**Water in its natural state**, that is, natural water left to its own nature.

**Of purification.** That is, of a purification to be performed under favorable auspices, and to be undertaken successfully and with heaven itself assenting. I therefore do not see why, with Junius, one should read *auspicii et mundationis*, “of auspices and purification.”

**To be medicated**, that is, to be imbued with medicinal power. Yet I think it should be understood in another sense, one that is more common and better here, as in *Aeneid* XI:

> But it had no power to heal (*medicari*) the wound  
> Of the Dardanian spear.

[Col. 1155B] **The rival of God**, namely, the Devil.

**By a sacrament**, or mystery, and even apart from the use and application of water in the washings thus far described.

**They know.** Others read *they are*; not badly, though *they know* seems to me more elegant and should therefore be retained.

**And whatever springs.** Springs bursting from caves or other shady places were believed to possess something divine—or, rather, some diabolical power; hence blind paganism ordinarily bestowed divine honor upon them. Seneca says of these in Epistle 41: “We venerate the sources of great rivers; the sudden eruption of an abundant stream from concealment has its altars; springs of warm water are worshiped, and either their darkness or their immense depth has made certain pools sacred.” At Rome there was also a spring sacred to the nymph Egeria at the foot of the Aventine Hill, of which Livy, bk. I, ch. 19, relates: “There was a grove whose center a perennial stream watered from a dark cave; because Numa very frequently withdrew there without witnesses . . . he consecrated the grove to the Camenae.” Plutarch adds [Col. 1155C] in his *Numa* that Numa placed the Vestal Virgins in charge of this spring, etc., as we reported above in the note **Temples**.

Accordingly, springs of this kind, because of some dreadful majesty—I know not what—of the places from which they welled forth, were altogether numbered among the gods; and in their honor particular sacred observances were established, such as the Fontinalia at Rome, customarily celebrated on October 3, and many others elsewhere.

Nor did they believe that a certain hidden divinity inhered only in beneficial springs, but also in harmful ones, which had to be propitiated through divine worship so that their destructive power—though it was in fact implanted in them by nature—might be averted. Of this kind were the waters of the Alcyonian marsh, mentioned by Pausanias toward the end of his *Corinth*, which dragged swimmers down to the very bottom; likewise the springs of the river Acidans, arising from Lapitha, a mountain of Arcadia, and exhaling so foul an odor that their very breath was sufficient to kill human beings, according to the same Pausanias in *Elis* I. I pass over many other such springs discussed by [Col. 1155D] Polemon in his book *On the Marvels of Sicily*, as well as by the author of the book *On Marvels*, commonly believed to be Aristotle, by Pliny, bk. XXXI, Solinus, ch. 31, and others.

**Streams.** “A stream,” Festus says, “is commonly the name for a slender flow of water produced not by expectation or design, but by its own natural impulse.” Others employ the word with other meanings.

**Pools.** *Piscinae* designated not only ἰχθυοτροφεῖα (*ichthyotropheia*), or fishponds, but also collections of cold water, gathered for swimming or pleasurable bathing into a fairly large place enclosed on every side, like a kind of artificial lake, even though otherwise devoid of fish. Thus Lampridius says of the emperor Alexander in his *Life*: “After being anointed, he bathed in such a way that he never, or only rarely, used hot baths, but always a pool”; and Victor, bishop of Tunnuna, says in his *Chronicle* of Arrianus Olympius: “He impiously ended his life in a pool of cold water.” Of this kind, too, was the Sheep Pool discussed at John 5 and the swimming pool of Siloam in John 9; we shall discuss them below.

[Col. 1156A] Furthermore, Tertullian himself testifies in *On the Shows*, ch. 8, that baths and the pools that formed one part of them and were nothing other than cold baths were consecrated to gods, or evil demons and idols: “The streets, the forum, the baths, the stables, and even our own houses are not entirely free from idols. Satan and his angels have filled the whole age”—that is, the world. Indeed, in *On Idolatry*, ch. 15, he also testifies: “We see even doors worshiped in the baths. . . . Whatever you do to a door, you will have done to an idol.” Thus, among the other filth of idols, the gentiles also had household gods of baths and doorways, and I know not what other filthy divinities, under whose most shameful auspices they might wash—or, more truly, be defiled with far fouler filth.

**Euripi.** *Euripus* was the particular name of that turbulent strait between Euboea and Attica which reverses itself seven times during the day and as many times during the night, alternately spewing out its waters and swallowing them again. After Aristotle had unsuccessfully investigated its causes, he is said to have wasted away from grief or, as others relate—though with little truth—to have thrown himself headlong into it. Subsequently, [Col. 1156B] this designation began to be extended to “trenches and channels with water,” as Lipsius says on Seneca, Epistle 83, such as were customarily found in gardens and praetorian residences. Indeed, water-basins generally into which aqueducts discharged were called εὔριποι (*euripoi*), either παρὰ τοῦ εὐριπίζεσθαι, “from being swept along like a Euripus,” because through them the waters readily rushed down to that place and were driven about in turbulent whirlpools, or, more truly, because they flowed around a certain portion of land as though it were an island. Pausanias says of these in *Laconia*, ch. 96: “The field in which the youths join battle is surrounded on all sides by a euripus, just as an island is by the sea.” Dionysius of Halicarnassus, bk. III, ch. 91, describes the Circus Maximus built by Tarquin as follows: εὔριπος εἰς ὑποδοχὴν ὕδατος ὀρώρυκται, βάθος τε καὶ πλάτος δεκάπους, that is: “A euripus has been dug around it to receive the waters, ten feet in depth and likewise in width.” Suetonius also says of this in *Julius*, ch. 39: “At the Circensian games, after the Circus area had been extended on either side and a euripus added around its circuit, young men of the highest nobility raced four-horse and two-horse chariots and trick-riding horses.” [Col. 1156C] Naval games were also presented there, water being introduced into the Circus itself through euripi—for larger channels and aqueducts were also so called. Indeed, the extravagance of certain emperors had grown to such an extent that Spartianus records of Heliogabalus: “He is said to have presented naval Circensian games in euripi filled with wine.” Moreover, these euripi too were consecrated to certain gods, as Tertullian testifies in *On the Shows*, ch. 10: “She therefore”—namely, the Great Mother, Ops, Tellus, or Cybele—“presides there over the euripus.”

**Cisterns.** This is the name given to underground receptacles for rainwater; Festus thinks that they are so called because they lie *cis*, or beneath, the ground.

**Wells.** Wells are deep receptacles of living water that continually wells up from certain hidden veins. The Aeolians formerly called them ποτήρια (*potēria*), ἀπὸ τοῦ ποτοῦ, “from drink”; hence some maintain that our *putei* were named from *potus*, “drink,” as though they were *potei*, that is, things supplying us with a most wholesome drink. Of this kind was the well in Homer, *Odyssey* X, from which Ulysses was to [Col. 1156D] summon from the underworld the shade of the seer Tiresias.

**To seize.** Namely, those who, as St. Justin Martyr says in *Apology* II, are λαμβανόμενοι καὶ ῥιπτούμενοι by the shades—or spirits—of the dead, “seized and hurled down,” and whom everyone calls δαιμονιολήπτους (*daimoniolēptous*), “demon-possessed,” *arreptitii*, “seized,” and μαινομένους (*mainomenous*), “raging mad.”

**Of a harmful spirit.** Certain particular spirits were assigned by the gentiles to all these springs, streams, pools, euripi, cisterns, wells, etc. Since demons appeared there in female form, they were also worshiped in this form and were believed to inhabit those caves watered by the outflow of springs. Thus Virgil, in *Aeneid* I, calls that Libyan

> . . . cave beneath overhanging rocks

the dwelling of the Nymphs. Pausanias likewise mentions in his *Boeotia* a particular cave belonging to the Cithaeronian Nymphs. Describing the Corycian cave in his *Phocis*, [Col. 1157A] he says: “Many streams flow here and there from living springs. The inhabitants of Parnassus regard it as sacred to the Corycian Nymphs.” Likewise, as the same author again testifies in his *Boeotia*, the Libethrian Nymphs were worshiped at the Libethrian spring. Other springs also had their own altars, shrines, or even temples consecrated to the Nymphs; these too were called *Nymphaea*, such as the one above the spring of the river Cytherus mentioned by Pausanias in *Elis* II. More particularly, the Nymphs presiding over rivers, pools, and wells were called Naiads, Ephydriads, and so forth.
