Comatas, too, in Theocritus, *Idyll* 5, swears by the Nymphs λιμνάδας (*limnadas*), “of the marshes.” And just as Orpheus calls the Nymphs daughters of Oceanus and Tethys, so Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII, considered them the mothers of rivers, because rivers arose from the sea:

> Nymphs, Laurentian Nymphs, from whom the rivers take their birth.

These Nymphs, moreover, were by no means always regarded as benevolent divinities, but had to be appeased with sacrifices lest they cause harm. [Col. 1157B] Hence in Theocritus, *Idyll* XIII, they were δειναὶ θεαὶ ἀγρώταις, “dread divinities to country folk,” as we shall presently see. Meanwhile, should anyone desire further information, he will find it in Natalis Comes, *Mythology*, bk. V, ch. 2, and also in our most learned Montfaucon, *L’Antiquité expliquée*, vol. I, part II, bk. IV, ch. 7.

**Half-dead.** Laurentius Valla, bk. IV, ch. 27, calls those *enecti* who have not already been killed and died but have very nearly reached that condition. Hence, when our author in *On Fasting*, ch. 7, mentions that severe fast of the Ninevites, during which even the cattle were *enecta*, Junius rightly explains these words as referring to beasts not already dead, but so emaciated by hunger through this fast—which, according to Jonah 3:7, was extended even to the cattle by decree of the king of Nineveh—that they were now nearer death than life; and he says that this is the proper meaning of the verb *enecare*.

**Driven mad by the Nymphs.** Daniel Heinsius, in his *Readings on Theocritus*, *Idyll* V, says as follows: “Whenever [Col. 1157C] antiquity mentioned the Nymphs, it prayed to be spared their anger, that is, madness or βλεποδαιμονία (*blepodaimonia*, ‘demon-sight’; for those to whom those goddesses appeared were believed to have lost their mental balance). The same thing was also believed to happen to seers, who were called νυμφολήπτους (*nympholēptous*, ‘seized by Nymphs’); our Latin authors, however, ordinarily call them not *nymphati* but *lymphati*.” Hence our author also says in *On the Soul*, ch. 50: “The demonic spring at Colophon makes people *lymphatici*,” or frenzied. On this see Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, bk. II, ch. 5.

**Hydrophobic.** They are called ὑδροφόβοι (*hydrophoboi*), παρὰ τὸ φοβεῖσθαι τὸ ὕδωρ, “from fearing water.” This happens especially to persons bitten by a rabid dog; their most pitiable condition is to be tormented by an extreme fear of water and simultaneously by an equal thirst. For the dreadful effects of this disease and other relevant matters, see Kircher, *Mundus Subterraneus*, bk. IX, section II, ch. 5. The gentiles formerly attributed all these things to evil spirits inhabiting the water.

**Profane.** In Holy Scripture the holy and the profane are customarily opposed; thus a person is here called profane [Col. 1157D] who has nothing whatever in common with holiness.

**Pool.** In the Greek text the word is κολυμβήθρα (*kolymbēthra*), by which *piscina*, in the sense discussed above in the note **Sprinkling**, signifies a bath or swimming pool.

**Bethsaida.** The Greek text of John 5:2 reads: Ἔστι δὲ ἐν Ἰεροσολύμοις ἐπὶ τῇ πφοβατικῇ κολυμβήθρᾳ, ἡ ἐπιλεγομένη ἑβραϊστὶ Βηθεσδὰ, πέντε στοὰς ἔχουσα, κ.τ.λ. [read contextually: προβατικῇ], “Now there is in Jerusalem, by the Sheep Pool, the one called in Hebrew Bethesda, having five porticoes,” etc. Our Vulgate renders this: “Now there is at Jerusalem a Sheep Pool, which in Hebrew is surnamed Bethsaida, having five porticoes,” etc. Here it should be noted that this pool is called *probatica* not from *probare*, “to test,” but ἀπὸ τῶν προβάτων, “from sheep”; for τὸ πρόβατον means “sheep” in Greek. Thus *probatica* here is equivalent to “ovine” or “belonging to sheep.” It was called the Sheep Pool because sheep and other animals intended for sacrifice were customarily washed in it, or because the entrails of animals already sacrificed were cleansed there. Others say that it was not the pool itself but the gate beside which it stood that was called the Sheep Gate—for in the Greek one reads ἐν, “in,” or, as other [Col. 1158A] manuscripts have it, ἐπὶ τῇ προβατικῇ, “at,” or rather “by, the Sheep [Gate],” perhaps the same one that at 2 Esdras 3:1 is called the Gate of the Flock. But these observations are offered ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ, “in passing.”

Moreover, this pool, which in the Greek text is called Bethesda—“house of mercy”—and in Latin manuscripts Bethsaida—“house of fishing”—may have been so called because it was once a fishpond.

**Stirred.** Some believed this angel to have been the archangel Raphael, whose name is interpreted “Medicine of GOD”: just as he had once been sent by GOD particularly to deliver Tobit from his blindness, so he was appointed to cure the more serious infirmities of other people as well. Whoever he was, one must suppose that he did not descend in any visible form, but merely imbued the water, by a singular command of GOD, with a medicinal power impressed upon it, as it were, in passing, and thus produced a visible sign of his presence.

**They precede.** A figure must always be better known [Col. 1158B] and better accommodated to comprehension. Hence, to prefigure spiritual things, we ordinarily choose bodily or sensible signs, through which we may, as it were, be led by the hand toward an understanding of spiritual realities and higher mysteries that would otherwise exceed all human comprehension.

Moreover, among the other Holy Fathers, St. Ambrose especially asserts in *On the Holy Spirit*, bk. I, ch. 7, that this pool was a figure of our BAPTISM:

> You also have it in the Gospel that at the appointed time an Angel descended into the swimming pool, and the water was stirred, and whoever first descended into the pool was made well. What did the Angel in this type announce except the descent of the Holy Spirit, which was to occur in our times and, when invoked by priestly prayers, consecrate the WATERS—those of Baptism, of course? That Angel, therefore, was the messenger of the Holy Spirit, because through spiritual grace medicine was to be brought to the weaknesses of our soul and mind.

And in *On Those Who Are Initiated into the Mysteries*, ch. 4, he says no less elegantly:

> For them an Angel descended into that pool; [Col. 1158C] for you, the Holy Spirit. For them a creature was stirred; for you, CHRIST himself, the LORD of creation, is at work. Then one person was cured; now all are healed. Therefore, that pool too was a figure, so that you might believe that divine power descends into this Font. Finally, that paralytic was awaiting a man. Whom, if not that Lord Jesus born of the Virgin, at whose advent it would no longer be a shadow that healed individuals, but the truth that healed all?

**The grace of God.** Namely, after the advent of Christ, the Author of grace.

**They healed.** Our author also uses the same verb in *To Scapula*, ch. 4: “How many honorable men have been healed either of demons or of illnesses.” See also *On Prescription*, ch. 38. Although this verb is not Ciceronian, St. Jerome is nevertheless known to have used it in the *Life of Hilarion*.

**The spirit.** Some read: “They minister healing to the spirit” (*Spiritui medentur*). But what prevents us from retaining the accusative *spiritum*, “the spirit,” as the object? For Terence too has in the *Phormio*: “Which, when circumstances are adverse, you are less [Col. 1158D] able to remedy.”

**They reform.** Simply for “they form,” just as he quite frequently uses *retractare*, “to handle again,” for *tractare*, “to handle,” and similarly uses other compounds in place of simple verbs.

**They delivered.** According to Tertullian’s judgment, therefore, that Angel descended only once each year; accordingly, he takes the words κατὰ καιρὸν, “at the appointed time,” in John 5:3 to mean the annual recurrence of the season.

**Death having been destroyed**, namely, the spiritual death of the soul.

**That is, the liability.** *Reatus*—a word unknown to Cicero and first employed by Messala, as Quintilian, bk. VIII, ch. 3, testifies—denotes an obligation for which someone is *reus*, that is, answerable or liable. Theologians ordinarily distinguish a twofold liability: namely, the liability of guilt, requiring satisfaction, and the liability of punishment, requiring the endurance of punishment. Hence the common saying: “He who has nothing in his purse”—with which, of course, to make satisfaction—“must pay with his hide,” with which he may endure the punishment.

[Col. 1159A] **Punishment.** Our author may be understood here in two ways: either as referring to the liability to punishment, upon whose removal the punishment itself no longer has any place; or, as I judge more likely, to the liability of guilt. In that case, the statement must by no means be understood universally, since it is certain among all theologians that, even after mortal guilt has been destroyed through repentance, a liability to punishment nevertheless remains—though, whereas it had formerly been eternal, it must now be discharged only temporally in purgatory. It is proper to Baptism alone that, when through it the liability for all antecedent guilt has been removed, every liability to punishment is simultaneously taken away.

**To the image of God.** He undoubtedly alludes to what God said at Gen. 1:26: “Let us make man to our image and likeness.” And: “God created man to his own image; to the image of God he created him.” There all the Greek interpreters render “image” by εἰκόνα (*eikona*) and “likeness” by ὁμοίωσιν (*homoiōsin*). Long ago, St. Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, q. 51, noted that, if we wish to speak strictly, a distinction exists between [Col. 1159B] these two:

> There are some who understand that the two expressions, “to the image” and “likeness,” were not used without reason, since, if they signified one thing, one term could have sufficed.

Above all, as St. Thomas explains at I, q. 93, art. 9, in the *corpus*, likeness is considered a preliminary to image insofar as it is more general than image. For, as he says at the cited question, art. 1, in the *corpus*:

> We must say, as St. Augustine says in *Eighty-Three Questions*, q. 74: “Where there is an image, there is immediately a likeness; but where there is a likeness, there is not immediately an image.”

“From this,” St. Thomas continues, “it is clear that likeness belongs to the nature of an image, while an image adds something to the nature of likeness, namely, that it is copied from another. For something is called an image because it is made in imitation of another. Hence an egg, however similar and equal it may be to another egg, is nevertheless not called its image, because it was not copied from that egg.” Yet he also discloses another meaning of likeness in the cited q. 93, art. 9, speaking thus [Col. 1159C]:

> It is also considered as subsequent to an image, insofar as it signifies a certain perfection of the image; for we say that someone’s image is like, or is not like, the person whose image it is.

Thus at Ps. 39:7 “image” is used of a certain fleeting—that is, imperfect—image: “Nevertheless man passes on in an image.” Among the Greeks, however, “likeness” is ordinarily used for an image that expresses its prototype precisely and, as it were, down to the last detail. Hence at Gen. 5:5 those words are employed to express the perfect likeness existing between Father and Son: “Adam begot [a son] to his image and likeness, and called his name Seth.”

Man, therefore, was made to the image of God not as regards his body—for he shares this with other animals, which nevertheless were not created to the image of God—but as regards the soul, which by its nature is spiritual, simple, immortal, and endowed with intellect and will, including freedom of the will, etc. Thus the soul displays within itself, [Col. 1159D] as in a kind of mirror, the attributes of God shining forth. Hence St. Augustine beautifully observes in *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, bk. II, ch. 7, that when God fashioned man from the clay of the earth, the words “to his image and likeness” were not added, because the formation of the body was then being described. “But the inner man”—that is, the soul, which is within the body—“was signified when it was said: ‘God made man to the image and likeness of God.’”

And this likeness is, as it were, the perfection and completion of that image, since it expresses not only the perfections of God but also, as it were, their finest and final features; and it even constitutes a certain symbol of the Most Holy Trinity. This is elegantly explained by the author of the book *On the Dignity of Man*, ch. 2, which was formerly ascribed to St. Ambrose. He says: “Just as the Son is begotten from the Father and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, so the will is generated from the intellect, and from these two in turn proceeds memory,” etc. But what is more splendid [Col. 1160A] than the passage in St. Augustine, *Confessions*, bk. XIII, ch. 2? He says:

> Who understands the omnipotent Trinity? And who does not speak of it, if indeed he understands it? Rare is the soul that, when speaking of it, knows what it is saying. . . . I would wish that people considered these three things within themselves: to be, to know, and to will. For I am, and I know, and I will; I am knowing and willing; and I know that I am and that I will to be; and I will to be and to know.

A golden confession!

There is also another image of God in the soul, one far more excellent because it is entirely supernatural, through which we approach God much more perfectly than through the gifts naturally implanted in us: namely, sanctifying grace. As our scholastics demonstrate, this is a formal participation in the divine essence and nature, through which we are called, and are, children of God. Furthermore, through faith our intellect knows him, and through charity embraces him toward whom it tends through hope. It is of this image that the Apostle must be understood when he says at Col. 3:9 ff.: “Stripping off the old man with his deeds and putting on the new, the one who is renewed unto knowledge, [Col. 1160B] according to the image of him who created him.” St. Ambrose, moreover, discusses both images beautifully and fully in *Hexaemeron*, bk. VI, ch. 8.

Finally, man was made in a singular manner to an image—namely, that of Christ. As St. Thomas notes at I, q. 93, art. 1, reply to objection 2:

> The Firstborn of every creature is the perfect image of God, perfectly representing him whose image he is: Man, not similar to God, but himself God. He is therefore called the image, and never “to the image.”

For the Apostle says at Rom. 8:29: “Those whom he foreknew and predestined to be made conformable to the image of his Son.” Likewise, at 1 Cor. 15:49, he speaks as follows: “As we have borne the image of the earthly”—Adam—“let us also bear the image of the Heavenly,” namely, Christ, whom immediately before, in v. 45, he had called “the last Adam, a life-giving Spirit.” Thus through Baptism man is restored to the image of God—not to that natural image, which he could not lose through the sin committed in Adam, but to the supernatural image of Grace, which he lost through Adam’s sin.

[Col. 1160C] **Is reckoned in eternity.** We human beings are the image of God in a representation so long as we see him through a mirror in an enigma; we are made his likeness when we see face to face, 1 Cor. 13:12. For “we know,” says John at 1 Ep. 3:2, “that, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is”—namely then, when “we all, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord,” 2 Cor. 3:18. And thus, finally, this statement of Tertullian must be understood: “The image in the representation, the likeness in eternity.”

**From his breath.** He undoubtedly alludes to Gen. 2:7: “God therefore formed man from the clay of the earth and breathed into his face”—literally, “into his nostrils,” as the principal organ of respiration—“the breath of life, and man became a living soul.” By “living soul” the life of the body is literally understood; but certain Holy Fathers explain it in the mystical sense as the life of the soul, which is sanctifying grace. Thus St. Ambrose, [Col. 1160D] *On Paradise*, ch. 5:

> Life, moreover, was, as the Apostle said (Col. 3:3), hidden with Christ in God. Man, therefore, was either in the shadow of life, on account of the figure of what was to come, etc., or he possessed a certain pledge of life, because he had the inbreathing of God, etc.

### Notes on Chapter VI

**Under an angel.** He appears to indicate the minister of baptism, alluding to that Angel at the Pool of Bethsaida in the preceding chapter.

**We are prepared.** But had he not said a little earlier that through baptism we receive the Holy Spirit whom we had lost through sin? Here, however, it must be carefully noted that Holy Scripture frequently distinguishes between the Holy Spirit and sanctifying Grace, which, having been lost through sin, we receive in baptism. It is certain, first of all, that the Apostles had already been baptized before the day of Pentecost, or had at least otherwise obtained the grace of the Holy Spirit; [Col. 1161A] and nevertheless it is only on the day of Pentecost that Acts 2:4 says of them: “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance.”

Next, at Acts 8:14 ff.: “When the Apostles who were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When these had come, they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit; for he had not yet come upon any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord.” They had therefore been baptized and cleansed of their sins through baptism; accordingly, they possessed the grace of the life-giving Holy Spirit. Yet they are said not yet to have had the Holy Spirit. “Then they laid their hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit.” The Apostles, therefore, received the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost not merely in some manner, but received his fullness, which not only flooded the soul but overflowed into the body itself through certain visible signs: “They were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance.” Likewise those Samaritans, [Col. 1161B] already baptized, received the HOLY SPIRIT through the laying on of hands at Acts 8:17—that is, his fullness.

And this is that Holy Spirit whom the impious Simon wished to purchase for himself with money, ibid., v. 18: “When Simon saw that through the laying on of the Apostles’ hands the HOLY SPIRIT was given, he offered them money,” etc. Another passage, Acts 19:5 ff., must also be explained in this way: “When they heard these things, certain Ephesians were baptized in the name of the Lord JESUS. And when Paul had laid his hands upon them”—after Baptism, of course—“the HOLY SPIRIT came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied.”

Furthermore, that laying on of hands performed upon the newly baptized was the very Sacrament of Confirmation. For just as through Baptism we are initiated into the Faith by the Holy Spirit through what may be called the first fruits of his grace, so through Confirmation we obtain the very Strength of Faith and the fullness of that Spirit, having now, through a new grace, become more mature [Col. 1161C] in the faith. Thus the Spirit who had been given invisibly through Baptism was also given visibly by the Apostles through Confirmation, together, namely, with the attached graces that we call “gratuitously given”: healing the sick, prophesying, interpreting, speaking in various tongues, etc., and other gifts of this kind, which at that time adhered to sacramental grace.

St. Justin, who suffered martyrdom in A.D. 166, and St. Irenaeus, who suffered martyrdom twelve years [Note: [Col. 1161D] **Twelve years.** This is an error by the commentator and easily corrected. He confuses the martyrdom of St. Irenaeus, by which he was crowned in A.D. 202, with the martyrdom of his predecessor St. Pothinus, which in fact is assigned to the year 178. EDD.] later, testify that these signs long continued in the Church: the former in *Apology* I and the *Dialogue with Trypho*, and the latter in *Against Heresies*, bk. V, ch. 6, and elsewhere. But it is sufficiently established that even toward the end of the second century such gratuitously given graces still flourished in some Churches, and that many people who were excessively credulous or otherwise incautious—because they failed properly to distinguish true prophecies from false—were deceived by Montanus and his wretched women, who rashly and deceitfully boasted of the gift of prophecy and the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Our own Tertullian in particular fell most disgracefully into the heresy of Montanus, [Col. 1161D] as we demonstrated in Critical Question 4 prefixed to the book *On Prescription*. See also what we said in the *Theological Miscellany*, *On the Church of Christ*, Disputation VI, no. XIII ff.

Thus, through Baptism, once the Holy Spirit has already been received—though invisibly—we are cleansed from sins through the infusion of grace; at the same time, we are prepared to receive that same Spirit more fully in the sacrament of Confirmation—not now, indeed, under visible signs of this kind, but with an invisible fullness and with strength of faith against internal and external temptations.

**The arbiter of Baptism.** I understand this as the minister, in whose arbitration and power, as it were, the administration of Baptism has been placed. In this sense our author says in *On Monogamy*, ch. 6: [Col. 1162A] “You have Moses, the arbiter of God at close hand.” Here, moreover, he again alludes quite clearly to the frequently mentioned history of the Sheep Pool in John 5. For just as the Angel there descended from heaven, stirring the waters, etc., and just as St. John the Baptist was sent as an Angel to preach and administer the baptism of repentance in the river Jordan, so now the priest, as another Angel officially appointed or sent for this purpose, prepares through the ministry of Baptism the way for the Holy Spirit to be infused more fully through Confirmation, as we have said.

**Faith obtains.** Not the faith of the baptizer or of the person baptized—for the effect of Baptism does not depend upon the work of the one performing it or of the subject receiving it; for who could require faith, or an act of faith, from an infant?—but the faith intrinsic to the Sacrament itself, as an *opus operatum* (“work wrought”), insofar as Baptism was instituted by Christ to be administered in the faith and name of the entire HOLY TRINITY. This faith is the intrinsic form of this Sacrament.

[Col. 1162B] **With the Holy Spirit.** Thus, for the substance and validity of this form, a distinct invocation of the three Persons of the Divinity is required, by which that Faith is sealed in Baptism, as our author likewise says in *On Idolatry*, ch. 12. Hence, from its sacramental form, Baptism is called by the ancient Fathers “the seal,” “the sign,” “the sealing of faith,” “the Sacrament of the Trinity,” “of Faith,” etc., as may be seen in Tournély, *Treatise on Baptism*, q. 1, art. 1, p. 146. Moreover, from this passage it is plainly gathered that already in Tertullian’s time the three Divine Persons necessarily had to be expressed in the form of Baptism, and that Baptism was by no means then conferred in the name of Christ alone. Thus he says in *Against Praxeas*, ch. 26: “Not once, but THREE TIMES, at each several name, we are dipped into the several PERSONS.”

**Through the blessing.** By the term “blessing” he understands the sacramental form of Baptism.

Arbiters of the faith. Some interpreters take considerable pains over this expression by comparing Tertullian’s own usage; [Col. 1162C] for in the *Apology against the Gentiles*, ch. 7, he seems to use *arbitri* for witnesses who are present at the performance of some action, saying: “Impious initiations likewise always exclude the profane” (that is, those who are strangers to those very impious superstitions) “and guard against arbiters” (namely, lest they be present as witnesses). And in the same work, ch. 16, he says: “It feared outside arbiters” (witnesses or observers) “of its vain worship.” And in *On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. 24, speaking of Christ transfigured, he says that “in the seclusion of the mountain, within the circuit of the cloud, he shone brightly before three arbiters.” But in the same book, ch. 21, he seems to take *arbiter* in the sense of “Author,” speaking thus of Christ: “The Arbiter and Master of this gracious discipline, the Illuminator and Guide of the human race, was proclaimed to be the Son of God.” See also what we said above concerning this word *arbiter*. In this passage, however, he seems to take “arbiters” for witnesses, perhaps alluding to 1 John 5:7: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the FATHER, the WORD, and the HOLY SPIRIT.”

Guarantors of salvation. This is, of course, in the sense in which, in the Epistle to the Hebrews 7:22, Jesus is said to have become [Col. 1162D] “the Guarantor of a better covenant.” Therefore the FATHER also, who sends the SON, and the HOLY SPIRIT, who was sent by the Son, will be Guarantors; for the Father through the Son, and the Son himself in the Holy Spirit, promised salvation to us.

Of the divine names, that is, of the Divine Persons—lest anyone attempt to wring Sabellianism from this phrase, as though there were merely names, with no distinction of realities in the Godhead. Now, just as the number of Persons is threefold, so too is the number of names, namely in the grammatical sense; but in the theological sense there is one Name, that is, one and the same dignity and authority in those three Persons. Accordingly, Baptism conferred “in the three names of the Father, the Son,” etc., would be invalid; it is therefore necessary that it be performed “in the Name of the Father and of the Son,” etc. On this matter the theologians should be consulted where they treat the form of Baptism.

Are pledged. This is not badly written *pignerentur* for *pignorentur*; for even in Cicero, *Philippic* IV, and indeed in an active sense, I find: “Mars himself is accustomed to claim as a pledge every most valiant man” [Col. 1163A] (that is, to claim him for himself and take him, as it were, in pledge). Here, however, our author takes it in a passive sense, for “to be given in pledge,” so that the meaning is: both the attestation of faith and the guarantee of salvation are confirmed through Baptism—to which these two things are, as it were, attached—as by a pledge now given.

Mention of the Church. Perhaps this should be understood to mean that a mention of the Church is necessarily made by implication as well, since it is to her that this pledge is given.

The body of the three exists, namely, united in the three Divine Persons and in faith in them.

### Notes on Chapter VII

With an anointing. He is by no means speaking here of the anointing of Confirmation (for he treats that in the following chapter), but of the rite which even today immediately follows Baptism. For after this the kiss of peace is given, and then the baptized person is anointed with chrism on the crown of the head. Indeed, St. Jerome says in his *Dialogue against the Luciferians* that presbyters are not permitted to baptize without the accompanying anointing with chrism.

I cannot refrain from transcribing here the rite of this [Col. 1163B] anointing as it is found in an ancient Pontifical of the local Metropolitan Church, cited by our Edmund Martène in *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, bk. I, ch. 1, art. 13, § 6: “When the infants have been lifted from the font—let the bishop or presbyter, after obtaining the chrism, make the sign of the cross with his thumb upon the crown of their heads, saying thus: ‘May God the Father Almighty—himself anoint you with the chrism of salvation in Christ Jesus our Lord (C. J. D. N.) unto eternal life. Peace be with you.’”

There was also another anointing preceding Baptism, by which those about to be baptized were anointed with oil upon the breast and shoulders. The Author of the *Recognitions*—whoever he may have been, certainly a very ancient writer—already mentions this anointing in bk. III: “Let each one of you be baptized in living waters, with the name of the Threefold Blessedness invoked over him, having first been thoroughly anointed with oil sanctified by prayer.” St. John Chrysostom also mentions this anointing in Homily 6 on Colossians 2, saying: “The person about to be baptized is anointed in the manner of athletes who are just about to enter the contest.” See [Col. 1163C] also the Author of *On the Sacraments*, bk. I, ch. 2, and bk. II, ch. 7, among the works of St. Ambrose. This anointing, however, was performed not with chrism but with the oil of catechumens. On this twofold anointing, the same Martène, in the place cited, will supply abundant material from the ancient so-called Latin *Ordines* and Rituals, as well as from the Greek Euchologia.

Moreover, the fact that the anointing appended to Baptism did not possess the character of sacramental Confirmation is evident even from this: Confirmation was conferred only by bishops—at least among the Latins—whereas that anointing, although performed with chrism, was administered even by presbyters, and not upon the forehead but upon the crown of the head.

He was anointed by Moses. For concerning the consecration of Aaron as priest, God himself commanded Moses in Exodus 29:7: “You shall pour the oil of blessing upon his head,” etc. Moreover, the ancients formerly used horns as vessels. Thus the anointing of kings was also performed with oil from a horn. “Fill your horn with oil,” etc., God said to Samuel in 1 Samuel 16:1, sending him to anoint David as king. “Samuel therefore took the HORN OF OIL [Col. 1163D] and anointed him in the midst of his brothers” (ibid., v. 13). Solomon likewise had been anointed by Zadok the high priest (1 Kings 1:39).

From chrism. *Christus* derives from κέχρισται, the third-person perfect passive of the verb χρίω, “I anoint”; while χρῖσμα is said to derive from the first-person perfect of the same verb, κέχρισμαι; and from ἀπὸ τοῦ χρίσματος, “from the anointing,” comes χριστός, “anointed.” Hence Isaiah 45:1: “Thus says the Lord to my ANOINTED”—from “he anointed”—“to my Christ Cyrus,” etc.

Anointing. Elsewhere χρῖσμα signifies the ointment itself with which an anointing is performed; hence Latin theologians also distinguish, in the Sacrament of Confirmation, between the chrism and the chrismation or anointing itself—that is, the application of the chrism—which the Greeks otherwise properly call χρῖσις. Yet I find that the Fathers use τὸ χρῖσμα indiscriminately for both the ointment and the anointing. Thus Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, bk. I, says concerning the ancient Lacedaemonians that they rightly regarded and called deceitful both deceitful garments and “anointings” (τὰ χρίσματα). [Col. 1164A] And in the *Paedagogus*, bk. II, after having said shortly before, οὐ θέμις δολερὰ εἵματα, καὶ χρίσματα εἰς τῆς ἀληθείας εἰσιέναι πόλιν, “It is unlawful for deceitful garments and ointments to enter the city of truth,” he writes shortly afterward: “Let a woman always be anointed together with the divine anointing of chastity” (τῷ τῆς σωφροσύνης χρίσματι συναλειφέσθω), “delighting in the holy ointment” (μύρῳ), namely, the Spirit. And in bk. IV he calls τὸ χρῖσμα τῆς εὐαρεστήσεως “the anointing of good pleasure,” that is, of a mind pleasing to God. But why multiply examples, when even in the New Testament τὸ χρῖσμα is taken for anointing? Thus 1 John 2:20: “And you have χρῖσμα, an anointing, from the Holy One.” And again in v. 27: “And the χρῖσμα, the anointing which you received from him, abides in you.”

By God the Father. Christ was anointed as Prophet, Priest, and King; for these alone were the three classes of men customarily anointed in antiquity. This anointing, however, was performed not with any visible chrism, but spiritually, by the Holy Spirit himself, namely when Christ, [Col. 1164B] having been baptized in the Jordan, immediately came up from the water; “and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the SPIRIT OF GOD descending like a dove and coming upon him. And behold, a voice from heaven said: THIS IS MY BELOVED SON, IN WHOM I AM WELL PLEASED” (Matthew 3:16–17). This, however, must not be understood as though the Holy Spirit anointed Christ at his Baptism with the fullness of his grace—for he already possessed it from the first instant of his conception, and it was incapable of any further increase—but as meaning that the Holy Spirit wished to display by some visible sign the anointing of Christ, consisting chiefly in the GRACE OF HEADSHIP and the HYPOSTATIC UNION, as something already accomplished long before. It is in this sense that Christ applied to himself in Luke 4:18 the words of Isaiah 61:1: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me.” Thus Peter too preached concerning Christ in Acts 10:38: “How God anointed him with the Holy Spirit,” etc.; St. Augustine, *On the Trinity*, bk. XV, ch. 26, explains this as follows: “Certainly not with visible oil, but with the gift of grace, [Col. 1164C] which is signified by the visible ointment with which the Church anoints the baptized. Nor indeed was Christ then anointed with the Holy Spirit when the Spirit descended upon him, after his Baptism, in the form of a dove. For then he deigned to prefigure his body, that is, his Church, in which the baptized especially receive the Holy Spirit; but he must be understood to have been anointed with that mystical and invisible anointing when the Word was made flesh,” etc. See the same author further.

We are delivered, though with this distinction: Baptism is a Sacrament washing away sins as stains of the soul, whereas that anointing belongs only to the rite following this Sacrament. It merely presents, as in a symbol of a past event, the deliverance effected by the power of baptismal grace, which spiritually anoints; it does not itself confer a new increase of grace.

A parallel passage occurs in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 8, where our author says: “The flesh is washed, so that the soul may be cleansed of stains. The flesh is anointed, so that the soul may be consecrated. The flesh is signed, so that the soul may be fortified. The flesh is overshadowed by the imposition of hands, [Col. 1164D] so that the soul also may be illuminated by the Spirit.” But these matters will presently be explained more fully.

### Notes on Chapter VIII

Is imposed. Two impositions of hands were formerly celebrated in connection with Baptism. One preceded not only Baptism but also the very anointing that belonged among the preliminary rites of Baptism—see the preceding chapter, note “With an anointing”—and it is frequently mentioned in the Latin baptismal *Ordines* presented by Edmund Martène in *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, bk. I, ch. 1, § 8. The other followed Baptism and was to be performed only by a bishop.

Here it must be understood that in the first centuries of the Church solemn Baptism—namely, that which was given only on Holy Saturday and the vigil of Pentecost—was administered by the bishops themselves, and that they immediately appended the SACRAMENT OF CONFIRMATION as a kind of completion. Hence St. Paulinus writes in his *Life of St. Ambrose*: [Col. 1165A] “He was also most vigorous in carrying out divine duties, so much so that five bishops after his death could scarcely perform what he had customarily accomplished for those being baptized.” That custom persisted for many centuries in the Church. But when the multitude of the faithful had grown excessively in the individual churches, and bishops had become exceedingly necessary for preaching the Gospel, the principle expressed by Paul in 1 Corinthians 1:17 also began to prevail: “Christ did not send me to baptize, but to PREACH THE GOSPEL.” Hence it came about that bishops could not always be present even at solemn Baptism to confirm the baptized immediately. For this reason, a manuscript Pontifical of the Church of Apamea in Syria, written in 1214 and reproduced by our Martène in *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, bk. I, ch. 2, art. 1, § 3, prescribes after all the rites of Baptism that, “IF THE BISHOP IS PRESENT, he must immediately confirm him”—the baptized person—“with chrism,” etc. Indeed, as early as the seventh century, few bishops performed the office of Baptism, being excessively occupied with other cares. Meanwhile, the same Martène, in the place cited, § 1, testifies that this practice of [Col. 1165B] confirming the newly baptized immediately was continued, at least in some churches, including Latin ones, nearly down to our own age. Among the Greeks the same custom persists even now: the Sacrament of Confirmation is appended immediately to Baptism, though it is administered not by a bishop but by the very presbyter who baptizes. On this matter Juenin should be consulted, Dissertation VII, *On Confirmation*, q. V, art. 2, § 1 ff.

Through a blessing, that is, a certain fixed form of words, such as must ordinarily be used in almost all the Sacraments at the Savior’s command, and which our author above, in ch. VI, likewise expressed by the word “blessing.”

Invoking the Holy Spirit. Moreover, this entire passage seems to favor the opinion of those who maintain that the imposition of hands alone—and not also anointing with chrism—is the matter of Confirmation. On this issue the dogmatic-scholastic theologians engage in much controversy, especially Tournély, *Treatise on the Sacrament of Confirmation*, q. 1, art. 3.

[Col. 1165C] Device, that is, a contrivance devised with skill. Thus our author says in *On the Spectacles*, ch. 10, that the demons, foreseeing their own interests from the beginning, inspired, among the other pollutions of idolatry, those ingenious devices of the arts belonging to spectacles. This is precisely the sense in which, in *On the Pallium*, ch. 1, he says that the Carthaginians marveled at the Roman battering ram, a machine of war, as a new and foreign “device,” that is, invention.

A spirit may be permitted. Certainly not a good spirit; for he is speaking of hydromancers, who drew predictions of future events from water. King Numa Pompilius is said to have been exceedingly devoted to this art. When he was preparing to regulate the religious institutions and rites of his Romans, since he appeared unable to seek counsel for himself in any other way, he was compelled to practice hydromancy, so that in the water he might see images of the gods—or rather, deceptions of demons—from whom he might hear what should be established and observed in sacred matters. So says St. Augustine, *The City of God*, bk. VII, ch. 35; and in the same place, after certain other remarks: “Because Numa Pompilius therefore *egesserit aquam*—that is, drew or carried out water—from which to practice hydromancy, he is said to have had as his wife the nymph Egeria—a decidedly chilly nomenclature. [Col. 1165D] For this is how events are customarily transformed into fables by being sprinkled with lies.”

Their incorporation, that is, their intimate conjunction—the conjunction, namely, of the water and that spirit.

With hands suitably placed above. That is, with hands imposed from above; for this was the rite of the hydromancers, who enchanted the waters and, as it were, surrendered them to the power of an evil spirit.

To animate. This entire sentence has the flavor of irony and alludes to the magical rites by which hydromancers customarily employ water for magical purposes. He says that they “animate” it with another—that is, with some higher and more powerful—spirit of such great splendor (just as hydromancers customarily boast that such glorious and illustrious effects are produced by that spirit); that is, they stir it up and render it, as it were, alive.

As an organ. That is, as a minister or instrument [Col. 1166A] subject to that spirit “obedientially,” as the Scholastics say, for the production of whatever effects it wishes.

Through holy hands, namely, through their imposition.

To fashion. *Modulari* means to arrange something according to a definite mode and measure, as we have already said above in ch. III, note “Fashioners.” By “spiritual sublimity,” moreover, he readily means the power of producing the sacramental grace of Confirmation, as though that power had been imparted to and inhered in the hands of the confirming bishop.

I shall relate here something that does not seem entirely foreign to our subject. Eunapius of Sardis, a pagan who around A.D. 380 was a sophist of no little renown among his own people, tells it concerning Iamblichus, a distinguished adherent of Platonic philosophy, in his *Lives of the Philosophers*: “Some time afterward, all agreed to go at the appointed season of the year to Gadara, a place of hot springs in Syria,” etc. “While Iamblichus was bathing there and the others were likewise occupied in bathing, a discussion arose concerning the baths, and Iamblichus said with a smile: ‘Although religious scruple prevents me [Col. 1166B] from disclosing these things, I shall nevertheless do so for your sake.’ At once he ordered his disciples to inquire of the local inhabitants by what names two of the smaller hot springs—though more elegant and beautiful than the others—had long ago been called. When they had carried out his command, they reported that one was named Love and the other Anteros, the god who avenges wrongs done to lovers. Immediately, after touching the water with his hand and murmuring a few little words, he summoned from the bottom of the spring a small boy, fair-skinned and of pleasing stature, with hair tinged like ruddy gold and the skin of his back gleaming, whose whole appearance was like that of one bathing or freshly bathed. His companions were astonished by the novelty of the event. ‘Let us pass,’ he said, ‘to the neighboring spring’; and rising at once, he went before them, absorbed in thought and with his face intent. There, performing the same actions as before, he called forth Love, who resembled the former boy in every respect except that his hair was darker, auburn, and spread across his neck. Both little boys crowded around Iamblichus, clinging to him in close embraces as though to their natural father. He immediately restored them to their own abodes, finished bathing, and departed,” [Col. 1166C] etc. Thus Eunapius.

These were, of course, fleeting apparitions of infernal spirits. No matter how much they pretended to have been washed and baptized, and though they were drawn from the waters by the hands of that magician, he was nevertheless unable to impose upon them the hands by which he might confirm them in some stable state.

Shaping, for “preshaping,” “figuring,” or simply “forming.” It is certainly in this last sense that I also find the verb used by Vitruvius, bk. VI: “The tragic stage is shaped”—this clearly should not be taken in a pejorative sense, but rather as “adorned”—“with columns, statues,” etc. Moreover, this entire passage is drawn from Genesis 48:13 ff., where: “He”—Joseph—“placed Ephraim at Israel’s left”—that is, Jacob’s, who had received the name Israel from the Angel with whom he had wrestled, Genesis 32:28—“but Manasseh at his own left, and thus at his father Jacob’s right, and brought them both to him. Jacob, stretching out his right hand, placed it upon the head of Ephraim, the younger brother, and his left hand upon the head of Manasseh, [Col. 1166D] who was the elder, crossing his hands. And Jacob blessed the sons of Joseph,” etc. Joseph, namely, placed both his sons before his father Jacob: the firstborn, Manasseh, at Joseph’s left, which directly faced Jacob’s right; but Ephraim at Joseph’s right and consequently at Jacob’s left. Joseph did not doubt that Jacob would place his right hand upon the one who had also been positioned on his right side—namely, Manasseh—and his left hand upon the other, namely Ephraim. But when Jacob placed his hands crosswise, that is, intersecting one another, and thus placed his right hand—which by nature has greater dignity because it is stronger—upon Ephraim, the second-born, and his left upon the firstborn Manasseh, Joseph attempted to correct what he thought an error by removing his father’s right hand from Ephraim’s head and transferring it to Manasseh’s. Jacob, however, undoubtedly conscious of a [Col. 1167A] higher Mystery, persisted in his intention and completed, in the same rite, the blessing he had already begun.

Which was to come to pass unto Christ. Those hands crossed in the form of a cross therefore foreshadowed the very Cross of Christ. MANASSEH was a figure of the Old Testament, as the firstborn—namely, in time; and because the Old Testament was itself a figure of the New Testament, Manasseh was thus A FIGURE of Christ himself, who in Colossians 1:15 is called “the Firstborn of every creature.” EPHRAIM, the second-born, represented the New Testament and was A FIGURE of Christ himself and of the Church, as something later—though again only in time—and, as it were, born second in Christ, but far greater in merits and privileges. In the Church there would be not the figure of the Cross, but the Cross itself: CHRIST CRUCIFIED. Therefore, although others read “which was to come to pass IN CHRIST,” I earnestly retain “which was to come to pass unto Christ”: namely, that which was to redound UNTO CHRIST, or to his Church THROUGH CHRIST.

Cleansed. Namely, through the washing that takes place in the Baptism of Christ.

[Col. 1167B] Blessed, namely, both sanctified through Baptism and its sacramental form, and thereafter confirmed through the imposition of hands. Moreover, this sentence may perhaps reasonably be seen as containing a tacit comparison, so that it can be explained thus: Just as the Holy Spirit descended in a certain manner upon the sons of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, who had been blessed by Jacob through the imposition of hands, so too the grace of Confirmation descends upon the baptized when the bishop imposes his hands upon them.

Descends. The connective “and” appears to have dropped out and should therefore be supplied here.

Dove. Some of the ancients believed this; but Aristotle, *History of Animals*, bk. II, and Pliny, bk. XI, ch. 27, who were themselves ancients, as well as all more recent anatomists, assert the contrary. Although doves, like other animals, also possess gall—the source of all anger and bitterness—it is well established that this gall is very temperate and boils up only when greatly provoked. In this sense St. Augustine says in Tractate VII on the Epistle of St. John: “The dove has no gall, yet it fights with beak and wings for its nest: it rages without bitterness.”

[Col. 1167C] Of the figure. For that descent of the Holy Spirit was prefigured by another dove, Noah’s dove in the Old Testament; and this dove was at the same time a certain preliminary figure of our Baptism.

Of the world. Thus he elegantly calls Noah’s Flood, which St. Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 40, *On Baptism*, aptly calls “a flood of sin.” For the whole world, previously filled and, as it were, inundated with sins and crimes, was cleansed from the filth of sin when the Flood came upon it under Noah and nearly the whole human race was miserably suffocated in the waters. In like manner, through the Baptism of Christ we are washed clean from original sin and from all other sins present before Baptism. That this same Baptism of ours was prefigured by that Flood is indeed evident from Holy Scripture itself, 1 Peter 3:20–21: “In [Col. 1167D] the days of Noah, while the Ark was being built, in which a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water. The like form of this”—the Apostle continues—“now saves you also: BAPTISM, not the removal of the filth of the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience to God through the Resurrection of Jesus Christ.” St. Augustine explains this further in *Against Faustus*, bk. XII, ch. 14: “Noah with his family is delivered through water and wood”—the ark—“just as the family of Christ is signed through Baptism by the Passion of the Cross.” And in the same book, ch. 17, he says: “The Flood came seven days after Noah entered the ark because we are baptized in hope of the future rest signified by the seventh day.” St. Basil the Great also compares Baptism to the Flood in Homily I on Psalm 28:10, saying: “The Prophet therefore calls the grace of Baptism a Flood, through which the soul, washed and purified from sins and having cast off the old man, thereafter becomes a dwelling fit for God in the Spirit.” He has similar remarks in Homily II on the same Psalm.

Herald of heavenly wrath. This passage is exceedingly difficult [Col. 1168A]: for how could the dove bearing the olive branch of peace have been the herald of heavenly wrath? Some therefore think that “grace” should be restored in place of “wrath.” Since the abbreviation *grae* is found in certain manuscripts, they say that this word was deformed into *irae* (“wrath”) by an ignorant scribe. Yet I think that “wrath” can also be maintained if we read it thus: “the dove announced to the earth peace from heavenly wrath”—that is, the wrath of heaven, which had formerly been angry but was now pacified—“as the herald” of that wrath now appeased, namely, announcing it and proclaiming it like a herald to the whole world.

Is held forth. Nothing is more widely known than that among the gentiles of old the olive branch itself was a symbol of peace. Especially pertinent here is the line of Virgil:

> And in her hand she holds forth the branch of the peace-bearing olive.

Thus, on a certain coin of the emperor Hadrian, a figure is seen with bent knee, extending its right hand to the Emperor himself and holding forth an olive branch in its left, with the [Col. 1168B] inscription: “TO THE RESTORER OF SPAIN,” namely, to the one who restored it to peace. Likewise, a certain coin of Severus Pius Augustus depicts a togate figure, similarly bearing an olive branch, with the added inscription: “TO THE FOUNDER OF PEACE.” No less do coins of Maximian and Philip the Elder display a figure of this kind; the former is inscribed “THE PEACE OF AUGUSTUS,” and the latter “ETERNAL PEACE.” Very many examples of this kind could be assembled here if space permitted.

By the same disposition, meaning “in the same manner” or “according to the same arrangement.”

To our flesh. For because it was formed from the earth—“the Lord God formed man from the slime of the earth,” Genesis 2:7—it is rightly called “earth.”

Bringing the peace of God. Concerning this dove, St. Ambrose says in *On Luke*, bk. II, ch. 3: “The grace of the laver requires simplicity, so that we may be simple as doves. The grace of the laver requires peace, which in the ancient type a dove once conveyed to that Ark which alone was immune from the Flood. [Col. 1168C] He who has now deigned to descend IN THE FORM OF A DOVE taught me of whom that dove was a type. He taught that in that branch and in that Ark there was a type of the peace of the Church: that amid the very floods of the World the HOLY SPIRIT should bring fruitful PEACE to his Church.” Thus St. Ambrose. That dove, therefore, brought an olive branch when the earth had already been cleansed from its filth; now, to those washed through Baptism, the Holy Spirit brings peace and grace of soul in the Sacrament of Confirmation and, by anointing the soul with oil, strengthens it for the struggle.

The Ark as a figure. In this allegorical meaning of the Ark, the ancient Fathers and interpreters agree almost universally. Of these I shall cite only two, Origen and St. Augustine. The former confirms it at length in Homily II on Genesis, from which I excerpt only a few words: “Just as it was then said to that Noah that he should build an Ark and bring into it not only his sons and relatives but also animals of various kinds, so too, at the consummation of the ages, the FATHER said to our NOAH, OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST, that he should make for himself an ARK of [Col. 1168D] squared timbers and give it dimensions filled with heavenly Sacraments,” etc. St. Augustine, moreover, speaks beautifully in *The City of God*, bk. XV, ch. 26: “God commands Noah, a righteous man, to build an ark in which he and his family might be delivered from the devastation of the Flood. This is undoubtedly a figure of the City of God journeying as a pilgrim in this world—that is, of the CHURCH—which is saved through the WOOD upon which hung the Mediator between God and men, the Man CHRIST JESUS.” See the same author further, both in this chapter and in the following ch. 27; likewise *Exposition of the Gospel of St. John*, Tractate VI; *Questions on the Gospels*, bk. II, q. 44; *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, ch. 19; but especially *Against Faustus*, bk. XII, ch. 14 ff., where he explains the Ark most fully as a figure of the Church. On the same subject one may also read St. Gregory the Great, Homily XVI on Ezekiel; Rupert of Deutz, *Commentary on Genesis*, bk. IV, ch. 71 ff.; and many others everywhere.

By a flood. Junius considers this passage corrupt and accordingly believes it should be restored thus: “If the world has also sinned again, in respect of which Baptism is badly compared, a flood [Col. 1169A] of fire is therefore appointed,” etc. He thus assigns the following meaning to the passage: “But if, after the singular grace of God was offered in Baptism, the world is carried into sins and plunges headlong into them altogether, by which deed it behaves most unjustly toward Baptism, and Baptism has been badly matched; therefore—that is, for this reason—a flood of fire is appointed for the world, so that just as it once perished when the waters overflowed, it may likewise one day be consumed by the fire of divine judgment.”

For my part, however, I would prefer to retain the text. It is admittedly somewhat obscure, but can be understood in this sufficiently suitable sense: “But the world nevertheless sinned again,” relapsing into its former sins—especially in the offspring of Ham, who treated his father so insultingly and whose son Canaan and his descendants, the Canaanites, were cursed by God himself (Genesis 9:25)—“in respect of which,” that is, by which circumstance or so that, “it is badly compared.” This does not mean that the earlier comparison was bad or unsuitable. Rather, not only is Baptism well compared to the Flood, since it cleanses all the filth of sins from the soul of each person just as the Flood cleansed it from the entire [Col. 1169B] world, but the world should also rightly be compared “in evil” to fire—that is, to the other flood which is to come upon it at the Last Judgment. “Therefore”—or for that reason—“a flood of fire is appointed,” etc. Recall what we said above in the note “Of the world.”

Is appointed for fire. The world, namely. On this matter St. Justin Martyr says in *Apology* II, p. 51 of my edition: Καὶ Σίβυλλα δὲ καὶ Ὑστάσπις, γενήσεσθαι τῶν φθαρτῶν ἀνάλωσιν διὰ πυρὸς ἔφασαν. Οἱ λεγόμενοι δὲ Στοϊκοὶ φιλόσοφοι, καὶ αὐτὸν τὸν Θεὸν εἰς πῦρ ἀναλύεσθαι δογματίζουσι, καὶ αὖ πάλιν κατὰ μεταβολὴν τὸν κόσμον γενέσθαι λέγουσι; that is: “Both the Sibyl and Hystaspes said that corruptible things would be consumed by fire. Those called Stoic philosophers teach that God himself will be dissolved into fire, and they say that the world will come into being anew through transformation.”

What, moreover, of Josephus, who in *Jewish Antiquities*, bk. I, ch. 3, affirms that Adam foretold a universal destruction of things, one by FIRE and the other by FLOOD? I willingly pass over the rest [Col. 1169C] concerning the two pillars, one of brick and the other of marble, of which at least one would escape either the fire or the waters. It is all too widely repeated and rests, so far as is known, almost entirely upon the testimony of this Josephus alone.

Meanwhile, it is certain that this opinion concerning the world’s destruction by fire permeated nearly all antiquity and was propagated even by the pagans Zeno, Pythagoras, Heraclitus, Sophocles, and others.

But see how this matter is supported by weighty testimonies of Holy Scripture. Of these I cite only one, clearer than the rest, from 2 Peter 3:5: “The heavens existed long ago, and the earth, standing out of water and through water by the word of God; through these the world that then existed perished, flooded by water. But the heavens and earth that now exist have been stored up by the same word and reserved for fire until the day of judgment and the destruction of ungodly men.” And shortly afterward: “The Day of the Lord will come like a thief; on that day the heavens will pass away with a great rushing sound, the elements will be dissolved by heat, and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up.” [Col. 1169D] Our most learned Calmet treats this subject in his introductory Dissertation *On the End of the World*, etc.

Restores. For thus it will be at the consummation of the age: “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all scandals and those who practice iniquity, and cast them into the furnace of fire” (Matthew 13:40–42).

What must be received. Those very figures of our Baptism—namely both the FLOOD and FIRE—should admonish us of what awaits in the next life those who fall after BAPTISM and are not afterward restored through Penance. For one must by no means agree with Montanus or Novatian that sins committed after Baptism are likewise incapable of forgiveness.

### Notes on Chapter IX

Supports supplied by nature, namely, the natural qualities that commend water above the other elements, which were discussed throughout ch. III.

[Col. 1170A] Privileges of grace. Gratuitous gifts superadded to that same nature, which were likewise discussed throughout ch. IV.

Solemn observances of discipline, namely, the rites customarily employed in Baptism by ordinance of the Church, as above in chs. VII and VIII.

Preliminary constructions, that is, preparations and antecedent ceremonies. Our author uses this word in this sense in *Against Hermogenes*, ch. 16: “Therefore, in the preliminary construction of this proposition,” etc. No less so in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 4: “Then the heretics begin immediately from that point, and from that point construct their preliminary argument.” See also *On Prescription against Heretics*, ch. XV.

Prayers, the formulas of prayer customarily employed especially in the blessing of the baptismal font or in Baptism itself. See above, ch. IV, note “God having been invoked.”

The sanctity of the water. Here he calls *religio* that sanctity which inheres in the baptismal water as a sacred thing destined for the Sacrament of Baptism.

Unencumbered. We properly call those persons “unencumbered” whose feet have been released and freed from chains as impediments.

[Col. 1170B] By the sacrament? Whatever Junius may object, the sentence must be read interrogatively.

From the world. Here “world” is taken in the pejorative sense, as St. James uses it in 4:4 of his Epistle: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world makes himself an enemy of GOD.” And St. Paul says of Christ in Galatians 1:4: “He gave himself for our sins, that he might rescue us from this present evil world.”

Their former ruler, as though another and far more merciless Pharaoh, who through sin exercised the cruelest dominion over the human race and still rules over individual sinners until they have been delivered from his tyranny through the water of Baptism. “When you were slaves of sin,” says the Apostle in Romans 6:20, “you were free from righteousness.” Read this entire chapter of the Apostle.

They leave behind, namely, by renouncing Satan and his pomps in Baptism. Moreover, the Apostle himself sufficiently declares in 1 Corinthians 10:1 ff. that the crossing of the Red Sea was a figure of our Baptism: “Our fathers [Col. 1170C] were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea.” Commenting on these words, St. Augustine says in *Against Faustus*, bk. XX, ch. 29: “The cloud and the Red Sea are assuredly Baptism. The enemies pursue from behind: past sins die.” St. Ambrose writes similarly in *On Those Who Are Initiated*, etc., ch. 3: “Do you observe that in that crossing of the Hebrews a figure of sacred Baptism was already present, in which the Egyptian perished and the Hebrew escaped? For what else are we taught daily in this Sacrament but that guilt is drowned and error abolished?” Thus Christians pass through Baptism as through the Red Sea into a new life. “The sea,” says Theodoret, as cited by Calmet on 1 Corinthians 10:2, “represented the sacred LAVER which those to be baptized enter; the cloud, the GRACE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT; Moses, the PRIEST who baptizes; the rod of this legislator, the CROSS OF JESUS CHRIST; the Israelites in the sea, the CHRISTIANS who are baptized; the drowned Egyptians and their leader Pharaoh, the demons cast down from the dominion they exercised over us.”

[Col. 1170D] Advantage. Latinius reads “for advantageous use,” and I do not oppose him. The common reading, however, can also be retained, although it is rather harsh, and “for its own advantage” can be understood as “for its own usefulness”—the usefulness that water customarily affords human beings through its pleasantness and clarity.

Of Moses, *Mosei* being used for *Mosis*, the genitive case.

Remedied. On this word see above, Chapter XV. Moreover, this episode is narrated in Exodus 15:23ff. as follows: “And they came to Marah, and they could not drink the waters of Marah, because they were bitter; hence he also gave the place a fitting name, calling it Marah, that is, ‘bitterness.’ … And the Lord showed him a piece of wood; and when he had cast it into the waters, they were turned to sweetness.”

Retro, “previously,” as often elsewhere.

Remedying. The ancient Fathers also interpret it thus, among them St. Ambrose, *On Those Who Are Initiated*, ch. 3:

> Marah, he says, was a very bitter spring; Moses cast wood into it, and it became sweet. For water without the preaching of the Lord’s cross—behold the wood—would be of no use for future salvation; but when it has been consecrated by the mystery of the saving Cross, it is then tempered for use as a spiritual washing and a saving drink. Therefore, just as Moses cast wood into that spring—that is, the Prophet—so into this font the priest casts the preaching of the Lord’s Cross, and the water becomes sweet unto grace.

[Col. 1171A]

Moreover, Junius thinks that this passage of Tertullian should be read thus: “the water of Baptism, namely, remedying by itself the most unhealthy veins.” But I firmly retain our reading. For it was not the water of Baptism that remedied those bitter waters, as though they were most unhealthy veins; rather, the wood—or Christ crucified upon the wood—converted those waters, which were destined for Baptism but were otherwise unhealthy, that is, contained nothing salutary or conducive to our salvation, into sweetness by itself, or by its own proper power, as a remedy for sins and for the salvation of our soul.

Flowed down. For when the people of Israel had come from the wilderness of Sin to Rephidim and, because of the bitter thirst afflicting them, had murmured against Moses, God commanded him to take the very rod with which he had previously divided the Red Sea and to strike the rock in order to draw water from it, etc.; Exodus 17:1ff. A similar miracle also occurred at Kadesh, as may be seen in Numbers 20:13ff. St. Paul had both in view in 1 Corinthians 10, explaining them thus:

> All drank the same spiritual drink—for they drank from a spiritual rock that followed them [ἔπινον γὰρ ἐκ πνευματικῆς ἀκολουθούσης πέτρας]. They drank, moreover, from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ—but with most of them, etc.

[Col. 1171B]

From this, not only the Rabbis but also quite a few Christian interpreters maintain that that rock, or at least the waters of that rock, thereafter always accompanied the Israelites in the wilderness. Thus our Author says in *On Patience*, ch. 5: “After the edible rain of manna, after the watery attendance of the rock,” etc. But what necessity is there to assert here so enormous a miracle, one by no means indicated by Moses? For the Apostle is not speaking here of that material rock which was at Rephidim, but of a spiritual rock—and thus only in a spiritual or mystical sense—namely Christ, prefigured by that rock, who as the living Rock continually accompanies Christians, the better Israelites, through the wilderness of this world, becoming for them a fountain of water springing up into eternal life; John 4:14. For this reason our Author rightly places this water, flowing forth from the rock at Rephidim, among the figures of our Baptism.

Be blessed. The passage is certainly obscure. Something seems to have dropped out and must be supplied. Accordingly, I think it should be read thus: “Water in Christ, in whom we see Baptism blessed”; this sense is sufficiently clear. But what does this mean, “Baptism is blessed”? It may be understood either of that very ancient rite, persisting even to our own times, namely the blessing of the baptismal font itself, which is customarily performed on Holy Saturday and the Vigil of Pentecost—see above, Chapter IV, note “God being invoked”—or of the very formula of Baptism, as in Chapter VI, note “Through the blessing.”

[Col. 1171C–D]

The grace of water, meaning its beauty or dignity, as in Chapter III, note “Or grace”; or its kindness, favor, or esteem with God, to whom water has always been more acceptable than the other elements, etc.

Confirmation, so that Baptism may be established or more strongly commended through water as its matter.

Water inaugurates, by changing it into wine, which was his first miracle: “Jesus made this the beginning of signs at Cana in Galilee,” etc.; John 2:11.

He invites to his water. For thus Jesus speaks to the Samaritan woman in John 4:14: “The water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.” And John 7:37: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.”

Concerning the agape. Ἀγάπη in Greek means “love.” Elsewhere *agapae* also means those charitable meals of the earliest Christians which they customarily celebrated before the consecration of the Holy Eucharist, both in memory of Christ’s Last Supper, at which he instituted that sacrament, and to foster mutual love. Paul sharply censures their abuse among certain people in 1 Corinthians 11:20ff.

[Col. 1172A]

He approves. Thus, in commending brotherly love in Matthew 10, the final verse, he says: “Whoever gives one of these little ones only a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple, amen I say to you, shall not lose his reward.”

Gladly. “But in the fourth watch of the night Jesus came to them, walking upon the sea”; Matthew 14:25.

He crosses the strait. “And entering into a boat, he crossed over and came into his own city”; Matthew 9:1. Similarly: “When they”—the disciples with Jesus—“had crossed over, they came into the land of Gennesaret”; Matthew 14:34.

Spear. “One of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out”; John 19:34. St. Ambrose teaches, on Luke 23, that Baptism was prefigured by this water:

> From that body, incorrupt though dead, there remained the life of all. For water and blood came forth: the former to wash clean, the latter to redeem.

And St. Augustine, *Tractate 120 on John*, accordingly says that Christ’s side was opened on the cross:

> So that there, as it were, the door of life might be opened, from which flowed the sacraments, without which no one enters into the life that is true life. That blood was shed for the remission of sins; that water tempers the saving cup: it supplies both washing and drink.

[Col. 1172B]

## Notes on Chapter X

Constantly, that is, “continuously” or “immediately”; as our Author likewise says of Christ in *On Patience*, ch. 3: “It was not enough that he even had his betrayer with him and did not immediately denounce him.” Elsewhere, however, he uses it for “boldly” and “fearlessly”; for example, in *On the Shows*, ch. 26, where a demon says from within a certain possessed woman: “I acted boldly, and indeed with perfect justice.”

Believing. He is certainly alluding to what appears in Isaiah 7:9, where the Hebrew text reads literally: “If you do not believe, neither shall you be faithful,” or “have confidence.” Symmachus translates it: Ἐὰν μὴ πιστεύσητε, οὐ διαμενεῖτε, “If you do not believe, you shall not endure”; and from this our Vulgate has: “If you do not believe, you shall not remain.” Theodoret has it somewhat differently: οὐδ’ οὐ μὴ πιστευθείητε, “You shall by no means be believed.” Finally, the Septuagint has: ἐὰν μὴ πιστεύσητε, οὐδὲ μὴ συνῆτε, “If you do not believe, you shall by no means understand”; in accordance with this wording John Chrysostom, Cyprian, Augustine, and other Fathers frequently cite the passage. That saying in John 6:69 also seems to accord with it, where Peter says to Christ: Καὶ ἡμεῖς πεπιστεύκαμεν, ἐγνώκαμεν κτλ., “And we have believed and have known that you are the Christ,” etc. And John 10:38: ἐὰν ἐμοὶ μὴ πιστεύητε, τοῖς ἔργοις πιστεύσατε, ἵνα γνῶτε, καὶ πιστεύσητε ὅτι ἐν ἐμοὶ ὁ Πατὴρ κτλ., “If you are unwilling to believe me, believe the works, so that you may know and believe that the Father is in me,” etc.

[Col. 1172C–D]

Accordingly, if we wish to understand the mysteries revealed by God, we must first believe, so that faith must precede and understanding follow from faith. Tertullian confirms this elsewhere as well, as in *On the Soldier’s Crown*, ch. 2: “I praise the faith which believes that a thing must be observed before it has learned it.” And in *Against Marcion* IV, ch. 20, after similarly employing that testimony of Isaiah, he immediately adds: “This was the faith which had also bestowed understanding.” Finally, in the same work, ch. 25, he confirms it again, saying: “He concealed it, after first supplying the prophetic instrument of obscurity, the understanding of which faith would merit; for unless you believe, you shall not understand.”

But what of our Protestants? They wish first to understand and then to believe, measuring their faith by the light of their own reason and paying no attention at all to the common saying: “The learner must believe”—before, that is, he understands what he is learning. See, then, the difference between us and them. They do not believe unless they understand; we believe in order that we may understand. This is what the Apostle admonishes us in 2 Corinthians 10:5: to be “destroying counsels”—human counsels—“and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God”—that is, against those things concerning God that become known to us through faith—“and bringing every understanding into captivity unto the obedience of Christ.”

[Col. 1173A]

By command, however. *Mandatus*, fourth declension, is found among the jurists. The word could therefore easily have adhered to Tertullian from civil jurisprudence; for we demonstrated in the epitome of his Life prefixed by us to the book *On Prescription* that he was highly skilled in civil law.

By condition. That is, according to its intrinsic nature or, as we otherwise say, according to its substance. That Baptism was therefore divine only extrinsically, namely with regard to that command of God by which it was administered by John. But it was not divine intrinsically and with regard to its own nature; rather, it was devoid of any power imparted to it.

It furnished. John’s Baptism therefore had no efficacy for producing anything supernatural in the soul, whereas Christ imparted to his Baptism the power to produce sanctifying grace and through it to abolish sins. John himself clearly indicated this difference between the two Baptisms in Mark 1:8, saying: “I have baptized you with water, but he shall baptize you with the Holy Spirit.”

[Col. 1173B]

It ministered beforehand. For just as John himself was merely the Forerunner of the Lord, preparing his way, Mark 1:2, so too John’s Baptism was merely a kind of precursor to Christ’s Baptism: through elicited acts of repentance it called people away from sins and disposed them toward a better life, but did not itself confer that life. Thus the author of *Twenty-two Responses to the Orthodox*, Response 2 to Question XXXVII, says: “John’s Baptism was the prelude to the Gospel of grace.” And St. Basil, *Homily 13, Exhortation to Baptism*, says: “John’s Baptism belonged to those being initiated; this one belongs to those being perfected. That one called away from sin; this one joins a person to God and makes him intimate with God.”

By power, or liberty, aided, namely, by the powers of grace.

To require. For faith, as the Council of Trent teaches in Session VI, *On Justification*, ch. [number absent in the source], is a certain disposition necessarily preceding repentance itself, as is explained there more fully. Thus, in Luke 7:29, “all the people hearing, and the publicans, justified God”—believing, namely, Christ as he so notably commended John’s qualities—“having been baptized with John’s Baptism.” And the Evangelist immediately continues: “But the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the counsel of God against themselves”—being unbelieving, namely, toward John as he preached a Baptism of repentance and toward Christ himself as he urged it so effectively—“not having been baptized by him.” Nor were they worthy of this Baptism of repentance, because they were destitute of faith, which they had so obstinately rejected.

[Col. 1173C]

Human. That is, a thing necessarily dependent on human choice and its free acts.

It is necessary. Equally human, namely, as he said above. See the note “By condition.” John’s Baptism therefore did no more than arouse repentance, by bestowing the helps of grace necessary for it; it did not itself efface sins. That had to be accomplished through an act of perfect repentance or contrition, as a work of the person acting.

If it had been heavenly. Just as Baptism conferred sanctifying grace itself and the remission of sins by a divine power intrinsic to itself—or, as we say, *ex opere operato*—as we have already said elsewhere.

God alone. This must indeed be understood of principal and authoritative power. Nevertheless, this power can also be communicated to human beings as instruments through whom sins are forgiven in Christ’s name and the Holy Spirit is conferred; and it is clear from John 20:22ff. that Christ communicated it to the Apostles, to their successors the bishops, and through these to priests. There Christ breathed upon the Apostles and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them,” etc.

[Col. 1173D–1174A]

Nevertheless, as St. Pacian says in Epistle 1 to Sympronianus: “What Christ does through his priests is his own power.” And in Epistle 3:

> What I do, I do not by my own right, but by the Lord’s; for we are God’s fellow workers. Therefore, whether we baptize, compel to repentance, or grant pardon to those who ask it, we administer this with Christ as its author.

These points had to be noted against our Protestants, who assert that priests possess no true power of forgiving sins, but merely a declaratory power regarding a remission already effected by God.

Would descend. “If I do not go away,” Christ says in John 16:7, “the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I shall send him to you.” Tertullian employs this testimony to prove that John’s Baptism could not yet confer the grace of the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit had not yet poured himself forth into the Church before Christ’s ascension into heaven. From this, quite a few even among our own maintain that neither did Baptism instituted by Christ possess the efficacy of conferring grace before the Passion and Resurrection—indeed, even before his Ascension. But more on this in the following chapter.

They had not even heard of him. In Acts 19:2ff., Paul says to his disciples: “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” But they said to him: “We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.” He said: “Into what, then, were you baptized?” They said: “Into John’s Baptism.” Paul then said: “John baptized the people with a Baptism of repentance,” etc.

[Col. 1174B]

From this it is easily inferred that John’s Baptism was not conferred in the name of the Holy Trinity; otherwise, they could not have been ignorant of the Holy Spirit, since they would previously have had to believe in him as the one through whose grace the remission of sins was to take place and sanctification be conferred upon the soul. These, therefore, were Ephesian Jews who had once been baptized by John in the Jordan and had meanwhile returned to Ephesus. Before Paul arrived there, they had heard nothing about Christ’s Baptism, hitherto conferred by the Apostles, nor about the laying on of hands—that is, the sacrament of Confirmation, which was then joined immediately to Baptism—nor about the gifts of the Holy Spirit accompanying it.

Paul clearly did not think John’s Baptism had sufficed for them, since through it they had not yet been initiated into Christ’s Church. Therefore Acts 19:5–6 adds: “When they had heard these things, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. And when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke with tongues and prophesied.” See, then, how much weaker John’s Baptism was than Christ’s.

The spirit of prophecy. For John was a prophet—indeed, as Christ told the crowds in Matthew 11:9, more than a prophet. See also ch. 21:26. For he prophesied, not—as the ancient prophets had—that Christ would come long afterward, but that he would come immediately after him.

The transfer. Namely, when Christ, baptized by John, saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him; Matthew 3:16.

[Col. 1174C]

To inquire. Namely, in Matthew 11:3, when John sent two of his disciples to Christ and said to him: “Are you he who is to come, or do we await another?” From this Tertullian believed that John later began to doubt whether Christ—whom he had so often and so openly proclaimed as the Messiah who was to come—was the true Messiah, even when Christ himself was exercising his ministry of preaching. Our Author sufficiently discloses this in *On Prescription*, ch. 8, and expresses it still more openly and at greater length in *Against Marcion* IV, ch. 18, where he says:

> While the Lord himself of powers, by the word and Spirit of the Father, was working and preaching upon earth, the portion of the Holy Spirit which, in accordance with the measure of the prophetic allotment, had operated in John in preparing the ways of the Lord, necessarily had now to withdraw from John, having been brought back—that is, recalled—into the Lord, as into the total sum of its mass, in whom, namely, the entire mass and fullness of grace resided.
