Accordingly, John was now an ordinary man, because, now left to himself by the prophetic spirit, he was now one of the crowd, etc.

[Col. 1174D–1175A]

Thus far, and further, Tertullian.

But other Fathers and interpreters more probably judge that John never doubted Christ. Rather, he sent his disciples—whom he had found reporting Christ’s miracles to him, yet perhaps still doubting his divinity—to question Christ, so that by his presence and by the miracles performed before them they might be fully convinced of his divinity. See also St. Ambrose on Luke, ch. 7, where he additionally offers mystical and allegorical meanings of that mission.

A candidate for remission. Among the Romans, those who aspired to public honors and went about among the individual tribes in the assemblies, soliciting votes for themselves, were called *candidati* from their white garment. Hence Tertullian says in *On Idolatry*, ch. 18: “Those who enjoyed familiarity with kings were called the kings’ ‘purple-clad men,’ just as among us candidates are so called from the white toga.”

This designation later began to be extended more widely, not because of similarity of dress but of office. Thus those who recited the prince’s letters and decrees in the senate were likewise called *candidati*, because this office gave them access to higher honors and to the magistracies themselves, as Ulpian teaches in the sole Law, §4, *Digest*, *On the Office of the Quaestor*. Likewise, younger men who were being trained in an apprenticeship and were shortly to leave adolescence were called *candidati*; in nearly this sense Quintilian, *Institutes*, Book V, calls them “candidates of eloquence.”

[Col. 1175B]

Accordingly, our Author also calls those people “candidates of the angels” in *On Prayer*, ch. 3, who have merited that heavenly utterance toward God and are learning the office of future glory, because such persons, according to Christ’s promise in Matthew 22:30, will be like God’s angels in heaven. Thus too in *To His Wife*, ch. 7, he calls one who is, as it were, undergoing an apprenticeship in the fear of God a “candidate of fear,” and elsewhere he has similar expressions. In the same way, therefore, our Author calls John’s Baptism a “candidate for remission,” because those initiated by it were prepared and disposed for Christ’s Baptism, through which full remission of sins takes place.

Moreover, in a worse sense, in *On the Crown*, ch. 7, he calls idolaters “candidates of the devil,” and in *On the Soul*, ch. 39, he calls certain offspring still in the mother’s womb “candidate progeny of demons.”

In Christ. Namely, in Christ’s Baptism.

It was declared. Namely, a remission that would occur not through the power of John’s Baptism itself, but through that of Christ’s Baptism which was afterward to follow; for this alone remitted sins *ex opere operato*, or by its own intrinsic power, as we have already said often elsewhere.

By the Spirit and fire. For thus John says in Luke 3:16: “I indeed baptize you with water; but one stronger than I shall come, and he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.” He certainly did not exclude water from Christ’s Baptism. John intended only to indicate that his washing was merely simple, performed outwardly with simple water, whereas in the future Baptism of Christ it would be elevated to a higher mystery and also to an interior washing of the soul, which cannot occur without the grace of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1175C]

But the question of what that Baptism “in the Holy Spirit and fire” (ἐν Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ καὶ πυρί) might be has exercised many and has even given some a serious occasion for error. For there were certain ancient heretics who thought that fire was to be understood simply and literally of our true elemental fire, and therefore that fire was to be employed in Baptism no less than water. Clement of Alexandria—or whoever else is the author of this writing—testifies thus in the *Prophetic Extracts*: ἔνιοι δὲ, ὥς φησιν Ἡρακλέων, πυρὶ τὰ ὦτα τῶν σφραγιζομένων κατεσημήνατο; that is: “Some, as Heracleon says, branded with fire the ears of those being sealed”—the baptized. The author of the poem *Against Marcion*, Book I, also records a certain fiery baptism of the heresiarch Valentinus, who “taught that one should be immersed twice, the body being passed through flame.”

St. Augustine too, in *On Heresies, to Quodvultdeus*, heresy 59, reports that the Seleucian heretics conferred Baptism by fire. Whatever the truth about these matters, it is certain that the Apostles never employed fire in Baptism, and therefore that it was by no means commanded by Christ; hence the Church has always abhorred this practice.

[Col. 1175D–1176A]

Accordingly, some Catholic interpreters judge more correctly that “in the Spirit and fire” denotes Christ’s own Baptism, upon which the Holy Spirit came in the form of a dove and at the same time—as St. Justin Martyr reports in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, p. 246 of my edition—κατελθόντος τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἐπὶ τὸ ὕδωρ, καὶ πῦρ ἀνήφθη ἐν τῷ Ἰορδάνῃ, that is: “When Jesus had descended into the water, fire was also kindled in the Jordan.”

But an invisible fire is also kindled in our Baptism, when the grace of the Holy Spirit flows into our hearts and, as St. Ambrose says in the final chapter of *On Elijah and Fasting*, consumes our sins and purifies the soul from their dross. Then there are those who, with St. Augustine on Psalm 65, understand it of the exorcisms customarily preceding our Baptism; for he says: “Why do unclean spirits so often cry out, ‘I burn,’ if that is not fire? But after the fire of exorcism one comes to Baptism.”

Others, with the author of the *Incomplete Work on Matthew*, Homily 3, take that Baptism of fire to designate, metaphorically, the tribulations and persecutions through which the constancy of the faithful righteous in faith and their patience in adversity are tested like gold in a furnace of fire. St. Basil, in his *Homily on Baptism*, maintains that this fire must be understood of the word of teaching, which both reproves the malice of sins and manifests the grace of justifications. These interpretations are sufficiently suitable, but only metaphorical.

Finally, our Tertullian explains it of the day of judgment and the infernal fire of the damned, as we shall see shortly.

[Col. 1176B]

Meanwhile I confess that I greatly prefer the opinion of those who understand it literally of the Holy Spirit’s visible descent in the form of fire, not only upon the Apostles but also upon their recently baptized disciples. A sufficiently brilliant and illustrious example of this occurs in Acts 11:15, where St. Peter says: “And when I had begun to speak, the Holy Spirit fell upon them, as also upon us at the beginning”—and thus also in the form of fire, just as he fell upon the Apostles on the day of Pentecost.

The best and entirely literal sense of St. John the Baptist’s words therefore seems to be this: “I indeed baptize you with water”—a barren element, namely, possessing no power of grace within itself—etc. “But he will baptize you”—not with water alone—“but in the Holy Spirit”—who makes the water of Baptism fruitful for the generation of grace—“and fire,” namely, with the graces of the Holy Spirit which will come upon you in fire through the laying on of hands.

This is that fiery Baptism which Christ himself foretold in Acts 1:5: “John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days hence.” And shortly afterward, v. 8: “You shall receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you,” etc.; and we know that this was fulfilled exactly ten days later, when the days of Pentecost were completed.

[Col. 1176C]

The faith of the water. That is, the faith which is directed toward water, or the Baptism of water, is stable, perseveres firmly, and perpetually bestows what is necessary for our salvation. Or: that water is faithful, keeping its promises, in the sense in which it was said in Isaiah 33:16: “His waters are faithful.” Or, finally, the sense is: only that faith is true and sincere in which we are washed unto salvation, etc.; but a feigned and unstable faith—one that is not serious and will soon be abandoned again—is immersed unto judgment.

Unto judgment. Tertullian seems to have drawn the sense of the text explained at greater length above from St. Paul, 1 Corinthians 3:13ff.:

> The work of each shall be made manifest; for the day of the Lord shall declare it, because it shall be revealed in fire; and the fire shall test what kind of work each has done. If anyone’s work remains—he shall receive a reward; if anyone’s work is burned, he shall suffer loss; but he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire.

The same thing had been foretold by Isaiah 4:4: “The Lord shall wash away the filth of the daughters of Zion—in the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning,” or fire. On this passage St. Basil says: “John’s Baptism was a cleansing of filth, but this is regeneration itself through the Holy Spirit; that testing, however, takes place through the fire of judgment.” And in *On the Holy Spirit, to Amphilochius*, ch. 35, he says: “The Baptism of fire is that testing which shall take place at the judgment.”

[Col. 1176D–1177A]

## Notes on Chapter XI

As though in fact. My edition has *because*, certainly with an obscure and corrupt sense; I therefore preferred to restore *as though* from other editions, so that the sentence instead expresses irony.

Had preached. When John said of Christ in Matthew 3:11, “He shall baptize you,” etc., he by no means added “by himself” or “with his own hands.”

He posted, that is, promulgated it or affixed it to the doors of the senate-house, etc. Its sense is surely that he ordered or caused it to be promulgated or affixed—namely, through another.

He is said to do it. According to that common rule of the jurists: “What anyone does through another is deemed to be done by himself.”

[Col. 1177B]

Moreover, *is ministered beforehand* is used by our Author in the same sense in which, in *On Prayer*, ch. 1, he called John Christ’s *pre-minister*, as one going before or ministering in advance. Apuleius likewise, in his *Apology*, called the tongue the pre-minister of lies and bitterness.

Through him. Namely, in his name and by his authority.

Into him. That is, into his power and name, so that you pass into Christ’s name and are henceforth to be called Christians. Thus St. Paul says in Galatians 3:27ff.: “As many of you as have been baptized in Christ”—in Greek, εἰς Χριστόν, “into Christ”—“have put on Christ. … For you are all one in Christ Jesus.” See further discussion in St. Basil’s cited *Homily on Baptism*.

He himself did not immerse. Nevertheless, there are Fathers who plausibly suppose that the Apostles—or at least their chief, Peter—were baptized by Christ’s own hand. Thus St. Augustine, in that very elegant Epistle 108 (now 265) to Seleuciana, *On the Baptism and Repentance of Peter*, says:

> Nor did he fail to perform the ministry of baptizing, so that he might have baptized servants through whom he would baptize others: he who did not fail to perform that memorable ministry of humility when he washed their feet and, when Peter asked that he wash not only his feet but also his hands and head, replied: “He who is washed has no need,” etc.

The entire epistle certainly deserves to be read on this subject.

[Col. 1177C]

He bestowed it by a word. For he absolved the paralytic in Matthew 9:2 and the woman in Luke 7:[48] with no other outward rite, but only with a few simple words, saying: “Your sins are forgiven you.”

He concealed it through humility. Thus, when Christ spoke directly of himself, he never openly called himself the Son of God but “the Son of Man,” as in Matthew 8:20, ch. 9:6, and frequently elsewhere. Hence, when in Luke 4:41 demons came out of many people, crying out and saying, “You are the Son of God,” he rebuked them and did not permit them to speak. And in John 8:54 he said: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing.”

They had built. For this was first built by the Apostles after they received the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost, when, after Peter’s first preaching, “those who received his word were baptized; and about three thousand souls were added on that day”; Acts 2:41.

With John’s Baptism. Tertullian was therefore of the opinion that before the Passion and Resurrection the Apostles administered only John’s Baptism, while Christ’s Baptism was first instituted afterward, as he affirms more explicitly a little later.

There were certainly Holy Fathers who followed this opinion of Tertullian, especially St. Chrysostom, Homily 28 on chapter 3 of St. John’s Gospel, and likewise St. Leo the Great, who writes in Epistle 4 to the bishops of Sicily:

> The Lord Jesus Christ himself, after he had risen from the dead, gave his disciples—in whom all the prelates of the Churches were being instructed—both the formula and the power of baptizing, saying: “Go, teach all nations,” etc. He could certainly have instructed them about this even before the Passion, had he not wished it to be properly understood that the grace of regeneration began from his Resurrection.

[Col. 1177D–1178A]

Some theologians afterward followed this opinion, and the Most Illustrious Melchior Cano, *On Theological Topics* VIII, ch. 5, strongly inclines toward it.

But St. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* III, q. 66, a. 2, teaches the contrary, following his Augustine, who speaks thus in the cited epistle to Seleuciana:

> Christ baptized, not by himself but through his disciples, whom we understand to have already been baptized, whether with John’s Baptism or, as is more credible, with Christ’s Baptism.

Augustine also affirms the latter absolutely in Tractates 5 and 13 on John and in *On the Origin of the Soul* III, ch. 9. If, therefore, the Apostles had received Christ’s Baptism while Christ was still alive, there is no doubt that they thereafter washed others only with that same Baptism. He judges, then, that the Apostles administered to their own people, even before the Passion, this Baptism of Christ which they had received.

Nor furnished. That is, while the washing with water had not yet been furnished with its own efficacy and power of washing away sins through baptismal grace.

The Resurrection. For Baptism was instituted by Christ to serve as a memorial of his Passion and Resurrection, as we shall immediately confirm.

Without his Resurrection. Thus the Apostle says in Romans 6:3ff.:

> Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized were baptized into his death? For we were buried together with him through Baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life, etc.

See also Colossians 2:12ff. Hence Christ says of himself in John 11:25: “I am the Resurrection and the Life.” For us, certainly, he was the resurrection from the death of sin to the life of grace.

[Col. 1178B]

On this subject it is also worthwhile to hear St. Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit* I, ch. 6, arguing so elegantly:

> In that element of the waters we are buried, so that, renewed through the Spirit, we may rise again. For in the water is the image of death, and in the Spirit is the pledge of life, so that the body dies through the water, which encloses the body as though in a kind of tomb, and through the power of the Spirit we are renewed from the death of sin.

See further discussion there.

## Notes on Chapter XII

Except Paul. He is recorded as having been baptized by Ananias in Acts 9:18. We do not find this disclosed in Holy Scripture concerning the other Apostles. Nevertheless, see what we said in the preceding chapter, note “They had built.”

Has put on. For already in the preceding chapter, note “With John’s Baptism,” our Author had taught that the other Apostles baptized not with Christ’s Baptism but only with John’s; consequently, they too could have received only John’s Baptism.

Concerning the danger to the others. The passage seems rather obscure to me, but it may perhaps be somewhat clarified from 1 Timothy 5:21, where the Apostle says:

> I testify before God … that you observe these things “without prejudgment” (χωρὶς προκρίματος), doing nothing “by inclining toward one side” (κατὰ πρόσκλησιν).

Πρόσκλησις properly means advocacy, by which one side is assisted more than another, as occurs in partiality.

[Col. 1178C–D]

It must not be concealed, however, that in many manuscripts, according to Calmet, the reading is πρόσκλισιν, which properly means an inclination or propensity, especially of the mind, and is equally pertinent to our subject. For the passage seems capable of being understood in precisely this sense: the other Apostles were exempted from that common law by a certain antecedent judgment and a singular propensity and favor of mind, so that thereafter their salvation would not be endangered by the absence and lack of Baptism. Thus the prescription, or law, concerning Baptism in John 3:5 never affected the Apostles, since they had already been exempted by God, but thereafter remained immovable only with respect to others.

Yet what need is there for so elaborate a circumlocution? Why might *prejudged* not rather be understood as “foreguarded,” that is, protected by some singular privilege against the danger to salvation?

Be rescinded. That is, for that law to be invalidated and revoked.

It has been established. The force of the entire argument raised against Baptism therefore seems to be this: if the Apostles did not receive Baptism and nevertheless attained salvation, then either they must have been specially exempted by Christ—though we read nowhere in the Gospel of such an exemption—or the gate of salvation also lies open to others who are unbaptized, and thus that law concerning the reception of Baptism possesses no binding force.

[Col. 1179A]

Such. Namely, the people who had devised this argument to overthrow the necessity of Baptism.

The wantonness of my pen, that is, that I should spontaneously devise such arguments, as though from the insolence of an innovating mind.

For one willing to be washed. For I greatly prefer this reading to “unwilling,” which my codex has; for although at first he had refused, doubtless as being unworthy, yet soon afterward he assented all the more readily.

They were destined. For after the Resurrection Christ was going to command the Apostles: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them,” etc. But Christ’s Baptism was the gateway to the Church, and a nearer and more [Col. 1179B] direct way to salvation than John’s baptism.

He was baptized. And indeed with John’s baptism, which in others was nothing but a baptism of repentance unto the remission of sins (Mark 1:4); but now, through Christ its institutor, it was being elevated to the character of a Sacrament, as our theologians more commonly hold.

It was not necessary. For it should not be said that the Apostles—being, of course, human beings—were at that time free from every sin that could be washed away through Baptism, and hence that they were not themselves subjects for the baptism of repentance.

Rivals [Aemuli], i.e., adversaries, enemies, or the envious, whom shortly afterward he calls those opposing the Lord. Thus also Our Author, in the *Apology*, ch. 21, speaks of fables as “rivals bent upon the destruction of the truth”; and similarly elsewhere quite often. It is established, however, that in other places this word is also taken in a favorable sense, for zealous imitators.

It is suggested, i.e., an argument is supplied—namely, one taught from the contrary, almost as though, according to Jesus Christ’s formulation, “the exception confirms the rule in [Col. 1179C] the contrary case.”

The discipline of religion, i.e., according to the discipline, rite, or ordinance of Religion. To discipline, moreover, belong all things ordained for common observance in the worship of God, whether by human beings appointed to govern the Church or by God himself; although those things that are only of human ordinance are called matters of mere discipline. And although in Tertullian elsewhere *disciplina* also means doctrine, nevertheless, in the stricter sense, that which proceeds from one who teaches seems to be called doctrine, while that doctrine, once received by learners and formed into their conduct, is called discipline.

Through patience. That is, the forbearance and permission by which he endures, or allows, these things to occur. In this sense Cicero says in the eighth action against Verres: “I shall not bear it, I shall not endure it, I shall not permit it”; and in Book I of *On Duties* he speaks of those who allow the people whom they ought to protect to be abandoned.

At the last. This is a Hellenism; for the Greeks customarily say ἐπ’ ἐσχάτων, “at the last,” which Latin writers commonly express by *tandem*, *ultimato*, or *denique*: “at length,” “finally,” or “lastly.” [Col. 1179D]

Provided only that it refers. For in John 13:10 Christ said to Peter: “He who has been WASHED needs only to wash his feet”; perhaps showing that we need only one washing of the body, or baptism, and that Baptism, once received, cannot afterward be repeated.

To deem. He seems here to use the verb *aestimare* in the sense of judging or deciding—as though it would be rash to make any unfavorable judgment concerning the salvation of the Apostles, even if perhaps they had not received Baptism.

Of enrollment. Or, of admission into the Apostolate.

A compendium of Baptism. That is, that singular prerogative would serve them in place of Baptism and, as by a compendium and shorter way, would supply it in advance.

Could confer. Junius judges that this entire passage was astonishingly mangled by an unskilled scribe through an inept transposition of words, and that it should accordingly be restored thus: “And thence the prerogative of inseparable familiarity WITH HIM [CUM ILLO] [Col. 1180A] could confer a compendium of Baptism. I suppose they followed him,” etc. Although I do not think this remedy for the passage should be rejected at all, I nevertheless think the received reading can also be sustained, so that the sense of the new sentence is: “With that”—namely, with that compendious supplement for Baptism—“they followed him,” etc.

Made whole. For he had used these words to the woman whom he delivered from the issue of blood, Matthew 9:22: “Take heart, daughter; your FAITH has made you whole.” He also addressed them to the Samaritan cleansed of leprosy, Luke 17:19, and shortly afterward, in ch. 18:42, to the blind man of Jericho whose sight he restored. And these obtained through that most living faith not merely bodily health, but far more the salvation of the soul—a faith to which salvation had already elsewhere and repeatedly been promised by Christ, as in John 3:16: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.” And in the same place, v. 36: “He who believes in the Son of Man has eternal life.” Nor is this surprising, since salvation had also been promised to Christ’s Baptism only when received [Col. 1180B] with faith: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe”—even if already baptized—“shall be condemned.”

Yet not baptized. For nowhere do we read that they had previously been baptized by Christ or by the Apostles.

Whose faith. That is, in what other persons, or among what others, faith is to be required. He immediately adds examples.

Raised up. Junius reads: “He who by one word,” etc. And indeed the context seems to require that the little word “who” at least be understood, in this way: “He who was raised up by one word of the Lord,” etc.

The tax booth. Τελώνιον, or, as Suidas has it, τελωνεῖον, strictly taken, is the place ἐν ᾧ, as he says, καθέζεται ὁ τελώνης, “in which the tax collector sits.” The latter, or *telonarius*, is so called ἀπὸ τοῦ τέλους—because among the Greeks τέλος sometimes also means a tax or tribute—and from ὠνεῖν, which among them means “to buy.” For in those times they generally held the taxes by purchasing the right to collect them for an annual payment; hence they were properly called τελῶναι, “purchasers of taxes,” [Col. 1180C] and among the Romans *publicani*, as persons charged with public money—money, namely, to be paid into the public treasury or farmed from it—or collectors acting under such officials. This latter class of men, because of their importunity and greed and the very wicked practices associated with them, was hated almost everywhere, but especially by the Jews, who more than others considered themselves freeborn and born for liberty, crying out against Christ himself in John 8:33: “We are Abraham’s seed; we have never served anyone.” Hence tax collectors or publicans of this kind were regarded as public sinners, indeed as heathens, from whose fellowship one ought likewise to abstain. Hence the Pharisees rose up against Christ and his disciples, Matthew 9:11, saying: “Why does your Teacher eat with publicans and sinners?” And in the same Evangelist, ch. 18:17, Christ himself, speaking to his disciples about fraternal correction, says: “If he will not hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a publican.”

Father. He alludes here to Peter and Andrew, to whom [Col. 1180D] Christ said: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men.” And they immediately left their nets and followed him, Matthew 4:20. Most especially, when he called James and John, they immediately left their nets and their father and followed him, ibid., v. 22. Indeed, they had also left their mother, who afterward, in Matthew 20:20, was so deeply concerned on their behalf about securing primacy in the kingdom of heaven.

He disregarded. Clement of Alexandria, in Book III of the *Stromata*, believed this to have been St. Philip the Apostle, who, when the Lord called him in Matthew 8:21–22, said: “Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father.” But Jesus said to him: “FOLLOW ME, and leave the dead to bury their dead.” Yet what prevents us from appending here that entire passage of Tertullian from *On Idolatry*, ch. 12, which also agrees with the examples cited above? “Even then,” he says, “it was demonstrated to us that pledges, crafts, and occupations must be abandoned for the Lord’s sake: when James and [Col. 1181A] John, called by the Lord, leave both father and boat; when Matthew is raised from the tax booth; when even burying one’s father was too slow for faith.” I promise, moreover, that one will not regret reading this entire chapter.

Which he heard. For the earlier calling of the disciple had already occurred previously—namely, Matthew 8:21—whereas only afterward, in Matthew 10:37, was this saying, “He who … father,” etc., pronounced by Christ.

## Notes on Chapter XIII

They provoke, i.e., stir up or draw forth.

Unless. “But only if” would be clearer.

Pleased. “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness,” Genesis 15:6. Upon these very words the Apostle says at Galatians 3:6: “Know, therefore, that those who are of faith are the sons of Abraham,” etc., etc. This faith, however, was certainly not a Sacrament in the proper sense.

They prevail. This is in the nature of a reply to the argument raised. It rests on the commonly received rule of law: “Later provisions derogate from earlier ones.”

[Col. 1181B] Enlarged, i.e., amplified and extended more widely, namely to more objects.

And his Resurrection. Namely, as things no longer future, but already past.

Sacrament, i.e., mystery, or mystery of faith.

The sealing of Baptism. For by Our Author himself, in *On the Shows*, ch. 24, it is called the “SEAL OF FAITH.” And in *On Repentance*, ch. 6, he says: “That washing is the sealing of faith”; and thus faith is reciprocally the sealing of Baptism. For, as St. Basil says in *On the Holy Spirit to Amphilochius*, ch. 12: “Faith is perfected through Baptism, while Baptism rests upon the foundation of faith,” etc. And in Book III *On the Holy Spirit against Eunomius*, he also calls Baptism the “SEAL OF FAITH.”

A certain garment of faith. Thus St. Gregory Nazianzen, in Oration 40, *On Baptism*, calls this Sacrament ἀφθαρσίας ἔνδυμα, “the garment of incorruption,” and, as he says a little afterward, αἰσχύνης κάλυμμα, “a covering of shame.” St. Cyril of Jerusalem also calls it a white garment, both because of the whiteness it imparts to the soul when the soot of sins has been wiped away [Col. 1181C], and because of the rite by which the baptized were immediately clothed in a white garment, which they were to wear for a fixed period. Even now the Rituals prescribe this in a certain manner both in the Baptism of infants and in that of adults, and the custom is still retained in the Church.

Previously. That is, before, namely in the Old Testament.

Bare. For that faith of the Old Law was in itself bare, empty, and void, and destitute of all intrinsic power for eternal salvation.

Power, i.e., force and efficacy.

Without its law. Namely, before that Old Law was fulfilled by the new Law of Christ.

Into the name. Matthew 28:19, where the Greek text reads altogether explicitly εἰς τὸ ὄνομα, “into the name,” while the Vulgate has “in the name.” It is well known, however, that among the Greeks εἰς is sometimes used for ἐν, as in Aeschines: εἰς τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καθέζομαι, “I sit in the assembly”; and no less so in Demosthenes and Xenophon. In this sense, therefore, our Vulgate [Col. 1181D] Translator understood εἰς τὸ ὄνομα, and theologians and interpreters generally have followed him.

It might, however, be asked here whether a Baptism conferred with this formula would be valid: “I baptize you into the name of the Father,” etc. I answer that it could at least appear doubtful, and therefore that, without grave sin—since the matter is likewise grave—the words “in the name” cannot be changed to “into the name”; hence such a Baptism should at least be repeated conditionally.

Some, however, think that an error lies hidden here, and that in other copies ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι, “in the name,” is actually found, so that the entire difficulty disappears of itself. Moreover, that law of Baptism was imposed by Christ not only upon the Apostles, that they should administer it, but also upon the nations, that they should receive it, Mark, last chapter, v. 16, in these words: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved”—the sense being that in the New Law salvation can be obtained in no other way than through Baptism.

## Notes on Chapter XIV

[Col. 1182A]

The household of Stephanas. For shortly beforehand he had said: “I give thanks to GOD that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius. I also baptized the household of Stephanas,” 1 Corinthians 1:14, 16. This Stephanas had been among the disciples of St. Paul.

He assigns, i.e., he ascribes his Baptism to him as though to its author or bestower. In nearly this sense he says in *Exhortation to Chastity*, ch. 16: “It was the old dispensation, which is assigned to the Gospel.” And Solinus: “Because of the odd-numbered days, January is allotted to the gods above; February, as being ominous, is allotted to the gods below.”

Apollo. Since some in the Corinthian Church had been baptized by Paul, others by Peter, and others by Apollo, a dispute and something like a schism had arisen among them, while some preferred their baptism to that of others as having been given by a more eminent minister. They said: “I indeed am of Paul; but I of Apollo; and I of Cephas; and I of Christ,” 1 Corinthians 1:12. But Paul reproved them all rather sharply, insisting that the efficacy of Baptism should be ascribed not to its ministers, [Col. 1182B] but to Christ alone as its sole author and institutor: “Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” And he presses these points much more forcefully in ch. 3:4ff.

Moreover, this Apollo—as he is described in Acts 18:24ff.—was a certain Jew, an Alexandrian by birth, an eloquent man and mighty in the Scriptures. Although he had not yet been initiated into Christ, but only with John’s baptism, nevertheless, being fervent in spirit, “he spoke and carefully taught the things concerning Jesus”; afterward Aquila and Priscilla explained to him the way of the Lord more carefully (Acts 18:25–26), and probably also initiated him with Christ’s Baptism. Accordingly, when he subsequently proceeded into Achaia and Corinth (ibid., v. 27, and ch. 19:1), and there joined many to the Church through Baptism, some of the Corinthians used this occasion to contend more zealously for his glory than was proper. This so displeased Apollo himself that, offended by it, he instead withdrew [Col. 1182C] to Crete with Zenas the lawyer, as St. Jerome testifies in his commentary on the Epistle to Titus, ch. 3; nor would he return until the dissenting Corinthians had been reconciled with one another. He is believed afterward to have been appointed their bishop, although others maintain that he became bishop of Caesarea, Iconium, Dura, or elsewhere.

Moreover, this name *Apollo* is not the same as that of the god Apollo. For the latter in Greek is Ἀπόλλων, ωνος, of the fifth declension, while the former is Ἀπολλώς—as it is written in the Greek copies—of the fourth Attic declension, whose genitive is Ἀπολλώ. Indeed, in the accusative too it is found retaining the same ending in Acts 19:1: Ἐγένετο δὲ ἐν τῷ τὸν Ἀπολλὼ εἶναι ἐν Κορίνθῳ, “And it happened while Apollo was at Corinth”; and Titus 3:13: Ζηνᾶν τὸν νομικὸν καὶ Ἀπολλὼ σπουδαίως πρόπεμψον, “Diligently send forward Zenas the lawyer and Apollo.” Or perhaps it was altogether indeclinable.

Peaceable. For his correction had the sole purpose of restoring peace and concord of mind among the Corinthians.

[Col. 1182D] To defend. Here it is readily taken to mean “to vindicate” or “to attribute.” It can also be explained as meaning “to defend himself and his own cause”; lest, therefore, he might appear to be doing this, he gives thanks to God that he baptized no one. See above, the note “The household of Stephanas.”

To baptize. For in Matthew, last chapter, v. 19, Christ himself commanded the Apostles: “Go therefore and TEACH all nations, BAPTIZING,” etc. And in Mark, last chapter, v. 15: “PREACH the Gospel to every creature. He who believes and is BAPTIZED,” etc. Teaching is therefore prior in the dignity and authority of institution, and baptizing subsequent; in other respects, however, Baptism has the greater excellence, as being that for which preaching itself serves solely as preparation.

## Notes on Chapter XV

Is discussed, i.e., whether anything further can be raised against Baptism, beyond those questions, namely, which we have already debated and examined.

I shall resume. *Retexere* here does not mean to undo a weaving again, as we read that Penelope formerly used to do, but to weave again or continue weaving—that is, to proceed in a matter once begun [Col. 1183A] and interrupted for a time.

I omitted. I think this refers to ch. 12, where he had begun to speak about the unity of Baptism. There he omitted, or interrupted, it, in the sense in which Horace said in the *Art of Poetry*:

> Let him defer most things and omit them for the present.

To cut through. That is, lest I should entirely separate the thoughts close at hand, or what remained to be said, and thus break off the whole web, as though cutting through it.

Baptism. Just as the Greeks say τὸ βάπτισμα, so certain Latin writers—not only our Tertullian, but also St. Ambrose throughout—customarily say *Baptismum, -mi* in the neuter gender.

One Church in heaven. He doubtless alludes to what the Apostle says in Ephesians 4:5: “One LORD, one FAITH, one BAPTISM.” For, as the same Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 12:13, “in ONE SPIRIT we were all baptized into ONE BODY.” Hence Clement [Col. 1183B] of Alexandria also says in Book IV of the *Stromata*, p. 326 of my edition: “The Lord washes believers through one Baptism into a wholly perfect communion, he who also comprehends the many baptisms of Moses in one Baptism.”

Our Author has, however, used a certain transposition of words here, mentioning Baptism in the second place and Faith in the third. Faith he seems to denote through the Church, of which the former is, as it were, the soul, while the latter is the proper seat of true Faith and Religion.

Nor is it surprising that he spoke of the Church “in heaven,” since throughout the Gospels it is called the Kingdom of heaven, as in Matthew 13:44: “The Kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed,” etc., etc.; and v. 31: “The Kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed,” etc. And so repeatedly in the same chapter, where it is certain that our Church is designated: ordained by God in heaven from eternity, planted by Christ on earth, united in the unity of Baptism, and finally consummated in heaven through vision and the love of fruition.

[Col. 1183C] For it was issued to us. Some understand it thus: “For that saying of Holy Scripture”—namely, about the Unity of Baptism, as immediately above—“was directed to us,” or has reference to us, Christ’s faithful.

Of communion. From this passage alone it is evident that the custom of abstaining from communion with heretics is most ancient in the Church. Add also *On Prescription*, ch. 30.

Us and them. He here lashes Cerdon, Marcion, Apelles, Hermogenes, and others of the same bran, who produced from their deranged brains two Gods—or indeed, as Valentinus did, a whole swarm of them. See *On Prescription*, chs. 7, 30, 33, and 40 at the end, and throughout the Appendix, ch. 49.

That is, the same. Here he attacks Valentinus in particular, who most impiously asserted that Christ was brought forth from the Demiurge and Sophia. See again *On Prescription*, ch. 7.

They do not possess. There are indeed some who strive to clear Tertullian here of every stain of error, as though he had spoken only of those heretics who adulterated the [Col. 1183D] legitimate form of Baptism, such as the Gnostics, Marcites, Cataphrygians, and others in Tertullian’s time. But it is clear that he speaks of heretics universally, and he confirms the same thing in *On Modesty*, ch. 19: “Among us,” he says, “the heretic, being equal to a heathen—indeed worse than a heathen—is admitted through the Baptism of truth,” that is, true Baptism, “after being cleansed of both persons,” namely, of that heathen and of the superimposed heretic—admitted, that is, to the Church.

It remains, therefore, that Tertullian erred seriously in the passage before us; nor does his argument establish its conclusion. For although those heretics discussed above erred monstrously concerning God and Christ, nevertheless, so long as they did not err in administering the Sacrament itself, but employed the same matter and form that our true Christ instituted in his true Church, this was the same Baptism, consisting of the same essential parts, as we call them, [Col. 1184A] and having the same Author. Our Baptism can therefore be conferred even outside our Church, if it is conferred duly and in the same manner as in our Church. For, as St. Augustine reasons in Book V *Against the Donatists*, ch. 26: “Just as it is said, ‘One Church, One Baptism,’ so it is said, ‘One Hope.’” The holy Doctor has in view Ephesians 4:1: “One body and One Spirit, as you were called in the One Hope of your calling,” and what immediately follows: “One Lord, One faith, One Baptism,” etc. “And yet,” he continues, “those who did not have One Hope possessed One Baptism; for how did those who said, ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die,’ asserting that there was no resurrection of the dead, have One Hope with the holy and the righteous?”

Therefore, those who do not have one faith and are not in one Church with us can nevertheless possess and confer one Baptism. For Baptism is the gateway and door of the Church, through which alone entrance into it lies open; it is therefore given to a person not because he already is, but so that he may be, in the Church. Just as a wicked minister of Baptism [Col. 1184B] does not have grace in himself and yet confers it upon another through Baptism, so too a heretic, even if perhaps he himself has not validly received Baptism, can nevertheless confer it validly upon another, open for him that door of the Church, and admit the other through it, while himself remaining outside the door. But we shall speak more conveniently and precisely about this matter in its proper place.

Meanwhile, however, what has been said makes it evident that the contrary opinion arose in the Church of Carthage as the second century was drawing to its close, and was afterward adopted by Agrippinus, its bishop, and much more forcefully confirmed by St. Cyprian. The history of those times is full of this matter, which our dogmatic theologians customarily present at greater length.

Yet a new doubt arises here: whether Agrippinus derived this error from Tertullian, or Tertullian from Agrippinus, for it is established that they were contemporaries. Although this matter cannot be defined with sufficient clarity amid such uncertainty about when Agrippinus began his episcopate, [Col. 1184C] we nevertheless judge it more probable that Tertullian was led into this opinion by Agrippinus, and consequently that Agrippinus was the first author of that error in Africa known to us.

Indeed, first, Vincent of Lérins, a writer of the fifth century, expressly testifies concerning Agrippinus in ch. 9 of his *Commonitorium* in these words: “First of all mortals”—in Africa, I understand, for it is established that the custom of rebaptizing heretics had already flourished in the East long before—“contrary to the divine Canon,” etc., “he judged that they should be rebaptized.”

Secondly, St. Cyprian also, in his Letter to Jubaianus, mentions Agrippinus as the very first: “Among us,” he says, “it is not a new and sudden practice to judge that those who come from the heretics to the Church should be baptized, since many years and a long age have now passed from the time when very many bishops, assembling together under Agrippinus, decreed this,” etc.

Thirdly, St. Augustine, speaking in Book II *On Baptism*, ch. 7, about the ancient custom of the Churches, says: “It is more truly believed to have begun to be corrupted through Agrippinus than to have been corrected.” But this corruption should instead have been imputed [Col. 1184D] to Tertullian if he had publicized this error before Agrippinus.

Fourthly and finally, Tertullian himself, at the very beginning of this chapter, sufficiently signifies by the words “for it was issued to us” that he had received this as something established by a solemn decree in the African Churches, and consequently had not invented it by his own ingenuity.

Others object, however, that since Tertullian wrote his book *On Baptism* while still a Catholic and, as we said in the *Critical Questions on On Prescription*, Question VII, around A.D. 197—when perhaps Agrippinus had not yet been appointed to the see of Carthage—and since the persecution begun against the Christians in 202 continued nearly until 213, a council certainly could not have been celebrated before that year—because during the persecution public assemblies of Christians had been prohibited with extreme severity by imperial edict—and hence only about eighteen years after the publication of the book *On Baptism*, when peace had finally been restored to the Church.

[Col. 1185A] Yet what prevents us, amid such uncertainty concerning the African bishops, from assigning the beginning of Agrippinus’s episcopate and the Council itself under Agrippinus before the year 196 [text uncertain: printed “166”]? This certainly seems more consistent with Cyprian’s testimony cited above. For in the Letter to Jubaianus already cited, he expressly testifies that “many years” and “a long age” had passed since the bishops assembled under Agrippinus, etc. But if this Council was held only after the persecution, namely in the year 215, [Col. 1186A] and that Letter was written only in 256, not very many years—only forty-one—and consequently not a long age, would have elapsed since that Council of Carthage under Agrippinus. But if we place this same Council in A.D. 194, it will be at least sixty-two years removed from the time when Cyprian wrote, a span that can finally constitute an age. It is better, however, to bring the whole matter, according to Pagi’s chronology—which we already adopted elsewhere in *On Prescription*—under a single view.

[Col. 1185B] You see, therefore, benevolent Reader, that in this system Agrippinus is neither placed too close to Cyprian nor removed an unduly great distance from him, and that the intervening interval could readily have been filled by Donatus, the intermediate bishop—perhaps, moreover, one or two others intervened as well.

Finally, just as this error brought no stain upon St. Cyprian and Agrippinus, so neither did it upon Tertullian, since the dogma that heretics should not be rebaptized had not yet been defined by the Church. Indeed, other Fathers distinguished by holiness of life also thought that this matter pertained solely to the discipline of the Church. Hence, even after the deaths of St. Stephen the Pontiff and St. Cyprian, this opinion and practice of rebaptizing heretics, or those coming from heresy to the Church, did not immediately fall into disuse; nor even after the First Council of Arles, held in 315, and the Council of Nicaea, celebrated in 325—although one or the other of these is believed to have been that plenary Council at which St. Augustine says, in Book I *On Baptism*, ch. 7 and elsewhere, that this controversy was fully settled. For even [Col. 1185C] St. Basil, who died only in 379, left the matter free to each Church, while himself still following the practice of the rebaptizers in his own Church, as Tournely admits in his *Treatise on the Sacraments in General*, q. 7, art. 2, p. 100 of my edition and following. But we shall deal with this matter elsewhere in due course.

In Greek. There can be no doubt that Tertullian was also highly proficient in the Greek language, and that he had previously written another book on Baptism in that language, in which he dealt chiefly with Baptism invalidly received from heretics and therefore to be repeated when they wished to come to our Church. Moreover, in *On the Soldier’s Crown*, ch. 6, he testifies that he had also treated the subject of the shows in Greek for the sake of those fond of spectacles; and immediately at the beginning of the book *On the Veiling of Virgins*, he clearly intimates that he had already treated this very argument in Greek. It is regrettable, however, that these and his other Greek works, long since consumed by age, have perished. [Col. 1186B]

Sins are washed away. Through Baptism, namely; sins committed afterward, however, must certainly be washed away by the tears of Repentance.

Jewish Israel. ISRAEL, as Our Author interprets it in Book IV *Against Marcion*, ch. 39, means “growing strong with God,” or, according to others, as though “he has prevailed over God.” The context of Genesis 32:28 itself also agrees very well, where the Angel says to Jacob: “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but () ISRAEL; because if () YOU HAVE BEEN STRONG, or have prevailed, () [Col. 1186C] AGAINST GOD, how much more shall you prevail against men!”

He is defiled. Innumerable washings were prescribed for the Jews in both Exodus and Leviticus, each of which it would certainly be superfluous labor to enumerate. Yet all these washings were of themselves powerless to cleanse the soul; they remedied only legal and bodily stains and impurities. They also had many other washings derived from the emptiest traditions and customarily observed even to the point of ostentation, as stated in Mark 7:3ff.: “The Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat unless they have frequently washed their hands, holding the tradition of the elders; and when they come from the marketplace, unless they are baptized, they do not eat; and there are many other things handed down to them to observe, the baptisms of cups and pitchers,” etc. Against these, therefore, Christ himself inveighs in the same place, v. 6: “Isaiah rightly prophesied about you hypocrites, as it is written: This people honors me with its lips, but its heart is far from me. . . . For leaving the commandment of God, you hold the tradition of men, the baptisms of pitchers and cups,” etc.

But in Hebrews 9:9ff., the Apostle, speaking of the old tabernacle and the gifts and sacrifices offered in it, says: “These cannot perfect the worshiper according to conscience, consisting only in foods and drinks, and various baptisms and ordinances of the flesh,” etc. [Col. 1187A]

Which does not make sport of sinners. The sense appears to be: which does not mock sinners with an ineffectual result, namely by disappointing those who place their hope in it and deservedly exposing them to ridicule, as happened through those sordid washings of the Pharisees.

It defiles. Superstitious washings of this kind washed the body, but at the same time infected the soul with a new stain, hypocrisy. [Col. 1187B] See the note “He is defiled.”

## Notes on Chapter XVI

One and the same. For it cannot be repeated.

To be baptized with a baptism. Luke 12:50, where he speaks of his impending Passion, which in Mark 10:38 he also designates by the name of Baptism, saying thus to the sons of Zebedee: “Can you drink the cup that I am to drink, or be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?”

He wrote. 1 John 5:6: “This is he who came by WATER and BLOOD, Jesus Christ; not in Water only, but in WATER and BLOOD.” Here some codices have δι’ ὕδατος, καὶ αἵματος, καὶ πνεύματος, i.e., “through water and blood and Spirit.” Others judge this last word superfluous and rightly omitted, because there immediately follows: “And it is the Spirit who testifies, because Christ is the Truth. For there are Three who bear testimony in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these Three are One. And there are three who bear testimony on earth: [Col. 1187C] the Spirit, the Water, and the Blood; and these three are one.”

Might be glorified. For thus St. Peter, reproaching the Jews for their faithlessness in Acts 3:13, says: “God glorified his Son Jesus, whom you delivered up . . . and you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead,” etc. Those words that St. Ambrose summarized so elegantly in his *Commentary on Luke*, ch. 22, accord wonderfully with these: “There are three witnesses, Water, Blood, and Spirit: Water for the washing; Blood for the price; Spirit for the resurrection.” Likewise, in Book I *On the Holy Spirit*, ch. 6: “Water is the witness of burial; Blood is the witness of death; Spirit is the witness of life.”

He doubtless drew these statements from the Apostle himself, who speaks thus in Romans 6:4: “For we were buried with him through Baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead, we too might walk in newness of life.” And in Colossians 2:12 he addresses his Colossians thus: “You were buried together in Baptism, in which you also rose again through faith in the operation of God, who raised him from the dead.” Thus it was only after his Passion and the shedding of his blood that Christ was glorified in the Resurrection, [Col. 1187D] as he himself declared to the disciples going to Emmaus, Luke 24:26: “Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer these things and so enter into his glory?”

The elect. He certainly alludes to Matthew 20:16 and 22:14: “Many are called, but few are chosen.”

He emitted. Namely, when one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, “and immediately there came forth Blood and Water,” John 19:34. See above, ch. 9, the note “Lance.”

Because. In the sense of “as.”

Had washed, i.e., had washed away their sins. Observe, however, the difference—if we wish to speak strictly—between *lavare*, “to wash,” and *lavari*, “to be washed.” “In baths,” says Varro in Book VIII *On the Latin Language*, “we both wash and are washed. But since usage was content with one of the two, we use ‘we are washed’ of the whole body, but ‘we wash’ of the parts, as when we say, ‘I wash my hands,’ and likewise the feet and other parts. Hence in the baths people do not correctly say, ‘I washed’; ‘I washed my hands’ is correct, but because ‘I am washed’ in the baths, the expression is ‘I have been washed.’”

[Col. 1188A] Might drink the Blood. To me, at least, there is no doubt that the Sacrament of the Holy Eucharist is indicated here, in which we drink the Blood of Our Lord Jesus Christ, not a figure of blood; for we are not said to be given figures of liquids to drink. Tertullian therefore judged that in that Sacrament we truly drink the Blood itself—the very Blood that flowed forth in Christ’s Passion, chiefly from his most sacred side. For concerning this he himself said in John 6:55ff.: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me,” etc. Also worthy of citation here is the passage from *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 8, where Our Author says: “The flesh feeds upon the body and blood of Christ, so that the soul may be made fat upon God.” He supposes the same thing in *On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. 13.

Baptism. For when the mouth is given the Eucharistic Blood to drink, the soul is also inwardly washed. But here he means rather the Baptism of martyrdom, in which our blood is poured out and, by virtue of Christ’s Blood shed for us in his Passion and upon the Cross, cleanses the soul from every stain of guilt and [Col. 1188B] punishment, no less than the Baptism of water itself. “The shedding of blood for Christ,” says St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, III, q. 66, art. 12, in the body of the article, “and the inward operation of the Holy Spirit are called Baptisms insofar as they produce the effect of the Baptism of water; while the Baptism of water has its efficacy from the Passion of Christ and the Holy Spirit.”

Represents. Not in a mere image and symbol, but in a present effect; for this is properly what “to represent” means, that is, to render the thing present. Thus Jesus Christ himself says that money is “represented” when it is produced and counted out on the spot. Our author himself likewise, in the last chapter of *On the Soldier’s Crown*, contrasts representation with a vision, or mere appearance: “If such are the images in the vision, what are the realities in the representation?”

But how the Baptism of blood supplies the place of, and produces the effect of, Baptism by water, we explained just above in the note “Baptism.” Add that the Baptism of martyrdom participates much more efficaciously in the power of Christ’s Passion [Col. 1188C]. For the Passion, as St. Thomas says (*Summa theologiae*, III, q. 66, a. 12, in the body of the article), operates in Baptism by water through a certain figurative representation, but in the Baptism of blood through imitation of the deed. This is assuredly not a simple representation, but a wonderfully efficacious manifestation of the thing itself in its power and effect. To this pertains Revelation 7:14: “These are they who came out of the great tribulation and washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.”

Restores. Baptism is lost with respect, namely, to its effect, when the baptized person again loses through mortal sin the innocence that he obtained in Baptism. It is recovered through martyrdom, by which the former innocence is fully restored, as we said above in the note “Baptism.”

## Notes on Chapter XVII

Little subject matter. This very brief treatise.

Of receiving. Concerning the minister and the subject, although he discusses the latter in the following chapter.

Bishop. That is, one who possesses the supreme [Col. 1188D] priesthood in his own Church and surpasses all the rest in the dignity of his authority. For since bishops alone are the true and genuine successors of the Apostles, they also succeeded to the right of those to whom it was particularly entrusted by Christ: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them,” etc. Matthew, last chapter, v. 19. Accordingly, in the earliest centuries of the Church, bishops administered Baptism publicly—that is, in the church itself—by right as something proper to themselves alone, as long as baptisteries had been erected only in cathedral churches. Nevertheless, even then presbyters are recorded as having assisted, and indeed as having baptized themselves whenever so great a multitude of persons to be baptized assembled that they could not have been attended to by the bishop alone. They did so, of course, at the bishop’s express command, while the bishop immediately afterward imparted the sacrament of Confirmation to those baptized. But later, when the number of the faithful had increased still further, especially in the larger dioceses, and access to [Col. 1189A] the cathedral baptistery had become more difficult for some, baptisteries were also erected in each parish church, to provide more securely for the salvation of souls. These were committed to the care and administration of each pastor, while bishops reserved to themselves only solemn Baptism, which was conferred no more than twice a year, leaving parish priests at other times the full right of baptizing.

Accordingly, this discipline always varied at different times, and even at the same time in different places. Thus in the second century St. Ignatius, Bishop of Antioch, says in his *Epistle to the Smyrnaeans*: Οὐκ ἐξόν ἐστι χωρὶς τοῦ Ἐπισκόπου, οὔτε βαπτίζειν, οὔτε προσφέρειν, κτλ., that is: “It is not lawful without the bishop”—meaning without his presence or command—“either to baptize or to make the offering,” etc. Presbyters therefore baptized even then, but only when furnished with the authority of their bishops. In the fourth century St. Ambrose, as Paulinus testifies in his *Life*, adhered so firmly to this custom that the work concerning those to be baptized which he had been accustomed to perform alone could scarcely be performed by five bishops after his death. Likewise in the fifth century, in [Col. 1189B] the *Instruction of the Clergy of Edessa to the Bishops Photius and Eustathius*, found in the Council of Chalcedon, Act X, they ask that Ibas, their bishop, be restored to them as soon as possible, especially since the saving festival of the holy day of Easter was approaching, on which, both because of the catechetical instructions—καὶ διὰ τοὺς ἀξιουμένους τοῦ ἁγίου βαπτίσματος χρεία τῆς αὐτοῦ παρουσίας, “and because of those deemed worthy of holy Baptism”—his presence was needed. Similarly, in the sixth century, in a letter written by the clergy of Italy to the Frankish legates in the year 552, they asked that Dacius, Bishop of Milan, finally be restored after fifteen or sixteen years, because, since almost all the bishops whom he was accustomed to ordain had died, an immense multitude of the people was dying without Baptism. In the same century St. Gregory the Great, in a letter to the Roman patrician, complains gravely against him because Blandus, Bishop of Orta, had now been detained by him for a long time at Ravenna. The chief cause of this complaint was that infants there were dying for their sins without Baptism. So too in the seventh century, at the Second Council of Seville [Col. 1189C], celebrated in 619, canon 7, it was decreed that presbyters were not permitted to enter the baptistery in the bishop’s presence, nor to immerse an infant while the bishop was present, etc. We therefore see how very tenaciously the bishops of certain Churches at those times guarded their right: they judged that it should not be communicated to presbyters even in their absence, perhaps because they considered Baptism without Confirmation, or the imposition of the bishop’s hands, not to be rightly professed.

Meanwhile, however, it gradually came about that public baptisteries were erected in parish churches as well. Bishops now commonly reserved to themselves only the power of conferring solemn Baptism, namely on Holy Saturday and the vigil of Pentecost, while they made a certain general right to confer Baptism outside those times available to presbyters and, as it were, annexed to the sacred ordination that presbyters received from bishops. Nor did even this form of discipline endure for long. When dioceses had expanded and the multitude of catechumens, etc., had increased excessively, solemn [Col. 1189D] Baptism also passed to presbyters. Thereafter it remained with the bishop almost solely in the Church of Milan—perhaps in memory of that singular zeal and example which St. Ambrose, as we recalled above, had so conspicuously displayed there—as our most learned Edmond Martène reports in Book I of *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, chapter I, article III, no. 3, from Constitution II of the Fourth Council of Milan, celebrated in 1575 under St. Charles Borromeo.

And deacons. Although the duty of baptizing was imposed by Christ upon the Apostles alone, Acts 8:12 nevertheless establishes that Philip, though only a deacon, baptized in Samaria—assuredly because the Apostles themselves had entrusted that duty to him. Moreover, ancient records testify that deacons, as persons immediately subordinate to presbyters, were not permitted to baptize without the presbyters’ command. Thus in the fifth century Pope Gelasius, in Letter V to the bishops of Lucania, chapter 5, says of deacons: “Let them not presume to baptize [Col. 1190A] without a bishop or presbyter, unless perhaps those aforementioned ministers are too far away”—that is, farther away than they could conveniently be approached to obtain permission—“and extreme necessity compels them.” In those earlier centuries there was not so great an abundance of priests that someone was always available to every particular congregation in villages and towns, or even in every city. And what had to be done if a priest was present but ill or otherwise impeded, or in sudden and extraordinary cases? The deacons—at least one of whom, according to Martène, Book I, chapter I, article 3, was required to reside in a church together with a presbyter—had to undertake that duty, readily commissioned by the presbyter.

Honor. Namely, the honor that each Church paid to its bishop as its hierarch, or rather spontaneously acknowledged as having been divinely conferred upon him.

Peace remains intact. But PEACE would not remain intact if the bishops’ authority were not preserved, with presbyters indiscriminately seizing upon every ecclesiastical duty [Col. 1190B] on their own authority; for bishops are those whom the Holy Spirit has appointed to govern the Church of God, etc. Accordingly, in Tertullian’s time this authority, as something quite recently derived from the Apostles, had been preserved for bishops, and in them rather for the Apostles themselves. Thus nothing was permitted in the administration of the sacraments—the treasures of the Church, deposited by Christ through the Apostles themselves and to be guarded by their successors—except at the commission of the lawful, immediate, and, as we say, direct successors of the Apostles, that is, the bishops. This was especially true in Baptism, concerning which the Apostles alone had been told: “Go, teach, baptize.”

Otherwise, that is, “in other circumstances,” or “but if not”; so that the meaning is: “But if the Church’s proper honor and the authority of those called and appointed to divine offices are not preserved, that right must equally be granted to the laity, with the whole order now thrown into confusion,” etc.

Can be given. For laypeople can confer no less perfect a Baptism than bishops and the others who baptized before them conferred.

[Col. 1190C] Hidden from anyone. Latinius, attempting to restore this wretchedly broken passage, reads it thus: “Unless bishops now,” etc., “are called learners or disciples”—that is, unless they have been specially called to this duty as disciples of the Lord, or at least as their true successors—“the Lord’s word ought not to be hidden from anyone”; rather, that command of the Lord (Matthew 28:19) will pertain equally to all: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them,” etc. This conjecture of Latinius is not inept.

Junius, however, retains the word *dicentes*, “saying,” and changes only the punctuation, beginning as follows: “Unless bishops now,” etc., “are called, saying: ‘The Lord’s word ought not to be hidden from anyone’; consequently Baptism also, equally God’s possession, can be administered by all. But how much more,” etc. He therefore wishes this entire context to be understood thus: “Unless perhaps—which is absurd—it should be decided that all who speak and affirm as follows are indiscriminately to be regarded as bishops, presbyters, and deacons: ‘Those whose business it is to proclaim God’s word and not to hide it also have the right to baptize; [Col. 1190D] but it is everyone’s business to proclaim God’s word; therefore it is also everyone’s business to baptize,’” etc.

This conjecture certainly seems to me happier and more acute than the preceding one of Latinius. The word *dicentes*, “saying,” should therefore refer to laypeople, as though Tertullian introduced them speaking and claiming Baptism for themselves no less than the preaching of the divine word. Perhaps they even considered that Christ’s saying in Matthew 10:27 was also addressed to them: “What you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops”; as though the Lord’s other saying, “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them,” which was addressed particularly to the Apostles alone, pertained in the form of a command to every other person, and thus the right to preach had also been granted to them by such a commission.

Equally. Namely, the word of God and its preaching.

God’s possession. *Census* does not properly mean annual revenue, but an assessment of each person’s goods entered in public registers, according to which taxes were imposed in a fixed proportion. Later, however [Col. 1191A], the word was also transferred to the taxes themselves that had to be paid. Hence in Matthew 17:23 Christ says: “From whom do the kings of the earth receive τέλη ἢ κῆνσον, tribute or census-tax?” Similarly, in Luke 20:22, when the Pharisees tempt Christ, they ask: “Is it lawful for us to give φόρον, tribute, to Caesar, or not?” In place of Luke’s φόρον, Matthew 22:17 and Mark 12:14 have κῆνσον, “census-tax,” which our Vulgate likewise renders as “tribute.”

In another sense it also signifies the registration or enumeration of each person’s goods, in which each individual declared his name and possessions. Thus Luke 2:1 says: “A decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled”—that is, assessed or entered in the census registers. And shortly afterward, v. 3: “All went to be registered, each to his own city.” And since the proportionate imposition of taxes arose from that census or registration, *census* is also used by our author in *Apology*, chapter 7, for origin, source, or profession: “The *census* of that discipline is from Tiberius.” Likewise in Book I *Against Marcion*, chapter 21: “You will find no [Col. 1191B] Church of apostolic *census* that professes Christianity in the Creator.” See also *On Prescription*, chapter 32. Likewise, in Book IV *Against Marcion*, chapter 40, speaking of the tribe of Judah, he says: “From whose tribe the carnal *census* of Christ was to proceed,” etc. Again in *Apology*, chapter 10, he says: “From him”—Saturn—“comes the *census* of all divinity, or of the greater or better-known divinity.” It is also established that the word is sometimes taken for the number ordinarily determined by an enumeration; in this sense he says in *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 4: “The whole *census* of the elements,” etc.

Finally, it is taken for substance, resources, or goods belonging to someone, as when he says in *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 25: “Thus the *census* of each substance exhibited man and God.” For shortly afterward there follows: “The distinctive character of the conditions, divine and human, was duly assigned according to the equally genuine reality of each nature.” Our author can therefore conveniently be understood in this sense when he calls Baptism “God’s *census*,” as something to be numbered among God’s own possessions.

Consecrated. Proper to the bishop, particularly assigned to him [Col. 1191C], and sanctified by God himself.

The bishop’s office. The force of the argument lies in this: laypeople should claim the right of baptizing all the less, since that right does not belong even to deacons or presbyters themselves without the bishop’s authority.

Rivalry. Some think that this passage should be punctuated thus: “The office of the episcopate is consecrated to bishops. Rivalry is the mother of schisms,” etc. But others rightly object to this tautology, ταυτολογία. The arrangement of this text that I have restored against my own manuscript must therefore be retained.

Is the mother of schisms. There are many and sufficiently lamentable examples of this in the Church, which it is not appropriate to recount here. See also our Tertullian in *On Prescription*, Critical Question IV.

Expedient. As though he wished to say: “Even if laypeople also possess the power to baptize, nevertheless it is not expedient for them to exercise it to the prejudice of the honor due to bishops. It is better that, out of reverence for the bishops’ preeminence, they abstain from exercising it.”

[Col. 1191D] You may use. Junius thinks these words were addressed only to presbyters and deacons. Indeed, St. Basil seems to have judged Baptism administered by laypeople wholly invalid and therefore to be repeated, in his First Canonical Epistle to Amphilochius, canon 1. From this very argument he attempts to prove that the Baptism of heretics is invalid—for after St. Cyprian, he had adhered to this position together with other Easterners—because those who had broken away from the Church, even if they were otherwise bishops or presbyters, had fallen back into the status of laypeople. “Those who have broken away,” he says, “have become laypeople and possess no power either to baptize or to ordain.” Therefore, he says, those baptized by them had been baptized by laypeople, and when they came to the Church they were ordered to be cleansed by the true Baptism of the Church.

But the context itself proves that Tertullian’s preceding words were spoken about laypeople, since immediately afterward he excludes only women from administering Baptism in a case of necessity. And certainly [Col. 1192A] it was always a most ancient custom in the Church that, in a case of necessity, when the bishop, presbyters, deacons, etc., were absent, laypeople also baptized.

Or of place. When in that place no bishop, presbyter, or even deacon is present, or when one cannot be summoned because of some other impediment.

Or of time. Namely, when delay would create an immediate danger that the person to be baptized might die in the meantime.

Condition. Namely, if some other legitimate cause requires that Baptism be imparted at once.

Steadfastness. *Constantia* here seems to be used for courage or firmness of mind, so that the meaning is: “For then it will be lawful to bring assistance courageously and fearlessly,” etc. Thus in Book V *Against Marcion*, chapter 1, he says: “With such *constantia* to proclaim another god.” It can also be taken for liberty or fitness, a meaning that agrees entirely with what is added immediately afterward. See also what we said above at chapter 10 concerning the word *constanter*. Whatever may be said of these interpretations, I would certainly prefer to understand *constantia* here as a stable and canonically established order and rule [Col. 1192B] relating to the person of the minister. That rule, like other ecclesiastical and human laws, has no application in a case of necessity.

To teach. He again alludes to what he recalled above in chapter 1 concerning Quintilla and her poisonous doctrine. He likewise complains bitterly about this insolence of women in *On Prescription*, chapter 41.

Moreover, some infer from this passage, not ineptly, that Tertullian wrote this book *On Baptism* while he was still truly orthodox. For after becoming a Montanist, he treated that talkative sex with much greater indulgence, and indeed with excessively tender reverence, although Paul himself in 1 Corinthians 14:34 condemned it to perpetual silence in the Church and could not adequately restrain it even so. To this also pertain the things we said in Critical Questions IV and V on *On Prescription*.

Will give birth for herself. A not inelegant metaphor, though not without sarcasm, directed against women who everywhere give birth to innovations in sacred matters. Moreover, when he speaks of “right,” [Col. 1192C] he does not thereby exclude every capacity of women to baptize, at least in a case of extreme necessity. Indeed, they are permitted and obliged to baptize if no man is present, or if modesty forbids Baptism to be administered by a man. It is clear from John Moschus—who flourished in the seventh century—*Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 3, that a case of necessity, at least extreme necessity, was not excluded even in those ancient times. There he asserts that it is contrary to the canons for deaconesses to baptize, except, of course, in a case of the strictest necessity. In such a case Tertullian’s own principle must certainly come into operation: “Since he will be guilty of the loss of a human being,” etc.

## Notes on Chapter XVIII

Former. Namely, Quintilla, whom he censured shortly before. He now calls her “former” because he had spoken about her at the very beginning of this book, and because she had already dared some time earlier to attack Baptism.

Was taking away, that is, had attempted to remove it from their midst.

On her own authority. By her own right—something that had not hitherto been tolerated even among male laypeople [Col. 1192D].

Falsely inscribed, that is, ψευδεπίγραφα, “pseudepigraphical,” or falsely entitled in his name: the *Journeys of Paul and Thecla*, whose spurious character no critic now doubts. These acts contain certain things wholly opposed to St. Paul’s teaching and many others that are entirely fabulous: for example, that Thecla was called by Paul to the apostolic duties of preaching the Gospel and baptizing, and that she performed both with more than masculine courage, etc. St. Jerome, however, says of these in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*: “We count the *Journeys of Paul and Thecla*, and the whole fable of the baptized lion”—though it has hitherto remained unknown whose work this was—“among the apocryphal Scriptures.” We know that they were likewise cast into the category of apocryphal writings by Pope Gelasius at the Roman Council held in 494.

But this spurious book must be carefully distinguished from other books commonly attributed to Basil, Bishop of Seleucia, who flourished in the middle of the fifth century. In treating them, Basnage, in his *Political-Ecclesiastical Annals* for A.D. 46, wishes to overturn completely the entire account [Col. 1193A] of St. Thecla’s deeds and miracles, although Baronius had long before established it much too forcefully under A.D. 47. But this is by no means the place to investigate these questions more laboriously.

From his own resources, that is, compiling material invented by his own mind.

Heaping up. I certainly do not think that he did this out of malice, but through a pious fraud and excessive zeal—that is, zeal lacking proper discretion—which also took possession of others around that time, especially the authors of certain Gospels. To secure authority for them, they attached the names of certain Apostles, as though those names would give value to such putrid wares.

Had departed from his position, that is, had been removed from the presbyterate and in some fashion reduced to the order of laypeople. Tertullian was the first to disclose this history, which was afterward affirmed by many others.

Near. He here calls something “near to faith” when it possesses great probability, so that it can prudently be believed with human faith [Col. 1193B].

Steadfastly, or freely and fearlessly. See above the note “Steadfastness,” and at chapter 10 the note “Steadfastly.”

Let them consult. “Let women keep silence in the Church; for they are not permitted to speak, but must be subject, as the Law says. But if they wish to learn anything, let them question their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in the Church.” Thus St. Paul, 1 Corinthians 14:34ff. Therefore, if they have learned anything in the Church, they are directed to their husbands, so that, if they have hesitated anywhere, they may be more fully instructed by them, or may be made more stable in teaching otherwise rightly received, against their natural volubility.

## Notes on Chapter XVIII

To be entrusted rashly, or to be administered indiscriminately to anyone. For it is like a pledge of salvation, which is ordinarily given both as security for a debt and to a creditor who will preserve it safely.

It is a duty, namely, to administer the same to others.

[Col. 1193C] Give to one who asks. “Give to everyone who asks of you,” says Christ, Luke 6:30.

Title. A *titulus* is elsewhere a certain mark, and as it were an inscription upon any action, by which it is rendered honorable and praiseworthy. Therefore, for both the request and the granting to be praiseworthy, each must have a title—that is, a reason and cause both for asking and for giving. The title for giving is the needful person’s request; the title for receiving is the petitioner’s need. Accordingly, Baptism must be conferred only upon those who ask for it, and not upon those who ask in just any manner, but upon those duly prepared to receive it, both through instruction in doctrine and through the fervor of a will that ardently desires it.

For almsgiving. What has just been said makes it sufficiently clear that, like alms, Baptism is to be given to those in need, but only to those who ask for it seriously. With respect to the Baptism of adults, this is necessary for it to be lawfully administered to someone; for validity, however, nothing is required except what is called a habitual intention to receive it [Col. 1193D]. But more on this elsewhere.

Express, that is, open. Thus our author says in *On the Shows*, chapter 3: “Certainly we nowhere find, in the same way as it is openly laid down, ‘You shall not kill,’” etc., “an equally express determination: ‘You shall not go to the circus,’” etc. And in Book II *To His Wife*, chapter 1, he says: “Now he does not advise, but expressly commands.” He likewise says: “It is a thoroughly examined and express judgment.”

Favor. He seems to have used *dignatio* for “grace,” following the example of Livy, Book II, who says of Appius: “Not long afterward he attained the favor of the leading men.”

Had intervened. See the entire sequence of this history carefully woven together in Acts, chapter 8.

To go on ahead. “But an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying: ‘Arise and go southward, to the road that descends from Jerusalem to Gaza.’” Acts 8:26.
