Here *praetendere* means to direct oneself there first, or to set out beforehand and, as it were, to occupy the road in advance so as to meet him; or it is used simply for *tendere*, “to proceed,” as our author often uses compounds in place of simple verbs [Col. 1194A].

Absorbed. “He had come to worship in Jerusalem and was returning, seated in his chariot and reading the prophet Isaiah.” Ibid., vv. 27ff. He was therefore fixed upon his reading with the greatest attention and, as it were, absorbed into it, so that Scripture seemed to receive the reader most intimately into itself. In almost the same sense our author says in *Apology*, chapter 18: “But so that we might approach both him”—GOD himself—“and his dispositions and wills more fully and deeply,” etc. And in *Exhortation to Chastity*, chapter 3, he says that the will of GOD must be considered deeply and with an abiding impression.

Apostle. From this very passage some have asserted that this Philip was an Apostle; but others, more commonly, place him among the seven deacons who were chosen by the Apostles in Acts 6:5. For if he was an Apostle, why was it necessary for Peter and John to be sent to the inhabitants of Samaria, who had recently been converted by this Philip, so that they might lay hands upon them and they might receive the Holy Spirit? Acts 8:17. For if Philip was an Apostle, could he not equally have given them the sacrament of Confirmation, whose administration then belonged to the Apostles alone—that is, to the bishops—by imparting it through the imposition of hands? He was therefore called an “apostle” as one specially sent by the Apostles properly so called, in the same sense in which Andronicus and Junia are called “notable among the apostles” by Paul in Romans 16:7.

Ordered. “But the Spirit said to Philip: ‘Go near and join yourself to this chariot.’” Acts 8:29.

At the right time. “Now the passage of Scripture that he was reading was this: ‘Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter,’” etc. Ibid., v. 32.

Invited. But who was invited? Was the eunuch taken up by Philip for Baptism after the exhortation, or was Philip taken up by the eunuch into the chariot? If we understand the former, the word *exhortatus* must be taken in a passive sense. This is not altogether unusual, since I also read in Cicero’s *Cato*: “He was urged at a banquet by a prostitute [Col. 1194C] to strike with the axe,” etc. But I prefer the latter interpretation. For after Philip had exhorted the eunuch, the latter asked Philip to come up and sit with him. Acts 8:31.

Is shown. “Then Philip opened his mouth and, beginning from this Scripture, preached Jesus to him.” Ibid., v. 35.

Does not delay. “‘Behold, water: what prevents me from being baptized?’ Philip said: ‘If you believe with your whole heart, you may.’ And he answered and said: ‘I BELIEVE that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.’” Ibid., vv. 36ff.

Is awaited. “And they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him.” Ibid., v. 38.

Is carried away. “But when they had come up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more,” etc. Ibid., v. 39.

Was baptized. Namely, only three days after his conversion, as is clear from Acts 9:9 and 18.

Host. For Ananias had been ordered to seek him in the house of Judas. Ibid., v. 11. Nothing further is known about who this man was [Col. 1194D].

## Notes on Chapter XVIII

Favors, that is, grace. See above.

Prerogatives, that is, singular preliminary dispositions and marvelous circumstances from which one may readily perceive what, and in what manner, God wishes human beings to do something outside the common order and rule.

To be deceived. A person asking for Baptism in a disorderly manner can deceive its minister, namely by approaching without a lawful disposition and not with a true intention, but only a feigned one. He can also deceive himself when he approaches out of immature zeal and believes himself impelled by God, although he has not yet been furnished with the necessary knowledge of the things to be believed so that he may receive it fruitfully.

It is more advantageous. In former times Baptism was postponed by many until adulthood, and sometimes almost until the end of life. Thus St. Martin, who had already become a catechumen at the age of [Col. 1195A] ten, was not baptized until eight years afterward, as Sulpicius Severus testifies in his *Life*, Book I, chapter 2. Some postponed it until the age of thirty, relying upon Christ’s example, as may be seen in St. Gregory Nazianzen’s *Oration on Holy Baptism*. The common opinion concerning the emperor Constantine is that he was baptized at Nicomedia shortly before his death. Likewise the emperor Constantius wished to be baptized by Euzoius at Antioch only at the very end of his life. What, moreover, of the fact that Theodosius the Great, after surviving many dangers in war, asked to be washed by Ascholius, Bishop of Thessalonica, only when he finally fell gravely ill? Perhaps our author himself, by ordering Baptism to be postponed through delay, was responsible for many people’s previously refusing Baptism, and doing so in good faith, out of excessive religious scruple and fear of conscience.

There were also those who delayed receiving Baptism with a worse intention, namely so that they might not afterward be bound by the severity of ecclesiastical laws and could thus sin more freely in the meantime. This policy, as rash, was rightly and most sharply censured by the two St. Gregories, Nazianzen and Nyssen, as well as by St. John Chrysostom and other Fathers [Col. 1195B].

As for the examples of others who formerly postponed Baptism excessively for other reasons, they have by no means been set before us for imitation. It should be enough for us to measure from them the gravity of the undertaking: we should neither rush into it suddenly nor receive those who rush into it in such a way, but should defer it until the desire has grown sufficiently and adequate testing has preceded it. Yet doing the same thing when a person already considers himself sufficiently prepared is not free from danger: drowsiness may meanwhile steal upon him, or the opportunity may afterward be lost. We know for certain that the younger Emperor Valentinian, overtaken by a violent death after delaying Baptism too long, was taken from this life while still a catechumen.

Finally, St. Basil should be heard on this subject in his *Exhortation to Baptism*, where, among many other things, he speaks as follows [Col. 1195C]:

> If the Church were distributing gold, you certainly would not say, “Send it tomorrow; you will give it tomorrow.” Rather, you would diligently and swiftly seek your portion and would bear delay with difficulty. But since the munificent King promises you, not the false coloring of some material thing, but the cleansing of the soul, you weave delays and excuses and offer impediments and reasons, though you ought to run to this gift.

And after other remarks:

> Indeed, if you were subject to public taxes, and a remission of debts were proclaimed everywhere to those liable, and someone then attempted to deprive you of this public benefit, you would grieve and cry out that you were being wrongfully deprived of your share in the common favor. But when not only remission of past things but also gifts for the future are openly offered, you do not listen, but injure yourself more than even enemies perhaps would injure you.

And again, shortly afterward:

> If some physician undertook, by certain devices and contrivances, to make you young again from being old, you would certainly take every care to come to the day on which you saw that you were to be restored to the flower of youth. But now, when it is announced that your soul, which you have rendered defiled by every crime, is to be renewed [Col. 1195D] and regenerated through Baptism, you so despise the benefit that you do not hasten of your own accord or go to meet the one who promises it.

And finally:

> Delay in approaching Baptism seems to cry out nothing other than this: “Let sin reign in me first, until at some point the Lord also reigns; let the members of injustice and the weapons of iniquity be with me, and afterward I shall also take up the weapons of righteousness for God,” etc.

Basil says these things against those who, although already duly instructed, contemplate continually postponing Baptism—and the same also applies to the sacrament of Penance.

Concerning little children. This opinion was certainly peculiar to Tertullian alone, since even while still a Catholic he was always inclined toward excessive scrupulousness and severity. Nor was it adopted by any of the ancient Fathers; still less did the Henricians, Peter Abelard, Peter of Bruys, the Anabaptists, or other heretics find any support in it. For they held that infants were wholly [Col. 1196A] incapable of receiving Baptism validly and that it therefore had to be repeated when they reached the use of reason. Tertullian’s statement, however, was only that of one advising against the practice. For that very reason it indicates unambiguously that a contrary custom existed even in the African Churches and at those same times, with only Tertullian, so far as we know, opposing it. His reasons were approved by none of his contemporaries or by any other of the holy Fathers, not even by St. Cyprian, who was otherwise so scrupulous concerning Baptism and who is nevertheless said to have constantly studied Tertullian as his teacher. For when Fidus, a bishop, raised the question and contended that little children should be baptized only after the eighth day, Cyprian, no longer taking any account of Tertullian’s argument, concluded as follows at the Council of Carthage of sixty-six bishops in the year 253: “No one agreed that infants ought to be baptized only after the eighth day from birth; rather, we all judged that God’s mercy and grace must be denied to no human being who has been born.” Thus he writes in his Letter 69 to Fidus.

[Col. 1196B] Moreover, St. Augustine is an abundant witness that paedobaptism, or the washing of little children, descends from apostolic practice and tradition. Speaking of little children in Sermon X *On the Words of the Apostle*, he says:

> They themselves are carried to the Church; and if they cannot run there on their own feet, they run on the feet of others so that they may be healed. Mother Church lends them the feet of others so that they may come, the heart of others so that they may believe, and the tongue of others so that they may confess. Thus, because those who are sick are burdened by another’s sin—namely Adam’s—when they are made healthy they may likewise be saved through another’s confession—namely that of the sponsor—made on their behalf. Therefore, let no one whisper alien doctrines to you. The Church has always had this practice and has always maintained it; she receives it from the faith of her forebears and preserves it steadfastly to the end.

In Book X *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 23, he confirms the same point, saying:

> The custom of Mother Church in baptizing little children is by no means to be despised, nor in any way to be regarded as superfluous; nor should it be believed at all unless it is an apostolic tradition.

A much earlier witness to this is Origen, who expressly says in his commentary on chapter 13 of the *Epistle to the Romans* [Col. 1196C]: “The Church received from the Apostles the tradition of giving Baptism even to little children.”

For this reason it was most salutarily decreed, and under severe penalties in several councils, that the Baptism of little children should not be delayed any longer, since sudden dangers of death can often overtake them. St. Charles Borromeo in particular decreed at the First Council of Milan that those responsible for the care of a newborn infant should ensure that the child was brought to the church to receive Baptism before the ninth day. If they neglected this, they were to incur the penalty of excommunication.

**Necessary.** These words, “If it is not so necessary,” Junius thinks may safely be omitted, and he testifies that they are in fact absent from many copies. But why may they not equally well be retained? They certainly yield a sufficiently appropriate sense: “If necessity does not press from some other quarter.”

**Sponsors.** They are otherwise called godparents (*patrini*), because they are, as it were, spiritual fathers, or sureties. Concerning them Saint Chrysostom, on Psalm XIV, says: “Immediately the priest exacts covenants and agreements from a tender age, [Col. 1196D] and questions the sponsor as surety for the minor,” etc. For they must undertake and answer on behalf of the infant, etc.; hence the aforesaid designation “sponsors” was also applied to them.

From this passage of Tertullian it is certainly evident that godparents had already been customarily employed in baptism from the most ancient usage and, as it were, from the very cradle of the Church, as Saint Basil, Epistle 128, Saint Augustine in numerous passages, and others everywhere likewise testify.

**They can.** That is, if the sponsors themselves should die before the baptized infant has attained the use of reason, so that he could be instructed by them concerning the obligation he contracted in baptism, or what those godparents promised on his behalf.

**Be deceived.** If meanwhile the infant, having grown to adulthood, drives out the grace of baptism by a wicked life, and thereafter refuses to fulfill in his own person, although he is now able to do so, the promises made for him, etc.

[Col. 1197A] **Christians.** They are to become such through baptism, by which, of course, initiation into the Christian people takes place.

**An innocent age.** Yet that age is in truth sufficiently guilty, since it is liable for original sin, which the soul contracts immediately upon its first infusion into the body. Nor is it likely that by this expression Tertullian intended to make infants immune from that sin, since in his treatise *On the Testimony of the Soul*, chapter 3, he says so explicitly: “Man, circumvented from the beginning by the devil so that he transgressed God’s commandment, and for that reason given over to death, thereafter made the ENTIRE RACE descended from his seed infected by him and the transmitter also of his condemnation.”

**Of sins.** Tertullian therefore called the age of infants innocent because they are free from actual sins, that is, sins committed by their own will; and he had believed that the chief end and power of baptism consisted in the remission of these sins, with respect both to guilt and to punishment. Since, therefore, there is only one baptism, and it cannot thereafter be repeated (chapter XV, note **They do not have**), and consequently in adults every guilt can indeed be erased through Penance, but not equally every punishment [Col. 1197B] (chapter V, note **Punishment**), Tertullian judged it better that baptism should be reserved until adulthood, so that then, together with original sin, all actual sins and the entire liability to the punishment due for them might be removed at once—whereas otherwise lengthy labors of penance and works of satisfaction would be required to remove it. Meanwhile, however, our author failed to consider that infants who die without baptism are thereby deprived of every further hope of salvation, a loss that can no longer be repaired by any means.

**In secular matters,** that is, in the affairs of this world, or temporal matters.

**Earthly substance,** that is, the administration of an inheritance and temporal possessions, is not entrusted to them, nor indeed can it be.

**Should divine things be entrusted?** Junius approves Latinius’s reading of these words interrogatively (*εἰρωτικῶς*), and I readily agree with him. Yet this argument of Tertullian is weak. The administration of their affairs cannot be entrusted to wards because [Col. 1197C] they are wholly incapable of it; nevertheless, goods acquired by inheritance pass to them. “As long as the heir is a child,” says the Apostle in Galatians 4:1, “he differs in no respect from a slave, although he is lord of all; but he is under tutors and administrators until the appointed time,” etc. Meanwhile, their goods stand in the greatest need of administration, and it is altogether necessary that there be someone to protect them and defend them against the injuries of others, etc. But once grace has been entrusted to an infant, and thereafter rests secure against every force, what administration does it require? For who will take away grace once received by an infant? Who will offer violence to him? Nothing is contrary or hostile to grace except sin subsequently committed by one’s own will; but how can this occur in an infant while he lacks the use of reason? Thus no snares threaten grace in the infant, whereas they must meanwhile be feared for his temporal goods. Those goods, therefore, need to be entrusted to another’s guardianship, as does the infant’s own person, which is plainly very exposed to injuries from others.

[Col. 1197D] **You may appear to have given.** Why should it not also be given to one who does not ask for it, so long as he cannot ask for it by himself, yet needs it for his salvation just as much as an adult who can ask? Will food, then, also be denied to an infant because, however necessary it may be to him, he cannot ask for it?

**Of delaying.** This opinion of Tertullian is extraordinary and displays his rigid disposition. It was never asserted by anyone else, and rests upon the same feeble argument that we examined above.

**Full maturity.** That is, when they are marriageable and mature enough for a husband.

**Wandering about.** I do not grasp this unless Tertullian means that, being without a companion and, as it were, a safeguard of her chastity, she is alone and therefore wanders among men.

**Let them be strengthened,** that is, if she has remained in widowhood for a longer period and surrounded herself with another protection by [Col. 1198A] withdrawing herself entirely from social company; if, by preserving the state of her widowhood for a longer time, she has acquired a somewhat firmer habit of continence and thereafter seriously and completely renounced marriage.

**Weight,** that is, the importance and gravity of the matter.

**The consequence.** The things that may follow baptism: namely, the danger of losing grace through sins—which, particularly because of the ingratitude joined to them, will be more serious after baptism than if committed before it—and the difficulty of recovering that grace. Perhaps our author here had in view the Apostle’s words in Hebrews 6:4:

> Ἀδύνατον τοὺς ἅπαξ φωτισθέντας, γευσαμένους τε τῆς δωρεᾶς τῆς ἐπουρανίου, καὶ μετόχους γενηθέντας πνεύματος ἁγίου . . . . καὶ παραπεσόντας, πάλιν ἀνακαινίζειν εἰς μετάνοιαν, ἀνασταυροῦντας ἑαυτοῖς τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ παραδειγματίζοντας.

That is:

> It is impossible for those who have once been ILLUMINATED—that is, baptized, as in chapter I, note **Blindness**—and have also tasted the heavenly gift and become partakers of the HOLY SPIRIT . . . and have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, since they crucify again for themselves [Col. 1198B] the Son of God and expose him to public disgrace.

Here *τὸ ἀδύνατον* (“the impossible”) signifies not what is absolutely impossible but what is difficult—that is, what cannot indeed be done by human means, but can be done by divine means, though with somewhat greater difficulty and with the danger of relapse. So in Mark 10:27, when the disciples ask who can be saved, Christ replies:

> Παρὰ ἀνθρώποις ἀδύνατον, ἀλλ’ οὐ παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ· πάντα γὰρ δυνατά ἐστι παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ.

That is:

> Among men—namely, by human powers—this is impossible, but not with GOD; for all things are possible with God.

Here he did not say “possible *for* GOD,” but “possible *with* GOD,” that is, through the powers of divine grace, by whose assistance nothing is now so arduous that it cannot be overcome and accomplished by us. “All things are possible to one who believes,” says Christ in Mark 9:23. For those baptized while still infants, therefore, the attainment of grace through baptism is certainly safer than its postponement would have been. In postponement there lies the danger of losing salvation so that it can no longer be recovered; in the baptized, grace is lost with greater difficulty [Col. 1198C] and, once lost, can at least be restored through Penance.

**Intact,** that is, obtained in its fullness through baptism and thereafter preserved without contamination.

**Concerning salvation.** “But he who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matthew 10:22).

### Notes on Chapter XIX

**It is preferable.** At the beginning of the Church no particular time was prescribed for baptism. “At first everyone taught,” says the author of the *Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians*, chapter IV, “and everyone baptized, whenever an opportunity arose on any day or at any time. For neither did PHILIP” (Acts 8) “seek a time or a day on which to baptize the eunuch. Nor did PAUL and SILAS” (Acts 16:33) “defer the time at which they baptized the jailer with all his household. Nor did PETER seek a particular day when he baptized Cornelius” (Acts 10:47ff.) “with his entire household. Thus, in order that the people might grow and multiply, permission was granted to all at the beginning both to evangelize and to baptize,” etc. “But when [Col. 1198D] the Church had embraced every place . . . it began to be governed by a different order and administration. Hence it is that now neither do deacons preach among the people, nor clerics or laypeople baptize, nor are believers immersed on just any day, unless they are sick.”

From this we see that it is not surprising if, in many other matters as well, the discipline that had existed in apostolic times, had been ordained by the Apostles themselves, and was then practiced, was nevertheless in many respects—namely, where no divine precept was attached—changed by the Church in the course of time, or augmented by the addition of further regulations. Such discipline was adapted variously and wisely to the requirements of different times and other circumstances, while those things belonging to the substance of the sacraments, since they are known to derive from a far higher and wholly divine institution, were always preserved unshaken.

But to return to our argument: from the most ancient times [Col. 1199A] the custom already prevailed that solemn baptism should be celebrated at EASTER and PENTECOST. Saint Siricius and Saint Gregory the Great, both supreme pontiffs, testify that this observance had proceeded from apostolic times themselves. The former, in his epistle to Himerius, Bishop of Tarragona, appeals to the custom of all the churches; the latter, in Epistle 136 to the bishops of Sicily, presents it as a rule instituted by the Apostles and handed down in the Church through an unbroken succession. According to Theophylact, *Commentary on Luke* 10, this very widespread practice endured almost until the end of the eleventh century. Finally it was entirely abrogated, and baptism was left to the discretion of its ministers, so that they might administer it whenever it seemed proper to them for a reasonable cause. This custom eventually prevailed among the Greeks as well, and indeed many centuries ago.

**The Passion of the Lord.** In his work *Against the Jews*, chapter 10, our author believed that *Pascha* was of Greek origin, derived from the Greek *πάσχω*, “I suffer.” In this matter he had Saint [Col. 1199B] Irenaeus before him, book IV *Against the Jews*, chapter 23, and several followers, especially Lactantius in book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 26, where he says:

> The sacrifice of the animal—the paschal lamb—is called *PASCHA* by the very people who perform it, *ἀπὸ τοῦ πάσχειν*, “from suffering,” because it is a figure of the PASSION,

etc.

Yet no one doubts that they were gravely mistaken concerning this etymology of the name, and that the word must be assigned to the Hebrews. For in Exodus 12:12 it is *PESACH*, from the root [Hebrew text missing in the supplied source]; and from this the Chaldeans, by adding their own suffix as they frequently do, made [form missing in the supplied source], *PISCHA* or *PASCHA*. The Septuagint also adopted this word, writing *πάσχα*, especially because its ending is Greek and is declined in the genitive with *-ατος*. Our Vulgate, however, used *PHASE*, because the harshness of the guttural letter is not very agreeable to Latin speakers. Hence the Vulgate also commonly cut it off in other proper names, especially disyllables: for *NOACH, THARACH,* and *CORACH* it wrote *Noe, Thare,* and *Chore*, etc.

Furthermore, *pesach, phase,* or *pascha* [Col. 1199C] means a PASSAGE or PASSING OVER. Hence Aquila translated *pascha* as *ὑπέρβασις*, “a crossing over” or “passing beyond,” while Symmachus rendered it *ὑπερμάχησις*, “defense”; but none of the Greek translators rendered it “Passion.” Finally, our Latin translator interprets Exodus 12:12 thus: “For it is the PHASE—that is, the PASSAGE—of the Lord.” The Hebrews were to celebrate the annual Passover in memory of the angel’s striking the firstborn of Egypt and passing untouched over, or passing by, only the houses of the Hebrews.

**We are immersed.** We have already shown in chapter XVI, note **Baptism**, 1188A, that Christ’s baptism derives all its efficacy from his Passion. See also chapter XI, note **The Resurrection**, 1178B.—**Without the resurrection.** Ibid.

**Will be interpreted.** It is used here passively, as in the author of the *Rhetoric to Herennius*, book II.

**Pentecost.** *Πεντηκοστή*—with *ἡμέρα*, “day,” understood—means “the fiftieth day.” From the day after the Sabbath (Leviticus 23:15), that is, from the second day of Unleavened Bread, seven weeks had to be counted, making forty-nine days. On [Col. 1199D] the fiftieth day the FEAST OF WEEKS was to be celebrated, which in our Church is called the FEAST OF PENTECOST. Just as it was formerly celebrated by the Jews in memory of the Law given to Moses on Mount Sinai—which is believed to have occurred on the fiftieth day after the feast of Passover, or the departure from Egypt (Exodus 19:1, 11)—so now in our Church the feast of Pentecost, that is, the fiftieth day after the feast of Easter, is celebrated in memory of the Holy Spirit’s descent upon the Apostles in tongues of fire (Acts 2:1ff.).

Since baptism is therefore the work of the Holy Spirit, who descended in the form of a dove upon Christ when he was baptized in the Jordan, and who in a special manner sanctified the waters—see above, chapter X, note [reference unclear in the source]—it is not surprising that the primitive Church appointed Pentecost, no less than Easter, as a time for solemnly conferring baptism. “Let all priests,” says Pope Siricius, cited above in the note **It is preferable**, “observe this rule if they do not wish to be severed from the solidity of the apostolic ROCK upon which Christ built the universal Church.”

[Col. 1200A] Since, however, this matter belonged purely to discipline, it is not surprising that even after the time of Siricius a different custom was observed elsewhere: on the NATIVITY OF THE LORD, when Avitus, Bishop of Vienne, testifies in his epistle to Clovis that Clovis, the first king of the Franks, was baptized; or on the EPIPHANY of the Lord, because on that day Christ himself was baptized by Saint John; and elsewhere, again, on the feast of SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST for a similar reason. Indeed, baptism was even administered on the feast days of the Apostles and Martyrs, not without opposition from the Roman Church, until at last, as the conditions of the times required, the individual churches were granted freedom in this matter. Nevertheless, according to the usage of almost the entire Church, the blessing of the baptismal font was restricted to HOLY SATURDAY of Easter and the VIGIL OF PENTECOST. On this subject Martène, *On the Rites of the Church*, book I, chapter 1, article 1; Juenin, *On Baptism*, question X, chapter 2; and many others may be consulted at greater length.

[Col. 1200B] **With waters.** That is, so that they may first have been solemnly blessed (chapter IV, note **God having been invoked**) and may always be prepared for the orderly administration of baptism to all.

**There is an interval.** From this it seems rightly to be inferred that throughout that intermediate period, namely from Easter to Pentecost, baptism was formerly customarily administered. I think this must be understood to mean that it was conferred solemnly at Easter and Pentecost, but during the intervening period only those were washed who had previously been hindered—for example by illness—or who had been absent for some other cause, as well as infants born during that intervening period, etc.

**Has been frequently celebrated,** that is, its annual commemoration was observed with frequent and more vivid remembrance.

**Dedicated,** that is, consecrated, or celebrated in religious worship amid hymns, prayers, thanksgivings, etc. From what has thus far been said, we clearly perceive that the feasts of EASTER and PENTECOST were instituted by the Apostles themselves, but [Col. 1200C] with rites different from those observed among the Hebrews and with different symbols, namely symbols of past events: Easter was to be celebrated in memory of Christ’s RESURRECTION, by which he raises us from the death of sin to the life of grace; Pentecost, in commemoration of the HOLY SPIRIT first poured out upon the Apostles and into the Church.

**Coming.** This must be understood of the Lord’s second coming, when he will come to judge the living and the dead.

**Partly disclosed.** That is, shown somewhat obscurely and, as it were, from a greater distance.

**Received back.** Some prefer *reciperato*, because it derives from *recipere*, “to receive.” But it is preferable to leave this dispute of grammarians undecided. It is sufficient here that the ASCENSION OF CHRIST, or his reception into heaven, is signified.

**At Pentecost.** For our author this name also denotes the entire period of fifty days between Easter and Pentecost. Hence in *On Idolatry*, chapter 14, he says: “Select the individual solemnities of the nations and arrange them in order: they will not be able to fill Pentecost.” [Col. 1200D] He also appears to be understood in that sense here. For Christ did not ascend into heaven on Pentecost if by that word one means the particular day, but during that intervening period, namely on the fortieth day after the Resurrection.

Moreover, the belief that the day of judgment will occur during Pentecost is Tertullian’s conjecture, weakly based on the words of Acts 1:11 cited above. For there it says only “in the same manner,” signifying the manner of his coming, not its time. For just as he ascended in glory and a cloud received him (Acts 1:9), so one day “they shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty” (Matthew 24:30). But why should we labor to determine something of which no one knows—not even the angels of heaven, but the Father alone (ibid., verse 36)?

**At the feast.** Jeremiah 31:8, where the Septuagint adds *ἐν ἑορτῇ φασέκ*, “at the solemnity of Phase,” or Passover. These words are absent from the Hebrew text and from all the other Greek versions—as Saint Jerome himself notes in his *Commentary on Jeremiah* at this passage [Col. 1201A]—and consequently also from our Latin Vulgate. Nor is it established by any testimony of Ezra, Nehemiah, or any other sacred writer that the Jews returned from the Babylonian captivity at the feast of Passover as they had once departed from Egyptian bondage; yet Jeremiah is speaking here of that return from Babylon. Hence this addition by the Seventy appears to have been introduced only for the sake of some mystical signification, fulfilled, of course, in Christ’s Passover and Passion, etc.

**Festive.** For it was called the SOLEMNITY OF WEEKS, as stated above in the note **Pentecost**.

**It makes no difference.** Time neither adds anything to nor takes anything from the effect of baptism, that is, grace; nor does one who receives baptism on a feast day acquire more grace than one who receives it on any other day. “One time is suited to one thing: one is proper for sleep, another for wakefulness, and likewise one for war and another for peace. The time for baptism is the whole of a person’s life,” says Saint Basil, Homily 13, *Exhortation to Baptism*.

### Notes on Chapter XX

**Frequent.** [Col. 1201B] Adults were admitted to baptism only when—apart, of course, from a case of urgent necessity—they had previously shown themselves worthy of this heavenly gift through various works of piety, especially works of penance, during their catechumenate. This was a time of probation and, as it were, a kind of novitiate before baptism. They also had to give great hope of their future perseverance in the grace once received. We have already discussed the catechumens and their classes in *On Prescription*, chapter XLI, and there is no leisure to repeat that material here. Catechumens were permitted to enter the church and pray with the others, and there before GOD to express their burning desire for baptism, etc. They were then dismissed from the church, while the deacon prayed to God for them, as is reported in book VIII, chapter 5 of the *Apostolic Constitutions*—whose author is not Saint Clement, but nevertheless some other very ancient writer:

> May the Lord mercifully hear their supplications and prayers; and, receiving their petitions, may he grant them assistance and fulfill the request of their hearts unto their benefit,

etc.

[Col. 1201C] **With fasts.** Thus the author of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book VII, chapter 23, likewise states: “Before baptism, let the person who is to be baptized FAST.” And below: “The person initiated into his”—Christ’s—“death, who is to be buried with him in baptism, must first FAST and afterward be baptized.” Saint Augustine likewise says in *On Faith and Works*, chapter 6: “Without doubt they would not be admitted to baptism if, during the very days in which they were to receive that grace, they were not purified by abstinence, FASTS, and exorcisms,” etc. The Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 85, also decreed: “Those to be baptized, after being tested for a long time by abstinence from wine and meat and by frequent imposition of hands, are to receive baptism.” For the more the body, weakened by fasting, is restrained, the more the soul is enlarged and becomes capable of receiving the grace of baptism with correspondingly greater abundance.

**With kneelings.** Kneelings are what the Greeks call *γονυπετεῖαι* or *γονυκλισίαι*, genuflections, customarily employed in prayer from the most ancient times. Hence in *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 3, our author speaks of worshiping “from the knees.” In *To Scapula*, chapter 4, he says: [Col. 1201D] “When have even droughts not been driven away by our kneelings and fastings?” etc.

Kneeling, therefore, is a sign of reverence, submission, or adoration. Thus Saint PETER, when about to raise Tabitha from the dead, “knelt down and prayed” (Acts 9:40). Saint PAUL, when about to depart from Miletus, “knelt down and prayed with them all,” etc. (Acts 20:36). The same Apostle says in Ephesians 3:14: “For this reason I bend my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Indeed, knees were also bent during prayer in the Old Testament. For when SOLOMON delivered that lengthy prayer at the dedication of the Temple in 3 Kings 8, he had fixed both knees upon the ground (ibid., verse 54). DANIEL, while praying, “bent his knees and worshiped and made confession before his God, as he had been accustomed to do before” (Daniel 6:10). Likewise EZRA said of himself: “I bent my knees and spread out my hands to the Lord” (Ezra 9:5). So too in the New Testament, those who approached Christ [Col. 1202A] to ask for the grace of healing made their request upon bended knee. Thus Matthew 17:14: “A man approached him, *γονυπετῶν αὐτῷ*, falling on his knees before him,” etc. And Mark 1:40: “A leper came to him, beseeching him, and *γονυπετῶν αὐτόν*, bending his knee, said to him,” etc. So too others elsewhere. What, moreover, of the fact that Christ himself on the Mount of Olives (Luke 22:41), *θεὶς τὰ γόνατα προσηύχετο*, “knelt down and prayed”? And this is he whom GOD exalted . . . “so that at the Name of JESUS, *πᾶν γόνυ κάμψῃ*, every knee should bend,” etc. (Philippians 2:10).

It is therefore especially fitting that those to be baptized should also fall upon their knees and pray to GOD for so illustrious a gift, through which, although they had previously fallen into sin, they are raised anew to salvation. For, as the author of the *Questions to the Orthodox*, reply to Question 115, says: *γονυκλισία σύμβολόν ἐστι τῆς ἐν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις πτώσεως*—“Bending the knees is a sign of the fall into sins.”

**With all-night vigils.** An all-night vigil, called *παννυχισμός* by the Greeks, properly speaking is a vigil of longer duration, continued through the entire night or at least a great part of it; [Col. 1202B] whereas a vigil simply so called is the suppression of sleep even for a shorter period. Martial accurately noted the distinction between the two in book V, Epigram 70:

> For keeping watch is easy; keeping watch all night is hard.

Hence Arnobius, book IV of the *Institutes*, says: “For whom those sacred all-night vigils and burdensome *pannychisms* are consecrated,” etc.

Here, however, we are by no means speaking of the all-night vigils of the gentiles, concerning which Cicero says in book II of *On the Laws*: “Thus Aristophanes assails the new gods and the all-night celebrations held in worshiping them,” etc. Tacitus also speaks of them (*Annals*, book V, chapter 44): “Women who had husbands celebrated sacred banquets and all-night vigils.” But away with such things, generally associated with the grossest obscenities! We must treat of far holier vigils, which were frequently observed in the earliest Church, as we learn sufficiently even from our Tertullian himself. These vigils were either public, celebrated by the entire assembly of a particular church, [Col. 1202C] or private, celebrated by individuals in their own homes. The former preceded every more solemn feast and also the commemorations of the martyrs. The latter were among the private works of penitents and were to be undertaken especially and more frequently by those preparing for baptism. Hence Saint Gregory Nazianzen, in his *Oration on Holy Baptism*, instructs the catechumen as follows:

> Good aids for obtaining the things you desire will be vigils, fasts, *chameuniae*—sleeping on the ground—prayers, tears, hardships, and assistance to the needy,

etc.

In the ancient Church fasts were always joined to these vigils. Later, however, when vigils were abolished because abuses had crept in, the fasts were retained together with the name alone of the vigils.

**Of sins.** Just as sins are remitted to no human beings in this order of providence without their first being retracted through some act of penance, so adults required certain acts of penance for the remission of actual sins provided by baptism, and therefore for the fruitful reception of baptism itself. [Col. 1202D] These acts had to be manifested by some outward sign, namely by public confession of sins. For the most ancient monuments likewise testify to this. Saint Justin Martyr, for example, says in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, page 177 of my edition, that even under the Old Testament washings did not profit unless those who received them had first repented:

> τοῦτο ἐκεῖνο πάλαι τὸ σωτήριον λουτρὸν ἦν ὃ εἵπετο τοῖς μεταγινώσκουσιν,

that is:

> This was that saving bath of old which followed upon those who repented.

After confirming this with an extended testimony from Isaiah, he adds:

> τοῦτ’ ἐκεῖνο τὸ βάπτισμα, τὸ μόνον καθαρίσαι τοὺς μετανοήσαντας δυνάμενον,

that is:

> This is that baptism which alone can purify those who repent.

How much more properly does he require this for our baptism in *Apology* II, page 73 of my edition, where he says:

> Εὔχεσθαί τε καὶ αἰτεῖν νηστεύοντες παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ τῶν προημαρτημένων ἄφεσιν διδάσκονται, ἡμῶν συνευχομένων καὶ συννηστευόντων αὐτοῖς· ἔπειτα ἄγονται ὑφ’ ἡμῶν ἔνθα ὕδωρ ἐστί, κ.τ.λ.

That is:

> They are taught, while fasting, to pray and ask GOD for the remission of their former sins [Col. 1203A]—yet how will they ask unless they confess those sins?—while we pray and fast together with them. Then they are led by us to the place where there is water,

etc.

This accords with what the very ancient author—formerly believed to have been Saint Jerome—of the *Sermon on Psalm 41 to the Newly Baptized* says:

> Throughout the whole of Lent they devoted themselves to prayer and fasting; they slept in sackcloth and ashes, seeking through confession of their sins the life they were to receive through baptism,

etc.

Eusebius, in the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 61, likewise reports that CONSTANTINE THE GREAT, EMPEROR, approached the reception of baptism after preparing himself in this manner:

> Having considered these things within himself, he fell upon the ground on bended knee, humbly begged pardon from GOD, and confessed his sins in the *martyrium*,

that is, in the place where the monuments or tombs of the martyrs were visited.

Lest we think so exalted an example had no followers, let us hear Socrates, a fifth-century writer. In book V of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 17, while treating of the destruction of the temple of Serapis, he says: “Very many more people embraced the Christian religion and, confessing their sins, [Col. 1203B] received the baptism of Christ.” Whether this confession, which adults had to make before baptism, concerned specific sins or was merely general is still disputed among critics. It is certain, however, that our sacramental Penance had no place among those preparing for baptism, since baptism itself is a kind of initiation into the remaining sacraments of our Church, granting a person the capacity validly to receive and administer them.

**Let them set forth,** that is, let them display an example in themselves. As Junius says at this passage, the metaphor is taken from merchants setting out their wares. Accordingly, in our baptism we too must display the baptism of John as the forerunner of Christ’s baptism. See above, chapter X, note **He administered beforehand**.

**Their sins.** Junius here reads *nunc*, “now,” in place of *non*, “not,” just as in book I of *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 1, where most manuscripts have: “Those who have heard him”—Christ—“prophesying until NOT long ago veil the virgins,” but Junius judges that NOW should be substituted. Reason itself certainly appears to require this, [Col. 1203C] especially because, as the critics report, that copyists’ error is also accustomed to occur very frequently in other writings.

**For.** This particle causes me to approve Junius’s emendation. For what conflict of flesh and spirit would there otherwise be if that public confession were NOT required? Moreover, from this very point I am almost led to believe that at that time this confession was not merely general but also particular, at least regarding sins already publicly committed. Otherwise, what difficulty would it have involved? See the note **Of sins** above.

**By conflict,** that is, mortification, which produces serious discomfort for our nature from that very conflict. “For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to one another” (Galatians 5:17). This humiliation weighs heavily upon each: upon the spirit because of its native nobility and excellence, and indeed also because of the pride implanted in it through sin; upon the flesh [Col. 1203D] because of its native sluggishness, which shrinks from such noble endeavors. For even toward these “the spirit is sometimes willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew 26:41).

**What he will obtain.** For when Christ preached on the mountain, he called those blessed who suffer persecution for righteousness, “because theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” “Blessed are you,” he continues, “when they revile you and say every evil thing against you,” etc. “Rejoice and exult, because your reward is abundant in heaven; for so they persecuted the Prophets,” etc. (Matthew 5:10ff.). This is also the lesson that Paul and Barnabas so earnestly impressed upon their hearers: “Through many tribulations”—or temptations—“we must enter the kingdom of GOD.” Some believe that Tertullian is instead referring here to Matthew 19:23: “A rich man will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty.”

**From the bath,** that is, after the bath.

**One must fast.** Just as Christ began his fast not before but [Col. 1204A] after baptism.

**Of salvation.** He means here the feast of Easter, which immediately follows Holy Saturday, formerly designated in a special manner as the day for solemn baptism (the preceding chapter). For the paschal jubilation is itself a mutual congratulation upon our salvation, which we, dead in Adam but rising with Christ to a new life, have recovered. Behold, therefore, the most ancient origin of paschal greetings, formerly a token of mutual charity among Christians, which the cunning spirit of this age customarily envelops in deceitful formulas of words and empty ceremonies.

Moreover, the sorrow of fasting is less suited to paschal joy, and accordingly the Church wished fasts to be excluded from these solemnities and indeed from the entire paschal season. Furthermore, the Church ordained that no Sunday should be darkened by fasting, since it wished that day also to be consecrated to the memory of the risen Christ. This is evident from canon 15 of Saint Peter of Alexandria, who flourished toward the end of the third century, [Col. 1204B] after approving the fasts on Wednesdays and Fridays, he says: “But as for the Lord’s Day, it is a joyful day, because Jesus Christ rose on that day.” What, moreover, of the fact that at the Council of Gangra, held in A.D. 370, canon 18, we find that even an anathema was pronounced upon those who, under the pretext of a more austere life, fasted on Sunday? This should not appear surprising, since they were regarded as sharing the practice of the Manichaeans and Priscillianists, who established Sunday as a regular day of fasting. Hence Saint Augustine, in Epistle 86 to Casulanus, when treating of the Saturday fast, etc., calls fasts of this kind “a great scandal” and “horrible.”

**Against him,** namely, against the tempter, the devil.

**With divine provisions,** namely, the manna that rained daily from heaven (Exodus 16:4ff.).

**Than God’s.** Namely, when that ungrateful and gluttonous people repeatedly lamented: “Who will give us meat to eat? . . . Our soul is dry; our eyes behold nothing but manna” (Numbers 11: [Col. 1204C] 4, 6).

**The water,** that is, his baptism in the Jordan.

**Of God.** Junius rightly judged this word redundant.

**By the word.** “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of GOD” (Matthew 4:4). This saying had been transferred here by Christ from Deuteronomy 8:3, where Moses, recalling to the people God’s blessings and the afflictions sent upon them in the desert, says: “He afflicted you with want and gave you manna as food . . . so that he might show you that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of GOD.” This is that figure of Israel from which our author said above that Christ turned the reproach back against the devil.

**To be struck down.** An elegant metaphor. Properly speaking, those are said to be “struck down” whose larger veins of the neck—which are otherwise customarily called *lisae*, and in Greek *σφραγῖτιδες*—are cut. Thus Celsus, book IV of *On Medicine*, chapter 1, says: “The *lisae*, according to Donatus, are the larger veins of the throat; [Col. 1204D] when these are severed, an animal immediately dies.” Hence *elisum* means something dead from such a cause. We likewise say of others carried off by a violent death that they were “struck down,” as Suetonius says in *Caligula*, chapter 26: “More than twenty Roman knights were struck down during that disturbance.” Cicero also uses “struck down by illness” in book V of the *Tusculan Disputations*.

**Birthday.** For it is “the bath of regeneration,” in accordance with Christ’s words to Nicodemus: “Unless a person is born anew, he cannot see the kingdom of GOD” (John 3:3). A person’s first birthday, therefore, is from his mother with respect to the body; the second is from GOD with respect to the soul, which, having died through sin, is reborn through baptism. These are they who were born “not of blood,” etc., “but BORN OF GOD” (John 1:13).

**Mother.** The Church may fittingly be understood here: “Jerusalem above, who is OUR MOTHER” (Galatians 4:26).

**Brothers.** “But we, BROTHERS, [Col. 1205A] like Isaac, are CHILDREN of promise” (ibid., verse 28).

**Possessions.** Not temporal possessions only, but especially the spiritual things necessary or wonderfully conducive to sustaining this new life.

It has been opened to you. Matt. 7:10 ff. And finally Christ adds there: “If you, then, though you are evil, [Col. 1206A] know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your FATHER who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him?”

**Of a sinner.** A remarkable example of humility! Yet how different Tertullian later became from his former self, swelling with the spirit of his Montanus—a spirit that did not, certainly, breathe upon him, but puffed him up!

[Col. 1205]

# DISSERTATION ON THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN BAPTISM AND PENANCE, THE AUTHOR OF THE FOLLOWING BOOK, AND THE DATE OF ITS COMPOSITION

**I.** Having therefore completed Tertullian’s *Book on Baptism*, we are now brought—not, indeed, according to the proper and customary order of our Sacraments, yet not by a leap [Col. 1205B] either—to his *Book on Penance*, which likewise is to be elucidated with certain notes. For the Author himself did not wholly pass over the intermediate Sacraments, Confirmation and the Eucharist. He treated the former, in Chapters VI and VII of his preceding book, by no means cursorily, as a kind of completion of Baptism; while the latter he at least touched upon briefly in Chapter XVI, as we noted there.

**II.** There is, moreover, a certain special connection, founded even upon necessity itself, between Baptism and Penance. For when GOD, the Creator of all things, had launched the First Man upon this universe as upon a vast open sea, and thereafter had appointed him, as it were, admiral of the sea for the whole human race, that man, swept away by the waves of his harmful desire, struck his ship upon the most unyielding rock of Original Sin [Col. 1205C] and caused the most wretched shipwreck not only of himself but of us all. The boundless GOODNESS of our SAVIOR then extended to us a first plank, BAPTISM, by grasping which we might rise again and reach the harbor of salvation. But because he foresaw that, even in this very harbor, there would be many shipwrecks among men who would again be engulfed by new waves, Christ, the same Institutor of the Sacraments, cast out to our enfeebled and excessively unstable will a second plank after shipwreck, PENANCE, by whose aid we might swim back once more to a safe shore. This, indeed, is that BAPTISM which the Council of Trent, Session XIV, Chapter 2, calls TOILSOME; for in it one must labor mightily through the arduous works of Penance, so that offenses may be washed away no longer in another’s font of water, but in [Col. 1205D] our own tears.

**III.** Accordingly, the following Book is joined to the preceding one all the more suitably because that earlier book ended with Penance itself as a preparation necessary for Baptism in adults, whereas this book, like a fitting joint, pursues the same subject more fully and also treats in greater detail that Penance which remains available to those who relapse after Baptism.

**IV.** There is, however, more than one difference between Baptism and Penance.

First, with respect to their end: Baptism was instituted chiefly to destroy original sin and, in adults, the other sins adhering to it; and then so that through it a person might be incorporated into the People of GOD and become a member of the Church. For no other entrance into that Church lies open than through this gate of Baptism, the first of all the Sacraments and one of the most necessary. [Col. 1206A] Penance, by contrast, must be employed to destroy actual sins, and especially those [Col. 1206B] committed subsequently, after Baptism.

Second, with respect to their effect: in Baptism, together with guilt, all liability to punishment is also removed, both eternal and temporal. Penance, however, does not have the same efficacy with regard to the latter; for temporal punishment remains to be discharged in purgatory unless full satisfaction for sins has been rendered in this life through works of penance.

Third, with respect to their intrinsic nature: Baptism is regeneration—spiritual, namely, and according to the soul—which, like carnal generation, can take place only once. Baptism therefore cannot be repeated in one who has once validly received it, since it is sealed with a kind of impressed seal, that is, a character. Penance, however, takes place in the form of a judgment in which a person, as the accused and at the same time his own accuser, [Col. 1206C] is absolved of his offenses. Just as an accused person may be brought before a human tribunal after each new offense and relapse, so one who falls after Baptism, once he has performed penance, must repeat it whenever he relapses again. Penance is therefore never sealed by any character, since the mercy of GOD is never afterward closed to him.

Fourth, with respect to necessity: Baptism is necessary for salvation for all human beings, even infants, who nevertheless are stained only by original sin. Penance, however, is necessary only for adults who are liable for sins committed by their own will, whether before or after Baptism. Nor can there be true and properly so-called penance for original sin, but only penance in the broader sense, namely any displeasure with [Col. 1206D] and detestation of a past evil. I deliberately pass over other differences, since my intention at present is to abstract from the Sacrament of Penance.

**V.** We must now come to the AUTHOR of this Book. No one either formerly doubted or now doubts that he was Tertullian. Erasmus of Rotterdam alone attempted to take it away from Tertullian, and only Beatus Rhenanus followed him; both relied upon this single and certainly rather weak argument: difference of style. I do not deny that the style in this book is somewhat more florid, but it does not differ greatly from that of the other works, even those which Tertullian wrote nearly at the end of his life, and the difference consists only in certain rather more brilliant allegories and metaphors. But if there were leisure to pluck similar blossoms from the other little plots of this same author, [Col. 1207A] I could easily weave whole garlands.

**VI.** Besides, critics of the highest reputation long ago perceived that from any mere discrepancy of style—unless supported by other and weightier arguments—an author can scarcely be rendered suspect, much less can any judgment be pronounced against him. Of these critics I cite even one, William Cave, who in the Prolegomena to his *Historia Literaria*, Section IV, no. 64, says that an argument for νοθεύσεως (*notheuseōs*), or spurious attribution, is supplied only when the style and the whole texture of the discourse are FAR DIFFERENT from the manner of expression employed by an author in his genuine works. Yet any reader will discover that it is so far from being greatly different that, apart from a few somewhat more animated phrases which scarcely occur in Tertullian’s other writings, that African and [Col. 1207B] concise mode of expression almost peculiar to Tertullian, that peculiar majesty of style, that abundance of meaning in almost every word, and that lofty eloquence—which, however harsh it may be, can nevertheless somehow draw even an unwilling reader toward itself—triumph no less in this book. I say nothing of other phrases so carefully reproduced from his other books, which I shall intentionally note in their proper places.

**VII.** Beatus Rhenanus himself then admits that the author of this book uses the same words and figures, that whoever he was undoubtedly belonged to Tertullian’s age, and that he was a most devoted student of Tertullian. Why, then, should he not be TERTULLIAN himself? For what other person could have reproduced his assuredly singular style, scarcely capable of imitation by anyone, so skillfully that he deceived St. Pacian, a writer of the fourth century, and all others for more than [Col. 1207C] eleven centuries down to Erasmus, into accepting him as Tertullian himself, while no one ever suspected from a difference of style that this Book had another author?

**VIII.** We therefore judge, finally, that nothing more can be inferred from that discrepancy of style, whatever its degree, than that Tertullian undertook this composition while he was still of more vigorous age and livelier talent. For minds of this fervent and agile kind are accustomed, like bees, to fly around among various flowers, to draw allegories and metaphors even from matters foreign to their subject, and carry them into their own hive, and so forth. Likewise, as age advances little by little, the style is accustomed to settle down and become more restrained and robust. Thus TULLY himself, the Prince of Orators, delivered his speeches for Publius Quinctius and Roscius of Ameria—the former his very first speech, delivered when he was twenty-six years old, [Col. 1207D] as Aulus Gellius reports in *Attic Nights*, Book XV, Chapter 28, and the latter in court in the following year. Some think that he sprinkled them, especially the latter, somewhat too freely with such florid ornaments—Malon, his last teacher, having vainly attempted to restrain from this verbal exuberance so vivid and flourishing a talent—although others even praise him for them. For as he gradually reached maturer age and this floral adornment fell away of its own accord, he ripened into fruits all the more enduring, and the more manly gravity and majesty of his eloquence was thereafter, as it were, consolidated.

**IX.** Finally, one will not easily find any writer who remains perpetually consistent with himself, especially if he has not carried his pen through one continuous work but across diverse and [Col. 1208A] unconnected subjects, at different times and with intervals of years. For one subject is by its very nature rather somber or humble and more barren, enough to blunt and depress even the vigor of a youthful talent, and before which the otherwise rich eloquence of men withers. Another subject, however, is more agreeable and pleasant and better suited to the author’s own disposition, and can sufficiently rouse and stimulate a talent otherwise rather languid. A final kind is so lively and diffuses something so radiant that it can kindle and inflame the writer completely, and even sometimes revive sparks long dormant beneath the gray ashes of old age. There are also other things that come to a writer from elsewhere and, as it were, obliquely, yet can sometimes do much to alter his disposition, [Col. 1208B] so to speak. Why, then, is it surprising if Tertullian too is not everywhere consistent with himself, but when he first turned to writing, though already of more mature age, used a somewhat more spirited style, which afterward settled down somewhat in his other books and compensated, as it were, by being adorned with a greater apparatus of learning? But let this have been said ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ (*hōs en parodōi*, “by way of digression”), although at somewhat excessive length.

**X.** But if the actual DATE of composition must now be designated somewhat more closely—although that cannot be done precisely—I think that this treatise was certainly committed to writing before A.D. 200, and probably in the year 197 or perhaps earlier. Certainly the dates of both this work and the other, *On Baptism*, were not far apart.

[Col. 1208C] **XI.** Whether, however, in the order of composition he placed the book *On Baptism* after this book *On Penance*, or this book after that one, can scarcely be determined. Yet it seems more probable to me that he placed this one afterward. For if he had written *On Penance* first, I believe that in the final chapter of *On Baptism*, where he discusses Penance as a preparation to be placed before Baptism, he would have made some mention of it as a subject already treated more fully elsewhere. Certainly in the book *On Baptism* itself, at the end of Chapter 15, he carefully refers his readers to another treatise on the same subject, previously composed in Greek. Who, then, will appear to judge wrongly if he says that Tertullian afterward adopted a new plan and undertook a fuller treatment, in a separate book, of this subject of Penance which he had treated somewhat briefly at the end of the book *On Baptism*? [Col. 1208D] He did so partly for the sake of catechumens, so that they might conceive a greater appreciation of the value of Baptism, which they would understand had to be obtained through such toilsome works of penance. Why, then, should they not afterward exercise themselves in these works with all the more ardent zeal, so that they might the more certainly obtain the so lavishly proposed reward of Baptism and its grace, and afterward preserve it all the more safely?

**XII.** Finally, we should hear the splendid judgment on this book delivered by Beatus Rhenanus himself, a man of great discernment, in the prefatory summary attached to it: namely, that this Commentary is such that theologians ought to learn it perfectly, “to the fingernail.” “For,” he continues, “it is an outstanding monument of antiquity: so holily [Col. 1209A] does it teach, so devoutly persuade, so insistently urge a matter supremely necessary to ecclesiastical discipline—*exomologesis*, that is, the act and ministry of Penance.” Certainly, just as we everywhere learn from Tertullian the traditions and discipline of the ancient Church, so here too, with signal [Col. 1210A] usefulness against our innovators, we are beautifully and solidly taught the manner of performing penance as it was customarily performed from the earliest centuries, and assuredly by apostolic institution. But let us now proceed to the subject itself.

[Col. 1209]

# BOOK ON PENANCE

**Chapter I.** Penance ought to concern only evil deeds, not good works.

**II.** True Penance is that which concerns evils, or offenses against GOD.

**III.** Penance must be performed for all sins, whether external or merely internal. [Col. 1209B]

**IV.** An exhortation to embrace Penance, which is as necessary to offenders as it is beneficial.

**V.** Penance must not be effaced by new sins, nor performed only in the mind, but also in actual deed.

**VI.** Catechumens are not therefore without need of penance merely because their sins are ultimately to be destroyed through Baptism itself. [Col. 1210A]

**VII.** Those who fall after Baptism must again perform penance.

**VIII.** That Penance must be performed as often as a person has sinned is confirmed by examples from Holy Scripture.

[Col. 1210B] **IX.** What *Exomologesis* is, and what its principal works are.

**X.** Public confession of sins must neither be a cause of shame nor be postponed.

**XI.** Nor should bodily hardships deter us from performing penance.

**XII.** The exhortation to penance is confirmed by examples set forth.

# Notes on Chapter I

[Col. 1209B]

**Penance.** According to St. Isidore, Bishop of Seville, *Origins*, Book IV, Chapter 19, *poenitentia* (“penance”) was so called as though it were *punientia* (“punishment”), because by repenting a person punishes in himself what he has done wrong. The author of the book *On True and False Penance*—formerly ascribed to St. Augustine—says almost the same in Chapter 19: [Col. 1209C] “To repent is the same as to maintain punishment, so that a person may continually punish in himself by taking vengeance upon what he committed by sinning.” In Greek it is called μετάνοια (*metanoia*), “a change of mind,” or of one’s former judgment, from μετανοεῖν (*metanoein*), which means “to understand afterward,” or “to become wise after the event.” In this same sense it is also called μετάγνωσις (*metagnōsis*), μετάγνοια (*metagnoia*), and μεταμέλεια (*metameleia*).

**This kind of men.** Here he censures the Gentiles, and especially their philosophers.

**We formerly were.** For Tertullian, born of Gentile parents and raised in paganism, did not turn to the Christian rites until he was already fairly advanced in age, as we indicated in the epitome of his Life prefixed to the book *On Prescription*, drawing upon his own testimony in the *Apology*, Chapter 18.

**By the light of God.** By faith, namely, which is the supernatural light of the soul.

**So far as nature extends**, that is, solely according to the guidance of natural reason, or so far as the light innate in our intellect itself extends.

[Col. 1209D] **Of the former judgment.** This is a general definition drawn from moral philosophy. He therefore says that penance is a movement, alteration, or certain affection of the mind, joined with a certain distress and arising from aversion to the former judgment or opinion from which something was done. For when someone now understands that he formerly acted less than rightly and thus incurred some loss or disadvantage, a certain movement afterward arises in his mind from the sense of that distress or offense. He therefore now changes and retracts his former judgment, having conceived displeasure with it and a certain hatred of it; and those philosophers suppose that the true nature of penance consists in this. Thus, some writers cited by Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, Book XVII, Chapter 1, say: “We customarily say that we repent when things we ourselves have done, or which were done by our will and counsel, afterward begin to displease us, and we change our judgment concerning them.”

**Nature**, or true conception and definition.

**Its Author.** Supply: “by rightly knowing him.” And how could those know him whose understanding was so blinded that they located Divinity in the stars, human beings, beasts, and every sort of basest creature? [Col. 1210B]

**Ordered.** For he made all these things according to the counsels of his infinite WISDOM.

**Strangers**, that is, those placed outside and alienated from knowledge of the true God.

**Storm.** We have already spoken of this florid allegory in the intervening Dissertation. [Col. 1210C]

**They dwell.** He also uses this verb in the book *Against the Valentinians*, Chapter 30: “He who dwelt in the world,” etc. But other manuscripts, and certainly better ones, have *diversentur*. Whichever form we believe Tertullian used, the expression will always be rendered more idiomatically in Latin by *conversentur*, “they dwell” or “associate.”

**To resolve.** In the sense of “to refute” or “to place beyond doubt.”

**Unto displeasure**, or it happens as something unwelcome, troublesome, or unpleasant. *Ingratia*, therefore—an obsolete word—is used here for displeasure at another’s deed. He also uses this word shortly afterward in Chapter 2. A parallel passage occurs in Book II *Against Marcion*, Chapter 24: “For it does not follow that, because a person repents from recollection of a great offense, and sometimes even from displeasure at some good work, God therefore does likewise.”

**Is inflicted.** In the sense of “is applied,” “expended,” “imposed,” “brought upon,” and so forth, as Plautus says in the *Captives*:

[Col. 1210D] “I shall appoint a day against them and inflict punishment.”

And Cicero says in *On His House*: “The Twelve Tables forbid laws to be imposed upon private persons.” Tacitus too, *Annals*, Book IV, Chapter 10, says of Drusus that, “when the poison had been drained, he increased suspicion, as though he were inflicting upon himself the death he had contrived for his father.” Again, Cicero in *For Rabirius* spoke of “the imposition of a fine.” Others understand *irrogare* in the sense of *erogare*, “to pay out,” whose meaning is almost the same as the former. We have already spoken of the word *erogare* in the book *On Prescription*, Chapter II, note “In the act,” though in a different sense. But let these matters be left to grammarians.

**On the contrary.** The word *contra* must certainly be marked with an accent, so as to mean “contrariwise” or “on the opposing side.”

# Notes on Chapter II

**Reason.** For reason is a thing of God and was given to us by divine gift, as our Author said above.

**Merits**, that is, considerations or grounds, in the sense in which jurists customarily speak of the “merits of a case.” It may also be understood here as utility [Col. 1211A] or benefit.

**They would weigh.** That is, weigh as though in a balance.

**They would maintain.** By not preparing for themselves material for repenting so often and so long.

**For salvation.** “For sorrow according to God produces a steadfast PENANCE UNTO SALVATION.” 2 Cor. 7:10.

**Inaugurated.** Elsewhere too our Author uses the verb *auspicor* passively. Thus in the book *On Patience*, Chapter 5, he says: “Since it is manifest that impatience was inaugurated together with malice, or malice by impatience.” And in the book *On the Soldier’s Crown*, Chapter 1: “There he laid aside his very heavy cloak, beginning to be relieved.” Properly, however, *auspicari* means “to watch birds”—for the ancients said *spicere* in place of *aspicere*, “to behold”—when from their flight, song, or feeding people took auspices. For they customarily undertook nothing without first consulting the birds, and only then believed that they had begun their business auspiciously and successfully, with favorable auspices and birds.

Among the ancients the active form *auspico* is also found, as [Col. 1211B] in Plautus’s *The Persian*: “I took the auspices for this day”; and in the work *Against Cato on His Consulship*: “After I had taken the auspices, and the army,” etc. But I am certainly excessive in these grammatical trifles.

**With a dowry.** He means Paradise and the other temporal gifts bestowed upon Adam.

**Had hastened**, that is, God had betaken himself promptly, or at a timely and appropriate moment. There appears to be a difference between “to mature” and “to hasten” or “accelerate”: the latter signifies mere speed, while the former signifies speed joined with deliberation. Thus delay is entirely absent from speed, but is mingled with maturation. Speed also sometimes does harm, whereas maturation never does. Hence the Greek maxim of Caesar Augustus was ΣΠΕΥΔΕ ΒΡΑΔΕΩΣ (*speude bradeōs*), “MAKE HASTE SLOWLY.” That is, he thought maturation coalesced, as it were, from two things otherwise opposed to one another: the speed of industriousness and the slowness of diligence. If these are duly proportioned, we call a business mature and say that it is now being done at the proper time. Thus also we call fruits that develop too quickly, as though nature were hurrying them forth, premature: they are rarely flavorful or durable. But those which grow by slower increments than is fitting mature more rarely and generally remain unripe, suitable neither for use nor for food. [Col. 1211C]

I do not, however, deny that *maturare* is sometimes used for “to hasten” or “act quickly.” That elegant statement found in St. Cyprian’s *Letter to Donatus* deserves to be cited here: “Receive what is perceived before it is learned and is not gathered through delays of time by prolonged cognition, but is imbibed through the short course of hastening grace.”

**Inaugurated.** On this word see the book *On Baptism*, Chapter XIX, note “Inaugurated.” Our Author generally uses this verb when he wishes to signify something new, as in the *Apology*, Chapter 12: “The body of your god is first inaugurated upon a gibbet”; and in the book *On the Soul*, Chapter 19, concerning a newborn infant: “Inaugurating all the senses at once,” he says, “sight by light, hearing by sound,” etc. Likewise, in the book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, Chapter 11, he says that “the universe”—this world—“was inaugurated by God.” In these and similar passages the word therefore seems to be understood as “to initiate”; in this sense he says that God inaugurated penance in himself as an example for us. [Col. 1211D]

Furthermore, repentance is predicated of God, like other properties of human affections of this kind, ἀνθρωποπαθῶς (*anthrōpopathōs*), “in an anthropopathic manner.” “In human beings,” says St. Augustine in Book II *To Simplicianus*, Question 2, “there is an act of repenting when a will is found that must be changed; but in a human being it is accompanied by mental pain, for he reproves in himself what he did rashly. Let us therefore remove,” he continues, “those things which arise from human weakness and ignorance, and let only the WILL that something should not be as it was remain. In this way there can be intimated to our mind the rule according to which it may be understood that GOD repents. For when he is said to repent, he wills that something should not be as he had made it to be. Yet while it existed, it was right that it should exist in that way; and when it is no longer permitted to exist in that way, it ought no longer so to exist. This is done by a perpetual and tranquil judgment of equity, by which God disposes all mutable things with an IMMUTABLE WILL.” Again, on Psalm 131: “When he changes his works through his immutable counsel, he is said to repent because of the change not in his counsel, [Col. 1212A] but in his work.” You will find similar statements in the same author’s *Eighty-Three Questions*, Question 52, and in the author of the book *On the Essence of Divinity* among the works of St. Augustine.

**Of acts of anger.** God indeed also becomes angry, but by no means as a human being does. “Human anger,” St. Augustine again says in Book II *To Simplicianus*, in the question cited, “is turbulent; but the anger of God, while he himself continually remains in TRANQUILLITY, executes vengeance upon the subjected creature with wondrous equity. . . . From human anger I remove the turbulent movement, so that the vigor of vengeance may remain; and thus, in some measure, I rise to a knowledge of what is called the ANGER OF GOD.” Shall I also add what he says in Book I *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*, Chapter 20? “When God repents, HE IS NOT CHANGED, yet he changes things; just as when he becomes angry, HE IS NOT CHANGED, yet he takes vengeance.”

**To his image**, that is, to the human being created in his image. Gen. 1:26 ff. Recall, if you wish, what we said fairly fully in Chapter V of *On Baptism*, note “To the image of God,” 1159A.

**Gathered.** As God said in Exod. 6:7: “I shall take you to myself as a people, and I shall be your God,” etc. So too [Col. 1212B] in very many other passages.

**He exhorted.** The books of Sacred History are full of these things; the books of Exodus and Judges in particular abound with examples of this kind.

**For prophesying.** Rhenanus says that this is a dative and means “in order to prophesy.”

**Sent forth.** For our Author, *emittere* means either simply “to send,” or, with greater emphasis, “to send forth from oneself,” so that they might prophesy in his own name, namely God’s.

**About to illuminate.** This was fulfilled on the day of Pentecost through those fiery tongues, when Peter shortly afterward declared in his address, Acts 2:17–18: “This is what was foretold through the prophet Joel: ‘And it shall be in the last days,’ says the Lord, ‘I shall pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy,’” etc. This is the very thing previously foretold in Isa. 44:3, where God says: “I shall pour out my Spirit upon your offspring,” etc. Furthermore, “to illuminate for the whole world” seems to have been taken from the Greek phrase in the Canticle [Col. 1212C] of Zechariah, Luke 1:[79]: ἐπιφᾶναι τοῖς ἐν σκότει καὶ σκιᾷ θανάτου καθημένοις (*epiphanai tois en skotei kai skiai thanatou kathēmenois*), that is, “TO ILLUMINATE—to bring light to—THOSE who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death.”

**Immersion**, or the baptism of penance, which John preached for the remission of sins. Mark 1:4.

**Appointed.** Namely, Gen. 12:3, where God says to Abraham: “In you all the kindreds of the earth shall be blessed.” And Isa. 41:8: “The offspring of Abraham, my friend, in whom I took hold of you from the ends of the earth . . . and said to you, ‘You are my servant; I have chosen you and have not rejected you,’” etc. And so very often elsewhere.

**Countersignature**, that is, the signature attached to that promise in the manner of a condition, so that the people of Israel would likewise bind themselves to keep that covenant.

**Might prepare**, in the sense of “might arrange” or “adapt,” as St. John admonishes: “Prepare the way of the Lord,” etc. Mark 1:3.

**Will draw near.** For thus John says to the people in the wilderness, Matt. 3:2: “Perform penance, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” [Col. 1212D]

**Ancient error.** Original Sin.

**Ignorance.** Sins committed through ignorance—that is, vincible and culpable ignorance.

**Sweeping.** Cleansing as if with brooms, for these are properly what we sweep with; thus Matt. 12:[44] says: “He finds it swept clean.”

**Scraping.** Those stains, or other things, which have settled somewhat more deeply are scraped off; hence we also speak of shaving a beard, etc.

**Lies open.** For receiving him in Baptism, but more fully through the subsequent imposition of Hands.

**Gladly.** Finding nothing now unseemly in this dwelling of his, but rather everything clean and worthy of himself.

**Cause.** The final cause, namely.

**This work.** *Opera* is used here for labor, as our Author likewise says in the book *On Patience*, Chapter 16: “This is the principle of patience, this its discipline, this its heavenly and true labor,” etc. And in the book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, Chapter 15: “Let them deny the fellowship of labors, so that they may deservedly deny the reward also.” [Col. 1213A]

**Benefits a human being**, that is, contributes to his advancement, as in the book *On Baptism*, Chapter VII.

**Its nature**, namely Penance.

**We learn.** For if this is unknown, the true nature of penance must necessarily be unknown. See above, Chapter I: “Therefore all who are ignorant of God,” etc.

**Be thrust upon.** By violently twisting penance, contrary to its own nature, so as to apply even to good works, which would thereafter be hindered by it.

**And**, in the sense of “also.”

**Let him see to it.** A form of expression frequently used by our Author.
