Thus in the *Apology*, Chapter 16, he says: “Let the appearance see to itself, provided the quality of the material is the same; let the form see to itself, provided it is the very body of God,” etc.; and in the book *On Patience*, Chapter 16: “Let his own people see to their own affairs”; and in the book *On the Shows*, Chapter 15: “Let the principal title of idolatry see to itself,” etc. We therefore generally use this phrase when we warn another who has been brought into some danger to take care concerning it and look after his own affair. [Col. 1213B] Thus Cicero says in the *Brutus*: “You will see to this,” that is, “I leave the care of this matter to you, lest, if anything happens otherwise, you impute it to me.” And Terence says in the *Brothers*: “I shall see to that”—as though he said, “That will be my concern.”

**Unto displeasure.** See Chapter I, note “Displeasure.” But what if I explain the sentence in this way: “Let the perverse opinion of men, certainly displeasing to others, see to itself,” etc.? Or: “If those whom we have benefited begin to displease us and to be ungrateful—that is, hateful—to us.”

**Forces penance.** The sense appears to be: “If it compels, drives, and twists penance, as though reluctant and contrary to its nature, even toward evil deeds.”

**Its pursuit.** The pursuit of favor is the desire to conciliate another’s favor and goodwill toward oneself, so that we may please the other and be pleasing—that is, acceptable—to him. For a person who confers a benefit upon another is rarely found either not to desire to please him or not to hope for and seek some advantage that will return to himself. Thus we love ourselves everywhere [Col. 1213C] and excessively.

**Mortal**, that is, temporal and destined at some point to end—both favor and displeasure, namely.

**Of gain.** Or profit and advantage, as the best Authors everywhere use the word.

**A debtor.** Of reward, namely.

**Evil.** Punishment, certainly.

**Rewarder**, that is, one who renders recompense.

**May decree**, in the sense of “may establish.” To decree is to establish something which cannot be violated with impunity.

**Must be rendered.** By repairing through satisfaction his supreme Right, which has been violated by sins.

**Private.** Latinius deletes *privatum* as otherwise introducing remarkable obscurity into the passage. I think, however, that it can be retained without difficulty, and understand “private” here as “one’s own,” as our Author says more explicitly in the book *On the Shows*, Chapter 10: “things which are private and proper to the stage,” etc. And Cicero says in Book III *On Ends*: “In speaking, nevertheless, they employ words that are, as it were, private and their own.”

**Duty.** What duty, however, can belong to malice except among those doctrines of which Tully says near the beginning of Book I *On Duties*: “There are certain schools which, by establishing ends of good and evil, throw every duty into confusion”? Here, however, our Author appears instead to have followed the etymology of the word, concerning which St. Ambrose says in Book I *On Duties*, Chapter 8: “We think that *officium* (‘duty’) is so called from *efficiendo* (‘performing’), as though it were *efficium*,” etc. In this sense even malice has its own “duty,” though improperly and only according to the name, being empty of the reality. Yet, as the words immediately following suggest, I rather think it should be understood thus: “It even expends upon goodness—or upon good works and benefits conferred upon another—the duty proper toward malice, namely that we should repent of evil.” [Col. 1213D]

**May be neglected.** See what was said at the end of Chapter I.

# Notes on Chapter III

**Spirit.** The soul, or its intellect.

[Col. 1214A] **Regard.** As though by rays emitted into it from God, the source of all Light.

**Precepts**, namely, precepts to be known.

**Must be reckoned.** Must be numbered among sins.

**May be a human being.** As consisting of body and soul.

**The two make one.** For the soul joined to the body makes one human being.

**Materials.** Or constituent parts, which are, as it were, the matter of the whole.

**A thing of God.** As he said above in Chapter I: “Reason is a thing of God.”

**Fashioned.** For God formed man—that is, his body—from the clay of the earth. Gen. 2:7.

**By his breath.** “And he breathed into his face the breath of life, and MAN became a living soul.” Ibid.

**Offends.** Tertullian did not mean by this that all sins are equal, as the Stoics thought. He meant only that because some sins are carnal and others spiritual—or some are committed through the body, while others subsist in the soul and its will alone—the greater gravity [Col. 1214B] of one sin over another must not be measured from this fact.

**Into judgment.** Namely, the fire of eternity; for “judgment” is here opposed to life—that is, eternal life. See what we said in the book *On Baptism*, Chapter X, note “Into judgment.”

**For that reason.**

**To expend.** Thus the body too must necessarily participate in penance, namely through perceptible and external acts and bodily afflictions, while the soul participates through inward sorrow, etc.

**Belongs to both.** For just as actions are said to belong to subjects, so neither the body alone nor the soul alone sins, but the Human Being, who is composed of body and soul and constitutes one subject or person. To this person actions, both good and evil, are imputed.

**Is performed.** Namely, by some external and perceptible work.

**Is thought.** And is retained merely within the mind.

**Is capable of being perceived.** “To be perceived” is not used here solely of the sense of touch, but also of perception by the other senses. [Col. 1214C] Furthermore, *contingi habet* (“has to be perceived”) in the sense of “can be perceived” is a Hellenism; for the Greeks customarily say, for example, οὐδεὶς εἰπεῖν ἔχει (*oudeis eipein echei*), “no one can speak.”

**Nor is apprehended.** That is, it is reached by no sense.

**Sins of the will.** Merely internal sins, namely.

**Mediocrity.** Human limitation, which, as though placed at the boundaries, cannot penetrate farther or reach the very heart of the matter. Human limitation, therefore, is such that it perceives only external acts—and not even these always or with sufficient certainty—while it is unable to look upon internal acts.

**Is not competent.** For even the Praetor himself does not judge internal things.

**Under God.** Namely, with no regard for God.

**Whence**, that is, through which thing and in whatever manner.

**May decide unto judgment.** For he first decides that one is to go to judgment before, in the judgment itself, he decides and pronounces sentence. Or perhaps he understands “judgment” here as condemnation itself and the punishment of eternal fire, as an example occurred above. Or, finally, this agrees with what appears at the beginning of the following Chapter: [Col. 1214D] “He appointed punishment THROUGH JUDGMENT.”

**Is the origin.** For otherwise it cannot be considered ours or imputed to us.

**When therefore.** Supply: “the will.”

**Is released.** This can be understood of the will, which is released or absolved from guilt; or of guilt itself, which is released, that is, removed. Thus we are also said “to release promises” when we remove and cancel their obligation by fulfilling them.

**Intercepts.** So that it cannot issue forth into the work itself and be consummated. For, as Festus says, a person *perpetrates* when he carries out and completes the work itself. The word is used especially of evil deeds, although we sometimes find it said even of good ones.

**It had done its own part.** Insofar as it lay within the will itself, efficaciously willing something, it had already accomplished it. Hence, as our Theologians commonly say, the external act does not superinduce a new species of sin upon the internal act; rather, [Col. 1215A] the former is the mere completion of the latter.

Addition to the law. For, to the sixth commandment of the Decalogue, by which adultery and so forth are forbidden, he also added a new commandment, by which even the inward will, although it has not been completed in deed, is made subject to guilt.

At close quarters. Or, in the act itself.

Would have defiled. “Everyone who looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart,” says Christ, Matthew 5:28.

To administer, i.e., to act, or in any manner whatsoever to contribute to the action.

Cancels out [*expungit*]. This word, which our author uses frequently, must be examined somewhat more carefully, since, unless it is properly understood, it can sometimes create great obscurity. First of all, it should be noted that creditors formerly wrote the names of their debtors upon wax tablets with a stylus. But when those debts had been discharged and the creditor’s claim thereby dissolved, they were accustomed either to pierce those names with points or to erase them with the reversed stylus, and thus to cancel them out [*expungere*]. Hence it came about [Col. 1215B] that this word, by a metaphor derived from that practice, was used to mean “to fulfill” and “to complete.”

But let us now produce examples from our Tertullian himself, and first of all the passage that he has in Book I *Against the Jews*, chapter 11, which is clearer than the rest: “Nor should they call into doubt or deny the things that we bring forward as written—so that those things foretold as destined to occur after Christ may be recognized as fulfilled. For,” he continues, “the dispensation would not be found completed [*expuncta*] unless he had come, after whom the things proclaimed were to be completed, and thereby proved to have been fulfilled.” So too in the same work, chapter 4, he has: “The abolition of fleshly circumcision and of the Old Law is shown to have been completed”—fulfilled and consummated—“in its own times.” Again, chapter 9: “The prophecy is understood to have been proclaimed just as it is believed to have been completed,” i.e., fulfilled. Likewise, chapter 12: “They will not have been prophesied concerning anyone other than him through whom we perceive them to have been completed.”

The word also recurs several times in the *Apology Against the Gentiles*, as in chapter 2: “The guilty man must discharge the debt of punishment”—i.e., that debt must be fulfilled by him [Col. 1215C], or the sentence pronounced against him must be carried into execution—“not be exempted from it.” And in chapter 15 he says that lust is “discharged,” that is, satisfied or completed. Likewise, chapter 20: “Prophecy, when foretelling the future among men, has but one tense, if perhaps it is distinguished while it is being fulfilled,” etc. And in chapter 21 he says of Christ, “who has now fulfilled [what was foretold] in the lowliness of the human condition.” Also in chapter 35: “For why do we, chaste, sober, and upright men, fulfill the vows and rejoicings of the Caesars?” Finally, chapter 48: “Then the whole human race will be restored, to discharge what it has deserved, whether good or evil, in this age.”

But let us examine the rest of his books as well. Thus in the book *On Patience*, chapter 14, he has: “He fulfilled every form of patience against every power of the devil.” And in the book *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 1: “The soldiers crowned with laurel were checked off in the camp.” For when they passed by in numerical order to receive the donative, after receiving it the names of the individuals were either marked with a point or wholly crossed out, as persons for whom that distribution had now been concluded and completed. In the book *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, chapter 6: “How many have been killed by robbers [Col. 1215D] with the sword, by enemies even upon the cross, first tortured, and indeed subjected to every indignity?” That is, with every indignity as it were consummated upon them. And in Book II *Against Marcion*, chapter 20: “He satisfied his people, in the straits of their expedition, with some consolation of tacit compensation,” or “fulfilled their need.” Thus in the book *On Prayer*, chapter 1, he calls the Gospel “the fulfiller of all former antiquity,” since in it, through Christ, all the things prefigured in the Old Law were fulfilled and consummated. Finally, in the book *On Idolatry*, chapter 16, he says: “If neither in the invocation nor in the sacrifice there is any designation of duty and fulfillment of my service”—that is, its performance and the fulfillment of the duty—“what then?” etc. Here you see that almost all these passages return to the same meaning. Therefore, by the phrase “the will fulfills the effect,” he meant that the very will to bring something about is already regarded as the deed itself fulfilled, as the context itself demonstrates. See also *On Prescription*, chapter 10.

[Col. 1216A] Satisfying. In the sense of filling out and completing.

May count as the deed, i.e., may be regarded as the deed.

## Notes on Chapter IV

Has pledged. Therefore, no kind of sin, however grave, is excluded from the hope of pardon and the fruit of repentance. This is again a clear indication that, when Tertullian wrote these words, he had not yet been corrupted by Montanus. For here he makes no distinction, as he does in the book *On Modesty*, chapter 2—when he was already an open Montanist—between remissible and irremissible sins. “According to this difference among offenses,” he continues there, “the condition of repentance is likewise distinguished. One kind will be able to obtain pardon, namely for a remissible offense; another will in no way be able to obtain it, namely for an irremissible offense.” He then proceeds to examine the various kinds of sins. But perhaps we shall treat this matter more fully elsewhere.

Repent, i.e., perform repentance; for in accordance with [Col. 1216B] this idiom our Vulgate translator twice uses *poeniteor* in the sense of a deponent verb: namely, Mark 1:15, where Christ says, “Repent” (the Greek has μετανοεῖτε, “repent”), “and believe the Gospel”; likewise Acts 3:19, where St. Peter says to the people, “Repent” (μετανοήσατε, “repent”) “and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out.” The Latins use the verb *poenitet* as an impersonal, more rarely as a personal verb, and scarcely ever as a deponent.

As I live. A formula by which God frequently swears by himself.

Preeminence. He uses this word in a bad sense for excellence, in the sense in which St. Paul, 1 Timothy 1:15, called himself the foremost among sinners, as though surpassing all others in the gravity of his sins.

I acknowledge. This was the voice of Tertullian while he still thought humbly of himself, not that of the proud Montanist insolently rising against the Church herself.

Faith, or faithfulness in saving. And hence [Col. 1216C] repentance was afterward called “the second plank after shipwreck.” St. Ambrose, or another author, beautifully imitated this passage in the *Epistle to a Fallen Virgin*, addressing her thus: “But you, who have now entered the contest of repentance, persevere bravely, wretched woman; cling to the plank like a SHIPWRECKED PERSON.” St. Jerome likewise, in Epistle VIII to Demetrias, speaking in the same way about repentance, says: “That plank, as it were, the SECOND AFTER SHIPWRECK for the wretched,” etc. And thereafter other holy Fathers adopted this phrase.

Will raise completely [*perlevabit*]. Some manuscripts read *perlavabit*, “will wash completely”; but unless I am mistaken, absurdly. For is someone who has sunk beneath the waves to be washed still further, or rather to be raised up and drawn out?

Will draw forward [*protelabit*]. *Protelare* means to advance or propel something *protelo*, that is, in a continuous draft, as oxen bound to the same yoke are accustomed to proceed with an equal and even impulse. Hence that long strap which binds them to the yoke was formerly called a *protelum*. From this comes Cato’s statement in *On Agriculture*: “Three oxen [Col. 1216D] will draw one plow in continuous draft.” There is no doubt that this word is of Greek origin and, as Donatus maintains, derived from πρό, “before,” and ἑλεῖν, “to draw.” Others derive it from τῆλε or τηλόθι, “far,” because in a *protelum* a rather lengthy drawing takes place. The word also has various figurative senses, concerning which the grammarians may be consulted, if one has leisure.

Unexpected. For the plank is sought in vain by a shipwrecked person unless it suddenly offers itself when hope is already at its last gasp.

Of minds, i.e., of wills. For will anyone value a servant’s obedience if it disagrees with his master’s will?

Through this, i.e., for this reason. Other manuscripts have “in proportion to this,” that is, “to so great a breadth of the subject.”

Constraints. Those, namely, of ability, time, or a treatment circumscribed in any other way.

It is good. And useful to us.

To listen. He takes it here in the sense of obeying. But I warn the [Col. 1217A] reader here to no purpose.

The advantage of the servant. Advantage, therefore, must be subordinated to the command. Yet this very thing is itself far more full of infinite advantage and reward: to have obeyed GOD when he commands, even without regard to advantage.

You turn it over. Or, you deliberate too anxiously within yourself; for that is what scrupulous people are accustomed to do.

He commands. What can be more powerful than these two little words, or more effective in thoroughly subjecting us so that we fulfill his commands?

He exhorts. But is “to exhort”—so familiar a word—greater than TO COMMAND? Indeed it is; for one who commands acts by his authority, but one who exhorts, even while commanding, is at the same time gracious: he presses his command, yet at the same time accommodates that very command to our weakness, and simultaneously shows that, in the very thing he has commanded, he is ready to help us fulfill it.

Salvation. This indeed can be wholly DIVINE and proper to the MERCY OF GOD alone.

[Col. 1217B] Saying, “As I live.” Passages of this kind are innumerable, especially in the Prophets.

By an oath. For “with a sworn oath.”

By an asseveration, i.e., by a promise, or perhaps better, by an assurance of fulfillment.

## Notes on Chapter V

To be unsealed. That is, after that repentance had been ratified and sealed by God through his grace, that seal must never again be broken by new sins, through expelling that grace once more.

Pretext. He also uses *praetextum* in the neuter gender in the book *On the Dress of Women*, chapter 9, where he says to the same women: “Do not claim unbridled license under the pretext of necessity,” etc. And in the book *Against the Valentinians*, chapter 9, he says: “under the pretext of affection for the Father,” etc.

You are separated, i.e., you withdraw from it, namely toward the knowledge of God.

You are glued to it. Made the more obstinate, the less you know.

[Col. 1217C] To fear. For just as the fear of the Lord is the beginning of WISDOM (Psalm 110:10), so too it is the beginning of repentance. Thus the Council of Trent, Session VI, *On Justification*, chapter 6, says concerning this: “They are disposed toward repentance when, understanding that they are sinners, they turn from the fear of DIVINE JUSTICE, by which they are profitably shaken, to consider the MERCY OF GOD,” etc. And again in Session XIV, chapter 4: “Attrition, conceived from fear of punishment, is an impulse of the HOLY SPIRIT by whose assistance the penitent prepares a way for himself toward justice.”

Obstinacy. Here he calls perseverance in evil “obstinacy,” by which the heart gradually hardens and wholly banishes the fear of God. For, as Ecclesiasticus 27:4 says, “Unless you hold yourself steadfastly in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overthrown.” Would that it could be restored from those most wretched ruins with equal ease and speed.

It is not permissible to remain ignorant. You will read nothing more elegant upon this subject than our Tertullian’s little book *On the Testimony of the Soul*, a work indeed weighty with substantial thoughts.

[Col. 1217D] By God’s gift. He refers again to what he had said above in chapter 1: “REASON IS A THING OF GOD.”

His rival. He meant the unhappy and excessively impudent ape of God. In the book *On Prescription*, chapter 40, you will read how this plotter against the human race long ago attempted to imitate the mysteries of God.

By returning. Or, by relapsing into former sins.

The Evil One. The devil, so called by way of eminence, as among the Greeks he is called ὁ Πονηρός, “the Evil One.” So too in the book *On Patience*, chapter 11, he says: “Joyful and widespread is the activity of the Evil One”; the context indicates that the devil is meant. And in the same work, chapter 14, he again says concerning him: “The Evil One was being torn apart, whom Job . . . was rending with great equanimity.” So too elsewhere. No less in the Lord’s Prayer, where in Matthew 6:13 Christ himself taught us, among other things, to pray, “but deliver us from evil,” the Greek text has ἀλλὰ ῥῦσαι ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ, “but deliver us from the Evil One”; by this expression most Latin as well as Greek Fathers understand the devil.

It is dangerous. As something scarcely to be set forth without [Col. 1218A] offending and scandalizing readers.

Edification. This is opposed to scandal: what scandal destroys, edification repairs.

After judging. This seems to mean the same as “with judgment,” which ought to be done only after serious deliberation and after the matter has been weighed on both sides.

Repentance. By which he now repents of his former repentance itself.

In act. The outward act, namely, as above, chapter 3, note “It is performed.”

In good faith, i.e., with the fear of God and faithfulness preserved unimpaired, and without prejudice to them.

With fear preserved. Bitter mockery!

It is a defense. He continues that sarcasm to this point.

Of hypocrites. Ὑπόκρισις otherwise means an actor’s impersonation, imitating the gestures of another person; hence an actor of this sort is also called a ὑποκριτής, “hypocrite” or “actor” [the printed reading *ὑποκρίσις* here is likely erroneous]. But in the idiom of Holy Scripture a hypocrite is one who outwardly displays uprightness in his conduct, but inwardly and beneath the skin, as they say, is wicked—[Col. 1218B] an unscrupulous pretender. Of such people the Poet says:

> Those who feign the Curii and live like Bacchanals.

Such above all were those against whom Christ warned us in Matthew 7:15: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves.” The Evangelists say more about them.

## Notes on Chapter VI

Mediocrity, i.e., our modest ability, as those who think humbly of themselves are accustomed to say. See also above, chapter 3.

That every. Junius wishes *omnis* here to be understood as *omneis*, as the ancients used to say for *omnes*. But those who think *omnis* should be referred to τὸ salutis, “the matter of salvation,” defend themselves by another passage of Tertullian, in the book *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 8: “EVERYTHING is whole and complete, lacking no part of itself.”

To novices. Here he means catechumens recently admitted to the first rank and therefore still [Col. 1218C] weak in faith.

Hangs over these people, or is appointed and directed toward them.

To water their ears. A rather florid metaphor concerning those who were admitted to hear the word of God in the Church, being placed among the catechumens in the rank of Hearers, of whom a little below.

Whelps. A *catulus* properly means a young dog or puppy, although I find it rightly applied to all brute animals—but only viviparous ones—while they are still young.

Perfect, i.e., with sight not yet perfected, as in the proverb: “A hurrying bitch gives birth to blind puppies.”

They crawl. This is a Hellenism, as from the Greek ἄδηλα ἕρπουσι, “they crawl uncertainly” or “into uncertainty,” nowhere planting sure and firm steps. Similar is the expression in the book *On Patience*, chapter 1: “those who live blind things,” for “those who live blindly.”

Indeed. Either *se*, “themselves,” must be understood, or it must certainly be inserted here.

[Col. 1218D] To enclose, i.e., to confine and, as it were, secure. For dogs endeavor to keep their whelps within their lairs so that, if they thoughtlessly stray, they do not in their blindness run into some obstacle and thereby suffer injury.

Of desiring. Because they are shortly to put an end to their evil desires, renouncing them in Baptism and being transformed from the old person into the new.

To grow old. An apt and elegant comparison for repentance.

They flatter, i.e., they flatter the beauty of the fruits, which they have still retained in part, by taking pleasure in it. See the book *On Baptism*, chapter 3, note “But grace,” 1147 B, and chapter 9, “The grace of water,” 1171 D.

Of the immersion, i.e., of Baptism, as frequently elsewhere.

The intervening time. Or intermediate time, namely between their conversion and Baptism itself, while they are still among the catechumens.

Furlough [*commeatum*]. A military term signifying permission granted to soldiers whereby, for reasons of health or other business, they may be absent from camp for a time. It also sometimes denotes the very period during which a soldier, having gone elsewhere, is absent from camp; indeed it is occasionally used for the provisions given as traveling supplies. Numerous examples occur in our author, as in the *Apology*, chapter 32: “We know that the overwhelming force threatening the whole world . . . is delayed by the furlough”—the period that God, as supreme Commander, will grant it—“of the Roman Empire.” It is used in the same sense in the book *Against Praxeas*, chapter 1: “But it too will again be rooted out during this reprieve,” etc. Thus in the *Apology*, chapter 46, he says that “the opportunity for deliberation” is often frustrated. And in the book *On Flight in Persecution*, chapter 9, he wishes us “to gain a reprieve.” Again, in Book II *Against Marcion*, chapter 10, he says: “By measuring out an interval for his operations, he acted according to the rationale of his goodness.” Finally, in the book *On the Soul*, chapter 30: “Because this span of life would not have equaled”—that is, would not have been equal and duly proportionate to—“a millennium,” being, of course, a far shorter time. For the rest, after *commeatum* understand “more” or “rather”; perhaps [Col. 1219B] this word has fallen out of the comparison, or is absent by an ellipsis frequent among the Greeks.

Than repentance. The particle *quam*, “than,” appears to require deletion; it was perhaps the work of a drowsy copyist.

To await. It seems to be used for “to wait for,” as in the book *Against the Jews*, chapter 6, where he says of Christ’s future coming: “Since he has not yet come, he must be awaited, until his coming is manifest.”

To emancipate. This example—continued still further here—could readily occur to Tertullian, since he had formerly been an advocate and was thoroughly practiced in legal affairs.

To adjudge. In the sense of “to give.” This is again a term proper to the forum. Thus Samuel Pitiscus, in his *Lexicon*, under the solemn formula of praetorian law, “I GIVE, I DECLARE, I ADJUDGE” (*DO, DICO, ADDICO*), cites a certain law from the ancients: “Whichever magistrate shall preside over the administration of justice in that colony, to that magistrate shall belong jurisdiction concerning that matter, the appointment of a judge, and ADJUDICATION.” Otherwise, “to adjudge” [Col. 1219C] properly belongs to a seller.

Institutes. For “establishes.”

By compensation. Indeed, through repentance the divine right violated by sin is repaired, and the injury inflicted upon it is compensated, insofar as the act of repentance has Christ’s satisfaction for us and his merits intimately joined to itself. Many of the Scholastics subsequently taught—and some still teach today—that what they call the formal character of repentance consists in the compensation of the aforesaid injury.

Lest an adulterer. Something must certainly be supplied by ellipsis.

The truth. As something to be examined more fully below.

We are absolved. This expression is ironic, as though absolution itself were proof either that true repentance had already been performed or that it was to be performed.

While pending, i.e., while still suspended.

Is foreseen. As though still impending.

Has been changed. Has now been transferred into another status. In this sense our author says in the book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 57: “Tell me, if you have changed your servant by granting him freedom,” etc.

[Col. 1219D] He charges it to himself. As recognizing himself still guilty of these things and therefore intending to perform repentance. But what was formerly more common among that thieving and fugitive class of men?

Discharged. Soldiers, after completing their lawful term of service—a specified number of years—were sent from camp or discharged from military service, thereafter released from their military oath. This was an honorable discharge; another kind, occasioned by illness or some other bodily defect, was called a medical discharge and was equivalent to the honorable one.

For marks, that is, military offenses by which he had been badly marked. If you prefer, you may take “marks” here as the punctures or brands with which recruits newly enrolled in military service were marked, so that, if they fled, they could be recognized by them and brought back beneath their standards and banners, to be subjected under military law to military punishment.

Vegetius, Book II, chapter 5, speaks thus of these marks: “Soldiers are inscribed with enduring [Col. 1220A] points in the skin”—points that will last and no longer be erased—“entered upon the rolls, and accustomed to swear the oath.” And Aëtius, a Greek physician, quoted by Lipsius in *On the Roman Military*, Book I, Dialogue 9, speaks as follows: Στίγματα καλοῦσι τὰ ἐπὶ τοῦ προσώπου, ἢ ἄλλου τινὸς μέρους τοῦ σώματος, ἐπιγραφόμενα, οἷα τῶν στρατευομένων ἐν τοῖς χερσί. That is: “They call ‘stigmata’ the marks inscribed upon the face or some other part of the body, such as those upon soldiers’ hands.” By these marks, therefore, soldiers were continually reminded of their duties for as long as they had to serve, and transgressors of those duties certainly had the gravest punishments to fear.

For those about to enter the water, or to be baptized. At that time Baptism was commonly performed by immersion, as our dogmatic theologians discuss at length. Thus the water was not then merely to be approached, but actually entered.

Safe. Secure and certain.

A sprinkling. Some prefer *asparginem*. We have said more about this word in the book *On Baptism*, chapter 5. For the rest, Tertullian seems here to allude to Baptism, [Col. 1220B] as it was formerly administered by sprinkling, especially to the clinically ill or bedridden; on this matter, consult again the dogmatic theologians treating the proximate matter of Baptism. It may also be understood thus: “even a single sprinkling”—that is, water sprinkled drop by drop—“not to speak of a whole abundance of water,” etc.

Will furnish. In the sense of “will impart.” It is not used in the legal sense in which someone lends his property to another for a time, to be returned afterward, but insofar as it signifies rendering to another an advantageous or useful service.

By theft. For “stealthily and secretly.”

To be circumvented. Or to be covered over with deceptions and cunning; in this sense someone is also said to be outwitted or circumvented by another. For, as he says in the book *On Baptism*, chapter 18, “Every petition is capable both of deceiving and of being deceived.”

God is light. An elegant statement indeed!

A symbol of death, i.e., Baptism, instituted by Christ as a commemorative sign of his Death and burial, [Col. 1220C] and indeed of his Resurrection as well, so that we too, having died in Adam and been buried with Christ through Baptism, might be raised from the death of sin to the LIFE OF GRACE. See the book *On Baptism*, chapter 11, note “Without his resurrection,” and chapter 16, note “Might be glorified.”

Permits. Junius rightly reads “promises,” although I think that “permits,” which is in my manuscript, can also be tolerated.

They fall away. From the grace obtained in Baptism, namely; we also know that many, forestalled by death, were not rarely prevented and disappointed even from obtaining it. See the book *On Baptism*, chapter 18, note “It is more advantageous.”

Having undertaken. That is, acting with faithless and inconstant, and therefore neither serious nor sincere, repentance.

About to fall. Such a person, namely, will be like the foolish man who builds his house upon sand, etc., Matthew 7:26.

Of the Hearers. This is a specific rank of catechumens, concerning which see above and perhaps elsewhere at greater length. Yet I think the word should be taken here simply for catechumens, [Col. 1220D] since he repeats it so often in the same sense.

For that reason. Or, for that cause.

As soon as. In the sense of “at the very first moment.”

As soon as you have examined him. Or, immediately when you have come to know him more closely and thoroughly.

You lie upon it. And continue to press upon it, as though from an excessively tenacious habit and custom. See the book *On Baptism*, chapter 11, note “Resurrection.”

Ignorant, i.e., while you did not yet know God.

Separates. Pamelius, according to Junius, reads from three manuscripts: “from the perfect word of God.” But what would that be? Is it not better to retain the reading of my manuscript, which may be explained quite suitably as follows: “What separates, distinguishes, and differentiates you from a servant of God already perfected through Baptism?” Nor does a catechumen possess anything exceptional in comparison with the baptized, as though the former could rush immediately into Baptism [Col. 1221A] without repentance for his own sins; indeed, he requires at least prior attrition in order to receive it fruitfully.

In good faith, i.e., with faithful and true repentance, not as in the preceding chapter, note “Of hypocrites.”

We have been washed. Inwardly, namely; although this is not always a perfect washing, but generally only one begun. For that repentance arising from fear which we call attrition does not of itself justify before Baptism is actually received; only perfect contrition arising from love of God above all things does so. Nevertheless, in the very long repentance that catechumens formerly had to perform before Baptism, it could scarcely happen that attrition did not at some point pass, as though through certain stages, into perfect contrition, so that someone might already be inwardly justified with his sins erased before actually receiving Baptism itself. Here one may consult what the Council of Trent, cited above, clearly explains in Session VI, *On Justification*, chapter 6.

Whole. Sincere and perfect; [Col. 1221B] this he calls the first—i.e., initial and begun—immersion or baptism, as we said immediately above.

As soon as. In the sense of “immediately when,” as above.

You have perceived, or have recognized.

From the waters, i.e., after Baptism, or after we have again emerged from the waters.

We have put on. For this is a necessary effect of Baptism and, as we call it, an effect *ex opere operato*; the Sacraments, like natural causes, necessarily operate in a properly disposed subject.

Obstructed, i.e., hindered on every side.

Bound. To Christ’s New Law, namely, after the baptized person’s renunciation of the devil and all his pomps.

For he who desires. Truly remarkable antitheses follow.

More fearful. Somewhat more shaken by the fear of GOD. See above.

Would promise in return. Simply for “would promise,” as our author [Col. 1221C] frequently uses similar compounds.

About to fulfill. Entirely correctly for the alternative form *praestiturus*, since *praestare* is taken to mean “to fulfill” or “to complete.”

## Notes on Chapter VII

To the Hearers. The author indicates clearly enough that what he has set forth thus far concerns the repentance to be performed before Baptism by Hearers or catechumens. Now, however, he turns to that kind of repentance which remains to be embraced by those who relapse after Baptism, as the “second plank after shipwreck,” as we said above.

Nothing now. Either “nothing now” concerns those who, after Baptism, are no longer conscious of anything worthy of repentance; or it should be referred to infants, who are incapable of actual sin and therefore of repentance.

Treating, that is, discussing. I am now weary of noting this so often.

To demonstrate, i.e., as though to point it out to persons invited to go on [Col. 1221D] sinning.

To that point. Or, to such an extent, or for that reason.

Let there now be open. Understand “a space”—namely, of time—or “a door,” or something similar.

Will have a way of escaping. The way of escape having, of course, been closed.

Will not have. The person himself, namely, who does not put an end to his offending.

Thus far. Thus far, or to this point. Or perhaps: Shall we Christians wait for the Gentiles themselves to set their god Terminus—faugh! a name not to be uttered without impiety—as a boundary to our sins?

To dangerous things. Others read “to dangers.” That is indeed plainer, but not so compelling that I must therefore abandon my manuscript.

They blame the sea. “He who suffers shipwreck twice wickedly accuses Neptune,” says Publilius, the writer of mimes.

They honor them by remembrance of the danger. A statement most elegantly expressed!

[Col. 1222A] To be a burden. An emphatic phrase, that is, well suited to arousing emotion.

To trample upon. To tread into it. But why multiply words? I take “trample upon” here simply for “tread upon,” or insult with one’s heels in utter contempt—and who will object?

A limit, i.e., restraint or restriction.

While it is extinguished. A most beautiful antithesis.

Works of death. Of that death, namely, which among all forms of death is the most terrible: the death of the soul.

Formerly his own. Previously his own, that is, the sinner’s.

About to judge. For St. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 6:3: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” Interpreters commonly understand this of evil or condemned spirits. “These,” our author says in the book *On the Apparel of Women*, chapter 2, “are those whom we shall judge; these are the angels whom we renounce in the laver.” And in the book *On Flight in Persecution*, chapter 10, he speaks thus: “Christian, you fear a man, though you ought to be feared by angels—since you are to judge angels—and ought to be feared by demons,” etc. Tertullian therefore speaks of these angels here as well.

[Col. 1222B] By deviations. Others read “by conditions,” which I cannot approve; Junius reads “by leadings astray,” a word our author uses in the book *On Prescription*, chapter 22. Indeed, this reading seems more consonant with the context, for we properly speak of leading someone from the road or straight path into trackless places, etc.

The door barred by a bolt. The word “barred” should not be referred to the bolt, but to the door, so that the sense is: “the door barred by the bolt of immersion or Baptism.” This is rightly stated because Baptism cannot be repeated; consequently, once someone has been baptized, this door no longer lies open to him for the pardon and remission of sins, as a door through which he might enter twice.

In vain. This expression is rather harsh, as though even repentance could not be repeated by the baptized after repeated relapses and consequently every hope of obtaining pardon anew were thereafter closed. But perhaps Tertullian meant to say no more [Col. 1222C] than that the more frequently someone has sinned, the more difficult sincere repentance becomes, and repentance worthy of pardon so many times. Indeed, immediately afterward he speaks more gently. But see rather below, chapter 9, “The defenses of nature,” 1169 D.

What you had received. A weighty statement indeed, to be deeply impressed upon the mind.

Lends. In the sense of gives and grants for your use.

You may restore, or recover; or reestablish.

Much more when enlarged. Here *nedum* must be explained as “much more.” I know that other meanings, and sometimes a negative force, are assigned to this otherwise sufficiently ambiguous word. But let these matters belong to the grammarians. Anyone will readily take “enlarged” here to mean “increased” or “extended.” Why say more, then? Here *nedum* will mean the same to me as “not to say when enlarged.”

Than to give. Because he who restores gives twice, by once again placing another in the same condition from which he had fallen.

[Col. 1222D] Not to have received. For nothing could be taken away from one who received nothing; therefore he feels no misery from a loss.

Of ill health. Unfavorable health, namely; for everyone knows that the word “health” is ambiguous. So too in the book *On Baptism*, chapter 5, he says: “Those who complained of ill health observed.”

## Notes on Chapter VIII

That. In the sense of “concerning that.”

Things sacrificed to idols [*idolothyta*] are the flesh of victims offered to idols, from εἴδωλον, “idol,” and θύω, “I offer” or “sacrifice.” Whoever ate of these offerings was therefore considered a participant in that sacrifice and polluted by it, as though sacrilegiously sharing the very religion of the Gentiles. For this reason, among other things, the eating of food sacrificed to idols was forbidden at the Council of Jerusalem, Acts 15, [Col. 1223A] because at that time it could scarcely take place without scandal. But once that circumstance had changed, eating such foods privately was by no means forbidden, since they could never in reality be polluted by idols or contaminated with impurity. And this is the very teaching of St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 10:27ff.:

> If any of the unbelievers invites you—to a meal, namely—and you are willing to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions for conscience’s sake. But if someone says, “This has been offered to idols,” do not eat it, for the sake of the one who informed you—lest, namely, he think it eaten in honor of his idols—and for conscience’s sake. I mean, however, not your own conscience but the other person’s, lest you become a scandal to another and injure his conscience.

Doubtful. I supply, “it would be,” or “it might appear.” For in former times the Apocalypse of St. John had not yet been universally received in the Church among the canonical books, that is, books of undoubted authority. Even Eusebius himself, as late as the fourth century, had doubts about it in Book III of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 33, believing with certain others that the author of this book [Col. 1223B] was not John the Evangelist but another John surnamed the Theologian. Since, therefore, it was not sufficiently established who this person was, or whether he had been inspired by the Holy Spirit, most Churches long hesitated to number the Apocalypse among the divine Scriptures. Indeed, the Council of Laodicea, held about A.D. 372, had not yet ventured to receive it into its canon. This was first done by the Council of Carthage in the year 397, and afterward Pope Innocent I finally proposed the complete canon of Holy Scripture.

Had been wearied by wandering. The little sheep, namely, exhausted from wandering about.

Relieves, i.e., diminishes.

Concealment. This seems to be used here for silence.

Aggravates. In the sense of increases.

## Notes on Chapter IX

Of one. Immediately before this, however, in chapter 8—and indeed already in chapter 5—Tertullian mentions only one repentance granted by the Church after Baptism, strictly excluding a further one. [Col. 1223C] Since he again insists upon this here, the matter seems to require somewhat more exact examination, though within the limits of our undertaking.

No one should suppose that this severity of discipline prevailed only in Tertullian’s time or only in the African Churches. First of all, ST. AUGUSTINE, that great LIGHT not merely of the African Church but of the WHOLE CHURCH, says in Epistle 54 to Macedonius:

> Although no place for the most humble repentance is granted in the Church to them—

he is speaking of those who, as he says shortly before, even after performing repentance and after reconciliation at the Altar, commit similar or graver offenses—

> nevertheless God does not forget his patience toward them.

And again, a little below:

> Although it has been cautiously and salutarily provided that a place for that most humble repentance should be granted ONCE in the Church, lest the medicine, if held cheap, should be less beneficial to the sick—a medicine that will have been all the less contemptible, etc.

Therefore, even in the fourth and fifth centuries, not only in the Church of Hippo but also in the other [Col. 1223D] Churches of Africa, such rigor prevailed that no one who relapsed into grave sins was admitted to a second *exomologesis*—that is, to be performed publicly, in the sight of the Church, and in the manner that our author subsequently describes in this very chapter and that St. Augustine above called “most humble.”

But what of CLEMENT regarding his Church of Alexandria and the other Churches subject to it? For in Book II of the *Stromata* he says:

> God, since he is rich in mercy, gave even to those who, after faith—

that is, after the faith received in Baptism—

> fall into some sin, μετάνοιαν δευτέραν, A SECOND REPENTANCE. If anyone, after his calling, has been tempted, driven by a certain violence, and cunningly circumvented, he will receive μίαν ἔτι μετάνοιαν ἀμετανόητον λάβῃ, ONE further REPENTANCE not to be repented of—

after which repentance, if he sins again, he will thereafter no longer be able to repent.

Origen himself, Clement’s disciple, likewise allowed no place for a second repentance after Baptism, as Dupin [Col. 1224A] testifies in the *Bibliothèque des auteurs ecclésiastiques*, vol. I, p. 216 of my edition.

But to speak also of the Churches of the West, St. Ambrose declares as follows in Book II of *On Penance*, ch. 10: “They are deservedly rebuked who think that penance should be performed repeatedly, who indulge themselves wantonly in Christ; for if they truly performed penance, they would not think it should afterwards be repeated, because, just as there is ONE BAPTISM, so there is ONE PENANCE—namely, that which is performed PUBLICLY.”

Accordingly, those guilty of certain graver crimes customarily received absolution only in the final struggle of death—indeed, as some plausibly believe, not even then—meaning solemn and public absolution, according to the discipline of most Churches.

Nor should this rigor, when account is taken of the times and other circumstances, be regarded as excessive or as displaying a kind of cruelty. For the greater strength of human nature at that time, its extreme corruption—especially among peoples recently converted to Christ’s Church—and its propensity toward certain kinds of offenses, particularly in the hotter [Col. 1224B] regions, needed to be restrained by a salutary terror from committing those offenses further and from performing penance too sluggishly. Otherwise, the Church’s laxity, which would then have been harmful, and the hope of obtaining pardon from her repeatedly might have encouraged new and more frequent relapses, with examples of this kind readily producing pernicious scandals among others also.

Furthermore, the penance of those who had relapsed after performing it once was judged not to have been sufficiently earnest and efficacious; and therefore the superiors of the Churches believed that no safe reliance could any longer be placed upon a second penance, whatever works might demonstrate it. Δόκησις τοίνυν μετανοίας, οὐ μετάνοια, τὸ πολλάκις αἰτεῖσθαι συγγνώμην, ἐφ’ οἷς πλημμελοῦμεν πολλάκις: “For it is the appearance of repentance, not repentance itself, repeatedly to ask pardon for those things in which we repeatedly offend,” as Clement of Alexandria again says in Book II of the *Stromata*. Consequently, it came about that persons who relapsed in this fashion were granted absolution only at the end of life—indeed, in at least some Churches, not even then, as many [Col. 1224C] plausibly believe. Yet those sinners, now fallen a second time, were not therefore to despair as though they must necessarily perish; for, as we read above from St. Augustine, they were left to the patience and mercy of God, so that through perfect contrition they might still be freed from their sins, if they truly and earnestly repented, and thereafter be saved. Indeed, it is highly probable that assistance was given to them, not only in the final struggle but even while they were still healthy and vigorous, through private sacramental absolution, according to the nature and requirements of their circumstances.

Yet these persons undoubtedly remained in a condition still sufficiently wretched and not to be envied by others, since they would henceforth lack both the public prayers of the Church, which were otherwise poured forth over public penitents, and, above all, communion in the Holy Eucharist. Finally, they would have to make satisfaction by suffering more severely and for a longer time in purgatory, unless they devoted themselves all the more earnestly to making satisfaction even in this life through internal acts of penance and external works of penance [Col. 1224D], undertaken voluntarily or at the judgment of priests.

For the rest, just as that severity of discipline was not the same in every Church, neither did it endure equally everywhere. In the Eastern Church, when, toward the close of the fourth century, Nectarius, Patriarch of Constantinople, abolished the public confession and penance of secret sins—and when the same practice, though later, prevailed in the Western Church—secret sins also were subjected only to secret confession. This could be repeated frequently and after any relapse, with the hope of again obtaining private absolution.

Eventually, the practice of public penance almost entirely fell into disuse, when even for public and more atrocious offenses nothing but private and secret penance was imposed in sacramental confession, as the circumstances of the times required; the offenses themselves, however, were left to the ecclesiastical judge to punish by canonical censures and the like. [Col. 1225A] For when that primitive fervor of the faithful had already cooled considerably, and their relaxed conscience had broken through the barriers of public penance, while the Church’s former rigor no longer seemed capable of being adapted to the political condition—and especially to the position of rulers—because of the hardness of their hearts, the Church, as a loving and provident mother, judged that she must at least come to the aid of her disobedient children’s salvation through leniency, and especially through opening more liberally the treasury of indulgences, by which that public penance could be supplied and compensated for. Let it suffice to have said these few things, despite the great breadth of this subject, in accordance with the purpose of our little work and as occasion prompted; the rest may be learned more fully from our dogmatic theologians.

From this it is now evident that the ancient severity of the Church in excluding a second penance lent no support whatever to the errors either of the Montanists or of the Novatians. For they attacked the Church’s very power to forgive the sins of those who relapsed after [Col. 1225B] Baptism, and attempted utterly to overthrow it. The Church, however, having received from Christ the POWER both of loosing and of binding, in Matthew 18:18 and John 20:23, regulated only the USE of each power, as something placed within her own discretion, so that at such a time, as often, and in such a manner as, when, and however frequently she judged it expedient, she might by her own authority and through her priests either forgive or retain the sins duly disclosed by penitents, while preserving inviolate all other things required for this sacrament by the institution of Christ himself.

**Quanto in arcto**: for *quanto arctius*, “the more constrainedly.”

**Tanto operosior probatio est**: that is, it must be demonstrated by correspondingly more numerous and arduous works of penance, so that proof may be given that it is earnest and sincere.

**Sola conscientia**: that is, by the mind alone, or by an internal act.

**Proferatur.** Junius reads *perferatur*, which I cannot disapprove; nevertheless, I prefer to retain the commonly received reading. [Col. 1225C]

**Aliquo etiam actu**: that is, by some external and perceptible act; for here he takes *actus* in the sense of a deed, as is gathered from the note **Agitur** on Chapter III.

**Exomologesis.** Ἐξομολόγησις (*exomologēsis*) is derived from ἐξομολογέω (*exomologeō*), which in the sacred writers properly means “to confess.” As Tertullian himself defines it in *On Prayer*, ch. 6, it is a petition for pardon, because one who asks pardon confesses an offense. It is useful to offer some examples. Thus in Psalm 27:7, where the Hebrew has [Hebrew text absent in the supplied source], Aquila translates: Καὶ ἀπὸ ἄσματός μου ἐξομολογήσομαι αὐτῷ, “And from my song I shall confess to him”; but the Septuagint has: Καὶ ἐκ θελήματός μου ἐξομολογήσομαι αὐτῷ, which our Vulgate renders: “And from my will I shall confess to him.” It does not say “IN my will,” but “FROM my will,” so that the confession is not retained merely within the will but is also outwardly manifested. So too in Psalm 29:10, where Symmachus renders the Hebrew thus: μὴ ἐξομολογήσεταί σοι κόνις, ἢ ἀπαγγελεῖ τὴν ἀλήθειάν σου; “Will dust confess to you, or proclaim your truth?” [Col. 1225D] Here, therefore, it signifies a confession that is a kind of proclamation, consisting in an external act and metaphorically applied to dust. Many other examples to this effect could be produced from the Old Law.

To come also to the New Testament, Matthew 3:6 says of John: “They were baptized by him, confessing [ἐξομολογούμενοι, *exomologoumenoi*] their sins.” This was certainly an external confession, demonstrated, that is, by external acts. For John did not administer his baptism indiscriminately, but only to those whose earnest repentance could be recognized from external works. So too Acts 19:18 states: “And many of those who believed came, confessing”—where again the word is ἐξομολογούμενοι—“and declaring,” externally, of course, “their deeds.” And what could be clearer than the Apostle’s words in Romans 10:10: “With the heart belief is made unto justice, but WITH THE MOUTH CONFESSION IS MADE [στόματι δὲ ὁμολογεῖται] unto salvation”? Although [Col. 1226A] I am not unaware that among secular writers the word is sometimes used in another sense, nevertheless in Holy Scripture ἐξομολόγησις is regularly expressed by confession performed with the mouth. Moreover, it is also used specifically for the confession of sins in 1 John 1:9: Ἐὰν ὁμολογῶμεν τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν, κ.τ.λ., “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all iniquity.” Likewise James 5:16: Ἐξομολογεῖσθε ἀλλήλοις τὰ παραπτώματα ὑμῶν, “Confess your sins to one another,” etc. Hence among Greek theologians *exomologesis*, used without qualification, is generally taken for the confession of sins, indeed for the entire penitential action insofar as it also includes works of satisfaction. In this very meaning it was transferred to the Latins also and has continued in the same use to the present.

But in the eighth century it began to be extended somewhat more broadly even to litanies, or public supplications, as St. Isidore bears witness in *Etymologies*, Book VI, ch. 19, near the end:

> The difference between LITANIES and EXOMOLOGESIS is that acts of exomologesis are performed solely for the confession of sins, whereas litanies are so called because they are used to entreat the Lord and obtain his mercy in some matter. But now both words are treated as having one meaning, and in common usage it makes no difference whether they are called litanies or exomologesis.

[Col. 1226B] Meanwhile, among the Easterners that ancient meaning remained, as is gathered from Chapter II of the first letter sent to the Lutherans in 1574 by Jeremiah, Patriarch of Constantinople; indeed, it is also still frequently employed by our Latin theologians today.

Nor have we dwelt somewhat longer upon this word without reason. For since our theologians regularly employ it particularly against the Calvinists, “one must proceed cautiously and prudently,” as Petavius observes in his *Annotations on St. Epiphanius*, at Heresy 89, “in interpreting this word, so that from the very context of the account we may judge in what sense it was employed by the Fathers.”

**Confessione**: that is, “through confession,” for this precedes satisfaction. An injury done to another is not repaired through satisfaction unless that very satisfaction has proceeded from a penitent heart and a confessing mouth. [Col. 1226C]

**Poenitentia nascitur.** Here he is speaking of the works of penance, which he enumerates more precisely immediately afterward.

**Prosternendi.** There were formerly four orders, or as it were degrees, of penitents: namely, the Weepers, the Hearers, the Prostrated, and the Co-standers.

The **WEEPERS** (προσκλαίοντες, *prosklaiontes*) were those who, outside the church door, beneath the portico or some lower part of its roof, clothed in sackcloth, sprinkled with ashes, etc., knelt or, in proportion to the gravity of their crimes, even lay prostrate with their whole body. Amid bitter tears, and sometimes amid sobbing and wailing, they implored those entering and leaving to assist them with prayers and to intercede with the bishop for their reception into the Church.

The **HEARERS** (ἀκροώμενοι, *akroōmenoi*, or “listeners”), having now been admitted within the church door, stood in the place called the νάρθηξ (*narthex*), or “rod”—as though designated specifically for those who were still under the rod of ecclesiastical discipline—which was separated from the church itself by wooden partitions or screens. They were admitted there to hear the divine Scriptures and other sacred readings, but were expelled again when the Mass of the catechumens began, as not yet worthy to share in the prayers of the rest of the faithful. [Col. 1226D]

The **PROSTRATED** (ὑποπίπτοντες, *hypopiptontes*) were those who were allowed a place within the church itself as far as the ambo, the place appointed for reading the Epistle and Gospel. They could thus both join their prayers to those of the rest of the faithful and, while kneeling or prostrate upon the ground, receive frequent impositions of hands—of which some believe at least the final one to have been sacramental, that is, an absolution from sins. But when the Oblation, which we call the Offertory, began, they were compelled to leave the church. [Col. 1227A] This order of the Prostrated was often called absolutely and simply “Penance” by the Latin Fathers, and the Prostrated themselves were called “penitents.” The first two classes were regarded merely as dispositions toward penance itself; but in this third class satisfaction itself was performed through laborious works of penance—fasts, vigils, and other practices tormenting the flesh—which were undertaken not now spontaneously and at one’s own discretion, but by ordinance of the Church herself, as she measured them in proportion to the offenders’ crimes. This may be seen in St. Pacian’s exceedingly beautiful *Exhortation to Penance*, in Juenin’s *Treatise on Penance*, Chapter IV, art. 3, and in others.

Finally, the **CO-STANDERS** (συνεστῶτες, *synestōtes*) were those who stood between the ambo and the sanctuary and were permitted, together with the rest of the faithful, to be present at the Sacrifice, but were excluded solely from participation in the sacred Table, or Eucharist, in order to prove their constancy.

Only when penitents had passed through these orders did they obtain public and solemn absolution from their offenses—an absolution that was finally sacramental—to be given by the bishop or, at his command, by a presbyter; thereafter they were restored to communion at the Holy Table and with the entire Church. [Col. 1227B]

Now, just as there is no doubt that from the times of the Apostles all Churches everywhere exercised great severity, admitting only those whom they had proved over a considerable period to be truly penitent from the heart, so it is also certain that neither the manner nor the order of admitting them was observed identically at all times or in every place. Certainly our Tertullian, otherwise so diligent in enumerating the traditions of his own times and the observances of discipline—especially those of the African Churches, already more rigorous than others—nevertheless nowhere makes an explicit distinction among those four classes.

Nor do they appear to have been in use in the Roman Church at that time. For Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, ch. 27, speaks only as follows concerning the penitent Natalius:

> In the morning he arose, clothed in haircloth and sackcloth and sprinkled with ashes, and with great grief and tears cast himself as a suppliant at the feet of Pope Zephyrinus—who held his see during Tertullian’s own period, from the year 197 to 217—and prostrated himself not only at the knees of the clergy but also at those of the laity, so that the Church of the merciful Christ, greatly moved with compassion for him, joined him in lamentation.

[Col. 1227C] Yet he—observe the rigor of the discipline of those times—although he employed many entreaties and displayed the marks of the blows he had endured, for he had been chastised very severely one night by an angel while living in the company of heretics, was only with difficulty at last received into communion in the Church. Yet no order of the aforesaid classes is recorded as having been observed here.

Observe also the custom of performing penance that prevailed in the Church of Carthage in the time of St. Cyprian, who came after Tertullian. Thus he says in his treatise *On the Lapsed*:

> One must pray more earnestly and make supplication, pass the day in mourning, spend the nights in vigils and weeping, occupy all one’s time with tearful lamentations, lie stretched upon the ground and cling to the ashes, roll in sackcloth and filth; after losing the garment of Christ, desire no garment any longer; after the devil’s food, prefer fasting; apply oneself to just works by which sins are purged; persist frequently in almsgiving, etc.

Here again no succession of those classes is observed—a matter St. Cyprian certainly would not have passed over in silence when he speaks so carefully elsewhere also, and indeed expressly, about the use of public penance. It is nevertheless more probable that those classes of penitents were introduced around Cyprian’s own time, not indeed in Africa but in the East. For St. Gregory, Bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus—commonly called the Wonderworker because of the holiness of his life and the multitude of miracles performed by him—who went to heaven in A.D. 265, is found to have been the first to enumerate them in his *Canonical Epistle*: provided, however, that its final canon belongs to Gregory himself, which some wish to doubt, and was not rather appended by some later Greek author. [Col. 1228A]

At least from the final canon of St. Basil the Great, Bishop of Caesarea, in his *Canonical Epistle to Amphilochius*, it is certain that this division of penance into four degrees—πρόσκλαυσις (*prosklausis*), weeping; ἀκρόασις (*akroasis*), hearing; ὑπόπτωσις (*hypoptōsis*), prostration; and σύστασις (*systasis*), standing together—already prevailed in the fourth century, for St. Basil is known to have departed to heaven in the year 379. But occasion has so carried me along that, contrary to the design of this little work I have undertaken, I have again become somewhat more prolix. Yet our dogmatic theologians will provide far more, especially that most learned work of Fr. Jean Morin, priest of the Congregation of the Oratory, the *Historical Commentary on the Discipline of Penance*, etc., in which he appears almost single-handedly to have exhausted this vast subject.

**Humilificandi.** In more classical Latin one would say *humiliandi*, “to be humbled.”

**Conversationem.** Here it is taken for the manner and mode of associating with people and conducting oneself among them, which the Greeks customarily call ὁμιλία (*homilia*).

[Col. 1228B] **Misericordiae illicem**: that is, something capable of attracting and eliciting God’s mercy. *Illex, illicis*, as Festus says, is a word derived from *illicere*, “to entice.” In this sense our author, *Apology*, ch. 41, calls the pagans “enticers of evils”; and in *On Patience*, ch. 13, he says that patience draws forth God’s clemency. There is also *illex, illegis*, meaning one who lives without law; but that is irrelevant to our subject.

**Habitu**: that is, in clothing.

**Sacco.** A sackcloth garment was a coarse robe woven from the rougher hair of goats, asses, or camels, and was worn as a sign of mourning. The word itself is of Hebrew origin; in that language a mournful garment of this kind is called [Hebrew term absent in the supplied source]. Thus in 2 Samuel 3:31 David said to Joab and to all the people: “Tear your garments, and gird yourselves with () SACKCLOTH.” And in 1 Kings 21:27, when Ahab heard the words of the prophet Elijah, “he covered his flesh with HAIRCLOTH, fasted, and slept IN SACKCLOTH,” etc. See also 2 Kings 14:1 and Nehemiah 9:1, as well as many other places.

[Col. 1228C] Moreover, this word passed from the Hebrews to the Greeks, and from them to the Latins. Thus St. John the Evangelist—writing, of course, in Greek—says in Revelation 6:12: “The sun became black like σάκκος τρίχινος,” or, as our Vulgate renders it, “HAIR SACKCLOTH.” What then? Is it not remarkable that the same word penetrated to the Italians, French, Spaniards, English, Flemings, Hungarians, etc., and that the same Hebrew word, *Sack*, even spread into Germany itself?

**Cineri incubare**: to lie upon ashes. Ashes also—that is, the dust of the earth—were used as a public sign of mourning, as almost innumerable examples, including those of the Old Testament, demonstrate. Especially notable are those found in the Book of Esther, such as 4:1 concerning Mordecai: “He tore his garments, was clothed in SACKCLOTH, AND sprinkled ASHES upon his head.” And in the same chapter, verse 3: “There was great mourning among the Jews, fasting, wailing, and weeping, many using SACKCLOTH AND ASHES as their bed.” Likewise Nehemiah 9:1: “The children of Israel assembled with fasting, in sackcloth, AND EARTH”—that is, the dust of the ground—“upon [Col. 1228D] them.”

**Corpus sordibus obscurare**: to darken the body with filth, by obscuring its brightness.

**Quae peccavit.** Nor is it unusual among Latin authors to construe the verb *peccare*, “to offend,” with an accusative. Thus in Plautus’ *Bacchides*: “If you had offended by a single syllable,” etc. There is something similar in Cicero, *On Duties*, Book I, where he says: “Many offenses are committed in the republic”; and in the *Paradoxes*: “Whatever offense is committed is committed in a disturbance of reason,” etc.

**Tractationi mutare**: for *retractare*, “to handle again,” as frequently elsewhere.

**Pura**: that is, simple. Thus in *On Patience*, ch. 13, he says: “Content with simple food and a pure drink of water.”

**Jejuniis preces alere**: to nourish prayers with fasts. An elegant metaphor, joined antithetically to fasting. And indeed, the more that is withdrawn from the body, the more the soul is to be nourished and, as it were, fattened.

**Mugire**: to bellow. A bellow, elsewhere proper to cattle, is here taken for wailing expressive of the greatest force of grief.

[Col. 1229A] **Charis.** Some manuscripts have *aris*, “altars”; but I have retained *charis*, or, as the ancients customarily wrote it, *caris*: that is, those dear to God, namely the devout faithful, and especially confessors and martyrs.

**Legationes dep. suae injungere**: to entrust to them embassies of his supplication. That is, so that they might intercede with God on behalf of the penitents. And why should those who are already beyond this mortality, nearer to God and indeed intimately united with him, not be all the more capable of doing this? Or why should they not hear our prayers? Why should God hear their prayers for us less than those of the living?

**Timore Dominum honoret**: let him honor the Lord by fear. For above, in Chapter VII, he had already said: “A man’s fear”—that is, when he salutarily fears God whom he has offended—“is honor to God.”

**Pronuntians sententiam**: pronouncing a sentence, as one to be delivered against a guilty person.

**Pro Dei indignatione fungatur**: that is, let him perform the office of God’s wrath and vengeance, forestalling it.

**Afflictione.** *Afflictio* affects the mind; *afflictatio*, as Cicero says in *Tusculan Disputations*, Book IV, is distress accompanied by torment of the body.

[Col. 1229B] **Non modo frustretur, sed expungat**: let it not merely elude but erase. One *frustrates* who avoids and evades; one *expunges* who utterly deletes and abolishes, barring every possibility of return. But how elegant are the antitheses that immediately follow! For the rest, we have spoken more fully above about the verb *expungere*, in the note **Expungit** on Chapter III.

### Notes on Chapter X

**Praesumo** is used here for “I think,” “I suppose,” or “I judge in anticipation.” Thus our author says in the *Apology*, ch. 2: “Since you prejudge our crimes from the confession of the name,” etc.

**Conscientiam**: that is, knowledge obtained from disclosure.

**Prodactae**: that is, rashly cast away or poured forth. Thus in *On the Soul*, ch. 48, he says: “They affirm that more certain and fully unfolded dreams occur toward the close of night, as though the vigor of souls were already emerging and sleep had been prolonged.”

[Col. 1229C] **Reformari**: that is, to be re-formed for salvation, by restoring it in oneself.

**Nae tu verecundia bonus**: “Truly, you are good through your modesty.” A sufficiently bitter irony.

**Expandens frontem**: spreading out the brow. The brow, as the index of the mind, is broadened by audacity.

**Ad deprecandum vero subducens**: but drawing it back when it comes to supplication. That same brow is lowered through dejection and faintheartedness.

**De detrimento ejus.** This is a ὑστερολογία (*hysterologia*, an inversion of natural word order), and should be restored to its proper order thus: “I incur more loss from it,” or “more of the loss that is customarily inflicted through it.”

**In risiloquio**: in mocking speech; the Greeks customarily call this σαρκασμός (*sarkasmos*) or εἰρωνεία (*eirōneia*), and the Latins *irrisio*, ridicule.

**Prostrato superscenditur**: one climbs over a person who has been laid low. Surely nothing baser or more ignoble can be said than that someone should wish to rise by depressing others when unable to do so by his own virtue.

**Spes.** I read *spes*, “hope,” most emphatically, in place of *species*, a word that must surely be expelled from this passage as utterly absurd here.

**Plausores**: that is, mockers. For he likewise has in the *Apology*, ch. 35: “Mockers are exposed every day.”

**Ad remedium conlabor et necesse est**: I must of necessity labor together toward the remedy. He is certainly alluding to Paul’s words in 1 Corinthians 12:26: “If one member suffers anything, all the members suffer together. Now you are the body of Christ, and members belonging to a member.” [Col. 1229D]

**Ecclesia vero Christus**: but the Church is Christ. For, as the Apostle again says in Ephesians 5:23: “Christ is the head of the Church”; and in Colossians 1:18: “He is the HEAD of the body, the CHURCH.”

**Christum exoras**: you entreat Christ. For Christ is sometimes taken not merely for the head of the Church, but for the head and members together—that is, for the entire body of the Church. Thus St. Augustine says in *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 69: “The whole may also rightly be called Christ—that is, the head together with his body, which is the CHURCH.” Hence the same author says in his *Letter to Honoratus on the Grace of the New Testament*, ch. 7: “The Church suffered in Christ when he suffered for the Church, just as he himself suffered in the Church when the Church suffered for him.” Again, in his exposition of Psalm 88, he argues thus:

> When he was already seated in heaven, he did not cry out from heaven, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute my servants?” nor “Why do you persecute [Col. 1230A] my saints?” nor “Why do you persecute my disciples?” but “Why do you persecute ME?” Therefore, just as, when no one was persecuting him as he sat in heaven, he cried, “Why do you persecute ME?” because the HEAD acknowledged his members, and love did not separate the HEAD from the union of his body, so, etc.

Thus, I say, to our subject: what is done to the brethren, the members of the Church, is done to CHRIST. For does he not himself say in Matthew 25:40: “As long as you did it to one of the least of these my brethren, you did it to ME”?

**Pollicetur**: he promises. An irony continued also through the following sentence.

**Conscientia**: for knowledge simply.

**Pervenire**: to arrive. This anticipates a certain minor objection.

**Malo**: by evil, namely through sin.

**Cauterio.** *Cauterium*, “cautery,” is not derived from *cavere*, “to take care,” but is of Greek origin: καυτήριον (*kautērion*) is named ἀπὸ τοῦ καίειν, “from burning,” because it possesses the power to burn, like the powder by which flesh is customarily eaten away when inserting issues (*fontanelles*) into the human body. [Col. 1230B] Hence something is called *cauteriatum*, “cauterized,” when it has, as it were, been burned and cut away by a cautery. Thus in 1 Timothy 4:2 the Apostle says: κεκαυτηριασμένοι τὴν συνείδησιν, “having their conscience cauterized”: once it had become rotten and corrupted by sins, it was burned and cut away by a cautery. See Calmet on this passage.

**Commendat**: he commends. Surely he could have said nothing more elegantly.

### Notes on Chapter XI

**Potiorem**: that is, the principal cause capable of deterring one from penance, as something pertaining to the soul, which is far more delicate and is often irritated much more sharply by certain comparatively slight things than the body is by far graver pains and even tortures.

**Sordulentos.** A rather rough-sounding word to Latin ears. But who would execrate it so vehemently when one finds even *sorditudo* used for *sordities*, “filth,” in Plautus’ *Poenulus*? [Col. 1230C]

**Deversari**: simply for *versari*, “to remain” or “to live,” as we have already observed repeatedly elsewhere regarding compounds of this kind.

**In asperitudine**: in roughness. The roughness of this noun would be tolerated only with difficulty by the more cultivated soil of Latium, as though it had been born in Africa’s parched deserts. Indeed, as the proverb has it, Africa always produces something new, and from of old carried its verbal monsters across the seas into foreign lands from time to time.

**Vanitate.** For when emaciation has been contracted through excessive fasting, all beauty seems, as it were, to vanish from the wasted face or become evanescent. Yet what loss is this, when by a kind of accretion the soul gains correspondingly greater beauty?

**In coccino**: in a scarlet-dyed garment. Although the Greek word otherwise signifies every kind of berry or grain in general, it particularly denotes the fruit of a certain tree not unlike the holm oak. In its berries, they say, a little worm of red color is born, from which wool or silk is customarily dyed scarlet or purple.

[Col. 1230D] Certainly the scarlet and purple colors seem to be treated interchangeably in the Gospel. For Matthew 27:28, speaking of the Jews mocking Christ as their king, says: “They placed around him χλαμίδα κοκκίνην, a SCARLET cloak”; but Mark 15:17 says: ἐνδύουσιν αὐτὸν πορφύραν, “They clothed him in PURPLE,” with whom John 19 also agrees: “They placed upon him ἱμάτιον πορφυροῦν, a purple garment.”

For the rest, there is no doubt that purple and scarlet are otherwise distinguished, if we speak more strictly. For we call that “purple” which is red but suffused with violet, whereas scarlet is brighter and more cheerful, such as is seen especially in the blooming color of young people’s blood.

**Tyrio**: Tyrian. This color is properly purple and was formerly the most precious of all. Concerning its inventor, Pollux, as cited by Samuel Pitiscus in his *Lexicon* under the word **PURPURA**, gives the following account:

> The Tyrians relate that Hercules was seized by love for a native nymph. The nymph’s name was Tyro. A dog accompanied Hercules; when it noticed a PURPLE SHELLFISH—a kind of precious mollusk—creeping among the rocks, it seized the protruding flesh in its teeth and used it for food, and the blood stained the dog’s lips scarlet. When its master returned to the girl, she saw the dog’s lips stained with an unfamiliar dye and declared that she would have nothing more to do with him unless he brought her a garment more splendid than that dog’s lips. Thus Hercules, having found the creature and collected its blood, brought the gift to the girl and was, as the Tyrians claim, the first inventor of scarlet dye.

[Col. 1231A] But St. Gregory Nazianzen, in Oration III against Julian, attributes the invention of this purple dye to a certain shepherd, saying:

> What? Will you not leave it to the Tyrians, from whom ἡ ποιμενικὴ κύων, ἡ τῇ κόχλῳ βρωθείσῃ, καὶ τὰ χείλη καθαιμαξάσῃ, τῷ ποιμένι τὸ ἄνθος γνωρίσασα—“that shepherd’s dog, which, after devouring the murex and staining its lips with blood, made the dye known to the shepherd”—presented through its mouth to you emperors that cloth, mournful and proud for the wicked?

For the rest, the purple robe was formerly peculiar to kings; it was later shared also with their household and with the nobles of the realm, as a sign that they had been admitted to participation in royal majesty. It is clear from Judges 8:26 that the kings of Midian used purple garments and that similar garments taken from them were sent as a gift to Gideon, judge of the Israelites. Daniel himself testifies in Chapter 5:4 that, when by his prophetic spirit he had revealed the hidden meaning of the writing shown to King Belshazzar, purple and a golden chain fell to him as a royal gift. Likewise, to omit other examples of the same kind, 1 Maccabees 10:20 records that Alexander Balas, king of Syria, rewarded Jonathan Maccabaeus with a golden crown and purple.

**Cedo**: used adverbially for “give” or “show me.”

**Acum crinibus distinguendis**: a pin for arranging the hair. This was an implement of women’s adornment, called a *hairpin* from its function and devised for fastening curls of hair. Martial writes of it in Book XIV, Epigram 24:
