> Let the pin fasten and support the scattered hair.

And in Book II, Epigram 66:

> Of the whole circle of her hair, one curl alone  
> Had gone astray, not properly fixed by the inserted pin.

[Col. 1231C] There was also another kind called the *discriminalis*, so named from separating the hair, as it were, strand by strand—with perverse and surely reprehensible industry. The distinction in hair between virgins and married women was that the former wore it curled, while the latter wore it parted from the forehead. Hence our author says in *On the Veiling of Virgins*, ch. 12:

> And as soon as they have understood themselves to be women . . . they turn—“sweep,” I almost wrote—the hair, and lift up their coiffure upon a more wanton pin—why not rather “insert it”?—professing their womanhood openly by hair parted from the forehead.

**Dentibus elimandis**: for polishing the teeth. In former times teeth also were customarily cleaned with powder; hence the verses in Apuleius, *Apology*, Book I, which he quotes from Catullus:

> I have sent, as you requested, a cleanser for the teeth,  
> A fine, whitening, noble little powder,  
> A smoother of the slightly swollen gum,  
> A sweeper-away of yesterday’s residue,  
> Lest any hideous stain of filth be seen  
> If perchance you smile with parted lips.

[Col. 1231D] **Bisulcum**: forked. He means scissors, an iron or bronze implement with two blades, etc., borrowed from tailors.

**Repastinandis.** A rustic word, especially proper to vine-dressers, who use *repastinare* for digging a field over again with the *pastinum*, likewise a forked implement, though of a very different kind: *den Acker umhacken*, “to hoe the field over.” Because a field is cleansed by digging it over again, foreign shrubs or stones being uprooted, any removal of impurities, including even the cutting of nails, is customarily called *repastinatio* by a metaphorical extension of the word. He is found to have used it in almost this sense for the cutting away of superfluous or harmful things in *On the Apparel of Women*, ch. 9: “How shall we be able to attain humility without cutting away the use of your riches or finery?” etc. Likewise in *On the Soul*, ch. 50: “No one will grant such power even to magic that it can remove death or, in the manner of a vine—meaning after the likeness of one—prune life back, with youth renewed.” Again, in *Against Marcion*, Book II, ch. 18: “So that the commission of injury might be pruned away by fear of immediate retaliation.” But in the *Exhortation to Chastity*, ch. 6, he also uses the word *repastinatio* for uprooting or cutting away.

**Coacti ruboris**: forced redness. Here he censures the cosmetics of soft and effeminate men, with which they are accustomed to repaint their former—indeed, now aged and as it were exhausted—beauty with a fresh falsehood, and thus to compel and, as it were, extort with rouge a blush already unwilling to appear.

**Balneas**: baths. Cicero himself also uses this noun as a feminine plural, as when in the speech *For Marcus Caelius* he mentions the Baths of Xenia. [Col. 1232B]

**Hortulani**: for *hortensis*, “of the garden.” This adjectival use of the word *hortulanus* will scarcely be found among other ancient authors.

**Senectutem vini**: the old age of wine. An elegant metaphor for signifying aged wine, which the ancients called “toothless,” as though lacking teeth, because of its mildness and the biting quality it had now cast off. Thus Plautus again in the *Poenulus*, Act III, scene 3:

> Water your years with toothless wine made mellow by age.

To make the age of wine known, tablets used to be hung from wine vessels, displaying the year and the consuls under whom each wine had been laid down. Hence Tibullus’ verse:

> Now bring me smoky Falernian wines from the time of an ancient consul.

Hence “consular wine” came to be used for the oldest and finest wine. Among these, the Opimian was most celebrated, named from the [Col. 1232C] consulship of Lucius Opimius—under whom, as Pliny testifies in Book XIV, ch. 14, there was an exceptionally fine vintage—and was praised especially by Petronius Arbiter in chapter 34. Cicero also mentions it in *On Famous Orators*, ch. 83, when discussing Falernian wine: wine neither so new that he would want it produced under the most recent consuls, nor, conversely, so old that he would seek Opimius and Anicius as consul. But since the consulship of Opimius fell in the year 632 from the founding of Rome, 119 before Christ, while Petronius died around A.D. 66, or 818 from the founding of Rome, it is clear that in Petronius’ time that wine could easily have been 180 years old.

But what is this compared with that wine which is preserved in the ancient castle called Schrofenstein, near Landeck in the County of Tyrol, and is said to have attained an age of more than four hundred years? Certainly, they report that the cask has now been overcome and eaten away by decay, while the wine itself is enclosed on every side by its own tartareous crust, so that it cannot leak out anywhere. And this wine—for I was permitted to taste some offered by a distinguished friend in the neighborhood—has a tartareous smell and taste, of which one might rightly say what the same [Col. 1232D] Cicero says in the passage cited: “Excessive age possesses neither the sweetness we seek, nor indeed is it any longer tolerable.” I except its spirits, which are thoroughly heroic and fit to rekindle the final sparks of old age. I have been pleased to mention these matters by way of a digression arising from the occasion.

**You should bestow upon your soul.** That is, you should be equally liberal and generous toward it. It is otherwise evident, however, that Tertullian held far too crude a conception of the soul. For throughout his *On the Soul*, and especially in chapter 38, he asserts that it grows to maturity at puberty no less than the body does; that there is also in the soul a desire for food; and, in chapter 9, that it is visible in a certain color, and so forth.

**Injured by sinning.** These words are undoubtedly ironic, directed against those who suppose that, even while indulging the body in everything, they can make satisfaction for their sins.

**They go about in a circuit**, that is, they walk about or make the rounds.

**Magistracies.** A magistracy is an office in the [Col. 1233A] commonwealth carrying the authority to pronounce judgment; among the Romans the term also sometimes denoted the very persons invested with such authority. There were many kinds of magistracies. There were urban magistrates, who administered justice in the City itself, and then provincial magistrates, who administered justice in the provinces subject to the Roman commonwealth, such as proconsuls, propraetors, legates of proconsuls and propraetors, provincial quaestors, and so forth. Among the urban magistrates there were also higher magistrates, who were elected in the Centuriate Assembly, such as consuls, censors, praetors, and so forth; and lower magistrates, who were customarily elected in the Tribal Assembly, such as urban quaestors, tribunes of the plebs, plebeian aediles, and so forth. In each of these classes there were ordinary and extraordinary magistrates. Thomas Dempster treats these matters fully and accurately throughout Book V, chapter 5, of his *Roman Antiquities*.

**Neither are they ashamed nor does it irk them.** We have already touched upon certain matters concerning candidates in the note “Candidate for remission” on chapter 10 of *On Baptism*. Now, however, it seems appropriate to say a few things briefly about them, recalling them, as it were, from their origins. Since it was customary for magistrates to be elected in the assemblies by the votes of the people, while [Col. 1233B] many among the people did not recognize by face or know the merits of the persons aspiring to those honors, the latter had to solicit the people’s votes by recounting their merits and presenting themselves in person. First, therefore, so that they might be recognized, they dressed in a gleaming white garment—the distinction between this and an ordinary white garment was that the former had been polished with a kind of chalk to a particular brilliance and greater splendor—and for a *trinundinum*, a period of twenty-seven days, since a market was customarily held in the forum every ninth day, they appeared on the Campus Martius, sitting upon the elevation called the Hill of the Gardens so that they might be more conspicuous. Then, as the people arrived, they went about among them, greeting everyone they met and winning them over by services of every kind.

This method of conciliating the people consisted chiefly of four parts: nomenclature, flattery, assiduity, and generosity.

Nomenclature consisted in knowing how to address every citizen by his own name; otherwise citizens might complain that they had thus far been neglected or had not been held in [Col. 1233C] the same regard as others. Since this was exceedingly difficult amid so great a multitude, every candidate enlisted assistants who would whisper to the office-seeker the names of individual passersby. They were called *nomenclatores*; Cicero, however, in his speech *For Murena* calls them *monitores* (“prompters”), and Festus calls them *fartores* (“stuffers”), because they secretly “stuffed,” as it were, the citizens’ names into the candidates’ ears. It was called flattery when they greeted people not merely by their proper names but also with more flattering forms of address, calling them fathers, brothers, patrons, and so forth, as though they were most closely bound to them. Assiduity consisted chiefly in canvassing, grasping hands, and soliciting votes. They canvassed, or made the rounds, in squares and streets, and not only at Rome but also in other Italian cities where they knew that many citizens were staying for business. They made these rounds either in person or through other friends enlisted to perform a share of this service and sent to those places, or already established there. Hand-grasping was performed by taking each person’s right hand, kissing it, kissing it fondly, [Col. 1233D] and so forth. It was called solicitation when, amid entreaties that were often downright offensively humble, they recalled benefits previously received from the people; they even bared scars that they might have received on the front of their chests in battle for the fatherland, and so forth; then they repeatedly begged that, in consideration of such things, the people would confer their votes upon them. Since they could not accomplish these things by themselves, they also employed other distinguished men, called *suffragatores* (“supporters”), who rehearsed the candidates’ virtues before the people, and so forth. To these services was added generosity, by which they won over the people through distributions, gifts thrown to the crowd, banquets, gladiatorial games, distributions of money previously deposited with intermediaries as a pledge of good faith, and so forth. It is known that some men at times exhausted their entire patrimonies through gifts of this kind.

Lest anyone suppose that we have exaggerated these matters unduly, it certainly seems pertinent to reproduce here several passages from Cicero, where Quintus Tullius instructs his brother [Col. 1234A] in the *Handbook of Electioneering for the Consulship* as follows:

> Many city-dwellers and industrious men, many freedmen influential and active in the forum, are engaged there; recruit those whom you can through your own efforts and those whom you can through mutual friends. Take care that they are eager for your success: exert yourself, seek them out, send people to them, and show that you regard yourself as having received the greatest favor from them. Then take account of the whole city, of every association of districts and neighborhoods. If you attach their leading men to your friendship, you will easily hold the rest of the multitude through them. Afterward, see that you have all Italy mapped out and comprehended in your mind and memory by tribes, and do not allow there to be any municipality, colony, prefecture, or indeed any place in Italy in which you do not have as strong a support as may suffice. Search out and investigate men from every region; get to know them, seek them out, secure them, and see that they campaign for you in their own neighborhoods and are, as it were, candidates on your behalf.

Do you imagine, however, that this business was finally completed merely by doing these things? Far from it: many more duties remained, which you will learn more exactly from Cicero in the same work, and it will be a pleasure to read him.

[Col. 1234B] But to what end have all these things been recounted, and at such length? Plainly so that the force of the argument which Tertullian presses so insistently here may be perceived all the more deeply. These burdens—so serious, so troublesome, so protracted, and almost insurmountable—had to be undertaken by the most eminent men in the Roman commonwealth, men who had already long rendered it the finest service. They bore them with such industry, such labor, and even such willingness, every sense of shame being easily overcome by the hope of honors; yet they were invited by no reward except one that was earthly, unstable, and afterward all too swiftly passing away, surrounded and, so to speak, purchased at the price of so many and such serious troubles and adversities. We, by contrast, though CHRISTIANS, blush to follow Christ, who “had to suffer these things and so enter into his glory” (Luke 24:26). Yet those candidates had committed no offense against the commonwealth but had instead rendered it excellent service; whereas our concern is the pardon of sins, the restoration of grace within us, and the HEAVENLY GLORY thereby attained and possessed for eternity.

[Col. 1234C] **Insults.** Who could believe that these candidates were not sometimes treated rather insultingly or disdainfully by certain men, perhaps enemies or less-than-friendly persons, given the license then enjoyed by the people; or even treated rather negligently by men who were otherwise their friends, amid interests so numerous and so divided? But let us hear Saint Cyprian, who in his *Letter to Donatus* describes these things most elegantly, as is his custom:

> The man who, conspicuous in brighter attire, appears to himself to shine in purple—at the price of what filth did he purchase his brilliance! What disdain of arrogant men did he first endure! What haughty doors did he besiege as a morning caller! How many insulting footsteps of puffed-up men did he precede, attended beforehand by wedges of clients, so that afterward a ceremonial procession of men greeting him might itself precede him—a procession subservient not to the man, but to his power?

And he continues in the same vein.

**Of their vows**, that is, of their desires.

**The ignobility of their garments.** For my part, I find nothing ignoble in this very kind of dress. Indeed, at other times those who were reckoned among the Romans as belonging to a more honorable station [Col. 1234D] and not to the common crowd customarily wore white garments. These were employed not merely when magistracies were being sought, but also in sacred rites, at more solemn banquets, at weddings, in military service, and in triumphs, as a symbol of moral purity, innocence, joy, integrity, and victory, as may be read at length in Johann Wilhelm Stucki, *Antiquities of Banquets*, Book II, chapter 26. I would therefore be more inclined to believe either that the remaining form of the garment worn by candidates differed from that of other people, or that it was made of the cheaper cloth customarily worn by the ignoble populace; or—and this I consider much more probable—that Tertullian is speaking of a period when the candidates’ condition had already fallen in esteem even among the Romans themselves and was regarded as ignoble, because ambition had by then corrupted everything excessively and was tending toward the public corruption of the commonwealth, so that it had become necessary to punish it even by public laws enacted against electoral canvassing.

[Col. 1235A] **They affect.** It is one thing to be disposed toward something and to seek it in moderation; it is quite another to affect it, that is, to be carried toward it by an immoderate desire and to press one’s inclination toward it with excessive solicitude beyond the bounds of what is right. Such is the custom of those who do not bring merits equal to the things desired, or suitable qualifications, yet strive to obtain their desires by every means. They are not unlike young birds which, though not yet sufficiently feathered, flap their wings prematurely and, with confidence far too immature, are seen attempting flight.

**They forestall them with salutations.** Thus they pursued their patrons even by nocturnal and excessively persistent exertions, pouring themselves into any atria they found open—or, more accurately, thrusting themselves in and all but breaking through. He calls these salutations “undigested,” because they were poured forth—or rather belched out—before the food from dinner had yet been properly digested.

**Diminishing themselves.** They made themselves smaller not merely by lowering the head, but by bending the whole body deeply, gaping like chameleons after the popular breeze they hoped to catch.

[Col. 1235B] **Distinguished by no banquets.** Indeed, in the note above on “Neither are they ashamed nor does it irk them,” we indicated that candidates—while their condition was still flourishing—sometimes provided the people with lavish and costly banquets, and so forth. But later, when plebeians too began to be mingled among the candidates, the kitchens themselves grew colder amid their slender and excessively hungry fortunes.

**Of the same flock.** Just as one who is not in the flock but lives alone is called *segrex*, “separate from the flock,” so here he calls *congreges* those who gather together with others, or belong to the flock. Thus Apuleius has in Book VIII of *The Golden Ass*: “The excellent shepherd at last allowed me to join the flock (*congregem*).”

**The fleeting joy of a single year.** It is well established that magistracies among the Romans, following the example of the Athenians, lasted only a year and were rarely extended for several years, almost never except under the emperor Tiberius; see Tacitus, *Annals*, Book I, chapter 80. For, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus says in *Roman Antiquities*, Book IV, chapter 79:

> The alternation of ruling and obeying, and the laying down of power before it corrupts the mind, restrains insolent dispositions [Col. 1235C] and does not permit the characters of rulers to become intoxicated by excessive license.

**The quest for axes and rods**, that is, the quest for the consulship or other magistracies; for here the sign is put metonymically for the thing signified.

The rods were several rounded staffs bound with a strap into a bundle, in which an axe was fixed with its blade projecting. These fasces, therefore, were granted as insignia to the higher magistrates. By them were signified those magistrates’ power of life and death through the axe, and the punishment through the rods of lighter crimes and offenses deserving flogging. When the consuls proceeded in public, fasces with axes were carried before them by an equal number of lictors; but when the consuls pronounced judgment in the forum, the lictors stood apart behind them. Vetulonia, a city of Etruria, is believed to have been the first to employ this custom. Silius Italicus says of it in Book VIII:

> And Vetulonia, once the glory of the Maeonian nation:  
> She first granted that twice six fasces should go before,  
> And joined to them as many axes, with silent terror.

**Of eternity.** Namely, of the eternal punishment to which we are to be condemned unless we return to our senses through repentance [Col. 1235D] while there is still time.

**The chastisement of diet.** This is accomplished through more frequent fasts.

**Attire**, that is, the cultivation of clothing, which is restrained by sackcloth and haircloth.

**They impose upon themselves.** Thus we Christians sometimes tend to be far more liberal toward human beings—and even prodigal in pouring out our possessions upon them—although we are often bound to them by no tie of gratitude and no debt requiring that an injury be repaired. They may consequently appear not so much enriched as burdened by our favors. Indeed, we ourselves are an excessive burden to ourselves, while in the meantime we bear Christ’s “easy yoke and light burden” (Matt. 11:30) with excessive impatience, or refuse it altogether. Yet if anyone owes God a debt because of an injury, he must not therefore despair as though he lacked the means to pay. For, as Saint Ambrose says in *On Repentance*, Book II, chapter 9:

> He who owes God possesses more resources for payment than one who owes a human being. [Col. 1236A] A human being demands money in return for money, and this is not always at the debtor’s disposal; God requires affection, which lies within your power. No one who owes GOD is poor unless he has made himself poor. And if he has nothing to sell, he has something with which to pay. Prayer, tears, and fasts are the property of a good debtor, and far richer than if someone were to tender money from the proceeds of estates without faith. Accordingly, no condition of debtors is better than that of those who are under obligation to God. In order to make satisfaction to God your creditor, you do not therefore have to sell yourself and all your possessions.

But God must be entreated with the servant in the Gospel, Matthew 18:26: “That servant therefore fell down and entreated him, saying: Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.” What, then, happened? “The master, having pity on that servant, released him and forgave him the debt.” How, then, was a man who had no means of repayment going to repay? He was to repay not from his own resources but from another’s—from the merits and satisfaction of our Christ; and yet these are not another’s, since Christ willed them to be ours.

Therefore, since those ambitious Roman candidates [Col. 1236B] so willingly undertook such great labors to obtain a fleeting dignity, how much better and more generously are we treated, since by the same effort—and one far lighter—we can both make satisfaction and at the same time invest profitably for ourselves in grace, the kingdom of heaven, and EVERLASTING GLORY. “Let magistrates now go their way”—thus I conclude with Saint Cyprian in the cited *Letter to Donatus*—“and consuls or proconsuls: let them glory in the insignia of a year-long dignity and in twelve fasces.”

**They bind with, as it were, a long rope.** Perhaps he has in view Proverbs 5:22 [Note: [Col. 1236D] Rather, Isaiah 5:18. See La Cerda on this passage, volume I of this work, column 1247. ED.]: “His own iniquities shall ensnare the wicked man, and he is bound by the cords of his own sins.” These ropes are indeed long and scarcely capable any longer of being broken. “From a perverse will,” says Saint Augustine in *Confessions*, Book VIII, chapter 5, confirming these things all too fully from his own experience, “lust was made; and when lust was served, habit was made; and when habit was not resisted, necessity was made”—a necessity, certainly, to be overcome by no human strength, but solely through the GRACE OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST.

## Notes on Chapter XII

[Col. 1236C]

**You reconsider**, used for “you consider,” as very often elsewhere. A person considers something in his mind when he thinks about confessing his sins and is now preparing to apply his mind seriously and effectively to that confession.

**Gehenna.** Gehenna is by no means, as some have thought, a Greek name, but a Hebrew one, signifying the same thing as “the Valley of Ennom.” Jeremiah 7:30–31 says of it:

> They built the high places of Tophet, which is in the VALLEY of the son of Ennom, that they might burn their sons and their daughters with fire, and so forth. Therefore, behold, the days are coming, and it shall no longer be called Tophet and the VALLEY of the son of ENNOM, but the Valley of Slaughter, and so forth.

“The Hebrews relate,” says Saint Jerome on this very text of Jeremiah, “that GEHENNA was named after this place (*gê hinnom*), because the entire people of the Jews perished there after offending God.” He explains the matter more fully in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 10:

> This valley, a small and level stretch of ground, was well watered, wooded, and full of delights, and within it was a grove consecrated to an idol—

MOLOCH, so often execrated by [Col. 1236D] Holy Scripture.

> The people had fallen into such madness that, forsaking the vicinity of the TEMPLE—

for this valley was close to Jerusalem—

> they offered victims there, and the rigor—

that is, their altogether monstrous and unspeakable cruelty—

> of religion—

namely, idolatrous religion—

> overcame the delights—

of that place, TOPHETH, named from DELIGHTS—

> and they burned their own sons for demons, or initiated them. And that place was called GEHENNOM, that is, the VALLEY of the children of HENNOM.

Thus Saint Jerome there. “Others report,” says the Latin translator of our Calmet in the *Biblical Dictionary*, under “Gehennom,” “that the city’s sewer was situated in that valley, where a perpetual fire was maintained for consuming carcasses and filth.”

**Do not hesitate.** The meaning is: do not deliberate with yourself for a long time over whether to seize upon this remedy or to postpone it any longer.

[Col. 1237A] **A treasury of eternal fire.** Thus he calls Gehenna, or hell; likewise in the *Apology Against the Nations*, chapter 47, he calls it “a subterranean TREASURY of hidden fire reserved for punishment.” Nor is this surprising, since all things preserved in certain repositories are sometimes called treasures. Thus Cicero, in *On the Orator*, calls memory “the treasury of all things.” Indeed, in Plautus I find even the expression “a treasury of evil.”

This word otherwise properly belongs to the Greeks, among whom θησαυρός (*thēsauros*, “treasure”) is thought by some to be derived from τιθέναι εἰς αὔριον (*tithenai eis aurion*, “to lay up for tomorrow,” or for future times), and by others from ἀπὸ τῆς θέσεως (*apo tēs theseōs*, “from the placing”)—namely, of gold—because gold in particular, and other precious things of that kind, are customarily hidden from the eyes and knowledge of other people and kept under stricter guard. I also find that ants and other animals which prepare and bury food for themselves for the winter were called by the Greeks θησαυριστικὰ τῆς τροφῆς ζῶα (*thēsauristika tēs trophēs zōa*), “animals that store up their food.”

That near the center of the earth there is an immense cavern filled with what resembles a fiery ocean raging in perpetual whirlwinds is the common conviction of natural philosophers. Moreover, [Col. 1237B] that this very place is hell is suggested by all those holy Fathers who believed that the souls of the damned are tormented by true and material fire—namely, as Saint Cyprian says in *On the Praise of Martyrdom*, “by torturing flames throughout the dreadful night of dense darkness, and by the perpetual raging fires of a smoking furnace,” and so forth. Read, if nothing else, Saint Augustine, *The City of God*, Book XXI, chapter 10.

Certainly, that treasury of infernal fire must be said to be hidden in some subterranean place, in the very bowels of the earth, until some other place more fitting than this presents itself: one most remote from that supreme and most radiant abode of the blessed, where nothing but “the shadow of death and everlasting horror dwells” (Job 10:22). Since the limbo of the Fathers itself, into which Christ descended to the underworld, was a subterranean place, why should we not assign to hell the lowest and deepest place of all within the earth’s bowels? There, by material fire, not only are those spirits and the souls of the damned even now tormented in marvelous but real ways, [Col. 1237C] but one day, after receiving back their bodies, they too will burn throughout all eternity, ever to be burned and never consumed.

**Little smoke-holes.** Thus, ironically, he calls the fire-spewing mountains scattered throughout the earth and already terrible in Tertullian’s time, especially Vesuvius and Etna, which not a few natural philosophers regard as the furnaces of hell. For they say that the central fire of our terrestrial globe is driven upward through fire-conducting channels into various other receptacles or fire-reservoirs, and from there is further forced through other conduits of this kind, variously intertwined, as far as the surface of our earth, until at last it finds an outlet through the cavernous vents of those mountains and sometimes discharges itself into the open air with incredible violence.

There are also some who say that the wailings of damned souls are sometimes heard in these mountains, though others regard this as entirely fabulous. I judge, however, that it could easily have happened that the subterranean roarings of these mountains, often heard even at a distance, impressed this terrifying apparition upon credulous and terror-stricken minds.

[Col. 1237D] In order that we may examine these little smoke-holes more deeply, it will be useful to draw certain details from an eyewitness, the immortal Athanasius Kircher, and from the preface to his *Subterranean World*, in his own words, lest I appear to have added anything. Driven by a desire to see the phenomenon, he overcame immense difficulties and struggled up to the summit of VESUVIUS, a mountain of Campania:

> I saw the entire crater illuminated by fire—horrible to relate!—amid an intolerable stench of burning sulfur and bitumen. Utterly stunned by this extraordinary spectacle, I believed that I was gazing upon the dwelling place of the infernal regions, in which nothing else seemed to be missing except the dreadful apparitions of demons. The mountain’s horrible roarings and rumblings could be perceived, together with an indescribable stench and smoke mingled with dusky globes of fire, which both the floor and sides of the mountain were continuously belching forth from eleven different places.

When he had prepared his *pantometrum* to measure that terrible crater, [Col. 1238A] he found that its circumference was nearly thirty thousand paces and its depth eight hundred paces.

He continues:

> The mountain, precipitous on every side in the form of a hollowed cylinder, descended around its circumference πρὸς τὰς ὀρθὰς (*pros tas orthas*), “at right angles.” In the center of the floor nature seemed to have established something like its own hearth—a true workshop of Vulcan’s kitchen, seething with an everlasting outpouring of smoke and flames, and occupied, by some hidden mechanism, in refining, separating, and burning sulfur, bitumen, and the other kinds of minerals, in preparation for the deadly devastation soon afterward to be produced. For the vapors enclosed within, as incapable of being contained as they were, shook off the burden placed upon them with such violence and force, accompanied by dreadful crashes, that the mountain seemed to be agitated by an earthquake. Whenever this occurred, the softer upper portions of the mountain, shaken and loosened by the tremor, fell like hills into the bottom of the abyss; and through the varied reflection of the sound they aroused such a crash as even a man of undaunted courage could scarcely endure. The matter continuously belched from [Col. 1238B] the center of the mountain formed what resembled a new mountain, furnished with a marvelous variety of streaks. The varied boiling of liquefied minerals shaped it, by their flow and color over every part of its circumference: now green from copper, then tawny from sulfur, arsenic, and sandarach; now red from cinnabar and red lead; now black from vitriol mixed with water, or ash-gray from the very ashes themselves. Thus it was fashioned by nature’s ingenious brush, and so forth.

Such is Kircher’s account of that Vesuvian smoke-hole. It ought not to seem surprising that the size and internal structure of its crater were described differently by different writers, since after every eruption, as was necessarily the case, it was found to have assumed a different appearance.

But now behold another smoke-hole of this kind: ETNA in Sicily, described by the same Athanasius, again as an eyewitness (*autoptēs*, αὐτόπτης). In Book IV of the *Subterranean World*, section I, chapters 8 and 9, he speaks as follows:

> At its highest summit the mountain opens into an enormous crater twelve Italian miles in circumference—

others assign it thirty, others again forty miles in circumference, and some fewer, [Col. 1238C] since this infernal crater gapes and expands to a greater or lesser degree at different times and according to the circumstances and effects of its horrible fury—

> and by a steep inward slope it narrows down toward Tartarus itself: a precipice horrible to behold, with flames and smoke bursting forth both from the depths and from the mountain’s side, accompanied by a dreadful roaring not unlike thunder. It is so fearsome that the mere imagination of imminent fire and ruin immediately dismays anyone, however daring and intrepid, and turns him away from what resembles an infernal abyss.

After another description of this immense chasm he continues:

> The gulf is so deep that it escapes every gaze, and is made fearsome by rocks rising like pyramids from its sides. And although those sides incline downward in a straight and perpendicular course, the rock faces descending in parallel, nevertheless, according to the laws of optics, because of the immense distance, they seem to converge at the center, and so forth. At the bottom—marvelous to relate!—I remember always observing, amid the continual belching forth of mineral matter, [Col. 1238D] what resembled a pool glittering with molten metal. The sides everywhere vomit forth perpetual smoke through corresponding passages in very many places, which at night we discovered to be kindled flame. The gulf is never without rumbling and roaring, and sometimes emits sounds so dreadful that they make even the mountain itself tremble. In a word, whoever desires to behold the marvelous power of GOD, the Best and Greatest, should approach mountains of this kind; and, astonished and stupefied by the ineffable effects of nature’s wonders, he will repeatedly be compelled to proclaim from the deepest affection of his heart: O DEPTH OF THE RICHES OF THE WISDOM AND KNOWLEDGE OF GOD! How incomprehensible are your judgments, and how unsearchable your ways! and so forth.

(Rom. 11:33.)

**They provoke blows.** The histories of all past ages attest that terrible destruction has been inflicted by mountains of this kind, which sometimes belch out entire conflagrations and seem to vomit forth hell itself—although a little later our author more correctly calls them only sparks from hell. [Col. 1239A] Thus Diodorus Siculus, in Book V of his *History*, relates that when Sicily was anciently inhabited by the SICANI, an eruption of Mount Etna burned all their crops and filled the entire neighboring region so deeply with ashes that, despairing of any further cultivation of their soil, they were compelled to withdraw into the western parts of the island, far from that mountain’s fury. Many centuries later, a new Italian people, the SICELS, as though ignorant of the disasters of the past, led a new colony across the strait into the deserted neighborhood of Etna.

See next what Cicero recounts in Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods* concerning the immense mass of ashes cast out from the burned-out bowels of the same mountain, which brought such dense darkness upon the entire surrounding country that for two days no man could recognize another. Saint Augustine also testifies in the final chapter of Book III of *The City of God*:

> We read that among them the sea grew so hot from Etna’s fires, which flowed from the mountain’s summit as far as the nearest shore, that [Col. 1239B] the rocks were burned and the pitch of ships was dissolved, and so forth.

Again, through the same surge of fire, Sicily was so completely filled with ash that it buried, crushed, and destroyed the roofs of the city of Catana. Moved to compassion by this disaster, the Romans remitted that city’s tribute for the year. What the horrible furies of Mount Etna were in the time of the two Plinys—that is, in the first century, in the year 76—we learn from two letters of the younger Pliny to Tacitus, the sixteenth and twentieth letters of Book VI. They cannot be read without immense agitation of mind, unless the horror of that spectacle is softened by the elegance of their style.

I do not mention here the eruption which in the year 812 drove the undaunted emperor CHARLEMAGNE from Sicily into Italy; nor the next one, which in 1537 vomited forth such an enormous quantity of sparks and ashes that they reached even across the sea into Italy and, if we believe Varenius, *Geography*, Book I, chapter 10, proposition 5, “ships at sea, though two hundred leagues distant from Sicily and sailing toward Venice, suffered damage.” [Col. 1239C] Nor do I mention anything about many other eruptions of this kind, certainly no less severe. Yet I cannot pass over two examples that occurred in the preceding century.

The first I excerpt from the account of Don Pietro Squillaci, a priest of Catana who was himself present during this disaster, as it appears in Kircher, Book IV, section I, chapter 9:

> When the entire surrounding country already seemed on the point of being overturned by dreadful convulsions of the earth, at last, on the eleventh of March—the year was 1669 from the birth of Christ—the mountain suddenly split open into three terrible chasms. The first of these vomited forth a vast quantity of fire and many stones, the very smallest of which equaled a weight of three *cantara*, or three hundredweights. The fiery matter, projected aloft, was dispersed at a distance of two miles—I always mean Italian miles—into the smallest particles and raged upon the ground below in the form of a fiery rain. Whenever the said furious mountain gaped open, it produced such crashing and such an earthquake that I cannot express its horror [Col. 1239D] in any words.

The crash was increased by the shouting of the lamenting people of Catana, to whom the world appeared to be ending. Those chasms vomited forth fire and sand in such quantity that the fields glowed red with living flame and the town of Catana, four miles from Etna, was covered, as it were, with blackened sand.

> All that fire, however, flowed away in two streams—

he would more accurately have called them rivers—

> which embraced and licked around Mountpelier—

although he had earlier said that its circumference was half a mile—

> so that it projected like an island or rock amid the flames. One of the principal streams buried the village of Mountpelier, so that every trace of it was erased. The entire fiery mass extended six miles in width, and near the beginnings of the two streams to a height of approximately four *canne*, more or less according to the variation of the terrain.

It is better, however, to read this entire account in Kircher, [Col. 1240A] where many other pertinent matters are explained at greater length. I promise that you will not do so without trembling of mind, if there is any piety in you—especially if you join to it the letters concerning the same eruption by Paolo Boccone of Palermo in Sicily and by Pierre Michon, otherwise known as the Abbé Bourdelot. Then indeed you will confess that the Mantuan poet was not stirred by excessive poetic frenzy when he poured forth his terrible song about this mountain in Book III of the *Aeneid*:

> . . . Etna thunders with horrific ruin,  
> And sometimes bursts into the air a cloud  
> Smoking with a pitch-black whirlwind and white-hot ash;  
> It lifts up globes of flame and licks the stars.  
> Sometimes, belching, it raises rocks  
> And the mountain’s torn-out entrails; with a groan  
> It heaps molten stones beneath the skies  
> And boils up from its deepest floor.

And yet those were only streams from this subterranean furnace, filled with an immense mass of liquefied minerals. [Col. 1240B] But what if you add other mountains, sometimes no less terrible than Etna? I do not mean Vesuvius in Campania alone, but Stromboli and Vulcano in the Lipari Islands, besides other fiery mountains of this kind in the Azores and the Canaries, islands of the Atlantic Ocean, and countless others. Finally, suppose you summon that terrible Hekla of farthest Iceland, a land seemingly congealed from ice itself. How immense a mass of fire do you think is required to inflame so many most capacious furnaces? If you combine them all into one, what else would you call Etna and Vesuvius but the little smoke-holes of that fiery Ocean raging in the more hidden recesses and innermost bowels of the earth?

How great, then, I ask, must be the force, the fury, and the heat of this Ocean, with so immense a mass of metals, minerals—each of which by itself customarily generates the greatest heat—and other combustible materials heaped together, as it were, into a single mass! Yet how very small—and this is truly astonishing—is the fear of it among many sinners!

Observe, however, what the fear [Col. 1240C] of merely temporal death could accomplish among those wretched people of Catana. “Lamentation,” Squillaci continues in his account, “disciplinary scourging, prayers, processions, fasts, abstinence, and expositions of the Forty Hours ceased in none of the churches, and produced such sorrow that the rocks themselves might have wept.” Yet the hearts of certain hardened sinners are now more stony than rocks, for they are not even moved by fear of eternal death.

But behold, once again, another little smoke-hole, and from it a conflagration bursting forth which not even the Ocean itself had been able to extinguish. The highest credibility for this incredible spectacle is nevertheless supplied by Fr. Ricciardus, S.J., who, as Kircher testifies in Book IV of the *Subterranean World*, “being present, saw everything with his own eyes, and afterward at Rome related to me orally the outcome of the entire affair, and wished it to be made known to posterity by written testimony.” Fr. Ricciardus’s account, as the highly renowned Kircher committed it with his pen to the memory of posterity, runs as follows:

> “If ever those fires enclosed within the bowels of the earth exerted their force, they did so most of all when, in the year [Col. 1240D] 1650, from September 24 to October 9, they shook that island”—it was Santorini, so called from St. Irene, Virgin and Martyr, to whom it is dedicated—“with so many enormous and frequent earthquakes that the people of Santorini, fearing imminent destruction, lay prostrate as suppliants at the altars day and night. Yet it is impossible either to state or explain how great a fear seized everyone when, after the barriers had been broken, those victorious flames struggled to force a path for themselves through the midst of the sea’s waves, about four Italian miles east of the island of Santorini. For the sea suddenly swelled upward to thirty cubits and, spreading widely over the neighboring lands, overturned everything in its path, so much so that in the very harbor of Candia, although it lies eighty miles away, it shattered both galleys and ships by its sudden assault. The air, meanwhile, infected by those foul-smelling, sulphurous vapors, began both to grow dark and to assume innumerable forms. Here fiery spears and flame-breathing swords [Col. 1241A] seemed to be brandished; there flashing arrows were discharged; here terrifying serpents and dragons seemed to fly about; there thunderbolts and lightning were stirred up, etc., etc.”

Furthermore, he continues, that fiery abyss vomited forth such a mass of pumice that the stones covered the entire surface of the sea. It is absolutely certain that they were carried as far as Smyrna and Constantinople and filled all the shores. The force of the conflagration was greatest during the first two months, since the neighboring sea appeared to boil like a seething pot, and enormous globes of flame and the densest smoke emerged day and night, etc., etc.

But what then? Should I think that another catastrophe ought to be passed over in silence—one similar to the former, indeed far more savage than all the rest—which the Ocean itself, where it flows among the Azores, exhibited in the preceding century? Here, then, are again the very words of Kircher, Book II of the *Subterranean World*, chapter XII, § 4:

> “Six miles from Pico—commonly called *Pico delle Camerine*—lies a place called *la Ferreria*. In that region of the Ocean, on a Saturday in the month of July 1638, fire erupted with such inexplicable violence that not even the Ocean sufficed to extinguish so great a conflagration, despite the fact that fishermen had previously and repeatedly ascertained the depth of the Ocean at that place to be 120 geometrical feet. [Col. 1241B] The area occupied by the boiling fire was as large as would suffice for sowing two *modii* of wheat. It erupted with such violence that, despite the aforementioned depth of the Ocean, it rose to the clouds and reached the upper region of the air, carrying up with it the water itself, sand, earth, rocks, and other enormous masses, which from a distance appeared—an appalling spectacle to those who beheld it—like tufts of cotton. When the material returned to the sea, it presented the appearance of molten pulp. From time to time, the force of raging nature hurled rocks of such immense size to a height of three spear-lengths that one would have said not rocks but entire mountains had been cast forth. Adding to the horror was the fact that, when those rocky mountains hurled aloft fell back and struck others wrested from the bowels of the sea, they burst with a terrible crash [Col. 1241C] into a thousand pieces; these, when afterward taken in hand, crumbled into black sand. Moreover, from the varied and immense quantity of ejected matter and the accumulation of innumerable rocks, a new island arose in the midst of the Ocean, and in its very deepest part. Small at first, measuring five *jugera*, it increased daily until, fourteen days later, it occupied a length of five miles. So great a multitude of fish perished in this conflagration that scarcely eight merchantmen of the Indies could have held them. Because they had been scattered far and wide over the island, the natives gathered them from a circuit of eighteen miles and buried them in extremely deep pits, lest their putrefaction cause some contagion. The smell of sulphur was perceptible over a distance of twenty-four miles.”

Thus Kircher, from the faithful eyewitness (*κατ’ αὐτοψίαν*, “according to direct observation”) report of the Fathers of the Society of Jesus.

### Now none remain

Among these was certainly Pompeii, said to have been founded by Hercules and formerly a Roman colony. Concerning it, our author likewise says in Book II of *On the Pallium*, chapter 2:

> By a cloud of this kind Etruria too was burned up in ancient Volsinii; and, that Campania might hope for all the more from its own mountains, Pompeii was torn away.

Likewise, in the *Apology*, chapter 40:

> Nor did Etruria and Campania complain about the Christians when Volsinii was drenched from heaven and Pompeii from its own mountain.

Tacitus likewise testifies concerning these matters in Book XV of the *Annals*, chapter 22, in these words:

> By an earthquake Pompeii, a celebrated town of Campania, collapsed in great part.

But anyone who wishes to know these events more precisely will find them in Dio Cassius’s *Roman History*, Book XVI, under Titus. And since I have once begun to be expansive and have already burst the narrow bounds of notes, what prevents me from excerpting from that author himself the following passages, which also lend credibility to what was said above, since readers will see that these things are not new, but occurred almost seventeen centuries ago? Xiphilinus, then, gives the following from his Dio:

> Then the sea began to roar at the same time, the whole sky resounded together, and an enormous and sudden crash was heard, as though mountains were collapsing together. Then immense stones first leapt forth and reached the highest summits, followed by a great quantity of fire [Col. 1242A] and smoke, so that it darkened the whole air and concealed the sun, just as though it had suffered an eclipse, etc. Some thought that the world was either being reduced to chaos or consumed by fire, etc., etc. So great was the quantity of ash that it filled the earth, the sea, and even the air itself. This caused great harm not only to human beings, estates, and livestock, but also destroyed all the fish and birds, and completely buried two entire cities, HERCULANEUM and POMPEII, while the people were seated in the theater—not, certainly, for the sake of some spectacle, but because they hoped for safety there and trusted that the place was better fortified against falling ruins.

And this is that very city, whether called Herculanum or Herculaneum, which Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book I of the *Roman Antiquities*, chapter 44, reports to have been founded by Hercules after his Spanish expedition. After it had been violently shaken under Nero in A.D. 63 and had collapsed in great part, and after it had been completely swallowed up around A.D. 80, it was discovered in the year 1713, and thus after sixteen full centuries. It has cast an immense light upon ancient history and enriched the treasury of Neapolitan antiquities with the richest additions of a new [Col. 1242B] and inestimable treasure. The entire literary world awaits with intense longing the fullest publication of it, which is now laboring under the press.

### *De die*

He meant *in dies*, “day by day” or “daily,” or, as we are otherwise accustomed to say, *de die in diem*, “from day to day.” In this sense our author also says in the *Apology*, chapter 16:

> You live in a novel fashion *de die*—from day to day.

So too Terence, in the *Adelphi*, spoke of “preparing a banquet *de die*,” that is, on each successive day.

### *Sperent*: “let them hope,” or “let them fear”

For *sperare*, “to hope”—just as hope is otherwise by its very nature joined with fear—was also customarily used among the ancients in this unfavorable sense. Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* I:

> If you despise the human race and mortal arms,  
> Yet fear the gods, who remember right and wrong.

And likewise Book IV:

> If I could have feared so great a grief as this—

### [Col. 1242C] *Ignis intrinsecus foeta*

Are the mountains themselves “pregnant”? But who would dare charge Tertullian with so great a grammatical lapse? Should one read *ignis intrinsecus foeti*, “pregnant inwardly with fire”? Yet in that case it would again be ambiguous whether *foeti* should be referred to the mountains, which are pregnant with fire—or rather made pregnant by fire—or to the fire, as though the fire itself were pregnant with sulphur, etc. Or is it preferable, with Latinius, to read *foetu*, “with offspring” or “with fecundity”? I myself certainly think so.

### *Nobis judicii*

That is, “for us of judgment”—of punishment, or of infernal penalty. See above, chapter III, the note on *In judicium*.

### Yet they are never ended

There is no age whose history does not recount such rages of mountains. As regards eruptions of Vesuvius, Kircher indeed supplies a chronicle of this kind, in which he reviews eighteen instances of Etna raging since the first arrival of the Janigenae in Sicily. Others enumerate more than twenty such grim instances of Vesuvius from the time of Christ down to our own. That these enormous furnaces are kindled with perpetual fire is made clearer than daylight by the continuous, dense volumes of smoke which they belch forth even while at rest.

[Col. 1242D] Furthermore, a difficult question has long exercised philosophers: from where come those perpetual conflagrations of such mountains, and the inexhaustible fuel required to sustain such fires through so many centuries? For it might seem that all the subterranean storehouses of fire, and hell itself, however immense, ought long ago to have been emptied through those fire-breathing vents.

Since a longer treatment of this matter lies outside our present purpose, we shall disclose our opinion only briefly.

First, we note that the material cast out by those dreadful convulsions of Etna accumulates chiefly upon the rim of its crater, and sometimes to such a height that it may appear to be a new mountain, or at least a considerable part of a mountain.

Second, this heap of ashes and other ejected matter, already impregnated by itself with various salts, is also commonly enriched by new subterranean additions through hidden channels, especially from the sea, as well as from melted snow—with which the summits of these [Col. 1243A] mountains are almost continually white—from the surrounding salt-laden and nitrous air, etc. This continues until the material, baked by the heat of the underlying fire and melted as though into a pulp, is driven into the utmost fury by subterranean air passages or even by water flowing in from subterranean reservoirs, etc. How great a disturbance even a single drop of water sprinkled upon molten metal in smelting furnaces can raise, and what an incredible devastation of everything it can produce, quite a few persons have at times learned at no small cost to themselves.

### Meanwhile, the punishments of the mountains

He calls “punishments of the mountains” the injuries inflicted by these very mountains, especially for the chastisement of sinners, etc.

### Not of the Judgment

He rather clearly intimates that final JUDGMENT, in which the whole world will be consumed by fire, as we said in *On Baptism*, chapter VIII, in the note “Destined for fire,” and in which the damned will hear that terrible sentence:

> Depart from me, accursed, into ETERNAL FIRE, etc.

Even now the SUPREME JUDGE threatens this through the [Col. 1243B] conflagrations of fire-breathing mountains.

### *Deputabit*

Simply for *putabit* or *aestimabit*, “will think” or “will reckon.” Thus our author also says in *Exhortation to Chastity*, chapter 6:

> It was the old dispensation, which in the Gospel is reckoned as new, etc.

So too Plautus, long before, had said in the *Amphitryon*:

> And let there be nothing for which all do not reckon me worthy.

Terence followed him in the *Hecyra*, where he writes:

> By Pollux, my master truly reckons my labor of little value.

### Sparks

By the same right by which he had called the immense craters of those fire-breathing mountains “little smoke-holes,” he now calls their conflagrations “sparks.” And sparks they certainly are if compared with that immense conflagration of HELL. When our sparks happen to burn our hands, the latter are withdrawn in pain at the first touch. Yet sinners have not yet immersed their hands—I will not say in molten lead, for how slight would that be!—but not even in those fiery torrents of Etna or Vesuvius, that is, in those “sparks,” although perhaps they are destined to burn eternally and never be consumed in that infernal abyss, the proper seat of the element of fire. [Col. 1243C]

### Of the inestimable hearth

That is, a hearth whose immense force of burning far surpasses not merely every estimate we can make, but all the powers of imagination.

### Missiles

In antiquity, *missilia* were gifts of coined gold and silver that were sometimes scattered among the people by emperors, or by the Senate and magistrates, in order profitably to win—or, to use a barbarous expression, to “collect”—their applause and favor. Indeed, objects of other kinds were also sometimes distributed as *missilia*, as Suetonius says in his *Caligula*:

> He also scattered largesses of various kinds.

Later, however, the word also passed into military usage, so that weapons discharged against enemies were likewise called *missilia*, “missiles.” Our author did not hesitate even to call thunderbolts *missilia* in Book II of *On the Pallium*, chapter 2.

### Practice-weapons

An *exercitor* is properly one who teaches another through exercise, as may be gathered from Plautus in the *Trinummus*: [Col. 1243D]

> This man, whoever he is, Curculio, is a trainer; he is teaching this man to run.

Hence those weapons discharged in military exercises and mock practice were called *exercitoria*, “practice-weapons,” and by Seneca, in Book II of *Natural Questions*, *lusoria*, “sporting weapons.”

### Of the Lord’s immersion

That is, of Baptism instituted by Christ the Lord.

### Memorials

*Monimenta*, “memorials,” are so called because they have been set up to admonish (*monere*) our mind to preserve the memory of past events. Junius here reads *munimenta*, “fortifications,” because they fortify us in advance against Gehenna.

### Second reserves

An elegant expression. For among the ancients the *subsidia*, “reserves,” were properly the third line in a battle formation, composed of the *triarii*, veterans, and the bravest soldiers. Placed at the rear, they would therefore settle down upon their knees beneath their standards, ready to come to the aid of an army that might be struggling and to restore its wavering line with fresh reinforcement. See Varro, *On the Latin Language*, Book IV.

### [Col. 1244A] Mute indeed

He calls “mute” those creatures that lack articulate speech.

### Souls

Here he uses *animae*, “souls,” for *animalia*, “animals,” as though employing a part for the whole.

### They recognize

For by the instinct of nature itself, divinely implanted in them, they avoid harmful things, seek wholesome ones, and, when they begin to fall ill, quickly look about for remedies. There can be no doubt that this instinct possesses something analogous to human reason.

### Delays

Among surgeons, a *mora* is a certain channel artificially hollowed out, into which a broken leg, already wrapped with bandages, is placed so that it may remain motionless there and “make a stay” (*moram trahere*). In the same way, arrows deeply fixed in the skin “make their stays” there, and sometimes irrevocably, namely when they have penetrated too deeply to be extracted or shaken out by the wounded animals themselves and thus recalled from the wound.

### With dittany

Aristotle indeed affirms this concerning wild goats in Book IX of the *History of Animals*, chapter 6, in these words:

> They say that in the island of Crete wild goats pierced by an arrow seek the herb dittany, for by this the barbed points are expelled from the body. [Col. 1244B]

He confirms the same thing in *On Marvelous Things Heard*, no. 4. Hence Virgil, *Aeneid* XII:

> Then Venus, the mother, shaken by her son’s undeserved pain,  
> Plucks dittany from Cretan Ida,  
> Its stem clothed in downy leaves and crowned  
> With purple flower. Those grasses are not unknown  
> To wild goats when swift arrows lodge in their backs.

But Pliny, Book VIII of the *Natural History*, chapter 27, transfers this to deer. Yet how many things are sometimes invented or reported with excessive credulity and are not verified! Certainly modern investigators of nature maintain profound silence on this matter, evidently possessing nothing from either their own or others’ sufficient experience by which they could properly establish the credibility of this belief of the ancients.

### To give them eyes

That is, to give them sight. For in this way our author also writes in the *Apology*, chapter 21:

> That he might give eyes, for the recognition of truth, to those already polished and deceived by refinement itself.

This verb, otherwise scarcely used by the ancients, was borrowed from his Tertullian by St. Cyprian in the treatise *On the Vanity of Idols*, near the end, where he speaks of the apostles, who gave eyes to the blind and ignorant for the recognition of truth. [Col. 1244C]

### From its own celandine

Aristotle, Book IV of *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter 6, asserts that swallows produce blind chicks, but says nothing about celandine. Pliny, however, affirms it in the passage cited, generally placing too much trust in the reports of others. This belief passed so thoroughly into popular opinion and adhered so tenaciously that even the very name of the swallows—for this bird is called *χελιδών* (*chelidōn*) in Greek—passed to that plant, which our Germans likewise call *Schwalben-Kraut* or *Schwalben-Wurtz*, “swallow-herb.” But the blindness of newly hatched birds—not only swallows but almost all birds, excepting aquatic species—is not properly blindness at all, but merely a covering of the eyelids, which after several days commonly separates gradually and frees the eyes from their coverings.

### Instituted for himself

That is, instituted for him, so that through repentance he might once again be restored to the grace of God.

### The Babylonian king

This is not that Nebuchadnezzar [Col. 1244D] who was otherwise called Saosduchin and who, in the year of the world 3347, defeated Arphaxad, king of the Medes, on the plain of Ragau; nor the other Nebuchadnezzar, otherwise called Nabopolassar, who is believed to have founded the kingdom of the Chaldeans in the year of the world 3378. Rather, it is the latter’s son Nebuchadnezzar, surnamed the Great, who succeeded to the kingdom in the year of the world 3399. He reduced Jehoiakim, king of Judah, to servitude (IV Kings 24:1); after besieging Jerusalem, he carried Jehoiachin into captivity when the latter voluntarily surrendered himself and all his people (ibid., v. 12 ff.); after Jerusalem had been captured, he killed the sons of Zedekiah, the last king of Judah, before his eyes, put out Zedekiah’s eyes, bound him in chains, and brought him to Babylon (IV Kings, final chapter, v. 7); finally, through Nebuzaradan, commander of his army, he burned the House of the Lord, the king’s house, the houses of Jerusalem, and every house with fire (ibid., v. 9), and thus completely extinguished and utterly overthrew the whole kingdom of Judah.

[Col. 1245A] When, as a result of this and the many other victories he had won over the Syrians, Phoenicians, Egypt, etc., he had become far more exalted and excessively unable to govern himself, God at last showed him in a dream the future penalties of his pride—a pride which could no longer be subdued by any other means. He saw a very tall and beautiful tree, cut down by the hand of an angel, stripped of all its ornament, with its root bound by a band of iron and bronze, etc. Daniel interpreted this dream and earnestly exhorted the king to repentance:

> Redeem your sins with alms, and your iniquities with mercies toward the poor; perhaps he will forgive your offenses.

But when the king too stubbornly refused to obey such salutary warnings, even after being granted an interval of twelve months, he was at last walking in the palace of Babylon and said:

> Is this not BABYLON THE GREAT, which I have built as the HOUSE OF THE KING, by the might of MY power and for the glory of MY splendor?

What then? While the words were still in the king’s mouth, a voice fell from heaven:

> TO YOU IT IS SAID, King Nebuchadnezzar: Your kingdom will pass away [Col. 1245B] from you; your dwelling will be with beasts and wild animals; you will eat hay like an ox; and seven times will pass over you, until you know that the MOST HIGH rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whomever he wills.

What happened next?

> In that same hour the sentence was fulfilled upon Nebuchadnezzar. He was driven from among men, ate hay like an ox, and his body was drenched with the dew of heaven, until his hair grew like that of eagles and his nails like those of birds.

After he had passed seven entire years among beasts in this most wretched condition and had been sufficiently humbled, he himself relates in what follows, at verse 33, what happened next:

> At that time my understanding returned to me, and I attained the honor and splendor of my kingdom, etc.; my magistrates sought me out, I was restored to my kingdom, and still greater magnificence was added to me.

### Like eagles’ talons

Our Vulgate mentions “the nails of birds,” namely birds of prey, among which eagles certainly stand out.

### [Col. 1245C] A leonine horror

Where our Vulgate has “like EAGLES,” the Septuagint has *λεόντων*, “of LIONS”; hence some in former times fell into the opinion that this king had been transformed into a lion.

### Displaying

There are many points in the history of this terrible metamorphosis which are debated rather contentiously among interpreters. They would certainly require more exact discussion if it were permissible once again—for this has already been done sufficiently elsewhere—to transgress the much narrower limits of our undertaking. Yet because our Tertullian set forth this most grievous example above all others, in order by its terror to compel sinners who presume far too proudly upon themselves to serious repentance, we cannot entirely refrain from dwelling upon it briefly.

I therefore assume, first, against Origen—who was otherwise far more devoted than was justifiable to allegorical senses, and was censured for this by St. Jerome in his *Commentary on Daniel* and thereafter by other interpreters—that this is not a mere allegory but an entirely true history. I am not unaware, however, that most of what is said about Nebuchadnezzar, as some maintain, in Isaiah 14 from verse 8 onward is also to be understood allegorically, according to the mind of the holy Fathers and of the Church herself, as referring to the most wretched expulsion from heaven of LUCIFER—the light-bearer, but one soon extinguished and now the king of darkness. [Col. 1245D]

Second, I assume that nothing can safely be asserted in this matter except what the historical wording in Daniel itself requires. Daniel, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, transmitted this event to us together with even its minute circumstances; consequently, God himself did not will that anything more should be known to us with certainty.

Third, I say that the Babylonian king was not actually changed into an ox or any other beast. For the human soul itself could not have been converted into the soul of an ox; that would certainly have been to change the essences of things. Nor, after the man’s soul had been expelled, did the soul [Col. 1246A] of an ox enter his body as though through some *μετεμψύχωσις* (*metempsychōsis*, transmigration of souls). That could not have occurred naturally, and the wording of the sacred text in no way compels recourse to a miracle. It signifies only that he ate hay LIKE AN OX, not that he changed into an actual ox. Do oxen have hair like eagles’ feathers, or nails like birds’ talons?

Furthermore, if he had assumed the true soul of an ox, Nebuchadnezzar would certainly have felt no punishment from it, nor could he have been brought thereby to knowledge of the true God, since he would have survived in body alone with no power of understanding remaining. Or will someone perhaps say that the soul of a brute was admitted, by a new miracle, into a partnership with the king’s soul in the same body? Or shall we say, finally, that the man’s soul meanwhile fled elsewhere and lived in exile somewhere outside every body—or was reduced entirely to nothing—and later returned by a right of restoration, or was reproduced, that is, newly created, entered its former body, and restored the king to himself? Who would dare devise such monstrosities of opinion?

Fourth, therefore, I say that the king’s transformation did not occur solely in his imagination, whereby he believed himself to be an ox and ate hay. It occurred plainly in the external bearing and appearance of his body, which assumed hair like that of eagles, nails like those of birds, etc. [Col. 1246B] I frame the hypothesis as follows.

First, Nebuchadnezzar was cast out from among men, that is, from their society; yet he did not therefore cease to be a human being. Rather, seized by sudden frenzy and madness, he lost the use of human reason, escaped or broke through the presence of his attendants and every guard, rushed into fields and forests, and, after his clothes had soon become tattered or—as madmen are accustomed to do—had been torn apart, wandered about aimlessly. Then, when human food was no longer available, since he had by then become wholly possessed by the imagination that he was an ox, he turned also to the ox’s fodder and ate hay LIKE AN OX.

Second, from this continual diet, so alien to a human being, there necessarily followed the most profound alteration of the blood, the other bodily fluids, the animal spirits, and that entire temperament, and at last even the outward condition of the whole body was disfigured. Through such a wild and long-continued diet it became savage and horrible in appearance: his hair resembled eagles’ feathers and his nails the talons of birds, so that Nebuchadnezzar, like an *ἀνθρωπόταυρος* (*anthrōpotauros*, “man-bull”), might at last have terrified not only human beings but even herds of oxen. [Col. 1246C] In this way, finally, it seems possible to satisfy Daniel’s account, as will be evident to anyone who weighs the fourth chapter carefully.

But what of the king during this most disastrous seven-year period? Did he retain the use of reason meanwhile and perceive the magnitude of his calamity, almost as Apuleius testifies about himself in his fabulous *Ass*? Our Tertullian indeed seems to have thought that he did, when he says that the king offered repentance for a LONG TIME—namely for as long as that unhappy condition lasted—and performed *exomologesis*, public penitential confession, through seven years of squalor.

Not a few others believe that intervals of reason at least shone upon the king with some frequency, so that he would from time to time recognize the misery of his condition. For, they say, that condition would not have been punitive if he had felt no distress whatever from it [Col. 1246D] and could not have compared it with the happiness of his former dignity, but instead had wandered with pleasure through fields and forests among wild animals in this depraved state of an alienated mind.

Yet, if I may frankly state my opinion, I incline to the view that the king was wholly deprived of the use of reason throughout that entire period of seven years. The sacred text does not compel us to think otherwise:

> Therefore, he says, AFTER THE END OF THE DAYS, I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted my eyes toward heaven—

He would have raised them more often if, during certain intervals of reason, he had recognized the unhappiness of his condition—

> —and MY UNDERSTANDING—

By this word the use of reason, or the mind’s consciousness and perception, is plainly denoted—

> —was restored to me, and I blessed the Most High, etc.

He confirms the same by that impassioned discourse in which, celebrating GOD’s praises, glory, power, and kingdom, he continues:

> AT THAT TIME my understanding returned to me, and my appearance returned to me, etc.

Thus only then [Col. 1247A] did he at last recognize God, when he recovered both his intellect and his former human appearance.

It is helpful to explain the matter further in this way. When those seven years had elapsed, the king awoke as though from a deep sleep. Those dark spirits which until then had besieged his mind from every side were dispersed—and this could not have happened so suddenly without a miracle. The memory of his monstrous pride and of the deeds he had committed with utmost wickedness because of it returned; the entire misery of his prolonged wretchedness and all its circumstances were vividly presented to his intellect. His pride was at last subdued, and he was driven to acknowledge the true God and to profess both his JUSTICE and his MERCY; thus, finally, he was converted, etc.

### Alas, what ill-treatment!

This is a Hellenism, for the Greeks frequently join the genitive to expressions of exclamation.

### God was receiving him

Did this king practice true repentance, profitable for eternal salvation, by which his sins were erased? And did he thereafter persevere in it and finally obtain salvation itself among the truly penitent? The matter is highly uncertain.

St. Jerome, in Letter VII to Laeta, and St. Augustine, in Letter CXXII—now CXI—to Victorianus, and especially the author of the book *On Predestination and Grace*, chapter 15, formerly attributed to St. Augustine, do seem to favor him. To others, however, that repentance is highly suspect, for they measure it by this king’s inconstant disposition. [Col. 1247B]

Certainly, after he had received from Daniel the interpretation of his dream concerning that STATUE composed of four metals, he was wholly astounded and burst out in these words:

> Truly your God is the GOD OF GODS and the LORD OF KINGS and a revealer of mysteries, etc. (Dan. 3:47)

But how unstable he was in his recognition of the true God, and with how great a pride he afterward swelled up again, is demonstrated by that second dream which followed—of the most beautiful tree soon to be cut down, etc. (Dan. 4)—and then by the terrible sentence pronounced against the king, condemning him to seven years of exile among beasts. For although God still granted him [Col. 1247C] an entire year in which to redeem his sins through almsgiving and other good works, we read that he did none of these things, but rather, swollen with fresh pride, boasted insolently of his own achievements.

And what happened besides? After he had spent seven full years among wild beasts in that most wretched bodily condition, and after he had recovered not only his former form but the kingdom itself, indeed increased with greater magnificence, what then? We read that he finally exclaimed:

> Now, therefore, I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise, magnify, and glorify the King of heaven, because all his works are true and his ways are judgments, and he is able to humble those who walk in pride.

Yet concerning repentance, sorrow of mind, detestation of his former life, a resolve upon a new and better one, etc., we read nothing. And these are precisely the things in which the nature of true and sincere repentance consists.

But how brief was even that acknowledgment of God and that humility? Behold a far greater madness of a mind swelling up anew—indeed a madness wholly incredible, were it not attested by the Prophet! Scarcely a year had elapsed [Col. 1247D], as the interpreters calculate, when:

> King Nebuchadnezzar made a golden statue, sixty cubits high, and set it up in the plain of Dura (Dan. 3:1, etc.).

This statue displayed the likeness either of Nabopolassar, his father, or of Bel, then the greatest of the Babylonian gods, or of Nebuchadnezzar himself; and by the publication of a most severe edict he ordered it to be worshiped. When those three young men, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, refused to commit this sacrilegious crime, he ordered them cast into a fiery furnace. When they were brought forth unharmed, the king, astounded by this new and enormous miracle, exclaimed:

> Blessed be the GOD OF GODS, who sent his angel, etc. (ibid., v. 95).

Indeed, by a public and extremely severe decree he restrained blasphemers against the God of Israel, publicly declaring:

> The MOST HIGH GOD has worked signs and wonders in my presence. It has therefore pleased me to proclaim his signs, because they are GREAT, and his wonders, because they are MIGHTY; his kingdom is an EVERLASTING KINGDOM, and his POWER endures from generation to generation [Col. 1248A] (ibid., v. 10).

This, however, is the very edict in which Nebuchadnezzar proceeds to recount the events that we cited above from Daniel 4 concerning his grim seven-year period in the forests. It is therefore necessary to conclude that the king’s metamorphosis—which should be carefully noted—occurred before this history of the three young men.

Who, I ask, could now promise himself that a king so inconstant possessed sincere and stable repentance, when Daniel thereafter maintains so profound a silence concerning his works, worthy fruits of repentance, and especially a blessed death? How different was the repentance of Manasseh, king of Judah! He was a most impious king, and perhaps even far more criminal than Nebuchadnezzar himself; nevertheless:

> After he was brought into distress, he prayed to the Lord his God and repented greatly before the God of his fathers; he prayed to him and earnestly besought him . . . and removed the foreign gods and the idol from the House of the Lord. . . . Moreover, he restored the altar of the Lord and sacrificed upon it victims, peace offerings, and praise; and he commanded Judah to serve the Lord God of Israel.

What similar things, I ask, do we read as recorded concerning Nebuchadnezzar? He indeed praised and magnified God, etc.; but did he pray, supplicate, and earnestly beseech him, etc.? [Col. 1248B]

And what, finally, if certain distinguished interpreters, including St. Jerome himself, wish the words of Isaiah 14—

> Hell beneath you was disturbed to meet you at your coming. . . . Your pride has been dragged down to hell, etc., etc.—

to be understood of Nebuchadnezzar? But it is better to leave either this king’s repentance and salvation or his damnation among those matters which God, like many other things of this kind, willed to remain unknown to us for the sake of salutary fear and thereby of greater constancy in repentance.

### The Egyptian emperor

That is, Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who is here called “emperor” in a broader sense, since, like other kings, he exercised supreme command over his subjects.

### Long denied to his Lord

For Moses had been commanded by God [Col. 1248C] to proclaim to Pharaoh in these words:

> The Lord God of the Hebrews has sent me to you, saying: Let my people go, that they may sacrifice to me in the desert; and until the present time you have refused to listen.

### By the cleaving of the sea

That is, by that division which the Greeks call *διχοτομία* (*dichotomia*, “bisection”). So too in Book II of *On the Pallium*, chapter 2, he speaks of “the wound of division,” and in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 19, of “the division of flesh and soul.” Solinus likewise used this word in chapter 36, saying:

> The Atlantic tide introduces into our sea the division—or severing—of the world.

### It was available as passable

*Liceo*, an ancient verb, has a passive meaning. Properly, a thing is said *licere* when it is valued at a definite price and offered for sale, while *liceri* means to value it and place a price upon it, as buyers do. Hence the poet’s line:

> The man who does not bid an *as* for me is not worth an *as* to me.

The sea therefore *licebat*, “was offered,” when it was presented by God to the Israelites [Col. 1248D] as passable for their crossing. Elsewhere Tertullian also uses *licere* for *liquere* or *patere*, “to be clear” or “to lie open,” as in *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 36:

> But concerning motion it will be clear elsewhere—
