that is, *liquebit*. Similarly, above in chapter VI, for *emendatos liquebit*, “it will be clear that they have been corrected,” some manuscripts substitute *licebit*.

### When the waves rolled back

The history of the crossing of the Red Sea—an event as fortunate and miraculous for the Israelites as it was fatal to the Egyptians and their Pharaoh—is universally familiar from Exodus 14.

Restored by *exomologesis*. *Exomologesis* differs from repentance as an external act differs from an internal one; for repentance is located in the mind of the person who grieves, whereas *exomologesis* is located in the mouth of the person who confesses and in the other works that outwardly manifest and demonstrate that inward repentance. Our author has already discussed these at length above, chapter IX.

[Col. 1249A] **Like Pharos.** Pharos was the name of that very lofty Egyptian tower, counted among the seven wonders of the world, which Ptolemy Philadelphus—or, at any rate, one of the Ptolemies—erected on the island of Pharos, seven stadia from the harbor of Alexandria and connected to the mainland by either a bridge or a causeway. He built it at the enormous cost, according to Pliny (*Natural History*, XXXIII, 12), of 800 talents—which, if I have calculated correctly, equal 1,200,000 of our thalers—in order to display fires to ships sailing by night, warning them of shoals and indicating the harbor entrance. From it, all towers—such as the one at Capri in Sicily which collapsed in an earthquake shortly before the death of the emperor Tiberius (Suetonius, *Tiberius*, 74); another which the emperor Claudius, according to the same author (*Claudius*, 21), had raised in imitation of the Alexandrian Pharos in the harbor at Ostia that he himself had excavated; and, finally, all those that still stand today in maritime cities and are customarily illuminated by nocturnal fires for the benefit of sailors—are called by the general name “Pharoses.” This name is not, as Isidore supposed (*Origins*, XV, 2), derived from Greek, ἀπὸ τοῦ [Col. 1249B] φωτὸς ὁρᾷν, “from seeing the light there,” but is more probably Egyptian in origin, having been transferred to that tower from the island itself, to which the name Pharos had long before adhered.

**Bearing every mark.** That is, marked in the worst possible way—namely, by as many sins as though they were brands burned into the soul. See another example of humility of this kind which Tertullian offered concerning himself at the end of the final chapter of *On Baptism*.

**To be silent about those things.** He means, as it were, that he finds it difficult to bring this treatise to an end and is breaking it off almost against his will.

[Col. 1250A] **The first, Adam**, that is, the originator and the first of all.

**Into Paradise.** In *Apology*, chapter 47, our Tertullian calls Paradise a place of divine delight appointed to receive the spirits of the saints. He believed that Paradise still existed, that it was situated beneath the Equator, and that it was enclosed on both sides by the torrid zone as by a wall of fire, and thus rendered inaccessible to mortals. St. Thomas, *Summa theologiae* II-II, q. 164, art. 2, ad 5, appears not to depart very far from this opinion. This word did not arise among the Greeks from παρὰ and δεύω, “from irrigating,” as Suidas maintains, but is of Persian—indeed Hebrew, or rather Chaldaean—origin, being derived from *pardes* [the immediately preceding etymological wording is corrupt in the source], which, according to the force of the word, signifies a garden of myrtles or, more generally, any exceptionally pleasant place.

But how was Adam restored through repentance to Paradise? Certainly not to that earthly Paradise from which he had been expelled and to which every return had been barred after God “placed before the paradise of pleasure [Col. 1250B] the Cherubim and a flaming, turning sword, to guard the way to the tree of life” (Gen. 3:24). Therefore that Paradise must be understood spiritually and mystically as the state of grace into which Adam was restored through repentance.

**He is not silent.** He still preaches to us by his example: amid toil, among thorns and thistles, and in the sweat of his face, as though performing perpetual works of repentance, he cultivated the earth and ate his bread from it. Thus he would serve as a lesson to us that only through the works of laborious repentance can one reach the **HEAVENLY PARADISE**, thereafter to inhabit it forever.

## Back Matter of the Volume

[Col. 1249]

# INDEX OF TERTULLIAN’S LATINITY

[Col. 1249C] We have already said a little, in the preface placed at the threshold of this edition, about the value of Tertullian’s Latin—though new, as no one denies, and generally inelegant and harsh. Dr. Lumper has more on this a little below; see, if you wish, vol. I, cols. 93–94. We have no intention of repeating these matters more fully here, nor will anyone suppose that a suitable place for a new dissertation is available at the extreme limits of our work. Readers should merely remember this above all: that attention must be paid to Tertullian’s novel expressions, since in them the new language of the Latin Church is born and bursts forth, as it were, in its first shoot. Nor should the first rudiments of a form of speech that has passed through the mouths of so many persons and centuries throughout the whole Christian world, continuing down to our own usage and enduring to the great praise of God and the salvation of souls, any longer be held in such contempt.

They should remember, moreover, that the unusual vocabulary of Tertullian’s Latin must be traced especially to three causes: first, to the difficult and utterly novel exposition of the Christian faith; next, to the bold use of Hellenisms, more frequent in Septimius because he was especially fond of writing in a Greek manner; [Col. 1249D] and finally, to his forensic practice and familiar expertise in the ancient Roman laws, through which he is very often found to have employed the pronouncements of jurists. To these must be added—as in other men whom nature has endowed exceptionally well—Tertullian’s innate disposition, spontaneously inclined toward unusual expressions, overflowing with the excessive abundance of his many fields of learning and, so to speak, belching from satiety, and finally willing to write rustically because of a certain inborn African roughness.

“What wonder is it,” says a recent author, “that the writings of Tertullian—a stern, impetuous, ardent man of luxuriant imagination and acute intellect—display the most evident marks of this disposition of his and have assumed an uncommon character? A harsh and obscure style of writing was characteristic of Africans. This therefore attached itself spontaneously to him as well. Yet in this very quality he is truly unique and always himself. Because of his difficult arrangement of words and his employment here and there of obsolete and novel terms, his discourse is often troublesome to readers. At one moment it creates disgust by its swollen grandiloquence; at another it produces obscurity by its broken composition. Yet if you excuse these features, I often seem to hear a man whom, in the gravity and fervor of his discourse, I would not judge inferior even to an orator of the Golden Age. Read the *Apologeticum*. Observe especially how, from its very beginning, he assails his opponents in vehement yet majestic language, stings them with acuteness, troubles their conscience, moves them to pity, and finally carries the mind away in admiration both of his own magnanimity and of the sublimity of the religion he is about to defend. Observe these things and, unless everything deceives me, you will thereby be abundantly persuaded that Tertullian, however great the stylistic faults from which he suffered, possessed outstanding eloquence.” Thus J. A. Coessen, *Commentatio de Tertulliano, Christi et religionis christianae adversus gentes apologeta* (“Dissertation on Tertullian as Apologist for Christ and the Christian Religion against the Gentiles”), *Annales Academiae* [Col. 1250D] *Rheno-Trajectinae*, 1823–1824.

No one, therefore, will find it surprising that all editors of Tertullian have compiled a glossary peculiar to him with such diligence. Moreover, from the many indexes of this kind furnished by the older editions, especially Rigault’s, we considered that the one which Christian Gottfried Schütz, professor of humane letters and eloquence at the University of Jena, appended to the Halle edition should be selected above all others. He rendered distinguished assistance to Salomon Semler in preparing the edition of Septimius. We have preferred his index to the others chiefly because, although it is somewhat shorter, or lists fewer words, it nevertheless probes the mysteries of Tertullian’s language more clearly through the abundance of its subject matter, its description of words, and the learning displayed in its definitions [Col. 1251A] and discussions. Not undeservedly, the author himself, with the agreement of most scholars highly experienced in patristic studies, considered it to serve as a continuous commentary. Words which are either missing here and there or insufficiently explained generally carry their own explanation with them, either in the fabric of the context or in the very copious notes of various scholars. Some, however, appear merely to have been cited so that they might be brought to notice—and not without deliberation, since it is not irrelevant to observe what formulas of expression Tertullian produced and what kind of language Christian literature fashioned for itself from its birth. —EDS.

The first numerals designate the volume; the second, the column; the third, the letter attached within the columns to the words cited.

# A

[Col. 1251A]

**A and Ω.** II, 935 B: “Thus the Lord also assumed for himself the two letters of Greece, the first and the last, as figures of the beginning and the end converging in himself,” etc.

**ABDICARE** (*to disown, repudiate*). II, 928 C: “Having voluntarily repudiated marriage, they grow old.” I: “The father, now bearing with his submissive son in turn, who had previously borne with his son when he was disobedient and defiant, [Col. 1251B] disowned him.”

**ABDICERE**, to disown, reject. II, 394 C: “Thus the Creator rejected everything sought from man.”

**ABHINC**, henceforth, from this point. II, 564 A: “What is written from this point onward.”

**ABIRE** (*to depart*). I, 1283 B: “As a woman whose husband has departed from affairs,” that is, has departed from life. Thus the Greeks customarily use the verbs οἴχεσθαι, κατοίχεσθαι, ἀπέρχεσθαι, and ὑπογίνεσθαι, that is, “to die”; all of them signify departure and withdrawal.—I, 615 C: “He has now departed and must return,” a proverb. For its meaning, see I, 209 B; 616 D.

**ABLUERE** (*to wash*), to baptize. II, 806 A: “The flesh is washed.” II, 1011 A: “It is not permitted to be washed again.”

**ABNOCTARE** (*to spend the night*). II, 749 B: “Among the Celts, to spend the night beside the tombs of brave men.…” [The text cited reads *adnoctare*.]

**ABOLEFACERE**, to abolish. I, 452 B: “To destroy a city by giving it the character of a tavern,” that is, to exchange civil and honorable order for the confusion of a tavern. Scaliger corrects it to *abolefacere*, κνίσσᾷν [“to fill with the savor or reek of burnt sacrifice”; reading uncertain]. I, 1308 A: “He could likewise have [Col. 1251C] abolished it,” etc.

**ABOMINAMENTUM** (*abomination*). II, 637 A: “The man cast away his golden abominations.”

**ABORTIVUS** (*abortive*). II, 564 A: “A defective and, so to speak, abortive birth.” Irenaeus: “Formless and without appearance, like an abortion.” II, 331 C: “The premature and, in a manner, abortive Marcionites.”

**ABRUMPERE** (*to break off*). II, 47: “He plainly breaks himself away from the Church of the authentic rule,” an expression used ἀμεταβάτως, “intransitively” [or “without transposition”].

**ABRUPTE** (*abruptly*). II, 165 C: “If we employ this proposition so abruptly in our assumptions.”

**ABRUPTUM** (*a precipice, chasm*). II, 507 A: “Here too I leap across the very broad chasm in the interrupted Scripture.” The expression is taken from those who prefer to shorten their journey by making a leap rather than incur a loss by walking along a more convenient route. Thus Scaliger on Cardan: “You fly across the largest field with the slightest leap.” Tertullian presently explains himself, II, 507 D: “You have removed so much from the Scriptures”; that is, you have cut out, rejected, and broken off so much that enormous gaps remain in the continuous text of the books. In book V against the same opponent: “How many pits he has made in the [Col. 1251D] epistle by removing what he wished.”

**ABRUPTUS**, harsh, obstinate. II, 77 A: “As concerning one who is harsh, headlong, and desirous of death.” II, 247 B: “More rugged than the Caucasus.” The Caucasus is a very extensive mountain of Scythia whose ridges, as Pliny says (*Natural History*, VI, 5), turn in the Colchian region of Pontus toward the Riphaean Mountains, one flank descending toward the Euxine and Maeotis, the other toward the Caspian and Hyrcanian seas, under various names. Virgil, *Aeneid* IV: “The bristling Caucasus begot you from its hard crags,” etc. By these words *abruptum* is explained when applied to a savage, hard, intractable, and inhospitable person. II, 432 C: “Moreover, nothing is so unreasonable as that another should provide it.” II, 657 B: “Otherwise harsh and absurd.”

**ABSOLESCERE** (*to fall out of use*). II, 921 C: “The seedbed of the race falls out of use,” that is, so that it ceases to exist in the accustomed and customary manner.

**ABSOLVERE** (*to release, remove*). II, 76 B: “He removes the exceedingly tiresome scout’s shoe from his feet,” that is, takes it off. Among the Romans, when soldiers were discharged as unworthy of the privileges and [Col. 1252A] honor of military service, their shoes, among other things, were customarily removed. Balduinus, *De Calceo*, chapter 24. See also **SPECULATORIA**. I, 572 A: “It has been settled concerning their weakness and mediocrity,” that is, it has been most clearly demonstrated that they possess no strength.

**ABSTINERE** (*to withhold*). I, 302 A: “Since women were so thoroughly withheld from wine [Col. 1252B],” using *abstinerentur* for *abstinerent*.

**ABSTRUERE**, to remove light by placing a structure before it. II, 38 C (15). See **OBSTRUERE**. II, 428 A: “And he denies that a lamp should be obstructed.”

**ABUSUS.** II, 970 B: “About to proceed from confinement to the contest, *abusus*,” that is, almost consumed and exhausted by long use. Rigault prefers *obesus*, but this lacks the authority of the manuscripts. Nonius: “*Obesus*: slender and thin, gnawed all around and emaciated.” Naevius: “With body and breast everywhere wasted, senseless in mind, oppressed by a drowsy, sluggish heaviness.” Gellius, *Attic Nights*, XIX, 7.

**ACACIA.** I, 13: “Which *acacia* promises,” that is, ἀκακία, “integrity, innocence.” Rigault prefers the alternative reading: “We have to put on this incorruptibility over the new man, which the monarchy promises.” He is alluding to Paul’s words in 1 Corinthians 15 and 2 Corinthians 5, which command Christians to hope confidently for the resurrection, which will clothe mortal bodies with immortality. For then it will come to pass that the souls of the blessed return to their bodies as to new dwellings—inasmuch as they are now eternal, [Col. 1252C] having been clothed with immortality as with a new garment, never thereafter to be worn away by any ages. By “monarchy” Septimius means God most good and most great, the sense in which he very frequently employed that word in his disputation *Against Praxeas*.

**ACATUS**, a small vessel. II, 469 A: “If you have never received stolen or illicit merchandise into your *acati*,” etc. Ἄκατος is a ship equipped for conducting trade. From it comes the diminutive ἀκάτιον, *acatium* (Pliny, *Natural History*, IX, 31). Here the author follows the entire procedure of nautical commerce with great precision, in order to strike Marcion more forcefully. For sailors receive merchandise under the merchants’ agreement; goods are delivered stamped with the mark of some title, or transmitted after being designated by a sign, loaded aboard, and so forth.

**ACCEDERE**, to equal. II, 1042 A: “But also Cleomachus, the boxer who had previously equaled the Tirynthian.” II, 76 A: “And a person from the ranks had now approached.” With Rigault one should read *decesserat*, “had withdrawn.” This was the soldier who was more steadfast than the other brethren—that is, his Christian fellow soldiers—[Col. 1252D] who had not wished to be exposed, judging that there was no betrayal of duty in so slight a concealment.

**ACCENDERE** (*to kindle*). II, 82 B: “He kindled sight in the eyes.”

**ACCENDONES**, trainers who incite gladiators to combat. II, 1050 A.

**ACCEPTABILIS** (*acceptable*). I, 585 A: “Yet how much more acceptable is our presumption.”

**ACCEPTO.** I, 347 A: “Your gods will carry it as received.” I, 569 A: “Therefore they remain silent and carry it as received.” II, 1011 A: “How much more does he credit as received those sins committed before the washing.”

**ACCESSIBILITAS** (*susceptibility*). II, 174 A: “So that we might also ascribe to the Son things contrary to him: mortality and susceptibility.”

**ACCIDENTIA** (*accident, incidental property*). II, 498 B: “For that which is ascribed is an accident; but the manifestation of the thing itself to which they happen precedes its accidents.” II, 665 B: “He suffered an accident of the spirit, for an ecstasy fell upon him,” etc.

**ACCURATUS** (*carefully attended*). I, 407 A: “What pasture is more carefully attended by them?” that is, the nourishment for which they have greater concern.

**ACERBUS** (*unripe*). II, 904 B: “Thus, before this indication, the matter is premature,” that is, immature. II, 229 A: “Just as the fig tree … [Col. 1253A] sheds its unripe figs,” from Revelation 6:13, τοὺς ὀλύνθους αὐτοῦ, “its late or unripe figs”; the Vulgate has *grossos suos*, “its unripe figs.” A *grossus* is a hard and unripe fig. Theodore Gaza, in his work *On Plants*, calls the wild fig ὄλυνθος.

**ACERBATUS** (*made more severe*). I, 533 A: “Redoubled scourges,” that is, doubled.

**ACERRA** (*incense-box*). I, 324 A: “Such as a cup, such as an incense-box.”

**ACERVUS** (*heap*). II, 103 C: “Winnowing the confused heap of the faithful.” I, 1271 A: “At every heap of messengers.”

**ACESCERE** (*to turn sour*). I, 474 A: “The air turns sour as so many tribes, curiae, and decuries belch”—something that commonly happens because of the multitude of people in theaters and spectacles.

**ACIES** (*edge; keen gaze; battle line*). II, 1643 B: “And to transfix with the gaze” means to look sharply and intently, with one’s eyes as though fixed upon the object: ἀτενὲς ὁρᾷν, “to gaze intently.” People who wear clothing alien to natural moderation, which turns them awry from an upright condition, openly offer themselves to be viewed—or rather ridiculed—and seem to wish to turn everyone’s eyes upon themselves. Yet the inspection or spectacle they seek is joined with reproach and insult toward those who wear such things, so that it is imputed to them not as praise but as a fault. To this is added in the same passage: “To point them out with the finger, to betray them with a nod.” II, 1006 C: “How drawn is the edge of the spiritual sword.” See **EXERTUS**. II, 1013 A: “Challenge them to the apostolic battle line.” II, 669 A: “So many ranks of pipes.”

**ACONITUM** (*aconite*). A poisonous plant; any kind of poison. II, 1030 A: “When every aconite of hostility has been uprooted.”

**ACOR** (*sourness*). II, 249 A: “With a little leaven he has corrupted the whole mass of faith by heretical sourness.” I, 1237 A: “Like fruits when they already begin to age into sourness or bitterness.”

**ACTOR**, one who conducts another’s business, an agent. II, 434 B: “He proposes an analogy involving agents.”

**ACTORIUM** (*forensic, pleading*): “a forensic proceeding concerning the soul.” II, 668 C.

**ACTRIX** (*actress; performer*). I, 650 B: “But if tragedies and comedies are performers of crimes and lusts.”

**ACTUS** (*act, activity, use*). II, 564 B: “Enthymesis arose from an act”—namely, the act by which Sophia burst forth to seek the Father, as the author says in chapter 9. I, 1313 A: “Thus, therefore, also regarding the use [Col. 1253C] of materials.” Tertullian calls the use of things created by God their *actus*: when we do something by means of them, when we employ them for an act or action, whatever kind it may be. I, 496 B: “For we now call your actions to witness concerning the judges.” II, 439 C: “Following the example of that servant who was removed from his office.” I, 670 B: “The smaller payment is compensated for by more frequent activity.”

**ACUS** (*needle*). I, 1246 A: “Show me the needle for arranging the hair.” II, 906 B: “And they arrange their hair with a more wanton needle.”

**ACUTUS** (*sharp*). II, 1048 A: “If I proceed to sharp weapons,” that is, if I proceed to fight you with sharp and decisive weapons, not with practice weapons that are blunt.

**AD**, in the sense “among” or “in the presence of.” I, 527 A: “But the profane and those who are not wholly with God.”

**ADDICERE** (*to adjudge, consign*). II, 120 A: “It is better that at some point you should not see your crowds than that you should consign them”—namely, to tributary servitude. I, 1237 A: “For at this price the Lord has determined to assign pardon”: a term proper to a seller. I, 438 A: “And thus adjudge us guilty of the charge.”

**ADDICTIO** (*adjudication*). II, 1015 A: “And the adjudication of all chastity.” [Col. 1253D] A praetor *addicit*, “adjudges,” when he commands that something belong to someone as his property.

**ADGENICULARI**, to fall at the knees. I, 1244 A: “And to fall at the knees of God’s altars.” Others read more correctly: “of God’s beloved ones” (*charis Dei*). By “God’s beloved ones” the martyrs are undoubtedly meant; penitents customarily petitioned them to restore them to the Church. See Tertullian, *To the Martyrs*: “Which some, not possessing peace, have been accustomed to seek from the martyrs”—namely, peace.

**ADGLUTINARE** (*to glue or join to*). I, 1235 A: “To such a degree are you glued to defiance.” II, 665 B: “And he shall be joined to his wife.” II, 684 B: “And he shall be joined to his woman.”

**ADHAERERE** (*to adhere*). II, 1047 A: “For the rest, it adheres to the shoulder.”

**ADHUC.** II, 54 A: “Even if I still remember,” that is, in addition, beyond the common rite.

**ADITUS**, one who has approached. II, 540 A: “For this reason they first torture one who has approached it”—namely, approached those sacred rites.

[Col. 1254A] **ADJUNGERE** (*to join*). II, 17 A: “Because it joins him to evils.” Junius prefers *adjugat*, that is, “binds under the same yoke,” just as Columella says that vine shoots are “yoked” (*adjugari*).

**ADJURARE** (*to adjure*). I, 692 A: “Whether you swear by idols or comply when adjured by another.” I, 448 A: “Moreover, we are accustomed to adjure demons, that is, genii.” II, 122 A: “Distrust of immediately marking, adjuring, and anointing the beast’s heel.”

**ADOLARI.** II, 806 B: “Religious offerings are made to God from the goods of the flesh,” that is, they render religious worship.

**ADOLATIO**, that is, *adulatio* in the usage of the ancients: worship of the gods that is not genuine but feigned.

**ADORARE.** II, 550 A: “Lest they be approved by seriousness,” that is, sanctioned. Junius prefers *adornentur*, “be adorned.” For if you apply seriousness to a frivolous thing, you will appear to adorn it; festive gaiety befits it. II, 218 A: “I venerate the fullness of Scripture.”

**ADSACRIFICIUM.** I, 686 A–B: “Suppose I am summoned, but my duty’s designation and the discharge of my service do not amount to participation in sacrifice—what then? I may attend if I please.” In these words he resolves the objection, “But [Col. 1254B] sacrifices are associated with these occasions,” by adopting the person of a Christian slave or freedman whom a pagan master had ordered to attend or present himself while either the master or his son sacrificed on the solemn occasion of assuming the toga of manhood or of a betrothal. “Suppose I am summoned,” he says, “provided that my duty and my service cannot be regarded as *adsacrificium*, that is, as the administration of, participation in, or consent to the sacrifice. Let him make use of both my service and my attendance: what is that to me? My conscience is intact in this matter; if I please, I may be present.”

For **ADSIGNARE** and **ADSISTERE**, see under the letter **ASS-**.

**ADSOLARE.** I, 363 B, note 1; 577 A: “If they *adsolant* the summit of majesty”—they depress it, dash it to the ground.

**ADVERSIO.** II, 299 C: “Now according to the *adversio* of the goodness to be directed,” that is, goodness to be directed in accordance with how each person turns his mind toward the goodness of God. Jurists call the right to receive fruits and apply them to one’s own uses *adversio*. Thus a carrier is said to hire a ship *in adversionem* when he hires it on the condition that its proceeds [Col. 1254C] accrue to the hirer himself.

**ADVIVERE** (*to live alongside*). I, 748 A: “Those who were then among them while they were living alongside them,” that is, while they were still living with them. II, 87 A: “What the idols themselves did for themselves while they were living alongside them,” that is, while they lived together with those who rendered them that worship.

**ADULARI** (*to flatter, indulge*). II, 972 A: “I must not only comply with him but also flatter him.” See **ADOLARI**. II, 976 B: “And at every hour they flatter those whom they greet.” II, 722 B: “For it [the body] alone rest flatteringly grants the end of labor,” that is, bestows it as an indulgence.

**ADULTER** (*adulterous, falsifying*). II, 30 A: “Only an adulterous sense opposes the truth,” that is, a perverse interpretation. II, 52 A: “An adulterous pen.” II, 198 A: “Altogether adulterous both in preaching and in flesh”: the flesh of Hermogenes was adulterous because he married repeatedly; his preaching was adulterous because through his heresy he had corrupted the faith and peace of the Church. I, 663 C: “For one who serves false gods is undoubtedly an adulterer against truth, because every falsehood is adultery.” I, 519 A: “But we promptly advance a prescription against our adulterers”—the heretics. II, 1000 C: “Itself also adulterous,” concerning the scripture known as *The Shepherd*. II, 156 B: “Let all adulterous crops be gathered.” I, 580 C: “Because we have fabricated an adulterous night.” [Col. 1254D]

**ADULTERARE** (*to adulterate*). I, 632 A: “But he who adulterates and courts”—namely, the truth. I, 519 A: “They adulterated it into philosophical sects.” II, 987 A: “He adulterates and violates himself.”

**ADULTERIUM** (*adultery, adulteration*). I, 519 B: “Adulterations of the saving discipline.” II, 51 A: “Adulterations of the Scriptures.” II, 401 A: “In this one place alone I marvel that Marcion’s hand was paralyzed in its adulteration,” that is, that, as though stupefied by its adulteration and corruption of the Scriptures, it lacked sensation. I, 1312 B: “Concerning the adulteration of unjust colors.”

**ADUMBRARE** (*to overshadow, veil*). II, 899 B: “Therefore so dangerous a face ought to be overshadowed,” that is, veiled. I, 645 A: “Later it was resolved to veil impiety with pleasure.” II, 1014 D: “Obscure things are illustrated by manifest things.”

**ADVOCARE** is the Greek παρακαλεῖν, “to exhort, console, summon to one’s aid.” II, 390 C: “To encourage the weak.”

**ADVOCATIO** properly means the company of patrons and friends [Col. 1255A] who attend someone in court. I, 270 A, C: “The advocacy of the Scriptures that is also to follow,” that is, their defense. II, 393 A: “Since you have received your consolation,” that is, παράκλησιν, “consolation.” I, 1267 A: “Accordingly, both consolation and laughter are promised to such persons.” II, 863 B: “Words of exhortation and advocacy,” that is, of consolation and aid. II, 93 B: “For whom the plea of necessity is most familiar,” that is, its allegation as an excuse. I, 270 A: “They employ hired advocacy.”

**ADVOCATOR**, παράκλητος, “advocate, comforter.” II, 393 A: “Just as I have proved him the advocate of beggars.”

**ADVOCATUS** (*advocate*). II, 931 A: “In this matter too you ought to recognize the Paraclete as advocate.” He alludes to the meaning of the word παράκλητος, “advocate”; but the author’s application is ridiculous. II, 972 A: “Insofar as he is Paraclete, that is, advocate.” I, 695 A: “No longer of advocates, but of angels.” By *advocati* he means those who gave a friend the benefit of their presence by affixing their seals, subscribing their names, and giving testimony. Thus Varro, *On Agriculture*, II, 5: “But you, Murrius, come as my advocate while I pay out the asses at the Parilia, so that if they later [Col. 1255B] demand them back from me, you may be able to bear witness.”

**AEDIFEX**, in place of *aedificator*, “builder.” I, 678 A: “From the likeness of that most provident builder.”

**AEDIFICARE**, to invite by setting forth an example. II, 540 A: “So that through the suspension of knowledge they may build up an opinion.” II, 139 C: “Admonishing by edifying them toward endurance of these things.” I, 1310 B: “They have learned to edify only this astonishment of women,” that is, to serve the work by doing and displaying something at which women may be astonished and marvel. II, 14 B: “To be built up toward ruin.” I, 624 B: “So that they may devote themselves to building up strength.”

**AEDIFICATIO** (*edification*). I, 1256 A: “No talkativeness in edification is disgraceful.”

**AEDIFICATORIUS** (*edificatory, building*). II, 782 B: “For the word that built death had crept into Eve while she was still a virgin.”

**AEMULATIO**, envy, hatred, and the distress experienced by the pagans when they saw their own numbers diminishing and the Christian religion gaining greater growth day by day. I, 277 A: “Once acquitted after the tribunal, he may laugh at your envy.” I, 308 A: “The Jews, from envy.” II, 52 A: “Proceeding, of course, from a cause of rivalry.” I, 536 A: [Col. 1255C] “The rivalry between the divine and the human matter,” that is, God thinks one way, man another. II, 408 A: “Rivalry with the law.” II, 928 A: “If anyone, through presumption concerning this providence of his, should provoke rivalry.” The meaning is that it is all the more possible, through God’s providence, for a woman to become pregnant if someone, by intercourse, challenges the assumption formed concerning her—that she is barren—as though intending to rival God, who makes barren women fruitful.

**AEMULUS** (*rival, opposed*). I, 277 B: “A certain principle of rival operation,” that is, actively rivalrous. See **RATIO**. II, 958 C: “In a rival manner,” that is, contrariwise. II, 278 B: “Who would not otherwise be fully good unless he were the rival of evil.”

**AENIGMA**, figure. II, 448 C: “Where, in the enigma of the stone.” II, 820 A: “Under the pretext of figures and enigmas.” II, 841 A: “So that the other kind cannot admit enigmas.”

**AEONEIUS.** II, 251 C: “Like the *oeoneian* sow.” Rigault emends this to *aeneian*. See **SCROFA**.

**AEQUIPARANTIA** (*equivalence*). II, 570 B: “Into rival equivalences of corporeal substances.”

[Col. 1255D] **AESCULAPIUS.** II, 1031 A: “Now to your Aesculapius.” He calls Aesculapius “yours” because he was especially worshiped in Africa and was believed to have been born of a Punic mother; previously he had belonged only to the people of Pergamum. The meaning is: the cloaks you once used were of the kind that even today the priests of Aesculapius employ.

**AESTIMARE** (*to estimate, perceive*). II, 82 B: “He perceived touch in the hands.” Rigault reads *extimavit* more correctly; see below.

**AESTIMATIO**, thought. I, 263–264 A: “And yet not even in this very way … toward consideration,” etc. [The parenthetical reference to Heumann is textually uncertain.] The meaning is: and yet they do not allow themselves to be admonished by this circumstance to consider whether perhaps truth underlies the doctrine commonly condemned. I, 1327 A: For *in aestimationem temporum*, “into an estimation of the times,” Rigault correctly restored *in extimatione temporum*, “at the extremity of the times,” that is, in the last times, at the end of the age.

**AESTUARE** (*to seethe, contend*). II, 134 C: “Since earthly offices also seethe over rank,” that is, contend for the dignity of rank [Col. 1256A] so that they may obtain first place. I, 497 A: “The prison always seethes with your people.”

**AESTUARIUM** (*surge, tideway*). I, 658 A: “What will you do when caught in that tideway of impious acclamations?”

**AETAS** (*age*). I, 316 A; 319 A: “Greater age,” that is, those greater in years. I, 1327 A: “Ages now brought to rest and drawn into the harbor of modesty.” In the same passage: “Because of the coldness of age.” II, 982 B: “Knowledge also has its ages in Christ.”

**AFFECTATIO**, imitation. I, 371 A: “But most of your people also, through imitation, sometimes,” etc.

**AFFECTIO**, προσποίησις, “assumption, affectation.” II, 1045 A: “Because of the different assumption of the dark garment.”

**AFFECTIOSUS** (*susceptible to impressions*). II, 682 B: “And it is naturally susceptible, lacking understanding.”

**AFFINIS** (*associated, participant*). II, 260 A: “And it is associated with both shamelessness and malice,” that is, a participant in them; so Cicero, *For Sulla*: “Associated with this suspicion.” II, 437 C: “Strangers and associated with no legal right.” I, 1261 A: “We shall be found participants in desire.” I, 1267 A: “Are those who are impatient participants in the same thing?” I, 674 A: “That they were participants in manifold idolatry.”

[Col. 1256B] **AFFINITAS** (*affinity, association*). I, 679 A: “So as not to proceed as far as associations with idolatry,” that is, to such a degree that we become participants in idolatry.

**AFFLATUS** (*breath*). II, 291 B: “The breath of God,” that is, the soul. II, 294 C: “Above all it must be maintained that the Greek Scripture specified this by naming ‘breath’ (πνοή), not ‘spirit’ (πνεῦμα).” I, 1231 B: “Other things completed by his breath.”

**Ἀγενεαλόγητος**, “without genealogy or kinship.” II, 73 A.

**AGERE** (*to act, perform, represent*). II, 26 B: “That Jesus Christ had acted,” that is, had assumed that human role and had performed everything foretold concerning Jesus Christ. II, 416 B: “And you act for him,” that is, you act as his representative and agent. II, 434 B: “To such an extent conducting his business.” II, 667 C: “But what are the dying said to yield—the *animus* or the *anima*?”

**AGINA**, Festus says, is the aperture into which the tongue of a balance is inserted—that is, the place in which the balance moves or turns. Hence those who are moved by a small profit are called *aginatores*. II, 234 B: “At what they call the middle point of the balance,” [Col. 1256C] concerning motion so evenly balanced that it inclines in neither direction and neither side outweighs the other.

**AGNITIO**, assent, approval. II, 155 B: “And from that recognition, peace.” II, 963 A: “Indeed, fasts will also obtain from God recognition of the mysteries,” that is, skill in interpreting sacred figures and images—namely, those divinely presented in dreams.

**AGNOSCERE**, to assent to, approve. II, 155 B: “Now acknowledging the prophecies of Montanus.”

**AGNOSCIBILIS** (*recognizable*). II, 877 A: “But it had preserved features recognizable to Peter.”

**AGONOTHETA**, ἀγωνοθέτης, the presiding official and judge of a contest—specifically a musical or dramatic contest. Those who presided over athletic contests were called *athlothetae*. II, 104 A: “Thus you will recognize that the judgment of the contest belongs to the same contest-president.” I, 624 A–B: “In which the living God is the contest-president.”

**Αἱρέσεις** (*haireseis*, “heresies”), so called by a Greek word from the meaning “choice,” which a person exercises either in establishing or in embracing them. II, 18 A.

[Col. 1256D] **Αἰών** (*aeon*). II, 550 B: Αἰῶνα τέλειον, “the perfect aeon.”

**ALIQUI**, in place of *aliquis*, “someone.” I, 315 A. This occurs very frequently.

**ALCINOUS**, king on the island of Corcyra. II, 1036 A. On his orchards, see Pliny, *Natural History*, XIX, 4, and Homer, *Odyssey*, VII.

**ALES** (*winged*), metaphorically meaning that something is exceedingly swift and swifter than any bird. I, 407 A: “Every spirit is winged.”

**ALEXANDER**, II, 1038 A, is Alexander Polyhistor, whom Suidas reports to have been a Milesian, to have been captured in war, to have served as a tutor in the household of Cornelius Lentulus, and afterward, upon being manumitted, to have been called by the name Cornelius. He appears to have written books for his mother concerning the affairs of the Phrygians and Egyptians. Richer understands the reference as being to the peoples of Alexandria and Africa.

**ALLECTIO** (*selection, enrollment*). II, 58 B: “A tested selection”—namely, of those to be admitted into ecclesiastical orders. For it was customary that this should be publicly announced before ordination. The announcement was made by posting their names and admonishing the people [Col. 1257A] that if anyone had any charge against them, he should prove it by manifest facts. Such was the Church’s tested selection, in contrast to the rash ordinations noted above among heretics. II, 514 B: “The Jews, however, are not sons of the Creator by nature, but by the selection of their fathers,” that is, by adoption.

**ALLEGERE**, to assume, adopt. I, 335 A: “On this side there is no ground for adopting humanity into divinity.” II, 808 A: “When the soul is adopted by God, it itself is what makes it possible for the soul to be adopted.”

**ALLEGORIA**, parable, enigma, figure. II, 421 C: “Through allegories and figures.” II, 835 B: “So that allegories may indeed be free of cloudiness.”

**ALLEGORICUS** (*allegorical*). II, 543 A: “An allegorical arrangement,” that is, figurative. See **CONVITIUM**. II, 996 A: “And when actors adapt allegorical gestures.” II, 836 A: “Allegorical Scriptures.”

**ALLEGORIZARE** (*to allegorize*). II, 401 A: “Which Christ allegorized in men.” II, 834 A: “We also maintain that the mention of garments in the Scriptures allegorizes the hope of the flesh.”

[Col. 1257B] **ALLOCUTIO** (*address*). II, 28 B: “The preface of an address,” that is, προσφώνησις, “an address or salutation.” II, 660 A: “Or addresses are delivered”—ὁμιλίαι, δημηγορίαι, “discourses, public speeches.”

**ALTEGRADIUS** (*high-stepping*). II, 913 A: “As though it were some beast rather than a bird … the other high-stepping creatures.”

**ALTERUTER** (*either of two; each of two*). I, 321 A: “From each of the two,” that is, from each party entering the contract. I, 471 A: “For one another,” that is, one in place of the other. II, 985 A: “Without either opposing alternative.”

**ALTILIS** (*fattened*). I, 651 A: “And because of Greece’s leisure you hate fattened men.” He means athletes or wrestlers, whom the directors of gymnasia customarily fed with the greatest care so that they might be distinguished by the utmost strength for contests. The Greeks were exceptionally devoted to such contests, enjoying leisure from public business. These, indeed, were the evils of a long peace. Septimius called them “fattened men,” just as Varro and Martial call cattle and hens *altiles*, meaning plump and fattened. I, 1246 B: “Seek out the enormous fattening of well-fed animals.”

**ALVEARIUM** (*trough*). II, 586 A: “Into the troughs of the mixture,” that is, basins and what are commonly called kneading-troughs.

[Col. 1257C] **ALVEUS**, belly, abdomen. I, 322 A: “The bellies of the bears themselves are sought.” II, 663 A: “And digested without bellies.”

**AMARE**, to be accustomed. II, 1033 A: “Being accustomed to dress according to the occasion.” II, 319 A: “But the unencumbered power of truth is accustomed to express itself in few words,” following the Greek usage φιλεῖ γενέσθαι, “is wont to occur.” I, 265 A: “They are accustomed to remain ignorant.” Heumann reads *amans*, “loving.” II, 133 B: “He was accustomed to invite to glory those whom he had called to salvation.”

**AMBITIO**, a wandering and manifold circuit. II, 978 B: “To them belongs the circuit of the body.” II, 900 A: “Because he did not naturally acquire the encircling covering of hair,” περιβόλην, “a covering.” II, 691 B: “The whole circumference of the belly.” II, 650 B: “But let the rivalry of each excellence see to itself,” that is, φιλοπρωτεία, “ambition for preeminence.”

**AMENTARE** (*to fit with a throwing-strap; hurl*). II, 439 C: “He hurled this proposition,” that is, he twisted and brandished it like a javelin. Lucan: “He fitted the javelin with a strap.” Hesychius: ἅμμα, δεσμός, “a fastening, a bond”; hence *amentum*, the strap of a javelin or spear.

**AMENTATIO** (*a fitting with straps; amenta*). I, 572 A: “By which you may fall upon your own swords and throwing-straps,” [Col. 1257D] that is, upon the straps attached to them.

AMENTIA (MADNESS). II, 684 B, “When God sent madness upon him”; thus he calls Adam’s sleep. See ECSTASY.

Ἀμήτωρ (*amētōr*), one who is without a mother. II, 73 A.

AMOR (LOVE). II, 247 A–B, “The loves of the Colchians”: love-philters, poisonous love-potions, and all other poisons. Compare Horace, *Odes* II.13.

AMPLIARE (TO ADJOURN; TO ENLARGE). I, 1318 A, “As though the Lord, by enlarging the law, does not distinguish it from the act of fornication.” II, 937 B, “That they may not only remain preserved, but also enlarged.” II, 76 B, “And the case was adjourned.” A case is said to be *ampliari* when its hearing is deferred or remitted to another time or another tribunal. Examples of adjourned cases occur in Livy, XLIII, where he says of M. Fitinnius: “After being twice adjourned, the defendant was acquitted at the third hearing.” And shortly afterward, concerning P. Furius Philus and M. Matienus: “Both were accused of the gravest crimes, and their cases were adjourned.”

AN, perhaps. I, 416 A, “Perhaps Christians,” that is, perhaps after becoming [Col. 1258A] Christians. The sense of the whole passage is: Believe them when, adjured by us, they speak the truth; for if they were permitted to lie, they would certainly do so whenever a Christian sought to establish the truth, lest they lose you, who are so profitable to them—or rather, lest at some future time they be driven from some possession of their own by you yourselves, if perhaps you became Christians.

ANABIBAZON, ἀναβιβάζων, “ascending”: among astrologers, the sign or natal planet (*planēta genethlios*, γενέθλιος) under which a person is conceived or born. II, 266 A, “For perhaps his Anabibazon stood in his way.”

ANDROMACHA (ANDROMACHE). II, 996 B, “For it has nothing to do with Andromache,” that is, nothing to do with Christ. Others regard this as proverbial, supposing that he is alluding to a play by some ancient tragedian entitled *Andromache*, and that the expression means nothing more than the phrases “Nothing to do with the verse,” “Nothing to do with Bacchus,” οὐδὲν πρὸς ἔπος, ἀπροσδιόνυσα—that is, irrelevant to the matter. For he compares the heretics with actors. Actors, adapting allegorical gestures to songs, represent things wholly remote from both the present play and the scene; likewise the heretics assign the same parables wherever they please, not [Col. 1258B] where they belong, and most effectively exclude them from their proper place. See PROVERBIAL FORMULAS, I, 210 D.

ANGELIFICARE (TO ANGELIFY). II, 832 B, “Re-formed and angelified in the kingdom of God.”

ANGINA (ANGINA). II, 732 B, “Or through compression of the liver there may be an angina of the mind,” that is, anguish of spirit.

ANGUSTIA (NARROW CIRCUMSTANCES). II, 905 A, “From narrow circumstances,” that is, from slender means or fortune.

ANIMA (SOUL). II, 228 B, “Swimming and flying souls.” II, 905 A, “Both in soul through expectation and in flesh through transformation,” that is: that virgin of yours is already married—already in soul through expectation of a husband, and married in flesh through the transformation of puberty. She is married in flesh and soul, just as in the phrase, “In face and shoulders like a god.” The meaning of the words that follow, “for whom you are preparing a second husband,” is this: your virgin, whom you consider a virgin, has ceased to be one because of her age—not, indeed, through being defiled by a man, but through age; accordingly, the husband to whom you give her will be her second.

ANIMALIS (ANIMAL; NATURAL), ψυχικός (*psychikos*). II, 953 C, “Recognize, then, the animal [Col. 1258C] faith, consisting entirely in zeal for the flesh.”

ANIMARE (TO ANIMATE; COLOR; GIVE LIFE OR SPIRIT). I, 1322 A, “Then the desirable heat of the sun, simultaneously animating and drying the hair.” *Animando* means “coloring,” as Lucretius speaks of “animated crops,” and Arnobius of “animated entrails.” I, 1202 B, “If waters know how to animate,” that is, to restore to a person the eternal life from which he had fallen through sinning. I, 1208 A, “To animate so great a brilliance with another spirit.” A machine is said to be animated when, through the modulations of a musician’s fingers, it releases in a brilliantly clear sound—distinguished by manifold variation—the breath compressed into water by pressure and embodied in it. Septimius, however, calls such breath “another spirit,” namely, a trained and articulated one. II, 994 C, “And you would believe that their mutual comparisons had animated them.” Colors are animated when they are so aptly placed together that each is enlivened by the vigor of the other.

ANIMATIO (ANIMATION). II, 556 B, “And the whole enthymesis, that is, animation together with passion,” etc. Irenaeus: “She laid aside her former intention, together with the passion that had befallen her.”

ANIMATRIX (ANIMATOR). II, 147 A, He calls perfect love the animator of confession, that is, that which incites, impels, and gives [Col. 1258D] courage to confess Christ.

ANNOTATIO (ASSIGNMENT), the charge that someone be lodged with care. I, 345 A, “Under the same assignment of the quaestor.”

ANNUS (YEAR). I, 487 A, “The year is in anxiety.” Zephyrus applies this to people’s anxiety concerning that year; but Tertullian seems to attribute anxiety and, as it were, travail not to people but to the year and season. II, 976 C, “When heaven stands amazed and the year is parched.”

ANNULUS (RING). I, 302 A, “The betrothal ring.” Tertullian says in this passage that it was golden. Pliny, however, *Natural History* XXX.1, teaches that this betrothal ring was made of iron. Kipping, *Roman Antiquities*, thinks Tertullian spoke according to the custom of his own age. Or did he rather misunderstand Pliny, who was speaking not of a betrothal ring but of a symbol of the frugality and modesty by which a bride or newly married woman was recalled to those ancient and uncouth Sabine women?

ANNUUS (ANNUAL). II, 79 B, “We make offerings for the dead and for birthdays on their annual day.”

[Col. 1259A] ANTECESSOR (FORERUNNER). II, 890 B, “He alone is the forerunner, because he alone comes after Christ”; concerning the Paraclete. II, 364 A, “Bereft of the protection of their predecessors.”

ANTECESSIVUM (ANTECEDENT). II, 894 G, “Both the subjective to the antecedent and the partial to the universal.”

ANTECURSOR (FORERUNNER). II, 825 A, “And thereafter the flower, the forerunner of the fruit.”

ANTELIUS. I, 684 A, “Among the Greeks also we read of Apollo θυραῖος (*thyraios*, ‘of the doorway’) and of the Antelii, demons who guard doorways.” Hesychius: Ἀντήλιοι θεοὶ, οἱ πρὸ τῶν θυρῶν ἱδρυμένοι. Εὐριπίδης, Μελεάγρῳ—“Antelian gods: those established before the doors. Euripides, in *Meleager*.” Then: ἀντήλιος, ὁ ἴσος τῷ ἡλίῳ φαινόμενος· καταχρηστικῶς δὲ ὁ ἀντικρὺ ἡλίου ἱδρυμένος βωμὸς ἢ θεός—“*Antēlios*: one appearing equal to the sun; by an extended use, an altar or god established directly opposite the sun.”

ANTELUCANUS (BEFORE DAWN). II, 79 B, “Even at assemblies before dawn.” I, 273 A, “Assemblies before dawn for singing to Christ.”

ANTENNA (YARDARM). II, 346 B, “For on the yardarm also, which forms part of the cross, the extremities are called horns.” Thus in Virgil: “We turn the horns of the sail-clad yardarms.”

ANTIAE are the front locks of hair hanging down from the forehead. II, 1042 A, “The molars shadowed among the forelocks.”

ANTICIPARE (TO ANTICIPATE). II, 858 B, “For every consummation and [Col. 1259B] perfection, although last in order, is anticipated in desire.”

ANTIQUITAS (ANTIQUITY). I, 515 A, “For the antiquity already established for the divine literature continues to benefit my argument.”

ANTIQUIUS (MORE ANCIENT; PRIOR). II, 213 B, “Something will have been more ancient than the Father,” that is, prior by nature, not in time, as the following words teach.

ANTISTARE (TO SURPASS; EXCEL; BE SUPERIOR). I, 442 A, “Who certainly live and surpass the dead.” II, 279 B, “For not even the continence of virginity excels.” With Rigault, read *virginitati*, “excels virginity.” II, 845 C, “But we surpass many sparrows.”

ANTISTATUS (ATTENDANT BODY). II, 563 B, “The commensurable attendant body of angels,” that is, the angels who are Soter’s attendants, standing before him or appearing to him in order to perform their ministries. He calls them “commensurable” because their kind could be compared with Soter’s substance. Junius interprets *antistatum* as προστασίαν (*prostasian*), “attendance” or “presidency.”

ANTISTES (PRESIDENT; CHIEF PRIEST). I, 259 B, “The chief priests of the Roman Empire.” Zephyrus understands this of the pontiffs themselves, whose authority administered sacred affairs, ceremonies, and, in short, all religion, [Col. 1259C] matters in the interpretation of which the highest concerns of the commonwealth were involved. Hence Cicero calls them “chiefs of public counsel” and “priests of the immortal gods.” Ancient inscriptions establish that the emperors themselves were also among them, since in those inscriptions they are called chief pontiffs.

ANTITHESIS (ANTITHESIS). II, 267 C, “For these are Marcion’s antitheses, that is, contrary oppositions.”

AORI, ἄωροι (*aōroi*), those who perish by an untimely death. II, 745 B.

Ἀπάτωρ (*apatōr*), one who is without a father. II, 73 A.

APEX, the insignia of priests: it was a sewn cap with which the flamens covered their heads. II, 1015 A; I, 363 A. II, 164 A, “An *apex* made of a ray”: by an analogy drawn from the caps of the flamens, he calls *apex* that threadlike thing which we see flashing amid darting rays when the sun shines, and in a manner hanging before our eyes. Lucretius calls them “weapons of daylight”; P. Varro, “darts”; Prudentius called them “points of the sun” or “of the rays.” II, 988 A, “Between the two most prominent summits of crimes.” II, 629 B, “Concerning, namely, the tips of Christ’s cross.” By “tips” he means what he calls [Col. 1259D] “horns” above.

APOCARTERESIS, ἀποκαρτέρησις (*apokarterēsis*), is the resolve and choice to die through abstinence from food and starvation. I, 512 A, “Lycurgus chose death by starvation as a hypocrite.” II, 262 B, “If through death by starvation you prove yourself a Marcionite,” that is: prove by the deed itself—by voluntary starvation and self-killing—that you are a hypocrite who rejects the Creator.

APORIATIO (PERPLEXITY), hesitation, fear, confusion. I, 69 A, “Conceived and uttered out of perplexity.”

APOSTOLICUS (APOSTOLIC). Hermogenes is called “apostolic” (II, 198 A), because, although the Apostle did not brand him in his mind, he nevertheless marked him by sharing his name. II, 472 B, “He confirms the Scripture of the Apostolic Acts.” It was customary among the ancient Fathers to call τὰς τῶν ἀποστόλων Πράξεις (“the Acts of the Apostles”) simply *Apostolica*, Ἀποστόλικα (“the Apostolic [books]”).

APOSTOLI (APOSTLES), whom this designation interprets as “those sent.” II, 52 A.

[Col. 1260A] APPARENTIA (APPEARANCE), ἐπιφάνεια (*epiphaneia*, “manifestation”). II, 268 A, “From the appearance of Christ down to Marcion’s audacity.”

APPARERE (TO ATTEND), to provide for, tend, or minister. I, 347 A, “For the soothsayer also attends upon the dead.” I, 527 A, “Another who attends upon God’s judgment,” that is, ministers to it. II, 814 C, “Rather to serve as a vessel for the soul.” I, 650 A, “Since ears and eyes attend upon the spirit.” Thus Cicero also calls the senses the mind’s attendants. I, 687 A, “Who attended upon idolatrous kings to the very end of their idolatry.”

APPARITIO (SERVICE). II, 59 A, “Devoted service.”

APPARITOR (ATTENDANT). I, 650 A, “Nor can the world be furnished, since its attendants are defiled”; he is speaking of the senses, the eyes and ears. See APPARERE.

APPENDIX (APPENDAGE). II, 744 A, “In paradise, to which even then the patriarchs and prophets [went as] appendages of the Lord’s resurrection.” II, 806 B, “And filth, the appendage of this duty”—fasting. II, 977 B, “Wantonness and luxury are, of course, the appendages of gluttony.”

APPLICARE (TO APPROACH; APPLY; ATTACH). II, 123 A, “They approach by means of the passions,” that is, they come near gently and softly. II, 502 D, “He attached an angel of Satan [Col. 1260B] to his apostle to buffet him.” I, 341 A, “The beasts whom you attach to Liber.”

APULIA. I, 652 B, “Because God has eyes even beyond the Apulias.” This word appears to signify the awnings used in theaters and amphitheaters for decoration and to ward off the scorching blows of the sun. These were sometimes purple, a color with which the finest wool was probably dyed, such as came from Apulia. Martial: “Apulian fleeces of the first quality.” Hence the awnings also acquired the name “Apulias.”

AQUA (WATER). I, 1202 A, “Water, a worthy vehicle for God.” I, 1224 A, “After the water,” that is, after baptism.

AQUARIOLUS (PROCURER). I, 495 A. Festus: “*Aquarioli* was the name given to the sordid attendants of unchaste women.” They also performed the role of pimps and arranged engagements for prostitutes. Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book XIV, chapter 12.

AQUATILIS (AQUATIC). I, 1259 A, “After the aquatic train that followed the rock, they despair of the Lord.”

AQUATIO (DRAWING OF WATER). II, 962 A, “Israel had sinned while drawing water [Col. 1260C] at Mizpah.”

AQUIGENUS (WATER-BORN). II, 299 B, “Among water-born and earth-born animals,” ὑδρογενῆ καὶ γηγενῆ τῶν ζώων, “the aquatic and terrestrial kinds of animals.”

AQUILEGUS (WATER-DRAWING). II, 707 A, “How greatly they will congratulate themselves upon their former and familiar water-drawing marks,” that is: beasts of burden—mules and asses—employed in turning these machines would congratulate themselves upon their condition if they ever happened to be changed into human beings, since they would then not sweat so greatly in turning these wheels. Vitruvius describes them. They were devices that drew up and poured out water by means of buckets.

AQUILEX (WATER ENGINEER) was the name given to the craftsman charged with finding, conducting, and managing water. II, 326 C, “God did not immediately promise that he would be a water engineer and farmer.”

AQUILICIA, sacred rites instituted for drawing forth and obtaining water. I, 487 A, “You sacrifice water-drawing rites to Jupiter.” This was a Roman custom, for among the Carthaginians Juno more properly presided over this concern. Compare chapter 33.

ARA (ALTAR). II, 1031 A, “After Pompey’s three altars,” namely, his triumphal altars—that is, his triumphs. I, 1182 A, “Will not your station be more solemn [Col. 1260D] if you have also stood at God’s altar?” He alludes to stations and employs a technical term of sacrificial ritual. An animal dedicated as a victim and awaiting sacrifice is said to “stand at the altar.” Virgil, *Georgics* II: “And the sacred he-goat, led by the horn, will stand at the altar.” I, 1286 A, “For God’s altar ought to be presented as clean.” Elsewhere he calls the Christian person God’s altar, from whose heart prayers are borne to God. Here, however, in a certain exceptional sense, he calls the heads of the ecclesiastical order God’s altar, because they convey the Church’s vows to God and through them the Christian Church customarily brings the sacrifices of its prayers before God. I, 677 B, “He will spit upon smoking altars and blow upon them.” II, 1048 A, “I am accustomed to prescribe remedies for morals from any ledge or altar.” Here, of course, it is the philosopher in the cloak who speaks, not the Christian. For a Christian could not be brought to leap upon an altar for the sake of making a speech, since Christians abhorred altars and sacrifices, and Christians passing by at that time would blow upon them. II, 136 C, “And the altar, a funeral pyre.”

[Col. 1261A] ARBITER (WITNESS; OBSERVER). II, 960 A, “He was going to lament those same leaders and arbiters of his,” that is, spectators and witnesses. II, 317 B–C, “With the Father as arbiter,” that is, witness. II, 414 A, “He takes three of the disciples as arbiters of the future vision and voice.”

ARBITRATRIX (ARBITRESS). II, 299 B, “Which was found in the Lord as arbitress of his works.”

ARBUSTUS (TREE-GROWN; ROBUST). II, 320 B, “He who made his affairs more tree-grown at their beginnings,” that is, one who managed his affairs in a more robust form—one, namely, who did not plant slips, but already-grown trees, and indeed larger trees, which produce fruit much earlier than slips.

ARCANUM (SECRET). I, 1297 A, “Whose secrets they preserve for the danger which they believe,” etc. By “the wives’ secrets” he means that pagan husbands do not betray their wives when they participate in Christian sacred rites. Those pagan husbands therefore preserve their wives’ secrets for the danger which they believe—that is, for the danger they believe threatens the Christian name, when persecution, as they hope, will blaze forth, so that they may then betray them if perhaps, through some hurt they have suffered, they desire their wives’ destruction. This is the meaning of “if perhaps they are hurt”: if perhaps [Col. 1261B] some injury to their feelings occurs, if there is some quarrel. See OBJECTION.

ARCHETYPUS (ARCHETYPAL). II, 548 A, “Archetypal teachers” are the principal and more ancient teachers.

ARCHIGALLUS, the chief of the Galli, the priests of Cybele, mother of the gods. I, 425 A. See EMPIRE. II, 815 A, “Either of the female sculptor or of the archigallus.”

ARCHIVA (ARCHIVES), journals, annals. I, 401 B, note 4, “You have it recorded in your archives.”

ARCHON, ἄρχων (*archōn*), prince or chief magistrate. II, 88 B; II, 215 A, ἄρχοντες (*archontes*), “rulers.”

Ἀρχή (*archē*, BEGINNING; PRINCIPALITY). II, 215 A, “ἀρχή denotes primacy not only in the ordering sense but also in the sense of power.” II, 551 A, Προαρχὴν and τὴν ἀρχὴν, “the pre-beginning” and “the beginning.” II, 579 A, “The earthy one, flesh by the substance of the ἀρχή, matter.” The Greek text of Irenaeus requires: “the earthy body by substance, flesh from matter.”

ARCUATUS (ARCHED). II, 122 A, “Rising with an arched rush”; concerning the scorpion.

ARCTARE (TO CONSTRAIN). II, 710 B, “Lest, after being committed to custody, you be constrained until the whole debt is discharged.”

[Col. 1261C] ARDOR (HEAT; BURNING). II, 106 B, “For when we are scorched by the heat of persecution.” II, 123 A, “And they are equipped at a fixed time, and at no other than that of the Gnostics’ heat.” I, 510 A, “I know also Phryne the prostitute, rutting beneath the heat of Diogenes as he lay upon her.”

AREA (OPEN GROUND; THRESHING FLOOR; BURIAL GROUND). I, 701 A, “Let there be no burial grounds; there were no threshing floors of their own.” He plays upon the word. For when that man cried, “Let there be no *areae*,” he meant burial grounds; when Tertullian replies, “There were no *areae* of their own,” he means threshing floors. *Area* is used for a cemetery. Pontius the Deacon, in the *Acts of Cyprian*: “He was buried in the *area* of the procurator Candidus.”

ARENA. I, 321 A, “A spectacle in the arena,” that is, a gladiatorial show. I, 467 A, “With the savagery of the arena.”

ARENARIUS NUMERORUM (ARITHMETICIAN), one who shows pupils various arithmetical combinations of numbers upon an abacus sprinkled with dust. II, 1050 A.

ARGUMENTARI (TO ARGUE; DEVISE), to proceed by subtleties or cleverly devise or expound something. I, 635 B, “Lest anyone think that we are arguing sophistically.” I, 639 B, “From it they devise the name of the Circus.”

[Col. 1261D] ARIDUS (DRY). II, 1040 A, “Dry fattening” is ξηροφαγία (*xērophagia*, “dry eating”), which was characteristic of athletes. II, 954 A, “Either late or dry foods.”

ARIES (BATTERING RAM). II, 800 B, “And everywhere this first ram is poised against us, by which the condition of the flesh is battered.” A ram is a beam suspended by ropes, its head sheathed in iron so that it appears to possess, like a ram, a very hard forehead; it is also drawn backward in the manner of a ram so that it may strike with greater force and bring down walls. Hence the verb *temperari* (“to be poised”), because skill and a certain balance were required in preparing and positioning it for its intended blows. The expression may be proverbial for: “A powerful argument is brought against us, one difficult to resolve; we are assaulted by open force,” just as rams and mines are contrasted with one another in arguments. II, 1031 B, “For the ram also,” etc.

ARITHMI, the Book of Numbers. II, 431 C.

[Col. 1262A] ARMARIUM (CABINET; ARCHIVE). I, 1307 B, “Because it is not admitted into the Jewish cabinet”—that is, into that canon of Scriptures which was preserved in the temple of the Hebrew people through the diligence of successive priests. Augustine so interprets it in *The City of God* XV.23. The same author, in book XII *Against Faustus*, says of the Jewish people: “What else is that nation but, as it were, the document chests of Christians, carrying the Law and the Prophets?” I, 670 B, “How much more quickly he constructs the cabinet.”

ARMARE (TO ARM). II, 687 B, “Which alone I could have armed as testimony to the fullness of the divinity.” II, 259 B, “He armed the knowledge of himself with so many works.”

ARTIFEX (ARTIST; PERFORMER). I, 655 B, “That artist of fists,” that is, a boxer. II, 762 B, “But the maker of the spectacle.” I, 636 A, “Hence the Romans borrow performers whom they have summoned,” that is, actors.

ARTUS (NARROW). II, 1030 C, “Nor narrow for the hands,” that is, more confined or constricted. See Cicero, *Against Catiline*. I, 1243 B, “How greatly the matter is in straits.”

ASINARIUS (ASS-WORSHIPER), a worshiper of an ass. I, 365 A; 577 C, “Because [Col. 1262B] among the worshipers of every kind of cattle and beast, we alone are ass-worshipers.”

ASINUS (ASS). II, 416 B, “The ass from Aesop’s well”: an inept fellow suddenly arriving and filling everything with his untimely braying.

ASPIS (ASP). II, 331 C, “The asp—as they say—borrows its poison from the viper.” Pliny says of the asp, *Natural History* VIII.23: “The necks of asps swell”; and “there is no remedy for their stroke, unless the affected parts are amputated immediately.” Its poison is, of course, so swift-acting. Of the viper, in the same book, chapter 39: “Among serpents, the viper alone is said to hide in the earth, while the others hide in hollows of trees or rocks”—but Aristotle, *History of Animals* V, gives the contrary account, saying that the viper hides beneath rocks while the other serpents conceal themselves in the earth. “All of them sleep without venom during their season of retreat.” In book VII, chapter 2, Pliny says that “the inhabitants of Mount Athos feed upon vipers’ flesh.” This is certainly evidence of a less effective poison. The proverb will therefore mean that the most pestilential creature [Col. 1262C] is instructed in wickedness by one less evil.

ASSECTATUS (PURSUED). II, 948 B, “And a widow pursued for some time,” that is, desired. Rhenanus reads *affectatae*, “desired.”

ASSENTATOR (ABettor; APPROVER). II, 206 A, “God is found to be an abettor of evil, one who assents to evil’s being done.” That is, although God recognizes matter as evil, he nevertheless uses it—as Hermogenes’ doctrine maintained—and either reinforces its depravity or at least ignores it. Junius conjectures *assectator*, “follower,” one who would have been obliged συνακολουθεῖν (*synakolouthein*), “to follow along with,” and endure the nature of matter.

ASSERTOR (CHAMPION; CLAIMANT), anyone who claims another into either free or servile status, a defender of another’s liberty. II, 273 C, “Such a claimant would also be condemned in the secular court.” I, 1287 A, “Whose champion disputed with the Lord,” that is, an advocate who undertakes to defend a person.

ASSIGNARE (TO ASSIGN; MARK; BIND). I, 1269 C, “And he assigns the virgin,” that is, he keeps her marked and bound by the chastity she shares with widows. I, 1272 A, “He assigns the public confession,” namely, to the repentance mentioned immediately before. II, 18 B, “But they faithfully assigned to the nations the discipline received from Christ.” [Col. 1262D] II, 1046 A, “And let him entrust the entire construction of the gathered fold to the restraining clasps.” III, 137 B, “Assigning the enduring stains of his blood to the flints.” II, 1023 B, “Discipline governs a person; power assigns him,” that is, points him out, displays him as distinguished, χαρακτηρίζει (*charaktērizei*, “characterizes” or “marks”).

ASSUMERE (TO ASSUME). I, 1236 B, “And they assume repentance.” A person is said to “assume repentance” when he professes his name among the hearers.

ATHENAE (ATHENS). II, 20 B, “What, then, has Athens to do with Jerusalem?” that is, what have philosophers to do with Christians?

ATTENTARE (TO ATTACK), to assail. II, 55 B: for the impious, proceeding from their own opinions, assail the understanding of the pious as though with the hand, and strive for this one thing: to transform truth into falsehood.

ATTONITUS (INTENSELY ALERT; ENTRANCED). II, 58 B, “An intensely alert diligence,” which is always afraid lest it commit some error. I, 656 B, “Entranced by mimes,” that is, attending to the mimes with an entranced mind.

[Col. 1263A] AVENA (WILD OAT). II, 156 A, “The Praxean wild oats.” He compares false doctrine to wild oats, for, as Pliny writes, the wild oat is a corruption of grain. In the same passage: “Those wild oats, indeed, had then shaken out their seed everywhere.”

AVOCATOR (ONE WHO CALLS AWAY). II, 762 B, “Not a raiser of the dead, but one who calls away the living,” that is, one who calls the living away from life to death, and from right faith to heresy.

AVOCATRIX (SEDUCTRESS). II, 647 C, “The seductress of all truth.”

AUCTOR (OWNER; PRINCIPAL), the lawful owner. II, 51 B, “And from the owners themselves,” that is, κυρίοις (*kyriois*, “lords”), the transferors of ownership. II, 113 B, “But since the principals themselves, who preside by authority, are those in whose hands lies the authority for maintaining the Church.” In the Glosses of Philoxenus, *auctor* is rendered ἀρχηγός (“leader”) and αὐθέντης (“master”); and in the books of the land surveyors, *auctores* is used absolutely for teachers and masters.

AUCTORAMENTUM (CONTRACTED SERVICE). I, 476 A, “Under contract to the belly.”

AUCTORARE (TO HIRE ONESELF OUT), to seek wages. I, 697 D, “Let us enter these contests as hired combatants.” *Auctorati* were those who, [Col. 1263B] for an offered wage or prize, had bound themselves and pledged their service as gladiators. I, 626 B, “Some have now hired themselves out even to the flames,” that is, bound themselves. II, 77 C, “And sufficiently hired under the protection of consent,” that is, confirmed and bound by its authority.

AUCTORITAS (AUTHORITY), supreme power in administering an empire. I, 258. II, 49 A, “Whence authority is also available to us,” that is: from that Church its institutions likewise furnish authority—κῦρος καὶ βεβαίωσις (*kyros kai bebaiōsis*, “validity and confirmation”)—to us Christians, just as do the other aforementioned and similar things; and that chair is available, etc. II, 977 A, “And they sigh at the authority of the star that delays,” that is, they grieve that the rising of the stars is delayed so long, since before it is unlawful to break the fast.

AUDIRE (TO BE HEARD OF; BE CELEBRATED). II, 1034 A, “It alone used to be heard of,” that is, formerly it was on everyone’s lips because of its fertility, and scarcely anything else was discussed. II, 796 A, “We shall know what the Sadducees hear from Christ,” that is, what name they are called and in what ways they are refuted. I, 1239 A, “Another among the hearers,” [Col. 1263C] that is, the catechumens.

AUDITUS (HEARING). II, 404 A, “Who raised up for hearing,” that is, for the hearing or for the purpose of hearing, by a Greek idiom: τῇ ἀκοῇ ἤγειρον, “they raised up for hearing.”

AURIGA (CHARIOTEER). II, 930 C, “Among others’ eunuchs and your own charioteers.” Rigault reads *perorigae tuae*. In Varro, *On Agriculture* II, where the mating of mares is discussed, *peroriga* means anyone who brings them to the stallion. Accordingly, he calls the Psychics *perorigae*, because, as he himself says, they pressed marriage upon people and, as it were, provoked sexual desire. Le Prieur prefers *urigae*, that is, those who, so to speak, aroused sexual desire. I, 641 B, “Deservedly they clothed idolatry even in charioteering colors,” that is, in their idolatrous games they assigned to their charioteers colors corresponding to the idols; for he calls these colors “charioteers,” just as Virgil, *Aeneid* XII, uses “charioteer sister” adjectivally. I, 661 A, “The charioteer wholly red upon the fiery wheel”; he alludes to the Red faction of the racers.

AURUGINARE (TO BECOME JAUNDICED). II, 675 C, “Those who become jaundiced from an excess of bile,” that is, suffer from jaundice. *Aurugo* means jaundice, from the color of gold. [Col. 1263D] An old glossary: ἴκτερος, “jaundice”; ἰκτερικός, *auruginosus*, “jaundiced,” one who suffers from that disease.

AUSPEX (AUSPICE; COMMANDER). II, 140 C, “As formerly, not under an auspice,” that is, under the person by whose command and leadership the affair was conducted. Rigault, however, dislikes this word and thinks nothing is missing except the name of a place.

AUT (OR). II, 164 E, “Thus he is either Father or Son,” that is: thus he is either the Father, who is designated by the word “Father” and not “Son”; or he is the Son, who is designated by the word “Son” and not “Father.” When the discourse concerns this or that person, the designation corresponds to the truth of the person. I, 1175 A, “Or how many arteries are needed”: *aut* means “otherwise,” in the Greek manner, for ἤ sometimes has this meaning.

AUTEM (BUT). The word itself is placed like a clasp—the connective particle attached to link the narrative together. II, 221 B.

Αὐτεξούσιον (*AUTEXOUSION*, SELF-DETERMINATION). II, 685 A, “Having within us the free power of choice subject to him, which is called αὐτεξούσιον.”

AUTHENTICUS (AUTHENTIC; ORIGINAL). II, 49 A, “Among whom their authentic letters [Col. 1264A] are read aloud,” that is, sounding forth the voice of each one in the same language in which they were written by the apostles. II, 546 B, “He broke away from the Church of the authentic rule.” II, 946 A, “Let us know plainly that it is not so in the authentic Greek text.”

AXIS. Festus: a round post around which a wheel turns. I, 531 A, “Bound to the post of half an axle.”

## B

BACCHANS (BACCHANTIC). II, 1043 B, “Worthily indeed, so that it might rustle something beneath the bacchantically raging garments.” “Bacchantic garments” are the purple robes proper to women celebrating the Bacchic rites.

BAJULI (BEARERS). I, 1281 B, “Nor German bearers.” German bearers, attendants of eminent men or more delicate women, carried them either seated in covered carriages or reclining in litters; the bearers were selected especially for their height.

BALTEUS or BALTEUM (BELT; ENCLOSING BARRIER). I, 634 B, “For they call the paths the pivots of the belts running around the circumference.” There were two kinds of path: one transverse, for those proceeding around the circumference; the other [Col. 1264B] straight, as though down the slope—as the author says—for those making their way around the seating area. The circuit nearest or surrounding the seating area belonged to the more distinguished spectators; the sloping section belonged to the common people surrounding that circuit. Tertullian relates that the circuit in which the senators’ orchestra stood was divided by belts and pivots.

It is established that the terms *baltei* or, more frequently, *baltea* were applied metaphorically to structures that served, as it were, as belts and barriers for other things, binding and securing them in their proper place. At public spectacles, likewise, *baltei* or *baltea* was the name given to the barriers between sections of seating, by which the στίχοι (*stichoi*), or rows, of senators, equestrians, and magistrates were divided so that they might watch comfortably—say, ten, fifteen, twenty, thirty, and so forth enclosed within each belt, according to their greater proximity to or distance from the circus or seating area, the length of the belts diminishing accordingly.

Each belt had two pivots of its own at either path. Through these the spectators entered from right and left; having entered, they closed them so that no one else could enter the belt. [Col. 1264C] By synecdoche they were called “pivots” because the doors turned and were mounted upon hinges, so that spectators—as the author also calls them in chapter 20—might have free entrance and exit when passing from the path into the belt or from the belt into the path. A similar arrangement existed among the common people, except that, in place of the more honorable belts, the people had plain seats, without barriers and handrails, and certain slight divisions between the paths in place of the pivots reserved for the more distinguished.

These, therefore, are the paths of which the author speaks: between those pivots and divisions, one could pass out of the spectacle—or in the opposite direction—from the stage and fore-stage, which were separated by a curtain, following the pivots of the belts around the circuit where the more distinguished sat, and following the divisions of the common people down the slope.

BAPTISMUS (BAPTISM). II, 1209 A, “After the baptism of the world,” that is, after the Flood. II, 1213 A, “When Paul alone of them had put on Christ’s baptism.” II, 1217 A, “The baptism of blood.”

BARBARIA (BARBAROUS LAND). II, 890 B, “Through Greece and certain [Col. 1264D] barbarous lands belonging to it.” By the “barbarous lands of Greece” he means certain regions outside or adjoining Greece with which the Greeks had dealings or wars. Horace: “Greece, colliding with barbarism in a protracted war.”

BARDUS (DULL). II, 230 B, “The painter is not duller than you.”

BASILIA, βασιλεία (*basileia*, KINGDOM). II, 350 B, “In the first division of the Kingdoms.” They divided the *Basiliai*, or “Kingdoms”—that is, the Books of Kingdoms—into two parts. The first comprised the two books entitled Samuel; the second, the two Books of Kings. Those who read “in the First Book of Kingdoms” are mistaken, for the passage occurs in the first division of the Kingdoms, in the second of the books entitled Samuel, chapter 7. II, 389 A, “So also previously in the Kingdoms.”

BAXA, a kind of gilded women’s shoe. II, 670 B; II, 1043 B, “The slipper and the *baxa* are gilded every day.”

BEKKOS. I, 570 B, “The first sound reported was *Bekkos*”; its interpretation is that it is the Phrygian word for bread.

BENEDICTUS (BLESSED). II, 42 A, “Under the episcopate of the blessed Eleutherus.” [Col. 1265A] Among the earliest Christians, “Blessed” was an eminent title. II, 1003 C, “The good shepherd and blessed Pope.”

BENEFICIARII was the name given to soldiers selected through the favor of the emperor for specified offices or duties; thus they attended upon the emperor in carrying out his commands. II, 118 C.

BENEFICIUM (BENEFIT). II, 1031 A, “The benefit of an injury.” The injury was inflicted upon Carthage in its destruction; the benefit consisted in permission to rebuild it.

BERYLLUS, βήρυλλος (*bēryllos*, BERYL), is one of the bright green gems found among the Indians. Pliny, *Natural History* XXXVII.5, gives one of its varieties as chrysoberyl, pale indeed, but shading into a golden color. Agricola, *On Fossils* VI, writes that chrysoberyl is also called “Choaspites.” Beryl is somewhat dimmer, with a radiance inclining toward gold. II, 660 B, “Nor therefore is there watery matter in beryls because they shimmer with a strained brilliance.”

BESTIA (BEAST). II, 261 B, “Those very beasts of your bed and mat”—bedbugs and fleas. II, 913 A, “Like a certain beast,” etc.: a circumlocution for the ostrich or “sparrow-camel,” [Col. 1265B] which Aristotle describes very well in *Parts of Animals* IV, and Pliny at the beginning of *Natural History* X.

BESTIARII, those who fought with beasts in the arena, whether condemned criminals or, when criminals were lacking, others matched against savage wild animals. I, 317 A. When they ate their last meal, a generous table was set before them. I, 492 A, “I do not recline at the public Liberalia, as is customary for beast-fighters eating their final supper.”

BIAEOTHANATI, βιαιοθάνατοι (*biaiothanatoi*), those whose souls are violently torn away through the savagery of punishments. II, 747 B.

BIBERE (TO DRINK). I, 471 A, “Who have drunk one spirit of holiness.” He contrasts them with those who, in the *Tablet of Cebes*, were said to drink error and ignorance. Shortly afterward: “To feast upon discipline.”

BISCULUM. I, 1246 B, “Some little piece of iron or bronze for digging around the nails.”

BLATTIRE (TO BABBLE), to speak incoherently and inanely. II, 1032 B, “As Silenus babbles into the ears of Midas.”

BOTRONATUS (CLUSTERED) describes a mass of hair arranged in clusters. Hesychius: [Col. 1265C] Βοτρυδὸν, ἑτέρα τῆς ἑτέρας ἐχομένη, ὡς οἱ βότρυες τὰς ῥάγας ἔχουσι πυκνὰς καὶ κατὰ συστροφήν, ἢ συνηγμένοι ὁμοῦ—“In clusters: one thing adjoining another, as bunches of grapes have their berries closely packed and twisted together, or gathered together in one mass.” I, 1329 A.

BOTULUS (SAUSAGE). II, 954 B, “The outer and inner sausages of the Psychics.” This is a bitter transferred epithet directed against the orthodox, as though he had said: “Those coarse, fat, and obese Psychics, resembling sausages, as tightly stuffed as sausages.” He was therefore justified in first asking pardon of their ears. For a sausage’s interior is crammed with a stuffing of meat, like the belly of some glutton, while its exterior is shamelessly distended in the manner of a penis, like that god of Horace made from a fig-tree trunk: “And the red stake projecting obscenely from his groin.”

BRABIUM, βραβεῖον (*brabeion*), a prize. I, 624 B, “The prize of angelic substance.”
