**MULSA.** II, 655 B, “No one ever poured honeyed water from Plato’s discourse into a person hesitating about the soul’s departure.” *Aqua mulsa*, *ὑδρόμελι* or *μελίκρατον*, is water mixed with honey. He alludes not only to the abundance but also to the honeyed or mellifluous quality of Plato’s eloquence. In the book *On the Soul*, he says of the same Plato: “On account of the honey of his eloquence.”

**MULTINUBENTIA,** polygamy (*πολυγαμία*). II, 953 C.

[Col. 1334C]

**MULTIVORANTIA,** gluttony or eating much (*πολυφαγία*). II, 953 C.

**MULUS.** I, 574 A, “This is to paint a mule from an ass,” a proverbial expression meaning to produce, after a model of follies, an example of similar follies, or to fabricate new falsehoods after old ones. For he adds: “and to copy Ptolemy from Valentinus.” Valentinus first devised these monstrous trifles. Ptolemy added something of his own, differing somewhat from his master. Hence the name of ass belongs to Valentinus, the author of this heresy, and that of mule to his disciple Ptolemy.

**MUNDITENENS,** world-ruler (*κοσμοκράτωρ*). II, 518 B; 576 A.

**MURTIA.** I, 640 A, “An idol also made the turning-posts ‘Murtian,’” that is, even the *metae Murtiae* were named after an idol. The Murtian turning-posts were the last turning-posts in the Circus Maximus, near the shrine of Murtia. Behind them stood the herald, who watched the contestants’ performances from that side and proclaimed those who had performed well or badly. They hold Murtia to have been the goddess of love, that is, Venus, etc. This Venus was first called “Myrtle Venus” or “Murtian Venus” from two myrtles—one patrician and the other plebeian—planted before the shrine of Quirinus, and was subsequently called Murtia. [Col. 1334D] Pliny recounts the story in *Natural History*, book XV, chap. 29. Varro mentions it in book IV of *On the Latin Language*. So Junius; but Rigault reads “the god of languor.” Augustine, *City of God* IV, chap. 16: “They called her the goddess Murcia, who would not move beyond due measure and would make a person, as Pomponius says, *marcidus*, that is, excessively sluggish.”

**MUTARE.** II, 229 A, “To be changed is to perish with respect to one’s former state”; things lose their former state when they are changed.

**MYSTERIA ATTICA.** I, 474 A, The “Attic mysteries” are the Eleusinian rites.

# N

**NASCIBILIS.** II, 349 A, “He denies that mine is mortal, although he acknowledges that it is capable of being born.”

**NASUS.** II, 984 B, “And one who is not mocked by the nose”: thus he rendered Paul’s expression in Galatians VI, *οὐ μυκτηρίζεται*, “is not mocked.” Hesychius: “*μυκτηρίζει*: he mocks, he ridicules, from making a contemptuous sound with the nostrils” (*μυκτηρίζει, χλευάζει, καταγελᾷ, ἀπὸ τοῦ μύζειν τοῖς μυκτῆρσι*).

[Col. 1335A]

**NATALES,** origin, beginning. I, 1256 B, “Therefore I detect the origin of impatience in the devil himself.” Thus, in book I *Against Marcion*, he spoke of “the origin of recognition,” and in *The Pallium*, of “the origin of the world.”

**NATATILIS.** II, 228 B, “So that swimming and flying creatures should arise from the waters.”

**NATURA.** I, 811 A, “And by the disposition of nature.” The Fulda manuscript has “of the divine nature”; and the person who supplied that collation—either Modius or Scioppius—made a note of it. This is certainly a weightier expression and more consonant with Christ’s words. I, 471 A, “By the right of nature, their one mother.”

**NATURALIS.** II, 894 B, “*Female* is a natural designation; *woman* is the general designation within the natural one.” “Natural designation” means one common by nature to all animals, which are distinguished by sex. “General” is that which distinguishes within the human race; beneath this comes the specific designation.

**NATURALITAS.** II, 722 B, “Who, then, will doubt the natural character of sleep?”

**NATURIFICATUS.** II, 584 B, “By kinship with the now naturalized spiritual condition.”

[Col. 1335B]

**NAUFRAGIUM.** I, 695 A, “Shipwreck is inescapable for those dashed against them”—Greek *ναυάγιον ἄφυκτον*, “a shipwreck that cannot be escaped.” Those who strike against reefs and wreck their ship cannot disentangle or extricate themselves from danger.

**NAVICULARIUS.** II, 374 B, “It would be another matter if he had deliberately chosen someone from the guild of shipowners.”

**NAVIGARE.** I, 695 A, “Among these reefs and bays, among these shallows and straits of idolatry, faith sails with the Spirit of God filling its sails.”

**NECESSARIUS.** I, 1310 A, “More numerous and more necessary services.” II, 768 A, “As though they brought something necessary to it,” in place of “something more necessary.” I, 1266 A, “Where the injury is greater, there the remedy for the injury is more necessary.” II, 1002 B, “Unless it is so that they may bind them perpetually to more necessary things.”

**NECESSITAS.** I, 273 A, “O judgment confounded by necessity,” that is, one which necessarily sins against justice in some respect. Or rather: Trajan, wishing to make allowance both for hatred against Christians and for the justice of their cause, properly satisfies neither. I, 275 A, The necessity [Col. 1335C] which unjust laws enacted against Christians impose upon judges. I, 345 A, “According as each has found domestic necessity a holier master.” The sense is: in truth they recognize that no good accrues to them from those gods who are themselves subject to a greater power—namely, domestic necessity. II, 385 C, “Since he adduces human necessity as though it were an advocate pleading in defense.” II, 93 A, “The condition of faith does not admit a plea of necessity.” II, 93 B, “Those for whom the advocacy of necessity is most familiar.”

**NEGARE.** II, 246 C, “Whose designation as ‘Euxine’ is belied by its nature,” that is, it deceives through the falsehood of its surname, since, because of the character of the place and the savagery of its nature, it ought to be called *Axenos* (*ἄξενος*, “inhospitable”). Ovid: “The Pontus which bears the lying surname Euxine.” II, 247 A, “All are denied,” that is, are restrained by ice and cannot flow. I, 324 A, “Otherwise they would have to be denied, if they had not tasted it,” that is, it would have to be denied that they were Christians if they did not taste the blood which they are so insistently said to crave.

**NEGATOR.** II, 95 A, “Thus, by surrendering my faith, I am found to be a denier.”

**NEGOTIUM.** II, 285 A, “But now God suffers trouble,” [Col. 1335D] that is, the rashness and audacity of the Marcionites cause trouble for God, since they fabricated for themselves another god distinct from the Omnipotent. II, 905 B, “For they send females into business at twelve years, but the male two years later,” that is, they establish that they are legally independent, as though releasing them from the restraints of another’s authority; they grant them the power to conduct business—a legal expression. II, 649 B, “From the business of inquisitiveness.” II, 888 B, “Now a concern peculiar to me, arising from the suffering occasioned by my opinion,” that is, I who was previously occupied in setting forth in Greek my opinion about the veiling of virgins. Junius explains it thus; but Rigault thinks that, in some disputation against the Greeks, Tertullian may have argued rather forcefully that virgins too ought to be veiled, and was met with Greek abuse and harassed as a heretic.

**NEOPHYTUS,** *νεόφυτος*, a person who has recently come to the Christian faith. II, 57 A; 268 B.

**NEPOTARI,** to live luxuriously and extravagantly. I, 513 A, “Beneath a grand façade of seriousness, he lives extravagantly.”

[Col. 1336A]

**NERVUS.** II, 786 B, “Through that umbilical cord,” that is, the joining of veins and arteries, insofar as their fibers converge and unite in the navel. I, 623 B, “The leg feels nothing in the *nervus*.” The *nervus* is a kind of wooden device by which separated and dislocated legs were broken or tortured. In the Law of the Twelve Tables: “Let him lead him away with him; let him bind him, either in a *nervus* or in fetters of fifteen pounds,” etc. An old glossary gives *nervus*: *ξυλοπέδη*, “wooden fetter.” I, 512, “Other sinews for incestuous lust.”

**NIDOR.** I, 407 A, “Their peculiar foods of smoke and blood,” through libations and sacrifices; but in this passage he may perhaps be speaking of sacrifices generally, not of necromantic sacrifices.

**NIMIETAS.** II, 236 A, “Incomprehensible because of the excessive magnitude of the conflict.”

**NOBILIS.** II, 150 C, “Are the Apostles’ writings, then, also well known?”—that is, are they not known to everyone, clear, and manifest? Ursinus’ copy has *mobiles* (“changeable”), that is, writings which mean something other than they sound, with one thing in the words and another in the meanings. Rigault nevertheless prefers the former reading. Junius reads *nubilae* (“clouded”), that is, covered by a cloud of obscurity and darkness so that they cannot be understood.

[Col. 1336B]

**NOEROS.** *Νοερός*, “mental,” “intellectual”; others read *noetos*, *νοητός*, “intelligible,” as in Irenaeus. II, 574 B.

**NOMEN,** the Christian religion. I, 278 A, “Let us be excluded from that name,” that is, let us cease to be called Christians and reject the Christian religion. I, 280 A, “Those who formerly, before this name,” that is, in earlier times, before they became Christians. I, 1252 A, “Persecuting the name together with its family,” that is, the Christian religion and its followers. I, 661 A, “Persecutors of the Lord’s name.” I, 525 A, “You, human being, so great a name,” that is, a thing of immense importance and great glory. II, 890 A, “And the whole scope of the name ‘tree’ is unfolded,” that is, everything signified by the word “tree.” II, 800 A, “And destined to perish from this designation too, thereafter into no designation.” After the corruption of our corpse, no designated name exists by which the matter that had constituted the human body may be marked. This he calls “the death of the designation.”

NICOLAITANS. II, 63 B, “Because that whole heresy of the Nicolaitans,” etc. They are indicated in Acts 20 by these words: “Speaking perverse things” (Λαλοῦντες διεστραμμένα). Tertullian in this passage, Epiphanius, *Heresies* XXV; Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* II and III; Jerome, the letter concerning Fabian and the letter to Ctesiphon; Eusebius, book III; Philastrius of Brescia, *Book on Heresies*; Theodoret, *Heretical Fables*, book III; Augustine, *Heresies* V; and countless others make Nicolaus, one of the seven deacons, the founder of this sect. [Col. 1336C] Ignatius, however, raises a doubt when he writes in his letter to the Trallians: “Flee also the falsely named Nicolaitans” (Φεύγετε καὶ τοὺς νικολαΐτας, τοὺς ψευδωνύμους). Add that most of those Fathers speak doubtfully about that Nicolaus, upon whom it was easy to cast the blame because of the filthiness of his life and his thoroughly corrupt morals.

MARK (*NOTA*). II, 17 B, “From temptations of a worse mark as well.” A metaphor from merchandise or kinds of wine, which were customarily distinguished by marks and recognized from them. II, 254 A, “Neither by the sound nor by the mark of this name,” that is, by the written form of the name. I, 1238 A, “What soldier, after being discharged from his camp, takes pains over his marks?” He means military marks by which a soldier is branded for military offenses—for example, if he has been absent without leave, a deserter, seditious, etc. I, 1248 B, “Since I am a sinner bearing every mark.”

[Col. 1336D] NEWNESS (*NOVELLITAS*), said of what has recently arisen. II, 157 A, “The very newness of yesterday’s Praxeas.” II, 697 C, “Nor does falsehood escape newness.”

NEW (*NOVELLUS*), recent. I, 392 A, “As being somewhat new.”

NOVIAN. II, 1042 B, “Novian’s Fullers.” The poet Novius produced a play entitled *The Fullers*, in which word there is an unspeakable obscenity.

NOVELTY (*NOVITAS*). II, 1030 C, He calls the Carthaginians “fortunate through novelty,” because Carthage had been granted Italic rights through the favor of the emperor Severus, during whose reign Tertullian wrote the treatise *On the Pallium*.

CULPABLE (*NOXIUS*). I, 372 A, “A culpable hireling.” Gothofredus takes *noxius* to mean “liable”; Rigaltius says that he acted dishonestly, because he had so often eluded the teeth of the beasts. In this passage I would rather understand *noxius* as someone who, although under no necessity of fighting with beasts and not condemned to them among the criminals, nevertheless, from desire for a little profit and for an agreed payment, handed himself over to the trainer.

[Col. 1337A] TO MARRY (*NUBERE*). II, 198 A, “She marries continually,” that is, she approves polygamy in every form and enjoins marriage without any distinction. Thus she defends God’s law in the service of lust.

CLOUDS. I, 417 A, “Otherwise, if you think this ought to be done, let him count the clouds while praying.” Christians generally assembled in open courts and, while praying there, looked up to heaven, without altars and without statues. The pagans therefore mocked them as though they were counting clouds in prayer.

CLOUDINESS (*NUBILUM*). II, 597 A, “The truth was overshadowed by a certain cloudiness in each person,” that is, the cloud of ignorance overshadowed the truth in the minds of individuals. II, 247 B, “More obscure than cloudiness.”

WALNUT GROVE (*NUCETUM*) is a place planted with walnut trees, from *nux* (“walnut”), just as *quercetum* comes from *quercus* (“oak”) and *lauretum* from *laurus* (“laurel”). II, 575 A, “Thus in heavenly matters too he presumed walnut groves.”

NAKEDNESS. II, 706 B, “Nor is nakedness granted to the ashes being punished,” because the ashes of assassins are not clothed or enclosed in an urn.

NAKED. II, 247 A, “Naked lust”: not covered, but exposed [Col. 1337B] to the spectators’ eyes. For the contrary statement follows: even when they conceal their lust, they are marked out to the judges by quivers suspended from the yoke of the wagon in which they indulge their lust. I, 301 A, “Naked theaters,” that is, without a roof. For they used to be covered to ward off the sun.

A THING OF NO ACCOUNT (*NULLIFICAMEN*), ἐξουθένημα. II, 330 A, “And the people’s thing of no account,” which at II, 639 A he also calls “the people’s rejection.”

NONE (*NULLUS*). II, 134 A, “The wounds are none,” that is, they are not reckoned as wounds, though they exist. Rigaltius retains the common reading, “the wounds are not none,” in this sense: there are no battles, because there is no enemy; nevertheless, there are not no wounds, because they struggle vigorously and bravely and are wounded.

TO NUMBER, equivalent to “to register.” II, 116 C, “Numbered in blood,” that is, those whose faces were marked with blood.

NUMERICALLY (*NUMEROSE*). II, 167 D, “So that he might speak numerically,” that is, in the plural, as he had previously said, “without the plural number.”

TO DISPLAY FOR SALE (*NUNDINARE*). II, 907 A, “I shall praise their vigor if they have put some example of virginity on sale even among the pagans,” that is, if they possess such constancy in their virginity that they dare also to set forth examples of it from which pagans may take something to imitate. The metaphor is from wares offered for everyone to see at markets.

MARKET-DISPLAYING (*NUNDINATITIUS*). II, 892 B, “Therefore, because of heads of this sort displayed at market,” that is, exposing themselves in public as though at a market.

*NUS*, νοῦς (“mind”). II, 62 A, Basilides says that the supreme god is named Abraxas, by whom was created Mind, which the Greeks call νοῦς. II, 552 A; 573 B, “He would represent that same demiurge as the son, νοῦς.” II, 666 A, “Accordingly, by *animus* also—or mind, which is νοῦς among the Greeks—we understand nothing other than an innate and implanted prompting of the soul,” etc.

NOWHERE (*NUSQUAM*). II, 228 B, “It will never happen,” from Isaiah 34:4, οὐδέποτε γενήσεται (“it will never happen”).

TO WAVER. I, 516 A, “Human scrupulousness, scorning faith, wavered all the more,” that is, by their uncertainty and instability they confused and disturbed even what they had found certain in the Scriptures.

[Col. 1337D] NOD (*NUTUS*). II, 1043 B, “To betray by a nod.” This belongs to people secretly mocking and disapproving something among themselves when it would be neither safe nor seemly to do so openly. Since they are permitted neither to turn their eyes upon the person nor to point with extended fingers, he can at least be indicated by a covert nod.

## O

*OBBA*, a kind of potbellied vessel with which libations were made to the spirits of the dead. I, 347 A.

TO REFUTE (*OBDUCERE*), or to catch and hold someone asserting contrary and mutually conflicting things. I, 501 A, “While he is refuted concerning the goodness of this sect.” II, 232 B, “And you will be refuted for making it corporeal and infinite.” II, 218 C, “The argument of the opposing side is refuted”—overcome and disproved. II, 270 B, “Produce, therefore, someone from among your own who possesses apostolic standing, [Col. 1338A] and you will have prevailed.” II, 344 A, “We have already prevailed concerning the names.” II, 797 A, “Accordingly, we too refute, having thereafter been refuted concerning God.” II, 993 B, “When I shall thus also have refuted the presumption of the opposing side.” It can also mean “to erase,” with a metaphor taken from account books, like “to strike out.” I, 531 A, “But we are erased,” that is, we die in battle, and you cast this against us.

BARRIER (*OBEX*). II, 143 C, “Nor will anyone dislodge the barrier of that prescription.”

TO FASTEN FIRMLY (*OBFIRMARE*). II, 688 C, “Even if he fixes no hunting spear firmly against it.”

TO SILT UP (*OBHUMARE*), II, 1033 B. Rivers are “silted up” when their channels are filled with mud so that they are thereby forced to alter their course. Others read “by overshadowing”; Latinius, “by walking about.”

TO LIE AGAINST (*OBJACERE*). II, 658 A, “Thus, therefore, even if corporeal things lie against corporeal things.”

ACCUSATION (*OBJECTIO*). I, 1297 A, “Whose dowries, through the accusation attached to the name, may provide the reward for silence,” etc.; that is, when the women are informed against because of the name and profession of the Christian religion, their husbands claim their dowries for themselves as payment for the silence they had maintained on their wives’ behalf for so long. Thus the husband himself, who had slyly spied out Christian secrets through the occasion of marriage, became arbiter of the dispute. Unless the wife was entirely ready to die, she necessarily had to forfeit either the faith pledged to Christ or her dowry.

[Col. 1338B] OFFERING (*OBLATIO*). II, 739 A, “What arises from the force of the offering,” that is, of the condition offered.

TO LATTICE (*OBLAQUEARE*), to draw out and extend in a latticed pattern. II, 805 A, “Lest you lattice it with silver as well.”

ENSNARED (*OBLEGATUS*). II, 971 B, “And bound, as I think, by all the enticements of this life as though they were worthier than eternal ones,” that is, baited on every side, nurtured amid pleasures, and growing sluggish in them.

BOND (*OBLIGAMENTUM*). II, 352 B, “When the bonds and burdens of the law were already being altered by evangelical freedom.” I, 684 A, “And every unclean spirit through the bond of consecration.” II, 98 A, “Not even subject to a veil, much less to a bond.”

[Col. 1338C] TO OBLITERATE. I, 1283 B, “But if they possess it, they ought to obliterate what they possess.” II, 933 C, “Therefore, if all those things obliterate the permission to marry.” II, 700 A, “Notorious wastelands have obliterated estates that were formerly most pleasant.” I, 1293 A, “For who could doubt that faith is daily obliterated through commerce with unbelief?”

BOUND (*OBNOXIUS*). II, 900 C, “Two laws bound to one another,” that is, joined to one another by what is, as it were, a covenant of nature. II, 452 A, “Releasing those bound by more violent contracts”; “entangled” (*obnexus*) is better.

ILL-OMENED (*OBSCOENUS*). II, 1031 A, “After the ill-omened portents of Gracchus,” that is, inauspicious and sinister omens: namely, a standard broken by the force of the winds although the standard-bearer resisted strenuously; and sacred offerings placed upon the altars scattered and cast beyond the boundaries of the city.

TO OBSERVE. II, 39 A, B, n. (1), “Since they themselves observed,” that is, since they remained consistent with themselves, having themselves taught the same thing in their letters. For he establishes the form of preaching from the form of the letters.

TO SEAL. I, 1283 B, “Those who immediately after the washing seal [Col. 1338D] their flesh,” that is, from baptism onward devote themselves to virginity and celibacy. I, 1327 A, “And they seal themselves for eunuchhood.” I, 675 A, “He seals the gods themselves with this name.” I, 677 B, “If we speak after faith has been sealed.”

ALTERED FROM USE (*OBSOLEFACTUS*). II, 905 A, “Her voice has been altered from use,” that is, changed and altered from its accustomed quality since it first began, as Nonius puts it, “to crow like a young cock.”

TO WEAR OUT (*OBSOLETARE*). I, 363 A, “They wear out the traces of majesty.” In the Fulda manuscript Havercamp reads “they level the summit to the ground” (*fastigium adsolant*), that is, make it equal to the soil; correctly. Compare I, 577 A; II, 135 A, “Those who had worn out the wedding garment,” that is, had rendered it worn out or had brought it in a worn-out state.

OBSTINACY, in a good sense, for constancy. I, 631 B, “To be trained for this constancy by renouncing pleasures.”

TO OBSTRUCT (*OBSTREPERE*). II, 82 C, “Although neither does extraordinary attire obstruct ordinary use,” that is, stand in its way. I, 630 B, “Such great outward consolations of the eyes or ears offer no obstruction to religion in the mind and conscience.” I, 654 B, “Even with the charm of pleasure obstructing.” I, 1326 A, “And let them obstruct the disciplines of chastity.”

[Col. 1339A] OBSTRUCTION (*OBSTREPITACULUM*). II, 268 A, “Against the obstructions of the opposing side.”

TO BIND (*OBSTRINGERE*). II, 57 A, “Now bound to the world.” He means those who held some prefecture among the pagans. For many Christians who had obtained some dignity or military office nevertheless discharged the duties of those honors; yet it did not seem right that they should be ordained to ecclesiastical offices.

TO BLOCK (*OBSTRUERE*). II, 38 B, “A lamp is not usually blocked under a bushel.” Junius and others prefer “hidden” (*abstrui*). *Abstruere* means to remove the light by placing a pile in front of it.

TO BLUNT (*OBTUNDERE*). II, 454 C, “David was not refuting the scribes’ error,” that is, disproving it. II, 169 B, “So that from this point I may now blunt your faith.”

TO BEFALL (*OBVENIRE*). II, 36 A, “Because Paul had befallen him as his adversary,” that is, had fallen to his lot as a servant given by God to the Church.

[Col. 1339B] HAPPENSTANCE (*OBVENIENTIA*). II, 584 C, “They add an argument from happenstance”: by *obvenientia* he means events that arise from elsewhere.

TO OVERSHADOW. II, 597 A, “The truth was overshadowed by a certain cloudiness in each person,” that is, in the minds of individuals the cloud of ignorance overshadowed the truth, especially if the noise of others who were equally overshadowed caused further confusion. II, 717 B, “Even now it overshadows and corrupts.”

OCCASION. II, 545 A, “From the occasion of divine abundance.” II, 886 B, “These women, however, could not dare this without some pretexts from the Scriptures.”

FIT FOR SLAUGHTER (*OCCISORIUS*). II, 705 B, “And whatever are to be butchered among those fit for slaughter,” that is, among those kinds of animals prepared for killing.

TO TAKE POSSESSION (*OCCUPARE*). I, 376 A, “It is less even than the eyes by which it is taken possession of”; for by his sight a person takes possession of whatever is placed before his eyes. II, 802 A, “Which first took possession of the designation ‘man.’” II, 802 B, “Consider again that God in his entirety has been taken possession of and dedicated to him.”

[Col. 1339C] TO ENCOUNTER (*OCCURRERE*). I, 500 A, “Deservedly, we alone encounter innocence,” that is, once we find it, we alone will embrace it. II, 42 B, “When he meets the condition of what was granted to him”—namely, repentance—that is, when he voluntarily presents himself anew to the Church.

EIGHT-HORSED (*OCTOJUGIS*). The Valentinian Ogdoad is so called; for he alludes to the circus games. II, 500 B, “Once, as they say, the starting-cloth has been dropped for that eight-horse team.”

TO GIVE SIGHT (*OCULARE*). Scaliger: ἐξομματοῦν (“to give eyes to”). I, 404 A, “Who would give sight to those already refined for recognition of the truth.” I, 1248 A, “He knows how to give them sight again.” II, 994 C, “In garments given sight by purple,” that is, illuminated by it. Thus Pliny says of the sun: “It gives sight to the other heavenly bodies.” The brilliance or radiance proper to purple is called “light.” Fabius, *Institutes* VIII: “A broad stripe and pieces of purple inserted in the proper place will bring light.” Horace, *Art of Poetry*: “One or two purple patches, to shine broadly, are sewn on.”

KEEN-SIGHTED (*OCULATUS*). “I think God is too keen-sighted from his higher position for anything below him to escape his notice.”

ODEUM. II, 851 C, “But very recently, in this city, [Col. 1339D] the foundations of an odeum were sacrilegiously laid upon so many ancient tombs.” He means either Carthage or Rome. Odea were places to which spectators sometimes withdrew from the theater if rain came on. Poems were also recited there, and grain for sale was customarily displayed. The foundations built upon the tombs are called sacrilegious because burial grounds were regarded as religious and sacred things. It followed from this that those who dug them up were guilty of sacrilege, and that the foundations of the odeum were sacrilegious, since for its sake things held sacred under the law of nations were seized for profane uses.

Οἰκονομία (“dispensation”). II, 156 B, “Yet under this dispensation, which we call οἰκονομία.” II, 158 A, “The mystery of the οἰκονομία,” concerning the doctrine of the Trinity.

OENOTRIA. Italy was so called from wine, not from any king of that name. This opinion agrees with Aristotle, *Politics* VII, and Strabo, book VI, who indicate it without making any mention of Oenotrius. I, 330 A.

[Col. 1340A] TO STUFF (*OFFARCINARE*). II, 418 C, “Besides being stuffed with loads of dough.” Exodus 12:34: “And the people took up their dough before it was leavened, their kneaded portions bound up in their garments upon their shoulders” (Ἀνέλαβε δὲ ὁ λαὸς τὸ σταῖς αὐτῶν πρὸ τοῦ ζυμωθῆναι, τὰ φυράματα αὐτῶν ἐνδεδεμένα ἐν τοῖς ἱματίοις αὐτῶν ἐπὶ τῶν ὤμων).

PRESENTATION (*OFFERENTIA*). II, 421 A, “Consider how the causes present themselves,” that is, according as the different causes present themselves.

TO OFFER. II, 922 B, “You both offer and baptize.” II, 942 C, “And she makes an offering on the annual days of his falling asleep.” II, 984 B, “And offering their affliction to God.”

OFFICIAL (*OFFICIALIS*). II, 93 A, “And the other reasons for official crowns,” which those who discharged certain offices and honors wore because of the necessity of their office.

OFFICE (*OFFICIUM*). II, 970 A, “He sends her forth to it with an official staff and retinue.” Among the jurists, *officium* is the very body of those who serve a magistrate; hence their expressions “to relinquish one’s staff” and “to hand over to the staff.” Tertullian uses it here in this sense. II, 137 B, “When the dedication of the imperial image compelled the crowd to its duty,” that is, [Col. 1340B] to the duty of idolatrous worship. II, 119 A, “If you have bought off the military offices,” that is, if with money you have won over to yourself soldiers exercising public authority. II, 713 A, “We believe that angels are divine offices,” that is, officials and administrators of offices. II, 719 C, “The resentment against the governor is more severe when his officials are assaulted.”

WORKSHOP (*OFFICINA*). II, 336 A, “Call the womb a sewer—the workshop for producing so great a living creature, namely, a human being.”

TO POUR DOWN THE THROAT (*OFFOCARE* or *OFFUCARE*), to give water to be swallowed down the throat, as Festus explains it. I, 695 A, “Whatever waves of it choke [him].”

TO AGGRAVATE (*ONERARE*). I, 1293 A, “The charge of contumacy is so greatly aggravated,” that is, it is so much graver and more atrocious. II, 928 A, “It is also recognized by outsiders and burdened with testimony.” II, 988 A, “He therefore aggravated adultery,” that is, he described adultery as a graver and more atrocious crime. This reading seems preferable to Latinius’s conjecture, “honored” (*honoravit*).

BURDENSOMENESS (*ONEROSITAS*). I, 1323 A, “So great a burdensomeness in arranging the head.” [Col. 1340C]

ONESIMUS. II, 588 A, “And perhaps you may give birth to some aeon named Onesimus.” He alludes to Philemon’s Onesimus, whom Paul begot in chains, as he himself writes to Philemon—that is, by an altogether heavenly birth, making a Christian from a Gentile and an upright man from a runaway. Septimius says mockingly: We expect that you, who are Marcus or Gaius—or at least, which suffices, a male—will give birth amid those unspeakable chains or embraces of the Valentinian angels. But what will you give birth to? Some Pauline Onesimus, no doubt? No, rather some monstrous scoundrel of Satan.

*ONOKOITĒS* (ὀνοκοίτης). I, 372 A, Properly one who copulates with an ass; then, that which is conceived from an ass and a human being. Thus the Septuagint translators frequently used κοίτης (“bed, intercourse”) for offspring, as did Paul in Romans 9:10. From the appearance of the body they mark this fictitious god as a kind of ὀνοκοίτης, shamefully begotten, as it were, of an adulteress. See Juvenal, *Satire* VI, verse 330; Suetonius, *Life of Domitian*, chapter 12; Martial I, 5.

BURDEN (*ONUS*). I, 515 A, “If it were not already a burden, I would regulate the size of the volume,” that is, its bulk and magnitude (ὄγκος, μέγεθος). [Col. 1340D]

TO WORK AT (*OPERARI*), to devote effort. I, 1520 A, “In which we work.” II, 762 C, “While he worked at curing weaknesses and defects.” I, 695 A, “Let it give the brethren an opportunity to work,” that is, an opportunity to do us good, so that through their assistance we may be protected from that necessity.

WORKER (*OPERARIUS*). I, 1271 A, “And so the devil is the worker of that victory of God.” I, 1274 A, “Workers for the belly”: he calls parasites this. II, 705 B, “And those to be wearied among working animals,” that is, among those kinds of animals prepared to perform labor.

OPERATION (*OPERATIO*). II, 907 A, “Or any operation of almsgiving”; so also “the operation of fasting.”

OPERATIVE (*OPERATRIX*). II, 739 A, “That very principle which produces death, though simple, is a force.”

WROUGHT (*OPERATUS*). I, 259 A, “A wrought persecution,” that is, a more violent and bitter one. Perhaps “aggravated” (*onerata*) would be better, so that the sense is: What prevents you from permitting the Christian sect to be defended [Col. 1341A] is the prejudgment by which you have condemned it so often.

ELABORATENESS (*OPEROSITAS*). I, 1328 A, “And elaborateness joined with rarity,” that is, workmanship and the craftsman’s fee. Irenaeus uses this word for labor and hardship in book V, chapter 19. I, 1184 A, “And elaborateness, the pander of the hair”;“ similarly I, 1151 A, “With the Gospel superimposed as the canceller of all former antiquity.” II, 1045 B, “The priestly apparatus,” etc. II, 651 A, “So great an elaborateness of persuasion.”

SKILLFULLY (*OPIFICE*). I, 158 A, “And so skillfully.” Rigaltius prefers “even craftsmen” (*etiam opifices*), which seems to agree better with what follows. Others read “even Opici” (*etiam opici*), that is, barbarians, because they spoke *opice*, that is, barbarously rather than in Latin, according to Pliny, book XXIX, chapter 1.

FULLNESS (*OPIMITAS*). II, 683 B, “Fullness hinders wisdom; thinness assists it.” II, 998 C, “And thus thereafter he feeds upon the fullness of the Lord’s body.”

OPINIONATED (*OPINIOSUS*), one who forms opinions. II, 447 A, “Let him see whether Christ will appear so opinionated to anyone”; so Cicero, *Academics*.

WORK (*OPUS*). I, 339 A, “In the very working,” that is, when they are cast, hammered, and engraved, and thus injured and wounded. [Col. 1341B]

PRAYER (*ORATIO*). II, 105 B, “But in the lawful prayer.” He calls that prayer “lawful” which Christ, skilled in heavenly law, prescribed for us. Thus Augustine spoke of “the lawful prayer” in *Sermon 125, On Time*.

ROUND TABLE (*ORBIS*), which the ancients called a *cilliba*. II, 1048 A, “For which Marcus Tullius bought a round citrus-wood table for five hundred thousand sesterces.” Citrus-wood tables were brought from Mauretania to Rome at incredible expense. Pliny, book XXXIII, chapter 11.

ORDER (*ORDO*). II, 39 B, “The whole order of the rule,” that is, an ordered form of Christian doctrine. In the same sense, II, 40 B, “The order of the Churches’ doctrine.” II, 947 B, “So that the people might know all the more that they must observe for themselves the order which produces the presiding officers.” He means the order of the once-married, from whom the presiding officers are chosen. Accordingly, he wished all the people to be once-married.

THE RISING (*ORIENS*). II, 545 A, “The Rising, a figure of Christ”; supply [Col. 1341C] “he loves.” For Christ is often understood by the word “Rising” in the sacred writings, as in Zechariah. He is called the Rising because he is the sun of righteousness rising from on high.

ADORNMENT (*ORNATUS*). I, 1309 A, “We call that adornment which ought to be called feminine uncleanness,” namely, care of the hair and skin.

MOMENTARY (*ORTANEUS*). II, 483 B, D, n. (1), “And certain signs even of momentary things.” *Ortanea* are things that are momentary and possess their being only in their arising: they arise and perish at once.

MOUTH (*OS*). I, 654 A, “But let him revisit the man, now exhausted, even for the spectacle of his mouth,” so that he may wish to look even upon the mouth and face of the dying man.

OSCILLATING DEVICE (*OSCILLUM*), an oscillation, αἰώρα, said of a machine poised for striking and assault. See Festus under this word. II, 1032 A.

OSTENTATIOUS (*OSTENTATITIUS*). II, 892 B, “The shamelessness of ostentatious virginity.”

IDLE (*OTIOSUS*). II, 76 A, “With an idle crown in his hand.” By “idle” he means useless and inappropriate. Thus in *To His Wife*: [Col. 1341D] “For us it is idle to beget children,” that is, it is useless and inappropriate for Christians to beget children while a tyrant rages against the Christian name.

## P

FOOD (*PABULUM*). I, 306 B, “And food from it,” that is, from the flesh of the slain infant. Havercamp proposes: “And with the food raw, from it and afterward,” etc.

PACIFYING (*PACATORIUS*). II, 435 C, “Judge a just and pacifying judgment.”

TRAINING (*PAEDAGOGATUS*). II, 563 A, “The training of the Holy Spirit,” that is, his ministry.

TRAINING-HOUSE (*PAEDAGOGIUM*), an assembly. I, 348 A, “Then concerning the imperial training-houses.” II, 554 A, “And a thousand other names from the training-house.” Following the custom of the imperial palace, he calls it a *paedagogium*, in which court boys were reared and instructed under the supervision of tutors.

[Col. 1342A] WINNOWING SHOVEL (*PALA*), an implement with which grain is winnowed and cleaned. II, 103 C, “This is that shovel which even now cleanses the Lord’s threshing floor.”

CLOAKED (*PALLIATUS*). II, 1049 A, “Cloaked discourse,” that is, philosophical and Christian discourse.

PALLIUM. II, 1031 B, “Of the now rounded pallium,” etc. You have exchanged your square cloak for a rounded cloak—that is, the Roman toga. Salmasius adduced as a witness particularly suited to this interpretation the ancient scholiast on Persius, who says that the toga is an unadorned pallium of rounded shape, with a broader and flowing fold.

STAKE (*PALUS*). II, 969 B, “But again you fix boundary stakes for God.” Writers on the regulation of boundaries teach that in certain regions stakes of holm oak, olive wood, and so forth were set up as boundary markers.

*PANGAPIPAN NIRAPIAM*. II, 563 A. The sense of this passage is perhaps: “Which miscellaneous work of Ptolemy would more properly have been called, after certain Attic *Curae*, a *Pankarpon* or *The Whole* (πάγκαρπον ἢ τὸ πᾶν).” [The lemma is textually corrupt.] By “Attic *Curae*” he means Greek books which, because their titles were devised with ambitious cleverness of this kind, were deservedly mocked in Pliny’s preface addressed to Vespasian. Πάγκαρπον means fruits of every kind. See Gellius, book XX, final chapter.

[Col. 1342B] BREAD (*PANIS*). II, 461 A, “Why, however, does he call bread his body?” I, 1160 A, “Then because his body is also reckoned to be in the bread.” II, 262 A, “Nor the bread by which he represents his own body.” II, 274 A, “Over another’s bread he performs thanksgiving to another God.” II, 370 B, “Behold, he first offers the bread of his teaching to the Israelites.” II, 80 A, “We suffer with distress if any portion even of our cup or bread falls to the ground.” II, 489 A, “Accordingly, we have already established in the Gospel the sacraments of the bread and the cup,” etc.

PAPA. II, 103 C, “Good shepherd and blessed papa,” that is, father—an appellation already at that time honorifically attributed to God’s devout servants and the ministers of the Church.

TENT (*PAPILIO*). I, 624 A, “But concerning tents spread out and tied down.” Tents and pavilions are spread out from their rolled-up state when erected in camp, and they are tied and fastened by ropes to stakes driven into the ground [Col. 1342C] so that they do not collapse when disturbed by the wind.

EQUAL (*PAR*). II, 204 A, “Equally” (*ex pari*), ἐξ ἴσου—that is, equally and alike. II, 398 A, “As one made equal to the law of my will,” that is, as though it were within my power to do whatever might be in my will and mind. II, 920 B, “And had provided for him”—Adam—“a necessary equal.” II, 107 C, “Which even amid evils is a corresponding good,” that is, the combination of good with evil, so that good and evil appear to make an equal pair in the same matter. Thus Festus says that the ancients fought “with matched horses,” meaning with two horses in a team.

PARACLETE. II, 156 A, “He put the Paraclete to flight,” that is, the spirit who is the author of special revelations. Montanus, if others are to be believed, proclaimed that a greater fullness of the Spirit dwelt in him than in the Apostles. But Baronius already observed that the school of Montanus remained harmless for some time and had disciples so commendable for holiness of conduct and so steadfast in martyrdom that nowhere else did anyone recognize more immediate powers of the divine presence. Indeed, that most learned cardinal rightly judged that Anicetus, then Roman pontiff, recognized these gifts of the divine Spirit in people who did not yet dissent in any respect from the rule of faith, granted peace to their churches, and, as Tertullian says, sent letters of peace. Praxeas, therefore, as Tertullian depicts him, did not cease from burdening Montanus’s disciples before the pontiff with fabricated charges—and even with accusations diminishing pontifical authority—until the already issued letters of peace or communion were recalled. Perhaps, then, some who were more than reasonably offended and indignant began to exalt and proclaim their Montanus to such a degree that they said that the Apostles indeed had possessed the Holy Spirit, but had not possessed the Paraclete; that this Paraclete of theirs had said more through Montanus than in Christ’s Gospel, and not merely more, but also better and greater things. We read these things concerning those called Cataphrygians in the *Catalogue of Heretics* customarily appended to Tertullian’s book *On Prescription against Heretics*. These reports sufficiently show that those Phrygians [Col. 1343A] attributed to their Montanus many things that he himself had never claimed. It thus becomes probable that Tertullian held Montanus’s doctrine as it originally was—indeed acceptable in its beginning to the more austere Christians—but not as it later became, when, embellished with Phrygian embroidery by the impostures and deceits of certain followers, it began everywhere to be spurned by the catholic Churches.

PARADISE. II, 856 A. “Namely, destined to lodge in paradise, not in the lower regions”; see LOWER REGIONS.

PREPARATION (*PARATURA*), constitution. I, 409 A, “To discern constitutions.” The sense of the whole passage is: beings dwelling and having their abode in the air, close to the stars and accustomed to the clouds, can know the constitution of the air and thus predict rains, drought, pestilence, and famine. I, 433 A, “That spirit belonging to the constitution of demons and angels.” I, 519 A, “This newly introduced preparation.” La Cerda understands the new sect of the Christians; Havercamp, more correctly with Rhenanus, the New Testament. II, 908 B, “According to the constitution of each Testament.” II, 570 B, “Into the corporeal constitution of matter.” II, 259 B, “He provided no preparation for himself by which he might be recognized,” that is, an adornment or outstanding element of creation through which he might be recognized by what was, as it were, his own apparatus and peculiar glory. [Col. 1343B] II, 284 C, “Thus one builds who lacks his own preparation,” that is, material made ready for building. II, 321 C, “To such an extent he lacked preparation that it could be believed.” II, 361 A, “Every thought and every preparation,” that is, every subject matter and apparatus of arguments. II, 906 B; 907 A, “But only those who are manifestly prepared parade their entire womanhood,” that is, they walk with uncovered heads, the principal part of manifest feminine preparation, which women customarily cover. II, 937 B, “So that we may discuss in order the whole of our preparation”: he means the writings of both Testaments. II, 769 A, “I must strike them back with their own preparation.” II, 723 B, “In these”—food and drink—“lies most of the preparation for sleep.” II, 77 A, “Shod with the preparation of the Gospel.”

ATTENDANT SPIRITS (*PAREDRI*) are evil spirits, wicked toward humankind, who

TO SPARE (*PARCERE*). I, 1283 B, “Since most pagan women spare the memory of their dearest husbands,” that is, [Col. 1343C] preserve it inviolate—namely, by abstaining from remarriage. are always in attendance upon someone and are familiar with him, II, 698 B.

TO PERFORM FUNERAL RITES (*PARENTARE*), to celebrate the due rites for parents. II, 927 B, “Perhaps those who perform funeral rites for him.” II, 795 B, “They perform funeral rites for the dead.” Pagans indeed did this, but Augustine establishes that Christians too in some places in his time repeatedly did so, in *City of God* VIII, chapter 27. They brought their meals to the memorials of the martyrs, prayed and made offerings so that they might eat, or even distributed some of the food to the needy. This practice, he says, is not followed by better Christians, and in most regions no such custom exists.

TO DISCHARGE (*PARERE*). II, 807 A, “Which can discharge so great a debt before Christ the Lord,” that is, render and pay so great a debt. A debtor obeys the summons of his creditor when he gives satisfaction. The one who demands commands; the one who provides what he promised obeys. II, 813 B, “Furthermore, to present the whole human being as a concretion of both substances,” that is, to make him present and produce him. I, 639 C, “Before these, three altars stand ready for three gods,” that is, they are at hand. I, 1203 A, “He made it present even in its own sacraments.” II, 654 B, “And his efforts are present externally, outside,” that is, they appear and are visible. [Col. 1343D] II, 191 C, “Such distinct proofs of each substance would not be presented”—that is, would not appear, in a forensic sense. II, 263 A, “How did the Lord appear from him in this world?”—that is, ὤφθη, ἐπεφάνη (“was seen,” “was manifested”): if the Lord could not exist here in substance, how could he exist in the appearance of substance?

TO MAKE EQUAL (*PARIARE*). II, 433 E, “Than one to whom they have made him equal in all respects.” II, 802 C, “He did not regard being equal to God as robbery,” τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ (“to be equal to God”). *Pariari* is a forensic term meaning “to become equal,” while *pariare* means “to make equal” or “to equate.” II, 700 C, “Because this supply would not have matched it,” that is, would not have made itself equal or corresponded to it on equal terms. II, 705 A, “Their natural qualities correspond; their substantial qualities do not.”

EQUALITY (*PARILITAS*). II, 252 B, “By this very fact supplying testimony to their equality and unity.” II, 804 A, “Moreover, is an example composed from diversity or from equality?”

EQUALLY (*PARITER*). I, 386 A, “He is equally of age,” a Hellenism: τὴν ἡλικίαν ἴσα ἐστί (“he is equal in age”).

[Col. 1344A] SMALL SHIELD (*PARMULA*). I, 321 A, “Blood caught in a small shield from the slashed thigh.” In Gorlaeus’s *Dactyliotheca*, volume II, no. 664, there is an engraving of a gem in which a small shield, or *parmula*, leans against Bellona’s altar and is intended to catch the blood. But it is also evident from the gem in Leonardo Agostini I, 171 that a small palm-shaped vessel (*palmula*), which others substitute in the text, was used in these rites. There a naked priest of Bellona is seen piercing his side with the blade held in his left hand and raising before Bellona’s image his right hand filled with the gore flowing from his slashed thigh.

PARRICIDE (*PARRICIDIUM*). I, 1282 B, “They are assaulted by abortive parricides, the conception being dissolved by drugs.” Similarly, in the book *On the Veiling of Virgins*, “infants fought down for some time by their mothers.”

PARTNER (*PARTIARIUS*). II, 274 B, “A partner in destruction.” II, 343 A, “Learn here also, together with the Jews who share your error.” II, 796 B, “Partners in their opinion,” κοινωνούς.

PASTURE (*PASCUA*), food. I, 407 A, “Which is a more carefully attended pasture for them,” that is, the food for which they have greater concern.

IN A SUFFERING MANNER (*PASSIBILITER*). II, 726 A, “How emotionally, anxiously, and sufferingly,”

[Col. 1344B] PASSION (*PASSIO*). II, 1010 B, “And of the one inviting to a passion contrary to flight.” II, 905 B, “The passion of marriage.” I, 842 A, “The things proclaimed concerning the passion of the kingdom, judgment, and resurrection.”

PASSIBLE (*PASSIONALIS*). I, 612 A, “For if God is angry, they say, he is corruptible and passible.”

INDISCRIMINATELY (*PASSIVE*), everywhere, in common, according to each person’s discretion. II, 956 A, “Yet let them circulate indiscriminately.”

PROMISCUITY (*PASSIVITAS*), indiscriminate frequency. II, 1044 A, “How many freedmen promiscuity brings forward for censure.” I, 325 A, “The promiscuity of luxury is a wandering Venus, roaming everywhere through lawful and unlawful things.” II, 234 B, “And it is not promiscuity,” that is, an affection flowing abroad indiscriminately and exposed to movements—dissolution and confusion. II, 585 B, “Concerning the promiscuity of life,” that is, a disorderly life spent according to lust, for which Irenaeus attests that the Valentinians were notorious. II, 397 C, “He permitted the promiscuity of my opinion,” that is, a common and indiscriminate principle, free to embrace any opinions whatsoever. II, 652 B, “They sometimes also possess intercourse of promiscuity,” [Col. 1344C] that is, the right of moving and passing back and forth indiscriminately, so that one is taken promiscuously in place of the other. II, 726 B, “And scattering all things in promiscuity,” that is, in the indiscriminate confusion and disturbance of things. II, 88 A, “Because promiscuity deceives,” that is, common usage, which prevails everywhere, deceives, so that corruption cannot be distinguished from the original condition, being in some fashion overshadowed and concealed by the indiscriminate use of everything.

PROMISCUOUSLY (*PASSIVITUS*), everywhere, commonly and indiscriminately among everyone. II, 1039 B, “Some, however, are promiscuously useful to everyone.”

COMMON (*PASSIVUS*), occurring everywhere, ordinary. II, 548 A, “Not with contrived leaders of common disciples.” II, 252 A, “An indiscriminate mode of life, of course.” I, 1277 B, “Through the permission then universally available,” that is, multiple marriages permitted everywhere. II, 936 B, “For your source in that passage is not indiscriminate,” that is, it is not wandering or unlimited, to be applied indiscriminately by you from any portion of Abraham’s history. II, 791 B, “Another common to all the others”—that is, ignoble, ordinary, shared. II, 985 A, “Without indiscriminate permission.”

[Col. 1344D] *PATAGIUM*, a golden stripe commonly sewn onto the upper part of a tunic. For married women it was called a *patagium*, and for men a *clavus*. II, 1036 B, “More gilded with a *patagium*.”

FATHER OF SACRED RITES (*PATER SACRORUM*), ἱεροφάντης (“hierophant”). See Meursius, *Eleusinia*, chapter XIII. I, 313 A.

**PATI** (“to undergo,” “to experience”), used of both favorable and adverse things, like the Greek πάσχειν. I, 376 B: “He experiences his own health.” I, 413 A: “Those who are thought to be affected by God,” that is, to be inspired or stirred; a circumlocution for τῶν ἐνθέων ἢ θεολήπτων, “the divinely inspired or God-possessed,” of whom three kinds are listed below: θεοφορούμενοι, “God-borne”; θεοπάρακτοι, “God-impelled”; and θεοπρόποι, “diviners.” II, 248 B: “The unhappy man experienced the impulse of this presumption.” II, 285 A: “But now it causes trouble,” that is, the rashness and audacity of the Marcionites—who fabricated for themselves another god distinct from the Almighty—causes trouble for God. II, 888 B: “Having now undergone the particular business of my opinion,” that is, “I who had previously been occupied in setting forth my opinion in Greek concerning the veiling of virgins”: Junius explains it thus. But Rigault thinks that, in some disputation [Col. 1345A] against the Greeks, when he had perhaps asserted rather vehemently that virgins also ought to be veiled, he was met with abuse from the Greeks and assailed as a heretic. II, 895 A: “Who has experienced a husband.” II, 904 B: “And to undergo marriage.” II, 652 B: “After the determination of the census, it undergoes the question of status.” II, 706 A: “Because a banquet undergoes funeral rites,” that is, because it is brought to the banquet, not to the tomb; expended upon the dinner, not upon the funeral.

**PATROCINIUM** (“patronage,” “support”). II, 543 A: “By the support of the compressed figure he conceals the sacrilege,” that is, in defense and confirmation of that shameful figure, made from compressed wool by felt-work; for this reason they put forward the venerable name of nature. See **CONVITIUM**. II, 668 A: “Of which I understand the mind to be the instrument, not the patronage,” that is, the governing faculty, as he called it at the beginning of the chapter.

**PATRUITUS.** II, 562 B: “And a discourse concerning paternal-uncle derivatives.” Irenaeus: πατρωνυμικός, “patronymic.” Junius prefers *de patritis*, “concerning paternal things,” as Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I, 19: “that philosophy inherited from father and grandfather.”

**PAUPERTINUS**, the same as *pauper*, “poor.” II, 262 A: “Because of [Col. 1345B] whom, into these impoverished elements.”

**PECCATELA** (“petty sin”). II, 719 A: “For persuading or commanding a petty sin.”

**PECTEN** (“comb”). II, 545 B: “The towers of Lamia and the combs of the sun.” These were children’s tales current at Carthage in Tertullian’s time, with which nurses restrained their little children from crying.

**PECUS** (“creature,” “animal”). II, 411 B: “Not called a creature after the figure,” that is, first a living, sentient body, newly furnished with its own form. Julius Firmicus uses the same word, book VII, chapter 1: “The creature, cut limb by limb within the mother’s womb, will be brought forth by physicians.” II, 486 A: “Through the likeness of the saving blood and of Christ’s sacrificial animal.” He alludes to the blood of the paschal lamb that was sprinkled upon the doorposts in Egypt. Exodus XII.

**PEJOR** (“worse”). I, 1300 A: “Because the Christian name pleases only the worse sort.” Tertullian says that things offensive to God are introduced by evil, and that this is made evident by the fact that, among the Gentiles, those especially who are of worse and more shameful life seek marriage with Christian women. Accordingly, pagans are found who do not shrink from such women—that is, Christians—so that they may destroy them, carry them off, and shut them out from the faith.

**PELLICEUS** (“of skin,” “leathern”). II, 578 A: “Meanwhile, they say that a fleshly surface was afterward woven over the earthy man, and that this is the tunic of skin, subject to sensation.” I, 1305 B: “And do you intend to adorn yourself over your tunics of skin?” II, 803 B: “For neither, as some maintain, were those tunics of skin which Adam,” etc.

**PELLITUS**, “clothed with skin.” II, 1038 A: “Clothed in skin, he is given to the world as one is given to the mines.”

**PENDERE** (“to remain pending”). II, 450 B: “Or from the recent Augustan census records, perhaps still pending at that time.” “At that time,” namely, when the blind man said: “Jesus, Son of David.” “Pending,” namely, the census tablets. Evidently censuses seem to have been conducted more than once under Augustus. And Septimius himself, in the book *Against the Jews*, appears to doubt whether Christ was enrolled in the census immediately upon his birth. II, 819 A: “One edict of God, I think, hangs before all men: the resurrection [Col. 1345D] of the dead.” Thus he calls the creed of the Christian faith; and above he said that this matter had been posted under a heading, alluding to the praetors’ edicts, which were customarily inscribed and displayed on the *album*, that is, a tablet. I, 648 B: “Then they depend upon the sign of the year.”

**PENDULUS** (“suspended,” “uncertain”). II, 708 A: “So that the concern of faith may be tested by suspenseful expectation.”

**PENES**, “among,” “in.” I, 314 B: “Infants are sacrificed to Saturn in Africa.”

**PENSUM**, the portion of work to be completed on any given day. II, 247 A: “They accomplish their allotted task with axes.”

**PENULA** (“cloak”). II, 76 B: “There the exceedingly burdened man laid aside his cloaks, beginning to be relieved.” It is established that cloaks were disliked because of their weight. Hence Septimius, taking occasion from this, says that that soldier, glorious in God, after laying aside the exceedingly heavy burden of pagan military service, then began to be relieved, as soon as he undertook Christ’s burden—which Christ himself taught to be light.

[Col. 1346A] **PEPO** (“melon,” figuratively “blockhead”). II, 702 B: “Why not rather so insipid a melon?” From proverbial usage it denotes an insipid person. II, 461 A: “But why does he call bread his body, and not rather the melon which Marcion had in place of a heart?”

**PER.** I, 403 B: “Through him and in him,” that is, according to his teaching and the religion instituted by God.

**PERDITRIX** (“destroying,” “ruinous”). II, 929 A: “After lust, the devil discovered even a ruinous chastity.”

**PERDOCERE** (“to teach thoroughly”). II, 546 A: “But neither do they teach thoroughly all whom they instruct.”

**PERDUCTOR** (“seducer,” “procurer”). I, 495 A: “First will come pimps, procurers, and brothel-attendants.” Procurers differ from pimps in that the latter bring willing women to someone, while the former drag unwilling women to him.

**PEREGRINARI** (“to travel abroad”). I, 388 A: “We must travel through the histories and literature of the world.” He conveys the delay and time spent in investigating the origins of other nations, while we travel in mind, not in body.

[Col. 1346B] **PEREMPTORIUS** (“peremptory,” “final”). II, 980 C: “I hear that an edict has also been posted, and indeed a peremptory one.”

**PEREMPTRIX** (“destroying”). II, 721 A: “Death, the destroyer of sensation.”

**PERENNARE** (“to endure perpetually”). II, 855 A: “But teeth also endure incorrupt.” I, 1233 B: “And it endures in the leaves,” that is, lasts perpetually.

**PERGULA** (“projecting gallery”). II, 550 B: “With gallery upon gallery built above.” *Pergulae* are στενὰ οἰκήματα, “narrow dwellings,” as the Glossary explains: narrow upper rooms projecting beyond the houses and extending outward by some portion of themselves, chiefly intended to provide convenient passage from one part of a house to another. Thus Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXI, chapter 3.

**PERICLITARI**, “to come near,” “to be not far from,” like the Greek κινδυνεύειν. II, 216 B: “And it does not come near being thought to have been made from something,” that is, it is not close to being thought to have arisen from something, etc. II, 77 A: “Finally, they mutter that so good and long a peace is in danger for them,” etc. The deed of this most courageous soldier was censured even by his Christian fellow-soldiers as an example of imprudent, headlong, and untimely courage. Reports circulated about him as a rash and reckless man eager to die, who, when questioned about his attire, had brought ill repute upon the Christian name and created danger, and by his rashness had come close to overthrowing the good and long peace which Christians then enjoyed. Septimius severely rebukes these words: “They mutter,” he says, “that so good and long a peace is being endangered for them.... [Col. 1346C] Nor do I doubt that some also mutter that the sacred Scriptures are already emigrating, unpacking their baggage, and preparing for flight from city to city.” The common text reads: “Nor do I doubt that certain Scriptures are emigrating”; but the oldest manuscript has: “Nor do I doubt that certain men the Scriptures are emigrating,” and the verb must be repeated from the preceding: “Nor do I doubt that certain men mutter the Scriptures,” etc.

**PERICULUM** (“danger,” “loss”). II, 174 A: “Without danger to the light,” that is, without loss.

**PERISCELIUM** (“anklet”) is a soft and ostentatious ornament of the legs. I, 1332 A. Juvenal calls it *pariscelis*.

**PERMOVERE** (“to disturb”). I, 1317 B: “Certainly they disturb scandal even by the spirit.” Rigault very correctly reads: “They disturb the spirit by scandal,” that is, they shake and disquiet it. For the saints possess the Spirit of God. Therefore, if they admit anything from evil, they disturb God’s Spirit; for the sake of a worldly thing they shake the spirit which they received from the Lord.

**PERONES**, rustic shoes suitable against snow, rain, and cold, made of rawhide and extending very high. II, 1046 B: “The rawhide shoes are called effeminate,” because luxury had rendered them effeminate. I, 1312 A: “And they desire to plunge pearls into the mud with rawhide shoes.” Pliny, book IX, chapter 35.

**PERPES**, “perpetual,” “continuous.” I, 378 A: “Into a fire equally perpetual and unbroken.”

**PERPETRABILIS** (“accomplishable”). I, 1289 B: “But how much more practicable it is to marry in the Lord,” for *perpetrabilius*, “more practicable,” or “more accomplishable,” after Greek usage. But the word is used in a favorable sense, as at I, 1288 A: “They are accomplished with zeal”; for, according to Festus, *perpetrat* means that one carries a thing through and completes it.

[Col. 1347A] **PERSONA** (“person”). II, 391 A: “The person of the name,” that is, that person to whom this name belongs.

**PERSONALITER** (“personally”). II, 551 A: ὑποστατικῶς, “hypostatically,” in respect of an individual person.

**PERSTRINGERE** (“to graze,” “to strike lightly”). The Latins use it of a superficial wound, not one driven deep, and also of the grazing, as it were, of lightning when it does not shatter or burn. I, 489 B: “If some things strike us too.”

**PERTINAX** (“persistent”). I, 671 B: “O divine sentence, persistent all the way to earth,” that is, one that prevails everywhere with the utmost constancy and binds men even here on earth, so that from this same sentence they judge that astrologers must be expelled.

**PERTINENTIUS** (“more directly,” “more deeply”). II, 374 C: “Which he wished to be recognized more directly,” that is, more deeply, or as referring most nearly to Christ.

[Col. 1347B] **PERTRACTUS** (“protracted”). I, 1159 A: “As a certain protracted duration in the age,” that is, an enduring and perpetual continuance, a prolongation of the age, as though the Lord were drawing it out at length.

**PHILOSOPHARI** (“to philosophize,” “to interpret philosophically”). II, 861 A: “The lions of Mithras philosophize the mysteries of a dry and burning nature,” that is, they interpret by philosophical reasoning that the lions in the mystery of Mithras are signs of a dry and burning nature.

**PHILYBA** is the inner bark of the linden, cut into strips. II, 1038 B: “A *tenus philyrae* is a band or snare and bond made from linden bark.” *Tenus* and *taenia*, however, are Greek words.

**PHYSCON.** II, 1042 B: “More impure than Physcon.” A proverbial expression concerning a man who gorges himself on every kind of luxury and lust. Ptolemy Physcon was the seventh Egyptian king descended from Lagus. After ruling at Cyrene, he succeeded his deceased brother Euergetes. In addition to more than bestial lust and cruelty—the crimes are related by Justin, book XXXVIII—his fat belly and the deformity of his body and face made him more like a beast than a man. This ugliness was increased, as if deliberately—or rather through lack of restraint—by the fineness of his transparent garment. He received from the circumstance the infamous name *Physcon*, as though “pot-bellied” and “brothel-attendant,” because of his devotion to his abdomen.

[Col. 1347C] **PIGMENTUM** (“pigment,” “drug,” “spice”). I, 676 A: “Even for men, for medicinal drugs.” For pigments are also useful in medicine; hence apothecaries were called *pigmentarii*. Julius Firmicus, book VIII, chapter 17: “Whoever shall have been born under this star will be snake-charmers, or persons accustomed to procure wholesome remedies for men from prepared herbal drugs belonging to Venus.” They also called seasonings *pigmenta*. Cassian, *Conferences* XV, chapter 3: “The bodies of the dead, embalmed with fragrant spices, are laid away in higher cells.” So too, near the end of Exodus XXXVII, what the Septuagint calls ἔργον μυρεψοῦ, “the work of a perfumer,” is called “the work of a *pigmentarius*.”

**PIPIARE** (“to pipe,” “to whimper”). II, 568 A: “Achamoth whimpered forth the heavenly rains,” that is, poured them out while whimpering. *Pipum* or *pipulum* means the wailing cry and whimper of one who weeps—the cry of a weeper in the language of the Oscans, as Festus says. II, 952 B: “And whimpering infants.”

[Col. 1347D] **PLAGA** (“stroke”). II, 130 C, 131 A: “This stroke was countered.” The expression is taken from gladiators, who either evade an opponent’s thrust by swerving their body or receive it on a small shield, so that the attempt is frustrated.

**PLAGIATOR**, a kidnapper who carries off a free person or slave. II, 273 C: “Such a claimant would be condemned even in the secular court, much more a kidnapper.”

**PLAGULA** (“cloth,” “panel”). II, 342 A: “I have not sewn a new piece of cloth onto an old garment.” Turnebus, I, 25, calls the *plagula* “patches.” *Plagulae* are curtains and textiles with which litters and couches were hung or wrapped, as in Suetonius, *Titus*, chapter 10: “when the curtains of the litter had been drawn aside.” Nonius interprets *plagulae* as large linen cloths, a couch-cover, and a litter-sheet; hence at II, 382 C he calls the addition *plagulae*.

**PLANE**, “indeed,” “rather,” “correctly.” I, 405 A: “Indeed, from the good,” that is, rather, he had a demon, but one that dissuaded him from the good. *Planius*, “more easily,” II, 1044 A: “By which they are more easily given.”

[Col. 1348A] **PLANUS**, “impostor.” II, 329 B: “Whom they considered an impostor in signs and a rival in teachings.” Cicero also uses the word in *For Cluentius* 26. It also occurs twice in Pliny, XXXV, 10. II, 342 C: “Or rather some impostor.”

**PLASMATOR** (“molder,” “creator”). II, 599 A: “The molder of man.”

**PLAUSOR** (“applauder”). I, 458 A: “Accomplices or applauders of criminal factions,” that is, supporters, helpers, or at least persons wishing for the same thing.

**PLAUTIOR**, “better suited for applause.” II, 1039 A: “Whereby shells, with their mossy woolliness, grow more luxuriantly shaggy.”

**PLENITUDO** (“fullness”). I, 500 A: “From fullness of knowledge,” Greek ἐκ τῆς πληροφορίας, “from full assurance.” II, 39 B: “That the Apostles were ignorant of the fullness of preaching,” that is, did not possess the highest and most perfect knowledge of the whole of Christian doctrine. II, 202 A: “Because, by not possessing the whole, it does not enter into the fullness of the comparison.” II, 218 A: “I adore the fullness of Scripture.” I, 653 A: “And the fullness of discipline owed to it.”

**PLENIUS**, “more perfectly.” I, 377 B.

[Col. 1348B] **PLUMBATUS** (“weighted with lead”). I, 440 A: “To be in lead-weighted hands.” Lead-weighted hands are soldered to some support of lead, so that they do not easily slip or gape open. This was required especially in the bending of the arms and the extension of the hands.

**PLURIMUM**, adverbially, for “for the most part.” II, 311 B: “For the most part from recollection of the offense.” Terence, *Phormio*: “I shall proceed home, where the greater part is.”

**POENICUM**, for *Poenum*, “a Punic man.” II, 1032 A: “Lest a Punic man among Romans either blush or grieve.”

**POENITENTIA** (“penance,” “repentance”). II, 42 B: “With the condition of the penance granted to him,” namely, of penance. A bishop, or the Church, was said to “grant penance” in the sense of imposing penance and its rules. II, 200 C: “From his repentance I shall turn it back against him.” Perhaps *ex peniculo illius*, “from his brush,” should be read, for the author continues in the allegory drawn from painting. A *peniculus* is a painter’s instrument with which colors are applied. The meaning, therefore, is: “From [Col. 1348C] his brush I shall turn it back against him, and shall take colors and outlines from him.”

**ΠΟΛΙΤΕΥΜΑ** (“commonwealth,” “citizenship”). “This is ours: citizenship in heaven,” II, 355 C.

**POLLINCTOR**, νεκρόκομος, νεκρολείπτης, “an undertaker,” one who anoints and tends the bodies of the dead. I, 347 A: “From a soothsayer, an undertaker.” II, 136 C: “And an undertaker-priest,” concerning one who sacrifices human beings.

**POLUCIBILIS** (“sumptuous”). II, 978 A: “Unless more sumptuous in catering,” that is, more elegant, lavish, and opulent.

**POLLUCTUM.** Varro, book V of *The Latin Language*: “When offerings from merchandise have been presented to Hercules upon the altar, then it is *polluctum*.” A *pollucta* and *pollucibilis* dinner is opulent and splendid. *Pollucere* means to consecrate, to sacrifice with a sumptuous banquet. I, 474 A.

**POMA** (“fruits”). I, 1344 A: “For to this end I know the fruits of the sea.” Thus he calls shellfish, because they were designed not for ostentation but for flavor and food.

**PONERE** (“to stop,” “to end”). II, 721 A: “So that the subject matter may stop there,” that is, so that this discourse concerning the soul may end there.

[Col. 1348D] **PONTICUS**, that is, Marcion. II, 248 A.

**POMPATICUS** (“pompous,” “processional”). I, 1326 A: “Thus to advance in pompous procession.”

**POMPATUS** (“more pompous”). I, 638 B: “But the apparatus of the circus games is somewhat more pompous.”

**POPINA** (“cookshop,” “tavern”). II, 970 B: “It is certainly your practice to furnish cookshops in prisons for martyrs of uncertain standing.” Lucian: Συνεκάθευδον μετ’ αὐτοῦ διαφθείροντες τοὺς δεσμοφύλακας, εἶτα δεῖπνα ποικίλα εἰσεκομίζετο, “They slept there with him after bribing the prison guards; then meals of various kinds were brought in.”

**POPULARIA** was the name given in the theater to the seats of the people or commoners, as distinguished from those of the equestrian order. I, 635 A: “And the separation of the commoners’ seats along the slope.” In the same way, the *equestria* were the seats of the knights.

**POPULARITAS** (“the general public,” “public consensus”). II, 257 B: “Finally, the greater consensus of the human race,” that is, the agreement of the nations. “Public consciousness”: II, 97 A: “The duties, honors, solemnities, and popular observances of the world.” II, 700 A: “By a council for relieving the public multitude.”

**PORTA** (“gate”). II, 540 A: “Since they also institute the gates five years beforehand”—anastrophe: *portas ante*, “the gates before,” instead of *ante portas*, “before the gates.” He says that they train those who are to be initiated for five years before they enter the gates and are sealed when about to enter them. Scaliger thinks the text should read: “since they institute *epopts* five years beforehand,” that is, masters of ceremonies to train and supervise the initiands in advance. For in sacred rites the ἐπόπται ἢ ἔφοροι, “overseers or supervisors,” were those who had already spent the prescribed time in the office of μύσται, “initiates”; hence Aristophanes uses ἐποπτεύειν, “to become an epopt.” In the same passage, “so many sighs for the gates,” that is, the whole object which they had desired for so long.

[Col. 1349A] **PORTARE** (“to carry”). The Greeks also regularly use it in the sense of “to take away.” II, 373 A.

**PORTIO**, that is, “counterpart,” “like.” I, 293 A: “Nero’s counterpart in cruelty”; thus “a counterpart of the edict” means a similar edict. I, 326 A: “From some portion of seed.” Havercamp reads *sparsione*, “dispersal,” καταβολὴ σπέρματος, “depositing of seed.” Compare Hebrews XI, 11. II, 965 C: “Restricted drink is the counterpart of xerophagy”; that is, under this restricted form of drink, dry food is also signified.

**PORTIONALE** (“partial”) is opposed to *summale*, “total.” II, 226 A; 964 B: “For by the exception of certain foods, the fast is partial.” II, 894 C: “And the partial to the universal.”

**POSTERITAS** (“posteriority”), that which crept in afterward. The Schoolmen rather unusually call it *posterioritas*. II, 44 A: “Posteriority belongs to falsehood.” II, 48 A: “With that aforementioned rope of posteriority preceding,” that is, the order of succession by which, as though by a rope, one climbs up to the apostolic Churches. II, 197 B: “For brevity’s sake, we are accustomed to plead posteriority against heretics,” that is, that they introduce a doctrine later than the doctrine of truth. II, 157 A: “The very posteriority of all heretics will now prove it.”

**POSTREMUS** (“last”). I, 1316 A: “The very last of all.”

**POSTUMARE** (“to be later”). I, 387 A: “Even if they are later than Moses.” II, 858 B: “For every consummation and perfection, although later in order, anticipates in effect.”

**POSTUMATUS** (“later status”). II, 590 A. It is opposed to priority.

**POSTUMUS** (“later,” “subsequent”). II, 121 A: “Whatever is propagated from the posterior part of the body.” II, 938 A: “And it was being prepared as though a later offspring.”

[Col. 1349C] **POTESTAS** (“power,” “authority”). I, 437 A: “In view of the immediately effective authority,” that is, the authority which represents and exercises in the world the role of divine power and can exact punishment at once. II, 371 A: “Because his word was in power,” that is, it was powerful.

**POTESTATIVUS** (“possessing authority”). II, 215 A: “It takes precedence not only as ordering but also as authoritative.”

**PRAE.** I, 436 A: “At hand,” that is, readily available.

**PRAEBERE**, “to render,” “to represent.” II, 233 B: “You wish what is uncompounded to be represented by compounded things.”

**PRAEBIBERE** (“to drink beforehand”). II, 122 A: “For some will also, by making haste, drink protection beforehand; but,” etc.; that is, they fortify themselves in advance with antidotes, amulets, and φυλακτήριοις potionibus, “protective potions,” but their power is dissolved by sexual intercourse and rendered ineffective.

**PRAECERPERE**, “to taste.” II, 158 B: “If I have had a taste of both languages.”

**PRAECIPITARE**, “to strike down,” “to cast down,” used of crops and fruits that are cast down before their proper time and ripeness. I, 406 A: “Some hidden defect in the air strikes it down while in flower.” *Praecipere*, “to forestall,” “to anticipate”: I, 489 A: “He does not anticipate [Col. 1349D] the separation,” that is, God does not forestall, before the time of the eternal judgment, the separation between the good and the evil, in which judgment partly consists.

**PRAECOQUUS** (“premature,” “unripe”). II, 1031 B: “Prematurely Roman,” that is, by an early and overhasty assumption of Roman dress. Others read *Romana praecoqua*, “premature Roman things,” that is, made Roman through surrender by an early and hasty decision. II, 331 C: “Premature and, as it were, abortive Marcionites.” II, 429 A: “So premature—indeed, so bitter—a love.”

**PRAEDAMNARE**, that is, “to condemn.” I, 283 A: “The word alone condemns both the unknown thing and its author in advance.” I, 1260 B: “He always justifies the poor and condemns the rich.”

**PRAEESSE** (“to prevail”). I, 522 A: “As though every line of reasoning did not prevail,” that is, as though the entire force of the arguments by which the alternation of human souls and their transmigration into other bodies is established and defended did not bind all the more if it is affirmed that souls are recalled each to its own body.

**PRAEFARI** (“to speak beforehand”), used of prophets. I, 378 B: “Concerning the office of speaking beforehand.” Rhenanus reads “of prophesying.” But the former is more genuinely Latin among those for whom seers *fari*, “utter,” and *profari*, “speak forth,” everywhere, when they *praefari*, “speak beforehand.” I, 413 A: “They speak beforehand with panting,” concerning the preliminary utterance which they made precede their prophecy. Compare Numbers XXIV, 3, and Donatus on Terence, *Phormio* IV, scene 4, at the words: “The diviner forbade it.”

[Col. 1350A] **PRAEFORMARE**, “to train very thoroughly,” “to train beyond others.” I, 266 A–B: “For how greatly they are trained for evil.” But Heumann, with Havercamp, reads *reformantur*, “are reformed.”

**PRAEFUGERE** (“to escape beforehand”). II, 706 B: “But even if the soul should escape before the final sword,” that is, if perhaps amid the tearing of beasts the soul should depart from the body before being driven out by the final sword-stroke.

**PRAEGNATUS**, “advanced pregnancy,” pregnancy near childbirth. II, 649 A; 650 C: “The young woman’s pregnancy and childbirth, of course.” II, 754 C: “Both conception and advanced pregnancy.”

**PRAEJUDICARE** (“to prejudge,” “to establish beforehand”). I, 265 A: “They prejudge that it is so,” that is, although they wish to remain ignorant, nevertheless in that force which they inflict upon themselves so as to persist in their ignorance, a certain knowledge—a prejudgment, namely—is implicit: that those things could not be hated if they were known more fully. II, 157 A: “By which judgment has equally been given beforehand against all heresies.” *Praejudicare* often means to give or foreshadow a preliminary judgment. II, 659 A: “This condition of bodily property has already prejudged concerning the other accidents of corporeality,” that is, the condition of bodily property will now constitute a certain manifest judgment for judging the other accidents of corporeality.

[Col. 1350B] **PRAELATIO** (“preference,” “superiority”). II, 801 C: “And greater by a hand because of its superiority, lest it be compared with the whole.” I, 573 A: “Preference for one cannot exist without insult to the other.”

**PRAELATOR** (“one who prefers”). II, 984 B: “The same one who prefers mercy.”

**PRAELUDERE**, the same as *proludere*, “to skirmish beforehand,” which in military affairs is ἀκροβολίζεσθαι. II, 324 A: “I shall have made these preliminary skirmishes.”

**PRAELUMINARE** (“to illuminate beforehand”). II, 841 B: “The parable pre-illuminated by the commentator on the Gospel.”

**PRAEMEDITATORIUM**, προμελετητήριον, “a place for preliminary practice.” II, 960 C: “It becomes a rehearsal room for privies.”

**PRAEMITTERE** (“to send ahead”). II, 970 B: “Having already sent ahead the juice of his blood,” namely, sent ahead to God, toward whom he himself is already hastening in his entirety. Thus elsewhere he spoke of a wife “sent ahead” and children “sent ahead,” who had already departed from the world.

[Col. 1350C] **PRAEPARATURA** (“preparation”). II, 402 B: “In John he had performed the preparation of the Lord’s ways”: preparation, παρασκευασμός, ἑτοιμασία.

**PRAESCRIBERE** (“to plead an exception”). II, 197 B: “For brevity’s sake, we are accustomed to plead posteriority against heretics.” II, 158 B: “Yet not on that account to plead an exception against the monarchy,” etc. II, 130 B: “An exception is pleaded against me, forbidding me to call any other God.” II, 256 A: “Pleading that God could not even have been unknown,” that is, by answering the opponents’ objections and refuting them. II, 888 B: “That truth requires this, against which no one can plead an exception,” that is, from which nothing can be detracted by any argument. II, 948 A: “Plead steadfastly that things commanded to certain persons are not commanded to all.” II, 849 A: “He prescribes everything,” that is, he comprehends everything within prescribed definitions. I, 307 A: “An exception is pleaded against you on the basis of your concealment.” I, 170 C: “See, therefore, how many things they prescribe for you.”

**PRAESCRIPTIO** (“legal exception,” “preliminary plea”). In forensic usage it signifies a refutation by which the defendant overturns his adversary’s accusation or turns it back upon him. Compare *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 35. He calls it “the prescription against heretics,” because we plead against the heretics on the very ground that they are heretics. Against them we oppose this single exception: that they bring forward doctrines contrary to the rule; and thus, as persons who ought not even to be heard, we exclude them from all disputation. II, 248 A: “Concerning the prescription of novelty.” II, 60 B: “To be repelled by definite, just, and necessary prescriptions.” He calls the prescriptions necessary because, in accordance with them, a judge must repel all who wish to bring an action. II, 157 B: “But with this prescription remaining intact”; for he had said before: “Whatever is first is true; whatever is later is adulterated.” II, 248 A: “Lest the summary method of prescription, invoked everywhere, be ascribed to lack of confidence.” By the “summary method of prescription” he means that thesis: “To such a degree is heresy,” etc.
