[Col. 1351A] **PRAESCRIPTIVE** (“by way of prescription”). II, 261 B: “Although it is so easy to meet it by way of prescription,” that is, by interposing a prescription through which I may exclude and destroy his entire action. What this prescription is, he shows in what follows.

**PRAESIDIUM** (“resources,” “property,” “private means”). I, 495 B: “Certainly with some resources.”

**PRAESIGNARE** (“to mark beforehand”). II, 260 A: “Which the Creator’s testimony had marked beforehand,” that is, had displayed a sign by which it might be recognized.

**PRAESPERARE** (“to hope for beforehand”). II, 513 A: “Therefore, he who was foretold was also hoped for beforehand”; Greek προελπίζειν.

**PRAESTANTIA** (“rendering,” “bestowal”). II, 302 B: “And the bestowal made on account of those who deserve it,” namely, by which he bestows rewards or punishments. II, 432 C: “Another commands them to remain secure concerning his performance.” In a bad sense: I, 1233 B: “For I recognize my own performance in sins.” II, 650 B: “But let the ambition for either superiority look to itself,” that is, φιλοπρωτεία, “love of preeminence.”

**PRAESTARE** (“to be preferable”). II, 281 C: “For whom it would be preferable to exist by cutting.” The meaning is: for which holiness it would be preferable—that is, more useful and desirable—to exist “by cutting,” that is, to be equal to marriage by cutting and excising it. “It would go better with us,” he says, “if ours were a holiness that led us to abolish marriage and made us exempt from marriage.”

[Col. 1351B] **PRAESTRUCTIM**, “by a prepared and fortified route.” II, 1038 A: “So that one might reach man by a prepared route.”

**PRAESUMERE**, “to suppose,” ὑπολαμβάνειν. I, 274 A: “Since you presume our crimes from the confession of the name.” I, 1317 B: “Wishing that it should continue in us, yet not presuming it.”

**PRAESUMPTIO** (“presumption,” “confidence”). II, 993 B: “When I have thus also overthrown the presumption of the opposing side.” I, 1237 A: “The presumption of baptism entails it,” that is, confidence that pardon will be obtained through baptism.

**PRAESUMPTORIE** (“presumptuously”). II, 462 B: “For Peter too uttered something presumptuously,” that is, with overconfident presumption.

**PRAETENDERE** (“to extend before,” “to put forward”). II, 619 B; 620 C, note 10: “And Judah extends before Israel”; *Jerusalem* should be read, from Zechariah XIV, [Col. 1351C] 14. *Praetendere* means to stretch before or opposite, or even in a circuit, as is explained in the following clause. II, 272 B: “I put forward another rule against him,” that is, I use another argument against him and unfold the rule of truth to him. II, 927 A: “We put forward the necessities of auxiliary means.” II, 80 A: “Tradition will be put before you as author.”

**PRAETER.** II, 572 A: *praeter haereticorum*, “except that of the heretics”; Greek πλήν, “except.” The heretics claimed the spiritual race for themselves. II, 169 C: “Except one God.”

**PRAETERESSE**, “to abstain,” “to renounce.” I, 466 A: “Since we also abstain from the very things concerning which they are conducted,” that is, since, moved by the conscience of our religion, we abstain from the very superstitions—or frenzy, lust, and cruelty—for the sake of which spectacles are conducted.

**PRAETRACTATUS** (“preliminary treatment”). II, 107 A: “And to determine it from this very preliminary treatment.”

**PRAEVELLERE** (“to tear away beforehand”). II, 150 A: “What does he tear away from it more effectively than martyrdoms?” Wherever God tears men away from idolatry, what does he tear away more effectively from idolatry, so as immediately to oppose what has been torn away to idolatry itself, than the martyrdoms of courageous Christians?

[Col. 1351D] **PRAEVENIRE** (“to anticipate”). II, 23 A: “He anticipates condemning.” A Hellenism. II, 312 B: “Therefore I fled beforehand to Tarshish.”

**PRAEVENTO.** II, 23 A. For this Latinius more correctly reads *praeverto*, and Rigault *praevenio*; both correspond to the Greek φθάνειν, “to anticipate.”

**PRAEVERTERE**, “to place before,” “to prefer.” II, 1045 B, as often in Plautus. II, 1028 B: “Who prefers the sinner’s repentance to his death.”

**PREMERE** (“to thresh”). II, 586 A: “He will have threshed the whole mass of his seed.”

**PRESSUS** (“deep,” “concentrated”). II, 1036 B: Purple is called *pressa* when it shines more purely and intensely, possessing the color of pressed and congealed blood and appearing blackish. II, 59 A: “More compelling testimonies.”

**PRINCIPALITAS** (“priority”), that which existed from the very beginning; the Schoolmen call it “priorness.” II, 44 A: “Toward the priority [Col. 1352A] of truth.” II, 668 A: “You have the priority of the soul.”

**PRIORATUS**, πρωτεῖον, “first place,” “primacy.” II, 546 B: “As minds are accustomed to be aroused by rivalry for first place.”

**PRISTINUS** (“former”). II, 970 B: “Which not even that Pristinus of yours, the non-Christian martyr, had attained.” Rigault thinks the text should read *pristinum vester*, “your former man,” that is, “one formerly yours,” just as at the beginning of the book *Against Praxeas* he said “a former teacher.” Many details in the story Septimius tells fit what Lucian relates concerning Peregrinus. For Lucian reports that Peregrinus too enjoyed reputation and esteem among the Christians for a time; that because of discourses about Christ which he delivered through the towns of Syria, he was arrested and cast into prison; and that there he was tended with the utmost care through the charity and devotion of the Christians, with meals of every kind brought in, and was soon afterward released from prison through the governor’s clemency. Later, however, he was expelled from Christian fellowship because of certain offenses, wandered through various cities practicing philosophy not without glory, and finally at Athens, driven by a mad craving for fame, summoned a crowd and, after delivering a lengthy discourse on contempt for death, leapt into a burning pyre and was seen no more. Septimius says that this martyr, whatever sort of man he was, was a “psychic,” that is, a Catholic, but not a Christian, because under torture he had denied Christ. Lucian writes that his Peregrinus was cast into prison because he worshiped Christ, τὸν μέγαν ἐκεῖνον ἄνθρωπον ἐν Παλαιστίνῃ ἀνασκολοπισθέντα, “that great man who was crucified in Palestine”; that the Christians immediately ran to him as to a brother and supplied every kind of consolation; and indeed that, after bribing the guards, they remained with him in prison and spent the night there.

[Col. 1352B] **PRO.** II, 1044 B: “The punishment was as for rape,” that is, the same punishment applied to so shameful a degradation as to rape.

**PROBARE** (“to demonstrate”). II, 191 A: “When he wished himself to be demonstrated.” Irenaeus: ὅτε οὖν ἠθέλησεν ἐπιδεῖξαι αὐτόν, “when, therefore, he wished to display himself.” Irenaeus’s Latin translator renders it *ostendere*, “to show.”

**PROBOLA**, προβολή, “emanation.” II, 162 D: “Προβολήν, that is, the bringing forth of one thing from another.” II, 163 B: “This will be the emanation of truth,” that is, the true generation of the Son. II, 163 A: “Valentinus distinguishes his emanations.”

**PROBUS** (“sound,” “excellent”). II, 1033 A: “Sound through calmness,” that is, sound by virtue of tranquility—tranquil, so that no one can justly complain of it. Latinius proposes *pronum*, “inclined.”

[Col. 1352C] **PROCEDERE** means to attend sacred rites, to go to a temple. I, 1294 A: “If one must attend the rites.”

**PROCLIVARE** (“to incline,” “to lean”). II, 234 B: “They inclined more toward the other.”

**PROCURARE** (“to administer,” “to serve”). II, 576 B: “For whom all heresies are administered,” ᾧ ἅπασαι αἱρέσεις οἰκονομοῦνται, “for whom all heresies are managed,” in forensic usage. II, 158 C: “Because it is administered through so many thousands of powers,” namely, the monarchy. II, 961 A: “Whom riches themselves serve.” II, 277 A: “But rivalry serves the liberation of man.” II, 799 A: “Under the pretext of administering,” that is, ministering to the emperors.

**PRODICIA** (“female betrayer,” “informer”). I, 567 A: “See what sort of informer you have suborned against us.” Here he calls her *prodicia*, whom in the *Apology* he calls an *index*, “informer.”

**PRODIGERE** (“to squander,” “to consume”). I, 525 A: “He may have squandered it into nothing,” that is, even though they may have acted extravagantly and prodigally in destroying and dissipating the body. Others read *redegerit*, “reduced.” I, 378 A: “When almost all the Creator’s ages have already been spent,” that is, carried onward. II, 483 B: “When this age has been spent,” that is, consumed. I, 1245 A: “To be restored to a salvation squandered,” that is, shamefully lavished, cast away, and lost.

[Col. 1352D] **PRODUCERE**, properly, of metals, “to extend,” “to hammer out.” I, 301 A: “And silver-bearing metals hammered out into dishes.” II, 609 A: “By which he brought them out of the land of Egypt,” for “led out.” II, 908 B: “Religion did not bring them forward,” that is, does not cause them to come into the Church of God and join themselves to it. I, 614 B: “And for this purpose brought them out onto the arena.” Athletes and gladiators are properly said to be “brought forward” into spectacles by the sponsors themselves who present the games.

**PRODUX** (“product,” “offshoot”). II, 786 B: “And the product of mutual intercourse.” He says *produx* just as above he said *tradux*, “offshoot.” Thus he calls the unity produced by mutual intercourse the “product of mutual intercourse”; or rather, that which springs apart from the joining of both when things that had been closely joined are torn from one another.

[Col. 1353A] **PROFERRE** (“to bring forth”). II, 163 A: “Was the Word of God brought forth, or not?”

**PROFESSIO**, ἀπογραφή, “declaration” or “registration,” used of merchants who declare their goods. I, 494 A: “How much is lost to taxation through the fraud and falsehood of your declarations.” II, 469 B: “But his declaration is completed by the authority of another.”

**PROFESSOR** (“declarant”). II, 469 B: “No one is both his own declarant and his own witness.”

**PROFLIGARE**, “to complete the greater part of a thing.” II, 503 B: “By how much the little work is briefly brought near completion,” that is, the more nearly this book is completed and brought to its end. Thus Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* V, 6: “The question has now been brought near completion and almost carried to its conclusion.”

**PROINDE**, the same as *perinde*, “just so,” as often in Cicero.

**PROLATIO** (“continuation,” “duration”; also “bringing forth”). II, 24 A: “Every prolongation of seeking and finding.” II, 552 A: “It received the function of its own propagation,” that is, procreation. II, 172 D: “That I introduce some προβολή, that is, a bringing forth of one thing from another”; “some extension belonging to sublimity and brightness.”

[Col. 1353B] **PROMA**, ταμεῖον, “storehouse.” II, 297 B: “You have filled your storehouses.”

**PROMULGARE** (“to make public law and bring into public use”). I, 534 B: “Who first introduced cherries from Pontus into public use in Italy.”

**PROMULSIS** (“serving vessel,” “platter”). II, 1048 B: “A five-hundred-pound platter,” that is, a dish made from five hundred pounds of silver.

**PRONUS**, construed with the dative. II, 234 C: “Inclined neither to evil nor to good.”

**PROPE.** II, 1033 A: “You come near denying that it is the same,” that is, you are not far from denying that it is the same.

**PROPERABILIS** (“rapid,” “hastening”). II, 722 A: “With rapidly advancing heat.”

**PROPERATUM**, something issued too hastily, or begun prematurely and left rough. II, 246 B. See Jerome, commentary on Obadiah.

**PROPRIE** (“properly,” “independently”). II, 664 B: “Not because it is properly spirit,” that is, apart from the soul and in itself.

[Col. 1353C] **PROPUDIOSUS**, unchaste, shameless. II, 1042 B, “Lest they too mutter something about your Caesars, who were equally shameless.”

**PROSAPIA** means lineage or family. Ancient gloss: *prosapies*, γενους καταγωγή, “descent of a family.” *Prosapia*, ἐκ προγόνων εὐγένεια καὶ συγγένεια, “nobility and kinship derived from one’s ancestors.”

**PROSCRIBERE.** II, 668 A, “Yet each writer has prefixed a notice of the form of his work and the main heading of his subject concerning the soul.” II, 101 A, “Proclaimed King of the Jews upon the cross,” i.e. declared so by the placard affixed by the provincial governor. II, 1008 A, “But it is uncertain to whom, because neither the person nor the case is specified.”

**PROSECARE**, to offer to God in sacrifice. I, 503 A, “Among the Gauls, those of more advanced age are sacrificed to Mercury.” I, 316 A, “Yet at the very end he ordered a cock to be sacrificed to Aesculapius.”

**PROSPECTE**, with the greatest foresight. I, 304 A, “Even concerning your gods themselves, what your fathers had decreed with foresight.”

**PROSPECTUS.** II, 98 A, “According to the Apostle’s foresight,” [Col. 1353D] i.e. as the Apostle providently determined.

**PROSPER.** II, 1030 C, “So prosperous in respect of their times,” a Tertullianic phrase, as is the expression below, “distinguished in their lusts.”

**PROSPEX.** I, 616 A, “An augur in omens, foresighted in events,” i.e. provident, prudent.

**PROSPICERE.** I, 425 A, “If she foresaw that she should pass over to her avengers.” The sense is: Cybele rightly passed over to the Romans together with her worship because she knew that perhaps the avengers of Ilium would arise from them. But how could she foresee so distant a turn of fortune when she could not discern the few days remaining in Aurelius’s destiny? II, 150 A, “Through which it foresees her rather than through the passions,” *tois pathēmasi prooratai* (τοῖς παθήμασι προορᾶται), in a Greek construction.

**PROSPICIAE.** II, 580 A, “Their *prospiciae*.” Ciaconius reads *prosiciae*. Festus: “*Prosicium*: that which, after being cut off, is cast away.” The Glossary: *Prosiciae*, αἱ τῶν θυμάτων ἀπάρχαι, “the first offerings from sacrificial victims”; and elsewhere, *prosiciae*, ἀκροθίνια, “first fruits” or “choice spoils.”

**PROSTARE.** II, 709 B, “Helen, made cheaper by having stood [Col. 1354A] for sale under a placard in the final extremity of degradation,” i.e. she had been a prostitute in an archway or public brothel, whose public placard advertised her infamy by notice.

**PROSTITUERE.** I, 502 A, “To expose useless lamps at midday.” Haverkamp, with the other interpreters, says that the expression is emphatic: the scant light of lamps and torches is “prostituted” when set against the most brilliant rays of the noonday sun. I should prefer, however, to interpret it as “to display openly.” II, 891 C, “Either to be covered or exposed,” i.e. to be set openly on view with the covering removed and to proceed without a veil before everyone’s eyes. II, 912 A, “To expose the whole face.”

**PROSTITUTIO**, public display or establishment. I, 433 A, “Under the public display of images.”

**PROTELARE.** II, 409 C, “But he prolonged the lives of six hundred thousand persons,” i.e. he continued, extended, and protracted the tenure of life and strength for six hundred thousand human beings. I, 1233 B, “And will prolong it to the harbor of divine mercy,” i.e. will conduct it as far as a harbor, however distant. [Col. 1354B] I, 630 A, “So as to prolong even ignorance into an opportunity,” i.e. such is the power of pleasures that it does not wish its man to be taught that spectacles must be avoided by a Christian for as long as an opportunity to view them may still be hoped for.

**PROVOCARE.** II, 88 A, “Summoning it”—namely, the common possession of instruments—“to the distinction between rational and irrational things,” i.e. requiring that it be suitably and prudently divided into two classes: the rational, whose construction and use are joined with reason, and the irrational, whose whole refinement lies outside and contrary to reason itself.

**PROXIME**, very recently, at the nearest preceding time. I, 372 A.

**PSYCHICUS.** II, 156 A, “And the bond remains among the Psychics.” The Psychics are contrasted with the Pneumatics, i.e. the “spiritual,” just as he contrasts “psychic faith” with spiritual discipline in *On Fasting*, chapter 1. The Montanists, or Cataphrygians, were called “spiritual” by their own party because they arrogated to themselves spiritual revelations and “inspired” (*enthousiōdeis*, ἐνθουσιώδεις) prophecies. Those, however, who denied that these extraordinary prophecies and revelations were ordinary occurrences [Col. 1354C] in the Church were called “Psychics,” from 1 Corinthians 2. Tertullian, however, in some measure followed a certain middle path. For, like a Montanist, he acknowledged the Paraclete, i.e. the regular spirit of extraordinary prophecies and revelations; he rigorously urged fasts, compelled martyrdoms by forbidding flight during persecutions, and condemned second marriages. But he abstained from the Montanists’ rites and from those impious and more atrocious proclamations concerning Montanus and Prisca. Hence Augustine, in *On Heresies, to Quodvultdeus*, distinguished the Tertullians or Tertullianists from the Montanists, who were also called *Kataphryges* (κατάφρυγες). II, 953 B; 954 B, “The outer and inner sausages of the Psychics.” I, 532 A, “Concerning which there is a dispute between us and the Psychics.”

**PTISSANA**, πτισάνη, peeled barley. The Greeks drenched barley with water and, while it was swelling, exposed it to the sun; then they pounded it in a mortar with a wooden pestle until it shed its husk and chaff. I, 532 A, [Col. 1354D] “After the pattern of barley-groats,” i.e. like *ptissana*.

**PUBLICARE**, to bring into public view. II, 112 B, “For he who is not made public among men is made public in the Lord.”

**PUBLICATIO.** II, 892 B, “Every public exposure of a good virgin is the suffering of violation,” i.e. the uncovering of her head.

**PULSARE.** I, 391 A, “The same Spirit strikes,” i.e. filled the minds of the prophets with truth and impelled them to foretell the future. II, 796 A, “Having knocked at salvation, though without entering truth,” i.e. the Platonists, champions of the immortality of souls, knocked upon salvation’s door, but, since they did not enter truth, remained ignorant of the character and manner of immortality. I, 609 B, “Then the philosophers are obtuse, when they knock at the doors of truth.”

**PULVIS.** I, 1306 A, “And that very black powder.” “Black powder” is what the Greeks and Latins called *calliblepharum*: it was made from burned leaves of roses and palms, from *ampelitis*, and from other substances, and was used to extend the beginnings of the eyes. [Col. 1355A] Junius reads *exodia*, i.e. the ends and outlines are extended with pigment to beautify the face.

**PUMEX.** II, 1042 A, “With the pumice of a mirror,” i.e. with a mirror polished with pumice, exceedingly smooth and highly polished.

**PUNIRE.** I, 1270 B, “Against every apparatus for overthrowing or punishing the faith.” “For punishing the faith,” i.e. for exercising and testing it by punishments and torments.

**PURGARE.** II, 427 C, “Elsewhere I prefer to clear away,” i.e. to refute and remove: a metaphor from agriculture. I, 306 A, “That I may clear for myself a road to plainer matters.”

**PURGATRIX.** I, 1205 A, “She purified herself with cleansing water.”

**PURUS.** I, 700 B, “We sacrifice as God commanded, with pure prayer, without incense and without a victim.” So too I, 1244 A, “To know only pure food and drink,” i.e. to use bread and water alone, without any other foods or seasonings. So Juvenal: “Where kings observe the festal Sabbaths with a bare foot,” i.e. with an uncovered foot. Thus “with pure prayer” means by prayer alone and unadorned, proceeding [Col. 1355B] from a holy and innocent mind. The Gentiles offered lifeless things or brute beasts, incense or oxen, to false gods; Christians offer the true God a rational soul that speaks praises and thanks to God. Athenagoras expressly explains this in his *Embassy for the Christians* to Antoninus and Commodus, also citing Paul’s words, in which he describes the victim as θυσίαν ζῶσαν, ἁγίαν, εὐάρεστον τῷ θεῷ, τὴν λογικὴν λατρείαν ἡμῶν, “a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God—our rational worship.” Tertullian himself says in the *Apologeticum*: “I offer to God the best and greater victim, which he himself commanded: prayer proceeding from chaste flesh, an innocent soul, and the Holy Spirit.” And in book IV, chapter 1, *Against Marcion*, on the words of Malachi, “A pure offering is offered to my name”: “namely, simple prayer from a pure conscience.” And in chapter 9 he says that a person ought to offer a gift to God at the temple—namely, prayer and thanksgiving in the Church through Christ Jesus, the universal priest of the Father. Minucius Felix, after saying, “We have no temples or altars,” adds: “A good disposition, a pure mind, and a sincere judgment are an acceptable victim. These are our sacrifices; these are God’s sacred rites.” [Col. 1355C] Finally, Justin, *Against Trypho the Jew*, testifies that our Eucharist is performed with pure prayer, or prayer alone. (These passages are found in Rigaltius.) I, 1269 A, “Content with simple nourishment and a pure drink of water.”

**PUSILLITAS**, smallness. II, 210 A, “Whatever power belongs to it rather than smallness,” i.e. “rather,” or “more,” than smallness. A very frequent Greek ellipsis.

**PUTATIVUS**, that which does not truly exist. II, 335 A, “The supposed corporeality in Christ.” II, 335 C, “To have assigned him a supposed nativity,” as though he had not truly and actually been born. II, 754 C, “Who introduced a merely apparent flesh of Christ.”

**PYCTES**, πύκτης, boxer. II, 134 A, “The boxer himself does not complain.” II, 978 B, “Boxers grow strong through dry diets.”

**PYRIPHLEGETHON**, the fiery river of the underworld, where the punishment is οἰμωγὴ τῶν ἐπὶ τοῦ πυρὸς ὀπτωμένων, i.e. “the wailing of those roasting in the fire,” as Lucian says in the *Necyomantia*. I, 520 A.

## Q

[Col. 1355D]

**QUA**, because, insofar as. I, 441 A, “They know, inasmuch as they are human, who also gave them a soul,” i.e. because, or insofar as, they are human beings, they also know from whom they received their soul. Or thus: they know who gave them the soul by which, of course, they are human and differ from brute beasts. I, 483 A, “If in any way the fruits of trees attempt anything there,” i.e. “if in any manner,” just as *aliqua* in Virgil means “in some manner.”

**QUAESTIO.** II, 581 A, “In questions concerning prepositions,” i.e. in the subtle examination of prepositions; hence in what follows he expounds and demonstrates *ex*, *per*, and similar terms. But the author treated the matter more fully in *On Prescription*, chapter 49. II, 172 C, “If I do not resolve this point through questions drawn from the Old Scripture.” II, 187 C, “After Philip and the whole substance of that question.” II, 307 A, “To love questions,” i.e. to apply oneself with complete zeal to those holy inquiries of which Isaiah later says, Καὶ δεῦτε, διελεχθῶμεν, “Come now, and let us reason together.”

[Col. 1356A] **QUANTI**, for *quot* (“how many”), just as *tanti* stands for *tot* (“so many”). I, 266 A; 281 A, “For how many are predisposed toward evil.” II, 179 C, “How many things I shall prescribe for you,” i.e. how very many. II, 253 C, “How many worthless slaves insult royal names.”

**QUANTO.** II, 219 B, “How much more he does not supply one to whom they may be ascribed,” i.e. *quanto magis non comparat*. II, 626 A, “And how much more incredible,” with “more” understood. II, 503 A, “The nearer this little work is to being dispatched briefly,” i.e. the nearer this book is to being completed and brought to an end.

**QUANTUM**, as concerns, if one considers. I, 281 A, “So far as interpretation is concerned.” II, 232 B, “Insofar as he is properly a painter.”

**QUATENUS**, equivalent to “because.” II, 226 B, “Because this pertains only to bodies,” etc. II, 176 B, “Because the Scriptures so teach,” i.e. since, seeing that.

**QUI.** II, 236 B, “As some beauty does,” i.e. some particular beauty.

**QUICQUID**, for anything whatever, anything at all. II, 43 B, “Whatever he corrects under this name.”

[Col. 1356B] **QUINIO.** II, 656 A, “Even in the civil law there is found a certain Greek woman who gave birth to a set of five sons.” “In the civil law,” i.e. in the books of the jurists, which the ancient grammarians also commonly cite in this manner. Pliny, *Natural History*, book VII, chapter 3: “There is also found in the Peloponnese a woman who four times gave birth to five children, and the greater part of each entire delivery survived.” Aristotle: Ἀνὰ πέντε γὰρ ἔτεκε, καὶ τὰ πολλὰ αὐτῶν ἐξετράφη, “For she bore five at a time, and most of them were reared.” He does not, however, mention the Peloponnese. Strabo too, drawing on the same Aristotle, tells the story differently in book XV, and Gellius differently in book X. Finally, Aristotle himself recalls that he spoke about the same matter elsewhere, in a passage no longer extant. Gaius, book I, *On Fideicommissaries*, as cited in Law 3, *On Doubtful Matters*, and Julianus, I, 36, *On Payments*, relate precisely the same story about an Alexandrian woman that our Septimius here relates about a Greek woman.

**QUINQUATRIA.** I, 674 A, “What schoolmaster is without a tablet of the seven idols? Yet he will attend the Quinquatria.” The *Quinquatria* are the festival days sacred to Minerva, [Col. 1356C] on the first of which sacrifices were made to Minerva, on the following three public shows were held, and on the fifth, finally, a purification. Ovid, *Fasti* III:

> One day lies between, and Minerva’s rites are held,  
> Which take their name from five days joined together.

The first of these days fell in March, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April; the last was commonly called the *Tubilustria*. All were celebrated with gifts called *Minervalia*, especially those that beginners and novices in every discipline presented to their teachers. Ovid, in the same place:

> You too, who by Phoebus’s art drive illnesses away,  
> Bring a few gifts from your stores to the goddess.  
> Nor you, the crowd deprived of a fierce teacher’s fee,  
> Despise her: she attracts new pupils.

These, then, were the Greater Quinquatria. On the Lesser, see Varro, book V, *On the Latin Language*, and Festus. The meaning is that there is no schoolmaster who does not have in his school or classroom a tablet of the seven idols, that is, [Col. 1356D] of the seven planets—the Moon, Mars, Mercury, and the others—from which the days of every week take their names. Or, if anyone should be found without such a tablet, he would nevertheless attend the Quinquatria. It is not worth the effort to investigate more carefully what use schoolmasters made of this tablet or register of the seven days. Perhaps it stated or indicated what had to be assigned to or recited by pupils on each day. Juvenal, *Satire* VII:

> Nothing succeeds for the Arcadian youth, whose wretched head  
> Dread Hannibal fills for me every sixth day.

On that day, evidently, the total for the entire week was collected. On the seventh day there was rest and leisure. Tertullian himself, *To the Nations* I, chapter 13: “It is certainly you who have admitted the Sun into the register of seven days, and from those days have chosen that one in preference—the day on which you either omit the bath or defer it until evening, or take care to have leisure and a meal.”

[Col. 1357A] **QUISQUE**, for *quisquis*, “whoever.” II, 611 B, “Or whoever succeeded him in inheriting the kingdom.”

**QUO.** II, 216 A, “In that there too he through whom all things were made is revealed,” i.e. *quod*, “that.” II, 522 B, “Wherefore neither does the Apostle here,” i.e. “for which reason.” II, 518 B, “To what end, then, do you give me two gods?” i.e. to what purpose, for what reason?

**QUOMODO**, in whatever manner, or by whatever means. II, 471 B, “But in whatever manner the Marcionites wish to be believed.”

## R

**RANUNCULUS.** I, 659 A, “As though drippings of honey came from a poisonous little frog,” i.e. as if someone were to press honeycomb together with the lungs of a poisonous toad; for honey mixed with poison would then drip forth—honey indeed, but poisoned. Juvenal, *Satire* I:

> …who, about to offer her thirsty husband  
> Mild Calenian wine, mixes a toad into it.

**RAPERE.** I, 266 A, “Whom it seizes,” with “evil” understood, i.e. those who pursue evil and perverse things. I, 1203 A, “Since every underlying material must necessarily seize the quality of that which hangs over it from above.”

[Col. 1357B] **RATIO.** I, 278 A, “A certain principle of rival activity,” i.e. a certain being actively engaged in rivalry. This is understood of the devil, who envies Christ’s Church. I, 526 A, “What principle governs the universe,” etc.; by “principle” is to be understood the wisdom of the supreme God. II, 122 A, “After the manner of torture,” i.e. in the form of torture. II, 143 C, “A certain rational principle has commanded us to treat these things too as sport,” i.e. reason itself compels and commands us to mock those dreams and trifles.

**RATO.** II, 710 A, “For no one holds this life duly accounted for except when all the things that charge it have been settled,” i.e. no life is held valid and entered into the accounts unless it has discharged and completed everything pertaining to the conduct of life. These are forensic expressions.

**REBELLARE.** II, 480 D, “What peace comes from one against whom there has been no rebellion?” i.e. against whom no rebellion has been committed.

**RECAPITULARE**, that is, to bring back to the beginning, or to review from the beginning. II, 512 C.

[Col. 1357C] **RECEPTUM.** II, 141 B, “And throughout the several stories of the heavens they begin to be examined concerning their reception.” Latinus proposes *de receptu*; Rigaltius, however, reads *de praecepto dispici*, “to be examined concerning the command,” i.e. inquiry and examination are made into whether we obeyed Christ’s command and whether we were steadfast in confessing Christ’s name before the authorities.

**RECIDIVATUS.** II, 796 A, “They certainly declared that the soul’s return is corporeal,” i.e. its restoration after a fall. II, 818 A, “Which promise the restoration of the flesh.” II, 837 C, “The restoration of the Jewish condition.” II, 697 A, “The Samian sage is Plato’s authority for the souls’ capacity to fly back through restoration.”

**RECIDIVUS**, revived, restored to life. II, 261 A, “They argue for the reliability of the returning year.” II, 424 B, “Awakened to the hope of eternal life by examples of restoration,” i.e. of things revived and renewed. Servius explains *recidiva* as things restored after a fall. Thus Virgil, “restored Pergama,” *Aeneid* IV, 7 and 10. Pliny, with the physicians, called recurring fevers *recidivae*, παλινδρόμους, ἀναπτομένας, “returning, flaring up again.” II, 810 B, “The entire creation is restored,” i.e. all created things are restored and renewed from the beginning. [Col. 1357D] II, 690 A, “Recollection itself after forgetfulness is memory restored.” II, 1022 A, “Thus adultery renewed from its former state.”

**RECIPROCARE.** II, 335 B, “To return all things in Christ to their head,” i.e. to their beginning. II, 78 C, “How long shall we draw the saw back and forth along this line?” See **LINEA**.

**RECIPROCICORNIS**, having horns curved backward and twisted, ἑλιξοκέρως, “spiral-horned.” II, 1031 B.

**RECOGITATUS.** II, 466 A, “In the recollection of those women.”

**RECOGNOSCERE**, to read carefully. I, 391 A, “While we suffer them, let them be read; while we read them carefully, they are verified,” i.e. all those things take place meanwhile as we read these words cursorily; but when we read carefully, we see that those earlier predictions are already verified by the outcome.

**RECORPORARE**, to transform into another body or another form. II, 804 A, “To re-embody it in stronger material.” II, 837 B, “And the flesh’s capacity to be re-embodied.” [Col. 1358A] II, 706 C, “For those who must be punished with labors and servile tasks will of course be re-embodied as asses and mules.”

**RECORPORATIO**, re-embodiment. II, 837 C.

**RECTOR.** II, 218 A, “I find the Word to be the arbiter of the ruler.” The Dijon manuscript reads: “I find the Word to be the arbiter of the creator.”

**RECUPERATIO.** II, 1022 C, “After recovery and reformation.” Here he uses *recuperatio* for treatment and healing, just as above he called impurity “irrecoverable.”

**RECUSARE**, to abandon. II, 1037 A, “When both scales and years are abandoned”; others read *recursantur*, “recur.” II, 336 A, “Clearly you have rejected the falsehood of the nativity,” i.e. you have refuted it by adducing grounds: a forensic term.

**REDANIMARE.** II, 811 B, “They should not be thought to be reanimated, but reformed.”

**REDANIMATIO**, reanimation. II, 837 C.

**REDINVENIRE.** II, 729 A, “Sophocles the tragedian rediscovered it through a dream.”

**REDIRE**, to be dissolved. II, 247 A, “Liquids return through fire,” [Col. 1358B] i.e. not even the liquids there are liquid unless, when fires are applied, they are dissolved into liquid; they are frozen, bound fast by frost.

**REFECTIO.** II, 798 B, “You abolish the restoration of the flesh precisely when we are asserting it,” i.e. its resurrection.

**REFICERE**, to be restored or replaced. II, 1047 A, “It easily directs itself, easily restores itself.” II, 809 C, “And surely he who made it is capable of restoring it.”

**REFRIGERARE.** I, 704 A, “We bring relief to the needy,” τοῖς πένησιν ἀναψύχομεν. A Hellenism. Varinus says: ἀναψύχω means τὸ τὸν λειποθυμοῦντα ἐπαναφέρω, ἢ τὸ ἀνάπτω καὶ ἀναλαμβάνω, “to revive one who is fainting, or to kindle and restore”; and *refrigerium* has the same sense in very many passages.

**REFRIGERIUM.** II, 708 A, “Through an eternal sentence both of punishment and of refreshment.”

**REFRIGESCENTIA.** II, 722 A, “But neither shall I admit any cooling.”

**REFORMATUS.** II, 563 A, “Re-formed as the guardian of the Aeons,” i.e. reformation.

**REFUGA.** II, 1309 B, “A fugitive from the mines is transformed”: one who removes himself [Col. 1358C] from the common lot of those condemned to the mines; or, as Rigaltius holds, one who, after being condemned to the mines, fled from them.

**REGIO.** II, 235 A, “From either region,” i.e. from the place or seat of each, namely good and evil.

**REGULA.** II, 26 B, “The rule of faith.” Here and elsewhere he calls *regula* what we commonly call the Apostles’ Creed: κανὼν τῆς ἀληθείας, σωμάτιον τῆς ἀληθείας, “rule of truth, body of truth,” in Irenaeus. II, 197 B, “The rule of truth.” II, 157 A, “That this rule had run its course from the beginning of the Gospel.” II, 254 B, “Because the rule of the supreme and great God, once established, forbids it,” i.e. once that rule is laid down, or that foundation cast, there cannot be two gods. II, 271 A, “I shall bring them under rules,” i.e. I shall bind in proper order and place the points relevant to explaining this question. II, 272 B, “I hold out another rule against him,” i.e. I employ another argument against him and unfold the rule of truth to him.

**RELIGIO.** I, 346 A, “Religion goes around the taverns begging.” Pamelius understands this of the priests of Cybele, who demanded alms door to door; Haverkamp, however, understands it of a public invitation to a lease and commends the words in *To the Nations* I, chapter 10: [Col. 1358D] “Trade is advertised by religion; sanctity begs for a lease.”

**RELIQUATIO.** II, 746 B, “There will be no remainder of times not yet established.”

**RELIQUATRIX.** II, 710 A, “Leaving a balance of sins,” i.e. owing an outstanding balance in the accounts. For *reliquatores* are persons who do not pay in full and completely what they owe someone, but remain debtors for some part of it.

**REMEABILIS.** II, 705 C; 706 A, “Indeed, just above they also affirm that it is capable of returning into bodies.”

**REMEDIARE**, to assist or remedy. II, 52 A, “We should remedy it by subtraction, addition, or transformation.” II, 447 A, “That they were therefore remedied,” restored to health. I, 703 B, “They have been healed either from demons or from illnesses.”

**REMISSA**, remission. II, 403 B, “We have spoken about the remission of sins.”

[Col. 1359A] **REMUNERARI**, used passively. I, 502 A, “They are rewarded with statues and salaries.”

**RENIDENTIA.** II, 733 B, “And their smiles during sleep,” i.e. laughter. For in the ancient Glossary *renidere* also means τὸ μειδιᾶν, “to smile.”

**RENUNTIARE**, to withdraw from a place that one had occupied without right. I, 404 A, “It follows that the false thing should withdraw.” II, 395 B, “And indeed this must immediately be declared,” i.e. stated. II, 103 A, “Being now about to declare it more fully in writing,” i.e. to define and declare it in my written response. II, 81 B, “These examples, therefore, will have made a counter-declaration,” i.e. an announcement will have been made in opposition and from the contrary side. II, 658 A, “For they say that for this reason too the soul must be declared incorporeal.”

**RENUNTIATIO.** II, 754 B, “Its declaration will furnish the rule for our resurrection,” i.e. a demonstration or declaration made by a pronouncement. I, 638 B, “Our single renunciation directed against idolatry.”

**REPASTINARE**, properly, to dig up again with a *pastinum*, the vine-dressers’ two-pronged implement. II, 303 C, “So that the commission of an injury might be rooted out by fear of an immediately impending retaliation.” [Col. 1359B] I, 1326 B, “Not digging up anew the use of your riches or refinements.” I, 1246 B, “And some two-pronged implement of iron or bronze for digging around the nails.” II, 735 A, “Or, after the manner of a vine, renew life by layering”—i.e. just as a farmer does with a vine, renewing it by a shoot—“with its age made new.”

**REPASTINATIO**, uprooting or cutting back, which is opposed to propagation. II, 921 B, “Not without a principle of propagation at the beginning and of uprooting at the end.”

**REPERCUTERE**, to turn an opponent’s own argument against him, like a missile which, rebounding from a shield, wounds the one who threw it and recoils upon him. I, 488 A, “This, you say, can also be turned back against your God.”

**REPERTRIX.** II, 394 B, “Nor does it impart joy to the Church that found it.”

**REPUERASCERE.** II, 544 A, B, “The Apostle too commands us to become children again.”

**REPUTESCERE.** II, 702 B, “Lest some condition of burial putrefy again.” See **CONDITIO**.

[Col. 1359C] **RES.** II, 1032 A, “Let the matter now come from elsewhere; let arguments now be sought elsewhere”: let us pass to other arguments, drawn from elsewhere.

**RESCULPERE.** II, 959 C, “For the first people had carved anew the first man’s crime.” Augustine, on Psalm 6: “For when we are converted, that is, when by changing our former life we carve the spirit anew.” Rufinus, on the same Psalm: “When we are converted, that is, when by changing our former life we are carved anew.”

**RESERARE**, to break and open. I, 308 A, “Who opened the bloodstained mouth for the judge?” i.e. that beastly gape of a man resembling a wild animal, closed by the row of teeth as though by a bar, was broken open by force, so that pieces of human flesh not yet sent down into the stomach might be discovered in the mouth.

**RESIGNARE**, to open, break open. I, 303 A, “Because they broke open the compartments of the wine cellar.” For they secured the cellars in which they stored wine and food not only with a bar but also with a seal. II, 782 A, “From the earth, that is, from flesh not yet opened to generation.” II, 378 A, “Jonathan, [Col. 1359D] Saul’s son, removed through supplication the guilt of breaking the fast.” He calls a fast that was to be infringed *resignatum*; for Jonathan had provided the occasion for violating the fast when he put honey to his mouth. II, 849 B, “For opening the Old Testament and confirming the New,” i.e. for explaining the Old and confirming the New. For wills were opened by unsealing and made binding by sealing.

**RESONARE.** II, 906 C, “Which sound publicly,” when a signal is given by trumpet or bell, concerning the three more notable public hours.

**RESPERGERE.** II, 1001 C, “The stains of flesh defiled again after baptism,” i.e. flesh sprinkled and stained again, namely with new filth after the washing.

**RESPONDERE.** II, 233 B, “That formless and uncultivated matter is reflected.” An image or object is said to *respondere* in a mirror in the sense that it is presented, represented, reflected, or rather displays itself opposite to be viewed. He therefore denies that matter is reflected in this ornamented [Col. 1360A] world, i.e. that it displays a corresponding answer and image of itself. II, 91 B, “And after Christ to answer to another master,” i.e. by entering into a new pledge to bind oneself to perform duties for a master other than Christ, who thinks and commands otherwise than he does.

**RESPONSIO.** II, 865 A, “For the soul is sanctified not by washing but by its answer.” The author calls *responsio* the pledge by which we in turn bind ourselves to the Lord who promises grace. The Apostle calls it ἐπερώτημα συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς, “the pledge of a good conscience,” from the reciprocal nature of the parties, in 1 Peter 3.

**RESUSCITARI**, to rise, said of stars. II, 1033 A, “The distinct confusion of the stars sometimes casts something down and sometimes raises it again.”

**RETRACTARE**, to refute. I, 280 A, “No one objects: is he not therefore good?” etc., i.e. no one refutes the words of those making the charge by saying, “See whether,” etc. II, 549 A, “They will be none other than those which are being refuted.” II, 136 C, “Nor does anyone object.” II, 403 B, “But we have not at once refuted the other matters by this proposition,” [Col. 1360B] i.e. we do not wish this proposition to be understood here as applying to the other arguments. *Retractare* often means to treat carefully and reconsider. II, 231 B, “We reconsidered something in what preceded.” I, 1255 B, “Who could ever discuss his goodness at length?” i.e. who could ever say enough about his goodness? But all the ancient copies read, *quis de bono ejus latere retractet*, i.e. who would consider concealing or privately suppressing his goodness? At I, 392 A, it means to censure: “Perhaps whether his standing is criticized on this ground.” For Tertullian says that the sect is carefully investigated for the sake of disparagement.

**RETRACTATUS.** II, 157 B, “A place must also be allowed for reconsiderations,” i.e. for more careful examination and refutation. II, 248 A, “That heretics must be convicted without an examination of their doctrines.” II, 474 A, “As was also proved in the examination of your Gospel.” II, 931 B, “In the general examination.”

**RETRO**, formerly. II, 246 B, “It was done by us formerly,” πεποίηται ἡμῖν, “it has been done by us.” A Hellenism. I, 432 A, “Those who formerly hated,” i.e. those who hated before now. So very frequently.

**RETROSIOR**, one who is farther back, i.e. older, more ancient. [Col. 1360C] I, 387 A, “Yet the very latest of them are found to be no more ancient than the foremost of your sages.”

**RHETORICARI.** II, 301 A, “Thus the heretics provoke us to engage in rhetoric as well as in philosophy.”

**RISILOQUIUM.** II, 1245 A, “When, among those about to mock him, it consists in derisive speech.”

**RIVALITAS.** II, 988 C, “How many rivalries shall I defend?” For very many lovers defend their beloved women from rivals by homicide, destroying those rivals by various kinds of death.

**ROBORATUS.** II, 691 A, “But how much stronger is the outcome of being refuted by women than of being approved?” Latinus, Rigaltius, and others read *ruboratior exitus*, “a more shameful outcome,” rather than *roboratior*. He calls an outcome *ruboratior* when it inflicts greater blushes and shame.

**ROMANITAS.** II, 1040 A, “If Romanness is the salvation of all,” etc., i.e. if embracing Roman customs is useful and glorious for all peoples, why do you now depart toward the Greeks through pursuits that are altogether dishonorable and useless?

[Col. 1360D] **ROMPHAEA**, ῥομφαία, sword. II, 745 A, “Unless it is because the sword that guards Paradise yields to no one.”

**RUCTARE.** I, 413 A, “Who are healed by belching.” Haverkamp reads “who are bent over.” This concerns seers who, after conceiving the divine power through sacrifices and the burning of whole offerings, are in labor pains and ὀδύναις, “agonies”; they therefore bend over while the spirit they have conceived strives to burst forth through their throats. II, 815 A, “Into whom some death has belched,” i.e. into whom someone, seized by the swift action of poison, breathed out his stricken soul with a belch while drinking.

**RUDIS.** II, 222 B, “That is crude which is imperfect.”

**RUMA**, also called *rumen*, is the breast in women; in certain animals, however, it is the projecting part of the throat through which swallowed food is brought back up, as Servius says—or, according to Nonius, the place in the belly into which food is received and from which it is returned. Festus: “The rumen is the part of the neck through which food is swallowed.” II, 800 A, “And from the crops of birds.”

[Col. 1361A] **RUMPERE.** I, 301 A, “Or of those who are still breaking whips,” on whose backs remain fresh traces of the whips broken during the beating; Persius wittily calls such persons “yesterday’s Quirites” in *Satire* III, 106.

**RUNCARE**, to root out completely, remove. II, 1035 B, “He undertook to root out and clear away.”

**RUNCINA**, an instrument with which a work was polished. I, 340 A.

**RUPEX**, uncultivated, rustic. II, 1041 A, “That man in the presence of a rustic.” I, 404 A, “Not those who were boors and still savage human beings.” II, 655 B, “But what will so many and such great souls of boors and barbarians do?”

**RUSSATUS.** II, 77 A, “And then reddened by hope of his own blood.” Military tunics were red, φοινικοὶ χιτῶνες, “scarlet tunics.” Here the soldier who became a Christian is said to be reddened, in place of his red tunic, by hope of his own blood, that is, by the hoped-for purple of martyrdom. Red military garments occur in Trebellius; and in Juvenal, “Lacerta in red.”

**RUSTARE.** *Ruscum* or *ruscus* denotes brambles and thorns; hence *ruscare* or *rustare*, and hence also *rustariae falces*, [Col. 1361B] sickles designed for uprooting thorns. II, 1035 B, “He undertook to root out and clear away.” Others read *ruspare*, i.e. “to search.”

## S

**SACERDOS.** II, 1045 A, “A priestly platform,” i.e. a platform belonging to a priest. Similarly I, 907 B, “a left-hand conscience,” i.e. a conscience aware of what is sinister. II, 926 C, “Through a priest ordained on the ground of monogamy, or even confirmed on the ground of virginity,” i.e. called to the priesthood from the number of the once-married, or from the number of virgins, ἀγάμων, “unmarried persons.”

**SACERDOTIUM.** II, 1031 A, priests.

**SACRAMENTUM**, religion. I, 363 B, “And from this learn the whole order of our religion,” i.e. advance to a knowledge of our religion. II, 623 B, “So too Jesus, because of the sacred significance of his name.” I, 520 A, “Only concerning our sacred rites.” II, 32 B, “One tradition of the same religion,” i.e. of the same Gospel. II, 38 A, “A silent mystery,” i.e. a more remote and secret sacred doctrine. II, 45 B, [Col. 1361C] “Because of a difference in doctrine.” II, 588 A, B, “I who have betrayed so great a mystery even by ridiculing it,” i.e. so great a secret, so arcane and hidden a doctrine. II, 594 A, “For the great mystery of the name.” Irenaeus: καὶ τοῦτ’ εἶναι τὸ μέγα καὶ ἀπόκρυφον μυστήριον, “and that this is the great and hidden mystery.” II, 157 B, the οἰκονομίας sacramentum, “mystery of the divine economy,” means the doctrine of the Trinity. II, 622 B, “Who was prepared among the representations of this mystery,” i.e. both so that he himself might be an image and so that he might be numbered among the types and images of Christ, of which there were very many under the Law in the Old Testament. II, 835 B, “For at that time this wood had a symbolic significance.” II, 138 B, “Lest antiquity perhaps had its own sacred ordinance,” i.e. lest someone suppose that martyrdoms were ordained for the Old Testament, not the New; for the Law, not the Gospel. Thus he speaks of the “sacrament of martyrdom.” II, 963 A, “But fasts will also obtain from God recognition of mysteries,” i.e. skill in interpreting sacred figures and images, namely those divinely presented in dreams. The *sacramenta*, therefore, are dreams sent by God. II, 964 C, “By what means recognition of mysteries might be obtained from God.” [Col. 1361D] II, 470 A, “The mysteries of these figures.” II, 660 A, “And it both sees and hears mysteries,” i.e. parables, enigmas, figures, and mysteries of the sort shown or suggested through dreams, by which God’s will is signified or disclosed. Irenaeus, book V, chapter 7, rendered ἄρρητα ῥήματα in Latin as *sermones inenarrabiles*, “words that cannot be uttered.” II, 973 A, “It is the law of the sacrament,” i.e. the law of Christian communion is that whatever belongs to any of our people belongs to us. II, 261 A, “Sacred signs of a dry and burning nature,” i.e. signs or mysteries. II, 280 A, “Not even the sacrament of his faith itself,” i.e. baptism. I, 1197 A, “Blessed is the sacrament of our water.” II, 317 C, Christ is called “the sacrament of human salvation.” II, 487 D, “Of what does he interpret it as a figure belonging to an alien sacrament?” i.e. a sacred sign given by an alien god. II, 943 C, “By presbyters and deacons of the same sacrament,” i.e. monogamists. II, 823 A, “So that it may be the form of the mystery,” concerning the resurrection. I, 1268 B, “Love is the supreme sacrament of faith.” I, 405 [Col. 1362A] A, “From its own consciousness the same soul makes a pronouncement from the word of the sacrament.” Haverkamp reads *animae eadem exsacramenti*: *exsacramentum* formed from *exsecrare*, so that the words mean: even the uneducated common people now frequently use, as a curse, the name of Satan, the author of this class—namely, of demons. A full stop must be placed after *generis*.

**SACRIFICIUM.** I, 1329 B, “Or a sacrifice is offered,” i.e. sacred prayers by which the pious present themselves to God, as Clement of Alexandria explains at length in *Stromata* VII, and Tertullian in *Apologeticum*, chapter 30, and *To Scapula*, chapter 2. I, 1303 A, “Sacrifices without scruple.” II, 927 A, “Your sacrifice will ascend with an unveiled brow.” See **PURUS**. II, 806 B, “For there are also sacrifices pleasing to God—I mean the struggles of the soul, fasts, late and dry foods, and the filth that accompanies this duty.” I, 1182 A, “Most people do not think that one should take part in the prayers of sacrifices.” He is speaking of fasts and the Eucharist, sacrifices which were celebrated especially with prayers.

**SAECULARIS.** II, 52 C, Secular writings are contrasted with the sacred Scriptures.

[Col. 1362B] **SAECULUM** (“age,” “world”). “Who made the age a body of times.” Zephyrus understands this of that indeterminate age in which neither earlier nor later was discerned, once it had been reduced to order and succession. Heraldus, however, prefers to understand it of the world: for the world is the body of times, from whose creation we number ages, years, months, and days; beyond it we cannot distinguish temporal successions, but there is eternity itself, and God himself is found to be both time and all things to himself. *Saeculum* may also simply be taken as a body of one hundred years. II, 57 A, “Now bound to the world.” See **OBSTRINGI**. II, 197 B, “In short, even to the present day the man exists and lives as a heretic concerning the world and nature as well,” i.e. his teaching is heretical in its treatment of the world and nature, since in Stoic fashion he makes matter eternal. II, 898 B, “Accordingly, let the age, God’s rival, see to it,” i.e. this impious age that strives against God—or else, “with nature as its guide, it will lead.” Pamelius understands this of Christians; Le Prieur, of the custom of the pagans, who cut off girls’ hair. II, 952 A, “From that final departure of the world.”

**SAEVUS** (“harsh”). II, 70 B, Cerdo’s other god; Irenaeus [Col. 1362C] renders it δίκαιον, “just,” i.e. one who presses his right to the utmost. For the utmost right is the utmost wrong.

**SALACITAS**, lust. II, 593 C, “Through voracity lust passes.”

**SALTICUS** (“dancing”). II, 137 B, “He is mutilated by an insulting slaughter for the profit of a dancing girl”: *puella saltica*, i.e. a little dancing girl, so called from dancing.

**SALTUS** (“leap”), concerning the incontinence of lust. I, 324 A, “Its companion is lust, whose leaps are everywhere,” etc.

**SALUTIFICATOR**, σωτήρ, “savior,” an author of salvation, as in Book V *Against Marcion*, chap. 15, II, 778 A: “Nor is there one savior, if there are two authors of salvation.”

**SAMIA**, a kind of cake regarded as a delicacy. II, 326 C, “That you would ever cook cakes and *samiae*”; others read *psamia*.

**SANGUINANS** (“bleeding”). II, 408 A, “Because the law excludes one from contact with a bleeding woman,” i.e. αἱμορροούσης, “a woman suffering a flow of blood.”

**SAPERE** (“to savor,” “to have the sense of”). II, 705 A, “Thus too the divine pronouncement has its proper sense.”

**SAPA**. II, 326 C, “Not, however, as though [producing] *sapa* from stones.” They called *sapa*—Varro says in Book I *On the Life of the Roman People*, as cited [Col. 1362D] by Nonius—what they had boiled down from must to half its original quantity.

**SAPIENTIA** (“wisdom”), the Christian religion. II, 1045 A, “When he first puts on this wisdom,” i.e. as soon as Christians assumed the cloak.

**SAPIENTIALIS** (“sapiential”). II, 670 A, “The vital and sapiential faculty, which they call τὸ ἡγεμονικόν,” that is, the ruling faculty.

**SAPOR** (“savor”). II, 851 A, “Not the substance itself, but the substance’s savor, by which the substance has savor”—with *sapit* used actively. So too *Against Marcion*, Book II, chap. 19: “through the same savor of suffering.”

**SARABARA**, a flowing garment worn by Persian nobles. Hesychius: Σαράβαρα, τὰ περὶ τὰς κνημίδας ἐνδύματα, “*sarabara*: garments worn around the shins.” I, 1171 A; II, 1043 A.

**SARMENTITII** (“faggot-men”). Why Christians were so called Tertullian himself explains at I, 531 A.

**SATIARE** (“to sate”). II, 124 B, “If it has sated the wound,” i.e. if the missile, driven into the wound, has penetrated it.

**SATURITAS** (“satiety”). II, 962 B, “Nor is there any cultivation of satiety in sackcloth.” [Col. 1363A] He says “cultivation of satiety” because joy proceeds from satiety, and from joy comes concern for more refined adornment, which is incompatible with the grimness of ashes and the harshness of sackcloth.

**SATURNALIA**. II, 119 A, “Christ commanded that such peace be purchased from the soldiers by Saturnalian gifts.” Either *Saturnalia* should be written, or it must be said that *Saturnalia munera*, “Saturnalian gifts,” are meant: these Christians sent to the soldiers or officials of the proconsul or governor on the occasion of the Saturnalian celebration, so that they might find them more favorable and merciful. The Saturnalia were days of gifts and New Year’s presents. Hence Martial’s line, 4:

> Sabellus had no Saturnalia more profitable  
> in ten years.

**SCAMMA**. Among the Greeks this denotes the arena in which athletes met in competition, because it was customarily surrounded by a trench, from σκάπτειν, “to dig.” Hence Jerome’s proverbial expression, addressed to Pammachius, “to depart from the *scamma* and the place of contest,” meaning to depart from one’s subject or cross the lines. I, 614 B, “And brought him forward into this arena.”

**SCANDALUM** (“scandal,” “stumbling block”). II, 320 C–D, “Before the scandal of Marcion.”

**SCANTINIA**, or the Scatinian law, enacted by Scatinius, tribune [Col. 1363B] of the plebs, against the passive and effeminate who practiced abominable sexual acts—that is, either themselves submitted to treatment as women or committed violence against boys. It prescribed a fine of ten thousand sesterces. Caelius, Epistle 13, writes that his enemies threatened him with prosecution under this law. II, 947 C, “Just as that man of yours from Uthina did not fear the Scantinian law.”

**SCAPULAE** (“shoulders”), the lower portions of mountains, which are often torn away by torrents and swept down together with them. II, 1033 A.

**SCENA** (“stage”). II, 336 A, “He ought to have run through the stage-play of the phantom.” The sense is: Marcion’s Christ ought to have served the stage completely and performed the play he had undertaken; for if he bore imaginary flesh, he ought also to have had [something else] imaginary—the object is absent from the supplied text—since in this way he would have run through the stage-play of the phantom.

**SCHOLA** (“school”). I, 455 A, “Schools of beasts”: the shows and circuses containing cages from which providers of games released lions, bears, and similar wild beasts trained to tear human beings apart, while men were trained to fight the beasts. During those spectacles, moreover, voices were sometimes heard [Col. 1363C] containing oblique attacks even upon their own Caesars.

**SCIAPODES** (“Shadow-Feet”). Hesychius: Σκιάποδες, οἱ ἐν Λιβύῃ πλατεῖς ἔχουσι τοὺς πόδας, καὶ ποιοῦσι σκιὰν αὐτοῖς ἐν καύματι, “The Shadow-Feet are those in Libya who have broad feet and use them to make shade for themselves in the heat.” And Stephanus of Byzantium: Σκίαποδες, ἔθνος Αἰθιοπικόν, ὡς Ἑκαταῖος ἐν περιηγήσει Αἰγύπτου, “The Shadow-Feet, an Ethiopian people, according to Hecataeus in his *Periegesis of Egypt*.” I, 570 A.

**SCIBILIS** (“knowable”). II, 511 A, “Not knowable to everyone.”

**SCIDIUM**. I, 621 A, “I shall test them with cheap wood-splinters.” *Scidia* are σχίδακες, κλάσματα ξύλων, “splinters, fragments of wood,” cheap pieces cut from felled trees. Vitruvius, Book II, chap. 1: “They block the gaps with splinters and mud.”

**SCINDERE** (“to split”). II, 368 C, “Within these he splits open the great and entire difference,” i.e. by splitting, as it were, he opens and exposes it, just as Cicero writes to Atticus of “splitting open his grief.”

**SCIRE** (“to know”), meaning “to be wise.” I, 436 A, “And rightly, if you know,” i.e. if you are wise; “so far as I know,” i.e. if I have any wisdom, if I remember correctly. I, 446 A, “Know from them,” i.e. learn and understand from them the source from which you wish to derive wisdom.

**SCOBINA**, an instrument for more polished adornment. Gloss: κοσμητήριον, “toilet implement.” I, 340 A.

**SCORTUM** (“hide”; ordinarily “prostitute”). II, 1042 A, “He has already portrayed Omphale represented in Hercules’ *scortum* [Col. 1363D].” This is understood of the lion’s skin, σκῦτος.

**SCRINIUM** (“archive”), a written document deposited and preserved in it. I, 381 A, “And meanwhile the sacred archive of a single prophet outlasts the ages.”

**SCRIPTURA** (“writing”). II, 585 A, “For us, in the writing of this seed.” Others read *inscriptura* as one word, i.e. ἐγγραφή, “enrollment,” by which, as he said above, we were enrolled in the class of the animal nature. Thus the enrollment of this seed is the rule laid down beforehand for the animal seed.

**SCROBULUS**. II, 903 A, “Or the *scrobuli* of the barbarians.” As Salmasius advised, this should read *stropulos*. According to Festus, *stropus*—also *stroppus* or *struppus*—is, as the philosopher Atteius thinks, a στρόφιον, “headband,” which priests wear on the head as an insignia; some say that it is a crown, or an insignia placed upon the head in lieu of a crown, such as a *strophilum*. From this come *stropiola* or *strophiola*, and *stropuli*. Le Prieur prefers *crobylos*. The commentator on Thucydides, Book I: κρώβυλος δ’ ἐστὶν εἶδος πλέγματος τῶν [Col. 1364A] τριχῶν ἀπὸ ἑτέρων εἰς ὀξὺ ἀπολῆγον, “A *crobylus* is a kind of interweaving of hair tapering from different parts to a point.” Hesychius: Κρώβυλος ὁ μαλλὸς τῶν παίδων, ἢ ὁ κόρυμβος τῆς ἐμπλοκῆς ἥ ἐστιν ἀνηνεγμένη ἀπὸ μέσου τοῦ μετώπου ἐπὶ τὴν κορυφήν· οὕτω δὲ ὁ ῥήτωρ Ἡγήσιππος, καὶ δήγγος ἐκαλεῖτο κρώβυλος, etc., “A *crobylus* is the lock of boys, or the topknot of braided hair carried upward from the middle of the forehead to the crown; so too the orator Hegesippus, and a *dēngos* was called a *crobylus*,” etc. See **CICADA**.

**SCROFA**, sow. II, 251 C, “Up to the offspring of thirty aeons it poured forth a swarm of divinity, like an aeonian sow.” Rigaltius emends this to “Aeneas’ sow,” for it alludes to that sow of Aeneas which, as Virgil says in *Aeneid* III,

> A huge sow found beneath the ilexes along the shore  
> lay there, having borne a litter of thirty young.

Rigaltius likewise reads in Jerome’s epistle to the Galatians, “As many offspring as Aeneas’ sow produced,” where the common text reads “the Aeonian sow.”

**SCRUPEUS**, rocky. II, 1011 A, “The rocky school is Chiron’s cave.”

**SCRUPULOSITAS** (“scrupulosity”). II, 39 B, “All these provocations to scrupulosity.” II, 957 B, “Toward every scrupulosity concerning food.” II, 905 A, “Descending from the constraints or scrupulosity,” i.e. from the peevishness of parents whom no one [Col. 1364B] pleases.

**SCRUPULOSUS** (“like little stones”). II, 1228 A, “God inflicted stony wounds upon the ears”—from which the little stones of gems might hang.

**SCYTALOSAGITTIPELLIGER** (“club-arrow-hide-bearer”), an epithet of Hercules, because he carried a club—in Greek σκυτάλη—arrows, and a lion’s hide. I, 1041 B.

**SECTA** (“sect,” “way”), in a favorable sense, of the Christian religion. I, 501 A, “While a veil is drawn over the goodness of this way.” II, 116 C, “Under the ancient redemption of his person and way.” II, 1008 C, “In the Apostle’s own way.” He used *secta* for conduct. Justinian does the same near the end of the title *On Legacies*, where he discusses shameful legacies: “The way of my times,” he says, “does not permit a testamentary disposition of this kind to be valid.” He therefore calls it “the Apostle’s way” in the same sense as, shortly afterward, “the Apostle’s nature and purpose,” the form and rule of his teachings. So above, “from Peter’s form.”

**SECUNDATUS** (“second rank”). II, 695 A, “If we give primacy to one and second rank to the other.”

**SECUNDUM** (“second”). I, 503 A, “Whom philosophers [Col. 1364C] assign as second after the gods,” i.e. they regard demons as occupying the place next after the gods. It is therefore no wonder that philosophers do not put demons to flight, since they are their friends, regarding them as second only to the gods.

**SEDATIO** (“cessation”). II, 441 A, “So that the cessation of the Law and the Prophets was effected by another power”: ἠρέμησις, “rest,” as though to say their placement in a seat of repose and leisure.

**SEMAXII** (“half-axle men”). Why Christians were so called Tertullian himself explains at I, 531 A.

**SEMEL**, ἐφάπαξ, ἁπαξαπλῶς, “once for all,” “altogether,” “utterly.” I, 328 A, and often.

**SEMINALE**, anything belonging to seed or derived from seed. II, 261 A, “The Great Mother reaped down into the earth together with the seed-bearing elements.”

**SEMITRACTATUS** (“half-treated”). II, 103 A, “I carried away with me a subject only half treated.”

**SEMPER** (“always”). II, 1029 C, “The rulers always of Africa.” A Hellenism, as in Terence: “And yesterday always gentleness.” Expressions of this kind are extremely frequent in Tertullian.

**SENECTUS** (“old age”). II, 133 B, “After the old age of the stadium,” i.e. after the stadium, or place appointed for contests, had undergone a kind of old age because it had not been frequented for many years. [Col. 1364D]

**SENESCERE** (“to grow old”). II, 1040 A, “The pursuits of the wrestling school growing old badly.” They are so called either because Severus revived them when they had nearly fallen into disuse, or because prizefighters rarely grow old.

**SENEX** (“old”). I, 527 A, “Old boys,” who preserved boyish virginity into old age.

**SENTENTIA** (“judgment,” “assertion”). II, 815 B, “Is it then a matter of fixing an assertion even upon little vessels and implements?” i.e. asserting it fearlessly and steadfastly.

**SENTENTIALITER** (“categorically”). II, 783 B, “Or because the Lord himself pronounced categorically and definitively.”

**SENTIRE** (“to feel,” “to direct one’s mind”). II, 276 C, “After so great an age he turned his thought toward man’s salvation,” i.e. directed his mind toward this plan. I, 1239 B, “So long as you have been disposed toward the Lord,” i.e. devoted to the Lord. I, 1264 A, “If, when afflicted by loss, we have felt impatiently.”

[Col. 1365A] **SENSUS** (“sense”). II, 213 B, “Sophia in sense.” Pithoeus’ book reads: “Sense and Sophia.” Junius proposes “Sophia’s sense.” II, 798 B, “It is indeed possible to be wise even through common conceptions in matters concerning God.” Common conceptions are κοιναὶ ἔννοιαι, or notions approved by the perception and consensus of nearly everyone.

**SEPIA** (“cuttlefish”). II, 306 A, “But indeed, these cuttlefish.” He aptly compares the Marcionites to cuttlefish. For, as Pliny relates in Book IX, chap. 29, cuttlefish are a kind of fish that, when they perceive themselves being caught, discharge ink—which serves them as blood—and hide themselves by darkening the water. In the same way, when the Marcionites perceive that they are being exposed, that is, when they are convicted of error, they spew darkness into this blasphemy and thus obstruct and divert their accuser by alleging things that blacken and obscure the Creator’s goodness.

**SEPTENTRIONES**, the constellation composed of seven stars which the Greeks called ἅμαξα, “the Wagon,” and ἄρκτος, “the Bear.” II, 771 B.

**SEQUESTRARE** (“to sequester”). II, 578 B, “He had sequestered it in his son the Demiurge,” [Col. 1365B] i.e. had preserved it set apart; a forensic term. II, 834 B, “Bodies treated with preserving spices are sequestered for burial, mausoleums, and monuments.” II, 848 B, “If [it is intended] rather to sequester faith in the future resurrection,” i.e. to confirm it securely, as though by the good faith of a stakeholder. II, 669 B, “And in what lodgings within the body they are sequestered,” i.e. in what seats the individual parts are kept. II, 759 B, “In whom every hope is sequestered.”

**SEQUESTRATORIUM**, a place where money is deposited and received. II, 872 C, “Because the earth too is a repository for seeds.”

**SERICUM**, silken clothing. II, 1042 A, “What that Hercules of Omphale’s must have been like in silk.” Richerius reads *in theristro*, i.e. θερινὸν ἱμάτιον, “a summer garment.”

**SI** (“if”) often means “as if,” “as though.” I, 406 A, “As if fruits, as if crops.” I, 438 A—or rather: “Let it first be established, then, whether they can impart these things.” II, 222 A, “The question, of course, is whether it was the earth that was made.” I, 467 A, “If perchance,” i.e. if there is perchance, as is supposed, any injury. II, 156 B, “If not,” i.e. but if in some respect it can no longer [Col. 1365C] be rooted out. II, 187 C, “If not, believe at least because of the works,” i.e. if by any argument or means, by any circumstance or cause.

**SIBYNA**, a kind of hunting spear, as the author explains at II, 361 C. Hesychius: σιβύνη, ὅπλον δόρατι παραπλήσιον, “a *sibyna*, a weapon resembling a spear”; and elsewhere, ζηβύνη, ὁλοσίδηροι ἄκοντες, “a *zēbyna*, javelins made entirely of iron”; and shortly afterward, ζιβύνη, ὁλοσίδηρον ἀκόντιον, ἢ λόγχη, ἢ σπάθη, ἢ μάχαιρα, “a *zibyna*, an all-iron javelin, or lance, or broad sword, or knife.” Festus explains it as a kind of Illyrian missile resembling a hunting spear. Ennius: “They remain, stabbing with curved daggers and *sibynae*.”

**SICCARE** (“to dry”). II, 577 B, “While the mud survived, it dried,” i.e. it was dried.

**SIGAEUM**, a promontory of the Troad; Achilles is believed to have been buried there.

**SIGERIUS**, a German by nationality and Domitian’s chamberlain, according to Dio. Though he had received very great favors from Caesar, he conspired with Parthenius, Stephanus, and others to kill Domitian. I, 457 A.

**SIGILLARIUM**. II, 563 A, “A figurine-maker’s shop,” just as a district of Rome was called *Sigillaria*, τὰ ἀγαλματοπωλεῖα, “the image-makers’ shops.” [Col. 1365D] Suetonius, *Claudius*, chap. 16, and *Nero*, chap. 28. II, 573 A, “And as though by an external puppet-master’s impulse,” i.e. he was moved to external actions by the internal direction of that other, just as articulated and self-moving figurines—νευρόσπαστα and αὐτόματα—are customarily moved by hidden craftsmanship and mechanical power. II, 654, “As though by a puppet’s motion, with an inward force moving the surface,” i.e. by an interior movement accomplished through a certain artifice and mechanical power.

**SIGNACULUM** (“mark,” “seal”). I, 392 A, “Concerning the bodily mark itself.” Minucius Felix: “Thus, finally, we are distinguished not by a mark upon the body, as you suppose, but by the sign of innocence and modesty.” II, 541 A, “The complete seal upon the tongue,” by which reverent silence was commanded. I, 656 A, “Against whom we abjure at the seal of faith,” i.e. in baptism we solemnly profess under oath that we have renounced her and will steadfastly continue to renounce her.

**SIGNARE** (“to seal”), to conceal. I, 401 A, “Midday was withdrawn when the sun sealed the world,” i.e. when it concealed and sealed away its light. Compare Job 9:7. II, 577 [Col. 1366A] A, “When Horus marked the final line.” II, 122 A, “Distrust in immediately sealing the heel of the beast,” where *signare* means to enclose as if under seal and keep shut. II, 282 B, “How will he have someone in whom to mark his goodness?” i.e. display it, someone upon whom he may bestow his goodness. I, 1296 A, “When you sign your little bed, when you sign your poor body”—with the sign of the cross. II, 927 B, “Sealed by age,” i.e. one who because of age is free from lust and will remain untouched.

**SIGNIFICANTIA** (“signification”). II, 549 B, “The significations will appear within the limits of the pages.” II, 304 C, “Not to touch upon any of the law’s hidden significations”—its spiritual significations, of course, etc. Rigaltius reads “of the signifying law.” “The hidden things of the signifying law,” i.e. the mysteries of the figurative law. He himself immediately explains it: “of the spiritual and prophetic law, of course.” II, 483 A, “But shadowed by significations.”

**SILICERNIUM**, a funeral banquet offered to old men. I, 347 A. See Donatus on Terence, *Adelphoe*, p. 299.

**SILVA** (“wood”). II, 51 A, “By what right, Marcion, do you fell my wood?” [Col. 1366B] i.e. why do you break into my possession? Why do you put your sickle into my harvest? I, 286 A, “You cut down and fell that entire old and squalid wood of laws with the new axes of imperial rescripts and edicts.” I, 244 A, “So that you may understand with how mighty an axe censorship cuts down, uproots, and eradicates the whole wood of lusts.”

**SIMPLICITAS** (“simplicity”). II, 543 A, “By beating themselves they scatter your simplicity,” i.e. they distract your simple mind, which deals straightforwardly with the truth, into various thoughts, beating their breasts just as though they agreed with the doctrine and were concerned solely and most earnestly with repentance. Rigaltius reads “your foolish simplicity,” with this sense: If you contend with them at close quarters, they will indeed beat themselves, but they will take care that nothing may be inferred from their self-beating except that they are foolishly simple; their chief concern will be to pass for foolishly simple rather than wicked.

**SIMPULUM**, a vessel used for pouring libations of wine at sacrifices; it is also called *simpuvium*. I, 347 A. See Kipping, *Roman Antiquities*.

[Col. 1366C] **SINGILARIUM**. See **SIGILLARIUM**.

**SINGULARIS**, μόνιος, “solitary.” I, 313 A, “Solitary Christians,” i.e. those alone who have neither mother nor sister living or at hand. Thus Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, Book III: “The solitary God.”

**SINGULARITER** (“singly”). II, 914 C, “To think about the end of your singularity,” i.e. about your own end, since you now live alone, having survived your wife.

**SIPARA**. These are hanging curtains belonging to girls and theaters. I, 368 A.

**SIPARIUM**, the curtain of a mime-show, which blocked the audience’s view while the acts of the plays were being changed. II, 563 B, “But beyond the curtain there is another tragic performance,” i.e. another tragic scene, another tragic act.

**SITIRE** (“to thirst”). II, 809 A, “Who perhaps still thirst to know God.” Those who do not yet know thirst, and therefore are ignorant. II, 835 B, “Nevertheless, they thirst for an interpretation of their own simplicity.” II, 886 D, “You will be able to thirst for no doctrine.” II, 723 B, “Adam first drank deeply of sleep [Col. 1366D] before he thirsted for rest.”

**SOL** (“sun”). II, 338 A, “I suppose, first anointed in the sun.” He alludes to ἡλίωσις, or exposure to the sun, whereby those who had been anointed warmed themselves to dry and strengthen their limbs. Persius, *Satire* 4:

> Or if, anointed, you idle and fix the sun upon your skin.

Junius prefers “at the bath-seat”; see that entry.

**SOLIDUM** (“the whole”). I, 1275 A, “Only see that you can receive the whole: this is entrusted to the good faith of my admonition.” He alludes to the capacity of husband and wife to take an entire inheritance, which was permitted only in certain cases under the Julian and Papian laws. On this matter title XVI appears among the fragments of Ulpian, III, 168: “And they believe that the unmarried and childless cannot receive the whole under God’s testament.” “To receive the whole” is ἴσων ἀξιοῦσθαι, “to be deemed worthy of equal rights,” which is the same as becoming sole heir and entering upon the entire inheritance. Under the Julian law this did not happen in the case of the unmarried, for their legacies lapsed and went to the treasury. Hence the Julian law was called the law of lapsing legacies.

**SOLIUM** (“throne”). II, 158 A, “And thus the Latins express the throne itself in vocal form.” The sense is that the name *solium* has now acquired that meaning in Latin ears. For *solium* is commonly said to derive from *sedere*, “to sit,” but *solium* also derives from *solus*, “alone,” so that it means the seat of one alone, the condition or dignity of one alone—monarchy. Of the same kind is this passage in Festus: “*Solia* are seats upon each of which no more than one person can sit; hence those who hold banquets for the gods are said to spread *solia*,” etc. II, 618 A, “I suppose, first anointed at the bath-seat.” *Solium*, so called from sitting, is a vessel in which people bathed while seated. See Suetonius, *Augustus*, chap. 82; Pliny, *Natural History*, Book XXVI, chap. 19.

**SOLOX**, coarse wool. I, 1042 B, “The coarse wool of a running-cloak.” Turnebus proposes: “the color of a running-cloak.”

**SOLUM** (“ground”). “Flesh upon the ground”: in solitude, in the sadness of desolation. Or: upon the bare earth, upon naked rock.

**SOPHISTA** (“sophist”). II, 548 A, “Miltiades, the sophist of the churches.” He is so called because he possessed great ability in disputing about subjects of every kind and passages of Scripture. II, 963 A, “All the sophists are troubled concerning the dream of the king of Babylon.” By “sophists” he means those elsewhere called wise men, interpreters of dreams, and diviners.

[Col. 1367B] **SORDES** (“filth”). II, 806 B, “And filth as an appendage of this duty”: an uncultivated squalor, as formerly in sackcloth and ashes, concerning which see *On Repentance*, chap. 9. II, 991 A, “The poison of lust adhered everywhere, and the cast filth”—this is the correct reading, not “lots”—“was incapable of being washed away, because the waters themselves had not yet been washed.” J. F. Gronovius, in his little book *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*, writes the following on this passage:

> Thus reads Ursinus’ manuscript; but closer to what was once commonly printed was: “milky filth not capable of possessing”; from which we shall plainly see what Scaliger’s hand fashioned: “and the filth of struggle not suitable for reins.” But we understand this no more readily.

“Milky” cannot be approved—not, I say, because of the κακέμφατον, “ill-sounding double meaning” (for many things in Tertullian could be censured under that name), but because that fluid belongs to the fig, not to its leaves, whose likeness he employs. Thus Jerome too, to Eustochium: “‘Increase and multiply’: this decree is fulfilled after paradise, nakedness, and the fig leaves that inaugurated the irritation of marriage.” I think it should read: “The poison of lust adhered everywhere, and hidden filth incapable of being washed away”—that is, concealed, [Col. 1367C] internal filth and, as he himself said, filth that adhered. As in the poet: “And he is consumed by a hidden fire.” Water was insufficient to wash this away: though powerful to cleanse external filth, it was itself also polluted by certain hidden stains before it was cleansed from them through Christ’s baptism. For those who take the conjunction *quod* as a pronoun referring back to *virus*, “poison,” are mistaken. This is a very common idea among the Fathers: Christ’s baptism sanctified the waters and, together with the Holy Spirit, made them capable of washing away those hidden and secret stains of original sin. Optatus of Milevis, Book I: “But Christ’s flesh, when it descended into and ascended from the Jordan, should not have been said by you to have been submerged. His flesh is found to be holier than the Jordan itself, so that by his descent he cleansed the water rather than being cleansed by it.” Jerome, urging Marcella to move to Bethlehem: “To see Lazarus come forth bound in his grave-clothes, and the streams of the Jordan made purer for the Lord’s washing.” In the epitaph of his mother Paula: “The Lord washed through his baptism waters polluted by the Flood and stained by the destruction of the entire human race.” [Col. 1367D]

**SOROR** (“sister”). II, 1031 A, The sister-city is Utica, a colony of the Tyrians. II, 739 A, “He tears apart the concretion of the sister substances.”

**SORS** (“lot”). II, 991 A, “And the cast lots”: read “filth”; see that entry.

**SPADO** (“eunuch”). II, 930 C, “Among alien eunuchs,” i.e. among heretics who abolish marriage. Heretics are alien and foreign to Catholics. He calls those who hate marriage eunuchs.

**SPADONATUS** (“eunuchhood”). I, 1327 A, “And they assign themselves to eunuchhood.”

**SPARSILE** (“scattered thing”). II, 984 A, “Such and so great are their scattered offerings.” Pamelius produced this reading from an English manuscript, and Pithoeus noted that the Reims manuscript read *spartilia*; others read *futilia*, “trifles.”

**SPARTEOLI** was the name given to soldiers who kept watch at Rome to ward off fires [Col. 1368A] and patrolled the districts of the city.
